Article Title: A theory of fairness, competition, and cooperation
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS; FORM GAMES; GROUP-SIZE; MARKET; EXPECTATIONS; RATIONALITY; PROVISION; BEHAVIOR; FIRMS; PAY
Abstract: There is strong evidence that people exploit their bargaining power in competitive markets but not in bilateral bargaining situations. There is also strong evidence that people exploit free-riding opportunities in voluntary cooperation games. Yet, when they are given the opportunity to punish free riders, stable cooperation is maintained, although punishment is costly for those who punish. This paper asks whether there is a simple common principle that can explain this puzzling evidence. We show that if some people care about equity the puzzles can be resolved. It turns out that the economic environment determines whether the fair types or the selfish types dominate equilibrium behavior.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter review of whether (1) the paper discusses that parameter at all and, if so, in what way (including any value it takes on in the paper’s examples), and (2) whether the paper makes predictions about how systematically varying that parameter would affect the difference that punishment makes (“the punishment treatment effect”), for either efficiency specifically or for other dependent variables. Note that the paper itself focuses on theoretical conditions for sustaining cooperation (and sometimes on final‐period behavior), rather than systematically manipulating parameters in an experiment. In many cases, it does not provide numerical effect sizes or direct statements about how altering parameters would change efficiency. Throughout, “not discussed” means the paper does not address that parameter in any systematic way, and “discussed but no systematic variation” means the paper mentions the parameter but does not analyze how changing it would affect the punishment treatment effect. The phrase “punishment treatment effect” is taken to mean how adding a punishment option changes group outcomes (especially cooperation and payoff).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. The paper refers extensively to n, the number of players, for settings such as the n‑player public goods game (with or without punishment), n‑player market games, and other examples.  
   • Does it predict how systematically varying it affects the punishment treatment effect (especially on efficiency)?  
     – The paper does discuss that having more players can make it harder or easier to enforce cooperation, but it does not provide a numerical effect size or a figure/table showing how efficiency changes with n. Overall, it establishes that large n can alter whether a few punishers can uphold high cooperation, but it does not systematically vary n in an experiment or provide explicit predictions about how changing n alone changes the punishment effect on total payoffs or efficiency.  

2) Number of rounds  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – The paper acknowledges repeated games (multiple rounds) and usually examines final‐period or steady‐state outcomes.  
   • Does it predict how systematically varying the number of rounds affects the punishment treatment effect?  
     – No. It does not present or derive formal results about changing the total number of rounds. It does not provide an effect size or discussion specific to how more or fewer rounds would alter the impact of punishment on efficiency.  

3) Is chat (communication) enabled between players?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Not in the sense of systematic “chat.” There is a passing mention (footnotes) that some earlier public goods studies allowed “cheap talk,” but the paper itself does not analyze chat or compare “chat vs. no chat.”  
   • Does it predict the effect of systematically varying communication on punishment’s impact?  
     – No, not discussed.  

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – The models sometimes treat cooperation as contributing “0 or y,” and other times as contributing continuously in [0, y]. But the authors do not focus on or systematically vary “forced all‑or‑nothing contribution.”  
   • Does it predict how changing all‐or‐nothing vs. continuous choice would affect punishment outcomes?  
     – No. This is not explicitly analyzed for the punishment effect on efficiency.  

5) Is the contribution default (i.e., do players “move money back” into their private account)?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. The paper’s exposition of public goods focuses on players choosing contributions from an endowment, but does not analyze “default choices” or moving funds “back.”  
   • Does it predict the effect of systematically varying a default arrangement?  
     – No, not discussed.  

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. The paper denotes it by “a” in public goods settings. It describes how a > 1/n makes full contribution socially optimal but not individually optimal for purely selfish agents.  
   • Does it predict how systematically varying MPCR affects the punishment treatment effect?  
     – The paper mentions that when “a” is higher, cooperation is more “tempting” (and can improve outcomes). Likewise, the paper’s theoretical propositions suggest that with punishment, it becomes easier to sustain high cooperation if “a” is large (and punishment is credible). However, no numeric “effect size” for efficiency is given, and there is no table or figure showing how the punishment/no‑punishment gap changes as “a” increases or decreases.  

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. Denoted by “c” in the public goods game with punishment. The punisher pays c×(punishment units).  
   • Does it predict how systematically varying the cost would affect the punishment treatment effect?  
     – Yes, in a theoretical sense: If c is too large, punishments become less credible because punishers will not want to spend heavily punishing. If c is small enough (i.e., c < certain thresholds in Proposition 5), punishers can credibly impose enough punishment to enforce high cooperation. The main predicted result is that sufficiently low c can transform a defecting equilibrium (no contributions) into one with high contributions (and thereby raise overall payoffs). A precise numeric impact on efficiency is not given, but the direction is that lower c facilitates higher cooperation and higher efficiency under punishment.  

8) Punishment magnitude (impact on the punished)  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – The formal model treats each punishment “unit” as imposing a cost of 1 on the punished and a cost of c to the punisher. However, the authors do not systematically vary that magnitude in the text; it is simply set to 1 (the punishee loses 1 token per punishment unit).  
   • Does it predict how changing that magnitude would affect the punishment treatment effect?  
     – The paper’s formal propositions depend on the idea that the punisher’s outlay is c while the punishee’s loss is 1 for each unit. There is no separate discussion of making that ratio bigger or smaller. So no direct claims are made about systematically varying the punishment magnitude for efficiency.  

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. The paper focuses on negative reciprocity (punishment). No reward mechanism is introduced or analyzed.  
   • Does it predict any effect of systematically varying reward vs. no reward?  
     – No, not discussed.  

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – No.  
    • Does it predict any effect of systematically varying reward cost?  
      – No, not discussed.  

11) Reward magnitude (the payoff to the rewarded)  
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – No.  
    • Does it predict any effect of systematically varying the reward magnitude?  
      – No, not discussed.  

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?  
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – The paper often references repeated‐game experiments (public goods or market games), typically with a set number of periods. However, it does not systematically examine “known vs. unknown horizon.”  
    • Does it predict how that knowledge would affect punishment’s impact on efficiency?  
      – No. It does not present those manipulations or a formal effect size.  

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much peers gained and lost each round)?  
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – In the public goods‐with‐punishment model, players do see one another’s contributions (and presumably the punishments imposed). But the paper does not systematically study “shown vs. not shown.”  
    • Does it predict how systematically varying outcome transparency would affect the punishment treatment effect?  
      – No, not discussed as a separate manipulation.  

14) When a player is punished, do they know who punished them?  
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – The text does not specify whether punishment is anonymous or identified. It does not compare “identified punisher” vs. “anonymous punisher.”  
    • Does it predict how that variation affects punishment’s influence on efficiency?  
      – No, not discussed.  

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who rewarded them?  
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – Rewards are not studied (see #9–11).  
    • Does it predict any effect of systematically varying reward visibility?  
      – No, not discussed.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper frequently refers to “overall payoffs,” “aggregate gains,” or “gains from trade,” and how punishment can lead to more cooperation and hence higher total payoff. Although “efficiency” is not always labeled as the ratio of realized to maximum possible payoffs, the logic is the same (e.g., a public goods game with full cooperation leads to the maximal group payoff). The paper also discusses other dependent variables—particularly contributions to the public good, acceptance thresholds in ultimatum games, and the fact of whether or not players punish. These are different from efficiency in that they do not always track total payoff directly, but the authors often connect them to payoff outcomes.  

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
     1) Number of players (n)  
     2) Number of rounds (multiple‐period experiments)  
     6) MPCR (denoted a)  
     7) Punishment cost (denoted c)  
     8) Punishment magnitude (implicitly 1 per unit)  
   • Not discussed at all or only extremely tangentially (and never varied):  
     3) Chat enabled?  
     4) All‐or‐nothing contribution?  
     5) Contribution default?  
     9) Whether reward is enabled?  
     10) Reward cost?  
     11) Reward magnitude?  
     12) Knowledge of the number of rounds?  
     13) Displaying peer outcomes?  
     14) Knowing the punisher’s identity?  
     15) Knowing the rewarder’s identity?  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when systematically varied?  
   • None of the parameters are experimentally varied within the same design in the paper for the explicit purpose of measuring changes in “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Instead, the paper develops theoretical conditions (e.g., c < certain thresholds, or a > 1/n) showing when punishment can sustain cooperation. That is more of a qualitative threshold analysis than a numerical “systematic variation.”  
   • In particular:  
     – MPCR (a): The paper discusses how higher a helps cooperation in both punishment and nonpunishment settings, but does not provide an effect‐size measure of how the punishment‐vs‐no‐punishment gap in payoff is altered by a.  
     – Punishment cost (c): The paper shows that if c is too high, punishment will not be credible and won’t raise efficiency. If c is below a certain bound, it can uphold high contributions. Again, the paper does not give an explicit effect‐size difference in group payoffs; it shows conditions under which punishment can or cannot work.  

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not provide direct numerical predictions, but it implies that:  
     – (1) If the number of players is large enough and few are willing to punish, sustaining cooperation (and thus raising efficiency) becomes harder; but the text does not quantify the effect on total payoff.  
     – (6) A higher MPCR (“a”) makes cooperation more valuable and thus likely strengthens the efficiency impact of punishment (because punishing defectors helps avoid the larger lost opportunity).  
     – (7) and (8) If the cost of punishing (c) is small relative to its impact on the punished (which is set at 1 per unit in their model), punishment is more credible, leading to higher efficiency gains from allowing punishment. Conversely, if punishment is too costly, its effect on efficiency gains will vanish.  
     – The paper does not provide meaningful predictions for how enabling chat, introducing rewards, or making contributions all‐or‐nothing would affect efficiency with punishment because those variations are not analyzed. In short, the paper’s statements about “parameters and their interactions” are limited to c and a (and partially n), written in broad theoretical terms with no direct numeric effect sizes.  

──────── This completes the requested analysis. ────────

Authors: Fehr, E; Gächter, S
Author Full Names: Fehr, E; Gächter, S
Article Title: Altruistic punishment in humans
Keywords Plus: INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; EVOLUTION; COOPERATION; HANDICAP
Abstract: Human cooperation is an evolutionary puzzle. Unlike other creatures, people frequently cooperate with genetically unrelated strangers, often in large groups, with people they will never meet again, and when reputation gains are small or absent. These patterns of cooperation cannot be explained by the nepotistic motives associated with the evolutionary theory of kin selection and the selfish motives associated with signalling theory or the theory of reciprocal altruism. Here we show experimentally that the altruistic punishment of defectors is a key motive for the explanation of cooperation. Altruistic punishment means that individuals punish, although the punishment is costly for them and yields no material gain. We show that cooperation flourishes if altruistic punishment is possible, and breaks down if it is ruled out. The evidence indicates that negative emotions towards defectors are the proximate mechanism behind altruistic punishment. These results suggest that future study of the evolution of human cooperation should include a strong focus on explaining altruistic punishment.

Abstract: Some of the most fundamental questions concerning our evolutionary origins, our social relations, and the organization of society are centred around issues of altruism and selfishness. Below each of the 15 parameters is treated separately.  For every parameter I first say whether the paper even TELLS us anything concrete about it and—if it does—what the value(s) are.  Second, I say whether the paper ever **systematically varies** that parameter in a punishment-versus-no-punishment comparison and therefore allows us to infer how changes in that parameter alter the *punishment treatment effect*.  Whenever numbers (effect sizes, cooperation rates, etc.) can be read directly from a figure or passage they are reported; otherwise I state explicitly that the paper is silent.  The word “efficiency’’ is used only when the paper itself uses or implies total (group) pay-off.

-------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes, several times.  
        – Public–goods experiments described in the review use groups of 4 (Fehr & Gächter 2002, Nature) and “larger groups’’ are discussed in the theoretical part.  
        – Fig. 4 (simulation) systematically varies group size n = 2 … 512.  
   • Systematically varied with respect to punishment effect?  
        – In the **simulation** of Fig. 4 group size is the only parameter that is explicitly varied (along with whether punishment of defectors or of defectors + non-punishers is allowed).  
        – Outcome: without punishment, cooperation collapses above n = 16; with punishment of defectors only, ≈40 % cooperation survives up to n = 32; with punishment of defectors **and** non-punishers, 70–80 % cooperation survives even for several-hundred-person groups.  
        – The paper never translates these cooperation rates into group efficiency numbers, so no efficiency effect size is given.

2.  Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Many laboratory studies cited last 10 rounds; the ultimatum-reputation study runs 10 rounds; some one-shot games are also reported.  
   • Systematic variation?  No.  The paper contrasts “one-shot’’ versus “repeated’’ settings qualitatively (“cooperation decays over 10 rounds’’) but never varies the number of rounds while holding everything else constant in a punishment treatment.

3.  Is chat enabled?  
   • Not mentioned anywhere.  No variation.

4.  All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Not mentioned.  The standard linear public good with continuous choices is assumed but never varied.

5.  Contribution default / “take’’ frame  
   • Not mentioned.

6.  MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned incidentally: in the trust game transfers are doubled (multiplication factor = 2).  No numerical MPCR is given for the public-goods experiments with punishment.  
   • Never systematically varied relative to punishment.

7.  Punishment cost (cost to punisher per unit)  
   • One concrete value is given for the third-party punishment game: 1 MU spent deducts 3 MU from the target.  
   • Not varied.

8.  Punishment magnitude (loss to target per unit)  
   • Value as above (3 MU per 1 MU spent) is stated once.  Not varied.

9.  Reward enabled?  
   • Yes, separate sections describe altruistic *rewarding* (gift-exchange, trust game).  However, reward is never placed in a factorial design with punishment so no punishment-treatment effect can be isolated.  No numbers on efficiency.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   • Neither is quantified; not varied.

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
   • The authors state that in all experiments “subjects were fully informed about whether future encounters were possible’’, but no treatment varies this knowledge.  No quantitative effect.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Not explicitly discussed; no variation.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed to the target?  
   • Third-party punishment game: the punisher is known only as “third party”, not by personal identity; ultimatum game responder identity obviously known by the proposer in that pair, but there is no treatment that varies this information.  So no systematic evidence.

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
   • Not discussed.

-------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables actually used  
   – The review almost always reports **cooperation / contribution rates, rejection (punishment) frequencies, or acceptance thresholds**.  
   – The word **efficiency** (group total pay-off relative to maximum) is *not* used in any table or figure; therefore efficiency is ­not a reported dependent variable.  Contributions and cooperation can be related to efficiency, but they are not identical.

B.  How many of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   – Seven: 1 (group size), 2 (rounds), 6 (multiplier, in one example), 7, 8 (punishment cost & magnitude), 9 (presence of reward), 12 (knowledge of horizon).  The other eight parameters receive no mention.

C.  For how many parameters is their *systematic* impact on a punishment treatment effect discussed?  
   – Only **one** parameter—group size (Parameter 1)—is systematically manipulated (in Fig. 4 simulations) together with different punishment rules.  Even here the outcome reported is *cooperation rate*, not efficiency, and the study is computational, not behavioural.  For the remaining 14 parameters the paper gives no systematic evidence on how varying that parameter changes the punishment treatment effect on **any** dependent variable.

D.  What predictions about the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency can be made from this paper alone?  
   • Because efficiency itself is never measured, only indirect conjectures can be drawn:  
        – Smaller groups (≤ 16) can achieve high cooperation with or without punishing non-punishers; hence punishment is likely to raise efficiency moderately.  
        – As group size grows, punishment of defectors alone ceases to stabilise cooperation, so the efficiency gain from introducing punishment should *decline* unless punishment of non-punishers (second-order punishment) is also allowed.  
        – If second-order punishment is available, introducing punishment is predicted (Fig. 4) to restore 70–80 % cooperation even in groups of several hundred, implying a large efficiency boost.  
        – No other clear‐cut predictions about the remaining 14 parameters can be derived from the text.

In short, the paper is a broad review of human altruism; apart from the simulation of different **group sizes** it provides virtually no quantitative basis for predicting how the other 14 listed design parameters would modulate the effect of punishment on group efficiency.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1) Number of players  
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes. Every group in the experiments has n = 4 players.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how varying it affects punishment’s impact on any dependent variable?  
     – No. The paper uses only groups of size 4 and makes no predictions about changing group size.

2) Number of rounds  
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes. Each treatment (punishment or no‐punishment) runs for 10 periods (rounds), and subjects know this.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how varying it affects punishment’s impact on any dependent variable?  
     – No. All experiments use exactly 10 periods for each condition. There is no discussion of experimentally varying the number of rounds.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The paper does not mention any free‐form chat or communication channels.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how varying it affects punishment’s impact on any dependent variable?  
     – No. The paper does not mention chat or how it might be manipulated.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. In the experiment, each subject can contribute any integer between 0 and 20 tokens, so it is not all‐or‐nothing.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how varying it affects punishment’s impact on any dependent variable?  
     – No. There is no mention of an all‐or‐nothing contribution format or of systematically varying contribution granularity.

5) Is the contribution default?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. Subjects simply decide an integer amount (0–20 tokens) to put into the public good. There is no “default” mechanism described.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how varying it affects punishment’s impact on any dependent variable?  
     – No. No mention is made of a contribution default or systematically varying it.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as the multiplication factor  
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes. The paper fixes a = 0.4 as the marginal payoff from each contributed token.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how varying it affects punishment’s impact on any dependent variable?  
     – No. They do not vary a; no predictive statements are made about changing it.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes. Table 2 shows the cost function c(p) (e.g., 1 token cost for 1 point of punishment, 2 tokens cost for 2 points, etc.), but this cost schedule is fixed.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how varying it affects punishment’s impact on any dependent variable?  
     – No. There is no discussion or manipulation of different punishment‐cost schedules.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes. Each punishment point reduces the punished player’s payoff by 10 percent of that period’s first‐stage payoff, up to a maximum of 10 points (100 percent).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how varying it affects punishment’s impact on any dependent variable?  
     – No. The 10 percent decrement per point is held constant. The paper does not analyze or predict changes to that percentage.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The experiment involves only punishment, with no mention of a reward mechanism.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how a reward option might affect outcomes?  
     – No. Not mentioned.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. No reward mechanism is included.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict its impact on punishment‐related outcomes?  
     – No. Not mentioned.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. Same as above: no rewards are used.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict its impact on punishment‐related outcomes?  
     – No. Not mentioned.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes. In all treatments, subjects know there are exactly 10 periods.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how changing knowledge of the horizon affects punishment’s impact?  
     – No. The horizon is always known and fixed.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?  
   • Discussed?  
     – Partially. In the no‐punishment condition, subjects only see total group contributions. In the punishment condition, they learn each group member’s contribution but not the exact punishment points assigned by others (only the points they themselves receive). They do not see full, detailed payoff breakdowns for peers.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary the information display or predict how changing it would affect punishment’s impact on any dependent variable?  
     – No. They do not manipulate information display, nor do they discuss how varying it might change punishment effects.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes. The design forbids identifying punishers. Subjects cannot tell which group member issued the punishment points.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary punisher anonymity or predict how changing it affects punishment’s impact?  
     – No. No variation or predictions.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. Rewards do not exist in this design, so this issue does not arise.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how it would affect punishment’s impact?  
     – No. Not mentioned.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are they different?

   • The paper’s main dependent variable is contribution (cooperation) levels. It also measures individual and group payoffs, especially to see how punishment changes net payoffs over time. Near the end, the authors examine whether adding punishment opportunities eventually yields higher “pecuniary efficiency” (i.e., higher average group payoff) despite the cost of punishing.  
   • Thus, the paper does consider total payoff (and payoff differences) and finds that, in later periods, the punishment treatment can result in higher average group payoffs compared to no punishment. However, they primarily discuss “contributions” and “average group payoff.” They do not formally define “efficiency” as “actual payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff,” but they do discuss relative payoff gains as a fraction of the no‐punishment payoff.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

   • Mentioned by the paper in some form (without systematically varying them):  
     1) Number of players (always 4).  
     2) Number of rounds (always 10).  
     6) MPCR (fixed at 0.4).  
     7) Punishment cost function (fixed per Table 2).  
     8) Punishment magnitude (10% payoff reduction per point).  
     12) Knowledge of the number of rounds (yes, known).  
     13) Partial information on contributions and punishments.  
     14) Punisher anonymity.  
   • Not mentioned at all or not used:  
     3) Chat, 4) All‐or‐nothing contributions, 5) Contribution default, 9) Reward presence, 10) Reward cost, 11) Reward magnitude, 15) Rewarder’s identity.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?

   • The short answer is none. The paper does not systematically vary any of the above parameters. In all cases (e.g., n=4, cost of punishment, fraction lost per punishment point, horizon=10, etc.), those features are fixed for the experiment. Hence, the paper provides no numerical effect sizes or formal predictions about how changing any parameter would alter the punishment treatment effect or efficiency.  

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

   • The paper itself does not vary the 15 parameters, so it presents virtually no direct evidence on how systematic changes in, say, group size, MPCR, or punishment cost might quantitatively alter the effect of punishment on efficiency. The only discussion of efficiency is that eventually, cooperation rises sufficiently (especially in Partner treatments) so that the higher contributions outweigh the cost of punishment, leading to higher group payoffs in later periods.  
   • As a result, strictly following what the paper says, one can make little to no prediction about how those 15 parameters would quantitatively affect efficiency if changed. The paper’s evidence only shows that, under the specific parameter settings (n=4, a=0.4, the stated cost function for punishment, etc.), punishment opportunities can raise contributions dramatically. Eventually, payoffs (and thus efficiency) can exceed those from a no‐punishment setting.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter analysis of what Elinor Ostrom’s paper “Collective Action and the Evolution of Social Norms” does and does not say about each of the 15 listed parameters, specifically with respect to (1) whether the paper mentions the parameter at all (and, if so, what relevant values or conditions it describes) and (2) whether it discusses the effect of systematically varying that parameter on any punishment treatment (i.e., the option to punish free riders), particularly its effect on group efficiency (total or average payoff relative to a theoretical maximum).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned? 
     – The paper refers to “groups” and sometimes uses examples of groups of 10 in a linear public goods experiment (p. 3–4). It does not provide details about systematically varying group size. 
   • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment? 
     – The paper does not discuss how changing the number of players would alter the punishment treatment effect (on efficiency or any other dependent variable).

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned?
     – Yes. The paper references finitely repeated public goods experiments with 10, 40, and 60 rounds (p. 6), and also describes decay in cooperation toward the last round. 
   • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment?
     – The paper does not link these different lengths of repetition to how punishment perse affects efficiency. It does discuss learning effects and decay in contribution, but not as a function of systematically varying the number of rounds for punishment’s sake.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned?
     – Yes. The paper discusses “face-to-face communication” versus no communication or minimal (computer messaging) settings (p. 6–7). It deems communication (“cheap talk”) a key factor influencing cooperation. 
   • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment?
     – While the paper notes that communication can boost cooperation and may include “tongue-lashings” or scolding as a mild form of punishment, it does not provide systematic or quantitative predictions about how varying communications options would change the punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned?
     – No. The paper focuses on linear public goods experiments in which participants choose how many units to contribute, not forced “all or nothing” choices. 
   • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment?
     – Not discussed.

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much of their endowment to move back into their hand)?
   • Mentioned?
     – No. The paper does not describe a default contribution rule or forced allocation mechanism of that sort.
   • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment?
     – Not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Mentioned?
     – The paper uses an example of each unit contributed yielding a certain “multiplication factor” (p. 3–4). It references a typical linear public goods payoff, but without elaborating different systematically varied MPCRs. 
   • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment?
     – Not discussed.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned?
     – The paper does mention that individuals “expend personal resources to punish” (p. 7), calling it “costly material payoffs” to sanction free riders. 
   • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment?
     – No. It does not analyze or quantify how different punishment costs alter outcomes, nor does it provide effect sizes.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   • Mentioned?
     – The paper mentions that punishment involves reducing a target’s payoff (p. 7–8), but does not specify any standard magnitude or systematically varied scale. 
   • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment?
     – Not discussed.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned?
     – The paper notes that some conditional cooperators may also be “willing rewarders” (p. 8). However, there is no detailed discussion about a separate “reward treatment” in the same structured way as punishment. 
   • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment?
     – Not discussed.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Mentioned?
      – No. The paper does not discuss the cost structure of rewards in a formal way.
    • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment?
      – Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)
    • Mentioned?
      – No. Similar to above, no systematic mention of magnitude or scale of rewards.
    • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment?
      – Not discussed.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
    • Mentioned?
      – Yes. The paper discusses “finitely repeated” public goods games in which players do know the final round (p. 4–6). 
    • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment?
      – The paper remarks on “backward induction” and cooperation decay in finite settings, but it does not analyze how knowledge of the final round specifically changes punishment’s efficacy or efficiency.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained or lost)?
    • Mentioned?
      – The paper often mentions participants “observing one another’s actions,” especially in the real world or in face-to-face experiments, but does not specify a systematic on-screen display of peer payoffs. 
    • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment?
      – Not discussed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Mentioned?
      – Punishment is discussed in general terms (p. 7–8) but the paper does not say whether or not the identity of the punisher is revealed. 
    • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment?
      – Not discussed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Mentioned?
      – No mention of whether the identity of a rewarder is revealed.
    • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment?
      – Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are they different?

   • The paper generally discusses individual or group “payoffs” in the context of public goods games but does not focus on “efficiency” (in the sense of total payoff ÷ maximum possible) as a core outcome. Rather, it focuses on cooperation rates, contributions, trust, and reciprocity as primary dependent variables. Payoffs are often mentioned in a qualitative sense (for instance, the temptation to free-ride), but the study’s emphasis is not on comparing actual total group payoff to the fully cooperative maximum.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

   • Mentioned in some form (though not always systematically):  
     – (2) Number of rounds  
     – (3) Chat enabled  
     – (6) Multiplication factor (only described in a typical example)  
     – (7)/(8) Punishment cost and magnitude (briefly noted but not varied)  
     – (9) Whether a reward is enabled (acknowledged in passing when describing “willing rewarders”)  
     – (12) Whether the number of rounds is known  
   • All others (1, 4, 5, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15) are either not mentioned at all or are only implied in passing without explicit detail.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?

   • None. Although the paper does discuss punishment in general and shows that individuals “expend personal resources to punish,” it does not examine how systematically varying any of the parameters changes punishment’s effects on cooperation or payoffs. There are no numerical effect sizes or formal experimental comparisons reported for any parameter manipulations.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

   • The paper does not provide systematic data or explicit theory linking the 15 parameters to the effect of a punishment mechanism on group efficiency. It does note, more generally, that allowing punishment often helps sustain cooperation, but no quantitative or parameter-specific predictions on efficiency can be drawn from the text. Accordingly, there is little basis here to predict how each of these 15 parameters and their interactions would shape punishment’s impact on overall efficiency.  

In short, the paper offers valuable insights into human behavior in social dilemmas and the role of punishment in sustaining cooperation, but it does not separately or systematically address how manipulating any of the 15 parameters would influence a punishment treatment’s effect on group efficiency.

Below we go through the 15 design parameters one by one and extract exactly what the paper says about each of them, focusing on (i) whether the parameter is mentioned at all, (ii) the value(s) actually implemented, and (iii) whether the authors **systematically vary** the parameter and report how that variation changes the *punishment-treatment effect* on any dependent variable (note that the paper almost never speaks of “efficiency” in the sense requested by the prompt).

----------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER SCAN
----------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  There are 2-player (second-party; SP) and 3-player (third-party; TP) versions of both the Dictator Game (DG) and the Prisoner’s Dilemma (PD).  
   • Values actually used  
        – SP conditions: 2 players (A,B).  
        – TP conditions: 3 players (A,B, C).  
   • Systematically varied?  Yes—the same groups of subjects play both a 2- and a 3-player version (order counter-balanced).  
   • Effect on the punishment treatment?  
        – Dictator Game (Fig. 5, Table 3): For every 10-point downward deviation from the egalitarian transfer, punishment by a second party rises by 4.54 deduction points (s.e.=0.87) whereas punishment by a third party rises by 2.07 deduction points (s.e.=0.61).  
        – Prisoner’s Dilemma (Tables 5-8): A defector is sanctioned on average 8.40 points by the second party but only 3.09 points by the third party if the partner cooperates (1.43 if the partner also defects). The fraction of punishers differs similarly (66.7 % vs. 58.7 % or 32.6 %).  
        – The paper never turns those numbers into “efficiency” (total payoff ÷ maximum payoff) but it does show (Fig. 6) that in the SP-DG low transfers are no longer profitable (punishment cancels the dictator’s gain) whereas they remain profitable in the TP-DG, implying lower total earnings—and hence lower efficiency—under TP than under SP, ceteris paribus.

2. Number of rounds  
   • One-shot in every treatment.  
   • Not varied → no information on its effect.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • None; anonymity assured.  
   • Not varied.

4. All-or-nothing contribution decision?  
   • Not applicable; the DG allows 0,10,…,50; the PD is binary (cooperate/defect) but this is never varied experimentally.  
   • No systematic manipulation.

5. Reversal/default framing (“withdraw from public fund”)?  
   • Not used.

6. Marginal Per Capita Return / Multiplication Factor  
   • Mentioned for the PD only: transferring 10 points is tripled (factor = 3).  
   • Single fixed value; not varied.

7. Punishment cost to punisher  
   • Fixed at 1 point per deduction point in every game.  
   • Not varied.

8. Punishment magnitude for target  
   • Fixed at 3 points lost by the target for every deduction point bought.  
   • Not varied.

9. Is a reward option present?  
   • No reward stage is ever implemented.  Parameter therefore absent.

10. Reward cost  
   • Not applicable.

11. Reward magnitude  
   • Not applicable.

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
   • Single round and common knowledge, but not manipulated.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Yes: third parties observe the first-stage actions before deciding on punishment; dictators see punishment totals after the fact.  
   • Always the same; not varied.

14. Do punished subjects learn the punisher’s identity?  
   • They do **not**; complete anonymity.  
   • Not varied.

15. Do rewarded subjects learn the rewarder’s identity?  
   • No rewards, so not applicable.

----------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
----------------------------------------------------------------
A. Does the paper analyse “group efficiency”?  
   – No.  The dependent variables are (i) amount of punishment (deduction points purchased), (ii) probability of punishing, (iii) dictators’ transfers, (iv) PD cooperation choices, and (v) individual earnings.  “Efficiency” (total or average payoff divided by maximum possible payoff) is **never** computed, although Fig. 6 does plot dictators’ *own* expected pay-offs.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   – 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14 are explicitly given a value.  Parameters 3-5 and 9-11, 15 are absent.  (8 parameters mentioned.)

C. Which parameters are *systematically varied* and linked to the punishment treatment effect?  
   – Only parameter 1 (number of players: 2 vs. 3).  No other parameter is experimentally manipulated.  Hence 1 out of 15.

D. What predictions about the punishment-treatment effect on **efficiency** can be drawn strictly from this paper?  
   – Because efficiency is never measured, very little can be said.  The one manipulable parameter (number of players) shows that moving from 2 to 3 players weakens punishment, keeps norm violations profitable, and therefore should *lower* efficiency relative to the 2-player (second-party) setting.  For all other parameters the paper provides no data, so no predictions can be made without venturing beyond the text.

(i) the raw change in average net yield from the CPR (“efficiency” in our terminology) and sometimes
(ii) the change after subtracting the resources consumed by fees and fines.  
Both figures are reproduced when given.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
• Mentioned?  Yes.  All experiments use n = 8.  
• Systematic variation?  No.  n is never varied, and no prediction is offered about varying it.  
• Numerical effect on punishment treatment effect?  None.

2. Number of rounds  
• Mentioned?  Yes.  Baseline sessions run 20 rounds; in some treatments additional rounds are played after round 20.  
• Subjects never know the exact end round.  
• Systematic variation?  No.  Round length is held constant and never analysed as an independent variable.  
• No prediction regarding punishment treatment effect.

3. Chat / face-to-face communication enabled?  
• Mentioned?  Yes.  Three levels are studied:  
  – No communication  
  – One-shot 10-minute discussion at round 10  
  – Repeated face-to-face discussion after every round from 11 on  
• Systematic variation?  Yes – this is one of the central manipulations.  
• Numerical results that speak to punishment treatment effect:  

  a) Sanctioning WITHOUT communication  
     Net CPR yield rises from –38 % (pre-sanction) to 37 % (post-sanction), but falls to 9 % once fees & fines are subtracted (Table 3; p. …).

  b) Sanctioning WITH a single communication round  
     Net CPR yield = 85 % before fees/fines and 67 % after (Table 3).  
     OWG does not present the matching “communication-only” figures in exactly the same periods, but the closest comparison is the “one-shot communication, 25 TK” line: 55 % net yield with no sanctioning.  Hence, adding punishment on top of one-shot communication raises average yield by ≈30 pp (from 55 % to 85 %), or ≈12 pp after fees/fines (from 55 % to 67 %).

  c) Endogenous choice of a sanctioning mechanism after a single communication round  
     – Groups that voted to add sanctioning: 93 % net yield, 90 % after fees/fines.  
     – Groups that did NOT add sanctioning: 56 % net yield (no sanction costs).  
     Punishment treatment effect ≈ +37 pp before sanctions costs and +34 pp after costs.

  d) Communication allowed from the very first period, sanctioning decided immediately  
     – Both groups voted for sanctioning.  Net yield ≈ 95 % before fees/fines, 94 % after.  
     There is no communication-only control for this exact schedule, so no separate effect size is available.

• OWG never expresses these differences as formal “predictions” of what would happen if the chat parameter were moved from one level to another, but the numbers above are the only direct evidence in the paper.

4. Contribution “all-or-nothing”?  
• Contribution is continuous in integer tokens (0–25 or 0–10).  
• Not varied; no predictions.

5. Contribution default / custom endowment move?  
• Not discussed or varied.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
• The public-goods technology is quadratic:  F(Σx) = 23Σx – 0.25(Σx)².  MPCR per token therefore declines with total investment.  
• These parameters are constant across treatments; only endowment (10 vs 25 tokens) changes.  
• No prediction is given about varying MPCR and its effect on punishment.

7. Cost to impose 1 unit of punishment  
• Discussed and varied.  Fee levels tried: 5 ¢, 10 ¢, 20 ¢, 40 ¢.  
• Finding: “The frequency of sanctions was inversely related to cost” (p. …).  
• OWG stops there; no separate statistics on how this cost variation changes the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine on target)  
• Discussed and varied.  Magnitudes tried: 10 ¢, 20 ¢, 40 ¢, 80 ¢.  
• No systematic efficiency results per magnitude; the only qualitative statement is that higher fines produced “dramatically increased” frequency of sanctions.

9. Reward enabled?  
• Not present.

10–11. Reward cost / reward magnitude  
• Not present.

12. Is the horizon known?  
• All subjects know the game is finite but not the exact number of rounds.  
• This parameter is fixed; no variation or prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
• Baseline: after each round a subject sees her own profits and the total group investment in the CPR.  
• Sanctioning treatments and one-shot-communication treatments: subjects also see every individual’s investment (by anonymous ID).  
• OWG reports that adding this individual-level information by itself “had no significant impact on observed yields” (footnote to p. …).  
• No quantitative analysis of how it moderates the punishment effect.

14. Is the punisher identified to the target?  
• Always anonymous: “any subject who was fined did not know the identity of those who imposed the fine.”  
• Not varied; no prediction.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
• No rewards exist.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables  
• OWG’s headline measure is “average net yield from the CPR as a percentage of the maximum possible net yield.”  
  That is exactly the definition of group efficiency which the user asks about.  
• Two auxiliary measures appear: (i) the same yield after subtracting fee and fine costs, and (ii) the “defection rate” (share of contributions above the agreed level).  These are conceptually different from efficiency.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
• Mentioned (10): 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14  
• Not mentioned at all (5): 5, 9, 10, 11, 15

C.  Parameters with any discussion of their EFFECT on the punishment treatment effect when *systematically varied*  
Strictly speaking, only parameter 3 (communication on/off/level) and, very briefly and qualitatively, parameters 7 and 8 (punishment fee and magnitude) receive such discussion.  
So: 3 parameters.

D.  What predictions can one make—solely on the basis of OWG—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?

• Communication (parameter 3).  Allowing **any** communication before or during a sanctioning phase roughly doubles or triples the efficiency gains of punishment and sharply reduces wasted sanction costs.  Repeated or earlier communication appears still better, but there is no clean counter-factual in OWG to quantify it exactly.

• Punishment cost (7) and magnitude (8).  Lower fees and/or higher fines make subjects punish more often; OWG does not tell us whether that extra punishment ultimately raises or lowers efficiency once the costs are counted, so no firm prediction is possible beyond “more punishment occurs.”

• All other parameters are fixed in the paper or not included.  OWG therefore provides no basis for predicting their influence on the punishment treatment effect.

Hence, apart from saying “communication strongly amplifies the efficiency benefit of adding punishment, while very high fee-to-fine ratios can wipe that benefit out,” the article supplies little leverage for forecasting the role of the other 13 parameters.

By treating models of human cooperation as classical spin models, a physicist can draw on familiar settings from statistical physics. Below I treat each of the 15 game-design parameters in turn.  
For every parameter I state

(a) whether the review paper mentions it at all, and, if so, in which part of the text / figure the concrete value(s) appear;  
(b) whether the paper derives or reports any **systematic** prediction about how changing that parameter alters the
size or the sign of the “punishment treatment effect’’ (i.e., the difference between outcomes in a version **with** vs. **without** peer- or pool-punishment);  
(c) whenever such a prediction is given, the numerical information that can be read directly from the figures or tables.

Because the paper is a broad review, most quantitative results come from phase-diagrams of evolutionary models; they are expressed in terms of “fractions of cooperators / punishers / defectors’’ rather than in terms of **group efficiency** (total payoff / maximum possible payoff of full cooperation).  Where nothing is said, I explicitly state “Not mentioned’’ and make no extrapolations.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players (group size)

• Mentioned?  Yes.  Laboratory studies are described with groups of 4 (section 2.3.1).  In all spatial models the default is G = 5 (section 3.1).  
• Systematic variation?  No.  G is kept fixed whenever punishment is analysed.  No figure varies G to show its impact on the punishment treatment effect.  
• Numerical effect size? None.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Number of rounds

• Mentioned?  Repeated versus one-shot games are discussed in section 2.1 and Fig. 3.  
• Systematic variation together with punishment?  No.  Punishment results are always for indefinitely repeated Monte-Carlo play; the number of periods is not a parameter that is swept.  
• Effect size? None.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Chat / communication enabled

• Not mentioned anywhere in connection with punishment.  
• No prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. All-or-nothing contribution rule

• Not mentioned.  
• No prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Contribution default (take-vs-give frame)

• Not mentioned.  
• No prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor r

• Mentioned throughout: r is the key parameter of every public-goods model (section 3.1).  
• Systematic variation with punishment?  Only partially.  
  – Peer punishment: in all phase diagrams r is fixed (e.g., r = 3.8 in Fig. 12).  
  – Pool punishment: one diagram (Fig. 19) keeps r = 2.0; another study uses r = 3.5 etc.  r is not scanned to show how the **difference between “no-punishment’’ and “punishment’’ efficiencies** changes.  
• No efficiency effect sizes are reported.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Punishment cost γ (per unit imposed)

• Mentioned?  Yes – γ is one axis in the peer-punishment fine-cost diagram (Fig. 12) and in the pool-punishment diagram (Fig. 19).  
• Systematically varied?  Yes, but the paper always reports **strategy composition** (C, D, P fractions) or phase boundaries, not efficiency.  
  Example: For peer punishment at r = 3.8, increasing γ from 0.1 to 0.65 moves the system across a discontinuous transition from a (C+D) phase to a (D+P) phase (Fig. 12).  
• Numerical thresholds:  
  – At γ ≈ 0.65 the critical fine β* for the transition satisfies β* ≈ 0.33 (inset of Fig. 12).  
  – Directed-percolation critical point for γ = 0.1 is β_c = 0.3262 (Fig. 13).  
• No efficiency data.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
8. Punishment magnitude β (fine)

• Mentioned exactly as above (orthogonal axis to γ).  
• Systematic variation?  Yes – phase boundaries in Fig. 12.  
• Quantitative information (peer punishment, γ = 0.1):  
  – When β rises from 0.2 to 0.5 the cooperative fraction ρ_{C+P} increases from ≈0 to ≈1 (inset Fig. 12).  
• No efficiency measure.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
9. Whether reward is enabled

• Mentioned: Between-treatment comparisons of “no reward’’ vs. “peer reward’’ vs. “reward + punishment’’ are described qualitatively in section 5.2.  
• No table/figure gives an efficiency contrast between “with reward’’ and “with punishment’’ for fixed parameter values.  
• No numerical prediction for our target outcome.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
10. Reward cost γ (per unit granted)

• Mentioned (parameter γ in Fig. 14).  
• Systematically varied?  Yes for peer rewarding, but again only strategy fractions are shown.  
  Example: at r = 2.0 and γ = 0.05, increasing β from 0.78 to 0.9 lets defectors re-enter through a cyclic (D+C+R) phase.  
• No efficiency effect reported.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
11. Reward magnitude β

• Same comment as above (Fig. 14 bottom panel).  No efficiency.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
12. Whether the number of rounds is known to players

• Not discussed.  No prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
13. Whether peer outcomes are shown

• Not discussed.  No prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
14. Whether the punished player learns who punished

• Mentioned only in passing when describing second- vs. third-party punishment (section 2.4), but the identity-revelation parameter is never manipulated.  
• No systematic prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
15. Whether the rewarded player learns who rewarded

• Not discussed.  No prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY REQUESTED BY THE USER
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Does the paper use “group efficiency’’ (total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  

   • In the bulk of the modelling work the reported dependent variable is the **stationary fraction of each strategy** (ρ_C, ρ_D …).  
   • “Average payoff’’ or “average income’’ is mentioned occasionally (e.g., tolerance model in section 9.1), but **no figure or table uses efficiency to characterise the punishment treatment effect**.  
   • Hence efficiency is referred to conceptually but is not an analysed outcome in the punishment studies.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  

   Parameters 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 are mentioned.  
   Parameters 3, 4, 5, 12, 13, 14, 15 are **not** mentioned.  
   Total mentioned: 8 of 15.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of **systematically varying** that parameter on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable)?

   • Systematic sweeps are shown for 6 parameters: r (6), punishment cost γ (7), punishment fine β (8), reward cost γ (10), reward magnitude β (11), and to a very limited extent the contrast “reward enabled’’ (9).  
   • However, none of these sweeps report efficiency; they report strategy-composition phase transitions.

D.  Predictions one could make—solely from this paper—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions affect the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency:

   Because efficiency is not analysed, only very rough qualitative statements are possible.  From the phase diagrams one may infer:  
   – Lower punishment cost γ and/or higher fine β promote phases in which defectors are absent; if payoffs were calculated, efficiency would presumably increase.  
   – Extremely high fines (peer punishment) can re-introduce defectors through cyclic dominance, so efficiency might peak at intermediate β.  
   – Enabling reward (with moderate cost) can likewise support cooperation, but if reward is too frequent / too large, cycling with defectors can lower efficiency.  
   Beyond these qualitative ideas, the review provides **no direct numbers or functional forms** linking any of the 15 listed parameters to changes in efficiency.  Consequently, data-driven prediction of the punishment treatment effect on efficiency is essentially impossible from this paper alone.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
In short, the review supplies a wealth of qualitative information on how γ, β, r determine which **strategies** survive, but it does **not** report efficiency, and it leaves seven of the user-specified parameters completely untouched.

Here is the systematic analysis of the 15 parameters presented in the paper concerning the effect of introducing punishment into a public goods game, focusing particularly on how these parameters may influence group efficiency:

### Analysis of Parameters

1. **Number of players**: The paper does not discuss the effect of varying the number of players on the punishment treatment effect.

2. **Number of rounds**: The paper employs a specific structure of 10 rounds but does not predict effects from varying this parameter.

3. **Is chat enabled between players?**: The paper does not mention this parameter or its influence on efficiency.

4. **Is the contribution "all or nothing"?**: The contribution model is based on varying amounts but does not discuss the potential effect of all-or-nothing contributions.

5. **Is the contribution default (if true, do players decide how much of their endowment to move from the public fund back into their hand)?**: This is not addressed in the paper.

6. **Marginal per capita return (MPCR)**: The paper states that each token invested yields a return of 0.4 tokens. It does not discuss how variations in MPCR might affect punishment effects but does consider that keeping all tokens (not contributing) is in participants' self-interest since contribution leads to a loss.

7. **Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment**: The cost of punishment was observed (1 token per unit imposed) but does not explore systematic variations on efficiency as a result.

8. **Punishment magnitude**: The deduction for each unit imposed was described (3 tokens lost per punishment unit), but there is no discussion on varying punishment magnitude and its effect on efficiency.

9. **Whether a reward is enabled**: The paper does not mention rewards in depth or explore their effects on efficiency.

10. **Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward**: This parameter is not discussed in terms of its effect on the punishment treatment.

11. **Reward magnitude**: Similarly, no insights are provided about rewards on punishment treatment effects.

12. **Is the number of rounds known to players?**: The paper does not specify if this influences punishment treatment effects.

13. **Are peer outcomes shown?**: The paper explains that participants are informed of peer contributions but does not relate this to efficiency.

14. **When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?**: Participants are not informed about punishers, which is noted but not analyzed regarding its impact on treatment effects.

15. **When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?**: This parameter is not mentioned.

### Summary

**A:** The paper does use group efficiency (actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff) as a dependent variable, along with cooperation rates and punishment expenditures. These dependent variables differ: efficiency relates to overall payoff, while cooperation rates measure participant contributions.

**B:** Of the 15 parameters, only parameters 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 12, and 13 are mentioned in the paper, but with limited detail in terms of systematic variation effects on efficiency.

**C:** The paper discusses systematic effects on the punishment treatment effect for:
- Only the marginal per capita return (this influences overall payoff but does not have numerical predictions).
- Punishment costs and magnitudes are described but without predictions based on systematic changes.

**D:** Predictions regarding how parameters and their interactions influence punishment treatment effect on efficiency based on the paper’s content are limited. Notably:
- The presence of punishment opportunities generally correlates with reduced cooperation in pools characterized by higher antisocial punishment.
- Antisocial punishment negatively correlates with the cooperative behavior observed, which may impact efficiency.
- Given the lack of direct correlation and effect size predictions for most parameters, one cannot confidently predict how systematic variations would positively or negatively affect efficiency beyond what's indicated regarding antisocial punishment and cooperation reductions. 

Overall, while the basic framework of the public goods game and punishment is discussed in detail, how each parameter specifically impacts the efficiency of the group in a systematic sense remains underexplored based on the current paper.

Parameter-by-parameter inspection
--------------------------------------------------------------------
(For every parameter I indicate ① whether the paper mentions it at all, and ② whether it reports what happens when the parameter is systematically varied **and** punishment is present.  Whenever the paper contains a numerical value or an explicit trend I cite the passage or figure.)

1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned generically: the authors contrast two-player PDs with “n-player” public-goods games (PGGs) (p. 6). No concrete n is ever given for the PGGs that include punishment.  
   (2) No systematic prediction about how changing n alters the punishment-treatment effect on *any* dependent variable, let alone efficiency.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Repeated interaction is discussed at length; continuation probability w is plotted in Fig. 2 for *pairwise* PDs. For PGGs that include punishment the paper just says they are “repeated” but gives no round numbers.

3. Chat allowed?  
   (1) Not mentioned anywhere.  
   (2) No prediction.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule?  
   (1) Not mentioned.  
   (2) No prediction.

5. Contribution default (withdrawal vs. contribution frame)  
   (1) Not mentioned.  
   (2) No prediction.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   (1) The authors note that in a standard PGG “all contributions are multiplied by some constant r (1 < r < n)” (p. 7). No value is supplied and r is never tied to punishment.

   (1) Also acknowledged only in passing; no figures.  
   (2) No systematic prediction.

9. Whether a *reward* option is enabled  
   (1) Explicitly discussed: “pairwise reward and punishment are both effective… higher payoffs are achieved when using reward (which creates benefit) than punishment (which destroys it)” (p. 7).

10. Cost to give a unit of reward  
    (1) Not specified.  
    (2) No prediction.

11. Magnitude of reward (benefit per unit)  
    (1) Not specified.  
    (2) No prediction.

12. Is the horizon known (finite vs. unknown number of rounds)?  
    (1) For dyadic PDs the continuation probability w is stated, which implicitly means the horizon is *not* known. For PGGs with punishment the paper says nothing.  
    (2) No prediction regarding the punishment-treatment effect.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    (1) For network experiments players “are typically presented in each round with the payoff and choice of each neighbor” (p. 11). Punishment PGGs are not linked to this information.

    (1) Not discussed.

Abstract: Both laboratory and field data suggest that people punish noncooperators even in one-shot interactions. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of whether and how the paper discusses each of the 15 specified features (and, if so, how it systematically varies them and reports any outcome measures). Throughout, please note that the paper’s main outcome measure is the long‐run average frequency of cooperation (or of punishment), rather than efficiency (i.e., actual total payoff divided by maximum possible payoff). Whenever the paper varies a parameter, it reports how it affects cooperation or punishment levels. It does not, however, directly measure or discuss “efficiency” as defined above.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Discussed? Yes. The model explicitly has groups of size n (e.g., Figures 1–4).  
   • Systematically varied? Yes. The paper shows how increasing n affects the maintenance of cooperation with and without punishment (e.g., Figure 1).  
   • Dependent variable(s) measured? Long‐run average frequency of cooperation (sometimes referred to as “the evolution of cooperation”), not efficiency.  
   • Any numerical effect sizes? The figures (e.g., Figure 1) show that for larger n (e.g., n up to “100 or 600”), punishment can still sustain cooperation more effectively than no‐punishment scenarios. However, no exact numeric “efficiency” values or effect sizes are given.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not analyze a repeated public‐goods game with a fixed or known number of rounds. It uses ongoing (multi‐period) simulation dynamics but does not treat “number of rounds” as a systematically varied game parameter.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussed? No. The paper makes no mention of in‐game communication or “chat.”

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Discussed? Implicitly yes, in the sense that the model is binary: an individual either cooperates (paying cost c) or defects. However, the paper does not label this as an “all or nothing” design; it is simply a binary model of cooperate vs. defect.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The authors do not compare different contribution formats. They only use the single binary format.

5. Is the contribution default?  
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not mention any default or forced contribution scheme.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor  
   • Discussed? Partly. The model frames a cooperative act as imparting benefit b (sometimes distributed as b/n). They occasionally vary b (in the sensitivity tests) to see how it affects the evolution of cooperation and punishment.  
   • Systematically varied? Yes, in a later “sensitivity analysis” where they consider per‐capita benefit = b/n. They do not directly speak of “MPCR,” but they do alter b (e.g., set it to 2c, 4c, 8c) in some variants.  
   • Dependent variable(s) measured? Frequency of cooperation, not efficiency.  
   • Any numerical effect sizes? They do not give exact numerical changes in “punishment treatment effect,” only qualitative results showing how cooperation remains viable under certain benefit‐to‐cost ratios.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussed? Yes. Throughout the paper, they denote this cost by k. Their baseline is k = 0.2.  
   • Systematically varied? Yes, they compare scenarios with k > 0, k = 0, or fixed vs. variable punishing costs in Figures 2 and 4. However, they do so primarily to see how cooperation fares, rather than measuring a shift in efficiency.  
   • Dependent variable(s) measured? Frequency of cooperation (and frequency of punishers), not efficiency.  
   • Any numerical effect sizes? No direct numeric “punishment‐treatment effect” on payoffs or efficiency is given. They show that when k is relatively low (and especially if it is proportional to the number of defectors), cooperation is much more easily sustained in large groups.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Discussed? Yes. The paper denotes this as p. Their baseline is p = 0.8 (i.e., the defector loses four times more than the punisher pays, since k = 0.2).  
   • Systematically varied? Yes (Figure 3). They compare p = 0.8 vs. a lower punishment magnitude (e.g., p = 0.4) and show that lower p makes defectors less disadvantaged, thereby causing cooperation (and punishment) to collapse more easily.  
   • Dependent variable(s) measured? Frequency of cooperation, not efficiency.  
   • Any numerical effect sizes? Only qualitative differences—for example, with p = 0.8, cooperation remains high for moderate group sizes; with lower p (like 0.4), cooperation frequencies plummet.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussed? No. The model involves only punishment. There is no mention of rewarding cooperative players.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Discussed? No. Not mentioned in the paper.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
   • Discussed? No. Not mentioned in the paper.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not describe any finite‐horizon or known‐end setting.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained or lost each round)?  
   • Discussed? Not in the usual “information display” sense. The model assumes individuals can imitate others based on payoff differences, but it does not treat “peer outcome visibility” as a varied parameter.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Discussed? No. The model does not address whether defectors learn who punished them.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Discussed? No. Again, rewards are not featured in this model, and no mention is made of identifying a rewarder.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   • The paper does not use “efficiency” (defined as total payoff divided by maximum possible payoff) as a dependent variable. Instead, it primarily reports the frequency of cooperation, the frequency of punishers, and occasionally refers to average payoffs only insofar as they influence imitation dynamics (i.e., individuals copy strategies with higher payoffs). Thus, cooperation frequency and punishment frequency are the primary outcome measures, which are not the same as efficiency.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
     (1) Number of players – yes  
     (4) All or nothing contributions – implicitly yes (binary choice model), though not varied  
     (6) MPCR or similar (benefit b) – yes  
     (7) Punishment cost k – yes  
     (8) Punishment magnitude p – yes  
   • None of the other parameters are discussed in the paper.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The paper systematically varies four parameters: (1) group size n, (6) the cooperative benefit parameter (b), (7) punishment cost k, and (8) punishment magnitude p. However, it always measures effects on “frequency of cooperation” (and punishers), not on “efficiency.”  
   • The paper does not systematically vary or discuss the others in relation to punishment treatment effects.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?
   • Because the paper never measures efficiency in the sense of total payoff versus maximum possible payoff, it provides limited direct evidence concerning how these parameters would affect “efficiency.” Its results do imply that when group size is too large (parameter 1) or when punishment is too weak/too costly (parameters 7 and 8), punishment will fail to maintain cooperation, which in turn would likely reduce efficiency in a real public‐goods setting. Similarly, if the effective “MPCR‐like” benefit (parameter 6) is high relative to costs, punishment can help sustain near‐universal cooperation, presumably improving efficiency in the real sense. Beyond those qualitative inferences, the paper provides no direct data on efficiency, so more precise predictions cannot be made from these results alone.
reference_APA: Boyd, R, Gintis, H, Bowles, S & Richerson, PJ (2003). The evolution of altruistic punishment. PROCEEDINGS OF THE NATIONAL ACADEMY OF SCIENCES OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA.

Abstract: The existence of social norms is one of the big unsolved problems in social cognitive science. Article Title: PUNISHMENT ALLOWS THE EVOLUTION OF COOPERATION (OR ANYTHING ELSE) IN SIZABLE GROUPS
Abstract: Existing models suggest that reciprocity is unlikely to evolve in large groups as a result of natural selection. In these models, reciprocators punish noncooperation by withholding future cooperation, and thus also penalize other cooperators in the group. Here, we analyze a model in which the response is some form of punishment that is directed solely at noncooperators. We refer to such alternative forms of punishment as retribution. We show that cooperation enforced by retribution can lead to the evolution of cooperation in two qualitatively different ways. (1) If benefits of cooperation to an individual are greater than the costs to a single individual of coercing the other n - 1 individuals to cooperate, then strategies which cooperate and punish noncooperators, strategies which cooperate only if punished, and, sometimes, strategies which cooperate but do not punish will coexist in the long run. (2) If the costs of being punished are large enough, moralistic strategies which cooperate, punish noncooperators, and punish those who do not punish noncooperators can be evolutionarily stable. We also show, however, that moralistic strategies can cause any individually costly behavior to be evolutionarily stable, whether or not it creates a group benefit.
