     – No numeric effect size.

14. Is the identity of the punisher revealed?  
15. Is the identity of the rewarder revealed?  
   • Not treated.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────
A. Dependent variables used  
   • The paper’s outcomes of interest are individual expected discounted payoffs and the set of “efficient’’ or “mutually beneficial’’ payoffs relative to the stage game.  
   • It never calculates “group efficiency’’ (total payoff ÷ social optimum) nor any treatment-effect difference in that variable.

B. How many of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   • 2 parameters:  
     1. Number of players (population size)  
     13. Visibility / public observability of actions (≈ peer-outcome display)

C. For how many parameters is a *systematic* effect on the punishment treatment effect discussed?  
   • 2 parameters, and only qualitatively:  
     – Population size:  With public observability, punishment effectiveness is population-independent; without observability, increasing population size eventually nullifies punishment’s ability to sustain cooperation (Proposition 3).  
     – Visibility of actions:  Switching from public observability to no information destroys the punishment mechanism in large groups; with full visibility, punishment can enforce any efficient outcome for all group sizes (Propositions 1–2).  
   • No numerical effect sizes are given.

D. Predictions that can be made *solely* on the basis of this paper  
   • Population size:  If players cannot observe others’ behaviour, larger groups sharply reduce (and ultimately eliminate) the positive efficiency impact of introducing punishment.  With full public observability, group size should not matter.  
   • Visibility of actions:  Allowing everyone to see everyone else’s actions is predicted to make punishment highly effective at sustaining efficiency; hiding such information makes punishment ineffective, especially in large populations.  
   • For every other listed parameter (round length, chat, cost/magnitude of punishment, rewards, contribution framing, MPCR, etc.) the paper offers no material whatsoever, so no predictions can be drawn from it.

In short, Kandori (1992) is a theoretical treatment of information transmission and population size in random-matching repeated games; it does not analyse the standard experimental design knobs (punishment cost, reward, MPCR, finite horizons, etc.).  Accordingly, very few of the user’s 15 parameters can be linked to the punishment‐treatment effect on efficiency from this paper alone.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter review of what (if anything) the Chen and Li paper (“Group Identity and Social Preferences”) says about each of the 15 specified design features, with special attention to whether the paper discusses systematic variation in these features and whether it makes any predictions (and provides effect sizes) about “punishment treatment effects” on any dependent variable—especially efficiency. Note that the paper itself does not study a repeated public goods game with peer‐imposed punishment; instead, it runs two‐person sequential allocation games (including “punishment” in the sense of negative reciprocity) and measures outcomes such as payoff differences, reciprocity, and social‐welfare‐maximizing choices. The paper does not analyze the 15 parameters in the context of a public goods game with third‐party or peer punishment. It also does not directly report effects on “efficiency” in a repeated public goods sense (i.e., total payoff relative to a social optimum from mutual cooperation plus punishment). Below, each parameter is addressed in turn.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   The paper reports that sessions had multiple participants, but the main analysis is of two‐person (A,B) sequential games. The “number of players” is never systematically varied as a treatment variable, nor is there any discussion of how changing the number of players would affect punishment or efficiency.

 • Any predictions about systematically varying it on punishment or efficiency?  
   No. The paper does not predict or measure how changing the number of players would affect a punishment treatment effect for any dependent variable.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Number of rounds
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   The paper does not study a repeated public goods game. While participants make decisions in multiple two‐person games, there is no discussion of systematically varying the “number of rounds.”

 • Any predictions about systematically varying it on punishment or efficiency?  
   No. No mention of how different round lengths or repeated interactions would affect the punishment treatment effect.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Is chat enabled between players?
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   Yes. Some treatments do involve a “chat” phase (the “Online Chat” stage), whereas others do not (“NoChat,” “NoHelp” treatments). The purpose is to see whether letting ingroup members chat increases group attachment or affects behavior toward ingroup versus outgroup partners.

 • Any predictions about systematically varying it on a “punishment treatment effect” (particularly on efficiency)?  
   The paper does test the presence vs. absence of chat, but it never frames it as a “punishment treatment” in a public‐goods sense. It looks instead at changes in two‐person reciprocity games (including negative reciprocity/punishment). Although the paper does measure how chat changes self‐reported group attachment and sometimes changes choices, it does not examine or predict how enabling chat would affect a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” There are no direct effect‐size estimates given for “punishment × chat” on an overall group efficiency metric.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   No. The experiment employs two‐person sequential allocation tasks, not an “all or nothing” design for contributions to any public good.

 • Any predictions about systematically varying it?  
   No. Not mentioned in the paper.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much of their endowment to move back into their hand)?
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   No. The experiments are not framed as a voluntary‐contribution public goods game, so there is no discussion of a “default” or forced contribution.

 • Any predictions about systematically varying it?  
   No. Not mentioned in the paper.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as a multiplication factor
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   No. There is no MPCR or “multiplication factor,” since these are not public goods games. Payoffs are set up in two‐person allocation tasks.

 • Any predictions about systematically varying it?  
   No. Not mentioned in the paper.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   Partly. In the paper’s negative‐reciprocity (punishment) games, the authors do refer to B’s “cost to punish” (the payoff difference if B chooses to reduce A’s payoff). While they do not call it “a single unit of punishment,” they do systematically vary how costly it is for B to choose a punishing action across the different two‐person game variants.

 • Any predictions about systematically varying it on a dependent variable? Effect sizes?  
   Yes—on the probability of punishing (i.e., negative reciprocity), not on “group efficiency.” Table 3, Panel B reports a logistic regression where a 100‐token increase in the punisher’s cost reduces the probability of punishing by 32.0% in the treatment sessions. The paper does not translate this into a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency,” nor does it connect it to a public goods scenario.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from a player per unit of punishment)
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   Yes. The paper calls it “Damage to A if B punishes.” This amount varies across the two‐person games, effectively changing the “severity” of a negative reciprocity action.

 • Any predictions about systematically varying it on a dependent variable? Effect sizes?  
   Yes—again for probability of punishing. The authors estimate that a 100‐token increase in the “damage to A” increases the likelihood of punishment by about 4.3% (in Table 3, Panel B). There is no reference to how that would alter “efficiency,” nor is there any “punishment treatment effect” in a public goods sense.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
9. Whether a reward is enabled
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   The paper does examine “positive reciprocity” or “reward,” but as part of the same set of two‐person sequential games—i.e., the possibility that B can choose an action that benefits A at some cost to B.

 • Any predictions about systematically varying “reward enabled” and its effect on punishment treatment or efficiency?
   The paper does not present separate “reward‐enabled vs. not” treatments. Instead, it discusses positive reciprocity in certain sub‐games. There is no systematic variation singled out as “reward on/off,” and no measure of how that changes a punishment treatment effect on overall efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   The paper refers to B’s “cost to reward” (the payoff difference if B chooses a more generous action). It is analyzed in Table 3, Panel A (the logistic regression on rewarding).

 • Any predictions about systematically varying that cost on punishment treatment or efficiency?
   The paper does give effect sizes for the probability of rewarding. But it does not link a systematically varied reward cost to any punishment‐based treatment effect, nor to a public‐goods‐style efficiency measure.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded to a player per unit of reward)
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   Yes—as “Benefit to A if B rewards.” For example, a 100‐token increase in that benefit increases B’s likelihood of rewarding A by 8.9% in the main treatment regressions.

 • Any predictions about systematically varying it on punishment treatment or efficiency?
   No. The paper identifies the relationship with the probability of rewarding but never discusses how this factor interacts with a punishment treatment to affect efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   No. The authors do not systematically vary or discuss “known vs. unknown rounds.” The two‐person games are played in a one‐shot manner (though repeated across many games), and the “end” is not the focus.

 • Any predictions about varying it on punishment treatment or efficiency?
   No mention in the paper.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost each round)?
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   The paper does talk about final payoffs for each participant, but it does not systematically vary or highlight “displaying peer outcomes” as a treatment factor.

 • Any predictions about varying it on punishment or efficiency?
   No. The paper does not explore that systematically.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   In these two‐person games, the “punisher” is always the other player (role B). There is no separate design in which a punishée does or does not know the punisher’s identity. So there is no systematic variation of anonymity.

 • Any predictions about systematically varying it?
   No. Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   As with punishment, the “rewarder” is always the other player in a two‐person game. There is no separate design that withholds that identity. So no separate variation is studied.

 • Any predictions about systematically varying it?
   No. Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   The paper does report individual payoffs and sometimes average (expected) payoffs across participants, and it does note that matching with an ingroup member increases average payoff relative to matching with an outgroup member. However, it does not use “group efficiency” in the usual public‐goods sense (i.e., total payoff / maximum possible from mutual cooperation). Instead, its main dependent variables in the two‐person games are (1) distribution‐preference parameters (charity and envy), (2) probability of rewarding/punishing (positive/negative reciprocity), and (3) the rate of choosing a social‐welfare‐maximizing action. These differ from “efficiency” in a repeated public goods scenario; the paper studies pairwise interactions rather than a repeated group contribution game.

B. Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
     (3) Is chat enabled;  
     (7) Punishment cost to impose punishment (they call it “cost to punish”);  
     (8) Punishment magnitude (they call it “damage to A if B punishes”);  
     (9–11) Reward presence/cost/magnitude are partially embedded in their positive reciprocity games, though not as a separate on/off treatment.  
   • The other parameters (1,2,4,5,6,12,13,14,15) are not discussed or systematically manipulated in their design.  

C. For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   Strictly speaking, the paper never frames any condition as a “punishment treatment” in a repeated public goods sense. However, it does investigate how certain cost or magnitude manipulations (7 and 8 above) affect the likelihood of punishing (i.e., negative reciprocity). The relevant effect sizes:  
   • (7) Punishment cost: A 100‐token cost increase reduces the probability of punishing by ~32%.  
   • (8) Punishment magnitude: A 100‐token increase in “damage to A” raises the probability of punishing by ~4.3%.  
   None of these analyses are about efficiency, nor do they measure a “punishment treatment effect” on total or average payoffs per se.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   The paper does not study a public goods setting or any formal measure of group “efficiency” under punishment; thus, there is insufficient basis to make specific predictions about how systematically varying those 15 parameters would change a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” The paper’s closest reference is that punishment likelihood (in a two‐person negative‐reciprocity sense) decreases as the punisher’s own cost goes up, and increases as the magnitude of harm to the target goes up. But no link is made to a public‐goods‐type efficiency measure. Consequently, one cannot infer meaningful predictions about how each of the 15 parameters would affect “efficiency” in a punishment‐based public goods game from this paper alone.
reference_APA: Chen, Yan & Li, Sherry Xin (2009). Group Identity and Social Preferences. AMERICAN ECONOMIC REVIEW.

Authors: Fehr, E; Fischbacher, U; Gächter, S
Author Full Names: Fehr, E; Fischbacher, U; Gächter, S
Article Title: Strong reciprocity, human cooperation, and the enforcement of social norms
Author Keywords: evolution; game theory; human cooperation; punishment; social norms; strong reciprocity
Keywords Plus: ULTIMATUM GAME; EVOLUTION; PUNISHMENT; FAIRNESS; BEHAVIOR; STAKES; TRUST
Abstract: This paper provides strong evidence challenging the self-interest assumption that dominates the behavioral sciences and much evolutionary thinking. The evidence indicates that many people have a tendency to voluntarily cooperate, if treated fairly, and to punish noncooperators. We call this behavioral propensity strong reciprocity and show empirically that it can lead to almost universal cooperation in circumstances in which purely self-interested behavior would cause a complete breakdown of cooperation. In addition, we show that people are willing to punish those who behaved unfairly towards a third person or who defected in a Prisoner's Dilemma game with a third person. This suggests that strong reciprocity is a powerful device for the enforcement of social norms involving, for example, food sharing or collective action. Strong reciprocity cannot be rationalized as an adaptive trait by the leading evolutionary theories of human cooperation (in other words, kin selection, reciprocal altruism, indirect reciprocity, and costly signaling theory). However, multilevel selection theories of cultural evolution are consistent with strong reciprocity.

Below is a point‐by‐point account of what the Fehr, Fischbacher, and Gächter (2002) paper says—or does not say—about each of the 15 parameters in relation to how introducing punishment in a public goods (or other) game might affect “efficiency.” When the paper explicitly discusses a parameter, I specify whether it is varied “systematically” (i.e., varied in a parametric design fashion) and whether the authors give any quantitative statements about payoffs or other outcomes under those variations. If the parameter is not addressed or if no systematic variation is provided, I state that as well.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of Players  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes, the paper reports different numbers of players in different games (e.g., 2‐player ultimatum bargaining games; 3‐player “third‐party punishment” games; 4‐player public goods games).  
     – However, it does not systematically vary the number of players (e.g., by running 2‐, 3‐, 4‐, 5‐, etc.‐player treatments to examine how that affects punishment’s impact).  
   • Does the paper make predictions about how varying the number of players affects the punishment treatment effect for any dependent variable?  
     – No. The paper mentions that cooperation can be sustained in 4‐person public goods games with punishment but does not provide any predictions for systematically changing group size.

2. Number of Rounds  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. The public goods games typically run for 10 periods, and the paper contrasts “one‐shot” games (e.g., certain ultimatum or single‐trial settings) with repeated‐period games.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary the number of rounds (e.g., 5 vs. 10 vs. 20) to see how that affects punishment?  
     – No. The authors do compare repeated‐interaction (“partner”) vs. random re‐matching (“stranger”) designs and note the difference in cooperation patterns over 10 rounds, but they do not systematically change the total number of rounds.  
   • Numerical effect sizes regarding systematically varying this parameter?  
     – None. No quantitative effect is reported from changing the length of the game as a formal design manipulation.

3. Is Chat Enabled between Players?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Indirectly—by insisting that interactions are fully anonymous and mentioning that subjects do not communicate except through their choices, they effectively state that no “chat” exists.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – No. There is no condition in which communication is allowed versus another condition where it is disallowed. No predictions are made.

4. Is the Contribution “All or Nothing”?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – The public goods games described allow participants to select how many tokens (0 to 20) to contribute, so it is not “all or nothing.” In the bilateral gift‐exchange setting, participants also choose actual effort along a continuous scale (0.1 to 1.0).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary an all‐or‐nothing format?  
     – No. There is no mention of an all‐or‐nothing contribution design, and no predictions are given for changing this parameter.

5. Is the Contribution Default (do players decide how much to move from a public fund back into their hand)?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. The experiments have an explicit “endowment” (tokens) and a choice of how many are invested in the public good, but the paper does not describe a default “automatic contribution” that players must pull back.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – Not addressed, and no predictions are made.

6. Marginal Per Capita Return (MPCR) or Related Parameters (e.g., multiplication factor)  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes, in the public goods game, each token contributed yields 0.4 tokens to each of the four group members. That is effectively an MPCR of 0.4.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary the MPCR?  
     – No. The paper uses MPCR = 0.4 but does not vary it to see how that changes punishment effects.  
   • Any numerical effect sizes about systematically changing MPCR?  
     – None. The authors do not manipulate MPCR within the paper.

7. Punishment Cost to Impose a Single Unit of Punishment  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. In one experiment, it costs the punisher 1 money unit per punishment point assigned (in another setup, a punisher can spend 1 money unit to reduce the target’s payoff by 2.5). In yet another variant, each punishment point reduces the target’s payoff by 10%.  
   • Is it systematically varied?  
     – No. Different experiments mention different punishment technologies, but the paper does not present a side‐by‐side systematic comparison. There is no parametric analysis of how different punishment‐cost levels affect outcomes.  
   • Any quantitative effect of systematically changing punishment cost?  
     – None reported.

8. Punishment Magnitude (coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. There are instances in which 1 punishment point reduces the target’s income by 3, or by 2.5, or by 10% of the target’s payoff.  
   • Is it systematically varied in an experimental design?  
     – No. The authors do not compare, for example, “10% pay reduction” vs. “20% pay reduction” in the same experiment. Different studies used different penalty rules, but no formal parametric contrasts.  
   • Any numerical effect from systematically changing punishment magnitude?  
     – No. The paper does not provide comparative effect sizes for different magnitudes.

9. Whether a Reward Is Enabled  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. One experimental variant gave the employer the ability to punish or reward the worker in a bilateral gift‐exchange.  
   • Is it systematically varied (presence vs. absence of rewards) in the paper to estimate an explicit treatment effect?  
     – The paper describes a setting with both punishments and rewards but does not show a dedicated “reward on vs. reward off” comparison that isolates how that factor alone shapes the punishment effect.  
   • Numerical effect size?  
     – None for systematically varying the presence of reward.

10. Reward Cost to Grant a Single Unit of Reward  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – In the gift‐exchange extension, it costs the “rewarder” 1 money unit to increase the recipient’s payoff by 2.5 money units.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – No, the cost is held constant in one setting; there is no parametric manipulation.  
   • Any effect size reported?  
     – No systematic effect size for different reward‐cost values.

11. Reward Magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted)  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Mentioned as 2.5 money units gained per 1 money unit spent by the rewarder in one experiment.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – No. They do not vary the reward multiplier in a controlled comparison.  
   • No effect on punishment or payoff is reported for systematically changing the reward multiplier.

12. Is the Number of Rounds Known to Players (i.e., do they know when the game ends)?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes, subjects in repeated‐period games are told there are 10 periods. Ultimatum and third‐party punishment games are also described as “one‐shot.”  
   • Is there a systematic variation of known vs. unknown horizon?  
     – No. The authors simply make it clear that subjects know the 10‐period horizon in the repeated games. There is no treatment that hides the horizon.  
   • No quantitative comparison about “known” vs. “unknown” horizon.

13. Are Peer Outcomes Shown (do players know how much peers gained and lost)?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Participants do see other group members’ contributions in the repeated public goods design and also see how many punishment points were assigned. The paper does not emphasize showing each other’s exact payoffs but does say that group members learn about others’ contribution decisions.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – No separate treatments with or without outcome disclosure.  
   • No effect size is reported for systematically hiding or revealing peer outcomes.

14. When a Player Is Punished, Do They Know Who the Specific Punisher Is?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. The authors explicitly say that identities remain anonymous, and players cannot trace who punished whom.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – No. There is no treatment where the punisher’s identity is revealed.  
   • No effect on punishment is reported for switching from anonymous to identified punishment.

15. When a Player Is Rewarded, Do They Know Who the Specific Rewarder Is?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – As with punishment, the design is anonymous. There is no condition in which the rewarder’s identity is revealed.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – None.  
   • No discussion of any effect size.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper’s primary outcome measures are:  
     – Contribution levels or cooperation rates (in public goods or gift‐exchange contexts).  
     – Punishment behavior (how much punishment is administered).  
     – Rejection rates (in ultimatum games).  
     – Third‐party punishment rates (in the 3‐person “third‐party punishment” game).  
   • While the authors sometimes note that punishments can raise overall payoffs (for example, in the bilateral “reward‐and‐punish” extension, total payoffs increased by 40% when punishment/reward was possible), their main dependent variables are typically contributions or punishment rates, not an explicit “efficiency” ratio. Thus, “efficiency” is not singled out as a formal dependent variable in the tables—most of their analysis focuses on how punishment fosters cooperation (contributions), and how strongly reciprocal behavior triggers punishment or reward.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned to some degree:  
     (1) Number of players (2 vs. 3 vs. 4 in different games),  
     (2) Number of rounds (1‐shot vs. 10‐period),  
     (3) No chat (games are anonymous),  
     (4) Continuous contributions (not all or nothing),  
     (6) MPCR = 0.4,  
     (7, 8) Punishment cost and magnitude,  
     (9) Presence of reward (in one gift‐exchange extension),  
     (10, 11) Reward cost and magnitude,  
     (12) Subjects do know the game length in repeated designs,  
     (13) Some outcome information is revealed (others’ contributions and punishment).  
     (14, 15) Punisher/rewarder identity was not revealed.  
   • Not really mentioned/used at all:  
     (5) A “default contribution” mechanism is never described.  
   • Hence the paper touches on 14 of the 15 parameters in some manner, but does not systematically manipulate them to measure how each influences “punishment treatment effects.”

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • The authors do not systematically vary any of the 15 listed parameters in a parametric “treatment effect” sense (like changing MPCR from 0.4 to 0.6, or changing the cost of punishment in a controlled design). Thus, there is no formal effect size from systematically changing these parameters while holding everything else constant.  
   • The only partial exceptions are:  
     – “Partner” vs. “Stranger” group composition (which is a difference in whether the same 4 players stay together or are re‐matched)—but that is not one of the 15 parameters listed. Even that was tested only as different matching protocols, not a manipulated factor in service of “parameter variation” as above.  
   • Therefore, strictly answering the question: none of the 15 parameters are systematically varied in the paper in order to quantify how each one shapes the punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency (or on contributions, payoffs, etc.). The paper primarily contrasts “no‐punishment” vs. “punishment” conditions (and in some experiments, also “reward” or “third‐party punishment”), but does not do parametric manipulations of the 15 items.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not systematically address most of these parameters, so one cannot derive a quantitative set of predictions about how each would change the punishment treatment’s impact on overall group efficiency.  
   • Based on the paper’s broader messages, one might qualitatively guess the following (though the authors do not claim this in a formal parametric sense):  
     – Increasing the number of rounds or making interactions stable (rather than random) tends to strengthen cooperation under punishment, which might raise total payoffs and efficiency.  
     – Higher punishment severity likely dissuades defection more strongly, potentially enhancing cooperation, though the direct cost of punishing can reduce net payoffs if punishment is too costly.  
     – Allowing rewards (alongside punishment) can induce over‐cooperation in bilateral gift‐exchange settings and might boost total payoffs, as noted in the example where they reported a 40% overall payoff increase in one extension.  
     – Beyond these broad statements, the paper does not provide enough direct empirical or theoretical detail to predict how other parameters (like enabling chat, varying MPCR, or revealing the punisher) would quantitatively shape efficiency.

In short, the paper rarely uses the explicit “efficiency” measure (total or average payoff divided by the payoff with full cooperation), nor does it systematically vary these 15 parameters to observe or predict changes specifically in a “punishment treatment effect.” The paper’s main focus is on how the availability of punishment (and reward, in one extension) influences cooperation, and how strong reciprocity manifests even in one‐shot or randomly matched environments.
reference_APA: Fehr, E, Fischbacher, U & Gächter, S (2002). Strong reciprocity, human cooperation, and the enforcement of social norms. HUMAN NATURE-AN INTERDISCIPLINARY BIOSOCIAL PERSPECTIVE.

Authors: CLUTTONBROCK, TH; PARKER, GA

Below I go through the 15 parameters one by one, quoting or paraphrasing only what appears in “Punishment in animal societies” (Clutton-Brock & Parker) and its boxes, figures and tables.

Parameter-by-parameter scan  

1  Number of players  
   (1) Discussed? Yes.  All formal models in Boxes 1-4 involve two individuals, “player 1” and “player 2.”  
   (2) Systematic variation? No.  The paper never analyses what would happen with three or more players, so no prediction can be extracted.

2  Number of rounds  
   (1) Discussed? Yes.  Each repeated game lasts N rounds; j of those are “training rounds” while the victim is still learning.  
   (2) Systematic variation? Only implicitly.  Several ESS conditions contain N (e.g., kc1 > j d1).  The authors do not vary N and report no effect sizes, so no quantitative prediction can be stated.

3  Is chat enabled?  
   (1) Not mentioned.  
   (2) No discussion, no prediction.

4  All-or-nothing contribution constraint  
   (1) Not literally addressed—the action set is Transgress vs. Desist (or Cooperate vs. Non-cooperate).  
   (2) No systematic variation; no prediction.

5  Contribution default (endowment moved back)  
   Not mentioned at all.

6  Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor  
   (1) Not mentioned.  Gains from transgressing or cooperating are labelled g1, g2, c1, c2, but these are one-person fitness effects, not group MPCRs.  
   (2) No systematic variation; no prediction.

7  Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   (1) Discussed.  It is d1 for the punisher.  Appears in every stability condition (e.g., kc1 > j d1).  
   (2) Systematic variation? Only qualitatively.  The authors state that if d1 is “small” relative to future gains, punishment can be an ESS.  They never report effect sizes for different d1 values, so no numerical prediction on efficiency can be extracted.

8  Punishment magnitude (damage to target per unit)  
   (1) Discussed.  Damage is d2 to the punished individual.  Conditions such as d2 > g2 appear repeatedly.  
   (2) Systematic variation? Qualitative only.  Larger d2 (holding d1 constant) makes punishment ESSs easier to satisfy; no numbers and no efficiency results are reported.

9  Whether a reward is enabled  
   Not mentioned.

10  Reward cost  
    Not mentioned.

11  Reward magnitude  
    Not mentioned.

12  Is the horizon known?  
    Not discussed.

13  Are peer outcomes shown?  
    Not discussed.

14  Is the punisher identified?  
    Not discussed.

15  Is the rewarder identified?  
    Not discussed.



------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables  
    The paper never measures “group efficiency” (actual total payoff ÷ maximum total payoff).  It analyses individual fitness pay-offs and derives conditions for Evolutionarily Stable Strategies (ESSs).  Thus the dependent variables are individual pay-offs, not efficiency, contribution level, or cooperation rate.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
    4 of the 15:  
      • #1 Number of players (always 2)  
      • #2 Number of rounds (symbol N, plus j and k = N-j)  
      • #7 Punishment cost to punisher (d1)  
      • #8 Punishment magnitude to target (d2)

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of systematically varying the parameter on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable)?  
    Zero.  All references to d1, d2, N, j, etc. are used to write boundary conditions (inequalities) for whether a punishment ESS exists; nowhere are those parameters systematically varied and linked to a measured “treatment effect,” let alone to efficiency.

D.  Predictions—if we had to forecast the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency using only this paper  
    • Because the model is strictly dyadic and not a public-goods setup, almost no direct translation to “group efficiency” is possible.  
    • Qualitatively one could say: lower punishment cost (d1) and/or higher punishment impact (d2) should make successful punishment—and hence compliance—more likely; that might raise the punisher’s payoff and possibly the joint payoff if costly conflicts are avoided after learning.  However, the paper does not state this in efficiency terms, provides no numbers, and gives no analysis of multi-person public goods.  
    • All other parameters (chat, MPCR, reward options, information conditions, etc.) are entirely absent, so no prediction can be made from this source alone.

In short, the article offers almost no usable information for predicting how the 15 canonical public-goods-game parameters will influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter survey of what Chaudhuri’s (2010) paper does and does not say about systematically varying each of the 15 listed factors (1)–(15), with respect to costly punishment in public‐goods settings. Throughout, “the paper” refers solely to the Chaudhuri (2010) survey that you provided. All references (e.g., Fehr & Gächter 2000, Gächter et al. 2008, Nikiforakis & Normann 2008) are as cited in that survey. Remember that the paper’s main focus is on contributions (or “cooperation”) and, at times, average or total payoffs. It does not systematically use “efficiency” (i.e., actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff) as a primary reported outcome, though it occasionally discusses net earnings or cost‐effectiveness. Any place where the paper discusses something other than efficiency (e.g., contributions, cooperation rates) is explicitly noted.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Yes. Various studies feature different group sizes (commonly 4‐person groups). One specific case is Carpenter (2007a), which looks at 5‐person vs. 10‐person groups to see how monitoring/punishment scales with group size.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying group size on the “punishment treatment effect” (especially on efficiency)?  
     – It reports that in Carpenter (2007a), larger groups (10 vs. 5) sometimes achieve higher or more stable contributions under certain monitoring conditions. However, the paper does not report explicit “efficiency” measures (i.e., total payoff vs. optimal payoff). Discussions focus on contribution rates rather than the punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency. No numerical effect size on efficiency is given.

2. Number of rounds
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Yes. Many of the cited experiments use 10 or 20 rounds; Gächter et al. (2008) specifically vary the time horizon from 10 rounds (P10) to 50 rounds (P50).  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematic variation in the number of rounds on the punishment treatment’s effect?  
     – Yes, for both contributions and earnings (which the paper sometimes equates to “payoffs”). Gächter et al. (2008) find that a longer horizon (50 rounds) leads to higher average contributions and also significantly higher net earnings with punishment compared to a 10‐round punishment treatment. The paper quantifies that per‐period contributions in P50 are about 25% higher than in P10 and about 50% higher than in the no‐punishment control of similar length, and that average net earnings are higher in P50. Although this is a payoff result, it is not explicitly framed as “efficiency” (i.e., payoff/maximum possible), but it is the closest numerical evidence on total payoffs.

3. Is chat (communication) enabled between players?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Yes. Several references show that face‐to‐face discussion or chat can boost contributions. Bochet et al. (2006) compare no‐communication vs. face‐to‐face vs. chat, sometimes combined with punishment.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying chat on the punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency?  
     – The paper reports that punishment plus robust communication often raises contributions very close to 100% of endowment, but it does not provide explicit numerical comparisons of “efficiency” (payoff versus maximum). The discussion is in terms of high cooperation or high contributions; no explicit effect size for efficiency is reported.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing” vs. choosing any amount?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – No. All studies surveyed use (or assume) a linear public good with continuous contribution choices from 0 to one’s entire endowment. There is no mention of a forced “all‐or‐nothing” regime.  
   • Any predictions about varying an all‐or‐nothing contribution format?  
     – No. The paper does not address this.

5. Is there a “contribution default” (e.g., forced or automatic transfer)?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – No. The paper does not mention any design where participants must “opt out” of contributing or have a default transfer from the public fund back to themselves, etc.  
   • Any predictions about systematically varying such a default?  
     – No coverage in the paper.

6. Marginal per‐capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Does the paper discuss MPCR?  
     – Yes. MPCR is foundational to linear public goods games. Ledyard (1995) is cited, and many of the surveyed experiments vary MPCR (examples: 0.3, 0.5, 0.75).  
   • Does the paper discuss how systematically varying MPCR affects the punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency?  
     – The paper does note that higher MPCR generally raises contributions and can alter the degree to which punishment fosters cooperation. However, explicit “efficiency” measures are not given (the focus remains on cooperation rates). No numeric effect on efficiency is provided.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit of punishment
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Yes. It discusses experiments where the punisher’s cost per “punishment point” is varied (e.g., Anderson & Putterman 2006 vary the “price” of imposing punishment).  
   • Does the paper present predictions or effect sizes regarding how systematically varying the cost of punishment affects efficiency?  
     – It primarily discusses how changes in the cost affect the “demand for punishment” and contributions; e.g., the law of demand for punishment (punish less when it costs more). But the paper does not give numerical estimates of changes in efficiency. It mostly reports changes in contributions or in raw “punishment expenditures.”

8. Punishment magnitude (income reduction per unit of punishment)
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Yes. One central theme is the “effectiveness” of punishment (how many tokens the target loses per punisher’s token). For example, Nikiforakis & Normann (2008) vary this from 1:1 up to 1:4.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about punishment magnitude’s effect on efficiency?  
     – Yes. The paper explicitly notes that only when punishment is sufficiently “high impact” (e.g., cost 1 but reduces the target’s payoff by 3 or 4) can it improve overall earnings above a no‐punishment baseline. For instance, at a 1:4 ratio, average group payoffs exceed those of the control. This is the clearest instance where the paper discusses systematic variation leading to an actual payoff (and thus approximate efficiency) increase. However, no single numeric “efficiency” ratio is reported; rather, it is stated that with 1:3 or 1:4, contributions remain ~90% of endowment and payoffs exceed the no‐punishment case.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Yes. Several experiments combine punishment and reward or allow for positive and negative “sanction” points (e.g., Gürerk et al. 2006, Sefton et al. 2007).  
   • Does the paper present predictions on systematically varying “reward enabled vs. disabled” for the punishment effect on efficiency?  
     – It discusses that the availability of rewards plus punishments can yield higher cooperation than punishment alone (Sefton et al. 2007). However, no explicit numeric effect on group efficiency is reported—only contributions. The paper does not isolate “punishment efficiency” under varied reward settings.

10. Reward cost to grant one unit of reward
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Briefly, yes, in studies where reward costs 1 token to the rewarder and gives +1 token to the recipient (e.g., Gürerk et al. 2006).  
   • Predictions about systematically varying that cost’s effect on punishment’s impact?  
     – No. The paper does not report any systematic variation of reward cost nor how that would change the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

11. Reward magnitude (tokens gained by recipient per unit of reward)
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – As above, typically it is a “1 token cost → +1 token to the rewarded.”  
   • Any predictions about how changing reward magnitude affects punishment treatment or efficiency?  
     – No. The paper does not cover systematically varying the payoff from each reward point.

12. Is the number of rounds known (do players know when the game ends)?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – The paper mentions that most repeated‐game studies have a public, fixed horizon (e.g., 10, 20, 50 rounds) or in some designs a random stopping rule. However, it does not specifically study “knowledge vs. ignorance of T” as a systematically varied factor for punishment.  
   • Predictions about that variation’s effect on punishment or efficiency?  
     – Not addressed in a systematic way.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (e.g., do players see exact contributions, earnings)?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Yes. In nearly all punishment designs, subjects see others’ contributions or can at least infer them before punishing. Some studies vary “monitoring fraction” (Carpenter 2007a), but the paper frames it in terms of who can punish whom.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying how much information is displayed and the resulting punishment–efficiency link?  
     – The paper discusses only that partial or full monitoring changes contribution trajectories. No numeric effect on payoff or efficiency is given.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who punished them?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Yes, extensively. Several references point out that revealing the punisher’s identity can lead to “counter‐punishment” or “antisocial punishment” (Nikiforakis 2008). In other designs (Cinyabuguma et al. 2005), punishee does not know who punished them.  
   • Does the paper make predictions on systematically varying “punisher identity revealed or not” for efficiency?  
     – The paper notes that revealing the punisher’s identity can undermine cooperation via revenge and antisocial punishment, but it does not quantify changes in total payoff or efficiency. The focus is on cooperation or contribution levels, not on payoff data.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who rewarded them?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – It does not explicitly address the anonymity of the rewarder.  
   • Any predicted effect on the punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency?  
     – No. This aspect is not covered.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are they different?  
   • The paper mostly reports “contributions” to the public good as the main dependent variable—often called “cooperation.” It also discusses “average earnings” or “payoffs” to see whether punishment is “cost‐effective.” True efficiency defined as “actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff” is mentioned only indirectly. Instances where net payoffs are higher in the punishment treatment are typically labeled in the paper as “more efficient,” but most references focus on contribution rates rather than formal efficiency ratios.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some capacity:  
     (1) Number of players, (2) Number of rounds, (3) Communication/chat, (6) MPCR, (7) Punishment cost, (8) Punishment magnitude, (9) Whether reward is enabled, (12) (some mention of horizon but not “knowledge vs. ignorance”), (13) Peer outcomes shown, and (14) Whether the punished player knows the punisher.  
   • Not mentioned (or only tangentially mentioned without any detail):  
     (4) All‐or‐nothing contributions, (5) Contribution default, (10) Reward cost systematically varied, (11) Reward magnitude systematically varied, (15) Whether rewarded players learn who rewarded them.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Clear systematic variation with explicit results:  
     – (2) Number of rounds (short vs. long horizon) → Focusing on net payoffs in Gächter et al. (2008).  
     – (7) Punishment cost → Some studies vary cost (Anderson & Putterman 2006, Carpenter 2007b), but the main findings concern changes in quantity of punishment or contributions rather than explicit efficiency.  
     – (8) Punishment magnitude → Nikiforakis & Normann (2008) systematically vary it (1:1 up to 1:4) and find that only high‐impact punishments raise payoffs above no‐punishment.  
   • Other parameters are either mentioned in passing or varied only to measure effects on contributions/cooperation, not on efficiency per se. No exact “treatment effect on efficiency” estimates are given except, informally, for (2) and (8), where the paper does note significantly higher total payoffs under certain punishment conditions.

D. If you were to make predictions about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   1) The paper does not discuss (4), (5), (10), (11), or (15) at all, so it provides no basis for predicting how these would affect efficiency.  
   2) It indicates that (2) a longer horizon can make peer punishment more effective both in raising contributions and in generating higher net earnings.  
   3) (7) & (8) must be balanced: punishment is only beneficial to total payoffs if it is relatively inexpensive for punishers but yields a sufficiently large payoff reduction to free‐riders. If penalty‐to‐cost ratios are too low, punishment reduces overall efficiency.  
   4) (1), (3), (6), (9), (12), (13), and (14) are shown to affect cooperation or whether participants punish, but their direct connections to “efficiency” as defined by total payoff/max payoff are either not reported or only hinted at.  

Hence, for many of the 15 parameters, the paper’s discussions concern cooperation levels rather than formal efficiency outcomes. Only for the cost‐effectiveness of punishment (param 7 vs. 8), the time horizon (param 2), and certain punishment‐design details do we see explicit references to higher or lower net earnings. For all other parameters, the paper does not provide sufficient information to draw fully confident conclusions about the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Below, each of the 15 design parameters is treated in turn.

For every parameter I report:

• Does the paper describe the parameter and, if so, what exact value or qualitative setting is used?  
• Does the paper say anything about what would happen to the **punishment treatment effect** if the parameter were systematically varied?  If yes, the stated or inferable numerical effect size is quoted (with the table / figure / page reference).  If no such claim appears, that is stated explicitly.

“Punishment-treatment effect’’ = (outcome with punishment) − (outcome without punishment), where the outcome of interest would have to be **efficiency** to match the user’s question.  The paper, however, generally reports mean contributions or cooperation rates, not efficiency.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned: Every experimental group contains 4 players (“each subject being grouped with three other subjects,” §3, description of Fehr & Gächter).  
   • Systematic-variation statement: none.  No prediction of how changing group size would alter the punishment-treatment effect. (The evolutionary section later simulates 8 vs 40 founders, but that is about the *population frequency of strong reciprocators*, not about an efficiency effect of punishment.)

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned: 10 rounds for Partner and Stranger treatments; 6 rounds for Perfect-Stranger because of subject-pool size (§3).  
   • Systematic-variation statement: none.  The paper never asks “What if the game had 20 rounds?” in connection with punishment effects.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Not mentioned; there is no description of any communication channel.  
   • Consequently no systematic-variation statement.

4. Contribution “all-or-nothing’’?  
   • Mentioned implicitly as “continuous choice’’: subjects can place “some number of the 20 points in the common account” (§3).  
   • No systematic-variation statement.

5. Contribution default / “endowment framed as public then reclaimed’’?  
   • Not mentioned.  No predictions.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned: Each point contributed returns 0.4 points to the contributor and 0.4 to each of the three team-mates (Fehr & Gächter design).  
   • No statement about varying the MPCR and its influence on the punishment-treatment effect.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   • Referred to only qualitatively (“by paying a ‘fee’, subjects could impose costs…”, §3, citing Ostrom et al.; “costly punishment,” §3 for Fehr & Gächter).  No numeric values given.  
   • No systematic-variation statement linking different punishment costs to changes in efficiency.

8. Punishment magnitude to the target  
   • Qualitatively noted (“impose costs,” “inflict harm”), but no numeric schedule appears.  
   • No systematic-variation prediction.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Not mentioned anywhere in the paper.  No predictions.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   • Not mentioned; therefore nothing about variation.

12. Finite horizon known?  
   • Yes: subjects “are informed … the experiment continues for exactly ten rounds.”  
   • No systematic-variation statement (e.g., hidden vs known horizon) vis-à-vis punishment’s impact.

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
   • Yes: after each round “the experimenter then tells the subjects how many points were contributed to the common account.” Individual earnings or identities are not revealed.  
   • No systematic-variation statement.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
   • Not stated.  The experiment is said to proceed under “strict anonymity,” suggesting that punishers are *not* identified, but this is not discussed further, nor is any variation of anonymity tested.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
   • Not applicable—no reward stage is used.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary

A. Dependent variables  
   • The laboratory part reports mean contributions (Fig. 1) and the *stability / change* of those contributions over time.  
   • The evolutionary model uses expected fitness (π) and the population frequency of a trait.  
   • **Group efficiency (total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff) is never computed or used as a dependent variable.**  Efficiency differs from contribution because, with MPCR < 1, 100 % contribution is still inefficient from an individual payoff perspective, even though it maximizes group payoff.  The paper does not present that calculation.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are at least mentioned?  
   Mentioned: 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14 (implicit anonymity).  → 9 of 15.  
   Not mentioned at all: 3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 15.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss *systematically varying* that parameter and the resulting punishment-treatment effect (for any dependent variable)?  
   • None (0/15).  The paper never manipulates any focal parameter across conditions to see how the with-punishment minus without-punishment difference changes.  The only manipulated factor in the cited experiment is *whether* punishment is available, and whether group membership is Partner/Stranger/Perfect-Stranger; none of the 15 listed parameters is systematically varied.

D. If one must nonetheless predict how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) will influence the punishment-treatment effect on **efficiency** using *only the content of this paper*, the information is extremely limited:  
   • The existence of punishment itself maintains or raises cooperation relative to a no-punishment baseline (Fig. 1).  Translating that into efficiency, one could assume “efficiency rises when punishment is allowed,” but no numeric mapping is given.  
   • The only hint of an interaction is that the *Partner* design (stable group) shows a larger absolute rise in contribution than the Stranger designs; this loosely suggests that anything making the group more stable/cohesive (parameter 2: longer repeated interaction, parameter 12: certainty about the horizon, parameter 1: smaller well-identified group) might amplify the punishment effect.  The paper gives no numbers, just the qualitative shape in Fig. 1.  
   • Beyond that, the model section emphasizes that high punishment *effectiveness* relative to its *cost* (large h, small c_r) makes cooperation sustainable, but those symbols do not map cleanly onto the 15 experimental design parameters except for the very general idea that *stronger, cheaper punishment* should increase efficiency.  No further predictions can be drawn.

Hence, on the basis of this paper alone, almost no quantitative or even directional prediction can be made for 14 of the 15 parameters, and only the very general statement “punishment increases efficiency more in stable groups” can be cautiously inferred for parameter sets that foster partner-like interaction.

Authors: Doebeli, M; Hauert, C
Author Full Names: Doebeli, M; Hauert, C
Article Title: Models of cooperation based on the Prisoner's Dilemma and the Snowdrift game
Author Keywords: continuous games; evolution of cooperation; game theory; iterated games; spatially structured; populations; Tragedy of the Commune
Keywords Plus: TIT-FOR-TAT; BY-PRODUCT MUTUALISM; PREDATOR INSPECTION; EVOLUTIONARY DYNAMICS; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; VISCOUS POPULATIONS; KIN-SELECTION; STRATEGIES; BEHAVIOR
Abstract: Understanding the mechanisms that can lead to the evolution of cooperation through natural selection is a core problem in biology. Among the various attempts at constructing a theory of cooperation, game theory has played a central role. Here, we review models of cooperation that are based on two simple games: the Prisoner's Dilemma, and the Snowdrift game. Both games are two-person games with two strategies, to cooperate and to defect, and both games are social dilemmas. In social dilemmas, cooperation is prone to exploitation by defectors, and the average payoff in populations at evolutionary equilibrium is lower than it would be in populations consisting of only cooperators. The difference between the games is that cooperation is not maintained in the Prisoner's Dilemma, but persists in the Snowdrift game at an intermediate frequency. As a consequence, insights gained from studying extensions of the two games differ substantially. We review the most salient results obtained from extensions such as iteration, spatial structure, continuously variable cooperative investments, and multi-person interactions. Bridging the gap between theoretical and empirical research is one of the main challenges for future studies of cooperation, and we conclude by pointing out a number of promising natural systems in which the theory can be tested experimentally.

Below I go through the 15 parameters one‐by‐one, quoting or paraphrasing only what is actually stated in the Doebeli & Hauert (2005) review and indicating whether the paper (i) mentions the parameter at all, and (ii) makes any prediction about how systematically varying that parameter would change the **punishment treatment effect** (i.e., the difference in efficiency between a Punishment and a No-Punishment condition).  “Efficiency” is never measured in the review, so whenever the paper speaks about other dependent variables (fraction of cooperators, evolutionary stability, basins of attraction, etc.) I flag that explicitly.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1. Number of players  
   (i) Mentioned.  The paper treats the two-player PD/SD and also their N-player extensions (Public Goods game; Box 3, Box 5).  
   (ii) No prediction about how changing group size alters *punishment* effects on efficiency.  Punishment is analysed only for the 2-player PD.

2. Number of rounds  
   (i) Mentioned repeatedly (Iterated PD and Iterated SD).  
   (ii) No statement that varying the number of rounds changes the *punishment* treatment effect (punishment is only analysed in a non-iterated two-stage PD with reputation).

3. Is chat enabled?  
   (i) Not mentioned.  
   (ii) No prediction.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   (i) Yes.  Binary (“all-or-nothing”) PD/SD are contrasted with “continuous” investment versions.  
   (ii) Punishment is never analysed in the continuous versions, so no prediction about this parameter’s impact on the punishment effect.

5. Contribution default / opt-out framing  
   (i) Not mentioned.  
   (ii) No prediction.

6. MPCR or multiplication factor  
   (i) Mentioned (Public Goods multiplier α; Box 3).  
   (ii) Never linked to punishment, so no prediction.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   (i) Explicitly discussed in Box 4 (“cost/fine ratio of punishment”).  
   (ii) Qualitative prediction:  Lower costs (or, equivalently, a smaller cost-to-fine ratio) enlarge the basin of attraction of the “social” strategy G₁ that both cooperates and punishes.  Conversely, high costs shrink that basin.  No numerical effect size or efficiency measure is reported.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine levied on the target)  
   (i) Also in Box 4 as the “fine” component in the cost/fine ratio.  
   (ii) Qualitative prediction:  Larger fines (holding cost constant) favour the cooperative equilibrium for the same reason as above.  No numbers and no efficiency statistics are provided.

9. Whether a reward option is enabled  
   (i) Mentioned briefly in Box 4: “rewarding mechanisms… lead to complicated dynamics.”  
   (ii) No systematic analysis, no prediction, and no efficiency measure.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   (i) Only generic statements that rewarding is “easily exploited”; no parameters singled out.  
   (ii) No prediction on punishment treatment effects.

12. Whether the horizon (number of rounds) is known  
   (i) Not mentioned.  
   (ii) No prediction.

13. Whether peer outcomes are publicly displayed  
   (i) Not mentioned.  
   (ii) No prediction.

14. Whether the punished player sees who punished them  
   (i) Reputation subsection (Box 4) assumes “individuals may learn about the punishing behaviour of their opponent,” implying that identities (or at least reputations) of punishers are known.  
   (ii) Qualitative statement: if punishers can be recognised, players can condition cooperation on that reputation and “punishment promotes cooperation … and can even enforce cooperation if the costs of cooperation exceed the benefits.”  Again, no efficiency metric nor numeric effect size is supplied.

15. Whether the rewarded player sees who rewarded them  
   (i) Not mentioned.  
   (ii) No prediction.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables actually analysed  
    – The paper uses: proportion of cooperators, strategy frequencies, evolutionary stability, basins of attraction, and sometimes individual/payoff dynamics in phase-plane diagrams.  
    – “Efficiency” (total group payoff divided by its maximum) is never reported.  Therefore, any links to efficiency must be inferred (and the authors make none).

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
    1 (players), 2 (rounds), 4 (all-or-nothing vs continuous), 6 (MPCR), 7 (punishment cost), 8 (punishment magnitude), 9 (reward enabled), and 14 (visibility/ reputation of punishers).  That is 8 of 15.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss the *systematic* effect of varying the parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
    Only 3: punishment cost (7), punishment magnitude (8), and visibility of punishers (14).  Even for these, the discussion is qualitative, refers to cooperation rates rather than efficiency, and provides no numeric effect sizes.

D.  If forced to predict the impact of the 15 parameters (and their interactions) on the punishment-induced change in efficiency based solely on this paper:  
    – Lower punishment costs and/or higher punishment fines (larger fine-to-cost ratio) together with reputational visibility of punishers should make the cooperative/punishing equilibrium more likely; hence efficiency *should* increase, but the magnitude is unknown.  
    – All other parameters receive no guidance from the paper; therefore no reliable prediction can be made for their main effects or interactions on efficiency.

In short, the review supplies only very limited and purely qualitative clues—restricted to the fine-to-cost ratio of punishment and to whether punishment reputations are observable.  For the majority of the 15 parameters, and for any quantitative prediction about efficiency, the paper is silent.

Below each of the 15 parameters I report exactly what can (and cannot) be extracted from the Gintis et al. (2003) article and its figures/tables.

FOR EVERY PARAMETER I ASK TWO QUESTIONS  
Q1. Is the parameter even mentioned (and, if so, what value or range is reported)?  
Q2. Does the paper **systematically vary** the parameter and tell us how this changes the
“punishment treatment effect” (PT-effect = payoff‐efficiency with punishment minus payoff‐efficiency without punishment)?  Numerical effect sizes are given whenever they can be inferred directly from the text or Fig. 2.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Number of players  
   Q1. Mentioned.  Examples: employer–employee game (2 players); public-goods game (4 players).  
   Q2. Not varied within a single experimental design, so no statement on how changing group size alters the PT-effect.

2.  Number of rounds  
   Q1. Mentioned.  Public-goods games are run for 6 or 10 rounds (one place says 10, another 6 and 10); earlier “typical” exposition refers to 10 rounds; Fehr & Gächter use 10.  
   Q2. No systematic comparison of 6 vs 10 vs anything else on the PT-effect.

3.  Chat (within-group communication)  
   Q1. Never mentioned.  
   Q2. No data, no prediction.

4.  “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
   Q1. Not mentioned; all public-goods descriptions involve continuous choice.  
   Q2. No data, no prediction.

5.  Contribution default / “take” frame  
   Q1. Not mentioned.  
   Q2. No data, no prediction.

6.  MPCR / multiplication factor  
   Q1. Implicitly 0.40 (each unit contributed returns 0.40 to each of four members ⇒ social multiplier = 1.6).  
   Q2. Held constant; no systematic variation, hence no prediction for PT-effect.

7.  Punishment cost (cost to punisher per unit)  
   Q1. The employer-employee game: cost = 1 point.  Public-goods punishment cost not numerically specified.  
   Q2. Cost never varied, so no statement on how changing cost influences the PT-effect.

8.  Punishment magnitude (loss inflicted per unit)  
   Q1. Employer-employee game: magnitude = 2.5 points per one-unit cost.  Public-goods magnitude not specified.  
   Q2. Not varied; no prediction for PT-effect.

9.  Presence of a reward option  
   Q1. Employer-employee game allows both punishment and reward.  Public-goods game does not.  
   Q2. Reward option is either absent (public-goods) or present (employer-employee) but never experimentally contrasted within one design.  No statement on how “adding–removing reward” alters the PT-effect on efficiency.

10. Reward cost  
    Q1. Employer-employee: cost = 1.  
    Q2. Not varied.

11. Reward magnitude  
    Q1. Employer-employee: +2.5 points per unit reward.  
    Q2. Not varied.

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
    Q1. Yes.  Subjects are explicitly told the total number of rounds in every public-goods design.  
    Q2. The paper does not contrast “known” vs “unknown” horizon, so no prediction for PT-effect.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    Q1. Subjects are told total group contribution each round; individual breakdown is not specified.  
    Q2. Not manipulated; no prediction for PT-effect.

14. Is the identity of the punisher revealed?  
    Q1. Repeatedly states that interactions are under “strict anonymity,” implying identities are concealed.  No further detail.  
    Q2. No manipulation, hence no prediction.

15. Is the identity of the rewarder revealed?  
    Q1. Same as (14); not explicitly discussed.  
    Q2. Not manipulated; no prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables used  
   – “Efficiency,” “net payoffs,” or “total payoffs” are mentioned only twice (e.g., employer-employee game: punishment + reward raise net payoffs by ~40 %).  
   – Much more space is devoted to “contribution level,” “effort,” and “cooperation” rates.  
   Hence, efficiency is referenced but is not the main dependent variable; contribution and cooperation are treated separately.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   10 of 15 (parameters 1, 2, 4, 6–12, 14) appear at least once in descriptive passages, although most are fixed at a single value.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss **systematic variation and its effect on the PT-effect**?  
   Zero.  The only genuine treatment contrast is “punishment allowed” vs “punishment forbidden,” holding all 15 parameters constant.  
   Thus, the article never tells us how changing any one of the 15 parameters alters the incremental effect of punishment on efficiency (or on any other dependent variable).

D.  Predictions one can make **solely from this paper** about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) influence the PT-effect on efficiency  
   – Virtually none.  Because none of the parameters are varied, the paper cannot support quantitative or even directional predictions for those parameters.  
   – The single robust statement that can be made is: “Allowing any costly peer-to-peer punishment under the conditions actually used (4-person group, MPCR = 0.4, 10 known rounds, anonymity maintained, no chat) dramatically increases both contributions and (in the employer-employee setting) net payoffs, i.e., raises efficiency.”  
   – Beyond that, any forecast about, for example, ‘lower punishment cost will amplify the PT-effect’ or ‘revealing punisher identity will weaken it’ would require bringing in outside evidence, which the instructions forbid.

In short, Gintis et al. (2003) convincingly document one big fact—“punishment boosts cooperation and sometimes payoffs under the exact conditions they study”—but they do not provide leverage for predicting how the magnitude of that boost will shift when any of the 15 design parameters are systematically tweaked.

⇒ Parameter discussed conceptually, no systematic variation, no efficiency result.

2. Number of rounds

⇒ Parameter discussed; no numbers and no treatment-effect estimate on efficiency when punishment is introduced.

• Not mentioned.  
⇒ No data, no prediction.

5. Endowment “default” rule (contribute first and retract later)  
• Not discussed.  
⇒ No data, no prediction.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
• Not discussed.  
⇒ No data, no prediction.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
• Repeatedly stresses that punishment is “costly for the punisher” and therefore second-order freeriding is a problem (pp. 16-17).  
• No numerical values; no parametric sweep; no efficiency numbers.  
⇒ Parameter acknowledged qualitatively but never varied or quantified.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss to the target per unit)  
• Implicitly invoked: “being punished is sufficiently costly so that cooperators have higher payoffs than defectors” (p. 31).  
• Again, purely conceptual; not systematically varied; no efficiency numbers.

• Rewards are not analysed.  
⇒ No data, no prediction.

• Not discussed.  
⇒ No data, no prediction.

• Not mentioned.

• Not mentioned.  
⇒ No data, no prediction.

• Not mentioned.  
⇒ No data, no prediction.

Summary  

A. Dependent variables  
• The paper does not use “group efficiency” in the experimental-economics sense (total payoff divided by the maximum).  The main dependent variables are (i) change in gene or cultural-trait frequency (Δx, Δφ), (ii) individual or group fitness in the evolutionary sense, and (iii) equilibrium stability (whether cooperation/punishment equilibria exist).  “Efficiency” in the payoff-maximising sense is therefore only an informal synonym for “higher mean group fitness,” not an explicit dependent variable.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
Four:  
1 (group size), 2 (number of rounds), 7 (punishment cost), 8 (punishment magnitude).  The other 11 parameters never appear.

C. Which parameters are systematically varied with respect to the punishment-treatment effect on ANY dependent variable?  
None.  The paper contains no systematic parameter sweep, no tables or figures manipulating any of the 15 parameters, and no numerical effect sizes for punishment on efficiency (or on any other dependent variable).

Almost none that are useful for forecasting the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.  The only verbal hints are:  
• If punishment is less costly to the punisher and/or more costly to the target (Parameters 7 & 8), then cooperation is more likely to be stable—hence efficiency “should” rise—but no magnitude is given.  
• Larger groups (Parameter 1) make reciprocity harder and therefore cooperation less stable; the paper does not show this specifically for punishment.  
• More rounds (Parameter 2) increase the between-group component in reciprocity models but, again, no quantitative link to punishment or efficiency.

Beyond these broad qualitative statements the paper provides no basis for quantitative prediction of how the 15 parameters, alone or in interaction, alter the punishment-treatment effect on group efficiency.

Abstract: Models of large-scale human cooperation take two forms. 'Indirect reciprocity'(1) occurs when individuals help others in order to uphold a reputation and so be included in future cooperation. In 'collective action'(2), individuals engage in costly behaviour that benefits the group as a whole. Although the evolution of indirect reciprocity is theoretically plausible(3-6), there is no consensus about how collective action evolves. Evidence suggests that punishing free riders can maintain cooperation(7-9), but why individuals should engage in costly punishment is unclear. Solutions to this 'second-order free rider problem' include meta-punishment(10), mutation(11), conformism(12), signalling(13-15) and group-selection(16-18).
