Below is a parameter-by-parameter inventory of what (if anything) the provided paper says with respect to each of the 15 public-goods-game parameters, and whether the paper makes any claims about systematically varying those parameters and how that might affect a punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency. Throughout, “punishment treatment effect” is taken to mean how adding a punishment option (or changing its details) influences efficiency (actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff if all cooperated). The paper by Panchanathan & Boyd (centered on “indirect reciprocity” and “collective action” with “Shunner,” “Defector,” and “Cooperator” strategies) does not report any experimental manipulations or data for a standard public goods game, nor does it discuss group “efficiency” as an outcome. Instead, its dependent variables are evolutionary stability, strategy frequencies, equilibrium conditions, and payoff dynamics in a theoretical model.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Discussed?  
     – Partially. The model is subdivided into groups of size n. Equation (1) in the paper depends on n, and examples use n = 30 or n = 100.  
   • Systematic variation and its effect on punishment treatment?  
     – The paper does not report any systematic variation of n in the sense of how it affects a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” It derives conditions under which certain strategies resist invasion (e.g., Shunner vs. Defector), but does not link changes in group size to changes in a measured punishment “treatment effect” or group efficiency.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Discussed?  
     – Partially. The paper’s model has a one-shot collective-action stage, then a repeated “mutual aid game” repeated on average 1/(1–w) times.  
   • Systematic variation and its effect on punishment treatment?  
     – They do vary w in illustrative examples (e.g., Figs. 1–3), but they never discuss an explicit “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” They analyze evolutionary stability (which strategies survive in equilibrium) rather than an outcome like total payoffs compared to a maximum. Thus, no discussion of how “longer or fewer rounds” systematically changes the punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. There is no mention of communication or “chat” of any kind.  
   • Systematic variation and its effect on punishment treatment?  
     – Not mentioned at all.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”? (i.e., forced total contribution vs. partial)  
   • Discussed?  
     – In their collective-action stage, individuals either contribute a net cost C or do not contribute at all. In that sense, it is an all-or-nothing decision.  
   • Systematic variation and its effect on punishment treatment?  
     – No. The paper does not explore partial contributions, nor does it systematically vary how contribution decisions are made. There is no discussion of the effect on any punishment outcome measure or efficiency.

5. Is the contribution default (e.g., do players decide how much to “uncontribute”)?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. There is no mention of default or reversed contributions.  
   • Systematic variation and its effect on punishment treatment?  
     – Not mentioned at all.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as a multiplication factor  
   • Discussed?  
     – The paper uses B to represent the total benefit created by the collective action, shared among group members, but does not frame it as an MPCR or systematically explore it.  
   • Systematic variation and its effect on punishment treatment?  
     – They show that “any behavior can be stabilized by linking it to indirect reciprocity if B < (long-term mutual-aid benefit).” However, they do not provide a table or figure documenting how systematically varying B alters a punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency. They do not report a numeric “punishment treatment effect” nor mention efficiency.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. In the paper’s model, punishing amounts to “withholding help” in the repeated mutual-aid stage; there is no separate cost spelled out as “coins spent to punish.”  
   • Systematic variation and its effect on punishment treatment?  
     – Not mentioned.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from punished players per unit punishment)  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. Again, the “punishment” is indirect: refusing mutual aid. The paper does not describe a numeric deduction inflicted on the target, nor a parametric “magnitude.”  
   • Systematic variation and its effect on punishment treatment?  
     – Not discussed.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The model involves only cooperation and withholding help (punishment). There is no mention of a reward mechanism.  
   • Systematic variation and its effect on punishment treatment?  
     – Not mentioned at all.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Discussed?  
      – No. There is no reward mechanism.  
    • Systematic variation and its effect on punishment treatment?  
      – Not mentioned at all.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
    • Discussed?  
      – No.  
    • Systematic variation and its effect on punishment treatment?  
      – Not mentioned.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    • Discussed?  
      – No. Theoretical players are said to play with probability w of continuation each period, but the paper does not treat knowledge of the horizon as a variable.  
    • Systematic variation and its effect on punishment treatment?  
      – Not mentioned.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much each peer gained or lost)?  
    • Discussed?  
      – The paper assumes “all group members know each individual’s behavioral history” so that indirect reciprocity can operate. There is no discussion of “peer payoffs,” only that everyone sees who helped and who didn’t.  
    • Systematic variation and its effect on punishment treatment?  
      – They do not systematically vary the presence/absence of that knowledge, nor do they link it with a measured punishment-effect outcome or efficiency.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Discussed?  
      – Not explicitly. It is assumed that decisions to withhold help are observable, but the paper does not analyze the effect of anonymity or identification.  
    • Systematic variation and its effect on punishment treatment?  
      – Not mentioned.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Discussed?  
      – No, because there is no reward mechanism in the model.  
    • Systematic variation and its effect on punishment treatment?  
      – Not mentioned.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • No. The paper does not discuss efficiency as “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff.” Its main dependent variables concern which strategies (Defector, Shunner, Cooperator, Reciprocator) are evolutionarily stable, how strategies invade or resist invasion, and how errors (implementation errors) affect equilibrium behavior.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Four parameters are at least obliquely mentioned:  
     – (1) “Number of players” (they use n = group size),  
     – (2) “Number of rounds” (modeled as repeated with probability w),  
     – (4) “Is the contribution all or nothing?” (it is indeed yes/no),  
     – (13) “Are peer outcomes shown?” (everyone’s contribution/helping behavior is known).  

   All other parameters (3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 15) are not explicitly discussed in ways relevant to a laboratory-style public goods game.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. The paper does not frame “punishment treatment” or “group efficiency” in the sense common to public-goods experiments. It derives conditions under which “Shunner” can outcompete “Defector,” or vice versa, but does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters to measure a “punishment treatment effect.”

Below, each of the 15 design parameters is treated in turn.  For every parameter I indicate  

(1) whether it is explicitly mentioned anywhere in the Van Lange et al. (2012) review, quoting or paraphrasing the relevant text, and  

(2) whether the authors say (or cite work saying) what would happen to the “punishment‐treatment effect” if the parameter were systematically varied.  
When possible I note the dependent variable to which the statement refers and copy any numerical effect size that can be inferred from the text, figure or table.  
If a point is not made in the paper, I state that explicitly.

------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Number of players (group size)  
(1) Mentioned.  In the section on “ostracism or social exclusion,” the authors write that “even the possibility of social exclusion is a powerful tool to increase cooperation, and that this threat might be more effective in small as opposed to large groups (e.g., Cinyabuguma et al., 2005; Kerr et al., 2009).”  
(2) Systematic variation?  Yes—small vs. large groups.  Direction: the effectiveness of the punishment option (social exclusion) on cooperation is predicted to be larger in small groups.  No numerical effect size is given.

2. Number of rounds  
(1) Repeated interaction and “multi-trial” games are discussed throughout, but the paper never tells us how many rounds were used in any study nor does it vary the number of rounds.  
(2) No prediction is offered about varying the number of rounds.

3. Chat enabled (communication)  
(1) Extensively discussed (“Communication can effectively promote cooperation …”).  
(2) The review does not link the availability of chat to the *incremental* effect of punishment.  It only says communication by itself helps cooperation.  No statement about the interaction with punishment.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) No discussion.

5. Contribution default (withdraw-versus-contribute framing)  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) No discussion.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
(1) Never specified.  
(2) No discussion.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
(1) Repeatedly mentioned.  Punishment is labeled “costly punishment”; Yamagishi’s work on “second-order public goods” is cited.  
(2) Systematic variation?  Indirectly.  The authors cite findings that “sanctions can decrease rather than increase cooperation, *especially if the sanctions are relatively low* (e.g., Gneezy & Rustichini, 2004; Mulder et al., 2006).”  Lower punishment levels normally coincide with lower costs, so the paper links *low* costs/magnitudes with a *smaller or even negative* punishment effect, but no numbers are provided.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine levied on target)  
(1) Same passages as above; “low sanctions can decrease rather than increase cooperation.”  
(2) Yes, direction only: very *low* punishment magnitudes can back-fire; higher magnitudes tend to increase cooperation relative to no-punishment baselines.  No numeric size given.

9. Whether a reward option is enabled  
(1) Mentioned.  A meta-analysis is cited showing that “rewards and punishments both have moderate positive effects on cooperation.”  
(2) The review does *not* say how simply adding a reward option changes the incremental effect of punishment.

10. Reward cost  
(1) The phrase “administering rewards and punishments is costly” appears, but costs are not varied.  
(2) No prediction.

11. Reward magnitude  
(1) Not discussed.  
(2) No prediction.

12. Whether the horizon (last round) is known  
(1) Not discussed.  
(2) No prediction.

13. Whether peer outcomes are shown  
(1) The review talks about “reputation” and “information about others,” but does not state whether payoff feedback was visible round by round.  
(2) No prediction.

14. Whether punished players learn who punished them (punisher identification)  
(1) The only related statement is that punishment can be “decentralized (by fellow members) rather than centralized (by an authority)”; who punished whom is not specified.  
(2) No prediction.

15. Whether rewarded players learn who rewarded them (rewarder identification)  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) No prediction.

------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
------------------------------------------------------------------

A.  Dependent variables used in the review  
The article is a *narrative* review, not an empirical paper.  It talks about (i) *cooperation rates / contributions*, (ii) *willingness to punish or reward*, (iii) *trust*, and occasionally total group outcomes, but it never defines or analyses *group efficiency* (total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff).  Thus “efficiency” per se is not a dependent variable in the review.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
Eight parameters are mentioned at all:  
1 (group size), 2 (rounds—indirectly), 3 (communication), 7 (punishment cost), 8 (punishment magnitude), 9 (reward option), 10 (reward cost – only in passing), 14 (centralised vs. decentralised punishment loosely related to punisher identity).

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss the *effect of systematically varying* the parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
Three:  
1. Group size (small vs. large → stronger punishment effect in small groups).  
7. Punishment cost (very low-cost/low-level sanctions can *reduce* cooperation).  
8. Punishment magnitude (same statement—very low magnitudes can back-fire).  
No numerical effect sizes are provided.

D.  Predictions one can reasonably make *solely from this paper* about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) influence the punishment effect on efficiency  

– Smaller groups should experience a larger positive efficiency gain from adding punishment (because exclusion works better in small groups).  
– Extremely low punishment levels (low cost, low magnitude) may yield *no* efficiency gain or even an efficiency loss.  Increasing punishment magnitude beyond this “too-low” zone should improve the treatment effect.  
– No other clear predictions are supported by statements in the review.  In particular, the authors give no guidance on the number of rounds, chat, MPCR, information conditions, or identity revelation with respect to how these would change the *incremental* impact of punishment on overall payoffs.

Taken together, the review provides only fragmentary qualitative guidance—mainly that punishment must be *strong enough* and that it works best in *small groups*—and it supplies no quantitative effect sizes for efficiency.
reference_APA: Van Lange, Paul A. M., Joireman, Jeff, Parks, Craig D. & Van Dijk, Eric (2013). The psychology of social dilemmas: A review. ORGANIZATIONAL BEHAVIOR AND HUMAN DECISION PROCESSES.

   • Mentioned?  NO.

------------------------------------------------------------------

A.  Dependent variables actually used in the paper  
   • The authors track:  
     – Individual expected payoff / “fitness”  
     – Average (group) payoff  
     – Fractions of strategy types (α for honest signallers, β for monitors)

   • Four parameters are explicitly present:  
     1. Number of players (n)  
     2. All-or-nothing contribution (binary signal)  
     6. MPCR-related public-good parameters (g, c)

D.  What predictions about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency can be made *solely* from this paper?

Below is an item-by-item analysis of the 15 parameters and whether (1) the paper explicitly discusses each parameter (and at what value, if given) and (2) whether it makes predictions about how systematically varying that parameter would affect the “punishment treatment effect” for any dependent variable (especially efficiency). All statements refer strictly to what is stated in the paper “The Competitive Advantage of Sanctioning Institutions” by Gürerk et al.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Discussed? The paper reports having 84 participants in total. There is no systematic variation of group size (they do not run separate treatments with different group sizes). Thus, it is not varied in the experiment.
   • Predictions from varying? The paper does not make or report any predictions about the effect of systematically varying the number of players on the punishment treatment effect for any dependent variable.

2. Number of rounds
   • Discussed? The game is played for 30 periods (rounds). This number is fixed and not varied across sessions.
   • Predictions from varying? The paper does not provide predictions on how changing the number of rounds would affect the punishment treatment effect.

3. Is chat enabled?
   • Discussed? The paper does not mention any live communication or “chat” functionality among participants. 
   • Predictions from varying? No predictions are given regarding any form of communication treatment or how it would affect punishment.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussed? Contributions are made on a continuous scale from 0 to 20 money units (MUs). “All or nothing” is not used in the experiment.
   • Predictions from varying? The paper does not discuss changing to an all-or-nothing format or how that would affect punishment.

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much of their endowment to move back to their hand)?
   • Discussed? In the experiment, each participant simply chooses any integer contribution between 0 and 20 MUs. There is no “default” mechanism reported, and no systematic variation of how contributions are decided.
   • Predictions from varying? None mentioned.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Discussed? The paper states that each group member “equally profits from the public good.” However, it does not provide a specific numeric MPCR or systematically vary that factor.
   • Predictions from varying? None mentioned.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussed? Yes. Each negative sanction token (punishment) costs the punisher 1 MU. The paper notes that punishing is costly.
   • Predictions from varying? Although the paper discusses that punishment is costly, it does not model or empirically test how systematically changing the cost of punishment (the 1 MU) would affect the punishment treatment effect.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   • Discussed? Yes. Each punishment token deducts 3 MUs from the punished individual. 
   • Predictions from varying? The experiment does not vary this 3-MU penalty. The paper does not provide predictions on how changing this magnitude would alter the punishment treatment effect.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussed? In the “sanctioning institution,” both negative (punishment) and positive (reward) sanctions are possible. Hence, reward is “enabled” in that institution’s rules. It is not enabled in the sanction-free institution.
   • Predictions from varying? The paper does not test or predict what would happen if researchers systematically allowed or disallowed rewards under otherwise identical conditions; it only reports that both positive and negative sanctions were available in the same “sanctioning institution.”

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Discussed? Yes. Assigning a single “positive sanction” token (reward) costs the reward-giver 1 MU.
   • Predictions from varying? There is no discussion or data on how altering the cost of reward would affect the punishment treatment.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)
   • Discussed? Yes. Each reward token gives the recipient 1 MU. 
   • Predictions from varying? The paper does not examine or predict how changing that 1-MU reward would alter the punishment treatment effect.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
   • Discussed? Participants play for 30 periods, but the paper does not explicitly describe whether participants knew in advance that the game would end after 30 rounds. There is no treatment manipulation about “knowing” versus “not knowing” the end.
   • Predictions from varying? No predictions are made about systematically changing participants’ knowledge of the horizon.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?
   • Discussed? The paper states that at the end of each period, participants receive “detailed (but anonymous) information about each of the other participants.” It includes contributions and resultant payoffs for each member of both institutions. However, this is fixed—there is no variation in disclosure level.
   • Predictions from varying? None are provided about how systematically changing the information display would affect punishment.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Discussed? The paper notes that all feedback is “anonymous.” There is no mention of revealing the identity of who punished whom. This was not varied experimentally.
   • Predictions from varying? None are given.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Discussed? As with punishment, the paper indicates that all information is anonymous. There is no mention of revealing the identity of who rewarded whom, and it was not varied.
   • Predictions from varying? None are given.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?  
   • The paper frequently references “payoffs” and also explicitly reports an “efficiency” measure—labeled “efficiency gains,” meaning actual total payoff relative to the maximum possible payoff (“95.8%” near the end for the sanctioning institution).  
   • Other dependent variables in the paper include (i) contribution levels to the public good, (ii) institution choice (sanctioning institution vs. sanction-free institution), and (iii) usage of sanction tokens. Contributions or cooperation rates are not identical to efficiency, because efficiency additionally accounts for the costs of punishment and the resulting net payoffs.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned explicitly with their fixed value in this single experiment:  
     (1) Number of players (84 total)  
     (2) Number of rounds (30 total)  
     (7) Punishment cost (1 MU per punishment token)  
     (8) Punishment magnitude (3 MUs deducted from the recipient per token)  
     (9) Whether a reward is enabled (yes, in the sanctioning institution only)  
     (10) Reward cost (1 MU)  
     (11) Reward magnitude (1 MU)  
     (13) Peer outcomes displayed (participants receive detailed but anonymous info)  

   • The remaining parameters—(3), (4), (5), (6), (12), (14), (15)—are either not discussed at all (e.g., chat) or only briefly described as fixed aspects of the design, but without explicit mention of any systematic variation.

C. For which and how many of these parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • The paper does not systematically vary any of the parameters. Consequently, it does not provide direct empirical or theoretical predictions about how changing those parameters would shift the punishment treatment effect.  
   • While the paper compares “sanctioning institution” vs. “sanction-free institution,” that is not a systematic variation of any single parameter in the sense of “Parameter 7 at multiple levels,” etc. It is instead a two-institution setup.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not explicitly discuss how systematically altering these parameters would influence the relationship between punishment and efficiency.  
   • The main relevant information is that punishment (costly to the punisher and penalizing the punished) eventually led to extremely high cooperation and high efficiency in the sanctioning institution—once enough participants chose that institution. However, the authors do not model what would happen if, for example, one changed the cost of punishment or the punishment magnitude.  
   • Overall, one can make little to no prediction, based strictly on this paper, regarding how each of the 15 parameters or their interactions would change the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency. The study’s focus was on the competition aspect between a punishment-enabled vs. a punishment-free institution, rather than systematically varying individual game parameters.

Below each of the 15 parameters I quote only what is explicitly in “Reward, Punishment, and Cooperation: A Meta-Analysis.”  
Whenever the paper supplies numbers I reproduce them exactly (page and/or table in parentheses).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players (group size)  
(1) Mentioned? Yes.  “The mode of group size was a four-person group … range two to 16” (Method – Coding Procedure).  
Values encountered: 2–16; mode = 4; mean≈4 (after deleting one 1,000-person outlier).  
(2) Systematic-variation test? Yes.  Meta-regression with the continuous group-size variable:  
 Punishment: b = -.01, Q(1)=0.15, p=.70 ⇒ no reliable moderation (Table 3 note).  
 Reward: b =.04, Q(1)=0.28, p=.35 ⇒ no reliable moderation (text).  
No separate efficiency data are reported.

2. Number of rounds (iterations)  
(1) Mentioned? Yes.  Two codings: (a) one-shot vs. iterated, (b) exact number of iterations.  
(2) Systematic-variation tests:  
 a. Categorical – Punishment:  
  • Partner-matching iterated d = 0.92  
  • Stranger-matching iterated d = 0.62  
  • One-shot d = 0.32   Q(2)=44.42, p<.02 (Table 3).  
 Reward:  
  • Iterated d = 0.81  
  • One-shot d = 0.16   Q(1)=13.03, p<.001 (Table 4).  
 b. Continuous – number of iterations:  
  Punishment: b =.005, Q(1)=3.38, p=.06 (ns in random-effects).  
  Reward: b =.003, Q(1)=1.10, p=.29 (ns random; significant b =.009, p=.01, in fixed-effects).  
No analysis of “known vs. unknown horizon.”

3. Is chat enabled? Not mentioned; no data; no predictions.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule? Not mentioned.

5. Contribution default / refund stage? Not mentioned.

6. Marginal Per-Capita Return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
Not coded or analyzed.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
(1) Mentioned? Yes—coded “Costly” vs. “Free.” 86 costly effect sizes, 39 free.  
(2) Systematic-variation test (Table 3):  
 Costly punishment d = 0.78 (95 % CI 0.66–0.91)  
 Free  punishment d = 0.52 (95 % CI 0.34–0.71)  
 Between-class Q(1)=5.41, p=.02 ⇒ Costly punishment yields a significantly larger treatment effect on cooperation.  
No efficiency numbers.

8. Punishment magnitude (cost-to-fine ratio)  
(1) Mentioned? Yes. Four ratios coded: 1:1, 1:2, 1:3, 1:4.  
(2) Systematic-variation test (Table 3): Q(3)=0.61, p=.89 ⇒ no detectable moderation of the punishment effect.  
Mean d’s: 0.87 (1:1), 0.76 (1:2), 0.84 (1:3), 0.90 (1:4).  

9. Whether a reward is enabled in the punishment treatment  
Not part of the meta-analysis; each effect size compares a pure punishment condition with a no-incentive control, so the presence/absence of rewards within punishment rounds is not examined.

10. Reward cost  
(1) Mentioned? Yes—same costly vs. free coding (8 costly, 18 free; Table 4).  
(2) Systematic-variation test:  
 Costly reward d = 0.97 (95 % CI 0.57–1.38)  
 Free    reward d = 0.32 (95 % CI 0.12–0.52)  
 Q(1)=8.07, p=.005 ⇒ costly rewards enhance the reward-treatment effect on cooperation.  

11. Reward magnitude  
Not coded; no analysis.

12. Do players know when the game ends? Not discussed.

13. Are peer payoffs shown? Not discussed.

14. Is the punisher identified? Not discussed (the paper notes most decentralized studies kept punishment anonymous but gives no moderator analysis).

15. Is the rewarder identified? Not discussed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
The meta-analysis uses “cooperation” (e.g., contribution level, take amount) as the sole dependent variable, expressed as standardized mean difference d between incentive and control.  
“Group efficiency/total payoff” is mentioned only conceptually in the Discussion; it is NOT analysed.

B. Parameters mentioned  
5 of the 15 parameters appear:  
1 (Group size), 2 (Number of rounds/iterations), 7 (Punishment cost), 8 (Punishment magnitude ratio), 10 (Reward cost).

C. Parameters systematically tested for their impact on the punishment treatment effect  
5 parameters are examined:  
• 1 Group size – tested, no significant moderation.  
• 2 Iterations – categorical and (marginally) continuous effects; punishment more effective in repeated play.  
• 7 Punishment cost – significant moderator (costly > free).  
• 8 Punishment magnitude (cost-to-fine) – tested, no effect.  
• 10 Reward cost – significant moderator for the reward-treatment effect (costly > free).  
No other parameters are analysed.

D. What can we predict about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment treatment effect on efficiency using only this paper?  
Because the paper rarely measures efficiency, only very tentative inferences are possible:  
– Higher punishment cost (Parameter 7) increases the cooperative effect and might therefore improve efficiency only if the behavioral gain outweighs the extra cost; the paper gives no direct test.  
– More rounds (Parameter 2) strengthen the cooperation effect of punishment; longer horizons may eventually allow punishment costs to be recouped, implying a possible rise in efficiency.  
– Group size, punishment magnitude, and the other 10 parameters provide no empirical basis here for efficiency predictions.  
Overall, the paper offers insufficient evidence to forecast changes in efficiency for 10 of the 15 parameters and only limited, indirect clues for the remaining five.
reference_APA: Balliet, Daniel, Mulder, Laetitia B. & Van Lange, Paul A. M. (2011). Reward, Punishment, and Cooperation: A Meta-Analysis. PSYCHOLOGICAL BULLETIN.

Authors: Fowler, JH; Christakis, NA
Author Full Names: Fowler, James H.; Christakis, Nicholas A.
Article Title: Cooperative behavior cascades in human social networks
Source Title: PROCEEDINGS OF THE NATIONAL ACADEMY OF SCIENCES OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
Author Keywords: behavioral economics; cooperation; public goods; social influence; pay-it-forward
Keywords Plus: CONDITIONAL COOPERATION; INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; PUBLIC-GOODS; EVOLUTION; DYNAMICS; SPREAD; GRAPHS; ALTRUISM; GAMES; MODEL
Abstract: Theoretical models suggest that social networks influence the evolution of cooperation, but to date there have been few experimental studies. Observational data suggest that a wide variety of behaviors may spread in human social networks, but subjects in such studies can choose to befriend people with similar behaviors, posing difficulty for causal inference. Here, we exploit a seminal set of laboratory experiments that originally showed that voluntary costly punishment can help sustain cooperation. In these experiments, subjects were randomly assigned to a sequence of different groups to play a series of single-shot public goods games with strangers; this feature allowed us to draw networks of interactions to explore how cooperative and uncooperative behaviors spread from person to person to person. We show that, in both an ordinary public goods game and in a public goods game with punishment, focal individuals are influenced by fellow group members' contribution behavior in future interactions with other individuals who were not a party to the initial interaction. Furthermore, this influence persists for multiple periods and spreads upto three degrees of separation(from person to person to person to person). The results suggest that each additional contribution a subject makes to the public good in the first period is tripled over the course of the experiment by other subjects who are directly or indirectly influenced to contribute more as a consequence. These results show experimentally that cooperative behavior cascades in human social networks.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what appears (or does not appear) in the paper by Fowler and Christakis (cited as ref. 37 in their references to Fehr and Gächter’s original experiments). All statements refer strictly to this text; none draw on outside sources or conjecture.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each group had 4 players.  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no discussion of altering the group size or testing different numbers of players.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency? Not discussed.  

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned? Yes. There were 6 rounds (called “periods”).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not indicate that the number of rounds was manipulated or analyzed in ways that would speak to the punishment effect on any dependent variable.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency? Not discussed.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not describe any open communication or “chat” between players; subjects only see contributions (and payoffs) from their group after the round ends.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency? Not discussed.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned? Indirectly. The experiment let participants contribute any whole‐number amount between 0 and 20 MUs; so, contributions were not forced to be “all or nothing.”  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency? Not discussed.  

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much to move from the public fund back to themselves)?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper describes a standard public goods game in which participants choose how much of their 20 MUs to contribute to the group, but there is no mention of default contribution rules or forced movement from the public fund.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency? Not discussed.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each MU contributed yields 0.4 MUs to each of the 4 group members (making the total “multiplication factor” 1.6).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper merely reports the factor used; there is no design or analysis that changes it.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency? Not discussed.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned? Yes. Spending 1 MU to punish reduces one’s own payoff by 1 MU. In these experiments, one could spend up to 10 MUs on punishing others.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency? Not discussed.  

8. Punishment magnitude (how many coins deducted from a punished player)
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each 1 MU spent on punishment reduces the punished player’s income by 3 MUs.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency? Not discussed.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned? No. The paper focuses on a “public goods game” and a “public goods game with punishment.” No reward mechanism is discussed.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency? Not discussed.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Mentioned? No. Rewards are not part of the design.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency? Not discussed.  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)
    • Mentioned? No. Rewards are not part of the design.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency? Not discussed.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
    • Mentioned? The experiment used 6 rounds, but the paper does not explicitly say whether or not subjects knew from the start there would be exactly 6.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency? Not discussed.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown?
    • Mentioned? Partially. Each subject can see how much each group member contributed, and the paper says that “contributions were revealed ... along with payoff outcomes.” Hence, subjects do see final payoffs at the end of each round.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency? Not discussed.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Mentioned? Indirectly. The paper says the experiment enforced strict anonymity, so subjects did not learn who punished them.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency? Not discussed.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Mentioned? No. Rewards are not part of the experiment; thus, this does not arise.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency? Not discussed.  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

SUMMARY

A: Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
• The paper’s main analytic focus is on individuals’ contributions (i.e., how many MUs they give to the public good) in subsequent periods. It also notes payoffs, but it does not frame results in terms of group efficiency (i.e., total payoff divided by the maximum possible). Instead, the key dependent variable is each subject’s contribution in the next period, plus analyses of how contributions “cascade” through the network.  

B: Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Parameters 1 (group size = 4), 2 (6 rounds), 6 (MPCR = 0.4 per person), 7 (1 MU punishment cost to punisher), and 8 (3 MUs deducted from punished player) are explicitly described. The paper also clarifies that subjects observed each other’s contributions and payoffs (parameter 13). Regarding punishment anonymity (parameter 14), it states that punishers were not identifiable. The remaining parameters are either not mentioned at all or not relevant to this particular experiment.  

C: For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• None. The paper does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters to examine changes in the punishment treatment effect. It examines only two fixed designs: a regular public goods game and one with punishment; within these, the any “systematic variation” of parameters such as group size or punishment magnitude is not performed.  

D: If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
• The paper itself confines its analysis to comparisons between a simple public goods game and a public goods game with punishment, emphasizing outcomes in terms of individual contributions. It does not examine or predict changes in group efficiency under systematic manipulations of those 15 parameters. Consequently, the study offers little to no direct basis for predicting how variations in these parameters or their interactions would affect the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.
reference_APA: Fowler, James H. & Christakis, Nicholas A. (2010). Cooperative behavior cascades in human social networks. PROCEEDINGS OF THE NATIONAL ACADEMY OF SCIENCES OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA.

Authors: Hauert, C; Traulsen, A; Brandt, H; Nowak, MA; Sigmund, K
Author Full Names: Hauert, Christoph; Traulsen, Arne; Brandt, Hannelore; Nowak, Martin A.; Sigmund, Karl
Article Title: Via freedom to coercion: The emergence of costly punishment
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; PUBLIC-GOODS; INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; HUMAN COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; DYNAMICS; TRAGEDY; COMMONS; HUMANS; GAMES
Abstract: In human societies, cooperative behavior in joint enterprises is often enforced through institutions that impose sanctions on defectors. Many experiments on so-called public goods games have shown that in the absence of such institutions, individuals are willing to punish defectors, even at a cost to themselves. Theoretical models confirm that social norms prescribing the punishment of uncooperative behavior are stable-once established, they prevent dissident minorities from spreading. But how can such costly punishing behavior gain a foothold in the population? A surprisingly simple model shows that if individuals have the option to stand aside and abstain from the joint endeavor, this paves the way for the emergence and establishment of cooperative behavior based on the punishment of defectors. Paradoxically, the freedom to withdraw from the common enterprise leads to enforcement of social norms. Joint enterprises that are compulsory rather than voluntary are less likely to lead to cooperation.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter summary of what (if anything) the Hauert et al. paper (“Via freedom to coercion: the emergence of costly punishment”) says about each of the 15 parameters, followed by the required four‐part summary.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The paper uses a population size M (e.g., M = 1000) and a subgroup of size N drawn to play the public goods game.  
   • Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment effects?  
     – No. The paper does note that for “large M,” punishing strategies can become established, but it does not present a systematic analysis (e.g., a table or figure) that shows how varying M changes the effect of punishment on efficiency (or on any other dependent variable).

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper models an ongoing evolutionary process rather than a discrete, repeated‐round game in the usual experimental sense. There is no discussion of how many rounds are played.  
   • Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment effects?  
     – No mention.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No.  
   • Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment effects?  
     – No mention.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes, effectively. Each participant either contributes a fixed amount c (cooperate/punish) or contributes nothing (defect).  
   • Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment effects?  
     – No. The paper assumes that each participant chooses whether to pay the cost c or not; it does not explore any alternative contribution schemes.

5. Is the contribution default?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper does not describe a default mechanism for contributing or not contributing.  
   • Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment effects?  
     – No mention.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. Denoted by r > 1 and multiplied by the sum of all contributions.  
   • Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment effects?  
     – The paper remarks that the main results are “robust” to changes in r but does not provide a systematic analysis of how varying r alone affects (a) efficiency or (b) the punishment treatment effect. There is no numerical effect size given.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. Denoted by γ (gamma). Punishers pay γ for each fine they impose.  
   • Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment effects?  
     – No. While γ is part of the model, the paper does not present systematic results showing how changing γ alone alters the treatment effect on efficiency or any other outcome variable.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted per unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. Denoted by β (beta). Defectors lose β for each punishment they receive.  
   • Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment effects?  
     – No. As with γ, β is discussed only to define the model, not systematically varied. No numerical effect size is provided.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Briefly. The authors note that in some contexts, “if punishment is combined with rewarding through indirect reciprocity,” punishment can be focused on the “worst offenders,” but the core model in the paper does not incorporate a formal reward mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment effects?  
     – No. There is no table/figure systematically analyzing rewards.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper never specifies a cost for rewarding; it only briefly references the possibility of rewards in other models.  
   • Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment effects?  
     – No mention.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No.  
   • Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment effects?  
     – No mention.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No.  
   • Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment effects?  
     – No mention.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see each other’s payoffs)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Only indirectly in the sense that players can imitate high payoffs, but no experimental design element (like “outcomes displayed on screen”) is discussed.  
   • Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment effects?  
     – No mention.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who punished them?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No.  
   • Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment effects?  
     – No mention.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who rewarded them?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No.  
   • Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment effects?  
     – No mention.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
• The paper’s principal outcomes center on which strategy (cooperator, defector, punisher, or non‐participant) dominates the population in the long run and on overall payoffs in a qualitative sense (e.g., whether the interaction yields “hardly any economic benefit” under defection). Although it alludes to higher total payoffs when prosocial strategies dominate, it does not explicitly measure “efficiency” as “actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff.” Its central dependent variables are the long‐run frequencies of strategies and the corresponding payoffs in evolutionary equilibrium—not a formal “efficiency” metric.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Mentioned explicitly:  
  – (1) Number of players (population size M)  
  – (4) All‐or‐nothing contribution structure (implicitly)  
  – (6) Multiplication factor r  
  – (7) Punishment cost γ  
  – (8) Punishment magnitude β  
  – (9) Brief reference to “reward” being possible in other models.  
• That is 6 out of the 15 parameters.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• None of the parameters are subjected to a fully systematic variation (with effect sizes) with respect to the “punishment treatment effect.” While the paper notes that certain results are “robust” to changes in r, σ, γ, and β, it does not provide numerical effect‐size estimates nor does it isolate a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”  
• Hence, zero of the 15 parameters are systematically varied in the sense of providing effect sizes regarding punishment’s impact on efficiency (or any dependent variable).

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
• The paper does not supply enough detail or data to make quantitative predictions regarding how systematically altering these 15 parameters would affect efficiency. Its main finding is that allowing voluntary participation (rather than forcing all players to take part) paves the way for punishment strategies to take over, which in turn can foster more cooperation and yield higher payoffs. Beyond that, no additional predictions—especially about how each of the 15 parameters might affect efficiency—can be made on the basis of the paper alone.
reference_APA: Hauert, Christoph, Traulsen, Arne, Brandt, Hannelore, Nowak, Martin A. & Sigmund, Karl (2007). Via freedom to coercion: The emergence of costly punishment. SCIENCE.

Authors: Henrich, J; Boyd, R
Author Full Names: Henrich, J; Boyd, R
Article Title: Why people punish defectors - Weak conformist transmission can stabilize costly enforcement of norms in cooperative dilemmas
Keywords Plus: SIZABLE GROUPS; EVOLUTION; SIZE
Abstract: In this paper, we present a cultural evolutionary model in which norms for cooperation and punishment are acquired via two cognitive mechanisms: (1) payoff-biased transmission a tendency to copy the most successful individual; and (2) conformist transmission-a tendency to copy the most frequent behavior in the population. We first show that if a finite number of punishment stages is permitted (e.g. two stages of punishment occur if some individuals punish people who fail to punish non-cooperators), then an arbitrarily small amount of conformist transmission will stabilize cooperative behavior by stabilizing punishment at some n-th stage. We then explain how, once cooperation is stabilized in one group, it may spread through a multi-group population via cultural group selection. Finally, once cooperation is prevalent, we show how prosocial genes favoring cooperation and punishment may invade in the wake of cultural group selection. (C) 2001 Academic Press.

Below I go through the fifteen design parameters, one‐by‐one, and report exactly what the Henrich & Boyd (2001) paper

• says about the parameter (value, definition, notation)  
• says about what would happen if that parameter were systematically varied, **specifically in terms of the “punishment treatment effect.”**

When the paper never mentions the parameter, or never links it to treatment effects, I say so explicitly.



--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER SCAN
--------------------------------------------------------------------

1.  Number of players  
    • Mentioned?  YES.  The model symbol N is the group size.  
    • Systematic-variation predictions?  YES (but not for “efficiency”).  
        – Key formula:  αᵢ ≈ (e φ / ρ)(N e)^{i–1}.  
        – Interpretation: with more players, it becomes harder (requires a larger conformist bias α) to stabilize punishment for i ≥ 2, so the incremental benefit of adding a punishment option shrinks.  
        – No explicit statement about total-payoff efficiency; the discussion is about whether cooperation and punishment are stable.

2.  Number of rounds  
    • Mentioned?  NO.  The paper analyses a single public-goods stage followed by i punishment stages; that is not the “number of rounds” in the usual experimental sense.  
    • Systematic-variation predictions?  NO.  (They do vary “number of punishment stages” i, but never the repeated-game horizon.)

3.  Chat between players  
    • Mentioned?  NO.  (No communication channel is modelled.)  
    • Predictions?  NO.

4.  All-or-nothing contributions  
    • Mentioned?  YES (implicitly).  Cooperation is dichotomous: “cooperate” vs “defect.”  
    • Systematic-variation predictions?  NO.  The authors never discuss a continuous contribution scale or compare it to the dichotomous one.

5.  Contribution default (reversible contributions)  
    • Mentioned?  NO.  
    • Predictions?  NO.

6.  MPCR / multiplication factor  
    • Mentioned?  PARTIALLY.  Benefit of one contribution is B, shared by N players, so MPCR = B/N.  
    • Systematic-variation predictions?  MINIMAL.  They require B > C for cooperation to raise payoffs, but they never trace how different MPCRs change the punishment treatment effect or efficiency.

7.  Punishment cost to impose (φ)  
    • Mentioned?  YES.  
    • Systematic-variation predictions?  YES.  
        – Larger φ raises the conformity threshold αᵢ (eqs. 6, 10, 12); therefore costly punishment is harder to stabilize and its efficiency benefit shrinks.  
        – For i = 1, α₁ ≈ e φ / ρ.  Thus a one-unit increase in φ increases α₁ linearly, but no exact numerical marginal effect on efficiency is given.

8.  Punishment magnitude (ρ)  
    • Mentioned?  YES.  
    • Systematic-variation predictions?  YES.  
        – ρ appears in the denominator of αᵢ.  Higher ρ lowers αᵢ, making punishment easier to stabilize.  
        – No direct efficiency numbers given.

9.  Whether a reward is enabled  
10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
    • Mentioned?  NO for all three.  Rewards never appear in the model, figures, or tables.  
    • Predictions?  NO.

12.  Whether the number of rounds is known  
    • Mentioned?  NO.  
    • Predictions?  NO.

13.  Whether peer outcomes are shown  
    • Mentioned?  NO.  
    • Predictions?  NO.

14.  Whether punishees learn the identity of the punisher  
    • Mentioned?  NO.  
    • Predictions?  NO.

15.  Whether rewardees learn the identity of the rewarder  
    • Mentioned?  NO.  
    • Predictions?  NO.



--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------

A.  Dependent variables in the paper  
    • Group efficiency (total payoff / maximum total) is **NOT** used.  
    • Main dependent variables:  
        – p₀, p₁, …, pᵢ : frequencies of cooperation and of punishers at each stage.  
        – Expected individual payoff b (sometimes used to compare equilibria).  
        – α thresholds for stability.  
      These differ from “efficiency” because they track behavioral frequencies or payoff differences, not the ratio of actual to maximal group earnings.

B.  How many of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
    5/15:  
      1 (Number of players N)  
      4 (All-or-nothing contributions, implicitly)  
      6 (MPCR via B and N)  
      7 (Punishment cost φ)  
      8 (Punishment magnitude ρ)

C.  How many parameters are linked to their *systematic* effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
    3/15:  
      1 (N), 7 (φ), 8 (ρ).  
    Even for these, the paper talks about stability of punishment and cooperation, not about efficiency or an experimental “treatment effect.”

D.  If one had to predict the punishment treatment effect on **efficiency** using only this paper  
    • Larger groups (N) → weaker or even negative treatment effect because higher N makes punishment harder to stabilize unless error rates are minuscule.  
    • More punishment stages (i) → stronger positive treatment effect because required conformist bias α falls sharply with i.  
    • Higher punishment cost to punisher (φ) → smaller or negative effect.  
    • Higher punishment magnitude on target (ρ) → larger positive effect.  
    • Variation in MPCR (B/N) or contribution cost C matters only insofar as B>C and C is not too large relative to ρ; precise efficiency predictions cannot be extracted.  
    • Nothing can be said, from this paper alone, about chat, reward, information disclosure, defaults, or contribution granularity.

In short, the paper is a theoretical stability analysis; it gives only indirect hints—through α-threshold formulas—about whether punishment will exist at all.  It provides virtually no direct leverage for predicting how the usual laboratory design parameters will change the **efficiency** gains from adding a punishment option.

Authors: Bernhard, H; Fischbacher, U; Fehr, E

Keywords Plus: INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; SOCIAL NORMS; EVOLUTION; PUNISHMENT; ENFORCEMENT; BEHAVIOR
Abstract: Social norms and the associated altruistic behaviours are decisive for the evolution of human cooperation(1-9) and the maintenance of social order(10), and they affect family life, politics(11) and economic interactions(12). However, as altruistic norm compliance and norm enforcement often emerge in the context of inter-group conflicts(13,14), they are likely to be shaped by parochialism(15) - a preference for favouring the members of one's ethnic, racial or language group. We have conducted punishment experiments(16), which allow 'impartial' observers to punish norm violators, with indigenous groups in Papua New Guinea. Here we show that these experiments confirm the prediction of parochialism. We found that punishers protect ingroup victims - who suffer from a norm violation - much more than they do outgroup victims, regardless of the norm violator's group affiliation. Norm violators also expect that punishers will be lenient if the latter belong to their social group. As a consequence, norm violations occur more often if the punisher and the norm violator belong to the same group. Our results are puzzling for evolutionary multi-level selection theories based on selective group extinction(2-5) as well as for theories of individual selection(17-19); they also indicate the need to explicitly examine the interactions between individuals stemming from different groups in evolutionary models.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter account based solely on the content of “Parochial altruism in humans” by Bernhard et al. (the paper excerpt you provided). The paper implements a one-shot, third-party punishment game among three players and varies group membership (whether player A, B, C belong to the same or different tribes). Aside from that, it does not systematically vary other features of the experimental design. Accordingly, for each of the 15 parameters, I note (1) whether the paper discusses it (and, if so, any fixed value it takes), and (2) whether it makes predictions about the effect of systematically varying the parameter on punishment outcomes (including efficiency or any other dependent variable). In nearly all cases, the paper does not discuss systematic variation of these parameters, nor does it measure efficiency (defined as total payoff / maximum possible payoff).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   – Mentioned? Yes. The experiment always has three players (A = “dictator,” B = “recipient,” C = “third-party punisher”).  
   – Systematically varied? No. The design always involves three players. The paper does not discuss how changing the number of players would affect punishment or efficiency.

2. Number of rounds  
   – Mentioned? It is a one-shot game (i.e., a single-round interaction).  
   – Systematically varied? No. They do not examine multiple rounds or how knowledge of multiple rounds might affect behavior.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   – Mentioned? The procedures indicate instructions were given verbally, but there is no mention of allowing or disallowing open-ended chat between players. The study is conducted under controlled conditions intended to prevent discussion about the game, so there is effectively no chat.  
   – Systematically varied? No. The paper does not manipulate communication channels.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   – Mentioned? No. The dictator can transfer any amount between 0 and 10 Kina in integer increments—so it is not an all-or-nothing design. However, the paper does not label this feature as a parameter, nor does it systematically vary it.  
   – Systematically varied? No.

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much to move back to themselves from a public pot)?  
   – Mentioned? Not in the sense described here. The paper is not a public-goods experiment with a default contribution; rather, it is a standard third-party punishment game in which the dictator decides how much to give (0–10 Kina) to the recipient.  
   – Systematically varied? No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor  
   – Mentioned? No. This is not described as a public-goods game with an MPCR.  
   – Systematically varied? No.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   – Mentioned? Yes. The paper states that the third party (player C) can spend 1 Kina on punishment, which reduces the dictator’s payoff by 3 Kina. In other words, the cost to the punisher for one “unit” of punishment is 1 Kina.  
   – Systematically varied? No. The cost is fixed at 1 Kina. There is no discussion of how varying this cost would alter punishment or efficiency.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   – Mentioned? Yes. For each 1 Kina spent on punishment, the dictator loses 3 Kina.  
   – Systematically varied? No. The 3:1 ratio is fixed. The paper does not discuss or predict how changing that ratio would affect outcomes.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   – Mentioned? Only punishment is discussed; there is no separate reward mechanism in the design.  
   – Systematically varied? No. Rewards are simply not part of the experiment.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    – Mentioned? No. Since no reward mechanism exists, no cost is discussed.  
    – Systematically varied? No.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
    – Mentioned? No. Again, reward is not part of the design.  
    – Systematically varied? No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    – Mentioned? It is specifically a “one-shot” game, so there is only a single decision round. The paper states that participants know they will not interact again in this game.  
    – Systematically varied? No. The game is always played once, with the knowledge that it does not continue.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much their peers gained/lost each round)?  
    – Mentioned? The third party sees how much the dictator decides to transfer. But the paper does not systematically vary what information is disclosed about payoffs; there is no separate condition with different payoff/display information.  
    – Systematically varied? No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    – Mentioned? The paper labels player C as the known third-party punisher in the sense that all roles are assigned, but it does not detail whether the dictator knows exactly who spent money on punishment (beyond the knowledge that it is the third-party). It does not systematically vary the punisher’s identity revelation.  
    – Systematically varied? No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    – Mentioned? Not applicable, as no reward mechanism exists in the design.  
    – Systematically varied? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Summary (A–D)

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   • The paper does not use the term “efficiency” (i.e., total payoff divided by maximum possible payoff) as a dependent variable. Instead, the authors focus on:  
     – Punishment decisions (how many Kina are spent punishing).  
     – Dictators’ transfer decisions (how many Kina are given from A to B).  
     – Expectations of punishment.  
   • Although total payoffs can be derived from the participants’ decisions, the paper does not explicitly report or analyze “efficiency” in the sense often used in public-goods or social-dilemma research.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form (though not systematically varied):  
     1. Number of players (always three).  
     7. Punishment cost (1 Kina spent by C).  
     8. Punishment magnitude (3 Kina deducted from A for each 1 Kina spent).  
     12. Number of rounds (one-shot, so effectively 1).  
   • All others are effectively not discussed in the sense of unique parameter values or variations.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss the effect on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable) when systematically varied?  
   • None. The study does not systematically manipulate any of those 15 parameters. Instead, the only variation is tribal group membership in each of the four conditions (ABC, BC, AB, AC).  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper itself provides no basis for predicting how varying these parameters would change efficiency. It only documents that third-party punishment in a one-shot game depends on group membership. Because none of the 15 parameters were varied, the paper offers little or no information about how such variations would affect “efficiency” (as specifically defined by total payoff / maximum possible payoff).  

In short, the paper focuses on group membership (ingroup vs. outgroup) in a one-shot game with fixed punishment rules. It does not explore or predict how changing any of the 15 listed parameters would affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Authors: Dreber, A; Rand, DG; Fudenberg, D; Nowak, MA
Author Full Names: Dreber, Anna; Rand, David G.; Fudenberg, Drew; Nowak, Martin A.
Article Title: Winners don't punish
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; REPEATED GAMES; COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; RECIPROCITY
Abstract: A key aspect of human behaviour is cooperation(1-7). We tend to help others even if costs are involved. We are more likely to help when the costs are small and the benefits for the other person significant. Cooperation leads to a tension between what is best for the individual and what is best for the group. A group does better if everyone cooperates, but each individual is tempted to defect. Recently there has been much interest in exploring the effect of costly punishment on human cooperation(8-23). Costly punishment means paying a cost for another individual to incur a cost. It has been suggested that costly punishment promotes cooperation even in non- repeated games and without any possibility of reputation effects(10). But most of our interactions are repeated and reputation is always at stake. Thus, if costly punishment is important in promoting cooperation, it must do so in a repeated setting. We have performed experiments in which, in each round of a repeated game, people choose between cooperation, defection and costly punishment. In control experiments, people could only cooperate or defect. Here we show that the option of costly punishment increases the amount of cooperation but not the average payoff of the group. Furthermore, there is a strong negative correlation between total payoff and use of costly punishment. Those people who gain the highest total payoff tend not to use costly punishment: winners don't punish. This suggests that costly punishment behaviour is maladaptive in cooperation games and might have evolved for other reasons.

5. Is the contribution default?

   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper calls it “b/c” (benefit‐to‐cost ratio) and uses either b/c = 2 (T1) or b/c = 3 (T2).

   • Numerical effect size on punishment treatment effect? They find that punishment increases cooperation frequency (e.g., from 21.2% up to 52.4% in T1, and from 43.0% up to 59.7% in T2), but there is “no significant difference in the average payoff” between control and treatment, regardless of b/c = 2 or 3. 7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned? Yes. Imposing punishment always costs the punisher 1 unit.

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are they different?

     1) Number of players (always 2, not varied)  
     2) Number of rounds (indefinite, not varied)  
     4) Contribution is effectively all‐or‐nothing (cooperate vs. defect vs. punish)

   • Only one parameter (parameter 6, the benefit‐to‐cost ratio) is systematically varied (b/c = 2 vs. b/c = 3). The authors report that although punishment raises cooperation levels in both conditions, it “does not increase the average payoff” in either. They do not frame it in terms of “efficiency,” but effectively there is zero payoff gain from adding punishment in both cases.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper explicitly concludes that allowing punishment does not increase the group’s average payoff for the two (b/c) ratios tested; hence there is no evidence (from these experiments) that punishment improves “efficiency.” There is no direct discussion at all of how the other parameters—number of players, known vs. unknown round length, presence/absence of communication, or reward features—would systematically alter the punishment effect. Thus, based solely on the paper, one can say little more than that punishment does not help the group‐level outcome (in payoff terms) under the tested conditions, and “winners don’t punish.” No further quantitative predictions regarding the 15 parameters or their interactions are provided.

Abstract: How do human groups maintain a high level of cooperation despite a low level of genetic relatedness among group members? We offer a model of cooperation and punishment that we call strong reciprocity: where members of a group benefit from mutual adherence to a social norm, strong reciprocators obey the norm and punish its violators, even though as a result they receive lower payoffs than other group members, such as selfish agents who violate the norm and do not punish, and pure cooperators who adhere to the norm but free-ride by never punishing. Below I walk through each of the fifteen design parameters, quoting or pointing to the exact passages, figures or tables in Bowles & Gintis (2003) that are relevant.  For every parameter I say

(i) whether the paper even mentions or instantiates the parameter, and  
(ii) whether the paper ever **systematically varies** it and then reports how that variation changes the “punishment-treatment effect’’ (or any other dependent variable).

Because the published study never compares a *no-punishment* baseline with a *punishment* treatment, strictly speaking it never reports a “punishment treatment effect’’ at all.  What it does report are the absolute levels of group‐average fitness (“average payoff”), shirking, and the frequencies of the three behavioural types inside a model that always allows costly peer punishment (ostracism) to occur.

────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
────────────────────────────────────────

1. Number of players in the group  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Notation n.  Baseline n = 20 (Table 1).  
   • Systematically varied?  Yes.  Third panel of Fig. 6 varies the *initial* n from ≈20 up to >120 and plots the resulting steady-state shirking rate.  
   • Effect reported?  Only on **shirking**, not on efficiency and not on any “treatment effect.”  Qualitative result: when n exceeds ≈120, Reciprocators “rarely invade,” shirking rises sharply, hence group fitness falls.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  Indirectly.  Simulations run for 30 000 periods; results are averaged over last 1000 periods (Fig. 3, Table 2).  
   • Varied?  No.  No predictions about varying the time horizon.

3. Chat / communication enabled  
   • Not mentioned at all.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
   • Mentioned?  Yes (work vs. shirk is binary).  
   • Varied?  No.  Always binary; no comparison with a continuous‐choice version.

5. “Contribution as default’’ framing  
   • Not mentioned.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  The product “b” is the gross benefit an agent produces if she works; cost of working is “c.”  Baseline b = 0.2, c = 0.1 (Table 1).  
   • Varied?  Not in any figure or table.  The authors state that “simulations show that it matters little how large this parameter is,” but they supply no systematic sweep.

7. Punishment cost to punisher  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  c_p = 0.1 baseline (Table 1).  
   • Systematically varied?  Yes.  Second panel of Fig. 6 varies c_p and plots steady-state shirking.  
   • Effect reported?  Only on shirking: as c_p rises, shirking rises (cooperation and implied efficiency fall).  No separate figures for efficiency and no contrast with a no-punishment baseline.

8. Punishment magnitude to target  
   • Model component?  The fitness loss from ostracism is denoted s (endogenous and heterogeneous).  s itself is *not* swept systematically; instead the authors change “fitness in pool” (ϕ₀) which indirectly changes the realized cost of being ostracised (first panel of Fig. 6).  
   • Because ϕ₀ is **not** one of our 15 parameters, and because s is not systematically manipulated, there is no entry here for parameter 8.

9. Reward enabled?  
10. Reward cost?  
11. Reward magnitude?  
   • The model has no reward stage, so none of these are mentioned or varied.

12. Finite horizon known to players  
13. Peer outcomes shown  
14. Identity of punisher known  
15. Identity of rewarder known  
   • None of these information-display parameters are treated in the paper.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────

A.  Dependent variables actually used  
   • Average group fitness (sometimes described as “average payoffs”).  
   • Average group shirking rate (inverse of cooperation).  
   • Population frequencies of Reciprocators, Cooperators, Selfish.  
   These three variables are *not* interchangeable: shirking is behavioural, frequencies are compositional, and fitness is an outcome.  “Efficiency” in the sense of (total payoff)/(payoff under full cooperation) is never explicitly calculated, although Fig. 2 plots “average payoffs” as a function of group composition.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   Parameters 1, 2, 4, 6, 7 and (through the construct s) loosely 8.  So at most 6/15.

C.  For how many of the 15 does the paper report the effect of **systematically varying** the parameter?  
   Two:  
   • Parameter 1 (group size) – varied in Fig. 6, effect shown on shirking.  
   • Parameter 7 (punishment cost) – varied in Fig. 6, effect shown on shirking.  
   Neither variation is tied to a punishment-vs-no-punishment comparison, so no punishment “treatment effect” per se is reported.

D.  What predictions (if any) can be made about the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency, *solely* from this paper?  
   • Smaller groups (n < ≈120) combined with low punishment costs (low c_p) *should* make punishment more effective at keeping shirking low and hence raise efficiency, because the simulations show lower shirking in that part of parameter space.  
   • High punishment costs or very large groups make Reciprocators unable to invade, so punishment would add little or nothing to efficiency in those regimes.  
   • For all other listed parameters (chat, reward, visibility, etc.) the paper gives no basis for prediction.

In short, Bowles & Gintis (2003) is rich on evolutionary dynamics but tells us almost nothing about how most of the 15 public-goods-game design choices would moderate the *efficiency impact* of adding punishment.
reference_APA: Bowles, S & Gintis, H (2004). The evolution of strong reciprocity: cooperation in heterogeneous populations. THEORETICAL POPULATION BIOLOGY.

Authors: Rand, DG; Dreber, A; Ellingsen, T; Fudenberg, D; Nowak, MA
Author Full Names: Rand, David G.; Dreber, Anna; Ellingsen, Tore; Fudenberg, Drew; Nowak, Martin A.
Article Title: Positive Interactions Promote Public Cooperation
Keywords Plus: REPEATED GAMES; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; COSTLY PUNISHMENT; SANCTIONS; EVOLUTION; GOODS; PROVISION; REWARDS; ORGANIZATIONS
Abstract: The public goods game is the classic laboratory paradigm for studying collective action problems. Each participant chooses how much to contribute to a common pool that returns benefits to all participants equally. The ideal outcome occurs if everybody contributes the maximum amount, but the self-interested strategy is not to contribute anything. Most previous studies have found punishment to be more effective than reward for maintaining cooperation in public goods games. The typical design of these studies, however, represses future consequences for today's actions. In an experimental setting, we compare public goods games followed by punishment, reward, or both in the setting of truly repeated games, in which player identities persist from round to round. We show that reward is as effective as punishment for maintaining public cooperation and leads to higher total earnings. Moreover, when both options are available, reward leads to increased contributions and payoff, whereas punishment has no effect on contributions and leads to lower payoff. We conclude that reward outperforms punishment in repeated public goods games and that human cooperation in such repeated settings is best supported by positive interactions with others.
