Below is a parameter-by-parameter analysis of whether (1) the paper discusses each of the 15 listed parameters (and, if so, any specific value it takes in their experiment) and (2) whether the paper makes predictions about how systematically varying that parameter would affect the “punishment treatment effect” for any outcome measure—especially efficiency (actual total payoff as a fraction of the maximum possible payoff). All statements are based solely on the content of the provided paper. If the paper does not discuss a parameter or its systematic variation, that is stated explicitly.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mention in paper? Yes. All groups had exactly 4 players.  
   • Systematic variation or effect on punishment? No. The paper does not vary group size, nor does it provide any prediction of how changing the group size would affect the punishment treatment effect for efficiency or any other measure.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mention in paper? Yes. It is a repeated game with an unspecified number of rounds. Participants were not told how many rounds would be played.  
   • Systematic variation or effect on punishment? No. The paper does not vary the number of rounds across conditions, nor does it predict how changing the number of rounds would affect the punishment treatment effect.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mention in paper? No. There is no mention of in-game “chat” or free-form communication. Players interacted anonymously via computer screens with no stated option for unstructured communication.  
   • Systematic variation or effect on punishment? No mention.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing” (forced full contribution or none)?
   • Mention in paper? The paper specifies that each participant receives 20 monetary units (MUs) and decides how many to contribute, implying a free, continuous choice between 0 and 20, rather than all or nothing.  
   • Systematic variation or effect on punishment? No. There is no all-or-nothing format, and no prediction about its effect was made.

5. Is the contribution default (do players move funds back into their hand)?
   • Mention in paper? No. The paper states participants start with 20 MUs and then decide how much to put into the public pool, with no mention of a “default” forced movement.  
   • Systematic variation or effect on punishment? No mention.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Mention in paper? Yes. The total contribution is multiplied by 1.6 and split among 4 players, implying an MPCR of 1.6/4 = 0.40.  
   • Systematic variation or effect on punishment? No. The paper keeps this factor at 1.6 and does not explore any variation or prediction about changing it.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mention in paper? The paper refers generally to punishment as “costly” and notes that punishing reduces both parties’ payoffs. However, it does not report a numeric cost.  
   • Systematic variation or effect on punishment? No. There is no systematic manipulation of the cost to punish, nor any prediction about altering it.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a target per unit punishment)
   • Mention in paper? The paper states that punishment “imposes costs” on the punished individual but gives no numerical deduction.  
   • Systematic variation or effect on punishment? No. The paper does not vary punishment magnitude, nor does it predict how changing that magnitude would affect outcomes.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mention in paper? Yes. The study has three main treatments beyond the control: PN (punishment only), RN (reward only), and RNP (reward or punishment). In PN, reward is disabled; in RN and RNP, reward is enabled.  
   • Systematic variation or effect on punishment? Partially, yes. Although “presence versus absence” of reward is manipulated across treatments, the paper does not systematically manipulate reward only to see how it alone changes the effect of adding punishment. Instead, it compares various combinations. Still, the paper does discuss how reward availability impacts group cooperation/efficiency compared to punishment alone. The paper reports that in PN (punishment only), average contributions and percentage of maximum possible payoff remain high (similarly high as with rewards), but total payoffs (a measure related to efficiency) are lower when only punishment is used. When reward is also available, punishment loses its effectiveness for raising contributions, and punishment use leads to lower payoffs. Numerically, Figure 1B indicates that with or without punishment, “reward” treatments achieve a similar fraction of maximum possible payoff to PN, but due to reward being generative rather than destructive, absolute payoffs are higher in reward conditions. The paper does not provide a single effect-size number for how enabling reward changes “the punishment treatment effect on efficiency,” but it does conclude that adding reward leads to higher overall earnings and that punishment alone yields less payoff.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Mention in paper? The paper notes that rewarding is “costly,” but no specific numerical cost is stated.  
   • Systematic variation or effect on punishment? No. The cost of reward is not systematically varied, nor is any prediction offered for changing it.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward)
   • Mention in paper? The experiment includes a “targeted” rewards stage where some positive amount is given, but no particular magnitude is reported.  
   • Systematic variation or effect on punishment? No. There is no manipulation of how large the reward is, nor as to its impact on punishment’s effectiveness.

12. Is the number of rounds known to the players (do they know when the game ends)?
   • Mention in paper? Yes. The paper explicitly says, “Subjects are not told the total number of rounds.”  
   • Systematic variation or effect on punishment? No. The paper does not vary whether the horizon is known or unknown. No prediction is offered about systematically altering participants’ knowledge of the final round.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained or lost)?
   • Mention in paper? The paper does mention that participants see how much others contributed in the public goods stage (and they can target punishment or reward accordingly), but it does not detail whether participants see exact payoffs or only contributions. There is no explicit mention that final payoff information per player is displayed.  
   • Systematic variation or effect on punishment? No. The paper does not systematically vary the amount of peer-outcome information participants receive.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Mention in paper? The authors contrast their design with typical studies where “subjects are often informed about the total amount of punishment they received, but not from whom.” Although they note that in their repeated setup, player identities persist, the paper does not explicitly confirm whether the punished individual sees who punished them.  
   • Systematic variation or effect on punishment? No. There is no explicit statement or variation of punisher-identifiability in the experiment.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Mention in paper? Same situation as with punishment. The text does not clearly specify whether recipients see who rewarded them, only that the second stage involves “targeted interactions,” presumably enabling or directing reward to a specific individual.  
   • Systematic variation or effect on punishment? No. The paper does not manipulate knowledge of who the rewarder is.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FINAL SUMMARY

A: Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • Yes. The paper reports two main measures related to what you call “efficiency”: (i) “percentage of the maximum possible payoff” (Figure 1B) and (ii) “average payoff” aggregated over the public goods game and the targeted interaction (Figure 1C). Additionally, the paper tracks “contributions to the public good,” which is not always the same as total efficiency.

B: Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned explicitly (with some specific value or condition in the design) are:  
     1) Number of players (always 4)  
     2) Number of rounds (unspecified but repeated, unknown to subjects)  
     4) Contribution is continuous, not all-or-nothing  
     6) MPCR/multiplication factor (1.6 total multiplier, implicitly MPCR=0.4)  
     7) Punishment is costly (but no numeric value given)  
     8) Punishment magnitude exists (unquantified)  
     9) Whether a reward is enabled or not (PN vs RN vs RNP vs Control)  
     10) Reward is also costly (no numeric value)  
     11) Reward magnitude exists (unquantified)  
     12) Number of rounds is not told to players  
     13) Some measure of peer behavior is shown (e.g., contributions), but payoffs are less clearly mentioned  
   • Parameters not mentioned at all or mentioned only as “not varied” or “not applicable” include:  
     3) Chat enabled? (no mention at all)  
     5) Contribution default? (no mention)  
     14), 15) Knowledge of exactly who punished/rewarded (not clearly stated or manipulated)

C: For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when the parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, no parameter is “systematically varied” along a numeric or design continuum in this paper, apart from the on/off presence of reward or punishment (Parameter 9). The paper compares four distinct conditions: Control (no targeted interactions), PN (punishment only), RN (reward only), and RNP (both punishment and reward).  
   • Thus, the one parameter for which the paper discusses a direct change in the presence or absence that relates to the “punishment treatment effect” on outcomes is:  
       9) Whether a reward is enabled (PN vs RN vs RNP).  
   • Even then, the paper frames it mainly in terms of comparing different treatments rather than systematically varying a single parameter to isolate incremental changes in punishment’s effect.

D: If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not provide direct evidence or discussion for most parameters. It focuses on repeated interactions and the availability of targeted rewarding vs. punishing, concluding that reward sustains high public-good contributions and yields higher group payoffs (or efficiency) than punishment alone.  
   • No data or explicit predictions are given for varying group size, number of rounds, chat, all-or-nothing contribution, systematically changing MPCR, the exact cost/magnitude of punishment or reward, or knowledge of who punishes or rewards.  
   • Therefore, for nearly all of the 15 parameters, the paper provides little or no basis for predicting how they would alter the punishment treatment effect on efficiency. The only direct conclusion from the paper is that enabling reward, either alone or alongside punishment, can maintain cooperation at least as well as punishment alone, and it yields higher absolute payoffs.  
   • Beyond that, no further quantitative predictions are made.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
reference_APA: Rand, David G., Dreber, Anna, Ellingsen, Tore, Fudenberg, Drew & Nowak, Martin A. (2009). Positive Interactions Promote Public Cooperation. SCIENCE.

Authors: Tenbrunsel, AE; Messick, DM
Author Full Names: Tenbrunsel, AE; Messick, DM
Article Title: Sanctioning systems, decision frames, and cooperation
Keywords Plus: BEHAVIOR; ORGANIZATIONS; SURVEILLANCE; INCENTIVES; DISCIPLINE; OWNERSHIP; DILEMMAS; REWARDS; WORK; FIRM
Abstract: Three studies are used to examine how surveillance and sanctioning systems affect cooperative behavior in dilemma situations. The first two studies demonstrate that a weak sanctioning system results in less cooperation than no sanctioning system; furthermore, results from the second study suggest that sanctions affect the type of decision people perceive they are making, prompting them to see it as a business rather than an ethical decision. The results from these studies are used to develop a theoretical model that postulates that the relationship between sanctions and cooperation is due to both a signaling effect, in which sanctions influence the type of decision that is perceived to be made, and a processing effect, in which the decision processing, including whether or not the strength of the sanction is considered, depends on the decision frame evoked. A third study provides support for the processing-effect hypothesis.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter account of whether (1) the paper even mentions the parameter (and, if so, what values it takes) and (2) whether it makes any prediction about how systematically varying that parameter would affect the “punishment treatment effect” (in the paper’s terms, the effect of having a sanctioning system) for any dependent variable. Throughout, please note that the paper never explicitly measures “efficiency” (total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff) as an outcome; rather, the authors focus primarily on cooperation rates, defection rates, expectations of others’ behavior, and decision frames.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
• Mentioned? Yes. Study 1 uses two players (a two-party prisoner’s dilemma); Studies 2 and 3 use multiple players (a multiparty social dilemma).  
• Systematically varied? No. The paper does not systematically manipulate or compare different group sizes nor discuss how varying group size would affect the sanction (punishment) treatment effect on cooperation or payoffs.

2. Number of rounds  
• Mentioned? Yes. Study 1 has four “production runs.” Studies 2 and 3 use a single-shot scenario.  
• Systematically varied? No. The paper does not systematically compare different numbers of rounds or speak to how changing the number of rounds affects the impact of sanctions on participants’ outcomes or cooperation.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
• Mentioned? No. There is no mention of any communication or chat feature in the paper.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Mentioned? The studies present cooperate/defect choices (e.g., “request an inspection vs. not,” “run scrubbers 80% vs. less”), but there is no analysis of partial vs. full contributions. Nor is there any systematic variation of “all or nothing.”  
• Systematically varied? No.

5. Is the contribution default?  
• Mentioned? No. The paper does not discuss any default contribution mechanism.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
• Mentioned? No. The authors do not mention MPCR, a multiplier, or any equivalent.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Mentioned? No. The paper focuses on fines imposed on the defector (“weak” vs. “strong” sanctions) but does not describe any cost to the “punisher” for imposing those fines. Hence, there is no discussion of systematically varying a “punisher’s cost.”

8. Punishment magnitude (coins or money deducted for each unit of punishment)  
• Mentioned? Yes. The paper explicitly compares “no sanction” vs. a “weak sanction” vs. a “strong sanction,” each corresponding to different fine amounts (e.g., US$30, US$50,000, US$2,000,000) or different probabilities of detection.  
• Systematically varied? Yes, in Studies 2 and 3, the authors differentiate a weak sanction (small fine, low detection probability) and a strong sanction (substantive fine, higher detection probability). Although they do not measure “efficiency,” they do report systematic effects on cooperation (i.e., the paper’s main dependent variable).  
  – For example, in Study 3:  
    • No-sanction condition: 64.4% cooperation  
    • Weak-sanction condition: 54.6% cooperation  
    • Strong-sanction condition: 79.5% cooperation  
  This is not framed as “group efficiency” but rather as cooperation rates. The paper does not provide numerical estimates of any direct payoff-efficiency ratio.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
• Mentioned? No. The experiments only describe sanctioning (punishment) conditions and do not introduce any form of reward for cooperating.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Mentioned? No. There is no discussion of any reward system or its cost.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded for each reward)  
• Mentioned? No. As above, the paper does not mention rewarding cooperators.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
• Mentioned? Partially. Study 1 participants are told there will be four production runs; Studies 2 and 3 are one-shot. However, there is no systematic manipulation of known vs. unknown lengths, nor any analysis of how that knowledge changes the impact of sanctions.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
• Mentioned? Partially. In Study 1, participants are told (after the second run) whether the other player cooperated or defected, but the paper does not systematically vary how much outcome information is revealed. They do not link this to any separate manipulation of punishment or “efficiency.”

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• Mentioned? No. Punishment is framed in terms of random inspection/fines conducted by “the division president” or “industry representatives,” not as peer-to-peer punishment. No systematic variation is discussed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
• Mentioned? No. The paper never addresses rewards or their disclosure.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
• The paper does not measure “group efficiency” or “total/average payoff” in the sense of dividing total payoff by a maximum possible payoff. Its main dependent variables are cooperation (e.g., whether or not participants choose to defect), expectations of others’ cooperativeness, and decision frames (e.g., “business” vs. “ethical”).

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Mentioned in some form:  
  – (1) Number of players (two-party vs. multiparty)  
  – (2) Number of rounds (Study 1 has four; Studies 2 & 3 are single-shot)  
  – (8) Punishment magnitude (weak vs. strong sanction)  
  – (13) Peer outcomes are partially revealed (cooperate/defect), though not systematically varied for punishment.  
• The paper does not mention or does not manipulate the remaining parameters.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• Only parameter (8), punishment magnitude, is systematically varied, examining its effect on cooperation rates (rather than “efficiency”). For the other parameters, the paper either does not mention them or does not systematically vary them in relation to punishment.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper, what would they be?  
• The paper never reports actual payoffs as a fraction of a maximum possible payoff (i.e., efficiency), so there is little direct basis for inferring how each parameter might shift “efficiency.” One might guess from the authors’ discussion that strong sanctions could raise cooperation and might therefore raise total group payoff—suggesting a higher efficiency—but the paper does not demonstrate or quantify that. For the vast majority of the 15 parameters, the paper simply provides no information to support any prediction about efficiency. As a result, very few (if any) concrete predictions can be made about how systematically varying those parameters would affect punishment’s influence on group efficiency.

Abstract: The existence of cooperation and social order among genetically unrelated individuals is a fundamental problem in the behavioural sciences. The prevailing approaches in biology and economics view cooperation exclusively as self-interested behaviour-unrelated individuals cooperate only if they face economic rewards or sanctions rendering cooperation a self-interested choice. Whether economic incentives are perceived as just or legitimate does not matter in these theories. Fairness-based altruism is, however, a powerful source of human cooperation. Here we show experimentally that the prevailing self-interest approach has serious shortcomings because it overlooks negative effects of sanctions on human altruism. Sanctions revealing selfish or greedy intentions destroy altruistic cooperation almost completely, whereas sanctions perceived as fair leave altruism intact. These findings challenge proximate and ultimate theories of human cooperation that neglect the distinction between fair and unfair sanctions, and they are probably relevant in all domains in which voluntary compliance matters-in relations between spouses, in the education of children, in business relations and organizations as well as in markets.

Author Keywords: collective action; economic games; evolutionary game theory; homophily; reciprocity
Keywords Plus: ANTISOCIAL PUNISHMENT; EVOLUTIONARY GAMES; RECIPROCITY; BEHAVIOR; MODEL; COEVOLUTION; SPREAD
Abstract: Human populations are both highly cooperative and highly organized. Human interactions are not random but rather are structured in social networks. Importantly, ties in these networks often are dynamic, changing in response to the behavior of one's social partners. This dynamic structure permits an important form of conditional action that has been explored theoretically but has received little empirical attention: People can respond to the cooperation and defection of those around them by making or breaking network links. Here, we present experimental evidence of the power of using strategic link formation and dissolution, and the network modification it entails, to stabilize cooperation in sizable groups. Our experiments explore large-scale cooperation, where subjects' cooperative actions are equally beneficial to all those with whom they interact. Consistent with previous research, we find that cooperation decays over time when social networks are shuffled randomly every round or are fixed across all rounds. We also find that, when networks are dynamic but are updated only infrequently, cooperation again fails. However, when subjects can update their network connections frequently, we see a qualitatively different outcome: Cooperation is maintained at a high level through network rewiring. Subjects preferentially break links with defectors and form new links with cooperators, creating an incentive to cooperate and leading to substantial changes in network structure. Our experiments confirm the predictions of a set of evolutionary game theoretic models and demonstrate the important role that dynamic social networks can play in supporting large- scale human cooperation.

Abstract: The scale of human cooperation is an evolutionary puzzle. All of the available evidence suggests that the societies of our Pliocene ancestors were like those of other social primates, and this means that human psychology has changed in ways that support larger, more cooperative societies that characterize modern humans. In this paper, we argue that cultural adaptation is a key factor in these changes. Below I go through the 15 listed design parameters one at a time and extract everything the paper says that is relevant for  
(1) the value that was actually implemented, and  
(2) whether the author makes – inside this paper – any quantitative or qualitative prediction about what would happen to the *punishment treatment effect* if that parameter were **systematically varied**.  
Whenever “punishment treatment effect” is mentioned I report it in terms actually used by the author (contribution, likelihood/intensity of punishment, likelihood/intensity of counter-punishment, individual earnings).  The paper never calculates the efficiency ratio “actual ÷ maximum,” so I translate efficiency claims into the author’s own payoff numbers when possible.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER EXTRACTION
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Discussed? Yes – groups of 4 (pp. 7-8).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  No prediction given for other group sizes.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Discussed? Yes – 10 periods per treatment (total 20 periods per session).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  Author does report within-game *period effects* (e.g., contributions fall over time in VCM and PCP but rise in P), yet the total horizon length is never manipulated, so no prediction about changing the horizon.

3. Chat / face-to-face communication  
   • Discussed? Yes – “decide simultaneously *and without communication*” (p. 7).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  No statement on what would happen if chat were allowed.

4. All-or-nothing contribution decision  
   • Discussed? Yes – subjects choose any integer 0–20 ECU (continuous choice).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  No claim about forcing all-or-nothing choices.

5. “Contribution default” (reversing the transfer)  
   • Discussed? No.  Not part of this experiment.  No prediction.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Discussed? Yes – each ECU placed in the public account yields 0.4 ECU back to *each* of 4 members (group return 1.6).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  No prediction provided for other MPCR values.

7. Cost to impose one unit of punishment  
   • Discussed? Yes – Table 2 gives the convex cost schedule (1 point costs 1 ECU; 10 points cost 30 ECU).  
   • Systematically varied? No empirical variation.  
   • Prediction? The author *states a qualitative prediction* (Hypothesis 1, p. 11): “As the cost of punishment increases, the quantity demanded of punishment will decrease … hence cooperation will become less stable.”  This is conceptual; no numerical effect size is presented.

8. Magnitude of a punishment point for the target  
   • Discussed? Yes – each point removes 10 % of the target’s stage-1 income, up to 100 %.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  No prediction for other magnitudes.

9. Existence of a reward option  
   • Discussed? No – rewards are absent in every treatment.

10. Cost of reward  
11. Magnitude of reward  
   • Discussed? Not applicable (no reward option).

12. Whether the number of rounds is common knowledge  
   • Discussed? Yes – subjects are told there will be exactly 10 periods.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

13. Peer-outcome visibility (who contributed how much, earnings, etc.)  
   • Discussed? Yes – after the contribution stage everyone sees each member’s contribution; after punishment they see total punishment received, etc.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

14. Whether the identity of the punisher is revealed  
   • Discussed? Yes – in P, only the *total* punishment received is shown; in PCP the victim is told how many points each individual assigned to him so that he can retaliate.  
   • Systematically varied *independently*? No.  The identity information changes only jointly with the introduction of the counter-punishment stage, so no separate causal prediction.

15. Whether the identity of the rewarder is revealed  
   • Discussed? Not applicable (no rewards).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables actually analysed  
    • Average or individual *earnings* (in ECU) – this is the closest the paper comes to “group efficiency,” but the efficiency ratio itself is never calculated.  
    • Contribution level & decision to contribute.  
    • Punishment likelihood and punishment intensity.  
    • Counter-punishment likelihood and intensity.  
    These variables are conceptually different: contribution measures cooperation, punishment variables measure enforcement activity, and earnings incorporate both benefits of cooperation and the monetary costs of punishment.

B.  Parameters mentioned at all (value given): 10 out of 15  
    Parameters 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14.  
    Parameters 5, 9, 10, 11, 15 are not mentioned.

C.  Parameters whose *systematic variation* is analysed for their impact on the punishment treatment effect: 0 out of 15.  
    The only experimental manipulation is the presence or absence of a second punishment stage (counter-punishment), which is not one of the listed 15 parameters.  The author does offer a **qualitative** prediction for Parameter 7 (“higher cost → fewer punishments → lower cooperation”), but that cost is not varied inside the experiment.

D.  Predictions one can legitimately offer – based **solely** on this paper – about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency:

    • Parameter 7 (punishment cost):  The paper argues (p. 11) that raising the cost lowers punishment frequency and thus weakens cooperation; therefore, higher cost should make the punishment treatment *less* efficient (or even negative relative to no-punishment baseline).  
    • Parameter 14 (punisher identity):  Revealing the punisher enables retaliation; the paper shows that once retaliation is possible, efficiency falls further.  Hence, making the punisher’s identity *more* salient is expected to reduce the positive (or increase the negative) punishment treatment effect.  
    • Time within a fixed horizon (related to Parameter 2):  Contributions tend to decay over periods in VCM and PCP but rise in P; thus the punishment-efficiency advantage of P grows later in the game, though the total horizon length itself was never manipulated.  
    For the remaining 12 parameters the paper supplies no direct evidence or explicit theoretical claim, so no prediction can be made from this source alone.

In short, the paper is rich in results about *whether* punishers can be counter-punished, but it leaves us with almost no leverage for forecasting how the usual structural design knobs (group size, MPCR, cost/magnitude schedules, communication, visibility, rewards, etc.) would modulate the net efficiency impact of punishment.
reference_APA: Nikiforakis, Nikos (2008). Punishment and counter-punishment in public good games: Can we really govern ourselves?. JOURNAL OF PUBLIC ECONOMICS.

Abstract: Rock is wrapped by paper, paper is cut by scissors and scissors are crushed by rock. This simple game is popular among children and adults to decide on trivial disputes that have no obvious winner, but cyclic dominance is also at the heart of predator-prey interactions, the mating strategy of side-blotched lizards, the overgrowth of marine sessile organisms and competition in microbial populations. Cyclical interactions also emerge spontaneously in evolutionary games entailing volunteering, reward, punishment, and in fact are common when the competing strategies are three or more, regardless of the particularities of the game. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of exactly what this paper says (and does not say) regarding each of the 15 listed parameters, followed by the required four‐part summary (A–D). Throughout, please note that the original paper does not use the term “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” It focuses on how punishment (and reward) can stabilize or destabilize cooperation under evolutionary (replicator) dynamics, often comparing “social” vs. “asocial” outcomes. There is no direct discussion of “efficiency” defined as total (or average) payoff relative to a maximum achievable payoff. Accordingly, all references to “effect on punishment treatment” below concern the paper’s discussion of stable or unstable cooperation under punishment.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned? Yes (the authors reduce the Public Goods Game to two players in their “minigame”).  
   • Systematically varied, or any predictions about its effect? No. They fix the analysis to two players. The paper does not discuss how changing the number of players might affect punishment’s impact.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned? Yes, indirectly: the Ultimatum Game is described as not repeated (“The game is not repeated”).  
   • Systematically varied, or any predictions about its effect? No. The paper does not analyze different numbers of rounds or how that might affect the punishment treatment.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Systematically varied, or any predictions? No mention at all.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned? Yes, but only insofar as they reduce each game to two binary choices (“minigames” with two options: cooperate or defect, punish or not, reward or not).  
   • Systematically varied, or any predictions? No. This binary (“all or nothing”) assumption is fixed; the paper does not evaluate different contribution formats.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Systematically varied, or any predictions? No mention at all.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Mentioned? The paper does say that in a general Public Goods Game, each contribution is multiplied by a factor r. However, they do not undertake any parametric analysis of r.  
   • Systematically varied, or any predictions? No. They do not vary r or discuss how changing r affects the treatment effect.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned? Yes. In the paper’s notation, the punisher’s cost is “γ.”  
   • Systematically varied, or any predictions? The paper explores conditions such as “2c < β − γ” (for stability of punishing cooperation). However, there is no explicit numerical effect size on efficiency. Instead, the paper shows that if γ is large, punishment is less likely to stabilize cooperation (and vice versa), but again only in the sense of which strategy equilibria occur.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   • Mentioned? Yes. In the paper’s notation, “β” is the fine imposed on the punished player.  
   • Systematically varied, or any predictions? They discuss inequalities like “c < β” and “2c < β − γ” affecting whether a “social” (punishing/cooperating) equilibrium is stable. They do not quantify a “treatment effect on efficiency” per se but show that changing β can shift whether punishment deters defection in evolutionary equilibrium.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned? Yes. They deal explicitly with “Public Goods with Reward” as a separate scenario.  
   • Systematically varied, or any predictions? The paper contrasts punishment vs. reward but does not treat “reward enabled vs. not enabled” as a continuous parameter. Instead, it analyzes these as two distinct cases (reward scenario vs. punishment scenario).

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Mentioned? Yes. In the reward scenario, the one who “returns part of the gift” pays a cost “γ.”  
   • Systematically varied, or any predictions? Like with punishment, they discuss how γ affects equilibria. They do not present any effect size in terms of efficiency.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)
   • Mentioned? Yes. In the paper’s notation, “β” appears as the payoff to the rewarded side. They also use expressions like “cost = –γ” to give “+β” to the other.  
   • Systematically varied, or any predictions? There is no direct modeling of how systematically varying β alone would change the “punishment (or reward) treatment effect.” Instead, they show that if β > c (etc.), certain equilibria arise, without quantifying changes in total payoff.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Systematically varied, or any predictions? No mention at all.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much others gained and lost each round)?
   • Mentioned? Not in these terms.  
   • Systematically varied, or any predictions? No mention at all.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Mentioned? Only indirectly: the paper talks about “reputation” and small probabilities that you learn another’s type. This is not the same as definitively revealing a punisher’s identity.  
   • Systematically varied, or any predictions? No direct mention that a punished player specifically learns who punished them. The paper uses parameters μ and ν to represent partial knowledge of the other’s type, but it does not discuss unmasking punisher identity.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Mentioned? Same as (14). The paper deals with a parameter for “the likelihood of knowing the other’s type,” but not specifically that the rewardee learns the rewarder’s identity.  
   • Systematically varied, or any predictions? No mention.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?

• The paper does not use “group efficiency” in the sense of actual payoff divided by a maximal possible payoff.  
• Its main focus is on how punishment or reward can stabilize or destabilize prosocial behavior under replicator dynamics. The authors discuss equilibria (e.g., “social” vs. “asocial”) and the frequency of cooperative vs. defecting strategies, not “efficiency.”  
• They do discuss payoffs in the sense of evolutionary success, but they do not frame it as “efficiency.”

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

• Mentioned in some form:  
   1 (Number of players) – specifically set to 2 in the minigame.  
   2 (Number of rounds) – only to note “not repeated,” no variation.  
   4 (All or nothing) – yes, in that they restrict to binary choices.  
   6 (Multiplication factor) – briefly noted (r), but never varied.  
   7 (Punishment cost, γ) – discussed extensively in formulas.  
   8 (Punishment magnitude, β) – also discussed.  
   9 (Whether reward is enabled) – they compare punishment vs. reward.  
   10 (Reward cost, γ) – same letter but in the reward context.  
   11 (Reward magnitude, β) – same letter but in the reward context.

• Not mentioned at all (or no relevant discussion):  
   3 (Chat enabled), 5 (Contribution default), 12 (Known # of rounds?), 13 (Peer outcomes shown?), 14 (Identity of punisher revealed?), 15 (Identity of rewarder revealed?).

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?

• The paper does not systematically vary any parameter in terms of a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” It does vary (in a theoretical sense) parameters such as c, γ, and β to check which equilibria emerge. But there are no numerical effect sizes or direct references to “efficiency.”  
• Thus, although parameters 7 (punishment cost γ) and 8 (punishment magnitude β) are central to their theoretical analysis of whether punishing cooperation can stabilize or not, the paper does not quantify these effects in terms of “efficiency.” Instead, it uses replicator‐dynamics stability and risk dominance as the outcome.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

• The paper does not provide results specifically linking these parameters to any ratio of total payoff versus maximum payoff.  
• It does indicate that if the cost of punishing (γ) is sufficiently low compared to the fine (β), cooperation may stabilize (i.e., the “social” outcome is reachable) rather than revert to the “asocial” outcome. One might infer that such a stable cooperative outcome could improve group payoffs, hence possibly raising efficiency—but the paper never states it in those terms.  
• Similarly, for reward, the paper shows more complex or oscillatory dynamics, suggesting that reward alone might be less reliably stabilizing. If stable cooperation is less often achieved, that can imply a lower payoff, thus (one might guess) lower efficiency. However, the authors do not formalize “efficiency” as a dependent variable in these analyses.  
• Because the paper’s modeling is purely in terms of evolutionary stability (rather than explicit total payoff), little or no precise prediction about “efficiency” can be extracted beyond guessing that the “social” equilibrium typically yields higher payoffs than the “asocial” one. 

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
reference_APA: Sigmund, K, Hauert, C & Nowak, MA (2001). Reward and punishment. PROCEEDINGS OF THE NATIONAL ACADEMY OF SCIENCES OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA.

Authors: Boyd, R; Gintis, H; Bowles, S
Author Full Names: Boyd, Robert; Gintis, Herbert; Bowles, Samuel
Article Title: Coordinated Punishment of Defectors Sustains Cooperation and Can Proliferate When Rare
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; STRONG RECIPROCITY; SIZABLE GROUPS; EVOLUTION; ENFORCEMENT; DOMINANCE; BEHAVIOR; HUMANS
Abstract: Because mutually beneficial cooperation may unravel unless most members of a group contribute, people often gang up on free-riders, punishing them when this is cost-effective in sustaining cooperation. In contrast, current models of the evolution of cooperation assume that punishment is uncoordinated and unconditional. These models have difficulty explaining the evolutionary emergence of punishment because rare unconditional punishers bear substantial costs and hence are eliminated. Moreover, in human behavioral experiments in which punishment is uncoordinated, the sum of costs to punishers and their targets often exceeds the benefits of the increased cooperation that results from the punishment of free-riders. As a result, cooperation sustained by punishment may actually reduce the average payoffs of group members in comparison with groups in which punishment of free-riders is not an option. Here, we present a model of coordinated punishment that is calibrated for ancestral human conditions and captures a further aspect of reality missing from both models and experiments: The total cost of punishing a free-rider declines as the number of punishers increases. We show that punishment can proliferate when rare, and when it does, it enhances group-average payoffs.

----------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
----------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned: Yes.  Example in Fig. 1: N = 4 (six groups of four).  Other examples use N ≥ 2 in general exposition.  
   • Systematic variation / prediction: No.  The paper uses only one group size per study and offers no comparative results across sizes.  No numerical effect size on the punishment treatment effect is reported.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned: Yes.  Main public-goods experiment: 10 periods without punishment followed by 10 with punishment.  
   • Systematic variation: No.  All groups face 10+10 periods; the authors do not compare different horizons.  
   • Prediction: None.  (They do assert conceptually that an “unknown” horizon could provide selfish incentives to punish, but they supply no data or quantitative prediction.)

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned: No.  No experiment in the paper allows participant communication.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Mentioned: No.  The contribution decision is continuous (0–Y).

5. “Contribution default” (take vs. give frame)  
   • Mentioned: No.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned: Yes.  In Fig. 1 M = 1.6 with N = 4 (MPCR = 0.40).  
   • Systematic variation: No.  Only one value is used; no comparison offered.

7. Punishment cost per unit  
   • Mentioned: Yes.  One punishment point costs the punisher 1 money unit.  
   • Systematic variation: No.  Same cost in every group; no data on alternative costs; no prediction.

8. Punishment magnitude per unit  
   • Mentioned: Yes.  One punishment point deducts 10 % (≈3 money units) from the target.  
   • Systematic variation / prediction: No.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Mentioned: No.  Only punishment is implemented.

10. Reward cost per unit  
    • Not mentioned.

11. Reward magnitude per unit  
    • Not mentioned.

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
    • Mentioned: Yes.  In Fehr & Gächter’s experiment subjects know there will be 20 rounds.  The authors contrast this with earlier studies that concealed the horizon, but they do not manipulate the variable themselves.  
    • Systematic variation / prediction: No direct experimental comparison; only verbal remarks.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mentioned: Yes.  After each period individual contributions are revealed so that punishment can be targeted.  
    • Systematic variation: No.  Always shown; no comparison when hidden.

14. Is the punisher identified to the target?  
    • Not explicitly stated, and never varied.  No prediction.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
    • Not applicable (no rewards).

----------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
----------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables actually used  
   • Cooperation / contribution rate (public-goods sections)  
   • Punishment points given and received  
   • Individual and total monetary payoffs in several sections (called “earnings,” sometimes discussed as “efficiency gains”)  
   • Effort in gift-exchange games  
   These variables are conceptually different.  The paper almost never computes “group efficiency” as the ratio (actual group payoff)/(maximum possible).  Where “efficiency” or “efficiency gains” is mentioned (e.g., long-term employment relations) it refers to higher total earnings, not that specific ratio.

B. Which of the 15 focal parameters are even mentioned?  
   7 of 15: 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of systematic variation on the punishment treatment effect?  
   Zero.  Not one of the 15 parameters is experimentally varied in more than one condition while keeping everything else constant so that its marginal impact on the punishment treatment effect could be estimated.

D. Implications for predicting punishment-treatment effects on efficiency, based solely on this paper  
   • The only solid qualitative result available is that “adding a costly punishment opportunity” raised cooperation almost to 100 % in a 20-round, N = 4, MPCR = 0.40 environment with a 1:3 (cost:impact) punishment technology and full feedback.  
   • Because no other values of the 15 parameters were explored, the paper provides virtually no leverage for forecasting how changing group size, horizon length, punishment cost, punishment magnitude, the visibility of outcomes, etc., would alter the efficiency effect of introducing punishment.

Abstract: Theoretical and empirical research highlights the role of punishment in promoting collaborative efforts(1-5). However, both the emergence and the stability of costly punishment are problematic issues. It is not clear how punishers can invade a society of defectors by social learning or natural selection, or how second-order free-riders (who contribute to the joint effort but not to the sanctions) can be prevented from drifting into a coercion-based regime and subverting cooperation. Here we compare the prevailing model of peer-punishment(6-8) with pool-punishment, which consists in committing resources, before the collaborative effort, to prepare sanctions against free-riders. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter review of what the paper by Sigmund et al. (2010) does—or does not—say regarding each of the 15 parameters, and whether the paper makes any predictions about their systematic variation and its impact on punishment’s effect on outcomes. As requested, the focus is on how these parameters might affect “efficiency” (defined as actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff), but the paper mainly discusses average (or total) payoff or prevalence of cooperation rather than efficiency per se.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Discussed? Yes. The paper uses groups of size N (with a numerical example N=5 in the figures).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not show how changing N systematically affects the punishment treatment effect on any dependent variable (including efficiency). No numerical effect size is given.

2. Number of rounds
   • Discussed? Yes, but only briefly. The authors note that many experiments last only a few rounds (e.g., 6–10), and that if the game continues sufficiently many rounds, cooperation may become common.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not present or analyze a systematic manipulation of the number of rounds. No effect size specific to efficiency is provided.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not mention communication or chat.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussed? Yes, implicitly. Players either contribute a fixed amount c to the public good or contribute nothing (a “yes–no” decision).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not explore changing this rule; no effect size is reported.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Discussed? No. There is no mention of defaults or forced decisions in that sense.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Discussed? Yes. The multiplication factor is r (> 1), for instance r=3 in the example simulations.  
   • Systematically varied? No. Although r is crucial in defining the social dilemma, the paper does not present results of systematically varying r to see its effect on punishment or efficiency.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit  
   • Discussed? Yes. For peer‐punishment, the cost is γ, often set to γ=0.7 in the examples. For pool‐punishment, there is a setup cost G=0.7 in the figures.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not systematically vary these costs to analyze the punishment treatment effect. No numeric effect size is provided.

8. Punishment magnitude (the deduction a punished player faces)
   • Discussed? Yes. For peer punishment, the fine is β per punisher (β=0.7 in examples). For pool punishment, a free‐rider is fined an amount B·Nv (B=0.7).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not systematically vary β or B to measure its impact on efficiency.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussed? No. The paper treats only punishment (peer vs. pool). Rewards are not addressed.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Discussed? No. Rewards are not addressed.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)
    • Discussed? No. Rewards are not addressed.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Discussed? No. The authors do not specify what players know about the duration. They only mention real‐life/experimental setups that sometimes had 6–10 rounds or more.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much peers gained or lost)?
    • Discussed? No. The paper does not describe information feedback of that kind.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Discussed? No. There is no mention of revealing who punished whom.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Discussed? No. Again, rewards are not considered, so this is not mentioned.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper largely discusses average (or total) payoff and cooperation rates. It does sometimes remark on overall “social cost” or “social payoff.” Strictly labeled “efficiency” measures—actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible—are not the central outcome in their tables/figures. The paper’s main dependent variables therefore include (i) average payoffs of different strategies, (ii) the prevalence of these strategies (cooperators vs. defectors, punishers vs. nonpunishers). These differ from efficiency in that the paper’s focus is on whether cooperation or punishment “dominates” and on the average payoff each strategy obtains, rather than an explicit ratio to the maximum possible group payoff.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned (at least in passing) are:  
     (1) Number of players (N)  
     (2) Number of rounds (briefly mentioned qualitatively)  
     (4) Whether contribution is all or nothing  
     (6) MPCR/multiplying factor (r)  
     (7) Punishment cost (γ or G)  
     (8) Punishment magnitude (β or B)  
   • In total, 6 of the 15 are mentioned in some form.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The paper presents no systematic variation of any of those 15 parameters and provides no explicit numerical effect sizes. Thus, 0 of the 15 parameters are systematically varied in the sense required to report a quantitative effect on punishment or efficiency.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not give enough data to predict how systematically altering these parameters would quantitatively change the effect of punishment on efficiency. It only discusses volunteer vs. compulsory participation, peer vs. pool punishment, and the presence vs. absence of second‐order punishment. Consequently, one can make little to no detailed prediction from this text alone about how each of the 15 parameters (beyond those explicitly addressed under single fixed values) might alter the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Abstract: What makes humans moral beings? This question can be understood either as a proximate how question or as an ultimate why question. The how question is about the mental and social mechanisms that produce moral judgments and interactions, and has been investigated by psychologists and social scientists. The why question is about the fitness consequences that explain why humans have morality, and has been discussed by evolutionary biologists in the context of the evolution of cooperation. Our goal here is to contribute to a fruitful articulation of such proximate and ultimate explanations of human morality. We develop an approach to morality as an adaptation to an environment in which individuals were in competition to be chosen and recruited in mutually advantageous cooperative interactions. In this environment, the best strategy is to treat others with impartiality and to share the costs and benefits of cooperation equally. Those who offer less than others will be left out of cooperation; conversely, those who offer more will be exploited by their partners. In line with this mutualistic approach, the study of a range of economic games involving property rights, collective actions, mutual help and punishment shows that participants' distributions aim at sharing the costs and benefits of interactions in an impartial way. In particular, the distribution of resources is influenced by effort and talent, and the perception of each participant's rights on the resources to be distributed.

Below every parameter is treated in exactly the same way.

FOR EACH PARAMETER  
(1) Does the paper mention the parameter?  If so, give the value used.  
(2) Does the paper either manipulate that parameter or otherwise report what would happen if one *systematically varied* it?  If yes, report the numerical effect on the punishment‐treatment effect (difference between a treatment **with** punishment and the otherwise identical treatment **without** punishment).  When the only outcome reported is “contribution” rather than “efficiency,” that is stated explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
(1) Mentioned: 4 per group.  
(2) Never varied; no prediction.

2. Number of rounds  
(1) Mentioned: 10 fixed periods.  
(2) Never varied; no prediction.

3. “Chat enabled” (mode of open verbal communication)  
(1) Mentioned and manipulated.  Four communication modes appear:  
    • No communication (B, R)  
    • Face-to-face (FF, FFwR)  
    • Anonymous on-line chat room (CR, CRwR)  
    • Numerical cheap talk (NCT, NCTwR)  
(2) Systematic variation exists.  Average earnings (≈ efficiency, maximum = 16) allow us to calculate the punishment-treatment effect, i.e.  
   Δ Efficiency = (With Punishment – Without Punishment).  

              No-com      Face-to-face     Chat room      Numerical  
   Avg. pay-off w/o P      12.85              15.77          14.88          12.84  
   Avg. pay-off with P     12.52              15.74          14.93          12.48  
   Δ (pay-off)            –0.33             –0.03          +0.05          –0.36  

   Hence, enabling punishment:  
   • lowers efficiency when there is **no communication** (–0.33)  
   • has essentially **no net effect** when communication is **face-to-face** (–0.03)  
   • has an almost **zero / slightly positive** effect when communication is **chat-room** (+0.05)  
   • again **reduces** efficiency when communication is restricted to **numerical cheap talk** (–0.36).  

   These are the only numerical effect sizes the paper allows one to infer that involve systematic parameter variation.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
(1) Mentioned only implicitly. Subjects choose any integer 0–10.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction.

5. “Contribution default / reduction stage that starts from full contribution”  
(1) Not used; not mentioned.  
(2) No prediction.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
(1) Mentioned: 0.4 per dollar in the public account (group size = 4 → social return 1.6).  
(2) Kept constant; no prediction.

7. Punishment cost to punisher  
(1) Mentioned: \$0.25 paid to reduce another’s payoff by \$1.  
(2) Never varied.  The paper does note qualitatively that these costs absorb most efficiency gains, but no systematic manipulation, hence no predictive effect size.

8. Punishment magnitude (damage to target)  
(1) Fixed at \$1 per punishment point.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction.

9. Reward enabled?  
(1) Not available in any treatment.  
(2) No prediction.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
(1) Not applicable.  
(2) No prediction.

12. Horizon known?  
(1) Yes.  Subjects are told there are exactly 10 periods.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction.

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
(1) Yes.  After each period the full contribution vector and pay-offs are displayed.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction.

14. Punisher identity revealed?  
(1) Yes, within-period letter codes (anonymised) reveal which *position* punished, but not the real identity; codes change each round.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction.

15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
(1) Not applicable.  
(2) No prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
   • The paper reports both “average contribution” and “average earnings.”  
   • “Efficiency” (actual ÷ maximum earnings) is never computed explicitly but is trivially obtained from earnings because the maximum possible is \$16 per period if everyone contributes the full endowment and nobody is punished.  
   • Contribution and earnings differ conceptually: contribution ignores the cost of punishing and therefore is not the same as efficiency.

B. Parameters mentioned (value stated)  
   1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14  → 10 of the 15 parameters appear in the text.

C. Parameters systematically varied and analysed for their effect on the punishment-treatment effect  
   Only parameter 3 (mode / presence of open communication) is actually varied in a way that interacts with the presence or absence of punishment.  Thus, 1 of the 15 parameters receives such analysis.

D. Predictions one can make about the 15 parameters’ impact on the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency, **solely from this paper**  

   • Open verbal communication (chat room or face-to-face) almost eliminates the efficiency losses usually caused by costly punishment; in a chat room it may even yield a tiny gain.  
   • Numerical cheap talk does not help; the punishment option again lowers efficiency.  
   • When no communication is allowed, introducing punishment reduces efficiency because the cost of punishment outweighs the extra public-good returns.  
   • Because every other parameter is held constant, the paper provides no basis for predicting how changing them (group size, MPCR, punishment cost/magnitude, horizon, information revelation, rewards, etc.) would alter the punishment-treatment effect.  Any such prediction would go beyond the evidence presented.

Below each of the 15 public-goods‐game parameters is examined in exactly the way the instructions request.

Parameter-by-parameter inspection  
(1) Number of players  
‒ The paper’s empirical work (blue jays, tamarins) and all theoretical discussion concern two-player iterated Prisoner’s Dilemmas. A value of N = 2 is therefore mentioned implicitly throughout (e.g., Fig. 1 caption: “Pairs of jays …”; Fig. 2 caption: “… pairs of tamarins …”).  
‒ The paper never varies the number of players, and it never analyses how changing N would alter a punishment treatment effect on any dependent variable, let alone efficiency. No effect size is given.

(2) Number of rounds  
‒ Repeated interaction is said to be necessary for reciprocity (“repeated opportunities for cooperative interaction”; p. 2).  
‒ The exact number of rounds is not reported; it is not manipulated; and no prediction is offered about how more or fewer rounds would change a punishment effect. No numerical effect size.

(3) Chat enabled between players  
‒ Never mentioned.

(4) All-or-nothing contribution rule  
‒ Not discussed.

(5) Contribution default / endowment kept vs. given  
‒ Not discussed.

(6) Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
‒ The public-goods framework and the notion of MPCR do not appear in the article.

(7) Punishment cost (to the punisher)  
‒ “Punishment” is introduced conceptually (Box 1) as a way to “impose costs on defection,” but no actual cost parameter, currency, or experiment is given. The cost is neither quantified nor varied; no prediction about varying it is supplied.

(8) Punishment magnitude (loss to target per unit)  
‒ Same as (7): discussed abstractly, never parametrised or varied.

(9) Whether reward is enabled  
‒ Mutual cooperation in the PD yields the standard payoff R, but no peer-to-peer reward option is studied. No systematic variation, no prediction.

(10) Reward cost  
‒ Not discussed.

(11) Reward magnitude  
‒ Not discussed.

(12) Are the total number of rounds common knowledge?  
‒ Not mentioned.

(13) Are peer outcomes shown?  
‒ Not mentioned.

(14) Identifiability of the punisher  
‒ Not mentioned.

(15) Identifiability of the rewarder  
‒ Not mentioned.


Summary requested by the user  

A. Dependent variables used  
The article never reports “group efficiency” (total payoff / maximum possible payoff). The main dependent variables are:  
• Proportion of cooperative choices (blue jay key-pecking; Fig. 1).  
• Frequency of altruistic tool pulls (tamarins; Fig. 2).  
• Hyperbolic discounting rate k across species (Fig. 3).  
These differ from efficiency because they track individual behaviour (cooperation choices, discounting rate) rather than aggregate monetary payoffs relative to a social optimum.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
Four are at least mentioned in passing:  
1. Number of players (always two).  
2. Number of rounds (only the fact that there are repetitions).  
7 & 8. Punishment cost and punishment magnitude (only qualitatively, no numbers).  
Hence 4/15 parameters are named, but none is experimentally manipulated.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of systematic variation on a punishment treatment effect for any dependent variable?  
Zero. No parameter is systematically varied with respect to punishment, and no effect sizes are given.

D. Predictions one could make for the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency, based solely on this paper  
The paper provides almost no direct leverage. About all that can be inferred is the following very generic expectation: punishment can in principle sustain cooperation when psychological constraints (e.g., cheater detection, memory) are met; therefore adding punishment might improve efficiency, but only if the cognitive burden on players is manageable. Because none of the 15 concrete design parameters is analysed, no quantitative or even directional predictions specific to those parameters—or to their interactions—can be made from the paper alone.

In short, the article is a general review of reciprocal altruism and cognitive limits, not an experimental study of punishment in public-goods games, so it yields virtually no parameter-specific guidance for forecasting punishment effects on group efficiency.

Abstract: Garrett Hardin's tragedy of the commons is an analogy that shows how individuals driven by self-interest can end up destroying the resource upon which they all depend. The proposed solutions for humans rely on highly advanced skills such as negotiation, which raises the question of how non-human organisms manage to resolve similar tragedies. Below is a point‐by‐point walk‐through of whether and how each of the 15 parameters is mentioned in the paper, and whether the authors make (a) any note of that parameter’s value in their own experiment, and (b) any prediction about systematically varying it and how that would affect a “punishment treatment effect.” Throughout, keep in mind that the paper focuses on a two‐person (proposer–responder) game with four variations (Dictator, Stick, Carrot, Carrot‐Stick) and does not present any formal analysis of “efficiency” as the ratio of actual to maximum possible payoffs (the paper mainly examines offers, demands for punishment and reward, and final payoffs per round, but does not frame results in terms of that efficiency measure).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper uses a two‐player game (one proposer and one responder).  
   • Systematically varied? No. It is always two players; there is no discussion of varying the number of players to study how that affects punishment.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned? Yes. The experiment always has 10 rounds, and subjects are randomly rematched each round.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not discuss changing the number of rounds to see how that would influence punishment.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned? No. There is no mention of any direct communication (chat) in the paper.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not enable chat, nor does it discuss how enabling or disabling chat could affect punishment’s impact.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned? No. Instead of “all or nothing,” the proposer chooses any offer from 40¢ to 240¢ out of $2.40.  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no discussion of forcing only two choices (all or nothing) or how that might affect punishment.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Mentioned? No. There is no discussion of whether there is a default amount to contribute or withdraw.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Mentioned? No. Unlike a public‐goods setting, this is not a linear‐public‐goods or MPCR framework.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned? Yes. In the Stick and Carrot‐Stick treatments, the responder can pay 1¢ to reduce the proposer’s payoff by 5¢.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The authors never change the cost factor of “1¢ for 5¢ punishment” across different sessions, nor do they discuss how systematically altering that cost would affect punishment.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted per unit of punishment)
   • Mentioned? Yes. It is fixed at 5¢ deducted from the proposer for every 1¢ spent by the responder.  
   • Systematically varied? No. They do not change the 5:1 ratio in different sessions, nor do they predict how varying it would affect punishment.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned? Yes. The presence or absence of reward (the “Carrot”) is one of the core treatment variations. The four conditions are: (1) Dictator (neither punishment nor reward), (2) Stick (punishment only), (3) Carrot (reward only), (4) Carrot‐Stick (both punishment and reward).  
   • Systematically varied? Yes, across the four treatments they do vary whether reward is enabled or not. This is central to their analysis of how the availability of reward, punishment, or both influences offers and final payoffs. They do not present a formal “punishment treatment effect on efficiency,” but they do compare how different treatments (with or without reward) lead to different outcomes.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Mentioned? Yes. In the Carrot and Carrot‐Stick treatments, responders pay 1¢ to increase the proposer’s payoff by 5¢.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The authors do not vary the 1¢ cost in different sessions and do not make predictions about how a different reward‐cost schedule would affect punishment’s impact.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward)
   • Mentioned? Yes. As with punishment magnitude, the ratio is 5:1 (5¢ to the proposer for every 1¢ spent by the responder).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not adjust this ratio across sessions.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
   • Mentioned? Yes. Subjects know there are 10 rounds total.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not examine what would happen if the horizon were unknown.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much peers gained or lost each round)?
   • Mentioned? Indirectly. Because this is a two‐player game, the responder sees the proposer’s offer. But there is no broader “group outcome” or “peer outcome” beyond these two roles, and it is not systematically varied.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Mentioned? The paper states that identities remain anonymous. In a two‐player setting, each responder’s action is effectively known to the proposer, but there is no separate parameter variation about identifying punishers.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Mentioned? Same as with punishment, the roles are known—there’s only one possible responder—but no parameter is varied.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?

The paper does not measure or report “group efficiency” as the fraction of the maximum possible payoff that is actually realized. Instead, it focuses on:  
• The proposer’s “offer” (how much out of $2.40 is transferred).  
• The frequency and magnitude of punishments and rewards (responder’s costly actions).  
• Final payoffs (proposer and responder) round by round.  
• “Cooperation” in the sense of how generous the offer is.  

Thus, although the authors discuss payoffs, they do not frame their primary dependent variable as “efficiency.”  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

Mentioned (in the sense that the paper explicitly states a fixed value or treatment condition):  
• (1) Number of players (always 2).  
• (2) Number of rounds (fixed at 10).  
• (7) Punishment cost (1¢ for 5¢ punishment).  
• (8) Punishment magnitude (5¢ is deducted per 1¢ spent).  
• (9) Reward enabled or not (central to their four treatments).  
• (10) Reward cost (1¢ for 5¢ reward).  
• (11) Reward magnitude (5¢ is added per 1¢ spent).  
• (12) Number of rounds known to players (yes, it is 10).  

Not mentioned or not applicable in the paper:  
• (3) Chat enabled (no reference).  
• (4) Contribution “all or nothing” (no).  
• (5) Contribution default (not discussed).  
• (6) MPCR or multiplication factor (not a linear public goods game).  
• (13) Are peer outcomes shown beyond the two‐player setting (not relevant here).  
• (14) & (15) Whether the punisher/rewarder is identified (only anonymity is mentioned, not systematically varied).  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?

They only systematically vary whether punishment is available and whether reward is available (parameter 9). They do not systematically vary any other parameter. Strictly speaking, the paper does not model “punishment treatment effect on efficiency,” but it does discuss how having (vs. not having) punishment and/or reward affects offers, payoff distributions, and the frequency/severity of punishment and reward.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

Because the paper does not track efficiency (actual total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff), it provides little basis for specific quantitative predictions. It shows:  
• Having punishment available (or not) can substantially shift the proposer’s behavior away from low offers.  
• Having both punishment and reward (Carrot‐Stick) leads to even more generous offers, indicating that these two tools can complement each other in raising cooperation.  

Beyond that, there is no direct discussion of systematically tweaking, for example, punishment magnitude or number of players to see how it would influence efficiency. Hence, the safest conclusion is that the paper offers limited guidance about how these 15 parameters, aside from the presence or absence of reward or punishment, would affect efficiency.
reference_APA: Andreoni, J, Harbaugh, W & Vesterlund, L (2003). The carrot or the stick: Rewards, punishments, and cooperation. AMERICAN ECONOMIC REVIEW.

Authors: Perugini, M; Gallucci, M; Presaghi, F; Ercolani, AP
Author Full Names: Perugini, M; Gallucci, M; Presaghi, F; Ercolani, AP
Article Title: The personal norm of reciprocity

Abstract: Reciprocity is here considered as an internalized social norm, and a questionnaire to measure individual differences in the internalized norm of reciprocity is presented. Author Full Names: Helbing, Dirk; Szolnoki, Attila; Perc, Matjaz; Szabo, Gyoergy
Article Title: Punish, but not too hard: how costly punishment spreads in the spatial public goods game
Keywords Plus: COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; DYNAMICS; EMERGENCE
Abstract: We study the evolution of cooperation in spatial public goods games where, besides the classical strategies of cooperation (C) and defection (D), we consider punishing cooperators (PC) or punishing defectors (PD) as an additional strategy. Using a minimalist modeling approach, our goal is to separately clarify and identify the consequences of the two punishing strategies. Since punishment is costly, punishing strategies lose the evolutionary competition in case of well-mixed interactions. When spatial interactions are taken into account, however, the outcome can be strikingly different, and cooperation may spread. The underlying mechanism depends on the character of the punishment strategy. In the case of cooperating punishers, increasing the fine results in a rising cooperation level. In contrast, in the presence of the PD strategy, the phase diagram exhibits a reentrant transition as the fine is increased. Accordingly, the level of cooperation shows a non-monotonous dependence on the fine. Remarkably, punishing strategies can spread in both cases, but based on largely different mechanisms, which depend on the cooperativeness (or not) of punishers.

A. Dependent variables used

    • “Co-operation level” ρC + ρPC.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?

C. For how many parameters is their *systematic* variation linked to a punishment-treatment effect?  
    Exactly 3: synergy factor r (6), punishment cost c (7), punishment fine f (8).

D. If we try to predict how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the **punishment treatment effect on efficiency** using only this paper:  
    • Because efficiency was never measured, predictions must be inferred indirectly: higher co-operation probably correlates with higher efficiency, but this is not demonstrated.
