Authors: Rockenbach, B; Milinski, M
Author Full Names: Rockenbach, Bettina; Milinski, Manfred
Article Title: The efficient interaction of indirect reciprocity and costly punishment
Keywords Plus: COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; REPUTATION; CUES
Abstract: Human cooperation in social dilemmas challenges researchers from various disciplines. Here we combine advances in experimental economics and evolutionary biology that separately have shown that costly punishment and reputation formation, respectively, induce cooperation in social dilemmas. The mechanisms of punishment and reputation, however, substantially differ in their means for 'disciplining' non-cooperators. Direct punishment incurs salient costs for both the punisher and the punished, whereas reputation mechanisms discipline by withholding action, immediately saving costs for the 'punisher'. Consequently, costly punishment may become extinct in environments in which effective reputation building - for example, through indirect reciprocity - provides a cheaper and powerful way to sustain cooperation. Unexpectedly, as we show here, punishment is maintained when a combination with reputation building is available, however, at a low level. Costly punishment acts are markedly reduced although not simply substituted by appreciating reputation. Indeed, the remaining punishment acts are concentrated on free-riders, who are most severely punished in the combination. When given a choice, subjects even prefer a combination of reputation building with costly punishment. The interaction between punishment and reputation building boosts cooperative efficiency. Because punishment and reputation building are omnipresent interacting forces in human societies, costly punishing should appear less destructive without losing its deterring force.

Where the paper does not address a parameter (or does not systematically vary it), that is stated explicitly. Numeric effect sizes are provided only when the paper itself presents measurable differences that one can directly infer. Please note that the term “punishment treatment effect” here is interpreted as how introducing costly punishment (alone or in combination with indirect reciprocity) changes outcomes such as cooperation, payoffs, or efficiency.

1) Number of players
• Discussion in paper: The design uses groups of eight subjects (p. 2, “Groups of eight subjects each played 20 periods…”).  
• Systematic variation or predicted effect: The paper does not systematically vary the group size (it is fixed at 8 throughout) and does not make predictions about how changing the number of players would affect punishment or efficiency.

2) Number of rounds
• Discussion in paper: All sessions last for 20 periods (p. 2, “Groups of eight subjects each played 20 periods…”).  
• Systematic variation or predicted effect: The paper does not vary the number of rounds; there is no discussion of how changing the length of the game might affect punishment treatment or efficiency.

3) Is chat enabled between players?
• Discussion in paper: There is no mention or use of verbal or text chat. All communication is limited to the game’s automated information displays.  
• Systematic variation or predicted effect: Not discussed.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
• Discussion in paper: Yes. Each subject can contribute either 0 or 10 money units (MUs) to the public good (p. 2, “each subject is endowed with 10 MUs and may contribute either 0 or 10 MUs”).  
• Systematic variation or predicted effect: The paper does not vary the contribution rules (they remain all or nothing throughout) and does not predict how changing this rule would affect the punishment treatment effect.

5) Is the contribution default (if true, do players decide how much of their endowment to move back into their hand)?
• Discussion in paper: Not described in those terms. Participants simply choose whether to keep or contribute 0 vs. 10 MUs from their endowment.  
• Systematic variation or predicted effect: Not discussed.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters
• Discussion in paper: The total contributions are multiplied by 1.6 and divided evenly among group members (p. 2, “The contributions are multiplied by 1.6…”).  
• Systematic variation or predicted effect: The paper does not vary this multiplier or discuss how changing it might influence the punishment treatment effect.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
• Discussion in paper: The cost to the punisher is 1 MU; each point of punishment spent reduces the punished subject’s income by 3 MUs (p. 2, “Punishing costs the punisher 1 MU and the punished subject 3 MUs.”).  
• Systematic variation or predicted effect: The paper does not vary these costs; there is no prediction about how changing the cost of punishment would affect the treatment effect.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed)
• Discussion in paper: The magnitude is 3 MUs deducted from the punished player per 1 MU spent by the punisher (p. 2).  
• Systematic variation or predicted effect: No systematic variation or discussion about changing the punishment ratio.

9) Whether a reward is enabled
• Discussion in paper: Yes—in the “PUN&IR” treatment, there is an indirect reciprocity (IR) stage where players can transfer 3 MUs (tripled to 9 MUs for the receiver). The paper refers to “helping” or “giving” in the IR stage, which acts as a reward mechanism for good contributors. This contrasts with the “PUN” treatment that has no IR stage.  
• Systematic variation or predicted effect: The only systematic manipulation of “reward” is whether the indirect reciprocity stage is present (PUN&IR) or absent (PUN). The authors do report that when punishment co‐occurs with indirect reciprocity (PUN&IR), overall efficiency is higher than with punishment alone (PUN). From Figure 4 and corresponding text (pp. 3–4), one can see that:  
  – In PUN&IR, subjects contributing 10 MUs to the public good often reach payoffs near the social optimum (27 MUs).  
  – In PUN alone, the payoff for those contributing 10 MUs was lower (on average about 24 MUs).  
  – Thus, enabling reward (indirect reciprocity) improves the net payoff of cooperators by roughly 3 MUs compared to punishment alone, while also lowering the overall use of costly punishment.  
  – The paper does not present a formal regression or marginal effect for “reward presence” but does show that PUN&IR yields higher group efficiency and less frequent—but more targeted—punishment.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
• Discussion in paper: The fixed cost is the 3 MUs that the sender forgoes if they decide to give help in the indirect reciprocity game (which then triples to 9 MUs for the receiver).  
• Systematic variation or predicted effect: The paper does not vary or systematically analyze changes in the reward‐cost parameter.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)
• Discussion in paper: If someone sends 3 MUs, the receiver gets 9 MUs (p. 2).  
• Systematic variation or predicted effect: The paper does not vary this ratio (or discuss manipulating it).

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
• Discussion in paper: Subjects know from instructions that they will play 20 periods (p. 2).  
• Systematic variation or predicted effect: No manipulation or prediction regarding unknown vs. known end rounds.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?
• Discussion in paper: Each player sees “anonymous summary information” about both groups at the end of each period, and in the IR stage, the sender sees the receiver’s contribution history. However, the paper does not study the effect of turning this information off or on.  
• Systematic variation or predicted effect: The paper does not vary or predict outcomes of changing the degree of outcome visibility.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
• Discussion in paper: Punishment is anonymous; subjects only see a summary of how many total points they received, not the source.  
• Systematic variation or predicted effect: Not discussed.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
• Discussion in paper: Reward (help in the IR stage) is also anonymous in terms of the giver’s identity.  
• Systematic variation or predicted effect: Not discussed.

Abstract: A growing number of field and experimental studies focus on the institutional arrangements by which individuals are able to solve collective action problems. Below is a parameter-by-parameter rundown based solely on the Sefton–Shupp–Walker paper you provided. For each of the 15 parameters, I note (1) whether the paper discusses that parameter (and, if so, what values or setup it uses), and (2) whether the paper makes predictions about the effect of systematically varying that parameter on the “punishment treatment effect” (in particular on efficiency, or on other outcomes if efficiency was not analyzed). “Punishment treatment effect” here refers to the effect of introducing punishment opportunities into a voluntary contributions mechanism.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Discussed?  
     – The paper states that each group has exactly four subjects.  
     – There is no variation in group size: all experimental treatments use four-person groups.
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – None. The paper does not vary the number of players or discuss how changing group size would affect punishment’s impact on efficiency.

2. Number of rounds
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes. Each session has 10 rounds in “Sequence I,” followed by 10 rounds in “Sequence II” (20 rounds total), all of which is common knowledge from the start.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – None. Although the authors discuss how behavior changes within these 20 rounds (e.g., “end of experiment decay”), the paper does not systematically vary the number of rounds across treatments or predict how changing the total number of rounds would alter punishment’s effect.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The study does not allow or mention any face-to-face or in-game free-form communication (“chat”) among participants, apart from seeing each other’s contribution decisions displayed anonymously.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – None. The paper does not address or manipulate communication.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussed?  
     – No. Subjects can allocate any number of tokens (0 through 6) to the public good in each round.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – None. The paper does not examine an all-or-nothing version of contributions.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Discussed?  
     – No. Subjects freely choose 0–6 tokens to put in the group account; there is no discussion of a forced “default” contribution or a forced reversal of the endowment.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – None.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes (implicitly). Each token in the group account yields 5 cents for each group member (20 cents total), whereas a token put in one’s private account yields 10 cents only to oneself. This is effectively an MPCR of 0.5.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – None. The MPCR is fixed at 0.5 throughout, and the paper does not consider or predict what would happen if MPCR changed.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes. In the “sanction” stage, spending 1 token to punish another player forfeits that token’s private value (10 cents) for the punisher. That is the cost of imposing punishment.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – None. The paper applies a 1:1 cost–impact ratio (the punisher sacrifices 10 cents, and the target loses 10 cents) but does not systematically vary it in the design or report predictions about higher/lower punisher costs.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player per punishment)
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes. Each punishment token reduces the other person’s earnings by 10 cents.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – None. Although the authors compare their 1:1 ratio to other studies with higher or nonlinear punishment costs, they do not vary this ratio in their own experiment.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes, extensively. The paper has a “Reward” treatment (where participants can spend tokens to reward others) and a “Sanction & Reward” treatment (where both punishment and reward are enabled).  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – Yes, but focused on comparing (a) baseline (no punishment, no reward), (b) sanction alone, (c) reward alone, and (d) sanction & reward together.  
     – The paper does discuss (1) how the sanction-only treatment affects efficiency over time, and (2) how adding reward-only differs and ultimately fails to sustain high allocation levels on its own, and (3) how combining reward and sanction can lead to higher average contributions and higher eventual earnings.  
     – They do not provide a single numerical “effect size” for how turning reward “on” or “off” changes the punishment effect specifically on efficiency. Instead, they note that the sanction & reward condition yields the highest contributions and eventually the highest earnings, suggesting a synergistic effect. No single numeric effect size is given in the text or tables for that synergy.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes. In the experiments with rewards, allocating a token to reward someone else costs the reward-giver that token’s private 10 cents. This is analogous to the punishment cost.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – None. They do not vary the cost of rewarding across treatments or predict how changes in that cost would influence punishment’s impact.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward)
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes. One reward token bestows +10 cents on the target.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – None. As with punishment magnitude, the paper uses a fixed ratio and does not systematically vary it or predict different costs/magnitudes.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes. Subjects know up front there are 20 total rounds (10 in Sequence I and 10 in Sequence II).  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – None. The paper does not vary the transparency or knowledge of ending conditions.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost)?
   • Discussed?  
     – Partly. The experiment does show each subject what each group member contributed (in anonymous random order), the total group contributions, and how many punishment/reward tokens they themselves received.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – None. The paper does not manipulate whether peer outcomes are hidden or shown.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the punisher is?
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes. The paper states that punished players see only the total number of punishment tokens received but cannot identify which specific member(s) punished them.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – None. This aspect is held constant (always anonymous).

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is?
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes, in parallel to punishment, the recipient sees only the total reward tokens received but not who gave them.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – None. Also held constant.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY OF FINDINGS AND IMPLICATIONS:

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how do they differ?
   • Yes. The authors explicitly track an “efficiency” measure (actual group earnings as a fraction of the maximum possible if everyone fully contributed, net of any cost of punishments or rewards).  
   • They also analyze group allocations (i.e., contributions to the public good), use of sanctions/rewards, and individual-level behaviors. “Efficiency” is not the same as “contributions”: for instance, punishing can raise contributions but shrink efficiency if punishments cost more than the contributions they induce.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?
   • The paper explicitly states the number of players (1), number of rounds (2), that there is no chat (3), that contributions can be any integer from 0–6 (hence not all-or-nothing) (4), that there is no forced contribution default (5), a fixed MPCR of 0.5 (6), the punishment cost (7) and magnitude (8), the presence or absence of reward (9), the reward cost (10) and magnitude (11), and that the number of rounds is finite and known (12).  
   • It also clarifies what each subject sees for peer outcomes (13) and that no one learns exactly who punished (14) or rewarded them (15).  
   • In total, all 15 parameters appear in the sense that the authors either specify a fixed choice for them or note that certain features are absent. However, for most parameters, there is no design variation.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each is systematically varied?
   • Only parameter #9 (whether or not rewards are enabled) is truly varied together with punishment in a factorial way (Baseline vs. Sanction vs. Reward vs. Sanction&Reward).  
   • The authors do observe that having both sanction and reward together can lead to higher sustained contributions and higher earnings, meaning a synergistic effect on “punishment’s impact” (i.e., the combined presence of reward modifies punishment’s ultimate effect on contributions and payoffs).  
   • No other parameter is systematically manipulated (e.g., group size, round lengths, punishment magnitude, cost of punishing) within this experiment.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?
   • The only robust evidence in this paper about systematically varying a parameter is that combining punishment with the availability of rewards (parameter #9) tends to produce the highest contributions and—in the later rounds—higher overall payoffs, indicating a net efficiency gain once the threat of punishment is established and large-scale use of punishment is no longer needed.  
   • For all other parameters (numbers of players, rounds, costs/magnitudes of punishment and reward, and so on), the paper does not provide direct predictions or effect sizes tied specifically to how changing those parameters would alter punishment’s effect on efficiency. They keep those design features fixed. Accordingly, one cannot reliably predict from this paper alone whether, for example, making punishment cheaper or more expensive, or changing the group size, would strengthen or weaken the efficiency impact of punishment.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Authors: Gächter, S; Herrmann, B
Author Full Names: Gaechter, Simon; Herrmann, Benedikt
Article Title: Reciprocity, culture and human cooperation: previous insights and a new cross-cultural experiment
Source Title: PHILOSOPHICAL TRANSACTIONS OF THE ROYAL SOCIETY B-BIOLOGICAL SCIENCES
Author Keywords: human cooperation; strong reciprocity; public goods experiments; culture; antisocial punishment
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS EXPERIMENTS; PUNISHING FREE-RIDERS; GROUP-SIZE; VOLUNTARY CONTRIBUTIONS; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; DECISION-MAKING; CONDITIONAL COOPERATION; STRATEGIC BEHAVIOR; COLLECTIVE ACTION; SOCIAL DILEMMAS
Abstract: Understanding the proximate and ultimate sources of human cooperation is a fundamental issue in all behavioural sciences. In this paper, we review the experimental evidence on how people solve cooperation problems. Existing studies show without doubt that direct and indirect reciprocity are important determinants of successful cooperation. We also discuss the insights from a large literature on the role of peer punishment in sustaining cooperation. The experiments demonstrate that many people are 'strong reciprocators' who are willing to cooperate and punish others even if there are no gains from future cooperation or any other reputational gains. We document this in new one-shot experiments, which we conducted in four cities in Russia and Switzerland. Our cross-cultural approach allows us furthermore to investigate how the cultural background influences strong reciprocity. Our results show that culture has a strong influence on positive and in especially strong negative reciprocity. In particular, we find large cross-cultural differences in 'antisocial punishment' of pro-social cooperators. Further cross-cultural research and experiments involving different socio-demographic groups document that the antisocial punishment is much more widespread than previously assumed. Understanding antisocial punishment is an important task for future research because antisocial punishment is a strong inhibitor of cooperation.

Below each of the 15 parameters I report exactly what can be learned from the paper.

For every parameter I state  
(1) whether the paper itself (including the studies it summarizes) actually describes the value that was implemented in the authors’ own experiments, and  
(2) whether the paper says anything about what would happen to the **punishment treatment effect on efficiency** (i.e. the difference in total‐group payoff between a condition with punishment and the otherwise identical condition without punishment) if that parameter were **systematically varied**.  Whenever the paper contains a quantitative estimate I reproduce it; if no number is given I report only the direction; if nothing at all is said I state this explicitly.

-------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
(1) Own experiment: fixed at 3. In the literature review many studies with 4 (e.g. Herrmann et al. 2008) or other sizes are mentioned.  
(2) The paper reports that “larger groups do not cooperate significantly less than smaller groups”, but this result refers to contribution levels, not to the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.  No claim or number is given for how changing group size would alter efficiency with punishment.

2. Number of rounds (length of the game)  
(1) Own experiment: strict one-shot (1 round).  In §3 the authors review 10-round and 50-round designs.  
(2) The only explicit statement about the punishment treatment effect on efficiency when the horizon is varied is in §3-(viii):  
• In 10-period games punishment “was detrimental” – average pay-offs were lower than in the no-punishment control.  
• In otherwise identical 50-period games “the opposite conclusion holds — cooperation is high and punishment costs negligible”, therefore pay-offs are higher than without punishment.  
No numerical efficiencies are reported, only the sign change.

3. Possibility of chat / free communication  
(1) Own experiment: no chat.  The review notes that communication greatly facilitates cooperation.  
(2) No statement is made about how allowing chat would change the punishment treatment effect on efficiency; the paper only says chat raises contributions when no punishment is available.

4. Contribution “all-or-nothing” versus continuous choice  
(1) Own experiment: continuous (0-20 tokens).  
(2) Not mentioned at all as a factor shaping punishment or efficiency.

5. Contribution-default / “take” frame  
Not mentioned.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR, multiplication factor)  
(1) Own experiment: MPCR = 0.5.  
(2) The review states that higher MPCR produces higher contributions, but gives no prediction about the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
(1) Own experiment: 1 token per punishment point.  
(2) §3-(iv) says punishment is “less likely used the more costly it is”, and implies effectiveness therefore falls, but no figures or efficiency comparison with the no-punishment baseline are provided.

8. Punishment magnitude for the target  
(1) Own experiment: each point reduces the target’s payoff by k ≥ 1; the exact k used by the authors is not given.  
(2) §3-(iv) says “severity of punishment … matters for the effectiveness of punishment to stabilise (or increase) cooperation” but does not translate this into an efficiency comparison.

9. Whether reward is enabled  
(1) Own experiment: no reward stage.  
(2) §3-(ix) reviews Sefton et al. (2007) and states that punishment raises contributions more than rewards do.  The discussion is about contributions, not efficiency; no treatment-effect numbers are reported.

10. Cost of a reward point  
Not discussed.

11. Magnitude of a reward point  
Not discussed.

12. Whether the horizon is common knowledge  
(1) Own experiment: trivially yes (one-shot).  
(2) Not analysed separately from parameter 2.

13. Whether peer outcomes are shown  
(1) Own experiment: yes – subjects see each other’s contributions before punishing.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction given.

14. Whether the punished player sees who punished them  
(1) Own experiment: no – punisher anonymity.  
(2) The paper never varies this dimension and gives no prediction.

15. Whether the rewarded player sees who rewarded them  
Not applicable / not discussed.

-------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY  

A. Dependent variables used in the paper  
• Contribution / cooperation rate  
• Punishment assigned / received  
• Individual or group earnings / pay-offs  
• The word “efficiency” is used descriptively (e.g. “punishment is an inefficient tool”) but no formal efficiency ratio is reported.  Therefore efficiency is discussed, but the actual dependent variables analysed are almost always contribution levels or earnings.

B. Parameters mentioned at all (value or description)  
Eight of the fifteen: 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 13, 14.

C. Parameters for which the paper discusses the **effect of systematically varying the parameter** on the punishment treatment effect (for any outcome variable)  
Only three:  
• 2 (Number of rounds) – sign of efficiency effect reverses between 10 and 50 rounds.  
• 7 (Punishment cost) – higher cost ⇒ less punishment and lower effectiveness (no numbers).  
• 8 (Punishment magnitude) – greater severity ⇒ greater effectiveness (no numbers).  
Hence 3/15 parameters receive any such discussion, and only parameter 2 is linked explicitly to efficiency.

D. What predictions can one make – based solely on this paper – about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  

• Long time horizon (many rounds) is the single condition under which the paper predicts that punishment will raise efficiency; with few rounds it is predicted to lower efficiency.  
• Higher punishment cost should weaken, and higher punishment magnitude should strengthen, any efficiency gains, but no direction for efficiency is given explicitly.  
• For all other parameters the paper is either silent or only discusses contributions; therefore no informed prediction about efficiency can be made from the paper’s contents alone.

Abstract: The puzzle of the emergence of cooperation between unrelated individuals is shared across diverse fields of behavioural sciences and economics. In this article we combine the public goods game originating in economics with evolutionary approaches traditionally used in biology. Instead of pairwise encounters, we consider the more complex case of groups of three interacting individuals. We show that territoriality is capable of promoting cooperative behaviour, as in the case of the Prisoner's Dilemma. Moreover, by adding punishment opportunities, the readiness to cooperate is greatly enhanced and asocial strategies can be largely suppressed. Finally, as soon as players carry a reputation for being willing or unwilling to punish, highly cooperative and fair outcomes are achieved. This group-beneficial result is obtained, intriguingly, by making individuals more likely to exploit their co-players if they can get away with it. Thus, less-cooperative individuals make more-cooperative societies.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter summary of what this particular paper (Brandt et al. “Punishment and reputation in spatial public goods games”) does or does not say, followed by the requested four‐part summary (A–D). In keeping with your instructions, I do not rely on anything external to the paper itself, and I note whether the paper discusses each parameter and whether it systematically varies that parameter and reports a punishment “treatment effect” (in this paper, primarily the effect on coexistence, thresholds for cooperation, and strategy frequencies) for any dependent variable. The paper does not measure “efficiency” per se (i.e., actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff); instead, it focuses on the fraction of cooperators, stability of cooperation, and thresholds for cooperative outcomes.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   – Discussed? Yes. The paper explicitly sets the number of players in each public‐goods interaction to 3 (n=3) on a hexagonal lattice.  
   – Systematically varied? No. They do not study what happens if n changes to 4, 5, etc. No “treatment effect” analysis for varying n is provided.

2. Number of rounds
   – Discussed? Not as a treatment. The paper uses a simulation with repeated “generations” (e.g., 3000 updates to relax, then 2000 measurements).  
   – Systematically varied? No. They do not vary the number of rounds to observe effects on punishment.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   – Discussed? No. The paper does not mention communication or chat.  
   – Systematically varied? No mention at all.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   – Discussed? Yes. The paper restricts choices to a binary “cooperate” (pay cost c) or “defect” (pay nothing).  
   – Systematically varied? No. They do not examine partial‐contribution options or compare them to all‐or‐nothing.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much to move back into their hand)?
   – Discussed? No. The paper only uses binary choices.  
   – Systematically varied? No mention at all.

6. Marginal per capita return (multiplication factor r)
   – Discussed? Yes, extensively. r is varied across a range (e.g., from below ≈1.35 up to ≈2.5 or more) to see when cooperation persists.  
   – Systematically varied? Yes. They examine how different values of r change thresholds for cooperative outcomes. Without punishment, cooperation requires r > 2.07; with punishment, the critical threshold drops to about 1.35, and with punishment plus reputation, further down to about 1.25.  
   – Effect size? The key finding is how the “threshold r₍c₎” for sustaining cooperation drops when punishment or punishment+reputation is introduced (e.g., from 2.07 down to ∼1.35 or 1.25). Although they do not frame this as a change in “efficiency,” it is the main systematic variation that they present.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   – Discussed? Somewhat. Denoted by γ (gamma). In nearly all illustrations they set γ=1.  
   – Systematically varied? No. They do not provide a table or figure showing how changing γ alone affects outcomes. Hence no quantitative “treatment effect” of varying γ is provided.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from a punished player)
   – Discussed? Yes. Denoted by β (beta). Often set to β=1.5.  
   – Systematically varied? Partially. The paper remarks that “when increasing the fines β,” the threshold r₍c₎ for establishing cooperation can drop below 1, forcing a (costly) cooperative outcome even when r < 1. They do not, however, provide numerical data for various β; they only describe the direction of the effect qualitatively.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   – Discussed? No. The paper considers only punishments (costly sanctions).  
   – Systematically varied? No mention at all.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit
    – Discussed? No.  
    – Systematically varied? No.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each reward)
    – Discussed? No.  
    – Systematically varied? No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
    – Discussed? No. The model is purely generational/spatial with no mention of round knowledge.  
    – Systematically varied? No mention at all.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained or lost)?
    – Discussed? No. The paper does not detail real‐time outcome visibility.  
    – Systematically varied? No mention at all.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    – Discussed? No.  
    – Systematically varied? No mention at all.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    – Discussed? No, and rewards are not part of the study.  
    – Systematically varied? No mention at all.
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Summary Responses (A–D):

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper does not explicitly measure or report “efficiency” as (total payoff) / (maximum possible payoff).  
   • The paper instead measures (i) strategic compositions of the population (e.g., fraction of cooperators and punishers vs. defectors), (ii) thresholds for coexistence, and (iii) bistability outcomes (full defection vs. mostly cooperative). These are different from efficiency measures.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned:  
     1 (group size = 3), 4 (binary “all or nothing” contributions), 6 (multiplication factor r), 7 (punishment cost γ), and 8 (punishment fine β).  
   • Not mentioned:  
     2, 3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15.  
   • Thus, 5 of the 15 are mentioned at all.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss systematic variation of that parameter and its effect on the punishment treatment (for any dependent variable)?  
   • Systematically varied and linked to punishment:  
       – (6) r (the multiplication factor): They show how the threshold r₍c₎ for establishing cooperation drops from ≈2.07 down to ≈1.35 when punishment is introduced, and to ≈1.25 when punishment is combined with reputation.  
       – (8) β (the punishment fine): They note that increasing β can push the cooperation threshold still lower (potentially below 1), although they do not provide a specific numeric series.  
   • No other parameters are systematically varied.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper, what would they be?  
   • Because the paper does not directly analyze total‐payoff efficiency, there is little basis for precise predictions of “group efficiency.” We only see how punishment interacts with r and β to lower the threshold for cooperation.  
   • From the text, one can infer that larger r, and/or larger β, strengthens cooperation and thus would presumably raise final payoffs—unless the cost of punishment (γ) is so high or r < 1, in which case the group might be forced into cooperation that is actually net‐costly.  
   • The paper does not discuss (and provides no evidence about) the other parameters, so we cannot make meaningful predictions for them.

Authors: Barclay, P

Article Title: Trustworthiness and competitive altruism can also solve the tragedy of the commons
Author Keywords: evolution; competitive altruism; game theory; trust; public goods
Keywords Plus: INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; PUNISHMENT; HUMANS
Abstract: The benefits of a good reputation can help explain why some individuals are willing to be altruistic in situations where they will not receive direct benefits. Recent experiments on indirect reciprocity have shown that when people stand to benefit from having a good reputation, they are more altruistic towards groups and charities. However, it is unknown whether indirect reciprocity is the only thing that can cause such an effect. Individuals may be altruistic because it will make them more trustworthy. In this study, I show that participants in a cooperative group game contribute more to their group when they expect to play a dyadic trust game afterwards, and that participants do tend to trust altruistic individuals more than nonaltruistic individuals. I also included a condition where participants had to choose only one person to trust (instead of being able to trust all players) in the dyadic trust game that followed the cooperative group game, and contributions towards the group were maintained best in this condition. This provides some evidence that competition for scarce reputational benefits can help maintain cooperative behaviour because of competitive altruism. (C) 2004 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

Below I go through the 15 requested design parameters one-by-one.  
For each parameter I state  

(1) Whether the paper even tells us the value that was used;  
(2) Whether the paper says anything—data, analysis, conjecture, figure or table—about how *changing* that parameter would alter the **punishment treatment effect** (i.e. the difference between the with-punishment and the without-punishment conditions).  
Whenever a numerical value can be read directly from the text, figures or tables I write it in brackets.  If no statement exists, I say so explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned: yes – fixed at 4 players per group.  
   (2) No discussion or prediction about varying the group size.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Mentioned: yes – two blocks of 10 periods each (10 without, then 10 with punishment).  
   (2) No claim about what would happen if the number of rounds were different.

3. Chat enabled?  
   (1) Reported: chat was not allowed; all interaction was anonymous and via computer.  
   (2) No discussion of enabling/disabling chat.

4. Contribution “all-or-nothing”?  
   (1) Reported: No – subjects chose any integer 0–20 tokens.  
   (2) No statement on switching to an all-or-nothing format.

5. Contribution default / take-back decision?  
   (1) Not part of the design; subjects made a standard endowment-to-public-good transfer.  
   (2) Not discussed.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   (1) Fixed MPCR = 0.4 (group multiplier 1.6).  
   (2) No analysis of higher or lower MPCRs.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   (1) Fixed at 1 token per punishment point.  
   (2) No statements on different punishment costs.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss to target per point)  
   (1) Fixed at 3 tokens.  
   (2) No statements on varying the magnitude.

9. Reward enabled?  
   (1) No – only costly punishment existed.  
   (2) No discussion of adding rewards.

10. Reward cost  
    Not applicable.

11. Reward magnitude  
    Not applicable.

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
    (1) Yes – subjects were told upfront that each stage lasts 10 periods.  
    (2) No comment on making the horizon unknown.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    (1) Yes – after each contribution stage subjects saw every member’s contribution and first-part income.  
    (2) No discussion of hiding or altering that information.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
    (1) No – subjects learned only “whether you have been assigned negative points”, not who did it; identities remained anonymous.  
    (2) No discussion of making punishment non-anonymous.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
    Not applicable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables actually used  
   • Mean contribution  
   • Mean punishment assigned  
   • “Punishment efficiency” or “social welfare” proxy: marginal effect of punishment (Δcontribution / average punishment).  

   The paper never reports **group efficiency** in the strict sense of (total payoff)/(maximum possible payoff). Contribution and punishment efficiency are therefore the main outcome measures, not efficiency as defined in the prompt.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   10 of them (1,2,3,4,6,7,8,12,13,14) are explicitly stated as fixed features of the design.  
   The remaining five parameters (5,9,10,11,15) are either inapplicable or not mentioned.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the *effect of systematically varying* that parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
   Zero.  All 15 parameters are held constant across treatments; the only factor that varies is ethnic composition.  No tables, figures or text examine what would happen if any of the 15 parameters were altered.

D. Implications for predicting punishment-treatment effects on true efficiency, given only this paper  
   • Because every one of the 15 parameters is fixed, the paper provides almost no direct leverage for forecasting how changing them would influence efficiency.  
   • The only qualitative hint is that with the specific setting used (4 players, 10 known rounds, MPCR 0.4, cost = 1, fine = 3, full feedback, anonymous punishment, no rewards), introducing punishment raised contributions everywhere but was *efficient* (marginal effect > 1) only when ethnic diversity was absent for Mongolians or present for both groups.  
   • One might cautiously infer that in any setting that keeps all these parameters unchanged, altering *ethnic composition* (a factor outside the 15-parameter list) matters more than tweaking the fixed design parameters.  
   • Beyond that, the paper provides no quantitative basis for predicting how efficiency would respond to, say, a higher fine, a lower cost, hidden identities, unknown horizon, or enabling rewards—the authors simply did not study those manipulations.

Hence, based solely on the evidence supplied, essentially no predictions about the 15 parameters and their interactions can be made.

Abstract: The efficiency of institutionalized punishment is studied by evaluating the stationary states in the spatial public goods game comprising unconditional defectors, cooperators, and cooperating pool punishers as the three competing strategies. Fines and costs of pool punishment are considered as the two main parameters determining the stationary distributions of strategies on the square lattice. Each player collects a payoff from five five-person public goods games, and the evolution of strategies is subsequently governed by imitation based on pairwise comparisons at a low level of noise. The impact of pool punishment on the evolution of cooperation in structured populations is significantly different from that reported previously for peer punishment. Representative phase diagrams reveal remarkably rich behavior, depending also on the value of the synergy factor that characterizes the efficiency of investments payed into the common pool. Besides traditional single- and two-strategy stationary states, a rock-paper-scissors type of cyclic dominance can emerge in strikingly different ways.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter accounting of what (if anything) the paper says about each of the 15 listed parameters and whether the paper makes predictions about the effect of systematically varying that parameter on the “punishment treatment effect.” Throughout, I use the paper’s notation: r (the “synergy factor”) is the multiplier of contributions to the public good, γ (gamma) is the cost of being a pool punisher, and β (beta) is the fine (punishment) imposed on defectors when at least one punisher is present in the group.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Discussed? No. The paper studies a large population arranged on a square lattice, but it does not compare or systematically vary finite “number of players”; it focuses on large system sizes.  
   • Predictions about varying it? No. The paper does not analyze how changing the number of players would affect any treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds
   • Discussed? No. The paper investigates a spatially extended model that is iterated until a stationary state, but does not treat “number of rounds” as a parameter for systematic variation.  
   • Predictions about varying it? No. There is no mention of a finite or known horizon, nor is there any systematic analysis of round-by-round effects.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussed? No.  
   • Predictions about varying it? No mention in the paper.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussed? No. Players contribute 1 if they are cooperators (or pool punishers), 0 if defectors. However, the paper never frames this as a parameter to vary; the game is simply defined that way with no alternative.  
   • Predictions about varying it? Not discussed.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Discussed? No.  
   • Predictions about varying it? Not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor
   • Discussed? Yes. The paper denotes this factor by r, which multiplies the contributions in each group.  
   • Predictions about varying it? Yes, and it is varied systematically (the paper presents analyses for r = 2.0, r = 3.5, and r = 3.8 in detail). The authors track how these different r values shift phase boundaries (e.g., about which strategies survive). However, they do not translate these findings into an explicit measure of group efficiency; rather, they examine the stationary frequencies of defectors, cooperators, and punishers. No explicit numerical “effect sizes” on payoff-based efficiency measures are given. Everything is reported in terms of strategy-phase diagrams and fractions of strategies.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussed? Partially. In the paper’s model of pool punishment, each punisher pays a lump-sum cost γ, irrespective of how many defectors are punished. That cost is not “per unit” in the sense of a typical peer-punishment game but rather a fixed cost.  
   • Predictions about varying it? Yes. The paper systematically varies γ (the punisher’s cost) and shows how changing γ, together with β (the punishment fine), alters which strategies dominate or coexist in the stationary state. These results appear in “full fine-cost phase diagrams” (e.g., Figs. 5, 10, and 12). Again, the paper focuses on which strategies survive and does not provide explicit payoff efficiency measures or exact numerical “effect sizes.” Instead, it shows how increasing γ makes punitive cooperation less likely to persist.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   • Discussed? Yes. In the paper, β (beta) is the punishment fine that each defector pays whenever there is at least one punisher.  
   • Predictions about varying it? Yes. β is systematically varied alongside γ in phase diagrams. The authors show transitions among strategy phases as β increases or decreases. While they discuss how large or small fines change the stationary mix of defectors, cooperators, and punishers, they do not report specific payoff-based effect sizes for “group efficiency.”

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussed? No. The study is strictly about (costly) pool punishment and does not include rewarding mechanisms.  
   • Predictions about varying it? No mention in the paper.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Discussed? No.  
    • Predictions about varying it? Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)
    • Discussed? No.  
    • Predictions about varying it? Not discussed.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Discussed? No. The focus is on stationary patterns in an ongoing evolutionary process.  
    • Predictions about varying it? No mention.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?
    • Discussed? No. The paper does not address the kind of information display or knowledge of other players’ payoffs.  
    • Predictions about varying it? Not discussed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Discussed? No.  
    • Predictions about varying it? Not discussed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Discussed? No (and there is no reward in the model).  
    • Predictions about varying it? Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper does not measure “efficiency” in the strict sense of (total payoff achieved) / (maximum possible payoff). Instead, it studies “the efficiency of institutionalized punishment” by analyzing which strategies (defectors, cooperators, punishers) survive in the stationary state. The main results are phase diagrams and frequencies (fractions) of each strategy, rather than direct measures of total/average payoff.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • The paper discusses and explicitly labels three out of the 15 parameters:  
       (6) The synergy factor r (analogous to the MPCR),  
       (7) The cost γ of pool punishment (though not “per unit” in the usual sense), and  
       (8) The punishment fine β.  
   • None of the other 12 parameters appear in the text.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The effect of r, γ, and β on the strategy frequencies is discussed at length. The authors provide phase diagrams showing how systematically varying (γ, β) for selected values of r changes the stationary distribution of defectors, cooperators, and punishers. They do not, however, frame the results in terms of net efficiency or overall payoff. Instead they focus on whether punishers die out, whether defectors dominate, or whether all three strategies coexist in a rock-paper-scissors cycle.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • Because the paper never calculates total or average payoffs, one can only infer indirectly. Generally, increased r (synergy) supports more cooperation and would presumably improve efficiency. A higher fine β and lower punisher cost γ can maintain higher levels of punishing (and thus less defection), which often implies more cooperation and presumably higher payoffs. Beyond these general inferences, the paper’s focus on strategy-frequency phase diagrams does not permit direct numerical predictions about group efficiency. No information is provided about the other parameters (1–5, 9–11, 12–15), so no predictions can be made for them based on this paper.

Abstract: A large literature shares the view that social norms shape human cooperation, but without a clean empirical identification of the relevant norms almost every behaviour can be rationalized as norm driven, thus rendering norms useless as an explanatory construct. Below is a parameter-by-parameter extraction of what the Fehr & Schurtenberger (2018) review actually says and, more importantly, what it does **not** say about how changing each parameter would influence the *punishment treatment effect* on **group efficiency** (total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff).

“Discussed” = the parameter is explicitly mentioned or can be unambiguously inferred from a cited experiment.  
“Systematic effect stated” = the paper makes an explicit prediction or reports a treatment comparison in which that parameter is deliberately varied.

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
• Discussed: Yes.  Fig. 3: “fixed groups of four subjects”. Other cited studies use 4-person groups as well.  
• Systematic effect stated: No.  The paper never varies group size or links size to how much punishment raises or lowers efficiency.

2. Number of rounds  
• Discussed: Yes.  Repeated games of 10 or 15 periods are repeatedly mentioned (e.g., decline over time; Fig. 3 has 15 periods; regularity 3 shows 10-period restarts).  
• Systematic effect stated: No.  No comparison of different horizon lengths on the punishment–control difference in efficiency.

3. Chat / pre-play communication  
• Discussed: Yes.  Regularity 1 (“if subjects can communicate… cooperation strongly increases”).  
• Systematic effect stated: No.  The paper only contrasts “communication vs no communication” in *games without punishment*; it never reports the punishment-with-chat versus punishment-without-chat efficiency gap.

4. All-or-nothing contribution decision  
• Discussed: No.  All referenced public-goods designs allow a continuous choice. No prediction given.

5. “Contribution default” (endowment removal instead of provision)  
• Discussed: No.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor  
• Discussed: No explicit values and no manipulation of the factor are reported.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
• Discussed: Yes, qualitatively (“costly punishment”, “high collateral cost”) but no concrete numbers.  
• Systematic effect stated: No.  No treatment varies the cost factor holding everything else constant.

8. Punishment magnitude (damage per unit)  
• Discussed: Qualitatively (e.g., “coins deducted”), not quantified.  
• Systematic effect stated: No.

9. Whether a reward option is enabled  
• Discussed: Yes.  Regularity 9 and Fig. 2d compare four conditions: Control (no sanctions), PN (punishment only), RN (reward only), RNP (reward + punishment).  
• Systematic effect stated: Partly.  The paper states that RN “leads to similarly high cooperation levels compared with PN and … RNP”.  It also notes that punishment’s high initial cost means *group welfare* does **not** immediately rise, whereas rewards raise cooperation without mentioning offsetting costs.  However, no explicit efficiency numbers are supplied, so the net *punishment treatment effect on efficiency* under “reward enabled” versus “reward disabled” is not quantified.

10. Reward cost  
• Discussed: No numerical value; never varied.

11. Reward magnitude  
• Discussed: No numerical value; never varied.

12. End-of-game horizon known  
• Discussed: No.

13. Peer outcomes shown  
• Discussed: Yes, indirectly.  In the reward treatments “subjects can observe the cooperation level of other group members” before rewarding.  Observation is therefore present, but the paper does not vary information revelation.  
• Systematic effect stated: No.

14. Punished player knows who punished  
• Discussed: No.

15. Rewarded player knows who rewarded  
• Discussed: No.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
• The review refers to “group welfare”, “overall welfare”, and “total payoff” (all synonyms of efficiency) and also to “cooperation rates” and “punishment costs”.  
• Contributions/cooperation rate = how much is put in the public good.  
• Efficiency/group welfare = monetary payoffs net of punishment/reward costs.  
• These are distinct; the authors stress that punishment often raises cooperation while *not* improving (or even lowering) welfare during the early periods.

B. Which parameters are mentioned?  
6 of 15:  1, 2, 3, 7, 9, 13.

C. Which parameters are *systematically varied* and tied to the punishment treatment effect?  
Only 1 of 15 (parameter 9: reward option).  Even here, the paper offers qualitative statements (high cooperation with or without punishment, lower cost with reward) but no numerical efficiency effect sizes.

D. What efficiency predictions can we make **solely** from this paper?  
• Enabling a *reward* option can generate the same high cooperation as punishment but likely with higher efficiency because it avoids the “high initial cost” of punishment.  
• Adding punishment without any normative or institutional constraints usually delays efficiency gains (costs exceed benefits for ≈ 10 rounds).  
• Providing a mechanism for *normative coordination* (subjects publicly state desired contribution norms) together with punishment lowers punishment usage and raises efficiency relative to “punishment only”.  
• Beyond these broad ideas, the paper offers *no evidence* on how varying group size, horizon length, sanction cost/magnitude, information conditions, or communication interact with punishment to affect efficiency.  Therefore, for the vast majority of the 15 parameters, the review does not allow quantitative or even directional predictions about the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.
reference_APA: Fehr, Ernst & Schurtenberger, Ivo (2018). Normative foundations of human cooperation. NATURE HUMAN BEHAVIOUR.

Authors: Guala, F
Author Full Names: Guala, Francesco
Article Title: Reciprocity: Weak or strong? What punishment experiments do (and do not) demonstrate
Author Keywords: Cooperation; evolution; experiments; punishment; reciprocity
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; NEURAL BASIS; CONDITIONAL COOPERATION; EVOLUTIONARY STABILITY; SOCIAL PREFERENCES; DECISION-MAKING; GROUP SELECTION; LOSS AVERSION; FOLK THEOREM
Abstract: Economists and biologists have proposed a distinction between two mechanisms - strong and weak reciprocity - that may explain the evolution of human sociality. Weak reciprocity theorists emphasize the benefits of long-term cooperation and the use of low-cost strategies to deter free-riders. Strong reciprocity theorists, in contrast, claim that cooperation in social dilemma games can be sustained by costly punishment mechanisms, even in one-shot and finitely repeated games. To support this claim, they have generated a large body of evidence concerning the willingness of experimental subjects to punish uncooperative free-riders at a cost to themselves. In this article, I distinguish between a narrow and a wide reading of the experimental evidence. Under the narrow reading, punishment experiments are just useful devices to measure psychological propensities in controlled laboratory conditions. Under the wide reading, they replicate a mechanism that supports cooperation also in real-world situations outside the laboratory. I argue that the wide interpretation must be tested using a combination of laboratory data and evidence about cooperation in the wild. In spite of some often-repeated claims, there is no evidence that cooperation in the small egalitarian societies studied by anthropologists is enforced by means of costly punishment. Moreover, studies by economic and social historians show that social dilemmas in the wild are typically solved by institutions that coordinate punishment, reduce its cost, and extend the horizon of cooperation. The lack of field evidence for costly punishment suggests important constraints about what forms of cooperation can or cannot be sustained by means of decentralised policing.

In diesem umfangreichen Austausch diskutieren Forscherinnen und Forscher die Rolle des sogenannten „starken Reziprozitätsprinzips“ – das heißt, einer Neigung, Verstößen gegen kooperative Normen auch auf eigene Kosten aktiv entgegenzuwirken. Im Zentrum steht die Frage, ob unkoordinierte, kostspielige Bestrafung tatsächlich im Feld (also „in der Wildnis“) zur Aufrechterhaltung von Kooperation beiträgt oder ob Menschen nicht vielmehr billigere und oft koordinierte Alternativen (z.B. öffentliche Bloßstellung, institutionalisierte Strafen, kollektive Maßnahmen) bevorzugen.

Francesco Guala argumentiert, dass Laborbefunde (z.B. in Public-Goods- oder Ultimatumspielen) die Existenz solcher Bestrafungsimpulse zwar gut belegen, aber dass die entscheidende Rolle teurer Einzelbestrafungen im realen Alltag eher fraglich ist. In Anthropologie und Feldstudien finden sich nur wenige Beispiele, die auf wirklich hohe, nicht kompensierte Kosten für Bestrafer schließen lassen. Häufig sind Vergeltungsschläge, kollektive Sanktionen oder Rufschädigung wirksamer – und deutlich risikoärmer.

In den Kommentaren wird einerseits verteidigt, dass stark reziprokes Verhalten durchaus existiert und unter bestimmten Bedingungen auch im Feld greift. Andererseits stimmen viele zu, dass Menschen häufiger kostengünstige und koordinierte Lösungen finden, während unkoordinierte, wirklich teure Sanktionen eher selten bleiben. Insgesamt wird klar, dass es weiterhin systematischer Feldstudien und sorgfältiger Experimente bedarf, um den genauen Stellenwert teurer Bestrafung in der menschlichen Kooperation zu bestimmen.

Abstract: This article generalizes a set of core design principles for the efficacy of groups that was originally derived for groups attempting to manage common-pool resources (CPRs) such as irrigation systems, forests, and fisheries. The dominant way of thinking until recently was that commons situations invariably result in the tragedy of overuse, requiring either privatization (when possible) or top-down regulation. Based on a worldwide database of CPR groups, Ostrom proposed a set of principles that broadly captured the essential aspects of the institutional arrangements that succeeded, as contrasted to groups whose efforts failed. Abstract: Third-party punishment (TPP)(1-7), in which unaffected observers punish selfishness, promotes cooperation by deterring defection. But why should individuals choose to bear the costs of punishing? We present a game theoretic model of TPP as a costly signal(8-10) of trustworthiness. Our model is based on individual differences in the costs and/ or benefits of being trustworthy. We argue that individuals for whom trustworthiness is payoff-maximizing will find TPP to be less net costly (for example, because mechanisms(11) that incentivize some individuals to be trustworthy also create benefits for deterring selfishness via TPP). We show that because of this relationship, it can be advantageous for individuals to punish selfishness in order to signal that they are not selfish themselves. We then empirically validate our model using economic game experiments. Furthermore, as predicted by our model, introducing a more informative signal-the opportunity to help directly-attenuates these signalling effects. When potential punishers have the chance to help, they are less likely to punish, and punishment is perceived as, and actually is, a weaker signal of trustworthiness. Costly helping, in contrast, is a strong and highly used signal even when TPP is also possible. Together, our model and experiments provide a formal reputational account of TPP, and demonstrate how the costs of punishing may be recouped by the long-run benefits of signalling one's trustworthiness.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?

These differ from efficiency because they focus on trust, trustworthiness, and signaling outcomes rather than maximizing total payoffs or calculating actual vs. maximum possible payoffs.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Three parameters are explicitly or implicitly mentioned in the context of the authors’ signaling framework and/or experimental manipulations:  
     7 (punishment cost), 9 (presence of helping, treated analogously to enabling a “reward”), and 10 (helping cost in the theoretical model).  
   • All other parameters receive no discussion in the paper.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The paper systematically varies:  
     – Parameter 9 (presence/absence of helping), in both the experiment (punishment‐only vs. punishment‐plus‐helping vs. helping‐only) and the model. They show numerically that adding helping greatly reduces punishment’s signaling value (16% vs. 4% difference in trust).  
   • The paper’s theoretical model also conceptually varies the cost of punishment (parameter 7) and the cost of helping (parameter 10) as “small” or “large,” though it does not report numerical effect sizes on “efficiency.” It reports how punishment and helping emerge as signals given different cost conditions, but it does not link these changes to a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not address efficiency, so it provides virtually no direct basis to predict how any of these parameters would affect “group efficiency” in a public‐goods‐style game.

     1. Punishment is more likely to emerge (and have stronger reputational impact) when the punishment cost is relatively small (i.e., easy to bear).  
     2. Introducing an alternative, more informative prosocial option (helping) reduces the usage and reputational impact of punishment.  
   • Beyond that, there is little in the paper about how varying any parameter would affect total payoffs or efficiency for the group.

A. Dependent variables used in the paper

Keywords Plus: INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; PUBLIC-GOODS; NEURAL BASIS; GAME-THEORY; EVOLUTION; FAIRNESS; COMPETITION; SANCTIONS; DEMAND
Abstract: Explaining the evolution and maintenance of cooperation among unrelated individuals is one of the fundamental problems in biology and the social sciences. Recent findings suggest that altruistic punishment is an important mechanism maintaining cooperation among humans. We experimentally explore the boundaries of altruistic punishment to maintain cooperation by varying both the cost and the impact of punishment, using an exceptionally extensive subject pool. Our results show that cooperation is only maintained if conditions for altruistic punishment are relatively favourable: low cost for the punisher and high impact on the punished. Our results indicate that punishment is strongly governed by its cost-to-impact ratio and that its effect on cooperation can be pinned down to one single variable: the threshold level of free-riding that goes unpunished. Additionally, actual pay-offs are the lowest when altruistic punishment maintains cooperation, because the pay-off destroyed through punishment exceeds the gains from increased cooperation. Our results are consistent with the interpretation that punishment decisions come from an amalgam of emotional response and cognitive cost-impact analysis and suggest that altruistic punishment alone can hardly maintain cooperation under multi-level natural selection. Uncovering the workings of altruistic punishment as has been done here is important because it helps predicting under which conditions altruistic punishment is expected to maintain cooperation.

Summary

 • Although they do not explicitly phrase it as “group efficiency” (i.e., payoff / maximum), they do analyze actual earnings in each condition and note clearly that the treatment with the greatest success in enforcing cooperation (T13) yields lower actual payoffs than no punishment. B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

   – (8) Punishment magnitude (impact to the punished).  
 • In doing so, they analyze how different “cost:impact” ratios (1:3, 1:1, 3:3, 3:1) affect (i) cooperation/contributions, (ii) punishment behavior, and (iii) actual payoffs in a treatment with punishment versus no punishment.  
 • The paper does not systematically vary or analyze the other parameters (such as group size or MPCR) for their effect on punishment.

   – When cost is low and magnitude is high (the T13 scenario), cooperation is highest over the rounds, but overall payoff (and thus efficiency) is actually lower than in the no‐punishment control.  
   – When punishment is less “effective” (e.g., cost is high and/or impact is low), punishment usage declines and cooperation decays, which also results in relatively low efficiency because contributions remain low; however, the group does not pay large punishment costs.  
 • For the other 13 parameters, the paper provides no direct or systematic empirical variance (e.g., group size is always 3, number of rounds always 6, etc.). Author Full Names: Falk, A; Fehr, E; Fischbacher, U
Article Title: Driving forces behind informal sanctions
Author Keywords: sanctioning; cooperation; social norm; reciprocity; fairness; spitefulness
Keywords Plus: FAIRNESS; PUNISHMENT
Abstract: This paper investigates the driving forces behind informal sanctions in cooperation games and the extent to which theories of fairness and reciprocity capture these forces. We find that cooperators' punishment is almost exclusively targeted toward the defectors, but the latter also impose a considerable amount of spiteful punishment on the cooperators. However, spiteful punishment vanishes if the punishers can no longer affect the payoff differences between themselves and the punished individual, whereas the cooperators even increase the resources devoted to punishment in this case. Our data also discriminate between different fairness principles. Fairness theories that are based on the assumption that players compare their own payoff to the group's average or the group's total payoff cannot explain the fact that cooperators target their punishment at the defectors. Fairness theories that assume that players aim to minimize payoff inequalities cannot explain the fact that cooperators punish defectors even if payoff inequalities cannot be reduced. Therefore, retaliation, i.e., the desire to harm those who committed unfair acts, seems to be the most important motive behind fairness-driven informal sanctions.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter summary of what the paper does (and does not) say, followed by the required four‐part summary (A–D).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
• Discussed? Yes. The experiment always involves three players in a one‐shot Prisoner’s Dilemma (PD).  
• Systematic variation? No. The paper does not compare different group sizes, so there is no discussion of how changing the number of players would affect punishment or efficiency.

2) Number of rounds  
• Discussed? Indirectly. The design is explicitly one‐shot.  
• Systematic variation? No. No multi‐round or repeated‐game treatments are conducted, so there is no discussion of how varying the number of rounds might affect punishment or efficiency.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
• Discussed? No. The paper states that all interactions were anonymous with no mention of any communication/chat.  
• Systematic variation? No. There is no mention of enabling or disabling chat, nor any prediction of how that would affect punishment or efficiency.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Discussed? Yes (implicitly). Participants either “cooperate” or “defect,” which is effectively an all‐or‐nothing contribution choice.  
• Systematic variation? No. The paper does not test partial contributions versus all‐or‐nothing, so it provides no predictions for changing that feature.

5) Is the contribution default (do players decide how much to move back into their hand from a public fund)?  
• Discussed? No. The paper’s PD game is a simple one‐shot “cooperate/defect” format and does not involve “default” contribution mechanisms.  
• Systematic variation? No mention.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor  
• Discussed? Only in that the paper provides a fixed payoff table for cooperating versus defecting; no explicit mention of a variable MPCR.  
• Systematic variation? No. The table (20, 32, 44, 12, 24, 36 payoffs) is fixed across treatments. The paper does not vary it to see how MPCR changes punishment or efficiency.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Discussed? Yes. In every treatment the cost to the punisher is always “1 token” per unit of punishment assigned.  
• Systematic variation? No. The cost remains the same (1 token), so there is no direct comparison of different punishment costs and their effects on efficiency.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
• Discussed? Yes. This is the key systematically varied parameter in the paper. In the “low‐sanction” condition, one point of punishment reduces the target’s payoff by f=1. In the “high‐sanction” condition, one point reduces a defector’s payoff by f=2.5 and a cooperator’s payoff by f=3.33.  
• Systematic variation? Yes. The paper shows how a higher punishment magnitude (f>1) allows defectors to gain payoff advantage over the punished person—leading to “spiteful” punishment by defectors—whereas in the low‐sanction condition (f=1), that spiteful punishment disappears. Numerical effects reported in the paper concern how many tokens are deducted on average or what fraction of players punish; the paper does not, however, link these changes in f to a specific measure of group efficiency.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
• Discussed? No. The paper studies only punishment (“assigning deduction points”) and does not mention any reward mechanism.  
• Systematic variation? No mention.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Discussed? No. Rewards are not used or mentioned.  
• Systematic variation? No.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)  
• Discussed? No. Rewards are not used or mentioned.  
• Systematic variation? No.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?  
• Discussed? Only insofar as it is a one‐shot game (so there is no “last round” knowledge to vary).  
• Systematic variation? No.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?  
• Discussed? Partially. After the PD decision, each subject sees who cooperated or defected and learns how much they themselves were punished. However, the paper does not describe showing everyone’s final payoffs, nor does it vary how much information is displayed.  
• Systematic variation? No.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• Discussed? They know that they received deduction points but not the punisher’s identity—interactions are anonymous.  
• Systematic variation? No. The paper does not study any condition where punisher identity is revealed.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
• Discussed? No. Rewards do not appear in the experiment.  
• Systematic variation? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY (A–D)

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
• The paper does not use group efficiency (actual total payoff / maximum possible) as its primary outcome. It focuses on (1) who punishes whom and by how much, (2) cooperation (fraction who choose “cooperate”), and (3) the presence of “spiteful” vs. “fairness‐driven” punishment. While it occasionally refers to payoffs (e.g., tokens lost), it does not report efficiency measures or systematically analyze total or average payoffs as the main dependent variable.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
• Mentioned in some form:  
  1) Number of players (always 3)  
  4) All‐or‐nothing contribution (cooperate or defect)  
  7) Punishment cost (1 token per deduction point)  
  8) Punishment magnitude (varied: f=1 vs. f=2.5 or 3.33)  
  13) Limited information display (players see others’ choices, but not systematically varied)  
• The other parameters (2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 15) are not discussed or are only incidentally stated (e.g., “one‐shot” for #2) without any systematic variation nor any direct link to a treatment effect.

C) For which and how many parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable) when that parameter is systematically varied?  
• Only one parameter—punishment magnitude (#8)—is explicitly and systematically varied (low‐sanction: f=1 vs. high‐sanction: f=2.5 or 3.33). The paper reports how it changes the prevalence of punishment by defectors (spiteful punishment appears only when f>1) and the severity of punishment by cooperators. However, the paper does not track how that variation changes overall group efficiency; instead, it documents changes in punishment behavior.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
• The paper does not discuss efficiency directly, nor does it offer explicit predictions of how varying those parameters would influence group efficiency. It reports that when punishment is more potent (f>1), defectors punish more often for spiteful reasons, while cooperators continue to punish defectors. That may or may not improve total earnings; the paper does not quantify efficiency outcomes. Accordingly, one cannot confidently project how any of the 15 parameters—other than the fact that changing punishment potency alters punishment behavior—would affect the group’s efficiency purely from this paper’s data.  

Overall, the paper principally investigates who punishes whom in a three‐player PD, rather than how efficiency changes under different parameter settings. Consequently, it provides no quantitative efficiency estimates or formal predictions linking those 15 parameters to group efficiency.
