Abstract: Situations where individuals have to contribute to joint efforts or share scarce resources are ubiquitous. Yet, without proper mechanisms to ensure cooperation, the evolutionary pressure to maximize individual success tends to create a tragedy of the commons (such as over-fishing or the destruction of our environment). This contribution addresses a number of related puzzles of human behavior with an evolutionary game theoretical approach as it has been successfully used to explain the behavior of other biological species many times, from bacteria to vertebrates. Our agent-based model distinguishes individuals applying four different behavioral strategies: non-cooperative individuals (defectors''), cooperative individuals abstaining from punishment efforts (called cooperators'' or second-order free-riders''), cooperators who punish noncooperative behavior (moralists''), and defectors, who punish other defectors despite being non-cooperative themselves (immoralists''). By considering spatial interactions with neighboring individuals, our model reveals several interesting effects: First, moralists can fully eliminate cooperators. This spreading of punishing behavior requires a segregation of behavioral strategies and solves the second-order free-rider problem''. Second, the system behavior changes its character significantly even after very long times (who laughs last laughs best effect''). Third, the presence of a number of defectors can largely accelerate the victory of moralists over non-punishing cooperators. Fourth, in order to succeed, moralists may profit from immoralists in a way that appears like an unholy collaboration''. Our findings suggest that the consideration of punishment strategies allows one to understand the establishment and spreading of moral behavior'' by means of game-theoretical concepts. This demonstrates that quantitative biological modeling approaches are powerful even in domains that have been addressed with non-mathematical concepts so far. The complex dynamics of certain social behaviors become understandable as the result of an evolutionary competition between different behavioral strategies.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter analysis based solely on the content of the Helbing et al. (2010) paper “Evolutionary Establishment of Moral and Double Moral Standards through Spatial Interactions,” with a focus on whether or how each parameter is mentioned and whether the paper makes any prediction about the effect of systematically varying it on the “punishment treatment effect” (i.e., how punishment affects outcomes). As requested, “efficiency” (actual total payoff ÷ maximum possible total payoff) is our primary concern; however, the paper itself does not explicitly analyze efficiency in those terms.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussion in paper?  
  – The model has local groups (“k+1” players) arranged on a lattice (with k = 4 neighbors in the main setup). It also briefly mentions testing k+1 = 9, 13, 21, or 25.  
• Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment?  
  – The paper does not systematically explore how changing the number of players/locations alters a “punishment treatment effect.” It only remarks that moralists can crowd out non‐punishers even when k+1 is larger than 5, but it does not tie this to any explicit effect on efficiency or any quantitative difference in “punishment treatment” specifically.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Number of rounds
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussion in paper?  
  – The paper uses an evolutionary model with many iterations (up to 10^7), but it does not treat this as discrete “rounds” that participants know about. There is no reference to “finite” vs. “infinite” horizon or whether rounds are known.  
• Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment?  
  – No. The paper does not discuss varying the number of rounds or any effect on punishment treatment or efficiency when changing the total iteration count.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Is chat enabled between players?
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussion in paper?  
  – No mention of communication or “chat.”  
• Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment?  
  – No mention or analysis of any communication channel.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussion in paper?  
  – Yes, implicitly. Participants are either cooperators (who contribute exactly 1) or defectors (who contribute 0). There is no partial contribution.  
• Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment?  
  – No. The paper does not examine what would happen if partial contributions were allowed. It is fixed as “all or nothing.”

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
5. Is there a contribution default (e.g., players choosing how much to move back)?
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussion in paper?  
  – No. Contributions are binary (cooperate at 1 or defect at 0). No mention of a default or of adjusting a fraction.  
• Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment?  
  – No. Not discussed at all.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussion in paper?  
  – Yes. The paper calls this the “synergy factor” r, which multiplies the sum of contributions. Figures 1–2 and others show results for r = 2.0, 3.5, 4.4, etc.  
• Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment?  
  – The paper systematically varies r and shows phase diagrams of which strategies (moralists, cooperators, defectors, immoralists) survive. However, it does not translate these findings into a direct “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Instead, it shows that higher r facilitates higher overall cooperation (especially moralists). There is no numerical effect size given for “efficiency” or for how “punishment treatment” specifically changes a payoff ratio.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussion in paper?  
  – Yes. Denoted by γ (gamma, effectively the total cost that punishing players pay). They vary γ in Figures 1–5 and text.  
• Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment?  
  – The paper systematically studies high vs. low γ and shows that punishment can promote the spread of moralists only if γ is not too high. Yet no explicit effect is given on “efficiency” measures (no ratio of actual vs. maximum payoff reported). Instead, they track final strategy fractions (e.g., moralists survive or take over).

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
8. Punishment magnitude (the penalty imposed on a target)
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussion in paper?  
  – Yes. Denoted by β (beta, the “punishment fine”). They systematically vary β in conjunction with γ and r.  
• Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment?  
  – Yes, extensive. The phase diagrams (Figure 1) show transitions (e.g., from a fully defector phase to a moralist‐dominated phase) depending on β. However, these results are framed in terms of which strategies persist, not an “efficiency” measure. No specific numeric effect on “treatment effect” or total payoffs is listed, only which strategies outcompete others.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
9. Whether a reward is enabled
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussion in paper?  
  – No. The paper only discusses punishment (cooperators who punish, defectors who may punish fellow defectors, etc.). There is no mention of rewarding.  
• Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment?  
  – Not addressed.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussion in paper?  
  – Not mentioned.  
• Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment?  
  – Not mentioned.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
11. Reward magnitude
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussion in paper?  
  – Not mentioned.  
• Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment?  
  – Not mentioned.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussion in paper?  
  – No. The study uses an evolutionary model without addressing whether participants know an end time.  
• Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment?  
  – Not mentioned.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
13. Are peer outcomes shown (e.g., do players see each other’s payoffs)?
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussion in paper?  
  – The model posits that individuals “imitate” higher payoffs locally, but the paper does not explore or vary how that information is displayed.  
• Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment?  
  – No. No mention of systematically varying transparency or displayed earnings.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
14. When a player is punished, do they know who punished them?
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussion in paper?  
  – There is no discussion. The paper simply models punishment costs and fines.  
• Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment?  
  – Not addressed.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who rewarded them?
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussion in paper?  
  – No mention of rewards or any “who rewarded whom.”  
• Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment?  
  – Not addressed.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how do these differ?  
   – The paper does not use “group efficiency” (actual total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff). Instead, it focuses on “which strategies survive” or “the fraction of each strategy” after long evolutionary times. Although the authors discuss escape from the “tragedy of the commons,” they do not provide an explicit efficiency ratio.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – Mentioned:  
     (1) Number of players (they work primarily with local groups of size 5 but also check larger)  
     (4) All‐or‐nothing contributions (implicitly)  
     (6) The synergy factor r (akin to MPCR)  
     (7) Punishment cost γ  
     (8) Punishment fine β  
   – Not mentioned (or mentioned only tangentially): 2, 3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   – They systematically vary r, γ, and β, but the paper frames outcomes in terms of eventual strategy compositions (e.g., whether moralists outcompete cooperators), not in terms of an efficiency measure or a “punishment treatment effect” specifically. No numeric “effect sizes” on efficiency are given.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper:  
   – The paper itself gives only indirect indications that higher r (stronger synergy), higher β (more severe punishment), and lower γ (cheaper punishment) yield more cooperation by moralists, presumably raising overall payoffs. However, it never directly analyzes the ratio of actual to maximum payoff. Consequently, there is little basis in the text to predict precise changes in “efficiency.” The paper does not address systematically varying the other parameters, so it provides no direct leverage to predict how they might affect efficiency.

Author Full Names: Purzycki, Benjamin Grant; Apicella, Caren; Atkinson, Quentin D.; Cohen, Emma; McNamara, Rita Anne; Willard, Aiyana K.; Xygalatas, Dimitris; Norenzayan, Ara; Henrich, Joseph
Article Title: Moralistic gods, supernatural punishment and the expansion of human sociality
Keywords Plus: COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; RELIGION; BELIEF
Abstract: Since the origins of agriculture, the scale of human cooperation and societal complexity has dramatically expanded(1,2). This fact challenges standard evolutionary explanations of prosociality because well-studied mechanisms of cooperation based on genetic relatedness, reciprocity and partner choice falter as people increasingly engage in fleeting transactions with genetically unrelated strangers in large anonymous groups. To explain this rapid expansion of prosociality, researchers have proposed several mechanisms(3,4). Here we focus on one key hypothesis: cognitive representations of gods as increasingly knowledgeable and punitive, and who sanction violators of interpersonal social norms, foster and sustain the expansion of cooperation, trust and fairness towards co-religionist strangers(5-8). We tested this hypothesis using extensive ethnographic interviews and two behavioural games designed to measure impartial rule-following among people (n = 591, observations = 35,400) from eight diverse communities from around the world: (1) inland Tanna, Vanuatu; (2) coastal Tanna, Vanuatu; (3) Yasawa, Fiji; (4) Lovu, Fiji; (5) Pesqueiro, Brazil; (6) Pointe aux Piments, Mauritius; (7) the Tyva Republic (Siberia), Russia; and (8) Hadzaland, Tanzania. Participants reported adherence to a wide array of world religious traditions including Christianity, Hinduism and Buddhism, as well as notably diverse local traditions, including animism and ancestor worship. Holding a range of relevant variables constant, the higher participants rated their moralistic gods as punitive and knowledgeable about human thoughts and actions, the more coins they allocated to geographically distant co-religionist strangers relative to both themselves and local co-religionists. Our results support the hypothesis that beliefs in moralistic, punitive and knowing gods increase impartial behaviour towards distant co-religionists, and therefore can contribute to the expansion of prosociality.

Authors: Ohtsuki, H; Iwasa, Y; Nowak, MA
Author Full Names: Ohtsuki, Hisashi; Iwasa, Yoh; Nowak, Martin A.
Article Title: Indirect reciprocity provides only a narrow margin of efficiency for costly punishment
Keywords Plus: SOCIAL NORMS; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; REPUTATION; HUMANS; RULES
Abstract: Indirect reciprocity(1-5) is a key mechanism for the evolution of human cooperation. Our behaviour towards other people depends not only on what they have done to us but also on what they have done to others. Indirect reciprocity works through reputation(5-17). The standard model of indirect reciprocity offers a binary choice: people can either cooperate or defect. Cooperation implies a cost for the donor and a benefit for the recipient. Defection has no cost and yields no benefit. Currently there is considerable interest in studying the effect of costly (or altruistic) punishment on human behaviour(18-25). Punishment implies a cost for the punished person. Costly punishment means that the punisher also pays a cost. It has been suggested that costly punishment between individuals can promote cooperation. Here we study the role of costly punishment in an explicit model of indirect reciprocity. We analyse all social norms, which depend on the action of the donor and the reputation of the recipient. We allow errors in assigning reputation and study gossip as a mechanism for establishing coherence. We characterize all strategies that allow the evolutionary stability of cooperation. Some of those strategies use costly punishment; others do not. We find that punishment strategies typically reduce the average payoff of the population. Consequently, there is only a small parameter region where costly punishment leads to an efficient equilibrium. In most cases the population does better by not using costly punishment. The efficient strategy for indirect reciprocity is to withhold help for defectors rather than punishing them.

Abstract: Maintaining the Earth's climate within habitable boundaries is probably the greatest public goods game played by humans. However,with > 6 billion players taking part, the game seems to rule out individual altruistic behavior. Thus, climate protection is a problem of sustaining a public resource that everybody is free to overuse, a tragedy of the commons problem that emerges in many social dilemmas. We perform a previously undescribed type of public goods experiment with human subjects contributing to a public pool. In contrast to the standard protocol, here the common pool is not divided among the participants; instead, it is promised that the pool will be invested to encourage people to reduce their fossil fuel use. We find a nonzero basic level of altruistic behavior, which is enhanced if the players are provided with expert information describing the state of knowledge in climate research. Furthermore, personal investments in climate protection increase substantially if players can invest publicly, thus gaining social reputation. This increase occurs because subjects reward other subjects' contributions to sustaining the climate, thus reinforcing their altruism. Therefore, altruism may convert to net personal benefit and to relaxing the dilemma if the gain in reputation is large enough. Below is a parameter-by-parameter summary based solely on the content of the referenced paper “Relational Contracts and the Nature of Market Interactions” by Brown, Falk, and Fehr. Throughout, please note that the paper does not study a public goods game or “punishment” in the sense of costly peer-punishment; instead, it focuses on repeated trading in labor‐market‐type interactions (complete vs. incomplete contracts). There is no systematic manipulation of “punishment costs,” “punishment magnitude,” etc. as would be typical in public-goods‐with-punishment experiments. Accordingly, the paper does not provide direct data or predictions about a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” for any of the 15 parameters.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – Yes. Each session had 10 workers and 7 firms (a total of 17 participants), with an excess supply of 3 workers.  
   • Systematic variation mentioned or predicted effects on “punishment treatment effect”?  
     – No. The paper does not vary the total number of players across conditions, nor does it mention any “punishment treatment.” No effect sizes are reported for how changing the number of players would alter a punishment treatment effect.

2) Number of rounds  
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – Yes. All sessions lasted for 15 trading periods (15 finite rounds).  
   • Systematic variation mentioned or predicted effects on “punishment treatment effect”?  
     – No. The paper uses 15 rounds uniformly and does not vary this number in a way that would speak to a punishment treatment.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – No. There is no mention of open chat or free-form communication. Participants can make offers (private or public), but not in a free-chat sense.  
   • Systematic variation mentioned or predicted effects?  
     – No. Not discussed.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – No. The paper’s design allows workers to choose an integer effort level from 1 to 10; it is not an “all-or-nothing” decision.  
   • Systematic variation mentioned or predicted effects?  
     – No. Not discussed.

5) Is the contribution default (e.g., are participants forced to move an endowment back into their hand)?  
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – No. There is no “default contribution” concept; participants choose wages/offers (firms) and effort levels (workers).  
   • Systematic variation mentioned or predicted effects?  
     – No. Not discussed.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor  
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – No. The study is not framed as a public goods experiment with an MPCR. Instead, payoffs follow the formula 10·e – w (for the firm) and w – c(e) (for the worker), with c(e) as an effort-cost function.  
   • Systematic variation mentioned or predicted effects?  
     – No. Not discussed.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – No. The paper does not study punishment in the sense of explicit peer-punishment costs or tokens.  
   • Systematic variation mentioned or predicted effects?  
     – No. Not discussed.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – No. While “firing” a worker (i.e., not renewing a contract) is sometimes described informally as a “discipline device,” the paper does not formalize it as a costed “punishment magnitude” in a public goods sense.  
   • Systematic variation mentioned or predicted effects?  
     – No. Not discussed.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – No. There is no designated “reward” mechanism in the sense of granting explicit bonus tokens to another player.  
   • Systematic variation mentioned or predicted effects?  
     – No. Not discussed.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Discussion in the paper?  
      – No. No such mechanism is studied.  
    • Systematic variation mentioned or predicted effects?  
      – No. Not discussed.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted to them)  
    • Discussion in the paper?  
      – No. Again, no direct “reward tokens” are mentioned.  
    • Systematic variation mentioned or predicted effects?  
      – No. Not discussed.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    • Discussion in the paper?  
      – Yes. Participants know there are 15 trading periods; the finite horizon is common knowledge.  
    • Systematic variation mentioned or predicted effects?  
      – No. The horizon length is fixed at 15, and there is no discussion of altering that horizon in ways that would speak to a punishment effect.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much others gained and lost)?  
    • Discussion in the paper?  
      – The paper states that only the trading partners in a given contract see each other’s payoffs and effort; other players do not see these details.  
    • Systematic variation mentioned or predicted effects?  
      – No. There is no condition varying the display of other peers’ outcomes. 

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Discussion in the paper?  
      – The study does not use a direct “punishment” protocol. “Firing” occurs if a firm decides not to renew a contract, but that is not framed as “who punished whom.” No systematic mention.  
    • Systematic variation mentioned or predicted effects?  
      – No. Not discussed.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Discussion in the paper?  
      – No official “rewarding” mechanism exists. Firms do make private offers to the same worker, but not as an explicit “reward” with known cost.  
    • Systematic variation mentioned or predicted effects?  
      – No. Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   – The paper occasionally refers to “efficiency” or total surplus (especially in Section 4.6 discussing “Efficiency and Distribution in Long-Term Relations”). The more common dependent variables, however, are wages, effort levels, profits, and the probability of contract renewal. “Efficiency,” as framed in many public goods studies (actual payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff), is not the paper’s primary focus, and it is not systematically analyzed in the sense of a “punishment treatment effect.” Thus, while “efficiency” and “earnings” do appear, the main dependent measures are (a) effort, (b) wages/rents, (c) firm profit, (d) worker earnings, and (e) contract renewal rates.  

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – Three parameters are explicitly referenced: (1) Number of players (fixed at 10 workers plus 7 firms), (2) Number of rounds (fixed at 15), and (12) Knowledge of the number of rounds (the participants know the game ends after 15 periods). The other 12 parameters are not mentioned in the paper.  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   – None. The paper does not invoke a treatment specifically called “punishment,” nor does it systematically vary those 15 parameters in a public-goods‐type framework. There is thus no discussion of a “punishment treatment effect” for any of those parameters.  

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   – The paper does not provide information about a public goods game or peer-punishment mechanism, so it offers no basis for predicting how those 15 parameters or their interactions would affect a “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency. Consequently, one can make little to no prediction on that topic from this paper alone.

Abstract: One-shot anonymous unselfishness in economic games is commonly explained by social preferences, which assume that people care about the monetary pay-offs of others. Abstract: Across the social sciences, a key question is how societies manage to enforce cooperative behavior in social dilemmas such as public goods provision or bilateral trade. According to an influential body of theories in psychology, anthropology, and evolutionary biology, the answer is that humans have evolved moral systems: packages of functional psychological and biological mechanisms that regulate economic behavior, including a belief in moralizing gods; moral values; negative reciprocity; and emotions of shame, guilt, and disgust. Based on a stylized model, this article empirically studies the structure and evolution of these moral traits as a function of historical heterogeneity in extended kinship relationships. The evidence shows that societies with a historically tightly knit kinship structure regulate behavior through communal moral values, revenge taking, emotions of external shame, and notions of purity and disgust. In loose kinship societies, on the other hand, cooperation appears to be enforced through universal moral values, internalized guilt, altruistic punishment, and an apparent rise and fall of moralizing religions. These patterns point to the presence of internally consistent but culturally variable functional moral systems. Consistent with the model, the relationship between kinship ties, economic development, and the structure of the mediating moral systems amplified over time.

     – Empirically, subjects in the experiments can choose to contribute in increments (e.g., 2 cents or 10-cent steps), not strictly “all or nothing.” In the model, contributions are simply “cooperate” (pay cost) or “defect,” or one can “opt out” as a loner.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. The paper does not explore a version with forced “all-or-nothing” contributions.  

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much of their endowment to move back)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No mention of any default contribution mechanism or forced transfer back to one’s own account.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Not applicable.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The paper uses r > 1 as the “cooperation multiplier” (analogous to MPCR × group size). They sample r from 1 < r < 5 in their 100,000-parameter sweeps.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Yes. They repeatedly emphasize that varying r affects whether cooperators or antisocial punishers dominate. Specifically, higher r facilitates cooperation and reduces antisocial punishment. There is no direct, numeric “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” provided, but the paper does show that high r correlates with higher cooperation and lower levels of destructive punishment.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. Denoted γ (gamma) in the model: the cost to the punisher. They include γ in the 100,000-parameter sweeps (0 < γ < 5).  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Yes, in the parameter sweeps. However, they only discuss qualitative outcomes (for example, “punishment is widespread,” or “punishment is destructive”) rather than giving a specific effect size on how systematically increasing γ alters the “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency.  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. Denoted β (beta) in the model: the cost inflicted on the punished. They impose γ < β < 5γ in their parameter sweeps.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Yes. The paper describes how large β makes punishment “strong” and can lock in whatever strategy is currently dominant (cooperator, defector, or loner), thereby not improving payoff efficiency overall. Small β (“mostly symbolic punishments”) can allow higher cooperation if r is also large. Again, there is no specific effect size on efficiency differences with and without punishment, only qualitative statements that large β fosters destructive stability that does not raise group payoffs.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper focuses entirely on punishment (no rewarding) and does not discuss introducing or removing reward.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Not applicable.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No; rewarding is not part of the design.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Not applicable.  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No; again, rewarding does not appear in the article.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Not applicable.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper’s experiments are one-shot. There is no explicit discussion of a multi-round game with known or unknown endpoint.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Not applicable.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much peers gained/lost each round)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – The experiments reveal peer contributions for the punishment stage (so that subjects can decide whom to punish). However, the article does not discuss any variation in whether outcomes are shown or concealed.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No; there is no systematic manipulation of the displayed information.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Not in the text provided; there is no discussion of punisher identity revelation.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Not applicable.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Not applicable, as rewarding does not appear in the paper.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Not applicable.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY  
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper’s central dependent variables are (1) the frequency of cooperation and (2) the frequency of different punishment strategies (including antisocial punishment). The authors also discuss how punishment affects average payoffs, noting that it is “destructive for all parties” and does not produce a payoff benefit once antisocial punishment is allowed.  
   • Although the authors do refer to overall payoffs, they do not give a direct measure labeled “efficiency” (actual total payoff divided by a hypothetical maximum). Rather, they highlight that “punishment does not increase cooperation or aggregate payoffs.” So they do speak about overall payoff but do not systematically analyze it as a standalone “efficiency” measure.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Discussed explicitly or included in their model/experiments:  
     – #1 (Number of players/group size, though not varied),  
     – #6 (cooperation multiplier r),  
     – #7 (punishment cost γ),  
     – #8 (punishment magnitude β).  
   • None of the other 11 parameters are discussed at all in the paper.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The paper actually carries out systematic parameter sweeps for r (parameter #6), γ (parameter #7), and β (parameter #8). Those three parameters are varied repeatedly, and the authors track how punishment strategies (antisocial, pro-social, etc.) invade or are invaded.  
   • However, they do not specifically report a “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency or payoff as a function of r, γ, or β in numerical effect sizes. They give qualitative findings only (e.g., “for large r and small β, cooperation is favored more often”).  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The authors do not directly measure the difference in efficiency with versus without punishment as a function of the 15 parameters. They only conclude that, once antisocial punishment is allowed, punishment no longer lifts overall payoffs in most parameter regions studied.  
   • From the paper, one can infer the following qualitative points:  
     – Having a higher “cooperation multiplier” (r) may help offset the destructive nature of punishment, in principle leading to somewhat better total payoffs under punishment; but the paper indicates that, even then, punishment’s positive impact on payoffs largely disappears once it can be directed at cooperators (antisocially).  
     – Making punishment less potent (i.e., reducing β) can allow more cooperation and may reduce the “self-interested, destructive” spiral. That in turn could slightly mitigate punishment’s negative impact on group payoffs.  
   • For all other parameters (number of players, number of rounds, communication, reward presence, etc.), the paper does not provide enough information to predict how they would affect the “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency.  

In short, the paper systematically examines only r, γ, and β. Even for those, it does not isolate a punishment-versus-no-punishment effect on total efficiency; rather, it concludes that punishment ceases to boost overall payoffs or cooperation once antisocial punishment is allowed, particularly for wide ranges of parameter values. Consequently, the text provides only limited guidance on predicting how any of the 15 parameters (beyond r, γ, β) would change the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Below I go through the 15 parameters in the order you listed them and report exactly what the paper says (and does *not* say) about each one with respect to the **punishment treatment effect**.  “Punishment-treatment effect’’ is interpreted as the difference between outcomes in a baseline public-goods game without punishment and in an otherwise identical game in which the option to punish is added.  When the paper analyses dependent variables other than efficiency I state this explicitly.

----------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
----------------------------------------------------------------

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes, implicitly.  Simulations are run on an L × L square lattice; L is not fixed in the text, but typical studies in this line of work use 200 ≤ L ≤ 400.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  The lattice size is only a technical detail; no results are reported for different values of L.  
   • Predicted influence on the punishment treatment effect?  None.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  No (the model runs to stationarity measured in Monte-Carlo steps).  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  
   • Predicted influence?  None.

3. Is chat enabled?  
   • Not modelled.  No effect discussed.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Yes.  A co-operator always contributes c = 1; a defector contributes 0.  
   • The paper never varies this feature, so no prediction is given for how changing it would alter the punishment effect.

5. Is contribution “default’’?  
   • Not part of the model; no discussion.

6. Marginal per–capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor r  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  r is *the* key parameter of the baseline game.  
   • Values used: r = 3.8 in Fig. 1 and in most punishment simulations; the text notes that r = 3.74 is the critical value at which cooperators first survive without punishment on a 5-person group (G = 5).  
   • Systematic variation?  Only qualitatively.  The author writes that “Similar phase diagrams can be obtained for smaller values of r, where, however, only strategy D survives at small values of the punishment fine.”  No full r-by-r grid is shown.  
   • Effect that *is* stated: when r is below the 3.74 threshold, adding punishment can create cooperation that would not exist otherwise; when r is above the threshold, punishment mostly changes *which* cooperative strategy survives (C vs P) but total cooperation is already high.  
   • Numerical effect sizes on efficiency?  None reported; dependent variable plotted is the *fraction of cooperators*.

7. Punishment cost γ (cost per unit of punishment delivered)  
   • Mentioned and systematically varied.  Fig. 1 inset shows γ = 0.10, 0.30, 0.65 at r = 3.8.  The main phase diagram uses γ on the vertical axis.  
   • Qualitative result: For a *given* fine β, higher γ weakens the punishment treatment effect; above a critical γ (≈ 0.65 at r = 3.8) punishment no longer helps and cooperators disappear.  
   • No efficiency data, only cooperation levels.  Effect sizes are therefore changes in ρC+P (fraction of cooperative strategies); exact numbers are not in the text.

8. Punishment magnitude β (fine per unit received)  
   • Mentioned and systematically varied (horizontal axis in Fig. 1).  
   • Qualitative result: Increasing β monotonically increases the fraction of cooperators for every γ that was studied, until punishers dominate completely.  
   • Again, only fractions of strategies are shown, not pay-offs or efficiency.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Reward is introduced only in Section 4 (“positive and negative reciprocity”) by allowing strategies R (reward-only) and B (both punish and reward).  The baseline punishment model of Section 3 has *no* reward option.  
   • The paper never toggles reward on/off while holding everything else constant, so no explicit “reward treatment effect’’ is identified.

10. Reward cost γ (cost per unit reward given)  
   • In the four-strategy model (D, P, R, B) the *same* γ is used for both punishment and reward.  γ is systematically varied in Fig. 2.  
   • Effect reported: Higher γ destroys the cyclic-dominance D+P+B phase and moves the system to a homogeneous D or B phase, either continuously (β = 0.37) or discontinuously (β = 0.55).  
   • No statement about total efficiency.

11. Reward magnitude β (benefit per unit reward received)  
   • β is again the *same parameter* that measures the size of rewards and fines.  Two β cross-sections are shown: β = 0.37 and β = 0.55 (Fig. 2).  
   • Qualitative result: Changing β alters the nature of the phase transition (continuous vs. discontinuous) when γ is raised, but the paper does not contrast “with vs. without punishment’’ here, nor does it quantify efficiency.

12. Do players know the number of rounds?  
   • Not part of the model; infinite-horizon simulations.  No discussion.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • The model is purely payoff-based strategy imitation; there is no information treatment to vary.

14. Do punished individuals know *who* punished them?  
   • The model assumes perfect local knowledge of strategies but does not model knowledge of *identity*; no variation, no discussion.

15. Do rewarded individuals know *who* rewarded them?  
   • Same as parameter 14: not modelled, no discussion.

----------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
----------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables  
   • The paper does *not* use “group efficiency’’ (total or mean payoff) as an outcome.  
   • Reported dependent variables are (i) fractions of each strategy at stationarity, and (ii) for the four-strategy model, the *amplitude of oscillations* in those fractions.  These are conceptually different from efficiency because they say nothing about the absolute size of total payoffs, only about how many players take which action.

B. Which of the 15 parameters appear in the paper?  
   • Explicitly: 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11.  
   • Implicit technical parameter: 1 (number of players) is fixed but never analysed.  
   • Total explicitly mentioned from your list: 7.

C. For how many of the 15 parameters does the paper analyse the *systematic* effect of varying that parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
   • Three parameters in the pure punishment model: r (6), γ (7), β (8).  
   • Two additional parameters when reward is present: γ (10, shared with 7) and β (11, shared with 8).  
   • Thus, 3 distinct parameters (r, γ, β) receive systematic variation in Section 3; β and γ are varied again in Section 4 when reward is also present.  No efficiency outcomes are provided.

D. What predictions can be made *solely* from the paper about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
   • Because the paper never measures efficiency, only rough qualitative inferences are possible:  
     – If MPCR r is well *below* the cooperative threshold (r < 3.74 for G = 5) adding punishment is expected to raise efficiency because it can create cooperation where none existed.  
     – For moderate r (≈ 3.8 in the paper) increasing the punishment *fine* β or decreasing the punishment *cost* γ should improve efficiency, because these changes move the system from defect-dominant to punisher-dominant phases.  
     – Once γ exceeds its critical value (≈ 0.65 at r = 3.8) punishment no longer helps, so the treatment effect on efficiency should vanish or even turn negative if punishment is costly but ineffective.  
     – All other listed parameters (1–5, 12–15) are not studied, so no prediction can be drawn from this paper alone about their influence on the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

That exhausts all statements that can be grounded directly in the text, figures, and tables of the provided paper.

Below each of the 15 design parameters I repeat the two questions required by the instructions.  
“Discussed?” = Is the parameter explicitly described anywhere in the article (figures, tables, text)?  
“Systematic-effect stated?” = Does the paper say what happens to the **punishment treatment effect** (for any dependent variable) when the parameter itself is **systematically varied**? --------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
• Discussed?  Yes – p. 3: “Six anonymous players are given $10 each.”  
• Systematic-effect stated?  No.  Only a single group size (6) is ever mentioned.

2. Number of rounds  
• Discussed?  Yes – Fig. 1 shows 6 rounds without punishment followed by 6 rounds with punishment.  
• Systematic-effect stated?  No.  Rounds are held constant; the author never varies or compares 4 vs 20 rounds, etc.

3. Is chat enabled?  
• Discussed?  No.  No mention of direct communication between subjects.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
• Discussed?  Yes – the author notes that in the Fehr-Gächter design “players can choose between different levels of contribution,” i.e. NOT all-or-nothing.  
• Systematic-effect stated?  No.

5. Contribution default / ‘take’ design  
• Discussed?  No.

6. Marginal-per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
• Discussed?  Yes – “the experimenter will triple the amount in the common pool … and distribute it equally among all six players” (multiplication factor = 3, MPCR = 0.5).  
• Systematic-effect stated?  No.  No alternative factors are described or compared.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
• Discussed?  Yes – several places say the punisher “must pay a fee.”  p. 12 explicitly contrasts a “1 : 3” fee-to-fine ratio with a “1 : 1” ratio.  
• Systematic-effect stated?  Yes.  Citing Ref. [59] the paper states that with a 1 : 1 ratio “contributors punish defectors vigorously … and the threat of punishment boosts contributions,” while defectors practically stop punishing.  With 1 : 3 the pattern is different (some defectors also punish).  No numerical efficiency numbers are given, but the qualitative effect is that lowering the fine-to-fee ratio (i.e. making punishment more expensive) changes who punishes while leaving the contribution-boosting effect intact.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine per unit)  
• Discussed?  Yes – implicitly in the same 1 : 3 vs 1 : 1 comparison (magnitude = 3 or 1).  
• Systematic-effect stated?  Yes – same quotation as above; higher magnitude (1 : 3) yields similar contribution levels with less total punishing by cooperators and some punishing by defectors.

9. Whether a reward option is enabled  
• Discussed?  Yes – whole section “The carrot” (Box 4) and Fig. 2 (PUN vs PUN&IR treatments).  
• Systematic-effect stated?  Yes.  
    – Andreoni et al. 4-treatment study: “Rewards alone prove ineffective.  Punishment alone induces 50 %-shares.  Adding rewards causes half the offers to exceed 50 % and more than a quarter to offer 100 %.”  
    – Milinski/Panchanathan & Boyd design: adding cost-free rewards delivered via indirect reciprocity “reduces the amount of direct, costly punishment … but does not eliminate it” and is “considerably more efficient in boosting contributions.” (Fig. 2).  No numeric efficiency value is reported.

10. Reward cost per unit  
• Discussed?  Only qualitatively – rewards in indirect reciprocity are described as “not costly.”  No numbers.  
• Systematic-effect stated?  No.

11. Reward magnitude per unit  
• Discussed?  No quantitative detail.  
• Systematic-effect stated?  No.

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
• Discussed?  Yes indirectly: repeated prisoner’s dilemma experiments are often designed so that “they are not told beforehand when the interaction will be over,” but this statement is made in the boxed lexicon, not in connection with the public-goods-with-punishment experiments.  
• Systematic-effect stated?  No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
• Discussed?  Not explicitly.  The standard Fehr-Gächter design does show contribution levels, but the article never talks about varying the information.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
• Discussed?  No.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
• Discussed?  No.

SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used in the article  
• The text refers to (i) “average contribution,” (ii) “average income / payoff,” and (iii) “efficiency” only in qualitative statements such as “in later rounds … this should yield a stable and economically efficient collaboration.”  
These variables are different: contribution is the amount put into the public fund; income is money actually earned; efficiency would be income relative to the social optimum.  Precise efficiency numbers are never reported.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
Seven clearly appear (1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9); parameters 10 & 12 are only alluded to in passing but without any numeric detail.

C. For how many parameters does the article tell us what happens when that parameter is systematically varied?  
Three:  
  • Punishment cost (7) and magnitude (8) via the 1 : 3 vs 1 : 1 comparison.  
  • Availability of a reward option (9) via the punishment-only / reward-only / both / neither and PUN vs PUN&IR designs.  
No other parameter is varied.

D. What predictions about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment treatment effect on **efficiency** can be made from this article alone?  

– Lower punishment costs or higher fine-to-fee ratios (1 : 3 instead of 1 : 1) should raise efficiency because they achieve similar contribution rates with less total expenditure on punishment.  
– Providing a cheap or cost-free reward mechanism (indirect reciprocity) alongside punishment should raise efficiency by substituting inexpensive rewards for costly fines.

Abstract: Among animals, Homo sapiens is unique in its capacity for widespread cooperation and prosocial behavior among large and genetically heterogeneous groups of individuals. Keywords Plus: ANTISOCIAL PUNISHMENT; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; STRONG RECIPROCITY; COSTLY PUNISHMENT; EVOLUTION; FIELD; GAME; PREFERENCES; TRAGEDY; INFANTS
Abstract: Understanding human cooperation is of major interest across the natural and social sciences. But it is unclear to what extent cooperation is actually a general concept. Most research on cooperation has implicitly assumed that a person's behaviour in one cooperative context is related to their behaviour in other settings, and at later times. However, there is little empirical evidence in support of this assumption. Here, we provide such evidence by collecting thousands of game decisions from over 1,400 individuals.    • Predictions under systematic variation?

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?

• The paper’s main measured outcomes are:

  – The authors sometimes refer to “success” in terms of payoff, and they discuss how payoffs correlate with action choices.  
  – They do not explicitly label “group efficiency” (i.e., total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff) but do compare payoff distributions across treatments.

  – Whether reward is enabled (Parameter 9) is implicitly “No.”

• The other parameters (3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15) are not implemented or systematically varied in any way.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when systematically varied?

• Strictly speaking, the paper does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters to see how the punishment treatment effect on payoff or efficiency changes.

• Hence, for none of the 15 parameters do they actually present a systematic variation and measured effect on punishment outcomes.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper, what would they be?

• The paper’s data show that under the single set of conditions tested (fixed punishment cost = 1, fixed magnitude = 4, repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma with a static network), adding punishment did not improve overall payoff relative to a no‐punishment static‐network scenario; in fact, it “diminished the benefits” of network reciprocity.

   • Simulations: the harm-to-cost ratio (6.35:1 baseline) was varied to 8:1 and 10:1 in robustness checks.  Authors state:  
     “Changing the punishment ratio … may change **levels** slightly but not the patterns …the difference between the No-monitoring and Single-monitoring conditions grows slightly in the low-MPCR treatment.’’  
     No numeric effect sizes and no efficiency calculation; still, the prediction is that varying the cost/harm ratio leaves the qualitative punishment treatment effect intact.

8. Punishment magnitude (harm to target)  
   • Directly tied to the cost schedule; magnitude is “10 % of gross earnings per point’’ in the lab.  Constant in the experiment.  
   • Varied only indirectly in the simulation robustness checks above.  Same comment as parameter 7.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • NEVER enabled.  No discussion.

10. Reward cost  
    • Not applicable.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Not applicable.

12. Do players know the number of rounds?  
    • YES – instructions state “The experiment is divided into 10 periods.”  
    • Not varied; no prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • YES – each subject sees every group member’s public and private investments after stage 1 and the total points awarded in stage 2.  
    • Not varied.

14. Do punished players learn the identity of punishers?  
    • They only see the **total** number of points received; identities are not revealed.  This is constant and never manipulated.

15. Do rewarded players learn the identity of rewarders?  
    • Not applicable (no rewards).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables actually analysed  
   – Individual contribution (main focus)  
   – Money spent on punishing  
   – Points received (severity of being punished)  
   – Change in contribution from t–1 to t  
   Group efficiency (total or average payoff divided by first-best) is **never calculated**.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are at least mentioned?  
   1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14  → 11 of 15 are mentioned in some form.  
   Only parameters 1 and 6 are deliberately varied in the experiment; parameters 7–8 are varied only in unreported simulation robustness checks.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss what happens to the punishment treatment effect when the parameter is **systematically varied**?  
   – Parameter 1 (group size): YES, but only for contributions, not for efficiency, and not as an interaction with the no-punishment baseline.  
   – Parameter 6 (MPCR): Contributions rise with MPCR, but again no explicit interaction with the punishment treatment.  
   – Parameters 7–8: Robustness simulations say qualitative punishment effect unchanged when the cost/harm ratio is moved to 8:1 or 10:1, but no numbers.  
   Hence at most **three** parameters (1, 6, 7/8) receive any statement about how their systematic variation might modify the punishment treatment effect, and only for contribution-based outcomes.

D. What predictions – limited strictly to the paper – can we make about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
   • The paper never measures efficiency, so direct quantitative predictions are impossible.  
   • Qualitatively, it suggests:  
     – Larger groups (5 → 10) will not reduce and may slightly enhance the efficiency gain from punishment, provided monitoring remains reasonably broad.  
     – A higher MPCR probably amplifies both contributions and the willingness to punish; it is *likely* (though untested) to enlarge the efficiency benefit of punishment because total surplus created by each contribution is larger.  
     – Making punishment cheaper and/or more damaging (higher harm-to-cost ratio) leaves the basic punishment effect intact, so efficiency changes little, although the gap between having and not having punishment might widen slightly when punishment is cheaper.  
   • For every other parameter (round length, chat, anonymity, rewards, information display, contribution granularity, framing), the paper gives **no evidence** on how they would move the efficiency impact of punishment.  Any forecast would therefore go beyond the article and must be left blank.

Abstract: One of the most elusive scientific challenges for over 150 years has been to explain why cooperation survives despite being a seemingly inferior strategy from an evolutionary point of view. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter rundown of (1) whether the paper by Wang et al. (cited as “Onymity promotes cooperation in social dilemma experiments”) mentions each of the 15 parameters (and if so, how), and (2) whether it contains any predictions about how systematically varying that parameter would affect the “punishment treatment effect” for any measured outcome. Throughout, “punishment treatment effect” is taken to mean how adding (or making use of) punishment changes outcomes relative to a setting without punishment, with special focus on efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned?  
     – The paper reports that 154 undergraduates participated (80 in T1—anonymous—and 74 in T2—onymous). However, it does not frame or systematically vary “number of players” as an experimental parameter.  
   • Predictions of effect if varied?  
     – None. No discussion of how changing group size would affect punishment’s impact on efficiency or any other outcome.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned?  
     – The paper uses an indefinite‐length repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma: in each pairwise interaction, there is a 75% probability of continuing to the next round, but the exact total number of rounds per interaction is not fixed and not known to participants in advance.  
   • Predictions of effect if varied?  
     – None. The authors do not systematically vary the number of rounds or predict how that variation would affect punishment’s role.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper never mentions any chat or communication channel except that in the “onymous” condition, participants see each other’s names.  
   • Predictions of effect if varied?  
     – None.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. This is a prisoner’s dilemma experiment with three discrete choices (cooperate, defect, punish). The authors do not discuss an “all or nothing” contribution rule.  
   • Predictions of effect if varied?  
     – None.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The experiment does not address any default choice. Each round, players explicitly choose among cooperate, defect, or punish.  
   • Predictions of effect if varied?  
     – None.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Mentioned?  
     – In the payoff matrix provided, cooperating costs 1 but gives the paired opponent 2. Defecting yields +1 to oneself and −1 to the opponent; punishing yields −1 to oneself and −4 to the opponent. However, the paper never refers to an explicit “marginal per capita return” or any multiplicative factor in the public‐goods sense; they present a 2 × 2 payoff structure adapted to a repeated PD with a punishment option, not a public goods game.  
   • Predictions of effect if varied?  
     – None. They do not systematically vary these payoff parameters.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. It is stated that punishing costs the punisher 1 unit. That value is used throughout.  
   • Predictions of effect if varied?  
     – None. The paper does not discuss changing this cost or any effect that might have on efficiency or the punishment treatment effect.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from the target per unit punished)
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. A punished player loses 4 units in the experiment.  
   • Predictions of effect if varied?  
     – None. The authors do not vary the magnitude of punishment or speculate about such variation.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The study only examines cooperation, defection, and punishment. There is no mention of a reward mechanism.  
   • Predictions of effect if varied?  
     – None.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Mentioned?  
      – No. As above, rewards do not feature in the design.  
    • Predictions of effect if varied?  
      – None.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward)
    • Mentioned?  
      – No. Same as above.  
    • Predictions of effect if varied?  
      – None.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Mentioned?  
      – Yes. Players do not know how many rounds each interaction will have; they only know that every round continues with 75% probability.  
    • Predictions of effect if varied?  
      – None. There is no systematic variation in “knowing the number of rounds.”

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained or lost)?
    • Mentioned?  
      – In both anonymous (T1) and onymous (T2), each participant sees the outcome of the last round and their own total payoff. The paper does not say that players see their partner’s entire payoff history, just the result of the previous round.  
    • Predictions of effect if varied?  
      – None. No systematic manipulation or predictions are presented on how revealing more or less outcome information might affect punishment’s impact.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Mentioned?  
      – Indirectly. In T2 (onymous treatment), participants see each other’s names and thus presumably can identify punishers more easily (since each round is between two named opponents). In T1, everything is anonymous, so they do not know exactly who the punisher is beyond the fact that “my current anonymous opponent punished me.”  
    • Predictions of effect if varied?  
      – None. The paper does not examine partial forms of punishment identification or how it alters the punishment effect on payoffs.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Mentioned?  
      – Not applicable. No reward scheme is used.  
    • Predictions of effect if varied?  
      – None.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper does not use the term “efficiency” in the sense of (actual total payoff)/(maximum possible payoff). Instead, it focuses on median payoff per round, overall payoff, and frequency of cooperation/defection/punishment. “Cooperation rate” and “frequency of punishment” are also key dependent variables. Thus:  
     – Dependent Variables in Paper: median payoff (or payoff per round), frequency of cooperation, frequency of defection, use of punishment.  
     – These are different from “efficiency” as defined in a typical public goods sense.  
   
B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
     1. Number of players (but not systematically varied).  
     2. Number of rounds (indefinite, 75% continuation chance).  
     6. Payoff setup akin to a PD (cooperation cost = 1, benefit = 2, etc.).  
     7. Punishment cost (1).  
     8. Punishment magnitude (4).  
     12. The number of rounds is not known to participants (indefinite).  
     13. Limited peer outcome display (players see their own payoff and the immediate result).  
     14. Identity of the punisher can be inferred in onymous treatment (where names are visible).  
   • Total: 8 parameters are mentioned in at least a descriptive sense. Note that none is varied systematically in the sense of “low vs. high cost of punishment,” “fewer vs. more players,” etc.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss the effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. The experiment does not systematically vary any of these parameters (e.g., no multiple cost levels, no multiple group sizes). There is no quantitative effect size reported for parameter manipulations other than comparing anonymity (T1) vs. onymity (T2). The difference between T1 and T2, however, focuses on revealing vs. concealing player identity; that factor is not among the 15 listed parameters in your question (it is closely related to #14, but the authors themselves do not frame it as a systematic variation of punisher identification alone—it also involves seeing names when cooperating or defecting).

D. If you were to make predictions on how these 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not discuss these parameters in a public‐goods‐game context or “efficiency” as you define it. Aside from stating that payoff (which you might loosely interpret as “effectiveness” or “benefit”) is not improved by punishment, the paper provides no direct theoretical or empirical basis for predicting how systematic changes in any of the 15 parameters would alter the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.  
   • Consequently, based strictly on this paper, no strong or specific predictions can be made for how these parameters would influence punishment’s impact on efficiency in a public goods game or even in the paper’s repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma setting.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Hence, the paper chiefly addresses anonymity vs. onymity and documents how removing anonymity promotes cooperation and payoff. It does not systematically vary or predict the influence of the 15 public‐goods‐game parameters listed in your query.

Abstract: Law backed by non-deterrent sanctions (mild law) has been hypothesized to achieve compliance because of norm activation. We experimentally investigate the effects of mild law in the provision of public goods by comparing it to severe law (deterrent sanctions) and no law.    • Mentioned? Yes. Three levels:

          • MildEnd accepted → 64% contribution, net efficiency ~62%.

          • SevereEnd accepted → 96% contribution, net efficiency ~96%.  
          • SevereEnd rejected → ~15% contribution in NoEnd(SEVERE).

    • Mentioned? No. The design has no reward option.

    • Mentioned? Indirectly. The paper clarifies it is a one-shot game known to participants (they know it ends immediately).  
    • Systematically varied or discussed regarding its effect on punishment treatment? No. It is simply fixed as a one-shot scenario.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much others gained or lost each round)?  
    • Mentioned? Not in the sense of real-time feedback. All decisions are anonymous, and the paper does not describe systematically displaying peer outcomes or varying the level of information about peer payoffs in any treatment.  
    • Systematically varied or discussed regarding its effect on punishment treatment? No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Mentioned? No. There is no “peer” punisher; it is a law that automatically deducts points from free-riders. The paper does not mention identifying any individual punisher.  
    • Systematically varied or discussed regarding its effect on punishment treatment? No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Mentioned? No. The paper involves no rewards at all.  
    • Systematically varied or discussed regarding its effect on punishment treatment? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • Yes. The authors measure both “gross” efficiency (based on contribution rates to the public good) and “net” efficiency (taking into account payoffs net of sanctions). They also measure individual contributions (cooperation) as a separate outcome. These dependent variables differ because high contributions can arise alongside punishment deductions, thus separating gross efficiency (contributions alone) from net efficiency (final payoffs after sanctions).

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned explicitly in some form:  
       1) Number of players (fixed at 3)  
       2) Number of rounds (fixed as a single, one-shot round)  
       6) MPCR (fixed at 0.5)  
       8) Punishment magnitude (0, 4, 14)  
     None of the other parameters (3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15) are discussed in any detail or systematically varied.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • Only parameter 8 (punishment magnitude) is systematically varied and linked directly to differences in contribution rate and efficiency (their main dependent variables).  
   • Although the paper also studies whether law is imposed exogenously or endogenously, that factor does not match any of the 15 listed parameters (it is a separate design factor in the paper).

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper only provides direct evidence for varying punishment magnitude (s = 0, 4, 14), showing that mild sanctions (4) do little to improve efficiency unless they are endogenously voted in, whereas severe sanctions (14) largely deter free-riding.  
   • For all other parameters (such as group size, number of rounds beyond one, use of chat, reward, revealing the punisher or rewarder, etc.), the paper does not provide discussion or data. Consequently, no predictions can be made about those parameters solely from what is reported in this paper.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

All statements above are taken strictly from the Tyran and Feld paper as provided, without reference to any external material or prior literature.

Abstract: An internal norm is a pattern of behavior enforced in part by internal sanctions, such as shame, guilt and loss of self-esteem, as opposed to purely external sanctions, such as material rewards and punishment. Public–goods‐type experiments are only touched on in passing in this review article.  
Except for a short textbook description of the “classical” public-goods game, no systematic manipulation of any game parameter is reported and no effect sizes are given.  Below each of the 15 parameters is examined strictly with respect to what appears in the paper.

─────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  The “classical experimental setup of the public-goods game” is said to have “four players”.  
   • Systematic variation / quantitative effect on a punishment treatment?  No.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  Repeated interaction is noted (“when the game is played repeatedly”), but the number of rounds is never stated.  
   • Systematic variation?  No.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned?  Not mentioned.  
   • Systematic variation?  No.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Mentioned?  Not mentioned.  
   • Systematic variation?  No.

5. Contribution default / endowment taken back?  
   • Mentioned?  Not mentioned.  
   • Systematic variation?  No.

6. MPCR (multiplication factor)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  The public pool is “doubled and divided equally”, so the marginal per-capita return is 0.5.  
   • Systematic variation?  No.

7. Punishment cost per unit  
   • Mentioned?  Costly punishment is repeatedly referred to (“costly punishment”, “the punisher bears the cost”), but no numerical value is provided.  
   • Systematic variation?  No.

8. Punishment magnitude per unit  
   • Mentioned?  Only conceptually (“sanction”, “chasing cleaners”), never quantified.  
   • Systematic variation?  No.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Mentioned?  The paper lists “reward” as one of several enforcement mechanisms, but gives no design details.  
   • Systematic variation?  No.

10. Reward cost per unit  
    • Mentioned?  Not quantified.  
    • Systematic variation?  No.

11. Reward magnitude per unit  
    • Mentioned?  Not quantified.  
    • Systematic variation?  No.

12. Do players know how many rounds remain?  
    • Mentioned?  Not mentioned.  
    • Systematic variation?  No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown / anonymity removed?  
    • Mentioned?  Yes.  It is stated that “making decisions anonymous leads in almost all conditions to a stark decrease in cooperation.”  
    • Systematic variation of anonymity?  The paper qualitatively contrasts anonymous vs. non-anonymous settings, but gives no numerical estimates and does not link it specifically to the *punishment* treatment effect.

14. Do punished players know the punisher?  
    • Mentioned?  Not mentioned.  
    • Systematic variation?  No.

15. Do rewarded players know the rewarder?  
    • Mentioned?  Not mentioned.  
    • Systematic variation?  No.

─────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used in the paper  
   • Group efficiency (total or average payoff): not analysed.  
   • Variables actually discussed: cooperation level (contribution levels), incidence of punishment/reward, reputation, success in cooperative tasks.  “Efficiency” is not equated with these variables, and no efficiency statistics appear.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   A total of 6:  
   (1) number of players (fixed at 4 in the textbook example);  
   (6) MPCR (fixed at 0.5 in the same example);  
   (7) punishment cost (qualitatively);  
   (8) punishment magnitude (qualitatively);  
   (9) presence of reward (qualitatively);  
   (13) anonymity vs. revealed behaviour (qualitatively).

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* that parameter on a punishment-treatment effect (for any dependent variable)?  
   Zero.  Only anonymity (13) is contrasted, but no systematic manipulation or quantitative impact on a punishment effect is reported.

D. Predictions that can be made about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency, based solely on this paper  
   The paper offers almost no basis for quantitative predictions.  Qualitatively one might infer:  
   • Having punishment available (regardless of its exact cost or magnitude) usually increases cooperation and therefore should raise efficiency.  
   • Removing social information (anonymity) undermines cooperation; thus parameter 13 (display of peer outcomes or identities) likely moderates the effectiveness of punishment.  
   Beyond these two broad statements the article contains insufficient information to predict how varying any of the 15 parameters or their interactions would change the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Abstract: We investigate the emergence and enforcement of contribution norms to public goods in homogeneous and heterogeneous groups. With survey data we demonstrate that uninvolved individuals hold well defined yet conflicting normative views of fair contribution rules related to efficiency, equality, and equity. In the experiment, in the absence of punishment no positive contribution norm is observed and all groups converge towards free-riding. With punishment, strong and stable differences in contributions emerge across group types and individuals in different roles. In some cases these differences result from the emergence of an efficiency norm where all fully contribute. In the cases where full efficiency is not attained, these differences result from the enforcement of different relative contribution norms. Hence, our experimental data show that, even in heterogeneous groups, individuals can overcome the collective action problem inherent in public good games by agreeing on and enforcing a contribution norm.
