Below each parameter is treated in the required “yes / no, value, predicted effect” format.  “Predicted effect” is understood as “what happens to the size (direction and, where possible, magnitude) of the punishment-treatment effect on **efficiency** (or whatever dependent variable the paper actually analyses) when the parameter is *systematically* varied”.  If the paper does not vary the parameter, or only mentions it in passing, this is stated explicitly.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
• Mentioned? Yes – every group has 3 players.  
• Systematically varied? No. The paper never explores 2-, 4-, …-player groups, so there is no prediction about how changing the group size would alter the punishment-treatment effect.  

2. Number of rounds  
• Mentioned? Yes – exactly 10 periods in every treatment.  
• Systematically varied? No.  No prediction given.  

3. Chat (pre-play or within-play communication)  
• Mentioned? No.  The word “chat”, “communication”, “cheap talk” or similar never appears in the design description.  
• Prediction? None.  

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
• Mentioned? Yes indirectly – subjects choose any integer amount between 0 and their individual upper bound; hence the game is NOT all-or-nothing.  
• Systematically varied? No.  No prediction.  

5. “Refund” or “default-contribution” framing (players decide how much to keep rather than how much to give)  
• Mentioned? No.  
• Prediction? None.  

6. Marginal Per-Capita Return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
• Mentioned? Yes – α = 0.50 for everyone in the “Equal”, “URE” and “UUE” groups; in “UMB” the high-benefit player has α = 0.75 while the two low-benefit players stay at 0.50.  
• Systematically varied? Partly – only one discrete change (0.50 → 0.75 for one role).  
• Observed / predicted effect on the punishment-treatment effect  
  – Without punishment, mean contribution of low players in UMB = 8.63 points; with punishment = 12.21 (+3.58).  
  – For high players in UMB the same comparison is 9.87 → 14.59 (+4.72).  
  – In “Equal” (α identical for all), the low-player lift is 4.21 → 16.22 (+12.01).  
  Thus when MPCR heterogeneity is introduced (α = 0.75 for one player) the *size* of the punishment-treatment effect on contributions falls sharply (roughly one-third of the lift achieved in the homogeneous game).  The paper never converts this into efficiency numbers, but it is clear that the *direction* is a reduction of the positive efficiency effect of punishment.  

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
• Mentioned? Yes – a punisher pays 1 point per point sent.  
• Systematically varied? No.  No prediction.  

8. Punishment magnitude (loss suffered by the target per unit sent)  
• Mentioned? Yes – the target loses 3 points per point received.  
• Systematically varied? No.  No prediction.  

9. Reward option available?  
• Mentioned? No – only punishment exists.  
• Prediction? None.  

10–11. Reward cost / reward magnitude  
• Not applicable.  

12. Is the horizon known?  
• Mentioned? Implicitly yes – subjects are told there are ten rounds (they answer comprehension questions about it).  
• Systematically varied? No.  No prediction.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
• Mentioned? Yes – after every contribution stage, each subject sees every group member’s contribution and period payoff.  
• Systematically varied? No.  No prediction.  

14. Is the identity of the punisher revealed?  
• Mentioned? Yes – explicitly *not* revealed (“subjects do not receive specific information concerning who punished whom”).  
• Systematically varied? No.  No prediction, and the authors give no speculation on what would happen if identities were disclosed.  

15. Is the identity of a rewarder revealed?  
• Not applicable (no rewards).  

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Use of “efficiency” as a dependent variable  
The paper talks extensively about the “efficiency norm” (i.e., everyone contributing fully) and labels groups that reach full contributions in ≥ 5 periods as “efficient”.  Nevertheless, the *reported dependent variables* are:  
 • Average contributions (by role and treatment)  
 • Amount of punishment points sent  
 • Binary classification of a group as “efficient” or “inefficient”  
 • Elicited normative judgments from the questionnaire.  
It never actually reports “total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff” in numbers, so “efficiency” in the strict sense is not an outcome variable; contribution is.  

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14 – nine parameters.  The other six (3, 5, 9–11, 15) are not mentioned.  

C. Which parameters are *systematically* varied and analysed for their impact on the punishment-treatment effect?  
Exactly one: parameter 6 (MPCR/benefit from the public good, via the UMB versus other group types).  No other parameter is varied, so for the remaining 14 there is no discussion of their causal impact on the punishment-treatment effect.  

D. Predictions that can be made (and their limits) based solely on the paper  
• Increasing heterogeneity in MPCR (giving one player a higher α) is likely to *dampen* the positive effect of punishment on group efficiency, because it dampens the increase in contributions produced by punishment (roughly one-third as big as in the homogeneous baseline).  
• Changing any of the other 14 parameters is outside the evidence base of the paper; therefore little or no prediction can be made about their influence on the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency.  One can merely note that punishment is highly effective when it can be applied at low cost (1) with a strong impact on the target (3), under anonymity, with full feedback on contributions, in a 3-player, 10-period game.  How that would change with different costs, magnitudes, group sizes, horizons, or information conditions remains open.
reference_APA: Reuben, Ernesto & Riedl, Arno (2013). Enforcement of contribution norms in public good games with heterogeneous populations. GAMES AND ECONOMIC BEHAVIOR.

1. Number of players

5. Contribution default rule  
   • Not mentioned; not applicable.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   • Not mentioned; not applicable.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   • Not explicitly discussed. The study recognises that the recipient, by rejecting, forgoes her own payoff (a cost), but this cost is not parameterised, varied, or analysed.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted per unit of punishment)  
   • Stated and varied indirectly through δ (the discount factor).  
        – Dictator game: δ = 1 → rejection cannot punish (magnitude = 0).  
        – Ultimatum game: δ = 0 → rejection removes the allocator’s entire offer (maximal magnitude).  
   • Effect of this variation (i.e., the “punishment treatment effect”) on the dependent variables actually analysed:  
        – Mean points kept by allocators fall from 64 (dictator) to 55 (ultimatum).  
        – Average change = -9.5 points to self; t(133)=6.5, Cohen’s d = 0.55.  
        – The size of this change is moderated by Honesty-Humility (β = -.20; unstandardised slope = -6.1 points per SD of Honesty-Humility).  
   • No efficiency measure is reported, so no efficiency effect is provided.

9. Reward enabled  
   • Not mentioned.

10. Reward cost  
    • Not mentioned.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Not mentioned.

12. Are the number of rounds known to players?  
    • Not mentioned; games are single-shot and presented as such, but this is not analysed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Not mentioned.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
    • Not applicable; recipients are hypothetical.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
    • Not applicable.


Summary

A. Use of “group efficiency” as a dependent variable?  
   No. The study reports (i) points allocated to self in each game, (ii) the mean of those two values, and (iii) the within-person difference between dictator and ultimatum allocations. These are distributional fairness measures, not efficiency (total or average payoff).

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
   Parameter 1 (players), Parameter 2 (rounds), and Parameter 8 (punishment magnitude/power via δ). 3 of 15 parameters are mentioned.

C. For which parameters is their *systematic variation* linked to the punishment treatment effect?  
   Only Parameter 8. The paper varies δ between 1 (no punishment) and 0 (maximal punishment) and quantifies how that shift changes behaviour. None of the other 14 parameters are systematically varied.

D. Predictions about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, based solely on this paper?  
   The paper offers virtually no leverage for predicting efficiency consequences, because (i) efficiency is never measured and (ii) only one parameter (punishment magnitude/power) is manipulated. All that can be inferred is that introducing a maximal, cost-imposing punishment opportunity (δ = 0) induces allocators to keep roughly 9–10 % fewer points for themselves, with the magnitude of this behavioural change shrinking as Honesty-Humility increases. No statements can be made about how any of the remaining 14 parameters—or interactions among parameters—would influence *efficiency* once punishment is introduced.

Below, each of the 15 design parameters is treated in turn.  
For every parameter I indicate (i) whether the review article ever mentions it and, if so, in what form, and (ii) whether the paper contains any prediction or empirical evidence about what happens when the parameter is systematically varied (especially with respect to the **punishment treatment effect**).  Citations refer to the page/paragraphs reproduced in the excerpt.

---------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
• Mentioned? Yes.  “Participants, usually in groups of between three and six…” (public-goods section).  
• Systematic variation? No.  The review supplies no comparison across different group sizes, hence no stated or implied effect on the punishment treatment effect (PTE).

2. Number of rounds  
• Mentioned? Yes.  The authors repeatedly contrast one-shot vs. repeated PGGs and also mention “large number of rounds” (Gächter et al. 2008).  
• Systematic variation? Partially.  
  – When the game is repeated, punishment “had effects over time, with players increasing their contributions after rounds of punishment” (Fehr & Gächter 2002).  
  – Punishment can eventually raise aggregate welfare “if the game is played for a large number of rounds” (Gächter et al. 2008), whereas in short or one-shot games it usually lowers welfare (Dreber et al. 2008; Ambrus & Greiner 2012).  
  – No numerical effect size is given, only the qualitative pattern above.

3. Chat enabled  
• Mentioned? No.  
• Systematic variation? No.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
• Mentioned? No.  
• Systematic variation? No.

5. “Reverse” PGG (contribution default)  
• Mentioned? No.  
• Systematic variation? No.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor  
• Mentioned? No.  
• Systematic variation? No.

7. Punishment cost (to the punisher)  
• Mentioned? Yes.  Punishment effects are “especially [large] when punishment was relatively cheap” (Egas & Riedl 2008; Nikiforakis & Normann 2008).  
• Systematic variation? Yes (qualitative only).  Lower cost → more punishment is used → higher contributions; the article does not state whether this raises efficiency, but it does imply that cheap punishment is more likely to change behaviour.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine inflicted)  
• Mentioned? Not directly; no manipulation or prediction reported.  
• Systematic variation? No.

9. Reward enabled  
• Mentioned? Briefly (“rewards and sanctions” in Walker & Halloran 2004).  
• Systematic variation? No explicit comparison of “punishment-only” vs “punishment + reward”, hence no prediction for the PTE.

10. Reward cost  
• Mentioned? No.  
• Systematic variation? No.

11. Reward magnitude  
• Mentioned? No.  
• Systematic variation? No.

12. End-round knowledge (do players know when the game ends?)  
• Mentioned? No explicit statement. One-shot vs final round behaviour is discussed, but horizon knowledge per se is not isolated as a parameter.  
• Systematic variation? No.

13. Peer outcomes displayed  
• Mentioned? No.  
• Systematic variation? No.

14. Punisher identity known  
• Mentioned? Yes, indirectly.  The review emphasises that in the canonical experiments “people can punish with impunity; that is, subjects cannot take revenge on the person who punished them… When subjects who are punished are permitted to punish the punishers, there is both less punishment and, consequently, less contribution…” (Nikiforakis 2008).  
• Systematic variation? Yes (qualitative).  Making the punisher identifiable and hence vulnerable to counter-punishment reduces both punishment and its effectiveness on cooperation; the article again does not provide numeric effect sizes nor efficiency figures.

15. Rewarder identity known  
• Mentioned? No.  
• Systematic variation? No.

SUMMARY  

A. Dependent variables in the paper  
• The review does refer to “aggregate welfare—overall payoffs” and to “group-wide outcomes”, which map directly onto the notion of efficiency.  
• More commonly it reports “contributions” or “cooperation rates”, and sometimes “punishment frequency”.  These variables are analytically distinct: contribution is the amount placed in the public account; efficiency is total pay-offs net of costs; punishment frequency is the behavioural mechanism, not the outcome.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned? 5 of them – #1, #2, #7, #9, #14.

C. Which parameters are discussed with respect to *systematic variation* in the punishment treatment effect? Only 3 –  
   • #2 (number of rounds: one-shot vs repeated; long vs short horizon),  
   • #7 (punishment cost: cheap vs expensive),  
   • #14 (identifiability of the punisher: impunity vs exposure to counter-punishment).  
   No numerical effect sizes are supplied.

D. What predictions can be made for efficiency based solely on this paper?  
• Long interactions (#2 high) slightly increase the chance that punishment eventually raises efficiency; short interactions mostly see efficiency fall.  
• Cheap punishment (#7 low) will more strongly raise contributions but may still reduce efficiency unless the horizon is very long.  
• Exposing the punisher’s identity (#14 identifiable) undermines both punishment use and its cooperative impact, so the PTE on efficiency should shrink or even reverse.  
• For the remaining 12 parameters the paper provides no direct information, so no evidence-based prediction can be made.

In short, the review gives only fragmentary guidance: horizon length, punishment cost, and protection of punishers jointly determine whether punishment will help or hurt efficiency; for all other design features the article is silent.

Below I go through the 15 parameters in the order given.  
For each parameter I state (i) whether the paper mentions the parameter and, if so, the value(s) it takes in the experiments that include punishment (i.e., a sanctioning institution) and (ii) whether the paper says anything about what would happen to the ***punishment-treatment effect*** (difference in outcomes between a baseline game and a game with peer punishment) if the parameter were systematically varied.  All numerical statements are taken directly from the text, tables or figures of the article.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (i) Mentioned.  All punish-ment designs reported by Ostrom et al. (1992, 1994) use eight players; the Casari & Plott (2003) replication also uses eight.  
   (ii) No systematic variation of group size is reported, hence no prediction about how changing group size would change the punishment-treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   (i) Mentioned: 20–30 rounds in total; punishment is introduced only after the first 10 rounds.  
   (ii) Not varied; no prediction offered.

3. Chat / face-to-face communication  
   (i) Mentioned.  Two punishment conditions are compared:  
        • “Sanctioning only’’ – no chat before sanctions (average gross group payoff = 39 % of the maximum; net payoff ≈ baseline once fees/fines are deducted).  
        • “Chat + sanctioning’’ – a single face-to-face meeting before sanctions (gross payoff = 85 % of the maximum; net payoff = 69 %).  
   (ii) Systematic variation: “no chat’’ vs “chat once before sanctioning.’’  The paper therefore predicts that enabling chat **increases** the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency by roughly +46 percentage-points of maximum possible pay-off (85 % – 39 %).  No finer-grained manipulation (multiple chats, length of chat, etc.) is reported.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
   (i) Tokens can be allocated continuously; the parameter is not discussed.  
   (ii) No prediction.

5. Contribution default / “take’’ frame  
   Not mentioned; no prediction.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   (i) A non-linear transformation function is fixed in every punishment experiment; it is never varied once punishment is available.  
   (ii) No prediction.

7. Punishment cost to assign one unit  
   (i) Systematically varied in the original sanctioning series: fees = \$0.05, 0.10, 0.20.  
   (ii) Reported effect: “Subjects assign more sanctions when the cost of sanctioning is lower.’’  Numerical efficiency figures broken down by each fee level are **not** given, so no numeric effect size on efficiency can be extracted.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine per unit)  
   (i) Systematically varied: fines = \$0.10 … \$0.80, generating fine-to-fee ratios from 2:1 up to 16:1.  Casari & Plott implement two regimes labelled “weak’’ and “strong’’ sanctions.  
        • Weak: efficiency rises above baseline but final numbers are not reported in the article (only that it is “closer to optimal’’).  
        • Strong: gross efficiency = 94 %, net efficiency after inspection fees = 76.9 %.  Baseline for the same subjects = 28.4 %.  
   (ii) Qualitative prediction: larger fines (or higher fine/fee ratios) induce more sanctioning and larger punishment-treatment effects on efficiency; very high inspection costs can undo part of the gain.  Quantitatively, in Casari & Plott moving from baseline to strong sanctions adds +65.6 percentage-points in gross efficiency (94 % – 28.4 %).

9. Reward option enabled  
   Not discussed.

10. Reward cost  
    Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude  
    Not discussed.

12. Finite horizon known to players  
    (i) Yes—subjects are told the total number of rounds; the parameter is fixed.  
    (ii) Not varied; no prediction.

13. Peer outcomes shown  
    (i) Baseline CPR game shows only the ***aggregate*** group investment; the punishment game reveals each individual’s investment so that others know exactly whom to sanction.  
    (ii) This shift is a prerequisite for punishment but is not itself systematically manipulated, so no separate prediction is offered.

14. Identity of punisher revealed  
    (i) In Casari & Plott the identity (and even the number) of inspectors is *not* revealed to the punished party.  In the original Ostrom et al. sanctioning design the article does not say whether identities are revealed.  
    (ii) No systematic variation, no prediction.

15. Identity of rewarder revealed  
    Not applicable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables  
    • Group efficiency (also called “percentage of the maximum” or “rent accrual”) – total group payoff divided by the theoretical maximum.  
    • Net efficiency – efficiency after subtracting the cost of monitoring, fees and fines.  
    • Individual or group contribution levels, defection rate, amount of sanctions imposed.  
    These measures are distinct: high contributions do not automatically imply high efficiency if sanctioning is excessively costly.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are *mentioned*?  
    Parameters 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14 are mentioned (9 of 15).

C.  For which parameters does the paper discuss how *systematic variation* changes the punishment-treatment effect?  
    • Parameter 3 (chat),  
    • Parameter 7 (punishment cost),  
    • Parameter 8 (punishment magnitude).  
    Thus 3 of the 15 parameters receive at least qualitative treatment; only Parameter 3 and the “weak vs strong’’ contrast under Parameter 8 allow a numerical change in efficiency to be read directly from the paper.

D.  Predictions one could make ***solely from this paper*** about how the 15 parameters and their interactions affect the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency  

    – Enabling even one brief round of face-to-face chat before punishment greatly amplifies the efficiency gain from punishment (≈ +45–50 pp of the maximum).  

    – Lowering the *cost* of punishing and/or increasing the *fine* (i.e., raising the fine-to-fee ratio) induces more punishment; in the one strong-versus-weak comparison available, moving to a stronger regime lifts gross efficiency by ≈ +65 pp (from 28 % to 94 %), though high monitoring fees can offset part of this gain in net terms.  

    – The paper offers **no evidence or predictions** about the effects of varying the other twelve parameters on the punishment-treatment effect.  Consequently, beyond the three points above, little or no prediction can be made from this source alone.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

 » Not mentioned. There is no experimental design or procedural detail on contributions from endowments.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
 » Not mentioned. The paper makes no reference to MPCR, multiplication factors, or how returns might be scaled in public goods contexts.

Abstract: Economic experiments have shown that punishment can increase public goods game contributions over time. However, the effectiveness of punishment is challenged by second-order free-riding and antisocial punishment. The latter implies that noncooperators punish cooperators, while the former implies unwillingness to shoulder the cost of punishment. Here, we extend the theory of cooperation in the spatial public goods game by considering four competing strategies, which are traditional cooperators and defectors, as well as cooperators who punish defectors and defectors who punish cooperators. Conversely, if synergistic effects are low and punishment is actively needed to sustain cooperation, antisocial punishment does is viable, but only if the cost-to-fine ratio is low. If the costs are relatively high, cooperation again dominates as a result of spatial pattern formation. A stable three-strategy phase that is sustained by the spontaneous emergence of cyclic dominance is also possible via the same route. The microscopic mechanism behind the reported evolutionary outcomes can be explained by the comparison of invasion rates that determine the stability of subsystem solutions. Below is a parameter-by-parameter summary of what (if anything) the paper says, followed by the four‐part summary requested. Throughout, note that the paper never reports results explicitly in terms of “efficiency” (i.e., actual total payoff / maximum possible total payoff). Instead, the authors focus on the stationary (long‐run) fractions of each strategy—cooperators, defectors, punishing cooperators, and punishing defectors—and how these fractions change as certain parameters (r, β, γ) vary.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned?  
     – The paper simulates a population arranged on an L×L lattice (with L ranging up to 6000).  
   • Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment?  
     – The paper does discuss that very small L can produce misleading results, but there is no systematic variation of “number of players” as an experimental variable. The authors do not report any numerical effect of changing the population size on the “punishment treatment effect,” nor do they frame results in terms of efficiency.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned?  
     – Not in the sense of a finitely repeated game. The paper uses an ongoing evolutionary model (Monte Carlo simulations) that runs until reaching a stationary solution, and does not treat the number of rounds as a systematically varied parameter.  
   • Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment?  
     – No mention.

3. Is chat enabled?
   • Mentioned?
     – No.  
   • Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment?
     – Not discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned?
     – Yes, in the sense that the model sets cooperators to contribute a fixed amount of 1, while defectors contribute 0. There is no option for in‐between contribution levels in this model.  
   • Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment?
     – The paper does not systematically vary this feature or discuss how moving away from all‐or‐nothing contributions would affect outcomes.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Mentioned?
     – No. There is no notion of a “default contribution” that players can move back into their private account.  
   • Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment?
     – Not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Mentioned?
     – Yes. The paper calls it r (the “multiplication factor”), and it is one of the main parameters they vary (e.g., r = 3.0 and r = 3.8 in most examples).  
   • Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment?
     – They do systematically vary r and show phase diagrams of strategies for different values of r (Figs. 1–3, 7). However, they do not measure “efficiency.” Instead, they report which strategies survive or go extinct. For example, they show that when r = 3.8 (where “network reciprocity” alone can sustain cooperation), antisocial punishment does not seriously hamper prosocial punishment. When r = 3.0 (where cooperation alone would ordinarily die out without punishment), second‐order free‐riding on antisocial punishment actually helps prosocial punishment survive.  
   – No numerical effect sizes on “efficiency” are given, only strategy‐fraction outcomes.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned?
     – Yes. Denoted by γ in the paper, referred to as the maximal cost of punishing.  
   • Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment?
     – The paper systematically varies γ (see the β–γ phase diagrams) and discusses how increasing or decreasing it affects which strategies persist (particularly the fraction of punishing cooperators vs. punishing defectors). They do not frame this in terms of total payoff or “efficiency,” but rather in terms of which mix of strategies (C, D, Pₐ, P_d) is stable. No explicit numerical “effect size” of γ on an efficiency metric is reported.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted per unit punishment)
   • Mentioned?
     – Yes. Denoted β, the maximal fine that can be imposed.  
   • Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment?
     – The paper systematically varies β (again see phase diagrams, e.g., in Figs. 1–2 for r = 3.8 and Figs. 3, 7 for r = 3.0). As β increases, prosocial punishment can become dominant at certain thresholds. But again, these threshold effects are described in terms of fraction of surviving strategies, not in terms of total efficiency or actual payoffs.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned?
     – No. The paper focuses solely on prosocial and antisocial punishment. Reward is mentioned only as background from other literature but not as part of the model or its results.  
   • Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment?
     – Not applicable.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Mentioned?
      – No.  
    • Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment?
      – Not applicable.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward)
    • Mentioned?
      – No.  
    • Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment?
      – Not applicable.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
    • Mentioned?
      – No. The model uses a stationary‐state evolutionary approach and does not treat knowledge of round endpoints.  
    • Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment?
      – Not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?
    • Mentioned?
      – No. The paper does not describe any display of how much each player gained or lost each round in a way that players “see” it.  
    • Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment?
      – Not discussed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Mentioned?
      – No.  
    • Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment?
      – Not discussed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Mentioned?
      – No, and rewarding is not part of the model.  
    • Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment?
      – Not applicable.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   – No. Although the basic notion of “payoff” exists, every result focuses on the stationary fraction of each strategy in the population. The key dependent variables in the paper are the long‐run densities (fractions) of nonpunishing cooperators, punishing cooperators, nonpunishing defectors, and punishing defectors. These fractions are not the same as group efficiency or total payoff.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   – The paper explicitly mentions and uses four of them:  
     (4) All‐or‐nothing contribution (by default in their model, though they do not vary it),  
     (6) Multiplication factor r,  
     (7) Punishment cost γ,  
     (8) Punishment fine β.  
   – The other 11 parameters in the list do not appear in the paper.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss the effect on the punishment treatment when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   – Only three are systematically varied:  
     • (6) r, the multiplication factor  
     • (7) γ, the punishment cost  
     • (8) β, the punishment fine  
   – The paper discusses how these three shape the existence of antisocial vs. prosocial punishment and how cooperators may or may not survive. It does not discuss these parameters’ impact on “efficiency” (actual payoff vs. maximum), but rather on the stationary fractions of each strategy.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   – Because the paper does not measure efficiency, it provides little direct guidance on how any of the 15 parameters affect actual total payoff or efficiency. All the reported results concern whether (and how) prosocial or antisocial punishment strategies survive in the evolutionary dynamics. One could infer that higher multiplication factors (r) and higher fines (β) at moderate costs (γ) help prosocial punishment become dominant; however, the paper never translates this into overall group efficiency. Thus, the paper itself offers almost no direct predictions about efficiency as traditionally defined.

Below I go through each of the 15 parameters exactly as requested.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1.  Number of players  
    • Mentioned? – Yes, several times.  
      – Stage A: Prisoner’s Dilemma is always played by 2 people.  
      – Stage B: PGG & PGP use 4; 3PDG uses 3; 3PPD uses 4; TG, DG, UG use 2.  
    • Systematic variation / predictions? – None. The numbers of players differ across games but are never experimentally varied nor linked to the “punishment treatment effect” (or to efficiency).

2.  Number of rounds  
    • Mentioned? – Yes.  The continuation probability δ differs between C-Culture (δ = 7/8, expected 8 rounds) and D-Culture (δ = 1/8, expected 1.14 rounds).  Total realised rounds ≈ 53 vs 51 in Exp. 1 and ≈ 40 in Exp. 2.  
    • Systematic variation / predictions? – The two δ values are part of the CCulture/D-Culture manipulation.  The paper reports that the high-δ setting produces much more Stage A cooperation (Figure 1; ≈ 80 % vs < 20 % by the end of Stage A).  However, no prediction is made about how further varying the number of rounds would influence the effect of adding punishment to a PGG or on efficiency.

3.  Chat enabled?  
    • Mentioned? – No.  No chat or communication channel is described.  
    • Systematic variation / predictions? – None.

4.  All-or-nothing contribution rule  
    • Mentioned? – No.  PGG and PGP allow a continuous contribution from 0-100 MU.  
    • Systematic variation / predictions? – None.

5.  “Contribution default” framing (take vs give)  
    • Mentioned? – No.  
    • Systematic variation / predictions? – None.

6.  MPCR / multiplication factor  
    • Mentioned? – Yes.  In both PGGs the factor is 1.6 (group of 4).  
    • Systematic variation / predictions? – Factor is fixed; no discussion of varying it.

7.  Punishment cost per unit  
    • Mentioned? – Yes.  In every punishment stage, 1 MU spent by a punisher (or rewarder) costs the punisher 1 MU.  
    • Systematic variation / predictions? – Cost is fixed; no analysis of what happens if it changes.

8.  Punishment magnitude per unit  
    • Mentioned? – Yes.  Each 1 MU spent removes 5 MU from the target.  
    • Systematic variation / predictions? – Fixed; no predictions for other magnitudes.

9.  Reward enabled?  
    • Mentioned? – Yes, only in the 3PPD game; reward is available in addition to punishment.  
    • Systematic variation / predictions? – Not varied (always allowed in 3PPD, never in PGP).  No predictions offered.

10. Reward cost  
    • Mentioned? – Yes, cost = 1 MU per rewarded unit.  
    • Systematic variation / predictions? – None.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Mentioned? – Yes, 1 MU granted increases the recipient’s payoff by 5 MU.  
    • Systematic variation / predictions? – None.

12.  Is the horizon known?  
    • Mentioned? – Implicit.  Stage A games end stochastically; subjects know the continuation probability but not the exact last round. No mention for PGG.  
    • Systematic variation / predictions? – None.

13.  Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mentioned? – Yes, in every round of Stage A subjects see both actions and earnings.  No special discussion for Stage B.  
    • Systematic variation / predictions? – None.

14.  Punishment anonymity (does target know punisher)?  
    • Mentioned? – Not stated.  Consequently no data.  
    • Systematic variation / predictions? – None.

15.  Reward anonymity (does target know rewarder)?  
    • Mentioned? – Not stated.  
    • Systematic variation / predictions? – None.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables used  
    • The paper never uses “group efficiency” (total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff) as an outcome.  
    • Main outcomes are:  
        – Stage A cooperation rate (% C decisions).  
        – Stage B transfers (fraction of endowment given in PGG, TG, DG, UG).  
        – Stage B punishment or reward (MU spent).  
        – Self-reported “inappropriateness” ratings.  
        – World-Values-Survey trust question.  
      These differ conceptually from efficiency because they focus on individual actions or expenditures rather than total earnings relative to the cooperative optimum.

B.  Parameters mentioned (value stated)  
    – 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13  → 9 of the 15.  
    – Parameters 3, 4, 5, 12, 14, 15 are not described (or only implicitly).

C.  Parameters whose systematic variation is analysed for their effect on ANY treatment effect  
    • None with respect to “introducing punishment” or efficiency.  
    • Parameter 2 (expected number of rounds via δ) is varied, and its impact on Stage A cooperation is quantified (≈ 80 % vs < 20 % cooperation), but the paper does not link this manipulation to the effect of punishment or to efficiency outcomes.  
    ⇒ 0 of the 15 parameters are systematically explored for their influence on a punishment treatment effect.

D.  Predicting the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency using only this paper  
    • The paper does not compare a “punishment” vs “no-punishment” public-goods game, nor does it compute efficiency.  Consequently it provides almost no direct guidance for predicting how any of the 15 parameters – singly or in interaction – would change the efficiency impact of adding punishment to a PGG.  
    • The only indirect hint is that when third-party punishment is possible (parameter set: cost = 1, magnitude = 5, anonymity unspecified) the willingness to punish depends on prior experience (C-Culture vs D-Culture).  One might tentatively predict that environments which foster cooperative norms (longer expected horizon, lower temptation) will enhance prosocial punishment and thereby have a better chance of raising efficiency when punishment is introduced.  Beyond that, the paper offers no systematic evidence.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Bottom line: The article is rich in behavioural results but it neither studies efficiency nor manipulates the 15 design features with respect to a punishment vs no-punishment comparison. Therefore it yields virtually no quantitative basis for forecasting how those features would alter the efficiency effect of introducing punishment in a public-goods game.

Abstract: Cooperation is crucial for the remarkable evolutionary success of the human species. Not surprisingly, some individuals are willing to bear additional costs in order to punish defectors. Below, “treatment effect of punishment” means the difference between a game with punishment (the adaptive-punishment model studied in the paper) and the same game without punishment (or, in some places, the previously studied “steady-punishment” variant).  
The requested dependent variable is efficiency, but the paper never measures efficiency. Every concrete result is expressed in terms of strategy frequencies (ρC , ρD) or phase boundaries. I therefore report the results exactly as they are stated, and note explicitly that no efficiency numbers are given.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECKLIST
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
 • Mentioned?  Yes.  The lattice contains L × L players (L from 200 to 7000).  
 • Systematically varied?  No.  L is changed only to avoid finite-size effects; no treatment effect is reported.

2. Number of rounds  
 • Mentioned?  Yes (“up to 10^7 Monte-Carlo steps”).  
 • Systematically varied?  No.

3. Chat enabled?  
 • Mentioned?  No.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
 • Mentioned?  Yes.  Players are either cooperators (contribute 1) or defectors (contribute 0); hence the game is all-or-nothing.  
 • Systematically varied?  No (always binary).

5. Contribution default / back-transfer?  
 • Mentioned?  No.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor r  
 • Mentioned?  Yes (called the “synergy factor” r).  
 • Systematically varied?  Yes.  r is the horizontal axis in all phase diagrams.  
 • Quantitative findings (all from Fig. 1):  
  – Without any punishment, cooperators survive only for r > 3.74 and dominate for r > 5.49 (values taken from text).  
  – With adaptive punishment, the critical r at which C survives is lowered.  Examples:  
   α = 0.1:  for every r there exists a Δ that produces full cooperation.  
   α = 1:  cooperators cannot survive below r = 2.48, no matter how large Δ is.  
   α = 2:  cooperators cannot dominate unless r ≥ 3.99.  
 • Effect on treatment:  Lower r (harder social dilemma) decreases the positive effect of punishment; higher r amplifies it.

7. Punishment cost per unit imposed (α Δ/k in the model, controlled by α)  
 • Mentioned?  Yes (parameter α).  
 • Systematically varied?  Yes.  Four values are analysed: α = 0.1, 0.5, 1, 2.  
 • Quantitative findings (again from Fig. 1):  
  – Low α (0.1) ⇒ even tiny Δ yields full cooperation.  
  – Moderate α (0.5) ⇒ a discontinuous jump to full C appears; e.g. at r = 1 the jump occurs at Δ ≈ 6.5.  
  – α = 1 sets the limit where fines equal costs; below r = 2.48 adaptive punishment fails at any Δ.  
  – α = 2 moves all C-only regions to r ≥ 3.99.  
 • Effect on treatment:  Raising α always weakens the punishment treatment effect.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine)  
 • Mentioned?  Yes.  The incremental step Δ determines the fine.  
 • Systematically varied?  Yes (vertical axis in Fig. 1).  
 • Quantitative findings (sampling from Fig. 1):  
  α = 0.5, r = 1  → C dominates for Δ > 6.5; mixed C + D for 2.7 < Δ < 6.5; D only below 2.7.  
  α = 1, r = 3  → mixed C + D above Δ ≈ 1.8; D only below.  
  α = 2, r = 4.5 → full C appears at Δ ≈ 1.8 (Fig. 4).  
 • Effect on treatment:  Larger Δ improves the punishment effect up to the point where cost (α) offsets it.

9. Reward enabled?  
 • Mentioned?  No.

10–11. Reward cost & magnitude  
 • Mentioned?  No.

12. Number of rounds known?  
 • Mentioned?  No (irrelevant for an infinite-horizon simulation).

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
 • Mentioned?  No.

14. Identity of punisher revealed?  
 • Mentioned?  No.

15. Identity of rewarder revealed?  
 • Mentioned?  No.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables actually used  
 • The paper does NOT use group efficiency (total or average payoff).  
 • Dependent variables used: stationary fractions of cooperators (ρC) and defectors (ρD); phase boundaries (type of absorbing state); qualitative spatial patterns (smooth vs. rough interfaces, cyclic dominance).  These differ from efficiency because they do not aggregate total payoffs; they measure who survives, not how large the pie is.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
 6 parameters: 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8.

C. Which parameters are systematically varied and their effect on the punishment treatment effect discussed?  
 3 parameters: 6 (synergy factor r), 7 (punishment cost α), 8 (fine size Δ).  
 No numerical efficiency effect sizes are available—only changes in survival or dominance of strategies.

D. If forced to predict the treatment effect on efficiency using only this paper:  
 • Higher r, larger Δ, and lower α should increase efficiency because they lead to full cooperation, and a fully cooperative group attains maximum possible payoff.  
 • All other listed parameters are never addressed, so no prediction can be supported for them.  
 • Interactions: α and Δ interact strongly (large fines help only if costs are not too high); r interacts with both (when r is high, even expensive punishment can pay off).  
 • Beyond these three variables the paper provides little or no guidance.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
Hence, only the multiplication factor (r), punishment cost (α), and punishment fine (Δ) are studied; everything else on the 15-item list is outside the scope of the article.

Authors: Price, ME; Cosmides, L; Tooby, J
Author Full Names: Price, ME; Cosmides, L; Tooby, J
Article Title: Punitive sentiment as an anti-free rider psychological device
Author Keywords: collective action; altruism; punishment; morality; cooperation; public goods; rational choice
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS; COOPERATION; RECIPROCITY; PUNISHMENT; ECONOMICS; MORALITY
Abstract: Those who contribute to a public good sometimes experience punitive sentiments toward others. But is the system that produces these sentiments an adaptation and, if so, which collective action problem was it designed to solve? Prior results from experimental economics show that acts of free riding are sometimes punished, that punishment deters free riding, and that the risk or actuality of punishment recruits higher levels of cooperation in a joint effort. This suggests that one function of punitive sentiments could be to recruit labor for collective actions. However, adaptations designed to cause participation in collective actions could not have evolved unless there were some mechanism that protected those who participated from having lower fitness than nonparticipating free riders. Therefore, a second possible function of punishment could be to eliminate or reverse fitness differentials that favor free rider designs over participant designs. To map the computational structure of this motivational adaptation (and hence identify its specific function) requires data that relate an individual's circumstances to his or her desire to punish. Herein, we report such data. The results indicate that the computational system that regulates one's level of punitive sentiment in collective action contexts is functionally specialized for removing the fitness advantage enjoyed by free riders rather than for labor recruitment or other functions. Results also support the hypothesis that a separate pro-reward motivational system exists that appears designed to handle the problem of labor recruitment. Rational choice counterexplanations for punitive sentiments were considered but eliminated on the basis of the evidence. (C) 2002 Elsevier Science Inc. All rights reserved.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter summary of what the paper by Ruff et al. (“Changing Social Norm Compliance With Noninvasive Brain Stimulation,” Science 342(6157): 482–484) does and does not say regarding (1) whether each parameter is mentioned at all (including any values used) and (2) whether the paper makes any predictions about what happens if one systematically varies that parameter—specifically with respect to the “punishment treatment effect.” Note that the paper’s main dependent variables are measures of norm-compliant behavior (transfers to another player), rather than group efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned status/value in paper: The experiment is framed as interactions between two individuals (Player A and Player B). Thus, two players interact in each decision round. 
   • Systematic variation or predictions regarding punishment effect: The paper does not systematically vary the number of players. No predictions are made about changing the number of players.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned status/value in paper: Although the experiment is repeated across multiple rounds, the paper does not specify the exact round count in the main text, nor does it highlight whether participants knew the total number of rounds.  
   • Systematic variation or predictions regarding punishment effect: None. The paper does not systematically vary or discuss how different numbers of rounds would affect punishment.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned status/value in paper: Not mentioned.  
   • Systematic variation or predictions regarding punishment effect: None.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned status/value in paper: Participants chose how many MUs to transfer, so there is a continuous choice from 0 up to the full amount they had received. This is not an “all or nothing” design.  
   • Systematic variation or predictions regarding punishment effect: None. The paper does not discuss varying whether the choice is “all or nothing.”

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much to move from a public fund back into their hand)?
   • Mentioned status/value in paper: Not mentioned. The paper does not discuss “default contributions” or a design in which participants “pull back” from a common fund.  
   • Systematic variation or predictions regarding punishment effect: None.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Mentioned status/value in paper: Not mentioned. The study setup involves transferring money to another player, not a classic public goods framework with a multiplication factor.  
   • Systematic variation or predictions regarding punishment effect: None.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned status/value in paper: The paper states that in punishment rounds, Player B can reduce Player A’s MUs, but no specific “cost” to Player B was provided.  
   • Systematic variation or predictions regarding punishment effect: None.

8. Punishment magnitude (the deducted coins per unit of punishment)
   • Mentioned status/value in paper: The paper indicates that Player B can reduce Player A’s MUs. It does not specify a per-unit magnitude or ratio by which B pays some cost to punish A.  
   • Systematic variation or predictions regarding punishment effect: None.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned status/value in paper: There is no mention of rewarding or “positive sanctions”; only punishment is considered.  
   • Systematic variation or predictions regarding punishment effect: None.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Mentioned status/value in paper: Not mentioned; no reward mechanism.  
    • Systematic variation or predictions regarding punishment effect: None.

11. Reward magnitude (the awarded coins per unit of reward)
    • Mentioned status/value in paper: Not mentioned; no reward mechanism.  
    • Systematic variation or predictions regarding punishment effect: None.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
    • Mentioned status/value in paper: Not mentioned in the paper.  
    • Systematic variation or predictions regarding punishment effect: None.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (i.e., do players see each other’s gains/losses)?
    • Mentioned status/value in paper: The paper does not discuss showing other participants’ detailed outcomes; it emphasizes “anonymous” play.  
    • Systematic variation or predictions regarding punishment effect: None.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Mentioned status/value in paper: The setting is described as “anonymous social interactions,” meaning the identity of the punisher is not revealed, but the paper does not systematically address different revelation regimes.  
    • Systematic variation or predictions regarding punishment effect: None.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Mentioned status/value in paper: Not applicable because no rewards are granted.  
    • Systematic variation or predictions regarding punishment effect: None.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────


SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper does not measure or discuss “group efficiency” or total/average payoffs as its main dependent variable. Its primary dependent variables focus on:  
     – Sanction-induced norm compliance (the difference in Player A’s transfer with vs. without punishment).  
     – Voluntary norm compliance (transfer in the baseline, no-punishment condition).

Article Title: Exploration dynamics in evolutionary games
Source Title: PROCEEDINGS OF THE NATIONAL ACADEMY OF SCIENCES OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
Author Keywords: cooperation; costly punishment; finite populations; mutation rates
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; COOPERATION; EMERGENCE
Abstract: Evolutionary game theory describes systems where individual success is based on the interaction with others. We consider a system in which players unconditionally imitate more successful strategies but sometimes also explore the available strategies at random. Most research has focused on how strategies spread via genetic reproduction or cultural imitation, but random exploration of the available set of strategies has received less attention so far. In genetic settings, the latter corresponds to mutations in the DNA, whereas in cultural evolution, it describes individuals experimenting with new behaviors. Genetic mutations typically occur with very small probabilities, but random exploration of available strategies in behavioral experiments is common. We term this phenomenon exploration dynamics'' to contrast it with the traditional focus on imitation. As an illustrative example of the emerging evolutionary dynamics, we consider a public goods game with cooperators and defectors and add punishers and the option to abstain from the enterprise in further scenarios. For small mutation rates, cooperation (and punishment) is possible only if interactions are voluntary, whereas moderate mutation rates can lead to high levels of cooperation even in compulsory public goods games. This phenomenon is investigated through numerical simulations and analytical approximations.

Authors: Baldassarri, D; Grossman, G
Author Full Names: Baldassarri, Delia; Grossman, Guy
Article Title: Centralized sanctioning and legitimate authority promote cooperation in humans
Source Title: PROCEEDINGS OF THE NATIONAL ACADEMY OF SCIENCES OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; EVOLUTION; INSTITUTIONS; ENFORCEMENT; EMERGENCE; WORLD
Abstract: Social sanctioning is widely considered a successful strategy to promote cooperation among humans. In situations in which individual and collective interests are at odds, incentives to free-ride induce individuals to refrain from contributing to public goods provision. Experimental evidence from public goods games shows that when endowed with sanctioning powers, conditional cooperators can discipline defectors, thus leading to greater levels of cooperation. However, extant evidence is based on peer punishment institutions, whereas in complex societies, systems of control are often centralized: for instance, we do not sanction our neighbors for driving too fast, the police do. Here we show the effect of centralized sanctioning and legitimate authority on cooperation. We designed an adaptation of the public goods game in which sanctioning power is given to a single monitor, and we experimentally manipulated the process by which the monitor is chosen. To increase the external validity of the study, we conducted lab-in-the-field experiments involving 1,543 Ugandan farmers from 50 producer cooperatives. This research provides evidence of the effectiveness of centralized sanctioning and demonstrates the causal effect of legitimacy on cooperation: participants are more responsive to the authority of an elected monitor than a randomly chosen monitor. Our essay contributes to the literature on the evolution of cooperation by introducing the idea of role differentiation. In complex societies, cooperative behavior is not only sustained by mechanisms of selection and reciprocity among peers, but also by the legitimacy that certain actors derive from their position in the social hierarchy.

Below is an item‐by‐item survey of whether (and how) the paper discusses each of the 15 parameters, followed by the required four‐part summary (A–D). Throughout, note that the paper’s main focus is on comparing a no‐punishment baseline to two centralized‐punishment regimes (randomly chosen monitor vs. elected monitor). Nowhere do the authors explicitly examine “efficiency” defined as (actual total payoff)/(maximum possible total payoff). Instead, their central outcome measure is the amount contributed to the public good (i.e., “contribution” or “cooperation”). They also use related measures such as “level of cooperation,” “compliance,” “responsiveness to monitors,” etc.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes, each session had 8–12 players.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how varying it affects the punishment treatment effect (for efficiency or any other outcome)?  
     – No. They needed at least eight participants for confidentiality reasons, but there is no systematic variation of group size in the design, and no predicted effect of changing group size.

2. Number of rounds
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. They ran six total rounds, with two “preliminary” rounds and four “post‐monitor” rounds.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how varying it affects the punishment treatment effect?  
     – No. They used six rounds for all sessions; there is no systematic manipulation of the number of rounds or discussion of how more or fewer rounds might affect results.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes, briefly: players were explicitly not allowed to talk once the game began.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how enabling/disabling chat would affect punishment treatment?  
     – No.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing,” or can participants contribute any amount?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – They used a standard public goods game with a continuous contribution choice (0–10 MUs). They do not force “all or nothing.”  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how changing to an all/nothing design would affect punishment treatment?  
     – No.

5. Is the contribution “default” (e.g., players must actively remove coins from a public fund)?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. They describe a typical setup: participants decide how to split each round’s 10 tokens between private and public accounts.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how that default might change the punishment treatment effect?  
     – No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. Contributions are doubled and then distributed evenly (“what is contributed to the public account is doubled…”).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how changing the multiplier would affect the punishment treatment effect?  
     – No.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes, the monitor can spend 1 MU to subtract 3 MUs from a targeted player.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how changing that cost would affect the outcome?  
     – No. The cost is fixed at 1 MU per act of sanction.

8. Punishment magnitude
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes, each “punishment” imposed by the monitor deducts 3 MUs from the punished player.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how changing that magnitude would affect the outcome?  
     – No. They set it at a 1‐to‐3 ratio and do not manipulate it.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – The authors reference prior literature where peer reward can matter, but they do not include a reward condition in their own design.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how adding a reward would affect the outcome?  
     – No.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – No, because there is no reward condition in the study.  
    • Does the paper systematically vary it?  
      – No.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – No, because there is no reward mechanism in their design.  
    • Does the paper systematically vary it?  
      – No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – They do not explicitly say whether participants were told there would be exactly six rounds, beyond describing the overall procedure.  
    • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict different effects for known vs. unknown end‐rounds?
      – No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see others’ gains/losses each round)?
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – They do not systematically discuss what exact payoff information participants saw, apart from stating that the game was played publicly, with the monitor’s identity known.  
    • Does the paper systematically vary it or discuss how changing that visibility might affect punishment outcomes?  
      – No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – Yes; there is a single monitor in centralized sanction conditions, so all players necessarily know who punished them. The authors mention that the monitor’s identity was public.  
    • Does the paper systematically vary punisher anonymity or make a prediction about the effect of changing that parameter?  
      – No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – No; no reward mechanism exists in this experiment.  
    • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict its effect?
      – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?  
   • The paper does talk generally about “efficiency,” “effectiveness,” or “advantage” of centralized sanctioning in a conceptual sense (especially to avoid overpunishment). However, the actual measured outcomes focus on:  
     – Contribution to the public good (i.e., how many tokens participants allocate to the group account each round), before and after monitors are introduced.  
     – Participants’ reactions to sanctioning and their “deference” to legitimate authority.  
   • The authors do not present the ratio of realized total payoff to maximum payoff (the user’s “efficiency” definition). Thus, “efficiency” in the paper’s text is not the same as the user’s requested outcome measure. The main dependent variables are:  
     – Individual contribution levels,  
     – Changes in contributions when punishment is introduced,  
     – Changes in contributions after being punished (“reaction to punishment”).

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned explicitly or implicitly:  
     (1) Number of players (8–12),  
     (2) Number of rounds (6),  
     (3) No opportunity to chat,  
     (4) Choice is not “all or nothing,”  
     (6) Multiplication factor of about 2,  
     (7) Punishment cost (1 MU),  
     (8) Punishment magnitude (3 MUs subtracted from the punished).  
   • A few others (such as 14: punisher identity is known) are mentioned in passing as part of design details.  
   • Altogether, the paper touches on various aspects of parameters 1–4, 6–8, and 14 (though primarily as design features, not as systematically manipulated factors).  
   • The rest (5, 9–13, 15) are not part of the design, or not discussed beyond a cursory mention (for instance, “reward” is mentioned only in background literature).

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The paper does NOT systematically vary any of the 15 parameters listed.  
   • Hence, it makes no direct predictions about how changing, for example, group size, cost‐to‐punish, number of rounds, or anonymity of punisher, would quantitatively shift the effect of punishment on any dependent variable.  
   • Therefore, the answer here is: none are systematically varied, so none have a tabulated or predicted numeric effect in this paper.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper, what would they be?  
   • Since the paper neither measures nor systematically analyzes “efficiency” in the sense of actual‐vs.‐maximum payoff, and since they do not systematically manipulate the 15 parameters, there is almost no direct basis for making specific predictions.  
   • The authors’ main point is that letting a central monitor punish defectors increases cooperation more than no punishment at all, and that “legitimacy” of punishment authority adds an incremental boost. However, that finding is tied to a single fixed cost‐and‐impact (1‐to‐3) punishment design, with a standard public goods multiplier of 2.  
   • Consequently, given the paper alone, one can say little or nothing about how the 15 parameters—and especially their interactions—might drive or dampen effects on efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Authors: Raihani, NJ; Thornton, A; Bshary, R

Article Title: Punishment and cooperation in nature
Keywords Plus: CLEANER FISH; EVOLUTIONARY STABILITY; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; STRONG RECIPROCITY; SERVICE QUALITY; PARTNER CONTROL; BEHAVIOR; MUTUALISM; MECHANISMS; DEFECTION
Abstract: Humans use punishment to promote cooperation in laboratory experiments but evidence that punishment plays a similar role in non-human animals is comparatively rare. In this article, we examine why this may be the case by reviewing evidence from both laboratory experiments on humans and ecologically relevant studies on non-human animals. Generally, punishment appears to be most probable if players differ in strength or strategic options. Although these conditions are common in nature, punishment (unlike other forms of aggression) involves immediate payoff reductions to both punisher and target, with net benefits to punishers contingent on cheats behaving more cooperatively in future interactions. In many cases, aggression yielding immediate benefits may suffice to deter cheats and might explain the relative scarcity of punishment in nature.

Below each of the 15 design parameters I quote or paraphrase every place in the paper that is relevant, then state whether the authors (i) merely mention the parameter, and (ii) give any explicit prediction about what would happen if the parameter were *systematically varied* (especially with respect to a punishment-vs-no-punishment treatment and, where possible, to **efficiency**).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
• Repeated throughout (e.g. “Punishment is most likely to evolve in … *symmetric n–player public-goods games or in asymmetric two-player* interactions”).  
• Systematic-variation prediction: Yes – the paper predicts that moving from 2-player to n-player interactions will *increase* the probability that punishment is used and will therefore enhance its “cooperation‐enforcing” effect. No numerical effect size is given and no statement is made about net **efficiency** (costs of punishment could offset gains).  

2. Number of rounds (time horizon)  
• “Short time horizons mean there are fewer opportunities for the punisher to benefit… whereas the net benefit … might be higher in more stable relationships.”  
• Systematic-variation prediction: Yes – more rounds (longer horizon) should strengthen the punishment treatment effect. No numbers; efficiency not explicitly computed.  

3. Chat enabled  
• Not mentioned.  No prediction.  

4. Contribution ‘all-or-nothing’ vs continuous  
• Section “Cheating: discrete or continuous?” – Punishment “most likely to occur where cheating is a discrete event”.  
• Systematic-variation prediction: Yes – making cooperation binary (all-or-nothing) should *increase* the effectiveness and use of punishment; making it continuous should decrease it. No numbers and no direct statement about efficiency.  

5. Contribution default / back-transfer design  
• Not mentioned.  No prediction.  

6. Marginal Per-Capita Return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
• Non-linear vs linear benefit functions are discussed (Volunteer’s Dilemma vs NPD), but the actual MPCR or factor is never specified, nor is it systematically varied.  No prediction.  

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
• Mentioned generically (“paying a small fee to impose a larger fine”).  
• Systematic-variation prediction: No quantitative prediction; only the qualitative point that high costs make punishment less beneficial. No numbers and nothing tied to efficiency.  

8. Punishment magnitude (fine suffered per unit)  
• Same generic wording (“larger fine”); Figure I in Box 2 shows a step-function benefit once the fine is large enough to cross a threshold.  
• Systematic-variation prediction: Qualitative – raising magnitude above the threshold yields no further benefit; below threshold yields none. No numbers, no efficiency statement.  

9. Whether a reward option exists  
• Not mentioned.  No prediction.  

10. Reward cost  
• Not mentioned.  No prediction.  

11. Reward magnitude  
• Not mentioned.  No prediction.  

12. Whether the number of rounds is known (end-game knowledge)  
• Not addressed.  No prediction.  

13. Whether peer outcomes are shown  
• Not addressed.  No prediction.  

14. Whether the punished player knows *who* punished her  
• Centralised vs peer punishment is discussed, but specific information disclosure is not.  No prediction.  

15. Whether the rewarded player knows the rewarder  
• Not mentioned.  No prediction.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY  

A. Dependent variables  
The review talks about (i) cooperation / contribution levels, (ii) punishment frequency, (iii) pay-offs of punishers vs non-punishers, and (iv) sometimes “net benefits”.  The paper never reports or analyses *group efficiency* (total payoff divided by the cooperative maximum). Efficiency therefore differs from the variables the authors actually use.

B. Parameters mentioned  
The text refers to 6 of the 15 parameters: 1, 2, 4, 7, 8, and—very indirectly—centralisation connected to 14.  The remaining 9 parameters are never discussed.

C. Parameters whose *systematic* variation is discussed  
Four parameters (1, 2, 4, 8) are the subject of explicit qualitative predictions.  None of the predictions are backed by numeric effect sizes or by efficiency data.

D. Plausible predictions for the punishment treatment effect on **efficiency**, using only the paper  

• More players (1) → likely stronger cooperation-boost from punishment; whether net efficiency rises depends on how large punishment costs are relative to the extra public-good benefit, which the paper does not quantify.  
• Longer horizons (2) → should increase efficiency gains from punishment because costs can be amortised over more rounds.  
• Discrete/all-or-nothing contributions (4) → punishment more effective; hence larger efficiency gain than in continuous games.  
• Very low punishment fines (8) → no effect; moderate fines above the “threshold” → positive effect; higher still → no further gain but added efficiency loss from cost.  
For all other parameters the paper supplies too little information to support any prediction.

Author Full Names: Szolnoki, Attila; Perc, Matjaz
Article Title: Correlation of Positive and Negative Reciprocity Fails to Confer an Evolutionary Advantage: Phase Transitions to Elementary Strategies
Keywords Plus: ANTISOCIAL PUNISHMENT; PROMOTE COOPERATION; COSTLY PUNISHMENT; SOCIAL NETWORKS; HUMAN-BEHAVIOR; EMERGENCE; DYNAMICS; GAMES; PLAY
Abstract: Economic experiments reveal that humans value cooperation and fairness. Punishing unfair behavior is therefore common, and according to the theory of strong reciprocity, it is also directly related to rewarding cooperative behavior. However, empirical data fail to confirm that positive and negative reciprocity are correlated. Inspired by this disagreement, we determine whether the combined application of reward and punishment is evolutionarily advantageous. We study a spatial public goods game, where in addition to the three elementary strategies of defection, rewarding, and punishment, a fourth strategy that combines the latter two competes for space. We find rich dynamical behavior that gives rise to intricate phase diagrams where continuous and discontinuous phase transitions occur in succession. Indirect territorial competition, spontaneous emergence of cyclic dominance, as well as divergent fluctuations of oscillations that terminate in an absorbing phase are observed. Yet, despite the high complexity of solutions, the combined strategy can survive only in very narrow and unrealistic parameter regions. Elementary strategies, either in pure or mixed phases, are much more common and likely to prevail. Our results highlight the importance of patterns and structure in human cooperation, which should be considered in future experiments.
