Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter summary based exclusively on the content of the provided paper by Szolnoki and Perc (2013). Throughout, please note that the paper focuses on evolutionary outcomes (which strategies persist in the population) rather than on group efficiency or total/average payoff. Where the paper does not address a parameter or its systematic variation directly, that is stated explicitly.

──────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
• Discussed? The paper uses large square lattices (up to L=7200 on a side), but it does not systematically vary “number of players” as a variable in order to study any treatment effect. The only mention of different system sizes is to check finite‐size effects.  
• Effect of systematically varying it? Not discussed. No results are given on how changing the number of players affects punishment or any other strategy.

2. Number of rounds
• Discussed? Not in the sense of a repeated‐game count. The evolutionary model proceeds for many Monte Carlo steps until a stationary state is reached, but the paper does not interpret this in terms of a finite or varying “number of rounds.”  
• Effect of systematically varying it? Not discussed.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
• Discussed? No. There is no mention of communication or chat in the model; it is strictly an evolutionary game on a lattice without player communication.  
• Effect of systematically varying it? Not discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
• Discussed? Indirectly yes: each cooperator contributes exactly 1 to the public good, while defectors contribute 0. Hence, in effect, the game is “all or nothing” from the outset.  
• Effect of systematically varying it? Not discussed. The authors fix contribution to 1 for all cooperators and do not report any attempt to vary this design.

5. Is the contribution default?
• Discussed? No. The paper does not address any default or continuous contribution decisions; cooperation always means contributing one fixed unit.  
• Effect of systematically varying it? Not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor
• Discussed? Yes. In this paper, the “synergy factor” r has the same role as the multiplier for the public good. The authors examine its values relative to thresholds (3.74, 5.49) where cooperators can survive or outcompete defectors if no punishment/reward is present. The paper highlights two primary cases: r=4.5 (“lenient conditions”) and r=2.5 (“harsh conditions”).  
• Effect of systematically varying it? The paper does show that at r=4.5, punishment alone generally outperforms combined strategies except in extremely narrow parameter regimes, and at r=2.5, a cyclic dominance among defectors, punishers, and the combined strategy can arise, again in specific ranges of cost and fine/reward. However, these findings concern strategy fractions rather than group efficiency. No numerical effect sizes for “efficiency” are given.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
• Discussed? Yes. Denoted by γ (gamma). Punishers pay cost γ/(G–1) per defector in their group. The paper systematically varies γ in phase diagrams.  
• Effect of systematically varying it? The authors track changes in stable strategy configurations—e.g., which strategies die out—rather than an “efficiency” outcome. They do not present a numeric effect of γ on “punishment treatment effect” in terms of total payoff or efficiency, only how γ shapes the presence or absence of punishing or combined strategies.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
• Discussed? Yes. Denoted by β (beta). Defectors incur cost β/(G–1) from each punisher. The paper systematically varies β (together with γ) in phase diagrams.  
• Effect of systematically varying it? As with γ, the paper focuses on how varying β changes which strategies (D, P, R, B) survive, rather than any explicit measure of group efficiency. No numeric effect size on efficiency is reported.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
• Discussed? The model includes two “rewarding” strategies (R and B). However, the authors do not treat “reward on vs. reward off” as a single toggle; rather, it is part of the four‐strategy setup (defect, punish, reward, or both). They do mention “in the absence of reward and punishment” only as a baseline.  
• Effect of systematically varying it? Not in the sense of toggling it on or off across conditions. Hence, there is no reported numeric effect on efficiency from enabling reward.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
• Discussed? Yes. The same parameter γ is used for the cost of punishing or rewarding. Again, they systematically vary γ but discuss outcomes in terms of stable strategy patterns, not efficiency.  
• Effect of systematically varying it? Same as parameter #7—no measure of “efficiency” is given.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)
• Discussed? Yes. The same parameter β is used for the reward an R or B cooperator pays to others. The paper systematically varies β, focusing on strategy fractions in the final population.  
• Effect of systematically varying it? The authors explore how different β values affect whether punishers, rewarders, or a combined strategy can survive. No explicit mention of efficiency or total payoff.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
• Discussed? No. This is purely a spatial evolutionary game; there is no mention of whether participants (there are no human participants here) do or do not know how many rounds remain.  
• Effect of systematically varying it? Not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much others gained/lost each round)?
• Discussed? No. There is no mention of any information display among real participants—these are simulations with deterministic payoff calculations.  
• Effect of systematically varying it? Not discussed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the punisher is?
• Discussed? No. The paper does not incorporate such informational details.  
• Effect of systematically varying it? Not discussed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is?
• Discussed? No. The paper does not incorporate such information.  
• Effect of systematically varying it? Not discussed.

──────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
No. The paper tracks which strategies (defect, punish, reward, or both) survive to form the stationary state. While individual or group payoffs are part of the game mechanics, the primary reported dependent variables are the stationary strategy fractions or phases (D, P, R, and B). These fractions differ from the concept of “group efficiency.”

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
Mentioned in some way:  
• #4 is implicitly fixed at “all or nothing” (not varied).  
• #6 (synergy factor r).  
• #7 (punishment cost γ).  
• #8 (punishment magnitude β).  
• #9, #10, #11 (rewarding is included via the same β and γ).  
The remaining parameters (#1, #2, #3, #5, #12–#15) are not addressed.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
They systematically vary (1) r (comparing r=4.5 vs. r=2.5), (2) γ (punishment/reward cost), and (3) β (punishment/reward magnitude). However, they do not measure a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Instead, they examine how these parameters alter final strategy compositions. No numerical effect sizes are linked to efficiency, only to which strategy or combination of strategies eventually takes over.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
Because the paper focuses on final strategy fractions rather than payoff‐based efficiency, it offers no direct evidence for how group efficiency changes with the 15 parameters. The chief insight is that punishment alone tends to outperform combined punishment‐and‐reward when running evolutionary simulations, except in narrow parameter regions. Absent specific numerical results on total payoff, one cannot draw strong conclusions about efficiency. Thus, there is little basis in this paper to predict how systematically changing each of the 15 parameters would alter the effect of punishment on group efficiency.

Authors: Kosfeld, M; Okada, A; Riedl, A
Author Full Names: Kosfeld, Michael; Okada, Akira; Riedl, Arno
Article Title: Institution Formation in Public Goods Games
Keywords Plus: PUNISHMENT; RECIPROCITY; PROVISION; MECHANISM; FAIRNESS; COOPERATION; COMPETITION; ALLOCATION; SANCTIONS; ECONOMICS
Abstract: Sanctioning institutions are of utmost importance for overcoming free-riding tendencies and enforcing outcomes that maximize group welfare in social dilemma situations. We investigate, theoretically and experimentally, the endogenous formation of institutions in public goods provision. Our theoretical analysis shows that players may form sanctioning institutions in equilibrium, including those governing only a subset of players. The experiment confirms that institutions are formed and that it positively affects cooperation and group welfare. However, the data also shows that success is not guaranteed. Players are unwilling to implement equilibrium institutions in which some players have the opportunity to free ride. Our results emphasize the role of fairness in the institution formation process. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter discussion, drawn strictly from the paper’s content (including its figures and tables), followed by the requested four‐part summary.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned? Yes. The experiment (Section II) uses groups of four players (n = 4).  
   • Systematically varied? No. All sessions use four‐player groups; the paper does not examine different group sizes.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (efficiency or otherwise)? Not discussed, because n is fixed at 4 in all treatments.  

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each experimental session spans 20 rounds (Section II).  
   • Systematically varied? No. It is always 20; the paper does not test other numbers of rounds.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (efficiency or otherwise)? Not discussed in terms of systematically varying the round count.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned? No. There is no indication that participants could communicate via free‐form chat.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (efficiency or otherwise)? Not discussed.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned? Partially. If an organization is implemented, its members must contribute their full endowment (p. 9–10). Nonmembers remain free to contribute any amount from 0 to w. Thus, for members, contribution is effectively “all” once they have joined the institution.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (efficiency or otherwise)? The paper does not study how changing from continuous to strictly all‐or‐nothing choices would affect punishment’s impact.  

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much of their endowment to move back)?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not discuss preset contribution defaults.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (efficiency or otherwise)? Not discussed.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper explicitly varies MPCR as a = 0.4 vs. a = 0.65 (Sections IIA–IIB).  
   • Systematically varied? Yes, these two values define the main “IF40” and “IF65” treatments.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (efficiency or otherwise)?  
     – The paper measures overall efficiency (group payoff as a fraction of the maximum) in an institution‐formation (punishment‐enabled) condition versus a control.  
     – For a = 0.4: Control group efficiency ≈ 25%, institution‐formation group efficiency ≈ 51% (p. 17–19).  
     – For a = 0.65: Control group efficiency ≈ 62%, institution‐formation group efficiency ≈ 70%.  
     – Thus, when punishment institutions are available, the increase in overall efficiency (relative to having no institution) appears larger at MPCR = 0.4 than at MPCR = 0.65 in absolute percentage‐point terms.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned? No. The experiment models punishment as centrally imposed with no explicit per‐unit cost to a peer “punisher.” Instead, each organization member shares a fixed total cost c = 2 of forming the institution (Sections I and II). There is no separate “punisher‐pays” parameter.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (efficiency or otherwise)? Not discussed.  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player per unit of punishment)
   • Mentioned? Yes. Once the institution is formed, if a member contributes less than w, their punishment equals w − gᵢ. (Equation (3), p. 5–6).  
   • Systematically varied? No. It is always that the shortfall from the full contribution is deducted.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (efficiency or otherwise)? The paper does not examine how alternative punishment formulas might alter the results.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned? No. The paper considers only a “punishing” institution.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (efficiency or otherwise)? Not discussed.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Mentioned? No. Only punishment is studied.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment (efficiency or otherwise)? Not applicable.  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward granted)
    • Mentioned? No. Only punishment is studied.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment (efficiency or otherwise)? Not applicable.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Mentioned? Yes. Subjects know that there are 20 rounds (Section II).  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment (efficiency or otherwise)? Not discussed in terms of systematically changing the horizon.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost each round)?
    • Mentioned? Partially. After each round, participants learn whether an institution was formed and see group contribution information (p. 8–9). However, the experiment does not systematically vary how or how much detail is displayed.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment (efficiency or otherwise)? Not discussed as a variable.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Mentioned? No. Punishment is enforced by a central “sanctioning organization,” not by a specific peer. The paper does not discuss revealing “who” sanctioned a free‐rider.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment (efficiency or otherwise)? Not discussed.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Mentioned? No. Rewards are not part of the design.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment (efficiency or otherwise)? Not applicable.  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Summary

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • Yes. The paper measures “efficiency” (group payoff relative to the maximum possible) and also discusses contribution levels. Contribution rate and overall efficiency often move in the same direction, but the paper explicitly tracks both.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned parameters:  
     1) Number of players (always four)  
     2) Number of rounds (always 20)  
     4) Contribution is effectively “all” for members once they join the institution  
     6) MPCR/multiplication factor (0.4 vs. 0.65)  
     8) Punishment magnitude (shortfall from full contribution)  
     12) Number of rounds is known  
     13) Some information on outcomes is shown (though not varied)  
   • Hence, 7 of the 15 parameters appear explicitly in the design or discussion.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Only parameter #6 (MPCR) is systematically varied (0.4 vs. 0.65). The paper shows that enabling punishment/organization formation improves efficiency substantially at both MPCR levels, but the absolute increase from no‐punishment control to punishment‐enabled is larger (in percentage‐point terms) at MPCR = 0.4 (25% to 51% efficiency) than at MPCR = 0.65 (62% to 70% efficiency). No other parameters are experimentally manipulated to gauge different impacts on punishment.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The only concrete predictions the paper gives come from varying the MPCR. The authors find that the option of forming a sanctioning institution raises efficiency more substantially (in absolute terms) at the lower MPCR (0.4), though efficiency in the no‐punishment baseline was also lower there.  
   • Apart from that, the paper does not make predictions about systematically altering the other parameters (e.g., group size, visibility of punisher, or a reward system). The experiment does not vary those features, so little or no firm prediction is possible for them based on this paper alone.

Authors: Arechar, AA; Gächter, S; Molleman, L
Author Full Names: Arechar, Antonio A.; Gaechter, Simon; Molleman, Lucas
Article Title: Conducting interactive experiments online
Author Keywords: Experimental methodology; Behavioral research; Internet experiments; Amazon Mechanical Turk; Public goods game; Punishment
Keywords Plus: MECHANICAL TURK; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; LAB; COOPERATION; POPULATION
Abstract: Online labor markets provide new opportunities for behavioral research, but conducting economic experiments online raises important methodological challenges. This particularly holds for interactive designs. In this paper, we provide a methodological discussion of the similarities and differences between interactive experiments conducted in the laboratory and online. To this end, we conduct a repeated public goods experiment with and without punishment using samples from the laboratory and the online platform Amazon Mechanical Turk. We chose to replicate this experiment because it is long and logistically complex. It therefore provides a good case study for discussing the methodological and practical challenges of online interactive experimentation. We find that basic behavioral patterns of cooperation and punishment in the laboratory are replicable online. The most important challenge of online interactive experiments is participant dropout. We discuss measures for reducing dropout and show that, for our case study, dropouts are exogenous to the experiment. We conclude that data quality for interactive experiments via the Internet is adequate and reliable, making online interactive experimentation a potentially valuable complement to laboratory studies.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter inventory of what the paper does (and does not) say about each of the 15 parameters and whether the authors systematically varied that parameter to test its impact on punishment’s effect on any outcome variable. At the end is the requested four-part summary (A–D).

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter (and its value)?  
     – Yes. The experiment is explicitly described as a “repeated four-person public goods game.” Thus, the number of players is 4.  
   • Does the paper make (or test) predictions about systematically varying the number of players?  
     – No. The paper does not vary group size; it only ever uses four-person groups (except for instances of attrition, which were not an intentional manipulation).

2. Number of rounds  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter (and its value)?  
     – Yes. There are 10 periods (rounds) in the “no-punishment” condition, followed by 10 periods in the “punishment” condition, for a total of 20 periods.  
   • Does the paper make (or test) predictions about varying the total or known number of rounds?  
     – No. The paper keeps the total number of rounds fixed at 20 (10 without punishment, 10 with punishment). It does not systematically alter the number of rounds to assess any effect on punishment.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Does the paper discuss whether chat was enabled?  
     – Yes. The paper notes that participants could not chat or communicate with one another (beyond the displayed onscreen information).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary the presence/absence of chat?  
     – No. There is no condition in which chat is turned on.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Does the paper discuss whether contributions are “all or nothing”?  
     – Yes, implicitly: each participant chooses how many (0–20) points to contribute out of 20. This is not an “all or nothing” contribution; instead, it is a continuous (integer-valued) choice.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary whether contributions are “all or nothing”?  
     – No. There is no manipulation of the contribution format.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much of their endowment to “move back”)?  
   • Does the paper discuss the existence of a “default” contribution rule or forced decisions?  
     – No. Participants simply decide how many points to contribute (0–20). There is no mention of a default or forced scheme.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary this feature?  
     – No. It is not varied.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as the multiplication factor  
   • Does the paper discuss the MPCR or multiplier?  
     – Yes. Contributions to the public good are multiplied by 1.6, and that total is then split equally among the four players (an MPCR of 1.6/4 = 0.4).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary the MPCR or multiplier?  
     – No. It remains fixed at 1.6, with no reported condition in which it is changed to test punishment effects.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Does the paper discuss punishment cost?  
     – Yes. Each deduction point assigned costs the punishing player 1 point.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary punishment cost?  
     – No. The cost is always 1 point per deduction point assigned.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Does the paper discuss punishment magnitude?  
     – Yes. Each deduction point imposed on a target costs that target 3 points.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary the punishment magnitude?  
     – No. It remains 3 throughout.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Does the paper talk about any reward mechanism?  
     – No. The design includes punishment only; there is no mention of rewards.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary a reward mechanism?  
     – No. There is no reward condition or variation.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Does the paper address this?  
      – No. Since there is no reward at all, it is not discussed.  
    • Does the paper systematically vary it?  
      – No.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins a player gets for each unit of reward)  
    • Does the paper address this?  
      – No. Same as above: no reward phase is used.  
    • Does the paper systematically vary it?  
      – No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    • Does the paper discuss this?  
      – Yes. Participants know there are two “parts”; each part is 10 periods, so it is standard in the design that they know each part has 10 rounds. However, they learn full details of Part 2 (punishment) only after finishing Part 1.  
    • Does the paper systematically vary whether the horizon is known?  
      – No. The same procedure is used for all sessions.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?  
    • Does the paper discuss this?  
      – Yes. After each period, participants see (1) their own contribution and earnings, (2) the average contribution in their group, (3) each group member’s individual contribution, and (in the punishment condition) (4) how much punishment they assigned or received in total.  
    • Does the paper systematically vary the visibility of peer outcomes?  
      – No. It is always displayed in the same way.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Does the paper discuss this?  
      – Yes, indirectly. The paper states that, at the end of a period, participants learn “the total number of points they assigned and received,” but not who specifically punished them. There is no indication that they see the punisher’s identity.  
    • Does the paper systematically vary whether the identity of the punisher is revealed?  
      – No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Does the paper discuss this?  
      – No. There is no reward mechanism in the design at all.  
    • Does the paper systematically vary it?  
      – No.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper’s main dependent variables are:  
     – Contributions (how many points participants invest in the public good).  
     – Punishment decisions (how often and how severely participants punish).  
     – Attrition rates (i.e., dropout).  
   • The paper does measure “efficiency” in the condition with punishment, reporting average payoffs (e.g., “Mean efficiency in the experimental condition with punishment was higher on MTurk…”). However, much of their discussion focuses on contributions and punishment frequencies rather than on systematic manipulations of efficiency.

B. Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned explicitly or implicitly with a specific value or setting:  
     1. Number of players (4).  
     2. Number of rounds (10 + 10).  
     3. Chat enabled? (No).  
     4. All-or-nothing contribution? (No, can contribute 0–20).  
     6. MPCR / multiplier (1.6).  
     7. Punishment cost (1 point).  
     8. Punishment magnitude (3 points).  
     12. Is the horizon known? (Yes, 10 periods each part).  
     13. Peer outcomes shown? (Yes, they see others’ contributions and total punishment assigned/received).  
     14. Do punished players know the punisher’s identity? (They do not).  
   • Mentioned as absent or not used:  
     9–11. Rewards.  
   • Not discussed as a varied feature:  
     5. Contribution default.  
     15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is? (No reward at all.)  

   In total, the authors explicitly address 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14 (ten parameters) in some form. They also note that parameters 9–11 and 15 (the reward items plus the identity of a rewarder) do not apply. They do not mention or vary parameter 5 (contribution “default”).

C. For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None of the parameters are actually “systematically varied” in the sense of designing multiple treatments that change only one parameter at a time. The authors keep all choice and punishment parameters fixed.  
   • Thus, they do not provide effect sizes of systematically varying any of the parameters on the punishment treatment effect (whether defined in terms of efficiency or anything else).  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

Authors: Chen, XJ; Szolnoki, A; Perc, M
Author Full Names: Chen, Xiaojie; Szolnoki, Attila; Perc, Matjaz
Article Title: Competition and cooperation among different punishing strategies in the spatial public goods game
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; EVOLUTION; RETALIATION; RECIPROCITY; DIVERSITY; EMERGENCE; OVERCOME; BEHAVIOR; PROMOTES
Abstract: Inspired by the fact that people have diverse propensities to punish wrongdoers, we study a spatial public goods game with defectors and different types of punishing cooperators. During the game, cooperators punish defectors with class-specific probabilities and subsequently share the associated costs of sanctioning. We show that in the presence of different punishing cooperators the highest level of public cooperation is always attainable through a selection mechanism. Interestingly, the selection does not necessarily favor the evolution of punishers who would be able to prevail on their own against the defectors, nor does it always hinder the evolution of punishers who would be unable to prevail on their own. Instead, the evolutionary success of punishing strategies depends sensitively on their invasion velocities, which in turn reveals fascinating examples of both competition and cooperation among them. Furthermore, we show that under favorable conditions, when punishment is not strictly necessary for the maintenance of public cooperation, the less aggressive, mild form of sanctioning is the sole victor of the selection process. Our work reveals that natural strategy selection cannot only promote, but sometimes also hinders competition among prosocial strategies.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter accounting of what the paper actually says (and does not say), followed by the required four‐part summary at the end.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Does the paper discuss it (and give a value)?  
     – The paper places players on an L×L square lattice with periodic boundary conditions. Although “number of players” = L×L, the paper does not treat this as a parameter of interest in any table/figure, nor is it systematically varied to see its effect on punishment.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about the effect of systematically varying the number of players on punishment (or any other dependent variable)?  
     – No. The paper does not explore how changing the population size would affect outcomes.

2. Number of rounds
   • Does the paper discuss it (and give a value)?  
     – The paper uses Monte Carlo simulations that run until a stationary state is reached; it does not specify “rounds” in the sense of a finite repeated public goods game.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about the effect of systematically varying the number of rounds on punishment (or any other dependent variable)?  
     – No. This is not mentioned at all.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Does the paper discuss it (and give a value)?  
     – No mention of any chat or communication among participants/players.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about the effect of systematically varying chat on punishment (or any other dependent variable)?  
     – No. It does not appear.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Does the paper discuss it (and give a value)?  
     – Cooperators contribute an amount c while defectors contribute nothing, but the paper does not present “all‐or‐nothing” as a manipulable design feature; it is simply the model’s definition of contribution.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about the effect of changing this parameter on punishment (or any other dependent variable)?  
     – No. The paper never systematically varies how contributions are made.

5. Is the contribution default (if true, do players decide how much to move back into their hand)?
   • Does the paper discuss it (and give a value)?  
     – No. Contributions are fixed at c by cooperators and 0 by defectors. There is no mention of a default or “return” mechanism.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about the effect of systematically varying this parameter on punishment (or any other dependent variable)?  
     – No mention.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor
   • Does the paper discuss it (and give a value)?  
     – Yes. The paper calls it the “enhancement factor” or “multiplication factor,” denoted by r. They examine r = 3.5, r = 4.0, and other nearby values.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about the effect of systematically varying r on punishment (or other variables)?  
     – Yes, but the paper examines the fraction of cooperators (or fraction of different punishing strategies) rather than “efficiency.” Example findings: at low r (e.g., r = 3.5), only strongly punishing cooperators can outcompete defectors unless multiple punishing types “cooperate” to hold off defectors. At higher r (e.g., r = 4.0), even milder forms of punishment can survive.  
   • Numerical effect size?  
     – The paper shows that for r above about 3.74, even non‐punishing cooperators can coexist with defectors; no explicit “effect size” on efficiency is given, but for reference, Figs. 2 and 5 show how the fraction of punishing strategies varies with r and the punishment fine α.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Does the paper discuss it (and give a value)?  
     – The model does not define a separate parameter for “punishment cost per unit” in isolation. Instead, the cost for punishing is tied to α times the number of defectors in one’s group, shared equally among punishers.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about the effect of systematically varying a separate cost‐to‐punisher parameter?  
     – No. The paper does not treat a distinct “cost‐to‐punish” parameter separate from α.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   • Does the paper discuss it (and give a value)?  
     – Yes. The paper’s main punishment parameter is α, called the “punishment fine” to defectors. It is varied systematically (e.g., α ranges from about 0.2 to above 0.4 in the figures).  
   • Does the paper make predictions about the effect of systematically varying α on punishment (or other dependent variables)?  
     – Yes. For example, Fig. 2 shows how different punishing strategies persist or not as α changes. Also Fig. 1, Fig. 5, etc. The dependent variable in the paper is fraction of different punishing/cooperative strategies, not efficiency per se. They repeatedly show that α has a “nonmonotonic” impact on how many punishing cooperators survive.  
   • Numerical effect size?  
     – The figures (esp. Fig. 1, Fig. 2, Fig. 5) show how, for example, cooperators can dominate when α is sufficiently large but not too large; they do not report a single effect‐size measure, but they do show thresholds (e.g., α ≈ 0.40, α ≈ 0.25, etc.) beyond which certain classes of punishers will or will not survive.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Does the paper discuss it (and give a value)?  
     – No mention of any reward mechanism.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying the enablement of reward?  
     – No. The study focuses on punishment only.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Does the paper discuss it (and give a value)?  
     – No.  
   • Any predictions?  
     – No mention.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)
   • Does the paper discuss it (and give a value)?  
     – No mention of reward magnitude.  
   • Any predictions?  
     – No mention.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
   • Does the paper discuss it (and give a value)?  
     – No. The evolutionary simulation continues until a stationary state; there is no mention of a finite or known horizon.  
   • Predictions about varying knowledge of the end of the game?
     – None.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost each round)?
   • Does the paper discuss it (and give a value)?  
     – The model is an evolutionary game where each player compares payoffs with neighbors to update their strategy, but the paper does not treat information display as a manipulated parameter—this is simply the standard learning rule.  
   • Predictions about systematically varying that information?  
     – No. Not addressed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Does the paper discuss it (and give a value)?  
     – No mention.  
   • Predictions about systematically varying punisher identification?  
     – Not discussed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Does the paper discuss it (and give a value)?  
     – Reward is not used at all; the paper does not mention it.  
   • Predictions about systematically varying rewarder identification?
     – Not applicable.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A: Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper focuses on strategy frequencies: how punishment‐capable cooperators, milder cooperators, or defectors populate the lattice at equilibrium. Although the text mentions that punishment can reduce overall payoffs, it does not use overall efficiency or total/average payoff as the main dependent variable. Instead, it reports fractions of cooperators (and fractions of various punishing strategies).  

B: Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned explicitly, in one form or another:  
     – (6) MPCR/multiplication factor (r).  
     – (8) Punishment magnitude (the paper’s “fine” α).  
   • The remaining parameters (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15) are either absent or not treated as variables to be manipulated.  

C: For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The paper systematically varies:  
     – (6) The synergy factor r (though they mainly show how this affects the fraction of different punishing classes—and thus cooperation—rather than “efficiency”).  
     – (8) The punishment fine α.  
   • Those two parameters are the only ones the paper truly varies to show impacts on outcomes. The outcomes analyzed are primarily fractions of strategies (punishing cooperators of various types vs. defectors).  

D: If you were to make predictions about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper never reports a direct measure of “group efficiency” = (actual total payoff) / (maximum possible total payoff). Hence one cannot glean precise quantitative predictions for that variable.  
   • Based on the simulation results for fractions of defectors/punishers, one can infer that increasing (6) r or using intermediate‐to‐moderate (8) α helps cooperators to thrive, which in many public goods models would imply higher efficiency. Very small α or excessively large α can expose punishers to high costs or let defectors prevail, presumably lowering overall efficiency.  
   • For the other 13 parameters—since they are not varied or in some cases not even mentioned—there is no basis in this paper to predict their roles for efficiency.

Abstract: We find that a process of voluntary association where individuals express a preference about whom they want to be associated with can create strong incentives to increase efficiency and contributions in provision of a public good. Below is a point‐by‐point analysis of how each of the 15 parameters from your list fares in the paper by Page, Putterman, and Unel (“Voluntary Association in Public Goods Experiments: Reciprocity, Mimicry and Efficiency”). In particular, for each parameter, I note whether (1) it is mentioned in the paper (and, if applicable, the value used in their experiment), and (2) whether the paper makes predictions about the effect of systematically varying that parameter on the punishment treatment effect for any dependent variable (including efficiency or any other dependent variables studied). I then conclude with the required four‐part summary.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned?: Yes. Each group always has 4 players (p. 7, Sec. 1.3). Sixteen subjects participated in each experimental session, and they were divided into four groups of four.  
   • Systematic variation or predictions?: No. The paper does not systematically vary group size nor does it predict how changing the number of players would affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency (or on any other outcome).

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned?: Yes. All sessions ran for 20 periods/rounds (p. 7, Sec. 1.3).  
   • Systematic variation or predictions?: No. The paper does not systematically vary the number of rounds nor predict how changing the number of rounds would affect the punishment treatment effect.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned?: Not discussed. There was no mention of any real‐time chat or in‐person discussion among participants.  
   • Systematic variation or predictions?: No mention and therefore no predictions.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned?: Indirectly. In the experiment, subjects chose an integer amount from 0 to 10 to contribute (p. 7), not strictly “all‐or‐nothing.”  
   • Systematic variation or predictions?: No. No systematic all‐or‐nothing design was tested or discussed.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Mentioned?: No. Participants explicitly decided how much of their endowment (0 to 10) to contribute; there was no mention of a “default” mechanism.  
   • Systematic variation or predictions?: No mention and thus no predictions.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Mentioned?: Yes. The paper uses a marginal per capita return of 0.4 (p. 7).  
   • Systematic variation or predictions?: No. They do not vary MPCR; hence no predictions about how changing MPCR would systematically affect the punishment treatment effect.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned?: Yes. In the punishment treatment, every dollar of reduction in another player’s earnings costs the punisher 25 experimental cents (p. 9, Sec. 1.3.3).  
   • Systematic variation or predictions?: No. The cost is fixed and not varied experimentally; no predictions are made about changing this cost.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted per unit of punishment)
   • Mentioned?: Yes. One unit of punishment deducted 1 experimental dollar from the target at a cost of 0.25 to the punisher (p. 9).  
   • Systematic variation or predictions?: No. It is fixed, and the paper does not discuss how changing the deduction magnitude would affect the punishment treatment effect.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned?: No. The study only discusses costly punishment; no reward option is provided.  
   • Systematic variation or predictions?: Not mentioned.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Mentioned?: No. There is no rewarding mechanism in these treatments.  
    • Systematic variation or predictions?: Not mentioned.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded to a player per unit of reward)
    • Mentioned?: No. As above, there is no reward stage or “positive sanction.”  
    • Systematic variation or predictions?: Not mentioned.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
    • Mentioned?: Yes. Subjects knew there were 20 periods in total (p. 7).  
    • Systematic variation or predictions?: No. The paper holds the finite horizon at 20 and does not explore hidden or uncertain lengths.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?
    • Mentioned?: Yes. In all treatments, each participant sees how much the other three group members contributed in each period (p. 7, Sec. 1.3.1). In the regrouping treatments, each participant also sees the average contribution for each of the other 15 players when ranking (p. 8, Sec. 1.3.2).  
    • Systematic variation or predictions?: No. They do display outcomes, but they do not systematically vary which outcomes are revealed or how that might affect the punishment treatment effect.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Mentioned?: Not explicitly. The paper specifies that players see how much they were punished (reduced) but does not say they learn who imposed it. Standard practice in these VCM‐with‐punishment designs is anonymity, and the paper does not deviate from that or systematically vary it.  
    • Systematic variation or predictions?: No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Mentioned?: Not applicable. No reward mechanism is present in any treatment.  
    • Systematic variation or predictions?: Not mentioned.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Summary Responses A–D

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   Yes. The paper explicitly reports “efficiency” as one of its main outcome measures, defined as observed earnings divided by the maximum possible earnings (p. 10, Table 2). The paper also discusses average contributions, average earnings, and final‐period contribution behaviors as additional measures (dependent variables). These other measures differ from efficiency in that “average contribution” is how much participants put into the public good on average, while “efficiency” factors in all payoffs net of any punishment costs.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   The paper mentions seven parameters in some fashion:  
   1) Number of players (4)  
   2) Number of rounds (20)  
   6) MPCR (0.4)  
   7) Punishment cost (0.25 per 1 dollar taken)  
   8) Punishment magnitude (1 dollar deducted from target’s payoff per unit)  
   12) The number of rounds is known (20)  
   13) Peer outcomes are shown (subjects observe others’ contributions)  
   The other parameters in the list (3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15) either do not appear in the paper or are not relevant to the study’s design.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   None. The experiment compares four treatments (baseline, punishment, regrouping, and combined punishment+regrouping), but does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters individually (for example, by changing group size, changing MPCR, or altering the punishment cost). Hence, the paper offers no direct predictions or effect sizes for how changing any single parameter would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency or on other outcomes.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   The paper offers no direct basis for predicting how systematic changes in these 15 parameters (e.g., changing the group size from 4 to 5, altering the cost/magnitude of punishment, or enabling rewards) might shift the punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency. The authors simply note that adding punishment in their design increases contributions but, because punishing consumes resources, punishment alone does not raise overall efficiency as much as regrouping does. Beyond their comparison of punishment versus no punishment (or regrouping versus no regrouping), there is little to no guidance in the text about how to forecast the impact of new parameter values or interactions on efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Overall, the paper does measure and report efficiency, but does not systematically manipulate or discuss variations of those 15 parameters beyond the baseline/punishment/regrouping/combined comparisons. Consequently, it makes no direct numerical predictions about how changing each parameter would affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Abstract: This paper examines cultural differences in individual decision-making in a corruption game. We define culture as an individual's accumulated experience, shaped by the social, institutional, and economic aspects of the environment in which the individual lives. Based on experiments run in Australia (Melbourne), India (Delhi), Indonesia (Jakarta) and Singapore, we find that there is a greater variation in the propensities to punish corrupt behavior than in the propensities to engage in corrupt behavior across cultures.          – Avg. efficiency 63 % in 0–30¢ set, 69 % in 0–120¢ set, 78 % in 30–70¢ set (Table 4).  
         – Hence cheaper punishment → more punishment and slightly more contribution, but lower efficiency.  
       • Contribution rises as price falls (Wilcoxon p≈.05 comparing 0–30¢ to other sets).

   (1) Fixed at 1 experimental dollar per unit.

    (1) Yes: subjects are told there are exactly 5 periods.  
    (2) Not varied; no predictions.

    (1) Yes: each subject sees every group member’s contribution; later he learns only the AGGREGATE punishment he received.

   • Contribution level – mean amount put in the public account.  
   • Quantity of punishment purchased – main focus of econometric tables.

     – Interpretation: Changing the number of players has no detectable impact on the punishment treatment effect on contributions.  
     – No efficiency data.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned.  Coded as “iterations” (range 1–50; M = 10.24).  
   • Systematically varied?  Yes – continuous moderator.  
     – Model 2: β = 0.33, p < .001.  (Across models β ≈ .26–.33, always p ≤ .005.)  
     – So every additional round is associated with a larger positive punishment effect on contributions; exact un-standardized change is not given.  
     – No efficiency analysis.

3. Is chat enabled?  
   • Not mentioned.  No value, no analysis.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule?  
   • Not mentioned.  All studies follow the standard Fehr-Gächter “continuous” choice protocol.  Never varied.

5. Contribution-default / “take” version?  
   • Not mentioned (all studies use the standard “give” version).  Never varied.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned only descriptively: each MU allocated to the group fund is multiplied by 1.5.  Identical in every study; never varied or analysed.

7. Punishment cost per unit  
   • Fixed at 1 MU in all the included experiments; mentioned but not varied, hence no analysis.

8. Punishment magnitude (penalty per unit)  
   • Fixed at 3 MU in all studies; mentioned but not varied.

9. Is a reward option enabled?  
   • Not part of the inclusion criteria; no paper in the meta-set allows rewards.  Not discussed, not analysed.

10. Reward cost per unit  
    • Not applicable (no reward option).

11. Reward magnitude per unit  
    • Not applicable.

12. Do players know the number of rounds?  
    • Not discussed.  The article never reports whether horizon is common knowledge, and no variation is analysed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • The Fehr-Gächter protocol always reveals each player’s contribution before punishment decisions, but this is fixed across studies and never treated as a moderator.

14. Is the identity of the punisher revealed?  
    • In the protocol the punisher remains anonymous.  Not varied, not analysed.

15. Is the identity of the rewarder revealed?  
    • Not applicable (no reward stage).

------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
   • The meta-analysis uses only one outcome: average contribution to the public good (converted to the standardized mean difference, d, between punishment and control).  
   • Total pay-off, efficiency, or any monetary welfare measure is never analysed.  Therefore “efficiency” ≠ the dependent variable employed in the paper.

B. Parameters merely mentioned  
   – Number of players, Number of rounds, MPCR, Punishment cost, Punishment magnitude.  
   – 5 out of 15.

C. Parameters whose systematic variation is actually analysed with respect to the punishment effect  
   – Number of players (non-significant).  
   – Number of rounds (significantly positive).  
   – 2 out of 15.

D. What can we predict—strictly from this paper—about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) will change the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
   • Very little, because the paper never measures efficiency.  
   • If we assume that higher contributions normally translate into higher efficiency (which is only true when the cost of punishment is negligible—an assumption the authors do not evaluate), then:  
     – More rounds should strengthen the positive impact of punishment on efficiency (β ≈ .30).  
     – Changing group size from 3 to 7 should have no reliable effect.  
   • For every other parameter (chat, contribution rule, default, MPCR, punishment/reward structure, information conditions) the paper provides no evidence or prediction.  Any forecast would have to rely on outside literature, which the current instructions forbid.

In short, the only clear, data-based statement this paper allows is: “Making the public-goods interaction last longer increases the (contribution-based) benefit of introducing peer punishment; changing the size of the group does not.”  No other parameter can be linked to punishment-induced efficiency changes on the basis of the present article alone.
reference_APA: Balliet, Daniel & Van Lange, Paul A. M. (2013). Trust, Punishment, and Cooperation Across 18 Societies: A Meta-Analysis. PERSPECTIVES ON PSYCHOLOGICAL SCIENCE.

Article Title: Punishment, counterpunishment and sanction enforcement in a social dilemma experiment
Author Keywords: public goods; sanction enforcement; counter punishment; information
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS PROVISION; MONETARY
Abstract: We present the results of an experiment that explores the sanctioning behavior of individuals who experience a social dilemma. In the game we study, players choose contribution levels to a public good and subsequently have multiple opportunities to reduce the earnings of the other members of the group. The treatments vary in terms of individuals' opportunities to (a) avenge sanctions that have been directed toward themselves, and (b) punish others' sanctioning behavior with respect to third parties. We find that individuals do avenge sanctions they have received, and this serves to decrease contribution levels. They also punish those who fail to sanction third parties, but the resulting increase in contributions is smaller than the decrease the avenging of sanctions induces. When there are five rounds of unrestricted sanctioning, contributions and welfare are significantly lower than when only one round of sanctioning opportunities exists, and welfare is lower than at a benchmark of zero cooperation.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what Denant‐Boemont et al. (2007) do (and do not) say and do (and do not) vary in their experiment, followed by the requested four‐part summary (A–D). In what follows, “the paper” refers strictly to Denant‐Boemont et al. (2007), and all statements reflect only what appears in that text.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. NUMBER OF PLAYERS  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The experiment always uses groups of size 4.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper keeps group size fixed at 4 in all treatments.  
   • Any stated effect of varying it on punishment treatment effect (for efficiency or any other outcome)? No.  

2. NUMBER OF ROUNDS  
   • Mentioned? Yes, in the sense that each session has 20 repeated periods (“rounds”).  
   • Systematically varied? No. All sessions and treatments use 20 repeated periods.  
   • Any stated effect of varying it on punishment treatment effect (for efficiency or any other outcome)? No. The paper does not compare, for example, 10 vs. 20 rounds.  
   • Note: Although the paper studies 1‑stage, 2‑stage, or 6‑stage punishment opportunities within each period, that is a separate design feature; the total number of repeated periods (20) does not change.  

3. IS CHAT ENABLED BETWEEN PLAYERS?  
   • Mentioned? Only insofar as the paper does not report any communication between participants.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Any stated effect? No.  

4. IS THE CONTRIBUTION “ALL OR NOTHING”?  
   • Mentioned? The paper states that each participant can contribute any amount (0 to 20 ECUs) to the public account.  
   • Systematically varied? No. It is never all‐or‐nothing.  
   • Any stated effect of varying it? No.  

5. IS THE CONTRIBUTION DEFAULT? (I.E., DO PLAYERS DECIDE HOW MUCH TO MOVE BACK TO THEIR HAND?)  
   • Mentioned? No. Participants actively choose an integer amount to contribute from 0 to 20. There is no “default” mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Any stated effect? No.  

6. MARGINAL PER CAPITA RETURN (MPCR) OR RELATED PARAMETERS SUCH AS MULTIPLICATION FACTOR  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each 1 ECU contributed yields 0.4 ECUs for each of the four participants. Thus the MPCR = 0.4 for the contributing individual.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The multiplier is 0.4 in all treatments.  
   • Any stated effect of varying it? No.  

7. PUNISHMENT COST TO IMPOSE A SINGLE UNIT OF PUNISHMENT  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each assigned punishment point imposes a cost on the punisher according to a cost function k(·), the same for all. The paper does not give each numeric cost explicitly in the text but refers to the Fehr & Gaechter (2000) scheme.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The cost remains the same in all treatments.  
   • Any stated effect? No, beyond noting that imposing punishment is always costly.  

8. PUNISHMENT MAGNITUDE (THE COINS DEDUCTED FOR EACH UNIT OF PUNISHMENT)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each point of punishment reduces 10 % of the target’s stage‐1 earnings, up to a cap of 10 total points (i.e. up to 100 %).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The magnitude is the same across treatments.  
   • Any stated effect? No.  

9. WHETHER A REWARD IS ENABLED  
   • Mentioned? No. The experiment only studies punishment; there is no reward option.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Any stated effect? No.  

10. REWARD COST TO GRANT A SINGLE UNIT OF REWARD  
    • Mentioned? No. Rewards are not implemented.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Any stated effect? No.  

11. REWARD MAGNITUDE (THE COINS AWARDED PER UNIT OF REWARD)  
    • Mentioned? No. Again, no rewards in this design.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Any stated effect? No.  

12. IS THE NUMBER OF ROUNDS KNOWN TO PLAYERS? (DO THEY KNOW WHEN THE GAME ENDS?)  
    • Mentioned? Yes. Participants know there are 20 periods in every treatment.  
    • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not compare “known” vs. “unknown” horizon.  
    • Any stated effect? No.  

13. ARE PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN (DO PLAYERS KNOW HOW MUCH PEERS GAINED AND LOST EACH ROUND)?  
    • Mentioned? Partially. In every treatment, participants see their own earnings each period, and they see the contribution decisions of others. They also see certain punishment allocations depending on the treatment. However, the paper does not say that they systematically vary the display of final earnings for each peer.  
    • Systematically varied? They do vary exactly what punishment information is shown. In “Full Information,” players see how much each person punished each other. In “Revenge Only,” players only learn who punished them, etc. But the paper does not vary whether or not final payoffs are displayed fully. Rather, it varies the ability to observe who sanctioned whom.  
    • Any stated effect of systematically varying full payoff displays? No direct discussion of how simply showing “peer outcomes” would affect efficiency. The variations in the paper are about who sees which punishment details (though that is more precisely parameter #14).  

14. WHEN A PLAYER IS PUNISHED, DO THEY KNOW WHO THE SPECIFIC PUNISHER IS?  
    • Mentioned? Yes. This is the core dimension that is indeed varied across treatments:  
      – Baseline: only one round of punishment, so effectively no direct knowledge of “who punished me” across multiple stages.  
      – Full Information: participants see precisely who punished whom in the second (and, if applicable, later) punishment stage(s).  
      – Revenge Only: you only see who punished you, not who punished others.  
      – No Revenge: you see how others punish third parties, but not who punished you.  
    • Systematically varied? Yes. This is a main experimental factor distinguishing Baseline, Full Information, Revenge Only, and No Revenge.  
    • Any stated effect on punishment treatment effect? Yes, extensively. For example, when punishers can be identified, counterpunishment occurs and reduces contributions (and thus reduces “welfare” or average earnings). In contrast, being unable to identify who punished you prevents or weakens counterpunishment, which can increase contributions. Effects reported (for contributions and “welfare”), but the paper does not quantify changes in “efficiency” as a fraction of the fully cooperative payoff. Rather, it reports changes in average payoff and average contribution.  

15. WHEN A PLAYER IS REWARDED, DO THEY KNOW WHO THE SPECIFIC REWARDER IS?  
    • Mentioned? No. Rewards do not figure in this experiment.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Any stated effect? No.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   • The paper focuses primarily on two dependent variables: (1) contributions to the public good and (2) group “welfare” or average/total payoff. The authors typically call it “welfare” or “earnings,” not explicitly “efficiency,” but the paper does compare welfare against various baselines.  
   • It also reports analyses of punishment behavior itself (e.g., “who punishes whom” and “how many points are assigned”). Thus, the study covers multiple outcomes: contributions, average monetary earnings (“welfare”), and punishment choices.  
   • The paper does not label “efficiency” as a separate measure; rather, it uses “welfare” or “earnings” to capture total or average payoff, which can be viewed as related to efficiency.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
     1 (players = 4), 2 (20 periods), 6 (MPCR = 0.4), 7 (punishment cost exists), 8 (punishment magnitude = 10 % per point), 12 (number of rounds is known = 20), 13/14 (information about punishment is manipulated across treatments).  
   • Not mentioned or set to “not used” (or equivalently set to a single value with no variation):  
     3 (no chat), 4 (not all‐or‐nothing), 5 (no default contribution rule), 9–11 (no rewards), 15 (no rewards, so no rewarder identity).  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect (for each dependent variable) when the parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The paper systematically varies only the treatment structure regarding who sees whom punishing (which is, in effect, parameter #14 and partially #13). It also varies whether there is 1 punishment stage (Baseline), 2 punishment stages (three variants: Full Information, No Revenge, Revenge Only), or 6 punishment stages (6SFI). But from the enumerated 15 parameters, the only directly varied dimension is the presence/change of punisher identification (#14) and partial differences in what punishment outcomes are visible (#13).  
   • The paper analyzes how these variations affect contributions and payoffs (“welfare”). Counterpunishment, sanction enforcement, and “full” vs. “limited” information about punisher identity produce different (“treatment”) effects on contributions and payoffs.  
   • No other enumerated parameter is systematically varied in the experiment.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • Because the paper does not vary most parameters (e.g., group size, MPCR, cost of punishment, etc.), it gives no direct evidence about how changing them would affect efficiency.  
   • The only clear findings relevant to “efficiency” (or group welfare) come from varying the punishment‐information structure (#14, and partly #13) and the number of punishment stages. Generally, once players know who punishes whom, counterpunishment rises, which reduces efficiency because it lowers contributions and is itself costly. Conversely, limited information about punisher identity reduces counterpunishment and often leads to better net outcomes. Multiple additional punishment stages (as in the 6‐stage Full Information treatment) decrease welfare further.  
   • Hence, apart from confirming that anonymity for punishers (or limiting the ability to target them) can sustain higher payoffs, the paper provides little or no basis for predicting how the other parameters would affect efficiency.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Reply ends here.
reference_APA: Denant-Boemont, Laurent, Masclet, David & Noussair, Charles N. (2007). Punishment, counterpunishment and sanction enforcement in a social dilemma experiment. ECONOMIC THEORY.

Abstract: Two experimental studies investigated the role of group identification in the selection of and cooperation with leaders to manage public good dilemmas. Below, each of the 15 parameters is treated in turn.  For every parameter I note  

(1) whether the paper mentions or fixes the parameter and, if so, the value(s) that can be read from the text, figures, or tables; and  

(2) whether the authors *systematically vary* that parameter and report how such variation changes the “punishment‐treatment effect.”  
(The only punishment treatment that appears in the article is the introduction of an *instrumental leader* who can fine the lowest contributor 220 pence per round.  There is no factorial manipulation of fine size, fine cost, etc.)

====================================================================  
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER EXTRACTION  
====================================================================

1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned.  All groups consist of 6 players in both studies.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction about changing group size.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Study 1: 1 actual contribution round (plus a prospective 2nd).  
       Study 2: 8 rounds (4 without, 4 with leader).  
   (2) Not experimentally varied; no prediction concerning more/fewer rounds.

3. Chat enabled?  
   (1) Not mentioned; no chat facility was provided.  
   (2) Not discussed.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   (1) Study 1: Yes (dichotomous “invest £3 or nothing”).  
       Study 2: No (continuous 0-300 pence).  
   (2) Although the two studies differ, the paper never treats this as an experimental factor, and no prediction is offered about how an all-or-nothing format would change the punishment effect.

5. “Contribution default” framing (refund decision)?  
   (1) Absent.  
   (2) Not discussed.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   (1) Step-level technology: If the group contributes ≥ £12, a £30 bonus is created (MPCR = £5/£3 ≈ 1.67 for a full contributor who keeps nothing).  
   (2) Held constant; no predictions about varying the MPCR.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   (1) Not given.  The external leader simply imposes the fine; no cost is stated.  
   (2) Not varied or analysed.

8. Punishment magnitude  
   (1) Stated: 220 pence fine levied on the lowest contributor each round.  
   (2) Only one magnitude used; not systematically varied; no prediction about larger/smaller fines.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   (1) Rewards are never available.  
   (2) Not discussed.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   → Not applicable (no rewards).

12. Whether the horizon is known  
   (1) Yes.  In Study 2 participants are told there will be eight sessions.  
   (2) Horizon length not varied; no prediction.

13. Whether peer outcomes are shown  
   (1) Participants are only told whether the *group* met the threshold; they do *not* see individual peers’ pay-offs.  
   (2) This visibility is fixed; no systematic manipulation or prediction.

14. Whether the punished player knows who the punisher is  
   (1) Yes.  Everyone knows the (external) leader is the punisher.  
   (2) Identity revelation not varied; no prediction.

15. Whether the rewarded player knows who the rewarder is  
   (1) N/A – no rewards.  
   (2) Not discussed.

====================================================================  
SUMMARY  
====================================================================

A.  Dependent variables  
    • The paper does **not** use “group efficiency” (aggregate pay-off divided by its maximum) at all.  
    • Primary behavioural DV: individual *contribution amount* (in pence or dichotomous invest/keep).  
    • Additional DVs: preference ratings for leader types, self-esteem, perceived leader legitimacy.  
    These variables differ conceptually from efficiency: efficiency incorporates both the public return and any punishment costs, whereas contribution level ignores monetary losses from fines and treats all contributed amounts as socially valuable.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
    8 of 15:  1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 13, 14.  (Parameters 3, 5, 7, 9, 10, 11, 15 are not mentioned.)

C.  For how many parameters does the paper *systematically vary the parameter* and link that variation to the punishment treatment effect?  
    Zero.  The only punishment treatment is whether an *instrumental leader with a fixed 220-pence fine* is present.  None of the 15 parameters is factorially varied to see how it moderates that treatment effect.

D.  Predicting the influence of the 15 parameters (and their interactions) on the punishment treatment effect on *efficiency*, using only this paper  
    • Because efficiency is never measured, and because none of the parameters is experimentally crossed with the punishment treatment, the paper allows almost no quantitative prediction.  
    • Qualitatively, one could infer:  
        – Presence of a *known* punisher who can levy a *substantial* fine (220 pence) raises contributions when compared with no punishment or with mere verbal encouragement, especially for low-identification groups.  
        – The size of the group (6) and the known finite horizon (8 rounds) are at least compatible with punishment working, but we cannot say whether different sizes or horizons would strengthen or weaken the effect.  
        – Because punishment is costless to the punisher in this design, any efficiency loss would arise solely from the victim’s fine; the paper does not compute that loss, so we cannot say whether efficiency rises or falls.  
    • For every other listed parameter (chat, MPCR, peer outcome visibility, rewards, etc.) the article offers no evidence from which to project an efficiency consequence.

In short, the article is informative about *who* punishes (an external leader) and *whether* punishment versus encouragement shifts **contributions**, but it provides virtually no leverage for predicting how the 15 protocol parameters, singly or jointly, would modulate the punishment treatment effect on group **efficiency**.
reference_APA: Van Vugt, M & De Cremer, D (1999). Leadership in social dilemmas: The effects of group identification on collective actions to provide public goods. JOURNAL OF PERSONALITY AND SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY.

Article Title: Human altruism: economic, neural, and evolutionary perspectives
Keywords Plus: STRONG RECIPROCITY; COOPERATION; PUNISHMENT; BEHAVIOR
Abstract: Human cooperation represents a spectacular outlier in the animal world. Unlike other creatures, humans frequently cooperate with genetically unrelated strangers, often in large groups, with people they will never meet again, and when reputation gains are small or absent. Experimental evidence and evolutionary models suggest that strong reciprocity, the behavioral propensity for altruistic punishment and altruistic rewarding, is of key importance for human cooperation. Here, we review both evidence documenting altruistic punishment and altruistic cooperation and recent brain imaging studies that combine the powerful tools of behavioral game theory with neuroilmaging techniques. These studies show that mutual cooperation and the punishment of defectors activate reward related neural circuits, suggesting that evolution has endowed humans with proximate mechanisms that render altruistic behavior psychologically rewarding.
