Below I go through the 15 focal parameters in exactly the order given.  
For each one I report

• Whether the review article mentions the parameter at all and, if so, what concrete value(s) or description(s) are given.  
• Whether the article reports or predicts what happens to the *punishment treatment effect* when the parameter is *systematically varied*.  
• If any quantitative effect size can be read off a figure or table, I state it; otherwise I note “no numerical effect reported”.

Because the paper is a short, broad review that synthesises results from many published and some unpublished studies, it almost never manipulates an individual parameter in a controlled fashion; instead it summarises qualitative findings. Whenever that is the case I state so explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned?  Yes – the text refers to “arbitrary number of players” in PGs, “large groups”, and the fact that the punishment-institution group “became rather large”. No specific size is given.  
   (2) Systematic variation and effect on punishment?  No. The review never reports a design in which group size is experimentally varied while holding everything else constant, so no prediction or effect size is provided.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Mentioned?  Yes – Figure 2 shows “30 periods”; the text contrasts “one-shot” with “repeated” games.  
   (2) Systematic variation?  No. The paper does not compare 10 vs 30 vs 50 rounds, etc., so no effect of changing the number of rounds on the punishment treatment effect is given.

3. Chat between players  
   (1) Mentioned?  No.  
   (2) Systematic variation?  Not applicable.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
   (1) Mentioned?  No.  
   (2) Systematic variation?  Not applicable.

5. Contribution default / endowment moved back  
   (1) Mentioned?  No.  
   (2) Systematic variation?  Not applicable.

6. MPCR or multiplication factor  
   (1) Mentioned?  No specific MPCR is ever stated.  
   (2) Systematic variation?  None.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   (1) Mentioned?  Yes – punishment is repeatedly described as “costly”. No numerical values are given.  
   (2) Systematic variation?  No. The cost level is never manipulated across treatments.

8. Punishment magnitude against the target  
   (1) Mentioned?  Only qualitatively (“reduce the other subjects’ income”, “the greater the free-riding the more the individual is punished”). No concrete deduction rate is reported.  
   (2) Systematic variation?  No.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   (1) Mentioned?  Yes – the review contrasts:  
       • a “punishment institution”  
       • a “no-punishment institution”  
       • a “reward institution”  
       • a “no-reward institution”  
       (Figure 2, panels a–d).  
   (2) Systematic variation and its effect?  Yes, but only for *reward vs. no reward*, not for varying reward *levels*. The pattern reported is:  
       – With voluntary institution choice, the punishment institution attains ~100 % contributions and maintains them;  
       – The reward institution shows a decay of cooperation similar to the baseline;  
       – Hence enabling *reward alone* does **not** create a positive treatment effect comparable to punishment.  
       No numerical efficiency ratio is given, only the contribution trajectories.

10. Reward cost  
   (1) Mentioned?  No numbers, only the phrase “costly rewarding”.  
   (2) Systematic variation?  None.

11. Reward magnitude  
   (1) Mentioned?  No.  
   (2) Systematic variation?  None.

12. Whether the horizon is known  
   (1) Mentioned?  No.  
   (2) Systematic variation?  None.

13. Whether peer outcomes are shown  
   (1) Mentioned?  Yes – players are “informed about others’ contributions” before punishing or rewarding.  
   (2) Systematic variation?  No. The availability of this information is kept constant within the cited studies.

14. Whether the punished player knows the punisher  
   (1) Mentioned?  The review notes that punishment occurs “even in interactions with completely anonymous strangers”, but it does not describe whether anonymity is *with respect to the punisher’s identity* inside the group.  
   (2) Systematic variation?  No.

15. Whether the rewarded player knows the rewarder  
   (1) Not mentioned.  
   (2) Systematic variation?  Not applicable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used  
   The review almost exclusively reports *contribution levels* or qualitative statements about “cooperation”. It occasionally remarks that certain choices “maximize joint payoff”, but it never reports *group efficiency* (total payoff divided by the cooperative maximum) as a measured variable. Thus the dependent variables discussed are:  
   – Contribution level / cooperation rate (primary)  
   – Incidence and severity of punishment or reward (secondary)  
   – Neural activation (for neuroimaging studies)  
   These differ from *efficiency* because they ignore the monetary cost of punishing or rewarding.

B. How many of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
   6 parameters are mentioned: 1, 2, 7, 8, 9, 13.

C. How many parameters are *systematically varied* in relation to the punishment treatment effect?  
   Only 1 parameter (parameter 9: “reward enabled”) is explicitly varied in the studies summarised, and even here the paper reports its impact on *cooperation*, not on efficiency. No numerical treatment-on-the-treated effect size is given.

D. Predictions one can make (and their limits)  
   Because the article provides almost no controlled parametric manipulations, it offers very little leverage for forecasting how each of the 15 parameters—or their interactions—will influence the punishment treatment effect on *efficiency*. The only cautious, paper-based predictions are:

   • Enabling costly *punishment* (while holding everything else constant) strongly increases cooperation and therefore is likely to raise efficiency, provided the dead-weight loss from punishment is not too large.

   • The main dependent variables are (i) the frequencies of defectors, cooperators, loners, and punishers, and (ii) their corresponding payoffs (or average payoff of the population). Authors: Gardner, A; West, SA

Article Title: Cooperation and punishment, especially in humans
Author Keywords: kin selection; neighbor-modulated fitness; repression of competition; public-goods game; human evolution; policing

Abstract: Explaining altruistic cooperation is one of the greatest challenges faced by sociologists, economists, and evolutionary biologists. The problem is determining why an individual would carry out a costly behavior that benefits another. Possible solutions to this problem include kinship, repeated interactions, and policing. Another solution that has recently received much attention is the threat of punishment. However, punishing behavior is often costly for the punisher, and so it is not immediately clear how costly punishment could evolve. We use a direct (neighbor-modulated) fitness approach to analyze when punishment is favored. This methodology reveals that, contrary to previous suggestions, relatedness between interacting individuals is not crucial to explaining cooperation through punishment. In fact, increasing relatedness directly disfavors punishing behavior. Instead, the crucial factor is a positive correlation between the punishment strategy of an individual and the cooperation it receives. This could arise in several ways, such as when facultative adjustment of behavior leads individuals to cooperate more when interacting with individuals who are more likely to punish. More generally, our results provide a clear example of how the fundamental factor driving the evolution of social traits is a correlation between social partners and how this can arise for reasons other than genealogical kinship.

Below is a point‐by‐point review of what the Gardner and West (2004) paper says regarding each of the 15 parameters and whether the authors discuss any systematic variation of that parameter and its predicted effect on punishment. Throughout, note that the paper does not report analyses in terms of “group efficiency” or “total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff,” so there are no direct statements about how these parameters affect “efficiency” in the usual public‐goods sense (see the final summary for details).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • What the paper says: The paper frequently uses group size “N.” In one example model, individuals form groups of size N, and the analysis shows that punishment can (or cannot) invade and be maintained depending on N.  
   • Systematic variation: Yes. The paper derives threshold conditions for when punishment can invade (for instance, d > (N−1)c in their eq. [14]) and when punishment is stable.  
   • Effect on “punishment treatment effect,” especially on efficiency: The paper does not discuss group “efficiency.” It analyzes whether punishment can invade or be evolutionarily stable. No numerical effect sizes are given in terms of payoff or efficiency; rather, the authors provide threshold inequalities (e.g., “punishment is unlikely to invade unless d > (N−1)c”).

2. Number of rounds  
   • What the paper says: The authors do note that repeated interactions can favor punishment in general theory, but they do not systematically vary or model the number of rounds.  
   • Systematic variation: No.  
   • Effect on punishment or efficiency: Not discussed.

3. Is chat (communication) enabled?  
   • What the paper says: Not mentioned at all.  
   • Systematic variation: No.  
   • Effect on punishment or efficiency: Not discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • What the paper says: The authors analyze a model in which individuals either cooperate or defect (a two‐strategy approach). They do not study partial‐contribution variations nor do they systematically compare “all‐or‐nothing” to a continuous choice.  
   • Systematic variation: No.  
   • Effect on punishment or efficiency: Not discussed.

5. Is the contribution default?  
   • What the paper says: There is no mention of a default mechanism for contributions (or a default “opt out”).  
   • Systematic variation: No.  
   • Effect on punishment or efficiency: Not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
   • What the paper says: The paper uses a “benefit of cooperation” parameter b, but it is not presented as an MPCR for a standard public‐goods game.  
   • Systematic variation: They do explore how a high benefit (b) might help cooperation, but the focus is on conditions for evolutionary stability rather than on efficiency outcomes.  
   • Effect on punishment or efficiency: They do not provide treatment‐effect estimates or an efficiency measure; only conditions (inequalities) under which punishment or cooperation is favored.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit (a)  
   • What the paper says: The cost a to the punisher is central to the authors’ models. For instance, they analyze how small or large a influences whether punishment can invade or be maintained (e.g., Figure 3 varies a).  
   • Systematic variation: Yes. They show that if a is too large, punishment is less likely to evolve or persist, but they do not translate this into an “efficiency” measure.  
   • Effect on punishment or efficiency: Discussed only in terms of evolutionary stability (e.g., whether punishment is an ESS); no direct statements on group efficiency.

8. Punishment magnitude (d)  
   • What the paper says: The authors denote d as “the fitness reduction suffered by a punished defector.” They systematically analyze how large d must be, relative to the cost of cooperation c, for punishment to be effective (e.g., d > c).  
   • Systematic variation: Yes. They provide threshold conditions (for instance, punishment can be stable if d > c).  
   • Effect on punishment or efficiency: Again, only in terms of “can punishment invade or remain stable?”—no numerical effect on efficiency is provided.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • What the paper says: The authors briefly mention that “rewarding” presumably has the opposite frequency dependence from punishing but do not model it fully or compare reward versus no‐reward treatments.  
   • Systematic variation: No.  
   • Effect on punishment or efficiency: Not discussed beyond a short conceptual statement that punishment is more common than reward in nature.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit  
   • What the paper says: Not discussed in any detail.  
   • Systematic variation: No.  
   • Effect on punishment or efficiency: Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude  
   • What the paper says: Not discussed in any detail.  
   • Systematic variation: No.  
   • Effect on punishment or efficiency: Not discussed.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
   • What the paper says: Not mentioned.  
   • Systematic variation: No.  
   • Effect on punishment or efficiency: Not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • What the paper says: Not mentioned (the authors do not consider real‐time displays of others’ payoffs or punishments).  
   • Systematic variation: No.  
   • Effect on punishment or efficiency: Not discussed.

14. When a player is punished, does the punished player know who punished them?  
   • What the paper says: Not mentioned.  
   • Systematic variation: No.  
   • Effect on punishment or efficiency: Not discussed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who rewarded them?  
   • What the paper says: Not mentioned.  
   • Systematic variation: No.  
   • Effect on punishment or efficiency: Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FINAL SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • No. The paper focuses on evolutionary stability conditions for cooperation and punishment (e.g., whether punishment can invade or persist) and on the direct fitness returns to individuals. They do discuss “mean fitness” in certain equations, but they never frame results in terms of “group efficiency” or “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff.” Thus, the paper’s primary dependent variables are:  
     – Whether cooperation is favored under certain conditions.  
     – Whether punishment is an evolutionary stable strategy under certain conditions.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Four parameters clearly appear in the analysis:  
     1) Number of players (group size N)  
     6) A cooperation‐benefit parameter b (analogous to a “multiplication” benefit, though not called MPCR)  
     7) Punishment cost a  
     8) Punishment magnitude d  
   • Reward is briefly mentioned conceptually (parameter 9), but not analyzed systematically with reward cost (10) or magnitude (11). None of the others are described at all.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, the authors only provide systematic analysis of how varying group size N, punishment cost a, and punishment magnitude d affect the ability of punishment to invade or remain stable. They do not discuss or quantify “treatment effects” on payoff/efficiency. Rather, they give threshold conditions under which punishment either can (or cannot) evolve and persist. They do not present numerical effect sizes for changes in total payoff or efficiency.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not address efficiency as typically defined in public‐goods experiments. Consequently, one cannot infer quantitative predictions for “efficiency” from this article. One might qualitatively guess (from the authors’ thresholds for stable punishment) that smaller cost of punishment (a), larger penalty (d), smaller group size (N), and a sufficiently large benefit of cooperation (b) would make punishment more likely to be stable; presumably that might improve cooperation, and hence “efficiency” if one were to map more cooperation onto higher group payoff. However, the paper itself does not frame or test this outcome in terms of group efficiency, so any efficiency‐based statement remains speculation not directly grounded in the authors’ data or figures.

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

     (1) Number of players (fixed at N = 10⁴).

Abstract: Much of human cooperation remains an evolutionary riddle. Unlike other animals, people frequently cooperate with non-relatives in large groups. Evolutionary models of large-scale cooperation require not just incentives for cooperation, but also a credible disincentive for free riding. Below is a point‐by‐point inventory of whether each of the 15 parameters is mentioned in the paper (and, if so, how), together with any discussion of systematically varying that parameter on “punishment treatment effects.” Throughout, I take “punishment treatment effect” to mean how having punishment (vs. not) and/or different punishment rules affects outcomes, while remembering that the paper’s focal dependent variables are contributions and profits (not the specific ratio of actual total payoff to the maximum possible payoff).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned? Yes. The experiment always used groups of four (p. 3).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not manipulate or compare different group sizes. No effect of varying group size is discussed.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned? Yes. They ran six rounds in the first (no-punishment) segment, followed by six rounds in the second segment (p. 3), for a total of 12 rounds.  
   • Systematically varied? No. They did not change the number of rounds across conditions; there is no discussion of how changing the number of rounds would affect the punishment treatment effect.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned? No. The text describes anonymous, computer-based interactions without mentioning any form of chat or messaging.  
   • Systematically varied? Not applicable; no discussion of chat.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned? Indirectly. The design let participants contribute any portion of their 20 MUs (p. 3), so it was not all or nothing.  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no mention of manipulating an all-or-nothing rule.

5. Is the contribution default (pulling from a fund back into the hand)?
   • Mentioned? No. Contributions were stated as “any amount from 0 to 20 MUs.” There is no mention of a “default contribution” mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied? Not applicable.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each MU contributed was doubled (making a total of 2) and then equally shared among four group members, yielding 0.5 per member (p. 3). Thus the MPCR = 0.5.  
   • Systematically varied? No. A single MPCR was used throughout, and the paper does not test how altering MPCR would change the punishment effect.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned? Yes. The cost to the punisher is called a “fee,” which can be paid up to 10 MUs. Each 1 MU spent reduces the target’s payoff by 3 MUs (p. 3).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper kept this cost fixed and does not examine different punishment costs.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   • Mentioned? Yes. It is three times the cost the punisher pays (p. 3).  
   • Systematically varied? No. They kept the ratio (1:3) constant. The authors note generally that “the success of punishing in this study is facilitated by the 1:3 ratio,” but they do not systematically vary that ratio in this experiment.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned? No. The experimental design concerns punishment vs. no punishment. There is no reward mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied? Not applicable.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Mentioned? No. Rewarding does not appear in this experiment.  
    • Systematically varied? Not applicable.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward)
    • Mentioned? No. No reward mechanism is used.  
    • Systematically varied? Not applicable.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Mentioned? Unclear in detail; the text does say participants “were not informed at the beginning of the first segment that there were two segments” (p. 3). Although that implies some limited or staggered knowledge, there is no explicit statement that the study systematically manipulated whether or not participants knew the exact number of rounds.  
    • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not test how the (un)certainty of the final round would affect punishment.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost each round)?
    • Mentioned? Partially. After each round, participants “received information on the contributions of other group members,” and, if punished, only learned the deductions from their own account (pp. 3–4). There is no full display of each peer’s payoff, just their contributions and one’s own punishment received.  
    • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not alter how much feedback is shown.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Mentioned? Yes. Interactions were anonymous, and participants only saw how many points they lost; they did not see who punished them (pp. 3–4).  
    • Systematically varied? No. The design kept punisher anonymity fixed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is?
    • Mentioned? No. Rewarding does not exist in this experiment, so there is no mention of anonymity in rewarding.  
    • Systematically varied? Not applicable.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A: Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
• The paper measures (1) contributions to the public good, (2) profits (payoffs) to individuals in each condition, and (3) punishing behavior (how often and how strongly participants punish). The text sometimes refers to “greater group profits” and “more profitable” conditions. However, the paper does not formalize “efficiency” as the ratio of total actual to total possible payoffs.  
• Thus, the main dependent variables are “contributions” and “profit,” plus the paper’s measures of “punishment use.” These differ from the narrower definition of efficiency = (actual payoffs / maximum possible payoffs).

B: Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Explicitly mentioned are:  
  1) Number of players (always four),  
  2) Number of rounds (6 per segment, 12 total),  
  6) MPCR (0.5),  
  7) Punishment cost (punisher pays 1 MU per unit),  
  8) Punishment magnitude (target loses 3 MUs per unit),  
  13) Partial peer-outcome display (they see contributions, not total payoffs),  
  14) Punisher identity not revealed.  
• All others (#3, #4, #5, #9, #10, #11, #12, #15) are either absent or only tangentially noted (e.g., #12 “not informed at the beginning about the second segment” but not truly varied).  
• Hence, seven parameters are clearly addressed in some way.

C: For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable, when the parameter is systematically varied?  
• The paper does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters.  
• Although parameters such as punishment cost (#7) and punishment magnitude (#8) are mentioned, they remain fixed at specific values (cost = 1, magnitude = 3 times that). The authors do not manipulate these to see how different values alter outcomes.  
• Therefore, none of the 15 parameters is tested in a systematic, “varied” way, and no numerical effect sizes from manipulating those parameters can be extracted from the paper.

D: If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
• The paper primarily contrasts “one punisher” vs. “all punishing” vs. “no punishment,” always with the same group size, same MPCR, same punishment costs, etc. It does not present direct evidence for how changes to those 15 parameters would affect group efficiency as a ratio of actual to maximum payoffs.  
• Consequently, there is little in the paper from which to predict how systematically varying (for instance) the number of rounds, enabling chat, changing the punishment ratio, or revealing the punisher’s identity would impact efficiency. The authors do note that the 1:3 cost‐to‐impact ratio helps sustain cooperation, implying that if punishment were more expensive (a smaller ratio), it would be less effective. However, that point is brought in mainly from earlier literature, not from within their own experimental manipulations.  
• In short, the paper does not provide enough direct evidence to make solid quantitative predictions about how varying any of the 15 parameters would change the “punishment‐treatment effect” on efficiency.

Below each of the 15 parameters I quote or paraphrase every sentence in the review that is even remotely relevant, and then state whether the paper (a) gives the concrete value actually used in the studies it summarizes, and (b) tells us what would happen to a *punishment treatment effect* (any dependent variable, let alone efficiency) if the parameter were to be **systematically varied**.

“Punishment treatment effect” = ( outcome in Punishment-condition − outcome in No-Punishment control )

────────────────────────────────────────
1. NUMBER OF PLAYERS  
• “N-person public good …” (Fig. 1a)  
a) The only value given is the symbol N (no number).  
b) No statement that changing N alters the punishment treatment effect.

2. NUMBER OF ROUNDS  
• “older work … focused on one-shot decisions … Experimental economics, and more recently psychology, has increasingly examined repeated decision making …”  
a) Values not specified (one-shot vs. ‘repeated’, no exact round counts).  
b) No claim that a longer or shorter horizon strengthens or weakens the effect of adding punishment.

3. CHAT / COMMUNICATION  
• Section “Communication” reviews that communication can raise cooperation.  
a) Presence/absence of chat is discussed qualitatively; no concrete chat protocol specified.  
b) No statement that adding punishment to a *chat* game produces a different treatment effect than adding it to a *no-chat* game.

4. ALL-OR-NOTHING CONTRIBUTION RULE  
No mention.

5. CONTRIBUTION DEFAULT (withdraw vs. give)  
No mention.

6. MPCR / MULTIPLICATION FACTOR  
• “Total contributions gain in value at factor k (with 1 < k/N < N).” (Fig. 1a)  
a) Only an inequality; no numeric k.  
b) No statement that a larger or smaller MPCR changes the punishment treatment effect.

7. COST TO IMPOSE 1 UNIT OF PUNISHMENT  
• “Punishment … is costly to the punisher but costlier … to the target, often at a 1:3 ratio.”  
a) Gives one common ratio (1 cost : 3 target loss).  
b) No comparison of that ratio with any other ratio; hence no prediction about varying cost.

8. MAGNITUDE OF PUNISHMENT PER UNIT  
Same single 1:3 ratio reference as above; again, no systematic variation.

9. WHETHER A REWARD OPTION IS ENABLED  
• Reward is repeatedly mentioned (“punishment (or reward) is costly …”, “third-party sanctioning … reward and punishment”).  
a) Presence noted, nothing more.  
b) The review never compares “punishment-only” vs “punishment-plus-reward” treatment effects.

10. COST OF 1 UNIT OF REWARD  
11. MAGNITUDE OF REWARD PER UNIT  
Both parameters only appear in the generic 1:3 “cost : benefit” description; not varied.

12. WHETHER THE NUMBER OF ROUNDS IS COMMON KNOWLEDGE  
Not mentioned.

13. PEER OUTCOME FEEDBACK  
• “participants receive, between decision rounds, feedback about the decisions made by others.”  
a) Feedback is indicated as present in ‘repeated games’; no details.  
b) No claim that the punishment treatment effect depends on giving or withholding that feedback.

14. PUNISHER IDENTITY REVEALED?  
• “third parties are more likely to punish when they can conceal their identity” (Rockenbach & Milinski 2011).  
a) Paper contrasts “concealed” vs “revealed” identity.  
b) It reports an effect on *propensity to punish*, not on the downstream **treatment effect** of punishment on efficiency (or any other dependent variable). No numbers.

15. REWARDER IDENTITY REVEALED?  
Not mentioned.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A.  Is group efficiency used as a dependent variable?  
No.  The review *defines* efficiency and often states that cooperation “increases welfare,” but the outcomes actually tabulated or plotted in the cited studies are almost always (i) individual or group contribution levels, (ii) punishment/reward decisions, or (iii) earnings.  None of the figures or tables in the review reports “efficiency = actual ÷ maximum possible.”

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
Ten: 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14.

C.  Which parameters are said to affect the *punishment treatment effect* **when systematically varied**?  
Strictly speaking, none.  Parameter 14 (punisher anonymity) is the only one for which the review describes a comparison of two values, but the outcome is “likelihood to punish,” not the treatment effect on contributions or efficiency.  So 0/15 (or 1/15 if one counts that oblique mention).

D.  Predictions one could make *solely from this review* about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency  
Because the review contains no direct evidence, the safest forecast is agnostic for all parameters.  The only very tentative hint is that *concealing the punisher’s identity* (Parameter 14) might lead to *more* punishment being used, which *could* raise contributions and thus efficiency—unless counter-punishment arises—but the review gives no data to quantify this, so even that prediction is shaky.  For every other parameter the review offers no guidance.

In short, the paper is an overview of mechanisms (sanctioning, reciprocity, communication) rather than a parametric study; it cannot be used to build a quantitative predictor of punishment’s effect on efficiency across the 15 design dimensions.

Abstract: The evolution of cooperation is one of the great puzzles in evolutionary biology. Punishment has been suggested as one solution to this problem. Here punishment is generally defined as incurring a cost to inflict harm on a wrong-doer. In the presence of punishers, cooperators can gain higher payoffs than non-cooperators. Therefore cooperation may evolve as long as punishment is prevalent in the population. Theoretical models have revealed that spatial structure can favor the co-evolution of punishment and cooperation, by allowing individuals to only play and compete with those in their immediate neighborhood. However, those models have usually assumed that punishment is always targeted at non-cooperators. In light of recent empirical evidence of punishment targeted at cooperators, we relax this assumption and study the effect of so-called 'anti-social punishment'. We find that evolution can favor anti-social punishment, and that when anti-social punishment is possible costly punishment no longer promotes cooperation. As there is no reason to assume that cooperators cannot be the target of punishment during evolution, our results demonstrate serious restrictions on the ability of costly punishment to allow the evolution of cooperation in spatially structured populations. Our results also help to make sense of the empirical observation that defectors will sometimes pay to punish cooperators. (C) 2010 Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved.

   • Mentioned?

   • Predictions about systematically varying it for the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
     The paper systematically varies z in a theoretical sense (including z → ∞, z = 4, etc.) and shows how it affects which strategies become evolutionarily stable (e.g., the condition β > zα in unstructured populations). No quantitative effect sizes regarding efficiency are given.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned?  
     No. The paper focuses on a single two‐stage interaction (cooperate/defect, then punish/no‐punish). It does not analyze multiple repeated rounds in the sense of a multi‐round public goods game.  
   • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
     Not discussed.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned?  
     No.  
   • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
     Not discussed.

   • Mentioned?

   • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
     No. The paper assumes a binary decision but never systematically varies that assumption to see how it would affect punishment’s impact on efficiency.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Mentioned?  
     No.  
   • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
     Not discussed.

   • Mentioned?

     Not discussed in terms of efficiency or a “punishment treatment effect.”

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment

Abstract: Social institutions often use rewards and penalties to promote cooperation. Here, we demonstrate that an institutional sanctioning policy we call 'first carrot, then stick' is unexpectedly successful in promoting cooperation. The policy switches the incentive from rewarding to punishing when the frequency of cooperators exceeds a threshold. We find that this policy establishes and recovers full cooperation at lower cost and under a wider range of conditions than either rewards or penalties alone, in both well-mixed and spatial populations. In particular, the spatial dynamics of cooperation make it evident how punishment acts as a 'booster stage' that capitalizes on and amplifies the pro-social effects of rewarding. Together, our results show that the adaptive hybridization of incentives offers the 'best of both worlds' by combining the effectiveness of rewarding in establishing cooperation with the effectiveness of punishing in recovering it, thereby providing a surprisingly inexpensive and widely applicable method of promoting cooperation.

Below, each of the 15 moderator-type parameters is treated in turn.  

For every parameter I state  

(1) Whether the paper mentions the parameter at all (and, if so, what concrete value(s) it uses);  
(2) Whether the paper systematically varies that parameter and, if it does, what the paper says about the consequence of such variation for the “punishment treatment effect” – i.e. for the difference between a condition with punishment (or “adaptive hybrid”) and a condition without punishment – on any dependent variable the authors analyse.  Numerical thresholds that can be read directly from the text, equations, tables or figures are reported where available.

────────────────────────────────────────

1. Number of players (group size, n)  
(1) Mentioned.  All analytic results are written for arbitrary n≥2; simulations fix n = 5.  
(2) n is not varied in figures or tables, but Eq. (2.5) derives the two incentive thresholds  
  δ– = F/(α n) and δ+ = F/α  (α = a for reward, b for punishment).  
Thus the model predicts that, holding everything else constant, larger n linearly lowers the δ– threshold at which punishment (or reward) starts to change the dynamics.  No efficiency numbers are reported, so no quantitative treatment-effect size on efficiency can be extracted.

2. Number of rounds  
(1) Not mentioned – the analysis is either infinite–time replicator dynamics or computer “generations”.  
(2) Not varied; no statements about its influence.

3. Chat enabled between players  
Not mentioned; not varied.

4. All-or-nothing contribution decision  
(1) Yes – players either “cooperate” (pay cost c) or “defect” (pay 0).  
(2) Never varied, so no information on how changing to a continuous choice would alter the punishment effect.

5. Contribution default / endowment refund  
Not mentioned.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor, r  
(1) Mentioned.  In all formulae r is the public-benefit factor; figures 2 a–l sweep r from 1.2 to 3.0 (horizontal axis).  
(2) Systematic variation: Figure 2 compares outcome regions (no cooperation vs. cooperation) for pure reward, pure punishment and adaptive hybrid as functions of r and δ.  Increasing r enlarges the parameter area where *punishment* (and hybrid) can lead to full cooperation.  No payoff-efficiency numbers are given.

7. Punishment cost (to impose one unit), here the share (1–w) δ of the institutional per-capita budget  
(1) Yes.  δ is always varied on the vertical axis of Figs. 1, 2, 3.  
(2) Systematic variation:  
 • Pure punishment: cooperation becomes globally stable once δ > F/(b n) (Eq. (2.5); with default parameters F=0.6, b=1 this is δ≈0.12).  
 • Adaptive hybrid: full cooperation arises when   
  max{F/(a n), F/(b n)} < δ < F/[a ∑k(1–x̂)k] (Eq. (3.3)).  
No explicit efficiency numbers are reported.

8. Punishment magnitude (leverage b)  
(1) Mentioned.  Two concrete values are shown: b=1 (Figs. 1c,e) and b=1.5 (Figs. 1d,f).  
(2) Systematic variation: raising b shifts both interior equilibria leftwards; i.e. a *smaller* δ is sufficient for punishment (and for the hybrid) to reach full cooperation (compare Fig. 1c with 1d).  No numerical efficiency outcomes.

9. Whether reward is enabled  
(1) Yes – three regimes are analysed: pure reward (w=1), pure punishment (w=0), and adaptive hybrid that switches from w=1 to w=0 at x = x̂.  
(2) Systematically contrasted.  Relative to pure punishment, allowing a prior reward phase greatly enlarges the (r, δ) area where cooperation can start from a single cooperator (Fig. 2e vs 2c).  No efficiency ratios are given.

10. Reward cost  
Same δ as for punishment.  See parameter 7: varying δ captures both reward and punishment budget variation, and the same qualitative statements apply.

11. Reward magnitude (leverage a)  
(1) Mentioned.  Baseline a = 1.  Authors also discuss the case a <b (they treat b = 1.5, a = 1).  
(2) Qualitative statement: if reward is *much less* efficient than punishment (a ≪ b) “punishing alone is sufficient… hybridization … is irrelevant” (§3.2).  No further numerical exploration, no efficiency data.

12. Finite vs. known number of rounds  
Not mentioned.

13. Peer-outcome information  
Only touched indirectly: in a robustness check the institution uses *local* vs. *global* cooperator frequency to decide w(x) (Electronic Suppl. Fig. S2).  No behavioural data; no efficiency numbers.

14. Punisher identity revealed  
Not mentioned.

15. Rewarder identity revealed  
Not mentioned.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables in the paper  
• Main analytic outcome: equilibrium *frequency of cooperators* x.  
• “Effectiveness”: whether full cooperation is attained (binary).  
• “Efficiency”: cumulative *institutional cost* until cooperation is established or recovered (Fig. 3) and the time required (text & ES Fig. S1).  
None of these equals the group-efficiency measure requested by the user (total payoff / maximum payoff). Group efficiency in that sense is never reported.

B. Parameters mentioned (8/15)  
1, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 (plus very tangentially 13).

C. Parameters that are *systematically varied* and whose variation is linked to a punishment-type treatment effect (5/15)  
6 (r), 7/10 (δ), 8 (b), 9 (switching reward on vs. off), 11 (a vs. b equality/inequality).  Numeric effect sizes are limited to the threshold formulas given above; no payoff efficiency numbers are provided.

D. What can we predict—solely from this paper—about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) affect the punishment treatment effect on *group efficiency*?  
• Because the authors never compute pay-offs relative to the social optimum, almost no direct inference about *efficiency* as defined by the user is possible.  
• Qualitatively, higher punishment leverage b or higher budget δ hasten full cooperation but also increase cost outlays; hence the sign of the effect on *efficiency* (payoff net of costs divided by optimum) is ambiguous.  
• Adding an initial reward phase (adaptive hybrid) is predicted to dominate pure punishment in cost-efficiency when cooperation has to *emerge*, but to be roughly cost-neutral once cooperation is already high.  
• Larger groups (n) lower the incentive threshold, suggesting a milder punishment suffices, so efficiency could improve with n, but the paper gives no numerical confirmation.  
• Higher MPCR r makes cooperation profitable even with smaller incentives, so any punishment cost might more readily be outweighed by the gain in social surplus; again no numbers are given.  
For all remaining parameters (2, 3, 5, 12–15) the paper provides no basis for prediction.

Consequently, while the paper yields rich information about *when* and *at what cost* punishment (or hybrid incentives) succeed in driving the population to full cooperation, it gives almost no quantitative guidance on how any of the 15 moderators would alter the *efficiency* treatment effect as defined by the user.
reference_APA: Chen, Xiaojie, Sasaki, Tatsuya, Braennstroem, Ake & Dieckmann, Ulf (2015). First carrot, then stick: how the adaptive hybridization of incentives promotes cooperation. JOURNAL OF THE ROYAL SOCIETY INTERFACE.

Article Title: Societal threat and cultural variation in the strength of social norms: An evolutionary basis

Abstract: The strengths of social norms vary considerably across cultures, yet little research has shown whether such differences have an evolutionary basis. Integrating research in cross-cultural psychology with evolutionary game theory, we show that groups that face a high degree of threat develop stronger norms for organizing social interaction, with a higher degree of norm-adherence and higher punishment for deviant behavior. This is the first work to show that different degrees of norm strength are evolutionarily adaptive to societal threat. Evolutionary game theoretic models of cultural adaptation may prove fruitful for exploring the causes of many other cultural differences that may be adaptive to particular ecological and historical contexts. 6. Marginal Per-Capita Return / multiplication factor r

• Mentioned?  Yes.  r is the synergy factor that multiplies the group contribution.

• Effect size on **punishment treatment effect**?

    • r ≈ 2.0 ⇒ Δₘ ≈ 1.0  
    • r ≈ 3.0 ⇒ Δₘ ≈ 0.5  
    • r ≈ 4.0 ⇒ Δₘ ≈ 0.35

• Effect size?  Same numbers already quoted under parameter 6: Fig. 7 gives the critical Δₘ that eliminates defectors for each r.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
9. “Reward enabled?”

• Mentioned?  Yes – rewarding is the main manipulation.  The paper also creates a direct comparison with punishment (Sec. 3.3).  
• Systematically varied?  Two separate models are run (reward model vs. punishment model).  Turning “reward on” versus “punishment on” is therefore a between-model condition, not a parameter sweep with numerical gradations.  
• Effect size?  Only Fig. 7 again: at α = 0.4, adaptive punishment needs a lower Δ to remove defectors than adaptive reward, implying a larger punishment treatment effect, but numerical pay-offs are not supplied.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
10. Reward cost (cost per unit given)

• Mentioned?  Same symbol α when the model is in “reward” mode.  
• Systematically varied?  Yes (Figs. 2, 5).  
• Effect size?  Analogous qualitative breakpoints as quoted for parameter 7, but again only phases, not pay-offs.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
11. Reward magnitude

• Mentioned?  Same symbol Δ in the reward model.  
• Systematically varied?  Yes (vertical axis in Figs. 2, 5; also the x-axis in Fig. 1).  
• Effect size?  From Fig. 1 (r = 2, α = 0.1):  
    Steady Rewarding: Defectors coexist for all Δ, even up to Δ = 4.  
    Adaptive Rewarding: Defectors extinct once Δ > ≈ 0.9.  
  No efficiency numbers are reported.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
12. End-round information (do players know the number of rounds)?

• Mentioned?  No.  
• Systematically varied?  No.  
• Effect size?  None.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
13. Are peer outcomes displayed?

• Mentioned?  No.  
• Systematically varied?  No.  
• Effect size?  None.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
14. Is the punisher known?

• Mentioned?  No.  
• Systematically varied?  No.  
• Effect size?  None.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
15. Is the rewarder known?

• Mentioned?  No.  
• Systematically varied?  No.  
• Effect size?  None.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
• The paper does **not** report “group efficiency” (total earnings divided by the cooperative optimum).  
• Reported variables are (i) stationary fractions of strategies (ρ_C, ρ_D, ρ_R or ρ_P), and (ii) the qualitative *phase* that survives (D, C, R, P, or combinations).  These are categorically different from efficiency.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
Seven of them: 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 (with 7 ≡ 10 and 8 ≡ 11, and 9 treated as a binary model choice).  Parameters 3, 5, 12, 13, 14, 15 are never mentioned.

C. For how many parameters is their *systematic* influence on the punishment treatment effect discussed?  
Three:  
• 6 (r), 7/10 (α, cost), and 8/11 (Δ, magnitude).  
The discussion is purely in terms of “which phase survives” or “minimum Δ needed to drive D extinct,” not in terms of pay-offs or efficiency.

D. If one had to predict how the 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment treatment effect on **efficiency**, relying only on this paper:

– Only r, α, and Δ can be said to matter, and the only concrete statements are:  
  • Lower r (weaker MPCR) makes punishment less effective (higher Δ required to eliminate defectors).  
  • Higher punishment cost α makes punishment less effective and can even remove punishing cooperators altogether.  
  • Higher punishment magnitude Δ strengthens the treatment effect up to the point defectors disappear.  
– No numerical relationship between these parameters and *efficiency* is provided anywhere.  
– For all other parameters (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 12-15) the paper gives no evidence that changing them would alter the punishment treatment effect.

In short, the article lets us say very little about efficiency; it only lets us infer that punishment is more potent than reward, and that its potency increases with larger MPCR (r), lower cost (α), and higher fine size (Δ). All other parameters remain a blank slate as far as this paper is concerned.

Where a numerical efficiency effect can be read directly from a table or figure I report it.  If the parameter is never varied (or not mentioned), I say so explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1.  Number of players  
    • Mentioned: Yes.  All games use “groups of four” (p. 4, Section 3.1).  
    • Systematically varied?  No.  There is no condition with a different group size, and no prediction about changing the size.  
    • Numerical effect size on efficiency when group size changes: None.

2.  Number of rounds  
    • Mentioned: Yes.  Each session has 20 periods (10 baseline + 10 treatment), p. 9.  
    • Systematically varied?  No.  All sessions use the same horizon, and the authors do not vary or predict effects of longer/shorter horizons (they only cite other studies that use 50 periods).  
    • Effect size: Not available.

3.  Chat enabled?  
    • Mentioned: No.  There is no chat or communication device in any treatment.  
    • Systematic variation / prediction: None.

4.  All–or–nothing contribution choice?  
    • Mentioned: Yes, implicitly.  Contributions are continuous from 0–5 tokens (Section 3.1).  
    • Varied or predicted?  No.

5.  “Contribution default” frame (endowment starts in public fund)?  
    • Not mentioned.  Endowment starts in the private account and can be moved to the public account.  
    • Varied / predicted?  No.

6.  Marginal-per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
    • Mentioned: Yes.  One token to the public good gives \$2 to each of the four members (MPCR = 0.667; multiplier = 8), Section 3.1.  
    • Varied or predicted?  No.  Only this single MPCR is used.

7.  Punishment cost (to the punisher)  
    • Mentioned: Yes.  
        – Peer-to-peer (P2P): Cost \$1 to reduce target’s payoff by \$3 (Section 3.4).  
        – Delegated “gun” mechanism: No per-shot cost; instead the group pays a hiring cost (8 tokens = \$2 per group ≈ \$0.50 per person) when the gun is hired (Sections 3.3, 5.1).  
    • Systematically varied?  No.  Only these fixed cost structures are studied.  
    • Prediction from varying cost?  None; authors only compare the fixed cost regimes.

8.  Punishment magnitude (deduction suffered by punished player)  
    • Mentioned: Yes.  
        – P2P: Each point deducts \$3.  
        – Gun mechanism: Variable, P = 3(g_y − g_z)+3 with a floor of \$3 (Section 3.2.1).  
    • Varied / predicted?  Not varied experimentally; no prediction about changing the magnitude.

9.  Reward enabled?  
    • Not used or discussed.

10. Reward cost  
    • Not applicable.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Not applicable.

12. Is the number of rounds known?  
    • The paper does not state that the horizon is hidden; in standard laboratory fashion subjects know the game length, but the authors never mention, vary, or theorise about this parameter.  
    • No systematic variation.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mentioned: Yes.  After each period subjects see all group members’ contributions and pay-offs (Sections 3.1–3.5).  
    • Varied / predicted?  No.

14. Do punished players learn who punished them?  
    • Mentioned: Yes (for P2P) punishments are anonymous (“anonymous information about …”, Section 3.4).  
    • Varied / predicted?  No.

15. Do rewarded players learn who rewarded them?  
    • Not applicable (no rewards).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
NUMERICAL “PUNISHMENT-TREATMENT EFFECTS” REPORTED IN THE PAPER

Because none of the 15 parameters are experimentally manipulated, the only measurable “treatment effects” in the paper come from switching the *type* of punishment regime, not from changing the parameter values themselves.  For completeness:

• Switching from the baseline no-punishment LPG game (average earnings \$23.82) to an exogenously imposed hired-gun game (GH) raises average earnings to \$37.28 (Table 2) – an efficiency gain of about \$13.46 per person, i.e., +56 % relative to baseline earnings.

• In the endogenous hiring game (G4H) the gun is actually hired in 85 % of periods, giving average earnings \$38.12 when hired and only \$19.55 when not hired (Table 2).  Hence, “hiring the gun” versus “not hiring” within the *same* parameter environment raises earnings by \$18.57.

• When the baseline already allows peer punishment, adding the option to hire the gun (G4H/P2P) raises average earnings from \$22.89 (P2P) to \$31.87 overall, and to \$36.14 in periods in which the gun is hired (Table 4).  The net welfare gain conditional on hiring is therefore \$13.25 (+58 %).

These numbers are consequences of *regime* changes, not of changes in any of the 15 listed parameters.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used  
   – Yes, the paper uses group or individual net earnings (i.e., efficiency) as its central welfare measure.  
   – Other dependent variables: (i) individual contribution to the public good; (ii) monetary cost of punishments.  Efficiency includes both contributions and punishment costs, so it differs from “contribution” alone.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 13, 14  →  8 parameters are described, but every one of them is *fixed*.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss their *systematic variation* and its effect on punishment treatment outcomes?  
   0.  None of the 15 parameters are systematically varied; therefore no effect sizes linked to parameter variation can be extracted.

D. What predictions (if any) can be made about how the 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency, **using only evidence in this paper**?  
   • Because the study holds all 15 parameters constant, the only safe prediction is that *when those parameters take exactly the values used here* (4 players, MPCR = 0.667, cost-benefit structure detailed above, anonymous one-shot peer punishment, etc.), delegating punishment to the “hired gun” raises efficiency relative to peer punishment or no punishment.  
   • The paper provides no basis for extrapolating how the size or sign of that effect would change if any of the parameters were altered (e.g., a different MPCR, more players, visible punishers, per-shot punishment fees, adding rewards, etc.).  Therefore, beyond the very restricted prediction just stated, **little or no additional prediction can be made** solely on the basis of the evidence reported.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
End of analysis.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter analysis based on the content of the provided paper. Throughout, “the paper” refers exclusively to “Intergroup Conflict and Intra-Group Punishment in an Experimental Contest Game,” by Abbink et al.

IMPORTANT NOTE ON TERMINOLOGY:  
• The paper’s main dependent variables are “contest expenditures,” “material losses,” and “rent dissipation” (ratio of total resources spent in the contest to the prize). The authors also discuss participants’ payoffs (earnings). They do compare punishment treatments to no‐punishment treatments, but they do not report the “efficiency” measure as (actual total payoff) / (maximum possible payoff of a fully cooperative group). Instead, they focus on how high conflict expenditures (and thus dissipation) become.  
• Where the paper does refer to “efficiency,” it is only in remarks that punishment makes group outcomes worse (less efficient) in these conflict games—unlike in many public goods games where punishment can raise efficiency. However, they do not provide a systematic measure labeled “efficiency” in the manner often used for public goods games.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) NUMBER OF PLAYERS  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – YES. The paper compares three main setups: (1:1), (1:4), and (4:4), referring to whether each “party” is one individual or a four‐person team. The authors also have a 4:4/40 treatment (same 4‐person teams, extended to 40 rounds).  
     – Values in the paper: 1 vs. 4 players per party.  

   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying the number of players for the “punishment treatment effect” on any dependent variable?  
     – PARTIALLY. The paper does consider a “4:4P” treatment (two teams of four each, with punishment). However, it never runs a 1:4 or 1:1 punishment treatment. Thus, although group size is discussed extensively (1 vs. 4) and “presence of punishment” is discussed (in 4:4 vs. 4:4P), the paper does not systematically compare punishment across different group sizes. The only punishment data come from 4:4P. Therefore, the paper does not show how systematically going from 1‐player to 4‐player teams changes the punishment effect.  
     – Quantitative effect sizes (for 4:4P vs. 4:4 without punishment): With punishment, final conflict expenditures can exceed twice the level of the no‐punishment case, and total material losses surpass 800% to 900% of the Nash‐equilibrium‐predicted level (Figures 5–6, Section IV).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2) NUMBER OF ROUNDS  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – YES. There are 20‐round sessions in most treatments and a 40‐round “4:4/40” condition.  

   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying the number of rounds for the punishment treatment effect?  
     – NO. While the authors do compare 4:4 (20 rounds) and 4:4/40 (40 rounds), they do not have a 4:4P (punishment) version extended to 40 rounds. Hence, there is no direct systematic variation of the time horizon under punishment vs. no punishment.  
     – They do note that in the 4:4P treatment (20 rounds), punishment usage remains steady even near the last round, indicating no typical “endgame effect,” but there is no parallel 4:4P/40 to compare.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3) IS CHAT ENABLED BETWEEN PLAYERS?  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – YES, but only to say there is NO chat. The design disallows communication among participants.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying chat for the punishment effect?  
     – NO. They never vary communication; that factor is held constant (no chat).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4) IS THE CONTRIBUTION “ALL OR NOTHING”?  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – The paper’s design lets each participant choose any integer from 0 to 1000 to invest in contest tokens. This is not “all or nothing.”  
     – They do not systematically vary it.  

   • Any predicted effect on punishment treatment?  
     – NO. This aspect is not varied or studied for punishment.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5) IS THE CONTRIBUTION DEFAULT (DO PLAYERS MOVE ENDOWMENT FROM PUBLIC TO PRIVATE)?  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – NO. The paper’s contest design is not about “default contributions” or moving funds out of a public account. Everyone simply decides how many contest tokens (0 to 1000) to buy.  
   • Any predicted effect?  
     – NO mention.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6) MARGINAL PER CAPITA RETURN (MPCR) OR RELATED MULTIPLICATION FACTOR  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – NO. Although the paper uses Tullock’s “lottery” contest function, it does not refer to MPCR or any public‐goods‐type “multiplication factor.”  
   • Any predicted effect?  
     – NO mention. The existing “multiplication factor” is simply how the lottery probability is determined from tokens, but it is not systematically varied.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7) PUNISHMENT COST TO IMPOSE A SINGLE UNIT  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – YES, it is fixed at 1 point per deduction token allocated by the punisher.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary that cost or make predictions about varying it?  
     – NO. The cost is always 1 point; the authors do not explore different punishment‐cost levels.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
8) PUNISHMENT MAGNITUDE (THE COINS DEDUCTED FROM A PLAYER WHO IS PUNISHED)  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – YES, it is fixed at 3 points deducted from the punished player’s payoff for each deduction token that player receives.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary that magnitude or predict its effect if varied?  
     – NO. They only use the fixed 3‐to‐1 ratio in the 4:4P treatment, with no parameter variation.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
9) WHETHER A REWARD IS ENABLED  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – NO. There is no reward—only punishment.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
10) REWARD COST TO GRANT A UNIT OF REWARD  
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
      – NO, because there is no reward condition.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
11) REWARD MAGNITUDE (COINS AWARDED PER UNIT REWARD)  
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
      – NO, for the same reason above.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
12) IS THE NUMBER OF ROUNDS KNOWN TO PLAYERS?  
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
      – YES. They explicitly tell participants the number of rounds (either 20 or 40).  
    • Do they systematically vary “known vs. unknown” horizon for the punishment effect?  
      – NO. All treatments have a known horizon. This is never manipulated to study punishment differently.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
13) ARE PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN (DO PLAYERS KNOW PEERS’ GAINS/LOSSES EACH ROUND)?  
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
      – PARTIALLY. Each participant sees how many contest tokens every teammate invests, whether their team won, and how many deduction tokens they personally received. They do see their own updated balance.  
    • Do they systematically vary the level of information shown for the punishment effect?  
      – NO. The design is fixed in what is displayed; no separate conditions are run.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
14) WHEN A PLAYER IS PUNISHED, DO THEY KNOW WHO THE SPECIFIC PUNISHER IS?  
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
      – They do not explicitly say that the punishee sees which particular teammate assigned tokens. The paper emphasizes anonymity within the team (players see each other’s ID numbers for investments but not real names). The instructions do not indicate that punishees learn the specific punisher.  
    • Any systematic variation?  
      – NO. Not varied.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
15) WHEN A PLAYER IS REWARDED, DO THEY KNOW WHO THE SPECIFIC REWARDER IS?  
    • The paper has no reward condition at all.  
    • Hence no discussion or variation.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY ANSWERS (A–D)

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?  
   • The paper focuses on “contest expenditures,” “material losses,” “rent dissipation” (i.e., how much of the prize is dissipated by conflict spending), and individual/team earnings. Although the authors say that punishment sometimes enhances efficiency in public‐goods experiments, their own analysis centers on how punishment in contests leads to very large waste (i.e., negative efficiency implications).  
   • Thus, they do not report a direct measure of efficiency = (actual total payoff) / (maximum possible payoff). Instead, they measure “rent dissipation” or “material losses,” which is their measure of how wasteful the contest has become.

B) Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   1. Number of players: MENTIONED (1 vs. 4).  
   2. Number of rounds: MENTIONED (20 vs. 40).  
   3. Is chat enabled? MENTIONED (communication is disallowed, never varied).  
   4. Contribution all or nothing? MENTIONED only implicitly (it is not all or nothing). Not varied.  
   5. Contribution default? NOT mentioned.  
   6. MPCR or multiplication factor? NOT mentioned.  
   7. Punishment cost to impose one unit? MENTIONED (1 point). Not varied.  
   8. Punishment magnitude? MENTIONED (3 points). Not varied.  
   9. Whether reward is enabled? NOT mentioned in the design (no reward).  
   10–11. Reward cost / magnitude? NOT mentioned.  
   12. Is the number of rounds known? MENTIONED (always known, either 20 or 40).  
   13. Are peer outcomes shown? PARTIALLY MENTIONED (they do see teammates’ contributions and final payoffs). Not varied.  
   14. Punishee knows who punished them? The paper suggests no direct identification. Not varied.  
   15. Punishee knows who rewarded them (if any)? NOT mentioned (no reward).  

C) For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • In terms of “systematic variation” specifically for punishment, the only change is from “no punishment” to “punishment” in a (4:4) condition.  
   • They do vary group size (1 vs. 4), but not with punishment for 1:1 or 1:4. They do vary the time horizon (20 vs. 40) but only in no‐punishment group contests.  
   • Hence, strictly speaking, the only parameter systematically varied to observe a direct “punishment treatment effect” is the presence vs. absence of punishment in the 4:4 setting.  

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, solely from this paper’s content, what would they be?  
   • The paper only shows that under 4:4 vs. 4:4P (punishment enabled), punishment severely increases conflict spending and reduces overall payoffs—implying lower efficiency in the presence of punishment.  
   • Because no other parameters (e.g., punishment cost, homogeneous vs. heterogeneous group sizes) are systematically manipulated alongside punishment, the paper does not provide evidence for how they might jointly moderate the punishment effect on efficiency.  
   • Therefore, one can say little beyond:  
       – In a 4:4 setting, introducing punishment raises conflict expenditures (often over twice the no‐punishment level) and pushes total losses above 800% of the (already high) equilibrium benchmark.  
       – No direct information is given about how changing other parameters (like punishment cost, group size + punishment, or enabling chat) would affect efficiency in this particular contest framework.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

This completes the requested analysis based solely on the content of Abbink et al.’s paper.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter summary of what (if anything) the paper by Bergstrom (“Evolution of Social Behavior: Individual and Group Selection”) says regarding that parameter and whether the paper makes any predictions about systematically varying it and its effect on the “punishment treatment effect” (i.e., how adding punishment to a public goods game increases or decreases the group’s efficiency).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. The paper often uses an N-player (or N-member) formulation for both prisoners’ dilemma and public goods settings (for instance, “N-player prisoners’ dilemma game,” “N-player linear public goods game,” and “groups of size N”). However, these discussions are in the context of evolutionary models (for example, the “haystack model”), not in the context of an experimental treatment manipulation.  
   • Does it predict effects of systematically varying this parameter on punishment treatment (for efficiency or any other outcome)?  
     – No. The paper does not discuss or measure how changing N would affect the outcome of a punishment-versus-no-punishment comparison. Its mentions of N serve only to set up theoretical arguments about when a game is or is not a prisoners’ dilemma.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Indirectly. The paper distinguishes between one-shot versus repeated (or indefinitely repeated) games and also discusses “long-lived” versus “short-lived” groups (sometimes parameterized by T, the “length of time” groups remain intact). However, these discussions focus on how the group might sustain cooperation over multiple generations.  
   • Does it predict effects of systematically varying this parameter on punishment treatment (for efficiency or any other outcome)?  
     – No. Although there is substantial discussion of repeated interaction helping sustain cooperation, there is no explicit modeling or empirical result on adding punishment and systematically varying the “number of rounds” per se. The paper does not quantify a “punishment treatment effect” in that context.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. There is no mention or analysis of communication (“chat”) in any experimental or theoretical sense.  
   • Does it predict effects of systematically varying this parameter on punishment treatment?  
     – No. Not discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?

Abstract: If individuals will cooperate with cooperators, and punish non-cooperators even at a cost to themselves, then this strong reciprocity could minimize the cheating that undermines cooperation. Second-party punishment is when you punish someone who defected on you; third-party punishment is when you punish someone who defected on someone else.    • Mentioned?

   • Mentioned?  
     – The paper frames the donation stage in terms of a benefit b and cost c. In many public goods settings, b/c can be analogous to an MPCR (if b > c). They pick typical numeric values (e.g., b = 4, c = 1) in examples.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?  
     – Not directly. They do not present a table or figure that systematically alters b/c to show changes in punishing‐based efficiency.    • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The parameter γ in the model is the cost to the punisher for applying punishment (and likewise the cost of providing a reward). They typically set γ = 2 in examples, subject to γ < b.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?  
     – They derive threshold conditions such as “μ > γ/(b + γ)” for certain strategies to invade. However, they do not provide numeric findings about “how efficiency changes” when γ changes; instead, they describe which equilibria or strategy mixtures emerge. No explicit data on “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”

8. PUNISHMENT MAGNITUDE (THE COINS DEDUCTED FROM THE TARGET)  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The paper denotes this as β. If someone is punished, they lose β; the punisher pays γ. In their examples, β = γ = 2.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?  
     – They do discuss how β relative to other parameters influences thresholds for stable or unstable equilibria (e.g., “c < β” or “γ ≤ β”). But they give no explicit numeric “change in group efficiency” when β is varied. Predictions are about strategy invasion or stability, not about changes in total payoff/efficiency from punishment per se.

   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes, extensively. The paper contrasts “punishment only” with “punishment + reward” treatments (Figures 3 and 4, sections 2–3).  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?  
     – Yes, in the sense that they examine two scenarios: (1) punishment only, (2) punishment + reward. They show that allowing reward speeds up the evolution of cooperation (the “catalytic effect”). Numerical “effect sizes” on efficiency are not given. Instead, they show that adding reward can help punishment‐based cooperation to arise more reliably (especially if the “information level” μ is low or moderate).    • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. Same parameter γ is also the cost to the rewarder (same as punishment cost).  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?  
     – Similar to item 7. They do not provide a quantitative change in efficiency from systematically varying γ. Instead, they give threshold inequalities for whether reward or punishment invades a population.

11. REWARD MAGNITUDE (TO THE RECIPIENT OF REWARD)  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. Same β as in punishment magnitude; it just adds β to the one being rewarded, while the rewarder pays γ.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?

12. IS THE NUMBER OF ROUNDS KNOWN TO PLAYERS?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Only indirectly. They reference repeated settings and infinite‐horizon population models; the text does not distinguish “known end dates” vs. “unknown.”  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?  
     – Not discussed.

13. ARE PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN (HOW MUCH PEERS GAIN/LOSE)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Not in the sense of “each co‐player’s payoff each round.” The paper primarily uses “information level” μ as the probability of knowing whether one’s opponent is an incentive‐using type (punisher/rewarder), not how much payoff they earned.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?  
     – No. They vary μ from 0 to 1, but not specifically whether “peer outcomes” are displayed. There is no mention of payoff‐display manipulations.

14. WHEN A PLAYER IS PUNISHED, DO THEY KNOW THE PUNISHER’S IDENTITY?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – The paper does discuss that building up a reputation as a punisher can matter. However, it does not explicitly say whether the punished party “knows who punished them.”

     – Not discussed.

15. WHEN A PLAYER IS REWARDED, DO THEY KNOW THE REWARDER’S IDENTITY?  
   • Mentioned?

     – Not discussed.

════════════════════════════════════════════
A. DOES THE PAPER USE GROUP EFFICIENCY (OR TOTAL/AVERAGE PAYOFF) AS A DEPENDENT VARIABLE? WHAT ARE THE DEPENDENT VARIABLES AND HOW ARE THESE DIFFERENT?  
   • Yes, the paper does at times talk about average payoffs and “efficiency” (they note that punishment may be costlier if many defect, etc.). However, the authors’ main analyses revolve around strategy stability, invasion possibilities, and thresholds for opportunistic strategies. They frequently discuss which strategies dominate in the long run (e.g., punisher vs. rewarder vs. defector), and how that affects overall payoffs.  
   • Hence, some outcomes (e.g., “Which strategies invade?” “Which states are stable?” “How quickly does cooperation arise?”) differ from measuring “efficiency.” Where the paper does speak of payoff, it does not provide explicit numerical “efficiency” measures (like actual payoff / maximum payoff) for each parameter; rather, it focuses on dynamic stability and how different incentive strategies can catalyze or block cooperation.

B. WHICH AND HOW MANY OF THE 15 PARAMETERS ARE MENTIONED IN THE PAPER?  
   • Mentioned clearly in some form:  
     1 (number of players) – yes, interpreted as 2 in their main model  
     2 (number of rounds) – acknowledged but not varied  
     4 (binary cooperation = “all or nothing”) – yes, as a fixed design  
     6 (benefit/cost akin to MPCR) – partial mention via b and c  
     7 (punishment cost) – yes, γ  
     8 (punishment magnitude) – yes, β  
     9 (whether reward is enabled) – yes, extensively discussed  
     10 (reward cost) – same γ as punishment  
     11 (reward magnitude) – same β as punishment’s magnitude  
   • The others (3, 5, 12, 13, 14, 15) are either not discussed at all or only mentioned tangentially without parameter variation.  
   • In total, nine of the 15 parameters (1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11) are at least mentioned. The remaining six are not meaningfully addressed.

C. FOR WHICH AND HOW MANY OF THE 15 PARAMETERS DOES THE PAPER DISCUSS THEIR EFFECT ON THE PUNISHMENT TREATMENT EFFECT WHEN SYSTEMATICALLY VARIED?  
   • Strictly as “punishment treatment effect on efficiency,” the paper never provides a direct numeric measure or effect size. Instead, for some parameters (particularly γ, β, and whether reward is possible) they give equilibrium/threshold conditions and discuss how easily punishment‐based strategies invade or stabilize.  
   • More specifically:  
     – (9) “Whether reward is enabled”: They compare “punishment only” vs. “punishment + reward” (Figures 3–4); although the paper frames it mostly in terms of faster emergence of cooperation, they imply that final average payoff (hence “efficiency”) is higher with both carrot and stick. No numeric “effect size” is given.  
     – (7, 8, 10, 11) “Cost and magnitude of punishment/reward” (γ, β): They analyze thresholds (e.g., μ > γ/(b+γ)), not changes in payoff ratio or explicit changes in efficiency.  
     – No other parameters are systematically varied to show direct impacts on an efficiency measure.  
   • Hence, only one parameter—(9), reward enabled vs. not—is overtly varied to compare outcomes with or without punishment. Even there, the outcome measure is typically which equilibrium emerges, not a stated quantitative difference in group efficiency.  
   • So effectively, just one of the 15 parameters (the presence or absence of reward) is expressly varied in the context of punishment’s impact on cooperation/average payoffs. The others are not varied in a way that yields a numeric “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”

D. IF YOU WERE TO MAKE PREDICTIONS ON HOW THE 15 PARAMETERS AND THEIR INTERACTIONS INFLUENCE THE PUNISHMENT TREATMENT EFFECT ON EFFICIENCY SOLELY BASED ON THIS PAPER, WHAT WOULD THEY BE?  
   • The paper itself offers limited direct discussion of “efficiency gains or losses from punishment.” Its main focus is on whether punishment (and reward) can stabilize cooperation, rather than on explicit efficiency ratios.  
   • Nonetheless, one might cautiously infer from the text that:  
     1) Allowing reward (parameter 9) alongside punishment tends to raise the likelihood that punishment will ultimately stabilize a high‐payoff outcome (and thus presumably raise group efficiency relative to a defection equilibrium).  
     2) If the cost of punishing/rewarding (γ) is too high or the magnitude of punishment/reward (β) is too low, punishment (and sometimes reward) may fail to emerge, which indirectly implies lower overall payoffs.  
     3) Varying other structural features (e.g., number of players, number of rounds, presence of communication) is largely unaddressed in this paper, so no predictions can be derived from the text.  
   • Overall, the paper does not provide numerical effect sizes or direct “efficiency” measures for any systematically varied parameter. Thus, one can make little to no precise numerical prediction of how these 15 parameters jointly influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency based solely on the paper’s content.

────────────────────────────────────────────
End of response.
