Article Title: Cooperation and assortativity with dynamic partner updating
Source Title: PROCEEDINGS OF THE NATIONAL ACADEMY OF SCIENCES OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
Author Keywords: network science; dynamic networks; web-based experiments
Keywords Plus: PRISONERS-DILEMMA GAMES; EVOLUTION; SELECTION
Abstract: The natural tendency for humans to make and break relationships is thought to facilitate the emergence of cooperation. In particular, allowing conditional cooperators to choose with whom they interact is believed to reinforce the rewards accruing to mutual cooperation while simultaneously excluding defectors. Here we report on a series of human subjects experiments in which groups of 24 participants played an iterated prisoner's dilemma game where, critically, they were also allowed to propose and delete links to players of their own choosing at some variable rate. Over a wide variety of parameter settings and initial conditions, we found that dynamic partner updating significantly increased the level of cooperation, the average payoffs to players, and the assortativity between cooperators. Even relatively slow update rates were sufficient to produce large effects, while subsequent increases to the update rate had progressively smaller, but still positive, effects. For standard prisoner's dilemma payoffs, we also found that assortativity resulted predominantly from cooperators avoiding defectors, not by severing ties with defecting partners, and that cooperation correspondingly suffered. Finally, by modifying the payoffs to satisfy two novel conditions, we found that cooperators did punish defectors by severing ties, leading to higher levels of cooperation that persisted for longer.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter review, based strictly on what appears (or does not appear) in the Wang, Suri, and Watts paper reproduced above. The paper studies a repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma game with dynamic partner “rewiring” (link formation and deletion), not a public goods game with explicit punishment or reward. Accordingly, most of the 15 public‐goods‐game parameters you list do not appear at all. Where a parameter is mentioned (e.g., number of players), the paper does not systematically vary it in ways relevant to a “punishment treatment effect.” Any references to “punishment” in the paper concern severing links (i.e., “implicit punishment” through ostracism), not a targeted mechanism that costs the punisher some amount and deducts points (or imposes a penalty) on the punished. Likewise, the paper discusses “cooperation” and “average payoffs” but does not use “efficiency” (as in actual/maximum payoff) as its focal dependent variable.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper specifies groups of 24 participants.  
   • Systematically varied or discussed for its effect on efficiency or on a punishment‐based treatment? No.  

2) Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? Yes. All experiments have 12 strategy‐update rounds (and some conditions insert “partner‐update turns” after r=1, 3, or 6 strategy rounds).  
   • Systematically varied for a punishment (or “punishment treatment”) effect? No. The paper does not discuss how varying the total number of rounds would alter any punishment‐treatment effect.  

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned? No. There is no mention of any in‐game discussion or chat.  

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • In the paper’s repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma, each player chooses either to cooperate or defect, which is indeed “all or nothing” in a binary sense. However, the paper does not treat this parameter as a variable to be manipulated, nor is it connected to any punishment‐treatment effect.  

5) Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much of their endowment to move from the fund back to themselves)?  
   • Not mentioned. The study is not framed in terms of a public‐goods‐type endowment or a default contribution.  

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
   • Not mentioned. The paper works with a Prisoner’s Dilemma payoff matrix (e.g., (C,C) = 4 points each, (C,D) = −1 for C, +7 for D, etc.), rather than a linear MPCR or “multiplier” used in many public goods experiments.

   • Not mentioned. There is no mechanism in which players pay a cost to punish others by reducing their payoffs. “Punishment” is discussed only in the sense of cutting ties (which does not involve a direct cost‐per‐punishment parameter).

   • Not mentioned. No explicit punishment or per‐unit deduction appears.

    • Not mentioned.

    • Not mentioned.

    • The paper does not explicitly say whether participants knew there would be 12 strategy‐update rounds. Typically in these experiments the total is common knowledge, but there is no direct statement. It is not systematically varied, nor is there any discussion of how varying that knowledge would affect (explicit) punishment treatment.  

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much their peers gained or lost)?  
    • The paper says participants see each other’s recent actions (cooperate or defect) and their own payoffs. It does not clearly say they see everyone else’s exact payoffs. The experiment does not systematically vary the display of outcomes, nor does it connect this parameter to a punishment treatment.  

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Not mentioned. There is no explicit punisher or punishment cost of the sort described in standard public goods “punishment” treatments.  

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Not mentioned. No reward mechanism is in place.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Summary of Findings

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are they different?  
   • The paper focuses primarily on (1) fraction of cooperating players (“cooperation level”) and (2) average (per‐player) payoff. It does not define or measure “efficiency” as “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff of a fully cooperative group.” Thus, although “payoff” is used, “efficiency” in the sense you define is not.  

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • (1) Number of players (24) appears.  
   • (2) Number of rounds (12) appears.  
   • (4) The game is “all‐or‐nothing” in the sense of cooperate vs. defect, but not varied as such.  
   • (13) A limited form of peer information is displayed (i.e., seeing others’ recent actions), but not systematically manipulated.  
   • No other parameter is mentioned in the sense of an explicit design choice that they manipulate or even hold fixed as part of a punishment treatment.  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the “punishment treatment effect” (for any dependent variable) when the parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, zero. The paper’s “punishment” is only in the sense of unilaterally deleting links in a Prisoner’s Dilemma, and none of the 15 public‐goods‐punishment parameters is varied or even discussed as a factor in a punishment‐treatment effect.  

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of this paper, what would they be?  
   • Because the paper does not address most of these parameters—nor does it measure efficiency in the manner you define—it provides no direct basis for predicting how systematically varying those 15 factors would affect a “punishment treatment effect” on group efficiency. Any such predictions would necessarily go beyond the paper’s content, which is limited to repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma with dynamic partner‐rewiring. Thus, we must conclude that little or no prediction about those 15 parameters, as you define them for a public goods setting, can be made solely from this paper.

Abstract: Parochial altruisma preference for altruistic behavior towards ingroup members and mistrust or hostility towards outgroup membersis a pervasive feature in human society and strongly shapes the enforcement of social norms. Since the uniqueness of human society critically depends on the enforcement of norms, the understanding of the neural circuitry of the impact of parochial altruism on social norm enforcement is key, but unexplored. To fill this gap, we measured brain activity with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) while subjects had the opportunity to punish ingroup members and outgroup members for violating social norms. Findings revealed that subjects' strong punishment of defecting outgroup members is associated with increased activity in a functionally connected network involved in sanction-related decisions (right orbitofrontal gyrus, right lateral prefrontal cortex, right dorsal caudatus). Moreover, the stronger the connectivity in this network, the more outgroup members are punished. In contrast, the much weaker punishment of ingroup members who committed the very same norm violation is associated with increased activity and connectivity in the mentalizing-network (dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, bilateral temporo-parietal junction), as if subjects tried to understand or justify ingroup members' behavior. Finally, connectivity analyses between the two networks suggest that the mentalizing-network modulates punishment by affecting the activity in the right orbitofrontal gyrus and right lateral prefrontal cortex, notably in the same areas showing enhanced activity and connectivity whenever third-parties strongly punished defecting outgroup members. Here we investigate the emergence and impact of different types of sanctioning to deter non-cooperative behaviour in climate agreements. We show that a bottom-up approach, in which parties create local institutions that punish free-riders, promotes the emergence of widespread cooperation, mostly when risk perception is low, as it is at present(3,7). On the contrary, global institutions provide, at best, marginal improvements regarding overall cooperation. Our results clearly suggest that a polycentric approach involving multiple institutions is more effective than that associated with a single, global one, indicating that such a bottom-up, self-organization approach, set up at a local scale, provides a better ground on which to attempt a solution for such a complex and global dilemma.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter summary based solely on the content of the provided paper by Vasconcelos et al. The paper focuses on a theoretical model of “collective-risk dilemmas” with punishment institutions at either the global or local (group) level, and it reports outcomes in terms of:  
• group achievement (ηG): the fraction of groups that successfully meet a threshold for contributing to (or “producing”) the public good, and  
• institution prevalence (ηI): how often in time punishment institutions (global or local) are active.  

Importantly, the paper does not directly measure or report “efficiency” (i.e., actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff), nor does it provide numerical results on how systematically varying each of the 15 parameters below would affect “efficiency.” Instead, it chiefly discusses the effects of varying risk perception (r) and whether punishment is organized globally or locally.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER DISCUSSION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. Number of players  
   • What the paper says: The model has a total population of size Z (often Z = 100 in their figures). Groups of size N = 4 are formed within that population to play the public goods game. The paper notes that “groups are small,” but does not report a systematic parameter sweep of Z or N that is then tied to a quantitative “punishment treatment effect.”  
   • Systematic variation / effect size on punishment treatment: The main text does not show explicit numerical results systematically varying Z or N. It does note qualitatively, “One can also show (Supplementary Information) that this result is even more pronounced in a scenario encompassing (many) small groups,” suggesting that smaller N can enhance local-punishment effectiveness. However, the paper does not provide a specific numeric effect size or discuss efficiency in this context.  

2. Number of rounds  
   • What the paper says: The model is framed in evolutionary (ongoing) terms with no fixed number of rounds. The text does not discuss or vary a finite time horizon or a known end of the game.  
   • Systematic variation / effect size on punishment treatment: Not mentioned.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • What the paper says: No mention of communication or “chat.”  
   • Systematic variation / effect size on punishment treatment: Not mentioned.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • What the paper says: Cooperator (C) and punisher (P) each pay a fraction c of an initial endowment b; defectors (D) pay nothing. The paper does not indicate any “all-or-nothing” design nor does it vary such a feature.  
   • Systematic variation / effect size on punishment treatment: Not mentioned.  

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much to move back into their hand)?  
   • What the paper says: No mention of any default or partial returns mechanism beyond the simple fraction c that cooperators/punishers always pay.  
   • Systematic variation / effect size on punishment treatment: Not mentioned.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
   • What the paper says: The paper frames contributions as a fraction c of one’s endowment b, with no direct reference to a traditional MPCR. It sets c/b = 0.1 in the figures.  
   • Systematic variation / effect size on punishment treatment: The paper does not systematically vary c, b, or any multiplier. No numeric effect on punishment outcome or efficiency is provided with respect to changing c/b.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • What the paper says: Punishers pay a “punishment tax” denoted πt in order to fund an institution. However, the paper does not analyze how varying πt affects outcomes. The figures typically set πt = 0.03.  
   • Systematic variation / effect size on punishment treatment: Not mentioned or quantified for efficiency or any other outcome.  

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted for each punishment)  
   • What the paper says: The paper defines πf (or Δ) as the fine for defectors whenever a punishment institution threshold is reached. This is central to the model but is not systematically varied in the reported results.  
   • Systematic variation / effect size on punishment treatment: Not mentioned or quantified for efficiency or any other outcome.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • What the paper says: The model only studies punishment. It does not discuss any reward mechanism.  
   • Systematic variation / effect size on punishment treatment: Not mentioned.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • What the paper says: No reward mechanism is presented.  
    • Systematic variation / effect size on punishment treatment: Not mentioned.  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)  
    • What the paper says: No reward mechanism is presented.  
    • Systematic variation / effect size on punishment treatment: Not mentioned.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players? (Do they know when it ends?)  
    • What the paper says: No mention. The evolutionary process has no fixed end.  
    • Systematic variation / effect size on punishment treatment: Not mentioned.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown? (Do players know how much peers gained/lost each round?)  
    • What the paper says: No mention of any real-time display of peer payoffs.  
    • Systematic variation / effect size on punishment treatment: Not mentioned.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • What the paper says: Punishment is administered by an “institution,” either global or local. The text does not address information about who imposed it.  
    • Systematic variation / effect size on punishment treatment: Not mentioned.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is?  
    • What the paper says: The paper does not implement rewards, so there is no discussion of knowledge of a rewarder.  
    • Systematic variation / effect size on punishment treatment: Not mentioned.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   • The paper does not use “group efficiency” (actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff) or total/average payoff as a primary measured outcome.  
   • The key dependent variables are:  
       – group achievement (ηG): fraction of groups that reach a required threshold of cooperators/punishers, thus successfully avoiding disaster.  
       – institution prevalence (ηI): fraction of time that a punishment institution (global or local) is supported.  
   • These are different from efficiency because they track how often the threshold is met or how often institutions exist, rather than payoffs relative to an ideal maximum.  

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
       1. Number of players (population size Z = 100, group size N = 4).  
       6. Contribution cost c/b = 0.1 (analogous to aspects of MPCR, though not labeled that way).  
       7. Punishment tax πt (punishers’ cost).  
       8. Punishment magnitude πf (the fine levied on defectors).  
   • None of the others (2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15) are discussed.  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The paper does not systematically vary or provide numeric effect sizes for any of the 15 parameters in relation to a “punishment treatment effect.”  
   • Although group size (parameter 1) is mentioned as small (N = 4), the paper’s main figures do not include a parameter sweep for N, πt, πf, or c/b that quantifies the outcome changes.  
   • Thus, strictly speaking, the paper does not show the effect of systematically varying any of these 15 parameters on “punishment treatment” for efficiency or other outcomes.  

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not address efficiency in the sense of payoffs relative to an ideal maximum and does not systematically vary these parameters. It mostly contrasts local versus global institutions under varying levels of risk.  
   • Consequently, there is little basis in the paper for predicting how those 15 parameters (or their interactions) would affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency. The only hint is that smaller groups (parameter 1) may favor the stability of local punishment and thereby could enhance cooperative outcomes—but even that is discussed in terms of “group achievement,” not efficiency.  

In short, the paper does not provide direct guidance for how systematically changing the 15 parameters would alter the effect of punishment on group efficiency. It mainly focuses on comparing local vs. global punishment institutions and shows how local punishments produce higher “group achievement” across a range of risk perceptions, without exploring the 15 parameters above in a systematic way.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what the Carpenter and Seki paper actually discusses. Throughout, please note that “systematically varying” a parameter refers to studying how changes in that parameter (e.g., different numbers of players, different punishment costs, etc.) affect outcomes. The paper runs a single experimental design (a repeated public‐goods game with a “social disapproval” option) plus a field productivity study of fishermen in Toyama Bay; it does not manipulate or compare different versions of these 15 parameters. Whenever the paper does not describe or systematically vary a given parameter, that is stated explicitly. All observations are based solely on the content of the provided text.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Discussed? Yes. The experiment was conducted in groups of four (p. 9–10 of the paper).  
   • Systematically varied? No. There was only one group size (four), with no variations across treatments. The paper does not explore how changing the number of players affects any outcome (including punishment or efficiency).  

2. Number of rounds
   • Discussed? Yes. There were 10 rounds total: the first 5 without social disapproval and the final 5 with social disapproval (p. 10).  
   • Systematically varied? No. Participants all played 10 rounds; the paper does not examine what would happen with a different number of rounds.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussed? Yes (indirectly). Participants were explicitly instructed not to speak or communicate with each other (pp. 9–10).  
   • Systematically varied? No. There was no treatment in which chat was allowed vs. disallowed.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussed? Yes. Each participant received 10 coins and decided how many of the 10 to contribute, with possible contributions ranging from 0 to 10 (pp. 9–10). This is not an “all or nothing” design.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not study how an all‐or‐nothing rule would change behavior.  

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much of their endowment to move back into their hands vs. a forced default out of the public fund)?
   • Discussed? Not in those terms. Participants simply receive 10 coins each round and freely decide how many to keep vs. contribute (p. 10). There is no “default contribution” framework in the sense of returning tokens from a group fund to one’s self.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor
   • Discussed? Yes. The common MPCR is 0.5 because all group contributions are doubled (multiplied by 2) and then shared equally among 4 players (p. 10).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The experiment uses only one MPCR (0.5) and does not compare it to any other factor.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussed? Yes. In the latter 5 rounds, participants can pay 10 yen to stamp an “unhappy face” for the group to see (pp. 10–12). That 10 yen is the cost to signal social disapproval.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The cost remains 10 yen in that single treatment; there is no variation in the cost of punishing.  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed)
   • Discussed? Yes, but the material punishment magnitude is zero: the “unhappy face” has no direct monetary effect on the punished. It is purely symbolic “shaming” (pp. 10–12).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not compare different magnitudes of monetary punishment.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussed? Not present. The experiment has only a social‐disapproval (“unhappy face”) option and no mention of a reward option (p. 12).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Discussed? Not applicable. No reward mechanism is used, so the paper does not address the cost of rewarding.  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted)
   • Discussed? Not applicable. No reward mechanism is used, so the paper does not address any reward magnitude.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
   • Discussed? Yes. Participants were told there would be 10 rounds (pp. 9–10, Appendix A).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?
   • Discussed? Yes. After each round, participants see a “report” that shows everyone’s contributions in random order, the total contributions, and each person’s share from the public good (pp. 10–11).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The experiment does not study what happens if this information were hidden vs. shown.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Discussed? Yes. They do NOT know. Punishment (social disapproval stamps) is anonymous (p. 12).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Discussed? Not applicable. There is no reward condition, so the paper does not address this.  

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary Responses

A: Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   • The paper’s main empirical outcomes are:  
     – In the lab portion: individual contributions to the public goods game, plus the occurrence of social disapproval (“punishment”).  
     – In the field portion: actual fishing productivity (kilograms of shrimp caught).  
   • Although the authors briefly mention “Pareto efficient” outcomes in describing public‐goods dilemmas, they do not measure efficiency as “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff”; rather, they measure (i) contribution levels in the game and (ii) fishing productivity. These are distinct from the standard “group efficiency” measure.  

B: Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned:  
     1. Number of players (4);  
     2. Number of rounds (10);  
     3. Chat (none allowed);  
     4. Not all‐or‐nothing (they can allocate any portion of 10 coins);  
     6. MPCR = 0.5;  
     7. Punishment cost = 10 yen;  
     8. Punishment magnitude = zero monetary penalty, but a public unhappy‐face signal;  
     12. Known number of rounds (10);  
     13. Peer outcomes are shown (in random order);  
     14. Punisher identity not revealed.  
   • Not mentioned or not present:  
     5. Contribution default mechanism;  
     9–11. Reward presence, cost, or magnitude;  
     15. Rewarder identity.  

C: For which and how many of these 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • The paper does not systematically vary any of the parameters. It runs one design with four players, 10 rounds, an MPCR of 0.5, a fixed punishment cost of 10 yen, zero monetary fine, and no reward. There is no table or figure in the paper that attempts to examine how changing any of these parameters would predictably alter contributions, productivity, or efficiency. Hence, none of the parameters are systematically varied to observe changes in the “punishment treatment effect.”  

D: If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not offer direct predictions for how changing any of the 15 parameters would affect group efficiency. It only presents one public‐goods setup (with a social‐disapproval option) and does not compare alternative designs. Consequently, there is little basis in the text for predicting how adjusting these 15 parameters (or their interactions) would shift a punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency.  

Accordingly, no inferences can be drawn from the paper on this specific point beyond the single design they implemented.
reference_APA: Carpenter, Jeffrey & Seki, Erika (2011). DO SOCIAL PREFERENCES INCREASE PRODUCTIVITY? FIELD EXPERIMENTAL EVIDENCE FROM FISHERMEN IN TOYAMA BAY. ECONOMIC INQUIRY.

Article Title: Grand Challenges in Social Physics: In Pursuit of Moral Behavior

Keywords Plus: ULTIMATUM GAME; EVOLUTION; PREFERENCES; COOPERATION; RECIPROCITY; PUNISHMENT; DECEPTION; FAIRNESS; EFFICIENCY; ORIGINS
Abstract: Methods of statistical physics have proven valuable for studying the evolution of cooperation in social dilemma games. However, recent empirical research shows that cooperative behavior in social dilemmas is only one kind of a more general class of behavior, namely moral behavior, which includes reciprocity, respecting others' property, honesty, equity, efficiency, as well as many others. Inspired by these experimental works, we here open up the path toward studying other forms of moral behavior with methods of statistical physics. We argue that this is a far-reaching direction for future research that can help us answer fundamental questions about human sociality. Why did our societies evolve as they did? What moral principles are more likely to emerge? What happens when different moral principles clash? Can we predict the break out of moral conflicts in advance and contribute to their solution? These are amongst the most important questions of our time, and methods of statistical physics could lead to new insights and contribute toward finding answers.

Abstract: Human behavior is strongly affected by culturally transmitted norms and values. Certain norms are internalized (i.e., acting according to a norm becomes an end in itself rather than merely a tool in achieving certain goals or avoiding social sanctions). Humans' capacity to internalize norms likely evolved in our ancestors to simplify solving certain challenges-including social ones. Here we study theoretically the evolutionary origins of the capacity to internalize norms. In our models, individuals can choose to participate in collective actions as well as punish free riders. In making their decisions, individuals attempt to maximize a utility function in which normative values are initially irrelevant but play an increasingly important role if the ability to internalize norms emerges. Using agent-based simulations, we show that norm internalization evolves under a wide range of conditions so that cooperation becomes instinctive. Norm internalization evolves much more easily and has much larger effects on behavior if groups promote peer punishment of free riders. Promoting only participation in collective actions is not effective. Typically, intermediate levels of norm internalization are most frequent but there are also cases with relatively small frequencies of oversocialized individuals willing to make extreme sacrifices for their groups no matter material costs, as well as undersocialized individuals completely immune to social norms. Evolving the ability to internalize norms was likely a crucial step on the path to large-scale human cooperation.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter analysis based solely on the content of the Gavrilets & Richerson (2017) paper “Collective action and the evolution of social norm internalization.” The focus is on whether the paper (a) discusses each parameter at all (and if so, what fixed value or range it is given), and (b) makes any predictions about how systematically varying that parameter would affect a “punishment treatment effect”—that is, what happens when punishment is introduced, particularly with respect to outcomes relevant to efficiency (understood as total or average payoff, or an analog). The paper does not itself use the term “efficiency” in the sense of “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff,” so whenever it addresses payoff/fitness, that is noted explicitly.

PARAMETER‑BY‑PARAMETER ANALYSIS

1) Number of players  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. The paper uses group size n (e.g., n = 8, 16, 24) in agent‐based simulations.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it and discuss effects on punishment or related outcomes?  
  – Yes. The authors explicitly vary n and present results in Figures 3 and 4. They show that in “us‐vs.‐them” games, larger n reduces norm internalization and punishment, whereas in “us‐vs.‐nature” games the relationship can be more mixed. They talk about how increasing n can undermine cooperation and punishment in certain conditions, but they do not report a numerical “effect size” for each increment in n.  
  – Although they do discuss payoffs (material payoff, fitness), they do not frame results in terms of “group efficiency.”  

2) Number of rounds  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – The Methods mention that each generation consists of Q repeated interactions (“rounds”), but there is no table or figure systematically varying Q.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it and discuss effects on punishment or any other outcome?  
  – No. The paper does not vary the number of rounds to study its impact on punishment or payoffs.  

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. There is no mention of chat or any communication protocol among players.  

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes, implicitly. Each individual’s production effort x is either 0 or 1 in the model, so the paper does use an “all or nothing” approach to contributions.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it and discuss effects on punishment or any other outcome?  
  – No. This setup is simply assumed in the model; there is no separate treatment varying the contribution format.  

5) Is the contribution default (a “take” vs. “give” framing)?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. The paper does not mention any variant such as “default contribution” or forced “take” vs. “give.”  

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – The paper uses a benefit parameter b (e.g., b = 1, b = 4) in both the “us‐vs.‐nature” and “us‐vs.‐them” models. This plays much the same role as an overall benefit (akin to a public‐good factor), but the authors do not call it MPCR.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it and discuss effects on punishment or any other outcome?  
  – Yes, to an extent. They do show results for different values of b (b = 1 vs. b = 4) for illustrative purposes. They discuss how higher b can help make cooperation more likely to evolve. However, they do not report a clear effect‐size estimate on payoff or punishment “treatment effect,” nor do they discuss it under the label “MPCR.”  

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. The authors use δ (“delta”) to denote the cost of punishing.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it and discuss effects on punishment or any other outcome?  
  – Yes, they mention that changes in δ and related cost terms can affect the likelihood of punishing free riders, but they provide no explicit effect‐size estimate for how systematically varying δ alone changes total payoffs or “efficiency.” Their summary plots (e.g., in the SI Appendix) show that if δ is too high, punishment (and hence cooperation) is undermined, but the paper does not quantify that effect size as, e.g., a regression coefficient.  

8) Punishment magnitude (the deduction per unit of punishment)  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – The paper’s parameter κ (“kappa”) is effectively the cost to the punished party. This can be interpreted as the “punishment magnitude.”  
• Does the paper systematically vary it and discuss effects on punishment or any other outcome?  
  – Yes. They present simulation results under various κ values. Generally, higher κ raises the stakes for free riders. The authors note that bigger costs to being punished can encourage more cooperation but do not provide a simple numeric effect size.  

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – They briefly contrast “punishment” vs. “reward” in general remarks, but they do not implement a formal “reward” mechanism in the model, nor do they vary a parameter enabling or disabling reward.  

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. Reward is not formally included as a model parameter in the text or tables.  

11) Reward magnitude (the award per unit of reward)  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. Same as above; they do not systematically analyze any reward magnitude parameter.  

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. There is no mention of players knowing the horizon or having incomplete/complete information about the number of rounds.  

13) Are peer outcomes shown (i.e., do players see how much others gained/lost)?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. The model assumes that each individual tracks overall group contributions enough to decide whether to punish. There is no separate parameter setting about the degree of transparency of peer payoffs.  

14) When a player is punished, do they know the punisher’s identity?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. The paper’s model does not involve a parameter for punisher identity disclosure.  

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know the rewarder’s identity?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. The paper does not feature any specific reward mechanism, so it does not discuss information about who gives a reward.  

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––  
SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
• The paper focuses on individual material payoff (π), average payoff within the group, and individual fitness (w). It does not use “group efficiency” = (actual total payoff) / (maximum possible payoff) as a stated metric. “Material payoff” is the total benefit minus costs an individual receives in each generation; “fitness” adds genetic/physiological costs. Thus these variables differ from a classical efficiency notion.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Mentioned in some form:  
  1) Number of players (n)  
  4) Contribution is binary (0 or 1)  
  6) Benefit parameter b (analogous to an overall multiplication factor)  
  7) Punishment cost δ  
  8) Punishment magnitude κ (the cost imposed on the punished)  
• Not mentioned or only mentioned but not used as a varied parameter:  
  – 2, 3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• The paper systematically varies n (Parameter 1), b (Parameter 6), δ (Parameter 7), and κ (Parameter 8) and discusses how those variations affect the emergence of punishment and cooperation. Punishment, in turn, affects average payoffs (though not framed as “efficiency”). Four parameters are thus systematically varied and connected to punishment/cooperation outcomes in the simulations.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
• The model discusses payoffs (material payoff, fitness), not “efficiency” in the strict public‐goods sense. Nonetheless, one can infer:  
  – (1) Larger groups can undermine the impact of punishment on cooperation in “us‐vs.‐them” contexts, possibly lowering average payoffs, whereas they can have mixed effects in “us‐vs.‐nature” contexts.  
  – (6) Higher benefit (b) generally promotes internalization and cooperation, which should elevate the payoff (and thus potentially increase efficiency).  
  – (7) & (8) Punishment‐related costs and magnitudes strongly influence willingness to punish and cooperate, which can have either a positive effect on payoffs (in “us‐vs.‐nature” games) or lead to overinvestment and lower net payoffs (in “us‐vs.‐them” games).  
  – The paper does not mention the other parameters at all (3, 5, 9–15) and thus no predictions can be made from the text regarding their effect on punishment or payoff.  
• Overall, the paper offers no quantitative conclusions about “efficiency,” and any predictions for those unmentioned parameters or for exact effect sizes cannot be made from the information provided.

Source Title: JOURNAL OF THE EUROPEAN ECONOMIC ASSOCIATION

Abstract: Many people contribute to public goods but stop doing so once they experience free riding. We test the hypothesis that groups whose members know that they are composed only of like-minded cooperators are able to maintain a higher cooperation level than the most cooperative, randomly composed groups. Our experiments confirm this hypothesis. We also predict that groups of like-minded free riders do not cooperate. Yet, we find a high level of strategic cooperation that eventually collapses. Our results underscore the importance of group composition and social learning by heterogeneously motivated agents to understand the dynamics of cooperation and free riding.

     No.  
   • Numerical effect size on punishment treatment effect?  
     None.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussion in paper?  
     Each unit of punishment costs the punisher 1 point. The paper identifies this cost but does not vary it.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     No; the cost is fixed at 1 point throughout.  
   • Numerical effect size on punishment treatment effect?  
     Not provided for different cost settings, since the cost was never varied.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Discussion in paper?  
     Each punishment point reduces the target’s payoff by 4 points. The paper notes this 1‐to‐4 ratio but does not manipulate it.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     No.  
   • Numerical effect size on punishment treatment effect?  
     None beyond the discussion that punishment is “relatively cheap” for the punisher (1 point costs the punisher, 4 points deducted from the punished).

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussion in paper?  
     The paper studies punishment only; no rewards are used.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     Not applicable.  
   • Numerical effect size on punishment treatment effect?  
     None.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Discussion in paper?  
      Not applicable; there is no reward.  
    • Systematic variation?  
      No.  
    • Numerical effect size on punishment treatment effect?  
      None.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
    • Discussion in paper?  
      Not applicable; there is no reward.  
    • Systematic variation?  
      No.  
    • Numerical effect size on punishment treatment effect?  
      None.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    • Discussion in paper?  
      Subjects know they will play two separate parts (“perfect‐strangers” matching). They are indeed informed that the experiment has these two parts, but the paper does not vary the informational condition (e.g., unknown end vs. known end).  
    • Systematic variation?  
      No; it is merely stated that the experiment ends after part 2.  
    • Numerical effect size on punishment treatment effect?  
      None.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost each round)?  
    • Discussion in paper?  
      Each player sees the other’s action (for instance, how many points were returned, how many punishment points were allocated). But there is no separate manipulation of visibility.  
    • Systematic variation?  
      No.  
    • Numerical effect size on punishment treatment effect?  
      None.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Discussion in paper?  
      Since each match is strictly between two players, the punished player knows that the other player is the punisher. There is no separate anonymity manipulation.  
    • Systematic variation?  
      No.  
    • Numerical effect size on punishment treatment effect?  
      None.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Discussion in paper?  
      Not applicable (no reward).  
    • Systematic variation?  
      No.  
    • Numerical effect size on punishment treatment effect?  
      None.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary (A–D)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper does not explicitly use the ratio of “actual total payoff divided by maximum possible total payoff” as its primary dependent variable.  
   • It does examine average earnings, frequencies of cooperation, and amounts of punishment and retaliation. It also collects self‐reported emotions (anger, guilt, etc.). Those outcomes differ from group efficiency because they focus on payoffs in raw (absolute) terms and behavioral frequencies rather than looking at efficiency as a fraction of the maximum possible total.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • The paper fixes certain parameters (it is a two‐person game; the cost of punishment is 1 point for the punisher, 4 points deducted from the punished; the multiplier in the “cooperate” option is 6; they run exactly two iterations), but it does not systematically explore or compare different values for them.  
   • In short, those parameters appear in a single fixed setting rather than being varied. No parameters among the 15 are really “systematically varied” in the design.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • In this paper, none of the 15 parameters are systematically manipulated. Hence the authors provide no direct, numerical predictions or effect sizes about how changing those parameters would affect punishment’s impact on any dependent variable (including efficiency).

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • Because the paper does not experimentally vary any of these 15 parameters, it offers little basis for predicting how changing them would shift the impact of punishment on group efficiency.  
   • The authors do note that punishment can raise cooperation but often does not raise overall earnings, implying that under the particular cost‐to‐punisher and benefit‐ of‐punishment settings used (1 point vs. 4 points), there can be significant “welfare loss” due to punitive escalation (retaliation). However, no systematic parametric analysis is provided. Therefore, beyond saying that punishment may fail to raise total payoffs under certain conditions, there is “little to no” concrete evidence in the paper to forecast how the 15 parameters or their interactions would alter the treatment effect on efficiency.

Below I walk through the 15 design parameters one by one, always asking two questions:

• Does the Henrich & Henrich paper (2006) mention the parameter or give a value for it?  
• Does the paper make any explicit prediction about what would happen to a “punishment‐treatment effect” (and especially to group efficiency) if the parameter were systematically varied?

If a point is not in the paper, I say so explicitly.  References such as “Eq. (3)” or “Table 1” are to the equations and the single table that actually appear in the article.

-------------------------------------------------
1  Number of players  
– Mentioned? Yes.  The paper repeatedly contrasts “dyads,” “triads,” “small groups (n ≤ 5)” and “n-person public-goods problems.”  
– Systematic prediction? Yes (qualitative only).  It argues that as n grows, both direct reciprocity and punishment become progressively weaker at sustaining cooperation, so the efficiency gain from introducing punishment should decline with larger groups.  No numeric effect size is given.

2  Number of rounds  
– Mentioned? Yes.  The probability of another round (ω) appears in Eq. (3).  
– Prediction for punishment? No.  ω is analysed for reciprocity, not for peer punishment.  The paper does not vary ω while holding “punishment treatment” constant.

3  Chat (free communication)  
– Mentioned? No.  There is no discussion of within-round chat or cheap talk.

4  All-or-nothing contribution rule  
– Mentioned? No.

5  “Refund” default (give-then-take-back)  
– Mentioned? No.

6  MPCR / multiplication factor  
– Mentioned? Only abstractly.  Benefits are denoted b, costs c, and the ratio b/c is said to influence whether cooperation can be sustained (e.g., generous vs. provokable strategies).  
– Punishment-specific prediction? No.  The article never varies b or c while analysing a punishment treatment.

7  Punishment cost to punisher  
– Mentioned? Yes, repeatedly (called “cost of punishing”).  
– Systematic prediction? Yes (qualitative).  Whenever the cost-to-punisher is low relative to the cost-to-target, punishment can be stabilised by conformist transmission and therefore produces higher cooperation and group gains.  No numbers are supplied.

8  Punishment magnitude (cost to target)  
– Mentioned? Yes, as “cost of being punished.”  
– Prediction? Yes (qualitative).  Larger deductions on the target, for a given small cost to the punisher, widen the gap between those two costs and therefore strengthen norm enforcement, yielding higher efficiency.  No quantitative gradient is reported.

9  Is a reward option present?  
– Mentioned? Only in passing (“help” or “reward” is contrasted with “punish” once).  No analysis.  
– No predictions.

10 Reward cost to giver  
11 Reward magnitude to receiver  
– Neither is analysed.

12  Are players told the total number of rounds?  
– Not mentioned.

13  Are peer outcomes (or reputations) shown?  
– Yes, in the sections on indirect reciprocity.  Accurate reputation flow (probability φ) underpins Eq. (4): φ b > c.  
– Punishment-specific prediction? Only indirectly.  The authors say that norms which punish “false gossip” raise φ and thereby allow higher cooperation, but they do not quantify an efficiency effect of adding punishment conditional on visibility.

14  Do punished players learn who punished them?  
– Not discussed.

15  Do rewarded players learn the identity of the rewarder?  
– Not discussed.

-------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A  Dependent variables actually used  
The article never measures “group efficiency” in an experiment.  Instead it uses theoretical variables:  
• Total or average fitness pay-offs (b and c) in stylised models  
• Probability of continuation (ω)  
• Accuracy of reputation flow (φ)  
• Relative cost of punishing versus being punished  
• Frequency of cooperators or punishers in the population  
These are analytically distinct from the empirical efficiency measure ( realised ÷ maximum pay-off ).

B  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
Five: #1 (group size), #2 (rounds/ω), #6 (b,c), #7 (punisher cost), #8 (punishment magnitude), and #13 (information about others).

C  For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* the parameter on a punishment-treatment effect?  
Three, and only qualitatively:  
– #1 Group size: larger n → weaker punishment effect.  
– #7 Punisher cost: lower cost → stronger punishment effect.  
– #8 Punishment magnitude: higher magnitude → stronger punishment effect.  
(No numeric effect sizes are provided.)

D  Predictions about the 15 parameters (and their interactions) for the efficiency impact of adding punishment, based solely on this paper  
• Biggest single moderator should be the ratio (cost-to-punisher)/(cost-to-target).  The smaller that ratio, the larger the predicted efficiency gain.  
• Punishment should raise efficiency more in dyads and very small groups than in large n-person public-goods games.  
• Visible, credible reputational information (high φ) indirectly amplifies punishment’s impact by making norm enforcement cheaper (gossip can substitute for costly material punishment).  
• The paper offers *no* guidance on chat, contribution defaults, all-or-nothing decisions, reward dimensions, knowledge of the horizon, or source‐identifiable punishment.  
• Because the paper is purely theoretical, there is little basis for interaction predictions beyond simple statements like “low punisher cost matters more in big groups” or “high φ can partially offset large group size.”

In short, the article provides only qualitative, theory-driven expectations for three of the 15 parameters and gives no numerical estimates of how much group efficiency would change when punishment is introduced under different laboratory designs.
reference_APA: Henrich, Joseph & Henrich, Natalie (2006). Culture, evolution and the puzzle of human cooperation. COGNITIVE SYSTEMS RESEARCH.

Below is an item-by-item account of what (if anything) the Brandt and Sigmund paper says about each of the 15 parameters and whether it discusses systematically varying them in relation to punishment and efficiency (or any other outcome). All references to “the paper” pertain only to the text provided (“Indirect reciprocity, image scoring, and moral hazara” by Brandt and Sigmund).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? The paper models a population of players in an evolutionary context but does not specify or systematically vary the number of players.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not discuss how changing the number of players would affect any punishment treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? Yes, in the sense that the authors examine whether the game has a constant number of rounds or a probability distribution of rounds, and they explore how a person’s probability of being observed (qₙ) might vary over their “lifetime” of rounds. However, this is framed as part of an evolutionary or asynchronous-entry model, not a discrete experimental setting where “the number of rounds” is manipulated in the usual sense.  
   • Systematically varied? They consider different assumptions about whether another round will occur, but there is no direct treatment of how varying the number of rounds systematically changes a “punishment treatment effect.” They discuss stable mixtures of strategies under different distributions of round lengths, but not in terms of how it affects “punishment vs. no-punishment” treatments on efficiency.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned? No. There is no discussion of communication, pre-play chat, or messaging.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned? The model in the paper is a binary decision (“help” or “not help”), but the paper does not describe this as an “all-or-nothing” forced contribution format in the sense of a typical public goods experiment.  
   • Systematically varied? No. They do not explore different ways of partial vs. full contributions.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much of their endowment to move from the public fund back into their hand)?  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper deals with a binary help-or-not-help action, not partial or default contributions.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? The paper discusses a cost c and benefit b of helping. These are closely related to the cost–benefit ratio (c/b), which sometimes plays a similar role to an MPCR in public goods contexts. However, the paper does not call this an “MPCR.”  
   • Systematically varied? Yes, in the sense that the paper analyzes thresholds such as q > c/(b·r) for certain equilibria to exist (where q is the probability of recognizing a partner’s score and r is the probability that a help attempt succeeds). But the authors do not frame this as a “punishment treatment” effect on efficiency; rather, they discuss whether stable cooperation via “discriminators” can exist under different c/b ratios.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? No. Although the authors refer to “costly punishment” in a broad sense (i.e., refusing to help is “costly” because it lowers one’s own reputation), there is no parameter or direct fee for imposing a punishment.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed on them)  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper’s notion of “punishment” is simply the refusal to help, resulting in a Bad score for the refuser, not a deduction of a specific payoff amount.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper only examines helping (which confers a benefit b) or not helping; it does not discuss separate “reward” mechanisms for punishing or encouraging cooperation.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted to them)  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
   • Mentioned? No. The authors analyze an evolutionary or continuous-entry model, not an experiment in which players are told exactly how many rounds remain.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?  
   • Mentioned? Not in payoff terms. The paper discusses a probability q that one observes the other’s “score” (Good/Bad), but not observing precise payoff outcomes.  
   • Systematically varied? They do examine the scenario where q can change with experience (qₙ), but they do not treat it as “peer outcome visibility.” They do not connect it to a punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper mainly analyzes payoffs (and the frequency of strategies in an evolutionary model). Although “average payoff” is discussed, there is no explicit use of “group efficiency” (i.e., achieved total payoff divided by a maximum possible payoff) as a primary outcome. The authors also track whether cooperation is stable (i.e., the fraction of discriminators and undiscriminating altruists vs. defectors) and what global payoff each strategy mix attains. Thus, “payoff” and “frequency of cooperators/defectors” are used, not “efficiency” in the public-goods sense.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • The paper briefly touches on (2) Number of rounds in the sense of indefinite vs. multiple-round assumptions and (6) cost–benefit parameters (c and b, which one could loosely relate to an MPCR). No other parameters from the list are explicitly mentioned.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, none are discussed in terms of a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” The authors do systematically examine how varying c/b (part of parameter 6) and the probability q of information changes the possibility of stable cooperation by “discriminators.” However, they do not frame it in terms of “punishment treatments” (as in experimental public goods with formal punishments) nor do they connect it to group efficiency metrics.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper provides insufficient information to predict how most of these 15 parameters would affect a formal “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency. It does discuss that a lower cost-to-benefit ratio (c/b) and higher probability of information (q) are conducive to stable cooperation by discriminating behaviors, but it does not relate these directly to “punishment treatment effects” in a public-goods sense, nor does it define “efficiency” as in total payoff relative to a maximum. Consequently, almost no direct predictions can be made for these 15 parameters, except the general point that lower c/b and higher monitoring (q) make “costly punishment” strategies (discrimination) more viable, which in turn could, in principle, yield higher payoffs on average.
reference_APA: Brandt, H & Sigmund, K (2005). Indirect reciprocity, image scoring, and moral hazard. PROCEEDINGS OF THE NATIONAL ACADEMY OF SCIENCES OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA.

Abstract: Two resource dilemmas, the commons dilemma, in which individuals take from a common resource, and the public goods problem, in which individuals give to a common good, were experimentally compared. Although they provide equivalent outcomes, the two dilemmas involve different frames of reference and are not psychologically equivalent. We also examined sanction systems, which involve contributions by individuals in the dilemma to provide rewards and penalties for cooperation. The results of Experiment 1 supported the hypothesis that public goods problems (''give dilemmas'') activate greater loss aversion and less cooperation than commons dilemmas (''take dilemmas''), and that this effect is moderated by sanction systems. The penalty sanction and especially the reward sanction produced greater cooperation. Also, as expected, loss aversion heightened exploitation: when the others were cooperative, a give dilemma generated less cooperation than a take dilemma. In Experiment 2, we extended the concept of frame and loss aversion to the structure of sanction systems, finding that subjects were more likely to contribute to a ''take sanction'' than to a ''give sanction.'' o1_summary:
Parameter-by-parameter extraction from “Framing in Resource Dilemmas: Loss Aversion and the Moderating Effects of Sanctions”

(Dependent variables actually analysed = amount “cooperated” or “taken”, i.e., contributions; no direct efficiency measure is reported.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
 • Mentioned? Yes – every session is an eight-person game (one real subject + seven computerised “others”).  
 • Systematically varied? No. All groups have 8 players; the paper makes no prediction about how changing group size would alter the punishment (sanction) treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
 • Mentioned? Yes – 12 trials (subjects were only told the game would last “10-20”).  
 • Systematically varied? No. No prediction about its effect.

3. Chat enabled?  
 • Mentioned? No. No discussion, no chat allowed, no predictions.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
 • Mentioned? Yes indirectly – subjects choose any integer 0-25 each round (so NOT all-or-nothing).  
 • Systematically varied? No. No prediction.

5. “Default” contribution direction (endowment moved back to self)?  
 • Mentioned? Frame is manipulated as GIVE versus TAKE, but there is no “default‐return” rule. Parameter not addressed.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
 • Mentioned? Implicitly – remaining public-fund tickets are doubled and equally divided (MPCR=2/8=0.25).  
 • Systematically varied? No. No prediction.

7. Cost to impose one punishment point  
 • Mentioned? Yes – each ticket contributed to the penalty fund costs 1 ticket.  
 • Systematically varied? No. No prediction.

8. Punishment magnitude  
 • Mentioned? Yes – total amount in penalty fund (pre-programmed 35–65 tickets) is subtracted from the least-co-operative person.  
 • Systematically varied? Not across experimental conditions; the size merely fluctuates inside a condition. The paper never analyses magnitude effects, so no prediction.

9. Reward enabled? (Presence/absence and type of sanction)  
 • Mentioned? Yes – three between-subject conditions: NONE, PENALTY, REWARD.  
 • Systematically varied? Yes.  
 • Reported effect (on cooperation, not efficiency):  
  Experiment 1, mean cooperation over 12 rounds (Table 1):  
   No sanction 9.7 (give+take pooled)  
   Penalty   13.9  
   Reward   20.8  
  ANOVA: F(2,183)=74.14, p<.0001.  
  Reward > Penalty > None.  
  Interaction: Reward (and Penalty) eliminate the usual frame difference between TAKE and GIVE games.  
 • No efficiency data, so no numeric effect on efficiency can be extracted.

10. Cost of a reward point  
 • Mentioned? Yes – 1 ticket per ticket placed in the reward fund.  
 • Systematically varied? No prediction.

11. Reward magnitude  
 • Mentioned? Yes – all tickets in the reward fund are transferred to the most co-operative player.  
 • Systematically varied? No. No prediction.

12. Are total rounds known?  
 • Mentioned? Yes – subjects are told only that there will be 10-20 rounds (uncertainty); never varied.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
 • Mentioned? Yes – feedback each round: own move, total of the 7 others, public-fund size, own personal fund, total others’ personal fund.  
 • Systematically varied? No.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
 • Mentioned? No – the sanction comes from an anonymous group fund; identity is never revealed; not varied.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
 • Mentioned? No – same anonymity; not varied.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables actually used  
 • The paper analyses “cooperation” (tickets given to the public fund in a give-frame or tickets left in the public fund in a take-frame) and “contributions to the sanction fund.”  
 • No variable labelled “efficiency,” “total payoff,” or “average payoff” is reported.

B. Parameters from the list that are explicitly described  
 Nine of the 15: 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 (i.e., 11 parameters) are at least mentioned descriptively.  
 Parameters 3, 5, 14, 15 are not mentioned at all.

C. Parameters that the paper systematically varies and links to the punishment treatment effect  
 Only one – parameter 9 (whether a reward condition, a penalty condition, or no sanction exists).  
 No other parameter is experimentally manipulated across levels, so we have 1/15 parameters with an observed effect; 0/15 regarding efficiency in particular.

D. Plausible predictions about efficiency based solely on this paper  
 • Because higher cooperation under reward and (to a lesser degree) penalty sanctions is documented, and because higher cooperation would normally raise group payoffs in this game, the best (though indirect) prediction is:  
  Reward sanctions > Penalty sanctions > No sanctions in terms of efficiency.  
 • The TAKE vs GIVE framing difference on efficiency should disappear once any sizeable sanction (penalty or reward) is present.  
 • No other concrete predictions can be derived about how changing group size, round length, punishment costs/magnitudes, identification, chat, information display, etc., would alter the efficiency effect—those variables were fixed or absent from the design and not theorised about.

In short, the paper only allows confident statements about parameter 9 (type/presence of the sanction). For the remaining 14 parameters and their interactions, the text gives no basis for forecasting how they would affect the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.
reference_APA: MCCUSKER, C & CARNEVALE, PJ (1995). FRAMING IN RESOURCE DILEMMAS - LOSS AVERSION AND THE MODERATING EFFECTS OF SANCTIONS. ORGANIZATIONAL BEHAVIOR AND HUMAN DECISION PROCESSES.

Keywords Plus: SOCIAL VALUE ORIENTATION; BETWEEN-GROUP COMMUNICATION; PRISONERS-DILEMMA GAME; STEP-LEVEL; GROUP-SIZE; N-PERSON; RESOURCE DILEMMAS; FUTURE CONSEQUENCES; STRUCTURAL-CHANGE; DECISION-MAKING
Abstract: One of the most continually vexing problems in society is the variability with which citizens support endeavors that are designed to help a great number of people. In this article, we examine the twin roles of cooperative and antagonistic behavior in this variability. We find that each plays an important role, though their contributions are, understandably, at odds. It is this opposition that produces seeming unpredictability in citizen response to collective need. In fact, we suggest that careful consideration of the research allows one to often predict when efforts to provide a collectively beneficial good will succeed and when they will fail. To understand the dynamics of participation in response to collective need, it is necessary to distinguish between the primary types of need situations. A public good is an entity that relies in whole or in part on contributions to be provided. Examples of public goods are charities and public broadcasting. Public goods require that citizens experience a short-term loss (of their contribution) in order to realize a long-term gain (of the good). However, because everyone can use the good once it is provided, there is also an incentive to not contribute, let others give, and then take advantage of their efforts. This state of affairs introduces a conflict between doing what is best for oneself and what is best for the group. In a public goods situation, cooperation and antagonism impact how one resolves this conflict. The other major type of need situation is a common-pool resource problem. Here, a good is fully provided at the outset, and citizens may sample from it. The resource is usually, but not necessarily, partially replenished. Examples of replenished resources are drinking water and trees; examples of resources that are functionally not replenished are oil and minerals. Common-pool resources allow citizens to experience a short-term gain (by getting what they want in the early life of the resource) but also present the possibility of a long-term loss (if the resource dries up). As with public goods, there is thus a conflict between, on the one hand, acting in one's best interest and taking as much as one wants all the time and, on the other, acting for the good of the group, which requires taking a lesser amount so that the replenishment rate can keep up with the rate of use. As with public goods, both cooperation and antagonism affect this decision. With these situations in mind, we can now dig deeply into the dynamics of both cooperation and antagonism. Cooperation is one of the most heavily studied aspects of human behavior, yet despite this attention, there is much that is not understood about it, including its fundamental base. There are a number of different perspectives on the base. Interdependence theory argues that cooperation is driven by how one interprets the subjective value of the outcomes that will result from various combinations of behaviors. A person who sees a potential result of 50 to you, 50 to me as We both would do well is more likely to cooperate than the person who sees it as I would not outgain the other person. Self-control theory suggests that cooperation is a function of how well a person can resist the impulse to benefit now and delay gratification. Evolutionary theory takes many forms but revolves around the extent to which cooperation is adaptive. Finally, the appropriateness framework takes a cognitive approach and assumes that cooperation is determined by a combination of social-cognitive (interpretation of self and the situation) and decision-heuristic factors. We propose that it is possible to integrate across these approaches and understand cooperation as a behavior that is influenced by all of these factors as well as other dynamics, such as cultural mores and personality traits. Antagonism, as it relates to the collective welfare, is a phenomenon with a lesser history but one that is clearly influential. A number of facets of antagonism are relevant. Power, and its abuse, is a major factor, and a specific application to collective goods is the notion of a gatekeeper, or a person who can completely determine whether a public good exists or a common-pool resource can be used. Gatekeepers tend to demand ample compensation from others in order for the good or resource to go forward. If this demand is resisted, as it often is, the end result is that the good is not provided or the resource not accessed. Another facet is the desire to see an out-group be harmed. Sometimes, this motivation is so strong that people will deny themselves a good outcome in order to see the harm occur. Why someone would want to see an out-group be harmed is debatable, but it may be attributable to a desire to be seen as a winner, or it may be a strategy designed to produce a net benefit for one's in-group. Emotions also play a role, with people tending to assume that out-group members have just basic emotions such as happiness and sadness and not secondary emotions such as guilt and shame. Because out-group members are emotionally simple, it is seen as acceptable to treat them badly. Complicating matters even further is that antagonism can sometimes be seen against in-group members who deviate, in either direction, from the group norm and against individuals who are behaving in a clearly selfless manner, like volunteers. A number of approaches have been proposed to the resolution of public goods problems. Structural solutions act to alter the basic dynamic of the dilemma by means of interventions such as rewards for cooperation, punishment for noncooperation, and selection of a single group member to chart a course of action for everyone. Third-party solutions involve the bringing in of an external agent to help determine how group members should behave. These agents may be more passive and merely suggest solutions, or they may be more active and dictate how decisions will be made, what decision will be made, or both. Finally, psychological solutions involve changing how people view the situation. We finish by discussing how policy makers can improve the chances of a publicly valuable good being supported. We particularly emphasize creation of a felt connection with future generations; clear demonstration of immediate and concrete consequences as a result of failure to provide the good; instillation of a sense of community; and isolation of the good from other, related issues. We also take up the general problem of distrust of those who establish policy and discuss some methods for helping minimize distrust.
