Below, each of the 15 design parameters is inspected in the light of the information that actually appears in the Parks-Joireman-Van Lange review.  “Mentions” means the parameter is described or at least alluded to.  “Systematic-variation prediction” means the authors (or the meta-analyses they cite) report, or clearly infer, what happens to a **punishment-vs.-no-punishment treatment effect** when the parameter is varied.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1. Number of players (group size)  
 • Mentioned: Yes – Table 3 (“Group size”) and surrounding text.  
 • Systematic-variation prediction for punishment?  No.  Group size is analysed for its main effect on cooperation; the paper never links it to the incremental effect of adding a punishment option.

2. Number of rounds / one-shot vs. iterated play  
 • Mentioned: Yes – Table 2 (“One-shot vs. iterated dilemmas”) and, crucially, in the sanctions subsection:  
  “rewards and punishments have roughly equal (medium-size) effects… with effects larger in iterated dilemmas involving repeated interactions with the same partner(s)” (Balliet et al., 2011).  
 • Systematic-variation prediction: Yes – Iterated play strengthens the punishment (and reward) treatment effect on cooperation.  No numerical effect size is given in the review.

3. Chat / communication allowed  
 • Mentioned: Yes – a full meta-analysis is summarised (Balliet 2010).  
 • Systematic-variation prediction for punishment?  No – communication is examined as a direct facilitator of cooperation, not as a moderator of punishment efficacy.

4. “All-or-nothing” forced contribution format  
 • Not mentioned.

5. “Contribution default” (withdraw vs. invest) framing  
 • Not mentioned.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor  
 • General incentive structure is discussed (fear & greed, MPCR-like manipulations), but never with respect to adding punishment; thus no systematic prediction for the punishment effect.

7. Cost to impose one unit of punishment  
 • Punishment is repeatedly labelled “costly,” but costs are never manipulated or analysed; no prediction is offered.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine levied per point)  
 • Not discussed.

9. Whether a reward option is enabled  
 • Mentioned: Yes – the sanctions section compares “reward” and “punishment.”  
 • Systematic-variation prediction: Yes – adding a *reward* option produces a treatment effect on cooperation of the same *average* magnitude as adding a punishment option (Balliet et al., 2011).  Again, no numeric estimate is given, and efficiency is not analysed.

10. Cost of rewarding  
 • Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude  
 • Not discussed.

12. Whether the number of rounds is common knowledge  
 • Not mentioned.

13. Whether peer outcomes are shown  
 • Identifiability of choices is covered, but visibility of pay-offs is not treated, and nothing is tied to punishment.

14. Whether the punished person sees who punished  
 • Not mentioned.

15. Whether the rewarded person sees who rewarded  
 • Not mentioned.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used in the article  
 • The review almost always talks about “cooperation,” “contribution” or “harvest level.”  
 • “Efficiency” (total or average pay-off relative to optimum) is referred to conceptually (e.g., “efficiency, self-interest, fairness, freedom” in Samuelson’s model) but is **not** measured or analysed as a dependent variable in any of the empirical summaries that include punishment.  Thus efficiency ≠ the variables actually reported.

B. Parameters merely mentioned (any value, any context): 6 of 15  
 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 13.

C. Parameters for which the paper gives a **systematic prediction about the punishment treatment effect** (any dependent variable): 2 of 15  
 • #2 Number of rounds – punishment (and reward) work better in iterated than in one-shot games.  
 • #9 Reward enabled – adding a *reward* option produces a treatment effect comparable (medium, positive) to adding punishment.

 No numerical effect sizes are provided in the review itself.

D. What can be predicted – strictly from this paper – about how the 15 parameters and their interactions will influence the punishment treatment effect on **efficiency**?  
 • Very little.  Efficiency is not analysed; only cooperation is.  The only clear moderators of the punishment treatment effect that the article identifies are (a) the game being repeated with the same partners and (b) replacing punishment with reward (or vice-versa), which yields roughly equal average improvements in cooperation.  For all other parameters (group size, communication, costs, magnitudes, information conditions, etc.) the review does not connect them to the incremental impact of punishment, so no evidence-based prediction can be made.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Key take-away:  Within this broad narrative review, punishment is discussed, but almost none of the 15 implementation details you are interested in (costs, magnitudes, information visibility, etc.) are analysed as moderators of its effect, and **efficiency** is not the focal outcome.

Authors: Szolnoki, A; Szabó, G; Czakó, L
Author Full Names: Szolnoki, Attila; Szabo, Gyoergy; Czako, Lilla
Article Title: Competition of individual and institutional punishments in spatial public goods games
Keywords Plus: PROMOTES COOPERATION; INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; EVOLUTION; EMERGENCE; DIVERSITY; MECHANISM; DYNAMICS; REWARD
Abstract: We have studied the evolution of strategies in spatial public goods games where both individual (peer) and institutional (pool) punishments are present in addition to unconditional defector and cooperator strategies. The evolution of strategy distribution is governed by imitation based on the random sequential comparison of neighbors' payoff for a fixed level of noise. Using numerical simulations, we evaluate the strategy frequencies and phase diagrams when varying the synergy factor, punishment cost, and fine. Our attention is focused on two extreme cases describing all the relevant behaviors in such a complex system. According to our numerical data peer punishers prevail and control the system behavior in a large segments of parameters while pool punishers can only survive in the limit of weak peer punishment when a rich variety of solutions is observed. Paradoxically, the two types of punishment may extinguish each other's impact, resulting in the triumph of defectors. The technical difficulties and suggested methods are briefly discussed.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what Szolnoki et al. (2011) do and do not say regarding each of the 15 parameters, followed by the required four‐part summary.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players
• Mentioned? They place players on a large square lattice with periodic boundaries of size L×L, and they do vary L (e.g., from 400×400 up to 7200×7200).  
• Systematically varied for punishment effect? No. They discuss increasing L to reduce finite‐size artifacts, not as a systematic parameter to see how punishment affects efficiency or total payoffs.

2) Number of rounds
• Mentioned? No. The paper uses an evolutionary (indefinite) model and does not specify or manipulate any finite number of rounds.  

3) Is chat enabled between players?
• Mentioned? No. There is no mention of any communication or chat among players.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
• Mentioned? They assume each cooperator or punisher contributes a fixed amount (= 1) to the public good; however, they do not describe it as a systematically varied parameter.  
• Systematically varied for punishment effect? No.

5) Is the contribution default?
• Mentioned? No. There is no mention of participants deciding how much to move “back” to themselves or any other default contribution mechanism.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication (synergy) factor
• Mentioned? Yes. The paper calls it the “synergy factor” r. They do systematically vary r (e.g., r = 2, 3.5, 3.8).  
• Effect on punishment treatment? They study how different r values change which strategy combinations survive (e.g., defector‐dominated vs. punisher‐dominated phases). They do not quantify “efficiency” as total‐payoff‐relative‐to‐max but explore how synergy factor shifts phase diagrams (Figs. 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9). They do not provide a numeric effect size regarding efficiency; they show thresholds and phase transitions in terms of final strategy frequencies.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
• Mentioned? Yes. For pool punishers, there is a constant cost γ; for peer punishers, the cost is γ multiplied by the number of defectors in the group and possibly by m, depending on the “hard” or “weak” limit. The paper systematically varies γ.  
• Effect on punishment treatment? They show phase transitions (e.g., from full defection to partial punisher coexistence) as a function of γ. They do not report how it changes “efficiency” but do detail thresholds and whether peers or pool punishers prevail under changing cost (Figs. 3–5, 8–9).

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted per punishment)
• Mentioned? Yes. Denoted by β (the “fine”). The paper varies β systematically and shows how different β levels change final strategic outcomes.  
• Effect on punishment treatment? They do not discuss “efficiency” per se but show how increasing β can enable or destroy stable punisher populations, or allow defectors to take over. Phase diagrams show transitions at specific β thresholds (Figs. 1–5, 7–9).

9) Whether a reward is enabled
• Mentioned? No. The paper deals with punishing strategies only; they do not include or vary reward.

10) Reward cost
• Mentioned? No, since reward is not considered.

11) Reward magnitude
• Mentioned? No, since reward is not considered.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?
• Mentioned? No. The model is purely evolutionary and does not discuss whether agents “know” the horizon or not.

13) Are peer outcomes shown?
• Mentioned? Not in the sense of an experimental display. The model’s imitation rule uses local payoff comparison, but the paper does not discuss systematically varying how (or if) outcomes are revealed. They simply assume update based on neighbors’ payoffs; there is no parameter about “information display.”

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
• Mentioned? No. The paper does not address knowledge of who applied the sanction.  

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
• Mentioned? No. There is no reward in the model, so this is not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?

• The paper does not measure “efficiency” (i.e., total group payoff / maximum possible payoff). Instead, the authors track the stationary frequencies of each strategy (defectors, cooperators, peer punishers, pool punishers) under varying synergy factors, costs, and fines.  
• They do refer to “elimination of the tragedy of the commons” and “which strategy dominates,” but they do not explicitly compute the group’s total payoff nor do they present “efficiency” as a fraction of a theoretical maximum payoff.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

• Mentioned clearly and used in some way:  
  (1) Number of players (L×L lattice sizes), (6) Synergy factor r, (7) Punishment cost (γ, plus factor m), (8) Punishment magnitude (β).  
• Not mentioned at all or not treated as variables:  
  (2), (3), (5), (9), (10), (11), (12), (13), (14), (15).  
• Mentioned as a fixed aspect but not varied:  
  (4) Contribution is always a fixed amount 1 for cooperators/punishers; they do not treat it as a varying parameter.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?

• The authors systematically vary three parameters: synergy factor r (parameter 6), punishment cost γ (parameter 7), and fine β (parameter 8). They provide phase diagrams for how those changes affect the final distribution of strategies (e.g., whether defectors are eliminated, whether punisher strategies survive). However, they do not frame their results in terms of “efficiency.”  
• No other parameter is systematically varied or directly tied to a punishment‐treatment outcome.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

• Because the paper does not measure total or average payoff, nor does it compare actual payoffs to a maximum possible payoff, one cannot make a direct numerical prediction about efficiency.  
• From the paper’s main results on strategy frequencies, one might guess that a higher synergy factor (r), a moderate punishment cost (γ), and a sufficiently large punishment fine (β) tend to reduce the fraction of defectors and thus could improve cooperation—and presumably could raise group payoffs. But the paper itself does not quantify that in terms of group efficiency.  
• No conclusions can be drawn about any other parameters (e.g., number of rounds, communication, reward) because the paper neither includes nor systematically varies them.  

In sum, the paper provides detailed results on how synergy factor, punishment cost, and punishment magnitude jointly shape which strategies survive in the long run, but it does not connect these to a formal measure of “efficiency.” Consequently, little can be stated about the exact punishment‐treatment effect on efficiency based on these results alone.

Authors: Houser, D; Xiao, E; McCabe, K; Smith, V
Author Full Names: Houser, Daniel; Xiao, Erte; McCabe, Kevin; Smith, Vernon
Article Title: When punishment fails: Research on sanctions, intentions and non-cooperation
Author Keywords: punishment; cooperation; trust; incentives; intentions; experiment
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS EXPERIMENTS; INTRINSIC MOTIVATION; COGNITIVE-DISSONANCE; EXTRINSIC INCENTIVES; RECIPROCITY; FAIRNESS; BEHAVIOR; MARKET; TRUST; ATTRIBUTIONS
Abstract: People can become less cooperative when threatened with sanctions, and previous research suggests both intentions and incentives underlie this effect. We report data from an experiment aimed at determining the relative importance of intentions and incentives in producing non-cooperative behavior. Participants play a one-shot investment experiment in pairs. Investors send an amount to trustees, request a return on this investment and, in some treatments, can threaten sanctions to enforce their requests. Decisions by trustees facing threats imposed (or not) by investors are compared to decisions by trustees facing threats imposed (or not) by nature. When not threatened, trustees typically decide to return a positive amount less than the investor requested. When threatened this decision becomes least common. If the request is large relative to the sanction then most trustees return nothing. If the request is small, trustees typically return the requested amount. These results do not vary with investors' intentions. (c) 2007 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

Below we walk through the 15 parameters one–by-one, citing exactly what can be found in Houser-Xiao-McCabe-Smith (2008) and whether the paper makes any prediction about how *systematically varying* that parameter would change the “punishment treatment effect.”  The punishment treatment effect is understood here as the difference (Threat – No-Threat) for whatever dependent variable the authors analyse.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Every game is a *pair* (1 investor, 1 trustee).  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  Always 2.  
   • Any prediction / effect size?  None.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  The experiment is explicitly *one-shot*.  
   • Varied?  No.  
   • Prediction?  None.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned?  Indirectly – the rules state “no talking at any time.”  
   • Varied?  No.  
   • Prediction?  None.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
   • Mentioned?  No.  Transfers and back-transfers are continuous (0–10).  
   • Prediction?  None.

5. Contribution default / “opt-out” framing  
   • Mentioned?  No.  
   • Prediction?  None.

6. Marginal-per-capita return / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Every MU sent by the investor is *tripled* (factor = 3).  
   • Varied?  No.  
   • Prediction?  None.

7. Punishment *cost to the punisher*  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Cost is zero to the investor; the 4-MU fine goes to the experimenter.  
   • Varied?  No.  
   • Prediction?  None.

8. Punishment *magnitude*  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Fixed deduction of 4 MU from the trustee.  
   • Varied?  No.  (The paper *does* discuss how a fixed 4-MU sanction interacts with high vs. low requests, but the magnitude itself is never changed.)  
   • Prediction under systematic variation?  Not given.

9. Whether a monetary *reward* option exists  
   • Mentioned?  No.  There is no reward stage.  
   • Prediction?  None.

10. Reward cost to grant 1 unit  
    • Not applicable.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Not applicable.

12. Whether the number of rounds is common knowledge  
    • Mentioned?  Yes – subjects know the game is played *once*.  
    • Varied?  No.  
    • Prediction?  None.

13. Whether peer outcomes are shown  
    • Mentioned?  Yes – each party sees the actual transfer / back-transfer after the decision sheet is returned, but the paper never varies this information.  
    • Prediction?  None.

14. Whether the punished party sees the *identity* of the punisher  
    • Mentioned?  Yes, and this is the *only* parameter the paper varies on purpose:  
      – Intention treatment: the trustee knows the sanction (or non-sanction) was *chosen* by the investor.  
      – Random treatment: the trustee knows the sanction was *randomly* assigned by Nature and that the investor is *unaware* of it at the time of her choice.  
    • Systematically varied?  Yes (two-level experimental factor).  
    • Prediction / effect size?  The authors *predict* and *find* that varying this parameter has essentially *no* effect on behaviour.  
      Numeric evidence (fair requests):  
      ‑ Mean % of tripled amount returned under threat  
        • Intentional threat: 31.9 %  
        • Random threat:     31.8 %  
        Difference ≈ 0; joint F-test, p = 0.93 (Table 2, Result 1).  
      ‑ Similarly, logit tests for complete defection or complete cooperation cannot reject equality (χ²(8)=6.1, p = 0.63).  
      Therefore, the paper’s best prediction is: revealing the punisher’s identity (and hence intentions) does *not* change the punishment treatment effect on any reported outcome.

15. Whether the rewarded party sees the identity of the rewarder  
    • Not applicable – no rewards.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use “group efficiency” (total payoff / maximum payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   – No.  Dependent variables are:  
     • Percentage of the tripled investment amount returned (continuous)  
     • Categorical cooperation types: complete cooperation (return ≥ request), weak non-cooperation (0 < return < request), complete defection (return = 0).  
     • Occasional reference to individual earnings, but the efficiency ratio is never computed.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are *mentioned*?  
   – 9 parameters: 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14.  

C. For which parameters does the paper analyse the effect of *systematically varying* the parameter on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable)?  
   – Exactly **one**: parameter 14 (knowledge of punisher identity / intentional vs. random threat).  
   – Effect: statistically zero for all reported outcomes.

D. Predictions you can make, based solely on this paper, about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) influence the punishment treatment effect on *efficiency*:  

   • Because efficiency is never measured, the only safe inference is that the authors found *no difference* between intentional and random punishment on cooperation or payoffs.  Hence one would predict *no change in efficiency* when varying parameter 14.  

   • For every other parameter the paper gives no data or theory that would allow a quantitative or even directional prediction about efficiency.  Any further guess would go beyond the evidence provided.

In short, the paper speaks only to whether *intentions* (parameter 14) matter; it concludes they do *not*.  Nothing else in the list of 15 parameters is experimentally manipulated or analysed with respect to the punishment treatment effect, let alone to overall group efficiency.

Authors: Perc, M
Author Full Names: Perc, Matjaz
Article Title: Sustainable institutionalized punishment requires elimination of second-order free-riders
Keywords Plus: COSTLY PUNISHMENT; INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; EVOLUTIONARY GAMES; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; HUMAN-BEHAVIOR; COOPERATION; REPUTATION; TRAGEDY; CARROT
Abstract: Although empirical and theoretical studies affirm that punishment can elevate collaborative efforts, its emergence and stability remain elusive. By peer-punishment the sanctioning is something an individual elects to do depending on the strategies in its neighborhood. The consequences of unsustainable efforts are therefore local. By pool-punishment, on the other hand, where resources for sanctioning are committed in advance and at large, the notion of sustainability has greater significance. In a population with free-riders, punishers must be strong in numbers to keep the punishment pool'' from emptying. Failure to do so renders the concept of institutionalized sanctioning futile. We show that pool-punishment in structured populations is sustainable, but only if second-order free-riders are sanctioned as well, and to a such degree that they cannot prevail. A discontinuous phase transition leads to an outbreak of sustainability when punishers subvert second-order free-riders in the competition against defectors.

Throughout, note that the paper focuses on the long‐run stability of different strategy mixes (punishers, cooperators, defectors) and on whether the “punishment pool” remains financially sustainable (Σ ≥ 0). The paper does not explicitly examine “efficiency” (actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff) as a dependent variable; instead, it considers the fractions of each strategy and the punishment‐pool balance. All statements below derive solely from the text, figures, and tables of the paper.

(1) Number of players
 • Mentioned?

(3) Is chat enabled between players?
 • Mentioned?

   – None.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
 • Mentioned?

 • Predictions from varying it?  
   – None. The paper does not investigate what would happen if partial contributions were allowed.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(5) Is the contribution default (do players decide how much of their endowment to move back)?
 • Mentioned?

 • Predictions from varying it?  
   – None.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related “multiplication factor”
 • Mentioned?  
   – Yes. The paper uses r as the “synergy factor,” which multiplies the total contributions in each local public‐goods group. This is referred to frequently (e.g., “Focusing first on the r−γ parameter plane…”).  
   – The authors systematically vary r; for instance, they note that in the absence of punishment, “cooperators survive only if r > 3.74, and crowd out defectors if r > 5.49.”  

 • Predictions from systematically varying r?  
   – They show phase diagrams (Figures 1–3) demonstrating how different combinations of r and the punishment fine γ produce different long‐run states (e.g., coexistence of punishers and defectors, or replacement of cooperators by punishers).  
   – Quantitatively, one example is that for sufficiently large r (depending also on γ), punishers can be sustained by eliminating second‐order free riders. For smaller r, punishers die out.  

 • Effect size(s)?  
   – In the text, they give several thresholds (e.g., r = 3.74 and r = 5.49) for different phase transitions in the absence of punishment. When punishment is present and γ is sufficiently large, these thresholds shift, allowing cooperation‐like behavior to survive at lower r.

   – None in this paper.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
 • Mentioned?

   – None.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward)
 • Mentioned?

   – None.

(12) Is the number of rounds known to players (i.e., do they know when the game ends)?
 • Mentioned?

 • Predictions from varying it?  
   – None.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players see each other’s payoffs)?
 • Mentioned?  
   – Not in the sense of “displaying outcomes.” The model uses local evolutionary updating, but there is no discussion of systematic variation in what they observe.  

 • Predictions from varying it?  
   – None.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
 • Mentioned?  
   – No. The model treats the punishment as institution‐wide (“the invisible hand” of pool punishment).  

 • Predictions from varying it?  
   – None.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
 • Mentioned?  
   – No reward mechanism is studied, so no mention.  

 • Predictions from varying it?  
   – None.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FINAL SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper does not use “efficiency” (actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff) as a stated dependent variable.  
   • Instead, the main dependent variables are: (1) the stationary fraction of each strategy type (punishers vs. cooperators vs. defectors), and (2) the pool‐punishment balance Σ (whether it remains nonnegative or goes negative, which the authors call “fully sustainable” vs. “conditionally sustainable” pool punishment).

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • The paper explicitly mentions (and defines in its model) four of them:  
       (4) Contributions are effectively “all or nothing.”  
       (6) The synergy factor r is extensively examined.  
       (7) The punisher’s cost per unit (β), though always set to 1.0.  
       (8) The punishment magnitude γ, which is systematically varied.  
   • The other 11 parameters (1, 2, 3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15) are either not mentioned at all or are mentioned only to note that no rewards or communication were modeled.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Two parameters are systematically varied and their impact on outcomes (fractions of each strategy and punishment‐pool sustainability) is analyzed:  
       – (6) The synergy factor r.  
       – (8) The punishment magnitude γ.  
   • The paper does not systematically vary the other parameters.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper never directly measures “efficiency” as total payoff / maximum payoff, so little concrete can be inferred.

Abstract: Cooperation among nonrelatives can be puzzling because cooperation often involves incurring costs to confer benefits on unrelated others. Punishment of noncooperators can sustain otherwise fragile cooperation, but the provision of punishment suffers from a second-order free-riding problem because nonpunishers can free ride on the benefits from costly punishment provided by others. One suggested solution to this problem is second-order punishment of nonpunishers; more generally, the threat or promise of higher order sanctions might maintain the lower order sanctions that enforce cooperation in collective action problems. Here the authors report on 3 experiments testing people's willingness to provide second-order sanctions by having participants play a cooperative game with opportunities to punish and reward each other. The authors found that people supported those who rewarded cooperators either by rewarding them or by punishing nonrewarders, but people did not support those who punished noncooperators-they did not reward punishers or punish nonpunishers. Furthermore, people did not approve of punishers more than they did nonpunishers, even when nonpunishers were clearly unwilling to use sanctions to support cooperation. The results suggest that people will much more readily support positive sanctions than they will support negative sanctions.

5.  Contribution default (recycling from public fund)?  
   (1) Not mentioned.

6.  MPCR / multiplication factor

   (1) Mentioned: the punisher paid C$1.

8.  Punishment magnitude  
   (1) Mentioned: each C$1 spent removed C$3 from the target.  
   (2) Not varied; no predictions.

9.  Reward enabled?  
   (1) Mentioned and **experimentally manipulated**.  
        • Study 1: between–subjects Punishment-only vs Reward-only.

        – Study 1, Reward condition: 30/49 participants rewarded the earlier rewarder vs 16/49 the non-rewarder (χ²(1)=16.33, p<.001); median extra reward to rewarder ≈ +15 ¢ (Wilcoxon S=76.5, p<.001).

10.  Reward cost  
    (1) Mentioned: C$1.  
    (2) Not varied; no predictions.

11.  Reward magnitude  
    (1) Mentioned: each C$1 awarded gave the target C$3.  
    (2) Not varied; no predictions.

12.  Are the number of rounds known?  
    (1) Subjects were explicitly told it was a one-shot game; they were NOT told in advance about the surprise sanction stages.  
    (2) Not varied; no predictions.

13.  Are peer outcomes shown?

14.  Is the punisher identified?  
    (1) Yes—players were identified by code names; subjects were told which coder-named cooperator had punished.  
    (2) Not varied; no predictions.

15.  Is the rewarder identified?  
    (1) Same as 14: the rewarder’s code name was shown.  
    (2) Not varied; no predictions.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY  

A.  Does the paper use “group efficiency” as a dependent variable?  
    No.  Dependent variables are (a) binary sanction decisions (who punished/rewarded whom), (b) amounts of money spent on punishment or reward, and (c) post-experimental likeability / trustworthiness ratings.  These are conceptually different from efficiency because they do not aggregate total payoffs relative to the maximum.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
    12 of 15: #1,2,3,4,6,7,8,9,10,11,13,14,15.  Parameters #5, #12 (in its “unknown horizon” sense), and #13–15 were not manipulated but are described.  

C.  For which parameters does the paper discuss the effect of **systematic variation** on the punishment treatment effect?  
    Only 1 parameter (#9, “Reward enabled?”).  The authors varied whether rewards, punishments, or both were available and reported how that changed (i) second-order sanctioning behavior and (ii) social evaluations.  No other parameter was experimentally varied or theoretically explored for differential effects.

D.  Predictions about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment treatment effect on **efficiency**, based solely on the paper  
    • The paper repeatedly notes that punishment removes net resources from the group whereas reward adds net resources; therefore, introducing punishment (holding all else constant) is expected to **decrease group efficiency**, whereas introducing reward is expected to increase it.

Abstract: The evolution and stability of helping behaviour has attracted great research efforts across disciplines. However, the field is also characterized by a great confusion over terminology and a number of disagreements, often between disciplines but also along taxonomic boundaries.    • Discussion in paper: Yes. A cost schedule, identical to Fehr and Gaechter (2000), is used (Table 1, p. 6). Costs are increasing in the total number of points a punisher assigns (e.g., 1 point costs 1 ECU, 2 points cost 2 ECU, … up to 10 points costing 30 ECU).  
   • Systematic variation or predictions? No. The paper does not vary these costs across sessions and does not predict how changing this cost schedule affects efficiency.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   • Discussion in paper: Yes. In MP and BP, each monetary‐punishment point reduces the punished player’s earnings from the first stage by 10% up to a maximum of 100% (p. 6).  
   • Systematic variation or predictions? No. The paper uses the same 10% increment for all sessions and does not examine how systematically altering it would affect efficiency.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussion in paper: No. The experiment only examines punishment (monetary and/or nonmonetary). There is no mention of a reward mechanism.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Discussion in paper: No. There is no reward system in this experiment.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)
   • Discussion in paper: No. Again, no reward system is present in the study.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
   • Discussion in paper: Yes. It is common knowledge that there are 15 total periods (pp. 5–6).  
   • Systematic variation or predictions? No. They do not manipulate whether the horizon is known or unknown. All sessions used a known, finite 15‐round horizon.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained or lost)?
   • Discussion in paper: Partially. Each subject sees how many ECUs each group member contributed (in random order, anonymized) and sees aggregate punishment points, but not the punisher’s identity (p. 7).  
   • Systematic variation or predictions? No. The paper does not vary how much information is shown or withheld in different sessions.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Discussion in paper: Yes. They explicitly state that only the total number of punishment points received is shown; the identity of the punisher(s) is hidden (p. 6).  
   • Systematic variation or predictions? No. No manipulation on whether punisher identity is revealed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Discussion in paper: Not applicable. There is no reward mechanism, so the question does not arise.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper frequently reports “earnings,” “overall welfare,” or “average payoff” at the group level, and it directly compares those payoffs under different punishment (MP, NP, BP) regimes (see Figures 1 and 2 and Table 2). Although it does not repeatedly use the term “efficiency” in the sense of “actual payoff divided by the maximum possible,” its measure of “overall welfare” or “earnings” serves a similar function.  
   • The paper also devotes significant attention to “contribution levels,” which can differ from “efficiency.” Contributions can rise, yet if punishment costs are high, overall payoffs (efficiency) may be lower; hence contribution and efficiency are not the same.  
   • Thus, the main dependent variables are (1) contribution levels (percentage of endowment contributed) and (2) average or total group earnings (“welfare”).

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned explicitly:  
     1 (Number of players = 4),  
     2 (Number of rounds = 15),  
     6 (MPCR = 0.4),  
     7 (Punishment cost schedule),  
     8 (Punishment magnitude = 10% per point),  
     12 (Players know there are 15 rounds),  
     13 (Players see others’ contributions in anonymized form),  
     14 (Punisher identity not revealed).  
   • Not present or not discussed:  
     3 (No formal chat mentioned),  
     4 and 5 (Not an all‐or‐nothing or default contribution),  
     9, 10, 11 (No reward system),  
     15 (Rewarder identity inapplicable).  
   • In total, the paper touches on 8 of the 15 parameters in some form.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. The experiment does not systematically vary any of those 15 parameters. Instead, it compares three punishment‐regime treatments (MP, NP, BP), each holding the above parameters fixed. There are no reported results about how changing any single parameter (e.g., altering group size, altering cost of punishment points, altering horizon length) would in itself affect the punishment treatment effect.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not provide direct evidence for systematic parameter changes beyond the three punishment treatments themselves. Consequently, there is little basis within these results for predicting how varying, for example, group size, the number of rounds, or the exact punishment cost schedule would affect efficiency.  
   • The main inference is that when monetary and nonmonetary punishment are both available (BP) under otherwise fixed conditions, average earnings (“welfare”) eventually become higher than in the single‐sanction systems (MP or NP). But the paper does not investigate how the 15 parameters, taken one by one or in combination, might alter that outcome.  
   • Therefore, based on this paper alone, we can make little to no quantitative prediction about how varying any of the 15 parameters would change the punishment treatment effect on efficiency. The paper’s focus is on whether adding a nonmonetary sanction to a monetary‐sanction regime (or vice versa) boosts cooperation and payoffs under one fixed configuration of parameters.

Article Title: The Role of a Common Is Moral Heuristic in the Stability and Change of Moral Norms

Abstract: Moral norms are fundamental for virtually all social interactions, including cooperation. Moral norms develop and change, but the mechanisms underlying when, and how, such changes occur are not well-described by theories of moral psychology. We tested, and confirmed, the hypothesis that the commonness of an observed behavior consistently influences its moral status, which we refer to as the common is moral (CIM) heuristic. In 9 experiments, we used an experimental model of dynamic social interaction that manipulated the commonness of altruistic and selfish behaviors to examine the change of peoples' moral judgments. We found that both altruistic and selfish behaviors were judged as more moral, and less deserving of punishment, when common than when rare, which could be explained by a classical formal model (social impact theory) of behavioral conformity. Furthermore, judgments of common versus rare behaviors were faster, indicating that they were computationally more efficient. Finally, we used agent-based computer simulations to investigate the endogenous population dynamics predicted to emerge if individuals use the CIM heuristic, and found that the CIM heuristic is sufficient for producing 2 hallmarks of real moral norms; stability and sudden changes. Below is a strictly documentary extraction of what the paper says (and does ​not​ say) about each of the 15 parameters in relation to any “punishment treatment effect.”  For completeness I also note whenever the authors analyse dependent variables other than efficiency.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1.  Number of players  
    • Mentioned?  Yes.  Experiments 1-4 used groups of 4; Experiments 6-7 used groups of 8.  
    • Systematically varied?  Yes (4 vs 8).  
    • Did the authors connect this variation to a ​punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  No.  
    • Reported effect (different DVs):  They report that moral- and punishment-judgement effects of commonness “did not differ for groups composed of four or eight players” (p. 17).  No numerical coefficient is given; no efficiency data are reported.

2.  Number of rounds  
    • Mentioned?  Yes – observers watched 40 one-shot interactions (20 trials per block).  
    • Varied?  No.  Always 40.  
    • Any link to punishment-treatment effect?  No.

3.  Chat enabled between players  
    • Mentioned?  No.

4.  All-or-nothing contribution rule  
    • Mentioned?  Yes – each simulated PGG player chose either “keep everything” (selfish) or “invest all” (altruistic).  
    • Varied?  No.  
    • Linked to punishment-treatment effect?  No.

5.  “Contribution default” (withdraw rather than give)  
    • Mentioned?  No.

6.  MPCR / multiplication factor  
    • Mentioned?  No payoff multiplier is specified anywhere in the paper.  No analysis uses MPCR.  No variation.

7.  Cost to impose one unit of punishment  
    • Mentioned?  Only in Experiment 9.  Participants spent their own bonus to buy “deduction points,” one point per monetary unit invested (exact cent value not reported).  
    • Varied?  No – fixed.  
    • Linked to punishment-treatment effect?  Not measured.

8.  Punishment magnitude (fine per unit)  
    • Mentioned?  Experiment 9: Each deduction point was multiplied by 5 and that amount was subtracted from the target’s earnings.  
    • Varied?  No.  
    • Linked to punishment-treatment effect?  No.

9.  Reward option enabled  
    • Mentioned?  No.

10. Cost of one unit of reward  
    • Mentioned?  No.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Mentioned?  No.

12. Horizon known (do players know when the game ends?)  
    • Mentioned?  Implicitly yes – observers were told they would watch 40 interactions, but this parameter was not manipulated.  No relation to punishment treatment.

13. Peer outcomes shown (payoffs displayed)  
    • Mentioned?  The paper only says observers saw each player’s ​choice​.  It never states that exact monetary outcomes were displayed.  Not varied; not analysed.

14. Punisher identity revealed  
    • Mentioned?  In Experiment 9, punishment was anonymous; identity not revealed.  Not varied.

15. Rewarder identity revealed  
    • Mentioned?  Not applicable (no reward).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables actually used  
    • Moral judgement (9-point scale)  
    • Desired (hypothetical) punishment (9-point scale)  
    • Reaction time of those judgements  
    • Probability of choosing the selfish/altruistic action (Experiment 8)  
    • Amount of ​costly​ third-party punishment purchased (Experiment 9)  
    The paper never measures “group efficiency” (total earnings divided by maximum possible).  Hence none of the reported effects are effects on efficiency.

B.  How many of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
    6 parameters (1, 2, 4, 6*, 7, 8) are mentioned at all.  (*MPCR only implicitly through the PGG label; no value given.)  The remaining 9 are completely absent.

C.  For how many parameters is any systematic variation analysed with respect to ​any​ dependent variable?  
    • Only Parameter 1 (number of players: 4 vs 8) is systematically varied.  
    • The paper shows this variation has ​no​ detectable effect on moral- or punishment-judgement outcomes.  
    • Zero parameters are analysed for their effect on a “punishment treatment effect,” and zero are analysed for effects on efficiency.

D.  What predictions about the 15 parameters’ influence on a punishment-treatment effect on efficiency can be made solely from this paper?  
    • Very little.  The paper never measures efficiency, never compares a punishment treatment to a no-punishment baseline, and never manipulates any of the key cost/magnitude parameters of punishment or reward.  Therefore it offers no empirical basis for forecasting how any of the 15 parameters—alone or in interaction—would change the ​efficiency​ impact of introducing peer punishment.  The only relevant fragment is that altering group size from 4 to 8 had no effect on judgement-level outcomes; by extrapolation one ​might​ guess that the efficiency effect of punishment would also be unchanged by modest shifts in group size, but the paper provides no data to support that conjecture.  In short, the paper supplies virtually no leverage for predicting punishment-treatment effects on group efficiency.

Keywords Plus: TIT-FOR-TAT; INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; COMPETITIVE ALTRUISM; COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; PUNISHMENT; TRAGEDY; BEHAVIOR; CARROT; CHOICE
Abstract: Decision rules of reciprocity include 'I help those who helped me' (direct reciprocity) and 'I help those who have helped others' (indirect reciprocity), i.e. I help those who have a reputation to care for others. A person's reputation is a score that members of a social group update whenever they see the person interacting or hear at best multiple gossip about the person's social interactions. Reputation is the current standing the person has gained from previous investments or refusal of investments in helping others. Is he a good guy, can I trust him or should I better avoid him as a social partner? A good reputation pays off by attracting help from others, even from strangers or members from another group, if the recipient's reputation is known. Any costly investment in others, i.e. direct help, donations to charity, investment in averting climate change, etc. increases a person's reputation. I shall argue and illustrate with examples that a person's known reputation functions like money that can be used whenever the person needs help. Whenever possible I will present tests of predictions of evolutionary theory, i.e. fitness maximizing strategies, mostly by economic experiments with humans.

Below I strictly summarize what can (and what cannot) be learned from the review by Milinski (2016) with respect to the 15 design parameters you listed and to the specific outcome “punishment-treatment effect on efficiency”.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER–BY–PARAMETER INSPECTION
--------------------------------------------------------------------
For every parameter I indicate

(1) Whether the paper even mentions the parameter, and, if it does, the value(s) that appear.
(2) Whether the paper says anything about what would happen **if that parameter were systematically varied** for any dependent variable, and especially for group efficiency (= realised pay-off / maximum pay-off).

P1. Number of players  
(1) Mentioned: yes. 4-person PG game is described as the “typical” design; groups of 6 (and occasionally 12) are also reported for specific experiments (e.g. Fig. 3, 4, 5, 6, 7).  
(2) No systematic manipulation or prediction. No effect size reported.

P2. Number of rounds  
(1) Mentioned incidentally (e.g. 16, 20 or 25 rounds in the cited studies).  
(2) Never varied systematically; no prediction given.

P3. Chat enabled  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) —  

P4. All-or-nothing contribution choice  
(1) Mentioned once: subjects can “invest anonymously either €1 **or nothing**”.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction.

P5. Contribution default / endowment moved back  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) —  

P6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
(1) Mentioned once: money in the account “is doubled” (implying MPCR = 0.5 in a 4-player game).  
(2) No manipulation; no prediction.

P7. Punishment cost  
(1) Example: “punisher pays €1”.  
(2) Not systematically varied; no prediction.

P8. Punishment magnitude  
(1) Example: “target loses €3”.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction.

P9. Reward possibility enabled  
(1) Yes. Several passages contrast “punishment” versus “reward” and report that, in initial votes, subjects tend to choose rewards, but experienced subjects prefer punishment.  
(2) The paper does not vary “reward on/off” within a punishment treatment and does not quantify any change in efficiency.

P10. Reward cost  
(1) Not specified.  
(2) No discussion.

P11. Reward magnitude  
(1) Not specified.  
(2) No discussion.

P12. End-known or unknown  
(1) Not reported.  
(2) —  

P13. Peer outcomes shown  
(1) Yes. Throughout the review it is emphasised that participants “could observe every interaction” or saw the “sequence of ‘yes’ and ‘no’”.  
(2) Not manipulated; no prediction.

P14. Punishee knows who punished  
(1) Not stated.  
(2) —  

P15. Rewardee knows who rewarded  
(1) Not stated.  
(2) —  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
DEPENDENT VARIABLES
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The review mainly talks about
•  contribution levels / cooperation rates  
•  amount of punishment or reward points  
•  “efficiency” only in passing (Section 11: “The interaction … boosts cooperative efficiency”, no numerical data shown—Fig. 7 only plots *sanctioning points*)  

Thus, most quantitative results in the paper concern cooperation or sanctioning, not efficiency as defined in your question.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Does the paper use group efficiency as a dependent variable?  
 Only briefly. Section 11 claims that combining reputation and punishment “boosts cooperative efficiency”, but the plotted figure concerns sanctioning points, not pay-offs. The standard dependent variables analysed in the cited work are (i) contributions/cooperation, and (ii) use of punishment or rewards.

B. Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
 7 of 15: 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 13.

C. For which parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* that parameter on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable)?  
 Zero. No parameter is experimentally varied in a way that permits estimating a marginal effect of that parameter on the “punishment treatment effect”. Consequently, no numerical effect sizes are provided.

D. What predictions about the 15 parameters and their interactions can be made **solely** from the review?  
 Very limited. All that can be inferred is:  
 •  Having any punishment option at all (cost ≈ 1, magnitude ≈ 3) typically raises cooperation, but at a cost that may cancel efficiency gains unless reputation mechanisms are also present.  
 •  Adding a parallel reputation mechanism (indirect reciprocity) “boosts efficiency” relative to punishment-only, but the review provides no quantitative estimate of the size of that boost nor the boundary conditions (group size, MPCR, etc.).  
 Beyond these qualitative statements, the paper offers no data for predicting how changing any of the 15 parameters—alone or in interaction—will alter the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

In short, the review is informative about the *existence* of reputation-punishment interactions, but it gives virtually no leverage for parameter-by-parameter quantitative prediction of efficiency effects.

Abstract: Prosocial behavior is crucial for functioning societies. However, its reliable scientific assessment and the understanding of its underlying structure are still a challenge. Below each of the 15 public-goods-game parameters we report exactly what the paper says (if anything).  We then state whether the authors ever *systematically varied* that parameter and, if so, whether they said anything about how such variation would change the “punishment-treatment effect” (i.e., the difference in outcomes between a punishment and a no-punishment condition).  Page, table or figure numbers are given in parentheses whenever the information is visible in the excerpt.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
GAME-STRUCTURE PARAMETERS
1.  Number of players  
    • Mentioned: Yes.  The “second-person punishment game” (2nd-PPG) involves 2 players (A and B).  The “third-person punishment game” (3rd-PPG) involves 3 players (A, B, C) (Methods section, “Game theoretical paradigms”).  
    • Systematically varied? No.  Only one group size per game is used.  No predictions about changing group size and the punishment treatment effect.

2.  Number of rounds  
    • Mentioned: Yes.  2nd-PPG: two rounds as A and three as B.  3rd-PPG: three rounds as C.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  No statements about how more or fewer rounds would alter the effect of punishment.

3.  Chat enabled?  
    • Mentioned: No.

4.  All-or-nothing contributions?  
    • Mentioned: No.  (In all games participants choose any integer number of monetary units.)

5.  Contribution default / endowment back-transfer design?  
    • Mentioned: No.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
MONETARY-STAKE PARAMETER
6.  Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
    • Mentioned: Partially.  In the trust game the amount sent is *tripled* before reaching the trustee (“TG … transferred amount would be tripled”, Methods).  This is not a public-goods MPCR and is never linked to punishment, so it is not informative for the requested prediction.  No systematic variation.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PEER-INCENTIVE PARAMETERS
7.  Punishment cost per unit  
    • Mentioned: Yes.  “Player B could invest MUs to punish Player A: for every assigned MU, three MUs were subtracted from Player A” (Methods, 2nd-PPG; identical in 3rd-PPG).  Thus the cost is fixed at 1 MU per punishment unit.  
    • Systematically varied? No.

8.  Punishment magnitude per unit  
    • Mentioned: Yes.  Fixed at 3 MUs deducted from the target for each MU spent by the punisher.  
    • Systematically varied? No.

9.  Reward enabled?  
    • Mentioned: No.

10. Reward cost per unit  
    • Mentioned: No.

11. Reward magnitude per unit  
    • Mentioned: No.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
INFORMATION-DISPLAY PARAMETERS
12. End-round information (finite-vs-indefinite horizon)  
    • Mentioned: Not explicitly.  Participants are simply told how many rounds a game contains, but this is not analysed or varied.

13. Peer-outcome feedback shown?  
    • Mentioned: Yes (implicitly).  In the punishment games, Player B (or C) sees how many MUs Player A offered before deciding on punishment.  This feedback is fixed; it is never varied experimentally, nor is its impact analysed.

14. Punishee knows the identity of the punisher?  
    • Mentioned: No explicit statement.  Given the 2-player set-up, the identity is obvious but never discussed, never varied.

15. Rewardee knows the identity of the rewarder?  
    • Mentioned: No (and reward is never used).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
A.  Dependent variables in the paper  
    • Efficiency (total or average payoff) is **not** used anywhere.  
    • Instead, the authors analyse:  
      – Monetary units *given* (DG, TG, etc.)  
      – MU *invested to punish* (2nd-PPG, 3rd-PPG)  
      – Helping frequency, reciprocity-effect size, cost-effect size (ZPG)  
      – Donation percentages, social-discounting parameter k, SVO choices, questionnaire scores.  
    These variables measure generosity, norm enforcement and self-reported prosociality; they are conceptually different from group efficiency.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
    • Parameter 1 (players), 2 (rounds), 6 (tripling factor in the trust game, loosely related), 7 (punishment cost = 1), 8 (punishment magnitude = 3), and 13 (peer-outcome feedback implicitly provided).  
    → 6 of 15 parameters appear at least once.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss how *systematically varying* them would change the punishment treatment effect (for **any** dependent variable)?  
    • None (0/15).  Every mentioned parameter is held constant; no prediction or empirical estimate of its variation exists.

D.  What predictions about the 15 parameters and their interactions can be made *solely from this paper* regarding the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
    • Very little to none.  The study does not use a public-goods framework, does not report efficiency, and never manipulates the listed parameters.  Hence the paper provides (i) no quantitative effect sizes and (ii) no qualitative hypotheses about how changing any of the 15 parameters would raise or lower the efficiency advantage (or disadvantage) of adding punishment.  Any further prediction would have to rely on external literature or speculation, which is outside the present task.

Abstract: Human cooperation may partly depend on the presence of individuals willing to incur personal costs to punish noncooperators. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter inventory, based strictly on the content of the Crockett et al. paper provided, followed by the requested four‐part summary. As the paper deals with an Ultimatum Game (UG) rather than a public goods game with punishment, it does not address most of the 15 parameters in the context of systematically varying them to study punishment’s effect on group efficiency. All references below are drawn solely from the text.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned? Yes (the Ultimatum Game is described as a two‐player game: proposer and responder).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not examine how changing the number of players affects punishment or any dependent variable. No effect size is reported.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned? Yes (participants played 48 one‐shot UG trials, each with a different “proposer” in a computer interface).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not analyze how varying the number of UG rounds alters punishment. No effect size is reported.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not mention enabling any real‐time communication or chat between players.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned? No. This paper discusses an Ultimatum Game (split‐the‐pie offers) rather than a public goods game with discrete all‐or‐nothing contributions. No systematic variation is described.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Mentioned? No. The UG does not force a default “move money back into a hand,” so this is not covered.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Mentioned? No. The experiment uses a simple UG split—there is no mention of a multiplication factor or MPCR.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned? Only in the general sense that rejecting an unfair offer is personally costly (the responder forfeits a payoff), but there is no parameter in the paper specifying a systematic “per‐unit” punishment cost. Nor is this parameter varied or assigned an effect size.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   • Mentioned? Not in a parametric sense. In the UG, if the responder rejects an unfair offer, both parties get nothing, but the paper does not describe systematic variation of “punishment magnitude” nor provide effect sizes.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned? No. There is no mention of a reward mechanism in the UG (only acceptance vs. rejection of offers).

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Mentioned? No. The experiment does not include any reward‐giving option.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)
   • Mentioned? No. Again, no reward mechanism is included in the described task.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
   • Mentioned? The method states that participants played 48 separate offers, but there is no indication that the effect of (or knowledge about) the total number of rounds was systematically varied or studied.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (e.g., do players see how much others gained or lost)?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not discuss showing other players’ outcomes from round to round. Each participant saw only their immediate split offers and responded accordingly.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Mentioned? No. Although participants see a photo of each purported proposer, the paper does not discuss whether the “punished” party (the proposer) learns who punished them. There is no systematic variation or effect size reported.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Mentioned? No. The design did not involve any reward mechanism or a notion of identifying a rewarder.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper does not use group efficiency, total payoff, or average payoff as a dependent variable. The key dependent variables are (1) the rejection rate of unfair offers (to index “altruistic punishment”) in the Ultimatum Game and (2) impulsive choice measured via delay discounting. The paper also discusses serotonin depletion and self‐control. These dependent variables are distinct from efficiency; there is no reference to actual total payoff or efficiency (actual/maximum) as an outcome measure.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Only two are mentioned at all:  
       1) Number of players (Parameter 1): The UG always has two players.  
       2) Number of rounds (Parameter 2): The experiment used 48 one‐shot trials.  
   • The remaining 13 parameters receive no mention or variation in this study.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • None of the parameters are systematically varied in the paper. Hence the paper provides no discussion or numerical effect sizes regarding how changing these parameters would affect punishment or any other dependent variable.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not analyze a public goods game, does not measure group efficiency, and does not systematically vary any of the listed parameters. Accordingly, it provides virtually no basis for predicting how varying them would affect a “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency. One can say little to nothing about how those parameters or their interactions would shape efficiency, based strictly on this paper’s information.

Abstract: The exclusion of freeriders from common privileges or public acceptance is widely found in the real world. Current models on the evolution of cooperation with incentives mostly assume peer sanctioning, whereby a punisher imposes penalties on freeriders at a cost to itself. It is well known that such costly punishment has two substantial difficulties. First, a rare punishing cooperator barely subverts the asocial society of freeriders, and second, natural selection often eliminates punishing cooperators in the presence of non-punishing cooperators (namely, 'second-order' freeriders). We present a game-theoretical model of social exclusion in which a punishing cooperator can exclude freeriders from benefit sharing. We show that such social exclusion can overcome the above-mentioned difficulties even if it is costly and stochastic. The results do not require a genetic relationship, repeated interaction, reputation or group selection. Instead, only a limited number of freeriders are required to prevent the second-order freeriders from eroding the social immune system.

Below each of the 15 design parameters we list  

(i) whether the paper ever mentions or fixes that parameter (and its value, if any), and  

(ii) whether the authors **systematically vary** that parameter and state what this does to the *punishment treatment effect* (i.e. the consequence of having a punishment option as compared with having none).  Every quotation, equation-number or figure reference is taken from the paper.  When no statement is made we say so explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players (group size, n)  
   (i) Discussed.  All analytical results are written for an arbitrary n ≥ 2.  In the main figures the authors set n = 5; in robustness checks they also use n = 4 and n = 10 (electronic supplementary material, figs S5–S6).  
   (ii) Systematically varied.  
        • Costly punishment (Fig. 1 & text): “the stable segment PK₀ expands with n” – i.e. a larger group makes it **easier** for punishment to sustain cooperation (lowers the required initial fraction of punishers).  
        • Social exclusion (supplementary figs S5–S6): “the limit exclusion cost γ̄ becomes more restricted as n increases” – i.e. in larger groups the exclusion cost must be even smaller if exclusion is to work.  
        Numerical expressions:  
          – Threshold fine β₀ = σ/(n-1) with σ = c(1 – r/n). β₀ falls as n rises.  
          – Threshold exclusion cost γ̄₀ = (r – 1)c/(n-1). γ̄₀ falls when n rises.  

2. Number of rounds  
   (i) Not mentioned – the model is an infinite‐horizon replicator dynamic.  
   (ii) No predictions.

3. Chat between players  
   (i) Not mentioned.  
   (ii) No predictions.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
   (i) Yes.  The game has only two pure actions: contribute c or contribute 0 (Section 2).  
   (ii) Never varied, so no prediction.

5. Contribution default (withdrawal framing)  
   (i) Not mentioned.  
   (ii) No predictions.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor (r)  
   (i) Discussed.  Assumed r > 1 and r < n; numerical illustrations use r = 3.  
   (ii) Analytically varied through threshold formulas, but no separate figure sweeps r.  
        • Costly punishment: β₀ = c(1 – r/n)/(n-1); higher r ⇒ lower β₀ ⇒ punishment becomes effective at smaller fines.  
        • Social exclusion: γ̄₀ = (r – 1)c/(n-1); higher r ⇒ higher γ̄₀ ⇒ exclusion can tolerate a larger cost.  
        These statements link r to the punishment treatment effect, although the paper gives no explicit efficiency numbers.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit (γ)  
   (i) Core parameter; default γ = 0.03 in Fig. 1.  
   (ii) Systematically varied: “decreasing γ … the minimal frequency of punishers out-competing defectors decreases” (Fig. 1a).  Lower γ makes punishment more potent; with very small γ punishers’ basin of attraction expands.

8. Punishment magnitude / fine per unit (β)  
   (i) Core parameter; β varied in Fig. 1a and formulas.  
   (ii) Systematically varied: must exceed β₀ = σ/(n-1) for punishment to matter; larger β shifts equilibrium R toward the defector vertex and enlarges the region in which punishers can prevail.  Finite β never suffices for punishers to *dominate* defectors – the game remains bi-stable.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   (i) Not mentioned.  
   (ii) No predictions.

10. Reward cost  
    Not mentioned; no predictions.

11. Reward magnitude  
    Not mentioned; no predictions.

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
    Not mentioned; no predictions.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    Not mentioned; no predictions.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
    Not mentioned; no predictions.

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
    Not mentioned; no predictions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables actually analysed  
    • Expected payoff of each strategy (P_C, P_D, P_P, P_E)  
    • Strategy frequencies (x, y, z) and the position of equilibria/basins of attraction  
    Group efficiency (total payoff ÷ maximum possible) is *not* directly reported; “optimal benefit” c(r-1) is used only as a reference point.  Thus efficiency, average payoff and contribution rate are different quantities in this paper.

B.  Parameters from the 15-item list that are even *mentioned*: 5 of 15  
    1 (group size), 4 (binary contribution rule), 6 (MPCR r), 7 (punishment cost γ), 8 (punishment magnitude β).

C.  Parameters whose systematic variation is linked to the punishment treatment effect: 4 of 15  
    1 (group size), 6 (r), 7 (γ), 8 (β).  The other 11 parameters receive no treatment-effect discussion.

D.  What can we predict – *only* from this paper – about how the 15 parameters and their interactions affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
    • Smaller punishment cost γ or larger fine β make costly punishment more *able* to push the population toward a cooperative equilibrium, but even then a fully efficient outcome is fragile (bistable and vulnerable to second-order free-riders).  
    • Social exclusion (modeled through cost γ̄ and success probability β̄) can, when cheap enough (γ̄ < γ̄₀) and/or sufficiently certain, generate global convergence to full cooperation, hence maximal efficiency.  
    • Larger groups (higher n) help costly punishment (lower β₀) but hurt social exclusion (lower γ̄₀ threshold).  
    • A higher multiplication factor r helps social exclusion (raises γ̄₀) and helps costly punishment by lowering β₀.  
    • No statements in the paper allow any prediction whatsoever about chat, number of rounds, rewards, visibility or framing variables, so from this source alone we must say “no basis for prediction” for parameters 2–3, 5, 9–15.

Article Title: Direct reciprocity with costly punishment: Generous tit-for-tat prevails
Author Keywords: Cooperation; Punishment; Evolution; Nash equilibrium analysis; Finite population size analysis; Computer simulation; Reciprocity

Abstract: The standard model for direct reciprocity is the repeated Prisoner's Dilemma, where in each round players choose between cooperation and defection. Here we extend the standard framework to include costly punishment. Now players have a choice between cooperation, defection and costly punishment. We study the set of all reactive strategies, where the behavior depends on what the other player has done in the previous round. We find all cooperative strategies that are Nash equilibria. If the cost of cooperation is greater than the cost of punishment, then the only cooperative Nash equilibrium is generous-tit-for-tat (GTFT), which does not use costly punishment. If the cost of cooperation is less than the cost of punishment, then there are infinitely many cooperative Nash equilibria and the response to defection can include costly punishment. We also perform computer simulations of evolutionary dynamics in populations of finite size. These simulations show that in the context of direct reciprocity, (i) natural selection prefers generous tit-for-tat over strategies that use costly punishment, and (ii) that costly punishment does not promote the evolution of cooperation.
