Below is a point‐by‐point review of whether (and how) the paper discusses each of the 15 public‐goods‐game parameters, followed by the required four‐part summary.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     Yes, but only in the context of a two‐player repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma (PD) and in an evolutionary simulation with population size N = 50. The text does not systematically vary the number of players, nor does it analyze how changing the number of players affects any “punishment treatment effect.”  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying this parameter on any dependent variable?  
     No. There is no analysis of varying the group size beyond stating that the repeated PD is pairwise, and that simulation populations have size 50.

2. Number of rounds
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     The paper sets the game to continue with probability w each round (a “geometric” or “indefinite” horizon). It sometimes uses w = 1 (effectively infinite repetition) or w < 1, but it does not treat the total number of rounds as a systematically varied parameter in the sense of (e.g.) “10 rounds vs. 20 rounds.”  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying the number of rounds for any dependent variable?  
     No. The paper does not explore “if you have 5 rounds vs. 50 rounds” or the impact of a known final round. Although w < 1 is sometimes used, the effect on punishment is not presented as a manipulation of a “number of rounds” parameter.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     No. There is no mention of communication or chat in the models or experiments.  
   • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
     No mention.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     No. The model is a repeated PD with three discrete actions (cooperate, defect, punish), not a public‐goods game with continuous or all‐or‐nothing contributions.  
   • Predictions?  
     No mention.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     No. There is no notion of a “default” contribution in the repeated PD framework.  
   • Predictions?  
     No mention.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     No. The model focuses on a 3×3 payoff matrix for single rounds of PD with punishment, not on a public‐goods multiplier.  
   • Predictions?  
     No mention.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter (α)?  
     Yes. The paper labels this “α” and examines what happens when α < c versus α > c. They also run evolutionary simulations that sometimes vary α (e.g., α = 0.1 vs. α = 10).  
   • Predictions about systematically varying α on any dependent variable?  
     Yes, they systematically vary α to see how it affects cooperation, usage of punishment, and total payoffs (which the authors often call “average payoff” or “total payoff,” rather than efficiency). They do not provide a numerical “effect size” for how α shifts a “punishment treatment effect,” but they do report that if α > c, punishment does not appear in winning strategies; if α < c, punishment can appear in a formal equilibrium but is still disfavored by evolutionary dynamics. No direct statements about “efficiency = actual payoff / maximum possible” are given.

8. Punishment magnitude (β)
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter (β)?  
     Yes. The paper varies β (the damage inflicted by punishment) and checks how that influences the frequency of punishment and cooperation in simulations.  
   • Predictions about systematically varying β on any dependent variable?  
     Yes, they show that although increasing β strengthens punishment’s sting, punishment strategies are still not evolutionary “winners,” and defection is used more often than punishment in response to defection. Again, no explicit numerical effect on “efficiency” is provided.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     No. There is no discussion of positive rewards or bonus payments.  
   • Predictions?  
     No mention.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
      No.  
    • Predictions?  
      No mention.

11. Reward magnitude
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
      No.  
    • Predictions?  
      No mention.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
      No. The model sets a continuation probability w but does not specifically address whether players know the exact ending condition.  
    • Predictions?  
      No mention.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
      No. It is strictly a two‐player repeated PD or a population simulation where each individual sees only who cooperated, defected, or punished them. There is no analysis of “peer outcomes shown” or hidden.  
    • Predictions?  
      No mention.

14. When a player is punished, does that player know who the specific punisher is?
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
      Not as a systematically varied factor. In a two‐player game, one immediately knows any punishment came from the other, but no separate manipulations or predictions are made.  
    • Predictions?  
      No mention.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
      No. The paper includes no reward mechanism.  
    • Predictions?  
      No mention.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper does not use “efficiency = (actual total payoff) / (maximum payoff under full cooperation).” Instead, it focuses on (i) the probability/frequency of choosing cooperate, defect, or punish, (ii) the expected or average total payoff over repeated interactions, and (iii) evolutionary stability (which strategies spread in finite populations). Thus, their “total payoff” is not reported as a fraction of a maximum possible payoff.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Parameter 1 (number of players) is mentioned only insofar as the basic repeated game is two‐player, and population‐level simulations use N = 50.  
   • Parameter 2 (number of rounds) is mentioned only implicitly as an indefinitely repeated game (with probability w of continuation).  
   • Parameter 7 (punishment cost α) and parameter 8 (punishment magnitude β) are discussed in detail and varied systematically.  
   • None of the other parameters (3–6, 9–15) are discussed in the sense of systematically changing them or analyzing their effect.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Only for parameter 7 (α) and parameter 8 (β) does the paper present systematic variation related to punishment. They show how α < c or α > c, and high or low β, affect usage of punishment and overall payoffs in repeated PD.  
   • There is no explicit numerical “effect size” for any “treatment effect on efficiency”; the discussion is more qualitative (including simulations showing that costly punishment does not raise one’s payoff).

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • Because the paper never measures “efficiency” in the sense of (actual total payoff) / (maximum possible payoff), and because it is a two‐player repeated PD (not a multi‐player public goods game), little can be concluded about how systematically varying these parameters would affect group efficiency. The paper’s core finding, however, is that costly punishment does not help stabilize cooperation or improve total payoffs under direct reciprocity; evolutionary simulations do not favor punishment use, especially when the cost of punishment is high. From these results alone, one would predict little or no improvement in “efficiency” due to punishment across most parameter values.

----------------------------------------------------------------------  
1. Number of players  
   (i) Yes.  Subjects are organised in groups of eight for matching, but the public–goods interaction itself is always a two–person game (each subject is paired with one partner each round).  
   (ii) The number of players is never varied, and no prediction is made about how changing it would alter the punishment treatment effect (for efficiency or for any other outcome).

2. Number of rounds  
   (i) Yes.  Experiment 1 and 2 run 20 rounds; Experiment 3 runs 20 rounds; Experiment 4 runs 11 rounds (10 pre-message + 1 post-message).  
   (ii) The paper never compares punishment effects across different horizons, so no prediction about systematic variation is given.

3. Chat enabled?  
   (i) Stated to be absent (“subjects interacted exclusively through individual computer terminals” and no mention of communication among them).  
   (ii) Not varied and no prediction supplied.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   (i) No.  Subjects may contribute any integer or decimal amount from 0 to 10 EP.  
   (ii) Not varied; no prediction.

5. Contribution default (endowment initially in the public account)?  
   (i) No.  Endowment is initially in the private hand; subjects move what they wish to the joint account.  
   (ii) Not varied; no prediction.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   (i) Yes.  For every 1 EP placed in the joint account the total return is 1.40 EP (0.70 EP to each of the two players).  This parameter is identical in all experiments.  
   (ii) Never varied; no prediction.

7. Punishment cost per unit  
   (i) Only in Experiment 2: it costs the punisher 0.25 EP to reduce the target’s payoff by 1 EP.  (No punishment was possible in Experiments 1, 3, 4.)  
   (ii) The cost is not varied; the authors give no prediction about how changing the cost would modify the punishment treatment effect.

8. Punishment magnitude (damage per unit)  
   (i) As above: 1 EP is removed from the target for each 0.25 EP paid.  
   (ii) Not varied; no prediction.

9. Reward enabled?  
   (i) No reward stage appears in any of the four experiments.  
   (ii) Not varied; no prediction.

10. Reward cost per unit  
11. Reward magnitude  
   (i-ii) Not applicable; the paper has no reward treatment.

12. Is the number of rounds known?  
   (i) Subjects are told all details of the game in advance, including that there will be 20 rounds (or 11 in Exp. 4).  
   (ii) Round knowledge is the same across conditions; no variation or prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   (i) Yes.  After each round subjects see their own and their partner’s contribution and payoff (and, when relevant, punishments delivered).  
   (ii) Not varied; no prediction.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
   (i) In the two-person interaction the target necessarily knows which of the two players punished; thus identity is known, but this is not manipulated.  
   (ii) No prediction about varying anonymity.

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
   (i-ii) Not applicable (no rewards).

----------------------------------------------------------------------  
SUMMARY  

A. Dependent variables  
   – The authors analyse: (a) contribution to the joint account; (b) amount of punishment points assigned.  
   – They occasionally translate higher contributions into higher payoffs (e.g., “associated with respective increases in payoffs of 9 % and 13 %”), but **group efficiency or total/average payoff is never used as an independent dependent variable in the statistical tests**.  Contribution and efficiency differ because efficiency depends on both contributions and the social return (1.4) whereas contribution is simply the amount given.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   Nine are explicitly specified (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14) although only 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14 have numerical values; parameters 3, 4, 5 are simply noted as absent/false.  Parameters 9, 10, 11, 15 are completely absent.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of **systematically varying** them on the punishment treatment effect (for any outcome)?  
   Zero.  None of the 15 parameters is systematically varied in the sense required.  The only design change that matters for punishment is the binary presence vs. absence of a punishment stage, but the underlying cost/magnitude parameters (7 and 8) are held fixed.

D. Predictions one can make, limited strictly to the paper  
   – With the particular punishment technology used (cost = 0.25, magnitude = 1), **allowing punishment raises contributions compared with no-punishment baselines**; the size of this effect on contributions before any moral message is positive but numerically small and declines over rounds (no efficiency numbers are provided).  
   – When a moral message is present, **punishment and moral suasion interact positively**: contributions stay high throughout the post-message phase, whereas either punishment alone (pre-message) or moral suasion alone (Exp. 1) fails to maintain them.  Hence the prediction is that “presence of punishment” (a compound of parameters 7–8 plus the mere availability of the stage) *increases* the treatment effect of punishment on efficiency when a strong moral appeal is simultaneously delivered.  
   – Beyond that, the paper furnishes **no quantitative or qualitative guidance** on how changing any of the 15 listed parameters (group size, MPCR, cost-to-punish, anonymity, rewards, chat, etc.) would alter the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Therefore, if one had to forecast the joint influence of the 15 parameters on efficiency solely from this article, the only firm statement would be: “Under the specific two-person, MPCR = 0.7 game studied, enabling low-cost punishment (0.25 → 1) together with a compelling moral message yields a larger and more persistent positive effect on efficiency-related outcomes than enabling punishment without such a message or providing the message without punishment.” No further parameter-level predictions can be justified from the paper.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter review of whether (1) the paper even discusses the parameter (and, if so, what value or setting it uses) and (2) whether the paper makes any prediction about systematically varying that parameter on the “punishment treatment effect”—in this case, the effect of punishment on any outcome measured in the paper. Throughout, recall that the paper examines punishment primarily in ultimatum games (both second- and third-party settings) and does not address “efficiency” (i.e., total payoff divided by the payoff of a fully cooperative group) as an outcome measure.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
• Mention in the paper: The paper reports experiments with (a) two players in a standard ultimatum game (proposer and responder) and (b) three participants in a “third-party punishment” setting (proposer, receiver, and observing punisher). However, the paper never systematically varies the number of players (e.g., comparing 2 vs. 4 vs. 8 players) nor predicts how changing that number would alter any punishment-related effects.  
• Prediction from systematic variation: Not discussed in the paper. No effect sizes given.

2) Number of rounds  
• Mention in the paper: The ultimatum and third-party punishment games cited are one-shot (single-round) interactions. The paper does not vary or compare multiple vs. single rounds, nor does it make statements about how repeated rounds would change punishment.  
• Prediction from systematic variation: Not discussed.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
• Mention in the paper: No. Players do not engage in any form of communication (chat) in the described experiments, and the paper does not discuss adding or removing communication.  
• Prediction from systematic variation: Not discussed.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Mention in the paper: No. In the ultimatum game design, proposers can offer varying proportions (e.g., 20%, 30%, 50%). This is not framed as an “all or nothing” decision, and the paper does not study an all-or-nothing variant.  
• Prediction from systematic variation: Not discussed.

5) Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much of their endowment to take back)?  
• Mention in the paper: No. The paper studies standard ultimatum and third-party games and does not incorporate a mechanism for “default contributions” from a public fund.  
• Prediction from systematic variation: Not discussed.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
• Mention in the paper: No. The tasks are ultimatum and third-party punishment games, not a public goods paradigm, so there is no mention of MPCR or a group multiplier.  
• Prediction from systematic variation: Not discussed.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Mention in the paper: Yes, but only in a fixed way for the third-party punishment game: participants can pay up to 0.50 (in British currency) to reduce the proposer’s payoff at a 1:3 ratio. However, the paper does not systematically manipulate the cost level (it is simply set at 1-to-3).  
• Prediction from systematic variation: Not discussed or estimated. No effect size given for changing that ratio.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed on them)  
• Mention in the paper: Yes, again only in the third-party punishment game. Every 0.50 a participant spends reduces the proposer’s payoff by 1.50 (a 1:3 ratio). As with the cost, this magnitude is not systematically varied.  
• Prediction from systematic variation: Not discussed or estimated. No effect size given.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
• Mention in the paper: No. The paper deals only with punishment (rejections in ultimatum games and payoff deductions in third-party settings). It does not include or discuss a reward mechanism.  
• Prediction from systematic variation: Not discussed.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Mention in the paper: No. There is no reward mechanism.  
• Prediction from systematic variation: Not discussed.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted to them)  
• Mention in the paper: No. Same as above.  
• Prediction from systematic variation: Not discussed.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
• Mention in the paper: The experimental design entails one-shot games, so there is effectively only one round. The paper does not discuss participants’ knowledge of multiple rounds or the impact of knowing (or not knowing) when a game ends.  
• Prediction from systematic variation: Not discussed.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?  
• Mention in the paper: Participants in both ultimatum and third-party designs see the proposed splits or offers. However, because these are one-shot interactions, the paper does not examine a repeated or dynamic display of peers’ outcomes across multiple rounds.  
• Prediction from systematic variation: Not discussed.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• Mention in the paper: In the ultimatum game, the proposer presumably knows the responder rejected the offer, but the paper never discusses whether or how knowledge of the “identity of the punisher” might change behavior (nor systematically varies that knowledge).  
• Prediction from systematic variation: Not discussed.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
• Mention in the paper: There is no reward condition, so this issue does not arise.  
• Prediction from systematic variation: Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use “group efficiency” (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?  
• The paper does not report group efficiency or total payoffs as a dependent measure.  
• The main dependent variables in the paper include:  
  – Whether participants reject or accept an ultimatum offer (second-party punishment).  
  – How much participants spend on third-party punishment.  
  – Reaction times for accepting or rejecting.  
  – Self-reported fairness ratings (post-task).  
  – Neural (fMRI) responses in specific brain regions.  

These variables differ from “efficiency” because they measure behavior (e.g., rejection rates), punishment spent, or brain activity, rather than the total or average earnings that could be compared against a fully cooperative benchmark.

B. Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• The paper explicitly identifies that there are two players in the standard ultimatum game and three in a third-party setup but does not systematically vary “number of players.”  
• It fixes “number of rounds” at one (but does not vary it).  
• It fixes the cost and magnitude of punishment (parameters 7 and 8) at a ratio of 1:3 in the third-party scenario, but again, does not vary them experimentally.  
• None of the other parameters (chat, rewards, MPCR, etc.) are mentioned at all.  

C. For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
• None. The study does not report any systematic variation of those 15 parameters (nor how changing them might affect punishment or efficiency).  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
• The paper provides no direct discussion or data on how any of those parameters (number of players, number of rounds, cost or magnitude of punishment, etc.) would affect the “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”  
• Consequently, no quantitative or qualitative predictions can be made about these parameters’ influences on efficiency as understood in a public goods or fully cooperative environment. The study focuses on second- vs. third-party punishment and serotonergic modulation of retaliatory vs. fairness-based motives, without exploring group-level efficiency outcomes.  

In short, the paper does not address how systematically varying any of the 15 parameters would affect efficiency under a punishment regime; it focuses on neural and behavioral measures (mostly acceptance/rejection decisions and neural responses) in one-shot ultimatum and third-party punishment settings.

Abstract: Self-interest frequently causes individuals engaged in joint enterprises to choose actions that are counterproductive. Free-riders can invade a society of cooperators, causing a tragedy of the commons. Such social dilemmas can be overcome by positive or negative incentives. Even though an incentive-providing institution may protect a cooperative society from invasion by free-riders, it cannot always convert a society of free-riders to cooperation. In the latter case, both norms, cooperation and defection, are stable: To avoid a collapse to full defection, cooperators must be sufficiently numerous initially. A society of free-riders is then caught in a social trap, and the institution is unable to provide an escape, except at a high, possibly prohibitive cost. Here, we analyze the interplay of (a) incentives provided by institutions and (b) the effects of voluntary participation. We show that this combination fundamentally improves the efficiency of incentives. In particular, optional participation allows institutions punishing free-riders to overcome the social dilemma at a much lower cost, and to promote a globally stable regime of cooperation. This removes the social trap and implies that whenever a society of cooperators cannot be invaded by free-riders, it will necessarily become established in the long run, through social learning, irrespective of the initial number of cooperators.    • Systematically varied with respect to punishment’s effect on efficiency? No. Although r appears in the formula for payoffs, there is no table or figure that varies r to examine efficiency under punishment.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned? No. The model frames punishment as an “institutional” mechanism, with costs subsumed into a general per capita incentive I. There is no separate parameter denoting “what it costs an individual punisher” (because players do not punish each other directly).  
   • Systematically varied? No.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted for each punishment unit)
   • Mentioned? Somewhat. The paper combines everything into a single per capita incentive I, which for punishment subtracts mI/mᴰ from defectors. However, it never calls this “punishment magnitude per unit.”  
   • Systematically varied with respect to punishment’s effect? Yes, but only in terms of “varying I from 0 up to c, etc.” The paper shows (Figs. 1, 2, 3) how increasing I changes which equilibrium is stable. The authors do not, however, present a numeric “treatment‐effect size on efficiency”; they show only how higher I can lead to full cooperation. No table or figure provides an explicit effect size for efficiency.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned? Yes, in direct contrast to punishment. The paper compares “rewarding” versus “punishing” across a range of I values.  
   • Systematically varied with respect to punishment’s effect on efficiency? The paper does systematically analyze “no reward” (punishment only) versus “reward” (punishment replaced by a reward institution). It compares outcomes (cooperator frequency, group welfare). However, no numerical “efficiency” effect size is given. Instead, the authors conclude that, in the presence of optional participation, punishing can achieve full cooperation at lower cost than rewarding.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Mentioned? Not as a distinct parameter. The authors again package everything into the total incentive I allocated to cooperators.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per reward unit)
   • Mentioned? Only as mI/mᴰ (punishing) versus mI/mᴯ (rewarding), but the paper refers to them collectively as “per capita incentive I.”  
   • Systematically varied with respect to efficiency? The paper does vary I, but not specifically the per‐reward magnitude. Numerical effect sizes for efficiency are not provided.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much peers gained/lost)?
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?  
   • The paper’s main outcome measures are (i) the frequency of cooperative versus noncooperative strategies and (ii) the “group welfare” or “long‐term average payoff” (sometimes called “payoff” or “average payoff” in the figures). These measures are not explicitly labeled “(actual total payoff) / (maximum possible payoff).” Hence the paper does not use “efficiency” in the strict sense of “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff,” even though it often refers to overall payoffs and “cost” or “benefit” outcomes.  
   • The authors also discuss whether the population converges to a state of full cooperation, partial cooperation, or defection. In short, “cooperator frequency” and “average payoff” are the main dependent variables, with “group welfare” used synonymously with average payoff. All differ from a formal “efficiency” ratio.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Four parameters are explicitly or implicitly mentioned:  
       (1) Number of players (n)  
       (4) All‐or‐nothing contribution (they model a binary choice)  
       (6) The multiplier r (similar to an MPCR concept)  
       (9) Whether a reward is enabled (versus punishment)  
   • The others (2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15) are either not discussed or only mentioned in passing without being clearly set as separate parameters.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable) when systematically varied?  
   • Strict systematic variation is applied only to the size of the institutional incentive, I (which one might loosely identify with punishment magnitude or reward magnitude). The paper then examines if outcomes converge to all‐cooperator, mixed, or all‐defector states. While this certainly bears on how punishment affects cooperation or payoffs, the authors do not present a numeric effect size for an “efficiency” measure. Rather, they show thresholds (I₋ = c/n, I₊ = c) for transitions in the dynamics.  
   • Formally among the listed 15 parameters, the closest match to “systematically varied” is parameter (8) or (11) if one equates them to “I,” but the paper itself does not label them as “punishment magnitude” or “reward magnitude per unit.” They simply examine I from 0 to c to see how the system’s equilibria shift.  
   • No other parameter in the 15‐item list is systematically varied to examine the punishment effect.

D. If you were to make predictions about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, solely based on the paper:  
   • The paper provides no explicit discussion of most parameters; hence almost no predictions can be made about how changing, for example, the number of rounds, default contributions, or information disclosure would affect punishment on efficiency.  
   • The one clear statement is that, if the group size n grows, the minimum per capita punishment incentive needed (I₋) to deter defection scales as c/n, so larger n lowers the required threshold. However, no direct efficiency ratio is provided.  
   • The paper strongly suggests that “punishing plus optional participation” can yield a fully cooperative outcome at lower cost (i.e., lower I) than rewarding. This implies that under standard scenarios, adding punishment can increase average payoffs, but the authors do not quantify that gain as a formal “efficiency” ratio.  
   • Beyond noting that punishing can establish full cooperation for smaller I than rewarding, and that the “cost” is c/n, almost no other parameter manipulations in the paper allow firm numerical predictions about efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Abstract: Although group membership has many privileges, members are expected to reciprocate those privileges. We tested whether in-group members would be punished more harshly than out-group members for marginal fairness norm violations within ultimatum game bargaining interactions. Participants considered monetary splits (of US$20) from in-group and out-group proposers, which ranged in proportion. Accepting an offer yielded the proposed payout; rejecting it caused each player to earn nothing-a punishment of the proposer at a personal cost. Below, each of the fifteen public-goods‐game parameters is checked, one at a time, against every piece of information contained in the article “For Members Only: In-group Punishment of Fairness Norm Violations in the Ultimatum Game.”  I report (1) whether the parameter is mentioned at all, (2) the exact value(s) used in the study (if any), and (3) whether the paper makes any statement—descriptive or predictive—about what would happen if the parameter were systematically varied, specifically with respect to the “punishment treatment effect.”  Whenever a numerical effect can be read directly from a figure, table, odds ratio, or text, I reproduce it.  If no information is available, I say so explicitly.

------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER AUDIT
------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Every interaction in the ultimatum game involves exactly two players (one proposer, one responder).  
   • Value used?  2 players per bargaining dyad.  
   • Systematic-variation discussion?  None.  The paper never varies, compares, or predicts anything about having more or fewer than two players, nor about its effect on punishment.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Each participant (always the responder) faced 10 “critical” offers (plus 6 fillers) in Study 1, and the same structure in Study 2.  
   • Value used?  10 critical rounds (offers) per participant.  
   • Systematic-variation discussion?  No.  The number of rounds is fixed and never analyzed as an independent variable.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned?  No.  There is no chat or any other form of communication beyond the offer itself.  
   • Systematic-variation discussion?  None.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule?  
   • Not applicable to an ultimatum game; never mentioned.

5. Contribution default / endowment move-back rule?  
   • Not applicable; never mentioned.

6. Marginal Per-Capita Return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Not applicable; never mentioned.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned implicitly.  Rejecting any offer costs the responder the amount she would have earned had she accepted.  
   • Values: If the offer is x, the cost of rejection to the responder is US\$x.  (E.g., rejecting an \$8 offer costs the responder \$8.)  
   • Systematic-variation discussion?  No.  The cost is a direct by-product of the offer size but is never manipulated independently.  The authors do not discuss what would happen if the cost were altered.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss inflicted on the target per unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned implicitly.  Rejection removes everything the proposer would have received (US\$20 – x).  
   • Values: If the offer is x, the proposer loses US\$20 – x.  
   • Systematic-variation discussion?  No separate manipulation or prediction.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Not mentioned; no reward option exists.

10. Reward cost  
    • Not applicable.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Not applicable.

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
    • Mentioned.  Participants are told they will interact “only once with each player,” and the total number of offers is shown trial-by-trial.  
    • Systematic-variation discussion?  None.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Not mentioned; responders see only the offer made to them, not what happens to others.  No systematic variation.

14. Is the identity of a punisher revealed to the punished player?  
    • Not explicitly addressed.  Avatars are shown during the offer, but the paper never specifies what the proposer sees after rejection nor manipulates this information.  No systematic variation.

15. Is the identity of a rewarder revealed to the rewarded player?  
    • Not applicable; no rewards.

------------------------------------------------------------------
NUMERICAL EFFECT SIZES REPORTED IN THE PAPER
------------------------------------------------------------------
The independent variables actually manipulated in the paper are (a) offer size and (b) proposer group membership (in-group vs. out-group).  Key logistic-regression odds ratios (ORs) reported for acceptance rates include:  

• Study 1, Race × \$8-offer interaction: OR = 0.17, Wald = 3.94, p = .047.  
• Simple slope for \$8 offer from White vs. \$10 offer: OR = 0.05, p = .007.  
• Simple slope for \$8 offer from Black vs. \$10 offer: OR = 0.29, p = .171.  
• Study 2, College-Group × \$8-offer interaction: OR = 0.18, Wald = 4.33, p = .037.  
• Simple slope for \$8 in-group vs. \$8 out-group: OR = 0.54, p = .015.

None of these results correspond to any of the fifteen public-goods parameters, so they cannot be used to parameterize a prediction model that focuses on public-goods punishment efficiency.

------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Does the paper analyze “group efficiency” (total or average payoff)?  
    • No.  The main dependent variable is binary offer acceptance vs. rejection.  Study 3 also collects perceived fairness, anger, proposer likability, competence, and exclusion intentions.  None of these is equivalent to group efficiency.

B.  Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are at least mentioned?  
    • Five:  #1 (number of players), #2 (number of rounds), #7 (punishment cost—implicitly), #8 (punishment magnitude—implicitly), and #12 (rounds known).  All other parameters (#3–6, 9–11, 13–15) are not mentioned at all.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of systematic variation on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable)?  
    • Zero.  No parameter from the list is experimentally varied or modeled, so no predictions or effect sizes about systematic variation are supplied.

D.  Predictions one could make—solely from this paper—about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency:  
    • The paper provides almost no leverage for such predictions.  Because every interaction is dyadic, single-shot (with respect to a given partner), anonymous, non-communicative, and always allows free rejection, there is no empirical basis here to estimate how changes in group size, repetition, communication, cost/magnitude of punishment, reward options, or information structure would modulate efficiency differences between a no-punishment and a punishment treatment.  The only inferable qualitative hint is that costly punishment does occur when the cost equals the whole foregone payoff (parameter #7) and the magnitude equals the entire proposer gain (parameter #8), but even that is shown only for hypothetical money and without any counterfactual “no-punishment” baseline.  Therefore, any efficiency-based forecasting for public-goods settings would, from this paper alone, be highly speculative and essentially unsupported.

Article Title: The coevolution of altruism and punishment: Role of the selfish punisher
Author Keywords: altruism; punishment; selfish punisher; lattice; score-dependent viability; score-dependent fertility

Abstract: Punishment is an important mechanism promoting the evolution of altruism among non-relatives. We investigate the coevolution of altruism and punitive behavior, considering four possible strategies: the altruist punisher (AP, a cooperator who punishes defectors), the altruist non-punisher (AN, a pure cooperator), the selfish punisher (SP, a defector who punishes defectors), and the selfish non-punisher (SN, a pure defector). In the viability model of a completely mixed population, SP first drives out SN, and hence it helps cooperators (AP and AN) to evolve. In contrast, in the fertility model of a completely mixed population, neither SP nor AN helps the evolution of cooperation. In both the viability and fertility models of a lattice-structured population, SP promotes the spread of AP. In contrast, AN discourages the evolution of AP. These results can be understood that punishment is a form of spite behavior, paying a cost to reduce the fitness of the opponents, and that different models give different magnitude of advantage to spite behavior. Abstract: Third-party intervention, such as when a crowd stops a mugger, is common. Yet it seems irrational because it has real costs but may provide no personal benefits. Below is a parameter-by-parameter assessment of whether and how the paper (Helbing et al., “Defector-accelerated cooperativeness and punishment in public goods games with mutations”) discusses or systematically varies each of the 15 listed parameters, and whether the paper makes predictions about how varying each parameter would affect the “punishment treatment effect” (i.e., how punishment changes outcomes compared to when punishment is not present). In the final summary (A–D), you will find a concise statement of (A) the paper’s dependent variables, (B) which parameters are mentioned, (C) for which parameters their effect on punishment is discussed under systematic variation, and (D) what the paper allows us to predict—if anything—about those parameters’ influence on efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER ASSESSMENT
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1) Number of players  
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – The model is played on an L×L square lattice (with L up to 1600), but the paper does not treat the number of players (or the lattice size) as a systematically varied parameter for the sake of comparing outcomes. The authors only mention using larger system sizes near phase boundaries to avoid random extinction of small clusters.  
   • Effect of varying it on punishment treatment or on any dependent variable?  
     – Not discussed. The paper does not provide predictions or effect sizes for how changing the total number of players would alter the impact of punishment.

2) Number of rounds  
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – The paper uses Monte Carlo simulation steps (MCS) to update strategies iteratively but does not describe a finite or known “number of rounds” (as might be used in an experimental setup).  
   • Effect of varying it on punishment treatment or on any dependent variable?  
     – Not discussed. There is no indication that the authors tested how systematically changing the number of rounds (or stopping times) affects punishment.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – Not addressed. The model is purely evolutionary; there is no mention of communication or “chat.”  
   • Effect of varying it?  
     – Not discussed.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – By design, cooperators contribute 1; defectors contribute 0. This is inherently an “all or nothing” contribution in the model.  
   • Systematic variation of this parameter?  
     – Not discussed. The paper does not explore partial contributions or changes to the “all or nothing” assumption.

5) Is the contribution default (players decide how much of their endowment to allocate)?  
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – Not addressed. The paper strictly deals with a fixed contribution (1 for cooperators, 0 for defectors).  
   • Effect of varying it?  
     – Not discussed.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor  
   • In this paper:  
     – The authors use a “synergy factor” r for the public good. They do mention critical values of r (e.g., r = 3.5, r ≈ 3.74, r > 5.45) at which the survival or extinction of particular strategies changes.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – The paper presents results for r = 3.5 (Figures 1 and 2) and references other values (3.74, 5.45) to explain when cooperators alone can or cannot survive among defectors. However, the reported dependent variable is the fraction of each strategy at equilibrium, not efficiency.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
     – The paper does not use “group efficiency” as an outcome measure when discussing changes in r. Instead, it highlights phase transitions (e.g., from pure defectors to punishing cooperators) for different r. No numerical effect size is reported regarding efficiency.  
     – Hence, the paper does not directly predict how varying r affects the “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment (c)  
   • In this paper:  
     – The cost of punishment is denoted c. It is systematically varied, and Figure 1 shows a phase diagram for c vs. f (the punishment fine). The authors discuss how c affects which strategies dominate (e.g., D vs. PC vs. PD).  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
     – The main result is how c helps determine whether punishing cooperators overcome defectors. However, the paper frames the outcome in terms of final strategy fractions, not efficiency.  
     – There are no numerical effect sizes tying c specifically to “efficiency,” only to which strategy eventually persists.

8) Punishment magnitude (f)  
   • In this paper:  
     – The punishment fine f is also systematically varied (together with c in a phase diagram).  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
     – The authors describe how increases in f can help punishing cooperators dominate defectors under spatial conditions, again focusing on strategy fractions.  
     – As with c, there is no explicit measurement of changes in group efficiency. The paper does not give an effect size for efficiency outcomes.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – Not mentioned. The model includes only punishment (fines) and does not incorporate rewards.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment?  
     – Not discussed.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Discussion in the paper?  
      – There is no reward mechanism in the model.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment?  
      – Not discussed.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded)  
    • Discussion in the paper?  
      – Also not included in the model.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment?  
      – Not discussed.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    • Discussion in the paper?  
      – Not addressed. The model is an indefinitely iterated evolutionary process without references to players’ knowledge of an end point.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment?  
      – Not discussed.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much peers gained/lost each round)?  
    • Discussion in the paper?  
      – The model uses local imitation based on payoff differences, but the paper does not examine or vary what players explicitly “see.”  
    • Effect on punishment treatment?  
      – Not discussed.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Discussion in the paper?  
      – Not mentioned. The paper’s update mechanism merely uses payoffs; there is no explicit information about who punished whom.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment?  
      – Not discussed.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Discussion in the paper?  
      – Rewarding is absent from the model.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment?  
      – Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FINAL SUMMARY (A–D)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different from one another?  
   – The paper does not use group efficiency or total/average payoff as its primary reported outcome. Payoffs appear only in the update rule (to determine strategy adoption), but the main dependent variables are the final fractions of each strategy (C, D, PC, PD) after convergence. This differs from “efficiency,” which would measure actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff. The paper does not explicitly analyze or report that ratio.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – The authors explicitly mention and incorporate three of the 15:  
     (i) Parameter 6 (Synergy factor r) – They discuss how different values of r affect which strategies survive.  
     (ii) Parameter 7 (Punishment cost c) – The paper systematically varies c in Figure 1 and in discussions.  
     (iii) Parameter 8 (Punishment fine f) – Also systematically varied in the same phase diagram.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   – Strictly speaking, the paper never quantifies a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Instead, it reports how varying r, c, and f changes the equilibrium fraction of punishing cooperators, defectors, etc. Thus, three parameters (6, 7, and 8) are systematically varied and linked to outcomes (fractions of strategies), but not to measured efficiency changes.  
   – No numerical effect sizes are given for efficiency (since efficiency is not the reported measure).

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   – Because the paper does not measure or discuss efficiency directly, it provides little basis for quantitative predictions about efficiency. One might infer that, whenever punishing cooperators become dominant (for suitable values of r, c, f), overall performance against defectors would improve, which usually implies higher total payoffs. However, the paper itself does not analyze or confirm this in terms of an efficiency metric. Thus, no firm predictions about any of the 15 parameters’ effects on efficiency can be drawn from the paper’s text and figures.

1. Number of players
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – The paper notes there were 10 pairs (20 total participants) in each session. However, this is simply a description of the experiment; the number of players was not systematically varied.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying this parameter for any dependent variable?  
     – No, there is no discussion or prediction about changing the group size and how that affects punishment (or any other outcome).  

2. Number of rounds
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Each participant made decisions in a one-shot Ultimatum Game and a one-shot Trust Game. The paper does not mention multi-round or repeated interaction.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying this parameter for any dependent variable?  
     – No, there is no mention of changing the number of rounds or its effect on punishment or efficiency.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No, the paper does not describe any communication or chat; the games were played anonymously using the strategy method.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about varying chat for any dependent variable?  
     – No, it does not address or vary this parameter.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No, the Ultimatum Game and the Trust Game involved incremental (in NIS 5 or NIS 10) divisions or transfers, not an all-or-nothing design.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about varying this parameter for any dependent variable?  
     – No, it does not.  

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much of their endowment to move back into their hand)?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No, there is no mention of a default contribution mechanism.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about varying this parameter?  
     – No, it does not.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – The paper states that in the Trust Game, the amount sent by Player A is tripled in transit and then Player B decides how much to return. However, this tripling factor is fixed, not varied.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying this factor and its effect on punishment or efficiency?  
     – No, there is no systematic variation or direct prediction.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – In the Ultimatum Game, rejection by Player B is costly because Player B loses her share. Thus, there is an inherent cost to punishing an unfair offer. However, the paper does not parameterize that cost as a standalone variable, nor is it varied.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about varying this parameter?  
     – No, it does not.  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – In the Ultimatum Game, if B rejects the offer, A loses the entire proposed division, and B also receives nothing. This magnitude is not described as a variable that the authors systematically manipulated; it is simply the standard Ultimatum Game rule.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about varying this parameter?  
     – No, it does not.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. In the Trust Game, Player B can reward Player A’s cooperation by returning more of the tripled transfer. However, they do not compare conditions with reward enabled versus disabled; the design always includes this possibility.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about varying the presence/absence of rewards?  
     – No, there is no condition in which reward is “off,” so no systematic variation or predictive discussion.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – In the Trust Game, any amount returned to A is costly to B (it reduces B’s payoff). The authors do not parameterize “per-unit” reward cost, and do not manipulate it.  
    • Does the paper make predictions about varying this parameter?  
      – No, it does not.  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – The “magnitude” of reward is simply the amount B returns. However, there is no separate multiplier or parameter that the authors vary; B’s reward is chosen from a continuous set of return amounts.  
    • Does the paper make predictions about varying this parameter?  
      – No, it does not.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – The paper does not mention round knowledge. The design is essentially single-shot for each game.  
    • Does the paper make predictions about varying this parameter?  
      – No, it does not.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost each round)?
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – There is no mention of revealing others’ outcomes beyond each participant’s own pairing. The focus is on Player B’s rejection or return decisions in each game.  
    • Does the paper make predictions about varying this parameter?  
      – No, it does not.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – No, the paper states that interactions were anonymous; it does not specify whether punishees learn the identity of punishers.  
    • Does the paper make predictions about varying this parameter?  
      – No, it does not.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – Similarly, anonymity prevented players from knowing one another’s identity; the paper does not state any further detail.  
    • Does the paper make predictions about varying this parameter?  
      – No, it does not.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?

• The paper does not explicitly measure or report “group efficiency” (i.e., actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff).  
• Instead, the dependent variables focus on individual second-mover behaviors in two games:  
  – In the Ultimatum Game, the dependent variable is whether Player B rejects or accepts a proposed division.  
  – In the Trust Game, the dependent variable is how much Player B returns to Player A (as a fraction of the amount originally sent).  
• These behaviors capture whether individuals are willing to pay costs to punish or reward, but they are not reported as measures of group-wide efficiency.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

• Strictly speaking, the paper only references or implies a fixed multiplier in the Trust Game (parameter 6) and the fact that reward and punishment are possible (parameters 9 and, implicitly, 7–8 and 10–11). However, none of these are systematically varied or discussed as parameters whose values change.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?

• No numerical effect size on the punishment (or reward) treatment effect is provided for changes in any of these parameters.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

• Because the paper does not manipulate or analyze these parameters, it provides little or no direct basis to predict how systematically varying them would affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.  
• The paper focuses on war versus peacetime, not on changing game structures, monetary stakes beyond a single tripling factor, peer incentive details, or information display. Accordingly, no conclusions can be drawn about these 15 parameters’ effects on efficiency.

Abstract: Punishment can stabilize costly cooperation and ensure the success of a common project that is threatened by free-riders. Punishment mechanisms can be classified into pool punishment, where the punishment act is carried out by a paid third party, (e. g. a police system or a sheriff), and peer punishment, where the punishment act is carried out by peers. Our experimental results show how organized punishment could have displaced individual punishment in human societies.

Abstract: Experiments have become a popular method to study altruism and cooperation in laboratory and, more recently, in field settings.    • Stated? Yes – continuous choice 0-100 points (p. 8).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

5. Contribution default / “take” version?  
   • Mentioned? No. Participants always decided how much of their 100-point endowment to contribute.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   • Stated? Yes – multiplication factor 1.5, so MPCR = 0.3 (p. 8).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

7. Punishment cost (per unit applied)  
   • Stated? Yes – cost = 1 point to punisher (p. 9 “for each point invested…”).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

8. Punishment magnitude (loss to target per unit)  
   • Stated? Yes – target loses 3 points per point invested (p. 9).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Mentioned? Yes – implicitly “no”; no reward option described in either scenario.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

10. Reward cost  
    • Not applicable / never mentioned.  

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Not applicable / never mentioned.  

12. Finite horizon known?  
    • Stated? Implied yes – subjects are told they play “the game” once (in each scenario).  
    • Systematically varied? No.  

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
    • Stated? Yes, but differently across the two scenarios.  
      – No-punishment condition: only total group contribution is revealed.  
      – Punishment condition: every individual’s contribution becomes visible.  
    • Systematically varied independently of punishment? No; it is bundled with the punishment manipulation, so the paper gives no separate prediction about varying this feature by itself.  

14. Punisher’s identity revealed?  
    • Not mentioned; cannot be inferred.  

15. Rewarder’s identity revealed?  
    • Not applicable (no rewards in the design).  

-------------------------------------------------
Numerical data on the punishment treatment effect actually reported

• Experiment 1: Mean contribution rises from 53.1 (SD = 28.5) to 63.9 (SD = 22.9); difference = 10.8 points, t(68)=-4.8, Cohen’s d ≈ 0.55.  
• Experiment 2: Mean contribution rises from 53.1 (SD = 28.7) to 66.2 (SD = 25.5); difference = 13.1 points, t(354)=-11.4, Cohen’s d ≈ 0.56.  
(The paper never translates this difference into group efficiency, and no efficiency numbers for the punishment condition are provided.)

-------------------------------------------------
Summary

A. Dependent variables  
   • The core dependent variable is INDIVIDUAL CONTRIBUTION.  
   • They also analyse the WITHIN-PERSON DIFFERENCE in contribution (punishment – no-punishment).  
   • A post-hoc simulation uses GROUP GAIN (total payoff minus initial endowments) but only for the no-punishment case.  
   • Group efficiency (actual payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff) is never computed; thus efficiency is not an analysed dependent variable in this paper.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   • Mentioned explicitly or implicitly: 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9 (absence of reward), 12, 13.  
   • Total mentioned: 9 of 15.  

C. For how many parameters does the paper examine how systematic variation affects the punishment treatment effect?  
   • Zero. None of the parameters are experimentally manipulated over multiple levels. The only manipulation is the presence vs. absence of punishment itself, which is not one of the listed 15 parameters. Consequently, the article offers no effect-size estimates for changing any of the 15 parameters.

D. Predictive leverage for efficiency based solely on this paper  
   • The paper supplies no direct evidence about efficiency changes when any of the 15 parameters vary, because none of them were varied.  
   • The only quantitative information that might inform efficiency is:  
       – MPCR = 0.3, group size = 5, mean contribution increase ≈ 10–13 points (out of 100) when punishment (with cost = 1, magnitude = 3) is introduced.  
       – If we mechanically transform the reported contribution increase into total payoffs under the experiment’s fixed parameters, we could approximate a modest positive efficiency effect of punishment, but the authors themselves never do this.  
   • Therefore, on the basis of the paper alone, we can make little to no prediction about how systematically changing any of the 15 design parameters (or their interactions) would amplify or dampen the punishment effect on efficiency. The study was designed to test a personality × punishment interaction, not to map the design space of public-goods institutions.

Authors: Wu, JH; Balliet, D; Van Lange, PAM
Author Full Names: Wu, Junhui; Balliet, Daniel; Van Lange, Paul A. M.
Article Title: Gossip Versus Punishment: The Efficiency of Reputation to Promote and Maintain Cooperation
Keywords Plus: SOCIAL DILEMMAS; INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; COSTLY PUNISHMENT; COMMUNICATION; SANCTIONS; TRUST
Abstract: Prior theory suggests that reputation spreading (e.g., gossip) and punishment are two key mechanisms to promote cooperation in groups, but no behavioral research has yet examined their relative effectiveness and efficiency in promoting and maintaining cooperation. To examine these issues, we observed participants interacting in a four-round public goods game (PGG) with or without gossip and punishment options, and a subsequent two-round trust game (TG). We manipulated gossip as the option to send notes about other group members to these members' future partners, and punishment as the option to assign deduction points to reduce other group members' outcomes with a fee-to-fine ratio of 1:3. Findings revealed that in the four-round PGG, the option to gossip increased both cooperation and individual earnings, whereas the option to punish had no overall effect on cooperation (but a positive effect on cooperation in the last two rounds of the PGG) and significantly decreased individual earnings. Importantly, the initial option to gossip made people more trusting and trustworthy in the subsequent TG when gossip was no longer possible, compared to the no-gossip condition. Thus, we provide some initial evidence that gossip may be more effective and efficient than punishment to promote and maintain cooperation.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter review of what this specific paper says (and does not say) with respect to (1) whether the paper explicitly discusses the parameter (and what value it takes if so) and (2) whether the paper makes any prediction about systematically varying that parameter and its effect on the punishment treatment effect (for efficiency or any other outcome). All statements are drawn directly from the paper as provided.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. NUMBER OF PLAYERS  
   • Discussed?  
     – The paper fixes group size at 4 players in the public goods game (PGG).  
     – There is no systematic variation of the number of players.  
   • Predictions about varying it?  
     – None. The paper does not discuss how changing group size would affect punishment’s impact on efficiency or any other outcome.

2. NUMBER OF ROUNDS  
   • Discussed?  
     – The paper implements 4 rounds of the PGG (followed by 2 rounds of a trust game).  
     – It notes that the effect of punishment on cooperation was only evident in the last two PGG rounds, but there is no systematic variation of the total number of rounds.  
   • Predictions about varying it?  
     – None. The authors do not speculate about how changing the number of rounds would influence punishment’s impact on efficiency.

3. IS CHAT ENABLED BETWEEN PLAYERS?  
   • Discussed?  
     – There is no condition in which players merely “chat.” Instead, there is a “gossip stage” in which participants can send a note about a group member to that member’s future partners. This is not direct groupwide chat or mutual messaging.  
     – The presence or absence of this gossip option is manipulated (no‐gossip vs. gossip).  
   • Predictions about varying it?  
     – The paper does not discuss systematically varying any generic “chat” feature. It only examines the presence versus absence of the gossip option.

4. IS THE CONTRIBUTION “ALL OR NOTHING”?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. In the PGG, participants can contribute any integer amount from 0 to 10.  
   • Predictions about varying it?  
     – None. The paper does not mention all‐or‐nothing rules, nor does it discuss how that format would affect punishment’s impact on efficiency.

5. IS THE CONTRIBUTION DEFAULT (DO PARTICIPANTS DECIDE HOW MUCH OF THEIR ENDOWMENT TO MOVE BACK INTO THEIR HAND)?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The paper uses a standard PGG procedure (contribute 0–10 points). There is no mention of a default contribution rule or reversing contributions.  
   • Predictions about varying it?  
     – None.

6. MARGINAL PER CAPITA RETURN (MPCR) OR RELATED MULTIPLICATION FACTOR  
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes. All contributions to the group account are doubled (multiplied by 2) and divided equally among group members.  
     – This factor (=2) is the same in all conditions; it is not varied.  
   • Predictions about varying it?  
     – None. The paper does not examine how changing the multiplication factor would affect punishment’s impact on efficiency.

7. PUNISHMENT COST TO IMPOSE A SINGLE UNIT OF PUNISHMENT  
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes. The experiment uses a cost of 1 point to the punisher for every deduction point assigned.  
     – This cost is not systematically varied; it is fixed at 1.  
   • Predictions about varying it?  
     – None. The paper does not explore how changing the cost‐to‐punisher would influence the punishment treatment effect.

8. PUNISHMENT MAGNITUDE (COINS DEDUCTED FROM A PLAYER FOR EACH UNIT OF PUNISHMENT)  
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes. Each deduction point costs the target 3 points, giving a fee‐to‐fine ratio of 1:3.  
     – The magnitude is not systematically varied.  
   • Predictions about varying it?  
     – None. The paper does not address how changing the 1:3 ratio would alter the effect of punishment on efficiency.

9. WHETHER A REWARD IS ENABLED  
   • Discussed?  
     – Not mentioned. There was no reward condition in this study.  
   • Predictions about varying it?  
     – None.

10. REWARD COST TO GRANT A SINGLE UNIT OF REWARD  
   • Discussed?  
     – Not applicable, as no reward mechanism is included in the experiment.  
   • Predictions about varying it?  
     – None.

11. REWARD MAGNITUDE (COINS AWARDED TO A PLAYER FOR EACH UNIT OF REWARD GRANTED)  
   • Discussed?  
     – Not applicable, as no reward mechanism is included in the experiment.  
   • Predictions about varying it?  
     – None.

12. IS THE NUMBER OF ROUNDS KNOWN TO PLAYERS (DO THEY KNOW WHEN THE GAME ENDS)?  
   • Discussed?  
     – The paper does not explicitly state whether participants knew the exact number of PGG rounds ex ante.  
   • Predictions about varying it?  
     – None.

13. ARE PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN (DO PLAYERS KNOW HOW MUCH THEIR PEERS GAINED AND LOST EACH ROUND)?  
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes. After each contribution stage, participants learn each member’s contribution and that member’s resulting earnings.  
     – The paper does not systematically vary how much outcome information is revealed.  
   • Predictions about varying it?  
     – None.

14. WHEN A PLAYER IS PUNISHED, DO THEY KNOW WHO THE SPECIFIC PUNISHER IS?  
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes. The paper states that punished players only see the total deduction points they receive, not who assigned them.  
     – This is not systematically varied.  
   • Predictions about varying it?  
     – None.

15. WHEN A PLAYER IS REWARDED, DO THEY KNOW WHO THE SPECIFIC REWARDER IS?  
   • Discussed?  
     – Not applicable, as there is no reward condition.  
   • Predictions about varying it?  
     – None.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables referenced, and how are these different?  
   • Yes. The paper measures “efficiency” or “welfare” in terms of participants’ total earnings (points) from the PGG. It also measures (a) cooperation/contribution levels in the PGG, and (b) subsequent trust/trustworthiness in a trust game. These variables are distinct: “cooperation” is how many points participants contributed; “efficiency” is how many total points participants earned; “trust” and “trustworthiness” are measured in the trust game. The authors explicitly note that punishment decreased total earnings (i.e., lowered efficiency), whereas gossip increased it.

B. Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form (though not necessarily systematically varied):  
     1. Number of players (fixed at 4).  
     2. Number of rounds (fixed at 4 in PGG, 2 in trust game).  
     3. Is chat enabled? (Not standard chat, but a “gossip” stage is introduced vs. no‐gossip.)  
     6. MPCR/multiplication factor (fixed at 2).  
     7. Punishment cost (1 point to punisher).  
     8. Punishment magnitude (3 points deducted from target).  
     13. Peer outcomes shown (yes, observed after each round).  
     14. Punisher identity known (no, they only see the total deductions).  
   • The other parameters (4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 15) are either not used at all or else mentioned only insofar as they do not apply (e.g., no reward).

C. For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Of the 15, the only actual “systematic variations” in the experiment are:  
     – (3) The presence or absence of gossip.  
     – The presence or absence of punishment, which relates to having (7) and (8) turned “on” vs. “off” in a yes/no sense (but not a variation in the punishment cost ratio itself).  
   • The paper does not systematically vary any other parameters (e.g., not the number of rounds, not the cost‐to‐fine ratio, not the group size, etc.). Thus only “no‐gossip vs. gossip” and “no‐punishment vs. punishment” are truly manipulated.  
   • For “punishment vs. no‐punishment,” the paper reports (1) no overall increase in cooperation by punishment across all four PGG rounds, although a positive effect emerges in later rounds, and (2) lower earnings (efficiency) under punishment.  
   • For “gossip vs. no‐gossip,” the paper reports (1) higher cooperation, (2) higher earnings (efficiency), and (3) greater trust and trustworthiness afterward.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not give explicit guidance on varying most of these parameters (such as changing group size, number of rounds, or the punishment cost/fine ratio). It only directly shows that “having some punishment vs. none,” by itself, reduced efficiency overall but did boost contributions in later rounds. “Having gossip vs. none” tended to increase contributions, increase total earnings, and have lasting impacts on trust.  
   • Thus, based on the paper alone, there is little or no evidence to predict how systematically changing the 15 parameters other than “punishment on/off” and “gossip on/off” would affect punishment’s impact on efficiency. The authors do not provide data or predictions on altering, for example, the cost/fine ratio, the MPCR, or the number of players.  
   • In short, aside from showing that punishment with a cost ratio of 1:3 hinders efficiency when used alone—and that adding gossip can counteract those losses—the paper offers no further systematic predictions about the other parameters or their interactions.
reference_APA: Wu, Junhui, Balliet, Daniel & Van Lange, Paul A. M. (2016). Gossip Versus Punishment: The Efficiency of Reputation to Promote and Maintain Cooperation. SCIENTIFIC REPORTS.

Abstract: Two studies were conducted to test reputation-based accounts of altruism which predict that the more people sacrifice to help others, the greater their ensuing benefits.
