Below I go through the 15 parameters one by one, restricting myself strictly to what appears in Nelissen (2008).

────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER‐BY‐PARAMETER CHECK
────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  The punishment vignette involves three “possible partners” (Players A, B, C) who had earlier observed an unfair split, and the subsequent trust-game interaction involves two players (the participant and the assigned partner).  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  The number of players is fixed; the paper contains no condition with a different group size.  No effect size is reported or implied.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  Indirectly.  All interactions (the third-party punishment situation and the trust game) are one-shot.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned?  No.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule?  
   • Mentioned?  No.  There is no public-goods contribution stage at all.

5. Contribution default / “take” frame?  
   • Mentioned?  No.

6. MPCR or multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  Partly.  In the trust game the participant’s transfer is tripled (multiplier = 3), but this parameter is never varied.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.

7. Punishment cost to imposer (per unit)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  “Every euro invested in punishment reduced the allocator’s payoff by €2.”  Hence the cost-per-unit to the punisher is €1.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  The unit cost is held constant; what is varied is the total amount a punisher chose to spend (0 vs €1.50) relative to his endowment.

8. Punishment magnitude (target-side loss per unit)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes, fixed at €2 per €1 spent.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.

9. Whether a reward option exists  
   • Mentioned?  No.

10. Reward cost per unit  
    • Mentioned?  No.

11. Reward magnitude per unit  
    • Mentioned?  No.

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
    • Mentioned?  No.  Not relevant in a one-shot design.

13. Are peer outcomes shown / information display about others?  
    • Mentioned?  Yes.  Participants are explicitly shown how much each potential partner spent on punishment.  
    • Systematically varied?  Partly.  Study 1 vs Study 2 manipulates whether the partners’ initial endowments (and therefore the “relative cost” of punishment) are displayed.  
      – Effect reported: When relative costs are visible, the strong punisher (spent €1.50 out of €5) is preferred 57 % of the time, versus 29 % for the non-punisher and 14 % for the weak punisher; χ²(2)=14.59, p<.001.  When relative costs are not visible, the preference disappears; χ²(2)=2.00, p=.40.  
      – Dependent variables affected: partner preference, not efficiency.

14. Is the identity of the punisher known?  
    • Mentioned?  Functionally yes (players are labelled A, B, C), but this factor is not varied.

15. Is the identity of a rewarder known?  
    • Mentioned?  No reward stage exists.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────
A.  Does the paper analyse group efficiency?  
    – No.  Dependent variables are (i) which partner is chosen, (ii) amount of money the participant transfers in a trust game, and (iii) perception ratings (fairness, friendliness, generosity).  None of these equals “efficiency” (total payoff divided by maximum possible).

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
    – Six:  #1 (players), #6 (multiplier = 3), #7 (cost = €1), #8 (magnitude = €2), #13 (visibility of punishment info / relative cost), #14 (punisher identity shown).  The remaining nine parameters never appear.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* the parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
    – Exactly one: parameter 13 (visibility of information about relative cost).  The paper shows that revealing endowments (thereby allowing observers to compute the relative cost of punishment) strongly changes the “punishment treatment effect” on partner choice; χ² and F statistics are provided for preference and transfer outcomes.  No systematic variations are reported for the other 14 parameters.

D.  Predictions that can be made (solely from this paper) about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency:  
    – The paper contains no data on efficiency, so very little can be inferred.  
    – The only tentative prediction is that making relative punishment costs *observable* (parameter 13) should enhance any positive reputation-based benefits of punishment, which *might* translate into higher future payoffs (and thus higher efficiency) for the punisher’s group.  
    – Because none of the other parameters were manipulated, the paper offers no basis for predicting how changing them would alter the punishment effect on efficiency.

In short, Nelissen (2008) tells us almost nothing about group efficiency and only addresses one of the 15 design parameters (information visibility) in a systematic way.
reference_APA: Nelissen, Rob M. A. (2008). The price you pay: cost-dependent reputation effects of altruistic punishment. EVOLUTION AND HUMAN BEHAVIOR.

Below I walk through the 15 design parameters, quoting or paraphrasing exactly what appears in the Anderies et al. paper.  For every parameter I indicate  

• Whether the parameter itself is reported in the paper (and, if so, the value actually used);  
• Whether the authors say anything – even informally – about how *changing* that parameter would alter the “punishment treatment effect” (i.e., the difference between the punishment and the no-punishment condition).  
Whenever the paper talks about a dependent variable other than **efficiency** I flag that explicitly.

-------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
-------------------------------------------------

1. Number of players in the group  
   • Mentioned.  The paper classifies “group size” as a standard micro-situational variable and states that “an increase in group size typically makes collective action more difficult.”  
   • No experiment in the paper systematically varies group size in a punishment treatment, and no numerical effect size is provided.  No direct link to efficiency is made.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Repeated vs. one-shot play is mentioned generically (“in a repeated game… groups approach the Nash equilibrium”).  
   • No systematic variation; no statement on how adding or subtracting rounds changes the *punishment* effect.

3. Chat / communication between players  
   • Explicitly discussed many times (“face-to-face communication has been shown to increase average earnings significantly”; “costly punishment has no positive effect if it is not combined with communication”).  
   • Direction of interaction with punishment:  
        – In classic static CPR games: allowing punishment by itself tends to *lower* net payoffs;  
        – In dynamic spatial CPR games, *punishment + communication* ≈ no positive efficiency effect unless communication is allowed.  
     No numeric magnitudes are given, but the qualitative prediction is clear: communication moderates the punishment effect.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
   • Not mentioned.

5. Contribution default / “refund” framing  
   • Not mentioned.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   • Not reported, nor is any manipulation of returns discussed.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   • Referred to in general language as “costly punishment”.  A single cost figure is never provided and the cost is never experimentally varied inside this paper.  
   • Only qualitative statement: because punishment is costly, its introduction *can* lower average earnings.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss to the target)  
   • Not reported, not varied.

9. Whether peer reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned only in passing when the authors list “reward” as a design possibility; no experiment here uses it, and no effect is discussed.

10–11. Reward cost / reward magnitude  
   • Not mentioned beyond the brief listing; no data, no effect.

12. Whether the horizon is common knowledge  
   • Not discussed.

13. Whether peer outcomes are displayed  
   • Baseline CPR experiments gave “aggregated information on the decisions of others,” but the paper never varies this dimension or links it to punishment.

14. Whether punished players know the identity of the punisher  
   • Not mentioned.

15. Whether rewarded players know the identity of the rewarder  
   • Not mentioned.


-------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
-------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables used  
   – The paper talks about (i) average earnings or “net average returns,” (ii) aggregate contributions / harvest effort, (iii) frequency of punishment events.  
   – **Efficiency** in the strict sense (total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff) is *not* explicitly calculated, although average earnings are reported qualitatively.

B.  Which parameters appear at all?  
   • 5 of the 15:  (1) group size, (2) rounds (implicitly), (3) communication, (7) punishment cost (only as “costly”), and (13) level of aggregate feedback.

C.  Which parameters are discussed in terms of *systematic variation* on the punishment treatment effect?  
   • Only 1 parameter – (3) Communication.  
   • Even here the evidence is qualitative: punishment lowers net earnings unless communication is allowed, in which case the combined treatment can raise or at least not lower earnings.  No numerical effect size is supplied.

D.  If we had to predict the punishment-efficiency link from this paper alone  
   • Communication: expect punishment to raise efficiency *only* when some form of face-to-face (or otherwise rich) communication is enabled; otherwise punishment likely reduces efficiency because of its direct cost.  
   • Group size: larger groups probably find it harder to use punishment efficiently, but the paper gives no direct evidence.  
   • All other parameters (round length, MPCR, cost/magnitude of punishment, reward options, information disclosure, identity revelation, etc.) are not covered, so no prediction can be made on the basis of the paper.

In short, the Anderies et al. article is primarily a methodological overview and contains almost no parameter-by-parameter evidence on how punishment influences group efficiency.  The only reasonably firm takeaway relevant to the 15-parameter schema is that *communication is a necessary complement for punishment to have a neutral or positive effect on payoffs; otherwise, costly punishment tends to lower group earnings.*

Keywords Plus: PUNISHMENT; COOPERATION; RECIPROCITY; SANCTIONS; PROVISION; MONETARY; DEMAND; GAMES
Abstract: A normative conflict arises when multiple plausible rules exist, specifying how one ought to behave in a given situation. In such cases, enforcing one normative rule can lead to a sequence of mutual retaliatory sanctions, which we refer to as a feud. We investigate the hypothesis that normative conflict enhances the likelihood of a feud in a public-good experiment. Normative conflict in our experiment arises from the fact that individuals derive different benefits from the public good. We find that punishment is much more likely to trigger counter-punishment and start a feud when there is a normative conflict, than it is in a setting in which all individuals derive the same benefit from the public good and no such conflict exists. While the possibility of a feud sustains cooperation, the cost of feuding fully offsets the efficiency gains from increased cooperation. Our results point to an important limitation of self-enforcement mechanisms. (C) 2012 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

Below, each of the 15 focal parameters is treated in turn.

For every parameter I indicate  

(1) Whether it is explicitly described in the paper (and, if so, its value in each treatment);  

(2) Whether the paper makes any prediction or supplies any empirical evidence about what would happen to the *punishment-treatment effect on group efficiency* if the parameter were systematically varied (i.e., taken to different levels).

Whenever the paper is silent, this is stated directly.

────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER SCAN
────────────────────────────────────────

GAME STRUCTURE  
1. Number of players  
   (1) Stated. All groups contain exactly 4 players.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction or evidence about changing group size.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Stated. Exactly 10 periods in every treatment; subjects know this.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction or evidence about changing the horizon.

3. Chat/communication allowed?  
   (1) Stated. “without communication” – chat disabled in every treatment.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction or evidence.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule?  
   (1) Continuous choice 0–20 ECU. (So the rule = “No”.)  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction or evidence.

5. Contribution default / “take back” design?  
   (1) Standard voluntary contribution mechanism: subjects *give* to the public account; no default and no “take-back”.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction or evidence.

MONETARY STAKES  
6. MPCR or related multiplication factor  
   (1) Stated and *varied across treatments*.  
       • Symmetric treatment: every player’s MPCR = 0.4.  
       • Asymmetric & No-Feud: two “high-return” players have MPCR 0.5, two “low-return” players MPCR 0.3.  
   (2) Systematic variation beyond these two levels is *not* undertaken, but the paper *does* link this heterogeneity to the punishment-treatment effect:

       – With heterogeneity (0.5/0.3) plus punishment (Asymmetric) average earnings = 21.59 ECU.  
       – With the same heterogeneity *but* punishment banned (No-Feud) earnings = 22.12 ECU.  
         ⇒ Introducing punishment *reduces* efficiency by ≈ 0.53 ECU and the difference is statistically insignificant.  

       – With *homogeneous* MPCR 0.4 plus punishment (Symmetric) earnings = 25.65 ECU.  
         ⇒ Switching from homogeneous to heterogeneous MPCR while retaining punishment lowers efficiency by ≈ 4.06 ECU (p = .07).  

       That is the only parameter whose variation is tied to an efficiency outcome.

PEER INCENTIVES  
7. Cost to impose one unit of punishment  
   (1) Stated. Flat fee of 1 ECU per period to activate punishment (allows unlimited points). Not varied.  
   (2) No predictions/evidence about other cost levels.

8. Punishment magnitude  
   (1) Stated. Each point deducts 1 ECU from the target. Not varied.  
   (2) No predictions/evidence.

9. “Reward enabled?”  
   (1) No. Reward stage absent in all treatments.  
   (2) Nothing discussed.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   – Not applicable; never introduced; no discussion.

INFORMATION DISPLAY  
12. Horizon known?  
   (1) Yes – subjects know the game lasts 10 periods.  
   (2) Not varied; no predictions/evidence.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   (1) Yes – after every stage, each player sees every other player’s contribution, earnings and punishment flows.  
   (2) Not varied; no predictions/evidence.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
   (1) Yes – unique IDs allow subjects to see exactly who punished whom in every stage.  
   (2) Not varied; no predictions/evidence.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
   – Not applicable (no rewards).

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use “group efficiency” (total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   Yes, average (and total) earnings are reported and used to assess efficiency.  
   Other dependent variables analysed are: individual contributions, likelihood & severity of (i) first-stage punishment, (ii) counter-punishment, number of punishment stages, incidence of feuds, and the proportion of subjects with negative period earnings. Efficiency is distinct from these behavioural measures.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
   10/15: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14.  
   Parameters 5, 9, 10, 11, 15 are not used or discussed.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss their *systematic* effect on the punishment-treatment effect?  
   Only 1/15 — parameter 6 (MPCR / heterogeneity). No other parameter is systematically varied, so there is no basis for quantitative predictions for the rest.

D. Prospects for predicting punishment-treatment effects on efficiency using only this paper  
   • Heterogeneous MPCR (high=0.5, low=0.3) in a setting that *allows* punishment produces no net efficiency gain relative to banning punishment, because extra cooperation is exactly offset by costly feuds.  
   • Homogeneous MPCR (0.4) with punishment increases efficiency relative to the heterogeneous case because far fewer counter-punishments and feuds occur.  
   • The paper provides no leverage for forecasting how any of the other 14 parameters—or interactions among them—would affect the efficiency impact of introducing punishment. Any further prediction would go beyond the presented evidence.

Below I go through the 15 concrete design parameters one‐by‐one and check (i) whether the paper ever states the value of the parameter and (ii) whether the paper derives or reports what happens to the **punishment treatment effect** when that parameter is *systematically varied*.  “Punishment treatment effect’’ would require a comparison **with vs. without punishment** and then a further comparison across different values of the given parameter.  Whenever the paper speaks about dependent variables other than efficiency I flag this explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1. Number of players in a group (N)  
   • Mentioned? – Yes, constantly (e.g., N = 4, 6, 8 in Figures 1, 2, 4, 5).  
   • Systematically varied for the punishment effect? – No.  Section 6 (sanctioning institutions) keeps N fixed at 4 in the punishment simulations; any N-variation is shown only for **no-punishment** settings (Sections 3–4).  No table/figure shows how changing N changes the *difference* between punished and unpunished conditions.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? – No.  The model is evolutionary and runs indefinitely; no fixed horizon is introduced.  
   • Systematic punishment effect? – Not applicable.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned? – No.  
   • Systematic punishment effect? – Not applicable.

4. “All-or-nothing’’ contributions?  
   • Mentioned? – Yes.  The model is binary: agents either contribute a fixed fraction cb or nothing.  
   • Systematically varied? – No; contribution discretisation is never manipulated, hence no punishment-effect estimate.

5. Rebate/“contribution default’’ frame?  
   • Mentioned? – No.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? – Not in those terms.  The benefit of meeting the threshold is that the player keeps her full endowment; that constant is never varied like an MPCR.  
   • Systematic punishment effect? – No.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   • Mentioned? – Yes.  Denoted π_tax (= 0.03 in Fig. 4).  
   • Systematically varied? – No.  Only that single value is used; there is no graph/table varying π_tax and contrasting treatments.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine on target)  
   • Mentioned? – Yes.  Denoted π_fine (= 0.30 in Fig. 4).  
   • Systematically varied? – No.  Again, fixed at one value.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Mentioned? – No reward mechanism appears.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   • Not mentioned.

12. Finite horizon known?  
   • Not mentioned.

13. Peer outcome visibility?  
   • Not mentioned.

14. Whether punished player learns who punished?  
   • Not mentioned.

15. Whether rewarded player learns who rewarded?  
   • Not mentioned.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Does the paper use “group efficiency’’ (total or average payoff / maximum payoff) as a dependent variable?  
    – No.  The main dependent variables are  
      • η_G (“group achievement’’): fraction of groups that reach the threshold;  
      • Fraction of cooperators in the stationary distribution;  
      • Gradient of selection;  
      • Occasionally average time that strategies persist.  
    None of these is an efficiency ratio.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned at all?  Four of them:  
      (1) group size N,  
      (4) binary vs. continuous contribution (always binary),  
      (7) punishment cost π_tax,  
      (8) punishment fine π_fine.  
    The other eleven parameters never appear.

C.  For how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss *systematically varying* the parameter **and** report what that does to the punishment treatment effect on any dependent variable?  
    – Zero.  No figure, table or sentence reports how the *difference* between punishment and no-punishment changes when any of the four mentioned parameters is varied.

D.  If forced to predict punishment-treatment effects on *efficiency* from this paper alone:  
    • The only qualitative statement available is that **local (group-level) punishment institutions outperform global ones** in raising η_G, especially when the perceived risk of collective failure is low and threshold requirements are strict.  
    • Because no other parameter is manipulated jointly with punishment, nothing can be said about the direction or size of punishment effects as N, π_tax, or π_fine change, nor about any interactions among the 15 listed parameters.  Hence, predictions beyond “local punishment helps more than global punishment” would be speculative and are not warranted by the text.

In short, the paper offers almost no leverage for forecasting how the 15 experimental design parameters—and certainly their interactions—modulate the effect of punishment on group efficiency.

Abstract: In a pairwise interaction, an individual who uses costly punishment must pay a cost in order that the opponent incurs a cost. Below is a parameter-by-parameter summary of what the paper (“Costly punishment does not always increase cooperation”) does and does not say about each of the 15 listed parameters and whether the paper links systematic variation of that parameter to the punishment treatment’s effect on any outcome (in particular, on efficiency). Throughout, please note that the study is actually a repeated two-player Prisoner’s Dilemma, not a multi-player public goods game, and there is no explicit systematic variation of most of these parameters.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of Players
 • Mention in Paper: Yes. The experiment is conducted with 2 players (a repeated two-player Prisoner’s Dilemma). 
 • Systematic Variation: No. The paper does not vary the number of players.
 • Effect on Punishment Treatment (or efficiency) When Varied: Not discussed.

2) Number of Rounds
 • Mention in Paper: Yes. The paper uses an indefinite horizon (there is a 0.75 probability another round will occur). Participants do not know when it will end. 
 • Systematic Variation: No. They do not systematically vary the number of rounds.
 • Effect on Punishment Treatment (or efficiency) When Varied: Not discussed.

3) Is Chat Enabled Between Players?
 • Mention in Paper: No. There is no mention of any discussion/chat feature.  
 • Systematic Variation: Not applicable.
 • Effect on Punishment Treatment (or efficiency) When Varied: Not discussed.

4) Is the Contribution “All or Nothing”?
 • Mention in Paper: Indirectly. The experiment is a discrete-choice repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma (cooperate, defect, or punish). 
 • Systematic Variation: No. There is no mention of varying from “all or nothing” to continuous amounts.
 • Effect on Punishment Treatment (or efficiency) When Varied: Not discussed.

5) Is the Contribution Default?
 • Mention in Paper: No. The paper does not describe any default contribution mechanism (typical of some public goods games). 
 • Systematic Variation: Not applicable.
 • Effect on Punishment Treatment (or efficiency) When Varied: Not discussed.

6) Marginal per Capita Return (MPCR) or Multiplication Factor
 • Mention in Paper: Partially. Instead of a classic “MPCR,” the authors run two different payoff structures (C1/T1 vs. C2/T2) where cooperating yields +1 for oneself and either +2 or +3 for the other. This is the closest analogue to varying the “return” of cooperation.
 • Systematic Variation: The study uses two sets of payoffs (labeled “1 & 2 units” vs. “1 & 3 units”), but does not extensively vary this factor beyond those two cases.
 • Effect on Punishment Treatment (or efficiency) When Varied: 
   – The authors measure cooperation frequency and average payoff. 
   – They do not explicitly discuss “efficiency = total payoff / maximum possible,” but they do show that in T1 (the 1 & 2 payoff structure) costly punishment lowers cooperation relative to control and lowers average payoff. In T2 (the 1 & 3 payoff structure), punishment does not significantly change cooperation or average payoff relative to control. 
   – No explicit numerical “efficiency” effect size is provided beyond these comparisons of cooperation frequency and average payoff.

7) Punishment Cost to Impose a Single Unit of Punishment
 • Mention in Paper: Yes. Punishing costs the punisher 1 unit.
 • Systematic Variation: No. It is fixed at 1 unit. 
 • Effect on Punishment Treatment (or efficiency) When Varied: Not discussed. No systematic variation in the paper.

8) Punishment Magnitude (the coins deducted from the punished player)
 • Mention in Paper: Yes. Punishment deducts 4 units from the target.
 • Systematic Variation: No. It is fixed at 4. 
 • Effect on Punishment Treatment (or efficiency) When Varied: Not discussed.

9) Whether a Reward Is Enabled
 • Mention in Paper: No. The experiments only involve costly punishment; reward is never made available.
 • Systematic Variation: Not applicable.
 • Effect on Punishment Treatment (or efficiency) When Varied: Not discussed.

10) Reward Cost per Unit
 • Mention in Paper: No. Rewards are not used in the experiment.
 • Systematic Variation: Not applicable.
 • Effect on Punishment Treatment (or efficiency) When Varied: Not discussed.

11) Reward Magnitude per Unit
 • Mention in Paper: No. Rewards are not used.
 • Systematic Variation: Not applicable.
 • Effect on Punishment Treatment (or efficiency) When Varied: Not discussed.

12) Is the Number of Rounds Known to Players?
 • Mention in Paper: Yes. Participants only know that each round continues with probability 0.75, so they do not know the exact number of rounds beforehand.
 • Systematic Variation: No. This is held constant throughout.
 • Effect on Punishment Treatment (or efficiency) When Varied: Not discussed.

13) Are Peer Outcomes Shown (Do Players Know How Much Others Gained/Lost)?
 • Mention in Paper: Yes. Each player sees the other’s choice and payoff at the end of each round in this two-player setting.
 • Systematic Variation: No.  
 • Effect on Punishment Treatment (or efficiency) When Varied: Not discussed.

14) When a Player Is Punished, Do They Know Who the Specific Punisher Is?
 • Mention in Paper: The design is a two-player game; each player sees the other’s choice (and thus knows whether they have been punished by the only possible punisher).
 • Systematic Variation: No.  
 • Effect on Punishment Treatment (or efficiency) When Varied: Not discussed.

15) When a Player Is Rewarded, Do They Know the Specific Rewarder?
 • Mention in Paper: No. There is no reward option in this experiment.
 • Systematic Variation: Not applicable.
 • Effect on Punishment Treatment (or efficiency) When Varied: Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different from one another?

 • The paper primarily reports (1) the frequency of cooperation and (2) the average payoff per round; it does not formally define efficiency as “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff.”  
 • The authors do discuss that when costly punishment is available, it can decrease the group’s total payoff (average payoff) because punishers lose points and those punished also lose points.  
 • So in this study, “average payoff” stands in for overall group benefit, whereas the frequency of cooperation is another key outcome. They do not present an explicit “efficiency ratio” but do speak about payoff levels and sum-payoff implications.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

 • Mentioned at least in passing:  
   – (1) Number of players (fixed at 2)  
   – (2) Number of rounds (indefinite with probability 0.75)  
   – (6) Payoff structure (two settings: T1 vs. T2)  
   – (7) Punishment cost (1)  
   – (8) Punishment magnitude (4)  
   – (12) Rounds not known in advance to participants  
   – (13) Peer outcomes (opponent’s choice and payoff) shown during the game  
   – (14) Punisher identity is known implicitly (2-player game)  
 • Not mentioned at all: (3) Chat, (4) All-or-nothing vs. continuous contributions, (5) Contribution default, (9) Reward presence, (10) Reward cost, (11) Reward magnitude, (15) Rewarder identity.  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?

 • Strictly “systematic variation” occurs only for the payoff structure: T1 vs. T2 (linked to parameter 6).  
 • For T1: The availability of costly punishment reduces cooperation frequency and reduces payoff compared to the control (no punishment).  
 • For T2: The availability of costly punishment does not significantly change cooperation frequency or payoff compared to the control.  
 • The authors do not systematically vary or discuss the effect of changing the other parameters with respect to punishment or any efficiency measure.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

 • The paper examines only two payoff structures for the repeated two-player Prisoner’s Dilemma, reporting that punishment sometimes reduces cooperation and average payoff (especially in the T1 payoff configuration). It does not explore how other parameters (number of players, presence of reward, different punishment costs or magnitudes, chat, etc.) might systematically affect efficiency.

However, no formal predictions about efficiency, nor any other parameters, are presented.  

Thus, based strictly on this paper, one can say very little about how systematically varying the 15 parameters (beyond the specific payoff differences they tested) would influence the punishment effect on efficiency.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter accounting of what is actually stated in Chen & Szolnoki (2018) concerning each of the 15 items in your list, followed by a summary (A–D) as requested. Throughout, please note that the paper’s main focus is on how a top‐down punishment (via an external inspector) and the resource’s own growth dynamics jointly determine the stationary fraction of cooperators and the stationary level of the common resource. The authors do not frame their results in terms of “group efficiency” (actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff) per se, and they likewise do not supply numerical “treatment effects” of punishment on efficiency. Instead, they analyze equilibrium strategy compositions and resource levels. Below, “not mentioned” means the paper simply does not discuss that parameter or any systematic variation of it for the punishment effect.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   – Mentioned? Yes. The paper denotes the number of individuals as N, and in examples uses N = 1000 or N = 100.  
   – Systematic variation? No. While N appears in the model (e.g., in resource‐consumption formulas), the paper does not systematically vary N to examine how changes in population size affect the impact of punishment on any outcome. No effect sizes are reported.

2. Number of rounds
   – Not mentioned. The paper uses continuous‐time (replicator) equations and does not treat the game as repeated for a known (or unknown) finite number of discrete rounds.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   – Not mentioned. No communication or “chat” channel is discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   – Mentioned only insofar as the model uses two pure strategies: “cooperator” (obeys the legal share) or “defector” (over‐harvests). There is no partial/continuous contribution level.  
   – Systematic variation? No. The paper simply fixes two strategies; it does not compare this binary setup to a variable or continuous‐choice contribution setting.

5. Is the contribution default?
   – Not mentioned. There is no discussion of any “default” mechanism by which players move endowments from or into a public fund.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   – The paper does not use “MPCR” explicitly, but it does study how the resource’s intrinsic growth rate r influences outcomes. For convenience, one can view r (and in part bₘ) as analogous to a “multiplier.”  
   – Systematic variation? Yes, they examine three regimes: r < eₐ (small r), intermediate r, and r > e_b (large r). They show qualitatively different final outcomes under punishment in each regime (Figs 2–4). However, they do not quantify a “treatment effect on efficiency.” Instead, they report whether punishment can stabilize a non‐depleted resource and higher cooperation for each r regime.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   – Not mentioned. In the paper’s model, punishment is instituted by an external (central) authority, and no explicit cost is borne by punishers themselves.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted for each unit of punishment)
   – Mentioned. The paper’s parameter β is the fine paid by a defector when caught. They do systematically vary p × β (inspection probability times fine) to see whether punishment can prevent over‐harvesting.  
   – Systematic variation? Yes, they derive threshold conditions in pβ that change the final evolutionary outcome. They do not, however, convert this into a numeric “treatment effect” on efficiency; instead, they discuss whether resource‐cooperator equilibria are stable or not, depending on pβ.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   – Not mentioned. The paper focuses solely on punishment (fines) and does not consider any reward mechanism.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    – Not mentioned. No reward mechanism is studied.

11. Reward magnitude
    – Not mentioned. Same as above.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
    – Not mentioned. Again, the model is framed in continuous time, not as a repeated game with a known or unknown horizon.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players learn one another’s payoffs)?
    – Not mentioned. Although each player’s payoff is computed, there is no discussion of players actually viewing one another’s outcomes.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    – Not mentioned. All punishment is centralized, not done peer‐to‐peer.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    – Not mentioned. No reward mechanism is present.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? 
   → The paper does not measure “efficiency” (total payoff / maximum possible payoff). Instead, it tracks (i) the fraction of cooperators in equilibrium and (ii) the resource abundance in equilibrium. Although these influence overall payoffs, the paper does not frame them as an “efficiency” ratio, nor does it report direct “treatment effects” on efficiency.

B. Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper? 
   → Four parameters appear explicitly:  
      (1) Number of players (N).  
      (4) Contribution is effectively “all or nothing” (cooperate or defect).  
      (6) Growth‐rate‐related parameter r (analogous to a multiplier).  
      (8) Punishment magnitude β (the fine).  

C. For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment (for any dependent variable) when each parameter is systematically varied?
   → Two are systematically varied and analyzed for their effect on final outcomes (fraction of cooperators and resource abundance):  
      • (6) The growth rate r (three regimes: small, intermediate, large).  
      • (8) The fine β (particularly pβ, the product of punishment‐detection probability and fine).  
   → The paper does not provide numerical “effect sizes” on efficiency; it provides qualitative transitions (e.g., stable full cooperation vs. mixed vs. defection states).

D. If you were to make predictions about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of this paper, what would they be?
   → The authors do not directly address efficiency as you have defined it, so only qualitative inferences are possible:  
      • If the resource growth rate r is too low, then even strong punishment may fail to sustain the resource (so “efficiency” would be low regardless of punishment).  
      • If the growth rate r is very high, the resource remains abundant even under defection, so punishment’s additional “efficiency” boost would be limited.  
      • At intermediate resource growth rates, stronger punishment (larger pβ) can induce a cooperative‐plus‐healthy‐resource equilibrium, which should improve total payoffs relative to no‐punishment cases, although the paper does not calculate the exact payoff ratio.  
      • None of the other parameters (like chat, reward, known rounds, etc.) are addressed and so no predictions can be made from this paper alone.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────

Hence, the paper discusses only a subset of your 15 parameters (N, binary‐strategy contribution, r, and β) and does not directly evaluate “efficiency.” It instead focuses on equilibrium population compositions (cooperators vs. defectors) and equilibrium resource levels under a top‐down inspection/punishment regime that depends on p×β and on the resource’s intrinsic growth rate r.

For every one of the 15 parameters I first state whether it is mentioned in the paper (and, if so, its value in the experiment), and then whether the paper gives any prediction or reported effect of *systematically varying* that parameter on the punishment-treatment effect.  
All numerical references come directly from the text, tables or figures reproduced in the paper.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1.  Number of players  
    • Mentioned: Yes. Each decision-making group contained 5 players.  
    • Systematically varied? No. All groups had the same size; no prediction or effect of changing group size is given.

2.  Number of rounds

    • Systematically varied? No. No prediction/effect of changing the number of rounds.

3.  Chat enabled?  
    • Mentioned: Yes. “No communication among subjects is allowed.”  
    • Systematically varied? No. No prediction/effect.

4.  All-or-nothing contribution?  
    • Mentioned: Yes. Subjects chose any integer from 0 to 20 tokens – not all-or-nothing.  
    • Systematically varied? No. No prediction/effect.

5.  “Contribution default” (withdrawal frame)?  
    • Mentioned: No. The paper never uses a withdrawal/default framing.  
    • Systematically varied? Not applicable.

6.  MPCR / multiplication factor  
    • Mentioned: Yes. a = 0.4 (marginal per-capita return).  
    • Systematically varied? No. No prediction/effect.

7.  Punishment cost per unit  
    • Mentioned: Yes. 1 token per punishment point. (In the Consensual treatment the cost is *waived* when a single request is not seconded, but the cost itself is still 1 when punishment is actually implemented.)  
    • Systematically varied? No. The cost rate is identical in all treatments; the paper gives no prediction about varying it.

8.  Punishment magnitude per unit  
    • Mentioned: Yes. Each point inflicted costs the target 3 tokens.  
    • Systematically varied? No. No prediction/effect.

9.  Reward enabled?  
    • Mentioned: No. There is no reward stage in any treatment.  
    • Systematically varied? Not applicable.

10. Reward cost per unit  
    • Mentioned: No.  
    • Systematically varied? Not applicable.

11. Reward magnitude per unit  
    • Mentioned: No.  
    • Systematically varied? Not applicable.

12. Do players know the number of rounds?  
    • Mentioned: Partially. Subjects were told the experiment had “two parts” but only the first part’s rules were explained at the outset. The paper never states that the exact total number of periods was revealed.  
    • Systematically varied? No. No prediction/effect.

13. Peer outcomes displayed?  
    • Mentioned: Yes. At the end of each period, every subject saw every group member’s contribution and earnings.  
    • Systematically varied? No. No prediction/effect.

14. Identity of the punisher revealed?  
    • Mentioned: Yes. Identities were *not* revealed; only aggregate punishment received was shown.  
    • Systematically varied? No. No prediction/effect.

15. Identity of the rewarder revealed?  
    • Mentioned: Not applicable (no rewards).  
    • Systematically varied? Not applicable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables used in the paper  
    • Group efficiency / total (net) payoff: Yes, called “net earnings” or “relative payoff (loss/gain).”  
    • Contribution level: Yes (average tokens contributed).  
    • Punishment rate / punishment points: Yes.  
    Differences: Contribution is a behavioral input; efficiency (net earnings) already subtracts punishment costs and is therefore a welfare measure; punishment rate is merely the amount of sanctioning activity.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even *mentioned*?  
    10 of 15 are mentioned (#1–4, 6–8, 12–14). Five (#5, 9–11, 15) are not mentioned.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* the parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
    Zero.  All three experimental treatments kept the 15 listed parameters constant; the only elements that changed (simultaneity vs. sequential timing, and the consensus requirement) are *not* among the 15 parameters in your list. Consequently the paper provides no numeric effect sizes for varying any of the 15 parameters.

D.  Predictions you could make—solely from this paper—about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency  
    • Because none of the 15 parameters were manipulated, the paper supplies virtually no direct evidence that could be extrapolated.  
    • At most one might *speculate* that keeping all of them fixed while altering the punishment institution (which is outside your parameter list) produced large efficiency differences; hence any of the 15 parameters that *interact* with the institution might matter. However, the paper itself gives no basis for saying *which* interactions or *how*.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Bottom line: the article is rich in results about *types of punishment rules*, but it does not vary—and therefore does not inform us about—the 15 specific parameters you list.

D.  Predictions one could make for efficiency solely from this paper  
Because the article never measures efficiency and never varies any of the 15 parameters, almost no parameter-specific predictions can be made. Abstract: Punishment of non-cooperators has been observed to promote cooperation. Such punishment is an evolutionary puzzle because it is costly to the punisher while beneficial to others, for example, through increased social cohesion. However, while it is well established that reputation plays a key role in human cooperation, the simple threat from a reputation of being a punisher may not have been sufficiently explored yet in order to explain the evolution of costly punishment. It mainly shows that punishment can evolve if (i) the cost of punishing (s) is not too high, (ii) the cost of being punished (e) is greater than the cost of cooperating (c), and (iii) the benefit of cooperating (b) exceeds s. To the extent that more stable cooperation can raise total payoff, one might guess that lower s, higher e, and higher b would enhance the net benefit of punishment and possibly raise efficiency. However, the paper never quantifies this as an efficiency ratio. For the other parameters, including group size, number of rounds, chat, reward presence, and so on, the paper does not discuss or provide evidence for how they would shift a punishment “treatment effect” on efficiency. Any further prediction would go beyond the text.

Abstract: Many interactions in modern human societies are among strangers. Explaining cooperation in such interactions is challenging. The two most prominent explanations critically depend on individuals' willingness to punish defectors: In models of direct punishment, individuals punish antisocial behavior at a personal cost, whereas in models of indirect reciprocity, they punish indirectly by withholding rewards. Below is a parameter-by-parameter summary, based strictly on the content of the Balafoutas et al. paper (“Direct and indirect punishment among strangers in the field”). In each case, I note whether (1) the parameter is explicitly discussed in any form in the paper (and if so, what value or range it takes), and (2) whether the paper makes predictions about how systematically varying that parameter would affect the “punishment treatment effect” (e.g., how punishment does or does not improve outcomes). For completeness, I include all 15 parameters, even though most are not mentioned or manipulated in the study.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Discussion: The paper does not describe any multi-player “public goods” setup with varying group sizes. In their field experiment, only one bystander at a time (the “observer”) is exposed to an enacted littering scenario and can respond.  
   • Systematic variation/predictions: Not discussed; no predictions or effect sizes are provided.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Discussion: The design is strictly one-shot per observer. There is no mention of repeated interactions or varying the number of rounds.  
   • Systematic variation/predictions: Not discussed; no predictions or effect sizes are provided.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussion: The paper never refers to free-form communication (“chat”) among participants. Interactions are limited to the confederates’ scripted statements.  
   • Systematic variation/predictions: Not discussed; no predictions or effect sizes are provided.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Discussion: There is no public-goods-contribution format. The scenario involves whether a bystander punishes or helps.  
   • Systematic variation/predictions: Not discussed; no predictions or effect sizes are provided.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much to move from the public fund to their hand)?  
   • Discussion: Not mentioned. This paper does not describe any choice of “contribution” to a public fund.  
   • Systematic variation/predictions: Not discussed; no predictions or effect sizes are provided.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
   • Discussion: There is no formal “public goods” multiplier or MPCR in this field experiment.  
   • Systematic variation/predictions: Not discussed; no predictions or effect sizes are provided.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussion: The paper does indicate qualitatively that direct punishment may have a “cost” (risk of retaliation, time, and effort). However, this cost is not numerically specified, nor is it manipulated experimentally.  
   • Systematic variation/predictions: The authors do not vary the punishment cost systematically and make no quantitative predictions about how changes in such cost would affect the overall impact of punishment on any outcome.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted for each unit of punishment)  
   • Discussion: The study’s “punishment” is a verbal scolding in a natural setting, not a monetary deduction. They acknowledge that it imposes a reputational or confrontation cost on the violator but do not define or manipulate an explicit “punishment magnitude.”  
   • Systematic variation/predictions: Not discussed; no predictions or effect sizes are provided.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussion: The authors discuss the possibility that “direct punishers might be rewarded” by fellow bystanders who could help them (e.g., picking up dropped books). They observe that no actual reward occurred. However, the study does not create or remove a formal “reward mechanism,” nor systematically vary that feature.  
   • Systematic variation/predictions: Not discussed; no predictions or effect sizes are provided.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Discussion: The cost of “reward” (e.g., bending down to help a punisher) is briefly noted as “low” but is never formally quantified or manipulated.  
    • Systematic variation/predictions: Not discussed; no predictions or effect sizes are provided.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each reward)  
    • Discussion: The field experiment design does not involve paying coins for helping or any numeric measure of reward.  
    • Systematic variation/predictions: Not discussed; no predictions or effect sizes are provided.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    • Discussion: The experiment is one-shot with an unsuspecting bystander. No mention of rounds or knowledge of an endpoint appears.  
    • Systematic variation/predictions: Not discussed; no predictions or effect sizes are provided.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much peers gained/lost each round)?  
    • Discussion: The setup does not present any monetary or payoff outcomes, so there is no “peer outcome” display.  
    • Systematic variation/predictions: Not discussed; no predictions or effect sizes are provided.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Discussion: Yes, in this field setting, the violator sees the punisher who scolds them. However, this is not systematically manipulated (it is always public, in-person).  
    • Systematic variation/predictions: Not discussed; no predictions or effect sizes are provided.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Discussion: The study measures whether a bystander helps a confederate who dropped books. That help is plainly observable if it occurs. There is no case where knowledge of a “secret rewarder” is systematically varied.  
    • Systematic variation/predictions: Not discussed; no predictions or effect sizes are provided.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary:

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • It does not. The main outcome measures are (i) how often a bystander punishes a norm violator (direct punishment), (ii) how often a bystander withholds help from the violator (indirect punishment), and (iii) how often a bystander helps someone who previously punished a violator (potential “reward”). The authors do not analyze total payoff or group efficiency but rather measure behavior such as “helping rates” and “direct punishment rates.”  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • The paper acknowledges in qualitative form that direct punishment has some personal “cost” (Parameter 7) and that reward could, in principle, exist but was never observed (Parameter 9). It also notes that the identity of the punisher is known (Parameter 14). However, the paper does not attach numerical values to these parameters nor systematically manipulate them. The other parameters (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, and 15) are not mentioned at all in the context of formal variation, numeric values, or design features.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. The authors did not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters and do not provide numerical effect sizes or formal predictions about how changing those parameters would shift the effect of punishment on cooperation, helping, or any other outcome.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper never addresses “efficiency” or “total payoff.” It focuses on whether direct punishment is rewardable, on indirect punishment through withholding help, and on the crowding out of direct punishment when indirect punishment is possible. Consequently, there is little or no basis in this study for predicting how systematic changes in the 15 parameters would affect efficiency. The authors’ main emphasis is on observed behaviors (like direct vs. indirect punishment) rather than payoff consequences for a group. One could only speculate—but the paper itself does not.  
   • Therefore, strictly following the paper, one must conclude that the authors do not provide enough evidence to predict the effect of any of the 15 parameters (or their interactions) on group efficiency.
reference_APA: Balafoutas, Loukas, Nikiforakis, Nikos & Rockenbach, Bettina (2014). Direct and indirect punishment among strangers in the field. PROCEEDINGS OF THE NATIONAL ACADEMY OF SCIENCES OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter accounting of what (if anything) this paper says about each of the 15 parameters in your list, followed by the required four‐part summary.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. All sessions use groups of three players (p. 5, Sect. 2.1 and 2.2). There is no variation across sessions: every group has three members.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying the number of players on the punishment treatment effect?  
  – No. There is no discussion of changing the number of players.

2. Number of rounds  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. It is explicitly a one‐shot game (p. 4–5, e.g. “… we study a one‐shot game”).  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying the number of rounds on the punishment treatment effect?  
  – No. They do not vary the number of rounds and do not analyze what would happen if the number of rounds changed.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. There is no mention of chat, communication, or messaging between players.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying chat?  
  – No mention.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes (indirectly): subjects may contribute any integer amount from 0 to 20 tokens; they are not forced only to contribute all or nothing (p. 5).  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying this parameter?  
  – No. It remains a continuous contribution choice from 0 to 20. No discussion of changing that to be all or nothing.

5. Is the contribution default?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. There is no mention of a “default” contribution mechanism.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying a contribution default?  
  – No mention.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. Each token contributed raises each group member’s payoff by 0.5 Guilders (p. 5). Thus, the MPCR is 0.5.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying the MPCR on the punishment treatment effect?  
  – No. The MPCR is fixed at 0.5 throughout. The paper does not vary it nor predict how changes in the MPCR would affect punishment.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. Punishing another player by 1 punishment point costs the punisher 1 Guilder (p. 6).  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying that cost?  
  – No. It is fixed at 1 Guilder in all sessions. The paper does not discuss changing it.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. Each punishment point imposed reduces the target’s payoff by 2 Guilders (p. 6).  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying punishment magnitude?  
  – No. It is held constant at 2; there is no discussion of changing it.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. There is no mention of any peer‐to‐peer “reward” mechanism.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying a reward option?  
  – No mention.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. Not discussed at all, since no reward mechanism is used.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying a reward cost?  
  – No mention.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward)  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. Rewards are never used, so no mention of reward magnitude.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying the reward magnitude?  
  – No mention.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Indirectly yes: since it is a one‐shot game, players know there is only that single round. They do not hide this.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying whether the number of rounds is known?  
  – No. The design is only one‐shot, with no variation.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained or lost each round)?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – They do see how much each person in their group contributed before punishment, and at the end they see how contributions translated into payoffs (p. 6–7). However, the paper does not systematically vary how or whether these outcomes are displayed.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying this parameter?  
  – No. They mention only one information condition.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – The paper does not explicitly say whether punishee identity information is revealed or kept hidden.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying punisher‐identification?  
  – No mention.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. There is no reward stage, so it never arises.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying whether rewarders are identified?  
  – No mention.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?  
• The paper does not use “group efficiency” (i.e., total/group payoff divided by the maximum possible) as a key outcome. The main dependent variables are: (1) punishment assigned, (2) self‐reported anger, (3) self‐reported guilt, and (4) contribution levels. Although the authors do record “payoff” for each individual, they do not report or analyze “efficiency” in the sense of total or average payoff relative to a maximum.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• The paper explicitly mentions five of them in its design: (1) number of players (=3), (2) number of rounds (=1, one‐shot), (6) MPCR (=0.5), (7) punishment cost (=1 Guilder), and (8) punishment magnitude (=2 Guilders).  
• The other ten parameters are either not mentioned or not relevant to their design.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• None. The paper does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters; they hold those five mentioned parameters fixed. Consequently, the authors do not provide any effect‐size estimates (or predictions) for changes in those parameters on punishment or on any other outcome variable.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
• The paper provides no direct evidence about group efficiency and does not analyze how varying those 15 parameters might affect efficiency. Hence, from this text alone, there is little basis for making predictions about efficiency. The results focus on punishment, anger, guilt, and contribution levels, not on total payoff or efficiency. Accordingly, there is almost no way to predict how systematically altering the listed parameters would change the punishment treatment’s effect on group efficiency.

Abstract: Communities often rely on sanctioning to induce public goods contributions. Past studies focus on how external agencies or peer sanctioning induce cooperation. In this article, we focus instead on the role played by centralized authorities, internal to the community. Combining lab-in-the-field experiments with observational data on 1,541 Ugandan farmers from 50 communities, we demonstrate the positive effect of internal centralized sanctioning authorities on cooperative behavior. We show that deference to authority in the controlled setting predicts cooperative behavior in the farmers natural environment, in which they face a similar social dilemma.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter account of what (if anything) the paper says regarding each of the 15 listed parameters and whether it discusses (a) the specific value used (if any) and (b) any predictions about how systematically varying that parameter would affect the punishment treatment effect. Throughout, “punishment treatment effect” refers to the effect of adding a centralized‐authority punishment regime on group outcomes. Note that the paper’s main outcome of interest is contribution (and sometimes cooperation in the farmers’ real‐life setting), rather than group efficiency (total or average payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff).

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players
   • Discussed?  
     – The paper does mention that, on average, 30 members from each farmer association took part in the experiment. However, it does not specify the exact size of each interacting group in the public goods game, nor does it say it varied that number of players.  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect?  
     – The paper does not systematically vary or make predictions about changing the number of players.

2) Number of rounds
   • Discussed?  
     – The experiment uses six rounds in total: two “preliminary” rounds without a monitor, followed by four rounds under the assigned/elected monitor condition.  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect?  
     – The paper does not vary the total number of rounds nor discuss how changing the number of rounds would affect punishment outcomes or efficiency.

3) Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussed?  
     – The paper states that participants were not allowed to talk to one another. There is no mention of having or enabling a “chat.”  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect?  
     – The paper does not systematically vary or discuss enabling chat.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussed?  
     – Contributions in the experiment range from 0 to 10 MUs in integer steps. Thus, it is not “all or nothing.”  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect?  
     – The paper does not vary whether contributions must be all or none, nor does it predict how imposing an all‐or‐nothing rule would affect punishment or efficiency.

5) Is the contribution default?
   • Discussed?  
     – The experiment does not use any “default” that automatically allocates part of one’s endowment. Participants freely decide how many of their 10 MUs to contribute.  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect?  
     – The paper does not discuss or vary a “default contribution” rule.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Discussed?  
     – The public good’s total is doubled and then divided evenly among the group, so the multiplier is effectively 2.  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect?  
     – The paper does not systematically vary the multiplier nor discuss any effect of doing so.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussed?  
     – The paper says the monitor pays 1 MU for each punishment imposed.  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect?  
     – The paper fixes that cost at 1 MU and does not evaluate how varying it would change the punishment effect.

8) Punishment magnitude
   • Discussed?  
     – Punishment deducts 3 MUs from the punished player each time it is imposed.  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect?  
     – The paper does not vary the 3‐MU deduction nor predict the impact of changing it.

9) Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussed?  
     – No rewards are used; the paper focuses only on punishment.  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect?  
     – Not mentioned at all.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Discussed?  
     – Not applicable; there is no reward mechanism in the study.  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect?  
     – Not mentioned.

11) Reward magnitude
   • Discussed?  
     – Not applicable; there is no reward mechanism in the study.  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect?  
     – Not mentioned.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
   • Discussed?  
     – The experiment proceeds for six rounds, but the paper does not report whether participants knew in advance that it would end exactly at six.  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect?  
     – No systematic variation or predictions about end‐round knowledge appear in the paper.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much peers gained or lost)?
   • Discussed?  
     – The experiment displays each contribution (lowest to highest) on a public board, but does not attach identities to each contribution. It does not specifically say whether players see each other’s final payoffs, only that they see the distribution of contributions.  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect?  
     – The paper does not vary how much information is shown, nor predict how changing that display would alter the punishment treatment effect.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Discussed?  
     – Because there is a single monitor, everyone knows that it is the monitor who punishes. The paper notes monitors stand in front and point out (publicly) which contribution levels will be punished, but do not name the specific players.  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect?  
     – The paper does not vary whether the punisher’s identity is hidden or revealed; there is no discussion of how such variation would affect outcomes.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Discussed?  
     – Not applicable; there is no reward mechanism in the experiment.  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect?  
     – Not mentioned.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Summary

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   – The paper does not report or analyze “efficiency” (i.e., total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff) as a dependent variable. Instead, the authors measure:  
     • Contribution (the amount each participant allocates to the public good).  
     • Cooperation in the real‐life farmer groups (e.g., how much of one’s harvest is sold collectively).  
   – Those measures differ from efficiency because they focus on how much is contributed or sold via the group, rather than on payoff maximization ratios.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – The paper explicitly gives or clarifies values for:  
     (1) Number of players (mentioned but not varied),  
     (2) Number of rounds (fixed at six, not varied),  
     (3) Chat (not allowed),  
     (7) Punishment cost = 1 MU,  
     (8) Punishment magnitude = 3 MUs,  
     (13) Peer contributions are revealed (distribution only),  
     (14) Everyone knows the punisher is the single monitor.  
   – For the remaining parameters (4, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 12, 15), either they do not arise at all or they are described only indirectly (e.g., “contribution is not all‐or‐nothing”); none is systematically manipulated.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   – None of the 15 parameters is systematically varied in the paper. They introduce punishment in two ways (random vs. elected monitor), but that manipulation does not align with any of the 15 parameters listed above (it is about whether the central punisher is chosen by lottery or by vote). Hence the paper does not provide systematic variation or effect‐size estimates for any of the 15 parameters.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper’s content, what would they be?  
   – The paper does not provide information or theory on varying those 15 parameters one by one, especially not with regard to efficiency. Its main finding is that introducing an internal‐authority punisher—and, in particular, electing that authority—raises contributions. The authors focus on contributions, not efficiency per se. Consequently, the paper offers little basis for predicting how systematically changing those 15 parameters (e.g., altering punishment cost or changing the number of rounds) would affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.  
   – Beyond noting that punishment (especially from an elected monitor) increases contributions, no direct discussions of efficiency or parameter variations appear. Therefore, the text does not enable firm predictions about those parameters’ or their interactions’ influence on efficiency.  

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Authors: Bingham, PM
Author Full Names: Bingham, PM
Article Title: Human uniqueness: A general theory
Keywords Plus: SOUTHERN-CALIFORNIA; RECIPROCAL ALTRUISM; TOOL-USE; EVOLUTION; ORIGINS; SPEARS; PUNISHMENT; COMPLEXITY; GRIPS; HAND
Abstract: The extensive, persistent ecological dominance of humans is unprecedented. We display a highly derived social adaptation involving uniquely extensive cooperation among nonclose Kin. Further, humans possess adaptive capabilities, including language, high cognitive function, and technological virtuosity not previously seen on this planet. Moreover, this suite of properties emerged and was refined very rapidly on a geological time scale. These diverse features of humans present what is referred to as the human uniqueness problem. A theoretical interpretation of these phenomena is one of the largest remaining challenges to the scientific enterprise. While many interpretations have been proposed-several containing important individual insights-none has yet proven robust or complete. A straightforward resolution of the human uniqueness problem is proposed. It is argued that coalitional enforcement is necessary and sufficient to allow extensive nonkin cooperation, leading to all major elements of human uniqueness. Coalitional enforcement arose uniquely in humans when the animals that founded the Home clade acquired the ability to kill or injure conspecifics from a substantial distance. This resulted from the evolution of hominid virtuosity at accurate, high-momentum throwing and clubbing; previously supposed to be adaptations for hunting, predator defense or individual aggression. No previous animal could reliably kill or injure conspecifics remotely. This ability dramatically reduced the individual cost of punishing noncooperative behavior by allowing these costs to be distributed among multiple cooperators. The capacity for coalitional enforcement drove the evolution of a cooperative social adaptation stably and autocatalytically from the origin of incipient Home about 2 million years ago through to the present moment-including socially supported, ultimately spectacular refinements in weaponry and social monitoring with attendant increases in efficiency of coalitional enforcement and thus in the extent of human cooperation. Its details rendered this evolutionary process very rapid. This theory is believed to be robust and relatively complete. For example, coalitional enforcement is necessary and sufficient to allow for the evolution of language in an ape. Further, given the likely functional organization of the ancestral vertebrate mind, the coalitional enforcement hypothesis predicts, in addition to genetic information the emergence of a second stream of design information in Home, susceptible to Darwinian selection. A novel source of design information has long been suspected on empirical and intuitive grounds to be responsible for the uniquely high level of human adaptive sophistication. The unprecedented cognitive power of human minds is also predicted by these implications of the theory. Lastly, the cognitive explosion associated with the relatively recent appearance of Behaviorally modern humans is predicted by the theory, as is the increasing size of human political units. The coalitional enforcement hypothesis and its immediate implications now enable the formerly elusive unification of diverse fields of study, including human biology, psychology, linguistics, paleontology, archaeology, anthropology, history, and economics.
