Below I go through the 15 design features one‐by-one and state, for each, what the paper actually says and whether it contains any prediction about **systematically varying** that feature and its consequence for a punishment treatment effect.  Whenever numbers or qualitative directions can be read directly from the text I quote them; otherwise I report “not mentioned”.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
--------------------------------------------------------------------

1.  Number of players  
    • Mentioned?  Yes.  The paper repeatedly contrasts a 1-versus-1 encounter with 10-versus-1 and 100-versus-1 “punisher-to-target” ratios (section 1c, Lanchester’s Law).  
    • Value(s) given?  Examples: 1, 10, 100 punishers.  
    • Prediction from systematic variation?  Yes, for *risk to a punisher*, not for efficiency.  
      – Moving from a 1:1 to a 10:1 ratio “reduces the risk of disability or death to any individual punisher to less than 1 %”.  
      – With a 100:1 ratio the risk falls to “less than one in 10 000”.  
      – The paper does **not** translate this into group efficiency or monetary pay-off.

2.  Number of rounds  
    • Mentioned?  No.  
    • Systematic-variation prediction?  No.

3.  Chat enabled?  
    • Mentioned?  No.  
    • Prediction?  No.

4.  All-or-nothing contribution?  
    • Mentioned?  No.  
    • Prediction?  No.

5.  Contribution default / “take” frame?  
    • Mentioned?  No.  
    • Prediction?  No.

6.  Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
    • Mentioned?  No.  
    • Prediction?  No.

7.  Punishment *cost* to impose one unit  
    • Mentioned?  Yes, qualitatively.  Section 1a uses a toy example: a co-operator is “willing to incur up to incrementally less than 3 units” of punishment cost in one scenario, <1 unit in another.  
    • Prediction from systematic variation?  Only the qualitative statement that distributing the cost across many punishers “profoundly” lowers individual cost and thereby makes punishment feasible.  No numerical dose–response or efficiency effect is provided.

8.  Punishment *magnitude* (damage done per unit)  
    • Mentioned?  Yes (must exceed benefits of parasitism), but only as a logical requirement.  No table, figure, or numerical gradient.  
    • Systematic-variation prediction?  No quantitative prediction; no link to efficiency.

9.  Reward enabled?  
10. Reward cost?  
11. Reward magnitude?  
    • Mentioned?  “Reward” is scarcely used; the argument is about punishment.  No treatment of enabling rewards or their cost/magnitude.  
    • Prediction?  No.

12.  Are the total number of rounds known?  
    • Mentioned?  No.  
    • Prediction?  No.

13.  Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mentioned?  No.  
    • Prediction?  No.

14.  Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
    • Mentioned?  Not directly.  Coalition punishment is described as *public* and collective, but the paper never manipulates anonymity, so no systematic prediction exists.

15.  Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
    • Mentioned?  No.  
    • Prediction?  No.


--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables actually used in the paper  
    • The paper never measures “group efficiency” (total pay-off ÷ maximum pay-off).  
    • Outcomes it does analyse are:  
      – Individual *risk* (probability of death or injury while punishing)  
      – Feasibility of stable *cooperation* (tertiary mutualism)  
      – Size of coalitions  
      – Evolutionary persistence of parasitism vs. cooperation  
    These are logically related to, but not identical with, economic efficiency.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
    • 1 (number of players / punisher-to-target ratio)  
    • 7 (punishment cost)  
    • 8 (punishment magnitude)  
    → 3 of 15 are mentioned at all; the other 12 are absent.

C.  For how many parameters is an effect of *systematic variation* on a punishment treatment reported?  
    • Only parameter 1 (size of the punishing coalition) is explicitly varied in examples that yield a numerical effect on *risk*.  
    • No parameter is linked to changes in *efficiency* or any economic pay-off measure.  
    So the answer is “1 parameter, and only for risk, not for efficiency”.

D.  Predicting the punishment treatment effect on efficiency **solely from this paper**  
    • Larger groups of punishers (parameter 1) should reduce the individual cost of punishment, which *may* let cooperation rise and therefore could raise efficiency; the paper does not quantify the magnitude for pay-offs.  
    • Lower individual punishment cost (parameter 7) should have the same qualitative direction.  
    • Bigger punishment magnitude (parameter 8) must exceed the benefit of free-riding; if it does, cooperation is stable.  Again the effect on efficiency is only implied, not computed.  
    • For the remaining 12 parameters the paper gives no basis at all for prediction.

In short, the article is a broad evolutionary theory piece; it is not an experimental public-goods-game paper.  Only the punisher-to-target ratio is explored numerically, and even there the outcome is individual *risk*, not group efficiency.  Therefore almost no direct, data-driven prediction about how the 15 laboratory design parameters would change the punishment treatment effect on efficiency can be extracted from this text.
reference_APA: Bingham, PM (1999). Human uniqueness: A general theory. QUARTERLY REVIEW OF BIOLOGY.

Article Title: Rewards and sanctions and the provision of public goods in one-shot settings
Author Keywords: public goods; rewards; sanctions
Abstract: A burgeoning literature in experimental studies of the Voluntary Contribution Mechanism focuses on the ability of institutions that allow the monitoring, sanctioning, and/or rewarding of others to facilitate cooperation. In this paper rewards and sanctions are examined in a one-shot VCM setting that so far has been unexplored in the literature. The study finds that while some subjects are willing to reward and sanction others at a personal cost, the opportunity to reward or sanction is ineffective in facilitating cooperation relative to previous experiments in which a repeated game environment is employed. The study also compares behavior in an environment in which the imposition of rewards and sanctions is certain to an environment in which imposition is uncertain. The expected value of the reward or sanction is kept constant across environments to focus simply on the effect of uncertainty about imposition. Uncertainty does not change behavior in a significant way, either in the level of cooperation or the willingness of individuals to impose rewards or sanctions.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter review, drawn strictly from the content of the Walker & Halloran paper, regarding (1) whether each parameter is mentioned and what value(s) it takes if so, and (2) whether the paper discusses any systematic variation of that parameter on the “punishment treatment effect,” especially as it relates to efficiency (actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff of a fully cooperative group). Any references to “the paper” below refer solely to the text you provided (“Rewards and Sanctions and the Provision of Public Goods in One‐Shot Settings”).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each group has exactly 4 players (p. 3, p. 5).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The experiments use strictly four‐person groups with no variation in group size. No effect on punishment treatment (or efficiency) is reported as a function of changing the number of players.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned? Yes. The experiment focuses on one‐shot settings; although subjects make decisions in “five decision situations,” each situation is itself one‐shot (p. 4).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not compare multiple‐round to single‐round environments. It does not study how varying the number of rounds affects punishment treatment or efficiency.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not discuss any form of real‐time chat or open communication among participants.  
   • Systematically varied? No mention of communication treatments; hence, no effect on punishment or efficiency is reported.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned? No. Each subject can allocate any number (0 to 10) of “blue” tokens to the public good. There is no forced “all or nothing.”  
   • Systematically varied? Not discussed; not manipulated.

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., players move tokens back to their hand)?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not address any default‐contribution mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied? Not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Mentioned? Yes. The per‐capita return is fixed at $0.50 (i.e., contributing 1 token yields $0.50 per person, or 2.00 total for the four‐person group) (p. 4–5).  
   • Systematically varied? No. It remains constant at 0.50, and the paper does not report manipulating that factor or its effect on punishment.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned? Yes, implicitly. Each “green” token used for punishment costs the punisher an opportunity to earn $0.20 in their private account (p. 5–6).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The cost of sacrificing a green token is always the same (20 cents). The paper does not discuss systematically altering the punishment cost or its direct effect on efficiency.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from the punished player)
   • Mentioned? Yes.  
     – Certain Sanction: Each green token lowers the other’s payoff by $0.20.  
     – Uncertain Sanction: Each green token has a 50% chance of lowering the other’s payoff by $0.40 and a 50% chance of doing nothing (p. 5–6). The expected deduction is $0.20.  
   • Systematically varied? Only in terms of “certain” vs. “uncertain,” but the expected magnitude in both cases is still $0.20. The paper finds no significant difference in efficiency when moving from certain to uncertain sanctions (Table 5, p. 13). Therefore, although these two variants exist, they are not shown to systematically affect the punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency in a statistically meaningful way.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned? Yes. They have Baseline (no reward or sanction), Certain Reward, and Uncertain Reward treatments (and similarly for sanctions).  
   • Systematically varied? Yes, in the sense that some conditions allow rewards while others do not. However, it is not studied in combination with a separate punishment condition (i.e., all “punishment” treatments are separate from all “reward” treatments). The paper finds that adding a reward mechanism does not improve efficiency relative to the one‐shot baseline (Table 5, p. 13–14).

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Mentioned? Yes, analogous to punishment cost. Each green token used to reward another gives up $0.20 in the rewarder’s private account (p. 5–6).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The cost remains 20 cents. No systematic variation is tested or reported.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded to the rewarded player)
   • Mentioned? Yes.  
     – Certain Reward: Each green token increases the target’s payoff by $0.20.  
     – Uncertain Reward: Each green token has a 50% chance of increasing the target’s payoff by $0.40 (and 50% chance of no effect), so expected magnitude = $0.20 (p. 5–6).  
   • Systematically varied? Only in terms of “certain” vs. “uncertain.” The expected value remains $0.20, and the paper concludes that this manipulation does not systematically boost efficiency (Table 5).

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
   • Mentioned? They are told decisions are one‐shot for each “decision situation,” so yes, it is known there is no repeat game within each situation.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not compare known vs. unknown horizons; there is no multi‐round design to manipulate in the main one‐shot comparisons.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much peers gained/lost)?
   • Mentioned? Partially. After first‐stage contributions, each subject sees everyone’s individual contributions and their own payoff (p. 5). However, they do not observe how others used rewards or sanctions in prior situations.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper keeps that feedback structure constant.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Mentioned? They never learn the identities of who punished or rewarded them (p. 5, note 6).  
   • Systematically varied? No. Not manipulated.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is?
   • Mentioned? Same as punishment: identities are not revealed (p. 5, note 6).  
   • Systematically varied? No. Not manipulated.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
END‐OF‐RESPONSE SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • Yes. The paper explicitly measures “allocative efficiency,” defined as total (or average) subject earnings relative to the maximum possible (Table 5, p. 13). The authors also track other dependent variables, primarily contribution levels (how many tokens each subject contributed to the public good) and the use of rewards/sanctions. They note that efficiency can differ from mere cooperation or contribution because punishment or reward imposes costs that lower total payoff.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form (even if not systematically varied):  
     1 (Number of players), 2 (Number of rounds), 6 (MPCR), 7 (Punishment cost), 8 (Punishment magnitude), 9 (Reward enabled?), 10 (Reward cost), 11 (Reward magnitude), 13 (Peer outcomes shown), 14 (Punisher identity known?), 15 (Rewarder identity known?).  
   • Not explicitly mentioned at all or effectively absent from discussion:  
     3 (Chat), 4 (All or nothing?), 5 (Contribution default?), 12 (Known vs. unknown number of rounds) – with the caveat that the paper simply treats each decision situation as a single known shot.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • The only systematic manipulations discussed are the presence vs. absence of sanctioning (Parameter 9 in reverse: “whether punishment is enabled or not,” though it is typically introduced as a separate treatment) and the certainty vs. uncertainty of sanctions or rewards (Parameters 8 and 11).  
   • Even in these cases, the paper’s main finding for efficiency is that neither punishment nor reward (certain or uncertain) improves one‐shot efficiency relative to the baseline. They do show slight numerical differences (Table 5), but no statistically significant efficiency gains.

D. If you were to predict how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, based solely on the paper’s content, what would those predictions be?  
   • The paper suggests that, in a purely one‐shot environment, allowing punishment does not raise efficiency because people do not adjust first‐stage contributions in anticipation of being punished (and imposing sanctions reduces total payoffs).  
   • Varying certainty vs. uncertainty of punishment (and similarly reward) does not yield consistent differences in either contributions or overall efficiency.  
   • The other parameters (e.g., group size, communication, cost of punishment, etc.) are not tested—so little or no prediction can be made from this paper alone about how systematically changing those would influence punishment’s net effect on efficiency.  

Based on this single paper, the overall conclusion is that punishment in a one‐shot public goods setting does not improve group efficiency, and changing the punishment/reward from certain to uncertain does not materially alter that finding. The authors do not provide results for other parameter variations beyond what they implemented.
reference_APA: Walker, JM & Halloran, MA (2004). Rewards and sanctions and the provision of public goods in one-shot settings. EXPERIMENTAL ECONOMICS.

Below, each of the 15 parameters is treated in turn.

For every parameter I state  
(i) whether the paper says anything at all about it and, if so, its value in the experiment, and  
(ii) whether the authors **systematically vary** that parameter (or observe natural variation in it) and, if so, what quantitative or qualitative effect they report on the *punishment treatment effect* (i.e. the difference that allowing punishment makes, especially to group efficiency).  
Whenever a parameter is not mentioned or not varied I say so explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1. Number of players  
(i) Mentioned. Groups are always of size 4.  
(ii) Never varied; no prediction or estimate of how changing group size would alter the effect of punishment on any outcome.

2. Number of rounds  
(i) Mentioned. Each session has 25 periods; subjects know this.  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction of how a different horizon would change the punishment effect.

3. Chat between players  
(i) Mentioned. “They were unable to communicate with others.” (p. 7)  
(ii) Not varied; no effect estimated.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
(i) Implicitly mentioned. Subjects choose any integer 0–10 to contribute, so the game is *not* all-or-nothing.  
(ii) Not varied; no effect estimated.

5. Contribution default / endowment moved back from the public fund  
(i) Not discussed. Only the standard “how much of your 10 tokens do you *contribute*” decision is used.  
(ii) Not applicable.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
(i) Stated. MPCR = 0.4 (group multiplier 1.6).  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
(i) Stated. It costs $0.25 to make the target lose $1.  
(ii) Fixed; no systematic variation or prediction.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine on target)  
(i) Stated. Each “point” of punishment reduces the target’s payoff by $1.  
(ii) Fixed; no variation or prediction.

9. Whether a reward option exists  
(i) Stated. *No reward stage* is available.  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
(i) Not applicable because no reward option is present.  
(ii) Not applicable.

12. Is the number of rounds common knowledge?  
(i) Yes. Subjects are told there will be 25 decisions.  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
(i) Yes. After the contribution stage each subject sees every other group member’s contribution; after the punishment stage final earnings are shown.  
(ii) Presentation of information is identical in all sessions; no variation.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
(i) Stated. Group members are labelled B–D, and the labels are randomly reassigned each period. Hence the punished player cannot identify the specific punisher.  
(ii) Fixed; no prediction.

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
(i) Not applicable (no rewards).  
(ii) Not applicable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables actually analysed  
– The paper’s core dependent variables are:
  • Individual contribution levels  
  • Punishment given and punishment received  
  • Changes in contribution from one period to the next  
  • Group earnings (occasionally referenced, but not tabulated)  

  “Efficiency” (total or average payoff divided by the cooperative optimum) is invoked in the *abstract* and in the discussion, but no efficiency measure or statistic is formally analysed in the results tables. Hence efficiency is conceptually present but not an outcome on which regressions are run.  

  Contribution and punishment are therefore distinct from efficiency in the reported analyses.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
11 of the 15 appear somewhere in the text: #1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 12, 13, 14.  
Parameters #5, 10, 11, 15 are not discussed (or are inapplicable).

C.  For how many parameters is the *effect of systematically varying the parameter* on the punishment treatment effect discussed?  
Zero. Every parameter is held constant across all sessions. The only experimental manipulation is *group-composition algorithms* (heterogeneous vs. homogeneous vs. random) which is **not** one of the 15 parameters listed. Consequently the paper makes no numerical or qualitative prediction of how changing any of the 15 parameters would alter the (hypothetical) difference between a “with-punishment” and a “without-punishment” condition.

D.  What predictions about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment treatment effect on efficiency can be drawn solely from this paper?  
Very few. Because none of the parameters is varied, the paper provides almost no direct evidence for how changing them would raise or lower efficiency when punishment is available. The only indirect hints are:  
– Perverse punishment (a behaviour, not a parameter) lowers earnings, so any parameter change that *increases* perverse punishment (e.g., making punishers identifiable, increasing fine-to-cost ratio, etc.) might reduce efficiency, but this is *not* analysed.  
– Conversely, punishment of low contributors raises their later contributions, suggesting that parameter changes which make such punishment cheaper or more effective *could* raise efficiency—but again this is speculative and not derived from systematic variation.

In short, the paper is informative about heterogeneity in *behaviour* under one fixed game structure, but it does not allow one to predict how the 15 design parameters listed would interact to change the efficiency impact of introducing punishment.

Authors: Cuesta, JA; Gracia-Lázaro, C; Ferrer, A; Moreno, Y; Sánchez, A

Article Title: Reputation drives cooperative behaviour and network formation in human groups
Keywords Plus: PROMOTE COOPERATION; EVOLUTION
Abstract: Cooperativeness is a defining feature of human nature. Theoreticians have suggested several mechanisms to explain this ubiquitous phenomenon, including reciprocity, reputation, and punishment, but the problem is still unsolved. Here we show, through experiments conducted with groups of people playing an iterated Prisoner's Dilemma on a dynamic network, that it is reputation what really fosters cooperation. While this mechanism has already been observed in unstructured populations, we find that it acts equally when interactions are given by a network that players can reconfigure dynamically. Furthermore, our observations reveal that memory also drives the network formation process, and cooperators assort more, with longer link lifetimes, the longer the past actions record. Our analysis demonstrates, for the first time, that reputation can be very well quantified as a weighted mean of the fractions of past cooperative acts and the last action performed. This finding has potential applications in collaborative systems and e-commerce.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter check of what, if anything, this paper says about systematically varying each of the 15 public‐goods‐game parameters (as listed in your question) and how that might affect a “punishment treatment effect,” especially with respect to efficiency. Throughout, note that the paper reports on an iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma with dynamic rewiring (and refers to breaking a link as “punishing a defector”), rather than a standard public goods game with costly punishment. Consequently, many of the 15 parameters simply do not appear in the paper at all.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   – Does the paper discuss this parameter?
     The authors do report the sizes of the groups in their experiments (17, 19, 21, 23, 24, and 25 participants).  
   – Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying this parameter on the punishment treatment effect (for efficiency or any other outcome)?
     No. Although different sessions had different group sizes, the paper does not present or analyze any systematic variation in group size on punishment or efficiency.

2. Number of rounds
   – Does the paper discuss this parameter?
     Yes. All experiments ran for 25 rounds, but participants were not told the exact total number of rounds.  
   – Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying the number of rounds?
     No. The paper does not compare treatments with different total rounds; it never examines how changing the round count affects punishment or efficiency.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   – Does the paper discuss this parameter?
     No mention of any real‐time communication or chat among participants.  
   – Any predictions?
     No.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   – Does the paper discuss this parameter?
     The study’s game is a binary choice each round: cooperate or defect. The authors do not frame this as “all or nothing contributions” to a public good; rather, it is a Prisoner’s Dilemma.  
   – Any predictions?
     No.

5. Is there a contribution default?
   – Does the paper discuss this parameter?
     No. Players make a binary cooperate/defect choice.  
   – Any predictions?
     No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   – Does the paper discuss this parameter?
     The payoff structure is 7 points for each cooperating neighbor (if one cooperates) or 10 points for each cooperating neighbor (if one defects). It is not described as an MPCR or multiplied payoff in a public‐goods sense.  
   – Any predictions about systematically varying it?
     No. The authors do not vary these payoff numbers across treatments.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   – Does the paper discuss this parameter?
     They treat “punishment” as breaking a link to a defector, but no explicit cost is paid by the punisher. There is no separate, monetary “punishment cost” anywhere.  
   – Any predictions?
     No.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a punished player)
   – Does the paper discuss this parameter?
     No. Again, “punishment” occurs via link removal, not by deducting a punished player’s payoff.  
   – Any predictions?
     No.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   – Does the paper discuss this parameter?
     No. The experiment only mentions cooperation versus defection and link rewiring; it does not include “rewards.”  
   – Any predictions?
     No.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    – Does the paper discuss this parameter?
      No. There is no reward mechanism.  
    – Any predictions?
      No.

11. Reward magnitude
    – Does the paper discuss this parameter?
      No.  
    – Any predictions?
      No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
    – Does the paper discuss this parameter?
      Yes. Specifically, participants did not know the total number of rounds (they only knew that each session would end at some point).  
    – Does the paper discuss systematically varying whether rounds are known?
      No. They do not vary this across treatments, so there is no analysis of its effect.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (e.g., how much peers gained/lost each round)?
    – Does the paper discuss this parameter?
      Participants do not see exact payoffs for others. Instead, they see (depending on the treatment) 0, 1, 3, or 5 of a given player’s past actions (C or D). The paper calls this “memory.”  
    – Does the paper give predictions or results about systematically varying it?
      The main systematic variation in the paper is the amount of memory (m = 0, 1, 3, or 5). However, the paper focuses on how that variation affects cooperation rates and network structure. It does not frame “punishment treatment effect” as a separate effect on group efficiency. Rather, it finds that when memory > 0, players punish defectors more effectively (by cutting links), leading to higher observed cooperation rates—but not discussed as “group efficiency.”

14. When a player is punished, do they know who punished them?
    – Does the paper discuss this parameter?
      The experiment does not say whether a cut link is labeled with the identity of who cut it. There is no explicit mention that the “punisher” is revealed.  
    – Any predictions?
      No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who rewarded them?
    – Does the paper discuss this parameter?
      There is no reward mechanism in the paper, so this is not discussed at all.  
    – Any predictions?
      No.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are its dependent variables and how are these different?
   • The paper does not present group efficiency—the ratio of total payoff to the maximal possible payoff—as a measured outcome.  
   • The primary dependent variables are (1) fraction of cooperative actions (the cooperation rate), (2) network connectivity (fraction of actual links relative to all possible links), and (3) link‐rewiring decisions (e.g., fraction of link proposals accepted, link lifetimes, etc.). These are conceptually different from “efficiency,” as they do not track total payoff relative to any maximum.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?
   • Mentioned in some form:  
     – Parameter 1 (number of players) is reported but not systematically varied with respect to punishment.  
     – Parameter 2 (number of rounds) is fixed at 25 and unknown to participants.  
     – Parameter 12 (whether the number of rounds is known) is discussed: it was not known.  
     – Parameter 13 (information display about peers) is partly addressed via “memory” (showing a small record of C/D actions).  
   • None of the others (3,4,5,6,7,8,9,10,11,14,15) are mentioned or manipulated in any standard “punishment in public goods” sense.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when systematically varied?
   • Strictly speaking, none. The study does systematically vary “memory” (m = 0, 1, 3, 5), but the authors neither use “punishment treatment effect” in the standard sense of a public‐goods punishment cost, nor do they measure group efficiency.  
   • Therefore, there is no direct discussion of systematic parameter variation on “punishment treatment effect” for efficiency or any other payoff measure.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper, what would they be?
   • Because the paper does not measure or mention group efficiency, nor does it detail costs and magnitudes of punishment or reward, almost no firm predictions can be made about how these 15 parameters would alter a punishment effect on efficiency. The paper shows only that giving players information on past actions (a “memory” parameter) can sustain cooperation through cutting links; but it does not connect that outcome explicitly to any efficiency measure.
reference_APA: Cuesta, Jose A., Gracia-Lazaro, Carlos, Ferrer, Alfredo, Moreno, Yamir & Sanchez, Angel (2015). Reputation drives cooperative behaviour and network formation in human groups. SCIENTIFIC REPORTS.

Authors: Szolnoki, A; Chen, XJ
Author Full Names: Szolnoki, Attila; Chen, Xiaojie
Article Title: Alliance formation with exclusion in the spatial public goods game
Keywords Plus: INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; COOPERATION; REWARD; PUNISHMENT; REPUTATION; BEHAVIOR
Abstract: Detecting defection and alarming partners about the possible danger could be essential to avoid being exploited. This act, however, may require a huge individual effort from those who take this job, hence such a strategy seems to be unfavorable. But structured populations can provide an opportunity where a largely unselfish excluder strategy can form an effective alliance with other cooperative strategies, hence they can sweep out defection. Interestingly, this alliance is functioning even at the extremely high cost of exclusion where the sole application of an exclusion strategy would be harmful otherwise. These results may explain why the emergence of extreme selfless behavior is not necessarily against individual selection but could be the result of an evolutionary process.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter accounting of what the paper does (and does not) say. As requested, all statements refer strictly to the content of the paper itself (Szolnoki & Chen, 2017) and its figures and tables.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Discussed? Yes (the paper arranges players on an L×L grid, and it varies L to check for finite-size effects).  
   • Systematic variation for the “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency or any other dependent variable?  
     – The paper does vary L, but it investigates the probability that a given strategy eventually takes over, or the coexistence of multiple strategies. It does not measure or report any “efficiency” outcome (actual payoff vs. maximum possible).  
     – No numerical effect size on a punishment treatment effect is given.  
   • Dependent variables measured instead of efficiency? The fraction of surviving strategies or the probability of strategy extinction.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Discussed? No. The model is an evolutionary (continuous-updating) game with no fixed number of rounds.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussed? No. There is no mention of communication or “chat.”  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Discussed? Yes, in effect. A cooperator contributes c = 1; a defector contributes 0. The paper uses these fixed values and does not study partial contributions.  
   • Systematic variation for the punishment treatment effect?  
     – No. The paper does not vary this feature and does not link it to any efficiency measure.  

5. Is the contribution “default” if players move endowment from the public fund to themselves?  
   • Discussed? No. Contributions are always c = 1 (cooperator) or 0 (defector).  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   • Discussed? Yes. The paper calls this the “synergy factor” r, and it is a primary parameter under study.  
   • Systematic variation for punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
     – r is varied (e.g., r = 3.8 vs. r = 2) to see if cooperators (including punishers or excluders) can survive. However, the paper reports final fractions of each strategy or the probability that defectors die out, not an efficiency ratio.  
     – No numeric effect on a “punishment treatment effect” for efficiency is provided.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussed? Yes, in effect. The paper calls this cost γ (gamma), describing the extra cost punishers pay when defectors are nearby.  
   • Systematic variation for the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
     – The paper discusses how varying γ can eliminate or favor punishers, but does not measure or report any treatment effect on “efficiency.”  
     – No numeric effect size on efficiency is provided.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a punished player)  
   • Discussed? Yes; the paper’s “fine” β (beta) is the maximum penalty defectors receive when punishers surround them.  
   • Systematic variation for the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
     – The paper explores how different β values help or hinder punisher strategies relative to defectors; it does not discuss or measure efficiency.  
     – No numeric effect size on efficiency is provided.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussed? No. The paper only studies punishment and exclusion strategies; there is no mention of rewards.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Discussed? No. Rewarding behavior does not appear in the study.  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a rewarded player)  
    • Discussed? No. Again, reward is not featured in the model.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    • Discussed? No. The paper sets up an evolutionary game with no mention of participants being informed of an end time.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much others gained or lost)?  
    • Discussed? No. While in the model each player’s payoff is used for imitative strategy updates, there is no discussion of displayed outcomes in an experimental sense. The paper does not systematically vary information disclosure.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Discussed? No. The paper does not address any identification of punishers.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Discussed? No. The model does not involve rewards at all.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total / average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • No. The main dependent variables discussed are the final fraction of each strategy in the population (e.g., fraction of defectors, punishers, excluders, cooperators) or the probability that defectors die out, not efficiency in terms of total payoff vs. maximum possible.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   • Mentioned:  
       (1) Number of players (via L×L, studying finite-size effects)  
       (4) Contribution is effectively all-or-nothing (c = 1 if cooperator)  
       (6) Marginal per capita return / synergy factor (r)  
       (7) Punishment cost (γ)  
       (8) Punishment magnitude (β)  
     That is 5 parameters in total.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None of the parameters are discussed with respect to an explicit “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” The paper never measures nor reports a ratio of actual total payoff to the maximum possible payoff. Instead, it examines final strategy frequencies and the probability of absorbing states. No numerical effect sizes on “efficiency” are provided.  

D. If you were to make predictions about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely from this paper’s content, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not measure nor define efficiency in the sense requested. It focuses on the survival/extinction of strategies, so it gives no direct basis for inferring changes in group payoff efficiency. Therefore, it provides little or no prediction on how those parameters (or their interactions) would alter a “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency. Any attempt to predict efficiency effects would go beyond what the authors report.

Authors: Drouvelis, M; Grosskopf, B
Author Full Names: Drouvelis, Michalis; Grosskopf, Brit
Article Title: The effects of induced emotions on pro-social behaviour
Author Keywords: Induced emotions; Anger; Happiness; Contribution; Punishment; Public goods experiments
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS; POSITIVE MOOD; PUNISHMENT; COOPERATION; INDUCTION; PROVISION; HAPPINESS; ANGER; LEAD
Abstract: Emotions are commonly experienced and expressed in human societies; however, their consequences on economic behaviour have received only limited attention. This paper investigates the effects of induced positive and negative emotions on cooperation and sanctioning behaviour in a one-shot voluntary contributions mechanism game, where personal and social interests are at odds. We concentrate on two specific emotions: anger and happiness. Our findings provide clear evidence that measures of social preferences are sensitive to subjects' current emotional states. Specifically, angry subjects contribute, on average, less than happy subjects and overall welfare as measured by average net earnings is lower when subjects are in an angry mood. We also find that how punishment is used is affected by moods: angry subjects punish harsher than happy subjects, ceteris paribus. These findings suggest that anger, when induced, can have a negative impact on economic behaviour. (C) 2015 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER–BY–PARAMETER CHECK

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  “Individuals randomly form groups of 3 members.”  
   • Systematic variation & predicted effect on punishment treatment effect? No.  The group size is fixed at 3; no predictions are offered about changing it.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  The game is explicitly “one-shot.”  
   • Systematic variation? No.

3. Is chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned? No.  The paper never refers to any messaging or chat option.  
   • Systematic variation? No.

4. Contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  Subjects choose any integer 0–20; hence contributions are continuous, not all-or-nothing.  
   • Systematic variation? No.

5. Contribution default / refund frame?  
   • Mentioned? No.  Players simply decide how many of their 20 tokens to contribute.  
   • Systematic variation? No.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  Each token contributed yields 0.5 ECU to every group member (MPCR = 0.5, group return = 1.5).  
   • Systematic variation? No.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  1 ECU per punishment point.  
   • Systematic variation? No.

8. Punishment magnitude (impact on target)  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  Each point removes 3 ECUs from the target.  
   • Systematic variation? No.

9. Is a reward option enabled?  
   • Mentioned? Yes—implicitly as “absent.”  Only costly punishment exists.  
   • Systematic variation? No.

10 & 11. Reward cost / reward magnitude  
   • Mentioned? No (because no reward option).  
   • Systematic variation? No.

12. Is the number of rounds known?  
   • Mentioned? Not directly, but subjects are told it is a one-shot game, hence they know when it ends.  
   • Systematic variation? No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  In Stage 2 “individuals are informed about the contributions of the other group members.”  
   • Systematic variation? No.

14. Is the punisher identified to the punished?  
   • Mentioned? No.  Identity disclosure is never discussed; standard anonymity is implied.  
   • Systematic variation? No.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
   • Not applicable (no rewards).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DEPENDENT VARIABLES USED IN THE PAPER

• “Contribution” – number of tokens transferred to the public good.  
• “Punishment assigned” – punishment points sent by a subject.  
• “Efficiency / overall welfare / average net earnings” – payoff after both stages, i.e., total group (or individual) earnings relative to the maximum.  
The paper repeatedly stresses that these are distinct: contributions measure provision; punishment measures sanctioning behaviour; earnings capture efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A.  Does the paper use group efficiency (total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
    Yes.  Average net earnings are analysed and explicitly referred to as “overall welfare” and “efficiency.”  Other dependent variables are contributions and punishment points.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
    8 of 15 are described: #1, #2, #4, #6, #7, #8, #12 (implicit), #13.  The remaining 7 are not mentioned (or are only implicitly absent, e.g., rewards).

C.  For which—and how many—of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when each parameter is systematically varied?  
    Zero.  None of the listed parameters are experimentally varied or analysed for their marginal impact on the punishment treatment effect for contributions, punishment usage, or efficiency.

D.  What predictions about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency can be made solely from this paper?  
    Very little.  Because every parameter in the list is held constant, the paper supplies no basis for quantitative or even directional predictions about changing group size, MPCR, punishment cost/magnitude, information structure, etc.  All observed differences in efficiency stem exclusively from the mood manipulation (anger vs. happiness) and from whether the punishment stage was announced—neither of which belongs to the 15 parameters in question.  Therefore, based solely on this paper, one cannot credibly predict how varying any of the 15 parameters (individually or interactively) would alter the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Authors: Delton, AW; Cosmides, L; Guemo, M; Robertson, TE; Tooby, J
Author Full Names: Delton, Andrew W.; Cosmides, Leda; Guemo, Marvin; Robertson, Theresa E.; Tooby, John
Article Title: The Psychosemantics of Free Riding: Dissecting the Architecture of a Moral Concept
Source Title: JOURNAL OF PERSONALITY AND SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY
Author Keywords: evolutionary psychology; cooperation; free riding; concepts; moral psychology
Keywords Plus: SOCIAL-EXCHANGE; COGNITIVE ADAPTATIONS; IMPRESSION-FORMATION; PUNITIVE SENTIMENT; EVOLUTION; COOPERATION; RECIPROCITY; PUNISHMENT; MODEL; SHUAR
Abstract: For collective action to evolve and be maintained by selection, the mind must be equipped with mechanisms designed to identify free riders individuals who do not contribute to a collective project but still benefit from it. Once identified, free riders must be either punished or excluded from future collective actions. But what criteria does the mind use to categorize someone as a free rider? An evolutionary analysis suggests that failure to contribute is not sufficient. Failure to contribute can occur by intention or accident, but the adaptive threat is posed by those who are motivated to benefit themselves at the expense of cooperators. In 6 experiments, we show that only individuals with exploitive intentions were categorized as free riders, even when holding their actual level of contribution constant (Studies 1 and 2). In contrast to an evolutionary model, rational choice and reinforcement theory suggest that different contribution levels (leading to different payoffs for their cooperative partners) should be key. When intentions were held constant, however, differences in contribution level were not used to categorize individuals as free riders, although some categorization occurred along a competence dimension (Study 3). Free rider categorization was not due to general tendencies to categorize (Study 4) or to mechanisms that track a broader class of intentional moral violations (Studies 5A and 5B). The results reveal the operation of an evolved concept with features tailored for solving the collective action problems faced by ancestral hunter-gatherers.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter discussion based solely on the content of the Markussen, Putterman, and Tyran paper (“Self-Organization for Collective Action: An Experimental Study of Voting on Sanction Regimes”) and its figures/tables. Each of the 15 parameters is listed in turn, indicating (1) whether the paper discusses or implements that parameter (including any value used) and (2) whether the paper makes predictions about the effect of systematically varying it on the punishment treatment effect for either efficiency or other dependent variables. Numerical effect sizes are included only where they can be inferred directly.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players
   • Discussed? The paper fixes the number of players at n = 5 in all sessions (see Section 3).  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no systematic variation in group size across treatments, and the paper does not predict how changing group size would alter the punishment treatment effect.  

2) Number of rounds
   • Discussed? Yes. Each phase consisted of 4 repeated periods. In most main treatments, there are 7 phases; in some robustness checks, 6 votes/phases. (Section 3)  
   • Systematically varied? Not in the sense of comparing different total lengths or different repeated games; the paper does not predict, in a structured way, how changing the total number of periods would affect the punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency.  

3) Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussed? No. There is no mention of free-form communication or “chat” being enabled.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussed? The paper allows contributions from 0 to 20 tokens (not merely all or none).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The experiment does not feature an all-or-nothing design.  

5) Is the contribution default?
   • Discussed? No. Each participant freely chooses how many tokens to contribute without a default rule.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Discussed? Yes. The MPCR is 0.4 (Section 3).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not explore different MPCR values, so it makes no predictions about the effect of systematically varying the MPCR on the punishment treatment effect.  

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussed? Yes, for informal (peer-to-peer) sanctions: it costs the punishing player 1 point to reduce the punished player’s payoff by either 4 points in the main treatments or 2 points in a robustness check. However, the “cost to impose” itself (1 point) is the same throughout; what varies is the ratio of that cost to the inflicted deduction.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper keeps the cost to the punisher at 1 point in all cases and does not formally vary that cost. Hence, it makes no predictions about how changing that cost alone (e.g., from 1 to 2) would affect the treatment effect.  

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed on them)
   • Discussed? Yes.  
       – Informal sanctions (IS): In the main experiment, each 1-point expenditure deducts 4 points from the target; in certain robustness checks, it deducts 2 points. (Section 5)  
       – Formal sanctions (FS): The parameter s = 0.8 or 0.4 (so that if someone allocates to the private account, they are fined s per coin). s = 0.8 is “deterrent,” s = 0.4 “non-deterrent.”  
   • Systematically varied? Yes, for formal sanctions (s = 0.4 or 0.8) and for informal sanctions (ratio 1:4 vs. 1:2).  
       – Effect (formal punishment, s): Higher s (0.8) is associated with higher contributions and, when “cheap” to implement (c = 2), yields higher average efficiency; when “expensive” (c = 8), efficiency suffers. The paper’s Figures 2–4 and related tables indicate that moving from 0.4 to 0.8 can raise contributions substantially but will not always raise efficiency if the fixed cost (c) is high.  
       – Effect (informal punishment, 4 vs. 2): With a ratio of 1:4, informal punishment is more “behaviorally deterrent.” Even when the ratio is 1:2, informal sanctions remain popular, though the paper does not give a single numerical effect size for how efficiency changes.    • Discussed? No. The design focuses on punishments only (formal and informal).

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Discussed? No. Rewards do not appear in the experiment.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)
    • Discussed? No.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Discussed? Yes. The game is finitely repeated, and participants know the structure.  
    • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not systematically alter the transparency of the endpoint.

    • Discussed? Yes. Players see others’ contribution decisions (and some information about punishments in the sense of total points of punishment received), but the paper does not vary the information condition.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?

    • Discussed? Not applicable. There is no reward mechanism in the design.

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned or fixed without systematic variation:  
       (1) Number of players (n = 5, not varied),  
       (2) Number of rounds (4 per phase, with 7 phases in main or 6 phases in some controls, not systematically varied as a treatment),  
       (3) No chat (fixed),  
       (4) Continuous contribution (not all-or-nothing),  
       (5) No contribution default,  
       (6) MPCR = 0.4 (fixed),  
       (7) Cost to impose 1 unit of peer punishment = 1 point (fixed),  
       (12) Rounds known to players (fixed),  
       (13) Peer outcomes are shown (fixed),  
       (14) Punisher’s identity is hidden (fixed).  
   • Systematically varied:  
       (8) Punishment magnitude: formal s = 0.8 (deterrent) vs. 0.4 (non-deterrent), and informal ratio 1:4 vs. 1:2 in robustness.  
       Also, for formal sanctions, a fixed cost c = 2 or c = 8 was systematically varied (though that fits under “cost of the scheme” more than under the 15 listed parameters, it does directly affect the “punishment treatment” condition).

       (9) Reward, (10) Reward cost, (11) Reward magnitude, and (15) Rewarder identity.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Parameter 8 (punishment magnitude) is systematically varied in two senses:  
       – Formal sanctions, going from s = 0.4 to s = 0.8, shows large increases in contributions and possible efficiency gains (especially if the scheme’s fixed cost is not too high).  
       – Informal sanctions in the robustness checks, going from a ratio of 1:4 down to 1:2, indicates that lower punishment strength can reduce the cost-effectiveness of peer punishment but does not eliminate its acceptance or its contribution effects.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper mainly highlights that:

     2) For informal punishment, lowering the effectiveness ratio from 1:4 to 1:2 still leaves peer punishment fairly popular, though its deterrent impact diminishes somewhat.  
     3) Other parameters (group size, number of rounds, knowledge of punisher identity, etc.) are not manipulated in this experiment, so little can be concluded from the paper itself about their effects on efficiency.

3. Chat (free communication)  
   – Not discussed at all.

4. All-or-nothing vs. continuous contribution  
   – Discussed?  Yes.  Section 3.1 models a discrete (all-or-nothing) choice {Cooperate, Defect}.  Section 3.2 extends this to a continuous effort level 0 ≤ p,q ≤ 1.  
   – Systematically varied?  The paper contrasts the two modelling styles but does not produce any comparative statics on the “punishment treatment effect” when one switches from discrete to continuous.  No numerical effect sizes are given.

5. Contribution default (endowment first placed in the public fund)  
   – Not mentioned.

6. MPCR / Multiplication factor (marginal return to one unit contributed)  
   – Closest analogue in the paper: the benefit parameter b (and sometimes the quadratic coefficients α₂, β₂, λ).  
   – Values mentioned: b = 10 or 8 in numeric examples (p. 19).  
   – Systematically varied?  Yes, but only qualitatively.  Propositions 4 and 5 state:  
        • “The higher profit the players can gain from the collaboration, the more collaboration effort they will contribute.”  
     No explicit efficiency or treatment-effect numbers are reported—only directional claims (↑b ⇒ ↑p*,q*).

7. Punishment cost to the person who punishes  
   – Not modelled.  Punishment is purely a deduction from the target; the punisher pays nothing.

8. Punishment magnitude (per-unit deduction suffered by the target)  
   – Modelled as δ (“social punishment”).  
   – Values/thresholds derived:  
        • Discrete model (Prop. 1): cooperation becomes the only evolutionarily stable equilibrium once δ ≥ c/2.  
        • Continuous model (Prop. 6 & Cor. 7): full cooperation when δ ≥ max{δ₁, δ₂} where closed-form expressions for δ₁, δ₂ are given in eqs. (17)–(18).  
   – Thus, the paper makes clear qualitative predictions: ↑δ moves the equilibrium from Defect (low efficiency) → Mixed → Cooperate (high efficiency).  No explicit “treatment effect on efficiency” numbers are computed, but the direction is unambiguous.

9. Whether a reward option is enabled  
10. Cost of rewarding  
11. Reward magnitude  
   – None of these three are ever mentioned; the models are punishment-only.

12. Whether the horizon is common knowledge  
   – Not discussed.

13. Whether peer outcomes are shown  
14. Whether the identity of a punisher is revealed  
15. Whether the identity of a rewarder is revealed  
   – None of these information-display parameters appear anywhere in the text, tables or figures.

SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Does the paper use group efficiency as a dependent variable?  
    • No.  Everything is expressed at the individual-payoff or equilibrium-strategy level (Π₁, Π₂, p*, q*).  
    • Dependent variables actually analysed: equilibrium effort levels (p,q); stability of the Nash equilibrium; individual expected payoffs.  “Efficiency” (total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff) is never computed.

B.  Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
    • Four:  
        (1) Number of players (always 2)  
        (4) All-or-nothing vs. continuous contribution  
        (6) MPCR/benefit parameter b (and related cost c, α₂, β₂, λ)  
        (8) Punishment magnitude δ  
      All other parameters (11 of 15) do not appear.

C.  For which parameters does the paper give predictions about their systematic effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
    • Only two:  
        – Parameter 6 analogue (benefit vs. cost): Higher b (or lower c) ⇒ higher cooperation ⇒ implied higher efficiency in the presence of punishment.  
        – Parameter 8 (punishment magnitude δ): When δ crosses the threshold c/2 (discrete model) or crosses max{δ₁,δ₂} (continuous model) the equilibrium flips from inefficient defection/mixed play to efficient full cooperation.  
      No numerical treatment-effect sizes in terms of efficiency are supplied.

D.  If we had to forecast the punishment-treatment effect on group efficiency using nothing but this paper:  
    • The only strong lever the paper isolates is δ.  Increasing δ beyond the critical level makes the group converge to full cooperation, so predicted efficiency jumps from below-optimal to 100 %.

    • All other parameters (group size, rounds, information display, rewards, etc.) are silent in the paper; therefore no evidence-based prediction is possible.

Abstract: Why did punishment and the use of reputation evolve in humans? However, these hypotheses lead to sharply divergent behavioral predictions in circumstances that have not yet been tested. Here we report results testing these rival predictions. These results are not consistent with the hypothesis that the psychology of punishment evolved to uphold group norms. The circumstances in which punishment is deployed and withheld-its circuit logic-support the hypothesis that it is generated by psychological mechanisms that evolved to benefit the punisher, by allowing him to bargain for better treatment.

Abstract: The sanctioning of norm-transgressors is a necessary-though often costly-task for maintaining a well-functioning society. Authors: Li, K; Cong, R; Wu, T; Wang, L
Author Full Names: Li, Kun; Cong, Rui; Wu, Te; Wang, Long
Article Title: Social exclusion in finite populations
Keywords Plus: COOPERATION; PUNISHMENT; EMERGENCE; GAME; RECIPROCITY; EVOLUTION
Abstract: Social exclusion, keeping free riders from benefit sharing, plays an important role in sustaining cooperation in our world. Here we propose two different exclusion regimes, namely, peer exclusion and pool exclusion, to investigate the evolution of social exclusion in finite populations. In the peer exclusion regime, each excluder expels all the defectors independently, and thus bears the total cost on his own, while in the pool exclusion regime, excluders spontaneously form an institution to carry out rejection of the free riders, and each excluder shares the cost equally. In a public goods game containing only excluders and defectors, it is found that peer excluders outperform pool excluders if the exclusion costs are small, and the situation is converse once the exclusion costs exceed some critical points, which holds true for all the selection intensities and different update rules. Moreover, excluders can dominate the whole population under a suitable parameters range in the presence of second-order free riders (cooperators), showing that exclusion has prominent advantages over common costly punishment. More importantly, our finding indicates that the group exclusion mechanism helps the cooperative union to survive under unfavorable conditions. Our results may give some insights into better understanding the prevalence of such a strategy in the real world and its significance in sustaining cooperation.

Article Title: Direct and indirect punishment of norm violations in daily life
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; 3RD-PARTY PUNISHMENT; SOCIAL-CONTROL; COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; DISGUST; REJECTION; GOSSIP; ANGER
Abstract: Across societies, humans punish norm violations. To date, research on the antecedents and consequences of punishment has largely relied upon agent-based modeling and laboratory experiments. Here, we report a longitudinal study documenting punishment responses to norm violations in daily life (k=1507; N=257) and test pre-registered hypotheses about the antecedents of direct punishment (i.e., confrontation) and indirect punishment (i.e., gossip and social exclusion). C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. The paper does not systematically vary any of these parameters, and it does not quantify or predict their effects on punishment (nor on efficiency).

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

It presents correlational and descriptive findings about real-world punishment (confrontation, gossip, or avoidance), not about how structural differences (e.g., number of players, repeated rounds, presence or cost of punishment, rewards, etc.) might shift efficiency outcomes. Below each of the 15 parameters is treated in exactly the same way:

• “Discussed?”  =  Did the paper even mention the parameter and (if so) what concrete value(s) were used?  
• “Systematic-effect?” =  Did the paper **vary the parameter on purpose** (or observe natural variation of it) and give a quantitative or qualitative statement about how that variation changes the *punishment treatment effect* (i.e., the difference between a condition with the possibility of punishment and a condition without)?  When any numerical comparison can be read directly from the paper, it is reproduced.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players in the game  
   • Discussed?  YES.  Baseline game = 2 players (A,B).  Two punishment treatments = 3 players (A,B, third-party C).  
   • Systematic-effect?  PARTLY.  Adding a third-party (hence punishment) raises A’s mean transfer from 3.73 to 6.02 (Punish-only) or 6.14 (Punish+Reward).  That is ≈ +2.3 points or +62 %.  The paper does not compute efficiency, so the precise efficiency gain is not reported.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Discussed?  YES.  Always 3 rounds; subjects know this; they are paid for one randomly chosen round.  
   • Systematic-effect?  NO.  The number of rounds is fixed; no predictions are made about changing it.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Discussed?  NO.  No chat is mentioned; no variation; no effect analysed.

4. Contribution “all-or-nothing”?  
   • Discussed?  NO.  A (and B) can choose any amount from 0–10 points.  Not varied.

5. Contribution default / “take” frame?  
   • Discussed?  NO.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Discussed?  YES.  Every point sent by A is multiplied by 3 when it reaches B (implicit marginal per-capita return = 3).  
   • Systematic-effect?  NO.  Factor is always 3; no predictions about changing it.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   • Discussed?  YES.  C sacrifices 1 point.  
   • Systematic-effect?  NO.  Cost is fixed at 1; never varied.

8. Punishment magnitude (deduction on target)  
   • Discussed?  YES.  Each point sacrificed by C reduces B’s payoff by 3 points.  
   • Systematic-effect?  NO.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussed?  YES.  Treatment-2: punishment only.  Treatment-3: punishment + reward.  
   • Systematic-effect?  YES.  Variation is deliberate and the paper states:  
     – A’s mean transfer: 6.02 (Punish-only) vs. 6.14 (Punish+Reward); difference statistically insignificant (Wilcoxon Z = 0.13).  
     – B’s mean transfer: 8.33 (Punish-only) vs. 6.99 (Punish+Reward); Chow test F = 2.315, p = 0.104 (one-tailed).  
     – C’s average spending: punishment 1.45 vs. 1.03, reward 0.86, total 1.89.  
     Effect on group efficiency is not reported.

10. Reward cost  
    • Discussed?  YES (Treatment-3).  C sacrifices 1 point to reward.  
    • Systematic-effect?  NO.  Never varied.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Discussed?  YES.  Each point sacrificed by C gives A 3 points.  
    • Systematic-effect?  NO.

12. Do players know the number of rounds?  
    • Discussed?  YES (they are told there are exactly 3 rounds).  
    • Systematic-effect?  NO.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Discussed?  PARTIALLY.  C sees both A’s and B’s decisions; A sees B’s decision in real time.  No cross-round feedback.  
    • Systematic-effect?  NO.

14. Does the punished player know who punished?  
    • Discussed?  NOT EXPLICITLY.  Numerical labels are used but the paper never analyses the informational aspect.  No variation.

15. Does the rewarded player know who rewarded?  
    • Discussed?  NOT EXPLICITLY.  No variation.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
   – The paper does **not** use “group efficiency” (total-payoff / maximum-possible total) as an outcome.  
   – Reported outcomes are:  
       • Amount sent by first mover A (proxy for “trust”).  
       • Amount returned by B (proxy for “trustworthiness”).  
       • Ratio returned / sent.  
       • Amount of punishment, amount of reward, total third-party sacrifice.  
     These are conceptually distinct from efficiency because they ignore both the size of the pie created by A’s transfer and the destruction of resources caused by C’s punishment/reward.

B. Parameters mentioned  
   9 of the 15 parameters appear at least once: 1,2,6,7,8,9,10,11,12 (and parameter 13 is implicitly present but never analysed).  

C. Parameters whose **systematic variation** is analysed for its effect on the punishment treatment effect  
   Only 2 parameters:  
   • Parameter 1 (Number of players / presence of a third party = presence vs. absence of punishment).  
   • Parameter 9 (Whether reward is enabled alongside punishment).  
   No other parameter is manipulated, so the paper provides no evidence on their interactive or marginal effects.

D. What predictions about the 15 parameters’ impact on the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency can we make from this paper alone?  
   • Adding a third party who can punish (moving from 2 to 3 players) markedly increases trusting behaviour; this almost certainly raises efficiency provided the resources the third party burns in punishing are not too large.  
   • Allowing reward in addition to punishment leaves A’s transfer unchanged, slightly lowers B’s return, and increases total third-party spending, so the net effect on efficiency is ambiguous and cannot be signed from the data given.  
   • For all other parameters (round length, chat, MPCR, punishment cost/magnitude, information revelation, etc.) the paper provides **no data or theory** on how changing them would alter the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.  Any further prediction would therefore require information outside the scope of this paper.

In short, the paper tells us that (i) introducing the *ability* to punish via a third party strongly boosts trusting behaviour, and (ii) letting that same third party also reward does not further raise trust and may even weaken the disciplining effect on responders.  Beyond those two insights the paper is silent about how other design parameters would modulate the efficiency impact of punishment.

Authors: Ostrom, E
Author Full Names: Ostrom, Elinor
Article Title: Building Trust to Solve Commons Dilemmas: Taking Small Steps to Test an Evolving Theory of Collective Action
Source Title: GAMES, GROUPS, AND THE GLOBAL GOOD
Keywords Plus: PRISONERS-DILEMMA; GROUP-SIZE; PROPERTY-RIGHTS; RATIONAL CHOICE; NEURAL BASIS; EVOLUTION; COOPERATION; RECIPROCITY; PREFERENCES; RESOURCE
Abstract: Extensive field research has found that when users of a resource do gain good feedback about the effect of their actions on a resource and can build norms of reciprocity and trustworthiness, they are frequently able to craft new institutions to solve puzzling dilemmas. We need to ask: How do different kinds of institutions support or undermine norms of reciprocity and trustworthiness? The finding from many field studies throughout the world that monitoring and graduated sanctions are close to universal in all robust common-pool resource (CPR) institutions is important as it tells us that without some external support of such institutions it is unlikely that reciprocity alone will allow individuals to solve CPR problems over time. On the other hand, the sanctions are graduated rather than initially severe. The current theory of crime deterrence - based on strict expected value theory - does not explain the graduated nature of these sanctions. But if people can learn to value trust and reciprocity and use them as fundamental norms for organizing their lives, they can agree on a set of rules that they agree to follow. Then graduated sanctions are a way of informing those, who have made an error or faced some emergency temptation, that others are watching and, if someone else were to break a rule, they would likely be observed. Thus, continuing to follow a positive norm of reciprocity is reasonable and it is then feasible to build trust over the long term.

Below I go through the 15 design parameters one by one, quoting or paraphrasing only what is contained in Elinor Ostrom’s “Building Trust to Solve Commons Dilemmas: Taking Small Steps to Test an Evolving Theory of Collective Action.”  
For every parameter I note

• Whether the paper even mentions the parameter and, if so, the value(s) actually used in any study the chapter cites or summarises;  
• Whether the chapter makes ANY prediction (qualitative or quantitative) about what would happen to the PUNISHMENT-TREATMENT EFFECT when that parameter is systematically varied;  
• The size of the effect if it can be read directly from the text, figures, or tables.  
When the chapter speaks about dependent variables other than efficiency (e.g., “joint returns,” “cooperation rate,” “over-harvesting”), I flag that explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER SCAN
--------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? ‑ Yes. 2-person games (Trust Game, Dictator) and 5-person common-pool-resource (CPR) games are described.  
   • Systematic variation & prediction? ‑ No. The chapter never compares 2 vs. 5 vs. larger groups while holding everything else constant, and it never links such variation to the punishment treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? ‑ Yes. The text contrasts one-shot with “repeated” interactions and distinguishes the first ten rounds vs. later rounds in Boero et al. (2008).  
   • Systematic variation & prediction about punishment? ‑ No. Repetition is discussed mainly in the context of communication or reputation, not in the context of adding punishment.

3. Chat (face-to-face or written communication)  
   • Mentioned? ‑ Yes. Allowing communication “drastically” reduces over-harvesting in CPR experiments (Ostrom et al. 1992).  
   • Prediction for punishment effect? ‑ None. Communication is analysed as its own treatment; the paper does not say how **adding punishment to a chat-enabled game** would interact to change efficiency.

4. All-or-nothing contributions  
   • Mentioned? ‑ No. There is no discussion of discrete vs. continuous contribution choices.

5. Contribution default (endowment returned vs. given)  
   • Mentioned? ‑ No.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? ‑ No.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   • Mentioned? ‑ Vaguely. The chapter refers to “costly punishment” and “graduated sanctions,” but gives no numbers.  
   • Prediction when cost is varied? ‑ No.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine per unit)  
   • Mentioned? ‑ Yes, in Rodriguez-Sickert et al. (2008): a “high fine” treatment vs. a “low fine” treatment in 5-person CPR experiments.  
   • Numerical values? ‑ Not reported; only the qualitative labels “high” and “low.”  
   • Systematic-variation prediction? – The only stated finding is that *there was **no difference*** in behaviour between the high-fine and low-fine groups.  No efficiency numbers are provided.  The dependent variable was resource extraction, not efficiency.

9. Reward enabled  
   • Mentioned? ‑ Yes, under the list of “micro-situational variables” (#10 in the list: “Participants can sanction (or reward) each other …”).  
   • Prediction for varying reward presence? ‑ No separate statement about adding rewards on top of punishment.

10. Reward cost  
    • Mentioned? ‑ No.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Mentioned? ‑ No.

12. Horizon known (known end round)  
    • Mentioned? ‑ No.

13. Peer-outcome visibility  
    • Mentioned? ‑ No explicit statement about whether subjects saw others’ pay-offs in the punishment treatments.

14. Punisher identity revealed  
    • Mentioned? ‑ No.

15. Rewarder identity revealed  
    • Mentioned? ‑ No.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables actually used  
   • “Group efficiency” (total pay-off divided by the cooperative maximum) is **not** employed directly.  
   • Reported outcomes include:  
     – Over-harvesting (resource extraction level)  
     – “Joint returns” / “higher incomes”  
     – Frequency or size of transfers (Trust/Dicator games)  
     – Presence or absence of punishment activity  
   These are related to but not identical with efficiency.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even *mentioned*?  
   7 parameters: 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 9, 10-ish (reward presence is mentioned though cost & size are not).

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss **the effect of systematically varying that parameter on the punishment treatment effect**?  
   • One parameter (Punishment magnitude, #8).  
   • Even here, the finding is qualitative (“no difference between high and low fine”) and the outcome is over-harvesting, not efficiency.

D. What predictions, restricted strictly to the information in this chapter, can be made about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency?  

   • Very little can be said.  The sole explicit piece of evidence is that once punishment is present at all, *raising or lowering the fine size* (within the range used by Rodriguez-Sickert et al.) did **not** further change outcomes, so one might predict a flat or very small marginal effect of punishment magnitude on efficiency in that narrow range.  
   • For every other parameter the chapter either offers no data or discusses them only outside a punishment context.  Hence, no further quantitative or even clear qualitative predictions about efficiency under punishment can be extracted from this source.

In short, the chapter is valuable for showing that the *presence* of monitoring and (costly) punishment often correlates with higher joint returns, but it almost never isolates individual design parameters or reports efficiency numbers in a way that lets one predict how manipulations of those parameters will change the **punishment treatment effect**.

Authors: Hilbe, C; Traulsen, A
Author Full Names: Hilbe, Christian; Traulsen, Arne
Article Title: Emergence of responsible sanctions without second order free riders, antisocial punishment or spite
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; COSTLY PUNISHMENT; COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; RECIPROCITY; BENEFITS
Abstract: While empirical evidence highlights the importance of punishment for cooperation in collective action, it remains disputed how responsible sanctions targeted predominantly at uncooperative subjects can evolve. Punishment is costly; in order to spread it typically requires local interactions, voluntary participation, or rewards. Moreover, theory and experiments indicate that some subjects abuse sanctioning opportunities by engaging in antisocial punishment (which harms cooperators), spiteful acts (harming everyone) or revenge (as a response to being punished). These arguments have led to the conclusion that punishment is maladaptive. Here, we use evolutionary game theory to show that this conclusion is premature: If interactions are non-anonymous, cooperation and punishment evolve even if initially rare, and sanctions are directed towards non-cooperators only. Thus, our willingness to punish free riders is ultimately a selfish decision rather than an altruistic act; punishment serves as a warning, showing that one is not willing to accept unfair treatments.

Below is a parameter–by–parameter analysis of whether (1) the paper discusses each of the 15 listed parameters (and, if so, with what values) and (2) whether the paper makes predictions about the effect of systematically varying that parameter on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable)—and particularly on efficiency.
