1) Number of players
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Partly. Most of the main analysis is framed in a two-player (pairwise) game, embedded in a well-mixed population of size n (see p. 2, “We study the transmission of strategies...in a finite population of size n.”). In supplementary sections (SI Text), the authors also mention that their arguments carry over to public goods games “between more than two players,” stating that the condition to sustain punishment grows more stringent with increased group size.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?  
     – The paper does not provide numerical results systematically varying the number of players in the sense of seeing how it would change “punishment treatment effect” on total payoffs or efficiency. They do note qualitatively that “large group sizes threaten the emergence and the stability of responsible peer punishment.” There is, however, no explicit analysis of how that alters group efficiency.

2) Number of rounds
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. The model is set up in an evolutionary (generational) context rather than a repeated, fixed-number-of-rounds game.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?  
     – Not discussed.

3) Is chat enabled?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. The paper does not mention communication between players (chat or messaging).  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?  
     – Not discussed.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – The main model considers a binary choice in the “helping stage”: donors either cooperate (pay cost c to give benefit b) or defect. This is effectively “all or nothing,” but the text does not label it that way.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?  
     – No. The paper does not systematically vary the nature of the contribution choice (i.e., no partial contributions).

5) Is the contribution default?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. There is no mention of participants first receiving an endowment and then choosing how much to contribute versus keep. It is strictly “cooperate (pay cost c) or not.”  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?  
     – Not discussed.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplier
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – For the two-player case, the parameter b is the benefit transferred to the co-player. In a multi-player public goods extension (SI Text), b would analogously reflect the “multiplier” that turns individual contributions into group benefits, but the paper does not call it an MPCR.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?  
     – The paper does not specifically tabulate how changing b shifts total payoffs or “efficiency.” They do note that for large populations, a threshold condition for the emergence of punishment is λ > γ/(γ + b). While this shows b’s importance for whether punishment persists, there is no direct discussion of group efficiency resulting from varying b.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. This is γ in their model, the cost to the punisher of imposing sanctions.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?  
     – The paper gives a threshold (e.g., Eq. (1)) involving γ, showing that when anonymity is low enough (i.e., λ surpasses a γ-dependent threshold), punishment can stabilize. However, they do not report numeric “treatment-effect-on-efficiency” estimates; instead they analyze which punishment type evolves at equilibrium. No direct measure of total payoffs or efficiency is given as γ varies.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from the punished player)
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. This is β in the model.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?  
     – Although β appears in thresholds and influences the payoffs of being punished, the paper explicitly states that in large populations, the condition for punishment to evolve “does not depend sensitively” on β. 9) Whether a reward is enabled
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – The authors mention that “the option to reward cooperators” has been considered in other studies but do not include rewards in their model.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?  
     – Not discussed, beyond noting in the literature review that some previous models allowed for rewarding.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. Same as above: no reward mechanism is analyzed in their main or supplemental models.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?  
     – Not discussed.

11) Reward magnitude
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. Rewarding is not part of their core setup.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?  
     – Not discussed.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. The discussion is in evolutionary (indefinitely repeated from a population perspective) terms and does not address participant knowledge of any horizon.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?  
     – Not discussed.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much their peers gained or lost each round)?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Not directly. The closest concept is that individuals may observe others’ punishment behavior (captured by probability λ). But the paper does not discuss visibility of exact payoffs or losses, only that it is “non-anonymous” enough for one’s punishing or defecting to become known.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?  
     – No. They do not systematically vary exactly how much payoff information is displayed. Rather, they vary λ (the probability you know something about your partner’s punishing propensity).

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Indirectly. The core claim is that “non-anonymity” fosters responsible punishment: knowing who punished whom matters for future reputations. But there is no design-level variation of “player sees punisher or not.” It is always presumed that punishment can be observed enough to generate reputational consequences.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?  
     – Not discussed; they treat non-anonymity (λ > 0) as a single dimension. They do not separate “victim knows punisher identity” from “third parties see punisher identity.”

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. The model does not include rewards.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?  
     – Not discussed.

   – The paper does not analyze payoffs aggregated at the group level, so only limited inferences can be drawn. In broad terms:  
     • Non-anonymity (parameter 14, or more loosely parameter 13) is crucial for responsible punishment to arise and deter defection. Such deterrence might improve group payoffs, but the paper does not quantify efficiency.

Abstract: Strong reciprocity, defined as a predisposition to help others and to punish those that are not helping, has been proposed as a potent force leading to the evolution of cooperation and altruism. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of whether this paper discusses each of the 15 listed features of public‐goods‐game experiments and, if so, whether it makes any predictions about systematically varying that feature’s effect on “punishment treatment” (especially with respect to group efficiency).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Discussed? The paper models “deme size” N in a population‐genetic framework (e.g., equations [11] and thereafter). This is loosely analogous to the number of players in a group.  
   • Effect of systematically varying on punishment treatment effect (for efficiency or otherwise)? The paper does examine how different N values affect whether punishment can invade, but it never measures any “punishment treatment effect” on group efficiency (i.e., the paper does not provide a numeric effect on total payoff or efficiency). It focuses instead on conditions under which punishment or “strong reciprocity” invades genetically or culturally.

2. Number of rounds
   • Discussed? No. The model assumes a life cycle with a helping stage and then a punishment stage, but it does not treat multi‐round or repeated interactions in the experimental sense.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussed? No. There is no mention of communication or “chat” among participants.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussed? No. Although the paper treats “helping” as a binary trait (help vs. no help), it does not discuss this as an “all or nothing” experimental rule, nor does it link it to a systematic variation of punishment effects on efficiency.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Discussed? No. The paper never mentions automatic or default contributions.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as the multiplication factor
   • Discussed? The paper introduces a “benefit of helping,” denoted B, which in some contexts could be viewed as analogous to a “multiplication factor.” However, the authors do not discuss “MPCR” per se.  
   • Effect of systematically varying on punishment treatment effect? Although the model examines how changes in B influence the invasion of helping/punishment, it does not report a “punishment treatment effect” on group efficiency or provide an effect‐size measure. All results occur in terms of evolutionary invasibility (changes in allele frequencies), not changes to group payoff efficiency.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussed? Yes. The paper uses Cₚ as the cost of punishing.  
   • Effect of systematically varying on punishment treatment effect? The model does analyze how different values of Cₚ affect whether punishment (and helping) can invade, but it does not quantify any resulting change in group efficiency or total payoff.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted)
   • Discussed? Yes. The paper calls it D (“the damage” a punisher inflicts).  
   • Effect of systematically varying on punishment treatment effect? The paper does study how changing D can favor or disfavor the evolutionary spread of punishment, but it does not explicitly discuss how D would affect any form of “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussed? No. The paper focuses solely on punishment (and helping). It does not mention rewarding behaviors.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Discussed? No. Not mentioned at all.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded)
    • Discussed? No. Also not mentioned.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
    • Discussed? No. The model does not consider repeated interactions or knowledge of a stopping round.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?
    • Discussed? No. The analysis does not involve observable outcomes in the sense of experimental feedback.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Discussed? No. There is no discussion of whether identities are revealed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Discussed? No. (And the paper does not treat reward at all.)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • No. The paper’s “dependent variables” are changes in gene frequencies or conditions of invasion for punishment and helping. It focuses on whether punishment (possibly coupled with helping) can invade under certain genetic or cultural transmission assumptions. These measures (invasion conditions, “fitness,” “fecundity”) are not the same as group efficiency.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Four are mentioned in some form:  
     1) “Number of players” as the “deme size” N.  
     6) “MPCR or related parameters” as the benefit of helping B (though not called MPCR).  
     7) “Punishment cost” as Cₚ.  
     8) “Punishment magnitude” as D.  
   • None of the remaining 11 parameters are discussed.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, the paper does not use the phrase “punishment treatment effect” or evaluate group efficiency as an outcome variable. Although it systematically varies N, B, Cₚ, and D in invasion analyses, it never gives an effect size relevant to a “treatment effect on efficiency.” It only analyzes whether punishment or helping invades genetically or culturally (i.e., changes in allele frequencies).

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   • The authors provide no direct statement about payoff efficiency (actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible). Their results concern evolutionary stability and invasion of punishing vs. non‐punishing strategies. Consequently, the paper offers no usable predictions about how varying each of the 15 parameters would affect a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” At most, it suggests that, in a population‐genetic sense, larger deme sizes, lower migration, and changes in the cost or severity of punishment can favor or disfavor the spread of punishment plus helping. But none of these statements are framed in terms of group efficiency or total payoff.  

Overall, therefore, the paper does not provide any quantitative or qualitative results on punishment’s impact on group efficiency when systematically varying the 15 parameters. It treats punishment and helping as genetically or culturally transmitted traits whose invasion is driven by direct or kin‐selected benefits, rather than changes in group‐level efficiency.

Below, each of the 15 design parameters is treated in turn.

For every parameter I report  
(1) whether the Lubell & Scholz (2001) article mentions the parameter and, if so, the value actually used in their experiments; and  
(2) whether the authors systematically vary that parameter and derive a prediction or a statistical result about how the **punishment treatment effect** (i.e., the difference between a “punishment’’ condition and a “no-punishment’’ condition) changes when the parameter itself is changed.  Whenever the paper provides a numerical estimate I cite the exact coefficient or mean difference and the table/figure in which it appears.

REMINDER: The paper’s dependent variable is always the **percentage of cooperative choices** (round-level cooperation).  “Efficiency’’ (total earnings ÷ maximum possible) is never analysed.

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Every game has 8 players (1 human subject + 7 computer-simulated).  
   • Varied?  No.  No prediction about how changing group size would alter any punishment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Games last 16–25 rounds; the true end is determined by a 0.25 continuation probability between rounds 16 and 24 (always ends by 25).  
   • Varied?  No.

3. Chat between players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – explicitly **not allowed**.  
   • Varied?  No prediction.

4. “All-or-nothing’’ contribution rule  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Subjects make a binary decision each round: invest \$4 (“cooperate’’) or invest \$0 (“defect’’).  
   • Varied?  No.

5. Contribution default / endowment refund frame  
   • Mentioned?  No.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  All invested money is doubled and then evenly divided: MPCR = 2 / 8 = 0.25.  
   • Varied?  No.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   • Mentioned?  Not applicable.  Punishment is imposed automatically by an external institution; players never pay to punish.  
   • Varied?  Not analysed.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine per unit)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Two separate “partial-deterrence’’ experiments vary the expected fine:  
     – Fixed-amount game: fine = \$0.10, \$1.00, or \$2.00, each with 50 % detection.  
     – Random-amount game: fine randomly drawn from \$0 to \$2 (uniform, 0.10 increments) with 50 % detection.  
     – Random-probability game: detection probability drawn from 0 to 0.50 (0.05 increments) for a fixed \$3 fine.  
   • Systematic prediction / result?  Yes.  Table 1 (p. 173) reports OLS coefficients:  
       • “Amount’’ coefficient = +23.37 (SE = 7.05, p<.01): every additional \$1 of expected fine raises average cooperation by 23.37 percentage points **for baseline subjects who were first-round defectors playing in a non-reciprocal environment**.  
       • Interaction “Reciprocity × Amount’’ = –16.13 (SE = 7.29, p<.05): the presence of reciprocity diminishes the fine’s effectiveness by 16.13 pp per \$1.  
       • Interaction “Cooperator × Amount’’ = –15.00 (SE = 7.70, p<.05): first-round cooperators respond 15 pp less per \$1 than first-round defectors.  
       • Combined, for first-round cooperators in a reciprocal environment the net slope is negative ( ≈ –7.6 pp per \$1), i.e. stronger fines **reduce** their cooperation.  
       • In the random-probability experiment, the coefficient on “Probability’’ is +55.63 (SE = 23.67, p<.05) with no significant interactions, so higher detection probability uniformly increases cooperation.  
     The article never converts these cooperation effects into efficiency terms.

9. Whether a reward institution exists  
   • Mentioned?  No.  Only penalties are studied.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   • Not mentioned or varied.

12. Do players know the number of rounds?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – they do **not** know; only told “at least 16 rounds.”  
   • Varied?  No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Mentioned?  Partly.  Each subject sees her own payoff history and (implicitly) how many others invested because group returns are displayed.  The information treatment is held constant; not varied.

14. Do punished players know who punished them?  
15. Do rewarded players know who rewarded them?  
   • Not applicable – punishment comes from an impersonal computer monitor.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A.  Does the paper use group efficiency?  
    – No.  Dependent variable = % of cooperative choices in rounds 2-16.  The authors occasionally report monetary payoffs in examples but do not analyse “efficiency.’’

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
    – Eleven: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 13, (and implicitly 14-15 as “not applicable’’), plus the absence of 5, 7, 9-11 is noted.  

C.  For which parameters is their *systematic* effect on a punishment treatment discussed?  
    – Only parameter 8 (punishment magnitude).  It is the sole dimension the authors vary deliberately and regress against cooperation.  No other parameter is manipulated to study its influence on the penalty treatment.  

D.  If we had to predict how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) will affect the punishment-treatment effect on **efficiency**, using *only* this paper:  
    – The paper gives evidence only for parameter 8.  Larger external fines increase cooperation—and therefore should raise efficiency—when:  
        • Subjects are first-round defectors, and  
        • The strategic environment is non-reciprocal.  
      The same fine can *lower* cooperation (and thus efficiency) among first-round cooperators when reciprocity is already present.  
    – For all other parameters the article supplies no data or theory beyond stating their fixed value, so no further efficiency predictions can be made from this source alone.

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?

     – No.

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much of their endowment to “move back into their hand” from a public fund)?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. The paper does not mention a design in which the default is to contribute and players must “opt out.”  
   • Does it make predictions about systematically varying such a default?  
     – No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – The paper’s public goods game example says: each $1 contributed generates $0.50 to each participant, implying an MPCR of 0.5. However, it is simply described, not varied.  
   • Does it make predictions about how systematically changing the MPCR affects punishment or efficiency?  
     – No.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. The theoretical sections model a cost w > 0 to the punisher and describe how this influences whether cooperation can be stabilized (e.g., “costly” punishment). In some experimental labor‐market settings, employers pay 1 to reduce or increase the employee’s payoff by 2.5.  
   • Does it make predictions about the effect of systematically varying that cost on the punishment treatment effect?  
     – The paper’s theoretical models do note that if punishment is very costly, fewer participants punish; in turn, this makes cooperation harder to sustain. However, there is no systematic, quantitative “effect size” reported for how changing w shifts efficiency or total payoffs. The paper does not provide numerical estimates about how directly varying the punishment cost would alter the overall “punishment treatment effect.”

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed)
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. In the theoretical model, punishment magnitude is denoted cₚ > 0 (the harm imposed on a defector). In the labor‐market experiment, imposing punishment reduces the employee’s payoff by 2.5.  
   • Does it make predictions about systematically varying this magnitude on the punishment‐efficiency relationship?  
     – The paper shows that if the magnitude cₚ is too low, it might fail to deter defection. However, it does not present numerical effect sizes or systematically vary cₚ in an experiment. Thus, there is no explicit quantitative relationship to group efficiency.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. In one version of the labor‐market experiment, “employers” can either reward or punish employees. The paper notes that punishment plus reward led, on average, to higher effort and a roughly 40% increase in net payoffs for all participants.  
   • Does it make predictions about systematically varying the “reward enabled vs. disabled” factor specifically on punishment’s effect?  
     – Not systematically. The paper reports an on/off condition (no reward/punishment vs. reward/punishment enabled) but does not isolate “reward only” or measure a specific “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” across multiple reward settings.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Briefly. In the labor‐market experiment, rewarding an employee typically costs the employer 1.  
   • Does it make predictions about how systematically changing this cost influences punishment or efficiency?  
     – No. The paper does not vary the reward cost experimentally nor provide a numerical effect scale.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. In the same labor‐market experiment, each 1 spent on a reward increases the employee’s payoff by 2.5.

   • Does the paper discuss it?

     – No.

   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Not explicitly. While the experiments do let participants observe or infer free‐riders in order to punish or reward them, the paper does not systematically address “revealing peer payoffs” nor vary that factor.  
   • Does it make predictions about varying the display of peer outcomes on punishment or efficiency?  
     – No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – In many of the paper’s reported experiments, punishment is anonymous; there is no discussion of systematically altering that anonymity (e.g., labeling punishers).  
   • Does it make predictions about this factor on the punishment treatment effect?  
     – No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – The same general anonymity conditions apply; the text does not detail knowledge of the rewarder’s identity nor does it systematically vary that detail.  
   • Does it make predictions about how that might affect punishment‐based outcomes or efficiency?  
     – No.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY:

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the actual dependent variables?  
   • The paper does discuss payoffs (e.g., net pay, total earnings) and measures cooperation rates or the fraction of contributors/punishers. It does not frame outcomes strictly as “efficiency = actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff.” In experiments (e.g., labor‐market, public goods), cooperation or average payoff is often highlighted. Thus, the key dependent variables are contributions, cooperation rates, and payoffs, rather than explicit “efficiency” ratios.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned (but not systematically varied):  
     – (1) Number of players (only described for specific designs),  
     – (2) Number of rounds (discussed in passing),  
     – (6) MPCR (0.5 in one standard public goods setup),  
     – (7) Punishment cost (modeled as w > 0 and also cost = 1 in the labor‐market experiment),  
     – (8) Punishment magnitude (cₚ > 0 or 2.5 in the labor‐market experiment),  
     – (9) Whether a reward is enabled (yes/no in one labor‐market design),  
     – (10) Reward cost (1 in that setting),  
     – (11) Reward magnitude (2.5 in that setting).  
   • Not mentioned at all:  
     – (3) Is chat enabled,  
     – (4) “All or nothing” contribution,  
     – (5) Contribution default,  
     – (12) Varying knowledge of the endpoint,  
     – (13) Display of peer outcomes,  
     – (14) Knowing the identity of the punisher,  
     – (15) Knowing the identity of the rewarder.

C. For which (and how many) parameters does the paper discuss a systematic effect on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable) when that parameter is varied?  
   • The paper does not report dedicated experiments or analyses systematically varying any of the 15 parameters. It mostly presents one‐off conditions or theoretical formulas (e.g., for the cost of punishing or magnitude of punishment). There is no table/figure that explicitly shows numeric effect sizes of systematically manipulated parameters on a “punishment treatment effect.”

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper links lower punishment cost (parameter 7) or larger punishment magnitude (parameter 8) with a higher likelihood of sustaining cooperation in its theoretical sections; presumably, that would also improve payoffs in public‐goods‐type settings. However, the authors do not provide direct efficiency ratios or systematic parametric tests.  
   • The presence of reward (parameter 9) was reported in one labor‐market design, and in combination with punishment it increased overall payoffs by about 40%. The paper does not isolate that effect purely as “reward only” nor systematically vary the cost or magnitude of reward to quantify the effect on an efficiency measure.  
   • Beyond those broad statements, the paper provides no empirical or tabulated results on how systematically altering these 15 parameters changes a punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency.  

In short, the paper discusses several of the parameters in general terms (particularly punishment cost, punishment magnitude, and the possibility of rewards), but it does not systematically vary any of them to quantify “punishment treatment effects” on efficiency. Consequently, the paper’s content alone allows very limited predictions about how those 15 factors or their interactions might shape punishment’s impact on group efficiency.

Authors: Liu, LJ; Wang, SX; Chen, XJ; Perc, M
Author Full Names: Liu, Linjie; Wang, Shengxian; Chen, Xiaojie; Perc, Matjaz
Article Title: Evolutionary dynamics in the public goods games with switching between punishment and exclusion
Keywords Plus: REPLICATOR DYNAMICS; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; COOPERATION; ENFORCEMENT; EMERGENCE; INSTITUTIONS; POPULATIONS; PROMOTES; DILEMMA; SOCIETY
Abstract: Pro-social punishment and exclusion are common means to elevate the level of cooperation among unrelated individuals. Indeed, it is worth pointing out that the combined use of these two strategies is quite common across human societies. However, it is still not known how a combined strategy where punishment and exclusion are switched can promote cooperation from the theoretical perspective. In this paper, we thus propose two different switching strategies, namely, peer switching that is based on peer punishment and peer exclusion, and pool switching that is based on pool punishment and pool exclusion. Individuals adopting the switching strategy will punish defectors when their numbers are below a threshold and exclude them otherwise. We show that an intermediate value of the threshold leads to a stable coexistence of cooperators, defectors, and players adopting the switching strategy in a well-mixed population, and this regardless of whether the pool-based or the peer-based switching strategy is introduced. Moreover, we show that the pure exclusion strategy alone is able to evoke a limit cycle attractor in the evolutionary dynamics, such that cooperation can coexist with other strategies. Throughout, please note that the paper’s main outcome measures concern the coexistence of strategies (cooperators, defectors, and switching strategies) and the fraction of cooperators. The authors do not measure or discuss “efficiency” (i.e., the group’s actual total payoff relative to the maximum possible payoff) as an outcome. Nor do they present numeric effect sizes for changes in efficiency. All references below are strictly to this paper’s content.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players (N)
• Discussed? Yes. The paper explicitly uses a group size N in all formulations (e.g., “In a group of N individuals”).  
• Value(s) or range mentioned? They typically set N=5 for illustrative figures (Figs. 1–4) but also analyze general N in their derivations.  
• Predictions from systematically varying N about the punishment treatment effect? The paper does include formulas parametrized by N (for example, “1 < r < N”), but it does not provide results or effect sizes about varying N in a way that measures changes in any sort of “punishment treatment effect” on payoffs or efficiency. No numeric effect on efficiency is given.  

2. Number of rounds  
• Discussed? No. The paper uses a replicator‐dynamics (infinite‐population) model without mentioning a finite or known number of rounds.  
• Any systematic variation or predictions? No.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
• Discussed? No; there is no mention of communication or “chat” in this paper.  
• Any systematic variation or predictions? No.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Discussed? Yes, implicitly. The setup is that “cooperators” pay a cost c to the public good and “defectors” pay nothing. This constitutes an all‐or‐nothing contribution structure.  
• Any systematic variation or predictions? The paper does not explore altering the contribution format. There is no systematic variation of this parameter or any effect size reported.  

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much to move back into their hand)?  
• Discussed? No. The paper only treats standard all‐or‐nothing cooperation or defection.  
• Any systematic variation or predictions? No.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor (r)  
• Discussed? Yes. The paper denotes r as the multiplication factor satisfying 1 < r < N.  
• Any systematic variation or predictions? They do analyze how r (along with N) enters the replicator equations. However, they do not present explicit “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” results; instead, r is used to show conditions for strategic coexistence or limit cycles. They do not give a numeric effect size for efficiency.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Discussed? Yes, in two variants: for peer‐based punishment, the cost is γ (gamma), and for pool‐based punishment, the cost is G. There is also a separate “monitoring cost” τ, sometimes in addition to a cost of exclusion cE or δ.  
• Any systematic variation or predictions? The paper sets values (e.g., γ=0.4, G=0.4) and includes them in the analysis, but does not systematically vary these costs in tables or figures to show how they might change total payoffs or efficiency. No numeric effect on an efficiency measure is given.  

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from a punished player)  
• Discussed? Yes. For peer‐based switching, the fine is β. For pool‐based switching, the fine is B.  
• Any systematic variation or predictions? The paper uses fixed values (e.g., β=0.4, B=0.4) in example simulations. There is no systematic sweep of β or B analyzing changes in efficiency, nor any numeric effect size on efficiency.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
• Discussed? No. The paper focuses on punishment and exclusion, not rewards.  
• Any systematic variation or predictions? No.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Discussed? No.  
• Any systematic variation or predictions? No.  

11. Reward magnitude  
• Discussed? No.  
• Any systematic variation or predictions? No.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
• Discussed? No.  
• Any systematic variation or predictions? No.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown, i.e., does each player see how much others earned or lost?  
• Discussed? No. The paper does not address how much information players see about others’ outcomes.  
• Any systematic variation or predictions? No.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who specifically punished them?  
• Discussed? No.  
• Any systematic variation or predictions? No.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who rewarded them?  
• Discussed? No. (And the paper does not use rewards.)  
• Any systematic variation or predictions? No.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?  
→ The paper does not measure or report “group efficiency” (or total or average payoff) as its central dependent variable. Instead, it uses replicator‐dynamics analyses to track stable strategy mixtures and the long‐term coexistence (or dominance) of cooperators, defectors, and switching strategies. While it does reference payoffs in the replicator equations, it does not provide an analysis of total efficiency nor does it interpret outcomes as “actual total payoff relative to the maximum possible.”

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
→ The paper explicitly mentions five of them:  
   (1) Number of players (N)  
   (4) All‐or‐nothing contributions (implicitly)  
   (6) The multiplication factor (r)  
   (7) Punishment cost (γ or G)  
   (8) Punishment magnitude (β or B)  
The remaining ten parameters receive no discussion.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
→ The paper does not systematically vary any of these five mentioned parameters for the purpose of quantifying how punishment affects “efficiency” or even total payoffs. Instead, the main systematic variation is of the switching threshold T (which is not one of the 15 listed parameters), analyzed for its impact on strategy coexistence. No numeric effect sizes on efficiency or payoff are provided.

D) If you were to make predictions, solely based on this paper, about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, what would they be?  
→ Because the authors do not examine total payoffs, let alone efficiency, and they do not report systematic parameter‐variation effects on payoffs, the paper offers little basis for predicting changes in group efficiency relative to a fully cooperative payoff. The results focus on fractions of strategies rather than efficiency. Accordingly, very few (if any) predictions about efficiency can be drawn from this article alone.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes, for peer punishment they use γ as the cost of punishing each free‐rider; for pool punishment, they use G as a fixed cost. In the main figures, γ = 0.4, G = 0.4.  
   • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – They note their conclusions (about which strategy dominates) hold for a “broad range” of costs, but they do not quantify any specific changes in efficiency. No numerical effect sizes or predictions about efficiency are given.  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed on them)  
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes, β for peer punishment and B for pool punishment often set to 0.4 in examples. The paper mentions that increasing β or B can change which strategy is favored if second‐order sanctioning is present.  
   • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – The authors note that “exclusion remains superior” for most moderate variations, but if punishment is “unrealistically high,” pool or peer punishers could prevail. They do not provide numerical effect sizes for any measure of efficiency, only for “strategy dominance.”  

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The paper addresses only “punishment” and “exclusion,” with no mention of enabling reward.  
   • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – None.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Discussed?  
      – No. There is no reward mechanism at all in this model.  
    • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
      – None.  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted to them)  
    • Discussed?  
      – No.  
    • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
      – None.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    • Discussed?  
      – No mention is made of this, as the study is framed in an evolutionary context.  
    • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
      – None.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?  
    • Discussed?  
      – No. The paper does not discuss any direct feedback or how outcomes are displayed.  
    • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
      – None.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Discussed?  
      – No. The paper treats punishment in a theoretical, evolutionary manner and does not mention identification of the punisher.  
    • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
      – None.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Discussed?  
      – No. Reward is not included in this model.  
    • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
      – None.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary (A–D)

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper does not use group efficiency or total/average payoff as a main dependent variable. Instead, it focuses on how different strategies (cooperators, punishers, excluders, defectors, and sometimes loners) fare in evolutionary competition. Its key outcome is the “stationary distribution” or “long‐run frequency” of each strategy in the population.  
   • Although the authors discuss payoffs (to define which strategy outperforms under evolutionary update rules), they never calculate efficiency as “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff.”  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned parameters:  
     1. Number of players (population size M, group size N)  
     4. All or nothing contribution  
     6. MPCR/multiplication factor r  
     7. Punishment cost (γ, G)  
     8. Punishment magnitude (β, B)  
   • These five are mentioned. All others (2, 3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15) are not discussed.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The authors do vary costs (γ, G) and fines (β, B) in a broad sense. However, they focus on which strategy survives rather than measuring a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” They do not quantify how these variations change group efficiency, nor do they present numerical effect sizes on efficiency (or any other clearly stated measure like total payoff).  
   • Hence, strictly speaking, there is no direct discussion linking any parameter’s systematic variation to the paper’s “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency. All references to variations address strategy dominance or coexistence, not efficiency.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not measure efficiency, so there is “little to no prediction” one can draw strictly from its text concerning how these parameters (or their interactions) affect efficiency. The authors primarily track mean frequencies of strategies, rather than total payoffs relative to a fully cooperative outcome. They do conclude that “exclusion” is more powerful than “punishment” in achieving cooperation, which might suggest greater overall efficiencies under exclusion (especially for moderate parameter values), but they do not present explicit data connecting parameters to group efficiency measurements.

Article Title: Perceptions of the appropriate response to norm violation in 57 societies
Keywords Plus: SOCIAL NORMS; CULTURAL-DIFFERENCES; PUNISHMENT; PREVALENCE; STRENGTH; ORIGINS
Abstract: Norm enforcement may be important for resolving conflicts and promoting cooperation. However, little is known about how preferred responses to norm violations vary across cultures and across domains. In a preregistered study of 57 countries (using convenience samples of 22,863 students and non-students), we measured perceptions of the appropriateness of various responses to a violation of a cooperative norm and to atypical social behaviors. Our findings highlight both cultural universals and cultural variation. We find a universal negative relation between appropriateness ratings of norm violations and appropriateness ratings of responses in the form of confrontation, social ostracism and gossip. Moreover, we find the country variation in the appropriateness of sanctions to be consistent across different norm violations but not across different sanctions. Specifically, in those countries where use of physical confrontation and social ostracism is rated as less appropriate, gossip is rated as more appropriate. Little is known about people's preferred responses to norm violations across countries. Here, in a study of 57 countries, the authors highlight cultural similarities and differences in people's perception of the appropriateness of norm violations.

Abstract: Some researchers have proposed that natural selection has given rise in humans to one or more adaptations for altruistically punishing on behalf of other individuals who have been treated unfairly, even when the punisher has no chance of benefiting via reciprocity or benefits to kin. Together, these findings suggest that the case for altruistic punishment in humans-a view that has gained increasing attention in the biological and social sciences-has been overstated.

(2) whether the paper says what would happen to the *punishment-treatment effect* if the parameter were **systematically varied**.  Whenever a numerical effect can be read directly from the paper, I reproduce it; otherwise I say so explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Yes – every game involved 3 players (dictator, recipient, third party).  
   (2) No prediction, and the number of players is never varied.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Yes – two rounds were played.  
   (2) No systematic variation; no prediction about changing the number of rounds.

3. Chat enabled?  
   (1) Not mentioned; no chat facility existed.  
   (2) No discussion or prediction.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
   (1) Not relevant; there is no contribution stage in this dictator/third-party design.  
   (2) Not discussed.

5. “Contribution default” or withdrawal rule  
   (1) Not relevant; not discussed.  
   (2) No prediction.

6. MPCR or multiplication factor  
   (1) Not applicable; there is no public-goods stage.  
   (2) No discussion.

7. Punishment cost (cost the punisher pays for one unit)  
   (1) Yes – the cost-to-punish ratio is 1 : 4 (each \$1 spent removes \$4 from the target).  
   (2) The paper *mentions* that “previous research has shown that punishment becomes more likely as the cost of punishment declines,” but the authors themselves do not vary this cost and offer no new quantitative estimate of how changing it would affect the treatment effect.

8. Punishment magnitude (damage per unit)  
   (1) Implied by the 1 : 4 ratio above (magnitude = 4× the punisher’s cost).  
   (2) Not varied, no prediction.

9. Reward enabled?  
   (1) Yes – subjects could also reward; this is highlighted as a design change meant to reduce demand effects.  
   (2) The authors do not study how *enabling vs. disabling* reward would change the (punishment) treatment effect; therefore no prediction.

10. Reward cost  
    (1) Yes – 1 : 1 (each \$1 given costs \$1).  
    (2) Not varied; no prediction.

11. Reward magnitude  
    (1) Equal to the cost (1 : 1).  
    (2) Not varied; no prediction.

12. Are the number of rounds known to the players?  
    (1) Yes – subjects were explicitly *not* told how many rounds there would be.  
    (2) The authors do not manipulate this information, so no prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    (1) Yes – after each round a screen displayed every player’s earnings.  
    (2) Not varied; no prediction.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
    (1) Indirectly yes – “players were identified consistently throughout,” so the target can infer who punished.  
    (2) Not varied; no prediction.

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
    (1) Same as 14 – identities remained constant; thus the recipient can identify the rewarder.  
    (2) Not varied; no prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables actually used  
   • Dollars punished or rewarded (behavioural).  
   • Whether punishment reached ≥ \$4 (deterrence threshold).  
   • Self-reported anger and envy.  
   • Two lexical-decision implicit measures (reported only in supplements).  
   ***Efficiency (group or total payoff) is never measured or analysed.***

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even *mentioned*?  
   10 of them: 1, 2, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14/15.  
   The paper is silent on 3, 4, 5, 6.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* that parameter on any punishment-treatment outcome?  
   None.  The sole partial exception is parameter 7 (punishment cost): the authors cite earlier literature saying lower costs increase punishment, but they themselves do not vary the cost nor supply an effect size.

D. What predictions about the 15 parameters and their interactions on the *punishment-treatment effect on efficiency* can be made from this paper alone?

The only hint is the external remark that lower punishment costs tend to raise the amount of punishment; but without knowing how punishment affects cooperation or payoffs in their design, even this does not translate into an efficiency prediction.    • Systematic variation? No. The experiment fixes the number of rounds at 10. The paper does not study or report how systematically changing the number of rounds affects any outcome, including the punishment effect.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned? No. There is no mention of communication/chat between the partners beyond the displayed choices.  
   • Systematic variation? No.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned? Indirectly, one can see that trustees can return any amount from 0 up to the tripled investment (rather than “all or nothing”). However, the paper does not explicitly discuss “all or nothing” setups.  
   • Systematic variation? No.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much of their endowment to move back into their hand)?  
   • Mentioned? No. The study focuses on investors sending some amount (which is tripled) and trustees deciding how much to return, but does not frame contributions as “default” or forced moves.

   • Mentioned? Yes. The amount the investor sends is multiplied by 3 before it reaches the trustee.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? Not clearly. The experiment uses a sanction threat in which the trustee loses 4 monetary units (MUs) if they fail to meet the investor’s requested return. Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS GAMES; STRUCTURED POPULATIONS; ANTISOCIAL PUNISHMENT; MULTIPLE STRATEGIES; COOPERATION; EMERGENCE; DYNAMICS; EQUILIBRIUM; MUTATIONS; DILEMMAS
Abstract: In evolutionary games, reproductive success is determined by payoffs. Weak selection means that even large differences in game outcomes translate into small fitness differences. Many results have been derived using weak selection approximations, in which perturbation analysis facilitates the derivation of analytical results. Here, we ask whether results derived under weak selection are also qualitatively valid for intermediate and strong selection. By qualitatively valid we mean that the ranking of strategies induced by an evolutionary process does not change when the intensity of selection increases. For two-strategy games, we show that the ranking obtained under weak selection cannot be carried over to higher selection intensity if the number of players exceeds two. For games with three (or more) strategies, previous examples for multiplayer games have shown that the ranking of strategies can change with the intensity of selection. In particular, rank changes imply that the most abundant strategy at one intensity of selection can become the least abundant for another. We show that this applies already to pairwise interactions for a broad class of evolutionary processes. Even when both weak and strong selection limits lead to consistent predictions, rank changes can occur for intermediate intensities of selection. To analyze how common such games are, we show numerically that for randomly drawn two-player games with three or more strategies, rank changes frequently occur and their likelihood increases rapidly with the number of strategies n. In particular, rank changes are almost certain for n >= 8, which jeopardizes the predictive power of results derived for weak selection.

Authors: Levin, SA

Article Title: Learning to live in a global commons: socioeconomic challenges for a sustainable environment
Keywords Plus: STRONG RECIPROCITY; EVOLUTION; DISPERSAL; STOICHIOMETRY; BIODIVERSITY; MAINTENANCE; COOPERATION; COMPETITION; PUNISHMENT
Abstract: Ecologists, economists and other social scientists have much incentive for interaction. First of all, ecological systems and socioeconomic systems are linked in their dynamics, and these linkages are key to coupling environmental protection and economic growth. Beyond this, however, are the obvious similarities in how ecological systems and socioeconomic systems function, and the common theoretical challenges in understanding their dynamics. This should not be surprising. Socioeconomic systems are in fact ecological systems, in which the familiar ecological phenomena of exploitation, cooperation and parasitism all can be identified as key features. Or, viewed from the opposite perspective, ecological systems are economic systems, in which competition for resources is key, and in which an evolutionary process shapes the individual agents to a distribution of specialization of function that leads to the emergence of flows and functionalities at higher levels of organization. Most fundamentally, ecological and socioeconomic systems alike are complex adaptive systems, in which patterns at the macroscopic level emerge from interactions and selection mechanisms mediated at many levels of organization, from individual agents to collectives to whole systems and even above. In such complex adaptive systems, robustness must be understood as emergent from selection processes operating at these many different levels, and the inherent nonlinearities can trigger sudden shifts in regimes that, in the case of the biosphere, can have major consequences for humanity. This lecture will explore the complex adaptive nature of ecosystems, and the implications for the robustness of ecosystem services on which we depend, and in particular examine the conditions under which cooperative behavior emerges. It will then turn attention to the socioeconomic systems in which environmental management is based, and ask what lessons can be learned from our examination of natural systems, and how we can modify social norms to achieve global cooperation in managing our common future. Below is an item‐by‐item analysis of what the paper by Fehr, Hoff, and Kshetramade (“Spite and Development”) does and does not say about each of the 15 parameters, together with whether the paper makes any prediction about systematically varying each parameter and its effect on punishment. Throughout, remember that the question asks specifically about how these parameters would affect the “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” The paper, however, does not study “efficiency” in the sense of actual total payoff divided by maximum possible payoff. Nor does it systematically vary these parameters. Instead, the paper focuses on one‐shot trust games with third‐party punishment and on stag hunt games (repeated over 10 rounds), examining punishment, cooperation, and spitefulness. The details are as follows.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
• Mentioned?  
  – Yes. In the trust game experiments, there are three players (A, B, C). In the stag hunt experiments, there are pairs of players.  
• Systematically varied?  
  – No. The paper does not systematically vary the number of players or analyze how changing this would affect punishment or any outcome.

2. Number of rounds  
• Mentioned?  
  – Yes. The trust game is played one‐shot, and the stag hunt game is played for ten rounds.  
• Systematically varied?  
  – No. They do not vary the number of rounds across conditions, nor do they study how changing the number of rounds would affect punishment.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
• Mentioned?  
  – No mention of chat in the paper. There is no discussion of whether communication is allowed or disallowed, nor is there any condition in which they vary chat.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Mentioned?  
  – Not in the context of a public goods game. The paper uses a binary trust game (A either keeps his 50 rupees or sends it all), but there is no mention of systematically varying an “all or nothing” contribution rule in a public‐goods sense.  
• Systematically varied?  
  – No.  

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much to move from the public fund back into their hand)?  
• Mentioned?  
  – No. The paper does not use a standard public goods design with a variable contribution level. Instead, it uses a binary trust decision (keep vs. send). No systematic variation is discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
• Mentioned?  
  – The trust game “triples the amount” that A sends, so effectively the 50 rupees become 150 extra for B (total 200 for B). However, this factor (3) is fixed.  
• Systematically varied?  
  – No. The paper does not compare different multiplication factors or analyze its effect on punishment.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Mentioned?  
  – Yes. In the third‐party punishment trust game, for every 2 rupees that player C spends, player B loses a 10‐rupee note.  
• Systematically varied?  
  – No. There is just one punishment‐cost condition. No effect of different cost levels is analyzed.

8. Punishment magnitude  
• Mentioned?  
  – Yes. The magnitude is 10 rupees lost by B for each 2 rupees spent by C.  
• Systematically varied?  
  – No. This parameter is fixed in the design, with no variation.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
• Mentioned?  
  – No. The paper discusses only punishment (including antisocial punishment) in trust or dictator‐style settings; reward is not mentioned.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Mentioned?  
  – No. There is no discussion of any reward mechanism.  

11. Reward magnitude  
• Mentioned?  
  – No. As above, rewards were not implemented or discussed.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
• Mentioned?  
  – The paper does not directly state whether players know the game length, but in the trust game it is explicitly one‐shot, and in the stag hunt, there are 10 rounds. There is no indication that round lengths or knowledge of them was systematically varied.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?  
• Mentioned?  
  – They do receive feedback in the repeated stag hunt about their partner’s choice. But for the trust game, the paper does not emphasize displaying others’ outcomes.  
• Systematically varied?  
  – No. The paper contains no discussion of varying the information structure to see its effect on punishment.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• Mentioned?  
  – The paper does not state that B is informed who punishes him. They only say that “C is the third party who can punish B.” They do not discuss whether B learns C’s identity.  
• Systematically varied?  
  – No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
• Mentioned?  
  – Not applicable. The experiments described do not include a reward condition.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A: Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
• The paper does occasionally note that certain actions “decrease total payoff,” but it does not measure efficiency as “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff.”  
• The main dependent variables examined are:  
  – Whether defection versus cooperation occurs (e.g., in the trust game or stag hunt).  
  – Frequency and intensity of punishment (including “antisocial” punishment).  
  – Distribution (or allocator) choices in dictator‐type games.  
• Thus, “efficiency” in the sense of a formal ratio is not the primary measured outcome, and the paper does not systematically compare total‐payoff outcomes to a maximum possible payoff.

B: Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Mentioned:  
  1. Number of players (fixed in each game).  
  2. Number of rounds (fixed as one‐shot or repeated 10 in the stag hunt).  
  6. Multiplication factor (tripled amount in the trust game).  
  7. Punishment cost (2 rupees per punishment).  
  8. Punishment magnitude (10 rupees lost per “unit” of punishment).  
• Not mentioned or not used:  
  3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15 (at least not in a way that is systematically manipulated or highlighted).

C: For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• None are systematically varied in the paper. The design fixes cost and magnitude of punishment, number of players, the single or repeated‐round format, and the multiplication factor. There is no table or figure reporting effect sizes for different parameter settings.

D: If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
• The paper does not provide any direct or quantitative basis for predicting how systematically changing the 15 parameters would affect “the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” The main takeaway is that in this particular setup, punishments—especially antisocial/spiteful punishment—tend to reduce total payoffs and cooperation. However, since none of the parameters are systematically manipulated, little to no precise prediction can be made from this paper alone on how varying them might change efficiency in a public goods game.

Below is a point‐by‐point inventory of whether (and how) each of the 15 parameters listed in your prompt appears in the paper by Cooper and Kühn, and whether the paper discusses systematic variation of that parameter’s effect on “punishment treatment effects” (particularly on efficiency, understood as total or average payoffs relative to the maximum possible). Following that inventory is the required four‐part summary (A–D).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER‐BY‐PARAMETER INVENTORY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes. In this experiment, each “round” matches two players (a “row” and a “column” player).  
   • Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment? No. The experiment always uses pairs (2 players). The paper does not vary group size, nor does it discuss how changing the number of players would affect any punishment mechanism or overall payoff/efficiency.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? Yes. There are 20 rounds (a “round” is the entire two‐period Bertrand game), though a couple of sessions ended slightly earlier.  
   • Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment? No. The design always fixes (at most) 20 rounds, does not systematically alter this, and does not analyze how changing the total number of rounds would affect punishment or efficiency.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned? Yes—this is one of the central variations in the paper (no communication, limited “pre‐period” messages, full preplay chat, or chat with renegotiation).  
   • Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment? Yes, the main treatment variation is precisely whether and how subjects can communicate. While the paper does not label it as a “public‐goods punishment treatment,” it does analyze how threats of “punishment” (choosing a low‐payoff action in Period 2) become more credible when rich chat is available. The authors measure how these communication treatments affect collusive outcomes and total payoffs (but they do not explicitly call this “efficiency”). No numerical “punishment‐treatment‐effect‐on‐efficiency” estimate is reported, though Tables and Figures show how open chat treatments yield higher joint payoffs relative to no‐chat or limited‐chat treatments.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned? No. The experiment is a repeated (two‐period) Bertrand game with three possible price choices each period. There is no mention of a forced “all or nothing” contribution regime.

5. Is the contribution default?  
   • Mentioned? No. Again, because the design is a Bertrand setting, there is no mention of a “default” contribution to a public fund.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? No. This is not a standard public goods setting. The paper’s payoff structure is a customized two‐period Bertrand matrix. It does not describe or vary any MPCR‐type multiplier.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? Only implicitly. “Punishment” in their experiment is accomplished by choosing a low price (Low) in Period 2, which lowers payoffs for both punisher and punishee. However, the authors do not systematically vary that cost. The same payoff matrix is used throughout, with no treatment that changes the cost of punishing.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted per unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned? Only implicitly, in that switching to a low price imposes a payoff loss on the “cheater.” There is no separate parameter for “units of punishment” or variation in punishment strength. The authors do not systematically alter the payoff matrix in different treatments to see how changing punishment magnitude affects outcomes.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned? No. The experiment does not include any reward mechanism (only threats and punishments by choosing lower prices).

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Mentioned? No. Rewards are not part of the design.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per reward)  
    • Mentioned? No. There is no reward mechanism at all.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    • Mentioned? Yes. Subjects are told they will play 20 rounds (in practice, some sessions ended earlier if two hours elapsed).  
    • Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment? No. They do not vary whether the horizon is known/unknown and do not analyze how “knowing the final round” changes the punishment outcome.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost each round)?  
    • Mentioned? Yes. After each period, players see both players’ prices and payoffs, so there is display of outcomes.  
    • Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment? No. The design does not vary whether players see each other’s payoffs. It is held constant throughout.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Mentioned? Not in the sense of a parameter. There is always exactly one opponent, so it is implicit who has “punished” by choosing Low. The authors do not systematically vary anonymity of punishment or identify different punishers in a multi‐player group.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Mentioned? No. Rewards do not appear in these experiments.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
REQUIRED SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   • The study measures collusion rates—i.e., whether subjects choose the collusive (“High”) price or deviate. It also frequently reports and analyzes monetary payoffs (including sums across both periods). Although the paper does not use the specific term “efficiency,” it does pay close attention to average and total payoffs as outcomes, as well as how punishments (choosing “Low”) reduce both players’ payoffs. Other main dependent variables include (i) the frequency of collusion (cooperative pricing) in Period 1, and (ii) the frequency of punishments in Period 2. Thus “collusion rate” and “payoffs” are the central outcome variables.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned explicitly in some form:  
     (1) Number of players (always 2),  
     (2) Number of rounds (always 20, or fewer if the session times out),  
     (3) Whether chat is enabled,  
     (12) Rounds are known to the players,  
     (13) Peer outcomes/payoffs are displayed each period.  
   • The other parameters—(4), (5), (6), (7), (8), (9), (10), (11), (14), and (15)—are either not relevant to their Bertrand setup or else not systematically introduced as a “parameter” that the paper measures or varies.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The only parameter truly varied is whether chat is enabled (and how). The authors compare No Communication, Limited Communication, Rich Preplay Chat, and Renegotiation (which includes interim chat). However, they do not frame this as “varying a punishment policy” in a public goods sense. Instead, they study how subjects threaten/execute punishments (choosing Low) depending on whether communication exists and how free‐form it is.  
   • They do not provide a numerical “punishment‐treatment‐effect‐on‐efficiency” estimate. Rather, they measure collusion rates and payoffs across different communication treatments. The systematic manipulations all center on parameter (3), “Is chat enabled?” The other parameters are not systematically manipulated to see how that changes punishments or payoffs.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not investigate a public‐goods model or manipulate most of those 15 parameters, so no direct predictions can be made for a standard “public goods game with punishment” beyond noting that richer communication is associated with more credible threats and thus more cooperative (higher‐payoff) outcomes in their two‐person Bertrand design.  
   • They do show that adding rich chat or renegotiation can drastically change behavior in a repeated setting with punishment threats—collusive outcomes remain higher, and total payoffs rise, even though formal “sanction costs” were not systematically varied.  
   • For all other listed parameters (like marginal per capita returns, reward magnitude, or the identity of punishers/rewarders), the paper provides no direct discussion or data to inform any predictions.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Below I walk through the fifteen design parameters point-by-point.  
For each parameter I state

(a) Whether the survey by Sethi & Somanathan (2003) mentions the parameter and, if so, the notation or numerical range the authors use; and  

(b) Whether the paper makes any quantitative or qualitative prediction about what happens to the **punishment treatment effect** (PTE) – i.e., the difference in group efficiency between a baseline public-goods game and the same game with peer punishment – when that parameter is **systematically varied**.

A “✓” means the item is mentioned; a “✗” means it is not.  “No PTE result” means the parameter is mentioned but the paper does **not** connect changes in that parameter to changes in the punishment treatment effect on efficiency (or on any other dependent variable).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players (group size)  
✓ Mentioned.  Two-person Prisoner’s Dilemma is analysed throughout; multi-person public-goods / common-pool games of size k are referenced (Gintis 2000; Sethi-Somanathan 2001).  
No PTE result.  The survey never traces how a larger or smaller k alters the efficiency gain from introducing peer punishment.

2. Number of rounds  
✓ Discussed repeatedly (infinite repetition vs. one-shot, finitely-repeated interactions).  
No PTE result.  No statement of how adding or subtracting rounds changes the punishment–efficiency link in public-goods settings.

3. Chat enabled?  
✗ Not discussed.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
✗ Not discussed.

5. Contribution default / “take” frame  
✗ Not discussed.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
✓ Implicitly present as the benefit–cost ratio β/α in the prisoner’s-dilemma notation.  
No PTE result.  Varying β or α is used only to state threshold conditions such as β > 2α or α/β < r; the effect on the efficiency impact of punishment is never worked out.

7. Punishment cost to punisher (γ)  
✓ Appears in Section 3.2 (costly sanctions game).  
No systematic PTE result.  γ is held fixed; the authors never graph or tabulate how efficiency changes as γ rises or falls.

8. Punishment magnitude on target (δ)  
✓ Appears in Section 3.2; a key threshold is δ > α for reciprocators to invade opportunists.  
Partial qualitative claim, but still **not** a treatment-effect result on efficiency.  The paper says that if δ > α, reciprocators can drive out optimisers, but it does not translate this into an efficiency differential between a punishment and a no-punishment condition, nor does it speak to marginal changes in δ once the threshold is crossed.

9. Reward enabled?  
✗ Not discussed.

10. Reward cost  
✗ Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude  
✗ Not discussed.

12. End-time known?  
✗ Not discussed.

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
✗ Not discussed.

14. Punisher identity revealed?  
✗ Not discussed.

15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
✗ Not discussed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary requested by the user
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables used in the paper  
– The survey is almost entirely theoretical and tracks (i) individual material pay-offs, (ii) population shares of strategy or preference types, and (iii) evolutionary stability.  
– “Efficiency” in the sense of *total group payoff relative to the cooperative maximum* is referred to only in passing (e.g., “mutual cooperation is efficient”) and **is never used as a measured dependent variable**.  
– Other dependent variables (contributions, cooperation rate, stability) are conceptually different from efficiency and receive most of the attention.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
Seven are mentioned at all:  1, 2, 6, 7, 8, (occasionally) group-formation processes related to 13–15, but the latter are not the exact parameters listed.  Strictly counting only the fifteen, the paper mentions 1, 2, 6, 7, 8 (five parameters).

C.  For how many parameters does the paper analyse how *systematic variation* changes the punishment treatment effect?  
Zero.  Although δ > α is an invasion threshold, the authors never compute or even qualitatively plot how varying δ, γ, group size, etc., changes the *incremental* efficiency gain from adding punishment to a public-goods game.

D.  What predictions about the 15 parameters and their interactions can be made **solely from this paper**?  
The survey is too general and too theoretical to support precise forecasting.  The few hints it provides are:  
– Larger punishment magnitude relative to the cost of cooperation (δ > α) is necessary for punishment-backed reciprocity to emerge; hence increasing δ from below to above α should, in principle, allow punishment to raise efficiency from zero (full defection) toward the cooperative benchmark.  
– High monitoring or punishment costs (γ or other “monitoring costs”) can let defectors out-perform reciprocators, implying a *lower* or even negative punishment treatment effect on efficiency when γ is large.  
– Very large groups, or groups in which reciprocators are rare, dilute the deterrent effect of punishment and may therefore weaken or overturn any positive efficiency effect.  
Beyond these qualitative statements, the paper offers **no quantitative guidance** on the size or direction of the punishment treatment effect as any of the 15 design parameters are varied, singly or in interaction.

In short, the paper supplies almost no direct leverage for predicting how the listed laboratory design parameters will modulate the efficiency impact of introducing punishment in public-goods games.

Authors: Raihani, NJ; Bshary, R
Author Full Names: Raihani, N. J.; Bshary, R.
Article Title: Resolving the iterated prisoner's dilemma: theory and reality
Author Keywords: cooperation; prisoner's dilemma; pseudo-reciprocity; punishment; reciprocity; tit-for-tat

Abstract: Pairs of unrelated individuals face a prisoner's dilemma if cooperation is the best mutual outcome, but each player does best to defect regardless of his partner's behaviour. Although mutual defection is the only evolutionarily stable strategy in one-shot games, cooperative solutions based on reciprocity can emerge in iterated games. Among the most prominent theoretical solutions are the so-called bookkeeping strategies, such as tit-for-tat, where individuals copy their partner's behaviour in the previous round. However, the lack of empirical data conforming to predicted strategies has prompted the suggestion that the iterated prisoner's dilemma (IPD) is neither a useful nor realistic basis for investigating cooperation. Here, we discuss several recent studies where authors have used the IPD framework to interpret their data. We evaluate the validity of their approach and highlight the diversity of proposed solutions. Strategies based on precise accounting are relatively uncommon, perhaps because the full set of assumptions of the IPD model are rarely satisfied. Instead, animals use a diverse array of strategies that apparently promote cooperation, despite the temptation to cheat. These include both positive and negative reciprocity, as well as long-term mutual investments based on 'friendships'. Although there are various gaps in these studies that remain to be filled, we argue that in most cases, individuals could theoretically benefit from cheating and that cooperation cannot therefore be explained with the concept of positive pseudo-reciprocity. We suggest that by incorporating empirical data into the theoretical framework, we may gain fundamental new insights into the evolution of mutual reciprocal investment in nature.

Abstract: Extortion is the practice of obtaining advantages through explicit forces and threats. Recently, it was demonstrated that even the repeated prisoner's dilemma, one of the key models to explain mutual cooperation, allows for implicit forms of extortion.
