Abstract: The present paper briefly describes and contrasts two different motivations crucially involved in decision making and cooperation, namely fairness-based and compassion-based motivation. Whereas both can lead to cooperation in comparable social situations, we suggest that they are driven by fundamentally different mechanisms and, overall, predict different behavioral outcomes. First, we provide a brief definition of each and discuss the relevant behavioral and neuroscientific literature with regards to cooperation in the context of economic games. We suggest that, whereas both fairness- and compassion-based motivation can support cooperation, fairness-based motivation leads to punishment in cases of norm violation, while compassion-based motivation can, in cases of defection, counteract a desire for revenge and buffer the decline into iterative noncooperation. However, those with compassion-based motivation alone may get exploited. Finally, we argue that the affective states underlying fairness-based and compassion-based motivation are fundamentally different, the former driven by anger or fear of being punished and the latter by a wish for the other person's well-being.

Authors: Boehm, C
Author Full Names: Boehm, C
Article Title: Impact of the human egalitarian syndrome on Darwinian selection mechanics
Keywords Plus: HUMAN-EVOLUTION; ALTRUISM; COMPETITION; DOMINANCE; COOPERATION; DECISIONS; SOCIALITY; SOCIETIES; BEHAVIOR; FORAGERS
Abstract: With nothing more than bin selection and reciprocal altruism theories to work with, the selection basis of human degrees of altruism and cooperation is often difficult to explain. However, during our prehistoric foraging phase, a highly stable egalitarian syndrome arose that had profound effects an Darwinian selection mechanics. The band's insistence on egalitarianism seriously damped male status rivalry and thereby reduced the intensity of selection within the group by reducing phenotypic variation at that level, while powerful social pressure to make decisions consensual at the band level had a similar effect. Consensual decisions also had another effect: they increased variation between groups because entire bands enacted their subsistence strategies collectively and the strategies varied between bands. By reducing the intensity of individual selection and boosting group effects, these behaviors provided a unique opportunity for altruistic genes to be established and maintained. In addition, the egalitarian custom of socially isolating or actively punishing lazy or cheating noncooperators reduced the free-rider problem. In combination. these phenotypic effects facilitated selection of altruistic genes in spite of some limited free riding. This selection scenario remained in place for thousands of generations, and the result was a shift in the balance of power between individual and group selection in favor of group effects. This new balance today is reflected in an ambivalent human nature that exhibits substantial altruism in addition to selfishness and nepotism.

Abstract: In this article we provide empirical support for anger as an underlying mechanism of costly punishment in three studies. A first study showed that participants punished other players more the less these players cooperated in a Public Goods Game and that this effect was mediated by experienced anger. A second study showed that participants appraised non-cooperation in a Sequential Trust Game (STG) as more unfair than cooperation and that they imposed more costly punishment on unfair others as compared to fair others. Moreover, a third study showed that following an anger induction in an unrelated task, participants imposed more costly punishment on unfair players in a subsequent STG.

Authors: Przepiorka, W; Diekmann, A
Author Full Names: Przepiorka, Wojtek; Diekmann, Andreas
Article Title: Individual heterogeneity and costly punishment: a volunteer's dilemma
Source Title: PROCEEDINGS OF THE ROYAL SOCIETY B-BIOLOGICAL SCIENCES
Author Keywords: evolution of cooperation; peer punishment; second-order free-rider problem; volunteer's dilemma; coordination; social norms
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS GAMES; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; STRONG RECIPROCITY; HUMAN COOPERATION; HUMANS; INSTITUTIONS; EVOLUTION; ENFORCEMENT; INCENTIVES; GOVERNANCE
Abstract: Social control and the enforcement of social norms glue a society together. It has been shown theoretically and empirically that informal punishment of wrongdoers fosters cooperation in human groups. Most of this research has focused on voluntary and uncoordinated punishment carried out by individual group members. However, as punishment is costly, it is an open question as to why humans engage in the punishment of wrongdoers even in one-time-only encounters. While evolved punitive preferences have been advocated as proximate explanations for such behaviour, the strategic nature of the punishment situation has remained underexplored. It has been suggested to conceive of the punishment situation as a volunteer's dilemma (VOD), where only one individual's action is necessary and sufficient to punish the wrongdoer. Here, we show experimentally that implementing the punishment situation as a VOD sustains cooperation in an environment where punishers and non-punishers coexist. Moreover, we show that punishment-cost heterogeneity allows individuals to tacitly agree on only the strongest group member carrying out the punishment, thereby increasing the effectiveness and efficiency of social norm enforcement. Our results corroborate that costly peer punishment can be explained without assuming punitive preferences and show that centralized sanctioning institutions can emerge from arbitrary individual differences.

Article Title: BACKWARD-LOOKING SOCIAL-CONTROL
Abstract: Rational-choice theorists stress the need for social control to overcome the free-rider problem in collective action. Critics counter that mechanisms for monitoring and enforcement are themselves public goods that presume collective action rather than explain it. In response, Heckathorn (1989) proposed an analytic solution based on ''hypocritical cooperation'' in which rational actors calculate the optimal allocation of resources between compliance with collective obligations and their enforcement. I relax these ''forward-looking'' behavioral assumptions and show how social control might evolve among ''backward-looking '' pragmatists. Computer simulations test the ability of various sanctioning regimes to generate cooperation as well as resist stampedes that risk overcooperation and needless sacrifice. External moral sanctions produce too little cooperation, while internalized sanctions produce too much. The best performer induced self-sustaining cooperation and then turned itself off once enforcement was no longer needed. This self-regulating system shows how collective rationality can obtain without the actors intending it.

Below I proceed through the 15 parameters one by one.  
For each parameter I indicate  

(1) Whether the Macy (1993) article ever mentions or operationalises the parameter and, if so, the value(s) it actually uses;  

(2) Whether the article gives any prediction – qualitative or quantitative – about what would happen to the “punishment-treatment effect” (i.e., the difference between a game with punishment and the same game without punishment) if the parameter were *systematically varied*.  Whenever the paper gives a precise numeric result I reproduce it, citing the relevant figure or passage; otherwise I state that no numeric effect size is available.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned.  All simulation examples use N = 100 players (e.g., Fig. 2, p. 828).  Group size also appears in every cost formula.  
   (2) Not systematically varied in the paper.  A qualitative statement is given (p. 833) that “the cost of side-payments increases about in line with the number who receive them,” so larger N should make material punishment (and reward) relatively less attractive, but no numeric effect size is reported.

2. Number of rounds (length of the repeated game)  
   (1) The word “iteration” is used, and figures display up to 60 iterations, but the horizon is never treated as a manipulable variable; it is simply long enough for learning dynamics to unfold.  
   (2) No systematic variation and no prediction.

3. Free chat between players  
   (1) Never mentioned.  
   (2) No prediction.

4. All-or-nothing contribution decision  
   (1) Explicitly assumed: “decisions to comply…are binary (non-divisible)” (p. 822).  
   (2) The paper never contrasts this with a continuous contribution schedule, so no prediction about varying it.

5. Contribution default / “take-back” frame  
   (1) Not discussed.  
   (2) No prediction.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   (1) Public-goods returns are captured by a *logistic S-curve* (Eq. 1), not by a linear MPCR.  Parameter values (slope = 10, mid-point = .5) are fixed across all runs.  
   (2) No systematic variation, hence no prediction.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   (1) Modelled through C′ij  = Vij′ / N^J′  (Eq. 5).  J′ is varied: 0 (very costly), .5 (moderate), or 1 (costless jointness).  
   (2) Systematic variation:  
       • Fig. 4 contrasts J′ = .5 (material sanctions) with J′ = 1 (costless moral pressure).  
       • Text (pp. 832–833) predicts that higher J′ (i.e., lower cost) increases the ability of punishment to push the group past the non-cooperative equilibrium and thus enlarges the punishment treatment effect.  No numeric efficiency figures are presented; the only numbers are contribution rates (e.g., ≈.80 with J′=1 versus ≈.45 with J′=.5).

8. Punishment magnitude (fine on target per “unit” sent)  
   (1) In Eq. 3, Sij = ± P′i^m .  The exponent m≥1 controls how sharply sanctions rise with the amount invested.  The paper compares m = 1 (linear, typical of material incentives) with m = 2 (accelerating, typical of moral pressure).  
   (2) Systematic variation: Higher m depresses the effectiveness of punishment at low enforcement levels (the “start-up problem”; see Fig. 4, dashed vs. solid lines).  No numeric efficiency effect is provided.

9. Whether a reward option exists  
   (1) Yes.  “Side-payments” to volunteers are the reward analogue (positive Sij ).  
   (2) The article predicts that adding rewards (as opposed to only punishments) helps to reach critical mass when m=1 and J′=.5, but if J′=0 the cost may outweigh the benefit (pp. 832–833, Fig. 4).  No numerical payoff or efficiency values are supplied—only the qualitative contrast that punishment-plus-reward succeeds in reaching ≈80 % contribution whereas punishment alone does not.

10. Reward cost  
    (1) Same cost function C′ij as for punishment; no further parameterisation.  Not varied independently.  
    (2) No prediction isolated from Parameter 7.

11. Reward magnitude  
    (1) Tied to the same Sij equation; not manipulated.  
    (2) No prediction.

12. Whether the number of rounds is announced  
    (1) Not mentioned.  
    (2) No prediction.

13. Whether peer outcomes (pay-offs) are shown  
    (1) In the simulation every agent “sees” the aggregate outcome Oi each period; there is no experimental treatment that withholds this information.  
    (2) Not varied, no prediction.

14. Whether punished players learn who punished them  
    (1) The model has *anonymous* sanctioning; identity is irrelevant.  
    (2) Not varied, no prediction.

15. Whether rewarded players learn who rewarded them  
    (1) Same as 14 – not modelled.  
    (2) No prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables used  
   • The paper does *not* report “group efficiency” (total payoff ÷ maximum possible).  
   • The reported dependent variables are:  
     – First-order contribution rate (percentage who contribute each round)  
     – Second-order contribution rate (percentage who punish/reward)  
     – Qualitative group outcome (“collective action success” vs. “failure”)  
   Contribution rate and efficiency are only indirectly related; efficiency is never computed.

B. Parameters mentioned  
   8 of 15 parameters are mentioned at all (1,2,4,6,7,8,9,13).  The other 7 are absent.

C. Parameters systematically varied for their *effect on the punishment treatment*  
   Only 3 parameters receive such treatment:  
   – Punishment cost (J′)  
   – Punishment magnitude curvature (m)  
   – Existence of rewards (Parameter 9)  
   For none of them does the paper supply an efficiency effect size; only contribution-rate trajectories are graphed.

D. What could we predict—*solely* from this paper—about the 15 parameters and their interactions on the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency?  
   • Lower punishment cost (higher J′) ⇒ larger positive effect of punishment on cooperation and therefore on efficiency.  
   • A more *linear* punishment technology (m≈1) beats an accelerating one (m>1) at low enforcement levels; hence, holding cost constant, smaller m should enlarge the treatment effect.  
   • Adding rewards can help reach critical mass when punishment costs are not too high, so “punishment + reward” may outperform “punishment-only” in efficiency – but if rewards are very costly (low J′) the advantage disappears.  
   • Larger groups (higher N) make material sanctions dearer and therefore shrink their efficiency advantage relative to moral sanctions.  
   • All other listed parameters are either fixed by assumption (binary choice, unlimited horizon, full outcome visibility) or never discussed; thus the paper offers no basis for prediction about them.

Abstract: We study evolutionarily stable outcomes for a class of games that admit cooperation and conflict as possible Nash equilibria.       – Not applicable. No reward mechanism.  
    • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict any effect of varying it?  
      – Not applicable.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins or benefit awarded for each unit of reward)
    • Discussion/Value in paper?  
      – Not applicable. No reward mechanism is used.  
    • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict any effect of varying it?  
      – Not applicable.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know exactly when the game ends)?
    • Discussion/Value in paper?  
      – The first 20‐round (no‐punishment) portion is presumably announced. However, there is a “surprise restart” at period 21 for punishment. The paper does not say that the total 40 rounds were known ahead of time.  
    • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict any effect of varying it?  
      – No. They do not manipulate whether the horizon is known or unknown, nor do they discuss how changing that knowledge would affect punishment’s impact on efficiency.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (i.e., do players see how much others gained/lost)?
    • Discussion/Value in paper?  
      – The star network structure means the peripheral players see only the central player’s contributions (and their own payoffs), and the central player sees each peripheral’s contribution. The paper does mention that everyone sees their own earnings but peripheral players do not directly see each other’s exact contributions.  
    • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict any effect of varying it?
      – No, there is only one information setup (the star network). No additional variation or predictions.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Discussion/Value in paper?  
      – The central player can only be punished by peripheral players, and the peripheral players can only be punished by the central player (due to the star network). However, the paper does not systematically manipulate whether the punishee knows the identity of the punisher.  
    • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict any effect of varying it?  
      – No. It is not one of their treatment variables and no separate predictions are made.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Discussion/Value in paper?  
      – Not applicable. The experiment does not include rewarding at all.  
    • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict any effect of varying it?  
      – No mention of reward.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • Yes. In Section 4.4 (“Efficiency”), the authors explicitly measure efficiency as actual group earnings as a percentage of the maximum possible. They also discuss (1) contributions to the public good and (2) punishment behavior/costs. Thus, the main dependent variables they examine are:  
     1) Contributions (or tokens allocated to the public fund)  
     2) Punishment (tokens spent and received)  
     3) Efficiency (payoffs net of punishment costs relative to the maximum possible)  

   These dependent variables differ in that contributions track how many tokens are put into the public good, whereas efficiency factors in both the benefits of cooperation and the costs of punishment.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
     (1) Number of players (fixed at 4)  
     (2) Number of rounds (40 total, but 20 followed by a “surprise” 20)  
     (6) MPCR = 0.5  
     (7) Punishment cost structure (Table 1)  
     (8) Punishment magnitude (10% payoff reduction per punishment token)  
     (13) Peer outcomes/information structure (star network)  
   • The other parameters (3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 15) are either not relevant or not varied in the authors’ design.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The authors do not systematically vary any of the above parameters. All are held fixed at the values described. Hence, none of the 15 parameters is truly “varied” in multiple conditions to see its impact on punishment’s effect on efficiency.  
   • Instead, the paper systematically varies only two features outside this specific 15‐item list:  
     – Whether the central position is assigned to a high‐status or low‐status person.  
     – Whether there is punishment at all (the second 20 rounds) versus no punishment (the first 20 rounds).  
   • Consequently, there are no numerical effect sizes in the paper that directly tie changes in any of the 15 parameters themselves to changes in the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   • Because the paper does not systematically vary or analyze these 15 parameters (beyond noting their fixed values), it offers little direct basis for predicting how varying them would affect the punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency. The only strong conclusion related to “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” is that it depends on how players use punishment and whether high‐status or low‐status individuals are at the center of the group.  
   • In short, the paper does not provide evidence that would allow precise or numerical predictions on how changes in any of the 15 parameters would alter the punishment treatment effect on efficiency. One could only tentatively speculate—but the paper itself gives no direct discussion or effect sizes on that point, so little to no prediction can be made from these results alone.

Below, each of the fifteen parameters is treated in turn.  
For every parameter I state (i) whether the paper ever mentions it (and, if so, its fixed value) and (ii) whether the paper *systematically varies* that parameter and reports how such variation changes the **punishment treatment effect** (i.e., the difference in efficiency ‑ or in any other dependent variable ‑ between “with-punishment” and “without-punishment” conditions).  Whenever the paper does give an effect size I quote the number and the source (table/figure); otherwise I explicitly say that no information is provided.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
(i) Mentioned: yes.  Groups of n = 3 (Section 2).  
(ii) Systematically varied: no.  No predictions or effect sizes.

2. Number of rounds  
(i) Mentioned: yes.  The experiment is one–shot (Part I and Part II are each single-round games).  
(ii) Systematically varied: no.  No predictions or effect sizes.

3. Chat enabled?  
(i) Mentioned: yes.  “Communication among participants was prohibited.” (Section 2)  
(ii) Systematically varied: no.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
(i) Mentioned implicitly.  Contributions could be any integer from 0 to 20 Guilders (standard linear PGG).  
(ii) Systematically varied: no.

5. Contribution default (backwards decision)?  
(i) Not mentioned.  
(ii) Not varied.

6. MPCR or related monetary-stakes parameter  
(i) MPCR γ = 0.5 is fixed (Section 2).  The *only* parameter the authors vary is the real-money **conversion rate** of the experimental currency (1 Guilder = 1.5 ZAR in LOW vs. 7.5 ZAR in HIGH, a 5× stake difference).  
(ii) Systematically varied: the conversion rate is varied, but MPCR itself is not.  The paper reports that this stake increase has **no statistically significant effect** on contributions or punishment (Table 1, Tobit regressions in Table 2).  Because efficiency is never calculated, no punishment-treatment-effect on efficiency is reported.

7. Punishment cost (to impose 1 unit)  
(i) Mentioned: fixed at 1 Guilder (Section 2).  
(ii) Systematically varied: no.

8. Punishment magnitude (deduction suffered per point)  
(i) Mentioned: fixed at 3 Guilders (Section 2).  
(ii) Systematically varied: no.

9. Reward enabled?  
(i) Mentioned implicitly: no reward stage exists.  
(ii) Not varied.

10. Reward cost  
(i) Not applicable / not mentioned.  
(ii) Not varied.

11. Reward magnitude  
(i) Not applicable / not mentioned.  
(ii) Not varied.

12. Is the number of rounds known?  
(i) Yes.  Subjects know each part is one-shot; this fact is common knowledge (Section 2).  
(ii) Not varied.

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
(i) Yes.  After the contribution stage players learn every group member’s contribution before deciding on punishment (Section 2).  
(ii) Not varied.

14. Is punisher identity revealed?  
(i) Mentioned: no.  “Group members would remain anonymous.” (Section 2)  
(ii) Not varied.

15. Is rewarder identity revealed?  
(i) Not applicable.  
(ii) Not varied.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary

A. Dependent variables used in the paper  
   – Contribution level (% of endowment contributed).  
   – Punishment behaviour (probability of punishing, mean punishment points, Tobit-estimated punishment demand).  
   – **Efficiency (total or average payoff) is *never* reported or analysed.**  
   Thus, contribution and punishment are the only dependent variables; they are conceptually different from efficiency because they ignore the costly nature of punishment and the social return from the public good.

B. How many of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   10 parameters are at least mentioned (1,2,3,4,6,7,8,12,13,14).  
   Five parameters (5,9,10,11,15) are not discussed.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss *systematic variation* and its effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
   Zero.  None of the fifteen parameters is systematically varied with respect to the punishment treatment effect on efficiency (or on any other outcome) in the paper.  The sole manipulation is stake size via a currency conversion rate, which is outside the listed parameters (MPCR is held constant).

D. Predictions one could make, *solely* from the content of this paper, about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency  
   The paper offers almost no basis for prediction.  Because no parameter on the list was varied, and efficiency was never measured, one can make **little to no prediction** about how changing any of the 15 parameters (individually or in interaction) would alter the efficiency impact of allowing punishment.  The only hint is that dramatically increasing the *real* stakes (five-fold) left average contributions and punishment behaviour unchanged; if one interprets “higher stakes” loosely as part of Parameter 6, that result would predict *no change* in efficiency from stake increases, but even that extrapolation is tenuous because efficiency itself was not calculated.

In short, the paper does not provide quantitative leverage for forecasting the punishment treatment effect on efficiency as a function of the listed parameters.

Authors: Grechenig, K; Nicklisch, A; Thöni, C
Author Full Names: Grechenig, Kristoffel; Nicklisch, Andreas; Thoeni, Christian
Article Title: Punishment Despite Reasonable Doubt-A Public Goods Experiment with Sanctions Under Uncertainty
Keywords Plus: PUNITIVE DAMAGES; CIVIL LITIGATION; PROOF; LAW; ENFORCEMENT; INFORMATION
Abstract: Under a great variety of legally relevant circumstances, people have to decide whether or not to cooperate when they face an incentive to defect. The law sometimes provides people with sanctioning mechanisms to enforce pro-social behavior. Experimental evidence on voluntary public goods provision shows that the option to punish others substantially improves cooperation, even if punishment is costly. However, these studies focus on situations where there is no uncertainty about the behavior of others. We investigate sanctions in a world with reasonable doubt about the contributions of others. Interestingly, people reveal a high willingness to punish even if their information about cooperation rates is highly inaccurate. If there is some nontrivial degree of noise, punishment (1) cannot establish cooperation high and (2) reduces welfare even below the level of a setting without punishment. Our findings suggest that sufficient information accuracy about others' behavior is crucial for the efficiency of sanction mechanisms. If a situation is characterized by low information accuracy, precluding sanctions, for example, through high standards of proof, is likely to be optimal.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter accounting of what the paper “Punishment Despite Reasonable Doubt: A Public Goods Experiment with Sanctions Under Uncertainty” does and does not say regarding each of the 15 listed parameters, together with whether the paper predicts the effect of systematically varying those parameters on the “punishment treatment effect.” Throughout, I adhere strictly to the content of this paper and do not draw on any outside sources.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Does the paper discuss it? Yes. All sessions use groups of four players.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict effects of varying it? No. The number of players is always 4 and is not varied.

2. Number of rounds
   • Does the paper discuss it? Yes. There are 10 periods (rounds).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict effects of varying it? No. All conditions run for 10 periods; the paper does not manipulate or analyze an effect of changing the number of rounds.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Does the paper discuss it? No. There is no mention of any open chat or communication channel between players.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it? No. It is not discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Does the paper discuss it? Yes, indirectly: each player chooses an integer from 0 to 20 to contribute. Hence, it is not all or nothing; one can contribute anywhere between 0 and 20 ECU.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict effects of varying it? No. The contribution decision is always 0–20 ECU, with no variations tested.

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much of their endowment to move from the public fund back into their hand)?
   • Does the paper discuss it? No. There is no mention of a default-contribution type of mechanism.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it? No. It never appears in the design or analysis.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor
   • Does the paper discuss it? Yes. The MPCR is constant at 0.4.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict effects of varying it? No. MPCR remains 0.4 throughout, and there is no discussion of varying it.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Does the paper discuss it? Yes. It costs 1 ECU (to the punisher) to impose 1 punishment point.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict effects of varying it? No. This cost is held fixed; there is no discussion of varying it.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed on them)
   • Does the paper discuss it? Yes. Each punishment point deducts 3 ECU from the punished player’s account.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict effects of varying it? No. This punishment magnitude (3 ECU) is fixed, and there is no discussion of systematically changing it.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Does the paper discuss it? No. The design includes only a punishment mechanism; rewards do not appear.  
   • Does the paper predict effects of varying it? No. The paper does not consider rewards.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Does the paper discuss it? No. Rewards are not part of the experiment.  
   • Does the paper predict effects of varying it? No. It is not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)
   • Does the paper discuss it? No. Rewards are never implemented in the design.  
   • Does the paper predict effects of varying it? No. It is not discussed.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
   • Does the paper discuss it? The design indicates a repeated game of 10 periods. Although the paper does not explicitly say “participants were told that there are 10 rounds,” it does state that it is a repeated game with exactly 10 periods, suggesting that this was common knowledge.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict effects of varying it? No. It remains 10 periods, with no separate condition for, say, unknown game length.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?
   • Does the paper discuss it? The paper explains that after each period, players see signals about others’ contributions, which may be noisy, and also see how many total punishment points they themselves received. However, they do not see who punished them or precise “gains/losses” of each other’s net payoffs.  
   • Does the paper predict effects of varying it? No. The main variation is the noise in signals of others’ contributions, not in the display of detailed peer earnings.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Does the paper discuss it? Yes. It explicitly states that “Players … receive no detailed information on who distributed points.” So punisher identity is kept hidden.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict effects of varying it? No. They do not change whether punisher identity is revealed; it is hidden in all relevant treatments.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Does the paper discuss it? No. There is no reward mechanism in this experiment, so this parameter does not arise.  
   • Does the paper predict effects of varying it? No. Rewarding is not part of the design.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Beyond those 15 parameters, the only systematic variation in the paper is:
• Whether a punishment mechanism is available or not.  
• Whether the “signal accuracy” about other players’ contributions (λ) is 1.0 (perfect), 0.9 (mild noise), or 0.5 (large noise).  

The chief “punishment treatment effect” in this paper is broadly how having punishment at various signal-accuracy levels affects outcomes (including “cooperation” and “welfare/efficiency”).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FINAL SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What other dependent variables are used, and how do these differ?  
• Yes. The authors explicitly measure “welfare” and “efficiency” (they refer to average payoffs, total payoffs, and “the fraction of possible efficiency gains” actually realized).  
• They also measure contributions (how many tokens each player invests in the public good) and punishment points used/received. These are conceptually distinct from efficiency, because overall efficiency depends on both positive (public good returns) and negative (punishment) payoffs.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Mentioned explicitly:  
  (1) Number of players (always 4).  
  (2) Number of rounds (always 10).  
  (4) Contribution is not “all or nothing” (though not “varied,” it is stated as 0–20 tokens).  
  (6) MPCR (0.4).  
  (7) Punishment cost (1 ECU).  
  (8) Punishment magnitude (3 ECU).  
  (14) Punisher identity is not revealed (mentioned, but not varied).  
• The paper does not mention or implement the other parameters in a way that systematically varies them.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• Strictly speaking, the paper does not systematically vary any of those 15 parameters, except for toggling the presence vs. absence of punishment (which relates loosely to parameters 7 and 8 but is not a direct variation of cost/magnitude themselves) and changing the noise level of signals (which is not one of the 15 listed parameters).  
• Hence, none of the originally listed 15 parameters is explicitly varied (e.g., changing the MPCR, changing group size, or changing punishment cost). The paper cannot (and does not) give effect sizes for systematically changing any of the 15 parameters.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
• The paper focuses on noise (signal accuracy) and presence/absence of punishment, rather than manipulating the 15 enumerated parameters. Thus, it provides little or no direct guidance for how systematically changing, say, “number of players” or “punishment magnitude” would affect efficiency.  
• One can only infer that if punishment becomes especially costly (parameter 7) or if punishment is especially large in impact (parameter 8), the efficiency losses from “erroneous” punishment might increase, much as they do in high-noise conditions. However, this inference is not directly tested in the paper.  
• In short, the paper does not give enough information to predict reliably how those 15 parameters or their interactions would affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, other than highlighting that the risk of “wrongful” punishment is a key channel reducing efficiency when punishment is available.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
reference_APA: Grechenig, Kristoffel, Nicklisch, Andreas & Thoeni, Christian (2010). Punishment Despite Reasonable Doubt-A Public Goods Experiment with Sanctions Under Uncertainty. JOURNAL OF EMPIRICAL LEGAL STUDIES.

Below each parameter is treated in turn.

For every parameter I report  

(1) Whether the paper explicitly gives its value / setting (and I quote the passage or give the table where it appears), and  

(2) Whether the paper makes any prediction or presents any evidence on what would happen to the **punishment-treatment effect on efficiency** (or on any other dependent variable) if that parameter were **systematically varied**.  If such a prediction exists I copy the numerical effect size; if not, I state “none”.

“Punishment-treatment effect” = outcome in a punishment treatment minus the outcome in the otherwise identical no-punishment treatment.

DEPENDENT VARIABLES USED BY THE PAPER  
The paper reports (i) average contribution, (ii) average earnings per person (sometimes called “efficiency”), (iii) punishment given / received, (iv) variances.  Only (ii) is an efficiency measure.

-----------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players in the group  
(1) Stated: groups of four.  (“…anonymous groups of four that stayed together for a total of 10 periods…”)  
(2) No parameter variation; no prediction.

2. Number of rounds  
(1) Stated: 10 periods.  
(2) No variation; no prediction.

3. Chat enabled?  
(1) All six treatments in this paper **do not** allow chat.  Chat is mentioned only as background referring to another paper (BPP 2006).  
(2) No prediction in this paper about adding or removing chat.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution?  
(1) Contributions are continuous integers 0–10.  This fact is implied but nowhere varied.  
(2) No prediction.

5. Contribution default / withdrawal frame?  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) No prediction.

6. Marginal-per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
(1) Stated: λ = 1.6 with n = 4 ⇒ MPCR = 0.40.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction.

7. Cost to impose one unit of punishment  
(1) Stated: “fixed cost of E$0.25 to the punisher per E$1 of earnings loss to the person punished.”  
(2) Single value, not varied.  The authors note that because punishment is costly, higher contributions in R do **not** raise earnings, but they do **not** investigate other cost levels, so no systematic prediction.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss to target per unit imposed)  
(1) Fixed at 1 (see #7 above).  
(2) Not varied; no prediction.

9. Whether a reward option is enabled  
(1) Not available in any treatment.  
(2) No prediction.

10. Cost of rewarding  
Not applicable.

11. Reward magnitude  
Not applicable.

12. Do players know the number of rounds?  
(1) The game is described as “a total of 10 periods”; the standard laboratory protocol makes this common knowledge, but the paper never contrasts it with an unknown-horizon design.  
(2) No prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
(1) Yes.  After each contribution stage subjects saw every group member’s contribution; after the punishment stage each subject saw how much s/he had been punished (not by whom).  
(2) Constant across treatments; no prediction.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
(1) No.  “Individuals were informed only of the reductions they themselves received, without knowing the identities of the punishers.”  
(2) Not varied; no prediction.

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
Not applicable (no rewards).

-----------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables actually analysed  
– Average contribution (behavioural)  
– Average monetary earnings per person (the paper sometimes calls this “efficiency”).  
– Dispersion measures and punishment flows.  
Contribution and efficiency move in different directions once punishment costs are taken into account: punishment raises contributions but leaves efficiency unchanged unless combined with the promise option.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are at least mentioned?  
Eight: 1, 2, 3 (only in background), 6, 7, 8, 13, 14.  The other seven are absent.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss how **systematically varying** that parameter would change the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable)?  
Zero.  Every mentioned parameter is held fixed; the paper varies only “communication structure” (none vs numerical announcements vs announcements + promise) and “institution” (punishment allowed vs not).

D. If one had to predict, relying **only** on the evidence in this paper, how the 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency, very little can be said.  The only qualitative inference supported is:

• With the specific cost/magnitude ratio used here (0.25 : 1), adding punishment raises contributions but does **not** raise efficiency unless an additional communication instrument (credible promises) is also available.  

Because no parameter among the 15 was experimentally manipulated, the paper provides no basis for extrapolating how changing any single parameter (group size, MPCR, punishment cost, information conditions, etc.) would alter that conclusion.
reference_APA: Bochet, Olivier & Putterman, Louis (2009). Not just babble: Opening the black box of communication in a voluntary contribution experiment. EUROPEAN ECONOMIC REVIEW.

Abstract: We model the coevolution of behavioral strategies and social learning rules in the context of a cooperative dilemma, a situation in which individuals must decide whether or not to subordinate their own interests to those of the group. There are two learning rules in our model, conformism and payoff-dependent imitation, which evolve by natural selection, and three behavioral strategies, cooperate, defect, and cooperate, plus punish defectors, which evolve under the influence of the prevailing learning rules. Below, each of the 15 public-goods-game parameters is considered in turn.

For each parameter I state  
(1) whether the paper even mentions it and, if so, the value(s) used;  
(2) whether the paper reports what happens when the parameter is **systematically varied** and, if so, how that affects the *punishment treatment effect* (i.e., the difference between a condition that allows punishment and one that does not).  
Whenever the paper’s figures/tables allow a numerical estimate, I give it; otherwise I simply note the qualitative pattern.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
--------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Number of players (group size)  
   1) Mentioned.  Baseline N = 64 (Table 1).  In all main figures N is systematically varied from small values (~4) up to at least 256.  
   2) Yes, the paper shows how varying N changes the gap between “punishment present” and “punishment absent.”  
      • Fig. 1A (cooperation):  
        – With *conformism present* the “punishment-plus-conformism” line (solid squares) lies well above the “conformism-only” line (triangles), and the gap **widens with N**.  
        – With *conformism absent* the “punishment-only” line (empty squares) is always above the “no-punishment/no-conformism” line (circles), but the gap **narrows with N** and eventually vanishes when N is very large.  
      • The dependent variable is *cooperation rate*, not efficiency; no numerical effect sizes are printed, only curves.  
      • Hence, group size is the **only parameter that the paper systematically varies and relates to a punishment effect**.

2. Number of rounds  
   1) Not mentioned; the model is a long-run evolutionary simulation, not a repeated finite-round public-goods game.  
   2) No discussion or prediction.

3. Chat enabled?  
   1) Not mentioned.  
   2) No discussion.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
   1) Implicitly mentioned: an individual either *cooperates* (pays cost c) or *defects*. This is indeed an all-or-nothing contribution structure.  
   2) The rule is fixed; there is **no systematic variation**, hence no prediction about its effect on punishment.

5. Contribution default (take vs. give frame)  
   1) Not mentioned.  
   2) No discussion.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   1) Not used; benefits of cooperation appear only indirectly via inter-group war success, not through an MPCR.  
   2) No discussion.

7. Punishment cost to punisher  
   1) Mentioned: k = 0.2 (Table 1).  
   2) Fixed; not systematically varied, so no prediction.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss to target per unit)  
   1) Mentioned: p = 0.8 (Table 1).  
   2) Fixed; no systematic variation or prediction.

9. Reward option present?  
   1) Not included.  
   2) No discussion.

10. Reward cost  
    Not included.

11. Reward magnitude  
    Not included.

12. Rounds known to players (finite-horizon information)  
    1) Not relevant; there is no round structure.  
    2) No discussion.

13. Peer outcomes shown  
    Not mentioned.

14. Punishee knows who punished  
    Not mentioned.

15. Reward recipient knows who rewarded  
    Not mentioned.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables used  
   • The paper does **not** report *group efficiency* (total or average payoff relative to the maximum).  
   • The main dependent variables are the *frequency of cooperation*, the *frequency of conformism*, and the *frequency of each strategy* (C, D, P).  
   • These differ from efficiency: a group could have high cooperation frequency yet, depending on parameter values, still achieve low total pay-off if punishers incur large costs.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   – Parameter 1 (Number of players)  
   – Parameter 4 (All-or-nothing contributions – fixed)  
   – Parameter 7 (Punishment cost k)  
   – Parameter 8 (Punishment magnitude p)  
   → 4 of the 15 are mentioned at all.

C. For which parameters does the paper discuss *systematic variation* and its impact on a punishment treatment effect?  
   – Only Parameter 1 (Number of players).  
   – So, 1 out of 15 parameters receives such treatment, and the outcome variable is *cooperation*, not efficiency.

D. Predictions one could make—restricted strictly to what the paper contains  
   • Larger group size (Parameter 1)  
     – With conformism present, adding punishment is predicted to **increase efficiency** (by proxy through higher cooperation) more and more as N grows.  
     – Without conformism, adding punishment helps mainly in small and medium groups; the benefit fades in very large groups.  
   • For Parameters 4, 7, 8 no variation is explored, so no prediction can be made beyond the single default values used.  
   • For the remaining 11 parameters the paper is silent; therefore **no prediction** about their main or interaction effects on efficiency can be extracted.

In short, the paper gives enough information to state that group size moderates the punishment effect on cooperation (and, by inference, would moderate efficiency), but provides virtually no guidance on how the other 14 parameters—or any interaction other than “group size × conformism × punishment”—would influence the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.
reference_APA: Guzman, Ricardo Andres, Rodriguez-Sickert, Carlos & Rowthorn, Robert (2007). When in Rome, do as the Romans do:: the coevolution of altruistic punishment, conformist learning, and cooperation. EVOLUTION AND HUMAN BEHAVIOR.

Authors: Raihani, NJ; Bshary, R
Author Full Names: Raihani, Nichola J.; Bshary, Redouan
Article Title: Third-party punishers are rewarded, but third-party helpers even more so
Author Keywords: Cooperation; indirect reciprocity; punishment; reputation
Keywords Plus: FALSE DISCOVERY RATE; INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; PUNISHMENT; COOPERATION; REPUTATION; EVOLUTION; RATHER; ANONYMITY; PARTNER
Abstract: Punishers can benefit from a tough reputation, where future partners cooperate because they fear repercussions. Alternatively, punishers might receive help from bystanders if their act is perceived as just and other-regarding. Third-party punishment of selfish individuals arguably fits these conditions, but it is not known whether third-party punishers are rewarded for their investments. Here, we show that third-party punishers are indeed rewarded by uninvolved bystanders. Third parties were presented with the outcome of a dictator game in which the dictator was either selfish or fair and were allocated to one of three treatments in which they could choose to do nothing or (1) punish the dictator, (2) help the receiver, or (3) choose between punishment and helping, respectively. A fourth player (bystander) then sees the third-party's decision and could choose to reward the third party or not. Third parties that punished selfish dictators were more likely to be rewarded by bystanders than third parties that took no action in response to a selfish dictator. However, helpful third parties were rewarded even more than third-party punishers. These results suggest that punishment could in principle evolve via indirect reciprocity, but also provide insights into why individuals typically prefer to invest in positive actions.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter inventory of what this particular paper does (and does not) say with respect to the 15 parameters of interest. Following that is a required four-part summary (A–D).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – Yes. The paper has a four-player setup: Dictator (Player 1), Receiver (Player 2), Third Party (Player 3), and Bystander (Player 4).  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or discuss varying it?  
  – No. The study always uses four players. The paper does not mention any effect, including on efficiency, of changing the number of players.

2. Number of rounds  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – Yes. It is a one-shot game (a single round).  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or discuss varying it?  
  – No. The paper does not manipulate or compare different numbers of rounds, nor does it discuss potential effects on treatment outcomes (or efficiency).

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – No. There is no mention of allowing or disallowing player communication or of chat features.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or discuss varying it?  
  – No.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – No. This is not a public goods design with partial or total contributions. The dictator simply chooses one of two splits.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or discuss varying it?  
  – No.

5. Is the contribution default?  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – No. (In a public goods game, this might mean “the player decides how much to move back into their hand,” etc.) Here, the game is a dictator-split format rather than a continuous or default-based contribution scheme.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or discuss varying it?  
  – No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – No. The design is not a repeated public goods game with a multiplier; it is a dictator game with a third-party/bystander component.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or discuss varying it?  
  – No.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – Yes, but only in the sense that, in the experiment, the third party pays 0.05 USD to reduce the dictator’s bonus by 0.20 USD.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or discuss varying it?  
  – No. The paper fixes the punishment cost at 0.05; there is no discussion of how the punishment cost might affect treatment effects or efficiency if varied.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted per unit punishment)  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – Yes, in this experiment it is 0.20 USD deducted from the dictator whenever a third party pays 0.05 USD.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or discuss varying it?  
  – No. The magnitude is fixed. No discussion of how systematically varying it would affect outcomes (including efficiency).

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – The paper does involve a bystander’s option to reward the third party, but it does not experimentally turn reward “on” vs. “off.” Bystanders always could pay 0.05 USD to reward the third party with 0.25 USD.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or discuss varying it?  
  – No. This aspect is always present; there is no condition in which rewarding is disabled.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – Yes; for bystanders, rewarding costs 0.05 USD.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or discuss varying it?  
  – No. There is no manipulation of different reward-cost levels, nor any discussion of how such variation might change results.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded per unit of reward)  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – Yes; the paper sets a fixed amount of 0.25 USD that the third party receives when the bystander pays 0.05 USD.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or discuss varying it?  
  – No. The paper does not explore the effect of systematically varying this magnitude.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – It is a one-shot game. The paper does not explore repeated or undisclosed end points.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or discuss varying it?  
  – No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much their peers gained/lost each round)?  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – In the design, the bystander is informed of the dictator’s action (fair/selfish) and the third party’s action (punish/help/do nothing) but there is no “systematic variation” of what is shown or hidden.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or discuss varying it?  
  – No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know the specific punisher?  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – No. The experiment does not focus on whether the punished dictator knows which specific person punished them.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or discuss varying it?  
  – No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know the specific rewarder?  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – No. The paper does not discuss whether the rewarded party knows exactly who rewarded them.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or discuss varying it?  
  – No.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   – No. The paper does not measure or report “efficiency” (actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff). Instead, it primarily measures whether and how often bystanders reward the third party. The authors also analyze whether the third party punishes, helps, or does nothing, and how that affects bystanders’ likelihood of giving a reward. These dependent variables (likelihood of receiving a reward, proportion choosing to punish or help, etc.) are not the same as group (in)efficiency.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – Mentioned (in a fixed way) are:  
       (1) Number of players (always four)  
       (2) Number of rounds (always one)  
       (7) Punishment cost (0.05 USD)  
       (8) Punishment magnitude (0.20 USD)  
       (9) Whether a reward is enabled (always yes)  
       (10) Reward cost (0.05 USD)  
       (11) Reward magnitude (0.25 USD)  
   – The other parameters (3–6, 12–15) either do not appear at all or appear without any discussion of being varied.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable, when the parameter is systematically varied?  
   – None. Although the paper fixes certain values for punishment and reward (e.g., cost and magnitude), it does not systematically vary any of these 15 parameters. Consequently, the paper does not provide numerical effect sizes related to parametric variation, nor does it link any of these parameters to changes in efficiency or other dependent variables when those parameters are varied.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper, what would they be?  
   – The paper does not address efficiency or how any of the 15 parameters, if manipulated, would alter it. Its focus is on whether third-party punishers or helpers gain social rewards (from bystanders). Therefore, it offers little basis for predicting how systematically changing any of the 15 parameters would affect the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.  

In short, this single paper investigates whether third-party punishment leads bystanders to reward the punisher, but does not discuss or test how changing parameters (e.g., group size, punishment cost, number of rounds) might influence group-level efficiency. Consequently, one cannot draw meaningful predictions about efficiency effects from it.
reference_APA: Raihani, Nichola J. & Bshary, Redouan (2015). Third-party punishers are rewarded, but third-party helpers even more so. EVOLUTION.

Authors: Jordan, J; McAuliffe, K; Rand, D
Author Full Names: Jordan, Jillian; McAuliffe, Katherine; Rand, David
Article Title: The effects of endowment size and strategy method on third party punishment
Author Keywords: Cooperation; Norm-enforcement; Strategy method; Emotions; Fairness; Economic games
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; FAIRNESS
Abstract: Numerous experiments have shown that people often engage in third-party punishment (3PP) of selfish behavior. This evidence has been used to argue that people respond to selfishness with anger, and get utility from punishing those who mistreat others. Elements of the standard 3PP experimental design, however, allow alternative explanations: it has been argued that 3PP could be motivated by envy (as selfish dictators earn high payoffs), or could be influenced by the use of the strategy method (which is known to influence second-party punishment). Here we test these alternatives by varying the third party's endowment and the use of the strategy method, and measuring punishment. We find that while third parties do report more envy when they have lower endowments, neither manipulation significantly affects punishment. We also show that punishment is associated with ratings of anger but not of envy. Thus, our results suggest that 3PP is not an artifact of self-focused envy or use of the strategy method. Instead, our findings are consistent with the hypothesis that 3PP is motivated by anger.

Abstract: In public-good provision, privileged groups enjoy the advantage that some of their members find it optimal to supply a positive amount of the public good. 2) Number of rounds  
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes. There are exactly 10 consecutive rounds (periods), and participants know this (pp. 7, 10).  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. The paper does not discuss varying the number of rounds, only that repeated interaction occurs over 10 periods. No predictions are made about changing the number of rounds.  

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The experiment does not mention any communication (“chat”) stage among participants.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No mention and no variation.  

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The paper uses a standard linear public-goods game where participants may contribute any integer from 0 to 20 tokens (p. 7). There is no “all or nothing” constraint.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. Not mentioned and not varied.  

5) Is the contribution default (where players remove from the public fund back to their private funds)?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. Each participant simply decides how many of their 20 tokens to contribute, and keeps the remainder. The instructions do not implement a “default” from the public fund back to the private fund.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No mention.  

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes, it is central to the paper. They compare “normal” groups (all have α = 0.5) and “privileged” groups (one member has α = 1.5, the others α = 0.5) (p. 8).  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Only in the sense of having two group types (normal vs. privileged). They do not vary α beyond 0.5/1.5.  
   • Predictions or effect size regarding the punishment treatment effect?  
     – Yes, the paper shows the difference in total contributions and payoffs when punishment is absent vs. present, under α = 0.5 (for all) vs. α = 1.5 for one person. Key numerical results (pp. 9–14):

   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. The cost is always 1 token. The paper does not state how changing this cost would affect the punishment treatment effect.  

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes. Each punishment point deducts 3 tokens from the punished player’s earnings (p. 8).  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. The punishment magnitude is fixed at 3 tokens lost per point. There is no discussion of how a systematic change in this magnitude would affect the punishment treatment effect.  

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The experiment involves only punishment. No separate reward mechanism is introduced.  

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. Rewards do not appear in the design.  

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. As above, no reward mechanism is included.  

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes. Participants are explicitly told there will be 10 rounds (p. 7).  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. The paper does not explore whether hiding the number of rounds would alter the punishment treatment effect.  

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained or lost each round)?  
   • Discussed?  
     – Limited. Participants see each other’s contributions and the total punishment points they receive (p. 8). However, the paper does not report that final payoffs of peers are shown in detail, only contributions and total punishment points assigned.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. There is no variation in how much information is revealed.  

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes. They do not know who punished them; they see only the total punishment points received (p. 8).  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. The paper keeps this information hidden in all punishment treatments.  

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. No reward mechanism is present.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how do these differ from one another?  
   • The paper reports total/average earnings (payouts) and also the distribution of earnings as dependent variables (pp. 14–16), as well as total contributions (a separate measure of cooperation).  
   • “Efficiency,” in the precise sense of actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff, is not reported explicitly as a ratio. Instead, the paper refers to total group earnings and payoff inequality. It also analyzes contribution rates. So “efficiency” in the sense of total surplus does appear, but often they discuss it in terms of overall payoffs or “material surplus.”  

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   Mentioned in some form:  
   1) Number of players (always 3)  
   2) Number of rounds (always 10)  
   6) Marginal per capita return (0.5 for normal, 1.5 for one “privileged” member)  
   7) Punishment cost (1 token)  
   8) Punishment magnitude (3 tokens deducted)  
   12) Players do know the fixed number of rounds  
   13) Participants see each other’s contributions and aggregate punishment points  
   14) Punishers are anonymous  
   The other parameters (3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 15) are not discussed or do not appear as part of the design.  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable) when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Only parameter #6 (the marginal per capita return) is varied to create “normal” vs. “privileged” groups. The paper directly discusses how this variation influences contributions, payoffs, and inequality when punishment is introduced. Effect sizes are reported (e.g., total contributions rise more strongly in normal than in privileged groups under punishment). No other parameter is systematically varied.  

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of this paper, what would they be?  
   • Since only the MPCR was varied in the experiment, the paper provides measurable insight only into how having a “high-benefit” member (α > 1 for one participant) changes the punishment treatment effect on total payoffs (and hence efficiency). The key finding is that punishment raises overall contributions substantially in normal groups (α = 0.5 for all) but has a far weaker impact in privileged groups (one α = 1.5) and consequently yields less additional total payoff for privileged groups.  
   • For the other parameters, the article does not supply direct evidence or systematic variation. The paper thus does not enable predictions about how changing group size, punishment cost/magnitude, knowledge of round length, or other factors (like enabling chat or different reward schemes) would quantitatively impact efficiency under punishment.  

In short, the paper’s experiment only varies one main feature (normal vs. privileged groups, i.e., α = 0.5 vs. one member having α = 1.5), and therefore predictions about all other parameters or more complex interactions cannot be made from this paper alone.

Below I strictly summarize what can – and what cannot – be extracted from the Hammerstein & Hagen paper with respect to each of the 15 design parameters and to the “punishment-treatment effect” (i.e., the change in outcomes produced by adding a punishment stage to a standard public-goods game).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER–BY–PARAMETER CHECK
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned: Yes.  The Fehr-&-Gächter game they recount is played by groups of four.  
   • Systematic variation / effect size: No.  The article offers no prediction about what would happen with 3, 5, … players.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned: Yes.  Each subject plays six one-shot public-goods interactions (groups are reshuffled each time).  
   • Systematic variation / effect size: No.

3. Is chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned: No.

4. All-or-nothing contributions?  
   • Mentioned: Yes, indirectly.  Subjects may “contribute an amount of their choosing,” so the design is NOT all-or-nothing.  
   • Systematic variation / effect size: No.

5. Contribution default (withdraw from a public fund)?  
   • Mentioned: No.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned: Vaguely.  They state that the experimenter “multiplies the total amount contributed,” but give no number.  
   • Systematic variation / effect size: No.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   • Mentioned: Qualitatively.  Punishment “is at a lesser cost to the punisher than to the target.”  No figure given.  
   • Systematic variation / effect size: No prediction about what happens if the cost were higher or lower.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss suffered by target per unit)  
   • Mentioned: Qualitatively (see item 7).  No number.  
   • Systematic variation / effect size: None.

9. Whether a reward option is enabled  
   • Mentioned: Rewards are referred to in a general discussion of “altruistic reward,” but the Fehr-&-Gächter game they summarize does NOT contain a reward stage.  
   • Systematic variation / effect size: No.

10. Reward cost  
    • Mentioned: No.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Mentioned: No.

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
    • Mentioned: Not explicitly.  The write-up never states whether participants knew there would be exactly six rounds, so no inference can be drawn.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mentioned: Partly.  After each round players “are informed of others’ contributions.”  The paper does not state that earnings/payoffs are shown.  
    • Systematic variation / effect size: None.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
    • Mentioned: Not specified.

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
    • Mentioned: Not applicable (no reward stage).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Numerical effect sizes**

The only quantitative statements given are descriptive, not the result of parameter variation:

• Baseline (no-punishment) condition: first-round mean contribution ≈ 50 % of the endowment; contributions decline over six rounds.  
• Punishment condition: contributions “start out even higher and then increase from round to round.”  > 80 % of subjects punish at least once; ~ ⅓ punish more than five times.  
• No efficiency (total-payoff / maximum-possible-payoff) numbers are reported, so no punishment-treatment effect on efficiency can be calculated.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables used in the paper  
   – Group efficiency (total or average payoff) is never reported.  
   – Reported variables: (i) individual/mean contribution levels, (ii) frequency of punishment acts, (iii) neuro-imaging activation levels in some ancillary studies.  “Contribution” and “frequency of punishment” are therefore the main behavioral outcomes; neither equals efficiency.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are at least mentioned?  
   7 of the 15: #1, #2, #4, #6 (name only), #7, #8, #13.  The remaining eight (3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 15) are absent or too vague to count.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* that parameter on the punishment-treatment effect (for any dependent variable)?  
   Zero.  The article never manipulates any of the 15 parameters; it merely contrasts “no punishment” versus “punishment” under one fixed parameter configuration.

D. Predictive guidance for efficiency, based solely on this paper  
   The paper only allows the following minimal, qualitative inference:  
   – Introducing a low-cost/high-impact punishment opportunity in a four-player, six-round public-goods game with full anonymity of partners and with feedback about others’ contributions tends to raise contributions over time relative to a no-punishment baseline.  
   – Because efficiency is monotonically related to contribution whenever the MPCR > 1, one can guess that efficiency would also rise under the described parameter set.  
   – No statement in the paper lets us predict how any *change* in the 15 listed parameters (e.g., more players, higher punishment cost, enabling chat, revealing punisher identity, etc.) would alter that efficiency gain.  Hence, beyond the single observed configuration, the paper provides virtually no basis for forecasting punishment-treatment effects on efficiency.

In short, the paper recounts one concrete example of a punishment-enhanced public-goods game but offers no systematic exploration of parameter space; therefore it supplies almost no usable quantitative input for predicting how each of the 15 design features (individually or in interaction) would influence the punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency.
reference_APA: Hammerstein, P & Hagen, EH (2005). The second wave of evolutionary economics in biology. TRENDS IN ECOLOGY & EVOLUTION.

Summary

Authors: Riehl, C; Frederickson, ME
Author Full Names: Riehl, Christina; Frederickson, Megan E.
Article Title: Cheating and punishment in cooperative animal societies
Source Title: PHILOSOPHICAL TRANSACTIONS OF THE ROYAL SOCIETY B-BIOLOGICAL SCIENCES
Author Keywords: cooperation; cheating; punishment; eusociality; policing; reciprocity
Keywords Plus: DIVISION-OF-LABOR; WORKER REPRODUCTION; EUSOCIAL HYMENOPTERA; HELPERS PAY; EXPERIMENTAL MANIPULATION; GENERALIZED RECIPROCITY; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; INDIVIDUAL VARIATION; BREEDING GROUPS; KIN SELECTION
Abstract: Cheaters-genotypes that gain a selective advantage by taking the benefits of the social contributions of others while avoiding the costs of cooperating-are thought to pose a major threat to the evolutionary stability of cooperative societies. In order for cheaters to undermine cooperation, cheating must be an adaptive strategy: cheaters must have higher fitness than cooperators, and their behaviour must reduce the fitness of their cooperative partners. It is frequently suggested that cheating is not adaptive because cooperators have evolved mechanisms to punish these behaviours, thereby reducing the fitness of selfish individuals. However, a simpler hypothesis is that such societies arise precisely because cooperative strategies have been favoured over selfish ones-hence, behaviours that have been interpreted as 'cheating' may not actually result in increased fitness, even when they go unpunished. Here, we review the empirical evidence for cheating behaviours in animal societies, including cooperatively breeding vertebrates and social insects, and we ask whether such behaviours are primarily limited by punishment. Our review suggests that both cheating and punishment are probably rarer than often supposed. Uncooperative individuals typically have lower, not higher, fitness than cooperators; and when evidence suggests that cheating may be adaptive, it is often limited by frequency-dependent selection rather than by punishment. When apparently punitive behaviours do occur, it remains an open question whether they evolved in order to limit cheating, or whether they arose before the evolution of cooperation.
