Below I go through each of the 15 public–goods-game (PGG) design parameters in the order given and state, strictly on the basis of the review by Riehl & Frederickson (2016):

• whether the paper explicitly mentions the parameter (and, if so, the value or range actually reported), and  
• whether the paper reports, models, or even speculates about how *systematically varying* that parameter would change the **punishment treatment effect** for any dependent variable (especially efficiency).  
When the answer is “no”, nothing further is invented.

-------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players (group size)  
– Mentioned? Yes.  Several passages note that free-riding becomes easier and more common in *larger* animal groups (e.g. laggards in lions, monkeys, dogs, wolves).  
– Systematic prediction for the punishment treatment effect? No.  The paper never links changes in group size to changes in the *efficacy* of punishment, let alone to efficiency. No effect sizes are given.

2. Number of rounds (length/repetition of the game)  
– Mentioned? Yes, indirectly.  The review reiterates the classic point that a single-shot Prisoner’s Dilemma favours defection whereas repeated interactions can support reciprocity.  
– Systematic prediction? No.  No quantitative or even qualitative statement is made about how adding or removing rounds would alter the impact of punishment on pay-offs or efficiency.

3. Chat between players  
– Mentioned? No.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
– Mentioned? No.

5. Contribution default (opt-out of giving vs. opt-in)  
– Mentioned? No.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor  
– Mentioned? No numerical parameter of that sort appears anywhere.

7. Punishment *cost* to the punisher  
– Mentioned? Only conceptually.  The review repeatedly describes punishment as “costly” or “aggressive”, but gives no numerical costs and does not vary the size of the cost.  
– Systematic prediction? No.

8. Punishment *magnitude* (loss to the target)  
– Mentioned? Conceptually (e.g. eviction, harassment, egg-eating), but never parameterised or varied.  
– Systematic prediction? No.

9. Whether a *reward* option exists  
– Mentioned? Yes, very briefly.  Positive reciprocity/partner choice is distinguished from costly punishment, but the paper never analyses the presence or absence of reward as an experimental factor.  
– Systematic prediction? No.

10. Reward cost  
– Mentioned? No.

11. Reward magnitude  
– Mentioned? No.

12. Whether the number of rounds is *known* to players  
– Mentioned? No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown? (feedback visibility)  
– Mentioned? Indirectly.  Dominant animals are said to “monitor” helper behaviour and can therefore identify non-contributors, but there is no explicit manipulation of information visibility, nor any systematic analysis of how more or less feedback would change punishment effects.  
– Systematic prediction? No.

14. Punisher identity revealed?  
– Mentioned? No.

15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
– Mentioned? No.

-------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used in the paper  
– The review is centred on *fitness* consequences in natural systems—e.g. number of offspring, survival, colony productivity.  
– Nowhere does the paper define or compute *group efficiency* in the PGG sense (total realised pay-off ÷ maximum possible pay-off).  
– Other dependent variables discussed: frequency of cheating, frequency of punishment, colony productivity, helper effort, etc. These differ conceptually from efficiency because they are not normalised against a theoretical optimum and often concern single actors, not group totals.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
Four:  
1 (group size), 2 (repetition), 7-8 (punishment cost and magnitude, only in a qualitative sense), and, tangentially, 9 (existence of a reward option) and 13 (some form of outcome monitoring).  None of the other nine parameters appear.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the *effect of systematic variation* on the punishment treatment effect?  
Zero.  The paper never manipulates any parameter experimentally and never offers regression coefficients, marginal effects, or even directional hypotheses linking a parameter change to a change in the *incremental* impact of punishment on any outcome, let alone efficiency.

D. What predictions, if any, can be extracted for how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) will influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
Based solely on this review, very few.  The only arguable hints are:  
• Larger groups (Parameter 1) tend to foster more free-riding, but the review explicitly states that empirical work “finds virtually no evidence that punishment suppresses free-riders” in such contexts, so no clear prediction for efficiency gains can be drawn.  
• Repetition of interaction (Parameter 2) is a *prerequisite* for reciprocity to work, but again no explicit link is made to punishment’s efficacy.  
Beyond these vague statements, the review offers no leverage for forecasting how any of the 15 design choices will amplify or dampen the efficiency impact of adding punishment to a PGG.

In short, the paper is a zoological review, not a PGG meta-analysis; it does not present the kinds of systematic experimental variations or quantitative results that would be needed to predict punishment treatment effects on efficiency across different game parameters.

Abstract: In the standard one-shot Prisoner's Dilemma game, participants often choose to cooperate, when the optimal strategy is to defect. Second, we report whether the authors ***systematically vary*** that parameter and, if they do, whether they give any quantitative or qualitative statement that links such variation to a “punishment-treatment effect”.  In the present paper the authors never run a no-punishment baseline, so strictly speaking they never report a *treatment effect of adding punishment*.  What they do report is how different parameters change the long-run composition of strategies in a model that already contains punishers.  When the paper makes such comparative-static statements we reproduce them, but we flag that they concern cooperation-rate (or “total cooperation density”) and not group efficiency.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players (group size)  
   • Mentioned?  YES.  Denoted N.  Typical values used in the figures: N = 4 or 5; in Fig. 3 they let N vary between 3 and 10.  
   • Systematically varied?  YES (see Fig. 3).  
   • Reported effect?  Increasing N “expands the area of full cooperation” and makes it easier for punishers + cooperators to drive out defectors.  No numerical effect size and no explicit link to efficiency or to a punishment-vs-no-punishment contrast.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  NO.  The model is a continuous-time replicator process with no finite horizon.  
   • Systematic variation?  Not applicable.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment?  None reported.

3. Chat (pre-play communication)  
   • Mentioned?  NO.  
   • Effect?  None.

4. All-or-nothing contribution decision  
   • Mentioned?  Implicitly YES (a snowdrift player is either a cooperator or a defector), but the paper never varies that feature.  
   • Effect?  None.

5. Contribution default (endowment framed as giving vs. keeping)  
   • Mentioned?  NO.  
   • Effect?  None.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor  
   • The snowdrift analogue is the cost-to-benefit ratio u = c/b.  
   • Mentioned?  YES (typical values: u = 0.18, 0.2, 0.25, 0.27).  
   • Systematically varied?  YES (see Fig. 1).  
   • Reported effect?  Lower u (i.e. higher gross return from cooperation) widens the region of full cooperation; higher u shrinks it.  No numbers and no efficiency or treatment-effect statement.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   • Parameter α (=α′/b).  Fixed at 0.01 in all simulations; never varied.  
   • Effect?  None reported.

8. Punishment magnitude for the target  
   • Parameter β (=β′/b).  Varied in Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 (e.g. β = 0.05, 0.06) and through the ratio β/α.  
   • Reported effect?  Larger β (or larger β/α) promotes full cooperation; below a critical β/α punishers disappear and the population settles on a cooperator–defector cycle.  No efficiency numbers, no treatment-effect numbers.

9. Whether a monetary reward option exists  
   • Mentioned?  NO (rewards are not in the model).  
   • Effect?  None.

10–11. Reward cost and reward magnitude  
   • Mentioned?  NO.  
   • Effect?  None.

12. Whether the number of rounds is common knowledge  
   • Not applicable in continuous-time replicator model.  
   • Effect?  None.

13. Visibility of peer pay-offs  
   • Not modelled or discussed.  
   • Effect?  None.

14. Whether the punished player learns who punished him  
   • Not modelled.  
   • Effect?  None.

15. Whether the rewarded player learns who rewarded him  
   • Not modelled.  
   • Effect?  None.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables actually used  
   • The paper never reports *group efficiency* (total realised payoff divided by the cooperative benchmark).  
   • Reported outcomes are:  
     – Frequencies of cooperators (x), defectors (y) and punishers (z).  
     – “Total cooperation density” f₍C⁺P₎ = x + z.  
   • These frequencies are not the same as efficiency.  The authors do display or discuss pay-off expressions in the algebra, but they never aggregate them into an efficiency statistic nor compare pay-offs across “with-punishment” vs “without-punishment” treatments.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
   • Mentioned: 1, 4 (implicitly), 6, 7, 8.  (5 parameters)  
   • Not mentioned: 2, 3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15.

C.  Which parameters are *systematically varied* and discussed with respect to any outcome?  
   • Varied: 1 (N), 6 (u), 8 (β or β/α).  (3 parameters)  
   • For none of them is an explicit punishment-treatment effect on efficiency reported; only changes in cooperation rates are described.

D.  What predictions about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment-treatment effect on **efficiency** can be made from this paper alone?  
   • Very limited.  The authors never compute efficiency and never contrast a punishment condition with a no-punishment baseline.  Assuming (i) that the “frozen phase” containing cooperators + punishers would generate higher average pay-offs than the “dynamical phase” containing cooperators + defectors, and (ii) that the absence of punishers is a rough proxy for “no-punishment”, one could *qualitatively* expect:  
       – Larger N, lower u, larger β or β/α would make punishment more likely to survive and hence *could* raise efficiency relative to an imagined no-punishment baseline.  
       – Variation in α, round length, communication, reward options, information conditions, etc. cannot be predicted because the paper is silent on them.  
   • No numerical magnitudes of the efficiency gains (or losses) can be extracted.

In short, the paper is informative about how group size, cost-benefit ratio and punishment severity influence whether punishers persist, but it does not report any punishment-treatment effect on group efficiency, nor does it cover 10 of the 15 design parameters listed.

Below I go through the fifteen public-goods–game parameters one by one and relate them to what is actually contained in the Wang et al. (2011) paper.  “Discussed” means the paper explicitly states the value of the parameter in at least one of its experiments.  “Systematically varied” means the authors deliberately manipulated that parameter and reported its impact on any dependent variable (punishment, anger, etc.).  Effect sizes are copied directly from the text, tables, or figures whenever the paper allows it.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Number of players  
   • Discussed: Yes.  
     – Ultimatum experiments: 2 players (offerer, responder).  
     – Third-party punishment experiments: 3 players (A, B, C).  
   • Systematically varied: No.  All experiments keep the player count fixed.  
   • Predicted effect on punishment treatment effect: None given.

2.  Number of rounds  
   • Discussed: No.  All interactions are one-shot; the paper never manipulates or even labels this as a variable.  
   • Systematically varied: No.  
   • Effect: Not discussed.

3.  Chat enabled between players  
   • Discussed: No mention of any chat or communication channel.  
   • Effect: Not discussed.

4.  “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
   • Not applicable; there are no public-goods contributions in this paper.  
   • Effect: Not discussed.

5.  Contribution default / withdrawal rule  
   • Not applicable.  
   • Effect: Not discussed.

6.  MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Not applicable; no public-goods stage.  
   • Effect: Not discussed.

7.  Punishment cost to the punisher  
   • Discussed: Yes.  
     – Ultimatum rejection: cost = loss of the offered amount (e.g., \$2 or \$1).  
     – Third-party punishment: 1 point used by Player C costs Player C exactly 1 point.  
   • Systematically varied: No.  The 1:1 cost is fixed; no manipulation.  
   • Effect: Not discussed.

8.  Punishment magnitude (damage to target per unit cost)  
   • Discussed: Yes.  
     – Third-party game: each point spent reduces the target’s payoff by 2 points (1:2 ratio).  
   • Systematically varied: No.  
   • Effect: Not discussed.

9.  Is a reward option enabled?  
   • Discussed: No.  
   • Effect: Not discussed.

10. Reward cost  
    • Not mentioned.  

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Not mentioned.

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
    • Not explicitly discussed.  All tasks are one-shot and framed as such; no variation.  
    • Effect: Not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Discussed: Yes (only in the third-party punishment set-up where Player C sees A’s transfer and B’s return).  
    • Systematically varied: No.  
    • Effect: Not discussed.

14. Do punished players know who punished them?  
    • Not mentioned; not manipulated.

15. Do rewarded players know who rewarded them?  
    • Not mentioned; not manipulated.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary

A.  Dependent variables used  
   • The paper does NOT use “group efficiency” (total or average payoff relative to the cooperative maximum).  
   • Main behavioral dependent variables:  
     – Ultimatum rejection rate (binary accept = 0 / reject = 1).  
     – Number of punishment points assigned by a third party.  
   • Psychological dependent variable: self-reported or coder-rated negative emotion (anger, disgust, scorn).  
   • Efficiency differs from these because the paper never computes total group earnings or ratios thereof.

B.  How many of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   • Four: (1) Number of players, (7) Punishment cost, (8) Punishment magnitude, (13) Visibility of peer outcomes.  

C.  How many parameters are systematically varied and linked to a punishment treatment effect?  
   • Zero.  None of the 15 public-goods parameters are experimentally manipulated.  All treatment effects in the article come from manipulating (i) time delay length and (ii) thought type (distraction, rumination, reappraisal), variables that are outside the 15-item list.

D.  What predictions can be made—strictly from this paper—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
   • Very little.  Because none of the parameters were manipulated, the paper provides no direct evidence or quantitative estimates that could be used to forecast how changing any of them would alter the efficiency impact of introducing punishment in a public-goods game.  At most one can infer:  
     – If punishment is extremely cheap to impose (Parameter 7) and highly damaging (Parameter 8), actors may punish a lot when angry, which would presumably lower efficiency; but the paper itself never states this outcome.  
   • Therefore, based solely on the article, there is insufficient information to generate specific, data-based predictions for any of the 15 parameters or their interactions on group efficiency.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Bottom line: The Wang et al. (2011) study is about how time delays and thought patterns influence costly punishment in ultimatum and third-party contexts.  It does not study public-goods parameters, group efficiency, or the systematic variation of any of the fifteen design features listed above.

Abstract: Cooperation in a large society of self-interested individuals is notoriously difficult to achieve when the externality of one individual's action is spread thin and wide on the whole society. This leads to the 'tragedy of the commons' in which rational action will ultimately make everyone worse-off. Traditional policies to promote cooperation involve Pigouvian taxation or subsidies that make individuals internalize the externality they incur. We introduce a new approach to achieving global cooperation by localizing externalities to one's peers in a social network, thus leveraging the power of peer-pressure to regulate behavior. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what (if anything) this paper (“Inducing Peer Pressure to Promote Cooperation,” Mani et al.) says about each of the 15 listed public‐goods‐game design features, followed by the required four‐part summary (A–D). Throughout, please note that the paper never uses the term “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” in the sense of “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff for a fully cooperative group.” It instead analyzes “social surplus,” “utility,” or “consumption” levels, and sometimes reports experimental increases in physical activity. All statements below refer only to what is explicitly in the paper.

────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes, but only in a single illustrative example of N = 100 agents (see “Illustrative example: promoting energy efficiency” section).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary this parameter or predict how varying it would affect the punishment treatment effect (for efficiency or any other dependent variable)?  
     – No. The paper does not vary the number of players in different conditions, nor does it relate this to a “punishment treatment effect.”  

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The theoretical model is cast as a two‐stage game (first peer‐pressure decisions, then action/consumption decisions) rather than a repeated‐rounds public goods game.  
   • Any predictions for systematically varying it?  
     – No.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. There is no discussion of enabling or disabling player chat.  
   • Any predictions for systematically varying it?  
     – No.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. Individuals in the paper’s model choose a continuous “action” (e.g., pollution level or consumption). The paper does not mention forced all‐or‐nothing contribution choices.  
   • Any predictions for systematically varying it?  
     – No.  

5. Is the contribution default (do players move their endowment back into their hand)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. There is no mention of a default contribution mechanism or anything similar.  
   • Any predictions for systematically varying it?  
     – No.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Not in the usual public‐goods‐game sense. The paper uses a negative‐externality framework rather than an MPCR.  
   • Any predictions for systematically varying it?  
     – No.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The paper models “cost of exerting peer pressure” (c) as a marginal cost to the punisher; this is the closest analogue to a “punishment cost.” Section “Equilibrium with peer pressure” and later sections analyze c. The illustrative example sets c = 1.  
   • Any predictions for systematically varying it?  
     – The paper shows that if c is too high, no one exerts peer pressure; if c is lower, peer pressure can reduce externalities and raise total (social) utility. However, it does not report an explicit “punishment treatment effect size” for changes in c, nor does it link c systematically to changes in group efficiency. Instead, it discusses the resulting equilibrium action/consumption or “social surplus.”  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player per punishment unit)  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Not as a separate parameter. The paper’s “peer pressure” enters utility through a bilinear term but is not broken into a distinct “punishment magnitude” separate from “punishment cost.”  
   • Any predictions for systematically varying it?  
     – No.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. Much of the paper discusses two reward mechanisms: (a) Pigouvian “direct rewards” to the polluter for reducing action, vs. (b) “social mechanism” rewards given to the polluter’s peers (i.e., peer‐reward setups).  
   • Any predictions for systematically varying it on punishment treatment effect?  
     – Not in the sense of “punishment treatment on efficiency.” The paper does compare outcomes when peer‐reward is implemented versus no peer‐reward, but it frames results in terms of social surplus or behavior change, not efficiency ratios. No numerical “punishment treatment effect size” is reported.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Mentioned?  
     – The paper does analyze a “redistribution loss” (denoted δ) that effectively increases the total cost of implementing a reward budget, but it does not label it “reward cost per unit” in the usual experimental‐economics sense.  
   • Any predictions for varying it?  
     – Yes, but only in terms of how a higher δ (the overhead for distributing rewards) changes the total cost under social vs. Pigouvian mechanisms. This is not tied to a standard public‐goods “punishment treatment effect.”  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward)  
   • Mentioned?  
     – The paper’s formal “social reward function” is r(…) = (α + β)(x − x*) in the model. They also vary “marginal reward” in the “Friends and Family” experiment (e.g., $0.012 vs. $0.0253, etc.).  
   • Any predictions for systematically varying it?  
     – They do show that reducing the reward rate in the peer‐reward condition can still outperform a Pigouvian approach if enough peer pressure is induced. However, this is analyzed in terms of equilibrium actions or social surplus, not as a “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency. No explicit effect size for “punishment treatment” is given.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (i.e., do they know when the game ends)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper’s model is a two‐stage game, but it is not a repeated multi‐round public goods game.  
   • Any predictions for systematically varying it?  
     – No.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know peer gains/losses every round)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – The paper assumes that peers know each other’s consumption/actions in order to apply pressure but does not treat this as a systematically varied parameter. In the “Friends and Family” experiment, there is a “peer‐see” condition, but the paper does not vary “information display” per se as an experimental design parameter.  
   • Any predictions for systematically varying it?  
     – No.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know the specific punisher?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No, the paper never discusses whether the identity of the punisher is revealed.  
   • Any predictions for systematically varying it?  
     – No.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know the specific rewarder?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No, there is no mention of whether rewarded players learn who specifically gave it.  
   • Any predictions for systematically varying it?  
     – No.  

────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper predominantly uses “social surplus” (sum of everyone’s utility) and also monitors individual consumption or activity changes. In one real‐world test, the outcome is “daily physical activity.” The paper does not discuss “group efficiency” = (actual total payoff) / (maximum possible payoff of full cooperation).  
   • The dependent variables the paper does discuss include:  
        – Social surplus (theoretical model).  
        – Consumption level (e.g., in the energy‐consumption example).  
        – Physical activity (in the “Friends and Family” experiment).  
     These differ from “efficiency” in the standard public‐goods‐game sense.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Parameter 1 (number of players) is mentioned only insofar as they give an example with N = 100.  
   • Parameter 7 (punishment cost) appears explicitly throughout as the cost c of exerting peer pressure.  
   • Parameter 9 (whether a reward is enabled) is central: The paper contrasts reward‐based social mechanisms (“peer‐reward”) vs. direct (Pigouvian) incentives vs. no reward.  
   • Parameter 10 (reward cost per unit) is loosely present as the “redistribution loss” δ, not exactly in the standard format but still a cost associated with giving out rewards.  
   • None of the other parameters is explicitly mentioned or given a numeric value.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable) when the parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, the paper never uses the phrase or setup “punishment treatment effect” in the standard public‐goods‐game sense. It analyzes how equilibrium consumption (or “social surplus”) changes when the cost of peer pressure c changes, or when different reward mechanisms are introduced.  
   • Hence no parameter is analyzed specifically in terms of “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” The closest is parameter 7 (cost of peer pressure): the paper shows that a lower c leads agents to exert more peer pressure, but it reports results for social surplus, consumption, or physical activity, not for group efficiency.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how these 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper’s focus on “peer pressure” cost (parameter 7) and on whether “peer reward” is enabled (parameter 9) suggests that if the cost of punishment is lower (i.e., c is smaller), or if peers receive enough reward to offset that cost, one might expect a larger increase in cooperation (hence presumably higher efficiency).  
   • Beyond that, the paper does not discuss systematically varying the other parameters (1–6, 8, 10–15) in a public‐goods‐game sense. Consequently, the paper provides no basis for predicting how those other parameters or their interactions would affect any punishment‐based “treatment effect on efficiency.”  

In short, the paper focuses on theoretical models of negative externalities with peer pressure, compares a “social mechanism” (rewarding peers) to a “Pigouvian mechanism,” and discusses social‐surplus outcomes rather than standard efficiency measures. It does not systematically address most of the 15 design parameters for a typical punishment‐enabled public goods game, nor does it offer explicit numerical estimates of a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”

Abstract: Humans are attracted to similar others. As a consequence, social networks are homogeneous in sociodemographic, intrapersonal, and other characteristics-a principle called homophily. Despite abundant evidence showing the importance of interpersonal similarity and homophily for human relationships, their behavioral correlates and cognitive foundations are poorly understood. Here, we show that perceived similarity substantially increases altruistic punishment, a key mechanism underlying human cooperation. Abstract: Studies that examine how helping behavior varies among individuals shed light on both the extent and the variation of human cooperative tendencies and the potential fragility of genealogical kinship in structuring prosociality. Here we explore the importance of both reciprocal altruism and kin selection in structuring cooperation in a contemporary African village context (Mpimbwe, Tanzania), where ethnographic observations suggest that traditional patterns of cooperation are becoming deeply eroded. Our analysis of the various ways in which people assist each other reveals that levels of helping are low. ────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players (group size)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  “When group size in a social dilemma increases, cooperation in a group often diminishes (Dawes, 1980; Kollock, 1998).”  
   • Systematically varied for a punishment treatment?  No.  The sentence is about *baseline* cooperation; punishment is not manipulated as a function of group size and no efficiency numbers are given.

2. Number of rounds (one-shot vs. finitely repeated / indefinitely repeated)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Many contrasts (e.g., “altruistic punishment encourages collective cooperation … especially in repeated social dilemmas”).  
   • Systematic variation tied to punishment?  Partly.  The review states that punishment is “especially” effective in *repeated* dilemmas (Balliet et al., 2011), implying that the punishment treatment effect should be larger with more rounds.  No numerical effect size or efficiency figure is provided.

3. Chat / communication between players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  “Communication can effectively promote cooperative behavior (Andreoni & Rao, 2011; Dawes et al., 1977 …).”  
   • Any link to punishment?  None.  No discussion of how adding chat changes the impact of a punishment option.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
   • Mentioned?  No.

5. Contribution default (withdraw vs. contribute frame)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes, but only for framing effects in *non-punishment* public-goods games (“take-some” vs. “give-some”).  No punishment treatment is involved, and no efficiency numbers are given.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  No explicit MPCR, multiplication factor or their variation is discussed in relation to punishment.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   • Mentioned?  Generally (“many individuals punishing opportunistic behavior at a cost to themselves”), but never quantified and never varied systematically.

8. Punishment magnitude (impact on the target)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes: “relatively small punishments can decrease cooperation (Gneezy & Rustichini, 2000)”.  
   • Systematic variation?  Only that *smaller* punishments hurt cooperation; the paper does not report an effect size or efficiency figure.

9. Whether a reward option is enabled  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Rewards are reviewed alongside punishments (“rewards are also important stimulants for cooperation”).  
   • Effect when varied?  Qualitative only (“sometimes more effective than punishment”; no efficiency data and no specific design parameters are given).

10. Reward cost to grant  
11. Reward magnitude received  
   • Mentioned?  Not at all.  The review never quantifies or systematically varies either dimension.

12. Whether the horizon (number of rounds) is known  
   • Mentioned?  No.  The paper contrasts one-shot vs. repeated games but never manipulates “end known vs. unknown” or links it to punishment.

13. Display of peer outcomes  
   • Mentioned?  No.

14. Punisher identity revealed  
15. Rewarder identity revealed  
   • Mentioned?  No for both.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────
A.  Dependent variables used in the paper  
    • The paper discusses cooperation rates, contribution levels, trust, rejection rates, punishment/reward behavior, etc.  
    • *Group efficiency* (total earnings as a % of the cooperative optimum) is **not** directly analysed anywhere.

B.  Parameters merely mentioned (whether or not linked to punishment)  
    6 of 15: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 9

C.  Parameters whose *systematic variation* is tied to a punishment treatment effect  
    Only 2 of 15, and only qualitatively:  
    • # of Rounds (2): punishment “especially” helpful in repeated games.  
    • Punishment Magnitude (8): very small fines can backfire.

D.  What can we predict—solely from this paper—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions determine the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
    • Repeated interactions (more rounds) should amplify any efficiency gains from adding a punishment option.  
    • Very small punishments may actually lower efficiency (because they cue a “market” rather than a “moral” frame).  
    • When punishments are absent, enabling rewards may produce similar or even larger efficiency benefits on occasion.  
    • Beyond those broad qualitative statements, the paper provides **no empirical basis** for predicting how the other 12 parameters—or any interactions among parameters—would alter the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Nonetheless, the remarks below address any portion of the paper relevant to systematic variation of each parameter—and whether the paper does or does not discuss such variation at all.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
• Discussed?: Yes, but not systematically varied. The paper describes theoretical setups and experiments where there are two‐person or four‐person groups (pp. 3–11). It also describes a “mini social reciprocity game” in which two groups of two or four players can punish within or across groups (pp. 10–14).  
• Systematic variation?: No. The paper does not systematically manipulate the group size to see how it affects any punishment‐related outcomes or payoffs.

2) Number of rounds  
• Discussed?: Briefly. The paper notes that standard public‐goods experiments often run for 10–20 rounds (p. 14), but it does not report an experimental design in which the number of rounds is changed from one treatment to another.  
• Systematic variation?: No. There is no study in the paper that changes how many rounds are played or analyzes this effect on punishment or on payoffs.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
• Discussed?: No. There is no mention of participant communication (chat) in any of the surveys or experimental protocols in the paper.  
• Systematic variation?: No mention; hence no systematic variation.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Discussed?: In the simple theoretical model in Section 2.1 (pp. 3–6), the authors assume contributions are all‐or‐nothing for illustrative purposes (50 EMUs either all contributed or all kept). However, the actual laboratory experiments described elsewhere typically let participants contribute any integer amount out of their endowment.  
• Systematic variation?: No. The paper does not compare one treatment with all‐or‐nothing contributions to another with continuous contribution decisions; the all‐or‐nothing framework is a theoretical simplification only.

5) Is there a “contribution default” (i.e., do participants move money back from a public fund)?  
• Discussed?: No. There is no mention of a default contribution mechanism in the paper.  
• Systematic variation?: No.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
• Discussed?: Yes, marginal returns are described for the standard public‐goods setting (typically 0.5 in their examples, p. 14).  
• Systematic variation?: No. The paper does not report any experiment that varies the MPCR to see how it changes punishment outcomes or payoffs.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Discussed?: Yes. In several places, including Carpenter (2002a) as cited (pp. 20–22), the “price” (the cost to the punisher) is systematically varied. For example, they examine arrangements in which it might cost the punisher 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, or 4 EMUs to destroy 1 EMU of the target’s earnings.  
• Systematic variation?: Yes. They systematically vary this cost/harm ratio in an experiment. Although they do not report a direct “efficiency” measure, they do show that punishment is nonzero even when the punisher must pay far more than the harm inflicted (i.e., cost > harm). They also estimate a price elasticity of demand for punishment of about –0.64 (p. 21), indicating that punishment does decline as the cost grows, but not to zero.

8) Punishment magnitude (payoff deducted from the target per unit sent by punisher)  
• Discussed?: Yes, as the “harm” in the cost‐to‐harm ratio. In the standard mutual‐monitoring experiments, 1 EMU spent on punishment reduces 2 EMUs of the target’s income (p. 8). In Carpenter (2002a), some treatments effectively make the harm inflicted be 1 EMU of damage while the cost can be 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, or 4 EMUs, thus changing the cost/harm ratio.  
• Systematic variation?: Yes, indirectly via changing that ratio. However, the paper’s main focus is the punisher’s cost rather than giving separate treatments that only change the harm inflicted. No direct effect sizes on “efficiency” are given, only on how punishment remains nonzero across different price/harm ratios.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
• Discussed?: Briefly. The Price, Cosmides, and Tooby (PCT) survey (pp. 16–17) includes a question asking whether individuals would “reward” someone who cooperates (e.g., who participates in a war draft). However, the experimental designs discussed do not include a reward stage.  
• Systematic variation?: No. The paper does not provide any instance in which a reward option is systematically manipulated.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Discussed?: No. The paper does not discuss a cost of giving rewards.  
• Systematic variation?: No.

11) Reward magnitude (the coin gain for the target per unit of reward)  
• Discussed?: No. The paper does not include any experiment that implements or systematically manipulates a reward magnitude for cooperation.  
• Systematic variation?: No.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?  
• Discussed?: The paper states that public‐goods experiments typically last for a known number of rounds (e.g., 10 or 20), but provides no separate manipulation or analysis of whether “knowing the final round” changes punishment effects.  
• Systematic variation?: No.

13) Are peer outcomes shown? (i.e., do players see each other’s payoffs?)  
• Discussed?: Yes, in the mutual monitoring experiments and social reciprocity experiments, participants see others’ decisions or at least see how much others contributed (pp. 14–15). They also see how much they themselves were punished, though not necessarily by whom.  
• Systematic variation?: No. The paper does not compare a “no‐feedback” to a “feedback” condition.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• Discussed?: Yes. In the social reciprocity experiment (p. 22), the punished player does not know which group the punishment came from. Similarly, in the mutual monitoring experiments, participants see how much they were punished but not the identity of the punisher.  
• Systematic variation?: No. There is no condition that compares “knowing the punisher’s identity” vs. “punisher remains anonymous.”

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is?  
• Discussed?: No. The paper does not implement reward experiments.  
• Systematic variation?: No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
• The paper primarily examines (1) players’ willingness to punish, (2) players’ contribution levels, and (3) average or individual payoffs. It does mention that contributing is “socially efficient,” but it does not formally present “efficiency” = (actual total payoff) / (maximum possible total payoff) as a measured dependent variable. Instead, measures such as “cooperation rate,” “contribution level,” and “punishment expenditures” are the core outcomes.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Mentioned in some form: (1) number of players (though not varied), (2) number of rounds (only as a typical design choice), (4) all‐or‐nothing contributions in a theoretical model, (6) MPCR = 0.5, (7) punishment cost, (8) punishment magnitude/harm, (9) whether a reward can occur (via survey question), (13) whether people see others’ outcomes/contributions, and (14) punisher identity visible or not. That covers 9 of the 15 parameters, though most are not manipulated.  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss effects on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable) when systematically varied?  
• Only two parameters—(7) the cost to impose punishment and (8) the punishment magnitude—are systematically varied (as the cost/harm ratio in Carpenter 2002a). The paper reports that when cost is very high (punisher pays more than the damage inflicted), punishment does not drop to zero; people still punish, contrary to simple “payoff differential” logic. No direct statistics on “efficiency” are reported.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely on the basis of this paper, what would they be?  
• The paper gives only limited guidance for predicting effects on efficiency. It consistently finds that punishment stabilizes or increases contributions relative to no‐punishment conditions, suggesting that efficiency could be higher when punishment is feasible—provided the cost of punishment does not outweigh the gains in cooperation. Beyond that, the only parameter systematically manipulated is the cost/harm ratio (parameters 7 and 8). The paper shows that people punish even when the cost of doing so is large, so one can cautiously infer that making punishment cheaper or more potent would increase the deterrent effect, potentially helping efficiency. For all other parameters, there is no direct discussion or evidence in the paper regarding their systematic variation or their effect on efficiency, so the paper does not allow strong predictions on those.

     – Amount (cost) of sanctions imposed.  
   • It does not analyze payoffs or efficiency ratios per se. Their “contribution” variable is conceptually distinct from efficiency in that it measures how many tokens participants contribute, rather than how large the total payoff is relative to its theoretical maximum.

Article Title: Third-party punishment increases cooperation in children through (misaligned) expectations and conditional cooperation
Source Title: PROCEEDINGS OF THE NATIONAL ACADEMY OF SCIENCES OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOOD EXPERIMENTS; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; SOCIAL NORMS; STRONG RECIPROCITY; YOUNG-CHILDREN; ENFORCEMENT; BEHAVIOR; HUMANS; CHIMPANZEES; EVOLUTION
Abstract: The human ability to establish cooperation, even in large groups of genetically unrelated strangers, depends upon the enforcement of cooperation norms. Third-party punishment is one important factor to explain high levels of cooperation among humans, although it is still somewhat disputed whether other animal species also use this mechanism for promoting cooperation. We study the effectiveness of third-party punishment to increase children's cooperative behavior in a large-scale cooperation game. Based on an experiment with 1,120 children, aged 7 to 11 y, we find that the threat of third-party punishment more than doubles cooperation rates, despite the fact that children are rarely willing to execute costly punishment. We can show that the higher cooperation levels with third-party punishment are driven by two components. First, cooperation is a rational (expected payoff-maximizing) response to incorrect beliefs about the punishment behavior of third parties. Second, cooperation is a conditionally cooperative reaction to correct beliefs that third party punishment will increase a partner's level of cooperation.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter review of what this paper says (and does not say) about each of the 15 listed parameters, followed by a four-part summary (A–D). Throughout, “the paper” and “this study” refer solely to the text you provided, entitled “Third-party punishment increases cooperation in children through (misaligned) expectations and conditional cooperation.”

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER ANALYSIS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1) Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The core experiment is a one-shot Prisoner’s Dilemma (PD) involving two players plus a third-party punisher. The paper explicitly describes a two-player PD (players 1 and 2) and a third party who can punish defection.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. The paper does not discuss what would happen if the group (or the number of third parties) were systematically varied. No predictions or effect sizes are given for changing this parameter.  

2) Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. It is a one-shot game (i.e., only 1 round). The paper repeatedly stresses that it is not repeated or iterated.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. The experiment always uses a single one-shot interaction; there is no condition with multiple rounds. No predictions or effect sizes are offered regarding how more or fewer rounds would affect the impact of punishment.  

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. There is no mention of any form of communication or chat between participants.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Not applicable.  

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes, albeit implicitly. Each child in the PD can either cooperate (invest their tokens) or defect (keep their tokens). That choice is effectively a binary decision.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. The paper does not manipulate whether participants can contribute partially versus “all or nothing.”  

5) Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much of their endowment to move from the public fund back)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. This study uses a standard two-player PD with a binary cooperate/defect choice. There is no mechanism involving partial contributions nor a default.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Not applicable.  

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as the multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. In the PD, if a child sends a token, that token is doubled for the partner, so effectively the relevant “multiplication” is 2.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. They do not change the doubling factor. No predictions or effect sizes are offered for how changing that factor would alter the punishment treatment effect.  

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The third party must spend 1 token (i.e., one unit of their own payoff) in order to punish a defector.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. The cost is always exactly 1 token. The paper does not discuss altering this cost or predict how that would affect cooperation or efficiency.  

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed)  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. Punishment is “all or nothing”: if a player in the PD is punished, they lose their entire PD payoff.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. It remains the same in all conditions, and the paper does not predict how changing the punishment severity would alter results.  

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Briefly, as a possibility for future research (the paper notes it would be interesting to see whether third-party reward might be as effective as third-party punishment). However, the experiment itself does not include any reward mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. No reward condition is used or varied.  

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. Since reward is not part of the design, the paper does not discuss reward cost.  

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted)  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. This is not part of the experimental design.  

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. Children know the PD is one-shot, so they know exactly when the game ends: after a single play.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. The paper does not vary whether the endpoint is known or unknown, nor does it make any predictions about such a variation.  

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Partially. The text states that children do not immediately see what their partner chose. Outcomes are revealed only after a delay of about three months. There is no real-time “outcome display.”  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. The timing or detail of payoff revelation is not systematically changed. The paper does not provide effect-size estimates or predictions for altering what is displayed.  

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The design is anonymous. Punished players do not learn the identity of their punisher (the paper says children were matched anonymously with a third party from another school).  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. The paper does not examine making the punisher’s identity public versus private.  

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. There is no reward mechanism in the first place, so the question of identifying a rewarder does not arise.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Not applicable.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FOUR-PART SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • Primary Dependent Variables: The paper mostly focuses on (i) cooperation rates, (ii) beliefs about punishment and about the other player’s cooperation, and (iii) actual punishment frequencies. It does also calculate average payoffs under each condition (Control vs. Third-Party Punishment) and concludes that larger payoffs (i.e., higher efficiency) result when a punishment threat exists.  
   • How They Differ:  
     – “Cooperation rate” is the proportion of children who choose to cooperate.  
     – “Beliefs” measure how often a child expects punishment or expects the partner to cooperate.  
     – “Efficiency/payoff” is discussed as the average token earnings across players net of any costs from punishment.  

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
     – (1) Number of players (2 + 1 punisher)  
     – (2) Number of rounds (one-shot)  
     – (4) All-or-nothing contributions (cooperate vs. defect)  
     – (6) Multiplication factor (2)  
     – (7) Punishment cost (1 token)  
     – (8) Punishment magnitude (entire payoff lost)  
     – (9) Reward is simply noted as a future research possibility (but not implemented)  
     – (12) Number of rounds known to players (they know it’s one-shot)  
     – (14) Punisher identity is anonymous  
   • Not mentioned or not part of the design (or only trivially so):  
     – (3) Chat (not discussed)  
     – (5) Contribution default (not applicable in a 2-choice PD)  
     – (10) Reward cost (no reward)  
     – (11) Reward magnitude (no reward)  
     – (13) Peer outcomes are not revealed in real time; no systematic variation  
     – (15) Rewarder identity not relevant (no reward)  
   • In total, at least 9 of the 15 parameters appear in some capacity, though many are not central to the design or systematically modified.  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. The paper does not systematically vary any of these parameters (e.g., it does not vary the cost of punishing, the group size, or the number of rounds). Therefore, it makes no direct predictions about how changing these parameters would affect the “punishment treatment effect” (i.e., the difference between Control and Third-Party Punishment in outcomes like cooperation or payoff).  

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper’s content, what would they be?  
   • Because none of the parameters were systematically varied, the paper provides little explicit guidance on how each factor would scale the treatment effect on efficiency.  
   • The main result linking punishment and efficiency is that the mere presence of a (rarely executed) punishment threat can substantially increase cooperation and thus payoff (and by extension, efficiency). Beyond that, the paper does not model any detailed interactions between the cost of punishment, the severity of punishment, the number of players, or other structural features in ways that would allow a numerical or theoretical prediction of how efficiency would change under different parameter values.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Those are all the statements that can be supported solely by the given paper. No other variations or predictions about the 15 parameters are discussed in the text.

Authors: Raihani, NJ; McAuliffe, K
Author Full Names: Raihani, N. J.; McAuliffe, K.
Article Title: Human punishment is motivated by inequity aversion, not a desire for reciprocity
Author Keywords: punishment; inequity aversion; reciprocity
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; NEURAL BASIS
Abstract: Humans involved in cooperative interactions willingly pay a cost to punish cheats. However, the proximate motives underpinning punitive behaviour are currently debated. Individuals who interact with cheats experience losses, but they also experience lower payoffs than the cheating partner. Thus, the negative emotions that trigger punishment may stem from a desire to reciprocate losses or from inequity aversion. Previous studies have not disentangled these possibilities. Here, we use an experimental approach to ask whether punishment is motivated by inequity aversion or by a desire for reciprocity. We show that humans punish cheats only when cheating produces disadvantageous inequity, while there is no evidence for reciprocity. This finding challenges the notion that punishment is motivated by a simple desire to reciprocally harm cheats and shows that victims compare their own payoffs with those of partners when making punishment decisions.

Authors: Chowdhury, SN; Kundu, S; Perc, M; Ghosh, D
Author Full Names: Chowdhury, Sayantan Nag; Kundu, Srilena; Perc, Matjaz; Ghosh, Dibakar
Article Title: Complex evolutionary dynamics due to punishment and free space in ecological multi-games
Source Title: PROCEEDINGS OF THE ROYAL SOCIETY A-MATHEMATICAL PHYSICAL AND ENGINEERING SCIENCES
Author Keywords: nonlinear dynamics; social dilemma; evolutionary game theory; cyclic dominance
Keywords Plus: PRISONERS-DILEMMA GAME; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; CHAOTIC ATTRACTORS; COOPERATION; PROMOTES; BIODIVERSITY; MAINTENANCE; REWARD
Abstract: The concurrence of ecological and evolutionary processes often arises as an integral part of various biological and social systems. We here study eco-evolutionary dynamics by adopting two paradigmatic metaphors of social dilemmas with contrasting outcomes. We use the Prisoner's Dilemma and Snowdrift games as the backbone of the proposed mathematical model. Since cooperation is a costly proposition in the face of the Darwinian theory of evolution, we go beyond the traditional framework by introducing punishment as an additional strategy. Punishers bare an additional cost from their own resources to try and discourage or prohibit free-riding from selfish defectors. Our model also incorporates the ecological signature of free space, which has an altruistic-like impact because it allows others to replicate and potentially thrive. We show that the consideration of these factors has broad implications for better understanding the emergent complex evolutionary dynamics. In particular, we report the simultaneous presence of different subpopulations through the spontaneous emergence of cyclic dominance, and we determine various stationary points using traditional game-theoretic concepts and stability analysis.

Below, each of the 15 design parameters is examined in the order requested.  
For every parameter I state (i) whether it is actually present in the paper, and if so in what form or value, and (ii) whether the paper says anything about what would happen if the parameter were systematically varied, particularly with respect to a punishment treatment effect.  Numbers that can be read directly from the figures are given where possible (the paper contains no numerical tables).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER SCAN  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  

1. Number of players  
   (i) Not mentioned.  The model is an infinite, well-mixed population (replicator differential equations).  
   (ii) No predictions.

2. Number of rounds  
   (i) Not mentioned.  Time is continuous and unbounded.  
   (ii) No predictions.

3. Chat enabled?  
   (i) Not mentioned.  
   (ii) No predictions.

4. “All or nothing’’ contribution rule?  
   (i) Not applicable – the paper is not a public–goods contribution model.  
   (ii) No predictions.

5. Contribution default / endowment rematching?  
   (i) Not applicable.  
   (ii) No predictions.

6. Marginal Per-Capita Return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   (i) Not mentioned.  Instead, pair-wise PD/SD pay-off parameters R,S,T,P are used.  
   (ii) No predictions.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit of punishment  
   (i) YES.  A single parameter δ (>0) is both the cost paid by the punisher and the fine imposed on the defector. Typical values explored: δ≈0–0.7 (see Fig. 3b).  
   (ii) YES.  Systematic variation in Fig. 3b shows:  
        • δ∈(0,0.115): no cooperators; only punishers and defectors coexist (stationary point E₅).  
        • δ≈0.115-0.7: all three types coexist (E₇).  
        • δ≥0.7: punishers disappear, leaving only cooperators and defectors (E₆).  
        Quantitative illustration (read from Fig. 3b, β=1.1, p=0.55, other parameters fixed):  
           – At δ=0.0: y≈0.25, z≈0.75, x=0.  
           – At δ=0.4: x≈0.45, y≈0.30, z≈0.25.  
           – At δ=0.7: x≈0.6,  y=0,     z≈0.4.  
        The paper, however, never translates these shifts into efficiency changes.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine deducted from the target)  
   (i) Same parameter δ; no separate magnitude parameter exists.  
   (ii) Same observations as in (7).

9. Reward enabled?  
   (i) Not present.  
   (ii) No predictions.

10. Reward cost  
    (i) Not present.  
    (ii) No predictions.

11. Reward magnitude  
    (i) Not present.  
    (ii) No predictions.

12. Are players told the number of rounds (horizon known)?  
    (i) Not applicable.  
    (ii) No predictions.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    (i) Not mentioned.  
    (ii) No predictions.

14. Is the identity of the punisher revealed?  
    (i) Not mentioned.  
    (ii) No predictions.

15. Is the identity of the rewarder revealed?  
    (i) Not mentioned.  
    (ii) No predictions.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
SUMMARY  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  

A.  Dependent variables actually analysed  
    – The paper NEVER reports “group efficiency’’ (total or average payoff relative to the cooperative optimum).  
    – Reported variables are: absolute fractions of Cooperators (x), Punishers (y), Defectors (z); sometimes relative fractions ⟨x⟩, ⟨y⟩, ⟨z⟩; qualitative dynamical states (fixed points, limit cycles, chaos).  Efficiency is not the same as any of these and is not computed.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters appear at all?  
    Only one experimental-style parameter appears: δ, which simultaneously plays the role of punishment cost (#7) and punishment magnitude (#8).  None of the other 13 parameters are mentioned.  Hence 1 (or, counting cost + magnitude separately, 2) of the 15 parameters appear.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper study the effect of systematic variation on any punishment treatment outcome?  
    Exactly one: δ (parameters #7/#8).  The outcome studied is the composition of strategies, not efficiency.  No other parameter from the list is examined.

D.  What predictions about efficiency can be made from this paper?  
    Almost none.  Because the authors never compute total pay-offs, one cannot extract a direct mapping from δ (or any other model parameter) to efficiency gains or losses from punishment.  At best, one can infer that:  
      • Low punishment cost/magnitude (small δ) yields zero cooperation and therefore low efficiency;  
      • Intermediate δ allows coexistence and thus should raise efficiency somewhat;  
      • Very high δ removes punishers and leaves a C–D mixture whose efficiency would depend on the precise C share, but no numbers are given.  
    For all other listed design parameters the paper is silent, so no evidence-based prediction is possible.

In short, the paper is almost entirely orthogonal to the 15-item design space of laboratory public-goods experiments.  Only the punishment cost/magnitude parameter (δ) is shared, and even for that variable the paper tracks strategy fractions rather than group efficiency.

Below, “punishment-treatment effect’’ always means the **difference** in an outcome when the possibility of peer punishment is present versus when it is absent (Game 1 versus Game 2 in this paper).  
All statements and numbers are copied or read directly from the text, its tables, or its figures.

────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes – always two players.  
   • Systematically varied? No (never changed), so no prediction about varying it.

2. Number of rounds (one-shot vs. repeated 20)  
   • Mentioned? Yes – “Single” treatments (1 round) and “Same” treatments (20 rounds).  
   • Systematically varied? Yes.  
   • Effect on punishment-treatment effect? The paper reports that repetition greatly raises cooperation/payoffs (Table II: SJM outcomes rise from 0.37 in Single 1 to 0.72 in Same 1; from 0.23 in Single 2 to 0.52 in Same 2).  However, the **increment attributable to punishment** (Game 1 – Game 2) is smaller in the repeated game (Same 1 vs. Same 2: 0.72–0.52 = +0.20) than in the one-shot game (Single 1 vs. Single 2: 0.37–0.23 = +0.14).  The paper does not translate these into efficiency numbers.

3. Chat allowed?  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • No information, no prediction.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Not relevant; never mentioned.

5. Contribution default / endowment retraction?  
   • Not relevant; never mentioned.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Not used in this bargaining study.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   • Mentioned? Implicitly yes.  In Game 1 the “down’’ move at x₅ gives (20, 20) instead of (60, 30) – i.e. the punisher (player 2) pays 10 to reduce player 1’s payoff by 40.  
   • Systematically varied? Only two discrete levels: “cost = 10, magnitude = 40’’ (Game 1) vs. “not available’’ (Game 2).  
   • Effect on punishment-treatment effect? Single play: SJM frequency 0.37 (Game 1) vs. 0.23 (Game 2); p<0.001.  Thus enabling costly punishment raises cooperation by 14 percentage points.  Repeated play: +20 percentage points as noted above.

8. Punishment magnitude (damage to target)  
   • Same comment as 7 (40-point loss in Game 1; not available in Game 2).  Not varied independently from cost.

9. Reward option enabled?  
   • Not present.

10–11. Reward cost / magnitude  
   • Not present.

12. Horizon known?  
   • Subjects “were told nothing about how many trials will be played’’ in the repeated treatments, whereas in the single-play treatments they obviously know the game ends after one move.  The horizon is therefore *implicitly* varied, but the paper never contrasts “known finite’’ vs. “known infinite’’ horizons holding the number of rounds constant; no quantitative prediction is offered.

13. Peer-outcome information (complete vs. private)  
   • Mentioned? Yes – “complete payoff information’’ versus “private information’’ treatments.  
   • Systematically varied? Yes (Same 1 vs. Private Same 1).  
   • Effect on punishment-treatment effect? With complete information (Same 1) left-branch play = 0.82 and SJM = 0.72; with private information these fall to 0.16 and 0.07.  The incidence of non-cooperative right-branch play is 0.18 (Same 1) versus 0.84 (Private 1).  No direct efficiency figure is reported, but the text states that “Private 1 yields by far the highest incidence of non-cooperative right game play.’’  The punishment option itself is *available* in both Private 1 and Same 1, so this manipulation shows that revealing peer payoffs is crucial for punishment to improve outcomes.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
   • Not applicable – only two players, identity is trivially known; not varied or discussed.

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
   • Not applicable – no rewards.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────
A. Dependent variables  
   • The paper never reports “group efficiency’’ (= total payoff / maximum total).  
   • Reported outcomes are:  
     – Frequency of left-branch play  
     – Frequency of the symmetric joint maximum (SJM: 50,50)  
     – Frequency of sub-game-perfect (SP: 40,40) outcomes  
     – Expected profit to each player conditional on a branch  
   These are related to, but not identical with, efficiency.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned? 6 of them:  
   1 (players), 2 (rounds), 7 & 8 (punishment cost & magnitude bundled together), 12 (horizon implicitly differs), 13 (peer-outcome visibility).

C. Which parameters are *systematically varied* and linked to a punishment-treatment effect? 3 groups (covering 4 numbered parameters):  
   • #2 Number of rounds (Single vs. Same)  
   • #7/8 Punishment cost & magnitude (present vs. absent)  
   • #13 Peer-outcome visibility (complete vs. private)  

D. Predictions that can be made *solely from this paper* about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would affect the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency:  
   • Allowing a direct‐punishment action that costs the punisher 10 and hurts the target by 40 (Game 1 vs. Game 2) raises cooperation and total payoffs; hence efficiency should rise by roughly the 14–20 percentage-point increases in SJM that are observed.  
   • Repetition (20 unknown-horizon rounds) amplifies cooperation in both punishment and no-punishment games, so the *incremental* advantage of having punishment persists but is not dramatically larger in repeated play.  
   • Hiding peer payoffs (private information) largely nullifies the benefit of the punishment option; efficiency would drop sharply.  
   • The paper provides no information to predict effects of chat, reward, MPCR, contribution formats, identity revelation, etc.; no prediction can be made for those parameters.

Beyond these limited points, the paper does not furnish enough evidence to forecast how the full set of 15 parameters or their higher-order interactions would influence the punishment-treatment effect on group efficiency.
reference_APA: McCabe, KA, Rassenti, SJ & Smith, VL (1998). Reciprocity, trust, and payoff privacy in extensive form bargaining. GAMES AND ECONOMIC BEHAVIOR.

Authors: Sääksvuori, L; Mappes, T; Puurtinen, M
Author Full Names: Saeaeksvuori, Lauri; Mappes, Tapio; Puurtinen, Mikael
Article Title: Costly punishment prevails in intergroup conflict
Source Title: PROCEEDINGS OF THE ROYAL SOCIETY B-BIOLOGICAL SCIENCES
Author Keywords: cooperation; group conflict; public goods; punishment
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; GROUP COMPETITION; PUBLIC GOOD; COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; SOCIETIES; ENFORCEMENT; PROVISION; SANCTIONS; BEHAVIORS
Abstract: Understanding how societies resolve conflicts between individual and common interests remains one of the most fundamental issues across disciplines. The observation that humans readily incur costs to sanction uncooperative individuals without tangible individual benefits has attracted considerable attention as a proximate cause as to why cooperative behaviours might evolve. However, the proliferation of individually costly punishment has been difficult to explain. Several studies over the last decade employing experimental designs with isolated groups have found clear evidence that the costs of punishment often nullify the benefits of increased cooperation, rendering the strong human tendency to punish a thorny evolutionary puzzle. Here, we show that group competition enhances the effectiveness of punishment so that when groups are in direct competition, individuals belonging to a group with punishment opportunity prevail over individuals in a group without this opportunity. In addition to competitive superiority in between-group competition, punishment reduces within-group variation in success, creating circumstances that are highly favourable for the evolution of accompanying group-functional behaviours. We find that the individual willingness to engage in costly punishment increases with tightening competitive pressure between groups. Our results suggest the importance of intergroup conflict behind the emergence of costly punishment and human cooperation.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter inventory of what (if anything) this particular paper says about each of the 15 listed variables. Following that is the requested four‐part summary. As instructed, all statements refer solely to what is reported or shown in the paper “Costly punishment prevails in intergroup conflict,” without drawing on any outside sources or assumptions.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Discussed? Yes. The paper reports that each group has 8 players, and that the design included either one group of 8 or two competing groups of 8.  
   • Systematically varied? No. All groups had 8 players, and the paper does not discuss varying this number or predict how changing the number of players would affect the punishment treatment effect (for efficiency or any other outcome).  

2. Number of rounds
   • Discussed? Yes. The game lasted for 30 periods in all treatments. The paper notes that 30 is sufficiently long that short‐horizon explanations for punishment’s ineffectiveness may not apply.  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no condition with a different number of rounds, and the paper does not model or predict how changing the number of rounds would affect punishment’s impact.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussed? Yes, in the sense that the paper explicitly states there was no communication or chat.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not enable chat in any treatment, nor does it discuss how enabling chat would change the punishment effect.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussed? Indirectly. The experiment allowed each participant to allocate between 0 and 20 monetary units (MUs) in any amount, so it was not “all or nothing.”  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not use or even mention an “all‐or‐nothing” rule, and there is no discussion of how such a rule would affect outcomes.  

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much of their endowment to move back into their hand)?
   • Discussed? Not directly. Participants freely chose how many MUs to allocate to the group account versus keep in their personal account, with no default or forced contribution.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not examine default rules and makes no predictions about their variation.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters (e.g., multiplication factor)
   • Discussed? Yes. The total group contribution was doubled (multiplied by 2) and then split among 8 players, which corresponds to an MPCR of 2/8 = 0.25.  
   • Systematically varied? No. All groups used the same multiplier (2), and there is no analysis of what would happen if it changed.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussed? Yes. In all “punishment” conditions, it cost the punisher 1 MU for each deduction point assigned.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The cost was always 1 MU per punishment point, and the paper does not explore higher or lower punishment costs.  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed)
   • Discussed? Yes. Each punishment point deducted 3 MUs from its target.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The deduction ratio was always 3:1 and was not altered across treatments. The paper does not discuss changing it.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussed? No. There is no mention of rewarding peers at all.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The experiment had only punishment or no‐punishment conditions.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Discussed? No. Rewards are not part of the design.  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted)
    • Discussed? No. Rewards are not part of the design.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Discussed? Implied. Participants played exactly 30 rounds, and from standard practice in such experiments, they would have been told it would last 30 rounds.  
    • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not explore unknown vs. known horizon or different endpoints.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost each round)?
    • Discussed? Yes. The paper states that participants observed each group member’s contribution and the resulting earnings (at least within their own group). In competitive settings, they also saw totals for the rival group.  
    • Systematically varied? No. This feedback procedure was the same across all treatments.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Discussed? Yes. The paper states that “participants were not informed about the individual punishment decisions of other participants,” so punisher identity was not revealed.  
    • Systematically varied? No. No treatment revealed punisher identity, and the paper does not discuss what would happen if it were revealed.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is?
    • Discussed? No. Rewards do not occur in this experiment, so there is nothing in the paper about whether the rewarder is revealed.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   • The authors do not use “efficiency” (actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff) as a formal dependent variable. Instead, they measure (i) net material payoffs (sometimes aggregated as total net payoffs), (ii) contributions/contribution rate, and (iii) variation in individuals’ payoffs within a group. These are distinct: for instance, “contribution rate” measures how many MUs participants put in the public good, whereas “net payoff” is how many MUs they keep after both gains from the public good and losses from punishment.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
     1 (Number of players: 8), 2 (Number of rounds: 30), 3 (Chat: excluded), 4 (All or nothing: not used; contributions are continuous), 6 (MPCR: effectively 0.25), 7 (Punishment cost: 1 MU), 8 (Punishment magnitude: 3 MUs), 12 (Number of rounds known: yes, 30), 13 (Peer outcomes shown: yes), and 14 (Punisher identity hidden: yes).  
   • Not applicable (or not mentioned at all):  
     5 (Contribution default), 9 (Reward used?), 10 (Reward cost), 11 (Reward magnitude), 15 (Rewarder identity).  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable, specifically when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None of the 15 parameters are systematically varied in this study. The paper only varies (i) whether a group has punishment or not and (ii) whether there is intergroup competition or not (and whether it is symmetric or asymmetric). Those variations do not match any of the 15 parameters in the list (they did not vary the punishment cost ratio, the number of rounds, the MPCR, etc.). Consequently, the paper does not provide effect sizes for systematically changing any of the 15 parameters on net payoffs (or on “efficiency”).  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of this paper, what would they be?  
   • Because the paper never manipulates these 15 parameters (other than having a fixed value for some of them) and does not theoretically model how changing them might shift the punishment effect on payoffs, there is essentially no direct basis here to predict how each parameter would increase or decrease “efficiency.” Almost all parameters remained constant across treatments, and the paper compares (a) punishment vs. no punishment, (b) competition vs. no competition, and (c) symmetric vs. asymmetric competition. Thus, there is little to no information on how systematically changing the 15 parameters would affect the punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
End of response.

Abstract: Well-functioning groups enforce social norms that restrain opportunism. We study how the assignment to the top or bottom of the caste system affects the altruistic punishment of norm violations.
