Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter inventory of what the paper “Caste and Punishment: The Legacy of Caste Culture in Norm Enforcement” does and does not discuss, followed by the requested four‐part summary (A–D).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Yes. Each “triple” in the experiment consists of exactly three players: A, B, and C.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how varying it would affect punishment or efficiency?  
     – No. They always use three‐person groups (A, B, C). There is no mention of experimental conditions with more or fewer players, nor any prediction about varying the group size.

2) Number of rounds  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Yes, in effect: this is a one‐shot (single‐round) sequential game.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how varying it would affect punishment or efficiency?  
     – No. All sessions are one‐shot. There is no mention of repeated interactions or of altering the number of rounds.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – No. There is no mention of any communication (chat or otherwise) between players A, B, and C.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how varying it would affect punishment or efficiency?  
     – No. Not mentioned.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Yes, effectively. Player A can either send his entire endowment (50 rupees) or opt out, and Player B can send 100 rupees back or send nothing. That is a binary (“all or nothing”) decision structure for both A and B.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how varying it would affect punishment or efficiency?  
     – No. The experiment kept the contribution choices strictly binary; there is no condition in which partial amounts could be contributed or returned.

5) Is the contribution default? (e.g., do players have to “undo” a contribution)  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – No. There is no default‐contribution mechanism discussed.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how varying it would affect punishment or efficiency?  
     – No. Not mentioned.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Yes. The endowment sent by A is tripled before it reaches B (i.e., from 50 rupees to 150, plus B’s own 50 rupees makes 200 total in B’s hand). So the effective “factor” is 3.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how varying it would affect punishment or efficiency?  
     – No. They do not vary this factor. The game always uses the same tripling.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Yes. Each “coin” C spends on punishment costs C two rupees.

   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?

   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?

     – No. Not mentioned.

The authors do mention broader implications for efficiency in a general sense—e.g., how caste‐dependent punishment “may impair the group’s ability to sustain cooperation”—but they do not report an explicit efficiency metric the way a typical public‐goods experiment might.  

   • In short, “efficiency” is not analyzed numerically as the key dependent variable; the paper’s main dependent variables are punishment behavior and cooperation rates.

       1) Number of players (always three).  
       2) Number of rounds (one‐shot).  
       4) Contributions/binary decisions (effectively “all or nothing”).  
       6) Multiplication factor (tripled endowment).  
       7) Punishment cost (2 rupees per punishment coin).  
       8) Punishment magnitude (10 rupees deducted per coin spent).  

   • Not discussed in any substantive way:  
       3), 5), 9), 10), 11), 12), 13), 14), 15.  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when the parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. The authors do not systematically vary any of the standard public‐goods or punishment parameters (e.g. the number of players, punishment cost or magnitude, number of rounds, etc.). Their “treatments” instead vary caste status (high‐castes vs. low‐castes) and the caste composition of the three‐person group.  

D) If you were to make predictions on how these 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not provide evidence or direct discussion for how changes in group size, round structure, chat availability, varying marginal‐returns, or altering punishment/reward parameters would quantitatively affect efficiency. All of those factors are held fixed while the study focuses on caste.  
   • Accordingly, strictly from this paper, one cannot infer numerical effect sizes or predictions about how systematically varying any of the listed 15 parameters would change the “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency. The paper’s central variation is instead whether the punisher and victim share high‐caste or low‐caste status (and whether B is in‐group/out‐group), not variation of typical public‐goods design parameters.  

In summary, the article is about how the pre‐existing social hierarchy (high‐caste vs. low‐caste) shapes third‐party punishment behavior, rather than about systematically manipulating parameters such as group size, number of rounds, punishment cost, or marginal return. Consequently, it offers no direct predictions for how changing those 15 parameters would affect efficiency.

Article Title: Evolution of public cooperation in a monitored society with implicated punishment and within-group enforcement
Keywords Plus: GROUP-SIZE; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; COLLECTIVE ACTION; ANTISOCIAL PUNISHMENT; DYNAMICS; PROMOTE; REWARD; GAMES
Abstract: Monitoring with implicated punishment is common in human societies to avert freeriding on common goods. But is it effective in promoting public cooperation? We show that the introduction of monitoring and implicated punishment is indeed effective, as it transforms the public goods game to a coordination game, thus rendering cooperation viable in infinite and finite well-mixed populations. We also show that the addition of within-group enforcement further promotes the evolution of public cooperation. However, although the group size in this context has nonlinear effects on collective action, an intermediate group size is least conductive to cooperative behaviour. This contradicts recent field observations, where an intermediate group size was declared optimal with the conjecture that group-size effects and within-group enforcement are responsible. Our theoretical research thus clarifies key aspects of monitoring with implicated punishment in human societies, and additionally, it reveals fundamental group-size effects that facilitate prosocial collective action.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter inventory of what the paper by Chen et al. (2015) does and does not say, focusing especially on whether they (i) mention a parameter at all (and at what value, if so), and (ii) discuss what happens if one systematically varies that parameter, particularly with respect to any “punishment treatment effect.” Throughout, note that the paper’s chief dependent variables are:  
• the fraction (or proportion) of cooperators in the population,  
• the stationary (long‐run) distribution of the number of cooperators, and  
• the “basin of attraction” toward full cooperation versus full defection.  

They do not report or analyze “efficiency” (i.e. total payoff relative to the payoff a fully cooperative group would achieve) as an outcome. Instead, they study how punishment parameters affect the evolutionary stability of cooperation.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
   – Discussed?  
     Yes. The paper refers to this as “group size N.” It is central to their model, and they do systematically vary it (see, e.g., Fig. 2d, Fig. 4d, Fig. 5d,h).  
   – Systematically varied for the punishment‐treatment effect?  
     The authors study how changing the group size N shifts the fraction of cooperators who survive evolutionarily (they do not speak in terms of “efficiency”). They find that an intermediate N is actually the least conducive to cooperation (whereas very small or very large N can promote it). They do not give any quantitative effect size for efficiency.  

2) Number of rounds  
   – Discussed?  
     No. The paper does not specify the number of rounds or whether the game is finitely or infinitely repeated in a behavioral‐experiment sense. Instead, they use evolutionary‐game dynamics (replicator equations, birth–death updating) with no explicit “rounds.”  
   – Systematically varied for the punishment‐treatment effect?  
     No mention at all.  

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   – Discussed?  
     No. There is no reference to communication or “chat.”  
   – Systematically varied for the punishment‐treatment effect?  
     Not mentioned.  

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   – Discussed?  
     Yes. The model is a standard two‐strategy public‐goods game (cooperate by paying cost c vs. defect by paying 0). This is, in effect, an all‐or‐nothing decision.  
   – Systematically varied for the punishment‐treatment effect?  
     No. They fix the contribution choice to be binary and do not explore partial‐contribution alternatives or vary that feature.  

5) Is the contribution default (do players “move” some endowment back)?  
   – Discussed?  
     No. The paper does not mention any default‐contribution mechanism or “endowment‐return” format.  
   – Systematically varied for the punishment‐treatment effect?  
     Not mentioned.  

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   – Discussed?  
     Yes. Denoted “r” in the paper. They note that the social dilemma is present when 1 < r < N. They sometimes use r = 3 in numerical examples.  
   – Systematically varied for the punishment‐treatment effect?  
     They do not systematically sweep r in the main figures (their parameter sweeps focus on p, d, q, and N). They therefore give no numerical effect size on how varying r changes the punishment treatment’s impact on cooperation.  

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   – Discussed?  
     Yes. Denoted “α” (alpha) in the model. In the main text they often set α = 0.3. They do comment in the Supplementary Information on larger values.  
   – Systematically varied for the punishment‐treatment effect?  
     They do not provide a focused, main‐text parametric sweep of α for “punishment treatment effects.” In supplementary figures, they do test higher α and see how it affects the fraction of cooperators (not efficiency). No numerical effect size is given for “efficiency,” and indeed they do not measure efficiency at all.  

8) Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from a player per unit of punishment)  
   – Discussed?  
     Partly. In their notation, “β” (beta) is the per‐defector punishment fine imposed by a punishing cooperator, and “d” is a group‐level sanction if at least one defector is found. Strictly speaking, “β” matches “punishment magnitude per unit.” They set it to 1.0 in their main examples but do not systematically sweep β in the main text.  
   – Systematically varied for the punishment‐treatment effect?  
     No. They acknowledge that β > α, but do not explore how varying β would shift outcomes. There is no measure or discussion of efficiency.  

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   – Discussed?  
     No. Although the paper mentions past work on reward, their own model includes only punishment (both peer and “implicated” group punishment).  
   – Systematically varied for the punishment‐treatment effect?  
     No.  

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    – Discussed?  
      No. Their model does not include any rewarding mechanisms.  
    – Systematically varied for the punishment‐treatment effect?  
      No.  

11) Reward magnitude (coins awarded per reward)  
    – Discussed?  
      No. For the same reason as above, they do not model rewards.  
    – Systematically varied for the punishment‐treatment effect?  
      No.  

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?  
    – Discussed?  
      No. The paper uses infinite‐population replicator dynamics or birth–death processes in finite populations; they do not discuss any horizon or whether it is known.  
    – Systematically varied for the punishment‐treatment effect?  
      No mention.  

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players see each other’s earnings)?  
    – Discussed?  
      No. The paper does not address what information individuals have about one another’s payoffs.  
    – Systematically varied for the punishment‐treatment effect?  
      No.  

14) When a player is punished, do they know who punished them?  
    – Discussed?  
      No. The model does not incorporate knowledge about the punisher’s identity.  
    – Systematically varied for the punishment‐treatment effect?  
      No mention.  

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who rewarded them?  
    – Discussed?  
      No. The model does not include any form of rewarding and does not discuss that informational question.  
    – Systematically varied for the punishment‐treatment effect?  
      No mention.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   The paper does not analyze “efficiency” in the sense of total payoff or total payoff divided by the fully cooperative total. Instead, it focuses on (i) the fraction of cooperators in the population over time, (ii) the gradient of selection, and (iii) the stationary distribution of the number of cooperators. While payoffs are defined for the replicator‐equation update rules, the authors do not present results about average or total payoffs as a stand‐alone outcome.  

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   Five of the 15 are explicitly mentioned:  
   1) Number of players (group size N),  
   4) Whether contributions are all or nothing (the paper uses a binary cooperate/defect model),  
   6) The MPCR or multiplication factor r,  
   7) The punishment cost to the punisher per unit (α),  
   8) The punishment magnitude deducted from the punished (β).  
   The other ten parameters are either not mentioned at all or not part of the model.  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable) when systematically varied?  
   • The paper systematically varies the group size N (parameter 1) and finds that an intermediate N is least conducive to cooperation.  
   • They also carry out parameter sweeps for the implicated‐punishment fine d and the probability p of being monitored, but those two are not in the user’s list of 15 (the user’s list does not include “d” or “p”).  
   • Although α (punishment cost, parameter 7) and β (punishment magnitude, parameter 8) appear in the model, the main‐text figures do not systematically vary them. They do explore larger α in the Supplementary Material, but only with respect to how it changes the fraction of cooperators. No effect size is given for any notion of “efficiency.”  
   • Thus, among the user’s 15 parameters, only the number of players (N) truly receives a parametric sweep in the main text.  

D) If you were to make predictions about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely from this paper, what would they be?  
   The paper never measures or reports efficiency, so it is not possible to quantify how changes in these parameters would alter total‐group payoff versus the fully cooperative benchmark. The authors focus instead on how frequently cooperation takes over evolutionarily (or fails to). If one were to guess about “efficiency,” one might correlate higher cooperation with higher efficiency, but the paper itself does not confirm or analyze that. Accordingly, based on the content of this paper alone, there is little to no direct basis for predicting how systematically varying any of the 15 parameters would affect the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.

Article Title: Fair and unfair punishers coexist in the Ultimatum Game
Keywords Plus: ANTISOCIAL PUNISHMENT; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; COSTLY PUNISHMENT; COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; SEROTONIN; RETALIATION; SIDE
Abstract: In the Ultimatum Game, a proposer suggests how to split a sum of money with a responder. If the responder rejects the proposal, both players get nothing. Rejection of unfair offers is regarded as a form of punishment implemented by fair-minded individuals, who are willing to impose the cooperation norm at a personal cost. However, recent research using other experimental frameworks has observed non-negligible levels of antisocial punishment by competitive, spiteful individuals, which can eventually undermine cooperation. Using two large-scale experiments, this note explores the nature of Ultimatum Game punishers by analyzing their behavior in a Dictator Game. In both studies, the coexistence of two entirely different sub-populations is confirmed: prosocial punishers on the one hand, who behave fairly as dictators, and spiteful (antisocial) punishers on the other, who are totally unfair. The finding has important implications regarding the evolution of cooperation and the behavioral underpinnings of stable social systems.

Below I go through the 15 public–goods-game (PGG) design parameters one by one, indicating (1) whether the Boehm paper even mentions the parameter and, if so, what is said, and (2) whether the paper makes any prediction about the effect of **systematically varying** that parameter on a punishment-vs-no-punishment treatment effect (in the paper’s own terms or ours).  Page, table and section references are supplied whenever something is actually mentioned.  Where nothing is said, that is stated explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  No.  The paper deals with real hunter-gatherer bands, not laboratory groups of a fixed size.  
   • Systematic-variation prediction?  None.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  No.  There is no repeated-game structure in the article.  
   • Prediction?  None.

3. Chat / communication allowed  
   • Mentioned?  No discussion of within-round chat or restricted/no chat.  
   • Prediction?  None.

4. All-or-nothing contributions  
   • Mentioned?  Not discussed; there is no “contribution stage” in the anthropological data.  
   • Prediction?  None.

5. Contribution default / endowment kept unless moved  
   • Mentioned?  Not discussed.  
   • Prediction?  None.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  Not discussed; there is no formal public-goods technology.  
   • Prediction?  None.

7. Punishment cost to punisher  
   • Mentioned?  The paper recognises that punishing can be “dangerous” or “costly” (e.g., group members “gang up” at some risk, p. 327), but gives no numbers or comparative cases.  
   • Systematic-variation prediction?  None.

8. Punishment magnitude (penalty to target per unit)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes, qualitatively.  Range runs from ridicule through ostracism to capital punishment (Table 1, items 4.2–4.44).  
   • Systematic-variation prediction?  None.  No claims that “stronger penalties will raise efficiency by X%.”

9. Whether a reward option exists  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  “Positive sanctioning” is discussed (pp. 329-330, 332-333).  Rewards include higher reputation, preferred marriage or trading partners, informal leadership.  
   • Systematic-variation prediction?  None.

10. Reward cost  
    • Mentioned?  No numerical or even qualitative treatment of costs to rewarders.  
    • Prediction?  None.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Mentioned?  Only that benefits can be “substantial”; no scale or comparison.  
    • Prediction?  None.

12. Whether the horizon (number of rounds) is known  
    • Mentioned?  No.  
    • Prediction?  None.

13. Whether peer outcomes are shown  
    • Mentioned?  No experimental analogue; not discussed.  
    • Prediction?  None.

14. Whether the punished player learns who punished them  
    • Mentioned?  Implicitly, yes: punishment in small bands is normally open and collective (“entire group kills culprit”, Table 1, item 4.43).  Anonymity is never mentioned.  
    • Systematic-variation prediction?  None.

15. Whether the rewarded player learns who rewarded them  
    • Mentioned?  Not directly.  Reputation-based rewards imply public knowledge but this is never contrasted with anonymity.  
    • Prediction?  None.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables actually used in the paper  
    • The paper never uses “group efficiency” (total or average payoff divided by maximum possible).  
    • Main outcomes are qualitative: (i) frequency of moral deviance categories, (ii) presence/absence and type of punishments, (iii) presence/absence of positive sanctioning of generosity, and (iv) hypothesised long-run genetic consequences.  These are conceptually very different from the PGG metrics of average contribution or efficiency.

B.  Which of the 15 design parameters are even **mentioned**?  
    • Four appear in a very loose, qualitative sense: 7 (cost to punishers, vaguely noted), 8 (punishment magnitude via ridicule → death), 9 (existence of rewards), 14 (punisher anonymity—implicitly “not anonymous”).  
    • The other 11 parameters are not touched at all.

C.  For which parameters does the paper discuss the effect of **systematically varying** that parameter on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable)?  
    • Zero.  No formal or informal comparative predictions are made across different values of any parameter.

D.  What predictions, if any, can be made **solely from this paper** about how the 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
    • The paper provides almost no leverage.  It does suggest in a broad, qualitative way that (i) harsher, publicly known punishments carried out collectively can reduce antisocial behaviour and support cooperation, and (ii) the presence of reward mechanisms may also foster generosity.  However, no magnitudes, trade-offs or interaction effects are specified.  Consequently, any quantitative prediction about efficiency changes in an experimental PGG as these 15 parameters vary would go far beyond the paper’s content.  In short, the paper offers too little to build parameter-level predictive models for efficiency.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Bottom line: The Boehm article is a qualitative, evolutionary anthropology account; it does not contain the experimental design elements, numerical treatment effects, or systematic manipulations needed to inform predictions about how the 15 PGG parameters would influence the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.
reference_APA: Boehm, Christopher (2008). Purposive Social Selection and the Evolution of Human Altruism. CROSS-CULTURAL RESEARCH.

Below each of the 15 parameters I state  

(1) whether the paper ever mentions the parameter and, if so, the value actually used in the experiment, and  

(2) whether the paper says anything about what would happen to the **punishment-treatment effect** (Observed vs. Unobserved punishment) if the parameter were systematically varied.  When a numerical effect can be read off a table or figure I quote it.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned.  Groups of 4 players.  
   (2) No statement at all about varying the group size, so no prediction.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Mentioned.  Two independent blocks of 10 periods each (20 periods in all).  
   (2) Not varied and no prediction about varying it.

3. Is chat enabled?  
   (1) Not mentioned → chat clearly not allowed.  
   (2) No discussion, hence no prediction.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   (1) Mentioned implicitly: subjects choose any integer 0–20, so “all-or-nothing = False.”  
   (2) No discussion of switching to an all-or-nothing regime.

5. “Contribution default” (take instead of give)?  
   (1) The game is the standard “give” frame.  Not otherwise discussed.  
   (2) No prediction.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   (1) Explicit: MPCR = 0.4.  
   (2) Nowhere do the authors vary or model changes in the MPCR, so no prediction for the treatment effect.

7. Punishment cost to inflict one unit  
   (1) Explicit: cost = 1 token per deduction point.  
   (2) The text contains only one qualitative remark: “As the ratio of effect per unit cost becomes larger, punishment becomes more common; at low enough ratios the possibility of punishment is not sufficient to maintain cooperation.”  
       • This is a general statement, not connected to the Observed-vs-Unobserved comparison, and it is not quantified.  
       • Therefore no usable prediction about the punishment-treatment effect.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss suffered per point)  
   (1) Explicit: each deduction point reduces the target’s payoff by 3 tokens.  
   (2) Same single qualitative remark as parameter 7, no quantitative or treatment-specific prediction.

9. Is a reward option enabled?  
   (1) Explicitly absent; only punishment exists.  
   (2) No prediction (rewards are never studied).

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   (1) Not used; never mentioned beyond acknowledging absence.  
   (2) No prediction.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
   (1) The instructions given to subjects state “After the tenth game you will be notified of your total income,” implying subjects know each block lasts ten periods.  
   (2) The number of known rounds is never varied; no prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   (1) Yes.  In BOTH treatments subjects always see every other group member’s Stage-1 contribution each period.  
   (2) What differs is whether *punishment outcomes* are shown each period.  
       • Observed treatment: after every period the victim sees the *total* punishment received that period.  
       • Unobserved treatment: victims learn their *cumulative* punishment only after ten periods.  
       • This is the sole systematic manipulation in the paper.  
       • Effect on efficiency (proxied by “income”): Table 3, col.(4) gives a coefficient of –1.158***, meaning mean income in Observed is 1.16 tokens lower than in Unobserved (pooled over periods).  
         ⇒ Withholding punishment information *increases* efficiency by ≈1.2 tokens per person per period.  
       • Effect on other outcomes: contributions are 4.27 tokens lower (col.(1)), fraction who punish 12.8 pp lower (col.(2)), punishment spending 0.34 tokens lower (col.(3)) when punishment is *observed*.  
       • Period-by-period estimates (Table 3, cols.(5)-(8)) show the efficiency gap is significant in several but not all periods (see p-values).  
       Thus parameter 13 is the only parameter for which the paper provides a clear, quantified treatment effect.

14. Does the punished player know WHO punished them?  
   (1) In both treatments, no: only the *aggregate* number of deduction points is revealed (and only with a delay in Unobserved).  
   (2) The identity dimension is never varied; no prediction.

15. If reward exists, does the rewarded player know who rewarded them?  
   (1) Not applicable (no reward option).  
   (2) No prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables actually analysed  
   • Contribution (tokens given)  
   • Indicator “punishes”  
   • Punishment expenditure  
   • Income (payoff) – this is the closest measure to group efficiency used in the paper.  
   The article never computes “efficiency = total payoff / maximum possible payoff,” so efficiency is *not* an explicit dependent variable.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   10 parameters: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 13, 14 (values stated); 10 & 11 explicitly absent.  Parameters 12 & 15 are implicit but not emphasized.  (Total mentioned: 12 of 15 in some form.)

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss how *systematic variation* would influence the punishment-treatment effect?  
   • Exactly ONE parameter—#13 (timing/visibility of peer outcomes)—is experimentally varied and its impact on payoff, contribution, and punishment variables is quantified.  
   • Parameters 7 and 8 receive a qualitative aside about how changing the punishment cost/benefit ratio influences cooperation *in general*, but not the treatment effect, not efficiency, and not quantitatively.  
   Thus: 1 parameter with a real, quantified analysis; 2 parameters with only non-quantified stray remarks; the remaining 12 parameters have no treatment-effect discussion.

D. Predictions one could make *solely from this paper* about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency  
   • The only supported prediction: If peer punishment information is delayed or withheld (parameter 13), efficiency rises by roughly 1.2 tokens per person per period under the payoff structure used here.  
   • For all other parameters the paper provides either no information or only very general statements, so no reliable prediction can be drawn about how changing them would alter the efficiency impact of adding punishment.
reference_APA: Fudenberg, Drew & Pathak, Parag A. (2010). Unobserved punishment supports cooperation. JOURNAL OF PUBLIC ECONOMICS.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter check based exclusively on the content of the paper “Punishing Unfairness: Rewarding or the Organization of a Reactively Aggressive Response?” and its figures, tables, and text. In particular, the paper examines an Ultimatum‐Game‐like “Social Fairness Game” in which participants can punish a partner for unfair offers. It reports primarily on neural activity (fMRI) and on how punishment decisions vary with perceived unfairness; it does not report on or manipulate most of the 15 parameters listed in your request, nor does it discuss group efficiency as an outcome. The details are as follows.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     The paper does not explicitly discuss “number of players” as a systematically varied parameter. It only states that the participant “encountered 12 partners,” but does not explore different group sizes nor how changing the number of total players affects outcomes.  
   • Does it make predictions about systematically varying “number of players” on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable)?  
     No. The paper does not mention systematically varying the number of players.

2. Number of rounds
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     The paper states that participants completed 120 trials (in four runs) but does not discuss varying the number of rounds.  
   • Does it make predictions about systematically varying “number of rounds”?  
     No. The paper does not systematically vary the number of rounds or analyze how changing that would affect punishment.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     No. There is no mention of participant chat or communication between players.  
   • Predictions about varying “chat enabled” on punishment treatment effect?  
     No. The paper does not mention or manipulate communication.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     No. The paper reports on an Ultimatum‐style game where the partner proposes how to split $20, but it does not frame it as an “all or nothing” contribution to a public good.  
   • Predictions about varying “all or nothing”?  
     No. It does not appear in the paper.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     No. The paper does not address any “default contribution” mechanism.  
   • Predictions about varying “contribution default” on punishment?  
     No. Not mentioned.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or similar multiplication factor
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     No. The study’s “Social Fairness Game” does not frame outcomes via a “multiplication factor” of the group pot (as in typical public goods games).  
   • Predictions about systematically varying MPCR?  
     No. Not mentioned.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     Yes, partly. In the paper’s task, the participant can spend from $1 up to $3 to punish. Each $1 of punishment cost results in $7 taken from the partner. This cost factor (to the punisher) is fixed; it is not manipulated.  
   • Predictions about systematically varying that cost on punishment outcomes?  
     No. While the paper does note the cost of punishment ($1 for each $7 deducted from the other player), it does not make or test predictions about what happens if that cost structure changes.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted for each unit of punishment)
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     Yes, they fix it at $7 deducted for each $1 spent by the punisher.  
   • Does it predict the effect of systematically varying the magnitude?  
     No. The magnitude is not experimentally varied, and the paper does not predict how its variation would affect results.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     No. The design focuses on punishment of unfair offers. It does not mention a reward mechanism.  
   • Predictions about rewards?  
     No. The paper makes no reference to any reward‐enabled variation for the other player.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?
      No. Rewards are not included in this paradigm.  
    • Predictions about systematically varying reward cost?  
      No. Not mentioned.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
      No. There is no reward condition in the reported study.  
    • Predictions about varying reward magnitude?  
      No. The paper does not address reward at all.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
      No. The paper does not specify whether participants knew precisely how many trials there would be.  
    • Predictions about varying that knowledge?  
      No. Not mentioned.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
      The paper mentions an “outcome‐phase” in which participants see how much they and their partner ended up with (e.g., “partner gets –$1, you get $0”). However, it does not mention systematically varying the manner or extent to which peer outcomes are shown.  
    • Predictions about systematically varying how peer outcomes are displayed?  
      No. The paper only reports that participants see the result of the transaction; there is no systematic manipulation discussed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the punisher is?
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
      No. It does not discuss any condition in which the punished player learns the punisher’s identity.  
    • Predictions about varying that knowledge?  
      No. Not addressed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is?
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?
      No. Rewarding was not part of the design.  
    • Predictions about systematically varying that knowledge?
      No. Not mentioned.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • No. The paper does not use group efficiency or total payoff as a chief dependent variable. Rather, it measures (a) neural activation in various brain regions, and (b) participants’ punishment decisions (i.e., how much they choose to spend to punish a partner). These dependent variables differ from efficiency. The paper never reports an “actual total payoff” relative to a maximum possible payoff.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Parameters #7 (“punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment”) and #8 (“punishment magnitude”) appear in the paper in a fixed ratio ($1 cost to punish = $7 deducted from the partner). All other parameters (#1, #2, #3, #4, #5, #6, #9, #10, #11, #12, #13, #14, #15) are either not mentioned at all or are mentioned only in passing (e.g., the presence of “120 trials” is stated, but not in a way that it is systematically analyzed or varied).  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. The paper does not systematically vary any parameter (including #7 and #8). Although #7 and #8 are part of the game rule (the participant pays $1 to deduct $7 from the proposer), the paper does not experimentally manipulate that ratio or compare multiple cost/magnitude conditions. Hence, it offers no discussion or numerical effect sizes for systematically varying any parameter in relation to punishment outcomes or efficiency.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper provides no direct basis to predict changes in efficiency. It focuses on neural correlates of punishment choices given a fixed cost and fixed punishment magnitude. 1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  The review cites “a one-shot Public Goods Game played by four players (Fehr & Gächter, 2002).”

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  The review contrasts “one-shot” with “repeated” public-goods interactions and notes that “if played repetitively, individual investments … decline … unless sanctions are in place … .”  
   • Systematic variation / prediction?  Partly.  It asserts qualitatively that introducing punishment prevents the usual across-round decline in contributions, but no numerical effect size is given and the variable “number of rounds” itself is never varied (e.g., 5 vs 20 rounds).  Dependent variable discussed is contribution level, not efficiency.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned?  No.  No reference to communication or chat between players.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
   • Mentioned?  No.

5. Contribution default (endowment automatically in public account, decision is to withdraw)  
   • Mentioned?  No.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  Only generically: in a public-goods description the multiplication factor is said to be “larger than one and smaller than the number of players.”  No value given, never varied.  No predictions.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher

   • Systematic variation / prediction?  None.

8. Punishment magnitude (deduction from target)  
   • Mentioned?  No numerical value; never varied; no predictions.

9. Whether a reward option is enabled  
   • Mentioned?  Only in other game paradigms (Trust Game, etc.) as “reward” in the lay sense of payoff, not as a peer-to-peer reward institution.  No public-goods reward mechanism is analysed.  No predictions.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   • Mentioned?  No.

12. Are players told how many rounds remain?  
   • Mentioned?  No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  In the Fehr & Gächter public-goods set-up players first learn “the investment of the other players” before deciding on punishment.  
   • Systematic variation / prediction?  No.  The presence of that information is a fixed feature; its absence/presence is never compared.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?

 • (1) Does the paper discuss it?  
   – The experiment is described as 10 rounds from the outset, but they do not state explicitly whether subjects know that it is exactly 10. It is implied that they do.  
 • (2) Any prediction about systematically varying whether the horizon is known or unknown?  
   – No.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown?
 • (1) Does the paper discuss it?  
   – Yes. Participants see how much bandwidth is created each round, observe each other’s investment decisions, and see real‐time file downloads in the “dashboard.”  
 • (2) Any prediction about systematically varying the extent of outcome visibility?  
   – No.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
 • (1) Does the paper discuss it?  
   – No direct punishment mechanism is implemented. Indirect “punishment” by lower investment is not accompanied by any identity revelation.  
 • (2) Any prediction about systematically varying this factor?  
   – No.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
 • (1) Does the paper discuss it?  
   – Rewarding does not occur in these experiments, so no.  
 • (2) Any prediction about varying knowledge of rewarder identity?  
   – No.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
 • The paper primarily reports total or average tokens earned, distribution of payoffs, and how these compare to a “social optimum.” They do not explicitly label it “efficiency,” though one can infer an efficiency‐type measure by comparing the group’s total payoff each round to the maximum possible payoff (the “cooperative optimum”).  
 • Other dependent variables the paper tracks include: (1) individual and group investment, (2) Gini coefficient of payoffs, (3) number of files downloaded, and (4) tokens earned by each position (A, B, …). These differ from “efficiency” because they do not necessarily represent the fraction of the maximum group payoff.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
 • Mentioned explicitly or implicitly in some form (but not always systematically varied):  
   1) Number of players (2 vs. 5)  
   2) Number of rounds (10)  
   3) Chat (always enabled)  
   4) Contribution is flexible (not all or nothing)  
   6) A mention of a production function (nonlinear), not labeled “MPCR”  
   12) Likely that participants know the game lasts 10 rounds (though not varied)  
   13) Basic peer information is shown (investments and bandwidth usage)  
 • The rest—parameters 5, 7–11, 14, and 15—are not discussed in the sense of a formal or systematic design feature for punishment or reward.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
 • The only truly systematic variation in the experiment is (#1) Number of players (2 vs. 5). Even there, the paper does not frame it as a “punishment treatment” but rather a difference in group size.  
 • They do not present or test a formal “punishment cost,” “punishment magnitude,” “reward,” or other such manipulations.  
 • Hence, effectively zero (0) parameters are discussed in terms of their effect on a dedicated “punishment treatment” or on “punishment treatment efficiency.”  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
 • Because the paper does not run or compare a “punishment” vs. “no punishment” arrangement—and does not systematically vary parameters such as cost or magnitude of punishing or rewarding—there is little basis to predict how changing any of the 15 parameters would alter a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”  
 • The one partial exception is that going from 2 players to 5 players shows that coordinating is more difficult (lower net payoff on average). They attribute that in part to the constraints of a larger group, but they do not quantify a “treatment effect” of punishment alone.  
 • Apart from that, the paper offers no direct guidance on how systematically altering these parameters (chat on/off, knowledge of rounds, reward presence, etc.) would affect efficiency under a punishment treatment.

Article Title: Punish and Voice: Punishment Enhances Cooperation when Combined with Norm-Signalling
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; SANCTIONS; MONETARY; BEHAVIOR
Abstract: Material punishment has been suggested to play a key role in sustaining human cooperation. Experimental findings, however, show that inflicting mere material costs does not always increase cooperation and may even have detrimental effects. Indeed, ethnographic evidence suggests that the most typical punishing strategies in human ecologies (e. g., gossip, derision, blame and criticism) naturally combine normative information with material punishment. Using laboratory experiments with humans, we show that the interaction of norm communication and material punishment leads to higher and more stable cooperation at a lower cost for the group than when used separately. In this work, we argue and provide experimental evidence that successful human cooperation is the outcome of the interaction between instrumental decision-making and the norm psychology humans are provided with. Norm psychology is a cognitive machinery to detect and reason upon norms that is characterized by a salience mechanism devoted to track how much a norm is prominent within a group. We test our hypothesis both in the laboratory and with an agent-based model. The agent-based model incorporates fundamental aspects of norm psychology absent from previous work. The combination of these methods allows us to provide an explanation for the proximate mechanisms behind the observed cooperative behaviour. The consistency between the two sources of data supports our hypothesis that cooperation is a product of norm psychology solicited by norm-signalling and coercive devices.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what the paper “Punish and Voice: Punishment Enhances Cooperation when Combined with Norm‐Signalling” (Andrighetto et al. 2013) says, or does not say, about each of the 15 parameters in relation to predicting the punishment treatment effect—especially on efficiency (actual total payoff over the maximum possible payoff), as requested. As instructed, all statements refer solely to what is contained in the paper (including its figures, tables, and text), without recourse to any outside sources.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of Players
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper states that “12 fixed groups of four subjects interact over thirty rounds.” Thus, each group has 4 players.  
   • Systematically Varied? No. The paper does not vary the group size across conditions.  
   • Effect on Punishment Treatment Effect? No predictions or results are provided on how changing the number of players would affect the punishment treatment effect on any dependent variable.

2. Number of Rounds
   • Mentioned? Yes. The experiment always consists of 30 rounds, divided into blocks (rounds 1–10, 11–20, and 21–30).  
   • Systematically Varied? No. The paper does not alter the total number of rounds; it is always 30.  
   • Effect on Punishment Treatment Effect? The authors do not discuss how varying the number of rounds would systematically affect the punishment treatment effect on cooperation, payoffs, or efficiency.

3. Is Chat Enabled between Players?
   • Mentioned? Partially. The authors do not allow open/free-form chat. Instead, in the “message” and “sanction” treatments, participants may send predetermined “normative messages” (one of three statements) to one another.  
   • Systematically Varied? The experiment does include a variation: no communication in the Punishment treatment, structured norm-relevant communication in the Message and Sanction treatments. However, there is no “free chat” condition nor a systematic parametric change in communication channels.  
   • Effect on Punishment Treatment Effect? The paper does compare treatments with versus without the ability to send a message, but it does not express results in terms of “efficiency” as a ratio of actual to maximum possible payoffs. Instead, it reports effects on average payoffs and on cooperation levels. No numerical effect size is given specifically for “efficiency” as defined above, though the paper does note that combined message + punishment yields higher average payoffs than punishment alone.

4. Is the Contribution “All or Nothing”?
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper clarifies that each player can contribute an integer amount “between 0 and 20.” That is not an all-or-nothing design.  
   • Systematically Varied? No. The contribution range is always 0–20 tokens.  
   • Effect on Punishment Treatment Effect? The authors do not discuss changing from continuous (0–20) to all-or-nothing or vice versa, so there is no consideration of this parameter’s effect.

5. Is the Contribution Default?
   • Mentioned? No. The study does not describe any default mechanism that automatically allocates or reverses endowments (e.g., “moving from the public fund back into one’s hand”).  
   • Systematically Varied? No.  
   • Effect on Punishment Treatment Effect? Not applicable; the paper does not address this at all.

6. Marginal Per Capita Return (MPCR) or Related Factor
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each player’s payoff formula contains a “0.4” multiplier on the sum of contributions (equivalent to an MPCR of 0.4).  
   • Systematically Varied? No. The MPCR is fixed at 0.4 (the paper does not examine multiple MPCR values).  
   • Effect on Punishment Treatment Effect? No discussion of how changing MPCR would change the relationship between punishment and cooperation or payoffs.

7. Punishment Cost to Impose a Single Unit of Punishment
   • Mentioned? Yes. One assigned punishment point costs the punisher 1 token.  
   • Systematically Varied? No. It stays at 1 token per punishment point; the paper does not test other cost levels.  
   • Effect on Punishment Treatment Effect? The authors do not study how changing this cost systematically would alter the punishment treatment’s outcomes.

8. Punishment Magnitude (the Cost Imposed on the Punished)
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each punishment point reduces the punished person’s payoff by 3 tokens.  
   • Systematically Varied? No. It is always 3 tokens lost by the punished for each point.  
   • Effect on Punishment Treatment Effect? The paper reports that punishment alone yields lower average payoffs than combined message + punishment, but it does not explore changes in the punishment deduction of 3 tokens.

9. Whether a Reward Is Enabled
   • Mentioned? No. The designs in the paper (Message, Punishment, and Sanction) do not include a reward mechanism.  
   • Systematically Varied? Not applicable.  
   • Effect on Punishment Treatment Effect? The paper does not consider rewards.

10. Reward Cost to Grant a Single Unit of Reward
   • Mentioned? No. Because no reward mechanism is present, no cost of rewarding is discussed.  
   • Systematically Varied? Not applicable.  
   • Effect on Punishment Treatment Effect? Not addressed.

11. Reward Magnitude
   • Mentioned? No. There is no monetary reward procedure in the experiment.  
   • Systematically Varied? Not applicable.  
   • Effect on Punishment Treatment Effect? Not addressed.

12. Is the Number of Rounds Known to Players?
   • Mentioned? Yes. The instructions say “The experiment has 30 rounds,” so participants do know the exact endpoint.  
   • Systematically Varied? No. They do not run a hidden-end or varied-end design.  
   • Effect on Punishment Treatment Effect? No discussion is given regarding how concealing or revealing the round length would systematically change punishment’s effect.

13. Are Peer Outcomes Shown?
   • Mentioned? Yes. After each round, participants see each group member’s contribution (and in punishment treatments, the punishment data).  
   • Systematically Varied? No. This is kept consistent throughout.  
   • Effect on Punishment Treatment Effect? The authors do not examine changes in whether or how outcomes are displayed.

14. When a Player Is Punished, Do They Know Who the Specific Punisher Is?
   • Mentioned? Yes. “Each punished group member is informed about the ID of all punishers at the end of each round.”  
   • Systematically Varied? No. Identification of punishers is always revealed if punishment occurs.  
   • Effect on Punishment Treatment Effect? The authors do not examine withholding punisher identity, so there is no discussion of how this might alter the efficiency outcome.

15. When a Player Is Rewarded, Do They Know Who the Specific Rewarder Is?
   • Mentioned? No. As with parameters 9–11, there is no reward mechanism at all in the design.  
   • Systematically Varied? Not applicable.  
   • Effect on Punishment Treatment Effect? Not addressed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the Paper Use Group Efficiency (or Total/Average Payoff) as a Dependent Variable? What Dependent Variables Appear?

• The paper does not explicitly use “efficiency” in the sense of “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff”; instead, it reports:  
  – Contribution levels (i.e., cooperation rates)  
  – Punishment usage (frequency, intensity)  
  – Average net earnings/payoffs.  

The authors compare mean payoffs across treatments (Sanction vs. Punishment vs. Message), which is not exactly the same as efficiency = (actual payoff)/(max payoff). Hence, “efficiency” is not directly reported. The main dependent variables in the paper are:  
  • Cooperation/contribution level.  
  • Punishment frequency and intensity.  
  • Average payoff/earnings.  

These variables differ in that contributions track how many tokens participants put into the public good, punishment usage tracks costly sanctioning, and payoffs track monetary outcomes—none of which is expressed as the fraction of a theoretical maximum.

B. Which (and How Many) of the 15 Parameters Are Mentioned in the Paper?

Mentioned in some form (with a fixed value or condition):
1 (4 players), 2 (30 rounds), 3 (a structured normative “message” in some treatments, but not free chat), 4 (choice is from 0 to 20, not “all or nothing”), 6 (MPCR = 0.4), 7 (1 token cost to punish), 8 (3 token deduction for the punished), 12 (participants know there are 30 rounds), 13 (peer outcomes are displayed), 14 (punished players see who punished them).  

Not mentioned or explicitly excluded:
5 (no contribution default mechanism), 9 (no rewards), 10 (no cost for rewards), 11 (no reward magnitude), 15 (no rewarder identity revealed, since no rewards exist).  

Hence, 10 parameters are discussed in some form (even if not systematically varied), and 5 are not mentioned.

C. For Which (and How Many) of the 15 Parameters Does the Paper Discuss Their Effect on the Punishment Treatment Effect When Each Parameter Is Systematically Varied?

None. Although the authors do compare different treatments (Message, Punishment, Sanction), they do not systematically vary any of the 15 detailed parameters (e.g., changing the punishment cost, altering group size, changing MPCR, enabling or disabling punisher anonymity, etc.). The paper therefore provides no direct numerical effect sizes or formal predictions about how systematically increasing/decreasing these parameters would alter the punishment treatment’s impact on cooperation, payoffs, or any ratio-based “efficiency.”

D. Predicted Influence of These 15 Parameters (and Their Interactions) on the Punishment Treatment Effect on Efficiency, Based Solely on the Paper

The paper’s key finding is that adding explicit norm communication (a “voice” or normative message) alongside material punishment yields higher cooperation and higher average payoffs than material punishment alone. Strictly from the content provided:  
• One might suspect that if communication becomes more informative or is combined with punishment, the group’s average payoff (and thus “efficiency”) would rise; if the cost of punishment or the severity of punishment became too high, payoffs might erode overall.  
• However, the paper does not offer evidence or modeling for changes in the other parameters—so, for most of the 15 parameters, the paper gives little to no basis from which to predict their effects on efficiency.  

Thus, apart from concluding that “combining norm communication and punishment is better than punishment alone,” no further predictions can be made with confidence from this paper about how varying the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would affect efficiency.

Below we walk through the 15 design parameters one-by-one, checking the Lippert & Spagnolo paper for  
(i) whether the parameter is explicitly described (and, if so, the value or values that appear) and  
(ii) whether the authors give any prediction about what would happen *if that parameter were systematically varied* to a different level, especially with respect to a “punishment treatment effect” on **group efficiency** (total pay-off ÷ first-best pay-off).  
Whenever the paper is silent we say so.

----------------------------------------------------------------------  
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
----------------------------------------------------------------------  

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  The set N = {1,…,n}. n is left completely generic.  
   • Systematic variation / prediction?  No. The model is written for any n; no comparative-static result links different n to the size of a “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency (or on any other outcome).

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  Yes — the interactions are infinitely repeated (δ<1).  
   • Systematic variation / prediction?  No. The horizon is always infinite; there is no analysis of what happens when the number of rounds is shortened or when the end is known.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  “Word-of-Mouth Communication” (WoM) is an environment in which agents can send voluntary, possibly false messages about past play. Two benchmark environments (“Public information” = full broadcast and “Private information without communication”) are defined by *prohibiting* such chat.  
   • Systematic variation / prediction?  Qualitatively yes.  The authors compare equilibria with WoM to equilibria without any communication and show:  
     – With WoM, Multilateral Repentance (MR) strategies are feasible and yield faster, more targeted punishment.  
     – MG (grim) strategies do *not* use chat even when it is available.  
     – Punishment becomes “optimal” (i.e. minimal discount factor needed for cooperation is lower) when WoM is switched on.  
   • Numerical effect size?  No numeric efficiency numbers or treatment-effect magnitudes are given.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
   • Mentioned?  No.  Not applicable (the stage game is a generic asymmetric PD with binary C / D).

5. Contribution default (refund frame, etc.)  
   • Mentioned?  No.

6. Marginal per capita return / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  No.  The paper never parameterises a public-goods production technology.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   • Mentioned?  No explicit variable captures a costly *instrument* of peer punishment.  “Punishment” occurs endogenously through playing D and thus forgoing the gains from cooperation; there is no separate cost parameter to the punisher.  
   • Variation / prediction?  None.

8. Punishment magnitude  
   • Mentioned?  No separate parameter.  The loss to the punished player is built into the PD pay-offs, but the paper never varies it.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned?  No (there is no stand-alone reward stage).

10. Reward cost  
    • Mentioned?  No.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Mentioned?  No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
    • Mentioned?  Indirectly: the game is infinitely repeated so the end is never reached or announced.  
    • Variation / prediction?  None.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mentioned?  Yes.  This is the essence of the “Public information” case (everyone sees everything) versus “Private information” (only own bilateral outcomes) versus WoM (only own outcomes plus voluntarily transmitted reports).  
    • Systematic variation / prediction?  Yes, qualitatively.  The paper proves:  
        – Closing a network plus *public* information sustains cooperation under certain payoff sums (Proposition 2.1).  
        – With only private monitoring MG still works but needs stricter conditions involving longer delays (Proposition 2.2).  
     Again, no numeric efficiency effects are reported.

14. Does a punished player know *who* punished?  
    • Mentioned?  Not as a design variable. In the model each bilateral link is perfectly observed by its two participants, so a defector always knows which neighbour switched to D. This is not varied or analysed.

15. Does a rewarded player know *who* rewarded?  
    • Mentioned?  Not applicable (no reward stage).

----------------------------------------------------------------------  
SUMMARY
----------------------------------------------------------------------  
A. Dependent variables  
   – The authors never compute “group efficiency” (= realized total payoff ÷ first-best total payoff).  
   – Outcomes they care about are: whether a given network of bilateral cooperations can be sustained; the minimum discount factor δ required; whether strategies are “optimal punishments”; and qualitative welfare during punishment phases.  
   – Hence “efficiency” in the sense requested by the user is not used.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   • Parameter 3 (communication on/off).  
   • Parameter 13 (visibility of others’ outcomes).  
   • The horizon (parameter 12) is implicitly fixed (infinite) but never varied.  
   → 2 of 15 parameters are explicitly described; none of the remaining 13 appear.

C. For how many parameters is *systematic variation* analysed with respect to any punishment effect?  
   • Parameter 3: yes—comparing “chat off” vs “chat on”.  
   • Parameter 13: yes—comparing “public” vs “private” monitoring.  
   • Even for these two parameters, the paper reports only qualitative statements about the possibility of sustaining cooperation and the discount-factor threshold, not quantitative treatment effects on efficiency.  
   → 2 parameters receive qualitative comparative-static treatment; 0 parameters receive numerical effect-size estimates.

D. What predictions about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment treatment effect on efficiency can be drawn solely from this paper?  
   • Enabling voluntary communication (parameter 3) and/or full public monitoring (parameter 13) should *improve* efficiency, because they allow faster, more targeted punishment and lower the discount factor required for cooperation.  
   • When communication is *disabled* and only private monitoring is available, punishment must rely on contagious grim-trigger behaviour, which is slower, more destructive and therefore yields lower efficiency.  
   • All other parameters (1,2,4-12,14,15) are simply not discussed, so no prediction can be made from this paper alone.

5. “CONTRIBUTION-DEFAULT / REFUND” FRAME  
(a) Not mentioned (standard “give” frame).  
(b) No discussion; no prediction.

6. MPCR (or related multiplication parameters)  
(a) Yes – determined by δ · a.  
    • Baseline: δ=0.5, a=1 for everyone.  
    • Valuation treatment: one “h-player” has δ=1.5, a=1.  
    • Capability treatment: one “h-player” has δ=0.5, a=3.  
    (Thus the *average* MPCR does not change across the three treatments; heterogeneity does.)  
(b) The paper does not systematically vary the *level* of MPCR, nor does it isolate MPCR heterogeneity as an independent manipulation. Consequently it makes no numerical prediction about how varying MPCR would change the punishment treatment effect. The only qualitative inference is that *heterogeneity* in marginal benefits can weaken the efficiency gains from punishment.

7. PUNISHMENT COST PER UNIT  
(a) Yes – 1 token to the punisher.  
(b) Fixed; no prediction.

8. PUNISHMENT MAGNITUDE PER UNIT  
(a) Yes – punished player loses 3 tokens.  
(b) Fixed; no prediction.

9. REWARD POSSIBILITY  
(a) No – rewards are not available.  
(b) Not discussed.

10. REWARD COST PER UNIT  
(a) n/a (no rewards).  
(b) n/a.

11. REWARD MAGNITUDE PER UNIT  
(a) n/a.  
(b) n/a.

12. IS THE HORIZON KNOWN?  
(a) Yes – players expect 10 rounds; the second block of 10 rounds is a surprise.  
(b) Horizon length/knowledge is not varied; no prediction.

13. PEER-OUTCOME FEEDBACK  
(a) Yes – after every round each player sees each group member’s individual contribution, punishment received, and payoff.  
(b) Constant across conditions; no prediction.

14. PUNISHER IDENTITY REVEALED  
(a) No – only the total number of punishment points received is shown.  
(b) Never varied; no prediction.

15. REWARDER IDENTITY REVEALED  
(a) n/a (no rewards).  
(b) n/a.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables used  
   • Sum of payoffs and its percentage of the social optimum (“social efficiency”).  
   • Mean contribution per player.  
   • Tokens spent on punishment.  
   • Within-group payoff inequality (s.d. of payoffs).  
   These variables are conceptually different: contributions ignore costs of punishment; efficiency folds in both contributions and punishment costs; inequality captures distribution, not total value.

B.  Parameters mentioned  
   9 of 15 are explicitly described (1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14).  
   The remaining 6 (3, 5, 9–11, 15) are either absent or not stated.

C.  Parameters whose *systematic variation* is analysed for their impact on the punishment treatment effect  
   None of the 15 parameters is experimentally varied in the paper.  
   Hence the paper offers **0** direct effect sizes of parameter variation on the punishment treatment effect for efficiency or any other dependent variable.

D.  What can be predicted – drawing only on the paper  
   • If Parameter 6 (MPCR) becomes *heterogeneous* in a way that gives some players a much higher private return than others while total returns remain constant (as in the Valuation treatment), the efficiency gain from punishment is likely to shrink or even turn negative because punishment is applied less systematically and antisocial punishment rises.  
   • If Parameter 6 becomes heterogeneous through higher *capability* (so that everyone benefits equally from any given contribution), punishment substantially raises efficiency because low contributors are reliably punished and high contributors are not antisocially targeted.  
   • Beyond this single qualitative statement about a particular *form* of MPCR heterogeneity, the paper provides no evidence that lets us forecast how changing any of the other 14 parameters—or their interactions—will modify the punishment treatment effect on efficiency. In short, apart from the special case of heterogeneous returns, the paper allows little to no prediction regarding the 15 parameters.
reference_APA: Koelle, Felix (2015). Heterogeneity and cooperation: The role of capability and valuation on public goods provision. JOURNAL OF ECONOMIC BEHAVIOR & ORGANIZATION.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter account of what is explicitly stated in the paper regarding (1) whether the paper discusses that parameter (and, if so, its value) and (2) whether there is any discussion in the paper about how systematically varying that parameter would affect “punishment treatment” outcomes. In this study, “punishment” refers to the external monetary penalty imposed by the regulator in the Low Penalty and High Penalty treatments.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players
   • Discussed? Yes. Each group has 5 players.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper always uses groups of size 5.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? The paper does not discuss how changing the group size would affect any outcome; it remains constant at 5. No numerical effect of changing group size is provided.

2) Number of rounds
   • Discussed? Yes. Each group plays 15 rounds, and the number of rounds is known to participants.  
   • Systematically varied? No, it is always 15.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed. The paper does not vary the number of rounds and provides no prediction for changing it.

3) Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussed? Yes. The paper explicitly states that verbal communication among participants was not permitted in any treatment; hence no “chat.”  
   • Systematically varied? No, it stays the same (no communication).  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed, as there is no variation in whether chat is enabled.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussed? Somewhat. Under the regulation treatments (Low Penalty and High Penalty), there is a requirement that everyone should “contribute all 25 tokens,” but participants can still deviate (they can choose from 0 to 25). It is not a forced “all or nothing” choice in practice.  
   • Systematically varied? No, there is no separate treatment that truly forces all or nothing; participants always have freedom to choose any amount.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed as a standalone factor.

5) Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much to move back to their hand)?
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not describe any “default” contribution mechanism or “reclaiming” from a public fund. Subjects simply choose how many tokens (0–25) to allocate to the group.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not mentioned.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Discussed? Yes. The paper sets the multiplier a = 2 and group size n = 5, so MPCR = a/n = 0.4.  
   • Systematically varied? No; it remains fixed at 0.4 in all treatments.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? The paper does not discuss how changing MPCR would affect punishment outcomes. No numerical effect for different MPCRs is provided.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment (i.e., cost to the punisher)
   • Discussed? No. Punishments in the paper are imposed by an external regulator, and there is no mention of a “cost to the punisher.”  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not mentioned.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each punished unit)
   • Discussed? Yes. This appears as the “penalty” s in the Low Penalty (s = 1) and High Penalty (s = 4) treatments.  
   • Systematically varied? Yes. The paper explicitly compares two levels (1 vs. 4) for s.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment?
       – Overview: Despite the fourfold increase in the penalty from s = 1 to s = 4, the paper reports that average contributions do not differ significantly between Low Penalty and High Penalty.  
       – Numerical Effect Size:  
         • Contributions: Low Penalty yields an average individual contribution of 18.2 tokens (out of 25); High Penalty yields 18.5 tokens. No statistically significant difference.  
         • Earnings: Low Penalty yields average expected earnings of 41.8 tokens; High Penalty yields 38.3 tokens. The higher penalty caused more fines for those who did not comply, thereby lowering overall earnings.  
       – Hence, increasing s from 1 to 4 does not improve group outcomes; on the contrary, actual earnings end up worse with the higher penalty.

9) Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussed? No. The paper implements no reward mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not mentioned.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Discussed? No. There is no reward treatment; thus, no mention of a reward cost.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not mentioned.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward granted)
   • Discussed? No. There is no reward mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not mentioned.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
   • Discussed? Yes. The design states that participants knew there would be 15 rounds.  
   • Systematically varied? No, it is fixed.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed as a systematically varied factor.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much their peers gained or lost each round)?
   • Discussed? Partially. In every treatment, all individual contributions are posted in random order (so that they cannot be linked to a specific person), but the paper does not systematically vary the extent of outcome visibility.  
   • In the “Shame” treatment, the randomly audited individual’s contribution and its consequence for the group is publicly revealed.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed as a design factor that was explicitly manipulated (beyond the difference between private vs. public revelation in Guilt vs. Shame).

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Discussed? No. Punisher identity is not really a feature here because the punisher is the external experiment monitor.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not mentioned.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Discussed? No, there is no reward mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not mentioned.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

SUMMARY RESPONSES

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper frequently analyzes total or average individual earnings (these are effectively group payoffs when aggregated) and also examines contribution levels as a separate outcome. Hence “average expected earnings” (or “social welfare”) is indeed reported. The authors sometimes refer to payoffs as “group welfare” or “social welfare,” akin to overall efficiency.  
   • They also measure individual contributions to the public good (another dependent variable). So “efficiency” in the sense of total payoff relative to the fully cooperative maximum is never directly tabulated as a ratio, but the paper does track total/average payoffs (similar in spirit to efficiency) and focuses as well on contributions.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Explicitly mentioned:  
     1) Number of players (n = 5).  
     2) Number of rounds (15).  
     3) Chat (no communication).  
     4) Reference to “all 25 tokens required” in regulation (though practically subjects can still choose 0–25).  
     6) MPCR = 0.4.  
     8) Punishment magnitude (s = 1 or s = 4).  
     12) Number of rounds known to participants.  
     13) Some display of individual contributions (random order) and random public revelation in the Shame treatment.  
   • Not mentioned or not used at all: parameters 5, 7, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15.  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Only parameter 8 (the punishment magnitude s = 1 vs. s = 4) is systematically varied in the two regulation (punishment) treatments. The paper reports how that variation impacts contributions and earnings (two dependent variables). Specifically, there is no significant difference in contributions between Low Penalty and High Penalty; however, earnings are actually lower in High Penalty due to heavier fines.  
   • No other parameter is systematically varied in a way that the paper links to the punishment treatment effect.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • Because only the penalty magnitude (parameter 8) was systematically varied, and the study found no improvement in overall payoffs from increasing the penalty, little else can be inferred about how the other parameters would affect efficiency.  
   • The data suggest that heavy penalties (s = 4) do not raise total group payoffs in practice—participants still shirk at similar rates, and those who deviate pay larger fines, lowering the overall group payoff.  
   • In general, the paper’s results show that other mechanisms (for instance, a “shame” treatment that publicly reveals low contributors) can outperform monetary punishment in terms of total payoffs.  
   • The paper does not systematically manipulate any other parameter, so no further predictions about how varying them would change punishment-based efficiency can be made from this text alone.
reference_APA: Claudia Lopez, Maria, Murphy, James J., Spraggon, John M. & Stranlund, John K. (2012). COMPARING THE EFFECTIVENESS OF REGULATION AND PRO-SOCIAL EMOTIONS TO ENHANCE COOPERATION: EXPERIMENTAL EVIDENCE FROM FISHING COMMUNITIES IN COLOMBIA. ECONOMIC INQUIRY.

Abstract: Experimental games-the dictator game and the ultimatum game-were played out among the Ju/'hoan Bushmen of the Kalahari. Subsequently, the experimenter tracked what the players did with the money earned in the games to see how it was used in games of everyday life. Players were stingy and did not punish in experimental games and were generous and did punish in games of life. The fact that the conditions of anonymity of the games removed cultural institutions and emotions governing sharing and reciprocity led Ju/'hoansi to reassess risks and benefits and play more selfishly. The findings underline the importance of cultural institutions such as sharing, reciprocity, and social sanctions (costly punishment) to provide the structure for other-regarding behavior to be expressed and to be rendered beneficial for the participants.
