Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter summary of what (if anything) Wiessner’s paper says about each of the 15 parameters and whether it discusses systematically varying that parameter’s effect on punishment (and especially on efficiency). Throughout, please note that Wiessner’s study involves dictator and ultimatum games in a small‐scale society (the Ju/’hoansi); it is not about public goods with punishment, nor does it analyze “efficiency” (in the sense of total group payoff relative to some maximum). References to punishment concern responder rejections in the ultimatum game and the everyday “punishment” that happens in Ju/’hoan village life, rather than a designed parameter (e.g., cost to punish and number of punishment tokens).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned? The paper implicitly mentions that each game has two players (a proposer and a responder for the ultimatum game, or proposer and recipient for the dictator game). There is no discussion of systematically varying the number of players, nor of any effect on punishment or efficiency.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned? The games described were single‐shot (each participant played the dictator game once, then the ultimatum game once). The paper does not discuss systematically varying the number of rounds, nor any predicted effect of changing how many rounds are played.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned? No. Participants were instructed not to reveal their decisions, and there is no mention of allowing (or preventing) communication as a variable. There is no systematic variation or prediction regarding chat.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned? No. In the dictator/ultimatum games, proposers choose any number of coins to offer (though Ju/’hoansi insisted that at least 1 coin must be given in the dictator game). There is no mention of systematically manipulating an all‐or‐nothing rule or discussing its effect.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Mentioned? No. These studies do not discuss settings in which players must “move” endowment in or out of a fund by default. No mention of systematically varying this.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Mentioned? No. Since these were dictator and ultimatum games, there is a simple one‐to‐one payoff with no multiplication factor. The paper does not mention anything like an MPCR or systematically varying it.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned? In the ultimatum game, a rejection “punishes” the proposer but also costs the responder a payoff. The paper does not describe this as systematically varied, nor does it present any predictions for how changing that cost would affect outcomes. There is only the general statement that bearing punishment costs (i.e., rejecting a low offer) is uncommon in this population.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   • Mentioned? Again, in the ultimatum game, rejecting an offer means no one receives anything (the “magnitude” is effectively the entire payoff). However, there is no discussion of systematically varying that punishment magnitude, nor any predicted effect on efficiency or other outcomes.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned? No. The paper’s experiments only involve the dictator game and the ultimatum game. There is no mention of any reward mechanism or systematically changing reward conditions.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Mentioned? No. Rewarding is not part of the design under discussion. No parameter manipulations or predictions are given.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)
    • Mentioned? No. As above, the paper does not discuss rewards.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
    • Mentioned? The paper does not discuss multiple rounds in the sense of strategic repeated play, so there is no mention of whether participants knew a round structure. No systematic manipulation or prediction is provided.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?
    • Mentioned? The paper states that each participant’s decision was private, and there was no knowledge of who offered how much. There is no discussion of systematically showing peer outcomes or varying the level of transparency.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Mentioned? The paper notes that the ultimatum game was anonymous: proposers and responders did not know each other’s identity. It does not discuss systematically changing whether punishment was anonymous or revealed, nor any predicted effect.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Mentioned? No. There is no formal “reward” in these experiments, so the paper does not address this.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • No, it does not. The main dependent variables are:  
     – The fraction of the stake offered by proposers in the dictator and ultimatum games.  
     – The frequency of rejections in the ultimatum game (to see whether people incur costs to punish).  
   • These differ from “efficiency” because they focus on proposers’ offers (split of the stake) and on whether responders reject offers, rather than on total payoffs relative to a maximum possible group payoff.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • At most, the paper implicitly references:  
     – (1) Number of players: two (proposer‐responder).  
     – (7) and (8) in the sense that ultimatum‐game punishment exists (responder rejection) and has a cost, but not as a systematically varied parameter.  
   • None of the parameters is explicitly discussed as a variable that is being manipulated or systematically varied, and no others are mentioned at all.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. The paper neither systematically varies any parameter nor makes numerical predictions about how varying them would affect punishment, contributions, or any notion of efficiency.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper provides no direct basis for predicting how varying these parameters would affect the punishment treatment effect on a group‐efficiency measure. It discusses only single‐shot dictator/ultimatum outcomes, plus anecdotal observations of punishment in everyday Ju/’hoan life. No direct information is given about changing game structure, monetary stakes, information, or reward “treatments.” Hence, there is little or no basis for making predictions solely from this paper’s content.
reference_APA: Wiessner, Polly (2009). Experimental Games and Games of Life among the Ju/'hoan Bushmen. CURRENT ANTHROPOLOGY.

Abstract: In a novel experimental design, we study public good games with dynamic interdependencies, where each agent's wealth at the end of period t serves as her endowment in t+1. Below each of the 15 parameters we state  
(i) whether the paper says anything about the parameter and, if so, the value(s) that were actually implemented, and  
(ii) whether the paper contains a prediction or an observed effect of systematically varying that parameter on the **punishment-treatment effect** (PUNISH minus NOPUNISH) for any dependent variable.  Whenever a numeric effect can be read directly from the paper we quote it and give the table or figure from which it can be taken.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
(i) Mentioned: all sessions use fixed groups of 4.  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction.

2. Number of rounds  
(i) Mentioned and systematically varied: sessions with 10 and with 15 rounds.  
(ii) Yes.  Wealth (their closest measure to efficiency) reacts differently to the availability of punishment depending on the horizon.  
   • 10-round games (Table 2, col. 1): PUNISH – NOPUNISH = +107 tokens (out of 3 075 maximum) – not significant.  
   • 15-round games (Table 2, col. 4): PUNISH – NOPUNISH = –790 tokens (p < 0.05).  
   Hence lengthening the horizon from 10 to 15 rounds turns the punishment effect on wealth from weakly positive/neutral to significantly negative (≈ –2.3 percentage-points of maximum possible group payoff).

3. Chat enabled  
(i) Explicitly ruled out; no chat.  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
(i) Participants choose any integer amount; not all-or-nothing.  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction.

5. Contribution default (withdrawal frame)  
(i) Not mentioned.  
(ii) No information.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
(i) Fixed at 1.5; with 4 players the one-shot MPCR = 1.5 / 4 = 0.375.  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction (authors only note that the possibility of exponential growth “has a similar effect to raising the MPCR”, but they never manipulate the MPCR).

7. Cost to impose one unit of punishment  
(i) Fixed: each token spent costs the punisher 1 and removes 3 from the target (so unit cost = 1/3 of the harm).  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction.

8. Punishment magnitude  
(i) Fixed: 3 tokens deducted per token spent.  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction.

9. Reward option enabled  
(i) Stated to be absent.  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction.

10. Cost of one unit of reward  
(i) Not applicable (no reward).  
(ii) —  

11. Magnitude of one unit of reward  
(i) Not applicable.  
(ii) —  

12. Is the horizon common knowledge?  
(i) Yes, subjects are told the exact length (10 or 15).  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
(i) Yes.  After each period subjects see every group member’s contribution, endowment and (in PUNISH) punishment decisions.  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
(i) Within a period, yes.  The screen shows who punished whom, but player labels are re-randomised from period to period.  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
(i) Not applicable.  
(ii) —  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary

A. Does the paper use “efficiency”?  
The authors’ main payoff-based dependent variable is called “wealth” (total tokens owned by the group at the start of the next period).  They occasionally compare this to the **maximum possible wealth** (fully cooperative path) but they never compute the ratio formally.  Other dependent variables are (i) individual or group contributions and (ii) inequality (Gini coefficient).  Efficiency in the strict sense ( realised pay-off ÷ maximum pay-off ) is therefore not directly reported, although wealth is monotonically related to it.

Abstract: Costly punishment of cheaters who contribute little or nothing to a cooperating group has been extensively studied, as an effective means to enforce cooperation. The prevailing view is that individuals use punishment to retaliate against transgressions of moral standards such as fairness or equity. However, there is much debate regarding the psychological underpinnings of costly punishment. Some authors suggest that costly punishment must be a product of humans' capacity for reasoning, self-control and long-term planning, whereas others argue that it is the result of an impulsive, present-oriented emotional drive. Here, we explore the inter-temporal preferences of punishers in a multilateral cooperation game and show that both interpretations might be right, as we can identify two different types of punishment: punishment of free-riders by cooperators, which is predicted by patience (future orientation); and free-riders' punishment of other free-riders, which is predicted by impatience (present orientation). Therefore, the picture is more complex as punishment by free-riders probably comes not from a reaction against a moral transgression, but instead from a competitive, spiteful drive. Thus, punishment grounded on morals may be related to lasting or delayed psychological incentives, whereas punishment triggered by competitive desires may be linked to short-run aspirations. These results indicate that the individual's time horizon is relevant for the type of social behaviour she opts for. Integrating such differences in inter-temporal preferences and the social behaviour of agents might help to achieve a better understanding of how human cooperation and punishment behaviour has evolved.

Authors: Chen, XJ; Perc, M
Author Full Names: Chen, Xiaojie; Perc, Matjaz
Article Title: Optimal distribution of incentives for public cooperation in heterogeneous interaction environments
Author Keywords: public cooperation; institutional reciprocity; scale-free network; punishment; reward
Keywords Plus: PRISONERS-DILEMMA GAME; SCALE-FREE NETWORKS; SOCIAL DILEMMAS; GOODS GAMES; ANTISOCIAL PUNISHMENT; EVOLUTIONARY DYNAMICS; PROMOTE COOPERATION; COMPLEX NETWORKS; REWARD; INSTITUTIONS
Abstract: In the framework of evolutionary games with institutional reciprocity, limited incentives are at disposal for rewarding cooperators and punishing defectors. In the simplest case, it can be assumed that, depending on their strategies, all players receive equal incentives from the common pool. The question arises, however, what is the optimal distribution of institutional incentives? How should we best reward and punish individuals for cooperation to thrive? We study this problem for the public goods game on a scale-free network. We show that if the synergetic effects of group interactions are weak, the level of cooperation in the population can be maximized simply by adopting the simplest equal distribution scheme. If synergetic effects are strong, however, it is best to reward high-degree nodes more than low-degree nodes. These distribution schemes for institutional rewards are independent of payoff normalization. For institutional punishment, however, the same optimization problem is more complex, and its solution depends on whether absolute or degree-normalized payoffs are used. We find that degree-normalized payoffs require high-degree nodes be punished more lenient than low-degree nodes. Conversely, if absolute payoffs count, then high-degree nodes should be punished stronger than low-degree nodes.

1) NUMBER OF PLAYERS
   • Mentioned?

   • Mentioned?  
     – Not in the sense of a repeated finite or known‐length experimental game. The paper models an evolutionary process on a network, rather than a repeated public goods game with a set number of rounds.

   • Mentioned?

   • Mentioned?

     – No.  

5) IS THE CONTRIBUTION DEFAULT?

   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes, referred to as “the enhancement factor r.”  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?

   • Numerical effect sizes?

12) IS THE NUMBER OF ROUNDS KNOWN TO PLAYERS?
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper runs an evolutionary game on a network, does not address whether participants know how many iterations/rounds there are.  

13) ARE PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN?
   • Mentioned?  
     – The paper does not describe any explicit disclosure of round‐by‐round outcomes. It simply uses an evolutionary update rule whereby players compare payoffs with neighbors. There is no mention of any “information treatments.”  

14) WHEN A PLAYER IS PUNISHED, DO THEY KNOW WHO PUNISHED THEM?
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. Punishment is institutional (centralized), so there is no mention of any punisher identity being revealed.  

15) WHEN A PLAYER IS REWARDED, DO THEY KNOW WHO REWARDED THEM?
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. Again, the reward is institutional, with no mention of a specific rewarding agent’s identity.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total / average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   – The paper does not measure group efficiency or total payoff in the sense of “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff.” Instead, it focuses on (i) the fraction of cooperators in the population (the primary outcome) and (ii) payoff differences between cooperators and defectors. These are not measures of collective efficiency.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – The paper explicitly or implicitly mentions:  
     1) Number of players (as the network size, N = 1,000 to 10,000).  
     4) That contribution is effectively “all or nothing” (cooperation = pay cost 1, defection = pay 0), though not labeled as such.  
     6) MPCR / multiplication factor (called “enhancement factor,” r).  
     8) Punishment magnitude is not labeled as such, but the paper does vary the incentive pool δ used to punish.  
     9) The presence of institutional reward (discussed as a separate treatment from punishment).  
   – None of the other parameters are concretely mentioned or varied in the sense of the paper’s model design.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss any effect on the punishment treatment (for any dependent variable) when the parameter is systematically varied?  
   – Two parameters receive explicit systematic variation in the punishment regime:  
     1) The enhancement factor r (parameter #6).  
     2) The total negative incentive pool δ (broadly related to “punishment magnitude,” though not in a per‐unit sense) plus α (the “distribution strength”), which determines whether high‐degree or low‐degree nodes get punished more.  
   – The paper does not supply a numerical “effect size” on efficiency or total payoff, but it does give contour plots of how these parameters influence the fraction of cooperators.

D) If you were to make predictions about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper’s content, what would they be?  
   – Because the paper does not analyze efficiency—and does not address most of the 15 parameters—one can say very little with confidence. The only robust statement derivable from their results is that, in harsher dilemmas (small r) or with insufficient punishment‐pool resources δ, punishment often fails to increase cooperation and thus would presumably fail to improve overall efficiency. In friendlier dilemmas (larger r) or with ample punishment resources δ, punishment can raise the fraction of cooperators and presumably would increase overall payoffs. However, since the paper never models or reports group efficiency, there is no direct quantitative relationship to draw between these parameters and “actual total payoff relative to the maximum possible payoff.”

────────────
Hence, based strictly on this paper, there is limited to no direct information on how systematically varying most of your 15 parameters would affect the punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency. The authors analyze cooperation rates, not efficiency, and primarily vary only r (enhancement factor) and δ, α (punishment/reward distribution parameters).

Abstract: It has been argued that punishment promotes the evolution of cooperation when mutation rates are high (i.e. when agents engage in 'exploration dynamics'). Mutations maintain a steady supply of agents that punish free-riders, and thus free-riders are at a disadvantage. Recent experiments, however, have demonstrated that free-riders sometimes also pay to punish cooperators. Inspired by these empirical results, theoretical work has explored evolutionary dynamics where mutants are rare, and found that punishment does not promote the evolution of cooperation when this 'anti-social punishment' is allowed. We find that for intermediate and high mutation rates, adding punishment does not promote cooperation in either compulsory or voluntary public goods games if anti-social punishment is possible. This is because mutations generate agents that punish cooperators just as frequently as agents that punish defectors, and these two effects cancel each other out. These results raise questions about the effectiveness of punishment for promoting cooperation when mutations are common, and highlight how decisions about which strategies to include in the strategy set can have profound effects on the resulting dynamics. Abstract: Public goods game has been widely studied on the formation mechanism of cooperation in social dilemmas. Extensive experimental and theoretical researches have shown that punishment can significantly facilitate cooperation. In nature and society, the individual continuously adjusts the degree of cooperation and severity of punishment. In this paper, the particle swarm optimization (PSO) is used for describing the learning rule of updating the input of cooperation and punishment cost.       1. Number of players (fixed at 10 000)  
      6. MPCR / enhancement factor r (varied)  
      7. Punishment cost per unit (implicitly fixed)

1. Number of players
   • Discussed? No. The paper never specifies how many players or agents are in a public goods game.    • Discussed? Only in a very general sense: “punishment is costly,” and the paper describes how punishment entails personal costs and can provoke retaliation. However, it never quantifies or systematically studies a specific per‐unit cost.

   • Discussed? No. The paper addresses negative sanctions (punishment, ostracism) and “gossip” as a mechanism to reduce cheating but does not examine a reward mechanism.

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?

Abstract: When choosing social partners, people prefer good cooperators (all else being equal). Given this preference, people wishing to be chosen can either increase their own cooperation to become more desirable or suppress others' cooperation to make them less desirable. Previous research shows that very cooperative people sometimes get punished (antisocial punishment) or criticized (do-gooder derogation) in many cultures. Here, we used a public-goods game with punishment to test whether antisocial punishment is used as a means of competing to be chosen by suppressing others' cooperation. As predicted, there was more antisocial punishment when participants were competing to be chosen for a subsequent cooperative task (a trust game) than without a subsequent task. This difference in antisocial punishment cannot be explained by differences in contributions, moralistic punishment, or confusion. This suggests that antisocial punishment is a social strategy that low cooperators use to avoid looking bad when high cooperators escalate cooperation.

    • Mentioned: YES – identities were hidden (“Participants were not told who punished them”).  
    • Systematically varied: NO, but the Discussion speculates that revealing identities might have reduced antisocial punishment. This is a conjecture, not an empirical manipulation; no effect size is provided.

    • Mentioned: NO – there was no reward stage.  
    • Systematically varied / predictions: NO.

SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables in the paper  
   • Group efficiency (total or average payoff) is NOT used.  
   • Reported DVs are:  
     – Antisocial punishment (L$ spent punishing higher or equal contributors)  
     – Moralistic punishment (L$ spent punishing lower contributors)  
     – Average contribution to the public good  
     – Trust-game choices and returns (markets condition only)  
   These differ from efficiency because they examine money spent or contributed, not the ratio of actual to potential group payoffs.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   • 9 of 15: #1, #2, #4, #6, #7, #8, #12, #13, #14.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss effects of *systematically varying* that parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
   • 0 of 15. None of the parameters are experimentally varied; therefore no numeric effect sizes for such variations exist in the paper.

D. Predictions one could make—based solely on this paper—about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency  
   • The paper provides almost no direct basis for prediction because it never measures efficiency and never varies the parameters.  
   • The only hint is speculative: revealing punisher identity (parameter 14) might weaken antisocial punishment, which in turn could raise efficiency, but this is conjecture only.  
   • For all other parameters the paper gives no empirical or theoretical statements about how changing them would alter the efficiency impact of adding punishment. Consequently, little to no prediction can be offered on the basis of this article alone.

Keywords Plus: STRONG RECIPROCITY; COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; PUNISHMENT; BEHAVIOR; ENFORCEMENT; PROVISION; QUEEN; LIONS
Abstract: Selfishness is seldom considered a group-beneficial strategy. In the typical evolutionary formulation, altruism benefits the group, selfishness undermines altruism, and the purpose of the model is to identify mechanisms, such as kinship or reciprocity, that enable altruism to evolve. Recent models have explored punishment as an important mechanism favoring the evolution of altruism, but punishment can be costly to the punisher, making it a form of second-order altruism. This model identifies a strategy called selfish punisher that involves behaving selfishly in first-order interactions and altruistically in second-order interactions by punishing other selfish individuals. Selfish punishers cause selfishness to be a self-limiting strategy, enabling altruists to coexist in a stable equilibrium. This polymorphism can be regarded as a division of labor, or mutualism, in which the benefits obtained by first-order selfishness help to pay for second-order altruism.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter review of what (if anything) this paper says about each of the 15 parameters and whether the paper makes predictions about how systematically varying them would affect the “punishment treatment effect.” Throughout, please note that the paper does not explicitly discuss “efficiency” in the sense of “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff.” Rather, it focuses on within-group (and sometimes between-group) fitness consequences of different punishment and cooperation strategies, along with conditions for different strategies to invade or remain stable.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
• Mentioned?: Yes. The paper refers to the group size as N.  
• Value(s) or how it appears: N > 1 (groups comprise multiple players).  
• Systematically varied?: Yes, in a qualitative sense:  
  – The paper states that decreasing group size N increases the discrepancy between the chances of being punished (or “expelled”) for selfish individuals and thereby favors “selfish punishers” over “selfish nonpunishers.”  
  – They provide an inequality showing how group size N can make certain equilibria more stable (see pp. 3–4 in the text, discussing “the equilibrium range is expanded with … decreasing group size N”).  
• Numerical effect size?: No single numeric effect size is provided. The effect is discussed qualitatively (smaller N helps maintain a stable “selfish punisher–altruistic nonpunisher” equilibrium).  
• Effect on punishment treatment?: They do not phrase it as “punishment treatment effect,” but they do predict that smaller groups make punishment strategies more viable, lowering free-riding within the group.

2) Number of rounds  
• Mentioned?: Yes, briefly. The main analytical model uses a single round. They do refer to a “multiround” simulation model in a prior reference (26), but that is not analyzed in detail here.  
• Value(s) or how it appears: One round in the formal model.  
• Systematically varied?: No. The paper fixes the model at one round and does not explore multiple-round variants within this article.  
• Numerical effect size?: None.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
• Mentioned?: No.  
• Systematically varied?: No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment?: Not discussed.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Mentioned?: Yes. On p. 2 (under “The Model”), the paper specifies that individuals either invest all of their endowment (altruist) or none (selfish).  
• Systematically varied?: No. That is simply the model assumption. The authors do not explore partial contributions in this article (though they cite a separate reference (26) that allows a continuum of endowment strategies).  
• Numerical effect size?: Not applicable.  
• Effect on punishment treatment?: No explicit discussion of how changing this assumption would alter punishment outcomes.

5) Is the contribution default (if true, do players decide how much of their endowment to move back)?  
• Mentioned?: No.  
• Systematically varied?: No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment?: Not discussed.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
• Mentioned?: Yes: the paper uses m as the “factor by which the combined investment in the public good is multiplied.”  
• Systematically varied?: Somewhat, in qualitative terms:  
  – The authors note that increasing the multiplication factor m can expand the equilibrium range that supports stable punishment.  
  – No precise numeric effect size is given, but the direction is: higher m makes cooperation more beneficial and helps sustain punishment strategies under some conditions.  
• Numerical effect size?: No single numeric value or effect size is given beyond qualitative statements.  
• Effect on punishment treatment?: A higher multiplier (m) generally makes cooperators more valuable to the group, which can in turn support scenarios in which punishment remains stable.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Mentioned?: Yes. The paper labels this cost c.  
• Systematically varied?: Yes, but only in qualitative or formula-based discussion:  
  – Altruistic punishers pay c for each selfish individual punished; selfish punishers pay c as well, but only when punishing others (and not themselves).  
  – If c is too large, punishment becomes harder to maintain.  
  – The paper gives inequalities indicating that punishment can stabilize under certain ranges of c relative to b, m, N, and the frequency of altruists.  
• Numerical effect size?: No. The paper provides inequalities rather than specific numeric outcomes.  
• Effect on punishment treatment?: Increasing c makes punishment harder to sustain; decreasing c helps maintain punishment strategies.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
• Mentioned?: Partially. In this model, if a selfish individual is punished, the “punishment” removes that individual’s entire payoff from that round. Effectively, punishment zeroes out the selfish individual’s gains.  
• Systematically varied?: No. The authors assume that the entire payoff is lost by a punished individual.  
• Numerical effect size?: None—there is no exploration of partial vs. total payoff removal.  
• Effect on punishment treatment?: They do not discuss how changing the fraction (rather than the entire payoff) might alter outcomes.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
• Mentioned?: No.  
• Systematically varied?: No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment?: Not discussed.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Mentioned?: No.  
• Systematically varied?: No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment?: Not discussed.

11) Reward magnitude  
• Mentioned?: No.  
• Systematically varied?: No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment?: Not discussed.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
• Mentioned?: No.  
• Systematically varied?: No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment?: Not discussed.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know others’ payoffs)?  
• Mentioned?: No.  
• Systematically varied?: No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment?: Not discussed.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• Mentioned?: No.  
• Systematically varied?: No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment?: Not discussed.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
• Mentioned?: No (and no reward is studied in the model).  
• Systematically varied?: No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment?: Not discussed.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
• The paper does not explicitly use “efficiency” = (actual total payoff) / (maximum possible total payoff). Instead, it tracks:  
  – Within-group fitness of each strategy (altruistic punisher, selfish punisher, altruistic nonpunisher, selfish nonpunisher).  
  – Conditions for stability or invasion of each strategy.  
• They also refer to group-level payoffs in a qualitative sense (not as a formal dependent variable distinct from individual fitness). Hence, “efficiency” in the strict sense is not specifically measured.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Mentioned in some form:  
  1) Number of players (N)  
  2) Number of rounds (not varied, but stated to be one)  
  4) Is contribution “all or nothing”? (yes, that is the model assumption)  
  6) Multiplication factor (m)  
  7) Punishment cost (c)  
  8) Punishment magnitude (effectively the entire payoff is lost)  
• Not mentioned at all:  
  3), 5), 9), 10), 11), 12), 13), 14), 15

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• The paper qualitatively (or via inequalities) varies:  
  – (1) Number of players N (discusses how smaller N favors punishment)  
  – (6) The multiplication factor m (higher m can stabilize punishment)  
  – (7) The punishment cost c (lower c can stabilize punishment)  
• For the other parameters it mentions, there is either no systematic variation (only a fixed assumption) or no mention of how they affect punishment stability or payoff outcomes.  
• Thus, the paper systematically discusses 3 of the parameters (1, 6, and 7) in terms of how changes in those parameters alter the viability or prevalence of punishment.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
• The authors never phrase their results in terms of “efficiency” or the ratio of actual vs. maximum payoff, so precise predictions about efficiency are limited. Still, from the discussion it is reasonable to infer:  
  – Smaller group sizes (Parameter 1) should enhance punishment’s effectiveness (and thus presumably enhance overall group success compared with no punishment) because selfish punisher strategies are more stable in smaller groups.  
  – Higher multiplication factors (Parameter 6) can make cooperation more profitable, which likely stabilizes punishment and thus (by preventing widespread free-riding) could lead to higher overall payoffs.  
  – Lower punishment cost (Parameter 7) makes punishers more viable, which in turn can preserve cooperation levels and could raise group outcomes.  
• For all other parameters, the paper does not provide enough information to predict any effect on efficiency (as strictly defined). Indeed, many of the parameters (chat, reward, knowledge of rounds, etc.) are simply not part of this model as presented. Consequently, little to no predictions can be made about them solely from this paper’s content.
reference_APA: Eldakar, Omar Tonsi & Wilson, David Sloan (2008). Selfishness as second-order altruism. PROCEEDINGS OF THE NATIONAL ACADEMY OF SCIENCES OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA.

Authors: Scheele, D; Mihov, Y; Schwederski, O; Maier, W; Hurlemann, R
Author Full Names: Scheele, Dirk; Mihov, Yoan; Schwederski, Olga; Maier, Wolfgang; Hurlemann, Ren
Article Title: A negative emotional and economic judgment bias in major depression
Source Title: EUROPEAN ARCHIVES OF PSYCHIATRY AND CLINICAL NEUROSCIENCE
Author Keywords: Altruistic punishment; Decision making; Emotion; Neuroeconomics; Major depression; Ultimatum game
Keywords Plus: DECISION-MAKING; UNFAIR OFFERS; NEURAL BASIS; ULTIMATUM; NEUROECONOMICS; METAANALYSIS; PUNISHMENT; RESPONSES; COGNITION; FAIRNESS
Abstract: Although major depression is projected to be among the top three causes of disability-adjusted life years lost in 2030, relatively little is known concerning the extent to which depressed mood states can bias social-economic decision making away from optimal outcomes. One experimental framework to study the interaction between negative emotion and social-economic decisions is the ultimatum game (UG), where the fair, cooperative player altruistically punishes the unfair, non-cooperative player. To assess a potential susceptibility of altruistic punishment to depressed mood, we repeatedly administered the UG task to a cohort of 20 currently depressed patients with a diagnosis of recurrent major depressive disorder and 20 healthy controls. Furthermore, valence and arousal ratings of emotionally laden pictures were obtained from all participants in order to assess a depressed mood-related distortion of emotion judgments. Compared to healthy controls, depressed patients over-sanctioned unfair proposals in the UG and judged emotional stimuli too negatively. Thus, major depression is associated with a negative emotional bias that hampers social-economic decision making and produces large personal costs.

Below is a point‐by‐point analysis of whether (and how) each of the 15 listed parameters appears in the paper, followed by the requested four‐part summary.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – The paper uses the Ultimatum Game (UG), which is explicitly a two‐person (proposer and responder) bargaining task. So it effectively has “2 players” in each exchange.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about the effect of systematically varying this parameter on punishment outcomes for any dependent variable?  
     – No, there is no systematic variation in the number of players, nor any discussion of how changing the number of players would affect measures of punishment.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – The paper notes that participants played 54 one‐shot UG trials (each trial had a new “proposer”), but it does not treat “number of rounds” as a systematically varied design feature.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about varying the number of rounds on the punishment outcome?  
     – No. It does not discuss or manipulate the number of rounds to explore its effect on punishment.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – No. There is no mention of real‐time interaction or chat among players.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about it?  
     – No.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – No. The paper studies an Ultimatum Game with various partial offers (0 € to 5.5 € out of 10 €), not an all‐or‐nothing contribution scheme.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about this?  
     – No.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much of their endowment to move back into their hand)?  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – No. Again, the paper deals with an Ultimatum Game setting where the proposer divides a pie and the responder accepts or rejects. There is no discussion of a “default contribution.”  
   • Does the paper make predictions about it?  
     – No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – No. The study deals only with a standard UG for 10 €, not with any public‐good “multiplication factor.”  
   • Does the paper make predictions about it?  
     – No.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – In the Ultimatum Game as implemented, if the responder rejects, everyone (both proposer and responder) receives 0, which could be viewed as a cost. However, the paper does not label or manipulate it as a “cost to impose punishment.” It is simply the standard UG payoff structure.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying that cost?  
     – No. There is no systematic variation or discussion of changing that cost.

8. Punishment magnitude (the amount deducted for each unit of punishment)  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – In a standard UG, “punishment” happens if the responder rejects the offer, which sets payoffs to zero. Yet the paper does not present or analyze different punishment magnitudes, nor does it systematically vary that magnitude.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about varying punishment magnitude?  
     – No.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – No. The experiment studies only “punishment” via rejections in the Ultimatum Game and does not consider any reward mechanism.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about it?  
     – No.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
      – No, it is not relevant to the Ultimatum Game set‐up they used.  
    • Does the paper make predictions?  
      – No.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
      – No. Again, no formal reward was part of their design.  
    • Does the paper make predictions about varying it?  
      – No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
      – The paper states that participants were instructed there would be “no repeated interactions” with the same partner: effectively a one‐shot UG repeated 54 times with different proposers. It does not systematically vary or analyze the topic of “known vs. unknown” number of rounds.  
    • Does the paper make predictions?  
      – No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost each round)?  
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
      – No. The paper indicates the responder sees an offer from each proposer but does not mention systematically displaying other outcome information or peer payoffs.  
    • Does the paper make predictions about varying that information?  
      – No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the punisher is?  
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
      – As a two‐player UG, the proposer would realize the responder rejected and thus “who punished them,” but the paper does not treat it as a systematically varied factor.  
    • Does the paper make predictions about varying anonymity of punishment?  
      – No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is?  
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
      – No. Rewards are not part of the study.  
    • Does the paper make predictions about it?  
      – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper does not use group efficiency or total/average payoff as a dependent variable. Instead, it measures:  
     – Rejection rate of UG offers (how often or under which conditions responders turn down a proposer’s offer),  
     – Fairness ratings (how fair participants judged each offer),  
     – Emotional ratings (valence and arousal judgments of emotional stimuli),  
     – Various clinical/depression severity measures.  
   • These differ from “group efficiency” because the paper focuses on individual rejection behavior and emotional biases, rather than overall group payoffs or the ratio of actual payoff to maximum possible payoff.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • At a literal level, only Parameter #1 (number of players = 2) and Parameter #2 (number of rounds = 54 one‐shot trials) receive mention, though simply as part of describing the Ultimatum Game design. Any resemblance to Parameter #7 or #8 is not presented as a “parameter” under systematic study; the paper does not explicitly treat them as adjustable factors. All other parameters (3–6, 9–15) either do not appear or are not discussed at all.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. The authors do not systematically vary any of those parameters, nor do they analyze how changes in them would affect “punishment treatment” or any other measure.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper provides no direct discussion of group efficiency or of systematically manipulating the parameters in question. Its focus is on how major depression shifts rejection rates and emotional judgments within a standard two‐person Ultimatum Game.  
   • Accordingly, there is little basis in the paper for predicting how varying those 15 parameters (e.g., changing the group size, enabling chat, altering punishment costs, etc.) would affect efficiency measures in a public goods framework. One can only note the authors’ finding that depressed patients show higher rejection rates for moderately unfair offers, which they interpret as “over‐punishment,” but the paper does not connect that to group or collective efficiency under varying design parameters.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
reference_APA: Scheele, Dirk, Mihov, Yoan, Schwederski, Olga, Maier, Wolfgang & Hurlemann, Ren (2013). A negative emotional and economic judgment bias in major depression. EUROPEAN ARCHIVES OF PSYCHIATRY AND CLINICAL NEUROSCIENCE.

Authors: Martinez-Vaquero, LA; Han, TA; Pereira, LM; Lenaerts, T
Author Full Names: Martinez-Vaquero, Luis A.; The Anh Han; Pereira, Lu-S Moniz; Lenaerts, Tom
Article Title: Apology and forgiveness evolve to resolve failures in cooperative agreements
Keywords Plus: TIT-FOR-TAT; WIN-STAY; EVOLUTION; PUNISHMENT; COMMITMENT; SYSTEM; ANGER
Abstract: Making agreements on how to behave has been shown to be an evolutionarily viable strategy in one-shot social dilemmas. However, in many situations agreements aim to establish long-term mutually beneficial interactions. Our analytical and numerical results reveal for the first time under which conditions revenge, apology and forgiveness can evolve and deal with mistakes within ongoing agreements in the context of the Iterated Prisoners Dilemma. We show that, when the agreement fails, participants prefer to take revenge by defecting in the subsisting encounters. Incorporating costly apology and forgiveness reveals that, even when mistakes are frequent, there exists a sincerity threshold for which mistakes will not lead to the destruction of the agreement, inducing even higher levels of cooperation. In short, even when to err is human, revenge, apology and forgiveness are evolutionarily viable strategies which play an important role in inducing cooperation in repeated dilemmas.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter check of what the paper actually says (if anything) about each of the 15 parameters and whether the paper makes any predictions about systematically varying them with respect to a “punishment treatment effect”—in particular, about how introducing punishment would change group efficiency. As requested, this analysis is restricted entirely to what is stated in the paper “Apology and forgiveness evolve to resolve failures in cooperative agreements,” without invoking prior literature or outside assumptions. Throughout, note that the paper analyzes an Iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma with commitments, apology, and forgiveness; it does not study a Public Goods Game with peer punishment/reward as framed by the 15 parameters.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – The paper sets a finite population of N = 100 individuals engaged in pairwise (two-player) repeated interactions. It does not study or vary the number of players in a group or discuss how it would affect anything called a “punishment treatment effect.”  
   • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – None. The paper does not systematically vary the number of players; no mention of efficiency impacts.

2. Number of rounds
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – The paper uses a repeated game with a continuation probability ω (so the expected number of rounds is 1/(1–ω)), but it does not frame this as a known fixed number of rounds from the players’ perspective.  
   • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – The authors do examine different values of ω (i.e., how likely the game is to continue), showing that higher ω makes commitments more beneficial. However, the paper does not describe these findings as a “punishment treatment effect,” nor does it discuss efficiency defined as (actual payoff)/(maximum payoff). Instead, it discusses how varying ω affects the dominance of strategies, the level of cooperation, and the presence of apology/forgiveness. No numerical effect size is given for an “efficiency” measure, only for strategy frequencies and cooperation rates.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – None. The paper never mentions any form of communication/chat among players.  
   • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – None.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – The paper analyzes a standard Iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma in which a player’s action each round is simply Cooperate or Defect (binary choice). It does not label this as “all-or-nothing contributions,” nor does it vary this feature.  
   • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – None.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – Not addressed. The paper does not discuss default contribution settings or any mechanism for automatically shifting funds between private and public accounts.  
   • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – None.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related factor
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – The paper analyzes a Donation game payoff matrix with parameters b (benefit) and c (cost), sometimes described as a “benefit-to-cost ratio b/c.” They do vary b/c (e.g., figures often use b/c = 2) in supplementary analyses.  
   • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – They show that higher b/c fosters more cooperation and makes commitments more successful. However, they do not describe these results in terms of a “punishment treatment effect” or “efficiency.” They report how different b/c values change strategy dominance and cooperation levels, not group-efficiency outcomes.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – The paper does not study peer punishment as in many Public Goods experiments. It focuses on “revenge” by defecting after a commitment is broken, but that is not modeled as a cost paid to punish someone; rather, it is simply switching the action to Defect. There is no parameter directly called “punishment cost to impose one unit of punishment.”  
   • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – None.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – The paper uses a “compensation” δ that a defector must pay if they break a commitment, but it is not framed as peer-administered punishment. It is an automatic transfer specified by the commitment agreement.  
   • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – The paper does examine different values of δ (e.g., δ = 4 in many figures), but solely in the context of whether commitments are viable. It does not link this to a “punishment treatment effect” or to efficiency. No numerical effect on “group efficiency” from systematically varying δ is discussed.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – The paper explicitly states that commitments are used as “an alternative to different forms of punishment or reward,” but it does not implement or test a reward mechanism.  
   • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – None. Reward is not studied in the paper’s models.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Discussion in the paper?  
      – Not addressed.  
    • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
      – None.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)
    • Discussion in the paper?  
      – Not addressed.  
    • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
      – None.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Discussion in the paper?  
      – The paper models an indefinite repeated game with probability ω of continuation. There is no statement that players know the exact round structure.  
    • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
      – None regarding knowledge of game length.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?
    • Discussion in the paper?  
      – The paper never discusses whether players observe each other’s payoffs.  
    • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
      – None.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Discussion in the paper?  
      – There is no standard “punisher.” The paper discusses “revenge” as mutual defection, but not a separate entity of a punisher who pays costs to punish. Hence, no mention.  
    • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
      – None.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Discussion in the paper?  
      – No reward mechanism is studied, and the paper does not address whether any actor is identified as a “rewarder.”  
    • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
      – None.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper does not use “efficiency” (actual total payoff / max possible total payoff) as a reported metric. Instead, it reports how strategies fare in terms of (i) the fraction of time they dominate the population (stationary distribution), (ii) cooperation levels, (iii) defection levels, and (iv) payoffs of particular strategies. These outcomes differ from measuring total or average payoff explicitly as a fraction of a theoretical maximum.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • The only close analog is parameter #6 (the benefit-cost ratio b/c in a two-player Donation game). The paper also has parameters such as the apology cost γ, arrangement cost ε, compensation δ, and probability of continuation ω, but none of these align directly with the user’s 15 parameters about a “public goods punishment” framework. No other parameter from the list is directly mentioned as stated.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, none. The paper is not about a “punishment treatment” in the sense of peer-punishment within a public goods game; it studies commitments and apology-forgiveness in a repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma. There is no text linking the 15 parameters to changes in “punishment treatment effect.”  
   • As a side note, the paper does systematically vary some game parameters (b/c, ε, δ, γ, α, and ω) but always with respect to how they influence the emergence of commitment-based cooperation, apology, and forgiveness—not with respect to a punishment treatment effect or efficiency measure.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of this paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper provides no direct discussion of group efficiency in a public goods setting with punishment and reward, so it gives no basis for predicting how systematically varying those 15 parameters would affect a “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency. Consequently, one cannot meaningfully infer predictions about those parameters or their interactions from this paper’s content.

Source Title: JOURNAL OF THE EUROPEAN ECONOMIC ASSOCIATION
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS; PUNISHMENT; COOPERATION; PROVISION
Abstract: The enforcement of social norms often requires that unaffected third parties sanction offenders. Given the renewed interest of economists in norms, the literature on third-party punishment is surprisingly thin. In this paper, we report the results of an experiment designed to replicate the anger-based punishment of directly affected second parties and evaluate two distinct explanations for third-party punishment: indignation and group reciprocity. We find evidence in favor of both, with the caveat that the incidence of indignation-driven sanctions is perhaps smaller than earlier studies have hinted. Furthermore, our results suggest that second parties use sanctions to promote conformism while third parties intervene primarily to promote efficiency.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account based strictly on what appears in the Carpenter & Matthews paper provided (“Norm Enforcement: Anger, Indignation, or Reciprocity?”). Afterward, you will find the required four‐part summary.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER‐BY‐PARAMETER DISCUSSION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

GAME STRUCTURE

1) Number of players  
   • Mention in paper? Yes. Each session has two groups of four participants (eight total).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper always uses groups of four and does not examine how changing this number might affect punishment or efficiency.

2) Number of rounds  
   • Mention in paper? Yes. The design is explicitly one‐shot (i.e., a single round).  
   • Systematically varied? No. They do not vary the number of rounds; there is only one round in every treatment.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mention in paper? No. The paper does not discuss any form of chat or communication between participants (beyond seeing others’ contributions/payoffs).  
   • Systematically varied? No mention, so no.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mention in paper? The design uses a 25‐token endowment from which participants can contribute any integer amount (0 up to 25). This is not an “all or nothing” format.  
   • Systematically varied? No. They do not compare an “all‐or‐nothing” treatment versus a free‐choice treatment.

5) Is the contribution default (i.e., are participants deciding how much to move back from the public fund)?  
   • Mention in paper? No. Contributions are described in the standard way (participants allocate some or all of their 25 tokens). There is no mention of having a “default” in the sense of forced transfer from the public pool.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

MONETARY STAKES

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related factor  
   • Mention in paper? Yes. They fix the MPCR at 0.5.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper uses 0.5 throughout, with no other MPCR values.

PEER INCENTIVES

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mention in paper? Yes. It costs 1 token (from the punisher’s payoff) to reduce the target’s payoff by 2 tokens.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The experiment does not vary that cost across conditions.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Mention in paper? Yes. Each token spent on punishing reduces the target’s payoff by 2 tokens.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The design keeps that ratio fixed at 1:2.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mention in paper? No. The experiment focuses exclusively on punishment; no reward mechanism is described.  
   • Systematically varied? No, because rewards are not part of the design.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Mention in paper? No. Same reason as above—no reward mechanism.  
    • Systematically varied? No.

11) Reward magnitude (coins awarded for each unit of reward)  
    • Mention in paper? No. Again, rewards do not appear in the design.  
    • Systematically varied? No.

INFORMATION DISPLAY

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?  
    • Mention in paper? Yes. Participants know it is a one‐shot game.  
    • Systematically varied? No. They do not compare “known” vs. “unknown” horizon.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (e.g., do players see others’ payoffs/gains/losses)?  
    • Mention in paper? Yes. After contributing, participants see others’ contributions (and in some treatments, how much was spent on punishment).  
    • Systematically varied? No. The same procedure is used in each treatment with the relevant punishment feedback.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Mention in paper? Yes, but only implicitly to say they do NOT reveal the punisher’s identity. Punishment is anonymous (e.g., in the sequential condition, the second group sees how much was spent in total but not who punished whom).  
    • Systematically varied? No. They do not compare “anonymous” vs. “identifiable” punishers.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Mention in paper? No, because there is no reward mechanism at all.  
    • Systematically varied? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
REQUIRED FOUR-PART SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper does not explicitly use “group efficiency” (actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff) as its measured dependent variable. Instead, its main dependent variables are:  
     – The amount each participant contributes (a continuous measure out of 25 tokens).  
     – Punishment decisions (SPP or TPP), measured by how many tokens participants spend to punish others.  
   • The authors do invoke the word “efficiency” in their discussion (they note that “third parties intervene primarily to promote efficiency”), but they do not formally measure or report “efficiency” as a separate ratio or statistic. So efficiency, in the sense of total payoff relative to the maximum, is not directly quantified.

B) Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
     1) Number of players (fixed at 4 per group, 8 total)  
     2) Number of rounds (1‐shot)  
     6) MPCR (0.5, fixed)  
     7) Punishment cost (1 token spent = 2 tokens deducted from target, but cost is 1)  
     8) Punishment magnitude (2 tokens deducted)  
     12) Knowledge of number of rounds (participants know it is one‐shot)  
     13) Peer outcomes shown (yes, after contributions, participants see others’ contributions, etc.)  
     14) Whether the punished know who the punisher is (the paper states punisher identity is not revealed)  
   • Not mentioned: parameters 3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 15 (these either do not arise at all in the experiment or are not relevant to its design).  
   • Total mentioned: 8 out of 15.

C) For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The experiment systematically varies the presence of second‐party vs. third‐party punishment (one‐way vs. two‐way, simultaneous vs. sequential). However, none of the listed 15 parameters (e.g., number of rounds, cost of punishment, MPCR, etc.) is explicitly varied over multiple values. Instead, the authors keep items like group size (4), cost of punishment (1 token), MPCR (0.5), etc., constant throughout.  
   • Thus, strictly speaking, the paper does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters listed. Consequently, it makes no numerical predictions about how varying them would change “the punishment treatment effect” on efficiency or other outcomes.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • Because the paper does not discuss varying these parameters (nor does it measure efficiency as a ratio), there is little direct basis for predicting how changing them would influence the effect of introducing punishment on group efficiency.  
   • The only clear takeaways are that the presence of third‐party punishment (vs. none or second‐party alone) tends to increase contributions and may thereby raise overall payoffs. But this is shown only under the specific, fixed parameter values: 4‐person groups, cost‐to‐magnitude ratio of 1:2, MPCR of 0.5, one‐shot game, and anonymous punishment. The authors do not speculate on how changes in, for example, the cost‐to‐magnitude ratio, the group size, or the number of rounds might systematically affect overall efficiency.  
   • Hence, the safest conclusion is that the paper itself provides little or no direct prediction about how systematically varying the 15 parameters would affect efficiency.

Authors: Sasaki, T; Uchida, S; Chen, XJ
Author Full Names: Sasaki, Tatsuya; Uchida, Satoshi; Chen, Xiaojie
Article Title: Voluntary rewards mediate the evolution of pool punishment for maintaining public goods in large populations
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; REPLICATOR DYNAMICS; SIMPSONS PARADOX; COOPERATION; CARROT; ENFORCEMENT; INCENTIVES; GAMES; INSTITUTIONS; GOVERNANCE
Abstract: Punishment is a popular tool when governing commons in situations where free riders would otherwise take over. It is well known that sanctioning systems, such as the police and courts, are costly and thus can suffer from those who free ride on other's efforts to maintain the sanctioning systems (second-order free riders). Previous game-theory studies showed that if populations are very large, pool punishment rarely emerges in public good games, even when participation is optional, because of second-order free riders. Here we show that a matching fund for rewarding cooperation leads to the emergence of pool punishment, despite the presence of second-order free riders. We demonstrate that reward funds can pave the way for a transition from a population of free riders to a population of pool punishers. A key factor in promoting the transition is also to reward those who contribute to pool punishment, yet not abstaining from participation. Reward funds eventually vanish in raising pool punishment, which is sustainable by punishing the second-order free riders. This suggests that considering the interdependence of reward and punishment may help to better understand the origins and transitions of social norms and institutions.

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper sets the public good interaction to occur in groups of size n ≥ 2 (e.g., n = 5 in Figures 1–4). Also, “very large populations” are considered in the replicator‐dynamics sense, but with subgroups of size n.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? No. The model is cast in infinite‐population replicator dynamics and does not specify a finite number of repeated rounds.  
   • Systematically varied? Not discussed.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned? No. There is no discussion of communication or chat.  
   • Systematically varied? Not discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned? The paper’s model effectively has a player either contribute (incurring a cost c1) or not. However, there is no separate treatment or label as “all or nothing,” nor any varying of that rule.  
   • Systematically varied? Not discussed.

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much to move back)?  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not address or manipulate any default option.  
   • Systematically varied? Not discussed.

   • Mentioned? Yes. Denoted r1 in the paper (also written as b1 = r1 c1). They use r1 > 1, and often 2 < r1 < n. They examine how it affects the stability of cooperation and punishment (e.g., Figures 1–4).

Still, they do not present results in terms of changes in “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Instead, they analyze the existence or stability of strategies. No numeric effect sizes for an “efficiency” outcome are given.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? Yes, denoted c3. The paper treats it as a cost a punisher must pay when contributing to the punishment fund.  
   • Systematically varied? Yes, c3 is studied, particularly in conjunction with r3, to see under which conditions punishers can invade. However, the paper does not quantify changes in “efficiency.” Instead, it examines whether punishment persists in equilibrium.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted per punishment)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Denoted b3 = r3 c3, with an additional weighting (kPC, kPR) for exactly how the punishment is assigned.  
   • Systematically varied? The paper examines how different values of r3 (and thus different punishment severity) affect which strategies dominate. They do not link it to a measured difference in group “efficiency”; rather, they focus on stability of punishment in the population.

9. Whether a reward is enabled

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Denoted c2, with b2 = r2 c2.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
   • Mentioned? No. The model is evolutionary and does not detail whether players know a final round.  
   • Systematically varied? Not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much others gained/lost)?  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not describe information feedback about others’ payoffs.  
   • Systematically varied? Not discussed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Mentioned? Not in the paper. The paper centers on “pool punishment,” which is implemented by a centralized fund, and does not mention revealing punisher identities.  
   • Systematically varied? Not discussed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Mentioned? Not in the paper. Reward is also modeled as a “pool” rather than personal reward.  
   • Systematically varied? Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The main dependent variables are the frequencies (or proportions) of strategies under replicator dynamics and the average payoff of each strategy or of the entire population. The paper does not explicitly define a ratio of actual total payoff to a maximum possible payoff (i.e., “group efficiency”). So “efficiency,” in the sense requested, is not directly measured.  
   • The paper’s dependent variables differ in that it often discusses whether full punishment or full defection becomes stable, or whether cycles occur. Payoffs are used as part of the replicator dynamics, but not as an explicit efficiency ratio.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form: (1) Number of players (n), (6) MPCR (r1), (7) Punishment cost (c3), (8) Punishment magnitude (r3 c3), (9) Whether reward is enabled, (10) Reward cost (c2), and (11) Reward magnitude (r2 c2).

   • In total, the paper explicitly discusses 7 of the 15 parameters.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?

Abstract: Although it is widely recognized that sanction increases cooperation in a public good game, comparatively little attention has been paid to a scenario in which agents have heterogeneous productivities (i.e. asymmetric impact on the group account).
