Below is a parameter-by-parameter analysis of what the paper by Tan (titled “Punishment in a Linear Public Good Game with Productivity Heterogeneity”) says about each of the 15 parameters. For each parameter, two questions are addressed:  
• Does the paper discuss the parameter (and, if so, does it specify a value)?  
• Does the paper say anything about how systematically varying that parameter affects the punishment treatment effect (i.e., how punishment changes outcomes such as efficiency or other variables)?  

Throughout, note that the paper’s central experimental manipulations compare a baseline public-goods setup with a homogeneous marginal per capita return (MPCR = 0.6) against a heterogeneous condition in which half of the group has MPCR = 0.9 and half has MPCR = 0.3 (still averaging to 0.6). The paper then layers punishment onto the heterogeneous condition. It does not systematically vary most of the other parameters.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
• Mentioned? Yes. The experiment uses four players per group throughout (“a four-person linear public good game”).  
• Systematically varied? No. The paper does not manipulate group size and does not predict how changing group size would alter punishment’s effect.

2. Number of rounds  
• Mentioned? Yes. Each session has 15 rounds.  
• Systematically varied? No. All sessions use the same number (15). The paper does not discuss varying the number of rounds or how that would affect punishment’s impact on efficiency.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
• Mentioned? Yes. The paper says that “communication was strictly forbidden,” so no chat is allowed.  
• Systematically varied? No. The paper does not discuss turning chat on or off nor the predicted effect of varying communication on punishment.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Mentioned? Indirectly. Subjects choose (from 0 to 10 tokens) how many tokens to contribute. It is not all-or-nothing.  
• Systematically varied? No. There is no mention of imposing an all-or-nothing rule or how that would change punishment’s effect.

5. Is the contribution default? (Do players decide how much of their endowment to move from the public fund back into their hand?)  
• Mentioned? No. The study follows a standard VCM structure; there is no default contribution, nor is that feature mentioned.  
• Systematically varied? No. The paper does not discuss this parameter at all.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
• Mentioned? Yes—this is the key parameter manipulated to create “productivity heterogeneity.” T1 has MPCR = 0.6 (for everyone), T2 has half at MPCR = 0.9 and half at MPCR = 0.3 (no punishment), and T3 repeats that heterogeneity but adds punishment.  
• Systematically varied? Partially. The study compares a homogeneous MPCR of 0.6 versus a combination of 0.9 and 0.3. It does not vary the MPCR in a wide range of values, but it does compare the homogeneous vs. heterogeneous case. Regarding punishment’s treatment effect, the heterogeneous group with punishment (T3) ends up with substantially higher contributions than the heterogeneous group without punishment (T2). However, efficiency (average payoff) does not uniformly increase in T3 because the costs of punishing offset the benefits. Numerical effect:  
  – T2 (heterogeneous, no punishment) has an average contribution of about 18.67% of subjects’ endowment.  
  – T3 (heterogeneous, with punishment) has an average contribution of about 49.33%.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Mentioned? Yes. Each “punishment point” sent costs the punisher 1 token.  
• Systematically varied? No. It is fixed at 1 token per point in T3. No predictions are made about how different punishment-cost levels would change the punishment treatment effect.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
• Mentioned? Yes. Each punishment point causes a 2-token deduction to the punishee.  
• Systematically varied? No. The magnitude is fixed at 2 tokens; no predictions are offered for other deductions.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
• Mentioned? Only insofar as the paper cites other studies that have used reward. The experiment itself does not enable rewards.  
• Systematically varied? No. No direct discussion of how introducing rewards (instead of or alongside punishment) might affect efficiency in this particular experiment.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Mentioned? No. Rewards are not implemented in the study, and the paper does not speculate on systematically varying the cost of rewards.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
• Mentioned? No. Again, rewards are not part of the design. The paper does not explore systematic variation.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
• Mentioned? Yes. The experiment clearly tells participants there are 15 rounds.  
• Systematically varied? No. The paper does not consider or discuss hidden vs. known endpoints.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?  
• Mentioned? Yes. At the end of each round, participants see everyone’s contributions and earnings and, in the punishment treatment, how many total punishment points they themselves received.  
• Systematically varied? No. There is no comparison with a hidden-information setting.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• Mentioned? Yes. The paper states that participants do not see who punished them. They only see the total points they received.  
• Systematically varied? No. The design never changes whether punishees see the identity of the punisher.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
• Mentioned? Only implicitly as part of references to other studies that have used rewards; in this experiment, there is no reward stage.  
• Systematically varied? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different from one another?  
• The paper measures contributions and also measures payoff (earnings). It does not explicitly define “efficiency” as “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff,” although it sometimes refers to “welfare” or “earnings” that could be seen as nearby concepts.  
• Dependent variables:  
  – Contribution level (fraction of tokens contributed)  
  – Earnings (average payoff per subject)  
• The paper notes that punishment led to higher contributions yet did not always improve average earnings, so the effect on “efficiency” can differ from the effect on “contribution.”

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Mentioned in some form: 1 (number of players), 2 (rounds), 3 (chat enabled?), 4 (not all-or-nothing), 5 (contribution style), 6 (MPCR), 7 (punishment cost), 8 (punishment magnitude), 9–11 (reward structure) only alluded to or stated as absent, 12 (rounds known), 13 (peer outcomes shown), 14 (punisher identity hidden), 15 (rewarder identity not applicable). Thus, nearly all are at least mentioned or implied, but many are mentioned only to say they are fixed or absent.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when systematically varied?  
• The only parameter remotely “systematically varied” is the structure of the MPCR across T1 and T2/T3 (Parameter #6). The paper thus discusses how having heterogeneous vs. homogeneous MPCR changes the impact of adding punishment on outcomes.  
• Cost or magnitude of punishment (#7 and #8) and so forth are not systematically varied; they are simply set to a particular value.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
• The paper only offers clear guidance on MPCR heterogeneity (#6). It shows that, for the specific cost and magnitude of punishment used, allowing punishment in a heterogeneous-MPCR environment raises contributions markedly but does not necessarily improve average payoffs over the entire session.  
• For most other parameters, the paper either fixes them (e.g., 4 players, 15 known rounds, cost of 1 per punishment point, etc.) or does not discuss them. Therefore, the paper provides little to no guidance on how systematically changing those other parameters or their interactions would affect punishment’s influence on efficiency.

Authors: Kamei, K; Putterman, L; Tyran, JR

Article Title: State or nature? Endogenous formal versus informal sanctions in the voluntary provision of public goods

Abstract: We investigate the endogenous formation of sanctioning institutions supposed to improve efficiency in the voluntary provision of public goods. Our paper parallels Markussen et al. (Rev Econ Stud 81:301-324, 2014) in that our experimental subjects vote over formal versus informal sanctions, but it goes beyond that paper by endogenizing the formal sanction scheme. We find that self-determined formal sanctions schemes are popular and efficient when they carry no up-front cost, but as in Markussen et al. informal sanctions are more popular and efficient than formal sanctions when adopting the latter entails such a cost. Practice improves the performance of sanction schemes: they become more targeted and deterrent with learning. Voters' characteristics, including their tendency to engage in perverse informal sanctioning, help to predict individual voting.

     14. Knowledge of the punisher’s identity (varied only in an additional “fuller info” treatment)  

   – Completely not mentioned or set to “not used”:  
     3 (Chat), 5 (Contribution default), 9–11 (Rewards), 15 (Reward identity).  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when systematically varied?  
   – The only parameter the authors explicitly and systematically vary that affects punishment’s impact on outcomes is #14 in their additional (“fuller information”) treatment. They compare standard anonymous punishment vs. identifying the punisher. The paper reports this does not diminish informal sanctions’ effectiveness.  
   – All other parameters appear in only one fixed form (e.g. 5 players, MPCR=0.4, punishment ratio=4, etc.) or are not present at all (no reward). The paper does not systematically vary them or provide effect sizes for them.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, solely based on this paper’s content, what would they be?  
   – The paper gives little direct basis for predicting how varying parameters 1–13 or 15 would shape punishment’s effect on efficiency, apart from these key points:  
     • Increasing or decreasing the fixed cost of a formal sanction system (which is tangentially related to #7–8 but not the same) strongly influences whether subjects adopt formal vs. informal punishment.  
     • Having more “information” about who punishes whom (#14) does not undermine effectiveness of informal sanctions in the paper’s design.  
     • Beyond that, the authors do not make or test systematic predictions for changes in group size, number of rounds, MPCR, or other dimensions. Hence, we have almost no quantitative effect sizes for changing those parameters.  

Overall, the study focuses on comparing “formal sanctions versus informal sanctions” under a fixed group size, fixed MPCR, and known horizon, sometimes with or without a fixed cost to operate formal sanctions. They do not systematically vary the 15 parameters (except partial variation of #14 in an extra treatment) in ways that would allow strong predictions about how each one might affect efficiency under punishment.

Authors: Muthukrishna, M; Francois, P; Pourahmadi, S; Henrich, J
Author Full Names: Muthukrishna, Michael; Francois, Patrick; Pourahmadi, Shayan; Henrich, Joseph
Article Title: Corrupting cooperation and how anti-corruption strategies may backfire
Keywords Plus: INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; PUNISHMENT; EVOLUTION; GAMES
Abstract: Understanding how humans sustain cooperation in large, anonymous societies remains a central question of both theoretical and practical importance. In the laboratory, experimental behavioural research using tools like public goods games suggests that cooperation can be sustained by institutional punishment-analogous to governments, police forces and other institutions that sanction free-riders on behalf of individuals in large societies(1-3). In the real world, however, corruption can undermine the effectiveness of these institutions(4-8). Levels of corruption correlate with institutional, economic and cultural factors, but the causal directions of these relationships are difficult to determine(5,6,8-10). Here, we experimentally model corruption by introducing the possibility of bribery. We investigate the effect of structural factors (a leader's punitive power and economic potential), anti-corruption strategies (transparency and leader investment in the public good) and cultural background. The results reveal that (1) corruption possibilities cause a large (25%) decrease in public good provisioning, (2) empowering leaders decreases cooperative contributions (in direct opposition to typical institutional punishment results), (3) growing up in a more corrupt society predicts more acceptance of bribes and (4) anti-corruption strategies are effective under some conditions, but can further decrease public good provisioning when leaders are weak and the economic potential is poor. These results suggest that a more nuanced approach to corruption is needed and that proposed panaceas, such as transparency, may actually be harmful in some contexts.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter accounting, based strictly on what appears in the paper (including its figures and tables) and on whether each parameter is (1) mentioned (with any value used) and (2) systematically varied for its effect on the “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency (or on other dependent variables, if at all). The paper primarily discusses “public good provisioning,” “contributions,” and “corruption” (namely, bribe‐taking), rather than “efficiency” in the sense of (total actual payoff) ÷ (maximum possible payoff). Where the paper does examine other outcomes, that is noted explicitly.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • Yes. Groups ranged from 4 to 7 players (Methods).  
   (b) Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
       • No. The paper does not systematically vary group size nor discuss how it affects the punishment treatment effect.  

2. Number of rounds
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • Yes. Each within‐subject condition was played for up to 10 rounds, potentially ending earlier at a random stopping point (Methods).  
   (b) Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
       • No. The paper does not discuss any systematic manipulation (e.g., 5 rounds vs. 15 rounds) nor any effect on punishment.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • No. No mention of participant chat or other direct communication among players.  
   (b) Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
       • No.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • The paper describes an endowment of 10 points that can be freely allocated; it does not mention an all‐or‐nothing option.  
   (b) Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
       • No.  

5. Is the contribution default (participants moving endowment back to hand)?
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • No. There is no mention of any forced “default” or automatically refunded contribution.  
   (b) Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
       • No.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters (e.g. multiplication factor)
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • Yes. The paper calls it “economic potential” with a low versus high multiplier (MPCR = 0.3 vs. 0.6).  
   (b) Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment (or other outcomes)?  
       • Yes, systematically varied between low (0.3) and high (0.6).  
       • The paper’s main dependent variable with respect to this manipulation is “public good provisioning” (i.e., average contributions). The authors do not use the term “efficiency” for these analyses; instead, they measure how contributions or bribery change under high vs. low economic potential.  
       • Numerically, in poor (low MPCR) contexts, bribery leads to especially reduced public good contributions (compared to the no‐bribery baseline), whereas richer (high MPCR) contexts still show a corruption‐driven decrease in contributions, but the absolute public good remains higher (Figures 2 and 3). The authors report a “25% drop” in average contributions overall (BG vs. IPGG), but that drop is more pronounced when the multiplier is low.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • The experiment uses a tax‐based system in which leaders punish out of a fixed “tax pool,” but the personal cost to leaders for assigning punishment is effectively minimal (their own share of the tax is small). The paper does not report or manipulate any explicit “punisher cost.”  
   (b) Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
       • No.  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player per unit of punishment)
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • Yes. The paper calls this the “punishment multiplier” or “leader power,” and there are two conditions: weak (1×) vs. strong (3×).  
   (b) Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment (or other outcomes)?  
       • Yes, systematically varied.  
       • For strong leaders (3× punishment multiplier), the paper finds that they become more likely to accept bribes (Odds Ratio ≈ 2.14 in Table 1) and, under bribery, reduce contributions relative to a no‐bribery institutional‐punishment condition (Figures 2 and 3).  
       • The paper frames these effects primarily in terms of changes in “contributions” and “public good provisioning,” not explicit “efficiency.”  

9–11. Whether a reward is enabled, the cost to grant a reward, and reward magnitude
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • No. The experiment includes no peer reward mechanism.  
   (b) Systematically varied?  
       • No.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • Yes. Players are not informed of the exact ending to avoid end‐game effects.  
   (b) Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
       • No.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much peers gained/lost each round)?
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • The paper does discuss “partial transparency” vs. “full transparency” as ways of displaying information about leader and player behavior. “Full transparency” reveals (anonymized) contributions, bribes, and what the leader chose. However, the paper does not explicitly say players see each other’s payoffs; rather, they see each other’s actions.  
   (b) Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment (or other outcomes)?  
       • Yes, in the sense that “transparency” is manipulated:  
         – Partial transparency: players see only the leader’s contribution to the public good.  
         – Full transparency: players also see all anonymized contributions/bribes and all leader decisions.  
       • Numerically, the paper reports that in contexts with stronger leaders or higher economic potential, these transparency treatments can partly mitigate the drop in contributions from bribery (Figures 2 and 3). In contrast, with weak leaders and poor economic potential, partial transparency can backfire by further reducing contributions.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know the identity of the punisher?
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • The punishment institution is always a single leader (publicly known) chosen each round, but there is no separate manipulation of whether the punished person knows who imposed the punishment.  
   (b) Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
       • No.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know the identity of the rewarder?
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • No. The study does not include rewards.  
   (b) Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
       • No.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (actual total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper does not explicitly use that ratio (“efficiency”) as a measured outcome. Instead, the authors focus on:  
     – Public good provisioning (average group contributions to the public pool)  
     – Leaders’ decisions to punish, to accept bribes, or to do nothing  
     – The overall drop in “cooperative contributions” in the presence of bribery  
   • They sometimes refer to “efficiency of public good provisioning,” but the central reported metrics are mean contributions or (z‐scored) contributions, not the exact ratio of (actual ÷ maximum) payoffs.  

B. Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form (though not necessarily manipulated):  
       1, 2, 6, 8, 12, 13, and possibly 14 (because the identity of the leader is known).  
   • Not mentioned or not at all used:  
       3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10, 11, 15.  

C. For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable) when systematically varied?  
   • Systematically varied and discussed:  
       – #6 (economic potential / MPCR)  
       – #8 (punishment magnitude / leader strength)  
       – #13 (transparency of actions — partial vs. full)  
   • In all other cases, either they are not varied or not mentioned.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper only directly addresses how low vs. high economic potential (MPCR), low vs. high punishment magnitude (leader strength), and partial vs. full transparency shape bribery, punishments, and contributions. It does not assess “efficiency” as a ratio. Consequently, firm predictions about efficiency are quite limited.  
   • From their results on public good contributions, one can infer that:  
       – Raising economic potential (parameter 6) might lessen the relative damage from corruption, because even if bribery persists, the bigger multiplier can still sustain higher total returns.  
       – Increasing punishment magnitude (parameter 8) without additional safeguards can backfire in a bribery environment, lowering group outcomes by enlarging the leader’s incentive to demand or accept bribes.  
       – Providing full transparency (related to parameter 13) can increase contributions (and thus “efficiency”) if leaders are strong or the economic potential is high, but can backfire when leaders are weak and economic potential is poor.  
   • For all other parameters, the paper provides no basis for prediction.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
reference_APA: Muthukrishna, Michael, Francois, Patrick, Pourahmadi, Shayan & Henrich, Joseph (2017). Corrupting cooperation and how anti-corruption strategies may backfire. NATURE HUMAN BEHAVIOUR.

Authors: Cason, TN; Gangadharan, L
Author Full Names: Cason, Timothy N.; Gangadharan, Lata
Article Title: Promoting cooperation in nonlinear social dilemmas through peer punishment
Author Keywords: Experiment; Voluntary contributions mechanism; Common pool resources; Public goods; Nonlinear returns
Keywords Plus: VOLUNTARY CONTRIBUTIONS MECHANISM; PUBLIC-GOODS; ENFORCEMENT; PROVISION; RESOURCES
Abstract: Many social dilemmas exhibit nonlinearities and equilibrium outcomes in the interior of the choice space. This paper reports a laboratory experiment studying whether peer punishment promotes socially efficient behavior in such environments, which have been ignored in most experimental studies of peer punishment. It compares the effectiveness of peer punishment in a linear public good game to the effectiveness of this decentralized enforcement mechanism in two nonlinear social dilemma games: a piecewise linear public good game and a common pool resource game. While peer punishment improves cooperation in these new environments, the impact of punishment is weaker and takes longer to be effective. This appears to be due to the greater complexity of the nonlinear settings, which makes socially optimal choices more difficult to identify.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter inventory of what the paper actually says (or does not say) about each of the 15 specified parameters, followed by the required four‐part summary.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes. All sessions use groups of n = 4.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not examine changing the group size.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (any dependent variable)? No. The paper keeps n = 4 fixed and does not discuss how varying n would affect the punishment treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? Yes. They conduct exactly 10 periods (rounds) in every treatment.  
   • Systematically varied? No. Always 10.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? The paper does not discuss changing the number of rounds, so no effect is reported for systematically varying this parameter.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned? Only in referencing Ostrom et al. (1992), where communication was important; but in the present study, no chat/communication is used.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed (no chat is used, and the paper does not vary this dimension).

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”? (i.e., forced to contribute the entire amount or nothing)  
   • Mentioned? Indirectly. In all treatments herein, participants choose any integer from 0 to 12 tokens to allocate to the public (or common) account. This is not an all‐or‐nothing design.  
   • Systematically varied? No. They always allow any integer allocation from 0 to 12.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? None discussed.

5. Is the contribution “default” in the sense that players move money from the public fund back to themselves?  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not describe a “default contribution” or a game structure in which players must actively remove money from a public fund.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor(s)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper studies three environments:  
     – Linear VCM with MPCR = 0.5 (a standard linear public good).  
     – Nonlinear VCM with piecewise MPCR (1.25 for first three tokens, 0.5 for next seven, 0.2 for last two).  
     – CPR environment with a quadratic group payoff rather than a constant MPCR.  
   • Systematically varied? They do compare these three distinct settings, but each is run at a fixed parameter choice. The paper does not, for example, vary MPCR within the same environment.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment for any dependent variable?  
     – On “contributions”: Punishment raises contributions most robustly in the linear VCM (higher and earlier), more weakly or more slowly in the two nonlinear environments (see Table 2 and Figure 2).  
     – On “efficiency”: The paper finds no statistically significant overall efficiency gain from punishment in any of the three environments (Figure 3). Punishment raises cooperation but also imposes punishment costs, so realized payoffs do not show a significant net improvement.  
     – Numerical effect sizes on contributions. From Table 2 (periods 6–10 average contributions):  
       → Linear VCM: No‐punishment groups contribute 4.87 tokens on average; punishment groups contribute 8.73.  
       → Nonlinear VCM: 4.93 (no punishment) vs. 6.77 (punishment).  
       → CPR: 7.59 (no punishment) vs. 6.97 (punishment).  
       Although these reflect different underlying MPCRs (or payoff functions), they give a sense of how the availability of punishment interacts with each environment’s marginal returns.  
     – For “efficiency,” none of these differences is statistically significant when comparing punishment vs. no punishment, because punishment costs offset gains from higher cooperation (Section 4.3).

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? Yes. It is fixed: assigning 1 “deduction point” costs the punisher 1 experimental dollar.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? The paper does not explore altering this cost. The cost is always 1.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each deduction point reduces the target’s payoff by 3 experimental dollars.  
   • Systematically varied? No—all treatments use the same 3:1 ratio of target’s loss to punisher’s cost.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed for a parametric variation, since it is held constant throughout.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned? No. They only study costly punishment; no rewarding institution is included.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not applicable (no rewards exist in the design).

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Mentioned? No. There is no reward stage in this experiment.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment? Not applicable.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted)  
    • Mentioned? No. Same as above—no reward in the game.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment? Not applicable.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    • Mentioned? Yes. Subjects are told there will be exactly 10 rounds, a known endpoint.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment? The paper does not discuss or manipulate whether the horizon is known or unknown.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost each round)?  
    • Mentioned? Partially. Players see each group member’s contribution and can assign punishment points, but they do NOT see who punished them. They do see the group’s total returns. The paper does not describe showing each individual’s net payoff after punishment.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment? No direct discussion of how changing the displayed information would affect punishment.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Mentioned? Yes. They do NOT know who punished them; punishment is assigned anonymously.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment? The paper does not vary whether punishment is revealed or anonymous, so no effect is discussed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Mentioned? No. Reward is never used, so this does not arise.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment? Not applicable.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • Yes. The paper explicitly reports an “efficiency index” that compares actual payoffs to the Nash‐equilibrium payoff and the socially optimal payoff.  
   • Other dependent variables? Contributions (or extraction in the CPR) and punishment behavior are also analyzed. Efficiency is different from the contribution rate because it accounts for the costly nature of punishment: even if contributions rise, punishment expenses can reduce overall payoffs.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form: (1) number of players (fixed at 4), (2) number of rounds (10), (3) communication (not used, but cited as important in other work), (4) contribution format (0–12 tokens, not all‐or‐nothing), (6) MPCR/nonlinear returns, (7) punishment cost, (8) punishment magnitude, (12) known number of rounds, (13) partial feedback on contributions, (14) anonymity of the punisher.  
   • The rest—(5), (9), (10), (11), (15)—are neither used nor varied.  
   • In total, the paper explicitly discusses or fixes aspects of 10 out of the 15 parameters, though it systematically varies only the payoff environment (linear VCM vs. nonlinear VCM vs. CPR) rather than single parameters in isolation.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable if the parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, the design varies the environment (linear vs. nonlinear vs. CPR), which corresponds to different payoff structures or marginal returns (parameter 6). The paper compares these three environments with or without punishment, observing smaller or slower impacts of punishment in the two nonlinear environments than in the linear one.  
   • No other parameter is systematically varied.  
   • Hence only parameter (6) (broadly, “MPCR or payoff structure”) is varied in a systematic way across the three environments, and the paper does discuss its effect on cooperation, punishment usage, and efficiency.

D. Based solely on the paper’s content, how would one predict the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?

   • The paper finds that when the basic punishment parameters (cost and magnitude) remain the same but the MPCR/payoff structure shifts from linear to nonlinear, punishment’s positive effect on contributions becomes slower, less intense, and does not yield a significant net efficiency advantage, mainly because punishment costs eat up the gains from higher cooperation.  
   • The paper does not provide evidence for how changing the number of players, the number of rounds, or allowing/not allowing communication would alter efficiency under punishment—those parameters were not varied.  
   • Nor does it provide results on “all-or-nothing” rules or reward‐based mechanisms.  
   • Consequently, for most of the 15 parameters, there is “little to no prediction” in this paper about how systematic changes would affect efficiency under punishment. The only clear experimental evidence on changing the environment (parameter 6) suggests that increased complexity and mid‐range equilibrium solutions make punishment less effective (and sometimes ineffective) in lifting group efficiency.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Authors: Hauser, M; McAuliffe, K; Blake, PR
Author Full Names: Hauser, Marc; McAuliffe, Katherine; Blake, Peter R.
Article Title: Evolving the ingredients for reciprocity and spite
Source Title: PHILOSOPHICAL TRANSACTIONS OF THE ROYAL SOCIETY B-BIOLOGICAL SCIENCES
Conference Title: Discussion Meeting on the Evolution of Society
Author Keywords: reciprocal altruism; spite; ultimate pressures; proximal constraints
Keywords Plus: GROOMING RECIPROCATION; FEMALE PRIMATES; HUMAN INFANTS; CHIMPANZEES; COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; ALTRUISM; PUNISHMENT; BEHAVIOR; FOOD
Abstract: Darwin never provided a satisfactory account of altruism, but posed the problem beautifully in light of the logic of natural selection. Hamilton and Williams delivered the necessary satisfaction by appealing to kinship, and Trivers showed that kinship was not necessary as long as the originally altruistic act was conditionally reciprocated. From the late 1970s to the present, the kinship theories in particular have been supported by considerable empirical data and elaborated to explore a number of other social interactions such as cooperation, selfishness and punishment, giving us what is now a rich description of the nature of social relationships among organisms. There are, however, two forms of theoretically possible social interactions-reciprocity and spite-that appear absent or nearly so in non-human vertebrates, despite considerable research efforts on a wide diversity of species. We suggest that the rather weak comparative evidence for these interactions is predicted once we consider the requisite socioecological pressures and psychological mechanisms. That is, a consideration of ultimate demands and proximate prerequisites leads to the prediction that reciprocity and spite should be rare in non-human animals, and common in humans. In particular, reciprocity and spite evolved in humans because of adaptive demands on cooperation among unrelated individuals living in large groups, and the integrative capacities of inequity detection, future-oriented decision-making and inhibitory control.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter check of whether (1) the cited paper (“Evolving the ingredients for reciprocity and spite” by Hauser, McAuliffe, and Blake) discusses the parameter at all (including providing any values) and (2) makes predictions about the effect of systematically varying that parameter on the punishment treatment effect for any dependent variable. Note that the paper primarily discusses theoretical and empirical perspectives on the evolution and proximate mechanisms of reciprocity, spite, and punishment in animals (including humans) rather than systematically manipulating specific parameters in a public-goods or experimental-punishment context.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  
     – The paper discusses that humans often live in large stable groups and non-human animals often live in smaller kin groups; however, it does not specify or manipulate the exact number of players in a game-like scenario.  
   • Any predictions from systematic variation?  
     – No. The paper does not systematically vary “number of players” nor provide a numerical effect size regarding punishment or any other dependent variable.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  
     – The paper notes that repeated interactions across time can support reciprocity (e.g., direct reciprocity depends on the possibility of future encounters), but it does not specify “number of rounds” in an experimental sense.  
   • Any predictions from systematic variation?  
     – No. There is no discussion of systematically varying the number of rounds or the effect on outcomes such as efficiency or payoffs.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No, there is no mention of communication protocols (like chat) in the paper.  
   • Any predictions from systematic variation?  
     – No mention or predictions.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No, there is no discussion of all-or-nothing contribution structures in the paper.  
   • Any predictions from systematic variation?  
     – No mention or predictions.

5. Is the contribution default (where players move part of their endowment back into their hand)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No, there is no discussion of any default contribution scheme.  
   • Any predictions from systematic variation?  
     – No mention or predictions.

6. Marginal Per Capita Return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No, the paper does not discuss MPCR or any direct analog, nor does it present a multiplier parameter.  
   • Any predictions from systematic variation?  
     – No mention or predictions.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned?  
     – The authors discuss that punishment can be personally costly, but there is no specific numerical cost or parameter studied.  
   • Any predictions from systematic variation?  
     – No. The paper does not systematically vary punishment cost or provide effect sizes regarding how changing punishment cost influences outcomes.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted)  
   • Mentioned?  
     – The paper indicates that punishment typically imposes costs on targets, but it does not introduce or vary a numeric “punishment magnitude.”  
   • Any predictions from systematic variation?  
     – No. No systematic manipulation or numeric effect sizes are provided.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Reward is discussed only insofar as some experiments (e.g., “nice stooges”) deliver beneficial outcomes, but there is no mention of an explicit “reward mechanism” akin to a public goods reward or bonus.  
   • Any predictions from systematic variation?  
     – No. The paper does not systematically vary a formal reward mechanism.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. There is no parameter in the paper addressing a “cost of reward.”  
   • Any predictions from systematic variation?  
     – No mention or predictions.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit)  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. Similar to above, there is no direct mention of systematically varying a reward magnitude.  
   • Any predictions from systematic variation?  
     – No mention or predictions.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper discusses repeated interactions in an evolutionary/biological sense but not in an experimental game format of “known vs. unknown” end rounds.  
   • Any predictions from systematic variation?  
     – No mention or predictions.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Although the paper discusses that non-human primates may track another’s behavior (e.g., “nice” vs. “mean” stooges) or observe outcomes, it does not formalize this as a parameter in a public-goods or punishment game.  
   • Any predictions from systematic variation?  
     – No. There is no systematic variation or effect size reported; they do not link “visibility of peer outcomes” to changes in punishment effect.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Punishment is discussed in general evolutionary terms—no experimental manipulations reveal whether the target knows the punisher’s identity.  
   • Any predictions from systematic variation?  
     – No mention or predictions.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. Similar to above, the paper does not address knowledge of the rewarder’s identity as a systematically varied factor.  
   • Any predictions from systematic variation?  
     – No mention or predictions.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper does not use “group efficiency” (i.e., actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff) as a dependent variable. Instead, it discusses cooperative outcomes, reciprocal altruism, spite, and punishment at a conceptual level. Dependent measures in the cited experiments include whether animals (or humans) choose to cooperate, defect, punish, or help in given tasks, rather than an explicit measure of efficiency.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Most are not mentioned at all. Some broad references to repeated interactions, costs/benefits of punishing, and group size appear only in passing (not as formal parameters). In short, none of the 15 parameters is addressed as a specific, quantifiable, or experimentally manipulated variable in the paper.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. The paper does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters for the express purpose of measuring changes in punishment or efficiency; no effect sizes for such variations are given.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper provides no basis for making direct quantitative or systematic predictions about how these 15 parameters would influence a punishment treatment effect on efficiency. The authors’ discussion of punishment, reciprocity, and spite concerns broad evolutionary and proximate factors, not parameter-by-parameter manipulations. Therefore, little to no predictive statement can be made about these parameters’ influence on efficiency from the paper alone.
reference_APA: Hauser, Marc, McAuliffe, Katherine & Blake, Peter R. (2009). Evolving the ingredients for reciprocity and spite. PHILOSOPHICAL TRANSACTIONS OF THE ROYAL SOCIETY B-BIOLOGICAL SCIENCES.

Authors: Lee, HW; Cleveland, C; Szolnoki, A
Author Full Names: Lee, Hsuan-Wei; Cleveland, Colin; Szolnoki, Attila
Article Title: Mercenary punishment in structured populations
Author Keywords: Cooperation; Public goods game; Punishment
Keywords Plus: EVOLUTIONARY GAMES; BEHAVIOR; DILEMMA
Abstract: Punishing those who refuse to participate in common efforts is a known and intensively studied way to maintain cooperation among self-interested agents. But this act is costly, hence punishers who are generally also engaged in the original joint venture, become vulnerable, which jeopardizes the effectiveness of this incentive. As an alternative, we may hire special players, whose only duty is to watch the population and punish defectors. Such a policelike or mercenary punishment can be maintained by a tax-based fund. If this tax is negligible, a cyclic dominance may emerge among different strategies. When this tax is relevant then this solution disappears. In the latter case, the fine level becomes a significant factor that determines whether punisher players coexist with cooperators or alternatively with defectors. The maximal average outcome can be reached at an intermediate cost value of punishment. Our observations highlight that we should take special care when such kind of punishment and accompanying tax are introduced to reach a collective goal. (C) 2021 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

o1_summary:
Below, each of the 15 parameters is dealt with in turn.

For every parameter I state  

(1) whether the paper explicitly mentions or manipulates it (and the values that appear), and  

(2) whether the paper says anything about **what would happen if the parameter were systematically varied** to the punishment-treatment effect on any dependent variable (especially efficiency / average payoff).  Numerical effect sizes are given whenever they can be read directly from a figure or table; when only qualitative statements are available I report them verbatim.

────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
────────────────────────────────────────

1. Number of players  
   1) Mentioned.  Simulations use a square lattice of size L × L with L = 200–800.  
   2) The paper does not link “more players” to a change in the **treatment effect on efficiency**.  The only systematic comment is that finite-size oscillations close to a phase boundary may erroneously wipe out coexistence (Fig. 3).  No quantitative treatment-effect estimate is given.

2. Number of rounds  
   1) Not discussed; the evolutionary process is run until a stationary state.  
   2) No statement.

3. Chat enabled  
   1) Not mentioned.  
   2) No statement.

4. All-or-nothing contribution decision  
   1) Implicitly present: a player either contributes the whole unit (C) or nothing (D, P).  This dimension is fixed; never varied.  
   2) No statement.

5. Contribution default / un-contribute option  
   1) Not part of the model.  
   2) No statement.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   1) The synergy factor r is the MPCR analogue.  The paper sets r = 3 throughout after noting that r < 3.74 makes cooperation impossible without punishment.  
   2) r is **not** systematically varied, so no treatment-effect prediction is provided.

7. Punishment cost (cost to impose one unit) – Gₚ  
   1) Central variable.  Scanned broadly; horizontal axes in Figs 1, 2, 3, 5, 6.  
   2) Main findings:  
      • At T = 0, β = 0.4 (Fig. 2) average payoff rises from ≈0 at Gₚ≈0 to a peak (≈0.22) at Gₚ≈0.3, then falls back to 0 once Gₚ ≥ 0.7.  
      • At T = 0.2, β = 0.2 (Fig. 6b) average payoff is maximised at an intermediate Gₚ (~0.9).  
      • Qualitative rule: “The maximal average outcome can be reached at an intermediate cost value of punishment.” (Abstract & Sec. 3.1)  
      • Phase composition shifts: low Gₚ → full P; medium Gₚ → P+C with high efficiency; still higher Gₚ → P+C+D (cyclic) or P+D; very high Gₚ → full D with zero (or negative, when T>0) efficiency.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine β)  
   1) Central variable.  Scanned vertically in Figs 1 and 5; two explicit cross-sections at β = 0.1 and β = 0.2 (Fig. 6).  
   2) Main findings:  
      • Low β (≤0.1) — even with punishment, the system ends in P+D; average payoff stays negative when T>0 because no C’s survive.  
      • Moderate β (≈0.2–0.4) — makes a P+C phase possible, leading to positive average payoff, provided Gₚ is not too large.  
      • “The fine level becomes a significant factor that determines whether punisher players coexist with cooperators or alternatively with defectors.” (Abstract)  
      No numerical efficiency curves across β are supplied; only phase boundaries.

9. Reward enabled?  
10. Reward cost?  
11. Reward magnitude?  
   1) Rewards are not modelled.  
   2) No statements.

12. End-known (known horizon)?  
   1) Not modelled.  
   2) No statements.

13. Peer outcome visibility  
   1) Not modelled.  
   2) No statements.

14. Punisher identity revealed  
   1) Not modelled.  
   2) No statements.

15. Rewarder identity revealed  
   1) Not applicable (no rewards).  
   2) No statements.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────
A. Dependent variables  
   • The paper reports (i) stationary fractions of C, D, P strategies and (ii) average payoff (total payoff divided by population size).  
   • It never computes *efficiency* in the “actual / maximum” sense used in the prompt, although average payoff is a close proxy once one realises that the maximum would be r · c (here 3) per player.  
   • Strategy fractions and average payoff therefore capture different aspects: payoff already incorporates cost, tax and fines, whereas the composition only shows how many contributors remain.

B. Parameters mentioned (out of 15)  
   5 parameters appear explicitly:  
   1. Number of players (system size)  
   4. Binary contribution rule (fixed)  
   6. MPCR r (fixed)  
   7. Punishment cost Gₚ (varied)  
   8. Punishment magnitude β (varied)

C. Parameters whose **systematic variation** is analysed for treatment effects  
   • Punishment cost Gₚ  
   • Punishment magnitude β  
   • (System size is varied for a methodological finite-size check but not linked to the treatment effect on efficiency.)  
   ⇒ 2 of the 15 parameters receive genuine systematic treatment-effect analysis.

D. Predictions one can make about the 15 parameters, based only on this paper  

   • 1. Number of players – Prediction: larger groups (bigger lattices) do not alter the final phase diagram but prevent artefactual extinction events near phase boundaries; no direct efficiency impact beyond that.  
   • 2. Number of rounds – No prediction.  
   • 3. Chat – No prediction.  
   • 4. All-or-nothing – Fixed; no basis for prediction.  
   • 5. Contribution default – Not modelled.  
   • 6. MPCR – Not varied; however, if r were ≥3.74 punishment would be redundant.  
   • 7. Punishment cost – Efficiency is hump-shaped: very low Gₚ → many punishers but no cooperators (efficiency low); intermediate Gₚ → coexistence of P and C and peak efficiency; high Gₚ → punishment collapses, system reverts to defection (efficiency ≈0 or negative if a tax is present).  
   • 8. Punishment magnitude – Needs to be “sufficiently large” in order to create the P+C phase; larger β pushes the efficiency-maximising window of Gₚ to the right.  
   • 9–11. Reward-related parameters – Not modelled, so no prediction.  
   • 12–15. Information-display parameters – Not modelled, so no prediction.

Hence, on the basis of this single paper, confident quantitative predictions can only be made for two parameters (punishment cost and punishment magnitude) and for their interaction with the tax level T (a variable outside the list of 15).  For the remaining 13 parameters the paper is silent, so any forecast of their influence on the punishment treatment effect on efficiency would be speculative.
reference_APA: Lee, Hsuan-Wei, Cleveland, Colin & Szolnoki, Attila (2022). Mercenary punishment in structured populations. APPLIED MATHEMATICS AND COMPUTATION.

Authors: Góis, AR; Santos, FP; Pacheco, JM; Santos, FC
Author Full Names: Gois, Antonio R.; Santos, Fernando P.; Pacheco, Jorge M.; Santos, Francisco C.
Article Title: Reward and punishment in climate change dilemmas
Keywords Plus: COORDINATION; COOPERATION; GOVERNANCE; EVOLUTION; DYNAMICS; TRAGEDY; CARROT; HUNT; RISK; GAME
Abstract: Mitigating climate change effects involves strategic decisions by individuals that may choose to limit their emissions at a cost. Everyone shares the ensuing benefits and thereby individuals can free ride on the effort of others, which may lead to the tragedy of the commons. For this reason, climate action can be conveniently formulated in terms of Public Goods Dilemmas often assuming that a minimum collective effort is required to ensure any benefit, and that decision-making may be contingent on the risk associated with future losses. Here we investigate the impact of reward and punishment in this type of collective endeavors - coined as collective-risk dilemmas - by means of a dynamic, evolutionary approach. We show that rewards (positive incentives) are essential to initiate cooperation, mostly when the perception of risk is low. On the other hand, we find that sanctions (negative incentives) are instrumental to maintain cooperation. Altogether, our results are gratifying, given the a-priori limitations of effectively implementing sanctions in international agreements. Finally, we show that whenever collective action is most challenging to succeed, the best results are obtained when both rewards and sanctions are synergistically combined into a single policy.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter analysis, based strictly on the content of the provided paper (Góis et al., “Reward and punishment in climate change dilemmas”). For each of the 15 parameters, I note whether the paper (1) even mentions it at all and (2) discusses any systematic variation of that parameter vis‐à‐vis the “punishment treatment effect.” Throughout, remember that the paper’s principal outcome measure is “average group achievement” (ηG), which is the fraction of times the group avoids losing its entire endowment, rather than group efficiency in the sense of total payoff divided by the full‐cooperation payoff. The paper does not report on “efficiency” per se, but rather on various other outcomes such as ηG, fraction of cooperators, etc.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The paper specifies a population size Z (often Z = 50) and a group size N (often N = 10).  
   • Systematic variation for punishment’s effect?  
     – The main text shows most examples with N = 10. In the Methods, the authors note that the “optimal switching point” between reward and punishment depends on N (Fig. 4 varies N), but they do not present numerical measures of how changing N alone alters the magnitude of the “punishment treatment effect” on outcomes like ηG. They only show how N affects the best way to combine reward and punishment. There is no direct quantitative effect size reported for varying N.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The study is an evolutionary model without a fixed or known number of rounds. There is no discussion of round‐by‐round play or how the game might end.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – Not discussed.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The model is theoretical/evolutionary; no mention of communication/chat.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – Not discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – The paper’s model has each individual either cooperate (pay cost cB) or defect (pay zero), so effectively it is an all‐or‐nothing contribution.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – They do not explore scenarios in which players may pick a contribution from a continuous range. Nor do they link different “all‐or‐nothing” settings to punishment’s effect or provide numerical effect sizes. So there is no systematic‐variation discussion.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much of their endowment to move back to their hand)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper frames choices simply as “cooperate or defect,” with no mention of a “default” or “opt‐out” style.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – Not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  
     – The paper departs from the linear‐public‐goods framework (which uses an MPCR); instead, it uses a threshold with probability r of “losing everything” if fewer than M cooperate. The authors refer to prior linear‐MPCR studies but do not adopt or vary an MPCR themselves.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – Not discussed.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper’s punishment is implemented by an institutional policy that deducts from a central budget. It does not model an out‐of‐pocket cost borne by the punisher.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – Not discussed.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player per unit punishment)  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The model uses a parameter b (termed “punishment efficiency”) that determines how strongly a defector is punished. In each group, the total punishment budget is N δ × (1 − w). A defector’s payoff is reduced by b(1 − w)Nδ / (N−j).  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – Somewhat. The authors do systematically vary the ratio a/b (reward vs. punishment efficiency) in Fig. 4 to see how it shifts the best “switching point” between Reward and Punishment. However, they do not provide a direct effect size linking changes in b alone to changes in the “punishment treatment effect” on ηG. Rather, they focus on how b affects the policy that switches from reward to punishment.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. This is central to the paper. They examine “pure‐Reward” (w=1), “pure‐Punishment” (w=0), or mixtures.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – Yes. Fig. 1 compares no incentives (black), pure‐Reward (blue), pure‐Punishment (red), and a combination (orange). They show that, depending on the risk level, punishment alone is less effective at lower risk but can sustain cooperation better when risk is high. No exact table of numerical effect sizes is given, but the figures show that enabling or disabling reward shifts average group achievement by up to 0.2–0.5 (roughly estimated) at certain risk values.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. Similar to punishment, the model assumes a central budget N δ that funds reward. The authors do not treat it as an individual cost a rewarder must pay.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit reward granted)  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The parameter a (“reward efficiency”) determines how strongly cooperators are rewarded. A cooperator’s payoff is incremented by a w N δ / j.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – As with punishment, the ratio a/b is varied in Fig. 4, which determines how soon one should switch from reward to punishment. The authors do not provide a numeric effect size for changes in a alone on a “punishment effect”; they only show how it shifts the optimal switching point. No direct data on group‐achievement changes solely from different a values is given.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper studies an ongoing evolutionary process, not a finite‐horizon or known‐end setting.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – Not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see one another’s payoffs)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. They assume individuals can compare payoffs enough to imitate successful peers, but the paper does not treat that as an experimentally varied parameter (e.g., partial vs. full information).  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – Not discussed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. Punishment is institutional, not peer‐to‐peer. The identity of a punisher is not mentioned.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – Not discussed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. As above, rewards come from a central pool. There is no mention of identifying the rewarder.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – Not discussed.

SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   – The paper does not explicitly track “efficiency” (total payoff ÷ maximum possible). Instead, the main dependent variable is the “average group achievement” (ηG), which is the fraction of groups that reach enough cooperators to avoid losing their endowment. They also discuss the fraction of cooperators in the population. Thus, the paper’s dependent variables differ from efficiency because they measure how often the public‐good threshold is met (or how many cooperators are in equilibrium), rather than total payoffs relative to a fully cooperative benchmark.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – Mentioned in some form:  
     • (1) Number of players (group size N = 10; population size Z = 50)  
     • (4) All‐or‐nothing contributions (cooperate vs. defect)  
     • (8) Punishment magnitude (b)  
     • (9) Whether a reward is enabled (they compare w=0 vs. w=1)  
     • (11) Reward magnitude (a)  
   – Partially referenced or assumed, but not systematically varied in a way bearing on a “punishment effect”: (1), (4), (8), (9), (11).  
   – Not mentioned or not relevant in the sense above: (2), (3), (5), (6), (7), (10), (12), (13), (14), (15).

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   – Strictly speaking, the paper systematically varies only two components relevant to punishment vs. reward policies in a way that could be called “systematic”:

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned in passing. The authors simulate on a 100×100 square lattice and sometimes a 200×200 lattice, but they do not systematically vary the number of players.  
   • No predictions or effect sizes are given regarding how changing the number of players would affect any dependent variable (including fraction of cooperators).

2. Number of rounds  
   • Not explicitly discussed as a parameter. The paper uses repeated updating over many time steps (up to 30,000), but does not systematically vary a finite “number of rounds” to see its effect.  
   • No predictions or effect sizes are provided about the effect of systematically varying the number of rounds.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Not mentioned at all.  
   • No predictions.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Not framed in these terms. The model is the Prisoner’s Dilemma with two discrete strategies (cooperate or defect), but there is no mention of “all or nothing” in a public-goods sense.  
   • No predictions.

5. Is the contribution default?  
   • Not mentioned. The paper does not discuss default contributions or decisions about moving endowments.  
   • No predictions.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor  
   • The paper’s main PD payoff parameter is b (the “temptation to defect”), which the authors systematically vary from values slightly above 1 to larger values. Although b is not called the MPCR, it serves a similar role in shifting payoffs.  
   • They do discuss how changing b systematically affects the fraction of cooperators (ρc). For example, Figures 3, 4, and 5 show that larger b reduces ρc unless punishment (α) is in a certain optimal range.  
   • They do not relate b to “efficiency.” They measure ρc, not group payoff.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • The paper combines (i) the cost to the punisher and (ii) the fine to the target into a single parameter α (“punishment fine”). Because punishment is mutual, α appears as a direct subtracted amount from the payoff of anyone facing an opposite-strategy neighbor.  
   • They systematically vary α from 0 up to values around 1.5 and study how ρc changes. They report that if α is too small or too large, cooperation can fail, while moderate α can lead to substantial increases in ρc. However, this is always in terms of fraction of cooperators rather than efficiency.  
   • Numerical effect sizes:  
     – For a well-mixed population (Fig. 1–2), there is a threshold αc above which cooperators take over (ρc → 1).  
     – On a square lattice (Figs. 3–10), moderate α often maximizes ρc, while very small or very large α leads to lower cooperation.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Not presented as a separate variable from the cost in this paper. The model does not distinguish a separate punisher cost (c) and punishee fine (f); α is treated as a single “punishment fine” that equally penalizes mismatched neighbors.  
   • No separate parameter for “punishment magnitude” is varied.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Not mentioned. The paper focuses solely on mutual punishment; there is no reward mechanism.  
   • No predictions.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Not mentioned.  
    • No predictions.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each reward)  
    • Not mentioned.  
    • No predictions.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    • Not mentioned.  
    • No predictions.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?  
    • Not explicitly stated in terms of “information display.” Presumably, individuals compare payoffs to update strategies under the Fermi rule, but the paper does not discuss any systematic variations in the information shown to players.  
    • No predictions.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Not discussed.  
    • No predictions.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Not applicable (no reward).  
    • No predictions.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper does not use “efficiency” (actual payoff / maximum payoff) or total payoff as its main outcome. Instead, it focuses on the fraction of cooperators (ρc). Payoffs are computed at the individual level to update strategies, but the aggregate measure reported is ρc. Thus, any references to “cooperation is enhanced” reflect an increase in ρc, not necessarily higher efficiency.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned or used, at least in passing:  
     – #1 (Number of players) is stated as 100×100 or 200×200 but not varied.  
     – #6 (Temptation to defect, b) is systematically varied.  
     – #7 (Punishment cost/fine, α) is systematically varied.  
   • The remaining parameters (#2, #3, #4, #5, #8, #9, #10, #11, #12, #13, #14, #15) are not discussed.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The paper systematically varies exactly two parameters: b (#6) and α (#7).  
   • The only reported dependent variable associated with these variations is the fraction of cooperators (ρc). The authors compare, for instance, α=0 (no punishment) versus α>0 (punishment present), showing how that difference (“the punishment effect”) changes ρc. There is no direct discussion of how these parameters change “efficiency” or total payoffs.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper’s results concern changes in ρc rather than efficiency. They do not measure total or maximum payoffs, nor do they derive a ratio indicating efficiency. Consequently, one cannot reliably predict how the 15 parameters or their interactions would affect efficiency. At most, one could posit that higher ρc might correlate with higher overall payoffs in a typical PD setting, but the paper itself provides no direct data or theoretical result on efficiency. Thus, strictly from the paper, there is little basis for predicting how these parameters and their interactions would change group efficiency.

Abstract: Rules regulating social behavior raise challenging questions about cultural evolution in part because they frequently confer group-level benefits. Whenever the article is silent I state that explicitly.

PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Number of players  
    • Name(s) used in the paper m₁ (players per G₁ community) and m₂ (number of G₁ communities that form a G₂ community); the total population size is N = m₁m₂ for the two–level model that is analysed most.  
    • Concrete values All numerical illustrations use m₁ = 20, m₂ = 20 (Fig. 3 & 4).  
    • Systematic variation? Only discussed qualitatively: “…when m₁ and m₂ are sufficiently large, punishers are always more abundant than defectors.” No table or figure shows the outcome for several different values, so no numerical slope or effect size is available.  
    • Predicted effect on the punishment treatment effect on efficiency Not reported; efficiency is never calculated.

2.  Number of rounds  
    • Not mentioned – the model is an infinite-time evolutionary Markov chain.

3.  Chat enabled?  
    • Not mentioned.

4.  “All-or-nothing” contribution decision  
    • The model is all-or-nothing by definition (cooperators pay c, defectors pay 0).  
    • No comparison to a continuous choice is made; hence no prediction for systematic variation.

5.  Contribution default / take-back frame  
    • Not mentioned.

6.  MPCR (or multiplication factor)  
    • Symbols used r₁ (level-1 multiplication factor) and k₁r₁ (the “effective enhancement factor” within a community).  
    • Values r₁ = 3 and k₁ = 0.5 (hence k₁r₁ = 1.5) in all numerical illustrations.  
    • Systematic statements The text states the qualitative threshold “Only when k₁r₁ > 1 can cooperation be favoured in the long run.” No figure varies r₁ or k₁; no quantitative effect size.  
    • Punishment treatment effect on efficiency Not analysed.

7.  Punishment cost to impose one unit  
    • Level-1 cost γ₁ and level-2 cost γ₂. Numerical illustrations: γ₁ = 0.5, γ₂ = 0.5.  
    • Qualitative condition “If m₁γ₁ ≫ c and m₂γ₂ ≫ c – ck₁r₁, then Φᴰᴾ² > Φᴾᴰ², so punishers are more abundant than defectors.” No explicit sweep across γ. No efficiency calculation.

8.  Punishment magnitude (fine on the target)  
    • Level-1 β₁ and level-2 β₂. Numerical illustrations: β₁ = 1.0, β₂ = 1.0.  
    • Qualitative condition identical to item 7 with β instead of γ. No systematic variation, no efficiency numbers.

9.  Reward enabled?  
10. Reward cost?  
11. Reward magnitude?  
    • Not part of the model; never mentioned.

12.  Is the number of rounds known?  
    • Not applicable (infinite-time evolutionary setting).

13.  Are peer outcomes shown?  
14.  Is the identity of the punisher revealed?  
15.  Is the identity of the rewarder revealed?  
    • None of these information-display variables appears in the article.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
DEPENDENT VARIABLES ACTUALLY USED
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The paper never computes “group efficiency” (total payoff ÷ maximum possible total payoff).  
Instead it uses:  
• Φ-values – fixation probabilities of one strategy invading another.  
• X_C, X_D, X_P – stationary probabilities that the population is homogeneously made of Cooperators, Defectors or Punishers (eq. 4, Fig. 3 & Fig. 4).  
“More abundant” or “prevalent” is always expressed in terms of these stationary probabilities.  
No payoff, welfare, or efficiency measure is reported.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Does the paper use group efficiency?  No.  
    Dependent variables: fixation probabilities (Φ) and stationary frequencies (X_C, X_D, X_P). These differ from efficiency because they describe where the population spends its time, not how much total payoff it earns.

B.  Which of the 15 focal parameters are even mentioned?  
    5 out of 15:  
    (1) number of players (m₁, m₂), (4) all-or-nothing contribution form (fixed in the model), (6) MPCR (r₁, k₁), (7) punishment cost (γ₁, γ₂), (8) punishment magnitude (β₁, β₂).  
    The remaining 10 parameters never appear.

C.  For how many of those 15 parameters does the article discuss how systematic variation affects any punishment treatment effect?  
    • 3 parameters receive at least a qualitative statement:  
      – number of players (m₁, m₂): “if both are sufficiently large, punishers dominate defectors.”  
      – MPCR (k₁r₁): cooperation/punishment can only prevail when k₁r₁ > 1.  
      – punishment cost & magnitude (γ, β): large enough β and γ (relative to c) are part of the condition for punishers beating defectors.  
    However, none of these discussions is linked to efficiency, and none is shown in a systematic numerical sweep; no quantitative effect sizes are provided.

D.  Predicted influence of the 15 parameters on the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, if one had to rely solely on this paper  
    • Because the paper never computes efficiency, almost no direct prediction can be made.  
    • Indirectly, one may guess that conditions that make punishers and/or cooperators more abundant (large m₁ & m₂, k₁r₁ > 1, sufficiently large β and γ) would probably raise efficiency relative to a baseline without punishment, but the article supplies no numbers, no model of total payoff, and no discussion of efficiency losses due to punishment costs.  
    • For the other 11 parameters (rounds, chat, reward system, information display, etc.) the paper gives no guidance at all.

Hence, from the supplied article alone, almost nothing quantitative – and only the broadest qualitative hints – can be said about how any of the 15 experimental design parameters would shift the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.
