   • Discussed in the paper? Yes, they specify the public‐goods multiplier as 1.6 for the total group contribution (each round’s total contribution is multiplied by 1.6 and split among the four players).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The MPCR is fixed (1.6). The paper does not investigate how changing this multiplier would affect outcomes, and no predictions are made about doing so.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussed in the paper? Not in the sense of peer punishment. Because punishment here is administered by an external institution, there is no cost borne by any “punisher.”  
   • Systematically varied? No. This cost is effectively zero for participants (the institution pays or deducts). No mention of systematically varying such costs appears.  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted for each unit of punishment)
   • Discussed in the paper? Yes. The magnitude of institutional punishment (and reward) varies across three “schemes”: Const, Up, and Down. In Const, the punishment (or reward) is 20 if selected; in Up, it ranges from 16 to 25.6; in Down, it ranges from 25.6 down to 16.  
   • Systematically varied as a parameter in the experiment? Yes—though it is presented as three different designs (Const, Up, Down) rather than a continuous parameter sweep.  
   • Predictions about effect on the “punishment treatment effect?”  
       – The paper focuses on changes in contribution. It reports that punishment‐only (“IP”), reward‐only (“IR”), or combined punishment+reward (“IRP”) differ in average contribution under each of Const, Up, and Down.  
       – Numerical effect sizes are given only for average contributions (e.g., IRP yields ~15.2–17.7 tokens contributed per round, IP yields ~10.8–12.6, IR yields ~8.3–9.2, Control ~7.6). The paper does not report or forecast how these changes translate into “efficiency,” nor does it give a formal “effect size” for efficiency.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussed in the paper? Yes. The experiment compares (i) punishment only, (ii) reward only, and (iii) both punishment and reward.  
   • Systematically varied? Yes, across “IP” (punishment‐only), “IR” (reward‐only), and “IRP” (punishment+reward).  
   • Predictions about effect on punishment treatment?  
       – The paper measures how average contributions differ when adding reward alone or punishment alone, or both. It finds IP treatment leads to higher average contribution than IR, and IRP is highest of all.  
       – Again, these are outcomes in terms of cooperation (contribution). There is no discussion of how it affects “efficiency.”  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Discussed in the paper? No. As with punishment cost, participants do not pay. The institution confers the reward.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)
   • Discussed in the paper? Yes, exactly as with punishment magnitude—Const, Up, and Down.  
   • Systematically varied as a parameter? Yes, in those three distinct designs.  
   • Predictions about effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
       – The paper compares how IR, IP, IRP fare in each design (Const, Up, Down). Numerical results are in terms of average contribution (Figure 1, tables in SI). No predictions about efficiency are provided.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
   • Discussed in the paper? The experiment is 50 rounds, but it is not explicitly stated that participants do (or do not) know the exact round count. The methods do not systematically examine “known vs. unknown” horizon.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown?
   • Discussed in the paper? Not explicitly. They do not describe any systematic variation of feedback about peer payoffs or contributions.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Discussed in the paper? Not relevant in this design: punishment is imposed by an institution. The identity of a “punisher” never arises.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is?
   • Discussed in the paper? Same as above. There is no peer who delivers the reward; it is assigned by the institution.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   • The paper does not employ group efficiency as a measured outcome. Instead, it focuses primarily on average individual contributions (i.e., cooperation) per round, the fraction of individuals cooperating/defecting/conforming, and players’ behavioral transitions across rounds. Although “payoff” is mentioned in theoretical derivations (and the paper notes that an institution’s reward and punishment can be “self‐financing”), the study does not systematically analyze total payoff or efficiency.  

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned explicitly:  
       – (1) Number of players (n=4, not varied)  
       – (2) Number of rounds (50, not varied)  
       – (6) MPCR/multiplication factor (1.6, not varied)  
       – (8) Punishment magnitude (varied across Const, Up, Down)  
       – (9) Reward presence or absence (compared IP, IR, IRP)  
       – (11) Reward magnitude (varied across Const, Up, Down)  
   • The remaining parameters (3, 4, 5, 7, 10, 12, 13, 14, 15) are either not discussed at all or not systematically varied in any way that the paper reports.  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect (for each dependent variable) when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The paper systematically varies:  
       – (8) Punishment magnitude (Const vs. Up vs. Down),  
       – (9) Whether rewards are enabled or not (treatments IP vs. IR vs. IRP),  
       – (11) Reward magnitude (Const vs. Up vs. Down).  
   • In all these cases, the paper reports effects on average contribution (cooperation), not on efficiency. It gives numerical values (e.g., round‐by‐round average contribution) but no “punishment‐treatment effect” in terms of total payoff or efficiency.  

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper’s content, what would they be?  
   • Because the paper does not analyze or quantify “efficiency” (actual payoff versus maximum), it offers no direct justification to predict how systematically changing any parameter would alter the punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency. Its results are confined to contribution/cooperation patterns.  
   • At most, one can infer that when punishment significantly raises contribution (as in IP or IRP treatments), the group’s total payoff under typical public‐goods assumptions would rise, presumably leading to higher efficiency—provided that the net “institutional” deduction or reward does not offset or consume the benefit. Yet the authors do not explicitly measure or model this trade‐off.  
   • In short, the paper does not provide enough details to predict changes in efficiency, so little to no prediction can be made solely from the contents of this study.

Authors: Raihani, NJ; Pinto, AI; Grutter, AS; Wismer, S; Bshary, R

Article Title: Male cleaner wrasses adjust punishment of female partners according to the stakes
Source Title: PROCEEDINGS OF THE ROYAL SOCIETY B-BIOLOGICAL SCIENCES
Author Keywords: cleaner fish; cooperation; Labroides dimidiatus; mutualism; punishment
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; COOPERATION; RECIPROCITY; EVOLUTION; FISH; BEHAVIOR; PAIRS
Abstract: Punishment is an important deterrent against cheating in cooperative interactions. In humans, the severity of cheating affects the strength of punishment which, in turn, affects the punished individual's future behaviour. Here, we show such flexible adjustments for the first time in a non-human species, the cleaner wrasse (Labroides dimidiatus), where males are known to punish female partners. We exposed pairs of cleaners to a model client offering two types of food, preferred 'prawn' items and less-preferred 'flake' items. Analogous to interactions with real clients, eating a preferred prawn item ('cheating') led to model client removal. We varied the extent to which female cheating caused pay-off reduction to the male and measured the corresponding severity of male punishment. Males punished females more severely when females cheated during interactions with high value, rather than low value, model clients; and when females were similar in size to the male. This pattern may arise because, in this protogynous hermaphrodite, cheating by similar-sized females may reduce size differences to the extent that females change sex and become reproductive competitors. In response to more severe punishment from males, females behaved more cooperatively. Our results show that punishment can be adjusted to circumstances and that such subtleties can have an important bearing on the outcome of cooperative interactions.

   • Discussed? No. While the fish either “cheat” (eat prawn) or feed more cooperatively (eat flake first), the paper does not frame their behavior as an “all‐or‐nothing contribution” in a public‐goods sense, nor does it systematically vary such a parameter.

   • Discussed? Partially. The study measures and describes the “intensity” or “severity” of punishment (number of aggressive chases per second) that males direct at females.    • Predictions about systematically varying this parameter?  
       – The paper does not systematically manipulate punishment magnitude exogenously. It does report that higher punishment intensity correlates with a greater subsequent reduction in female cheating. Specifically, “the more severe the punishment, the less likely females were to eat prawn again” (effect size = −9.8 ± 4.1, p = 0.003), but this is a correlation from male behavior rather than a researcher‐imposed treatment.

    • Discussed? Punishment is an immediate physical chase by the male, so the female necessarily observes who chases her. The paper does not analyze or manipulate whether such information is known or hidden.  
    • Predictions about systematically varying this parameter? None.

    • Discussed? No; again, there is no reward mechanism in the paper.  
    • Predictions about systematically varying this parameter? None.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary (A–D)

A: Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   • The study does not use “group efficiency,” “total payoff,” or “average payoff” as a dependent variable.  
   • Instead, the main dependent variables are (1) the severity/intensity of male punishment (i.e., number of chases per second directed at a cheating female) and (2) how the female’s subsequent behavior changes (e.g., whether the female cheats again by eating prawn). These revolve around cooperation (cheating vs. not cheating), not overall payoff or efficiency.

B: Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • None of the canonical public-goods-game parameters (1–7, 9–15) are explicitly discussed in the sense of systematic experimental manipulation.  
   • Punishment “magnitude” (parameter #8) aligns partly with “punishment intensity” in the paper, but it is not exogenously controlled; it is measured natural behavior, not an experimentally varied design factor.

C: For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The paper never systematically varies any of the 15 parameters. It only measures punishment intensity that arises naturally under different conditions (high‐ vs. low‐value clients, smaller vs. similar‐sized females). Hence, it does not experimentally isolate how changing any parameter would alter a “punishment treatment effect.”  
   • The one partial parallel is parameter #8 (punishment magnitude), but even there, the paper does not treat it as a systematically varied factor; it is simply observed to be correlated with how much the female subsequently cheats.

D: If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • There is little to no direct basis in this paper for predicting how any of the 15 public‐goods parameters, alone or in combination, would affect efficiency. The paper’s key result is that more severe punishment (more intense chases) correlates with lower immediate cheating in this particular fish context. There is no discussion of overall group payoff, total earnings, or efficiency in a public‐goods sense.

Author Full Names: Li, Kun; Szolnoki, Attila; Cong, Rui; Wang, Long
Article Title: The coevolution of overconfidence and bluffing in the resource competition game
Keywords Plus: EVOLUTIONARY DYNAMICS; PRISONERS-DILEMMA; COOPERATION; PUNISHMENT; EMERGENCE; RECIPROCITY; NETWORKS
Abstract: Resources are often limited, therefore it is essential how convincingly competitors present their claims for them. Beside a player's natural capacity, here overconfidence and bluffing may also play a decisive role and influence how to share a restricted reward. While bluff provides clear, but risky advantage, overconfidence, as a form of self-deception, could be harmful to its user. Still, it is a long-standing puzzle why these potentially damaging biases are maintained and evolving to a high level in the human society. Within the framework of evolutionary game theory, we present a simple version of resource competition game in which the coevolution of overconfidence and bluffing is fundamental, which is capable to explain their prevalence in structured populations. Interestingly, bluffing seems apt to evolve to higher level than corresponding overconfidence and in general the former is less resistant to punishment than the latter. Moreover, topological feature of the social network plays an intricate role in the spreading of overconfidence and bluffing. While the heterogeneity of interactions facilitates bluffing, it also increases efficiency of adequate punishment against overconfident behavior. Furthermore, increasing the degree of homogeneous networks can trigger similar effect. We also observed that having high real capability may accommodate both bluffing ability and overconfidence simultaneously.

Abstract: In dealing with peer punishment as a cooperation enforcement device, laboratory studies have typically concentrated on discretionary sanctioning, allowing players to castigate each other arbitrarily. (ii) Whether the paper makes any prediction (numerical or qualitative) about what would happen to the *punishment treatment effect* if the parameter were **systematically varied**.  “Punishment treatment effect” is understood here as the change in outcome (e.g., earnings/efficiency, contribution, etc.) that is attributable to giving subjects the possibility to punish under the particular institution being studied.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (i) Mentioned: groups of N = 4 (p. 8).  
   (ii) Not varied; no predictions about changing group size.

2. Number of rounds  
   (i) Mentioned: T = 20 finitely-repeated periods, and subjects were told this (p. 8–9).  
   (ii) Fixed; no predictions about a different horizon.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   (i) Not mentioned; all interaction is through the programmed interface only.  
   (ii) No discussion, no predictions.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution format?  
   (i) Discussed implicitly: subjects choose any integer 0–20 tokens (continuous choice, not all-or-nothing).  
   (ii) Not varied; no predictions.

5. Contribution default / reversal frame (take from public fund)?  
   (i) Never mentioned.  
   (ii) No discussion, no predictions.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   (i) Explicit: each contributed token yields 0.4 tokens to *each* of four players (MPCR = 0.4; group return = 1.6).  
   (ii) MPCR is the same in every treatment; paper offers no predictions about changing it.

7. Punishment cost per unit  
   (i) Yes: Table 2 gives a convex schedule (1 point costs 1 token, 2 points cost 2, …, 10 points cost 30).  
   (ii) Cost schedule is never altered; no predictions of varying costs.

8. Punishment magnitude (damage per unit)  
   (i) Yes: every punishment point *received* reduces the target’s stage-1 earnings by 10 %; maximum 100 %.  
   (ii) Not varied; no predictions of changing the deduction rate.

9. Reward enabled?  
   (i) Not available in any treatment.  
   (ii) No discussion, no predictions.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   (i) & (ii) Not applicable (rewards never appear).

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
   (i) Yes: subjects were told there would be 20 periods.  
   (ii) This feature is fixed; no predictions about uncertainty over the horizon.

13. Are peer outcomes / contributions shown?  
   (i) Central design feature.  
       • Baseline: full feedback – each player sees every individual contribution.  
       • Full-R (restricted, “legitimate” punishment): identical full feedback.  
       • Partial-R (restricted): only the *average* contribution and the contributions of people who gave **less** than the observer are shown.  
   (ii) Systematically varied.  Main findings:  
       • With legitimacy-based punishment, removing information about the *higher* contributors “is sufficient to generate a dramatic decline in cooperation rates and earnings” (Abstract; Result 3).  
       • Quantitatively, mean contribution falls from 14.53 (Full-R) to 8.33 (Partial-R) tokens (Table 3).  
       • Average earnings likewise fall (Fig. 4); Wilcoxon z = 2.89, p = 0.003 (Full-R > Partial-R).  
       Hence, more complete information about peers’ contribution **increases** the punishment treatment effect on both cooperation and efficiency under the legitimacy rule.

14. Does a punished player learn who punished them?  
   (i) Yes, discussed: punishment is anonymous in all treatments; punishees never learn the identity of their punisher (p. 9).  
   (ii) Not varied; no predictions.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who rewarded them?  
   (i) Rewards do not exist; therefore not discussed.  
   (ii) No predictions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   – Yes.  “Average earnings” (tokens) are reported and compared across treatments (e.g., Fig. 4; Result 5).  
   – Other dependent variables: individual contribution level, change in contribution, number of punishment points given/received.  Contributions measure cooperation; earnings capture efficiency; punishment points capture deterrence activity; these variables are analytically distinct.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14  →  9 parameters.

C. For which parameters does the paper discuss the **effect of systematically varying** the parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
   Only parameter 13 (information about peer contributions).  So: 1 of 15 parameters.

D. Predictions that can be made *solely* from this paper with respect to efficiency:  
   • Providing *full* information about every peer’s contribution (parameter 13) *amplifies* the positive impact of legitimacy-based punishment on both cooperation and average earnings; withholding information about higher contributors largely nullifies the efficiency gain.  
   • For all other listed parameters the paper gives no direct evidence or theoretical argument about how changing them would alter the punishment treatment effect.  Consequently, no reliable predictions can be offered for parameters 1–12 and 14–15 beyond the specific fixed values used in the experiment.
reference_APA: Faillo, Marco, Grieco, Daniela & Zarri, Luca (2013). Legitimate punishment, feedback, and the enforcement of cooperation. GAMES AND ECONOMIC BEHAVIOR.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter analysis based solely on the content of the provided paper by Anderson and Stafford. Throughout, please note that the paper does not explicitly analyze “efficiency,” defined as the actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff; rather, it focuses on “group contributions” (the total amount allocated to the public good) and on individuals’ decisions to comply by contributing. Where possible, numerical effect sizes on group contribution are taken directly from the paper’s regressions and tables, but no measure of “efficiency” as defined in the question is given.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper uses groups of 10 subjects in each experimental session.  
   • Systematically varied? No. It is fixed at 10 in every session.  
   • Any predicted effect on the punishment treatment (for group contribution or otherwise)? No. There is no discussion of how varying the number of players would affect outcomes.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each session involves 20 decision-making “scenarios” or “rounds.”  
   • Systematically varied? No. All sessions have 20. The paper does compare a “One-Time” versus a “Repeated” treatment, but the actual number of rounds (20) is not changed.  
   • Any predicted effect on the punishment treatment? The paper does not systematically manipulate the number of rounds, so there is no predicted or measured effect of changing that number.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned? No. There is no mention of any communication or chat among participants.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed at all.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper instead allows any allocation from $0 to $5; it is not an all-or-nothing decision.  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no all-or-nothing variant.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much to move back into their hand)?  
   • Mentioned? Not in these terms. All subjects make a continuous choice from $0 to $5.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

6. MPCR (Marginal Per Capita Return) or related multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper states that the return on group contributions is doubled and shared among ten players (making the MPCR = 0.20).  
   • Systematically varied? No. MPCR = 0.20 in all conditions.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? The paper does not vary the MPCR, so no direct prediction of how changing it would affect the punishment treatment.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? No. Punishment is administered by the experimenter (a top-down regulator), and there is no mention of a cost that punishers themselves must pay.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed in the paper.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper calls this “punishment severity” (s), which can be 1, 2, 3, or 4.  
   • Systematically varied? Yes. They explicitly vary severity from 1 to 4, in combination with different punishment probabilities.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? The paper reports effects on group contribution (not on efficiency).  
       – In Table 3, random-effects tobit regressions show that punishment severity has a (statistically) significant positive effect on group contribution.  
       – For the One-Time treatment, the coefficient on Punishment Severity is 0.79 (p < 0.05), with a marginal effect of 0.50; for the Repeated treatment, it is 1.17 (p < 0.05), with a marginal effect of 0.53.  
       – The authors conclude that severity has a larger quantitative impact on group contribution than probability (though both are positive).

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned? No. There is no discussion of any reward instrument or positive sanction.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Mentioned? No.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
    • Mentioned? No.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
    • Mentioned? Yes. Subjects know there are 20 decision-making scenarios.  
    • Systematically varied? No. The number of rounds (20) is fixed and always common knowledge.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment? There is no discussion of how systematically changing knowledge of the number of rounds would affect treatment outcomes.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost each round)?  
    • Mentioned? Partially. In the Repeated treatment, participants learn the total group contribution and see who was punished (by letter), but they do not see each individual’s exact payoff or contribution. In the One-Time treatment, no interim feedback is given.  
    • Systematically varied? The paper contrasts One-Time (no feedback) versus Repeated (with feedback). However, they do not treat “information display” itself as a systematically isolated factor; it is bundled with repetition.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment? The paper does not provide a separate analysis of how purely changing peer-outcome feedback alters the punishment treatment effect. They do note that in the Repeated setting, contribution patterns differ partly because participants see some feedback between rounds, but there is no explicit “systematic variation” to isolate the feedback effect on punishment outcomes.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Mentioned? No. Punishment is externally imposed by the experimenter, so there is no “who” among peers.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Mentioned? No. There is no reward mechanism in the design.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FINAL SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper’s primary dependent variables are:  
       – Group contribution (the total amount allocated to the public good)  
       – Individual compliance decisions (how much each subject contributes)  
     The authors also track individual earnings, but they do not measure or report an explicit “efficiency” ratio (actual total payoff / maximum payoff).  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Discussed:  
       1) Number of players (fixed at 10)  
       2) Number of rounds (fixed at 20)  
       6) MPCR (fixed at 0.20)  
       8) Punishment magnitude (called punishment severity)  
       12) Number of rounds is known to subjects  
       13) Some information about group-level outcomes is revealed in the Repeated treatment  
   • Not mentioned or not relevant to this design:  
       3) Chat enabled, 4) All-or-nothing, 5) Contribution default, 7) Punishment cost to punisher,  
       9) Reward enabled, 10) Reward cost, 11) Reward magnitude, 14) Punisher identity, 15) Rewarder identity  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when systematically varied?  
   • Only two parameters are systematically varied:  
       – Punishment probability (listed in the paper as “p” ranging from 10% to 90%)  
       – Punishment magnitude (punishment severity “s” ranging from 1 to 4)  
   • Their effects are discussed in terms of group contribution (not efficiency). The paper gives regression coefficients for both probability and severity (Table 3) but does not measure “efficiency.”

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper provides no direct analysis of efficiency. It does show that higher punishment severity and higher punishment probability both increase group contributions (which could, in principle, raise group efficiency if one interprets “more contribution” as closer to the social optimum).  
   • Because only probability and severity are systematically varied, the safest statements about a potential “efficiency” measure would be that increasing either probability or severity of punishment likely boosts contributions and thus presumably moves the group closer to socially optimal outcomes. The paper, however, provides no numerical ratio for actual payoff vs. maximum payoff.  
   • No guidance can be drawn from this paper regarding the other parameters (e.g., changing group size, enabling chat, introducing rewards, or altering MPCR), because the paper neither manipulates them nor speculates on their effect on any efficiency measure.  
   • In summary, there is little that can be concluded about “efficiency” specifically, beyond the fact that increasing either punishment probability or punishment severity is associated with more contribution (and presumably more total surplus), with severity having the larger quantitative effect in this particular design.
reference_APA: Anderson, LR & Stafford, SL (2003). Punishment in a regulatory setting: Experimental evidence from the VCM. JOURNAL OF REGULATORY ECONOMICS.

Abstract: Impersonal cooperation among strangers enables societies to create valuable public goods, such as infrastructure, public services, and democracy. Below I go through the 15 design parameters one‐by‐one and report exactly what the paper says about each of them and, crucially, whether the paper ever links **systematic variation of that parameter to the SIZE of a punishment treatment effect on group efficiency** (or on any other dependent variable).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1. Number of players (group size)  
   • Mentioned? YES.  Coded as “group size (log-transformed)”, ranging from 2 to 324 (Mdn = 3.5).  
   • Systematic prediction about the punishment treatment effect? NO.  
   • Other results: In the global meta-regression, group size had no significant main effect on cooperation (b = -0.042, p = .186).

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? YES.  Coded as “Repetitions” (one-shot vs. repeated).  
   • Systematic prediction about punishment effect? NO.  
   • Other results: Repetitions was not significant in the global sample (b = 0.034, p = .343).

3. Is chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned? YES.  Coded as “Communication (present vs. absent/mixed)”.  
   • Systematic prediction about punishment effect? NO.  
   • Other results: Communication increased baseline cooperation (b = 0.532, p < .001).

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
   • Mentioned? YES.  Captured by “Number of choice options” (dichotomous vs. continuous).  
   • Systematic prediction about punishment effect? NO.  
   • Other results: Continuous choice raised cooperation (b = 0.128, p = .001).

5. Contribution default (withdrawal from a public pool)  
   • Mentioned? NO.  
   • Prediction? NO.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? PARTIALLY.  Pay-off structure summarized by the K-index (0–1; higher = less conflict).  
   • Systematic prediction about punishment effect? NO.  
   • Other results: Higher K strongly increased baseline cooperation (b = 0.737, p < .001).

7. Punishment cost per unit  
   • Mentioned? NO (the database only codes whether *some* sanction mechanism exists).  
   • Prediction about punishment effect? NO.

8. Punishment magnitude per unit  
   • Mentioned? NO.  
   • Prediction? NO.

9. Whether a reward option exists  
   • Mentioned? NO (punishment and reward are lumped together in the “Sanctions present” dummy).  
   • Prediction about punishment effect? NO.

10. Reward cost per unit  
   • Mentioned? NO.  
   • Prediction? NO.

11. Reward magnitude per unit  
   • Mentioned? NO.  
   • Prediction? NO.

12. End-game known (do players know the last round)?  
   • Mentioned? NO.  
   • Prediction? NO.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Mentioned? NO.  
   • Prediction? NO.

14. Do punished players learn the punisher’s identity?  
   • Mentioned? NO.  
   • Prediction? NO.

15. Do rewarded players learn the rewarder’s identity?  
   • Mentioned? NO.  
   • Prediction? NO.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
   • The paper’s only dependent variable is “cooperation rate” (logit-transformed proportion contributed or binary cooperate/defect).  
   • It never analyzes group efficiency, total group payoff, or average individual payoff.  
   • Thus “efficiency” ≠ the variable used.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   Six: (1) group size, (2) number of rounds (repetitions), (3) chat, (4) all-or-nothing vs. continuous choice, (6) MPCR proxy (K-index), and a coarse presence/absence of sanctions (touches tangentially on 7–11 but without costs/magnitudes).

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss **their effect on the punishment treatment effect**?  
   Zero.  The study never separates “punishment” vs. “no-punishment” conditions to compute a treatment effect, let alone efficiency.

D. Predictions you could make (solely from this paper) about how the 15 parameters – singly or in interaction – influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency  
   • The paper offers virtually no evidence that can be generalized to punishment-induced changes in efficiency.  
   • All you can infer is descriptive: cooperation tends to be higher when the game’s structural incentives are more benign (higher K), when chat is allowed, when sanctions of *some* kind are available, and when choices are continuous.  
   • Whether these factors would amplify or dampen the *incremental* effect of introducing punishment on *efficiency* is left completely unresolved by the authors.  Any prediction would have to be speculative and lie outside the paper’s content.

In short, the paper is informative about baseline cooperation but says nothing about how punishment, let alone the 15 specific design parameters, modulates group efficiency.

Author Full Names: Sterelny, Kim
Article Title: Cooperation, Culture, and Conflict
Source Title: BRITISH JOURNAL FOR THE PHILOSOPHY OF SCIENCE
Keywords Plus: WEALTH TRANSMISSION; HUNTER-GATHERERS; GROUP SELECTION; EVOLUTION; PUNISHMENT; RECIPROCITY; ORIGINS; COEVOLUTION; MORTALITY; MIND
Abstract: In this article I develop a big picture of the evolution of human cooperation, and contrast it to an alternative based on group selection. The crucial claim is that hominin history has seen two major transitions in cooperation, and hence poses two deep puzzles about the origins and stability of cooperation. The first is the transition from great ape social lives to the lives of Pleistocene cooperative foragers; the second is the stability of the social contract through the early Holocene transition to complex hierarchical societies. The first of these transitions is driven, at least initially, by individual advantage: cooperation paid off for individual foragers, initially through mutualist interaction, then through reciprocation. This argument leads to a reanalysis of the role of violence and the nature of the freeriding threat to cooperation. But the conditions that select for cooperative individuals in the Pleistocene were eroded in the Pleistocene-Holocene transition. So we need an alternative account of the survival, and indeed the expansion, of cooperation in the Holocene. Group selection driven by intercommunal conflict really may well be central to this second transition.

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different from one another?

Its focus is on whether cooperation persists or collapses, how free‐rider threats (especially from “bullies”) are contained, and the role of group selection in different historical periods. These outcomes (such as “origins and stability of cooperation”) differ from a measurable concept like “group efficiency” in a public goods game.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

Article Title: High strength-of-ties and low mobility enable the evolution of third-party punishment
Source Title: PROCEEDINGS OF THE ROYAL SOCIETY B-BIOLOGICAL SCIENCES
Author Keywords: third-party punishment; evolutionary game theory; structured populations
Keywords Plus: ANTISOCIAL PUNISHMENT; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; RESIDENTIAL-MOBILITY; REPLICATOR DYNAMICS; COOPERATION; SELF; REPUTATION; REWARD; GAME
Abstract: As punishment can be essential to cooperation and norm maintenance but costly to the punisher, many evolutionary game-theoretic studies have explored how direct punishment can evolve in populations. Compared to direct punishment, in which an agent acts to punish another for an interaction in which both parties were involved, the evolution of third-party punishment (3PP) is even more puzzling, because the punishing agent itself was not involved in the original interaction. Despite significant empirical studies of 3PP, little is known about the conditions under which it can evolve. We find that punishment reputation is not, by itself, sufficient for the evolution of 3PP. Drawing on research streams in sociology and psychology, we implement a structured population model and show that high strength-of-ties and low mobility are critical for the evolution of responsible 3PP. Only in such settings of high social-structural constraint are punishers able to induce self-interested agents toward cooperation, making responsible 3PP ultimately beneficial to individuals as well as the collective. Our results illuminate the conditions under which 3PP is evolutionarily adaptive in populations. Responsible 3PP can evolve and induce cooperation in cases where other mechanisms alone fail to do so.

Below, each of the 15 public–goods-game parameters is examined in the light of what is actually contained in Roos et al. (2014).  
For every parameter I state  

(1) Whether the paper even introduces that parameter (and its value, if any), and  
(2) Whether the paper reports or predicts what would happen to the **punishment treatment effect** when the parameter is systematically varied.  
“Punishment treatment effect’’ is understood here as the difference between a setting **with** punishment and an otherwise identical setting **without** punishment.  
Whenever the paper reports a numerical pattern I quote it; if nothing is said, I say so explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------  
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER

1. Number of players in the group  
   (1) Mentioned only once: all simulations use a population of 1 000 agents (p. 7, Fig. 2 caption).  
   (2) Never varied; no statements about how changing population size would change any treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) There is no finite “round’’; the evolutionary model runs for 5 000 generations and is then averaged.  
   (2) Not varied; no predictions.

3. Is chat enabled?  
   (1) Not part of the model.  
   (2) No discussion.

4. All-or-nothing contributions?  
   (1) Yes.  Each dyadic “cooperation game’’ is binary: agents either “Cooperate’’ (pay cost c) or “Defect’’ (pay 0).  
   (2) The binary nature is fixed; the effect of switching to a continuous contribution scale is never explored.

5. Is the contribution a default that can be moved back?  
   (1) Not applicable.  
   (2) No discussion.

6. Marginal-per-capita return / Multiplication factor  
   (1) The analogue is the benefit of cooperation b (with cost c = 1).  b is systematically varied in Figure 1 (surface plots).  
       Values displayed: b≈2 to b≈8.  
   (2) Effect reported (though not on “efficiency’’ but on *proportion of responsible 3PP* and *cooperation rate*):  
       • At average node degree d = 4 (high strength-of-ties) and mobility m = 0, the long-run proportion of responsible punishers is ≈1 for any b≥3 and falls below 1 for b≈2.  
       • At low strength-of-ties (d = 14) or high mobility (m≥0.2) the proportion is ≈0 across all b.  
       No efficiency numbers are given; therefore no direct numerical treatment effect on efficiency can be extracted.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher (λ)  
   (1) Fixed at λ = 1 in every simulation (Fig. 1 caption and elsewhere).  
   (2) Never varied; no predictions.

8. Punishment magnitude to the target (ρ)  
   (1) Fixed at ρ = 3.  
   (2) Never varied; no predictions.

9. Are rewards possible?  
   (1) No reward stage exists.  
   (2) No discussion.

10. Reward cost  
    Not applicable.

11. Reward magnitude  
    Not applicable.

12. Is the horizon (number of rounds) common knowledge?  
    (1) No such notion; the evolutionary model is indefinite.  
    (2) No discussion.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    (1) Agents *do* know each neighbour’s **punishment strategy** (this is labelled “punishment reputation’’), but they do *not* observe monetary outcomes.  
    (2) The effect of hiding or showing reputation/outcomes is not varied; no predictions.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed to the punished?  
    (1) Not modelled.  Pay-offs accrue automatically; reputation is assumed to be public, but who carried out any single act is irrelevant.  
    (2) No discussion.

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
    Not applicable (no rewards).

--------------------------------------------------------------------  
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables actually analysed  
   • Proportion of *responsible third-party punishers* in the population  
   • Cooperation rate (percentage of cooperative actions)  
   • The authors state qualitatively that overall pay-off increases when responsible 3PP emerges, but they never graph or tabulate *efficiency* (total pay-off divided by the cooperative maximum).  
   Thus, **efficiency is not used as an outcome variable in the paper**.

B. Which of the 15 parameters appear anywhere in the paper?  
   5 of 15:  
   (1) Number of players (fixed = 1 000)  
   (4) All-or-nothing contributions (binary cooperate/defect)  
   (6) Benefit-of-cooperation parameter b (MPCR analogue)  
   (7) Punishment cost λ (fixed)  
   (8) Punishment magnitude ρ (fixed)

C. For how many parameters does the paper examine the *effect of systematically varying* that parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
   Only **one** parameter—the benefit-of-cooperation b (parameter 6).  
   Even here, the reported outcome is *proportion of responsible punishers* / *cooperation*, not efficiency.

D. Predictions one can make, restricted strictly to what the paper shows  
   • Higher MPCR / larger benefit b makes it easier for punishment to induce cooperation; therefore, if one were to compute efficiency, the *increment* created by adding punishment should increase with b under high strength-of-ties/low mobility, but would remain near zero under low strength-of-ties or high mobility.  
   • Because λ and ρ were never varied, the paper supplies no basis for predicting how changing punishment cost or severity would affect efficiency.  
   • No information is provided on any of the remaining 13 parameters, so **no further predictions about their main or interaction effects on efficiency can be extracted from this paper.**

In short, the article is almost entirely orthogonal to the 15-parameter framework of laboratory public-goods games: it varies population-structure variables (strength-of-ties and mobility) that are *not* on the list, and it tracks cooperation and strategy frequencies rather than economic efficiency.

Abstract: Economic interactions often take place in open communities, where agents are free to leave in order to join a more preferred community. Tiebout (1956) conjectured that voting with feet might generate considerable efficiency gains, since individuals with different preferences sort themselves into those communities that suit them most. Below we walk through the list of 15 parameters exactly in the order given in the prompt.  
For each parameter we state  

(1) whether (and where) the paper explicitly mentions the parameter and its value, and  
(2) whether the paper provides any prediction or quantitative evidence on how *systematically varying* that parameter would change the “punishment treatment effect” (i.e., the difference in outcomes between a setting **with** and **without** peer-punishment).  Numerical effect sizes are reported whenever they can be read directly from the paper’s text, figures or tables.

---------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned: yes.  Every independent “population” contains 12 players (p. 8, Section 3.1).  
   (2) Systematic variation: none.  The number of players is fixed at 12 in every condition; no prediction is offered about changing it.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Mentioned: yes.  Exactly 30 periods (p. 6, §3.3 “The game described above is repeated for 30 periods”).  
   (2) No variation and no prediction.

3. Chat enabled?  
   (1) Mentioned: yes.  “No communication is allowed” (Appendix A, “Please notice”).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

4. All-or-nothing contribution decision?  
   (1) Mentioned: yes.  Subjects can choose any integer contribution 0–20 tokens (p. 4, “Each player … may contribute an integer amount …”).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

5. “Contribution default / withdrawal” option  
   (1) Not mentioned at all – the game is the standard VCM where tokens begin in the private account and can be *added* to the public project.  
   (2) No discussion.

6. Marginal Per-Capita Return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   (1) Mentioned: yes.  MPCR = a = R/n with R fixed at 1.6; Table 1 lists a for n = 2…12.  MPCR therefore *changes endogenously* when community size changes.  
   (2) Not *systematically* varied by the experimenters.  In the discussion of Result 6 (p. 12) the authors note that a lower MPCR “decreases the individual monetary incentives to contribute” and cite Isaac & Walker (1988), but they give no numerical estimate of the effect inside their own data, nor any prediction about exogenously changing MPCR.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   (1) Mentioned: yes.  One punishment point costs the punisher 1 token (p. 4).  
   (2) Fixed; no prediction about varying it.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss suffered by the target)  
   (1) Mentioned: yes.  Each punishment point deducts 3 tokens from the target (p. 4).  
   (2) Fixed; no prediction.

9. Whether a reward option exists  
   (1) Mentioned: yes.  VF-REW has only rewards; VF-PUN has only punishment.  
   (2) *Systematic variation:* The paper directly contrasts these two regimes.  
       • Mean contribution (across 30 periods and both communities) is 14.5 tokens in VF-PUN vs 10.0 in VF-REW (p. 9, Result 1), a *45 % higher* contribution level with punishment.  
       • Efficiency (total payoff divided by the cooperative optimum) is *not* reported, so only contribution data are available.  
       • Therefore the only quantitative effect size we can extract is: ΔContributions ≈ +4.5 tokens (or +45 %) when “reward” is replaced by “punishment”.  No efficiency number is provided.

10. Reward cost to rewarder  
    (1) Mentioned: yes, cost = 1 token (p. 4).  
    (2) Fixed; no prediction.

11. Reward magnitude (gain to recipient)  
    (1) Mentioned: yes, +3 tokens (p. 4).  
    (2) Fixed; no prediction.

12. Is the time horizon known?  
    (1) Mentioned: yes.  Participants are told that there will be 30 rounds (Appendix A).  
    (2) Not varied; no prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes displayed?  
    (1) Mentioned: yes.  At the end of every round, players see each member’s contribution, punish/reward points sent & received, and payoffs in *both* communities (p. 5 and Appendix A).  
    (2) Fixed; no prediction.

14. Knowledge of the identity of a punisher  
    (1) Mentioned: yes.  The display order is randomly reshuffled each period so identity is *concealed* (“it is not possible to identify any group member”, Appendix A).  
    (2) Not varied; no prediction.

15. Knowledge of the identity of a rewarder  
    (1) Same as (14): identity is concealed.  
    (2) Not varied; no prediction.

---------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables used  
    The paper’s main dependent variables are  
      • Contribution (tokens invested in the public good).  
      • Switching choice (whether a subject moves between communities).  
      • Punishment / reward tokens sent and received.  
    Efficiency (total or average payoff relative to the cooperative maximum) is *mentioned* in the abstract and discussion but is **never reported or analysed quantitatively** in the results tables or figures.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are at least mentioned?  
    14 of 15.  The only parameter completely absent is #5 (contribution default / withdrawal).

C.  For how many parameters does the paper examine the effect of *systematic variation* on the punishment treatment effect?  
    Just 2 of 15.  
      • Parameter 9 (Reward enabled vs. not) – varied between VF-REW and VF-PUN.  Effect size on contributions: +45 % for punishment relative to reward.  
      • Parameter 6 (MPCR) varies *endogenously* with community size, but this is not an experimental manipulation and no quantitative causal estimate is given.  Hence, strictly speaking, only parameter 9 is systematically varied.

D.  Predictions you could legitimately make about the punishment-treatment effect on **efficiency**, solely from this paper  
    • Allowing subjects to *self-select* into a punishment-enabled institution (open communities) greatly increases contribution levels, and in the authors’ verbal interpretation also “improves efficiency”, relative to (i) forced allocation to punishment, (ii) fixed-size punishment groups, or (iii) a reward-only institution.  
    • Because efficiency data are not shown, one must *infer* that higher contributions with punishment would translate into higher efficiency unless punishment costs outweigh the contribution gains; the paper does not provide the exact balance.  
    • The study offers no evidence on how changing group size, MPCR, punishment cost/magnitude, horizon length, anonymity, or communication would modulate that efficiency gain.  Therefore, beyond the single insight that “punishment beats reward when people can vote with their feet”, the paper supplies **little to no quantitative basis** for predicting how the other 14 parameters (or their interactions) would affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.
reference_APA: Guererk, Oezguer, Irlenbusch, Bernd & Rockenbach, Bettina (2014). On cooperation in open communities. JOURNAL OF PUBLIC ECONOMICS.

Authors: Harrell, A; Simpson, B
Author Full Names: Harrell, Ashley; Simpson, Brent
Article Title: The Dynamics of Prosocial Leadership: Power and Influence in Collective Action Groups
Keywords Plus: SOCIAL DILEMMAS; PUBLIC-GOODS; INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; COOPERATION; PUNISHMENT; PROVISION; EXPECTATIONS; ORIENTATION; INCENTIVES; SANCTIONS
Abstract: This paper bridges insights from theories of collective action, power, and influence to address the conditions under which group leaders solve collective action problems. We show how leaders' behaviors impact the success of collective action groups as a whole via both power and influence processes. In a laboratory experiment, groups first completed a baseline measure of cooperation in a public good dilemma without punishment. In a second phase, the capacity to punish was introduced. One condition, the peer-sanctioning condition, was equivalent to the prevailing solution in the experimental literature on collective action, where the ability to punish others is distributed equally among all group members. In the other two conditions, only a single group leader could punish; we varied whether the person assigned to lead was other-regarding (prosocial) or self-regarding (proself). The results support our prediction that prosocial leaders increase their contributions to the group after ascending to leadership, while proself leaders reduce their contributions. Further, as expected, rank-and-file group members are influenced by leaders' contribution behaviors; as a result, prosocial-led groups as a whole were substantially more productive than proself-led groups. Indeed, as predicted, prosocial leaders were even more effective in maintaining large group contributions than the standard peer-sanctioning system. These findings suggest that putting power and influence in the right hands solves collective action problems and promotes collective welfare.

Abstract: Many communities rely upon ostracism to enforce cooperation: if an individual shirks in one relationship, her innocent neighbors share information about her guilt in order to shun her, while continuing to cooperate among themselves. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter inventory of what (if anything) the paper “Ostracism and Forgiveness” by S. Nageeb All and David A. Miller says about each of the 15 public‐goods‐game parameters you listed—specifically focusing on whether the paper:  
• discusses (and, if so, gives a value for) the parameter, and  
• makes any predictions about systematically varying that parameter’s effect on the “punishment treatment effect” for any dependent variable (especially efficiency).  

Because the paper does not actually study a standard public goods game with numeric punishment costs or contributions, nearly all of the canonical “public goods parameters” go unmentioned. Wherever the paper does not discuss a parameter, or does not provide any predictions for how changing it would affect punishment (much less efficiency), that is stated explicitly.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The paper considers a society of n ≥ 3 players (e.g., see Section II).  
     – It also presents a three‐player illustrative example (Section I) and generalizes to n players (n ≥ 3).  
   • Any prediction from varying this parameter?  
     – The paper does derive a condition “r < 2λ(n – 3)” in Theorem 2 that ensures a “temporary ostracism” equilibrium yields higher payoffs than permanent ostracism. However, this discussion is framed in terms of overall feasibility of certain equilibria rather than any explicit change in a “punishment treatment effect.”  
     – No numeric “effect size” is given on how more (or fewer) players systematically shift a “punishment treatment effect.”  
     – The paper does not use the term “efficiency” for these outcomes, and it does not quantify how n influences a difference between “with‐punishment” vs. “no‐punishment” treatments in a public goods–style experiment.  

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper models an ongoing (potentially infinite‐horizon) setting with interactions arriving stochastically (Poisson processes). It does not discuss a finite or known number of rounds, nor systematically vary the number of rounds.  
   • Any prediction from varying this parameter?  
     – No mention.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned?  
     – Not in the sense of “chat” as in typical public goods experiments. The paper does analyze “evidentiary communication” between partners (i.e., revealing subsets of one’s private history).  
   • Any prediction from varying this parameter?  
     – No. The paper does not treat “having chat vs. no chat” as a systematically varied parameter.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper studies a “variable stakes” framework for repeated interactions. There is no mention of forced all‐or‐nothing contributions.  
   • Any prediction?  
     – No mention.

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., do players start with endowments and move money back)?
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The model uses a repeated‐game approach (with chosen effort levels / stakes), not a standard “endowment → contribution” public goods paradigm.  
   • Any prediction?  
     – No mention.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The authors’ setting does not employ the classic linear public goods MPCR; instead, they use T(φ) and V(φ) as effort‐benefit functions.  
   • Any prediction?  
     – No mention.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper examines ostracism (refusal to cooperate with a deviator) but does not parametrize a “cost” of punishing that is paid by the punisher.  
   • Any prediction?  
     – No mention.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted for each unit of punishment)
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. Punishment here appears in the form of permanently or temporarily ostracizing someone, rather than deducting numeric units.  
   • Any prediction?  
     – No mention.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned?  
     – Briefly. The paper’s “Rewarding Whistleblowers through Asymmetric Play” extension (Section IV) acknowledges that one could offer higher continuation payoffs to a whistleblower.  
   • Any prediction from systematically varying reward vs. no reward?  
     – No. The paper does not provide data or models that systematically vary “reward enabled vs. disabled.” No numeric effect size is given.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Mentioned?  
      – No. While “rewarding whistleblowers” is discussed, the authors do not formalize a cost‐per‐reward unit.  
    • Any prediction?  
      – No mention.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded per unit of reward)
    • Mentioned?  
      – No. Same reasoning: the text mentions the possibility of “benefiting a whistleblower” but not any fixed or explicit magnitude.  
    • Any prediction?  
      – No mention.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Mentioned?  
      – No. The model uses indefinite or ongoing interactions.  
    • Any prediction?  
      – No mention.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained or lost each round)?
    • Mentioned?  
      – Not in these terms. The authors assume private monitoring (only each pair sees its own interaction) and rely on strategic “gossip” about deviations. No systematic variation of information display is studied.  
    • Any prediction?  
      – No mention.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Mentioned?  
      – The paper does presume that if you are ostracized, you experience refusal to cooperate from your partners, but it does not systematically vary “visibility” of the punisher.  
    • Any prediction?  
      – No mention.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Mentioned?  
      – No. There is no standard “rewarder” role.  
    • Any prediction?  
      – No mention.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   • The paper focuses on players’ equilibrium payoffs and the highest “stakes” (effort levels) that can be sustained under different enforcement regimes (bilateral vs. permanent ostracism vs. temporary ostracism with forgiveness). Although these payoffs speak to how cooperation might increase, the paper does not use the term “group efficiency” or compute a ratio of “actual total payoff” to “maximum possible payoff.”  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Only two parameters receive explicit mention in any direct sense:  
     (1) The number of players (n).  
     (9) The possibility of rewarding someone (in an extension), though not as an on/off parameter in a standard public goods sense.  
   • All other parameters (including number of rounds, MPCR, punishment cost, punishment magnitude, reward cost/magnitude, known vs. unknown horizon, etc.) do not appear.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, the paper only provides a systematic condition involving the number of players n—namely that when n is large (and r < 2λ(n – 3)), temporary ostracism can outperform permanent ostracism. However, it never frames this in terms of a numeric “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency. There is no effect‐size statistic, only an inequality describing when an improved equilibrium is feasible.  
   • Thus, effectively none of the 15 parameters are discussed in a way that directly maps onto your request (i.e., “systematically vary a parameter to see how punishment treatments raise or lower efficiency”).  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of this paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper’s content does not map cleanly onto typical public goods–experiment parameters (e.g., punishment cost/magnitude, MPCR, or number of rounds). The central takeaways revolve around how permanent vs. temporary ostracism can or cannot exceed bilateral enforcement as a way to incentivize cooperation, given private and strategic communication.  
   • Consequently, the paper offers little basis for predicting the punishment treatment effect on “efficiency” for any of the 15 parameters except to note that with more players (n) and sufficient patience (r small relative to λ), one can sustain higher effort (i.e., more cooperation) under a “forgiveness” regime. This is still not reported in terms of efficiency, nor is it reported as an effect of systematically varying each parameter in a standard public goods sense.  

In short, the bulk of your listed parameters go completely undiscussed, and no numeric estimates or direct efficiency comparisons appear for any.

Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS; ETHNORACIAL DIVERSITY; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; FIELD EXPERIMENT; 2ND-GENERATION; GERMANY; TRUST; CITY
Abstract: Recent waves of immigration to Western nations have fueled a debate over the consequences of ethnic diversity for social cohesion. One prominent argument in this debate holds that diversity is detrimental to trust and cooperation because individuals in heterogeneous communities face difficulties in enforcing social norms across ethnic lines. We examine this proposition in a field experiment involving real-life interactions among residents of multiethnic German neighborhoods. We find significant ethnic asymmetries in the pattern of norm enforcement: Members of the majority native German population are more active in sanctioning norm violations, while ethnic minorities are more likely to find themselves the target of sanctions. We interpret these results in light of prevailing status inequalities between ethnic minorities and the native majority. We further calculate that, as a result of ethnic discrimination, social control is likely to rise in communities with moderate minority population shares.

Authors: Leimar, O
Author Full Names: Leimar, O
Article Title: Repeated games: A state space approach
Keywords Plus: REPEATED PRISONERS-DILEMMA; EXTENSIVE 2-PERSON GAMES; TIT-FOR-TAT; EVOLUTIONARY STABILITY; FINITE AUTOMATA; STRATEGY; COOPERATION
Abstract: Repeated games, such as the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma (IPD), are often used as idealised models of social interactions. Here, I develop a state space approach to the study of two-player, repeated games. A strategy is represented by way of a state space, where a player's choice of action depends on the current state, and where the actions performed can cause transitions from one state to another. This kind of representation provides a possible link between a game theoretical analysis and concepts from mechanistically oriented ethology, where an individual's state is viewed as made up of motivational variables. Using the concept of a limit ESS for a game in the extensive form, I derive a number of fundamental results for state space strategies. Conditions ensuring purity of a limit ESS are given, as well as a characterisation of the most important class of pure limit ESSs. The theoretical analysis covers games with and without a role asymmetry and also games where players move alternately. To illustrate the state space approach, I apply the theoretical results to three examples. First, for the role symmetric IPD, I find a great number of pure limit ESSs, and relate these to the strategies most frequently studied previously. I also discuss whether there can be randomised limit ESSs, concluding that although this is possible, none have been found so far. Second, as a game possessing a role asymmetry, I study a simplified model of social dominance. I concentrate on the question of whether punishment administered by a dominant can determine the allocation of a resource between the dominant and a subdominant. The game turns out to have limit ESSs with this property, but there are also stable strategies where the dominant lacks control. Third, I analyse an alternating Prisoner's Dilemma, which is a natural model to investigate the evolution of reciprocal altruism. No stable strategy for this game has been described previously. Of the limit ESSs I find, one is of particular interest, in that it closely corresponds to the notion of reciprocal altruism as conceived by Trivers. (C) 1997 Academic Press Limited.

Below I go through the 15 parameters one‐by‐one.  
For each parameter I state  

(1) whether it is mentioned in the paper and, if so, what concrete value(s) or symbol(s) are given;  

(2) whether the paper makes any prediction about how *systematically varying* that parameter would change the “punishment treatment effect.”  
Because the paper never measures “efficiency” (total group payoff divided by the cooperative maximum) and never runs a punishment-versus-no-punishment comparison, I interpret “punishment treatment effect” here as “whether strategies that contain a punishment component can be evolutionary stable (limit-ESS) and under which parameter ranges.”  If the paper does not link the parameter to that question, I report “no prediction.”  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
(1) Mentioned: All games analysed are **two-player** (IPD, dominance game, alternating PD).  
(2) No variation; no prediction.

2. Number of rounds (or length of the interaction)  
(1) Replaced by the continuation probability ω (0<ω<1).  
    • Many explicit values: ω = 0.34, ω = 0.99 in Table 2; algebraic thresholds such as ω > (T–R)/(R–P) for Pavlov, ω > (T–R)/(T–P) for Grim, ω > c/b for Reciprocity, etc.  
(2) Yes—systematic predictions:  
    – Pavlov is a limit-ESS only when ω > (T–R)/(R–P).  
    – Grim is a limit-ESS when ω > (T–R)/(T–P).  
    – CTFT requires both ω > (T–R)/(R–S) and ω > (P–S)/(R–S).  
    – Reciprocity (alternating PD) is a limit-ESS when ω > c/b.  
    Hence increasing “round length” (larger ω) enlarges the parameter region in which punishment-using strategies are stable; shortening the interaction makes them unstable.

3. Chat enabled?  
(1) Not mentioned (no communication in any model).  
(2) No prediction.

4. All-or-nothing contribution format  
(1) Not part of the paper.  
(2) No prediction.

5. Contribution default / endowment framing  
(1) Not part of the paper.  
(2) No prediction.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
(1) Not used. Pay-offs are expressed only with the usual PD symbols (T,R,P,S) or with cost/benefit (c,b).  
(2) No prediction.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
(1) Appears only in the dominance game as the parameter **c** (e.g., c = 0.3 in one numerical illustration; general constraints 0 < c < v).  
(2) No systematic variation.  The paper states a condition (0 < c < v) but does not trace how changing *c* alters stability beyond that inequality.

8. Punishment magnitude to the target  
(1) Appears as **d** in the dominance game.  A stability condition for the “Quarrel” strategy requires d > 2v.  
(2) Some qualitative prediction: higher d (relative to v) broadens the range in which punishment maintains dominance (Quarrel is a limit-ESS when d > 2v and ω high).  Beyond this inequality no systematic mapping is given.

9. Whether a reward option is enabled  
(1) Never mentioned.  
(2) No prediction.

10. Reward cost  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) No prediction.

11. Reward magnitude  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) No prediction.

12. Do players know the final round?  
(1) Not discussed.  All models assume indefinite horizon with continuation probability ω, which players are presumed to know.  
(2) No prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
(1) Not discussed.  
(2) No prediction.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
(1) Not applicable—two-player setting makes identity obvious.  
(2) No prediction.

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
(1) Not applicable—reward option absent.  
(2) No prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY  

A. Dependent variables  
• The paper does **not** use “group efficiency.”  
• Main dependent concepts: (i) evolutionary stability (limit-ESS vs. not), (ii) expected stationary pay-off W(x) for each role/state, (iii) number of limit-ESS strategies that exist for given parameters (Table 2).  These differ from efficiency because they concern strategy stability, not realized total pay-offs relative to a cooperative benchmark.

B. Parameters that are mentioned  
4 of 15:  
1 (Number of players = 2), 2 (Round length via ω), 7 (Punishment cost c), 8 (Punishment magnitude d).  All others are absent.

C. Parameters for which *systematic* effects on punishment stability are analysed  
Only 2 of 15:  
• Parameter 2 (ω) – several explicit functional thresholds.  
• Parameter 8 (d) – one inequality (d > 2v) determining when punishment can stabilise dominance.  
(Parameters 7, 1 only appear descriptively, not varied.)

D. Predicting the punishment treatment effect on **efficiency** using only this paper  
The paper gives virtually no direct leverage:  
– Efficiency is never computed.  
– “Punishment” is embedded in specific strategies (Grim, CTFT, Tyranny, etc.) and their stability hinges mainly on ω and, in one model, on d relative to v.  
Therefore, the safest prediction is extremely limited: longer expected interactions (higher ω) and more severe punishment of the target relative to its cost (high d, low c) make punishment-based strategies more likely to be stable; but the consequences for efficiency (total pay-off relative to the cooperative maximum) cannot be quantified from what is provided.

In short, only the continuation probability (round length) and, in one model, the punishment magnitude relative to the benefit, are systematically linked to whether punishment “works.”  No other of the 15 design parameters is analysed, and the paper never measures efficiency, so no further prediction is possible.

Abstract: Recent years have seen an explosion in the diversity of partner control mechanisms hypothesised to stabilise cooperative behaviour among unrelated individuals. Game theory suggests numerous strategies, each with specific decision rules that allow cooperators to control a non-contributing partner. This diversity of hypothetical strategies seems likely to reflect diversity in the types of intraspecific cooperation and interspecific mutualism that exist in nature. It is therefore important to provide a framework that explains similarities and differences between the various hypothetical strategies and that predicts how key parameters that describe the natural history of natural systems favour different control mechanisms.    • Discussion in the paper?

     No. The model runs until absorption in either P (paladin) or U (unreformable), and the paper does not analyze how altering the total rounds would affect results.

   • Discussion in the paper?

   • Discussion in the paper?

   • Discussion in the paper?  
     No. Rehabilitation resources come from a general program, not from peer rewarders.  
   • Systematically varied or predicted effect?  
     No. Not mentioned.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   No. The paper does not use “efficiency” in the sense of total payoff or payoff relative to a maximum. Instead, it reports the following dependent variables:  
   • P/U ratio (paladins vs. unreformables) at final equilibrium.  
   • Total number of crimes per player.  
   • Total number of punishments per player.  
   • Recidivism rate.  
   These differ from an “efficiency” measure because they do not track payoff or group welfare in the standard public‐goods sense; the paper focuses on population shares and the incidence of crime.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   1) Number of players (N=400) is briefly mentioned, but not varied.  
   8) Punishment magnitude (θ) is a main parameter.  
   9) Whether a reward is enabled is captured by whether h>0.  
   11) Reward magnitude is effectively h.  
   The remaining parameters (2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 10, 12, 13, 14, 15) are not discussed as such.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on punishment treatment when systematically varied?  
   • Punishment magnitude (θ, parameter #8).  
   • Presence and magnitude of a “carrot” (h, parameter #9 and #11).  
   In total, the paper systematically varies two broadly corresponding parameters (θ, h). It compares outcome measures such as P/U for different values of θ and h. No other parameter is systematically varied.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?
   Because “efficiency” (in the conventional public‐goods sense) is never measured or discussed, and because most of the listed parameters are not even mentioned in this paper, there is little basis for making predictions. The only partial insight is that increasing punishment magnitude (θ) and enabling adequate rehabilitation (larger h, over a suitable time τ) jointly reduces crime, increases the fraction of “reformed” individuals, and decreases recidivism. If one were to interpret “efficiency” as “improved social outcome” in some broad sense, one could predict that a balanced combination of punishment and rehabilitation (with intermediate duration τ), as shown in the paper’s figures and discussion, would be most beneficial. No predictions can be made for the other parameters from the content of this paper.

Article Title: Human punishment is motivated by both a desire for revenge and a desire for equality
Author Keywords: Cooperation; Punishment; Inequity aversion; Altruism; Economic game; Revenge; Inequality aversion

Abstract: Humans willingly pay a cost to punish defecting partners in experimental games. However, the psychological motives underpinning punishment are unclear. Punishment could stem from the desire to reciprocally harm a cheat (i.e. revenge) which is arguably indicative of a deterrent function. Alternatively, punishment could be motivated by the desire to redress the balance between punisher and cheat. Such a desire for equality might be more indicative of a fitness-leveling function. We used a two player experimental game to disentangle these two possibilities. In this game, one player could choose to steal $0.20 from their partner. Depending on the treatment, players interacting with a stealing partner experienced either advantageous inequality, equal outcomes or disadvantageous inequality. Players could punish stealing partners, but some players had access to effective punishment (1:3 fee to fine) whereas others could only use ineffective punishment (1:1). Players who had access to effective punishment could reduce disadvantageous inequality by tailoring their investment in punishment whereas ineffective punishment did not change the relative payoffs of the individuals in the game but could be used to exact revenge. Players punished regardless of whether stealing created outcome inequality or whether punishment was ineffective at removing payoff differentials, suggesting that punishment was at least partly motivated by the desire to inflict reciprocal harm. However, in the effective punishment condition, players' tendency to punish increased if stealing resulted in disadvantageous inequality and, when possible, punishers tailored their investment in punishment to create equal outcomes. Together these findings suggest that punishment is motivated by both a desire for revenge and a desire for equality. The implications of these findings are discussed. (C) 2015 Elsevier Inc.       – “Ineffective” condition: fine = $0.05 ⇒ 1 : 1 fee-to-fine ratio.

    • Systematic variation?  Yes – 2 levels.  
      Reported effects (dependent variable = proportion of P1s who punish):  
          P2 stole & created disadvantageous inequality →  
            – Ineffective: 10 % punished (0.10 ± 0.02)  
            – Effective:   34 % punished (0.34 ± 0.02)  
          P2 stole & no disadvantageous inequality →  
            – Ineffective: 6 %  
            – Effective: 19 %  
      Thus, increasing punishment magnitude (holding cost fixed) markedly raised the tendency to punish.  
      The paper does not translate this into changes in payoff or efficiency.

9.  Reward enabled?  
    • No reward option exists in the design.  Not mentioned.

10. Reward cost  
    • Not applicable.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Not applicable.

    • Players are told it is a one-shot game.  Not varied; no prediction.
