    • P1 is told P2’s action and the monetary outcomes; P2 sees the punishment points assigned.  
    • This information structure is fixed; not experimentally varied; no prediction.

14. Whether the punished player learns the identity of the punisher  
    • Not explicitly stated.  Interaction is anonymous and only two people are involved, but this factor is not manipulated or analysed.

15. Whether a rewarded player learns the identity of the rewarder  
    • Not applicable (no reward option).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables used  
    – Binary decision to punish (yes/no).  
    – Number of punishment points purchased.

    8 of 15 are mentioned at least in passing:

    • The only concrete evidence is that when the fine imposed on the target per unit of punishment is tripled (holding the cost to the punisher constant), people punish much more often and tailor the amount they buy so as to equalise payoffs when that is possible.

Abstract: In social interactions, decision makers are often unaware of their interdependence with others, precluding the realization of shared long-term benefits. In an experiment, pairs of participants played an Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma under various conditions involving differing levels of interdependence information. Each pair was assigned to one of four conditions: No-Info players saw their own actions and outcomes, but were not told that they interacted with another person; Min-Info players knew they interacted with another person but still without seeing the other's actions or outcomes; Mid-Info players discovered the other's actions and outcomes as they were revealed over time; and Max-Info players were also shown a complete payoff matrix mapping actions to outcomes from the outset and throughout the game. With higher levels of interdependence information, we found increased individual cooperation and mutual cooperation, driven by increased reciprocating cooperation (in response to a counterpart's cooperation). Furthermore, joint performance and satisfaction were higher for pairs with more information. We discuss how awareness of interdependence may encourage cooperative behavior in real-world interactions. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter summary of what the paper does or does not discuss regarding (a) the parameter itself (and any values used in the study) and (b) any predictions about systematically varying that parameter on the “punishment treatment effect” for efficiency (or any other relevant dependent variable). Throughout, note that the paper studies an Iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma (IPD) with pairs of participants and varying “interdependence information,” rather than a public goods game with a formal punishment mechanism. Consequently, although the paper occasionally uses words like “punishment” (in reference to defecting in response to a partner’s defection), it does not examine any explicit punishment treatment, nor does it measure its impact on group efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Discussed? Yes. The experiment used pairs (two players).  
   • Any systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment? No. The paper kept the game strictly two‐player; it did not vary the number of players or discuss any effect on a punishment treatment.

2. Number of rounds
   • Discussed? Yes. Participants played 200 rounds, but the number was not revealed to them.  
   • Any systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment? No. The paper did not systematically vary the number of rounds nor link it to any punishment treatment effect.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussed? No. There is no mention of any chat or communication channel between players.  
   • Any systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment? No.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussed? Indirectly. In each round of the IPD, participants choose one of two actions (A or B), which is effectively a binary choice.  
   • Any systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment? No. The binary choice was not manipulated, and the paper does not study this in terms of a punishment mechanism or efficiency.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much to move back to their private account)?
   • Discussed? No. The IPD used a simple 2×2 payoff matrix with choices labeled A or B. There was no default contribution aspect.  
   • Any systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment? No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as a multiplication factor
   • Discussed? No. The payoff matrix remained fixed (–1, –1; 10, –10; –10, 10; 1, 1), and there was no mention of manipulating a multiplication factor or MPCR.  
   • Any systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment? No.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussed? No. Although the paper uses the phrase “punishing defection,” it is only in the sense of responding to defection by defecting in the next round (a kind of “negative reciprocity”), not a formal cost‐based punishment.  
   • Any systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment? No.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   • Discussed? No. There is no mechanism for deducting coins as punishment.  
   • Any systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment? No.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussed? No. Participants only saw a two‐action IPD with no additional reward mechanism.  
   • Any systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment? No.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Discussed? No. No formal reward mechanism was introduced.  
    • Any systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment? No.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward granted)
    • Discussed? No. No mention of a reward system at all.  
    • Any systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment? No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Discussed? Yes. The participants did not know the total number of rounds (200).  
    • Any systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment? No. The study did not systematically vary this knowledge, and it made no predictions about punishment treatments.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much their peers gained/lost each round)?
    • Discussed? Yes. In the “Mid‐Info” and “Max‐Info” conditions, participants saw both the other player’s action and outcome each round; in “Min‐Info,” they knew there was another player but did not see the other’s actions/outcomes; in “No‐Info,” they did not even know they were interacting with a partner.  
    • Any systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment? They systematically varied information disclosure but did not analyze it as a “punishment treatment.” The paper discusses how greater information changes cooperation rates and pair performance, not an explicit punishment regime or group efficiency measure.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Discussed? No. There is no formal punishment regime, and the paper does not address identifying a punisher.  
    • Any systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment? No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Discussed? No. No such mechanism exists here.  
    • Any systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper never explicitly measures “group efficiency” (actual payoffs divided by the maximum possible payoff); instead, it looks at:  
     – (1) Individual cooperation rate (frequency of choosing Action B).  
     – (2) Mutual cooperation rate (frequency of both choosing B).  
     – (3) Pair‐level performance (sum of the two players’ payoffs over 200 rounds).  
     – (4) Sum of the two players’ satisfaction ratings at the end.  
   • These are conceptually different from “efficiency” in a public goods or punishment‐based paradigm.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned or used in some form:  
     – Parameter 1 (Number of players): Always 2.  
     – Parameter 2 (Number of rounds): Fixed at 200, unknown to participants.  
     – Parameter 12 (Is the number of rounds known?): They explicitly state players do not know.  
     – Parameter 13 (Are peer outcomes shown?): This was systematically varied across conditions.  
   • The paper does not mention or manipulate the other parameters in the sense of a public goods game or punishment mechanism.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. The paper does not implement a punishment treatment (with a cost or magnitude) and does not analyze its effect on efficiency. Although “punishing defection” (by defecting back) is observed behaviorally, there is no systematic manipulation of a punishment parameter, nor any link to a public goods notion of “group efficiency.”

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not contain evidence or discussion directly addressing how introducing a punishment mechanism, or changing parameters such as the number of players or rounds, would affect group efficiency. Consequently, based solely on this text, there is little or no basis to predict how systematically varying the 15 parameters might influence any “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency. The paper’s findings center on how different levels of information (i.e., knowledge of the other’s actions, payoffs, and game structure) influence cooperation in a two‐player IPD—rather than on how punishment in a public goods game would behave under different conditions.

Below I go through the 15 parameters one-by-one and follow the five instructions literally.

────────────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER‐BY‐PARAMETER CHECK
────────────────────────────────────────────────
For each parameter I state  

(1) “Mentioned?” – whether the paper even specifies the parameter and, if so, the value(s) used;  

(2) “Systematically varied?” – whether the paper reports what happens when the parameter is deliberately changed over several levels;  

(3) “Effect on the punishment treatment effect?” – whether the paper links that variation to the **difference between a punishment and a no-punishment condition** (or any other dependent variable).  When numerical effect sizes can be read directly off a table or figure, I quote them; otherwise I keep the statement qualitative.  When the paper looks only at cooperation or average investment (not efficiency) I note that explicitly.

1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned: Yes.  A fixed lattice of N = 10 000 players (periodic 100 × 100).  
   (2) Systematically varied: No.  
   (3) Effect on punishment treatment effect: Not discussed.

2. Number of rounds (length of the game)  
   (1) Mentioned: No finite round structure; the model runs for 10 000 “generations” and then another 1 000 for statistics.  
   (2) Systematically varied: No.  
   (3) No discussion.

3. Chat enabled?  
   (1) Not mentioned.  
   (2) Not varied.  
   (3) No discussion.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   (1) Explicitly NOT all-or-nothing; the game is continuous (0 ≤ s ≤ 1).  
   (2) Not varied – only the continuous version is studied.  
   (3) No discussion.

5. Contribution default / “opt-out” frame  
   Not mentioned at all.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor (“synergy factor” r)  
   (1) Mentioned: baseline r = 4.0; Appendix B varies r.  
   (2) Systematically varied: Yes, in Appendix B (see Fig. 8).  
   (3) Effect reported: Only the **level of cooperation (average investment)** is plotted.  As r rises, cooperation increases, both when tolerance is fixed and when tolerance co-evolves.  No comparison to a no-punishment baseline is given, so no quantitative “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” is reported.

7. Punishment cost per unit (α)  
   (1) Mentioned: Yes; α ranges roughly 0–1 in Figs. 1, 2, 5.  
   (2) Systematically varied: Yes (α on the x-axis of the contour plots).  
   (3) Reported effects:  
       • For fixed tolerance h = 0.1, cooperation is high only when α is “very low or zero” (Fig. 1a).  
       • For h = 0.3, cooperation is high in most of the area where α < β (Fig. 1b).  
       • Fig. 2 (α = 0.2) shows how tolerance moderates the effect.  
       Quantitative values are colour gradients only; no numeric efficiency data.

8. Punishment magnitude / fine (β)  
   (1) Mentioned: Yes; β varied 0–1 in the same figures.  
   (2) Systematically varied: Yes.  
   (3) Effects: Increasing β (holding α fixed) “always” increases cooperation (average investment) (Fig. 1).  Again no efficiency numbers.

9. Reward enabled?  
   (1) Not in the model.  
   (2) Not varied.  
   (3) No discussion.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   Both absent.

12. Are the number of rounds known to players?  
   Not relevant / not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   Not discussed.

14. Punished player knows who punished them?  
   Not discussed.

15. Rewarded player knows who rewarded them?  
   Not applicable.

────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Dependent variables actually used  
   • Average investment (plotted in all main figures).  
   • Average tolerance (Fig. 5b) when tolerance is allowed to co-evolve.  
   • Investment distribution snapshots.  

   The paper never reports **group efficiency, total group payoff, or average payoff**.  Thus any statements about efficiency would be extrapolations, not in the paper.

B. How many of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   4 of 15:  
   – Parameter 6 (synergy factor r)  
   – Parameter 7 (punishment cost α)  
   – Parameter 8 (punishment fine β)  
   – Parameter 4 is implicitly “continuous, not all-or-nothing”, but not varied.  

   The remaining 11 parameters never appear.

C. How many parameters are *systematically varied* and linked to a treatment effect?  
   3 of 15 (6, 7, 8).  
   Even for these three, the paper only shows how they change **average investment** inside the punishment condition, or across α–β space, but it never gives a direct before-vs-after “punishment treatment effect on efficiency”.

D. Predicting punishment-treatment effects on efficiency using only this paper  
   The only safe (but still indirect) predictions are:  
   • Lower punishment cost α and/or higher fine β should raise cooperation, and therefore would likely raise efficiency if efficiency were measured.  
   • Raising the synergy factor r should raise cooperation and hence efficiency.  
   • Extremely low tolerance (h close to 0) destroys cooperation even when punishment is available; moderate tolerance maximises cooperation (Fig. 2).  
   • When α > β, punishment becomes “unreasonable” and cooperation collapses; efficiency would probably fall below the no-punishment baseline because costs are paid but cooperation is not gained.  

   Beyond those qualitative points, the paper contains no data that allow numerical predictions about efficiency, nor about any of the other 11 parameters or their interactions.

Below, each of the 15 parameters is treated in turn.  
For every parameter I report (1) whether it is mentioned anywhere in the paper, and, if so, what concrete value or qualitative description is given; and (2) whether the paper says anything about how **systematically varying** that parameter changes the size or the direction of the *punishment treatment effect* (and, where possible, whether any numerical effect size can be extracted).

────────────────────────────────────────  
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER SCAN
────────────────────────────────────────  

1. Number of players (group size)  
   (1) Mentioned qualitatively.  Page “Conceptual framework … micro-situational variables” states that “larger groups will make it more difficult to evaluate the trustworthiness of all other participants and make it easier to free-ride.”  
   (2) No systematic variation, no numbers, and no link to the punishment treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Implicitly referred to as “time horizons” in the list of micro-situational variables.  
   (2) Never manipulated, no predictions tied to punishment, no effect size.

3. Chat enabled (cheap talk)  
   (1) Explicitly mentioned.  Cheap talk is described as communication “face-to-face or in chat-rooms on the internet.”  
   (2) The paper states that adding cheap talk “leads to much higher earnings as a group” relative to a no-communication baseline *and* that high earnings can also be obtained when costly punishment is available.  However, the effect is not decomposed into (a) punishment-only, (b) chat-only, or (c) punishment × chat interactions.  No numerical effect size is provided.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
   (1) Not discussed.  
   (2) No predictions or data.

5. Contribution default / “give-back” design  
   (1) Not discussed.  
   (2) No predictions or data.

6. MPCR (marginal per-capita return) or multiplication factor  
   (1) Not discussed.  
   (2) No predictions or data.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   (1) The term “costly punishment” is used, which logically implies a positive cost, but no specific value is given.  
   (2) No systematic manipulation or quantitative results.

8. Punishment magnitude (damage done per unit)  
   (1) Not discussed.  
   (2) No predictions or data.

9. Reward enabled  
   (1) Outside of a brief listing of “graduated sanctions” and “conditional cooperation,” the word “reward” never appears in the sense of a peer-to-peer positive transfer.  
   (2) No predictions or data.

10. Reward cost  
   (1) Not discussed.  
   (2) No predictions or data.

11. Reward magnitude  
   (1) Not discussed.  
   (2) No predictions or data.

12. Is the number of rounds common knowledge?  
   (1) Not discussed.  
   (2) No predictions or data.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   (1) Not discussed.  
   (2) No predictions or data.

14. Is the punisher identified (who punished whom)?  
   (1) Not discussed.  
   (2) No predictions or data.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
   (1) Not discussed.  
   (2) No predictions or data.

────────────────────────────────────────  
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────  

A. Dependent variables actually used in the paper  
   • “Group earnings” / “total earnings”  
   • “Harvesting rate” (amount extracted)  
   • “Cooperation” (a qualitative term)  
   The word “efficiency” (total payoff ÷ optimum payoff) never appears. Earnings, harvesting rate, and cooperation are conceptually different from efficiency, although higher efficiency would generally require higher earnings *and* lower extraction.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   Five: 1 (group size), 2 (rounds as time horizon), 3 (chat/cheap talk), 7 (punishment cost, only implicit), 8 (punishment magnitude, implicit by omission).  The remaining ten parameters are not mentioned at all.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the *systematic* effect of varying the parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
   Zero.  The closest the paper gets is a qualitative statement that allowing cheap talk or costly punishment—in unspecified forms—leads to higher group earnings than the no-institution baseline.  No parameter is varied in a gradient fashion, no interaction terms are explored, and no numerical estimates are given.

D. What predictions can be made—*solely* from this paper—about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
   • Cheap talk (parameter 3) is *likely* to enhance the overall gains achievable with punishment, because both institutions are individually said to raise earnings relative to baseline.  
   • Larger group size (parameter 1) is *likely* to blunt the effectiveness of any institution—including punishment—because it “makes it more difficult to evaluate trustworthiness.”  
   • Longer or more certain time horizons (parameter 2) *may* help maintain cooperation, but the paper offers only a conjecture, not a test.  
   • For every other parameter (4–6, 7–15) the paper supplies no evidence or arguments that would allow a directional prediction limited to punishment’s impact on efficiency.  
   In short, the document provides almost no basis for quantitative or even directional predictions once the full set of 15 design parameters is introduced.

Thus, if one had to forecast punishment’s effect on efficiency using *only* this paper, one would have extremely limited guidance—essentially just the qualitative hunch that (i) combining punishment with communication is good and (ii) large groups are harder to govern. All other parameter effects remain indeterminate.

Authors: Jiang, LL; Perc, M; Szolnoki, A
Author Full Names: Jiang, Luo-Luo; Perc, Matjaz; Szolnoki, Attila
Article Title: If Cooperation Is Likely Punish Mildly: Insights from Economic Experiments Based on the Snowdrift Game
Keywords Plus: ANTISOCIAL PUNISHMENT; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; HUMAN-BEHAVIOR; EVOLUTION; CARROT; REWARD; RECIPROCITY; SANCTIONS; EMERGENCE; DYNAMICS
Abstract: Punishment may deter antisocial behavior. Yet to punish is costly, and the costs often do not offset the gains that are due to elevated levels of cooperation. However, the effectiveness of punishment depends not only on how costly it is, but also on the circumstances defining the social dilemma. Using the snowdrift game as the basis, we have conducted a series of economic experiments to determine whether severe punishment is more effective than mild punishment. We have observed that severe punishment is not necessarily more effective, even if the cost of punishment is identical in both cases. The benefits of severe punishment become evident only under extremely adverse conditions, when to cooperate is highly improbable in the absence of sanctions. If cooperation is likely, mild punishment is not less effective and leads to higher average payoffs, and is thus the much preferred alternative. Presented results suggest that the positive effects of punishment stem not only from imposed fines, but may also have a psychological background. Small fines can do wonders in motivating us to chose cooperation over defection, but without the paralyzing effect that may be brought about by large fines. The later should be utilized only when absolutely necessary.

Below is an item‐by‐item analysis of how each of the 15 parameters relates to the findings reported in the paper by Jiang et al. (2013). All statements refer strictly to what is actually stated (or not stated) in the paper. Numbers in parentheses (e.g., “p. …”) refer to page or figure/table references only when directly evident from the paper excerpt provided.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of Players
   • Mentioned? Yes. The experiment always uses groups of five players (p. 5 “groups of five”).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not vary the group size; it remains fixed at five.  
   • Any prediction about how changing this parameter would affect punishment treatment? No. The paper does not discuss or predict how changing the number of players would alter punishment’s effect on any dependent variable.

2. Number of Rounds
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each session has 25 periods/rounds (p. 9 “Each subject played 25 periods…”).  
   • Systematically varied? No. No changes in the number of periods were reported.  
   • Any prediction about how changing this parameter would affect punishment treatment? No. There is no discussion of systematically varying the number of rounds nor any prediction about its effect.

3. Is Chat Enabled Between Players?
   • Mentioned? No. There is no mention of any communication or “chat” enabled between players.  
   • Any prediction? No. The paper does not provide any prediction or result related to enabling or disabling chat.

4. Is the Contribution “All or Nothing”?
   • Mentioned? Yes, implicitly. The experiment is a Snowdrift game with a binary choice of “cooperate” or “defect” (e.g., p. 4 “They can either … start shoveling (cooperate) or … remain in the car (defect).”).  
   • Systematically varied? No. They do not shift between discrete vs. continuous contribution.  
   • Any prediction about systematically changing this? No. The paper does not discuss variations of cooperation options beyond the standard two‐choice setting.

5. Is the Contribution Default?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not mention a default contribution mechanism or any variant where participants “move funds back to their hand.” They either cooperate or defect.  
   • Any prediction? No.

6. Marginal Per Capita Return (Multiplication Factor) or Related Parameters
   • Mentioned? Yes, via the cost‐to‐benefit ratio r (p. 3–5). That ratio was systematically varied: r ∈ {0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 0.9} in the no‐punishment treatments, and at r = 0.2 or r = 0.8 in the punishment treatments.  
   • Systematically varied? Yes. They explicitly study how different r values influence outcomes.  
   • Predictions or findings on punishment effect?  
     – At low r (e.g., r = 0.2), cooperation is already relatively likely. Adding severe punishment (fine = 4) does not improve cooperation rates beyond what mild punishment (fine = 2) achieves, and also reduces average payoffs more (Fig. 3a, 3c).  
     – At high r (e.g., r = 0.8), cooperation is initially rare. Severe punishment (fine = 4) substantially raises cooperation and pushes average payoff above the mild‐punishment condition (fine = 2), making it worthwhile (Fig. 3b, 3d).  

   While they do not use the word “efficiency,” the paper’s discussion of “average payoff” is likely the closest measure to group welfare or efficiency in these experiments.

   • Numerical effect sizes stated or inferable:  
     – At r = 0.2, average payoffs (95% CI) with mild punishment (p = 2) ≈ (3.41, 3.56) vs. severe punishment (p = 4) ≈ (3.09, 3.40). Cooperation levels for p = 2 vs. p = 4 also overlap (≈ 0.65–0.89).  
     – At r = 0.8, average payoff is higher for severe punishment (≈ 2.0+ range) than for mild punishment (≈ 1.3–1.7 range). Also, cooperation rates roughly double under severe punishment.

7. Punishment Cost to Impose a Single Unit of Punishment
   • Mentioned? Yes. The cost to the punisher is always 1 (p. 6 “the punisher’s profit was reduced by a single unit”).  
   • Systematically varied? No. This cost remains constant.  
   • Any prediction about varying it? No. The paper does not speculate on how changes in the punisher’s cost might affect outcomes.

8. Punishment Magnitude (Coins Deducted from the Punished)
   • Mentioned? Yes. This is the key parameter p taking values p = 2 (mild punishment) and p = 4 (severe punishment).  
   • Systematically varied? Yes, for two treatments (Treatment II: p = 2 vs. Treatment III: p = 4).  
   • Predictions/findings:  
     – At low r = 0.2, severe punishment (p = 4) does not improve cooperation beyond mild punishment (p = 2) and reduces overall payoffs more.  
     – At high r = 0.8, severe punishment strongly increases cooperation compared to mild punishment and lifts average payoffs above no‐punishment and mild‐punishment levels (Figs. 3–6).  
   • Numerical effect sizes stated or inferable:  
     – “Effectiveness of punishment” (percentage of defectors switching to cooperate) at r = 0.8 is significantly higher for p = 4 (≈ 11%) than for p = 2 (≈ 8%) (Fig. 6b).  
     – Confidence intervals of average payoff also differ across p = 2 vs. p = 4 (Fig. 3d and discussion).

9. Whether a Reward is Enabled
   • Mentioned? Briefly in the introduction as part of broader literature on “stick vs. carrot.”  
   • Used or systematically varied? No. The experiment did not incorporate any reward.  
   • Any prediction about systematically varying reward? No.

10. Reward Cost to Grant a Single Unit of Reward
    • Mentioned? No. There was no reward implemented.  
    • Any discussion or prediction? No.

11. Reward Magnitude
    • Mentioned? No. Not implemented in the experiment.  
    • Any discussion or prediction? No.

12. Is the Number of Rounds Known to Players?
    • Mentioned? The paper states participants played 25 rounds, but it does not say whether they knew this in advance. Usually they would, but the article does not explicitly confirm it.  
    • Systematically varied or any effect discussed? No.

13. Are Peer Outcomes Shown?
    • Mentioned? The paper indicates each subject sees their own payoff and presumably knows if punishment happened for defectors, but it does not detail whether they see others’ exact payoffs or just know there was punishment.  
    • Systematically varied or any effect discussed? No.

14. When Punished, Does a Player Know Who the Punisher Is?
    • Mentioned? No. The text only says that if at least one cooperator chose to punish, all defectors in the group incur the fine. There is no statement that identifies an individual punisher to the punished.  
    • Any prediction about varying punisher identity disclosure? No.

15. When Rewarded, Does a Player Know Who the Rewarder Is?
    • Mentioned? No. There is no reward in the experiment, hence no mention.  
    • Any prediction? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Dependent Variables in the Paper and Relation to Efficiency  
   The paper does not explicitly measure “group efficiency” (= actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff). Instead, it reports:  
   • Frequency (rate) of cooperation (fC).  
   • Average payoff (sometimes also called “average profit” or “group welfare”).  
   • How often (and under what conditions) defectors switch to cooperation.  
   While “average payoff” is related to overall welfare, the paper does not use the term “efficiency” or compute “actual payoff / maximum payoff.” The main dependent variables differ in that the cooperation rate is about behavior (fraction of cooperators), whereas payoff measures monetary outcomes.

B. Which and How Many of the Fifteen Parameters Are Mentioned?  
   The paper explicitly mentions:  
   (1) Number of players (always 5),  
   (2) Number of rounds (always 25),  
   (6) Cost‐to‐benefit ratio (related to MPCR),  
   (7) Punishment cost to punisher (fixed at 1),  
   (8) Punishment magnitude p (2 vs. 4).  
   The paper does not mention parameters 3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12 (beyond stating 25 rounds), 13, 14, 15 in any way that describes systematically varying or measuring their effect. Overall, 5 of the 15 are mentioned, though only parameters #6 and #8 are truly varied.

C. For Which and How Many of the Fifteen Parameters Does the Paper Discuss Systematic Variation and Its Effect on the Punishment Treatment?  
   • Parameter #6 (the cost‐to‐benefit ratio r) is systematically varied (multiple values without punishment; r = 0.2 and 0.8 with punishment) and the paper reports that the ability of punishment (mild or severe) to raise cooperation or payoff depends strongly on whether r is low (punishment less crucial, mild is better) or high (punishment is more important, severe is better).  
   • Parameter #8 (punishment magnitude p) is systematically varied (p = 2 vs. p = 4), and the paper shows that a higher fine only improves outcomes when r is high. Otherwise, the severe fine (p = 4) lowers average payoff compared to mild punishment.  

   No other parameters are varied or discussed in terms of how their systematic changes would affect the punishment treatment effect. Thus, 2 of the 15 parameters (#6 and #8) are systematically varied and analyzed.

D. Predictions About How the 15 Parameters and Their Interactions Might Influence the Punishment Treatment Effect on Efficiency, Solely From This Paper  
   • Cost‐to‐benefit ratio (parameter #6) is central. The paper’s data suggest that if the game environment is already favorable to cooperation (low cost‐to‐benefit ratio), severe punishment does not yield sufficiently higher cooperation to offset its negative payoff impact. Conversely, if the environment is unfavorable to cooperation (high cost‐to‐benefit ratio), a more severe punishment level can boost cooperation and raise overall payoffs above what mild punishment or no punishment can achieve.  
   • Punishment magnitude (parameter #8) interacts with parameter #6: if r is low, mild punishment is enough to maintain cooperation with higher average payoffs; if r is high, severe punishment yields higher cooperation and higher average payoffs than mild punishment.  
   • The paper provides no discussion or data regarding systematically altering any of the other 13 parameters (beyond #6 and #8), so no further predictions about efficiency can be made from this particular study.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
reference_APA: Jiang, Luo-Luo, Perc, Matjaz & Szolnoki, Attila (2013). If Cooperation Is Likely Punish Mildly: Insights from Economic Experiments Based on the Snowdrift Game. PLOS ONE.

Abstract: Some peer punishment technologies may bias experimental results in unwanted ways. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter summary based on the content of the Casari (2005) paper. Following that, you will find the required four‐point summary (A–D). Please note that the paper’s chief focus is on how a “variable fine‐to‐fee ratio” can confound interpretations of punishment behavior; it does not systematically examine group efficiency as an outcome, nor does it discuss most of the 15 parameters that you listed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER DISCUSSION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

GAME STRUCTURE

1) Number of players.  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper notes that Fehr and Gächter (2000) run a public‐goods experiment in groups of four, while Carpenter (2002b) compares groups of size 5 vs. 10.  
   • Effect of systematic variation? The paper does not report how varying group size affects any “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency. It does cite Carpenter (2002b) to show that with the Fehr–Gächter (FG) punishment technology, shifting from five‐person to ten‐person groups changes the fine‐to‐fee ratio but did not significantly affect “punishment patterns.” That discussion focuses on punishment usage/frequency, not on efficiency. No numerical effect sizes on efficiency are provided.

2) Number of rounds.  
   • Mentioned? Yes, but only incidentally. Fehr and Gächter (2000) ran 10‐round sessions, some with “partner” matching and some “stranger.”  
   • Effect of systematic variation? The paper does not discuss systematically varying the number of rounds, nor does it provide any effect sizes or predictions regarding efficiency.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not discuss communication or chat.  
   • Effect of systematic variation? Not applicable (not mentioned).

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned? Indirectly, only insofar as the original FG design uses a contribution range [0 … 20]. There is no all‐or‐nothing constraint.  
   • Effect of systematic variation? Not discussed; the paper does not examine or predict how shifting from continuous contributions to all‐or‐nothing would affect punishment or efficiency.

5) Is there a contribution default?  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Effect of systematic variation? Not applicable.

MONETARY STAKES

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplier.  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Denoted by “a,” it is 0.4 in Fehr–Gächter (2000), and Carpenter (2002b) varies it from 0.30 to 0.75.  
   • Effect of systematic variation? The paper observes that changing “a” within the FG technology changes the fine‐to‐fee ratio. It notes that in Carpenter’s setup, shifting “a” from 0.30 to 0.75 leads to higher fine‐to‐fee ratios, which can alter punishment behaviors. However, there is no reported effect size and no direct statement about efficiency.

PEER INCENTIVES

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment.  
   • Mentioned? Yes. In FG (2000), the paper reproduces the cost schedule of punishment points (Table 2).  
   • Effect of systematic variation? The paper does not test or report how exogenously changing that cost schedule would affect efficiency or any other dependent variable. It only warns that the FG technology’s varying fine‐to‐fee ratio (arising partly from that cost schedule) may confound the interpretation of results.

8) Punishment magnitude (coins deducted per unit).  
   • Mentioned? Yes. In FG (2000), each punishment point reduces the target’s payoff by 10% of the target’s first‐stage earnings.  
   • Effect of systematic variation? Not discussed. The paper does not present any systematic manipulation of punishment magnitude nor any effect size linking that manipulation to efficiency.

9) Whether a reward is enabled.  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Effect of systematic variation? Not applicable.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward.  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Effect of systematic variation? Not applicable.

11) Reward magnitude (coins awarded per unit).  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Effect of systematic variation? Not applicable.

INFORMATION DISPLAY

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?  
   • Mentioned? The paper does not clarify whether FG’s participants knew it was 10 rounds or not.  
   • Effect of systematic variation? Not discussed.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players see peers’ gains/losses)?  
   • Mentioned? Indirectly. Fehr and Gächter’s setup entails observing others’ contributions for punishment decisions, but the paper does not systematically explore or vary that dimension.  
   • Effect of systematic variation? Not discussed.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Effect of systematic variation? Not applicable.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Mentioned? No (and there is no reward mechanism in the experiment).  
   • Effect of systematic variation? Not applicable.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FOUR‐POINT SUMMARY (A–D)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A) DOES THE PAPER USE GROUP EFFICIENCY AS A DEPENDENT VARIABLE? WHAT ARE THE DEPENDENT VARIABLES, AND HOW ARE THEY DIFFERENT?  
   • The paper (Casari, 2005) does not measure group efficiency (actual vs. maximum payoff) as a primary dependent variable. Rather, it focuses on:  
     – Punishment decisions (who punishes whom, how many points are assigned).  
     – The free‐rider vs. cooperator status of punishers/punished.  
     – The fine‐to‐fee ratio’s confounding role in interpreting punishment data.  
   • The paper does at times mention that in prior studies, cooperation could reach “nearly efficient” levels, but Casari’s re‐analysis is specifically about punishment use or received punishment, not about efficiency.

B) WHICH AND HOW MANY OF THE 15 PARAMETERS ARE MENTIONED IN THE PAPER?  
   • Mentioned explicitly or in passing:  
     1) Number of players (groups of four for FG; groups of five vs. ten in Carpenter).  
     2) Number of rounds (FG used ten rounds, though not systematically varied).  
     6) MPCR (denoted “a,” ex. 0.4 in FG, 0.3 or 0.75 in Carpenter).  
     7) Punishment cost schedule (Table 2, c(pᵢʲ) values).  
     8) Punishment magnitude (10% earnings deduction per punishment point).  
   • The remaining 10 parameters (3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15) are not discussed.

C) FOR WHICH AND HOW MANY OF THE 15 PARAMETERS DOES THE PAPER DISCUSS THEIR EFFECT ON THE “PUNISHMENT TREATMENT EFFECT” (FOR ANY DEPENDENT VARIABLE) WHEN SYSTEMATICALLY VARIED?  
   • Strictly speaking, the paper never frames results in terms of “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” It does note:  
     – (1) Number of players: Carpenter (2002b) varied group size under the FG technology but found “no significant differences” in punishment patterns. This is about punishing behavior, not efficiency. No numeric effect size on efficiency is given.  
     – (6) MPCR: Changing “a” is said to change the fine‐to‐fee ratio, which can alter punishment usage. However, the paper does not provide quantitative effect sizes on how that variation changes efficiency nor does it present a formal measure of the “treatment effect.”  
   • Other parameters are not systematically varied in the paper.

D) IF YOU WERE TO MAKE PREDICTIONS ON HOW THE 15 PARAMETERS AND THEIR INTERACTIONS INFLUENCE THE PUNISHMENT TREATMENT EFFECT ON EFFICIENCY SOLELY BASED ON THIS PAPER, WHAT WOULD THEY BE?  
   • The paper provides little basis for direct statements on efficiency. It underscored that a higher fine‐to‐fee ratio tends to increase usage of punishment, but it did not measure total payoffs or efficiency directly.  
   • We can only infer that if group size or MPCR changes make the fine‐to‐fee ratio higher, punishing behavior may intensify; whether that translates into higher or lower efficiency is not demonstrated in this study. Casari (2005) warns primarily that a non‐constant fine‐to‐fee ratio may bias or confound cause‐and‐effect interpretations about punishment.  

In short, there is insufficient discussion in Casari (2005) to predict how each of the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would affect efficiency under a punishment regime. The main lesson from the paper is that one must keep the fine‐to‐fee ratio constant if one aims to analyze how punishment itself influences outcomes (including efficiency). Beyond that caution, this paper does not systematically investigate how those parameters shape efficiency.
reference_APA: Casari, M (2005). On the design of peer punishment experiments. EXPERIMENTAL ECONOMICS.

Authors: Zhu, PC; Guo, H; Zhang, HL; Han, Y; Wang, Z; Chu, C
Author Full Names: Zhu, Peican; Guo, Hao; Zhang, Hailun; Han, Ying; Wang, Zhen; Chu, Chen
Article Title: The role of punishment in the spatial public goods game
Author Keywords: Peer punishment; Pool punishment; Evolutionary dynamics; Spatial games
Keywords Plus: PRISONERS-DILEMMA; COOPERATION; EMERGENCE; COEVOLUTION; EVOLUTION; NETWORKS; PROMOTES
Abstract: Though contradicting with natural selection, cooperative behaviors widely exist in practice and seem to be an effective measure to maintain the functioning of complex systems. As revealed by previous studies, punishment is capable of promoting cooperation and therefore various types of punishment are proposed. Previously, scholars mainly focus on investigating either peer punishment or pool punishment, whereas in social and biological systems, an individual might function as different roles when facing different players. Thus, we mainly investigate these two types of punishment together and the effects of punishment-type transfer on the evolutionary dynamics are further provided with sufficient analyses in this manuscript. Role of different type of punishment on cooperation seems to be related to the number of punishers (being denoted as T) among corresponding neighbors. Simulations are conducted in order to investigate the effect of threshold reflecting the punishment-type switching on evolutionary dynamics, while peer punishment is proved to be more effective than pool punishment in promoting cooperation. We hope our findings here can shed some lights on the investigation of punishment.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what the paper does (and does not) say about each of the 15 experimental or design parameters in relation to punishment and efficiency. Throughout, “the paper” refers only to the text, figures, and tables actually provided above. No additional sources or interpretations are used.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The authors place the game on an L×L lattice (with L up to 1500), resulting in L² players.  
   • Systematically varied for the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
     – No. They only note that they increase L (the lattice size) to avoid finite‐size artifacts and do not analyze how changing the number of players affects punishment outcomes or efficiency. No effect sizes or predictions about efficiency appear.

2) Number of rounds
   • Mentioned?  
     – No specific mention of a finite set of rounds or repeated discrete periods as in some experimental designs. The paper uses “Monte Carlo steps” in a spatial evolutionary model but does not treat the number of rounds as a parameter whose variation is studied.  
   • Systematically varied for the punishment treatment effect?  
     – No. No discussion in terms of round‐by‐round or finite‐horizon effects; they only consider long‐run stationary states.

3) Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned?  
     – No.  
   • Systematically varied for punishment effect?  
     – No mention at all.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned?  
     – The paper has each cooperator contribute c = 1; defectors contribute c = 0. Punishers also contribute c = 1 plus a cost for punishing. This is effectively an “all or nothing” scheme, but the paper does not label it as such.  
   • Systematically varied for punishment effect?  
     – No. They do not report changing this feature or predicting how changing it would affect punishment or efficiency.

5) Is the contribution a default (players must move money back if they do not want to contribute)?
   • Mentioned?  
     – No.  
   • Systematically varied for punishment effect?  
     – No mention at all.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The paper uses a “multiplication factor” r, which they vary from 3.0 to 5.0 in their simulations.  
   • Systematically varied for the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
     – They do systematically vary r and report how that changes strategy mixes (fractions of cooperators, punishers, and defectors). However, they do not measure or report “efficiency” (total payoff / maximum possible) or any explicit total‐payoff outcome. Instead, they discuss how, for different values of r, cooperation or defection dominates, or how punishers survive. No numeric effect size on efficiency is given.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned?  
     – The paper uses γ = 0.05 as the cost parameter for punishing, but it is a constant in the simulations.  
   • Systematically varied for punishment effect?  
     – No. They do not explore how changing γ would affect outcomes, nor do they provide effect sizes or predictions for such changes.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted for each unit of punishment)
   • Mentioned?  
     – The paper sets β = 0.5 as a fine on each defector.  
   • Systematically varied for punishment effect?  
     – No. The authors do not report any systematic variation of β. They simply fix it at 0.5.

9) Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper focuses only on punishment; rewards do not appear anywhere.  
   • Systematically varied for punishment effect?  
     – No mention at all.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Mentioned?  
      – No.  
    • Systematically varied for punishment effect?  
      – No mention at all.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)
    • Mentioned?  
      – No.  
    • Systematically varied for punishment effect?  
      – No mention at all.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Mentioned?  
      – No.  
    • Systematically varied for punishment effect?  
      – No mention at all.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much others gained/lost)?
    • Mentioned?  
      – No direct statement about displaying outcomes.  
    • Systematically varied for punishment effect?  
      – No mention at all.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who punished them?
    • Mentioned?  
      – No.  
    • Systematically varied for punishment effect?  
      – No mention at all.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who specifically rewarded them?
    • Mentioned?  
      – No. As noted, no rewards are implemented.  
    • Systematically varied for punishment effect?  
      – No mention at all.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?  
   – The paper does not discuss “group efficiency,” total payoff, or average payoff. Its core dependent variables are the long‐run fractions (frequencies) of cooperators, defectors, and punishers on the lattice. Although it discusses how punishment promotes cooperation, there is no explicit measure of actual total payoff or its ratio to the fully cooperative payoff.

B) Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – Four parameters are mentioned (albeit not always formally named):  
     1) Number of players (L²).  
     6) The multiplication factor r (analogous to MPCR).  
     7) The punishment cost γ (fixed at 0.05).  
     8) The punishment magnitude β (fixed at 0.5).  
   – The rest are not discussed at all.

C) For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable, specifically when the parameter is systematically varied?  
   – Only one parameter is systematically varied: the multiplication factor r (#6). The paper reports how varying r changes the fractions of cooperators, punishers, and defectors. Even then, the authors do not measure efficiency as an outcome variable. There is no systematic variation reported for any other parameter.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   – The paper does not analyze efficiency at all, so it offers little or no direct guidance on how these parameters would shift total payoffs versus the maximum possible. From the simulations, one can infer that higher r fosters more cooperation (and presumably higher total group payoff), so a larger multiplication factor might be expected to raise efficiency under punishment. For all other parameters, the authors do not provide predictions or data about how systematically changing them would affect efficiency (they keep costs and fines fixed, omit rewards, do not vary group size or number of rounds, etc.). Thus, there is almost no basis for predicting the effect on efficiency of any further parameter or parameter interaction beyond noting that higher r appears to encourage more cooperation, which could translate into higher efficiency.

Authors: Riedl, A; Rohde, IMT; Strobel, M
Author Full Names: Riedl, Arno; Rohde, Ingrid M. T.; Strobel, Martin
Article Title: Efficient Coordination in Weakest-Link Games
Author Keywords: Efficient coordination; Weakest-link; Minimum effort; Neighbourhood choice; Experiment
Keywords Plus: PUNISHMENT; FAILURE; COOPERATION; LEADERSHIP; SELECTION; EXAMPLE; SHOT
Abstract: Coordination problems resembling weakest-link games with multiple Pareto ranked equilibria are ubiquitous in the economy and society. This makes it important to understand if and when agents are able to coordinate efficiently. Existing research on weakest-link games shows an overwhelming inability of people to coordinate on efficient equilibria, especially in larger groups. We show experimentally that freedom of neighbourhood choice overcomes the problem and leads to fully efficient coordination. This implies substantial welfare effects with achieved welfare being about 50% higher in games with neighbourhood choice than without it. We identify exclusion of low effort providers who in response start providing high effort as the simple but effective mechanism enforcing efficient coordination. A variety of other treatments show that the efficiency result as well as the identified mechanism are robust to changes in the information condition, payoff specification, and a substantial increase in group size. Moreover, we find that neighbourhood choice boosts efficiency even when exclusion does not materially affect the excluded agent. Our results are widely applicable on the societal and organizational level, e.g. containment of diseases, fight against terrorism, and co-authorship networks.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter inventory of what the paper actually says (or does not say) about each of the 15 listed features, with special attention to whether (a) the paper even mentions or implements that feature, (b) the paper systematically varies it, and (c) if so, whether the paper reports an effect on “punishment” (in the paper’s setting, “exclusion”) and the resulting impact on efficiency or other outcomes. All statements refer strictly to what appears in the paper “Efficient Coordination in Weakest‐Link Games” by Riedl, Rohde, and Strobel.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   – Mentioned? Yes.  
     • In the main experiment, groups of size 8 (BT vs. NT) are studied.  
     • The paper also studies groups of size 24 in two additional treatments (BT‐XL vs. NT‐XL).  
   – Systematically varied? Yes: the authors compare n=8 groups to n=24 groups.  
   – Effect on “punishment treatment” (i.e. neighborhood‐choice/exclusion) and efficiency?  
     • For n=8: without neighborhood choice (BT), efficiency declines over time; with neighborhood choice (NT), efficiency converges near the maximum.  
     • For n=24: again, without neighborhood choice (BT‐XL), the group collapses to the lowest effort and low efficiency; with neighborhood choice (NT‐XL), the group converges to the highest effort and achieves very high efficiency.  
     • Although the paper does not give a numeric “effect size” labeled as “punishment effect,” the payoff (welfare) difference is large (about 61% higher total payoff in NT‐XL vs. BT‐XL).  

2. Number of rounds
   – Mentioned? Yes.  
     • All experiments use 30 repeated rounds.  
   – Systematically varied? No. No treatment changes the number of rounds from 30.  
   – Effect on punishment treatment and efficiency?  
     • The paper does not study how “increasing” or “decreasing” the number of rounds affects the exclusion/punishment mechanism or efficiency.  
     • The authors do note an endgame effect near the final round, but this is not varied experimentally.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   – Mentioned? No.  
     • The paper does not discuss enabling general (“open”) chat or messaging; there is no mention of player‐to‐player discussion.  
   – Systematically varied? No. No mention of chat at all, so nothing is systematically varied.  
   – Effect on punishment treatment and efficiency? Not discussed.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   – Mentioned? No.  
     • The paper uses a weakest‐link (minimum‐effort) coordination game with 7 discrete effort levels (1 through 7). There is nothing about forced “all in or 0.”  
   – Systematically varied? No.  
   – Effect on punishment treatment and efficiency? Not discussed.  

5. Is the contribution default (players decide how much to move from public fund back to themselves)?
   – Mentioned? No.  
     • There is no mention of a “default” mechanism of contribution: participants explicitly choose their effort between 1 and 7.  
   – Systematically varied? No.  
   – Effect on punishment treatment and efficiency? Not discussed.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   – Mentioned? Partially.  
     • The paper sets parameters a=20, b=10, c=60 in its baseline; the ratio “a/b>1” encourages higher effort equilibria.  
     • In an “alternative payoff” (NT‐AP) treatment, benefits are still proportional to neighborhood size but costs are not, effectively changing the cost‐benefit ratio.  
   – Systematically varied? Yes, in the sense that NT‐AP changes the payoff function compared to NT. The authors highlight that making costs independent of neighborhood size can raise the cost‐to‐benefit ratio for small neighborhoods.  
   – Effect on punishment treatment and efficiency?  
     • Even in NT‐AP, group outcomes remain substantially more efficient than the baseline treatment with no neighborhood choice (BT).  
     • The paper does not provide a single numerical “punishment‐effect size” for changing the cost‐to‐benefit ratio but does report somewhat lower average effort in NT‐AP (yet still far higher than in BT).  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   – Mentioned? Only implicitly.  
     • “Punishment” occurs via unilateral exclusion (dropping someone from one’s neighborhood). The paper measures ex post whether excluding someone was personally costly or beneficial.  
     • They do not treat this cost as a preset “per‐unit” parameter. Instead, it emerges from the payoff function given the neighborhood’s minimum effort.  
   – Systematically varied? No. They measure realized costs of exclusion but do not manipulate a “punishment‐cost” parameter across treatments.  
   – Effect on punishment treatment and efficiency? Not separately studied as a parametric variation.  

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from the punished)
   – Mentioned? Only implicitly.  
     • Being excluded can be costly for the excluded, but this is again an outcome of the payoff formula (fewer interactions lower one’s earnings).  
   – Systematically varied? No.  
   – Effect on punishment treatment and efficiency? Not separately modeled as a “punishment‐magnitude” parameter.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   – Mentioned? No.  
     • The paper does not feature any separate reward mechanism or “positive” peer sanction.  
   – Systematically varied? No.  
   – Effect on punishment treatment and efficiency? Not discussed.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   – Mentioned? No.  
     • No reward mechanism at all.  
   – Systematically varied? No.  
   – Effect on punishment treatment and efficiency? Not applicable.  

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded for each unit of reward)
   – Mentioned? No.  
     • Again, there is no reward option in these experiments.  
   – Systematically varied? No.  
   – Effect on punishment treatment and efficiency? Not applicable.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
   – Mentioned? Yes.  
     • In the experiments, players know in advance that there are 30 rounds (a fixed and known horizon).  
   – Systematically varied? No.  
   – Effect on punishment treatment and efficiency?  
     • The paper does not compare “known horizon” vs. “unknown horizon,” so no results on systematically varying it.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see each other’s payoffs or gains/losses)?
   – Mentioned? Yes, in two ways:  
     • In the main NT treatment, each player sees all effort choices in all previous rounds.  
     • In the NT‐IL (“information loss”) treatment, one only sees the effort history of those with whom one has actually interacted.  
   – Systematically varied? Yes. The authors compare “full information” (NT) to “restricted information” (NT‐IL).  
   – Effect on punishment treatment and efficiency (broadly, on exclusion)?  
     • The paper finds that even with severely restricted information (NT‐IL), participants still exclude low‐effort neighbors, low‐effort neighbors raise effort thereafter, and aggregate outcomes converge to high efficiency—virtually the same as with full information.  
     • No numeric “punishment‐effect size” is given, but they do show that restricted information does not undermine the beneficial effect of exclusion for group welfare.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   – Mentioned? Yes, implicitly.  
     • A subject can tell exactly which other subject did not choose to interact with them (or “dropped” them). The instructions’ screenshots show that players see proposals (or lack of proposals) at the pairwise level.  
   – Systematically varied? No. They never hide the identity of an excluder.  
   – Effect on punishment treatment and efficiency? Not separately studied via any variation.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   – Mentioned? No.
     • There is no rewarding mechanism; thus no mention of seeing “who rewarded whom.”  
   – Systematically varied? No.  
   – Effect on punishment treatment and efficiency? Not applicable.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • Yes. The paper reports and analyzes:  
     – Minimum effort chosen in the group (not the same as efficiency).  
     – Average effort (also not the same as efficiency).  
     – Actual welfare (the sum of payoffs) and a comparison to the maximum possible (which corresponds to “full efficiency”).  
   • Hence, although the authors often focus on measures like “average (or minimum) effort,” they do also explicitly use total payoff (welfare) and the percentage of the optimal (fully efficient) payoff.

B. Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form: (1) Number of players, (2) Number of rounds (but not varied), (6) Cost‐benefit parameters akin to “marginal returns,” (7) & (8) “punishment” costs and magnitudes only as outcomes of exclusion (not set exogenously), (12) Players know the total number of rounds, (13) Peer information is displayed to varying extents, (14) The identity of excluders is known.  
   • Not mentioned at all or not relevant under these authors’ design: (3), (4), (5), (9), (10), (11), (15).  

C. For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Systematically varied parameters (with discussion of how they affect exclusion/punishment‐type behavior and efficiency):  
     1) Number of players (8 vs. 24).  
     6) Payoff specification (NT vs. NT‐AP).  
     13) Extent of information about peer effort choices (NT vs. NT‐IL).  
   • For each of these, the paper shows that enabling exclusion (i.e. their neighborhood‐choice treatments) preserves or boosts group welfare to near‐efficient levels, regardless of group size, payoff specification, or information feedback.  
   • No other parameter is systematically varied for the purpose of measuring the “punishment treatment” effect.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper’s main finding is that free‐form “exclusion” of low‐effort participants (whether it is materially costly or not) is sufficient to sustain very high effort and high welfare most of the time. Hence:  
     – Larger group size (Parameter 1) does not undermine the effectiveness of exclusion; the paper’s results show that neighborhood choice still pushes the entire group to high efficiency even with n=24.  
     – Changing the cost‐benefit ratio (Parameter 6) from the baseline to the “NT‐AP” alternative payoff does reduce average effort slightly, but still remains far above the no‐exclusion baseline.  
     – Restricting how much one can see of others’ efforts (Parameter 13) does not break the efficiency‐enhancing effect of exclusion: even with “information loss,” participants still converge to high effort.  
   • The paper does not address chat (3), all‐or‐nothing (4), default contributions (5), or separate reward mechanisms (9–11, 15). Nor does it manipulate the number of rounds (2) or whether the horizon is known (12). Thus, no predictions can be made from this paper alone regarding how those unmentioned factors would affect punishment or efficiency.  

All of the above is drawn solely from the content of “Efficient Coordination in Weakest‐Link Games.”
reference_APA: Riedl, Arno, Rohde, Ingrid M. T. & Strobel, Martin (2016). Efficient Coordination in Weakest-Link Games. REVIEW OF ECONOMIC STUDIES.

Authors: Stewart, AJ; Parsons, TL; Plotkin, JB
Author Full Names: Stewart, Alexander J.; Parsons, Todd L.; Plotkin, Joshua B.
Article Title: Evolutionary consequences of behavioral diversity
Source Title: PROCEEDINGS OF THE NATIONAL ACADEMY OF SCIENCES OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
Author Keywords: behavioral diversity; cooperation; evolution; rock-paper-scissors; game theory
Keywords Plus: ZERO-DETERMINANT STRATEGIES; ITERATED PRISONERS-DILEMMA; TIT-FOR-TAT; MEMORY SIZE; WIN-STAY; COOPERATION; PUNISHMENT; EXTORTION; GAME; BIODIVERSITY
Abstract: Iterated games provide a framework to describe social interactions among groups of individuals. This body of work has focused primarily on individuals who face a simple binary choice, such as cooperate or defect. Real individuals, however, can exhibit behavioral diversity, varying their input to a social interaction both qualitatively and quantitatively. Here we explore how access to a greater diversity of behavioral choices impacts the evolution of social dynamics in populations. We show that, in public goods games, some simple strategies that choose between only two possible actions can resist invasion by all multichoice invaders, even while engaging in relatively little punishment. More generally, access to a larger repertoire of behavioral choices results in a more rugged fitness landscape, with populations able to stabilize cooperation at multiple levels of investment. As a result, increased behavioral choice facilitates cooperation when returns on investments are low, but it hinders cooperation when returns on investments are high. Finally, we analyze iterated rock-paper-scissors games, the nontransitive payoff structure of which means that unilateral control is difficult to achieve. Despite this, we find that a large proportion of multichoice strategies can invade and resist invasion by single-choice strategies-so that even well-mixed populations will tend to evolve and maintain behavioral diversity.

Below is a point‐by‐point inventory of what the paper by Stewart, Parsons, and Plotkin (2016) actually discusses with respect to the 15 listed parameters, together with whether the paper makes (or does not make) any predictions about how systematically varying each parameter would affect a “punishment treatment effect,” especially as it relates to overall payoff or “efficiency.” Where the paper is silent, no extrapolations are made beyond what the authors actually stated.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – The paper’s formal model is an iterated two‑player game, analyzed in a large well‑mixed population of size N. It does not present a standard laboratory “public goods game” with multiple players simultaneously interacting in a group. Instead, each individual in a population of size N plays pairwise (two‑player) interactions.  
     – The authors do examine how population size N can affect the evolutionary stability of certain strategies (e.g., Fig. 2 explores different values of N).  
   • Does the paper predict how systematically varying the number of players would affect a punishment treatment effect (for efficiency or any other dependent variable)?  
     – No. The paper never frames results in terms of a “punishment treatment effect,” nor does it discuss how changing the group size in a multi‑person public goods game would alter such an effect. They only note how a larger population size (N) can make certain two‑choice cooperative strategies more or less robust.

2) Number of rounds  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – The paper does not use a fixed, finite number of rounds in the sense of a normal laboratory experiment. Rather, it typically considers infinitely repeated interactions (or a long, discounted horizon).  
   • Predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – None. The paper does not investigate how varying the number of rounds (or whether participants know the horizon) would affect “punishment” or efficiency.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No.  
   • Predictions if systematically varied?  
     – Not mentioned; no predictions given.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Discussed?  
     – Not in the sense of a forced “all or nothing” design. The article compares two‑choice “cooperate or defect” models versus multichoice/continuous models, but it does not impose or study an inflexible “all or nothing” parameter.  
   • Predictions if systematically varied?  
     – None. The paper does not address forced all‑or‑nothing contributions.

5) Is the contribution default? (i.e., moving money back from the public fund)  
   • Discussed?  
     – No mention of any default or forced endowment return.  
   • Predictions if systematically varied?  
     – Not discussed; no predictions.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
   • Does the paper discuss this?  
     – Yes. Their “r” is effectively the factor by which public investments are multiplied before being shared (B = r × C). The paper systematically studies how varying r (from just above 1 to nearly 2 or beyond) affects the stability of cooperation.  
   • Does it predict systematic variation on any punishment treatment effect?  
     – They do not examine a punishment “treatment” in the usual sense. Instead, they show that when r is higher (i.e., it is more profitable to cooperate), certain two‑choice cooperative strategies can resist invasion even by more elaborate multichoice mutants. They frame the result in terms of overall cooperation or payoff, not as a “punishment effect.” They report no numeric “effect size” for a punishment treatment, only how different r values lead to changes in the evolutionary stability of cooperation or lower/higher investment equilibria.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. Although the paper uses the word “punishment” colloquially (reducing one’s contribution to retaliate), none of the typical lab‐experiment parameters (e.g., a fixed cost for punishing another player) appear.  
   • Predictions if systematically varied?

Abstract: Alone and together, climatic changes, population growth, and economic scarcity create shared problems that can be tackled effectively through cooperation and coordination. Perhaps because cooperation is fragile and easily breaks down, societies also provide individual solutions to shared problems, such as privatized healthcare or retirement planning. But how does the availability of individual solutions affect free-riding and the efficient creation of public goods? We confronted groups of individuals with a shared problem that could be solved either individually or collectively. Across different cost-benefit ratios of individually versus collectively solving the shared problem, individuals display a remarkable tendency toward group-independent, individual solutions. Below I go through the 15 requested design parameters one by one, extracting only what can be read in Nicklisch-Grechenig-Thöni (2016, “Information-sensitive Leviathans”).  For every parameter I state  

(1) whether the paper explicitly reports the parameter’s value or otherwise comments on it, and  
(2) whether the paper makes any prediction (ex-ante) or inference (ex-post) about how *systematically varying* that parameter would change the **punishment treatment effect**—i.e., the effect of having a punishment option (DecPun or CenPun) relative to NoPun—on *any* dependent variable, and in particular on group efficiency (total pay-off / maximum possible).

Because the authors vary only one design element (the accuracy of contribution signals, λ), none of the 15 parameters below is experimentally manipulated; consequently the paper contains no effect-size estimates for varying any of the 15 parameters.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER EXTRACTION
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Stated: 10 citizens + 1 authority per matching group (p. 6).  
   (2) Never varied; no discussion of how other group sizes would alter the punishment treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Stated: 32 periods, organised in eight four-period “phases” (p. 11).  
   (2) Not varied; no predictions about longer or shorter horizons.

3. Chat (free communication)  
   (1) Authors do not allow chat; the term never appears.  
   (2) No discussion of what enabling chat would do.

4. “All-or-nothing” contributions  
   (1) Contributions are discrete in 2-ECU steps from 0 to 20 (p. 6); i.e., *not* all-or-nothing.  
   (2) Not varied; no predictions about forcing all-or-nothing moves.

5. Contribution default / “opt-out” framing  
   (1) Not mentioned.  
   (2) Therefore no predictions.

6. Marginal-per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   (1) Each contributed ECU is multiplied by 1.6 and then divided among citizens present in the institution (p. 6). MPCR = 1.6 / group size.  
   (2) Held constant; no claims about other MPCRs.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   (1) Fixed at 1 ECU per point in both institutions (p. 7). In CenPun the cost is borne collectively by all other citizens.  
   (2) Not varied; no predictions.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss to target)  
   (1) Fixed at 3 ECU per punishment point (p. 7).  
   (2) Not varied; no predictions.

9. Reward enabled?  
   (1) No reward stage exists; never mentioned.  
   (2) Not discussed.

10. Reward cost  
   – Not applicable.

11. Reward magnitude  
   – Not applicable.

12. Are players told the number of rounds?  
   (1) Yes. Participants know the game lasts exactly 32 rounds (p. 11).  
   (2) This information is not manipulated; no discussion of uncertainty about the horizon.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   (1) In each period players see signals of every citizen’s contribution; at the start of a new phase they see, for every institution, the *number of citizens, mean contribution and mean profit* in each previous period (p. 12, Fig. A2).  
   (2) Level of feedback is fixed; authors never vary the amount or the aggregation level of outcome information.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
   (1) In DecPun punished citizens learn only the *total* punishment received and not which peer(s) punished them (p. 12). In CenPun the identity of the authority is common knowledge, so the origin of punishment is known.  
   (2) This anonymity difference is built-in, not manipulated. The authors note that anonymity makes targeted revenge difficult (p. 24) but offer no systematic test of how relaxing anonymity would affect efficiency.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
   – Not applicable (no rewards).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Use of “efficiency” as a dependent variable  
   • The paper reports *average individual profit* (and by construction total profit) but never divides it by the maximum possible payoff, so the efficiency ratio sensu stricto is not calculated.  
   • Other dependent variables: institutional choice (share of citizens in each regime), contribution level, total punishment, and the distribution of “misguided” vs. “free-rider” punishment.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are explicitly mentioned?  
   10 of 15: #1, #2, #3 (implicitly “no”), #4, #6, #7, #8, #12, #13, #14.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper explore the effect of *systematically varying* that parameter on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable)?  
   Zero.  None of the 15 parameters is experimentally manipulated; consequently no causal statements or effect sizes are provided for changes in those parameters.

D.  What predictions can we make—using only this paper—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
   • Because none of the parameters was varied, the paper lends almost no direct evidence for such predictions.  
   • Indirectly, one might conjecture (again, solely based on scattered remarks in the text):  
     – Larger groups might require steeper punishment schedules to deter free-riding (Eq. 7, p. 8), suggesting a potentially lower efficiency gain from punishment (#1).  
     – Higher MPCR would lower the needed punishment to sustain cooperation (Eq. 7), possibly increasing punishment’s efficiency advantage (#6).  
     – Identifying punishers (#14) could increase retaliatory cycles under imperfect information (authors allude to revenge motives), possibly decreasing efficiency, but this is speculative because not tested.  
   • For all other parameters the paper offers no basis for even a directional guess.

In short, the study is informative about how *signal accuracy* (a variable outside the present 15-item list) interacts with centralized vs. decentralized punishment, but it does not provide evidence about how changing any of the 15 listed design features would modify the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

D. Predictions one could make about the punishment-treatment effect on *efficiency* using only this review  

   • Turning reward “on” (so that punishment and reward can both be used) should raise efficiency when (i) cooperation is initially rare and (ii) the environment is noisy.  
   • Relying on punishment alone—especially *peer* punishment—often lowers efficiency because it directly removes target payoffs and can trigger retaliation.  
   • Costs and magnitudes of punishment/reward, the MPCR, information conditions, group size, number of rounds, chat, etc. cannot be linked to efficiency effects from the material in the review; the paper provides no evidence or even conjectures specific to those parameters.  

   Hence, any further prediction about how the 15 parameters or their interactions influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency would be speculative and is not warranted by the content of the paper.
