Article Title: Cultural group selection and human cooperation: a conceptual and empirical review
Author Keywords: Cultural group selection; cooperation; culture; norm psychology; institutions; altruism
Keywords Plus: STRONG RECIPROCITY; 3RD-PARTY PUNISHMENT; POLITICAL COMPLEXITY; EVOLUTIONARY-THEORY; HAMILTONS RULE; TRANSMISSION; ALTRUISM; NORMS; INSTITUTIONS; POPULATION
Abstract: Cultural group selection has been proposed as an explanation for humans' highly cooperative nature. This theory argues that social learning mechanisms, combined with rewards and punishment, can stabilise any group behaviour, cooperative or not. Equilibrium selection can then operate, resulting in cooperative groups outcompeting less-cooperative groups. This process may explain the widespread cooperation between non-kin observed in humans, which is sometimes claimed to be altruistic. This review explores the assumptions of cultural group selection to assess whether it provides a convincing explanation for human cooperation. Although competition between cultural groups certainly occurs, it is unclear whether this process depends on specific social learning mechanisms (e.g. conformism) or a norm psychology (to indiscriminately punish norm-violators) to stabilise groups at different equilibria as proposed by existing cultural group selection models. Rather than unquestioningly adopt group norms and institutions, individuals and groups appear to evaluate, design and shape them for self-interested reasons (where possible). As individual fitness is frequently tied to group fitness, this often coincides with constructing group-beneficial norms and institutions, especially when groups are in conflict. While culture is a vital component underlying our species' success, the extent to which current conceptions of cultural group selection reflect human cooperative evolution remains unclear.

• Whether the parameter is explicitly mentioned or instantiated anywhere in the text, tables or figures, and (if so) what fixed value or qualitative description is given.  
• Whether the paper makes any prediction about what would happen to a *punishment-treatment effect* if that parameter were **systematically varied**.  
• Any quantitative effect size that can be extracted (none were found).  

Throughout, “punishment-treatment effect” means the change in some outcome when a punishment stage is added to a baseline PGG.

-------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players (group size)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes, but only illustratively.  Figure 2 uses dyads (n = 2) inside a toy population of 8.  
   • Systematic-variation prediction?  No.  The paper gives no statement about how changing group size would alter the punishment effect on any outcome.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  No.  
   • Prediction if varied?  Not discussed.

3. Chat / communication allowed?  
   • Mentioned?  No.  
   • Prediction?  Not discussed.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
   • Mentioned?  No.  
   • Prediction?  Not discussed.

5. Contribution default / opt-out framing  
   • Mentioned?  No.  
   • Prediction?  Not discussed.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  No PGG language is used.  The only numbers (b = 3, c = 1) occur in Figure 2’s dyadic Prisoner-Dilemma example, not a public goods game.  
   • Prediction if MPCR changes?  Not discussed.

7. Punishment cost to punisher  
   • Mentioned?  Only qualitatively (“cost of being punished must exceed the cost of doing X”; “punishers may keep fines”).  No numerical value.  
   • Prediction if cost is varied?  None.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss to target per unit)  
   • Mentioned?  Only in the same qualitative statements; no value given.  
   • Systematic-variation prediction?  None.

9. Whether a reward option is available  
   • Mentioned?  Rewards are referenced in passing (“three Rs – reputation, reciprocation and retribution (and reward) can stabilise any behaviour”).  
   • Prediction if reward were toggled?  None.

10. Reward cost to giver  
    • Mentioned?  No numerical or conceptual detail.  
    • Prediction?  None.

11. Reward magnitude to recipient  
    • Mentioned?  No.  
    • Prediction?  None.

12. Whether the horizon (number of rounds) is known  
    • Mentioned?  No.  
    • Prediction?  None.

13. Whether peer outcomes are shown each round  
    • Mentioned?  No.  
    • Prediction?  None.

14. Punishment anonymity (does target know who punished?)  
    • Mentioned?  No.  
    • Prediction?  None.

15. Reward anonymity (does target know who rewarded?)  
    • Mentioned?  No.  
    • Prediction?  None.

-------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY  

A.  Dependent variables actually used in the paper  
    • The paper is a conceptual review; its “dependent variables” are theoretical constructs: individual fitness (biological), cultural fitness, group fitness and pay-offs in toy examples.  
    • “Efficiency” (total pay-off ÷ maximum possible pay-off) is *never* used.  When pay-offs are shown (Figure 2), they are illustrative, not empirical.  So none of the quantitative outcomes map cleanly onto the efficiency measure typically used in PGG experiments.

B.  Which of the 15 design parameters are mentioned at all?  
    • Four:  (1) number of players (only as “groups of two”), (7) punishment cost, (8) punishment magnitude, (9) presence of reward.  
    • The other eleven parameters are completely absent.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss the *effect of systematically varying* the parameter on a punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable)?  
    • Zero.  The review never manipulates or varies any PGG design feature; it simply states, in words, that “punishment can stabilise any behaviour provided the costs of being punished exceed the costs of doing X,” without modelling how different parameter levels would modify outcomes.

D.  What usable predictions can be made *solely* on the basis of this paper about how these 15 parameters (and their interactions) change the punishment treatment effect on **efficiency**?  
    • Very little.  The paper provides no empirical data, no formal models of public-goods efficiency, and no parameter sweeps.  The only qualitative hint is that punishment must be sufficiently *cost-effective* (loss to target > cost to punisher) to stabilise cooperation; from that one might infer that raising punishment magnitude or lowering punishment cost could increase efficiency, but the paper gives no numerical guidance and does not tie the argument to the efficiency metric.  For all other parameters (group size, MPCR, information conditions, chat, horizons, reward structure, etc.) the paper offers no basis for prediction.

In short, the review is invaluable for broad theorising about punishment, norms and cultural group selection, but it offers virtually no parameter-level leverage for forecasting punishment treatment effects on group efficiency in public-goods experiments.

Abstract: Violators of cooperation norms may be informally punished by their peers. How such norm enforcement is judged by others can be regarded as a meta-norm (i.e., a second-order norm). We examined whether meta-norms about peer punishment vary across cultures by having students in eight countries judge animations in which an agent who over-harvested a common resource was punished either by a single peer or by the entire peer group. Whether the punishment was retributive or restorative varied between two studies, and findings were largely consistent across these two types of punishment. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what (if anything) the paper says about each of the 15 listed design features and whether it makes any predictions about systematically varying them. All information comes solely from the paper as provided. In brief, the study focuses on the Dictator Game (DG), the Ultimatum Game (UG), and the Third‐Party Punishment Game (3PPG), run as one‐shot interactions in different societies. Its dependent variables are DG offers (generosity), UG minimum acceptable offers (2PP), and 3PPG minimum acceptable offers (3PP). There is no discussion of group efficiency (in the sense of total payoff divided by maximum possible payoff) nor any discussion of systematically varying the 15 parameters. Details appear below.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Mentioned in the paper?  
  – The paper describes a 2‐player Ultimatum Game (UG) and a 3‐player Third‐Party Punishment Game (3PPG). Hence, two or three players are involved, depending on the game.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying this parameter (effect on punishment treatment, etc.)?  
  – No. The paper does not discuss what would happen if the number of players were varied beyond these standard 2‐ and 3‐player setups.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Number of rounds
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Mentioned in the paper?  
  – The paper explicitly states that these are “one‐shot” (single‐round) games.  
• Systematic variation or predicted effect on punishment treatment?  
  – No. There is no discussion or manipulation of repeated rounds or how altering the number of rounds might change outcomes.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Is chat enabled between players?
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Mentioned in the paper?  
  – No mention of any communication between players is made; the games are described as anonymous.  
• Systematic variation or predicted effect?  
  – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4. Is the contribution "all or nothing"?
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Mentioned in the paper?  
  – No. The Dictator Game and Ultimatum Game allow offers anywhere from 0% to 100% of the stake; there is no restriction to “all or nothing.”  
• Systematic variation or predicted effect?  
  – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much to move back into their own hand)?
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Mentioned in the paper?  
  – No. Participants simply choose how much to offer (as the first player) or whether to accept/reject (as the second), not described in terms of “default contribution.”  
• Systematic variation or predicted effect?  
  – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Mentioned in the paper?  
  – No. These games (DG, UG, 3PPG) do not discuss a “multiplication factor” or MPCR of the sort found in typical public goods or linear voluntary contribution mechanisms.  
• Systematic variation or predicted effect?  
  – No.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

• Mentioned in the paper?  
  – No.  
• Systematic variation or predicted effect?  
  – No.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded per unit of reward)

• Mentioned in the paper?  
  – No.

  – No.

  – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FINAL SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   – The paper does not measure efficiency as “actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff.” Instead, it examines:  
     • DG offer (a measure of generosity)  
     • UG minimum acceptable offer (2PP)  
     • 3PPG minimum acceptable offer (3PP).

All references to “punishment” rely on standard UG (2PP) or 3PPG frameworks without experimental manipulations of these parameters.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

Authors: Grimalda, G; Pondorfer, A; Tracer, DP

Abstract: Human cooperation is enigmatic, as organisms are expected, by evolutionary and economic theory, to act principally in their own interests. However, cooperation requires individuals to sacrifice resources for each other's benefit. We conducted a series of novel experiments in a foraging society where social institutions make the study of social image and punishment particularly salient. Participants played simple cooperation games where they could punish non-cooperators, promote a positive social image or do so in combination with one another. Authors: Gao, L; Wang, Z; Pansini, R; Li, YT; Wang, RW
Author Full Names: Gao, Lei; Wang, Zhen; Pansini, Riccardo; Li, Yao-Tang; Wang, Rui-Wu
Article Title: Collective punishment is more effective than collective reward for promoting cooperation
Keywords Plus: HOST SANCTIONS; SNOWDRIFT GAME; EVOLUTION; MUTUALISM; DYNAMICS; BEHAVIOR; CONSEQUENCES; STRATEGIES; EMERGENCE; CONFLICT
Abstract: Collective punishment and reward are usually regarded as two potential mechanisms to explain the evolution of cooperation. Both scenarios, however, seem problematic to understand cooperative behavior, because they can raise the second-order free-rider problem and many organisms are not able to discriminate less cooperating individuals. Even though they have been proved to increase cooperation, there has been a debate about which one being more effective. To address this issue, we resort to the N-player evolutionary snowdrift game (NESG), where a collective punishment/reward mechanism is added by allowing some players to display punishment/reward towards all remaining players. By means of numerous simulations and analyses, we find that collective punishment is more effective in promoting cooperation for a relatively high initial frequency of cooperation or for a relatively small group. When the intensity of punishment exceeds a certain threshold, a stable state of full cooperation emerges for both small and large groups. In contrast, such state does not appear for large groups playing a NESG with reward mechanism. In the case of mutualistic interactions, finally, our results show the new payoff with collective punishment/reward can lead to the coexistence of cooperators and defectors when discrimination between these two is not possible.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter account of what (if anything) the paper says about each of the 15 parameters and whether it makes predictions about the effect of systematically varying that parameter on the punishment treatment effect. Throughout, note that the paper focuses on cooperation frequencies (and, at times, “full cooperation” states), not on efficiency (total payoff / maximum possible payoff). In places where the paper discusses “all-cooperator” states or stable equilibria, this is still about cooperation itself, not efficiency.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
1) Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper uses “group size” N throughout, systematically studying both smaller groups (e.g., N = 3, 5) and larger groups (e.g., N = 20).  
   • Effect of systematic variation? Yes (for cooperation frequency, not efficiency).  
     – Main findings:  
       – With collective punishment, sufficiently large punishment intensity can drive cooperation to a stable “all-cooperator” state even for large N.  
       – With collective reward, sustaining “all-cooperator” states becomes more difficult as N grows.  
     – The paper does not report a numerical “efficiency” effect size; it instead reports changes in cooperation frequency and stability of “all cooperator” equilibria.

2) Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? No. There is no discussion of discrete rounds or of how many rounds the players might face.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned? No. The model does not address communication or chat.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper models contributions in terms of a continuous “cooperation” vs. “defection” strategy in the multiplayer snowdrift framework; it does not present an “all or nothing” forced contribution regimen.

5) Is the contribution default?  
   • Mentioned? No. There is no discussion of default contribution or forced contribution designs.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? Not in those terms. The paper relies on cost-to-benefit ratios (c/b) in a snowdrift game context, not on a public-goods MPCR.  
   • Effect of systematic variation? The paper varies c/b (and N), but without referring to MPCR or a standard public-goods multiplier. There is no mention of how this relates specifically to a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? Only in a lumped sense (the paper’s parameter p captures “punishment intensity,” and sometimes r·p is used for the cost to punishers). However, the paper does not explicitly dissect “cost per unit of punishment” in the typical public goods sense.  
   • Effect of systematic variation? Yes, but only on cooperation frequency. The paper systematically varies p/b.  
     – Main finding: if p/b exceeds a certain threshold, a stable state of full cooperation can emerge (in small or large groups).  
     – No mention of an explicit effect size on efficiency, only on how likely the population is to converge to high cooperation.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player per unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned? Similarly lumped into the same “punishment intensity” p. The model uses terms like p(1 − 1/(N–k+1)) for the additional cost imposed. There is no place where they break out “cost” vs. “magnitude” in separate parameters.  
   • Effect of systematic variation? The paper does vary p (and thus the overall punishment inflicted), showing that stronger punishment makes all-cooperator outcomes more likely. Again, reported in terms of cooperation frequency, not efficiency.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper compares a “collective reward” mechanism to a “collective punishment” mechanism.  
   • Effect of systematic variation? The paper does consider switching from no reward to a reward regime, but it focuses on comparing reward vs. punishment for cooperation outcomes. It does not discuss efficiency outcomes.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Mentioned? Not as a standalone “cost per unit.” The paper instead defines a parameter w (or w/b) to represent the perceived intensity of the reward.  
   • Effect of systematic variation? Yes, they vary w/b and show that higher reward intensity can promote cooperation in smaller groups. However, as N grows large, reward alone is less likely to produce full cooperation; again, the paper reports no efficiency measures.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
   • Mentioned? As above, w is treated in a single parameter that captures the overall effect of reward. The paper does not separately model “cost” vs. “magnitude” as distinct variables.  
   • Effect of systematic variation? Same as parameter 10: higher w/b promotes cooperation more strongly (for small N), with no specific reference to efficiency.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper uses a replicator-dynamics framework rather than a finitely-repeated game. There is no discussion of round knowledge.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (i.e., do players see how much others gained/lost)?  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not discuss the information structure about peer outcomes.

14) When a player is punished, do they know the specific punisher’s identity?  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper emphasizes that discrimination of individual defectors is absent, but does not examine the identity of punishers at all.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Mentioned? No. Same as above; the paper does not address whether a rewarded player knows who gave the reward.

FINAL SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper focuses on the fraction of cooperators, stability of “all-cooperator” states, or mixed equilibria under punishment or reward. It does not explicitly measure efficiency (actual total payoff / max possible payoff). Thus, while they discuss whether the group can converge to full cooperation, they do not present efficiency metrics per se.  
   • Key dependent variables: (1) The frequency of cooperation at equilibrium, (2) whether “all-cooperator” states are stable, and (3) how these outcomes change as punishment or reward intensity increases.  
   • These are different from an “efficiency” measure, since the paper tracks cooperation levels and not actual or normalized payoffs.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
   • Mentioned in some form are:  
     – (1) Number of players (group size N)  
     – (7) & (8) Punishment parameters (lumped into p)  
     – (9) Whether a reward is enabled  
     – (10) & (11) Reward parameters (lumped into w)  
   • The other parameters (2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 12, 13, 14, 15) are not discussed.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when the parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Systematically varied with respect to punishment or reward outcomes (cooperation frequency), but not efficiency, are:  
     – (1) Number of players (group size N)  
     – (7)/(8) Punishment intensity p  
     – (9)/(10)/(11) Enabling and scaling reward (parameter w)  
   • No other parameters are systematically varied in the paper.

D) If you were to make predictions on how these 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • Because the paper does not measure or report efficiency, one cannot directly conclude how efficiency responds to variations in group size, punishment cost/magnitude, or reward cost/magnitude. The paper only shows that higher punishment intensity or smaller group size can drive cooperation closer to 100%. If one assumes that higher cooperation would usually raise efficiency in a public-goods-like setting, then the results might imply that collective punishment (especially when sufficiently strong) would yield higher overall efficiency than collective reward, particularly in larger groups. However, the paper itself does not quantify this.  
   • Beyond that, the paper provides no information to predict how the other parameters (number of rounds, chat, knowledge of others, etc.) would affect efficiency.

Article Title: Games of corruption: How to suppress illegal logging
Author Keywords: Line segments of equilibria; Bistability; Exploration-induced-equilibrium; Information
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; COOPERATION; INSTITUTIONS; ENFORCEMENT; RECIPROCITY; COMMUNITY; EMERGENCE; EFFICIENT; EVOLUTION
Abstract: Corruption is one of the most serious obstacles for ecosystem management and biodiversity conservation. In particular, more than half of the loss of forested area in many tropical countries is due to illegal logging, with corruption implicated in a lack of enforcement. Here we study an evolutionary game model to analyze the illegal harvesting of forest trees, coupled with the corruption of rule enforcers. We consider several types of harvesters, who may or may not be committed towards supporting an enforcer service, and who may cooperate (log legally) or defect (log illegally). We also consider two types of rule enforcers, honest and corrupt: while honest enforcers fulfill their function, corrupt enforcers accept bribes from defecting harvesters and refrain from fining them. We report three key findings. First, in the absence of strategy exploration, the harvester-enforcer dynamics are bistable: one continuum of equilibria consists of defecting harvesters and a low fraction of honest enforcers, while another consists of cooperating harvesters and a high fraction of honest enforcers. Both continua attract nearby strategy mixtures. Second, even a small rate of strategy exploration removes this bistability, rendering one of the outcomes globally stable. It is the relative rate of exploration among enforcers that then determines whether most harvesters cooperate or defect and most enforcers are honest or corrupt, respectively. This suggests that the education of enforcers, causing their more frequent trialing of honest conduct, can be a potent means of curbing corruption. Third, if information on corrupt enforcers is available, and players react opportunistically to it, the domain of attraction of cooperative outcomes widens considerably. We conclude by discussing policy implications of our results. (C) 2014 Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussed? The paper does model cooperation vs. defection as two discrete choices (e.g., “harvesters may log illegally or legally”). However, it does not present this as “all or nothing” in the sense of partial‐vs‐full contributions, nor does it systematically compare different contribution formats.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation? None. Although harvesters are either cooperators or defectors, the paper does not study how varying that binary nature would affect outcomes.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much of their endowment to move back into their hand)?
   • Discussed? No.  
     – There is no mention of defaults or partial return of an endowment.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation? None.

   • Discussed? No.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussed? No.  
     – The paper describes a fee s that harvesters pay to hire an enforcer, plus other parameters for the enforcer’s payoff, but not a per‐unit cost to “punish” as in peer‐punishment models.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation? None.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed on them)
   • Discussed? Partially.  
     – The model has a penalty A for defecting harvesters if the enforcer is honest (e.g., sections 2 and 3). A is larger than b (the benefit of cooperation to the co‐player). However, the paper does not describe a “unit‐by‐unit” imposition of punishment.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation? The paper does not systematically vary A to see how that would affect a “punishment treatment effect.” Although there are threshold conditions (A > b, etc.), the paper does not report numerical effect sizes or direct implications for changes in A on “efficiency.”

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussed? No.  
     – The paper does not mention adding rewards to counterbalance punishments.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation? None.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Discussed? No.  
     – No mention of reward systems.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation? None.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted to them)
   • Discussed? No.  
     – Rewards per se do not appear in this model.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation? None.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
   • Discussed? No.  
     – Again, the model is replicator‐based and has no finite‐round design.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation? None.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much others gained/lost each round)?
   • Discussed? No.  
     – The only comparison is via payoff‐based imitation (“social learning”), but the paper never describes whether harvesters explicitly see others’ incomes.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation? None.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Discussed? No.  
     – The paper models a hired‐enforcer framework without addressing punisher identity revelation.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation? None.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Discussed? No; and reward is not even in scope.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation? None.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ADDITIONAL NOTE: The paper does discuss “information on corrupt enforcers” (section 5). This is about being able to recognize whether an enforcer is corrupt or honest with some probability p. However, this is not the same as showing peer outcomes (parameter 13) or revealing who administered punishment (parameters 14 or 15). Instead, it is a parameter p that affects whether a corrupt enforcer is recognized as such. None of the 15 listed parameters address “the probability of identifying a corrupt enforcer,” so that particular variation (p) does not match any of the given items.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The main dependent variables in the paper are the frequencies (fractions) of different harvester strategies (cooperators vs. defectors) and of different enforcer types (honest vs. corrupt), all tracked via replicator equations.  
   • Although “payoffs” appear in the replicator dynamics, the paper does not present “group efficiency” (i.e., actual total payoff/maximum possible payoff) as a measured dependent variable. B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • None of the 15 parameters are explicitly discussed in the sense that the paper either sets or varies them directly. The model uses separate parameters (A, b, c, s, B, p, etc.) that do not correspond to those 15.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. The paper does not take any of those 15 parameters, vary them, and analyze how “punishment” changes efficiency or any other measure.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper provides no direct basis for linking any of those 15 parameters to group‐efficiency outcomes under punishment. Because it does not describe or manipulate these factors, one cannot infer how they might affect a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Hence, no meaningful predictions can be made solely from the content of the paper.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter summary of what can (and cannot) be gleaned from the paper about each of the 15 listed parameters, along with the paper’s actual focus and whether it makes (or does not make) any predictions about altering each parameter’s effect on punishment and efficiency:

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
• Discussed?  
  – The paper does consider a population of “players” (M) and random matching among them for pairwise interactions.  
  – It also considers a population of “umpires” (N).  
• Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment‐effect predictions?  
  – The paper does examine how increasing population size tends to dampen the cyclic swings in corruption. However, it does not connect this explicitly to any measure of “group efficiency” (actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff). Nor does it quantify a “punishment treatment effect” (the difference in payoff outcomes with vs. without punishment) as a function of changing M or N.  

2. Number of rounds  
• Discussed?  
  – No. The model is presented in an evolutionary (potentially infinite‐horizon) setting. The paper does not mention a specific finite number of rounds, nor whether participants know the horizon.  
• Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment‐effect predictions?  
  – No. There is no discussion of changing the number of rounds.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
• Discussed?  
  – No. There is no mention of any communication or “chat” between players.  
• Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment‐effect predictions?  
  – No.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Discussed?  
  – The paper focuses on a “donation game” (cooperate vs. defect), but it does not explicitly highlight or vary a forced binary contribution vs. partial contribution. There is no direct statement about “all‐or‐nothing” contributions as a systematic parameter.  
• Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment‐effect predictions?  
  – No.  

5. Is the contribution default? (i.e., do players move endowment from the public fund back to private?)  
• Discussed?  
  – No mention of any “default” mechanism. The paper frames each interaction as a cost–benefit donation choice (C or D), not a default contribution–withdrawal.  
• Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment‐effect predictions?  
  – No.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
• Discussed?  
  – The paper uses a “benefit b” and “cost c” in a two‐player donation game, rather than a multi‐player MPCR common in typical public‐goods experiments.  
• Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment‐effect predictions?  
  – No. The parameter b is occasionally changed, but not in a way that is framed as an MPCR or systematically linked to an “efficiency” measure.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Discussed?  
  – Not in the sense of the typical “peer punishment cost” from standard public‐goods experiments. In this model, an “umpire” punishes defectors and collects fees, but there is no explicit mention of a separate cost borne by the umpire for punishing.  
• Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment‐effect predictions?  
  – No.  

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed)  
• Discussed?  
  – Yes, the paper calls the fine on defectors “A.” Whenever an honest umpire catches a defector, the defector pays A.  
• Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment‐effect predictions?  
  – The paper does vary A to illustrate changes in the dynamic of corruption vs. honesty (e.g., Figures 1 and 3 mention A = 2 vs. A = 0.7).  
  – However, there is no explicit calculation or statement about how changing A alters a “punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.” Instead, the paper focuses on whether corruption cycles are damped or sustained under different parameter values.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
• Discussed?  
  – No. No reward mechanism is included in the model (only punishment or bribery).  
• Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment‐effect predictions?  
  – No.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Discussed?  
  – No. Rewarding is not modeled.  
• Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment‐effect predictions?  
  – No.  

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded for each unit of reward)  
• Discussed?  
  – No. Same as above.  
• Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment‐effect predictions?  
  – No.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
• Discussed?  
  – No. The paper does not deal with finite‐horizon or known‐end settings.  
• Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment‐effect predictions?  
  – No.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained or lost)?  
• Discussed?  
  – No. The model is strictly about frequency‐dependent payoffs in an evolutionary dynamic. There is no mention of players seeing each other’s outcomes.  
• Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment‐effect predictions?  
  – No.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• Discussed?  
  – The “punisher” in the model is an institution (an “umpire”), so the question of identifying a peer punisher does not arise.  
• Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment‐effect predictions?  
  – No.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
• Discussed?  
  – No reward of any kind is modeled, so this is not mentioned.  
• Systematically varied for punishment‐treatment‐effect predictions?  
  – No.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary  
A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   – The paper frames everything in terms of evolutionary stability, strategy frequencies, and cycles of corruption vs. honesty. It does discuss payoffs in passing (e.g., average payoffs of strategies) but does not present “group efficiency” (actual total payoff divided by the fully cooperative payoff) as a tracked dependent variable. Instead, the main outcomes are the prevalence of corruption vs. honesty among umpires and cooperation vs. defection among players, along with the resulting cycles.  
   
B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – The paper only mentions:  
     • (1) Number of players (M) in passing,  
     • (8) Punishment magnitude (A), though it is just called the fine.  
   – Parameters such as (b, c, f, h, B) appear, but these do not map onto the 15 listed parameters except that A aligns with “punishment magnitude.”  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable) when systematically varied?  
   – Strictly speaking, none are explicitly linked to a measured difference in “efficiency” or a “punishment treatment effect.” The paper does systematically vary A to show that different fine levels can change the dynamic from cycles to stable equilibria. But it does not frame doing so as altering a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”  

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   – The paper offers little direct guidance about group efficiency. It focuses on the strategic and evolutionary interplay between bribery, honest punishment, and players’ decisions to cooperate or defect. Because it does not analyze how total payoffs compare to a “fully cooperative” benchmark, almost no prediction can be made about group‐efficiency impacts from systematically varying these parameters.  
   – The only partial hint is that higher penalties (A) for defectors and lower monitoring costs (h) to players can help sustain more cooperation and thus presumably raise overall payoffs compared to a fully corrupt regime. However, the paper does not quantify efficiency or the change in outcomes relative to a no‐punishment baseline. Consequently, no precise predictions for “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” can be extracted from this paper.

Article Title: The choice of institutions to solve cooperation problems: a survey of experimental research
Author Keywords: Literature review; Experiments; Cooperation; Public goods; Endogenous institutional choice; Voting
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS; MINIMUM PARTICIPATION; COLLECTIVE CHOICE; TAX EVASION; PUNISHMENT; PROVISION; COALITIONS; SANCTIONS; RULES; GAME
Abstract: A growing experimental literature studies the endogenous choice of institutions to solve cooperation problems arising in prisoners' dilemmas, public goods games, and common pool resource games. Participants in these experiments have the opportunity to influence the rules of the game before they play the game. In this paper, we review the experimental literature of the last 20 years on the choice of institutions and describe what has been learned about the quality and the determinants of institutional choice. Cooperative subjects and subjects with optimistic beliefs about others often vote in favor of the institution. Almost all institutions improve cooperation if they are implemented, but they are not always implemented by the players. Institutional costs, remaining free-riding incentives, and a lack of learning opportunities are identified as the most important barriers. Unresolved cooperation problems, like global climate change, are often characterized by these barriers. The experimental results also show that cooperation tends to be higher under endogenously chosen institutions than exogenously imposed institutions. However, a significant share of players fails to implement the institution and they often perform poorly, which is why we cannot conclude that letting people choose is better than enforcing institutions from outside.

   – No. Although some designs force a full contribution under certain “institutions,” the paper does not treat “all or nothing” contributions as a systematically varied parameter.  
 • Does the paper predict an effect for punishment and efficiency?  
   – No. No mention of such a systematic variation.

5) Is the contribution default?
 • Does the paper mention or vary a “default contribution” that participants must actively reverse?  
   – No.  
 • Any predictions about how a default shapes punishment’s efficiency effect?  
   – No.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
 • Does the paper discuss MPCR/multiplication factor?  
   – Yes, for instance Kosfeld et al. (2009) compare high vs. low MPCR in a public goods setting, but not specifically to isolate the “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”  
 • Does the paper predict how systematically varying MPCR affects a punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency?  
   – No direct prediction or effect size is given. The paper notes that MPCR can alter whether participants adopt an institution, but does not analyze “punishment on efficiency” as a function of MPCR changes.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
 • Does the paper discuss punishment cost?  
   – Yes. Several studies vary how “cheap” or “expensive” it is to punish; e.g., Sutter et al. (2010) compare “low leverage” vs. “high leverage” in punishing. Markussen et al. (2014), Kamei et al. (2015), and others compare formal and informal punishments, sometimes cheap, sometimes costly.  
 • Does the paper give numeric effect sizes about how systematically changing punishment cost shifts the punishment‐vs‐no‐punishment effect on efficiency?  
   – No. The paper does note that cheaper (less costly) punishment is “more popular” or “more effective” at raising cooperation/payoffs, but it does not present quantitative estimates for how that affects efficiency (actual ÷ maximum).

8) Punishment magnitude (the deducted amount per unit of punishment)
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   – Yes, implicitly, in terms of “deterrent vs. non‐deterrent” punishments. Studies label punishments as “mild” (non‐deterrent) or “severe” (deterrent).  
 • Does the paper quantify how systematically varying magnitude changes the punishment effect on efficiency?  
   – No. It reports that “deterrent” punishments can bring cooperation close to 100%, but numeric effect sizes for efficiency changes are not reported.

9) Whether a reward is enabled
 • Does the paper discuss availability of rewards?  
   – Yes. Some studies give subjects a choice between a punishment option, a reward option, or neither (e.g., Sutter et al. 2010; Gürerk et al. 2014).  
 • Does the paper predict or quantify how toggling reward on/off changes the “punishment treatment effect on efficiency”?  
   – No. The paper only notes that reward alone tends to be less effective than punishment for raising cooperation, but does not provide numbers tied specifically to efficiency under punishment as a function of reward availability.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   – Only in broad terms of “high” vs. “low leverage” for rewarding (Sutter et al. 2010).  
 • Does the paper give effect sizes linking changes in reward cost to the punishment treatment effect?  
   – No. It does not systematically assess punish/reward cost variations for efficiency gains from punishment measures.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward)
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   – As above, only in the sense of “high reward leverage” or “low reward leverage,” but not singled out as an isolated parameter.  
 • Does the paper analyze or give numeric effects on punishment’s efficiency?  
   – No.

12) Is the number of rounds known (do players know when the game ends)?
 • Does the paper discuss this systematically?  
   – No. Some experiments presumably reveal the number of rounds; others do not. The paper does not isolate “known end round” as a systematically varied factor for a punishment effect.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much peers gained or lost)?
 • Does the paper discuss whether players observe each other’s payoffs?  
   – Yes, many designs do give feedback on payoffs or contributions (e.g., players see how each “institution” group performed).  
 • Does the paper detail how systematically changing that information display affects the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
   – No explicit effect‐size discussion. It notes that feedback fosters learning and fosters migration into punishment institutions, but does not quantify an efficiency effect.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who punished them specifically?
 • Does the paper discuss this?  
   – No. The paper’s punished participants often see someone punished them, but there is no systematic variation of whether the identity of the punisher is revealed, nor any effect on efficiency reported.

15) When rewarded, do they know who rewarded them specifically?
 • Does the paper discuss this?
   – No. As with (14), there is no systematic mention of individual rewarder identity or its effect on punishment’s impact.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY (A–D)

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how do they differ?  
   • The paper sometimes refers to “efficiency,” sometimes to group payoffs, sometimes to cooperation or contribution rates. It seldom measures efficiency strictly as (actual total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff). In many cases, “higher cooperation” or “higher average payoff” is used interchangeably with “improved efficiency.” Nonetheless, the paper does not consistently maintain a single “efficiency” measure—it uses cooperation rates, payoffs, or “efficiency rate” somewhat interchangeably, noting they can differ.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some fashion:  
     1) Number of players (varies across studies, but not systematically analyzed),  
     2) Number of rounds (often repeated vs. one‐shot),  
     6) MPCR / multiplication factor (e.g., Kosfeld et al. 2009),  
     7–8) Punishment cost and magnitude (the paper distinguishes expensive vs. cheap, deterrent vs. non‐deterrent),  
     9–11) Reward presence, cost, and magnitude (similarly, “low leverage” vs. “high leverage” reward, but without separate effect sizes),  
     13) Visibility of others’ outcomes or performance is commonly reported, but not as a systematically manipulated parameter.  

   • Not explicitly mentioned or varied:  
     3) Chat, if enabled or disabled, is occasionally noted (Ostrom et al. 1992) but not systematically studied for punishment’s effect.  
     4) “All or nothing” contributions.  
     5) Default contribution.  
     12) Whether the number of rounds is known in the sense of a “known horizon.”  
     14–15) Whether punishees/rewardees know exactly who punished/rewarded them.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • Strictly none. Although the paper notes that punishment tends to raise cooperation and can raise payoffs (sometimes labeled efficiency), it does not present a systematic “Parameter X → effect on punishment’s impact on efficiency” for any of the 15 dimensions. At most, the paper comments that “cheaper or more deterrent” punishment fosters stronger cooperation and payoff gains, but it does not give effect sizes or an explicit formula for how the punishment “treatment effect” on efficiency changes with those manipulated costs or magnitudes.

D. If you were to make predictions about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper itself provides little direct basis for parameter‐by‐parameter predictions about punishment’s effect on efficiency. It does observe that punishments that are more “deterrent” or cheaper can raise payoffs (and thus “efficiency”), and that repeated play with punishment can sustain high cooperation. Beyond these broad suggestions, the paper does not supply numeric estimates or systematic analyses that link each of your 15 parameters to the strength of the punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency.  
   • In short, one cannot glean detailed predictions from this survey alone about how each parameter (or their interactions) would alter the effect of introducing punishment on efficiency. The survey mostly aggregates findings on whether people adopt various institutions, how cooperation and payoff change, and whether those changes differ when institutions are chosen endogenously or exogenously. But it does not break down those results by systematically manipulated parameters such as number of players, cost‐per‐unit punishment, or availability of chat.

────────────────────────────────────────

Hence, based strictly on this survey article, there is little to no direct, parameter‐by‐parameter predictive content about how punishment would affect efficiency under variations in your 15 features. The paper primarily discusses overall cooperation levels and payoffs (sometimes termed efficiency), without isolating each parameter’s impact on a punish‐versus‐no‐punish comparison.

Abstract: We use skin conductance responses and self-reported hedonic valence to study the emotional basis of cooperation and punishment in a social dilemma. We argue that the availability of sanctions sets in motion a virtuous emotional circle that accompanies cooperation. Emotional reaction to free riding leads cooperators to apply sanctions. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter rundown of what the paper says and does not say, focusing strictly on its own content (including figures and tables) and on whether it discusses each parameter and/or makes systematic predictions about how varying that parameter would affect the “punishment treatment effect.” Throughout, remember that the paper itself never uses the term “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Instead, its main comparisons and analyses concern “contributions,” “punishment behavior,” “skin conductance responses (SCR),” and “hedonic valence,” rather than manipulated changes in total payoffs relative to a maximum or any other efficiency measure.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players
 • Discussed? Yes. Groups always have four players.  
 • Systematically varied or predicted about? No. The paper uses only n=4 players per group and does not study how changing the group size would affect any outcome (including contributions or punishment).

2) Number of rounds
 • Discussed? Yes. All sessions have 20 periods; participants know the game lasts exactly 20 rounds.  
 • Systematically varied or predicted about? No. There is no treatment with a different number of rounds, and the paper offers no predictions about varying the length of the interaction.

3) Is chat enabled between players?
 • Discussed? Yes, but only to say that communication is forbidden (“Communicating with the other participants during the experiment is strictly forbidden…”).  
 • Systematically varied or predicted about? No. The paper does not examine changing or allowing chat and gives no predictions for it.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
 • Discussed? Yes, indirectly. Each participant can contribute any whole‐integer amount from 0 to 20. This is not an all‐or‐nothing rule.  
 • Systematically varied or predicted about? No. The paper keeps this continuous choice (0–20) fixed and does not discuss what would happen if it were changed to an all‐or‐nothing contribution rule.

5) Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much of their endowment to move from the public fund back into their hand), or some variant?
 • Discussed? Not really. The design simply allocates 20 tokens to each subject every period, who then chooses how many tokens to place in the group account. No alternative or “default contribution” rule is studied.  
 • Systematically varied or predicted about? No mention at all.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
 • Discussed? Yes. The paper sets the group multiplier at 1.6, meaning each individual receives 0.4 per token contributed to the public good.  
 • Systematically varied or predicted about? No. They leave it fixed at 1.6 and do not explore what would happen at different MPCR values.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
 • Discussed? Yes, in Table 1. A convex cost schedule is used (1 point = 1 ECU cost, 2 points = 2 ECU, 3 points = 4 ECU, etc.).  
 • Systematically varied or predicted about? No. The paper always uses the same discrete, convex cost structure and does not compare multiple punishment‐cost regimes.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
 • Discussed? Yes, also in Table 1. Each point assigned reduces the target’s payoff by 10%.  
 • Systematically varied or predicted about? No. This 10%‐per‐point system is constant; the paper does not explore how altering it would change outcomes.

9) Whether a reward is enabled
 • Discussed? Briefly, only insofar as the design description makes it clear that no rewards are available (only punishment).  
 • Systematically varied or predicted about? No. There is no reward treatment, so the paper provides no discussion of or predictions about rewards.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
 • Discussed? No. There is no mention of any reward mechanism; the paper only studies punishment.  
 • Systematically varied or predicted about? No.

11) Reward magnitude
 • Discussed? No. Same as above: the experiment does not include reward, so nothing is said about how reward magnitude might change outcomes.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?
 • Discussed? Yes. Subjects in all treatments know there are 20 periods.  
 • Systematically varied or predicted about? No. The paper does not explore hidden endpoints or indefinite horizons.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (e.g., how much each peer gained or lost)?
 • Discussed? Partly. The experiment shows each subject the total contribution to the group fund and each group member’s individual contribution (with scrambled IDs). They also learn if they were punished and by how many total points (though not who punished them).  
 • Systematically varied or predicted about? No. The same feedback structure applies to all sessions, and there is no discussion of systematically altering what information is shown.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
 • Discussed? Yes. The paper explicitly states that the identity of the punisher is never revealed (“it was not possible for a participant to identify who had punished him”).  
 • Systematically varied or predicted about? No. This anonymity is never changed or compared to an alternative.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is?
 • Discussed? No. The experiment has no reward stage, so there is also no mention of whether a rewarder’s identity would be revealed or not.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
• The paper does not explicitly measure or report “efficiency” in the sense of (actual total payoff) / (maximum possible total payoff).  
• The authors do speak about individual payoffs in passing (e.g., reducing some or all of a participant’s payoff via punishment) and note that “the maximum feasible group payoff” would arise if everyone contributed fully. However, the core dependent variables studied are:  
  – Contribution levels (how many tokens contributed out of 20)  
  – Punishment points assigned  
  – Emotional measures, including skin conductance responses (SCR) and self‐reported valence  
• Thus, they do not formally treat “efficiency” as their main measure, and they do not report an efficiency ratio.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
Mentioned in some form:  
1 (group size of 4), 2 (20 rounds), 3 (no communication allowed), 4 (not constrained to all‐or‐nothing), 6 (MPCR=0.4), 7 (punishment cost schedule), 8 (each punishment point = 10% payoff reduction), 9 (reward is not enabled), 12 (number of rounds is known), 13 (participants see each other’s contributions and punishment points received), and 14 (punisher identity is not revealed).  
Not discussed or not present at all:  
5 (no “default contribution” condition), 10 (cost of reward), 11 (magnitude of reward), 15 (rewarder identity).  
So, in total, the paper touches on 10 of the 15 parameters in its description but does not systematically vary any of them.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect, specifically when that parameter is systematically varied?  
• The paper does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters. It keeps group size, number of rounds, cost and magnitude of punishment, and all other features fixed. Consequently, it provides no direct predictions or effect sizes about how changing any one parameter would alter the size or direction of a punishment‐based treatment effect on cooperation, payoffs, or efficiency.  
• Numerically, therefore, the count is zero: no parameter is experimentally manipulated in multiple ways other than “no punishment” vs. “punishment.” That contrast (Baseline vs. Sanction treatment) is the sole major manipulation, but it is not among the 15 parameters listed (it is simply the presence/absence of a punishment stage).

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper’s content, what would they be?  
• The paper does not connect systematic changes in those parameters to group efficiency. Its focus is on how participants’ emotions relate to cooperation and punishment under two fixed conditions (Baseline vs. Sanction), rather than on parameter shifts.  
• Since it never studies or forecasts changes in group size, MPCR, punishment cost schedules, or any other factor besides “no punishment” vs. “punishment,” one cannot draw more than very general speculation (e.g., that shifting the cost or the effectiveness of punishment might influence willingness to punish or to cooperate). But the study itself provides no direct evidence or numerical estimates. Thus, based strictly on the text, one can make little to no specific prediction about how systematically altering any of the 15 parameters would change the punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency.

Article Title: Empathy Moderates the Effect of Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation of the Right Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex on Costly Punishment
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; DECISION-MAKING; ULTIMATUM GAME; NEURAL BASIS; PSYCHOPATHY; COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; CHOICE; BASES
Abstract: Humans incur considerable costs to punish unfairness directed towards themselves or others. Recent studies using repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) suggest that the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) is causally involved in such strategic decisions. Presently, two partly divergent hypotheses are discussed, suggesting either that the right DLPFC is necessary to control selfish motives by implementing culturally transmitted social norms, or is involved in suppressing emotion-driven prepotent responses to perceived unfairness. Accordingly, we studied the role of the DLPFC in costly (i.e. third party) punishment by applying rTMS to the left and right DLPFC before playing a Dictator Game with the option to punish observed unfair behavior (DG-P). In addition, sham stimulation took place. Individual differences in empathy were assessed with the German version of the Interpersonal Reactivity Index. Costly punishment increased (non-significantly) upon disruption of the right - but not the left - DLPFC as compared to sham stimulation. However, empathy emerged as a highly significant moderator variable of the effect of rTMS over the right, but not left, DLPFC, suggesting that the right DLPFC is involved in controlling prepotent emotional responses to observed unfairness, depending on individual differences in empathy.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter review, based strictly on the content of Nelissen and Mulder (2013). All references to “the paper” or “the article” below refer solely to the text provided. Throughout, note that the dependent variable they focus on is “contributions to the group fund” (i.e., cooperation), not efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper states there were four players (p. 5: “a four‐player interaction”).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The experiment fixed the group size at four; there is no discussion or prediction about how varying the number of players would alter any punishment effects.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper describes 10 total rounds (plus a practice round). Participants were told they would not know the exact number of rounds (p. 5–6).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The number of rounds was fixed and not experimentally changed.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned? No. The article never refers to any chat or direct communication (other than disapproval messages in the social‐punishment condition). There is no separate variable about enabling or disabling live chat.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned? Indirectly. Participants could invest “some amount” of their 4 Euro endowment (p. 5). This implies a continuous choice from 0 to 4, not all‐or‐nothing.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not vary whether contributions must be all or nothing.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much of their endowment to move from the public fund back into their hand)?
   • Mentioned? No. Participants were simply told they could invest from their 4 Euro. There is no discussion of forced default contributions or reversing a default.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplier
   • Mentioned? Yes. Contributions were multiplied by 1.5 then evenly split among four players (p. 5).  
   • Systematically varied? No. They used a fixed multiplier of 1.5 and did not discuss how changing that number would affect cooperation or punishment effects.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned? Yes. Imposing a financial fine “did not reduce the punishing players’ payoff” (p. 6), so the cost to the punisher was zero.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The experiment did not manipulate different punishment costs.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from a punished player)
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each fine was 1 Euro (and could be imposed by up to three other players, so a maximum of 3 Euros deducted).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The magnitude was always 1 Euro. The paper does not discuss how changing this magnitude would modulate punishment effects.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned? No. The design compared a financial‐sanction condition and a social‐disapproval condition with a control. No reward mechanism was introduced.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Mentioned? No. There was no reward treatment in the paper.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded to a rewarded player)
    • Mentioned? No. Again, no reward treatment was used.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Mentioned? Yes. The paper explicitly stated that participants were told they would not know the number of rounds beforehand (p. 5).  
    • Systematically varied? No. There was just one procedure in which they did not know.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained or lost)?
    • Mentioned? Partly. After each round, “individual contributions were displayed on screen,” but not in a way that each contribution could be matched to a specific individual consistently (p. 5). So participants saw how much was contributed by “player X, Y, Z” but not who was who.  
    • Systematically varied? No. The same display rule was used throughout.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Mentioned? Yes. The paper states that punished players only learned “the number of players that had imposed a fine or had expressed disapproval” (p. 6). They did not learn the punisher’s identity.  
    • Systematically varied? No. This was constant in the design.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Mentioned? No. This experiment had no reward mechanism, so it is not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Summary of Required Points:

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?

   The paper does not use or report “efficiency,” defined as actual total payoff over the maximum possible total payoff of a fully cooperative group. Its main dependent variable is the “contribution” (i.e., how many Euros each participant invests into the public good). The paper also tracks the frequency of punishment assigned. Although payoffs were mentioned (participants would be paid from a randomly selected round), the analysis focuses almost exclusively on contributions to the group fund as the behavioral measure of cooperation.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

   Mentioned (in some fashion): (1) Number of players, (2) Number of rounds, (6) MPCR (the 1.5 multiplier), (7) Punishment cost (zero), (8) Punishment magnitude (1 Euro), (12) Whether the number of rounds is known (it is not), (13) Whether peer outcomes are shown (in anonymous form), and (14) Whether the punished know who punished them (they do not). That is 8 of the 15.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?

   None. The paper does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters (e.g., it does not vary the number of players, the cost of punishment, the magnitude of fines, etc.). Its main variation is whether participants can impose financial sanctions, impose social disapproval, or no punishment at all. Hence it has no direct, parametric predictions (with numerical effect sizes) about changing any of the 15 listed parameters.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

   The paper does not address efficiency, nor does it vary any of the 15 parameters. Hence very little can be inferred or predicted about how systematically changing them would alter the effect of punishment on efficiency. The study’s findings are specific to a fixed group size (4), a fixed multiplier (1.5), zero cost of punishment, and a fixed punishment magnitude (1 Euro). Because “efficiency” was neither measured nor discussed, the paper does not provide a basis for drawing parameter‐by‐parameter predictions about efficiency. Any such statements would go beyond the paper’s content, so no clear predictions can be offered.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter check against what appears explicitly in the paper “Freedom, enforcement, and the social dilemma of strong altruism” by De Silva et al. (2009). For each of the 15 parameters, I note (a) whether the paper discusses it (and, if so, in what form and with what values) and (b) whether it makes any predictions about how systematically varying that parameter would affect the “punishment treatment effect” on any outcome measure. As per your instructions, I focus strictly on what the paper itself says, without adding any outside information or speculation.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
• In the paper, two notions of “number of players” appear:  
  – Group size N (the sample of players who have the option to participate in the public good).  
  – Total population size M (the overall population from which groups of size N are drawn).  
• The paper uses N = 5 in its figures (e.g., Figure 1 and Figure 3) and sets M = 100 in various finite‐population simulations (Figures 2 and 3).  
• Although the paper does show simulations for particular values of N and M, it does not provide a systematic exploration (e.g., a table or figure) tracking how changes in either N or M would alter a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” The authors do not give a numerical effect size tied specifically to efficiency.  

2) Number of rounds  
• The paper does not mention rounds in the sense of a repeated game with a known or unknown stopping point. The model is set up in an evolutionary framework, sometimes with a Moran process, without specifying any finite number of rounds.  
• No systematic variations of “number of rounds” are discussed.  

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
• There is no mention of communication or “chat” among players.  

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Yes. Each participant either contributes a fixed cost c or does not contribute at all. In that sense, contributions are “all or nothing.”  
• The paper does not, however, examine systematically varying this rule; it is simply part of their model setup (either you pay cost c or you don’t). No numerical effect size is provided.  

5) Is the contribution default (the ability to move one’s endowment from the public fund back to oneself)?  
• The paper does not discuss any default mechanism where players automatically contribute or retract some portion of an endowment.  

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
• The paper uses r (> 1) as the multiplication factor on contributions. Examples include r = 3 in several figures and numerical simulations.  
• Although r is important in shaping outcomes, the paper does not present a systematic set of results (tables, effect sizes) on how different r values specifically change the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.  

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• The parameter γ (gamma) is the cost a punisher pays to fine defectors. The examples use γ = 1 or γ = 0.3.  
• The paper notes that punishment can succeed when c + γ < β (N − 1). However, it does not quantify how varying γ alone changes “group efficiency.” Instead, it discusses how γ shapes the stability of punishers vs. defectors. No specific effect size on efficiency is given.  

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed)  
• The parameter β (beta) is the fine deducted from a defector when punishers act. The paper states that punishers can dominate if β is large enough (relative to c and γ).  
• Again, there is no explicit measure of how varying β systematically changes the “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency. The paper focuses on which strategies prevail, not the ratio of total payoff to the maximum possible.  

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
• The paper does not include a reward mechanism. It briefly mentions in broader context that “other forms of sanctions or positive incentives are possible,” but it does not implement or analyze rewards.  

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Not discussed, since no reward mechanism is modeled.  

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted)  
• Also not discussed, for the same reason.  

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
• The paper’s models are evolutionary and do not describe any finite‐horizon or known‐ending scenario. No discussion of known vs. unknown time horizons.  

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much peers gained/lost)?  
• The paper does not consider any visibility conditions of other players’ outcomes or payoffs.  

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• Not mentioned or modeled.  

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
• Not applicable; there is no reward mechanism in this paper.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the paper’s dependent variables, and how do they differ?  
• The paper’s primary focus is on the evolutionary stability or frequencies of strategies—namely, how punishers, cooperators, defectors, and nonparticipants invade or dominate over time. Payoffs clearly matter in determining which strategies spread, but they do not explicitly track “efficiency” as “actual total payoff divided by maximum possible payoff.”  
• The paper does discuss average payoffs within each strategy, but it does not define or use “group efficiency” as a main outcome. The authors emphasize “which strategy (punisher, defector, cooperator, nonparticipant) eventually dominates the population most of the time.”

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Mentioned parameters:  
  1) Number of players (group size N, population size M)  
  4) All‐or‐nothing contributions (implicitly part of the model)  
  6) Multiplication factor r  
  7) Punishment cost γ  
  8) Punishment magnitude β  

• Not mentioned or used:  
  2) Number of rounds  
  3) Chat  
  5) Default contribution mechanism  
  9) Reward enabled  
  10) Reward cost  
  11) Reward magnitude  
  12) Known number of rounds  
  13) Visibility of peer outcomes  
  14) Punisher identity revealed  
  15) Rewarder identity revealed  

Hence, 5 of the 15 parameters receive explicit modeling or discussion (1, 4, 6, 7, 8).

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• The paper does analyze how punishment may or may not be stable depending on relations among parameters such as r, c, β, γ, N, and whether participation is voluntary or compulsory. However, it does not provide a systematic variation of any parameter that is then directly linked to a measured “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”  
• Instead, the authors look at whether punishers take over the population, how often, and under what conditions. No numerical effect sizes or tables quantify changes in efficiency as a function of systematic parameter variation.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
• Because the paper does not measure efficiency (as a ratio of actual to maximal group payoff) and does not systematically vary the 15 parameters to track changes in efficiency, the paper gives little basis for making quantified predictions.  
• Qualitatively, the paper does imply that optional participation (“freedom”) plus effective punishment can lead to higher overall payoffs than occur when defection is rampant. However, there are no direct statements or numerical estimates in terms of “efficiency” or “punishment treatment effect” for each of the 15 parameters.  
• In short, one cannot form a detailed prediction of how these parameters and their interactions would affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency from this paper alone. The authors focus on whether punishers prevail (and thereby raise cooperation rates) rather than on explicit efficiency measures.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Abstract: Strong reciprocity is an effective way to promote cooperation.
