Following that, you will find the required four-part summary (A–D).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
• Mentioned? Yes. The ultimatum game (UG) has two players (proposer and responder). The third-party punishment game (TPPG) has three players (proposer, receiver, and punisher).  
• Systematically varied, or predictions about efficiency? No. The paper does not discuss changing the number of players beyond these basic designs, nor does it analyze how varying the number would affect punishment or overall payoffs/efficiency.

2. Number of rounds
• Mentioned? Indirectly. The games were effectively played once (one-shot). There is no repeated/multi-round design.  
• Systematically varied, or predictions about efficiency? No. The paper does not discuss manipulating the number of rounds or how that would affect punishment or efficiency.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
• Mentioned? No. There is no discussion of whether participants could communicate during the game.  
• Systematically varied, or predictions about efficiency? No.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
• Mentioned? No. In the UG, DG, and TPPG, players could choose percentages (0% to 100%, in increments of 10%). There is no all-or-nothing structure.  
• Systematically varied, or predictions about efficiency? No.

5. Is the contribution default (players withdrawing from a public fund)?
• Mentioned? No. Because these are not public-goods games (they are DG/UG/TPPG), there is no design element regarding a “default” contribution.  
• Systematically varied, or predictions about efficiency? No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters (e.g., multiplication factor)
• Mentioned? No. The study did not use a public-goods game where an MPCR or multiplication factor is typically reported.  
• Systematically varied, or predictions about efficiency? No.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
• Mentioned? Partially. In the TPPG, the “punisher” (P3) can pay 20% of his or her endowment to reduce the proposer’s payoff by three times that amount. However, the paper does not refer to it as a “cost per unit” but rather a single fixed decision: pay 20% or pay nothing.  
• Systematically varied, or predictions about efficiency? No. There is no systematic manipulation of that cost.

8. Punishment magnitude (the deduction a punished player receives per unit of punishment)
• Mentioned? Partially. The TPPG multiplier is 3: if the punisher pays 20%, the proposer loses three times that amount. But this multiplier is fixed.  
• Systematically varied, or predictions about efficiency? No. The paper does not examine what would happen if the multiplier changed.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
• Mentioned? No. There is no discussion of positive rewards or “reward treatments.”  
• Systematically varied, or predictions about efficiency? No.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
• Mentioned? No.  
• Systematically varied, or predictions about efficiency? No.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward)
• Mentioned? No.  
• Systematically varied, or predictions about efficiency? No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
• Mentioned? The text implies it was a one-shot game and that participants knew there was no repetition, but the paper does not discuss any systematic variation or effect of that knowledge.  
• Systematically varied, or predictions about efficiency? No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?
• Mentioned? Not explicitly. The paper does not state whether participants could see or learn about others’ exact payoffs during or after each decision.  
• Systematically varied, or predictions about efficiency? No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
• Mentioned? Not explicitly. There is no statement about whether the punisher’s identity in the TPPG was revealed.  
• Systematically varied, or predictions about efficiency? No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
• Mentioned? No, and there was no reward mechanism in these games.  
• Systematically varied, or predictions about efficiency? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A–D Summary

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
• The paper occasionally discusses “group earnings,” particularly that Hadza group earnings in the ultimatum game were low because many low offers were rejected. However, formal “efficiency” (actual payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff in a fully cooperative scenario) is not set out as a dedicated outcome measure.  
• The primary dependent variables in the paper are (1) the amount of money offered by proposers, (2) acceptance/rejection decisions by responders, and (3) the punishment (or lack thereof) imposed by third parties.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Three parameters appear explicitly or implicitly:  
  – (1) The number of players (two in UG, three in TPPG)  
  – (7) Punishment cost (punisher pays 20%)  
  – (8) Punishment magnitude (the proposer loses 3× the amount paid by the punisher)  
• Other parameters (e.g., number of rounds, possibility of chat, MPCR, rewards) are not discussed at all.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• None. Although the paper describes the TPPG’s punishment cost and magnitude, it does not vary these factors (or any other parameters) systematically. There is no reported effect size or formal modeling of how changing these parameters might alter group payoff or “punishment treatment effects.”

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
• The paper provides virtually no direct basis for predicting how systematically changing these parameters would shift the punishment treatment effect on efficiency. It reports only the single design used (with fixed costs and magnitudes), and no further manipulations or predictions about public-goods contexts or different cost–benefit ratios. Therefore, based on this paper alone, one can make little to no specific prediction about how these 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the effect of punishment on group efficiency.

   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not treat a separate enforcement cost for the government beyond its general “strict governance cost.”  
   • Predicted effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed on them)  
   • Discussed? Yes. The paper’s parameter “P” is the penalty (punishment) imposed on enterprises if they violate regulations.  
   • Systematically varied? Partly, in numerical simulations (P = 2, 4, 6). This only shows how larger penalties lead enterprises to switch faster to “strict implementation.”  
   • Predicted effect on punishment treatment effect (for efficiency)? The paper does not measure efficiency or a “punishment treatment effect.” It only shows qualitatively that increasing P accelerates convergence to strict enterprise compliance. No numeric effect size on efficiency is given.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussed? Yes. The model includes a reward H that the local government gives the public to encourage supervision, and a subsidy αC₃ for enterprises that comply.  
   • Systematically varied? The paper does not compare a “reward on” vs. “reward off” scenario directly, but it does treat reward parameters as part of the model.  
   • Predicted effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed. The paper does not examine how enabling reward interacts specifically with punishment for “efficiency.”

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Discussed? In the paper’s payoff formulation, H is subtracted from the local government’s payoff when it rewards the public. That effectively acts as the government’s “cost” per unit of reward.  
   • Systematically varied? The paper does vary H in simulations (1, 2, 3), but it does not label H as a “cost parameter” separate from reward magnitude—rather, it is the reward itself.  
   • Predicted effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed with respect to efficiency; the paper only shows that as H rises, the public’s supervision rate grows.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted to them)  
   • Discussed? Yes. The model calls this H (for the public) and αC₃ (for enterprises).  
   • Systematically varied? Yes, for H (values 1, 2, 3). The paper shows that a larger H increases the public’s inclination to supervise, though it slows the local government’s adoption of strict governance (because of budget concerns).  
   • Predicted effect on punishment treatment effect (for efficiency)? Not discussed in those terms.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
   • Discussed? No. The paper is not framed in those terms.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Predicted effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much others gained/lost each round)?  
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not address information disclosure among players.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Predicted effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not analyze the informational aspects of identifying the punisher.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Predicted effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Discussed? No. The model merely stipulates that the local government provides H or a subsidy; there is no analysis of whether the recipient knows who gave it.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Predicted effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   No. The paper examines replicator‐dynamic stability for each party’s strategy (strict vs. nonstrict governance, strict vs. nonstrict implementation, and supervision vs. nonsupervision). It reports payoffs for the local government, enterprises, and the public, but does not calculate group efficiency (actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff). Thus, it never reports or analyzes “efficiency” as the outcome.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   1) Number of players (#1) is implicitly fixed at three (local government, enterprises, public).  
   2) Punishment magnitude (#8), labeled P, is discussed and varied in the simulations.  
   3) Whether a reward is enabled (#9) is present: the paper includes a reward (H to the public, αC₃ to enterprises).  
   4) Reward cost/magnitude (#10 and #11) appears as H (for the public) and αC₃ (for enterprises). H is varied in simulations.  

   Altogether, four parameter “categories” (#1, #8, #9, #10/#11) appear, though the paper does not link any of these to group efficiency or “punishment treatment effect” in the public‐goods sense.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   The paper does not discuss a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Nor does it compare “punishment vs. no‐punishment” conditions in terms of collective payoffs.  
   – Parameter #8 (punishment magnitude P) is systematically varied, but only its effect on enterprises’ behavior is reported.  
   – Parameter #11 (reward magnitude H) is also varied to see how it affects the public’s strategy (and the local government’s).  
   However, none of these variations are linked to an efficiency measure or a “treatment effect” in the sense of comparing total group payoffs to a fully cooperative benchmark.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of this paper, what would they be?  
   The paper provides no direct evidence about efficiency, and it never quantifies a “punishment treatment effect.” All numerical simulations focus on how quickly each of the three parties converges to “strict” or “supervision” strategies. Because the paper never references total payoffs versus a maximum possible payoff, there is insufficient basis here to make predictions about how varying the 15 parameters would shift group efficiency under a punishment treatment. One can only note that increasing the magnitude of the penalty (P) or the rewards (H) can encourage more “cooperative” strategies (strict implementation, etc.), which, by analogy to some forms of public‐goods reasoning, might improve overall outcomes. But the paper itself does not address or measure these effects in terms of efficiency. Consequently, little or no prediction is possible strictly from this paper’s text.

Authors: Sigmund, K; Hauert, C; Traulsen, A; De Silva, H
Author Full Names: Sigmund, Karl; Hauert, Christoph; Traulsen, Arne; De Silva, Hannelore
Article Title: Social Control and the Social Contract: The Emergence of Sanctioning Systems for Collective Action
Author Keywords: Evolutionary game theory; Public goods games; Cooperation; Costly punishment; Social dilemma; Voluntary interactions
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC GOOD GAMES; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; STRUCTURED POPULATIONS; 2ND-ORDER PUNISHMENT; EVOLUTIONARY GAME; PRISONERS-DILEMMA; HOST SANCTIONS; NEURAL BASIS; GOODS; COOPERATION
Abstract: Punishment of free-riders is generally viewed as an important factor in promoting cooperation. But since it is often costly to sanction exploiters, the emergence of such a behavior and its stability raise interesting problems. Players who do not contribute to the sanctions, but profit from the increased level of cooperation caused by them, act as second-order exploiters and threaten the joint enterprise. In this paper, we review the role of voluntary participation in establishing and upholding cooperation with or without punishment. In particular, we deal with two distinct forms of punishment, namely peer punishment and pool punishment, and compare their stability and their efficiency. The emergence and upkeep of collaborative undertakings can strongly depend on whether participation is voluntary or mandatory. The possibility to opt out of a joint enterprise often helps in curbing exploiters and boosting pro-social behavior.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter examination of what this paper does and does not say about systematically varying each of the 15 parameters with respect to any “treatment effect” of punishment on group efficiency. Throughout, “efficiency” is understood as actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff for a fully cooperative group, per your request. Where the paper addresses dependent variables other than efficiency (e.g., strategy frequencies, fixation probabilities, oscillatory dynamics), that is noted explicitly.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The paper frequently uses N to denote the size of a group sampled to play the public goods game, and M for the overall population size. Examples include N = 5, N = 8, and M = 100 in various simulations.  
   • Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
     – No. Although the text sometimes considers different values of N and references large M (e.g., M = 100 or 1,000) and N ≥ 2, it does not present a systematic variation of “number of players” or a resulting quantitative effect on efficiency (or any other variable) caused by changing N or M. The paper primarily uses fixed illustration values rather than exploring how changing N or M alone would alter efficiency.  

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Not in a way that is modeled as a focal parameter. The text refers to repeated or multiple rounds in general terms (including references to “a few rounds” in sections about experiment findings from other work), but it does not examine how a varying number of rounds specifically alters the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.  
   • Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
     – No. There is no section or set of results showing how different round counts change the punishing regime’s impact on efficiency (or any other dependent variable).  

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. There is no mention of communication channels, structured or unstructured, in the paper’s models or simulations.  
   • Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
     – No.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes, effectively. In the core models, each participating player either contributes a fixed amount c or contributes nothing. There is no partial contribution in the paper’s main framework.  
   • Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
     – No. The paper adopts this “all or nothing” approach but never explores how changing it (e.g., allowing graded contributions) would alter punishment’s effect on efficiency.  

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much of their endowment to move back into their hand)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper’s public goods models assume a fixed cost c if contributing. There is no mention of giving players a continuous or customized default contribution level.  
   • Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
     – No.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The paper uses r > 1 as a multiplication factor on contributed resources, which in many public goods formulations is related to the MPCR.  
   • Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
     – Not in a formal, tabular, or figure-based sense for efficiency. Although different parts of the text use particular r values (e.g., r = 3, r = 5) to illustrate outcomes, the paper does not give a systematic analysis (e.g., a table) showing how varying r shifts the punishment treatment effect on any dependent variable, including efficiency.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The paper denotes γ for the per-unit cost of imposing a fine in the peer-punishment mechanism and G for the extra fee in the pool-punishment scenario (though G can be interpreted slightly differently).  
   • Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
     – The paper discusses how higher or lower punishment costs can favor or undermine the stability of punishers, but it does not provide specific quantitative effect sizes for how changes in γ or G translate into changes in efficiency or total payoff. Results revolve mainly around whether punishers can invade or fixate, not direct measures of efficiency. There is no numerical effect size on efficiency reported.  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted for each unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The paper labels that β for peer punishment (and B for pool punishment).  
   • Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
     – The paper relies on inequalities (e.g., c < (N–1)β) to explain when punishment can be stable or invade. It does not present numerical effect-size estimates on group efficiency; rather, it shows that certain threshold relationships allow punishers to prevail. No systematic table or figure ties different β or B values to a specific efficiency outcome.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. All analyses are restricted to punishment (peer or pool), with no mention of any reward mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
     – No.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Mentioned?  
      – No. Rewarding is not part of any model in the paper.  
    • Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
      – No.  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
    • Mentioned?  
      – No. Again, no rewarded-based designs appear in the paper.  
    • Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
      – No.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    • Mentioned?  
      – No. The paper’s theoretical models are not framed in terms of participants’ knowledge about terminal rounds.  
    • Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
      – No.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost each round)?  
    • Mentioned?  
      – The paper notes that interactions occur under anonymity assumptions and does not delve into displaying or hiding specific outcome information.  
    • Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
      – No.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Mentioned?  
      – The paper references “anonymous” interactions and does not specify how punishers might be identified.  
    • Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
      – No.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Mentioned?  
      – Not at all, since the text does not cover rewards.  
    • Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
      – No.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A: Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper occasionally refers to “efficiency” (e.g., cooperative populations can generate higher payoffs) and “overall income,” but its main focus is on strategy dynamics (whether punishers or defectors take over, or whether populations cycle) rather than systematically measuring and reporting “group efficiency” as a numeric ratio.  
   • The typical dependent variables are:  
     – Strategy frequencies in the population (e.g., fraction of punishers vs. defectors vs. non-participants)  
     – Fixation or invasion probabilities (which strategy eventually dominates)  
     – Cyclic dominance or stable equilibria among strategies  
   • These differ from efficiency in that they do not explicitly quantify total payoff relative to the theoretical maximum payoff that full cooperation could achieve.

B: Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
     (1) Number of players (group size N, total population M),  
     (4) All-or-nothing contributions (implicitly),  
     (6) Multiplication factor r,  
     (7) Punishment cost (γ, G),  
     (8) Punishment magnitude (β, B).  
   • The rest (2, 3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15) do not appear as focal discussion points in any of the paper’s models, tables, or figures.  

C: For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None are systematically varied and then linked directly to a numeric change in “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”  
   • Parameters (6), (7), and (8) are discussed in the sense of threshold conditions or inequalities (e.g., c + G < (N–1)B for pool punishers to succeed), but without reporting an explicit, quantitative effect on efficiency per se.  

D: If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • Because the text does not systematically analyze or report efficiency metrics, almost no direct predictions can be made about how changing these parameters would shift the ratio of actual to maximum payoff. The paper instead focuses on whether punishers invade or persist as a strategy, or how populations transition among punishers, defectors, and non-participants.  
   • Consequently, one can only infer generally that:  
     – If punishment parameters (cost, magnitude) favor the stable presence of punishers, the population’s average payoff tends to be higher (implying likely greater efficiency than under all-defect states), but the paper never quantifies that in ratio form.  
     – Voluntary participation (parameter not on your list but heavily featured in the paper) helps punishers maintain cooperation; that mechanism might increase efficiency relative to mandatory settings, but again the paper does not supply a numeric effect size for this efficiency gain.  
   • Overall, the paper’s models and discussions do not enable precise statements on how each of the 15 parameters, let alone their interactions, numerically influences efficiency.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Abstract: Cooperative behaviour has been extensively studied as a choice between cooperation and defection. However, the possibility to not participate is also frequently available. This type of problem can be studied through the optional public goods game. The introduction of the 'Loner' strategy' allows players to withdraw from the game, which leads to a cooperator-defector-loner cycle. While pro-social punishment can help increase cooperation, anti-social punishment-where defectors punish cooperators-causes its downfall in both experimental and theoretical studies. In this paper, we introduce social norms that allow agents to condition their behaviour to the reputation of their peers. We benchmark this with respect both to the standard optional public goods game and to the variant where all types of punishment are allowed. We find that a social norm imposing a more moderate reputational penalty for opting out than for defecting increases cooperation. When, besides reputation, punishment is also possible, the two mechanisms work synergically under all social norms that do not assign to loners a strictly worse reputation than to defectors. Under this latter set-up, the high levels of cooperation are sustained by conditional strategies, which largely reduce the use of pro-social punishment and almost completely eliminate anti-social punishment. This article is part of the theme issue 'The language of cooperation: reputation and honest signalling'.

Below, each of the 15 design parameters is considered in turn.

For every parameter I state  
(1) whether the paper says anything about it (and, if so, the value(s) used), and  
(2) whether the paper reports what would happen to the **punishment-treatment effect** (i.e. the difference between a condition with punishment and an otherwise identical condition without punishment) when that parameter is systematically varied.  When the paper shows numbers I report them; when the paper only gives a qualitative statement I reproduce that; when it is silent I say so explicitly.

------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players in the population  
(1) Mentioned.  All baseline simulations use N = 1000.  
(2) Not varied, and no prediction is made about how changing N would alter the punishment-treatment effect on any outcome.

2. Number of rounds in the game  
(1) The model is indefinitely repeated; after every round the group continues with probability Ω and is dissolved otherwise.  Baseline Ω = 10/11.  
(2) Ω is systematically varied in robustness checks (electronic-suppl. Fig. S21).  The paper shows that, as long as Ω ≠ 0, the joint “reputation + punishment’’ condition keeps cooperation high.  However it never isolates the *increment* produced by adding punishment, so no separate punishment-treatment effect is reported.

3. Is chat enabled?  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) No discussion, no prediction.

4. “All-or-nothing’’ contributions  
(1) Yes.  Contribution is binary: c or 0.  This feature is fixed.  
(2) Never varied, no prediction.

5. “Contribution default’’ (take vs. give frame)  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) No prediction.

6. Marginal-per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor r  
(1) Baseline r = 3; r is systematically varied in robustness checks (suppl. Fig. S17).  
(2) The figures show that, over the whole range examined (r ≈ 2–5), the *reputation + punishment* condition produces higher cooperation and higher average payoff than *punishment-only*.  The paper does not translate this into “efficiency’’ and does not report numeric treatment-effect sizes, so no quantitative effect can be extracted.

7. Punishment cost γ  
(1) Baseline γ = 1.  Varied in robustness checks (suppl. Fig. S20).  
(2) Same qualitative result as for r: lowering or raising γ changes absolute cooperation levels, but the paper does not isolate how the incremental effect of adding punishment varies with γ.

8. Punishment magnitude β  
(1) Baseline β = 2.  Varied in robustness checks (suppl. Fig. S20).  
(2) Same comment as for γ: no explicit punishment-treatment effect is given.

9. Is a reward option present?  
(1) Rewards are never included.  
(2) No prediction.

10. Reward cost  
Not applicable.

11. Reward magnitude  
Not applicable.

12. Is the horizon known?  
(1) Not discussed.  Players are programmed agents; the model specifies Ω but does not speak of players’ knowledge about the final round.  
(2) No prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
(1) Pay-offs and reputations are common knowledge by assumption (“we assume actions are observed without error… so that players’ resulting reputations are common knowledge”).  
(2) Not varied; no prediction.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) No prediction.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
Not applicable (no rewards).

------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Does the paper use “efficiency’’ as a dependent variable?  
• Not explicitly.  The main dependent variables are  
  – proportion of cooperative actions,  
  – strategy frequencies,  
  – “population fitness’’ = average payoff.  
Population fitness is close to, but not normalised into, the efficiency measure requested.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
Six: 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8.

C.  For which parameters does the paper *systematically vary* the parameter and give any statement about its impact on the punishment-treatment effect?  
Three: 6 (r), 7 (γ), 8 (β).  
Even for these, the paper only shows that the combination of reputation + punishment dominates the other conditions across the range; it never gives numeric treatment-effect estimates.

D.  What predictions can be made—solely from this paper—about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) will influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency?  

The paper allows only very cautious, qualitative predictions:  
• Changing r, γ or β alters overall cooperation and pay-offs, but the *direction* of the incremental benefit of adding punishment (with reputation already present) is always positive in the explored range, so no sign-reversal is expected.  
• None of the other 12 parameters is analysed; the paper provides no basis for predicting how they interact with punishment to affect efficiency.

Beyond these few qualitative statements, the paper offers little that can be used to forecast the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency when the 15 parameters are manipulated.

Authors: Powers, ST; Lehmann, L
Author Full Names: Powers, Simon T.; Lehmann, Laurent
Article Title: When is bigger better? The effects of group size on the evolution of helping behaviours
Author Keywords: sociality; cooperation; altruism; reciprocity; punishment; relatedness; cultural evolution; group size; diminishing returns; institutions
Keywords Plus: DENSITY-DEPENDENT SURVIVAL; PUBLIC-GOODS; CULTURAL-EVOLUTION; COOPERATIVE BEHAVIOR; INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; VISCOUS POPULATIONS; PAROCHIAL ALTRUISM; SELFISH SENTINELS; INCLUSIVE FITNESS; SOCIAL EVOLUTION
Abstract: Understanding the evolution of sociality in humans and other species requires understanding how selection on social behaviour varies with group size. However, the effects of group size are frequently obscured in the theoretical literature, which often makes assumptions that are at odds with empirical findings. In particular, mechanisms are suggested as supporting large-scale cooperation when they would in fact rapidly become ineffective with increasing group size. Here we review the literature on the evolution of helping behaviours (cooperation and altruism), and frame it using a simple synthetic model that allows us to delineate how the three main components of the selection pressure on helping must vary with increasing group size. The first component is the marginal benefit of helping to group members, which determines both direct fitness benefits to the actor and indirect fitness benefits to recipients. While this is often assumed to be independent of group size, marginal benefits are in practice likely to be maximal at intermediate group sizes for many types of collective action problems, and will eventually become very small in large groups due to the law of decreasing marginal returns. The second component is the response of social partners on the past play of an actor, which underlies conditional behaviour under repeated social interactions. We argue that under realistic conditions on the transmission of information in a population, this response on past play decreases rapidly with increasing group size so that reciprocity alone (whether direct, indirect, or generalised) cannot sustain cooperation in very large groups. The final component is the relatedness between actor and recipient, which, according to the rules of inheritance, again decreases rapidly with increasing group size. These results explain why helping behaviours in very large social groups are limited to cases where the number of reproducing individuals is small, as in social insects, or where there are social institutions that can promote (possibly through sanctioning) large-scale cooperation, as in human societies. Finally, we discuss how individually devised institutions can foster the transition from small-scale to large-scale cooperative groups in human evolution.

Below each of the 15 design parameters we list what can ‒ and cannot ‒ be extracted from Powers & Lehmann (2017) with respect to a “punishment-treatment effect”.  Citations in brackets refer to the section or figure where the statement appears (e.g. “II-2” = Section II, sub-section 2).

PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK  

1. Number of players (group size, 𝒩)  
   • Discussed? Yes – it is the focal variable of the whole paper (every main section).  
   • Value(s) used? Treated symbolically; examples in Figs. 1–4 run from 𝒩 ≈ 1 to several hundred.  
   • Prediction when systematically varied? Yes.  For punishment the authors state:  
     – The per-capita loss a defector suffers from pool-punishment, P𝒩, “must decrease with the absolute number of non-helpers in the group” (II-2).  
     – Therefore “it becomes more difficult for punishment to invade as group size increases” and “the effect of punishment decreases with group size when helpers are rare” (II-2).  
     Quantitative size: no numerical slope, only the qualitative 1/𝒩 decline (“on the order of 1/𝒩”).  

2. Number of rounds  
   • Discussed? Repeated vs one-shot interactions are contrasted many times, but the actual number of rounds is never specified or varied.  
   • Systematic prediction? No.  The paper only distinguishes “repeated” vs “one-shot”.  

3. Chat enabled? (free communication)  
   • Discussed? Not as an experimental switch.  Communication is mentioned only as part of institution building or gossip, not as an on/off parameter in a game.  
   • Prediction? None.  

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
   • Not mentioned.  

5. Contribution default / “take” frame  
   • Not mentioned.  

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   • Discussed? Yes – as the “marginal product of helping” M𝒩.  
   • Systematic prediction for punishment? No.  Variation in marginal returns is analysed for direct benefit models (linear vs diminishing vs sigmoidal), but the paper never links MPCR variation to the incremental effect of adding punishment.  

7. Punishment-cost to punisher  
   • Mentioned qualitatively (“investment into punishment”, II-2), but never parameterised or varied.  No effect sizes.  

8. Punishment magnitude (damage to target per unit)  
   • Covered as P𝒩.  P𝒩 itself is said to fall with group size – but the authors do not vary the magnitude independently of 𝒩, nor give a functional form beyond “declines ∝ 1/𝒩 when non-helpers are common”.  No direct statement on varying the magnitude while keeping other factors constant.  

9–11. Reward presence, reward cost, reward magnitude  
   • Totally absent.  The word “reward” never appears in any technical sense.  

12. Knowledge of the horizon (# rounds known)  
   • Not discussed.  

13. Peer-outcome visibility (who earned what)  
   • Visibility is treated only in the context of reputation for indirect reciprocity, not in punishment experiments.  No systematic variation.  

14. Punisher identity revealed?  
   • Not treated.  

15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
   • Not treated.  


--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables used  
   – The article never uses “group efficiency” (total realised payoff ÷ maximal payoff).  
   – Its key dependent quantities are:  
     • Direct marginal benefit to self, D𝒩  
     • Marginal benefit to others, B𝒩  
     • Responsiveness coefficient, ρ𝒩  
     • Scaled relatedness, κ𝒩  
     • Per-capita punishment cost to a defector, P𝒩  
   These are evolutionary fitness components, not behavioural payoffs, contributions, or efficiencies in the experimental-economics sense.

B.  Which of the 15 design parameters are even mentioned?  
   • Mentioned: 1 (group size), 2 (round structure, but only qualitatively), 6 (MPCR conceptually), 7–8 (punishment cost and magnitude, qualitatively), 13 (information about others, but only for reputation).  
   • Total mentioned: 5 of 15.  

C.  Which parameters are systematically varied in the paper *and* linked to a punishment-treatment effect?  
   • Only parameter 1 (group size).  No numerical effect size is given, but the qualitative prediction is clear: increasing 𝒩 weakens the efficacy of punishment and makes its evolutionary invasion harder.  
   • Count: 1 of 15.  

D.  If we had to predict the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency using only this paper:  
   – Prediction 1: Adding punishment in *small* groups should markedly raise efficiency because P𝒩 > C is attainable; in large groups the same institution has little effect, so the treatment effect shrinks roughly with 1/𝒩.  
   – Prediction 2: Any manipulation that increases the *per-capita* impact of sanctions (e.g. higher magnitude or lower cost) would increase efficiency, but the paper offers no explicit guidance on functional form.  
   – Beyond group size, the paper provides insufficient information to forecast how other listed parameters or their interactions will moderate the punishment effect on efficiency.

In short, the review by Powers & Lehmann is centered on how *group size* shapes evolutionary pressures.  For the specific experimental design parameters listed in the prompt, it yields a clear qualitative prediction only for parameter 1; the remaining 14 parameters receive no actionable treatment with respect to how punishment affects efficiency.
reference_APA: Powers, Simon T. & Lehmann, Laurent (2017). When is bigger better? The effects of group size on the evolution of helping behaviours. BIOLOGICAL REVIEWS.

Authors: Wang, SX; Chen, XJ; Xiao, ZL; Szolnoki, A

Article Title: Decentralized incentives for general well-being in networked public goods game
Author Keywords: Cooperation; Evolutionary game theory; Decentralized incentives; Optimal control theory; Pair approximation approach
Keywords Plus: EVOLUTIONARY DYNAMICS; COOPERATION; POPULATION; STRATEGY; REWARD
Abstract: Prosocial incentives are recognized as effective tools to promote public cooperation. But their usage is costly, hence we need to find an optimal policy that offers the best outcome for a minimal cost. This problem has attracted extensive attention of scholars from many fields, and it has been studied intensively in well-mixed populations. Yet, the system behavior in the case of group interactions where decentralized incentives are involved is rather unexplored. To fill this gap, we consider the possible consequences of decentralized rewarding and punishing incentives in a spatially arranged population where players play public goods game with their neighbors. Importantly, both time-independent and dynamically varying cases are checked. With the help of pair approximation approach, we derive the dynamical equations under weak selection and obtain theoretical conditions of the minimally requested amounts for the expected outcome. By using optimal control theory, we also devise an index function to quantify the executing costs and obtain the optimal dynamical punishing and rewarding protocols. In addition, both numerical calculations and Monte Carlo simulations support that the optimal dynamical rewarding scheme requires a lower cumulative cost than the punishing alternative if the initial cooperation level is below a threshold value. Otherwise, the usage of punishment is more efficient. (C) 2022 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

Below every parameter you will find two short subsections:  
(i) “Mentioned ?” – whether the paper even mentions or fixes the parameter, together with the concrete value(s) that appear.  
(ii) “Systematic-variation prediction ?” – whether the authors explicitly explore *changes* in that parameter and report how such changes modify the *punishment treatment effect* (or any other dependent variable).  Wherever the paper gives a numerical effect size I cite the equation, table or figure.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players (group size n)  
(i) Mentioned ?  Yes.  General theory is written for any n ≥ 2; all numerical illustrations use n = 5 (see caption of Figs. 1–3).  
(ii) Systematic-variation prediction ?  No.  Although n appears symbolically in the optimal‐punishment formula  
     u*P(t)=2(n–r)c/n·(1–x)/(1–xⁿ) (Eq. B.8), the paper never varies n or comments on what would happen to efficiency, cooperation or cost when n changes.

2. Number of rounds  
(i) Mentioned ?  No.  The model is continuous time; the concept “number of rounds’’ is absent.  
(ii) Systematic-variation prediction ?  No.

3. Chat enabled?  
(i) Mentioned ?  No.  
(ii) Systematic-variation prediction ?  No.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
(i) Mentioned ?  Yes.  The public-goods game is binary: a “cooperator contributes c, a defector contributes 0’’ (Sec. 2.1).  The parameter itself is not varied.  
(ii) Systematic-variation prediction ?  No.

5. Contribution default / extraction frame  
(i) Mentioned ?  No.  
(ii) Systematic-variation prediction ?  No.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor  
(i) Mentioned ?  Yes.  The synergy factor r (>1) enters all payoff equations; numerical work fixes r = 3.  
(ii) Systematic-variation prediction ?  No.  r is never swept or analysed for its influence on punishment efficacy.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit  
(i) Mentioned ?  No direct analogue.  The institution’s *total* cost is the quadratic objective J=∫½(nu)²dt, but “cost per unit’’ is not parameterised.  
(ii) Systematic-variation prediction ?  No.

8. Punishment magnitude per unit  
(i) Mentioned ?  Yes indirectly.  Payoff reduction for a defector is b nu/(nD+1) with leverage b.  The paper fixes b = 1 and never varies it.  
(ii) Systematic-variation prediction ?  No.

9. Reward enabled?  
(i) Mentioned ?  Yes.  Two separate models are analysed: reward‐only and punishment-only.  In the punishment-only treatment, reward is “off’’.  
(ii) Systematic-variation prediction ?  No.  The study does not look at mixed regimes nor at how “turning reward on’’ would change the punishment effect.

10. Reward cost per unit  
(i) Mentioned ?  No explicit parameter.  Same quadratic cost function J, but no per-unit parameter.  
(ii) Systematic-variation prediction ?  No.

11. Reward magnitude per unit  
(i) Mentioned ?  Yes.  Bonus to a co-operator is a nu/(nC+1); a is fixed at 1.  
(ii) Systematic-variation prediction ?  No.

12. End-game known?  
(i) Mentioned ?  No.  
(ii) Systematic-variation prediction ?  No.

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
(i) Mentioned ?  No.  
(ii) Systematic-variation prediction ?  No.

14. Punisher identity revealed?  
(i) Mentioned ?  No (punishment is institutional, not peer-to-peer).  
(ii) Systematic-variation prediction ?  No.

15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
(i) Mentioned ?  No.  
(ii) Systematic-variation prediction ?  No.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables actually analysed  
• Fraction of cooperators x(t).  
• Cumulative *institutional cost* J.  
Group efficiency, total payoff, or average payoff are *not* analysed; the paper briefly cites “average payoff’’ only inside payoff equations but never reports it as an outcome.

B. Parameters from the 15-item list that are even mentioned = 6  
(#1 group size n, #4 binary contribution, #6 synergy factor r, #8 punishment leverage b fixed at 1, #9 reward on/off, #11 reward leverage a fixed at 1).

C. Parameters for which the authors discuss *systematically varying* them and reporting an effect on the punishment treatment effect = 0.  
No tables, figures or text explore sweeps of n, r, a, b, etc.

D. Prediction horizon restricted to paper content  
Given that only fixed single values are used and no comparative statics are carried out, the paper allows almost **no quantitative prediction** about how any of the 15 experimental design parameters (or their interactions) would change the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.  The sole qualitative hint is that, *for whatever values of n and r one plugs into the analytical formulas*, the optimal institutional punishment strategy achieves the target cooperation level at a lower cumulative monetary cost than the optimal reward strategy.  Because efficiency (total payoff relative to the social optimum) is never computed, even this cost advantage cannot be translated into an efficiency prediction.

Hence, based solely on this paper, the safest forecast is: “Insufficient information—no credible prediction about how the 15 parameters or their interactions would alter the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”
reference_APA: Wang, Shengxian, Chen, Xiaojie, Xiao, Zhilong & Szolnoki, Attila (2022). Decentralized incentives for general well-being in networked public goods game. APPLIED MATHEMATICS AND COMPUTATION.

Below, each of the 15 design parameters is treated in turn.  
For every parameter I report  

(1) Whether the paper mentions the parameter at all (and, if so, the fixed value actually used in the experiment), and  

(2) Whether the paper makes any prediction or provides any evidence on what would happen to the *punishment-treatment effect* (the difference between the “with-punishment’’ and “no-punishment’’ conditions) **if that parameter were systematically varied**.  Whenever a numerical effect size can be read directly from a figure or a table I give it, but only when the author(s) do so.

Because the paper studies *trust games, one-shot prisoner’s dilemmas and a third-party-punishment stage*, the only “punishment-treatment effect’’ that is actually reported is the change in the *cooperation rate* (not efficiency) when third-party punishment is introduced in the prisoner’s-dilemma stage.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned implicitly. Each prisoner’s-dilemma involves 2 players; the punishment stage adds a *third-party punisher*. Value is fixed; never varied.  
   (2) No prediction or evidence on how changing the number of players would change the punishment-treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) One-shot games only. Value = 1; never varied.  
   (2) No prediction.

3. Chat enabled?  
   (1) No chat. (No communication allowed; students were “prohibited from speaking”.)  
   (2) No prediction.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   (1) Yes for the prisoner’s dilemma (binary send vs. keep); no for the trust game. This feature is fixed.  
   (2) No prediction.

5. Contribution default / “withdraw-from-public-fund’’?  
   (1) Not applicable; not discussed.  
   (2) No prediction.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   (1) Prisoner’s dilemma: transfer is doubled (MPCR = 2).  
       Trust game: amount sent is tripled.  
       Both factors are fixed; never varied.  
   (2) No prediction.

7. Punishment cost per unit  
   (1) Fixed at 1 (punisher pays €1 per deduction point).  
   (2) No prediction.

8. Punishment magnitude per unit  
   (1) Fixed at 3 (target loses €3 per deduction point).  
   (2) No prediction.

9. Reward enabled?  
   (1) No reward option in any stage.  
   (2) No prediction.

10. Reward cost  
    (1) Not applicable.  
    (2) No prediction.

11. Reward magnitude  
    (1) Not applicable.  
    (2) No prediction.

12. Finite horizon known?  
    (1) Subjects are told each game is one-shot and independent. Horizon length not manipulated.  
    (2) No prediction.

13. Peer outcomes displayed?  
    (1) Not described. Pay-offs were paid in sealed envelopes days later; interim outcomes were not revealed.  
    (2) No prediction.

14. Punisher identity revealed?  
    (1) No – punishment is anonymous.  
    (2) No prediction.

15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
    (1) Not applicable (no reward).  
    (2) No prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables used  
    • Trust (amount sent)  
    • Trustworthiness (amount returned)  
    • Cooperation rate in prisoner’s dilemma (with and without punishment)  
    • Dictator giving (altruism)  
    • In-group-favoritism measures (within-subject differences)  
    • Punishment levels/frequencies  
    The paper **does not** use “group efficiency’’ (total or average pay-off relative to the social optimum) as a dependent variable.

B.  Parameters merely *mentioned* (values fixed): 10 of 15  
    1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9 (as “not enabled’’), 12, 14  
    Parameters 5, 10, 11, 13, 15 are not mentioned at all.

C.  Parameters for which the paper discusses the effect of *systematic variation* on the punishment-treatment effect: **0**.  
    The study reports one punishment treatment (cost = 1, magnitude = 3) and never varies any design feature.

D.  What can be predicted — only from this paper — about how the 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency?  
    • Because efficiency is never analysed, the paper offers **no direct evidence** that links any parameter to *efficiency-based* treatment effects.  
    • The only observable treatment effect is that adding third-party punishment raises the *cooperation rate* in a two-player prisoner’s dilemma by roughly 9 pp in high-Mafia schools (51 % → about 60 %) and by roughly 13 pp in low-Mafia schools (60 % → about 73 %) (Fig. 2, Panel B).  
    • With no parameter variation, one cannot infer how changing MPCR, punishment cost/magnitude, group size, information, etc. would alter that effect — let alone efficiency.  
    • Thus, based solely on the content of this paper, virtually **no predictive leverage** exists for any of the 15 parameters or their interactions with respect to the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency.

Below I go through each of the 15 parameters in turn, following the five requested rules.  I refer to the equations, tables and figures that actually appear in the paper (“Fig. 1”, “Fig. 3”, the Appendix, etc.).  Unless a number is printed in the paper I report “no numerical effect size”.

────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? – YES.  Denoted N throughout (e.g., N = 5 in Figs. 1-3; algebra treats N as a symbol).  
   • Systematic variation? – NO.  All numerical illustrations fix N = 5, and no comparative statics in N are reported, so no prediction about how changing N would modify the punishment treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? – NO.  The model is an infinite-time replicator system, so the notion of finitely many rounds never appears.  
   • Systematic variation? – Not applicable.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned? – NO.  
   • Systematic variation? – Not applicable.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Mentioned? – INDIRECTLY.  The model assumes a binary decision—strategy C always contributes c = 1, D never contributes.  However the paper never varies this assumption or contrasts it with a continuous-choice game.  
   • Systematic variation? – NO.

5. Contribution default / endowment moved back?  
   • Mentioned? – NO.

6. Marginal Per-Capita Return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? – YES.  Denoted r (set to r = 3 in all numerical work).  
   • Systematic variation? – NO.  r is fixed; there is no figure or table that sweeps r, so no prediction is offered.

7. Punishment cost per unit imposed  
   • Mentioned? – YES.  Denoted M (M = 0.5 in all figures; appears symbolically in inequalities).  
   • Systematic variation? – NO.  Although inequalities such as “M < β(N − 1)” are derived, the paper never shows what happens when M itself is changed.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine per unit received)  
   • Mentioned? – YES.  Denoted β (β = 0.3 in all numerical work).  
   • Systematic variation? – NO.  β is fixed.

9. Reward enabled (yes/no)  
   • Mentioned? – PARTIALLY.  The whole model is a “combined reward-and-punishment” scheme; there is no separate treatment that entirely removes rewards, so the paper does not study an ON/OFF switch for rewards.

10. Reward cost to grant one unit  
    • Mentioned? – NO.  All rewards (bounties) come from a common tax pool; no separate “cost-per-reward” parameter exists.

11. Reward magnitude (coins the target receives)  
    • Mentioned? – YES.  Denoted b and explicitly varied in Fig. 3 over b = 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 10.  
    • Systematic variation? – YES.  
      Qualitative prediction from Fig. 3 and the surrounding text:  
      – With very small b = 0.1, punishers cannot beat defectors; the only stable equilibrium lies on the CD edge (punishment ineffective).  
      – With intermediate b = 0.3 or 0.5, both a CP-edge and a CD-edge equilibrium are stable; punishers survive but cooperation does not dominate.  
      – With very large b = 10, punishers and defectors coexist on the DP edge; cooperators disappear and the original punishment effect is “more severely detrimental”.  
      Numerical effect size on efficiency is NOT provided (no total-payoff numbers are printed).

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
    • Mentioned? – NO.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mentioned? – NO.

14. Do punished players observe who punished them?  
    • Mentioned? – NO.

15. Do rewarded players observe who rewarded them?  
    • Mentioned? – NO.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────
A.  Dependent variables used  
    • Group efficiency / total or average payoff – NOT used.  
    • Variables actually analysed – frequencies of strategies (x = C, y = D, z = P), locations and stability of equilibrium points, and vague verbal statements about “level of cooperation”.  These are conceptually different from efficiency because they do not sum the payoffs of all group members.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned? – 6 of them  
    (#1 N, #4 binary contribution (implicitly), #6 r, #7 M, #8 β, #11 b).

Below I go through the 15 parameters one-by-one, always sticking strictly to what is said or plotted in the paper.

─────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
─────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned?  YES – always 10 000 players on a 100 × 100 lattice.  
   (2) Systematically varied?  NO – it is kept fixed, so no prediction of how changing it would alter any punishment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Mentioned?  YES – simulations normally run 50 000 steps (plus 500 further steps for averaging).  
   (2) Systematically varied?  NO – therefore the paper offers no claim about its influence on the punishment treatment effect.

3. Is chat enabled?  
   (1) Mentioned?  NO.  
   (2) No discussion, no prediction.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   (1) Mentioned?  YES – explicitly “individuals have continuous strategic space”; so the answer is NO (not all-or-nothing).  
   (2) They never switch to an all-or-nothing version, so no prediction.

5. Contribution default (give-to-private instead of give-to-public)?  
   (1) Mentioned?  NO.  
   (2) No discussion.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor r  
   (1) Mentioned?  YES – central independent variable; varied from about 1.5 to 3 in most figures.  
   (2) Systematic variation?  YES – dozens of “average cooperation vs r” curves are shown.  
       • Self-punishment: smaller r needs stronger guilt (γ) or lower tolerance (h_IT) to lift cooperation.  
       • Peer-punishment: larger r almost always increases cooperation; for very low r (<2) heavy punishment may back-fire (Fig. 7).  
       Numerical effect sizes are only visible graphically; no coefficients are reported.

7. Punishment cost (α)  
   (1) Mentioned?  YES – α is the cost to the punisher per target.  
   (2) Systematic variation?  PARTLY – Fig. 9 varies the pair (α, β) simultaneously:  
       (0.05, 0.15), (0.10, 0.20), (0.15, 0.25), (0.20, 0.30).  
       Because α and β move together the independent impact of α cannot be isolated; nevertheless the curves show that the joint increase boosts cooperation for almost the full r-range.

8. Punishment magnitude (β)  
   (1) Mentioned?  YES – β is the fine taken from the punished player per case.  
   (2) Systematic variation?  YES – same Fig. 9. Larger β (together with larger α) monotonically raises cooperation; with β = 0.30 the group reaches ≈100 % cooperation already at r≈1.5. No numeric regression result is provided.

9. Reward enabled?  
   (1) Mentioned?  NO – rewards are not part of the model.  
   (2) No discussion.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   Same as (9): not mentioned or varied.

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
   Not applicable – infinite-horizon simulation; not mentioned.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   Not explicitly discussed; the model presumes agents observe neighbours’ pay-offs when they imitate but this visibility is never varied. Hence no prediction.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
15. Is the rewarder identified?  
   Not modelled; no statements.

─────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
─────────────────────────────────────────
A. Dependent variables  
   • The paper’s key outcome is the “average cooperation level”  ḡ  (mean contribution).  
   • Pay-offs are defined but the authors never compute group efficiency (total or average pay-off divided by the maximal possible).  
   • Therefore “efficiency” as asked by the user is NOT used; the only analysed dependent variable is contribution.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   6 of them: 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8.  (The remaining 9 are absent.)

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of systematically varying that parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
   • MPCR r (parameter 6) – YES.  
   • Punishment cost α (parameter 7) – PARTIALLY (jointly with β).  
   • Punishment magnitude β (parameter 8) – YES.  
   So 3 parameters (2½ if one counts α only partially).  None of the other 12 parameters are varied.

D. What could one predict about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency, using only this paper?

   – MPCR r: Higher r should increase efficiency under punishment except when r is extremely low and social tolerance is extremely strict (peer-punishment back-fires).  
   – Lower tolerance thresholds (h_IT or h_ST) make punishment kick in more often; this reliably raises cooperation and hence should raise efficiency, except under peer-punishment with very low r where it may reduce efficiency because punishment costs eat up benefits.  
   – Stronger fines β (together with the associated cost α) improve cooperation and therefore would be expected to raise efficiency until costs start offsetting gains (the paper does not calculate that tipping point).  
   – Higher punishment cost α was never isolated; based on intuition within the model it probably lowers efficiency, but the paper provides no direct evidence.  
   – All other listed parameters are either fixed or absent; no prediction can be made from the paper.

In short, the paper only lets us form predictions about MPCR and the two monetary punishment parameters; for the other 12 design features it gives no information relevant to forecasting efficiency effects.

PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned: Groups of four (Sect. 2 “participants are matched in groups of four”).

   (2) The authors *speculate* that results would be “rather negligible” if punishment were costly, but they do not provide a test or a quantitative prediction. No systematic variation.

8. Punishment magnitude per unit  
   (1) Fixed: each point chosen reduces target’s payoff by 1; maximum 10 points (Sect. 2).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

9. Reward enabled?

11. Reward magnitude

14. Is the identity of a punisher revealed to the punished?  
   (1) The paper never states whether identities are revealed; likely anonymous.  
   (2) Not discussed.

15. Is the identity of a rewarder revealed?  
   (1, 2) Not applicable (no reward).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables actually analysed  
    • Strength (slope) of conditional cooperation  
    • Probability of being classified a conditional co-operator vs. free rider  
    • Punishment slope (sensitivity of punishment to others’ contributions)  
    • Incidence of conditional punishing vs. unconditional punishing

Below is a parameter-by-parameter account, based strictly on the content of the paper. For each of the 15 parameters, I note whether (1) the paper mentions it (and, if so, how it is implemented) and (2) whether it systematically varies that parameter and discusses any effect on the “punishment treatment effect.” Throughout, recall that the paper’s main focus is on defection rates, punishment rates, and the coordination/“efficiency” of punishment (whether punishment is carried out by exactly one person), rather than on explicit measures of group efficiency as “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff.”

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of Players
   • Mentioned? Yes. The experiment always uses groups of four.  
   • Systematically Varied? No. The number of players (4) does not change across conditions; the paper does not discuss how varying group size would affect punishment or efficiency.

2. Number of Rounds
   • Mentioned? Yes. There are 30 rounds total: 15 rounds in part 1 (no penalty) and 15 rounds in part 2 (with penalty).  
   • Systematically Varied? No. It is always 30 rounds, split into the same two parts for all conditions. The paper does not study how changing the total number of rounds would affect punishment or efficiency.

3. Is Chat Enabled Between Players?
   • Mentioned? No. There is no suggestion that participants communicate or chat with one another, and no condition in which communication varies.  
   • Systematically Varied? No.

4. Is the Contribution “All or Nothing”?
   • Mentioned? Yes (in effect). Players choose whether to “steal” or “not steal,” and whether to “punish” or “not punish”; there is no partial contribution or partial punishment.  
   • Systematically Varied? No. The paper does not examine or discuss changing this all-or-nothing setup.

5. Is the Contribution Default?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not discuss any default contribution setting, nor do participants slide money back from a public fund.  
   • Systematically Varied? No.

6. Marginal Per Capita Return (MPCR) or Related Multiplication Factor
   • Mentioned? No. The study frames defection-and-punishment as a “step-level public good” problem. There is no linear public good or MPCR parameter varied.  
   • Systematically Varied? No.

7. Punishment Cost to Impose a Single Unit of Punishment
   • Mentioned? Yes, very centrally. The experiment labels these costs K, which differ in “missing hero dilemma” (MHD) vs. “volunteer’s dilemma” (VOD), and also in asymmetric vs. symmetric conditions. In the MHD: K > U. In the VOD: K < U. They further vary whether one person has K < others (asymmetric) or all have the same K (symmetric).  
   • Systematically Varied? Yes. The paper looks closely at four conditions: (i) symmetric MHD, (ii) asymmetric MHD, (iii) symmetric VOD, and (iv) asymmetric VOD. This is a between-subject variation of the costs. The paper discusses how lower-cost “strong” members end up punishing more often, and how that shapes defection rates and the overall “efficiency” of punishment (i.e., fewer redundant punishers). They do not provide numeric “efficiency” measures (such as total payoff / maximum payoff), but they do report that in the asymmetric VOD, punishment is more efficiently carried out by exactly one punisher, and defection rates are lower.

8. Punishment Magnitude (Coins Deducted from the Target per Unit Punishment)
   • Mentioned? Yes. In the second half of the experiment, a penalty P=60 MU is imposed on the thief if at least one person punishes. In the first half, P=0.  
   • Systematically Varied? Yes, within-subject across rounds 1–15 (P=0) vs. rounds 16–30 (P=60). The paper discusses how introducing the penalty drastically reduces defection rates in all conditions. However, the article mostly reports changes in rates of defection and punishment, not in an explicit measure of group payoff efficiency.

9. Whether a Reward Is Enabled
   • Mentioned? No. The design involves only punishment and no reward mechanism.  
   • Systematically Varied? No.

10. Reward Cost to Grant a Single Unit of Reward
   • Mentioned? No; there is no reward.  
   • Systematically Varied? No.

11. Reward Magnitude
   • Mentioned? No; there is no reward.  
   • Systematically Varied? No.

12. Is the Number of Rounds Known to Players?
   • Mentioned? The paper indicates 30 rounds, with 15 in each part. It does imply that participants know there are two parts of 15 rounds each.  
   • Systematically Varied? No. The number of rounds is the same across sessions, so there is no analysis of how knowledge vs. uncertainty of the horizon affects punishment or efficiency.

13. Are Peer Outcomes Shown?
   • Mentioned? Yes. All participants receive full feedback on who stole (if anyone did) and who punished.  
   • Systematically Varied? No. This feedback setup is constant across all conditions.

14. When a Player Is Punished, Do They Know Who the Specific Punisher Is?
   • Mentioned? Yes. Participants see how every group member decided at the end of each round (i.e., who punished and who did not).  
   • Systematically Varied? No.

15. When a Player Is Rewarded, Do They Know Who the Specific Rewarder Is?
   • Mentioned? No, and no such reward mechanism is used.  
   • Systematically Varied? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   The paper uses “punishment rates,” “defection (stealing) rates,” and whether punishment is carried out by exactly one punisher (which the authors refer to as more “efficient” punishment). While they use the word “efficient” (and talk about net cost to the group), they do not formally measure “group efficiency” as “actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff.” Instead, they track:  
   • Punishment at the individual and group level,  
   • Defection rates,  
   • Number of punishers per defection (to see if punishing is redundant or done by exactly one person).  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   The paper explicitly mentions or specifies seven of the parameters:  
   (1) The number of players (always 4).  
   (2) The number of rounds (30).  
   (4) That choices (steal or punish) are effectively all-or-nothing.  
   (7) Punishment cost (K) — systematically varied across MHD/VOD and symmetric/asymmetric.  
   (8) Punishment magnitude (P=0 or 60) — varied between the two halves of the experiment.  
   (13) Peer outcomes shown (yes, everyone sees who did what).  
   (14) Punisher identity revealed (yes, decisions are revealed by player).  

   The other parameters (3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 12, 15) are either not mentioned at all or are mentioned tangentially but not manipulated or analyzed.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   The paper systematically manipulates two:  
   • Punishment cost (parameter 7) across four between-subject conditions (MHD vs. VOD × symmetric vs. asymmetric).  
   • Punishment magnitude (parameter 8) via a within-subject penalty difference (P=0 for the first 15 rounds vs. P=60 for the next 15).  

   In both cases, the discussion focuses on how these variations affect defection rates and punishment rates (and whether punishment is carried out by exactly one person). Although the authors label fewer redundant punishers as “more efficient” second-order public good production, they do not provide a direct measure of aggregate payoff efficiency.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper:  
   • The paper only gives information on two parameters (7 and 8) in a systematically varied manner. For the other 13 parameters, it says little or nothing about varying them.  
   • Lower punishment cost (especially for one “strong” punisher) appears to make punishment more frequent, more “efficiently” handled by a single punisher, and thus lowers defection. Those effects plausibly translate into higher group payoff than if everyone has the same high cost.  
   • Adding a penalty (higher punishment magnitude) also reduces defection substantially (particularly in the volunteer’s dilemma), which likely raises group payoffs.  
   • Beyond that, the paper does not provide enough detail to predict how the other parameters or their interactions might shift the punishment treatment effect on strict “efficiency” measures. The authors mainly document changes in defection rates and number of punishers rather than explicit payoffs.

Abstract: Unelected officials with coercive powers (e.g., police, prosecutors, bureaucrats) vary markedly in the extent to which citizens view their actions as legitimate.
