Below is a point‐by‐point inventory of whether (and how) each of the 15 listed parameters is addressed in the Dickson, Gordon, and Huber paper, followed by the required four‐part summary (A–D). The paper’s focus was on how an “authority” (paid either a fixed salary or by appropriating collected penalties) punishes citizens in a repeated public‐goods setting and how other citizens’ willingness to help or hinder this punishment reflects “legitimacy.” Crucially, the study varied only (1) the authority’s compensation scheme and (2) the transparency of information about who contributed. The rest of the commonly listed parameters (e.g., the cost or magnitude of punishment, number of players, number of rounds) were not systematically varied. As required, this response does not draw on any information outside the paper itself.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Discussed? The experiment always uses groups of 5 (one authority and four citizens). The paper does not vary group size.  
   • Effect of systematically varying? Not studied; the paper makes no predictions about changing group size.  

2. Number of rounds
   • Discussed? Every session lasts 20 repeated periods.  
   • Effect of systematically varying? Not studied; the paper does not discuss changing the number of rounds.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussed? Not mentioned at all.  
   • Effect of systematically varying? Not discussed.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussed? Yes, each citizen chooses either to contribute the entire 20‐token endowment or contribute nothing; that is indeed a binary (all‐or‐nothing) decision.  
   • Effect of systematically varying? They did not manipulate the binary structure; no predictions are made about changing this.  

5. Is the contribution default? (i.e., do players decide how much of their endowment to move out of a public fund?)
   • Discussed? The experiment uses a strict contribute‐or‐keep design (20 tokens or 0), with no partial amounts. There is no notion of “default” moves.  
   • Effect of systematically varying? Not studied or discussed in the paper.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Discussed? Yes, they state that each of the five group members receives 0.4×(total contributed), meaning the MPCR is 0.4 for citizens (and the authority also benefits 0.4×(total contributed) in the salary treatments, plus or minus other components). However, the paper does not systematically vary the MPCR.  
   • Effect of systematically varying? Not studied; no predictions are made about changing MPCR.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussed? In the experiment, the authority always pays 2 tokens to impose punishment. This cost remains fixed.  
   • Effect of systematically varying? Not studied; no commentary on how changes in that cost would affect outcomes.  

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   • Discussed? The punished player loses 30 tokens (if enforcement is successful). This amount never varies.  
   • Effect of systematically varying? Not studied, and no predictions are advanced about changing that magnitude.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussed? The experiment does not include any reward mechanism.  
   • Effect of systematically varying? Not discussed, as the design only included punishment.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Discussed? Not applicable, since no rewards are used.  
    • Effect of systematically varying? Not discussed.  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted)
    • Discussed? Not applicable, since no rewards are used.  
    • Effect of systematically varying? Not discussed.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Discussed? Subjects are told there are 20 periods; the paper does not report any attempts to hide or vary the ending.  
    • Effect of systematically varying? Not discussed in the paper.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost each round)?
    • Discussed? This maps onto the full‐versus‐limited‐information manipulation. In the “full information” condition, citizens see who contributed and who did not, plus who was targeted. In the “limited information” condition, they see only that someone was targeted but not whether the target contributed.  
    • Effect of systematically varying? Yes, they systematically vary the information display: “full information” vs. “limited information.”  
      – Dependent variables discussed under this manipulation: contribution levels, citizen willingness to help/hinder the authority (their measure of legitimacy), and overall payoff patterns.  
      – Numerical effect sizes:  
         • Moving from full to limited information sharply reduces contributions when the authority is on a fixed salary (compare Figures 3 vs. 7 and associated discussion).  
         • For instance, under salary × full information, citizens contributed about 2.46 times per period on average; under salary × limited information, it was lower (about 1.82 times per period, as implied by figures and discussion).  
         • Under limited information, citizen “net assistance” to the authority also drops in the salary condition (Table 4, columns 3–4).  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Discussed? There is always exactly one punisher (the “authority”), so in practice everyone knows who punishes (it is the authority by design). The paper does not discuss varying whether the punisher’s identity is hidden.  
    • Effect of systematically varying? No parameter variation or prediction on that.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Discussed? Not applicable; the experiment does not involve rewards.  
    • Effect of systematically varying? Not discussed.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper reports average payoffs per period for citizens and authorities, so total/average payoffs appear in the analysis. However, the central focus is on (a) how often citizens contribute (the “contribution rate”) and (b) how often they assist or hinder the authority (their “legitimacy” measure).  
   • These payoffs and “legitimacy” measures differ from standard “efficiency” metrics in public‐goods experiments (i.e., total payoff relative to a fully cooperative maximum). The term “efficiency” as such is not emphasized, nor is it systematically measured as “actual ÷ optimal total payoff.”  

B. Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned explicitly (though not necessarily varied): #1 (number of players = 5), #2 (number of rounds = 20), #4 (binary/all‐or‐nothing contribution), #6 (MPCR = 0.4), #7 (punishment cost = 2), #8 (punishment magnitude = 30), #12 (subjects know there are 20 periods), #13 (information display varied). That is 8 parameters at least briefly described.  
   • The other 7 parameters are not used at all (chat, default contribution style, reward presence/cost/magnitude, punisher identity hidden, rewarder identity hidden).  

C. For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when varying the parameter systematically?  
   • Strictly speaking, the authors do not study a “punishment treatment effect” in the sense of comparing “with‐punishment” versus “no‐punishment.” Punishment is always present via the authority. They do, however, systematically vary parameter #13 (the “transparency” of peer outcomes, i.e., full vs. limited information). They analyze how this variation changes contribution rates, citizen intervention, and realized payoffs—and interpret these patterns in terms of “legitimacy.”  
   • No other parameter is systematically manipulated.  

D. Predictions about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence punishment’s effect on efficiency, based solely on the paper:  
   • The experiment manipulates only (1) whether the authority is salaried or gains from “appropriated” penalties, and (2) whether citizens receive full vs. limited information about who contributed. Nothing else is varied.  
   • Consequently, the paper does not provide direct guidance on how changing the other parameters (e.g., number of players, punishment cost, punishment magnitude, presence of rewards, or knowledge of the game’s end) would influence “efficiency.”  
   • For the two factors they do manipulate:  
      – When citizens have full information, a salaried authority elicits substantially more citizen assistance (hence stronger deterrence) than an appropriator authority—yet overall contribution rates and payoffs end up quite similar across the two.  
      – When citizens have only limited information, contributions drop significantly under a salaried authority, but remain higher under an appropriator authority, suggesting that “transparency” interacts with how officials are compensated to affect cooperation and payoffs.  
   • Beyond these two insights, the paper offers no predictions about systematically varying any other feature.

Abstract: Are people more prosocial in a religious context? We addressed this question through an experiment. However, these insights do not arise from manipulating the classic parameters (7–8) or (9–11); they arise from the three membership rules that the paper labels as different “treatments.”  
   • Therefore, on the narrow question of “how do the 15 parameters and interactions influence a punishment effect on efficiency in this paper,” the most accurate conclusion, based strictly on the text, is that no direct or numerical predictions can be made.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Summary Answers:

A. The paper does not directly use “efficiency” (actual payoff divided by maximum possible) as a main dependent variable. Instead, its main outcomes are (a) contributions, (b) group size/composition, and (c) participant earnings. These three are different from a formal “efficiency ratio,” though the authors do occasionally compare earnings to a group‐optimal payoff level.

B. Parameters explicitly mentioned: #1 (12 players), #2 (20 rounds), #4 (choice is a 0–15 integer, not all‐or‐nothing), #6 (1.5 multiplier and nonlinear costs, but not systematically varied), #12 (the finite number of rounds is known), #13 (subjects see partial information about average group contributions). C. The paper does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters to examine a “punishment treatment effect.” Indeed, no standard punishment or reward mechanism is introduced, so there is no direct numeric effect size for any parameter’s impact on punishment.

Because the paper neither sets up nor measures a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency,” it provides no basis for predictions about systematically varying those 15 parameters for that purpose. The authors only discuss that “restricted entry” can act like a punishment for low contributors (by barring entry) and “restricted exit” can act like a punishment for high contributors (by trapping them). Beyond that qualitative observation, nothing in the text allows one to make specific predictions about how those 15 parameters (or their interactions) would affect efficiency if one added a punishment mechanism.

Those are the relevant details as presented in the paper itself.

Abstract: Ethnic groups are thought to be particularly good at enforcing cooperative behavior, in part because social networks among coethnics are favorable to peer sanctioning schemes, resulting in observed outcomes like higher public goods provision in ethnically homogeneous areas and infrequent interethnic conflict. This article formalizes this process, accounting for networks that spread news relevant to sanctioning from peer to peer. Below I walk through each of the 15 design parameters and state, strictly on the basis of the paper by dos Santos & Wedekind (2015):

• whether the parameter is mentioned and, if so, the value(s) that are actually used;  
• whether the paper systematically varies that parameter and reports how the variation changes the “punishment-treatment effect.”  
(The authors never run a “with–punishment vs. without-punishment” treatment; the closest comparison they make is between three DIFFERENT reputation systems—generosity-scoring, punishment-scoring, reward-scoring.  Their main dependent variable is cooperation frequency, not efficiency.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players (group size, n)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Typical values shown in Fig. 1 run from n ≈ 5 up to at least n ≈ 20 (exact tick labels not printed in the excerpt, but multiple sizes are simulated).  
   • Systematically varied? Yes; Fig. 1 plots cooperation frequency against n.  
   • Effect on “punishment-treatment effect”? They do NOT compare “no-punishment” to “punishment,” so no treatment effect on efficiency is reported.  What Fig. 1 does show is that under punishment-scoring larger n lowers cooperation, though the decline is less steep than under generosity-scoring.  No numeric effect size on efficiency exists.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  Each individual plays m = 5 interactions per generation.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • No information on any treatment effect.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Not mentioned at all → no information.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Yes.  Contribution is strictly binary (contribute cost c or defect).  
   • Never varied.

5. Contribution default / endowment pulled back?  
   • Not mentioned.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR, factor r)  
   • Mentioned.  Baselines such as r = 0.9 n and r = 0.66 n are used.  
   • r is adjusted in a few places (main text and Appendix A8–A9) but only to show that the qualitative ranking of reputation systems is unchanged.  No systematic sweep and no efficiency numbers, hence no treatment-effect estimate.

7. Punishment cost (α)  
   • Mentioned.  Baseline α = 0.1; other α (not printed in main text) appear in Appendix figs.  
   • Varied jointly with β in “different punishment ratios,” but only qualitatively (“cooperation could also emerge more easily for different punishment ratios,” Figs. A8–A9).  No numerical effect on efficiency or on a punishment-vs-baseline treatment.

8. Punishment magnitude (β)  
   • Mentioned.  Baseline β = 0.3 or β = 0.5 depending on figure.  
   • Same limited qualitative variation as for α; no efficiency or treatment-effect numbers.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Yes.  A separate “reward-scoring” scenario replaces punishment with reward.  
   • Not used to estimate any punishment-treatment effect—the whole punishment stage is removed, so no comparison within punishment conditions.

10. Reward cost (cost per unit reward)  
    • α again, but in reward model.  Fixed; not varied.

11. Reward magnitude (benefit per unit reward)  
    • β again, but in reward model.  Fixed; not varied.

12. Are the number of rounds known to players?  
    • Not discussed (the simulation assumes infinite-horizon evolutionary play with no end-game awareness).

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Yes: “Each interaction is public, and everybody knows everybody’s reputation.”  
    • Never varied.

14. Is the identity of the punisher revealed?  
    • Yes: reputation is based on “who punished defectors in their last interaction,” so identities are revealed.  
    • Not varied.

15. Is the identity of the rewarder revealed?  
    • Analogous statement in reward model.  Not varied.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables used  
   • The paper never reports group efficiency (total payoff / maximum payoff).  
   • Main DV: cooperation frequency (proportion of contributors in the PGG).  
   • They also track strategy frequencies (e.g., proportion of punishers) but do not call these dependent variables in the statistical sense.  
   • Efficiency, earnings, or pay-offs are not plotted or analysed.

B. Which of the 15 parameters appear?  
   • 10 of 15 are explicitly mentioned: 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15 (chat, contribution default, knowledge of horizon are absent).  
   • Only two—group size (1) and punishment parameters α, β (7, 8)—are ever varied, and only group size is varied systematically in the main text.

C. For how many parameters is the effect of systematic variation on the punishment-treatment effect reported?  
   • Zero.  Because there is no “with-punishment vs. without-punishment” comparison and no efficiency measure, the paper gives no quantitative treatment-effect estimates for any of the 15 parameters.

D. Forecasts you could make about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency, based solely on this paper  
   • Almost none.  The paper shows that when a punishment-based reputation rule is in force, larger groups still cooperate more than under a generosity-based rule, suggesting that if one compared “no-punishment” (but generosity scoring) to “with-punishment” (and punishment scoring) the efficiency gain from adding punishment probably shrinks with group size but remains positive.  Beyond that qualitative guess, the article supplies no data that let us quantify how any of the 15 parameters, alone or in interaction, would change the efficiency effect of introducing punishment.

In short, the paper is informative about how reputation mechanisms built on punitive actions can sustain cooperation, but it does not give usable estimates for predicting the efficiency impact of adding punishment under different experimental parameter choices.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter survey of what (if anything) the paper “Spatial Evolution of Social Norms in a Common-Pool Resource Game” says, first about whether the parameter is even mentioned, and second about whether the paper makes any predictions about systematically varying that parameter and how it would affect a “punishment treatment effect.” As instructed, “punishment treatment effect” is understood here as how introducing punishment (enforcers) would change some outcome—ideally group efficiency, but at least payoffs or cooperation. Where the paper is silent, I state that explicitly.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  
     Yes. The paper denotes the total number of agents by n, studies various values (e.g., n = 5, 8, 9, 100), and explores how the number of agents shapes the existence of particular equilibria (e.g., D–E or C–D–E equilibria).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it and predict an effect on a punishment “treatment effect” for efficiency (or any other dependent variable)?  
     The paper does systematically vary n to show that certain punish/punished (enforcer–defector) equilibria only arise above specific thresholds (for instance, n ≥ 5 or n ≥ 9). However, it does not connect those findings directly to a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Instead, the paper frames results in terms of whether enforcers can coexist with defectors/cooperators, not how much total payoffs or efficiency change due to punishers.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  
     The paper uses discrete “time steps” (or “rounds”) for its evolutionary updates, and sometimes goes up to 200 time steps in simulations. However, it does not study finite vs. infinite horizons in the sense of a repeated public‐goods experiment, nor does it discuss whether agents know when the game ends.  
   • Systematically varied for punishment effect on efficiency (or other outcomes)?  
     No. The paper does not systematically vary the number of rounds, nor does it compare how a known vs. unknown ending influences punishment.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned?  
     No. The paper does not discuss any form of communication or “chat.”  
   • Effect of systematically varying it?  
     Not discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned?  
     No. The paper discusses “cooperators” who use low effort xL and “defectors” who use high effort xH, but it does not present this as an “all‐or‐nothing” forced choice, nor does it use that language.  
   • Effect of systematically varying it?  
     Not discussed.

5. Is the contribution default (in the sense of a default endowment returned to the player)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     No. The paper does not describe participants deciding how much of their endowment to transfer to themselves from a public fund, nor mention defaults.  
   • Effect of systematically varying it?  
     Not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  
     The paper uses a concave harvest function F(X) and sometimes writes Z(X) = F(X)/X – w, but it does not use or vary a standard “MPCR” factor as in typical linear public goods games. Its functional forms (e.g., N^½ X^½) are not treated like an MPCR that is systematically tuned.  
   • Effect of systematically varying it?  
     Not discussed in terms of “punishment treatment effect.” The paper only notes that more intense exploitation reduces returns for everyone, but does not link this to a formal MPCR measure or a direct measure of efficiency changes under punishment.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned?  
     Yes. Denoted by γ (“gamma”). The paper devotes considerable discussion to how γ compares to δ (the penalty inflicted on defectors).  
   • Effect of systematically varying it with respect to punishment outcomes?  
     The paper does systematically vary γ (in both propositions and simulations) to show which equilibria (D–E, C–D–E, etc.) arise or disappear. However, it does not tie these results to an explicit “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Instead, it focuses on whether enforcers persist, how many defectors remain, etc. No numerical effect size on “efficiency” is reported.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned?  
     Yes. Denoted by δ (“delta”). It is the sanction that defectors pay whenever an enforcer punishes them.  
   • Effect of systematically varying it?  
     Yes. The paper systematically varies δ and reports how that changes frequencies of outcomes (D, C–E, C–D–E, blinking states, etc.). It does not provide an explicit effect size on efficiency. Instead, it reports (for example) that for certain ranges of δ, the likelihood of stable coexistence of enforcers and defectors goes up or down.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned?  
     No. The model is only about “punishing” defectors, not rewarding cooperators.  
   • Effect of systematically varying it?  
     Not discussed.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Mentioned?  
     No.  
   • Effect of systematically varying it?  
     Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward)  
   • Mentioned?  
     No.  
   • Effect of systematically varying it?  
     Not discussed.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
   • Mentioned?  
     No. The paper does not address whether agents know the total duration of the game or the update horizons.  
   • Effect of systematically varying it?  
     Not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much others gained or lost)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     Partly. The paper states that an agent only observes payoffs (or average payoffs) of neighbors on a circle. This local information is central to the imitation step (“they imitate the strategy in their neighborhood with the highest payoff on average”).  
   • Effect of systematically varying that information?  
     The paper does not systematically vary “information display,” so no direct effect on “punishment treatment” is discussed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who punished them?  
   • Mentioned?  
     The paper does say that a defector is punished by any enforcer in the adjacent neighborhood. It does not detail whether the punished defector knows the specific punisher’s identity.  
   • Effect of systematically varying it?  
     Not discussed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is?  
   • Mentioned?  
     Not applicable. There is no reward mechanism in the model.  
   • Effect of systematically varying it?  
     Not discussed.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper does not measure “group efficiency” the way it is often defined in public‐goods experiments (i.e., actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff). Instead, it analyzes payoffs of different strategy types (cooperators, defectors, enforcers) and whether cooperators/enforcers can persist. It sometimes refers to Pareto‐efficient or socially optimal effort levels, but most results are framed in terms of whether cooperation strategies survive in equilibrium, rather than explicitly calculating “group efficiency.”  

   • The paper’s other dependent variables.  
     – Existence and stability of “C–D–E” equilibria vs. losing or retaining enforcers.  
     – Frequencies of ending up in certain configurations (D‐only, C–E, C–D–E, “cycling,” etc.).  

B. Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Explicitly mentioned:  
     1. Number of players (n).  
     7. Punishment cost (γ).  
     8. Punishment magnitude (δ).  
     13. Limited mention that agents see neighbors’ payoffs (though not varied experimentally).  
   • None of the others (2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 15) are substantively mentioned or varied.

C. For which (and how many) parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, the paper never uses “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency. It does, however, systematically vary the number of players n, the punishment cost γ, and the punishment magnitude δ to see whether enforcers (and thus punishment) survive in equilibrium. This is three parameters (1, 7, 8).  
   • Even then, the paper reports these parameters’ effects on equilibrium frequencies or the presence of stable enforcers, not a numerical effect size on group efficiency. No table or figure in the paper gives a direct measure of “efficiency change” from punishment.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not supply a direct measure of efficiency or a formal “punishment treatment effect.” Its focus is on which equilibria (C, D, E, or mixed) emerge and survive.  
   • The only parameters the paper clearly ties to the punishment mechanism are n, γ (punishment cost), and δ (punishment inflicted). From the paper’s analysis, one might infer that heavier punishment (larger δ) can help stabilize “enforcer” strategies and thereby reduce overall exploitation—which presumably could improve group outcomes if we labeled that “efficiency.” Similarly, a lower cost to punish (γ) can facilitate stable punishment. But the paper does not quantify by how much total payoffs, or a percentage of maximum payoff, increase or decrease.  
   • All other parameters listed in the user’s question are either unmentioned or not explored in connection to punishment or efficiency. Thus, based solely on this paper, one cannot make further predictions about them.
reference_APA: Noailly, Joelle, Withagen, Cees A. & van den Bergh, Jeroen C. J. M. (2007). Spatial evolution of social norms in a common-pool resource game. ENVIRONMENTAL & RESOURCE ECONOMICS.

Authors: Berger, J; Hevenstone, D
Author Full Names: Berger, Joel; Hevenstone, Debra
Article Title: Norm enforcement in the city revisited: An international field experiment of altruistic punishment, norm maintenance, and broken windows
Author Keywords: Broken windows; field experiment; norm enforcement; punishment; social control
Keywords Plus: PEOPLES REACTIONS; COLLECTIVE ACTION; SOCIAL-CONTROL; COOPERATION; DISORDER; DEMAND; EVOLUTION; SANCTIONS; BEHAVIOR
Abstract: In laboratory experiments, people are willing to sanction norms at a costa behavioral tendency called altruistic punishment. However, the degree to which these findings can be generalized to real-world interactions is still debated. Only a small number of field experiments have been conducted, and initial results suggest that punishment is less frequent outside of the lab. This study replicates one of the first field experiments on altruistic punishment and builds ties to research on norm compliance and the broken windows theory. The original study addressed the enforcement of the anti-littering norm in Athens. We replicate this study in Bern, Zurich, and New York City. As an extension, we investigate how the experimental context (clean vs littered) impacts social norm enforcement. As a second extension, we investigate how opportunity structure impacts the maintenance of the anti-littering norm. Findings indicate that norms are universally enforced, although significantly less than in the standard laboratory experiment, and that enforcement is significantly more common in Switzerland than in New York. Moreover, individuals prefer more subtle forms of enforcement to direct punishment. Abstract: Background. Paranoia involves thoughts and beliefs about the harmful intent of others but the social consequences have been much less studied. We investigated whether paranoia predicts maladaptive social behaviour in terms of cooperative and punitive behaviour using experimental game theory paradigms, and examined whether reduced cooperation is best explained in terms of distrust as previous studies have claimed. Methods. We recruited a large population sample (N = 2132) online. All participants completed the Green et al. Paranoid Thoughts Scale and (i) a Dictator Game and (ii) an Ultimatum Game, the former with an option for costly punishment. Following distrust-based accounts, we predicted highly paranoid people would make higher offers when the outcome depended on receiving a positive response from their partner (Ultimatum Game) but no difference when the partner's response was irrelevant (Dictator Game). We also predicted paranoia would increase punitive responses. Predictions were pre-registered in advance of data collection. Data and materials are open access. Results. Highly paranoid participants actually made lower offers than non-paranoid participants both in the Dictator Game and in the Ultimatum Game. Paranoia positively predicted punitive responses. Conclusions. These findings suggest that distrust is not the best explanation for reduced cooperation in paranoia and alternative explanations, such as increased self-interest, may apply. However, the tendency to attribute harmful intent to partners was important in motivating punitive responses. Below I go through the 15 parameters in the order given and follow the requested format.  
For each parameter I state  

(1) whether the paper even mentions or fixes that parameter (and, if so, its value), and  
(2) whether the paper makes any prediction or provides any numerical evidence about **systematically varying** that parameter on the *punishment treatment effect* (for any dependent variable the authors analyse – note that none of their DVs is group-efficiency).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned.  All sessions involve three roles: two first-order decision makers (A, B) whose choices are observed, and one third-party “observer/sanctioner” (C).  The number of players is always 3.  
   (2) Never varied; no predictions or effect sizes reported.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) One-shot game (single round) in both experiments.  
   (2) Not varied; no predictions.

3. Chat enabled between players  
   (1) Not mentioned; no chat was allowed.  
   (2) Not discussed.

4. All-or-nothing contribution constraint  
   (1) Not used.  A & B could choose any integer 0-100 coins (continuous choice).  
   (2) Not discussed.

5. Contribution default / endowment moved *back* from public fund  
   (1) Not part of the design.  
   (2) Not discussed.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   (1) Fixed.  In the Public-Good frame each contributed coin is multiplied by 1.5 and then split equally, so MPCR = 0.75.  An isomorphic 1.5 multiplier applies to remaining coins in the Common-Resource frame.  
   (2) Not varied; no predictions.

7. Punishment cost (to punisher)  
   (1) Fixed at 1 coin per unit.  
   (2) Not varied; no predictions.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss to target per unit)  
   (1) Fixed at 3 coins per unit.  
   (2) Not varied; no predictions.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   (1) Explicitly manipulated.  
       • Experiment 1: between-subject design – participants were forced either to *only* punish (decrement coins) or *only* reward (increment coins).  
       • Experiment 2: within-subject *choice* condition – reward and punishment were both available and the subject chose which to use.  
   (2) Yes, the paper predicts and reports effects of this manipulation, although the authors’ dependent variables are (a) the binary *decision to sanction* and (b) *sanction size*, not efficiency.  Main findings:

       Experiment 1 (forced-choice)  
       – Probability of sanctioning: reward 86.8 % vs punishment 66.1 % (Logit: B = 1.224, OR = 3.40, p = .009).  
       – Mean sanction size: reward 30.31 coins vs punishment 11.47 coins (F = 30.29, p < .001, η² = .19).

       Experiment 2 (free choice)  
       – Among sanctioners, 77.6 % chose reward, 22.4 % chose punishment (OR ≈ 3.46).  
       – Mean reward size 38.87 coins; mean punishment size 15.75 coins.

10. Reward cost  
    (1) Fixed at 1 coin per unit.  
    (2) Not varied; no predictions.

11. Reward magnitude  
    (1) Fixed at +3 coins per unit.  
    (2) Not varied; no predictions.

12. Do players know the number of rounds?  
    (1) Not relevant – single-shot.  
    (2) Not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    (1) Yes.  The observer is told exactly how many coins each of A and B contributed/harvested.  Value is constant across conditions.  
    (2) Not varied; no predictions.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
    (1) Not mentioned; presumably anonymous.  
    (2) Not discussed.

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
    (1) Not mentioned; presumably anonymous.  
    (2) Not discussed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY  

A. Does the paper use group efficiency as a dependent variable?  
   No.  Dependent variables are:  
   • “Choice to sanction” (binary: yes/no)  
   • “Sanction size” (number of coins given as reward or taken as punishment)  
   These variables capture the *willingness to sanction*. They are conceptually different from group efficiency, total payoff, contribution rate, etc.; the paper never reports efficiency numbers.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
   9 of 15: 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13.

C. For how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their *systematic variation* and its effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
   Only 1 parameter – #9 (reward enabled vs. punishment only) – is experimentally varied and analysed.  No other parameter is manipulated.

D. What predictions can be made, solely from this paper, about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) will influence the punishment treatment effect on *efficiency*?  
   • The paper offers virtually no guidance for efficiency; it never measures pay-offs of the group.  
   • All fixed parameters (1-8, 10-15) are held constant, so the authors make no claims about what would happen if they changed.  
   • The only clear implication is that giving participants the *option* to reward instead of punish (parameter 9) greatly reduces the frequency and size of punishment.  If, in a public-goods game, punishment is the only sanction available, one might expect more punishment than when both reward and punishment are available.  Whether this raises or lowers *efficiency* is unknown, because the paper does not connect sanction frequency/size to final pay-offs.  
   Hence, apart from expecting “less punishment when reward is enabled,” the paper provides almost no basis for predicting efficiency effects of the 15 parameters or their interactions.

Abstract: Strong reciprocity explains prosocial cooperation by the presence of individuals who incur costs to help those who helped them ('strong positive reciprocity') and to punish those who wronged them ('strong negative reciprocity').    – Mentioned? Yes, implicitly. The design is one-shot (plus a prior classification phase that does not feed back into the main interaction).

   – Systematically varied? No. The paper does not discuss any variation in the number of rounds or its effect on punishment or efficiency.

3. Is chat enabled between players?

   – Mentioned? No. The standard public-goods procedure is used: participants have 20 tokens and decide how many they want to put into the group project; there is no mention of a “default” mechanism.  
   – Systematically varied? No.

   – Mentioned? Yes. The paper states that contributions are multiplied by 1.6 and then split among the four group members.  
   – Any specific value(s)? 1.6.

Abstract: Although positive incentives for cooperators and/or negative incentives for free-riders in social dilemmas play an important role in maintaining cooperation, there is still the outstanding issue of who should pay the cost of incentives. The second-order free-rider problem, in which players who do not provide the incentives dominate in a game, is a well-known academic challenge. In order to meet this challenge, we devise and analyze a meta-incentive game that integrates positive incentives (rewards) and negative incentives (punishments) with second-order incentives, which are incentives for other players' incentives. The critical assumption of our model is that players who tend to provide incentives to other players for their cooperative or non-cooperative behavior also tend to provide incentives to their incentive behaviors. In this paper, we solve the replicator dynamics for a simple version of the game and analytically categorize the game types into four groups. We find that the second-order free-rider problem is completely resolved without any third-order or higher (meta) incentive under the assumption. To do so, a second-order costly incentive, which is given individually (peer-to-peer) after playing donation games, is needed. The paper concludes that (1) second-order incentives for first-order reward are necessary for cooperative regimes, (2) a system without first-order rewards cannot maintain a cooperative regime, (3) a system with first-order rewards and no incentives for rewards is the worst because it never reaches cooperation, and (4) a system with rewards for incentives is more likely to be a cooperative regime than a system with punishments for incentives when the cost-effect ratio of incentives is sufficiently large. This solution is general and strong in the sense that the game does not need any centralized institution or proactive system for incentives.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what, if anything, the Okada et al. (2015) paper says about each of the 15 parameters in relation to punishment and efficiency. Throughout, “the paper” refers solely to the text of Okada et al. (2015) as provided in your prompt.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – The paper assumes an infinitely large, well‐mixed population (i.e., effectively “infinite” players). It does not discuss varying the number of players.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – None. The paper does not analyze changing the number of players, nor does it link this to any treatment‐effect measure (including efficiency).

2. Number of rounds
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – Not mentioned at all.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – None.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – Not mentioned.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – None.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – The basic “donation game” in their model is a binary choice to cooperate (help) or defect (not help). While that is indeed “all or nothing,” the paper does not discuss experimentally or theoretically varying that feature.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – None.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – Not mentioned.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – None.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – The paper uses a cost of donation c = 1 and a benefit b to the recipient. However, it does not systematically vary b or examine a “multiplication factor” (MPCR).  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – None.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – Yes. Denoted as P1 (first‐order punishment cost) or Pp (second‐order), but ultimately folded into their key ratio μ (the “incentive cost‐effect ratio”). They do examine how different μ values affect whether cooperation can be stable.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – The paper focuses on whether cooperation (or “cooperative regimes”) can be maintained, rather than on group efficiency per se. It does not quantify an “effect size” on efficiency or total payoff from changing punishment cost. No numerical effect on efficiency is given.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player per unit of punishment)
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – Yes. Denoted as F1 (first‐order punishment “fine”) or Fp (second‐order). Also subsumed within μ.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – Same as #7 above: the paper discusses how different values of the fine/cost ratio can stabilize or destabilize cooperation, but does not give quantitative predictions about efficiency. No explicit numerical effect on efficiency is reported.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – Yes. Rewards (A1, R1, etc.) and their presence/absence figure centrally in the “24 possible configurations” of the meta‐incentive game. The paper contrasts punishment‐only systems with those that include reward and shows that second‐order incentives for first‐order reward are crucial for stable cooperation.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – They do discuss that enabling reward (especially if backed by meta‐incentives) can help maintain cooperation. However, they do not present numerical measures of how “enabling/disabling reward” changes efficiency. Their findings are about stable vs. unstable cooperation rather than explicit total‐payoff ratios.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – Yes. Denoted as R1 (cost of first‐order reward) and similarly Rr (cost of second‐order reward), etc. Again, folded into μ and δ in the simplified model.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – The paper’s main predictions concern whether cooperation equilibria are stable. None of the analyses provide quantitative “efficiency” outcomes (e.g., how payoffs scale) from systematic variation of reward cost alone.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – Yes. Denoted as A1 (first‐order reward) and similarly Ar (second‐order). As with punishment, the ratio μ = (reward or punishment magnitude)/(cost) is the key parameter in their analysis.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – Again, the paper focuses on describing conditions under which cooperation is stable. No explicit effect sizes or direct measures of efficiency are reported.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – Not mentioned.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – None.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much peers gained/lost each round)?
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – The model assumes all players have “perfect” information about who cooperated and who gave incentives but does not discuss manipulating the visibility of outcomes.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – None.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – Not explicitly mentioned, other than stating “peer‐to‐peer incentives” in a well‐mixed population with “perfect information.” They do not discuss varying the anonymity or identifiability of punishers.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – None.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is?
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – Same as #14: not varied or explicitly discussed.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – None.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are they different?  
   – The paper does not present group efficiency in the sense of “actual total payoff divided by maximum possible payoff.” Although “efficiency” is mentioned in a qualitative sense (e.g., trading off efficiency for stability, or seeking an “efficient” incentive level), the main dependent variables throughout are the stability of cooperation and the frequencies of different strategies in the population under replicator dynamics. So the paper’s analyses revolve around whether particular incentive configurations yield stable cooperative equilibria, not around numerical efficiency measures.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – Seven parameters appear in some form:  
       (1) Number of players (infinite population is assumed)  
       (4) All or nothing contribution (the base donation game is binary, though not varied)  
       (7) Punishment cost (P1, Pp, part of the incentive‐cost ratio μ)  
       (8) Punishment magnitude (F1, Fp, also part of μ)  
       (9) Whether reward is enabled (explicitly compared: punishment‐only vs. punishment‐plus‐reward)  
       (10) Reward cost (R1, Rr, etc.)  
       (11) Reward magnitude (A1, Ar, etc.)  
   – The remaining eight parameters (#2, #3, #5, #6, #12, #13, #14, #15) receive no meaningful discussion or are not varied.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   – The paper primarily studies punishment and/or reward cost/magnitude collectively via the ratio μ and the discount factor δ. It uses these to determine whether cooperation stabilizes. However, it does not link changes in these parameters to a quantitative “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Instead, it shows how large/small μ and δ must be for stable cooperation to emerge under different incentive configurations. No numerical effect sizes are provided in terms of efficiency or payoffs.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   – The paper provides no direct modeling or data on final payoffs versus the maximum possible, so one cannot derive numerical predictions for efficiency. About all one can say is that if an incentive system (punishment alone, reward alone, or combined) has a sufficiently high cost‐effect ratio (μ) and if it includes second‐order rewards for rewarding, then cooperation can stabilize—and presumably yields higher overall payoffs (and thus higher efficiency). Beyond that, the paper does not give explicit guidance for how each of the 15 parameters or their interactions would quantitatively shift a punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency.

1. Number of players (group size)  
(1) Mentioned several times.  Key sentence: “evolutionary game theory shows that … volunteers … emerge sooner in smaller groups than in larger groups [22].”  The authors also recommend subdividing large on-line networks into smaller “sub-groups.”  No concrete numbers are given.

(1) Not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?

(1) Not discussed.  
(2) No prediction.

15. Do rewarded players learn the identity of their rewarder?  
(1) Not discussed.  
(2) No prediction.

-------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables actually used in the paper  
The article is a narrative review; it does not present original experimental data.  Thus no dependent variables are *measured* by the authors.  Variables discussed in cited work include contribution level, emergence time of volunteers, adoption of pro-environmental practices, reputation scores, etc.  “Group efficiency” (total or average payoff relative to optimum) is never reported as a dependent variable.

B. How many of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
Six are mentioned in any form:  
1 (group size), 2 (repeated vs one-shot), 3 (communication), 7 (costly punishment is possible), 9 (rewards can be provided), 13 (visibility of peer outcomes).

Zero.  The only quantitative directional statement (“volunteers emerge sooner in smaller groups”) involves group size but is silent on punishment.  No tables or figures provide effect sizes for any of the 15 parameters.

• Allowing repeated interaction (more rounds) and making peers’ actions visible (parameter 13) should increase the baseline cooperation level; whether that strengthens or weakens the *incremental* benefit of punishment is not addressed.  
• Enabling communication (parameter 3) is viewed as helpful for cooperation, but no link is drawn to punishment efficacy.  
Beyond these broad guesses, the paper offers no basis for quantitative or even directional predictions about how systematic changes in any of the 15 parameters, alone or in combination, would move the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Abstract: Recent experimental studies seem to concur that gossip is good for groups by showing that gossip stems from prosocial motives to protect group members from non-cooperators. Thus, these studies emphasize the bright side of gossip. However, scattered studies point to detrimental outcomes of gossip for individuals and groups, arguing that a dark side of gossip exists. To understand the implications of gossip for cooperation in groups, both the dark and bright side of gossip must be illuminated. We investigated both sides of gossip in two scenario studies. Participants showed a higher group protection motivation in response to gossip when imagining gossiping to a potential victim of a norm violator compared to a non-victim. They showed a higher emotion venting motivation when imagining gossiping to a non-victim compared to a potential victim. Both these gossip motives were related to an increased tendency to gossip. In Study 2 (N = 104), we manipulated whether participants were the targets or observers of gossip and whether the gossip was true or false. Results showed that targets of negative gossip intended to increase their work effort in the short run, but only when the gossip was true. Furthermore, gossip targets reported lower long-term cooperative intentions toward their workgroup regardless of gossip veracity. This paper demonstrates that gossip has both a dark and bright side and that situational factors and agent perspectives determine which side prevails.

Abstract: Explaining the evolution of cooperation remains one of the greatest problems for both biology and social science. The classical theories of cooperation suggest that cooperation equilibrium or evolutionary stable strategy between partners can be maintained through genetic similarity or reciprocity relatedness. These classical theories are based on an assumption that partners interact symmetrically with equal payoffs in a game of cooperation interaction. However, the payoff between partners is usually not equal and therefore they often interact asymmetrically in real cooperative systems. With the Hawk-Dove model, we find that the probability of cooperation between cooperative partners will depend closely on the payoff ratio. The higher the payoff ratio between recipients and cooperative actors, the greater will be the probability of cooperation interaction between involved partners. The greatest probability of conflict between cooperative partners will occur when the payoff between partners is equal. The results show that this asymmetric relationship is one of the key dynamics of the evolution of cooperation, and that pure cooperation strategy (i.e., Nash equilibrium) does not exist in asymmetrical cooperation systems, which well explains the direct conflict observed in almost all of the well documented cooperation systems. The model developed here shows that the cost-to-benefit ratio of cooperation is also negatively correlated with the probability of cooperation interaction. A smaller cost-to-benefit ratio of cooperation might be created by the limited dispersal ability or exit cost of the partners involved, and it will make the punishment of the non-cooperative individuals by the recipient more credible, and therefore make it more possible to maintain stable cooperation interaction.

   • Prediction from paper about varying this parameter on punishment treatment effect?  
     No. This is not addressed in the paper.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussion in paper?  
     The paper deals with Hawk-Dove payoff matrices, not public goods contributions. It does not describe “all-or-nothing” contributions.  
   • Prediction from paper about varying this parameter on punishment treatment effect?  
     No. Nothing is stated in the paper.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much to move from the public fund back into their hand)?
   • Discussion in paper?  
     The study does not address a public goods setup or a contribution default; it uses the Hawk-Dove model.  
   • Prediction from paper about varying this parameter on punishment treatment effect?  
     No. Unmentioned in the paper.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factors
   • Discussion in paper?  
     The paper uses the ratio m = v/c (benefit to cost of conflict) but does not frame this as a “marginal per capita return.” It does not treat the public goods MPCR concept.  
   • Prediction from paper about varying this parameter on punishment treatment effect?  
     No. While the paper examines how changing m affects the frequency of cooperation in the Hawk-Dove game, it never analyzes an external “punishment treatment” or group efficiency in a public goods sense.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussion in paper?  
     The paper uses “c” as the cost incurred during a Hawk-Dove conflict, but does not treat or label it as “punishment cost.” Although the text refers to “dominant or host might implement a strategy to punish,” it does not provide any numeric cost or systematic manipulation of an explicit punishment-cost parameter.  
   • Prediction from paper about varying this parameter on punishment treatment effect?  
     No. The paper does not systematically vary a punishment-cost parameter in the sense of public goods punishment.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed on them)
   • Discussion in paper?  
     Although “P = (v - c)/2” appears in the classical Hawk-Dove payoff matrix, that “punishment” is just the payoff to both hawks meeting (i.e., a conflict cost), not an imposed peer-punishment. The paper does not discuss a parameter that sets “punishment magnitude” in a public-goods sense.  
   • Prediction from paper about varying this parameter on punishment treatment effect?  
     No. It is not addressed.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussion in paper?  
     The paper briefly references that a dominant individual “might ... reward cooperating individuals,” but provides no formula or explicit parameter for “reward.”  
   • Prediction from paper about varying this parameter on punishment treatment effect?  
     No. The text does not systematically vary or measure the effect of enabling a reward as in a public goods experiment.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Discussion in paper?  
      No explicit mention about a cost paid by the rewarder (e.g., cost to the host or dominant to reward) or any relevant parameter variation.  
    • Prediction from paper about varying this parameter on punishment treatment effect?  
      No.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward)
    • Discussion in paper?  
      The paper does not discuss a formal reward parameter or how varying it influences cooperation.  
    • Prediction from paper about varying this parameter on punishment treatment effect?  
      No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Discussion in paper?  
      The paper does not address repeated-play knowledge or whether game endpoints are common knowledge.  
    • Prediction from paper about varying this parameter on punishment treatment effect?  
      No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost each round)?
    • Discussion in paper?  
      No. The paper does not discuss the observability of other players’ payoffs.  
    • Prediction from paper about varying this parameter on punishment treatment effect?  
      No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Discussion in paper?  
      No. There is no concept of direct punisher identity or any mention of how knowledge of punisher identity might matter.  
    • Prediction from paper about varying this parameter on punishment treatment effect?  
      No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Discussion in paper?  
      No. Same as above, no mention.  
    • Prediction from paper about systematically varying this parameter on punishment treatment effect?  
      No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper examines payoff matrices in a Hawk-Dove game, as well as the probability/frequency of cooperation (x₀) under different cost-benefit and asymmetry conditions. It does discuss individual expected payoffs, but does not measure “group efficiency” as total payoff divided by the maximum possible cooperative payoff. Its main dependent variables include the mixed-strategy frequency of cooperation and the associated Nash equilibrium payoffs. These are not the same as group efficiency.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • None of the 15 parameters are explicitly mentioned in the context of a public-goods or punishment-treatment experiment. The paper does talk generally about “punishment” by a dominant or host but does not define or systematically vary any of the 15 parameters as listed (e.g., cost to punish, magnitude, MPCR, etc.).

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. The paper does not systematically vary or analyze any of the 15 parameters in terms of a “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency or on any other outcome measure. There is no numerical effect size reported for any of the 15 parameters.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not provide enough information to form predictions specific to introducing punishment in a public goods game or how that would influence efficiency according to each of these 15 parameters. Consequently, no predictions can be drawn from this paper alone regarding the systematic variation of those parameters on efficiency.
reference_APA: Wang RuiWu, He JunZhou, Wang YaQiang, Shi Lei & Li YaoTang (2010). Asymmetric interaction will facilitate the evolution of cooperation. SCIENCE CHINA-LIFE SCIENCES.

Abstract: The study of warfare from an evolutionary perspective has expanded rapidly over the last couple of decades. However, it has tended to focus on the ancestral origins, prevalence, and instruments of war rather than adaptationist analyses of its underlying psychology. I argue that our evolved coalitional psychology may contain a set of distinct evolved heuristics designed specifically for offensive and defensive coalitional aggression. Data from two survey experiments are presented, in which subjects were given scenarios depicting offensive or defensive aggression and were told to make decisions, for example, regarding their willingness to participate in the conflict, their opinions of others who did not choose to participate, and their expectations benefit. The results indicate that humans do indeed distinguish readily between these two domains and that their willingness to participate, as well as their emotional responses toward others, is highly contingent upon this informational cue in adaptively relevant ways. In addition, and consistent with parental investment theory, data reveal a range of sex differences in attitudes toward coalitional aggression in the two conflict domains. Beyond the study of warfare, this project has implications for our understanding of the relationship between individual behavior and group dynamics, as well as for our understanding of the mechanisms by which the psychological framing of political events can lead to important social outcomes.

Below, each of the 15 public-goods-game (PGG) design parameters is treated in turn.

For every parameter I report  
(1) whether it is mentioned in the article at all (including in theory sections), and, if so, what fixed value or qualitative assumption is implied;  
(2) whether the authors **systematically vary** the parameter and report a quantitative impact on any “punishment treatment effect.”  (No such treatment effect is ever computed, so the answer will usually be “No.”)  
If a parameter is never mentioned I state that explicitly.

----------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? ‑- No.  
   • Systematically varied? ‑- No.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? ‑- No.  
   • Systematically varied? ‑- No.

3. Is chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned? ‑- No.  
   • Systematically varied? ‑- No.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule?  
   • Mentioned? ‑- No.  
   • Systematically varied? ‑- No.

5. Contribution default / endowment “take-back” frame?  
   • Mentioned? ‑- No.  
   • Systematically varied? ‑- No.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? ‑- No.  
   • Systematically varied? ‑- No.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   • Mentioned?  Only at a verbal, theoretical level (“punishment reverses the fitness differential … participants incur a cost,” etc.).  No numeric value or experimental manipulation is supplied.  
   • Systematically varied? ‑- No.

8. Punishment magnitude to the target  
   • Mentioned?  Only conceptually (“coins deducted,” “reverse fitness differential”), never quantified or manipulated.  
   • Systematically varied? ‑- No.

9. Whether a reward option is enabled  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  “Reward sentiment” toward contributors is measured via survey items in both scenarios, so rewards are implicitly “enabled.” The option is **not** compared with a “no-reward” condition.  
   • Systematically varied? ‑- No.

10. Reward cost to giver  
    • Mentioned?  Theoretical discussion only (e.g., rewarding is “costly” and therefore rare).  No numbers, no manipulation.  
    • Systematically varied? ‑- No.

11. Reward magnitude to recipient  
    • Mentioned?  Only conceptually; never quantified or manipulated.  
    • Systematically varied? ‑- No.

12. Finite horizon known to subjects?  
    • Mentioned? ‑- No.  
    • Systematically varied? ‑- No.

13. Are peer outcomes displayed?  
    • Mentioned? ‑- No.  
    • Systematically varied? ‑- No.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
    • Mentioned? ‑- No.  
    • Systematically varied? ‑- No.

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
    • Mentioned? ‑- No.  
    • Systematically varied? ‑- No.

----------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables used  
    • The paper never measures “group efficiency” (total payoff / maximum payoff).  
    • Reported dependent variables are:  
        – Willingness to participate in coalitional aggression  
        – Expected personal benefit  
        – Expected group benefit  
        – Punitive sentiment toward non-participants  
        – Reward sentiment toward participants  
        – (in Study 2) Expected probability of success  
      These variables capture attitudes and intentions, not realized monetary payoffs, so they are conceptually distinct from efficiency.

B.  Which of the 15 design parameters appear anywhere in the paper?  
    • Parameter 7 (punishment cost) – mentioned conceptually  
    • Parameter 8 (punishment magnitude) – mentioned conceptually  
    • Parameter 9 (reward option) – implicitly present  
    Total mentioned: 3 of 15, all in purely verbal discussion.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper report the effect of **systematically varying** the parameter on any punishment treatment effect?  
    • None (0/15).  No parameter is experimentally manipulated, nor is any treatment‐control contrast on actual punishment behavior or on efficiency reported.

D.  If one had to forecast how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency **using only this paper**, almost no direct guidance is available.  The only qualitative insight is that punishment (and reward) may promote cooperation more strongly when:  
    • the underlying collective good is truly public (the authors’ “defense” frames) versus partly privatizable (their “offense” frames), and  
    • the group faces a labor shortage (analogous to low contribution levels).  
   Translating that intuition back to a standard PGG, one could very tentatively predict that punishment will raise efficiency more when MPCR is high (public-good benefits widely shared) and when current contributions are low (labor insufficient).  No statements can be made from the paper about numerical costs or magnitudes of punishment, number of players, rounds, information disclosure, etc.

In short, the article offers rich psychological theory about when humans *want* to punish or reward, but it provides virtually no experimental leverage on the 15 design parameters relevant to the punishment treatment effect on efficiency in laboratory public-goods games.

Abstract: To promote cooperation, people often rely on the administration of sanctions. However, from previous research we know that those in control of sanctions are generally reluctant to punish non-cooperative choice behavior and prefer to reward cooperative choice behavior, which is consistent with the do-no-harm principle. Below we go through the 15 public–goods-game parameters one at a time.  
For each parameter we state

(i) whether it appears anywhere in the paper and, if so, the value(s) that were actually used;  
(ii) whether the authors **systematically varied** that parameter and reported what such variation does to the punishment-treatment effect for any dependent variable (and, if so, the numeric effect that can be read from the tables or figures).  
Whenever nothing is said in the paper we say so explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (i) Mentioned.  Experiment 1: 4 players; Experiments 2 & 3: 5 players (the target “Person C” plus 4 others).  
   (ii) Never varied.  No prediction about changing group size on any outcome, let alone on efficiency.

2. Number of rounds  
   (i) All three experiments are one-shot; participants know this.  
   (ii) Not varied; no predictions.

3. Chat enabled?  
   (i) No chat is ever allowed; the word “chat” never occurs.  
   (ii) Not discussed, not varied, no predictions.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   (i) Contributions/harvests were continuous (0–10 chips).  
   (ii) Not varied; no predictions.

5. Contribution default / endowment relocation?  
   (i) Such a rule is never used or mentioned.  
   (ii) Not applicable.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   (i) Exp 1: remaining chips are doubled then split among 4 → MPCR = 0.50.  
       Exp 2 & 3: remaining chips doubled then split among 5 → MPCR = 0.40.  
   (ii) MPCR is fixed in each study and never manipulated; no predictions.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   (i) Always zero.  “Participants could administer the punishment without any cost to themselves.”  
   (ii) Not varied; no predictions.

8. Punishment magnitude  
   (i) Exp 1: fixed fine = #chips harvested by Person C (here 10).  
       Exp 2 & 3: 0–100 decrement points, €0.01 each; decided by the actor(s).  
   (ii) Magnitude is chosen by participants but never manipulated by the experimenter; authors give no prediction about how changing the maximum or slope would alter treatment effects.

9. Reward enabled?  
   (i) Yes – sanction type was Punishment vs Reward in Exp 1 & 2.  
   (ii) The paper compares punishment to reward, but never compares “punishment present” to “punishment absent,” so it does not estimate a punishment-treatment effect on efficiency.

10. Reward cost  
    (i) Always zero.  
    (ii) Not varied; no predictions.

11. Reward magnitude  
    (i) Mirrors punishment magnitude: fixed bonus = #chips left (Exp 1); 0–100 increment points worth €0.01 each (Exp 2).  
    (ii) Not experimentally varied; no predictions.

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
    (i) Yes – one-shot and explicitly stated.  
    (ii) Not varied; no predictions.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    (i) Participants are shown Person C’s harvest (and therefore own payoff component). No condition hides or reveals more information.  
    (ii) Not varied; no predictions.

14. Does the punished player learn who punished?  
    (i) Directly addressed in Experiment 3 via the Accountability manipulation.  
        • Accountable: everyone learns each actor’s decision and explanation.  
        • Unaccountable: only the net number of decrement points is revealed; individual decisions remain private.  
    (ii) Systematically varied.  Effect on *punishment size*:  
        – Table 3: Individual-Accountable mean = 41.9 points, Individual-Unaccountable = 49.3.  
        – Joint-Accountable = 58.4, Joint-Unaccountable = 55.3.  
        The Accountability main effect on punishment size is not significant (F = 0.20, p = .656).  
        Crucially, the paper never calculates efficiency, so no effect on efficiency can be extracted.

15. Does the rewarded player learn who rewarded?  
    (i) Not treated at all.  
    (ii) No discussion or prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used  
   The paper never analyses group efficiency, total pay-off or any welfare measure.  
   Dependent variables are:  
   • Sanction vote (yes/no) – Exp 1  
   • Number of decrement/increment points assigned – Exp 2 & 3  
   • Self-reports: felt personal responsibility, external accountability, entitlement.  
   These are conceptually different from efficiency because they capture decisions or psychological states, not pay-offs realised in the public-goods game.

B. Parameters mentioned (any statement of their value): 11 of 15  
   1,2,4,6,7,8,9,10,11,12,14 are described.  
   Parameters 3,5,15 are not mentioned; parameter 13 is implicit but never discussed as a design element.

C. Parameters whose *systematic variation* and *effect on the punishment-treatment effect* are analysed: 1 of 15 (parameter 14).  
   Even there, the outcome is not efficiency and the effect is statistically nil.

D. Predictions one can make about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) will influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency, **using only this paper**: very limited.  
   • Personal identification of the punisher (parameter 14) appears to have little or no impact on the size of punishment, hence we would predict little or no impact on efficiency.  
   • For all other parameters the paper supplies no information, so no evidence-based prediction can be made.

In short, the paper is about *who* makes the punishment decision (individual vs group, accountable vs unaccountable), not about how classic public-goods design parameters affect the efficiency consequences of introducing punishment.
