Parameter-by-parameter extraction from the paper (“Resource scarcity and democratic elections in commons dilemmas: An experiment on forest use in Ethiopia”)

For each of the 15 parameters we indicate  

(1) whether the paper even reports the parameter (value, range, or wording) and  

(2) whether the paper says what would happen to the **punishment treatment effect** (i.e. the difference between “with-punishment” and “without-punishment” conditions) if that parameter were systematically changed.  If numerical effect sizes can be read straight off the paper, they are given; otherwise “not reported”.  “Punishment treatment effect” is interpreted exactly as in the user prompt: change in group efficiency (or any other dependent variable the authors actually analyse) caused by adding punishment.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Stated: always 5 players per group (26 sessions).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction about how changing the group size would alter the punishment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Stated: 10 rounds in Game 1, 10 rounds in Game 2.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction about its influence on the punishment effect.

3. Chat/communication enabled  
   (1) Reported: “We did not allow for interpersonal communication.”  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
   (1) Not applicable—subjects choose any integer harvest between 0 and a ceiling.  
   (2) Not discussed.

5. Contribution default / rollback framing  
   (1) Not used.  
   (2) Not discussed.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor (return from the public fund)  
   (1) There is no linear public-goods technology. Pay-offs are price per harvested tree (0.5 or 1 ETB) plus a share of the remaining stock; a 10 % biological growth rate is fixed.  
   (2) Not varied in a way that is linked to punishment; no prediction about punishment effect.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   (1) Not applicable—punishment is done by the experimenter with no cost to any peer.  
   (2) Not discussed.

8. Punishment magnitude (money/trees deducted per unit)  
   (1) Fixed: “The amount of trees deducted is twice whatever that person collected beyond the amount allowed”. Probability of detection = 1/5.  
   (2) Magnitude never varied; no prediction about what would happen if it were.

9. Reward enabled?  
   (1) No reward mechanism exists.  
   (2) Not discussed.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   (1) & (2) Not applicable.

12. Number of rounds known in advance  
   (1) Subjects are told the game lasts ten rounds.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

13. Peer outcomes shown  
   (1) Yes: after every round subjects are told the *total* group harvest.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

14. Punisher identity revealed?  
   (1) Not relevant: no peer punisher.  
   (2) Not discussed.

15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
   (1) Not relevant.  
   (2) Not discussed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
What the paper actually does manipulate

• Scarcity (initial stock = 101 vs 51).  
• Institutional mode: second game is either  
  – Election (group majority vote may accept or reject the pre-specified sanction),  
  – Imposition (same sanction forced),  
  – Control (no sanction, no vote).  

Those manipulations are not any of the 15 parameters requested above, so strictly speaking the article contains **no systematic variation of any of the 15 parameters** with respect to punishment magnitude, cost, information, etc.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary answers requested

A. Dependent variables used  
   – Main analysed variable: Harvest Ratio (HR) = individual harvest ÷ maximum allowed that round.  
   – Additional variables discussed: resource stock remaining, frequency of resource collapse.  
   – “Efficiency” (total earnings ÷ maximum possible earnings of a fully cooperative group) appears only in Table 3 as a *theoretical* benchmark; it is **not** the variable the regressions analyse.  

B. Which of the 15 parameters are merely mentioned in the paper?  
   7 out of 15: 1 (group size), 2 (number of rounds), 3 (chat), 6 (returns/growth rate), 8 (punishment magnitude), 12 (rounds known), 13 (peer outcomes shown).

C. For how many of the 15 parameters does the paper study how *systematically varying* that parameter changes the punishment treatment effect for **any** dependent variable?  
   Zero.  No parameter in the list is experimentally varied in more than one level so no causal statements can be made within the paper about their impact on the punishment effect.

D. Predictions one could still attempt (purely from the paper) about how the 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment effect on efficiency  

Given the absence of any direct evidence in the paper, only very tentative, qualitative conjectures can be made:

• The written results show that *imposed* sanctions under high resource abundance tended to increase harvesting (reduce cooperation), while *elected* sanctions reduced harvesting.  If we map that back onto “efficiency”, this suggests that when punishment is externally imposed **and** the resource is plentiful, efficiency may actually fall, whereas when groups democratically legitimise the same punishment rule efficiency may rise.  
• Because all groups have 5 players, 10 known rounds, no chat, fixed and mild punishment magnitude, etc., nothing can be inferred about how changing any of those specific parameter values would alter the punishment effect.  

In short, the paper furnishes almost no leverage for predicting how the 15 canonical public-goods design parameters will interact with punishment to affect group efficiency.

Article Title: People prefer coordinated punishment in cooperative interactions
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; STRONG RECIPROCITY; EVOLUTION; ENFORCEMENT; DEFECTORS; INSTITUTIONS; EMOTIONS; BENEFITS; GOVERN; NORMS
Abstract: Human groups can often maintain high levels of cooperation despite the threat of exploitation by individuals who reap the benefits of cooperation without contributing to its costs(1-4). Prominent theoretical models suggest that cooperation is particularly likely to thrive if people join forces to curb free riding and punish their non-contributing peers in a coordinated fashion(5). However, it is unclear whether and, if so, how people actually condition their punishment of peers on punishment behaviour by others. Here we provide direct evidence that many people prefer coordinated punishment. With two large-scale decision-making experiments (total n = 4,320), we create minimal and controlled conditions to examine preferences for conditional punishment and cleanly identify how the punishment decisions of individuals are impacted by the punishment behaviour by others. We find that the most frequent preference is to punish a peer only if another (third) individual does so as well. Coordinated punishment is particularly common among participants who shy away from initiating punishment. With an additional experiment we further show that preferences for conditional punishment are unrelated to well-studied preferences for conditional cooperation. Our results highlight the importance of conditional preferences in both positive and negative reciprocity, and they provide strong empirical support for theories that explain cooperation based on coordinated punishment.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter rundown based solely on the content of the provided paper (“People prefer coordinated punishment in cooperative interactions”). For each of the 15 parameters, I note (1) whether (and how) the paper mentions the parameter (and what value is used, if any); and (2) whether it makes any prediction or provides any numerical effect sizes about what would happen if that parameter were systematically varied with respect to the punishment treatment effect (especially on efficiency or on any other outcome variables). “Systematically varied” means that the paper actually manipulates that parameter across conditions or makes explicit theoretical predictions about changing it. Whenever the paper does not address a parameter or its effect, I state this explicitly.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • What the paper says: The study uses 3‐person groups (two Punishers and one Target).  
   • Systematic variation/predictions: The paper does not systematically vary the number of players, nor does it discuss how changing group size would affect punishment’s impact on efficiency (or any other dependent variable).

2. Number of rounds
   • What the paper says: The interaction is one‐shot (single round).  
   • Systematic variation/predictions: The paper does not vary the number of rounds or discuss how repeating vs. one‐shot would affect punishment outcomes.

3. Is chat enabled?
   • What the paper says: There is no mention of chat or open communication. Participants do not communicate with one another aside from making their decisions as instructed.  
   • Systematic variation/predictions: None.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • What the paper says: Yes. It is a binary linear public goods game in which each player either cooperates (contributes) or defects (contributes nothing).  
   • Systematic variation/predictions: The paper does not test different contribution formats. It reports only the single binary “all‐or‐nothing” approach.

5. Is the contribution default (do participants decide how much of their endowment to move back)?
   • What the paper says: There is no mention of any default contribution mechanism. Participants simply choose to cooperate or defect; there is no partial or “move‐back” decision.  
   • Systematic variation/predictions: None.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters
   • What the paper says: The payoff structure is fixed: an individual who defects earns 5 monetary units (MU) personally (and 0 for others), whereas a cooperator earns 2 MU for each group member (2 for self, 2 for each of the other two). In other words, there is a fixed payoff rule and no systematic changes to these payoffs.  
   • Systematic variation/predictions: None.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • What the paper says: A punisher pays 1 MU to punish, which imposes a 3 MU deduction on the punished player. This cost is the same throughout the experiments.  
   • Systematic variation/predictions: The paper does not vary this cost, nor does it make predictions about changing it.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player per unit punishment)
   • What the paper says: Each punishment costs the target 3 MU. If two punishers both punish, the total deduction is 6 MU.  
   • Systematic variation/predictions: The paper does not vary or discuss systematically changing the punishment magnitude.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • What the paper says: The study focuses solely on punishment; no reward mechanism is present.  
   • Systematic variation/predictions: None.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • What the paper says: Not discussed. No rewards are used.  
    • Systematic variation/predictions: None.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)
    • What the paper says: Not discussed. No rewards are used.  
    • Systematic variation/predictions: None.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • What the paper says: Yes. Participants know it is a one‐shot interaction (so they know the game ends after this single decision).  
    • Systematic variation/predictions: There is no mention of systematically varying the horizon or discussing multi‐round variants.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?
    • What the paper says: Punishers see whether the Target cooperated or defected; however, the paper does not report that participants see each other’s final or running payoffs, nor does it systematically vary information about outcomes.  
    • Systematic variation/predictions: None.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • What the paper says: The paper does not indicate that Targets learn the identity of the punisher. It does not systematically vary whether the punisher’s identity is revealed.  
    • Systematic variation/predictions: None.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • What the paper says: Not applicable—no rewards are used, and the paper does not discuss this.  
    • Systematic variation/predictions: None.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A: Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper does not report “efficiency” (total payoff divided by the maximum possible) as a main dependent variable. Instead, it measures and reports:  
       – Punishment decisions (binary: punish or not).  
       – Cooperation decisions (also binary).  
       – Anger ratings (self‐reported).  
     Although the paper mentions that punishment can promote cooperation and discusses payoffs in its background motivations, it does not present a formal efficiency metric or total/average payoffs as a primary outcome.

B: Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form (though not varied):  
       (1) Number of players (fixed at 3)  
       (2) Number of rounds (one‐shot)  
       (4) Contribution is all or nothing (binary)  
       (7) Punishment cost (1 MU)  
       (8) Punishment magnitude (3 MU deducted from target)  
       (12) The number of rounds is known (one‐shot)  
     • The rest (3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15) are either not used, not relevant, or not explicitly varied.

C: For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The paper does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters. There are therefore no explicit predictions or numerical effect sizes tied to parameter manipulations (including efficiency).  

D: If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • Because the paper never systematically manipulated these parameters or analyzed efficiency as a dependent variable, it offers no direct guidance on how any of these 15 parameters would affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency. Hence, one cannot draw numerical or firm predictions about parameter variations from this particular study’s data and discussions. The paper’s main focus is on (a) whether people punish conditionally on others punishing, and (b) how that conditionality relates to anger and unconditional punishment choices, rather than on group efficiency under varied experimental parameters.

Article Title: Selfish punishment: Altruism can be maintained by competition among cheaters
Author Keywords: altruism; selfish; punishment; cooperation; public goods
Keywords Plus: STRONG RECIPROCITY; COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; BEHAVIOR; HUMANS
Abstract: Altruistic punishment refers to a class of behaviors that deters cheating at a cost to the punisher, making it a form of second-order altruism. Usually, it is assumed that the punishers are themselves solid citizens who refrain from cheating. We show in a simulation model that altruism and punishment paradoxically become negatively correlated, leading to a form of selfish punishment. Examples of selfish punishment can be found in organisms as diverse as wasps, birds, and humans. (C) 2007 Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved.

Below I go through the 15 parameters one‐by‐one, quoting only what can be extracted from Eldakar, Farrell & Wilson (2007).  For each parameter I state  

(1) whether the paper mentions it and, if so, its value(s), and  
(2) whether the paper **systematically varies** it and reports how that variation changes any “punishment treatment effect.”  Whenever a numerical effect can be read directly from a table or figure I give it; otherwise I simply report the qualitative direction.  I also remind the reader whenever the paper analyses a dependent variable other than **efficiency** (total or average payoff).

------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Number of players (group size, N)  
   (1) Mentioned.  Default N = 4 (Table 1).  Figure 5 varies N from 2 to 10.  
   (2) Systematically varied.  Figure 5 shows that as N increases, equilibrium altruism and punishment both drop; the negative correlation between the two traits becomes strongest at N ≈ 7 and then weakens slightly.  The paper does **not** translate this into any efficiency measure nor into a “punishment-minus-no-punishment” treatment effect.  No numerical effect sizes on efficiency are given.

2.  Number of rounds (R)  
   (1) Mentioned.  Default R = 6 (Table 1).  Figure 6 varies R from 1 to 10.  
   (2) Systematically varied.  With R = 1 both altruism and punishment collapse to (almost) zero; with larger R both traits rise and the (negative) correlation moves toward zero.  Again, nothing is said about efficiency or about the difference between a punishment and a no-punishment treatment.

3.  Chat enabled?  
   Not mentioned at all.

4.  “All-or-nothing” contribution?  
   Contributions are continuous 0–1.  Not varied; no discussion of an all-or-nothing regime.

5.  Contribution default / “take” frame?  
   Not mentioned.

6.  MPCR / multiplication factor  
   The group fund is “doubled” (paragraph in §2), i.e., MPCR = 0.5.  This factor is never varied.

7.  Punishment cost to the punisher (C)  
   (1) Mentioned.  Default C = 40 (Table 1) which the authors interpret as “80 % of one’s endowment” in Figs 1–3.  
   (2) Systematically varied in Figure 4.  As C rises, mean altruism and punishment both fall and the altruism–punishment correlation becomes more negative.  No efficiency data, and no explicit comparison of “with punishment” vs “without punishment.”

8.  Punishment magnitude (fine levied on the target)  
   The model uses **exclusion** rather than a coin fine; magnitude is captured by D, the probability that detection leads to removal.  D is given a default value of 0.5 but is only mentioned anecdotally (“If the capacity for punishment is eliminated by setting D = 0 …”).  It is **not** systematically varied.

9.  Whether a reward is enabled  
   Not in the model.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   Not in the model.

12. Are the number of rounds known to players?  
   Not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   Assumption: players “know the total contribution of other members but not the contribution of each individual.”  This information structure is fixed; it is not varied.

14. Do punished players know who punished them?  
   Not mentioned; there is no such option in the model.

15. Do rewarded players know who rewarded them?  
   Not applicable—no reward option in the model.

------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY  

A. Dependent variables.  The paper follows the time path of three quantities:  
   • Mean altruism level (A) in the population.  
   • Mean punishment level (P).  
   • The correlation between A and P.  
   It never reports **group efficiency** (total or average payoff / maximum possible payoff) and never reports simple cooperation rates in the usual experimental-economics sense.  Thus “efficiency” as defined in the prompt is **not** analysed.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   5 of 15:  (1) group size, (2) number of rounds, (6) MPCR (fixed at 2×), (7) punishment cost, (8) punishment magnitude (probability D).  Parameters 3,4,5,9–15 are absent.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of **systematically varying** that parameter on any punishment treatment effect?  
   3 parameters:  
      • Group size N (Fig 5)  
      • Number of rounds R (Fig 6)  
      • Punishment cost C (Fig 4)  
   For none of them is efficiency analysed; the outcomes are mean A, mean P, and their correlation.

D. Predictions one could make—limited strictly to what appears in the paper—about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) alter the punishment treatment effect on efficiency:

   – Because efficiency itself is never measured, the paper offers almost no direct guidance.  
   – Indirectly, higher mean altruism should raise efficiency, while higher mean punishment lowers individual payoffs but (through deterring cheating) probably raises group payoffs.  If one accepts that heuristic, the figures imply:  
      • Smaller groups (N ≈ 4) → higher A, moderate P → probably higher efficiency than larger groups.  
      • More rounds (larger R) → higher A and lower P → higher efficiency.  
      • Lower punishment costs (small C) → higher A, higher P correlation close to zero → likely higher efficiency than when C is high (because very high C reduces A and P).  
   – No statements (and therefore no predictions) can be made from the paper about chat, reward, information conditions, MPCR variation, contribution default, or identity revelation.  For those 12 parameters the paper provides no basis even for a directional guess.

In short, the article is concerned with the evolutionary covariance between altruism and punishment, not with efficiency, so it can inform only very crude, second-hand guesses about how three of the fifteen parameters might shift efficiency when punishment is introduced.
reference_APA: Eldakar, Omar Tonsi, Farrell, Dene Leo & Wilson, David Sloan (2007). Selfish punishment: Altruism can be maintained by competition among cheaters. JOURNAL OF THEORETICAL BIOLOGY.

Authors: Dercole, F; De Carli, M; Della Rossa, F; Papadopoulos, AV
Author Full Names: Dercole, Fabio; De Carli, Marco; Della Rossa, Fabio; Papadopoulos, Alessandro V.
Article Title: Overpunishing is not necessary to fix cooperation in voluntary public goods games
Author Keywords: Altruistic punishment; Finite populations; Fixation of cooperation; Public goods games; Replicator dynamics
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; ANTISOCIAL PUNISHMENT; EVOLUTION; DEFECTORS
Abstract: The fixation of cooperation among unrelated individuals is one of the fundamental problems in biology and social sciences. It is investigated by means of public goods games, the generalization of the prisoner's dilemma to more than two players. In compulsory public goods games, defect is the dominant strategy, while voluntary participation overcomes the social dilemma by allowing a cyclic coexistence of cooperators, defectors, and non-participants. Experimental and theoretical research has shown how the combination of voluntary participation and altruistic punishment-punishing antisocial behaviors at a personal cost-provides a solution to the problem, as long as antisocial punishment-the punishing of cooperators-is not allowed. Altruistic punishment can invade at low participation and pave the way to the fixation of cooperation. Specifically, defectors are overpunished, in the sense that their payoff is reduced by a sanction proportional to the number of punishers in the game. Here we show that qualitatively equivalent results can be achieved with a milder punishing mechanism, where defectors only risk a fixed penalty per round-as in many real situations-and the cost of punishment is shared among the punishers. The payoffs for the four strategies-cooperate, defect, abstain, and cooperate-&-punish-are derived and the corresponding replicator dynamics analyzed in full detail. (c) 2012 Elsevier Ltd. Below, each of the 15 design parameters is treated in turn.

For every parameter I ask:

• Does the paper even define or use the parameter?  If so, what concrete value-range is reported?  
• Does the paper ever say what would happen to the *punishment treatment effect* (i.e., the difference between a public–goods game **with** punishment and one **without** punishment) if that parameter were systematically varied?  
• If such a statement exists, is a numerical effect size (slope, marginal effect, percentage-point change, etc.) that could be read directly from a table or figure available?

The dependent variables actually analysed in the article are also named explicitly each time so that they are not mistaken for “efficiency”.

─────────────────────────────────────────

1. Number of players in the group (N)  
   • Mentioned? ‑- YES.  Core model parameter, range explored: 2 < N ≤ 100; basic run N = 5; an alternative run N = 4 (Fig. 1d,e).  
   • Prediction under systematic variation? ‑- YES, but only for the share of initial states that end in **fixation of cooperation** (called attractor A).  In the Discussion (§5) the authors state: “the fixation of cooperation … is enhanced by enlarging the group of interacting players (parameter N)”.  
   • Numerical effect size? ‑- NO specific numbers are printed; Fig. 4 shows a monotone upward shift of the green curve as N rises but axes are not in absolute units.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? – NO.  The model is infinite-horizon (replicator dynamics); no finite-round condition is studied.  
   • Therefore no predictions and no effect sizes.

3. Chat / communication enabled  
   • Not modelled, never mentioned ⇒ no predictions.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
   • Assumed to be all-or-nothing (each co-operator pays c, defectors pay 0) but **never varied**, so no treatment-effect prediction.

5. “Contribution default” (endowment kept unless actively moved)  
   • Not mentioned, not varied.

6. Marginal per-capita return r (multiplication factor)  
   • Mentioned? ‑- YES.  Range used: 2 < r ≤ 50 (note (iii), Sect. 2); basic run r = 3.  
   • Prediction? ‑- YES.  Sect. 5: increasing r “exacerbates the reward” and *increases* the fraction of initial states that end in cooperation fixation.  
   • Effect size? – NO explicit slope; Fig. 4 shows the green curve (cooperation-fixation basin) rising with r, but no numeric coefficients.

7. Punishment cost to punisher (γ)  
   • Mentioned? – YES.  Range (0, 50); basic run γ = 1.  
   • Prediction? – YES.  γ plays a key role in the trans-critical and pitch-fork bifurcations that determine whether the equilibrium Q is a saddle or a repellor (Appendix A.3).  Qualitatively, a *higher* γ (costlier punishment) makes fixation of cooperation harder; a *lower* γ can turn Q into a saddle, creating larger basins leading to cooperation.  
   • Numerical effect size? – NO single number; only inequalities, e.g. “2 γ > (r−2)c” in Table A2.

8. Punishment magnitude β (fine paid by target)  
   • Mentioned? – YES.  Range (0, 50]; basic run β = 1.2.  
   • Prediction? – YES.  There is an explicit threshold β_min = (N−r)/(N(N−1))·c.  β must exceed β_min for any stable co-existence of co-operators and punishers (Eq. 5).  Increasing β above that threshold enlarges the basin of attraction for cooperation fixation (Fig. 1 and Fig. 4).  
   • Numerical effect size? – Threshold is numeric (β_min); beyond that no quantitative slope is provided.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Not in the model ⇒ no predictions.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
    • Both not in the model ⇒ no predictions.

12. Finite or known horizon (rounds known)  
    • Not modelled ⇒ no predictions.

13. Peer outcome visibility  
    • Perfect information is assumed but never varied ⇒ no predictions.

14. Whether the punished party learns who punished  
15. Whether the rewarded party learns who rewarded  
    • Not modelled ⇒ no predictions.

─────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables actually analysed  
   • The paper never uses **group efficiency** (total-payoff / maximum-payoff) as an outcome.  
   • Outcomes studied are:  
      1. Fractions of initial conditions that eventually reach each attractor:  
          A – fixation of cooperation (mix of co-operators & punishers on x-w edge),  
          B – rock-paper-scissors limit cycle with *no* punishers,  
          C – loner equilibrium.  
      2. Local stability properties of equilibrium Q and bifurcation points (no direct welfare interpretation).  
   These are not interchangeable with efficiency.

B. Which of the 15 parameters appear at all? – 4 of them:  
   1 (N), 4 (all-or-nothing, but fixed), 6 (r), 7 (γ), 8 (β).  
   (The “all-or-nothing” rule is fixed and never varied; so only 4 are genuinely present.)

C. Which parameters are *systematically varied* and connected to a punishment-treatment effect on any dependent variable? – 4 parameters:  
   1 (N), 6 (r), 7 (γ), 8 (β).  
   In every case the paper only supplies qualitative directions (larger N, r, β → more cooperation fixation; larger γ → less), never numeric effect sizes, and never with respect to efficiency.

D. What can we predict, *solely from this paper*, about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would affect the punishment-treatment effect on **efficiency**?  
   • Because the article never measures efficiency, we cannot derive quantitative predictions.  
   • Qualitatively, parameters that enlarge the basin leading to cooperation fixation (large N, r, β; small γ) would probably raise efficiency because the cooperative attractor yields higher individual payoffs than the other attractors, but the paper does not compute the payoffs of those attractors relative to the social optimum, so even this statement goes beyond the text.  
   • For the remaining 11 parameters the paper gives no information whatsoever, so no prediction can be made.

In short, the study is about evolutionary stability and basin sizes, not about efficiency; only four of the fifteen design parameters are examined, and even for those the findings are qualitative and concern cooperation fixation rather than efficiency improvements.
reference_APA: Dercole, Fabio, De Carli, Marco, Della Rossa, Fabio & Papadopoulos, Alessandro V. (2013). Overpunishing is not necessary to fix cooperation in voluntary public goods games. JOURNAL OF THEORETICAL BIOLOGY.

Authors: Quan, J; Cui, SH; Chen, WM; Wang, XJ
Author Full Names: Quan, Ji; Cui, Shihui; Chen, Wenman; Wang, Xianjia
Article Title: Reputation-based probabilistic punishment on the evolution of cooperation in the spatial public goods game
Author Keywords: Evolutionary game; Cooperation; Probabilistic punishment; Reputation
Keywords Plus: PROMOTES COOPERATION; DYNAMICS
Abstract: Low-reputation defectors are more likely to be punished than defectors with high repu-tations. Motivated by this reality, this paper proposes a new mechanism, the reputation -based probabilistic punishment, into the spatial public goods game model. In this mech-anism, players with time-dependent reputations are divided into two types, good players with reputations higher than the reputation threshold and bad players with reputations lower than the threshold. A defector considered a good player is less likely to be punished than a defector considered a bad player. Based on these assumptions, we systematically explore how this mechanism influences the evolution of cooperation. Through extensive simulations, we verify that a higher value of the reputation threshold is more conducive to promoting and maintaining cooperation. Moreover, increasing the cost of being pun-ished could effectively encourage players to take cooperative behaviors. Simulation results show that both increasing the punishment intensity and increasing the punishment fine could increase the cost of being punished and are beneficial to the promotion of cooper-ation. Additionally, in the structured population, the distributions of strategies, reputation, and payoff in the evolutionary stable state are mainly present in the form of clusters.(c) 2022 Elsevier Inc. Below, each of the 15 design parameters is treated in turn.  For every parameter I state  
(1) whether it appears in the paper (and its value if it does), and  
(2) whether the paper systematically varies the parameter and reports how that variation changes the *punishment treatment effect* (the difference in outcomes between a game *with* punishment and an otherwise-identical game *without* punishment).  Whenever the paper gives a numerical effect size I quote it; otherwise I simply note the qualitative pattern or say that nothing is reported.  I limit myself strictly to what is in the paper.

-------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned.  All simulations use a 100 × 100 lattice, i.e. N = 10 000.  
   (2) Never varied; no comparison to a no-punishment baseline ⇒ no information on the punishment treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) The evolutionary process is run for up to 10 000 time steps, but “rounds” in the experimental-economics sense are not defined.  
   (2) Not varied; no treatment-effect information.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   (1) Not mentioned.  
   (2) No information.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
   (1) Present.  Every C or PC always contributes exactly one unit; D contributes zero.  The rule is fixed.  
   (2) Not varied; no treatment-effect information.

5. Contribution default / endowment retrieved from the public pool  
   (1) Not modelled.  
   (2) No information.

6. MPCR (multiplication factor r)  
   (1) Yes.  “Enhancement factor” r is varied from 0 to 5.5 in Figures 1, 2, 7.  
   (2) Varying r changes the *frequency of cooperation* ρ(C + PC).  Example from Fig. 1a (Z = 98, b = 0, α = 0.1, β = 1.0):  
        r = 0 → ρ ≈ 0.07  
        r = 2 → ρ ≈ 0.55  
        r ≥ 5.5 → ρ ≈ 1  

       The paper never compares these outcomes to a game *without* punishment, so no punishment-treatment effect on efficiency is reported.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit (α)  
   (1) Yes.  Default α = 0.1; varied 0.1 – 0.5 in Fig. 10.  
   (2) Higher α shifts the β-threshold at which full cooperation appears.  E.g., at r = 3.5 and Z = 98, full cooperation is reached at  
        α = 0.1 → β ≈ 0.19  
        α = 0.2 → β ≈ 0.22  
        α = 0.3 → β ≈ 0.31  
        α = 0.4 → β ≈ 0.43  
        α = 0.5 → β ≈ 0.57  

       No comparison to a no-punishment baseline; thus no treatment-effect data.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine β)  
   (1) Yes.  Varied 0.1 – 0.8 in Fig. 10.  
   (2) With r = 3.5, Z = 98, b = 0 the cooperation rate moves from 0 to 1 as β crosses the α-specific thresholds listed above.  Again, no treatment-effect information on efficiency.

9. Reward enabled  
   (1) Not included.  
   (2) No information.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   (1)(2) Not included; no information.

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
14. Is the punisher identified?  
15. Is the rewarder identified?  
   (1)(2) None of these information-display parameters are modelled; the paper is silent on them.

-------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used  
   – ρ(C + PC): frequency of cooperative strategies (cooperators + punishers).  
   – Distributions/means of individual payoff.  
   – Distributions of reputation.  
   – *Group efficiency* (total payoff ÷ maximum possible) is *not* explicitly computed.  Average payoff snapshots are shown but never normalised to the cooperative optimum.

B. Which of the 15 parameters appear at all?  
   6 of 15: 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8.

C. Which of the 15 parameters are systematically varied *and* linked to any outcome (even if not efficiency or not a treatment effect)?  
   3 of 15: 6 (r), 7 (α), 8 (β).  
   For none of them does the paper provide a punishment-treatment effect on efficiency because the study never reports a baseline without punishment.

D. Predicting the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency from this paper alone  
   The study makes no direct comparison between “punishment” and “no-punishment,” so it offers virtually no guidance on how any of the 15 parameters would alter the *incremental* change in efficiency produced by introducing punishment.  At most we can infer that larger r, smaller α, and larger β tend to raise cooperation and average payoff within the punishment regime, so one might *guess* that, relative to a no-punishment baseline, punishment would (i) improve efficiency more when r is low (because the baseline is worst there) and (ii) improve efficiency less when α is very high (because punishers pay heavy costs).  Beyond these loose qualitative guesses the paper provides no quantitative leverage for predicting treatment effects on efficiency, and it says nothing about the other 12 parameters or any interactions between parameters.

-------------------------------------------------
Therefore, if one’s goal is to forecast how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the *punishment treatment effect on efficiency*, this paper supplies almost no usable evidence; only parameters 6, 7 and 8 are touched upon, and even for them the necessary no-punishment baseline is missing.

Abstract: Finding ways to overcome the temptation to exploit one another is still a challenge in behavioural sciences. In the framework of evolutionary game theory, punishing strategies are frequently used to promote cooperation in competitive environments. Here, we introduce altruistic punishers in the spatial public goods game. This strategy acts as a cooperator in the absence of defectors, otherwise it will punish all defectors in their vicinity while bearing a cost to do so. We observe three distinct behaviours in our model: i) in the absence of punishers, cooperators (who don't punish defectors) are driven to extinction by defectors for most parameter values; ii) clusters of punishers thrive by sharing the punishment costs when these are low; iii) for higher punishment costs, punishers, when alone, are subject to exploitation but in the presence of cooperators can form a symbiotic spatial structure that benefits both. This last observation is our main finding since neither cooperation nor punishment alone can survive the defector strategy in this parameter region and the specificity of the symbiotic spatial configuration shows that lattice topology plays a central role in sustaining cooperation. Below, I follow the five requested steps.  Everything is taken exclusively from Flores et al. (2021); no outside evidence or conjecture is added.

────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER–BY–PARAMETER CHECK
────────────────────────────────────────
For each of the 15 parameters I indicate  

(1)  WHETHER the paper even specifies the parameter (and, if so, with what value or range).  
(2)  WHETHER the paper **systematically varies** that parameter and draws any conclusion about how such variation changes the “punishment treatment effect”.  
The only dependent variables ever analysed in the paper are explicitly named.

1. Number of players in the group who decide simultaneously  
 (1) Mentioned.  The authors fix a square lattice L × L with L = 100, i.e. 10 000 players. Group size for payoff calculation is G = 5 (focal site plus its four von-Neumann neighbours).  
 (2) Not varied, no statements about changing L or G on the punishment effect.

2. Number of rounds (time steps)  
 (1) They let the simulation run up to t_max = 10⁶ Monte-Carlo steps, or until defectors disappear.  
 (2) Not varied; no claims about its influence.

3. Chat / communication allowed  
 (1) Never mentioned.  
 (2) No discussion.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
 (1) Yes.  Contribution is binary: cooperators and punishers each invest c = 1, defectors invest 0.  
 (2) The rule is fixed; its variation is not explored.

5. “Contribution default” framing (players withdraw rather than deposit)  
 (1) Not mentioned.  
 (2) No discussion.

6. Marginal-per-capita-return (MPCR) / multiplication factor r  
 (1) Core parameter.  They vary r and always plot it as r/G.  
 (2) Systematically varied.  
     • Fig. 1: For γ = 0 the onset of altruism occurs at r/G ≈ 0.9; for 0 < γ < 0.2 the threshold falls (exact values visible in Fig. 1); for 0.2 < γ < 0.8 the threshold rises; for γ > 1 it falls again due to “symbiosis”.  
     • Fig. 3 gives a phase diagram in (r/G, γ) space.  
  All dependent variables discussed are fractions of strategy types; **efficiency is never reported**.

7. Punishment cost to punisher (per punished unit)  
 (1) Denoted γ, and set equal to the fine δ for simplicity (γ = δ).  
 (2) Core manipulated variable.  γ ranges from 0 up to ≈ 2.  
     • Fig. 2a plots final ρ = ρ_C + ρ_P against γ for several r’s.  
     • Qualitative finding: increasing γ first promotes, then harms, then (for γ > 1) again promotes altruism because of the “symbiosis” pattern.  
     • No numerical efficiency data are given.

8. Punishment magnitude to the target (fine)  
 (1) Also γ (since γ = δ).  
 (2) Same variation and conclusions as in #7.

9. Reward availability  
 (1) Not present.  
 (2) No discussion.

10. Reward cost  
 (1) Not present.  
 (2) No discussion.

11. Reward magnitude  
 (1) Not present.  
 (2) No discussion.

12. Do players know the number of rounds?  
 (1) Irrelevant in the evolutionary simulation; not mentioned.  
 (2) No discussion.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
 (1) Not discussed.  
 (2) No discussion.

14. Is the identity of the punisher revealed?  
 (1) Not discussed.  Agents simply feel a fine; they never identify sources.  
 (2) No discussion.

15. Is the identity of the rewarder revealed?  
 (1) Not present.  
 (2) No discussion.

────────────────────────────────────────
REQUESTED SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────
A.  Dependent variables used  
 • Fraction of cooperators ρ_C, fraction of punishers ρ_P, and especially their sum ρ = ρ_C + ρ_P (“fraction of altruistic strategies”).  
 • No measure of group efficiency, total payoff, or average payoff is ever plotted or tabulated.  
 Hence efficiency is conceptually distinct and is **absent** from the paper.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
 6 (r), 7 (punishment cost), 8 (punishment magnitude—identical to #7), 1 (number of players) and 4 (all-or-nothing contribution rule) are at least specified.  That is 5 of the 15.  The remaining 10 are never mentioned.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of **systematically varying** the parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
 Exactly two underlying parameters are systematically manipulated and analysed:  
  • MPCR / multiplication factor r (#6)  
  • Punishment cost = punishment magnitude γ (#7 & #8)  
 No other parameter is varied.

D.  If one had to predict how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency, using solely this paper:  
 • Because efficiency is never measured, only indirect guesses are possible.  Higher ρ generally implies more contributors, but punishers also bear extra costs, so efficiency and ρ are not perfectly aligned.  
 • Low to moderate γ (≈ 0.1–0.2) combined with moderate r/G (> 0.7) is likely to raise efficiency, because punishment induces cooperation at a relatively small cost.  
 • Intermediate γ (≈ 0.4–1) can lower efficiency: punishment is costly yet fails to secure universal cooperation—defectors may still survive, and punishers pay high fees.  
 • Very high γ (> 1) plus r/G between 0.6 and 0.95 yields the “symbiosis” state with high cooperation; net efficiency is uncertain—cooperation is high but punishers pay large fines.  
 • No guidance at all is available for the other 12/15 parameters; the paper provides **no basis** for predicting their main or interaction effects on efficiency.

In short, Flores et al. (2021) is informative about how varying the benefit-to-cost ratio r and the punishment parameter γ reshapes the prevalence of cooperative strategies; it gives **no direct evidence** on group efficiency and says nothing about the remaining experimental-design parameters.

Article Title: Evolutionary game dynamics in multiagent systems with prosocial and antisocial exclusion strategies
Author Keywords: Cooperation; Social exclusion; Costly punishment; Second-order sanctioning
Keywords Plus: REPLICATOR DYNAMICS; COOPERATION; PUNISHMENT; EMERGENCE; PROMOTES
Abstract: Cooperation is very important in human society and identified as an essential principle of evolution, but how to promote cooperation among rational individuals remains a huge challenge. Recent works have found that prosocial exclusion can work as a powerful control strategy to promote cooperation effectively. However, it remains unclear whether prosocial exclusion can still favor cooperation when antisocial exclusion is introduced. And does prosocial exclusion have evolutionary advantages when comparing with prosocial and antisocial punishment strategies? Below I go through the 15 design parameters one by one, referring only to what is explicitly contained in “Evolutionary game dynamics in multi-agent systems with prosocial and antisocial exclusion strategies.”  For each parameter I state  

• whether it is mentioned in the paper, and, if so, the value(s) used;  
• whether the paper systematically varies that parameter and reports how such variation changes the *punishment treatment effect* (or any other outcome);  
• any numerical effect size that can be read directly from a figure, table, or formula.

Because the paper is theoretical, its main outcome variables are *stationary distributions* (long-run frequencies) of strategies, not group efficiency.

-------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER

1. Number of players in a group (N)  
   – Mentioned?  Yes.  A fixed value N = 5 is used in all numerical illustrations (Figs. 1-4); formulas are written for generic N.  
   – Systematically varied?  No.  All plots use N = 5; no comparative statics over N are reported.  
   – Effect size on punishment treatment effect?  None reported.

2. Number of rounds  
   – Mentioned?  No.  The model is an evolutionary process with no discrete finite number of rounds.

3. Chat enabled  
   – Mentioned?  No.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution choice  
   – Mentioned?  Implicitly yes: a *cooperator* always contributes a fixed cost c, a *defector* contributes 0.  Contribution level is not variable.  
   – Systematically varied?  No.  (Parameter treated as fixed.)

5. Contribution default / endowment-back decision  
   – Mentioned?  No.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor (r)  
   – Mentioned?  Yes.  Fixed at r = 3 in every figure and table (stated p. 14 and in captions of Figs. 1-4).  Authors state that “main results remain valid if r is approximately changed,” but they do not show any calculations for other r.  
   – Systematically varied?  No.  
   – Effect size?  Not reported.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher (G_P, G_A)  
   – Mentioned?  Yes.  Table 1 lists G_P and G_A; numerical work sets G_P = G_A = 0.4 (Fig. 4 caption).  
   – Systematically varied?  No.  
   – Effect size?  None.

8. Punishment magnitude to the target (B_P, B_A)  
   – Mentioned?  Yes.  Table 1; numerical work fixes B_P = B_A = 0.4 (Fig. 4 caption).  
   – Systematically varied?  No.  
   – Effect size?  None.

9. Reward enabled  
   – Mentioned?  No (the paper studies punishment and exclusion only).

10. Reward cost  
    – Mentioned?  No.

11. Reward magnitude  
    – Mentioned?  No.

12. Whether the number of rounds is known  
    – Mentioned?  No.

13. Whether peer outcomes are shown  
    – Mentioned?  No.

14. Whether the punished player knows the identity of the punisher  
    – Mentioned?  No.

15. Whether the rewarded player knows the identity of the rewarder  
    – Mentioned?  No.

-------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables used  
    – The paper does *not* use group efficiency (total payoff / maximum payoff) as an outcome.  
    – Outcomes reported: stationary distribution (long-run frequency) of each strategy under mutation-selection dynamics; occasionally aggregate “level of cooperation” (sum of cooperative strategy frequencies).  These are distinct from efficiency because they do not aggregate payoffs across strategies, nor do they normalise by the social optimum.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
    4 parameters:  
    (1) group size N, (6) multiplication factor r, (7) punishment cost, (8) punishment magnitude.  
    All other 11 parameters do not appear.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss how *systematically varying* them affects the punishment treatment effect (for any outcome)?  
    Zero.  None of the parameters are systematically varied.  Every parameter that does appear is held fixed in the figures and tables.

D.  What predictions can be made—*solely from this paper*—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
    • Because efficiency is never calculated, the paper offers no direct basis for predicting efficiency changes.  
    • The only qualitative statements that might indirectly relate to efficiency are:  
      – Prosocial pool exclusion tends to eliminate defectors (which might raise efficiency if payoffs were calculated).  
      – Antisocial pool exclusion alone lets defectors dominate, lowering cooperation.  
      – Adding prosocial exclusion alongside antisocial exclusion still allows prosocial exclusion to prevail.  
      – When the full set of strategies is available, prosocial pool exclusion dominates all others under both first- and second-order sanctioning.  
    • These conclusions are derived at *fixed* parameter values; no comparative statics are given.  
    • Therefore, beyond noting that efficiency would presumably track the frequency of cooperative versus defective strategies, the paper provides almost no quantitative leverage for forecasting how changes in any of the 15 experimental parameters would modify the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

In short, the paper is valuable for understanding evolutionary dominance relations among exclusion and punishment strategies, but it does not speak to most of the listed experimental design parameters, nor does it offer numerical predictions about group efficiency under systematic parameter variation.

Article Title: Sympathy and Punishment: Evolution of Cooperation in Public Goods Game
Source Title: JASSS-THE JOURNAL OF ARTIFICIAL SOCIETIES AND SOCIAL SIMULATION

Keywords Plus: INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; BEHAVIOR
Abstract: An important way to maintain human cooperation is punishing defection. However, since punishment is costly, how can it arise and evolve given that individuals who contribute but do not punish fare better than the punishers? This leads to a violation of causality, since the evolution of punishment is prior to the one of cooperation behaviour in evolutionary dynamics. Our public goods game computer simulations based on generalized Moran Process, show that, if there exists a 'behaviour-based sympathy' that compensates those who punish at a personal cost, the way for the emergence and establishment of punishing behaviour is paved. In this way, the causality violation dissipates. Among humans sympathy can be expressed in many ways such as care, praise, solace, ethical support, admiration, and sometimes even adoration; in our computer simulations, we use a small amount of transfer payment to express 'behaviour-based sympathy'. Our conclusions indicate that, there exists coevolution of sympathy, punishment and cooperation. According to classical philosophy literature, sympathy is a key factor in morality and justice is embodied by punishment; in modern societies, both the moral norms and the judicial system, the representations of sympathy and punishment, play an essential role in stable social cooperation.

Abstract: With the introduction of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and related technologies in our daily lives, fear and anxiety about their misuse as well as their inherent biases, incorporated during their creation, have led to a demand for governance and associated regulation. Abstract: Punishing defectors is an important means of stabilizing cooperation. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter summary of whether (1) the paper mentions each parameter (and, if so, what value or setting it uses) and (2) whether the paper makes predictions about the effect of systematically varying that parameter on “the punishment treatment effect.” In this paper, “punishment treatment effect” would mean the impact of punishment on any outcome variable the authors analyze (e.g., cooperation level). Crucially, the authors do not discuss “efficiency” (i.e., total payoff / maximum possible payoff) in any of their mathematical or simulation results, nor do they present how varying parameters would change group efficiency as such.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes, in the sense that they examine a square lattice with 30×30 = 900 sites (or individuals). They also refer to a “well‐mixed population,” which can be thought of as large or infinite.  
   • Effect of systematically varying?  
     – Not addressed. The paper does not report results for different population sizes or discuss how changes in number of players would affect punishment’s impact on any outcome variable.

2) Number of rounds
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The model is framed as a continuous birth–death process rather than a finite repeated game with a specified number of rounds.  
   • Effect of systematically varying?  
     – Not addressed.

3) Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned?  
     – No.  
   • Effect of systematically varying?  
     – Not addressed.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes, indirectly, in that the model uses continuous (from 0 up to some positive value) cooperation levels, not an “all or nothing” choice.  
   • Effect of systematically varying?  
     – Not addressed. The model never switches to all‐or‐nothing contributions; it simply assumes continuous cooperation.

5) Is the contribution default (e.g., do players decide how much of their endowment to move back into their hand)?
   • Mentioned?  
     – No.  
   • Effect of systematically varying?  
     – Not addressed.

6) MPCR (marginal per capita return) or related multiplication factor
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. There is a birth‐rate function enhanced by neighbors’ cooperation, but no standard public‐goods “multiplier” or MPCR is modeled.  
   • Effect of systematically varying?  
     – Not addressed.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned?  
     – The paper does define a cost of punishment, Cp(pi) = ap [pi]^ep, and systematically explores parameter ep to see if punishment costs are decelerating, linear, or accelerating.  
   • Effect of systematically varying?  
     – Yes, for cooperation (but not explicitly for “efficiency”):  
       – If punishment is “too expensive” (ep large/accelerating), punishment and cooperation collapse.  
       – If punishment is relatively cheaper (linear or decelerating), punishment can co‐evolve with cooperation.  
     – No numerical effect sizes are given for “efficiency” or total payoffs; the paper focuses on cooperation levels.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The paper calls it “punishment severity” (p0). It is one of the four evolving traits (cooperation level c, threshold c0, strictness s, and severity p0).  
   • Effect of systematically varying?  
     – They do not present a simple parameter sweep of p0 alone; rather, p0 evolves endogenously. They show that when punishment severity increases (and is not too costly), cooperation often “runs away” to higher levels.  
     – Again, the analysis concerns cooperation levels, not group efficiency. No numerical effect sizes for efficiency are reported.

9) Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned?  
     – No.  
   • Effect of systematically varying?  
     – Not addressed.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Mentioned?  
      – No.  
    • Effect of systematically varying?  
      – Not addressed.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)
    • Mentioned?  
      – No.  
    • Effect of systematically varying?  
      – Not addressed.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?
    • Mentioned?  
      – No. The authors do not use a finite‐round repeated game structure.  
    • Effect of systematically varying?  
      – Not addressed.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much others gained/lost each round)?
    • Mentioned?  
      – No. Although the model includes “perception errors” regarding cooperation levels, there is no systematic discussion of displaying payoffs or outcomes to neighbors.  
    • Effect of systematically varying?  
      – Not addressed.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Mentioned?  
      – No.  
    • Effect of systematically varying?  
      – Not addressed.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Mentioned?  
      – No.  
    • Effect of systematically varying?  
      – Not addressed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary of the Paper’s Use of Dependent Variables and Parameters
A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   – No. The authors never refer to or report “efficiency” = (total payoff / maximum possible payoff). Rather, they track:  
     (1) Cooperation level (c).  
     (2) Punishment threshold (c0).  
     (3) Punishment strictness (s).  
     (4) Punishment severity (p0).  
   In short, their primary dependent variable is the population’s average cooperation level. They also mention costs to individuals, but not group‐level efficiency.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – Mentioned at all:  
     • (1) Number of players: They fix it at 30×30 in a lattice or consider a well‐mixed population.  
     • (4) Is contribution “all or nothing”? They do the opposite (continuous cooperation), though they do not vary that.  
     • (7) Punishment cost: They give it a functional form and vary the exponent (ep).  
     • (8) Punishment magnitude: They model it as “punishment severity” (p0).  
   – The rest (2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15) are not mentioned.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   – Strictly speaking, “punishment treatment effect” is not the authors’ term, nor do they connect punishment directly to group efficiency. However, they do systematically investigate how variations in punishment cost (parameter 7) and in punishment severity (parameter 8) influence the evolution of cooperation levels in the population.  
   – They do not provide numerical effect sizes in terms of “efficiency” or total payoff, only qualitative statements (e.g., if punishing is too expensive, both punishment and cooperation collapse).

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   – The paper does not address efficiency at all, so one can only speculate that higher cooperation might sometimes raise total payoffs and thereby raise efficiency. However, because no direct measure of efficiency exists in the paper’s results, very little can be inferred about how systematically varying these parameters would affect group efficiency.  
   – The main mentionable points are:  
     • When punishment is less costly (parameter 7 not too large), punishment evolves and elicits high cooperation. If one assumes higher cooperation correlates with higher overall payoffs, then one might guess efficiency would be higher.  
     • When punishment severity (parameter 8) is high and its cost is not prohibitive, cooperation can “run away” to very large levels. Again, this may or may not translate to higher efficiency in a strict payoff sense, since the authors do not measure or report that outcome.  
   – Otherwise, the paper provides no further guidance on efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Hence, based solely on this paper, there is almost no direct basis for predicting how the 15 parameters or their interactions would affect “efficiency,” as the authors focus on the evolution of cooperation (and related punishment traits) rather than on group‐level payoff or efficiency.

Article Title: The Effect of Power Asymmetries on Cooperation and Punishment in a Prisoner's Dilemma Game
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC GOOD GAMES; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; EVOLUTION; ENFORCEMENT; SANCTIONS; GOODS; RETALIATION; RECIPROCITY; PROVISION; COERCION
Abstract: Recent work has suggested that punishment is detrimental because punishment provokes retaliation, not cooperation, resulting in lower overall payoffs. These findings may stem from the unrealistic assumption that all players are equal: in reality individuals are expected to vary in the power with which they can punish defectors. Here, we allowed strong players to interact with weak players in an iterated prisoner's dilemma game with punishment. Defecting players were most likely to switch to cooperation if the partner cooperated: adding punishment yielded no additional benefit and, under some circumstances, increased the chance that the partner would both defect and retaliate against the punisher. Our findings show that, in a two-player game, cooperation begets cooperation and that punishment does not seem to yield any additional benefits. Further work should explore whether strong punishers might prevail in multi-player games.

   – Whether players punish.

   4) “All or nothing” contribution – yes (cooperate vs. defect are binary).

   3) Chat – not used.  
   5) Default contribution – not used.  
   6) MPCR or multiplier – not used (a single payoff matrix was used).  
   9) Reward – not used.  
   10) Reward cost – not used.  
   11) Reward magnitude – not used.  
   15) Knowledge of rewarder – not used.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
 • The study effectively compares (a) symmetric vs. (b) asymmetric power conditions; that is the only systematic variation relevant to punishment magnitude and cost ratio (parameter 8). They do so to see whether strong vs. weak punishment changes outcomes (cooperation, retaliation, opting out). However, they never analyze an “efficiency” outcome.  
 • No other parameter is systematically varied to gauge changes in punishment’s effect.  
 • Hence, only one parameter (8: Punishment magnitude / power asymmetry) is systematically manipulated. Even then, the authors limit their analysis to cooperation, punishment, retaliation, and opting out, not efficiency.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of this paper, what would they be?

 • The main takeaway from the paper is that, in this two‐player Prisoner’s Dilemma setting, punishment does not reliably increase cooperation and can even backfire (leading to more defection or retaliation), particularly when “strong” punishment is used.

 • Because the paper does not systematically vary the other parameters, it contains no direct evidence or explicit predictions about how parameters 1–7 and 9–15 would affect group efficiency under a punishment scheme. The conclusions must remain that the paper offers little to no basis for strong efficiency predictions regarding those parameters.

Keywords Plus: COLLECTIVE ACTION; UNCERTAINTY; RISK
Abstract: Global coordination for the preservation of a common good, such as climate, is one of the most prominent challenges of modern societies. In this manuscript, we use the framework of evolutionary game theory to investigate whether a polycentric structure of multiple small-scale agreements provides a viable solution to solve global dilemmas as climate change governance. We review a stochastic model which incorporates a threshold game of collective action and the idea of risky goods, capturing essential features unveiled in recent experiments. We show how reducing uncertainty both in terms of the perception of disaster and in terms of goals induce a transition to cooperation. Taking into account wealth inequality, we explore the impact of the homophily, potentially present in the network of influence of the rich and the poor, in the different contributions of the players. Finally, we discuss the impact of polycentric sanctioning institutions, showing how such a scenario also proves to be more efficient than a single global institution.

 • Does the paper discuss it?

 • Any predictions?  
   – No.

13) Are peer outcomes shown?  
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   – The text mentions that agents imitate strategies based on payoffs they “observe,” but it does not explore different information‐revelation conditions.  
 • Any predictions about systematically varying that information display?  
   – No.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
 • Does the paper discuss it?

 • Any predictions?

 • Does the paper discuss it?

Summary (A–D)

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how do these differ?

Most analyses center on the fraction of cooperators (or punishers) and how close the group is to meeting a threshold.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
 • Four parameters receive mention:  
   1) Number of players (group size N)  
   4) The fact that contributions are effectively all‐or‐nothing (cooperate or defect)  
   7) A punishment tax or cost (πt), though not framed as “cost per unit punishing”  
   8) A punishment fine (πf).  
 • None of the other 11 parameters are discussed.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?

The paper does not provide numerical effect sizes for any parameter manipulation related to punishment.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

No further parameter‐by‐parameter quantitative predictions can be made.

Below is a point‐by‐point analysis of whether and how the paper discusses or systematically varies each of the 15 parameters you listed (in the context of punishment in a public‐goods‐type setting) and what the paper says about any resulting effect on efficiency (actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff). As will be seen, the paper is in fact a theoretical study of a two‐player repeated trust game with private information, not an experimental public goods game. The paper does not systematically vary the 15 parameters you listed, nor does it present predictions specifically about a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” as typically defined for public goods games. Rather, it focuses on how trust and various forms of reciprocity can sustain or improve total payoffs (sometimes termed “cooperative gains”) in a two‐player setting.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Discussed or mentioned in paper?  
     – Yes. The paper analyzes a game with exactly two players (player a and player b).  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it (e.g., 2 vs. 4 vs. 10) and its effect on punishment?  
     – No. There is no mention of changing the number of players; the game is always two‐player.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Discussed or mentioned in paper?  
     – The paper studies an infinitely repeated interaction with a discount factor β. It does not treat the number of rounds as a finite, manipulable parameter.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it and predict effects on punishment treatment?  
     – No. The paper allows for an infinite‐horizon repeated game; there is no systematic variation of the “length” of the game.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussed or mentioned in paper?  
     – No. The paper does not discuss whether players can chat or communicate outside the structure of sending or not sending income.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Discussed or mentioned in paper?  
     – The paper’s trust game allows an investor to send x ∈ [0,1]. Hence it is not “all or nothing,” nor does the paper force that choice.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary “all or nothing” vs. partial contributions?  
     – No. It simply assumes that players can choose any x ∈ [0,1].

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much to move back into their hand)?  
   • Discussed or mentioned in paper?  
     – No. The paper does not discuss a default mechanism for contributions, nor does it systematically vary such a parameter.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
   • Discussed or mentioned in paper?  
     – The paper has a parameter k > 1, multiplied by an investment x. With probability q, the investment yields kx; otherwise the investment fails. They assume qk > 1 so that on average the investment is beneficial.  
   • Any systematic variation of that factor for the purpose of measuring a punishment effect on efficiency?  
     – No. Although the paper examines how total payoffs depend on qk > 1, it does not discuss “punishment treatment effects” under different multipliers in the sense of a public goods experiment.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussed or mentioned in paper?  
     – The paper uses the term “punishment” to mean “symmetric punishment phases” (e.g., reverting to autarky or a worse payoff), but it does not model the cost of punishing in the sense of tokens spent to punish.  
   • Any effect of systematically varying a “punishment cost” on efficiency?  
     – No. That kind of explicit cost (à la a standard public goods experiment where punishing another player costs the punisher) does not appear.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player per unit of punishment)  
   • Discussed or mentioned in paper?  
     – Again, “punishment” is discussed qualitatively as a switch to a worse equilibrium payoff, not as a per‐unit deduction.  
   • Any predictions from systematically varying a “punishment magnitude”?  
     – No. The paper does not present numerical or experimental manipulations of that sort.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussed or mentioned in paper?  
     – The paper talks about “immediate reciprocity” (i.e., trustee sending something back right away) and “dynamic reciprocity” (favors returned in future periods). Those do function like “rewards,” but they are not framed as an on–off “reward treatment.”  
   • Does the paper systematically vary reward vs. no‐reward treatments?  
     – No. There is no separate parameter toggling “reward on” or “reward off.”

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Discussed or mentioned in paper?  
     – No. There is no explicit “cost” to reward analyzed.  
   • Any effect of varying it on punishment or efficiency?  
     – No.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded per unit of reward)  
   • Discussed or mentioned in paper?  
     – The trustee can reciprocate up to kx (the total possible returns), but there is no separate “unit reward” parameter.  
   • Effect of systematically varying?  
     – No mention of that.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
   • Discussed or mentioned in paper?  
     – The paper models an infinite‐horizon repeated trust game, generally interpreted as indefinite. There is no discussion of players knowing or not knowing a finite endpoint.  
   • Any predictions from systematically varying a known vs. unknown horizon?  
     – No. The paper does not treat that.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much others gained/lost)?  
   • Discussed or mentioned in paper?  
     – The analysis concerns what each player privately observes (the success or failure of the investment if they are the trustee) vs. what is publicly observed (the amount transferred). It does not systematically address “showing peer outcomes” in a sense relevant to a public goods experiment.  
   • Any predictions from systematically varying that degree of outcome visibility?  
     – No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Discussed or mentioned in paper?  
     – Not applicable in the sense the paper discusses. Their “punishment” is a grim or partial grim shift to worse payoffs, not something done by a single punisher with known identity.  
   • Any systematic variation?  
     – No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Discussed or mentioned in paper?  
     – Similar to the above: the paper’s “reward” is immediate or future reciprocity, but it does not revolve around “knowing who rewarded.”  
   • Any systematic variation?  
     – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper does not use “group efficiency” defined as (actual total payoff) / (maximum possible payoff) in the standard public goods sense. It does, however, focus on total (joint) payoffs of the two players relative to an autarky (Nash) payoff and relative to a “first‐best” payoff. It also uses each player’s long‐run utility (payoff) as a dependent variable. Strictly speaking, the analysis is about sustaining or improving total outcomes in a repeated trust game, not “efficiency” measured as a fraction of the fully cooperative group outcome.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Only Parameter #1 (number of players = 2) is explicitly fixed. The paper also has parameters that resemble a “multiplication factor” (k) and a “probability of success” (q), but these are not framed as an MPCR in a public goods sense. None of the other parameters (e.g., chat, known number of rounds, punishment cost, reward cost) appear as adjustable or systematically manipulated variables.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. The paper does not systematically vary or report quantitative “treatment effects” of changes in these parameters—especially not in a public‐goods‐experiment sense of “punishment treatments” or “efficiency changes.” Instead, it presents theoretical constructions showing how trust and reciprocity can emerge and how certain forms of “punishment” (like reverting to autarky) can sustain cooperation, without analyzing a per‐unit punishment cost or reward magnitude.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not provide grounds for making such predictions. It does not address these 15 parameters in the typical public goods “punishment treatment” sense, nor does it quantify an “efficiency” ratio for them. Consequently, there is little or no basis in the paper for predicting how systematically varying those parameters might alter a punishment effect on efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
reference_APA: Abdulkadiroglu, Atila & Bagwell, Kyle (2013). Trust, Reciprocity, and Favors in Cooperative Relationships. AMERICAN ECONOMIC JOURNAL-MICROECONOMICS.

Authors: García, J; Traulsen, A
Author Full Names: Garcia, Julian; Traulsen, Arne
Article Title: Evolution of coordinated punishment to enforce cooperation from an unbiased strategy space
Source Title: JOURNAL OF THE ROYAL SOCIETY INTERFACE
Author Keywords: collective action; punishment; evolution; cooperation
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS; POOL PUNISHMENT; EMERGENCE; INSTITUTIONS; PROVISION; DYNAMICS
Abstract: The emergence and maintenance of punishment to protect the commons remains an open puzzle in social and biological sciences. Even in societies where pro-social punishing is common, some individuals seek to cheat the system if they see a chance to do so-and public goods are often maintained in spite of cheaters who do not contribute. We present a model accounting for all possible strategies in a public goods game with punishment. While most models of punishment restrict the set of possible behaviours, excluding seemingly paradoxical anti-social strategies from the start, we show that these strategies can play an important role in explaining large-scale cooperation as observed in human societies. We find that coordinated punishment can emerge from individual interactions, but the stability of the associated institutions is limited owing to anti-social and opportunistic behaviour. In particular, coordinated anti-social punishment can undermine cooperation if individuals cannot condition their behaviour on the existence of institutions that punish. Only when we allow for observability and conditional behaviours do anti-social strategies no longer threaten cooperation. This is due to a stable coexistence of a minority supporting pro-social institutions and those who only cooperate if such institutions are in place. This minority of supporters is enough to guarantee substantial cooperation under a wide range of conditions. Our findings resonate with the empirical observation that public goods are resilient to opportunistic cheaters in large groups of unrelated individuals. They also highlight the importance of letting evolution, and not modellers, decide which strategies matter.

PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER

   • Yes. Denoted n; default n = 5 (Fig. 2 caption).

     Effect shown: as n increases the *probability that an implemented

2. Number of rounds  
   • Not mentioned (the model is evolutionary across generations, not a

   • Yes. Fixed cost γ to support a pool, default γ = 0.7.  
   • Systematically varied jointly with n in Fig. 3c.

     Numerical values are displayed as a surface but exact point estimates
     are not tabulated.  
     No statement on efficiency or on the size of a
     punishment-versus-no-punishment effect.

   • Yes. β = 1.5 in all simulations.  
   • Not varied; consequently no effect reported.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
10. Reward cost
