   • Rewards are never modelled, so no effects.

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
   • Not applicable; infinite evolutionary horizon. Not mentioned.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Not discussed; no effect.

14. Does a punished player know who punished?  
   • Not discussed; no effect.

15. Does a rewarded player know who rewarded?  
   • Not discussed; no effect.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables used  
   • The paper never analyses *group efficiency* (total pay-off divided by the
     social optimum).  
   • Dependent variables actually reported:  
     – Fraction of cooperators / defectors / loners (Fig. 2b, Fig. 3b).  
     – Stationary probabilities of each strategy.  
     – Probability that a pro-social punishment pool is implemented
       (Fig. 3c).  
     – Pay-off equations are written, but aggregate efficiency is not plotted
       or discussed.  
     Hence “efficiency” in the strict sense is absent, and the variables
     differ from one another (counts of strategies vs. probabilities vs.
     algebraic pay-offs).

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   6 of 15:  
   (1) group size n, (4) all-or-nothing contribution (yes, but not a numeric
       parameter), (6) MPCR r, (7) punishment cost γ,  
   (8) punishment magnitude β, (12) – (15) are all *not* mentioned, and all
   reward-related parameters (9-11) are absent.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematic
   variation* on the punishment-treatment effect?  
   Only 2 parameters (1: group size; 7: punishment cost).  
   Even for these, the outcome presented is the probability that a pool gets
   implemented or the equilibrium share of supporters, not efficiency, and no
   numeric effect size of a “with-punishment minus without-punishment”
   contrast is supplied.

D. Predictions one could make—restricted strictly to what the paper gives  
   • Larger groups and higher pool costs each reduce the likelihood that a
     pro-social punishment institution is active; if one equates “treatment
     effect on efficiency” with “efficiency advantage created by punishment,”

     Consequently, beyond the qualitative statement above, the paper offers
     little basis for predicting how the full set of 15 parameters or their
     interactions will shape the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency.

group size and punishment cost, but it does not study efficiency directly and
it leaves almost all of the specified design parameters untouched.

Below I go through the 15 design parameters one by one and stick strictly to what is stated in the paper “The role of leaders in inducing and maintaining cooperation: The CC strategy”.

For each parameter I answer two questions.  
(1) Is the parameter explicitly mentioned or can its value be inferred?  
(2) Does the paper predict what would happen to the *punishment treatment effect* if that parameter were systematically varied?  When a numerical effect can be taken directly from a table or figure I quote it; otherwise I say none is given.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Number of players  
   (1) YES.  In all laboratory games that contain punishment the interacting group is two **contributors** plus (in the third-party–punishment game) one **leader** (=3 persons). In the sequential Prisoner’s Dilemma and the 2-person public-goods game there are exactly two players.  
   (2) NO.  The paper never varies the number of players and never links it to any punishment-vs-no-punishment comparison.

2.  Number of rounds  
   (1) YES/IMPLICIT.  Most games are explicitly *one-shot*; the “sorting” experiment runs 20 rounds, but that experiment does **not** contain a punishment treatment.  
   (2) NO.  No systematic variation of the horizon is analysed in connection with punishment.

3.  Chat enabled?  
   (1) NO.  The word “chat”, “communication” or “cheap talk” never appears.  
   (2) –.

4.  All-or-nothing contribution?  
   (1) YES.  Contributions in the lab public-goods games are *continuous*: 0–6 Birr or 0–10 experimental units, so the answer is “no, they are **not** forced to be all-or-nothing”.  
   (2) NO.  The paper does not study what would happen if the choice were binary.

5.  Contribution default (reverse PG frame)?  
   (1) NO mention.  
   (2) –.

6.  MPCR / multiplication factor  
   (1) YES.  In the 2-player PG the marginal per-capita return is 0.75; in the Falk-Kosfeld principal–agent game it is 2 for the principal per unit invested by the agent.  
   (2) NO.  MPCR is never varied and no prediction is made about how changing it would alter the punishment treatment effect.

7.  Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   (1) YES.  In the leader punishment game it costs the leader 1 Birr per deduction point.  
   (2) NO.  That cost is fixed; there is no systematic manipulation and therefore no prediction of how changing the cost would alter the treatment effect.

8.  Punishment magnitude (fine per unit)  
   (1) YES.  One deduction point reduces a member’s payoff by 3 Birr.  
   (2) NO.  Magnitude is never varied; no prediction is offered.

9.  Reward enabled?  
   (1) NO.  Rewards are not implemented in any of the paper’s own experiments.  They are only mentioned in passing (“an alternative instrument … may be the reward of cooperation”).  
   (2) –.

10. Reward cost  
   (1) Not applicable (see 9).  
   (2) –.

11. Reward magnitude  
   (1) Not applicable.  
   (2) –.

12. Is the length of the game known to subjects?  
   (1) NO explicit statement for any punishment game.  The sequential PD and two-person PGs are one-shot, so the question is moot; for the sorting experiment (no punishment) subjects know the total of 20 rounds.  
   (2) NO.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   (1) PARTIAL.  In the third-party punishment game, the leader sees each member’s contribution; the paper never states whether members learn each other’s payoffs.  
   (2) NO systematic variation or prediction.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
   (1) YES.  The paper states that group members “did not learn the actual punishment decisions of their leader”.  Thus identity is *not* revealed.  
   (2) NO.  There is no treatment in which identity is revealed, so no prediction.

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
   (1) Not applicable (no rewards).  
   (2) –.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables actually used  
   • Forest-management performance (Potential-Crop-Trees per hectare) – a field measure of real cooperation outcomes.  
   • Individual investments/contributions in various lab games.  
   • Principals’ and agents’ payoffs in the principal–agent game.  
   The paper does **not** compute efficiency in the sense of “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff”, nor does it report total group payoffs with and without punishment treatments.  Hence “efficiency” as defined in the user prompt is not a reported dependent variable.

B.  Of the 15 design parameters, 10 are at least briefly mentioned or their value can be inferred: 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14; the remaining 5 (3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 15) are not mentioned.

C.  For **none** of the 15 parameters does the paper give a numerical or directional prediction about how *systematically varying* that parameter would change the punishment treatment effect on any dependent variable.  The paper never implements a punishment-vs-no-punishment comparison in which a parameter is varied.

D.  What can we predict—solely from this paper—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  Very little.  The text contains no evidence that changing group size, horizon, MPCR, punishment cost, etc., would strengthen or weaken (let alone reverse) the effect of allowing punishment on efficiency.  At best we can restate the qualitative insight that (i) some mechanism for punishment, especially if executed by prosocial leaders, can raise cooperation and real-world outcomes, while (ii) antisocial punishment can lower them.  Beyond that, the paper offers no basis for parameter-by-parameter quantitative predictions about efficiency.
reference_APA: Kosfeld, Michael (2020). The role of leaders in inducing and maintaining cooperation: The CC strategy. LEADERSHIP QUARTERLY.

The strong interaction between these systems can bring about regime shifts which in the extreme can lead to the collapse of social cooperation and the extinction of ecological resources. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what (if anything) the Casari & Luini (2012) paper says. The focus of the paper is on comparing “one‐to‐one” versus “sequential” punishment designs with respect to the amount of punishment administered, how people choose to punish (instrumentally vs. expressively), and how that relates to contribution decisions in a public‐goods setting. The paper does not measure nor predict “efficiency” (in the sense of total payoff relative to the maximum possible payoff) and does not systematically vary most of the 15 parameters listed in your request. Any mention below is solely limited to what the authors actually report.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned? Yes. Groups of exactly three players (“teams of three”) are formed in each period. The paper also notes that each session has 15 participants, who are randomly rematched into five groups of three.  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no condition in which the group size changes.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each session lasts 24 “periods.” Part 1 has four periods (no punishment), then two 10‐period blocks with different punishment designs (one‐to‐one vs. sequential), so 24 in total.  
   • Systematically varied? No. They do not vary the total number of periods across conditions or sessions.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned? Yes, in the sense that the authors explicitly state there is no communication. “No communication among subjects was allowed.”  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no treatment with or without chat; it is simply disallowed in all conditions.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned? Not in those terms. The paper describes a standard voluntary‐contribution mechanism in which each player can contribute any integer amount between 0 and 20 tokens.  
   • Systematically varied? No. Contributions are not forced to be “all or nothing” in any condition.

5. Is the contribution default (are players deciding how much to move from the public fund back into their hand)?
   • Mentioned? No. Participants simply choose how many of their 20 tokens to contribute to the public good. There is no mention of a “default” mechanism or forced withholding.  
   • Systematically varied? No mention at all.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper sets a = 0.6 for the public‐good multiplier. That is, each token contributed returns 0.6 tokens to each group member.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The MPCR is fixed at 0.6 in all conditions.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned? Yes. It is c = 1/4. That means each punishment point costs 0.25 tokens to the punisher.  
   • Systematically varied? No. This cost is the same throughout the experiment.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   • Mentioned? Yes. If a punisher assigns p points, the punished person’s payoff is reduced by p, and the punisher pays 0.25 × p.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The ratio of 1:1 damage (p points of payoff lost per punishment point) does not change across conditions.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned? No. They only study punishment. There is no reward mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Mentioned? No. Rewards do not appear in the design at all.  
    • Systematically varied? No.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)
    • Mentioned? No. Again, there is no reward mechanism.  
    • Systematically varied? No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Mentioned? Indirectly. Each session had 24 periods, and participants were told the experiment had three parts. However, the paper does not explicitly say whether participants knew in advance the exact total number of periods. It does state that participants were informed when instructions for the next part began.  
    • Systematically varied? No. There is no condition in which the horizon is changed or kept hidden.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?
    • Mentioned? Yes. After each public‐good stage, players see how much everyone in their group contributed, and after punishment, they see the total punishment assigned.  
    • Systematically varied? No. This is the same in all conditions.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Mentioned? Yes, indirectly. The paper states that punishment is done anonymously: “No subject was informed of the identity of the other group members.” Although they do see if they were punished, they do not learn exactly who punished them.  
    • Systematically varied? No. Anonymity does not change.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Mentioned? No. As noted above, no rewards are used at all, so this does not arise.  
    • Systematically varied? No.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Regarding predictions about systematically varying any of the above parameters to see how it would affect a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency,” the paper does not provide such predictions. Its central comparison is between “one‐to‐one” and “sequential” punishment rules under a single set of parameter values (group size fixed at 3, MPCR = 0.6, cost of punishment = 0.25, etc.). The authors do discuss how punishment affects contributions and punishment patterns, but not how it affects “efficiency” as defined (actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff). There is also no new treatment where those 15 parameters are individually or jointly changed to observe changes in efficiency outcomes; they simply keep those parameters fixed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The authors refer to “group payoffs” and note that total payoffs would be maximized by full cooperation. However, they do not systematically measure or report a “group efficiency” ratio, nor do they focus on total payoff as the paper’s main dependent variable. Instead, they mainly measure (1) how much punishment is administered, (2) how punishment decisions differ between one‐to‐one and sequential punishment, and (3) how much people contribute to the public good. So while payoffs are described to explain theoretical predictions, the paper’s reported results center on punishment and contribution behavior, not “efficiency” in the sense of total payoff / maximum possible payoff.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned (but not systematically varied):  
     1) Number of players (fixed: 3 per group, 15 in a session),  
     2) Number of rounds (24),  
     3) Chat is disallowed,  
     4) Contributions are not all‐or‐nothing,  
     6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR = 0.6),  
     7) Punishment cost (0.25 per point),  
     8) Punishment magnitude (1:1 damage),  
     12) They mention 24 periods existed, although not a systematic factor,  
     13) Peer outcomes shown,  
     14) The identity of the punisher is hidden.  
   • Not mentioned or not applicable:  
     5) “Contribution default” is not discussed,  
     9–11) No rewards, so reward parameters do not appear,  
     15) No rewards, so no mention of rewarder identity.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. The paper does not systematically vary any of these parameters. It holds them constant and only varies the structure of punishment (one‐to‐one vs. sequential). Hence there is no discussion of how changing those parameters would affect the “punishment treatment effect” on any outcome measure.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not provide grounds for making such predictions. It does not study efficiency as a dependent variable, nor does it experimentally vary those 15 parameters. Its focus is on whether punishment is “instrumental” or “expressive” under two specific implementations. Therefore, there is little to no basis in the paper for predicting how changing those parameters would affect punishment’s effect on efficiency.
reference_APA: Casari, Marco & Luini, Luigi (2012). Peer punishment in teams: expressive or instrumental choice?. EXPERIMENTAL ECONOMICS.

Authors: Bone, JE; Wallace, B; Bshary, R; Raihani, NJ

Article Title: Power Asymmetries and Punishment in a Prisoner's Dilemma with Variable Cooperative Investment
Keywords Plus: 3RD-PARTY PUNISHMENT; COUNTER-PUNISHMENT; PARTNER CONTROL; CLEANER; COERCION
Abstract: In many two-player games, players that invest in punishment finish with lower payoffs than those who abstain from punishing. These results question the effectiveness of punishment at promoting cooperation, especially when retaliation is possible. It has been suggested that these findings may stem from the unrealistic assumption that all players are equal in terms of power. However, a previous empirical study which incorporated power asymmetries into an iterated prisoner's dilemma (IPD) game failed to show that power asymmetries stabilize cooperation when punishment is possible. Instead, players cooperated in response to their partner cooperating, and punishment did not yield any additional increase in tendency to cooperate. Nevertheless, this previous study only allowed an all-or-nothing-rather than a variable-cooperation investment. It is possible that power asymmetries increase the effectiveness of punishment from strong players only when players are able to vary their investment in cooperation. We tested this hypothesis using a modified IPD game which allowed players to vary their investment in cooperation in response to being punished. As in the previous study, punishment from strong players did not increase cooperation under any circumstances. Thus, in two-player games with symmetric strategy sets, punishment does not appear to increase cooperation.

Below is a point‐by‐point summary of how (and whether) the Bone et al. (2016) paper mentions or varies each of the 15 parameters you listed, and whether the paper makes any claims about how changing those parameters would affect punishment’s impact on group efficiency (or on any other dependent variable). All statements refer solely to what is reported in the paper itself, including its figures and tables.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The experiment is strictly a two‐player iterated game.  
   • Systematically varied? No. They always use two players. The paper does not discuss what would happen if the number of players changed.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (for any dependent variable)? Not discussed.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each game was 50 rounds, although participants were told it could end between 20 and 100 (to avoid end‐game effects).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed. The paper does not analyze how altering the number of rounds would affect punishment outcomes.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned? No. There is no mention of any chat or direct communication between participants.  
   • Systematically varied? Not applicable.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper explicitly states that, unlike an earlier study by the same authors, this one used a variable‐investment version of the prisoner’s dilemma (i.e., not all-or-nothing).  
   • Systematically varied? No. In this study, every participant makes a variable contribution choice. There is no condition in which the authors revert to all‐or‐nothing.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? They do not measure efficiency and make no explicit claims on how systematically varying all‐or‐nothing versus variable formats would alter punishment’s effect. Their main point is simply that the current study used a variable‐investment setup.

5. Is the contribution default (push vs. pull)?  
   • Mentioned? No. There is no mention of a default contribution or a “push/pull” framing.  
   • Systematically varied? Not applicable.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? Not under those terms. The payoffs stem from a two‐player matrix (Table 1 in the paper) rather than a public goods multiplier.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The cost for a player to punish is always 1 unit, for both “weak” and “strong” players.  
   • Systematically varied? No. It is fixed at 1.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? The paper does examine how punishment is used, but does not vary the punishment cost. No efficiency metric is calculated.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player who is punished)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. A “weak” player inflicts a 1‐unit fine when punishing; a “strong” player inflicts a 6‐unit fine.  
   • Systematically varied? The paper always uses 1:1 for weak and 1:6 for strong. Those are the two power “types,” but they do not otherwise manipulate or systematically explore different ratios (e.g., 1:2 vs. 1:6 vs. 1:10).  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? The central focus is that strong vs. weak punishment might matter, but the authors do not measure group efficiency. They conclude that, even with this power asymmetry, punishment seldom led to higher cooperation or payoffs. No numerical effect sizes on efficiency are given (they do not measure efficiency).

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned? No. The game only allows punishment, not reward.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

10. Reward cost  
   • Mentioned? No. Rewards do not feature in the design.  
   • Systematically varied? Not applicable.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude  
   • Mentioned? No. Rewards are not part of the game.  
   • Systematically varied? Not applicable.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The participants were told the game would last “somewhere between 20 and 100” rounds (the actual number was 50). Therefore participants did not know the exact endpoint.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed. They do not analyze how systematically revealing vs. concealing the final round would affect punishment.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each round, players see their own and their partner’s decisions and payoffs.  
   • Systematically varied? No. Everyone sees the same outcome information.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? The paper does not connect this display to any variation in punishment effectiveness or efficiency.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Mentioned? Implicitly yes, because it is strictly a two‐player interaction: being punished can only come from one’s single partner. There is no separate condition where punisher identity is hidden.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed in terms of how systematically concealing vs. revealing punisher identity would affect outcomes.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Mentioned? No. There is no reward option, so whether a rewarder is identified is not discussed.  
   • Systematically varied? Not applicable.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A: Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • No. The authors explicitly focus on behavioral outcomes: mean cooperation level, propensity to punish, changes in cooperation following punishment, and retaliation. They do note final earnings (e.g., average payment), but they do not analyze efficiency (actual total payoff / maximum payoff) as a dependent variable.

B: Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • The paper explicitly mentions or describes eight of them in some form:  
     1) Number of players (always two),  
     2) Number of rounds (50, with participants told 20–100),  
     4) Contribution structure (variable, not all-or-nothing),  
     7) Punishment cost (fixed at 1 unit),  
     8) Punishment magnitude (1 unit vs. 6 units),  
     12) Whether the exact number of rounds is known (they do not know the precise end),  
     13) Peer outcomes displayed (yes),  
     14) Knowledge of who punished (implicit, two-player setup).  
   • The other parameters—3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, and 15—are not mentioned in the study or not applicable (e.g., no rewards).

C: For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, the only parameter they manipulated in a comparative sense was whether players were weak or strong (which bundles punishment magnitude at 1 vs. 6). They also presented “symmetric” vs. “asymmetric” pairings (weak–weak, strong–strong, or weak–strong). However, they did not measure efficiency, and they did not systematically vary any parameter across multiple levels beyond those two player types.  
   • Therefore, the paper does not provide effect sizes or predictions on efficiency for systematically varying any of the parameters. Instead, it reports that actual punishment (as opposed to the threat of it) did not raise cooperation or reduce retaliation, regardless of whether players were weak or strong.

D: If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper’s content, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not measure group efficiency at all, and its main claim is that punishment from strong or weak partners did not succeed in boosting cooperation once the game was underway. Hence, it provides no direct inference on overall efficiency.  
   • Beyond noting that weak players cooperated more against strong partners (which the authors interpret as a possible effect of the threat of high‐impact punishment), the study does not quantify total or group payoffs. It therefore offers little basis for predicting how any of the listed parameters or their interactions might systematically raise or lower a group’s overall efficiency.  
   • Consequently, based strictly on the information in Bone et al. (2016), one can say very little about how those 15 parameters—individually or jointly—would affect punishment’s impact on total payoff or efficiency. The authors themselves emphasize that they focused on cooperation behavior, not on payoff or efficiency metrics.

Below is a systematic walkthrough of each of the 15 parameters, indicating whether (1) the paper discusses that parameter (and what specific value or setup it uses, if any) and (2) the paper makes any predictions about the effect of systematically varying that parameter on the “punishment treatment effect.” (Throughout, “punishment treatment effect” is understood to mean how introducing punishment into the game would, if at all, change outcomes—in particular, whether it yields stronger or weaker cooperation or payoffs.)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     Yes. The paper explicitly models two “producers” (Producer 1 and Producer 2).  
   • Any systematic variation or prediction?  
     No. The paper keeps the number of players fixed at two and does not discuss what happens if that number changes.

2. Number of rounds
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     No. The paper refers generally to an “evolutionary” or repeatedly played game but never specifies the exact number of rounds.  
   • Any systematic variation or prediction?  
     No.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     No.  
   • Any systematic variation or prediction?  
     No.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     No. Although the paper frames choices as “cooperate (C)” or “compete (D),” it does not invoke a public-goods framing of “all-or-nothing contributions.”  
   • Any systematic variation or prediction?  
     No.

5. Is the contribution default (players move some portion back to their own possession)?
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     No.  
   • Any systematic variation or prediction?  
     No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters (e.g., multiplication factor)
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     No. The paper introduces “Δπ” as extra payoff from cooperation, but this is not explicitly framed as an MPCR in a public goods sense, and there is no mention of “multiplying” each player’s contribution.  
   • Any systematic variation or prediction?  
     No.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     Not specifically. The paper does introduce a penalty “pQ,” but it is not framed as “the cost to the punisher” to impose one unit of punishment. Instead, “pQ” is the amount subtracted from the defector’s payoff; no cost is charged to the punisher.  
   • Any systematic variation or prediction?  
     No. The paper does not discuss systematically varying a punishment “cost” to the punisher.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed)
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     Partially. The paper sets up a punishing mechanism in which a defector (the noncooperator) pays an amount “pQ” to the partner who was defected upon. If “pQ” is high enough, it can change the game’s equilibrium.  
   • Any systematic variation or prediction for the punishment treatment effect?  
     The paper does say that, if pQ > max(c1 + f1, c2 + f2), then the only stable equilibrium is mutual cooperation. However, there is no numerical effect size reported, nor is there explicit reference to a shift in “group efficiency.” It simply shows that if the penalty is large enough, the system evolves to cooperation.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     Yes. The paper calls it an “incentive mechanism” (e.g., V is the reward or subsidy).  
   • Any systematic variation or prediction?  
     The paper states that if V > max(c1 + f1, c2 + f2), mutual cooperation is a uniquely stable outcome. There is no mention of how changing V would quantitatively affect efficiency.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     No. While the paper discusses providing a reward V to cooperators, it never frames how costly that reward is to the rewarder.  
   • Any systematic variation or prediction?  
     No.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted)
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     Partially. The paper uses V as the total reward given to cooperators to encourage cooperation.  
   • Any systematic variation or prediction for the punishment treatment effect?  
     The paper does not treat reward and punishment jointly in the sense of “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” It does say that if V is large enough, cooperation becomes stable. But it gives no quantitative effect on payoffs or efficiency beyond noting the stable-cooperation outcome.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     No.  
   • Any systematic variation or prediction?  
     No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     No.  
   • Any systematic variation or prediction?  
     No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     No.  
   • Any systematic variation or prediction?  
     No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     No.  
   • Any systematic variation or prediction?  
     No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper does not use “group efficiency,” “total payoff,” or “average payoff” as its reported dependent variable. Instead, it uses evolutionary stable strategies, focusing on whether the end state is “cooperate” or “compete,” along with certain payoff comparisons. While the paper does describe changes in payoffs, it does not frame these in terms of total/average payoff or efficiency.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   1) Number of players (Param #1) is mentioned: always two producers.  
   2) Punishment magnitude (Param #8) is discussed (pQ).  
   3) Whether a reward is enabled (Param #9) is discussed (the paper calls it an “incentive mechanism”).  
   4) Reward magnitude (Param #11) is discussed (V).  
   Everything else is not explicitly addressed. Thus, 4 of the 15 parameters are mentioned.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The paper only discusses parameter #8 (punishment magnitude, pQ) in a way that is close to “systematic variation”: it states that if the punishment is large enough (pQ > certain threshold), the unique stable outcome is cooperation. However, there is no numeric effect size given, and no reference to “group efficiency.”  
   • Similarly, for parameter #9 and #11 (reward enablement and reward magnitude), the paper states that if V is large enough, the unique stable outcome is cooperation. Again, no numeric effect size on efficiency is provided.  
   • The paper does not quantify how these parameter variations affect “punishment treatment effect” in terms of total payoff or efficiency outcomes.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not directly measure “efficiency” or “actual total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff.” It limits itself to whether cooperation or noncooperation is the stable outcome. No numerical effect sizes on payoffs are provided.  
   • Consequently, based solely on this paper, it is not possible to make a detailed quantitative prediction about how systematically varying each of the 15 parameters (or their interactions) would change group efficiency. The primary qualitative takeaway is that larger punishment “pQ” or larger reward “V” can stabilize cooperation. If one assumes cooperation yields higher total payoffs, then one might infer that sufficiently high punishment or reward would likely increase efficiency—but the paper does not explicitly confirm this.  

In short, the paper only discusses a few of the 15 parameters (number of players, punishment magnitude, reward enablement, reward magnitude) and gives qualitative conditions under which cooperation becomes stabilized, but it does not measure or predict changes in efficiency (as total payoff / maximum payoff). Therefore, beyond guessing that “higher punishments or rewards probably boost overall collaborative payoffs,” the paper provides little to no quantitative basis for the effect on efficiency.

Article Title: The effects of contemporaneous peer punishment on cooperation with the future
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; 3RD-PARTY PUNISHMENT; STRONG RECIPROCITY; EVOLUTION; ENFORCEMENT; INEQUALITY; ECONOMICS; TIME
Abstract: We use a laboratory version of the intergenerational goods game (IGG) to investigate whether peer punishment facilitates the successful provision of multigenerational public goods. In our experiment, groups (generations) decide sequentially about the provision of a multigenerational public good through the voluntary contributions of their members. Successful provision requires that contributions meet a threshold and exclusively benefits members of future generations. Provision costs are borne only by the current generation. We compare a baseline condition without a punishment institution to a treatment condition where peer punishment can be inflicted exclusively on members of the same generation but not on members of past or future generations. We find that without punishment the likelihood of reaching the contribution threshold is low and that making punishment available within a generation is partially successful in sustaining cooperation in a succession of multiple generations. Little is known about decentralized institutions that could facilitate cooperation for the sake of future generations. Here, the authors show that allowing for peer punishment within a generation is only partially successful in facilitating cooperation for the sake of later generations.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter review of what the paper actually states and whether it makes any predictions about how systematically varying each parameter would affect the “punishment treatment effect.” In doing so, I focus exclusively on what is reported in the paper (including its figures and tables). “Punishment treatment effect” here means how introducing a punishment option changes outcomes relative to a no‐punishment baseline.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter (and give its value)?  
     – Yes. Each session has 12 participants, divided into four groups of three.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it (i.e., changing the number of players)?  
     – No. There is no discussion of how changing group size or session size would affect punishment’s impact.

2) Number of rounds
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter (and give its value)?  
     – Yes. The game is designed with up to four generations (called “groups” in the paper). Generations 1, 2, and 3 make a contribution decision; generation 4 does not make a decision but can earn money if generation 3 contributes enough.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No. The experiment always had at most four successive groups. There is no mention of examining additional or fewer generations/rounds to see how that would change the punishment effect.

3) Is chat enabled between players?
   • Does the paper discuss this?  
     – No. The paper does not mention any form of player communication or “chat.”  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No. It is never addressed.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Does the paper discuss this?  
     – The paper states that each participant can divide their endowment (up to €10) in any amount between their private account and the group account. Hence, it is not an all-or-nothing design.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No. The paper does not discuss forcing “all or nothing” or partially changing contributions. No effect of that is analyzed.

5) Is the contribution default?
   • Does the paper discuss this?  
     – No. There is no mention of a “default” or forced contribution setting.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No. Not addressed.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Does the paper discuss this?  
     – No. This is a threshold public goods game, not a standard linear public goods game with an MPCR.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying the MPCR or threshold?  
     – While they do explain that the threshold is €15 out of a €30 group endowment, they do not systematically vary the threshold or any “multiplication factor.” There is no discussion of how varying it would change the punishment effect.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter (and give its value)?  
     – Yes. It costs €1 for the punisher to impose one “punishment point.”  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No. The cost is fixed at €1 per point. The paper does not discuss how different punishment-cost levels would change the punishment effect.

8) Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from a player per unit imposed)
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter (and give its value)?  
     – Yes. Each punishment point deducts €3 from the punished person (fine-to-fee ratio of 3:1).  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No. The fine ratio (3:1) is fixed. They do not examine alternative magnitudes or model how that would alter the treatment effect.

9) Whether a reward is enabled
   • Does the paper discuss this?  
     – No. The design involves only punishment, no rewards.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying a reward option?  
     – No. Reward is absent and never discussed as a variant.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Does the paper discuss this?  
      – No. There is no reward mechanism at all.  
    • Predictions?  
      – None.

11) Reward magnitude (coins earned by the rewarded player)
    • Does the paper discuss this?  
      – No. Same as above: no reward mechanism in play.  
    • Predictions?  
      – None.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know the game length)?
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter (and give its value)?  
      – Yes. Subjects know that there can be up to four groups in sequence.  
    • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying the information about the end of the game?  
      – No. They do not examine treatments in which the end is unknown or ambiguous. No mention of systematically testing different known horizons.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost)?
    • Does the paper discuss this?  
      – Yes. After each group’s contribution stage, participants see each other’s contributions in that group. The text says they are not told about other groups’ results, but do learn if their own group reached the threshold.  
    • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying this feedback format?  
      – No. It is simply part of the design and not systematically manipulated.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Does the paper discuss this?  
      – The paper states that each player is “identifiable by a number” during punishment, but does not explicitly say whether punished players see which numbered person punished them. This detail is not varied.  
    • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying anonymity of punishers?  
      – No. Not mentioned at all.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is?
    • Does the paper discuss this?
      – No. There is no reward mechanism.  
    • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying knowledge of rewarders?
      – No. Not relevant to this design.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Summary (A–D)

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper reports on “aggregate earnings,” “share of sustained generations,” and “propensity to meet the threshold,” among other outcomes. They do not explicitly calculate efficiency as “actual payoff / maximum possible payoff,” nor do they label their payoff measure as “efficiency.”  
   • Dependent variables they do discuss include: (1) whether the threshold is reached and subsequent generations are sustained, (2) individual contributions, and (3) total earnings (sometimes referred to as “aggregate earnings”). The paper also notes that the punishment mechanism does not lead to statistically higher total average earnings for participants, because punishment costs offset some of the gains from cooperation.  
   • Hence, the paper’s main measures differ from a formal “efficiency ratio.”

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • The paper explicitly states or clarifies the following parameters (though not always labeling them exactly as “parameters” in the text):  
     1) Number of players (they fix the group size at 3, 12 per session).  
     2) Number of rounds (up to four groups in a sequence).  
     7) Punishment cost (1 euro per punishment point).  
     8) Punishment magnitude (3 euros deducted per punishment point).  
     12) Whether the total number of groups (rounds) is known (it is announced).  
     13) Whether peer outcomes (contributions) are shown (they are).  
   • All others are either not used or not mentioned in any detail. That means the paper touches on 6 of the 15 parameters in some form (1, 2, 7, 8, 12, 13).

C) For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for any dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. The experiment does not systematically vary any of these parameters (the design is the same for all subjects within each treatment: no-punishment vs. punishment). The cost of punishment, its magnitude, and the known number of groups are all held constant. The paper does not manipulate group size or feedback structure or any other item.  
   • Hence, no parameter is systematically “varied” (e.g., different values across treatments) to test how that variation changes the punishment effect on cooperation or earnings. The only main variation is the presence vs. absence of punishment itself.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper itself does not provide direct guidance on what would happen if any of these 15 parameters changed. It simply reports that, under its fixed settings, punishment approximately doubles the chance that future generations get funded but does not generate significantly higher total earnings on average once punishment costs are subtracted.  
   • Therefore, strictly following the paper’s discussion, one cannot make clear predictions about how systematically altering group size, thresholds, punishment-cost ratios, or any other design parameter would change the effect of punishment on eventual efficiency. The paper does not investigate those dimensions and offers no explicit or numerical effect sizes for hypothetical variations.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Abstract: The provision of public goods motivates the creation of institutions designed to compel individuals to cooperate. Peer punishment mechanisms have garnered particular attention and suggest that groups are able to self-govern. Research suggests that the effectiveness of peer punishment depends on a group's capacity to establish and enforce contribution norms. Below I go through the 15 parameters one‐by‐one, always sticking strictly to what is reported in Kingsley (2016).

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each group contains n = 4 players (Sec. 2, eq. (1)).  
   • Systematic variation / prediction? No. The number of players is fixed; the paper makes no prediction about how changing n would alter the punishment treatment effect on any dependent variable.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? Yes. 15 paid periods after one practice round (Sec. 2).  
   • Systematic variation / prediction? No. The length is never varied between treatments, though the author sometimes separates “early” (1-8) and “late” (9-15) periods post-hoc. No prediction about how a different horizon would change the punishment effect is offered.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned? No. There is no reference to any communication stage; therefore chat is disabled.  
   • Predictions? None.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution?  
   • Mentioned? Yes indirectly. Players choose any integer amount of their endowment to put in the group account (continuous choice).  
   • Predictions? None. The study does not compare to an all-or-nothing variant.

5. “Contribution default / refund” framing?  
   • Mentioned? No. Players simply decide how much of their own endowment to contribute; no refund or default framing is used.  
   • Predictions? None.

6. MPCR (or multiplication factor)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Pay-off function is non-linear: π_i = w(e_i–x_i) + 1/n[aΣx_j – b(Σx_j)^2] with w = 1, a = 6, b = 0.025 (Sec. 2). That yields an interior social optimum of 100 EDs per group (MPCR varies with total contributions).  
   • Predictions? None. a and b are fixed; no statement about how different return schedules would alter punishment effectiveness.

7. Punishment cost per “point”  
   • Mentioned? Yes. A subject pays 1 ED to impose one unit of punishment (Sec. 2).  
   • Predictions? None. Cost is fixed; varying it is never analysed.

8. Punishment magnitude (“fine” per unit)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. 1 ED paid removes 3 EDs from the target (Sec. 2, eq. (2)).  
   • Predictions? None.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Mentioned? Yes (implicitly). There is no reward stage; only punishment exists.  
   • Predictions? None.

10–11. Reward cost / magnitude  
   • Not applicable: no reward option is present; therefore nothing is mentioned or predicted.

12. Is the number of rounds common knowledge?  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Subjects are told there will be 15 paid periods (Sec. 2).  
   • Predictions? No comparison to an unknown-horizon design.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Mentioned? Partially. After the contribution stage players see each group member’s contribution (labelled by a random ID each round). They also see their own earnings; the paper does not say that they observe others’ earnings.  
   • Predictions? No systematic variation.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
   • Mentioned? Not explicitly. Subjects choose whom to punish by current-round ID, but the text does not state whether the recipient sees who punished them. Consequently no causal claim is made about varying identity revelation.

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
   • Not applicable (no reward stage).

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables actually used  
   • Group efficiency (total or average payoff divided by its maximum) is NOT directly reported.  
   • Main dependent variables:  
     – Contribution level (EDs contributed)  
     – Earnings / payoffs (before and after punishment costs)  
     – Amount of punishment imposed  
   These differ conceptually: contributions measure cooperative input, earnings measure monetary welfare, and punishment imposed measures enforcement effort. Efficiency, defined as realised divided by maximum possible earnings, would combine the last two but is never calculated.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   Eight are explicitly referenced (1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13). The other seven (3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15) are either absent or designated “not applicable.”

C. For how many parameters does the article discuss the effect of SYSTEMATICALLY VARYING the parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
   Zero. None of the eight mentioned parameters are varied across treatments, so no effect sizes for such variation exist. The sole treatment variable in the paper is endowment heterogeneity, which is outside the present 15-parameter list.

D. What predictions—restricted solely to the paper’s contents—can be made about how these 15 parameters (and their interactions) will change the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
   The paper offers virtually no basis for prediction. Since none of the parameters are manipulated, the study contains no empirical or theoretical statements about how changing any of them would increase or decrease the efficiency effect of punishment. Therefore, based only on Kingsley (2016), one must conclude that there is insufficient information to forecast how any of the 15 parameters, individually or in interaction, would influence the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.

Below I go through the 15 design parameters one-by-one, quoting or paraphrasing only what appears in “Cooperation in the commons with unobservable actions.”  For every parameter I state  

(a) whether the paper even mentions or fixes the parameter, and  
(b) whether the paper says what would happen to the **punishment treatment effect** (the difference between a game *with* and *without* punishment) if that parameter were systematically varied.  When a numerical pattern can be read from a figure or table I reproduce it.

-------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
-------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Number of players  
• Mentioned? Yes.  The model is built for an arbitrary N ≥ 3 (Section 2).  Numerical illustrations use N = 3 and N = 4 (Figs. 2 & 3).  
• Systematic prediction? Yes.  
  – Fig. 2 plots, for each N, the minimum discount factor δ needed for the two-part punishment equilibrium to exist (Assumption 2) and the minimum δ for the punishment phase itself to be self-enforcing (Assumption 3).  
  – Qualitative result (p. 20): “cooperation could be easier to support with four players than with three … ultimately, however, as group size rises further the former effect dominates and cooperation becomes more difficult to support.”  
  – Thus the predicted punishment treatment effect on efficiency is:  
     • N = 2 not analysed (model requires N ≥ 3).  
     • N = 3 → 4 positive (punishment becomes feasible for a wider δ-range; Fig. 3 shows that at δ = 0.90 the punishment phase is self-enforcing for N = 4 but not for N = 3).  
     • N > ≈4 negative (need a larger δ; fewer parameter combinations satisfy both Assumptions 2 & 3).  
  No exact slope coefficients are reported, only the boundary curves in Fig. 2.

2. Number of rounds  
• Mentioned? The theoretical game is infinite-horizon (discrete time t = 0,1,…). No finite-round condition is ever varied.  
• Prediction? None.

3. Chat / communication  
• Mentioned or varied? No.  
• Prediction? None.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
(Not relevant, the decision variable is a continuous harvest level.)  
• Mentioned? No.  
• Prediction? None.

5. “Contribution default” framing  
• Mentioned? No.  
• Prediction? None.

6. Marginal Per-Capita Return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
• Mentioned? No.  The model instead has a price p and a cost function c(s); neither is varied in the punishment analysis.  
• Prediction? None.

7. Punishment cost to punisher  
• Mentioned? Only implicitly: during the harsh one-period punishment each player “incurs one-period negative profits” (p. 9).  There is no free parameter that is systematically varied.  
• Prediction? None.

8. Punishment magnitude (how much the target loses per unit)  
• Mentioned? Endogenously determined; not an independent parameter.  
• Prediction? None.

9–11. Reward option, reward cost, reward magnitude  
• Mentioned? No.  
• Prediction? None.

12. Are the number of rounds common knowledge?  
• The horizon is infinite and that fact is not varied.  
• Prediction? None.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (i.e., is individual behaviour observable)?  
• Mentioned? Yes.  Core assumption: “player i cannot observe h_jt for j ≠ i … punishment must be symmetric” (p. 5).  
• Prediction when varied? No.  This information structure is fixed; the paper only *contrasts* it with earlier papers that assumed perfect monitoring.

14. Is the identity of the punisher revealed?  
• Not applicable; punishment is group-wide and symmetric.  Not discussed as a variable.

15. Is the identity of a rewarder revealed?  
• Not applicable, not discussed.

-------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
-------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables actually analysed  
– Individual or group **present-value payoffs** (v for cooperation; π for a one-shot deviation).  
– Whether **full cooperation** (first-best harvest path) can be sustained as a sub-game-perfect equilibrium.  
– The paper never reports the *ratio* “actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff,” so the term “efficiency” is used qualitatively, not as the exact metric requested in the prompt.  No tables or figures give efficiency percentages.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are explicitly mentioned?  2 of 15  
   #1 Number of players  
   #13 Observability of peer outcomes (fixed at “aggregate only, no individual info”)

C. Which parameters are *systematically varied* and linked to the punishment treatment effect?  1 of 15  
   #1 Number of players – varied analytically (N) and in Figs. 2 & 3.

D. What predictions can we make—restricted strictly to evidence in this paper—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions will influence the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency?

• #1 Number of players  
  – Increasing N from very small values (3 → 4 in the example) can *improve* the punishment treatment effect because harsher symmetric punishment becomes self-enforcing (Assumption 3 starts to hold) and therefore cooperation—and hence efficiency—can be sustained where it could not before.  
  – Beyond that intermediate range, further increases in N shrink each player’s cooperative share, increase the temptation to defect, raise the δ-threshold (Assumption 2), and thus *reduce* the ability of punishment to boost efficiency.

• #2–#15  
  – The paper provides no direct comparative-static results.  Therefore, based solely on this source, we cannot make any informed prediction about how changing those 14 parameters would alter the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

In short, the paper gives us useful, albeit qualitative, guidance only for Parameter 1 (group size).  For the remaining 14 parameters it either fixes them, ignores them, or treats them outside the scope of its analysis; consequently almost no prediction about their influence on the punishment treatment effect on efficiency can be drawn from this paper alone.

Abstract: Partner choice is likely to be an important mechanism for the maintenance of cooperation in many mutualisms, and cleaner mutualisms among fish have been a model system for testing predictions of partner choice theories. Fish seeking to be cleaned ( clients) face two potential problems: cleaners may cheat them by feeding on tissue or mucous, and they may have to wait for service from a cleaner. The results indicate that cleaners give ornate butterflyfish, Chaetodon ornatissimus, priority of access to their services when these clients can switch partners; however, ornate butterflyfish are not cheated less often when they have access to multiple cleaner stations, and they frequently respond to cheating by aggressively chasing cleaners. In combination with previous work, these results indicate that partner choice influences cooperative interactions between bluestreak cleaner wrasse and their clients, but that some clients with the ability to switch partners may use other strategies (i.e. punishment) to limit cheating by cleaners. Parameter-by-parameter extraction from Dong, Sasaki & Zhang (2019)

For every parameter we first say whether it is explicitly modelled in the paper and, if so, how.  
Second, we list any statement or figure that allows us to infer what would happen to the
punishment–minus–control effect on **group efficiency** (the authors’ “group average fitness”)
when that parameter is systematically varied.

1. Number of players in a group (n)  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  All formal results contain n.  Figures 2–3 use n = 4 and 8.  
   • Systematic variation? Figure 3 varies n (two rows: n = 4 and n = 8).  The colour code
     shows which institution (Reward, Punishment, IRP0.5, IRPmax) gives the
     highest efficiency.  Increasing n does not qualitatively change the
     ranking: under small decision errors IP beats IR only for a
     narrow intermediate range of the incentive size (C_I) but
     under intermediate/large errors IR dominates for every n.
     No numerical effect sizes are reported.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? No (the model is an infinitely repeated population process).  
   • Systematic variation? No.

3. Chat possibility  
   • Not mentioned.

4. All-or-nothing contribution decision  
   • Mentioned? Yes: each player either contributes the fixed amount c or nothing.  
   • Systematic variation? No (always binary).

5. Contribution default / “retraction” frame  
   • Not mentioned.

6. Marginal Per-Capita Return (multiplication factor r)  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  r is in every equation; Figure 3 has columns with r = 2 and r = 3.  
   • Systematic variation? Yes (Figure 3).  Result: the identity of the
     efficiency-maximising institution is insensitive to r; IR dominates
     for intermediate/large errors, and for small errors IP/IRP can win
     only in a narrow C_I band.  No numerical magnitudes reported.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   • Institutional setting: every player pays the fixed entry fee C_I
     before the game starts.  Thus C_I is the (shared) cost of enabling
     one “unit” of punishment or reward.  
   • Systematic variation? Yes.  C_I is the main x-axis in Figures 1e,
     2c, 2d and Figure 3.  
     – Without decision errors (Fig. 1e):  
       • C_I ≤ C_I⁻ (0 – 0.125 in the numerical example) ➔ IR yields
         higher efficiency than IP (punishment reduces pay-off).  
       • C_I⁻ < C_I < C_I⁺ (0.125 – 0.5) ➔ IRPmax beats both IR and IP.  
       • C_I ≥ C_I⁺ ➔ IR again dominates.  
     – With decision errors μ = 0.01:  
       sequence of most efficient institutions as C_I rises:
       IR → IP → IRP0.5 → IRPmax → IR.  
     – With μ ≥ 0.1 IR is always most efficient regardless of C_I.

8. Punishment magnitude per unit  
   • Determined endogenously: each defector loses (C_I · n)/n_D.  Not
     varied independently of C_I, so no separate results.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Central object of study (IR vs IP vs IRP).  
   • Systematic variation? Yes – the three incentive regimes and the
     parameter α (share of the budget devoted to reward).  
     – α = 0 (IP), α = 1 (IR), 0 < α < 1 (IRP).  
     – Fig. 1c–e derive the stability and efficiency of IRP as α varies.
       Max-efficient α is α_max = [n – (n – r)c / (n C_I)] / (n – 1).
     – The authors never translate this into a numeric treatment-effect
       size but do state that IRP is never superior once decision errors
       exceed the “small” range.

10–11. Reward cost and reward magnitude per unit  
   • Both tied to the same entry fee C_I; not varied separately.

12. Knowledge of the number of rounds  
   • Not mentioned.

13. Feedback about peer outcomes  
   • Not mentioned.

14–15. Identity of punisher / rewarder revealed  
   • Not applicable (centralized institution).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
   • The paper’s efficiency variable is “group average fitness at the
     stable equilibrium”.  
   • They also track “cooperation level” (equilibrium share of
     contributors).  The two variables are analytically distinct: punishment
     can raise cooperation while lowering fitness.

B. Which of the 15 parameters appear?  
   6 parameters: 1 (group size n), 4 (binary contribution), 6 (MPCR r),
   7 (entry fee C_I that finances punishment/reward), 8/11 (resulting
   magnitudes, but not independent), and 9 (whether reward is enabled and
   α, the reward fraction).

C. Which parameters are **systematically varied** and linked to the
   punishment treatment effect on any dependent variable?  
   • 3 parameters: n, r, and C_I are each varied in figures.  
   • Parameter 9 is varied by switching across IR, IP and IRP and by
     varying α.  
   (Total: 4 of 15.)

   Numerical effect sizes are not given; only qualitative regions (which
   incentive yields the highest efficiency).

D. Predictions that can be made for the 15 parameters, based solely on
   this paper  

   – Punishment cost / incentive size (C_I) is the strongest moderator:
     with no decision errors, punishment (or mixed) can improve efficiency
     only for an intermediate range of C_I; with realistic errors it
     basically never raises efficiency.  

   – Decision errors (μ) are decisive but are not one of the 15
     parameters supplied by the user; once μ ≥ 0.1, reward always beats
     punishment irrespective of n, r or C_I.

   – Larger group size n or larger MPCR r do **not** overturn that
     qualitative conclusion; they only slightly shift the C_I thresholds.  

   – Parameters not modelled (rounds, chat, visibility, identity
     disclosure, etc.) cannot be linked to any prediction—no evidence is
     provided.  

   Consequently, if one had to forecast the punishment treatment effect on
   efficiency using only this paper, the only confident statements would be
   that (i) increasing the universal punishment budget (C_I) beyond a low
   threshold quickly makes punishment counter-productive once decision
   errors exist, and (ii) toggling on a reward component (α > 0) or
   switching to pure reward (α = 1) typically restores or maximises
   efficiency.  Little or no prediction can be made for the remaining
   parameters because they are not addressed in the study.

A: Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different from one another?

Below I go through the list of 15 parameters one‐by‐one, quoting only what can be found in the paper “Impact of punishment on the evolution of cooperation in spatial prisoner’s dilemma game.”  For every parameter I state  
(1) whether it is mentioned in the paper and, if so, the value(s) used, and  
(2) whether the paper reports what would happen if the parameter were **systematically varied** to see how the *punishment treatment effect* changes.  Numerical effect sizes are given whenever they can be read directly from the figures or text.  I purposely do not add any information that is not in the article.

-------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER 1 – Number of players  
(1) Mentioned.  Simulations are run on a 400 × 400 lattice (160 000 players) after stating the model is defined on an L × L lattice in general.  
(2) Not systematically varied; no results on how changing group size alters the punishment treatment effect on any outcome.

PARAMETER 2 – Number of rounds  
(1) Mentioned.  Each run lasts 50 000 Monte-Carlo (MC) steps; the last 5 000 steps are averaged for statistics.  
(2) Never varied; no discussion of how a different horizon changes any treatment effect.

PARAMETER 3 – Chat enabled?  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) Not applicable.

PARAMETER 4 – “All-or-nothing” contribution decision  
(1) Implicitly “yes.”  A Prisoner’s Dilemma has a binary choice C or D, i.e., contribute (cooperate) or not.  
(2) The paper never varies this design feature, so no treatment-effect predictions.

PARAMETER 5 – Contribution default (take-out vs. put-in frame)  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) Not applicable.

PARAMETER 6 – MPCR / multiplication factor  
(1) Not used; the study is a Prisoner’s Dilemma, not a linear public-goods game.  
(2) Not applicable.

PARAMETER 7 – Punishment cost to the punisher  
(1) Not modeled.  “Punishment” is implemented automatically by reducing the punished player’s fitness coefficient; there is **no cost to any punishing individual**.  
(2) Therefore the effect of varying the punishment cost is never studied.

PARAMETER 8 – Punishment magnitude (how much the target loses per unit)  
(1) Directly modeled by the “punishment rate” α.  The target’s fitness coefficient is multiplied by (1 – α) whenever his own payoff is below the neighbours’ average.  Studied values: α = 0 (no punishment), 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 0.10 (exact values visible in Fig. 1a).  
(2) Systematically varied and clear effects are reported:

   • Fig. 1a: For any fixed memory length M = 5, higher α shifts both cooperative-dominance threshold b_C1 and extinction threshold b_C2 upward.  
   • Fig. 2: At b = 1.15 and K = 0.1, the phase diagram in the α × M plane shows a transition from pure-D (low α, low M) → mixed (intermediate) → pure-C (higher α and/or M).  
   • Fig. 4: At α = 0.03 the long-run co‐operator fraction stabilises below 1; at α = 0.08 it quickly converges to 1.  Quantitative values can be read approximately: for b = 1.15, α = 0 the stationary ρ_C ≈ 0; α ≈ 0.03 gives ρ_C ≈ 0.8; α ≈ 0.08 gives ρ_C = 1.

   These results are all in terms of the fraction of cooperators ρ_C (not efficiency).

PARAMETERS 9 – 11 – Reward enabled, reward cost, reward magnitude  
(1) Rewards are never included in the model.  
(2) No discussion.

PARAMETERS 12 – 15 – Information conditions  
(1) None of these information-display variables (known end-round, outcome feedback, identity of punisher/rewarder) are discussed.  
(2) No treatment-effect results.

-------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY  

A. Dependent variables in the paper  
   • Fraction of cooperators ρ_C (primary outcome drawn in all figures).  
   • Standard deviation of the individual fitness coefficient SD(φ) (used to quantify heterogeneity).  
   Group efficiency (total or average payoff relative to the cooperative optimum) is **not** measured.

B. How many of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   4 parameters:  
   – #1 Number of players (fixed)  
   – #2 Number of rounds (fixed)  
   – #4 Binary cooperate/defect choice (fixed)  
   – #8 Punishment magnitude α (varied)

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* them on the punishment treatment effect?  
   Exactly 1 parameter: #8 Punishment magnitude α.  (And even here the outcome is ρ_C, not efficiency.)

D. What predictions about the punishment-treatment effect on **efficiency** can be made solely from this paper?  
   • Because the paper never reports payoffs, total payoffs, or efficiency, only very indirect inferences can be drawn.  The only solid qualitative prediction is that larger punishment magnitude (higher α) – especially when combined with a non-zero memory length M – drives the system toward full cooperation, which would *likely* raise efficiency relative to the no-punishment condition.  
   • For all other listed parameters (group size, horizon, communication, reward presence, information conditions, etc.) the paper offers no guidance, so no prediction can be made from this source alone.

A.  Dependent variables actually used  
    • P_c – P_d (payoff difference between strategies)  
    • x_c (fraction of cooperators)  
    • Sometimes average cooperation over both network layers  
    Group efficiency (total or average payoff divided by the maximum possible) is NEVER calculated.

B.  Parameters from the list that are mentioned (5/15)  
    1, 4, 6 (via b and c), 7 (α), 8 (β).

C.  Parameters whose systematic variation is analysed with respect to outcomes while punishment is in force (2/15)  
    • 1.  Number of players N – varied; larger N weakens cooperation.  
    • 7.  Punishment cost α – varied; higher α reduces cooperation and thus would reduce efficiency.  
    (No other listed parameter is both varied and linked to a punishment-related outcome.)

    • If punishment is already present, raising its COST (α) will lower cooperation and therefore lower efficiency; lowering α has the opposite effect.

    • The paper gives no information about how changing the punishment magnitude β, enabling chat, showing outcomes, allowing rewards, etc. would alter efficiency, so no prediction can be drawn for those parameters from this source alone.

Authors: Huang, F; Chen, XJ; Wang, L
Author Full Names: Huang, Feng; Chen, Xiaojie; Wang, Long
Article Title: Conditional punishment is a double-edged sword in promoting cooperation
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS; INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; EVOLUTIONARY DYNAMICS; GAME; STRATEGIES; SELECTION; FINITE
Abstract: Punishment is widely recognized as an effective approach for averting from exploitation by free-riders in human society. However, punishment is costly, and thus rational individuals are unwilling to take the punishing action, resulting in the second-order free-rider problem. Recent experimental study evidences that individuals prefer conditional punishment, and their punishing decision depends on other members' punishing decisions. In this work, we thus propose a theoretical model for conditional punishment and investigate how such conditional punishment influences cooperation in the public goods game. Considering conditional punishers only take the punishing action when the number of unconditional punishers exceeds a threshold number, we demonstrate that such conditional punishment induces the effect of a double-edged sword on the evolution of cooperation both in well-mixed and structured populations. Specifically, when it is relatively easy for conditional punishers to engage in the punishment activity corresponding to a low threshold value, cooperation can be promoted in comparison with the case without conditional punishment. Whereas when it is relatively difficult for conditional punishers to engage in the punishment activity corresponding to a high threshold value, cooperation is inhibited in comparison with the case without conditional punishment. Moreover, we verify that such double-edged sword effect exists in a wide range of model parameters and can be still observed in other different punishment regimes.
