Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what (if anything) the Fehl et al. (2012) paper1 says about each of the 15 study‐design parameters and whether it reports (a) any actual values used and (b) any systematic variation of that parameter’s effect on punishment’s impact—especially on efficiency. Following that is the required summary (A–D).

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
1. NUMBER OF PLAYERS
• Mentioned? Yes.  
  – The public‐goods (PG) game used subgroups of four; the prisoner’s‐dilemma (PD) game used subgroups of two.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
  – The paper compares pairs (in the PD) vs. groups of four (in the PG), but it does not systematically manipulate different group sizes to analyze how that would affect punishment outcomes. Therefore, no numerical effect sizes tied to varying group size are provided.  
• Any prediction about its effect on punishment’s impact (for efficiency or otherwise)? They do note that punishment was more frequent in the group environment (PG) than in dyads (PD), but they do not provide a formal analysis linking “number of players” to “efficiency.”

2. NUMBER OF ROUNDS
• Mentioned? Yes.  
  – Each “period” of the PG had 1 contribution round followed by 5 punishment rounds (3 periods total). The PD had 5 periods, each with 1 PD round followed by 5 punishment rounds.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
  – The experiment included these fixed numbers of rounds. There is no discussion of how systematically increasing or decreasing rounds would affect punishment or efficiency.  
• Any prediction about its effect? The paper notes that participants did not know how many rounds of punishment or social interaction there would be, and it discusses a “last‐round effect” for punishment investment. However, it does not present a systematic analysis of varying the number of rounds to predict changes in efficiency.

3. IS CHAT ENABLED BETWEEN PLAYERS?
• Mentioned? No.  
  – There was no real‐time communication (chat) mentioned.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any prediction? None.  

4. IS THE CONTRIBUTION “ALL OR NOTHING”?
• Mentioned? Yes.  
  – Both the PG and PD were binary: participants contributed either €1 or €0.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
  – They implemented a binary design but did not compare it with continuous‐contribution versions in the same study.  
• Any prediction about effect on efficiency? None in the paper.

5. IS THE CONTRIBUTION DEFAULT?
• Mentioned? No.  
  – There is no mention of a “default” option for contributions (e.g., automatically contributing unless one opts out).  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any prediction? None.

6. MARGINAL PER CAPITA RETURN (MPCR) OR RELATED MULTIPLIER
• Mentioned? Yes.  
  – The multiplier was 1.6 in both the PG and PD.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any prediction about effect? None. They do not discuss how changing 1.6 to some other factor would alter the result.

7. PUNISHMENT COST TO IMPOSE A SINGLE UNIT
• Mentioned? Yes.  
  – In the PG, assigning 1 “point” of punishment cost the punisher €0.10 and imposed a €0.30 fine on the target (3:1 ratio). In the PD, 1 punishment point cost the punisher €0.50 and fined the target €1.50.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any prediction? No. The paper did not manipulate this cost to see differences in outcomes.

8. PUNISHMENT MAGNITUDE (HOW MUCH THE TARGET LOSES PER UNIT)
• Mentioned? Yes.  
  – In the PG, for each punishment point assigned by the punisher, the target lost thrice that monetary unit (3:1 ratio). In the PD, for each punishment point assigned, the target lost €1.50.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any prediction? None.

9. WHETHER A REWARD IS ENABLED
• Mentioned? No.  
  – No reward mechanism was included in either game.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any prediction? None.

10. REWARD COST TO GRANT A SINGLE UNIT
• Mentioned? No.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any prediction? None.

11. REWARD MAGNITUDE (HOW MUCH THE TARGET GAINS PER UNIT)
• Mentioned? No.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any prediction? None.

12. IS THE NUMBER OF ROUNDS KNOWN TO PLAYERS?
• Mentioned? Yes.  
  – The authors explicitly state that participants did not know how many punishment rounds or how many total rounds there would be.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any prediction? The paper notes that the uncertainty of ending fostered “last‐round” spikes in punishment, but they do not systematically test or quantify how revealing vs. concealing the round number would change the effect on efficiency.

13. ARE PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN?
• Mentioned? Yes.  
  – In the PG, participants saw who contributed and who did not, and also who punished whom and how much, for every punishment round. In the PD, a participant saw whether the partner contributed and likewise saw the partner’s punishment decisions.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any prediction? None.

14. WHEN A PLAYER IS PUNISHED, DO THEY KNOW WHO THE SPECIFIC PUNISHER IS?
• Mentioned? Yes.  
  – The paper states that participants “knew exactly who punished whom with how much.”  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any prediction? None. Although the paper discusses that the visibility of punishment begets vendettas, it does not systematically vary anonymity.

15. WHEN A PLAYER IS REWARDED, DO THEY KNOW THE REWARDER?
• Mentioned? No (no reward condition).  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any prediction? None.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?

• The paper mostly reports contribution rates (cooperation) and punishment/counter‐punishment frequencies, as well as monetary earnings (payoffs). The authors do not compute efficiency as “(actual total payoff) ÷ (maximum possible total payoff).”  
• Hence, although the paper does address “earnings,” it does not explicitly frame them as “group efficiency.” Its main outcome measures are:  
  1) Cooperation level (i.e., proportion contributing),  
  2) Punishment and vendetta patterns,  
  3) Participants’ final earnings (payoffs).  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

• Eight of the 15 appear explicitly in some capacity:  
  1 (Number of players), 2 (Number of rounds), 4 (All‐or‐nothing contributions), 6 (Multiplier), 7 (Punishment cost), 8 (Punishment magnitude), 12 (Whether the number of rounds is known), 13 (Peer outcomes shown), and 14 (Punisher identity revealed).  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?

• In this study, none of the parameters were systematically varied (i.e., manipulated across multiple values in a design specifically to observe changes). Rather, the experiment had fixed settings (e.g., one subgroup size in PG vs. another in PD, a fixed punishment cost, etc.).  
• Consequently, there are no numerical effect sizes or direct predictions in the paper about how changing any of these 15 parameters, one by one, would alter punishment’s effect on efficiency or on any other outcome variable.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

• The paper offers only limited hints:  
  – The comparison between 2‐player (PD) and 4‐player (PG) setups suggests that more players can lead to more frequent punishment and higher rates of counter‐punishment. That in turn can promote cooperation but also reduce individual payoffs (due to vendettas).  
  – Punishment rounds create a “last‐round effect,” suggesting that if participants know a final round is imminent, punishment bursts may occur.  
  – Overall, retaliatory punishment (vendettas) was very costly and likely lowers earnings. One might therefore predict that any parameter increasing the likelihood or severity of vendettas (e.g., larger punishment magnitude or lower anonymity) could decrease efficiency.  
• However, because the paper does not run any systematic variations of these 15 parameters, it does not yield clear or quantitative predictions specific to “efficiency,” and so one must conclude that the evidence to make such predictions is very limited.

Authors: Ozono, H; Jin, N; Watabe, M; Shimizu, K
Author Full Names: Ozono, Hiroki; Jin, Nobuhito; Watabe, Motoki; Shimizu, Kazumi
Article Title: Solving the second-order free rider problem in a public goods game: An experiment using a leader support system
Keywords Plus: SANCTIONING SYSTEM; PUNISHMENT; COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; RECIPROCITY; PROVISION
Abstract: Punishment of non-cooperators-free riders-can lead to high cooperation in public goods games (PGG). However, second-order free riders, who do not pay punishment costs, reduce the effectiveness of punishment. Here we introduce a leader support system, in which one group leader can freely punish group followers using capital pooled through the support of group followers. In our experiment, participants engage in three stages repeatedly: a PGG stage in which followers decide to cooperate for their group; a support stage in which followers decide whether to support the leader; and a punishment stage in which the leader can punish any follower. We compare a support-present condition with a no-support condition, in which there is an external source for the leader's punishment. The results show that punishment occurs more frequently in the support-present condition than the no-support condition. Within the former, both higher cooperation and higher support for a leader are achieved under linkage-type leaders-who punish both non-cooperators and non-supporters. In addition, linkage-type leaders themselves earn higher profits than other leader types because they withdraw more support. This means that leaders who effectively punish followers could increase their own benefits and the second-order free rider problem would be solved.

Instead, it primarily reports (1) the proportion of times the group reaches the step‐level threshold (“success rate”) and (2) average contributions, along with some payoff details. These are not formal efficiency ratios, though higher success on the public good threshold does tend to yield higher average total payoffs.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
     1 (number of players = 5),  
     2 (number of rounds = 14),  
     3 (chat = disallowed),  
     4 (participants choose an integer from 0–10 rather than “all or nothing”),  
     5 (participants freely decide their contribution; no default is given),  
     6 (the “threshold” design implies a fixed payoff of 12 if ≥31 is contributed, but this is not systematically varied),  
     7 and 8 (the centralized mechanism’s cost is 3 to everyone, and the fine is 6 to anyone contributing <6),  
     12 (the number of rounds is known in advance),  
     13 (players see the sum of contributions, but not each peer’s payoff).  
   • None of those parameters are varied systematically except whether the mechanism is on or off (and how it is removed—automatic vs. by vote). The paper does not systematically manipulate any of the other parameters.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when the parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, the only systematic variations are:  
     – Having no centralized sanctioning mechanism (baseline, BL) vs. having one (AR or VR) in rounds 1–7,  
     – Removing it automatically (AR) or by vote (VR) in rounds 8–14.  
   • The paper reports how these variations affect success rates and contributions. There is no discussion of systematically varying the cost or magnitude of punishment, the group size, communication channels, or any other parameter.  

   • Numerical effect sizes (for success rate in providing the public good):  
     – In rounds 1–7:  7% in BL vs. 89% in AR and 87% in VR (Table 1).  
     – In rounds 8–14: 0% in BL vs. 65% in AR and 48% in VR.  

D. Predictions for how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, based solely on this paper  
   • The paper only examines one dimension of punishment (the presence of a centralized mechanism, then its removal). It does not speak to how altering any of the other 15 parameters (e.g., number of players, changing the fine magnitude, enabling rewards, etc.) would systematically affect efficiency or total payoff. Consequently, based on this paper alone, we can say little about other parameters’ influences.  
   • The main lesson the paper furnishes is that having a “strong” centralized punishment mechanism (with a high success rate in enforcing contributions early on) can train or “educate” groups so that when that mechanism is later removed, higher cooperation (and hence higher payoffs) sometimes persists. Voting vs. automatic removal does not improve outcomes; in fact, the group with “automatic removal” maintained higher cooperation on average in the second half.  

   Thus, for most parameters, the paper provides no direct prediction or effect size regarding how they might change the punishment treatment effect on efficiency. Only the on/off presence of the centralized sanctioning mechanism (and how it is removed) is tested.

Article Title: The role of ventromedial prefrontal cortex and temporo-parietal junction in third-party punishment behavior
Author Keywords: tDCS; VMPFC; TPJ; Altruistic punishment; Antisocial punishment
Keywords Plus: DIRECT-CURRENT STIMULATION; NONINVASIVE BRAIN-STIMULATION; ECONOMIC DECISION-MAKING; BIOLOGICAL MARKETS; PAROCHIAL ALTRUISM; NEURAL BASIS; TEMPOROPARIETAL JUNCTION; COSTLY PUNISHMENT; PARTNER CHOICE; SOCIAL NORMS
Abstract: Third parties punish, sacrificing personal interests, offenders who violate either fairness or cooperation norms. This behavior is defined altruistic punishment and the degree of punishment typically increases with the severity of the norm violation. An opposite and apparently paradoxical behavior, namely anti-social punishment, is the tendency to spend own money to punish cooperative or fair behaviors. Previous fMRI studies correlated punishment behavior with increased activation of brain areas belonging to the reward system (e.g. the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, VMPFC), the mentalizing (e.g. the temporoparietal junction, TPJ) and central-executive networks. In the present study, we aimed M investigating the causal role of VMPFC and TPJ in punishment behaviors through the application of anodal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS). Sixty healthy participants were randomly assigned to three tDCS conditions: (1) anodal tDCS over VMPFC, (2) anodal tDCS over right TPJ (rTPJ), (3) sham stimulation. At the end of the stimulation, participants played a third-party punishment game, consisting in viewing a series of fair or unfair monetary allocations between unknown proposers and recipients. Participants were asked whether and how much they would punish the proposers using their own monetary endowment. To test membership effects, proposers and recipients could be either Italian or Chinese. Anodal tDCS over VMPFC increased altruistic punishment behavior whereas anodal tDCS over rTPJ increased anti-social punishment choices compared with sham condition, while membership did not influence participant's choices. Our results support the idea that the two types of punishment behaviors rely upon different brain regions, suggesting that reward and mentalizing systems underlie, respectively, altruistic and anti-social punishment behaviors.

Below is a point‐by‐point analysis of whether, and how, each of the 15 parameters is mentioned or systematically varied in the paper, followed by a four‐part summary (A–D). In keeping with your instructions, all statements refer strictly to the content of the paper. No additional literature or conjecture is introduced.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players
   • Mentioned? The paper describes a “third‐party punishment game” with three roles (dictator, recipient, third‐party punisher), but does not systematically vary the number of players. The only mention of other players is the statement that participants believed they were playing with additional individuals, though the game effectively featured a Dictator (A), a Receiver (B), and a Punisher (C).
   • Effect of varying this parameter? Not discussed. No predictions in the paper about how changing the number of players would alter punishment or efficiency.

2) Number of rounds
   • Mentioned? The paper says that participants played 160 trials of the task, but does not frame these as “rounds” in the sense of systematically varying their number. 
   • Effect of varying this parameter? Not discussed. No predictions offered.

3) Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned? No. This paper does not describe any communication or chat feature among participants.
   • Effect of varying this parameter? Not discussed.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned? The dictator can choose any transfer between 0 and 20 tokens, so it is not “all or nothing.” However, the paper does not systematically vary or test an “all or nothing” contribution format.
   • Effect of varying this parameter? Not discussed.

5) Is the contribution default (do players decide how much of their endowment to move from the public fund back to their hand)?
   • Mentioned? No. The game is described as a variant of the Dictator Game in which the dictator directly chooses how many tokens to give. There is no mention of a “default contribution” mechanic or systematically varying it.
   • Effect of varying this parameter? Not discussed.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not describe any multiplication factor, as it is not a public goods design with an MPCR; it is a third‐party punishment game where transfers are made one‐to‐one.
   • Effect of varying this parameter? Not discussed.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper states that for every two tokens subtracted from the dictator, the punisher must pay one token. This ratio is the fixed “cost” structure. 
   • Systematically varied? No. The cost does not change across conditions; there is no discussion of varying it.

8) Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   • Mentioned? Yes, indirectly. Participants can subtract 2, 4, 6, 8, or 10 tokens, which is the “magnitude” of punishment. 
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not experiment with different punishment magnitudes (it is always the same set of possible subtractions).

9) Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned? The paper focuses exclusively on punishment (there is no reward option in the game). 
   • Effect of varying or introducing rewards? Not discussed.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Mentioned? No. Rewards were not part of the design.
    • Effect of varying this parameter? Not discussed.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)
    • Mentioned? No. Again, no reward mechanism was used in the study.
    • Effect of varying this parameter? Not discussed.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Mentioned? No. The paper does not indicate whether participants knew exactly how many trials (“rounds”) they would play, nor does it vary that factor.
    • Effect of varying this parameter? Not discussed.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?
    • Mentioned? The punisher sees how many tokens the dictator transfers to the receiver. However, the paper does not discuss showing other players’ payoffs in detail, nor is there any systematic variation of what is revealed.
    • Effect of varying this parameter? Not discussed.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Mentioned? No. The paper does not report whether the dictator learns the identity of the punisher, and it does not systematically vary anonymity or identification.
    • Effect of varying this parameter? Not discussed.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Mentioned? Not applicable. The study did not use rewards, so there is no mention of whether the rewarded party sees who rewarded them.
    • Effect of varying this parameter? Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • No. The paper’s dependent variables are:  
     – The binary decision to punish or not (i.e., whether the third party subtracts tokens).  
     – The amount of punishment imposed (i.e., how many tokens are subtracted).  
   • The paper does not use or report “group efficiency,” “total payoff,” or “average payoff” as a central outcome. Instead, it focuses on punishment decisions in fair vs. unfair offers.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned (in some fashion):  
     – (1) Number of players (they mention three roles, though not systematically varied)  
     – (7) Punishment cost (fixed cost of 1 token per 2 tokens deducted)  
     – (8) Punishment magnitude (2, 4, 6, 8, or 10 tokens could be subtracted)  
     – (9–11) Reward not enabled (mentioned implicitly that it is absent).  
   • All other parameters (2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 12, 13, 14, 15) either receive no mention or are not systematically manipulated.  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The paper does not systematically vary any of these parameters. Accordingly, it does not present effect sizes for systematically changing the cost, magnitude, or any other parameter. Its principal manipulation was the site of transcranial direct current stimulation (VMPFC vs. TPJ vs. sham), not any of the 15 parameters above.  

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not discuss efficiency or total payoff and does not vary any of the 15 parameters. Consequently, it does not provide evidence to form predictions about how changes in those parameters would affect punishment’s impact on group efficiency. Virtually no direct guidance for efficiency predictions can be drawn from this text alone.

Authors: Singh, M; Boomsma, JJ
Author Full Names: Singh, Manvir; Boomsma, Jacobus J.
Article Title: Policing and punishment across the domains of social evolution
Keywords Plus: REPRODUCTIVE CONFLICT; WORKER REPRODUCTION; LIFE-HISTORIES; HOST SANCTIONS; BLOOD REVENGE; PONERINE ANT; DOMINANCE; COOPERATION; BEHAVIOR; QUEEN
Abstract: Several decades of research in humans, other vertebrates, and social insects have offered fascinating insights into the dynamics of punishment (and its subset, policing), but authors have only rarely addressed whether there are fundamental joint principles underlying the maintenance of these behaviors. Here we present a punisher/bystander approach rooted in inclusive fitness logic to predict which individuals should take on punishing roles in animal societies. We apply our scheme to societies of eusocial Hymenoptera and nonhuman vertebrate social breeders, and we outline potential extensions for understanding conflict regulation among cells in metazoan bodies and unrelated individuals in human societies. We highlight that: 1) no social unit is expected to express punishment behavior unless it collects positive inclusive fitness benefits that surpass alternative benefits of bystanding; 2) punishment with public good benefits can be maintained through either direct fitness benefits (coercion) or indirect fitness benefits (correction) or both; 3) differences across social systems in the distributions of power, relatedness, and reproductive options drive variation in the extent to which individuals actively punish; and 4) inclusive fitness logic captures many punishment-relevant evolutionary and ecological variables in a single framework that appears to apply across very different types of social arrangements.

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?

   • The paper’s dependent variables (in a broad sense) are: (1) whether punishment is expressed (who punishes, under what conditions), (2) the role of power asymmetries, (3) the extent of conflict or conflict suppression within a group, and (4) how these factors align with inclusive fitness benefits. Authors: Giardini, F
Author Full Names: Giardini, Francesca
Article Title: Deterrence and transmission as mechanisms ensuring reliability of gossip
Author Keywords: Gossip; Reputation; Cooperation; Evolution
Keywords Plus: INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; REPUTATION DYNAMICS; EVOLUTION; COOPERATION; CUES
Abstract: Spreading information about the members of one's group is one of the most universal human behaviors. Thanks to gossip, individuals can acquire the information about their peers without sustaining the burden of costly interactions with cheaters, but they can also create and revise social bonds. Gossip has also several positive functions at the group level, promoting cohesion and norm compliance. However, gossip can be unreliable, and can be used to damage others' reputation or to circulate false information, thus becoming detrimental to people involved and useless for the group. In this work, we propose a theoretical model in which reliability of gossip depends on the joint functioning of two distinct mechanisms. Thanks to the first, i.e., deterrence, individuals tend to avoid informational cheating because they fear punishment and the disruption of social bonds. On the other hand, transmission provides humans with the opportunity of reducing the consequences of cheating through a manipulation of the source of gossip.

       • No. The paper does not discuss whether participants have a default contribution or must actively adjust it.  
   (2) Systematic variation and predicted effect?  
       • No. No predictions are given.  

6. MARGINAL PER CAPITA RETURN (MPCR) OR MULTIPLICATION FACTOR  
   (1) Mentioned?  
       • No. Although the paper mentions “cooperation,” it does not specify a linear public goods or multiplier structure, nor anything about an MPCR.  
   (2) Systematic variation and predicted effect?  
       • No. Nothing on how changing the multiplication factor would change punishment’s effect.  

7. PUNISHMENT COST TO IMPOSE A SINGLE UNIT OF PUNISHMENT  
   (1) Mentioned?  
       • The paper refers to “the possibility of punishing false informers” or “the fear of punishment,” but it never quantifies a cost to the punisher, nor does it describe a per‐unit punishment cost in a typical public goods or lab‐experiment sense.  
   (2) Systematic variation and predicted effect?  
       • No. The paper does not propose or analyze how systematically changing punishment cost would influence outcomes or efficiency.  

8. PUNISHMENT MAGNITUDE (THE COINS DEDUCTED FOR EACH UNIT)  
   (1) Mentioned?  
       • The paper uses the term “punishment” in a general sense (e.g., social exclusion). It does not quantify or model a numeric punishment magnitude.  
   (2) Systematic variation and predicted effect?  
       • No. The paper gives no analytic or empirical result on how punishment magnitude influences any outcome.  

9. WHETHER A REWARD IS ENABLED  
   (1) Mentioned?  
       • No. Reward is not discussed in the paper, which focuses on deterrence based on fear of punishment, not on prosocial reward.  
   (2) Systematic variation and predicted effect?  
       • No. No mention of systematically introducing or removing reward and the effect on behavior.  

10. REWARD COST TO GRANT A SINGLE UNIT OF REWARD  
    (1) Mentioned?  
        • No. The paper does not discuss the cost of reward.  
    (2) Systematic variation and predicted effect?  
        • No. No mention or predictions about this.  

11. REWARD MAGNITUDE (THE COINS AWARDED FOR EACH UNIT OF REWARD)  
    (1) Mentioned?  
        • No. Same as above; reward magnitude is not discussed.  
    (2) Systematic variation and predicted effect?  
        • No. The paper does not explore or predict how reward magnitudes might affect a punishment treatment effect.  

12. IS THE NUMBER OF ROUNDS KNOWN TO PLAYERS (DO THEY KNOW WHEN THE GAME ENDS)?  
    (1) Mentioned?  
        • No. The paper does not reference whether participants know how many rounds remain—there is no mention of an endgame effect.  
    (2) Systematic variation and predicted effect?  
        • No. Nothing is said about how knowledge of round structure would alter punishment impacts.  

13. ARE PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN (DO PLAYERS KNOW HOW MUCH EACH PEER GAINS/LOSES)?  
    (1) Mentioned?  
        • Although the paper is about information transmission, it does not discuss real‐time displays of peer outcomes in an experimental sense.  
    (2) Systematic variation and predicted effect?  
        • No. There is no direct analysis of systematically showing or not showing peer outcomes.  

14. WHEN A PLAYER IS PUNISHED, DO THEY KNOW WHO THE SPECIFIC PUNISHER IS?  
    (1) Mentioned?  
        • The paper discusses being punished by receivers or by the gossiped agent, but not in terms of an explicit game parameter that is turned on or off. It generally notes that punishment can come from multiple sources.  
    (2) Systematic variation and predicted effect?  
        • No. There is no formal discussion of “transparent punisher identity” versus “anonymous punisher.”  

15. WHEN A PLAYER IS REWARDED, DO THEY KNOW WHO THE SPECIFIC REWARDER IS?  
    (1) Mentioned?  
        • No. The paper does not discuss any reward mechanism or whether the identity of a rewarder is transparent.  
    (2) Systematic variation and predicted effect?  
        • No. The paper does not speak to this parameter at all.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY RESPONSES

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper does not use or report “group efficiency” (defined as the ratio of actual total payoff to the maximum possible). It does mention “average payoffs” and “cooperation” in agent‐based simulations and in references to economic games (e.g., higher payoffs associated with the possibility of reliable gossip), but it does not formally label efficiency as a dependent variable.  
   • Its primary focus is on reliability of gossip, how deterrence and transmission contribute to the stability of gossip in human groups, and how false gossip is punished or avoided.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • The paper uses the concept of “punishment” in broad terms (i.e., fear of social exclusion or retaliation), but it does not mention any specific 1–15 parameter (such as “punishment cost,” “punishment magnitude,” “number of players,” “MPCR,” etc.) in a formal or numeric sense. Strictly speaking, none of the 15 parameters are specified or given values in this paper.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The paper does not systematically vary any of these 15 parameters. Therefore, there is no direct empirical or theoretical discussion of how changing any of them would affect a punishment‐treatment impact (whether on efficiency, payoff, or cooperation).  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not provide enough detail to make predictions about public‐goods‐game parameters or how systematically varying them would affect group efficiency under punishment. It discusses deterrence (punishment risk) and transmission (the ability to pass or conceal the source of gossip) as general mechanisms, but not in a way that maps onto the 15 parameters in a typical punishment‐vs.‐no‐punishment public goods experiment. Consequently, there is little or no direct basis in the text for predicting how these parameters or their interactions shape a punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

In short, the Giardini (2011) paper does not address the 15 parameters of typical public goods games with punishment. It focuses instead on theoretical modeling of gossip reliability, emphasizing (1) deterrence (fear of punishment for false gossip) and (2) transmission (the ability to obscure responsibility for gossip) as key mechanisms explaining why gossip persists. Beyond referencing broad ideas of social exclusion as punishment, it does not detail punishment or reward parameters in a manner that would allow predictions about their effect on group efficiency.

Keywords Plus: COORDINATION FAILURE; STRATEGIC UNCERTAINTY; GAMES; SELECTION; EVOLUTION
Abstract: Second-order free riders, who do not owe punishment cost to first-order free riders in public goods games, lead to low cooperation. Previous studies suggest that for stable cooperation, it is critical to have a pool punishment system with second-order punishment, which gathers resources from group members and punishes second-order free riders as well as first-order free riders. In this study, we focus on the priority of punishment. We hypothesize that the pool punishment system that prioritizes second-order punishment is more likely to achieve cooperation than the system that prioritizes first-order punishment, because the former is more likely to obtain sufficient punishment resources. In the experiments, we compare four pool punishment systems: 1To2 (first-order punishment to second-order punishment), 2To1 (second-order punishment to first-order punishment), 1ONLY (first-order punishment only), and 2ONLY (second-order punishment only). We find that the 2To1 and 2ONLY systems can receive more support than the 1To2 and 1ONLY systems and only the 2To1 system can achieve high cooperation. However, the effect of priority of second-order punishment is observed only when the punishment ratio (PR) is low (Experiment 1), not high (Experiment 2), in which the punishment resource is relatively abundant.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter analysis of what the paper says (or does not say) about each of the 15 game‐design parameters and whether the paper reports any systematic variation of that parameter, along with any stated or implied effects on punishment or other outcomes. Throughout, keep in mind that the paper itself does not use or report “efficiency” (actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff) as a dependent variable; instead, it tracks outcomes such as total PGG (public goods) contribution, total support for the punishment system, group profit, and the punishment system’s surplus.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
• Mentioned? Yes. In all experiments, each group has four members.  
• Systematically varied? No. The paper uses groups of four throughout and does not vary group size.  
• Any predicted effect on punishment treatment (for efficiency or any other outcome)? No. The paper does not discuss how changing the number of players might affect punishment or any dependent variable.

2) Number of rounds  
• Mentioned? Yes. All groups play 15 repeated periods (rounds).  
• Systematically varied? No. The study always uses 15 rounds.  
• Any predicted effect on punishment treatment? No. Although the paper notes that behavior can change in the final (15th) period, it does not systematically manipulate the number of rounds nor make predictions about varying it.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
• Mentioned? No. There is no mention anywhere in the paper of allowing discussion or chat among participants.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any predicted effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Mentioned? Indirectly: The paper explicitly states that each player can contribute anywhere from 0 to 20 tokens in the PGG, in increments of 1. Thus contributions are not restricted to “all or nothing.”  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any predicted effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

5) Is the contribution default (where players decide how much to move from the public fund back to their hand)?  
• Mentioned? No. Players simply decide how many tokens to contribute out of 20, from 0 to 20.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any predicted effect? Not discussed.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor  
• Mentioned? The PGG multiplier is a constant 1.6 and is not varied. However, the paper does systematically vary the “punishment ratio” (PR), which multiplies the total tokens provided to the punishment fund by either 1 (in Experiment 1) or 3 (in Experiment 2).  
• Systematically varied? Yes, but only in the sense that the authors change PR = 1 vs. PR = 3 (Experiment 1 vs. Experiment 2). The PGG’s own multiplier (1.6) is not varied, but the punishment resource multiplier (the “punishment ratio”) is.  
• Any predicted effect on punishment treatment? Yes. Under PR=1, prioritizing second‐order punishment (“2To1” in the paper) leads to significantly higher cooperation levels in the PGG compared to prioritizing first‐order punishment (“1To2”); under PR=3, both priority orders achieve similarly high support and cooperation. Numerically (from Figures 2 and 3 in the paper), in Experiment 1 (PR=1), the “2To1” condition shows total PGG contributions around 60–65 tokens in the second half of the game, while “1To2” is lower (around 40). In Experiment 2 (PR=3), the difference between “2To1” and “1To2” disappears, and both lead to similarly high PGG contributions.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Mentioned? The system uses up as many tokens as it deducts from a punished player, but there is no separate parameter (like “1 token for the punisher to remove 3 tokens from the target,” etc.).  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any predicted effect? Not discussed.

8) Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
• Mentioned? The pool punishment system reduces a free‐rider’s tokens down to zero (if enough punishment resources exist); it is effectively a 1:1 drain on the punishment fund for each coin deducted. That was not varied.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any predicted effect? Not discussed.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
• Mentioned? No. The study involves only punishment; there is no mention of any reward mechanism.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any predicted effect? Not discussed.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Mentioned? No.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any predicted effect? Not discussed.

11) Reward magnitude (coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
• Mentioned? No.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any predicted effect? Not discussed.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
• Mentioned? Yes. Participants were explicitly told that the game would be repeated exactly 15 times.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any predicted effect on punishment treatment? No. The paper does not compare “known vs. unknown” horizon.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?  
• Mentioned? The paper states that players see who is punished in a given round and by how much, and also see the PGG results at the end of each period.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any predicted effect? Not discussed beyond noting that participants know who was punished.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• Mentioned? The punishment is administered by a central “pool system,” so there is no information about any specific individual punisher. The paper does not discuss systematically varying whether the punisher’s identity is revealed.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any predicted effect? Not discussed.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
• Mentioned? No, because there is no reward in this design.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any effect? Not applicable.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY RESPONSE

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
• The paper does not report “efficiency” in the sense of “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff.” Instead, it examines:  
  – Total PGG contribution (sum of contributions to the public good).  
  – Total support for the punishment system (how many tokens participants devote to punishment).  
  – Group profit (sum of tokens retained after the PGG and any punishments).  
  – Surplus of the system (total punishment tokens provided minus total tokens spent on punishment).  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Mentioned in some form (even if only a fixed value) are:  
  1) Number of players (fixed at 4).  
  2) Number of rounds (fixed at 15).  
  6) Multiplication factor for the PGG (fixed at 1.6) and the punishment ratio (PR), which is systematically varied (1 vs. 3).  
  12) Players know there are 15 rounds.  
  13) Partial outcome information (punishment feedback) is shown.  
• The remaining parameters (3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15) are either not mentioned at all or simply do not appear as design variations in the paper.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• Only one parameter is truly “systematically varied” and analyzed in detail: the punishment ratio (PR = 1 vs. 3). The paper discusses how that variation modulates the impact of “priority of second‐ vs. first‐order punishment” on outcomes such as PGG contribution and group profit. Strictly speaking, none of the other 15 listed parameters are systematically varied.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper, what would they be?  
• The paper does not discuss efficiency per se, nor does it systematically manipulate 14 of the 15 listed parameters. Its only systematic manipulation is the punishment ratio (which they call PR).  
• From the findings, one might guess that when the system’s punishment resources become more abundant (i.e., PR is larger), any added punishment regime may more reliably sustain cooperation or reduce free riding. If resources are scarce (low PR), then prioritizing second‐order punishment can induce higher cooperation—but the paper does not translate this directly into “efficiency” (they instead note that group profit may remain relatively low due to high punishment costs).  
• For the remaining parameters (e.g., number of players, presence of chat, etc.), the paper does not offer any explicit predictions or data. Hence, little or no prediction on how they influence efficiency can be made solely from this text.
reference_APA: Ozono, Hiroki, Kamijo, Yoshio & Shimizu, Kazumi (2017). Punishing second-order free riders before first-order free riders: The effect of pool punishment priority on cooperation. SCIENTIFIC REPORTS.

Abstract: Punishment widely exists in social and biological systems and it has been proved to be an effective way to promote cooperation in evolutionary game in previous work. In this paper, we introduce a new mechanism of punishment that the punishment fine can be multiplied if there are several punishers decide to punish a defector, which leads to a low payoff of defector and promotes the level of cooperation. This mechanism can simulate group hunt which is common in natural animal world, for example, in biological system, a pack of animal in which every individual cooperates with each other can hunt a prey which is stronger than an individual inside the pack. A pack of wolves can make the process of hunt easier than the hunt implemented by a lone wolf, inspired by which we construct this mechanism of punishment to simulate the group punishment. Interestingly, we find that this mechanism can dramatically promotes the level of cooperation when we compare the simulation result with traditional evolutionary public good game. Below, each of the 15 design parameters is treated in turn.

For every parameter I state  
(1) whether the paper mentions it and, if so, what concrete value(s) are used;  
(2) whether the authors **systematically vary** that parameter and report how this changes the *punishment-treatment effect* (i.e., the difference between “with punishment” and “without punishment”).  Whenever the paper contains a numerical pattern that can be read directly from a figure or table I reproduce the approximate effect-size.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
(1) Mentioned. A square lattice of size 100 × 100 is used, so N = 10 000.  
(2) Never varied; no results about how changing N alters the punishment effect.

2. Number of rounds (length of the game)  
(1) The evolutionary simulation is run for 20 000 Monte-Carlo steps (MCS) and pay-offs are averaged over the final 5 000 MCS.  
(2) Not varied; no results.

3. Chat enabled?  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) No discussion.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule?  
(1) Yes. “Cooperators contribute 1 … defectors contribute nothing.”  
(2) Fixed; not varied; no discussion of its impact on punishment.

5. Contribution default / endowment recall?  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) No discussion.

6. Marginal per–capita return / multiplication factor (MPCR, called r or r/G)  
(1) Mentioned and **systematically varied** from r = 0 to 5 (Fig. 1 & Fig. 3). Group size G = 5, so r/G ranges from 0 to 1.0.  
(2) Effect on punishment treatment:

    • Fig. 1 compares β = 0 (no punishment) with β = 0.2, 0.5, 1.0.  
      – Without punishment (β = 0) cooperation starts to appear only once r/G ≈ 0.75.  
      – With β = 1.0 the same onset occurs already at r/G ≈ 0.40.  
      – Thus, for any r, the *difference* in cooperation between “punishment” and “no-punishment” becomes larger the smaller r/G is.  
    • Fig. 3 (contour plot) shows that increasing r monotonically increases the final co-operation fraction for every positive β, but again the incremental benefit of punishment is largest at intermediate r.

No efficiency numbers are supplied, only the fraction of cooperators.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
(1) Defined but not independently parameterised. Cost to each punisher is β·N_D/N_P.  
(2) Because cost is completely determined by β, it is not varied separately from β; no isolated results.

8. Punishment magnitude to the target  
(1) Controlled by the single parameter β.  
(2) **Systematically varied** (β = 0, 0.2, 0.5, 1.0).  
    • Fig. 1: At r/G = 0.6, increasing β from 0 → 0.2 → 0.5 → 1.0 raises the co-operation fraction from ≈0 → 0.30 → 0.55 → 1.0.  
    • Fig. 2 (time series at r = 3.75): steady-state co-operation: β = 0.2 → 0.40; β = 0.5 → 0.55; β = 1.0 → 0.80.  
Hence, higher β consistently magnifies the punishment treatment effect.

9. Reward enabled?  
(1) Not present.  
(2) No discussion.

10. Reward cost  
(1) Not present.  
(2) —  

11. Reward magnitude  
(1) Not present.  
(2) —  

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
(1) Not meaningful in an infinite-horizon evolutionary model; not mentioned.  
(2) —  

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) —  

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) —  

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) —  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Is group efficiency used as a dependent variable?  
No. The paper’s sole outcome variable is the fraction of cooperators ρ_c (sometimes over time, sometimes at equilibrium). Pay-offs are calculated internally for strategy updating but are never reported as “total payoff”, “average payoff”, or “efficiency”.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
Six: (1) number of players, (2) number of rounds/MCS, (4) all-or-nothing contribution rule, (6) MPCR r, (7) punishment cost (implicitly via β), (8) punishment magnitude β.

C. For how many parameters is their effect on the punishment treatment effect *systematically varied*?  
Two: parameter 6 (MPCR r) and parameter 8 (punishment magnitude β).  
Neither efficiency nor any other pay-off-based measure is analysed; only the co-operation rate.

D. Predictions that can be made (and their limitations)  
• Increasing β (punishment magnitude & cost) strongly increases the positive effect of punishment on co-operation; at β ≈ 1, full co-operation is reached in most of the explored r-range.  
• Increasing MPCR r also increases co-operation, but the marginal benefit of adding punishment is largest at low–to-moderate r.  
• Because efficiency is not reported, the only inference one can hazard is that, if total pay-off were positively (and roughly linearly) related to the number of cooperators, then higher β and higher r would both raise efficiency, with β having the larger incremental influence.  
• No statements can be made about any of the remaining 13 parameters (or about interactions other than r × β), because the paper provides no evidence whatsoever on them.

In short, the paper allows reasonably confident qualitative predictions for just two parameters (r and β) and provides no leverage for the other thirteen.

PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER REVIEW
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned: Yes. Each group has 6 players (3 “near-site” and 3 “far-site”).  
   (2) Systematically varied? No. No statements or data on how changing the group size would alter the punishment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Mentioned: Yes. Exactly 30 periods; this is common knowledge.  
   (2) Varied? No. The paper only notes that punishment spikes in period 30; it does not explore other horizon lengths.

3. Chat enabled?  
   (1) Mentioned: No. No in-game communication is ever allowed.  
   (2) Varied? No.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
   (1) Mentioned: Indirectly. Emissions are continuous from 0 to 125, so the rule is *not* all-or-nothing.  
   (2) Varied? No.

5. Contribution default (endowment automatically contributed)?  
   (1) Not mentioned.  
   (2) Not varied.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   (1) Not used. Instead payoffs come from a quadratic benefit function and heterogeneous transfer coefficients (Tf = 0.24, Tn = 0.36).  
   (2) Not varied, and no prediction is given about changing them.

7. Punishment cost (to punisher)  
   (1) Mentioned: 0.5 Experimental \$ per deduction point. Chosen to create a 3:1 fine-to-cost ratio.  
   (2) Not varied. The authors *speculate* that “stronger punishment may be needed,” but offer no data or quantified prediction.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine suffered by target)  
   (1) Mentioned: 1.5 Experimental \$ per point.  
   (2) Not varied; no predictive statements on varying it.

9. Reward enabled?  
   (1) Mentioned: No. Rewards are never available.  
   (2) Not varied.

10. Reward cost  
    N/A.

11. Reward magnitude  
    N/A.

12. Are number of rounds known?  
    (1) Yes – 30 rounds announced in advance.  
    (2) Not varied. Authors merely observe an end-period punishment spike.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    (1) Yes. After each period subjects see the exact emissions of the two neighbors at their own location, total location emissions, total ambient pollution, own payoff, and (when applicable) total punishment received/assigned.  
    (2) Not varied. No statement on altering the information display.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
    (1) Yes, indirectly: the paper states that punishment is *anonymous*; targets only see the total points received, not who sent them.  
    (2) Not varied.

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
    N/A – no rewards.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables used  
   • Efficiency (realized surplus ÷ 109.2 maximum) – the paper’s main welfare measure.  
   • Individual pollution (emission choice).  
   • Environmental damages (aggregate ambient pollution).  
   • Punishment behaviour (points assigned/received).  
   These variables are distinct: higher contributions (lower emissions) can raise efficiency, but efficiency is also reduced by dead-weight losses from punishment itself – which is why the study finds that punishment may lower variance without raising efficiency.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even *mentioned*?  
   8 of 15 are mentioned in some form: 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14.  
   The remaining 7 (3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 15 and the “default” aspect of 5) receive no mention.

C. For how many parameters does the paper *systematically vary the parameter and report its impact on the punishment treatment effect*?  
   Zero.  The only factor that is varied is the presence/absence of a **group-tax** instrument, which is outside the list of 15 parameters.  Consequently the paper contains **no effect sizes** describing how any of the 15 parameters moderate the impact of punishment on efficiency or any other outcome.

D. Predictions one can make about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment-efficiency link, based solely on this paper  
   • Because nothing is experimentally varied, the paper provides almost no leverage for forecasting how changes in these parameters would alter the punishment treatment effect.  
   • The authors *speculate* (without data) that “stronger punishment” (i.e., different values for parameters 7 & 8) might be necessary in their heterogeneous, non-linear environment.  
   • They also note that the *known* final period induces high “emotional” punishment, hinting that parameter 12 (time horizon) could matter, but again no systematic evidence is supplied.  
   • For all other parameters the paper is silent; any prediction would go beyond the evidence.

In short, the study demonstrates that in a 6-person, 30-round game with a 0.5-to-1.5 punishment cost/fine structure, allowing punishment raises efficiency only marginally (≈ +2.5 pp without the tax, ≈ +3.2 pp with the tax) and never significantly; but it offers **no data at all** on whether altering any of the 15 design parameters would strengthen, weaken, or reverse that punishment effect.

   • Mentioned?

   • Mentioned?

   • Systematically varied, with predictions for punishment effect?  
     – No mention.

5) Is the contribution default (do players decide how much of their endowment to move)?  
   • Mentioned?

   • Mentioned?

     – No mention.

8) Punishment magnitude (how many coins are deducted from the target per unit)  
   • Mentioned?

     – The paper systematically varies P_A and P_B in the numerical examples and shows how different values lead to different stable equilibria of cooperation vs. noncooperation.      – No mention.

Summary of Findings

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?

Instead, it focuses on whether enterprise and university/research‐institute populations stabilize on “positive cooperation” or “negative cooperation.” Government’s payoffs are also tracked. However, there is no explicit measure or discussion of group efficiency in the sense typically used in public‐goods experiments.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

One could say that “reward enabled” (parameter 9) is implicitly modeled as part of the financial‐intervention scenario, but there is no separate “reward on/off” parameter. All other parameters in the list (for example, number of players, number of rounds, chat, or whether punishers are identified) do not appear in the paper.

   • The authors systematically vary P_A, P_B (punishment magnitudes) and f_A, f_B (reward magnitudes), but only with respect to whether cooperation eventually stabilizes; they do not measure “efficiency” or a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Thus, although they do systematically change those parameters, they do not do so in a way that maps onto the standard notion of “punishment treatment effect” used in many public‐goods‐game experiments, and they do not measure group efficiency.

Consequently, based on this paper alone, one can make little to no prediction about how systematically varying those 15 parameters would affect efficiency in a public‐goods‐game sense.

     2) More extensive peer monitoring (bigger z) makes the threat of collective punishment more credible, thus raising payoffs and enabling a more “efficient” outcome in the sense of sustaining high effort.

   • Discussed? The authors implement a payoff matrix with R = 1, P = S = 0, and T = b (> 1). Hence “b” can be considered analogous to the “temptation to defect” or “relevant multiplication” in other PD/public‐goods contexts.  
   • Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment? Yes, they systematically vary b roughly in the range 1.05 to 2.0 and show phase diagrams (Figs. 4–6) illustrating how b interacts with punishment probabilities to determine whether full cooperation or full defection ultimately prevails. The authors do measure final fraction of cooperators and average payoff, but they do not measure or report any “efficiency” ratio. No numeric “effect size” on efficiency is given; rather, they show transitions to all‐cooperator or all‐defector states for different values of b.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussed? Yes; it is fixed at 1 payoff unit to the punisher.  
   • Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment? No. The authors do not analyze different punishment‐cost levels.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from a punished player)
   • Discussed? Yes; it is fixed at 3 payoff units lost by the punished player.  
   • Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment? No.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussed? No, not in the simulations. The authors focus solely on punishment, though they briefly mention that other authors have studied reward mechanisms.  
   • Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment? No.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Discussed? Not applicable (no reward).  
   • Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment? No.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded)
   • Discussed? Not applicable (no reward).  
   • Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment? No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
   • Discussed? No.  
   • Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment? No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see others’ payoffs)?
   • Discussed? The model has each player compare payoffs with one neighbor during the update step, but there is no explicit mention of controlling or systematically varying how much payoff information is revealed.  
   • Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment? No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Discussed? No.  
   • Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment? No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Discussed? Not applicable, as no reward mechanism is implemented.  
   • Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Dependent variables used in the paper and differences among them  
   The paper does not use the term “group efficiency” or measure total payoff relative to a maximum possible payoff. Instead, it treats (1) the fraction of cooperators (sometimes called the average level of cooperation) and (2) the average payoff per individual as the key outcomes, often showing which stable state (all‐C or all‐D) emerges. The authors do note “maximum payoff” in the sense of what a fully cooperative population could earn, but they do not present it as an efficiency ratio. Hence the main dependent variables are:  
   • Fraction of cooperators in the population (or final state: all C vs. all D).  
   • Average (or mean) payoff in the population.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   Four parameters are explicitly mentioned:  
   (1) Number of players (Parameter 1) – set to N=1000 (not varied).  
   (2) Temptation to defect b (akin to a multiplication factor, Parameter 6) – systematically varied.  
   (3) Punishment cost (Parameter 7) – fixed at 1 payoff unit.  
   (4) Punishment magnitude (Parameter 8) – fixed at 3 payoff units.  
   The remaining eleven parameters are not mentioned in the paper’s modeling or analysis.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss systematic variation of their effect on the “punishment treatment effect” for any dependent variable?  
   Only parameter 6 (temptation to defect b) is systematically varied, and the results are shown with and without social/nonsocial punishment. The paper reports how changes in b, together with different punishment probabilities, push the final outcome to all cooperation or all defection, and how this influences average payoff. No other parameter is tested through a systematic range of values.

D. Predictions for the influence of these 15 parameters and their interactions on punishment’s effect on efficiency, based solely on the paper  
   The paper does not analyze efficiency as you define it, so it provides no direct numeric effect sizes on how each parameter would shift actual payoffs relative to a fully cooperative maximum.  
   • The authors do show that increasing the temptation to defect (b) can worsen cooperation (and thus lower eventual average payoffs) unless social punishment is strong enough.  
   • Punishment cost and magnitude remain fixed, so there is no indication of how varying them would change efficiency.  
   • The other parameters—from group size and number of rounds to information display and reward—are either absent or unvaried in this study. Consequently, the paper provides little to no basis for predicting how those parameters would shape the effect of punishment on efficiency.  

In short, because the article focuses on fraction of cooperators and average payoff (rather than total‐payoff‐to‐its‐maximum ratio), the paper gives no direct discussion of how systematically varying the 15 listed parameters would affect “efficiency” in the specific sense you require.

Below I go through the 15 design parameters one-by-one.  
For each parameter I state  

• whether the paper ever mentions it (and, if so, the value that is actually used), and  
• whether the authors report what happens when the parameter is systematically varied and how that influences the *punishment‐treatment effect* (i.e., the difference between a condition with peer punishment and the baseline without it).  
When numbers can be read straight off a figure I note the approximate effect size; otherwise I simply record the qualitative direction that the authors state or plot.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned?  Yes.  They label the population size n and put the agents on a scale-free network, but the numerical value is never given.  
   (2) Systematically varied?  No.  No predictions or data on how changing n alters the impact of punishment.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Mentioned?  Only implicitly: the simulation runs for “time steps”.  
   (2) Systematically varied?  No.

3. Chat enabled?  
   (1) Not part of the model.  
   (2) No discussion.

4. All-or-nothing contributions?  
   (1) Yes.  Cooperators always contribute the full endowment (c = 10); defectors contribute 0.  
   (2) Not varied, so no prediction about its effect on punishment.

5. Contribution default / endowment kept unless moved?  
   (1) Not in the model.  
   (2) No discussion.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor of the public good  
   (1) Yes.  They call it the enhancement factor r and fix it at r = 0.3 for *all* reported simulations.  
   (2) Not varied, so no statement about how r would moderate the punishment treatment effect (the authors merely note that even with a small r, punishment can push contributions up to the maximum).

7. Punishment cost to the imposer  
   (1) Yes.  Labeled s (“penalty factor”).  
       Typical values in the figures span roughly s = 0.5 … 2.5 (exact tick marks are not printed).  
   (2) Systematically varied?  Yes (Fig. 1a for IDR; Fig. 4 for CDR).  
       Effect: Higher s ⇒ larger *punishment treatment effect* on contribution.  
       – IDR, Fig. 1a: raising s from ≈0.5 to ≈2.5 moves steady-state mean contribution from ≈2/10 up to 10/10 (≈+8 units).  
       – CDR, Fig. 4 shows the same monotone increase on the s–k heat-map.  
       Efficiency is not reported, so no efficiency effect can be extracted.

8. Punishment magnitude received by the target  
   (1) Yes.  The multiplication factor k (each punishment costs the punisher s and removes k · s from the target).  
       Values tried: k = 1,2,3.  
   (2) Systematically varied?  Yes (Fig. 1b, Fig. 4).  
       Effect: Higher k ⇒ stronger punishment treatment effect on contribution.  
       – IDR, Fig. 1b: k from 1→3 raises the final contribution roughly from ≈3/10 to 10/10.  
       – CDR, Fig. 4: same monotone pattern.  
       No efficiency data.

9. Reward enabled?  
   (1) Yes.  Separate *reward‐only* simulations are run (Fig. 2).  
   (2) Systematically varied?  They compare “reward only” to “punishment only” but do *not* combine them, so there is no systematic manipulation of a “reward ON / OFF” factor inside a punishment treatment.  
       What we can glean: replacing punishment by reward also raises contributions, but the text says “punishment is marginally more effective than reward.”

10. Reward cost to rewarder  
    (1) Same parameter s when the model is run in “reward” mode.  
    (2) Varied in Fig. 2a.  Higher s again leads to higher contributions under reward, but this says nothing about the punishment treatment effect.

11. Reward magnitude earned by target  
    (1) Same parameter k, varied in Fig. 2b.  
    (2) Same comment as for #10.

12. Do players know the number of rounds?  
    Not in the model – no mention.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    Not modelled – no mention.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
    Not modelled – no mention.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
    Not modelled – no mention.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used  
   – The paper primarily reports *average contribution* over time.  
   – Payoff is discussed in equations but no payoff or efficiency results are plotted.  
   – Therefore *group efficiency* (total or average payoff relative to the maximum) is *not* used as an outcome in the reported results.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   8 of 15 (1,2,4,6,7,8,9,10/11).  Parameters 3,5,12,13,14,15 are completely absent.

C. For how many parameters does the paper *systematically vary* them and link that variation to the punishment treatment effect?  
   Only 2 parameters in the punishment domain:  
   – Punishment cost s (#7)  
   – Punishment magnitude k (#8)  
   Both are varied for IDR and CDR and shown to elevate contributions as they increase.  
   (Strictly speaking the authors also vary the share of punishers p_T and the sanction threshold p_S, but those are not on your 15-item list.)

D. What predictions can be made – *restricted to the information in this paper* – about how the 15 parameters and their interactions will influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?

   – Because efficiency itself is never measured, the only safe prediction is via the proxy “higher contributions should mechanically raise efficiency whenever r > 0”.  
   – From the parameters the paper *does* study we can therefore say:  
       • Larger punishment cost to the punisher (s) is predicted to *increase* the punishment treatment effect on efficiency (through higher contributions).  
       • Larger punishment magnitude to the target (k) is predicted to *increase* the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.  
       • A higher fraction of potential punishers/rewarders (p_T, though not on the 15-list) or a lower collective threshold (p_S) would have the same qualitative impact.  
   – For all other parameters (1-6,9-15) the paper provides no empirical or simulated evidence, so no prediction can be made strictly from this source.

In short, the paper tells us that making punishment harsher (either by raising what it costs the punished or by letting more people mete it out) pushes contributions to the maximum, which would in turn push efficiency up, but it is silent about how any of the other design features would moderate that effect.
reference_APA: Baker, F & Rachlin, H (2002). Teaching and learning in a probabilistic prisoner's dilemma. BEHAVIOURAL PROCESSES.

Abstract: Centralized sanctioning institutions have been shown to emerge naturally through social learning, displace all other forms of punishment and lead to stable cooperation. However, this result provokes a number of questions. If centralized sanctioning is so successful, then why do many highly authoritarian states suffer from low levels of cooperation? Why do states with high levels of public good provision tend to rely more on citizen-driven peer punishment? Here, we consider how corruption influences the evolution of cooperation and punishment. Below, “the paper” always refers to Abdallah et al. (2014) “Corruption drives the emergence of civil society.”  
The authors study an evolutionary‐game simulation of a Public-Goods Game (PGG) that includes peer–punishers, pool-punishers, corruptors, and (in a later extension) hybrid punishers.  The main outcome variables the authors actually report are (i) the stationary proportions of the different strategy types and (ii) the implied level of “cooperation” (share of individuals who contribute c to the PGG).  Efficiency (total payoff divided by the cooperative optimum) is never reported.

PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1. Number of players in the group (N)  
   • Mentioned: Yes.  Baseline simulation N = 5; population size M = 100.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  N is held fixed.  No effect size is reported for varying N.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned: No.  The model runs for S = 100,000 imitation events, but this is not interpreted as a finite, known number of game rounds.  No systematic variation.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Not mentioned.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution?  
   • Yes.  Players either contribute the fixed amount c or 0.  No variation: contribution is always binary.

5. Contribution default / endowment moved back?  
   • Not mentioned.

6. MPCR (multiplication factor r)  
   • Mentioned: r = 3.0 in all simulations.  
   • Not varied.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit (peer-punishers’ γ; pool-punishers’ G)  
   • Mentioned: γ = 0.7, G = 0.7 in baseline.  
   • Not systematically varied in the main text, although the ESM states that results are “robust” to changing γ.  No numerical effect sizes.

8. Punishment magnitude (β for peer; B for pool)  
   • Mentioned and SYSTEMATICALLY VARIED.  B is the key policy lever in the paper.  
   • Effect reported (Figure 2a):  
     – Low B (<(M-1)/(N-1)G ≈ 17.5 when M = 100, N = 5, G = 0.7): Peer-punishers ≈ 93 % of the population; corruptors ≈ 1 %; cooperation high.  
     – High B (e.g. B = 7 in text; Figure 1c, 2a “strong punishment”): Pool-punishers 35 %, corruptors 19 %, peer-punishers 10 %, defectors-loners increase; cooperation declines.  
   • Qualitative conclusion: Increasing B (the severity of second-order centralized punishment) eventually lowers cooperation once corruption is possible.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Not mentioned.

10. Reward cost  
    • Not mentioned.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Not mentioned.

12. Finite horizon known to players?  
    • Not applicable.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Not discussed.

14. Punisher identity revealed?  
    • Not discussed.

15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
    • Not discussed.


----------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
   • Efficiency (total or average payoff) is NOT used.  
   • The paper reports (i) stationary frequencies of strategies and (ii) the resulting share of cooperative actions.  “Cooperation” ≠ “efficiency”; the authors never compute total pay-offs relative to the cooperative maximum.

B. Parameters the paper mentions (any value given): 1, 4, 6, 7, 8.  That is 5 of 15.

C. Parameters whose *systematic variation* is analyzed for their impact on the treatment effect of punishment: only parameter 8 (punishment magnitude B).  So 1 of 15.

D. Predictions one can make about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency, based solely on this paper:

   – Punishment magnitude B: If corruption is possible, higher B ultimately *reduces* cooperation and would therefore reduce efficiency.  
   – Presence or absence of corruption/hybrid strategies (not in the 15 parameters) mediates this effect.  
   – For all other listed parameters, the paper provides no evidence or discussion from which to infer how changing them would alter the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.  Any prediction beyond B would be speculative.

In short, aside from showing that very severe centralized punishment backfires when bribery is possible, the paper offers little guidance on how the 15 experimental design parameters would influence the efficiency impact of a punishment treatment.

Abstract: Altruistic punishment, which occurs when an individual incurs a cost to punish in response to unfairness or a norm violation, may play a role in perpetuating cooperation.
