• whether the paper even mentions the parameter and, if so, what concrete value(s) or description are given;  
• whether the paper presents evidence or arguments about how *systematically varying* that parameter would change the *punishment-treatment effect* (the difference in outcomes between a baseline game and a punishment game).  
When the paper is silent, I say so explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  YES, indirectly.  The review distinguishes “second-party” (2-player) and “third-party” (3-player) punishment.  
   • Systematic-variation prediction?  NO.  The paper does not compare punishment effects across different group sizes or provide any quantitative effect size.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  NO.  All tasks reviewed are one-shot exchanges (ultimatum game, dictator game, trust game).  
   • Systematic-variation prediction?  NO.

3. Chat enabled between players  
   • Mentioned?  NO.  
   • Prediction?  NO.

4. All-or-nothing contribution decision  
   • Mentioned?  NO (and the paper never discusses contribution stages at all).  
   • Prediction?  NO.

5. Contribution default / endowment-back choice  
   • Mentioned?  NO.  
   • Prediction?  NO.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  NO.  
   • Prediction?  NO.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   • Mentioned?  YES, generically.  The review repeatedly calls punishment “costly” and states that “participants forgo a monetary reward to punish.”  No numerical values are supplied.  
   • Systematic-variation prediction?  NO.  The authors do not report how changing the cost coefficient alters behavior, neural activity, or efficiency.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from the target per unit)  
   • Mentioned?  YES, generically (e.g., “reducing the norm violator’s payout,” “the impact of the punishment itself on the opponent”).  No exact magnitudes are given.  
   • Systematic-variation prediction?  NO.

9. Reward enabled  
   • Mentioned?  YES.  Several cited studies compare “punishment” and “reward” blocks, but the review never analyses how merely toggling reward on/off changes group outcomes.  
   • Systematic-variation prediction?  NO.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   • Mentioned?  NO numerical specification, no discussion of varying these parameters.  
   • Systematic-variation prediction?  NO.

12. Is the number of rounds common knowledge?  
   • Mentioned?  NO.  
   • Prediction?  NO.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Mentioned?  NO explicit statement.  (UG and DG inherently reveal an offer size, but the paper never treats visibility as an experimental factor.)  
   • Prediction?  NO.

14. Punisher identity revealed  
   • Mentioned?  NO.  
   • Prediction?  NO.

15. Rewarder identity revealed  
   • Mentioned?  NO.  
   • Prediction?  NO.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables actually used in the paper  
   • The review is about *neural activation* (BOLD, PET, electrophysiology) and *behavioral decisions* such as “reject unfair offer,” “amount invested in punishment,” or “acceptance rate of unfair offers.”  
   • *Group efficiency (total payoff / maximum possible payoff)* is never measured or analyzed.  Thus the dependent variables differ fundamentally from efficiency: they track individual neural or choice outcomes, not collective payoffs.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   • 4 parameters receive any mention at all:  
     (1) Number of players (2 vs 3)  
     (7) Cost to punish (qualitative)  
     (8) Punishment magnitude (qualitative)  
     (9) Whether a reward option exists  
   • The other 11 parameters are completely absent.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* that parameter on any punishment-treatment effect (for any dependent variable)?  
   • Zero.  No tables, figures, or text provide effect sizes or even verbal predictions that “if X rises, the punishment effect on Y will increase/decrease.”

D. What predictions can be made—*solely on the basis of this paper*—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment-treatment effect on *efficiency*?  
   • The paper gives essentially no basis for quantitative or even qualitative predictions about efficiency.  Its entire focus is on neural mechanisms underlying the individual decision to punish, not on group-level payoffs. In short, the neuroscience review is almost entirely orthogonal to the public-goods-game design parameters listed and provides no systematic evidence or estimates that would help forecast the punishment treatment’s impact on group efficiency.

Abstract: The field of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is going through a period of great expectations, introducing a certain level of anxiety in research, business and also policy. This anxiety is further energised by an AI race narrative that makes people believe they might be missing out. Whether real or not, a belief in this narrative may be detrimental as some stake-holders will feel obliged to cut corners on safety precautions, or ignore societal consequences just to win. Starting from a baseline model that describes a broad class of technology races where winners draw a significant benefit compared to others (such as AI advances, patent race, pharmaceutical technologies), we investigate here how positive (rewards) and negative (punishments) incentives may beneficially influence the outcomes. We uncover conditions in which punishment is either capable of reducing the development speed of unsafe participants or has the capacity to reduce innovation through over-regulation. Alternatively, we show that, in several scenarios, rewarding those that follow safety measures may increase the development speed while ensuring safe choices. Moreover, in the latter regimes, rewards do not suffer from the issue of over-regulation as is the case for punishment. Overall, our findings provide valuable insights into the nature and kinds of regulatory actions most suitable to improve safety compliance in the contexts of both smooth and sudden technological shifts.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter inventory of what this particular paper (Han et al. 2021, PLOS ONE) does or does not say, followed by the requested four‐part summary (A–D). Throughout, note that the paper’s focus is on a 2‐strategy (SAFE vs. UNSAFE) “innovation race” model with optional “peer punishment” or “peer reward,” rather than on a standard public goods game. Moreover, the paper does not measure “efficiency” as “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff,” and it does not systematically vary most of the 15 parameters as one would in a typical experimental public goods setting.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned?  
     – The authors use a well‐mixed population of size Z = 100, and pairwise interactions occur in repeated 2‐player matchups.  
     – They do not vary “number of players” per group. They do not report how changing Z or using groups larger than 2 would affect anything.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment if systematically varied?  
     – Not discussed. No predictions or effect sizes are provided.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned?  
     – The paper uses an “average” or expected number of development rounds W (e.g., W = 100 in simulations).  
     – They do not systematically vary W in the figures or tables to show a punishment‐efficiency relationship.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment if systematically varied?  
     – Not discussed for any dependent variable in the sense of a dedicated figure or table showing changes in punishment’s effect. No effect size is provided.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned?  
     – Not at all. There is no mention of communication channels or chat.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment if systematically varied?  
     – Not discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned?  
     – The paper frames each round’s choice as either SAFE or UNSAFE: a binary choice, not a partial‐contribution scheme.  
     – They do not refer to it as “all or nothing” in the sense of standard public goods; they simply define two discrete actions.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment if systematically varied?  
     – Not discussed; there is no analysis of partial vs. complete contributions.

5. Is the contribution default (do players move endowment back to hand)?
   • Mentioned?  
     – Not at all. No such default or endowment is discussed in this paper.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment if systematically varied?  
     – Not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Mentioned?  
     – The authors do not use a public‐goods MPCR. Instead, they define a “speed” parameter s (> 1) for UNSAFE actions. This is not cast as an MPCR.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment if systematically varied?  
     – They do vary s in some theoretical boundaries (e.g., s = 1.5 in examples), but they do not link it to changes in “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The paper denotes a punishment‐imposer’s “speed cost” as sα. Imposing punishment reduces the punisher’s own development speed by sα.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment if systematically varied (for any dependent variable)?  
     – Yes, the paper systematically varies sα and shows how it influences the fraction of unsafe players (“AU frequency”), not efficiency. See Fig. 5 (bottom row).  
     – Numerical results show that if punishment is very “cost‐efficient” (small sα, large effect on the punished party), punishment can strongly reduce UNSAFE choices–sometimes undesirably so in scenarios where UNSAFE was collectively preferred (their “Region III”).  
     – No numerical effect size is given for “efficiency.” Plots show AU frequency only.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from the punished player)
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The paper uses sβ as the penalty inflicted on UNSAFE players’ speed. This is the magnitude by which the punishee’s speed is reduced.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment if systematically varied (for any dependent variable)?  
     – Yes, varied systematically alongside sα in Fig. 5 (bottom row). They report how “AU frequency” changes.  
     – They do not measure efficiency, only the fraction of unsafe vs. safe players.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The paper models a “reward strategy” (RS) that, if it sees SAFE in the co‐player, boosts that co‐player’s speed.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment if systematically varied?  
     – The paper does examine “reward alone” and “reward + punishment” scenarios. However, it never measures “efficiency” as a dependent variable. Results focus on how reward influences “AU frequency.”

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. In the model, the rewarder’s own speed is reduced by sα. This is the cost of conferring a positive speed boost on the other.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment if systematically varied?  
     – Reward is examined in parallel to punishment but does not systematically alter “punishment’s effect on efficiency.” They do show how reward’s cost (sα) affects “AU frequency” (see Fig. 5, top row).

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded to the rewarded player)
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. This is sβ in the reward case, increasing the SAFE co‐player’s speed by sβ.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment if systematically varied?  
     – Reward magnitude is varied, but not specifically to see how it modulates “punishment treatment.” Rather, they see how reward alone (or combined with punishment) changes the fraction of UNSAFE players. No measure of efficiency is given.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
   • Mentioned?  
     – Not addressed. The model has an expected number of rounds W, not a discussion of whether players know W or not.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment if systematically varied?  
     – Not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much others gained or lost)?
   • Mentioned?  
     – Not addressed. No mention of revealing payoffs or losses.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment if systematically varied?  
     – Not discussed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who punished them?
   • Mentioned?  
     – Not addressed. The paper does not discuss identifying punishers.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment if systematically varied?  
     – Not discussed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who rewarded them?
   • Mentioned?  
     – Not addressed. The paper does not discuss identifying rewarders.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment if systematically varied?  
     – Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper’s main dependent variables are either (i) the fraction (or frequency) of UNSAFE (AU) strategies in the population at long run (their Figs. 3–5) or (ii) risk‐dominance conditions for safe vs. unsafe.  
   • They do mention “average payoff” here and there (the game‐theoretic notion of payoff), but they do not discuss “group efficiency” = (actual total payoff) / (maximum possible total payoff).  
   • Hence the paper’s “dependent variables” differ from efficiency. Most results are presented as “AU frequency” or which strategy is adopted at high frequency.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Explicitly mentioned and used:  
       – (1) Number of players, but only in the sense of a population size Z = 100, not systematically varied.  
       – (2) Number of rounds W, but typically fixed at 100.  
       – (7, 8) Punishment cost (sα) and punishment magnitude (sβ).  
       – (9, 10, 11) Reward presence, reward cost (sα), reward magnitude (sβ).  
     • The rest (3, 4, 5, 6 [as MPCR], 12, 13, 14, 15) do not appear as such, or are not systematically varied, or are not discussed at all in the context of a public goods framework.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on “the punishment treatment effect” when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The authors only systematically vary punishment cost (sα) and punishment magnitude (sβ) (parameters 7 and 8 in your list). They show how these shifts change the fraction of unsafe players.  
   • They do not measure or report “efficiency” changes. Instead, their dependent variable is “AU frequency.”  
   • Hence only two of the 15 parameters (7, 8) are directly varied to see how punishment changes outcomes (though the outcome is not efficiency).

D. If you were to make predictions of how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely from the content of this paper, what could you say?  
   • The paper does not present or discuss a ratio of total payoff to a maximum possible payoff. It reports changes in who ends up SAFE vs. UNSAFE. Thus, there is no direct statement about “group efficiency.”  
   • They do show that if punishment is cheap for the punisher (small sα) and strongly reduces speed of the punished (large sβ), then fewer players end up being UNSAFE; they call it “strong regulation.” In some parameter regions, that might “improve overall safety” but the paper never quantifies it as an efficiency ratio.  
   • Consequently, one cannot draw numerical or explicit predictions for how each of the 15 parameters drives efficiency, since the paper does not track efficiency. Little to no further prediction is possible from this text alone.
reference_APA: The Anh Han, Pereira, Luis Moniz, Lenaerts, Tom & Santos, Francisco C. (2021). Mediating artificial intelligence developments through negative and positive incentives. PLOS ONE.

Authors: Han, TA; Duong, MH; Perc, M
Author Full Names: Han, The Anh; Duong, Manh Hong; Perc, Matjaz
Article Title: Evolutionary mechanisms that promote cooperation may not promote social welfare
Source Title: JOURNAL OF THE ROYAL SOCIETY INTERFACE
Author Keywords: social welfare; cost efficiency; reward; punishment; evolution of cooperation; social dilemma
Keywords Plus: PRISONERS-DILEMMA; PUNISHMENT; EMERGENCE; DYNAMICS; TRUST; GAME
Abstract: Understanding the emergence of prosocial behaviours among self-interested individuals is an important problem in many scientific disciplines. Various mechanisms have been proposed to explain the evolution of such behaviours, primarily seeking the conditions under which a given mechanism can induce highest levels of cooperation. As these mechanisms usually involve costs that alter individual pay-offs, it is, however, possible that aiming for highest levels of cooperation might be detrimental for social welfare-the latter broadly defined as the total population pay-off, taking into account all costs involved for inducing increased prosocial behaviours. Herein, by comparing stochastic evolutionary models of two well-established mechanisms of prosocial behaviour-namely, peer and institutional incentives-we demonstrate that the objectives of maximizing cooperation and of maximizing social welfare are often misaligned. First, while peer punishment is often more effective than peer reward in promoting cooperation-especially with a higher impact-to-cost ratio-the opposite is true for social welfare. In fact, welfare typically decreases (increases) with this ratio for punishment (reward). Second, for institutional incentives, while maintaining similar levels of cooperation, rewards result in positive social welfare across a much broader range of parameters. Furthermore, both types of incentives often achieve optimal social welfare when their impact is moderate rather than maximal, indicating that careful planning is essential for costly institutional mechanisms to optimize social outcomes. These findings are consistent across varying mutation rates, selection intensities and game configurations. Overall, we argue for the need of adopting social welfare as the main optimization objective when designing and implementing evolutionary mechanisms for social and collective goods.

Below, each of the 15 design parameters is treated in turn.

For every parameter we report  
(1) whether it is explicitly instantiated in the paper, giving the value(s) used;  
(2) whether the paper **systematically varies** that parameter and, if so, what happens to the *punishment treatment effect* (i.e., how the presence of punishment changes the dependent variable that is being tracked).  When an approximate numerical effect can be read directly from a figure or table, it is given; otherwise “n.a.” is stated.

Because the paper studies evolutionary‐game–theoretic models—not laboratory public-goods experiments—many of the requested parameters are simply absent.

────────────────────────────────────────

1. Number of players in the group  
   (1) Mentioned.  Population size N = 50 in all simulations.  
   (2) Not varied.  No predictions on how changing N would alter the punishment treatment effect.  

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Not in the model: interactions are one-shot Prisoner’s Dilemmas played in an infinite evolutionary process.  
   (2) No discussion.  

3. Chat enabled?  
   Not mentioned.  

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   (1) Implicitly yes: the PD offers only the binary actions C or D.  
   (2) No variation; no discussion of alternative contribution technologies.  

5. Contribution default / extraction game?  
   Not mentioned.  

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   Not part of the PD model; not discussed.  

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   (1) Peer punishment: cost ε = 1 (fixed).  
       Institutional punishment: cost per unit is δ / b.  Three values of the efficiency parameter b are shown (e.g., b = 1, 2, 3).  
   (2) ε itself is not varied, but b is.  Increasing b (i.e., making punishment cheaper for the institution) enlarges the parameter region in which punishment yields *positive* social welfare, yet even at b = 3 the paper shows (Fig. 2c) that very large δ again lowers welfare.  No numeric slope is provided.  

8. Punishment magnitude (δ)  
   (1) Explicit.  In peer incentives Fig. 1 the ratio δ / ε is scanned from 0 to 5.  In institutional incentives Fig. 2 δ is varied on both axes (exact grid not specified but covers roughly 0–2.5).  
   (2) Peer punishment: as δ / ε rises, cooperation increases (left panels of Fig. 1) but social welfare **decreases** (right panels).  E.g. at β = 0.1, going from δ / ε = 0 to 5 raises cooperation from ≈0.33 to ≈0.9, while SW falls by ≈0.25 (visual estimate).  
       Institutional punishment: welfare is negative for small b unless δ is in an *intermediate* range; too small or too large δ is bad (Fig. 2a).  No numeric table is provided.  

9. Reward enabled?  
   (1) Yes.  Separate peer-reward and institutional-reward models are analysed.  
   (2) Switching from punishment to reward keeps cooperation the same (institutional case) or lowers it slightly (peer case) but **raises social welfare** across most of the parameter space (Figs. 1 & 2).  Example: at β = 0.1 and δ / ε = 3, peer punishment gives SW ≈1.1 whereas peer reward gives SW ≈1.35 (visual estimate).  

10. Reward cost to the rewarder  
    (1) Peer reward: ε = 1 (fixed).  
        Institutional reward: cost per unit is δ / a.  Values a = 0.7, 1, 1.3 (>1 means cheaper reward) are shown.  
    (2) Varying a systematically shifts the welfare surface in Fig. 2b–d.  Larger a (cheaper reward) monotonically raises social welfare for any δ; smaller a yields an inverted-U with an optimal intermediate δ.  No exact effect sizes are tabulated.  

11. Reward magnitude (δ)  
    (1) Same δ as under punishment; varied identically.  
    (2) Peer reward: raising δ increases both cooperation and welfare (Fig. 1, right column).  
        Institutional reward: for a > 1, the best welfare is at the *largest* δ displayed; for a ≤ 1, the optimum lies at an intermediate δ (Fig. 2b–d).  

12. Horizon known?  
    Not modelled.  

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
    Not modelled.  

14. Punisher identity known?  
    Not modelled.  

15. Rewarder identity known?  
    Not modelled.  

────────────────────────────────────────

SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables used  
    – Social welfare (SW): total population payoff, *not* divided by the theoretical maximum.  
    – f_C: long-run frequency of cooperation.  
    The paper does not report “group efficiency” as defined in the prompt; SW and f_C are distinct.  

B.  Parameters mentioned (6/15)  
    1, 4, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11.  

C.  Parameters whose *systematic variation* is analysed for their effect on punishment treatment (4/15)  
    8 (punishment magnitude δ), 10 (reward cost efficiency a), 11 (reward magnitude δ), and, indirectly, 7 (punishment cost efficiency b).  No other parameter is varied.  

D.  What can we predict about the 15 parameters and their interactions, *using only this paper*?  
    – Larger punishment magnitude (δ) makes punishment better at raising cooperation but worse (peer) or non-monotonic (institutional) for efficiency.  
    – Making punishment cheaper (higher b) helps welfare, yet even then an intermediate δ is optimal.  
    – Reward, whenever available, is predicted to dominate punishment on efficiency unless rewards are extremely costly (low a).  
    – All other parameters (group size, rounds, information conditions, etc.) receive no treatment, so no prediction can be drawn from this paper alone.

Article Title: NON-MONETARY INCENTIVES AND OPPORTUNISTIC BEHAVIOR: EVIDENCE FROM A LABORATORY PUBLIC GOOD GAME

Abstract: This study reports data from a laboratory experiment that investigates the incentive effect of three distinct social communication schemes on free-riding behavior. We use performance-based approval and disapproval ratings and a linear public good game to address the above issues. The treatments vary in terms of subjects' opportunities to anonymously assign (1) only the approval ratings to other group members, (2) only the disapproval ratings to other group members, and (3) either the approval or the disapproval ratings to other group members (but not both to the same group member), after they play a standard linear public good game. Despite the Nash prediction of zero individual contribution in all three treatments, the data show that the disapproval points generate significantly higher contribution than the approval points. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter review of what this particular paper (Dugar, “Non‐Monetary Incentives and Opportunistic Behavior: Evidence from a Laboratory Public Good Game”) does—and does not—say about each of the 15 listed parameters. Throughout, I use the term “punishment treatment effect” to refer to the impact of having a punishment (in this paper, “disapproval points”) on some outcome relative to not having punishment.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. Groups are of size four. Each experimental session had 12 total participants in the lab, broken into three groups of four.  
     – Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it?  
       → No. The number of players per group is always fixed at four, and the paper does not study how changing group size would affect punishment’s impact on efficiency or on any other outcome.

2. Number of rounds
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. Each session lasts 15 periods (rounds).  
     – Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it?  
       → No. All sessions use 15 periods. The paper does not manipulate or compare different numbers of rounds, so there is no prediction about how changing from, say, 10 to 20 rounds would alter the effect of punishment.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – The paper notes that subjects do not interact face‐to‐face or via chat; they only interact by assigning approval or disapproval points electronically.  
     – Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it?  
       → No. There is no “chat‐enabled” versus “not chat‐enabled” comparison, so the paper makes no predictions on how allowing open chat might change the punishment treatment effect.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. Contributions are in integer tokens out of an endowment of 20 tokens (i.e., any amount between 0 and 20). There is no forced “all or nothing” rule.  
     – Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it?  
       → No. The paper uses a standard linear public good game with continuous (0 to 20) contribution options.

5. Is the contribution default (if true, do players decide how much to move back to themselves after seeing some default)? 
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. Subjects explicitly choose how many tokens (0–20) to contribute. There is no mention of any “default” contribution or forced action.  
     – Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it?  
       → No. This parameter does not appear.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. The MPCR is 0.4, meaning each token contributed to the public good yields 0.4 tokens to each of the four group members.  
     – Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it?  
       → No. The MPCR is fixed at 0.4 in all sessions. The paper does not explore how changing the MPCR would influence punishment’s effect.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – The experiment labels “disapproval points” as the non‐monetary punishment. These points are costless for punishers to assign.  
     – Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it?  
       → No. The cost remains zero throughout all punishment treatments. The paper does not discuss changing that cost.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – The disapproval points have no direct monetary effect on the recipient’s payoff in this experiment (i.e., there is no payoff deduction).  
     – Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it?  
       → No. The “magnitude” of punishment is fixed at “purely symbolic,” with no actual payoff reduction; hence the paper does not address varying the point‐to‐payoff deduction rate.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. The experiment includes (a) a Disapproval‐only treatment, (b) an Approval‐only treatment, (c) an Approval‐Disapproval treatment, and (d) a Baseline (no points at all). Thus, presence or absence of (non‐monetary) rewards is indeed manipulated.  
     – Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it?  
       → The paper’s primary “systematic variations” across treatments are:  
          1) Disapproval Only (punishment only),  
          2) Approval Only (reward only),  
          3) Approval‐Disapproval (both reward and punishment).  
         However, the paper does not present incremental or parametric variations of the reward instrument itself (like different intensities); it only switches on/off the availability of non‐monetary rewards or punishments.

   • Numerical effect size that can be inferred from the paper (for punishment vs. no‐punishment, but focusing on “reward presence” for efficiency or payoff):  
     – The paper documents that “disapproval only” yields significantly higher average contribution (and thus average payoff) compared to the Baseline (no‐reward/no‐punishment) or the Approval‐only. Reward alone (Approval‐only) has a smaller effect than punishment alone. When both (Approval + Disapproval) are allowed, that yields the highest contributions (hence highest average payoffs).

     Note: The paper generally reports average contributions and earnings, not a ratio of actual to maximal possible payoff. However, the data (Figures 1, 2, and Tables 1–2) show that enabling punishment (disapproval) or combining it with reward yields higher group payoffs than not enabling it.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – The “approval points” are costless to assign, just as disapproval points are costless.  
     – Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it?  
       → No. The cost is always zero in the experiment.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – As with disapproval, approval points do not alter the recipient’s monetary payoff. These points are entirely payoff‐neutral.  
     – Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it?  
       → No. There is no change in the “magnitude” across different conditions. The treatment manipulates only the presence versus absence of the reward points, not their monetary effect.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. Subjects know from the start that the game lasts 15 periods: it is a finitely repeated public good game.  
     – Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it?  
       → No. It is always 15 in all treatments, with no discussion of how incomplete knowledge might affect results.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained or lost each round)?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. At the end of each period, each subject sees (i) the distribution of contributions by group members that period, (ii) the aggregate approval or disapproval points each group member received, and (iii) their own earnings. However, individuals’ private payoffs are not labeled by personal ID.  
     – Does the paper systematically vary the visibility of peer outcomes or make predictions about varying it?  
       → No. The paper does not manipulate how much outcome information is given. It is held constant across treatments.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. They make it clear that punishment is anonymous: a punished player sees only aggregate disapproval points, not the identity of the punisher.  
     – Does the paper systematically vary that anonymity, or predict how it would alter the punishment effect?  
       → No. It is always anonymous.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. Similarly, approval is also anonymous: a rewarded player sees only how many total approval points they got, but not from whom.  
     – Does the paper systematically vary that anonymity, or predict how it would alter the effect?  
       → No. It is always anonymous.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY:

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?

   – The paper primarily reports (1) individual contributions to the public good and (2) individual (and thus group) payoffs. Total payoff is essentially group welfare in this setting. They do sometimes refer to “welfare” or “group welfare,” which is the sum of payoffs. However, they do not explicitly use the ratio “(actual total payoff) / (maximum possible total payoff)” as the metric of “efficiency.” Instead, they discuss “earnings” (i.e., average or total payoffs) and “contribution levels” (i.e., percentage of endowment contributed).  
   – So the main dependent variables are:  
       • Contribution (the number of tokens put into the public good)  
       • Average individual earnings (or group payoff)  
     These are not labeled “efficiency,” but a higher group payoff is interpreted as “more welfare.”

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

   – Mentioned explicitly or implicitly:  
       1) Number of players: fixed at 4 per group.  
       2) Number of rounds: fixed at 15.  
       3) (Implied) No chat: they specify no face‐to‐face communication or free‐form chat.  
       6) MPCR = 0.4.  
       7) Punishment cost = 0 (they call it disapproval points, costless).  
       8) Punishment magnitude = 0 in payoff terms.  
       9) Whether a reward is enabled: yes, manipulated across treatments (approval absent vs. present).  
       10) Reward cost = 0.  
       11) Reward magnitude = 0 in payoff terms.  
       12) Number of rounds known to players = yes (15).  
       13) Peer outcomes shown? Yes, they see how much others contributed plus the total disapproval/approval points.  
       14) Identity of punisher is unknown.  
       15) Identity of rewarder is unknown.  

   – Not mentioned at all or not manipulated:  
       4) “All or nothing” forced contribution format: not used.  
       5) “Contribution default”: not used.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?

   – The paper only systematically manipulates the presence or absence of non‐monetary punishment (Parameter 9, in combination with the presence or absence of approval “reward”). Specifically, the paper compares:  
       • Baseline (no punishment, no reward)  
       • Disapproval‐only (punishment)  
       • Approval‐only (reward)  
       • Approval‐Disapproval combined.  
   – This means only Parameter 9 (“Whether a reward is enabled”) and, implicitly, the presence/absence of punishment are systematically varied.  
   – The other parameters (e.g., group size, cost/magnitude of punishment, cost/magnitude of reward, number of rounds, etc.) are held constant, not varied.

   • Effect sizes (for the presence of punishment vs. not) are reported in terms of average or final‐round contribution and payoff (Table 2, Figures 1–2), not in terms of an explicit efficiency ratio. For example:  
       – Average individual contribution in the Disapproval‐only treatment is about 9.02 tokens; in the Baseline it is 5.79 tokens, and in the Approval‐only it is 6.59 tokens (Table 1).  
       – Contributions (and hence payoffs) are highest of all (11.89 tokens) in the combined Approval‐Disapproval treatment.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

   – Because the paper does not experimentally vary most of the 15 parameters, one cannot draw data‐based conclusions about how changes in group size, number of rounds, or the exact numeric cost/magnitude of punishment or reward would shift “efficiency.”  
   – The single clear takeaway from the paper is that enabling non‐monetary punishment alone raises contributions and payoffs relative to no punishment or reward, and that combining non‐monetary punishment with non‐monetary reward raises contributions/payoffs even more.  
   – Beyond that, the paper provides little or no basis for predicting how the other parameters (e.g., bigger group size, different MPCR, known vs. unknown number of rounds, revealing punisher identity, etc.) would affect the punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

• ⟨P⟩ – average payoff in the population

B. Which of the 15 parameters appear anywhere in the paper?

Below, each of the 15 listed parameters is addressed in turn, strictly according to what appears (or does not appear) in the provided paper. When the paper does not mention a parameter at all, or does not analyze any systematic variation of it, that is stated directly. References to “Figures” and “Tables” below refer only to those within the text of the paper itself, not external material.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER DISCUSSION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. Number of players  
   • Mention in paper: The paper focuses on intergovernmental cooperation among five entities: the Ministry of Water Resources (MWR) and four local governments (Henan Province, Hebei Province, Beijing, and Tianjin). Hence, it implicitly has five “players” in its evolutionary game framework.  
   • Systematic variation: The paper does not systematically vary the number of players to see how that changes any treatment effect (including punishment). No numerical effect sizes are given for changing the number of players.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mention in paper: The paper does not specify how many times the game is played (number of rounds) or whether it is finitely or indefinitely repeated.  
   • Systematic variation: Not discussed.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mention in paper: The paper does not discuss chat or any communication mechanism among players.  
   • Systematic variation: Not discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mention in paper: The paper describes each local government choosing “strong” or “weak” willingness to cooperate, but it never frames this as an “all-or-nothing contribution” to a public good.  
   • Systematic variation: Not discussed.

5. Is the contribution default?  
   • Mention in paper: The paper does not mention default contribution rules (e.g., automatically contributing unless one opts out).  
   • Systematic variation: Not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Mention in paper: The paper introduces a term α > 1 to scale local governments’ payoffs if both choose “strong willingness,” but never uses (nor labels) it as an MPCR or “public goods” multiplier in the sense of a standard public goods game.  
   • Systematic variation: While α appears in the payoff functions (Tables 1 and 2 in the paper), the paper does not discuss α as a stand-in for a “marginal per capita return,” nor does it link α to a punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mention in paper: Punishment is presented in the form of a “penalty” (P) that MWR applies when local governments show weak willingness, and there is also MWR’s cost of supervision (M for weak supervision, mM for strong supervision). However, the paper does not describe a separate “cost per unit of punishment” in the sense of, for instance, 1 coin to punish 1 coin from someone else. Instead, M and mM are general supervision cost parameters, not singled out as an incremental “per-unit” cost.  
   • Systematic variation: The paper explores conditions under which “ωP > mM” or “ωP < mM,” etc., but does not frame this as systematically varying a per-punishment cost to see effects on total group efficiency. No effect sizes are given that link a “punishment cost per unit” to changes in efficiency or any other variable.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted for each unit of punishment)  
   • Mention in paper: The “penalty” P that local governments suffer when caught with weak willingness can be viewed as a punishment magnitude. The paper analyzes conditions such as “σcᵢ – (ε + ηπᵢ) > P” or “λF > (θ–β)C,” but does not interpret P as “units of punishment.”  
   • Systematic variation: Although the paper evaluates different inequalities (e.g., P compared to other terms in Table 3’s equilibrium conditions), it does not provide a systematic numeric variation of P that is then tied to a “treatment effect.” There is no explicit effect size stated for how changing P alone shifts total efficiency.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mention in paper: The paper does refer to “ε” as an increased “political achievement score” for local governments that are strongly implementing policies under strong MWR supervision. However, the paper does not frame this as a “reward treatment” being turned on or off.  
   • Systematic variation: No mention of systematically enabling or disabling a reward mechanism to measure its effect on punishment or efficiency.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Mention in paper: No mention is made of any separate cost specifically for granting ε (the paper frames M as a cost of supervision, not a cost of granting a reward).  
   • Systematic variation: Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)  
   • Mention in paper: The paper’s notation “ε” captures some gain (e.g., improved evaluation score) for local governments showing strong willingness while supervised. This is not explicitly called “reward magnitude” nor do they depict it as a standard public-goods “reward.”  
   • Systematic variation: The paper does compare strong vs. weak supervision scenarios and mentions ε in the payoff matrix. However, it does not systematically vary ε to isolate a “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
   • Mention in paper: Not discussed.  
   • Systematic variation: Not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much their peers gained/lost)?  
   • Mention in paper: Although local governments can observe each other’s “weak” or “strong” willingness, the paper does not say that they see each other’s payoffs or losses.  
   • Systematic variation: Not discussed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Mention in paper: The punisher is consistently MWR in the model, so by design local governments know that MWR is behind the penalty. There is no separate concealment or anonymity dimension.  
   • Systematic variation: Not discussed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Mention in paper: Similar to Parameter 14, any “reward” or beneficial evaluation score (ε) comes uniquely from the MWR. The paper distinguishes no separate condition of anonymity.  
   • Systematic variation: Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper’s stated goal is to improve the “efficiency of emergency management.” However, it does not analyze “efficiency” in the specific experimental-economics sense of “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible.” Instead, it relies on evolutionary-stable-strategy (ESS) conditions and payoff functions for local governments and MWR.  
   • The dependent variables examined in the analyses are the evolving probabilities of each strategy (e.g., strong vs. weak willingness), along with payoffs (profits and costs) for local governments and MWR. “Profit” or “penalty” in the paper differs from a direct measure of group efficiency.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Parameter (1), “Number of players,” appears insofar as the paper defines 5 players (MWR plus 4 local governments).  
   • Parameters (7) and (8), “Punishment cost” and “Punishment magnitude,” bear partial resemblance to M and P in the paper (supervision cost and penalty).  
   • Parameters (9) and (11), “Whether a reward is enabled” and “Reward magnitude,” loosely align with the presence of ε in the payoff matrix, but the paper does not label it or treat it formally as a “reward system.”  
   • No other parameters (2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 13, 14, 15) are explicitly mentioned as such.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, the paper does not frame “punishment treatment effect” the way a public goods experiment would. It analyzes conditions (like whether P is larger or smaller than certain cost terms) that shift equilibrium outcomes. But it does not provide a direct numeric “treatment effect” on total payoffs or on a measure of efficiency as these parameters vary. Consequently, there are no explicit effect sizes in the sense of “vary parameter X by one unit and see outcome Y.”  
   • In sum, none of the 15 parameters are systematically varied in a way that the paper ties to a measured “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper itself gives insufficient basis to isolate “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” in a public-goods sense. It does not compare how group payoffs might rise or fall solely because of a penalty’s presence or magnitude.  
   • Given the paper’s content, one can say little beyond the following: increasing the penalty P above a certain threshold can encourage local governments to choose “strong willingness” (which the paper interprets as more effective emergency management). But any precise prediction on total efficiency or group payoff—especially as a ratio of actual to maximum possible payoff—cannot be drawn from the paper’s analyses alone.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(end)

Authors: Mieth, L; Buchner, A; Bell, R
Author Full Names: Mieth, Laura; Buchner, Axel; Bell, Raoul
Article Title: Moral labels increase cooperation and costly punishment in a Prisoner's Dilemma game with punishment option
Keywords Plus: SOCIAL DILEMMAS; EVOLUTION; BEHAVIOR; PROGRAM; POWER
Abstract: To determine the role of moral norms in cooperation and punishment, we examined the effects of a moral-framing manipulation in a Prisoner's Dilemma game with a costly punishment option. In each round of the game, participants decided whether to cooperate or to defect. The Prisoner's Dilemma game was identical for all participants with the exception that the behavioral options were paired with moral labels (I cooperate and I cheat) in the moral-framing condition and with neutral labels (A and B) in the neutral-framing condition. After each round of the Prisoner's Dilemma game, participants had the opportunity to invest some of their money to punish their partners. In two experiments, moral framing increased moral and hypocritical punishment: participants were more likely to punish partners for defection when moral labels were used than when neutral labels were used. When the participants' cooperation was enforced by their partners' moral punishment, moral framing did not only increase moral and hypocritical punishment but also cooperation. The results suggest that moral framing activates a cooperative norm that specifically increases moral and hypocritical punishment. Furthermore, the experience of moral punishment by the partners may increase the importance of social norms for cooperation, which may explain why moral framing effects on cooperation were found only when participants were subject to moral punishment.

Abstract: One of the important topics in public choice is how people's free-riding behavior could differ by group size in collective action dilemmas. Such over-punishment results from third party punishers' conditional punishment behaviors: their punishment intensity is positively correlated with their beliefs on the peers' punitive actions. Below I go through the fifteen parameters one by one, referring only to what is stated in the Kamei (2018) paper “Group size effect and over-punishment in the case of third-party enforcement of social norms”.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Discussed?  YES.  Four values are used: total group size N = 3, 4, 6, 12 (i.e. 1, 2, 4 or 10 third-party punishers).  
   • Systematic variation?  YES – this is the central treatment variable.  
   • Effect on the “punishment treatment effect”?  
        – Punishment per punisher in scenario (b) (defector vs. co-operator) falls slightly as N grows (Table 3, col. 2):  
              N=3→4:  –1.028 points (p<.01)  
              N=3→6:  –0.542 (ns)  
              N=3→12: –1.382 (p<.01)  
        – Total punishment received by a defector nonetheless rises sharply because there are more punishers (Result 4; Appendix Table A.5).  
        – Efficiency (total pay-off) consequences (Fig. 3):  
              • N = 3: Unique NE is mutual defection; expected pay-off of a co-operator 26.60, defector 29.07.  
              • N = 4: Coordination game; mutual cooperation becomes an NE.  
              • N = 6: Mutual cooperation is the unique NE; expected pay-off co-operate 35.27, defect 12.34.  
              • N = 12: Over-punishment – a defector’s expected pay-off −26.7, even a co-operator’s expected pay-off 13.42 → “huge efficiency loss”.  
        – In short, more third-party punishers first raise efficiency (by deterring defection) but, at very large N, reduce efficiency through over-punishment and some punishment of cooperators.

2. Number of rounds  
   • One-shot game only; never varied; no predictions.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • No communication allowed; not varied; no predictions.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • The PD choice is binary (send 10 or keep 10) but this feature is constant; no discussion of varying it.

5. Contribution default / “give-back” frame?  
   • Not used, not discussed.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Not applicable (the stage-1 game is a Prisoner’s Dilemma, not a linear public-goods game).  No variation, no predictions.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   • Constant: 1 point per unit of punishment.  Mentioned (Section 2.1) but never varied; no predictions.

8. Punishment magnitude (damage per unit)  
   • Constant: each punishment point deducts 3 points from the target.  Mentioned but not varied; no predictions.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Rewards never available; not discussed.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   • Not applicable.

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
   • Only one round; players know this.  Constant; no variation or predictions.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Third parties are told exactly what each PD player did; PD players do not learn individual punisher behaviour.  Setting is fixed; not varied.

14. Are punishers identified?  
   • No – punishment is anonymous.  This is stated but never varied; no predictions.

15. Are rewarders identified?  
   • Not relevant (no rewards).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables used  
   – Main outcomes analysed:  
       • PD players’ cooperation decision (“Send 10” yes/no)  
       • Punishment frequency and punishment points per third-party punisher  
       • Expected monetary pay-offs after punishment (often displayed in payoff matrices)  
   – “Group efficiency” (total pay-off divided by the maximum possible) is talked about qualitatively (“huge efficiency loss”) but is never computed as a separate dependent variable.  Hence efficiency is mentioned conceptually, whereas the statistical analyses focus on cooperation, punishment intensity and individual/expected pay-offs.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   – Parameter 1 (Number of players) – central treatment variable  
   – Parameters 7 & 8 (punishment cost and magnitude) – described but fixed  
   – Parameter 14 (punisher anonymity) – described but fixed  
   – Parameter 12 (round information) – implicitly fixed (one-shot)  
   Total mentioned: 5 out of 15.  Only parameter 1 is actually manipulated.

C. For how many parameters is the effect of systematic variation on the punishment treatment effect discussed?  
   – Only parameter 1 (Number of players).  1 out of 15.

D. Predictions you can make (solely from this paper) about how the parameters will influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency  
   – Number of players: Rising N first increases the efficiency benefit of adding punishment (because deterrence becomes effective) but, beyond a point (10 third-party punishers in this design), efficiency declines due to over-punishment and occasional punishment of cooperators.  
   – All other parameters: The paper provides no evidence or theory about how varying them would change efficiency once punishment is introduced.  Any prediction would be speculation, so none can be made on the basis of this paper alone.

Hence, outside of group size, the paper offers little guidance for predicting how the other 14 parameters or their interactions would modify the effect of punishment on group efficiency.

Abstract: Mechanisms and conditions for the spontaneous emergence of cooperation in multi-player social dilemma games remain an open question. This paper focuses on stochastic evolutionary optional public goods games with different exclusion strategies. We introduce four strategy types in the population, namely, cooperation, defection, loner and exclusion. Synchronous and asynchronous exclusion forms have been compared in finite-sized, well-mixed and structured populations. In addition, we verify that the asynchronous exclusion mechanism is indeed better than the synchronous exclusion mechanism in all cases. The benefits of the asynchronous exclusion are measured by comparing the probability that the system chooses the cooperative states in the two situations. In the well-mixed population cases, only when the investment amplification factor is small and the probability of exclusion success is high will the asynchronous exclusion mechanism have a relatively large advantage in promoting cooperation. However, in the structured population cases, the range of the investment amplification factor, in which the asynchronous exclusion mechanism has relatively large advantages in promoting cooperation, is somewhat different and is mainly in the middle of the interval under our parameters. Our study further corroborated that when non-participation and exclusion strategies exist, a structured population does not necessarily promote cooperation compared with a well-mixed population for some parameter combinations.    • Mentioned?

For example, Figures 2–4 show how changing r (along with other parameters) alters the probability that the population ends up in a cooperative state. They report that when r is small and the exclusion‐success probability (β) is large, asynchronous exclusion (one form of “punishment”) can have a bigger advantage in helping cooperators. 14) When a player is punished, do they know who the punisher is?  
    • Mentioned?  
      – No.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is?  
    • Mentioned?  
      – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────

FINAL SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   – The paper does not measure “group efficiency” or “total payoff.” Its main outcomes are the probability/frequency of each strategy in the final population state—specifically, how often cooperators prevail. These are not the same as efficiency, which would require comparing actual total payoff to the maximum possible.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   – The paper mentions two of them directly: (1) the number of players (M) and (6) the multiplication factor r. It also implicitly discusses the cost of “punishment” (parameter 7) but only through the function cE = 0.2 × 10^β, rather than as an independently varied parameter. All other listed parameters (2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15) are either not discussed or not systematically varied.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   – Only one parameter in the list—the multiplication factor r—is systematically varied in a way that the authors relate to how “punishment” (exclusion) changes cooperation outcomes. Although cE is discussed, it is not systematically varied apart from being tied to β. Neither the paper nor its figures quantify a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency,” but they do show how varying r (and β, which is not on your list) changes the probability that cooperators dominate under synchronous vs. asynchronous exclusion.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely from the paper’s content, what would they be?  
   – The paper provides no direct measures or discussions of “efficiency” (total payoff relative to the maximum). It reports how certain parameter changes (particularly r and β) affect the probability of the system reaching a cooperative state under different exclusion rules. Therefore, there is little or no information about how the 15 parameters would specifically affect the “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” The main take‐away from the paper is that asynchronous exclusion can foster more cooperation than synchronous exclusion (especially when r is relatively small and β is high), but the authors do not link this advantage to aggregate payoffs or efficiency.    • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not compare different ways of restricting contribution choices.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency? Not discussed.  

5. Is the contribution default (if true, do players decide how much to “move back” from a public fund)?  
   • Mentioned? No. There is no mention of a default‐based design or an endowment that is automatically contributed and can be taken back.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency? Not discussed.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper sets the MPCR (a) to 0.5 in a group of three.  
   • Systematically varied? No; it is fixed at 0.5.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency? Not discussed in terms of systematically changing the MPCR.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The cost is 1 point per unit of punishment assigned.  
   • Systematically varied? No; it is always 1 point.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency? Not discussed in terms of varying the cost.  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins/points deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed on them)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each unit of punishment reduces the target’s payoff by 3 points.  
   • Systematically varied? No; it is always 3 points.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency? Not discussed with respect to changing that magnitude.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned? No. The experiment has no reward mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency? Not discussed.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Mentioned? No. Rewards are not implemented, so no cost is discussed.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency? Not discussed.  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins/points awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted to them)  
    • Mentioned? No. Rewards are not implemented, so no magnitude is discussed.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency? Not discussed.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    • Mentioned? Yes, each game is one‐shot, so they know there is only one round for that game.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency? Not discussed.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?  
    • Mentioned? The paper states that in the strategy‐method elicitation, people see the other players’ (hypothetical) contribution levels. Subjects do learn final payoffs only at the end but do not see feedback round by round. There is no systematic manipulation of what is displayed.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency? Not discussed.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Mentioned? The paper does not report that any identifying information was revealed about who punished whom.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency? Not discussed.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Mentioned? No, since there is no reward mechanism.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency? Not discussed.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FINAL SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper does refer to “earnings” or “payoffs,” and it notes that full contribution is “socially efficient,” but it does not present a formal measure of “group efficiency” (such as the ratio of total actual payoff to the maximum possible payoff). Instead, the main dependent variables in the paper are:  
     – Contribution levels (including “unconditional” and “conditional” contributions).  
     – Punishment decisions (and whether punishment is “antisocial” vs. directed toward lower contributors).  
     – Classification of subjects (free‐riders, conditional cooperators, etc.).  
   • Thus, although the paper acknowledges the efficient outcome, it does not quantify efficiency as a separate dependent variable in the manner that is sometimes done (e.g., total payoff / maximum possible payoff).  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned explicitly in the design (though not systematically varied):  
     1 (number of players = 3), 2 (number of rounds = 1, i.e., one‐shot), 4 (absence of a continuous range, instead four discrete contribution choices), 6 (MPCR = 0.5), 7 (punishment cost = 1), 8 (punishment magnitude = 3), and 12 (players know it is one‐shot).  
   • That is 7 parameters mentioned in some way.  
   • The other 8 parameters (3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15) either do not apply (e.g., chat, reward) or are not explicitly varied (information display about punishment identity, etc.).  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The paper does not systematically vary any of the listed parameters (participants all face the same cost to punish, the same punishment magnitude, the same MPCR, etc.).  
   • Consequently, there is no discussion of how systematically changing any of the parameters would change the punishment treatment effect, for either efficiency or the other outcomes.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not provide direct evidence on group efficiency. It is mostly concerned with how punishment influences contributions and how punishers respond to (in)equalities in contribution.  
   • Since no parameters are varied, one cannot infer from the paper alone how changes in the number of players, rounds, punishment cost, or other parameters would quantitatively affect overall efficiency.  
   • The main inference one can draw is that when punishment is introduced (compared to no‐punishment), it tends to increase contribution on average. If we equate higher contribution with higher total payoff (given MPCR > 0), then punishment plausibly increases efficiency. But because the paper does not present explicit efficiency measures, there is “little to no prediction” about how systematically adjusting each of the 15 parameters (or their interactions) would affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.
reference_APA: Cheung, Stephen L. (2014). New insights into conditional cooperation and punishment from a strategy method experiment. EXPERIMENTAL ECONOMICS.

Below I go through the 15 parameters one by one, strictly reporting what the paper actually says and, where possible, whether the paper predicts what would happen if the parameter were systematically varied for any dependent variable, in particular for a “punishment-treatment effect” on **efficiency** (total pay-off divided by the maximum possible).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. NUMBER OF PLAYERS (group size n)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  All results are written for an n-person group.  
   • Value(s)?  n is left symbolic; occasionally the authors refer to “sufficiently large n.”  
   • Systematic variation & predicted effect?  No explicit comparative-static result on how changing n alters the difference between a game **with** and **without** punishment, nor on efficiency.  n only appears as an algebraic factor in formulas.

2. NUMBER OF ROUNDS  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – the model is explicitly one-shot; the authors contrast this with repeated games used elsewhere.  
   • Systematic variation?  None.  No multi-round variant is analysed, so no prediction.

3. IS CHAT ENABLED?  
   • Mentioned?  No.  Not modelled and never discussed.

4. ALL-OR-NOTHING CONTRIBUTION?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes, implicitly.  Effort eᵢ ∈ [0,1] is continuous, so the contribution **is not** all-or-nothing.  
   • Systematic variation?  None – only the continuous case is analysed.

5. “CONTRIBUTION DEFAULT” (withdraw vs. give)?  
   • Mentioned?  No.

6. MPCR (φ = q/n)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  φ is kept symbolic and bounded by 1/n < φ < 1.  
   • Systematic variation?  Partially.  Many inequalities (e.g. 2λφ<1 vs. 2λφ>1) determine whether punishment can sustain cooperation, but the paper never computes the size of a punishment treatment effect on efficiency as φ changes.  Only qualitative statements such as “if 2λφ>1 full contribution is always a Nash equilibrium even without punishment” are made.

7. COST TO IMPOSE 1 UNIT OF PUNISHMENT  
   • Mentioned?  Yes: c(s) = ½ s².  Fixed; not varied.  
   • Systematic variation?  None.

8. PUNISHMENT MAGNITUDE (how much the target loses per unit)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes: the variable s_{ji} itself is the loss to j.  The loss–per–unit ratio is fixed at 1.  
   • Systematic variation?  None.

9. REWARD ENABLED?  
   • Mentioned?  Only in a short speculative paragraph (“A further extension would be to consider rewarding…”) but not modelled.  No results, no variation.

10. REWARD COST  
11. REWARD MAGNITUDE  
   • Mentioned?  No.

12. ARE THE NUMBER OF ROUNDS KNOWN?  
   • One-shot model ⇒ question irrelevant, not discussed.

13. ARE PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes, implicitly: everyone observes others’ contributions before punishing.  
   • Systematic variation?  No.

14. IS THE PUNISHER’S IDENTITY KNOWN?  
   • Mentioned?  Not in the model.  Some outside experiments are cited where the identity was hidden, but nothing is modelled or predicted.

15. IS THE REWARDER’S IDENTITY KNOWN?  
   • Not applicable (no rewards modelled).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A.  Dependent variables used  
    • The paper’s central dependent variable is the Nash-equilibrium **contribution level** e*.  
    • It also analyses the “sum of benefits from the public project net of contribution and punishment costs” (joint surplus / average payoff).  
    • Efficiency in the sense of “actual ÷ maximum possible payoff” is mentioned descriptively, but no explicit efficiency ratio is calculated in the algebra or the figures.  Hence contribution and net surplus, not efficiency per se, are the formal outcomes.

B.  How many of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
    7 of 15: 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 13.  The remaining eight (3, 5, 9–12, 14, 15) never enter the model.

C.  How many parameters are systematically varied and linked to a **punishment treatment effect**?  
    Strictly speaking, none.  φ and n do appear in comparative-static inequalities, but the paper never reports “with-punishment minus without-punishment” changes in efficiency (or even in contribution) as those parameters are moved.  Every formal comparative static is about how altruism (a) or reciprocity (λ) changes equilibrium behaviour **within** a punishment environment.

D.  What predictions can we make about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency using only this paper?  
    • Little to nothing.  The model holds every parameter on the above list constant except φ and n, and efficiency is not computed.  
    • The only indirect hints are:  
        – If 2λφ > 1, punishment adds nothing (full cooperation already Nash); hence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency would be zero in that φ-region.  
        – When 2λφ < 1, punishment can raise contributions, so efficiency would presumably be higher with punishment, but the size of the improvement is not quantified as a function of φ or any other of the 15 parameters.  
        – All other listed parameters are simply not part of the model, so no prediction can be made.

In short, the paper is a theoretical exploration of how **preferences (altruism a and reciprocity λ)** interact with the existence of a punishment option; it does not study how structural, monetary-stake, peer-incentive, or information-display parameters change the punishment treatment effect on efficiency. Therefore virtually no usable quantitative predictions regarding the 15 specific parameters can be extracted.
reference_APA: Hwang, Sung-Ha & Bowles, Samuel (2012). Is altruism bad for cooperation?. JOURNAL OF ECONOMIC BEHAVIOR & ORGANIZATION.

Authors: Gavrilets, S

Article Title: The dynamics of injunctive social norms
Author Keywords: social norms; cooperation; punishment; decision-making; values
Keywords Plus: COLLECTIVE ACTION; PUNISHMENT; EVOLUTION; CONSERVE; MODELS; ENERGY
Abstract: Injunctive social norms are behaviours that one is expected to follow and expects others to follow in a given social situation; they are maintained by the threat of disapproval or punishment and by the process of internalization. Injunctive norms govern all aspects of our social life but the understanding of their effects on individual and group behaviour is currently rather incomplete. Here I develop a general mathematical approach describing the dynamics of injunctive norms in heterogeneous groups. My approach captures various costs and benefits, both material and normative, associated with norm-related behaviours including punishment and disapproval by others. It also allows for errors in decision-making and explicitly accounts for differences between individuals in their values, beliefs about the population state, and sensitivity to the actions of others. In addition, it enables one to study the consequences of mixing populations with different normative values and the effects of persuasive interventions. I describe how interactions of these factors affect individual and group behaviour. As an illustration, I consider policies developed by practitioners to abolish the norms of footbinding and female genital cutting, to decrease college students' drinking, and to increase pro-environmental behaviours. The theory developed here can be used for achieving a better understanding of historical and current social processes as well as for developing practical policies better accounting for human social behaviour.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?

Keywords Plus: SOCIAL DISORGANIZATION THEORY; COOPERATION; EMERGENCE; COHESION; DISORDER
Abstract: The prevalence of antisocial behavior varies across time and place. The likelihood of committing such behavior is affected by, and also affects, the local social environment. To further our understanding of this dynamic process, we conducted two studies of antisocial behavior, punishment, and social norms. These studies took place in two neighborhoods in Newcastle Upon Tyne, England. According to a previous study, Neighborhood A enjoys relatively low frequencies of antisocial behavior and crime and high levels of social capital. In contrast, Neighborhood B is characterized by relatively high frequencies of antisocial behavior and crime and low levels of social capital. In Study 1, we used an economic game to assess neighborhood differences in theft, third-party punishment (3PP) of theft, and expectation of 3PP. Participants also reported their perceived neighborhood frequency of cooperative norm violation (cheating). Participants in Neighborhood B thought that their neighbors commonly cheat but did not condone cheating. They stole more money from their neighbors in the game, and were less punitive of those who did, than the residents of Neighborhood A. Perceived cheating was positively associated with theft, negatively associated with the expectation of 3PP, and central to the neighborhood difference. Lower trust in one's neighbors and a greater subjective value of the monetary cost of punishment contributed to the reduced punishment observed in Neighborhood B. In Study 2, we examined the causality of cooperative norm violation on expectation of 3PP with a norms manipulation. Residents in Neighborhood B who were informed that cheating is locally uncommon were more expectant of 3PP. In sum, our results provide support for three potentially simultaneous positive feedback mechanisms by which the perception that others are behaving antisocially can lead to further antisocial behavior: (1) motivation to avoid being suckered, (2) decreased punishment of antisocial behavior, and (3) decreased expectation of punishment of antisocial behavior.    The paper never reports “group efficiency” (total or average payoff relative to maximum).  Hence efficiency is not analysed.

B.  Which of the 15 design parameters appear at all?  
   – 6 of them are explicitly described (1, 2, 7, 8, 12, 14).  
   – The remaining 9 are absent or not applicable.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss what happens when the parameter is **systematically varied**?  
   – For none of the 15 parameters are there experimental manipulations across different values.  
   – The only quasi-variation is individual heterogeneity in the *subjective* cost of £2 (parameter 7), used to predict punitiveness, but this is correlational, not an experimental change in the rule of the game.

D.  What predictions (if any) can be made—*solely from this paper*—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency?  
   • Because efficiency itself was never measured, and because none of the 15 parameters were experimentally varied, the paper gives almost no leverage for forecasting how changing those parameters would alter the efficiency gain (or loss) caused by allowing punishment.  
   • The only qualitative hint concerns parameter 7: raising the **perceived** cost of punishing (or making punishment objectively dearer) should reduce the amount of punishment delivered; if less punishment induces more antisocial behaviour, efficiency would probably fall.  Conversely, lowering the cost might increase punishment and (if deterrence works) raise efficiency.  
   • All other parameters are untouched; therefore the paper provides insufficient evidence to predict their separate or interactive effects on the punishment treatment effect.

In short, the study is informative about how neighbourhood context, perceived norms and subjective costs are associated with theft, punishment and expectations, but it does not manipulate any of the canonical public-goods design parameters and does not analyse efficiency.

Abstract: People often punish norm violations. In what cases is such punishment viewed as normative-a behavior that we should or even must engage in?
