Keywords Plus: MORAL HAZARD; JOB DESIGN; INFORMATION; PERFORMANCE; COLLUSION; IMPACT; ORGANIZATIONS; PRODUCTIVITY; DEMOGRAPHY; OWNERSHIP
Abstract: We study optimal team design. In our model, a principal assigns either heterogeneous agents to a team (a diverse team) or homogenous agents to a team (a specialized team) to perform repeated team production. We assume that specialized teams exhibit a productive substitutability (e.g., interchangeable efforts with decreasing returns to total effort), whereas diverse teams exhibit a productive complementarity (e.g., crossfunctional teams). Diverse teams have an inherent advantage in fostering desirable implicit/relational incentives that team members can provide to each other (tacit cooperation). In contrast, specialization both complicates the provision of cooperative incentives by altering the punishment agents can impose on each other for short expected career horizons and fosters undesirable implicit incentives (tacit collusion) for long expected horizons. As a result, expected compensation is first decreasing and then increasing in the discount factor for specialized teams, while expected compensation is always decreasing in the discount factor for diverse teams. We use our results to develop empirical implications about the association between team tenure and team composition, pay-for-performance sensitivity, and team culture.

Below I go through the 15 parameters one‐by‐one, reporting exactly what can (and cannot) be found in the paper “Optimal Team Composition: Diversity to Foster Implicit Team Incentives” (Glover & Kim, 2021).  Wherever possible I quote or paraphrase the relevant sentence(s) or equation(s) and state whether the paper makes any **systematic** prediction about varying that parameter on a *punishment* treatment effect—especially on group-level efficiency (actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff of full cooperation).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Number of players  
    • Mentioned?  YES.  Each “team” always has exactly two agents (p. 4 “…two agents make a binary effort decision…”).  
    • Values? Always fixed at 2; never varied.  
    • Systematic prediction on punishment treatment effect?  NO.  The paper never studies what happens if the group were larger or smaller.

2.  Number of rounds  
    • Mentioned?  INDIRECTLY.  Interactions are modeled as an infinitely repeated game with common discount factor δ.  
    • Value? “Permanently assigned … for all future periods” (p. 5).  
    • Systematic variation?  NO.  The horizon is never finitely truncated nor varied; only the discount factor is varied and that is not mapped to a known finite number of rounds.

3.  Chat enabled between players?  
    • Mentioned?  NO.

4.  Contribution “all-or-nothing”?  
    • Mentioned?  NO.  The model uses continuous or binary *effort* choices, not public-goods contributions.

5.  Contribution default / endowment framing?  
    • Mentioned?  NO.

6.  MPCR (marginal per-capita return) or equivalent “multiplication factor” in public-goods games  
    • Mentioned?  NO.  Output is a *probability of project success* f(ei,ej) multiplied by S, not an MPCR.

7.  Punishment cost to the punisher  
    • Mentioned?  NO.  “Punishment” is only implicit (grim-trigger reversion to a low-effort equilibrium).  There is no explicit costly peer sanction.

8.  Punishment magnitude (monetary loss per unit punishment)  
    • Mentioned?  NO.

9.  Reward enabled?  
    • Mentioned?  NO.

10. Reward cost  
    • Mentioned?  NO.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Mentioned?  NO.

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
    • Mentioned?  NO finite horizon is ever assumed; horizon is infinite.  Whether this is *known* is moot.

13. Peer outcomes shown (do agents observe others’ results)?  
    • Mentioned?  PARTIALLY.  Agents perfectly observe *each other’s effort choices* (“because of their proximity … each agent can observe the effort choice of the other”, p. 5).  
    • Systematic variation?  NO.  Monitoring is assumed perfect and never varied.

14. Whether punished player knows who punished them  
    • Mentioned?  NO.  There is no explicit punisher.

15. Whether rewarded player knows who rewarded them  
    • Mentioned?  NO.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  DEPENDENT VARIABLES USED IN THE PAPER
--------------------------------------------------------------------
• Expected wage / expected compensation (per-agent)  
• Principal’s expected per-period payoff (2 f(2) S − 4 E[w])  
• Probability of success f(ei,ej)  

The paper *does not* report, model, or optimise “group efficiency” in the public-goods sense (actual total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff).  Instead it concentrates on cost of providing incentives (wages) and the principal’s net payoff.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
B.  WHICH OF THE 15 PARAMETERS ARE EVEN MENTIONED?
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Only parameter 1 (number of players = 2) is explicitly specified.   
Parameter 13 (whether actions are observable) appears as an *assumption*, not as a variable.  
All other 13 parameters are absent.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
C.  PARAMETERS FOR WHICH THE PAPER DISCUSSES *SYSTEMATIC VARIATION* ON A PUNISHMENT TREATMENT EFFECT
--------------------------------------------------------------------
None (0/15).  No punishment treatment is implemented, and no parameter is systematically varied in that context.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
D.  WHAT CAN WE PREDICT—SOLELY FROM THIS PAPER—ABOUT HOW THOSE 15 PARAMETERS AND THEIR INTERACTIONS WOULD AFFECT THE PUNISHMENT TREATMENT EFFECT ON **EFFICIENCY**?
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Essentially nothing.  The paper is a theoretical analysis of team diversity in a repeated principal–agent model; it contains no public-goods game, no peer-to-peer costly punishment, and no efficiency ratio of realised vs. socially optimal payoff.  Consequently it offers no basis for predicting how any of the listed public-goods design parameters (chat, MPCR, punishment cost/magnitude, reward schemes, information disclosure, known horizon, etc.) would alter a *punishment* treatment effect on group efficiency.

In summary, this paper is not informative for the requested prediction task: (i) efficiency is not a reported dependent variable, (ii) punishment is not a treatment, and (iii) only one of the 15 experimental design parameters even appears (trivially fixed).

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are *mentioned*?

C.  For which parameters does the paper discuss their *systematic* effect on the punishment-treatment effect (for any dependent variable)?  
    2 out of 15:  
       • Parameter 7 (punishment cost T): higher T → higher p → lowers μ* (Proposition a).  
       • Parameter 8 (punishment magnitude C): higher C → lower p (via dp/dC = –D/(2C²)).  
    These effects are given analytically for p and μ*, not for efficiency.

D.  Predictions one could make **solely from this paper** about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) will influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency:  
    • The paper gives no direct information about pay-offs or efficiency, so almost no quantitative prediction about efficiency is possible.

    • For all other parameters (1-6, 9-15) the paper is silent, so no prediction can be grounded in the text.

Abstract: We extend the recent experimental literature on incomplete punishment networks in linear public goods games. Irrelevant – reward absent.

(2) Horizon knowledge never varied or analysed.

Keywords Plus: IMPLICIT ASSOCIATION TEST; PUNITIVE SENTIMENT; SOCIAL-EXCHANGE; PUNISHMENT; EVOLUTION; COGNITION; RECIPROCITY; BEHAVIOR; PSYCHOLOGY; STRATEGIES
Abstract: People regularly free ride on collective benefits, consuming them without contributing to their creation. In response, free riders are often moralized, becoming targets of negative moral judgments, anger, ostracism, or punishment. Moralization can change free riders' behavior (e.g., encouraging them to contribute or discouraging them from taking future benefits) or it can motivate others, including moralizers, to avoid or exclude free riders; these effects of moralization are critical to sustaining human cooperation. Based on theories of error management and fundamental social domains from evolutionary psychology, we propose that the decision to moralize is a cue-driven process. One cue investigated in past work is observing a person illicitly consume collective benefits. Here, we test whether the mind uses a 2nd cue: merely opting out of contributing. Use of this cue creates a phenomenon of preventive moralization: moralization of people who have not yet exploited collective benefits but who might-or might not-in the future. We tested for preventive moralization across 9 studies using implicit and explicit measures of moralization, a behavioral measure of costly punishment, mediation analyses of the underlying processes, and a nationally representative sample of almost 1,000 U.S. adults. Results revealed that merely opting out of contributing to the creation of exploitable collective benefits-despite not actually exploiting collective benefits-elicited moralization. Results further showed that preventive moralization is not due to the moralization of selfishness or deviance but instead follows from the uncertainty inherent in moralization decisions. These results imply that even people who will never exploit collective benefits can nonetheless be targets of moralization. We discuss implications for social and political dynamics.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
    6 out of 15: 1, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11.

C.  Which parameters are **systematically varied** and connected to the punishment treatment effect?  
    Only 3: 8, 10, 11 (all captured by the single variable α).

    – Parameter 1 (number of players) is varied for robustness only; no efficiency change is attributed to it.

D.  What can we predict—restricted solely to this paper?  
    • Moderate punishment/reward magnitude (α roughly between 0.1 and 0.6) together with a medium-to-high information level q (≈0.4–0.8) yields the highest efficiency because it lets SC–SD alliances form and keeps second-order free riders (C) in check.

Abstract: Evolutionary game dynamics in finite populations assumes that all mutations are equally likely, i.e., if there are n strategies a single mutation can result in any strategy with probability 1/n. However, in biological systems it seems natural that not all mutations can arise from a given state. Certain mutations may be far away, or even be unreachable given the current composition of an evolving population. These distances between strategies (or genotypes) define a topology of mutations that so far has been neglected in evolutionary game theory. In this paper we re-evaluate classic results in the evolution of cooperation departing from the assumption of uniform mutations. We examine two cases: the evolution of reciprocal strategies in a repeated prisoner's dilemma, and the evolution of altruistic punishment in a public goods game. In both cases, alternative but reasonable mutation kernels shift known results in the direction of less cooperation. We therefore show that assuming uniform mutations has a substantial impact on the fate of an evolving population. Our results call for a reassessment of the model-less approach to mutations in evolutionary dynamics.

     – Yes, they label it r (the total pot in the public goods game is multiplied by r). They use r = 3 in numerical examples.  
   • Systematic variation or predictions?  
     – No. They do not systematically vary r nor do they discuss how its variation would affect a punishment treatment effect.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mention in paper?  
     – Yes, they denote a punisher’s per‐defector cost as γ (e.g., γ = 0.3 in their simulations).  
   • Systematic variation or predictions?  
     – No. They set γ at 0.3 but do not systematically vary it or provide effect sizes for how changing γ alters punishment’s impact on long‐run outcomes.  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed)  
   • Mention in paper?  
     – Yes, denoted β (most examples use β = 1).  
   • Systematic variation or predictions?  
     – No. They do not systematically vary β or predict changes in punishment treatment effects under different β values.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mention in paper?  
     – No. Rewards do not appear in their models or discussion.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Mention in paper?  
      – No. They do not study any reward mechanism.  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)  
    • Mention in paper?  
      – No. Similarly, no mention in the paper.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    • Mention in paper?  
      – No. The repeated game uses a continuation probability δ, not a prespecified known endpoint. The authors never address whether players know that δ or a specific final round.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mention in paper?  
      – No. They do not discuss any explicit feedback or payoff observability among players.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Mention in paper?  
      – No. There is no mention of that possibility or of anonymity versus revealed punishers.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Mention in paper?  
      – No. Rewards are not part of the model, and no such parameter is discussed.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A–D SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?

   • The paper does not explicitly use “group efficiency” (i.e., actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff) as a dependent variable.  
   • Instead, their primary dependent variables are (i) the long‐run “abundance” or stationary fraction of each strategy (e.g., fraction of time spent in punishing versus nonpunishing states), and (ii) sometimes average payoffs in the evolutionary model. These are not the same as group efficiency.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

   • Mentioned to some degree:  
     1. Number of players (N and subgroup size n)  
     4. All‐or‐nothing contribution (implicitly: cooperators pay cost c, defectors pay 0)  
     6. MPCR‐like factor r  
     7. Punishment cost (γ)  
     8. Punishment magnitude (β)  
   • Not mentioned at all (or only indirectly stated to be absent):  
     2, 3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?

   • None. The paper does not report any explicit systematic variation of these parameters for the purpose of estimating or predicting a “punishment treatment effect,” whether on efficiency or on any other outcome.  

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

   • The paper provides no direct discussion of “efficiency” per se, nor does it systematically vary any of the 15 parameters to measure how these changes alter punishment’s impact. Consequently, on the basis of this paper alone, one can make little or no firm prediction about how each of the 15 parameters—or their interactions—would affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.  
   • In short, there is not enough information in this paper to draw definite conclusions about how each of the 15 parameters would shape the effect of punishment on group efficiency.

Authors: Takesue, H
Author Full Names: Takesue, H.
Article Title: Evolutionary prisoner's dilemma games on the network with punishment and opportunistic partner switching
Keywords Plus: PROMOTES COOPERATION; REPUTATION; COEVOLUTION; BEHAVIOR
Abstract: Punishment and partner switching are two well-studied mechanisms that support the evolution of cooperation. Observation of human behaviour suggests that the extent to which punishment is adopted depends on the usage of alternative mechanisms, including partner switching. In this study, we investigate the combined effect of punishment and partner switching in evolutionary prisoner's dilemma games conducted on a network. In the model, agents are located on the network and participate in the prisoner's dilemma games with punishment. In addition, they can opportunistically switch interaction partners to improve their payoff. Our Monte Carlo simulation showed that a large frequency of punishers is required to suppress defectors when the frequency of partner switching is low. In contrast, cooperation is the most abundant strategy when the frequency of partner switching is high regardless of the strength of punishment. Interestingly, cooperators become abundant not because they avoid the cost of inflicting punishment and earn a larger average payoff per game but rather because they have more numerous opportunities to be referred to as a role agent by defectors. Our results imply that the fluidity of social relationships has a profound effect on the adopted strategy in maintaining cooperation. Copyright (C) EPLA, 2018

Below I go through the 15 parameters one-by-one, quoting exactly what the paper says (or does not say) about each and, when possible, pointing to the relevant figure/table.  For every parameter I indicate whether the authors ever look at what happens when the parameter is systematically varied and whether this is tied to the **punishment treatment effect** (i.e., the change that would be observed when a punishment option is present vs. absent).  If a numerical effect size can be read directly from a figure or table I reproduce it; otherwise I state that no numerical effect size is provided.

────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
────────────────────────────────────────

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned: Yes.  “Parameters: N = 50 000” appears in every figure caption.  
   • Systematic variation & link to punishment effect: No.  The value is held constant; no figures/tables contrast different N’s.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned: Yes.  Each run lasts 10 000 × N Monte-Carlo periods and statistics are averaged over the next 20 000 × N periods.  
   • Systematic variation: No.  Rounds are never varied, nor are they tied to the punishment treatment effect.

3. Chat between players  
   • Mentioned: No.  The model is fully formal and contains no communication channel.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
   • Mentioned: Yes (implicitly).  The model is a binary Prisoner’s Dilemma: agents either “cooperate” (pay the cooperation cost) or “defect” (pay nothing); there is no continuous contribution choice.  
   • Systematic variation: No.  The binary rule is fixed; its effect is not evaluated.

5. Contribution default (withdrawal option)  
   • Mentioned: No.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor  
   • Closest analogue in the paper: the temptation to defect, b (1 < b < 2).  
   • Mentioned: Yes.  b is systematically varied in fig. 1.  
   • Predictions about punishment treatment effect: Only partial.  Fig. 1 shows that (ρ_C + ρ_P) falls as b rises, and the slope depends on punishment strength (α) and partner-switch rate (w).  However, there is no baseline *without punishment*, so the “treatment effect” of adding punishment cannot be isolated.  No numeric slope or regression is given.

7. Punishment cost (γ)  
   • Mentioned: Yes.  Default γ = 0.05; γ = 0, 0.5 are used in fig. 6.  
   • Systematic variation: Yes (fig. 6).  
   • Prediction: Higher γ shifts the composition toward cooperators and away from punishers when w is large (fig. 6b).  Exact numbers are only visible graphically; e.g. at w = 0.8 and α = 0 the cooperator share is ≈0.48 at γ = 0 and ≈0.62 at γ = 0.5.  Again no baseline without punishment is offered.

8. Punishment magnitude (α)  
   • Mentioned: Yes.  Extensively varied (α = 0, 0.1, 0.17, 0.24, 0.35, 0.5, 0.51, 0.88) in figs. 1–3, 6, 8.  
   • Systematic variation: Yes.  
   • Prediction:  
     – When partner switching is slow (w ≈ 0.1) stronger punishment (larger α) is *required* for cooperators + punishers to survive (fig. 3).  
     – When partner switching is fast (w ≥ 0.4) varying α has almost no effect on strategy frequencies (fig. 3).  
     – Numerical example from fig. 2a (w = 0.1):  α = 0.51 yields ρ_C ≈ 0.32, ρ_P ≈ 0.55, ρ_D ≈ 0.13; with α = 0.17 the defector share is ≈0.9.  Again no direct “with-punishment vs. without-punishment” contrast is provided.

9. Reward enabled  
   • Mentioned: No.  Only costly punishment is modelled.

10. Reward cost  
    • Mentioned: No.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Mentioned: No.

12. End-time known  
    • Mentioned: No.  Evolutionary simulations are infinite-horizon and the question of “known number of rounds” never arises.

13. Peer outcomes displayed  
    • Mentioned: No.

14. Punisher identity revealed  
    • Mentioned: No.

15. Rewarder identity revealed  
    • Mentioned: No.



────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────
A. Dependent variables.  
   – The paper never reports “group efficiency” (total actual payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff).  
   – Main dependent variables:  
     • ρ_C, ρ_P, ρ_D (population frequencies of cooperators, punishers, defectors)  
     • π_C, π_P, π_D (average *per-game* payoffs by strategy)  
     • Counts of strategy switches (n_{D→C}, n_{D→P}, etc.)  
   These are different from efficiency because they give no direct information on total surplus created.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  Six:  
   1 (number of players), 2 (round count), 4 (all-or-nothing cooperation, but fixed), 6 (b), 7 (γ), 8 (α).

C. For how many parameters does the paper *systematically vary* the parameter and discuss its effect on any dependent variable?  Three: 6 (b), 7 (γ), and 8 (α).  None of these analyses isolate the “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”

D. What predictions can be made—strictly from this paper—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions will affect the punishment treatment effect on *efficiency*?  
   • Almost none, because the authors never compute efficiency and never compare a “punishment” condition to a “no-punishment” baseline.  
   • One can only infer, indirectly, that when α is large and/or when w is large, total defection is curbed; hence efficiency would *probably* rise, but no quantitative relationship is given.  
   • For all other listed parameters (chat, knowledge of rounds, reward presence, etc.) the paper provides no information at all, so no prediction can be grounded in this source.

In short, the paper is useful for understanding how punishment strength, punishment cost, partner-switch frequency, and temptation to defect jointly shape the *composition* of strategies—but it does **not** report, let alone model, the effect of those parameters on the punishment treatment effect with respect to efficiency.

Authors: Gao, SP; Du, JM; Liang, JL
Author Full Names: Gao, Shiping; Du, Jinming; Liang, Jinling
Article Title: Evolution of cooperation under punishment
Keywords Plus: ANTISOCIAL PUNISHMENT; EMERGENCE; RULES; INSTITUTIONS; RECIPROCITY; PROMOTE
Abstract: Punishment has been considered as an effective mechanism for promoting and sustaining cooperation. In most existing models, punishment always comes as a third strategy alongside cooperation and defection, and it is commonly assumed to be executed based on individual decision rules rather than collective decision rules. Differently from previous works, we employ a democratic procedure by which cooperators cast votes independently and simultaneously for whether to impose punishment on defectors, and we establish a relationship between the cooperators' willingness to punish defectors (WTPD) and whether the punishment is inflicted on defectors. The results illustrate that the population can evolve to full cooperation under consensual punishment. It is noteworthy that, compared with autonomous punishment, whether consensual punishment is more in favor of cooperation crucially depends on the minimum number of votes required for punishment execution as well as the cooperators' WTPD. Our findings highlight the importance of collective decision making in the evolution of cooperation and may provide a mathematical framework for explaining the prevalence of democracy in modern societies.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter inventory based strictly on the content of the provided paper. Because the paper focuses on the replicator‐dynamic analyses of cooperation (specifically, on the fraction of cooperators and conditions under which cooperators come to dominate), it does not provide a direct analysis of how punishment affects group efficiency (i.e., the actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff), nor does it discuss most of the 15 parameters listed. Where parameters are mentioned at all, their effects are analyzed with respect to outcomes such as cooperation level or evolutionary stability, rather than efficiency. Numerical “effect sizes,” when reported, concern the interior fixed points or basin of attraction in the fraction of cooperators over time—again, not efficiency metrics. Below is how each parameter is (or is not) addressed in the paper, followed by the requested four‐part summary.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   – Mentioned? Yes. The paper denotes the group size by N.  
   – Does the paper systematically vary it? Yes, in several parts of the analysis and tables, N is varied (e.g., N = 5, 10, 20, 50).  
   – Any prediction or numeric effect on “punishment treatment effect on efficiency”?  
     • No. The authors do vary N but only discuss how this affects the fraction of cooperators and the replicator‐dynamic equilibria; they do not report efficiency outcomes or effect sizes regarding efficiency.  

2. Number of rounds  
   – Mentioned? No. There is no mention of multiple discrete rounds or a known/unknown end of play.  

3. Is chat enabled?  
   – Mentioned? No. The paper does not discuss any form of communication or chat.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   – Mentioned? The model assumes that “cooperators” contribute a fixed amount c and “defectors” contribute 0, but the paper does not systematically vary whether contributions are forced to be all‐or‐nothing. The authors do not analyze other contribution rules.  

5. Is the contribution default?  
   – Mentioned? No. The paper does not address having a default contribution or optional retraction from the public fund.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   – Mentioned? Yes. The paper refers to a parameter r (the “enforcement factor” or multiplier in the public goods game).  
   – Does the paper systematically vary it? Yes. It appears in tables and figures where r = 1.2, 2, 3, 4, etc.  
   – Any prediction or numeric effect on “punishment treatment effect on efficiency”?  
     • No. The authors discuss how increasing r can promote cooperation (e.g., expanding the basin of attraction to full cooperation), but do not give any quantitative effect on group efficiency.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   – Mentioned? Yes. The paper’s parameter α (alpha) represents the cost of punishing.  
   – Does the paper systematically vary it? Yes, in tables and figures.  
   – Any prediction or numeric effect on “punishment treatment effect on efficiency”?  
     • No. Variation of α is discussed only insofar as it helps or hinders achieving a stable high‐cooperation equilibrium. The paper does not mention efficiency.  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed)  
   – Mentioned? Yes. The paper’s parameter β (beta) represents this fine or penalty.  
   – Does the paper systematically vary it? Yes, in tables and figures (e.g., β = 1.5, 2, etc.).  
   – Any prediction or numeric effect on “punishment treatment effect on efficiency”?  
     • No. The discussion focuses on how β influences when defection can be suppressed, not on overall efficiency.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   – Mentioned? No. Apart from noting that some other experiments in the literature consider reward, the paper itself does not model or vary reward.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   – Mentioned? No.  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)  
   – Mentioned? No.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
   – Mentioned? No. There is no mention of participants knowing (or not knowing) when the game ends.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see others’ gains/losses each round)?  
   – Mentioned? No.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   – Mentioned? No.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   – Mentioned? No.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   The paper does not measure “group efficiency.” Its dependent variables center on:  
   • Fraction (or proportion) of cooperators evolving under various parameters.  
   • Average payoff of cooperators vs. defectors in replicator‐dynamic terms.  
   These are not explicitly framed as “group efficiency.”  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   Four:  
   1) Number of players (N).  
   2) MPCR or multiplication factor (r).  
   3) Punishment cost (α).  
   4) Punishment magnitude (β).  
   None of the other eleven parameters is discussed.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The paper only analyzes how the above four parameters (N, r, α, β) shape the fraction of cooperators (and sometimes the stability of full vs. partial cooperation).  
   • It never reports a numeric effect specifically on “punishment treatment effect” for “efficiency.” Instead, the outcome measure is the fraction of cooperators.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper provides no direct statements linking punishment to efficiency.  
   • It does imply that raising r and β, or lowering α (and sometimes lowering N), strengthens the basin of attraction to full cooperation—suggesting higher overall payoffs might follow when cooperators dominate.  
   • However, because punishment itself exacts costs, the net gain in total payoff (efficiency) versus a fully cooperative, no‐punishment scenario is never assessed. The paper never quantifies overall payoff or efficiency in these scenarios, only the evolution of cooperation and payoff differences between cooperators and defectors.  

Thus, little to no prediction about “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” can be made purely from the contents of this paper.

Authors: Singh, M; Garfield, ZH
Author Full Names: Singh, Manvir; Garfield, Zachary H.
Article Title: Evidence for third-party mediation but not punishment in Mentawai justice
Keywords Plus: COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; PSYCHOLOGY; LEADERSHIP; SOCIETIES
Abstract: Researchers argue that third parties help sustain human cooperation, yet how they contribute remains unclear, especially in small-scale, politically decentralized societies. Studying justice among Mentawai horticulturalists in Indonesia, we examined evidence for punishment and mediation by third parties. Across a sample of 444 transgressions, we find no evidence of direct third-party punishment. Most victims and aggrieved parties demanded payment, and if a transgressor faced punishment, this was never imposed by third parties. We find little evidence of indirect sanctions by third parties. Nearly 20% of transgressions were followed by no payment, and as predicted by dyadic models of sanctions, payments were less likely when transgressions were among related individuals. Approximately 75% of non-governmental mediators called were third parties, especially shamans and elders, and mediators were called more as cooperation was threatened. Our findings suggest that, among the Mentawai, institutionalized penalties function more to restore dyadic cooperation than to enforce norms. Singh and Garfield studied 444 transgressions among the Mentawai (Indonesia) and find evidence of third-party mediation but not punishment. They suggest that, for the Mentawai, penalties serve to restore cooperation more than enforce norms.

It also discusses how those evolve or fail to evolve under different parameter settings. Any references to “payoff” or “score” in the paper are used primarily for evolutionary updating (death–birth events) rather than to measure efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of Players  
   – Discussed?  
     The paper sets up a population of N×N individuals (with N=50), but it does not systematically vary the number of players, nor does it analyze different group sizes or total population sizes as a parameter.

   – Discussed?  
     The model runs for 1,000,000 generations under an evolutionary simulation, but there is no concept of a repeated multi‐round (finitely or infinitely repeated) public goods game.      Not discussed. The paper does not explore varying how many times the same set of players interacts.

   – Discussed?  
     Not mentioned.

     Not mentioned.

     Not mentioned.

     None.

6. Marginal Per Capita Return (MPCR) or Multiplication Factor  
   – Discussed?

   – Predictions of Systematic Variation (Any Dependent Variable)?  
     They analyze how higher or lower r affects the evolution of cooperation in the presence of punishment (for instance, Figures 5 and 6 plot the steady‐state levels of cooperation, punishment severity, threshold, and strictness as r is varied). Note that they do not directly measure “group efficiency” as total payoff/maximum payoff. Instead, they track whether cooperation and punishment evolve.  
     Numeric Effect Sizes?  
     The paper provides color gradients (Figures 5 and 6) but does not provide explicit numeric effect sizes regarding the difference between with‐ vs. without‐punishment outcomes. Its primary focus is on whether cooperation and punishment reach high or low levels for given r.

7. Punishment Cost to Impose a Single Unit of Punishment  
   – Discussed?  
     The paper’s notation for the cost to punish is tied to f (punishment severity) and the exponential term that depends on the opponent’s cooperation level.    – Discussed?

   – Predictions of Systematic Variation (Any Dependent Variable)?

     Numeric Effect Sizes?

    – Discussed?

    – Predictions of Systematic Variation?  
      None.

14. When a Player Is Punished, Do They Know Who Punished Them?  
    – Discussed?  
      Not mentioned. The model does not include knowledge or anonymity details about punishment.  
    – Predictions of Systematic Variation?  
      None.

15. When a Player Is Rewarded, Do They Know Who Rewarded Them?  
    – Discussed?  
      Not mentioned. The model does not include any rewards.  
    – Predictions of Systematic Variation?  
      None.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   No. The main dependent variables are an individual’s continuous cooperation level (x), punishment severity (f), punishment threshold (u), and “strictness” (a). Although the paper does compute a “score” (payoff from the public goods plus/minus punishment costs), that score is used strictly for the evolutionary birth–death process, not for measuring efficiency as “actual total payoff over maximum total payoff.” Hence, “cooperation level” ≠ “efficiency.”

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned as fixed (group size = 4) but not varied: Number of players.  
   • Systematically varied in the paper:  
       – #6 MPCR (the “efficiency of public goods,” denoted r).  
       – #8 Punishment magnitude (via β).  
   • The rest (#1, #2, #3, #4, #5, #7, #9–#15) are either not discussed at all or merely set to particular values without any examination of their systematic variation.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   Only two:  
   • #6 (r) is systematically varied, and the paper shows its effects on whether cooperation and punishment evolve.  
   • #8 (β) is systematically varied, and the paper shows that a sufficiently large β is required for high cooperation/punishment.  
   No other parameters are systematically manipulated; the paper presents no numerical “effect sizes” regarding group efficiency.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper, what would they be?  
   Because the paper does not measure or report efficiency, there is no direct information about “the treatment effect on group efficiency.” One might infer that higher punishment magnitude (β) or appropriate levels of r would facilitate cooperation, which in some real‐world sense could improve group‐wide outcomes. However, the paper does not frame or quantify those outcomes as “efficiency.” With the limited discussion available, we thus cannot specify numerical or definitive predictions for how each of the 15 parameters and their interactions would affect a punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency. The paper primarily shows that:  
   – Under spatial structure, strict punishment fosters high cooperation;  
   – Under random mixing, more graduated (“less strict”) punishment fosters high cooperation;  
   – Neither scenario is explicitly connected to efficiency measurements in the sense of total/maximum payoff.  

Those are the only predictions we can offer based on the content of the paper alone.

   a) Discussion in the paper:

    a) Discussion in the paper:  
       – There is no reward mechanism in these experiments, so not mentioned.  
    b) Predictions about varying rewarder identification:  
       – Not discussed.

FINAL SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables?

   – The paper also mentions “cooperation” or “contributions” as important but conceptually distinct from efficiency, since one can have punishment arising in ways that do not necessarily elevate group payoffs.

     (1) Number of players,  
     (2) Number of rounds,

Abstract: In explaining the pressing issue in biology and social sciences how cooperation emerges in a population of self-interested individuals, researchers recently pay intensive attentions to the role altruistic punishment plays. However, as higher-order cooperators, survival of punishers is puzzling due to their extra cost in regulating norm violators. Previous works have highlighted the importance of individual mobility in promoting cooperation. Yet its effect on punishers remains to be explored. In this work we incorporate this feature into modeling the behavior of punishers, who are endowed with a choice between leaving current place or staying and punishing defectors. Results indicate that optimal mobility level of punishers is closely related to the cost of punishing. For considerably large cost, there exists medium tendency of migration which favors the survival of punishers. This holds for both the direct competition between punishers and defectors and the case where cooperators are involved, and can also be observed when various types of punishers with different mobility tendencies fight against defectors simultaneously. For cheap punishment, mobility does not provide with punishers more advantage even when they are initially rare. We hope our work provide more insight into understanding the role individual mobility plays in promoting public cooperation.

Abstract: This article examines the rules and practices of waiting in line as a system of informal order, showing that despite its reputation for drudgery, the queue offers rich insights about social norms and the psychology of cooperation. Abstract: Broken windows: the metaphor has changed New York and Los Angeles. Yet it is far from undisputed whether the broken windows policy was causal for reducing crime. The scope of the theory is not confined to crime. The theory claims that crime is inextricably linked to social order more generally. PARAMETER‐BY‐PARAMETER DISCUSSION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1) Number of players  
   • Not mentioned in the paper.

2) Number of rounds

3) Is chat enabled between players?

4) Is the contribution "all or nothing"?  
   • Not mentioned in the paper.  
   • No predictions or effect sizes are given for making contributions all‐or‐nothing.

5) Is the contribution default?  
   • Not mentioned in the paper.  
   • No predictions or effect sizes are given about any default contribution mechanic.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
   • Not discussed at all in the paper.  
   • No predictions about MPCR or similar parameters.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussed in the paper as the parameter c (“the cost associated with policing”).  
   • The paper systematically varies c in its theoretical analysis (Figures 1–3). However, the paper does not use “efficiency” (total payoff ÷ maximum payoff) as its dependent measure; instead, it examines how c influences the evolutionary stability of three strategies (Honest, Cheat, and Police).  
   • Example effect sizes (all drawn directly from text and figures, referring to stable equilibria in proportions of strategies rather than “efficiency”):  
       – In Figure 1(a), with c = 0.5, p = 2, b = 3, and θ = 1, the population converges to (H ≈ 1/3, P ≈ 1/2, C ≈ 1/6).  
       – If c is larger or if other parameters are set unfavorably, the population may spiral toward all cheating or other mixed equilibria.  
   • No explicit mention of group efficiency is provided.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Discussed in the paper as the parameter p (“the punishment associated with cheating if caught”).  
   • Systematically varied in Figures 1–3 in combination with other parameters. When p is increased, cheating becomes riskier, and equilibria tend to have fewer cheaters. Several numerical examples appear in the text:  
       – With p = 2, b = 3, c = 0.5, the stable mix is (H ≈ 1/3, P ≈ 1/2, C ≈ 1/6).  
       – With p = 4, b = 5, c = 0.5, the stable mix is (H ≈ 0.65, P ≈ 0.25, C ≈ 0.10).  
       – With p = 6, b = 7, c = 0.5, the stable mix is (H ≈ 0.76, P ≈ 0.167, C ≈ 0.071).  
   • Again, the paper does not relate these changes in p to a measure of “efficiency,” but rather to changes in strategy frequencies.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussed in the paper via the benefit parameter b > 0 (“the benefit to the punisher when they catch a cheat”).  
   • The paper differentiates “opportunistic punishment” (b > 0) from “altruistic punishment” (b = 0). It shows that when b = 0 (purely altruistic punishment), policing fails and the population tends toward cheating. With b > 0, punishment can sustain a stable mix of honest and policing strategies.  
   • No mention of efficiency as a dependent variable, only the equilibrium mix of strategies.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Not discussed in the paper.  
   • There is no separate cost for “rewarding” in the model—only the cost c for policing/punishing.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
   • Not discussed as a separate “rewarding‐cooperator” mechanism. The paper’s b parameter is strictly the payoff to the punisher, rather than a separate “reward magnitude for good behavior.”  
   • No predictions about a stand‐alone reward‐granting mechanism.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?  
   • Not mentioned in the paper.  
   • No predictions given about this.

13) Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • The paper assumes that misreported or “cheating” research can be uncovered by policing, but it does not systematically vary how much or which outcome information is shown.  
   • No effect sizes or predictions for systematically altering information display.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Not mentioned in the paper.  
   • No predictions given.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Not mentioned in the paper (and the model does not address direct “rewarding” of cooperators).  
   • No predictions given.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FOUR‐PART SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper does discuss payoffs (it refers to them as a “fitness” or “expected payoff” in a game‐theoretic sense) but never defines or measures “efficiency” as (total payoff) ÷ (maximum possible payoff).  
   • Its main dependent variables are the proportions of scientists adopting each of the three strategies (Honest, Police, Cheat) over time. The paper also refers to average fitness but does not use “efficiency” or “group efficiency” as a named outcome metric.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Three parameters appear explicitly (although in the paper’s own notation):  
       – Parameter 7, “punishment cost” (c).  
       – Parameter 8, “punishment magnitude” (p).  
       – Parameter 9, “whether a reward is enabled” (captured by b > 0).  
   • None of the others (1–6, 10–15) are discussed or varied in this study.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for any dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Only for the three parameters above (7: cost c, 8: punishment magnitude p, and 9: presence of reward b). The paper systematically varies them to show how different (c, p, b) values shift the long‐run proportions of policing, honesty, and cheating. It does not address “efficiency” or provide an effect size on efficiency; it focuses on strategy shares and stability/cycling.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not analyze efficiency, so it provides little to no direct basis for predictions about actual total payoff or total group efficiency. It centers on whether punishment (with reward for policing) can sustain honesty or whether the group collapses into widespread cheating. Consequently:  
       – Parameters 7, 8, and 9 (c, p, b) appear crucial for preventing universal cheating in the model—and might be expected to influence overall payoffs if one equates “more honesty” with “higher group welfare.”  
       – However, the paper never directly measures or reports group efficiency, so one cannot make a firm efficiency prediction beyond the general idea that more cheating likely reduces group‐wide welfare.  
   • For all the other parameters (1–6, 10–15), nothing in this paper offers guidance on how they might alter a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”

Article Title: Conditions for the Emergence of Shared Norms in Populations with Incompatible Preferences
Keywords Plus: COLLECTIVE ACTION; COMPUTATIONAL MODEL; LOCAL CONVERGENCE; GROUP-PERFORMANCE; SOCIAL NORMS; PUNISHMENT; COOPERATION; REPUTATION; GAMES; COORDINATION
Abstract: Understanding norms is a key challenge in sociology. Nevertheless, there is a lack of dynamical models explaining how one of several possible behaviors is established as a norm and under what conditions. Analysing an agent-based model, we identify interesting parameter dependencies that imply when two behaviors will coexist or when a shared norm will emerge in a heterogeneous society, where different populations have incompatible preferences. Our model highlights the importance of randomness, spatial interactions, non-linear dynamics, and self-organization. It can also explain the emergence of unpopular norms that do not maximize the collective benefit. Furthermore, we compare behavior-based with preference-based punishment and find interesting results concerning hypocritical punishment. Strikingly, pressuring others to perform the same public behavior as oneself is more effective in promoting norms than pressuring others to meet one's own private preference. Finally, we show that adaptive group pressure exerted by randomly occuring, local majorities may create norms under conditions where different behaviors would normally coexist.

Below is an item‐by‐item account of what the paper by Helbing et al. (2014) does or does not say about each of the 15 parameters you listed, followed by the requested four‐part summary (A–D). Throughout, “the paper” refers exclusively to the text and figures from Helbing et al. (2014) as provided.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Discussed? No. The paper does use an agent‐based model on a grid, but it does not specify or systematically vary the total number of players for purposes of comparison.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment? No. There is no exploration of how changing the number of players would affect any treatment effect, and no numerical effect sizes are reported.

2. Number of rounds
   • Discussed? No. The model in the paper evolves in (simulation) time steps, but there is no notion of discrete “rounds” in the sense of a repeated public goods game.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment? No. The paper does not address this parameter.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussed? No.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment? No.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussed? No.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment? No.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Discussed? No.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment? No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Discussed? No. The paper uses a payoff structure based on two parameters A and B and does not employ the standard MPCR concept.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment? No.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussed? Yes (the paper denotes it as C, sometimes combined into L = (k+1)·C).  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment? Yes, but not for “efficiency” per se. The paper systematically varies C (and hence L) to explore how punishment can enforce a single norm or fail to do so (e.g., Figures 8 and 9). No numerical effect size on “group efficiency” is given; rather, the discussion focuses on whether a shared behavior (a norm) emerges and on the proportions of punishers.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted for each unit of punishment imposed)
   • Discussed? Yes (the paper sets F = k · C, so F depends on C).  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment? Yes, in conjunction with the punishment cost C, but again only in terms of whether norms form. The paper does not report an effect size on “efficiency” but shows that higher punishment levels L = (k+1)C can shift the system from coexistence of behaviors to near‐unanimous adoption of one norm (Figures 8 and 9).

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussed? No.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment? No.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Discussed? No.  
    • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment? No.

11. Reward magnitude
    • Discussed? No.  
    • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment? No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
    • Discussed? No.  
    • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment? No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?
    • Discussed? No. The paper does not specify information feedback of how much each peer gained or lost.  
    • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment? No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Discussed? No.  
    • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment? No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Discussed? No.  
    • Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?

The paper does not use “group efficiency” (actual total payoff / maximum possible total payoff) as its primary dependent variable. Instead, it studies whether one behavior eventually becomes a “shared norm,” the coexistence of behaviors, or the fraction of individuals performing certain actions. The main outcome variables include:  
• Whether a single norm (consensus) emerges or multiple behaviors persist.  
• The fraction of the population that adopts each behavior.  
• Occasional references to individuals’ payoffs (e.g., Figure 4 shows average payoff over time), but not framed as “efficiency.”  

These variables differ from efficiency in that they do not measure how close the group’s total payoff is to a theoretical maximum; instead, they reflect the dynamics of norm formation, path dependence, and local versus global consensus.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

• Only two of the 15 parameters appear:  
  (7) Punishment cost (C).  
  (8) Punishment magnitude (F = k·C).  

No other parameters from the list are mentioned.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?

• The paper systematically varies exactly two parameters in its discussion:  
  (7) Punishment cost C (and the combined punishment level L = (k+1)C).  
  (8) Punishment magnitude F (through F = k·C).  

• This variation is related to whether or not a norm is established—i.e., how likely the population is to end up in behavioral consensus—rather than any direct measure of “efficiency.”

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

The paper does not analyze group efficiency and does not address most of the 15 parameters. Consequently, it provides almost no basis for predicting how those parameters would affect a punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency in a public goods game. Even for punishment cost (parameter 7) and punishment magnitude (parameter 8), the paper focuses on whether one behavior becomes a norm. Although one might guess that enforcing behavioral consensus could influence total payoff, the paper presents no direct analysis or effect sizes for “efficiency.” Thus, little can be concluded regarding all 15 parameters’ (or their interactions’) influence on the punishment treatment effect for efficiency.

Authors: Weibull, JW; Salomonsson, M

Article Title: Natural selection and social preferences

Keywords Plus: EVOLUTIONARILY STABLE STRATEGIES; MULTILEVEL SELECTION; COMPETITION; MUTATION; BEHAVIOR; HISTORY
Abstract: A large number of individuals are randomly matched into groups, where each group plays a finite symmetric game. Individuals breed true. The expected number of surviving offspring depends on own material payoff, but may also, due to cooperative breeding and/or reproductive competition, depend on the material payoffs to other group members. The induced population dynamic is equivalent with the replicator dynamic for a game with payoffs derived from those in the original game. We apply this selection dynamic to a number of examples, including prisoners' dilemma games with and without a punishment option, coordination games, and hawk-dove games. For each of these, we compare the outcomes with those obtained under the standard replicator dynamic. By way of a revealed-p reference argument, our selection dynamic can explain certain altruistic and spiteful behaviors that are consistent with individuals having social preferences. Below I follow the requested five-step format.  All statements are taken verbatim or are direct logical implications from the contents, figures and equations of “Natural Selection and Social Preferences” (Weibull & Salomonsson, 2005).  No outside sources are used.

-------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER–BY–PARAMETER CHECK
-------------------------------------------------
(1) Number of players  
• Mentioned?  Yes – every formal and numerical example is a two-player (n = 2) game (Sections 2–3).  
• Systematically varied?  No.  The paper never analyses n ≠ 2, so no prediction on how changing n alters the punishment treatment effect.

(2) Number of rounds  
• Mentioned?  No.  All games are one-shot (or one shot + a punishment stage) and the number of repetitions is never varied.  
• Prediction?  None.

(3) Chat enabled?  
• Mentioned?  Not at all.  
• Prediction?  None.

(4) “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
• Mentioned?  Yes – cooperation (C) versus defection (D) is binary (Sections 3.1 & 3.2).  
• Prediction when varied?  Not discussed; only the binary case is analysed.

(5) Contribution default / disclose rule  
• Mentioned?  No.  
• Prediction?  None.

(6) MPCR / multiplication factor  
• Mentioned?  Only indirectly.  In the payoff matrix  
    Π = [[2, a], [b, 1]]  
“a” and “b” play the role of returns to own and others’ contributions, but the authors never call them MPCR and never connect them to the punishment treatment effect.  
• Prediction?  None that links systematic changes in a or b to the *difference* between punishment and no-punishment treatments.

(7) Punishment cost to the punisher (c)  
• Mentioned?  Yes – see Eq. (17) and Figs. 5–7.  
• Systematic variation?  Indirectly.  Equations and figures show how the size of the “co‐operative Nash-equilibrium component” expands as c falls (because CP then becomes less dominated by CN).  For example, in Fig. 6 (c = 0.3) the upper bound of that component is p̄≈0.75, versus ≈0.63 in Fig. 5 (same d but defined by the material game).  
• Numerical effect on *efficiency*?  Not provided.  Dependent variables are population shares and dynamical attractors, not efficiency, so no effect size on efficiency can be extracted.

(8) Punishment magnitude (d)  
• Mentioned?  Yes – see same sections.  “Harsh” punishment is defined by b – d < 2.  
• Systematic variation?  Yes – the condition b – d determines whether a cooperative equilibrium component exists at all.  Stronger punishment (smaller b – d) increases the likelihood that the population converges to cooperation (Fig. 7).  
• Numerical efficiency effect?  No number is reported; same caveat as (7).

(9) Whether a reward option is enabled  
• Mentioned?  Yes – Section 4 analyses a decision node where the acting player may *reward* (r > 0) or *punish* (r < 0).  
• Systematic variation?  Only a static inequality (Eq. 21) is derived; the paper does not run dynamics with and without rewards, so no prediction on treatment effects.

(10) Reward cost (c in Section 4)  
• Mentioned?  Yes in Eq. (21).  
• Systematic variation?  Only algebraically; no dynamic or payoff results are produced.

(11) Reward magnitude (r)  
• Same status as (10).

(12) Finite-horizon known?  Not mentioned.

(13) Peer outcomes shown?  Not mentioned.

(14) Punisher identified?  Not mentioned.

(15) Rewarder identified?  Not mentioned.

-------------------------------------------------
REQUESTED SUMMARY
-------------------------------------------------
A.  Does the paper use group *efficiency* (total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
No.  The principal dependent variables are  
• the *derived* fitness payoffs (φ(·,·));  
• the fraction of the population playing each pure strategy (replicator share x);  
• the type and stability of stationary states (Nash equilibria, attractors).  
“Efficiency” in the experimental-economics sense (actual-over-maximum total payoff) never appears.

B.  Which (and how many) of the 15 listed design parameters are even mentioned?  
Parameter numbers 1, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11 – eight in total.

C.  For which (how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* that parameter on the punishment treatment effect for any dependent variable?  
Only for two parameters: 7 (punishment cost) and 8 (punishment magnitude).  Even for these, the outcome variable is *cooperative population share / stability*, not efficiency.

D.  If forced to predict, solely from this paper, how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency:  
• Lower punishment cost (7) and larger punishment magnitude (8) are predicted to enlarge the basin of attraction of cooperative states.  If one equates “more cooperation” with “higher efficiency,” then lower c and/or higher d should make the punishment treatment raise efficiency by more.  
• The model gives no lever to predict anything about parameters 2, 3, 5, 12–15.  
• Number of players (1) might matter because all proofs assume n = 2; with n > 2 the derivations do not hold, so no prediction can be extracted.  
• Binary versus continuous contributions (4) is fixed; no comparative-static result is available.  
• Rewards (9–11) can substitute for punishments when the fitness function φ is *positively* responsive to the other’s material payoff (co-operative breeding), but the paper provides only a static inequality (21).  Efficiency implications remain undefined.  

Hence, on the basis of the present paper alone, one can make only very weak, purely qualitative efficiency predictions and only for punishment cost and magnitude; for the other 13 parameters the paper is silent.
reference_APA: Weibull, JW & Salomonsson, M (2006). Natural selection and social preferences. JOURNAL OF THEORETICAL BIOLOGY.

Authors: Li, XH; Molleman, L; van Dolder, D
Author Full Names: Li, Xueheng; Molleman, Lucas; van Dolder, Dennie
Article Title: Do descriptive social norms drive peer punishment? Conditional punishment strategies and their impact on cooperation
Author Keywords: Cooperation; Peer punishment; Decision-making experiment; Sanctioning; Online experiment; Conditional strategies
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; EVOLUTION; RECIPROCITY; BEHAVIOR; CULTURE; EMERGENCE; INFORMATION; STRANGERS; FAIRNESS
Abstract: Peer punishment is widely considered a key mechanism supporting cooperation in human groups. Although much research shows that human behavior is shaped by the prevailing social norms, little is known about how punishment decisions are impacted by the social context. We present a set of large-scale incentivized experiments in which participants (999 American participants recruited via Amazon Mechanical Turk) could punish their partner conditional on either the level of cooperation or the level of punishment displayed by others who previously interacted in the same setting. While many participants punish independently of levels of cooperation or punishment, a substantial portion punishes free riding more severely when cooperation is more common ('norm enforcement'), or when free riding is more severely punished by others ('conformist punishment'). With a dynamic model we demonstrate that conditional punishment strategies can substantially promote cooperation. In particular, conformist punishment helps cooperation to gain a foothold in a population, and norm enforcement helps to maintain cooperation at high levels. Our results provide solid empirical evidence of conditional punishment strategies and illustrate their possible implications for the dynamics of human cooperation.

Below, “mentioned” means that the paper gives an explicit value or description for the parameter.  
“Systematically varied / effect estimated” means the paper reports what happens when the parameter itself is exogenously changed (e.g., two treatment levels of group size).  
All page, table, or figure references are to the single paper reproduced above.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------  
PARAMETER–BY–PARAMETER CHECK  

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned: Yes – every interaction is a two-person Prisoner’s Dilemma (Section 2.1).  
   • Systematically varied / effect estimated: No. The study only uses dyads, so no inference about changing group size on any outcome, let alone on the “punishment treatment effect.”

2. Number of rounds (length of interaction)  
   • Mentioned: Yes – the game is one-shot (two sequential stages within the single round).  
   • Systematically varied: No.

3. Chat (pre-play communication)  
   • Mentioned: No – there is no opportunity for chat and this is never discussed.  
   • Systematically varied: No.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution decision  
   • Mentioned: Yes – cooperation is binary (“cooperate” vs. “defect”) (Section 2.1).  
   • Systematically varied: No.

5. “Contribution default / withdrawal from a fund”  
   • Mentioned: No – not relevant to a binary PD.  
   • Systematically varied: No.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned: Indirectly – the payoff matrix is fixed: mutual C = 18 points each; unilateral D = 25/9; mutual D = 16/16.  
   • Systematically varied: No.

7. Punishment cost (per unit)  
   • Mentioned: Yes – 1 point to the punisher per deduction point assigned (Section 2.1).  
   • Systematically varied: No.

8. Punishment magnitude (per unit)  
   • Mentioned: Yes – 3 points deducted from the target per deduction point (Section 2.1).  
   • Systematically varied: No.

9. Presence of a reward option  
   • Mentioned: No – only punishment is possible.  
   • Systematically varied: No.

10. Reward cost (per unit)  
    • Not applicable.  

11. Reward magnitude (per unit)  
    • Not applicable.

12. Whether the number of rounds is known  
    • Mentioned: Yes – because the game is announced as one-shot, participants trivially know when it ends (only one decision per stage).  
    • Systematically varied: No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mentioned: Partly – participants are told the partner’s Stage-1 action (cooperate/defect) before deciding whether to punish. They are also shown payoff-irrelevant “reference-group” statistics.  
    • Systematically varied: No treatment contrasts in which feedback visibility differs.

14. Is the identity of the punisher revealed?  
    • Mentioned: Not explicitly. Because there are only two players, the recipient could in principle infer who punished, but the paper never discusses identity revelation, and it is not varied.

15. Is the identity of the rewarder revealed?  
    • Not applicable (no reward option).

---------------------------------------------------------------------------  
EFFECT OF ANY PARAMETER ON A “PUNISHMENT TREATMENT EFFECT”  

The paper never compares “with-punishment” versus “without-punishment” treatments, never reports efficiency (total or average payoff as a fraction of the cooperative maximum), and never manipulates any of the 15 parameters. Accordingly, it contains no numerical estimates of how changing any parameter would alter the punishment treatment effect on efficiency—or on any other dependent variable.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------  
SUMMARY  

A. Dependent variables used  
   • Cooperation rate (fraction of players choosing “cooperate”).  
   • Punishment intensity (deduction points assigned).  
   • No measure of group efficiency, total payoff, or average payoff is reported.

B. Parameters mentioned  
   Seven of the 15 parameters are explicitly described (1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12; parameter 13 is only partially touched upon). The remaining parameters are absent or not applicable.

C. Parameters whose systematic variation is analysed  
   Zero. The study fixes all parameters; therefore it yields no empirical or simulated effect sizes for changing any of them on any “punishment treatment effect.”

D. Predictive leverage for the present task  
   Because the paper:  
   • does not study public-goods settings;  
   • does not manipulate the existence of punishment or any of the 15 structural parameters;  
   • and does not report efficiency,  
   it offers virtually no direct evidence for forecasting how introducing punishment will change efficiency as a function of those parameters. At best, one could note that the punishment technology used (cost = 1, impact = 3) still allowed substantial cooperation (≈ 66 %) and moderate punishment (≈ 2.5 points on average) in dyads. Extrapolating to larger groups, multiple rounds, or different punishment costs/impacts would, however, go beyond the data provided.

Hence, based solely on this paper, little to no prediction can be made about how any of the 15 parameters—or their interactions—will shape the efficiency effect of adding punishment to a public-goods game.

Author Full Names: De Geest, Lawrence R.; Stranlund, John K.; Spraggon, John M.
Article Title: Deterring poaching of a common pool resource
Author Keywords: Common pool resources; Deterrence; Experiments; Poaching; Sanctions

Abstract: We present results from common pool resource experiments designed to examine the ability of a group of resource users, called insiders, to simultaneously manage their own exploitation and defend their resource from encroachment by outsiders. The insiders can use communication, peer monitoring and sanctions to coordinate their decisions. In addition, they can sanction any outsiders they observe. We vary the insiders' ability to observe and sanction the outsiders from no observability to partial and full observability. We find a striking non-monotonicity between observability of the outsiders and levels of poaching. Poaching was higher under partial monitoring than zero monitoring, and was lower and more stable under full monitoring. Although full observability allowed the insiders to better coordinate their own harvests, they were unable to fully deter poaching because their sanctions were far too low and they were unwilling to punish low levels of poaching. Below I go through the 15 parameters one at a time.  
For each parameter I report  

(1) Whether the paper explicitly states the parameter and, if so, its value(s);  
(2) Whether the paper makes ANY prediction (ex-ante or ex-post) about how *systematically varying* that parameter would influence the “punishment treatment effect”.  
Because the study does not include a “no-punishment” baseline, the only way the authors can speak to a “punishment treatment effect” is indirectly—by comparing the three monitoring treatments that all *allow* punishment but differ in how easy it is to *direct it at outsiders*.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
(1) Yes. 8 per group‐of-groups (5 insiders, 3 outsiders).  
(2) No systematic variation; no predictions.

2. Number of rounds  
(1) Yes. 15 periods; subjects were told this.  
(2) Not varied; no predictions tied to changing the horizon.

3. Chat enabled?  
(1) Yes. Insiders may chat in every odd-numbered period; outsiders never.  
(2) Chat opportunity is held fixed; no predictions about changing it.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
(1) Explicitly continuous: each subject chooses 0–12 tokens to invest.  
(2) Not varied; no predictions.

5. “Contribution default” (withdrawal vs. deposit frame)  
(1) Not explicitly discussed as a design dimension; subjects *invest* up to 12 tokens.  
(2) No discussion; no predictions.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor  
(1) Non-linear CPR technology with a = 31, b = 0.4; the resulting return schedule is shown in Table 1 and the “Initial Payoff Table”.  
(2) Not varied; the paper cites earlier work that varied linear vs. non-linear payoffs, but makes no new prediction here.

7. Punishment cost per unit  
(1) Yes. One laboratory dollar to the punisher.  
(2) Not varied; no predictions about changing it.

8. Punishment magnitude per unit  
(1) Yes. Each point deducts 3 dollars from the target.  
(2) Not varied; no predictions about changing it.

9. Reward enabled?  
(1) No. Rewards are absent.  
(2) Consequently no predictions.

10 & 11. Reward cost and magnitude  
(1) Not applicable.  
(2) No discussion.

12. Is the number of rounds known?  
(1) Yes, subjects were told there would be 15 periods.  
(2) Not varied; no predictions.

13. Peer-outcome visibility (monitoring)  
(1) YES. This is the *only* parameter the authors manipulate:  
 • Zero Monitoring – insiders cannot see any outsider’s harvests.  
 • Partial Monitoring – each insider sees 1 randomly chosen outsider.  
 • Full Monitoring – insiders see all 3 outsiders.  
(2) Predictions and empirical effects:  
 Predicted: More visibility ⇒ stronger deterrence, lower poaching, higher insider pay-offs/efficiency.  
 Observed numerical effects (selected):  
  – Average outsider harvests (Table 3):  
   Zero 6.83 Partial 7.98 Full 5.99  
   Thus, compared with Zero, Full lowers outsider harvests by −0.84 tokens; compared with Partial, Full lowers them by −1.99 tokens.  
  – Final *insider* efficiency (Table 8):  
   Zero 0.23 Partial 0.08 Full 0.32  
   Hence, moving from Zero→Full raises insider efficiency by +0.09; moving from Partial→Full raises it by +0.24; moving from Zero→Partial *reduces* it by −0.15.  
  – Final *outsider* efficiency (Table 9):  
   Zero 0.46 Partial 0.29 Full 0.32.  
  These are the only systematic effect sizes the paper provides.

14. Punisher identity known?  
(1) Yes. The standard Fehr-Gächter anonymity is used: targets do *not* know who punished them.  
(2) Not varied; the authors only remark that anonymity “may have important consequences”, but give no prediction of varying it.

15. Rewarder identity known?  
(1) Not applicable (no rewards).  
(2) No discussion.
