Below I go through the fifteen parameters one‐by‐one and match them to what is – and is not – said in Kamei & Putterman (2015).  “Discussed” means the paper gives the parameter’s value or changes it across treatments; “Systematic effect” means the paper makes an explicit prediction or reports an estimated effect of **varying that single parameter** on any dependent variable.  Where a numerical effect can be read directly from a table or figure, I provide it.  All page, table and figure references are to the paper reproduced above.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   – Discussed?  Yes.  All sessions use groups of four.  
   – Systematic effect examined?  No.  Group size is never varied, so no prediction or effect size is reported.

2. Number of rounds  
   – Discussed?  Yes.  Fifteen periods in every treatment.  
   – Systematic effect?  No.  

3. Chat enabled?  
   – Discussed?  Not mentioned; chat is never available.  
   – Systematic effect?  No.  

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
   – Discussed?  The game is a standard linear VCM; subjects choose any integer 0–20, so the rule is continuous, not all-or-nothing.  Not varied.  
   – Systematic effect?  No.  

5. Contribution default (refund frame)  
   – Discussed?  Not mentioned.  
   – Systematic effect?  No.  

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   – Discussed?  Yes.  Each token in the public account yields 0.4 to each of the four members (total multiplier 1.6).  Not varied.  
   – Systematic effect?  No.  

7. Punishment cost (cost to send one unit)  
   – Discussed?  Yes.  Cost = 1 point in all treatments.  
   – Systematic effect?  No.  

8. Punishment magnitude (loss to target per unit)  
   – Discussed?  Yes.  Loss = 3 points in all treatments.  
   – Systematic effect?  No.  

9–11. Reward system (enabled, cost, magnitude)  
   – Discussed?  Rewards are never available, so all three parameters are absent.  
   – Systematic effect?  No.  

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
   – Discussed?  Subjects are told there will be 15 periods in every treatment.  Not varied.  
   – Systematic effect?  No.  

13. Peer outcomes shown (full payoff information)  
   – Discussed?  Every treatment shows everyone’s **contributions** each period.  Whether earnings are shown is not stated, and the extent of punishment information (who punished whom) is dealt with under Parameter 14.  The paper never varies payoff visibility per se.  
   – Systematic effect?  No.  

14. Does a punished player know the identity of her punisher?  
   – Discussed?  Yes.  This is a core treatment variable.  
       • Reference treatments (both fixed-ID and random-ID): NO (code “N” in Table 1).  
       • EGO and FULL treatments: YES – but scope differs.  “E” = a player is told who punished her; “F” = everyone sees every dyad.  
   – Systematic effect?  Partly.  Identity revelation is always bundled with other design changes (fixed vs. random IDs, number of stages, history display), so the paper never isolates its **own** causal effect.  Still, Table 1 lets us read treatment-level differences in average group **earnings** (a proxy for efficiency).  Comparing each “N” reference to its corresponding “identity-revealing” treatments:  
       • Random-ID block:  
         – Reference (random-ID, N): 26.6 points per person per period  
         – EGO2 (identity revealed, 2 stages): 28.0  ( +1.4 )  
         – EGO3 (identity revealed, 3 stages): 23.5  ( –3.1 )  
         – EGO3hist (identity revealed + history): 26.6  ( 0 )  
       • Fixed-ID block:  
         – Reference (fixed-ID, N): 25.5  
         – FULL2 (identity revealed to all, 2 stages): 28.3  ( +2.8 )  
         – FULL3: 26.4  ( +0.9 )  
         – FULL3hist: 29.5  ( +4.0 )  
     The authors’ summary (Result 1, p. 16) is that identity revelation **combined with ego-centric design and a dedicated counter-punishment stage** hurts efficiency (EGO3), while identity revelation **combined with full information and/or history** helps (FULL3hist, FULL2).  No single-parameter causal estimate is given.

15. When a player is rewarded, does she know who rewarded her?  
   – Not applicable (no reward).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables in the paper  
   • Group **efficiency / earnings**: reported as average points earned per subject (e.g., Table 1, Fig. 2).  
   • **Contribution level**: average tokens placed in the public account (same sources).  
   • The two variables differ: contribution is a behavioral input; earnings incorporate both cooperation benefits and punishment costs.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   – Parameters 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13 and 14 are mentioned (10 of 15).  
   – Only Parameter 14 (punisher identity known) is actually varied.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of **systematically varying** that parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
   – Exactly one: Parameter 14, and even here the variation is confounded with other design changes.  No numeric “partial” effect is estimated.

D.  What predictions about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment-efficiency link can be made **solely from this paper**?  
   • Parameter 14 (identity revelation) matters, but only in interaction with:  
       – whether information is ego-centric or full,  
       – whether IDs persist across periods,  
       – whether there is a separate counter-punishment stage, and  
       – whether past histories are displayed.  
     Identity revelation paired with ego-centric information and an immediate retaliation stage lowers efficiency; paired with full information and/or history, it raises efficiency.  
   • For the remaining 14 parameters the paper gives no basis for prediction because they are held constant (or absent).  Therefore, using this paper alone, little or nothing can be said about how changing the number of players, MPCR, punishment magnitude, presence of rewards, etc., would alter the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

8. Punishment magnitude (per point)

15. Do rewarded players learn who rewarded them?  
    Not applicable (no rewards).

SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────

A.  Use of “efficiency” as a dependent variable?

      • Individual contribution levels  
      • Average (group) contributions  
      • Punishment points assigned / punishment “slopes”

Below is a parameter-by-parameter analysis of the research paper by Nakao and Machery (2012). Following the instructions, the focus is strictly on what appears in the paper, and no additional inferences have been made beyond the paper’s content. Where the paper is silent, that is stated explicitly.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Discussion in paper?  
     The paper does not mention any specific number of players or individuals in a public-goods‐type game. Instead, it refers generally to pairs or groups of organisms across various species. No concrete “two-player” or “n-player” setup is described in the way public goods games often do.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     Not discussed at all.

2. Number of rounds
   • Discussion in paper?  
     The paper does not refer to any concept akin to “rounds” in a repeated game.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     Not discussed at all.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussion in paper?  
     The paper never mentions communication or “chat” in the sense of experimental participants talking to each other.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     Not discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussion in paper?  
     The paper does not talk about contributions being all or nothing (i.e., forced full contribution or zero contribution).  
   • Systematic variation?  
     Not discussed.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Discussion in paper?  
     There is no mention of a “default” endowment or whether players/organisms automatically contribute and can pull back some portion.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     Not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Discussion in paper?  
     No mention of MPCR, multipliers, or any typical public goods multiplier.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     Not discussed.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussion in paper?  
     The paper frequently refers to punishment having some “cost to the punisher” (e.g., short-term costs such as time, energy, risk of retaliation), but it does not operationalize this as a per-unit, numerical “cost.” There is no systematic or quantitative statement like “cost = X tokens.”  
   • Systematic variation?  
     There is no experiment or table showing a numeric variation of this cost; hence no predicted effect on the punishment treatment effect (in terms of efficiency or any other measured variable).

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed)
   • Discussion in paper?  
     The paper speaks of the “harm” or “cost” imposed on violators (sometimes severe, e.g. evicting them from the group), but there is no single quantifiable “magnitude” parameter measured in the style of a public goods game.  
   • Systematic variation?
     Not discussed as a systematically varied factor.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussion in paper?  
     No mention of rewarding, bonus payments, or positive reinforcement as an alternative to punishment.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     Not discussed.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Discussion in paper?  
      The paper does not refer to any form of reward cost.  
    • Systematic variation?  
      Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude
    • Discussion in paper?  
      No mention.  
    • Systematic variation?  
      Not discussed.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Discussion in paper?  
      Not discussed. The paper deals with evolutionary contexts rather than controlled, round-based experiments.  
    • Systematic variation?  
      No mention.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?
    • Discussion in paper?  
      Not discussed. The paper’s examples concern whether an organism “detects” cheating, but there is no systematic treatment of how or whether “gains/losses” are displayed.  
    • Systematic variation?  
      Not discussed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Discussion in paper?  
      The paper does sometimes note whether the punishee “detects” being punished (e.g., wasps receiving aggression, subordinates evicted by dominants). However, there is no discussion akin to anonymity or knowledge of punisher identity in a lab-experiment sense.  
    • Systematic variation?  
      Not discussed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Discussion in paper?  
      Reward is never discussed, so there is no mention of punishees or rewardees identifying who rewarded them.  
    • Systematic variation?  
      Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?

   The paper does not use group efficiency, total payoff, or average payoff as a dependent variable. Instead, it focuses on evolutionary fitness, costs, and benefits of punishment (often in terms of reproductive success, survival, or reduced exploitation). These are distinct from “efficiency” in a typical public goods experiment. The primary outcome measure is fitness-for both the punisher and punishee—rather than collective payoffs or social welfare.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

   • The paper conceptually addresses punishment’s cost to the punisher (Parameter 7) and the magnitude of punishment to the punishee (Parameter 8), but does not quantify them. No other parameters (1–6, 9–15) appear explicitly in the sense of a public goods game framework.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?

   None. While cost to the punisher (7) and cost imposed on the punishee (8) appear in qualitative form, the paper does not systematically vary them (e.g., no table or figure manipulating these costs step-by-step). It makes no direct predictions or measured effect sizes regarding changes in “punishment treatment effect” for any metric (whether fitness or efficiency) if either parameter changed.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

   The paper does not analyze the notion of “group efficiency” at all. It focuses on whether punishment can evolve (in evolutionary terms) and on whether or not punishment changes a punishee’s subsequent behavior. It is therefore not possible to make any data-based predictions from this paper about how systematically varying these 15 design parameters would affect group efficiency. Consequently, one must conclude that the paper provides little to no direct basis for predicting the punishment treatment effect on efficiency for a public goods game.

Authors: Li, J; Liu, Y; Wang, Z; Xia, HX
Author Full Names: Li, Juan; Liu, Yi; Wang, Zhen; Xia, Haoxiang
Article Title: Egoistic punishment outcompetes altruistic punishment in the spatial public goods game
Abstract: The evolution of costly punishment is a puzzle due to cooperators' second-order free-riding. Previous studies have proposed many solutions mainly focused on reducing the punishment cost or punishing second-order free riders directly or indirectly. We attempt to explain this confusion from the perspective of punishment motivation, which is why the punisher is willing to pay the cost. The answer is that the punisher is egoistic. Egoistic punishment aims to protect punishers' own cooperative benefits shared by the defectors. In such case, egoistic punishers would pay a cost in punishing defectors and retrieve lost payoffs from defectors. Here, we examined the evolution and performance of egoistic punishment and compared it with typical altruistic punishment using classic peer-punishment and pool-punishment modes. Results showed egoistic punishment can evolve and effectively promote cooperation within a large parameter range, whether in a well-mixed or structured population, or through peer-punishment or pool-punishment modes. This result is also robust to different strategy-updating rules. The evolution under the pool-punishment mechanism is more complicated. The influence of parameters is counter-intuitive because of cycle dominance; namely, the cost is the key factor to control the level of cooperation and the fine determines the ratio of the punishers and cooperators. Compared with altruistic punishment, egoistic punishment can promote cooperation in a lower-fine and higher-cost area, especially in the pool punishment mode, and the egoistic punishers have stronger survivability. Egoistic punishers represent the natural fairness in a social system. Results revealed that focusing on individual equity can significantly promote collective cooperation. This study provides another explanation for the evolution of costly punishment.

Author Full Names: Murase, Yohsuke; Baek, Seung Ki
Article Title: Five rules for friendly rivalry in direct reciprocity
Abstract: Direct reciprocity is one of the key mechanisms accounting for cooperation in our social life. According to recent understanding, most of classical strategies for direct reciprocity fall into one of two classes, 'partners' or 'rivals'. A 'partner' is a generous strategy achieving mutual cooperation, and a 'rival' never lets the co-player become better off. They have different working conditions: For example, partners show good performance in a large population, whereas rivals do in head-to-head matches. By means of exhaustive enumeration, we demonstrate the existence of strategies that act as both partners and rivals. Among them, we focus on a human-interpretable strategy, named 'CAPRI' after its five characteristic ingredients, i.e., cooperate, accept, punish, recover, and defect otherwise. Our evolutionary simulation shows excellent performance of CAPRI in a broad range of environmental conditions.

Abstract: The collective action problem can easily undermine cooperation in groups. Recent work has shown that within-group heterogeneity can under some conditions promote voluntary provisioning of collective goods. Here we generalize this work for the case when individuals can not only contribute to the production of collective goods, but also punish free-riders. To do this, we extend the standard theory by allowing individuals to have limited foresight so they can anticipate actions of their group-mates. For humans, this is a realistic assumption because we possess a theory of mind. We use agent-based simulations to study collective actions that aim to overcome challenges from nature or win competition with neighboring groups. We contrast the dynamics of collective action in egalitarian and hierarchical groups. We show that foresight allows groups to overcome both the first- and second-order free-rider problems. While foresight increases cooperation, it does not necessarily result in higher payoffs. We show that while between-group conflicts promotes within-group cooperation, the effects of cultural group selection on cooperation are relatively small. Our models predict the emergence of a division of labor in which more powerful individuals specialize in punishment while less powerful individuals mostly contribute to the production of collective goods.

  – The paper does compare outcomes in the presence vs. absence of punishment (Sections 2.2, 3.2), but it does not present a numerical “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Instead, it reports changes in total group effort and individual payoffs (Figs. 2, 4, 5, 6, and discussion).  
  – There is no explicit numeric effect size for “efficiency” (the ratio of actual total payoff to the maximal payoff) as a function of group size. The authors focus on total effort, payoffs, and how punishment changes with group size, not on a formal “efficiency” ratio.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2) Number of rounds.  
• Does the paper discuss it? No. The model uses an event‐driven, continuous‐time simulation rather than a discrete multi‐round setting with a known or unknown ending. The paper does not treat “number of rounds” as a variable.

• Does it make predictions about systematically varying it? The paper systematically varies the benefit parameter b (also in Table 1, typically 0.0 to 2.0) and shows how that affects total group effort or payoffs (e.g., Fig. 3). However, there is no explicit measure of a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency”; rather, they report how higher b leads to higher contributions and more punishment. • There is no systematic variation of “information display” in the paper, so no predictions are offered on that topic.

• No predictions given.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is?  
• Does the paper discuss it? No. Rewards do not appear in the model, so the paper does not address this.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?  
• The paper focuses on total group effort, individual (absolute) payoffs, and individuals’ relative share of payoffs. It occasionally discusses whether foresight or punishment increase or decrease payoffs overall. However, it does not explicitly use “efficiency” defined as (actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff). Thus, while it measures payoffs, it does not present an efficiency ratio as a key dependent variable.  

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Mentioned in some explicit form:  
  (1) Number of players: yes, as “group size,” systematically varied (N = 4, 8, 16).  
  (6) Benefit/cost terms (akin to an MPCR), but not labeled as such: “b” is varied, “c” is fixed, but they do not call it MPCR.  
  (7)–(8) Punishment cost/magnitude are described as formulas (δᵢⱼ and κᵢⱼ), but not systematically varied.  
• The other parameters (2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15) are not mentioned in the sense of being varied or studied.  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• Strictly speaking, the paper systematically varies only two parameters from your list: (1) group size N, and (6) the benefit parameter b (loosely related to an MPCR concept). It discusses how those changes affect overall cooperation and payoff outcomes in punishment vs. no‐punishment models. However, it never calculates an explicit “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” There is no numerical “effect size” for an efficiency measure.  

D) If you were to make predictions on how these 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper’s content, what would they be?  
• The paper never expresses an “efficiency” ratio and does not report numeric comparisons of “with vs. without punishment” specifically in those terms. It mainly reports changes in total effort and payoff shares. Therefore, at best one can infer:  
  – Larger group sizes generally make it more difficult to maintain punishment and cohesive cooperation; this might reduce any efficiency gains from punishment.  
  – Higher benefit parameters (b) can increase overall cooperation and punishment activities, but the net effect on payoffs is mixed because punishment imposes costs. The resulting effect on an “efficiency” ratio is not quantified.  
  – Other listed parameters (e.g., whether there is chat, reward, who sees the punisher’s identity, etc.) are not discussed at all, so no prediction can be made from this paper alone.  

In short, the paper provides many results on punishment and cooperation but does not directly measure “efficiency” (actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff), nor does it systematically vary most of the 15 parameters you listed. Consequently, only limited predictions can be made about how those 15 parameters would affect a punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency based on this single paper.

Article Title: Evolution of cooperation by the introduction of the probabilistic peer-punishment based on the difference of payoff
Keywords Plus: ANTISOCIAL PUNISHMENT; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; GAMES
Abstract: There are two types of costly punishment, i.e. peer-punishment and pool-punishment. While peer-punishment applies direct face to face punishment, pool-punishment is based on multi-point, collective interaction among group members. Regarding those two types of costly punishment, peer-punishment is especially considered to have the flaws that it lowers the average payoff of all players as well as pool-punishment does, and facilitates antisocial behaviour like retaliation of a defector on a cooperator. Here, this study proposes the new peer-punishment that punishment to an opponent player works at high probability when an opponent one is uncooperative, and the difference of payoff between a player and an opponent one becomes large in order to prevent such antisocial behaviour. It is natural to think that players of high payoff do not expect to punish others of lower payoff because they do not have any complaints regarding their economic wealth. The author shows that the introduction of the proposed peer-punishment increases both the number of cooperative players and the average payoff of all players in various types of topology of connections between players.

   • Mentioned? Yes. Denoted by r, which multiplies a player’s payoff P(i). Specifically, punishing another player subtracts r×P(i) both from the punisher’s payoff and from the punishee’s payoff. The paper chooses r = 0.15.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Mentioned? No. The paper does not discuss whether the identity of the punisher is revealed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Mentioned? No. There is no reward mechanism at all, so this is not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned parameters are:  
     (1) Number of players (N).  
     (2) Number of rounds (generations).  
     (4) All-or-nothing contribution (implicitly, as a two-strategy Prisoner’s Dilemma).  
     (6) MPCR/multiplication-factor-like parameter, b = 1.5.  
     (7) Punishment cost (coefficient r).  
     (8) Punishment magnitude (also governed by r).  
   • None of the other parameters (3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15) are discussed.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when the parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The paper does not provide systematic “variations” or effect-size estimates for any of the 15 parameters. It mentions that different topologies (regular, random, scale-free) were tested, and that r was selected from 0 to 0.3. However, no table or figure directly reports how changing any of these 15 parameters alone shifts the punishment treatment effect, nor does the paper give numerical effect sizes (e.g., no partial η² or regression coefficient).  
   • As a result, strictly speaking, zero of the 15 parameters are varied in a way that is reported with explicit predictions or effect sizes for “punishment treatment effect” on either average payoff or cooperation.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper focuses only on how the proposed peer-punishment affects number of cooperators and average payoff in a spatial Prisoner’s Dilemma, not on efficiency (defined as total payoff / maximum possible payoff). There is no direct information about how systematically altering the 15 parameters would change efficiency.  
   • Notably, the author emphasizes that when punishment is present (with r = 0.15), the average payoff is higher than without punishment. This suggests the proposed punishment improves overall payoffs, which might also improve “efficiency.” But there is no formal modeling of “maximum possible payoff” nor any quantification of partial parameter changes.  
   • Consequently, the paper provides too little detail for any firm prediction on most of the 15 parameters’ effects on efficiency. Any further conclusion would go beyond what is stated in the paper.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Answer Summary:  
A. The paper’s dependent variables are primarily (1) the number/frequency of cooperative players and (2) the average payoff of all players. It does not explicitly measure “efficiency” (total ÷ maximum) or “group efficiency.”  
B. Six of the 15 parameters (1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8) are mentioned in some way.  
C. Zero of the 15 parameters are systematically varied with a reported effect size on how they change the punishment treatment effect; the paper does not present explicit numerical results on parameter-by-parameter variations.  
D. Based solely on this paper, little to no firm prediction can be made about how systematically changing these 15 parameters would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, because the paper does not address efficiency as you define it nor systematically compare changes in those parameters.

Because the paper deals with Enga warfare and peacemaking rather than laboratory-style public goods experiments, it contains no explicit discussion of systematic parameter variations or “punishment treatment effects” on efficiency. Whenever the paper does not mention the parameter or its effect, that is indicated as such.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not discuss any form of “number of players” in a public-goods or game-theoretic sense.  
   • Effect of varying this parameter on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not describe interactions in discrete “rounds” or anything analogous.  
   • Effect of varying this parameter on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does discuss many forms of communication (e.g., oratory, mockery, singing, mediation), but never in the sense of enabling or disabling “chat” as one would do in a controlled experiment.  
   • Effect of varying this parameter on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned? No. The research does not involve choices about contributing “all or nothing” to a communal fund.  
   • Effect of varying this parameter on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not address contribution defaults or anything resembling that mechanic in a public goods game.  
   • Effect of varying this parameter on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Mentioned? No. Nothing in the paper equates to a formal marginal-per-capita-return or multiplication factor.  
   • Effect of varying this parameter on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit of punishment
   • Mentioned? No. Although the paper discusses the general idea of sanctioning or “punishing” free riders in small-scale societies, it does not specify any numeric or operational “cost to punish,” nor does it systematically analyze varying that cost.  
   • Effect of varying this parameter on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted per unit of punishment)
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not present or analyze anything like a “punishment magnitude” in terms of coins or other uniform metrics.  
   • Effect of varying this parameter on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned? No. The paper discusses positive actions such as compensation and peacemaking, but it does not describe a formal “reward mechanism” akin to a public goods experiment.  
   • Effect of varying this parameter on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

10. Reward cost to grant one unit of reward
   • Mentioned? No. There is no formal notion of incurring a cost to reward in the paper’s ethnographic context.  
   • Effect of varying this parameter on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded per unit of reward)
   • Mentioned? No. While the paper discusses distribution of pigs and other wealth in peacemaking, it does not present a concept of a “reward magnitude” that is systematically varied in a public goods sense.  
   • Effect of varying this parameter on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
   • Mentioned? No. There is no notion of “rounds,” “round endpoints,” or knowledge of rounds in the sense of repeated game protocols.  
   • Effect of varying this parameter on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?
   • Mentioned? No. While Enga clans are aware of each other’s gains and losses in war, the text does not discuss any kind of controlled information feedback akin to “showing peer outcomes” each round.  
   • Effect of varying this parameter on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Mentioned? No. There is no direct mention of anonymity, identification, or other aspects of “who punished whom.”  
   • Effect of varying this parameter on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Mentioned? No. Although exchanges and compensation are very public in Enga society, the paper does not address “rewarder identification” in any laboratory or game-framework sense.  
   • Effect of varying this parameter on punishment treatment? Not discussed.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Summary

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What dependent variables does it use, and how do they differ?  
   – The paper never refers to group efficiency (in the sense of “actual total payoffs divided by the maximum possible payoff”). Rather, it looks at warfare and peacemaking among the Enga: the decisions that lead to escalating conflict or restoring peace, how populations resettle, how compensation is paid, and how rituals are conducted. The main “outcomes” are reductions in violence, continuity of trade and exchange, or successful compensation. These are sociopolitical results, not group-efficiency metrics.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – None. The paper does not mention any of the 15 parameters in the context of a public goods game or numeric experimental variations.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   – None. The paper does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters, nor does it discuss such variation’s impact on a punishment treatment effect—whether on efficiency or any other variable.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper, what would they be?  
   – The paper provides no basis for making any predictions about how changes in the 15 specified parameters would affect a “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency. The entire discussion is rooted in Enga warfare, peacemaking, and compensation rather than experimental game parameters and outcomes. Consequently, no predictions can be made from this text alone apart from stating that the topic is not addressed.

Authors: Vukov, J; Pinheiro, FL; Santos, FC; Pacheco, JM
Author Full Names: Vukov, Jeromos; Pinheiro, Flavio L.; Santos, Francisco C.; Pacheco, Jorge M.
Article Title: Reward from Punishment Does Not Emerge at All Costs
Keywords Plus: PRISONERS-DILEMMA GAME; EVOLUTIONARY DYNAMICS; INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; COOPERATION; DIVERSITY; BEHAVIOR; PROMOTES; TRAGEDY
Abstract: The conundrum of cooperation has received increasing attention during the last decade. In this quest, the role of altruistic punishment has been identified as a mechanism promoting cooperation. Here we investigate the role of altruistic punishment on the emergence and maintenance of cooperation in structured populations exhibiting connectivity patterns recently identified as key elements of social networks. We do so in the framework of Evolutionary Game Theory, employing the Prisoner's Dilemma and the Stag-Hunt metaphors to model the conflict between individual and collective interests regarding cooperation. We find that the impact of altruistic punishment strongly depends on the ratio q/p between the cost of punishing a defecting partner (q) and the actual punishment incurred by the partner (p). We show that whenever q/p<1, altruistic punishment turns out to be detrimental for cooperation for a wide range of payoff parameters, when compared to the scenario without punishment. The results imply that while locally, the introduction of peer punishment may seem to reduce the chances of free-riding, realistic population structure may drive the population towards the opposite scenario. Hence, structured populations effectively reduce the expected beneficial contribution of punishment to the emergence of cooperation which, if not carefully dosed, may in fact hinder the chances of widespread cooperation.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter summary of what the Vukov et al. (2013) paper does and does not say about each of the 15 listed public‐goods‐game parameters, followed by the required four‐point summary (A–D). Throughout, note that the paper studies an evolutionary Prisoner’s Dilemma or Stag‐Hunt game on a scale‐free network and focuses on the final fraction of cooperators (or a related area‐based “cooperation‐index” Ω) rather than on group efficiency (i.e., total‐payoff‐relative‐to‐maximal‐payoff).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of Players  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The paper fixes the population size at 1000 agents (nodes) in each simulation (p. 5, “Scale‐free networks … with 10^3 nodes”).  
   • Systematically varied or any stated effect on punishment treatment?  
     – No. They do not vary population size; there is no discussion about how changing the number of players affects punishment outcomes.

2. Number of Rounds  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper analyzes evolutionary dynamics until fixation (or a final stable fraction of cooperators) and does not treat a finite or known number of “rounds” of interaction.

3. Is Chat Enabled Between Players?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. No mention of communication or chat.

4. Is the Contribution “All or Nothing”?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – The game is a two‐strategy model (cooperate vs. defect), but the paper does not frame this as “all or nothing” contributions in a public‐goods sense, nor do they systematically vary partial vs. entire contributions. No explicit mention of “all or nothing.”

5. Is the Contribution Default (Reverse Decision of Endowment)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. There is no discussion of default moves or endowment reallocation.

6. Marginal Per Capita Return (MPCR) or Multiplication Factor  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper uses pairwise Prisoner’s Dilemma or Stag‐Hunt payoff parameters (T, R, S, P), not a group‐based MPCR or multiplier.

7. Punishment Cost to Impose (Cost to the Punisher)  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. Labeled q in the paper (p. 2–3).  
   • Systematically varied or any effect on punishment treatment?  
     – Yes. They examine q over a range of values. They find that the ratio q/p is critical to whether punishment helps or hinders cooperation. Although their dependent variable is the fraction of cooperators (or Ω), not efficiency, they do systematically vary q and show that when q/p < 0.54, punishment tends to enhance cooperation (pp. 3–5, Figs. 3–4).

8. Punishment Magnitude (Deduction Imposed on the Punishee)  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. Labeled p in the paper.  
   • Systematically varied or any effect on punishment treatment?  
     – Yes. They explore multiple (p, q) pairs and show that altruistic punishment occurs when p > q, but even then, whether it helps or hurts cooperation depends sensitively on p vs. q. A main result is that, on average, if q/p < 0.54, punishment enhances cooperation; else it is detrimental (p. 5, Fig. 4).

9. Whether a Reward Is Enabled  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. Although “reward” is mentioned in a broad sense in the title or in passing (e.g., “Reward from Punishment Does Not Emerge…”), the actual model does not incorporate a separate reward mechanism. There is no systematic variation of a reward parameter.

10. Reward Cost to Grant a Single Unit of Reward  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper’s analysis does not include a standalone reward mechanism or cost for rewarding.

11. Reward Magnitude (Coins Awarded to the Recipient)  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. Same as above (no explicit reward strategy is included).

12. Is the Number of Rounds Known to Players?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The model is evolutionary; there is no finite‐round design or known end.

13. Are Peer Outcomes Shown (Do Players Know Others’ Gains/Losses Each Round)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The model uses evolutionary imitation based on payoffs but does not discuss any explicit “information display” to players about peers’ outcomes.

14. When a Player is Punished, Do They Know the Specific Punisher?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The authors do not address information about who punishes whom.

15. When a Player is Rewarded, Do They Know the Specific Rewarder?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper does not include a reward mechanism, so this is not addressed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper does not use group efficiency or total payoff as its main outcome. Instead, it reports the fraction of cooperators at end of the evolutionary process, as well as an area‐based index Ω measuring the fraction of (T, S) parameter space for which cooperators exceed 50%.  
   • They do compute payoffs as part of the evolutionary reproduction rule, but the main metrics reported are (i) final fraction of cooperators and (ii) Ω. These differ from efficiency because the authors do not divide total payoff by the maximum possible group payoff.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Three parameters (#1, #7, #8) are explicitly mentioned.  
     – #1 (Number of players) is fixed at 1000.  
     – #7 (Punishment cost q) is used and varied.  
     – #8 (Punishment magnitude p) is used and varied.  
   • All other parameters are not discussed in the paper.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Only two parameters (#7: punishment cost q and #8: punishment magnitude p) are systematically varied. The paper explores their combined effect, focusing on how q/p influences whether punishment drives cooperation up or down. Even there, the outcome variable is “fraction of cooperators” (or the cooperation‐index Ω), not efficiency.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not analyze group efficiency; it analyzes cooperation levels. Nonetheless, we might infer that if punishment promotes cooperation for q/p < 0.54 (in an evolutionary sense), it could in many setups translate into higher collective payoffs, but the paper gives no direct evidence or formula for efficiency.  
   • Apart from q and p, none of the other parameters receive any discussion in this paper; therefore, the paper provides little or no basis for making predictions about how those other parameters (number of rounds, chat, reward availability, etc.) would affect efficiency or any cooperation‐related measure.
reference_APA: Vukov, Jeromos, Pinheiro, Flavio L., Santos, Francisco C. & Pacheco, Jorge M. (2013). Reward from Punishment Does Not Emerge at All Costs. PLOS COMPUTATIONAL BIOLOGY.

Authors: Wardil, L; da Silva, JKL
Author Full Names: Wardil, Lucas; da Silva, Jafferson K. L.
Article Title: Distinguishing the opponents promotes cooperation in well-mixed populations
Keywords Plus: INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; EVOLUTIONARY GAMES; PUNISHMENT
Abstract: Cooperation has been widely studied when an individual strategy is adopted against all coplayers. In this context, some extra mechanisms, such as punishment, reward, memory, and network reciprocity must be introduced in order to keep cooperators alive. Here, we adopt a different point of view. We study the adoption of different strategies against different opponents instead of adoption of the same strategy against all of them. In the context of the prisoner dilemma, we consider an evolutionary process in which strategies that provide more benefits are imitated and the players replace the strategy used in one of the interactions furnishing the worst payoff. Individuals are set in a well-mixed population, so that network reciprocity effect is excluded and both synchronous and asynchronous updates are analyzed. As a consequence of the replacement rule, we show that mutual cooperation is never destroyed and the initial fraction of mutual cooperation is a lower bound for the level of cooperation. We show by simulation and mean-field analysis that (i) cooperation dominates for synchronous update and (ii) only the initial mutual cooperation is maintained for asynchronous update. As a side effect of the replacement rule, an implicit punishment mechanism comes up in a way that exploitations are always neutralized providing evolutionary stability for cooperation.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what (if anything) the paper says about each of the 15 public‐goods‐game parameters you listed, followed by the required four‐point summary.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     Yes. The paper uses N to denote the population size (e.g., N = 3, N = 40, N = 100) and varies it to examine how cooperation evolves for synchronous and asynchronous updates in a prisoner’s dilemma setting.  
   • Does the paper predict the effect of systematically varying this parameter on the punishment treatment effect (or on any dependent variable)?  
     The paper does examine how different values of N affect the fraction of cooperation (f_c) over time and the stability of cooperation. However, there is no mention of an explicit “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Instead, they track how N influences the fraction of cooperation and when (or if) cooperation takes over. No numerical effect size is provided with respect to “punishment treatment effect,” because the paper frames “implicit punishment” as a strategy‐replacement dynamic rather than a costly or explicit punishment of the kind one typically sees in a public‐goods or experimental‐economics setting.

2. Number of rounds
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     The paper does not refer to a finite or known number of rounds, nor does it manipulate a round count. It speaks of synchronous or asynchronous “updating” and looks at time evolution but does not fix or vary a known end point.  
   • Does the paper predict the effect of systematically varying it (for any dependent variable)?  
     No. There is no discussion of changing the length of interaction or having participants know (or not know) the game length.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     No, it does not mention communication or chat.
   • Any predicted effect if varied?  
     No, not discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     The paper describes a prisoner’s dilemma in which players choose C or D in each pairwise interaction, but it does not mention systematically varying between “all‐or‐nothing” or partial contributions.  
   • Any predicted effect if varied?  
     No. They use a fixed two‐strategy (C or D) prisoner’s‐dilemma setup.

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., are participants moving some portion of their endowment)?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     No, the paper does not mention a default contribution scheme or partial‐endowment mechanism.  
   • Any predicted effect if varied?  
     No, not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     Not in the typical public‐goods sense. Instead, the paper uses “b” (> 1) as the temptation to defect in the prisoner’s dilemma payoff. They do note that “b” can vary, but they conclude that varying b “has no effect in the simulations and in the mean‐field results” beyond establishing that b > 1 for a prisoner’s dilemma.  
   • Any predicted effect if varied?  
     No effect on “punishment treatment” is analyzed; the paper explicitly says that changes in b do not alter the main qualitative outcome (they do not frame it as an MPCR nor do they link it to efficiency).

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     No. Although they refer to an “implicit punishment” (the act of switching from C to D against a defector), there is no explicit punishment cost parameter.  
   • Any predicted effect if varied?  
     No, not discussed.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted for each unit of punishment)
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     No. The paper’s “implicit punishment” does not involve any specified deduction of coins or cost from the deviant player; instead, they model replacement of strategies.  
   • Any predicted effect if varied?  
     No, not discussed.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     The text briefly mentions reward in its Introduction (as one of several mechanisms studied in the literature), but it does not appear as a varied parameter in their model or results.  
   • Any predicted effect if varied?  
     No, the paper never introduces or systematically investigates a reward mechanism.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      No.  
    • Any predicted effect if varied?  
      No, not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded to a player per unit of reward)
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      No.  
    • Any predicted effect if varied?  
      No, not discussed.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      No. They do not mention participants learning about round counts or the game’s ending.  
    • Any predicted effect if varied?  
      No, not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much their peers gained or lost)?
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      No. There is an imitation rule based on payoffs, but the paper does not treat it as players “seeing” outcomes in a public‐goods expository sense.  
    • Any predicted effect if varied?  
      No, not discussed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who punished them?  
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      No explicit mention of “knowing who punished.” The model has “implicit punishment,” but they do not discuss identification of the punisher.  
    • Any predicted effect if varied?  
      No, not discussed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who rewarded them?
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      No. Same reasoning as above with reward not being a parameter.  
    • Any predicted effect if varied?  
      No, not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   The paper does not present “group efficiency” in the sense of total payoffs relative to a maximum possible payoff. They focus on (i) fraction of cooperative strategies (“fraction of cooperation”) across the population and (ii) stability of cooperation or defection. At times, they discuss individual payoffs to define the evolutionary imitation process, but the paper’s primary reported dependent variable is fraction of cooperation (f_c), not group efficiency.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   Of the 15, only two are explicitly mentioned in any detail:  
   1) Number of players (Parameter 1), which they denote by N.  
   2) A defection‐temptation parameter b (loosely analogous to a “multiplication factor,” Parameter 6, although the authors do not frame it that way for a public goods game).  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   None. The paper discusses parameter variation only with respect to how it influences the fraction of cooperation under an “implicit punishment” (strategy‐replacement) rule; it does not link any parameter to an explicit “punishment treatment effect” or to efficiency.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   The paper gives no direct information about efficiency, explicit punishment costs, punishment magnitudes, or any of the standard public‐goods‐game implications for these parameters. Consequently, there is insufficient basis in the paper to predict how systematically varying those 15 parameters, individually or in combination, would affect a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” One can at most note that they find larger populations take longer to converge toward high cooperation (or remain at a lower bound under asynchronous updating), but this is reported only in terms of cooperation rates, not efficiency.

Authors: Zhang, JL; Cao, M
Author Full Names: Zhang, Jianlei; Cao, Ming
Article Title: Strategy Competition Dynamics of Multi-Agent Systems in the Framework of Evolutionary Game Theory
Source Title: IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON CIRCUITS AND SYSTEMS II-EXPRESS BRIEFS
Author Keywords: Game theory; multi-agent system; evolution dynamics
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; DIRECT RECIPROCITY; COOPERATION
Abstract: There is the recent boom in investigating the control of evolutionary games in multi-agent systems, where personal interests and collective interests often conflict. Using evolutionary game theory to study the behaviors of multi-agent systems yields an interdisciplinary topic which has received an increasing amount of attention. Findings in real-world multi-agent systems show that individuals have multiple choices, and this diversity shapes the emergence and transmission of strategy, disease, innovation, and opinion in various social populations. In this sense, the simplified theoretical models in previous studies need to be enriched, though the difficulty of theoretical analysis may increase correspondingly. Here, our objective is to theoretically establish a scenario of four strategies, including competition among the cooperatives, defection with probabilistic punishment, speculation insured by some policy, and loner. And the possible results of strategy evolution are analyzed in detail. Depending on the initial condition, the state converges either to a domination of cooperators, or to a rock-scissors-paper type heteroclinic cycle of three strategies.

Abstract: Cooperation based on mutual investments can occur between unrelated individuals when they are engaged in repeated interactions. Individuals then need to use a conditional strategy to deter their interaction partners from defecting. Responding to defection such that the future payoff of a defector is reduced relative to cooperating with it is called a partner control mechanism. Three main partner control mechanisms are (i) to switch from cooperation to defection when being defected ('positive reciprocity'), (ii) to actively reduce the payoff of a defecting partner ('punishment'), or (iii) to stop interacting and switch partner ('partner switching'). We show that random interactions in an unstructured population and a high number of rounds increase the likelihood that selection favours partner switching. In contrast, interactions localized in small groups (without genetic structure) increase the likelihood that selection favours punishment and/or positive reciprocity. This study thus highlights the importance of comparing different control mechanisms for cooperation under different conditions.

2. Number of rounds

   • Mentioned? No.

   • Mentioned? No.

5. Contribution default / rollback rule  
   • Mentioned? No.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? No. The PD uses fixed benefit B_h = 2 and cost C_h = 1, but these are not varied systematically in the text or main figures.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   • Mentioned? Yes, C_p (baseline = 1).  
   • Systematic variation? Yes, in supplementary analyses and Fig. S4. Doubling C_p causes punishment to lose its dominance (positive reciprocity takes over when T is small). No quantitative change in efficiency is given.

8. Punishment magnitude to the target  
   • Mentioned? Yes, D_p (baseline = 2).  
   • Systematic variation? Yes, in sensitivity analyses (text says “if payoff reduction is reduced… punishment is replaced by positive reciprocity or switching”). Exact numerical effect sizes are not printed in the main paper.

9. Reward option present  
   • Mentioned? No.

10–11. Reward cost and reward magnitude  
   • Mentioned? No.

12. End-game information (round number known)  
   • Mentioned? No.

13. Peer outcome visibility  
   • Mentioned? No.

14. Punisher identity revealed  
   • Mentioned? No.

15. Rewarder identity revealed  
   • Mentioned? No.

────────────────────────────────────────
Summary  
A. Use of “efficiency”?  
   • The paper never reports group efficiency, total payoff, or average payoff per capita.  
   • Dependent variables used: (i) frequency of mutual cooperation; (ii) frequency of each strategy class. These differ from efficiency because they ignore the costs paid for punishing or switching.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
   • 4 parameters: (1) number of players (fixed at 2), (2) number of rounds (T), (7) punishment cost, (8) punishment magnitude.  

C. For how many parameters is the effect of systematic variation on the punishment treatment effect discussed?  
   • None with respect to efficiency (because efficiency is never measured).  
   • With respect to the prevalence of punishment (a different dependent variable), systematic variation is shown for 3 parameters: number of rounds, punishment cost, and punishment magnitude. Group size (which is related to but not identical with “number of players in the game”) is also varied and strongly affects whether punishment or switching dominates.

D. Predicting the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment treatment effect on efficiency using only this paper  
   • Very limited predictions are possible because efficiency was not calculated. One can only *infer* that parameters which make punishment dominant (few rounds, small groups, low punishment cost, high punishment magnitude) are conditions under which adding a punishment option is more likely to raise cooperation, and hence *might* increase efficiency—providing the efficiency loss from punishment costs themselves does not outweigh the cooperation gain. Conversely, many rounds and large groups push the system toward partner switching; in that regime punishment is rare, so introducing it would likely have little or even negative effect on efficiency. For the remaining 11 parameters (chat, reward, information display, contribution rules, etc.) the paper gives no data, so no prediction can be made.

In short: the article is useful for understanding how rounds, group size, and punishment efficiency parameters shape the *frequency* of punishment, but it offers almost no direct guidance on how any of the 15 public-goods parameters would alter the *punishment treatment effect on efficiency*.

4. CONTRIBUTION “ALL OR NOTHING” VERSUS CONTINUOUS

5. IS THERE A “CONTRIBUTION DEFAULT”?

6. MARGINAL PER CAPITA RETURN (MPCR) OR SIMILAR MULTIPLICATION FACTOR
• Mentioned? Only indirectly when referring to public goods payoffs in general (e.g., that “contributions” may or may not yield a net benefit).  
• Does the paper give a systematic treatment or effect size for MPCR? No. The paper does not provide or vary any numerical “multiplication factor.”

7. PUNISHMENT COST TO THE PUNISHER
• Mentioned? Yes. Punishment is broadly described as an “investment” or short‐term costly act (for example, a client ‘chases’ a cheating cleaner, which imposes an energetic/ opportunity cost on the punisher).  
• Systematic variation? No. The paper does not present or test different levels of punishment costs, so it provides no effect sizes or predictions about varying the cost.

8. PUNISHMENT MAGNITUDE (HOW MUCH IS TAKEN FROM THE TARGET)
• Mentioned? Only in general terms. The paper notes that punishment can reduce the cheater’s payoff (e.g., a chased cleaner fish foregoes foraging), but it does not discuss specific “magnitudes” or how varying the magnitude would affect outcomes.  
• Systematic variation? No. No quantitative manipulation is reported.

9. WHETHER A REWARD IS ENABLED
• Mentioned? Yes, in the sense that humans can also reward cooperators and that “reward” is one of the theoretical partner‐control mechanisms (e.g., “positive reciprocity”).  
• Systematic variation? No. Although reward is acknowledged (for example, references to experiments where humans sometimes “pay to reward”), there is no discussion of systematically varying a reward option or its effect on overall punishment efficacy.

• Systematic variation? No. No effect sizes or predictions about toggling “peer‐outcome visibility” are provided.

14. WHEN A PLAYER IS PUNISHED, DO THEY KNOW THE PUNISHER’S IDENTITY?
• Mentioned? In the fish‐cleaner examples, “punishment” by chasing is obviously known to the punishee, but the paper does not link this to a systematically varied parameter in a game‐experiment sense.

15. WHEN A PLAYER IS REWARDED, DO THEY KNOW THE REWARDER’S IDENTITY?

• The paper does not explicitly address the other parameters in any systematic or numerical way.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the “punishment treatment effect” (for any dependent variable) when the parameter is systematically varied?

D) If you were to predict how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would those predictions be?

Its coverage of punishment and cooperation is largely conceptual, illustrating that punishment can increase cooperative behaviors in some contexts (e.g., repeated interactions, or when bystanders adjust their behavior through image scoring) without quantifying changes in total payoffs or efficiency.    Group efficiency (total or average pay-off divided by the maximum feasible pay-off) is never reported.

B. Parameters from the list that the paper even mentions: 4 of 15  
   (1) Number of players, (2) Number of rounds, (4) Binary (all-or-nothing) contribution rule, (6) Gain factor r.

C. Parameters for which the paper reports the effect of systematic variation on any outcome: 1 of 15  
   Only parameter 6 (gain factor r) is systematically varied, and its effect is reported on cooperation rates, not on efficiency and not as a treatment–control difference.

D. What can be predicted—solely from this paper—about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency?  
   • The paper supplies no baseline condition without punishment, so no actual “treatment effect” can be calculated.  
   • Efficiency is not measured; hence no direct statements allow prediction.  
   • The only relevant hint is that higher multiplication factors (larger r) “amplify the cooperation-promoting effect” of the punishment-cum-reward rule.  By implication, if efficiency were monotonically related to cooperation, one might expect a larger positive punishment-treatment effect on efficiency when r is large.  
   • For the remaining 14 parameters the paper is silent; therefore no prediction can be made from this source alone.

In short, the article is about how a specific probabilistic, reputation-based punishment rule shapes the *level of cooperation* under different synergy factors; it does not analyse efficiency and does not provide parameter-by-parameter treatment-effect estimates for any of the 15 design variables listed.

Abstract: Sponsored search advertising (SSA) markets have witnessed soaring bid prices from advertisers, which have been considered to be a potential challenge to the long-term stability, profitability and effectiveness of the SSA ecosystem. One approach to addressing this challenge is identifying cooperative and stable bidding strategies for competing advertisers with the objective of reaching socially optimal outcomes in repeated SSA auctions. Although useful in analyzing advertiSers' bidding behavior in single auction sessions, static game-theoretic analysis and simulation studies in the extant SSA literature offer only limited insights for characterizing the long-term evolutionary dynamics and stability of advertisers' bidding behavior. In this paper, we address this problem by applying evolutionary game theory and Coevolutionary simulation. Our key finding is that a group of nice and retaliatory (NR) strategies can promote stable cooperation among competing advertisers. Advertisers using NR strategies will never deviate from cooperation first (nice) and always punish their rivals' deviations using competitive bids (retaliatory). The NR strategies are shown to be able to encourage advertisers to decrease their bids to obtain revenue that is equal to that awarded under the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves (VCG) auction mechanism and are further shown to alleviate bid inflation effectively at the system level. 6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  NO.  Again, not a public-goods context.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   • Mentioned?  Not as a parameter.  “Punishment” takes the form of retaliatory high bids in the NR strategy, but there is no explicit cost parameter and no quantitative exploration.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss for target)  
   • Mentioned?  NO parameter; magnitude is implicit in “switching to the UBNE bid,” but never formalised or varied.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Mentioned?  NO.

10. Reward cost  
    • Mentioned?  NO.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Mentioned?  NO.

12. Are the number of rounds common knowledge?  
    • Mentioned?  NO.  The paper does not state whether players know T in the finite-horizon simulations; this is not analysed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mentioned?  PARTIALLY.  The theoretical model assumes complete information: each advertiser knows rivals’ bids, values and CTRs.  However, the paper never manipulates the information condition, so there is no treatment effect.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
    • Mentioned?  NO explicit statement.  In the NR strategy every rival “punishes” by bidding aggressively, but the paper never treats identifiability as a variable.

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
    • Mentioned?  NO.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────
A. Dependent variables  
   • The paper does NOT use “group efficiency” (total payoff divided by maximum possible) as an outcome.  
   • Main dependent variables:  
        – Individual advertiser revenue (discounted sum)  
        – Bid levels (convergence to GEAE vs. UBNE)  
   These are conceptually different from efficiency; the paper never reports efficiency ratios.

B. Parameters actually mentioned (out of 15)  
   • Parameter 1 (Number of players)  
   • Parameter 2 (Number of rounds / periods)  
   • Parameter 13 (“Peer outcomes known”) in the sense of complete information  
   Total mentioned: 3.

   • None (0/15).  No parameter is experimentally or analytically varied to measure how it changes the effect of turning “punishment” on versus off.

Authors: de Jong, S; Tuyls, K
Author Full Names: de Jong, Steven; Tuyls, Karl
Article Title: Human-inspired computational fairness
Author Keywords: Multi-agent systems; Reinforcement learning; Fairness; Human-inspired mechanisms; Social dilemmas
Keywords Plus: INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; SOCIAL DILEMMAS; COOPERATION; AGREEMENT; EMERGENCE; TRAGEDY
Abstract: In many common tasks for multi-agent systems, assuming individually rational agents leads to inferior solutions. Numerous researchers found that fairness needs to be considered in addition to individual reward, and proposed valuable computational models of fairness. In this paper, we argue that there are two opportunities for improvement. First, existing models are not specifically tailored to addressing a class of tasks named social dilemmas, even though such tasks are quite common in the context of multi-agent systems. Second, the models generally rely on the assumption that all agents will and can adhere to these models, which is not always the case. We therefore present a novel computational model, i.e., human-inspired computational fairness. Upon being confronted with social dilemmas, humans may apply a number of fully decentralized sanctioning mechanisms to ensure that optimal, fair solutions emerge, even though some participants may be deciding purely on the basis of individual reward. In this paper, we show how these human mechanisms may be computationally modelled, such that fair and optimal solutions emerge from agents being confronted with social dilemmas.
