Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter inventory of what this particular paper says—and does not say—about systematically varying each of the 15 listed factors with respect to how punishment affects “efficiency” (understood as actual total payoff divided by the payoff of a fully cooperative group). Because the paper does not explicitly track that ratio as a dependent variable, the discussion below indicates whether the authors (a) mention the parameter at all (and, if so, the value(s) used) and (b) make any predictions about changing that parameter’s values and how it might alter the effect of punishment on outcomes. Where the paper is silent, that is stated plainly.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes. The paper explores Ultimatum Games with 2–3 players in some examples, and Public Goods Games with as many as 50, 100, 200, 500, or 10,000 agents.  
   • Systematically varied for punishment’s effect on efficiency?  
     – They do systematically vary the number of players/agents and report how outcomes (e.g., convergent strategy profiles) change. However, they do not frame their results in terms of “efficiency = (actual total payoff)/(maximum possible payoff).” Instead, they report measures such as “average strategy,” “the percentage of pairwise games in which neighbors converge on a mutually compatible strategy,” and so on. The paper does not supply a numerical effect size for efficiency or formally predict how changing group size alters the “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”  

2) Number of rounds  
   • Discussed?  
     – Partially. They do mention repeating the game many times (e.g., 2,000 or 6,000×n iterations).  
   • Systematically varied for punishment’s effect on efficiency?  
     – No. Although the authors refer to repeated interactions allowing agents to learn cooperative strategies, the paper does not examine variations in the total number of rounds in order to see how that changes the effect of punishment on efficiency.  

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. There is no mention of any communication, messaging, or “chat.”  
   • Systematically varied for punishment’s effect on efficiency?  
     – No. No mention at all.  

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Discussed?  
     – Only to note that the paper generally uses a continuous space of actions (not just two discrete choices like “all” vs. “nothing”).  
   • Systematically varied for punishment’s effect on efficiency?  
     – No. They do not test how restricting contributions to “all or nothing” alters punishment or outcomes.  

5) Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much to move back to themselves)?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The paper never addresses any notion of a “default” contribution mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied for punishment’s effect on efficiency?  
     – No mention at all.  

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor in the Public Goods Game  
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes, they set r = 1.5 in the Public Goods Game as an example of the “factor by which the common pool is multiplied.”  
   • Systematically varied for punishment’s effect on efficiency?  
     – No. They do not sweep across different values of r to examine how that changes punishment’s impact on efficiency.  

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussed?  
     – They do mention that in human experiments (and in their modeling), an agent might pay a cost c to reduce another’s payoff by a larger amount e.  
   • Systematically varied for punishment’s effect on efficiency?  
     – No. They do not systematically vary the cost parameter c and track how that numerically changes group outcomes or “efficiency.”  

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted per unit punishment)  
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes. The paper sets e = 3 in some of its PGG examples (so that each punishment reduces the target’s payoff by 3).  
   • Systematically varied for punishment’s effect on efficiency?  
     – No. They do not explore multiple values of e or provide any quantitative “efficiency” effects.  

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The focus is entirely on punishment and/or “withholding action.” They do not consider a reward mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied for punishment’s effect on efficiency?  
     – No.  

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Discussed?  
      – No. The authors do not introduce a reward mechanism at all.  
    • Systematically varied for punishment’s effect on efficiency?  
      – No.  

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit reward)  
    • Discussed?  
      – No. As above, there is no reward mechanism in these models.  
    • Systematically varied for punishment’s effect on efficiency?  
      – No.  

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?  
    • Discussed?  
      – No. The researchers do not address whether participants know how many times the game will be repeated.  
    • Systematically varied for punishment’s effect on efficiency?  
      – No.  

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players see each other’s gains/losses)?  
    • Discussed?  
      – Implicitly, yes. The computational models assume that each agent knows the other’s payoff so it can decide whether it feels exploited.  
    • Systematically varied for punishment’s effect on efficiency?  
      – No. There is no discussion of exploring different information‐revelation conditions.  

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Discussed?  
      – No. The paper never addresses anonymity or identification of the punisher.  
    • Systematically varied for punishment’s effect on efficiency?  
      – No.  

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Discussed?  
      – No. As there is no mention of rewards, the paper does not discuss who sees or knows about a rewarder’s identity.  
    • Systematically varied for punishment’s effect on efficiency?  
      – Not applicable.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper does not explicitly use “efficiency = actual total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff.” Instead, it discusses outcome measures such as:  
     – The learned (final) strategies that agents adopt in Ultimatum and Public Goods Games.  
     – How many repeated interactions (games) are needed for learning to converge.  
     – Whether agents end up with near‐cooperative splits in the Public Goods Game.  
     – “Performance” in the sense of how many pairs of agents converge on a compatible (nonpunished) strategy.  
   • They do occasionally frame certain outcomes as “closer to the fair or optimal solution” (e.g., fully cooperative group in the PGG), but they do not track that ratio as a formal dependent variable.  

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned to some degree (though not necessarily with any systematic variation of punishment effects on efficiency):  
       1) Number of players  
       2) Number of rounds (only in the sense that the game is repeated many times, but not systematically varied)  
       6) Multiplication factor (r = 1.5, but not varied)  
       7) Punishment cost c (mentioned, not varied)  
       8) Punishment magnitude e (mentioned, not varied)  
       13) Peer outcomes appear to be known (implicitly), but not varied  
   • Not mentioned at all (or mentioned only to say it is not used) for the rest:  
       3), 4), 5), 9), 10), 11), 12), 14), 15  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, none of the parameters are systematically varied in order to measure how “punishment treatment” changes “efficiency.” The authors do vary the number of players (Parameter 1), the population composition (e.g., fraction of fixed‐strategy agents), and sometimes the presence or absence of the rewiring option; but they do not cast these as manipulations of “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” The paper reports changes in “average strategies,” “fraction of games with a matching strategy,” and other measures, rather than a ratio of payoffs to the cooperative maximum.  

D) Predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, based exclusively on the paper’s content  
   • The paper does not explicitly define “efficiency” or provide formula‐based predictions of how changing each parameter will shift the ratio of actual‐to‐maximum group payoff. Although it discusses how various design choices (e.g., punishing defectors or withholding action in a network) foster higher cooperation, it never translates those outcomes into an “efficiency” ratio.  
   • Consequently, one can say the paper allows only limited inferences about how systematically varying the 15 parameters would shape the punishment effect on efficiency. It does show that (1) punishment plus “withholding action” can push groups toward more cooperative strategies, and (2) changes in group size or population composition do not undermine that result. But beyond that, the paper does not quantify or predict how each parameter individually causes numerical changes in the ratio (actual payoff ÷ maximum payoff).  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
reference_APA: de Jong, Steven & Tuyls, Karl (2011). Human-inspired computational fairness. AUTONOMOUS AGENTS AND MULTI-AGENT SYSTEMS.

Authors: Brosig, J; Weimann, J; Yang, CL
Author Full Names: Brosig, J; Weimann, J; Yang, CL
Article Title: Communication, reputation, and punishment in sequential bargaining experiments

Keywords Plus: PRISONERS-DILEMMA; FAIRNESS; BEHAVIOR; CONSEQUENCES; COOPERATION; PREFERENCES; RECIPROCITY; TRUST; TRUTH
Abstract: Experiments on sequential bargaining have shown that subjects' behavior is far from the equilibrium prediction. Whereas previous models explain these deviations by some kind of social preferences, we investigate an alternative interpretation of behavior based on the assumption of bounded rational self-interest. Our analyses reveal that, in line with this interpretation, bargaining outcomes depend on subjects' payoff consequences from punishment. However, after preplay communication, we find a much weaker effect of these payoff consequences and a tremendous increase in the number of equal splits. This communication effect can be attributed to reputation effects only to a minor degree, if at all.

----------------------------------------------------------------
Parameter-by-parameter extraction from the paper
----------------------------------------------------------------
(“✓” = explicitly discussed in the paper; “✗” = not mentioned)

1. Number of players  
    ✓ Always two (first-mover / second-mover).  
    Systematically varied? ✗ (never varied → no prediction).

2. Number of rounds  
    ✓ All games are one-shot (single round).  
    Varied? ✗ → no prediction.

3. Chat / pre-play communication  
    ✓ Three conditions: NONE, E-MAIL (anonymous written chat), VIDEO (face-to-face).  
    Systematic effects reported:  
    • No-chat ⇒ only 1 of 18 A-moves was rewarded; equal-split (A2) almost never realised.  
    • E-mail ⇒ 83 % of first movers chose A; 70 % of those A-moves were rewarded.  
    • Video ⇒ 97 % (game H), 89 % (M), 77 % (L) chose A; ≥ 91 % of A-moves were rewarded.  
    Thus introducing chat, and making it less anonymous, raises the frequency of the efficient equal-split outcome and almost eliminates punishment.  
    Numerical effect on punishment (game H):  
      – NONE: 42 % of the 24 B-moves were punished.  
      – E-MAIL: 5 of 7 B-moves were punished (≈ 71 %).  
      – VIDEO: 0 of 1 B-move was punished.  
    (The sample for B-moves becomes tiny in the communication treatments because most first movers switch to A.)

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
    ✗ Not used – choices are binary (A vs B, then 1 vs 2).

5. Contribution default / endowment withdrawal  
    ✗ Not used.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR)  
    ✗ Not applicable; the study is not a voluntary-contribution public-goods game.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
    ✓ Captured through “PunEff” = first-mover’s loss ÷ second-mover’s cost.  
    Values: game H (PunEff = 7) vs games M & L (PunEff = 2).  
    Systematic effect (no-communication condition):  
      PunEff 7 ⇒ 42 % of B-moves punished (10/24).  
      PunEff 2 ⇒ 0 % of B-moves punished (0/20).  
    After communication PunEff no longer matters (no significant differences).  
    Inference for efficiency: in the absence of communication, a higher PunEff leads to more punishment and hence lower joint pay-offs; with communication the effect disappears.

8. Punishment magnitude (victim’s loss per unit)  
    ✗ Not reported separately; only the PunEff ratio is given.

9. Presence of a reward option  
    ✓ Second movers can reward (choose 2 in the A-sub-game).  
    Varied? ✗; reward is always available.

10–11. Reward cost & magnitude  
    ✗ Not isolated or varied.

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
    ✓ Yes – always one-shot. Not varied.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    ✓ Both players know the full payoff matrix and observe the realised outcome, but this aspect is never varied.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
    ✓ Trivially yes (only the matched second mover can punish). Not varied.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
    ✓ Same as 14. Not varied.

----------------------------------------------------------------
Summary answers requested
----------------------------------------------------------------
A. Does the paper use “group efficiency” as a dependent variable?  
    The authors speak of the “efficient equal-split outcome A2” and of “efficiency of outcomes”, but they never compute the formal efficiency ratio ( realised total payoff ÷ maximum possible total payoff ). Their explicit dependent variables are:  
    • prop(A) – share of first movers choosing A  
    • prop(2 | A) – share of second movers rewarding  
    • prop(1 | B) – share of second movers punishing  
    • Frequency of the realised outcome categories (A1, A2, B1, B2)  
    These variables are related to, but not identical with, group efficiency.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
    8 of 15: #1, #2, #3, #7, #8 (implicitly), #9, #13, #14, #15.  
    Only #3 (communication) and #7 (punishment cost/efficiency) are deliberately varied.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss their *systematic* effect on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable)?  
    2 parameters.  
    • #7 Punishment cost/efficiency: Higher efficiency (PunEff = 7 vs 2) → sharp rise in actual punishment (42 % → 0 %) when there is no communication; no effect with communication.  
    • #3 Chat/communication: None → E-mail → Video form a clear monotonic pattern: more communication and less anonymity sharply reduce punishment frequency and increase realisation of the equal-split (efficient) outcome.

D. Predictions one can make – **using only this paper** – about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency:

1 Number of players – no evidence; cannot predict.  
2 Number of rounds – only one-shot examined; cannot predict multi-round effects.  
3 Chat enabled – Expect large positive impact on efficiency (especially if video/face-to-face) by virtually eliminating punishment and producing equal splits.  
4 All-or-nothing contributions – not studied; no prediction.  
5 Contribution default – not studied.  
6 MPCR – not studied.  
7 Punishment cost (or its ratio to inflicted loss) – With no communication, cheaper/more efficient punishment (higher PunEff) increases actual punishment and therefore *lowers* efficiency; with communication this lever becomes irrelevant.  
8 Punishment magnitude – not isolated; no separate prediction beyond what is implied by PunEff.  
9 Reward availability – always ON, so no comparative data; no prediction about turning it OFF.  
10–11 Reward cost & magnitude – not discussed; no prediction.  
12 Round-number information – not varied; no prediction.  
13 Displaying peer outcomes – not varied; no prediction.  
14/15 Identifiability of punisher/rewarder – held constant; no prediction.

In short, the paper only justifies two robust qualitative expectations for efficiency:  
  (i) Communication (especially non-anonymous) greatly improves efficiency by crowding out punishment and promoting rewards.  
  (ii) When there is no communication, making punishment cheaper for the punisher (or more damaging for the target) encourages punishment and therefore worsens efficiency.  
For the other thirteen parameters the paper offers little or nothing for forecasting their impact.

Authors: Wang, Q; Liu, LJ; Chen, XJ
Author Full Names: Wang, Qiang; Liu, Linjie; Chen, Xiaojie
Article Title: Evolutionary Dynamics of Cooperation in the Public Goods Game with Individual Disguise and Peer Punishment
Author Keywords: Cooperation; Peer punishment; Individual disguise; Replicator equations; Stochastic evolutionary dynamics
Keywords Plus: REPLICATOR DYNAMICS; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; COLLECTIVE ACTION; COMPETITION; GOVERNANCE; IMITATION; REWARD; FINITE; ALLOWS
Abstract: The phenomenon of individual disguise is ubiquitous in the real world. Recent evidences show that peer punishment is successful to stabilize cooperation among selfish individuals. However, it is unclear whether peer punishment is still able to stabilize cooperation when individual disguise for escaping being punished is considered. In this paper, we thus introduce individual disguise of defectors into the public goods game with peer punishment and aim to explore how peer punishment influences the evolutionary dynamics of cooperation, defection, and punishment in this scenario. We consider both cases of infinite and finite populations. In infinite populations, by using replicator equations, we find that although low disguise cost can hinder public cooperation, peer punishment still plays a positive role in promoting the evolution of cooperation, no matter whether second-order punishment is considered or not. We further demonstrate that the larger fine on defectors or the smaller the cost of punishment, the easier to establish a state of full punishment. In addition, in finite populations we reveal that the population spends most of the time in the region of defection for low disguise cost, and the population spends most of the time in the region of cooperation for high disguise. When second-order punishment is not considered, the punishment strategy does not have evolutionary advantage, whereas when second-order punishment is considered, the population can evolve toward regime of punishment and spends most of the time in the monomorphic states with widespread punishment or cooperation.

Below I go through the 15 pre-specified design parameters one by one, quoting or pointing to the relevant place in the paper whenever something is said, and stating explicitly when nothing at all is said.

The dependent variables that the paper analyses are always called “fitness’’ (individual or group average).  The term *efficiency* is never used, but in a two–person Prisoner’s Dilemma with the particular pay-off numbers the authors use, fitness of the pair is numerically identical to “group efficiency’’ as normally defined (total pay-off divided by the maximum possible total).  When I speak of “the punishment treatment effect’’ I follow the paper’s logic:  the “treatment’’ is the presence of costly peer punishment (negative reciprocity); the “effect’’ is the difference in fitness between the world with punishment and the world without.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1.  Number of players  
   • Mentioned: yes – the underlying game is explicitly a *two-player* Prisoner’s Dilemma (Table 1, §2).  
   • Systematic variation? none – the number of players is kept fixed at 2 throughout.

2.  Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned: yes – the authors start from a *one-shot* PD.  
   • No systematic variation is analysed.  Repeated interaction is mentioned only for motivation in the introduction.

3.  Chat enabled?  
   • Not mentioned at all.

4.  All-or-nothing contribution choice?  
   • Yes – cooperation (C) or defection (D) is strictly binary (§2).  
   • No variation analysed; the binary structure is assumed throughout.

5.  Contribution default / refund frame?  
   • Not mentioned.

6.  MPCR / multiplication factor (i.e., baseline material pay-offs)  
   • A specific PD payoff matrix is fixed (C,C gives 1 each; D,C gives 2/-1; etc.).  
   • Although the authors note that their qualitative results “hold for other PD pay-offs’’ (§2), they never *vary* the pay-offs, so no numerical comparative statics are derived.

7.  Cost to impose one unit of punishment  
   • Central to the model.  Cost per unit is c h, with 0 < c < 1 (§2).  
   • Effect of varying c:  For a given anger parameter v, punishment deters defection and raises efficiency if and only if v > c (p. 6, text around Table 2 and Fig. 1).  Lower c therefore unambiguously *increases* the punishment treatment effect on efficiency; raising c weakens it.  No exact elasticities are reported.

8.  Punishment magnitude (harm per unit)  
   • Harm = h and the optimal h* chosen by a punisher is v/c (§2).  
   • Varying v therefore co-varies h.  The paper does give systematic predictions:  
        – Holding c fixed, larger v rotates the “advantage of cooperating’’ curve upward (Fig. 1) and makes the efficient all-C equilibrium more likely.  
        – However, at the group level the authors later show that *too much* v is inefficient; the group-optimal v^o is b − 2 (Proposition 2).  Hence the treatment effect on efficiency is hump-shaped in v: it first rises as v increases above c, peaks at v = v^o, then falls.  No numeric slope is provided.

9.  Reward enabled?  
10. Cost of reward  
11. Magnitude of reward  
   • Rewards are never modelled or even mentioned, so nothing can be said.

12.  Finite horizon known?  
13.  Peer outcomes shown?  
14.  Punisher identity revealed?  
15.  Rewarder identity revealed?  
   • None of these information-display dimensions are discussed anywhere in the article.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables  
   • Individual fitness W(.)  
   • Group average fitness W^g(.)  
   • “Efficiency’’ in the usual experimental-economics sense never appears as a term, but group fitness is numerically equivalent in their 2-player PD.  
   • Contribution rates, cooperation rates etc. are discussed only insofar as they feed into fitness; they are not the main outcomes.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   • Six:  #1 (players = 2), #2 (rounds = 1), #4 (binary choice), #6 (pay-off matrix fixed), #7 (punishment cost c), #8 (punishment magnitude via h = v/c).  The other nine are completely absent.

C.  For how many parameters is a *systematic* effect on the punishment treatment effect analysed?  
   • Two:  #7 (cost c) and #8 (magnitude / anger v).  For both, qualitative comparative statics are worked out; no other parameter receives such treatment.

D.  Predictions one could make, *only* from this paper, about how the 15 parameters and their interactions affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency  
   • Lower punishment cost c (#7) => larger positive treatment effect; if c rises above v, punishment ceases to sustain efficiency.  
   • Higher punishment magnitude (operationalised as higher v, #8) increases the treatment effect up to the group-optimal point v^o = b − 2, after which further increases reduce efficiency.  
   • All other parameters (#1,2,4,6) are fixed in the model, so no prediction about variation is supported.  
   • For the nine parameters that never appear, the paper provides no basis for prediction.

Abstract: While the evolution of cooperation has been widely studied, little attention has been devoted to adversarial settings wherein one actor can directly harm another.    • These variables differ from efficiency because they track strategy composition, crime rates, and transitions toward Utopia or Dystopia, rather than group-level payoff efficiency.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Most of the 15 are either not mentioned or appear only incidentally in describing the fixed design (e.g., number of rounds, anonymity, the stolen amount αδ, etc.). None are truly “systematically varied” in the sense of a formal treatment that compares multiple values of that parameter.  
   • The paper does mention the cost of retaliation for failed reporting (ε) being different across two parameter profiles (A vs. B), and a fixed punishment cost to the criminal (θ = 45). These parameters, however, do not map directly onto the 15 parameters listed (they do not, for example, alter “punishment cost to the punisher” or “punishment magnitude” in multiple steps).  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None of the 15 parameters are systematically varied in the sense of changing them to multiple values to see how the punishment treatment effect changes.  
   • The only partial variation is the switch between parameter Profile A and B, changing the cost of failed reporting; yet this is never explicitly framed as “systematically varying a punishment parameter” to observe changes in group efficiency or “punishment treatment effect.” The paper rather looks at how the presence or absence of the Informant strategy affects whether the group converges to high or low crime.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • Because the paper does not study total or average payoffs relative to a maximum or systematically examine how changing each parameter affects punishment, there is virtually no direct basis in the paper to predict how modifications to (1)–(15) would affect efficiency.  
   • The main robust finding the paper does supply is that allowing (vs. disallowing) an “Informant” strategy is critical in moving the system from high crime to low crime, which indirectly suggests it improves overall outcomes for players. However, the paper does not translate that insight into formal efficiency measures.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Thus, based strictly on the paper, there is no direct discussion of how any of the listed 15 parameters—when systematically varied—would affect a “punishment treatment effect” on group efficiency. The paper’s principal finding instead is that having the Informant strategy available crucially enables transitions to and maintenance of a low-crime equilibrium.

Authors: Xie, K; Liu, TJ
Author Full Names: Xie, Kai; Liu, Tingjin
Article Title: The regulation of good and evi promotes cooperation in public goods game
Author Keywords: Cooperation; Evolution game; Heterogeneity payoff distribution; Punishing evil and promoting good; Reputation mechanism
Keywords Plus: REPUTATION; EVOLUTION; PUNISHMENT
Abstract: The topic of how to solve cooperation dilemmas has been intensively investigated. Numerous mechanisms have been presented to promote cooperation level by introducing various third-party strategies. This paper considers the more realistic strategy named punishing evil and promoting good (PEPG) in the public goods game, whose fundamental action is cooperation. Players selecting this strategy can not only reward cooperators but also penalize defectors, effectively amalgamating the advantages of both rewarders and punishers. Moreover, distinct strategic choices lead to dynamic changes in players' reputation, which in turn significantly influence their income distribution. Notably, individuals with elevated reputation are entitled to allocate more benefits rather than homogeneous distribution. Simulation experiments demonstrate that the PEPG strategy is pivotal in eliminating defectors and fostering cooperative behavior. Importantly, three intriguing phenomena are displayed in this research, including the resurgence of defectors, the polarization of reputation and the disparities of payoffs, all of which help us understand the emergence of cooperation in the real world.

Below, each of the 15 design parameters is checked against the contents of the paper “The regulation of good and evil promotes cooperation in public goods game.”  
For every parameter we state  

• Whether the paper even mentions or fixes that parameter (value, label, or qualitative description).  
• Whether the paper ever varies that parameter ​systematically and reports an effect on any treatment that contains punishment (their PEPG strategy).  
• Whether a numerical effect size can be extracted for the punishment‐treatment effect, and on which dependent variable(s).  
Whenever the paper is silent we say so explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER SCAN
--------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned: Yes. They use a 200 × 200 spatial lattice ⇒ 40 000 players.  
   • Systematically varied? No. Population size is fixed.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? None reported.

2. Number of rounds (time steps)  
   • Mentioned: Yes. Each simulation runs 10 000 iterations; the final 1 000 are used for measurement, and 50 independent trials are averaged.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? None reported.

3. Chat between players  
   • Mentioned: No.  
   • Effect: Not discussed.

4. All-or-nothing contribution decision  
   • Mentioned: Yes implicitly. Agents either “invest the unit cost c = 1” (cooperate) or “contribute nothing” (defect); PEPG also invests c = 1.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not analysed.

5. “Contribution default” (withdrawal from the public pool)  
   • Mentioned: No.  
   • Effect: Not discussed.

6. Marginal Per-Capita Return / multiplication factor (called enhancement factor r)  
   • Mentioned: Yes. They explore r = 2, 3, 4, 4.8 and display a full heat-map over r ∈ [3.2,5] alongside parameter a.  
   • Systematically varied? Yes – r is the main exogenous variable.  
   • Reported effect (dependent variable = cooperation frequency f_c): Higher r decreases the critical threshold for cooperation and raises f_c.  
     – Example: Fig. 1a shows that when a = 2, f_c is ≈0 at r = 2 and ≈1 at r = 4.  
   • Numerical effect size on efficiency? Not given; efficiency was not computed.

7. Punishment cost per unit (β)  
   • Mentioned: Yes. β = 0.1 fixed in nearly all simulations. An auxiliary comparison sets β = 0 (together with γ = 0) to create a “no reward/ no punishment” baseline.  
   • Systematically varied? No (only the β = 0 switch is shown, but not as a gradient).  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? No quantitative trend reported.

8. Punishment magnitude per unit (γ – the fine inflicted on defectors)  
   • Mentioned: Yes, labeled “bonus-penalty value γ, 0<γ<1”.  
   • Systematically varied? Yes. γ takes 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 in different figures.  
   • Reported effect (dependent variable = f_c): In the heat maps (Fig. 8) higher γ shrinks the low-cooperation (green) region; i.e. larger punishment magnitude amplifies the positive punishment‐treatment effect on cooperation.  
   • No efficiency numbers reported.

9. Whether any reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned: Yes. PEPG simultaneously punishes defectors and rewards cooperators. Turning γ = β = 0 disables both actions.  
   • Systematically varied? Only two states (enabled vs disabled).  
   • Effect: With γ = β = 0 cooperation resembles a standard PGG; enabling reward/punishment (γ>0) yields markedly higher f_c (Fig. 1a vs Fig. 1b). No efficiency metric.

10. Reward cost per unit (β again)  
    • Same remarks as parameter 7. Not varied.

11. Reward magnitude per unit (γ again)  
    • Same remarks as parameter 8. In this model the same γ governs both the fine on defectors and the bonus to cooperators, so the reward-magnitude trend equals the punishment-magnitude trend.

12. Knowledge of the number of rounds  
    • Mentioned: No.  
    • Effect: Not discussed.

13. Visibility of peer outcomes after each round  
    • Mentioned: No.  
    • Effect: Not discussed.

14. Identification of the punisher  
    • Mentioned: No.  
    • Effect: Not discussed.

15. Identification of the rewarder  
    • Mentioned: No.  
    • Effect: Not discussed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (total or average payoff / maximum)?  
   • No. The paper’s main dependent variables are  
     – Cooperation level f_c (fraction of cooperators + PEPG)  
     – Instantaneous cooperation time-series f_c(k)  
     – Distribution of reputation values  
     – Average payoffs of cooperators/defectors ( \bar p_{c,p} and \bar p_d ).  
   These variables are different from “efficiency” because they are not normalised to the social optimum; the paper never reports “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff.”

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   • Mentioned: 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11   (nine parameters, although 7&10 share β, 8&11 share γ).  
   • Not mentioned at all: 3, 5, 12, 13, 14, 15.

C. Which parameters are systematically varied and linked to the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable)?  
   • Varying r (parameter 6) – clear monotonic effect on cooperation.  
   • Varying γ (parameters 8 & 11) – clear monotonic effect on cooperation.  
   • Switching reward/punishment on vs off (parameter 9) – large discrete effect on cooperation.  
   In total, 2 unique continuous parameters (r, γ) plus one on/off switch are analysed. No efficiency statistics are given.

D. Predictions one could make for the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency, strictly from the paper’s contents:  
   • Because higher r and higher γ strongly increase cooperation levels, and because the paper also shows that, whenever cooperation dominates, the average payoff of cooperators exceeds that of defectors, it is reasonable to predict that efficiency would likewise increase with r and γ and with the mere presence of the reward-and-punishment option.  
   • The paper does not give any evidence about how β, population size, number of rounds, or any information-display parameters influence payoffs, so no prediction can be made for those factors.  
   • Interactions: The heat-map of f_c (Fig. 8) indicates that the joint effect of (r, a, γ) is non-additive: large γ can compensate partially for smaller r. Translating that into efficiency terms would predict positive two-way interactions (r × γ, a × γ) on efficiency as well, but the paper gives no numbers.  
   • For all other parameters (chat, identification of punishers, etc.) the paper supplies no basis for prediction, so the correct forecast is “no prediction possible.”

In short, the only solid, paper-based expectations about efficiency are:  
– Enabling punishment/reward (γ>0) should raise efficiency relative to the no-punishment baseline.  
– Within the punishment condition, larger γ and larger r should monotonically increase efficiency.  
Beyond that, the paper is silent.

Authors: Nakamaru, M; Yokoyama, A
Author Full Names: Nakamaru, Mayuko; Yokoyama, Akira
Article Title: The Effect of Ostracism and Optional Participation on the Evolution of Cooperation in the Voluntary Public Goods Game
Keywords Plus: RECIPROCITY; DYNAMICS; ASSOCIATION; REPUTATION; REWARD
Abstract: Not only animals, plants and microbes but also humans cooperate in groups. The evolution of cooperation in a group is an evolutionary puzzle, because defectors always obtain a higher benefit than cooperators. When people participate in a group, they evaluate group member's reputations and then decide whether to participate in it. In some groups, membership is open to all who are willing to participate in the group. In other groups, a candidate is excluded from membership if group members regard the candidate's reputation as bad. We developed an evolutionary game model and investigated how participation in groups and ostracism influence the evolution of cooperation in groups when group members play the voluntary public goods game, by means of computer simulation. When group membership is open to all candidates and those candidates can decide whether to participate in a group, cooperation cannot be sustainable. However, cooperation is sustainable when a candidate cannot be a member unless all group members admit them to membership. Therefore, it is not participation in a group but rather ostracism, which functions as costless punishment on defectors, that is essential to sustain cooperation in the voluntary public goods game.

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?

  4) Is the contribution all or nothing (yes, always)  
  6) MPCR/multiplier (b)

  – Number of rounds (h)  
  – MPCR/multiplier (b)  
• Strictly speaking, they do not present a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Instead, they analyze how ostracism (interpretable as costless punishment) affects the proportion of cooperators under different values of N, h, and b. No numeric effect sizes are directly reported, only qualitative or figure-based outcomes (e.g., “cooperation becomes more stable for larger h or larger b”).

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

They do show that exclusion (costless punishment) boosts cooperation, which in principle might also raise total payoffs if cooperation yields higher group returns. For the other parameters (e.g., punishment cost, revelation of the punisher, reward mechanisms, etc.), the paper does not address them at all, so no predictions can be drawn from this source.

Article Title: Honesty and dishonesty in gossip strategies: a fitness interdependence analysis
Source Title: PHILOSOPHICAL TRANSACTIONS OF THE ROYAL SOCIETY B-BIOLOGICAL SCIENCES
Author Keywords: reputation; cooperation; dishonest gossip; fitness interdependence; modelling approach
Keywords Plus: INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; EVOLUTIONARY PSYCHOLOGY; 3RD-PARTY PUNISHMENT; SOCIAL-INTERACTION; COOPERATION; REPUTATION; EXPRESSIONS; COMPETITION; GENEROSITY; PERCEPTION
Abstract: Gossip, or sharing information about absent others, has been identified as an effective solution to free rider problems in situations with conflicting interests. Yet, the information transmitted via gossip can be biased, because gossipers may send dishonest information about others for personal gains. Such dishonest gossip makes reputation-based cooperation more difficult to evolve. But when are people likely to share honest or dishonest gossip? We build formal models to provide the theoretical foundation for individuals' gossip strategies, taking into account the gossiper's fitness interdependence with the receiver and the target. Our models across four different games suggest a very simple rule: when there is a perfect match (mismatch) between fitness interdependence and the effect of honest gossip, the gossiper should always be honest (dishonest); however, in the case of a partial match, the gossiper should make a choice based on their fitness interdependence with the receiver and the target and the marginal cost/benefit in terms of pay-off differences caused by possible choices of the receiver and the target in the game. Moreover, gossipers can use this simple rule to make optimal decisions even under noise. We discuss empirical examples that support the predictions of our model and potential extensions. This article is part of the theme issue 'The language of cooperation: reputation and honest signalling'.

Below I go through the 15 design parameters one‐by‐one and state, strictly on the basis of the Wu et al. (2021) article,  

(1) whether the paper ever mentions the parameter and, if so, what exact value(s) are used or assumed, and  
(2) whether the paper makes any prediction about how *systematically varying* that parameter would change the *punishment-treatment effect* on any dependent variable (and, if so, what numerical effect size can be inferred).  

Because the article is a modelling paper on gossip honesty—not an experimental paper on public-goods punishment—almost none of the required information is provided. I nevertheless list every parameter explicitly so that the absence of coverage is transparent.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
GAME-STRUCTURE PARAMETERS
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Every formal model involves exactly three strategic actors (gossiper, receiver, target) plus, in the second stage, a two-player game between receiver and target.  
   • Systematic variation / prediction? No. The paper never studies what happens if the number of players is 4, 5, etc., nor links this to a punishment treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? Yes, implicitly: all games are modelled as *one-shot* interactions.  
   • Systematic variation / prediction? No. No multi-round or end-game knowledge manipulations are analysed.

3. Is chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned? No. There is no reference to free-form chat or communication channels.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Mentioned? No. The public-goods contribution decision is never modelled.

5. Contribution-default framing?  
   • Mentioned? No.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
MONETARY-STAKES PARAMETER
--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? No. There is no public-goods production function in the paper.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PEER-INCENTIVE PARAMETERS
--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Punishment *cost* (cost to punisher per unit)  
   • Mentioned? Partially. In the punishment game the variable *c* denotes the *cost of punishing* borne by the (future) receiver. Typical values in the figures are *c = 1*.  
   • Systematic variation? No. The model never sweeps *c* over a range to see how a punishment *treatment effect* on any outcome would change. *c* only appears symbolically in an inequality determining when the gossiper is honest.

8. Punishment *magnitude* (fine on punished player)  
   • Mentioned? Yes, denoted γ (gamma); in figures γ = 1.  
   • Systematic variation? No. Again, γ is not systematically varied nor linked to group efficiency.

9. Is a reward option enabled?  
   • Mentioned? No.

10. Reward cost  
    • Mentioned? No.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Mentioned? No.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
INFORMATION-DISPLAY PARAMETERS
--------------------------------------------------------------------
12. Is the horizon (number of rounds) known?  
    • Mentioned? No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mentioned? No.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
    • Mentioned? No.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
    • Mentioned? No.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
ADDITIONAL NOTES ON DEPENDENT VARIABLES
--------------------------------------------------------------------
• The *only* behavioural outcome the modelling paper analyses is the binary choice of the *gossiper* to send *honest vs. dishonest* information.  
• The article also computes whether honest gossip is an equilibrium strategy under different constellations of *fitness interdependence* (V_gr, V_gt) and game pay-offs.  
• No variable labelled “group efficiency,” “total payoff,” or “average group payoff” is ever used.  
• Consequently, no “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” is reported or forecast.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Does the paper use group efficiency as a dependent variable?  
   • No. Dependent variables are (i) whether the gossiper is honest or dishonest and (ii) the underlying incentive structure that makes honesty an equilibrium. These differ conceptually from efficiency, contributions, or cooperation rates.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are *mentioned*?  
   • Five:  
     – #1 (number of players fixed at 3/2)  
     – #2 (number of rounds fixed at 1)  
     – #7 (punishment cost c)  
     – #8 (punishment magnitude γ)  
     – None of the remaining ten parameters appear.  
   • So, 5 / 15 parameters are at least touched upon.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* them on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable)?  
   • Zero. The paper never runs or simulates parameter sweeps; it simply states symbolic inequalities. No numerical marginal effect of changing c, γ, or any other parameter on any treatment effect is derived.

D. Predictions that could be made—solely from the paper—about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) influence the punishment treatment effect on *efficiency*:  
   • The paper provides virtually no basis for such predictions. Its entire focus is on gossip honesty, not on efficiency in public-goods games with punishment.  
   • At best, one could speculate that higher punishment *cost* (c) or higher punishment *magnitude* (γ) would shift the honesty–dishonesty boundary for gossip, but even that is only with respect to gossip decisions, not efficiency.  
   • Therefore, any attempt to forecast the punishment treatment effect on efficiency from this article would be almost entirely uninformed.

In short, Wu et al. (2021) does not supply the information required to model how the 15 experimental design parameters would alter the efficiency impact of introducing punishment in a public-goods game.

   Not applicable; never mentioned; never varied.

12. Do players know the number of rounds?  
   (1) Yes.  They are explicitly told each part is one-shot and independent (Section 4).  
   (2) No discussion of hiding that information or varying horizon length.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   (1) Part II: after contributions, every subject learns the two other players’ contribution levels (Section 4).  No pay-offs were shown, only contributions.

   (1) The paper never says.  Standard phrasing (“subjects can punish other group members individually”) suggests anonymity, but the article never states it.

   Not applicable (no rewards in the design).

Summary requested by the user
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables actually analysed  
   • The paper never analyses **group efficiency** (total or average pay-off divided by the social optimum).  
   • Main dependent variables: (i) individual contribution level (Part I and Part II), (ii) individual punishment points assigned, (iii) some derived measures (proportion of zero contribution, “spiteful” punishment ratio, individual earnings). B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   8 of 15: #1, #2, #3, #4, #6, #7, #8, #12, #13 (identity of punisher #14 is only implicit and never clarified).  The other parameters are simply absent.

Abstract: Games of public good provision, collective action, and collusion share concern for the free rider that shirks on its obligations. According to the folk theorem. the free rider problem can be resolved through punishment mechanisms. Versions of the folk theorem have been applied when monitoring is imperfect. Empirical evidence contradicts this theory: while often subjects cooperate significantly, rarely is all shirking eliminated. To reconcile theory with empirical evidence, I provide a theoretical basis for the inability of participants in collective action problems to attain full compliance. I construct a general class of compliance models with imperfect monitoring through a common signal. I derive sufficient conditions - on both the utility of agents and the monitoring capabilities - under which slippage from full compliance is unavoidable, showing the limits of the folk theorem logic. The paper is purely theoretical, focuses on the possibility (or impossibility) of achieving full compliance in repeated public‐goods‐type settings with imperfect monitoring, and does not present experiments or systematic parametric variations. Below, I indicate for each parameter whether it is (1) mentioned at all in the paper and, if so, how, and (2) whether the paper makes any predictions about systematically varying it.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

   – Mentioned?

   – Any systematic variation / predicted effect on “punishment treatment effect”?  
     The paper does not provide a quantitative or tabular analysis of how increasing or decreasing the number of players systematically changes the outcome for efficiency or any other dependent variable. It does note conceptually that if the number of participants increases (e.g., in a cartel), each individual’s contribution to or deviation from the collective outcome becomes harder to detect. However, it does not offer a numerical effect size for “punishment treatment” on efficiency or other measures as n varies.

2. Number of rounds
   – Mentioned?  
     The paper discusses an indefinitely repeated (infinite‐horizon) game. It does not analyze a known, finite number of rounds, nor does it vary that number systematically.  
   – Any systematic variation / predicted effect on “punishment treatment effect”?  
     No. All formal analysis pertains to infinite or indefinite repetition (i.e., unknown end). There is no discussion of changing or comparing different finite round lengths.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   – Mentioned?

   – Any systematic variation / predicted effect?

   – Mentioned?

   – Any systematic variation / predicted effect?  
     No. The paper’s entire thrust is that continuous spaces allow partial compliance; it does not systematically manipulate a forced all‐or‐nothing regime.

   – Mentioned?

   – Any systematic variation / predicted effect?

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment

  12) Indefinite or infinite repetition (players do not know the game’s end).  

• The paper does not explicitly mention or analyze the others (3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15) in any parametric or design‐feature sense.  

Hence, of the 15 parameters, only a few (1, 2 in the sense infiniteness, 4, 12) appear at all, and even those appear only in passing or for broad theoretical setup rather than systematic design variation.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?

• None of the parameters are systematically varied in order to isolate a “punishment treatment effect” the way an experimental or quantitative paper might do.  
• The paper provides general arguments about why, in an n‐player setting with imperfect information, full compliance will slip to partial compliance, but it never tabulates or numerically estimates an effect of systematically changing any of the 15 parameters.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

• The paper does not support strong numerical or specific directional predictions for “efficiency.” It primarily predicts that wherever there is imperfect monitoring, full compliance is almost never sustained. Overall, the paper is a theoretical inquiry into the inevitability of “partial” rather than “full” compliance in imperfectly monitored public‐goods scenarios. Abstract: Large-scale cooperation is a hallmark of our species and appears to be unique among primates. SUMMARY
----------------------------------------------------------------

   • Self-control measures (delay discounting and go/no-go RT differences)

Abstract: Laboratory attempts to identify relationships between personality and cooperative behaviour in humans have generated inconsistent results. This may partially stem from different practices in psychology and economics laboratories, with both hypothetical players and incentives typical only in the former. Another possible cause is insufficient consideration of the contexts within which social dilemmas occur. Real social dilemmas are often governed by institutions that change the payoff structure via rewards and punishments. However, such 'strong situations' will not necessarily suppress the effects of personality. On the contrary, they may affect some personalities differentially. Extraversion and neuroticism, reflecting variation in reward and punishment sensitivity, should predict modification of cooperative behaviour following changes to the payoff structure. We investigate interactions between personality and a punishment situation via two versions of a public goods game. We find that, even in a strong situation, personality matters and, moreover, it is related to strategic shifts in cooperation. Extraversion is associated with a shift from free-riding to cooperation in the presence of punishment, agreeableness is associated with initially higher contributions regardless of game, and, contrary to our predictions, neuroticism is associated with lower contributions regardless of game. Results should lead to new hypotheses that relate variation in biological functioning to individual differences in cooperative behaviour and that consider three-way interactions among personality, institutional context and sociocultural background.

Abstract: We conduct an experiment where participants choose between actions that provide private benefits but may also impose losses on others. Three legal environments are compared: no law, strict liability for harm caused to third parties, and an efficiently designed negligence rule where damages are paid only when the harmful action generates a net social loss. Legal obligations are either perfectly enforced (Severe Law) or only weakly so (Mild Law), i.e., expected sanctions are then nondeterrent. PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players

2. Number of rounds

1. Number of players

        • invite more nuisance suits (Sect. 6.1),

        • under some information structures push the equilibrium to pure legal sanctions (Proposition 2).  
       Numerical illustration (Table 1, p. 12): raising d from 20→30 raises “deterrence” from \$5→\$15 and expected litigation cost from \$5→\$12.5 (benefit-cost ratio rises from 1.00→1.20).  Note: the paper never reports “group efficiency”; it reports deterrence and expected cost.

   (i)  Not mentioned.  
   (ii) No prediction.

10. Reward cost  
    (i)  Not mentioned.  
    (ii) No prediction.

11. Reward magnitude  
    (i)  Not mentioned.  
    (ii) No prediction.

12. Are players told the number of rounds?  
    (i)  Infinite horizon is common knowledge.  
    (ii) Not varied; no prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?

14. Do punished subjects learn who punished them?  
    (i)  Not mentioned.  
    (ii) No prediction.

15. Do rewarded subjects learn who rewarded them?  
    (i)  Not mentioned.  
    (ii) No prediction.

   • Buyer’s surplus U  
   • Total welfare W (=V+U)  
   • “Deterrence” (expected monetary penalty on the firm when it delivers low quality)  
   • Expected litigation cost

Below, each of the 15 requested parameters is considered in turn.  For every parameter I state  

(i)  whether it is mentioned anywhere in the paper (including figures, tables, or text) and what concrete value(s) are used, and  

(ii) whether the paper investigates how *systematically varying* that parameter changes “the punishment-treatment effect’’—i.e., the difference that the possibility of punishment makes, relative to a game without punishment.  Whenever the paper offers numerical information I reproduce (or closely approximate) it and cite the relevant figure.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
--------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Number of players  
   (i) Mentioned.  Simulation lattices of 30 × 30 (N = 900), 60 × 60 (N = 3600) and 90 × 90 (N = 8100) are used (p. 9, Fig. 3 caption).  
   (ii) Not systematically varied to study any treatment effect; authors merely note that the results are “the same” across these sizes.  No numerical treatment effect is reported.

2. Number of rounds  
   (i) Not mentioned: the evolutionary model iterates indefinitely; only “time steps” or Monte-Carlo steps (MCS) are referred to.  
   (ii) No discussion of systematic variation.

3. Chat enabled?  
   Not mentioned; no human subjects.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   The model is tri-strategic (C, D, P) and hence binary at the act level, but the paper never treats “all-or-nothing” as a manipulable parameter, nor varies it.

5. Contribution default?  
   Not applicable / not mentioned.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   Corresponds to the “cost-to-benefit ratio” r ∈ (0, 1).  
   (i) Extensively mentioned; r is swept from 0 to 1 in Figs. 1, 2, 4 and across two-dimensional (r, β) phase diagrams (Fig. 3).  
   (ii) r is systematically varied, but only *within the punishment game itself*.  The paper never contrasts “a game with punishment vs. the same game without punishment” at different r’s, so no treatment-effect estimate is given.  Numerical results reported are frequencies of C, D, P (e.g., Fig. 1 shows at α = 0.01, β = 0.05: fp rises from ≈0.33 at r = 0.02 to ≈1 at r ≈ 0.24, then falls to 0 by r ≈ 0.67).

7. Punishment cost (cost to impose one unit)  
   (i) The paper’s symbol α.  Two concrete values are used: α = 0.01 (Figs. 1, 2a-c, 4a) and α = 0.10 (phase diagram Fig. 3; Fig. 4b).  
   (ii) There is *no* systematic sweep of α; only two discrete values are illustrated and they are not compared in terms of a treatment effect.  No numerical effect sizes are reported.

8. Punishment magnitude (penalty suffered per unit)  
   (i) Symbol β.  Extensively varied:  
       • In Fig. 1–2–4: β = 0.05.  
       • In phase diagrams (Fig. 3) β is swept continuously from 0.1 to 1.0 against r.  
   (ii) Again, outcomes reported are strategy frequencies and phase composition, not the incremental efficiency gain/loss due to adding punishment.  No treatment-effect numbers are provided.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   Not mentioned.

10. Reward cost  
    Not mentioned.

11. Reward magnitude  
    Not mentioned.

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
    Not applicable; infinite-horizon evolutionary simulation.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    Not modelled.

14. Do punished players know the punisher?  
    Not modelled.

15. Do rewarded players know the rewarder?  
    Not modelled.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------

A.  Dependent variables actually used  
    • fc, fd, fp = long-run frequencies of Cooperators, Defectors and Punishers.  
    • Derived “phases’’ (AllC, AllD, C + P, D + P, C + D + P, etc.).  
    • No measure of *group efficiency* (total or average payoff) is ever reported.  
      Frequencies and phase labels differ conceptually from efficiency: one can
      have the same frequency mix but different absolute payoffs, and vice-versa.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters appear?  
    4 parameters:  
      #1 (N), #6 (r), #7 (α), #8 (β).

C.  For how many parameters is a *systematic* effect on the punishment-treatment
   effect discussed?  
    Strictly speaking, none.  r and β are systematically varied, but always
    *within* a punishment-enabled game; the paper never contrasts those results
    with a no-punishment baseline, so no treatment-effect estimate is produced.
    For α only two illustrative values are used; N is mentioned but not varied
    for analytical purposes.

D.  Predicting the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency on the sole basis of
   this paper  
    • The paper provides *no efficiency data at all*, so quantitative prediction
      is impossible.  
    • Qualitatively, one could *guess* that efficiency would track the share of
      cooperators plus punishers (since C and P both contribute) and be harmed
      by larger fractions of D.  Hence:  
        – Low r and moderate-to-high β (region “C + P’’ in Fig. 3) might raise

        – Very high r or very low β leads to AllD, so punishment would have no
          efficiency benefit and could even reduce payoffs through its cost.  
    • Beyond these generalities the paper offers no basis for modelling how any
      of the remaining 11 parameters—or interactions among the full set of 15—
      would influence efficiency.

In short, the article concentrates on evolutionary frequencies of strategies on a lattice and does not report, let alone model, the impact of any of the 15 experimental-design parameters on *group efficiency* when punishment is introduced.

For each parameter I state

When numerical information that can be translated into an effect size is available in the paper’s tables/figures I cite it; otherwise I state that no such number can be inferred.

(2) Not varied; no prediction or data on how changing group size would change the punishment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
(1) Reported: 20 rounds. Subjects know this.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction about how a different horizon would change the punishment effect.

3. Chat enabled?  
(1) Reported implicitly: no communication allowed (“it is not allowed to communicate with other participants”).  
(2) Not varied; no prediction.

4. Contribution “all-or-nothing”?  
(1) Reported: no. Each player chooses any integer 0–20.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction.

5. Contribution default / “take” frame?  
(1) Players start with 20 and decide how much to *contribute*; there is no default that they subsequently “take back”.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
(1) Reported: total multiplier 1.6 → MPCR = .40.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
(1) Reported: 1 point per punishment point (punisher’s own budget decreases by exactly the number of points sent).  
(2) Not varied; no prediction of how changing that cost would alter the punishment effect.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss per point to target)  
(1) Reported: –3 points to the target for every point sent.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction.

9. Reward enabled?  
(1) Yes in REW treatments; absent in all other treatments.  
(2) Reward presence is *varied* (P-REW vs P; L-REW vs L). However, the paper never compares a punishment treatment with and without rewards, so no statement is made on how enabling rewards changes the *punishment* effect.

10. Reward cost  
(1) Reported: 1 point per reward point.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction.

11. Reward magnitude  
(1) Reported: +3 points to the recipient per point sent.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction.

12. Finite horizon known?  
(1) Yes. Subjects know there are 20 periods.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction.

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
(1) Yes. After every round every player sees “individual contributions and pay-offs”; in Stage 2 the leader (or each peer in the peer-treatments) also sees contributions before allocating points.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction.

14. Do punished players know who punished them?  
(1) Partially discussed.  
    • In leader-punish (L-PUN) followers know the deduction came from the leader, because only the leader can punish.  
    • In peer-punish (P-PUN) subjects see for each group member “assigned or received points”, but the order of members is randomised each round so identities cannot be tracked across rounds.  
(2) This information structure is *not* manipulated; no prediction.

15. Do rewarded players know who rewarded them?  
(1) Same structure as for punishment (leader known in L-REW; partially anonymised peers in P-REW).  
(2) Not manipulated; no prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used  
   • The paper’s main dependent variable is *average contribution*.  
   • It also reports *net pay-offs* (after rewards/punishments) and sometimes “pay-offs from the public-good stage”.  
   • *Efficiency* (total pay-off divided by the first-best total) is never explicitly constructed nor analysed.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   All 15 parameters appear in the description of the design (values are listed above).

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss how *systematically varying* the parameter changes the punishment treatment effect?  
   Zero. Punishment itself is treated as a binary treatment factor (present vs absent), but none of the parameters in the list is varied *within punishment treatments* so as to study its marginal impact on the punishment effect.

D. What predictions can be made—based **solely** on this paper—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment effect on efficiency?

Consequently it offers virtually no systematic information on how changing those structural parameters would amplify or dampen the punishment treatment’s effect on group efficiency.

Below we go through the 15 moderator-variables one by one, extracting only what the paper actually says.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER EXTRACTION  

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Every game analysed is a 2-player game (“2×2 bimatrix game”; “two–player mini public-goods game”).  
   • Systematic variation?  None.  The paper never studies what happens when the number of players is changed, nor links it to any punishment-treatment effect.  

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  No.  All games are analysed as one-shot static games; the word “round” never occurs.  
   • Systematic variation?  Not applicable.  

3. Chat / communication  
   • Mentioned?  No.  Never discussed.  

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution decision  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  In the mini-PGG each subject either “sends a benefit b at cost a” (C) or does not (D); this is a binary (“all-or-nothing”) move.  
   • Systematic variation?  No.  The paper keeps this binary structure fixed.  

5. Contribution default / refund rule  
   • Mentioned?  No.  

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or related payoff parameters  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  In the mini-PGG the relevant payoff parameters are the cost of cooperation a and the benefit b (the MPCR is b/2 in a 2-player game).  
   • Systematic variation?  Yes, partially.  Inequality (51) shows how the cost of cooperation a enters the threshold at which punishment can make the cooperative equilibrium the limiting QRE:  

        2 β  >  4 a + α + √(8 a α + α²)          (Eq. 51)

     Thus, as a rises (holding α and β fixed) the RHS increases, making it harder for punishment to sustain cooperation.  A special case the authors spell out is a = α ⇒ β > 4 a.  No explicit numerical effect on efficiency is reported – only on equilibrium selection.  

7. Punishment cost (α)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – cost to the punisher.  
   • Systematic variation?  Yes.  α enters the same threshold (Eq. 51).  Two limits are discussed:  
        – If α = a the threshold becomes β > 4 α.  
        – If α ≫ a the threshold simplifies to β > α.  
     Lower α therefore makes cooperative (and potentially more efficient) equilibria easier to select through punishment, but the paper never calculates total pay-off/efficiency.  

8. Punishment magnitude / fine (β)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – the loss imposed on the punished player.  
   • Systematic variation?  Yes.  A larger β pushes the system across the threshold in Eq. 51 so that the cooperative equilibrium is the limiting QRE.  Numerical illustration: with a = α = 1, cooperation is selected once β > 4.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned?  No.  No rewarding option is modelled.  

10. Reward cost  
    • Mentioned?  No.  

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Mentioned?  No.  

12. Do subjects know the number of rounds?  
    • Mentioned?  No.  (One-shot framework.)  

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mentioned?  No.  

14. Do punished players learn who punished them?  
    • Mentioned?  No.  

15. Do rewarded players learn who rewarded them?  
    • Mentioned?  No.  

------------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY  

A.  Dependent variables used  
    – Group efficiency / total or average payoff: NOT used.  
    – Variables actually analysed:  
        • Which Nash equilibrium is selected as the limiting QRE.  
        • The probabilities of cooperation (x) and of punishing (y) along the QRE path.  
      These variables are conceptually different from efficiency; the paper never reports pay-off sums or percentages of the social optimum attained.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
    5 parameters:  
       (1) number of players (fixed at 2),  
       (4) binary/all-or-nothing contribution,  
       (6) cost/benefit of cooperation (a, b),  
       (7) punishment cost (α),  
       (8) punishment magnitude (β).

C.  For how many of those does the paper analyse the *effect of systematic variation* on a punishment treatment?  
    3 parameters:  6 (a), 7 (α), 8 (β).  
    – All three enter inequality (51), which identifies when allowing punishment changes the limiting QRE from the asocial equilibrium (defection, no punishment) to a cooperative equilibrium that includes punishment.  
    – No efficiency figures are produced; only equilibrium selection and frequencies of cooperation/punishment are given (e.g., Fig. 3).  

D.  What predictions (restricted to what the paper offers) could one make about the 15 parameters and their interactions on the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency?  
    • Because efficiency itself is never calculated, the paper allows only indirect inferences:  
        – If parameters (β high, α low, a low) place the game above the threshold in Eq. 51, the limiting QRE becomes cooperative-with-punishment.  Since cooperation yields higher total pay-offs than mutual defection in a PGG, one would *expect* higher efficiency in those parameter regions, but the paper does not quantify the gain.  
        – Raising β or lowering α (while holding the other parameters fixed) therefore should *increase* the punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency; the opposite changes should decrease it.  
        – Changes in the other 12 parameters are not treated, so no prediction can be drawn solely from this paper.  Hence, for most of the 15 moderators we must state that the paper gives no basis for prediction.

Abstract: Two books edited by members of the MacArthur Norms and Preferences Network (an interdisciplinary group, mainly anthropologists and economists) are reviewed here. These books in large part reflect a renewed interest in group selection that has occurred among these researchers: they promote the theory that human cooperative behavior evolved via selective processes which favored biological and/or cultural group-level adaptations as opposed to individual-level adaptations. In support of this theory, an impressive collection of cross-cultural data are presented which suggest that participants in experimental economic games often do not behave as self-interested income maximizers; this lack of self-interest is regarded as evidence of group selection. In this review, problems with these data and with the theory are discussed. On the data side, it is argued that even if a behavior seems individually-maladaptive in a game context, there is no reason to believe that it would have been that way in ancestral contexts, since the environments of experimental games do not at all resemble those in which ancestral humans would have interacted cooperatively. And on the theory side, it is argued that it is premature to invoke group selection in order to explain human cooperation, because more parsimonious individual-level theories have not yet been exhausted. In summary, these books represent ambitious interdisciplinary contributions on an important topic, and they include unique and useful data; however, they do not make a convincing case that the evolution of human cooperation required group selection.

Abstract: Studies to date on the role of social exclusion in public cooperation have mainly focused on the peer or pool sanctioning types of excluding free-riders from the share of common goods. Besides, previous modeling methods of either peer or pool exclusion often presuppose some particular forms of feedback between the individual or collective efforts and the efficiency of social exclusion and, therefore, cannot comprehensively evaluate their effects on the evolution of cooperation in the social dilemma situations.
