Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what is or is not discussed in the Wang and Perc (2022) paper “Replicator dynamics of public goods games with global exclusion” (Chaos 32, 073132). In keeping with your instructions, each of the 15 parameters is addressed in turn—first, whether the paper (1) mentions it (and, if so, with what value) and (2) makes any predictions about the effect of systematically varying it on “the punishment treatment effect” (here understood as how adding a punishing mechanism affects outcomes), especially with respect to “efficiency” (actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff). Where the paper does speak to a variable in some form, it does so in manifold dynamical terms (e.g., stable states, replicator flows) rather than under the heading of “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Where the paper is silent, the answer is simply that it does not appear, and no effect size or direct prediction is provided.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   – Discussed? Yes. The paper sets the group size to N in the public goods game (Section II and throughout).  
   – Systematic variation? The paper analyzes replicator dynamics for a general N and, in numerical illustrations, often sets N = 5. They do not, however, link varying N to any explicit “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Instead, they explore how different N values enter into their classifications of fixed points and phase transitions. They provide no numerical effect size concerning how changing N alters any efficiency measure.

2. Number of rounds
   – Discussed? No. The paper places the game in an infinite‐population, infinite‐time replicator‐dynamic setting. It does not mention discrete repeated rounds, nor does it analyze how knowledge of a final round would alter outcomes.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   – Discussed? No. There is no mention of communication or “chat” between players.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   – Discussed? The model uses the standard public goods assumption that “cooperators contribute 1, defectors contribute 0” (e.g., Section I). This is effectively an all‐or‐nothing contribution setting.  
   – Systematic variation? They do not systematically vary from “all or nothing” to partial contributions, nor do they connect “all or nothing” to any measured punishment‐treatment effect.

5. Is the contribution default?
   – Discussed? No. The paper does not address any default or forced‐choice version of contributions.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   – Discussed? Yes. The paper denotes this factor by r ∈ (1, N).  
   – Systematic variation? The authors do analyze how r enters their stability and phase‐classification results, but never in terms of efficiency changes strictly attributable to a “punishment solution” versus “no‐punishment.” Instead, r influences whether cooperators can invade defectors, or how excluders fare in equilibrium. They present no numeric effect size linking r‐variation to any “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   – Discussed? Partially, in that the model includes a cost of being a “global excluder,” cGE (Section II). This is a fixed extra cost paid by each individual who attempts global exclusion of free‐riders. That is the closest analogue to “punishment cost.”  
   – Systematic variation? Yes, cGE is varied extensively, and many “phases” of the replicator dynamics are classified under different intervals of cGE. However, the text never frames cGE’s variation explicitly as “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Rather, they examine whether cooperators, defectors, and/or global excluders dominate, coexist, or cycle, for different cGE. No numeric effect size is given that translates directly into changes in group efficiency.

8. Punishment magnitude
   – Discussed? Not in the sense of a separate parameter specifying how much payoff is deducted from a punished individual. In the model, if excluders succeed in building the institution, defectors in that group get zero share of the good (Section II). This “magnitude” is not introduced as a tunable quantity; it is effectively the entire payoff that defectors would have received. The paper does not treat it as a systematically varied parameter, nor provide effect sizes for efficiency.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   – Discussed? No. The model addresses only “global exclusion” as a sanctioning mechanism. No direct rewarding of cooperators appears.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    – Discussed? No. The paper does not consider rewards or their cost.

11. Reward magnitude
    – Discussed? No. As above, there is no rewarding mechanism in the model.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
    – Discussed? No. The framework is a continuous‐time (replicator) infinite‐horizon approach, so no mention of finite or known horizon.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?
    – Discussed? No. The population is described by frequencies of strategies, but there is no mention of players seeing one another’s payoffs round by round.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    – Discussed? No. There is no mention of any informational condition about “who punished whom.” Sanctioning is implemented at a global‐institution level.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    – Discussed? No. As the paper contains no reward mechanism at all, it does not address this question.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   – The paper’s focal measures come from replicator‐dynamic equilibria and stability (e.g., which strategies dominate or coexist, and whether the population settles into homogeneous states or cyclic orbits). Although the paper does define an average population payoff, it does not report “efficiency” as actual‐to‐max payoff. Nor does it describe the effect of “punishment” on efficiency per se. Thus, “efficiency” (as fraction of the fully cooperative outcome) is not a primary reported outcome.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – The paper explicitly discusses:  
     • (1) Number of players, denoted by N.  
     • (6) Multiplication factor r.  
     • (7) Cost of being a punisher (analogous to cGE).  
   – None of the remaining 12 parameters appear in this paper.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   – Although the paper does vary N, r, and cGE systematically, it does so to classify phases of the replicator dynamics (e.g., stable orbits, heteroclinic cycles) rather than to quantify a “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency or payoff. No direct measure of how any parameter shifts “punishment’s effect on efficiency” is presented, and no numerical effect size on efficiency is given.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely on the content of this paper, what would they be?  
   – The paper does not speak to most of these parameters (2–5, 9–15) at all, so no prediction can be drawn from it. For the three it does address (N, r, cGE), the authors only show how they shift the stability and coexistence of cooperators, defectors, and global excluders, rather than reporting any ratio of actual group payoff to maximum payoff. Consequently, one cannot infer from the paper how systematically varying N, r, and cGE would change “efficiency” in the sense of total‐payoff‐relative‐to‐the‐fully‐cooperative benchmark. The authors do show conditions under which a punishing/excluding strategy can proliferate along with cooperators (hence mitigating free‐riding), but they do not connect those conditions to an explicit efficiency metric. Absent that, no numerical predictions about punishment’s net effect on efficiency can be made based solely on this paper.

Article Title: Identity, Kinship, and the Evolution of Cooperation

Abstract: Extensive cooperation among biologically unrelated individuals is uniquely human. It would be surprising if this uniqueness were not related to other uniquely human characteristics, yet current theories of human cooperation tend to ignore the human aspects of human behavior. This paper presents a theory of cooperation that draws on social, cultural, and psychological aspects of human uniqueness for which current theories have little or no explanation. This identity is linked to basic survival instincts by emotions that are mentally experienced as culture-laden feelings.    • Mentioned? No. There is no reward mechanism in this design.  
   • Systematically varied or discussed for its effect on punishment treatment? No.

11. Reward magnitude
   • Mentioned? No. Same as above—no reward mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied or discussed for its effect on punishment treatment? No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
   • Mentioned? Yes. Players know there are exactly 20 rounds.  
   • Systematically varied or discussed for its effect on punishment treatment? No. They do not compare a known‐horizon to an unknown‐horizon variant; only one horizon (20 rounds) is used.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much their peers gained or lost each round)?
   • Mentioned? Partially. Each player sees the contributions of each other player and the group total, then later sees a summary of threat schedules or actual punishment assigned in some conditions. However, the paper does not systematically vary what information is displayed.  
   • Systematically varied or discussed for its effect on punishment treatment? No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper explicitly states that players do not observe who punished them. Identities remain anonymous.  
   • Systematically varied or discussed for its effect on punishment treatment? No. The authors do not vary whether punisher identity is revealed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is?
   • Mentioned? No. Rewarding is not part of the experiment.  
   • Systematically varied or discussed for its effect on punishment treatment? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   Yes. The authors often refer to the “overall welfare,” “final payoff,” or “earnings” of the group, which align with measures of efficiency. However, they also emphasize other dependent variables, such as the contribution level to the public good and the number of punishment points assigned. These latter measures are not identical to efficiency, since punishment can raise contributions but still reduce overall payoffs if its costs outweigh its benefits in early periods.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   The paper explicitly mentions parameters 1 (fixed at 4 players), 2 (20 rounds), 6 (MPCR = 0.4), 7–8 (punishment cost and magnitude, systematically varied as Low‐Effectiveness vs. High‐Effectiveness), 12 (the 20‐round horizon is known to participants), 13 (players do see one another’s contributions, among other information), and 14 (punishment is anonymous). That is a total of 8 parameters mentioned in some form. The other 7 parameters (3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 15) are not implemented or not discussed in this specific experiment.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   Only parameters 7 and 8 (the punishment‐cost and punishment‐magnitude combination) are actually varied between Low‐Effectiveness (LE) and High‐Effectiveness (HE). The paper discusses how increasing punishment effectiveness (i.e., a 1:2 cost‐to‐target ratio rather than 1:1) strengthens contributions induced by punishment and by threats—but can also raise punishment costs to the group. So exactly 2 parameters are systematically varied and analyzed for their effect on punishment and efficiency.

D. Predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, based solely on the paper:  
   • The paper indicates that as punishment becomes more “effective” (i.e., costlier to the punished relative to the punisher’s cost), threats are more credible, punishment raises contributions more firmly, but early‐round payoffs may still be dragged down by the cost of punishing. Over enough rounds, average efficiency can improve, especially in later stages.  
   • For all other parameters—such as group size, number of rounds, communication structure (chat vs. threats), contribution format (“all or nothing” vs. continuous), reward systems, and knowledge of who punishes—this study does not vary them or make predictions about how they would shape the punishment treatment effect on efficiency. The paper provides no direct data from which to infer how changes in those unvaried parameters would alter the impact of punishment on total payoffs. Consequently, little to no prediction can be made about the unvaried parameters based on the content of this paper alone.

Below I go through the 15 design parameters, strictly summarising what this single article says about (a) the value actually used in the experiment and (b) whether the paper examines what would happen if the parameter were systematically varied for the purpose of predicting the “punishment treatment effect’’ (difference between any punishment condition and the no-punishment baseline).  Whenever possible I quote or paraphrase the numerical information contained in the text, figures or tables.

-----------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
 (a) Always four players per group.  
 (b) Never varied; no prediction (or data) about how changing group size would alter the punishment treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds (periods)  
 (a) 24 periods in total (6 under each of the four systems).  
 (b) Not experimentally varied.  The authors do show that the gap between “no-punishment’’ and “with-punishment’’ widens over the six periods within a block (Fig. 1), but they do not ask what would happen if the *total* number of periods were 12, 30, etc.

3. Chat enabled?  
 (a) No chat; all interaction is via the z-Tree interface.  
 (b) Not discussed; no prediction.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
 (a) No.  Participants choose any integer amount from 0 up to their endowment.  
 (b) Not discussed; no prediction.

5. Contribution “default’’ reversal?  
 (a) Standard PGG: decide how much to *send* to the public fund; nothing is said about a “withdraw’’ frame.  
 (b) Not discussed; no prediction.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
 (a) Each MU invested is multiplied by 1.6 and then equally divided → MPCR = 1.6/4 = 0.40.  
 (b) Held constant; no analysis of different MPCRs.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
 (a) Peer & democratic: 1 MU paid by the punisher.  
  Central: cost is shared—0.2 MU borne by each of the other three players for every 0.6 MU fine imposed.  
 (b) The cost level differs *across* systems but is not manipulated independently; the paper never asks “what if the cost were 0.5 MU or 2 MU?”  Hence no systematic prediction.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine per unit)  
 (a) Peer & democratic: punished player loses 2 MU for every 1 MU spent.  
  Central: 0.6 MU deducted per MU *not* contributed.  
 (b) Again, differences are confounded with the type of system; there is no systematic variation of the fine rate itself.

9–11. Reward enabled / reward cost / reward magnitude  
 (a) No reward option in any condition.  
 (b) Not discussed.

12. Is the number of rounds known?  
 (a) Yes.  Subjects were explicitly told they would play 24 periods (six per system).  
 (b) Not varied; no prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
 (a) Yes. After each contribution stage, subjects see every group member’s contribution and income.  
 (b) Not varied; no prediction.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
 (a) No.  IDs are reshuffled each period and only the *total* punishment a target receives is displayed.  
 (b) Not varied; no prediction.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
 (a) Not applicable (no reward).  
 (b) Not discussed.

-----------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A: Dependent variables used  
 • Relative contribution (% of own endowment put in the public account)  
 • Money-unit profit per period  
 • Satisfaction ratings  
 • Fairness ratings  
 The paper does NOT compute “efficiency’’ in the sense of (actual total payoff)/(maximum possible payoff).  Profit is related but not identical to efficiency because the denominator (the maximum) is never used.

B: Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
 Eight parameters are explicitly described: 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13 and 14.

C: For how many parameters does the paper analyse the effect of *systematically varying* the parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
 None (0/15).  The only experimental manipulations are (i) symmetry vs. asymmetry of endowments and (ii) type of punishment system.  Neither manipulation corresponds to an independent, systematic sweep of any of the 15 parameters.

D: Predicting the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency using only this paper  
 Because efficiency is never reported, only indirect inferences can be made:  
 • With the specific settings used (4 players, MPCR = 0.40, cost-to-fine ≈ 1:2, known 24-period horizon, anonymous punishers), peer punishment raises contributions strongly but *reduces* total profit; democratic punishment raises contributions a bit more and leaves profit statistically unchanged; central punishment raises contributions moderately and also leaves profit statistically unchanged.  
 • Hence, in these circumstances, introducing punishment is unlikely to *increase* efficiency unless the costs of punishment are very small or the game is much longer, but the paper supplies no direct data for alternative parameter combinations.  Consequently, apart from noting that very similar parameter settings produced no efficiency gains (and sometimes losses), the article offers little basis for further predictions about how the 15 parameters or their interactions would influence the punishment effect on efficiency.

Below, each of the 15 parameters is treated in turn.

For every parameter we state  
(1) whether the paper even mentions it and, if so, the value(s) actually used in the experiments, and  
(2) whether the paper says anything—numerical or verbal—about how *changing* that parameter would alter the **punishment-treatment effect** (i.e., the efficiency gain or loss produced by allowing peer punishment versus not allowing it).  All citations to “Table 1”, “Table 2”, “Table 3”, or specific text are to the paper reproduced above.  If nothing is said, that is reported explicitly.

------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
(1) Mentioned.  Both studies use groups of four (“groups of four players”, §2.1.2).  
(2) No statement or data on how using a different group size would change the punishment treatment effect on any outcome (efficiency or otherwise).

2. Number of rounds  
(1) Mentioned.  Study 1: two rounds; Study 2: one round (see Fig. 1 and §3.1).  
(2) The paper never analyses “number of rounds” as an independent variable that is *systematically varied*; the authors run the two designs but do not compare them on efficiency or on a “punishment treatment effect.”

3. Chat enabled?  
(1) Not mentioned (there was no chat).  
(2) No discussion of what enabling chat would do.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
(1) Mentioned only implicitly: contributions are continuous from 0 to 400 cents (§2.1.2).  
(2) No speculation or data on switching to an all-or-nothing format.

5. Contribution “default” design?  
(1) Not used; the standard PGG design is followed.  
(2) No mention.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
(1) Mentioned: each cent contributed is doubled and divided among four, so MPCR = 0.50 (§2.1.2).  
(2) No analysis of what would happen if MPCR were higher or lower.

7. Cost to impose one unit of punishment  
(1) Mentioned: cost = 1 (cost-to-impact ratio 1 : 4, §2.1.2).  
(2) No discussion of how changing that cost would affect the punishment treatment effect.

8. Punishment magnitude per unit purchased  
(1) Mentioned: every cent spent removes four cents from the target (impact = 4, §2.1.2).  
(2) No statement on the consequences of other impact levels.

9. Reward enabled?  
(1) Not enabled; never discussed.  
(2) No analysis.

10. Reward cost  
(1) Not applicable.  
(2) No analysis.

11. Reward magnitude  
(1) Not applicable.  
(2) No analysis.

12. Is the number of rounds common knowledge?  
(1) Yes.  Participants knew in advance the exact length of the game (two rounds in Study 1; one round in Study 2, §2.1.3).  
(2) The paper does not address what would happen if the horizon were unknown.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
(1) Yes.  After each contribution stage participants saw every group member’s contribution (§2.1.3).  
(2) No claims about withholding that information.

14. Is the identity of the punisher revealed to the punished?  
(1) Ambiguous.  The paper states that “individual identifiers were maintained … to allow for reputation building” (§2.1.2) but never says whether the actual *punishing* player was revealed.  
(2) No analysis of varying identifiability.

15. Is the identity of the rewarder revealed?  
(1) Not applicable (no rewards).  
(2) No analysis.

------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY  

A. Does the paper study *efficiency*?  
 No.  Dependent variables are (i) contribution level, (ii) the binary decision to punish, (iii) punishment investment (in cents), (iv) decision time, and (v) self-reported affect.  “Efficiency” (total or average payoff relative to the cooperative maximum) is never reported.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
 7 of them: #1, #2, #4, #6, #7, #8, #12, #13 (possible mention of #14 but unclear).

C. For how many parameters does the paper examine the effect of *systematically varying* the parameter on the punishment treatment effect for any dependent variable?  
 Zero.  None of the parameters are experimentally varied with the express purpose of estimating how they change the impact of a punishment option, and efficiency is never measured.

D. Predictive take-aways that can be made *solely* from this paper  
 • Because no baseline “no-punishment” condition and no efficiency data are supplied, the paper offers almost no leverage for predicting how any of the 15 parameters – singly or in interaction – would affect the efficiency change caused by introducing punishment.  
 • The only dimension that differed across the two studies was “number of rounds,” but even here the authors present no comparative statistics on efficiency, so no prediction can be drawn.  
 • Consequently, any attempt to forecast the punishment treatment effect on efficiency on the basis of this article alone would be speculative; the paper simply does not provide relevant evidence.

In short, the article is informative about psychological moderators of *how much people punish*, but it offers virtually no information about how design parameters of a public-goods environment would alter the *efficiency* consequences of adding a punishment option.

Below is an item-by-item summary of whether and how the paper discusses each of the 15 listed parameters (1–15), along with any mention of systematically varying them and the effect on punishment’s impact—especially with regard to efficiency. The paper by Strang and Park (referred to here simply as “the paper”) focuses heavily on general factors that influence cooperation/punishment and on neural/psychological mechanisms, rather than on systematic variations in public‐goods‐game parameters or on explicit measures of group efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) NUMBER OF PLAYERS  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – Yes. It briefly notes that cooperation levels can depend on group size (e.g., “it is highest in small groups”), referring to prior behavioral findings on public goods games.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying the number of players for punishment’s effect (on efficiency or otherwise)?  
  – No. It does not provide any quantitative effect size or a systematic manipulation of number of players.  

2) NUMBER OF ROUNDS  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – Yes. The paper mentions repeated interactions versus one-shot interactions and notes that cooperation can be higher in repeated interactions or decline without punishment across multiple rounds.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying the number of rounds for punishment’s effect (on efficiency or otherwise)?  
  – No. Although it notes that punishment stabilizes or maintains cooperation in repeated games, there is no systematic analysis of how different round lengths quantitatively change punishment’s impact on total payoffs or efficiency.  

3) IS CHAT ENABLED BETWEEN PLAYERS?  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – No. There is no mention of chat or communication channels between participants.  

4) IS THE CONTRIBUTION “ALL OR NOTHING”?  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – Somewhat. It distinguishes the Prisoner’s Dilemma (in which players must either cooperate fully or defect fully) from the standard public goods game (where one can contribute “part, all, or none”).  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying an all‐or‐nothing contribution structure for punishment’s effect?  
  – No. It only notes the Prisoner’s Dilemma as an example; no effect sizes or efficiency outcomes for different contribution rules are discussed.  

5) IS THE CONTRIBUTION DEFAULT (E.G., DO PLAYERS “PULL BACK” FUNDS)?  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – No. The paper does not mention any design in which the default is to contribute, and players must actively remove or “pull back” funds.  

6) MARGINAL PER CAPITA RETURN (MPCR) OR RELATED MULTIPLICATION FACTOR  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – Yes. It mentions the “multiplying factor (f)” in both the public goods game and the Prisoner’s Dilemma.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying MPCR/factor for the punishment treatment effect?  
  – No. It simply describes that the contributions are multiplied but does not systematically examine different values of f or relate them to punishment’s impact on efficiency.  

7) PUNISHMENT COST TO IMPOSE A SINGLE UNIT OF PUNISHMENT  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – Yes. It notes that “participants have to invest part of their own payoff in order to decrease the noncooperator’s payoff” and that “usually a punishment ratio of 1:3 is applied.”  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying this cost ratio for the punishment effect (on efficiency or any other dependent variable)?  
  – No. The paper only mentions the typical ratio (1:3) but does not discuss how different punishment‐cost variations would affect outcomes. No effect sizes are provided.  

8) PUNISHMENT MAGNITUDE (COINS DEDUCTED PER UNIT OF PUNISHMENT)  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – Yes, implicitly, in describing the 1:3 ratio (the punisher pays 1 unit; the target loses 3).  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying punishment magnitude?  
  – No. As above, it only notes the standard ratio without analyzing how changes would affect efficiency or other outcomes.  

9) WHETHER A REWARD IS ENABLED  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – No. The paper focuses on the punishment side of maintaining cooperation. It does not discuss any design where peer-to-peer rewards are offered.  

10) REWARD COST TO GRANT A SINGLE UNIT OF REWARD  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – No. It does not discuss reward costs or systematically compare punishment versus reward.  

11) REWARD MAGNITUDE (COINS AWARDED PER UNIT OF REWARD)  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – No. Same as above; the paper does not address rewards or their magnitude.  

12) IS THE NUMBER OF ROUNDS KNOWN TO PLAYERS?  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – No. It contrasts one‐shot versus repeated games but does not specify whether participants have common knowledge about how many rounds will be played.  

13) ARE PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN (E.G., HOW MUCH OTHERS GAIN/LOSE EACH ROUND)?  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – No. Although it does mention “anonymous” versus “non-anonymous” designs in general (and how anonymity affects cooperation), it does not detail whether peer outcomes are displayed.  

14) WHEN A PLAYER IS PUNISHED, DO THEY KNOW WHO THE SPECIFIC PUNISHER IS?  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – No. It addresses second‐ and third‐party punishment in broad terms but does not say whether the punished player sees the punisher’s identity.  

15) WHEN A PLAYER IS REWARDED, DO THEY KNOW WHO THE SPECIFIC REWARDER IS?  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – No. Rewarding is not a focus of the paper, so there is no mention of whether the rewarder’s identity is revealed.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY  
A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper does not explicitly use a measure of “group efficiency” (actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff). It does discuss “payoff,” “cooperation rates,” “punishment behavior,” and “subjective happiness/emotional responses,” as well as neural activation in various brain regions. These are treated as distinct dependent variables (cooperation rate ≠ efficiency, punishment ≠ cooperation, etc.), and none is framed explicitly as a ratio of actual total payoff to maximum payoff.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned to some extent: #1 (number of players), #2 (number of rounds), #4 (all‐or‐nothing contribution in the Prisoner’s Dilemma), #6 (the multiplication factor f), #7 (punishment cost), and #8 (punishment magnitude).  
   • Not mentioned: #3, #5, #9, #10, #11, #12, #13, #14, and #15.  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each is systematically varied?  
   • None. Although the paper points out typical setups—for instance, that a 1:3 punishment ratio is “usually” applied—it does not analyze or predict how systematically varying these parameters would alter punishment’s effect on any outcome (efficiency or otherwise). No numerical effect sizes are provided.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not offer direct predictions about efficiency (in the sense of group payoff relative to the maximum) under punishment. Instead, it emphasizes general tendencies: punishment stabilizes cooperation, cooperation tends to be higher in small groups or with repeated play, etc. There is minimal to no basis for quantitatively predicting how each parameter and its interactions would change efficiency, beyond the general notion that punishment options often foster cooperation—which might, in principle, improve total payoffs or preserve cooperation over time.  

Accordingly, the paper by Strang and Park does not systematically vary or quantify these 15 parameters with respect to efficiency outcomes. Their primary focus is on psychological and neural mechanisms (especially emotion, punishment, brain activity) rather than on parametric manipulations of public‐goods‐game designs and their direct impact on group efficiency.

Abstract: The evolutionary foundations of helping among nonkin in humans have been the object of intense debates in the past decades. One thesis has had a prominent influence in this debate: the suggestion that genuine altruism, strictly defined as a form of help that comes at a net fitness cost for the benefactor, might have evolved owing to cultural transmission. Abstract: To explore damages rules' deterrent effect we use a public good experiment to tailor punishment to rules used in civil litigation. The experimental treatments are analogous to: (1) damages limited to harm to an individual, (2) damages limited to harm to a group, such as in class actions, and (3) treble damages.    • Discussed? Yes. The experiment always lasts 30 periods (rounds).

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned at all? No. There is no statement that participants can send messages to one another, nor is there any condition with or without chat.  
   • Systematic variation? No. The paper is silent on this.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned at all? Indirectly, the paper shows that each participant chooses any integer from 0 to 20 to contribute. Thus, it is not an all‐or‐nothing design.  
   • Systematic variation? No. The paper does not study switching from “continuous” to “all or nothing” contributions.

5. Is the contribution default (participants decide how much to move back to themselves)?
   • Mentioned at all? No. All participants choose any integer from 0 to 20 to contribute. No default or forced contribution rule is discussed, so no systematic variation or prediction is reported.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Discussed? Yes. The paper sets the MPCR at 0.4, so each player gains 0.4 times the sum of all contributions.  
   • Systematic variation? No. It is held constant at 0.4 in all treatments, and the paper does not discuss changing it.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussed? Yes, implicitly. In the experiment, the “active player” pays no cost to claim “damages” from another player; imposing damages is costless to the active player.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player per unit of punishment)
   • Discussed? Yes, extensively. The paper frames it as “damages” rather than per‐unit punishment, but effectively they vary how much can be taken from low contributors:
        – “Compensatory” (up to 0.4 × the shortfall)  
        – “Class action” (up to 0.6 × the shortfall)  
        – “Treble damages” (up to 1.2 × the shortfall).  
   • Systematic variation? Yes. The paper systematically alters the maximum damages that can be imposed. However, the paper always analyzes effects on (i) contributions to the public good and (ii) individual or group profit—never on “efficiency” defined as total payoff / maximum payoff.

Abstract: Potential Pareto Public Goods create an aggregate benefit to society while harming some members of the community. As the overall benefit outweighs the harm incurred, provision may lead to Pareto improvement if the gains from cooperation are used to compensate the harmed parties. Such situations are ubiquitous, e.g., in not-in-my-backyard (NIMBY) problems. We study experimentally voluntary contributions to Potential Pareto Public Goods, in which provision is efficient but harms a minority in the group. We test the effects of punishment and reward institutions, with and without communication. We find that contributions to Potential Pareto Public Goods are not viewed as unequivocally socially desirable and do hot increase with communication or punishment. With the reward institution, communication facilitates compensation, undoing the harm imposed on the minority player by majority contributions. Consequently, contributions are no longer viewed as socially undesirable, and majority contributions increase. Taken together, our results establish that perceptions and behavior in voluntary contributions to Potential Pareto Public Goods are dramatically different than with universal public goods that benefit all members of the community. We suggest that the underlying mechanism is team reasoning: individuals consider what is good for the group, and play their part in achieving that goal. (C) 2016 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

Author Keywords: Online communities; Collaborative groups; Social applications; Free riding; Game theory; Tit for Tat
Abstract: In this paper, we address the problem of the free riding behaviour that takes advantage of collaborative educational social groups without contributing back to other participants posts. Free riders are active users who ask questions and draw knowledge from the community but provide very limited or no contributions back to it. Since the survival of a collaborative educational community is highly dependent on its active users and their contributions, motivating free riding users to take an active part would naturally augment the value the community provides and ensure its survivability. As a solution, we formally analyse the impact of the free riding behaviour by means of repeated game theory where classical and generous Tit for Tat are used. Such analysis shows the impact of such behaviour on educational communities and raises the need for other strategies that motivate free riding users to cooperate under the threat of being punished by cooperative ones; hence, we introduce reputation based Tit for Tat strategies. Article Title: The Norm-Signaling Effects of Group Punishment: Combining Agent-Based Simulation and Laboratory Experiments
Author Keywords: norms; punishment; cooperation; agent-based simulation; laboratory experiments
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; COOPERATION; ENFORCEMENT; SANCTIONS; MONETARY
Abstract: Punishment plays a crucial role in favoring and maintaining social order. Recent studies emphasize the effect of the norm-signaling function of punishment. However, very little attention has been paid so far to the potential of group punishment. We claim that when inflicted by an entire group, the recipient of punishment views it as expressing norms. The experiments performed in this work provide evidence that humans are motivated not only by material incentives that punishment imposes but also by normative information that it conveys. The same material incentive has a different effect on the individuals' future compliance depending on the way it is implemented, having a stronger effect when it also conveys normative information. We put forward the hypothesis that by inflicting equal material incentives, group punishment is more effective in enhancing compliance than uncoordinated punishment, because it takes advantage of the norm-signaling function of punishment. In support of our hypothesis, we present cross-methodological data, that is, data obtained through agent-based simulation and laboratory experiments with human subjects. The combination of these two methods allows us to provide an explanation for the proximate mechanisms generating the cooperative behavior observed in the laboratory experiment.

Parameter-by-parameter extraction from the paper
------------------------------------------------
(For each parameter I first say whether the paper even **mentions** it and, if so, what value is used; second, whether the paper makes any **prediction under a systematic variation** of the parameter for the punishment-treatment effect (PTE).  “PTE” here means the difference between the punishment and the no-punishment conditions on any outcome.)

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned: groups of four (one human + three computer confederates).  
   • Systematic variation / prediction: none. Group size is fixed at 4; the authors only say they “intend to vary the size of the group in future work.”

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned: 40.  
   • Not varied; no prediction. The only distinction is descriptive (Rounds 1-9 vs. 10-40).

3. Chat / communication enabled?  
   • Mentioned: expressly disabled (“Participants could not communicate”).  
   • Not varied; no prediction.

4. Contribution “all-or-nothing”?  
   • Mentioned: yes — at the first stage each subject chooses either to contribute (C) or defect (D); no continuous choice.  
   • Not varied; no prediction.

5. Contribution default / withdrawal frame  
   • Not mentioned.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Implicitly mentioned through Table 1 pay-off matrix (each additional contributor raises everyone’s earnings by 5).  
   • Not varied; no prediction.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   • Mentioned qualitatively: punishing “also inflicts a cost to the punisher” (size not reported).  
   • Held constant; not varied; no prediction.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss to target per unit)  
   • Mentioned: being punished “reduces the punished subject’s payoff to zero” (for the single round in which it is applied).  
   • Held constant; not varied; no prediction.

9. Is a reward option enabled?  
   • Not mentioned; reward option is absent.

10. Reward cost  
    • Not applicable / not mentioned.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Not applicable / not mentioned.

12. Is the number of rounds known to the players?  
    • Mentioned: yes — subjects know the game lasts 40 rounds.  
    • Not varied; no prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mentioned: after each contribution stage “participants are informed about their individual earnings and the decisions and earnings of the other participants.”  
    • Not varied; no prediction.

14. Is the punisher identified to the target?  
    • Mentioned: no — anonymity is preserved to avoid reputational effects.  
    • Not varied; no prediction.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
    • Not applicable; reward absent.

------------------------------------------------
Summary
------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables actually analysed  
   • The paper does **not** compute or report group efficiency (total or average payoff divided by the cooperative maximum).  
   • Dependent variables used:  
     – Contribution / cooperation rate (fraction of contributions).  
     – Non-punished defector rate (fraction of defectors who escape punishment).  
   These are behavioural frequencies, not payoffs or efficiency.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   Parameters 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14 (10 out of 15) are stated.  
   Parameters 5, 9, 10, 11, 15 are not discussed.

C. Which parameters are *systematically varied* and linked to the punishment-treatment effect?  
   • None of the 15 listed parameters.  
   • The sole manipulated independent variable in the study is the **number of punishers** (0, 1, 2, 3), which is *not* on the user-supplied list. Therefore 0/15 parameters receive any causal analysis of their effect on the PTE.

D. What predictions about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency can be made *solely from this paper*?  
   Because the paper never varies any of the listed parameters and never measures efficiency, almost no parameter-specific prediction can be drawn. The only cautious, paper-based inferences one might venture are:  
   • If peer outcomes (parameter 13) were *not* shown, the authors’ norm-signalling argument could be weaker, so the positive contribution effect they observe with group punishment might shrink — but the paper itself does not test this.  
   • Revealing punisher identity (parameter 14) might introduce reputational channels the authors explicitly excluded; again this is speculative and untested.  
   Beyond those qualitative remarks, the paper provides **insufficient evidence to predict how varying any of the 15 parameters, singly or in interaction, would change the impact of punishment on group efficiency.**

Hence, for the purpose of forecasting efficiency effects, the study offers little guidance with respect to the 15 parameters enumerated above.

Abstract: Do opportunities to punish non-punishers help to stabilize cooperation? Or do opportunities to punish punishers harm cooperation and its benefits by deterring first order punishment and wasting resources? Below I go through the 15 parameters one-by-one, saying (i) whether the paper ever states the value of the parameter and (ii) whether the paper reports what happens when the parameter is systematically changed and how that change alters the punishment-treatment effect.  “Punishment-treatment effect’’ always means the difference between a condition with a punishment stage and a condition without it.  Whenever the paper speaks about variables other than group efficiency (e.g., contributions), I note this explicitly.  All statements are taken directly from the paper text, figures or tables reproduced in the prompt.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (i) Stated: yes – fixed groups of four.  
   (ii) Systematically varied: no.  No prediction or estimate of how moving from 4 to any other size would change the punishment-treatment effect on any variable.

2. Number of rounds  
   (i) Stated: yes – 15 periods.  
   (ii) Not varied – no prediction.

3. Chat enabled?  
   (i) Not mentioned.  (No indication that chat was ever available.)  
   (ii) Not varied – no prediction.

4. “All-or-nothing’’ contribution rule  
   (i) Stated indirectly – standard voluntary contribution mechanism in which each subject “allocates funds between a private account and a group account.’’  Hence contributions are continuous, not all-or-nothing.  
   (ii) Not varied – no prediction.

5. “Reverse” contribution default (participants withdraw from a public fund)  
   (i) Not mentioned.  
   (ii) Not varied – no prediction.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   (i) Not reported anywhere in the paper text provided.  
   (ii) Not varied – no prediction.

7. Punishment cost per unit  
   (i) Numerical value never given in the excerpt.  
   (ii) Not varied – no prediction.

8. Punishment magnitude per unit  
   (i) Numerical value never given.  
   (ii) Not varied – no prediction.

9. Whether a reward option exists  
   (i) Stated implicitly – there is no reward stage in any treatment.  
   (ii) Not varied – no prediction.

10. Reward cost per unit  
11. Reward magnitude per unit  
   Both not applicable (no reward option).

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
   (i) Not stated explicitly, but the design description (“standard … design of 15 periods in fixed groups”) and the use of a finite-period public-goods game strongly suggest subjects knew the horizon.  Nevertheless, the paper never says so.  
   (ii) Not varied – no prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   (i) Yes.  
       – Baseline & Punish 1: after stage-1 contributions, each player sees every group member’s contribution.  
       – Punish 2: each target of punishment sees who punished her and by how much, but information about punishment between other dyads is hidden.  
       – Punish 2′: full “matrix” of who punished whom is revealed to everyone, and a reminder screen of earlier periods is added.  
   (ii) Systematic variation: yes – the step from Punish 2 to Punish 2′ enlarges the set of peer-outcome information.  
       Effect on punishment-treatment effect:   Figure 2 shows that, relative to Baseline, average earnings are significantly higher in Punish 1 (p = 0.031) and marginally higher in Punish 2′ (p = 0.065); earnings in Punish 2 are also above Baseline but not significantly so (exact p-value not given).  However, “there is no statistically significant difference in earnings between any two punishment treatments,” which means adding the extra information in Punish 2′ does not significantly change the punishment-treatment effect on earnings or on contributions.  No numerical effect size (in payoffs or efficiency units) is provided beyond the statement of non-significance.  Hence the paper’s prediction is: enlarging peer-outcome information (parameter 13) from the Punish 2 to the Punish 2′ level has no detectable impact on either contributions or earnings.

14. Does a punished player learn the punisher’s identity?  
   (i) Yes – in both Punish 2 and Punish 2′ the target sees the identity and amount of each punishment received.  
   (ii) Not varied – no prediction.

15. Does a rewarded player learn the rewarder’s identity?  
   Not applicable (no reward stage).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables  
    • The paper reports (i) mean contribution per period and (ii) mean earnings per subject.  
    • “Efficiency’’ (total payoff as a percentage of the maximum) is never computed, but mean earnings are a direct proxy.  Therefore, the paper does use an efficiency-related dependent variable (earnings) but discusses it separately from contributions.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are at least mentioned?  
    Seven: 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 13, 14.  Of these, only parameter 13 is actually manipulated across treatments.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of systematic variation on the punishment-treatment effect?  
    Exactly one – parameter 13 (peer-outcome information).  The paper reports that expanding the information set (Punish 2′ vs. Punish 2) produces no significant change in either contributions or earnings, i.e., no change in the punishment-treatment effect.

D.  What predictions can be made, drawing only on this paper, about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency?  
    • Parameter 13: Altering the detail and reach of information about others’ punishment actions does not materially change the efficiency gain produced by adding a punishment stage.  
    • All other parameters: the paper offers no evidence or prediction.  Therefore, based solely on this article, we have essentially no basis for predicting how variations in number of players, number of rounds, MPCR, punishment cost and magnitude, availability of rewards, anonymity of punishers, etc., would affect the punishment-treatment effect on group efficiency.

Author Full Names: Bicskei, Marianna; Lankau, Matthias; Bizer, Kilian
Article Title: Negative reciprocity and its relation to anger-like emotions in identity-homogeneous and -heterogeneous groups
Author Keywords: Social identity; Emotions; Experiment; Public goods; Negative reciprocity
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS; SOCIAL CATEGORIZATION; DECISION-MAKING; COOPERATION; PUNISHMENT; ECONOMICS; DIVERSITY; FAIRNESS; BEHAVIOR; POWER
Abstract: Several studies have shown that social identity fosters the provision of public goods and enhances the willingness to reciprocate the cooperative behavior of group members. Nonetheless, the question of how social identity affects negative reciprocity in identity-homogeneous and-heterogeneous groups has only received little attention. Consequently, we seek to fill this gap by examining whether social identity affects individuals' willingness to sanction deviating group members in a public good context. Moreover, we devote particular attention to the role of anger-like emotions in negative reciprocity. To test our hypotheses, we employ one-shot public good games in a strategy method with punishment opportunity and induced social identity. Our results indicate that members of identity-homogeneous groups are prone to reveal less negative reciprocity than identity-heterogeneous groups when they face contributions smaller than their own. We also find that anger-like emotions much more strongly influence punishment behavior when individuals are matched with members of different identities than in identity homogenous groups. These findings contribute to an increased understanding of the nature of social identity and its impact on reciprocity, improving economists' ability to predict behavior while taking emotions into consideration. Article Title: Intention Modulates the Effect of Punishment Threat in Norm Enforcement via the Lateral Orbitofrontal Cortex
Author Keywords: intention; lateral orbitofrontal cortex; norm compliance; punishment threat; tDCS
Keywords Plus: PREFRONTAL CORTEX; STIMULATION; SANCTIONS; OTHERS; FMRI
Abstract: Although economic theories suggest that punishment threat is crucial for maintaining social norms, counterexamples are noted in which punishment threat hinders norm compliance. Such discrepancy may arise from the intention behind the threat: unintentionally introduced punishment threat facilitates, whereas intentionally introduced punishment threat hinders, norm compliance. Here, we combined a dictator game and fMRI to investigate how intention modulates the effect of punishment threat on norm compliance and the neural substrates of this modulation. We also investigated whether this modulation can be influenced by brain stimulation. Human participants divided an amount of money between themselves and a partner. The partner (intentionally) or a computer program (unintentionally) decided to retain or waive the right to punish the participant upon selfish distribution. Compared with the unintentional condition, participants allocated more when the partner intentionally waived the power of punishment, but less when the partner retained such power. The right lateral orbitofrontal cortex (rLOFC) showed higher activation when the partner waived compared with when the computer waived or when the partner retained the power. The functional connectivity between the rLOFC and the brain network associated with intention/mentalizing processing was predictive of the allocation difference induced by intention. Moreover, inhibition or activation of the rLOFC by brain stimulation decreased or increased, respectively, the participants' reliance on the partner's intention during monetary allocation. These findings demonstrate that the perceived intention of punishment threat plays a crucial role in norm compliance and that the LOFC is casually involved in the implementation of intention-based cooperative decisions.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter accounting of what (if anything) this paper says about each of the 15 parameters and whether the authors report or predict any effect of systematically varying that parameter on the “punishment treatment effect,” understood here as how introducing a punishment option changes behavior (especially compared to no‐punishment conditions). As requested, all information is taken solely from the content of the paper by Zhang et al. (2016), without bringing in additional literature or assumptions.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper studies one “allocator” (the participant) and one “responder” (a partner or a computer “decider”). However, it does not systematically vary the number of players (it is always effectively two in the actual interaction).  
   • Any predicted effect of varying it on the punishment treatment effect? No. The paper does not discuss what would happen if the number of players changed, nor does it provide effect sizes for such a manipulation.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned? The authors do state that participants played 64 total trials in two blocks of 32. However, they do not treat “number of rounds” as a manipulated factor.  
   • Any predicted effect of varying it on punishment’s impact? No. The paper does not examine how changing the total number of rounds would alter the effect of punishment in any dependent measure.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned? No. There is no mention of textual or verbal chat.  
   • Any predicted effect of varying it? No. The paper does not address this parameter.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned? The paper indicates that participants could allocate anywhere between 0 and 20 yuan to the partner in increments of 2 yuan (i.e., not all‐or‐nothing).  
   • Any predicted effect if it were varied? No. The paper does not discuss how forcing an “all‐or‐nothing” choice might affect punishment outcomes.

5. Is the contribution default (do players move money from the public fund back into their hand)?
   • Mentioned? Not in that sense. Participants simply choose how many yuan (0–20) to give up. No “default” contribution level is systematically varied or analyzed.  
   • Any predicted effect of varying it? No mention.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplier  
   • Mentioned? No. This is a dictator‐style allocation game, not a public‐goods setup with a multiplier.  
   • Any predicted effect of varying it? The paper does not address MPCR or any multiplication factor.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? The paper does not discuss a “cost to the punisher.” Rather, the participant (allocator) loses 4 yuan if punished, but there is no mention that the one imposing punishment also pays a cost.  
   • Any predicted effect of systematically varying that cost? None given.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   • Mentioned? The study used a fixed 4 yuan punishment.  
   • Any predicted effect of varying it? The authors note that punishment intensity can matter in principle (they cite prior findings), but they do not systematically manipulate the punishment amount here and provide no effect‐size estimates for changing it.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned? No. The experiment only discusses punishment (retain vs. waive). No reward mechanism was implemented.  
   • Any predicted effect of rewards? No discussion in this paper.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Mentioned? No. Rewards were not used.  
    • Any predicted effect? Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)
    • Mentioned? No. Again, no reward mechanism is deployed.  
    • Any predicted effect? Not discussed.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Mentioned? The paper does not indicate whether participants knew the exact total number of trials.  
    • Any predicted effect if it were varied? Not addressed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much their peers gained/lost)?
    • Mentioned? The authors state that trial‐by‐trial payoffs were not revealed, so peer outcomes were not displayed.  
    • Any predicted effect? No. The paper does not discuss systematically varying the visibility of others’ outcomes.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Mentioned? Participants do know whether the decision to “retain” or “waive” punishment comes from a “partner” (other human) or a “computer program.” However, the authors do not treat it as a manipulation of anonymity; rather, the entire experiment centers on whether punishment is “intentional” (from the partner) or “unintentional” (from a computer).  
    • Any predicted effect of varying punisher identification itself? No. The experiment always makes it clear who decides (partner vs. computer), but they do not systematically vary anonymity or identifiability.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Mentioned? No. There is no reward condition.  
    • Any predicted effect? Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   • The paper does not use “group efficiency” or “total payoff” as its main dependent measure. Instead, the authors measure how much money participants allocate to their partner (as a proxy for “norm compliance”), participants’ self‐reported emotional states, and (via neuroimaging) activation in certain brain areas. These outcomes (allocation amounts, emotions, neural activity) differ from “efficiency,” which would compare total payoffs to a theoretical maximum.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Parameters explicitly or implicitly mentioned:  
     (1) Number of players (always two plus confederates),  
     (2) Number of rounds (64 trials, but not manipulated),  
     (4) Whether contribution is all‐or‐nothing (it is not, but that is simply the setup),  
     (8) Punishment magnitude (fixed at 4 yuan),  
     (14) Knowledge of the punisher’s identity (partner vs. computer) insofar as participants could see that it was the “partner” or the “computer” who retained/waived punishment.  
   • No other parameters in the list are described or manipulated.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • In this study, none of the 15 parameters above were systematically varied for the purpose of analyzing how changes in that parameter alone would alter punishment’s effect on behavior or payoff. The authors instead manipulated (a) who decided on punishment threat (partner vs. computer) and (b) whether the threat was retained or waived. That particular manipulation does not match any of the 15 parameters as they are listed (it is somewhat related to whether one knows the identity of the punisher, but the paper does not treat that as a “parameter variation” akin to #14). Thus, effectively zero of the parameters (in the sense of the above list) were systematically varied in a way that the paper links to changes in punishment effectiveness.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not provide evidence or discussion on systematically altering any of the 15 parameters (other than using a fixed punishment and telling participants whether a partner or a computer was responsible), nor does it speak about “efficiency” as an outcome. Consequently, there is little basis to predict how these 15 parameters, individually or in combination, would affect punishment’s net impact on group efficiency. The authors do note that punishment intensity can matter, but they do not vary it. Otherwise, no systematic guidance about these parameters is offered. Hence, based purely on this paper, one can make no or minimal prediction on how those 15 parameters or their interactions would affect efficiency.
reference_APA: Zhang, Yuan, Yu, Hongbo, Yin, Yunlu & Zhou, Xiaolin (2016). Intention Modulates the Effect of Punishment Threat in Norm Enforcement via the Lateral Orbitofrontal Cortex. JOURNAL OF NEUROSCIENCE.

Authors: Wu, JH; Balliet, D; Peperkoorn, LS; Romano, A; Van Lange, PAM
Author Full Names: Wu, Junhui; Balliet, Daniel; Peperkoorn, Leonard S.; Romano, Angelo; Van Lange, Paul A. M.
Article Title: Cooperation in Groups of Different Sizes: The Effects of Punishment and Reputation-Based Partner Choice
Author Keywords: group size; public goods game; reputation-based partner choice; punishment; cooperation
Keywords Plus: SOCIAL VALUE ORIENTATION; INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; PUBLIC-GOODS; SUSTAINING COOPERATION; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; COMPETITIVE ALTRUISM; PROMOTE COOPERATION; COLLECTIVE ACTION; EVOLUTION; DILEMMAS
Abstract: Reputation and punishment are two distinct mechanisms that facilitate cooperation among strangers. However, empirical research on their effectiveness is mainly limited to relatively small groups and does not address how they enhance cooperation in relatively larger groups. We address this gap in the literature by testing hypotheses from competing perspectives about the extent to which reputation-based partner choice and punishment enhance cooperation in both small and large groups. Prior work recognizes that an increase in group size is accompanied by a change in the incentive structure, which determines whether the temptation (extra benefit for each person from non-cooperation over cooperation, regardless of others' choices) or gain (extra benefit for each person from full cooperation over full non-cooperation) remains constant or varies with group size. Thus, we first test how group size affects cooperation when temptation or gain increases with group size (Study 1), and then move on to testing predictions on the effectiveness of reputation and punishment across different group sizes (Study 2). In Study 1 (N = 820), we randomly assigned participants to play an online one-shot public goods game in groups of 4, 20, or 40, while keeping the marginal group return or marginal per capita return fixed across groups, in which case the temptation or gain increased with group size. In Study 2 (N = 1,132), we further compared a public goods situation involving a punishment or reputation mechanism with an anonymous situation across group sizes, while the marginal group return was fixed across groups. Overall, we found that when temptation increased with group size, 20-person groups cooperated significantly less than 4-person groups in one-shot interactions, and that this effect was explained by lower expectation of others' cooperation, less perceived collective efficacy, and greater perceived conflict. However, 40-person and 4-person groups did not vary in one-shot cooperation. Importantly, reputation-based partner choice and punishment invariably promoted one-shot cooperation in groups of different sizes. These findings suggest no simple effect of group size on cooperation and underscore the utility of reputation and punishment in fostering cooperation (at least in one-shot interactions) regardless of the size of groups.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter summary of what appears in Wu et al. (2020), with special attention to whether the paper (1) discusses each parameter (and, if so, what value or condition it takes) and (2) makes any prediction about how systematically varying that parameter would affect the “punishment treatment effect.” Note that the paper measures and reports effects on cooperation (and several psychological variables), but does not measure or report effects on group efficiency (i.e., total payoff or payoff relative to a fully cooperative outcome).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
• Mentioned? Yes.  
  – In both studies, group size was experimentally varied among 4, 20, or 40 persons.  
• Systematically varied to predict punishment treatment effect? Yes, but only for cooperation (not efficiency).  
  – Study 2 compared a punishment condition to a control condition across group sizes (4, 20, 40). The authors found that punishment increased cooperation in all three group sizes, and the interaction “group size × punishment” was not statistically significant.  
  – Numerically, in Study 2’s logistic regressions (Table 2), punishment versus control had an overall coefficient b = 0.53, p = 0.001, OR = 1.70, with no reliably different effect across the three group sizes.  

2) Number of rounds  
• Mentioned? Yes, as “one-shot” (so there was exactly 1 round).  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed, since there was no variation (only a single round in all conditions).

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
• Mentioned? Not discussed at all.  
• Systematically varied? No.  

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Mentioned? Yes, but not varied as an experimental factor.  
  – Study 1: Participants could choose any number of tokens (0 through 20) to contribute.  
  – Study 2: Participants had exactly two choices (contribute all 20 tokens, or 0).  
• The paper does not pivot any analyses or predictions on systematically changing the all-or-nothing rule, nor does it discuss how this would influence punishing.  

5) Is there a contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much of their endowment to move back to themselves)?  
• Mentioned? No.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• No predictions offered.  

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters (e.g., multiplication factor)  
• Mentioned? Yes.  
  – Study 1 experimentally held either MGR (“marginal group return,” 1.6) or MPCR (0.4) fixed across groups.  
  – Study 2 always held MGR = 1.6 fixed.  
• Systematically varied to predict punishment effect?  
  – In Study 2, the punishment condition was carried out only under fixed MGR = 1.6. So MPCR was not varied in the punishment analyses, and there is no reported effect of varying MPCR on punishment effectiveness.  
  – No predictions about how systematically changing MPCR or MGR would alter the punishment treatment effect.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Mentioned? Yes.  
  – In Study 2, each deduction point (the “unit of punishment”) costs the punisher 1 token.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
  – The cost was always 1 token; there is no analysis of how changing that cost would affect punishment’s impact.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
• Mentioned? Yes.  
  – In Study 2, each unit of punishment deducted 3 tokens from the target.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
  – The ratio (1:3) was fixed; no predictions were made about altering it.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
• Mentioned? No.  
  – The paper contrasted a punishment condition and a reputation condition, but not a formal “reward” (bonus) mechanism or prosocial reward per se.  
• Systematically varied? No.  

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Mentioned? No.  
• Systematically varied? No.  

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
• Mentioned? No.  
• Systematically varied? No.  

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know if and when the game ends)?  
• Mentioned? Yes, implicitly.  
  – All interactions were one-shot; thus, participants knew there was only one interaction.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• No predictions about systematically changing round knowledge.  

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained or lost each round)?  
• Mentioned? Only briefly.  
  – In Study 2, participants were told they would see “some or all members’ decisions” prior to punishment or partner choice, but the paper does not systematically vary the visibility of others’ outcomes.  
• No analysis or predictions about varying this factor for the punishment effect.  

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• Mentioned? Not addressed.  
• Systematically varied? No.  

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
• Mentioned? N/A because no reward treatment was implemented.  
• Systematically varied? No.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • No. The paper focuses on cooperation (the proportion of tokens contributed or the proportion of cooperators), as well as three psychological variables: expected others’ cooperation, perceived collective efficacy, and perceived conflict. There is no separate measure of group efficiency or total payoff in the results.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • The paper explicitly discusses six of them:  
     (1) Number of players (varied at 4, 20, 40),  
     (2) Number of rounds (one-shot),  
     (4) Whether the contribution decision is all-or-nothing (Study 2) or continuous (Study 1),  
     (6) MPCR or related payoff parameters (MPCR = 0.4, MGR = 1.6),  
     (7) Punishment cost (1 token),  
     (8) Punishment magnitude (3 tokens deducted from the target per 1 token spent).  
   • Parameters 3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, and 15 are either not mentioned at all or not systematically varied.  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • Only one parameter—(1) Number of players—was both systematically varied and used to test the impact of punishment (vs. control) on cooperation.  
     – The key result: Punishment significantly increased cooperation in 4-, 20-, and 40-person groups, with no reliable interaction between group size and punishment.  
   • None of the other parameters were systematically varied (in combination with punishment) to observe changes in any dependent variable.  

D) If we were to make predictions about how all 15 parameters and their interactions might influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, based solely on this paper, what could we say?  
   • The paper does not measure or report group efficiency at all, so it offers no direct evidence for the effect of punishment on efficiency. The only systematically varied factor relevant to punishment was group size, and the authors found that punishment increased cooperation similarly across sizes. Because the paper does not quantify total payoffs or efficiency, we cannot make firm predictions about how those 15 parameters or their interactions would affect the punishment treatment effect on actual group efficiency.  
   • In short, the paper provides no direct information on how systematically altering any parameters beyond group size might shape punishment’s effect on efficiency, and even for group size, the outcome measure is cooperation rather than efficiency. Consequently, little to no prediction can be made about punishment’s effect on efficiency from this paper alone.

Authors: Tanaka, T; Camerer, CF
Author Full Names: Tanaka, Tomomi; Camerer, Colin F.
Article Title: Trait perceptions influence economic out-group bias: lab and field evidence from Vietnam
Author Keywords: Behavioral economics; Stereotypes; Field experiments; Trust; Group affiliation; Ingroup-outgroup
Keywords Plus: POSTAPARTHEID SOUTH-AFRICA; SOCIAL PREFERENCES; 3RD-PARTY PUNISHMENT; RACIAL STEREOTYPES; NORM ENFORCEMENT; GROUP MEMBERSHIP; DISCRIMINATION; IDENTITY; TRUST; COOPERATION
Abstract: Group favoritism is typically directed toward in-group members and against out-group members, but these cross-group effects often vary. Little is known about why group effects on economic choices vary. We use a survey method developed in social psychology to measure stereotyped attitudes of one group toward another. These attitudes are then associated with prosociality in five experimental games (also using an unusual amount of individual-level sociodemographic control). We present evidence from an artificial field experiment of a majority group with high status (Vietnamese) exhibiting no disfavoritism toward a lower-status out-group (Khmer) and typical disfavoritism to a second out-group (Chinese). Both Vietnamese and Chinese groups see the Khmer as warm but incompetent, attitudes which seem to activate empathy rather than contempt. The results suggest that measuring between-group stereotype attitudes can be used to predict the sign of cross-group favoritism in other natural settings.
