Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what the paper does (and does not) say about each of the 15 listed features of a public‐goods‐with‐punishment design. Because the paper in question does not actually study a repeated public goods game with punishment, almost all of these parameters are simply not discussed. The paper does include one “third‐party punishment” (3PP) game, which is a single‐shot, three‐player variant of a dictator game (not a repeated public goods game). Where relevant, references to that 3PP game are noted.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned? Indirectly. The paper’s third‐party punishment game has three players (one dictator, one recipient, and one punisher).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not vary the number of players. There is no public goods game here, only single‐shot, three‐player 3PP.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned? Only insofar as the 3PP (and other games) are played in single‐shot format.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not examine multi‐round or repeated treatments.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned? No. The experiments did not involve free‐form communication (“chat”) among participants.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper studies dictator‐type allocations, an “envy” game, etc., but not an all‐or‐nothing structure in a public goods sense.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

5. Is the contribution “default” (where players must actively move money out of a public fund)?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper’s behavior‐allocation games involve sending or keeping money in a simple one‐shot manner; there is no mention of a default contribution mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Mentioned? No. The paper uses a simple multiplier in the trust game (doubling or tripling a transferred amount), but there is no mention of MPCR in a public goods context.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned? Yes, but only in the specific 3PP game. In that game, the punisher forfeits 1,000 dong of their endowment to reduce the dictator’s payoff by 3,000 dong.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The cost (1,000 dong) is fixed and never manipulated.

8. Punishment magnitude (the amount deducted from the target per unit of punishment)
   • Mentioned? Yes, again only in the 3PP game: punishing deducts 3,000 dong from the dictator.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The magnitude (3,000 dong) is fixed in the single 3PP game design.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned? No. None of the games provided a mechanism for rewarding other players.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Mentioned? No (no reward mechanism was studied).  
    • Systematically varied? No.

11. Reward magnitude (the amount awarded for each unit of reward granted)
    • Mentioned? No (no reward mechanism was studied).  
    • Systematically varied? No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
    • Mentioned? The games are single‐shot, so there is only “one round.” There is no condition of known versus unknown horizons.  
    • Systematically varied? No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much others gained/lost each round)?
    • Mentioned? The paper does not discuss whether participants learn the specific payoffs of peers in a repeated sense, only that final outcomes were communicated at the end of each single‐shot game.  
    • Systematically varied? No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Mentioned? The paper does not clarify whether punished dictators knew the specific identity of who punished them, beyond knowing there is a third‐party punisher in the 3PP game.  
    • Systematically varied? No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is?
    • Mentioned? No. The design does not include a reward.  
    • Systematically varied? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use “group efficiency” (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper does not use (or report) a ratio of actual to maximum possible payoff in a manner typical of “efficiency” in public goods studies.  
   • Its main dependent variables are individual game decisions in dictator/envious allocations, third‐party punishment thresholds (the “minimum accepted” offer), trust/reciprocity choices, and coalition formation choices. The authors do at times note average payoffs by group or mention “earnings,” but not in the sense of studying or modeling group efficiency as the key outcome.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Slight references appear for:  
     (1) Number of players – the 3PP game has three players.  
     (7) Punishment cost – fixed at 1,000 dong.  
     (8) Punishment magnitude – fixed at 3,000 dong.  
   • The remaining 12 parameters are not discussed in the paper.

C. For which and how many of those 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • None. The paper does not systematically vary the number of players, punishment cost, or punishment magnitude (or any other parameter), and provides no discussion or predictions about how changing those parameters would affect any treatment effect (whether on “efficiency” or on any other dependent variable).  
   • In other words, there is zero systematic variation of the 15 parameters in this study.

Abstract: Institutional punishment plays a central role in human societies. Yet research in evolutionary game theory has focused almost exclusively on peer punishment. Here we present a model for the evolution of institutional punishment. We consider a set of states (kingdoms), each consisting of a number of individuals (subjects) and a single leader (king). Subjects choose how much to pay to the king as tribute. The king chooses how much to punish his subjects based on their tribute payment level, in an effort to exact as much tribute as possible. We find the existence of both coercive Nash equilibria with punishment and high tribute payments, and noncoercive Nash equilibria with no punishment and no tribute payments. We also examine stochastic coevolutionary dynamics using agent-based simulations. We find that within a single state, the more intensely the king punishes, the more subjects evolve to pay in tribute. The king earns the most when both punishment is strong and subjects are accurate in their learning. When we consider co-evolution occurring at the level of the king as well as the subject, we see that kings evolve to punish heavily, as long as subjects are sufficiently accurate and frequent in their learning, and learn predominately from subjects in the same kingdom. If citizens have error-prone learning and/or are slow to update their strategies, however, selection leads to kings who punish little. Thus confusion is collectively beneficial for subjects. In sum, we show circumstances under which natural selection can favor the emergence of institutional punishment as a tool of coercion.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter review of what (if anything) the paper says about each of the 15 listed factors. In virtually all cases, the paper does not explicitly refer to “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” or systematically vary that parameter with the express purpose of measuring how it affects efficiency. Instead, the paper develops a theoretical model of kings (who can punish) and subjects (who can pay tribute), and compares outcomes under different forms of evolutionary dynamics. Any references below to “efficiency” or total payoffs are drawn directly from the paper’s discussion of aggregate payoffs.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – Yes, the paper considers a fixed number n of subjects per kingdom. It analyzes n = 10 versus n = 100 in one section (see Fig. 1).  

• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it and the effect on punishment treatment (for efficiency or any other dependent variable)?  
  – The paper does not systematically explore how changes in n alter the difference between punishment and no‐punishment (i.e., the “punishment treatment effect”). It does report that the outcome patterns for n=10 and n=100 are very similar (they “have little effect”), and so uses n=10 for computational simplicity.  
  – There is no quantitative effect size given, nor any formal discussion of how varying n would change total payoffs or efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Number of rounds
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – No, the model is set up as an indefinitely iterated evolutionary process. There is no statement about a finite or known number of rounds of play that would ever be revealed to subjects or kings.  

• Any prediction of its systematic variation?  
  – No, the paper does not mention or vary the number of rounds, nor does it analyze the effect of such variation on punishment or efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Is chat enabled between players?
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – No, there is no mention of any communication or “chat” among the subjects or between subject and king.  

• Any prediction of its systematic variation?  
  – No mention.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – The paper lets each subject’s tribute be p ∈ [0, 1], which is a continuous fraction of her income. It never imposes an “all‐or‐nothing” rule.  

• Any prediction of its systematic variation?  
  – No, there is no variation; the model always uses a continuous amount of tribute.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5. Is the contribution default (do players move from public fund back to hand)?
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – No, the setup is simply that each subject produces 1 unit of income and decides what fraction (p) of that income to send to the king. There is no alternative formulation where “contribution” is the default.  

• Any prediction of its systematic variation?  
  – No mention.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – No, this is not a standard public‐goods model with a multiplier. The paper never uses a factor analogous to MPCR.  

• Any prediction of its systematic variation?  
  – No mention.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – The “cost of punishing” and the “punishment inflicted” are both governed by the same parameter s in a linear function. Specifically, punishing a subject who deviates by (1 − p) costs the king s·(1 − p), and the subject also loses s·(1 − p). Hence it is effectively a 1:1 cost‐to‐damage ratio.  
  – However, the paper does not separate “cost to punisher” and “cost imposed on target” as two distinct parameters. Everything is wrapped into s.  

• Any prediction of its systematic variation?  
  – They do systematically vary s from 0 to 3 or 0 to 10. Changes in s affect how strongly the king punishes (and thus how much it costs him each time he punishes). But the paper frames this more directly as “punishment strength” (see parameter 8 below).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted per unit)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – Yes, the parameter s is exactly the variable that determines punishment magnitude for each increment (1−p). The paper systematically manipulates and analyzes s ∈ [0,3] or [0,10].  

• Does the paper make predictions about how systematically varying s affects “punishment treatment” outcomes (any dependent variable, including total payoff and efficiency)?  
  – Yes. The paper shows (Figs. 1, 2, 3) that increasing s leads to more tribute (p) from subjects, lower subject payoffs, and—for sufficiently large s and sufficiently high subject “intelligence”—the emergence of “coercive equilibria.”  
  – It notes that in a world with no errors, both a no‐punishment equilibrium and a full‐punishment (“coercive”) equilibrium can have the same total payoff. With any error, the coercive arrangement (high s) becomes less efficient overall because punishment costs are incurred.  
  – The paper does not provide a single numeric estimate of “treatment effect” on total payoff. Instead, it states qualitatively that with high s and even small error, overall payoffs—which can be seen as efficiency—are lower in the coercive equilibrium than in the noncoercive one.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – No, there is no mention of rewards. The paper focuses entirely on punishment.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – No. There is no reward stage in the model.  

• Any prediction of its systematic variation?  
  – No mention.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – No. There is no notion of subjects knowing a fixed end; the model is an ongoing evolutionary process.  

• Any prediction of its systematic variation?  
  – No mention.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see each other’s gains/losses)?
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – The model has “pairwise comparison” evolutionary updating, so in principle each learner sees another’s payoff. But the paper does not treat this as an experimentally varied parameter (“visibility of peer outcomes” is not manipulated).  

• Any prediction of its systematic variation?  
  – No mention.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
14. When a player is punished, does he/she know who the punisher is?
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – No. The paper assumes a single “king” punishes, so the identity of the punisher is clear by definition—but this is never varied as a factor.  

• Any prediction of its systematic variation?  
  – No mention.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
15. When a player is rewarded, does he/she know who the rewarder is?
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – No reward stage is modeled, so there is no discussion of whether the identity of a rewarder is revealed.  

• Any prediction of its systematic variation?  
  – No mention.


────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are its dependent variables, and how are these different from one another?

• The paper’s main outcome measures are:  
  – Each subject’s payoff (labelled π).  
  – Each king’s payoff (labelled Π).  
  – The paper also discusses total (aggregate) payoffs, noting that with no error, both a “noncoercive” (p=0) and a “coercive” (p=1) equilibrium can in principle be equally efficient (no punishment actually happens if all subjects comply). Once errors occur, the coercive equilibrium becomes strictly less efficient due to punishment outlays.  
• Those payoffs are not framed in terms of a “group efficiency” ratio (i.e., actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff), but the paper does discuss how total payoffs can suffer when punishment is large and there are mistakes.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

• Parameter 1 (number of players) is mentioned (they compare n=10 vs. n=100).  
• Parameters 7–8 (cost/magnitude of punishment) appear in the paper as the single parameter s.  
• None of the other 12 parameters are addressed.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when the parameter is systematically varied?

• Only parameter 8 (punishment magnitude s) is systematically varied with respect to its effect on outcomes (including total payoffs). The paper shows that higher s can lead to more coerced tribute, which can reduce subjects’ payoff, often increase the king’s payoff (once subjects comply), and lower total payoffs in the presence of any error.  
• Parameter 1 (number of players n) is varied (n=10 vs. n=100), but the paper does not link that variation explicitly to any difference in “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency; it simply notes the results are largely the same for n=10 or n=100.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper’s content, what would they be?

• The only concrete guidance comes from the paper’s analysis of punishment strength (parameter 8). There, the model says that when s is zero, there is no punishment; when s>1 and players make mistakes, total payoffs (and thus efficiency) fall relative to the no‐punishment equilibrium because punishment costs are borne by the king, and everyone’s final payoff is dragged down.  
• For the other 14 parameters, the paper simply does not provide direct discussion or results from which to infer systematic predictions.

Abstract: We examine how trust is sustained in large societies with random matching, when records of past transgressions are retained for a finite length of time. Abstract: Recently, behaviors that seem to function as punishment or apology have been reported among non-human primates as well as humans. Such behaviors appear to play an important role in maintaining cooperation between individuals. Therefore, the evolution of these behaviors should be examined from the viewpoint of the evolution of cooperation. The iterated prisoner's dilemma (IPD) game is generally considered to be a standard model for the evolution of cooperation. In the present study, strategies accompanied by punishment-like attacks or apology-like behavior were introduced into the common IPD simulation. Punishment and apology were represented by the P signal and the AS signal given immediately after defection. A strategy with the P and AS signals, named the pPAS strategy, was proved to be an evolutionarily stable strategy under certain conditions. Numerical simulations were carried out according to different assigned values of the costs of punishment and apology. The simulations showed that pPAS could dominate the population (1) when the cost of giving P is relatively small, (2) when the cost of receiving P is relatively large, or (3) when the cost of giving AS is relatively large.      1) The average (expected) payoff in the population when a strategy dominates.  
     2) Evolutionary stability or whether a given strategy (e.g., pPAS) can invade and dominate.  
   – These differ from “efficiency” in that they report the average points per individual (e.g., 2.97, 2.94, etc.) rather than the ratio of (actual total payoff)/(maximum possible total payoff).

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – Five are explicitly mentioned or used:  
     1) Number of players (=2) [Parameter #1].  
     2) Number of rounds (infinite / w=0.99), though not systematically varied [#2].  
     3) T (temptation payoff) as part of the IPD payoff matrix, which loosely corresponds to a “related parameter” under #6.  
     4) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment (K1) [#7].  
     5) Punishment magnitude/cost to the defector (K2) [#8].  
   – All others (parameters #3–5, #9–11, and #12–15) are either not mentioned or not varied.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   – Three parameters are explicitly varied to observe their effect on outcomes involving punishment:  
     (a) T (the “temptation” payoff, part of #6 in your list),  
     (b) K1 (punishment cost to the punisher) [(#7)],  
     (c) K2 (punishment cost to the punishee) [(#8)].  
   – When these shift, they change whether pPAS or GTFT or AllD dominates, and thereby change the resulting average payoff.  
   – The paper does not provide a single numerical “effect size” but does show how low K1, high K2, or lower T fosters pPAS.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

     1) Fewer players (#1) or indefinite rounds (#2) are simply assumed; they are not varied, so no direct predictions.  
     2) Larger T (under #6) makes punishment‐apology systems more vulnerable to certain “deceptive” strategies, while lower T (3.5) lets pPAS thrive more easily, maintaining high average payoffs.  
     3) Lower cost of giving punishment (#7 = K1) favors stable cooperation with pPAS; higher cost can undercut it.  
     4) Higher cost to be punished (#8 = K2) makes punishment more deterrent, again favoring pPAS.  
   – No predictions can be formed from the paper about the remaining parameters, since they are not addressed.

Article Title: Local and Global Interactions in an Evolutionary Resource Game
Author Keywords: Common property; Cooperation; Evolutionary game theory; Global interactions; Local interactions; Social norms
Abstract: Conditions for the emergence of cooperation in a spatial common-pool resource game are studied. This combines in a unique way local and global interactions. A fixed number of harvesters are located on a spatial grid. Harvesters choose among three strategies: defection, cooperation, and enforcement. Individual payoffs are affected by both global factors, namely, aggregate harvest and resource stock level, and local factors, such as the imposition of sanctions on neighbors by enforcers. The evolution of strategies in the population is driven by social learning through imitation, based on local interaction or locally available information. Numerous types of equilibria exist in these settings. An important new finding is that clusters of cooperators and enforcers can survive among large groups of defectors. We discuss how the results contrast with the non-spatial, but otherwise similar, game of Sethi and Somanathan (American Economic Review 86(4): 766-789, 1996).

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what, if anything, the paper by Noailly et al. (2008) says about each of the 15 listed parameters and whether it makes any prediction about systematically varying them in relation to a “punishment treatment effect”—which, in your terms, would be how punishment changes outcomes (especially “efficiency”) compared to no punishment.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
1. Number of players  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  Yes. The paper uses m to denote the population (number of harvesters). Most simulations use m = 100 arranged on a 10×10 grid, but Section 3.5 systematically varies m (from 36 up to 121).  
• Any prediction about systematically varying it and its effect on the punishment treatment (for efficiency or any outcome)?  
  The paper shows how a larger population size can foster the persistence of enforcers (punishers) and more mixed “cooperative” equilibria. However, it does not quantify any impact on “group efficiency” per se (they do not measure “actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff”). Instead, they measure which strategies survive. No numeric effect size on efficiency is given.

2. Number of rounds  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  The authors typically run the model for 50 rounds (or sometimes 500 or more to check stability), but they do not systematically vary the number of rounds to see how it would affect a punishment‐versus‐no‐punishment treatment effect on efficiency.  
• Any prediction about varying it?  
  No. They do not link the number of rounds to any measure of punishment’s effect on efficiency.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  No. There is no mention of communication or “chat” among players.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  No. Players choose discrete “high” (defect) or “low” (cooperate) effort, but this is never referred to as an “all‐or‐nothing” enforceable contribution scheme.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much of their endowment to move from the public fund back “into their hand”)?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  No. The paper does not use or mention a default mechanism of that sort.

6. Marginal per capita return or a related multiplication factor  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  No. The authors use a harvest function F(X) = α X^β N₀^(1−β). Although F is somewhat analogous to a production or “multiplication” function, they neither label nor study it as an MPCR or linear multiplier, nor do they link it to a standard public‐goods‐game “return.” Hence, no mention of an MPCR.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  Yes. They use γ (gamma) as the per‐defector cost paid by an “enforcer” to punish.  
• Any prediction about systematically varying it?  
  They set γ = 0.1 in their main simulations and do not do a systematic variation of γ. Thus, there is no direct, numeric result about how changing γ would alter the punishment effect on payoffs or “efficiency.”

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from a player per unit of punishment)  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  Yes. They denote it by δ (delta). In Section 3.5, the authors do systematically vary δ from 0.1 up to 1.5 and show how it influences the frequency of equilibria dominated by defectors vs. those that sustain cooperators/enforcers.  
• Any prediction about its effect on punishment vs. no‐punishment outcomes (for efficiency or otherwise)?  
  They do not measure an explicit “treatment effect on efficiency.” Instead, they track which strategies eventually dominate. Higher δ tends to deter defection because punishers impose stronger sanctions, so cooperators and enforcers persist more often. The paper does not provide a numerical change in total payoff or “efficiency.”

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  No. Only punishment (“enforcement”) is considered, not rewards.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  No. The model does not include rewards.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward)  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  No. Again, no reward mechanism appears.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  No. There is no mention whether players know how long the interaction lasts.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see others’ payoffs)?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  Yes. Each agent observes the payoffs of its local neighbors in order to imitate the most successful strategy.  
• Any prediction about systematically varying this?  
  No. The paper’s setup always assumes local payoff observation. It does not systematically remove or alter that information display.

14. When a player is punished, do they know the specific punisher?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  Not in the sense of “identifying who punished.” The model simply states that enforcers punish defectors in their neighborhood but does not discuss knowledge of the punisher’s identity.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know the specific rewarder?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  No. They do not analyze rewards at all.

SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?  
   • The paper does not explicitly measure “group efficiency,” i.e., total payoff divided by the theoretical maximum, nor does it label or analyze a punishment “treatment effect” on efficiency. Instead, the main outcomes are which strategies (defect, cooperate, enforce) survive in equilibrium (D, E, C, or combinations). They also track payoffs at the individual level but not in the form of group‐efficiency comparisons.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned:  
     1. Number of players, m  
     7. Punishment cost (γ), although not systematically varied  
     8. Punishment magnitude (δ), which is systematically varied  
     13. Peer outcomes are visible for local imitation (but not varied).  
   • The paper does not discuss or vary the other parameters.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • They systematically vary only two parameters in relation to punishment and look at resulting equilibria (defectors vs. cooperators/enforcers):  
     1. Number of players (m).  
     8. Punishment magnitude (δ).  
   • However, they never directly measure a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Instead, they track how often large‐scale defection versus enforcement/cooperation emerges under different values of m and δ.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   • The authors never present “efficiency” calculations, so strictly from this paper one cannot quantify how introducing punishment changes “group efficiency.” The paper does imply that higher δ (punishment magnitude) makes it more likely that enforcers and cooperators persist, presumably boosting collective outcomes in many configurations. Larger populations (m) can also allow more spatial clustering of enforcers and cooperators. But beyond noting these qualitative results—that bigger δ and larger m often foster more cooperative equilibrium—the paper does not estimate or report numeric changes in total payoff or efficiency from punishment. Consequently, one cannot reliably predict a numerical treatment effect on efficiency from this paper’s text alone.

Authors: Engelmann, D; Nikiforakis, N
Author Full Names: Engelmann, Dirk; Nikiforakis, Nikos
Article Title: In the long-run we are all dead: on the benefits of peer punishment in rich environments
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS EXPERIMENTS; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; COUNTER-PUNISHMENT; GOOD GAMES; COOPERATION; ENFORCEMENT; RECIPROCITY; HUMANS
Abstract: We investigate whether peer punishment is an efficient mechanism for enforcing cooperation in an experiment with a long time horizon. Previous evidence suggests that the costs of peer punishment can be outweighed by the benefits of higher cooperation if (i) there is a sufficiently long time horizon and (ii) punishment cannot be avenged. However, in most instances in daily life, when individuals interact for an extended period of time, punishment can be retaliated. We use a design that imposes minimal restrictions on who can punish whom or when, and allows participants to employ a wide range of punishment strategies including retaliation of punishment. Similar to previous research, we find that, when punishment cannot be avenged, peer punishment leads to higher earnings relative to a baseline treatment without any punishment opportunities. However, in the more general setting, we find no evidence of group earnings increasing systematically or significantly over time relative to the baseline treatment. Our results raise questions under what conditions peer punishment can be an efficient mechanism for enforcing cooperation.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter account of what the Engelmann & Nikiforakis (2015) paper does (and does not) say regarding each of the 15 listed factors and how these factors might affect the “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency (i.e., the actual total payoff relative to the maximum possible payoff under full cooperation). Throughout, I refer only to what is actually stated in the paper, including its figures and tables, without bringing in any other studies or my own inferences.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
 • Mentioned? The paper uses groups of four players in every treatment (No Punishment, Standard Punishment, Rich Punishment).  
 • Systematically varied? No. All groups have size four. There is no discussion in the paper about what happens if this parameter is varied.

2. Number of rounds
 • Mentioned? Yes. Each treatment (NP, SP, and RP) lasts 30 periods. The paper also references previous 50-period designs for comparison, but does not itself use more or fewer than 30.  
 • Systematically varied? No. They do not run different numbers of rounds across treatments. While they discuss how a “long time horizon” can help punishment offset its costs, they do not manipulate the exact number of rounds experimentally.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
 • Mentioned? No. There is no mention that participants are allowed to chat or communicate.  
 • Systematically varied? No. The paper makes no statements about changing or enabling chat.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
 • Mentioned? Not explicitly. The experiment is a linear public-good game (participants can contribute any integer amount 0–20), rather than an all-or-nothing format.  
 • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not discuss changing this feature.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much of their endowment to move back into their hand)?
 • Mentioned? Not explicitly. The design is described as a standard linear public-good game with the usual “choose your contribution from 0 to 20.” There is no mention of forced default allocations or any variant of that sort.  
 • Systematically varied? No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor
 • Mentioned? Yes. The group account multiplies contributions by 1.6, which is then divided equally among 4 players, so the MPCR is 0.4.  
 • Systematically varied? No. The paper keeps MPCR = 0.4 throughout. No predictions are made about varying the MPCR.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
 • Mentioned? Yes. In the punishment treatments (SP, RP), it costs 1 ECU to assign 1 punishment point.  
 • Systematically varied? No. It is held constant at 1 ECU per punishment point. The paper does not discuss changing this cost.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed on them)
 • Mentioned? Yes. Each punishment point reduces the punished individual’s payoff by 3 ECU.  
 • Systematically varied? No. The ratio of 1 ECU cost to the punisher and 3 ECU deducted from the punished is constant. The paper does not discuss changing this ratio.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
 • Mentioned? No. There is no reward stage or reward option in any treatment.  
 • Systematically varied? Not applicable.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
 • Mentioned? No. Not applicable, as the paper does not study any reward mechanism.

11. Reward magnitude
 • Mentioned? No. Again, not applicable.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
 • Mentioned? Yes. In all three treatments, participants know that the game ends after 30 periods.  
 • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not compare “known” vs. “unknown” horizon.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much their peers gained or lost each round)?
 • Mentioned? Partially. After each period, players see the contribution of everyone else and, when punishment is present, see how many punishment points each player assigned and received within that same period (SP) or across multiple stages (RP).  
 • Systematically varied? Not as an isolated factor. The difference between “Standard Punishment” (SP) and “Rich Punishment” (RP) also involves changing ID anonymity across periods, but the paper does not isolate or systematically vary “information display.”

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
 • Mentioned? Yes, but not as an isolated treatment variable.  
   – In SP, IDs are randomized each new period, preventing across-period identification (and thus meta-strategies). However, within a single period, players see exactly who punished whom.  
   – In RP, identification numbers stay the same across periods, so people can observe who punished whom both within and across periods.  
 • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not discuss how turning this knowledge on or off would affect efficiency, aside from noting it is part of the overall difference between SP and RP.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
 • Mentioned? No. There is no reward action.  
 • Systematically varied? Not applicable.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DEPENDENT VARIABLES AND OTHER NOTES FROM THE PAPER

• Although the paper’s title, abstract, and discussion refer to “efficiency,” the primary analysis is in terms of realized group earnings (which are the sum of individual payoffs in each period, or their average). That is not exactly the same as “efficiency = total payoff / (maximum possible payoff),” though conceptually related. The authors also measure contributions (i.e., how many ECUs are contributed to the public good) and punishment expenditures (i.e., number of punishment points assigned). They do not expressly compute an “efficiency ratio”; instead, they compare average group earnings across treatments.  
• The paper contrasts three treatments:  
  – No Punishment (NP)  
  – Standard Punishment (SP)  
  – Rich Punishment (RP)  
  …but does not systematically vary the 15 parameters one by one.  
• Numerical effect sizes in the paper focus on:  
  – SP vs. NP: After enough rounds, SP eventually achieves statistically higher average earnings than NP.  
  – RP vs. NP: RP does not achieve a statistically higher average payoff than NP by the end of 30 periods; half the groups sustain very high contributions, while the other half unravel into low contributions and/or feuds.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper mainly tracks group earnings (which can be considered a measure of total or average payoff). It also compares levels of contributions. “Efficiency” is discussed conceptually as higher group earnings net of punishment costs, but the paper does not specifically calculate an efficiency ratio (actual total payoffs divided by the maximum possible).

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned: (1) number of players (always 4), (2) number of rounds (30), (6) MPCR (= 0.4), (7) cost to punish (= 1 ECU), (8) punishment magnitude (= 3 ECU), (12) known horizon (30 rounds), (13) peer outcomes shown (contributors and punishment points assigned), and (14) whether the punisher is revealed (it is revealed, but with different anonymity rules in SP vs. RP).  
   • Not mentioned at all or not applicable: (3), (4), (5), (9), (10), (11), and (15).

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None of the 15 parameters is systematically varied in the paper. In other words, the study does not manipulate group size, the punishment cost ratio, the horizon length, or whether punishers remain anonymous, etc., in a one-parameter-at-a-time way. Instead, the paper compares three fixed designs (NP, SP, RP) that differ in several respects at once. There are therefore no numerical effect sizes in the paper that isolate the impact of varying any of the 15 parameters alone.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • Because the paper does not experimentally vary any of these parameters as isolated treatments, it offers little direct basis for predictions about systematically altering them. The paper primarily concludes that, even with a “long horizon,” if punishers can be identified and can retaliate, gains in group earnings may fail to emerge. Beyond that, the authors do not provide any explicit predictions about how changing group size, MPCR, punishment magnitude, or other parameters (like chat, reward mechanisms, or anonymity) would alter the effect of punishment on efficiency. Thus, one can make no firm predictions from this paper alone.
reference_APA: Engelmann, Dirk & Nikiforakis, Nikos (2015). In the long-run we are all dead: on the benefits of peer punishment in rich environments. SOCIAL CHOICE AND WELFARE.

Authors: Ozono, H; Kamijo, Y; Shimizu, K
Author Full Names: Ozono, Hiroki; Kamijo, Yoshio; Shimizu, Kazumi
Article Title: The role of peer reward and punishment for public goods problems in a localized society
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; COOPERATION; GOVERNANCE; BENEFITS; TRAGEDY
Abstract: Cooperation in social dilemmas can be sustained if individuals are effectively rewarded or punished from peers within the group. However, as group size increases, we inevitably face localization, in which a global group is divided into several localized groups. In such societies, members can reward and punish only neighbors within the same localized group, while cooperation for social dilemmas should be solved through global group involvement. In this situation, the global group and the local group are not always equal in terms of welfare, and situations can arise in which cooperation is beneficial for the global group but not for the local group. We predict that in such a locally inefficient situation, peer reward and punishment cannot function to sustain global cooperation. We conducted an experiment in which 16 group members played a public goods game incorporating peer reward and punishment. We manipulated the range of peer reward and punishment (only local members/all global members) and payoff structure (locally efficient/locally inefficient). We found that high cooperation was not achieved and that peer reward and punishment did not function when, and only when, the group was divided into localized groups and the payoff structure was locally inefficient.

1. Number of players
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – Yes. The experiment varies group size (4 vs. 16 players). In the BASE condition, there is a single group of 4. In the Local0.1, Local0.4, and Global0.1 conditions, there are 16 players.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it, and if so, does it make predictions about the punishment treatment effect?  
  – The paper does systematically change the number of players across these conditions. However, it does not explicitly report how “varying the number of players” by itself alters the effect of punishment on efficiency. Instead, the paper focuses on how different conditions (some with 4 vs. 16 players) affect average profit and contributions, but does not provide a numerical effect size about how that variation alone changes “punishment treatment effect.”  

2. Number of rounds
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – The paper specifies 15 rounds (periods).  
• Does the paper systematically vary it, and if so, does it make predictions about the punishment treatment effect?  
  – No. All conditions use 15 rounds. The paper notes end‐of‐game effects in round 15, but does not manipulate the total number of rounds as an experimental factor and does not provide a punishment‐effect prediction tied specifically to changing the number of rounds.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – No mention of chat or communication of that sort. There is no discussion of letting players communicate except for the obligatory numeric feedback.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – The paper states that participants can contribute any integer amount from 0 to 20 tokens. It is not an all‐or‐nothing format, and the paper does not manipulate this.  

5. Is the contribution default?
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – No. The contribution decision is from 0 to 20, with no mention of a forced default or “uncontributing by default.”  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – Yes. This is the central manipulated variable across conditions (e.g., MPCR = 0.1 vs. 0.4 vs. 1.6 vs. 6.4).  
• Does the paper systematically vary it, and if so, does it make predictions about the punishment treatment effect?  
  – Yes, the MPCR differs by condition:  
    • BASE condition: 4 players; total contributions multiplied by 1.6 and shared.  
    • Local0.1: 16 players; MPCR of individual is 0.1, multiplication factor is 1.6 for the global group.  
    • Local0.4: 16 players; MPCR of individual is 0.4, multiplication factor is 6.4 for the global group.  
    • Global0.1: 16 players; MPCR of individual is 0.1, multiplication factor is 1.6 for the global group, but peer interactions are with all 16.  

  The paper finds that, in the “locally inefficient” scenario (Local0.1), both punishment and reward are less effective at boosting cooperation (and hence profit). However, it does not report a numeric effect size specifically for how punishment alone changes “efficiency” in the sense of actual‐to‐maximum payoff. Instead, it reports that low MPCR at the local group level (Local0.1) makes punishment and reward less effective at sustaining cooperation.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – Yes, the cost is 1 token for each unit of punishment.  
• Is it systematically varied?  
  – No. The cost is fixed at 1 token in all conditions, with no discussion of how changing that cost would alter the punishment effect.  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed on them)
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – Yes. Each punishment token deducts 3 tokens from the target.  
• Is it systematically varied, and are there predictions about its effect?  
  – No. The punishment magnitude (3 tokens) remains constant, with no variation across conditions. There is no reported effect of systematically changing it.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – Yes, in the sense that the experiment always has both peer reward and punishment.  
• Is it systematically varied?  
  – No. The presence of a reward option is always “on.” The paper does not look at any condition where reward is disabled, so there is no direct comparison or effect size.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – Yes, the cost is 1 token to the rewarder.  
• Is it systematically varied?  
  – No. It is held constant; the paper makes no predictions about changing the cost.  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted to them)
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – Yes, the rewarded player gains 3 tokens for each unit of reward.  
• Is it systematically varied?  
  – No. It is fixed at 3 across all conditions, so the paper does not evaluate how altering it would affect punishment or efficiency.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – Yes, all participants are explicitly told there are 15 periods.  
• Is it systematically varied?  
  – No. There is no condition in which the game length is unknown. The paper does not assess how that variation would influence punishment’s effect.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – The paper mentions that participants see others’ contributions and see from whom they received punishment or reward.  
• Is it systematically varied?  
  – No. Everyone in all conditions can see these outcomes; there is no manipulation test.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – Yes, the methods state that participants “receive feedback concerning from which other participants they received punishment.”  
• Is it systematically varied?  
  – No, it is always revealed. The paper does not discuss systematically changing anonymity.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
  – The same as #14: it is revealed to the receiver who gave the reward.  
• Is it systematically varied?  
  – No. There is no manipulation of whether the reward is anonymous.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
• The paper does not use “group efficiency” defined explicitly as “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff” in its analyses. Instead, the main dependent variables are:  
  – Average PGG contribution.  
  – Average profit (also analyzed in “adjusted” form for comparability).  
  – Average amount of reward and punishment.  
  – Whether cooperators are rewarded more or punished less than non‐cooperators.  
These differ from an efficiency ratio in that they do not directly compare observed total payoffs to the payoff that would arise from perfect cooperation.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• The paper explicitly discusses the following parameters:  
  1) Number of players (4 or 16).  
  2) Number of rounds (always 15, though not systematically manipulated).  
  6) MPCR (the main systematically varied factor alongside group structure).  
  7) Punishment cost = 1 token (mentioned but not varied).  
  8) Punishment magnitude = 3 tokens (mentioned but not varied).  
  9) Whether a reward is enabled (always enabled).  
  10) Reward cost = 1 token (mentioned but not varied).  
  11) Reward magnitude = 3 tokens (mentioned but not varied).  
  14) and 15) Players do know who punished/rewarded them (mentioned but not varied).  
The others (chat, “all or nothing” contribution, etc.) are either not manipulated or not discussed.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• Strictly speaking, the paper only systematically varies:  
  – (1) Number of players (4 vs. 16).  
  – (6) MPCR / multiplication factor (0.1 vs. 0.4 vs. 1.6 vs. 6.4 in different groupings).  
• However, the discussion focuses largely on how these manipulations affect overall cooperation, rewards, punishments, and profits—not on a formal “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” The authors do not provide a numerical effect size that directly links changes in either parameter to punishment’s impact on “efficiency.”  
• They do find that when the local MPCR < 1 (i.e., “local inefficiency”), both reward and punishment have weaker effects on cooperation and overall payoffs.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
• The paper itself does not measure efficiency as “actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff.” Consequently, it offers little direct guidance for many of these parameters.  
• Still, one can tentatively infer from the discussion of “locally inefficient” vs. “locally efficient” that when the local‐level MPCR < 1, punishment (and reward) become far less effective at raising cooperation. If one views “efficiency” in a broad sense, the implication is that local inefficiency limits the beneficial effect of punishment on group payoffs.  
• Beyond that, the paper provides no basis for predicting how systematically varying the other parameters (e.g., punishment magnitude, number of rounds, anonymity, etc.) would affect punishment’s impact on efficiency. It never directly addresses these other factors.  

Overall, the paper primarily compares several specific conditions and does not give dedicated analyses of “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” per se for each of the 15 parameters. Most parameters are either not varied or not discussed in any detail regarding how they would shape punishment’s effect on “efficiency.”
reference_APA: Ozono, Hiroki, Kamijo, Yoshio & Shimizu, Kazumi (2020). The role of peer reward and punishment for public goods problems in a localized society. SCIENTIFIC REPORTS.

  • General verbal claims:  
   – If E < c, cooperation stays low;  
   – If E > c, cooperation is high;

 Not in model; no prediction.

 Not discussed.

 Not discussed.

14. Punisher identity revealed?  
 Not discussed.

15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
 Not discussed.

SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used  
 • \bar p = average probability of “positive cooperation.”  
 • \bar U = average payoff per neighbour link.  
 The paper does **not** compute *group efficiency* (actual / maximum payoff), nor any total-payoff ratio.  
 Hence “efficiency” in the sense requested by the user is absent.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
 1 (number of players, descriptively), 8 (punishment magnitude).  
 All others are absent or not applicable. → 2 of 15 mentioned, but only one (parameter 8) is actually manipulated.

C. Which parameters are *systematically varied* and linked to the punishment treatment effect?  
 Only parameter 8 (punishment magnitude E).  
 No other parameter is varied in a way that isolates its impact on the “punishment treatment effect” (or any effect).

 Because *efficiency* is never measured, only indirect inference is possible. Assuming that higher \bar U would map monotonically onto higher efficiency, the paper lets us predict the following:

Abstract: The role of punishments in promoting cooperation is an important issue. We incorporate costly punishments into the snowdrift game (SG) by introducing a third punishing (P) character, and study the effects. • whether the paper ever mentions the parameter, and if so the value(s) that actually appear in the text, tables or figures;  
• whether the paper contains any statement (numerical or verbal) about what would happen **if that parameter were systematically varied** to the “punishment treatment effect” (i.e., the difference between the Punishment and No-Punishment conditions).  
Whenever the paper talks about a dependent variable other than efficiency I note that explicitly.

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned.  All simulations use N = 30 000; the analytical part treats an infinite well-mixed population (replicator dynamics).  
   • No results on what happens when N is varied; hence no prediction for the punishment treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Not mentioned (the model runs until a steady state).  
   • No predictions.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Not mentioned.  
   • No predictions.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution?  
   • Not mentioned.  The game is a 2-player Snowdrift game with pure strategies C, D, P.  
   • No predictions.

5. Contribution default / back-transfer?  
   • Not mentioned.  
   • No predictions.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor (here: cost-to-benefit ratio r)  
   • Extensively discussed.  r is varied from 0 to 1; Figures 1 & 3 plot steady-state frequencies against r.  
   • Prediction when r is varied (dependent variable = cooperation frequency, not efficiency):  
        – There exists a critical r_c that depends on α and β.  
        – For r < r_c the punishment treatment eliminates all defectors; the population settles on a C+P mixture (D frequency 0).  
        – For r > r_c the long-run state is the **same** as in the no-punishment Snowdrift game (C and D coexist, P vanishes).  
        – Example with α = 0.1, β = 0.5: r_c ≈ 0.20.  
        – Hence the “treatment effect” on cooperation is +r when r<r_c (e.g., at r=0.15 cooperation rises from 0.85 in the baseline SG to 1.00 with punishment) and ~0 for r>r_c.  
   • No efficiency measure is reported; only frequencies and average fitness are shown.

7. Punishment cost (α)  
   • Mentioned; typical values 0.1 (Figs 1-3) and 0.2 (Fig 4 & analytic section).  
   • Analytic expressions show that larger α shrinks the region in which punishers survive (e.g., the stability condition for a P-C state involves α+β).  However the paper does **not** present systematic sweeps of α or quantitative effect sizes.

8. Punishment magnitude (β)  
   • Mentioned; values 0.5 and 0.8 appear.  
   • Analytic results: the invasion condition involves r/β, so increasing β makes it harder for defectors to invade and therefore enlarges the parameter space where punishment is effective.  No systematic numerical sweep or effect size is provided.

9. Reward enabled?  
10. Reward cost?  
11. Reward magnitude?  
   • Not present at all in the paper; no predictions.

12. Finite/known horizon?  
   • Not mentioned; infinite horizon implicit.  No predictions.

13. Peer outcome visibility?  
14. Identity of punisher known?  
15. Identity of rewarder known?  
   • Not mentioned; no predictions.

────────────────────────────────────────
Summary  

A. Dependent variables used in the paper  
   – Frequencies of Cooperators (f_C), Punishers (f_P) and Defectors (f_D).  
   – Sometimes “average fitness” is computed, but solely as an intermediate step.  
   – **Group efficiency (total or average payoff divided by the cooperative optimum) is never reported.**  
   Hence the dependent variables studied are cooperation frequencies, not efficiency.

B. How many of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   4 parameters appear:  
      (1) number of players N,  
      (6) cost-to-benefit ratio r,  
      (7) punishment cost α,  
      (8) punishment magnitude β.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of **systematically varying** the parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
   – Only one parameter (r) is systematically varied with numerical results.  
   – α and β are in the analytic formulas and verbal discussion, but lack systematic variation or numerical effect sizes.  
   – So: 1 parameter with systematic quantitative evidence, 2 additional parameters with qualitative analytic statements.

D. If forced to predict the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency using only this paper  
   – The paper gives no direct efficiency numbers, so predictions are necessarily indirect.  
   – Efficiency should mirror cooperation frequency under the Snowdrift payoffs used.  
        • For r < r_c (low cost-to-benefit ratio) punishment should raise efficiency to its maximum because D agents disappear.  
        • For r > r_c punishment will **not** change efficiency relative to the baseline game.  
   – Higher α (costlier punishment) should reduce or eliminate the efficiency gains because punishers die out more easily.  
   – Higher β (stronger punishment) should enlarge the region where punishment boosts efficiency.  
   – No prediction can be made about the other eleven parameters; they are absent from the paper.

In short, the article is almost entirely about how r, α and β determine whether punishers survive, using cooperation frequency as the outcome.  It provides no direct information on group efficiency and no information on the remaining twelve design parameters.

Abstract: We explore whether lawful cooperation in buyer groups facilitates collusion in the product market. Buyer groups purchase inputs more economically. The paper does not transform these output changes into efficiency figures, so the impact on efficiency is not quantified.

4. ALL-OR-NOTHING CONTRIBUTION  
(i) Not relevant; no binary contribution decision exists.  
(ii) Not discussed.

5. CONTRIBUTION DEFAULT  
(i) Not relevant.  
(ii) Not discussed.

6. MPCR / MULTIPLICATION FACTOR  
(i) Not part of the design; the game is Cournot, not a linear public good.  
(ii) Not discussed.

7. PUNISHMENT COST‐TO‐PUNISHER  
(i) Implicit.  In Closed buyer groups two firms can “exclude” the third; the excluding firms do not pay any explicit monetary cost (Section 3).  The value is fixed and never manipulated.  
(ii) Because it is fixed, no systematic-variation prediction is made.

8. PUNISHMENT MAGNITUDE  
(i) Implicit.  Exclusion raises the target’s marginal cost from 10 to 22 (Section 4).  Fixed.  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction.

9. REWARD ENABLED  
(i) Rewards do not exist in this experiment.  
(ii) Not discussed.

10. REWARD COST  
11. REWARD MAGNITUDE  
(i) & (ii) Not applicable; see #9.

12. ROUND NUMBER KNOWN  
(i) Participants know there will be 7 initial rounds and “at least 20” further rounds, after which continuation is random.  Hence they have partial but not complete horizon knowledge (Section 4).  
(ii) The degree of horizon knowledge is not varied; no prediction.

13. PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN  
(i) Yes.  After every period subjects see the buyer-group decisions, all quantities and each firm’s profit (Section 4).  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction.

14. PUNISHER IDENTIFIED  
(i) Not clearly specified.  Subjects know which firm is excluded but the text never says they learn which two firms proposed the exclusion.  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction.

15. REWARDER IDENTIFIED  
(i) No rewards; not mentioned.  
(ii) Not applicable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY  

A. Dependent variables  
– The paper does **not** use “group efficiency” (total payoff / maximum possible payoff) as a dependent variable.  
– Main dependent variables: (i) firm-level output, (ii) industry output, (iii) whether exclusion is suggested or implemented, (iv) welfare (consumer + producer surplus, computed ex-post).  These differ from efficiency because they do not normalise by the first-best benchmark.

B. Parameters mentioned  
7 of the 15 parameters appear anywhere in the paper: #1, #2, #3, #7, #8, #12, #13.

C. Parameters whose *systematic variation* is analysed for their impact on the punishment treatment effect  
Only 1 of the 15 parameters—#3 (Chat enabled)—is experimentally varied and analysed in conjunction with the punishment institution (Closed buyer groups).  The Talk dummy lowers firm-level output by about 6.6 units (Table 3) but the Talk × Closed interaction is not significant; effects on efficiency are not reported.

D. What can be predicted—purely from this paper—about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
• Because efficiency itself is never reported, no direct quantitative prediction can be made.  
• Qualitatively, the paper suggests that adding a *cost-free, high-magnitude* punishment option (exclusion) reduces output and therefore lowers efficiency when demand is linear.  Varying #7 or #8 might therefore affect efficiency, but the experiment offers no data on different cost or magnitude levels, so no directional estimate can be given.  
• Enabling chat (#3) further strengthens collusion; if efficiency is measured as total surplus relative to the joint-profit maximum, efficiency would decline, but the size of the change is unknown.  
• For all other parameters the paper contains no information, so no prediction—beyond “unknown”—is possible.

In short, the study only lets us say with confidence that (a) giving subjects an exclusion-based punishment mechanism and (b) allowing them to chat both move outcomes away from the competitive benchmark; everything else remains uninformative with respect to efficiency.

SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables actually analysed

   – Average contribution **among insiders**  
   – Average **total** contribution (called “effectiveness”)  
   – Number of punishment points allocated  
   – The paper does *not* present group efficiency (payoff divided by maximum possible payoff) as an outcome.  
   These variables differ conceptually: participation concerns entry, insider contribution concerns compliance, total contribution combines the two, and punishment points measure enforcement activity.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are *mentioned*?  
   10 of 15 are mentioned (1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14).  
   Five (5, 9, 10, 11, 15) are not used at all.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of **systematically varying** the parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
   Zero.  None of the parameters is experimentally or theoretically varied, so no causal statements or effect sizes are supplied.

D. What predictions (restricted to the paper’s content) can be made about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?

Below, the term “punishment-treatment effect’’ means the *difference* between a world in which peer–punishment is possible and an otherwise identical world in which it is not.  
In the Safarzynska (2013) paper there is **no such experimental contrast** – punishers, cooperators and defectors always coexist in the same simulation environment.  Consequently, almost none of the 15 public-goods parameters were designed or analysed with the goal of estimating a punishment-treatment effect on efficiency.  Where the paper *does* vary a parameter, it reports the consequences for (i) the long-run population share of harvest-conserving types (punishers + non-punishing cooperators) and (ii) the probability that a group collapses through resource exhaustion.  These two outcomes, not efficiency, are the paper’s focal dependent variables.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Parameter-by-parameter extraction from the paper
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players in a group  
   – Discussed: yes.  Fixed baseline = 20; systematically varied 5-50 (Fig. 6).  
   – Effect analysed: yes, on conservation frequency and collapse risk.  No estimate of a punishment-treatment effect or efficiency effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   – Mentioned: a simulation lasts 10 000 time steps.  
   – Not varied; no effect analysed.

3. Chat between players  
   – Not mentioned.

4. “All-or-nothing’’ contribution rule  
   – Model uses two discrete effort levels (low vs. high), but this rule is not varied; no effect analysed.

5. Contribution default / refund rule  
   – Not applicable; not mentioned.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   – No MPCR.  Related ecological parameters are the intrinsic growth rate r and effort productivities eℓ = 0.001 and eʜ (0.002–0.009 explored, Fig. 7).  
   – Varying eʜ was analysed, but only for its direct impact on conservation and collapse, not on a punishment-treatment effect.

7. Punishment *cost* (to the punisher)  
   – Parameter c, baseline 0.1.  Analytically discussed, but *not* varied in simulations; hence no systematic effect reported.

8. Punishment *magnitude* (fine inflicted on the target)  
   – Parameter d, baseline 0.1, varied 0.1–0.9 (Fig. 7).  Higher d increased conservation and lowered collapse probability when the population already had ≥ 50 % conservation.  No efficiency or treatment-effect estimate.

9–11. Reward availability, reward cost, reward magnitude  
   – Rewards do not exist in the model; no discussion.

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
   – Irrelevant in the simulation; not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   – Not discussed.

14. Punisher identity revealed?  
   – Not discussed.

15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
   – Not applicable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Required summary
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables actually used  
    • Long-run average frequency of resource-conserving individuals (punishers + cooperators).  
    • Probability / frequency of group collapse through resource exhaustion.  
    • Occasionally, within-group replicator dynamics.  
    **Efficiency (total payoff ÷ maximum payoff) is never computed.**  
    Contributions, cooperation rates and efficiency therefore are not measured interchangeably in this paper.

B.  Parameters mentioned (out of the 15)  
    1, 2, 4 (implicitly), 6 (via eℓ/eʜ and resource growth r), 7, 8.  
    Total = **7**.

C.  Parameters whose *systematic variation* is analysed for any outcome  
    1 (group size), 6 (eʜ), 8 (punishment magnitude).  
    Total = **3**, and the outcomes are conservation share and collapse risk, never efficiency nor a punishment-treatment contrast.

D.  What can we predict – solely from this paper – about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency?  
    • The paper gives **no direct evidence** on efficiency and no comparison of “with punishment’’ vs. “without punishment.’’  
    • Indirectly, larger punishment magnitudes (parameter 8) and larger group sizes (parameter 1, once above a threshold) *increase* resource conservation and *decrease* collapse risk; if one equated “more conservation / fewer collapses’’ with “higher efficiency,’’ then greater d and sufficiently large n might raise efficiency in a setting that allows punishment.  
    • Higher extraction productivity eʜ (parameter 6 analogue) paradoxically also increases conservation in the long run (because it speeds up collapse of all-defector groups), again suggesting a possible positive effect on eventual efficiency when punishment is possible.  
    • No information is available for the remaining 12 parameters, so no prediction can be made for them.

In short, the paper is largely *orthogonal* to the experimental-design parameters listed in the prompt, and it does not deliver numeric or qualitative estimates of any punishment-treatment effect on efficiency.
reference_APA: Safarzynska, Karolina (2013). The coevolution of culture and environment. JOURNAL OF THEORETICAL BIOLOGY.

Abstract: Mediation is a popular process to prevent conflicts over common resources, but there is little clean insight into its effectiveness and mechanisms. Below, each of the 15 design-parameters is treated in turn.  For every parameter I state  

(1) whether it is explicitly described in the paper and, if so, with what value(s);  
(2) whether the paper contains any prediction or empirical evidence about what would happen if that parameter were **systematically varied** to a different level, specifically with respect to the “punishment treatment effect” on **efficiency** (combined payoff of the two resource users relative to the cooperative maximum).

Whenever a numerical effect can be read‐off from a table or figure, I provide it.  In all other cases I explicitly say that the paper is silent.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned.  Two resource users (A & B); sometimes a third, non-contributing mediator (C). No other group sizes appear.  
   (2) Not varied.  No prediction on how changing the number of players would alter the punishment treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Fixed at 3 rounds in all treatments.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

3. Chat enabled between players  
   (1) Three regimes are used.  
       • “noM” – no chat.  
       • “C/noM” – direct A↔B chat, no mediator.  
       • “Com” – only **indirect** chat (C with each player separately).  
       • “C/P” – indirect chat **plus** punishment.  
   (2) Systematic variation exists.  The paper offers two clear findings about efficiency:

       a.  Adding *direct* chat (C/noM) to the no-chat baseline (noM) raises combined payoff from 46.50 to 67.85 points (Table 2), i.e. an efficiency gain of 21.35 / 80 ≈ +26.7 percentage-points of the cooperative maximum.

       b.  Adding chat to an existing punishment option (Pun → C/P) raises combined payoff from 48.88 to 73.86 points, an efficiency gain of 24.98 / 80 ≈ +31.2 percentage-points.

       The text interprets this as a *synergy* between punishment and communication (“Prediction 3”).

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
   (1) Not applicable.  Players may withdraw any integer number of balls (0–20).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

5. Contribution default (re-allocation from public to private)  
   Not mentioned.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   Not a public-goods setting; ball values (1,2,3,4) are fixed; never varied; no prediction.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   (1) Described and manipulated indirectly through the *interest* treatments:  
       • Impartial mediator: cost = 0.5 points per 1-point deduction.  
       • Biased mediator: cost differs (0.667 vs 0.333 depending on whom she fines).  
       • “No-stakes” mediator: same 0.5-point cost, but her own earnings are fixed, so punishment yields her no direct benefit.  
   (2) This is the only parameter—besides chat—that is experimentally varied.  Table 4 shows that changing the punishment cost/incentive structure has **no statistically significant effect** on combined efficiency:  

       Impartial 73.86, Biased 74.57, No-stakes 70.73 (points after punishment; all ≈ 89–93 % of maximum).  Hence the paper predicts *little or no sensitivity* of efficiency to moderate changes in punishment cost in the presence of communication.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine per unit)  
   (1) Always 1-for-1 (each deduction removes 1 point from the target).  
   (2) Never varied; no prediction.

9. Reward option enabled  
10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   Not implemented; authors explicitly say rewards were excluded.  No predictions.

12. End-of-game known  
   (1) Players are told there are exactly 3 rounds.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

13. Peer outcomes shown  
   (1) Yes – after every round all players see each other’s withdrawals, current payoffs and punishments.  
   (2) Constant; no prediction.

14. Punishee knows the punisher  
   (1) Always yes; the only punisher is the (identified) mediator C.  
   (2) Not varied.

15. Rewardee knows the rewarder  
   Not applicable (no rewards).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
   • The paper’s main efficiency metric is “overall performance of A and B after punishment” (total points earned by the two resource users).  
   • It also reports “conflict incidence,” “inequality / Gini,” “punishment points,” etc.  
   • “Efficiency” (combined payoff) is **not** identical to “contribution”, “withdrawn balls,” or “inequality”; the authors treat these as separate outcomes.

B. Parameters mentioned (any value given): 8 of 15  
   1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14.

C. Parameters whose **systematic variation** is analysed for their effect on the punishment treatment effect: 2 of 15  
   • Parameter 3 (communication/chat) – strong positive interaction with punishment.  
   • Parameter 7 (punishment cost via mediator incentives) – no detectable effect within the tested range.

D. What can we predict—solely from this paper—about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?

   • The only robust, paper-based prediction is that punishment **by itself** (with the cost–benefit structure used) does **not** improve efficiency, but **punishment × communication** strongly does (+31 percentage-points).  
   • Moderate changes in the punisher’s cost structure (0.5 vs 0.667 vs 0.333 cost per point, or eliminating her monetary stake) do **not** materially change the punishment effect, provided communication is present.  
   • For all other parameters the paper offers no evidence, so—remaining faithful to the instructions—we can make **no prediction** about their individual or interactive influence on the punishment treatment effect.

Hence, if one had to forecast efficiency solely with this paper in hand, the key levers would be:  
   1) ensure some form of real-time communication/caucusing, and  
   2) retain a credible punishment option;  
all other design choices listed in the 15-parameter set would be treated as unknowns.
