Authors: Bruhin, A; Janizzi, K; Thöni, C
Author Full Names: Bruhin, Adrian; Janizzi, Kelly; Thoeni, Christian
Article Title: Uncovering the heterogeneity behind cross-cultural variation in antisocial punishment
Author Keywords: Antisocial punishment; Public good games; Finite mixture models; Heterogeneity; Cultural variation
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS; SOCIAL PREFERENCES; COOPERATION; BELIEFS; CRITERION; CLUSTERS; BEHAVIOR; NUMBER
Abstract: Antisocial punishment in public good games, i.e., punishment of individuals who contributed the same or more than their punisher, varies substantially across cultures. We exploit the data of Herrmann et al. (2008) and implement an empirical strategy based on a finite mixture model to uncover the heterogeneity behind this variation. After we exclude 17.7% Type N subjects who never punish, estimating the finite mixture model reveals two distinct punisher types among the remaining subjects: 30.3% Type AF subjects who engage in antisocial punishment as well as free rider punishment and 52.0% Type F subjects who engage exclusively in free rider punishment. Moreover, we find that in cultures with high levels of antisocial punishment, Type AF subjects are more frequent. Despite the parsimony of this classification, the number of Type AF in a group predicts mean earnings in that group and enhances our understanding of the large variation in the effectiveness of peer punishment across cultures. – Not varied; no prediction.

– No reward stage exists; not applicable.

A. Dependent variables used  
– The paper never computes “group efficiency” (payoff divided by maximum).  
– It does analyse:

  • Latent “inclination” parameters estimated by the finite-mixture Tobit.  
  • Mean group earnings (absolute tokens) – used as their proxy for the “effectiveness of peer punishment.”  
  • Contributions.  
These variables are therefore different from the formal efficiency ratio requested in the prompt.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
9 of them: (1) players, (2) rounds, (4) contribution scale, (6) MPCR, (7) punishment cost, (8) punishment magnitude, (12) known horizon, (13) peer information, (14) anonymity of punisher.

2. Number of rounds

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution?

   (ii) No discussion of what would happen if the cost were positive or varied.

   (ii) No speculation on unknown or longer horizons.

   (i) One-shot with no feedback; children do *not* learn others’ contributions or payoffs.  
   (ii) No analysis of revealing or hiding such information.

   (i) Not relevant: punishment is imposed by an impersonal rule (“magician” or “subtraction rule”).  
   (ii) No discussion of identifying punishers.

15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
   – Not applicable (no rewards).

Summary requested by the user
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Use of “group efficiency” as a dependent variable?  
    • The paper never reports group efficiency (total or average payoff divided by the social optimum).  
    • The only behavioural dependent variables are:  
        – Contribution level in NoLaw, ExoLaw, EndoLaw (labelled Contri_NoLaw, Contri_ExoLaw, Contri_EndoLaw).  
        – Binary vote for punishment in EndoLaw (reported only descriptively).  
      Thus “efficiency” is *not* analysed, and contribution is not the same as efficiency because the punishment rule subtracts tokens (lowering payoffs even when contributions rise).

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are explicitly mentioned?  
    9 of 15: 1 (players), 2 (rounds), 3 (chat), 4 (all-or-nothing), 5 (default), 6 (MPCR), 7 (punishment cost), 8 (punishment magnitude), 12 (horizon).  
    The remaining six (9–11, 13–15) are either not present or not discussed.

    Zero.  The study keeps every listed parameter fixed; the only design variation is between “no punishment”, “exogenous punishment” and “endogenous punishment”.  Hence it provides no quantitative or qualitative predictions about how changing any of the 15 parameters would alter the punishment effect on *any* dependent variable (let alone on efficiency).

D.  What predictions about the 15 parameters and their interactions can be made *solely* from this paper?  
    Very few:  
    • Introducing a cost-free, automatic punishment that deducts 2 tokens (parameter bundle 7–8) *raises contributions* by roughly 2.5–2.8 tokens (Tables 8–10), but the paper does not translate this into efficiency and does not examine alternative punishment costs or magnitudes.

In short: the article is rich in behavioural results about *who* (left-behind vs. non-left-behind children) responds to a specific punishment rule, but it does not explore design‐parameter space. 6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
 a. Not mentioned.  
 b. No discussion.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
 a. Punishment is referred to abstractly (“individuals who don’t participate are punished by withdrawal of future help”), but no cost parameter is introduced.  
 b. Neither values nor sweeps are provided.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss to the target)  
 a. Not parameterised; punishment is modelled as “withdrawal of future help,” i.e., a qualitative shift from good to bad standing.  
 b. No quantitative treatment.

9. Whether a reward option exists  
 a. Never mentioned.  
 b. No discussion.

10. Reward cost  
 a.–b. Not mentioned.

11. Reward magnitude  
 a.–b. Not mentioned.

12. Is the horizon known?  
 a. The horizon is uncertain (continuation probability w); whether players *know* when the game ends is never discussed.  
 b. No systematic variation.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
 a. The punishment model assumes that third parties “observe the signal and subsequent behaviour” and pool their evidence, but visibility of monetary pay-offs is never a variable.  
 b. No systematic variation.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
 a. Not addressed.  
 b. No discussion.

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
 a.–b. Not addressed.
--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used  
 – Main dependent variable: evolutionary stability of *honest signalling* (captured by the inequality p a /[p a + (1–p) b] > T_L / T_H).  
 – Auxiliary quantities: T_H, T_L (expected waiting times until a player falls out of good standing), and the probability that a lie is detected (e) or a truthful statement is mis-classified (ε).  
 The paper never reports “group efficiency,” “average group payoff,” or any welfare normalised to the first-best, so efficiency is absent.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
 2 parameters:  
   (1) Number of players (n, but only in the punishment extension).  
   (2) Number of rounds / length of the repeated interaction (w, T).

C. For how many of the 15 parameters does the paper tell us how *systematic variation* affects the punishment treatment effect?  
 None.  Length of play (w) and group size (n) are each discussed, but the authors do not present results that cross those values **between** a “no-punishment” and a “punishment” condition, so no numeric treatment-effect estimates exist.

D. Predictions one could make—solely from this paper—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions will influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency in a public-goods game  
 Given that the article does not model a public-goods environment, does not measure efficiency, and quantifies almost none of the 15 parameters, very little can be predicted:

 • Longer expected interaction lengths (higher w) generally make punishment-free cooperation harder to sustain; therefore the *incremental* benefit of adding punishment *may* grow with w.  
 • A larger monitoring community (higher n) improves detection and therefore should magnify the benefit of punishment.  
 Beyond these two qualitative statements, the paper offers no information on any of the other 13 parameters, provides no effect sizes, and therefore yields no further predictive leverage.

In short, the article is almost entirely orthogonal to the 15 public-goods design variables and provides essentially no quantitative guidance for forecasting how changes in those variables would alter a punishment treatment’s impact on group efficiency.

(1) whether the paper even mentions or implicitly fixes the parameter and, if so, with which value;  
(2) whether the paper says anything about what would happen if the parameter were **systematically varied** to estimate a punishment-treatment effect on any dependent variable (efficiency or otherwise).  Numerical effect sizes are supplied only when the paper allows it.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER SCAN
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Implicitly fixed.  Each experimental interaction involves 3 persons: Villager 1, Villager 2, and the Water-Point Leader (WPL) as a third-party punisher.  
   (2) No systematic variation; no predictions.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) One-shot (single round).  
   (2) Not varied; no predictions.

3. Chat enabled?  
   (1) No.  Choices were made privately with no mention of communication.  
   (2) Not discussed; no predictions.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule?  
   (1) Not applicable.  The task is a Trust Game, not a PGG.  
   (2) Not discussed.

5. Contribution default / endowment moved back?  
   (1) Not applicable.  
   (2) Not discussed.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor of the public fund  
   (1) Not applicable.  The closest analogous value is the Trust-Game payoff structure (10,5/35,20/20), but the paper does not frame it as an MPCR.  
   (2) Not varied; no predictions.

7. Punishment cost per unit  
   (1) Stated: “Every dollar (N$) spent on punishment by the WPL …”.  Cost = 1 N$ for the punisher.  
   (2) Held constant; no analysis of varying it.

8. Punishment magnitude per unit  
   (1) “… reduces the second villager’s earnings by three times as much …”.  Magnitude = 3 N$ deducted from target for every 1 N$ spent by punisher.  
   (2) Held constant; no discussion of varying it.

9. Reward enabled?  
   (1) No reward option is provided.  
   (2) Not discussed.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   (1) Not applicable.  
   (2) Not discussed.

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
   (1) Yes: participants know it is one-shot; nothing is ever hidden.  
   (2) Not varied; no predictions.

13. Are peer outcomes displayed?  
   (1) Not explicitly stated.  The design description does not say that villagers see each other’s payoffs; only their own.  
   (2) Not discussed.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
   (1) Yes.  Each villager was told “the name of the leader they were matched with”.  Hence punisher identity is common knowledge, but this was not experimentally manipulated.  
   (2) No discussion of varying anonymity.

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
   (1) Not applicable (no reward).  
   (2) Not discussed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables used  
   – The paper does **not** use “group efficiency” (total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff) anywhere.  
   – Main dependent variables:  
     • Pro-social punishment (PSP) frequency & intensity  
     • Anti-social punishment (ASP) frequency & intensity  
     • Villager satisfaction with the leader (5-point Likert & binary)  
     • Leaders’ attitudinal measures (Likert items)  
   – These variables differ from efficiency: they capture norm enforcement, attitudes and satisfaction, not aggregate payoffs relative to a cooperative benchmark.

B. Parameters mentioned (at least fixed): 6 of 15  
   #1, #2, #7, #8, #12, #14.

C. Parameters whose **systematic variation** is analysed for its effect on any punishment treatment effect: 0 of 15.  
   The experiment keeps all design parameters fixed; the study’s comparisons hinge on leader gender and other socio-demographic variables, not on game-design manipulations.

D. Predictions one could make—solely from this paper—about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency:  
   The paper offers virtually no basis for such predictions.  Because (i) efficiency is never measured, and (ii) none of the parameters is experimentally varied, the only extremely tentative inferences are:  
   – If cost-to-fine ratio stayed at 1:3 (parameter #7/#8) and leaders punish rather mildly (especially females), we might expect only modest efficiency gains compared with a no-punishment baseline, but the paper does not quantify this.  
   – Revealing the punisher’s identity (#14) was compatible with some level of punishment; we cannot say whether anonymity would raise or lower efficiency.  
   – One-shot interaction (#2) combined with known identity (#14) still produced punishment; again, no efficiency data are available.  
   Beyond these vague remarks, the paper does not allow credible predictions about efficiency effects of changing any of the 15 parameters.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
In short, the article is mainly a field study of leadership and gender, using a fixed one-shot trust-cum-punishment game as a measurement tool, not as a treatment.  It therefore provides no experimental evidence or quantitative predictions about how varying standard PGG design parameters would alter the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.

Below, I go through each of the 15 parameters in turn, sticking strictly to what appears in “Time-dependent effects hinder cooperation on the public goods game.”  
For every parameter I state  

(1) whether the paper mentions the parameter and (when it does) the value(s) used, and  
(2) whether the paper says anything about how *systematically varying* that parameter influences the punishment-treatment effect (i.e., the difference between a game **with** punishment and a game **without** punishment).  When the paper varies the parameter only inside a game that already contains punishment, I note that as well, because technically that is *not* a punishment-treatment comparison.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
(1) Mentioned.  The authors use a square lattice with L = 300 (default) so N = L² = 90 000 players; in the delay section they reduce it to L = 100 (N = 10 000).  
(2) Not systematically varied; no prediction about its influence on any punishment-treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
(1) They let the simulation run for 5000 Monte-Carlo Steps (MCS) and occasionally longer; one MCS ≙ N asynchronous imitation attempts.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction.

3. Chat enabled  
Not mentioned at all.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
(1) Mentioned implicitly.  Cooperators and punishers “contribute an amount of 1,” defectors contribute 0.  So the contribution choice is indeed all-or-nothing.  
(2) Never varied; no prediction.

5. Contribution-default framing (withdraw from public pot)  
Not mentioned.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor r  
(1) Central to the paper.  They  

   • vary r statically (Fig. 1) from about 2.4 up to 4.2,  
   • let r oscillate in time: r(t)=r₀+r₁ sin(2πωt/L²) with r₀≈3.6–4.0, r₁ up to ≈1.0, and ω from 10⁻⁵ to ≈0.1 MCS⁻¹.

(2) What is varied is r **inside games that already include punishers**.  The authors do not run a “no-punishment” baseline, so there is no direct punishment-treatment contrast.  Still, they report:  

   • Static r (Fig. 1): For pool punishment at K = 0.5, punishers begin to dominate once r ≳3.3; for peer punishment defectors go extinct roughly at r≈3.2–3.4.  
   • Oscillating r (Figs. 2–3): Large amplitude oscillations (high r₁) or low-frequency oscillations make defection dominate; very high-frequency oscillations have little effect.  Quantitatively, the “all-defectors” phase boundary in Fig. 3 gives the critical amplitude r₁* as a rising function of ω and of r₀, but exact numbers are only read off graphically (e.g., at ω=0.001 and r₀=3.6, r₁*≈0.55).

Again, this is *not* a treatment-effect estimate; it is an effect of r conditional on punishment already being present.

7. Punishment cost (γ)  
(1) Fixed at γ = 0.0125.  
(2) Never varied; no prediction.

8. Punishment magnitude (β)  
(1) Fixed at β = 0.125.  
(2) Never varied; no prediction.

9–11. Reward enabled / reward cost / reward magnitude  
Not implemented or mentioned.

12. Horizon known (are the number of rounds common knowledge?)  
Not discussed.

13. Peer outcomes shown  
Not discussed.

14. Punisher identity revealed  
Not discussed.

15. Rewarder identity revealed  
Not applicable because there is no rewarding.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY  

A. Does the paper use “group efficiency” (total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
No.  The dependent variables analysed are the *frequencies* of the three strategies (cooperators, defectors, punishers) over time.  Although individual pay-offs are computed to update strategies, efficiency (actual total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff) is never reported.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
Seven:  
1 (number of players), 2 (rounds), 4 (all-or-nothing contributions), 6 (MPCR r), 7 (punishment cost), 8 (punishment magnitude), and implicitly 12 (finite horizon, though not discussed).  The remaining eight parameters are absent.

C. For which parameters does the paper discuss how *systematically varying* them affects the punishment-treatment effect for any dependent variable?  
Strictly speaking, zero.  The only parameter the authors *systematically vary* is the multiplication factor r (including its oscillatory amplitude and frequency), but they always keep punishment in the game, so they do not compare to a no-punishment baseline.  Therefore, none of the 15 parameters is analysed with respect to a true punishment-treatment contrast.

D. Predictions one could make—solely from this paper—about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency:

• Parameter 6 (MPCR r) is the only one the paper clearly links to cooperation.  Higher constant r, or oscillations with small amplitude/high frequency, should *increase* cooperation and therefore probably *increase* efficiency under punishment.  Large low-frequency oscillations should do the opposite.  

• The paper provides no information that lets one predict how changing any of the other 14 parameters would alter the efficiency gain (or loss) from introducing punishment.

Hence, based only on this study, almost no quantitative prediction about the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency can be made beyond the qualitative statement that favourable, stable, or increasing r is likely to amplify whatever efficiency benefit punishment may yield, whereas time-instability in r and delays in punishment probably erode that benefit.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter inventory of what the paper actually says (or does not say) regarding each of the 15 listed public-goods-game parameters in relation to a “punishment treatment effect.” Note that the study in the paper is not structured as a standard public goods experiment and does not systematically vary these parameters to test their influence on efficiency; instead, its focus is a multi-agent foraging environment with a built-in mechanism for punishing (and thereby discouraging) taboo berry consumption.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
• Mention in the paper?  
  – Yes. The environment features eight agents at a time in each episode, sampled from a population of 12.  
• Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment mentioned?  
  – No. The paper does not systematically manipulate the number of players to assess any impact on punishment or group efficiency.

2) Number of rounds  
• Mention in the paper?  
  – The paper refers to 1,000-step “episodes,” which reset.  
• Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment mentioned?  
  – No. There is no systematic variation (e.g., no shorter vs. longer episodes) to measure how it affects punishment or efficiency.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
• Mention in the paper?  
  – No. The paper does not describe or use any communication or chat channel between agents.  
• Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment mentioned?  
  – Not discussed at all.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Mention in the paper?  
  – No. There is no mention of forced “all-or-nothing” contributions. Agents learn via general navigation and punishment beams in a foraging environment.  
• Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment mentioned?  
  – Not applicable.

5) Is the contribution default (endowment moved from a public fund)?  
• Mention in the paper?  
  – No. The study is not modeled on players moving endowments in or out of a public good.  
• Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment mentioned?  
  – Not applicable.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
• Mention in the paper?  
  – No. The paper uses a reward structure for berry consumption, not a standard linear public goods multiplier.  
• Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment mentioned?  
  – Not applicable.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Mention in the paper?  
  – Yes. Using the “punishing beam” costs the punisher 20 points.  
• Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment mentioned?  
  – It is not varied. The paper keeps it fixed at 20 points, and does not analyze how manipulating this cost might change group efficiency or punishment outcomes.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from the punished player)  
• Mention in the paper?  
  – Yes. The punished agent loses 35 points if struck by the punishing beam.  
• Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment mentioned?  
  – No variation. The paper keeps it at 35 points and does not explore its systematic effect on efficiency.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
• Mention in the paper?  
  – There is no separate “prosocial” or “bonus” reward. The only “reward” for punishing is that the punishing player avoids the usual −20 cost and instead nets +15 (having “spent” 20 but gained 35). However, there is no stand-alone reward mechanism for rewarding good behavior.  
• Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment mentioned?  
  – Not applicable as a separate design parameter.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Mention in the paper?  
  – No. There is no free-standing reward-beam or “reward cost.”  
• Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment mentioned?  
  – Not applicable.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
• Mention in the paper?  
  – Not in the sense of a direct “rewarding” system.  
• Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment mentioned?  
  – Not applicable.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
• Mention in the paper?  
  – The paper does not specify whether agents “know” the episode length. Agents learn from repeated 1,000-step episodes, but the authors do not analyze knowledge of horizon.  
• Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment mentioned?  
  – Not discussed.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (e.g., do players see others’ payoffs)?  
• Mention in the paper?  
  – The environment does not display payoff amounts of peers; the only social signal is “marking” a taboo violator’s color and the possibility of punishing that marked player.  
• Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment mentioned?  
  – No. The paper does not explore different forms of payoff visibility.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• Mention in the paper?  
  – The text does not explicitly state that the punished agent “knows” who fired the beam; the environment is visually interactive, but punisher-identity knowledge is not explored.  
• Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment mentioned?  
  – Not discussed.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
• Mention in the paper?  
  – The setup has no dedicated “rewarder,” so this is not covered.  
• Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment mentioned?  
  – Not applicable.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY  
A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
• The main outcome measure in the paper is the group’s total net reward (sum of all player rewards minus the costs of punishment). The authors do compare total group return across conditions (no rules, one important rule, or one important plus one silly rule). However, they do not frame it as “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff.”  
• Additional dependent variables in the paper include time spent poisoned, number of taboo berries eaten, and frequency of punishment events. These measures differ from efficiency per se, because they track how well agents learn to avoid a toxic berry (compliance) or how often they punish norm violations.

Abstract: We introduce the possibility of coercive punishment by specialized enforcers into a model of community enforcement. We assume that, just as regular agents need to be given incentives to cooperate with each other, specialized enforcers need to be given incentives to carry out costly punishments. We fully characterize optimal equilibria in the model. When the specialized enforcement technology is sufficiently effective, cooperation is best sustained by a one-time enforcer punishment equilibrium, where any deviation by a regular agent is punished only once, and only by enforcers. The reason why there is no community enforcement following deviations by regular agents is that such a response, by reducing future cooperation, would decrease the amount of punishment that enforcers are willing to impose on deviators. Conversely, when the specialized enforcement technology is less effective, optimal equilibria involve a mix of specialized enforcement and community enforcement (which might take the form of ostracism). ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. NUMBER OF PLAYERS  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. The paper analyzes a “small group model” (k+1 players) and a “large group model” ((k+l)n players).  
   • Does the paper make any predictions about systematically varying this parameter and its effect on a punishment treatment effect (on cooperation or on efficiency)?  
     – The paper does examine how larger groups (versus smaller groups) can shape whether specialized or community enforcement is optimal, but it frames the result in terms of “maximal level of cooperation” or “social welfare,” not an explicit “treatment effect on efficiency.” No numeric effect sizes are given.  

2. NUMBER OF ROUNDS  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – The baseline analysis uses a repeated (potentially infinite-horizon) framework with a common discount factor δ; it does not use a finite known number of rounds.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying the number of rounds on a punishment treatment effect?  
     – No. The paper does not discuss changing the number of rounds or whether the game length is known.  

3. IS CHAT ENABLED BETWEEN PLAYERS?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. There is no mention of player communication or chat in the model.  
   • Predictions of systematically varying it?  
     – Not discussed.  

4. IS THE CONTRIBUTION “ALL OR NOTHING”?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. Producers in the model choose effort levels x ≥ 0 from a continuum. There is no mention of an all-or-nothing contribution mechanism.  
   • Predictions of systematically varying it?  
     – Not discussed.  

5. IS THE CONTRIBUTION DEFAULT (E.G., DECIDE HOW MUCH TO MOVE BACK TO THE HAND)?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. The model simply assumes producers pick a cooperation level x ≥ 0. There is no notion of “default” contributions.  
   • Predictions of systematically varying it?  
     – Not discussed.  

6. MARGINAL PER CAPITA RETURN (MPCR) OR RELATED FACTORS  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – The paper calls its production/benefit function f(x), which is strictly concave, bounded, and differentiable. This is loosely analogous to the productivity or “social benefit” side of cooperation, but it is not formalized as a standard MPCR.  
   • Predictions about systematically varying MPCR/f(x) on any punishment treatment effect?  
     – The paper does not give numeric effect sizes or use “punishment treatment effect” language. It shows that if production is more or less effective (i.e., changes in f), then maximum equilibrium cooperation can shift, but there is no direct statement of how that modifies an “efficiency treatment effect.”  

7. PUNISHMENT COST TO IMPOSE A SINGLE UNIT OF PUNISHMENT  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes, at length. An enforcer who punishes at level y > 0 pays a personal cost of y. The function g(y) translates that y into disutility g(y) felt by the punished producer. This punishment technology (g) is a central element of the model.  
   • Predictions of systematically varying it?  
     – The paper systematically examines how more or less effective specialized enforcement (i.e., cheaper or costlier punishing) shapes whether “specialized enforcement” alone or in combination with “community enforcement” is optimal (in the sense of sustaining higher cooperation).    • Does the paper discuss it?

   • Predictions of systematically varying it?  
     – The analysis hinges heavily on whether g is steep: the paper’s main theoretical results compare “pure specialized enforcement” versus “mixed” strategies depending on that shape. No numeric effect size for “treatment effect on efficiency” is presented, only for levels of cooperation.

    • Does the paper discuss it?

11. REWARD MAGNITUDE  
    • Does the paper discuss it?

    • Predictions of systematically varying it?  
      – Not discussed.  

12. IS THE NUMBER OF ROUNDS KNOWN TO PLAYERS?

    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – Yes. The paper devotes significant attention to the monitoring structure, contrasting “perfect monitoring” (everyone sees all outcomes) versus “private monitoring” (individuals only see matches they participate in, or possibly partners’ last matches).  
    • Predictions of systematically varying it?  
      – This is central to their discussion of sustaining cooperation (e.g., one-time enforcer punishment works differently under perfect versus private monitoring). 14. WHEN A PLAYER IS PUNISHED, DOES THAT PLAYER KNOW WHO THE SPECIFIC PUNISHER IS?  
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – The paper states that, in each match, participants see who does what in that match (cooperative effort, punishment choices, etc.). However, there is no systematic variation in “anonymous” vs. “identified” aspects of punishment.  
    • Predictions of systematically varying it?  
      – Not discussed as a separate lever; no numeric effect size.  

15. WHEN A PLAYER IS REWARDED, DOES THAT PLAYER KNOW WHO THE REWARDER IS?  
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – No. There is no notion of rewards in the model, so no mention.  
    • Predictions of systematically varying it?  
      – Not discussed.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?  
   – The paper’s main dependent variable is the “maximum level of cooperation” that can be sustained in equilibrium. A closely related quantity is the resulting “social welfare” (i.e., total or average payoff). However, the authors do not specifically measure “efficiency” in the sense of (actual total payoff) / (maximum possible payoff) for a fully cooperative group. They also do not label anything a “punishment treatment effect.”  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

     1) Number of players (discussed in small vs. large group)  
     6) Production benefits via f(x), albeit not named “MPCR”

Instead, it looks at how various technical conditions (especially on the punishment technology g and group size k) shape whether “pure specialized enforcement” or “community enforcement” partly remains. There is no numeric effect-size table; the authors give only theoretical thresholds (like g′(y) ≥ 1) for switching to purely specialized punishments. Strictly speaking, none of the 15 parameters is discussed in the narrow sense of “the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”  

D. If you were to make predictions on how these 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

But the paper itself never formalizes these results as explicit coefficients or quantitative effect sizes for an “efficiency treatment effect.” Thus, the predictions would remain qualitative rather than numerical.

Abstract: According to Turnbull's 1972 ethnography The Mountain People, the Ik of Uganda had a culture of selfishness that made them uncooperative. His claims contrast with two widely accepted principles in evolutionary biology, that humans cooperate on larger scales than other species and that culture is an important facilitator of such cooperation. We use recently collected data to examine Ik culture and its influence on Ik behaviour. Turnbull's observations of selfishness were not necessarily inaccurate but they occurred during a severe famine. Cooperation re-emerged when people once again had enough resources to share. Accordingly, Ik donations in unframed Dictator Games are on par with average donations in Dictator Games played by people around the world. Furthermore, Ik culture includes traits that encourage sharing with those in need and a belief in supernatural punishment of selfishness. When these traits are used to frame Dictator Games, the average amounts given by Ik players increase. Turnbull's claim that the Ik have a culture of selfishness can be rejected. Cooperative norms are resilient, and the consensus among scholars that humans are remarkably cooperative and that human cooperation is supported by culture can remain intact.

As you will see, the paper reports only on one-shot Dictator Games (not Public Goods Games) among the Ik; there is no mention of systematically varying any of these 15 parameters in the context of a punishment mechanism or group efficiency.    • Not applicable.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Not applicable.  
   • As with punishment, there is no experimental reward mechanism. The paper does not discuss systematically revealing any rewarder’s identity.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • No. The paper measures amounts allocated in a one-shot Dictator Game (i.e., the percentage of the endowment donated). This is treated as a measure of generosity. Although the word “cooperation” appears in qualitative discussions, the study never calculates or reports “group efficiency,” “total payoff,” “average payoff,” or related measures.  

   • Other dependent variables brely mentioned: average donation in different framing conditions (control, needy recipient, supernatural punishment, combined). These are not measures of efficiency.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • None of the 15 parameters (as they pertain to typical public goods/punishment designs) are actually mentioned or measured.  
   • Any references to “punishment” in the paper concern participants’ belief in supernatural spirits, not an experimentally administered public-goods-style penalty.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. The paper does not systematically vary or even mention these parameters.

   • The paper provides no direct basis for making any prediction. It does not examine a public goods game, does not assess efficiency, and does not alter any of the 15 parameters. Abstract: Social learning is often proposed as an important driver of the evolution of human cooperation. In this view, cooperation in other species might be restricted because it mostly relies on individually learned or innate behaviours. Here, we show that juvenile cleaner fish (Labroides dimidiatus) can learn socially about cheating consequences in an experimental paradigm that mimics cleaners' cooperative interactions with client fish. Juvenile cleaners that had observed adults interacting with model clients learned to (1) behave more cooperatively after observing clients fleeing in response to cheating; (2) prefer clients that were tolerant to cheating; but (3) did not copy adults' arbitrary feeding preferences. They further show that negative responses to cheating can potentially shape the reputation of cheated individuals, influencing cooperation dynamics in interaction networks. Cleaner fish can cheat clients for higher rewards but this comes with a risk of punishment. Here, Truskanov et al. show that juvenile cleaner fish can learn by observing adults to behave more cooperatively themselves but also to prefer clients that are more tolerant to cheating.

Below I go through the 15 pre-specified design parameters one by one and extract only what the Yang & Fu (2020) paper actually says.   
“Punishment treatment effect’’ = outcome in the punishment condition minus outcome in the no-punishment (L = 0) baseline.  
The paper’s only outcome that is plotted or tabulated is the cooperation level ρ (= total contribution divided by the maximum possible contribution).  Group efficiency (total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff) is never reported.

──────────────────────────────  
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  A 100 × 100 lattice → 10 000 players.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  Always 10 000.  No predictions about varying it.  

2. Number of rounds  
   • The model is an infinite-horizon evolutionary simulation; time steps run until equilibrium.  
   • Not varied; no predictions about changing the horizon length.  

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Never mentioned; the model has no communication.  

4. Contribution “all-or-nothing’’?  
   • Explicitly NOT all-or-nothing: strategies are continuous, s ∈ [0,1].  
   • The paper never switches between discrete and continuous contributions, so no prediction about varying this parameter.  

5. Contribution default / endowment return decision?  
   • Not discussed.  

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   • Implemented as the group enhancement factor r.  
   • Systematically varied (Figs. 1 & 6).  
     – In Fig. 1 (synchronous updating, α = 0.2) r ranges roughly 2 – 6.  
     – In Fig. 6 (asynchronous updating, α = 0.2) a similar range is used.  
   • Reported effect (dependent variable = cooperation level ρ):  
       For every fixed punishment rule L, ρ rises monotonically with r.  
   • Punishment treatment effect:  
       • For L = 1 and L = 2 (≤ half of the group punished) ρ_L − ρ_L=0 is positive for the whole r-range.  
       • For L = 3 and L = 4 (> half punished) ρ_L − ρ_L=0 is negative for the whole r-range.  
     Numerical values must be eyeballed; e.g. at r≈4 in Fig. 1  
       – L=0: ρ≈0.30  
       – L=1: ρ≈0.70  (treatment lift ≈ +0.40)  
       – L=2: ρ≈0.55  (lift ≈ +0.25)  
       – L=3: ρ≈0.05  (lift ≈ –0.25)  
       – L=4: ρ≈0       (lift ≈ –0.30)  

7. Punishment cost per unit  
   • Defined as β = L α / (5–L).  Cost is therefore fully determined by L and α.  
   • Not manipulated independently; no separate prediction.  

8. Punishment magnitude (fine, α)  
   • Systematically varied in Fig. 4 (α from 0.1 to ~1.6).  
   • Effects (dependent variable = ρ, r is held fixed):  
       – When the punished players are the minority (L=1 or 2, r=3) ρ rises with α.  
         Example, L=2: α=0.2→ρ≈0.17, α=0.8→ρ≈0.50, α=1.6→ρ≈0.80.  
       – When the punished players are the majority (L=3 or 4, r=8) ρ falls with α.  
         Example, L=4: α=0.1→ρ≈0.55, α=0.5→ρ≈0.25, α=0.9→ρ≈0.00.  
   • Hence the sign of the punishment treatment effect changes with α and L.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Not in the model.  

10. Reward cost  
    • Not in the model.  

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Not in the model.  

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
    • Not relevant to the evolutionary model; not discussed.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Not mentioned.  

14. Is the punisher identified?  
    • Not mentioned; punishment is implemented mechanically.  

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
    • Not applicable.  

──────────────────────────────  
Summary requested  

A.  Dependent variables  
    • The paper uses “cooperation level’’ ρ = Σ s_i / N.  
    • Total or average PAYOFF or “efficiency’’ is never reported.  
    • Therefore efficiency and cooperation are not interchangeable here; only cooperation is measured.  

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
    5 parameters:  
    (1) number of players (fixed 10 000)  
    (4) contribution all-or-nothing (fixed “no”)  
    (6) MPCR/enhancement factor r (varied)  
    (7) punishment cost (implied by L and α)  
    (8) punishment magnitude α (varied)  

C.  For how many parameters does the paper examine the effect of SYSTEMATIC VARIATION on the punishment treatment effect?  
    2 parameters:  
    • Parameter 6 (MPCR r) – varied in Figs. 1 & 6.  
    • Parameter 8 (punishment magnitude α) – varied in Fig. 4.  
    No other parameter is systematically varied.  

D.  Predicted impact on the punishment treatment effect on efficiency (if one had to extrapolate from the paper alone)  
    • The study offers no efficiency data, so any prediction must be indirect.  
    • It shows that when the punished minority is ≤ half of the group (L ≤ 2), higher α and higher r both improve cooperation relative to the no-punishment baseline; when the punished majority is > half (L ≥ 3), the opposite occurs.  
    • Because higher cooperation usually correlates with higher payoffs in a PGG, one can tentatively predict the same qualitative pattern for efficiency:  
        – High r and/or high α with small L → positive efficiency treatment effect.  
        – High α with large L → negative efficiency treatment effect.  
    • The paper offers no information on the remaining 13 parameters or on any interactions beyond (r × L) and (α × L), so no further predictions can be made from this source alone.

Authors: Jaffe, K
Author Full Names: Jaffe, K
Article Title: Altruism, altruistic punishment and social investment
Keywords Plus: EVOLUTION; COOPERATION; MECHANISM; BEHAVIOR
Abstract: The concept of altruism is used in very different forms by computer scientists, economists, philosophers, social scientists, psychologists and biologists. Yet, in order to be useful in social simulations, the concept altruism requires a more precise meaning. A quantitative formulation is proposed here, based on the cost/benefit analysis of the altruist and of society at large. This formulation is applied in the analysis of the social dynamic working of behaviors that have been called altruistic punishments, using the agent based computer model Sociodynamica. The simulations suggest that altruistic punishment on its own cannot maintain altruistic behaviors. Altruistic behavior is sustainable in the long term only if these behaviors trigger synergetic forces in society that eventually make them produce benefits to most individuals. The simulations suggest however that altruistic punishment may work as a social investment, and is thus better called decentralized social punishment. This behavior is very efficient in enforcing social norms. The efficiency of decentralized social punishment in enforcing norms was dependent on the type of labor structured of the virtual society. I conclude that what is called altruistic punishment emerges as a type of social investment that can evolve either through individual and/or group selection, as a successful device for changing or enforcing norms in a society. Social simulations will help us in better understanding the underlying dynamic working of such devices.

Authors: Pfattheicher, S; Böhm, R; Kesberg, R
Author Full Names: Pfattheicher, Stefan; Boehm, Robert; Kesberg, Rebekka
Article Title: The Advantage of Democratic Peer Punishment in Sustaining Cooperation within Groups
Author Keywords: democratic punishment; peer punishment; public goods game; social dilemma; voting
Keywords Plus: COSTLY PUNISHMENT; PUBLIC-GOODS; ANTISOCIAL PUNISHMENT; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; PARTICIPATION; TRUST; SATISFACTION; SANCTIONS; SADISM
Abstract: In social dilemma situations, individuals benefit from uncooperative behavior while exploiting resources of the collective. One prominent solution to prevent uncooperative behavior and to increase cooperation is to establish a system of costly peer punishment, that is, the possibility for every individual involved in the dilemma to impose costly punishment on interaction partners. However, recent research revealed that, in contrast to a situation without punishment, peer punishment is inefficient and maladaptive in the sense that the total payoff is reduced and punishment of cooperative individuals (i.e., antisocial punishment) is possible. In the present work, we propose that a system of democratic peer punishment, that is, direct and equal participation of each individual in the punishment decision-making process with punishment only executed when a majority has voted for its execution, can address the shortcomings of a peer punishment system. Using iterated public goods games, we show higher cooperation levels, higher total payoffs, and reduced executed punishment in the democratic compared with a peer punishment system. Moreover, we document that fairness perceptions, satisfaction, and interpersonal trust are increased in the democratic punishment system. Implications for how cooperation and democratic punishment systems may evolve are discussed. Copyright (c) 2018 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.

Authors: Przepiorka, W; Diekmann, A
Author Full Names: Przepiorka, Wojtek; Diekmann, Andreas
Article Title: Heterogeneous groups overcome the diffusion of responsibility problem in social norm enforcement
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS GAMES; GROUP-SIZE; VOLUNTEERS DILEMMA; BYSTANDER INTERVENTION; COLLECTIVE ACTION; COOPERATION; PUNISHMENT; PROVISION; CHIMPANZEES; INCENTIVES
Abstract: Social norms promote cooperation in everyday life because many people are willing to negatively sanction norm breakers at a cost to themselves. However, a norm violation may persist if only one person is required to sanction the norm breaker and everyone expects someone else to do it. Here we employ the volunteer's dilemma game (VOD) to model this diffusion of responsibility in social norm enforcement. The symmetric VOD is a binary choice game in which all actors have the same costs of and benefits from cooperation and only one actor's cooperation is required to provide the collective good for the group. The asymmetric VOD differs from the symmetric VOD in one (strong) actor having lower costs of cooperation. In a laboratory experiment, we find that, in line with the diffusion of responsibility hypothesis, subjects' propensities to sanction the norm breaker decrease with group size in the symmetric VOD. In the asymmetric VOD, groups tacitly coordinate on the strong subject to sanction the norm breaker alone. Although at first lower in larger groups, strong subjects' sanctioning rates increase over time and reach equally high levels across different group sizes. Our results show that heterogeneous groups can be more effective in achieving norm compliance than groups of all equals because they naturally evade diffusion of responsibility in social norm enforcement.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what the paper by Przepiorka and Diekmann (2018) does (and does not) say, focusing on whether the authors (1) discuss the parameter at all, (2) give that parameter a particular value and/or systematically vary it, and (3) make any predictions about how varying that parameter would affect the “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency (as defined in your question: the actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff if everyone cooperated). Note that the paper never uses that precise ratio as a dependent variable; it instead measures outcomes such as the proportion of theft, the proportion of sanctioning decisions, and whether exactly one person sanctions (“efficient sanctioning”), but it does not compute group efficiency in the sense of total payoff–to–maximum payoff. Wherever the paper does not address a parameter or says nothing about how varying it would affect a punishment‐versus‐no‐punishment “treatment effect” on efficiency, this is stated explicitly.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Discussed? Yes. The experiment uses either 2‐person groups (1 thief + 1 potential “victim”) or 5‐person groups (1 thief + 4 victims).  
   • Values / systematic variation? Yes. They systematically compare n = 2 to n = 5.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect (on efficiency)? The paper does not measure efficiency as total payoff / maximum payoff, nor does it discuss how increasing “n” changes a “punishment‐treatment effect” on that ratio. Instead, they report:  
     – Individual sanctioning drops from n=2 to n=5 in the symmetric game (diffusion of responsibility) and is somewhat high in the asymmetric game for “strong” players.  
     – They do label “exactly one punisher” as an “efficient” outcome for sanctioning, but this is not presented as a payoff‐based measure of group efficiency. The authors do not provide an effect size in terms of payoff efficiency.  

2. Number of rounds
   • Discussed? Yes. They run 30 rounds total (15 rounds in a “no‐penalty” version; 15 rounds in a “penalty” version).  
   • Values / systematic variation? The total of 30 rounds is fixed; the within‐subject design has 15 no‐penalty rounds, then 15 that introduce a 60 MU penalty for the thief.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect (on efficiency)? The paper does not discuss systematically varying the total number of rounds beyond that fixed design; they also do not compute or report group efficiency as a ratio outcome. The authors do discuss “learning” over blocks of 5 rounds, but not in terms of payoff efficiency or a punishment‐treatment effect on that measure.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussed? No. There is no mention in the paper of any chat or communication among subjects.  
   • Values / systematic variation? Not applicable.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect (on efficiency)? Not applicable.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussed? Yes (indirectly). In their “stealing game with a sanctioning option,” a potential victim’s decision is binary: either sanction (= “volunteer”) or not sanction.  
   • Values / systematic variation? No. The game is always implemented as a binary choice (sanction or not), so there is no variation in whether it might be continuous.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect (on efficiency)? Not discussed. They do not vary the binary‐versus‐continuous format, nor do they measure efficiency as total payoff–to–maximum payoff.  

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., deciding how much to withdraw or keep)?
   • Discussed? No. This parameter does not appear in the paper; there is no “default contribution” or partial contribution.  
   • Values / systematic variation? Not applicable.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect (on efficiency)? Not applicable.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Discussed? No. The experiment is a volunteer’s dilemma “stealing game,” not a linear public‐goods game with an MPCR.  
   • Values / systematic variation? Not applicable.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect (on efficiency)? Not applicable.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussed? Yes. It is central to their “symmetric” vs “asymmetric” VOD conditions. The cost of sanctioning is K=25 for everyone in the symmetric game, and K=25 for “strong” vs K=35 for “weak” players in the asymmetric game.  
   • Values / systematic variation? Yes, but only in the sense of two fixed cost levels in the asymmetric condition (25 vs 35) and a single cost in the symmetric condition (25).  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect (on efficiency)? They do not measure or predict changes in payoff‐efficiency as a function of changing K. They only test how it changes sanctioning propensities (i.e., “strong” vs “weak”). No efficiency ratio is discussed.  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted for each unit of punishment)
   • Discussed? Partly. The “punishment” is that a thief must return the stolen 50 MU per victim to all victims if at least one punishes, and in the second phase, an additional penalty of 60 MU is imposed on the thief if at least one victim punishes.  
   • Values / systematic variation? The authors compare “no penalty” (first 15 rounds) to “penalty=60 MU” (last 15 rounds). They do not, however, systematically vary the magnitude of the penalty in different treatments (it is simply 0 vs 60).  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect (on efficiency)? Not stated. The authors report only how introducing a 60 MU penalty reduces theft. They do not discuss total‐payoff efficiency from systematically varying the magnitude.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussed? No. The study examines only “negative sanctioning” (punishment). No reward mechanism is ever introduced.  
   • Values / systematic variation? Not applicable.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect (on efficiency)? Not applicable.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Discussed? No. There is no mention of rewarding others.  
    • Values / systematic variation? Not applicable.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment effect (on efficiency)? Not applicable.  

11. Reward magnitude
    • Discussed? No. As above, no reward mechanism is examined.  
    • Values / systematic variation? Not applicable.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment effect (on efficiency)? Not applicable.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
    • Discussed? The paper does not explicitly say whether subjects are told exactly how many rounds. However, there is no mention that the round count is hidden. Typically, the instructions do state up front that the experiment lasts for 30 rounds.  
    • Values / systematic variation? No. There is no across‐treatment variation in whether the horizon is known or unknown.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment effect (on efficiency)? Not discussed.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown?
    • Discussed? The authors do not systematically vary the information that players see about others’ payoffs. They do not highlight any design factor where some see or do not see payoff details of others.  
    • Values / systematic variation? Not applicable.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment effect (on efficiency)? Not applicable.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who punished them?
    • Discussed? No. The paper does not mention any variation on revealing punisher identities.  
    • Values / systematic variation? Not applicable.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment effect (on efficiency)? Not applicable.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is?
    • Discussed? No. There is no reward condition, so the paper does not address this parameter.  
    • Values / systematic variation? Not applicable.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment effect (on efficiency)? Not applicable.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper does not use “group efficiency” in the sense of total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff if all cooperated. Instead, it uses these primary dependent variables:  
     – Stealing rate (frequency of norm violations).  
     – Individual sanctioning rate (how often a “victim” chooses to punish).  
     – Group sanctioning rate (whether at least one victim chooses to punish).  
     – “Efficient sanctioning rate” = probability that exactly one victim punishes.  
   • These variables are not the same as a payoff‐based efficiency ratio.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned or set at fixed values without systematic variation:  
       (2) Number of rounds (fixed at 30).  
       (4) All‐or‐nothing decisions (binary).  
   • Mentioned and systematically varied:  
       (1) Number of players (n=2 vs n=5).  
       (7) Punishment cost (25 for everyone in the symmetric game; 25 vs 35 for “strong” vs “weak” in the asymmetric game).  
       (8) Punishment magnitude changes from no penalty (0 MU) to penalty (60 MU) across two phases, though not varied across treatments.  
   • All other parameters (3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 12 beyond being fixed/not hidden, 13, 14, 15) are either not mentioned at all or not manipulated.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The authors do systematically vary (1) Number of Players, (7) Punishment Cost, and effectively have a before/after difference for (8) Punishment Magnitude (0 MU penalty vs 60 MU penalty). However, they do not refer to “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” as you define it. Rather, for these parameters the paper discusses changes in the probability of sanctioning and norm enforcement (not the ratio of total payoff to maximum payoff).  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • Because the paper never calculates or reports payoff‐based efficiency, very little can be concluded about how these parameters would affect “efficiency” in the way you define it. The only partial proxy is the paper’s “efficient sanctioning rate” (where exactly one person punishes). Although that is not a payoff ratio, it does suggest that smaller groups (n=2) and asymmetric cost structures (one “strong” subject) tend to result in more “efficient” single‐person punishment, at least after some learning.  
   • Apart from that partial inference, the paper does not provide direct evidence or theoretical discussion on total payoff–to–maximum payoff measures. One therefore cannot make quantitative or confident predictions about group‐efficiency outcomes for any of the 15 parameters.

Authors: Guo, ZY; Guo, R; Xu, CY; Wu, Z
Author Full Names: Guo, Ziyan; Guo, Rui; Xu, Chengyi; Wu, Zhen
Article Title: Reflexive or reflective? Group bias in third-party punishment in Chinese and Western cultures
Author Keywords: Third-party punishment; Group bias; Time pressure; Cognitive load; Group identity; Cultural difference
Keywords Plus: BLACK SHEEP; INGROUP FAVORITISM; INTERGROUP BIAS; PAROCHIAL ALTRUISM; GROUP MEMBERSHIP; SOCIAL NORMS; IMPACT; GUILT; PSYCHOLOGY; EMOTIONS
Abstract: Third-party punishment (TPP) is critical for promoting cooperation and maintaining societal stability by deterring norm violations. Research has shown that TPP is influenced by ingroup bias, whereby people punish outgroup norm violators more severely than ingroups. The current study examined the social-cognitive mechanisms of the ingroup bias in TPP using a dual-process framework from a cross-cultural perspective. We asked whether people from different cultures were predisposed to ingroup bias, and whether this bias would change through reflection. To investigate this issue, we conducted five experiments employing economic games in Chinese and Western adults (total n = 1300) and a single-paper meta-analysis. Participants observed that ingroup and outgroup members allocated resources unfairly, and then decided how much money to deduct as punishment toward allocators in the reflexive or reflective modes (by manipulating response time constraint or cognitive load). Across a range of experimental designs, results provided converging evidence that Chinese and Western participants both exhibited ingroup favoritism in the reflexive mode, but behaved differently in the reflective mode: Chinese participants remained punishing ingroups less than outgroups, although they felt guilty and spent longer time dealing with ingroup violations; by contrast, ingroup favoritism decreased in the Western sample, especially among high group identifiers. These findings suggest that ingroup favoritism during TPP is reflexive and culturally universal, but it is manifested in different ways to meet specific cultural expectations when punishers make decisions in the reflective mode. This study thus deepens our understanding of how and why TPP is group-biased.

Abstract: This paper proposes a new class of incentive mechanisms aiming at compelling self-interested users in online communities to cooperate with each other by exchanging resources or services. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter accounting of what the paper actually discusses (and what it does not) regarding the 15 public‐goods‐game design parameters you listed, together with whether the paper makes any statements about systematically varying those parameters and predicting their effects on “punishment treatment” and, in particular, on group efficiency. References to “Tables” and “Figures” below are to those in the paper itself (“Robust Reputation Protocol Design for Online Communities: A Stochastic Stability Analysis,” by Zhang & van der Schaar).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. The paper consistently denotes the community size by N (e.g., Section II, “We consider an online community consisting of N users…”).  
     – However, it does not report any systematic variation of N to see how changes in community size would affect punishment or efficiency. The number of players is taken as a given constant (in examples, N=1000).  
   • Does it predict anything about systematically varying it?  
     – No. The paper does not discuss varying N to see how that impacts the “punishment treatment effect” or any other variable.

2. Number of rounds
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Not in the sense of a finite or known number of rounds. The paper analyzes an (effectively) infinite‐horizon repeated matching model with a discount factor δ. There is no discussion of a finite “number of rounds” or whether that number is known to players.  
   • Does it predict anything about systematically varying it?  
     – No. The paper does not consider making the game shorter or longer in a controlled way nor reports any effect sizes of doing so.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. There is no mention of communication or “chat” among participants.  
   • Does it predict anything about systematically varying it?  
     – No mention at all.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – The paper analyzes a “gift‐giving” stage game in which the server’s action is binary (0 or 1), i.e. either refuses to provide service (0) or fully provides it (1). In that sense it is indeed an “all or nothing” decision.  
   • Does it predict anything about systematically varying it?  
     – No. The model is fixed to a binary action (Table I). The paper does not discuss changing that structure.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. The paper does not describe any “default” from the public fund to a private account or anything similar.  
   • Does it predict anything about systematically varying it?  
     – No mention at all.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Not in the usual “MPCR” sense of a public‐goods game. Instead, the benefit to the recipient is denoted b and the cost to the provider is c, with b > c so that supplying is socially efficient.  
   • Does it predict anything about systematically varying it?  
     – The paper does present results for different values of b and c (e.g., in Table II), but it does not treat these as an MPCR or measure their “punishment treatment effect.” Rather, it examines how the protocol (especially parameter β) supports a fully cooperative outcome. There is no explicit discussion of systematically varying b/c as a lever on punishment efficacy, beyond illustrating numerical examples.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. The model has no cost paid by “punishers.” Punishment is implemented automatically by lowering a deviant’s reputation with probability β; there is no notion of exact “punishment cost” to other players or to a punisher.  
   • Does it predict anything about systematically varying it?  
     – No mention at all of a punisher’s out‐of‐pocket cost.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted for each unit of punishment)
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Not in the sense of direct monetary deductions. “Punishment” in the paper is losing one’s reputation (reset to 0) with probability β upon deviance. That is not framed as a numerical “deduction of coins” or a cost that the punishee pays.  
   • Does it predict anything about systematically varying it?  
     – The paper does systematically study how changing β (the probability of reputation reset) affects long‐run cooperation (see especially Theorem 2, Table III). However, it is never framed as “punishment magnitude in coins,” so there is no direct effect‐size statement about “units of punishment” in a standard public‐goods‐game sense.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – The paper’s “reward” is that if a user complies with the social rule, the user’s reputation is incremented by 1 (not exceeding L). It is always “enabled” in the sense that individuals can increase their reputation from 0 up to L.  
   • Does it predict anything about systematically varying it?  
     – No. That “reward” process (reputation increments) is an intrinsic part of the protocol; the paper does not study turning that reward on or off.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. The model has no notion of a “rewarder” who pays a cost for granting positive reputation; it is an automatic protocol.  
   • Does it predict anything about systematically varying it?  
     – No mention at all.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Same as above: there is no direct coin transfer. Reputation “goes up by 1” with probability 1 for compliance (unless at maximum L).  
   • Does it predict anything about systematically varying it?  
     – No. The paper only considers the effect of having L reputational “levels,” not any direct monetary reward size.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. The game is modeled with an infinite sequence (discount factor δ). The paper does not discuss whether players know any terminal period.  
   • Does it predict anything about systematically varying it?  
     – No mention at all.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained or lost each round)?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Not in the sense of “payoff outcomes.” Rather, individuals do observe (or at least the protocol broadcasts) the distribution of reputation states (Section III). That is not the same as seeing exact coin payoffs or who lost/gained each round.  
   • Does it predict anything about systematically varying it?  
     – No. The paper fixes the assumption that the community state (the distribution of reputations) is known, not systematically changed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. The punishment is automatic (reset to reputation 0 with probability β). There is no mention of players learning “who” inflicted that punishment.  
   • Does it predict anything about systematically varying it?  
     – No mention at all.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Same as above: it is a protocol that automatically increments reputation from θ to θ+1 (if one follows the social rule), not an identified “rewarder.”  
   • Does it predict anything about systematically varying it?  
     – No mention at all.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary (A–D)

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • Yes. The paper couches its main objective in terms of achieving “social welfare” = b – c (the maximum if everyone cooperates) and reports average social welfare normalized by that maximum (for instance in Table II). It also uses “stochastically stable equilibria” to indicate whether the community attains that maximal payoff in the long run. Note that the paper’s “social welfare” or “average social welfare” is effectively the same as group efficiency in a repeated gift‐giving context.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper (at all)?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
     (1) Number of Players (N).  
     (4) All‐or‐nothing structure (the server either supplies (1) or not (0)).  
     • Also, the paper implicitly discusses “punishment severity” via β, and “reward” as reputation increments, but not as any cost‐of‐punishment or cost‐of‐reward variables.  

   • All the rest—(2) Number of rounds, (3) Chat, (5) Default contributions, (6) MPCR, (7) Punishment cost to punisher, (8) A monetary punishment “magnitude,” (9) On/off reward, (10) Reward cost, (11) Reward magnitude in coins, (12) Known vs. unknown final round, (13) Full peer‐outcome displays, (14) Identity of punisher known, (15) Identity of rewarder known—are not discussed in any direct sense.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on (or systematically varying them for) the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable?  
   • Strictly speaking, none of the 15 parameters (as listed) are systematically varied in the usual “public‐goods‐punishment” sense. The only parameter the paper truly varies to see an effect on long‐run efficiency is β (the probability that a deviation leads to reputation reset). That is not listed exactly among your items as “punishment cost or magnitude” but is the paper’s analog of “punishment severity.”  
   • Hence, the paper does not present effect sizes for systematically varying your labeled parameters (1–15). It only gives numerical examples for b, c, and β (see Tables II–III), showing how different β values (within certain ranges) can sustain or fail to sustain high efficiency.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not examine or even mention most of those 15 parameters in the usual sense of a public‐goods experiment. Therefore, on nearly all of them—number of rounds, chat/no chat, peer‐outcome visibility, identity of punisher or rewarder, etc.—the paper provides no direct guidance.  
   • The only insight consistent with the paper concerns “punishment strength”: in Zhang & van der Schaar’s model, if punishment (i.e. reputation reset) is too weak (β too small), cooperation unravels. If punishment is too zealously strong (β exceeding a critical threshold), full defection can also emerge stochastically. A moderate range of β (strictly between c/(δb) and a higher critical value) sustains high efficiency.  
   • Beyond that β result, the paper itself does not enable predictions on how your other 15 parameters would alter the “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Thus, apart from recognizing that the paper uses a binary “all or nothing” action (Parameter 4), a fixed community size N (Parameter 1), and a “punishment severity” β (which does not map directly onto the “punishment cost” or “punishment magnitude” items from your list), there is no direct mention of systematically varying any of those 15 parameters to measure effects on efficiency. The paper’s focus is on reputation‐protocol design (L, H, β) in an infinite‐horizon setting, with the principal result being that moderate but not extreme “punishment probability” β can stochastically stabilize full cooperation.

Abstract: Spatial public goods game is a popular metaphor to model the dilemma of collective cooperation on graphs, yet the non-excludable property of public goods has seldom been considered in previous models. Based upon a coevolutionary model where agents play public goods games and adjust their partnerships, the present model incorporates the non-excludable property of public goods: agents are able to adjust their participation in the games hosted by others, whereas they cannot exclude others from their own games. In the coevolution, a directed and dynamical network which represents partnerships among autonomous agents is evolved. We find that non-excludable property counteracts the positive effect of partner switching, i.e., the equilibrium level of cooperation is lower than that in the situation of excludable public goods game. Therefore, we study the effect of individual punishment that cooperative agents pay a personal cost to decrease benefits of those defective neighbors who participate in their hosted games.
