Below I track the 15 parameters one‐by‐one and state exactly what the paper says about each of them and, when possible, how systematically varying the parameter is shown to affect the *punishment-treatment effect* (i.e., the difference between the “with–punishment” and the “no-punishment” conditions).  All page, figure and table references are to the single paper reproduced above.

------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  YES – lattice of size 32 × 32 (≈1 000 agents) in the main simulations; the authors also show a 100-agent and a 2 500-agent sample for visualisation (Fig. 2 and Fig. 3).  
   • Systematically varied?  NO.  Group size is held fixed in all punishment vs. no-punishment comparisons, so no effect on the punishment-treatment effect is reported.

2.  Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  NO.  The model runs for 50 000 Monte-Carlo (MC) steps before data are collected, but this horizon is never varied and never linked to punishment.

3.  Chat enabled  
   • Mentioned?  NO.

4.  “All or nothing” contribution rule  
   • Mentioned?  YES – each agent either *cooperates* (contributes cost c = 1) or *defects* (contributes 0).  
   • Varied?  NO.  No discussion of how changing to a continuous contribution level would alter the punishment-treatment effect.

5.  Contribution default / endowment back-transfer  
   • Mentioned?  NO.

6.  Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor (r)  
   • Mentioned?  YES – r is the *only* game-payoff parameter that is varied systematically in the article (Figs. 4, 5, 6, 7).  
   • Systematic variation and link to punishment?  YES.  
        – Fig. 4: ρ_C vs. r in non-excludable game *without* punishment.  
        – Fig. 6: ρ_C vs. r in non-excludable game *with* punishment (φ = 3).  
        The visual gap between the two figures is the punishment-treatment effect.  Across all values displayed (roughly r ≈ 4.0 – 6.0), introducing punishment lifts ρ_C from very low levels (≈0–0.2 depending on W) to moderate/high levels (≈0.5–0.9).  Exact numeric differences are not tabulated, so only qualitative effect sizes can be extracted (“large positive”).  Efficiency itself is not reported.

7.  Punishment *cost* to the punisher  
   • Mentioned?  YES – fixed at c = 1 per punishment act (Section 3.2, Eqn. for Δf(i)).  
   • Varied?  NO.  No statement on how changing the cost would influence the punishment-treatment effect.

8.  Punishment *magnitude* to the target  
   • Mentioned?  YES – parameter φ (called “punishment amplification factor”) multiplies the cost c, so each punished defector loses φ·c shared among all punished defectors in that focal group.  
   • Systematic variation and link to punishment?  YES – Fig. 7 plots ρ_C vs. r for several φ values (exact legend values not numerically printed, but visually three curves, e.g., φ = 1, 2, 3).  Higher φ → higher ρ_C at every r tested, hence the punishment-treatment effect is stronger when punishment is harsher.  No numeric efficiency outcomes are provided.

9.  Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned?  NO.

10. Reward cost  
   • Mentioned?  NO.

11. Reward magnitude  
   • Mentioned?  NO.

12. Horizon known (finite or unknown number of rounds)  
   • Mentioned?  NO.

13. Peer-outcome feedback shown  
   • Mentioned?  NO.

14. Punisher identity revealed  
   • Mentioned?  The model assumes agents *know* who is in their IN-neighbourhood (punishers) because punishment is executed pair-wise, but this is never treated as a manipulable information condition, nor is it varied.  Therefore NO systematic evidence.

15. Rewarder identity revealed  
   • Mentioned?  NO (rewards are absent).

------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary requested in points A–D
------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables used  
   – The paper never reports *efficiency* (total or average payoff / maximum possible).  
   – The key dependent variable is ρ_C, the equilibrium fraction of cooperators.  
   – Secondary descriptive measures: indegree distributions (Table 1, Fig. 3).  
   – Efficiency, contribution amount (continuous) or monetary payoff per se are *not* analysed.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   1, 4, 6, 7, 8  → 5 out of 15.

C.  For which parameters does the paper *systematically vary the parameter* and report its effect on the punishment-treatment effect (for any DV)?  
   • Parameter 6 (MPCR r).  
   • Parameter 8 (Punishment magnitude φ).  
   That is 2 out of 15.

D.  Predictions that can be made *solely* from the contents of this paper about how these parameters (and their interactions) influence the punishment-treatment effect on **efficiency**:  
   – Because efficiency is never measured, the only way to infer anything is to assume that higher ρ_C roughly translates into higher efficiency (which is true only when r > 1).  Under that caveat:  
        • Introducing costly punishment in a non-excludable PGG markedly *increases* ρ_C and would therefore be predicted to *increase* efficiency, the gain being larger as r (MPCR) increases.  
        • The efficiency gain from punishment should itself grow with the punishment magnitude φ (because larger φ gives higher ρ_C).  
   – For all other parameters (number of players, rounds, communication, etc.) the paper offers *no evidence* or discussion, so no prediction can be made from this source alone.

In short, the paper only allows confident, qualitative predictions for two parameters (MPCR and punishment magnitude) and is silent on the remaining thirteen with respect to their impact on the efficiency effect of punishment.

Authors: Simpson, B; Willer, R; Harrell, A

Article Title: The Enforcement of Moral Boundaries Promotes Cooperation and Prosocial Behavior in Groups
Keywords Plus: SOCIAL DILEMMAS; PUNISHMENT; REWARD; TRUST; SANCTIONS; SYSTEMS
Abstract: The threat of free-riding makes the marshalling of cooperation from group members a fundamental challenge of social life. Where classical social science theory saw the enforcement of moral boundaries as a critical way by which group members regulate one another's self-interest and build cooperation, moral judgments have most often been studied as processes internal to individuals. Here we investigate how the interpersonal expression of positive and negative moral judgments encourages cooperation in groups and prosocial behavior between group members. In a laboratory experiment, groups whose members could make moral judgments achieved greater cooperation than groups with no capacity to sanction, levels comparable to those of groups featuring costly material sanctions. In addition, members of moral judgment groups subsequently showed more interpersonal trust, trustworthiness, and generosity than all other groups. These findings extend prior work on peer enforcement, highlighting how the enforcement of moral boundaries offers an efficient solution to cooperation problems and promotes prosocial behavior between group members.

   • Mentioned? Yes. The experiment is conducted in four‐person groups.

   • Mentioned? Yes. There are nine rounds of the public goods game (PGG), plus a subsequent one‐shot PGG (making ten total).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The study uses the same fixed number of rounds (nine + a final one‐shot).  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed for variations in the number of rounds.

   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not addressed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned? Implicitly no. Participants contribute any amount from 0 to 20 MUs.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not addressed.

   • Mentioned? No. There is no mention of a default contribution mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters (e.g. multiplication factor)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Contributions to the public good are doubled (multiplied by 2) and then distributed evenly among the four group members. This implies each contributed MU yields 0.5 MU back to the contributor on average.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The factor of 2 is the same throughout.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed for variations in this factor.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment

Abstract: To understand the human capacity for psychological altruism, one requires a proper understanding of how people actually think and feel. Article Title: Gains to cooperation drive the evolution of egalitarianism
Keywords Plus: INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; BEHAVIOR; STRATEGY; HUNTER; HUMANS; LOGIC; GAMES; ACHE
Abstract: What conditions favour egalitarianism, that is, muted hierarchies with relatively equal distributions of resources? Here, we combine the hawk-dove and prisoner's dilemma games to model the effects of economic defensibility, costs of competition and gains from cooperation on egalitarianism, operationalized as the absence of hawks. We show that a 'leveller' strategy, which punishes hawkishness in the hawk-dove game with defection in the prisoner's dilemma, can be evolutionarily stable provided that the gains from cooperation are high relative to the benefits of hawkishness. Under these conditions, rare mutant levellers select for hawks that acquiesce to punishment by playing dove. If these 'acquiescent hawks' become common, levellers outperform hawks and establish a new egalitarian equilibrium. An analysis of human foraging groups corroborates these results, as groups with a greater reliance on cooperation are more egalitarian. Cooperation fosters greater equality when individuals can withhold its benefits from would-be dominant individuals. What conditions favour egalitarianism? Hooper et al. develop and validate empirically a game theory model showing that cooperation fosters greater equality when individuals can withhold its benefits from would-be dominant individuals.

Abstract: Global cooperation becomes more and more important in times of increased environmental awareness. Article Title: Two ways to overcome the three social dilemmas of indirect reciprocity
Keywords Plus: EVOLUTION; COOPERATION; PUNISHMENT; MAINTAIN
Abstract: Indirect reciprocity is one of the main principles of evolving cooperation in a social dilemma situation. In reciprocity, a positive score is given to cooperative behaviour while a negative score is given to non-cooperative behaviour, and the dilemma is resolved by selectively cooperating only with those with positive scores. However, many studies have shown that non-cooperation with those who have not cooperated also downgrades one's reputation; they have called this situation the scoring dilemma. To address this dilemma, the notion of justified punishments has been considered. The notion of justified punishment allows good individuals who defect against bad co-players to keep their standing. Despite numerous studies on justified punishment, it is unknown whether this solution leads to a new type of dilemma because reputations may be downgraded when the intent of punishment is not correctly communicated. The dilemma of punishment has so far been rarely analysed, and thus, the complete solution of the mechanism for evolving cooperation using the principle of indirect reciprocity has not been found yet. Here, we identify sufficient conditions to overcome each of the three dilemmas including the dilemma of punishment to maintain stable cooperation by using the framework of evolutionary game theory. This condition includes the principle of detecting free riders, which resolves the social dilemma, the principle of justification, which resolves the scoring dilemma, and the principle of generosity, which resolves the dilemma of punishment. A norm that satisfies these principles can stably maintain social cooperation. Our insights may offer a general assessment principle that applies to a wide range of subjects, from individual actions to national decisions.

   • Does it systematically vary this parameter or report its effect on the punishment treatment?  
     – No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – Not directly discussed. The evolutionary update rule implies that players can “imitate” neighbors’ strategies, but there is no mention of systematically varying or displaying payoff information in a controlled manner.  
   • Does it systematically vary this parameter or report its effect on the punishment treatment?  
     – No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – The model does not define an individual punisher. Punishment arises automatically when two interdependent partners choose different strategies.  
   • Does it systematically vary this parameter or report its effect on the punishment treatment?  
     – No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     – Not applicable. The paper does not include any reward mechanism.  
   • Does it systematically vary this parameter or report its effect on the punishment treatment?  
     – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary of key questions

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?

   – The paper does not use “group efficiency” (actual total payoff / maximum possible total payoff if everyone cooperates) as a primary dependent variable. It focuses mainly on:  
     1) Fraction (frequency) of cooperators (i.e., what proportion of the population cooperates).  
     2) Average fitness of different “strategy couples” in Figures 3–4 (where “fitness” for an individual depends partly on its own payoffs and partly on its partner’s payoff).  
   – These differ from “efficiency” because one can have high cooperation rates without necessarily referring to the explicit ratio of actual total payoff to the maximum payoff. “Fitness” in the paper is an individual‐level measure used to update strategies in the evolutionary dynamics, not a group‐level efficiency measure.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

   – Parameter 6 (Marginal per capita return or synergy factor) is effectively the “temptation to defect,” b.  
   – Parameter 8 (Punishment magnitude) is the paper’s main parameter, u, which reduces payoffs when two partners’ strategies differ.  
   – The paper does note the total number of players is L×L on each layer (parameter 1), but it does not systematically vary it to measure punishment effects.  
   – No other parameters among the 15 appear in the design or results (i.e., chat, reward, knowledge of rounds, etc. are not discussed).

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?

   – Two parameters are systematically varied and discussed in relation to cooperation (not efficiency):  
     1) b (parameter 6 in your list).  
     2) u (parameter 8 in your list).  
   – The paper shows how cooperation rates change when b and u vary, but does not translate those changes into “efficiency” or any explicit group‐efficiency measure.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

   – Because the paper reports no direct measure of group efficiency, strict predictions about efficiency (in the sense of total payoff relative to the fully cooperative maximum) cannot be made. Nearly all discussion centers on the fraction of cooperators and average (individual) fitness.  
   – From the paper’s results on fraction of cooperators, one might guess that, for moderate ranges of punishment magnitude u, cooperation (and possibly total payoff) could be enhanced somewhat—but the paper does not quantify that in efficiency terms.  
   – Apart from b (temptation to defect) and u (punishment magnitude), no other parameters (e.g., round numbers, default contributions, reward, etc.) are addressed, so the paper provides little or no basis for predicting how those unmentioned parameters would affect efficiency under a punishment policy.  

In short, the paper’s sole significant systematic variations are in the temptation to defect (b) and the punishment factor (u). Everything else either is not mentioned or is held fixed without discussion of its effects. Consequently, it yields almost no direct information for predicting how those 15 parameters might shape the punishment treatment effect on “efficiency,” since the authors focus on cooperation rates, not the ratio of total to maximum payoff.

Authors: Ohdaira, T
Author Full Names: Ohdaira, Tetsushi
Article Title: The probabilistic pool punishment proportional to the difference of payoff outperforms previous pool and peer punishment
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; EVOLUTION; COOPERATION; REWARD
Abstract: The public goods game is a multiplayer version of the prisoner's dilemma game. In the public goods game, punishment on defectors is necessary to encourage cooperation. There are two types of punishment: peer punishment and pool punishment. Comparing pool punishment with peer punishment, pool punishment is disadvantageous in comparison with peer punishment because pool punishment incurs fixed costs especially if second-order free riders (those who invest in public goods but do not punish defectors) are not punished. In order to eliminate such a flaw of pool punishment, this study proposes the probabilistic pool punishment proportional to the difference of payoff. In the proposed pool punishment, each punisher pays the cost to the punishment pool with the probability proportional to the difference of payoff between his/her payoff and the average payoff of his/her opponents. Comparing the proposed pool punishment with previous pool and peer punishment, in pool punishment of previous studies, cooperators who do not punish defectors become dominant instead of pool punishers with fixed costs. However, in the proposed pool punishment, more punishers and less cooperators coexist, and such state is more robust against the invasion of defectors due to mutation than those of previous pool and peer punishment. The average payoff is also comparable to peer punishment of previous studies.

Article Title: Heterogeneous groups cooperate in public good problems despite normative disagreements about individual contribution levels
Keywords Plus: CONDITIONAL COOPERATION; SOCIAL NORMS; PUNISHMENT; CONFLICT; PREFERENCES; STABILITY; EVOLUTION; BEHAVIOR; IMPACT; LIMITS
Abstract: Norms can promote human cooperation to provide public goods. Yet, the potential of norms to promote cooperation may be limited to homogeneous groups in which all members benefit equally from the public good. Individual heterogeneity in the benefits of public good provision is commonly conjectured to bring about normative disagreements that harm cooperation. However, the role of these normative disagreements remains unclear because they are rarely directly measured or manipulated. In a laboratory experiment, we first measure participants' views on the appropriate way to contribute to a public good with heterogeneous returns. We then use this information to sort people into groups that either agree or disagree on these views, thereby manipulating group-level disagreement on normative views. Participants subsequently make several incentivized contribution decisions in a public goods game with peer punishment. We find that although there are considerable disagreements about individual contribution levels in heterogeneous groups, these disagreements do not impede cooperation. While cooperation is maintained because low contributors are punished, participants do not use punishment to impose their normative views on others. The contribution levels at which groups cooperate strongly relate to the average normative views of these groups.

1. Number of players

2. Number of rounds
   • What the paper does: The study uses exactly 10 rounds for the main part analyzed (p. 5, “Participants play the PGG in fixed groups of three for 10 rounds.…”).

   • Systematic variation or predictions: No mention of a “default contribution” parameter or how varying it might affect punishment or efficiency.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor
   • What the paper does: Uses a total multiplication factor of 1.75, split among the three players. For two players, the return mᵢ = 0.50; for one player, mᵢ = 0.75 (p. 6).

Abstract: Well-enforced norms create an opportunity for norm breakers to cooperate in ventures requiring trust. (1) Explicitly varied from 1 to 20 (e.g., Figs. 1 & 2).  
(2) Effect of punishment:  
• In 1–2 round enterprises TR has little or negative value: the extra cost (0.2) is not recouped.  
• From ≈5 rounds on, conditional cooperation with punishment (TR or exiting strategies) dominates free-riding, raising average pay-offs.

(1) Not mentioned.

(1) Yes.  “Cooperate” = contribute 1 unit; “defect” = 0.  Binary throughout.

5. Contribution default (withdrawal from public fund)  
(1) Not part of the game.  
(2) No effect reported.

(1) Two payoff structures are analysed.  
 a. “Hard” game: fixed cost F = 2 (Table 1).

(2) Effect of punishment when the game becomes easier (F=0.5):  
 • All strategies earn higher absolute pay-offs.

 • Average score with TR ≈ 0.5; without TR (Free-Rider only) ≈ 0.35.  So punishment raises payoffs by ≈ 0.15 per period (≈ +43 %).

(1) Cost is 0.2 units for TR; not otherwise varied.  
(2) No systematic variation → no statement.

(2) Effect: increasing the magnitude from 2 to 3 stabilises cooperation in 3-round games that were previously chaotic (compare Figs. 5 & 6).

 Not in the model → no effects.

(1) Implied: all players see their *own* payoff; TR also knows who defected.

(1) Not discussed.  
(2) No information.

 Not applicable (no rewards).

C. Which parameters are *systematically varied* and linked to the punishment-treatment effect?  
 • Parameter 2 (rounds)  
 • Parameter 6 (payoff structure / MPCR)

    – Qualitative results: Increasing b raises both cooperation rate and average payoff under most social norms; social norms N4 and N7 fail to maintain cooperation at low b.  
    – Numerical effect size: Not given in a table; only curves are shown in fig. 3.  
    – No comparison of “with-punishment” vs “without-punishment”; therefore no direct statement about the *punishment treatment effect* on efficiency.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit (α)  

  • Mentioned?  Yes.  Fixed at α = 1 in all reported simulations.  
  • Varied?  No.  
  • No effect estimates.

8. Punishment magnitude / fine on target (β)  

  • Mentioned?  Yes.  Varied in fig. 4 (β from 1.5 up to 5).  
  • Effects reported  
    – Dependent variables: cooperation rate and average payoff.  
    – Qualitative: Higher β tends to increase cooperation but often *decreases* average payoff; under social norm N9 payoffs stay relatively high even when β is large.  
    – No explicit efficiency ratio and no explicit comparison to a “no-punishment” baseline.

9. Presence of a monetary reward stage  

  • Not included in the model; therefore no effects.

10. Reward cost  

  • Not included.

11. Reward magnitude  

  • Not included.

12. Do players know the number of rounds?  

  • Not modelled; no effects.

13. Are peer outcomes shown? (Feedback visibility)  

  • Closest model parameter is the observation probability q (probability that a by-stander sees the donor’s move).  
  • Mentioned?  Yes, and systematically varied in fig. 2 (q from 0.1 up to 1.0).  
  • Effects reported  
    – Higher q increases cooperation and usually increases average payoff, except under norm N5 in private reputation, where payoff first becomes negative and only later positive.  
    – No efficiency ratio and no punishment-treatment comparison.

14. Do punished players learn the identity of the punisher?  

  • Not modelled.

15. Do rewarded players learn the identity of the rewarder?  

  • Not modelled.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY  

A.  Dependent variables used in the paper  
   • “Cooperation rate” – the proportion of interactions in which donors cooperate.  
   • “Average payoff” (also called “average social welfare”) – mean monetary payoff per individual.  
   • The paper does *not* report “group efficiency” in the sense of actual payoff divided by the maximum possible if everyone cooperated.  Hence efficiency is never computed directly.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   • Mentioned (7 parameters): 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 13 (via q), plus a parameter outside the list (error rate ε).  
   • Not mentioned at all (8 parameters): 3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 15.

C.  For how many parameters is *systematic variation* shown and an effect discussed?  
   • Four parameters are systematically varied:  
        – 6 (benefit b) – fig. 3  
        – 8 (fine β) – fig. 4  
        – 13 / q (observation probability) – fig. 2  
        – An extra parameter outside the list, the execution error ε – fig. 5  
   • For none of these does the paper compute or discuss the *punishment treatment effect on efficiency*; they only show cooperation rate and average payoff under settings that always allow punishment.

D.  What predictions about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency can be made *solely* from this paper?  

Very little.  The study never contrasts a “punishment” treatment with a “no-punishment” treatment, nor does it ever calculate efficiency.  Consequently:

   • Parameters 6 (benefit), 8 (fine) and 13/q (information visibility) clearly interact with punishment *because punishment is present*, but we are not told how those same parameters would change outcomes **without** punishment, which is needed to isolate any punishment-treatment effect.  
   • For all remaining parameters there is either no variation or no mention.

Therefore, based solely on Quan et al. (2019) the safest prediction is that we *cannot* reliably forecast how any of the 15 parameters (individually or in interaction) will modify the punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency.  The paper provides qualitative hints – e.g., large fines can raise cooperation yet lower welfare, and more observation raises both – but it does not supply the comparative baseline necessary to compute an efficiency-based treatment effect.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter inventory of what (if anything) the paper by Bortolotti, Casari, and Pancotto actually says about each of the 15 design features in relation to the effect of adding a punishment stage. Following that, you will find a required four‐part summary (A–D).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The experiment used groups of N=4 (p. 8 in the paper).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not report nor predict how changing group size would affect punishment or any outcome.  

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each participant first played eight rounds (periods) of a standard public‐goods game (PGG‐Standard), followed by eight rounds of a PGG with punishment (PGG‐Punishment).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not discuss how different numbers of rounds might affect the punishment treatment effect.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned? No. There is no mention of allowing public or private communication among participants.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned? Indirectly. Each subject could contribute 0, 6, 14, or 20 tokens (p. 8). That is not a strict all‐or‐nothing setup; participants had four discrete choices.  
   • Systematically varied? No. No predictions are given about changing from discrete‐choice to strictly all‐or‐nothing.  

5. Is the contribution “default”? (i.e., do players move their endowment back to themselves, rather than choosing a contribution?)  
   • Mentioned? No. There is no discussion of a “default” contribution mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR; or multiplication factor)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The MPCR is given as a = 0.5 (p. 8).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not explore alternative MPCR values or predict how changing it would affect the punishment treatment.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? Yes. A punisher pays 1 token per “point” of punishment assigned (p. 8).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not discuss how relaxing or tightening this cost would affect any outcome.  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted per unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. For each point of punishment received, the target loses 4 tokens (p. 8).  
   • Systematically varied? No. No predictions are offered about changing the severity of a punishment point.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned? No. The experiment does not enable any type of reward.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Mentioned? Not applicable (no rewards).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

11. Reward magnitude  
   • Mentioned? Not applicable (no rewards).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
   • Mentioned? It is stated the game was played for 8 periods in each phase (p. 8). In standard repeated‐game designs of this kind, participants are typically told how many periods they will play. The paper does not explicitly say “the horizon was unknown” or “the horizon was known,” but it does say “each subject first played 8 periods” and “then 8 periods.”  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no discussion or manipulation of known vs. unknown horizons.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (how much each peer gained/lost each round)?  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper states that at the end of each period, participants saw “individual contributions and earnings for each group member” (p. 8).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not consider removing or altering this feedback.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The punisher’s identity was not revealed (p. 8).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Mentioned? Not applicable; there was no reward mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   The paper never reports “efficiency” as (total payoff)/(maximum possible payoff). Instead, its measures of outcome include individual contributions (to the public good), the amount of punishment assigned/received (i.e., minus tokens), and participants’ earnings per period. Although the authors do state how payoffs change (e.g., punishment lowered earnings more drastically for the general population than for students), they never present specific measures of efficiency, nor do they treat total or average payoff as an explicit dependent variable in the sense of “efficiency.”  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   Eight parameters arise in the design description:  
   1) number of players (= 4),  
   2) number of rounds (= 8 repeated periods for each stage),  
   6) MPCR (= 0.5),  
   7) punishment cost (= 1 token per punishment point),  
   8) punishment magnitude (= 4 tokens deducted from the target per point),  
   12) (implicitly) participants appear to know they are playing 8 rounds,  
   13) peer outcomes are shown, and  
   14) punisher identity is concealed.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when systematically varied?  
   The paper does not systematically vary any of these eight parameters (nor the others). It does not offer predictions or numerical effect sizes for how changing the group size, MPCR, cost of punishing, or other factors would affect either “efficiency” or any other outcome measure.  

D. If you were to make predictions about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   The paper provides no direct guidance about altering any of the 15 parameters. It keeps all structural features (group size, MPCR, punishment cost, punishment magnitude, etc.) fixed, and hence there is no empirical or theoretical discussion within the article that would allow reliable predictions about how systematically varying those parameters would change the punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency. Consequently, one cannot infer from the paper how, for example, increasing or decreasing the punishment cost or the group size might alter efficiency. The data and the authors’ interpretations focus instead on comparing two different human populations (students vs. general population) under one fixed set of design parameters. Without further evidence or explicit statements in the article, little or no prediction can be made about parameter variations and their effect on efficiency.

Authors: Quan, J; Chen, XY; Yang, WJ; Wang, XJ
Author Full Names: Quan, Ji; Chen, Xinyue; Yang, Wenjun; Wang, Xianjia
Article Title: Cooperation dynamics in spatial public goods games with graded punishment mechanism
Author Keywords: Spatial public good game; Evolutionary game theory; Graded punishment; Cooperation
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; PROMOTES COOPERATION; EVOLUTIONARY DYNAMICS; REWARD
Abstract: Punishment, as an incentive mechanism, was normally carried out with a certain fixed probability in previous studies. But in a real legal society, recidivists are punished more than first offenders. Learning from this idea, we introduce a new form of graded punishment in the spatial public goods game, in which the punishment probability changes dynamically according to the number of consecutive defections in the games. Our logic is that the more times a player defects continuously, the greater the probability that he will be punished. To demonstrate the effect of the graded punishment mechanism, we serve the traditional fixed probability punishment as the reference model. By comparing the simulation results of the two models, we find that graded punishment can solve social dilemmas, and in most cases, it is more conducive to cooperation than traditional probabilistic punishment. However, with the increase in the punishment cost or the decline of the fine, the advantage of graded punishment weakens. Additionally, if the initial punishment probability is small enough and the punishment cost is close to the fine, the effect of the graded punishment is not as good as the traditional punishment. Therefore, it has pros and cons in promoting cooperation. These results provide a new perspective on the punishment mechanism in promoting cooperation and establish a basis for choosing more effective incentives.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account based strictly on the content of the provided paper by Quan et al. (2023). The paper’s central focus is on how introducing “graded punishment” (where punishment probability increases with repeated defection) affects the level of cooperation in a spatial public goods game, compared to “traditional,” fixed‐probability punishment. As requested, I include whether each of the 15 parameters is (1) discussed in the paper at all, including any fixed values used, and (2) whether the paper makes predictions (including numerical effect sizes, if any) about systematically varying the parameter and its effect on “the punishment treatment effect.” Note that the paper’s main outcome variable is the fraction of cooperators (and punishers) in the population, rather than efficiency (actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff). Where the paper does not address a parameter’s effect, I explicitly state so and refrain from any speculation beyond what is in the text.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes, the paper uses N = 10,000 players arranged on a 100×100 lattice (page 5).  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. The paper fixes N = 10,000 and does not discuss how changing the population size would affect cooperation or punishment.  
   • Any effect size predicted for the punishment treatment?  
     – No. The paper does not vary or analyze different numbers of players.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned?  
     – The paper uses Monte Carlo steps (MCS) in a simulation, going up to 10⁴ or 10⁵ steps until convergence (pages 5–6).  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. Although they sometimes run more steps for special parameters, they do not vary the “number of rounds” as a treatment condition, nor do they discuss how it influences punishment or cooperation.  
   • Any effect size predicted?  
     – No.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. There is no mention of communication or chat between players.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Not applicable.  
   • Any effect size predicted?  
     – No.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned?  
     – The paper has each cooperator contribute exactly 1 unit to the public fund, and defectors contribute 0. This is effectively an “all or nothing” contribution (page 2).  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. It is held constant throughout.  
   • Any effect size predicted?  
     – No.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much to move back)?
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. There is no mention of any “default” mechanism or partial contribution.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Not applicable.  
   • Any effect size predicted?  
     – No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The paper calls it the “enhancement factor” r. They systematically vary r in some of the figures (e.g., r ∈ [2.0, 4.5]) (pages 6–8).  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Yes. They show that increasing r generally helps cooperation, because cooperation becomes relatively more profitable, and it can widen the region in which full cooperation emerges (Figures 5–6, 10).  
   • Any effect size on “punishment treatment effect”?  
     – The paper only compares how graded vs. traditional punishment fosters higher final cooperation when r changes. They do not track “efficiency” as actual payoff / maximum payoff, so no explicit numerical “effect size” is given for efficiency. Instead, they show the fraction of cooperators (and punishers) in stable states.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. Denoted as α (“alpha”). This is systematically varied (e.g., α from 0.1 to 0.6 in Figures 1–2, and sometimes 0.4 in Figures 5–6, etc.).  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Yes. They examine how increasing α affects cooperation under both graded and traditional punishment (Figures 1–2).  
   • Any effect size on “punishment treatment effect”?  
     – Not in terms of efficiency; rather, they repeatedly show that higher α (cost to punish) makes it harder for the punishment strategy to survive and reduces cooperation. The paper gives transitions in the fraction of cooperators in Figures 1–2, but no direct mention of total payoff or efficiency.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a punished player)
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. Denoted as β (“beta”), referred to as the “fine.” This is systematically varied (commonly from 0.1 to 1.0 in Figures 1–2, 5–6).  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Yes. They examine how increasing β generally boosts cooperation, since defectors get fined more.  
   • Any effect size on “punishment treatment effect”?  
     – They focus on transitions in the fraction of cooperators versus defectors. No direct measure of efficiency is reported. They do give fine‐by‐fine thresholds at which full cooperation or partial cooperation emerges.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned?  
     – The paper very briefly notes that reward is another type of incentive in the literature but does not incorporate it in the model (it is purely about punishment).  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. They do not enable or disable reward in the actual simulations.  
   • Any effect size predicted?  
     – No.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Mentioned?  
     – No.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Not applicable.  
   • Any effect size predicted?  
     – No.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded to a rewarded player)
   • Mentioned?  
     – No.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Not applicable.  
   • Any effect size predicted?  
     – No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. There is no discussion of player knowledge side; the paper strictly focuses on repeated Monte Carlo simulations.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No.  
   • Any effect size predicted?  
     – No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost)?
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper does not discuss any direct feedback or display of other players’ payoffs beyond the local imitation rule (players only compare payoffs but no explicit mention that outcomes are “displayed”).  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No.  
   • Any effect size predicted?  
     – No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who punishes them?
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper does not discuss whether the punished individual learns the specific punisher’s identity.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No.  
   • Any effect size predicted?  
     – No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who rewards them?
   • Mentioned?  
     – No, and the paper does not include a reward mechanism at all.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Not applicable.  
   • Any effect size predicted?  
     – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different from one another?  
   – The paper does not use “group efficiency” (actual total payoff over the maximum possible payoff) as an outcome measure. Instead, its principal dependent variable is the fraction (density) of cooperators, sometimes combined cooperators plus punishers (ρc). They also discuss stability of full‐defection vs. full‐cooperation states, as well as partial coexistence. Occasionally, they note that punishers may reduce “social welfare,” but they do not provide any explicit measure of efficiency.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – Mentioned in some form (even if only fixed):  
     1) Number of players (N=10,000, fixed),  
     2) Number of rounds (via MCS, but not varied),  
     4) Contributions are effectively “all or nothing,”  
     6) Enhancement factor r,  
     7) Punishment cost α,  
     8) Punishment magnitude (fine) β.  
   – All others (3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15) are either not mentioned at all or only briefly stated as existing in prior literature. Hence 6 out of 15 parameters appear, though only r, α, and β are systematically varied.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when the parameter is systematically varied?  
   – Exactly three: the enhancement factor r (param #6), the punishment cost α (param #7), and the punishment fine β (param #8). The paper systematically varies these to compare “graded punishment” vs. “traditional (fixed‐probability) punishment,” looking at resulting fractions of cooperative strategies. No direct efficiency measurement is given, and no other parameter is systematically varied to show a direct effect on punishment’s impact.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of this paper, what would they be?  
   – The paper focuses on cooperation density rather than efficiency, so we cannot directly extrapolate effect‐size predictions about total payoffs or payoff ratios. Based on the paper’s arguments, one might expect that:  
     • Higher enhancement factor (r) increases cooperation under both fixed‐probability and graded punishment, potentially improving efficiency if one assumes that more cooperation leads to higher group payoff.  
     • Higher punishment cost (α) generally makes punishment more expensive for punishers, which could reduce the net benefits (and possibly reduce efficiency).  
     • Higher punishment fine (β) makes defectors’ payoffs drop more, encouraging cooperation overall; if punishment cost does not grow too large, it could improve cooperation rates (and possibly efficiency).  
     • If the initial punishment probability is small and the cost of punishing (α) is too close to the fine (β), the “graded” approach can perform worse in terms of sustaining cooperation.  
   – For all other parameters (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15) the paper offers no basis to predict how they might influence efficiency, since they are not systematically studied there.   

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
reference_APA: Quan, Ji, Chen, Xinyue, Yang, Wenjun & Wang, Xianjia (2023). Cooperation dynamics in spatial public goods games with graded punishment mechanism. NONLINEAR DYNAMICS.

Authors: Francés-Gómez, P; Sacconi, L; Faillo, M
Author Full Names: Frances-Gomez, Pedro; Sacconi, Lorenzo; Faillo, Marco
Article Title: Experimental economics as a method for normative business ethics
Keywords Plus: BEHAVIORAL ETHICS; SEPARATION THESIS; SOCIAL-CONTRACT; JUSTICE; COOPERATION; ALLOCATIONS; RECIPROCITY; PUNISHMENT; RAWLS
Abstract: We advance the thesis that the method of experimental economics can make significant contributions to normative, as opposed to descriptive, business ethics. We contend that there are two basic ways in which experimental economics may make this contribution, and we exemplify these ways by pointing to experimental support of social contract theory as rational foundation for business ethics. These two ways are: (1) adding psychological realism; and (2) testing some quasi-empirical assumptions present in normative theory. In order to make good our methodological claim, we first describe the methodological rules of experimental economics, distinguishing this method from other behavioral business ethics approaches. We also contemplate the possible objection that empirical methods cannot bear on normative ethics because there is no way of bridging the gap between descriptive theory (how people behave) and normative theory (how people ought to behave).

• Systematically varied with predictions for efficiency?: No. All experiments let participants choose any integer amount; the paper does not test forcing an “all or nothing” format.

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., do players “move” their endowment back)?  
• Discussed?: No. The experiment simply gives each active participant 20 ECUs; they may allocate anywhere from 0 to 20 to the public fund. There is no mention of a forced‐default or default‐contribution design.  
• Systematically varied with predictions for efficiency?: No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
• Discussed?: Yes. The MPCR is 0.4. If a player contributes 1 ECU, each active participant (including that player) receives 0.4 ECUs.  
• Systematically varied with predictions for efficiency?: No. The paper uses 0.4 throughout and does not explore how changes in that factor affect the punishment treatment effect.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Discussed?: Yes, but in a fixed way. Whenever the authority decides to punish a given contributor in a particular round, it costs the authority 1 ECU total (no matter how many ECU‐points are subtracted from that single contributor). The authority may punish multiple contributors in a round, in which case each punished player costs the authority 1 ECU.  
• Systematically varied with predictions for efficiency?: No. The paper keeps that cost at 1 ECU per punished person and does not investigate how changing this cost would alter the punishment treatment’s effect.

8. Punishment magnitude (the deducted amount)  
• Discussed?: Yes, but again in a fixed way. The authority can subtract up to 80 ECUs from each active participant’s income and can distribute up to 80 total punishment points across the group each round.  
• Systematically varied with predictions for efficiency?: No. No alternative punishment magnitudes are tested or predicted.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
• Discussed?: No. Only punishment is included. There is no reward mechanism in any treatment.  
• Systematically varied with predictions for efficiency?: No.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Discussed?: No. Rewards do not figure into the design and are never varied.

11. Reward magnitude  
• Discussed?: No. As above, there is no reward mechanism.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
• Discussed?: Yes. Participants are told there will be 10 rounds in the baseline and most treatments. In the “experienced judge” extension, the same judge undergoes a second 10‐round sequence, and that is also announced.  
• Systematically varied with predictions for efficiency?: No. The paper does not experimentally manipulate whether the game length is known or unknown.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much others gained/lost)?  
• Discussed?: Yes, all active participants see how everyone in their group contributed and how much punishment was assigned, along with everyone’s period income.  
• Systematically varied with predictions for efficiency?: No. This display of outcomes is always present, and no alternative is tested.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• Discussed?: Yes, and the answer is no—they do not know the punisher’s identity. Authorities remain anonymous.  
• Systematically varied with predictions for efficiency?: No. The experiment never reveals the punisher’s identity, nor does it vary the anonymity procedure.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
• Discussed?: No, there is no reward option at all.  
• Systematically varied with predictions for efficiency?: No.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?  
• The paper does not use “group efficiency” (actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff) as its central dependent variable. Although the experimenters note what the fully cooperative outcome would earn and do compare actual payoffs to that level, their main outcome measures are:  
  – Contribution behavior (how many ECUs each participant contributes).  
  – Punishment behavior itself (who punishes whom, punishment “certainty,” punishment “severity”).  
  – Whether an authority’s personal social value orientation (SVO) moderates their punishment decisions.  
• Hence, the experiment’s key dependent variables differ from a pure efficiency ratio. The authors sometimes mention participants’ payoffs or incomes, but the principal focus is on punishment choices and contribution levels.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Mentioned (in a fixed form) or described in passing are:  
  1. Number of players  
  2. Number of rounds  
  4. Whether contributions are “all or nothing” (they are not; participants choose from 0 to 20)  
  6. MPCR (fixed at 0.4)  
  7. Punishment cost (1 ECU per punished person)  
  8. Punishment magnitude (up to 80 ECUs per participant per round)  
  12. Number of rounds is known  
  13. Peer outcomes are displayed  
  14. The punisher is anonymous.  

• The paper does not mention or does not implement any variation in:  
  3. Chat (not used); 5. Contribution default (not used); 9. Reward option (not used); 10 & 11. Reward cost/magnitude (not used); 15. Rewarder identity (not used).

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• None of the parameters is truly “systematically” varied (e.g., tested at multiple levels) with respect to how that variation might change the punishment treatment effect (especially with respect to efficiency). All relevant parameters in the public‐goods setup (e.g., MPCR = 0.4, punishment cost = 1) remain fixed. The authors do introduce new frames (calling the authority a “judge” or “public official”), adding an “announcement” step, or using “elected” vs. “appointed” judges. But those manipulations do not match any of the 15 parameters you listed (e.g., MPCR, punishment cost) insofar as systematically varying them.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
• The paper makes no direct claims or quantitative predictions about how altering those 15 parameters would affect efficiency, because the experiment does not vary them. Consequently, based on what is reported, one cannot make informed predictions for how systematically changing, for instance, the marginal per capita return or the cost/magnitude of punishment would shift group efficiency. The paper’s key variations are in labeling the authority, letting them announce a policy, electing them, or making them “experienced,” all of which lie outside the 15 parameters you enumerated.  

Hence, there is little to no direct evidence in this paper about the 15 parameters’ or their interactions’ effect on the punishment treatment’s impact on group efficiency.

Authors: Wang, YF; Vasilakos, AV; Ma, JH
Author Full Names: Wang, Yufeng; Vasilakos, Athanasios V.; Ma, Jianhua
Article Title: VPEF: A Simple and Effective Incentive Mechanism in Community-Based Autonomous Networks
Source Title: IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON NETWORK AND SERVICE MANAGEMENT
Author Keywords: Community-based autonomous networks; evolutionary game theory; incentive mechanism; voluntary principle; entry fee
Abstract: This paper focuses on incentivizing cooperative behavior in community-based autonomous networking environments (like mobile social networks, etc.), in which through dynamically forming virtual and/or physical communities, users voluntarily participate in and contribute resources (or provide services) to the community while consuming. Specifically, we proposed a simple but effective EGT (Evolutionary Game Theory)based mechanism, VPEF (Voluntary Principle and round-based Entry Fee), to drive the networking environment into cooperative. VPEF builds incentive mechanism as two simple system rules: The first is VP meaning that all behaviors are voluntarily conducted by users: Users voluntarily participate (after paying round-based entry fee), voluntarily contribute resource, and voluntarily punish other defectors (incurring extra cost to those so-called punishers); The second is EF meaning that an arbitrarily small round-based entry fee is set for each user who wants to participate in the community. We presented a generic analytical framework of evolutionary dynamics to model VPEF scheme, and theoretically proved that VPEF scheme's efficiency loss defined as the ratio of system time, in which no users will provide resource, is 4/(8 + M). M is the number of users in community-based collaborative system. Finally, the simulated results using content availability as an example verified our theoretical analysis.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what this paper (referred to here as “the paper”) does and does not say, followed by the requested four‐part summary.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Discussed? Yes. The paper denotes M as “the number of users” (or “the size of the community”) in a community‐based collaborative system.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary this parameter? Yes. In Figures 2, 3, 4, 5, and especially Figure 6, M takes on values such as 500, 1000, etc.  
   • Does it predict an effect on punishment treatment for any dependent variable? Yes, it derives a closed‐form expression for “efficiency loss” = 4 / (8 + M). In the paper’s terminology, large M lowers the fraction of time spent in a no‐contribution (defecting/loner) state and thus improves overall outcomes. Numerically:  
       – Efficiency loss is 4 / (8 + M).  
       – Consequently, the fraction of time in the “punisher” state is (2 + M) / (8 + M).  
     These are exact formulas from the paper (Theorem 1, Appendix I). However, the paper does not compare “punishment vs. no‐punishment” conditions. It instead analyzes steady‐state probabilities under its single proposed punishment‐based mechanism (VPEF).  

2. Number of rounds  
   • Discussed? Mentioned, but not systematically varied. The paper states that VPEF proceeds in multiple “rounds” (e.g., “VPEF is divided into multiple rounds”) but does not systematically manipulate the total number of rounds, nor does it provide predictions about how changes in the total number of rounds affect efficiency or any punishment‐treatment measure.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not mention communication or chat among participants at all.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Discussed? The paper does assume that each cooperator or punisher invests the same resource cost c_s (no partial amounts are modeled), but it never explicitly calls this an “all or nothing” mechanism. It also does not vary whether the contribution is fully discrete vs. continuous. Nor does it analyze how toggling “all or nothing” affects outcomes.  

5. Is the contribution default? (i.e., can participants move a fraction back into their hand by default?)  
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not mention any notion of reversing or moving an unused portion of an endowment back into a personal account.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
   • Discussed? Yes. The paper uses α (alpha) as a “multiplexing/diversity factor,” which serves the same role as a group‐benefits “amplification” parameter.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary α? Yes. In Figure 5, they vary α from 1 to 10 and track the fraction of time that the system spends in each strategy (punisher, cooperator, defector, loner).  
   • Numerical effect relevant to punishment or efficiency? Yes. The paper reports:  
       – If α = 1 (no net benefit from pooling), almost everyone remains a loner (“L”) and there is effectively no cooperation.  
       – For α > 1, the system tends to evolve toward punishers (“P”). There is no direct numeric “treatment effect size” given for efficiency; instead, the authors show that once α exceeds 1, punishers dominate most of the time.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussed? The paper uses c_u as the punisher’s “incurred cost for punishment.”  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper introduces c_u in the model but does not present any figure or table where c_u is changed systematically to measure the effect on outcomes.  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed)  
   • Discussed? Yes. Denoted c_p, the penalty inflicted on a defector. However, the paper often re‐expresses c_p in terms of an exogenous probability p_b (the probability that a defection is caught) times other factors.  
   • Systematically varied? Only indirectly, through varying p_b from 0 to 1 in Figure 3. A higher p_b effectively makes punishment “bite” harder because more defectors are discovered and penalized.  
   • Effect on outcomes? With low p_b, defection frequently goes unpunished, so punishment is less effective; with high p_b, punishers dominate. Again, the paper reports fractions of time spent in each strategy, not “efficiency” per se, but these fractions are tied to the same underlying model (they do not present a direct “punishment vs. no‐punishment effect size on total payoff,” only the time distribution across strategies).  

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not mention rewards of any kind.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Discussed? No. The paper does not mention any reward cost.  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted)  
    • Discussed? No. The paper does not mention any reward magnitude.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
    • Discussed? No. The paper does not address whether participants do or do not know the final round.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much others gained or lost)?  
    • Discussed? No. The paper does not describe explicit feedback about others’ payoffs beyond noting that punishers succeed in identifying defectors with probability p_b. It does not analyze showing or hiding payoffs to peers in general.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Discussed? No. Not mentioned.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Discussed? No. Not mentioned, and no reward is discussed.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables? How are these different?  
   • The paper defines an “efficiency loss” = 4 / (8 + M) under its strong‐selection analytical model, where M is the total number of users. This is essentially the fraction of time the system spends with no contributions (defectors or loners). Hence it does treat “efficiency” as one of its main theoretical results.  
   • In actual simulations, the paper mainly tracks time‐averaged proportions of each strategy (punisher, defector, cooperator, loner) rather than explicitly showing total or average payoff. It interprets “punisher dominance” as a desirable outcome, but it does not always label that as “efficiency.”  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
       1. Number of players (M)  
       2. Number of rounds (stated but not varied)  
       4. Contribution style is effectively a single mandatory cost c_s, but not framed as “all or nothing.”  
       6. Multiplication factor (α)  
       7. Punishment cost (c_u)  
       8. Punishment magnitude (c_p, partly manifested via p_b)  
   • Not mentioned at all or not in a way that matches the question:  
       3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, the paper does not compare “punishment” vs. “no punishment” as separate treatments. Rather, it studies a single four‐strategy evolutionary game that includes punishers. The parameters that it actually varies systematically (through figures or formulas) and then measures changes in either “time in punisher state” or “efficiency loss” are:  
       1. Number of players, M (Figures 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; formula for efficiency loss 4 / (8 + M))  
       6. Multiplication factor, α (Figure 5)  
       8. Probability p_b of detecting defectors (Figure 3), which by extension varies punishment’s efficacy.  
   • The paper does present explicit numeric relationships or plots showing how each of these changes the fraction of time the population ends up with punishers vs. defectors vs. loners.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper gives a precise formula for overall “efficiency loss” as 4 / (8 + M) under strong selection, so that increasing M should reduce the long‐run inefficiency.  
   • An increase in the multiplication factor α above 1 generally pushes the population toward punishers in almost all simulations. If α = 1 or below, no one contributes.  
   • If the probability p_b of detecting defectors is too low, punishment fails to gain traction; if p_b is near 1, punishers dominate.  
   • The other parameters (number of rounds, chat, reward structure, etc.) are either not investigated or not mentioned. The paper does not provide evidence to predict their effects on efficiency.  

Therefore, for most of the 15 parameters, the paper provides little or no predictive guidance, other than for: (1) number of players, (6) the multiplication factor, and (8) the probability of detecting defectors.
reference_APA: Wang, Yufeng, Vasilakos, Athanasios V. & Ma, Jianhua (2015). VPEF: A Simple and Effective Incentive Mechanism in Community-Based Autonomous Networks. IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON NETWORK AND SERVICE MANAGEMENT.

Abstract: Across human societies, people are sometimes willing to punish norm violators. Such punishment can take the form of revenge from victims, seemingly altruistic intervention from third parties, or legitimized sanctioning from institutional representatives. Although prior work has documented cross-cultural regularities in norm enforcement, substantial variation exists in the prevalence and forms of punishment across societies. Such cross-societal variation may arise from universal psychological mechanisms responding to different socio-ecological conditions, or from cultural evolutionary processes, resulting in different norm enforcement systems. To provide a more complete view of the shared and unique aspects of punishment across societies, we review prior research in anthropology, economics and psychology, and take a first step towards integrating the plethora of socio-ecological and cultural factors proposed to explain cross-societal variation in norm enforcement.      – None. The paper does not discuss how changing the number of agents would affect punishment or its impact on any dependent variable.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  
     – The simulations run for a certain number of time steps (e.g., 500). The paper does not treat “rounds” explicitly as in a repeated public goods game, and does not systematically vary the number of time steps.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation?  
     – None.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. There is no discussion of communication or “chat” among agents.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation?  
     – None.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. Contributions (donations) in the model can vary continuously (from 0 to 10 deciles of food wealth), rather than being forced all-or-nothing.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation?  
     – None.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much to move from a public fund back to themselves)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper does not discuss default contributions or a mechanism where endowments must be reclaimed from the public pool.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation?  
     – None.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related “multiplication factor”  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Not in the sense of a classic public goods multiplier. The paper uses a “Gain” parameter for “egoistic reciprocity” (ASt = 2), but it is not analyzed as a systematic group-level multiplier.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation?  
     – None specific to an MPCR. The paper does not provide a numerical effect size or direct discussion of how varying “Gain” would change punishment outcomes in a way that maps onto typical MPCR variations.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The paper has a “Cost” gene (Cost = 1 to 5 food units), paid by both punisher and punished. Some simulations experiment with “Cost = 0” or “Cost paid only by the punished.”  
   • Predictions about systematic variation?  
     – The paper shows qualitatively that when the cost for the punisher is high (both punisher and punished pay equally), punishment becomes rarer, and generosity tends to be low. When the punisher does not pay (only the punished does), punishment is more common and generosity is higher. There is no numerical effect size for “efficiency” reported; the discussion is framed in terms of stable pro-social behavior or high generosity vs. defection, rather than total payoffs or efficiency ratios.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Partially, but not as a separate parameter from #7. In the model, “Cost” applies equally to both punisher and punished. There is no separate parameter for “punishment magnitude” over and above the cost to the punisher.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation?  
     – None separately from cost. The paper does not treat the punishee’s penalty as distinct from the punisher’s cost.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The model does not include a distinct “reward” action that agents can direct to others. “ASt = 2” (egoistic reciprocity) is more a built-in synergy than a peer-to-peer reward mechanism.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation?  
     – None.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Mentioned?  
      – No. There is no parameter for giving rewards at a cost to the rewarding player.  
    • Predictions about systematic variation?  
      – None.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted)  
    • Mentioned?  
      – No. The paper does not model a separate “reward magnitude.”  
    • Predictions about systematic variation?  
      – None.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players? (Do they know when the game ends?)  
    • Mentioned?  
      – No. The simulation simply runs for a certain number of steps. There is no mention of agents “knowing” how long it will last.  
    • Predictions about systematic variation?  
      – None.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost each round)?  
    • Mentioned?  
      – No. The paper does not address whether agents see each other’s payoffs or contributions, other than the local information used for punishment or donation when agents come within 20 pixels.  
    • Predictions about systematic variation?  
      – None.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Mentioned?  
      – No. There is no explicit mention of anonymity vs. direct identification in the paper.  
    • Predictions about systematic variation?  
      – None.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Mentioned?  
      – No. As above, there is no formal reward mechanism discussed, and no mention of knowledge of the rewarder.  
    • Predictions about systematic variation?  
      – None.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different from one another?  
   – The paper does not use group efficiency (i.e., actual total payoff divided by a maximal possible payoff) as a dependent variable. Its main outcomes concern the prevalence of different agent “types” (punishers vs. non-punishers, generous vs. selfish, shameful vs. shameless), and how these evolve over time. The paper sometimes refers to “pro-social behavior” or “generosity” and notes that “aggregate wealth” has been studied in Sociodynamica in other work, but it does not provide a ratio-based efficiency measure.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – Of the 15 listed, two appear in some form:  
     1) The number of players (kept at a maximum of 1000, not varied)  
     2) The punishment cost (#7), modeled as “Cost,” which both punishers and punished pay.  
   – All other parameters (1–15), as stated, are either not mentioned at all or are not distinctly separated from the “Cost” parameter (e.g., there is no separate punishment magnitude).  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   – The paper discusses systematic variation only for the punishment cost (#7). It shows that high cost to punishers discourages punishment and generally leads to lower population-wide generosity; low or zero cost to punishers enables punishers to thrive and results in higher generosity. However, the paper does not report any numerical effect size on efficiency or on total payoffs.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   – The paper does not directly speak of “efficiency” as defined for a public goods game. It indicates that lowering the punisher’s cost increases punishment and generosity, which might, by extension, lead to more cooperative or pro-social outcomes (and potentially higher average payoffs). Beyond this, there is no information in the paper about how any of the other parameters (number of players, number of rounds, rewards, information display, etc.) would affect efficiency. Hence, there is little basis in the paper to predict how the 15 parameters or their interactions would shape the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.
