Below I go through the 15 parameters one by one, always stating  

(i) whether the parameter is explicitly mentioned in the paper, and, if so, what concrete value(s) are used;  
(ii) whether the authors **systematically vary** the parameter and report what that does to any treatment effect of punishment.  
The term “treatment effect of punishment” is interpreted exactly as in the paper: the consequences of adding a punishment option to the public-goods environment.  The paper’s main outcome variables are the stationary frequency of each strategy (P, C, D, L) and sometimes the average payoff of a strategy; no direct efficiency measure (actual ÷ maximum payoff) is ever reported.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   – Mentioned.  Two numbers are used:  
     • N  = number of players in a group (e.g. 50 in most figures; varied from 10 → 100 in Fig. 11).  
     • M = total population size (500 in most runs; varied from 50 → 1000 in Fig. 12).  
   – Systematically varied (Fig. 11 and Fig. 12).  Varying N or M had **virtually no influence** on the time the system spends in the Punisher (P) state; hence no change is predicted for a punishment-treatment effect on efficiency (none is reported).

2. Number of rounds  
   – Mentioned only descriptively (“10⁵ evolutionary rounds”, “many rounds”).  
   – Not systematically varied; no effect reported.

3. Chat enabled?  
   – Never mentioned.  No variation, no effect.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution?  
   – Yes.  Every peer either contributes the whole unit (is C or P) or nothing (is D).  
   – This design aspect is fixed; not varied; no effect reported.

5. Contribution default / withdraw from public fund?  
   – Not present; not discussed.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   – Implemented as α₁ (punishment scheme) and α₂ (reward scheme). Typical values: α₁ = 10, α₂ = 5.  
   – Systematically varied only in the **reward** scheme (Fig. 7).  No systematic variation in the punishment scheme, so no information about the punishment treatment effect.

7. Punishment cost to impose (c_u)  
   – Values given (standard c_u = 0.1).  
   – Systematically increased (Fig. 9: 0 → 1).  Result: even very high costs did **not** reduce the dominance of Punishers; therefore no reduction in (unreported) efficiency is predicted.

8. Punishment magnitude (c_p, the fine on the target)  
   – Fixed at 0.2 in all analyses; not varied; no reported effect.

9. Reward enabled?  
   – Yes, a reward treatment is analysed, but the paper never toggles reward ON/OFF inside the punishment treatment.  Hence no crosstalk with punishment treatment effect is analysed.

10. Reward cost (c_r)  
    – Two cases: c_r > 0 (standard runs) and c_r = 0 (“zero-cost reward”).  
    – Systematically varied only inside the reward scheme.  No data about interaction with punishment.

11. Reward magnitude (b_r)  
    – Varied 0 → 0.3 in reward scheme (Fig. 8).  Again, no link to punishment treatment effect.

12. Do players know the number of rounds?  
    – Not discussed; constant; no effect.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    – The design stipulates that players see only the amount of punishment they receive, not who sent it.  This is fixed; not varied.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
    – Always anonymous (“subjects are often informed about the total amount of punishment they received, but not from whom”).  Not varied.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
    – Same as 14: anonymity is fixed; not varied.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY  

A.  Dependent variables actually used  
    • Stationary frequency (time average) of each strategy (P, C, D, L).  
    • Occasionally the **average payoff of a strategy**.  
    • The paper never computes “group efficiency” = realised / maximum payoff; hence efficiency is not a dependent variable in the paper.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are at least mentioned?  
    Parameters 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15.  (11 of 15).  
    Parameters 3, 5, 12, 13 are not mentioned.

C.  For which parameters is a **systematic variation** analysed for any dependent variable?  
    • #1 (N and M) – varied, but only shows no effect on strategy frequencies.  
    • #6 (benefit/multiplication) – varied, but only inside reward scheme.  
    • #7 (punishment cost) – varied; high costs still leave Punishers dominant.  
    • #10 (reward cost, including c_r = 0) – varied inside reward scheme.  
    • #11 (reward magnitude) – varied inside reward scheme.  
    That is 5 of the 15 parameters; none of the variations are linked to a measured efficiency outcome.

D.  What predictions about the 15 parameters and their interactions can be made **solely on the basis of this paper** with respect to the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?

    – Because the paper never measures efficiency, only indirect guesses are possible.  
    – Parameters that the paper itself varied (#1, #7) did **not** alter the dominance of Punishers; therefore little or no change in efficiency would be predicted.  
    – Parameters never varied (#2, #3, #4, #5, #8, #12-#15) provide no information; no prediction can be made.  
    – Reward-related parameters (#9-#11) are irrelevant for the punishment treatment effect unless the designer switches from punishment to reward, which is outside the treatment definition.  

    In short, the paper provides **very limited leverage** for forecasting how any of the 15 parameters – alone or in interaction – would alter the impact of adding punishment on group efficiency.
reference_APA: Wang, Yufeng, Nakao, Akihiro, Vasilakos, Athanasios V. & Ma, Jianhua (2011). On the effectiveness of service differentiation based resource-provision incentive mechanisms in dynamic and autonomous P2P networks. COMPUTER NETWORKS.

(1) whether the paper even reports the parameter (and, if so, its value), and  
(2) whether the paper says anything about how **systematically varying** that parameter would change the *punishment treatment effect* – i.e., the increment (positive or negative) in some outcome that is attributable to the possibility of punishing.

Because the paper never compares “no-punishment” with “punishment,” its “treatment effect” is always the difference between alternative *ways* of granting punishment power (unrestricted vs. single punisher, random vs. top contributor, 1-period vs. 4-period tenure, etc.).  Whenever the paper stays silent, “Not mentioned” is stated explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned: groups of four (N = 4) throughout.  
   • No systematic variation → no prediction about varying N.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned: 20 rounds in every treatment.  
   • Not varied; no prediction.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Not mentioned (there is no chat).  
   • No prediction.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution?  
   • Contributions chosen continuously from 0–20 tokens.  
   • Not varied; no prediction.

5. “Contribution-default” (withdrawal instead of giving)?  
   • Not part of the design; standard endowment-allocation task.  
   • No prediction.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   • Stated: each token contributed returns 0.4 tokens to *each* player (MPCR = 0.4).  
   • Held constant; no prediction about other MPCRs.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   • Stated: convex cost function (1,2,4,6,9,…30 for 0–10 points).  
   • Fixed across treatments; no prediction about other costs.

8. Punishment magnitude per unit  
   • Stated: each point received reduces victim’s Stage-1 earnings by 10 %.  
   • Fixed; no prediction.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Rewards are never available.  
   • No prediction.

10. Reward cost per unit  
    • Not applicable; never used.

11. Reward magnitude per unit  
    • Not applicable.

12. Are the number of rounds common knowledge?  
    • Participants know the game is 20 rounds (implied by instructions).  
    • Not varied; no prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Yes – every player sees every other member’s contribution each period.  
    • Same in all treatments; no prediction on varying this visibility.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
    • No – punishment is anonymous in *all* treatments.  
    • Not varied; no prediction.

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
    • Not applicable (no rewards).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
What the paper *does* vary (none of which appears in the 15-item list)

   • Decentralised vs. single-punisher (“centralised”) punishment  
   • Criterion for selecting the single punisher (random vs. top contributor)  
   • Tenure of the punisher (1 round vs. 4 rounds)  
   • Immunity rules (who cannot be punished)

These institutional variables, not the 15 listed parameters, drive all of the reported effects on contributions and earnings.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Use of “efficiency” as a dependent variable?  
    • The paper never reports efficiency as “actual ÷ maximum possible.”  
    • Reported outcomes: mean contributions, mean punishment points, and mean *earnings* (total pay-offs).  Earnings ≠ efficiency because the denominator (maximum possible group pay-off) is never used.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
    • 8 of 15: (1) group size = 4, (2) rounds = 20, (6) MPCR = 0.4, (7) punishment cost schedule, (8) punishment magnitude 10 % per point, (12) horizon known, (13) peer contributions displayed, (14) punishment anonymous.  
    • The remaining 7 parameters (3,4,5,9,10,11,15) are not discussed.

C.  For how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss effects of *systematically varying* them on any punishment treatment effect?  
    • Zero.  Every mentioned parameter is held constant; the authors never vary them nor speculate about doing so.

D.  Predictions that can be made about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, using *only* this paper:  
    • Very little can be said. “Punishment treatment effect’’ is taken to mean the difference between the outcome with mutual punishment (α > 0) and without punishment (α = 0).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned: the authors simulate a 100 × 100 lattice (10 000 players) and state that results are “qualitatively unchanged” on a 200 × 200 lattice.  
   • Systematic variation: NO. No equation, figure or table varies the group size to see how it changes the punishment effect.  
   • Effect size: none reported.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Not discussed. They run 50 000 updating steps to reach stationarity but never vary that number.  
   • No predictions.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Not mentioned.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule?  
   • Not mentioned.

5. Contribution default / refund mechanism?  
   • Not mentioned.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor  
   • Closest analogue in the paper is the “temptation to defect’’ r in the snow-drift payoff matrix.  
   • r is systematically varied (0 < r < 1).  
   • Findings (punishment treatment effect on fraction of cooperators ρ₍c₎):  
        – Well-mixed: with α = 0, ρ₍c₎ = 1 – r.  
        – With punishment (α > 0):  
              * If α < 0.5, ρ₍c₎ still decreases smoothly with r, always lying above the α = 0 curve when r < α and below it when r > 1 – α.  
              * If α ≥ 0.5, a discontinuous drop occurs at r = 0.5: ρ₍c₎ jumps from 1 to 0.  
        – Structured lattice: the discontinuity appears at r ≈ 0.52 for α = 1.5 (Fig 3a).  
   • No efficiency measure is reported, so no quantitative efficiency effect is provided.

7. Punishment cost per unit  
   • Not modeled separately; the paper explicitly states that “the cost of punishment can be absorbed into the punishment fine”.  
   • Not varied independently; no effect size.

8. Punishment magnitude per unit  
   • Represented by the single parameter α (“punishment fine”).  
   • Systematically varied from α = 0 to ≈ 1.5.  
   • Findings (treatment effect on ρ₍c₎):  
        – For fixed r = 0.3 (weak temptation): ρ₍c₎ rises monotonically with α and reaches 1 at α ≈ 0.4 (Fig 4a).  
        – For r = 0.54 (moderate): ρ₍c₎ is non-monotonic; maximum cooperation (ρ₍c₎ ≈ 1) occurs around α ≈ 1.0, while both lower (α ≈ 0) and higher (α ≈ 1.5) fines lead to lower cooperation (~0.55 and ~0.35 respectively; Fig 4a).  
        – For r = 0.67 (strong temptation): ρ₍c₎ declines with α; at α ≈ 0.3 cooperation is ≈ 0.2 and approaches 0 for α > 0.6 (Fig 4a).  
   • In well-mixed populations similar qualitative results hold with the discontinuity at α = 0.5.  
   • No efficiency figures.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • No reward in the model.

10–11. Reward cost & reward magnitude  
   • Not present.

12. Is the number of rounds known?  
   • Not applicable (infinite horizon evolutionary model).

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Not discussed.

14. Is the punisher known?  
   • Punishment is automatic and mutual; no information-revelation dimension is modeled.

15. Is the rewarder known?  
   • Not applicable (no rewards).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
   – The paper never reports group efficiency, total payoff, or average payoff.  
   – Sole dependent variable used for results is the steady-state fraction of cooperators ρ₍c₎.  
   – Time-series ρ₍c₎(t) are also shown. Efficiency and contribution amounts are therefore not the same variable here.

    (2) Not varied.

    (2) Not varied.

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
    (1) N/A – single round.  
    (2) Not varied.

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
    (1) “Observability” IS manipulated.  In the “knowledge/random” and “knowledge/choice” treatments, the Bystander is told how much the third-party invested; in “anonymous/random” they are not.  
    (2) The study reports that observability (vs anonymity) raises mean third-party investment by \$0.05 (GLM estimate = 0.05, p = 0.008) in the punishment condition and by the same amount in the help condition. ------------------------------------------------------------------
Parameter-by-parameter inspection
------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned symbolically as N in the graduated-punishment model, but never varied or tabulated.  
   • No prediction about how changing N alters the *punishment treatment effect* (PTE) on efficiency or any other outcome.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Not mentioned.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Not mentioned.

4. All-or-nothing contributions?  
   • Not mentioned.

5. Contribution default / endowment moved back?  
   • Not mentioned.

6. MPCR or multiplication factor  
   • Not mentioned.

7. Punishment *cost to impose*  
   • In the graduated-punishment section the authors explicitly “ignore” the individual cost of imposing pool punishment (“its cost is evenly assigned, therefore ignoring the cost has no difference in our model setting”).  
   • No systematic variation; no PTE prediction.

8. Punishment magnitude (per-unit fine)  
   • Denoted P. It is the single parameter the paper varies systematically.  
   • Core result: optimal punishment P* that maximises *per-capita social welfare* (their efficiency metric) is  
        – P* = 0   if private benefit B > social harm H  
        – P* → ∞  if B < H   (under the baseline QRE model with no evaluation errors)  
        – With evaluation errors (ε₁, ε₂) and heterogeneous β, P* ≈ B + √[H/(ε₁  β̄)]   (Eq. 20).  
   • They graph P* as a function of H (Fig. 7).  But they never compare “with-punishment” vs “no-punishment” treatments; they only choose the welfare-maximising P*.  Therefore they give no direct estimate of the *incremental* PTE on efficiency.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   • Rewards never appear.

12. End-time known?  
13. Peer outcomes shown?  
14. Punisher identified?  
15. Rewarder identified?  
   • None are discussed.

------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables actually used  
   • “Per-capita social welfare” (or total welfare Φ/N); this equals the sum of pay-offs and is closest to the efficiency concept requested.  
   • Other outcomes in other sections of the paper: number of tourists (T), resource level (X), social concern (y).  
   • The paper does *not* measure “contribution rate,” “cooperation rate,” or experimental “group efficiency” in a public-goods game; it is entirely theoretical.

B. Coverage of the 15 parameters  
   • Six of the 15 appear at all:  
       (1) Number of players (symbol N, not varied)  
       (7) Punishment cost (mentioned only to say it is ignored)  
       (8) Punishment magnitude P (varied)  
       (12-15) None.  
   • Nine parameters receive no mention.

C. Parameters *systematically varied* with respect to the punishment treatment effect  
   • Only parameter 8 (punishment magnitude).  
   • And even for #8 the paper varies it in order to *find* the welfare-maximising level; it never contrasts punishment vs. no-punishment treatments.

D. What can be predicted—solely from this paper—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
   • Practically nothing for 14 of the 15 parameters; they are absent.  
   • For parameter 8 we can say: “If punishment is set at the paper’s optimal graduated level (roughly proportional to √H when H≫B), per-capita welfare is higher than if no punishment is used; the size of the gain rises with the square root of the external harm H and falls with the false-accusation error rate ε₁ and with mean sensitivity β̄.”  
   • Because no control (no-punishment) scenario is numerically worked out, the exact treatment *effect* cannot be extracted.  Hence, beyond the qualitative statement above, reliable quantitative predictions about PTE on efficiency cannot be made from this paper alone.

------------------------------------------------------------------
Bottom line: The paper is a theoretical ecology piece, not a public-goods-experiment paper.  Only the punishment-magnitude parameter is analysed, and even that analysis optimises welfare rather than reporting a punishment-vs-no-punishment treatment effect.

Abstract: Natural selection designs some social behaviors to depend on flexible learning processes, whereas others are relatively rigid or reflexive. What determines the balance between these two approaches? We offer a detailed case study in the context of a two-player game with antisocial behavior and retaliatory punishment. Below is a parameter-by-parameter review based strictly on what appears in the paper “Evolution of flexibility and rigidity in retaliatory punishment,” by Morris, MacGlashan, Littman, and Cushman. Each parameter is listed alongside (1) whether the paper discusses it (and, if so, the specific value or range mentioned) and (2) whether the paper makes any prediction about the effect of systematically varying that parameter on the “punishment treatment effect.” Note that the paper never uses the phrase “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” nor does it explicitly measure “efficiency” (defined as total actual payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff). Instead, the paper examines outcomes such as whether punishment evolves, whether agents steal/punish in repeated interactions, payoffs of each strategy, and convergence to equilibria.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
   • Discussion: The paper explicitly studies a two-player steal/punish game (e.g., “We model the dynamic between antisocial behavior and retaliatory punishment in repeated relationships.”).  
   • Systematic variation or prediction: The paper does not systematically vary the number of players. There is no discussion of how changing the number of players would affect punishment’s impact.

2) Number of rounds  
   • Discussion: The model uses repeated interactions for N rounds and occasionally uses examples (e.g., “our findings clarify punishment's adaptive basis in repeated relationships”). The empirical experiment uses 20-round and 10–20-round designs.  
   • Systematic variation or prediction: The paper does not provide any systematic manipulation of “number of rounds” in a way that would allow direct predictions about changing this parameter to gauge a punishment effect.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussion: No mention of chat or communication in the text.  
   • Systematic variation or prediction: Not discussed.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Discussion: The thief chooses either “steal” or “do nothing,” and the victim chooses “punish” or “do nothing.” This amounts to binary actions per role, but nowhere does the paper describe it as an “all-or-nothing” parameter in the sense of forcibly contributing all or nothing to a public good.  
   • Systematic variation or prediction: Not discussed as a varying parameter.

5) Is the contribution default? (i.e., do players decide how much to move from the public fund back into their hand?)  
   • Discussion: Not applicable, as the paper studies a two-action steal/punish game rather than a public-goods setup with partial contributions.  
   • Systematic variation or prediction: Not discussed.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
   • Discussion: The paper does not feature public-goods or MPCR frameworks. It revolves around pairwise “steal or don’t” and “punish or don’t,” with payoff parameters s (value of stealing), c (cost of punishing), and p (punishment magnitude).  
   • Systematic variation or prediction: Not discussed.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussion: Yes. The paper labels this cost c (e.g., “the victim may either punish (paying a cost −c) to inflict a cost −p on the thief)”).  
   • Systematic variation or prediction: Yes. The paper systematically varies c in simulation. For instance, in the reinforcement-learning (RL) simulations, c ranges from 0.1 to 10 in Figure 4. They report that as c increases, flexible victims become more “vulnerable” to suboptimal learning (i.e., failing to punish), and rigid punishment is more likely to evolve. Numeric effect sizes appear in Figures 3 and 4, showing how often populations converge on a strategy favoring punishment when c is varied.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed on them)  
   • Discussion: Yes. The paper labels this magnitude p (the cost inflicted on the thief when punished).  
   • Systematic variation or prediction: Yes. The paper includes p in the payoff equations (along with s, c). The text discusses that greater p can make punishment more likely to succeed (less likely the thief persists in stealing). In their RL simulations (Table S1), p is sampled from ranges such as 5–15 in some runs. They do not give a single “summary effect size,” but they demonstrate that increasing p can tip the thief/victim learning race toward punishing.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussion: No. The paper focuses exclusively on a steal/punish game. They mention “reward-based decision-making” in the neuroscience sense (i.e., “punishment is intrinsically rewarding for the punisher”) but do not model a separate “reward the other player” mechanism.  
   • Systematic variation or prediction: Not discussed as a parameter.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Discussion: Not discussed; no explicit rewarding of one’s partner is included in the model.  
    • Systematic variation or prediction: Not discussed.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted)  
    • Discussion: Not discussed; again, there is no separate prosocial reward mechanism.  
    • Systematic variation or prediction: Not discussed.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    • Discussion: In the human experiment, participants “do not know the game lengths” for certain sets of rounds. But the paper does not systematically compare “known vs. unknown” round endpoints.  
    • Systematic variation or prediction: Not discussed as a treatment variable.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much their peers gained/lost each round)?  
    • Discussion: For the human participants, each round’s outcome is displayed (“Participants are then informed of their partner’s decision”). Because it is a two-player game, each sees the other’s choice and payoff changes. However, there is no focus on systematically varying the information display.  
    • Systematic variation or prediction: Not discussed.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Discussion: In the two-player design, each participant knows the other’s action. The paper does not treat anonymity or identification of the punisher as a systematically varied factor.  
    • Systematic variation or prediction: Not discussed.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Discussion: There is no reward function for the second actor (other than “punish”).  
    • Systematic variation or prediction: Not discussed.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper does not use “group efficiency” in the sense of (actual total payoff ÷ maximum possible total payoff). Instead, it tracks each strategy’s payoff and the overall evolutionary stability of punishment vs. stealing. Dependent variables in the study include (1) whether a population converges to rigid or flexible punishment/stealing strategies, (2) how often the thief “steals” vs. the victim “punishes,” and (3) individual payoffs used to determine evolutionary success. These are not expressed as “efficiency.”

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned to any degree:  
     – (#1) Number of players: Always 2, but not systematically varied.  
     – (#2) Number of rounds: Used (N = 20 or so in experiments, or unspecified in simulations), but not systematically varied to assess punishment effects.  
     – (#7) Punishment cost c: Discussed in detail, systematically varied in simulations.  
     – (#8) Punishment magnitude p: Discussed in detail, systematically varied in simulations.  
   • None of the remaining parameters (3, 4, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15) are used as a systematically varied factor in the paper’s models or experiments.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking about “systematic variation,” the paper systematically varies (7) punishment cost c and (8) punishment magnitude p during its agent-based and Q-learning simulations. It shows how these variations affect whether punishment evolves or how often punishment arises in equilibrium.  
   • Therefore, only 2 parameters (#7 and #8) are systematically varied to show how they alter punishment outcomes (albeit not labeled “punishment treatment effect on efficiency”).

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not analyze group efficiency directly, so little can be inferred about “actual ÷ maximum possible payoff.”  
   • From the paper’s modeling of repeated steal/punish interactions, one might guess that when punishment’s cost (c) is large relative to its deterrent effect (p), flexible punishers frequently fail to deter stealing (leading to lower overall payoffs). Conversely, a larger punishment magnitude p discourages theft more reliably, potentially raising average payoffs. But again, the paper does not quantify “maximum possible payoff,” so any statement about “efficiency” must be speculative.  
   • No other parameters (e.g., number of players, number of rounds, whether chat is enabled, etc.) are tested or varied in a way that would allow direct predictions about efficiency.  

Overall, the paper studies two-player repeat interactions and focuses on whether punishment becomes rigid or flexible, not on a group-efficiency measure. Consequently, it offers limited or no direct guidance on the effect of systematically changing most of the 15 public-goods parameters on group efficiency.
reference_APA: Morris, Adam, MacGlashan, James, Littman, Michael L. & Cushman, Fiery (2017). Evolution of flexibility and rigidity in retaliatory punishment. PROCEEDINGS OF THE NATIONAL ACADEMY OF SCIENCES OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account, based strictly on what appears in the paper by Sasaki (2013). Following that, you will find the required four‐point summary (A–D). Throughout, note that the paper’s main focus is on how an institutional incentive parameter δ (the per‐capita “punishment” or “reward” level) and the option to refrain from playing jointly shape the long‐run evolutionary outcomes (such as everyone eventually cooperating, everyone defecting, or nobody participating). The paper does not explicitly analyze how these outcomes translate into a formal “efficiency” measure (i.e., the group’s total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff). Whenever the paper does refer to average or total payoffs, it is usually in the course of describing evolutionary stability rather than “efficiency” per se.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
• Mentioned? Yes. The model is defined for n ≥ 2.  
• Systematically varied? Yes, in a theoretical sense: the paper contrasts the case n = 2 with n > 2 (see, e.g., Sect. “3.4 Degenerate Dynamics for Pairwise Interactions with n=2”).  
• Effect on the punishment treatment (for any dependent variable)? The paper does not explicitly quantify “efficiency” but does note that when n is larger, the threshold level of punishment needed to induce full cooperation is smaller (δ– = c/n). No numerical effect sizes regarding “efficiency” are given, only the threshold expression c/n.

2. Number of rounds  
• Mentioned? No. The paper sets up a replicator‐dynamics (infinite‐population) model with no reference to discrete repeated rounds or a known/unknown horizon. There is no discussion of round‐by‐round play or its effect.

3. Is chat enabled (communication among players)?  
• Mentioned? No. The paper does not address any communication, discussion, or chat channels among players.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Mentioned? Yes. The paper explicitly models cooperation as contributing a fixed amount c or contributing nothing, i.e., a binary decision (cooperate or defect).  
• Systematically varied? No. The analysis never alters whether it is “all or nothing”; it remains fixed at a binary choice throughout. There is no discussion of how changing that setup might affect punishment.

5. Is the contribution “default” in the sense that participants must actively move money back to themselves?  
• Mentioned? No. There is no mention of any “default” mechanism. The paper simply uses a straightforward contribute‐or‐not (cooperate vs. defect) scheme.

6. MPCR or related multiplication factor  
• Mentioned? Yes. The paper uses r > 1 as the multiplier on contributed amounts (e.g., (r–1)c is the net benefit if all in a group cooperate).  
• Systematically varied? Not in the sense of a parametric sweep. It is treated as a given parameter. The paper does not present results on how systematically varying r (MPCR) changes the punishment treatment effect.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit of punishment (i.e., the cost paid by the punisher)  
• Mentioned? No. Punishment is assumed to be provided by a centralized (state‐like) authority. The paper does not include a separate “cost for the punisher”; hence there is no discussion of systematically varying a per‐punishment cost.

8. Punishment magnitude (the deducted amount per unit of punishment)  
• Mentioned? Yes, effectively captured by δ in the “punishment” condition.  
• Systematically varied? Yes. A central focus is how different ranges of δ (from 0 up to c) affect stability of cooperation vs. defection vs. non‐participation. Although the paper does not frame it as “efficiency,” it shows that if δ ≥ c/n, even starting from many defectors, full cooperation can take over when participation is optional (whereas it would remain bi‐stable under compulsory participation). No explicit numerical effect sizes on efficiency are given, only the key threshold δ– = c/n and the higher threshold δ+ = c.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
• Mentioned? Yes. The paper compares the “punishment” scenario to the “reward” scenario and also to “no incentives.”  
• Systematically varied? In effect, the paper sets up three conditions: no incentives, punishment incentives, and reward incentives. It does not treat “reward on/off” as a parameter that takes multiple numeric values; rather, it analyzes the overall difference between having a reward mechanism vs. not having one.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Mentioned? In the model, the parameter δ also represents the institutional (per‐capita) total reward that cooperators receive (if “rewards” are used).  
• Systematically varied? Yes, again as δ from 0 to c. However, the paper does not give an explicit measure of how those changes in δ shift “efficiency.” Instead, it shows that under rewards, optional participation tends to lead to all non‐participating (unless δ is large), rather than full cooperation.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded to a player per unit of reward)  
• Mentioned? Yes, but as part of the same δ parameter.  
• Systematically varied? Yes; the paper’s main comparison is how different δ values affect whether cooperators and defectors can stably coexist, or whether one side takes over. No direct efficiency measure is given, only stable states.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
• Mentioned? No. The paper offers a replicator‐dynamics model with no mention of knowledge about discrete rounds or horizon.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
• Mentioned? No. There is no mention of participants seeing one another’s payoffs or contributions.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who punished them?  
• Mentioned? No. All punishing is institutional, so there is no discussion of identifying individual punishers.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who rewarded them?  
• Mentioned? No. All rewarding is likewise institutional, with no mention of identifying individual rewarders.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
• The paper focuses on replicator dynamics and on which strategy (cooperate, defect, or not participate) eventually takes over. Although it sometimes refers to “group welfare” or “payoff,” it does not define or measure “efficiency” (the ratio of actual payoff to the theoretical maximum) as a primary dependent variable.  
• Other dependent variables: The descriptive results concern whether the final outcome is full cooperation, full defection, coexistence of cooperation/defection, or wholesale non‐participation.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Mentioned in some form: (1) Number of players (n), (4) All‐or‐nothing contributions, (6) Multiplication factor (r), (8) Punishment magnitude (δ in the punishment model), (9) Reward enabled (they compare “reward” vs. “punishment” vs. no incentives), (10) Reward cost (also δ), and (11) Reward magnitude (δ again).  
• None of the remaining parameters (2, 3, 5, 7, 12, 13, 14, 15) are discussed.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• The main systematically varied parameter is δ (punishment or reward incentive level). The paper analyzes how raising δ above certain thresholds changes the evolutionary outcomes (from stable defection to bi‐stability to stable cooperation under punishment, or to stable coexistence under rewards, etc.). These results implicitly bear on “efficiency” only insofar as stable cooperation might yield high payoffs, but the paper does not present an explicit efficiency metric.  
• The number of players (n) is also discussed for n ≥ 2, and the paper shows that a key threshold δ– = c/n for punishment determines whether cooperation can invade. This again is stated in terms of stability of cooperation, not an explicit “punishment‐treatment‐effect on efficiency.”

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
• The paper does not measure efficiency numerically. However, one can infer:  
  – Increasing δ (the institutional penalty on defectors) past δ– = c/n tends to ensure that populations end up at full cooperation when participation is optional. In principle, that yields maximal group payoff (and so presumably maximal efficiency).  
  – For n > 2, having a larger group (larger n) lowers the required δ– = c/n (making it cheaper, in per‐capita terms, to create full cooperation). That would presumably improve efficiency under punishment if δ is set appropriately.  
  – Turning on rewards (rather than punishment) and varying δ does not so readily produce all‐cooperator outcomes under optional participation. Hence, the paper suggests that reward treatments alone tend to yield far less cooperative (and thus less efficient) final states than do punishments with the same δ.  
• Beyond that, the paper offers no direct discussion of how the other parameters (such as number of rounds, peer‐outcome visibility, chat, etc.) might affect efficiency under punishment, so no further predictions can be made from this source alone.
reference_APA: Sasaki, Tatsuya (2014). The Evolution of Cooperation Through Institutional Incentives and Optional Participation. DYNAMIC GAMES AND APPLICATIONS.

Authors: Kaiping, GA; Jacobs, GS; Cox, SJ; Sluckin, TJ
Author Full Names: Kaiping, G. A.; Jacobs, G. S.; Cox, S. J.; Sluckin, T. J.
Article Title: Nonequivalence of updating rules in evolutionary games under high mutation rates
Keywords Plus: FIXATION PROBABILITY; PRISONERS-DILEMMA; COOPERATION; DYNAMICS; PUNISHMENT; MUTANT; GRAPHS
Abstract: Moran processes are often used to model selection in evolutionary simulations. The updating rule in Moran processes is a birth-death process, i.e., selection according to fitness of an individual to give birth, followed by the death of a random individual. For well-mixed populations with only two strategies this updating rule is known to be equivalent to selecting unfit individuals for death and then selecting randomly for procreation (biased death-birth process). It is, however, known that this equivalence does not hold when considering structured populations. Here we study whether changing the updating rule can also have an effect in well-mixed populations in the presence of more than two strategies and high mutation rates. We find, using three models from different areas of evolutionary simulation, that the choice of updating rule can change model results. We show, e. g., that going from the birth-death process to the death-birth process can change a public goods game with punishment from containing mostly defectors to having a majority of cooperative strategies. From the examples given we derive guidelines indicating when the choice of the updating rule can be expected to have an impact on the results of the model.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter review of what this paper does—and does not—say about each of the 15 listed public‐goods‐game (PGG) parameters (focusing on punishment and efficiency). As instructed, all statements refer only to the content of the Kaiping et al. paper itself (Phys. Rev. E 90, 042726), and no other sources.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
   • Discussed?  
     – The paper frequently uses an overall population size N (for example, N = 40 or 50 or 100 in various illustrations). However, it treats N as the size of a well‐mixed evolutionary population rather than “players” in a repeated PGG experiment.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – The paper does not present or discuss systematically varying N to see how punishment would affect “efficiency.” No effect sizes on efficiency (or any other dependent variable) are reported for changes in N.

2) Number of rounds  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The paper models population updates in discrete time but does not specify or manipulate a finite or known number of rounds.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – Not mentioned.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The paper makes no mention of communication or chat.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – Not mentioned.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The paper’s public goods game model defines cost/benefit formulas for cooperating vs. defecting vs. punishing (and, in other references, “loner”), but it does not discuss an all‐or‐nothing contribution rule.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – Not mentioned.

5) Is the contribution default? (i.e., do players decide how much to move back into their personal fund?)  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The paper does not describe partial vs. full contributions or default options.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – Not mentioned.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Discussed?  
     – Partially. In “Model 3: Public goods game with punishment,” the paper uses r = 2.8 as a multiplying factor for the public good.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – The paper does not systematically vary r to quantify how that would shift any outcome, let alone “efficiency.”

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussed?  
     – Partially. The paper’s Model 3 uses a “punishment cost” (γ) to punish defectors, set to γ = 0.6 in the example.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – No. The paper presents only one set of parameter values (e.g., r = 2.8, c = 0.8, β = 1.5, γ = 0.6) and does not discuss how systematically changing γ would affect outcomes.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Discussed?  
     – Partially. The paper calls this “the fine β” imposed on defectors; it takes β = 1.5 in the example.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – No. The authors do not analyze how different β values would systematically alter punishment outcomes.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The example public goods model includes a “punisher” strategy, but no reward‐granting strategy.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – Not mentioned.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The paper does not incorporate a reward mechanism.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – Not mentioned.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)  
   • Discussed?  
     – No.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – Not mentioned.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The paper treats an ongoing evolutionary process, not a repeated game with a known horizon.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – Not mentioned.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much others gained/lost)?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – Not mentioned.

14) When punished, does the punished player know who punished them?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. Information feedback of this form is not modeled.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – Not mentioned.

15) When rewarded, does the rewarded player know who rewarded them?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. Rewarding is not modeled in the paper.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation?  
     – Not mentioned.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper does not use “group efficiency” (actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff) or any group‐level payoff measure as a dependent variable. Instead, it mainly measures evolutionary outcomes such as stationary distributions of strategies, fixation times, and frequencies of cooperators and defectors.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Four parameters are mentioned in some way:  
     – (1) Number of players (N),  
     – (6) MPCR/multiplication factor (r),  
     – (7) Punishment cost (γ),  
     – (8) Punishment magnitude (β).  
   • The other 11 parameters are not mentioned at all.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. The paper does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters to assess how punishing affects any measure of payoff or “efficiency.” It only presents single‐value examples of (N, r, c, β, γ).

D) If you were to make predictions on how these 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper:  
   • The paper provides no direct evidence or quantitative estimates of efficiency changes when systematically varying any of these parameters. Thus, there is effectively no basis in the paper from which to predict how those 15 parameters, or their interactions, would affect a punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency.

Authors: Wang, Z; Li, RD; Jin, X; Ding, H
Author Full Names: Wang, Zhen; Li, Ruodan; Jin, Xing; Ding, Hong
Article Title: Emergence of Social Norms in Metanorms Game With High-Order Interaction Topology
Source Title: IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON COMPUTATIONAL SOCIAL SYSTEMS
Author Keywords: Hypertext systems; Games; Topology; Heuristic algorithms; Network topology; Standards; Sociology; High-order interaction; hypergraph; learning; metanorms game model; punishment
Abstract: In an autonomous system, rational agents aim to maximize their benefits. Rational agents gradually give up cooperation with others and only request services, which leads to the phenomenon of free-riding. This phenomenon generally exists in the real society and application system. Therefore, how to reduce the behavior, which is similar to free-riding, has become an important research topic. In addition, the traditional pairwise interaction network cannot truly reflect the interaction properties of cooperative events. Social norms provide an effective way to promote cooperation for autonomous systems. Axelrod's metanorm game model achieves the emergence of social norms by conducting punishment to connivance based on punishing defection. However, links in networks only allow for pairwise interactions. Therefore, we introduce hypergraphs, which are more suitable to reflect group interaction to model metanorm games. The establishment efforts of norms are examined on hypergraphs (uniform random hypergraph (URH), hyperdegree-heterogeneous random hypergraphs, and real-world hypergraphs). We show that the difference in group sizes affects norms emergence of agents and realize the establishment of social norms on URH. To a certain extent, the probability of being seen is positively correlated with agents' vengefulness and learning time and negatively correlated with boldness. However, the usage of the boldness and vengefulness learning (BV-learning) algorithm on HRHs cannot make norms emergence because leavers cannot participate in learning and the fixed learning step. Therefore, we propose the dynamic relevance BV-learning algorithm to overcome the aforementioned problems, so hub agents and leavers can jointly establish better social norms. We also verify the evolution process of agents' cooperation rate by BV-learning and the dynamic relevance BV-learning, respectively, which demonstrate that the establishment of social norms can indeed promote agents' cooperation. Finally, in order to illustrate the universality of the dynamic relevance BV-learning clearly, we study norms establishment on real-world hypergraphs by and compare it with BV-learning. It can be found that the dynamic relevance BV-learning can effectively establish social norms on real-world hypergraphs.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
GAME-STRUCTURE

1. Number of players  
   • Stated once in Table I: “N = 1000”.  
   • Fixed in every simulation; never varied; no prediction.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Table I: “R = 1 000 000”.

3. Chat enabled?

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Not relevant (there is no public-good contribution choice).

5. Contribution default / endowment reclaim?  
   • Not relevant.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
MONETARY STAKES

6. Marginal-per-capita-return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • The game is a metanorm game, not a linear public-goods game; no MPCR appears.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PEER INCENTIVES

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   • Constant parameter “E = –2” (Table I, Algorithm 1).  
   • Never varied; no numerical prediction attached to changing it.

8. Punishment magnitude on the target  
   • Constant parameter “P = –9” (Table I, Algorithm 1).  
   • Never varied; no prediction.

9. Reward enabled?  
10. Reward cost?  
11. Reward magnitude?  
   • The model contains *no reward stage*.  All three items are absent.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
INFORMATION DISPLAY

12. Are the number of rounds known to players?  
   • Not discussed (agents are artificial learners that simply iterate).

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Each agent reads neighbours’ Total Scores when updating (Algorithms 2 & 3), but this is hard-coded and never manipulated.  No systematic variation or prediction.

14. Is the identity of a punisher revealed?  
15. Is the identity of a rewarder revealed?  
   • Not discussed; rewards do not exist.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary answers required by the prompt
--------------------------------------

A.  Dependent variables used  
    • The paper never reports “group efficiency” (total realised payoff ÷ maximum cooperative payoff).  
    • Reported outcomes are:  
      – Average Boldness (B)  
      – Average Vengefulness (V)  
      – Cooperation Rate (CR)  
      – Occasionally average Total Score (TS) components (DS, HS, PS, POS).  
    These are behavioural or individual-payoff measures, not efficiency.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
    • #1 Number of players (fixed at 1000)  
    • #2 Number of rounds (fixed at 1 000 000)  
    • #7 Punishment cost (E = –2)  
    • #8 Punishment magnitude (P = –9)  
    • #13 Peer outcomes shown (implicitly “yes”, but never varied)  
    → 5 of the 15 appear, but only as fixed background settings.

C.  For how many of the 15 parameters does the paper *systematically vary* the parameter and link it to the punishment treatment effect on any dependent variable?  
    • None (0/15).  All parameters are held constant; no effect-size estimates are provided.

D.  What predictions can be made — *solely from this paper* — about how those 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
    • The paper offers no data, theory, or discussion that connects any of the 15 listed parameters to changes in efficiency (or even includes an efficiency measure).  
    • Consequently, based strictly on the paper, virtually no prediction can be made.  At most one can note that very large punishment costs (E) or very small punishment magnitudes (P) *might* reduce cooperation and therefore reduce efficiency, but the authors never explore this.  For the other 13 parameters the paper is completely silent.

In short, the paper studies how group size per hyperlink (G), network topology and a learning rule affect boldness, vengefulness and cooperation, but it does not manipulate or analyse any of the 15 experimental design parameters listed above, nor does it report efficiency.

Authors: Inglis, RF; West, S; Buckling, A
Author Full Names: Inglis, R. Fredrik; West, Stuart; Buckling, Angus
Article Title: An experimental study of strong reciprocity in bacteria
Author Keywords: Pseudomonas aeruginosa; bacteriocin; siderophore
Keywords Plus: ROCK-PAPER-SCISSORS; PSEUDOMONAS-AERUGINOSA; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; COOPERATION; VIRULENCE; SPITE; EVOLUTION; GREENBEARDS; COMPETITION; DISPERSAL
Abstract: Strong reciprocity, whereby cooperators punish non-cooperators, may help to explain the evolutionary success of cooperative behaviours. However, theory suggests that selection for strong reciprocity can depend upon tight genetic linkage between cooperation and punishment, to avoid the strategy being outcompeted by non-punishing cooperators. We tested this hypothesis using experimental populations of the bacterium Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which cooperate by producing iron-scavenging siderophores and, in this context, punish non-cooperators with toxins. Consistent with theory, we show that cooperative punishers can indeed invade cheats, but only when the traits are tightly linked. These results emphasize that punishment is only likely to be favoured when the punishment itself leads to a direct or indirect fitness benefit to the actor.

Below, each of the 15 design variables is treated separately.  For every variable I indicate  

(i) whether the review article explicitly mentions it and, if so, what concrete value or design choice is described, and  

(ii) whether the article contains any prediction or evidence about how **systematically varying** that variable changes the *punishment‐treatment effect* – i.e. the difference in outcomes between a baseline public–goods game and the same game with peer punishment added.  Whenever the article differentiates between dependent variables (efficiency vs. contribution, etc.) I note that as well.  No claims beyond what is written in the article are introduced.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
 (i) Not stated; the paper only speaks of “multiperson” or “group” games.  
 (ii) No predictions.

2. Number of rounds  
 (i) “Finitely repeated”, “multiple periods”, “first period onward”; no concrete number.  
 (ii) No predictions about varying the length or its influence on punishment.

3. Is chat enabled?  
 (i) Yes.  Section 2.2 reports that cheap‐talk communication (especially face-to-face) “substantially increases efficiency”, citing Isaac & Walker 1988a, Ostrom et al. 1992, etc.  
 (ii) The article never combines communication with a punishment treatment in the same experimental design, so no prediction about the *punishment* treatment effect is given.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
 (i) Not mentioned.  
 (ii) No predictions.

5. Contribution default / “take” vs “give” frames  
 (i) The review devotes a subsection to “give” vs “take” and framing (Andreoni 1995b; Khadjavi & Lange 2013) but this is entirely about the *baseline* public-goods game, not about punishment.  
 (ii) No prediction for the punishment treatment effect.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
 (i) Described qualitatively: the factor is chosen “larger than 1 for the group but smaller than 1 for the individual”.  No numerical values.  
 (ii) No statements on how changing the MPCR modifies the punishment treatment effect.

7. Punishment cost (to the punisher)  
 (i) Not discussed.  
 (ii) No predictions.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss per unit inflicted)  
 (i) Not discussed.  
 (ii) No predictions.

9. Whether a reward option is enabled  
 (i) Yes.  The paper repeatedly contrasts “punishment and/or rewards”.  
 (ii) Findings about rewards are presented (effectiveness disappears when reciprocal rewarding is possible), but no experiment is cited that systematically varies *reward presence* while holding punishment fixed, so there is no quantitative statement about how adding rewards changes the *punishment* treatment effect on efficiency.

10. Reward cost  
 (i) Not reported.  
 (ii) No predictions.

11. Reward magnitude  
 (i) Not reported.  
 (ii) No predictions.

12. Whether the horizon (number of rounds) is common knowledge  
 (i) Not mentioned.  
 (ii) No predictions.

13. Whether peer outcomes are shown  
 (i) Not mentioned.  
 (ii) No predictions.

14. Whether the punished player is told **who** punished her  
 (i) Yes, indirectly.  “Subjects’ identity labels remain constant within periods but are randomly changed between periods.”  This describes a design in which the target *can* identify the punisher during a period, but cannot build a long-run record across periods.  
 (ii) Systematic variation is discussed:  
 • Nikiforakis (2008) adds a *second* punishment stage (making retaliation feasible) while keeping identities constant over periods.  Result: “Hardly any punishments are imposed and efficiency … is as low as if punishments could not be imposed.”  
 Interpretation from the review: letting punishers be identifiable across time (so counter-punishment is possible) largely eliminates the positive punishment treatment effect on efficiency.  
 Quantitative sizes are not provided in the review, only the qualitative statement that efficiency falls “as low as” the no-punishment baseline.

15. Whether the rewarded player is told **who** rewarded her  
 (i) Same design logic as (14).  The article states that when identities stay constant across periods, “free riders … exchange reward tokens with other free riders; the reward institution loses its effectiveness.”  
 (ii) Thus, making rewarders identifiable over time removes the (positive) treatment effect of adding rewards.  This is again qualitative; no numerical effect size is given.  It is not directly about punishment, but it shows an analogous identity effect for rewards.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used  
 • Yes, the paper repeatedly uses **efficiency / group payoffs** (“group payoffs are much greater…”, “the impact of punishments on efficiency is culturally dependent”).  
 • It also uses **contribution level / cooperation rate**, **net contributions**, **price efficiency** in permit markets, etc.  These are conceptually distinct: efficiency equals realised total payoff relative to the social optimum, whereas contribution level is the amount placed in the public account.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
 5 parameters: (3) chat, (6) MPCR (qualitatively), (9) reward enabled, (14) punisher identity, (15) rewarder identity.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss *systematic variation* and its effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
 2 parameters:  
 • (14) Identity of punisher across periods (variation: reset vs. fixed)  
 • (15) Identity of rewarder across periods (variation: reset vs. fixed)  
 In both cases only qualitative statements are given; no numerical effect sizes on efficiency are reported.  No other parameter is systematically varied in relation to the punishment treatment.

D. Predictions one can make – restricted to what the review actually says  
 • Keeping player identities constant across periods (so that punished players can identify and retaliate) is predicted to *eliminate* or strongly reduce any efficiency gains from introducing punishment.  
 • Analogously, letting identities remain constant allows reciprocal rewarding and therefore destroys the positive effect of rewards.  
 • The review gives no basis for predicting how changes in group size, number of rounds, MPCR, punishment cost/magnitude, information disclosure, or contribution framing will modify the punishment treatment effect on efficiency. ─────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
• Mentioned?  Yes.  A and B play a Prisoner’s Dilemma; C is an uninvolved third‐party (3 participants per group, with only A and B creating the social dilemma).  
• Value actually used: 2 “implicated” players (plus 1 observer).

2. Number of rounds  
• Mentioned?  Yes.  Exactly 20 periods.  
• Systematically varied?  No.  No prediction or data on what would happen if the horizon were shorter or longer.

3. Is chat enabled?  
• Mentioned?  Not discussed; there is no chat in either treatment.  
• Systematically varied?  No.

4. All-or-nothing contribution decision?  
• Mentioned?  Implicitly yes.  “Option I” (cooperate) vs “Option II” (defect) is a binary choice.  
• Systematically varied?  No.  No statement about moving to a continuous contribution scale.

5. Contribution default / “take” vs “give” frame  
• Mentioned?  Not applicable in this PD design; not discussed.  
• Systematically varied?  No.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
• Mentioned?  The paper supplies an explicit PD pay-off matrix (Table 1) but does not label it as an MPCR.  
• Systematically varied?  No.  Only a single matrix is used, so no inference about other MPCRs.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
• Mentioned?  Yes.  It costs the punisher 1 token to deduct 3 tokens from the target.  
• Systematically varied?  No.  No alternate cost schedules are studied or predicted.

8. Punishment magnitude per unit  
• Mentioned?  Yes.  Each unit removes 3 tokens from the target (maximum 40 tokens can be removed per period).  
• Systematically varied?  No.

9. Reward enabled?  
• Mentioned?  No.  There is no reward stage in either treatment.  
• Systematically varied?  Not applicable.

10. Reward cost per unit  
• Mentioned?  Not applicable (no rewards).

11. Reward magnitude per unit  
• Mentioned?  Not applicable (no rewards).

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
• Mentioned?  Subjects are told the interaction lasts 20 periods (“for 20 periods”).  
• Systematically varied?  No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
• Mentioned?  Yes.  “All the decisions are revealed to each player at the end of each period.”  
• Systematically varied?  No.

14. Is the identity of a punisher revealed?  
• Mentioned?  Yes.  With only two PD players, the target can infer who punished. Proposals are also visible, even when vetoed in the TPA treatment.  
• Systematically varied?  No.

15. Is the identity of a rewarder revealed?  
• Mentioned?  Not applicable (no rewards).

─────────────────────────────────────────
Effect-size information contained in the paper
(These describe the single manipulation actually run: baseline peer punishment vs. peer punishment requiring third-party approval.)

• Average cooperation rate: 0.70 (baseline) vs 0.47 (TPA); Mann-Whitney p < 0.05.  
• Average earnings: 25.30 vs 23.52 tokens; p < 0.10.  
  (Efficiency sensu stricto—payoff divided by group maximum—is not computed, but average earnings decline by ≈1.78 tokens when punishment needs approval.)  
• Punishment on defectors (expected enforced amount): 6.13 vs 3.75 tokens (p < 0.10).  
• Antisocial punishment (expected enforced amount on cooperators): 1.90 vs 0.91 tokens (p < 0.05).

Because none of the 15 parameters above is manipulated, the paper offers no statistical estimate of how changing any of them would alter the treatment effect.

─────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A.  Use of “efficiency” as a dependent variable?  
    – The paper reports mean earnings per person and cooperation rate.  
    – It never defines or reports “group efficiency” as (actual / maximum possible).  
    – Thus, the dependent variables are (i) cooperation rate and (ii) average earnings. These differ conceptually from efficiency because they are not normalised by the social optimum.

B.  How many of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
    – Eleven are at least mentioned or their value can be inferred (1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14; parameter 3 is implicitly “no chat”).  
    – Four parameters (5, 9, 10, 11, 15) are irrelevant to this design and not discussed.

C.  How many parameters are systematically varied and linked to the punishment-treatment effect?  
    – Zero.  The only manipulation in the study is an institutional feature outside the list—the presence or absence of third-party approval.  Therefore the paper provides no direct evidence on how varying any of the 15 parameters changes the punishment treatment effect on any outcome.

D.  Predicted influence of the 15 parameters on the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, based solely on this paper  
    – The paper does not give enough information to offer quantitative predictions for any of the 15 parameters.  
    – Qualitatively, one could conjecture (although the paper never states it) that anything which raises the frequency or severity of punishment on defectors relative to cooperators would raise cooperation and hence average earnings, while the reverse would lower them.  However, because the study never changes cost ratios, group size, horizon length, information flow, or any other of the listed factors, these remain unsubstantiated.  
    – In short, based solely on the paper, little to no prediction can be made about how changing the 15 parameters or their interactions would alter the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Abstract: A large body of empirical evidence suggests that altruistic punishment abounds in human societies. Based on such evidence, it is suggested that punishment serves an important role in promoting cooperation in humans and possibly other species. However, as punishment is costly, its evolution is subject to the same problem that it tries to address. To suppress this so-called second-order free-rider problem, known theoretical models on the evolution of punishment resort to one of the few established mechanisms for the evolution of cooperation. This leaves the question of whether altruistic punishment can evolve and give rise to the evolution of cooperation in the absence of such auxiliary cooperation-favoring mechanisms unaddressed. Here, by considering a population of individuals who play a public goods game, followed by a public punishing game, introduced here, we show that altruistic punishment indeed evolves and promotes cooperation in the absence of a cooperation-favoring mechanism. In our model, the punishment pool is considered a public resource whose resources are used for punishment. We show that the evolution of a punishing institution is facilitated when resources in the punishment pool, instead of being wasted, are used to reward punishers when there is nobody to punish. Besides, we show that higher returns to the public resource or punishment pool facilitate the evolution of prosocial instead of antisocial punishment. We also show that an optimal cost of investment in the punishment pool facilitates the evolution of prosocial punishment. Finally, our analysis shows that being close to a physical phase transition facilitates the evolution of altruistic punishment.

• Thus, effectively just one parameter—group size—is taken up in any detail. There is no numerical effect size or formula for how that parameter influences a punishment-based outcome.

D: If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of this paper, what would they be?  
• Little direct prediction is possible. For Parameter 1 (Number of players), the paper suggests that as groups grow, punishment becomes costlier to carry out (due to memory and monitoring constraints), making the overall punishment-based enforcement of cooperation more difficult—potentially reducing any efficiency gains from a punishment mechanism.  
• Beyond group size, the paper does not discuss (for example) the cost of punishing, the magnitude of punishments, or the presence of rewards. Nor does it discuss varied numbers of rounds or whether those rounds are announced. So for the majority of the parameters, there is no information suitable for making a prediction about how they would affect punishment or efficiency.  
• Therefore, aside from the general statement that larger groups tend to face escalating punishment costs (and can in some cases be “more efficient” in producing public goods or less efficient depending on how punishment is deployed), no further predictions can be made solely on the basis of this paper.

   • Not mentioned.  No predictions.

14. Is the identity of the punisher revealed?  
   • Not mentioned.

15. Is the identity of the rewarder revealed?  
   • Not mentioned.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────
A.  Dependent variables actually used  
    • Stationary proportion of cooperators ρ (and binary indicators “global cooperation” vs. “global defection”).  
    • No measure of group efficiency, average payoff, or total payoff appears anywhere in the text, figures, or tables.

B.  Parameters from the list that appear at all: 4 (binary contribution is assumed), 1 (N), 8 (π), and, tangentially, 13 (full information is assumed).  That is 4 of 15.
