Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter summary of what the paper actually says (or does not say) about each of the 15 listed features, followed by the required four‐part concluding summary.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   Yes. Throughout the experiment, groups of size N = 4 or N = 8 are studied.  
   In fact, varying the number of players (from 4 to 8) is one of the main treatment variables in the study.  
 • Does the paper make predictions about the effect of systematically varying it on the “punishment treatment effect”?  
   The paper does not use the phrase “punishment treatment effect” explicitly, but it does analyze what happens when the number of players increases under different probabilities of exclusion (which the authors frame as “social sanctions”). The main reported outcome is the frequency of “free riding” (choosing the low‐effort action).  
   – For small groups (N=4), the authors find that nearly everyone exerts high effort; punishment/exclusion probability matters little.  
   – For larger groups (N=8), participants are much more likely to free‐ride unless the exclusion probability is sufficiently high.  

2) Number of rounds
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   Yes. All sessions have 20 rounds/periods.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary the number of rounds or discuss how changing it would affect punishment/exclusion?  
   No. The number of rounds (20) is the same in all treatments, and the paper does not discuss varying it.  

3) Is chat enabled between players?
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   Yes, in the sense that the paper explicitly forbids any communication among participants.  
 • Is it systematically varied?  
   No. There is no treatment in which participants can chat, so the paper gives no evidence on how communication would affect exclusion/punishment or efficiency.  

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   Yes. The experiment is set up so that each player either chooses the high‐effort action (A) or the low‐effort action (B). That amounts to an all‐or‐nothing decision with respect to “cooperating” on quality.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary that feature?  
   No. It remains all or nothing in all treatments; hence, no predictions are made about other contribution formats.  

5) Is the contribution default (e.g., does one move a “public fund” into a private fund)?
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   No. The study’s design is a straightforward action‐A vs. action‐B game, with no mention of a “default contribution” or a mechanism whereby participants move endowments between private/public accounts.  

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   The authors do analyze how the collective rent (and thus payoffs) depends on the share of players choosing the costly action, but they label the main quality‐rent parameter as a = 10 rather than calling it “MPCR,” and they do not systematically change that parameter in the experiment.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary it or quantify its effect on punishment or efficiency?  
   No. The experiment uses fixed values (e.g., a = 10, cA = 4, etc.) and does not compare different “MPCR‐like” multipliers.  

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   No. In this design, if a subject is caught free‐riding, that player is excluded from the collective rent. There is no separate “punisher” who pays a cost, so the paper never reports a “cost per punishment.”  

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted for each punishment unit)
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   There is no incremental “punishment magnitude.” Punishment takes the form of a complete loss of the cooperative share in that round (0 payoff from the collective). The authors do not treat that as a punisher‐imposed parameter and do not systematically vary its size in the manner typical of a per‐unit punishment.  

9) Whether a reward is enabled
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   No. Only exclusion (a penalty) occurs, with no mention of any “reward” mechanism.  

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   No. Rewards do not appear in the design.  

11) Reward magnitude
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   No. No reward mechanism.  

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   Yes. Each session is exactly 20 rounds, and this is common knowledge (the participants know it will end after period 20).  
 • Does the paper systematically vary whether the round horizon is known or unknown?  
   No. It is always known, with no variations.  

13) Are peer outcomes shown (i.e., do players see how much each peer gained or lost)?
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   The paper states that after each round, every player sees (i) her own payoff and (ii) the number (or frequency) of people choosing the high‐effort action, but not each peer’s exact payoff individually.  
 • Does it systematically vary the display of peer outcomes?  
   No. The study keeps the information display constant.  

14) When a player is punished, do they know who specifically punished them?
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   No. Punishment is automatic exclusion from the rent if caught. There is no notion of a “punisher,” so the experiment does not reveal any punisher identity.  

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who specifically rewarded them?
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   No. There is no reward mechanism in the experiment at all.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   • The paper does not frame its findings in terms of “efficiency” or an “actual payoff / maximum payoff” ratio. Instead, the authors measure:  
     – The frequency of free‐riding (the proportion of players choosing the low‐effort option).  
     – The average payoff (they sometimes refer to “payoffs,” “collective rent,” or “mean free riding rates”).  
   • Thus, although total payoff is tracked as part of each subject’s earnings, the paper’s main reported outcome is the fraction of “shirking” or “free‐riding,” rather than an efficiency metric.  

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned (even if only to fix it at one value):  
     1) Number of players (N = 4 or 8).  
     2) Number of rounds (always 20, known to participants).  
     3) No communication allowed (mentioned, but not varied).  
     4) Contribution is “all or nothing” (A vs. B).  
     6) The payoff structure does depend on a parameter “a=10,” but not labeled as MPCR.  
     8) “Punishment” is an all‐or‐nothing exclusion, though never labeled as “magnitude per punishment unit.”  
     12) The number of rounds is known (20).  
     13) Players see the frequency of high‐effort actions, not full details of each peer.  
   • The paper does not mention or manipulate explicitly:  
     5) Contribution default, 7) Punishment cost per unit, 9–11) Any reward aspect, 14–15) Identity of punisher or rewarder (there is no such peer‐determined mechanism).  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment (i.e., exclusion) when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Systematically varied and explicitly analyzed:  
     1) Number of players (4 vs. 8).  
       – Shows large vs. small group differences in free‐riding under different exclusion probabilities.  
     8) Probability of “punishment” (exclusion), which in the paper is denoted θ.  
       – This is by far the main “punishment” variable: when θ is larger, free‐riding falls sharply (for N=8).  
   • No other parameter from the list is systematically varied in relation to punishment.  

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The experiment sheds direct light on only two systematically varied dimensions as they relate to “punishment” (i.e., exclusion): group size (N) and exclusion probability (θ). The paper also shows how a higher fixed payoff (p) influences whether subjects choose the costly action, but that is separate from any formal “punishment cost” or “punishment magnitude” parameter.  
   • For all remaining parameters (chat, partial vs. all‐or‐nothing contributions, whether the punisher is known, or whether a reward exists, etc.), the paper does not analyze or even propose how they would affect any efficiency measure. Consequently, the paper allows little or no prediction about them.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Hence, within the confines of this paper alone, the clearest conclusions about “punishment” (exclusion from collective rents) concern how a bigger group size tends to worsen cooperation absent a sufficiently large exclusion probability, and how higher exclusion probability (the closest thing in the paper to a “punishment treatment”) significantly reduces free‐riding. The rest of the listed parameters are either not discussed or not varied in the study.

Article Title: Emotion and intergroup cooperation: How verbal expressions of guilt, shame, and pride influence behavior in a social dilemma

Keywords Plus: CENTIPEDE GAME; DECISION-MAKING; UNFAIR OFFERS; INFORMATION; ANGER; INDIVIDUALS; APPRAISAL; REGRET; TRUST; POWER
Abstract: In interpersonal relations, it is known that expressing self-conscious emotions such as guilt and shame following a transgression is beneficial to reconciliation. In the current research, we examine whether this also applies to intergroup relations. Groups of three persons played an intergroup version of the centipede game, in which one party can cooperate with or exploit another party. In Study 1, two groups played six rounds of this game in each of two phases. Between phases, groups rated how much guilt, shame, and pride they experienced in relation to how they had performed in Phase 1; these ratings were shared with the opposing group. Groups expressing high levels of guilt and shame were associated with greater cooperation in Phase 2, whereas groups expressing high levels of pride were associated with lower cooperation in Phase 2. In Study 2, all groups played against a group programmed to behave in an exploitative way in Phase 1. This group then expressed shame, pride, or no emotion (control) about its performance. Cooperation in Phase 2 was significantly higher in the shame than in the pride condition, and altruistic punishment was highest in the pride condition and lowest in the shame condition. Between them, these studies show that emotional expression plays an important role in repairing intergroup relationships and in particular that expressing shame about a transgression enhances intergroup cooperation following a transgression.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what (if anything) the paper says (or does not say) about each of the 15 parameters in your list. Where the paper does mention a parameter, I note whether it was systematically varied and whether the paper reports any effect on punishment treatments (in particular, on anything resembling “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency or on any other dependent variable). The paper’s two studies focused on a centipede‐type game played in groups (Studies 1 and 2) and on how expressive displays of guilt, shame, or pride influenced cooperation (and, in the second study, “altruistic punishment”). The authors did not investigate public‐goods‐game parameters such as marginal per capita return, nor did they manipulate monetary‐punishment parameters. They also did not report on “efficiency” in the sense of total payoff relative to the maximum possible. Instead, they measured cooperation outcomes (e.g., number of steals, number of tickets won) and altruistic punishment.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players
 • Mentioned? Yes, but only insofar as each group had three persons (two groups played against each other).  
 • Systematically varied? No. The same size (two groups of three) was used throughout each study.  
 • Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

2) Number of rounds
 • Mentioned? Yes. In Study 1, each phase of the centipede game had six rounds; in Study 2, each phase had two rounds.  
 • Systematically varied? No. The authors did not manipulate different numbers of rounds to test its effects.  
 • Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

3) Is chat enabled between players?
 • Mentioned? The paper did allow a brief “interactive communication stage” between phases, but this was limited to sharing self‐reports of guilt, shame, or pride (or in one condition, no emotion). The paper does not use real‐time chat or text exchange so that players strategize freely.  
 • Systematically varied? No. The paper did not compare different forms or amounts of chat.  
 • Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed as a systematically varied factor.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
 • Mentioned? No. The paper used a sequential “go/stop” (centipede) format, not a public‐goods format in which participants choose an amount to contribute.  
 • Systematically varied? No.  
 • Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

5) Is the contribution default?
 • Mentioned? No. The paper does not use any default contribution or re‐investment format.  
 • Systematically varied? No.  
 • Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factors
 • Mentioned? No. This was not a public‐goods design; it was a centipede game design. The paper does not discuss an MPCR or any multiplier.  
 • Systematically varied? No.  
 • Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
 • Mentioned? The second study includes a single altruistic‐punishment measure at the end, where participants could “give up” tickets to remove double that number of tickets from the other group. However, no cost‐per‐punishment “unit” was systematically manipulated; that ratio (1:2) was simply fixed.  
 • Systematically varied? No.  
 • Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed as a systematic manipulation.

8) Punishment magnitude (coins deducted for each unit of punishment)
 • Mentioned? Study 2 used a fixed ratio in which two tickets are deducted from the other group for each one ticket the punisher forgoes. But there was no variation of the magnitude.  
 • Systematically varied? No.  
 • Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed as a systematic manipulation.

9) Whether a reward is enabled
 • Mentioned? No. The authors did not include, allow, or discuss rewarding behavior.  
 • Systematically varied? No.  
 • Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
 • Mentioned? No. Same as above: the paper does not address rewards.  
 • Systematically varied? No.  
 • Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded)
 • Mentioned? No. Rewards were not included.  
 • Systematically varied? No.  
 • Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
 • Mentioned? Both studies refer to a “finite” number of rounds (6 in each phase of Study 1, 2 in each phase of Study 2), but the paper does not specifically highlight whether the participants were or were not told that number. Typically, players knew the structure of each phase.  
 • Systematically varied? No.  
 • Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much peers gained/lost each round)?
 • Mentioned? Yes, in the sense that participants (groups) could see how many total “tickets” they had after each round, and they generally knew the other group’s final ticket counts. However, the paper does not highlight any systematic variation of how or whether peer outcomes were displayed.  
 • Systematically varied? No.  
 • Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed as a systematic manipulation.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
 • Mentioned? No. The paper’s altruistic punishment measure is done by deciding how many tickets to sacrifice to reduce the other group’s tickets, but it does not mention whether participants see exactly who on the other side punished them.  
 • Systematically varied? No.  
 • Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
 • Mentioned? No. No reward mechanism is included in the design.  
 • Systematically varied? No.  
 • Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
 • The paper does not report “efficiency” in the sense of (actual total payoff) ÷ (maximum possible payoff). Instead, its dependent variables are:  
   – Number of tickets won (by each group).  
   – Average node exit in the centipede game.  
   – Number of steals (noncooperative moves).  
   – Percentage of cooperative moves.  
   – Altruistic punishment (whether participants give up tickets to penalize the other group).  
 • While number of tickets won might sometimes be interpreted as payoff, the paper never references “group efficiency” or a ratio of actual payoff to potential maximum payoff.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
 • The paper’s design inherently involves parameters #1 (Number of players), #2 (Number of rounds), #3 (some limited form of communication—but not “chat” in a typical sense), #7–8 (a fixed cost‐magnitude ratio for altruistic punishment in Study 2), and #13 (players see final ticket counts).  
 • However, none of these are systematically manipulated to see how they alone affect any outcome.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
 • In short, none. The paper does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters. The only punishment‐related manipulation is participants’ opportunity to punish, at a fixed 1‐to‐2 cost‐benefit ratio; that ratio is never varied.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
 • Because the paper does not manipulate these parameters, it provides little to no direct basis for predicting each parameter’s effect on a punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency. The studies focus instead on whether emotional expressions of guilt, shame, or pride affect subsequent cooperation or altruistic punishment. The authors do not explore how structural elements (numbers of players, rounds, or punishment cost and magnitude) might jointly influence outcomes such as total efficiency.  
 • Accordingly, from this paper alone, one cannot reliably make predictions about how systematically varying these 15 parameters would affect a punishment treatment’s impact on group efficiency. The paper is silent on this question.

Overall, this article examines expressions of guilt, shame, and pride in a repeated (two‐phase) intergroup centipede game. Below I go through the 15 design parameters exactly in the requested order.

For every parameter I state  

(1) whether it is mentioned in the paper and, if so, the value that was actually implemented, and  

(2) whether the paper contains any prediction or estimate for what would happen to the *punishment-treatment effect* **if that parameter were systematically varied**.  Whenever a numerical coefficient can be read from a table I cite it, but only when it explicitly refers to a systematic change in the parameter.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER SCAN
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned.  Each decision making unit is a *sub-group of four*.  
   (2) Never varied; no prediction about changing the group size.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Fixed at 20 periods, organised in four 5-period “stages”.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction about having more or fewer rounds.  
       (The “stage 3-4” dummy in Table 2 only captures within-game
       learning, not a manipulation of the total horizon.)

3. Chat / communication  
   (1) No chat was allowed; not discussed further.  
   (2) No variation, no prediction.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution vs. continuous choice  
   (1) Subjects chose any integer from 1 to 8 nets (continuous).
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

5. Contribution default (endowment automatically goes to public fund)  
   (1) Not part of the design; not mentioned.  
   (2) No prediction.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   (1) Pay-off function uses the constants p₁ = 18 and p₂ = 12, but the
       marginal return is *never experimentally changed*.  
   (2) No prediction.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher per unit  
   (1) Constant and known: 1 point per punishment point assigned.  
   (2) Never varied; no prediction.

8. Punishment magnitude for the target per unit  
   (1) Zero monetary deduction; punishment is purely symbolic
       (“flags”).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

9. Possibility of *rewards*  
   (1) Rewards are not available; not discussed further.  
   (2) No prediction.

10. Cost to grant one unit of reward  
    (1) Not applicable.  
    (2) No prediction.

11. Magnitude of reward received  
    (1) Not applicable.  
    (2) No prediction.

12. Is the end-round known?  
    (1) Subjects were explicitly told the game lasts 20 rounds.  
    (2) Not varied; no prediction about making the horizon unknown.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    (1) Always shown: after every period each player learns the *total*
        number of nets chosen by the other three and sees any flags
        displayed.  
    (2) No manipulation of information disclosure; no prediction.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
    (1) No; punishment is anonymous.  
    (2) Not varied; no prediction.

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
    (1) Not applicable (there are no rewards).  
    (2) No prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
NUMERICAL EFFECT SIZES ACTUALLY REPORTED
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Because none of the 15 parameters is varied, the only numerical
treatment effects given in the paper relate to *whether punishment is
available or not* (and to whether the group is “in-group” or “mixed”).
Example: in Table 2, “mixed-group × NMP” has a coefficient of –0.414,
meaning that when punishment is possible in mixed groups subjects use
0.414 fewer nets (≈20 % of one standard deviation).  This is *not* an
effect of changing any of the 15 parameters; it is merely the main
treatment of the study.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Does the paper study *group efficiency*?  
    No.  The dependent variables are  
      • individual extraction level (number of nets),  
      • punishment points assigned,  
      • flags received (yellow / orange / red), and  
      • period-to-period changes in extraction.  
    Efficiency (total or average payoff as a share of the social
    optimum) is never computed.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are *mentioned*?  
    8 of 15: #1, #2, #4, #6, #7, #8, #12, #13, #14.  
    (They are *described* but never manipulated.)  Parameters #3, #5,
    #9, #10, #11, #15 are not mentioned or not applicable.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss their *systematic*
   effect on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent
   variable)?  
   Zero.  No parameter among the 15 is experimentally varied, hence no
   systematic effect is estimated.

D.  Predictions one could make about how the 15 parameters (and their
   interactions) would influence the punishment treatment effect on
   **efficiency**, using *only* this paper:  
   The paper offers virtually no direct evidence.  All that can be
   cautiously inferred is:  
   • Introducing punishment *at all* can reduce extraction in the
     specific setting studied (four-person CPR, 20 known rounds, cost 1
     to the punisher, zero material cost to the target, anonymous,
     partial information).  
   • The presence of punishment is more effective when the group is a
     “mixed” community rather than an “in-group”; this contextual
     moderator is *not* among the 15 parameters.  
   • No statements, qualitative or quantitative, are made about what
     would happen if any of the 15 parameters were increased, decreased
     or toggled.  
   Hence any prediction about those parameters’ influence on *efficiency*
   must be labelled “no basis in the paper”.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
In short, the paper is informative about *whether* symbolic punishment
works in one specific field setting, but it does **not** provide
leverage for forecasting how changing standard design parameters (group
size, marginal return, cost/magnitude of punishment, information
structure, etc.) would alter the punishment effect on efficiency.
reference_APA: de Melo, Gioia & Piaggio, Matias (2015). The perils of peer punishment: Evidence from a common pool resource framed field experiment. ECOLOGICAL ECONOMICS.

Abstract: In four bargaining games with an option to punish, participants could avoid punishment by shifting the blame for an unfair offer on a random coin flip. Punishments were not affected by whether the results of the coin flip could be verified, nor by beliefs about whether a coin had actually been flipped (Studies 1-3). Alternative explanations of reluctance to punish hypocrites, such as free-riding from altruistic punishment (Study 2), or feelings of gratitude (Study 3) were not supported. Independent third parties were also less punitive toward those who blamed the coin (Study 4). Similar results were found in an online vignette study run with a more representative sample (Study 5). In sum, these findings suggest that hypocrisy thrives because it can deter punishment. (c) 2015 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

Below, each of the 15 public-goods parameters is treated in turn.  
For every parameter I state (i) whether the paper says anything about it (and, if so, what concrete value or set-up is used) and (ii) whether the authors give any prediction or evidence about what would happen if the parameter were systematically varied – in particular, how such variation would change the **punishment treatment effect** (i.e., the difference that the availability of punishment makes).

----------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
(i) Mentioned.  Studies 1-3 use two players (proposer & responder).  Study 4 adds a third-party “judge” so that three roles are present.  Study 5 is hypothetical but still framed as a two-player game.  
(ii) No systematic manipulation.  The coin-blame effect is shown separately for 2-player (second-party) and 3-player (third-party) settings, but the paper never contrasts these two settings in order to estimate how “adding a third party” changes the size of the punishment effect on any payoff-based outcome, let alone efficiency.

2. Number of rounds  
(i) Explicitly one round; every ultimatum interaction is one-shot.  
(ii) Never varied, no predictions.

3. Chat enabled?  
(i) Not mentioned; no chat was permitted.  
(ii) Not discussed.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
(i) Not relevant to the ultimatum game used; nothing said.  
(ii) Not discussed.

5. Contribution default?  
(i) Not relevant; nothing said.  
(ii) Not discussed.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor  
(i) Not applicable; no public good.  
(ii) Not discussed.

7. Punishment cost per unit  
(i) Only Study 4 specifies that the judge spends 1 cent to deduct 3 cents from the proposer.  
(ii) Fixed; never varied; no predictions.

8. Punishment magnitude per unit  
(i) See #7: 3 cents deducted for every 1 cent spent.  
(ii) Fixed; never varied; no predictions.

9. Reward enabled?  
(i) Study 4 allowed judges to reward as well as punish, but reward behaviour is reported only to say it was not affected by the coin condition.  
(ii) The possibility of reward is never varied experimentally.

10. Reward cost per unit  
(i) Stated only in passing (“another 100 cent could be used for rewarding”) but no exact per-unit conversion is given.  
(ii) Not varied; no predictions.

11. Reward magnitude per unit  
(i) Not specified beyond the general 100-cent budget.  
(ii) Not varied.

12. Is the number of rounds known?  
(i) Implied yes – players are told it is a single, one-shot game.  
(ii) Not varied.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
(i) By design, responders and judges are informed of the monetary division, so they do see pay-offs.  
(ii) This information condition is never varied or analysed.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
(i) No; the lab set-up keeps everyone anonymous.  
(ii) Not discussed.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
(i) Same as #14: anonymity; not discussed.  
(ii) Not discussed.

----------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY  

A.  Dependent variables.  
   – The paper does **not** use group efficiency (total or average pay-off divided by the maximum) as an outcome.  
   – Main dependent variables are (a) rejection rate of unfair offers (binary second-party punishment), (b) amount of money spent on punishment by third parties, and (c) respondents’ beliefs about whether the proposer really flipped the coin.  These are conceptually different from efficiency because they do not aggregate group pay-offs.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   7 of them appear in some form (#1, #2, #7, #8, #9, #10, #11; #12 and #13 are only implicit).  The remaining parameters (#3–6, #14, #15) are absent.

C.  Which parameters are *systematically varied* and linked to the punishment treatment effect?  
   None of the 15 parameters is experimentally manipulated with the aim of tracing its influence on the punishment effect.  The paper’s only manipulations concern (a) whether the proposer blames a coin and (b) whether the coin result can be verified – factors that do not map onto the 15-item list.

D.  What predictions about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment-efficiency link can be made from this paper alone?  
   Essentially none.  Because efficiency is never measured and none of the listed structural, monetary-stake, or information parameters is varied, the paper supplies virtually no basis for forecasting how altering those parameters would amplify or dampen the impact of punishment on efficiency in a public-goods setting.  The only (very indirect) hint is that the presence of a third-party punisher (parameter 1) did not eliminate the deterrence effect of “blaming the coin,” suggesting that going from 2 to 3 players might not qualitatively change how uncertainty over culpability moderates punishment, but even this inference concerns rejection rates, not efficiency.

In short, the article is informative about how *moral doubt* can suppress punishment, but it offers almost no leverage for predicting how the 15 public-goods design parameters or their interactions would shape the effect of introducing punishment on group efficiency.

Authors: Skatova, A; Ferguson, E
Author Full Names: Skatova, Anya; Ferguson, Eamonn
Article Title: Individual differences in behavioural inhibition explain free riding in public good games when punishment is expected but not implemented
Author Keywords: Cooperation; Free riding; Punishment risk; Behavioural inhibition; Individual differences
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; COSTLY PUNISHMENT; SOCIAL DILEMMAS; BIS/BAS SCALES; COOPERATION; REWARD; UNCERTAINTY; THREAT; ACTIVATION
Abstract: Background: The literature on social dilemmas and punishment focuses on the behaviour of the punisher. However, to fully explain the effect of punishment on cooperation, it is important to understand the psychological mechanisms influencing the behaviour of those who expect to be punished. This paper examines whether the expectation of punishment, rather than the implementation of punishment is sufficient to prevent individuals from free riding. Individual differences in the punishment sensitivity have been linked to both threat responses (flight, fight, fear system, or the FFFS) and to the response to the uncertainty of punishment (BIS-anxiety). The paper, therefore, examines if individual differences in BIS-anxiety and FFFS can explain some of the variability in free riding in the face of implemented and non-implemented punishment. Methods: Participants took part in a series of one-shot Public Goods Games (PGGs) facing two punishment conditions (implemented and non-implemented) and two standard non-punishment PGGs. The punishment was implemented as a centralized authority punishment (i.e., if one participant contributed less than their group members, they were automatically fined). Individual contribution levels and presence/absence of zero contributions indexed free riding. Individual differences in behavioural inhibition were assessed. Results: Individuals contributed more under the threat of punishment (both implemented and non-implemented). However, individuals contributed less when the punishment was not implemented compared to when it was. Those scoring high in BIS-anxiety contributed more when the punishment expectations were not implemented. This effect was not observed for FFFS. Conclusion: Supporting previous research, punishment had a powerful effect in increasing contribution levels in the PGGs. However, when expected punishment was not implemented, individual differences in punishment sensitivity, specifically in BIS-anxiety, were related to fewer contributions (increased free riding) as compared to the situation when punishment was not implemented. This has implications for our understanding of why some people cannot resist the temptation to free ride, even when facing possible punishment for their actions. Our findings suggest that the diminished functioning of mechanisms, associated with trait behavioural inhibition, can partly explain such behaviours.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what this particular paper says (or does not say) regarding (1) the parameter itself and (2) any predictions the paper makes about systematically varying that parameter on the “punishment treatment effect.” Note that the paper’s sole focus is on whether punishment (centralized authority) is actually implemented or not, and on how that influences individual contributions (rather than group efficiency). All statements refer strictly to what appears in the text, figures, and analyses of the paper.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned? Yes. All public goods games (PGGs) in this study were played in groups of four.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper keeps the group size fixed at four and does not discuss changing the number of players or its effect on punishment.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned? Yes. The experiment used multiple “blocks,” each containing a certain number of one‐shot “trials.” However, the exact number of trials per block was not itself an experimental factor.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not systematically manipulate or compare different round lengths. It does not predict how changing the number of rounds would alter the punishment effect.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not report any communication (chat) among participants.  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no discussion about enabling or disabling chat.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned? Indirectly. Each participant could contribute any integer amount between 0 and 20 MUs. There was no “all‐or‐nothing” constraint.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not manipulate contribution style. It only notes that participants freely chose their contribution from 0 to 20 MUs.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not discuss having a default contribution that participants must opt in or out of (or move funds back from a public pot).  
   • Systematically varied? No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Mentioned? Yes, effectively. The payoff formula shows a 0.5 multiplier on the sum of group contributions.  
   • Systematically varied? No. A single MPCR (0.5) is used throughout, and the paper does not predict how different multipliers would affect punishment efficacy.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned? No. In this design, the “punisher” is a central authority, not a peer paying any cost. The study does not address how imposing punishment might cost the punisher.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not manipulate or quantify any cost borne by punishers.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted per unit of punishment)
   • Mentioned? Only in general terms. The experiment imposes “a fine” if participants contribute less than the group average in certain trials—but nowhere does the paper specify the numerical magnitude of that fine.  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no discussion or manipulation of different fine sizes.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned? No. The paper only describes punishment (fines for undercontribution); no reward mechanism is introduced.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Mentioned? No. Rewards do not appear in the design.  
    • Systematically varied? No.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded per unit of reward)
    • Mentioned? No. Again, the paper does not use or mention any rewards.  
    • Systematically varied? No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do players know when the game ends)?
    • Mentioned? Yes, in that participants were not explicitly told how many blocks or trials there would be.  
    • Systematically varied? No. There is no discussion of comparing “known” versus “unknown” endpoints to see how it influences punishment.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (i.e., do players see how much each of their peers gained/lost)?
    • Mentioned? Partially. Participants saw the average contribution of the group, plus their own payoffs. They did not see individual peers’ gains or losses.  
    • Systematically varied? No. The study does not manipulate the level of information about others’ outcomes.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Mentioned? The punisher is a central authority (not a peer). There is no mention that participants learn anything about a specific punisher’s identity (and indeed there is no “other player” punisher).  
    • Systematically varied? No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Mentioned? No. There is no reward mechanism in this paper.  
    • Systematically varied? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?
   • The paper does not use “group efficiency” (total payoff / maximum possible payoff) as a dependent variable. Instead, it uses (a) individual contribution levels to a public good, and (b) whether participants contributed zero on at least one trial (free riding). These outcomes are both related to cooperation, but they are not measures of group efficiency or total payoff.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?
   • Parameters 1 (number of players), 2 (number of rounds), and 6 (multiplication factor of 0.5) are explicitly mentioned in the paper. The remaining parameters (3–5, 7–15) either do not appear at all or appear only in passing as fixed features (without numeric details or discussion of variation).

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?
   • None. The only manipulation was whether punishment was “implemented” or “non-implemented,” but this does not map onto any of the 15 parameters as they were defined in your list (e.g., they did not vary punishment magnitude, cost, or group size). Consequently, the paper provides no discussion of how systematically changing any specific parameter (among the 15 listed) would alter punishment’s effects on cooperation or efficiency.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?
   • The paper gives no direct evidence or theoretical discussion about how varying group size, number of rounds, the MPCR, punishment cost, or punishment magnitude, etc., would affect group efficiency. Its focus is on whether contributions change under the threat of central authority punishment that may or may not be implemented. Because the study does not examine efficiency or vary these parameters, one can make almost no prediction from this paper alone; it does not offer guidance on how any of the 15 parameters would systematically alter the effect of punishment on group efficiency.

────────────
(end of answer)

Authors: Fang, X; Chen, XJ
Author Full Names: Fang, Xing; Chen, Xiaojie
Article Title: Evolutionary dynamics of trust in the N-player trust game with individual reward and punishment
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS; COOPERATION
Abstract: Trust plays an important role in human society. However, how does trust evolve is a huge challenge. The trust game is a well-known paradigm to measure the evolution of trust in a population. Reward and punishment as the common types of incentives can be used to improve the trustworthiness. However, it remains unclear how reward and punishment actually influence the evolutionary dynamics of trust. Here, we introduce individual reward and punishment into the N-player trust game model in an infinite well-mixed population, where investors use a part of the returned fund to reward trustworthy trustees and meanwhile punish untrustworthy trustees. We then investigate the evolutionary dynamics of trust by means of replicator equations. We show that the introduction of reward and punishment can lead to the stable coexistence state of investors and trustworthy trustees, which indicates that the evolution of trust can be greatly promoted. We reveal that the attraction domain of the coexistence state becomes larger as investors increase the incentive strength from the returned fund for reward and punishment. In addition, we find that the increase of the reward coefficient can enlarge the attraction domain of the coexistence state, which implies that reward can better promote the evolution of trust than punishment.

Below is a point‐by‐point account of what the paper by Fang and Chen (2021) does and does not say about each of the 15 parameters in relation to the “punishment treatment effect” (in particular, with respect to overall efficiency). Throughout, “the paper” refers exclusively to the text, figures, and tables that were provided.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players
   • Discussed? Yes. The paper consistently denotes the group size by N, with figures often using N = 20 as an example.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying N and how that affects the punishment treatment effect (especially on efficiency)?  
     – The paper analyzes replicator dynamics for a general N in its mathematical derivations, discusses some sensitivity to N, and notes that certain expressions (e.g., a₂₂ < 0) can depend on N. However, it does not relate those derivations to any measure of “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” and provides no numerical effect sizes tied to varying N.  

2) Number of rounds
   • Discussed? No. The paper models an infinite well‐mixed population and does not mention a finite or known number of rounds.  
   • Systematic variation or effect size? Not mentioned.  

3) Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussed? No. There is no reference to any communication or chat.  
   • Systematic variation or effect size? Not mentioned.  

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussed? No. The paper focuses on a trust game with parameters tᵥ, Rₜ, Rᵤ, etc., rather than an “all‐or‐nothing” contribution mechanism.  
   • Systematic variation or effect size? Not mentioned.  

5) Is the contribution default?
   • Discussed? No. There is no mention of a default (automatic) contribution or the ability to pull back endowment.  
   • Systematic variation or effect size? Not mentioned.  

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Discussed? Partially. The paper uses Rₜ and Rᵤ as the amounts that trustworthy vs. untrustworthy trustees return (or keep) and defines r = (Rᵤ – Rₜ)/Rₜ. These can be viewed as parameters that scale returns, loosely analogous to a “multiplying factor.”  
   • Systematic variation or effect size? The paper does analyze some cases (e.g., the condition αp > r) but never connects these results explicitly to a “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency and does not provide numerical effect sizes for how altering Rₜ, Rᵤ, or r changes overall/payoff efficiency.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussed? No. The model’s approach is that a fraction p of the investors’ returned fund is used for incentives, and some fraction (1 – α) of it ends up punishing untrustworthy trustees, but there is no standalone mention of a direct, per‐unit “cost” to the punisher.  
   • Systematic variation or effect size? Not mentioned.  

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted for each unit of punishment)
   • Discussed? Yes, but only implicitly as part of the formula for how the incentive budget is split. The paper indicates that untrustworthy trustees are fined by (1 – α)pRₜ(…) but does not single out “punishment magnitude per unit” or analyze its systematic variation separately from α and p.  
   • Systematic variation or effect size? The paper does not isolate punishment‐magnitude variation or link it to a “punishment treatment effect” (nor to efficiency).  

9) Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussed? Yes. The paper explicitly studies a model in which both reward and punishment can be introduced. It notes that α = 0 corresponds to using all incentive budget for punishment, while α = 1 corresponds to all budget for reward.  
   • Systematic variation or effect size? The paper does consider different α but does not provide a numerical effect on “efficiency.” Rather, it reports changes in stable coexistence states of (investor, trustworthy trustee) strategies.  

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Discussed? No. As with punishment cost, there is no direct parameter specifying a personal cost each time a reward is conferred. The total budget for reward is αp(…) drawn from the returned fund.  
   • Systematic variation or effect size? Not mentioned.  

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)
   • Discussed? Yes, but only as part of αpRₜ(…)—the fraction of the incentive budget used for rewarding trustworthy trustees.  
   • Systematic variation or effect size? The paper does vary α from 0 to 1 and p from 0 to 1, but it does not quantify changes in terms of “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”  

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not touch on knowledge of or finite vs. infinite horizon.  
   • Systematic variation or effect size? Not mentioned.  

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players see each other’s gains/losses)?
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not address real‐time information disclosure.  
   • Systematic variation or effect size? Not mentioned.  

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the punisher is?
   • Discussed? No. There is no mention of whether players learn the source of punishment.  
   • Systematic variation or effect size? Not mentioned.  

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is?
   • Discussed? No. There is no mention of whether players see who gave the reward.  
   • Systematic variation or effect size? Not mentioned.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper does not measure or report a ratio of “actual total payoff” to a “maximum possible total payoff.” Instead, it uses replicator‐equation analyses of whether (and under what conditions) the population converges to all‐untrustworthy trustees (U) vs. a boundary coexistence of investors (I) and trustworthy trustees (T). Although payoffs per strategy are part of the theoretical model, “efficiency” as typically defined in public‐goods or social‐dilemma contexts is not explicitly analyzed. Thus, the chief dependent variables in the paper are the equilibrium frequencies of different strategies (I, T, U) and the stability properties or “basin of attraction.”

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned explicitly or used in their model: 1 (N), 6 (returns/multipliers, via Rₜ, Rᵤ, and r), 8 and 11 in an implicit way (punishment and reward magnitudes) as functions of α and p, and 9 (reward is enabled).  
   • The remaining parameters (2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 10, 12, 13, 14, and 15) are not addressed.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The authors do examine p (the “incentive strength”) and α (fraction of the incentive budget allocated to reward vs. punishment), which jointly determine how much individuals are punished or rewarded. However, they do not label this “the punishment treatment effect,” nor do they provide numerical effect sizes for changes in “efficiency.” Instead, they describe how varying p and α affects the stability of (I,T,U) mixtures. No other parameter is systematically varied for the explicit purpose of describing a “punishment treatment effect,” and no direct discussion of efficiency is provided.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper provides no direct discussions or measurements of efficiency. Its main results concern which strategy mixtures become stable. Thus, there is insufficient information in the text to predict changes in “group efficiency” or “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” for any of the 15 parameters in a quantitative sense. The best the paper offers is that larger “incentive strength” p and a higher “reward coefficient” α lead to a larger basin of attraction for states featuring trust and trustworthiness—suggesting that, if efficiency were measured, it might increase in those cases. Apart from that, the paper has insufficient details to draw further efficiency‐based conclusions.
reference_APA: Fang, Xing & Chen, Xiaojie (2021). Evolutionary dynamics of trust in the N-player trust game with individual reward and punishment. EUROPEAN PHYSICAL JOURNAL B.

Below, each of the 15 parameters is treated in turn.  For every parameter I indicate  

(1) Whether it is described in the paper and, if so, its implemented value(s);  
(2) Whether the paper reports or predicts what would happen to the *punishment treatment effect* if that parameter were **systematically varied**.  All numerical information is taken directly from the text, the two figures, or Tables 1–2.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER SCAN
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Number of players  
   (1) Yes.  Groups consist of 4 players (1 designated punisher “D” + 3 non-punishers).  
   (2) No systematic variation; no prediction.

2.  Number of rounds  
   (1) Yes. 30 rounds in both studies.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

3.  Chat enabled?  
   (1) Mentioned only implicitly (“participants were shown a blank screen asking them to wait”).  No chat allowed.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

4.  All-or-nothing contributions?  
   (1) No. Subjects freely allocate 0–20 tokens.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

5.  Contribution *default* (endowment first in public fund)?  
   (1) Not mentioned. All tokens start in private hands.  
   (2) No discussion; no prediction.

6.  MPCR / multiplication factor  
   (1) Yes. MPCR = 0.5 (equivalent to group multiplication factor of 2).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

7.  Punishment *cost* per unit  
   (1) Yes. Costless to the punisher (“Each token could be used … Unused tokens were not added to the payoff of D”).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

8.  Punishment *magnitude* per unit  
   (1) Yes. One token deducted from target for each punishment token used.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

9.  Reward enabled?  
   (1) No; there is no reward option.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

10. Reward cost  
   (1) N/A (reward absent).  
   (2) N/A.

11. Reward magnitude  
   (1) N/A (reward absent).  
   (2) N/A.

12. Round horizon known?  
   (1) Subjects are told the game has 30 rounds (instructions mention “each session consisted of thirty rounds”).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
   (1) Yes, and *this* parameter is varied across the two studies.  
         • Study 1: Only the punisher sees everyone’s contributions; the three non-punishers see only their own information (low-information condition).  
         • Study 2: Contributions of every player are public knowledge (full-information condition).  
   (2) Effect of variation: The authors report almost identical results for both conditions—punishers still contribute less and enforce higher norms.  However, they do **not** compute any “punishment minus no-punishment” treatment effect (there is no baseline without punishment), so no quantitative change in *efficiency* (or any other treatment effect) is given.  The only statement is qualitative: “The findings of Study One are qualitatively replicated in a full information setting.”

14. Victim knows who punished them?  
   (1) Yes.  The punisher is a fixed, publicly known role (“referred to as ‘D’ ”).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

15. Victim knows who rewarded them?  
   (1) N/A (reward absent).  
   (2) N/A.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables actually analysed  
   • Mean individual contribution to the public account  
   • Imposed contribution norm (maximum contribution punished)  
   • Difference between punisher and non-punisher contributions over time  
The paper never computes group efficiency (total or average payoff divided by the cooperative optimum).  Therefore “efficiency” is **not** used as a dependent variable, and the reported variables are conceptually different.

B.  How many of the 15 parameters are *mentioned*?  
   8 out of 15: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14 are explicitly or implicitly stated; parameters 5, 9–11, 15 are absent.

C.  For how many parameters is their *systematic variation* analysed with respect to the punishment treatment effect on any dependent variable?  
   Only 1 parameter (Parameter 13: peer-outcome visibility) is varied.  The paper reports that making contributions public versus private leaves the qualitative pattern unchanged.  No numerical treatment-effect size on efficiency (or on any “punishment vs. no-punishment” comparison) is provided.

D.  Predictive value for the 15 parameters with respect to the punishment treatment effect on efficiency  
   The paper gives virtually no leverage.  Because there is no “no-punishment” control, no efficiency measure, and only one parameter is varied qualitatively, one can make *almost no data-driven prediction* about how any of the 15 parameters—or their interactions—would alter the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.  The sole hint is that revealing everyone’s contributions (Parameter 13) seems *not* to change the basic behavioural pattern generated by costless, designated punishment, so one might very tentatively predict little or no effect of that parameter on efficiency.  For all other parameters, the paper is silent.

In short, the study documents that costless, designated punishment sustains high group contributions while simultaneously allowing punishers to free-ride, but it does not provide treatment-effect estimates on efficiency nor systematic parameter sweeps that would allow further prediction.
reference_APA: Hoeft, Leonard & Mill, Wladislaw (2017). An experimental investigation of designated punishment behavior in public goods. ECONOMICS LETTERS.

Below, each of the 15 parameters is treated in turn.  For every parameter I first state what the paper actually implements (if anything), and then whether the authors vary that parameter and, if so, what happens to the “punishment-treatment effect”.  Where the paper reports numbers I quote them exactly from the relevant table or figure.

(Throughout I use the paper’s own dependent variables: contribution rate, received‐punishment points and net profits.  The paper never reports the formal “efficiency” ratio, although net profits are mechanically bounded above by 75 points per player.)

PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1. Number of players  
• Implemented: 5 players per group (p. 8).  
• Systematically varied? No.  No results on how changing the group size would influence the treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
• Implemented: 20 (p. 8).  
• Systematically varied? No.  No predictions about a different horizon.

3. Chat enabled?  
• Implemented: No chat is ever mentioned or allowed.  
• Systematically varied? No.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule?  
• Implemented: Yes.  Subjects choose between contributing their entire 50-point endowment or keeping all 50 points (p. 8).  
• Systematically varied? No.

5. Contribution default (opt-out framing)?  
• Not used.  No default manipulation; subjects actively choose.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
• Implemented: Each contributed 50 points yields 5 × 15 = 75 total; hence MPCR = 0.3 (p. 8).  
• Systematically varied? No.

7. Cost to impose one unit of punishment  
• Implemented: 5 points to the punisher in every treatment (p. 9).  
• Systematically varied? No.

8. Punishment magnitude per “unit”  
• Implemented:  
  – Individual punishment: 15 points deducted from the target.  
  – Democratic / Dictator punishment: when punishment is implemented the target loses 60 (15 × 4) points (p. 9).  
• Systematically varied? Indirectly, yes: magnitude differs across the three punishment institutions.  
• Effect on net profits (“efficiency” proxy):  
  No-noise condition (Table 1):  
  – Individual (15-point hits): 53.72  
  – Democratic (60-point hits, but majority filter): 65.18  
  – Dictator (60-point hits, no filter): 49.61  
  Hence a larger potential magnitude raises efficiency only when combined with the majority-vote filter; it lowers (or does not raise) efficiency under a dictator.  The paper does not isolate “magnitude” per se, so no ceteris-paribus estimate is possible.

9. Presence of a reward option  
10. Cost of one reward unit  
11. Reward magnitude  
• Rewards are never available; none of these parameters appear.

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
• Implemented: Yes – they are told upfront that there are 20 rounds.  
• Systematically varied? No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown / observability accuracy?  
• Implemented and varied: Two information environments.  
  – “No Noise”: contributions are displayed truthfully.  
  – “Noise”: each contribution is mis-reported as “no contribution” with 10 % probability (p. 8).  
• Effect sizes on net profits (Table 1):  
  Individual punishment: 53.72 → 50.92 (Δ = –2.80)  
  Democratic punishment: 65.18 → 57.97 (Δ = –7.21)  
  Dictator punishment: 49.61 → 45.93 (Δ = –3.68)  
  Regression model 6 (Table 3) confirms the drop is statistically significant only for Democratic punishment (Noise × DemPun, p = 0.002).

14. Does the punished player learn who punished?  
• Implemented: Yes.  Group members have fixed IDs and are told “about the punishments and votes in their group” (p. 9).  
• Systematically varied? No.

15. Does the rewarded player learn who rewarded?  
• Not applicable (no rewards).

-------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used  
The paper analyses (i) probability of contribution, (ii) punishment points received, and (iii) net profits (average payoff per round).  “Efficiency” (total payoff ÷ social optimum) is never reported, although net profits are bounded above by the efficient level of 75 points.

B. Coverage of the 15 parameters  
Nine parameters are explicitly mentioned: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14.  Six parameters (5, 9–11, 15) never appear.

C. Parameters whose *systematic* variation is analysed for their effect on the punishment treatment effect  
Exactly two:  
• Parameter 8 (punishment magnitude) – varied indirectly via the comparison of Individual vs Democratic vs Dictator punishment.  
• Parameter 13 (observability accuracy) – varied directly (perfect vs 10 % noise).  
All other parameters are fixed; no causal statements about changing them are made.

D. What can we predict – solely from this paper – about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency?  
• Lower observability accuracy (Parameter 13) reliably reduces efficiency when punishment is available, and the drop is especially large under majority-vote punishment.  
• A high punishment magnitude (Parameter 8) can either improve or harm efficiency, depending on the institutional filter that accompanies it: majority voting + high magnitude delivered the best pay-offs; a dictator + the same high magnitude did not.  
• For every other parameter the paper provides no evidence, so no prediction anchored in this paper can be made.
reference_APA: Ambrus, Attila & Greiner, Ben (2019). Individual, Dictator, and Democratic punishment in public good games with perfect and imperfect observability. JOURNAL OF PUBLIC ECONOMICS.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter accounting of what the paper by Jeffrey R. Vincent (“Spatial dynamics, social norms, and the opportunity of the commons”) does and does not say with respect to the 15 parameters and the question of how varying them would affect the “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency in a public goods game. Throughout, “the paper” refers solely to Vincent’s article, as quoted in full in the prompt.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     No. The paper never specifies any number of players in a controlled or experimental game.  
   • Does the paper predict how varying it might affect punishment or any dependent variable?  
     No. It does not mention or systematically vary “number of players.”

2. Number of rounds
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     No. The paper does not mention repeated rounds or any specifics about repeated interactions in a game-theoretic experiment setting.  
   • Does the paper predict an effect of varying the number of rounds?  
     No. It provides no predictions on this parameter.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     No. The paper does not reference communication technologies, chat, or cheap talk in a public goods experiment.  
   • Does the paper predict an effect of enabling chat?  
     No. The paper does not mention this at all.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     No. The paper does not reference forced contributions or binary contribution choices in a public goods context.  
   • Does the paper predict any effect of making contributions all or nothing?  
     No. It provides no such discussion.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much to move from a public fund back to their hand)?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     No. The entire notion of “default” or “conditional” contributions is not mentioned.  
   • Does the paper predict an effect of systematically varying this parameter on punishment treatment?  
     No. There is no mention.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     No. While it reviews “multiplying” effects in fisheries or resource growth (e.g., fish population dynamics), it does not present anything resembling a marginal per capita return in a public goods game.  
   • Does the paper predict an effect of systematically varying the MPCR on punishment treatment?  
     No. It does not address this in a game-theoretic or experimental sense.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     The paper does discuss punishments and sanctions in a high-level sense (e.g., “Sanctions were geared to the seriousness of the violations,” references to fines, “economic incentives,” “prices,” “detectives,” and “patrols”). However, it does not provide a formal or numerical “cost” per unit punishment, as would be typical in a public goods experiment.  
   • Does the paper predict how systematically varying the cost-to-punish affects punishment treatment for efficiency or any other variable?  
     No. It mentions punishments exist but does not quantify or predict the effect of changing punishment cost.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     It discusses real-world systems of fines and sanctions (e.g., “small fines to expulsion” in historical Japanese forest management). It does not, however, present a controlled or systematically varied “punishment magnitude.”  
   • Does the paper predict any effect of systematically varying punishment magnitude?  
     No. It references the importance of sanctions in real-life cooperative outcomes but does not quantify or systematically vary “magnitude.”

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     Very briefly. The abstract and discussion mention that “Successful examples of resource management systems back up norms with economic incentives: rewards for good behavior and punishments for bad.” The paper thus acknowledges that both punishments and rewards can be used.  
   • Does the paper predict the effect of systematically enabling or disabling a reward mechanism on punishment or on efficiency?  
     No. The paper states that rewards can matter but does not present any experimental or formal variation or effect size.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
      No. The paper never addresses how costly it might be to reward, nor any systematic variation.  
    • Does the paper predict the effect of systematically varying the cost of rewards on punishment or efficiency?  
      No. It does not mention such an analysis.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted)
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
      No. Beyond general comments that rewards can exist, there is no mention of “reward magnitude.”  
    • Does the paper predict how systematically varying reward magnitude affects punishment or efficiency?  
      No. No details or predictions on this parameter.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
      No. The paper’s discussions of repeated interactions are general (e.g., real-world fishers interacting repeatedly) but not in the style of controlled game parameters.  
    • Does the paper predict an effect of whether the end is known or unknown?  
      No. It never addresses this point.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much each other gained or lost)?
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
      No. The paper does not address the question of whether participants in a game (or a resource management setting) see each other’s exact payoffs or outcomes.  
    • Does the paper predict an effect of systematically varying whether outcomes are displayed?
      No. It does not discuss this.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
      No. Although the paper mentions that real-world sanctions exist, it does not specify whether the punished party learns who punished them in any formal sense.  
    • Does the paper predict an effect of systematically varying this attribution of punishment?
      No. It is not mentioned.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Does the paper discuss this parameter?
      No. As with the previous question on punishment, the paper does not explore whether knowledge of the rewarder is provided.  
    • Does the paper predict any effect when participants know who rewarded them versus anonymous rewarding?
      No. It does not discuss this point.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?

• The paper frequently discusses overall “win-win opportunities,” “long-run profits,” “economic outcomes,” and “resource stock levels” in real-world commons management. However, it does not present these as experimentally measured dependent variables in a lab-style public goods game.  
• It speaks of a “tragedy of the commons,” fish catches, and forest outcomes in real ecosystems. 8. Punishment magnitude (loss to target per unit)  
   (1) Only referred to abstractly (“hurt more” vs. “hurt less”). Never quantified.  
   (2) No prediction.

9. Reward enabled?  
   (1) Rewards are mentioned once (trustees “send back money” ‑ a reward), but not within a public-goods-with-punishment paradigm.  
   (2) No prediction about adding rewards to a punishment treatment.

10. Reward cost  
    (1) Not mentioned.  
    (2) No prediction.

11. Reward magnitude  
    (1) Not mentioned.  
    (2) No prediction.

12. End-round information (known horizon)  
    (1) Known vs. unknown horizon is not treated.  
    (2) No prediction.

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
    (1) Cited Fehr & Fischbacher (2003) ultimatum study where proposers could *observe* responders’ past accepts/rejects. This is observation of *behaviour* rather than “peer outcomes” in a public-goods sense.  
    (2) No statement on how visibility of others’ pay-offs affects punishment’s efficiency impact.

14. Punishee knows punisher identity?  
    (1) The importance of being able to “recognise commitment to punishment” is stressed, but no design where identity revelation is systematically manipulated.  
    (2) No prediction.

15. Rewardee knows rewarder identity?  
    (1) Not discussed.  
    (2) No prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables actually used  
   • The paper is theoretical. It talks about fitness, individual pay-offs, rejection rates, cooperation rates, trust sent/returned, and presence of punishment.  
   • “Group efficiency” (total or average pay-off divided by the maximum) is *not* used as an outcome variable in any figure or table.  
   • Thus, efficiency is *conceptually* mentioned (e.g., punishment can “sustain cooperation” and thereby *could* raise joint fitness), but it is never measured.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even *mentioned*?  
   5 of 15 appear at least in passing:  
   – #1 number of players (binary vs. n player)  
   – #2 number of rounds (one-shot vs. repeated)  
   – #7 punishment cost (qualitatively)  
   – #8 punishment magnitude (qualitatively)  
   – #13 some form of outcome/behaviour visibility

C. For how many parameters does the paper *systematically vary* them and link them to a punishment-treatment effect?  
   Zero. 0/15.  No tables, no figures, and no numerical effect sizes are provided for any systematic variation.

D. What predictions about the 15 parameters—restricted strictly to what can be inferred from the paper—can be made about their impact on the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency?

   • Because the paper never reports efficiency outcomes under different parameter settings, only very broad qualitative conjectures can be extracted:
     – Punishment *could* raise efficiency if commitment to punish is recognisable and if opportunists respond by cooperating; if recognition is impossible, costly punishment may lower efficiency.  
     – Higher punishment cost (#7) or lower punishment magnitude (#8) would, by simple arithmetic, make it harder for punishment to be individually advantageous; thus efficiency gains would be less likely.  
     – The paper hints that repeated interaction (#2) or opportunities for partner choice (not among the 15 parameters) facilitate the positive effect of punishment, but no gradients or numbers are supplied.

   Beyond these loose statements, the paper provides insufficient detail to generate quantitative or even ordinal predictions about how any of the 15 parameters—or their interactions—shape the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.

In short, the article is a conceptual/theoretical essay on commitment; it does not experimentally or computationally manipulate the 15 design parameters, nor does it measure efficiency, so it offers almost no direct leverage for forecasting punishment treatment effects on efficiency as a function of those parameters.

Article Title: The source of punishment matters: Third-party punishment restrains observers from selfish behaviors better than does second-party punishment by shaping norm perceptions
Keywords Plus: COOPERATION; GAME
Abstract: Punishment aims to deter individuals' selfish behaviors, but it can occasionally backfire. Some scholars have proposed promoting prosocial behaviors using punishment that communicates positive social norms because it provides additional motivation. However, it is unclear which factors affect the norm expressive function of punishment. This study proposes that third-party punishment communicates more positive normative information, and thus, promotes more prosocial behavior in observers than does second-party punishment. Using dictator games, we investigated the effects of second-party punishment compared to third-party punishment of another's unfair sharing on observers' norm perceptions and subsequent sharing decision-making. Two experiments consistently found that third-party punishment was more effective than second-party punishment at inducing observers' beliefs that unfair distribution was unusual (descriptive norm) and unacceptable (injunctive norm). The altered descriptive but not injunctive norm perception further guided individuals' own sharing behaviors. Taken together, these results suggest that third-party punishment might be better than second-party punishment at decreasing selfish behaviors by shaping individuals' norm perceptions, especially descriptive norm perception, regarding the relevant behaviors.
