Below is a parameter-by-parameter analysis based solely on the content of the Chen et al. (2020) paper. For each parameter, I note whether (1) the paper discusses it (and how), and (2) whether the paper makes predictions about the effect of systematically varying that parameter on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable, including efficiency). Numerical effect sizes are included only when the paper specifically reports or implies them.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
 • Discussion in paper?  
   The paper uses a dictator game with either two players (dictator and recipient) or three players (dictator, recipient, and third-party punisher). However, the authors do not systematically vary the number of players (e.g., testing 2 vs. 3 vs. 4). Rather, they compare second-party punishment (SPP, which implicitly has two players: the offender and offended) versus third-party punishment (TPP, which brings in a third party).  
 • Predictions from systematic variation?  
   No. The paper does not discuss how changing the total number of players would affect punishment outcomes.

2. Number of rounds
 • Discussion in paper?  
   All experiments are one-shot (single-round) dictator games. The paper does not mention multiple rounds or whether participants would know or not know the number of rounds.  
 • Predictions from systematic variation?  
   No. The paper does not discuss the impact of varying the number of rounds.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
 • Discussion in paper?  
   The paper does not use or mention any “chat” in the sense of open communication. They only describe recipients’ or third parties’ “messages”/“feedback,” but do not systematically manipulate open discussion.  
 • Predictions from systematic variation?  
   No. The paper does not address enabling or disabling a free-form chat.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
 • Discussion in paper?  
   The paper describes a dictator game with multiple possible transfer amounts (e.g., 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 points in Experiment 1), not an all-or-nothing format.  
 • Predictions from systematic variation?  
   No. The paper does not discuss an all-or-nothing contribution rule or how that might influence punishment.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much of their endowment to move from the public fund back to their hand)?
 • Discussion in paper?  
   Not relevant; this is not a public goods design. The paper uses a standard dictator game in which the dictator chooses how many points (or lottery tickets) to transfer, rather than moving money in or out of a fund.  
 • Predictions from systematic variation?  
   No. Not mentioned in the paper.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factors
 • Discussion in paper?  
   Not used. This is a one-shot dictator game, so MPCR is irrelevant.  
 • Predictions from systematic variation?  
   No. Not mentioned.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
 • Discussion in paper?  
   Experiment 2 describes that in second-party punishment (SPP), the recipient can pay 1 coin to reduce the dictator’s payoff by 3 coins. In third-party punishment (TPP), a similar cost structure is noted; that third parties can intervene at some personal cost. However, the paper uses a fixed cost in each scenario and does not systematically vary cost levels.  
 • Predictions from systematic variation?  
   No. The paper does not discuss how changing the punishment cost would affect outcomes; it simply holds the cost fixed in the second experiment.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
 • Discussion in paper?  
   Again, in Experiment 2, the dictator loses 3 coins when the punisher (recipient or third party) intervenes. This magnitude is fixed.  
 • Predictions from systematic variation?  
   No. There is no mention of systematically varying or testing different magnitudes.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
 • Discussion in paper?  
   The study focuses entirely on punishment (verbal or monetary). Rewards are not examined.  
 • Predictions from systematic variation?  
   No. Not mentioned at all.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
 • Discussion in paper?  
   Not used. The paper does not include any reward mechanism.  
 • Predictions from systematic variation?  
   No. Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)
 • Discussion in paper?  
   Not used. The paper does not include any reward mechanism.  
 • Predictions from systematic variation?  
   No. Not discussed.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
 • Discussion in paper?  
   The paper describes one-shot games; presumably, participants know it is only one round, but there is no explicit manipulation or discussion of “knowing vs. not knowing.”  
 • Predictions from systematic variation?  
   No. Not mentioned.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?
 • Discussion in paper?  
   The paper does not systematically manipulate the display of others’ outcomes. Participants do see that the dictator “unfairly” divided the amount, but that is part of the scenario. No mention of systematically varying the display of peers’ payoffs.  
 • Predictions from systematic variation?  
   No. Not discussed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
 • Discussion in paper?  
   The text states that in both experiments, players remain anonymous. However, participants are told in the manipulation that either the injured party (SPP) or a third party (TPP) delivered punishment. There is no separate systematic variation of punisher anonymity or identifiability beyond “second-party” vs. “third-party.”  
 • Predictions from systematic variation?  
   No. The paper does not mention systematically altering punisher identification.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
 • Discussion in paper?  
   The paper does not involve any reward mechanism.  
 • Predictions from systematic variation?  
   No. Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A: Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
 • The paper does not report or analyze group efficiency or total/average payoff.  
 • Instead, the paper examines (1) norm perceptions (descriptive and injunctive norms) and (2) individual sharing behavior (how many points or lottery tickets the dictator allocates). These are distinct from efficiency, as they measure beliefs and individual prosocial tendencies, not the ratio of actual total payoff to maximum payoff.

B: Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
 • Mentioned in some form:  
   – Parameter 1 (# players): The game uses 2 or 3 players, but not systematically varied beyond the second- vs. third-party punishment distinction.  
   – Parameter 7 (punishment cost) and Parameter 8 (punishment magnitude): Both are set to particular fixed values in Experiment 2, but not explored across multiple levels.  
 • The other parameters are not discussed or mentioned substantively.

C: For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
 • The paper does not systematically vary any of the parameters above.  
 • Consequently, there is no discussion of the effect of systematically varying any of the 15 parameters on punishment outcomes (whether for efficiency or any other measure).

D: If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
 • The paper does not address efficiency at all (nor do the authors discuss how systematically changing game structure, stakes, or information affects any efficiency-related outcome). Therefore, there is insufficient information to predict how the 15 parameters or their interactions might influence a punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency. The experiments focus on how third-party versus second-party punishment affects norm perceptions and individual sharing. Thus, no clear predictions can be made regarding those 15 parameters’ influence on “efficiency.”

Abstract: This paper reports results of an experiment designed to investigate the nature of cooperation and punishment. Subjects are matched in a series of two-person, two-stage games with a sequential equilibrium that supports first-stage cooperation with a credible threat of subsequent punishment. Below is a point‐by‐point examination of how (if at all) the paper discusses and/or systematically varies each of the 15 parameters that you listed, followed by the required summary (A–D).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Does the paper discuss it? Yes. All sessions involve exactly two players (a “row” player and a “column” player).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it, or predict the effect of varying it? No. The experiment always uses two‐person matchups and does not vary the number of players.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Does the paper discuss it? Yes. Each session has 20 two‐stage games (so “20 rounds” in the sense of 20 repeated plays, each of which has two sequential decisions).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it, or predict the effect of varying it? No. Although the paper describes that there are four five‐game “sequences,” it does not manipulate the total number of rounds as a treatment.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Does the paper discuss it? No. There is no mention of communication or chat between participants.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it, or predict the effect of varying it? No. Not mentioned at all.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Does the paper discuss it? No. The paper focuses on choices (R1/R2, C1/C2, etc.) in a matrix game, not on a partial‐versus‐all‐or‐nothing contribution mechanism.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it, or predict the effect if it were varied? No. Not mentioned.

5. Is the contribution default (do players move money out of a public fund by default)?  
   • Does the paper discuss it? No. The experiment uses a matrix payoff structure rather than a “default contribution” setup.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it, or predict the effect if it were varied? No. Not mentioned.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Does the paper discuss it? No. The study is framed as a two‐stage game with specified payoff matrices, not as a public‐goods MPCR setup.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it, or predict the effect if it were varied? No. Not mentioned.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Does the paper discuss it? The experiment does refer to “punishment” choices (e.g., R4) and shows different payoffs, so there is an implicit “cost” to the punisher in some payoffs. However, the paper never labels or measures this explicitly as a “punishment cost.”  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it, or predict the effect of varying it? No. Different payoff designs (“U,” “D,” “N,” and “F”) do alter second‐stage payoffs, but they do not single out “punishment cost” as a systematically varied parameter.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted when punishing)  
   • Does the paper discuss it? The second‐stage payoff matrix does allow “R” to reduce “C”’s payoff (and vice versa), and some treatments differ (nickel vs. dime designs, or whether the punishment outcome is Pareto dominated). But the paper does not label this difference as “punishment magnitude” per se.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it, or predict the effect of systematically varying it? No. While the “U,” “D,” and “N” designs do result in different payoff outcomes when punishment is chosen, the authors do not provide formal predictions for how changing only the size of the punishment would affect outcomes, nor do they provide numeric effect sizes on efficiency.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Does the paper discuss it? Yes. The second‐stage matrix always includes a “reward” option (e.g., choosing R3/C4 after cooperation). The paper labels some outcomes “reward” or “punish.”  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it, or predict the effect of enabling/disabling reward? No. All main treatments (except for the “flat” stage) allow reward and punishment. The paper does not treat “reward on” vs. “reward off” as a separate factor.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Does the paper discuss it? Not explicitly. As in punishment, the matrix payoff changes if one chooses a more “rewarding” action (e.g., R3 instead of R4), but there is no designated “cost to reward” described in the study.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it, or predict the effect of varying it? No. Not mentioned.

11. Reward magnitude (how many coins are awarded)  
   • Does the paper discuss it? Only in the sense that R3/C4 might yield a higher payoff to the other player, but there is no direct label “reward magnitude.”  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it, or predict the effect of varying it? No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
   • Does the paper discuss it? Yes, participants are instructed they will play 20 two‐stage games. However, there is no mention of unknown or surprise endings.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it, or predict the effect of varying it? No. They do not manipulate known vs. unknown horizon.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see each other’s payoffs)?  
   • Does the paper discuss it? Participants do see each other’s choices (R1 or R2, etc.) and payoffs after each two‐stage game. But it is simply part of the design.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it, or predict the effect of varying it? No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know the specific punisher?  
   • Does the paper discuss it? The design is a two‐person game with anonymous IDs, but each player sees the other’s action (R3 vs. R4, etc.). There is no separate mention of “identifying the punisher” because each match is just two people.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it, or predict the effect of varying it? No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Does the paper discuss it? Same as above: it is inherently known, since there are only two players, but not discussed as a separate design feature.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it, or predict the effect of varying it? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper does not use “group efficiency” (actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff) as its focal dependent variable. Instead, it measures:  
     – The incidence (frequency) of first‐stage “cooperation” (R1 or C1).  
     – Second‐stage “punish” (R4 if the other defected) and “reward” (R3 if the other cooperated) propensities.  
   • Although the paper reports numerical payoffs in tables, it does not frame them in terms of an “efficiency” ratio.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
     (1) Number of players (always 2),  
     (2) Number of rounds (20 games),  
     (9) Whether a reward is enabled (always possible except in the “flat” second stage, but not systematically varied).  
   • The rest are either not discussed at all or simply part of a fixed design choice (e.g., participants do see others’ choices, but that is not systematically manipulated).

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for any dependent variable when each is systematically varied?  
   • None. Although the study varies certain second‐stage payoff structures (“U,” “D,” “N,” and “F”) and compares how frequently subjects punish/reward or cooperate, it never frames these manipulations as “systematically varying punishment cost” or “reward magnitude,” etc. Nor does it measure an explicit “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”  
   • Thus, there is no direct numerical effect size reported for how any of the 15 parameters would influence a punishment treatment effect.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely on the paper’s content, what would they be?  
   • The paper’s data do not enable specific predictions about group efficiency. Its focus is on cooperation rates and second‐stage punish/reward behavior.  
   • No parametric manipulations of chat, group size, MPCR, or the visibility of punishers/rewarders appear. The authors do not quantify how changes in, for example, “punishment magnitude” alone affect total payoffs.  
   • Consequently, little to no prediction about how those 15 parameters (and their interactions) would affect efficiency can be made strictly from this paper.

Article Title: Retaliation and the role for punishment in the evolution of cooperation

Abstract: Models of evolutionary game theory have shown that punishment may be an adaptive behaviour in environments characterised by a social-dilemma situation. Experimental evidence closely corresponds to this finding but questions the cooperation-enhancing effect of punishment if players are allowed to retaliate against their punishers. Below each of the 15 design parameters we state  

(i) whether it is mentioned in Wolff (2012) and, if so, the (fixed) value(s) that are used in the baseline model or in simulations;  
(ii) whether the paper *systematically* varies that parameter and gives a prediction about how the *presence of punishment* (the “punishment treatment”) changes some dependent variable when the parameter is moved.  
Whenever a closed-form threshold or inequality is derived we reproduce it, because that is the only numeric information the paper contains.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
(i) Yes.  The main model fixes N = 3 (p. 4, Sec. 2.2). A large-N variant is only sketched in Appendix B; no numbers are reported.  
(ii) Not varied.  No prediction about how changing N would alter the effect of punishment on any outcome.

2. Number of rounds  
(i) The game is *infinitely repeated* with continuation probability π (Sec. 2).  
(ii) Yes.  π is systematically changed in the analytical results and in Figs. 1 & 3.  
     • Punishment is *stable* only when  
       π < π_max = (2p + 2k – c)/(2p + 2k)     (Prop. 1).  
       Once π exceeds that value, retaliation spreads and the “punishment treatment effect” on cooperation/payoffs (and hence efficiency) collapses.  
     • When π is high *and* mutations occur, punishment can still *raise* cooperation in the mixed equilibrium, but only modestly (Result 1; Fig. 3). No explicit efficiency number is reported.

3. Chat between players  
(i) Not mentioned.  
(ii) No predictions.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
(i) Yes.  Contributions are binary (cooperate or defect) (Sec. 2).  
(ii) Not varied; no predictions.

5. Contribution default / “take” frame  
(i) Not discussed.  
(ii) No predictions.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor (b and c)  
(i) Yes.  A co-operator pays c and creates total benefit b (equivalently MPCR = b/(N–1)c when N = 3). Baseline simulations use c = 1, b = 4 (Figs. 1-3).  
(ii) Varied analytically:  
     • Conditional co-operators can invade defectors only if b and π satisfy  
       b² – 4c(b–c)/π > 0   (Eq. 3).  
     • Full-cooperation equilibria with punishment exist only if b ≤ 2c/π when π is at its upper stability bound (Prop. 2).  
     Higher b therefore weakens the *need* for punishment and shrinks the predicted incremental efficiency gain from introducing it.

7. Punishment cost to punisher (k)  
(i) Yes.  Baseline k = ½.  
(ii) Varied in all analytical thresholds:  
     • Punishers can invade defectors iff           c + 2k < π(b – c)/(1 – π)  (Eq. 4).  
     • π_max above falls with k; raising k makes punishment cease to help.  
     • A c ≥ 2k/3 condition (Prop. 4) guarantees parameter regions in which punishment is *necessary* (though not permanently present) to reach the partially cooperative equilibrium.  
     Therefore larger k lowers or reverses the punishment treatment effect on cooperation/payoffs.

8. Punishment magnitude p  
(i) Yes.  Baseline p = 3⁄2 or 6⁄7 in different figures.  
(ii) Systematically appears in all key inequalities:  
     • Full cooperation with punishment requires          c < 2p  (Prop. 2).  
     • π_max = (2p + 2k – c)/(2p + 2k) increases in p, so stronger sanctions enlarge the π-region where punishment still works.  
     Hence increasing p strengthens, and decreasing p weakens, the predicted efficiency gain from punishment.

9. Reward enabled  
(i) Not discussed.  
(ii) No predictions.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
(i,ii) Not discussed; no predictions.

12. Do players know the final round?  
(i) Not directly addressed.  The model assumes an indefinite horizon with common knowledge of continuation probability.  
(ii) Not varied; no predictions.

13. Visibility of peer outcomes  
14. Identification of punisher  
15. Identification of rewarder  
(i) None of these information-display parameters are mentioned.  
(ii) No predictions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables – does the paper use *efficiency*?  
• The paper’s outcomes are (i) evolutionary stability of strategies, (ii) cooperation (contribution) rates, (iii) stationary type frequencies, and (iv) expected *payoff* of each type.  
• ‘Efficiency’—total group payoff divided by the first-best payoff—is never explicitly calculated. Payoff is discussed only at the level of individual strategy types, not the group as a whole. Thus “efficiency” in the sense requested is absent.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
6 of them: 1 (N), 2 (rounds/π), 4 (binary contribution), 6 (MPCR via b and c), 7 (k), 8 (p).

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* the parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
4 parameters: π (parameter 2), MPCR / b and c (parameter 6), punishment cost k (parameter 7), and punishment magnitude p (parameter 8).  
No quantitative efficiency effects are given; only threshold conditions and qualitative statements about whether punishment can stabilise cooperation.

D. Predicting the punishment-treatment effect on *efficiency* from the paper alone  
• Efficiency will increase relative to a no-punishment baseline only when all four conditions hold simultaneously:  
   (i) π < (2p + 2k – c)/(2p + 2k) (punishers are not wiped out by retaliation);  
   (ii) c < 2p (punishment hurts more than contributing);  
   (iii) c + 2k < π(b – c)/(1 – π) (punishers can spread in a defecting population);  
   (iv) The benefit parameter b is not so large that conditional co-operators could achieve high cooperation unaided.  
• Raising p or lowering k or c makes these inequalities easier to satisfy and therefore should enlarge the positive efficiency effect of adding punishment; doing the reverse should shrink or erase it.  
• Increasing π helps conditional co-operators directly but eventually eliminates the need (and the stability) of punishment; hence the marginal efficiency gain from punishment is inverted-U shaped in π.  
• The paper gives no leverage for predicting interactions with any of the remaining nine parameters, nor any numeric magnitude of the efficiency change.

In short, the paper lets us predict only *qualitative* directions (or threshold crossings) for four of the fifteen design variables; for the other eleven variables it provides no information at all about how they would influence the effect of introducing punishment on group efficiency.

Abstract: Settlers flocking to boomtowns on the American western frontier were faced with the same task that communities in weak states across the globe face in contemporary times: self-governance. Peer sanctions can enforce cooperation in these environments, but their efficacy depends on the social networks that transmit information from peer to peer. The author uses a game-theoretic model to show that peripheral network positions can generate such strong incentives to misbehave that persistent cheating occurs in equilibrium. The model reveals that groups maintaining high levels of cooperation that face shocks to their strategic environment or to their network can ratchet down into less cooperative equilibria in which the most peripheral become ostracized. Below is a point‐by‐point inventory of whether and how each of the fifteen parameters you listed appears in (or is systematically varied by) the Jennifer M. Larson (2017) article “Why the West Became Wild: Informal Governance with Incomplete Networks.” As you will see, the paper is not actually about a standard public‐goods game with a separate “punishment treatment condition,” nor does it provide direct measures of efficiency. Instead, it studies a repeated prisoner’s dilemma in an indefinitely long horizon, where “punishment” is embedded in a peer‐sanctioning (gossip) mechanism. Consequently, almost none of your specific 15 parameters are discussed or varied in the way one typically sees in a lab‐based public‐goods‐with‐punishment experiment.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter (and, if so, what values are used)?  
     – Yes. The paper denotes the number of players by n and considers “society” to be a finite set N = {1, …, n}. It also discusses how population size can grow or shrink (section “Shocks Due to Population Change”).  
   • Does the paper make predictions about the effect of systematically varying the number of players on a “punishment treatment effect” (for any dependent variable)?  
     – The paper does not compare a “punishment” versus “no‐punishment” treatment, so it never reports a “punishment treatment effect.” It does, however, discuss how larger or smaller population sizes might strain or facilitate informal enforcement of cooperation. No numerical effect sizes for “efficiency” (or for a punishment‐treatment contrast) are given.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Discussed?  
     – The paper models an infinite‐horizon repeated game. It does not consider a finite number of rounds, nor does it examine or vary whether participants know when the game ends.  
   • Predictions about varying it?  
     – No. There is no systematic variation of the number of rounds.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The paper does not discuss any form of “chat.” Gossip is modeled as a mechanical, exogenous transmission of “negative judgments” through a social network, but not as a freely enabled “chat” among players.  
   • Predictions about varying it?  
     – No. There is no variation of “chat” in the paper.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The paper studies a repeated prisoner’s dilemma in which the action set is simply cooperate (c) or defect (d). The notion of a continuous or “all‐or‐nothing” contribution does not appear.  
   • Predictions about varying it?  
     – No.

5. Is the contribution default? (That is, do players decide how much of their endowment to move from the public fund back into their hand?)  
   • Discussed?

     – No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
   • Discussed?  
     – Not in public‐goods‐game terms. The paper uses payoffs (1 for mutual cooperation, 0 for mutual defection, −β and α otherwise) and does not refer to any MPCR or multiplication factor.

   • Discussed?

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Discussed?

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained or lost each round)?  
   • Discussed?  
     – The model has private pairwise observations, plus the spread of “negative judgments” via the network. There is no mention of displaying payoffs or showing outcomes systematically.

     – No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Discussed?  
     – Not in these terms. The paper does not examine the identity of the punisher. It assumes punishment is recognized (if the defector meets someone who heard the gossip), but does not study the effect of the target’s knowing who dealt the punishment.  
   • Predictions about varying it?  
     – No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. Rewards never appear.  
   • Predictions?  
     – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?  
   • The paper never uses “efficiency” ≈ (actual total payoff)/(maximum possible payoff) as a dependent variable. Instead, all of the analyses refer to whether cooperation vs. defection is sustained, who defects persistently, whether the group transitions into a “less cooperative equilibrium,” and so forth.  
   • The dependent measures there are best described as (i) overall level of cooperation, (ii) how widely misbehavior spreads, and (iii) who becomes “ostracized.” These do not translate to an explicit measure of efficiency.

B. Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
   • Only the number of players (parameter #1) clearly appears, in that the article sets n players in the model. The paper also parameterizes payoffs (α, β, δ), but these do not match your #7 or #8 (punishment cost, punishment magnitude) or #6 (MPCR). None of the other parameters is mentioned.

C. For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect (for each dependent variable) when systematically varied?

The paper does not compare a “punishment” vs. “no‐punishment” condition, nor does it measure an effect on “efficiency.” It does analyze how population growth or decline may strain or facilitate cooperation, but that is not framed as systematically varying “punishment treatment.”

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions might influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not provide enough detail to predict a formal “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” at all. Inferences could be loosely drawn that increasing group size (parameter #1) may make cooperation harder to enforce, thus lowering efficiency, but the paper does not speak in terms of a dedicated punishment‐treatment variable or an efficiency ratio. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter review of whether (1) the paper discusses the parameter (and, if so, whether it gives the parameter’s value) and (2) whether the paper makes predictions about the effect of systematically varying that parameter on the “punishment treatment effect” (i.e., what the paper calls rejections or payoff differences when punishments are possible). Where the paper discusses dependent variables other than efficiency, that is explicitly noted. Throughout, “the punishment treatment effect” in the paper corresponds to comparing “open response” (where responders’ rejections are revealed immediately to proposers) versus “covered response” (where proposers never learn in real time who punished them).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
• Discussed? The paper reports sessions typically having 16 participants (eight proposers and eight responders), but it does not systematically vary the number of players.  
• Effect of systematic variation? Not discussed; no predictions are made.

2. Number of rounds
• Discussed? Yes, the paper uses exactly eight rounds in every session. However, there is no systematic variation in the number of rounds (e.g., they do not compare 8 vs. 10).  
• Effect of systematic variation? Not discussed. The paper does analyze how behavior (e.g., rejection rates) changes over the eight fixed rounds, but it does not manipulate the total number of rounds.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
• Discussed? No. The paper does not mention chat or any communication among participants (beyond the minimal instructions).  
• Effect of systematic variation? Not discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
• Discussed? Responders can only accept or reject if an unfair offer is made (8–2 split), and cannot reject an equal split (5–5). This is a “mini‐ultimatum” format, but the paper does not describe it as “all or nothing” in the sense of a public goods contribution.  
• Effect of systematic variation? Not discussed.

5. Is the contribution default?
• Discussed? No. There is no mention of a “default contribution” mechanism in this ultimatum setting.  
• Effect of systematic variation? Not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
• Discussed? No. The experiment is framed as a 10‐point pie for an ultimatum division, not a public‐goods‐style “multiplication.”  
• Effect of systematic variation? Not discussed.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
• Discussed? The experiment has a “costly punishment” in the sense that responders forgo their payoff (they earn 0) if they reject an unfair offer. However, the paper does not manipulate or vary that cost.  
• Effect of systematic variation? Not discussed.

8. Punishment magnitude
• Discussed? The “magnitude” of the punishment is also fixed: if the responder rejects, both parties earn 0 instead of the offered division. This is not systematically varied.  
• Effect of systematic variation? Not discussed.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
• Discussed? No. There is no reward mechanism in the experiment.  
• Effect of systematic variation? Not discussed.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
• Discussed? No. No reward is used or varied.  
• Effect of systematic variation? Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude
• Discussed? No. As with (9) and (10), there is no reward mechanism at all.  
• Effect of systematic variation? Not discussed.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
• Discussed? Yes, participants are explicitly told the experiment lasts for eight rounds.  
• Effect of systematic variation? Not discussed; there was no treatment that hid the total number of rounds.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much their peers gained and lost)?
• Discussed? Yes, this is central to the paper’s two‐treatment comparison: in the “open response” treatment, proposers immediately see if their offer was accepted or rejected (i.e., they see the outcome of each round). In the “covered response” treatment, the proposer sees only a question mark and learns their total payoff only after all rounds are over.  
• Effect of systematic variation? Yes, they systematically compare “open” vs. “covered” responses. For dependent variables such as rejection rates (and also total payoffs—i.e., efficiency), the paper finds:  
  – Covered response treatment → lower rejection rate (22.5% on average) and higher total payoff (i.e., higher efficiency)  
  – Open response treatment → higher rejection rate (40.6% on average) and lower total payoff  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
• Discussed? Effectively yes, because in the “open” treatment the proposer immediately sees the rejection (and thus knows the identity of that round’s partner who rejected). In the “covered” treatment, they do not.  
• Effect of systematic variation? Yes, in tandem with #13, they vary whether punishment is visible in real time. The paper shows that knowledge of the punisher’s action leads to higher overall rejection rates in early rounds, but also reduces the frequency of unfair offers over time. However, for efficiency, the open treatment (where punishment is visible) ultimately has lower total payoffs. Numerically, the open‐treatment rejection rate is about 18 percentage points higher (40.6% vs. 22.5%) than the covered treatment.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
• Discussed? No. Rewards do not appear in this design.  
• Effect of systematic variation? Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A: Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
• Yes. The paper explicitly discusses total payoffs for both the proposer and responder together as a measure of efficiency. It also looks at average payoffs for each role, as well as:  
  – Rejection rates (the fraction of unfair offers turned down)  
  – Rates of equal offers by proposers  
  – Payoffs for proposers and responders separately  
These variables differ from efficiency because, for example, rejection rates focus on how often punishment occurs, whereas efficiency focuses on total earnings.

B: Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• The paper mentions or sets values for:  
  – (2) Number of rounds is fixed at 8.  
  – (12) The number of rounds is known to participants.  
  – (13) Peer outcomes are shown (or not) in the open vs. covered response.  
  – (14) Whether a punished proposer knows who punished them is effectively varied by the open vs. covered mechanism.  
All other parameters (1, 3–11, 15) are either not mentioned or not varied.

C: For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• Only parameters (13) and (14) are systematically varied (together, as “open vs. covered”). For these, the paper reports:  
  – Significantly higher rejection rates (≈40.6% vs. 22.5%) under open feedback, leading to lower total efficiency.  
  – More fairness‐minded offers in some open‐treatment sessions if responders harshly punish unfair offers, but overall lower efficiency because of the frequent costly rejections.

D: If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
• The paper only directly compares “open” vs. “covered” feedback. It does not offer evidence on varying the other parameters (e.g., changing the number of players, enabling rewards, changing the cost of punishment). Consequently, from this paper alone, one can say:  
  – Making punishment visible in real time (open) increases rejection rates and lowers efficiency relative to concealing punishment details (covered).  
  – For all other parameters, the paper provides no direct grounds to predict how they would affect efficiency or punishment.

Keywords Plus: SPENDING MONEY; COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; PROSOCIALITY; FRAMEWORK; EMOTIONS; FAIRNESS; TRAGEDY; MATTERS
Abstract: Previous research on money and prosociality has described a monotonic pattern, showing that money reduces generosity. The present research aimed to examine whether money differently impairs generosity when arising from altruistic versus egoistic motives. To this end, we employed economic games designed to study generosity (e.g., the Dictator game) and varied experimental currency (i.e., money vs. candy/food). The results (N = 850) showed that although money made people ignore others when others were not crucial for their future gain, generosity was not impacted when egoistic motives (Study 1: avoiding sanctions; Studies 2 and 3: building reputation) were present. In other words, although people in general showed flexible prosociality by adjusting their generosity level according to game type, this was much more strongly the case when money rather than candy/food was the currency. In addition, we demonstrate a boundary condition of money on flexible generosity, namely imbuing money with prosocial meaning (Study 3). Some implications are discussed.

Article Title: Punishment Leads to Cooperative Behavior in Structured Societies
Author Keywords: Continuous prisoner's dilemma; agent-based model; altruistic punishment; strong reciprocity; game theory; small-world network; scale-free network
Keywords Plus: STRONG RECIPROCITY; COLLECTIVE ACTION; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; POPULATION VISCOSITY; PRISONERS-DILEMMA; STRONG TIES; EVOLUTION; FAILURE; ORIGIN; SUSTAINABILITY
Abstract: Altruistic punishment occurs when an agent incurs a cost to punish another but receives no material benefit for doing so. Despite the seeming irrationality of such behavior, humans in laboratory settings routinely pay to punish others even in anonymous, one-shot settings. Costly punishment is ubiquitous among social organisms in general and is increasingly accepted as a mechanism for the evolution of cooperation. Yet if it is true that punishment explains cooperation, the evolution of altruistic punishment remains a mystery In a series of computer simulations I give agents the ability to punish one another while playing a continuous prisoner's dilemma. In simulations without social structure, expected behavior evolves agents do not punish and consequently no cooperation evolves. Likewise, in simulations with social structure but no ability to punish, no cooperation evolves. However, in simulations where agents are both embedded in a social structure and have the option to inflict costly punishment, cooperation evolves quite readily. This suggests a simple and broadly applicable explanation of cooperation for social organisms that have nonrandom social structure and a predisposition to punish one another. Results with scale-free networks further suggest that nodal degree distribution plays an important role in determining whether cooperation will evolve in a structured population.

Below, each of the 15 design parameters is examined in the order given.  
For every parameter I report (1) whether the paper says anything about it and, if so, the value that is used, and (2) whether the paper *systematically varies* the parameter and, if so, what happens to the *punishment-treatment effect* (i.e., the difference between the punishment and the no-punishment condition).  All numerical statements are taken directly from the text, tables, or figures.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned.  A fixed population of 400 agents (Table 2).  In every single CPD game only **two** players interact (plus one observer).  
   (2) Never varied, so no prediction about its effect on the punishment treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Mentioned.  Each simulation lasts 10 000 generations; within every generation each agent initiates 3 one-shot games (Table 2).  
   (2) Not varied, so no prediction.

3. Is chat enabled?  
   (1) Not mentioned; the simulated agents have no communication channel.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution?  
   (1) No.  The game is a *continuous* prisoners’ dilemma (Section 2.1) with $x\in[0,1]$.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

5. Contribution default / “refund stage”?  
   (1) Not present in the model.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   (1) Fixed at $r=1.5$ (Table 2).  
   (2) Never varied, so no prediction.

7. Punishment *cost* to impose a single unit  
   (1) Present.  Every agent carries an individual cost parameter $c_i\in[0,1]$ that mutates endogenously (Section 2.2).  
   (2) The experimenter never sets different exogenous values of $c$; therefore there is no systematic manipulation and no prediction about its effect.

8. Punishment *magnitude* – coins deducted per punished unit  
   (1) Present.  Labelled the *punishment multiplier* $M$ (Table 2).  
       • Range systematically explored: 0 ≤ M ≤ 6 in steps of 0.01 (single runs) and 0.5 (100 replications); extra spot checks at M = 5 000.  
   (2) YES – this is the *only* parameter the paper systematically varies.  
       Observed punishment-treatment effect (dependent variable = **mean contribution**, not efficiency):  
       – On regular lattices and small-world networks a sharp transition from ≈ 0 to ≈ 1 occurs when M crosses a network-specific threshold:  
         • Linear network (degree = 2): transition ≈ M = 1.5  
         • von Neumann (degree = 4): ≈ 1.8  
         • Hexagonal (degree = 6): ≈ 2.2  
         • Moore (degree = 8): ≈ 2.8  
       – On a complete (well-mixed) network *no* transition even at M = 5 000 (Figure 1a, Table 4).  
       – On scale-free networks contributions rise only modestly (mean 0.49 at M = 0 to 0.67 at M = 4; Figure 1d & Table 3).  
       – Random and random-regular networks show intermediate patterns (Table 3).  
       The paper does not translate these contribution changes into efficiency changes, but—because pay-offs rise monotonically with contribution—efficiency would track the same qualitative pattern.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   (1) Not included in the model.  
   (2) Not varied; no predictions.

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
   (1) Not modelled (agents have no foresight).  
   (2) Not varied; no predictions.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   (1) Not modelled.  
   (2) Not varied; no predictions.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
   (1) Not discussed.  In the code an observer *k* punishes *i*, but there is no information transmission rule, and this aspect is never varied.  
   (2) No prediction.

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
   (1) Not applicable (no rewards).  
   (2) No prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY  

A. Dependent variables used  
   – Mean contribution (primary).  
   – No measure of *group efficiency* or of total/average payoff is ever reported.  Because efficiency ≠ contribution when MPCR < 1, the two measures differ conceptually, but only contribution is analysed.

B. How many of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   5 parameters: #1, #2, #6, #7, and #8.

C. How many parameters are *systematically varied* and linked to a punishment treatment effect?  
   Only **one** parameter – Punishment magnitude (parameter 8).

D. Predicted influence on efficiency (if we had to infer it from the paper)  
   – Raising punishment magnitude M above a network-specific threshold should push efficiency from very low to nearly maximal levels *provided the population is structured* (linear, von Neumann, hexagonal, Moore, small-world, random-regular).  
   – In well-mixed (complete) networks, even enormous M does *not* improve efficiency.  
   – In scale-free networks the effect is modest; efficiency is expected to stay intermediate for any realistic M.  
   – For the remaining 14 parameters the paper offers no basis for prediction; therefore, on the basis of this paper alone, little or nothing can be said about their individual or interactive impact on the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Abstract: Metanorms is a mechanism proposed to promote cooperation in social dilemmas. Recent experimental results show that network structures that underlie social interactions influence the emergence of norms that promote cooperation. We generalize Axelrod's analysis of metanorms dynamics to interactions unfolding on networks through simulation and mathematical modeling. Network topology strongly influences the effectiveness of the metanorms mechanism in establishing cooperation. In particular, we find that average degree, clustering coefficient and the average number of triplets per node play key roles in sustaining or collapsing cooperation.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter walkthrough based strictly on the Galán et al. (2011) paper “Axelrod’s Metanorm Games on Networks.” For each of the 15 parameters listed, the response states (1) whether the paper addresses that parameter at all (and, if so, what value or setting it adopts), and (2) whether the paper makes predictions about systematically varying that parameter and its effect on punishment or cooperation. The focus is on how each parameter, if mentioned, might affect a “punishment treatment effect,” specifically on group efficiency (even though the paper itself does not use “efficiency” as its main variable).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Discussed? Yes. The paper fixes the number of agents at 50. It does so to facilitate certain social‐network structures and statistics.  
   • Systematically varied or predictive effect? No. They do not vary the number of players, nor do they make predictions about how changing it would affect any punishment‐related outcome.

2. Number of rounds
   • Discussed? Yes. Each “generation” consists of four rounds in which agents decide to defect or cooperate, punish, and meta‐punish; then many generations are run.  
   • Systematically varied or predictive effect? No. The paper does not vary the number of rounds or make predictions about how doing so alters punishment outcomes.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussed? No. There is no mention of communication or chat between agents.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussed? Yes, implicitly. Agents either cooperate or defect (a binary choice).  
   • Systematically varied or predictive effect? No. The model consistently uses that binary cooperate/defect framework and does not explore other contribution rules.

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., do players move endowment from the public fund back to themselves)?
   • Discussed? No. The paper’s game is not framed as contributing money to a public account. Defection/cooperation is a binary choice that affects payoffs directly without partial contribution decisions.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not use an MPCR or multiplier typical of linear public‐goods games.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussed? Yes. The paper sets a punisher’s “enforcement cost” to E = −2.  
   • Systematically varied or predictive effect? No. The cost is held fixed; there is no reported exploration of how varying E would affect punishment or total payoffs.

8. Punishment magnitude (the amount deducted from the punished)
   • Discussed? Yes. The paper sets Punishment payoff = P = −9 (the defector loses 9 units if punished).  
   • Systematically varied or predictive effect? No. They do not change this value to see how it would affect outcomes.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussed? No. The paper studies a punishment/metapunishment setting and does not introduce any reward mechanism.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Discussed? No. Rewards do not appear in the paper.

11. Reward magnitude
   • Discussed? No. As above, no reward mechanism is included.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
   • Discussed? No. The paper states a repeated (four‐round) scenario each generation, but does not describe whether agents know the overall horizon. There is no mention of systematic variation of this factor.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know others’ payoffs)?
   • Discussed? No. While agents “observe” defection (with certain probability) in order to punish, the paper does not state that complete payoff information is displayed to peers.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Discussed? No. The modeling focuses on whether punishment is “observed” in a metanorm sense, but the paper does not address whether the punished player knows the exact identity of the punisher.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not have reward, so this does not arise.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?  
   • The paper does not use “group efficiency” (actual total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff) as its main dependent variable. Instead, it focuses on whether cooperation (via low boldness and high vengefulness) emerges or collapses, often measured as the fraction of time the system spends in a “norm establishment” zone versus a “norm collapse” zone. The authors also track individual expected payoffs in their theoretical derivations, but their primary outcome variables are the stability of norms and the fraction of time spent in cooperation or defection states.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   • Mentioned in some way:  
     (1) Number of players (fixed at 50)  
     (2) Number of rounds (4 rounds per generation)  
     (4) All‐or‐nothing contribution (binary cooperate vs. defect)  
     (7) Punishment cost = −2  
     (8) Punishment magnitude = −9  
   • The other 10 parameters (3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15) are not mentioned in the paper.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when systematically varied, for any dependent variable?  
   • None of these parameters is systematically varied for the sake of comparing punishment versus no‐punishment conditions, nor does the paper present effect sizes for different values of any parameter. The paper holds them fixed in its simulations and focuses on variations in network topology (e.g., average degree, clustering, number of triplets).

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not provide direct findings about changes in group efficiency, nor does it systematically vary any of the 15 parameters. Accordingly, no firm predictions can be drawn for how those parameters or their interactions affect a punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency. The paper’s key systematic variations involve network structures (e.g., degree, clustering), not the standard public‐goods parameters. Thus, on the basis of this paper alone, one can make little or no prediction about how the 15 parameters or their combinations would affect efficiency in a punishment‐enabled public good or metanorm game.

Authors: Perry, L; Gavrilets, S
Author Full Names: Perry, Logan; Gavrilets, Sergey
Article Title: Foresight in a Game of Leadership
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS; PRISONERS-DILEMMA; COLLECTIVE ACTION; EVOLUTION; COOPERATION; PUNISHMENT; EMERGENCE; ORIGINS
Abstract: Leadership can be effective in promoting cooperation within a group, but as the saying goes heavy is the head that wears the crown. A lot of debate still surrounds exactly what motivates individuals to expend the effort necessary to lead their groupmates. Evolutionary game theoretic models represent individual's thought processes by strategy update protocols. The most common of these are random mutation, individual learning, selective imitation, and myopic optimization. Recently we introduced a new strategy update protocol - foresight - which takes into account future payoffs, and how groupmates respond to one's own strategies. Here we apply our approach to a new 2 x 2 game, where one player, a leader, ensures via inspection and punishment that the other player, a subordinate, produces collective good. We compare the levels of inspection and production predicted by Nash Equilibrium, Quantal Response Equilibrium, level-k cognition, fictitious play, reinforcement learning, selective payoff-biased imitation, and foresight. We show that only foresight and selective imitation are effective at promoting contribution by the subordinate and inspection and punishment by the leader. The role of selective imitation in cultural and social evolution is well appreciated. In line with our prior findings, foresight is a viable alternative route to cooperation.

Even there, it does not link these to any measure of “efficiency,” nor does it give explicit effect sizes. Instead it uses inequalities (e.g., k < θb − h) that determine whether the leader punishes or not.

Parameter-by-parameter extraction from Gao et al. (2015)

(For every parameter the two bullets correspond to instruction 3-(1) “Is it in the paper?” and 3-(2) “Is a systematic variation analysed and, if so, what numerical effect is reported?”)  
The page, figure or equation where the material appears is given in brackets.

1. Number of players in the group  
• Yes. The population size N is explicitly modelled (e.g. N = 100 in Figs. 1–5; analytical results for N → ∞ and for the minimum N = 2, Appendix E).  
• Systematic variation: Appendix E derives closed-form conditions that depend on N.  
  – For peer pro-social punishment to beat defection in large populations: β > 2c + α.  
  – For pool pro-social punishment to beat defection as N → ∞: β > 0 (Eq. E-3).  
  – With N = 2 the same dominance requires β > b + c + α.  
  Hence increasing N widens the parameter range in which punishment promotes cooperation. The paper does not translate this into group efficiency.

2. Number of rounds  
• Not mentioned; the model is an infinite-horizon Moran process.

3. Chat enabled  
• Not mentioned.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
• Not mentioned.

5. Contribution default option  
• Not mentioned.

6. Marginal Per-Capita Return / multiplication factor (here: benefit–cost structure b and c)  
• Yes. b and c (cost-to-benefit ratio c/b) are central parameters (Fig. 1 varies c/b; Figs. 2 & 4 vary c and keep b constant).  
• Systematic variation:  
  – Fig. 1 shows abundances of strategies as c/b moves from 0 to 1. Cooperation and pro-social punishment drop monotonically with c/b, defection rises.  
  – Fig. 4 panels vary c on the horizontal axis and α on the vertical; higher c shrinks the region where punishment helps.  
  No numerical effect on efficiency is reported.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher (α)  
• Yes (α = 5, 10 etc.; varied in Fig. 4, Appendix E).  
• Systematic variation: Higher α lowers the stationary abundance of pro-social punishers and raises that of second-order free-riders and defectors (Fig. 4). Exact inequality for peer punishers vs. defectors: N(β – α) > 2b + 2(N–1)c.  

8. Punishment magnitude / fine (β)  
• Yes (β = 10, 30; varied in Fig. 2 and in analytic inequalities).  
• Systematic variation:  
  – Increasing β enlarges the region in which pro-social punishment (especially pool) out-competes defection (Fig. 2; β enters the inequalities quoted under parameter 1).  
  – No efficiency numbers are given.

9. Reward enabled?  
• Not in the model.

10. Reward cost  
• Not in the model.

11. Reward magnitude  
• Not in the model.

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
• Not relevant; infinite Moran process.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
• Not addressed.

14. Do punished players know who punished them?  
• Implicitly addressed through the “pattern” of punishment.  
  – Peer punishment reveals the punisher; pool punishment hides identity (Section 3.1, discussion of retaliation).  
• Systematic variation: The whole paper contrasts the two patterns. Pool punishment (hidden identity) consistently produces higher cooperation than peer punishment when other parameters are kept constant (Figs. 1–3). No numerical efficiency figures are given.

15. Do rewarded players know who rewarded them?  
• Not applicable (no rewards).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary requested in points A–D

A. Dependent variables  
The paper does not use group efficiency (total or average payoff relative to the social optimum) as an outcome. The dependent variables are:  
• Stationary abundance (long-run frequency) of each strategy (main variable in Figs. 1, 2, 4).  
• Fixation probability and fixation time between homogeneous states (Figs. 3, 5).  
These differ from efficiency because they say nothing about aggregate payoffs; they only describe evolutionary success of strategies.

B. Which of the 15 parameters occur?  
Five:  
1 (population size N), 6 (b and c), 7 (punishment cost α), 8 (punishment fine β), 14 (identity of punisher implicitly via pattern). The remaining ten parameters are not mentioned.

C. For how many of the 15 parameters is the effect of systematic variation on the punishment treatment effect analysed?  
Four (or five if the identity point is counted): N, b/c, α, β, and the punishment pattern (linked to parameter 14). All analyses concern strategy abundance, not efficiency.

D. Predictions—if one nevertheless had to forecast the impact on group efficiency using only this paper  
Because efficiency is never measured, only very cautious qualitative extrapolations are possible:  
• Larger groups (higher N) and larger fines β relative to cost α should make punishment more effective at raising cooperation and hence presumably efficiency, especially when punishment is centralised (pool).  
• High costs of cooperation (high c) or high punishment cost α erode the beneficial effect.  
• Revealing the punisher’s identity (peer punishment) undermines the efficiency gain; hiding identity (pool punishment) preserves it.  
Beyond these broad tendencies, the paper offers little basis for quantifying the punishment treatment effect on efficiency or for modelling interactions among the 15 parameters.

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are they different?

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter review of whether (1) the paper by Rebers and Koopmans (“Altruistic Punishment and Between‐Group Competition…”) addresses each of the 15 parameters in any way (and, if so, what values or conditions they used) and (2) whether the paper makes any claim—numerical or otherwise—about systematically varying that parameter and predicting how it would affect the “punishment treatment effect,” especially with respect to efficiency. In this study, Rebers and Koopmans primarily compare single‐group versus intergroup public‐goods conditions (n‐person Prisoner’s Dilemmas) that allow punishment, but they do not systematically manipulate most of the parameters listed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned?: Yes. The authors ran groups of six individuals in a group (and two groups of six in the intergroup condition).  
   • Values used or varied?: The paper does not systematically vary the number of players; it remains fixed at six per group.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency) if varied?: No discussion.  

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned?: Yes. They use only a single contribution round plus one punishment stage (two‐stage design).  
   • Values used or varied?: No. They do not systematically explore multiple or varying rounds.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency) if varied?: Not discussed.  

3. Is chat enabled?
   • Mentioned?: No. There is no discussion of communication or “chat” between players.  
   • Systematically varied?: No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency) if varied?: Not discussed.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned?: The design effectively makes the contribution decision a binary one: each participant either keeps their €2 (“defect”) or puts all €2 into the group pot (“cooperate”).  
   • Systematically varied?: No. They do not alter this feature. It is the same across conditions.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency) if varied?: Not discussed.  

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much to move back into private hands)?
   • Mentioned?: No. The authors do not mention any “default contribution” mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied?: No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency) if varied?: Not discussed.  

6. MPCR (marginal per capita return) or related parameters (e.g., multiplication factors)
   • Mentioned?: Only insofar as the payoff tables define how much each individual earns if they put money in the group account. In the single‐group conditions, putting in €2 yields a certain payoff to each group member (e.g., €0.60 per member in some tables). Between‐group condition shifts share of a €43.20 bonus.  
   • Systematically varied?: Partly. The authors use a “single‐group‐low‐payoff” and “single‐group‐high‐payoff” condition, but they do not frame it as varying the MPCR in a formal sense, and they do not examine how that variation affects punishment’s impact on efficiency. Their main interest is single‐group versus intergroup, not MPCR variation per se.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency) if varied?: Not specifically modeled or discussed.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned?: Yes. Each €0.10 spent on punishment reduces the targeted person’s payoff by €0.30. Hence, the cost imposed on the punisher is 1/3 of the damage inflicted.  
   • Systematically varied?: No. They fix a 1:3 ratio (punisher pays 1; target loses 3).  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency) if varied?: Not discussed.  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   • Mentioned?: Yes. As above, the target loses €0.30 if the punisher spends €0.10.  
   • Systematically varied?: No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency) if varied?: Not discussed.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Mentioned?: No. Not applicable (there is no reward option).  
    • Systematically varied?: No.

    • Mentioned?: No. Same as above; no reward mechanism is present.  
    • Systematically varied?: No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency) if varied?: Not discussed.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
    • Mentioned?: They refer to one‐shot contribution plus a punishment stage. Presumably, participants do know from the instructions that there is no repetition beyond that.  
    • Systematically varied?: No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency) if varied?: Not discussed.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost each round)?
    • Mentioned?: Participants do see how many cooperators and defectors were in their own group before deciding on punishment. The paper does not indicate that participants see exact earnings of each peer, but they do see enough to know who cooperated/defected.  
    • Systematically varied?: No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Mentioned?: The experiment is described as anonymous; the authors do not report that the punishee learns the identity of who punished them.  
    • Systematically varied?: No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency) if varied?: Not discussed.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Mentioned?: Not applicable—there is no reward treatment.  
    • Systematically varied?: No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency) if varied?: Not discussed.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The main dependent variables examined are:  
     – Whether individuals cooperated (contributed) or defected.  
     – How much money individuals spent on punishing “defectors” vs. punishing “cooperators.”  
   • The paper occasionally refers to “group welfare” or how perverse punishment reduces group efficiency but does not systematically measure or analyze “efficiency” as (actual payoff / maximum payoff).  
   • Hence, the authors do not treat group efficiency (in the sense of total or average payoff realized) as their primary or formal dependent variable. Their dependent variables differ accordingly: they focus on the amount spent on punishing and the rate of cooperation, not on efficiency per se.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
       1. Number of players (fixed at six per group).  
       2. Number of rounds (one contribution stage + one punishment stage).  
       4. All‐or‐nothing contribution (participants put €2 in or keep €2).  
       6. MPCR‐type payoff structure (though they frame it in payoff tables).  
       7. Punishment cost (fixed ratio 1:3).  
       8. Punishment magnitude (meeting that 1:3 cost‐to‐impact ratio).  
     The other parameters (3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15) are either absent or not discussed beyond minimal references to anonymity or knowledge of cooperators/defectors, and no parameter is truly varied in a systematic, experimental sense except for the limited payoff differences among single‐group‐low, single‐group‐high, and the intergroup competition condition.

C. For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?
   • Strictly speaking, the authors do not systematically manipulate any of the 15 parameters to test how that variance affects punishment’s impact on “efficiency.” Their only systematic manipulations are:  
     – Single‐group (low payoff) vs. single‐group (high payoff) vs. intergroup competition.  
   • Even for that manipulation, they measure cooperation levels and punishment expenditures, not efficiency. They do not provide any numerical effect size for how varying, say, the punishment cost or the number of players would change the effect of punishment on efficiency.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?
   • The paper does not provide enough information to make firm predictions about how most of the 15 parameters would affect efficiency in a punishment game. Their focus is on comparing single‐group vs. intergroup conditions (i.e., presence or absence of between‐group competition) with respect to punishment of cooperators or defectors, not on systematically analyzing how those parameters shape overall payoffs or group efficiency.  
   • Accordingly, one can make little or no prediction for most parameters, as the study merely fixes them and does not discuss their broader impact on efficiency. The only qualitative takeaway (regarding efficiency) is that intergroup competition raised punishment of defectors (which in repeated games might increase efficiency in principle), and that “perverse” punishment of cooperators is not heightened by intergroup competition. Beyond that, the paper does not offer predictions for other parameters.

Abstract: Enhancing human cooperation in the use of limited and depletable resources is of central concern to environmental management and human welfare. Below, each of the 15 parameters is treated in turn.  For every parameter I state (1) whether it appears in the paper and, if so, its value; and (2) whether the paper makes any prediction or reports any evidence about how *systematically varying* that parameter would change the *punishment treatment effect* (i.e., the difference in outcomes between a “punishment” and a “no-punishment” condition).  Page, figure and table references are given where they are available in the text you provided.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER SCAN
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
 (1) Mentioned: yes.  Five players per session (Study 1 and Study 2, Method sections).  
 (2) Systematic-variation discussion: none.  Only one group size is used; the authors never speculate on how using four, six, etc. players would alter the punishment treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
 (1) Mentioned: yes.  Twenty rounds are always played (Method, Study 1 and Study 2).  
 (2) No systematic variation; no predictions.

3. Chat enabled?  
 (1) Mentioned implicitly: players sit in enclosed cubicles with *no* interaction (Study 1 Procedure).  
 (2) No variation; no predictions.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
 (1) Not relevant/mentioned.  Players choose any integer 0-30 points each round; this is a continuous choice.  
 (2) No discussion.

5. “Contribution default” framing (withdraw from public fund vs. contribute to it)  
 Not mentioned; not varied.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
 Not used.  The task is a common-pool (resource dilemma) game, not a public-goods game; no MPCR is defined.

7. Punishment cost to punisher  
 (1) Mentioned: yes, but only in Study 2.  Participants may pay \$0, \$1, \$2, or \$3 (cost to themselves) (Study 2 Procedure).  
 (2) Not experimentally varied by the researchers.  Participants simply choose a level; the authors do not analyse how changing the *schedule* of costs would alter the punishment treatment effect.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine on target per unit cost)  
 (1) Mentioned: fixed at a 1 : 3 ratio.  Every \$1 spent fines the target \$3 (Study 2 Procedure).  
 (2) No variation; no predictions.

9. Whether a reward option exists  
 (1) Not present.  Only punishment is offered.  
 (2) No discussion.

10. Reward cost  
 Not applicable.

11. Reward magnitude  
 Not applicable.

12. Whether the number of rounds is known to players  
 (1) Yes, but only implicitly.  The round number (“Round 1”, “Round 2”, …) is displayed on each screen, so subjects can infer how far they are, but the text never states that an *unknown-horizon* variant was tried.  
 (2) No systematic manipulation; no predictions.

13. Whether peer outcomes are shown  
 (1) Study 1: peer outcomes are *not* shown.  
 (2) Study 2: after each round subjects are told which player took the most points and how many points that player took (Procedure).  
 No systematic manipulation; no predictions about varying the *amount* of information and its effect on punishment.

14. Whether punished players learn the identity of the punisher  
 Not mentioned.  The text only says “we are going to give you the opportunity to fine a player of your choosing,” with no information on feedback to the target.  No manipulation; no predictions.

15. Whether rewarded players learn the identity of the rewarder  
 Not applicable because there is no reward option.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables actually analysed  
 • Total points *taken* by each participant across 20 rounds (individual consumption).  
 • Amount each participant *spent on punishment* (Study 2 only).  
 The paper never reports group efficiency (total earnings divided by the cooperative maximum) nor average pay-offs.  Therefore any result that speaks about “efficiency” must be inferred, not observed.

B.  Coverage of the 15 parameters  
 The manuscript explicitly mentions 6 of the 15 parameters (1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 13).  The remaining 9 are absent or irrelevant.

C.  Parameters whose *systematic variation* is analysed for their effect on the punishment treatment effect  
 None (0/15).  Every mentioned parameter is held constant; the paper offers no experimental or theoretical statements about how changing those parameters would alter the effect of introducing punishment.

D.  What predictions about the 15 parameters can be made *solely* from this paper?  
 Because the authors did not vary the parameters and did not theorise about them, almost no parameter-specific prediction can be made.  The only qualitative hint is that punishment, as implemented (cost = \$1–\$3; fine = 3×cost), had *very little* behavioural impact: subjects spent on average only about \$0.48 and this spending did **not** differ between the cricket (moral-value) and control conditions.  Hence, within the narrow range tested, punishment had negligible influence on consumption or efficiency.  Whether that would change with a different group size, longer/shorter horizon, cheaper punishment, identifiable punishers, etc. is left entirely open by the paper.

In short, the article is informative about how *adding non-monetary moral value to the resource* changes cooperation, but it sheds virtually no light on how any of the 15 structural parameters—and certainly not their interactions—would modulate the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.

Abstract: Studying social dilemmas prompts the question of how cooperation can emerge in situations where individuals are expected to act selfishly. Here, in the framework of the one-shot Public Goods Game (PGG), we introduce the concept that individuals can adjust their behaviour based on the cooperative commitments made by other players in the group prior to the actual PGG interaction.
