Below I list the 15 experimental‐design parameters, indicate what the paper says about each one, and, whenever possible, report what happens when the parameter is systematically varied in the PUNISHMENT condition (ω = 0).  “Punishment treatment effect” is interpreted exactly as in the paper: the change in outcomes when institutional punishment (δ > 0, ω = 0) is switched on, relative to a benchmark with no incentives (δ = 0).

Because the paper never reports “group efficiency” (total earnings / maximum possible total earnings) the only dependent variables for which the authors supply results are

• cooperation frequency (sometimes called “cooperative density”)  
• strategy frequencies (shares of the eight commitment strategies)  
• critical r-values at which cooperation survives or dominates

Whenever the paper gives numbers these come from Figures 3–5 (punishment) or Figure 4 (critical r).  Exact numerical values are not printed in the text, so only rough values can be read off.

───────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
───────────────────────────────────────────

1. Number of players (group size in the public-goods interaction)  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  Every focal player plus its four von Neumann neighbours form a group, so G = 5.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  G is held constant at 5; the paper makes no prediction about changing it.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? None reported.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? No.  The model is explicitly “one-shot”; evolutionary time is handled through Monte-Carlo steps, not repeated rounds seen by the same subjects.  
   • No predictions.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Not mentioned; not modelled; no predictions.

4. All–or–nothing contribution?  
   • Yes.  Contribution is binary (cooperate = pay cost c = 1; defect = pay 0).  
   • Not varied, so no prediction about its variation.

5. Contribution default (withdrawal from a public endowment)?  
   • Not present; no prediction.

6. Marginal Per-Capita Return (MPCR) / multiplication factor r  
   • Yes, systematically varied, typically 1 < r < 6.  
   • Punishment results (Figures 3 & 4):  
        – Without punishment the classical lattice PGG needs r ≈ 3.9 for cooperation to survive.  
        – Adding punishment (δ > 0, ω = 0) lowers that critical r; how far it is lowered depends on the commitment threshold τ and on δ:  
             ▸ τ = 5 & strong punishment (δ ≈ 0.25): cooperation survives down to r ≈ 1.1.  
             ▸ τ = 4 & δ ≈ 0.19: critical r is around 2.2.  
             ▸ τ = 2 & δ ≈ 0.19: critical r only moves a little (≈ 3.4).  
   • Thus, smaller r becomes viable when both δ and τ are high; the paper offers no efficiency numbers but plainly shows higher cooperation frequencies.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   • The institutional mechanism imposes no individual cost on the punisher; the whole group pays a budget G δ.  Hence the cost is not an independent parameter and is never varied.  
   • No prediction.

8. Punishment magnitude / strength (δ when ω = 0)  
   • Yes, varied from 0 to ≈ 0.3.  
   • Findings (Fig. 3):  
        – Increasing δ increases cooperation until a plateau is reached; the plateau is reached faster for low τ.  
        – Effect sizes are visual, not numeric.  Example for τ = 4: raising δ from 0.05 to 0.25 moves the critical r from ≈ 3.5 down to ≈ 1.4.  
        – Very high δ plus high τ can even stabilise cooperation at r ≈ 1.1 (almost no social return).  
   • No payoff or efficiency numbers are given.

9. Reward enabled? (whether ω = 1 instead of 0)  
   • Yes.  Section 3.3 sets ω = 1 to study reward.  
   • The paper does not contrast “punishment only” versus “punishment + reward” for the same run, so no direct statement about reward’s influence on the punishment treatment effect.

10. Reward cost to grant one unit  
11. Reward magnitude  
   • Both fold into the same parameter δ when ω = 1.  Variation of δ is discussed only for the reward-only treatment, not for punishment, so they do not inform the punishment treatment effect.

12. Horizon known to players?  
   • Not modelled; no predictions.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Not modelled; no predictions.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
15. Is the rewarder identified?  
   • Not modelled; punishment and reward are administered anonymously by the “institution”.  No predictions.

───────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
───────────────────────────────────────────

A.  Dependent variables used  
    • Cooperation frequency (and closely related strategy frequencies)  
    • Critical MPCR r at which cooperation survives / dominates  
    Group efficiency or total payoff is never reported, so results cannot be translated directly into efficiency gains.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
    8 of them: 1, 4, 6, 7/8 (treated together in the model), 9, 10, 11.  The remaining seven (2, 3, 5, 12, 13, 14, 15) are absent.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper report the effect of SYSTEMATIC VARIATION on the punishment treatment effect?  
    Only two:  
        • Parameter 6 (MPCR r)  
        • Parameter 8 (punishment strength δ)  
    Their interaction with the commitment threshold τ (a variable not on your list) is crucial in all reported results.

D.  What predictions can be made, restricted to the paper’s content, about how the 15 parameters jointly influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
    • The paper contains no efficiency data; therefore, no firm quantitative prediction about efficiency can be made.  
    • Qualitatively, stronger punishment (higher δ) and harder public-goods environments (lower r) interact with a HIGH commitment threshold to raise cooperation; if higher cooperation translates into higher efficiency, one would expect efficiency gains under those same conditions.  
    • For all other listed parameters (group size, number of rounds, chat, contribution format, visibility, identity disclosure, etc.) the paper offers no information, so no prediction—beyond “unknown”—can be made.

In short, the only systematic levers studied in the paper that matter for the punishment treatment effect are the multiplication factor r and the institutional punishment strength δ; everything else is either fixed or outside the model.

   • Discussion: Again, the study is framed in terms of Prisoner’s Dilemma interactions and does not involve a default contribution to a public fund.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussion: The paper’s central parameter is r, 0 ≤ r ≤ 1, which scales how much payoff the punisher invests (and simultaneously how much the target loses). Specifically, if P(i) is the punisher’s payoff, rP(i) is deducted from both the punisher and the punished in the relevant condition.  
   • Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment: Yes. The paper systematically varies r from 0.0 to 1.0. The paper repeatedly shows that moderate to higher values of r can increase the average payoff (especially when accompanied by the coevolutionary mechanism of breaking and creating connections). However, no explicit ratio of “actual total payoff” over “maximum possible total payoff” is provided, so only the average payoff (and number of cooperators) is given.    • Discussion: In the model, the same parameter r sets both how costly it is to punish and how severe the punishment is (rP(i)). The paper does not separate “cost to punisher” from “deduction for the punished” as two independent parameters; both are governed by r.  
   • Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment: The systematic variation is the same as for parameter #7; no additional separate variation is discussed.

Article Title: The Hard Problem of Cooperation
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS GAMES; SOCIAL DILEMMAS; PEOPLES REACTIONS; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; RATIONAL CHOICE; BEHAVIOR; SOCIETIES; TRUST; INSTITUTIONS; ORIENTATION
Abstract: Based on individual variation in cooperative inclinations, we define the hard problem of cooperation as that of achieving high levels of cooperation in a group of non-cooperative types. Can the hard problem be solved by institutions with monitoring and sanctions? In a laboratory experiment we find that the answer is affirmative if the institution is imposed on the group but negative if development of the institution is left to the group to vote on. In the experiment, participants were divided into groups of either cooperative types or non-cooperative types depending on their behavior in a public goods game. In these homogeneous groups they repeatedly played a public goods game regulated by an institution that incorporated several of the key properties identified by Ostrom: operational rules, monitoring, rewards, punishments, and (in one condition) change of rules. When change of rules was not possible and punishments were set to be high, groups of both types generally abided by operational rules demanding high contributions to the common good, and thereby achieved high levels of payoffs. Under less severe rules, both types of groups did worse but non-cooperative types did worst. Thus, non-cooperative groups profited the most from being governed by an institution demanding high contributions and employing high punishments. Nevertheless, in a condition where change of rules through voting was made possible, development of the institution in this direction was more often voted down in groups of non-cooperative types. We discuss the relevance of the hard problem and fit our results into a bigger picture of institutional and individual determinants of cooperative behavior.

2) Number of rounds
 • Mentioned? Yes. They used several fixed blocks of rounds:  
   – First phase: four rounds of an unregulated public goods game.  
   – Second phase: 16 rounds in the “evolving institution” condition.  
   – Third phase: two blocks of four rounds each (weak vs. strong institution).  
   – Finally, four rounds with no institution.  
 • Systematically varied? No. Although the experiment had different stages with different round lengths, the paper does not examine how different total round lengths or different knowledge of these lengths would affect punishment. There is no reported systematic manipulation of round number to test its effect on punishment or on treatment effects.

3) Is chat (communication) enabled between players?
 • Mentioned? Only briefly in a general introduction (p.2–3) where the authors note that “communication…facilitates cooperation.”  
 • Systematically varied? No. There was no condition in which players were allowed to chat directly or not; no manipulation of communication was performed. The paper does not discuss any effect of chat on punishment.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
 • Mentioned? Indirectly, the paper explains that each player decides how many of their ten tokens to contribute (anywhere from 0 to 10). This is not an all‐or‐nothing setup; players can contribute any integer amount.  
 • Systematically varied? No. There is no mention of a version where participants are forced to contribute everything or nothing. The paper does not discuss any systematic variation from continuous choice to all‐or‐nothing.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters
 • Mentioned? Yes. The paper’s multiplication factor is M=2, with N=4, so the MPCR=2/4=0.5.  
 • Systematically varied? No. M=2 is fixed throughout. The paper does not examine how systematically changing MPCR would affect punishment’s impact.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
 • Mentioned? Somewhat. The paper sets a “monitoring cost” of C=1 token; monitoring leads automatically to punishment if the target’s contribution is below the threshold.

 • Mentioned? Yes, and systematically varied. The fine F takes low values (F=2) in the “weak institution” but can rise up to F=10 in the “strong institution,” and in the “evolving institution” condition can move from F=2 up to F=9 depending on voting (p.8–9).

 • Mentioned? No explicit statement. The experiment’s instructions do not say that punishees learn who monitored them; it appears anonymous.  
 • Systematically varied? No. The paper makes no mention of changing whether identity of the punisher is revealed.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who rewarded them (is the rewarder’s identity revealed)?
 • Mentioned? No. Similarly, the identity of the monitor who discovered the cheater seems not revealed.  
 • Systematically varied? No. There is no discussion of altering that information.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY  
A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   • The paper regularly reports “payoff” (average tokens earned) and also reports “contributions” and “monitoring rate.” It does not use “efficiency” in the sense of “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff,” nor does it label its main variable as “efficiency.” Instead, the key outcome variables are (1) payoff and (2) contribution. These differ from a formal measure of “efficiency”: payoff may be lower or higher than the maximum possible but is not presented as a fraction of that maximum.  

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned at all (even if only fixed):  
     (1) Number of players (N=4).  
     (2) Number of rounds (various fixed amounts in each stage).  
     (4) They do note that players can contribute any integer 0–10, so the game is not “all or nothing,” but there is no special discussion of that as a parameter.  
     (6) MPCR factor M=2 (i.e., 0.5 per capita return).  
     (7) Punishment cost to monitor: 1 token.  
     (8) Punishment magnitude F (varies from 2 → 9 or 10).  
     (9) Reward is enabled (R=3).  
     (11) Reward magnitude is 3 tokens.  
     (12) Rounds are known.  
     (13) Some peer outcome information is shown (aggregates).  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when systematically varied?  
   • Only parameter (8), the fine/punishment magnitude F, is truly manipulated (weak vs. strong vs. evolving from low to high). Author Full Names: Griffin, Christopher; Belmonte, Andrew
Article Title: Cyclic public goods games: Compensated coexistence among mutual cheaters stabilized by optimized penalty taxation
Keywords Plus: SOCIAL DILEMMAS; COOPERATION; DYNAMICS
Abstract: We study the problem of stabilized coexistence in a three-species public goods game in which each species simultaneously contributes to one public good while freeloading off another public good (cheating). The proportional population growth is governed by an appropriately modified replicator equation, depending on the returns from the public goods and the cost. We show that the replicator dynamic has at most one interior unstable fixed point and that the population becomes dominated by a single species. We then show that by applying an externally imposed penalty, or tax on success can stabilize the interior fixed point, allowing for the symbiotic coexistence of all species. We show that the interior fixed point is the point of globally minimal total population growth in both the taxed and untaxed cases. We then formulate an optimal taxation problem and show that it admits a quasilinearization, resulting in novel necessary conditions for the optimal control. In particular, the optimal control problem governing the tax rate must solve a certain second-order ordinary differential equation.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or a similar multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? No. The authors instead use a sigmoidal production function relating group investment to water availability; they do not treat an MPCR or factor as a parameter to be varied. No predictions are made.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? Yes. It is fixed at 1 token per use (shared if multiple punishers target the same player).  
   • Systematic variation discussed? No. This cost is not varied across sessions. No predictions about how changing the cost of punishing would affect the treatment’s impact on payoffs or efficiency.  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The experiment imposes a 4‐token fine on the punished player with 2/3 probability.  
   • Systematic variation discussed? No. The fine amount (4 tokens) is fixed throughout. The paper does not discuss what would happen if this were changed.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned? No. The study had no reward treatment. No predictions are made.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Mentioned? No. There is no reward mechanism in the paper. No predictions.  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded)  
    • Mentioned? No. Likewise, no mention of offering rewards.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
    • Mentioned? Yes. Players did not know how long the game would last. However, it was not used as a systematically varied factor for analyzing punishment outcomes. No explicit predictions were made about manipulating whether round length was known.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (does each player know how much others gained or lost)?  
    • Mentioned? Yes. After each round, players saw how many tokens each person invested and how much water each extracted. The authors note that this “social information” may have boosted cooperation.  
    • Systematic variation discussed? No. The experiment always provided this information; they did not test a scenario where it was hidden. No predictions are made about toggling it.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Mentioned? Not stated explicitly. The paper does not say whether the identity of the punisher is revealed to the punished. There is no systematic variation or analysis.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Mentioned? No. There is no reward treatment in the paper.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?  
   • The paper measures each individual’s total tokens earned, as well as each group’s total earnings (“group welfare”). It sometimes compares realized outcomes to the social optimum, which is effectively a measure of efficiency. The authors also examine inequality of earnings (Gini coefficients), investment levels, and extraction levels. “Efficiency” in the strict sense (actual group payoff divided by the maximum possible) is not always the explicit statistic presented, but the authors do repeatedly consider how close groups come to the social optimum.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • The paper explicitly mentions and uses seven parameters:  
     1 (number of players = 5), 2 (number of rounds = baseline 7, treatment 8–11), 3 (chat enabled in the “communication” treatment), 7 (punishment cost = 1 token), 8 (punishment magnitude = 4 tokens), 12 (number of rounds unknown), 13 (peer decisions and payoffs displayed).  
   • The paper does not mention or use the remaining eight parameters (4, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15) in its design.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. Although the paper does compare baseline rounds to a punishment‐enabled treatment, it does not systematically vary any of those 15 parameters to examine how that variation alters punishment’s effect on efficiency (or on any other outcome).  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • Because no parameters above were varied systematically, and because the paper contains no numerical forecasts for how changes in these parameters would shift the punishment effect, it provides little basis for any prediction regarding how such changes would affect group efficiency. Indeed, the sole punishment configuration tested tended to reduce group payoffs (partly through water “wastage”), but no deeper claim is made about how changing the punishment cost, punishment magnitude, group size, communication setting, or other parameters would strengthen or weaken that effect. Consequently, there is effectively no direct guidance in the paper for how these 15 parameters (or their interactions) might alter the punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency.

Article Title: Justice Sensitivity and Cooperation Dynamics in Repeated Public Good Games

Abstract: It is frequently observed that despite individual incentives to free ride, humans decide to cooperate with each other to increase social payoffs. In the current research, we address the effects of individual differences in justice sensitivity on cooperation. Using incentivized repeated public good games, we find that individual differences in justice sensitivity-the ease of perceiving, remembering, and reacting to injustice from the perspectives of an observer, beneficiary, or perpetrator, but not victim-substantially predicts cooperation in the absence of a punishment option. In contrast, when costly punishment is allowed for, cooperation becomes strategic as it also aims at avoiding subsequent punishment. If such a sanctioning mechanism is in place, justice sensitivity no longer predicts cooperation. The results regarding the degree of cooperation as reaction to initial non-cooperation of one's counterparts highlight the role of justice-concerning personality traits for the sufficient provision of public goods, as sanctioning institutions are not always possible, effective, or suitable.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter review of what the paper says (or does not say) about each of the 15 parameters, followed by the requested four‐part summary.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) NUMBER OF PLAYERS  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter? Yes. The experiment always uses groups of four players interacting over multiple rounds (p. 8).  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it? No. There was no manipulation of group size, and no predictions about its effect on punishment or efficiency.

2) NUMBER OF ROUNDS  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter? Yes. The experiment runs for 10 rounds (p. 8). Participants are aware that it ends after those 10 rounds (p. 8).  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it? No. The paper does not vary the number of rounds. It does mention a “last‐round effect” (p. 12) but does not systematically manipulate round length or horizon.

3) IS CHAT ENABLED BETWEEN PLAYERS?  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter? No. There is no mention of any chat, communication, or messaging between participants.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it? No. The paper does not address chat at all.

4) IS THE CONTRIBUTION “ALL OR NOTHING”?  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter? The study uses the standard linear Public Goods Game in which each participant can contribute any integer amount between 0 and 20 tokens (pp. 6, 8, Appendix). This is not an “all or nothing” format.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it? No. The paper does not introduce a forced all‐or‐nothing choice and does not predict how making it “all or nothing” might affect outcomes.

5) IS THE CONTRIBUTION DEFAULT (I.E., PLAYERS DECIDE HOW MUCH OF THEIR ENDOWMENT TO MOVE BACK)?  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter? Participants decide how many of the 20 tokens to contribute to the public good (pp. 8–9). There is no mention of a “default” or forced reversed decision.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it? No. It is only reported as a standard “choose 0–20 tokens” procedure.

6) MARGINAL PER CAPITA RETURN (MPCR) OR RELATED MULTIPLICATION FACTOR  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter? Yes. The total contribution is multiplied by 1.6 and then split among the four players, giving each an individual share of 0.4 per token contributed (p. 8).  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it? No. Only one multiplication factor (1.6) is used, with no systematic variation.

7) PUNISHMENT COST TO IMPOSE A SINGLE UNIT OF PUNISHMENT  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter? Yes. The cost schedule is reproduced from Fehr & Gächter (2002), showing that distributing punishment points is “costly” to the punisher (Table on p. 10 of the Instructions).  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it? No. The cost rule is the same throughout. The paper does not examine how different cost structures change outcomes.

8) PUNISHMENT MAGNITUDE (THE COINS DEDUCTED FROM A PLAYER PER UNIT OF PUNISHMENT)  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter? Yes. Each punishment point deducts 10% of the punished player’s first‐stage income, up to 100% if 10 or more total points are assigned (pp. 9–10).  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it? No. There is no manipulation of the severity of punishment or its functional form.

9) WHETHER A REWARD IS ENABLED  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter? No. The study uses only punishment or no‐punishment. There is no reward or bonus mechanism to increase others’ payoffs.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it? No.

10) REWARD COST TO GRANT A SINGLE UNIT OF REWARD  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter? No. There is no mention of a reward stage or cost of rewarding.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it? No.

11) REWARD MAGNITUDE (THE COINS AWARDED TO A PLAYER FOR EACH UNIT OF REWARD)  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter? No. Rewards do not appear in the design.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it? No.

12) IS THE NUMBER OF ROUNDS KNOWN TO PLAYERS?  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter? Yes, participants know the game length is 10 rounds (p. 8).  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it? No. The game length is fixed and not experimentally manipulated.

13) ARE PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN (DO PLAYERS KNOW HOW MUCH THEIR PEERS GAINED/LOST EACH ROUND)?  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter? Partially. After each round, participants see how much everyone contributed (and in the punishment condition, they can observe how many punishment points each player received and assigned). They also see their own earnings. However, the paper does not examine systematically altering the information displayed.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it? No. There is only one information condition.

14) WHEN A PLAYER IS PUNISHED, DO THEY KNOW WHO THE SPECIFIC PUNISHER IS?  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter? They make clear that decisions are anonymous (p. 6, p. 16). There is no indication that the punished player learns the identity of the punisher.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it? No.

15) WHEN A PLAYER IS REWARDED, DO THEY KNOW WHO THE SPECIFIC REWARDER IS?  
• Does the paper discuss this parameter? This is not applicable because there is no reward phase.  
• Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying it? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
• The study primarily measures individual and group contributions to the public good. It also reports payoff levels (p. 7, p. 12) and maximum possible payoff (16 euros on average if everyone contributed fully), but the term “efficiency” (actual payoff divided by maximum possible) is not used as the focal dependent variable. The paper’s main dependent variable is contribution behavior. It also reports participants’ actual earnings, but efficiency (in the sense of the ratio between actual and maximum payoffs) is not separately analyzed as a distinct outcome.  

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Mentioned in some form:  
  (1) Number of players (fixed at 4),  
  (2) Number of rounds (fixed at 10),  
  (6) MPCR = 0.4 for each token,  
  (7) Punishment cost schedule,  
  (8) Punishment magnitude.  
• The other parameters (3–5, 9–11, and 12–15) are either not manipulated or appear only as fixed conditions (e.g., downward anonymity). In total, 5 of the 15 parameters are explicitly reported (though not all are deeply analyzed).

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• None. The paper uses only a two‐condition design (punishment vs. no punishment). It does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters (e.g., group size, cost, or magnitude of punishment) to compare outcomes. Thus, there is no quantitative or qualitative prediction or effect size regarding how changes in these 15 parameters would alter the punishment treatment effect.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
• The paper does not discuss systematic variations of the 15 parameters, so it offers no direct basis for predicting how different group sizes, different MPCRs, different punishment costs, etc., would shift efficiency. Apart from noting that punishment strongly increases contributions (and thus increases total payoffs), the study does not provide numerical effect sizes for how altering one of those parameters would further impact efficiency. Therefore, based solely on this paper, one can make little to no specific prediction about how systematically varying these parameters would affect overall efficiency. The only solid finding is that enabling a punishing mechanism increases contributions relative to no‐punishment—but the paper does not extend that to systematically vary or analyze any of the 15 parameters in question.

Authors: Dannenberg, A; Haita-Falah, C; Zitzelsberger, S
Author Full Names: Dannenberg, Astrid; Haita-Falah, Corina; Zitzelsberger, Sonja
Article Title: Voting on the threat of exclusion in a public goods experiment
Author Keywords: Public goods experiment; Cooperation; Ostracism; Institutional choice; Social preferences
Keywords Plus: OSTRACISM; COOPERATION; PUNISHMENT; SANCTIONS; BENEFITS; FAIRNESS; LEGAL; GAME
Abstract: Ostracism is practiced by virtually all societies around the world as a means of enforcing cooperation. In this paper, we use a public goods experiment to study whether groups choose to implement an institution that allows for the exclusion of members. We distinguish between a costless exclusion institution and a costly exclusion institution that, if chosen, reduces the endowment of all players. We also provide a comparison with an exclusion institution that is exogenously imposed upon groups. A significant share of the experimental groups choose the exclusion institution, even when it comes at a cost, and the support for the institution increases over time. Average contributions to the public good are significantly higher when the exclusion option is available, not only because low contributors are excluded but also because high contributors sustain a higher cooperation level under the exclusion institution. Subjects who vote in favor of the exclusion institution contribute more than those who vote against it, but only when the institution is implemented. These results are largely inconsistent with standard economic theory but can be better explained by assuming heterogeneous groups in which some players have selfish and others have social preferences.

Abstract: Scheler (1973) proposed a model of punishment intended to re-establish a reconciled relationship between a harm doer and the person(s) harmed. Punishment was followed by genuine forgiveness, seeking genuine repentance from the harm doer, leading to the reconciliation of the relationship. This paper proposed that only a punisher having the character of a Knight of Faith (Kierkegaard 1985) could effectively implement this punishment process. It is argued that this process is more effective in achieving reconciliation and re-establishing effective relationships than traditional retributive approaches as typified by the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, enacted in response to the Enron and WorldCom scandals.

Article Title: Triggers for cooperative behavior in the thermodynamic limit: A case study in Public goods game
Abstract: In this work, we aim to answer the question: what triggers cooperative behavior in the thermodynamic limit by taking recourse to the Public goods game. Using the idea of mapping the 1D Ising model Hamiltonian with nearest neighbor coupling to payoffs in game theory, we calculate the Magnetization of the game in the thermodynamic limit. We observe that punishment acts as an external field for the two player Public goods game triggering cooperation or provide strategy, while cost can be a trigger for suppressing cooperation or free riding. Finally, reward also acts as a trigger for providing, while the role of inverse temperature (fluctuations in choices) is to introduce randomness in strategic choices.

Abstract: An important part of the debate about self versus state-governance involves a discussion about enforcement mechanisms. While some scholars argue that private enforcement mechanisms work sufficiently well in supporting cooperation, others cite the downfalls of private mechanisms so as to legitimize government enforcement. This paper focuses on the interplay between government and private enforcement mechanisms. Using an experimental approach, we demonstrate two results. Authors: Roberts, G
Author Full Names: Roberts, Gilbert
Article Title: When Punishment Pays
Keywords Plus: STRONG RECIPROCITY; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; COSTLY PUNISHMENT; NEURAL BASIS; EVOLUTION; COOPERATION; BEHAVIOR; SELECTION; BENEFITS
Abstract: Explaining cooperation in groups remains a key problem because reciprocity breaks down between more than two. Punishing individuals who contribute little provides a potential answer but changes the dilemma to why pay the costs of punishing which, like cooperation itself, provides a public good. Nevertheless, people are observed to punish others in behavioural economic games, posing a problem for existing theory which highlights the difficulty in explaining the spread and persistence of punishment. Here, I consider the apparent mismatch between theory and evidence and show by means of instructive analysis and simulation how much of the experimental evidence for punishment comes from scenarios in which punishers may expect to obtain a net benefit from punishing free-riders. In repeated games within groups, punishment works by imposing costs on defectors so that it pays them to switch to cooperating. Both punishers and non-punishers then benefit from the resulting increase in cooperation, hence investing in punishment can constitute a social dilemma. However, I show the conditions in which the benefits of increased cooperation are so great that they more than offset the costs of punishing, thereby removing the temptation to free-ride on others' investments and making punishment explicable in terms of direct self-interest. Crucially, this is because of the leveraging effect imposed in typical studies whereby people can pay a small cost to inflict a heavy loss on a punished individual. In contrast to previous models suggesting punishment is disadvantaged when rare, I show it can invade until it comes into a producer-scrounger equilibrium with non-punishers. I conclude that adding punishment to an iterated public goods game can solve the problem of achieving cooperation by removing the social dilemma.

In line with your instructions, all references below rely solely on the text, figures, and tables in Roberts (2013), and all mentions of “efficiency” (defined as actual total payoff divided by the fully cooperative payoff) are noted carefully.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players (group size)
   • Discussed? Yes. The paper uses group size g as a core parameter (most simulations use g = 3, with some results given for g = 8 and g = 20).  
   • Systematic variation or prediction of its effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
     – The author shows analytically and via simulations that as group size increases, punishment can still “pay” (i.e., become self‐interested) only if the synergy factor k is large enough to satisfy the inequality k > g·p / (p + q). That condition ensures that punishment can help sustain cooperation.  
     – However, the paper never reports the effects in terms of group “efficiency” (i.e., total payoff over maximum possible). Instead, it focuses on whether punishment can invade, how much cooperation emerges, and whether punishers vs. non‐punishers get higher or lower average payoffs.  
     – No numerical effect size is provided for how group size alone changes “the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”

2) Number of rounds
   • Discussed? Yes. The paper repeatedly emphasizes repeated interactions; simulations use m = 20 by default, but the author checks m = 1, 4, 20, 30.  
   • Systematic variation or prediction of its effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
     – The paper reports that with only 1 round (m=1), punishment does not elevate cooperation or payoff. Increasing the number of meetings (e.g., from 1 to 4 or more) makes punishment far more likely to “pay,” because there is time for defectors to switch to cooperation after being punished. Hence, cooperation rises sharply once m ≥ 4.  
     – Again, these results are reported in terms of proportions of cooperators and punishers, not explicitly in terms of group efficiency. No quantitative effect size is given for efficiency.

3) Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussed? No. The paper makes no mention of communication or “chat” between participants. There is no statement about systematically varying communication.

   • No direct statement is given about systematically manipulating “all or nothing” rules, and no effect size is reported.

5) Is the contribution default?
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not mention any default rules about how much of one’s endowment is “automatically contributed” or “moved back from a public fund.” No systematic variation of such a design.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters (e.g., multiplication factor)
   • Discussed? Yes. Roberts (2013) uses a parameter k that multiplies the group’s total contribution and then divides that by group size g. This is effectively the synergy factor.  
   • Systematic variation or prediction of its effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
     – Yes. For instance, Table 2 (“The leveraging effect of cost to benefit ratios…”) varies k/g (which is the per‐capita return) and also varies p and q. The paper shows that if k > g·p / (p + q), punishment increases cooperation markedly and can be self‐interested (i.e., beneficial to the punisher).  
     – Although these outcomes are described in terms of the percentage of cooperators and punishers, no separate measure of “efficiency” is reported. No numeric effect size for “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” is given.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment (p)
   • Discussed? Yes. The entire analysis hinges on p (the punisher’s cost) vs. q (the cost inflicted on the punished). The paper examines scenarios with, for example, p=1, q=3, and also lower values (p=0.2) or matched values (p=1, q=1).  
   • Systematic variation or prediction of its effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
     – Yes, in Table 2 and throughout the simulations, p is systematically varied alongside q and the synergy factor. The central finding is that punishment can stabilize cooperation (and yield higher group payoffs) when p < q · (b / c).

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Discussed? No. No mention of rewards or their costs.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)
    • Discussed? No. Same as above; no mention of a reward stage.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much others gained or lost)?
    • Discussed? No. There is no mention of revealing peer payoffs or peer outcomes.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who specifically punished them?
    • Discussed? No. There is no discussion of anonymity vs. identification of the punisher.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who rewarded them?
    • Discussed? No. Reward is not considered in the paper at all, so nothing is stated here.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   • The paper’s central dependent variables are proportions of cooperators, proportions of punishers, and average (or total) payoff each type of agent achieves. B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Five parameters appear explicitly:  
       1) Number of players (group size g).  
       2) Number of rounds (m).  
       6) MPCR or multiplication factor (k, or equivalently b and c).  
       7) Punishment cost p.  
       8) Punishment magnitude q.  
   • All other parameters, including whether chat is enabled, whether contributions are “all or nothing,” reward structure, knowledge of punisher identity, etc., are not discussed.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each is systematically varied?  
   • The paper systematically varies:  
       – Group size (Parameter 1).  
       – Number of rounds (Parameter 2).  
       – The MPCR or factor (Parameter 6).  
       – Punishment cost p (Parameter 7).  
       – Punishment magnitude q (Parameter 8).  
   • The dependent variables under these manipulations are (i) whether punishment can invade or be stable, (ii) proportions of cooperators and punishers, and (iii) average individual payoffs. The paper does not give an explicit numeric “treatment effect” on efficiency for these parameters.  

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   • Because the paper never reports efficiency as “actual total payoff / maximum payoff,” direct inferences are limited. Nonetheless, Roberts (2013) strongly indicates that:  
       1) Smaller group sizes and higher MPCRs (k/g) make it more likely that punishment raises cooperation, which in turn raises payoffs. This would presumably raise efficiency if punishment prompts nearly full cooperation.  
       2) More rounds (larger m) help punishment “pay” because there is time for defectors to switch to cooperation, so punishment likely yields higher overall payoffs (and hence would improve efficiency) in repeated settings.  
       3) Punishment can be self‐interested if p < q · (b / c). Whenever that threshold is met, adding punishment substantially increases cooperation; presumably this would also increase efficiency.  
       4) None of the other parameters (chat, reward, knowledge of punisher, etc.) can be inferred from the paper, as they are not mentioned.  

In short, Roberts (2013) gives us a clear picture of how group size, number of rounds, and certain cost–benefit parameters (p, q, k) influence whether punishment becomes stable and increases cooperation. However, the paper does not directly measure “efficiency,” so it offers no numerical effect sizes on the punishment treatment effect in terms of actual‐versus‐maximum payoffs.

   • The paper does not use “group efficiency” (actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff) as its primary dependent variable.  
   • Instead, it discusses “cooperation” (e.g., whether players contribute in public goods games) and “punishment willingness” or “defection.” It also presents payoff calculations in illustrative scenarios—e.g., how cooperators’ versus defectors’ payoffs compare after various punishment methods—but it does not report or predict “efficiency” per se as distinct from those payoff considerations.  

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
     1) Number of players (the paper references 4 vs. 30)  
     7) Punishment cost ratio (indirectly, cost‐to‐punisher is 1, cost‐to‐defector is 2 in TPP)  
     8) Punishment magnitude (the defector loses 2 units of payoff)  
     13) Are peer outcomes shown? (indirectly, referring to Milinski et al.’s design)  
   • None of the remaining 11 parameters are discussed.  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None of the parameters are discussed in terms of systematically varying them. The paper uses fixed scenarios (e.g., 4 players vs. 30 players, cost ratio 1:2, etc.) to illustrate arguments about reciprocity and punishment but does not report a quantitative or predictive model about how those variations change a punishment “treatment effect.”  

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not give explicit guidance for predicting changes in efficiency based on systematic parameter changes. Its examples concern (1) small vs. larger groups, and (2) the difference between punishing by “exclusion from future cooperation” (TPR) versus “direct costly punishment” (TPP). It emphasizes that depending on how many cooperators vs. defectors are present, one punishment method may be “overpunishing” or “underpunishing.” However, there is no direct statement about overall efficiency gains/losses in a strict sense—and certainly no numerical effect sizes. Consequently, one cannot predict how the 15 parameters, individually or in interaction, would alter a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” using only evidence from this paper. Beyond that, the paper offers little or no basis for quantitative predictions.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter check of what this paper (Mieth et al.) does and does not say with respect to the 15 public‐goods‐game parameters you listed. Afterward, you will find the required four‐part summary.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. NUMBER OF PLAYERS
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   – Yes, but only in the sense that the authors use a two‐player (dyadic) version of a Prisoner’s Dilemma game with a punishment option. There is one “participant” and one “partner” in each interaction.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how changing it would affect punishment’s effect?  
   – No. The paper does not vary “number of players” nor predict any effect of changing this parameter on punishment or on any outcome variable.

2. NUMBER OF ROUNDS
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   – They conduct multiple one‐shot interactions: each participant plays exactly 40 trials (20 interactions with female faces, 20 with male faces). However, there is no multi‐round interaction with the same partner.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how changing it would affect punishment’s effect?  
   – No. The number of trials is fixed (40). The paper does not test or predict how different numbers of rounds/trials would affect the results.

3. IS CHAT ENABLED?
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   – No. There is no mention of any chat, messaging, or discussion between participants in these experiments.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict its effect?  
   – No mention at all.

4. IS THE CONTRIBUTION “ALL OR NOTHING”?
 • Does the paper discuss it or set it?  
   – Yes. The game is a Prisoner’s Dilemma with a binary cooperate/defect choice; cooperating costs 30 cents, defecting costs 0 cents. So contributions are “all or nothing.”  
 • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how changing it would affect punishment’s effect?  
   – No. This aspect is held constant across all trials and experiments, with no reported variations or predictions about changing this parameter.

5. IS THE CONTRIBUTION DEFAULT?
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   – No. Participants simply make a binary decision each trial (cooperate or defect); there is no mention of setting one’s own “default” or shifting one’s endowment.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict any effect?  
   – No mention at all.

6. MARGINAL PER CAPITA RETURN (MPCR) OR MULTIPLICATION FACTOR
 • Does the paper discuss it or set it?  
   – Yes, indirectly. The authors mention a 1/3 “bonus” from the combined contributions, which is then split evenly, resulting in typical Prisoner’s Dilemma payoffs.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict its effect?  
   – No. The factor is fixed (1/3) throughout. There is no discussion of how a changed MPCR would influence punishment’s effects.

7. PUNISHMENT COST TO IMPOSE A SINGLE UNIT OF PUNISHMENT
 • Does the paper discuss it or set it?  
   – Yes. It costs the participant 1 cent for each “unit” of punishment imposed, and each cent spent subtracts 10 cents from the partner’s balance.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict its effect?  
   – No. The cost is always 1:10 and is never varied experimentally. The paper does not predict how altering that ratio would affect punishment or any dependent variable.

8. PUNISHMENT MAGNITUDE (DEDUCTION PER UNIT OF PUNISHMENT)
 • Does the paper discuss it or set it?  
   – Yes. As noted, 1 cent spent imposes 10 cents of punishment on the other’s account.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict its effect?  
   – No. They keep that magnitude constant (10 cents deducted per 1 cent spent) and do not speculate on alternatives.

9. WHETHER A REWARD IS ENABLED
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   – No. There is no mention of any prosocial reward mechanism, only a punishment option.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict its effect?  
   – No mention at all.

10. REWARD COST TO GRANT A SINGLE UNIT OF REWARD
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   – No. Rewards are not part of the design.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict its effect?  
   – No mention at all.

11. REWARD MAGNITUDE (AWARDED FOR EACH UNIT OF REWARD)
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   – No. Rewards are not part of the design.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict its effect?  
   – No mention at all.

12. IS THE NUMBER OF ROUNDS KNOWN TO PLAYERS?
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   – The paper does not specify whether participants explicitly knew “40 total trials” in a way that might affect their strategic thinking. The authors do not highlight any variation or concealment of the number of trials.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict its effect?  
   – No mention of systematically manipulating round‐number information or how that would matter for punishment.

13. ARE PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN (I.E., DOES EACH PLAYER KNOW ITS PEERS’ GAINS/LOSSES)?
 • Does the paper discuss it or set it?  
   – Yes. After each trial, participants see how many cents the partner gained/lost and see updated balances. However, it is simply displayed to them as part of the Prisoner’s Dilemma framing; it is not manipulated or varied.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict its effect?  
   – No. The display is constant throughout the study, with no mention of comparing different information‐disclosure conditions.

14. WHEN A PLAYER IS PUNISHED, DO THEY KNOW WHO THE SPECIFIC PUNISHER IS?
 • Does the paper discuss it or set it?  
   – Since each “partner” is just the single opponent on a given trial, participants can see that the punishment came from that partner (or from the participant’s side). However, the authors do not treat this as a condition or vary it.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict its effect?  
   – No. They do not manipulate whether the punisher is anonymous.

15. WHEN A PLAYER IS REWARDED, DO THEY KNOW WHO THE REWARDER IS?
 • Does the paper discuss it or set it?  
   – No. Rewarding does not exist in this design.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict its effect?  
   – Not applicable.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   – No. The authors never measure or report “group efficiency,” “total payoff relative to the maximum,” or “group‐level efficiency.” Instead, they study:  
     • The participant’s probability of cooperation.  
     • The probability of each “type” of punishment (moralistic, hypocritical, irrational, antisocial).  
     • The total (aggregated) amount of money spent on punishment.  
     • The harshness (i.e., how many cents spent) once punishment is chosen.  
   These outcomes differ from efficiency because they do not gauge whether the group payoff is near or far from the maximal cooperative outcome.

B) Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   – Mentioned in passing or fixed in the design:  
     • (1) Number of players → Always two, not varied.  
     • (2) Number of rounds → Always 40 one‐shot encounters, not varied.  
     • (4) Contribution is all or nothing (cooperate vs. defect).  
     • (6) MPCR or factor → 1/3.  
     • (7) Punishment cost → 1 cent per unit.  
     • (8) Punishment magnitude → 10 cents deducted per 1 cent spent.  
     • (13) Peer outcomes shown → Yes, but not systematically varied.  
   – Not mentioned (or not part of the design at all): (3), (5), (9), (10), (11), (12), (14), (15).  
   Overall, the paper references or sets 7 of the 15 parameters (without varying them).

C) For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when systematically varied?  
   – None. The authors do not systematically manipulate any of these parameters. Thus, there is no direct discussion within the paper of how changing any of these 15 parameters would affect punishment’s impact on any outcome variable (efficiency or otherwise). The text only reports results under a single, fixed setting of each parameter (e.g., the punishment ratio remains at 1:10; the game is always two‐player, etc.).

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   – The paper never measures efficiency, never varies these parameters, and never connects them to efficiency. Accordingly, it offers no direct basis to predict how changes in these 15 parameters would alter the impact of punishment on group efficiency. Any speculation about those parameters’ effects on efficiency would go beyond what the text provides. The safest conclusion is that little to no prediction can be made solely from the present paper’s content.
reference_APA: Mieth, Laura, Buchner, Axel & Bell, Raoul (2017). Effects of Gender on Costly Punishment. JOURNAL OF BEHAVIORAL DECISION MAKING.

Below I go through the requested 15 design parameters one‐by‐one and check what the paper actually says about each of them, always keeping in mind that the outcome studied in the article is the evolutionary success (stationary abundance, fixation probability, fixation time) of a *strategy* that combines in-group cooperation with out-group punishment (called “CP” in the paper).  
Whenever the authors talk about “payoff” I report it, but I always point out that the paper never reports *group efficiency* (total earnings divided by the cooperative optimum) and never analyses any *treatment effect* obtained by *adding* a punishment stage to an otherwise identical public–goods game.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players (group size)  
   • Discussed? YES.  The population size N is varied in the analytical expressions and in Figs. 2 & 3 (examples: N = 10, 20; the surface plot in Fig. 3 spans N≈5–100).  
   • Systematic prediction? YES, but only for the *stationary probability of the CP strategy*, not for efficiency.  
     – For low mutation and weak selection the critical benefit-to-cost ratio that makes CP more frequent than ¼ is given by b > g(N)·c + f(N)(α–γ) where g(N)↓3 and f(N)↓1 as N increases (Appendix B).  
     – Qualitative effect: larger N lowers the threshold b and therefore *helps* CP; no numbers about efficiency are given.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? NO.  The evolutionary model is a continuous Moran process; there is no “round” parameter.

3. Is chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned? NO.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Mentioned? NO.

5. Contribution default / endowment framing?  
   • Mentioned? NO.

6. MPCR (multiplication factor of a public good)  
   • Not literally used, but the analogue in the paper is the *benefit of cooperation* b and the *cost* c.  
   • Systematic prediction? YES, again only for CP abundance.  
     – Key inequalities:  
       • Low mutation, large N: CP favoured if  
         b > c                       when c < (γ–α)/2  
         b > 3c + (α–γ)   otherwise.  
       – Numerical values shown in Fig. 1 (panels a–d) and Fig. 2. No efficiency results.

7. Punishment cost (to punisher)  
   • Parameter α in the model.  
   • Systematic prediction? YES (for CP abundance). Lower α (holding γ fixed) expands the parameter region in which CP is favoured. Explicit expressions are contained in the same inequalities reported under (6) (α always enters through γ–α).

8. Punishment magnitude (fine imposed)  
   • Parameter γ.  
   • Systematic prediction? YES.  A larger γ (holding α fixed) favours CP; if γ–α is very large the condition for CP collapses to the ordinary altruism condition b > c (text, Sect. 3.1).

9. Reward enabled?  
10. Reward cost?  
11. Reward magnitude?  
   • Mentioned? NO for all three.  Rewards do not appear in the model.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
14. Do punished players know the punisher?  
15. Do rewarded players know the rewarder?  
   • Mentioned? NO for all four.  The model is not an experiment with information treatments.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used in the paper  
   • Stationary *probability* (abundance) of each strategy (main focus is CP).  
   • Fixation probability and fixation time.  
   • Average pay-off of each strategy under high mutation (used only to show CP is never favoured in that limit).  
   • *Group efficiency, total payoff, or average payoff of the group as a percentage of the cooperative optimum is never reported.*

B. How many of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   • Mentioned: 4 out of 15 →  
     (1) Number of players (N)  
     (6) Benefit & cost of cooperation (analogue of MPCR)  
     (7) Punishment cost α  
     (8) Punishment magnitude γ  
   • All other parameters are absent.

C. How many parameters are *systematically varied* and analysed for their impact on a punishment treatment effect?  
   • Strictly speaking, *zero*.  The paper never defines a “punishment treatment effect” and never measures efficiency.  
   • The four mentioned parameters *are* systematically varied, but only to predict which parameter combinations make the punishing-cooperator strategy more abundant than ¼ of the stationary state.

D. What predictions about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment treatment effect on efficiency can be made solely from this paper?  
   • Practically none.  Because the paper gives no efficiency data and no treatment contrast (with-punishment vs. without-punishment), it is impossible to translate its results into quantitative or even qualitative predictions about *group efficiency*.  
   • At best, one could conjecture that parameter sets (large γ–α, moderate b/c, moderate-to-large N, low mutation) that make the punishing-cooperator strategy common might *indirectly* raise efficiency relative to a no-punishment scenario, but this is not demonstrated in the paper and therefore cannot be asserted on the requested “paper-only” basis.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
In short, the article is an analytical study of evolutionary stability of a parochial-altruism strategy, not an experimental study of punishment treatments, and it offers no direct evidence about how any of the 15 design parameters would change the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.
reference_APA: Gao, Shiping, Wu, Te & Wang, Long (2015). Emergence of parochial altruism in well-mixed populations. PHYSICS LETTERS A.

Below, each of the 15 parameters is treated in turn.

For every parameter we report  
(i) whether the paper mentions or fixes the parameter (including its value, if given) and  
(ii) whether the paper systematically varies that parameter and links those variations to the **punishment treatment effect** (i.e. the difference between a game with punishment and the most comparable version without punishment).  Whenever the paper provides quantitative information we cite the relevant figure or equation; otherwise we describe the result qualitatively.  When the paper is silent we say so explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. NUMBER OF PLAYERS (-group size N)  
(i) Mentioned.  Most simulations use N = 5; Fig. 1 once uses N = 6.  
(ii) Not systematically varied.  The authors make only one qualitative remark (“with the increment of size the loner will become a beneficial selection…”), but no simulation, figure, table or numerical effect size is supplied, and no explicit comparison between “with-punishment” and “no-punishment” conditions is reported.

2. NUMBER OF ROUNDS  
(i) Not mentioned.  The model is an evolutionary dynamical system; time is continuous, not a finite sequence of rounds.  
(ii) No variation, no prediction.

3. CHAT ENABLED?  
Not mentioned at all.

4. ALL-OR-NOTHING CONTRIBUTION?  
(i) Implicitly fixed at “all” (cooperators and punishers always invest the full cost c, defectors invest 0).  
(ii) Never varied, no prediction.

5. CONTRIBUTION DEFAULT / WITHDRAWAL FRAME?  
Not discussed.

6. MPCR / MULTIPLICATION FACTOR r  
(i) Mentioned and numerically varied.  Typical parameter set: c = 1, r ranges in Figs. 5 & 6.  
(ii) Systematically varied in Fig. 5 (three panels):

   • Fig. 5a  – compulsory PGG (no loner, no punishment)  
   • Fig. 5b  – voluntary PGG without punishment  
   • Fig. 5c  – voluntary PGG **with** punishment  

   Comparison of Fig. 5b vs Fig. 5c therefore isolates the punishment treatment effect as r changes.  Qualitative results only: as r increases, the frequency of cooperators (and cooperators + punishers combined) grows faster when punishment is available; defectors fall.  No efficiency measure or exact numbers are printed; curves are presented graphically, without a table.

   Fig. 6 reports pay-offs as a function of r **only for the punished game**, so the incremental effect on efficiency cannot be extracted.

7. COST TO IMPOSE PUNISHMENT (γ)  
(i) Mentioned.  Fixed at γ = 0.3 in all examples.  
(ii) Never varied, no prediction.

8. PUNISHMENT MAGNITUDE (β)  
(i) Mentioned.  Fixed at β = 1.0.  
(ii) Never varied, no prediction.

9. REWARD ENABLED?  
Not part of the model; rewards are absent, so there is no discussion.

10–11. REWARD COST / REWARD MAGNITUDE  
Not applicable (no reward option).

12. IS THE NUMBER OF ROUNDS KNOWN?  
Not relevant to the evolutionary model; not discussed.

13. ARE PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN?  
Not discussed.

14. IS THE PUNISHER IDENTIFIED?  
Not discussed.

15. IS THE REWARDER IDENTIFIED?  
Not discussed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables used  
   • Strategy frequencies (proportions of C, D, P, L).  
   • Individual pay-offs for each strategy type.  
   • Average (population-mean) pay-off (Fig. 6).  
   The paper never computes “group efficiency” in the sense of (total realised pay-off) ÷ (maximum possible pay-off of full cooperation).  Consequently, all results concern different dependent variables from the one requested.

B.  Parameters mentioned (at least once): 4 of 15  
   1 (group size N)  
   6 (MPCR r)  
   7 (punishment cost γ)  
   8 (punishment magnitude β)

C.  Parameters whose **systematic variation** is analysed with respect to a punishment treatment effect: 1 of 15  
   • Parameter 6 (MPCR r): Fig. 5 compares games with and without punishment over several r-values and shows that punishment raises cooperation frequencies when r is larger, though no numerical coefficients are provided.  

   No other parameter is varied in a way that isolates a punishment treatment effect.

D.  What can be predicted—solely from this paper—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?

   • Because efficiency itself is never measured, the paper allows only indirect conjectures.  The lone parameter whose variation is studied (r) raises both cooperation and average pay-off in the punished game; hence one may cautiously predict that a higher MPCR will increase the punishment treatment’s positive impact on efficiency.  

   • The authors hint (without data) that larger groups may make loners more attractive; absent new simulations, the efficiency effect of punishment in bigger groups remains unknown.  

   • No evidence is given about punishment cost, punishment magnitude, any reward parameters, communication, information conditions, number of rounds, or contribution framing, so no predictions about those factors can be extracted from the paper.

   Therefore, based on the provided article alone, almost no quantitative prediction about the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency can be made, except the qualitative expectation that a larger multiplication factor r should strengthen that effect.

Abstract: Third-party punishment can promote fair behavior. However, the mechanisms by which this happens are unclear. Third-party punishment may increase fair behavior by providing direct feedback, helping shape the behavior of those punished, or through an influence on reputation, by encouraging the transgressor to behave appropriately before a third-party audience. Below, each of the 15 candidate moderator-parameters is treated in turn.  For every parameter I indicate  

(1) whether it is explicitly described in the article (and, if so, its value), and  
(2) whether the paper contains any prediction or empirical estimate for how **changing** that parameter would alter the size of the “punishment treatment effect’’ (Direct-Feedback condition minus the control condition(s)).  Numerical effect‐sizes are quoted exactly as they appear in the text or in Table 1.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Number of players  
    • Mentioned?  YES.  Each game involves three roles: the child dictator, an absent peer recipient, and (depending on condition) a third-party observer or punisher.  The number of players is fixed at 3 in every condition.  
    • Systematic variation / prediction?  NO.  The study never manipulates the number of players nor speculates on how adding or removing players would change the punishment effect.

2.  Number of rounds  
    • Mentioned?  YES.  Every child makes 6 forced-choice allocations (called “trials”).  
    • Systematic variation / prediction?  PARTIALLY.  Although the total number of rounds is not varied between groups, **trial number is analysed as a continuous moderator**.  
        – Model 3 (Table 1) reports a significant Condition × Trial interaction:  
          • Direct-Feedback vs. Baseline: OR = 2.45 (SE = 0.25, z = 3.55, p < .001).  
          • Direct-Feedback vs. Reputation: OR = 2.18 (SE = 0.25, z = 3.13, p = .002).  
        – Interpretation given by authors: additional opportunities for punishment across rounds magnify the punishment treatment effect.  
        – No estimate is given for what would happen if the game had, say, 20 vs. 2 rounds; therefore only a within-experiment (z-scored-trial) effect is available.

3.  Chat enabled between players  
    • Mentioned?  NO.  Children never communicate with peers or with the punisher/observer beyond the scripted demonstration.  
    • Systematic variation / prediction?  NO.

4.  All-or-nothing contribution format  
    • Mentioned?  YES, indirectly.  The task is a forced-choice dictator game (only two discrete allocations per trial).  However this “all-or-nothing’’ feature is not contrasted with a continuous-choice format.  
    • Systematic variation / prediction?  NO.

5.  Contribution default (endowment already in the public fund)  
    • Mentioned?  NO.  Not relevant to the design.

6.  MPCR / multiplication factor  
    • Mentioned?  NO.

7.  Punishment **cost** to punisher  
    • Mentioned?  YES.  Each time the experimenter punishes, she forfeits one of her own tokens (cannot exchange it for candy).  Cost = 1 token.  
    • Systematic variation / prediction?  NO.  Cost is held constant.

8.  Punishment **magnitude** (loss imposed on target)  
    • Mentioned?  YES.  When punished, the child loses **all** tokens from that trial, while the recipient still receives hers.  
    • Systematic variation / prediction?  NO.  Magnitude is fixed; no dose–response analysis is reported.

9.  Reward enabled  
    • Mentioned?  NO.  There is no reward option in any condition.

10. Reward cost  
    • Mentioned?  NO.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Mentioned?  NO.

12. Horizon known (are subjects told how many rounds remain?)  
    • Mentioned?  NOT EXPLICITLY.  The paper never states whether children were informed there would be exactly six trials.  
    • Systematic variation / prediction?  NO.

13. Peer-outcome visibility  
    • Mentioned?  YES (constant).  After each decision the child sees both her own and the recipient’s token bag.  
    • Systematic variation / prediction?  NO.

14. Punisher identity revealed  
    • Mentioned?  YES.  The punisher is an adult experimenter sitting next to the child; identity is always known.  
    • Systematic variation / prediction?  NO.

15. Rewarder identity revealed  
    • Mentioned?  NO (because no reward).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables used  
    • The study’s sole quantitative DV is the binary choice of the **fairer vs. less-fair** allocation (coded as “less-selfish = 1, more-selfish = 0”).  
    • “Fairness’’ is thus measured as the proportion of trials in which the child selects the fairer split.  
    • No measure of group-level **efficiency** (total or average payoff) is reported or analysed.

B.  How many of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
    • Eight:  (1) number of players, (2) number of rounds, (4) forced-choice format, (7) punishment cost, (8) punishment magnitude, (13) peer-outcome visibility, (14) punisher identity, plus indirectly that no reward is available (9–11, 15 absent).  

C.  How many parameters are analysed for their **systematic** impact on the punishment treatment effect?  
    • Exactly ONE: parameter 2 (trial / round number).  The paper provides odds‐ratios showing that, relative to controls, the punishment effect grows over successive trials.

D.  If forced to predict how the full set of 15 parameters (and their interactions) would shape the punishment treatment effect on group **efficiency**, using only evidence in this article:  
    • The only clear prediction is that giving players **multiple repeated rounds** (parameter 2) should strengthen the efficiency gain from allowing punishment, because fairness rises over time in the Direct-Feedback condition.  
    • For all other parameters the paper is silent; therefore no evidence-based prediction can be made about their main effects or interactions on efficiency.  Any additional forecast would require information outside the scope of the present article and must be left unspecified.

Below I step through the 15 design parameters in the order given by the prompt.  
For each parameter I state  

(1) Whether the parameter appears anywhere in Fishman (2006) and, if so, the value(s) actually used in the model.  
(2) Whether the paper **systematically varies** that parameter and, if it does, whether any numerical effect on a *punishment treatment effect* is reported.  I quote or point to the relevant figure / equation whenever possible.  
“Punishment-treatment effect” is taken to mean the difference in some outcome between a situation **with** punishment and an otherwise identical situation **without** punishment.  The paper’s closest analogue is the comparison of an “empathic-retaliator” strategy (ER, which does retaliate—i.e., punishes defection) with strategies that do not retaliate (UA—unconditional altruist) or that retaliate differently (UD—unconditional defector, TFT—tit-for-tat).

Because the paper studies **pairwise direct reciprocity** and never studies public-goods groups, almost all public-goods design parameters below are simply **not present**.

------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Always exactly 2; hard-wired by the direct-reciprocity model.  
   (2) Never varied.  No effect sizes reported.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Rounds per lifetime are stochastic, Poisson distributed with mean μ (called “the parameter of the pertinent Poisson distribution”).  
   (2) μ is systematically varied.  Figures 1–4 show how increasing μ affects several quantities that in turn determine when the *punishing* ER strategy is an ESS.  
       • Fig. 1: γ(μ)↑ with μ. ER becomes ESS when c < γ.  
       • Fig. 2: ξ(μ)↓ with μ (ξ is the unstable interior equilibrium between ER and UD).  
       • Fig. 3: δ(μ)↓ with μ (probability that ER is ESS when UA can mutate to TFT).  
     Numeric example from text: “ER is an ESS whenever μ is sufficiently large; γ→1 as μ→∞.”  No direct statement about *group efficiency*.

3. Chat enabled?  
   Not mentioned.  Not varied.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   Not mentioned.

5. Contribution default (endowment first placed in public fund)?  
   Not mentioned.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   Not applicable.  Model has a fixed dyadic benefit of 1 and cost c.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   Not parameterised.  “Punishment” is modeled as **withholding the cooperative act** (retaliatory defection).  The only cost is the opportunity cost of foregone benefit, and that cost is not treated as an explicit, variable parameter.

8. Punishment magnitude  
   Not parameterised.

9. Reward enabled?  
   Not in the model.

10. Reward cost  
    Not in the model.

11. Reward magnitude  
    Not in the model.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
    Not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    Not discussed.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
    Not discussed.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
    Not applicable.

------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY  

A. Dependent variables  
   The paper never reports “group efficiency” (total payoff ÷ maximum possible).  Instead it analyses  
   • Expected *individual* payoffs (π-values).  
   • Whether a strategy is an ESS, a global attractor, or can be invaded (replicator dynamics).  
   • Interior equilibrium frequency ξ of ER.  
   These are conceptually different from efficiency because they concern evolutionary stability, not aggregate payoffs relative to the social optimum.

B. Which of the 15 parameters appear at all?  
   2 of 15.  
   • #1 (players) is implicitly 2.  
   • #2 (rounds) appears via μ.  
   All other 13 parameters are absent.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss **systematic variation** and its impact on a punishment treatment effect?  
   Only 1 parameter (#2, number of rounds via μ).  
   Increasing μ increases the parameter region in which the punishing ER strategy is an ESS and lowers the chance that ER is out-competed by TFT mutants (Figs. 1–3).  No quantitative effect on efficiency is provided.

D. Predictions one could make—*restricted solely to the paper’s content*—about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence a punishment-treatment effect on efficiency:  

   • The paper allows a qualitative prediction for parameter #2 only: *more rounds (higher μ) make a punishing strategy more evolutionarily stable relative to non-punishing ones; if higher stability translated into greater aggregate payoffs, efficiency could rise with μ.*  However, no efficiency metric is calculated, so even this prediction is speculative.  

   • For the other 14 parameters the paper offers **no information whatsoever**.  Therefore, based only on this paper, no further predictions can be made about how they or their interactions affect the efficiency impact of introducing punishment.

In short, Fishman (2006) is a theoretical analysis of pairwise direct reciprocity; it does not study public-goods punishment, group efficiency, or 13 of the 15 design parameters listed in the prompt.

Abstract: Trust game is a common framework for studying trust behavior between unrelated individuals. Previous theoretical research has found that network structure or reputation can promote trust and cooperation, but these studies often assume that interactions between players are one-time and investors have no choice but to invest, which is inconsistent with reality. Here we introduce the conditional investment strategy and government management into a repeated N-player trust game, where investors can make investment decisions based on the investment environment and the government plays the role of a regulator. We find that the introduction of the conditional investment strategy and incentives can prompt the evolution of trust. Besides, we reveal that as punishment intensity increases, not only can trust emerge but investment behavior can also be maintained. Furthermore, we verify the above theoretical results by numerical simulations.
