Below, every one of the 15 public-goods‐game (PGG) design parameters is inspected against what is **explicitly contained in the paper “N-player repeated evolutionary trust game under government management.”**  
For each parameter we state  

(1) Whether the paper even mentions the parameter and, if so, what value(s) are used;  
(2) Whether the paper says what would happen to the **punishment treatment effect** (i.e., the difference between the game with punishment/reward and the game without it) if that parameter were **systematically varied.**  
Whenever the paper gives a numerical condition (e.g., a threshold) we report it verbatim; when no information is given we say so.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Parameter-by-parameter inspection
---------------------------------

1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned. Two population sizes are defined: number of investors \(N_I\) and number of trustees \(N_T\). Baseline simulations use \(N_I=10\). Theoretical results distinguish the cases “\(N_T>1\)” and “\(N_T=1\)”.  
   (2) Systematic variation of \(N_T\) is analysed analytically.  
       • For \(N_T>1\) the punishment threshold that allows an interior equilibrium with trust is  
         \(\delta>\delta^{*}= \dfrac{(1-r)^2 R + 2r(1-r)T}{R(1-r)+rT(N_T+1)}\).  
         Thus, increasing \(N_T\) lowers the required \(\delta^{*}\) (because the denominator grows with \(N_T\)).  
       • For the extreme case \(N_T=1\) the dynamics are qualitatively different (a centre with closed orbits and no asymptotically stable interior point).  
       No efficiency measure is reported, so the paper gives no direct numbers for “efficiency treatment effect,” only for strategy composition.  

2. Number of rounds (time horizon)  
   (1) Mentioned. A continuation probability \(\omega\) is used; the expected number of rounds is \(R=1/(1-\omega)\). A fixed index \(T\) denotes the round at which the government starts to punish. Baseline example: \(R=10\) (\(\omega=0.9\)) and \(T=5\).  
   (2) The paper does not plot or tabulate how changing \(R\) or \(T\) alters the punishment treatment effect. They enter algebraically in \(\delta^{*}\) (above) but the authors never explore the comparative statics. No quantitative prediction is given.

3. Chat enabled?  
   Not mentioned at all → no prediction.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   Not discussed. (Investors pay a fixed unit “1” when they invest, but the authors never compare this with a continuous contribution mode.)

5. Contribution default / leading frame?  
   Not discussed.

6. MPCR (multiplication factor)  
   (1) Mentioned as the “relative productivity” parameter \(r\;(0<r<1)\). Baseline \(r=0.8\).  
   (2) Appears algebraically in every payoff and in \(\delta^{*}\) but its effect is not systematically explored. No plots or tables vary \(r\), so no quantitative prediction about the punishment treatment effect is provided.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   Not defined. Punishment is meted out by “the government,” not by peers; the model does not assign a cost to any human decision maker. No prediction possible.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine per unit)  
   (1) Central to the paper. Denoted \(\delta\). Values used in figures: 0.02, 0.06, 0.10, 0.22, 0.30.  
   (2) Systematically varied. Main analytical results:  
       • If \(0<\delta\le (1-r)/N_T\) the only stable equilibrium is (cautious investors, untrustworthy trustees) → punishment has **no positive treatment effect** on trust or efficiency.  
       • If \((1-r)/N_T <\delta \le \delta^{*}\) a boundary equilibrium \((0,y^{*})\) becomes stable. Some trustees are trustworthy but investors remain cautious → moderate positive effect.  
       • If \(\delta^{*}<\delta<1-r\) an interior equilibrium \((x^{**},y^{**})\) is asymptotically stable; both trust and unconditional investment coexist → largest positive effect predicted.  
       • If \(\delta\ge 1-r\) the boundary equilibrium disappears but the interior point persists; the paper calls this “can still maintain a high level of trust,” again implying a positive treatment effect.  
       No total-payoff/efficiency numbers are printed, so the magnitude of the efficiency change is unknown.

9. Reward enabled?  
   (1) Yes. Reporting an untrustworthy trustee yields the same amount \(\delta\) as a bonus to the reporter. Rewards are always “on”; no condition without rewards is examined.  
   (2) Because reward is never switched off, the paper contains no prediction about enabling vs. disabling rewards.

10. Reward cost to grant one unit  
    Not modelled—the bonus comes from a government pool with no cost to the investor. No prediction.

11. Reward magnitude  
    Same parameter \(\delta\) as for punishment. See point 8 for how varying \(\delta\) alters outcomes. The separate effect of “reward size holding punishment fixed” is not investigated.

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
    Not discussed; the model uses an undisclosed continuation probability. No prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    The government publicly announces “the number of untrustworthy trustees,” but individual payoffs are not shown. The paper never varies this information structure; no prediction.

14. Punisher identity revealed?  
    Not applicable—punisher is the government. No prediction.

15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
    As above; no prediction.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY
--------

A. Dependent variables  
   – The paper does **not** use “group efficiency” (total payoff divided by maximum possible payoff) as an outcome.  
   – Outcomes analysed are the **population shares of four strategies:** unthinking investors, cautious investors, trustworthy trustees, untrustworthy trustees. Payoffs are written down symbolically but never aggregated into an efficiency metric. Thus “efficiency” ≠ “trust level” in this paper.

B. Which of the 15 parameters appear?  
   • Explicitly treated: 1 (number of players—investors & trustees), 2 (rounds via \(R\) & \(T\)), 6 (MPCR \(r\)), 8 & 11 (punishment/reward magnitude \(\delta\)), 9 (reward is enabled).  
   • Mentioned implicitly or fixed at zero cost: none of the remaining parameters.  
   → 6 of 15 parameters are mentioned at all.

C. Which parameters are **systematically varied** and linked to the punishment treatment effect?  
   • Punishment/Reward magnitude \(\delta\) (Parameter 8/11) – Fully analysed.  
   • Number of trustees (part of Parameter 1) – Two separate analytical cases \(N_T>1\) vs \(N_T=1\).  
   No other parameter is varied.  
   → 2 of 15 parameters receive systematic “treatment-effect” discussion.

D. Predictions for the punishment treatment effect on efficiency (if one had to infer it)  
   The paper gives almost no information that can be converted into an efficiency metric, so very little can be predicted. All we know is:  
   • Increasing \(\delta\) past two thresholds \((1-r)/N_T\) and \(\delta^{*}\) successively induces (i) the appearance of some trustworthy behaviour and (ii) a stable coexistence with unconditional investment, both of which would likely raise efficiency relative to the no-punishment baseline.  
   • Larger \(N_T\), larger \(R\), and larger \(r\) all lower the critical \(\delta^{*}\) needed, so, ceteris paribus, they **amplify** the (positive) punishment treatment effect.  
   Beyond those qualitative statements, the paper offers no numbers that translate strategy composition into actual efficiency levels, so precise quantitative predictions cannot be made.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Abstract: Recently, exploration on how to sustain cooperation based on indirect reciprocity has obtained considerable concern. Below, each of the 15 parameters is considered in turn.

For every parameter we state  

(i) whether the paper even mentions it (and, if so, the value actually used), and  

(ii) whether the paper says anything about what would happen to the *punishment-treatment effect* if that parameter were *systematically varied*.

The punishment-treatment effect we have in mind is the change in **efficiency** (total group payoff relative to the social optimum) that arises when a punishment institution is present as opposed to when it is absent (StdPun, CTP0, CTP1, CTP5 vs. VCM).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  All sessions use n = 4.  
   • Systematic-variation prediction?  Only in the theoretical section.  
     –  𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐧 (the minimum number of “conditional co-operative enforcers” required to sustain cooperation) is  
        𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐧 = int[ 1 + ((1+α)(n−1) − α/c)/(α+β) ] + 1.  
        Thus, ceteris paribus, larger n ⇒ larger 𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐧 ⇒ it becomes harder for punishment to raise efficiency.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  Yes (20 rounds, fixed).  
   • Prediction?  None.  No systematic variation.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned?  Not at all.  There was no chat.  
   • Prediction?  None.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes—implicitly rejected.  Subjects could contribute any integer 0–20.  
   • Prediction?  None.

5. Contribution default / “take-back” frame?  
   • Mentioned?  No.  
   • Prediction?  None.

6. MPCR (marginal per-capita return)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  a = 0.5.  
   • Prediction?  None.

7. Punishment cost to impose 1 unit  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  A punisher pays 1 token to reduce the target’s payoff by 3 (c = 1/3 in FS notation).  
   • Systematic-variation prediction?  Purely theoretical.  In the formula for 𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐧 above, a higher c ⇒ higher 𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐧.  If c exceeds α/[(1+α)(n−1)] the required number of enforcers exceeds 1; if c falls below that threshold, one enforcer suffices.  That prediction links c negatively to the efficiency-boost that punishment can deliver.  No numerical estimates beyond the threshold condition are given and the parameter was **not** varied experimentally.

8. Punishment magnitude (victim loss per unit)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  3 tokens per unit.  
   • Prediction?  None.

9. Whether reward is enabled  
10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   • Mentioned?  No (there is no reward stage).  
   • Prediction?  None.

12. Is the horizon known?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Subjects were explicitly told there would be 20 (and only 20) rounds.  
   • Prediction?  None.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  After every contribution stage subjects saw each other’s contributions (listed in descending order) and, after the punishment stage, the *total* punishment they themselves received.  
   • Prediction?  None.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  The identity is **not** revealed (“no subject identifiers were used”).  
   • Prediction?  None.

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
   • Mentioned?  Not applicable (no rewards).  
   • Prediction?  None.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables  
    – Group efficiency / earnings (tokens per group per round) – used throughout Figures 5 and 9 and Table 5.  
    – Contribution level (group total or individual) – the main behavioural outcome.  
    – Punishment decisions (frequency and magnitude) and participation in the punishment stage.  
    – “Efficiency” is literally measured as realised total tokens; no normalisation by the social optimum is done, so efficiency and contribution are *not* the same dependent variable.

B.  Parameters that appear in the paper (8 of 15)  
    1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14.

C.  Parameters for which the paper contains *any* discussion of how varying them would change the punishment-treatment effect (2 of 15, and only in theory)  
    – # 1 Number of players (n) – via formula for 𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐧.  
    – # 7 Punishment cost (c) – same formula and related discussion.  
    No experimental evidence is supplied because neither parameter is varied in the data.

D.  What predictions about the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency can we make *solely* from this paper?  
    • Lower punishment cost (smaller c) or smaller group size (n) should reduce 𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐧, making credible punishment easier and therefore *increasing* efficiency gains from punishment.  
    • All other listed parameters are kept fixed in the study, and the paper provides no guidance on how varying them would matter; hence, beyond the two theoretical comparative-statics above, little to no prediction can be extracted.

Abstract: This paper introduces a special cooperation strategy with both punishment and reward capabilities and analyzes the effect of this strategy on cooperation evolution. Below each of the fifteen experimental‐design parameters is checked against the contents of the Pan-Wang-He paper.  For every parameter we report  

(1) Whether the paper even mentions or codes the parameter, and the value(s) used;  
(2) Whether the paper says what would happen to the *punishment treatment effect* (i.e., the change that is attributable to allowing punishment) **when that parameter is systematically varied**; if so, the qualitative or quantitative pattern is copied from the figures/tables.

Because the authors never compute *group efficiency* (total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff of a fully cooperative group) we have to rely on the only outcomes they do report—fractions of “ordinary cooperators” (C), “special cooperators” (SC, who punish and reward), “defectors” (D) and the sum of C+SC—when we talk about “treatment effects.”  Wherever the word “efficiency” would normally be used, the paper instead reports “proportion of cooperators.”  We flag this difference explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned.  A 400 × 400 square lattice → 160,000 players.  
   (2) Never varied; no prediction about how changing group size would alter the impact of punishment.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Fixed at 10,000 Monte-Carlo steps (average of last 1,000 recorded).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

3. Chat enabled?  
   (1) Not mentioned at all.  
   (2) No prediction.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule?  
   (1) Not relevant; the model is a pairwise PD matrix, not a continuous PGG.  
   (2) No prediction.

5. Contribution default / withdrawal rule?  
   (1) Not mentioned.  
   (2) No prediction.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   (1) Not in the model.  The closest analogue is the PD temptation parameter b (=T) which the authors *do* vary (1.0 ≤ b ≤ 2.0).  
   (2) They do report how raising b modifies cooperation, but never frame it as “punishment treatment vs. no-punishment.”  Thus no direct statement about MPCR-like parameters on the punishment effect.

7. Punishment *cost* to the punisher  
   (1) Not parameterised.  Special cooperators actually gain α from defectors; they do NOT pay a cost to punish.  
   (2) Therefore no prediction.

8. Punishment *magnitude* (loss inflicted on the target)  
   (1) Explicit parameter α (0.0–1.0).  
   (2) Systematically varied throughout Figs. 2, 3, 6, 8, 9.  Main pattern (for the dependent variable “total fraction of cooperators”, not efficiency):  
       • When α is very low, enabling punishment does **nothing**—cooperation ≈ 0.  
       • Increasing α into a *moderate* band produces the largest positive punishment treatment effect (sharp rise of C+SC up to ≈ 0.8–1.0 in Fig. 8).  
       • Further increases beyond that band reduce cooperation again (down-turn in Fig. 2 and the ridge in Fig. 8).  
     No numerical slope is given, only these qualitative “∩-shaped” trends.

9. Is *reward* enabled?  
   (1) Always enabled in the sense that γ can be set to 0.  The paper never compares a treatment with *punishment only* to the same game with reward turned off but punishment left on.  
   (2) No separate on/off comparison; therefore the paper provides no leverage on how simply “switching on” reward modulates the *punishment* effect.

10. Reward cost to giver  
    (1) Same parameter γ: the SC loses γ when rewarding C.  Not separated from reward magnitude.  
    (2) Not independently varied; no prediction.

11. Reward magnitude γ  
    (1) Systematically varied 0.0–1.0.  
    (2) Joint effect with punishment (Figs. 2, 3, 8, 9):  
        • At low α, changing γ has *zero* effect.  
        • At moderate α, higher γ *raises* the fraction of ordinary cooperators (Fig. 2b, Fig. 3, bright diagonal in Fig. 9a-c).  
        • At high α, further increases of γ *lower* cooperation (“over-rewarding” undermines the benefit; Fig. 2, Fig. 3).  
      Again, no numeric coefficients.

12. Are the number of rounds known to players?  
    (1) Not modelled (evolutionary simulation).  
    (2) No prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    (1) Not discussed.  
    (2) No prediction.

14. Do punishees learn who punished them?  
    (1) Not in the model.  
    (2) No prediction.

15. Do rewardees learn who rewarded them?  
    (1) Not in the model.  
    (2) No prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Does the paper use *group efficiency* as a dependent variable?  
   • No.  All dependent variables are fractions of strategies: proportion of ordinary cooperators (C), special cooperators (SC), defectors (D), and the sum C+SC.  These are *not* payoffs and therefore not the same as efficiency.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   • Six: 1 (number of players), 2 (rounds), 6* (temptation b, analogous but not identical to MPCR), 8 (punishment magnitude α), 9/11 (reward on & magnitude γ).  The remaining nine parameters never appear.

C. For which parameters does the paper discuss *systematic variation* and its effect on the punishment treatment effect (for any DV)?  
   • Two unequivocally:  
     – Punishment magnitude α (parameter 8)  
     – Reward magnitude γ (parameter 11)  
   • Temptation b (loosely tied to parameter 6) is also varied, but the paper never frames it as altering the *punishment* treatment effect, only as altering overall cooperation.  
   Hence: 2 of the 15 parameters receive direct systematic-variation analysis linked to punishment.

D. Predicting how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) will influence the punishment-treatment effect on *efficiency*, using only this paper:  
   • Because efficiency was never calculated, the only safe inference is that conditions producing more cooperators (especially more *total* cooperators C+SC) would probably yield higher efficiency *if* payoffs were re-computed.  
   • The paper suggests an inverted-U relationship for punishment magnitude α and a non-monotonic (sometimes positive, sometimes negative) interaction between α and reward magnitude γ.  
   • All other parameters either stay fixed or are absent, so the paper offers no basis for prediction about them.  Any further forecast would require assumptions not contained in the article.
reference_APA: Pan, Qiuhui, Wang, Yue & He, Mingfeng (2022). Impacts of special cooperation strategy with reward and punishment mechanism on cooperation evolution. CHAOS SOLITONS & FRACTALS.

Below I go through the 15 public-goods parameters one at a time and report exactly what can – and cannot – be learned from Fiedler & Haruvy (2016).

────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER EXTRACTION
────────────────────────────────────────

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  Groups have two players (Proposer A, Responder B) in the benchmark treatment and three players (A, B plus one Third-party C) in the monitoring, punishment and reward treatments.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  “Two vs. three” is a pre-condition for having punishment, not a factor whose levels are crossed with punishment.  The paper never estimates how changing the group size beyond those fixed values would change the *punishment treatment effect* on any outcome, let alone efficiency.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? Yes: exactly 10 rounds in every session.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  No prediction about more or fewer rounds.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned? No.  There is no chat or communication channel other than the standard feedback screens.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule?  
   • Mentioned? No.  Not relevant in a trust game.

5. Contribution default / endowment moved back?  
   • Mentioned? No.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  The amount sent by A is multiplied by three before B receives it.  This multiplier is fixed at 3 in all treatments.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  No prediction given about different multipliers.

7. Cost to impose one unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  1 Lab-Euro (L€) spent by C.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  Held constant, no discussion of what would happen if the cost were higher or lower.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss to target per unit)  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  Every L€ spent by C deducts 3 L€ from the target.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Mentioned? Yes: four mechanisms are compared – No third party, Monitoring only, Punishment, and Reward.  
   • Systematically varied relative to punishment? Reward is a separate treatment; its presence is never crossed with punishment, so there is no estimate of an interaction “reward × punishment” on efficiency.  The only comparison is that reward has *no aggregate advantage* over monitoring or punishment.

10. Cost to grant one unit of reward  
    • Mentioned? Yes.  1 L€ to C.  
    • Systematically varied? No.

11. Reward magnitude (gain to target per unit)  
    • Mentioned? Yes.  3 L€ added to the target.  
    • Systematically varied? No.

12. Do players know the number of rounds?  
    • Mentioned? Yes.  Subjects are explicitly told the game lasts 10 rounds.  
    • Systematically varied? No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mentioned? Yes.  After each round each participant sees the investment, the return, and (when applicable) the punishment/reward that directly concerns him or her.  
    • Systematically varied? No.

14. Do punished players know who punished them?  
    • Mentioned? Partially.  Players know *that* the third party punished them but not the punisher’s personal identity (all roles are anonymous).  There is only one third-party in the group, so the source is obvious but not personally identified.  
    • Systematically varied? No.

15. Do rewarded players know who rewarded them?  
    • Same answer as 14.  Mentioned but never varied.

────────────────────────────────────────
NUMERICAL EFFECTS THAT ARE ACTUALLY REPORTED
────────────────────────────────────────

The only quantitative “punishment treatment effects” directly observable in the paper are on:

• Amount sent by A  
• Proportion returned by B  
• (Indirectly) total pay-offs, discussed qualitatively

Example (Table 1):  
Random partner, No-third-party vs. Punishment  
 Amount sent rises from 4.97 L€ to 5.79 L€ (+0.82 L€, ≈ +16%).  
Fixed partner, No-third-party vs. Punishment  
 Amount sent rises from 6.32 L€ to 7.59 L€ (+1.27 L€, ≈ +20%).

The paper acknowledges “greater efficiency” but never reports the efficiency ratio (total payoff / maximum possible payoff) or any regression that uses efficiency as the dependent variable.  All regressions (Tables 2–3) use ΔAmount Sent or ΔProportion Returned or C’s Transfers.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────
A.  Dependent variables used  
    • Amount sent (investment)  
    • Proportion returned  
    • Transfers by the third party  
    • “Efficiency” is only mentioned descriptively; it is never computed or analysed as an outcome variable. So efficiency, contribution and cooperation are *not* treated as the same.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned (value stated)?  
    10 of them: 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, and implicitly 14/15.  Five parameters (3, 4, 5, 14, 15) are either absent or only implicitly present.

C.  For how many parameters is the effect of *systematically varying* that parameter on the punishment treatment effect discussed?  
    Zero.  None of the parameters are experimentally manipulated in more than one level *within* a punishment treatment, so no systematic parameter-sensitivity of the punishment effect is estimated.

D.  Predictions you can make (and their limits)  
    • Because the paper finds that monitoring alone produces almost the same aggregate outcomes as punishment, any parameter that merely *adds* punishment to a situation with strong monitoring cues is unlikely to raise efficiency much.  
    • Fixed matching (repeated partners) seems to amplify the size of the punishment effect on “amount sent” (+20 % vs. +16 %), so one might cautiously predict that variables which strengthen repeated-interaction incentives (e.g., smaller groups, longer horizons) could make punishment more efficiency-enhancing.  
    • Beyond that, the study offers no data for predicting how changing costs, magnitudes, MPCR, information disclosure, chat, group size above three, etc., would shift the efficiency impact of punishment.  Any further prediction would have to come from outside evidence, not from this paper.

In short: The article tells us *that* third-party punishment can raise investments and returns a bit, and that most of the gain comes from the mere fact of being monitored – but it tells us almost nothing about how the size of that effect would vary with the 15 public-goods design parameters listed above.

PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
────────────────────────────────────────

Parameter 1. Number of players  
(1) Mentioned?  Yes – the model assumes “an **infinitely large and uniformly mixed population**.”  
(2) Systematic variation?  No.  The population size is treated as a constant; no results show how changing it alters any punishment effect.

Parameter 2. Number of rounds  
(1) Mentioned?  Implicitly infinite continuous time via the replicator equations; no discrete “round” structure.  
(2) Systematic variation?  No.

Parameter 3. Chat enabled?  
Not mentioned; therefore no variation or prediction.

Parameter 4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
Not mentioned.

Parameter 5. Contribution default (endowment retrieval)?  
Not mentioned.

Parameter 6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
Not mentioned; the paper studies a Prisoner’s Dilemma, not a linear public-goods game.

Parameter 7. Punishment cost to impose one unit (α)  
(1) Mentioned?  Yes – denoted α, “the cost for the quasi-defector to reward or punish.”  
Typical values used: α = 0.1 in most figures; in Fig. 6 α is systematically swept from ≈0 to 1.  
(2) Systematic variation and predicted effect?  Yes.  
• Fig. 6a-c (heat maps of co-operator share ρ_C as a function of α and γ) show:  
  – When α is very small, co-operators survive.  
  – As α increases, ρ_C first rises slightly, then drops sharply to zero once α passes a threshold (exact threshold depends on γ and b).  
Numerical illustration (Fig. 6b, b = 1.5): at γ ≈ 0.5 the switch from positive ρ_C to ρ_C = 0 occurs around α ≈ 0.25.  
Effect on punishment treatment: Higher punishment cost quickly erodes the cooperation-promoting effect of punishment; beyond a critical α the “punishment treatment effect” disappears.

Parameter 8. Punishment magnitude (γ)  
(1) Mentioned?  Yes – denoted γ, “the punishment fine.” Values varied 0.0–0.8 (Fig. 3) and on heat maps (Fig. 6).  
(2) Systematic variation and predicted effect?  Yes.  
Findings (all on ρ_C):  
• With β = 0.3 (Fig. 3a) or 0.5 (Fig. 3b) and δ = 0.3, increasing γ from 0 to 0.2 introduces co-operation when temptation b is moderate (≈1.1).  
• Beyond moderate γ (≈0.4–0.6) additional increases generate little or no further rise in ρ_C (“limited effect”).  
Effect size example (Fig. 3c, b = 1.2, β = 0.7): ρ_C climbs from 0 at γ = 0.1 to ≈0.48 at γ = 0.5, then levels off for γ ≥ 0.5.  
Interpretation: punishment magnitude helps at first, but the marginal benefit saturates.

Parameter 9. Reward enabled?  
(1) Mentioned?  Yes – reward exists whenever β>0.  
(2) Systematic variation?  Implicitly yes: figures compare β=0 (no reward) with β>0. Predictions: without reward (β=0) punishment alone is insufficient to sustain cooperation when γ is low; adding reward can “ameliorate the limited impact of punishment” (Abstract; §3, Fig. 4c).

Parameter 10. Reward cost (identical α)  
Same α as Parameter 7, so variation described under Parameter 7.

Parameter 11. Reward magnitude (β)  
(1) Mentioned?  Yes – varied between 0.3 and 0.9 (Figs 2, 4, 7).  
(2) Systematic variation and predicted effect?  Yes.  
Main findings:  
• At moderate temptation b (Fig. 4a, b = 1.3) ρ_C rises with β up to a peak then falls (“moderate reward best”).  
• At high temptation (b = 1.9) increasing β monotonically increases ρ_C (Fig. 4a).  
• With fixed γ, Fig. 4b shows that higher β pushes the minimum b at which cooperation emerges to larger values.  
Effect sizes (Fig. 4a, b=1.5): ρ_C ≈0 at β = 0.1, ≈0.55 at β ≈ 0.6, then drops back to ≈0.3 at β ≈ 0.9.

Parameter 12. Rounds known to players?  
Not mentioned.

Parameter 13. Peer outcome visibility?  
Not mentioned.

Parameter 14. Punisher identity known?  
Not mentioned.

Parameter 15. Rewarder identity known?  
Not mentioned.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────

A. Dependent variables  
The paper does **not** use “group efficiency” (total or average payoff divided by maximum) as an outcome.  The explicitly reported dependent variables are:  
• ρ_C  – fraction of cooperators in the stationary state or after time-evolution.  
• ρ_D, ρ_QD – fractions of defectors and quasi-defectors.  
Efficiency or monetary pay-off is discussed qualitatively but never measured or plotted.

B. How many of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
5 of 15:  
7 (punishment cost α), 8 (punishment magnitude γ), 9 (reward enabled via β>0), 10 (reward cost α), 11 (reward magnitude β).  
Parameter 1 is described but never varied.  All others are absent.

C. How many parameters are **systematically varied** and linked to the punishment treatment effect?  
Exactly 3:  
• α (parameters 7 & 10)  
• γ (parameter 8)  
• β (parameter 11)  
For each, the paper gives qualitative and curve-level quantitative evidence (no regression coefficients) on how changing the parameter alters the ability of punishment (and reward) to raise the co-operation rate.

D. What predictions can be made—solely from this paper—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions will influence the punishment treatment effect on group **efficiency**?  

Because the paper never measures efficiency, only co-operation rates, any efficiency-based prediction must be indirect and tentative: higher ρ_C in a Prisoner’s Dilemma normally implies higher group payoff, so trends in ρ_C likely translate into similar trends in efficiency.  With that caveat:

• Lower punishment cost α is predicted to strengthen the punishment treatment effect; once α exceeds a threshold, the effect collapses.  
• Increasing punishment magnitude γ helps at first but plateaus; at very high temptation b its marginal impact on efficiency is negligible.  
• Reward magnitude β has a non-monotonic effect at low/medium b (moderate β best) and a positive effect at high b; thus β can partially compensate for the limited returns of high γ.  
• Interactions: the benefit of raising γ is larger when β is low; the benefit of β is larger when γ is moderate (Fig. 7 heat maps).  
• For all other parameters (1–6, 12–15) the paper gives no information, so no prediction can be made.

Hence, based solely on the paper, useful efficiency predictions are confined to the three incentive parameters (α, γ, β) and their pairwise interactions; nothing can be inferred about the remaining twelve parameters.
reference_APA: Pan, Qiuhui, Wang, Yue, Chen, Qin, Gao, Liyan & He, Mingfeng (2022). Effects of quasi-defection strategy on cooperation evolution in social dilemma. PHYSICS LETTERS A.

Abstract: Today, economic experiments are well accepted in mainstream economics. They are also widely applied in ecological economics, often focusing on institutions. Yet, many empirical studies in this field lack a sound theoretical foundation of institutions and institutional change. In this paper, I show that in a structure-agency framework three theoretical viewpoints on institutions can be distinguished. They can be viewed as (1) structures that shape incentives, (2) cognitive media, embedded in beliefs and cognition of agents, or (3) evolving from a process of agents' choices and structural aspects. Abstract: Punishments are meant to deter bad acts, but we commonly only punish those we catch. At some point in time, a society chooses how to catch bad acts. Below I go through the 15 parameters exactly in the order requested.  
For each parameter I first note whether the paper even mentions it and, if it does, what concrete value(s) are used.  
Second, I state whether the authors **systematically vary** that parameter and, if so, what quantitative effect of the variation on any outcome variable (contribution, net‐earnings, etc.) can be read out of the tables or figures.  Wherever a numerical effect can be taken straight from the paper I give the figure and the table, otherwise I write “none”.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
1. NUMBER OF PLAYERS  
(1) Mentioned: yes. All groups have four players (fixed groups of four, 10 periods).  
(2) Systematically varied: no. There is no alternative group size and no statement about how changing the size would modify the punishment treatment effect. Numerical effect: none.

2. NUMBER OF ROUNDS  
(1) Mentioned: yes. Every session lasts 10 periods and subjects know this.  
(2) Systematically varied: no. No prediction about changing the horizon. Numerical effect: none.

3. CHAT ENABLED?  
(1) Mentioned only implicitly: the instructions allow no direct communication; the only information flow is what the monitoring technology reveals.  
(2) Not varied and no prediction. Numerical effect: none.

4. “ALL-OR-NOTHING” CONTRIBUTION RULE  
(1) Mentioned: yes. Subjects may contribute any integer amount from 0 to 5 tokens, so the game is *not* all-or-nothing.  
(2) Not varied; no statement on how switching to all-or-nothing would matter. Numerical effect: none.

5. CONTRIBUTION DEFAULT / REFUND FRAME  
(1) Not used; subjects decide how many tokens to *contribute* (not how many to withdraw).  
(2) Not varied; no prediction. Numerical effect: none.

6. MPCR / MULTIPLICATION FACTOR  
(1) Mentioned: each token invested in the public account yields \$1 to each of the 4 players (social return = \$4, MPCR = 1 for a single participant, 0.25 relative to the marginal private return of 2).  
(2) Not varied and no prediction about varying MPCR. Numerical effect: none.

7. PUNISHMENT COST (to punisher, per point)  
(1) Mentioned: fixed at \$1 for each punishment point.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction. Numerical effect: none.

8. PUNISHMENT MAGNITUDE (loss to target per point)  
(1) Mentioned: fixed at \$3 per punishment point.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction. Numerical effect: none.

9. REWARD ENABLED?  
(1) Not present. Only punishments exist in all treatments.  
(2) Therefore not varied; no prediction. Numerical effect: none.

10. REWARD COST  
(1) Not applicable.  
(2) Not varied. Numerical effect: none.

11. REWARD MAGNITUDE  
(1) Not applicable.  
(2) Not varied. Numerical effect: none.

12. IS THE NUMBER OF ROUNDS KNOWN?  
(1) Mentioned: yes, subjects are explicitly told there will be 10 periods.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction. Numerical effect: none.

13. ARE PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN?  
(1) Mentioned and *indirectly* varied through the four monitoring treatments.  
    • Exogenous GroupMonitor: on average 2.38 of the 4 members are monitored and their full contribution/earning vector is broadcast to everyone (Table 1).  
    • Endogenous GroupMonitor: almost nobody is monitored (0.03 on average).  
    • Exogenous PeerMonitor: 2.50 members monitored, but each monitored player is seen by only one neighbour.  
    • Endogenous PeerMonitor: 0.86 members monitored and information is still local.  
(2) Quantitative effect of *realised* visibility on subsequent contribution is reported in Table 4:  
    – When monitoring is purely *exogenous* an additional person monitored in period t-1 changes period t contribution by +0.011 tokens (statistically nil).  
    – When monitoring is *endogenous* an additional person monitored in period t-1 raises period t contribution by +0.609 tokens (p<0.01).  
    No efficiency measure is supplied, so the effect on efficiency cannot be computed from the paper.

14. DOES THE TARGET KNOW WHO PUNISHED THEM?  
(1) Mentioned: after the punishment stage each subject sees “costs of punishments they received” but *not* the identity of the punisher. The identity is therefore **never revealed** in any treatment.  
(2) Not varied and no prediction about changing this rule. Numerical effect: none.

15. DOES THE TARGET KNOW WHO REWARDED THEM?  
(1) Not applicable – there are no rewards.  
(2) Not varied. Numerical effect: none.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables actually used  
   – Public contributions (tokens)  
   – % of subjects giving all 5 tokens  
   – % of subjects giving 0 tokens  
   – Number monitored  
   – Willingness-to-pay to monitor  
   – Total punishments (costs paid + costs received)  
   – Net earnings (individual monetary payoff)  
   The paper does **not** report “group efficiency” (total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff). Net earnings are individual, not group, and are not normalised.

B. Parameters mentioned  
   10 of the 15 parameters are explicitly described (1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,12,13,14).  
   Rewards (9,10,11) and the “default/refund” frame (5) are only mentioned insofar as they are *absent*.

C. Parameters *systematically varied* and linked to an outcome  
   Strictly speaking, none of the 15 canonical parameters is isolated and systematically varied.  
   The only quasi-variation that can be quantified is Parameter 13 (visibility of peer outcomes) via the different monitoring regimes. The paper reports a +0.609 token rise in next-period contributions per extra player monitored when monitoring is endogenous, but gives no numbers for efficiency. No other parameter in the list is varied.

D. What can be predicted (for **efficiency**) from this paper alone?  
   • Because efficiency is not reported, only indirect inferences are possible.  
   • Endogenous Group-level monitoring produced much lower contributions yet slightly *higher* net earnings than Exogenous Group monitoring (Table 1: 14.25 vs 13.78). Thus one might (very cautiously) predict that, holding all other parameters at the paper’s values, moving from exogenous to endogenous Group monitoring would not raise efficiency despite a ∼44 % fall in cooperation – the saved monitoring and punishment costs roughly offset the lost public-good returns.  
   • Endogenous Peer monitoring delivered almost the same contributions and slightly higher payoffs than Exogenous Peer monitoring; hence efficiency would presumably not change appreciably.  
   • The only parameter that the paper links to behaviour is #13: extra visibility generated endogenously (not exogenously) increases contributions, so greater endogenous visibility is likely to raise efficiency. Numerically: ≈ 0.6 additional tokens contributed per extra player monitored.  
   • For every other parameter (1-12, 14-15) the paper provides no evidence from which to predict how changing that parameter would alter the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

In short, the paper is about *who chooses* to monitor and *what information flows*, not about the 15 structural parameters listed above. Only visibility of peer outcomes (#13) shows a measurable (but still “contributions-only”) effect, and even that is conditional on monitoring being endogenous. For efficiency the paper offers almost no direct guidance.

Below each of the 15 parameters is treated in exactly the same way:

• “Mentioned?” = Does the paper explicitly describe the parameter or give its value?  
• “Systematically varied?” = Did the authors deliberately manipulate that parameter across two or more conditions?  
• “Any numeric effect on a punishment-treatment effect?” = Did the paper report how changing that parameter changes the *incremental* impact of punishment on any dependent variable?  When numbers are available they are reproduced from the appropriate table or figure.

(Whenever the paper reports something other than *efficiency* I state that fact explicitly.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes – every group is a dyad (2 players: “subjects A and B”).  
   • Systematically varied? No – always 2.  
   • Any numeric effect on a punishment-treatment effect? No.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? No discrete “rounds”; the experiment ran for six timed *segments* totalling four hours.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Any numeric effect? No.

3. Is chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned? Yes – “communication” was OFF in Segment III (“Pre-talk”), ON in Segment V (“Talk”), and OFF again in Segment VI (“Post-talk”).  
   • Systematically varied? Yes (within-group manipulation).  
   • Any numeric effect? Not on *efficiency*; the authors only report  
      – mean % time on the cooperative task, and  
      – mean amount of money given (+) or taken (–).  
     Example (Table 4, males):  
       • Punishment use (mean “–”) drops from 17.3 to 7.0 when chat is turned on.  
       • % time on cooperation rises from 44 % to 87 %.  
     Nothing in the paper translates these into a treatment effect on *efficiency*, and no separate “punishment vs. no-punishment” condition is crossed with the chat manipulation.

4. All-or-nothing contribution choice  
   • Mentioned? No – the choice is binary (cooperative task vs. individual task) but the parameter is never labelled or varied.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Numeric effect? No.

5. Contribution default (endowment automatically goes to the public fund)  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Numeric effect? No.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? Indirectly.  In Segments III-VI the per-pull reinforcement is 0.1¢ to A and 0.7¢ to B on the cooperative task; on the individual task both get 0.2¢.  
   • Systematically varied? Yes across segments I–II versus III–VI (equal payoffs versus inequity), but the change is confounded with many other design features and *never analysed*.  
   • Numeric effect on punishment-treatment? None reported.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   • Mentioned? Yes – it is zero (“pressing the (–) button simply subtracted one count from A’s total”).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Numeric effect? No.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss suffered by the target per unit)  
   • Mentioned? Yes – one cent per press.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Numeric effect? No.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Mentioned? Yes – the (+) button is always present in the segments that contain punishment.  
   • Systematically varied? No (although individual subjects *choose* whether to use it).  
   • Numeric effect? No.

10. Reward cost  
    • Mentioned? Yes – one cent is removed from B for each cent given to A.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Numeric effect? No.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Mentioned? Yes – one cent goes to A per press.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Numeric effect? No.

12. Is the number of rounds (or duration) known to players?  
    • Mentioned? Not stated.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Numeric effect? No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mentioned? Yes – each subject’s panel displays both players’ cumulative earnings.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Numeric effect? No.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
    • Mentioned? Implicitly yes (only B can punish so A knows the source), but the paper never discusses it explicitly or manipulates anonymity.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Numeric effect? No.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
    • Same as (14) – implicitly yes, never discussed or varied, no numeric effect reported.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
   • The paper never calculates “group efficiency” (total actual payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff).  
   • Reported DVs are:  
      1. Mean % of time the dyad spends on the cooperative task.  
      2. Whether or not the group attains “steady-state cooperation.”  
      3. Total amount of money *given* (reward) and *taken* (punishment).  
   These are behaviour-level or strategy-use measures, not payoff-level efficiency measures.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   Parameters 1, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15.  (11 of 15)

C. For how many parameters does the paper analyse the effect of *systematically varying* that parameter on a punishment-treatment effect?  
   Only one parameter – communication (parameter 3) – is actually manipulated.  
   Even there, the authors do not calculate a separate “punishment treatment effect”; they merely show how the *presence of communication* alters (i) usage of punishment and (ii) cooperation rates.  
   Therefore: 0 of the 15 parameters are analysed for their impact on a quantified punishment-treatment effect on **any** dependent variable.

D. Predictions one could make (strictly from this paper) about how the 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment-treatment effect on *efficiency*:  
   • The paper provides almost no basis for quantitative prediction.  
   • Qualitatively, one might infer that enabling communication (parameter 3) will *reduce the incidence of punishment* and *raise cooperation*, which in turn could make punishment *less necessary* but *also less damaging* to efficiency.  
   • No other parameter is varied or analysed in a way that allows even qualitative inference about its interaction with punishment on efficiency.  
   In short, beyond guessing that “communication dampens punishment’s negative impact,” the paper supplies virtually no information for predicting how the 15 parameters (individually or jointly) shape the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.

-----------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
-----------------------------------------------------------------

1. Number of players  
   • Stated: All sessions are dyads: one “principal” P and one “agent” A (Section 2.1).  
   • Variation: none.  
   • Effect on punishment-treatment: not discussed.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Stated: T = 15, common knowledge (Abstract, §2.1).  
   • Variation: none.  
   • Effects discussed: Authors report time trends (demands and punishment rise) but never compare games with different T, so no prediction about a treatment effect.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Never mentioned.  
   • No variation, no prediction.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Not applicable – there is no voluntary public-good contribution stage in this extortion game.  
   • No prediction.

5. Contribution default / withdrawal frame  
   • Not applicable.  
   • No prediction.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Not applicable (no public-goods production technology).  
   • No prediction.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   • Fixed at 10 points for the principal irrespective of the damage y she inflicts (Section 2.1).  
   • Variation: none within the experiment.  
   • The Discussion (§3, §5) speculates that “low costs” might explain persistence of punishment and contrasts the present 1 : 16 cost-to-damage ratio with Jung et al. (1994) 90 : 70.  This is a post-hoc remark, not a systematic manipulation, so no effect size can be inferred.

8. Punishment magnitude (damage per unit)  
   • Within a round P chooses any y∈[0,160]; the *maximum* possible magnitude (160) is fixed by design.  
   • Systematic experimental variation: none across treatments; however, *behavioral* variation is analysed.  
   • Findings about dependent variables other than efficiency:  
     – 90 % of rejections are punished; 70 % of those punishments are maximal (Table 3).  
     – For the majority of agents (Type 3) a larger y in the previous round *lowers* the next-round acceptance probability by ≈14 percentage points (Table 6; p. 14).  
   • Effect on group efficiency is not computed; thus no treatment-effect prediction.

9. Reward enabled?  
10. Reward cost?  
11. Reward magnitude?  
   • Rewards are not part of the design; none of the three parameters is mentioned or varied.

12. Is the number of rounds common knowledge?  
   • Yes – “The time horizon (T = 15) is common knowledge” (§2.1).  
   • Not varied; no prediction about efficiency differences.

13. Peer-outcome feedback shown?  
   • Subjects observe all numerical outcomes generated by the stage game (implicitly clear from the game description and the z-Tree implementation).  No alternative feedback condition is used.  
   • No prediction.

14. Punisher identity known?  
   • Trivially yes: each dyad has exactly one principal; anonymity across pairs is preserved but not within a pair.  Not varied.  
   • No prediction.

15. Rewarder identity known?  
   • Not applicable (no reward option).

-----------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
-----------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables actually analysed  
   • The paper reports (i) principals’ demands, (ii) agents’ acceptance decisions, (iii) punishment choices, and (iv) monetary pay-offs.  Combined earnings (24.14 € out of the 30 € maximum, ≈ 80 % efficiency) are reported once (§5) but **efficiency is never treated as the main dependent variable** and is never linked to the presence vs. absence of punishment.  Other dependent variables (contribution, cooperation rate) do not appear.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   – Mentioned: 1, 2, 7, 8, 12, 14 (6 parameters).  
   – Not mentioned: 3, 4, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 13, 15.

C. Which parameters are *systematically varied* and analysed for their effect on the punishment-treatment effect?  
   • None of the 15 parameters is experimentally manipulated across treatments; consequently the paper presents **0** direct estimates of how varying any parameter shifts the punishment treatment effect on any dependent variable (including efficiency).  
   • The only within-game variation analysed is behaviour-driven variation in punishment magnitude (parameter 8) and its effect on acceptance rates, not on efficiency.

D. What predictions can be drawn **solely** from this paper about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency?  
   • Very little can be predicted, because there is no baseline game without punishment and no systematic parameter manipulation.  The only qualitative hint is speculative: “low punishment costs” (parameter 7) seem to sustain frequent and severe punishment and therefore lower agents’ pay-offs, which, holding principals’ pay-offs roughly constant, would mildly **reduce efficiency**.  Beyond this conjecture, the paper supplies no evidence enabling further predictions about any of the 15 parameters or their interactions.

In short, the paper is informative about behaviour *within* a single punishment design but provides almost no leverage for forecasting how changes in the 15 listed design variables would alter the punishment-treatment effect on group efficiency.

Below I go through the 15 meta-parameters one by one, extracting exactly what the paper says and, where possible, the quantitative consequences for the *punishment-treatment effect* (i.e. the difference in outcomes between conditions **with** and **without** punishment).  “Efficiency’’ is understood as the group’s total (or average) monetary payoff relative to the maximum attainable payoff.

────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   – Stated?  Yes: groups of four (p. 11, Sect. 2.2).  
   – Systematically varied?  No.  No prediction about how changing the group size would alter the punishment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   – Stated?  Yes: 20 periods, split into two 10-period parts (§2.3).  
   – Systematically varied?  No.  The authors do not analyse how a different horizon would affect the punishment effect.

3. Chat (verbal communication) enabled?  
   – Stated?  Yes, and **this is the only parameter that is experimentally varied.**  
     • ComEarly: chat in periods 1, 4, 7 (part 1 only) *plus* punishment in both parts.  
     • ComLate: chat only in periods 11, 14, 17 (part 2) *plus* punishment in both parts.  
     • ComOnly: chat in both parts but **no punishment** at all.  
   – Effect of systematically varying chat on the punishment treatment effect?  Yes.  
     • When chat is present (compare ComEarly vs. ComOnly, part 1)  
       – Average contribution rises from 11.26 to 15.19 (+3.93).  
       – Average earnings rise from 29.01 to 31.45 (+2.44).  
       → Net punishment-treatment effect on efficiency ≈ +2.44 ECU per player.  
     • When chat is absent (no condition without punishment exists, so the paper cannot isolate the punishment effect under “no chat’’).  
     • Timing: Giving chat *after* a 10-period punishment history (ComLate) improves contributions (11.94→15.41) and earnings (24.34→29.72) but still leaves total earnings well below the early-chat condition (31.66 vs 27.04 over 20 periods).  Hence early chat magnifies the positive punishment effect on efficiency; late chat only partly restores it.

4. “All-or-nothing’’ contribution?  
   – Stated?  No; subjects choose any integer 0–20.  
   – No variation, no prediction.

5. Contribution default / reversal of decision frame  
   – Not used, not discussed.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   – Stated?  Yes: two “types’’ with m = 0.6 or 0.3 (heterogeneity).  
   – Systematically varied?  No (fixed within the experiment).  No predictions about altering MPCR on the punishment effect.

7. Punishment cost to punisher  
   – Stated?  Flat fee of 1 ECU per period if at least one point is assigned (§2.3.1).  
   – Not varied; no prediction of varying the fee.

8. Punishment magnitude (damage per point)  
   – Stated?  1 ECU taken from target per point.  
   – Not varied; no prediction.

9. Reward option present?  
   – No.  Not mentioned (only in literature review as “not used here’’).

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   – Not applicable.

12. Are players told the number of rounds?  
   – Players know each part lasts 10 rounds and that a second part will follow, but do *not* know in advance what the second part will entail.  
   – Constant across treatments; no systematic variation.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   – Yes: contributions, provisional earnings, punishment points assigned/received reported every stage (§2.3.1).  
   – Not varied.

14. Is punisher identity revealed?  
   – Yes: each stage shows “the number of points each group member has assigned to them’’—effectively revealing identity (§2.3.1).  
   – Not varied; no discussion of changing it.

15. Is rewarder identity revealed?  
   – Not applicable (no reward stage).

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────
A.  Dependent variables  
    • The paper uses (i) *average contributions*, (ii) *average earnings / total group earnings* (= efficiency), and occasionally (iii) *amount of punishment* and *presence of feuds*.  
    • Contributions measure cooperation but do not equal efficiency because punishment expenditures reduce earnings.  Efficiency is explicitly reported as “earnings’’ or “group earnings.’’

B.  Parameters mentioned (9/15)  
    1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14.  (Parameters 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 15 are absent.)

C.  Parameters whose *systematic variation* is analysed for their impact on the punishment treatment effect (1/15)  
    – Parameter 3 (chat enabled / timing).  No other parameter is experimentally manipulated.

D.  Predictions one can make *solely from this paper* about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency  

    • Enabling real-time chat before punishment starts (early chat) amplifies the positive punishment effect on efficiency (≈ +2.4 ECU per player in this design) because covenants are formed and punishment is scarcely needed.  
    • Delaying chat until after a history of punishment sharply reduces this benefit; punishment costs remain high, so the punishment effect on efficiency is smaller and sometimes negative.  
    • Without chat, the paper provides no direct evidence, but the first 10 rounds of ComLate (punishment without chat) suggest that punishment alone can *reduce* efficiency relative to an unavailable baseline (earnings 24.34 ECU vs. 29.01 ECU when chat-only).  
    • Nothing in the paper allows predictions about changing the number of players, rounds, MPCR, punishment cost/magnitude, rewards, visibility parameters, or contribution framing.  These remain “no-prediction’’ areas given the present evidence.

Therefore, apart from “early chat is essential for punishment to raise efficiency,’’ the paper offers little leverage for forecasting how the other 14 parameters—or any higher-order interactions—would modify the punishment treatment effect.

Below, I go through each of the 15 design parameters, state what the paper says about them, and whether the paper makes (or allows us to infer) any prediction about how *changing* that parameter would alter the punishment-treatment effect.  Whenever a numerical effect of the punishment treatment can be read directly from a table or figure I report it, but only for the parameter values actually used in the study.  “Punishment treatment effect” refers to the difference between the “control-mechanism ON’’ and “control-mechanism OFF’’ conditions.

----------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1.  Number of players  
    • Mentioned?  Yes.  Each subject is matched with the pre-recorded decisions of 3 others (groups of 4).  
    • Systematically varied?  No.  No statements or predictions about varying group size.

2.  Number of rounds  
    • Mentioned?  Yes (one-shot; four independent scenarios, no feedback).  
    • Systematically varied?  No.

3.  Chat enabled?  
    • Mentioned?  Implicitly: none allowed.  
    • Systematically varied?  No.

4.  All-or-nothing contribution?  
    • Mentioned?  The text first writes “$x_i\in\{0,10\}$’’ but immediately afterwards says participants “decide how many monetary units to transfer,” and later tables show average contributions taking on many values between 0 and 10.  Hence the game is a *continuous* contribution game (not all-or-nothing).  
    • Systematically varied?  No.

5.  Contribution default (withdraw vs. contribute)?  
    • Mentioned?  Yes: Subjects start with 10 units in their private envelope and *move* any amount to the group envelope.  Thus the default is zero contribution.  
    • Systematically varied?  No.

6.  MPCR or multiplication factor  
    • Mentioned?  Yes.  Each unit placed in the public envelope is multiplied by 1.5 and each of the 4 players receives ¼ of the total.  MPCR = 0.375.  
    • Systematically varied?  No.

7.  Punishment cost to *impose* one unit  
    • Mentioned?  The only cost is a *flat* fee of 1 point that each subject pays if she elects to be in the “control-mechanism’’ regime; no marginal cost per punishment point.  
    • Systematically varied?  No.  Therefore no prediction about varying that cost.

8.  Punishment magnitude (loss per punishment unit)  
    • Mentioned?  Stated to be “proportional to the deviation from the group average” and drawn from a distribution of pilot strategies, but no numbers given.  
    • Systematically varied?  No.

9.  Reward enabled?  
    • Mentioned?  There is *no peer-to-peer reward*.  However, ¼ of all collected fines is *automatically* added to the public account (a form of ex-post rebate, not a strategic reward).  
    • Systematically varied?  No.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
    • Not applicable (see #9).

12.  Do players know the number of rounds?  
    • Mentioned?  They know each decision is one-shot; yes.  
    • Systematically varied?  No.

13.  Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mentioned?  “No feedback was given between the games.”  So outcomes are *not* shown.  
    • Systematically varied?  No.

14.  Is punisher identity revealed?  
    • Mentioned?  The “control” punishment is impersonal and anonymous.  Identity not revealed.  
    • Systematically varied?  No.

15.  Is rewarder identity revealed?  
    • Not applicable (no rewards).

----------------------------------------------------------------
NUMERICAL PUNISHMENT-TREATMENT EFFECTS OBSERVED (FOR THE SINGLE DESIGN USED)

Dependent variable in the paper = “contribution out of 10 points.”

• When *paired with own-type partners*  
  – Cooperative farmers: contribution rises by ≈0.7 points (Table 4, Panel A, col 1; n.s.).  
  – Private-mill farmers: coefficient ≈0 (Table 4).  

• When *paired with other-type partners*  
  – Cooperative farmers: contribution rises by ≈3 points (Table 4, Panel B, col 1; ***p < 0.01).  
  – Private-mill farmers: essentially no change (interaction term −3.04 cancels the main +3.0, Table 4).

No efficiency measure is reported, so no efficiency effect can be calculated from the paper.

----------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Does the paper use *group efficiency* as a dependent variable?  
    No.  Only “contribution to the public good (0–10)” is analysed.  No payoff, total profit, or efficiency variable is reported.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are *mentioned*?  
    12 of 15: parameters 1–8, 9 (in the limited automatic-rebate sense), and 12–14.  Parameters 10, 11, 15 are not applicable / not mentioned.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* the parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
    Zero.  None of the 15 parameters is experimentally manipulated in more than one value, so the paper contains no predictions, statistical or theoretical, about varying them.

D.  If I had to predict how the 15 parameters or their interactions would influence the punishment-treatment effect on *efficiency*, using only this paper, I could say very little.  The only clear qualitative insight is that, in the single design studied, introducing punishment raises contributions for cooperative-mill farmers when they expect to interact with “out-group’’ partners, and has little effect otherwise.  Because the paper never reports payoffs, I cannot even be sure whether this raises or lowers efficiency (the 1-point entry fee and the unknown fine sizes make that ambiguous).  Hence:  
    • Parameters linked to *group identity* (not in the list) appear crucial; none of the 15 parameters directly captures that.  
    • For all 15 listed parameters, the paper provides no data that would allow a directional prediction for efficiency once those parameters are changed.

In short, the study is informative about *who* benefits from punishment in one concrete implementation, but gives almost no leverage for forecasting how design variations (the 15 parameters) would affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.
reference_APA: Hopfensitz, Astrid & Miquel-Florensa, Josepa (2017). Mill ownership and farmer's cooperative behavior: the case of Costa Rica coffee farmers. JOURNAL OF INSTITUTIONAL ECONOMICS.

Abstract: Social norms govern human behavior and usually change slowly over time. While individuals' willingness to sanction others is decisive for the enforcement of social norms and thus social stability, little is known about individual sanctioning behavior related to newly introduced social norms. During the COVID-19 pandemic, governments have used various tools to rapidly and actively introduce the new norm of wearing a face mask; this offers a unique setting to study the determinants of individuals' willingness to sanction a cooperation norm. Below I catalogue what the paper actually says (and does **not** say) about each of the 15 design parameters and the way they influence the “punishment treatment effect’’ – i.e. the difference between a condition **with** punishment and a condition **without** punishment.  
Unless explicitly indicated, the only dependent variables for which numerical comparisons are available are (i) the average cooperation (contribution) rate and (ii) the average payoff reported in Fig. 1.  “Efficiency’’ in the strict sense of “payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff’’ is never reported.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players in the group (n)  
   • Discussed? Yes. Baseline n = 3; also n = 4 and n = 5 are run.  
   • Systematic variation & effect sizes? Yes.  
     – Cooperation:  
        n=3 ASP-only vs None +2.0 pp (72.6 % – 70.6 %)  
        n=4 ASP-only vs None +1.3 pp (48.9 % – 47.6 %)  
        n=5 ASP-only vs None −0.9 pp (6.9 % – 7.8 %)  
     – Payoff: only n=3 reported (0.637 vs 0.634, +0.003).  
     Prediction: the positive punishment effect fades and turns negative once groups reach five members.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? Groups are re-drawn each “round’’ in an evolutionary Moran process, but the number of rounds is not a variable; simulations always last 50 000 update events.  
   • No systematic variation; no predictions.

3. Is chat enabled?  
   • Not mentioned; no predictions.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Yes. Action set is binary (contribute 1 or 0). The paper never varies this feature, so no prediction is offered.

5. Contribution default (reversing the frame)  
   • Not used.

6. Marginal per-capita return (multiplication factor R)  
   • Discussed? Yes. Baseline R = 1.9; Table 1 varies R = 1.5–2.3; Fig. 4b samples R ∈ [1.1, 2.9].  
   • Systematic variation & effect:  
     – Table 1 (ASP-only vs None) differences in cooperation:  
        R=1.5 +3.89 pp  
        R=1.7 +3.11 pp  
        R=1.9 +2.04 pp  
        R=2.1 +1.36 pp  
        R=2.3 +0.98 pp  
     – Narrative (Fig. 4b): Effect turns negative only when R is low **and** mutation μ is high.  
     Prediction: lower MPCR strengthens the positive effect of punishment up to a point.

7. Punishment cost to punisher (k)  
   • Discussed? Yes. Baseline k = 0.1; Fig. 4c samples k ∈ [0, 0.3].  
   • Systematic variation: Fig. 4c shows the sign of the treatment effect over the k–d plane. The text states that the effect becomes negative “if punishment is cheap but very effective”. No numerical deltas are printed.

8. Punishment magnitude to target (d)  
   • Discussed? Yes. Baseline d = 0.5; Table 1 varies d = 0.2–0.8; Fig. 4c samples d ∈ [1.5 k, 5 k].  
   • Systematic variation:  
     – Table 1 (ASP-only vs None) cooperation differences:  
        d=0.2 +1.39 pp  
        d=0.35 +1.80 pp  
        d=0.5  +2.04 pp  
        d=0.65 +2.14 pp  
        d=0.8  +2.35 pp  
     – Combined with k, very large d and very small k can flip the sign (Fig. 4c).

9. Reward enabled?  
   • No rewards exist in the model, hence no discussion.

10.–11. Reward cost / magnitude  
   • Not applicable.

12. Is the horizon known?  
   • Not modelled; the evolutionary process is indefinite.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Assumed yes (players “learn others’ contributions”), but this is fixed; no variation, no prediction.

14. Punisher anonymity  
   • Not addressed.

15. Rewarder anonymity  
   • Not relevant (no rewards).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Use of “efficiency’’?  
   The paper reports (i) average cooperation rates and (ii) average payoffs.  
   The classic efficiency metric (actual total payoff ÷ social optimum) is **not** reported, so average payoff is only a proxy.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
   6 of them: 1, 4, 6, 7, 8, 13.

C. Which parameters are systematically varied and linked to the punishment treatment effect?  
   4 parameters: 1 (group size), 6 (MPCR R), 7 (punishment cost k), 8 (punishment magnitude d).

D. What predictions about the punishment-efficiency effect can be made solely from this paper?  
   • Small groups (n ≤ 4) ⇒ punishment tends to raise cooperation and (slightly) payoff; at n = 5 the effect can become negative.  
   • Lower MPCR (harder social dilemma) ⇒ larger positive effect; very low R combined with high mutation may reverse the sign.  
   • Increasing d while holding k constant moderately strengthens the positive effect, unless k is so low that punishment becomes “cheap and lethal”, in which case the effect can turn negative.  
   • Reducing k (punishment cheaper) is beneficial only up to the point where k is very small relative to d; beyond that the treatment effect can become negative.  
   • No statements can be made about any of the other 11 parameters; the paper provides no data or theory on them.

Hence, except for the four parameters above, the paper offers little guidance for predicting how design choices will influence the punishment treatment effect on true group efficiency.
reference_APA: Schunk, Daniel & Wagner, Valentin (2021). What determines the willingness to sanction violations of newly introduced social norms: Personality traits or economic preferences? evidence from the COVID-19 crisis. JOURNAL OF BEHAVIORAL AND EXPERIMENTAL ECONOMICS.
