Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter analysis of how (and whether) the paper discusses each of the 15 listed parameters with respect to any “punishment” treatment effect. In this experiment, there is no standard monetary punishment with a cost and magnitude (such as a typical “pay one coin to reduce another’s payoff by three coins”). Instead, “exclusion” is the only mechanism of removing someone from the benefits of future interaction; it is instituted through costless voting. Consequently, the paper does not report typical “punishment costs” or “punishment magnitude” effects.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper fixes groups of five players (one in position C, four in periphery).  
   • Systematically varied? No. Groups always have five members, so there is no discussion of how changing the number of players would affect any punishment treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each block has 5 rounds, and there are 5 blocks. Thus, the game is finitely repeated for 25 total rounds (5 rounds × 5 blocks).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not alter (e.g., shorten or lengthen) the number of rounds to test its effect, so no predictions about varying this parameter on any (punishment) treatment effect are given.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not permit or discuss any real‐time communication or chat.  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no mention of enabling or disabling chat, hence no reported effect on punishment or exclusion behavior.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned? Yes, indirectly. The paper specifies that each player chooses a contribution between 0 and 50 in a linear public‐goods format. This is a continuous decision, not all‐or‐nothing.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not change the format of contributions from continuous to all‐or‐nothing, and it makes no predictions about that change.

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., do players “opt out” of moving money back to themselves)?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not discuss any such default mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no mention or manipulation of a “default” contribution design.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplier
   • Mentioned? Yes. The MPCR is fixed at 0.6 for each point contributed to the public good.  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no discussion of altering MPCR and no reported impact of systematically varying it on any punishment‐related effect.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned? No. Exclusion votes are cast at no cost to the voter; there is no cost parameter for punishment.  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no discussion of a cost or how varying that cost would affect a punishment treatment effect.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted for each unit of punishment)
   • Mentioned? No. The paper discusses only “exclusion,” which completely removes a player from future rounds if a majority votes to exclude, but there is no incremental “punishment magnitude.”  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no parameter for partial or per‐unit punishment and no predictions about varying it.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not include or discuss any reward mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied? No. No mention of enabling or disabling rewards.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Mentioned? No. The experiment does not involve rewarding, so there is no parameter for a reward “cost.”  
   • Systematically varied? No. No discussion here.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded to a player per unit of reward)
   • Mentioned? No. There is no provision for rewarding, so no mention of payout increments for such a mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied? No. Absent from the paper.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each participant knows there are 5 rounds in each block (and 5 blocks total).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not experimentally change whether the horizon is known.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (e.g., do players see others’ payoffs or contributions)?
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper states that at the end of each round, each player sees every other in‐group (non‐excluded) player’s contribution. They also see how many votes were cast.  
   • Systematically varied? No. Everyone sees this information; the paper does not compare different information‐revelation conditions.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Mentioned? Partially. In this experiment, “punishment” means being excluded, but players do not learn specifically who voted against them, only the total number of votes. Thus, no individual punisher is revealed.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not manipulate whether punisher identity is revealed or hidden.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Mentioned? No. No reward mechanism exists in this setup, so this is not discussed.  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no mention of revealing or concealing a “rewarder’s” identity.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper often discusses “contribution” and “earnings” as measured outcomes. It also directly addresses “efficiency” in terms of aggregated payoffs and notes whether total group earnings are higher or lower under certain conditions (e.g., with or without “centrality,” with or without “exclusion”).  
   • “Contribution” (how much is invested in the public good) is distinct from “efficiency” (how large total payoffs are, net of any exclusion losses). “Earnings” is the individual‐level payoff. The authors highlight that “centrality does not reduce overall efficiency.”

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned:  
       (1) Number of players (always 5),  
       (2) Number of rounds (5 rounds per block),  
       (4) Continuous (0–50) contribution,  
       (6) MPCR = 0.6,  
       (12) The finite horizon is known,  
       (13) Information on others’ contributions is revealed,  
       (14) Exclusion votes are anonymous (so the “punisher” is not identified).  
   • In total, 7 of the 15 parameters are at least mentioned in some form.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None of the parameters are systematically varied for a “punishment” cost/magnitude design. The paper’s “punishment” is an on/off exclusion vote with zero cost. Hence, no parameter is experimentally manipulated to evaluate a range of punishment intensities or costs.  
   • The paper varies only whether “exclusion” is possible and whether “centrality” is present, neither of which matches the standard parametric punishments 7–8. Thus, strictly speaking, there are 0 parameters for which the paper discusses systematic variation of a “punishment treatment effect.”

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not systematically assess changes in monetary punishment cost or magnitude, nor does it use rewards. It fixes the group size, rounds, MPCR, and knowledge conditions. Consequently, there is little direct evidence to predict how varying these parameters would affect a “punishment” treatment effect on efficiency.  
   • The one relevant takeaway is that the paper’s costless exclusion voting (no mention of unit‐by‐unit punishment cost or magnitude) can increase contributions, and that having a “central” member does not reduce overall payoffs even though the central player free rides more. Beyond that, the paper’s data and text do not provide specific guidance on systematically altering any of the 15 listed parameters for standard punishment or reward designs.  

Accordingly, the paper yields only limited to no prediction for how most of the 15 parameters would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, as it never systematically manipulates them in the context of standard punishment or reward.
reference_APA: van Leeuwen, Boris, Ramalingam, Abhijit, Rojo Arjona, David & Schram, Arthur (2019). Centrality and cooperation in networks. EXPERIMENTAL ECONOMICS.

Authors: Yamamoto, H; Okada, I
Author Full Names: Yamamoto, Hitoshi; Okada, Isamu
Article Title: How to keep punishment to maintain cooperation: Introducing social vaccine
Source Title: PHYSICA A-STATISTICAL MECHANICS AND ITS APPLICATIONS
Author Keywords: Evolutionary game theory; Social dilemma; Free-rider problem; Agent based simulation; Social vaccine
Keywords Plus: ANTISOCIAL PUNISHMENT; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; EVOLUTIONARY APPROACH; EXPLORATION DYNAMICS; INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; MAINTENANCE; ENFORCEMENT; DEFECTORS; OVERCOME; NORMS
Abstract: Although there is much support for the punishment system as a sophisticated approach to resolving social dilemmas, more than a few researchers have also pointed out the limitations of such an approach. Second-order free riding is a serious issue facing the punishment system. Various pioneering works have suggested that an anti-social behavior or noise stemming from a mutation may, surprisingly, be helpful for avoiding second-order freeloaders. Below I go through the fifteen design parameters one‐by-one, referring only to what is actually written, plotted or tabulated in “How to keep punishment to maintain cooperation: Introducing social vaccine.”

PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER SCAN  

1. Number of players  
   • Discussed? Yes.  The authors set N = 20 in all analytic work (Figs. 2-4) and then vary N = 20, 40, 60, 80, 100 in Sec. 3.3 / Fig. 10.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on the “punishment treatment effect”?  
     – “Treatment” in the paper means adding a social-vaccine punisher–defector.  
     – Outcome reported is average boldness (probability of defection), not efficiency.  
     – Without vaccine: cooperation fails when N < 40; with vaccine: cooperation is stable for every N tested (upper vs. lower panel of Fig. 10).  No numerical efficiency figures are provided.

2. Number of rounds (length of the repeated interaction)  
   • Discussed? Indirectly.  The simulation runs for 10², 10³, 10⁴ or 10⁵ “generations.”  
   • Effect if varied? Without the social vaccine, longer runs increase the likelihood that cooperation collapses; with the vaccine, the run length no longer matters (Fig. 10).  Again the outcome is boldness, not efficiency.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Not mentioned.  No variation, no effect reported.

4. Contribution “all-or-nothing”?  
   • Yes.  Players simply “cooperate” or “defect.”  This is fixed and never varied, so no effect is estimated.

5. Contribution default / take-back format?  
   • Not mentioned.

6. MPCR (multiplication factor, marginal per-capita return)  
   • The paper uses the public-goods equivalent “temptation to defect,” T.  
     – T is systematically varied: T = 1 … 6 (Sec. 3.2; Figs. 5–8).  
   • Effect of varying T:  
     – Without vaccine the meta-norm system always collapses (average boldness → 1) for every T tested (Figs. 5, 6).  
     – With vaccine, cooperation is “robustly maintained regardless of the values of T” (Fig. 7, Fig. 8).  No numeric efficiency measures are given.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   • Labeled E (and M E for meta-punishment).  Operational range E = −1 … −6.  
   • Effect when varied:  
     – Without vaccine, cooperation persists only when |E| < 2; otherwise it collapses (Fig. 6).  
     – With vaccine, cooperation is maintained over the full range, although the final defection ratio rises as |E| grows (text below Fig. 8 and Fig. 9).

8. Punishment magnitude (fine imposed on target)  
   • Labeled P (= M P) and fixed at −9 throughout.  Not varied; therefore no effect reported.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Not included.

10. Reward cost?  
11. Reward magnitude?  
   • Not included.

12. Endpoint known (do players know the last round)?  
   • Not discussed.

13. Peer outcome visibility (do players see others’ payoffs)?  
   • Not discussed explicitly; the only information channel is probabilistic detection (parameter s), which is fixed and outside the list of 15.

14. Punisher identification  
15. Rewarder identification  
   • Not discussed.

----------------------------------------------------------------------  
SUMMARY  

A. Dependent variables used  
   – Group efficiency or total/average payoff is mentioned once (“average payoffs are equal to those of perfect cooperative regimes”) but no data are shown.  
   – All figures plot average boldness (defection rate) and sometimes vengefulness.  
   – Therefore efficiency is not actually measured; the principal dependent variables are (i) boldness, (ii) vengefulness.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
   – Mentioned: 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8.  (6 parameters.)  
   – Not mentioned: 3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15.

C. Which parameters are systematically varied and their impact on the punishment treatment effect discussed?  
   – Varied: 1 (population size), 2 (number of generations), 6 (T / MPCR proxy), 7 (punishment cost E).  (4 parameters.)  
   – For these four, the paper compares outcomes with vs. without the “punishment treatment” (the social-vaccine mechanism).  Effects are presented only for boldness, not for efficiency, and no numerical effect sizes are supplied.

D. Predictions you can make about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, using only this paper  
   – Large population sizes and/or the presence of a social vaccine are necessary for punishment to translate into sustained cooperation; therefore efficiency gains from punishment are predicted only when N ≳ 40, or whenever a social vaccine is present, regardless of N.  
   – High punishment costs (large |E|) erode but do not eliminate the vaccine’s effectiveness; expect somewhat lower efficiency when punishment is very costly.  
   – Varying the temptation to defect (T) does not alter the vaccine’s qualitative success; thus efficiency should stay high across T once the vaccine (and hence punishment) is in place.  
   – The paper offers no basis for predicting any effect of chat, contribution format, rewards, information display, or identification of punishers/rewarders.  For those parameters the safest prediction, on the sole basis of the paper, is “no information / cannot predict.”

Hence, using this paper alone, only coarse qualitative forecasts about parameters 1, 2, 6 and 7 are possible; for the remaining eleven parameters the paper provides no grounds for prediction.

------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Number of players (group size)  
    (1) Mentioned.  Simulations are run on networks that contain L² nodes.  Default lattice: L = 100 (10 000 players).  Robustness checks vary L from 50² to 400².

2. Number of rounds

4. All-or-nothing contribution?

5. Contribution default / endowment moved back?  
    Not mentioned → No prediction.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
    (1) YES.  In this PD formulation it is captured by the “dilemma strength” r = c/(b–c) (0 < r ≤ 1).  r is *systematically varied* in every main figure (e.g., Fig. 2).

      No efficiency numbers are reported.

7. Punishment cost to impose (γ)  
    (1) Mentioned; fixed at γ = 0.1 throughout the main text.  
    (2) Never varied → no prediction.

8. Punishment magnitude / fine (β)  
    (1) Mentioned; fixed at β = 0.3.  
    (2) Never varied → no prediction.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
    Not included.

10. Reward cost  
    Not included.

11. Reward magnitude  
    Not included.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
    Not discussed; the model assumes anonymous one-shot interactions embedded in an evolutionary process.  No variation.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    The only information players use is payoffs of a randomly chosen neighbour (for Fermi imitation) and/or action frequencies (for conformist imitation).  There is no on/off manipulation of an “information display” parameter.  No prediction.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
    Not discussed.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
    Not discussed.

------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables used  
    – Fractions (densities) of the four strategies C, D, CP, DP.  
    – Sometimes aggregated as “cooperative actors” (C + CP).  
    – No measure of **group efficiency / total payoff** is ever computed.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
    3 of 15:  
        1. Number of players (network size)  
        6. MPCR / dilemma strength r  
        7. Punishment cost (γ)  
        8. Punishment magnitude (β)  
    (γ and β are mentioned but *not varied*).

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* that parameter on the punishment-treatment effect?  
    Only 2 parameters:  
        – Parameter 1 (network size): varied in robustness checks; effect reported as “little difference.”  
        – Parameter 6 (MPCR / r): extensively varied; quantitative thresholds for CP dominance given above.  
    No other parameters are systematically varied.

D. If one had to predict how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency *using only this paper*:  
    – Almost no direct prediction can be made because the paper never measures efficiency.

Below I go through the fifteen parameters one‐by‐one, strictly extracting what the Robbett (2016) paper tells us about  

(1) whether the parameter is mentioned (and what concrete value is used) and  
(2) whether the paper says anything about how *changing* that parameter would alter the **punishment treatment effect** – i.e. the difference between a “Sanctions’’ treatment and the Baseline for any outcome variable.  
Whenever possible I quote the numerical treatment effect the paper reports.  All page, table and figure references are to the pdf you supplied.

──────────  
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned – All groups have exactly 3 players.  
   • Systematic variation? None. No statement on how changing group size would modify the punishment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned – 10 rounds (known to subjects).  
   • No variation; no prediction about its influence on the punishment effect.

3. Chat (communication) enabled?  
   • Mentioned – Three separate “communication’’ treatments (Restricted vs. Unrestricted vs. none).  
   • BUT the paper never combines chat *with* punishment, so it contains no evidence or prediction on how adding or removing chat would change the **punishment vs. baseline** difference. The parameter is therefore *not* linked to the punishment treatment effect.

4. Contribution “all-or-nothing’’?  
   • Not mentioned. Contributions are 0–4 tokens, freely chosen. No variation, no prediction.

5. Contribution default / take-back frame?  
   • Not used. No discussion.

6. MPCR or equivalent multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned – Each contributed token yields 10 points to each of the three players (so MPCR=10/1 in absolute points; in the usual normalized scale MPCR=10/50=0.20 because 50 points = US$1).  
   • Held constant; no discussion of varying it and thus no prediction for the punishment effect.

7. Punishment cost (per unit)  
   • Mentioned – Cost = 1 point.  
   • Fixed; the paper does not vary the cost and gives no prediction about what would happen if the cost were changed.

8. Punishment magnitude (impact on target per unit)  
   • Mentioned – Each point spent reduces the target’s payoff by 3 points.  
   • Fixed; again, no systematic variation or prediction.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • No. Only costly punishment is available in the “Sanctions’’ treatment.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   • Not applicable – no rewards in any treatment.

12. Number of rounds known to players?  
   • Mentioned – Yes, always common knowledge.  
   • Not varied; no statement on how uncertainty about the horizon would affect punishment’s impact.

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
   • Mentioned – After every period subjects see each group member’s *contribution* (not payoff). Presented in three unlabeled boxes whose order is reshuffled each period.  
   • Always the same; not varied; no prediction about its effect on punishment.

14. Punishee knows the identity of the punisher?  
   • Punishment is entered anonymously (typed below each unlabeled contribution box). The target therefore **does not** know which co-player punished her.  
   • This anonymity feature is constant; no comparison to an identified-punisher condition, hence no prediction.

15. Rewarder identity known?  
   • Not applicable (no reward option).

──────────  
WHAT THE PAPER ACTUALLY TELLS US ABOUT THE *SIZE* OF THE PUNISHMENT TREATMENT EFFECT

Two environments are studied:  
• Private Incentives (others do *not* know your type)  
• Observable Incentives (types common knowledge)

In each environment there is a Baseline and a Sanctions treatment.  
Dependent variable used in all reported regressions is *total group contribution*; efficiency is shown only descriptively (Figure 5).

Private Incentives (Table 1, col. 1)  
 Punishment effect on total contributions = +0.380 tokens (SE = 0.694) – statistically insignificant (p≈0.59).

Observable Incentives (Table 2, col. 1)  
 Punishment effect = +0.507 tokens (SE = 0.705) – also insignificant (p≈0.29).

Thus, with the single cost=1, impact=3 punishment technology used, *introducing* punishment raises group contributions by roughly half a token at best, and never significantly, in either information environment.

The paper does not explore any parameter change (group size, cost, magnitude, identity, etc.) that could strengthen or weaken that effect, so no further quantitative predictions are available.

──────────  
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
   • The core regressions use *total group contribution* and type-specific contributions.  
   • Figure 5 additionally reports *efficiency* ((actual payoff – Nash payoff)/(max – Nash)).

Abstract: How are norms maintained? Axelrod (in Am. Political Sci.       • Vengefulness (probability of punishing a defector)

   (1) Mentioned? Yes.  Both the PD and the PD-TPP are strictly one-shot.  
   (2) Systematic variation? No.  Only one round is ever played.

3. IS CHAT ENABLED?  
   (1) Mentioned? Implicitly.  All interactions are anonymous, on paper, with no communication.  
   (2) Systematic variation? No.

4. “ALL-OR-NOTHING” CONTRIBUTION?  
   (1) Mentioned? Yes.  A (or B) either keeps all 10 tokens or sends all 10; there is no continuous choice.  
   (2) Systematic variation? No.

5. “CONTRIBUTION DEFAULT” FRAME?  
   Not used or mentioned.

6. MPCR / MULTIPLICATION FACTOR  
   (1) Mentioned? Yes.  Tokens sent are tripled (factor 3).  
   (2) Systematic variation? No.

7. PUNISHMENT COST (per deduction point)  
   (1) Mentioned? Yes.  The C player pays 1 token per deduction point.  
   (2) Systematic variation? No.

8. PUNISHMENT MAGNITUDE  
   (1) Mentioned? Yes.  Every deduction point imposed on A or B reduces the target’s payoff by 3 tokens.  
   (2) Systematic variation? No.

9–11. REWARD ENABLED / COST / MAGNITUDE  
   The experiment contains no reward option; these parameters are not mentioned.

12. ARE THE NUMBER OF ROUNDS KNOWN?  
   (1) Mentioned? Only indirectly.  Because the game is explicitly one-shot, subjects know exactly when it ends.  
   (2) Systematic variation? No.

13. ARE PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN?  
   (1) Mentioned? Yes.  Final pay-offs were posted afterwards (in prison recreation areas or on a web site for students).  
   (2) Systematic variation? No.  There is no alternative information regime studied.

14. IS THE PUNISHER’S IDENTITY REVEALED?  
   (1) Mentioned? Yes.  The design keeps complete anonymity; A and B never learn which specific C punished them.  
   (2) Systematic variation? No.

15. IS THE REWARDER’S IDENTITY REVEALED?  
   Not applicable (no rewards).

-------------------------------------------------
Observed punishment-treatment effects that can be read directly from Table 1 (dependent variable = “percentage who cooperate”):

• Students: 67.5 % → 34.8 % (change = –32.7 p.p.; χ², p < 0.01)  
• Ordinary criminals: 50.0 % → 66.7 % (change = +16.7 p.p.; n.s.)  
• Camorristi: 86.7 % → 65.2 % (change = –21.5 p.p.; p < 0.01)

Those are the only numerical treatment effects that the paper reports.  No other parameter is manipulated.

-------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables used in the paper  
   • Cooperation / “probability to cooperate” (binary)  
   • Amount of punishment chosen by the third party  
   • Attitudinal indices (cooperation, reciprocity, locus of control)  
   The paper never reports “group efficiency”, total payoff, or average payoff, so efficiency is not analysed.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   9 of them: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 14 (13 is described but not really framed as a design parameter).  Parameters 5, 9, 10, 11, 15 are absent.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of **systematically varying** that parameter on the punishment-treatment effect?  
   Zero.  No parameter is varied independently of the punishment manipulation, hence no causal statements about parameter changes can be extracted.

D.  Predictions about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency, based solely on this paper  
   • Because efficiency itself is never measured, the paper provides no direct guidance.  
   • The only qualitative insight is that, with the specific parameter constellation used (tripling factor 3, punishment cost 1, punishment impact 3, one-shot, anonymous), introducing punishment lowered cooperation for students and Camorristi but raised it for ordinary criminals.  
   • Since other parameters were held fixed, the paper offers **little to no basis** for forecasting what would happen if any of the 15 parameters (or their combinations) were changed.  Any such prediction would go beyond the evidence presented.

On this base, the theory of asymmetric evolutionary game with hierarchical punishment is extend. And its impact on the evolution of cooperation is studied. Below, each of the 15 public-goods parameters is treated in turn.

For every parameter we state  
(1) whether it is explicitly mentioned anywhere in the article and, if so, what concrete value(s) are used;  
(2) whether the paper systematically varies that parameter and reports its impact on the *punishment treatment effect* (i.e., the difference between runs with hierarchical punishment and runs without it).  Whenever a numerical effect can be read directly off a figure or table, it is supplied; otherwise “not quantified” is given.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned.  Simulations are run on square lattices of size N = L × L with L = 100 (thus N = 10 000).  
   (2) N is kept constant; no results are shown for other sizes, so no prediction is made about how changing N would alter the punishment treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Only the technical detail that each realisation is run for 10^5 time-steps (plus 10^4 for averaging).  
   (2) The number of rounds is never varied; no prediction is offered.

3. Chat enabled?  
   (1) Not mentioned.  
   (2) Not discussed.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   (1) Not mentioned – contributions do not exist because the paper studies a two-player Prisoner’s Dilemma (PD), not a public-goods game.  
   (2) Not discussed.

5. Contribution default / withdrawal rule  
   (1) Not applicable.  
   (2) Not discussed.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   (1) Not mentioned.  The closest analogue is the temptation-to-defect parameter b in the PD; values between 1.05 and 1.5 are explored, but that parameter is not one of the listed 15.  
   (2) No MPCR is used.

7. Punishment cost (to the punisher)  
   (1) Yes.  The cost is fixed at γ = 0.1 throughout the paper.  
   (2) γ is never varied, so there is no prediction of how changing γ would affect the punishment treatment effect.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine paid by target)  
   (1) Yes.  β is the central control parameter.  Values examined include β = 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9.  
   (2) Systematically varied and compared to the *no-punishment* baseline (called the “traditional model”).  
       Dependent variable: fraction of cooperators ρ_C (not efficiency).  
       Qualitative findings:  
       • For small temptation (b < 1.05), increasing β from 0.1 → ≥0.5 **reduces** ρ_C, because punishers replace cooperators.  
       • For larger temptation (b ≥ 1.1), increasing β **increases** ρ_C; the treatment effect becomes strongly positive (e.g., at b = 1.2   ρ_C ≈ 0 with β = 0.1 versus ≈ 0.45 with β = 0.9 ≈ +0.45).  
       • A “reverse” or crossing pattern is reported: the ranking of ρ_C for β = 0.1 vs. β = 0.5 changes sign as b grows.  
       Numerical effect sizes that can be eyeballed from Fig. 1:  

       b = 1.1 : β = 0.1 → ρ_C ≈ 0.18 ; β = 0.9 → ρ_C ≈ 0.30  (Δ ≈ +0.12)  
       b = 1.2 : β = 0.1 → ρ_C ≈ 0.00 ; β = 0.9 → ρ_C ≈ 0.45  (Δ ≈ +0.45)  
       b = 1.5 : β = 0.1 → ρ_C ≈ 0.00 ; β = 0.9 → ρ_C ≈ 0.07  (Δ ≈ +0.07)  

       Again, the paper never reports group efficiency.

9. Reward enabled?  
   (1) Not present.  
   (2) Not discussed.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   (1–2) Not present and not discussed.

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
   (1) Not applicable in an evolutionary simulation with indefinite time-steps.  
   (2) Not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
14. Is the punisher identified?  
15. Is the rewarder identified?  
   (1) None are mentioned; the model provides no information channels beyond payoff comparison.  
   (2) Not discussed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
   • The study tracks the fraction of cooperators (ρ_C), fraction of punishers, and spatial patterns.  
   • Total or average payoff – i.e., *group efficiency* – is **never** reported.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   3 out of 15:  
   (1) Number of players (fixed at 10 000)  
   (7) Punishment cost γ (fixed)  
   (8) Punishment magnitude β (varied)

C. For how many parameters is a systematic effect on the punishment treatment effect analysed?  
   Exactly 1: Parameter 8 (punishment magnitude).  No other listed parameter is systematically varied.

D. Predicting the punishment treatment effect on *efficiency* using only this paper  
   The article does not measure efficiency, so only very tentative extrapolations are possible:  
   • A larger punishment magnitude β is likely to *increase* efficiency when temptation to defect is high, because it rescues cooperation; when temptation is low, stronger β could *lower* efficiency by converting cost-free cooperators into costly punishers.  
   • Varying any of the remaining 14 parameters is outside the scope of the paper; therefore no evidence-based prediction can be made for them or for higher-order interactions.

In short, the paper gives usable guidance only for the single parameter “punishment magnitude”, and only with respect to the *cooperation rate*, not group efficiency.

Author Full Names: Xie, Enhui; Liu, Mengdie; Liu, Jieqiong; Gao, Xiaoxue; Li, Xianchun
Article Title: Neural mechanisms of the mood effects on third-party responses to injustice after unfair experiences
Author Keywords: DLPFC; mood; third-party response to injustice; unfair experience
Keywords Plus: SOCIAL VALUE ORIENTATION; DECISION-MAKING; PUNISHMENT; COOPERATION; FAIRNESS; COMPENSATION; BEHAVIOR; ANGER
Abstract: Behavioral decision theory argues that humans can adjust their third-party responses (e.g., punishment and compensation) to injustice by integrating unfair experiences. Typically, the mood plays an important role in such a decision-making process. However, the underlying neurocognitive bases remain largely unclear. We first employ a modified third-party justice game in which an allocator split an amount of money between oneself and a receiver. The participants can reapportion the money as observers by choosing from the following three costly options: compensate the receiver, accept the current allocation, or punish the allocator. Then, a second-party pseudo interaction is conducted where participants receive more (i.e., advantageous unfair experience) or less (i.e., disadvantageous unfair experience) than others. Finally, participants perform the third-party justice game again after unfair experiences. Here, we use functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to measure participants' brain activities during third-party responses to injustice. We find participants compensate more to the receiver after advantageous unfair experience, which involved enhanced positive emotion, weakened sense of unfairness, and is linked with increased activity in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (rDLPFC). In contrast, participants punish more on the allocator after disadvantageous unfair experience, which might primarily stem from their negative emotional responses, strong sense of unfairness, and is associated with significantly decreased activity in the rDLPFC. Our results suggest that third-party compensation and punishment involved differential psychological and neural bases. Our findings highlight the crucial roles of second-party unfair experiences and the corresponding mood responses in third-party responses to unfairness, and unravel the intermediate neural architecture.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of whether the paper discusses each of the 15 listed public‐goods‐game parameters (and if so, any predictions or evidence about systematically varying them), followed by the required four‐part summary.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
• Mentioned?  
  – The paper states that 60 participants took part, paired up in two‐person sessions, with each participant acting as a “third party” observing two other players (allocator and receiver). However, the paper does not systematically vary the number of players nor discuss how changing this number would affect any outcome.  
• Predictions about varying it?  
  – None.  

2) Number of rounds  
• Mentioned?  
  – The paper uses 40 trials per session (three sessions total), but does not vary the number of trials/rounds. It never explores how altering the number of rounds would change punishment or efficiency.  
• Predictions about varying it?  
  – None.  

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
• Mentioned?  
  – No. There is no reference in the paper to participants communicating with one another by chat or any other channel.  
• Predictions about varying it?  
  – None.  

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Mentioned?  
  – No. The study involves a “third‐party justice game” with discrete choices (punish, compensate, accept). There is no mention of forced all‐or‐nothing contributions and no systematic variation of such a design.  
• Predictions about varying it?  
  – None.  

5) Is the contribution default? (i.e., do players choose to move money back to themselves?)  
• Mentioned?  
  – No. The study design has participants pay a fixed cost to choose among three options (accept, punish, or compensate). There is no discussion of a “default contribution” parameter in the sense of a public‐goods‐game setting.  
• Predictions about varying it?  
  – None.  

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
• Mentioned?  
  – No. The paper does not study a public goods scenario of multiplied returns. The game focuses on redistributing a fixed endowment, not on MPCR.  
• Predictions about varying it?  
  – None.  

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Mentioned?  
  – The paper uses a flat cost of 3 yuan whenever participants choose punish, compensate, or accept. It does not vary that cost.  
• Predictions about varying it?  
  – None. No systematic variation or predictions about changing that cost.  

8) Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from a player per unit of punishment)  
• Mentioned?  
  – The study’s “punish” choice deducts from the unfair party’s outcome, but the exact magnitude is not varied systematically. The cost to the punisher is always 3 yuan.  
• Predictions about varying it?  
  – None.  

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
• Mentioned?  
  – Not in those terms. The paper discusses “compensation,” but does not describe a separate reward mechanism or compare “reward enabled” vs. “reward disabled” conditions.  
• Predictions about varying it?  
  – None.  

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Mentioned?  
  – No. The paper does not provide a separate “reward” cost—only a fixed 3 yuan cost for “compensation,” “punishment,” or “accept.”  
• Predictions about varying it?  
  – None.  

11) Reward magnitude (coins awarded per unit of reward)  
• Mentioned?  
  – No. As above, “compensation” is not systematically varied in size; nor is there a separate “reward magnitude.”  
• Predictions about varying it?  
  – None.  

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
• Mentioned?  
  – The text does not explicitly discuss whether participants knew exactly how many trials lay ahead. There is no analysis of transparency vs. uncertainty about the total number of rounds.  
• Predictions about varying it?  
  – None.  

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much their peers gained/lost each round)?  
• Mentioned?  
  – The study does show participants how money is allocated (e.g., “7:3”) to two other individuals. However, it does not systematically vary the amount or clarity of this information.  
• Predictions about varying it?  
  – None.  

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• Mentioned?  
  – Not addressed. The paper says that participants observe allocations and can punish, but does not indicate whether the punished party learns an identity.  
• Predictions about varying it?  
  – None.  

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
• Mentioned?  
  – Not addressed. As with punishment, it is not discussed whether anonymity is maintained.  
• Predictions about varying it?  
  – None.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Summary:

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are they different?  
   – The paper does not use group efficiency (actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff) as a dependent variable. Its main behavioral dependent variables are the proportion of “third‐party punishment,” “third‐party compensation,” or “accept” choices; it also measures self‐reported mood and neural activity. These are distinct from “efficiency” because they focus on how people respond to unfair splits and how their mood and brain activity correlate with those responses, rather than measuring total payoff or payoff ratios.  

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – The paper briefly mentions a fixed cost for punishing/compensating (Parameter 7) but does not discuss systematically varying that cost. It also describes that participants see the allocations (related to Parameter 13), but again without any systematic variation. None of the other parameters (1–6, 8–12, 14, 15) are discussed in a way that directly relates to changing those parameters.  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   – None. Although the paper does use a punishment option, it never varies punishment cost, number of players, or any other parameter, nor does it provide numerical effect sizes for changing any of these parameters.  

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   – The paper does not provide information on efficiency or on systematically varying any of the 15 parameters. Consequently, it offers no clear basis for predicting how changes in the 15 parameters might alter the effect of punishment on efficiency. One therefore cannot draw meaningful predictions about group efficiency from this study’s data or discussion.

Authors: Konishi, N; Oe, T; Shimizu, H; Tanaka, K; Ohtsubo, Y
Author Full Names: Konishi, Naoki; Oe, Tomoko; Shimizu, Hiroshi; Tanaka, Kanako; Ohtsubo, Yohsuke
Article Title: Perceived Shared Condemnation Intensifies Punitive Moral Emotions
Keywords Plus: 3RD-PARTY PUNISHMENT; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; SOCIAL NORMS; ANGER; COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; DISGUST; ENFORCEMENT; DEFECTORS; COMMUNITY
Abstract: Punishment facilitates large-scale cooperation among humans, but how punishers, who incur an extra cost of punishment, can successfully compete with non-punishers, who free-ride on the punisher's policing, poses an evolutionary puzzle. One answer is by coordinating punishment to minimise its cost. Notice, however, that in order to effectively coordinate their punishment, potential punishers must know in advance whether others would also be willing to punish a particular norm violator. Such knowledge might hinder coordination by tempting potential punishers to free-ride on other punishers. Previous research suggests that moral emotions, such as moral outrage and moral disgust, serve as a commitment device and drive people to carry out the costly act of punishment. Accordingly, we tested whether the perception of socially shared condemnation (i.e., knowledge that others also condemn a particular violator) would amplify moral outrage and moral disgust, and diminish empathy for the violator. Study 1 (scenario-based study) revealed that perceived shared condemnation was correlated positively with moral outrage and moral disgust, and negatively with empathy. Study 2 experimentally demonstrated that information indicating that others also condemn a particular norm violation amplified moral outrage. Lastly, Study 3 (autobiographical recall study) confirmed the external validity of the finding.

SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper does not examine group efficiency, total payoff, or average payoff. The authors focus on moral emotions (moral outrage, moral disgust, empathy) and self-reported likelihood of intervention or punishment. These variables differ from efficiency-based measures because they emphasize psychological or emotional reactions and self-reported punitive intentions rather than payoffs or resource allocations in a public goods context.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter discussion of what (if anything) this paper says about each of the 15 public‐goods‐game parameters, followed by the requested four‐part summary (A–D). Throughout, note that the paper by Nolan (2017) focuses on how the presence (vs. absence) of a “formal sanctioning system” (regulatory or market‐based) affects participants’ use of “informal sanctions”—that is, guilt and disapproval toward defectors—and several other psychological variables. The paper does not measure or discuss “efficiency” (actual vs. maximum possible payoff) as a dependent variable, nor does it systematically vary most parameters common to public‐goods‐game designs.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
• Discussed? Yes. In the lab experiment (Study 1), participants were led to believe they were in an eight‐person group.  
• Systematically varied? No. The paper does not manipulate or compare different group sizes; it only fixes the size at eight.  
• Any reported effect on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable)? No. The paper does not test different numbers of players.

2. Number of rounds  
• Discussed? Somewhat. The lab game ran for five rounds, but the “critical” comparison was over the first three.  
• Systematically varied? No. All participants followed the same round structure.  
• Any reported effect on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable)? No. The paper does not compare different numbers of rounds.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
• Discussed? Yes, but only as a minor procedural detail. In Study 1, after receiving feedback about other players’ cooperation/defection, participants could send text messages or emoticons to a defector/cooperator.  
• Systematically varied? No. Everyone had that option.  
• Any reported effect on punishment? No systematic discussion of “chat” as a manipulated parameter.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Discussed? The paper’s design shows that participants could choose any number of points (0 to 10) to contribute. They were not constrained to “all or nothing.”  
• Systematically varied? No. The choice was always from 0 to 10.  
• Any reported effect on punishment? Not discussed.

5. Is the contribution default?  
• Discussed? No. The paper makes no mention of default contribution settings (e.g., forced or automatic contributions).  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any reported effect on punishment? Not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor  
• Discussed? The design specifies that contributions to the “group account” are doubled before being split among the eight members. That implies a multiplier of 2, with each point in the group account effectively yielding 0.25 back per contributor.  
• Systematically varied? No. It is fixed at 2.  
• Any reported effect on punishment? Not discussed.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Discussed? Briefly. In Study 1, participants could “deduct points” from a defector’s account at a cost of 0.25 point per 1 point deducted. Also, in the regulatory condition, participants risked losing one point if detected defecting.  
• Systematically varied? No. The paper uses a single cost structure in the lab; it never changes this cost.  
• Any reported effect on the punishment treatment effect? No. They do not study different punishment‐cost levels.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
• Discussed? Some mention of a “1‐point deduction” in the regulatory condition, and “you can subtract (or add) points to another’s account at 1 point per 0.25 cost.”  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any reported effect on punishment? No. The paper does not vary or compare different punishment magnitudes.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
• Discussed? Slightly. In Study 1, participants could also “add” points to a cooperator’s account. But “reward” was not a focal construct; the analysis centers on punishing defectors.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any reported effect on punishment or efficiency? No.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Discussed? The same 0.25‐point cost applied to add or subtract a single point from another’s account.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any reported effect on punishment? No.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
• Discussed? The magnitude was 1 point for each reward action (at a 0.25 cost), but not systematically varied.  
• Any reported effect on punishment? No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
• Discussed? The paper states that participants proceeded through five rounds but focuses on the first three. It does not explicitly say whether participants were told about the total number in advance or how certain they were about the end.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any reported effect on punishment? No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained or lost each round)?  
• Discussed? Partly. Participants received contrived feedback: “one person contributed three points, another contributed nine points.” They did see those outcomes. But the paper does not vary how or whether outcomes were displayed.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any reported effect on punishment? Not separately discussed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• Discussed? Not in detail. The procedures do not clarify that the punished individual sees the identity of the punisher. This was not manipulated or emphasized.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any reported effect on punishment? No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
• Discussed? Same as above. The paper does not dwell on whether recipients learn who rewarded them.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any reported effect on punishment? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
• No. The paper does not analyze efficiency (i.e., total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff).  
• What are the dependent variables, and how are these different from efficiency?  
  – In Study 1, dependent variables included participants’ willingness to cooperate (their point contributions), the extent of guilt and shame (labeled “internal sanctions”), disapproval of non‐cooperators (“indirect social sanctions”), willingness to send punishing emoticons or deduct points (“direct social sanctions”), expectations about how others will cooperate, perceived choice (intrinsic motivation), and decision frame (economic vs. ethical).  
  – In Study 2, dependent variables included levels of guilt for not recycling, perceived social approval/disapproval for different levels of recycling, willingness to confront neighbors who do not recycle, and attributions about others’ reasons for recycling.  
• In short, the paper focuses on internal and social sanctions, trust, and framing, not on group efficiency.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• The paper explicitly mentions:  
  1) Number of players (fixed at 8),  
  2) Number of rounds (5 total, with analyses focusing on the first 3),  
  3) A sort of “chat” (messages/emoticons) is allowed,  
  6) A fixed multiplier (2× on group contributions),  
  7–8) A fixed punishment cost (deducting 1 point costs 0.25) and fixed magnitude (1 point).  
• It briefly notes there is also an option to reward, but does not explore that systematically.  
• All other parameters (e.g., “all or nothing” contributions, knowledge of final round, identity of punisher, etc.) appear only as procedural details or brief mentions. None are manipulated systematically.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• Strictly speaking, none. The paper’s main manipulation is the presence/absence/type (regulatory vs. market‐based) of a formal sanctioning system, not a systematic variation of the above 15 parameters.  
• Therefore, no effect sizes or predictions are provided for systematically varying any of the 15 parameters on punishment or “efficiency.”  

D. If you were to make predictions on how these 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
• The paper offers no direct evidence or discussion dealing with “efficiency” as an outcome. It also never systematically manipulates the 15 parameters. Consequently, there is minimal basis for any specific prediction, beyond the general finding that introducing an external “formal sanctioning system” can sometimes buttress (increase) informal sanctions like guilt and disapproval of noncooperators.  
• In short, the paper does not provide enough information to predict how varying the 15 parameters (e.g., changing group size, adjusting the punishment cost, or the marginal per capita return) might quantitatively affect the treatment effect on group efficiency.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Article Title: Evolution of cooperation through adaptive interaction in a spatial prisoner's dilemma game
Source Title: PHYSICA A-STATISTICAL MECHANICS AND ITS APPLICATIONS
Author Keywords: Evolution of cooperation; Adaptive interaction; Disconnecting strength
Keywords Plus: SOCIAL NETWORKS; PUNISHMENT
Abstract: In this paper, we study the effect of adaptive interaction on the evolution of cooperation in a spatial prisoner's dilemma game. The connections of players are co-evolutionary with cooperation; whether adjacent players can play the prisoner's dilemma game is associated with the strategies they took in the preceding round. If a player defected in the preceding round, his neighbors will refuse to play the prisoner's dilemma game with him in accordance with a certain probability distribution. We use the disconnecting strength to represent this probability. We discuss the evolution of cooperation with different values of temptation to defect, sucker's payoff and disconnecting strength. The simulation results show that cooperation can be significantly enhanced through increasing the value of the disconnecting strength. In addition, the increase in disconnecting strength can improve the cooperators' ability to resist the increase in temptation and the decrease in reward. We study the parameter ranges for three different evolutionary results: cooperators extinction, defectors extinction, cooperator and defector co-existence. Meanwhile, we recruited volunteers and designed a human behavioral experiment to verify the theoretical simulation results. The punishment of disconnection has a positive effect on cooperation. A higher disconnecting strength will enhance cooperation more significantly. Our research findings reveal some significant insights into efficient mechanisms of the evolution of cooperation. Abstract: Background: Allowing players to punish their opponents in Public Goods Game sustains cooperation within a group and thus brings advantage to the cooperative individuals. However, the possibility of punishment of the co-players can result in antisocial punishment, the punishment of those players who contribute the most in the group. To better understand why antisocial punishment exists, it must be determined who are the anti-social punishers and who are their primary targets. Methods: For resolving these questions we increased the number of players in a group from usual four to twelve. Each group played six rounds of the standard Public Goods Game and six rounds of the Public Goods Game with punishment. Each player in each round received 20 CZK ($ 1.25). Players (N=118) were rematched after each round so that they would not take into consideration opponents' past behavior. Results: The amount of the punishment received correlated negatively with the contribution (p= -0.665, p<0.001). However, this correlation was positive for players in the highest contributors-quartile (p =0.254, p<0.001). Therefore, the graph of relation between the contribution given and punishment obtained was U-shaped (R-2=0.678, p<0.001) with the inflection point near the left boarder of the upper quartile. The antisocial punishment was present in all groups, and in eight out of ten groups the Justine Effect (the positive correlation between the contribution to the public pool and the risk of suffering punishment in the subpopulation of altruistic players) emerged. In our sample, 22.5% subjects, all of them Free riders and low contributors, punished the altruistic players. Conclusions: The results of our experimental game-study revealed the existence of the Justine effect - the positive correlation between the contribution to the public pool by a subpopulation of the most altruistic players, and the amount of punishment these players obtained from free-riders.

   •  Not stated.  The design section does not say whether players see the stranger’s monetary outcome; the authors only say payoffs follow Table 1.  The feature is neither varied nor analyzed.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
   •  Not applicable—no real punishment or reward is ever implemented.

----------------------------------------------------------------
NUMERICAL EFFECT SIZES REPORTED IN THE PAPER
----------------------------------------------------------------
Because there is **no punishment treatment** in the behavioral game, the paper reports *zero* effect sizes linking any of the 15 parameters to a “punishment treatment effect” on any dependent variable, let alone on efficiency.  All coefficients and figures relate instead to:
•  The likelihood of cooperating in the PD, predicted by survey-based beliefs about *community norms* (especially “retaliatory sanctions”).  
•  Heterogeneity across five Chinese cities.

----------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
----------------------------------------------------------------
A. Does the paper study group efficiency?  
   •  No.  Dependent variable = binary “cooperate” vs. “defect” in a one-shot PD.  
   •  Efficiency (total or average payoff relative to the cooperative optimum) is never computed.  Thus “efficiency,” “contribution level,” and “cooperation rate” are absent or conflated with the single binary choice.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   •  #1 (players = 2), #2 (rounds = 1), #4 (binary action set in PD), #12 (rounds known), #7–8 (punishment/retribution referenced abstractly in vignettes).  
   •  That is 6 of 15, and only as background description—none are manipulated.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the *punishment treatment effect*?  
   •  Zero.  No punishment treatment exists.

D. If forced to predict how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency using *only* this paper, little can be said:  
   •  The article contains no controlled punishment stage, no efficiency data, and no systematic parameter sweeps.  
   •  All that can cautiously be inferred is that beliefs about the *existence* of retaliatory punishment in outside life correlate positively with baseline cooperation in a two-person one-shot PD—suggesting that if a formal punishment option were later added, willingness to cooperate might increase in communities where people anticipate retaliation.  There is, however, no numerical basis for estimating magnitude, nor any insight into cost-effectiveness or efficiency consequences.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter account of what, if anything, the paper by Krasnow and Delton (2016) says about each of the 15 parameters, together with any discussion (or lack thereof) of how systematically varying that parameter would affect the “punishment treatment effect”—in other words, whether the paper addresses how introducing punishment would increase or decrease group efficiency (actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff). Throughout, I use the term “punishment treatment effect” simply to refer to how punishment might change cooperation or payoffs. The paper itself does not speak in terms of “group efficiency,” nor does it present outcome data in a way that can be translated directly into efficiency measures. I will nonetheless note whenever they discuss (a) the parameter at all and (b) whether they mention how systematically changing it might affect punishment’s impact. Numerical effect sizes are not provided in the paper for any parameter.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
• Mentioned?: Yes, in the sense that the paper discusses groups of varying sizes—up to 25—in agent-based models.  
• Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?: The paper states that the authors “allowed evolution to work on quantitative individual differences” in punitive tendencies in groups ranging up to size 25, but they do not connect this explicitly to efficiency, nor do they provide specific effect sizes. They do say their models find that punishment can evolve in group settings up to that size, but they do not measure or report how group size systematically changes the magnitude of a “punishment treatment effect” on total payoffs or efficiency.

2) Number of rounds  
• Mentioned?: The paper refers to one-shot vs. repeated interactions but does not specify a controlled, discrete number of rounds as a design parameter in a public goods game.  
• Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?: No direct mention of systematically varying the number of rounds, nor of how that variation would affect punishment’s impact on efficiency. They do discuss conceptually that “life is long enough that… later cooperation repeats,” but there is no formal discussion of how changing the exact number of rounds alters total payoffs or efficiency.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
• Mentioned?: No. The authors do not mention any form of intra-group communication or chat.  
• Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?: No mention.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Mentioned?: No. The authors discuss “cooperation” in general but do not refer to forced “all or nothing” contributions.  
• Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?: No mention.

5) Is the contribution default? (i.e., deciding how much of one’s endowment to move from the public fund back into one’s hand)  
• Mentioned?: No.  
• Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?: No mention.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
• Mentioned?: No. The authors do not present or manipulate a typical “MPCR” factor from public goods game designs.  
• Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?: No mention.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Mentioned?: Yes, but only qualitatively. The paper states that punishment is “costly” due to time, effort, and risk of retaliation, and that this cost is relevant to its evolution.  
• Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?: The paper does not provide any table or figure systematically varying punishment cost or showing effect sizes. They mention that in their simulations “punishment is probabilistic rather than all-or-none (lowering costs),” and that this matters for seeing whether punishment evolves, but they do not quantify increases or decreases in group payoffs or efficiency.

8) Punishment magnitude (i.e., how many coins are deducted from a player per unit of punishment)  
• Mentioned?: The idea that punishment involves “costs” or “negative payoffs” to the target is implicit; however, no specific “magnitude” is analyzed.  
• Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?: Not discussed in a systematic, quantitative way.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
• Mentioned?: No. The article talks exclusively about punishment (the “stick”) vs. cooperation (the “carrot”), but not about peer-driven reward.  
• Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?: No mention.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Mentioned?: No.  
• Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?: No mention.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward)  
• Mentioned?: No.  
• Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?: No mention.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players? (Do they know when the game ends?)  
• Mentioned?: Indirectly, the authors compare “one-shot” vs. “repeated” interactions under uncertainty, but they do not discuss whether participants have knowledge of when or how the interaction ends in a typical experiment.  
• Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?: No. They do not link any knowledge-of-end condition with a measured effect on efficiency.

13) Are peer outcomes shown? (Do players know how much their peers gained or lost each round?)  
• Mentioned?: No. The paper does not mention the disclosure or visibility of peers’ gains in an experimental design.  
• Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?: No mention.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who punished them?  
• Mentioned?: The authors do talk about “anonymous” vs. non-anonymous contexts, noting that laboratory tasks sometimes use “one-shot, anonymous punishment.” However, they do not systematically manipulate or measure how knowledge of the punisher’s identity shifts payoffs or efficiency.  
• Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?: No formal analysis. They simply note that the real-world ancestral ecology rarely would have guaranteed anonymity.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who rewarded them?  
• Mentioned?: No, as reward is not addressed in this paper.  
• Systematic variation and effect on punishment treatment?: No mention.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?  
• The paper does not use group efficiency or total/average payoff as a clearly reported dependent variable. Instead, it discusses cooperation, generosity, and punishment (including whether these behaviors “evolve” in an agent-based simulation). It also refers more broadly to whether punishment supports group cooperation. None of these are directly equated to “efficiency” as defined by actual vs. maximum payoff.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• “Number of players” (parameter 1) is mentioned (they discuss groups up to size 25).  
• “Punishment cost” (parameter 7) is mentioned qualitatively.  
• “When a player is punished, do they know who punished them?” (parameter 14) is indirectly alluded to via talk of “anonymous punishment,” but not in a systematic parametric sense.  
• No other parameters among the 15 are explicitly discussed.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• None of the parameters are explicitly and quantitatively varied in the paper for their effect on a “punishment treatment effect” or on “efficiency.” The authors discuss modeling different group sizes and mention punishment cost generally, but they do not provide any analysis or effect sizes regarding punishment’s effect on total payoffs or efficiency under systematic changes of these parameters.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
• The paper does not include enough explicit analysis to make strong predictions. It treats punishment largely in qualitative or evolutionary terms (e.g., that punishment can help stabilize cooperation and that some willingness to punish evolves in larger groups). However, no direct statements about efficiency outcomes (actual vs. maximum payoff) are made. Consequently, there is little to no basis from the paper’s content alone to predict how varying any of these 15 parameters would quantitatively affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.  

In short, the paper primarily advances an argument about how punishment (and generosity) can be adaptive and why “apparently irrational” prosocial or punitive acts might still be generated by evolved psychological mechanisms. It does not, however, systematically track or report an “efficiency” measure or the specific parameters that would allow one to calculate it.
reference_APA: Krasnow, Max M. & Delton, Andrew W. (2016). Are Humans Too Generous and Too Punitive? Using Psychological Principles to Further Debates about Human Social Evolution. FRONTIERS IN PSYCHOLOGY.

Below I go through the fifteen design parameters in the exact order given.  
For each parameter I state  

(1) whether the paper even mentions the parameter and, if so, the value actually used in the experiment; and  
(2) whether the paper makes – or allows us to infer – any prediction about how **systematically varying** that parameter would change the *punishment-treatment effect* (i.e., the difference in efficiency/earnings between a public-goods game **with** punishment and the same game **without** punishment).

I rely strictly on what is written in the article, its tables and its figures.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned: yes. Each public-goods group has four players.  
   (2) No variation and no prediction.  

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Mentioned: yes. The game lasts five repeated rounds.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction about different horizons.  

3. Chat (free communication)  
   (1) Mentioned implicitly: “participants were not allowed to communicate”.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.  

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
   (1) Mentioned: contributions are 0–10 points in one-point steps (standard continuous choice).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.  

5. Contribution default / refund format  
   (1) The default is zero; subjects actively choose how many of their 10 tokens to put in the public fund.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.  

6. MPCR (or multiplication factor)  
   (1) Explicit: every point sent to the group account is multiplied to 2 and then divided among four members ⇒ MPCR = 0.5.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction about higher/lower MPCRs.  

7. Cost to impose one unit of punishment  
   (1) Explicit: 2 points for the punisher.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.  

8. Magnitude of one unit of punishment  
   (1) Explicit: 5 points deducted from the target.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.  

9. Presence of a reward option  
   (1) Explicitly absent: only costly **punishment** (“disapproval cards”) exists.  
   (2) Reward is never introduced, so there is no discussion of how adding rewards would affect efficiency.  

10. Cost to grant one reward  
11. Magnitude of one reward  
   (1) Not applicable in the design; not discussed.  
   (2) Therefore no predictions.  

12. Whether the horizon is common knowledge  
   (1) The design states “who repeatedly interact for five rounds”; participants are instructed, so the horizon is known.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.  

13. Information about peer outcomes  
   (1) Yes: after each contribution stage subjects see every other player’s individual contribution before choosing punishment; after the punishment stage they only see how many disapproval cards they received, not who sent them.  
   (2) The information structure is fixed; the article does not explore alternative feedback regimes.  

14. Whether the punished know the identity of the punisher  
   (1) Explicit: “they do not know the punishers’ identity.”  
   (2) Identification is not varied; the authors do not speculate on what would happen if identity were revealed.  

15. Whether the rewarded know the identity of the rewarder  
   (1) Not applicable (no rewards).  
   (2) No prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY  

A. Dependent variables actually analysed  
   – Trust-game transfers (sender and receiver)  
   – Public-goods contributions  
   – Probability/amount of punishment  
   – Group total earnings over the five rounds (Table 7).  
   “Efficiency” in the textbook sense (total payoff ÷ social optimum) is **not** computed, but total earnings per group serve as a direct proxy.  

B. Which of the 15 parameters are at least mentioned?  
   10 of them: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14.  
   (Rewards and their two cost/magnitude parameters, plus chat and default, are only mentioned by stating they do not exist.)  

C. For how many parameters does the paper study the effect of *systematically varying* the parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
   Zero. Every one of the 15 parameters is held constant across treatments; the only experimental variation concerns **ethnic composition of the group**, which is outside the present 15-parameter list.  

D. What can we predict – solely from this paper – about how varying the 15 parameters would change the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
   Very little. Because none of the parameters were varied, the paper provides no within-study evidence. All we can glean indirectly is that, given the specific parameter constellation used (4 players, 5 known rounds, MPCR = 0.5, punishment cost = 2, impact = 5, anonymous punishers, no chat, no rewards), punishment sometimes lowers total earnings in ethnically mixed groups relative to homogeneous groups.  
   Extrapolating beyond that design would require external evidence that the authors do not supply. Hence, no reliable predictions about the direction, let alone the size, of punishment-treatment effects when any of the 15 parameters are changed can be made from this paper alone.

Abstract: The effect of sanctions on cooperation depends on social and cultural norms. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter inventory of what appears (and what does not) in the Fatas and Mateu (2015) paper. The paper compares two public‐goods environments—one with a linear production function (VCM) and the other in which the minimum contribution determines the group outcome (WLM). It introduces punishment partway through each game (in a second block of 20 rounds), thereby comparing behavior with vs. without punishment. However, it does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters listed in your request—other than switching the production function itself (which is not one of the 15). Accordingly, any inferences about “systematically varying” a parameter cannot be drawn from the study, since no such systematic manipulations were conducted.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players
 • Mentioned or used?  
   – Yes. Each group has 4 players (p. 7 and elsewhere).  
 • Systematically varied?  
   – No; the experiment keeps group size fixed at 4.  
 • Any predictions or effect sizes about varying group size?  
   – None.

2) Number of rounds
 • Mentioned or used?  
   – Yes. There are 20 rounds with no punishment, followed by 20 rounds with punishment (p. 7–8). Each block length (20 rounds) is known to participants.  
 • Systematically varied?  
   – No; the study simply runs two 20‐round blocks.  
 • Any predictions or effect sizes about varying the number of rounds?  
   – None.

3) Is chat enabled between players?
 • Mentioned or used?  
   – No; the paper does not mention allowing any form of in‐game communication (“chat”).  
 • Systematically varied?  
   – No.  
 • Any predictions?  
   – None.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
 • Mentioned or used?  
   – It is explicitly not “all or nothing.” Participants choose any amount (0–50 ECUs).  
 • Systematically varied?  
   – No.  
 • Any predictions?  
   – None.

5) Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much of their endowment to move back to their hand from the public fund)?
 • Mentioned or used?  
   – No. The task is framed as a standard “how much to contribute” decision, with no special “default” rule.  
 • Systematically varied?  
   – No.  
 • Any predictions?  
   – None.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
 • Mentioned or used?  
   – Yes, for the linear VCM, the MPCR is 0.5 (p. 7). In the WLM, “b = 0.5” enters the payoff via the minimum contribution.  
 • Systematically varied?  
   – No; MPCR is fixed at 0.5 in all VCM sessions.  
 • Any predictions or effect sizes about changing the MPCR?  
   – None.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
 • Mentioned or used?  
   – Yes. Each punishment point costs the punisher 2 ECUs (p. 9).  
 • Systematically varied?  
   – No; it is fixed.  
 • Any predictions or effect sizes about varying that cost?  
   – None.

8) Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from the punished player)
 • Mentioned or used?  
   – Yes. Each single unit of punishment reduces the punished player’s payoff by 6 ECUs (p. 9).  
 • Systematically varied?  
   – No.  
 • Any predictions?  
   – None.

9) Whether a reward is enabled
 • Mentioned or used?  
   – The experiment does not include a reward stage; there is only punishment.  
 • Systematically varied?  
   – No.

 • Mentioned or used?  
   – No; no rewards were used.  
 • Systematically varied?  
   – No.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded)
 • Mentioned or used?  
   – No; no rewards were used.

   – No.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
 • Mentioned or used?  
   – Yes. Each block is known to last 20 rounds (p. 7–8), although the “surprise” was that a second block of 20 appeared.  
 • Systematically varied?  
   – No.  
 • Any predictions?  
   – None for systematically changing the known horizon.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much others gained or lost)?
 • Mentioned or used?  
   – Yes. After each round, subjects see each player’s contribution and their own payoff. They see total punishment inflicted on them but not who sent it (p. 9).  
 • Systematically varied?  
   – No.  
 • Any predictions?

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
