 • Systematically varied?  
   – No.  
 • Any predictions?  
   – None.
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • Yes. The authors measure “efficiency” by comparing actual group earnings (or total payoff) to the no‐contribution baseline and, in some figures, to the maximum payoff if everyone fully contributed. They also report intermediate measures such as contribution rates or “% of maximum” provision of the public good. Hence, the authors discuss:  
     – Provision of the public good (percentage of the maximum possible).  
     – Actual earnings (to assess net welfare after punishment costs).  
     – Antisocial vs. social punishment frequencies.  
   • These are distinct from “efficiency” in that the paper focuses heavily on “provision” and “cooperation” as well, but they do ultimately examine net gains in payoffs, thus addressing efficiency/welfare directly.

B) Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned:  
     1 (group size = 4), 2 (20 rounds per block), 6 (MPCR = 0.5), 7 (punishment cost = 2), 8 (punishment magnitude = 6), 12 (the 20‐round blocks are known), 13 (individual contributions/earnings are displayed), 14 (identity of punisher is hidden).

Abstract: From small communities to entire nations and society at large, inequality in wealth, social status, and power is one of the most pervasive and tenacious features of the social world. What causes inequality to emerge and persist? In this study, we investigate how the structure and rules of our interactions can increase inequality in social groups. Specifically, we look into the effects of four structural conditions-network structure, network fluidity, reputation tracking, and punishment institutions-on the distribution of earnings in network cooperation games. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter analysis following your requested structure. All statements refer strictly to what appears in the Lefebvre & Stenger (2020) paper (“Short‐ & long‐term effects of monetary and non-monetary incentives to cooperate in public good games: An experiment”) and its figures and tables. Where the paper does not address a parameter or does not provide specific predictions about systematically varying it, that is stated explicitly. The paper’s main focus is on how punishments and rewards (both monetary and non‐monetary) affect contributions over a 30‐round repeated public‐good experiment and on whether those effects persist after the incentive is withdrawn (Periods 16–30). Critically, the paper studies “contributions” (and, secondarily, payoffs), rather than the specific measure of group efficiency (actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff). It does not provide a direct analysis of how systematically varying the following parameters would affect “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER DISCUSSION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1) Number of players  
   • Discussed? Yes, the paper fixes group size at 4 players per group.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not vary the group size. No predictions or effect sizes are discussed about changing the number of players.

2) Number of rounds  
   • Discussed? Yes. Their main design has 30 total periods (two sequences, each of 15 periods). In four main treatments, punishment or reward is available in the first 15 periods, then removed for the last 15.  
   • The paper also describes three supplemental treatments (MR-10, MR-20, MR-NA) which adjust the length of the “reward phase”—10 periods or 20 periods or an uncertain end. However, it does not explicitly analyze how doing so impacts “efficiency”; rather, it reports how average contributions differ across these variants (see Figure 4).  
   • Systematically varied for punishment treatment effect? Not specifically. They do not present a quantitative link of “number of rounds” to a punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency or on payoffs. There is no numeric effect size on “efficiency” reported.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussed? Yes, in that the paper states there is “no possibility of communicating.”  
   • Systematically varied? No. Thus, there is no discussion of how enabling/ disabling chat would change punishment’s (or any incentive’s) impact.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Discussed? Yes, the paper describes a classic linear public‐goods game where participants choose how many tokens (0 to 20) to contribute, so it is not “all or nothing.”  
   • Systematically varied? No. No predictions or effect sizes are offered about changing to an “all‐or‐nothing” mechanism.

5) Is the contribution default (e.g., do players move a default amount from the public fund)?  
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not describe or manipulate any default contribution mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Discussed? Yes. Each token invested yields 0.4 tokens for each of the four group members, equivalent to a 1.6 total multiplier on a single token contributed.  
   • Systematically varied? No. They always use MPCR=0.4 and do not present how varying it would affect punishment or efficiency. No effect sizes are given.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussed? Yes. In the Monetary Punishment (MP) treatment, each punishment point costs the punisher 0.25 tokens.  
   • Systematically varied? No. They used the same “0.25 cost” throughout. The paper does not offer predictions or effect sizes for other cost/impact ratios.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted per punishment point)  
   • Discussed? Yes. In the Monetary Punishment treatment, each punishment point removes 1 token from the punished player’s earnings.  
   • Systematically varied? No. No predictions or effect sizes for changing the magnitude are given.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussed? Yes, they have separate Reward treatments (Monetary Reward, MR, and Non‐monetary Reward, NMR). In the Baseline and Punishment treatments, there is no reward.  
   • Systematically varied for its effect on the punishment treatment? Not exactly. Rewards are studied as a separate condition, not combined with punishment. The paper does not discuss “punishment treatment effect” specifically under the condition that a reward is or is not simultaneously enabled.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Discussed? Yes. In Monetary Reward (MR), it costs 0.25 tokens to grant 1 token of reward.  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no manipulation of the cost ratio.

11) Reward magnitude (coins awarded per unit of reward)  
   • Discussed? Yes. In MR, each reward point gives +1 token to the rewarded individual’s payoff.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not present predictions or effect sizes for changing it.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?  
   • Discussed? Yes, the paper states that apart from one additional treatment with an uncertain end (MR-NA), the experiment is finitely repeated with the final period known to participants.  
   • Systematically varied? Only in MR‐NA (uncertain ending). The paper reports that uncertainty reduced contributions overall but does not quantify an “efficiency” effect nor systematically compare punishment treatments under known vs. unknown lengths.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much others gained or lost)?  
   • Discussed? The experiment reveals each group member’s contribution amount (in ascending order), but not their final payoff or how many sanctions/rewards the others received.  
   • Systematically varied? No. That display rule is kept constant; there is no discussion of changing it.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Discussed? Explicitly stated as “no.” The paper says subjects only learn how many punishment points they received in total but cannot identify who assigned them.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Discussed? Similarly “no.” Subjects see the total number of reward points they receive but cannot identify who allocated them.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper’s main dependent variables are individual contribution levels, group contribution levels, and, secondarily, payoffs. They do not report “group efficiency” as the ratio of total payoff to the maximum possible payoff; “contribution” is not the same as “efficiency.” Where they discuss “payoffs,” it is mainly in the context of how punishments or rewards adjust an individual’s earnings, not the group’s efficiency ratio.

B) Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned: (1) Number of players = 4; (2) Number of rounds = 30 (with some additional variations for reward-length and uncertain end); (3) No chat allowed; (4) Contributions are a continuous choice, not all‐or‐nothing; (6) MPCR=0.4; (7) Punishment cost=0.25; (8) Punishment magnitude=1 token per point; (9) Rewards are either absent or present in certain treatments; (10) Reward cost=0.25; (11) Reward magnitude=+1 token per point; (12) The number of rounds is known except in the MR‐NA variant; (13) Peers see others’ contributions; (14) Punishers remain anonymous; (15) Rewarders remain anonymous.  
   • Not mentioned as a design parameter: (5) The “contribution default” was not manipulated or discussed.

C) For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on a punishment treatment effect when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The study does not systematically vary any of the standard structural or incentive parameters (1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15) to analyze how that variation alone modifies the punishment effect.  
   • The only partial exception is parameter (2), “Number of rounds (or length of the incentive phase).” They do run extra conditions (MR-10, MR-20, MR-NA) but these revolve around reward lengths—not specifically how systematically varying the total rounds changes the punishment treatment effect.  
   • Hence, explicitly for “punishment treatment effect,” the paper offers no numerical effect sizes that come from systematically varying one parameter at a time.

D) If you were to make predictions (on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency) solely based on the content of this paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper presents no direct evidence for how varying these parameters would shift “efficiency,” nor does it model total payoff relative to the maximum possible payoff. It mainly reports that, with fixed settings of four players, 0.4 MPCR, and 0.25 punishment/reward cost, monetary punishment leads to higher average contributions than non‐monetary punishment, suggesting it is more “effective” at raising contributions.  
   • Once punishment is removed, contributions remain higher than the no-punishment baseline, indicating a persistence in contributions. However, the authors do not specify how changing the group size, the cost of punishment, or other structural parameters would shift that persistence or the ratio “actual payoff / maximum payoff.”  
   • Consequently, the paper provides little basis for predicting how systematically varying any of these 15 parameters—aside from introducing or removing punishments or rewards—would affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

   • The sole quantitative dependent variable is the fraction of cooperators, f_c.  
   • Snap-shots of spatial strategy distributions are also shown.

B. Parameters mentioned (any value stated)  
   4 of 15:  
      #1 Number of players  
      #2 Number of rounds  
      #7 Punishment cost (ρ)  
      #8 Punishment magnitude (β)

C. Parameters whose **systematic variation** is linked to the punishment treatment effect  
   Only 1 of 15 – parameter #7 (punishment cost ρ).  
   All other parameters are either held fixed or absent.

D. What can be predicted—solely from this paper—about the 15 parameters’ impacts on the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
   • Because efficiency is never measured, the paper allows **very limited inference**.  
   • The only directional cue is that lowering the cost of punishment (ρ) strongly increases cooperation, so—*if* higher cooperation translated into higher efficiency—one would expect a positive PTE at low ρ and a smaller or even negative PTE at high ρ.  
   • For all other parameters (1–6, 8–15) the paper provides no evidence that would support any prediction about efficiency.

Hence, beyond “low punishment cost is beneficial,” the article supplies almost no information for forecasting how the 15 design variables or their interactions would modulate the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.

Article Title: Altruistic Punishment and Impulsivity in Parkinson's Disease: A Social Neuroscience Perspective
Author Keywords: impulsive behavior; altruistic punishment; Parkinson's disease; social cognition; social norms; ingroup and outgroup contexts; default mode network (DMN); functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI)
Keywords Plus: DEFAULT MODE NETWORK; CONTROL DISORDERS; CLINICAL-FEATURES; CINGULATE CORTEX; DECISION-MAKING; NEURAL BASIS; COOPERATION; DYSKINESIAS; REWARD; INHIBITION
Abstract: Non-motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease (PD) are of increasing interest in clinical and psychological research. Disinhibition-the inability to inhibit inappropriate behavior-leads to social and emotional impairments, including impulsive behavior and disregard for social conventions and decision-making behavior. In recent years, the latter has been investigated using economic exchanges during social interactions. Altruistic punishment-to punish someone who violates group norms even if it foresees a personal cost-is one of the most useful and fruitful paradigms; it allows to maintain a cooperation system within social groups. Alterations of this cognitive ability negatively impact the quality of life of the individual and social stability. Social neuroscience has suggested association between impulsive behaviors and altruistic punishment. Neuroimaging research aimed at exploring functional networks and intrinsic functional connectivity went in this direction. To date, little is known about these issues in neurodegenerative diseases such as PD. Dopamine replacement treatment and dopamine-agonists have been associated with impulse-control disorder and impulsive-compulsive behavior able to affect social decision-making. Frontal-executive dysfunction determines an alteration of social functioning through a mechanism of subversion of online action-monitoring, which associates disinhibition with volition. Genetic polymorphisms, alterations of the nigro-striatal substance, and impairment in the medial prefrontal cortex and in the Default mode network (DMN) seem to be able to explain these mechanisms. This theoretical perspective article aims to present these topics in order to encourage an interdisciplinary discussion capable of generating new research and developing rehabilitative intervention to improve social decision-making in PD patients.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter analysis based solely on what is stated in the paper “Altruistic Punishment and Impulsivity in Parkinson’s Disease: A Social Neuroscience Perspective” by Morese and Palermo (2020). The references to other studies (e.g., Djamshidian et al., 2011; de Quervain et al., 2004) are mentioned in the paper itself. No information outside the paper has been used.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
1. Number of players
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     The paper mentions an experimental procedure (citing Djamshidian et al., 2011) in which participants believed they were playing a trust game online. It states that “eight participants played with one trustee per round,” but it does not otherwise discuss varying the number of players.  
   • Does it make predictions about systematically varying this parameter for any dependent variable (including efficiency)?  
     No. There is no discussion of systematically varying the number of players.

2. Number of rounds
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     The description of the trust game in Djamshidian et al. (2011) mentions multiple rounds, but the paper does not elaborate on manipulating or systematically varying the number of rounds.  
   • Does it make predictions about systematically varying this parameter for any dependent variable?  
     No. There is no discussion of how changing the number of rounds might affect punishment or any other dependent variable.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     No. There is no mention of any communication or chat mechanism in the game.  
   • Does it make predictions about systematically varying this parameter?  
     No. It is not discussed at all.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     No. Although the paper mentions players in a trust game deciding “whether to share part of his or her money,” it does not characterize this as an all‐or‐nothing contribution and does not discuss any systematic variation.  
   • Does it make predictions about systematically varying this parameter?  
     No. This parameter is not addressed in the paper.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     No. There is no mention of default contribution schemes or forced contribution settings in the trust task.  
   • Does it make predictions about systematically varying this parameter?  
     No. Not mentioned at all.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     The paper states that the sum exchanged was quadrupled in the trust game (citing Djamshidian et al., 2011), but it does not delve into MPCR concepts as in a typical public‐goods paradigm.  
   • Does it make predictions about systematically varying this parameter?  
     No. The paper does not discuss how systematically altering the multiplication factor would change punishment behaviors.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     The paper, referencing Djamshidian et al. (2011), notes that “the punisher loses £1 for every £2 used to punish.” However, there is no discussion of adjusting this cost across conditions.  
   • Does it make predictions about systematically varying this parameter?  
     No. The paper only reports the cost used in the task but does not discuss its systematic variation.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     The paper indicates that each act of punishment deducts £2 from the target, at the cost of £1 to the punisher, but does not explore different magnitudes of punishment.  
   • Does it make predictions about systematically varying this parameter?  
     No. It is not systematically explored; no effect size or prediction is given for varying the punishment magnitude.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     No. While “reward” is referred to throughout the paper in the context of neural reward circuitry, there is no mention of any experimental condition in which players can reward peers in the game.  
   • Does it make predictions about systematically varying this parameter?  
     No. The possibility of rewarding other players to promote cooperation or measure its effect on punishment is not mentioned.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     No. The paper does not mention any reward‐based mechanism in the game design.  
   • Does it make predictions about systematically varying this parameter?  
     No. Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     No. Similarly, there is no mention of any systematically varied reward magnitude.  
   • Does it make predictions about systematically varying this parameter?  
     No. Not mentioned.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     No. The paper does not specify whether players were informed of how many total rounds the trust game would have.  
   • Does it make predictions about systematically varying this parameter?  
     No. There is no discussion of it.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     The paper notes that participants observed others’ fair/unfair behavior and decided whether to punish, but it does not describe systematically varying the way outcomes were displayed.  
   • Does it make predictions about systematically varying this parameter?  
     No. The paper does not address changes in how information is displayed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     No. It references a scenario in which players believed they were playing online, but it does not mention whether punishment was anonymous or revealed.  
   • Does it make predictions about systematically varying this parameter?  
     No. The paper does not address this.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     No. As there was no rewarding mechanism in the game, there is no discussion of whether the rewarded player knows the rewarder.  
   • Does it make predictions about systematically varying this parameter?  
     No. Not discussed.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper does not use group efficiency or a total/average payoff measure as its dependent variable in the sense of “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff.”  
   • The key dependent variables mentioned are related to punishment decisions (e.g., how frequently and how strongly participants punish) and to impulsivity or impulse‐control behaviors in Parkinson’s disease. The paper does not equate these measures to “efficiency.”

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Parameters mentioned (but not systematically varied) include:
     – Number of players (Parameter 1): referenced as “eight participants” but not varied.  
     – Punishment cost (Parameter 7) and Punishment magnitude (Parameter 8): set at £1 cost for every £2 inflicted, but not varied.  
   • None of the other 12 parameters are mentioned in the sense of explicit, deliberate variation or condition.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. The paper does not describe any systematic manipulation of these parameters, nor does it present effect sizes for how changing these parameters would affect punishment or efficiency.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper provides no direct evidence for making predictions on how systematically varying any of the 15 parameters would change punishment’s effect on group efficiency. Its central focus is on the neurobiological and impulsivity aspects of altruistic punishment in PD. Thus, there is little to no basis within this paper alone to predict how these parameters or their interactions would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Authors: Eichenseer, M
Author Full Names: Eichenseer, Michael
Article Title: Leading-by-example in public goods experiments: What do we know?
Author Keywords: Leading-by-example; Public goods game; Survey; Literature review; Meta-analysis; Lab experiments
Keywords Plus: SEQUENTIAL CONTRIBUTIONS; VOLUNTARY LEADERSHIP; AUTHENTIC LEADERSHIP; ETHICAL LEADERSHIP; FIELD EVIDENCE; COOPERATION; PROVISION; HETEROGENEITY; RECIPROCITY; PREFERENCES
Abstract: This meta-analysis explores whether leading-by-example increases contributions in public goods experiments. I find that leadership overall improves public good provision significantly, whereas leaders benefit less than followers. The reason is that followers match the leader's contributions imperfectly and, on average, only contribute about 79% of the leader's contribution. Consequently, only a small proportion of group members are willing to bear the burden of leadership. Despite this, leaders are usually not worse off compared to an average player in a simultaneous game without a leader. In general, leadership becomes more effective when one adds transactional elements like punishment and reward, whereas it becomes less effective if there is frequent change (rotating leadership).

Below “punishment-treatment effect” (PTE) always means  
   ( average efficiency with a punishment option – average efficiency without a punishment option ).

For every parameter i = 1 … 15 I state  
   (1) whether the paper explicitly gives the parameter’s value / range, and  
   (2) whether the paper says what would happen to the PTE if the parameter were systematically changed.  
   A numerical effect is quoted only when the paper itself reports it.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   (1) Yes. Group size varies from 2 to 8; reported in all meta-regressions (mean 3.9, SD 0.9).  
   (2) No prediction on how changing group size would alter the PTE.  
       (The paper only controls for group size in regressions on cooperation level.)

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Yes. Games last 4–20 periods (mean = 14.2).  
   (2) No statement on the PTE.

3. Chat enabled between players  
   (1) Indirectly. “Leading-by-words/cheap talk” is coded (12 % of treatments).  
   (2) The paper never compares “punishment + chat” with “punishment + no-chat,” hence no PTE prediction.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
   (1) Not mentioned; all reviewed VCMs use continuous contribution choices.  
   (2) No information.

5. Contribution default / “reversal” decision  
   (1) Not mentioned.  
   (2) No information.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR)  
   (1) Yes. Range 0.33–0.83; entered as a control in all regressions.  
   (2) No claim about how MPCR moderates the punishment effect.

7. Cost of imposing one unit of punishment  
   (1) Not reported; the meta-analysis only has a dummy “centralised punishment allowed”.  
   (2) No prediction. Cost levels are never varied systematically.

8. Magnitude of punishment per unit  
   (1) Not reported.  
   (2) No prediction.

9. Reward enabled (yes/no)  
   (1) Yes. “Centralised reward” and “Peer reward” dummies appear.  
   (2) Effect on PTE?  No.  The paper estimates how the mere presence of a reward option changes efficiency (coefficient = +0.148 for centralised reward in Table 1) but never interacts this with “punishment present”, so it does not give an effect on the punishment treatment.

10. Cost of granting one unit of reward  
11. Magnitude of reward per unit  
   Same as 7–8: not reported; no prediction.

12. Horizon known (common knowledge of final round)  
   (1) Not discussed; experiments follow the standard finite-known-horizon design but this is never varied.  
   (2) No prediction.

13. Peer outcomes shown each round  
   (1) Visibility of others’ contributions is necessary in sequential designs and is sometimes varied (e.g., Figuières et al. 2012 compare sequential with/without info).  
   (2) The paper never analyses whether showing pay-offs changes the *punishment* effect.

14. Punished player learns identity of punisher  
15. Rewarded player learns identity of rewarder  
   (1) Not mentioned.  
   (2) No prediction.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
   – “Cooperation level” = average group contribution ÷ social optimum (the paper also calls this “group efficiency”).  
   – Contribution ratio (followers/leaders).  
   – Leader pay-offs relative to simultaneous baseline.  
   – Gini index of pay-offs.  
   These variables differ: efficiency is total welfare relative to the optimum, whereas contribution ratio and Gini concern distributional issues.

B. Parameters actually mentioned: 1, 2, 3 (cheap-talk proxy), 6, 7 (presence of punishment, not its cost), 9 (presence of reward), 13 (information about prior moves). 8 of the 15 are at least named; exact values are given only for 1, 2, 6.

C. Parameters for which the paper discusses *systematic* effects on the punishment treatment: effectively none.  
   – The paper estimates a main effect of “centralised punishment allowed” on efficiency (coefficient ≈ +0.26) and of “peer punishment allowed” (≈ +0.47), but it never analyses how altering any of the 15 parameters changes that effect.  
   Hence 0/15 parameters meet the “systematic variation of PTE” criterion.

D. What predictions can be made, based solely on this paper?  Very few.  
   • If a leader is given exclusive punishment power, efficiency rises by about 26 percentage points on the 0–1 scale, independent of the other listed parameters.  
   • Allowing *peer* punishment raises efficiency even more (≈ +0.47).  
   • No quantitative or qualitative guidance is provided on how group size, MPCR, number of rounds, communication, or any information-display feature would *moderate* that punishment benefit.  
   • Therefore, outside the crude “punishment on/off” dummy, the paper offers almost no basis for predicting how the 15 parameters or their interactions will influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Article Title: Corrupt third parties undermine trust and prosocial behaviour between people
Keywords Plus: 3RD-PARTY PUNISHMENT; COOPERATION; HONESTY; INSTITUTIONS; STATE; POWER
Abstract: Corruption is a pervasive phenomenon that affects the quality of institutions, undermines economic growth and exacerbates inequalities around the globe. Here we tested whether perceiving representatives of institutions as corrupt undermines trust and subsequent prosocial behaviour among strangers. We developed an experimental game paradigm modelling representatives as third-party punishers to manipulate or assess corruption and examine its relationship with trust and prosociality (trust behaviour, cooperation and generosity). In a sequential dyadic die-rolling task, the participants observed the dishonest behaviour of a target who would subsequently serve as a third-party punisher in a trust game (Study 1a, N = 540), in a prisoner's dilemma (Study 1b, N = 503) and in dictator games (Studies 2-4, N = 765, pre-registered). Across these five studies, perceiving a third party as corrupt undermined interpersonal trust and, in turn, prosocial behaviour. These findings contribute to our understanding of the critical role that representatives of institutions play in shaping cooperative relationships in modern societies. Across five studies, Spadaro et al. show that perceiving representatives of institutions as corrupt is associated with lower interpersonal trust and prosocial behaviour among strangers.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter analysis, based solely on the content of “Corrupt third parties undermine trust and prosocial behaviour between people.” For each parameter, I note (1) whether the paper explicitly discusses it (and, if so, how), and (2) whether the paper makes any predictions about how systematically varying that parameter would affect “the punishment treatment effect” for any dependent variable, including numerical effect sizes if reported. As the paper does not use the term “punishment treatment effect on efficiency,” I also indicate whenever no mention is made of an effect on efficiency, and whenever mention is made only of effects on other dependent variables (primarily trust and cooperation).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes, the paper describes dyads (first mover and second mover) and also a “third-party punisher” (TPP). Participants observe or interact with the second mover, who later serves as TPP in subsequent economic games.  
   • Systematically varied or predicting effect on punishment treatment? No. The paper does not systematically vary the total number of players, nor does it provide any discussion or effect size regarding how changing the number of players would affect any “punishment treatment effect.”

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? Yes, the die-rolling phase (Phase 1) typically consists of 10 rounds (Studies 1a, 1b). Then, Phase 2 is a one-shot decision.  
   • Systematically varied or predicting effect on punishment treatment? No. The paper does not explore varying the number of rounds as an experimental factor, nor is there any reported effect of doing so.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned? Yes. In Study 1b, the paper includes a 2 (Corruption: honest vs. corrupt TPP) × 2 (Communication: present vs. absent) design, so there is a condition in which participants could send a message to the partner before deciding in the Prisoner’s Dilemma.  
   • Systematically varied or predicting effect on punishment treatment? Partially. The presence/absence of chat is manipulated, but the focus is on trust and cooperation outcomes rather than “efficiency.” The paper does not report specific effect sizes for how communication changes a “punishment treatment effect,” nor does it frame the results in terms of group efficiency. The main text indicates that corruption undermines trust, and the supplementary materials discuss the chat factor, but there is no separate, numerical “punishment-treatment-effect” estimate.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not mention any all-or-nothing contribution structure (e.g., no forced full-contribution design).

5. Is the contribution default? (i.e., do players decide how much to move from public to private)  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper never discusses a contribution-default parameter.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? Briefly. For example, in the trust game, any amount sent is tripled for the trustee, but this factor (3×) is simply part of the standard trust game design.  
   • Systematically varied or predicting effect on punishment treatment? No. The paper does not systematically vary the multiplier (or anything akin to MPCR) and makes no predictions or effect sizes related to doing so.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? Yes, but only in generic terms: the TPP “can invest part of their endowment” to reduce others’ payoffs. The exact cost structure is not manipulated.  
   • Systematically varied or predicting effect on punishment treatment? Not at all. The paper does not vary the per-unit cost of punishment and provides no effect-size estimates for changing this cost.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned? Only as a general, fixed option in which the TPP reduces others’ earnings at some personal cost. The details remain constant within each study.  
   • Systematically varied or predicting effect on punishment treatment? No. There is no manipulation or discussion of how altering the punishment’s impact per unit would affect trust, cooperation, or efficiency.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned? No. All five studies use a third-party punisher (TPP) design but do not incorporate any reward mechanism.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Mentioned? No. No rewards are introduced or discussed.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)  
   • Mentioned? No. As above, the paper deals only with punishment, not rewarding.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
   • Mentioned? Yes, participants learn the structure: they see that Phase 1 has 10 rounds of die-rolling, and Phase 2 is one-shot.  
   • Systematically varied or predicting effect on punishment treatment? No. The paper does not manipulate whether the total number of rounds is known or unknown.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much others gained or lost)?  
   • Mentioned? Indirectly, yes. Participants do see the second mover’s (later TPP’s) claimed die-roll outcomes in Phase 1. They also learn that the TPP can punish in Phase 2. But there is no separate manipulation or direct discussion of systematically varying how much peer information is revealed.  
   • Systematically varied or predicting effect on punishment treatment? No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Mentioned? Only to the extent that participants know there is a “third-party punisher” seat. The paper does not explicitly address whether the identity behind the punishment is revealed in detail, nor does it manipulate or compare anonymity.  
   • Systematically varied or predicting effect on punishment treatment? No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Mentioned? No. Rewarding is never part of the design.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────

SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   • The paper does not measure “group efficiency,” nor does it discuss total or average payoffs relative to a fully cooperative benchmark. Instead, it focuses on two main dependent variables: (1) interpersonal trust (as measured by a multi-item scale) and (2) cooperation (operationalized as the amount given to another player, e.g., in a trust game, prisoner’s dilemma, or dictator game). “Trust” refers to participants’ beliefs and expectations about a partner’s trustworthiness, while “cooperation” refers to how much they actually transfer or contribute to the other player.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • At least some aspect of parameters #1 (number of players), #2 (number of rounds), #3 (chat/communication), #6 (a multiplier in the trust game, though not labeled MPCR), #7 (punishment cost), #8 (punishment magnitude), #12 (participants know the number of rounds in the die-rolling phase), and #13 (outcomes are revealed in Phase 1) are mentioned. Parameters #4, #5, #9, #10, #11, and #15 are not discussed at all. Parameter #14 receives only cursory reference (they know there is a TPP) but is not explored experimentally.  

C. For which and how many parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The paper does not frame any findings in terms of a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”  
   • The only parameter that is explicitly varied in a factorial design (beyond corruption vs. honesty) is #3 (communication present vs. absent in Study 1b). Even there, the analyses focus on interpersonal trust and cooperation with or without communication; no separate “punishment treatment effect” is calculated or provided. No numerical effect sizes are reported for systematically varying any of these 15 parameters on a punishment-based outcome.

D. If one were to predict how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely from this paper’s content, what would those predictions be?  
   • The paper provides no direct data or discussion about changing any of these parameters in order to predict changes in efficiency. Its central finding is that perceived corruption of a third-party punisher undermines interpersonal trust and reduces cooperation with a stranger. Beyond that, it gives little or no basis for predicting how systematically varying any of the 15 listed parameters would affect a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Thus, based strictly on this text, one can make no or only minimal predictions regarding efficiency.

Authors: Lv, SJ; Li, JY; Zhao, CH
Author Full Names: Lv, Shaojie; Li, Jiaying; Zhao, Changheng
Article Title: The evolution of cooperation in voluntary public goods game with shared-punishment
Author Keywords: Public goods game; Shared-punishment; Voluntary participation; Evolutionary game
Keywords Plus: DYNAMICS; POLYMORPHISM; STRATEGIES; ALTRUISM
Abstract: A large number of theoretical and experimental studies have shown that punishment and voluntary participation can promote cooperation, which offers an explanation for the emergence of cooperation. In this paper, individuals can freely choose whether to participate in the public goods game, and cooperators perform both cooperation and punishment. On the one hand, cooperators invest in public goods, and on the other hand, they punish the defectors and share the cost of punishment. Furthermore, considering the impact of population structure, we investigate the evolution of cooperation in well-mixed populations with the replicator dynamics and structured populations with the Fermi update rule, respectively. Our results indicate that the evolution of cooperation is obviously different between the two populations. In well-mixed populations, the voluntary participation mechanism prevents defection from becoming an evolutionary stable strategy. When the fine is low, the strategy of non-participation will be the only evolutionary stable strategy. With the increase of the fine, both cooperation and non-participation will be the evolutionary stable strategies. When the fine is high, cooperation will become the only evolutionary stable strategy. In structured populations, cooperators, defectors and loners can coexist under mild punishment, which means that population structure is favorable to the emergence of cooperation. However, cooperators occupy the population with higher fine threshold compared to well-mixed populations, which indicates that population structure is not always favorable to the evolution of cooperation.

• the replicator-dynamic equilibria (fractions of C, D, L) in well-mixed populations,

Abstract: We use decision-making experiments with human participants to study cooperation in a laboratory public goods game. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what the paper does—and does not—say about each of the 15 parameters in relation to the punishment treatment and its effects on efficiency (actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff). All statements refer strictly to this paper (Chaudhuri & Paichayontvijit) and its tables/figures, without invoking prior literature or external sources.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Yes. In all sessions, groups have 4 players (p. 4, “participants are placed into groups of four…”).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary this parameter (e.g., 2 vs. 4 vs. 8 players) and predict how it affects the punishment treatment?  
     – No. The number of players is fixed at 4; there is no separate condition with a different group size. Hence the paper provides no discussion of how changing group size would affect the punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency.

2. Number of rounds
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Yes. Two experiments are reported: Experiment 1 spans 20 rounds total (with interventions after round 10), and Experiment 2 spans 30 rounds total (with interventions after round 10).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary this parameter in relation to punishment?  
     – Yes. Experiment 1 uses 20 rounds total; Experiment 2 uses 30 rounds. Punishment is included in both experiments. Hence, the horizon is longer in Experiment 2.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (any dependent variable)?  
     – Qualitative findings: In both experiments, punishment starts with lower efficiency but tends to improve over time. By round 30 (Experiment 2), punishment shows an upward trend but does not clearly surpass the “restart recommendation” treatment. The paper reports no exact numerical “effect size” for how going from 20 to 30 rounds changes the effectiveness of punishment—only that the longer horizon allows punishment to catch up more than in a shorter horizon.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – No. The paper does not mention any real‐time chat or communication among participants (beyond the experimenter reading out instructions, which is not player‐to‐player chat).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it?  
     – No; the paper provides no condition in which participants can or cannot chat. Hence there is no discussion of how chat might affect the punishment treatment.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – No. Contributions range from 0 to 10 tokens (in whole units). Participants are free to choose any integer from 0 to 10. “All or nothing” is not imposed, nor is it varied.  
   • Any systematic variation?  
     – No.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – No. All decisions require an active choice each round; there is no mention of a “default” that gets moved back to private hands or anything similar.  
   • Any systematic variation?  
     – No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Yes. The MPCR is 0.5 (p. 4, “Tokens contributed to the public account are doubled (i.e., multiplied by 2) and redistributed equally…”).  
   • Any systematic variation?  
     – No. The paper fixes the MPCR at 0.5 and does not examine any other multiplication factors.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Yes. Each point of punishment sent costs the punisher NZ$0.05 (Table 2).  
   • Any systematic variation?  
     – No. The paper always uses that same cost structure, so there is no separate treatment that changes the punishment cost.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins/earnings deducted per unit of punishment)
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Yes. Each punishment point received reduces the target’s earnings by 10% for that round (Table 2).  
   • Any systematic variation?  
     – No. The paper uses this same 10% mechanism throughout and does not compare it with, e.g., 5% or 30%.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Not in the sense of an actual “reward” institution. The only non‐punishment intervention is a “recommendation” (exhortative message). There is no reward treatment.  
   • Any systematic variation?  
     – No. The paper does not implement a reward condition at all.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – No. There is no reward treatment.  
   • Any systematic variation?  
     – No.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – No. There is no reward treatment.  
   • Any systematic variation?  
     – No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Yes. In standard punishment and recommendation conditions, participants know there are 20 rounds in Experiment 1, and 30 in Experiment 2. For the special “restart” treatment (recommendation + a surprise extension after 12 rounds), participants only initially know about 12 post‐intervention rounds, then are asked to continue for 8 more. However, that “surprise” aspect applies to the recommendation treatment only, not to punishment.  
   • Any systematic variation in punishment treatments?  
     – No. For the punishment groups, the total horizon is always known (20 or 30). The paper does not systematically compare “known vs. unknown” horizon for punishment.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Partially. The standard public goods setup reveals each group member’s contribution (in tokens) and each participant’s own payoff. The paper does not say that players see each other’s final payoffs from all sources, but they do see each other’s contributions each round (p. 4, “Participants get to observe the individual contributions… and their own earnings…”).  
   • Any systematic variation?  
     – No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Yes. The paper explicitly states that punishers remain anonymous (p. 5, “Participants are not aware of the identity of punishers thereby ruling out targeted punishments as revenge…”).  
   • Any systematic variation?  
     – No. All punishment treatments maintain anonymity.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – No. The paper has no reward treatment, so it does not address whether rewarders are identified.  
   • Any systematic variation?  
     – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   – Yes. The main dependent variable in the figures and table is “efficiency,” measured as average earnings in NZ$ (max possible is NZ$1 per round if all contribute). The paper also discusses contribution rates, but explicitly distinguishes “efficiency” (monetary payoffs) from contribution level.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – Mentioned parameters (in some form) are:  
       (1) Number of players (always 4; not varied),  
       (2) Number of rounds (20 vs. 30 across experiments),  
       (6) MPCR = 0.5 (fixed, not varied),  
       (7) Punishment cost per point,  
       (8) Punishment magnitude (10% earnings reduction per point),  
       (12) Whether the total number of rounds is known to participants,  
       (13) Whether peer outcomes are shown,  
       (14) Whether punishment is anonymous.  
     Thus 8 of the 15 parameters receive at least some mention. The other 7 are not discussed or are not in the design.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect (for each dependent variable) when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   – Only one parameter (2: Number of rounds) is explicitly varied across different punishment conditions (20‐round vs. 30‐round). The paper examines how a longer horizon helps punishment effectiveness “catch up” in later rounds, though it does not provide a precise numeric “effect size.” The other parameters appear only in a single fixed setting (e.g., cost to punish is always the same), so there is no systematic variation of them.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   – The one clear prediction from the paper is that longer repeated interaction (i.e., more rounds) can eventually improve punishment’s impact on efficiency, because punishment tends to “take time” to become effective. Beyond that, the authors do not systematically vary other parameters (e.g., group size, cost‐to‐punish ratio, or anonymity of punishers). Therefore, the paper provides little or no basis for predictions about how changes in those other 14 parameters (and their interactions) would alter the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.
reference_APA: Chaudhuri, Ananish & Paichayontvijit, Tirnud (2017). On the long-run efficacy of punishments and recommendations in a laboratory public goods game. SCIENTIFIC REPORTS.

Authors: Guo, T; Du, CP; Shi, L
Author Full Names: Guo, Tian; Du, Chunpeng; Shi, Lei
Article Title: Evolution of cooperation on interdependent networks: The impact of asymmetric punishment
Author Keywords: Interdependent networks; Punishment; Cooperation; Asymmetric
Keywords Plus: TIT-FOR-TAT; PRISONERS-DILEMMA GAME; WIN-STAY; COSTLY PUNISHMENT; LOSE-SHIFT; ANTISOCIAL PUNISHMENT; HOST SANCTIONS; RECIPROCITY; REPUTATION; MECHANISM
Abstract: The role of costly punishment in shaping the evolution of cooperation has long been a subject of debate, given its contested effectiveness due to challenges posed by second-order free-riders and antisocial punishment. However, these conclusions have predominantly arisen from scenarios characterized by symmetry, where individuals possess the ability to mutually impose punishment. In this study, we delve into the impact of asymmetric punishment on the development of cooperation within interdependent networks. Notably, our approach involves the exclusive application of punishment between players situated on different network layers, with no punitive interactions occurring within the same network layer. A critical distinction lies in the fact that punitive authority resides solely with the upper-layer players, while the reverse is not true. Specifically, we investigate two modes of punishment: (i) pro-social punishment, where cooperators penalize defectors, and (ii) anti-social punishment, wherein defectors penalize cooperators. Through extensive numerical simulations, we unveil a synchronization phenomenon of strategies within the two networks when the costs of punishment are comparatively high. This synchronization gives rise to the gradual emergence of cooperative clusters, resulting in higher payoffs for the individuals involved. Conversely, when punishment costs are relatively low, the synchronization phenomenon does not manifest, and the evolution of cooperation takes a divergent course. In summary, our findings enrich the theory of punishment by underscoring the pivotal role played by asymmetric punishment in molding cooperative behavior.

Below I go through the 15 parameters one‐by‐one, quoting exactly what the paper contains and, whenever possible, what the paper allows us to infer about the *punishment-treatment effect* (PTE).  “PTE” here simply means the difference between a *punishment* condition (α > 0) and a *no-punishment* condition (α = 0).  The only dependent variables the authors actually report are the fraction of cooperators (ρC) and, in a few figures, the frequency of punishment events—never group efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
────────────────────────────────────────

1.  Number of players  
    • Mentioned? Yes. Two L × L lattices; L varied from 400 to 1 000.  
    • Systematically varied wrt PTE? No. L is only varied “to avoid finite-size effects.” No results relate L to the size or sign of the punishment effect.

2.  Number of rounds (length of play)  
    • Mentioned? No fixed number of rounds is defined; the simulation runs until a stationary state.  
    • Systematic variation? None.  

3.  Chat enabled?  
    • Not mentioned.  

4.  All-or-nothing contribution choice?  
    • Not applicable (the model is a Prisoner’s Dilemma, not a public-goods contribution).  

5.  Contribution default?  
    • Not applicable.  

6.  Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor (PGG)  
    • Directly absent, but the model’s *temptation to defect* b plays the analogous role of “dilemma strength.”  
    • Systematic variation? Yes. b ranges roughly 1.0–1.35 (Fig. 2).  
    • Effect on PTE? Higher b weakens the effect of punishment.  
      – At α = 0.8 cooperation is 100 % up to b≈1.35, after which it collapses (Fig. 2).  
      – At any given α, raising b shifts the “full-cooperation” region to the left and requires higher α for the same outcome (Fig. 3).  
      – Numerical effect sizes are given only graphically (colour map), not in coefficients.

7.  Punishment cost (to the punisher)  
    • Implemented as α·Px. α is the **only** parameter varied in most figures.  
    • Systematic variation? Yes. α=0 (no punishment) up to ~1.0.  
    • Effect on PTE? Strongly positive: increasing α monotonically raises ρC (Fig. 3). For the benchmark cost-to-fine ratio 1:1, full cooperation emerges beyond α≈0.26 (b=1.02) or α≈0.55 (b=1.10).  

8.  Punishment magnitude (fine on the target)  
    • Studied via different cost-to-fine ratios: 1:1, 1:3, 1:5 (Fig. 7).  
    • Systematic variation? Yes.  
    • Effect on PTE? Larger fines (1:3, 1:5) dominate or match the baseline 1:1 across all α. With b=1.02, ρC is always ≥ the 1:1 case; with b=1.20, the three curves are almost indistinguishable but still ordered 1:5 ≥ 1:3 ≥ 1:1. No numerical pay-off data are provided.

9.  Reward enabled?  
    • Mentioned briefly in Sec. 3 and Fig. 8. A parallel “reward factor” (also called α) is introduced only for qualitative comparison.  
    • Systematic variation? Reward factor mapped against b (Fig. 8), but not combined with punishment.  
    • Effect on PTE? Not analysed; the comparison shows that when b is small, punishment attains higher ρC than reward, but when b is large the opposite is true. No efficiency data.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
    • Neither is spelled out; no systematic variation.

12.  Do players know the number of rounds?  
    • Not relevant (infinite-horizon simulation).

13.  Are peer outcomes shown?  
14.  Do punished players learn the identity of the punisher?  
15.  Do rewarded players learn the identity of the rewarder?  
    • None of these information-display variables are modelled or discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────
A. Dependent variables  
   – Group efficiency is *never* reported.  
   – Reported variables: (i) fraction of cooperators ρC; (ii) frequency of punishment events (inset of Figs. 4-5).  
   – No pay-off or welfare measure is provided, so “efficiency” cannot be computed from the paper.

B. Parameters explicitly mentioned (value given at least once): 6 of 15  
   (1) number of players (L) (6) dilemma strength b (7) punishment cost α  
   (8) punishment magnitude via cost-to-fine ratio (9) existence of reward (it is compared)  
   (10–11) reward parameters are implied but never quantified.  
   The remaining 9 parameters are not mentioned at all.

C. Parameters whose *systematic* variation and impact on the punishment treatment effect are analysed: 3  
   – Dilemma strength b (analogous to parameter 6)  
   – Punishment cost α (parameter 7)  
   – Punishment fine magnitude (parameter 8)  
   No numerical regression coefficients are given; effects are read qualitatively from the figures.

D. Predicted influence on *efficiency*—if one tried to extrapolate from what is reported  
   – Because efficiency equals average payoff and the paper never reports payoffs, only tentative qualitative guesses are possible.  
   – Greater punishment cost (higher α) raises cooperation to 100 %, so **efficiency would likely rise** for all but the largest b.  
   – Larger punishment fines (higher cost-to-fine ratios) speed up or slightly enlarge the cooperation region, so they should also **increase efficiency** relative to 1:1.  
   – A stronger dilemma (higher b) lowers cooperation and therefore would **reduce efficiency**, unless α is large enough to offset it.  
   – For every other parameter (1-5, 9-15) the paper provides no evidence, hence no prediction can be made on efficiency.

In short, only three of the fifteen parameters are explored, and even for those the paper talks exclusively about cooperation rates, not about group efficiency.

Below each of the 15 design parameters I state  
(1) whether the parameter or something directly equivalent appears in the paper (and with what value(s)), and  
(2) whether the paper **systematically varies** the parameter and, if so, what effect this variation is reported to have on the “punishment-treatment effect” (PT-effect).  The authors do not study efficiency; instead they study (i) equilibrium composition of strategies and (ii) sizes of the basins of attraction of three long-run states: all-Punishers (P), all-Defectors (D) and a P–C coexistence.  Where the paper gives a numerical threshold (e.g. “α*≈0.96”), I reproduce it, but no quantitative effect sizes (e.g. β-coefficients) are provided in the article.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players (group size)  
   (1) Mentioned.  The baseline analysis fixes G = 5.  
   (2) Never varied; no prediction on PT-effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Not mentioned; model is continuous-time replicator dynamics.  
   (2) Not discussed.

3. Is chat enabled?  
   Not mentioned; never varied.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
   (1) The model hard-codes an all-or-nothing rule: a co-operator (or punisher) contributes c, a defector contributes 0.  
   (2) Rule not varied; no prediction.

5. Contribution default / exit option  
   Not mentioned.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   (1) Appears as the “synergy factor” r, set to r = 3 in all figures.  
   (2) Never varied.

7. Punishment cost (β)  
   (1) Explicitly included; baseline β = 0.7 but systematically varied in Fig. 5 (β = 0.4, 0.7, 1).  
   (2) Reported qualitative effect: holding fine α constant, increasing β “decreases the basin of attraction of the full-punishment state”.  Hence a higher β weakens the PT-effect (no numerical effect size given).

8. Punishment magnitude / fine (α)  
   (1) Explicitly included; baseline α = 0.7 but systematically varied in Fig. 5 (α = 0.4, 0.7, 1).  
   (2) Reported qualitative effect: for any fixed β, increasing α “increases the basin of attraction of the full-punishment state”.  Thus a higher α strengthens the PT-effect.

9. Reward enabled (yes/no)  
   (1) A reward mechanism is always on, implemented through the “resource-allocation” rule once group contributions exceed the threshold λ.  
   (2) The paper never switches reward off, so no comparison is available.

10. Reward cost to grant reward  
    Not modelled; players incur no explicit cost when reward is allocated.

11. Reward magnitude (a, b)  
    (1) Implemented as reward weights:  
        a = weight for cooperators (0 ≤ a < 1),  
        b = weight for defectors (0 ≤ b < a).  
        Baseline a = 0.7, b = 0.3 but both are systematically varied (Figs. 3–4).  
    (2) Effects:  
        • Critical value a* ≈ 0.96.  If a > a* the system shifts from full-punishment towards Punisher–Cooperator coexistence, decreasing the PT-effect.  
        • Critical value b* ≈ 0.64.  If b > b* defectors prevail, eliminating the PT-effect.  
        • For b fixed and a < a*, increasing a leaves the PT-effect roughly unchanged; for a fixed and below a*, increasing b reduces the PT-effect gradually.

12. Rounds known to players  
    Not applicable.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    Not modelled.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
    Not modelled.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
    Not modelled.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY  

A.  Dependent variables  
    The paper does **not** report or analyse group efficiency, total payoff, or average payoff.  Dependent variables are (i) fixed points of the replicator dynamics (which strategy set survives) and (ii) relative sizes of basins of attraction leading to the full-punishment, full-defection, or P–C coexistence states.  These differ from efficiency because they refer to long-run composition, not to realised payoffs.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
    7 of 15: 1 (G), 4 (all-or-nothing rule), 6 (r), 7 (β), 8 (α), 9 (reward always on), 11 (reward weights a, b).

C.  Which parameters are **systematically varied** and their effect on the PT-effect discussed?  
    3 of 15: 7 (β), 8 (α), 11 (a, b).

D.  Predictions one could make about efficiency solely from this paper  
    Because efficiency is never computed, only indirect conjectures can be made:  
    • Larger punishment fines (α) should raise efficiency if we assume that states with more punishers/co-operators are more efficient than states dominated by defectors.  
    • Higher punishment costs (β) should lower efficiency for the same reason.  
    • Very large cooperative reward weight (a > 0.96) or large defector reward weight (b > 0.64) are predicted to erode punishment and therefore (again indirectly) to reduce eventual efficiency.  
    • For all remaining parameters (1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 12-15) the paper offers no basis for a prediction.

Authors: Darcet, D; Sornette, D
Author Full Names: Darcet, D.; Sornette, D.
Article Title: Quantitative determination of the level of cooperation in the presence of punishment in three public good experiments
Source Title: JOURNAL OF ECONOMIC INTERACTION AND COORDINATION
Keywords Plus: CULTURAL-GROUP SELECTION; LARGE-SCALE COOPERATION; COEVOLUTIONARY PROCESSES; INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; EVOLUTION; ALTRUISM; BEHAVIOR; TRUST; BRAIN; GAME
Abstract: Strong reciprocity is a fundamental human characteristic associated with our extraordinary sociality and cooperation. Laboratory experiments on social dilemma games and many field studies have quantified well-defined levels of cooperation and propensity to punish/reward. The level of cooperation is observed to be strongly dependent on the availability of punishments and/or rewards. Here, we propose an operational approach based on the evolutionary selection of prosocial behaviors to explain the quantitative level of the propensity to punish in three experimental set-ups. A simple cost/benefit analysis at the level of a single agent, who anticipates the action of her fellows, determines an optimal level of altruistic punishment, which explains quantitatively experimental results on a third-party punishment game, the ultimatum game and an altruistic punishment game. We also report numerical simulations of an evolutionary agent-based model of repeated agent interactions with feedback by punishments, which confirms that the propensity to punish is a robust emergent property selected by the evolutionary rules of the model. The cost-benefit reasoning is not to be taken literally but rather to embody the result of the selection pressure of co-evolving agents that have make them converge to their preferences (which can be seen as either hard-wired and/or culturally selected). In this view, the prosocial preference of humans is a collective emergent process, robustly selected by adaptation and selection. Our main contribution is to use evolutionary feedback selection to quantify the value of the prosocial propensity to punish, and test this prediction on three different experimental set-ups.

Below is an item‐by‐item survey of what the paper does and does not say regarding each of the 15 parameters—and, in particular, whether it discusses how systematically varying these parameters would affect a “punishment treatment effect.” In keeping with the request, “punishment treatment effect” here is understood as how punishment changes outcomes relative to no‐punishment conditions. The paper frequently reports effects on cooperation levels, rejection rates, overall contributions, and other measures, but it does not explicitly define or track “efficiency” as the ratio of actual to maximum possible payoffs.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER‐BY‐PARAMETER DISCUSSION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1) Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  
   • Where/How? The paper analyzes three laboratory games with differing numbers of players (n=2 in the ultimatum game, n=3 in the third‐party punishment game, n=4 in Fehr & Gächter’s public‐good‐with‐punishment experiment) and also runs an agent‐based model for n up to 8.  
   • Systematically varied and effect on punishment treatment? The paper does show (in its agent‐based model) how the emergent punishment parameter k depends on n (Fig. 5). However, it does not tie this explicitly to a measured “efficiency” outcome; it focuses on contributions and punishment propensities rather than efficiency per se. No numerical effect size for an efficiency measure is given.

2) Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? Yes, but only in a descriptive sense.  
   • Where/How? Fehr & Gächter’s experiment ran six periods; the agent‐based model sometimes runs T=500 repeated interactions.  
   • Systematically varied and effect on punishment treatment? The paper does not examine how changing the total number of rounds would alter punishment’s effect. There is no separate analysis or numerical effect size for “if the game is repeated different numbers of times.”

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Systematically varied and effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed at all.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned? Indirectly, the paper states that subjects can choose any integer investment from 0 up to some maximum (e.g., up to 20 MUs), so it is not “all or nothing.”  
   • Systematically varied and effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

5) Is there a “contribution default” (do people move money out of a public fund)?  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Systematically varied and effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  
   • Where/How? In the Fehr & Gächter public‐goods experiment, the paper uses a factor r₁ = 1.6 and divides its product among four players.  
   • Systematically varied and effect on punishment treatment? The paper does not provide or analyze data varying the MPCR. It offers no numerical effect size linking different MPCRs to the punishment treatment effect.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  
   • Where/How? In the main experiments, each MU spent on punishing directly costs the punisher 1 MU. The paper calls that the cost “mⱼ→ᵢ.”  
   • Systematically varied and effect on punishment treatment? The studies and figures do not vary this cost. No numerical effect size is given for how changing the per‐unit‐punishment cost alone would modify outcomes.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player per unit punishment)  
   • Mentioned? Yes, prominently, as rₚ (the “punishment efficiency”).  
   • Where/How? In Fehr & Gächter’s setup, rₚ = 3. The paper also studies rₚ = 3.5 or rₚ in the range 1–4.5 in its agent‐based model.  
   • Systematically varied and effect on punishment treatment? Yes. The agent‐based model systematically varies rₚ and shows how that changes the level of cooperation and the emergent punishment parameter k (see Fig. 6). However, the paper does not report an “efficiency” ratio in these simulations, so there is no direct numerical effect size on efficiency. Instead, it discusses how higher rₚ tends to stabilize high contributions (i.e., fosters cooperation).  

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned? Yes, but only conceptually.  
   • Where/How? The paper notes that one can do a parallel analysis of “feedback by reward” instead of punishment and briefly references that “punishment vs. reward” might both evolve.  
   • Systematically varied and effect on punishment treatment? No. The paper does not provide data or tables where reward is systematically turned on or off, nor does it tie this to efficiency measures.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Mentioned? Only in a general, theoretical sense (it would be symmetric to punishment cost), with no specific numeric manipulations.  
   • Systematically varied and effect on punishment treatment? Not systematically tested.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player per unit of reward)  
   • Mentioned? Only at the level of theoretical symmetry with punishment.  
   • Systematically varied and effect on punishment treatment? Not tested in the paper.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when it ends)?  
   • Mentioned? The paper does not say whether subjects explicitly know the total number of rounds. It reports only that there are multiple periods in the experiments.  
   • Systematically varied and effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players see each other’s gains/losses)?  
   • Mentioned? Indirectly. In Fehr & Gächter’s setup, individuals must see others’ contributions in order to punish them. The text implies that such information is displayed, but the paper does not investigate systematically changing what is disclosed.  
   • Systematically varied and effect on punishment treatment? No.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Mentioned? Not in any detail. The paper does not describe whether that is revealed.  
   • Systematically varied and effect on punishment treatment? No information.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Systematically varied and effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FINAL SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?  
   • The paper does not use “group efficiency” in a strict sense (actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff). It discusses average payoffs, cooperation rates, willingness to punish, and punisher/punishee expenditures in various public‐good or bargaining games. While higher cooperation typically implies higher total payoffs, “efficiency” as the fraction of maximum possible group payoff is not a reported metric in the text.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned: #1 (number of players), #2 (number of rounds, though not systematically varied), #6 (MPCR or multiplication factor), #7 (punisher’s cost), #8 (punishment magnitude, rₚ), and #9 (whether reward is enabled, discussed conceptually). The paper also alludes to #10 and #11 (reward cost and magnitude) in an entirely theoretical sense.  
   • Not mentioned or given any focus: #3 (chat), #4 (all‐or‐nothing), #5 (contribution default), #12 (whether the number of rounds is known), #13 (systematic manipulations of revealed outcomes), #14 (knowledge of who punished), and #15 (knowledge of who rewarded).

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • The only parameter the paper clearly varies in a systematic fashion (in its agent‐based simulations) is #8, the punishment magnitude/effectiveness rₚ. It shows how boosting rₚ brings about more cooperation (and thus higher payoffs) in the repeated public‐goods setup. However, the paper does not frame this difference as a change in “efficiency,” nor does it present a numeric “punishment treatment effect size” for payoffs.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper’s content, what would they be?  
   • The paper never reports an explicit measure of efficiency, so it offers no solid basis to compute how varying each parameter alters “(treatment) with punishment” minus “(treatment) without punishment” in efficiency terms. It does suggest that higher punishment magnitude (rₚ) can induce significantly more cooperation (and thus higher total payoffs). Beyond that, there is no direct guidance in the paper on how each of the other parameters—if manipulated—would quantitatively shift an efficiency ratio.  

In short, the paper focuses on cooperation, punishment expenditures, and (in some passages) overall payoffs, but does not provide explicit numerical results linking each parameter to an “efficiency” measure. Consequently, one can say little about how introducing punishment will raise or lower efficiency when systematically altering these 15 parameters, other than the general statement (supported by the agent‐based results) that higher punishment efficacy (rₚ) supports significantly higher cooperation.
reference_APA: Darcet, D. & Sornette, D. (2008). Quantitative determination of the level of cooperation in the presence of punishment in three public good experiments. JOURNAL OF ECONOMIC INTERACTION AND COORDINATION.

Authors: Dannenberg, A
Author Full Names: Dannenberg, Astrid
Article Title: Non-binding agreements in public goods experiments
Keywords Plus: SOCIAL DILEMMAS; COMMUNICATION; COOPERATION; PUNISHMENT; COMMITMENT; COALITIONS; COVENANTS
Abstract: This article presents experimental evidence on the effects of non-binding agreements on co-operation in public goods games. In particular, it compares first-best agreements that require full co-operation by all players and second-best agreements that require only a minimum contribution level rather than full co-operation. The results show that when there is no punishment opportunity, second-best agreements work better than first-best agreements because they are more likely to be formed and kept. First-best agreements form at the beginning of the game, but non-compliant behaviour by some players causes co-operation to collapse. This result is reversed when there is a punishment opportunity. In this case, first-best agreements work better than second-best agreements as they allow groups to establish a common behavioural standard, deter violations, and achieve very high levels of co-operation.
