Authors: Wegmann, J; Musshoff, O
Author Full Names: Wegmann, Johannes; Musshoff, Oliver
Article Title: Groundwater management institutions in the face of rapid urbanization - Results of a framed field experiment in Bengaluru, India
Author Keywords: Common pool resource management; Monitoring; Sanctioning; Urbanization
Keywords Plus: COLLECTIVE ACTION; RESOURCE; HETEROGENEITY; COOPERATION; BEHAVIOR
Abstract: Many aquifers in semi-arid and arid regions with rapid urbanization are over-exploited or even at the point of depletion. Driven by the increased demand for food and other agricultural products, irrigated agriculture constitutes the biggest user of groundwater, and has thus contributed to this critical situation. In this paper, we compare different designs of groundwater management institutions in order to avoid aquifer over-exploitation and ensure secure water sources. We assess externally imposed reward-based and punishment rules as well as communication on their effectiveness to reduce water extraction behavior of groundwater users. Moreover, we evaluate how different user types affect the outcome of these institutional designs. To do so, we conducted a framed field experiment with 600 households along the rural-urban interface of the fast growing city of Bengaluru, India. Results indicate that all treatments can prolong the life of the resource but reward-based and punishment rules seem to be more effective than communication. Parameter-by-parameter extraction from Wegmann & Mußhoff (2020) with respect to the **punishment-versus-control treatment effect on group efficiency**

1. Number of players  
   • Discussed? Yes – every group contained exactly 4 players.  
   • Systematically varied? No – always four, so the paper makes no prediction about changing this number.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Discussed? Yes – two sequences of 5 periods (10 periods total).  
   • Systematically varied? No – held constant; no prediction about varying it.

3. Chat between players  
   • Discussed? Yes – only the “communication” treatment allowed 5 minutes of discussion before each round; chat was **not** allowed in the punishment treatment.  
   • Systematically varied with punishment? No – the paper gives no data in which punishment is combined with (or compared across different levels of) chat, so no prediction on its marginal effect on the punishment treatment.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
   • Discussed? No – pumping hours were chosen on a 17-point scale (0–8 h in 0.5-h steps). Nothing said about forcing all-or-nothing.

5. Contribution default / endowment “rollback”  
   • Not mentioned; not applicable to this CPR design.

6. Marginal Per-Capita Return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Not used (the game is framed as profit from pumping governed by a quadratic benefit function). No MPCR is reported or manipulated.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   • Not applicable – punishment is imposed by an external regulator; no peer cost is specified or varied.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine per unit)  
   • Discussed? Yes – 100 tokens are deducted for every hour a monitored subject pumps above the 1-hour quota.  
   • Systematically varied? No – always 100 tokens; no prediction about changing the magnitude.

9. Reward enabled  
   • Yes, but only in a separate “reward” treatment. Not combined with punishment, so irrelevant for the punishment effect.

10. Reward cost  
    • Not applicable (external regulator funds it).

11. Reward magnitude  
    • 200 tokens to one randomly audited compliant subject; not systematically varied and not coupled to punishment.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
    • Discussed – the number of periods was deliberately **not** announced.  
    • No variation; no prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Partly – the new groundwater level (group-level state) was publicly announced. Individual profits stayed private. The visibility parameter was not manipulated, so there is no prediction.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
    • Not relevant – punishment is administered by an impersonal external regulator; no identity is revealed.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
    • Same as 14 – external regulator, no identity.

Effect-size information that can be read directly from the paper (all refer to the treatment–control difference in the five-period treatment sequence):

• Mean social-efficiency score  
  – Control: 89 %  
  – Punishment: 97 %  
  – Thus punishment raises efficiency by 8 percentage points (Table 4; t-test p < 0.01).

• Average pumping hours (ordered-probit coefficient)  
  – Punishment coefficient −0.85 (p < 0.01) relative to control (Table 3, model 2). The paper does not convert this into efficiency units beyond the social-efficiency score above.

No other parameter in the list is systematically manipulated, so no other numerical effect sizes exist.


SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
   – Yes, the paper explicitly uses “social efficiency” (actual group pay-offs divided by the optimum) as one dependent variable.  
   – It also analyses individual pumping hours (extraction level). Efficiency and extraction are different: extraction is a direct behavioural measure; efficiency is a welfare outcome derived from pay-offs.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   – 1, 2, 3, 8, 12, 13 (6 parameters). All others are either absent or not applicable.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of **systematically varying** that parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
   – Zero. The punishment treatment is implemented with one fixed setting for every parameter.

D. Predictions that can be made solely from this paper about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency  
   – Because only one configuration is studied, the paper offers almost no leverage for extrapolating parameter effects. The only inferable points are:  
     • With 4 players, 5 undisclosed rounds, a 1-hour quota and a 100-token fine, punishment improves efficiency by ~8 pp relative to the no-rule control.  
     • Allowing pre-play communication (parameter 3) in the *absence* of punishment yields a much smaller efficiency gain (≈1 pp), but the interaction between communication and punishment is not studied; no prediction can be made.  
     • No evidence is supplied to say whether a larger (or smaller) fine, more players, public identification of punishers, known end time, etc., would strengthen or weaken punishment’s efficiency advantage. Therefore, beyond the single observed data point, no additional predictions are possible from this source alone.

Article Title: CREATION OF SOCIAL ORDER IN ETHNIC CONFLICT
Author Keywords: costly monitoring; ethnic conflict; in-group policing; social matching game; social order
Keywords Plus: COOPERATION; VIOLENCE
Abstract: This article develops a model of random matching with costly monitoring to demonstrate that the threat of ethnic conflict can function to create an in-group policing mechanism which helps enforce inter-ethnic social order. Instead of regarding ethnic conflict as a form of collective penalty on an unidentified wrongdoer and his ethnic brethren (Fearon and Laitin, 1996), we argue that ethnic conflict is triggered by a wrongdoing because avengers seek to take advantage of in-group networks for detecting and punishing the culprit. Our theory predicts that the success of inter-ethnic cooperation hinges on the quality of in-group policing. As a consequence, a group with lower-quality policing tends to have more frequent and longer disputes with other groups.

Below is a point‐by‐point account of whether and how each of the 15 listed parameters is addressed in the paper by Nakao (cited as “the paper” below), together with whether the paper discusses any systematic effect of that parameter on what you have called the “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Throughout, I use the paper’s own terminology (e.g., “in‐group policing,” “out‐group conflict,” “ex ante payoff,” “comparative statics”) without bringing in additional information or assumptions beyond what appears in the text.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
• Discussed? Yes. The paper assumes two groups, each with n individuals (see especially Section 2.1, which defines groups A and B with n people each).  
• Systematically varied for any punishment‐treatment effect? The paper does note qualitatively that sustaining cooperation becomes more difficult as n (“group size”) gets large, but it does not present a separate, quantitative “treatment effect on efficiency” from introducing punishment as n changes. Instead, it discusses conditions under which cooperation can or cannot be sustained in large groups. There is no table or figure showing a numerical “punishment effect” as n varies.

2. Number of rounds
• Discussed? Not in the usual “public goods” sense (e.g., 10 or 20 total rounds). The paper uses a repeated or indefinitely repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma model with discount factor δ, so there is no finite, known number of rounds. However, it does introduce T^(out), the length (in periods) of “ethnic conflict,” and T^(in), the length of “in‐group punishment.”  
• Systematically varied for any punishment‐treatment effect? Partly. In Tables (e.g. Table 3), the paper varies T^(out) (the “length of ethnic conflict”) and shows how that impacts ex ante payoffs. There is no direct reference to “efficiency = total payoff / max payoff,” but the paper does give numeric results for average or per‐period payoffs under different T^(out). That is the closest it comes to “systematic variation of rounds,” though it never explicitly calls the difference in payoff a “punishment treatment effect.”  

3. Is chat enabled between players?
• Discussed? No. The paper does not mention any form of free‐form communication or “chat” as an experimental or game‐design variable.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
• Discussed? The paper models a Prisoner’s Dilemma in which each player either Cooperates or Defects. Although that is, in effect, a binary action, the paper does not treat this as a design parameter that is systematically varied, nor does it link it to a punishment‐treatment effect on efficiency.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much of their endowment to move)?
• Discussed? No. The paper does not describe a “default contribution” mechanism.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
• Discussed? No. The paper uses a Prisoner’s Dilemma payoff structure with parameters α and β, but it does not present those as a “public‐good multiplier” or an MPCR. It does not speak of systematically altering a group‐level multiplier as a variable for punishment treatments.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
• Discussed? Not in the typical “one unit of punishment” sense. The paper instead treats “monitoring cost” (m or m_I) as a membership tax that finances the probability r(m) of identifying a defector within the group. It does not present a per‐punishment‐token cost. Hence there is no table or figure showing how a per‐unit punishment cost changes efficiency.  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted per unit of punishment)
• Discussed? No. There is no notion of a “1‐to‐x” or “1‐to‐3” punishment magnitude in coins. Rather, once a culprit is identified in the paper’s model, that individual faces a “punishment phase” (reduced future payoffs), but the paper does not treat that phase as a numeric, per‐unit fine.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled
• Discussed? No. The paper never mentions rewarding or a “carrot” mechanism.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
• Discussed? No. The paper does not consider rewards at all.  

11. Reward magnitude
• Discussed? No. Same as above; no mention of rewards.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
• Discussed? Not in the sense of a finite‐round game. The paper uses an indefinitely repeated (or infinitely repeated) framework and does not specify whether players “know” a final round.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much others gained each round)?
• Discussed? No. The paper does specify that actions within a group are perfectly observed by all peers, but it never discusses how “payoff outcomes” or “gains/losses” are displayed or withheld. It also does not treat this as something the model systematically varies.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
• Discussed? No. The paper’s focus is on whether the identity of a defector becomes known, not on linking the identity of punisher to punishee.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
• Discussed? No. Again, rewards do not appear in the model.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   • The paper does not use the term “efficiency = (actual total payoff) / (max possible payoff).” Instead, it focuses on “ex ante expected payoffs” (often separated into in‐group payoff and out‐group payoff) and on whether cooperation or conflict arises. The theoretical model’s key outcomes are: (1) whether groups maintain cooperation (vs. suffering ethnic conflict); (2) what the average or expected payoff is in equilibrium; (3) how costly monitoring and conflict durations affect those payoffs.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned at all:  
     (1) Number of players (n) is mentioned.  
     (2) Number of rounds is not directly discussed as a finite horizon, but T^(out) (length of “ethnic conflict”) is treated as a parameter in comparative statics.  
     • The paper does not mention or treat the other parameters (#3, #4, #5, #6 [as an MPCR], #7, #8, #9, #10, #11, #12, #13, #14, #15) in the sense enumerated by your list.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when that parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None are framed by the authors explicitly as “the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Instead, the paper derives conditions under which “peer policing + threat of conflict” sustains cooperation. In partial analogy, T^(out) (length of external conflict) and group size n do appear in the theoretical inequalities. Still, the paper does not present a numeric “treatment effect” (punishment vs. no‐punishment) specifically for efficiency.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • Because the paper does not use “treatment effect on efficiency” or measure “efficiency” as total over maximum payoff, it offers very little direct guidance on how systematically varying these 15 parameters would shift that ratio. It does suggest that:  
     – Larger group size (Parameter 1) tends to make cooperation harder to sustain.  
     – Longer or stronger conflicts (a stand‐in for Parameter 2) can substitute somewhat for costly internal policing, raising overall payoffs if monitoring is otherwise expensive, but the paper does not quantify this as “efficiency.”  
     – Other parameters (e.g., chat, reward, knowledge of punisher) are not addressed at all, so no predictions can be formed from the text.  

In short, the paper focuses on a repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma with in‐group policing and out‐group conflict, not on a standard public goods setup with a measured “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Consequently, it provides only very limited information about how your 15 listed parameters would drive efficiency outcomes in a public‐goods‐type “punishment treatment.”
reference_APA: Nakao, Keisuke (2009). CREATION OF SOCIAL ORDER IN ETHNIC CONFLICT. JOURNAL OF THEORETICAL POLITICS.

Authors: Kimbrough, EO; Rubin, J
Author Full Names: Kimbrough, Erik O.; Rubin, Jared
Article Title: Sustaining Group Reputation
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS; TRUST; COOPERATION; INSTITUTIONS; EXCHANGE; TRUSTWORTHINESS; PUNISHMENT; ECONOMICS; IDENTITY; SHADOW
Abstract: When individuals trade with strangers, there is a temptation to renege on agreements. If repeated interaction or exogenous enforcement is unavailable, societies often solve this problem via institutions that rely on group, rather than individual, reputation. Groups can employ two mechanisms to uphold reputation that are unavailable to individuals: information sharing and in-group punishment. We design a laboratory experiment to distinguish the roles of these mechanisms when individual reputations are unobservable. Subjects are split into groups and play a trust game with random re-matching, where only the group identity of one's partner is known. Treatments differ by whether information about group members' transactions is shared and whether in-group punishment is possible. We find that information sharing encourages path dependence via group reputation: good (bad) behavior results in greater (fewer) gains from exchange in the future. However, the mere threat of in-group punishment is enough to discourage bad behavior.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter accounting, based strictly on what appears in the paper “Sustaining Group Reputation.” Throughout, remember that the paper studies a repeated trust game (investment game) with random re‐matching, not a public goods game, and it does not report an explicit measure of “efficiency” defined as actual payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff. Instead, it reports variables such as amount sent, amount returned, and total (or average) payoffs.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Whether mentioned?  
     – Yes. Each session has 16 subjects split into 2 groups (colors) of 8, with 4 senders and 4 receivers in each color.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. The paper keeps group size/session size constant (16 per session); it does not discuss varying the number of players.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
     – Not discussed; there is no analysis of changing the number of players.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Whether mentioned?  
     – Yes. Ten rounds (periods) are played in each session. The experiment ends before the scheduled time so that subjects do not know when the final round occurs.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. The paper treats 10 rounds as a fixed design feature and does not explore altering the number of rounds.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
     – Not discussed; the paper does not predict how changing the number of rounds would affect punishment.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Whether mentioned?  
     – The paper does allow the receiver to send a single non‐binding “message” (an intended return percentage) before the sender chooses how much to send. However, there is no free‐format or open “chat” between players, and the paper does not treat “chat” as a systematically varied factor.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
     – Not discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Whether mentioned?  
     – No. Instead of an “all or nothing” choice, the sender can send any integer amount from 0 to 10.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
     – Not discussed.

5. Is the contribution default (are players forced to move money back)?  
   • Whether mentioned?  
     – No. Senders freely choose how much to send (0–10). Receivers freely choose how much to return (0 up to what they receive). No “default” mechanism is discussed.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
     – Not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Whether mentioned?  
     – Yes, the paper states that whatever senders choose to send is tripled (a factor of 3) and given to the receiver.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. The multiplier is always 3.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
     – Not discussed; the paper does not analyze changing the multiplier.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Whether mentioned?  
     – The experiment includes a “jury” mechanism. To file a dispute, a sender pays 2 ECU. If the majority of jurors vote to convict, the defendant (receiver) pays the shortfall plus that 2 ECU back to the sender.  
     – In an appendix “Jury‐Info‐Pay” treatment, jurors themselves must pay a cost to vote, but that was only a robustness check, not a systematic variation of the punishment cost itself.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No main treatment systematically changes the 2‐ECU dispute cost or cost per unit of punishment.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
     – Not discussed (beyond the specific 2‐ECU cost in the jury treatments).

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Whether mentioned?  
     – If convicted, the receiver must pay the unpaid promised amount plus 2 ECU to reimburse the sender for the dispute cost. There is no concept of “per‐unit” punishment, only one lumpsum remedy.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
     – Not discussed.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Whether mentioned?  
     – None of the treatments include reward of any kind.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
     – Not applicable.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Whether mentioned?  
      – No. There is no reward.  
    • Systematically varied?  
      – No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
      – Not applicable.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted)  
    • Whether mentioned?  
      – No.  
    • Systematically varied?  
      – No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
      – Not applicable.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    • Whether mentioned?  
      – Yes. Subjects are told there are multiple periods, but not the total count (the session ends before the time slot is up, to limit end‐game effects).  
    • Systematically varied?  
      – No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
      – Not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much their peers gained or lost)?  
    • Whether mentioned?  
      – Yes. This is the “Info” vs. “No Info” dimension of the 2×2 design. In “No Info,” subjects learn only their own outcome each round; in “Info,” they also see the outcomes of other same‐color (in‐group) players.  
    • Systematically varied?  
      – Yes. The main design uses “No Info” vs. “Info.”  
    • Effect on punishment treatment effect (on any dependent variable)?  
      – The paper consistently finds that adding “Info” fosters path dependence: knowing that other in‐group members were cheated encourages senders to withhold trust from that out‐group. However, it does not systematically report an “efficiency” ratio; it reports total payoffs, amounts sent, amounts returned, etc. Numerically, the paper indicates that “Info” alone does not raise average returns or trust as much as the presence of the jury. Instead, “Info” intersects with the jury treatment to create an additive positive effect on overall payoffs.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Whether mentioned?  
      – The paper’s “jury” mechanism involves a vote among the three in‐group receivers. Votes are anonymous. Hence the punished receiver does not see exactly who voted to convict or acquit.  
    • Systematically varied?  
      – No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
      – Not discussed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Whether mentioned?  
      – No, there is no reward mechanism.  
    • Systematically varied?  
      – No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
      – Not applicable.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   • The experiment measures variables such as:  
     – Amount sent by the sender.  
     – Amount returned by the receiver.  
     – Total payoff (also referred to as total welfare).  
     – Rate of “cheating” (returning less than promised).  
   • The paper does discuss overall welfare (the sum of senders’ and receivers’ payoffs) but does not frame it as “efficiency” (actual payoff / maximum payoff). Thus, “efficiency” in the strict sense of payoff divided by the cooperative maximum is not directly reported.  

B. Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned but not varied:  
     (1) Number of players (always 16 per session).  
     (2) Number of rounds (10, not known to subjects).  
     (6) Multiplication factor (always 3).  
     (7) Punishment cost (2 ECU to file a dispute).  
     (8) Punishment magnitude (repayment of unfulfilled promise plus 2 ECU).  
     (12) Number of rounds unknown to participants.  
     (14) Punisher identity not revealed.  
   • Not mentioned at all or discussed only to say it was not used:  
     (4) All‐or‐nothing contribution (the experiment uses 0–10 continuous choice).  
     (5) Contribution default (none).  
     (9–11) Reward not used.  
     (15) Rewarder identity not used.  
   • Systematically varied:  
     (3) Chat is not exactly varied, only a single “message” mechanism, so it is not a factor.  
     (13) Peer outcomes shown (“Info”) vs. hidden (“No Info”). This is explicitly varied.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • Only parameter 13—the presence/absence of information about peer outcomes—is directly manipulated. The paper devotes substantial discussion to how “information sharing” (vs. no such information) and the presence (or absence) of the “jury” mechanism interact to affect total payoffs, amount sent, and amount returned. However, they do not treat the cost or magnitude of punishment as a systematically varied factor.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper:  
   • Because the study does not measure efficiency (i.e., payoff / maximum) but rather total payoffs, amounts sent, and amounts returned, the paper offers no direct guidance on many of these parameters (e.g., changing the group size, changing punishment cost, changing the multiplier, etc.). It neither varies them nor predicts how varying them would affect “punishment treatment effect.”  
   • The only systematic comparison is between “Info” vs. “No Info” and “Jury” vs. “No Jury.” The findings suggest that, if punishment is available and the group can share outcome information, total payoffs are higher. That pattern would plausibly (though not proven in this paper) generalize to higher efficiency as well. Beyond that, the paper provides little evidence on other parameters.  

In short, there is limited predictive content for these 15 parameters in relation to punishment’s effect on efficiency; the experimental design only varies (1) the presence or absence of a jury punishment mechanism and (2) whether or not group members share outcome information. All other parameters remain unchanged or unmentioned in the paper.
reference_APA: Kimbrough, Erik O. & Rubin, Jared (2015). Sustaining Group Reputation. JOURNAL OF LAW ECONOMICS & ORGANIZATION.

Authors: Bshary, A; Bshary, R
Author Full Names: Bshary, Andrea; Bshary, Redouan
Article Title: Interactions Between Sabre-Tooth Blennies and Their Reef Fish Victims: Effects Of Enforced Repeated Game Structure and Local Abundance on Victim Aggression
Keywords Plus: CLEANER FISH; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; LABROIDES-DIMIDIATUS; INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; EVOLUTION; COOPERATION; SELECTION; MUTUALISM; BENEFITS; BEHAVIOR
Abstract: The conditions under which humans benefit from contributing to a public good have attracted great interest; in particular the potential role of punishment of cheaters is hotly debated. In contrast, similar studies on other animals are lacking. In this study, we describe for the first time how the course of interactions between parasitic sabre-tooth blennies (the cheaters) and their reef fish victims can be used to study both punishment and the emergence of public goods. Sabre tooth blennies (Plagiotremus sp.) sneak up from behind to bite off small pieces of scales and/or mucus from other fish. Victims regularly show spontaneous aggression as well as aggressive responses to blenny attacks. In a between species comparison, we tested how the probability of chasing a blenny is affected by (1) the option of avoiding interactions with a blenny by avoiding its small territory, and (2) variation in local abundance of conspecifics. We found that resident victim species are more aggressive towards blennies than visiting species. This difference persisted when we controlled for victim size and territoriality, suggesting that it is the enforced repeated game structure that causes residents to chase blennies. In residents, we also found a negative correlation between aggression towards blennies and local abundance, which suggests that the benefits of chasing are diluted with increasing local abundance. We discuss the implication of these results for future studies.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter accounting of what the paper says (if anything) regarding each of the 15 public‐goods‐game parameters, focusing specifically on (1) whether the paper discusses the parameter at all (and, if so, the value or range used) and (2) whether it makes any predictions about how systematically varying that parameter would affect the “punishment treatment effect.” In keeping with your instructions, all statements are based solely on the content of this single paper, and numerical effect sizes on efficiency are provided only if the paper itself supplies such data (it does not).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   a) Mention in paper?  
      • The paper does not frame the system explicitly by “number of players.”  
      • However, it does examine “local abundance” of victim fish (i.e., group size on a reef patch). This is somewhat analogous to changing the number of participants exposed to blennies, but the authors never call it “number of players” or treat it as a parameter in a controlled public goods game.  
   b) Effect of systematically varying it on punishment treatment effect?  
      • The paper does not use the term “punishment treatment effect” or measure efficiency. It reports only that higher local abundance correlates with a lower propensity to aggress against (i.e., “punish”) biting blennies. There is no reference to how this would affect efficiency, and no effect size regarding efficiency is given.

2. Number of rounds  
   a) Mention in paper?  
      • The paper discusses the idea of an “enforced repeated game structure” for resident victim fish (as opposed to “one‐off” or very infrequent interactions for visiting fish). That is the closest mention to “number of rounds,” but there is no explicit statement of an actual round count.  
   b) Effect of systematically varying it on punishment treatment effect?  
      • No. The authors do not experimentally vary the length of repeated interactions or observe how different lengths might change any efficiency measure or even aggression per se. They note only that resident fish cannot easily escape repeated encounters.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   a) Mention in paper?  
      • No. There is no talk of communication or “chat” among fish.  
   b) Effect of systematically varying it on punishment treatment effect?  
      • Not discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   a) Mention in paper?  
      • No. The study does not discuss any “all or nothing” contribution scenario.  
   b) Effect of systematically varying it on punishment treatment effect?  
      • Not discussed.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much to move from the public fund back into their hand)?  
   a) Mention in paper?  
      • No. There is no mention of an endowment or default contribution.  
   b) Effect of systematically varying it on punishment treatment effect?  
      • Not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   a) Mention in paper?  
      • No. The paper uses no explicit economic or payoff‐multiplication term.  
   b) Effect of systematically varying it on punishment treatment effect?  
      • Not discussed.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   a) Mention in paper?  
      • The paper assumes there is some cost when victim fish chase the blenny (e.g., time/energy cost), but provides no numeric quantification or explicit parameter for “cost of punishment.”  
   b) Effect of systematically varying it on punishment treatment effect?  
      • Not discussed. There is no systematic variation or explicit measure of how changing the cost would influence aggression or any efficiency measure.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   a) Mention in paper?  
      • No. While “aggression” is framed as a presumed punishment, no numerical magnitude (e.g., “units of damage”) is given.  
   b) Effect of systematically varying it on punishment treatment effect?  
      • Not discussed.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   a) Mention in paper?  
      • No. There is no mention of any reward mechanism.  
   b) Effect of systematically varying it on punishment treatment effect?  
      • Not discussed.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    a) Mention in paper?  
       • No. Reward is not studied in this system.  
    b) Effect of systematically varying it on punishment treatment effect?  
       • Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
    a) Mention in paper?  
       • No.  
    b) Effect of systematically varying it on punishment treatment effect?  
       • Not discussed.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    a) Mention in paper?  
       • No. The authors do not address whether fish “know” or anticipate the number of future interactions.  
    b) Effect of systematically varying it on punishment treatment effect?  
       • Not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much peers gained/lost)?  
    a) Mention in paper?  
       • No.  
    b) Effect of systematically varying it on punishment treatment effect?  
       • Not discussed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    a) Mention in paper?  
       • The paper notes that blennies are often chased immediately by the victim they just bit, so presumably the blenny “knows” which fish chased it in that instant. However, there is no dedicated discussion about anonymity vs. identifiability of punishers.  
    b) Effect of systematically varying it on punishment treatment effect?  
       • Not discussed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    a) Mention in paper?  
       • Rewarding is not part of the study.  
    b) Effect of systematically varying it on punishment treatment effect?  
       • Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?  
   • The paper does not measure or report group efficiency, total payoff, or average payoff.  
   • Instead, it measures the frequency of victim fish aggression (punishment) toward biting sabre‐tooth blennies, broken down into three categories (unprovoked aggression, aggression in response to an attempted bite, and aggression in response to an actual bite).

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Only two appear to have any close parallels:  
     1) “Number of players” loosely corresponds to “local abundance” (group size), which they do measure.  
     2) “Number of rounds” loosely corresponds to repeated vs. non‐repeated interactions (resident vs. visiting fish).  
   • All other parameters (3–5, 6, 7–8, 9–11, 12–15) are not mentioned in a way that maps onto any controlled variation or any standard public‐goods‐game variable.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, none. The authors do not systematically manipulate any parameter in an experimental sense. They only observe correlations between local abundance (possible proxy for “number of players”) and aggression. Thus, there is no direct analysis of how varying these parameters influences “punishment treatment effect” or efficiency.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, solely based on this paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not provide any direct measurement or modeling of efficiency. It discusses that aggression (punishment) may produce a public good in the sense of deterring the blenny from attacking that victim group in the future, but does not formally track total payoffs or “efficiency.” Consequently, one can make little to no prediction about how systematically altering any of the 15 parameters would affect group efficiency, beyond noting that high local abundance (large “number of players”) is correlated with lower aggression—and that repeated interactions (for resident fish) appear to increase punishment. No quantitative or numerical effect sizes on efficiency are given.
reference_APA: Bshary, Andrea & Bshary, Redouan (2010). Interactions Between Sabre-Tooth Blennies and Their Reef Fish Victims: Effects Of Enforced Repeated Game Structure and Local Abundance on Victim Aggression. ETHOLOGY.

Authors: Rob, R; Yang, HX
Author Full Names: Rob, Rafael; Yang, Huanxing
Article Title: Long-term relationships as safeguards
Author Keywords: Community games; Information flows; Heterogeneity of types; Long-term relationships
Keywords Plus: REPEATED GAMES; STARTING SMALL; SOCIAL NORMS; COOPERATION
Abstract: We analyze a repeated prisoners' dilemma game played in a community setting with heterogeneous types. The setting is such that individuals choose whether to continue interacting with their present partner, or separate and seek a new partner. Players' types are not directly observed, but may be imperfectly inferred from observed behavior. We focus on a class of equilibria that satisfy zero tolerance and fresh start. We find that the punishment for defecting and the reward for cooperating are driven by the formation and the dissolution of long-term, high-paying relationships: an individual who defects, aborts a long-term relationship that he is in, or that he might have entered into, is thrown into short-term interactions with individuals who are likely to defect and, consequently, receives low payoffs. On the flip side, an individual who cooperates, enters into or prolongs a long-term interaction with a partner who cooperates and, consequently, receives high payoffs.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter review of what the paper by Rob and Yang (titled “Long‐term relationships as safeguards”) does or does not say regarding each of the 15 specific public‐goods‐game parameters and their predicted effect on the “punishment treatment effect” (i.e., how introducing punishment changes group efficiency). The paper itself studies a repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma in an indefinitely lived community with heterogeneous player types (some cooperate unconditionally, others defect unconditionally, and the rest strategically choose to cooperate or defect), focusing on whether “good,” “bad,” or mixed‐strategy equilibria emerge under different distributions of types. Throughout, “punishment” in their model arises endogenously because defectors are forced into more short‐lived or “stranger” relationships rather than through any explicit peer-imposed punishment with a known token cost or magnitude.

Below, for each parameter, I first state whether the paper:  
• (1) Mentions/discusses it (and with what value, if it does).  
• (2) Makes predictions about the effect of systematically varying that parameter on the punishment treatment effect for any dependent variable (and, if so, provides a numerical effect size).  

As you will see, the paper does not actually investigate a public goods game, does not speak of “group efficiency” per se (they speak instead of “social welfare,” “average payoff,” or “total per-period payoff”), does not use “punishment treatment” in the sense of imposing token-based punishments on peers, and does not systematically vary the 15 parameters below. Hence nearly all entries will indicate that the parameter is not mentioned or not varied.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   (1) Mention/Value in paper?  
       • The paper assumes a continuum of measure 1 of infinitely lived players. There is no finite-number specification and no systematic variation of the number of players.  
   (2) Effect of systematically varying this parameter on punishment treatment effect?  
       • Not discussed. No numerical effect size is provided.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Mention/Value in paper?  
       • The setting is an infinite-horizon repeated game (discrete infinite time). The paper does not treat the number of rounds as a parameter that can vary.  
   (2) Effect of systematically varying this parameter on punishment treatment effect?  
       • Not discussed.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   (1) Mention/Value in paper?  
       • Not mentioned at all.  
   (2) Effect of systematically varying this parameter on punishment treatment effect?  
       • Not discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   (1) Mention/Value in paper?  
       • Not mentioned. The paper analyzes a Prisoner’s Dilemma with payoffs a, b, l, etc.; it does not frame it as an “all-or-nothing contribution” game.  
   (2) Effect of systematically varying this parameter on punishment treatment effect?  
       • Not discussed.

5. Is the contribution default? (i.e., do players choose how much of their endowment to move back into their hand?)  
   (1) Mention/Value in paper?  
       • Not mentioned.  
   (2) Effect of systematically varying this parameter on punishment treatment effect?  
       • Not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor for the public good  
   (1) Mention/Value in paper?  
       • Not mentioned. The repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma payoffs use parameters a, b, and l, which do not represent an MPCR or a public-goods multiplier.  
   (2) Effect of systematically varying this parameter on punishment treatment effect?  
       • Not discussed.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   (1) Mention/Value in paper?  
       • Not mentioned in the sense of a token-based or monetary cost. In their model, “punishment” is that a defector is dropped by a partner and must re-enter a “stranger” phase. There is no explicit, player-imposed “cost” to the punisher.  
   (2) Effect of systematically varying this parameter on punishment treatment effect?  
       • Not discussed.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from a punished player)  
   (1) Mention/Value in paper?  
       • Not mentioned in the sense of a peer-to-peer punishment magnitude. The paper’s “defector gets matched into new short-term encounters” is not cast as a deduction of coins by other players.  
   (2) Effect of systematically varying this parameter on punishment treatment effect?  
       • Not discussed.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   (1) Mention/Value in paper?  
       • The word “reward” appears in a different sense: “the reward for cooperating” is that one remains in a profitable, longer-term relationship. However, there is no explicit, token-based reward mechanism under a punisher/rewarder’s control.  
   (2) Effect of systematically varying this parameter on punishment treatment effect?  
       • Not discussed.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    (1) Mention/Value in paper?  
        • Not mentioned.  
    (2) Effect of systematically varying this parameter on punishment treatment effect?  
        • Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
    (1) Mention/Value in paper?  
        • Not mentioned in a token-based sense.  
    (2) Effect of systematically varying this parameter on punishment treatment effect?  
        • Not discussed.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    (1) Mention/Value in paper?  
        • The horizon is infinite, and there is no discussion of known or unknown finite endpoints.  
    (2) Effect of systematically varying this parameter on punishment treatment effect?  
        • Not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?  
    (1) Mention/Value in paper?  
        • Each player sees only their own partner’s choices (cooperate or defect). No mention of learning others’ outcomes.  
    (2) Effect of systematically varying this display of peer outcomes?  
        • Not discussed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    (1) Mention/Value in paper?  
        • Not applicable. Punishment is effectively “being forced into short-term matches” rather than a direct punisher. There is no discussion about identification of a punisher.  
    (2) Effect of systematically varying whether a punisher can be identified?  
        • Not discussed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    (1) Mention/Value in paper?  
        • Not applicable. There is no direct rewarder.  
    (2) Effect of systematically varying whether a rewarder can be identified?  
        • Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
▌ A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper does not use the term “group efficiency,” but it does use “social welfare,” “total per-period payoff,” and “average payoff in the community” as outcome variables. It also considers individual discounted payoffs for each player type.  
   • Hence, “social welfare” or “average payoff” is akin to total/average payoffs of the population. The paper does not frame this as “actual payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff,” so it does not label this ratio as “efficiency.”  

   What are the dependent variables, and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper focuses largely on whether the “good equilibrium,” “bad equilibrium,” or a mixed strategy equilibrium exists under various distributions of player types.  
   • It then examines the resulting average payoff (or “social welfare”) at those equilibria.  
   • Thus, “existence of equilibria” and “social welfare” (average payoff) are the paper’s main dependent variables. They do not call either one “efficiency.”

▌ B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • The paper does mention that there is a continuum of players (so item 1—number of players—is implicitly infinite).  
   • It also mentions that the horizon is infinite (so item 2—number of rounds—is infinite), but it does not treat that as a systematically varied parameter.  
   • As for all other parameters (3 through 15), they are not mentioned in the sense of public-goods protocols, punishment tokens, or reward tokens.  

   In total, only items (1) and (2) are mentioned in passing (infinite population, infinite horizon), but not in a way resembling a standard public goods experiment design. None of the remaining parameters (3–15) appear in the paper.

▌ C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when that parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The paper does not present any systematic variation of items 1–15 in the context of “punishment treatment effect,” nor does it even present a “punishment treatment” in the public-goods sense. Their “punishment” is an endogenous shift into a less profitable match. They do not systematically manipulate cost or magnitude of such a punishment.  
   • Hence, there is no discussion of how any of these 15 parameters would affect a “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency (or any other dependent variable) if varied.  

   So: Zero out of these 15 parameters are systematically varied for studying the effect on a punishment treatment.

▌ D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • Because the paper does not treat a public goods game, does not define “punishment treatment effect” in the sense of a costed punishment mechanism, and does not systematically vary any of these 15 parameters, little to no prediction can be made purely from the paper’s content about how those parameters or their interactions would affect efficiency.  
   • The paper addresses how the fraction of “bad” vs. “good” types in a population can sustain or undermine cooperation in a repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma, but it does not map onto these 15 parameters from a standard public goods experiment design.  

   Consequently, there is no basis in this paper alone for making predictions on how parameters 1–15 or their interactions would shape a punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Answering strictly from the paper by Rob and Yang (2008), none of the fifteen listed public‐goods‐game design parameters is systematically varied or analyzed for its effect on “punishment treatment” or on “efficiency.” The paper does not describe a public goods game nor implement external punishment or reward costs/magnitudes; instead, it studies repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma relationships with endogenous matching and type heterogeneity. Thus, no quantitative or qualitative predictions about the 15 parameters’ influences on a “punishment treatment effect” can be drawn from this source alone.
reference_APA: Rob, Rafael & Yang, Huanxing (2010). Long-term relationships as safeguards. ECONOMIC THEORY.

Authors: Röhl, T; Röhl, C; Schuster, HG; Traulsen, A
Author Full Names: Roehl, Torsten; Roehl, Claudia; Schuster, Heinz Georg; Traulsen, Arne
Article Title: Impact of fraud on the mean-field dynamics of cooperative social systems
Keywords Plus: INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; EVOLUTIONARY GAMES; PRISONERS-DILEMMA; BOLTZMANN-LIKE; INDIVIDUALS; POPULATIONS; PUNISHMENT; EMERGENCE; SELECTION; NETWORKS
Abstract: The evolution of costly cooperation between selfish individuals seems to contradict Darwinian selection, as it reduces the fitness of a cooperating individual. However, several mechanisms such as repeated interactions or spatial structure can lead to the evolution of cooperation. One such mechanism for the evolution of cooperation, in particular among humans, is indirect reciprocity, in which individuals base their decision to cooperate on the reputation of the potential receiver, which has been established in previous interactions. Cooperation can evolve in these systems if individuals preferably cooperate with those that have shown to be cooperative in the past. We analyze the impact of fake reputations or fraud on the dynamics of reputation and on the success of the reputation system itself, using a mean-field description for evolutionary games given by the replicator equation. This allows us to classify the qualitative dynamics of our model analytically. Our results show that cooperation based on indirect reciprocity is robust with respect to fake reputations and can even be enhanced by them. We conclude that fraud per se does not necessarily have a detrimental effect on social systems.

o1_summary:
Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter summary of what (if anything) the paper says about each of the 15 specified features of a “public goods game with punishment” and how (if at all) the paper discusses systematically varying those features’ impact on punishment and payoffs. Throughout, note that the paper itself does not use the language of a standard “punishment” public‐goods experiment; instead, it analyzes “discriminators,” “defectors,” and “scammers” in an indirect reciprocity framework with a penalty ρ imposed on scammers if discovered with probability α. Nevertheless, the table below follows the requested 15 parameters strictly:

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players
   • Not discussed in the paper. The model is effectively a mean‐field (replicator) approach, and no specific finite group size or systematic variation in player number is analyzed.

2) Number of rounds
   • Discussed and explicitly varied. The parameter n represents how many times (rounds) reputations can change (Sec. II and Fig. 1). The paper examines how greater n can favor discriminators (cooperators) over defectors or scammers, because more rounds allow a "good" reputation to pay off in later rounds.  
   • The paper does not, however, tie this to “punishment treatment effect on efficiency”; rather, it focuses on how payoffs and strategy frequencies change with n. No numerical “effect size on efficiency” is provided.

3) Is chat enabled between players?
   • Not discussed.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • The paper’s model posits that a donor either pays a cost c or does not pay it (i.e., cooperates or does not cooperate), but there is no explicit discussion that this is systematically varied or that it is “forced all or nothing.” It is simply part of the model’s structure with no separate analysis of different contribution rules.

5) Is the contribution default (do players decide how much to move from the public fund into their hand)?
   • Not discussed; there is no mention of any default contribution mechanism.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • The paper uses a cost‐benefit framework (cost c, benefit b). The ratio c / b appears frequently (e.g., Secs. II–III) and is identified as a key parameter affecting whether cooperation is favored. Although not labeled MPCR or “multiplication factor,” the cost‐benefit ratio serves the same role.  
   • The paper systematically varies c / b but does not explicitly frame it in terms of a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Rather, higher benefit relative to cost (b >> c) can enhance the success of cooperative or discriminatory strategies. No numeric “effect size on efficiency” is given.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Not discussed. The paper does not have a model of “punishers” who pay a personal cost; discovery of scammers and penalty ρ is imposed “by the community” without mention of any cost to the punisher.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   • This is discussed in terms of the penalty ρ a scammer must pay if caught (Sec. II). The paper systematically varies ρ (alongside detection probability α) to see under what conditions scamming outperforms or is outperformed by other strategies.  
   • No direct statement about “group efficiency” from varying ρ is given, but the paper shows that increasing ρ helps suppress scammers, thereby favoring cooperation in certain parameter regions.

9) Whether a reward is enabled
   • Not discussed. The paper does not feature a fourth strategy or any mention of a rewarding mechanism.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Not discussed.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)
    • Not discussed.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Not discussed. The paper treats n as a fixed parameter for the model but does not mention whether participants know n or not.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much others gained/lost each round)?
    • Not discussed. The model’s assumption is that a player’s reputation (good or bad) is publicly observable, but there is no mention of showing payoffs or specifically how such information is displayed round by round.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Not discussed. Punishment (paying penalty ρ) occurs automatically upon discovery; the paper does not model knowledge of who imposed it.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Not discussed; no reward mechanism is included.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A) Dependent variables in the paper and how they differ:  
   • The paper’s main dependent variables are the average (or accumulated) payoffs of the three strategies (discriminators, defectors, scammers) and the frequencies of these strategies in the population under the replicator dynamics.  
   • The paper does not use the term “group efficiency” (i.e., actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible). Instead, it focuses on whether cooperation can persist given differing cost, benefit, penalty, detection probability, and number of rounds.  
   • Thus, “efficiency” as typically defined in a public‐goods experiment is not reported. The closest analog is the average payoff across the population.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   • Three of the 15 are explicitly mentioned:  
       (2) Number of rounds (n).  
       (6) Cost‐benefit ratio (c and b) (analogous to an MPCR factor).  
       (8) Punishment magnitude (here, the penalty ρ).  
   • The other 12 parameters are not discussed in the paper.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when the parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, the paper never refers to a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Instead, it looks at how strategy payoffs are altered by detection probability α, penalty ρ, number of rounds n, and cost–benefit ratio c / b.  
   • Of the listed parameters, only parameters (2), (6), and (8) appear in the paper’s analyses at all. But the paper does not couch them in terms of “punishment treatment effect” on “efficiency,” nor does it provide explicit numerical effect sizes for “efficiency.”

D) Predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency,” based solely on the paper:  
   • Because the authors do not analyze “efficiency” nor a standard “peer punishment” mechanism, very little can be concluded about the classic “punishment treatment effect” from these results. The main points that might speak to group‐level outcomes are:  
       – (2) More rounds (n) can favor cooperative strategies in the presence of a reputational penalty, which could in principle increase total payoffs.  
       – (6) A favorable cost–benefit ratio (b ≫ c) makes cooperation more robust and, in the presence of penalizing scammers, could raise overall population payoff.  
       – (8) A higher penalty ρ makes scamming less profitable and thus can help sustain cooperation and higher average payoffs, presumably enhancing “efficiency.”  
   • Apart from those three aspects, the paper provides no information from which to predict how the remaining 12 parameters would affect punishment (or “punishment treatment effect on efficiency”).  

In short, there is almost no basis in this particular paper for extending predictions about many of the usual design parameters of a public goods game (chat, revealing punisher identity, rewards, etc.) or about how “efficiency” specifically would change. The paper’s focus is on average payoffs of competing strategies under varied detection probability, cost–benefit ratio, and number of rounds, rather than on group efficiency per se.
reference_APA: Roehl, Torsten, Roehl, Claudia, Schuster, Heinz Georg & Traulsen, Arne (2007). Impact of fraud on the mean-field dynamics of cooperative social systems. PHYSICAL REVIEW E.

Authors: Shreedhar, G; Tavoni, A; Marchiori, C
Author Full Names: Shreedhar, Ganga; Tavoni, Alessandro; Marchiori, Carmen
Article Title: Monitoring and punishment networks in an experimental common pool resource dilemma
Author Keywords: common pool resources; monitoring; networks; punishment
Keywords Plus: EQUIVALENT PUBLIC GOOD; PEER PUNISHMENT; CONDITIONAL COOPERATION; SOCIAL PREFERENCES; GOODS; MANAGEMENT; LEADERSHIP; ECONOMICS; GAMES
Abstract: With the aid of a lab experiment, we explored how imperfect monitoring and punishment networks impacted appropriation, punishment and beliefs in a common pool resource appropriation dilemma. We studied the differences between the complete network (with perfect monitoring and punishment, in which everyone can observe and punish everyone else) and two 'imperfect' networks (that systematically reduce the number of subjects who could monitor and punish others): the directed and undirected circle networks. We found that free riders were punished in all treatments, but the network topology impacted the type of punishment: the undirected circle induced more severe punishment and prosocial punishment compared to the other two networks. Both imperfect networks were more efficient because the larger punishment capacity available in the complete network elicited higher punishment amount.

Below is an item‐by‐item accounting of whether and how each of the 15 parameters is mentioned or systematically varied in the paper, followed by the required four‐part summary.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. The paper always uses four players (“n=4”) in each group.  
• Is it systematically varied or do the authors predict its effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
  – No. The group size is held constant; the paper offers no prediction about changing the number of players.

2. Number of rounds  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. Each session has 15 rounds, and this is common knowledge.  
• Is it systematically varied or do the authors predict its effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
  – No. The paper uses exactly 15 rounds without experimental variation. The authors do not make specific predictions about other possible numbers of rounds.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – The paper does not allow or discuss any real‐time chat/communication among participants.  
• Is it systematically varied or do the authors predict its effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
  – No mention. No predictions or results about enabling/disabling chat.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. Participants choose any integer from 0 to 25 tokens for the common account (i.e., not “all or nothing”).  
• Is it systematically varied or do the authors predict its effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
  – No. The paper does not study any forced “all or nothing” design.

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., do participants move endowment from the public fund back)?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. The game endowment is 25 tokens, and participants privately choose how many to place into the common account.  
• Is it systematically varied or do the authors predict its effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
  – No mention. No default is manipulated or discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – The study uses a nonlinear payoff function F(X) = aX – bX² (table 2 mentions a=0.25, b=5, w=4).  
• Is it systematically varied or do the authors predict its effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
  – No. There is no experimental variation of these parameters across treatments.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. It is fixed at 1 token per punishment point for the punisher (“c_a = 1”).  
• Is it systematically varied or do the authors predict its effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
  – No. It is held constant at a 1:3 fee‐to‐fine ratio. No predictions for changes to that cost.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from the punished player)  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. Each punishment point deducts 3 tokens from the target (“c_r = 3”).  
• Is it systematically varied or do the authors predict its effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
  – No. No variations or systematic predictions about changing this deduction.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. The experiment considers only punishment; no reward mechanism is used.  
• Is it systematically varied or do the authors predict its effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
  – No mention.

10. Reward cost to the rewarder  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. Rewarding is not part of the design.  
• Is it systematically varied or do the authors predict its effect?  
  – No mention.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded)  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. Again, no reward mechanism is present.  
• Is it systematically varied or do the authors predict its effect?  
  – No mention.

12. Is the number of rounds known to the players (do they know when the game ends)?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. “An experimental session consisted of 15 decision‐rounds, and this was common knowledge.”  
• Is it systematically varied or do the authors predict its effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
  – No. The experiment keeps this constant (targeting a one‐shot logic in stranger‐matching), and no separate predictions are made for varying known vs. unknown round lengths.

13. Are peer outcomes shown to players (e.g., how much each peer gained or lost each round)?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. In stage two, each player sees how many tokens their “network neighbors” allocated to the public/private account. In the Complete Network (CN), they see everyone’s allocations; in the Undirected Circle (UCN) and Directed Circle (DCN), they see only those they can monitor.  
• Is it systematically varied or do the authors predict its effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
  – Yes, in effect, because perfect vs. imperfect (circle) network structures vary how much each participant can see (and hence punish). The main paper result is that the “imperfect” circle networks end up with slightly higher efficiency (net payoffs) than the “complete” network, primarily because the complete network’s high punishment capacity leads to heavier—but often inefficient—punishment. Numerically, the paper’s Table 3 shows:  
    – CN average net payoff: about 172 tokens  
    – UCN average net payoff: about 189 tokens  
    – DCN average net payoff: about 189 tokens  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes, but only to say that identities are anonymized in the stranger‐matching design; the punished do not learn exactly who punished them.  
• Is it systematically varied or do the authors predict its effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
  – No. There is no separate condition where identification of punishers differs.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No, because reward is not part of the design.  
• Is it systematically varied or do the authors predict its effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
  – No mention.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
• Yes, the paper explicitly uses “net payoffs” as a measure of efficiency. The main dependent variables are (1) individual appropriation (how many tokens placed in the common account), (2) punishment (amount, severity, incidence), (3) net payoffs (efficiency), and (4) beliefs. The authors note that sometimes “cooperation” or “appropriation” is not the same as net payoff; punishing can raise cooperation yet reduce net payoffs if punishment costs are high.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Mentioned in some form (but not varied):  
  1) Number of players (always 4).  
  2) Number of rounds (always 15).  
  6) Nonlinear payoff parameters (akin to MPCR but not linearly varied).  
  7) Punishment cost (1 token).  
  8) Punishment magnitude (3 tokens deducted).  
  12) Participants know there are 15 rounds.  
  13) Participants see outcomes only of those they are allowed to monitor (this changes with network structure).  
  14) Punisher identity is not revealed.  
• Not mentioned/Not used at all:  
  3) Chat (or communication).  
  4) All‐or‐nothing contribution.  
  5) Default contribution mechanism.  
  9, 10, 11) Rewards (not used).  
  15) Rewarder identity (not applicable).

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• Only one parameter is truly manipulated in the experiment: the network structure (part of parameter 13 about feedback on peers), resulting in Complete vs. Undirected Circle vs. Directed Circle monitoring/punishment. By design, that manipulation affects how many peers one can observe and punish. The paper discusses how that leads to differences in efficiency, punishment levels, and appropriation but does not systematically vary the other parameters.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
• The paper only shows that making peer monitoring and punishment “imperfect” by removing some links (Undirected or Directed Circle) can slightly increase net payoffs compared to a Complete Network, mainly because the latter’s overall punishment capacity is so large that it often reduces payoffs through costly punishment. Apart from that finding, the paper does not analyze systematic variations in the other parameters and does not provide enough evidence to predict how changing them (e.g., altering group size, number of rounds, punishment cost, enabling rewards, etc.) would change efficiency.  

Consequently, one can say little else about how any other parameter (or combination of parameters) would affect efficiency, based solely on this paper’s content.

Authors: Bigoni, M; Potters, J; Spagnolo, G
Author Full Names: Bigoni, Maria; Potters, Jan; Spagnolo, Giancarlo
Article Title: Frequency of interaction, communication and collusion: an experiment
Author Keywords: Cartels; Cournot oligopoly; Flexibility; Imperfect monitoring; Repeated games
Keywords Plus: INFINITELY REPEATED GAMES; COOPERATION; TIME
Abstract: The frequency of interaction facilitates collusion by reducing gains from defection. Theory has shown that under imperfect monitoring flexibility may hinder cooperation by inducing punishment after too few noisy signals, making collusion impossible in many environments (Sannikov and Skrzypacz in Am Econ Rev 97:1794-1823, 2007). The interplay of these forces should generate an inverse U-shaped effect of flexibility on collusion. We test for the first time these theoretical predictions-central to antitrust policy-in a laboratory experiment featuring an indefinitely repeated Cournot duopoly, with different degrees of flexibility. Results turn out to depend crucially on whether subjects can communicate with each other at the beginning of a supergame (explicit collusion) or not (tacit collusion). Without communication, the incidence of collusion is low throughout and not significantly related to flexibility; when subjects are allowed to communicate, collusion is more common throughout and significantly more frequent in the treatment with intermediate flexibility than in the treatments with low or high flexibility.
