Below is a point‐by‐point inventory of whether and how this paper addresses each of the 15 parameters in relation to any “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency. As requested, all statements refer strictly to what is actually contained in the paper itself (i.e., no additional sources or speculation). The paper studies an indefinitely repeated Cournot duopoly with or without pre‐play communication (chat). It does not present a public goods game, does not implement peer‐to‐peer punishment or rewards, and does not measure a ratio of group payoff to a “fully cooperative” benchmark. Therefore, almost none of the 15 parameters is varied with respect to any punishment‐based treatment. Where the paper does discuss or vary a parameter, that is noted below.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
 • Mentioned?  Yes. The experiment features two players (a duopoly).  
 • Systematic variation affecting punishment treatment effect?  No. The paper does not vary the number of players, nor does it discuss any punishment treatment effect for different numbers of players.

2. Number of rounds
 • Mentioned?  Yes, but only in the sense that the game is an indefinitely repeated Cournot duopoly (random termination).  
 • Systematic variation affecting punishment treatment effect?  No. Apart from running multiple indefinite‐length supergames, the paper does not systematically vary the total number of rounds in order to study a punishment treatment effect.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
 • Mentioned?  Yes. The paper runs treatments with and without communication (chat).  
 • Systematic variation affecting punishment treatment effect?  The paper discusses how the ability to communicate vastly increases collusion rates, but it does not frame this as a “punishment treatment” nor measure “punishment costs” or “punishment magnitudes.” Hence, it does not examine a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” No numerical talk of an effect size for “punishment treatment” is given, because punishment is not formally implemented as in a public‐goods‐plus‐sanctions design.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
 • Mentioned?  No. The paper studies quantity choices in a Cournot game (either 3 or 4), not a binary or “all or nothing” contribution game.  
 • Systematic variation affecting punishment treatment effect?  Not discussed.

5. Is the contribution default (are players deciding how much to move back into their hand)?
 • Mentioned?  No. There is no mechanism resembling “default” contributions.  
 • Systematic variation affecting punishment treatment effect?  Not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
 • Mentioned?  No. The paper examines price and profit in a Cournot setting and does not describe any MPCR‐type parameter relevant to a public goods game.  
 • Systematic variation affecting punishment treatment effect?  Not discussed.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
 • Mentioned?  No. Participants do not penalize one another with any formal punishment tool.  
 • Systematic variation affecting punishment treatment effect?  Not discussed (no punishment‐cost parameter exists).

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted per punishment)
 • Mentioned?  No. There is no direct punishment rule or “units of punishment.”  
 • Systematic variation affecting punishment treatment effect?  Not discussed.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
 • Mentioned?  No. There is no reward mechanism in the experiment.  
 • Systematic variation affecting punishment treatment effect?  Not discussed.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
 • Mentioned?  No. No formal reward system exists.  
 • Systematic variation affecting punishment treatment effect?  Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded per reward)
 • Mentioned?  No. Again, no reward system exists.  
 • Systematic variation affecting punishment treatment effect?  Not discussed.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
 • Mentioned?  Yes. The game uses an indefinite horizon with random continuation probability; subjects do not know which round will be the last.  
 • Systematic variation affecting punishment treatment effect?  No. The experiment does not vary whether or not the horizon is known; it remains indefinite in all sessions.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much their peers gained/lost)?
 • Mentioned?  Partially. Subjects see only the common market price each period (plus their own payoffs). They do not see the competitor’s payoffs.  
 • Systematic variation affecting punishment treatment effect?  Not discussed; the paper does not alter what is shown in a way to test punishment.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
 • Mentioned?  No. There is no direct punishment mechanism, so nothing is said about identifying the punisher.  
 • Systematic variation affecting punishment treatment effect?  Not discussed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
 • Mentioned?  No. There is no direct reward mechanism, so nothing is said about rewarder identification.  
 • Systematic variation affecting punishment treatment effect?  Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────


SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper focuses on “cooperation” (collusive choices), price outcomes, and players’ profits. While it does report and compare average payoffs, it does not use the term “group efficiency” in the sense of (actual total payoff) / (maximum possible total payoff). Instead, the main dependent variables include:  
     – Cooperation (collusion) rate.  
     – Price outcomes.  
     – Length of initial cooperation.  
     – Individual and average profits.  
   • These measures differ from one another: “cooperation rate” looks at how often both players choose a “collusive” quantity, whereas average profit is a monetary measure. The paper does not convert these into an efficiency ratio relative to a “fully cooperative” standard, nor does it measure a “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Parameter 1 (Number of players) and Parameter 2 (Number of rounds) are implicitly or explicitly described (but not systematically varied for punishment).  
   • Parameter 3 (Is chat enabled?) is explicitly manipulated (two conditions: chat vs. no chat).  
   • Parameter 12 (Is the number of rounds known to players?) is discussed (subjects face an indefinite horizon with random continuation).  
   • The other 11 parameters (4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15) are either not used in this Cournot‐duopoly design or not varied in a way that would speak to a formal “punishment treatment.”

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. Although the paper uses the concept of “punishment strategies” (e.g., defecting if one observes a suspiciously low price), there is no “punishment treatment” with a direct cost/magnitude of punishment or reward. Hence, the effects of systematically varying any parameter on a “punishment treatment effect” are not examined.

D. Predictions for how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, solely based on this paper’s content:  
   • The paper does not provide a framework in which explicit “punishment” or “reward” (akin to public good sanctioning) is implemented. Consequently, it offers little or no direct basis for predicting how systematically varying these 15 parameters would alter a punishment treatment effect on efficiency. Any attempt at such a prediction would go beyond what the authors actually investigated.

Authors: Fischer, S; Grechenig, K; Meier, N
Author Full Names: Fischer, Sven; Grechenig, Kristoffel; Meier, Nicolas
Article Title: Monopolizing Sanctioning Power under Noise Eliminates Perverse Punishment But Does Not Increase Cooperation
Author Keywords: cooperation; public good; centralized punishment; imperfect information; anti-social punishment; perverse punishment
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC GOOD EXPERIMENTS; GOODS; ENFORCEMENT; HUMANS; PROVISION; PRIVATE; LEGAL; GAMES
Abstract: We run several experiments which allow us to compare cooperation under perfect and imperfect information in a centralized and decentralized punishment regime. Under perfect and extremely noisy information, aggregate behavior does not differ between institutions. Under intermediate noise, punishment escalates in the decentralized peer-to-peer punishment regime which badly affects efficiency while sustaining cooperation for longer. Only decentralized punishment is often directed at cooperators (perverse punishment). We report several, sometimes subtle, differences in punishment behavior, and how contributions react.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter response concerning whether (1) the paper discusses each of the 15 parameters (and, if so, the value it takes), and (2) whether the paper makes predictions about the effect of systematically varying that parameter on the treatment effect of punishment (specifically, on efficiency or any other dependent variable). Because the paper itself only manipulates the punishment institution (decentralized vs. centralized) and the noise in contribution signals (λ = 1, 0.75, 0.50), it does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters listed in your query. Therefore, no systematic effect of changing these parameters on the punishment treatment effect is offered in the paper.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   – Discussion: The paper fixes groups of five (four “C-participants” and one “authority”).  
   – Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment: Not varied; no predictions offered.

2. Number of rounds  
   – Discussion: All sessions have 30 rounds in a partners design, and although the authors compare early vs. late rounds in their analysis, the total number of rounds is never varied experimentally.  
   – Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment: Not varied; no predictions offered.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   – Discussion: The paper does not mention chat or any other form of communication.  
   – Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment: Not varied; no predictions offered.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   – Discussion: Contributions range over discrete increments {0, 2, 4, …, 20}. This is neither “all or nothing” nor tuned experimentally.  
   – Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment: Not varied; no predictions offered.

5. Is the contribution default?  
   – Discussion: There is no mention in the paper of a default contribution mechanism (e.g., automatic contributions or “refund” decisions).  
   – Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment: Not varied; no predictions offered.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   – Discussion: The MPCR is 0.4 for every treatment.  
   – Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment: Not varied; no predictions offered.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   – Discussion: In decentralized punishment (DEC), each punishment point sent costs the sender 1 token. In centralized punishment (CEN), each point issued by the authority similarly costs the authority 1 token. However, this cost is kept constant across all conditions.  
   – Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment: Not varied; no predictions offered.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   – Discussion: Each imposed punishment point deducts 3 tokens from the punished individual. This magnitude is also constant across all conditions.  
   – Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment: Not varied; no predictions offered.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   – Discussion: The paper does not include any reward mechanism; only punishment is studied.  
   – Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment: Not applicable.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    – Discussion: No reward is used in the experiment.  
    – Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment: Not applicable.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward)  
    – Discussion: No reward is used in the experiment.  
    – Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment: Not applicable.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
    – Discussion: Yes. Participants know there are 30 total rounds. The design is a standard, finitely repeated public‐good game.  
    – Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment: Not varied; no predictions offered.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained or lost each round)?  
    – Discussion: Participants do see signals about how much each other participant contributed, but this signal is accurate only with probability λ = 1, 0.75, or 0.50. Apart from that, the paper does not show complete peer payoffs; only partial information (the noisy or accurate contributions) is given.  
    – Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment: The paper does systematically vary the noise (λ) in the signals about contributions, and this affects punishment behavior and efficiency. However, this manipulation is framed only as varying the accuracy of the contribution signal, not as changing the visibility of “peer payoffs.” Hence, none of the 15 listed parameters (as stated) is systematically varied, but the level of signal noise is. The paper does discuss how noise affects efficiency under decentralized vs. centralized punishment, but that manipulation is independent of the 15 parameters in your list.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    – Discussion: In decentralized punishment, recipients cannot identify the individual punisher. In centralized punishment, there is only one authority who punishes. That design feature is constant in each institution and not varied across sessions.  
    – Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment: Not varied; no predictions offered.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    – Discussion: No reward mechanism is included, so not applicable.  
    – Systematic variation or effect on punishment treatment: Not applicable.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY  

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • Yes. The paper explicitly reports “efficiency” (the authors define it as total earnings, minus fixed endowments, aggregated over all participants including the authority). They also measure contributions and the total punishment used. Hence, key dependent variables in the paper are contributions, punishment, and overall efficiency. The authors note that “efficiency” can differ from “cooperation” (or average contribution), and they report each separately.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned (but not varied):  
       1. Number of players (always 5)  
       2. Number of rounds (always 30)  
       6. MPCR (always 0.4)  
       7. Punishment cost per point (always 1)  
       8. Punishment magnitude (always 3)  
       12. Number of rounds known (yes, 30)  
       14. Whether a punished player knows the punisher (varies by institution but not experimentally manipulated)  
   • Not mentioned or not relevant:  
       3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 13 (in the sense of full payoff visibility), 15  

   Altogether, the paper touches on 7 of the 15 parameters (1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 12, 14) as fixed design features but does not treat them as experimental variations.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. The study does not systematically vary any of those 15 parameters. The only systematic variations are (a) whether punishment is decentralized or centralized and (b) the noise level in contribution signals (λ = 1, 0.75, 0.50). Consequently, the paper does not provide quantitative effect sizes for manipulating any of the 15 parameters listed.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not discuss or test changes in any of the 15 parameters. Hence, it offers no direct guidance about how systematically varying them (e.g., changing the number of players, changing the punishment cost, changing whether chat is enabled, etc.) would alter the effect of punishment on efficiency. The authors focus on contrasts between decentralized vs. centralized punishment at different levels of signal noise and note that under intermediate noise (λ = 0.75) the decentralized regime can escalate punishment. Beyond that, the paper makes no predictions relevant to your 15 parameters, so little to no reliable prediction can be made about how they might influence efficiency.

Authors: Sääksvuori, L
Author Full Names: Saeaeksvuori, Lauri
Article Title: Intergroup conflict, ostracism, and the evolution of cooperation under free migration
Author Keywords: Cooperation; Group conflict; Group formation; Ostracism; Social behavior
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS; GROUP SELECTION; GROUP COMPETITION; FIELD EXPERIMENT; PUNISHMENT; BEHAVIOR; GAME; CHIMPANZEES; EXCLUSION; SOCIETIES
Abstract: Theoretical investigations and quasi-experimental evidence from modern conflict areas suggest that intergroup conflict and ostracism play a pivotal role in the evolution of cooperation. However, there is little direct evidence about the influence of intergroup conflict on human social behavior in the presence of endogenous group formation and unrestricted migration. This study introduces an experiment to examine the impact of intergroup conflict and ostracism on group formation, and human cooperation in a dynamic environment where group size, the occurrence of intergroup hostility and the threat of ostracism are endogenously determined. Here, we show that intergroup conflict may inhibit merging into single large human coalitions. The threat of ostracism is shown to increase the average group size and cooperation within the society. In addition, we find that competitive pressure between groups decreases the likelihood of social exclusion. Our results suggest that free migration between groups suppresses the impact of between-group competition on within-group cooperation. Moreover, our results stress the role of ostracism as a means to repress competition within groups and enhance group success in competition against other groups.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter summary based strictly on the Sääksvuori (2014) paper you provided (“Intergroup conflict, ostracism, and the evolution of cooperation under free migration”). All references to “punishment” in that paper concern ostracism by majority vote, rather than costly punishment of the usual type (e.g., paying 1 coin to reduce someone else’s payoff). Likewise, the paper does not implement or systematically vary the standard “punishment” or “reward” parameters that often appear in public‐goods experiments. Accordingly, here is what the paper says (or does not say) for each of the 15 parameters listed in your request, followed by the required four‐part summary (A–D).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. In all treatments, each “society” has 12 players. These societies are subdivided into groups (e.g., 4 groups of 3 to start), and players can migrate or form new groups.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying this parameter on the punishment treatment effect (ostracism)?  
  – No. The number of players is fixed at 12 in every session; the paper does not vary it or predict how changing it would affect ostracism’s impact on efficiency (or any dependent variable).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Number of rounds
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. Each experimental session proceeds for 20 rounds (periods).  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying the number of rounds?  
  – No. It always uses 20 rounds and does not explore how a different number of rounds would affect ostracism, net payoffs, or cooperation.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Is chat enabled between players?
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Briefly. The paper states that participants were prevented from communicating or seeing one another; there was no explicit chat.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying chat?  
  – No. There is no treatment in which chat is enabled, nor is there any discussion of varying chat to see how it would affect the “punishment” (ostracism) treatment.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes, indirectly. Each player can contribute any amount from 0 to 20 monetary units (MUs). It is not all‐or‐nothing.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying this parameter?  
  – No. The contribution decision is always a free choice of how many MUs to allocate, and the paper does not study an all‐or‐nothing format.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5. Is the contribution default?
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. Participants simply choose how many of their 20 MUs to contribute; no mention is made of a default contribution or reversing that choice.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying a default contribution format?  
  – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. Table 2 shows a schedule of MPCR that depends on actual group size. For instance, with 12 people in one group the MPCR is 0.275, whereas with 2 people it is 0.65, and so on.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying MPCR on the punishment (ostracism) effect?  
  – No. The MPCR is determined by group size according to the same schedule in all treatments. There is no separate systematic variation of the MPCR.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Not in the typical sense of paying to punish. The only “punishment” is ostracism, carried out by majority vote. There is no stated per‐unit cost to the punisher.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying a punishment cost?  
  – No. The paper does not mention any such cost or systematically vary it.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. Ostracism removes a person from the group but does not deduct specified coins in the sense of “punishment points.”  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying punishment magnitude?  
  – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
9. Whether a reward is enabled
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. The design does not allow any “reward” mechanism; only ostracism is studied as a social sanction.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying reward?  
  – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
  – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
  – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – It appears participants know there are 20 rounds, because instructions mention “the experiment is repeated for 20 periods.”  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying knowledge of the final round?  
  – No. There are no treatments in which this knowledge is altered or studied in relation to the ostracism mechanism.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
13. Are peer outcomes shown (i.e., do players see each other’s payoffs)?
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Partially. Players see individual contributions of members of their own group and see average contributions in all existing groups. They do not see other players’ total payoffs in detail, only group or average allocations.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying the extent of outcome visibility?  
  – No. The paper implements only one information regime; no variation or predictions are discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. Ostracized players learn how many total votes were cast against them, but not who voted. The identity of individual punishers is never revealed.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying this?
  – No. The design is fixed; there is no condition that varies whether ostracized players see the identity of voters.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss it?
  – No. The experiment does not have a reward mechanism.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?
  – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A–D Summary
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper reports “net average pay‐offs” (see Figure 1(c)) and also repeatedly discusses average contributions, group size, and other measures. However, it does not explicitly report “efficiency” as total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff, nor does it focus on that ratio. It primarily tracks (1) net average payoff, (2) average contribution, and (3) group size. These dependent variables differ from “efficiency” in the strict sense, although one can infer that higher average payoff is closer to the social optimum.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
     1) Number of players (fixed at 12)  
     2) Number of rounds (fixed at 20)  
     6) MPCR (depends on group size per Table 2, but not varied as a separate treatment)  
     12) Known number of rounds (yes, presumably known to participants)  
     13) Some outcome information is shown (group‐level or individual contributions)  
     14) Punished players see the number of ostracism votes but not who voted.  
   • The others (3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 15) are either not used or not systematically varied.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when the parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, none. The paper does compare “no ostracism” vs. “ostracism” treatments, but these do not map onto the classic cost/magnitude “punishment” parameters (#7, #8). No other parameter in the list is systematically manipulated to see its effect on ostracism’s impact. Hence, there is no direct discussion of how changing the listed parameters would quantitatively alter ostracism’s effect on average payoff or contributions.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not supply evidence about varying these specific parameters (1–15) beyond noting that adding “ostracism” in general raised cooperativeness and increased average group size (and thus higher payoffs). It does not experimentally vary punishment cost, punishment magnitude, or chat, nor does it vary the number of players or rounds in a way that would let one measure changes in efficiency. Consequently, on the evidence provided, one can only note that “having ostracism at all” led to higher average payoff. Little to no specific prediction about how systematically changing any of the 15 parameters (e.g., changing group size from 12 to some other number, changing round length, or changing punishment cost) would affect efficiency can be drawn from the paper.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
End of response

• Not mentioned.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?

  – This is a statement about *reward vs. punishment*, not about how “turning reward on” changes the **punishment** treatment effect, so it does not yield a prediction for the parameter “reward enabled” when the focus is on punishment.

10. Reward cost per unit (cost to rewarder)  
• Present as H_SR = 2.5 (Fig. 3).  
• Not varied; no prediction.

11. Reward magnitude (benefit to target)

• Not mentioned.

• Not mentioned.

• Not mentioned.  
• No prediction.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables.  
   • The paper never reports “group efficiency” (total or average payoff divided by the cooperative optimum).

B.  Parameters from the list that the paper actually mentions: 8 of 15

D.  What can we predict about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment treatment effect on *efficiency*, using only this paper?

Below I go through the 15 parameters one-by-one and report exactly what the paper says about each of them and, where possible, what it implies for the
“punishment treatment effect” (i.e., the change in group efficiency that is produced when a punishment option is added).

----------------------------------------------------------------------  
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK‐LIST  

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned: Yes. Every group has 6 players (Table 1, Sect. 3).  
   • Systematically varied? No. All sessions use the same size, so the paper makes no prediction about how changing group size would alter the punishment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned: Yes. All groups play 30 periods (Sect. 3.1).  
   • Systematically varied? No. No prediction about its influence on the punishment effect.

3. Chat enabled? (non-binding communication)  
   • Mentioned: Yes. Two of the four treatments contain 5-minute chat periods before rounds 11 and 21 (“Covenants” and “Swords & Covenants”).  
   • Systematically varied? Yes – presence vs. absence of chat is the only parameter that is experimentally manipulated in a way that interacts with punishment.  
     – Empirical result:  
       • Without chat: adding punishment (“Swords”) raises mean yield/efficiency by 0 (M-W p = 0.34 for periods 11-30).  
       • With chat: adding punishment on top of chat (compare “Swords & Covenants” with “Covenants”) also raises efficiency by ~0 except for a small uptick in the very last 5 periods (M-W p = 0.043 for periods 26-30 only).  
     – Qualitative prediction: Enabling chat neutralises the usefulness of punishment; the punishment treatment effect on efficiency is therefore predicted to be ≈ 0 in the presence of chat.

4. All-or-nothing contribution choice  
   • Mentioned: No. Extraction is continuous 0–125. No discussion of varying this feature.

5. Contribution default / endowment framing  
   • Mentioned: No.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned: Yes indirectly. The external damage factor α = 0.05 (marginal group cost 0.30) is fixed.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

7. Punishment cost per unit  
   • Mentioned: Yes. Cost = 0.5 experimental$ per deduction point (Sect. 3.2).  
   • Systematically varied? No inside the experiment, though the authors compare the chosen ratio (fee-to-fine = 1:3) to OWG’s 1:2 or 1:4. No prediction about varying it.

8. Punishment magnitude per unit  
   • Mentioned: Yes. Each point removes 1.5 experimental$ from the target (Sect. 3.2).  
   • Systematically varied? No.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Mentioned: No. No rewards in any treatment.

10–11. Reward cost & magnitude  
   • Mentioned: No.

12. Horizon known?  
   • Mentioned: Yes. Subjects are told there will be 30 periods (Appendix instructions).  
   • Systematically varied? No.

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
   • Mentioned: Yes. After each round everyone sees all extraction numbers; after punishment they see total points they received (Sect. 3.3).  
   • Systematically varied? No.

14. Punisher identity revealed?  
   • Mentioned: Yes. The punished player learns only the total points, not who punished (Sect. 3.3).  
   • Systematically varied? No.

15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
   • Not applicable (no rewards).

----------------------------------------------------------------------  
SUMMARY  

A. Dependent variables  
   • The paper’s headline measure is “yield” = (total payoff actually obtained) / (maximum possible payoff) – this is exactly group efficiency as defined by the user.  
   • They also discuss (i) efficiency after accounting for the dead-weight loss of punishment, (ii) individual extraction levels, and (iii) number of punishment points assigned. These variables are conceptually different: extraction is a behavioural input, punishment points are a cost, yield/efficiency is the ultimate welfare outcome.

B. Parameters that are explicitly mentioned (9 of 15): 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14.

C. Parameters whose systematic variation is analysed for their effect on the punishment treatment effect: only 1 of 15 (Parameter 3 – chat/communication).

D. Predictions about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, based solely on this paper:  
   • Enabling chat (Parameter 3) is predicted to drive the punishment treatment effect to (approximately) zero, because communication alone already achieves near-maximum efficiency and punishment becomes redundant.  
   • For all other parameters the paper provides no direct evidence or formal prediction. Therefore, based solely on this source, little or no prediction can be made about how varying group size, punishment cost/magnitude, horizon, visibility, rewards, etc. would modulate the efficiency impact of punishment.

Abstract: Cooperation in groups often requires individual members to make costly contributions that benefit the group as a whole. Prior research suggests that shared norms can help to support ingroup cooperation by prescribing common standards of how much to contribute. These common standards may be disrupted when groups undergo membership change, i.e., when members from outgroups enter the ingroup. When newcomers and incumbents have different notions about how much to contribute, a normative disagreement ensues that could undermine cooperation and the extent to which individuals identify with the group. In a laboratory experiment, we manipulate whether newcomers and incumbents disagree about how much to contribute in a public goods game with peer punishment. We examine whether normative disagreement between newcomers and incumbents affects newcomer-incumbent relations in terms of group identification, the emergence of a social norm, and costly punishment. The main goal is to test whether normative disagreement and the resulting newcomer-incumbent relations harm cooperation in terms of contributions to the common good. We find that normative disagreement between newcomers and incumbents negatively affects the emergence of a shared social norm and lowers feelings of group identification. Contrary to expectations, normative disagreement does not affect cooperation negatively. Instead, participants adjust their behavior to each other's standards, using punishment for norm enforcement. This punishment is especially directed at low-contributing newcomers, leading them to conform to the incumbents' higher contribution standards.

   • Held constant; no discussion of other magnitudes.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Explicitly absent; only punishment is available (§3.1).  
   • Hence no values or predictions.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   • Not applicable (rewards not implemented).

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
   • They are told there will be “10 rounds” in part 1 and another set of 10 after the reshuffle (§3.3).  
   • Not varied; no prediction about uncertainty vs certainty of the horizon.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Yes. After each round “the contributions and payoffs of each member are communicated to all group members” (§3.1).  
   • No variation; no prediction about hiding vs showing.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
   • No. “We do not let participants see who punished whom” (§3.1).  
   • Not varied; no prediction of the alternative case.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
   • Not applicable (no rewards).

SUMMARY
————————————————————————
A. Dependent variables used  
   • The paper does NOT analyse group efficiency (total payoff / maximum payoff).  
   • Main dependent variables:  
     – Contribution level (MU or % of endowment)  
     – Punishment sent / received  
     – Group identification (Likert index)  
     – Social-norm strength (overlap in normative expectations)  
   These variables capture behaviour, sanctioning and subjective perceptions; none are identical to efficiency.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   • Mentioned: 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14  → 8 parameters.  
   • Not mentioned at all: 3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 15.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of SYSTEMATICALLY VARYING that parameter on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable)?  
   • Zero. Every mentioned parameter is fixed. No experimental or analytical variation of the 15 parameters is linked to changes in the punishment treatment effect.

D. What predictions—restricted solely to information in the paper—can be made about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency?  
   • Very limited. The study never measures efficiency and never varies any of the listed parameters, so it offers virtually no direct evidence for how changing them would amplify or dampen the efficiency impact of punishment.  
   • The only indirect hint is that anonymity of punishers (parameter 14) is said to “curb punishment driven by revenge motives,” implying that identifiable punishment could work differently—but no efficiency data are provided.  
   • Likewise, heterogeneous MPCRs (parameter 6) are described as creating divergent norms, which in turn influence how punishment is used, but again efficiency is not measured.  
   • For all other parameters the paper is silent, so no substantive prediction can be drawn from this source alone.

Hence, the paper is largely uninformative for forecasting how the 15 design parameters would modulate the effect of introducing punishment on group efficiency.

Abstract: Economic experiments have suggested that cooperative humans will altruistically match local levels of cooperation (conditional cooperation) and pay to punish non-cooperators (altruistic punishment). Evolutionary models have suggested that if altruists punish non-altruists this could favour the evolution of costly helping behaviours (cooperation) among strangers. An often-key requirement is that helping behaviours and punishing behaviours form one single conjoined trait (strong reciprocity). Previous economics experiments have provided support for the hypothesis that punishment and cooperation form one conjoined, altruistically motivated, trait. However, such a conjoined trait may be evolutionarily unstable, and previous experiments have confounded a fear of being punished with being surrounded by cooperators, two factors that could favour cooperation. Here, we experimentally decouple the fear of punishment from a cooperative environment and allow cooperation and punishment behaviour to freely separate (420 participants). We show, that if a minority of individuals is made immune to punishment, they (i) learn to stop cooperating on average despite being surrounded by high levels of cooperation, contradicting the idea of conditional cooperation and (ii) often continue to punish, 'hypocritically', showing that cooperation and punishment do not form one, altruistically motivated, linked trait.

Abstract: Social dilemmas are among the most puzzling issues in the biological and social sciences. Extensive theoretical efforts have been made in various realms such as economics, biology, mathematics, and even physics to figure out solution mechanisms to the dilemma in recent decades. Although punishment is thought to be a key mechanism, evolutionary game theory has revealed that the simplest form of punishment called peer punishment is useless to solve the dilemma, since peer punishment itself is costly. In the literature, more complex types of punishment, such as pool punishment or institutional punishment, have been exploited as effective mechanisms. So far, mechanisms that enable peer punishment to function as a solution to the social dilemma remain unclear. In this paper, we propose a theoretical way for peer punishment to work as a solution mechanism for the dilemma by incorporating prospect theory into evolutionary game theory. Prospect theory models human beings as agents that estimate small probabilities and loss of profit as greater than they actually are; thus, those agents feel that punishments are more frequent and harsher than they really are. We show that this kind of cognitive distortion makes players decide to cooperate to avoid being punished and that the cooperative state achieved by this mechanism is globally stable as well as evolutionarily stable in a wide range of parameter values.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what the paper says (and does not say) regarding each of the 15 items you listed, followed by the requested four‐part summary.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • What the paper says: The model assumes an “infinitely large, well‐mixed population.” Players are randomly paired to play a donation‐punishment (two‐player) game, but there is no variation in finite group size.  
   • Systematic variation discussed? No. The paper does not discuss changing the number of players and provides no predicted effect on any outcome from varying this parameter.

2. Number of rounds  
   • What the paper says: The analysis uses “time evolution” under the replicator equation. The text does not treat the game as a finite or known number of rounds.  
   • Systematic variation discussed? No. The paper does not vary the number of rounds, nor does it predict any effect on punishment, efficiency, or any other variable from changing the number of rounds.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • What the paper says: There is no mention of communication or chat.  
   • Systematic variation discussed? No.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • What the paper says: The paper’s “donation game” is indeed all‐or‐nothing (either cooperate [pay cost c] or defect). However, they do not treat this parameter as something that can be varied—it is simply the game’s fixed design.  
   • Systematic variation discussed? No.

5. Is the contribution “default” (do players choose an amount to pull back to themselves)?  
   • What the paper says: Not discussed. The paper uses a simple binary donation game with no partial‐contribution mechanism.  
   • Systematic variation discussed? No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters (multiplication factor)  
   • What the paper says: The paper frames it as a two‐player donation game with benefit b to the other and cost c to oneself. No mention of a “public goods” multiplication factor (MPCR).  
   • Systematic variation discussed? No.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • What the paper says: Denoted r in the model (the cost a punisher pays). The paper sets r = 1 (together with c = 1) and does not report results from systematically varying r.  
   • Systematic variation discussed? No. They fix r = 1 and do not predict the effect of varying it.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed)  
   • What the paper says: Denoted s in the paper. This parameter is central to the analysis; they do vary s in their figures and investigate whether cooperation (CN) or defection (DN) is stable, depending on s and on an error‐rate parameter ε.  
   • Systematic variation discussed for any dependent variable? Yes, but only for “stability of cooperation” versus “defection,” not for efficiency. The paper plots different regions in (ε, s/s_max) space; once s is large enough (relative to c and ε), cooperation can become stable under “prospect theory” assumptions. Numerical effect sizes are given in figures as domains of stability rather than payoffs or efficiency measures. No discussion appears about total group payoff or efficiency.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • What the paper says: Nothing. The paper focuses entirely on punishment, with no reward mechanism.  
   • Systematic variation discussed? No.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • What the paper says: Not discussed (no reward in the model).  
   • Systematic variation discussed? No.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted)  
   • What the paper says: Not discussed (no reward in the model).  
   • Systematic variation discussed? No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
   • What the paper says: They assume an infinitely repeated or “time‐evolving” setting with no mention of known endpoints.  
   • Systematic variation discussed? No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost)?  
   • What the paper says: The paper does not mention any display of payoff information to the participants.  
   • Systematic variation discussed? No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • What the paper says: Not discussed. The model is well‐mixed and does not focus on punishment visibility or anonymity.  
   • Systematic variation discussed? No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • What the paper says: Not applicable; there is no reward in the model.  
   • Systematic variation discussed? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?  
   • The paper does not use group efficiency or group total payoff as a measured dependent variable. Instead, it studies the population’s evolutionary dynamics, focusing on which strategy (cooperate‐punish [CP], cooperate‐not‐punish [CN], defect‐punish [DP], or defect‐not‐punish [DN]) becomes stable over time.  
   • “Efficiency” is not addressed. Instead, the paper’s key outcome is whether the population converges to cooperation or defection (and under what conditions).

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
     1. Number of players – They assume an infinite population, but do not vary it.  
     4. All or nothing – Yes, the paper is an all‐or‐nothing donation game by design.  
     7. Punishment cost – Denoted r, set equal to 1, but not varied.  
     8. Punishment magnitude – Denoted s, this is explicitly varied in the paper.  
   • The remaining parameters (2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15) either do not appear or are not varied.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Only one parameter is clearly and systematically varied in the analysis: punishment magnitude s (parameter 8).  
   • The paper does discuss how changing s (in conjunction with the error rate ε) alters whether the population converges to defection or cooperation. However, it does not link changes in s to any measure of efficiency or total payoff, only to the stability of one strategy over the other.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper provides no direct data or models on efficiency or total payoffs, so it offers no direct evidence for how each parameter (or their interactions) would shift “group efficiency.” Its focus is on the conditions for stable cooperation under prospect theory, rather than on aggregate payoffs.  
   • Hence, based solely on this article, there is little or no basis for predicting how the 15 parameters would affect the “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency.

Abstract: Insights from experimental psychology and economics have rarely been applied to the study of international law and never to the study of international legal theory. This article applies them to socio-legal international theory that has grosso modo two important background paradigms with several variants: rationalist and constructivist. In both paradigms, the interest in understanding and explaining international law by uncovering causal mechanisms in international cooperation and compliance and in asking how cooperation is sustained in a system as decentralized as international law is paramount. In both, fundamental assumptions regarding the behaviour of actors are made. However; regardless of the theoretical standpoint, both fall short of experimental evidence about their behavioural assumptions. The article uses experimental evidence provided by public good games as a conceptualization of how social order is constructed and upheld in systems without central authority such as international law. It aims to illuminate the behavioural basis of important building blocks of international cooperation and law by discussing the preferences of states and strategic interaction, reciprocity, sanctions, communication and trust as well as consent and legitimacy, reflecting on what the experimental insights teach us on the assumptions of rationalist and constructivist approaches to international legal theory.    • Discussion in the paper?

   • Predictions about varying this parameter?  
     None given.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     The paper discusses the importance of “communication,” “cheap talk,” and “face-to-face communication” for increasing cooperation (e.g. pp. 14–15). Nonetheless, it does not report or cite any data on systematically turning communication on vs. off, nor does it quantify the effect of communication on punishment or efficiency.  
   • Predictions about varying this parameter?  
     None given, beyond the general statement that communication is not merely “cheap talk” and fosters cooperation.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Discussion in the paper?

   • Predictions about varying this parameter?

   • Discussion in the paper?

     None.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment.  
   • Discussion in the paper?  
     The paper frequently notes that “punishment” in public good games is “costly to the punisher” (e.g. pp. 3, 10, 16). However, it does not provide or cite data on how manipulating the exact cost of punishment alters the punishment effect or efficiency.

     None.

   • Discussion in the paper?

   • Discussion in the paper?

SUMMARY (A–D)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A) Does the paper use “group efficiency” (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?

Below I go through the 15 parameters exactly in the requested order.

Numerical effect sizes are quoted whenever the paper contains them.  If the paper is silent, I say so.

------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
• Mentioned: yes – every public-goods game consisted of **4 players** (p. 6).  
• Systematic variation / prediction: none.  The group size is fixed and never compared to other sizes.

2. Number of rounds  
• Mentioned: yes – each game lasted **25 rounds** (p. 6).  
• Systematic variation / prediction: none.  Round length is constant.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
• Mentioned: ordinary free-form chat is **never allowed**.  Only in the very last tournament did two rule sets permit a *unanimous vote on a non-binding covenant*; this is not chat in the usual sense (section 3.3).  
• Systematic variation / prediction: none.  No comparison of “chat on” vs. “chat off” is made.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
• Mentioned: contributions are **continuous 0–20 tokens** (p. 6).  
• Systematic variation / prediction: none.

5. Contribution default / refund frame?  
• Not mentioned at all.

6. Marginal Per-Capita Return (MPCR)  
• Mentioned: MPCR = **0.4** (total multiplier 1.6) (p. 6).  
• Systematic variation / prediction: none.

7. Punishment cost (to the punisher)  
• Mentioned indirectly.  Each self-designed rule incurred “rule costs”, and some of those costs were tied to punishment mechanisms, but the costs differ from rule set to rule set and are never reported in a way that lets us link *cost size* to *treatment effect*.  
• Systematic variation / prediction: none.

8. Punishment magnitude (impact on target)  
• As in (7), magnitudes differ across rule sets (e.g., lowest contributor loses X tokens, redistributed to others) but are not reported in a way that lets us map larger vs. smaller magnitudes onto efficiency changes.  
• Systematic variation / prediction: none.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
• Mentioned: three rule sets contained a “big bonus” paid to the top contributor at the end (section 3.1).  
• Systematic variation / prediction: none.  The paper never isolates “punishment + reward” vs. “punishment only”.

10. Reward cost  
• Not reported.

11. Reward magnitude  
• Not reported.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
• Mentioned: yes – 25 rounds was common knowledge, but the paper never alters this.  
• Systematic variation / prediction: none.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
• Mentioned: yes.  Rule sets either  
  – revealed individual contributions (coded “ID”), or  
  – concealed them and showed only the sum (coded “noIndFB”), or  
  – in two cases hid even the sum (“noFB”).  
• Systematic variation / prediction: partially.  
  – The authors compute a “component-efficiency index”. For “noIndFB” the index is +0.091 for rule sets 1-3 and –0.040 for rule set 4 (Table 2).  
  – That index is relative efficiency, **not** a punishment-treatment effect.  The paper never reports “punishment effect conditional on feedback”, so no numerical treatment effect is available.

14. Do the punished know who punished them?  
• Peer punishment occurs only in one rule set; identity revelation is not described.  No analysis.

15. Do the rewarded know who rewarded them?  
• As above, not described; no analysis.

Summary requested in points A-D
------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables used  
• Yes, the paper explicitly uses **group efficiency** (sum of pay-offs divided by the social optimum).  
• It also reports **average contribution levels**.  Contributions and efficiency are not the same because the rule sets carry costs, so a rule can raise contributions while lowering efficiency (and vice versa).

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
Eight parameters appear:  
1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 13.  The remaining seven (5, 7, 8, 10, 11, 14, 15) are either absent or only indirectly referenced without concrete values.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* the parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
Strictly speaking, for **none**.  
• The only quantitative comparisons that resemble “systematic variation” are the component-efficiency indices for “pun” (presence vs. absence) and “noIndFB” (concealing individual feedback).  However, these indices compare whole rule sets, not a clean punishment-vs-no-punishment manipulation, so they are *not* a true punishment treatment effect in the usual sense.  No other parameter is varied in a controlled manner.

D. If one had to predict how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, relying **only** on this paper:  
• Little can be predicted with confidence. ------------------------------------------------------------------
In short, the study is exploratory and descriptive; it does not manipulate the 15 listed parameters, so it offers almost no direct guidance for predicting the *punishment treatment effect on efficiency* when those parameters change.

Throughout, please note that the paper’s main dependent variable is the fraction (or rate) of cooperators (“cooperation level”) rather than total efficiency or payoff.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned? Yes. The authors use an L×L regular lattice with L=100, so there are 10,000 players in total.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not examine what happens if the number of players changes, nor does it tie changes in the number of players to a “punishment treatment effect” (and certainly not to efficiency).

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned? Indirectly. They use discrete time steps (up to 10,000 or more) until the fraction of cooperators stabilizes, but they do not treat the “number of rounds” as a parameter to be varied.  
   • Systematically varied or predicted effect? No. They do not discuss how changing the number of rounds would alter outcomes.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned? No. There is no mention of any sort of communication or chat among players.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each player is either a cooperator (contributes 1) or a defector (contributes 0).  
   • Systematically varied or predicted effect? No. The model fixes this at 1 vs. 0 and does not investigate partial contribution or any alternative; the paper offers no predictions about varying whether contributions are all-or-nothing.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not discuss any “default contribution” mechanism. Each cooperator simply donates a fixed amount of 1.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper refers to a “synergy factor,” r, which multiplies the group’s contribution before it is evenly split.  
   • Systematically varied? Yes. Their figures vary r from about 2.5–3 up to around 4 or so, and they compare these conditions to the baseline public-goods game.  
   • Dependent variable(s) affected? They measure the fraction of cooperators (not efficiency). For example, they note that with their payoff-transfer mechanism, “global cooperation can be achieved at r=2.7,” whereas in a traditional PGG, one might need r=4.6 to see the same high level of cooperation.  
   • Numerical effect size on efficiency? Not reported. They never measure efficiency (total payoff ÷ maximum payoff). They only report how the fraction of cooperators depends on r.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned? No. In their mechanism, payoffs are automatically transferred from low-ranked (punished) to high-ranked (rewarded) individuals, and there is no explicit “cost” paid by punishers themselves.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed on them)
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does discuss that a fraction s of payoffs is transferred away from lower-ranking individuals, which functions as a “punishment,” but they do not treat it as a “per-unit-of-punishment” parameter. There is no standard “punishment magnitude” of the sort often studied in experimental public-goods games.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned? Only in the sense that high-ranking individuals automatically receive payoffs transferred from low-ranking ones (an endogenous “reward”), but they do not compare “reward enabled” vs. “reward disabled.”  
   • Systematically varied or predicted effect? No. The mechanism is always on, so there is no on/off discussion.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Mentioned? No. Because the mechanism automatically moves payoffs from low- to high-ranking individuals, there is no separate “reward cost” that a person must pay.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward granted)
   • Mentioned? No direct mention of “reward magnitude” as a cost-based parameter. While the paper does discuss what fraction of payoffs is transferred (via “transfer strength,” s), they never frame it as a “reward magnitude” akin to typical reward-institution studies and do not analyze it as such.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not describe whether players know when the game ends.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost each round)?
   • Mentioned? No. The authors do say that players’ reputation rankings are public, but there is no mention of players seeing each other’s numeric payoffs or outcomes.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Mentioned? No. There is no discussion of any punisher identity being revealed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Mentioned? No. There is no discussion of any rewarder identity being revealed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • No. The paper’s main outcome is the fraction of cooperators (sometimes called cooperation rate). It does not use efficiency = (actual total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff of a fully cooperative group) as a measured outcome.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • (1) Number of players → Mentioned but not systematically varied.  
   • (4) Is the contribution all or nothing? → Yes, it is all or nothing (1 or 0).  
   • (6) MPCR (synergy factor r) → Explicitly mentioned and systematically varied.  
   • (9) Whether a reward is enabled → In effect, there is always “reward,” but not toggled on/off.  
   • None of the others are discussed in the sense of that specific parameter, so effectively 4 of the 15 appear in some form.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Only parameter (6), the synergy factor r, is truly varied in the simulations and explicitly analyzed. However, they never discuss the effect of varying r on any “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Instead, they show how varying r changes the fraction of cooperators in the presence of their (combined) punishment-and-reward mechanism.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper, what would they be?  
   • The authors do not measure efficiency, so no direct statements can be made from their text. They do show that higher synergy factors lead to faster or more widespread cooperation, and presumably that might correlate with higher efficiency, but they never compute such an outcome. For all other parameters, there is no discussion in the paper of how systematically varying them would affect any measure of efficiency. Thus, the paper provides little to no basis for predicting how these 15 parameters (or their interactions) affect a “punishment treatment effect” specifically on efficiency.

The paper never reports group efficiency, so no efficiency effect sizes exist.

1. Number of players  
(1) Mentioned once. A square lattice of size L = 300 (therefore 90 000 players).  
(2) Not varied; no predictions.

2. Number of rounds  
(1) The evolutionary simulations run 10 000–15 000 Monte-Carlo steps; these steps are not framed as “rounds” known to the players.  
(2) Not varied; no predictions.

3. Is chat enabled?  
Not mentioned.

(1) Yes.  In every group each individual either “co-operates” by paying cost = 1 or “defects” by paying 0.  
(2) Not varied; no predictions.

5. Contribution default / endowment moved back?  
Not part of the model.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
(1) Called the “normalised amplification factor” φ = F/G, with 0 < φ < 1.  
(2) Systematically varied over the full [0,1] range (see Fig. 1, Fig. 2, Fig. 4, Fig. 6, Fig. 7).  The paper reports:

   • With punishment present (c₃ > 0.5), raising φ from 0.14 to 0.16 produces an “explosive” jump in co-operation abundance from ≈0 to ≈1 (Fig. 1).  
   • With no punishment (c₃ = 0), co-operators survive only for φ ≳ 0.4.  
   • For intermediate c₃ (0.3) the cross-section in Fig. 4 shows a step-wise pattern: at φ ≈ 0.16 the system moves from 0 co-operation to ≈0.35; at φ ≈ 0.19 it moves further to ≈0.55; full co-operation is reached only for φ ≥ 0.65.  

The paper never translates these changes into treatment-effect estimates on efficiency.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
Not modelled: the co-operator who receives compensation never pays to impose it.

(1) Posterior-compensation parameter c₃ (0 ≤ c₃ ≤ 1) is exactly the amount a defector must pay when inside an effective agreement; the same c₃ is divided among the in-agreement co-operators.  
(2) c₃ is systematically varied:

   • For every φ the surface in Fig. 1 shows how higher c₃ enlarges the co-operation region.  
   • Example from Fig. 1: at φ = 0.15, increasing c₃ from 0.45 to 0.6 raises co-operation from ≈0 to ≈1.  
   • Example from Fig. 7 (φ = 0.45): between c₃ = 0.00 and 0.04 co-operation inside agreements falls from ≈0.45 to ≈0.25; at c₃ ≈ 0.11 the system switches to almost 0 co-operation; for c₃ > 0.15 co-operation rises again, reaching ≈0.8 by c₃ = 0.3.

9. Reward enabled?  
Not present.

10. Reward cost  
Not present.

11. Reward magnitude  
Not present.

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
Not addressed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
Not addressed.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
Not addressed (there is no separate punisher).

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
Not addressed.

SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables.  
 • The paper never reports “group efficiency” (total or average payoff divided by the cooperative optimum).  
 • Two dependent variables are analysed:  
  (a) “Co-operation abundance” = fraction of players currently cooperating.  
  (b) “Effective-agreement rate” = fraction of groups whose prior agreement reaches the threshold T.  
 These differ conceptually from efficiency and from each other: (a) is a behaviour; (b) is an institutional outcome.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
 7 of them: #1, #2, #4, #6, #8, #12 (implicitly unknown), and #13–15 (implicitly absent).  
 Values are fixed for #1, #2, #4; systematically varied only for #6 (φ) and #8 (c₃).

 • Efficiency itself is never computed, so only qualitative extrapolations are possible.

   • Discussed? Yes. Each group in the experiment has eight players.

2. Number of rounds
   • Discussed? Yes. The experiment has 30 rounds total: 15 “baseline” rounds, followed by either another 15 baseline rounds or 15 ostracism‐enabled rounds.  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no treatment in which the total or partial number of rounds is systematically changed, so the paper does not forecast how altering the number of rounds would affect the punishment treatment effect.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussed? Yes, but only to say that communication was prohibited.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The study does not enable chat in any group, nor does it predict the impact of changing that rule.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussed? No. Subjects choose any integer number of “months” (0 to 8) to fish. The experiment does not force an all‐or‐nothing decision, nor does the paper mention systematically varying a binary (all‐or‐nothing) rule.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Discussed? No. There is no mention of a “default” amount contributed before players take action. The paper does not study or predict any effect of changing default rules.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Discussed? Partially. The common‐pool payoff is derived from a piecewise linear function, F(x). However, this parameter is not described as an MPCR in a public‐goods sense, and it is fixed rather than varied.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The production (payoff) function remains the same throughout. The paper does not predict how changing it would affect the punishment treatment.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussed? Indirectly. The experiment introduces a cost to the remaining group members each time a person is ostracized, ensuring that excluding someone is always costly. However, only that one cost‐level is used.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not compare different cost‐levels. Therefore, it does not predict how changing the cost would alter the punishment treatment effect.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted per unit of punishment)
   • Discussed? In effect, being punished means expulsion from the game: a subject who is ostracized earns no further payoffs in subsequent rounds. That is the “magnitude” of punishment.  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no condition in which the severity of ostracism changes. The paper does not attempt to see how the punishment effect might differ if, for instance, ostracism were shorter or less severe.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussed? No. The game is only about overfishing and/or ostracism, with no reward mechanism. The paper never mentions introducing rewards.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Discussed? No. There is no reward mechanism in the design, so the paper does not discuss possible costs of rewarding.

   • Discussed? No. Rewarding does not appear in the experiment, and the paper does not address it.

   • Systematically varied? No. The paper uses the same known‐length design; no condition involves unknown or different round counts.

   • Discussed? Partially. Each player is told how many months each other member fished in every round, and also sees who (if anyone) has been ostracized. Players do see their own payoff but the paper does not systematically vary the level of feedback provided.

   • Discussed? In effect, no. The paper notes that everyone sees the total votes cast and that excluded players learn how many votes they received, but not who voted for them.

   • Discussed? No. There is no reward condition.

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?

The paper’s main dependent variable is the amount of overfishing (the total number of “months fished” beyond the social optimum) within each group. It also tracks how many votes a participant receives, and whether certain participants are ostracized. Although the payoffs are defined mathematically, the paper does not explicitly present “group efficiency” or “total payoff / maximum possible payoff.” Put differently, it focuses on total (or average) “months fished” compared to the social optimum, rather than directly reporting efficiency.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

The experiment necessarily involves (1) a fixed number of players (eight), (2) a fixed number of rounds (30, known to participants), (3) no chat, (6) a fixed payoff function (akin to a fixed MPCR), (7)/(8) a single punishment cost and magnitude (costly ostracism), (12) a known horizon of 30 rounds, and (13) some information disclosure about group fishing levels. None. The paper implements only one change across conditions: the presence (vs. absence) of ostracism as a punishment mechanism. Consequently, no explicit “parameter‐by‐parameter” effect on punishment’s impact can be gleaned from the paper.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

The paper shows that switching from “no ostracism” to “ostracism allowed” drives actual fishing closer to the social optimum, which implies likely gains in group payoffs (and, by extension, efficiency). Because the paper does not vary any other parameters, it does not suggest how changing, say, group size, punishment costs, reward mechanisms, round length, or information disclosure might strengthen or weaken that effect. On those details, the paper remains silent, so we cannot make further predictions without going beyond what the authors have actually reported.
