Abstract: This paper investigates whether providing strong cooperation incentives only at the outset of a group interaction spills over to later periods to ensure cooperation in the long run. We study a repeated linear public-good game with punishment opportunities and a parameter change after the first ten (of twenty) rounds. Below, the 15 design parameters are taken in the order given by the user.  
For each parameter I state  

(1) whether it is mentioned in the Bruttel-Friehe paper and, if so, the exact value(s) used, and  
(2) whether the paper makes *any* prediction or empirical statement about what would happen if that parameter were *systematically varied* with respect to the “punishment treatment effect.”  
(The experiment contains punishment in every treatment, so in practice the paper never contrasts “with-punishment” versus “without-punishment”; instead it looks at how changing α or β influences contributions when punishment opportunities are present.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned: fixed groups of four.  
   (2) No systematic variation, no predictions.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Mentioned: 20 rounds; subjects knew this.  
   (2) Not varied across treatments, no predictions.

3. Chat enabled?  
   (1) Mentioned implicitly: “without the possibility of communicating.”  
   (2) Not varied, no predictions.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution decision?  
   (1) Mentioned by implication: subjects choose any integer 0-20 (continuous choice).  
   (2) Not varied, no predictions.

5. Default contribution / endowment return?  
   (1) Decision is framed as contributing out of an endowment; no default pull-back mechanism.  
   (2) Not varied, no predictions.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR, α/4)  
   (1) Central treatment variable.  
       • HIGHRETURN: α1-10 = 2 (MPCR = 0.50)  
       • BASE and LOWCOST: α1-10 = 1.2 (MPCR = 0.30)  
       • All treatments: α11-20 = 1.2 (MPCR = 0.30)  
   (2) Systematically varied. Empirical findings (Fig. 1, Table 2):  
       • Rounds 1-10: high α raises mean contribution by ≈ 8.7 points (Tobit coef., p<0.01).  
       • After α drops from 2→1.2 in round 11 the contribution advantage disappears within two rounds; by rounds 13-20 contributions are statistically indistinguishable from BASE and trend below it (interaction term –1.10 points per round, p<0.01).  
       • The paper never computes efficiency, so no efficiency effect is given.

7. Cost of imposing punishment (β)  
   (1) Central treatment variable.  
       • LOWCOST: β1-10 = 0.25; BASE & HIGHRETURN: β1-10 = 0.50  
       • All treatments: β11-20 = 0.50  
   (2) Systematically varied. Findings (Table 2, Table 4):  
       • Rounds 1-10: Lower β does *not* significantly raise contributions (+4.0 points, p≈0.28) but does increase punishment usage (+1.72 points, p≈0.07).  
       • When β rises to 0.50 in round 11, punishment falls (–1.75 points, p≈0.09) and contributions decline sharply (interaction –1.35 points per round, p<0.01).  
       • No efficiency numbers reported.

8. Punishment magnitude  
   (1) Fixed at “each point deducted lowers the target’s payoff by one point.”  
   (2) Not varied, no predictions.

9. Reward enabled  
10. Cost of reward  
11. Reward magnitude  
   (1) Rewards are *not* available; none of these parameters appear.  
   (2) No discussion or prediction.

12. Horizon known?  
   (1) Yes – subjects were told there would be exactly 20 rounds and that “a parameter might change after round 10.”  
   (2) Not varied, no predictions.

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
   (1) Yes – after Stage 1 each player sees every group member’s contribution and payoff πᵢ; after Stage 2 they also see punishment given/received and final payoff Πᵢ.  
   (2) Not varied, no predictions.

14. Punisher identity revealed?  
   (1) No – player IDs are randomly re-drawn each round “to avoid reputation formation,” so punishment is anonymous.  
   (2) Not varied, no predictions.

15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
   (1) Irrelevant (no rewards).  
   (2) Not discussed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY  

A. Dependent variables actually analysed  
   • Individual contribution to the public good (primary).  
   • Punishment points assigned/received.  
   • Beliefs about future average contributions.  
   Efficiency (total or average payoff, or payoff/max-possible-payoff) is *never* reported or analysed. Thus “efficiency” ≠ the paper’s dependent variables.

B. Parameters of the 15 that are at least mentioned: 10 (numbers 1,2,3,4,6,7,8,12,13,14).  

C. Parameters whose *systematic* variation is analysed with respect to any treatment effect: 2 (MPCR α and punishment cost β). Even for these, the outcomes reported are contributions and punishment, not efficiency.

D. What can be predicted—solely from this paper—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the *punishment treatment effect on efficiency*? Very little, because (i) efficiency is not measured, and (ii) there is no treatment without punishment to generate a “punishment effect.” Tentative inferences if one were forced to translate the contribution results into efficiency terms:  
   • A higher MPCR (α) in the presence of punishment boosts efficiency while it lasts but may lead to *lower* post-change efficiency because contributions crash and punishing still costs resources.  
   • Lower punishment cost initially creates more punishment but not higher contributions; once the cost rises, both punishment and contributions fall, so efficiency is likely worse than the constant-cost baseline.  
   • No evidence is provided for any of the other 13 parameters; therefore no prediction can be made on efficiency effects tied to them.

In short: only α and β are studied; their influence is documented for contributions and punishment, not for efficiency, and no parameter is linked to a “punishment vs. no-punishment” contrast within the paper.

Author Full Names: Zhao, Shanshan; Pan, Qiuhui; Zhu, Wenqiang; He, Mingfeng
Article Title: How punishing evil and promoting good promotes cooperation in social dilemma
Author Keywords: Punishing evil and promoting good strategy; Replicator dynamics equation; Social dilemma; Well-mixed population; Cooperation evolutionary
Keywords Plus: PUNISHMENT; EVOLUTION; DYNAMICS
Abstract: In this paper, based on the social dilemma model, we introduce the punishing evil and promoting good strategy, whose basic strategy is to cooperate, while to obtain benefits at the cost of payment. Specifically, when the person who punishes evil and promotes good plays a game with the cooperator, his contributions will bring the same benefits to both parties, reflecting the promoting good. However, when the person who punishes evil and promotes good plays a game with the defector, making the benefit of the defector loss and become his own benefit, reflecting the punishing evil. The results show that when only the role of punishing evil is considered, increasing punishment strength can easily make those punishing evil and promoting good and ordinary cooperators appear. But only increasing the punishment is not enough to weed out the defectors. When only the effect of promoting good is considered, under a smaller temptation to defection, the increase of the reward strength can transform the system from a full defection state to a full coop-eration state. Whereas when the temptation is greater, the increase in the reward is not enough for the cooperator to survive and only defectors exist in the system at this time. In addition, there exist combinations of minimum values of punishment and reward that bring the system to a defector-free state. In conclusion, our study finds effective intervals for promoting the development of those who punish evil and promote good and ordinary cooperators, respectively.(c) 2022 Elsevier Inc. 6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   • Closest analogue is the “temptation to defect” parameter b (1 < b ≤ 2).  
     Values used: b = 1.2, 1.4, 1.6, 1.8 in Figs. 2–7; varied continuously in stability analysis.  
   • Systematic variation?  Yes – the paper plots how changing b alters the fractions of each strategy *under given punishment or reward levels*.  However, it never calculates efficiency and never contrasts “punishment” vs “no-punishment” payoffs, so no punishment-treatment effect on efficiency is reported.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   • Cost is the fixed “payment” γ paid by the SC (punish-and-reward) player.  γ is set to 0.2 in all numerical simulations; the analytical section lets 0 ≤ γ ≤ 1.  
   • Systematic variation?  Only indirectly in the analytical stability conditions; all simulations keep γ fixed, so no treatment-effect curve is given.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine per unit)  
   • Parameter α₂ (0 ≤ α₂ ≤ 1).  Simulations use α₂ = 0 … 1; specific vertical slices at 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 (Figs. 3 & 6) and heat-maps (Fig. 7).  
   • Systematic variation?  Yes, but only on the **fractions of strategies**.  No efficiency or treatment-effect numbers are provided.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Yes – cases with α₁>0 (reward) vs α₁=0 (no reward) are analysed.  
   • Systematic variation?  α₁ is swept from 0 to 1, again only for strategy-fractions, not efficiency.

10. Reward cost per unit  
    • Same fixed γ (=0.2 in simulations).  Not varied.

11. Reward magnitude (bonus per unit)  
    • Parameter α₁ (0 ≤ α₁ ≤ 1), varied exactly as described for parameter 9.

12. Horizon known (do players know the last round)?  
    • Not discussed.

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
    • Not discussed.

14. Punished player knows the identity of the punisher?  
    • Not discussed.

15. Rewarded player knows the identity of the rewarder?  
    • Not discussed.



--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables actually used  
   • The paper follows deterministic replicator dynamics and reports:  
     – x, y, z: population shares of the three strategies (SC, C, D).  
   • “Efficiency”, “total payoff” or “average group payoff” never appears as an outcome variable.  All figures and tables plot strategy frequencies only.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   – Mentioned in some form: 6 (b), 7 (γ), 8 (α₂), 9 (reward on/off), 10 (γ again), 11 (α₁).  
   – Not mentioned at all: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 12, 13, 14, 15.  
   Total mentioned: 6 / 15.

C. For how many parameters does the paper *systematically vary* them and link that variation to any punishment-treatment effect?  
   – None for efficiency (because efficiency is never examined).  
   – For other outcomes (strategy shares) the paper systematically varies 6 (b), 8 (α₂), and 11 (α₁).  
   Count relative to efficiency: 0 / 15.  
   Count relative to *any* outcome: 3 / 15.

D. Predictions one could plausibly make—strictly from this paper—about the parameters’ impact on the punishment treatment effect on **efficiency**  
   • The paper gives no efficiency numbers, no baseline (no-punishment) vs punishment comparison, and thus no quantitative or qualitative link to efficiency.  
   • Therefore, based solely on the paper, almost no prediction can be made for any of the 15 parameters or their interactions with respect to efficiency.  At best one might conjecture that higher α₂ or α₁ (when γ is moderate) would raise cooperation and thereby *could* raise efficiency, but that remains unexplored in the text.  Consequently, predictions must be classed as “cannot say” for all 15 parameters.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
BOTTOM LINE  
The article studies how reward strength (α₁), punishment strength (α₂), temptation (b) and cost (γ) move the *fractions* of three strategy types within a replicator-dynamics model.  It never measures group efficiency, never contrasts a punishment treatment with a no-punishment baseline, and never addresses the majority of the 15 laboratory design parameters listed in the prompt.

Article Title: Static and dynamic underinvestment: An experimental investigation

Abstract: In this paper, we analyze a stylized version of an environment with public goods, dynamic linkages, and legislative bargaining. Our theoretical framework studies the provision of a durable public good as a modified two-period version of Battaglini et al. (2012). The experimental design allows us to disentangle inefficiencies that would result in a one-shot world (static inefficiencies) from additional inefficiencies that emerge in an environment in which decisions in the present affect future periods (dynamic inefficiencies). The quantitative predictions of the bargaining model with respect to the share of dynamic inefficiencies are closest to the data when dynamic linkages are high. To the extent that behavior is different from the model's predictions, a systematic pattern emerges namely, the use of strategic cooperation, whereby groups increase the efficiency of current proposals by selectively punishing, in future proposals, individuals who propose highly inefficient allocations. Below I walk through each of the 15 requested design parameters and relate them to what is (and is not) contained in Agranov et al. (2016).  I keep strictly to the information in the paper.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  All committees have n = 3 members.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Any link to a punishment treatment effect? No punishment exists.

2. Number of rounds (within a game)  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  Each “match’’ lasts exactly two periods; subjects play ten independent matches.  
   • Varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not applicable.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned? No.  There is no in-game communication channel reported.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Mentioned? Implicitly no.  Players can choose any split of the 200-token budget between private and public allocations.  
   • Varied? No.  
   • Relation to punishment? Not discussed.

5. Endowment-return (“contribution default”) framing  
   • Mentioned? No.  The task is framed as allocating a budget, not as moving money back to self.  No default mechanism is reported.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  Public-good utility is u(g)=5√g, so the marginal return is diminishing; there is no constant MPCR.  
   • Varied? No (A=5, α=½ fixed).  
   • Punishment effect? Not discussed.

7. Punishment cost per unit  
8. Punishment magnitude per unit  
   • Mentioned? Not at all.  The experiment contains no punishment stage.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   • Mentioned? No.  No reward stage exists.

12. Is the horizon known?  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  Subjects are explicitly told the game lasts two periods.  
   • Varied? No.  No punishment linkage discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Mentioned? Yes (p. 17—the full history of allocations and votes is continuously visible on screen).  
   • Varied? No.  No punishment analysis.

14. Are punishers identified?  
15. Are rewarders identified?  
   • Not applicable; no punishment or reward mechanism is present.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Does the paper use **group efficiency** as a dependent variable?  
   • It talks repeatedly about “inefficiencies’’—static, dynamic, total—defined as the gap between actual investment (or welfare) and the planner’s optimum.  
   • Dependent variables actually analysed:  
     – Public investment in period 1 and period 2 (in % of budget)  
     – Welfare measure W (aggregate pay-off above a no-investment baseline)  
   • These are differences from optimum, not the ratio “actual / maximum”.  
   • No other dependent variable (e.g., punishment frequency) is used.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are explicitly mentioned? 6 of them  
   1, 2, 4, 6, 12, 13.  
   (Parameters 3, 5, 7-11, 14, 15 are never mentioned.)

C. For how many parameters does the paper study **systematic variation of the parameter on the punishment treatment effect** (for any dependent variable)?  
   • Zero.  There is no punishment treatment in the paper.

D. Predictions one could make—using only this paper—about how the 15 parameters (and interactions) would influence a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency’’:  
   • The paper offers no empirical or theoretical material on punishment, punishment costs, or how any design factor moderates a punishment-induced change in efficiency.  
   • Consequently, the only safe prediction is: “no clear prediction can be made from this paper alone.”  Any substantive conjecture would require evidence outside the paper’s scope.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
In short, Agranov et al. (2016) is a study of dynamic versus static under-investment in a bargaining environment with no punishment or reward functionality.  None of the 15 listed parameters is analysed in relation to a punishment treatment effect, and the paper provides no numerical effect sizes that could be transferred to such a question.

Below, each of the fifteen design parameters is treated in turn.  For every parameter I report   
(1) whether the paper even refers to it and, if so, the values used, and   
(2) whether the paper makes any prediction about the *systematic* effect of changing that parameter on **the punishment treatment effect** (in the sense of “difference between a game with and without punishment’’).  When the paper instead reports results for some *other* dependent variable (e.g., lower bounds on the discount factor, number of defectors, contact-rate φ, etc.) I note that explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1. Number of players  
  (1) Yes.  The model has N=2n ≥ 4 agents.  Fig. 1 traces the lower-bound β* for N = 4, 20, 40.  
  (2) The paper shows that the lower bound on the discount factor β* needed to sustain grim-trigger cooperation rises with N (Proposition 1, Fig. 1).  This is **not** a treatment-effect estimate; the baseline “no-punishment’’ game is never analysed, and no efficiency numbers are reported.

2. Number of rounds  
  (1) Indirectly.  The horizon is *indefinite* (infinite repetition with continuation probability β).  
  (2) No systematic comparison across horizons; no treatment effect.

3. Is chat enabled?  
  (1) Not mentioned.  
  (2) No effect reported.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
  (1) Not mentioned (the stage game is a binary Prisoner’s Dilemma with C or D).  
  (2) No effect reported.

5. “Contribution default’’ formulation  
  (1) Not applicable; not discussed.  
  (2) No effect reported.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
  (1) Not used.  The stage-game payoffs are written generically as (c,d,g,l).  
  (2) No effect reported.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
  (1) Not part of the model.  Agents punish simply by switching to D, which has no parameterised monetary cost beyond the usual payoff structure.  
  (2) No effect reported.

8. Punishment magnitude on the target  
  (1) Not parameterised.  The loss to the punished player is whatever results from being defected against.  
  (2) No effect reported.

9-11. Reward availability / reward cost / reward magnitude  
  Not modelled; no discussion.

12. Whether the number of rounds is known  
  (1) Indefinite horizon assumed; players never know when the game ends.  
  (2) No comparison with a finite-known horizon; hence no treatment effect.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  (Observability of others’ actions/payoffs)  
  (1) Partially.  Players always see the action of their match partner and, with probability parameterised by a = 0…N-2, also see a other randomly chosen agents’ *actions* (not payoffs).  
  (2) Corollary 1 & 2: increasing a lowers both  
      • the β-threshold needed for cooperation (β(a) ≤ β*)  
      • the minimum off-equilibrium cooperation cost l(β,k; a).  
     These are predictions about equilibrium *in the punishment regime itself*, not about a treatment effect vs. a no-punishment baseline.  No numeric efficiency changes are given.

14. Victim knows who punished?  
  (1) No.  Agents are anonymous; identities are unobservable.  
  (2) No effect reported.

15. Victim knows who rewarded?  
  (1) No (rewards absent).  
  (2) No effect reported.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used  
   – The paper does *not* report group efficiency (total-payoff ÷ maximum possible).  
   – Main dependent objects are: continuation payoffs v_k, contact rate φ_k, the number of defectors k, and lower bounds on β and l that make grim-trigger obeyed.  These are incentive-compatibility statistics, not efficiency measures.

B. Which of the 15 parameters appear at all?  
   2 parameters clearly appear:  
   • # 1 Number of players N  
   • # 13 Observability (a) – loosely maps onto “peer outcomes shown’’  
   The remaining 13 parameters are absent.

C. For how many parameters does the paper give predictions under systematic variation?  
   2 parameters (N and a).  Even there, the predictions concern equilibrium-sustaining bounds (β*, l) rather than the *punishment treatment effect* on efficiency or contributions.

D. What can be predicted—solely from this paper—about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
   • Larger N makes it *harder* to sustain punishment-supported cooperation (β* goes up), so if one could compare to a no-punishment baseline, one would expect the efficiency gain from adding punishment to *fall* with N.  
   • Greater observability a makes cooperation easier (β* and l thresholds fall).  Hence the efficiency gain from adding punishment would *rise* with a.  
   • For all other parameters the paper is silent; no prediction can be made.  In particular, nothing is said about monetary stakes (MPCR), explicit punishment/reward prices or magnitudes, chatting, finite horizons, or identification of punishers/rewarders.

Beyond these two qualitative statements, the paper offers no quantitative estimates of how any of the 15 parameters would change *efficiency* when a punishment option is introduced.
reference_APA: Camera, Gabriele & Gioffre, Alessandro (2014). A tractable analysis of contagious equilibria. JOURNAL OF MATHEMATICAL ECONOMICS.

Authors: Schlaepfer, A
Author Full Names: Schlaepfer, Alain
Article Title: The emergence and selection of reputation systems that drive cooperative behaviour
Source Title: PROCEEDINGS OF THE ROYAL SOCIETY B-BIOLOGICAL SCIENCES
Author Keywords: evolution of cooperation; indirect reciprocity; reputation; punishment
Keywords Plus: INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; COSTLY PUNISHMENT; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; REPEATED GAMES; EVOLUTION; GOSSIP; INFORMATION; SOCIETIES; HUMANS
Abstract: Reputational concerns are believed to play a crucial role in explaining cooperative behaviour among non-kin humans. Individuals cooperate to avoid a negative social image, if being branded as defector reduces pay-offs from future interactions. Similarly, individuals sanction defectors to gain a reputation as punisher, prompting future co-players to cooperate. But reputation can only effectively support cooperation if a sufficient number of individuals condition their strategies on their co-players' reputation, and if a sufficient number of group members are willing to record and transmit the relevant information about past actions. Using computer simulations, this paper argues that starting from a pool of non-cooperative individuals, a reputation system based on punishment is likely to emerge and to be the driver of the initial evolution of cooperative behaviour. However, once cooperation is established in a group, it will be sustained mainly through a reputation mechanism based on cooperative actions.

Below I walk through the 15 public-goods‐game parameters one by one, stating exactly what the Schlaepfer (2018) paper says (or does not say) about each parameter and, when possible, whether the paper reports how *systematically varying* that parameter changes any “punishment treatment effect.”  I keep the wording as close as possible to the paper and cite the relevant part of the text, figures or tables when available.

------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1. Number of players (group size)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Table 1 lists N = 100 as the “size of generation.”  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  All simulations reported in the main text keep N = 100, and no figure/table reports results for alternative N.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  None reported.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  Partly.  The model fixes an *expected* number of lifetime interactions m = 30 (Table 1).  
   • Systematically varied?  Yes, but only in the electronic supplementary figure (“Figure 1 in the electronic supplementary material … varying … group size (m)”).  No numerical values are given in the main paper.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  Not discussed; only overall cooperation rates are plotted, and no efficiency numbers or treatment-effect estimates are presented.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned?  No.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  First-stage choice is binary: “contribute y or defect” (Methods §2).  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  Not discussed.

5. Contribution default (reversing the action frame)?  
   • Mentioned?  No.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Parameter r (public-good multiplier) = 1.6 in Table 1.  
   • Systematically varied?  Yes (supplementary figure varies r).  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  The paper only says that the qualitative ranking of cooperation rates (pun-rep > both-rep > coop-rep) “holds across all parametrizations.” No efficiency or treatment-effect numbers are reported.

7. Punishment cost (to punisher)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  k = 0.2 (Table 1).  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  Not reported.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss to target)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  p = 0.5 (Table 1).  
   • Systematically varied?  Yes (supplementary figure varies p).  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  Not quantified; only cooperation rates are plotted.

9. Is a reward option available?  
   • Mentioned?  No.

10. Reward cost  
   • Mentioned?  No.

11. Reward magnitude  
   • Mentioned?  No.

12. Are players told the number of rounds?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes—implicitly.  The model assumes “individuals … may condition their strategies on their opponent’s reputation, but not on the number of interactions that have occurred within a generation, since the latter is unknown.”  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  Not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown each round?  
   • Mentioned?  Not directly.  Instead the paper studies whether reputation information can be *bought* at cost ρ and spread through a gossip channel γ.  No explicit statement about showing others’ pay-offs.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  Not reported.

14. When a player is punished, do they learn who punished them?  
   • Mentioned?  No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they learn who rewarded them?  
   • Mentioned?  No.

------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used in the paper  
   • The main outcome is the *share of cooperative acts* (Figures 1, 3).  
   • Additional outcomes: share of players using a given reputation type (Figures 2, 3, 4) and frequency of punishment types (Table 2).  
   • *Efficiency* (group pay-off / maximum) is **not** reported anywhere.

B. Parameters from the user’s list that the paper explicitly mentions: 6 of 15  
   (1) number of players, (2) number of rounds/interactions, (4) all-or-nothing contribution, (6) MPCR, (7) punishment cost, (8) punishment magnitude.

C. Parameters whose *systematic variation* is analysed: 3 of 15  
   (2) number of rounds/interactions (m) – only in supplementary figure,  
   (6) MPCR (r) – supplementary figure,  
   (8) punishment magnitude (p) – supplementary figure.  
   Even for those three, the paper only plots overall cooperation rates; it never computes a punishment-treatment effect on efficiency (or on any variable).

D. Predictions that can be made for the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency *solely* from this paper  
   • Very little can be said.  The study never removes punishment altogether, so no “with-punishment vs. no-punishment” contrast—and therefore no treatment effect—can be extracted.  
   • The strongest qualitative takeaway is that *allowing players to build punishment-based reputations* raises cooperation relative to a setting where only cooperation-based reputations exist.  If higher cooperation translated one-for-one into higher efficiency (an assumption not tested), then giving access to punishment-based reputation should improve efficiency.  
   • Changes in MPCR (r), punishment severity (p) and expected number of interactions (m) do not reverse that qualitative ordering, but the paper provides no numbers that allow one to predict the *magnitude* of any efficiency change.  
   • For the remaining 12 parameters the paper says nothing that would let us predict their effect (or interaction effects) on efficiency.

In short, the paper is informative about how reputation spreads and how that affects the *rate of cooperation*, but it does **not** report group efficiency and it never isolates a “punishment treatment effect.” Consequently, the paper offers almost no direct leverage for forecasting how the 15 experimental design parameters will influence the efficiency impact of introducing punishment in a standard public-goods game.
reference_APA: Schlaepfer, Alain (2018). The emergence and selection of reputation systems that drive cooperative behaviour. PROCEEDINGS OF THE ROYAL SOCIETY B-BIOLOGICAL SCIENCES.

Authors: Vasconcelos, VV; Dannenberg, A; Levin, SA
Author Full Names: Vasconcelos, Vitor V.; Dannenberg, Astrid; Levin, Simon A.
Article Title: Punishment institutions selected and sustained through voting and learning
Keywords Plus: COSTLY PUNISHMENT; COLLECTIVE ACTION; COOPERATION; RECIPROCITY; GOVERNANCE
Abstract: In virtually all human societies, the sustained provision of public goods is enforced through punishment. This can happen, for example, via a legal system (formal punishment institutions) or individual-level reciprocity (informal punishment institutions). However, targeting and enforcement of punishment is usually costly, leaving a permanent temptation for individuals to avoid the costs. Here, we show that costly punishment institutions can be adopted through voting and learning but suffer an existential threat if the decision-making process to implement the punishment institution is not aligned with the scale of the public good, creating unavoidable free-riding incentives. We design a model where individuals vote in favour of or against the institution, either with their feet or group vote, to govern public goods at different scales. Learning occurs through the accumulation of one's experiences and observations of other members in the population, but it may be limited due to memory and information constraints. We show-across scales of the decision-making process and public good-under which conditions punishment institutions are adopted and promote cooperation. Using a meta-study approach, we compare the model to existing experimental results, which largely confirm the key results of the model.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter inventory based strictly on the contents of the paper. “Discussed” means the paper explicitly mentions the parameter in its model or in the experiments it reviews. “Systematically varied” means the paper reports how changing that parameter (and that parameter alone) alters the effect of punishment (of any kind) on outcomes in the model or experiments. All references to “effects” below refer to what the paper itself reports; no extrapolations or outside findings are added.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1) Number of players  
• Discussed? Yes. The paper’s model has a population of size Z in which groups of size n ≤ Z play the public‐goods game (e.g., n = 5 and Z = 100 in local scenarios, or n = Z in global scenarios).  
• Systematically varied for a punishment‐treatment effect? No. Although the model allows for different n and Z, the main text holds n and Z fixed in examples (n = 5, Z = 100 for local scenarios; n = Z in global scenarios) and does not report how varying n or Z alone affects punishment or efficiency.

2) Number of rounds  
• Discussed? Yes, insofar as the paper simulates a repeated game (e.g., “5 × 10^4 generations”), and the experiments in the meta‐study also use repeated settings.  
• Systematically varied for a punishment‐treatment effect? No. The paper does not systematically change the number of rounds or generations to see how that alters punishment’s impact.

3) Is chat (communication) enabled between players?  
• Discussed? No. There is no mention of any chat or explicit messaging among players in either the model or the experiments surveyed.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Discussed? Yes. In the model, individuals “either cooperate, C, by contributing a fixed amount c, or defect, D, by contributing nothing.” That is effectively an all‐or‐nothing contribution.  
• Systematically varied for a punishment‐treatment effect? No. The paper does not report any scenario with partial‐contribution choices.

5) Is the contribution “default” (do players decide how much of their endowment to keep vs. give)?  
• Discussed? No. The paper describes only a strict contribute‐or‐not choice. There is no mention of any variable default contribution.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
• Discussed? Yes. The model repeatedly uses “F/n” as the per‐capita multiplier on contributions (they set F/n = 0.5 in their main simulations).  
• Systematically varied for a punishment‐treatment effect? Not in the main text. They note in passing (Methods and Supplementary) that they can vary F or F/n, but the main text holds it fixed and does not present systematic variation or effect sizes.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Discussed? Partly. In this paper’s model, punishers pay a membership fee cI to join the institution rather than a per‐unit punishment fee. There is no separate, incremental “cost per unit punished.”  
• Systematically varied for a punishment‐treatment effect? No. The membership cost cI is mentioned but is held fixed, and the paper does not report systematic effects of varying it.

8) Punishment magnitude (the amount deducted from a punished player)  
• Discussed? Yes, effectively via the parameter FΙ (sometimes written F1). Defectors in the institution are “impaired” proportionally to FΙ times the summed membership fee.  
• Systematically varied for a punishment‐treatment effect? No. They generally set FΙ = 5 in the main examples and do not show how changing FΙ alone shifts outcomes.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
• Discussed? No. The paper treats only punishment institutions. Rewards do not appear.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Discussed? No (same reason as #9).

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)  
• Discussed? No (same reason as #9).

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
• Discussed? No. The paper does not say whether participants (in model or experiments) know how many rounds there will be.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (i.e., do players learn how much others gained/lost)?  
• Discussed? Yes, the paper explicitly contrasts “local information” (players observe only their own group) versus “global information” (players also see interactions they did not participate in).  
• Systematically varied for a punishment‐treatment effect? Yes, they do compare local‐ vs. global‐information conditions and show how that changes the fraction of people who cooperate and/or adopt the institution. However, the paper does not provide a numerical “efficiency effect size”; rather, the outcome reported is whether the institution is adopted and the resulting cooperation levels.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• Discussed? No. Punishment is modeled as an institution enforcing fines collectively, so the paper does not mention identifying an individual punisher.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
• Discussed? No. The model and experiments reviewed do not involve rewards or rewarders.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary of Key Points

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?  
   • The main outcomes in the paper’s model are (i) whether punishment institutions are adopted (the fraction of individuals choosing or voting for them) and (ii) cooperation rates (who contributes vs. defects). Although individual payoffs enter the agents’ learning, the paper’s figures and main results focus on cooperation levels and institutional adoption rather than on “efficiency” in the sense of total payoff divided by the maximum possible. Hence “efficiency,” as the user defines it, is not a main reported dependent variable in the paper.

B) Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
     (1) Number of players (n, Z), (2) Number of rounds (implicit as repeated), (4) All‐or‐nothing contributions, (6) MPCR (F/n), (7) Punishment “cost” (though modeled as a membership fee cI), (8) Punishment magnitude (FΙ), and (13) Peer outcomes shown (local vs. global information).  
   • Not mentioned or not relevant:  
     (3), (5), (9), (10), (11), (12), (14), (15).  

C) For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • In the main text (Figures 2 and 3), the paper systematically varies “information display” (local vs. global) and “memory length,” neither of which directly appears on the 15‐item list (they are not exactly the same as #13, though they overlap with it). Of the user’s 15 parameters, only #13 (information display to peers) clearly maps onto the paper’s local‐ vs. global‐information distinction, and that is varied systematically. The reported effect is on cooperation and institution adoption, not on “efficiency.”  
   • The other parameters are mentioned but either held fixed or not systematically varied with respect to punishment’s effect on outcomes. No numerical effect sizes on “efficiency” or on “punishment treatment effect” are given for any of the 15 parameters.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper’s focus is on whether (and under which conditions) punishment institutions become established and spur cooperation, not on how varying each parameter changes net efficiency. Because the paper does not quantify “efficiency” as total/maximum payoff, there is little to no direct basis here for predicting how those 15 parameters (e.g., group size, number of rounds, punishment cost, etc.) would affect efficiency.  
   • The only systematic variation directly addressed is local‐ vs. global‐information availability (#13). Even in that case, the paper’s results are framed in terms of sustained cooperation and adoption of the institution, rather than the ratio of actual total payoff to maximum possible payoff. Thus, the paper provides almost no explicit predictions for efficiency effects under each parameter.

Author Full Names: Pan, Xiaofei; Houser, Daniel
Article Title: Why trust out-groups? The role of punishment under uncertainty
Author Keywords: Group identity; Trust; Punishment; Belief; Uncertainty
Keywords Plus: COOPERATION; ECONOMICS; IDENTITY; SANCTIONS; BIAS
Abstract: We conducted a hidden-effort trust game, in which we assigned subjects to one of two groups. The groups, which were formed through two different group formation processes, included a social group that required sharing and exchange among its members, and a non-social group that did not. Once assigned, subjects participated in the game with members from both groups, either with or without the opportunity to punish a trustee who may have defected on them. We found that for investors in the non-social group, the opportunity to punish a trustee worked to promote trust, but only when the trustee was a member of the other group. For the social group, the opportunity to punish had no effect on the investors' trust decisions, regardless of the trustee's group. We provide a theoretical framework to explain this asymmetric effect of punishment on trust. Our results suggest that groups with identities founded in sharing and exchange-a feature of globalized societies may find it less necessary to engage in costly punishment. As a result, they may enjoy gains in economic efficiency. (C) 2018 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

   • Mentioned: Yes. Cost = 0 (the investor can cut 6 units from B “at no cost to herself”).  
   • Systematic variation / predictions: No. Cost is fixed; the paper never studies other cost levels. It only compares “punishment possible (cost = 0)” vs. “punishment impossible”.

8. Punishment magnitude (tokens lost by the target per unit)  
   • Mentioned: Yes. Magnitude = 6.  
   • Systematic variation / predictions: No.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned: Yes—rewarding is **not** available.  
   • Systematic variation / predictions: No.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   • Not applicable (no reward option).

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
   • Mentioned: Yes. Subjects are told there are exactly two periods.  
   • Systematic variation / predictions: None.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Mentioned indirectly: Investors observe their own payoff but never observe the trustee’s action; trustees do not learn the investor’s reduction decision until payment. No cross-sectional feedback is provided.  
   • Systematic variation / predictions: None.

14. Do punished players learn the punisher’s identity?  
   • Not reported. No variation or prediction.

15. Do rewarded players learn the rewarder’s identity?  
   • Not applicable (no reward).

Effect sizes actually reported (not “systematic” variations of the parameter but a switch from “punishment impossible” to “punishment possible”)

• For Non-social investors facing out-group trustees, allowing cost-free punishment raises the trust rate from 0.29 to 0.56 (Table 2, Fig. 4; Δ ≈ +0.27).  
• No statistically significant change in any other investor–partner pairing.  
• The study does not compute efficiency (total earnings / maximum possible), so no efficiency effect is reported.

========================================================
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used  
   – Trust (binary choice IN vs. OUT)  
   – Reciprocity (trustee’s choice ROLL vs. DON’T ROLL)  
   – Punishment frequency (whether investor deducts 6)  
   – Beliefs (elicited expectations)  
   The paper never presents group efficiency, total payoff, or average payoff as an outcome, although the abstract talks loosely about “gains in economic efficiency”.

B. Parameters from the 15-item list that are at least mentioned: 6 of 15 (1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 12).  

C. Parameters whose **systematic variation** is analysed with respect to the punishment treatment effect: strictly speaking, none. The only “variation” is whether punishment is prohibited or allowed (cost = 0, magnitude = 6). No parameter is studied at more than one value.

D. What can we say—solely from this paper—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?

• The paper’s only clear finding is that introducing a cost-free, moderate-severity punishment option can raise trust (and hence would tend to raise efficiency) **only** when (i) the group size is two, (ii) punishment is free to the punisher, (iii) magnitude is 6, and (iv) the investor belongs to a “Non-social” identity group and the trustee to the out-group.  
• Because no other parameter was varied, the paper provides essentially **no information** on how changing the number of players, round length, communication, contribution rules, punishment cost, punishment severity, rewards, information disclosure, or identity revelation would modify the efficiency impact of punishment. Any prediction about those factors would have to come from other sources, not from this paper.

Abstract: Both experimental and theoretical studies have shown that punishment plays an important role in promoting cooperation. Various forms of punishment are proposed to explain why costly punishment could be maintained in the population and stabilize cooperation. Here we consider an altruistic behavior that cooperators perform cooperation and punishment simultaneously and share the punishment cost. We investigate the role of punishment cost shared among cooperators in the evolution of cooperation in public goods game. We show that the punishment can promote and stabilize cooperation when the penalty imposed on defectors is large enough compared to the punishment cost incurred by cooperators in well mixed populations. In structured populations, cooperation could emerge under lower fine threshold and coexist with defection. However, as the penalty increases, cooperation will have a larger basin of attraction in the well-mixed population than that in the structured population. Our analytical and simulated results indicate that punishment indeed can effectively promote the evolution of cooperation. We also find that population structure can promote the coexistence of cooperation and defection but not always be beneficial to cooperation. (C) 2019 Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved.

Below I go through the fifteen parameters one by one, extracting only what is written or shown in Wang & Lv (2019).  For every parameter I (1) note whether it appears in the model, figures or tables and, if so, its value(s), and (2) state whether the paper says anything about what **happens when that parameter is systematically varied** with respect to the “punishment-treatment effect” (i.e., the difference between a game with punishment and a game without punishment).  When the paper analyses some other dependent variable (most often the equilibrium fraction of cooperators) I point that out explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players in the group (N)
   1) Mentioned: Yes.  It is a core variable in the analytical model (group size N ≥ 2).  Empirical illustrations use N = 5, 10 (Figs. 1–3) and N = 10 000 for simulations on networks (Fig. 6).
   2) Systematic variation: Yes.  
      •  In the well-mixed analysis, the stability threshold for cooperation is
            β > 1 + α – r/N  (full cooperation stable)  
            β < 1 + α/N – r/N  (full defection stable).  
         Thus, as N increases the cooperative region shrinks (Fig. 4).  
      •  Figs. 1–3 compare N = 5 vs. 10 and show that larger N accelerates fixation at full defection when parameters are such that defection is ultimately stable, and slows fixation at full cooperation when cooperation is ultimately stable.  
      •  No “punishment vs. no-punishment” comparison is provided, only the dynamics **with** punishment, so no numerical “treatment effect” on efficiency can be extracted.

2. Number of rounds  
   1) Not mentioned (the model is an infinite-time evolutionary process).  
   2) No discussion.

3. Chat enabled?  
   1) Not mentioned.  
   2) No discussion.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   1) Yes.  Players choose “Cooperate” (contribute cost c = 1) or “Defect” (contribute 0).  The paper does not vary this rule.  
   2) No systematic variation.

5. Contribution default / endowment pulled back?  
   1) Not mentioned.  
   2) No discussion.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor (r)  
   1) Mentioned.  r appears in all payoff formulas.  Numerical illustrations use r = 1.5, while the algebra keeps r as a symbol (1 < r < N).  
   2) Although r is an explicit parameter in the analytical threshold expressions above, the paper does not present figures or tables in which r is systematically varied.  Therefore no quantitative prediction of how varying r changes the punishment treatment effect is supplied.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit (α)  
   1) Mentioned.  α is the *total* punishment cost that is shared equally by cooperators (each pays α/n_c).  Values used include α = 0.4, 0.5, 0.6 (Fig. 2b, Fig. 6).  
   2) Systematic variation: Yes.  
      •  From Fig. 4 and the threshold conditions, increasing α shifts both boundary surfaces upward, reducing the parameter space where cooperation is stable and enlarging the region where defection is stable.  
      •  Fig. 2b (two α values) and Fig. 6 (α on the horizontal axis) show that higher α lowers the equilibrium frequency of cooperators.  
      •  Again, no baseline “no-punishment” condition is analysed, so the paper does not report a punishment-treatment effect on efficiency.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine β)  
   1) Mentioned.  β is the fixed fine each defector pays.  Values range from β ≈ 0.7 to 1.5 in the figures; Fig. 5 and Fig. 6 sweep β widely.  
   2) Systematic variation: Yes.  
      •  Higher β enlarges the cooperative basin and ultimately guarantees full cooperation once β > 1 + α – r/N (Fig. 3, Fig. 4).  
      •  Fig. 5 compares well-mixed vs. structured populations as β varies.  
      •  Fig. 6 shows cooperation levels increasing monotonically with β across several networks.  
      •  No efficiency-based treatment effect is reported.

9. Reward enabled?  
10. Reward cost?  
11. Reward magnitude?  
   For all three: 1) Not in the model. 2) No discussion.

12. Number of rounds known to players?  
13. Peer outcomes shown?  
14. Punisher identity revealed?  
15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
   For all four information/display variables: 1) Not in the model. 2) No discussion.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Does the paper use *efficiency* (total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
    No.  The dependent variable throughout is the *frequency of cooperators* (or, equivalently, the evolutionary equilibrium of strategies).  Payoffs are used only to drive evolutionary dynamics; they are not analysed as outcomes in their own right.  Therefore “efficiency” is never reported.

B.  Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
    Five: (1) Number of players N, (4) All-or-nothing contribution (fixed, not varied), (6) MPCR r, (7) Punishment cost α, (8) Punishment magnitude β.

C.  For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* the parameter on any dependent variable?  
    Three: N, α and β.  All three are varied analytically (threshold formulas) and graphically (Figs. 1–6).  No systematic variation is presented for r, and none for the remaining twelve parameters.

D.  If forced to predict how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on *efficiency* using only this paper:  
    •  The paper gives no direct evidence about efficiency, so any prediction must be indirect.  
    •  Larger fines (β) and smaller punishment costs (α) increase the prevalence of cooperation; if we assume average payoff rises with cooperation, then efficiency should rise with higher β and fall with higher α.  
    •  Smaller groups (lower N) favour cooperation under punishment; thus efficiency would be higher in smaller groups, all else equal.  
    •  The remaining twelve parameters are not addressed; the paper offers no basis for prediction about them or about their interactions.  
    •  Interaction predictions (e.g., β × α) are implicitly given by the two threshold inequalities, but no quantitative efficiency outcomes are provided.  Hence only qualitative statements (higher β relative to α improves cooperation, and probably efficiency) can be made.

In short, the paper focuses on how N, α and β shape the equilibrium frequency of cooperators under shared-cost punishment; it does not measure payoffs or efficiency, and it does not manipulate the other twelve parameters in the list.

Article Title: Increasing returns to scale: The solution to the second-order social dilemma
Keywords Plus: GROUP SELECTION; PUNISHMENT; COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; EMERGENCE; BEHAVIOR; RATHER
Abstract: Humans benefit from extensive cooperation; however, the existence of free-riders may cause cooperation to collapse. This is called the social dilemma. It has been shown that punishing free-riders is an effective way of resolving this problem. Because punishment is costly, this gives rise to the second-order social dilemma. Without exception, existing solutions rely on some stringent assumptions. This paper proposes, under very mild conditions, a simple model of a public goods game featuring increasing returns to scale. We find that punishers stand out and even dominate the population provided that the degree of increasing returns to scale is large enough; consequently, the second-order social dilemma dissipates. Historical evidence shows that people are more willing to cooperate with others and punish defectors when they suffer from either internal or external menaces. During the prehistoric age, the abundance of contributors was decisive in joint endeavours such as fighting floods, defending territory, and hunting. These situations serve as favourable examples of public goods games in which the degrees of increasing returns to scale are undoubtedly very large. Our findings show that natural selection has endowed human kind with a tendency to pursue justice and punish defection that deviates from social norms.

  – They show that if r (and/or the “degree of increasing returns to scale” α) is large enough, punishers (and cooperation) can dominate. For example, increasing r shifts the threshold for α at which punishment becomes evolutionarily stable.  
  – The paper reports no explicit “efficiency” measure or numeric effect size for efficiency. Instead, the main outcome is whether punishers dominate and defectors go extinct.

7) Punishment cost  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. They label it γ (gamma) in their model (“cost of punishment”). Figure 4(g) shows how systematically varying γ affects the fraction of punishers, cooperators, and defectors.  
• Predictions about systematically varying it?  
  – Increasing γ undermines punishers’ success; punishers fare worse with higher punishment cost. Again, the paper does not report an explicit efficiency measure or numeric effect on efficiency.

8) Punishment magnitude  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. They label it δ (delta, “strength of punishment”). Figure 4(f) shows how systematically varying δ affects the fraction of each strategy.  
• Predictions about systematically varying it?  
  – Increasing δ helps punishers defeat defectors. As δ increases, a punisher‐based regime becomes more stable. No direct statement on group efficiency is given, only on whether punishers dominate.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – The introduction does briefly mention that “reward is another solution” discussed in prior work, but the model itself does not include or vary any form of reward.  
• Predictions about systematically varying it?  
  – No. They do not incorporate rewards into the analysis.

10) Reward cost  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. The paper does not model reward at all.  
• Predictions about systematically varying it?  
  – Not mentioned.

11) Reward magnitude  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. Same as parameter 10: rewarding is not modeled.  
• Predictions about systematically varying it?  
  – Not mentioned.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. There is no mention of a finite or known horizon.  
• Predictions about systematically varying it?  
  – Not mentioned.

13) Are peer outcomes shown?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No mention is made of whether players see each other’s payoffs.  
• Predictions about systematically varying it?  
  – Not mentioned.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the punisher is?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No.  
• Predictions about systematically varying it?  
  – Not mentioned.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No.  
• Predictions about systematically varying it?  
  – Not mentioned.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FINAL SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   – It does not use “group efficiency” (actual payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff) as a measured or reported outcome. Instead, it reports (1) the fraction of time each strategy occupies the population (i.e., fixation probabilities under different configurations) and (2) how punishers or cooperators can dominate defectors under increasing returns to scale. These are not the same as efficiency.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – Four of them appear in some form:  
     • (1) Number of players (M and N), though not varied, is mentioned.  
     • (6) MPCR (labeled r) is explicitly analyzed.  
     • (7) Punishment cost (γ) is analyzed.  
     • (8) Punishment magnitude (δ) is analyzed.  
   – The others (2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15) are not discussed in the sense of being modeled or varied.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the “punishment treatment effect” when systematically varied?  
   – The paper systematically varies three parameters—r (the multiplier), γ (the punishment cost), and δ (the punishment magnitude). It reports how these affect the dominance of punishers (versus defectors or cooperators). However, it never presents an explicit treatment‐effect calculation for efficiency.  
   – The number of players (1) is mentioned but not varied in their figures or tables.

D) Predictions for how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence punishment’s effect on efficiency, based solely on the paper’s content:  
   – Because the paper does not measure efficiency and only shows how punishers can (or cannot) invade and remain stable, one can infer relatively little about efficiency per se. The main inference is that higher r, higher δ, and lower γ favor punishers, thereby making defection less likely. If one assumes stable punisher dominance correlates with higher payoffs for the group, then we might guess that (r ↑, δ ↑, γ ↓) would improve efficiency. But the paper itself does not quantify these relationships as efficiency metrics, so we cannot confidently predict exact efficiency outcomes from its data.

Keywords Plus: PROCEDURAL JUSTICE; COOPERATION; PUNISHMENT; ENFORCEMENT; BEHAVIOR
Abstract: To what extent do individuals' perceptions of legitimacy affect their intrinsic motivations to comply with an authority? Answering this question has critical implications for law enforcement but is challenging because actions or institutions that affect intrinsic motivations typically also affect extrinsic, material ones. To disentangle these, we propose an experimental approach that separately identifies the effect of an authority's costly action to improve enforcement fairness on citizen behavior through both intrinsic and extrinsic channels. In experiment 1, the authority's simple attempt to institute fairer enforcement increases prosocial behavior by 10 to 12 percentage points via the intrinsic channel. A follow-up experiment demonstrates that this is not motivated by citizen attempts to pay back authorities. Our findings provide causally credible evidence that an authority's actions can directly shape citizens' behavior by enhancing her legitimacy and have important implications in policy domains where this conflicts with other incentives.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter inventory of what, if anything, this paper says about each of the 15 listed features in relation to punishment and to outcomes. Following that is the requested summary (A–D).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
• Mentioned? Yes. Each experimental group has five total players: four “citizens” and one “authority.”  
• Systematically varied? No. The group size is always five; the paper does not discuss experimentally changing it.  
• Any stated effect on punishment or efficiency? No.  

2) Number of rounds  
• Mentioned? Yes. Each experiment ran for 20 “periods,” and subjects knew this.  
• Systematically varied? No. The paper does not manipulate the number of rounds.  
• Any stated effect on punishment or efficiency? No. (They do report how contribution rates evolve over the 20 rounds, but there is no systematic experimental variation of the number of periods.)  

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
• Mentioned? No. The paper does not indicate any communication or “chat” being enabled.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any stated effect? No.  

4) Is contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Mentioned? Yes. Citizens choose whether to contribute their 20‐token endowment in full or not contribute (keep it).  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any stated effect on punishment or efficiency? No. (They simply fix this binary choice format throughout.)  

5) Is the contribution “default”? (i.e., can players move part of their endowment back to themselves?)  
• Mentioned? No. There is no mention of any “default” mechanism or partial contribution.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any stated effect? No.  

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
• Mentioned? Yes. The MPCR is fixed at 0.4 (i.e., each 20‐token contribution yields 8 tokens back to each member, including the authority).  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any stated effect on punishment or efficiency? No. The MPCR is simply a constant parameter in their design.  

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Mentioned? No. The experiments do not analyze any separate cost to the authority for punishing. They study only whether the authority makes a “small” or “big” accuracy investment (not framed as a per‐punishment cost).  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any stated effect? No.  

8) Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from a player)  
• Mentioned? Yes. Whenever the authority (in the role of central punisher) penalizes a citizen, −24 tokens are imposed.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any stated effect on efficiency? No. The paper keeps the 24‐token deduction fixed; they do not study varying that deduction.  

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
• Mentioned? No. The paper does not include or discuss any reward mechanism.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any stated effect? No.  

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Mentioned? No. There is no mention of rewarding at all.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any stated effect? No.  

11) Reward magnitude (coin benefit to a rewarded player)  
• Mentioned? No. Same as above: no reward mechanism is discussed.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any stated effect? No.  

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?  
• Mentioned? Yes. Participants knew up front that there were 20 total periods.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any stated effect on punishment or efficiency? No direct discussion about varying round knowledge.  

13) Are peer outcomes shown to players each round? (i.e., do they see others’ payoffs?)  
• Mentioned? No explicit statement that participants see each other’s total payoffs or losses. They only learn the authority’s strategy and the realized accuracy level.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any stated effect? No.  

14) When a player is punished, do they know who punished them (the punisher’s identity)?  
• Mentioned? Not systematically. In the experiment, the “punisher” is always the central authority. There is no condition in which punishment is hidden—or attributed to another peer.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any stated effect? No.  

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who rewarded them (the rewarder’s identity)?  
• Mentioned? No. There is no reward mechanism in the experiments.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any stated effect? No.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY  
A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how do these differ?  
• The paper does not measure or report an explicit “efficiency” metric defined as total actual payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff. Instead, the key outcome variables are citizens’ “contribution” (binary: contribute the 20‐token endowment or not) and “compliance”/“cooperation” choices in a public good game. The authors also analyze how accuracy of detection, enforcement rules, and “legitimating” choices (big vs. small investment in accuracy) affect the likelihood of citizens’ contributing.  
• Thus, although the word “efficiency” appears in the background discussion (e.g., referencing prior work), the authors themselves focus on contribution behavior, not an efficiency ratio.  

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Mentioned parameters:  
  1) Number of players (always 5)  
  2) Number of rounds (always 20)  
  4) All or nothing contribution (binary choice)  
  6) MPCR = 0.4  
  8) Punishment magnitude = 24 tokens  
  12) The number of rounds is known (20)  

• That is six parameters (1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12).  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the “punishment treatment effect” when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• None of the 15 parameters above are systematically varied in different conditions in this paper (e.g., the punishment magnitude of 24 tokens is fixed rather than varied; the MPCR is fixed at 0.4, etc.).  
• Consequently, the paper does not provide any effect‐size estimates for systematically varying these parameters.  

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper, what would they be?  
• The paper does not give direct guidance about how any of the 15 parameters, individually or in combination, would affect efficiency if they were varied. It keeps those parameters fixed and focuses on “legitimacy” (big vs. small enforcement‐accuracy investment) plus the resultant accuracy levels.  
• Hence, based solely on the content of this paper, there is little basis to predict how systematically changing any of the 15 parameters would alter the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Abstract: Traffic congestion is increasingly deteriorating people's travel experience, and accordingly the relationship between travel mode selection and subjective well-being has become a hot issue of concern. Article Title: Suppressing defection by increasing temptation: The impact of smart cooperators on a social dilemma situation
Author Keywords: Social dilemmas; Cooperation; Cyclic dominance
Keywords Plus: RECIPROCITY; REWARD
Abstract: In a social dilemma situation, where individual and collective interests are in conflict, it sounds a reasonable assumption that the presence of super or smart players, who simultaneously punish defection and reward cooperation without allowing exploitation, could solve the basic problem. The behavior of such a multi-strategy system, however, is more subtle than it is firstly anticipated. When exploring the complete parameter space we find that the emergence of cyclic dominance among strategies is rather common, which results in several counter-intuitive phenomena. For example, the defection level can be lowered at higher temptation, or weaker punishment provides better conditions for smart players. Our study indicates that smart cooperators can unexpectedly thrive under high temptation, emphasizing the complexity of strategic interactions. This study suggests that the principles governing these interactions can be applied to other moral behaviors, such as truth-telling and honesty, providing valuable insights for future research in multi -agent systems.

Below I go through the 15 public-goods‐game parameters one at a time and relate them to what is (and is not) said in the paper “Suppressing defection by increasing temptation: The impact of smart cooperators on a social dilemma situation.”

Important terminology  
•  “Punishment treatment effect’’ would normally mean the difference between an environment with and without punishment.  
•  The paper never runs such a comparison. Punishment (and reward) are always “built into’’ the smart-cooperator (M) strategy and no baseline “no-punishment’’ condition is analysed.  
•  The paper’s only dependent variables are the long-run (stationary) fractions of the three strategies D, C and M on a spatial lattice. Group efficiency, total payoff and average payoff are never reported.

Because of that, whenever I write “No prediction on punishment-treatment effect’’ below, this is simply because the paper never measures that quantity.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned: Yes. A square lattice of size L = 1000 (sometimes 1200) ⇒ N = L² ≈ 10⁶–1.4 × 10⁶.  
   (2) Systematically varied? No. L is fixed; no predictions offered.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Not an experimental round structure; instead the model is run for 10⁴ Monte-Carlo steps.  
   (2) Not varied; no predictions.

3. Chat enabled?  
   (1) Not mentioned.  
   (2) No predictions.

4. “All-or-nothing’’ contribution rule  
   (1) The game is a binary Prisoner’s Dilemma (cooperate vs defect) – effectively “all or nothing”, but the paper never discusses varying this rule.  
   (2) No predictions.

5. Contribution default (endowment moved back)  
   (1) Not applicable.  
   (2) No predictions.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor  
   (1) The closest analogue is T, the “temptation to defect” payoff. Values are varied from ~1.0 to 2.5.  
   (2) Systematic variation: YES.  
       • Fig. 1 shows that increasing T from 1.0 to 2.0 lowers the stationary fraction of D and raises M.  
       • Heat maps in Fig. 2 repeat this for many (T,W) pairs.  
       • No efficiency numbers; no punishment-treatment effect is calculated.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   (1) No separate per-use cost is modelled. The only cost is a flat “maintenance cost’’ G borne continuously by M.  
   (2) Therefore no predictions about varying a per-unit punishment cost.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from target)  
   (1) YES. Denoted U in the payoff matrix; varied from 0 to 1 (see Fig. 4).  
   (2) Systematic variation: YES.  
       • Fig. 4: Raising U slightly reduces D, strongly lowers M, and raises C.  
       • No efficiency data; no explicit punishment-treatment effect calculated.

9. Reward enabled?  
   (1) Reward is always “on’’—M gives reward W to C. No on/off manipulation.  
   (2) No predictions about switching it on/off.

10. Reward cost (cost to giver per unit)  
    (1) Not separated; folded into G.  
    (2) No predictions.

11. Reward magnitude (coins given)  
    (1) YES. Denoted W; varied jointly with T in Fig. 2.  
    (2) Systematic variation: YES.  
        • Higher W, especially when G is low, benefits C and harms M; D remains rare.  
        • Again, no efficiency or punishment-treatment effect reported.

12. Do players know the number of rounds?  
    (1) Not applicable to this evolutionary model.  
    (2) No predictions.

13. Are peer outcomes shown each round?  
    (1) Not discussed.  
    (2) No predictions.

14. Do punished players know who punished them?  
    (1) Not modelled.

Abstract: Humans often behave altruistically towards strangers with no chance of reciprocation. From an evolutionary perspective, this is puzzling. The evolution of altruistic cooperative behavior-in which an organism's action reduces its fitness and increases the fitness of another organism (e.g. by sharing food)-only makes sense when it is directed at genetically related organisms (kin selection) or when one can expect the favor to be returned (reciprocal altruism). Therefore, evolutionary theorists such as Sober and Wilson have argued that we should revise Neo-Darwininian evolutionary theory. They argue that human altruism evolved through group selection in which groups of altruists were naturally selected because they had a comparative advantage over other groups. The heated debate between advocates and critics of group selection often suffers from a lack of conceptual clarity. In response, I set out to clearly distinguish 'genetic' from 'cultural' group selection (developed by Boyd, Richerson & Henrich) and argue that the latter does not face the potentially debilitating problems plaguing the former. I defend the claim that human altruistic dispositions evolved through cultural group selection and gene-culture coevolution and offer empirical evidence in support. I also argue that actual altruistic behavior often goes beyond the kind of behavior humans have evolved to display. Conscious and voluntary reasoning processes, I show, have an important role in altruistic behavior. This is often overlooked in the scientific literature on human altruism.

Unless explicitly noted, the paper never translates results into “efficiency’’ (total payoff / first–best payoff); when it does not, I state the variable used (usually “contribution’’).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. NUMBER OF PLAYERS ( n )
• Mentioned?  Yes.  Section 3.1 analyses a public-goods game with n ≥ 2; §3.2 (the only section that actually contains a punishment treatment) is restricted to n = 2.
• Systematic predictions?  Not for the punishment treatment effect.  In §3.2 n is fixed at 2, so no comparative statics.  In §3.1 the author shows how n changes the condition under which compliers give voluntarily, but there is no punishment stage there.

2. NUMBER OF ROUNDS
• Mentioned?  No.
• No predictions.

3. IS CHAT ENABLED?
• Not mentioned.

4. ALL-OR-NOTHING CONTRIBUTION?
• Not mentioned – all examples with punishment assume a continuous choice 0 ≤ c ≤ endowment.

5. “REVERSAL’’ (CONTRIBUTION AS DEFAULT)?
• Not mentioned.

6. MARGINAL PER CAPITA RETURN  ( γ )
• Mentioned?  Yes – core parameter in all public-goods examples.
• Systematic punishment-effect prediction?  Yes, in §3.2.
  ‑ The introduction of punishment raises each player’s contribution by  
       Δc = c̄_s = κ · g ⁄ [(1–γ) φ]            (eq. 8 in text)  
    where κ is the fraction of compliers, g the guilt parameter and φ the punishment cost.
  ‑ Hence the size of the punishment treatment effect is ∂Δc/∂γ  =  κ g ⁄ [(1–γ)² φ]  > 0.  Larger MPCR makes punishment more effective.
  ‑ The paper stops at contributions; it never converts this into efficiency numbers.

7. PUNISHMENT COST PER UNIT  ( φ )
• Mentioned?  Yes – linear cost parameter in §3.2.
• Systematic prediction?  Yes.  From the same formula,
       Δc = κ g ⁄ [(1–γ) φ] ,
  so ∂Δc/∂φ  = –κ g ⁄ [(1–γ) φ²]  < 0.  Cheaper punishment (lower φ) magnifies the treatment effect.
• No explicit efficiency calculation is given.

8. PUNISHMENT MAGNITUDE PER UNIT
• The model fixes the damage per unit of punishment at 1 monetary unit; this parameter is not varied, and no treatment-effect prediction is made.

9. IS A REWARD OPTION AVAILABLE?
10. REWARD COST
11. REWARD MAGNITUDE
• Rewards are never introduced; no discussion.

12. ARE THE NUMBER OF ROUNDS COMMON KNOWLEDGE?
• Not discussed.

13. ARE PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN?
• Not discussed.

14. IS THE PUNISHER IDENTIFIED?
15. IS THE REWARDER IDENTIFIED?
• Not discussed.

SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables used
   – The paper’s theoretical examples track (i) individual contributions to the public good and (ii) expected utility / “welfare’’.  
   – “Efficiency’’ in the sense of (total realised payoff) ÷ (payoff under full cooperation) is never computed.  Therefore all numeric results are in contribution units, not efficiency units.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters appear?
   4 parameters:  
      #1 (n), #6 (γ), #7 (φ), #8 (punishment effect per unit).  
   (γ and φ are explicit; n and the fixed punishment magnitude are implicit.)

C.  For how many parameters does the paper state how systematic variation changes the punishment treatment effect?
   Exactly 2 parameters – γ and φ.  The predicted effect is
        Δ contribution  =  κ g ⁄ [(1–γ) φ] ,
   so larger γ or smaller φ give a larger treatment effect.  No other parameter is analysed in this way, and no efficiency calculation is supplied.

D.  If one had to forecast the influence of the 15 parameters on the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency solely from this paper:

• Lower punishment cost (φ) → stronger positive effect.
