Below, each of the 15 parameters is examined in the order given.  For each parameter I state  

(1) whether the paper ever mentions the parameter and, if so, what value(s) are described; and  
(2) whether the paper makes any prediction or reports any *systematic* manipulation of that parameter and its impact on the “punishment-treatment effect” (i.e., the difference in outcomes between a condition *with* versus *without* punishment).  Numerical effect sizes are provided only when they can be read directly from the text, tables, or figures.  If nothing is said, that is stated explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned.  “A typical PG experiment involves groups with four members….”  Two-player PD/TG games are also described.  
   (2) No study in the paper systematically varies group size while holding everything else constant and then compares the punishment-versus-no-punishment difference.  No quantitative effect is reported.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Mentioned.  Most repeated PG studies cited last “about 15 rounds”; Andreoni’s restart design is described as two blocks of 10 rounds.  
   (2) No experiment varies the *length* of the game conditional on the presence of punishment.  The paper only notes that, *given* a fixed horizon, contributions decay without punishment but stay near 100 % with punishment.

3. Chat enabled  
   (1) Not mentioned anywhere.  
   (2) No discussion or data.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution versus continuous choice  
   (1) Mentioned only tangentially: the simultaneous PD is said to require choosing “all 20 points or nothing,” whereas the standard PG allows any amount.  
   (2) No systematic variation of this feature in a punishment design; no effect sizes.

5. Contribution default / “take” game  
   (1) Not mentioned.  
   (2) No discussion.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   (1) Illustrated once: each token invested yields 0.4 to every group member (group return = 1.6).  
   (2) No experiment varies the MPCR while studying punishment; no quantitative results.

7. Cost to impose one unit of punishment  
   (1) Described: “Each deduction point costs a player one point….”  
   (2) Cost is not experimentally manipulated; no statement of how changing the cost would alter the punishment treatment effect.

8. Magnitude of punishment (loss to target per unit)  
   (1) Described: “…decreases the earnings of the punished player by more, for example 3 points.”  
   (2) The 3-to-1 ratio is treated as fixed; no systematic variation or prediction.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   (1) Rewards are mentioned only anecdotally (e.g., “whether a reward is enabled” is never discussed).  
   (2) No data, no predictions.

10. Cost to grant a unit of reward  
    Same as #9 – not discussed.

11. Magnitude of reward  
    Same as #9 – not discussed.

12. Are the number of rounds known to players?  
    (1) Not stated; standard PG instructions are summarized but whether the horizon is common knowledge is never made explicit.  
    (2) No variation or prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    (1) Yes for punishment treatments: “In the second stage each member … gets to see the other member’s contributions….”  
    (2) Visibility is held constant; the effect of *changing* feedback on the punishment treatment effect is not analyzed.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
    (1) Yes—punishers remain anonymous: “while still preserving anonymity.”  
    (2) Anonymity is never relaxed or varied; no effect sizes.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
    Same as #9 – no discussion.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary

A.  Dependent variables  
    The paper is primarily concerned with
    • Individual contribution / cooperation rate  
    • Frequency and intensity of punishment  
    • Self-reported affect and neural activation  
    • Occasionally “group income” is illustrated, but *group efficiency (total payoff ÷ maximum possible)* is never used as the outcome of any statistical test.  Thus “efficiency” is not treated as a dependent variable in the reported evidence, even though the authors use efficiency examples rhetorically.

B.  Parameters merely *mentioned* (with at least one concrete value): 8 of 15  
    1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 13, 14

C.  Parameters whose *systematic* variation is linked to the punishment treatment effect: essentially 0 of 15  
    The paper contrasts “no punishment” vs. “punishment” regimes but does not vary any of the listed parameters inside punishment designs.  The closest is “one-shot vs. repeated,” but the horizon itself is never parametrically manipulated; instead, behavior is just tracked over existing rounds.

D.  What can be predicted—strictly from material in this paper—about how the 15 parameters (and interactions) influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?

    • Adding a punishment stage (cost = 1, efficacy = 3) in a repeated four-player PG keeps contributions near 100 % through the final round, whereas without punishment contributions fall toward 0.  Hence, *conditional on those exact parameter values,* the treatment effect on efficiency is large and positive.  
    • Because no study in the paper alters any other parameter while holding everything else fixed, the paper supplies virtually no leverage for predicting how changing group size, MPCR, punishment cost/magnitude ratio, information conditions, or any interaction among the 15 parameters would modulate the efficiency gain from punishment.  
    • The only qualitative guidance offered is the warning that punishment *reduces* efficiency when it is mis-directed (e.g., when above-average contributors are punished) or when its mere availability is perceived as distrust, but these statements are not tied to any of the fifteen concrete parameters listed above.

In short, the survey demonstrates **that** costly peer punishment can prevent the collapse of cooperation, thereby greatly increasing efficiency, but it provides almost **no quantitative or systematic evidence** about how tweaking any of the 15 experimental design parameters would amplify or dampen that effect.

A. Dependent variables used

   • “Group efficiency” in the public-goods sense (actual total payoff divided by the maximal cooperative total payoff) is *not* defined nor used.  Therefore the dependent variables differ from the efficiency measure requested in the prompt.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   • Only 3 of them appear at all:  
     1. Number of players (fixed N)  
     2. Number of rounds (implicitly infinite)  
     12. Knowledge of the horizon (yes, infinite)  
   • All other 12 parameters (3–11, 13–15) are absent.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* the parameter on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable)?  
   • Zero.  No parameter is systematically varied in a “with-punishment vs. without-punishment” sense, and no treatment effect on efficiency (or on any other dependent variable) is computed.

D. Predictions that can be made, solely from this paper, about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency  
   • The paper offers essentially no leverage to predict the punishment treatment effect for any of the 15 experimental design parameters because (i) the environment is a trust game, not a public-goods game; (ii) sanctions are endogenous refusals to cooperate, not costly peer punishment; (iii) no punishment-vs.-no-punishment comparison is analysed; and (iv) efficiency is not measured as in public-goods studies. Abstract: In many real-world social dilemmas the surplus from insider cooperation can be stolen by outsiders. Below I walk through the 15 design parameters, extracting only what the paper actually says.  For every parameter I note  

(i) whether it is explicitly described (and its value, if given);  
(ii) whether the authors ever vary it or discuss how **varying** it would change the “punishment treatment effect” (the difference in some outcome with vs. without punishment).

The outcomes the paper studies are listed first so you can see what the “treatment effect” is measured on.

DEPENDENT VARIABLES THAT THE PAPER REPORTS  
– “Allocation” (the amount insiders put in / take from the group account).  
– “Co-operation Index” (a rescaled version of Allocation used to compare PG and CPR).  
– Gross surplus, surplus net of theft, and surplus lost to theft.  
– Individual profit / payoff.  
– Sanctions supplied, deterrence ratio, outsider theft levels.  

“Group efficiency” (total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff) is never calculated; when the words “efficiency” or “welfare” appear they refer only to payoffs, not to the efficiency ratio.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER EXTRACTION
--------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned: 4 insiders (+ 2 outsiders in theft treatments).  
   • Never varied; no prediction about varying it.

2. Number of rounds  
   • 15 periods. Known to subjects.  
   • Never varied; no prediction.

3. Chat / communication  
   • No chat is permitted (subjects only see on-screen information).  
   • Not varied; no prediction.

4. “All-or-nothing” vs. continuous contribution  
   • Contributions/appropriations are continuous from 0 to the whole endowment.  
   • Not varied; no prediction.

5. “Contribution default” (take-back vs. give-to)  
   • Not discussed; decision screen simply asks how much to put in Account 1 vs. a private account.  
   • No variation; no prediction.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Non-linear production: V(G)=aG – bG² with a=6, b=0.025.  
   • The parameters are fixed; no statements on changing them.

7. Cost to impose 1 unit of punishment  
   • 1 experimental $ spent by an insider removes 3 from the outsider (“1:3 technology”).  
   • Fixed; never varied; no predictions.

8. Punishment magnitude per unit  
   • See #7 (3-for-1). Fixed.  
   • Not varied; no prediction.

9. Reward option  
   • No reward stage exists.  
   • Not discussed; no prediction.

10–11. Reward cost and magnitude  
   • Not applicable (no reward).

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
   • Yes (subjects told there will be 15).  
   • Not varied; no prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Yes.  
     – Outsiders observe total insider surplus before deciding how much to steal.  
     – Insiders see each outsider’s theft amount and payoff before sanctioning.  
   • Always the same; no discussion of altering it.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
   • The paper never states whether outsiders learn *who* punished them; the software description simply says outsiders “were informed of their final pay-offs” after sanctions.  No mention of identity revelation; therefore no usable information and no variation.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
   • Not applicable (no reward).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Does the study use “efficiency” as a dependent variable?  
   • No.  Outcomes are Allocation, Cooperation Index, profits, surplus, sanctions, theft, etc.  “Efficiency” in the strict sense (total payoff ÷ maximum possible) is never computed.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
   • Mentioned (with fixed values): 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13.  
   • Not mentioned / not applicable: 5, 9, 10, 11, 14 (unclear), 15.  
   So 9 of 15 are at least described.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* the parameter on the punishment treatment effect for any dependent variable?  
   • Zero.  Every parameter is held constant; the paper never manipulates or models treatment-effect differences that would arise if these parameters changed.

D.  What predictions—restricted strictly to the content of this paper—can we make about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
   • Very little.  The experiment only tells us that with the single parameter constellation they implement, allowing insiders to punish outsiders **does not** raise group payoffs enough to offset punishment costs and residual theft; hence efficiency does not improve.  Because none of the 15 parameters is varied, the paper offers no evidence that changing them would alter that conclusion.  Any further prediction would go beyond what is stated.

In short, the paper fixes the game environment and never explores parameter changes, so it yields no quantitative or qualitative guidance on how those parameters would moderate the effect of punishment on group efficiency.

Below we go through the list of 15 parameters one‐by‐one, restricting ourselves strictly to what is contained in “Fostering cooperation through the enhancement of own vulnerability.”

FOR EACH PARAMETER  

1. Number of players  
   – Discussed?  Yes.  Every game is played by exactly two players (a 2×2 Prisoner’s Dilemma).  
   – Systematically varied?  No.  No prediction about what would happen with 3, 4 … n players.  

2. Number of rounds  
   – Discussed?  Yes.  Exactly 50 rounds in every treatment.  
   – Systematically varied?  No.  No statement on how changing the length of the horizon would alter the punishment treatment effect.  

3. Chat enabled?  
   – Mentioned?  No.  There is no reference to any form of chat or free discussion.  
   – Effect predicted?  None.  

4. All-or-nothing contribution decision  
   – Mentioned?  Yes implicitly.  The action space is {Cooperate, Defect}, i.e. an all-or-nothing choice.  
   – Varied?  No.  No prediction about switching to a continuous contribution scale.  

5. Contribution default / “withdraw from a default contribution”  
   – Not mentioned.  

6. Marginal Per-Capita Return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   – Not used.  Pay-offs are fixed money amounts (55-70-25-5).  No parameter is varied.  

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit of punishment  
   – Discussed?  Yes.  The cost is a fixed 4 points per punishment act (p = 4).  
   – Varied?  No.  The paper never considers a different cost, so no prediction is offered.  

8. Punishment magnitude (loss per unit inflicted)  
   – Discussed?  Yes, and this is the core endogenous variable.  Each player first chooses an “own possible punishment level” x ∈ [0,50].  
   – Systematic variation & predicted effect?  Yes.  
        • Theory: If x < 15 (= t – c) a player remains a defector; 15 ≤ x ≤ ≈20–25 makes her a conditional co-operator; x > 20–25 makes her an unconditional co-operator.  
        • Data:  In the second half of the experiment, cooperation frequency rises sharply once both players set x ≥ 15.  Fig. 3 (Gradual) shows ≈55 % cooperation when 15 ≤ x ≤ 25 for both players, rising to ≈80 % when both choose x ≥ 45.  
        • Efficiency:  Fig. 7 demonstrates that average earnings begin to rise once x ≥ 15 and keep rising with x in Gradual; in Leap the peak is around x ≈ 20.  
        → Numerical effect that can be read directly: moving from “both x ≤ 5” to “both 15 ≤ x ≤ 25” raises cooperation from roughly 0–5 % to roughly 34 % in Leap and 55 % in Gradual (second-half data, p < 0.05 in a fixed-effects logit).  Efficiency improves in parallel (Fig. 4).  

9. Whether a reward option is enabled  
   – Not mentioned, not present, no effect estimated.  

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   – Not applicable.  

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
   – Yes, they are told there are 50 rounds.  Not varied; no predictions about uncertainty of horizon.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   – Yes.  A “social history screen” reveals the last 10 rounds of every pair inside the 8-person matching group (own & partner punishment levels, actions, punishments).  
   – Varied?  No.  No comparison to a treatment without this information.  

14. Do punished players know who punished them?  
   – Yes in the trivial sense that there are only two people in a pair; the punished player knows it was the partner.  The paper never varies anonymity of the punisher.  

15. Do rewarded players know who rewarded them?  
   – Not relevant (no rewards).  



SUMMARY  

A. Dependent variables used  
   • Efficiency (round payoff / 110, Fig. 4).  
   • Cooperation rate (% of C choices), Table 4.  
   • Frequencies of the specific outcomes C-C, C-D, D-D.  
   These measures are distinct: cooperation is an action; efficiency incorporates both actions and punishment costs.  

B. Which of the 15 parameters are at least mentioned?  
   1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14  → 8 of 15.  

C. For which parameters does the paper discuss the effect of systematically varying the parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
   Only parameter 8 (punishment magnitude).  None of the other 14 parameters are experimentally or theoretically varied in a way that lets the authors compute a treatment effect.  

D. Predictions we can make (solely from this paper) about how the 15 parameters and their interactions affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency  

   – Allowing players to set higher punishment magnitudes (parameter 8) above the threshold of ≈15 raises both cooperation and efficiency, provided the two players’ choices are aligned.  
   – Giving players the chance to match each other’s punishment levels gradually (mechanism difference, not one of the listed 15 parameters but operationalised through the dispersion of parameter 8) leads to still higher punishment levels, fewer C-D mismatches, higher cooperation, and hence higher efficiency than a one-shot (Leap) choice.  
   – Holding everything else fixed, extremely high punishment levels do not reduce efficiency in Gradual (they coincide with very high cooperation) but can reduce expected earnings in Leap because they carry greater variance when the partner does not match them (Fig. 7).  
   – Nothing in the paper lets us say what would happen if we changed any of the following: number of players, number of rounds, communication, MPCR, punishment cost, reward possibilities, information conditions, or identification of punishers.  For those 14 parameters we must admit that the paper provides no basis for prediction.

Abstract: Collective risk social dilemmas are at the heart of the most pressing global challenges we are facing today, including climate change mitigation and the overuse of natural resources. Below is a parameter-by-parameter summary of what is (and is not) discussed in the paper with respect to the 15 parameters in question, followed by the required four‐part summary (A–D). In what follows, “the paper” refers exclusively to the provided article by Jiang et al. (2023). All statements below derive solely from that text. “Systematically varying” a parameter means that the authors deliberately changed its value across different conditions in order to measure its effect on outcomes. “Punishment treatment effect” refers, in the spirit of your request, to any discussion of how introducing or changing punishment parameters affects outcomes (though the paper itself does not use the phrase “punishment treatment effect” in precisely those terms). Also note that the paper does not define “efficiency” as (actual total payoff) ÷ (maximum possible payoff), but rather focuses on whether the target sum is achieved, average investments, and the fraction of failed groups.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players                                  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper devotes extensive discussion to groups of sizes M = 2, 5, and 10.  
   • Systematically varied? Yes. The authors explicitly study how increasing group size (2 → 5 → 10) affects outcomes in the presence of punishment.  
   • Effect on the punishment treatment (for the paper’s dependent variables)?  
     – The authors measure how often groups fail to reach the target (“failure probability”) and how much they contribute on average. They find that, for the same punishment probability p, larger groups generally contribute less on average and thus fail more frequently (unless the punishment probability is extremely high, p = 1).  
     – Numeric effect sizes in the paper center on “fraction of failures,” “average investment,” and whether the target is reached. For instance, Fig. 3 shows that when p < 1, higher M yields more failures; only when p = 1 could even large groups (M = 10) reliably reach the target.  
   • No direct statement about “efficiency” (in the sense of total payoffs ÷ maximum possible) is provided.  

2. Number of rounds                                   
   • Mentioned? Yes, all experiments use 10 rounds.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper always uses 10 rounds and does not study how changing the number of rounds affects punishment.  
   • No predictions about varying the number of rounds are given.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?                    
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not indicate that any form of intra-group communication or chat was allowed.  
   • No predictions about varying chat.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?              
   • Mentioned? Partially. Each participant can contribute 0, 1, or 2 MU. This is neither strictly continuous nor purely “all or nothing.”  
   • Not systematically varied. The authors do not change the set {0, 1, 2} to study different contribution rules.  

5. Is the contribution default?                       
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not describe any “default” mechanism (e.g., a participant having to exert effort to retract a default contribution).  
   • No predictions.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR)                  
   • Mentioned? Not as such. The experiment is framed in terms of a “target sum” (10 × M) that must be reached, rather than an MPCR or multiplication factor.  
   • Not systematically varied. No predictions concerning changes in MPCR.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper sets a punishment cost of 1 MU for each free-rider fined in a round, but that 1 MU is shared evenly among all group members.  
   • Systematically varied? No. It is kept constant at 1 MU per free rider, with no reported manipulations of that cost.  
   • No predictions about changing that cost.  

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted per unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper fixes the punishment fine at 3 MU per free-rider (when punishment occurs).  
   • Systematically varied? No. It remains 3 MU throughout all experiments.  
   • No predictions about altering that fine.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled                         
   • Mentioned? No, not in the experiments. The paper only discusses punishment; no reward mechanism is present.  
   • No predictions on reward.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward       
    • Not applicable. No reward mechanism is studied.  

11. Reward magnitude                                   
    • Not applicable. No reward mechanism is studied.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?          
    • Mentioned? The experiment always ran for 10 rounds, and the participants appear to have been informed that there would be 10 rounds total.  
    • Systematically varied? No. They did not compare “known” vs. “unknown” horizon. No predictions.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown?                           
    • Mentioned? Only partial. After each round, participants see their own contribution, the group’s total contribution for that round, and the gap to the target. They do not see others’ individual earnings or punishments in detail.  
    • Not systematically varied, and no predictions about altering the information display.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know the punisher?  
    • Mentioned? No. The experiment imposes fines probabilistically (with probability p). There is no identification of who is responsible for punishing.  
    • No predictions.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know the rewarder?  
    • Not applicable. No reward is used in the design.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The article does not present a direct measure of “efficiency” defined as (actual total payoff) ÷ (maximum possible payoff). Instead, its main dependent variables include (1) whether the final target is attained (or the “failure probability” of not reaching that target), (2) the average amount contributed to the public pool, (3) final payoffs if the target is (or is not) reached, and (4) how many players choose “selfish,” “fair-share,” or “altruistic” contributions (0, 1, or 2 MU respectively).  
   • “Failure probability” differs from “efficiency,” and “average payoff” (also discussed) is not the same as that ratio-based definition of efficiency.  

B. Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
     – (1) Number of players (M) is a central focus, varied systematically.  
     – (2) Number of rounds is always 10 (discussed but not varied).  
     – (7) Punishment cost is set to 1 MU.  
     – (8) Punishment magnitude is 3 MU.  
     – (12) Number of rounds known (10).  
     – (13) Limited outcome information is displayed.  
   • All other parameters (#3, #4, #5, #6, #9, #10, #11, #14, #15) are effectively absent (no mention, no manipulation, or no real discussion).  

C. For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect, for any measured dependent variable, when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Only Parameter 1 (Number of players) is truly “systematically varied.” The authors run separate sessions with M = 2, 5, and 10. They measure how the punishment mechanism’s effects (on fraction of free‐riders, average investment, fraction of failures) depend on M.  
   • The paper keeps all other parameters fixed (e.g., 10 rounds, a 3 MU fine, a 1 MU punishing cost, no rewards) and does not systematically vary them, so there is no discussion of how systematically changing them would affect punishment for any dependent variable.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The authors do not directly address “efficiency” in the sense of total payoff / maximum payoff, nor do they systematically vary most of the parameters. They do show that larger group sizes (Parameter 1) have a greater risk of failing to reach the collective target unless the probability of punishment is extremely high (p ≈ 1).  
   • Consequently, if one were to make predictions about efficiency (not directly measured in the paper), one would guess that, for larger groups, punishment has to be very “certain” in order for payoffs to be high (i.e., to avoid failure). Keywords Plus: FIELD EXPERIMENT; PUNISHMENT; ENFORCEMENT; TRUST; PROVISION; GAMES
Abstract: In this paper, we analyze the nature of cooperation in different corruption regimes. In a laboratory experiment with university students in Mexico, individuals play first a corruption game and then a public goods game. The corruption game is divided into three groups: high- and low-monitoring scenarios as well as a control group not exposed to the game. The public goods game is divided into three groups: the standard game, a game with centralized punishment executed by an exogenously assigned leader, and a game similar to the second one, but adding the possibility of counter-punishment. There are four key results. First, there is more corruption in the low-monitoring group. Second, in the public goods game there is less cooperation in the low-monitoring group than in the group with more intensive monitoring. Third, the option of punishment increases cooperation, but the sensitivity to punishment is greater in the high-monitoring (low-corruption) group. Fourth, the option of counter-punishment of the leader decreases cooperation. Our results highlight the importance of corruption in decreasing trust and social capital and show the difficulty of promoting cooperation when corruption is prevalent.

Abstract: The question of how altruism can evolve despite its local disadvantage to selfishness has produced a wealth of theoretical and empirical research capturing the attention of scientists across disciplines for decades. One feature that has remained consistent through this outpouring of knowledge has been that researchers have looked to the altruists themselves for mechanisms by which altruism can curtail selfishness. An alternative perspective may be that just as altruists want to limit selfishness in the population, so may the selfish individuals themselves. These alternative perspectives have been most evident in the fairly recent development of enforcement strategies. Punishment can effectively limit selfishness in the population, but it is not free. Thus, when punishment evolves among altruists, the double costs of exploitation from cheaters and punishment make the evolution of punishment problematic. Here we show that punishment can more readily invade selfish populations when associated with selfishness, whereas altruistic punishers cannot. Thereafter, the establishment of altruism because of enforcement by selfish punishers provides the ideal invasion conditions for altruistic punishment, effectively creating a transition of punishment from selfishness to altruistic. Thus, from chaotic beginnings, a little hypocrisy may go a long way in the evolution and maintenance of altruism.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter summary of what (if anything) the paper says regarding each of the 15 parameters, whether the paper systematically varies them, and whether it connects these variations to any “punishment treatment effect.” Note that the paper’s main focus is on the evolutionary success of “selfish punishment” versus “altruistic punishment” in maintaining cooperation (or “altruism”) in agent‐based models. The paper explicitly examines how varying certain model inputs (group size, number of iterations, cost of punishment, and cost of solitary behavior) affects the spread of punishment strategies and ultimately the fraction of cooperators in the population. However, it does not use the term “efficiency” (i.e., actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff) and it does not report explicit numeric effect sizes on total payoffs. Instead, it largely reports changes in strategies’ frequency and relative fitness.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper refers to “group size” (n) and a total population size (N).  
   • Systematically varied? Yes. In Figure 9 and related text, the authors vary group size and show that smaller groups facilitate the invasion/effectiveness of both selfish and altruistic punishment (because punishment has a larger impact on the within‐group composition). Larger groups hamper punishment’s ability to stabilize cooperation.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (any dependent variable)? Yes, it discusses that decreasing group size strongly aids the “invasion of punishment,” whereas larger group size works against it. No numerical effect size on total payoff or “efficiency” is given.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper calls this “iterations” (I), the number of repeated interactions within groups before reproduction/migration.  
   • Systematically varied? Yes. The authors vary the number of iterations from 6, 10 (baseline), and 14 (see Figure 8).  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (any dependent variable)? Yes. Increasing the number of rounds promotes the effectiveness of punishment (because groups remain together longer, so punishers can remove cheaters more thoroughly, and group selection effects have more time to build up). Again, no numeric effect size on efficiency is provided.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not discuss communication or chat among agents.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned? The model is, in effect, an “all‐or‐nothing” contribution game: “altruists” always contribute their entire resource in each round, while “selfish” individuals contribute nothing.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper sets all altruists to contribute and all selfish types to withhold; there is no variation around partial vs. full contributions. There is also no discussion of how changing this assumption would affect the punishment treatment.

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much to move back into their hand)?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not discuss any default contribution mechanism or partial endowment return.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper denotes a multiplier m > 1 on contributed resources.  
   • Systematically varied? No. They state the multiplier is greater than 1 to ensure that contributions (when made by altruists) pay off at the group level, but they do not report different values of m or systematically vary it.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed beyond noting that m > 1 fosters a meaningful public‐goods setting; no numerical results are presented for different m.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper uses “C” to denote the cost of punishment to the punisher.  
   • Systematically varied? Yes. In Figure 6, they examine C = 5%, 20% (baseline), and 40% of the resource.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (any dependent variable)? Yes. With higher punishment cost, punishment is less able to invade and stabilize altruism; lowering the cost favors altruistic punishment over selfish punishment. The paper gives no explicit numeric “efficiency” measure but does note that higher C hinders the “success” of punishment.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins taken from the punished player)
   • Mentioned? Only in the sense that punishment expels cheaters from group interactions entirely. That is effectively a “binary” or all‐or‐nothing penalty (not a graduated subtraction of coins).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not report tests of different punishment‐severity levels other than expulsion.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned? No. The paper only discusses punishing transgressors (expulsion) and does not add any reward protocol.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Mentioned? No. The paper does not include a reward mechanism.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)
    • Mentioned? No. The paper does not include a reward mechanism.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
    • Mentioned? No. The paper models repeated interactions for a fixed number of iterations but does not state whether agents “know” this.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (i.e., do players see how much their peers gained and lost)?
    • Mentioned? No. The paper does not include any explicit discussion about information feedback of others’ payoffs.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Mentioned? No. The paper does not address whether individuals learn who punished them.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Mentioned? No. As with parameters 9–11, the paper does not include any reward mechanism or knowledge thereof.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper primarily tracks the evolutionary success (i.e., final frequencies) of different punishment‐and‐cooperation strategies and their fitness (payoff). While it does discuss “group productivity,” “group fitness,” and “payoff,” it does not use “efficiency” (ratio of actual total payoff to maximum payoff of a fully cooperative group) as a direct reported outcome. Thus, the dependent variables in the paper are mainly (1) the frequency/evolutionary stability of punishment strategies (selfish vs. altruistic) over time, and (2) the resulting “fitness” or payoff. These differ from a formal “efficiency” measure.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   • Mentioned:  
     #1 (Number of players/group size),  
     #2 (Number of rounds/iterations),  
     #4 (game structure is effectively all‐or‐nothing, but not varied),  
     #6 (multiplier m > 1, not varied),  
     #7 (punishment cost C),  
     #8 (punishment magnitude—expulsion, but not varied).  
   • Not mentioned at all:  
     #3 (chat), #5 (contribution default), #9–#11 (reward structure), #12–#15 (information display parameters).  
   • Hence 6 of the parameters appear in some form (though not necessarily systematically varied).

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • Three parameters are actually varied in the simulations and discussed in detail:  
       (1) Group size (#1).  
       (2) Number of rounds/iterations (#2).  
       (3) Punishment cost (#7).  
   • No exact numeric impact on total payoffs (“efficiency”) is provided, but the paper reports whether punishment successfully invades and stabilizes cooperation under these variations.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper:  
   • The paper provides enough discussion to predict that smaller groups, longer rounds (more iterations), and lower punishment costs all make punishment more likely to stabilize cooperation (which would presumably increase a group’s average payoff—hence likely improving efficiency).  
   • The remaining parameters (chat, partial vs. full contributions, reward, knowledge of other players’ outcomes, etc.) are not addressed, so we have no evidence from this paper to predict their effect on efficiency. Any statement beyond these limited insights would go beyond what the paper itself says.

Author Full Names: Perez, Irene; Yu, David J.; Janssen, Marco A.; Anderies, John M.
Article Title: Social roles and performance of social-ecological systems: evidence from behavioral lab experiments
Author Keywords: behavioral experiments; communication; irrigation systems; lab experiments; qualitative comparative analysis; social-ecological networks; social-ecological systems; social roles
Keywords Plus: COLLECTIVE ACTION; COMMUNICATION; COOPERATION; COMMONS; MANAGEMENT; GOVERNANCE; PUNISHMENT; DILEMMAS; NETWORK
Abstract: Social roles are thought to play an important role in determining the capacity for collective action in a community regarding the use of shared resources. Here we report on the results of a study using a behavioral experimental approach regarding the relationship between social roles and the performance of social-ecological systems. The computer-based irrigation experiment that was the basis of this study mimics the decisions faced by farmers in small-scale irrigation systems. In each of 20 rounds, which are analogous to growing seasons, participants face a two-stage commons dilemma. First they must decide how much to invest in the public infrastructure, e.g., canals and water diversion structures. Second, they must decide how much to extract from the water made available by that public infrastructure. Each round begins with a 60-second communication period before the players make their investment and extraction decisions. By analyzing the chat messages exchanged among participants during the communication stage of the experiment, we coded up to three roles per participant using the scheme of seven roles known to be important in the literature: leader, knowledge generator, connector, follower, moralist, enforcer, and observer. Our study supports the importance of certain social roles (e.g., connector) previously highlighted by several case study analyses. However, using qualitative comparative analysis we found that none of the individual roles was sufficient for groups to succeed, i.e., to reach a certain level of group production. Instead, we found that a combination of at least five roles was necessary for success. In addition, in the context of upstream-downstream asymmetry, we observed a pattern in which social roles assumed by participants tended to differ by their positions. Although our work generated some interesting insights, further research is needed to determine how robust our findings are to different action situations, such as biophysical context, social network, and resource uncertainty.

The paper studies an irrigation game with asymmetric positions and real‐time coordination; it does not implement or systematically vary any explicit “punishment treatment” (such as costly sanctions) in the sense of a standard public goods game with punishment. Therefore, for each parameter, all references to “punishment treatment effect,” “punishment cost,” “punishment magnitude,” etc., are absent unless explicitly noted. In the paper, the word “enforcer” appears as a coded role—someone who threatens not to contribute—but there is no formal or systematic manipulation of a punishment mechanism.

   – Discussed? Yes. There is a 60‐second communication stage before each round in which players can send typed messages. However, the paper’s design specifically restricts chat so that each participant can communicate only with immediate neighbors.

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?

• The paper primarily measures “group performance” via total water extracted (EXT) by all players combined. It also considers other measures such as total group investment, final earnings, and (in an appendix) the percentage of maximum possible earnings.  
• “Infrastructure efficiency” is also mentioned (a percentage that determines water availability), but it is not the same as “group efficiency” in the sense of “actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff.” The paper does note in Appendix 2 that “percentage of the maximum earning” was used as another indicator, but the core indicator is total group extraction (EXT).  
• Therefore, although the authors mention “efficiency” in describing the infrastructure’s functioning, their main dependent variables are total extraction, total investment, and final earnings—not specifically a “treatment effect on group efficiency” from punishment.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

• Mentioned or given a fixed value:  
  1) Number of players (always 5).  
  2) Number of rounds (20 total).  
  3) Chat is enabled in a particular neighbor‐only format.  
  4) Contribution is not “all or nothing” (players invest any integer tokens 0–10).  
  12) The game lasts 20 rounds, but the paper does not specify whether subjects knew it would end exactly at 20.  
  13) Some peer information is shown (neighbors’ investments and appropriation statuses).  

• Not mentioned or not present at all:  
  5) Contribution default, 6) MPCR in the usual sense, 7) Punishment cost, 8) Punishment magnitude, 9) Reward presence, 10) Reward cost, 11) Reward magnitude, 14) Punisher identity revealed, 15) Rewarder identity revealed.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?

• None. The paper does not present any formal “punishment treatment” or manipulate parameters related to punishment or reward. As a result, it does not report any effect sizes or predictions about changing these 15 parameters with respect to a punishment treatment effect.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

• The paper provides no direct basis for predicting how systematically changing any of these 15 parameters would affect a punishment‐based treatment’s impact on group efficiency. The experiment does not include a formal punishment mechanism with specified cost/magnitude, nor does it vary number of players, number of rounds, or chat conditions in a way linked to punishment. Consequently, one cannot infer any punishment‐treatment‐efficiency predictions from this paper. The safest conclusion is that the paper offers little to no prediction on those points.

Abstract: We study impersonal exchange and ask how agents can behave honestly in anonymous transactions without contracts. We analyze repeated anonymous random matching games, where agents observe only their own transactions. Little is known about cooperation in this setting beyond the prisoner's dilemma. The paper is a purely theoretical analysis of anonymous, random-matching repeated games.  It is not an experiment and it never studies a “punishment treatment effect” on group efficiency in a public–goods game.  Consequently, virtually none of the 15 design parameters that matter in experimental public-goods games appear in the text, figures or tables.  Below is a parameter-by-parameter checklist that adheres strictly to what the paper does (and, more importantly, does not) say.

----------------------------------------------------------------
CHECK OF THE 15 PARAMETERS
----------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Players are partitioned into two “communities,” each of size M (Section 3.1).  
   • Systematic variation & effect on punishment treatment?  The paper derives a minimum community size  (call it M̲) needed for its equilibrium construction (Proposition 2 and Section 3.4).  This has nothing to do with an experimental “punishment treatment,” let alone with group efficiency.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  Only in the sense that the repeated game is infinite; the authors divide play into three “phases” whose lengths (Tᴵ and Tᴵᴵ) are chosen endogenously.  
   • No discussion of varying a finite horizon or of any treatment effect.

3. Chat allowed?  
   • Not mentioned.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Not mentioned (the stage games studied are general; the illustrative “product-choice” game has binary actions, but this is not tied to any public-goods design nor to punishment).

5. Contribution default / endowment return?  
   • Not mentioned.

6. MPCR or multiplier  
   • Not mentioned.

7. Cost to impose punishment  
8. Magnitude of punishment  
9. Presence of a reward option  
10. Cost to reward  
11. Magnitude of reward  
   • None of these five parameters appear anywhere in the paper.  Punishment here is strategic “Nash reversion,” not a costly peer-to-peer sanction with adjustable parameters.

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
   • The game is infinite; calendar time is common knowledge (Section 7.1).  No discussion of varying this.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • The informational structure is “private monitoring”: each player observes only his own match; never sees others’ payoffs.  No variation studied.

14. Is the identity of a punisher revealed?  
15. Is the identity of a rewarder revealed?  
   • Not applicable; there are no peer sanctions or rewards in the usual experimental sense.

----------------------------------------------------------------
A–D SUMMARY
----------------------------------------------------------------
A: Dependent variables in the paper  
   • The authors are interested in equilibrium payoffs (vectors in ℝ²) and whether play can approximate the Pareto-efficient stage-game outcome.  
   • They never compute “group efficiency” in the experimental sense ( realised total payoff / maximum possible payoff ), nor do they measure contributions or cooperation rates.

B: How many of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   • Only 3:  
     – #1 (number of players, called M)  
     – #2 (rounds, but only as “infinite” with internally chosen phase lengths)  
     – #13 (information display: players do NOT see peer outcomes)  
   • The other 12 parameters are not mentioned at all.

C: For how many parameters is there any discussion of *systematically varying* the parameter and measuring a punishment treatment effect?  
   • Zero.  The paper never runs (or even imagines) a punishment vs. no-punishment comparison on efficiency, so there are no effect sizes, no figures, no tables that bear on any of the 15 parameters in that sense.

D: Predictive content for a public-goods punishment treatment based solely on this paper  
   • Almost none.  The model analyses strategic “community enforcement” via infinite-horizon Nash reversion, not the costly peer-punishment institutions used in laboratory public-goods experiments.  Therefore, the paper provides no numerical or directional predictions about how manipulating the 15 experimental parameters would change the efficiency impact of adding punishment.  The only weak hint is that a larger population (higher M) makes grim-trigger-style punishment harder and requires higher patience; but even that result is framed for abstract repeated games, not for efficiency in a punishment treatment.

In short, the paper does not supply usable empirical leverage on any of the 15 design parameters with respect to a punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter analysis based solely on the content of the provided paper and how (if at all) it discusses each of the 15 public‐goods‐game parameters in relation to punishment, reward, or efficiency. In short, the paper does not frame its field study in terms of a public goods experiment with systematic parameter variations, nor does it speak directly of “efficiency” (i.e., total group payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff), or a “punishment treatment effect.” It focuses instead on the plausibility of sustaining mutual help (i.e., cooperation) in an overlapping‐generations (OLG) labor union setting under limited observability. Any references to costs, benefits, rewards, or punishments are discussed in a qualitative sense (e.g., “helping” or “not helping”), rather than as an experimentally varied parameter.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Discussion in paper?  
     The paper does mention that the Tokyo Managers' Union has a membership that fluctuates (Example: 231 members at one time; ~100 enter and ~100 exit in a year), but it never systematically varies or experimentally manipulates “number of players.”  
   • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency when varied?  
     Not discussed. No numerical effect sizes or predictions are provided.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Discussion in paper?  
     The paper treats the union as an OLG repeated game with a continual inflow and outflow of members. It does not treat the interaction as a fixed series of rounds with a known end.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency when varied?  
     Not discussed.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussion in paper?  
     The paper does not set up a specific “chat” feature as in a lab experiment. It only notes that members meet occasionally (e.g., in monthly or bimonthly meetings), but there is no systematic analysis of “chat or no chat.”  
   • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency when varied?  
     Not discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Discussion in paper?  
     The paper does not use a public‐goods‐style “contribution” framework. “Helping” takes many forms (e.g., attending protests or hearings), but these are not formalized as all‐or‐nothing decisions.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency when varied?  
     Not discussed.

5. Is the contribution default (choose how much to move from the public fund)?  
   • Discussion in paper?  
     No. The paper does not frame help in terms of default or partial contributions.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency when varied?  
     Not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
   • Discussion in paper?  
     The paper speaks only informally about the “benefit” b and “cost” c of helping in a repeated interaction. It does not use or vary an MPCR factor, and it does not connect b and c to any group‐efficiency measure.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency when varied?  
     Not discussed as a systematic variation. The paper only notes that cooperation may be sustained if b > 8c in a particular illustrative model (not as an experimental result but as a mathematical condition for one possible equilibrium).

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussion in paper?  
     The paper repeatedly uses the terms “reward” or “punish” conceptually (e.g., refusing help to a member who does not help others), but it does not define any explicit “cost to punish” or treat it as a parameter.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency when varied?  
     Not discussed.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted per punishment unit)  
   • Discussion in paper?  
     No explicit mention of a formal punishment‐magnitude parameter. “Punishment” in the union is effectively “being left with no one to help you,” not a parametric penalty.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency when varied?  
     Not discussed.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussion in paper?  
     The paper talks about “helping” as a general way of rewarding cooperative members, but it is not set up as an experimentally toggled or measured “reward is on/off” variable.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency when varied?  
     Not discussed.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Discussion in paper?  
      The cost of helping is referred to generally (time, effort, missing work), but there is no systematic parameter for “reward cost.”  
    • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency when varied?  
      Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded for each reward)  
    • Discussion in paper?  
      Same as above—there is no mention of any formal payoff magnitude for a “reward.” The paper frames help as a reciprocal act, but not as a numeric reward.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency when varied?  
      Not discussed.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    • Discussion in paper?  
      The union context is indefinite, continuous inflow/outflow. The paper does not speak of members “knowing the final round” or not.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency when varied?  
      Not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained or lost)?  
    • Discussion in paper?  
      The study emphasizes “limited observability,” noting that union members do NOT systematically know how much or how often others have helped. No formal display of outcomes is discussed.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency when varied?  
      Not discussed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Discussion in paper?  
      There is no direct discussion of a “punisher” identity being revealed. “Punishment” here mostly means not receiving help, and no systematic variation of “transparent” vs. “anonymous” punishment is analyzed.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency when varied?  
      Not discussed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Discussion in paper?  
      In principle, people see who shows up at their protest or hearing, but the paper does not treat “visibility of the rewarder” as a systematically varied parameter.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment or efficiency when varied?  
      Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary:

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper does not use “group efficiency” (i.e., actual total payoff over maximum possible payoff) as a dependent variable. Its focus is on whether cooperation (helping) can be sustained in a union despite high turnover, rather than on measuring efficiency in a public‐goods‐game sense. The outcomes of interest are:  
     – Observed cooperation (e.g., members attending each other’s labor dispute protests, legal hearings, etc.)  
     – Qualitative descriptions of how members reciprocate help under limited observability.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Strictly speaking, none of the 15 public‐goods‐game parameters (1–15) appear either in name or in a systematically varied fashion in the paper. The authors do invoke a notional “cost” (c) and “benefit” (b) of helping, but this is not formalized as MPCR or as a custom “punishment magnitude,” “reward cost,” etc.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. The paper does not systematically vary or discuss any of these 15 parameters, nor does it present effect sizes for changes in parameters on outcomes such as efficiency or cooperation rate.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper provides almost no basis for making such predictions. It does not treat its setting as a controlled public goods game with parametric manipulation. Author Keywords: Evolutionary game; Cooperation; Q-learning; Social punishment; Multilayer network
Keywords Plus: GAMES; DYNAMICS; MEMORY
Abstract: Cooperative dynamics are crucial in balancing individual and collective behaviors, with evolutionary game theory providing deep insights into this complex interplay. Complex social systems are often characterized by their multilayered structures, within which agents assume diverse roles, interacting and coupling through feedback, profoundly influencing each other across different domains. Given the efficacy of reinforcement learning in analyzing game-theoretic behaviors, we introduce a novel inter-layer feedback mechanism with selfadapting Q-learning algorithm, to explore the evolution of cooperative behaviors within multilayered network structures. One layer is named the classic layer, which comprises cooperators and defectors, while the other layer is named the management layer and contains punishers and inactive individuals. Based on self-adapting Q-learning, agents in management layer decide whether to choose punishment action through the proposed inter-layer feedback mechanism, which induces a game transition in the classic layer. The agents' strategies in classic layer provide feedback to management layer's agents and influence their strategy choices. Simulation results reveal that the lower punishment cost and greater punishment severity and reputation factors can facilitate the evolution of cooperation. Furthermore, the critical effect of the self-adapting Q-learning algorithm under the inter-layer feedback mechanism enables agents to engage in introspective learning, rather than mere imitation. Finally, the variations in the Q-value and state transition probabilities are explored that the interlayer feedback mechanism incrementally increases the Q-value of cooperators over time, thereby augmenting the frequency of cooperation within the entire process from a microscopic perspective. This research aims to offer crucial insights into the dynamics of cooperative behavior within the social punishment dilemma through the perspectives of artificial intelligence.

     – p = 0.5 & β = 0.5 ⇒ Full cooperation and sustainable resource.  
     – With very high intrinsic growth r and low p, even β = 0.5 does **not** eliminate full defection.

Abstract: Social expectations guide people's evaluations of others' behaviors, but the origins of these expectations remain unclear. It is traditionally thought that people's expectations depend on their past observations of others' behavior, and people harshly judge atypical behavior. Here, we considered that social expectations are also influenced by a drive for reciprocity, and people evaluate others' actions by reflecting on their own decisions. To compare these views, we performed four studies. Study 1 used an Ultimatum Game task where participants alternated Responder and Proposer roles. Modeling participants' expectations suggested they evaluated the fairness of received offers via comparisons to their own offers. Study 2 replicated these findings and showed that observing selfish behavior (lowball offers) only promoted acceptance of selfishness if observers started acting selfishly themselves. Study 3 generalized the findings, demonstrating that they also arise in the Public Goods Game, emerge cross-culturally, and apply to antisocial punishment whereby selfish players punish generosity. Finally, Study 4 introduced the Trust Game and showed that participants trusted players who reciprocated their behavior, even if it was selfish, as much as they trusted generous players. Overall, this research shows that social expectations and evaluations are rooted in drives for reciprocity. This carries theoretical implications, speaking to a parallel in the mechanisms driving both decision-making and social evaluations, along with practical importance for understanding and promoting cooperation.

Below I list each of the 15 design parameters and report, strictly on the basis of the paper you supplied,

• whether the parameter is ever described (and its value, if it is)  
• whether the authors ever **systematically vary** that parameter, or predict/estimate what would happen to a *punishment-treatment effect* (for any dependent variable) if the parameter were varied.  
When a numerical value is given in the text, table, or figure, I reproduce it; when a statistical effect of varying the parameter is reported, I give the coefficient or test statistic and its location in the paper.

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned: yes.  Study 1, 2, 4 use a 2-player Ultimatum Game; Study 3 uses a 4-player Public Goods Game.  
   • Systematically varied: no.  The paper never manipulates group size, nor models how changing it would alter the punishment treatment effect.  No effect size available.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned: yes.  Study 1 = 384 trials; Study 2 = 144 trials; Study 3 = 10 rounds; Study 4 = 60–120 trials (5 or 10 blocks of 12).  
   • Systematically varied: no.  Round length differs across studies for logistical reasons only; no predictions or estimates of its causal impact on punishment or efficiency.

3. Chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned: no.  No chat or communication channel is ever described.

4. “All-or-nothing” contributions  
   • Mentioned: indirectly.  In the UG participants choose among five discrete splits; in the PGG they can contribute any number of the 20 tokens (0–20).  
   • Systematically varied: no, and the all-or-nothing feature is never analysed as an experimental factor.

5. Contribution default / take-frame vs give-frame  
   • Mentioned: no.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned: yes.  In the PGG the pot is “increased to 160 % of its original value” (MPCR = 0.4 for each of four players).  
   • Systematically varied: no.  Only the single value 1.6 is used; there is no analysis of how a different MPCR would alter punishment or efficiency.

7. Punishment cost (actor side)  
   • Mentioned: yes.  
     – UG: Responder “rejects” at the cost of forgoing the proposed amount (implicit, not quantified).  
     – PGG: “Each token spent would lead to the targeted player losing three tokens” (cost = 1 token).  
   • Systematically varied: no.  No alternative cost levels and no predictions of their influence are provided.

8. Punishment magnitude (target side)  
   • Mentioned: yes.  
     – UG rejection removes the entire proposed payoff from both players.  
     – PGG: 1 token spent → 3-token deduction.  
   • Systematically varied: no; no estimates reported.

9. Whether a reward option is enabled  
   • Mentioned: no.  The experiments use punishment (and acceptance), never peer reward.

10. Reward cost  
   • Mentioned: no.

11. Reward magnitude  
   • Mentioned: no.

12. Whether the number of rounds is common knowledge  
   • Mentioned: not explicitly.  The text does not report telling subjects whether the game length was known or unknown, nor does it vary that information.

13. Peer outcomes shown  
   • Mentioned: yes.  In UG subjects see whether the opponent accepted/rejected and the amount kept/given; in PGG they see every player’s contribution each round.  
   • Systematically varied: no.  Visibility is fixed in each game; no comparison to a hidden-information condition is made.

14. Whether the punisher’s identity is revealed  
   • Mentioned: yes for the PGG (“Participants were told of punishments directed toward them but were *not* told who specifically punished them”).  
   • Systematically varied: no.

15. Whether the rewarder’s identity is revealed  
   • Not applicable (no reward stage), therefore never mentioned.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A.  Use of “group efficiency” as a dependent variable?  
    • No.  The paper analyses rejection likelihood (UG), tokens spent on punishment (PGG), Trust-Game investments, proposed offers, and contributions.  “Efficiency” (total or average payoff divided by the cooperative optimum) is never computed or discussed.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
    • Seven parameters appear: 1, 2, 4 (implicitly), 6, 7, 8, 13, 14.  The remaining eight (3, 5, 9-12, 15) are never discussed.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper examine the effect of *systematically varying* the parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
    • Zero.  None of the 15 parameters is experimentally manipulated or modelled as a moderator of the punishment treatment effect on *any* dependent variable, let alone on efficiency.  Consequently no numerical effect sizes of such variations are available.

D.  Predictions that can be made (and their limits) about how these parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, **based solely on the paper**:  
    • Because the authors never study efficiency and never vary any of the listed parameters, the paper supplies almost no direct basis for forecasting how changes in those parameters would raise or lower group efficiency when punishment is available.  
    • The only (very indirect) hints are:  
        – Punishment occurs in both 2-player and 4-player games, but nothing in the results compares the *magnitude* of its behavioural or welfare effects across those group sizes.  
        – Changing MPCR, punishment cost, punishment magnitude, visibility of punisher identity, etc., could plausibly matter, but the paper offers no data or theorising specific to such manipulations.  
    • Therefore, any quantitative or even qualitative prediction about how the 15 parameters (alone or in interaction) affect the punishment-induced change in *efficiency* would have to come from literature other than this paper.  On the evidence provided here, little to no prediction can be made.

Article Title: Shadow of conflict: How past conflict influences group cooperation and the use of punishment
Source Title: ORGANIZATIONAL BEHAVIOR AND HUMAN DECISION PROCESSES
Author Keywords: Conflict; Conflict resolution; Cooperation; Behavioral spill-over; Punishment
Keywords Plus: CUTTHROAT COOPERATION; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; INTEGRATIVE MODEL; RECONCILIATION; IDENTITY; PERPETRATOR; DIVERSITY; VICTIM; NEEDS; PROSOCIALITY
Abstract: Intergroup conflict profoundly affects the welfare of groups and can deteriorate intergroup relations long after the conflict is over. Here, we experimentally investigate how the experience of an intergroup conflict influences the ability of groups to establish cooperation after conflict. We induced conflict by using a repeated attackerdefender game in which groups of four are divided into two 'attackers' that can invest resources to take away resources from the other two participants in the role of 'defenders.' After the conflict, groups engaged in a repeated public goods game with peer-punishment, in which group members could invest resources to benefit the group and punish other group members for their decisions. Previous conflict did not significantly reduce group cooperation compared to a control treatment in which groups did not experience the intergroup conflict. However, when having experienced an intergroup conflict, individuals punished free-riding during the repeated public goods game less harshly and did not react to punishment by previous attackers, ultimately reducing group welfare. This result reveals an important boundary condition for peer punishment institutions. Peer punishment is less able to efficiently promote cooperation amid a 'shadow of conflict.' In a third treatment, we tested whether such 'maladaptive' punishment patterns induced by previous conflict can be mitigated by hiding the group members' conflict roles during the subsequent public goods provision game. We find more cooperation when individuals could not identify each other as (previous) attackers and defenders and maladaptive punishment patterns disappeared. Results suggest that intergroup conflict undermines past perpetrators' legitimacy to enforce cooperation norms. More generally, results reveal that past conflict can reduce the effectiveness of institutions for managing the commons.

   • Mentioned: Yes – cost = 1 unit to the punisher.

    • Not applicable (no reward).

12. Do players know the number of remaining rounds?  
    • Mentioned: Yes – the round counter (“round x of 15”) was constantly visible.  
    • Systematic variation discussed: No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mentioned: Yes – after each stage subjects saw every player’s contributions, payoffs, punishment given and received.  
    • Systematic variation discussed: No.

14. Is the identity of each punisher revealed to the target?  
    • Mentioned: Yes – the feedback screen displayed how many deduction points each specific group member assigned.  
    • Systematic variation discussed: No.

15. Is the identity of each rewarder revealed?  
    • Not applicable (no reward stage).

----------------------------------------------------------------
Summary requested in items A – D
----------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables used in the paper  
   • The paper’s main outcome variables are (i) cooperation (amount contributed), (ii) earnings/payoffs (contributions + public good return – punishment costs – punishment received), and several punishment-process measures (punishment given, received, reaction to punishment).  
   • “Efficiency” in the sense of “total group payoff divided by maximum possible payoff” is NOT explicitly computed, although earnings are a direct ingredient of efficiency.  Thus, earnings and efficiency are related but not identical in the paper.

Abstract: Cooperation in modern society is based on mutual trust and reputation information can well reflect people's social image. Good social norms encourage people to cooperate with high-reputation (or called 'good') individuals and severely punish those who defect 'good' individuals. However, the existing research lacks a unified criterion of how to evaluate the behavior when interacting with low-reputation (or called 'bad') people. Based on public goods games, we focus on exploring second-order social norms that can improve the evolution of cooperation in this study. Parameters to control the reward and punishment intensity through increasing or decreasing one's reputation when interacting with 'bad' individuals are introduced. Simulation results show that this reward and punishment mechanism through reputation can effectively promote the evolution of cooperation in both well-mixed and latticed populations. Under certain high-reputation threshold environments, a well-mixed population structure can even promote cooperation more significantly than a lattice network. However, increasing reward intensity for cooperating with 'bad' individuals cannot further improve cooperation, but in a high-reputation threshold environment, increasing punishment intensity for defecting 'bad' individuals can further improve cooperation. Below, each of the 15 parameters is treated in turn.  
For every parameter I state  

(1) whether the paper even mentions the parameter and, if so, what concrete value(s) are used;  
(2) whether the authors **systematically vary** that parameter and draw a causal conclusion about how the change modifies the **punishment treatment effect** (i.e., the difference between the ‘traditional model with no reputation-based reward/punishment’ and the model that contains the reward-and-punishment module).  Whenever an approximate numerical effect can be read from a figure or table, it is given.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
(1) Mentioned.  Main simulations: lattice of size L = 100 × 100 ⇒ N = 10 000.  Robustness check: well–mixed population with N = 10 000.  
(2) Not varied.  No statement on how changing N would alter the punishment treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
(1) Only that simulations normally run 10⁴ MCS (sometimes 5 × 10⁴).  
(2) Not varied, no prediction.

3. Chat enabled?  
Not mentioned.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
(1) Fixed at c = 1 for every co-operator, 0 for every defector → yes, all-or-nothing.  
(2) Not varied.

5. Contribution default (give-back option)  
Not mentioned.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor r  
(1) Central parameter.  r is scanned widely (≈1.3–6).  
(2) Yes – systematically varied.  Main result: adding the reward-&-punishment module dramatically lowers the critical r at which cooperation and hence efficiency can emerge.  
    • Baseline (no reputation mechanism): cooperation starts only at r ≈ 3.75 and full cooperation at r ≈ 5.5 (Fig. 9, w = 1).  
    • With reward + punishment, Panel 1(d):  
        – Z = 10 ⇒ cooperation appears at r ≈ 2.7 (Δ ≈ –1.0)  
        – Z = 30 ⇒ r ≈ 2.5 (Δ ≈ –1.3)  
        – Z = 50 ⇒ r ≈ 2.1 (Δ ≈ –1.6)  
        – Z = 90 ⇒ r ≈ 1.4 (Δ ≈ –2.3)  
        – Z = 98 ⇒ r ≈ 1.3 (Δ ≈ –2.4)  
   The lower r, the larger the treatment advantage over the baseline; however the paper gives no direct efficiency numbers, only ρ_c.

7. Punishment cost to punisher  
No monetary or reputational cost to the punisher is modelled; parameter absent.

8. Punishment magnitude  
(1) Punishment for ‘defecting a bad individual’ is P₂ ∈ {0,1,2,3}.  A constant –5 is used for ‘defecting a good individual’.  
(2) Yes – P₂ is systematically varied (Fig. 4, Figs. 5–7).  
    • High-threshold environment (Z = 90 or 98): raising P₂ from 1 to 3 reduces the critical r for cooperation by ≈0.2–0.3 and quickly drives defectors to extinction (Fig. 4 bottom rows; Fig. 6).  
    • Low-threshold environment (Z = 10 or 30): changing P₂ has “no significant effect”; the r–ρ_c curves almost coincide (Fig. 4, top rows).  
   No group-efficiency data reported; only ρ_c.

9. Reward enabled  
(1) Four treatments are compared (Fig. 1): neither reward nor punishment, punishment-only, reward-only, and reward+punishment.  
(2) Yes – qualitative conclusions:  
    • Reward+punishment > baseline.  
    • Reward-only or punishment-only can even under-perform baseline (Panels 1(b)&(c)).  
   No numbers on efficiency; only ρ_c.

10. Reward cost  
Not modelled.

11. Reward magnitude  
(1) P₁ (increase in reputation for ‘cooperate with a bad individual’) varied from 1 to 5 (Fig. 4 columns).  
(2) Yes – authors report that “increasing P₁ above 1 does **not** further improve cooperation”; the r thresholds remain unchanged.  Hence no detectable effect on the punishment treatment effect.

12. Number of rounds known  
Not mentioned.

13. Peer outcomes shown  
Not mentioned.

14. Punisher identity known  
Not applicable.

15. Rewarder identity known  
Not applicable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY  
A. Dependent variables  
– Main dependent variable: frequency of cooperators (ρ_c).  
– Secondary variables: average payoff per strategy and average reputation (Fig. 2b), but the *group efficiency* (total payoff / maximal payoff) is **never explicitly computed**. Payoff and efficiency are therefore not interchangeable in this paper.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
Six: #1, #4, #6, #8, #9, #11.  (The rest are absent.)

C. For how many parameters is a *systematic* variation linked to the punishment treatment effect?  
Three: #6 (MPCR), #8 (punishment magnitude), #11/#9 (reward magnitude / presence).  Effects are all reported in terms of changes in ρ_c; no efficiency figures are given.

D. Predictions (efficiency-focused) that can be made **solely from the paper**  
Because the paper hardly reports group payoffs, only a few tentative efficiency-related statements are possible:  
1. Lower multiplication factors r will gain most in efficiency from adding the punishment module because cooperation can arise at r ≈1.3–2.7 instead of 3.75.  
2. In high-threshold environments (Z ≥ 90), increasing punishment magnitude (P₂) should further raise efficiency by wiping out defectors; in low-threshold environments it should not matter.  
3. Turning reward on without punishment, or vice-versa, is likely to *reduce* efficiency relative to the full combination or even to the baseline.  
4. Once reward is on, making it larger (P₁>1) does not change outcomes, so no additional efficiency gains are expected.  
5. No inference can be drawn for the remaining 11 parameters because they are not analysed.

In short, the paper allows confident efficiency predictions for only three of the fifteen parameters, and only in the indirect sense that higher cooperation frequencies normally translate into higher efficiency. All other parameters are either kept constant or not discussed, so the paper offers little guidance on their influence.

Abstract: We investigate the effect of voice exercised through comment-based participation on individual public goods provision.
