conditions and reports how the **punishment treatment effect** (adding enforcement) changes.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   ✓  Five participants per group: 4 contributors + 1 rule-maker (p. 9, §3).  
   Systematic variation? No. The size is fixed, so the paper gives no prediction about how changing the group size would alter the punishment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   ✓  Stage 2 has 5 games × 5 rounds = 25 rounds (Table 1).  
   No variation. No predictions.

3. Chat enabled?  
   ✓  “Subjects were not permitted to communicate in any way…” (§3). Always false; no variation or prediction.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   ✓  Players choose any whole number 0–25 (Appendix A description). Always continuous; no variation.

5. Contribution default / refund frame  
   –  Not used or discussed.

6. MPCR (multiplication factor)  
   ✓  Fixed at 0.4 (p. 10). Not varied; no predictions.

7. Cost to impose 1 unit of peer punishment  
   –  No peer punishment at all. The exogenous fine carries no cost for players, but that cost is not a treatment variable. No systematic variation.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss per unit imposed)  
   ✓  Fine = 25 points, applied with 50 % probability (§3). Magnitude never changed, so the paper does not predict how altering the magnitude would alter the punishment effect.

9–11. Reward enabled / reward cost / reward magnitude  
   –  No rewards in any treatment.

12. Is the horizon known?  
   ✓  Players are told each game has 5 rounds; the schedule is common knowledge (implicit in instructions). Horizon length is never varied; no predictions.

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
   ✓  End-of-round summary shows each peer’s contribution and sanction status (§3). This visibility is constant; no predictions.

14. Do punished players learn who punished them?  
   –  Not applicable (punishment is by the software).

15. Do rewarded players learn who rewarded them?  
   –  Not applicable.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
NUMERICAL EFFECTS THAT CAN BE LINKED TO ANY OF THE 15 PARAMETERS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Because none of the 15 parameters is systematically varied, no direct numerical effect of a parameter change on the **punishment treatment effect** (enforcement vs. no enforcement) can be extracted.  
The only “punishment treatment effect” the paper reports is the **presence vs. absence** of enforcement:

• Enforcement only vs. control: +3.13 points to individual contribution (Table 2, model 1).  
• Comment + enforcement vs. comment only: +5.99 points (Table 2, model 1).  
These results are tied to a single fixed punishment design (magnitude = 25, probability = 0.5), so they do not speak to parameters 7-8.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Dependent variables  
   • Group efficiency / total or average payoff: NOT measured.  
   • Reported DVs: (i) individual contribution level, (ii) binary and relative non-compliance,
     (iii) chosen minimum-contribution rule (MCR).  
     These differ from “efficiency”: they reflect behaviour, not earnings relative to the social optimum.

B. Parameters mentioned (9/15)  
   1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7 (implicitly zero cost), 8, 12, 13 are described.  
   Parameters 5, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15 are not mentioned.

C. Parameters whose **systematic variation** is analysed for their impact on the punishment treatment effect: 0/15.  
   The paper keeps every listed parameter constant; only the presence/absence of enforcement and comments is manipulated.

D. Predicting punishment-treatment effects on efficiency using only this paper  
   • The paper offers almost no leverage: efficiency is never computed, and none of the 15 parameters is varied.  
   • The only qualitative inference possible is that, with the specific fixed settings (5 players, MPCR = 0.4, fine = 25 with 50 % probability, full information), introducing enforcement raises contributions; adding comments further amplifies this.  
   • Beyond that, the paper gives **little to no basis** for predicting how changing group size, MPCR, fine size, horizon length, information, etc. would influence the efficiency effect of punishment, because those dimensions were never varied or analysed.

Hence, while the study is informative about *whether* enforcement helps under one specific design, it provides no systematic evidence to forecast how the 15 detailed parameters (or their interactions) would modulate the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Below I go through the 15 design-features one by one, quoting exactly what the paper tells us and noting whether it ever shows what would happen if the feature were systematically varied with and without punishment.  “Punishment treatment effect” ( PTE ) is understood as the difference between an environment that contains a peer-punishment option and an otherwise identical environment that does not.  The paper never actually runs such a comparison, so in every case the best we can do is to note whether the authors vary the parameter at all and, if they do, what dependent variable(s) they examine (cooperation rate, reward share, etc.).


────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. NUMBER OF PLAYERS (GROUP SIZE)
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  A parameter “G” sets initial group size and therefore average carrying capacity.  
     ‑ Baseline G = 20 (Table 1).  
     ‑ Figure 4c varies G from 10 to 100.
   • Systematic variation & numerical effect?  
     The only reported outcome is the stationary fraction of cooperators (not efficiency and not the punishment treatment effect).  Figure 4c shows that larger G → lower cooperation, but exact numbers are not given in the text.  No comparison to a “no-punishment” baseline is provided, so no PTE can be inferred.

2. NUMBER OF ROUNDS
   • Mentioned?  No.  Generations are infinite and non-overlapping; no finite “round” structure is modelled.
   • Systematic variation?  None.

3. IS CHAT ENABLED?
   • Not mentioned or modelled.

4. ALL-OR-NOTHING CONTRIBUTION?
   • Yes, but fixed.  Agents are either “cooperate” (pay C, deliver B) or “defect” (pay 0, deliver 0).  
   • Never varied.

5. “CONTRIBUTION-DEFAULT / WITHDRAW” FRAME?
   • Not mentioned; not modelled.

6. MPCR / MULTIPLICATION FACTOR
   • Benefit of cooperating B = 0.9, Cost C = 0.1 (Table 1).  
   • These parameters are kept constant; no systematic variation, no PTE.

7. COST TO IMPOSE ONE UNIT OF PUNISHMENT
8. PUNISHMENT MAGNITUDE PER UNIT
   • The model folds both quantities into one “institutional efficiency” parameter E that applies to *both* reward and punishment.  No separate cost or magnitude parameters exist, and the authors do not isolate punishment from reward.  
   • They do vary E (Figures 4a and 5b).  Larger E ⇒ higher cooperation.  Again, no baseline without punishment, so no PTE.

9. IS A REWARD OPTION ENABLED?
   • Always enabled; never switched off; no comparison to a punishment-only or no-reward condition.

10. COST TO GRANT A UNIT OF REWARD
11. REWARD MAGNITUDE
   • As with punishment, both are absorbed into E and never examined separately.

12. ARE THE NUMBER OF ROUNDS COMMON KNOWLEDGE?
13. ARE PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN?
14. IS THE PUNISHER IDENTIFIED?
15. IS THE REWARDER IDENTIFIED?
   • None of these information-display variables appear in the model or text.
   • No systematic variation whatsoever.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables used
    • The paper’s main outcomes are (i) fraction of cooperators in the stationary distribution, (ii) average group preference parameters h and r, and sometimes (iii) group carrying capacity.  
    • It never reports “group efficiency” (total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff), nor total payoff, nor the direct payoff difference between punishment and no-punishment treatments.

B.  How many of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?
    • 4 of 15:  (1) group size G, (4) all-or-nothing contribution (binary action is fixed, not varied), (6) MPCR-like variables B and C (not varied), and (7-11) combined indirectly via E.  
    • The remaining 11 parameters are absent.

C.  How many parameters are *systematically varied* and linked to any outcome?
    • Two:  group size G (parameter 1) and institutional efficiency E (which is not on the user’s list but is the only parameter that loosely maps onto punishment/reward “cost–benefit”).  
    • Neither variation is analysed in terms of a punishment treatment effect, only in terms of equilibrium cooperation.

D.  What predictions can be made about the PTE on efficiency solely from this paper?
    • Very little.  Because no condition without punishment is ever simulated, the magnitude—let alone the sign—of the punishment treatment effect on efficiency cannot be extracted.  
    • The paper does suggest that, when punishment (and reward) can be coordinated institutionally and when the conversion efficiency E is high enough, cooperation (and hence total group payoff) can be sustained; when E or group size is unfavourable, cooperation collapses.  But these statements concern absolute cooperation levels, not the incremental effect of adding punishment to an otherwise identical game.

In short, the paper is valuable for modelling the *endogenous* evolution of institutional rules, but it does not furnish quantitative or even qualitative leverage for predicting how any of the 15 experimental design parameters – singly or in interaction – would alter the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Article Title: Cooperation, conformity, and the coevolutionary problem of trait associations

Abstract: In large scale social systems, coordinated or cooperative outcomes become difficult because encounters between kin or repeated encounters between friends are infrequent. Even punishment of noncooperators does not entirely alleviate the dilemma. One important mechanism for achieving cooperative outcomes in such social systems is conformist bias where individuals copy the behavior performed by the majority of their group mates. Conformist bias enhances group competition by both stabilizing behaviors within groups and increasing variance between groups. Due to this group competition effect, conformist bias is thought to have been an important driver of human social complexity and cultural diversity. However, conformist bias only evolves indirectly through associations with other traits, and I show that such associations are more difficult to obtain than previously expected. Specifically, I show that initial measures of population structure must be strong in order for a strong association between conformist bias and cooperative behaviors (cooperation and costly punishment) to evolve and for these traits to reach high frequencies. Additionally, the required initial level of association does not evolve de novo in simulations run over long timescales. This suggests that the coevolution of cooperative behaviors and conformist bias alone may not explain the high levels of cooperation within human groups, though conformist bias may still play an important role in combination with other social and demographic forces. ----------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER–BY–PARAMETER INSPECTION
----------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players in a group  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Groups are of size N and the paper runs the model for N = 4, 16, 64, 256 (Table 1; Figs. 2–4).  
   • Systematic variation studied?  Yes.  The only parameter of the 15 that is actually varied in the paper is N.  
   • Reported consequences of that variation?  
     – Dependent variables examined: median allele frequencies of “cooperate,” “punish,” and “conform” (Figs. 2, 4).  
     – Qualitative result: Larger N lowers the threshold F_ST needed for the joint rise of cooperation and punishment (Fig. 2). For N = 64 or 256, a within–group F_ST ≳ 0.2 is enough; for N = 4 the threshold is higher.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  No.  The model runs for many “time steps,” but nothing equivalent to an experimental “round” is defined, and its length is not manipulated.  
   • Systematic variation?  None.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned?  No.  
   • Systematic variation?  None.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Mentioned?  Implicitly yes.  Each individual either “cooperates” (contributes) or does not – a binary choice.  
   • Systematic variation?  No.  The binary structure is fixed; it is never compared with a continuous-contribution version.

5. Contribution default / refund frame  
   • Mentioned?  No.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  Not directly.  The game pay­off is encoded with a fixed cost of cooperation c_C = 0.2 (Table 1); the benefit side is embedded in the group conflict rule and is not parameterised as an MPCR.  
   • Systematic variation?  None.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   • Mentioned?  Yes: c_R = 0.2 (Table 1).  
   • Systematic variation?  No.  c_R is fixed.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss to target)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes: c_P = 0.8 (Table 1).  
   • Systematic variation?  No.  c_P is fixed.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Mentioned?  No.  There is no reward institution in the model.  
   • Systematic variation?  None.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   • Both not applicable (no rewards).

12. Horizon known (do players know when the game ends)?  
   • Mentioned?  No analogue in the model; not discussed.  
   • Systematic variation?  None.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Mentioned?  Very indirectly.  “Pay-off based learners” can observe a partner’s pay-off, but whether that information is public or private is not varied.  
   • Systematic variation?  None.

14. Is the punisher identified to the target?  
   • Mentioned?  No.  
   • Systematic variation?  None.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
   • Not applicable (no rewards).

----------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
----------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables  
    • The paper never reports group efficiency, total pay-off, or any pay-off-based efficiency measure.  
    • Reported outcomes are:  
        – Allele (or strategy) frequency of Cooperation, Punishment, Conformist bias

Abstract: We experimentally study punishment patterns across network structures, and their effect on cooperation. In a repeated public goods setting, subjects can only observe and punish their neighbors. Centralized structures (like the star network) outperform other incomplete networks and reach contribution levels like the ones observed in a complete network. Below is a parameter-by-parameter account, based strictly on the content of the provided paper. For each of the 15 parameters, I state:  
• Whether the paper discusses it (and if so, what specific value or setting it takes).  
• Whether the paper makes any prediction about the effect of systematically varying that parameter on the punishment treatment effect (i.e., the difference in efficiency when punishment is introduced) for any dependent variable.  

————————————————————————————————————————  
1) Number of players  
• Mentioned? Yes. Every experimental group has exactly four players (p. 8, Section III, “a group G is composed by four agents”). This is not varied in the experiment; all sessions use groups of size four.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Prediction about its effect if varied? The paper does not discuss how changing the number of players would affect punishment or efficiency.  

2) Number of rounds  
• Mentioned? Yes. Each session has 20 rounds of the baseline VCM (no-punishment) followed by an unannounced restart of another 20 rounds with punishment (pp. 8–9).  
• Systematically varied? No. All groups play 20 rounds in each phase (VCM, then punishment). Although an end-game effect is tested (using a P20 dummy in their regressions), there is no systematic manipulation of the number of rounds.  
• Prediction about its effect if varied? The paper does not provide any prediction on how changing the total number of rounds (e.g., 10 vs. 30) would affect the punishment treatment effect.  

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
• Mentioned? No. The paper does not enable or discuss any chat or communication between participants.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Prediction about its effect if varied? Not discussed.  

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Mentioned? No. Contributions in the experiments range continuously from 0 to 50 ECUs (p. 8), so it is not an “all or nothing” design.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Prediction about its effect if varied? Not discussed.  

5) Is the contribution default (players deciding how much to “move back” vs. “give”)?  
• Mentioned? The paper follows a standard voluntary contribution (i.e., from 0 to 50 tokens offered to the public good). There is no separate mechanism of “deciding how much to move back,” and no mention of a “default” contribution that participants must alter.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Prediction about its effect if varied? Not discussed.  

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
• Mentioned? Yes. The “return” from the contribution is a 0.5 factor (p. 8: “Each ECU contributed to the group account yields a payoff of 0.5 ECU to each group member.”).  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Prediction about its effect if varied? Not discussed.  

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Mentioned? Yes. Table 1 (p. 9) shows the cost function K(Pin): if a punisher assigns P points, they pay a cost that increases in steps (2, 4, 8, 12, … ). However, this cost function is fixed for all punishment rounds.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Prediction about its effect if varied? Not discussed.  

8) Punishment magnitude (amount deducted from a punished player)  
• Mentioned? Yes. Each punishment point the target receives reduces 10% of that target’s Stage 1 payoff, up to 100% (p. 9). This is a fixed rule and is not changed across treatments.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Prediction about its effect if varied? Not discussed.  

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
• Mentioned? No. The experiment only studies punishment; no reward mechanism is included.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Prediction about its effect if varied? Not discussed.  

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Mentioned? No. There is no reward.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Prediction about its effect if varied? Not discussed.  

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
• Mentioned? No. There is no reward in these sessions.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Prediction about its effect if varied? Not discussed.  

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?  
• Mentioned? Yes. Participants are told there are 20 rounds in each part (p. 8–9 documents it is a “finitely repeated” game). They do not vary whether the horizon is known or unknown.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Prediction about its effect if varied? Not discussed.  

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players see others’ earnings)?  
• Mentioned? Participants see how much their “neighbors” contributed in the previous stage and the total number of punishment points they received (p. 9). They also see their own payoff breakdown. However, the paper does not manipulate or vary what information is shown.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Prediction about its effect if varied? Not discussed.  

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• Mentioned? The paper states that participants only see “the aggregate number of points they receive” (p. 9). They do not see who punished them or how many points each punisher assigned. This is not manipulated across treatments.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Prediction about its effect if varied? Not discussed.  

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
• Mentioned? No. As the experiment does not involve rewards, this question does not arise.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Prediction about its effect if varied? Not discussed.  

————————————————————————————————————————  
FINAL SUMMARY  

A: Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
• Yes, the paper uses “efficiency” in terms of participants’ earnings (payoffs) as a key dependent variable (pp. 3–4, Section IV.C, Table 9, Table 10).  
• The paper also analyzes contributions to the public good and punishment patterns. Hence, the paper’s main dependent variables are (1) contributions, (2) punishment assigned/received, and (3) payoffs (efficiency). “Efficiency” measures are not identical to “contributions” (since payoffs can be reduced by punishment costs), nor to punishment rates alone.  

B: Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Mentioned explicitly (though not varied):  
  (1) Number of players (always 4)  
  (2) Number of rounds (always 20 + 20)  
  (6) MPCR (fixed at 0.5)  
  (7) Punishment cost schedule (from Table 1)  
  (8) Punishment magnitude (10% payoff reduction per point)  
  (12) Knowledge of the number of rounds (participants know the game ends at 20 rounds in each phase)  
  (13) Players see neighbors’ contributions and total group contribution; they do not see full identities.  
  (14) Players do not see who punished them.  

• Not mentioned (or not present) at all:  
  (3), (4), (5), (9), (10), (11), (15).  

C: For which and how many of these 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
• None are systematically varied in the experiment (the network structure is varied, but that is not among the 15 listed parameters). Hence, the paper offers no direct discussion of how changing any of these 15 parameters would alter the “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency, nor does it provide numeric estimates of parameter-by-parameter effects.  

D: If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on content of this paper, what would they be?  
• The paper does not present systematic manipulations or direct empirical predictions regarding these 15 game parameters. It therefore provides no basis for making meaningful predictions about how any of them (e.g., number of players, punishment cost function, punishment magnitude, or allowing for reward) would affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency. The only meaningful takeaway about efficiency arises from comparing four different network structures; none of those structures corresponds directly to a systematic variation of the 15 parameters. Consequently, from the paper alone, one can make little to no prediction about how changing any of the 15 parameters would affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Article Title: Defectors, not norm violators, are punished by third-parties
Author Keywords: cooperation; punishment; social; norms; cheats; sanction
Abstract: Punishment of defectors and cooperators is prevalent when their behaviour deviates from the social norm. Why atypical behaviour is more likely to be punished than typical behaviour remains unclear. One possible proximate explanation is that individuals simply dislike norm violators. However, an alternative possibility exists: individuals may be more likely to punish atypical behaviour, because the cost of punishment generally increases with the number of individuals that are punished. We used a public goods game with third-party punishment to test whether punishment of defectors was reduced when defecting was typical, as predicted if punishment is responsive to norm violation. The cost of punishment was fixed, regardless of the number of players punished, meaning that it was not more costly to punish typical, relative to atypical, behaviour. Under these conditions, atypical behaviourwas not punished more often than typical behaviour. In fact, most punishment was targeted at defectors, irrespective of whether defecting was typical or atypical. We suggest that the reduced punishment of defectors when they are common might often be explained in terms of the costs to the punisher, rather than responses to norm violators.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter inventory of what Chen (2012) does and does not say, followed by the requested four‐part summary.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER‐BY‐PARAMETER DISCUSSION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  
     – The paper uses a one‐superior/one‐subordinate setup (p. 45), but does not systematically vary the number of players.  
   • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment effect?  
     – Not discussed.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. All participants played 20 rounds (p. 45), split into two blocks of 10.  
   • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment effect?  
     – Not discussed. The paper does not examine how changing the total number of rounds would affect any outcome.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. There is no mention of participant communication/chat; instructions came from the experimenter, and interactions were computer‐mediated without interpersonal chat.  
   • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment effect?  
     – Not discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The “report” in this study can vary in five‐dollar increments between $700 and $900 (p. 46). The paper does not treat it as all‐or‐nothing nor discuss systematically varying that format.  
   • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment effect?  
     – Not discussed.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much of their endowment to move)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The experiment concerns budget “reports” rather than contributions from a personal endowment, and no mention of default choices is made.  
   • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment effect?  
     – Not discussed.

6. MPCR (marginal per capita return) or multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper frames each project’s gross revenue as $1,000 independent of the declared budget, and there is no discussion of an MPCR or related multiplier.  
   • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment effect?  
     – Not discussed.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Mentioned implicitly: in the stick and carrot‐stick treatments, the “cost” to punish is always $1 (p. 47).  
   • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment effect?  
     – Not discussed. The cost remains $1 throughout and is never varied. The paper does not examine how changing that $1 cost would alter outcomes.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The “stick” (punishment) and “carrot‐stick” (punishment plus reward) treatments include two different punishment levels: −$5 in the first 10 rounds and −$2 in the second 10 rounds (pp. 47–48).  
   • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment effect?  
     – Yes, for “slack creation” (not for “efficiency”). In the stick treatment, the mean proportion of slack retained (PSR) rose from 0.389 with the large (−$5) punishment to 0.536 with the smaller (−$2) punishment (Table 1, p. 49). The paper interprets that as larger punishments reducing self‐serving behavior more effectively.  
   – Numerical effect size (in terms of PSR)  
     – Under the stick treatment, the difference between first 10 rounds (punishment = −$5) and second 10 rounds (punishment = −$2) was about 0.389 vs. 0.536 PSR (p < 0.10, Table 3).

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. Several conditions include a reward or no reward (the carrot and carrot‐stick treatments vs. the others).  
   • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment effect?  
     – The paper does compare “carrot only,” “stick only,” “carrot‐stick,” and “hands‐off,” but it does not speak of reward presence specifically as it affects “punishment treatment.” Instead, it notes that the combination of reward + punishment (“carrot‐stick”) is most effective in reducing slack creation overall (pp. 50–51). There is no direct discussion of how toggling “reward enabled or not” alone changes the effect of punishment on efficiency.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Mentioned?  
     – As with punishment, the cost to the “superior” of giving a reward is $1 (p. 47).  
   • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment effect?  
     – Not discussed. That $1 cost is not altered in the experiment.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. In the carrot and carrot‐stick treatments, the reward magnitude changes from +$5 in the first 10 rounds to +$2 in the second 10 rounds (p. 47).  
   • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment effect?  
     – The paper measures the effect on slack creation in “carrot only” and “carrot‐stick,” but not specifically on any “punishment” effect alone.  
     – Numerically, in the carrot treatment, the proportion of slack retained is 0.471 (first 10 rounds with +$5) vs. 0.517 (second 10 rounds with +$2) (Table 1, p. 49). That is not statistically significant, so the paper concludes that changing reward magnitude alone has little impact on reducing slack creation (pp. 50–51).

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes, participants are informed up front that there will be 20 rounds (p. 46).  
   • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment effect?  
     – Not discussed. The design keeps the total of 20 rounds fixed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see each other’s payoffs)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. This experiment is one‐superior/one‐subordinate, with no observation of other subordinates’ outcomes.  
   • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment effect?  
     – Not discussed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know specifically who punished them?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Not as a separate manipulation. The paper simply states that a (computer‐simulated) superior punishes or rewards. There is no discussion of varying whether the identity of the punisher is revealed.  
   • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment effect?  
     – Not discussed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know specifically who rewarded them?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Same as above. The design uses a single, computer‐implemented superior. No variation of “known identity” is discussed.  
   • Effect of systematic variation on punishment treatment effect?  
     – Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FOUR‐PART SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are they different?  
   • The paper does not measure group efficiency or total/average payoff. Instead, its main dependent variable is the “proportion of slack retained” (PSR), which reflects how much cost padding the subordinate includes in the reported budget. This is distinct from efficiency or overall payoff.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
     (2) Number of rounds (fixed at 20),  
     (7) Punishment cost (fixed at $1),  
     (8) Punishment magnitude (varied from −$5 to −$2),  
     (9) Whether a reward is enabled (yes/no across “carrot” vs. “stick”),  
     (10) Reward cost (fixed at $1),  
     (11) Reward magnitude (varied from +$5 to +$2).  
   • The other parameters (1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 12, 13, 14, 15) are either not mentioned or appear in passing but are not systematically varied.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Only parameter 8 (punishment magnitude) is systematically varied in a way that the paper analyzes in detail for differences in slack creation (first 10 rounds = −$5 vs. second 10 rounds = −$2).  
   • The paper does systematically vary reward magnitude (parameter 11), but that primarily speaks to the “carrot” or “carrot‐stick” frameworks rather than how punishment’s effect changes.  
   • No other parameters are systematically varied or analyzed for their impact on punishment’s effect.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • Because the study focuses on slack creation (PSR) and does not measure efficiency, the paper gives limited basis for direct predictions about group efficiency.  
   • Its main finding is that higher punishment magnitude (−$5 vs. −$2) reduces slack creation more strongly, suggesting that, were we to apply these results to a public‐goods‐type setting, larger punishment is more likely to improve efficiency relative to smaller punishment.  
   • The paper also finds that rewards alone do not do much to reduce slack creation, so we could predict that “reward only” regimens have little efficiency impact, while combined punishment and reward (“carrot‐stick”) could have a more substantial effect.  
   • Other parameters (like the number of players, presence of chat, details about information, etc.) are not discussed with respect to efficiency or even with respect to varying punishment effects, so no predictions can be made solely from this paper.
reference_APA: Chen, Mien-Ling (2012). The Effect of Leader Reward and Punishment Behaviors on Subordinates' Budget Reports. ENGINEERING ECONOMIST.

Authors: Shen, C; Song, Z; Shi, L; Tanimoto, J; Wang, Z
Author Full Names: Shen, Chen; Song, Zhao; Shi, Lei; Tanimoto, Jun; Wang, Zhen
Article Title: Exit options sustain altruistic punishment and decrease the second-order free-riders, but it is not a panacea
Author Keywords: evolutionary game theory; altruistic punishment; coexistence; cyclic dominance; bi-stable
Keywords Plus: COOPERATION; PROMOTES; EMERGENCE; EVOLUTION; CARROT
Abstract: Why do humans punish free riders at their own expense? This behavior represents an evolutionary puzzle in human societies. This study explores the role of exit strategies in fostering altruistic punishment within evolutionary game theory. We extend the traditional prisoner's dilemma model by incorporating exiters, players who opt out for a small payoff while nullifying their opponent's payoff, and altruistic punishers who cooperate and punish non-cooperators. Our findings indicate that in well-mixed populations, exiters destabilize defection but do not promote altruistic punishment. In social networks, however, exiters enable altruistic punishment via cyclic dominance among altruistic punishers, defectors, and exiters. Notably, this cyclic dominance is sensitive to exit payoffs; adjustments can lead to cyclic dominance of non-punishing cooperators, defectors, and exiters, or to a bi-stable state between these two types of cyclic dominance. These results highlight the nuanced impact of exiters on altruistic punishment, emphasizing the need for careful incentivization of exit behavior. While exiters can support altruistic punishment in networked populations, their effectiveness is not a panacea and is highly sensitive to exit payoffs, indicating limits to the voluntary participation mechanism.

9. Reward enabled?  
   Not included.

10. Cost of reward  
    Not included.

11. Reward magnitude  
    Not included.

12. Whether the number of rounds is known  
    Not applicable / not mentioned.

13. Whether peer outcomes are shown  
    Not mentioned.

14. Whether punishees learn who punished them  
    Not mentioned.

15. Whether rewardees learn who rewarded them  
    Not mentioned.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables actually used  
   • The authors analyse stationary **fractions of strategies** (AP, NC, D, E), phase diagrams, fixation probabilities and, only implicitly, expected pay-offs that determine those fractions.  
   • They do NOT report “group efficiency” (total or average payoff divided by the cooperative optimum).  
   • Thus “efficiency” is absent; strategy shares and stability classes are the main outcomes.

B. Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters appear at all?  
   – Parameter 1 (population size)  
   – Parameter 6 (benefit/multiplication b)  
   – Parameter 7 (punishment cost γ)  
   – Parameter 8 (punishment fine β)

However, the paper provides no numeric payoff totals, so quantitative predictions cannot be made.

Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; KIN SELECTION; COOPERATION; ENFORCEMENT; BEHAVIOR; DESIGN
Abstract: Cooperation has long been an enigma in the life and social sciences. A possible explanation for the phenomenon is the recently developed idea of strong reciprocity in which agents altruistically reward those that cooperate and altruistically punish those that do not. The acts are altruistic in the sense that when agents punish or reward they incur a cost but receive no material benefit. Both experimentalists and modelers have focused primarily on third-party altruistic punishment mechanisms yet rarely discuss how they establish a cost for punishing. As the number of immediate neighbors increased, mean offers fell but still remained significantly greater than that predicted by standard economic theory.     – “Contribution” or “public-good provision” is the dominant outcome throughout the article.  
    – “Efficiency” (total payoff divided by the social optimum) is referenced only anecdotally (“full efficiency levels”, “almost 90 % of full contribution”, etc.) and never formally analyzed.  
    – Other outcomes mentioned: frequency of punishment, antisocial punishment, partner selection, etc.  
      Hence, **efficiency is not the main reported dependent variable; contribution is.**

B.  Parameters merely mentioned (value or definition given)  
    8 of 15:  1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 13, 14.

C.  Parameters whose **systematic variation** is linked to the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable)  
    3 (communication on/off)  
    7 & 8 jointly (punishment price / magnitude)  
    13 (visibility / information structure)  
    Total = 3 parameters.

D.  If forced to predict how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment-treatment effect on group efficiency, relying **only** on the article:

    • Communication (param 3) is predicted to strengthen the positive punishment effect because “punishment supplements anonymous communication and fosters contributions to almost full efficiency.”  
    • Lower punishment effectiveness (high cost or low magnitude; params 7-8) still reverses the usual contribution decline, so punishment should help efficiency even when expensive, though perhaps a bit less.  
    • Limited information about peer actions (param 13) substantially weakens punishment’s effectiveness, so efficiency gains should shrink in incomplete or sparse information networks.  
    • For every other parameter (1,2,4,5,6,9–12,14,15) the paper gives too little or no evidence to make a defensible prediction.

That is the full extent of what can be concluded from this single article.

Below you will find, for each of the 15 parameters, (1) whether the Kocher & Matzat paper even mentions the parameter and, if so, its realized value(s); and (2) whether the paper offers any **prediction or empirical estimate of what would happen if the parameter were systematically varied with respect to the “punishment-treatment effect.”**  “Punishment-treatment effect” is taken to mean the difference between an institutional environment that allows peer-to-peer punishment and one that does not (standard VCM or reward-only VCM).

PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1. Number of players  
   – Mentioned: Yes. Groups of n = 4. Not varied.  
   – Systematic-variation prediction: None.

2. Number of rounds  
   – Mentioned: Yes. Ten periods in each of Parts II and III. Not varied.  
   – Prediction: None.

3. Chat enabled?  
   – Mentioned: Yes (“We did not allow any communication”). Always “No.”  
   – Prediction: None.

4. “All-or-nothing” contributions?  
   – Mentioned: Yes, implicitly. Subjects choose any integer from 0–20, i.e., continuous, not all-or-nothing. Not varied.  
   – Prediction: None.

5. Contribution default / “opt-out”?  
   – Not mentioned at all. No prediction.

6. MPCR (marginal per-capita return)  
   – Mentioned: Yes. γ = 0.4. Not varied.  
   – Prediction: None.

7. Punishment cost per point  
   – Mentioned: Yes. Always 1 token to the punisher. Not varied.  
   – Prediction: None.

8. Punishment magnitude (tokens lost by target per point)  
   – Mentioned & systematically **endogenously** varied: L = −1,−2,−3,−4,−5 (subjects most often picked L = −5).  
   – Predictions / estimates:  
       • Theory (§5.2): higher |L| makes cooperation easier and should raise contributions; efficiency effect ambiguous.  
       • Data (Table 6, partner treatment): coefficient = +1.850 tokens contributed for each one-unit increase in |L| (p<.01).  
         Stranger treatment: +1.289 (p<.01).  
       • No separate estimate for efficiency; average profits are lower under punishment than under reward at every observed L.

9. “Reward enabled?”  
   – Mentioned: Yes. Three institutions compared: standard VCM (no reward), VCM+Punishment, VCM+Reward.  
   – Prediction / estimate: Enabling reward rather than punishment raises efficiency.  
       • Partner sessions (Table 5): mean profit 23.91 tokens with reward vs 19.69 with punishment (Δ = +4.22).  
       • Stranger: 22.67 vs 18.82 (Δ = +3.85).  
       • Paper explicitly states: “VCM with reward is the most efficient institution… although punishment yields higher contributions.”

10. Reward cost per point  
    – Mentioned: Yes. Cost = 1 token. Not varied.  
    – Prediction: None.

11. Reward magnitude  
    – Mentioned & systematically varied: L = +1 or +2 (subjects overwhelmingly chose +2).  
    – Predictions / estimates:  
        • Theory (§5.3): larger L makes positive contributions easier to enforce.  
        • Data (Table 6, partner): coefficient = +1.827 tokens per extra reward unit (p<.01); stranger +0.849 (p<.01).  
        • No direct efficiency estimate by reward-magnitude level.

12. Do players know the number of rounds?  
    – Mentioned: Yes (subjects were told there would be 10 rounds). Not varied.  
    – Prediction: None.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    – Mentioned: Yes. After each period players saw every group member’s contribution and the number of punish/reward points received. Not varied.  
    – Prediction: None.

14. Do punished players learn who punished them?  
    – Mentioned: Yes—they explicitly do **not** learn the identity. Not varied.  
    – Prediction: None.

15. Do rewarded players learn who rewarded them?  
    – Mentioned: Same as 14: identity is hidden. Not varied.  
    – Prediction: None.


SUMMARY

A.  Does the paper analyse group efficiency?  
    – It reports “profits” (average tokens earned) and calls the reward institution “the most efficient.”  
    – Dependent variables used: (i) individual/group contributions, (ii) individual/group profits (“efficiency”), (iii) frequency of punishment/reward decisions, (iv) subjects’ votes.  Contributions and profits are analytically distinct; profits already incorporate the cost of punishing/rewarding, whereas contributions do not.

B.  Parameters mentioned: 14 of the 15 (all except #5).  Only #8 and #11 are actually varied; #9 is varied in the broader sense that some sessions have punishment and others reward.

C.  Parameters for which the paper gives predictions or empirical estimates of their *systematic* impact on the punishment treatment effect:  
    – #8 Punishment magnitude (clear theory + regression coefficients).  
    – #11 Reward magnitude (theory + coefficients).  
    – #9 Reward enabled (institution comparison: effect sizes on profits).  
    That is 3 of 15 parameters.

D.  If one had to forecast the punishment-treatment effect on **efficiency** using nothing but this paper:  
    – Increasing punishment-magnitude (|L|) will raise contributions but (because punishment itself is costly and used often) is unlikely to raise, and may lower, efficiency relative to either a weaker punishment or to a reward institution.  
    – Enabling reward (instead of punishment) reliably increases efficiency by roughly 4 tokens per person in 10-round groups of four with γ = 0.4.  
    – Most other parameters are held constant in the study; the paper offers no basis for predicting how changing them (number of players, MPCR, chat, knowledge of identity, etc.) would interact with punishment to affect efficiency.  Therefore, beyond the few leverage-related findings, the paper provides little to no guidance on the remaining parameters.

Below each of the 15 design parameters is treated in exactly the same way:

• “Value in this paper” = the setting actually used in every treatment.  
• “Systematic variation?” = Did the authors deliberately change that parameter (or a very close operationalisation of it) across treatments?  
• “Prediction / effect size?” = Whether the paper offers an explicit hypothesis or reports an empirical effect that follows from **varying** that parameter.  Where possible, the most direct numerical evidence (taken from the paper’s figures / tables) is quoted, but only when the paper itself allows such an inference.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   – Value in this paper: 4 per group.  
   – Systematic variation? No; fixed in all sessions.  
   – Prediction / effect size? None.

2. Number of rounds  
   – Value: 15 repetitions of the two–stage game.  
   – Systematic variation? No.  
   – Prediction / effect size? None.  The authors merely include “Period” in regressions (Table 3) to show that contributions usually fall over time (except in the circle network), but they never consider different lengths.

3. Is chat enabled?  
   – Value: No chat or communication channel is mentioned; only computerised decision screens.  
   – Systematic variation? No.  
   – Prediction / effect size? None.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   – Value: No. Subjects freely allocate any integer 0–20 tokens to the group account.  
   – Systematic variation? No.  
   – Prediction / effect size? None.

5. “Contribution–default” framing (withdraw from public fund)?  
   – Value: Standard VCM: subjects **invest** in the group account; nothing to “withdraw”.  
   – Systematic variation? No.  
   – Prediction / effect size? None.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   – Value: Two types exist in every period: low = 0.3, high = 0.7.  A subject’s type is randomly re-assigned each round.  
   – Systematic variation? Yes (within every group and across periods).  
   – Prediction / effect size? YES, for contribution and punishment but **not** for efficiency:

     Hypothesis 3 (p. 10): “Whatever punishment network the subject participates in, the individual contribution increases with the MPCR.”  
     Empirical effect (Table 2): High-MPCR subjects give 4.03 tokens in a complete network vs 1.89 tokens for low-MPCR subjects; similar gaps in other networks.  
     Effect on efficiency is never calculated separately for different MPCR compositions, so no efficiency effect size is given.

7. Punishment cost (to punisher)  
   – Value: 1 token per punishment point (binary: 0 or 1).  
   – Systematic variation? No.  
   – Prediction / effect size? None.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss to target)  
   – Value: each punishment deducts 3 tokens from the target.  
   – Systematic variation? No.  
   – Prediction / effect size? None.

9. Is a monetary reward possible?  
   – Value: No reward stage.  
   – Systematic variation? –  
   – Prediction / effect size? None.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   – Not applicable (no reward stage).

12. Is the horizon known?  
   – Value: The instructions state the game “was repeated over 15 periods”; hence subjects knew the fixed length.  
   – Systematic variation? No.  
   – Prediction / effect size? None.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   – Value: Each subject sees (i) the exact first-stage contributions of the players he/she **can** punish, (ii) aggregate group contribution, and (iii) total number of punishments they sent and received.  Final pay-offs of others are **not** shown.  
   – Systematic variation? No.  
   – Prediction / effect size? None.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
   – Value: No. The punished player only learns the **number** of punishments received, not who sent them.  
   – Systematic variation? No.  
   – Prediction / effect size? None.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
   – Not applicable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables used  
   – YES, the study explicitly analyses “efficiency” (they label it “group payoffs”): total tokens earned by the four players divided by the maximum of 160 tokens (Figure 6; Table 7).  
   – Other dependent variables: group contribution, individual contribution, punishment amount, punishment severity (received punishments / potential punishers), likelihood of being punished.  Efficiency is payoff-based, the others are behavioural and therefore conceptually distinct.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   – Mentioned (value stated): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14.  (11 out of 15.)  
   – Not mentioned at all: 9, 10, 11, 15.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of **systematically varying** them on the punishment treatment effect?  
   – Only 1 parameter (MPCR, #6) is deliberately varied.  The paper predicts and measures its effect on contribution and punishment (not on efficiency).  None of the remaining 14 parameters is varied, so no causal claims are made.

D.  If we must predict how the 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency **using only this paper**, we can say very little:

   – The paper’s single robust efficiency result is that altering the **punishment network topology** (not one of the 15 listed parameters) matters: incomplete networks (circle and homo-pairwise) yield higher efficiency than a complete network.  
   – The only listed parameter that is manipulated (MPCR heterogeneity) shows that high-MPCR players contribute more, but the authors did not compute separate efficiency numbers by MPCR type, so we cannot quantify an efficiency impact.  
   – For all other parameters (number of players, punishment price, punishment magnitude, information conditions, rewards, etc.) the paper provides no data or theory beyond reporting their fixed values; therefore no prediction can be grounded in the text.

In short, with respect to efficiency, the study teaches us almost exclusively about the role of network structure (outside the present 15-parameter list) and offers no direct leverage for forecasting how changing any of the 15 parameters would alter the punishment treatment effect.

Authors: Moreno, SFGY; Gutierrez-Garcia, JO
Author Full Names: Gongora y Moreno, Sergio F.; Octavio Gutierrez-Garcia, J.
Article Title: Collective action in organizational structures
Author Keywords: Collective action; Cooperation; Public goods games; Organizational research; Agent-based simulation
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS; VOLUNTARY CONTRIBUTIONS; COOPERATION; PUNISHMENT; RECIPROCITY; PROVISION; DYNAMICS; SIZE
Abstract: Public goods games played by a group of individuals collectively performing actions towards a common interest characterize social dilemmas where both competition and cooperation are present. By using agent-based simulation, this paper investigates how collective action in the form of repeated n-person linear public goods games is affected when the interaction of individuals is driven by the underlying hierarchical structure of an organization. The proposed agent-based simulation model is based on generally known empirical findings about public goods games and takes into account that individuals may change their profiles from conditional cooperators to rational egoists or vice versa. To do so, a fuzzy logic system was designed to allow the cumulative modification of agents' profiles in the presence of vague variables such as individuals' attitude towards group pressure and/or their perception about the cooperation of others. From the simulation results, it can be concluded that collective action is affected by the structural characteristics of hierarchical organizations. The major findings are as follows: (1) Cooperation in organizational structures is fostered when there is a collegial model defining the structure of the punishment mechanisms employed by organizations. (2) Having multiple, and small organizational units fosters group pressure and highlights the positive perception about the cooperation of others, resulting in organizations achieving relatively high aggregate contribution levels. (3) The greater the number of levels, the higher the aggregate contribution level of an organization when effective sanctioning systems are introduced.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter inventory of what the paper does and does not say about each of the 15 public‐goods‐game design parameters in relation to punishment and its effects. Because the paper focuses almost entirely on contribution levels (and occasionally on utility at the individual level) rather than on group efficiency (i.e., total payoff / maximum possible payoff), there is no direct discussion of how modifying these parameters would affect “efficiency.” Some parameters are mentioned in passing; none are systematically varied for the stated purpose of measuring a punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency. Where relevant numerical details do appear (e.g., a 40% fine), these refer only to the model’s fixed choices and not to experiments that vary the parameter.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussed?  
  – Yes, indirectly. The paper refers to an “organizational size” that can go up to 5000 agents, and this size emerges from how many levels and what span of control each unit has (Sect. 4.1).  
  – However, the paper does not label this as “number of players” in a direct parameter sense; rather, it distinguishes organizations by their number of hierarchical levels and the span of control within each level.  
• Systematically varied for its effect on the punishment treatment?  
  – The authors vary the number of total agents only through the structure (1–4 levels, units of 4/8/12). They do not isolate “number of players” on its own, nor do they measure any specific effect of “number of players” on punishment treatment outcomes. The reported dependent variable is “aggregate contribution level,” not efficiency, and there is no separate numeric “treatment effect” reported for number of players.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Number of rounds
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussed?  
  – Yes, but fixed at 20 rounds. The paper justifies 20 rounds by standard practice in public goods experiments (Sect. 6).  
• Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
  – No. The paper does not vary the number of rounds; it is kept at 20 in all simulations.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Is chat enabled between players?
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussed?  
  – The authors note that “face‐to‐face communication” or “chat” can increase cooperation (Finding 9 in Sect. 3) but explicitly say they do not simulate it.  
• Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
  – No, they do not enable chat at all in their model, nor do they vary this parameter.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussed?  
  – No. The model uses continuous contributions from 0–100% of an endowment (Sects. 5.2–5.3). There is no mention of an all‐or‐nothing format.  
• Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
  – No mention at all.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5. Is the contribution default (i.e., do players move some default amount into their hand)?
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussed?  
  – No. All contributions are chosen each round according to the model’s rules; there is no notion of a “default” forced contribution that one must move back or forth.  
• Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
  – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussed?  
  – The paper states that the game is “linear” (Sects. 1 and 3) so that a player’s payoff is (own endowment – own contribution) + (average contribution of the group). They do not label this with an MPCR or show a numerical multiplier.  
• Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
  – No. No multipliers are changed or tested; the linear form is simply fixed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussed?  
  – Yes. The paper defines each punishment mechanism’s cost to the punisher (e.g., “the cost incurred by the supervisor is determined by dividing his/her endowment by the number of subordinates,” Sect. 5.4).  
• Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
  – No. These rules are built into the four punishment mechanisms but never varied experimentally. No numeric effect on efficiency or total payoff is reported.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussed?  
  – Yes. A fine of “p%” of the endowment is imposed (Sect. 5.4), and that p is set to 40%.  
• Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
  – No. The 40% penalty is chosen once; the paper does not vary it to see how that changes outcomes.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
9. Whether a reward is enabled
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussed?  
  – The authors mention only punishment, not reward, and suggest exploring combinations of “reward/punishment mechanisms” as a future direction (Sect. 8).  
• Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
  – No. Rewards do not appear in the simulation.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussed?  
  – No. Rewards are not present in the simulation.  
• Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
  – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussed?  
  – No. Same as above; no reward mechanism was implemented.  
• Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
  – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussed?  
  – Yes. The paper implements a “last round is announced” dynamic (Finding 3 in Sect. 3) and hard‐codes 20 rounds, with 70% of the players contributing zero in the last round.  
• Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
  – No. The paper keeps this feature constant.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost)?
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussed?  
  – Indirectly. Each agent updates its “perception about the cooperation of others,” which includes noticing others’ contributions (Sects. 4.2 and 5.1).  
• Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
  – No. This is simply part of the model’s assumptions.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussed?  
  – Not really. The paper does not specify whether the punished agent sees the punisher’s identity.  
• Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
  – No mention.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Discussed?  
  – No. As with (9)–(11), there is no reward mechanism in the simulations.  
• Systematically varied for its effect on punishment treatment?  
  – No.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

========================================
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
What dependent variables does it use, and how do these differ?
----------------------------------------
The paper does not discuss “group efficiency” as a ratio of (total payoff) / (maximum possible payoff). Instead, it reports:  
• The average contribution level per round.  
• The aggregate contribution level (the average of the per‐round averages).  
• Occasional mention of an individual’s “utility” in simple linear form.  

Those measures differ from efficiency. In particular, the authors never compute the fraction of the maximum possible group payoff.

========================================
B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?
----------------------------------------
Seven parameters are mentioned in some form:  
• (1) Number of players (as “organizational size”),  
• (2) Number of rounds (fixed at 20),  
• (6) MPCR/multiplication factor (called “a linear public goods game,” but no varying factor),  
• (7) Punishment cost to the punisher,  
• (8) Punishment magnitude (set to 40%),  
• (12) Number of rounds known,  
• (13) Peer outcomes shown (represented in agent “perception”).  

However, none of these is experimentally manipulated across multiple values for the purpose of gauging effects on “efficiency.” The remaining parameters either do not appear or are mentioned only to say they are out of scope.

========================================
C. For which and how many of these 15 parameters does the paper discuss a systematic effect on the “punishment treatment effect” for any dependent variable when that parameter is varied?
----------------------------------------
Strictly speaking, none of the 15 parameters is systematically varied purely to measure changes in the punishment treatment’s impact on contributions (or any other outcome). Instead, the authors systematically vary only the organizational structure (number of hierarchical levels, span of control) and the “type of punishment mechanism.” Those variations are not part of the 15‐item list above and are used to study changes in contribution levels (not “efficiency”). Consequently, there is no numerical effect size reported for systematically varying parameters #1–#15 with respect to punishment effects.

========================================
D. If you were to make predictions on how these 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?
----------------------------------------
The paper does not measure group efficiency and never manipulates those 15 parameters with a view to reporting an “efficiency” outcome. Hence, there is little direct basis to predict how systematically varying any of them—especially those never mentioned—would affect the punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency. One can only note the paper’s broader theme: sanctioning mechanisms that punish free riders more comprehensively (in their examples) led to higher contribution levels. But there is no direct statement or data linking these specific parameters to changes in efficiency. Therefore, based solely on this paper’s contents, almost no concrete prediction can be made about how changing the 15 parameters would alter the punishment effect on efficiency.

Parameter-by-parameter extraction from the paper  
(Only what is explicitly written – nothing extrapolated)  

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned: Yes. A fixed 100 × 100 square lattice ⇒ N = 10 000.

2. Number of rounds (time horizon)  
   • Mentioned: Yes. Simulations run up to T = 1000 Monte-Carlo steps (each step is N elementary strategy updates).

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned: No.  

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Mentioned: Yes. Players choose one of three discrete strategies: C contributes c = 1, D contributes 0, P contributes 1 and can punish. No continuous contribution choice exists.  
   • Systematic variation / prediction: None.  

5. Contribution default / “opt-out” framing?  
   • Mentioned: No.  

6. Marginal per-capita return (synergy factor r)  
   • Mentioned and varied: Yes. Main values used: 2.5, 2.8, 3.0; the heat-maps keep r fixed at either 2.5 or 3.0 when other parameters are swept.  
   • Prediction (dependent variable = cooperation rate, not efficiency):  
        – Raising r from 2.5 to 2.8 sharply accelerates the time at which betrayers (D) disappear.  
        – Beyond r ≈ 3.0 the marginal speed-up flattens because more surviving cooperators give betrayers resources, slowing complete elimination (described in Fig. 4).  
        – Numerical illustration (Fig. 4): At r = 2.5 betrayers survive ~400-500 T; at r = 3.0 betrayers die out before 200 T. No total-payoff/efficiency numbers are reported.  

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit (α)  
   • Mentioned and varied: Yes. Range 0.0–1.5 in heat-maps.  
   • Prediction (again in terms of eventual share of C+P):  
        – For a given fine d, lowering α enlarges the parameter region that converges to “global cooperation” (all C/P).  
        – Threshold examples from Fig. 6(a): with α = 0.61 cooperation becomes stable if d ≥ 0.61; with α = 1.19 the threshold is d ≈ 1.10.  
        – Fig. 7 snapshots show that increasing α from 0.8→1.4 delays elimination of betrayers and leaves fewer cooperators in the final state.  

8. Punishment magnitude / fine (d)  
   • Mentioned and varied: Yes. Range 0.25–1.5.  
   • Prediction:  
        – For r = 2.5 a fine below ≈0.6 cannot suppress betrayers even when α=0.  
        – Above that, higher d compensates for higher α.  
        – Cross-section in Fig. 6(b): at d=0.92 the system tolerates α up to ≈1.22.  

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Mentioned: No. There is no rewarding stage in the model.  

10–11. Reward cost, reward magnitude  
   • Mentioned: No.  

12. Do players know the number of rounds?  
   • Mentioned: No. (The model is an infinite-horizon evolutionary simulation; no information variable of this kind exists.)  

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Mentioned: No explicit statement.  

14. Punisher identified?  
   • Mentioned: No.  

15. Rewarder identified?  
   • Mentioned: N/A (no rewards implemented).  


SUMMARY  

A. Dependent variables  
   – The paper reports fractions of the three strategies (C, P, D) over time and the final stationary frequencies.  
   – Total or average payoff (“efficiency”) is never computed; it is only discussed qualitatively (“higher earnings”, “global cooperation”).  
   – Therefore efficiency is not an actual dependent variable in this paper.  

B. Parameters from the list that appear at all: 6 (r), 7 (α), 8 (d), plus fixed values for 1, 2, 4. Five of the fifteen are mentioned; the other ten are absent.  

C. Parameters whose *systematic* variation is analysed for their effect on the punishment treatment effect (measured as cooperation level, not efficiency): three – r (6), α (7), d (8). No systematic variation is performed for the other twelve.  

D. Ability to predict the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency using only this paper  
   – Efficiency itself is never operationalised, so quantitative predictions are impossible.

Abstract: In this paper we focus on inefficient product quality arising from a free-riding problem in agricultural cooperatives. Abstract: Institutions can be strong or weak. But what does this mean? Equilibrium theories equate institutions with behavioural regularities. C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
Strictly speaking, none. The paper describes some variations (e.g., cost–penalty ratios in the simulations), but it does not analyze a “punishment versus no‐punishment treatment” difference in terms of efficiency or provide numeric effect sizes on such a treatment effect. Instead, it focuses on how punishment (mainly from centrally placed individuals) increases cooperation and how that pattern holds for different cost ratios and network sizes. The paper never reports “efficiency” as a measured outcome.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
The paper itself provides little or no direct evidence about group efficiency, nor does it systematically compare “punishment vs. no‐punishment” under each parameter. The authors focus on how punishment from central players promotes cooperation in heterogeneous networks, not on how total payoffs compare to the theoretical maximum. Consequently, there is insufficient information in this paper to make meaningful predictions about the effect of systematically varying these 15 parameters—either singly or in interaction—on any measure of efficiency. One can only say that punishment from well‐connected “central” players tends to maintain higher cooperation levels in these networks, but even that is presented in terms of cooperation and fairness, not efficiency.

Article Title: Evolving Righteousness in a Corrupt World
Keywords Plus: SOCIAL-STATUS; PUNISHMENT; EVOLUTION; ALTRUISM; EMOTION; COOPERATION; EXPRESSION; QUEEN; POWER
Abstract: Punishment offers a powerful mechanism for the maintenance of cooperation in human and animal societies, but the maintenance of costly punishment itself remains problematic. Game theory has shown that corruption, where punishers can defect without being punished themselves, may sustain cooperation. However, in many human societies and some insect ones, high levels of cooperation coexist with low levels of corruption, and such societies show greater wellbeing than societies with high corruption. Here we show that small payments from cooperators to punishers can destabilize corrupt societies and lead to the spread of punishment without corruption (righteousness). Righteousness can prevail even in the face of persistent power inequalities. The resultant righteous societies are highly stable and have higher wellbeing than corrupt ones. This result may help to explain the persistence of costly punishing behavior, and indicates that corruption is a sub-optimal tool for maintaining cooperation in human societies.
