Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter analysis based solely on the content of the Duéñez-Guzmán and Sadedin (2012) paper (“Evolving Righteousness in a Corrupt World”). Each of the 15 parameters is listed along with what (if anything) the paper says about it, and whether the paper explicitly discusses or predicts any systematic effect of that parameter on the “punishment treatment effect.” In the paper itself, the authors mainly explore how adding a small positive “payment” (e) from cooperators to punishers interacts with two punishment‐related parameters (p and q), plus a punisher’s own punishment cost (c), to affect stable equilibria (“righteousness,” “corruption,” or “defection”) and overall population well‐being (sometimes described as “higher wellbeing” or “higher payoff”). They do not frame their results specifically in terms of “efficiency” (i.e., total payoff / maximum possible payoff). Whenever the text below says “no mention,” it means the paper does not describe or attempt to vary that parameter in any way.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. The model uses replicator dynamics (effectively an infinite population). The paper does not mention any finite number of players or vary group size.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No.  

2. Number of rounds  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. Time is modeled continuously via replicator dynamics; the paper does not discuss discrete rounds or repeated‐game settings.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. The paper models a 4‐strategy evolutionary game with replication, not a linear public good or partial‐contribution design.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No.  

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much of their endowment to move from the public fund back into their hand)?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as a multiplication factor  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. Although the authors mention payoff parameters (t, r, s) from the Prisoner’s Dilemma, they do not use or mention an MPCR or group multiplier typical of public goods games.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes, this is denoted c in the model (“the cost experienced by a punisher when punishing another individual”).  
     – In the main simulations, c is set at 0.2, and the authors note from a previous model [20] that the existence and stability of equilibria did not depend strongly on c alone.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No explicit prediction for how systematically varying c changes the “treatment effect” on any outcome. The authors do note that changing c can affect basins of attraction, but they do not give a numerical effect size nor do they link c directly to “efficiency.”  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed on them)  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes, in fact, the authors use two punishment‐magnitude parameters:  
       • p: punishment inflicted on a non‐punishing defector.  
       • q: punishment inflicted on a punishing defector (i.e., a defector who also punishes).  
     – These are central to the paper’s analysis; see Figs. 2 and 3.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – Yes. The paper systematically explores pairs of (p, q) from 1 to 10 and analyzes which equilibrium (defection, corruption, righteousness) is stable and how large each equilibrium’s “basin of attraction” is.  
     – The authors do not express these findings explicitly in terms of “efficiency,” but they state that a “righteous” equilibrium yields higher wellbeing (i.e., higher overall payoff) than a “corruption” equilibrium, and corruption yields higher payoff than outright defection.  
     – Numerical effect sizes are shown only as phase‐space diagrams (Figs. 2 and 3) rather than as a single effect‐size number for how p and q affect “punishment treatment.”  

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. The only “positive” transfer in the model is an unconditional small payment e to punishers from cooperators, which is not treated as a separate “reward” mechanism.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No.  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see others’ payoffs)?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No.  

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?

   • The paper does not explicitly use the term “efficiency” as total‐payoff‐divided‐by‐max‐possible‐payoff. Instead, it discusses:  
     1) The equilibrium payoffs of the population (sometimes called “net wellbeing” or “cumulative payoff”).  
     2) Equilibrium strategy compositions (defection, corruption, righteousness).  
   • The authors do state that “righteousness” yields higher wellbeing (i.e., higher total payoff) than “corrupt” societies, and both exceed “defection.” But they never call that ratio or difference “efficiency” in the text.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

   • Mentioned explicitly:  
       – Parameter 7 (the punishment cost to impose a single unit: c).  
       – Parameter 8 (the punishment magnitude deducted from a non‐punishing defector: p, and from a punishing defector: q).  
     So three parameters (c, p, and q) from within the broad category of “punishment cost and punishment magnitude” are clearly discussed, but these map onto two or three of the user’s listed items (7 and 8).  
   • None of the other 12 parameters appear in the paper.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?

   • Only p and q (under the user’s parameter #8) are actually varied systematically and analyzed in terms of their impact on whether punishment leads to a “righteous” equilibrium (which has higher total payoff) vs. a “corruption” equilibrium vs. full defection. The paper presents phase diagrams (Figures 2 and 3) varying p and q from 1 to 10.  
   • The cost c (parameter #7) is mentioned but not systematically varied in the main figures; the paper sets c = 0.2 and discusses only qualitatively how it can influence equilibria.  
   • No other parameters in the list are systematically varied.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

   • The paper only provides firm analysis for varying punishment‐magnitude parameters (p, q) and, to a much lesser extent, the cost c. Its central finding is that sufficiently large and more “egalitarian” punishment of all defectors (p ≈ q and both ≥ (t − r)) can lead to stable “righteousness” (universal cooperation with universal punishing), which yields higher overall payoffs.  
   • Beyond these observations, the paper does not discuss other parameters from the given list. Hence, there is little basis to predict their influence on “efficiency” (in the sense of total‐payoff / max‐payoff).  
   • Concretely, the paper suggests that if punishment magnitudes against all defectors are both high and approximately equal, then introducing punishment can increase the group’s total payoff. If punishers can remain corrupt (larger p, smaller q, or a major power imbalance), then lock‐in to corruption or defection occurs and overall payoff is lower.  
   • For the other 12 parameters, the paper does not mention or provide enough information to predict their influence on punishment’s effect on efficiency.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────  
(End of response)

Authors: Nicklisch, A; Wolff, I
Author Full Names: Nicklisch, Andreas; Wolff, Irenaeus
Article Title: COOPERATION NORMS IN MULTIPLE-STAGE PUNISHMENT
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS EXPERIMENTS; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; COLLECTIVE CHOICE; SOCIAL NORMS; PROVISION; SANCTIONS; ENFORCEMENT; RECIPROCITY; SITUATIONS; MECHANISM
Abstract: We analyze the interplay between cooperation norms and people's punishment behavior in a social-dilemma game with multiple punishment stages. By combining multiple punishment stages with self-contained episodes of interaction, we are able to disentangle the effects of retaliation and norm-related punishment. An additional treatment provides information on the norms bystanders use in judging punishment actions. Partly confirming previous findings, punishment behavior and bystanders' opinions are guided by an absolute norm. This norm is consistent over decisions and punishment stages and requires full contributions. In the first punishment stage, our results suggest a higher personal involvement of punishers, leading to a nonlinearity defined by the punishers' contribution. In later punishment stages, the personal-involvement effect vanishes and retaliation kicks in. Bystanders generally apply the same criteria as punishers in all stages.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter inventory of what is actually done or mentioned in the paper by Nicklisch and Wolff (2011). In all cases, unless otherwise noted, the paper does not systematically vary the parameter in question and does not make predictions about how varying that parameter would affect the “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency (i.e., actual total payoff relative to the maximum possible). The experiment in the paper compares only two treatments—BASIC vs. OPINION—both of which use the same core design features.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Discussed? Yes. They fix the group size at 4 (p. 7).  
   • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No. They do not vary the group size; there is no discussion of how changing the number of players would affect punishment or payoffs.

2. Number of rounds
   • Discussed? Yes. They fix 10 repeated rounds (p. 9).  
   • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No. All sessions use 10 rounds, and the paper does not theorize about how changing the total number of rounds would alter the punishment effect on efficiency.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussed? Not as “chat.” The instructions show there was no free-form communication.  
   • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No mention of enabling or disabling real-time chat, so no effect is discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussed? Indirectly, contributions can range from 0 to 20, so the experiment does not force all-or-nothing (p. 8).  
   • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No. No mention of testing an all-or-nothing rule.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much of their endowment to “move back” to themselves vs. defaulting to the public good)?
   • Discussed? Not in these specific terms. Participants simply choose any integer from 0 to 20 to contribute.  
   • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No. There is no mention of default contributions or how they might affect punishment.

6. MPCR (marginal per capita return) or multiplication factor
   • Discussed? Yes. They set the return α = 0.4, with 4 players, in all sessions (p. 7).  
   • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No. They do not vary α, nor do they predict how changing α would alter punishment’s impact on efficiency.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussed? Yes. The experiment uses a specific cost schedule from Fehr and Gächter (2000) (Table 1, p. 12).  
   • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No. The cost function is fixed for all sessions, and the paper does not discuss altering it.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted per unit of punishment)
   • Discussed? Yes. Each point of punishment reduces the target’s payoff by 10% (p. 8). Maximum 10 points means a 100% reduction of first-stage payoff.  
   • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No. They do not alter the 10% deduction rate. No predictions are given for changes in that rate.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussed? No. The paper’s design includes only punishment opportunities; there is no reward mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Discussed? No, because no reward mechanism is used.  
    • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded per unit of reward)
    • Discussed? No. There is no reward system in the design.  
    • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
    • Discussed? Yes. Participants know there are exactly 10 rounds (p. 9).  
    • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No. There is no testing or discussion of unknown vs. known round lengths.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost)?
    • Discussed? Yes. All players are shown others’ contributions, payoff changes from punishment, and how many points each player received (pp. 8–9).  
    • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No. This information is always provided, not manipulated.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Discussed? Yes. Players see which group member (by ID) assigned points to them (p. 8).  
    • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No. No condition hides the punisher’s identity.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Discussed? Not applicable. No rewards are used.  
    • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • They do examine average payoff (pp. 15–16), sometimes referring to it as “efficiency.” However, they do not formally define efficiency as the ratio of actual total payoff to the maximum possible. They also look at contributions, announcements of punishment, and actual punishment points assigned. Thus, their key dependent variables are (1) average payoff, (2) individual payoff, (3) contribution levels, (4) punishment announcements, (5) punishment intensity, and (6) bystanders’ approval of punishment.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Eight are explicitly mentioned in the design or instructions:  
      (1) Number of players (fixed at n = 4)  
      (2) Number of rounds (fixed at 10)  
      (6) MPCR α = 0.4 (fixed)  
      (7) Punishment cost function (fixed from Fehr & Gächter)  
      (8) Punishment magnitude (10% payoff reduction per point)  
      (12) Rounds are known (10 total)  
      (13) Peer outcomes are displayed  
      (14) Punisher identity is revealed  
   • The remaining seven parameters (3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, and 15) are either not used or not relevant for this design.

C. For which and how many of these 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • None. The paper does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters listed. Therefore, no quantitative or predictive effect sizes are given for changing those parameters.

D. If you were to make predictions on how these 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper:  
   • The authors do not provide direct evidence or model-based statements about varying any of these parameters. Their experiment compares only BASIC vs. OPINION (bystanders can voice their approval or rejection of a punishment announcement), but that variation does not align with any of the 15 parameters above. Consequently, one cannot infer how systematically tweaking those 15 parameters would alter the effect of punishment on efficiency. The paper’s data simply do not speak to that question.

Authors: Bahbouhi, JE; Bouderba, SI; Elkouay, A; Moussa, N
Author Full Names: Bahbouhi, Jalal Eddine; Bouderba, Saif Islam; Elkouay, Abdelali; Moussa, Najem
Article Title: Effects of individual and collective decision rule on cooperation in public goods game
Author Keywords: Evolutionary game theory; Public goods game; Punishment; Reward; Free riders
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; PRISONERS-DILEMMA; REPLICATOR DYNAMICS; REWARD; REPUTATION; EVOLUTION; RECIPROCITY; CARROT; INSTITUTIONS; SANCTIONS
Abstract: Research on public goods game has traditionally focused on studying the effects of punishment and reward in experimental settings, commonly known as standard games. However, these standard games often examine isolated interactions among individuals, leading to varying results based on factors such as the population studied, number of participants, and geographical context. Consequently, the understanding of cooperation evolution remains imprecise. To address this limitation, we are trying to generalize these experimental studies, we employ an agent-based model in this study to simulate interactions in public goods game and explore the influence of punishment and reward on the evolution of cooperation. Unlike standard games, evolutionary games offer a more comprehensive framework to capture and analyze a broader range of strategic interactions and behaviors. In our approach, we introduce two methods for applying punishment or reward: Individual Punishment or Reward and Collective Punishment or Reward. Under the first method, actors can individually reward or punish each other based on their contributions or free-riding behavior towards the collective good. In the second method, decisions for punishment or reward are made collectively after achieving a consensus or agreement among the members of the group. We provide a model for comparing Individual Decision Rule and Collective Decision Rule under punishment and reward, to study their effects on the evolution of contributions. Consistent with recent experimental findings, our results indicate that these mechanisms lead to a significant increase in contributions compared to the outcomes observed in standard public goods game. Additionally, we demonstrate the significant role of rewards in promoting contribution within public goods game.

Below every parameter is treated separately.

For each parameter I report  
(1) whether it is **explicitly described in the paper and, if so, the value that was used**, and  
(2) whether the paper gives **any prediction or numerical evidence about what would happen if that parameter were systematically varied** for any dependent variable (contribution, punishment, pay-off, “efficiency”, etc.).  
If nothing is said, that is stated explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players in the public-goods group  
   (1) Mentioned. Exactly four “players” (either four individuals or four 3-person teams) formed a group.  
   (2) Held constant; no prediction about varying it.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Mentioned. Ten rounds in Part II (no‐punishment) and ten rounds in Part III (punishment); plus a one-shot Part I.  
   (2) Fixed; no prediction about changing the horizon.

3. Is chat enabled?  
   (1) Mentioned. No chat or face-to-face communication was allowed; only proposal entry was possible.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction about enabling chat.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   (1) Mentioned. Contributions were integer 0-20 tokens; therefore NOT all-or-nothing.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

5. “Contribution default” (players withdraw from a public fund by default)?  
   (1) Not the case here. Subjects decided how many tokens (0-20) to INVEST; no default withdrawal frame.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   (1) Mentioned. MPCR = 0.4 (group multiplier 1.6).  
   (2) Held constant; no prediction about higher or lower MPCR.

7. Punishment cost to punisher per unit  
   (1) Mentioned. 1 token.  
   (2) Fixed; no prediction about alternative costs.

8. Punishment magnitude (tokens deducted from target per unit)  
   (1) Mentioned. 3 tokens.  
   (2) Fixed; no prediction about alternative magnitudes.

9. Is a reward option enabled?  
   (1) Not present.  
   (2) Not discussed.

10. Reward cost per unit  
    (1) Not applicable.  
    (2) Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude  
    (1) Not applicable.  
    (2) Not discussed.

12. Do players know the number of rounds?  
    (1) Yes. The game was announced as finitely repeated for exactly ten periods in each part.  
    (2) Not varied; no prediction about uncertainty.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    (1) Yes. After each period participants saw their own pay-offs and anonymised contributions (and punishments in Part III) of every other player/team.  
    (2) Not varied; no prediction.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
    (1) No. Punishment was completely anonymous.  
    (2) Not varied; no prediction.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
    (1) Not applicable (no rewards).  
    (2) Not discussed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used  
   • Contributions (tokens invested)  
   • Punishment (tokens spent, probability, social vs. anti-social)  
   • Net profits (= monetary pay-off after contributions and punishment)  
   Efficiency in the sense of “actual total pay-off divided by the maximum possible pay-off” is **not** explicitly analysed; net profit is the closest proxy the authors use.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are at least mentioned?  
   10 of them: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14.  
   Parameters 5, 9, 10, 11, 15 are not part of the design.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect that *systematic variation* of that parameter would have on the punishment treatment effect?  
   Zero. Every parameter listed above is fixed; the authors supply no theoretical or empirical claims about what would happen if any of them were changed.

D. What predictions can be made—based solely on this paper—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions will influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency?  
   Very little. The experiment compares “no-punishment” (Part II) with “punishment enabled” (Part III) under one single combination of the 15 parameters. Therefore:
   • Under the exact setting used (4 players, MPCR = 0.4, anonymous costly punishment 1→3, no chat, known 10-round horizon, feedback shown) adding punishment raised average contributions (≈ +1.5×) but also created costly sanctions; net profits rose slightly only for unanimity teams and fell for individuals.  
   • Because none of the 15 parameters was varied, the paper provides virtually no leverage for predicting how changing any of them (alone or in interaction) would shift the efficiency impact of introducing punishment.  
   • All that can be cautiously inferred is that, *when punishment is anonymous and costs 1 to impose 3, and when groups consist of unanimity-ruled 3-person teams that act as one player in a 4-player public-goods game*, punishment can coexist with higher contributions and (for those teams) higher net pay-offs. Beyond that specific configuration the paper is silent.

Article Title: Local stability of cooperation in a continuous model of indirect reciprocity
Keywords Plus: SOCIAL NORMS; EVOLUTION
Abstract: Reputation is a powerful mechanism to enforce cooperation among unrelated individuals through indirect reciprocity, but it suffers from disagreement originating from private assessment, noise, and incomplete information. In this work, we investigate stability of cooperation in the donation game by regarding each player's reputation and behaviour as continuous variables. Through perturbative calculation, we derive a condition that a social norm should satisfy to give penalties to its close variants, provided that everyone initially cooperates with a good reputation, and this result is supported by numerical simulation. A crucial factor of the condition is whether a well-reputed player's donation to an ill-reputed co-player is appreciated by other members of the society, and the condition can be reduced to a threshold for the benefit-cost ratio of cooperation which depends on the reputational sensitivity to a donor's behaviour as well as on the behavioural sensitivity to a recipient's reputation. (i) Yes. Main values analysed: r = 3.5 (“low”) and r = 4 (“high”). They remind the reader that without punishment cooperators need r > 3.74 to survive.

(i) Central variable; vertical axis in the same phase diagrams.  
(ii) Systematically varied (≈ 0–1). Reported thresholds (for α = 0.01, r = 3.5):  
   • β1 ≈ 0.376 – below this IAC cannot survive.  
   • β2 ≈ 0.662 – above this cooperators survive again (C+IAC coexistence).  
   • In the IAD model additional thresholds β4 ≈ 0.035, β5 ≈ 0.396 distinguish D+IAD, C+IAD+D and IAC+D phases.

Neither mentioned or varied.

A. Does the paper use group efficiency?

(1 group size), (4 all-or-nothing contribution), 6 (r), 7 (α), 8 (β), 13 (visibility of pay-offs).

Authors: Harrell, A; Wolff, T
Author Full Names: Harrell, Ashley; Wolff, Tom
Article Title: Cooperation in Networked Collective-Action Groups: Information Access and Norm Enforcement in Groups of Different Sizes
Author Keywords: cooperation; collective action; experiments; networks; social networks
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; SOCIAL DILEMMAS; PROVISION; DYNAMICS
Abstract: Norms, typically enforced via sanctions, are key to resolving collective-action problems. But it is often impossible to know what each individual member is contributing to group efforts and enforce cooperation accordingly. Especially as group size increases, people commonly have access to the behaviors of-and can sanction-only those to whom they are tied in a broader network. Here we integrate two streams of research: one conceptualizing ties in networked collective-action groups as access to information about what others are doing and a second where ties represent information plus opportunities to enforce cooperation via punishment. While both have pointed to the cooperation benefits of more ties in the network, we argue that these benefits will depend on group size and whether ties provide access to information about what others are doing or whether they also entail opportunities for norm enforcement. Our experiment demonstrates that densely tied information networks facilitate cooperation but only when the group size is small. When people can also enforce their ties' cooperation, however, densely tied networks particularly benefit larger groups. The results demonstrate how network-level properties and individual-level tie patterns intersect to promote contributions in small and large collective-action groups.

Below, each of the 15 parameters is treated in the same order in which they were given.  For every parameter I first say whether the paper mentions it and (if mentioned) what concrete value(s) it takes in the experiment.  I then state whether the paper **systematically varies** the parameter and, if so, what the paper actually reports about its impact on the “punishment treatment effect.”  Throughout I quote or reference exact coefficient estimates (mostly the B-coefficients reported in Tables 1 and 2 as well as the overall model in the on-line appendix Table S2).  The term “punishment-treatment effect” is interpreted exactly as in the paper: the causal effect of adding a punishment stage to an otherwise identical public–goods phase.

Important: The paper’s principal dependent variable is **average contribution per round**; earnings/profits and punishment sent are examined secondarily.  The word “efficiency” (actual total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff) never appears in the paper, and no efficiency measure is reported.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Parameter-by-parameter reading of the paper
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. NUMBER OF PLAYERS  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Two experimental conditions: “small” groups of 3–5 (M ≈ 3.81) and “large” groups of 7–9 (M ≈ 7.83).  
   • Systematically varied?  Yes (between-group manipulation).  
   • Reported influence on the punishment treatment effect?  Yes.  
        – Three-way interaction “Group size × Network density × Punishment” in the global model (Table S2, Model 2): B = 2.10, p = .02.  
        – In the information-and-punishment phases (Table 2) the key coefficient is the four-way slope “Large group × Dense × Round”: B = 0.51, p < .001.  Interpretation: with punishment present, large groups in dense networks raise contributions by ≈0.51 tokens per additional round, whereas large groups in sparse networks *decrease* by ≈0.35 tokens per round (simple slope reported in text).  Small groups hardly change with density when punishment is available.  
        No efficiency numbers are given.

2. NUMBER OF ROUNDS  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Seven rounds per phase, four phases = 28 rounds total.  
   • Systematically varied?  No (fixed at 7 within a phase).  “Round” is treated as a time variable, not an experimental manipulation.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment?  Not applicable.

3. IS CHAT ENABLED?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  “Participants were prevented from communicating with others …” (p. 11).  Value = “No chat.”  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  No statements about how enabling chat would change a punishment treatment.

4. ALL-OR-NOTHING CONTRIBUTION?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes, implicitly.  Subjects choose any integer from 0 to 20.  Not varied.  No predictions.

5. CONTRIBUTION DEFAULT (REFUND OPTION)?  
   • Not mentioned; not manipulated.

6. MPCR / MULTIPLICATION FACTOR  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Each point in the group fund is doubled, then divided equally.  Therefore MPCR = 2 / N (≈0.25 to 0.67 depending on N).  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  No discussion of changing the multiplication factor.

7. PUNISHMENT COST PER UNIT  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  “It cost one point to deduct three points from an alter’s earnings.”  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  No statements about alternative costs.

8. PUNISHMENT MAGNITUDE PER UNIT  
   • Mentioned?  Yes: 3 points are deducted from target for each 1 point spent.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.

9. REWARD ENABLED?  
   • Mentioned?  Not at all.  No rewards in this design.

10. REWARD COST  
11. REWARD MAGNITUDE  
   • Not applicable (no reward stage).

12. ARE NUMBER OF ROUNDS KNOWN?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  “To avoid end-game effects, participants were not told in advance exactly how many rounds they would complete.”  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  No prediction.

13. ARE PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes, and **systematically varied** via the network-density manipulation.  
        – Fully dense (all alters visible) versus sparse (Erdős–Rényi p ≈ 0.43) networks.  
   • Reported influence on punishment treatment?  Yes.  
        – INFORMATION-ONLY phases: Dense boosts contributions in small groups but *reduces* them in large groups over time.  Coefficient “Large × Dense × Round” = –0.56, p = .002 (Table 1).  
        – INFORMATION-AND-PUNISHMENT phases: Dense helps both sizes but especially large groups.  “Large × Dense × Round” = +0.51, p < .001 (Table 2).  
        – Efficiency not reported; profits are mentioned: Dense networks start with lower profits (B = –3.46, p = .03 in Round 1) but over seven rounds profit rises faster than in sparse (B = +1.05, p < .001).  The profit result does not interact with group size.

14. IS THE PUNISHER IDENTIFIED?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  “Participants … were unable to see their connections’ individual deduction decisions.”  Therefore punisher identity is hidden.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  No prediction.

15. IS THE REWARDER IDENTIFIED?  
   • Not applicable (no rewards).

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

A.  Dependent variables actually analysed  
   – Main DV: Contribution level per round.  
   – Secondary DVs: (i) punishment sent, (ii) punishment received, (iii) round-by-round profits.  
   – **Group efficiency (total or average payoff divided by the cooperative optimum) is never computed.**  Profits are *not* normalised by the cooperative benchmark and therefore differ conceptually from efficiency.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even *mentioned*?  
   Mentioned: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14.  (10 parameters)  
   Not mentioned: 5, 9, 10, 11, 15.

C.  Which parameters are *systematically varied* and analysed for their effect on the punishment treatment?  
   Only two:  
   • Parameter 1 (group size) – between-groups manipulation.  
   • Parameter 13 (visibility of peer outcomes via network density) – within-group manipulation.  
   For neither parameter does the paper report *efficiency* effects; only contribution, punishment, and profit effects.

D.  If forced to predict the punishment-treatment effect on **efficiency** from this paper alone:  
   • Large, fully-dense information-and-punishment networks are expected to yield the biggest positive treatment effect (because they end with the highest contributions and, after a few rounds, higher profits).  
   • Small groups will gain less from adding punishment; dense vs. sparse hardly matters once punishment is available.  
   • When no punishment is available, making the information network dense can *lower* efficiency in large groups (contributions collapse) but raise it in small groups (contributions grow).  
   • All other parameters (MPCR, punishment cost ratio, anonymity of punishers, communication, round knowledge, etc.) are held constant in the study, so the paper provides **no basis** for predicting how changing them would move efficiency.

In short, the paper gives strong, quantitative guidance for only two of the fifteen design parameters—group size and information visibility—and only for outcomes in **contribution and profit**, not formally defined efficiency.  For the remaining thirteen parameters, no systematic evidence or prediction about the punishment treatment effect is provided.

Abstract: Authorities rely on reports from private citizens to detect and enforce more than a trivial portion of effective law-breaking. The present article is the first to study the cultural aspect of peer reporting experimentally. By collecting data in a post-Soviet country (Moldova), we focus in particular on how the Soviet legacy of using citizens as private informants may have a long-lasting effect on their willingness to cooperate with state authorities. We then contrast those effects with peer reporting behavior in France, a Western society. Our results suggest that participants in Moldova view cooperation with authorities as less socially acceptable than their counterparts in France. Our results also suggest that participants in Moldova engage less frequently in peer reporting than individuals in France. However, we also find that less peer reporting does not necessarily imply less tax compliance. Participants in both countries exhibit very similar tax compliance rates. We explain the effect of peer reporting on tax compliance in Moldova using the country's past experience during the Soviet era, when being reported to authorities was common and carried grave consequences.

Abstract: Fairness norms and resulting behaviours are an important prerequisite for cooperation in human societies. At the same time, financial incentives are commonly used to motivate social behaviours, yet it remains unclear how financial incentives affect fairness-based behaviours. Combining a decision paradigm from behavioural economics with hierarchical drift-diffusion modelling, we investigated the effect of different financial incentives on two types of fairness-based decisions in four experimental groups. In two groups, participants divided points between themselves and a disadvantaged person, inciting fairness-based compensation behaviour, in two other groups they divided points between themselves and a fairness violator, inciting fairness-based punishment behaviour.  • The paper provides evidence that *larger individual monetary incentives* (parameter 6/11) reliably change decision behaviour, so it is reasonable to predict that in a public-goods-with-punishment setting the *size* of monetary stakes will also modulate any punishment treatment effect on efficiency, although the sign could depend on whether the incentive is aligned or in conflict with cooperation.  
 • For the remaining 14 parameters the paper offers no data, theory, or speculation, so no prediction grounded in the paper can be made.

Authors: Wang, CY; Cui, WF
Author Full Names: Wang, Canyou; Cui, Weifang
Article Title: Supervision for the Public Health Services for Older Adults Under the Background of Government Purchasing: An Evolutionary Game Analysis Framework
Author Keywords: public health services; older adults; supervision; government purchasing; evolutionary game

Abstract: As an important measure to involve services for older adults, the government procurement practices have become a key link for public health services. However, the information asymmetry between public health service purchasers and public health service undertakers triggers a supervision dilemma. Based on this background, this study uses the evolutionary game theory to analyze the symbiotic evolution between local governments and public health service institutions under different reward and punishment mechanisms, explore game evolution, strategy adjustment, and influencing factors of different game subjects, and analyze the necessity and appropriate intensity of dynamic rewards and punishment mechanisms. The results show that: under the static condition, the penalty can change the strategies of local governments to a certain extent, but it is still difficult to achieve complete self-discipline management of public health service institutions. For three dynamic mechanisms, a dynamic reward mechanism is more conducive to adopting a self-discipline behavior of public health service institutions, which is helpful to realize the supervision of public health services for older adults. Also, there is a positive correlation between the proportion of public health service institutions who adopt a self-discipline behavior strategy and the maximum punishment intensity, and a negative correlation with the reward intensity. Below is a parameter-by-parameter analysis of whether (1) the paper discusses each of the 15 listed parameters (and, if so, what its value is) and (2) whether the paper makes predictions about systematically varying that parameter on the effect of punishment (for any outcome measure, including but not limited to efficiency). References to “the paper” mean only the text and figures provided in “Supervision for the Public Health Services for Older Adults Under the Background of Government Purchasing: An Evolutionary Game Analysis.”

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. The paper considers two populations (local governments and public health service institutions) in an evolutionary game but does not specify the total number of players.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict effects on punishment?  
     – No mention or variation.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. Although the analysis is “evolutionary,” the paper does not specify a discrete number of rounds or whether that number is known.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict effects on punishment?  
     – No mention or variation.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. The paper does not discuss communication or chat between the players.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict effects on punishment?  
     – No mention or variation.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. The paper uses discrete strategies (“self-discipline” versus “fraud” for public health service institutions; “positive supervision” versus “passive supervision” for governments) but does not frame these as “all-or-nothing contributions” in a public goods sense.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict effects on punishment?  
     – No mention or variation.

5. Is the contribution default?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. There is no mention of a default contribution scheme.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict effects on punishment?  
     – No mention or variation.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. The paper does not use concepts such as an MPCR or a multiplication factor; it does not analyze a classic public goods production function.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict effects on punishment?  
     – No mention or variation.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Not in per-unit terms. The paper includes a government “cost of supervision” (I), but that is a lump-sum effort cost, not a per-unit cost of punishing.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict effects on punishment?  
     – No. The paper does not treat a “cost to punish” per unit as a separate parameter or vary it in that manner.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player per unit punishment)  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. The paper uses P as the penalty inflicted on a public health service institution (PHSI) when it engages in “fraud behavior.”  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict effects on punishment for any dependent variable?  
     – Yes. The paper analyzes different ranges of P (e.g., P < I, I < P < C+ΔL−S, P > max(I, C+ΔL−S)) and shows how these different regimes lead to different equilibria in terms of “self-discipline” proportions x and “positive supervision” proportions y.  
     – Numerical effect sizes: The paper does not provide an exact numeric effect size on group efficiency, but it shows through figures (Figures 1–3) and simulation that when P becomes large enough, the equilibrium can cycle or converge to different (x, y) levels. However, it does not quantify efficiency changes.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. The paper includes a reward term S, paid by local governments to PHSIs that adopt “self-discipline behavior.”  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict effects on punishment?  
     – Yes, in the sense that S interacts with the penalty P (particularly in dynamic reward and penalty regimes) to alter strategy equilibria. Figures 4–6 show how systematically changing S (and P) affects the fraction of self-discipline and supervision, but not efficiency per se.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. Although S is the reward amount, no separate “per-unit cost” of granting S is described. The analysis treats S itself as the magnitude of the reward to PHSIs, rather than a separate cost parameter for local governments.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict effects on the punishment treatment effect?  
     – The paper varies S but does not detail a per-unit cost of S to the rewarder.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes, as S.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict effects on punishment?  
     – Yes, in both static and dynamic reward models. They show that varying S can change the final fraction of local governments implementing “positive supervision” and the fraction of PHSIs choosing “self-discipline,” but they do not connect this to efficiency.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. There is no mention of whether participants know the end of the interaction.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict effects on punishment?  
     – No mention or variation.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know their peers’ payoffs)?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. The paper does not describe informational conditions about others’ payoffs.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict effects on punishment?  
     – No mention or variation.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. The paper does not discuss whether PHSIs learn the identity of punishing local governments.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict effects on punishment?  
     – No mention or variation.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. The paper does not discuss whether PHSIs learn which local government issued a reward.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict effects on punishment?  
     – No mention or variation.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are they different?  
   • The paper does not mention “group efficiency” in the sense of actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff. Instead, the main outcomes are the evolutionary stable strategies (ESS) and the equilibrium proportions of PHSIs choosing “self-discipline” (x) and local governments adopting “positive supervision” (y). The paper also analyzes payoff expressions, but does not define or measure “efficiency.”

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Discussed parameters:  
       – Punishment magnitude (P)  
       – Whether a reward is enabled (yes)  
       – Reward magnitude (S)  
   • Indirectly mentioned: cost of supervision (I), cost of self-discipline (C), and extra gains from fraud (ΔL) appear in the paper, but they do not match exactly any of the 15 listed items except for (7) and (8) in a very approximate sense.  
   • All other parameters among the 15 are not mentioned.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • Only two parameters—(8) “punishment magnitude” (P) and (9)/(11) “reward is enabled”/“reward magnitude” (S)—are systematically varied. The paper examines how changing P or S changes the equilibrium proportions (x, y). This analysis is not framed in terms of “efficiency” or total payoff; rather, it concerns whether self-discipline or supervision emerges in the population.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of this paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper never reports efficiency—only evolutionary equilibria in terms of proportions of particular strategies. Therefore, based on the information given, one cannot make quantitative predictions about how changing these parameters would increase or decrease group efficiency. Only qualitative inferences can be made, such as “higher penalties (P) can deter fraudulent behavior but may still lead to cyclical behavior unless combined with dynamic incentives,” and “higher rewards (S) can affect the fraction of self-discipline.” However, no direct statement about overall efficiency (as defined in public goods games) is provided in the paper.  

Hence, apart from noting that P and S alter equilibrium strategy choices, the paper does not supply enough details to predict changes in efficiency. One would have to say that the paper provides little to no direct basis for predicting the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.
reference_APA: Wang, Canyou & Cui, Weifang (2022). Supervision for the Public Health Services for Older Adults Under the Background of Government Purchasing: An Evolutionary Game Analysis Framework. FRONTIERS IN PUBLIC HEALTH.

Authors: Hua, SJ; Liu, LJ

Article Title: Governance of risky public goods under the threat of ostracism
Author Keywords: Cooperation; Evolutionary game theory; Punishment; Social exclusion

Abstract: How to enforce cooperation among unrelated agents is one of the main concerns in distributed artificial intelligence. The limited success of existing efforts to achieve large-scale cooperation is partly related to the lack of strong sanctioning mechanism to restrain defective agents who undermine cooperation. Here we use the framework of evolutionary game theory to investigate the emergence of cooperation in collective risk dilemma (CRD) through the implementation of instrumental ostracism on defective agents. By analyzing the stochastic model, we find that instrumental ostracism can better promote the emergence of widespread cooperation than punishment. Such advantage is more obvious when the risk is relatively low. Furthermore, we verify that the polycentric sanctioning institutions including punishment and ostracism are more effective than a single global one in improving the level of cooperation. Our model can be applied to many collective action problems, such as climate change and vaccination in Covid-19, so as to further provide some suggestions for decision makers. & COPY; 2023 Elsevier B.V. Abstract: 'Personal responsibility', one of the basic principles of social governance, requires one to be accountable for what one does. However, personal responsibility is far from the only norm ruling human interactions, especially in social and economic activities. In many collective communities such as among enterprise colleagues and family members, one's personal interests are often bound to others'-once one member breaks the rule, a group of people have to bear the punishment or sanction. Such a mechanism is termed 'joint liability'. Although many real-world cases have evidenced that joint liability can help to maintain collective collaboration, a deep and systematic theoretical analysis on how and when it promotes cooperation remains lacking. Here, we use evolutionary game theory to model an interacting system with joint liability, where one's losing credit could deteriorate the reputation of the whole group. We provide the analytical condition to predict when cooperation evolves and analytically prove that in the presence of punishment, being jointly liable greatly promotes cooperation. Our work stresses that joint liability is of great significance in promoting current economic prosperity.

Below I go through the 15 pre-specified public-goods-game parameters one by one and report exactly what the paper says (and does not say) about each of them.  I keep a strict separation between (i) simple descriptive information (whether the parameter appears in the model and, if so, which value is used) and (ii) any statement in the paper about what would happen if that parameter were **systematically varied**.  Whenever a numerical effect can be read from a figure, table or formula I cite it explicitly.  I never go beyond what the text, figures or equations in the paper allow.

------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  The population size is denoted N.  Most simulations use N = 100; Fig. 4b,d varies N from ≈30 to 300; §3.2 also analyses the limit N → ∞.  
   • Systematic-variation prediction? Yes, but only for the dependent variable “stationary abundance of cooperators/punishers/defectors”, **not for efficiency**.  
     –  Fig. 4b (analysis) and Fig. 4d (simulations) show an inverted-U shape: “an intermediate population size N is most beneficial to the evolution of cooperators and punishers”.  
     –  No efficiency measure and no explicit “punishment treatment effect” is reported.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? No.  The model is an evolutionary process with an unlimited succession of generations; the notion of finitely many rounds does not occur.  
   • Systematic-variation prediction? No.

3. Is chat enabled?  
   • Not mentioned.  No predictions.

4. All-or-nothing contribution choice?  
   • Not mentioned.  No predictions.

5. Contribution default / “take” frame?  
   • Not mentioned.  No predictions.

6. Marginal Per-Capita Return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • The standard MPCR of a public-goods game does not appear.  The paper uses individual benefit b and cost c in a loan-repayment setting.  
   • No statements connect anything equivalent to an MPCR with punishment treatment effects.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit (γ)  
   • Mentioned? Yes (γ).  Typical values: γ = 0.3 (Figs. 2–5), γ = 0.5 (Fig. 6).  
   • Systematic-variation prediction? Yes, analytically.  
     –  Key result (eq. 3.1, finite populations): altruists are favoured if β − γ > 4c(δ − δ ln δ).  Lower γ, holding β constant, relaxes the condition.  
     –  Special cases:  
       • With joint liability at minimal tolerability (m = 1 ⇒ δ≈0): altruists evolve if β > γ.  
       • Without joint liability (m = N ⇒ δ = 1): altruists evolve if β > γ + 4c.  
   • Again, this is expressed in terms of *abundance*, not efficiency, and the paper never plots γ while holding everything else constant to show a “punishment treatment effect”.

8. Punishment magnitude (β)  
   • Mentioned? Yes (β).  Typical values: β = 2 (Figs. 2–5), β = 6 (Fig. 6).  
   • Systematic-variation prediction? Yes, by the same inequalities as for γ.  Larger β (for fixed γ) makes it easier for cooperation to evolve.  
     –  No figure systematically sweeps β, but the analytic threshold β − γ > … is explicit.  
   • No efficiency results.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Not mentioned.  No predictions.

10. Reward cost  
    • Not mentioned.  No predictions.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Not mentioned.  No predictions.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
    • Not applicable; no finite-horizon game.  No predictions.

13. Are peer pay-offs shown?  
    • Not discussed.  No predictions.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
    • Not discussed.  No predictions.

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
    • Not discussed.  No predictions.

------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
------------------------------------------------------------------

A. Does the paper use *group efficiency* as a dependent variable?  
   – No.  The analysed dependent variables are:  
     • Fixation probability ρ of invading types.  
     • Stationary/average abundance of punishers, cooperators, defectors.  
     • Location of equilibria in replicator dynamics.  
   “Efficiency” (actual total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff) is never reported, so these variables are conceptually distinct from efficiency.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
   – 3 out of 15:  
     1 (Number of players N)  
     7 (Punishment cost γ)  
     8 (Punishment magnitude β)

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* that parameter on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable)?  
   – Also 3 (the same three).  
     • N is varied in Fig. 4 (effect on abundance).  
     • γ and β are varied analytically in the threshold inequalities.  
   – None of these analyses use “efficiency” as the outcome; they use abundance or invasion probability.

D. If forced to predict how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency *solely* from the paper:  
   –  Very little can be said.  The only defensible qualitative inferences are:  
     • Larger β relative to γ should, by fostering more punishment-supported cooperation, *tend* to raise efficiency.  
     • Extremely small or extremely large N dampens cooperation; medium N enhances it, so efficiency might peak at intermediate group sizes.  
     • All other listed parameters (chat, rewards, visibility, etc.) are completely absent from the model; the paper gives **no basis** for predicting their impact on efficiency or on any punishment effect.

In short, the paper is highly informative about how β, γ and population size influence evolutionary *cooperation*, but it provides no direct evidence—numerical or verbal—on how any of the 15 parameters would change the *punishment treatment effect on group efficiency*.
reference_APA: Wang, Guocheng, Su, Qi & Wang, Long (2022). Evolution of cooperation with joint liability. JOURNAL OF THE ROYAL SOCIETY INTERFACE.

Abstract: Influential individuals are introduced and integrated with the public goods game (PGG) to investigate their influence on the emergence and evolution of cooperation. In the model, some influential individuals whose behaviors can be controlled by us are introduced into a homogeneous population on a square lattice. The influential individuals can play three kinds of roles: I. exemplar, II. supervisor with the power to punish defectors, and III. supervisor with the power to reward cooperative co-players. It is found that the existence of influential individuals who play Role I turns out to be detrimental to cooperation and that the larger the number of influential individuals is, the more difficult it is for cooperation to be maintained. For those playing supervisory roles, both punishment and reward are found to be effective ways for the influential individuals to promote and stabilize cooperative behavior. By comparing the critical costs and the mean payoffs for a low multiplication factor under the role of punishment and the role of reward, it is found that reward is a more effective intervention measure than punishment for influential individuals seeking to improve cooperation and that reward leads to a higher mean payoff. Below the 15 parameters are inspected one‐by-one in the exact order given.  
For each parameter I report  

(1) whether it is mentioned in the paper and, if so, the value(s) that appear;  
(2) whether the paper reports what will happen to the *punishment treatment effect* when that parameter is systematically varied.  Whenever the paper contains a quantitative statement or a figure that allows one to read off a numerical effect, I reproduce it; otherwise I quote the qualitative claim.  If the parameter is not mentioned or no prediction is made, this is stated explicitly.

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
(1) Mentioned: Yes.  The authors fix a 100 × 100 square lattice, i.e. N = 10 000 normal players and d · N influential players.  
(2) Systematic variation: No.  N is never changed, so no prediction about how varying N would modify the punishment treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
(1) Mentioned: Only indirectly.  Simulations are run “until the system achieves its steady state” and the outcome is read after 2 500 or 35 000 time steps, but the number of rounds is never treated as an experimental parameter.  
(2) Systematic variation: No.

3. Is chat enabled?  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) No prediction.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
(1) Mentioned implicitly.  Cooperators invest a fixed amount c = 1, defectors invest 0.  There is no option to contribute an intermediate amount.  
(2) No variation, hence no prediction.

5. Contribution default (retraction option)  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) No prediction.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor r  
(1) Mentioned and varied.  Fig. 1 varies r from roughly 1.0 up to 4.0 in the role-I baseline; Figs. 2–4 hold r at either 1.2 or 1.5 while varying punishment or reward.  
(2) Prediction on punishment treatment effect: Yes.  
    • For Role II (punishment) the *critical fine Vp* above which punishment succeeds falls as r rises (Fig. 2).  Qualitatively, higher r increases the effectiveness of punishment.  
    • No numerical slope is given, but Fig. 2 shows that at r = 1.2 the critical Vp is ≈ 4, whereas at r = 1.5 it is ≈ 2.7.  Thus ΔVp/Δr ≈ –4.3 per unit increase in r (rough read-off).  
    • The same qualitative statement holds for reward (Role III, Fig. 3), but that is not a punishment treatment, so strictly speaking it is outside the punishment treatment effect.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
(1) Mentioned.  The punisher pays nothing; “the cost is derived from society.”  
(2) Never varied; no prediction.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine Vp paid by the target)  
(1) Mentioned and systematically varied.  Vp is the horizontal axis in Fig. 2 (range 0–5).  
(2) Prediction: Yes.  For both r = 1.2 and r = 1.5, increasing Vp raises the fraction of cooperators ρc once Vp exceeds a critical threshold.  When Vp < threshold, punishment has *no* positive treatment effect; when Vp > threshold, the treatment effect turns positive and grows monotonically with Vp until ρc ≈ 1.

9. Whether a reward mechanism is enabled  
(1) Mentioned.  Role II (punishment) vs. Role III (reward).  
(2) Prediction about punishment treatment effect: Indirect.  The paper shows that for the *same* cost V the reward regime attains higher cooperation than the punishment regime (Fig. 4).  That comparison implies that *removing* reward (i.e. staying with punishment only) yields a lower efficiency than enabling reward.  However, this statement is about “punishment vs. reward,” not “punishment vs. no-punishment,” so the paper gives no clean estimate of an interaction.

10. Reward cost to grant one unit  
(1) Mentioned: as with punishment, the rewarder pays nothing.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction on punishment treatment effect.

11. Reward magnitude (Vr)  
(1) Mentioned and varied in Fig. 3, but this is part of the reward regime, not the punishment regime.  
(2) No prediction for the punishment treatment effect.

12. Are the number of rounds known to players?  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) No prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
(1) Not discussed.  
(2) No prediction.

14. Are punishers identified?  
(1) Not discussed.  The model merely deducts Vp; no information disclosure is modelled.  
(2) No prediction.

15. Are rewarders identified?  
(1) Not discussed.  
(2) No prediction.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used  
   – Fraction of cooperators, ρc (most of the paper)  
   – Mean payoff (Fig. 5)  
   The paper never reports “efficiency” in the strict sense (actual / maximal group payoff).  Mean payoff is related but not identical; ρc measures strategy composition, not payoffs.

B. Parameters out of the 15 that are *mentioned* in the paper: 1, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11  → 8 parameters.

C. Parameters for which the paper *systematically varies the parameter and reports its effect on the punishment treatment effect* (for *any* dependent variable):  
   – 6 (MPCR r)  
   – 8 (punishment magnitude Vp)  
   So 2 out of 15 parameters receive such discussion.

D. Predictions that can be made about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, *based solely on this paper*:

   • Higher MPCR r strengthens the positive impact of punishment on cooperation and on mean payoff, because the critical fine needed to make punishment effective falls as r rises.  
   • Larger punishment magnitude Vp (once above the critical threshold) monotonically increases the positive punishment treatment effect.  
   • All other parameters are either fixed or absent from the model; the paper provides no basis for predicting their influence on efficiency.  Therefore, beyond the two statements above, little can be said about the remaining 13 parameters or about higher-order interactions.

That exhausts what can be extracted from the paper without introducing outside information.
reference_APA: Zhuang, Qian, Wang, Dong, Fan, Ying & Di, Zengru (2012). Evolution of cooperation in a heterogeneous population with influential individuals. PHYSICA A-STATISTICAL MECHANICS AND ITS APPLICATIONS.

Authors: De Dreu, CKW; Gross, J; Romano, A
Author Full Names: De Dreu, Carsten K. W.; Gross, Joerg; Romano, Angelo
Article Title: Group Formation and the Evolution of Human Social Organization
Author Keywords: social evolution; public goods; group processes; intergroup relations
Keywords Plus: PROMOTE COOPERATION; PAROCHIAL ALTRUISM; PROSOCIAL BEHAVIOR; DIRECT RECIPROCITY; CARRYING-CAPACITY; DECISION-MAKING; PUNISHMENT; CONFLICT; GAMES; PREJUDICE
Abstract: Humans operate in groups that are oftentimes nested in multilayered collectives such as work units within departments and companies, neighborhoods within cities, and regions within nation states. With psychological science mostly focusing on proximate reasons for individuals to join existing groups and how existing groups function, we still poorly understand why groups form ex nihilo, how groups evolve into complex multilayered social structures, and what explains fission-fusion dynamics. Here we address group formation and the evolution of social organization at both the proximate and ultimate level of analysis. Building on models of fitness interdependence and cooperation, we propose that socioecologies can create positive interdependencies among strangers and pave the way for the formation of stable coalitions and groups through reciprocity and reputation-based partner selection. Such groups are marked by in-group bounded, parochial cooperation together with an array of social institutions for managing the commons, allowing groups to scale in size and complexity while avoiding the breakdown of cooperation. Our analysis reveals how distinct group cultures can endogenously emerge from reciprocal cooperation, shows that social identification and group commitment are likely consequences rather than causes of group cooperation, and explains when intergroup relations gravitate toward peaceful coexistence, integration, or conflict.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter summary for the 15 features (game structure, monetary stakes, peer incentives, and information display). Following that, you will find the four‐point summary (A–D) requested. Throughout, I refer only to what appears in the provided paper by De Dreu et al. (no other sources). I also note instances where the paper mentions dependent variables other than efficiency (e.g., cooperation, free riding). Whenever the paper does not discuss a given parameter or its systematic variation, I say so explicitly.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Discussion: The paper does not specify or manipulate the number of players in any experimental game. Although there is general discussion of “larger” versus “smaller” groups, there is no mention of systematically varying the exact group size or number of players in a public goods–type game.  
   • Predicted effect (if any): Not discussed; no predictions.

2. Number of rounds
   • Discussion: The paper frequently mentions “repeated interactions” and the notion that cooperation can evolve over multiple encounters, but it does not specify or vary the exact number of rounds in a formal experiment.  
   • Predicted effect (if any): Not discussed; no predictions.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussion: The paper mentions that individuals can “exchange information” in the form of gossip, but it does not specifically report any study where real‐time chat is enabled or disabled.  
   • Predicted effect (if any): Not discussed; no predictions.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussion: The authors do not mention a design in which participants must contribute all or nothing to a public good. Their discussion of cooperation is general, with no mention of forced “all or nothing” choices.  
   • Predicted effect (if any): Not discussed; no predictions.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Discussion: There is no mention in the paper of a default contribution rule or mechanism (such as deciding how much of one’s endowment to move back into a private account).  
   • Predicted effect (if any): Not discussed; no predictions.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as a multiplication factor
   • Discussion: The authors mention cost and benefit parameters in dyadic helping (with b > c), but do not present or vary an MPCR or multiplication factor in a standard public goods game sense.  
   • Predicted effect (if any): Not discussed; no predictions.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussion: The paper discusses punishment in broad, qualitative terms (e.g., to deter free riding), but provides no specific numerical cost that is systematically manipulated.  
   • Predicted effect (if any): Not discussed; no predictions.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   • Discussion: The paper refers to punishment’s ability to deter free riding but does not specify or manipulate its exact magnitude in a formal game setting.  
   • Predicted effect (if any): Not discussed; no predictions.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussion: The authors do mention that “groups can … reward others for being cooperative,” but they do not analyze or systematically vary the presence/absence of a reward mechanism in an experiment.  
   • Predicted effect (if any): Not discussed; no predictions.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Discussion: Reward is discussed only in general (“material or symbolic rewards”); the paper does not discuss a numeric reward cost or any variation of it.  
   • Predicted effect (if any): Not discussed; no predictions.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)
   • Discussion: Likewise, although reward is noted, there is no specification of a manipulative design in which reward magnitude is systematically increased or decreased.  
   • Predicted effect (if any): Not discussed; no predictions.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
   • Discussion: While repeated interactions are considered important, the paper never describes an experiment with known versus unknown horizon, nor does it analyze how making the number of rounds known would affect outcomes.  
   • Predicted effect (if any): Not discussed; no predictions.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much their peers gained and lost each round)?
   • Discussion: The paper describes that group members may monitor whether and how much others contribute, but it does not discuss an experimental design in which peer outcomes are systematically displayed or hidden, nor does it provide predictions about varying that kind of feedback.  
   • Predicted effect (if any): Not discussed; no predictions.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Discussion: Punishment is discussed as a deterrent, but there is no mention of whether punishees learn the exact identity of the punisher.  
   • Predicted effect (if any): Not discussed; no predictions.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Discussion: Again, while rewards are mentioned, there is no statement about whether the recipient learns the identity of the rewarder.  
   • Predicted effect (if any): Not discussed; no predictions.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Summary (A–D)

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different from one another?  
   – The paper does not explicitly use “efficiency” (total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff) as a dependent variable. It mainly discusses “cooperation,” “free riding,” “club goods,” and “collective action” as outcomes or dependent measures, including whether participants help (cooperate) or not and how groups maintain their “commons.” These are conceptually different from directly measuring total group payoff relative to a maximum.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – The existence of punishment and reward is mentioned in general terms (parameters #7, #8, #9, #10, #11) but without quantitative discussion of costs or magnitudes or how these might be systematically manipulated. None of the other parameters (1–6 and 12–15) are discussed at all. Thus, while “punishment” and “reward” are acknowledged, none of the 15 parameters is truly singled out in a way that matches the typical public goods–experiment design details (no repeated‐round treatments, no stake‐variation, no cost‐coefficients, etc.).

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   – The paper does not report any systematic variation of any parameter; hence it provides no quantitative (or even qualitative) predictions about how any of these 15 parameters, when varied, would affect a “punishment treatment effect” on cooperation, free riding, or efficiency.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   – The paper does not address varying these parameters, so there is effectively no guidance for making parameter‐by‐parameter or interaction predictions regarding how punishment might alter efficiency. The authors do state broadly that the possibility of punishment (and related social enforcement) can help “better maintain … club goods,” but it never quantifies or systematically analyzes how altering any of the 15 design features would specifically change outcomes. Hence, based solely on this paper, one cannot draw conclusions about the punishment treatment effect on efficiency under systematic parameter manipulations.

Authors: Kaiping, GA; Cox, SJ; Sluckin, TJ
Author Full Names: Kaiping, G. A.; Cox, S. J.; Sluckin, T. J.
Article Title: Cooperation and punishment in community-structured populations with migration
Author Keywords: Public goods game with punishment; Group selection; Community-structured population; Migration
Keywords Plus: EVOLUTION; DYNAMICS; GAMES
Abstract: The stable presence of punishing strategies in various cooperative species is a persistent puzzle in the study of the evolution of cooperation. To investigate the effect of group competition, we study the evolutionary dynamics of the Public Goods Game with punishment in a metapopulation that consists of separate communities. In addition to (a) well-mixed non-interacting communities, we model three distinct types of interaction between communities, (b) Migration independent of fitness; (c) Competition between whole communities, where entire communities replace each other depending on average fitness; (d) Migration where the probability of an offspring replacing an individual in another community depends on fitness. We use stochastic simulations to study the long-run frequencies of strategies with these interactions, subject to high mutation and migration rates. In cases (a) and (b), the transition between cooperation/punishment and defection regimes occurs for similar parameter values; with migration (b), the transitions are steeper due to higher total mixing. Fitness-based migration (d) by contrast can help support cooperation, changing the locations of transitions, but while group selection (c) does stabilise cooperation over much of the parameter space, fitness-based migration (d) acts as a proxy for group selection only in a smaller region.
