Below each of the 15 parameters I state  

(i) whether the paper ever mentions (or fixes) the parameter and, if so, the value(s) it uses, and  

(ii) whether the paper ever shows what happens when that parameter is *systematically varied* and how this changes the *punishment treatment effect*.  
(The only places in the paper where “punishment” is switched off are the simulations in which the authors set β = γ = 0.  The dependent variables they report are almost exclusively the long-run *frequencies of strategies* rather than efficiency.)

----------------------------------------------------------------  
GAME-STRUCTURE PARAMETERS  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
1. Number of players in the group (N)  
   i. Mentioned constantly.  Default N = 50 (Table 1).  Heat-map in Fig. 5 varies N from ≃20 up to ≃150.  
   ii. Fig. 5 (group-competition model) shows that, with punishment switched *on*, larger N quickly destroys cooperation if local selection w₁ is strong, whereas under weak local selection cooperation survives even for very large N.  
       • No simulations without punishment at the same N are reported, so the paper never reports a *punishment treatment effect* as a function of N.  Only frequencies of C, D, P with punishment are shown.

2. Number of rounds  
   i. Not mentioned (the model is an infinite-time Markov process).  
   ii. No discussion.

3. Chat between players  
   i / ii. Not mentioned.

4. All-or-nothing contribution  
   i. Yes.  Contribution is binary: an agent either pays c or pays nothing (Section 1).  This is fixed; never varied.  
   ii. No variation, hence no treatment effect.

5. Rebate / contribution default  
   i / ii. Not mentioned.

----------------------------------------------------------------  
MONETARY-STAKE PARAMETER  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) — labelled r  
   i. Default r = 3 (Table 1).  
   ii. Fig. 7d (fitness-based migration model) varies r (exact scale not printed, but ~1.5–5).  In that model, higher r increases payoff differentials *between* communities, so cooperators become slightly more common and punishers slightly less common; defectors stay low.  
       • The same r-range is *not* simulated with punishment turned off, so no punishment treatment effect is reported.  The authors only note that r is “irrelevant” in well-mixed and constant-migration models because all players in a community receive the same Π.

----------------------------------------------------------------  
PEER-INCENTIVE PARAMETERS  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
7. Punishment cost to punisher (γ)  
   i. Default γ = 5 (Table 1).  γ is systematically varied in:  
      • Fig. 3b (constant migration)  
      • Fig. 9 (comparison of group-conflict vs. fitness-based migration)  
   ii. Qualitative findings:  
      – Constant migration (Fig. 3b): very low γ makes punishers abundant and defectors scarce; increasing γ first crowds out P (more C) and eventually lets D dominate.  
      – Fitness-based migration (Fig. 9): as γ rises, punishers become rarer and *cooperators* replace them; defector share stays low.  
      – Group conflict (Fig. 9): frequencies of C and P are almost flat across γ.  
      The paper never repeats the γ-sweep with β = γ = 0, so we again lack a direct punishment-treatment effect on efficiency or on strategy frequencies.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine β)  
   i. Fixed at β = 20 (Table 1).  Not systematically varied.  
   ii. No discussion beyond stating that setting β = γ = 0 disables punishment.

9. Presence of a reward option  
10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   i / ii. Rewards never appear in the model.

----------------------------------------------------------------  
INFORMATION-DISPLAY PARAMETERS  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
12. End-round information about remaining number of rounds  
13. Display of peer outcomes  
14. Identification of punisher  
15. Identification of rewarder  
   i / ii. None of these are modelled or discussed.

----------------------------------------------------------------  
SUMMARY  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
A.  Use of “efficiency” as a dependent variable?  
    No.  The paper’s outputs are almost exclusively the *long-run average frequencies* of the three strategies (Cooperate, Defect, Punish).  Sometimes the authors plot the *mean payoff* of a community only as an intermediate quantity needed for between-community selection, but they never divide that by the theoretical maximum, so they never compute “group efficiency” in the sense requested.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
    6 of them:  
    (1) number of players N, (4) binary contribution (fixed), (6) MPCR r,  
    (7) punishment cost γ, (8) punishment fine β, and the “presence/absence of punishment” implicitly controlled by setting β = γ = 0.  
    The other 9 parameters are absent.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper give *systematic* results on their effect when the parameter is varied?  
    Four: N, r, γ, and (trivially) the on/off switch for punishment itself.  
    None of these analyses report efficiency; all report strategy frequencies, and only γ and the on/off switch compare “punishment on” vs. “punishment off.”  No numerical effect sizes on efficiency are provided anywhere.

D.  What predictions about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment treatment effect on efficiency can be made *solely* from this paper?  
    • Because efficiency is never calculated, the paper offers almost no direct guidance.  
    • The qualitative takeaway is simply that *having* punishment (β, γ > 0) versus *not having* punishment (β = γ = 0) is crucial: with punishment, defectors can be suppressed under some population-structuring mechanisms (migration, group conflict, fitness-based migration); without punishment, defectors dominate.  
    • Higher punishment *cost* γ weakens the prevalence of punishers; whether that helps or hurts efficiency cannot be inferred.  
    • Larger groups (N) undermine cooperation under strong within-group selection but not under weak selection; again no efficiency numbers are available.  
    • Changes in r reshape payoffs between communities and therefore can slightly bolster cooperation in the fitness-based migration model, but efficiency consequences are unknown.  
    • Nothing whatsoever can be said, from this paper alone, about parameters 2, 3, 5, 9-15.

Hence, if forced to predict efficiency effects, the only evidence here is that “turning on” punishment in structured populations *can* raise cooperation levels, particularly under group conflict or fitness-based migration, but the paper gives no numerical basis for translating that into efficiency terms and no information about the remaining parameters.

Authors: Ringsmuth, AK; Lade, SJ; Schlüter, M
Author Full Names: Ringsmuth, Andrew K.; Lade, Steven J.; Schluter, Maja
Article Title: Cross-scale cooperation enables sustainable use of a common-pool resource
Source Title: PROCEEDINGS OF THE ROYAL SOCIETY B-BIOLOGICAL SCIENCES
Author Keywords: cooperation; social-ecological system; cross-scale interactions; multiscale analysis; common-pool resource; resource management
Keywords Plus: SOCIAL-ECOLOGICAL SYSTEMS; GOVERNANCE; CONNECTIVITY; RESILIENCE; MULTISCALE; FRAMEWORK
Abstract: In social-ecological systems (SESs), social and biophysical dynamics interact within and between the levels of organization at multiple spatial and temporal scales. Cross-scale interactions (CSIs) are interdependences between processes at different scales, generating behaviour unpredictable at single scales. Understanding CSIs is important for improving SES governance, but they remain understudied. Theoretical models are needed that capture essential features while being simple enough to yield insights into mechanisms. In a stylized model, we study CSIs in a two-level system of weakly interacting communities harvesting a common-pool resource. Community members adaptively conform to, or defect from, a norm of socially optimal harvesting, enforced through social sanctioning both within and between communities. We find that each subsystem's dynamics depend sensitively on the other despite interactions being much weaker between subsystems than within them. When interaction is purely biophysical, stably high cooperation in one community can cause cooperation in the other to collapse. However, even weak social interaction can prevent the collapse of cooperation and instead cause collapse of defection. We identify conditions under which subsystem-level cooperation produces desirable system-level outcomes. Our findings expand evidence that collaboration is important for sustainably managing shared resources, showing its importance even when resource sharing and social relationships are weak.

Below, each of the fifteen public-goods‐game design parameters is considered in turn.  For every parameter I report

(1) whether it is mentioned anywhere in Ringsmuth et al. (2019),  
(2) the value(s) the paper actually uses (if any), and  
(3) whether the paper makes a prediction about how *systematically varying* that parameter would change the “punishment treatment effect”.  When the paper speaks about variables other than efficiency (e.g. cooperation rate) I note that explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players (group size)  
   – Mentioned? Yes.  Each community contains n players; the main text sets n = 50 in Fig. 2 and keeps n constant elsewhere.  
   – Prediction when varied? No.  The paper does not vary n systematically and gives no quantitative or qualitative prediction for how changing n would alter any “punishment treatment effect”.  (In §S6 they merely state that the main results are “robust to variations in n”.)

2. Number of rounds  
   – Mentioned? No.  The model is continuous-time until an equilibrium is reached; “rounds” never appear.

3. Chat / communication between players  
   – Mentioned? Partly.  The authors distinguish two norm-setting scenarios: “collaborative” (communities *share resource information while setting the norm*) and “uncollaborative”.  That is not the free, within-round chat typical of public-goods experiments, so parameter 3 in the strict sense is **not** present.  
   – Prediction? None for chat.  The collaborative/non-collaborative distinction *is* analysed, but it is treated as a modelling assumption, not something whose continuous variation is examined.

4. “All-or-nothing” contributions  
   – Mentioned? No.

5. Contribution default / endowment kept unless moved  
   – Mentioned? No.

6. MPCR or multiplication factor  
   – Mentioned? No.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   – Mentioned? Yes—assumed to be 0 (“we assume that cooperators bear no cost for sanctioning defectors”).  
   – Prediction when varied? No.  The cost is fixed at zero for the entire paper.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine suffered per unit punishment)  
   – Mentioned? Yes.  The per-capita sanction experienced by a defector is controlled by parameter s (maximum sanctioning) together with parameters g, T and the social coupling λ.  s is fixed at 0.0068 in the main text (derived from h = 0.34 in Tavoni et al.).  
   – Prediction when *systematically* varied? No.  Although Figures 3–5 show that *increasing* the overall sanction actually received (via λ) can lead to phase transitions (collapse of defection), the magnitude parameter s itself is never varied; therefore no quantitative effect size is reported.

9. Reward enabled  
10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   – Mentioned? Not at all.  Rewards do not exist in the model.

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
14. Is the punisher identified?  
15. Is the rewarder identified?  
   – Mentioned? No for all four.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables used in the paper  
   ‑ Group efficiency (total or average payoff relative to maximum) is **not** measured.  
   ‑ Main outcomes:  
     • ϕ = fraction of cooperators in each community (social state).  
     • ρ = resource stock (biophysical state).  
   These variables are analysed via their *equilibrium* (fixed-point) values and by the composition of the “stability landscape” (which attractors—C, D, Ċ, Ď—exist).  Total payoff, average payoff and efficiency are never computed, so the link to efficiency remains unspecified.

B. Which of the 15 design parameters are even mentioned?  
   3 parameters:  
   (1) group size n  
   (7) punishment cost (fixed at 0)  
   (8) punishment magnitude s, g, T (held constant)  
   None of the remaining 12 parameters appears.

C. Which parameters are *systematically varied* to study their impact on any punishment treatment effect?  
   Strictly speaking, **none** of the 15.  The paper systematically varies *coupling strengths* (δ for resource diffusion, λ for social sanction spill-over) and *effort factors* μ, but those are outside the requested list.  Therefore 0 / 15 parameters are studied in the required way.

D. What predictions can be made—based solely on this paper—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
   • Because efficiency itself is never analysed, the paper offers no direct guidance.  
   • For parameters it does mention (#1, #7, #8) the authors neither compute efficiency nor compare “punishment” vs. “no-punishment” treatments, so no numerical effect sizes are available.  
   • Indirectly, one might infer that larger n or larger s would *increase* sanctioning capacity and thus help sustain cooperation, which *could* raise efficiency, but that inference is not made in the text, and would violate instruction 1.  Consequently, **little to no prediction can be made** from this paper about how any of the 15 parameters would modify the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

In short, the Ringsmuth et al. model is valuable for understanding how *cross-scale couplings* δ and λ change cooperation equilibria, but it offers virtually no direct evidence about the standard public-goods-experiment design parameters listed above, nor about efficiency as a dependent variable.

Below each parameter is treated in turn.

For every parameter we state  

(i) whether the paper ever defines or uses the parameter, giving the symbols and numerical values that actually appear in the text, tables or figures;  

(ii) whether the paper explores what happens when that parameter is *systematically varied* and, if so, what quantitative or qualitative effect is reported on any dependent variable; and  

(iii) whether the paper links that variation to the *punishment treatment effect on group efficiency*.  
Whenever the paper speaks about other dependent variables (most frequently “fraction of cooperators” or “evolutionary stable states”), this is noted explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players in the public-goods group  
   (i) Yes.  In well-mixed populations the group size is denoted G; in structured populations each focal game has k+1 players.  Numerical values used: G = 5 (Fig. 3b) and G ranging from 2–10 in Fig. 2; k = 2,3,4, … in Figs. 5 & 6.  
   (ii) Systematic variation: Fig. 2 (x* vs. G) and Fig. 3b (phase diagram in ω–G space).  Increasing G decreases the attraction basin of full cooperation at first and increases it later (synergistic punishment, ω>1).  For discounting (ω<1) larger G is always bad for cooperation.  
   (iii) No efficiency calculation and no comparison with a “no-punishment” baseline, so no direct statement about the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

2. Number of rounds  
   (i) Not mentioned.  Infinite-time replicator dynamics are assumed.  
   (ii) Not varied.  
   (iii) No discussion.

3. Is chat enabled?  
   Not mentioned; not varied; no discussion.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   (i) Yes.  Players choose C (contribute 1) or D (contribute 0).  The setting is fixed and never varied.  
   (ii–iii) No variation, no efficiency analysis.

5. Contribution default direction  
   Not mentioned; not varied; no discussion.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor r  
   (i) Yes.  Symbol r; examples 1.5 (Figs. 1,2,3b), 2.5 (Figs. 4,5,6), 4.5 (Fig. 4c).  
   (ii) Systematic variation: Fig. 3a (ω–r phase diagram).  Larger r expands the parameter region in which cooperation and defection are bi-stable and enlarges the attraction basin of full cooperation.  
   (iii) No efficiency or treatment-effect calculation.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   (i) Model parameter α (“each co-operator pays a fixed cost α to the punishment pool”).  Values used: 0.5 (Figs. 1–3,5,6), 0.4, 0.1 (Fig. 4).  
   (ii) Only threshold inequalities are stated ((k+1)(1+α) …); one set of pictures changes α between panels of Fig. 4.  There is no systematic graph α-vs-outcome.  
   (iii) No efficiency analysis.

8. Punishment magnitude  
   (i) Parameter β (maximum fine) together with the non-linear factor ω.  Values: β = 0.9 (Figs. 1,3,5,6a), 1.3 (Fig. 6b), 1.5 (Fig. 4b), 2.3 (Fig. 6c), 7 (Fig. 4c).  
   (ii) Systematically varied in Fig. 5 (equilibria vs. β) and Fig. 6 (interior equilibrium vs. k for several β).  Larger β always shrinks the unstable equilibrium and therefore enlarges the attraction basin of cooperation (both for discounting and synergy).  Interaction with k: under synergy, the sign of the k-effect reverses at higher β.  
   (iii) No efficiency/treatment-effect numbers.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   Not present; no variation; no discussion.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   Not present.

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
   Not applicable in an infinite horizon evolutionary model; not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   Not discussed.

14. Do punished players learn the identity of the punisher?  
15. Do rewarded players learn the identity of the rewarder?  
   Not discussed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary requested in items A-D
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables used  
    The paper does NOT report group efficiency (total payoff divided by the cooperative maximum).  The dependent variables are  
      • fraction of cooperators in the population (x or p_C);  
      • locations and stability of equilibria (x = 0, x = 1, interior x*);  
      • size of the attraction basin of full cooperation.  
    These differ from efficiency because they track strategy frequencies, not realised payoffs relative to an optimum.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
    Five:  
      1. Number of players (G or k+1)  
      4. All-or-nothing contribution (fixed, binary)  
      6. MPCR / multiplication factor r  
      7. Punishment cost α  
      8. Punishment magnitude β (plus the non-linear modifier ω, which is not in the original list but is central to the model)  
    The other ten parameters are absent.

C.  For how many parameters is the effect of *systematically varying* the parameter on the punishment treatment effect discussed?  
    Strictly speaking, none.  The paper never computes a punishment-minus-no-punishment treatment difference, nor does it evaluate efficiency.  
    If we look at other reported dependent variables (co-operation rate / equilibria) instead, systematic variation is shown for three parameters:  
      • Number of players G (Fig. 2, Fig. 3b)  
      • Multiplication factor r (Fig. 3a)  
      • Punishment magnitude β (Figs. 5 & 6)  
    Punishment cost α is only altered across isolated examples, not scanned systematically, and the all-or-nothing rule is not varied.

D.  Predictions one could make (only from content of this paper) about how the 15 parameters and their interactions affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency  

    Because efficiency is never computed, only indirect inferences are possible: higher long-run cooperation would normally raise efficiency if punishment costs are not too large.  Based solely on the paper:

    • Increasing β (punishment severity) should *increase* the treatment effect on efficiency, because it broadens the basin in which the population ends in full cooperation.  
    • Increasing r (MPCR) has the same qualitative influence.  
    • Increasing group size G (or degree k) has a non-monotonic influence under synergy (ω>1) and a negative influence under discounting (ω<1).  Therefore, no simple directional prediction can be made without knowing ω.  
    • Higher punishment cost α tends to undermine cooperation (appears in destabilising inequalities), so the efficiency gain from punishment would likely *decrease* when α is larger.  
    • All remaining parameters (2,3,5,9–15) are not discussed, so no prediction can be drawn from the paper.

    In short, only very tentative, cooperation-based statements can be offered; the paper provides almost no direct leverage for quantitative predictions about the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Authors: Vromen, J
Author Full Names: Vromen, Jack
Article Title: Ultimate and proximate explanations of strong reciprocity
Source Title: HISTORY AND PHILOSOPHY OF THE LIFE SCIENCES
Author Keywords: Strong reciprocity; Ultimate explanation; Proximate explanation; Reciprocal causation
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; EVOLUTIONARY-THEORY; COOPERATION; DISTINCTION; BIOLOGY
Abstract: Strong reciprocity (SR) has recently been subject to heated debate. In this debate, the West camp'' (West et al. in Evol Hum Behav 32(4): 231-262, 2011), which is critical of the case for SR, and the Laland camp'' (Laland et al. in Science, 334(6062): 1512-1516, 2011, Biol Philos 28(5): 719-745, 2013), which is sympathetic to the case of SR, seem to take diametrically opposed positions. The West camp criticizes advocates of SR for conflating proximate and ultimate causation. SR is said to be a proximate mechanism that is put forward by its advocates as an ultimate explanation of human cooperation. The West camp thus accuses advocates of SR for not heeding Mayr's original distinction between ultimate and proximate causation. The Laland camp praises advocates of SR for revising Mayr's distinction. Advocates of SR are said to replace Mayr's uni-directional view on the relation between ultimate and proximate causes by the bi-directional one of reciprocal causation. The paper argues that both the West camp and the Laland camp misrepresent what advocates of SR are up to. The West camp is right that SR is a proximate cause of human cooperation. But rather than putting forward SR as an ultimate explanation, as the West camp argues, advocates of SR believe that SR itself is in need of ultimate explanation. Advocates of SR tend to take gene-culture co-evolutionary theory as the correct meta-theoretical framework for advancing ultimate explanations of SR. Appearances notwithstanding, gene-culture coevolutionary theory does not imply Laland et al.' s notion of reciprocal causation. Reciprocal causation'' suggests that proximate and ultimate causes interact simultaneously, while advocates of SR assume that they interact sequentially. I end by arguing that the best way to understand the debate is by disambiguating Mayr's ultimate-proximate distinction. I propose to reserve ultimate'' and proximate'' for different sorts of explanations, and to use other terms for distinguishing different kinds of causes and different parts of the total causal chain producing behavior.

Article Title: Race for Power in Public Good Games with Unequal, Unstable Punishment Power
Author Keywords: public goods; social comparison; punishment; cooperation; social dilemmas; power
Keywords Plus: SOCIAL-COMPARISON PROCESSES; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; COOPERATION; PSYCHOLOGY; COMPETITION; INCENTIVES; MOTIVATION; DILEMMAS; SELF
Abstract: Decentralized punishment can maintain contributions to a public good at a high level. This positive effect holds even for situations involving inequality in punishment power, meaning that the relative costs for punishment differ between persons. We extend this line of research by examining the additional influence of instability of and thus potential competition for punishment power in public good experiments. As in previous research, inequality is operationalized by assigning the role of a 'strong player' to one group member, who can punish others at a reduced cost compared to other players. Instability is operationalized by the fact that the role assignment can change across rounds and is contingent on behavior in previous rounds. Three experiments show that under unequal, unstable (punishment-) power, individuals behave more competitively and engage in a race for power resulting in detrimental effects for the group. Specifically, we find that (i) unstable power goes along with a disproportionate use of punishment; (ii) not inequality by itself but rather the combination of instability and inequality causes this effect; and (iii) this excessive use of punishment is found not only when the role of the strong player is assigned to individuals who previously behaved rather selfishly but also when prosocial behavior leads to the top, speaking for a generalizability of our findings. Below is a parameter-by-parameter analysis based solely on the provided paper “Race for Power in Public Good Games with Unequal, Unstable Punishment Power.” In each case, I indicate (1) whether and how the paper mentions the parameter (including any fixed value used), and (2) whether the paper makes predictions (or provides data) about systematically varying that parameter’s effect on the “punishment treatment effect” (in this paper, that would refer to how punishment changes outcomes such as efficiency, contributions, or other measures). Where the paper does not address a parameter or does not vary it, I state so explicitly.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mention in paper: Yes. All experiments use groups of 4 players.  
   • Systematic variation or predictions: No. The number of players is held constant at 4. The paper does not discuss or test how changing group size would affect punishment or efficiency.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mention in paper: Yes. All experiments feature 10 rounds of the public goods game.  
   • Systematic variation or predictions: No. The paper does not systematically vary the number of rounds, nor does it predict how changing the number of rounds would affect the punishment treatment effect.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mention in paper: No. There is no mention of allowing player chat (textual or otherwise).  
   • Systematic variation or predictions: No. Not discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mention in paper: No. In the experiments, players can contribute any integer amount (0 to 20 Talers).  
   • Systematic variation or predictions: No. The “all or nothing” format is never used or discussed.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Mention in paper: No. The paper always allows players to choose freely how much to contribute (0–20 Talers). There is no forced or default contribution.  
   • Systematic variation or predictions: No. Not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplier
   • Mention in paper: Yes. The MPCR is 0.4 (the group multiplier is 1.6, split equally among 4 players).  
   • Systematic variation or predictions: No. The paper does not vary the MPCR or multiplier or discuss how changing it would affect punishment or efficiency.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mention in paper: Yes. It costs 1 Taler per punishment point to the punisher, in all conditions.  
   • Systematic variation or predictions: No. This cost is fixed; the paper does not alter it or discuss the effect of changing the cost.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted per unit punishment)
   • Mention in paper: Yes. Punishment “power” differs between “strong” (Type A) and “weak” (Type B) players. In unequal-power conditions, a strong player’s punishment magnitude is 4 Talers per point; a weak player’s punishment magnitude is 1 Taler per point.  
   • Systematic variation or predictions: Partly. The paper compares “equal punishment” (everyone’s magnitude = 1) to “unequal punishment” (one player with magnitude = 4). However, the paper does not vary the magnitude across multiple levels (it is only 1 vs. 4). The main systematic variation is whether that unequal power is stable or unstable. The authors do measure how those unequal-power setups affect outcomes such as contribution, the use of punishment, and overall efficiency. Numerical effect sizes (e.g., differences in “round wins”) are reported for comparisons of stable vs. unstable setups, not for a direct gradient of punishment magnitudes.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mention in paper: No. The study deals only with punishment; there is no mention of a reward mechanism.  
   • Systematic variation or predictions: No.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Mention in paper: No.  
   • Systematic variation or predictions: No.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward)
   • Mention in paper: No.  
   • Systematic variation or predictions: No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
   • Mention in paper: Yes. Participants know there will be 10 rounds.  
   • Systematic variation or predictions: No. The paper does not vary or manipulate whether the game length is known.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much others gained or lost)?
   • Mention in paper: Partly. All participants see each other’s contributions each round (and can see some “rank” information in certain conditions).  
   • Systematic variation or predictions: A partial manipulation appears in Experiment 2, where “rank info” is shown in some conditions but withheld in an “equal, no rank info” control condition. However, the paper does not treat “peer outcome visibility” as a primary factor systematically varied for the punishment effect alone—it mainly focuses on how “rank info” fosters competition when power is unstable. The paper reports that even small manipulations such as rank visibility can affect punishment usage, but there is no direct measure of its effect on “punishment treatment vs. no punishment.” Instead, it is folded into the designs that examine stable vs. unstable power.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Mention in paper: Yes, but only to say that ID numbers are reshuffled every round, making it impossible to identify the specific punisher.  
   • Systematic variation or predictions: No. The paper does not manipulate whether punishees learn who punished them.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Mention in paper: No. There is no reward mechanism.  
   • Systematic variation or predictions: No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary of the Paper’s Design and Findings

A. Dependent variables in the paper, including group efficiency:
   • The paper does measure (1) contributions to the public good, (2) total or average “round win” (which is effectively each player’s payoff in each round), and (3) punishment points assigned. Group efficiency is frequently referenced and captured by total (or average) payoff net of any punishment expenditures.  
   • The authors also track “cooperation” via contribution rates, but they explicitly note that efficiency can differ from simple contribution measures when a lot of punishment is wasted. Thus, “efficiency” sometimes decreases even when contributions remain the same, if punishment expenditures become excessive.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned?
   • The paper mentions the following parameters in some form:  
       (1) Number of players (fixed at 4),  
       (2) Number of rounds (fixed at 10),  
       (6) MPCR (fixed at 0.4),  
       (7) Punishment cost (fixed at 1 Taler per point),  
       (8) Punishment magnitude (1 vs. 4 in “weak vs. strong” players),  
       (12) Known length of game (10 rounds known),  
       (13) Peer outcomes or rank information (partially varied in one of the experiments).  
   • None of the other parameters (3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15) are systematically manipulated or even discussed in terms of variation.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when each parameter is systematically varied?
   • (8) Punishment magnitude is tied to “unequal power” vs. “equal power” designs. However, it is always either “everyone has magnitude=1” (equal) or “one strong player with magnitude=4, others have magnitude=1” (unequal). The paper’s main focus is whether that power asymmetry is stable or unstable. The authors do not present a gradient of punishment magnitudes, so the effect of systematically varying the magnitude alone is not examined. Instead, the effect is always bundled with stable vs. unstable roles.  
   • (13) In one condition, participants do not see their rank order; in the other conditions, they do. This rank-information difference partially modifies punishment usage, but it is not framed in the paper as a direct test of how “information display” alone shifts efficiency under punishment vs. no punishment. Instead, it is a supporting condition comparing “equal, rank info” vs. “equal, no rank info” and “unequal stable” vs. “unequal unstable.” Numerical differences (regressions) are reported in the text and tables, but there is no dedicated table showing “the punishment treatment effect with vs. without rank info” specifically for efficiency. Rather, you see references in Figures 2 and 3 (Experiment 2) to how “no rank info” yields somewhat fewer punishment points than “rank info,” but that is again always in combination with stable vs. unstable power.  
   • No other parameters from the list are systematically varied to isolate or estimate an effect on punishment or efficiency.

D. Predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, based solely on the paper:
   • The paper is narrowly focused on comparing (a) equal vs. unequal punishment power and (b) stable vs. unstable assignments of that power, with a side condition on rank-information display. It does not examine other parameters (e.g., group size, reward availability, or changes to MPCR) in a systematic way.  
   • Hence, from this paper alone, one cannot extrapolate how those other 15 parameters or their interactions would affect efficiency. The only fairly robust prediction that emerges is that making punishment power both unequal and unstable tends to reduce overall efficiency—because “weak” players (and sometimes the “strong” player) use punishment in a counterproductive, competitive way.  
   • Likewise, the paper suggests that adding rank information can increase punishing or “races for power,” but no formal prediction is made about systematically changing how information is displayed beyond the specific presence or absence of rank info.  
   • Therefore, beyond the results tied to “(8) punishment magnitude (unequal vs. equal),” “stability vs. instability of that inequality,” and the presence of “(13) rank info vs. no rank info,” little can be concluded about the rest of the 15 parameters.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Answering the four summary questions explicitly:

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   • Yes. The paper uses “round win” and “efficiency” (total payoff net of costs) as outcome measures. It also measures contributions (cooperation level) and assigned punishment. “Efficiency” can deviate from “contributions” if punishment costs become large.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned: (1), (2), (6), (7), (8), (12), (13). (Items 3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 14, and 15 are either not mentioned or not varied.)

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when the parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Practically only (8) and (13) receive anything close to systematic variation (equal vs. unequal punishment power, stable vs. unstable, and presence vs. absence of rank info). Even so, the paper bundles the manipulation of “punishment magnitude” (unequal vs. equal) with “stability” or “instability,” and rank info is only tested in some conditions. There is no separate, across-the-board exploration of each parameter’s effect on the punishment treatment.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency based solely on this paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not systematically address most of the parameters, so little can be predicted for them. The main, clear result is that “unequal + unstable punishment power” leads to excessive use of punishment and lower efficiency compared to stable or equal-power designs. A smaller, related finding is that showing rank information can foster competition, sometimes increasing punishment and lowering payoff. Beyond that, the paper provides no guidance on how changing group size, number of rounds, or adding rewards (etc.) might affect efficiency or the punishment treatment effect.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

All statements above reflect only what is contained in the given paper.
reference_APA: Dorrough, Angela, Gloeckner, Andreas & Lee, Borah (2017). Race for Power in Public Good Games with Unequal, Unstable Punishment Power. JOURNAL OF BEHAVIORAL DECISION MAKING.

Abstract: A peer punisher directly imposes fines upon defectors at a cost to himself. It is one of the mechanisms promoting cooperation, which is ubiquitous in nature. Parameter-by-parameter extraction from Sui et al. “Multiple tolerances dilute the second order cooperative dilemma”

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players in a group (M)
   • Discussed: yes.  Values used most often are M = 3 and M = 4; general formulas for any M are given.  
   • Systematic-variation results:
        – Critical fine that makes “punishment as a whole” more abundant than in neutrality  
          ω_crit | 3 = 1.25 v + 1.5 (1 − r/3)  (Eq. C.16)  
          ω_crit | 4 = 1.40 v + 1.2 (1 − r/4)  (Eq. C.31)  
        – Comparing ω_crit | 3 and ω_crit | 4 shows that larger groups (M = 4) favour punishment provided  
          0.15 v + 0.20 r < 0.30 (Fig. 6).  
        – Abundance differences within punishers: for M = 3,  π_P1 − π_P2 ≈ (N/48)(2ω−v)β  
          (Appendix C.2); for M = 4,  π_P1 − π_P2 ≈ (N/100)(3ω−v)β and  
          π_P2 − π_P3 ≈ (N/50)(ω−v)β (Appendix C.3).  
   • Dependent variables: stationary average abundance of each strategy; not efficiency.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Not mentioned; game is modelled as an indefinitely repeated evolutionary process.

3. Chat between players  
   • Not mentioned.

4. All-or-nothing contribution  
   • Mentioned but fixed.  Every co-operator or punisher “contributes a fixed amount 1” (Sec. 2).  
   • No systematic variation; no effect estimates.

5. Contribution default / return decision  
   • Not mentioned.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor r  
   • Discussed and systematically varied.  
   • Enters every analytical inequality via (1 − r/M).  Higher r lowers ω_crit, i.e. makes punishment prevail with a smaller fine.  Example for M = 3: ∂ω_crit/∂r = −0.5; for M = 4: ∂ω_crit/∂r = −0.30.  
   • Fig. 7 varies r/M from 0.25 to 0.8 and shows how strategy abundances change; no efficiency data are shown.

7. Cost to punish v  
   • Discussed and varied.  
   • Appears linearly in every threshold:  
        ω_crit | 3 increases 1.25 units for each unit rise in v;  
        ω_crit | 4 increases 1.40 units per unit v.  
   • In abundance contrasts, higher v lowers (2ω−v), (3ω−v) etc., therefore weakens the dominance of less-tolerant punishers.

8. Punishment magnitude ω  
   • Discussed and varied from 0.4 to 1.6 in simulations (Figs. 2 & 4).  
   • Larger ω always increases the relative (and total) abundance of punishers.  Exact linear effects shown above for π differences.  
   • Critical ω values derived:  
        M = 3, P1 favoured if ω > v + (1 − r/3);  
        M = 3, P2 favoured if ω > 2v + 3(1 − r/3);  
        M = 4, analogous formulas (see C.23-C.28).

9. Reward enabled  
10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   • Not included anywhere in the paper.

12. End-round information (known horizon)  
13. Feedback on peer outcomes  
14. Punisher identity revealed  
15. Rewarder identity revealed  
   • None of these information-display parameters are mentioned.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables used  
    – Stationary average abundance of each strategy (π_i).  
    – Critical punishment fine ω_crit derived from those abundances.  
    – Occasional reference to individual payoffs but no aggregate “efficiency” (total or average group payoff) is analysed.  Thus “efficiency” as defined by the user does not appear in the paper.

B.  Parameters from the list that are mentioned: 5 of 15  
    (1) group size M, (4) all-or-nothing contribution (fixed, not varied),  
    (6) MPCR r, (7) punishment cost v, (8) punishment magnitude ω.

C.  Parameters whose systematic variation is analysed with respect to the punishment treatment effect (in terms of strategy abundance, not efficiency): 4 of 15  
    (1) group size, (6) r, (7) v, (8) ω.  
    Exact analytical effect sizes are given by the inequalities and linear coefficients reproduced above.

D.  What can be inferred—strictly from this paper—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
    • The paper never measures efficiency, so direct predictions are impossible.  
    • Indirectly, greater abundance of punishers relative to defectors is likely to raise efficiency (because punishers still cooperate), so parameters that enhance punishment abundance (larger ω, lower v, higher r, and in some parameter regions larger M) would probably increase efficiency.  
    • No information is available for parameters 2,3,5,9-15, therefore no prediction can be made for them solely on the basis of this paper.

In short, the study provides detailed analytical results for how group size, the public-goods multiplication factor, and the cost and magnitude of punishment jointly determine when punishment strategies proliferate, but it does not report group efficiency, nor does it address any of the information-display or reward-related parameters listed by the user.

Authors: Murase, Y; Baek, SK
Author Full Names: Murase, Yohsuke; Baek, Seung Ki
Article Title: Friendly-rivalry solution to the iterated n-person public-goods game
Keywords Plus: PRISONERS-DILEMMA; EVOLUTION; COOPERATION; GENEROSITY; STRATEGIES; EXTORTION; CYCLES
Abstract: Author summary How to maintain cooperation among a number of self-interested individuals is a difficult problem, especially if they can sometimes commit error. In this work, we propose a strategy for the iterated n-person public-goods game based on the following five rules: Cooperate if everyone did, accept punishment for your own mistake, punish others' defection, recover cooperation if you find a chance, and defect in all the other circumstances. These rules are not far from actual human behavior, and the resulting strategy guarantees three advantages: First, if everyone uses it, full cooperation is recovered even if error occurs with small probability. Second, the player of this strategy always never obtains a lower long-term payoff than any of the co-players. Third, if the co-players are unconditional cooperators, it obtains a strictly higher long-term payoff than theirs. Therefore, if everyone uses this strategy, no one has a reason to change it. Furthermore, our simulation shows that this strategy will become highly abundant over long time scales due to its robustness against the invasion of other strategies. In this sense, the repeated social dilemma is solved for an arbitrary number of players. Repeated interaction promotes cooperation among rational individuals under the shadow of future, but it is hard to maintain cooperation when a large number of error-prone individuals are involved. One way to construct a cooperative Nash equilibrium is to find a 'friendly-rivalry' strategy, which aims at full cooperation but never allows the co-players to be better off. Recently it has been shown that for the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma in the presence of error, a friendly rival can be designed with the following five rules: Cooperate if everyone did, accept punishment for your own mistake, punish defection, recover cooperation if you find a chance, and defect in all the other circumstances. In this work, we construct such a friendly-rivalry strategy for the iterated n-person public-goods game by generalizing those five rules. The resulting strategy makes a decision with referring to the previous m = 2n - 1 rounds. A friendly-rivalry strategy for n = 2 inherently has evolutionary robustness in the sense that no mutant strategy has higher fixation probability in this population than that of a neutral mutant. Our evolutionary simulation indeed shows excellent performance of the proposed strategy in a broad range of environmental conditions when n = 2 and 3.

Below is an analysis of how the 15 parameters listed in your prompt appear in—and are discussed by—the Murase and Baek (2021) paper. The focus is on whether the paper explicitly (1) addresses each parameter, (2) provides any systematic variation of that parameter, and (3) links that variation to any “punishment treatment effect” on group efficiency (i.e., actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff under full cooperation). Throughout, note that the paper does not run an experiment or treatment explicitly labeled as “punishment” versus “no punishment,” nor does it provide measured or simulated increases/decreases in efficiency from adding a punishment mechanism. Instead, it introduces a theoretical strategy (“CAPRI-n”) that includes a rule labeled “punish others’ defection,” but no separate cost or magnitude is modeled for administering punishment. Consequently, the paper does not report a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” in the sense requested.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER DISCUSSION  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. Number of players  
   • Discussed? Yes. The entire paper focuses on an n-person public-goods game, with particular emphasis on n = 2, 3, and 4 in simulations.  
   • Systematic variation? Yes, but not in terms of a punishment treatment effect. The paper examines how the proposed CAPRI-n strategy operates for varying n; it does not compare “punishment versus no punishment” treatments. No numeric effect size is presented regarding “punishment treatment effects” for varying n.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Discussed? Indirectly. The game is modeled as infinitely repeated (the paper assumes an indefinite sequence of rounds).  
   • Systematic variation regarding punishment effect? No. The paper does not systematically vary the number of rounds (finite vs. infinite) or discuss how that might affect punishment. No numerical effect sizes are reported.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussed? No. There is no mention of any communication or chat between players in this paper.  
   • Systematic variation regarding punishment effect? No.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Discussed? Players choose between two discrete actions (cooperate or defect), but the paper does not frame this as “literally all or nothing” nor vary it. It is simply a two-action setup.  
   • Systematic variation regarding punishment effect? No.

5. Is the contribution default (such that players decide how much of their endowment to move back)?  
   • Discussed? No. The paper studies a discrete-action public-goods game: contribute or not. There is no mention of partial contributions or of adjusting a default.  
   • Systematic variation regarding punishment effect? No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as the multiplication factor  
   • Discussed? Yes. The paper uses a multiplication factor ρ strictly between 1 and n, and in the simulations, they also use a “benefit” parameter b related to ρ.  
   • Systematic variation regarding punishment effect? They vary b (e.g., b = 2, 3, …) and ρ in evolutionary simulations, but never in the sense of measuring a “punishment treatment effect.” No numeric effect size is given for a “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency as ρ or b changes.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not introduce a separate, quantifiable cost of punishment; “punishment” in CAPRI-n is simply switching to defection without an explicit cost to the punisher.  
   • Systematic variation regarding punishment effect? No.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a target)  
   • Discussed? No. The strategy calls for “punish others’ defection” by defecting but does not formalize a separate cost taken from the punished player’s payoff.  
   • Systematic variation regarding punishment effect? No.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussed? No. There is no mention of rewarding others in the sense of bestowing positive payoffs or transfers.  
   • Systematic variation regarding punishment effect? No.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Discussed? No.  
    • Systematic variation regarding punishment effect? No.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
    • Discussed? No.  
    • Systematic variation regarding punishment effect? No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    • Discussed? Not explicitly. The model is of an infinitely repeated game with no known end.  
    • Systematic variation regarding punishment effect? No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?  
    • Discussed? No. The paper does not describe any information-display conditions.  
    • Systematic variation regarding punishment effect? No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Discussed? No. The paper does not address knowledge of who defected as “punishment.”  
    • Systematic variation regarding punishment effect? No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Discussed? No. The paper does not involve reward or knowledge of it.  
    • Systematic variation regarding punishment effect? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper does use an “efficiency” criterion—meaning that if everyone adopts the CAPRI-n strategy, the group will tend toward full cooperation. However, the paper never measures “group efficiency” strictly as (actual total payoff)/(maximum total payoff) in a labeled “treatment.” It also uses other dependent measures such as long-term payoff (individual or average) and fixation probabilities in evolutionary simulations. They do not run separate “punishment vs. no-punishment” conditions; thus, they do not compare a measured “treatment effect” on efficiency.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned:  
       1) Number of players (the paper studies n = 2, 3, 4)  
       6) The multiplication factor ρ (and b, which is related)  
     • None of the other 13 parameters are discussed in any direct sense.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. The paper does not discuss “punishment treatment effects” or systematically compare payoffs in a special “punishment enabled” vs. “no punishment” scenario.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not compare a punishment treatment to a non-punishment baseline, so it offers no direct evidence from which to estimate a “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency. We therefore cannot predict how systematically altering these parameters would change efficiency gains or losses specifically tied to a punishment mechanism.

Abstract: Most observed institutional arrangements, in governments, firms, and other organizations, acknowledge the effectiveness of imposing sanctioning institutions and monitoring policies to achieve particular goals. However, less attention has been paid to the influences of the delegation mechanism of sanctioning power. In particular, it remains unclear whether the mechanism influences the legitimacy of the authority/institution, in centralized institutional arrangements. We report laboratory-experimental results of a public goods game that compare the performance of exogenous (i.e., the Leviathan) versus endogenous (i.e., the Democracy) delegation of sanctioning power. Observed differences are not statistically significant, regardless of the effectiveness of sanctions imposed, tested in two experiments with different punishment/cost functions. Democratic schemes in centralized power environments should not be taken for granted. Experimental evidence contradicts the common belief of a robust causal relationship between indirect democratic institutions, collective action, and economic outcomes.

Below is an item‐by‐item analysis of what the paper says (and does not say) about each of the 15 parameters you listed. All statements refer solely to the content of the paper “The effects of centralized power and institutional legitimacy on collective action,” including its figures and tables. Throughout, “punishment treatment effect” refers to the difference made by introducing punishment (the “tax/punishment environment”) relative to a baseline without punishment (the “VCM” phase). Note that the paper measures and reports primarily (1) contributions to the public good and (2) net payoffs (or profits). Although net payoffs can be interpreted as a measure of efficiency, the paper never explicitly defines “efficiency” as the actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff of a fully cooperative group. The authors also do not systematically vary most of the 15 parameters. Where they do vary a parameter (namely, the punishment cost and punishment magnitude), they report effects on contributions and payoffs, but not always in a way framed as “efficiency.” Below is the detailed breakdown:

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • What the paper does:  
     – All experimental groups consist of 5 players.  
     – This is not varied.  
   • Does the paper predict or discuss how systematically varying the number of players would affect the punishment treatment effect (on any outcome)?  
     – No.  

2. Number of rounds  
   • What the paper does:  
     – Each experiment has 10 rounds in Phase 1 (baseline VCM) and 10 rounds in Phase 2 (punishment).  
     – This is not varied: every session uses exactly 20 total rounds (10 pre‐punishment, 10 with punishment).  
   • Does the paper predict or discuss how systematically varying the number of rounds would affect the punishment treatment effect?  
     – No.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • What the paper does:  
     – No mention of any real‐time chat or communication among players.  
     – No variation in whether chat is present; no chat was used.  
   • Does the paper predict or discuss how systematically varying chat would affect the punishment treatment effect?  
     – No.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • What the paper does:  
     – Players can contribute any integer from 0 up to their entire endowment of 20 ECUs.  
     – “All or nothing” is never used or mentioned.  
   • Does the paper predict or discuss how systematically forcing “all or nothing” contributions would affect the punishment treatment effect?  
     – No.  

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much to “move back” from the public fund)?  
   • What the paper does:  
     – The experiment uses the usual “how much you contribute out of 20” format.  
     – There is no discussion of a “default” contribution mechanism.  
   • Does the paper predict or discuss how systematically varying this would affect punishment outcomes?  
     – No.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor  
   • What the paper does:  
     – The MPCR is fixed at 0.4 in both phases of all sessions.  
   • Does the paper predict or discuss how systematically varying the MPCR would affect the punishment treatment effect?  
     – No.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • What the paper does:  
     – This is systematically varied across two experiments:  
       (a) Main experiment: The cost is 1:1 (one point from the group/manager to reduce one point of the target’s payoff).  
       (b) Second experiment: The cost is cheaper at 3:1 (one point from the group/manager reduces the target’s payoff by three).  
     – The paper presents results for each experiment separately.  
   • Does the paper provide a numeric effect of systematically varying punishment cost on the punishment treatment effect?  
     – The paper does not offer a single “elasticity” or dose‐response figure for cost of punishment. Instead, it runs two stand‐alone experiments. Key findings relevant to net payoffs (the paper’s proxy for efficiency) under each cost condition:  
       (1) In the main experiment (1:1 cost), introducing punishment increased average net payoffs (comparing baseline VCM vs. punishment), but there was no statistically significant difference in net payoffs between Democracy and Leviathan.  
       (2) In the second experiment (3:1 cost), again net payoffs improved under punishment, with no significant difference between Democracy and Leviathan.  
       (3) The authors do not pool or regress cost as a continuous variable, so they do not give a precise “effect size” purely as a function of cost.  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • What the paper does:  
     – Linked to the cost above, the magnitude is 1 point per unit in the main experiment, and 3 points per unit in the second experiment.  
   • Does the paper predict or discuss how systematically varying the magnitude alone would affect the punishment treatment effect?  
     – Apart from running two separate cost‐magnitude designs, the paper does not discuss or model what would happen if the magnitude were on a continuum or systematically changed.  
     – They only report that in both designs, punishment significantly raises contributions relative to VCM, but does not produce a significant difference between Democracy and Leviathan in net payoffs.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • What the paper does:  
     – There is no reward mechanism in this study.  
   • Does the paper predict or discuss how systematically varying a reward mechanism would affect the punishment treatment effect?  
     – No.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • What the paper does:  
     – No reward mechanism, so no cost of reward.  
   • Does the paper predict or discuss it?  
     – No.  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded)  
   • What the paper does:  
     – Again, no reward mechanism.  
   • Does the paper predict or discuss it?  
     – No.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
   • What the paper does:  
     – Subjects know there are 10 rounds in Phase 1 and 10 rounds in Phase 2.  
     – The authors do not systematically vary whether the time horizon is known.  
   • Does the paper predict or discuss how systematically varying end‐of‐game knowledge would affect the punishment treatment effect?  
     – No.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?  
   • What the paper does:  
     – Each player sees how many ECUs each group member contributed, in random order, at the end of each round. In the punishment phase, they also see how many total punishment points were used, but not who received them (except if they personally were punished, they see how many points they lost).  
   • Does the paper predict or discuss how systematically varying this information display would affect the punishment treatment effect?  
     – They give no direct predictions about “more vs. less” information beyond the implemented design.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • What the paper does:  
     – No. The “manager” (the centralized punisher) remains anonymous; punished players do not learn which person in their group punished them.  
   • Does the paper predict or discuss how systematically varying punisher identification would affect outcomes?  
     – No.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • What the paper does:  
     – No reward procedure exists in the design, so this does not apply.  
   • Does the paper discuss any systematic variation of a rewarder’s identity revelation?  
     – No.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY RESPONSES

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   • The paper’s reported outcomes are primarily:  
     1) Contribution to the public good.  
     2) Net payoff (profits).  
   • Although “net payoff” can be taken as a measure of how well the group is doing economically, the paper never explicitly calls it “efficiency” in the sense of “actual total payoff ÷ the maximum possible payoff.” Thus, “efficiency” (as you define it above) is not directly measured, even though net payoffs serve a similar function.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned (but not systematically varied):  
     – (1) Number of players: always 5.  
     – (2) Number of rounds: always 10 + 10 = 20 total.  
     – (6) MPCR: fixed at 0.4.  
     – (12) Participants do know there will be 10 rounds in each phase.  
     – (13) Peers’ contributions are displayed each round, and at the end of each round total punishment is shown in random order.  
     – (14) The punished player does not see the identity of the punisher.  
   • Systematically varied in separate experimental conditions:  
     – (7) Punishment cost (1:1 vs. 3:1)  
     – (8) Punishment magnitude (1 point vs. 3 points deducted per punishment unit)  
   • Not mentioned or not used:  
     – (3) Chat not used.  
     – (4) “All or nothing” forced contributions not used.  
     – (5) No “contribution default” mechanism.  
     – (9) Reward is not used.  
     – (10) Reward cost is not used.  
     – (11) Reward magnitude is not used.  
     – (15) No reward at all, so no knowledge of a rewarder’s identity.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Only parameters 7 (punishment cost) and 8 (punishment magnitude) are systematically varied.  
   • Effect sizes from the paper regarding net payoffs (the paper’s nearest proxy to “efficiency”):  
     – Main experiment (cost = 1:1, magnitude = 1):  
       • Leviathan: net payoffs rise by 3.59 ECUs when adding punishment (Table 2, Panel C).  
       • Democracy: net payoffs rise by 4.72 ECUs (Table 2, Panel C).  
       • Difference‐in‐difference = 1.125 (p = 0.232), not significant.  
     – Second experiment (cost = 3:1, magnitude = 3):  
       • Leviathan: net payoffs rise by 6.63 ECUs (Table 3, Panel C).  
       • Democracy: net payoffs rise by 5.07 ECUs.  
       • Difference‐in‐difference = –1.154 (p = 0.381), not significant.  
   • The authors conclude that while punishment (of either cost structure) raises payoffs relative to no‐punishment, whether punishment is delegated “democratically” or “exogenously” does not change net payoffs in a statistically significant way.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not systematically vary most parameters and does not provide any discussion for them. Hence, no prediction can be made from the paper on parameters 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, or 15 regarding their effect on efficiency.  
   • The only systematic variation pertains to punishment cost (7) and punishment magnitude (8). In both cost–magnitude settings tested, punishment improved net payoffs versus no‐punishment. However, the paper shows no systematic advantage for one version of centralized punishment over the other (i.e., Democracy vs. Leviathan) in terms of net payoffs. There is also no clear evidence in the paper that the higher magnitude/lower cost (3:1) yields higher “efficiency” gains than the 1:1 setting, beyond the fact that net payoffs did increase from baseline in both. The authors do not link that increase explicitly to an “efficiency ratio,” nor do they claim strong differences between the two cost conditions.  

────────────  
Overall, then, the paper only discusses systematic variation for punishment cost and magnitude, and it finds that while punishment in either cost–magnitude condition significantly raises net payoffs (and contributions) relative to no‐punishment, it sees no reliable difference between an endogenously chosen punisher (“Democracy”) versus an exogenously assigned punisher (“Leviathan”). The paper does not provide predictions for how any of the other parameters you listed would systematically affect efficiency under punishment.

Authors: Clavien, C; Tanner, CJ; Clément, F; Chapuisat, M
Author Full Names: Clavien, Christine; Tanner, Colby J.; Clement, Fabrice; Chapuisat, Michel
Article Title: Choosy Moral Punishers
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; STRONG RECIPROCITY; COSTLY PUNISHMENT; POPULATIONS; COOPERATION; ENFORCEMENT; MOTIVATION; SOCIETIES; EVOLUTION; FAIRNESS
Abstract: The punishment of social misconduct is a powerful mechanism for stabilizing high levels of cooperation among unrelated individuals. It is regularly assumed that humans have a universal disposition to punish social norm violators, which is sometimes labelled universal structure of human morality or pure aversion to social betrayal. Here we present evidence that, contrary to this hypothesis, the propensity to punish a moral norm violator varies among participants with different career trajectories. In anonymous real-life conditions, future teachers punished a talented but immoral young violinist: they voted against her in an important music competition when they had been informed of her previous blatant misconduct toward fellow violin students. In contrast, future police officers and high school students did not punish. This variation among socio-professional categories indicates that the punishment of norm violators is not entirely explained by an aversion to social betrayal. We suggest that context specificity plays an important role in normative behaviour; people seem inclined to enforce social norms only in situations that are familiar, relevant for their social category, and possibly strategically advantageous.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter accounting of what the paper by Chassang and Zehnder (titled “Rewards and punishments: Informal contracting through social preferences”) does and does not say regarding each of the 15 specified parameters. Note that the paper never analyzes a standard public goods game, never uses the particular 15 parameters listed, and never reports a numerical “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency (understood as total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff of a fully cooperative group). Accordingly, all 15 parameters either go unmentioned or receive no systematic treatment in the paper.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
   • Not mentioned in the paper. The authors study interactions among a single principal, one active agent, and one passive player, without systematically varying the total number of players.

2) Number of rounds  
   • Not mentioned. The paper analyzes a single interaction (ex post transfers within one principal–agent–passive‐player setting), with no repeated‐round structure discussed or varied.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Not mentioned or analyzed in the paper.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Not mentioned. The paper involves a continuous transfer T in [−Tmax, Tmax], but there is no “contribution” variable (nor a mention of forcing it to be “all or nothing”).

5) Is the contribution default (if true, do players decide how much to move back into their hand)?  
   • Not mentioned. There is no mechanism in the paper resembling a “default contribution level” that participants could adjust.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
   • Not mentioned. Although the authors do distinguish “positive” and “negative externality environments,” no standard MPCR‐style factor is used or systematically varied.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Not mentioned in the sense of a discrete “per‐unit” punishment cost. The paper’s “λ” parameter reflects a general efficiency loss from any transfer (reward or punishment), but this is not treated as a “cost per unit of punishment” in the usual experimental‐economics sense, nor is it systematically varied to study an effect on “punishment treatment” in a public goods game.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment imposed)  
   • Not mentioned. While the paper discusses “punitive transfers,” there is no discrete punishment‐points‐per‐coin framework nor any systematic variation of it.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Not separated from punishment as an on–off choice. The principal can implement positive or negative transfers, but the possibility of enabling/disabling reward is not discussed or varied.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Not mentioned. As with punishment, the paper models a single “efficiency cost” coefficient λ for all transfers (positive or negative), not a reward‐specific cost systematically varied.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted)  
   • Not mentioned in the sense of discrete reward units. The paper’s transfer T covers both rewards and punishments but is not varied per “unit of reward.”

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
   • Not mentioned. The model is single‐interaction; no repeated‐game or known‐horizon framework is studied.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?  
   • Not mentioned. Only the principal’s information set about the agent’s possible “pro‐social” vs. “non‐pro‐social” action is discussed. There is no systematic exploration of showing/hiding outcomes to peers.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Not mentioned. The model has one principal who always makes reward/punishment decisions, so there is no analysis of whether the punished party knows the punisher’s identity.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Not mentioned for the same reason as parameter 14.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?

The paper’s focus is theoretical, examining how a principal’s social preferences and ex post transfers can (partially) induce a pro‐social action by an agent. While the authors do use the language of “efficiency” in a theoretical sense—comparing equilibrium outcomes to a “first‐best” or “ex ante optimal” arrangement—they do not measure “group efficiency” in the manner of experimental public goods games (i.e., total payoff as a fraction of the payoff under full cooperation). Instead, the main dependent variables are:  
• whether the agent chooses the pro‐social action,  
• the sum of payoffs (sometimes called “share of the efficient surplus”),  
• the difference between equilibrium outcomes and ex ante optimal surplus.  

Hence they do talk of “efficiency” (e.g., “bounded away from first‐best” or “partially internalized”), but not as “actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff of a fully cooperative group.”

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

None. The paper does not mention or systematically manipulate any of the 15 parameters listed above.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?

For none. The authors do not discuss (nor report) the effect of systematically varying any of those 15.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

Because the paper does not address any of the 15 parameters or how they might be systematically varied, it is not possible to draw predictions from its content on how those parameters (or their interactions) would affect a “punishment treatment effect” on group efficiency. The paper’s theoretical framework simply does not cover these features of experimental public goods designs, so no meaningful prediction can be made solely from its text.
reference_APA: Chassang, Sylvain & Zehnder, Christian (2016). Rewards and punishments: Informal contracting through social preferences. THEORETICAL ECONOMICS.

Abstract: We study how communication affects cooperation in an experimental public goods environment with punishment and counter-punishment opportunities. Participants interacted over 30 rounds in fixed groups with fixed identifiers that allowed them to trace other group members' behavior over time. The two dimensions of communication we study are asking for a specific contribution level and having to express oneself when choosing to counter-punish. We conduct four experimental treatments, all involving a contribution stage, a punishment stage, and a counter-punishment stage in each round. In the first treatment communication is not possible at any of the stages. The second treatment allows participants to ask for a contribution level at the punishment stage and in the third treatment participants are required to send a message if they decide to counter-punish. The fourth combines the two communication channels of the second and third treatments. We find that the three treatments involving communication at any of the two relevant stages lead to significantly higher contributions than the baseline treatment. We find no difference between the three treatments with communication. We also relate our results to previous results from treatments without counter-punishment opportunities and do not find that the presence of counter-punishment leads to lower cooperation level. The overall pattern of results shows that given fixed identifiers the key factor is the presence of communication. Whenever communication is possible contributions and earnings are higher than when it is not, regardless of counter-punishment opportunities.
