Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what (if anything) the paper says about each of the 15 listed factors and whether the authors vary it in a way that would allow inferences about its impact on how punishment affects efficiency. All references (including numeric effect sizes) come strictly from the text, tables, and figures of the paper itself. Parenthetical references to “Treatment 1, 2, 3, 4” (or “T1,” etc.) follow the paper’s terminology.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1) Number of players  
• Mentioned? Yes. The paper fixes groups of four participants in all sessions (p. 7–8).  
• Systematically varied? No. The paper does not alter group size, nor does it predict how changing group size would affect punishment’s impact on efficiency.  

2) Number of rounds  
• Mentioned? Yes. Each session has 30 rounds in total, divided into three blocks of 10 (p. 7–8).  
• Systematically varied? No. All treatments use 30 rounds; the paper does not explore how changing that number influences the impact of punishment on efficiency.  

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
• Mentioned? Yes. The paper’s key design feature is whether participants can send messages (what the authors call “communication”) during either the punishment stage or the counter-punishment stage (or both) (p. 5–6).  
• Systematically varied? Yes.  
  – Treatment 1: No communication.  
  – Treatment 2: Communication (a normative message) is allowed alongside punishment.  
  – Treatment 3: Counter-punishers must send a free-form message when counter-punishing.  
  – Treatment 4: Both forms of communication (the normative message and the forced message when counter-punishing) are enabled.  
• Effects on punishment treatment (including efficiency)?  
  – The paper reports that adding either sort of communication substantially boosts contributions and raises earnings relative to no‐communication treatments (Tables 2, 3, 6–9; Figures 1–4). In other words, once punishment is introduced, having some form of communication offsets the usual negative effects of punishment/counter-punishment on group payoffs.  
  – Numerical effect sizes on earnings for Block 2 (rounds 11–20) can be inferred from Table 3 (p. 14):  
    • No communication (T1) had lower average earnings (e.g., 22.64 in Block 2).  
    • Communication treatments (T2, T3, T4) had higher average earnings in Block 2 (26.55, 25.66, and 25.71, respectively), a difference of roughly 3 to 4 monetary units on a baseline of about 22–23 units.  

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Mentioned? Indirectly. Participants choose any integer from 0 to 20 tokens to contribute (p. 7). They are not restricted to all-or-nothing contributions.  
• Systematically varied? No. No discussion of forcing all-or-nothing contributions or how that would change the effect of punishment on efficiency.  

5) Is the contribution default?  
• Mentioned? No. The paper does not discuss a “default” contribution or any systematic shifting of endowment back to one’s hand.  

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
• Mentioned? Yes. Payoffs (p. 7) use the formula 20 − Ci + 0.4 × (sum of contributions). Thus the MPCR is 0.4.  
• Systematically varied? No. MPCR is fixed at 0.4 in all treatments; no predicted effects of changing it.  

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Mentioned? Yes. Imposing one punishment point costs the punisher 1 unit (p. 8).  
• Systematically varied? No. The cost of 1 is used consistently; there is no discussion of how different costs would alter efficiency.  

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
• Mentioned? Yes. Each assigned punishment point costs the punished player 3 units (p. 8).  
• Systematically varied? No. Always 3; the paper does not discuss varying it or its effect on efficiency.  

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
• Mentioned? No. There is no reward mechanism in these experiments, so no discussion or variation of rewards.  

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Mentioned? No. Not applicable, since rewards do not appear.  

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
• Mentioned? No. Not applicable, as no reward mechanism is used.  

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?  
• Mentioned? Yes. Participants are told from the start there are 30 rounds (p. 7).  
• Systematically varied? No. No discussion of changing that information.  

13) Are peer outcomes shown? (Do players see how much others gained or lost?)  
• Mentioned? Partial. After each stage, everyone sees each other’s contributions and learns who punished whom, but the paper does not systematically manipulate the level of outcome information (p. 7–8). No separate discussion about modifying this information and its effect on efficiency.  

14) When a player is punished, do they know who specifically punished them?  
• Mentioned? Yes. Punished group members learn which IDs assigned punishment to them (p. 8). This is the same across all treatments.  
• Systematically varied? No.  

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who specifically rewarded them?  
• Mentioned? No. The experiment does not include reward, so this does not arise.  

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
• Yes. The paper explicitly reports “earnings” or payoffs (Tables 3, 6–9) and also frequently discusses contribution levels. Punishment and counter-punishment usage is measured as well. Hence, “efficiency” is tracked as average earnings (the authors refer to “the bottom line” or “overall earnings”), but they also analyze contributions and punishment behavior as additional dependent variables.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Mentioned:  
  1) Number of players (fixed at 4),  
  2) Number of rounds (30),  
  3) Chat/communication possibility (varied),  
  6) MPCR = 0.4,  
  7) Punishment cost = 1,  
  8) Punishment magnitude = 3,  
  12) Rounds are known,  
  13) Some outcome/feedback info is displayed (not varied),  
  14) Punisher identity is revealed.  
• Not mentioned or not applicable: 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 15.  
• Hence 9 out of the 15 are at least noted in the paper (3 is the only one truly varied).

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• Only one parameter—parameter (3), the presence or absence of communication—was systematically varied and analyzed for its impact on the “punishment + counter-punishment” treatment’s effect on contribution and earnings. None of the other 14 parameters were systematically varied or predicted to alter the punishment treatment effect in this paper.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
• The paper’s only clear inference is that permitting communication (parameter 3) has a major positive impact: it neutralizes the otherwise efficiency‐reducing effect of adding counter‐punishment opportunities. In treatments without communication, punishment plus counter‐punishment lowers earnings; in treatments with communication—of any type—contributions and efficiency rise substantially.  
• On all other parameters, the paper either keeps them fixed or does not discuss how changing them might influence the effect of punishment on efficiency. Hence, little to no prediction can be made from the paper about parameter changes other than the presence/absence of communication.

Abstract: Explanations for biological evolution in terms of changes in gene frequencies refer to outcomes rather than process. Integrating epigenetic studies with older evolutionary theories has drawn attention to the ways in which evolution occurs. Adaptation at the level of the gene is giving way to adaptation at the level of the organism and higher-order assemblages of organisms. Authors: Zheng, XT; Nie, PY

Article Title: Effective Punishment Needs Legitimacy
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC GOOD GAMES; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; GROUP-SIZE; COOPERATION; GOODS; PROVISION; EVOLUTION; ENFORCEMENT
Abstract: Perverse punishment may hinder cooperation. Perverse punishment includes retaliation punishment and non-retaliation punishment, hereafter other perverse punishment. We design two treatments of contributing to a public good: anonymous punishment (AP) and public punisher ID to the punishee (PPID) treatments. Retaliation is possible in PPID, but not in AP. PPID does generate more retaliation punishments. We also find that contributions in PPID are relatively stable across different group sizes, while voluntary contributions mechanism (VCM) and AP are more sensitive to changes in group size. We explain the effectiveness of the punishment scheme by the legitimacy of a punishment. In PPID, the possibility of retaliation makes a subject deliberate more on the legitimacy of a punishment when he/she is contemplating imposing one, which leads to less perverse punishment and a higher level of cooperation in our experiment. This effect is more prominent in larger groups when targeting the punisher becomes harder without knowing the punisher's ID in AP. In particular, while the effect of whether a subject is punished on the increment of contribution is not statistically significant, the number of punishers does increase the amount of contribution significantly.

1. NUMBER OF PLAYERS  
   • Discussed? Yes. The experiment includes groups of size 4, 8, or 12 (see Table 1).  
   • Systematically varied? Yes. They explicitly run treatments with these three different group sizes and compare outcomes.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (and on efficiency)?  
     – The paper reports that Anonymous Punishment (AP) yields higher average efficiency than Public Punisher ID (PPID) for 4‐person groups (85.55% vs. 78.25%), but for 8‐ and 12‐person groups, PPID yields a higher efficiency than AP (80.60% vs. 76.10% for 8‐person groups; 78.05% vs. 61.35% for 12‐person groups; see Table 8).  
     – In other words, when group size grows, AP’s efficiency drops more sharply, whereas PPID remains relatively more effective.  

2. NUMBER OF ROUNDS  
   • Discussed? Yes. There are 10 rounds of voluntary contributions mechanism (VCM) and 30 rounds of VCM with punishment (AP or PPID).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper keeps the total number of rounds fixed (10 + 30).  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (and on efficiency)? They do not test how a changing total number of rounds alone would affect efficiency; no numerical effects are given.  

3. IS CHAT ENABLED BETWEEN PLAYERS?  
   • Discussed? Yes, briefly: the paper states that “communication was not allowed.”  
   • Systematically varied? No. They do not compare a chat‐enabled versus non‐chat‐enabled condition.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (and on efficiency)? Not mentioned.  

4. IS THE CONTRIBUTION “ALL OR NOTHING”?  
   • Discussed? Only insofar as the paper states that players can contribute “any number between 0 and 10,” including decimals. So it is not all or nothing.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (and on efficiency)? Not discussed.  

5. IS THE CONTRIBUTION DEFAULT (DO PLAYERS DECIDE HOW MUCH TO REMOVE FROM A PUBLIC FUND)?  
   • Discussed? No. The contribution is a standard voluntary contribution mechanism where subjects input how much to contribute from a 10‐EMU endowment. There is no “default removal” format.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (and on efficiency)? Not discussed.  

6. MARGINAL PER CAPITA RETURN (MPCR) OR RELATED MULTIPLICATION FACTOR  
   • Discussed? Yes. They double (×2) the group account and split it evenly (so effectively MPCR = 0.5).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The MPCR remains the same across all conditions.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (and on efficiency)? Not analyzed as a factor that is varied.  

7. PUNISHMENT COST TO IMPOSE A SINGLE UNIT OF PUNISHMENT  
   • Discussed? Yes. Each 1 EMU spent on punishment by the punisher costs the punisher 1 EMU.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (and on efficiency)? Not reported for changing this cost.  

8. PUNISHMENT MAGNITUDE (THE COINS DEDUCTED FROM THE PUNISHEE PER UNIT)  
   • Discussed? Yes. Each 1 EMU spent on punishment reduces 2 EMUs from the punished player.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (and on efficiency)? Not discussed in terms of systematically varying the magnitude.  

9. WHETHER A REWARD IS ENABLED  
   • Discussed? No. Only punishment is studied; no positive reward or “reward stage” is mentioned.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

10. REWARD COST TO GRANT A SINGLE UNIT OF REWARD  
    • Discussed? No (no rewards in the design).  
    • Systematically varied? No.  

11. REWARD MAGNITUDE (THE COINS AWARDED FOR EACH UNIT OF REWARD)  
    • Discussed? No (no rewards in the design).  
    • Systematically varied? No.  

12. IS THE NUMBER OF ROUNDS KNOWN TO PLAYERS (DO THEY KNOW WHEN THE GAME ENDS)?  
    • Discussed? Yes. Participants know there are 40 periods (10 + 30).  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment (and on efficiency)? Not discussed.  

13. ARE PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN? (DO PLAYERS KNOW HOW MUCH OTHERS GAINED/LOST?)  
    • Discussed? Yes, they see others’ contributions (in descending order) and punishment outcomes.  
    • Systematically varied? Not exactly. The main variation is whether IDs are revealed to the punishee (Parameter 14). Otherwise, all treatments show how much each person contributed (anonymously listed in AP, with ID in PPID).  
    • Effect on punishment treatment (and on efficiency)? Not discussed as an isolated, systematically varied factor.  

14. WHEN A PLAYER IS PUNISHED, DO THEY KNOW WHO THE SPECIFIC PUNISHER IS?  
    • Discussed? Yes. This is the paper’s key manipulation (AP vs. PPID).  
    • Systematically varied? Yes. AP conceals the punisher’s identity; PPID reveals the punisher’s ID to the punishee.  
    • Effect on punishment treatment (and on efficiency)?  
      – In 4‐person groups, AP yields slightly higher efficiency (85.55%) than PPID (78.25%).  
      – In 8‐ and 12‐person groups, PPID yields higher efficiency (80.60% vs. 76.10% in 8‐member; 78.05% vs. 61.35% in 12‐member) (Table 8).  
      – This difference is attributed to punishment “legitimacy”: AP tends to create more “perverse” or “irrational” punishment in large groups, whereas PPID fosters more carefully targeted punishment (at the risk of retaliation), which ultimately leads to higher efficiency for bigger groups.  

15. WHEN A PLAYER IS REWARDED, DO THEY KNOW WHO THE REWARDER IS?  
    • Discussed? No. There is no reward mechanism in the experiment.  
    • Systematically varied? No.

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • Yes. The paper reports (1) contributions, (2) total or average earnings per round, and (3) an “efficiency” measure (actual total payoff compared to the maximum possible payoff). These dependent variables differ: “contributions” measure how much of the endowment is put into the public good, while “efficiency” and “earnings” measure (respectively) the ratio of realized payoffs to theoretical maximum and the monetary outcomes.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
     1 (group size),  
     2 (number of rounds stated but not varied),  
     3 (chat disabled, not varied),  
     4 (contribution is not all‐or‐nothing, but not varied),  
     5 (no “default” mechanism, but they mention standard free contribution),  
     6 (MPCR = 0.5, not varied),  
     7 & 8 (punishment cost and magnitude set at 1 EMU spent → 2 EMUs deducted, not varied),  
     12 (finite/known rounds),  
     13 (basic outcome information is displayed),  
     14 (punisher identity revealed vs. not) is explicitly varied.  
   • Not mentioned:  
     9, 10, 11, 15 (no reward mechanism at all).  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • Only two are truly “systematically varied” in ways the authors analyze for their effect on outcomes:  
     1 (group size varied across 4, 8, 12),  
     14 (punisher identity hidden vs. revealed: AP vs. PPID).  
   • They present how these two variations affect punishment patterns, contributions, and eventually earnings/efficiency (see especially Table 8). Numerical effect sizes, in terms of average efficiency, are given for each group size by treatment (AP vs. PPID).  

D. Predictions about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, based solely on the paper:  
   • The paper provides detailed evidence only for (1) group size and (14) anonymous vs. identified punishment. Its main finding is that, for large groups, revealing the punisher’s identity (PPID) leads to higher efficiency than anonymous punishment (AP), whereas for small groups (4 members) AP does slightly better.  
   • Other parameters (e.g., number of rounds, punishment cost, etc.) are not experimentally changed in this study, so no direct prediction can be drawn from this paper about what would happen if those were systematically varied. The authors do not provide effect‐size estimates for any such variation beyond what they themselves manipulated (group size and punisher ID).  
   • Consequently, aside from the discussion of group sizes and anonymity (AP vs. PPID), the paper gives little or no basis for predicting how changes in the other parameters would alter the relationship between punishment and efficiency.

Authors: Bodnar, T; Salathé, M
Author Full Names: Bodnar, Todd; Salathe, Marcel
Article Title: Governing the Global Commons with Local Institutions
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS EXPERIMENTS; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; GAMES; COOPERATION; DYNAMICS; STRATEGIES; TRAGEDY; HUMANS
Abstract: Most problems faced by modern human society have two characteristics in common - they are tragedy-of-the-commons type of problems, and they are global problems. Tragedy-of-the-commons type of problems are those where a commonly shared resource is overexploited by free riders at the expense of everyone sharing the resource. The exploitation of global resources such as clean air and water, political stability and peace, etc. underlies many of the most pressing human problems. Punishment of free riding behavior is one of the most frequently used strategies to combat the problem, but the spatial reach of sanctioning institutions is often more limited than the spatial effects of overexploitation. Here, we analyze a general game theoretical model to assess under what circumstances sanctioning institutions with limited reach can maintain the larger commons. We find that the effect of the spatial reach has a strong effect on whether and how the commons can be maintained, and that the transitions between those outcomes are characterized by phase transitions. The latter indicates that a small change in the reach of sanctioning systems can profoundly change the way the global commons can be managed.

Most of the paper’s focus is on whether “the commons can be maintained” under different forms of punishment and on the long‐run distribution of strategies (cooperators, defectors, punishers, or nonparticipants). The authors refer to “the payoff” in order to determine whether a new strategy can invade, and they show “phase transitions” in strategy frequencies. B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – The paper explicitly touches upon five of them:  
     1) Number of players (M),  
     4) Whether the contribution is effectively all or nothing (they assume it is, via a fixed c),  
     6) The multiplication factor r,  
     7) Punishment costs (γ for peer punishment, β for pool punishment),  
     8) Punishment magnitudes (g for peer punishment, b for pool punishment).

Abstract: Imposing sanctions on non-compliant parties to international agreements is advocated as a remedy for international cooperation failure. Nevertheless, sanctions are costly, and rational choice theory predicts their ineffectiveness in improving cooperation. 9. Reward enabled  
(1) No – there is *only* punishment (called “sanctions”).  
(2) Not discussed.

10. Reward cost  
(1) N/A (no rewards).  
(2) N/A.

(1) N/A.  
(2) N/A.

(1) Yes – subjects were told there would be 10 rounds.

(1) Yes – after every round each subject saw every other player’s contribution history (and, in S treatments, all sanctions).  
(2) Feedback format is fixed; not varied; no prediction.

(2) Identification rule is fixed; not varied; no prediction.

(1) N/A (no rewards).  
(2) N/A.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependence on **efficiency**  
• The paper’s principal dependent variables are  
 – Probability of Loss Avoidance (PLA) = group-level cooperation;  
 – Individual contributions;  
 – Amount of sanctioning;  
 – (Occasionally) total pay-offs.  
• “Efficiency” in the sense of total or average pay-offs is touched on only briefly (“payoffs were significantly higher in NS than S”, SM §1.8).  The authors do not present efficiency as their core outcome, and never compute “actual ÷ maximum possible” efficiency.

B. Which parameters are mentioned?  
The paper explicitly states fixed values for 9 of the 15 parameters (1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14).  The remaining 6 (3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 15) are absent or not applicable.

C. Which parameters are *systematically varied* and analysed for their influence on the punishment treatment effect?  
None.  All 15 parameters are held constant throughout the experiment, so the paper offers 0 such analyses and 0 numerical effect sizes for any parameter variation.

D. What predictions can be made about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment treatment effect on *efficiency*, using only this paper?  
Very little.  Because the study only manipulated “Sanctions present vs absent” and “National vs International composition (Open/Blind)”, while holding every one of the 15 design parameters fixed, the paper provides no empirical or theoretical basis for forecasting how changes in any of those 15 parameters would alter the efficiency impact of punishment. Abstract: This study investigates the effect of social rewards and sanctions on cooperation by examining a voluntary contribution mechanism used in conjunction with ex post communication. The experiment consists of two stages. In the first stage, paired subjects play a standard public-good game; in the second, each of them evaluates his or her partner's contribution in the first stage and sends a free-form written message to him or her. The experimental results show that the mere presence of an opportunity to praise or blame is not enough to promote cooperation. However, once subjects actually experience being blamed, they contribute significantly more in the following round. When disapproval is expressed in the subject's own words, unlike in previous studies, social sanctions were found to have a stronger impact on cooperation. The experience of being praised, in contrast, does not have such an effect. These results suggest that subjects may be more sensitive to the disutility of being blamed than to the utility of being praised.

Below each of the 15 parameters is treated in exactly the same way.

For every parameter I state  

(1) whether the paper ever mentions or fixes the parameter (and, if so, the value that was actually used in the experiment), and  

(2) whether the paper makes any prediction or produces any numerical evidence about what would happen to the **punishment treatment effect** if that parameter were **systematically varied**.  
When a numerical effect can be read directly from a table or figure I report it; otherwise I explicitly say that nothing is said.

────────────────────────────────────────

PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned: Yes – every group is a pair (n = 2).  
   • Systematic-variation prediction: None.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned: Yes – exactly two rounds were played. Subjects learned about the second round only after the first was over.  
   • Systematic-variation prediction: None.

3. Is chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned: Yes – only in the SRS treatment, and only *after* the contribution decision, subjects could send one free-form text message.  
   • Systematic-variation prediction: None. The paper never varies the presence/absence of chat beyond the single comparison “message allowed (SRS) vs. not allowed (B & MRS).”

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
   • Mentioned (implicitly): No. Subjects chose any integer from 0 to 20, so the rule was *not* all-or-nothing.  
   • Systematic-variation prediction: None.

5. Contribution default (withdrawal frame)  
   • Mentioned: Not at all.  
   • Systematic-variation prediction: Not applicable.

6. MPCR or multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned: Yes – a = 0.7.  
   • Systematic-variation prediction: None.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   • Mentioned:  
     – Social sanctions: cost = 0.  
     – Monetary sanctions: cost = 1 (punisher loses one unit for each point).  
   • Systematic-variation prediction: Not systematic, but the paper *does* give two isolated data points:  
     β̂ (effect of *experiencing* a social sanction on subsequent contribution) = +5.671 (Table 3, column “SRS”, p < 0.10).  
     β̂ (effect of *experiencing* a monetary sanction) = –4.556 (Table 3, column “MRS”, n.s.).  
     The author never claims this difference is due to the cost level per se, and no continuous variation in the cost parameter is attempted.

8. Punishment magnitude (damage suffered by the target per unit)  
   • Mentioned: Monetary sanctions: 1-for-1; social sanctions: purely verbal (no monetary deduction).  
   • Systematic-variation prediction: None.

9. Whether reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned: Yes – enabled in SRS and MRS, absent in the baseline B.  
   • Systematic-variation prediction: No. The coefficient on “reward received” is –2.042 (SRS) and +3.791 (MRS) but both are statistically insignificant (Table 3). The paper never varies “reward enabled” beyond the single on/off comparison.

10. Reward cost  
    • Mentioned: 0 (social) vs. 1 (monetary).  
    • Systematic-variation prediction: None.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Mentioned: 1-for-1 in MRS; undefined non-monetary for SRS.  
    • Systematic-variation prediction: None.

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
    • Mentioned: Yes – they are *not* known in advance; subjects only learn that a second round exists after finishing the first.  
    • Systematic-variation prediction: None.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mentioned: Players see both investments but only their own payoff, not their partner’s payoff.  
    • Systematic-variation prediction: None.

14. Is the identity of the punisher revealed?  
    • Mentioned: Yes – with only two players, the target always knows who did it; in SRS the message arrives with the partner’s ID, in MRS the points come from the partner.  
    • Systematic-variation prediction: None.

15. Is the identity of the rewarder revealed?  
    • Same as 14 – always revealed.  
    • Systematic-variation prediction: None.

────────────────────────────────────────

SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables actually used  
   – Average individual contribution in each round (Figure 1).  
   – Change in individual contribution between Round 1 and Round 2 (Tobit estimates, Table 3).  
   – Frequency and size of rewards/sanctions (Figure 2).  
   The paper never reports group efficiency, total payoff, or average payoff, so “efficiency” is **not** a dependent variable in this study.

B. Parameters mentioned  
   14 of the 15 parameters appear in the description (all except #5 “contribution default”).

C. Parameters whose *systematic variation* is analyzed with respect to the punishment treatment effect  
   Strictly speaking, **zero** parameters are varied along more than one controlled level. The paper offers two isolated data points for parameter 7 (cost of punishment) and parameter 10 (cost of reward) via the comparison “social (cost = 0) vs. monetary (cost = 1),” but that is not a systematic manipulation in the sense of a parametric sweep.

D. What can we predict about efficiency, based solely on this paper?  
   Very little. The paper never computes efficiency, so one must extrapolate from contribution effects. All we can say is:  
   • Allowing *cost-free* social sanctions (and revealing them) increased subsequent contributions by about 5.7 tokens on a 0-20 scale, while costly monetary sanctions did not.  
   • Rewards, whether costly or cost-free, had no detectable effect.  
   • Therefore, if group efficiency is a monotone function of aggregate contributions (with MPCR = 0.7), we would expect *greater* efficiency when punishment is (i) cost-free and (ii) expressed in an identifiable, verbal form, and **no** efficiency gain when punishment is costly and purely monetary.  
   Beyond these qualitative statements, the paper offers no evidence on how any of the 15 parameters or their interactions would quantitatively influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Authors: Bravo, G; Squazzoni, F
Author Full Names: Bravo, Giangiacomo; Squazzoni, Flaminio
Article Title: Exit, Punishment and Rewards in Commons Dilemmas: An Experimental Study
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS; HUMAN COOPERATION; CHOICE; SANCTIONS; CARROT; STICK; PROVISION; PEOPLE
Abstract: Commons dilemmas are interaction situations where a common good is provided or exploited by a group of individuals so that optimal collective outcomes clash with private interests. Although in these situations, social norms and institutions exist that might help individuals to cooperate, little is known about the interaction effects between positive and negative incentives and exit options by individuals. We performed a modified public good game experiment to examine the effect of exit, rewards and punishment, as well as the interplay between exit and rewards and punishment. We found that punishment had a stronger effect than rewards on cooperation if considered by itself, whereas rewards had a stronger effect when combined with voluntary participation. This can be explained in terms of the 'framing effect', i.e., as the combination of exit and rewards might induce people to attach higher expected payoffs to cooperative strategies and expect better behaviour from others.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter account of what the Bravo and Squazzoni (2013) paper does (and does not) say with regard to each of the 15 parameters, followed by a four-part summary as requested. Throughout, “the paper” refers only to the content of the Bravo and Squazzoni (2013) article, including its figures and tables.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   a) Mentioned?  
      • Yes. All sessions are played in groups of six.  
   b) Systematically varied?  
      • No. The paper keeps group size fixed at six; it does not study different group sizes.  
   c) Effect on punishment treatment effect (especially on efficiency)?  
      • Not discussed. No predictions are made about changing the number of players.

2. Number of rounds  
   a) Mentioned?  
      • Yes. There are 10 introductory rounds, then 10 “treatment” rounds (20 rounds total).  
   b) Systematically varied?  
      • No. They always run exactly 10 + 10 rounds; there is no condition with, for example, fewer or more rounds.  
   c) Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
      • Not discussed. The paper does not predict nor measure how changing the total number of rounds would affect any outcome.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   a) Mentioned?  
      • Yes, but only to say that there was no communication at all; the paper does not enable or compare any form of chat.  
   b) Systematically varied?  
      • No; there is no treatment involving chat.  
   c) Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
      • Not discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   a) Mentioned?  
      • Yes. Participants either “help” (pay 10 MU) or “do not help” (pay 0 MU). There is no partial amount choice.  
   b) Systematically varied?  
      • No; there is only a single all-or-nothing design throughout.  
   c) Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
      • Not discussed. The paper does not compare different ways of contributing.

5. Is the contribution default (do players move their endowment back to themselves vs. choose how much to contribute)?  
   a) Mentioned?  
      • The experiment always gives each participant 100 MU and allows them a binary help/no-help choice. There is no “default contribution” mechanism described.  
   b) Systematically varied?  
      • No.  
   c) Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
      • Not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplier of the public good  
   a) Mentioned?  
      • The paper’s setup yields 10 MU cost by the helper to generate a total of 20 MU distributed among 5 other players. This is effectively a constant multiplier for others.  
   b) Systematically varied?  
      • No; it stays fixed.  
   c) Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
      • Not discussed. They do not study different multipliers.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   a) Mentioned?  
      • The paper’s “negative incentive” is centrally imposed (−5 MU for defectors). There is no cost borne by peers who punish, because the punishment is enforced externally.  
   b) Systematically varied?  
      • No. It is always costless for the punisher (the “institution”).  
   c) Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
      • Not discussed as a systematically varied parameter.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted for each unit of punishment)  
   a) Mentioned?  
      • Yes. Under the negative-incentive condition, 5 MU is deducted from non-helpers.  
   b) Systematically varied?  
      • Not across multiple deduction sizes. The experiment compares “no punishment” (null) vs. “punishment = 5 MU.” There is no other (e.g., 3 MU or 10 MU) condition.  
   c) Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
      • The paper does compare “null” vs. “negative incentive” treatments. In terms of efficiency (final profit as a fraction of the optimum, see Figure 3b in the paper):  
        – No-Null yields about 58% of the theoretical optimum, whereas No-Neg yields about 67%.  
        – That is the nearest numeric effect size on (group) efficiency from adding punishment (5 MU) vs. no punishment.  
      • They do not analyze any other punishment magnitudes.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   a) Mentioned?  
      • Yes. This is the “positive incentive” condition (+5 MU to helpers).  
   b) Systematically varied?  
      • Yes. They have three conditions: null (no incentive), negative incentive (punishment), or positive incentive (reward).  
   c) Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
      • They do compare positive vs. negative incentives, but not specifically how “adding reward” changes “punishment’s” effect. Punishment and reward never co-occur in the same treatment; each is tested separately.  
      • Hence no condition directly combines “punishment plus reward,” so there is no explicit measure of “reward’s presence” altering the punishment effect.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   a) Mentioned?  
      • The institution automatically grants +5 MU to anyone who helps, at no cost to the helper. It is not paid by other players.  
   b) Systematically varied?  
      • No; it remains fixed at one setting.  
   c) Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
      • Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded for each unit of reward)  
   a) Mentioned?  
      • Always +5 MU.  
   b) Systematically varied?  
      • No. Only one reward amount is used.  
   c) Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
      • Not discussed. No range of reward sizes is tested.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
   a) Mentioned?  
      • Yes. Participants are explicitly told there are 10 introductory and then 10 additional periods.  
   b) Systematically varied?  
      • No; the game length is the same for everyone.  
   c) Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
      • Not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained or lost each round)?  
   a) Mentioned?  
      • The paper states that players see only aggregate group results, not individual peer-by-peer outcomes.  
   b) Systematically varied?  
      • No.  
   c) Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
      • Not discussed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   a) Mentioned?  
      • Not in the sense of player-to-player visibility. Punishment is imposed “externally,” so a punisher identity never appears.  
   b) Systematically varied?  
      • No.  
   c) Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
      • Not discussed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   a) Mentioned?  
      • Similarly, “rewards” happen automatically from the experimenter.  
   b) Systematically varied?  
      • No.  
   c) Effect on punishment treatment effect?  
      • Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • Yes. Besides “cooperation” (the fraction of participants who choose to help), the paper also measures final profits and reports “profit as a proportion of the theoretical optimum,” which they interpret as an efficiency measure. So they have at least two key dependent variables: cooperation rate and efficiency (final payoff relative to maximum possible).

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   • The paper mentions in passing that there are 6 players (1), 10+10 rounds (2), no communication (3), all-or-nothing contributions (4), a fixed (implicit) MPCR (6), a fixed punishment magnitude of 5 MU (8), and a fixed reward of 5 MU (9, 11).  
   • However, it only truly and deliberately manipulates two experimental factors: (i) exit vs. no exit, and (ii) incentive type (null, negative, or positive). Thus, a few parameters (numbers 5, 7, 10, 12–15) appear or are implicitly set, but are not truly discussed or varied. In total, the paper concretely uses (and manipulates) only a subset of parameter 8 (presence/absence of punishment) and parameter 9 (presence/absence of rewards).

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, the only aspect resembling “systematic variation” in punishment is going from “no punishment” to “punishment = 5 MU.” That partly relates to parameter 8 (“punishment magnitude”). The paper shows that going from null-incentive to negative-incentive changes group efficiency from 58% to 67% (Table 2 and Figure 3b).  
   • None of the other parameters (1–7, 9–15) are systematically varied in different values or levels (beyond “present vs. not present”) to test how they affect the punishment treatment effect. Rewards (parameter 9) are indeed manipulated, but not specifically to see how it alters punishment’s effect; positive incentives and negative incentives occur in separate conditions.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper gives little direct guidance about varying parameters beyond “punishment present” vs. “punishment absent” (and similarly “reward present” vs. “reward absent”). We see that adding even a moderate punishment (a 5 MU fine) boosts cooperation and can raise total earnings (relative to the no-incentive baseline).  
   • Because the paper does not examine other levels of punishment magnitude or cost, nor other group sizes, nor communication, nor different knowledge conditions, we cannot reliably predict how changing those parameters would alter the punishment effect on efficiency. The same is true for the all-or-nothing rule, which is never varied.  
   • For the few conditions that are tested, the data imply that including punishment (especially when no exit option is introduced) can raise cooperation and efficiency. However, the paper does not address deeper interactions with any of the other untested parameters, so the safest conclusion is that we have very limited ability to make further predictions from this particular study alone.
reference_APA: Bravo, Giangiacomo & Squazzoni, Flaminio (2013). Exit, Punishment and Rewards in Commons Dilemmas: An Experimental Study. PLOS ONE.

Authors: Hetzer, M; Sornette, D
Author Full Names: Hetzer, Moritz; Sornette, Didier
Article Title: An Evolutionary Model of Cooperation, Fairness and Altruistic Punishment in Public Good Games
Keywords Plus: INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; COSTLY PUNISHMENT; DECISION-MAKING; EXPERIMENTAL ECONOMICS; PREFERENCES; DYNAMICS; NASH; POPULATIONS; COMPETITION; CONFORMITY
Abstract: We identify and explain the mechanisms that account for the emergence of fairness preferences and altruistic punishment in voluntary contribution mechanisms by combining an evolutionary perspective together with an expected utility model. We aim at filling a gap between the literature on the theory of evolution applied to cooperation and punishment, and the empirical findings from experimental economics. The approach is motivated by previous findings on other-regarding behavior, the co-evolution of culture, genes and social norms, as well as bounded rationality. Our first result reveals the emergence of two distinct evolutionary regimes that force agents to converge either to a defection state or to a state of coordination, depending on the predominant set of self-or other-regarding preferences. Our second result indicates that subjects in laboratory experiments of public goods games with punishment coordinate and punish defectors as a result of an aversion against disadvantageous inequitable outcomes. Our third finding identifies disadvantageous inequity aversion as evolutionary dominant and stable in a heterogeneous population of agents endowed initially only with purely selfregarding preferences. We validate our model using previously obtained results from three independently conducted experiments of public goods games with punishment.

Abstract: In prisoner's dilemma game (shortly, PD game), punishment is most frequently used to promote cooperation. However, outcome varies when different punishment approaches are applied. Each point indicates whether the paper (1) explicitly discusses the parameter and, if so, what value (or range of values) is used, and (2) whether the paper makes any predictions (including effect sizes, if given) about systematically varying that parameter on the “punishment treatment effect”—that is, how adding punishment (versus having no punishment) influences the outcome measures in the paper. As the instructions note, the paper’s main outcome measures are “fraction of cooperation (ρC)” and “average payoff.” The paper does not use the term “efficiency” (actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff); instead, it reports average (or total) payoffs. Where no discussion exists, it is stated explicitly.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players
   • Discussion: The paper fixes the population on an L×L square lattice with L = 100 (i.e., 10,000 players). It does not systematically vary the number of players.  
   • Prediction when varied: Not discussed.

2. Number of rounds
   • Discussion: The authors run the evolutionary game over many time steps until a stationary state is reached, but they do not specify a set number of rounds, nor do they discuss any finite or known horizon.  
   • Prediction when varied: Not discussed.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussion: The paper does not mention any communication or “chat” between players.  
   • Prediction when varied: Not discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussion: The paper studies a standard Prisoner’s Dilemma (PD) game, where each player chooses to “cooperate” or “defect.” There is no mention of forced “all or nothing” contributions in a public goods sense.  
   • Prediction when varied: Not discussed.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Discussion: Not applicable, as the paper does not model decisions to move an endowment in or out of a public fund.  
   • Prediction when varied: Not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Discussion: The parameter “b” (temptation to defect) is varied between 1 and 2, but it is not framed as an MPCR (it is a standard PD payoff parameter).  
   • Prediction when varied: They do systematically vary b, but only to observe how it interacts with punishment intensity; they do not call it “MPCR,” and they do not treat it as a public-goods-multiplication factor.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussion: The model charges no direct cost to individual punishers; instead, the cost of punishment is paid out of a collective “public benefit fund” that is raised by taxing players. The paper does not report systematically varying any per-punishment cost borne by individual punishers.  
   • Prediction when varied: Not discussed (no direct or explicit variation of punishment cost).

8. Punishment magnitude (the deducted coins or payoff from a punished player for each unit of punishment)
   • Discussion: This is the key parameter “p” (0 < p < 1), called “punishment intensity.” The punished player loses p×b payoff units if punished, where b is the temptation. In the paper’s model, p also determines the fraction of defectors who are punished, because punishment range q = 1 – p.  
   • Prediction when varied: Yes, systematically varied (p = 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.5, 0.8, etc.).  
        – Dependent variables studied: Fraction of cooperation (ρC) and average payoff.  
        – Effect size (qualitative):  
           ► Without punishment (p=0), ρC is close to 0 at high b.  
           ► At moderate p (about 0.4–0.5), ρC can approach 1.  
           ► “Slight intensity” p around 0.2 typically yields higher fraction of cooperators and higher average payoff than “severe intensity” p around 0.8.  
           ► They also find that if p is too high or too low, ρC decreases; moderate intensities yield the highest ρC and payoff.  
        – Although they do not use the term “efficiency,” they do report that slight punishment intensity consistently yields higher average payoff than severe intensity when punishment is in effect.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussion: The paper focuses exclusively on punishment and does not study or mention any reward mechanism.  
   • Prediction when varied: Not discussed.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Discussion: Not applicable (no reward mechanism).  
    • Prediction when varied: Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)
    • Discussion: Not applicable (no reward mechanism).  
    • Prediction when varied: Not discussed.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
    • Discussion: The paper does not mention whether players know how many rounds will be played; it does not address a finite versus infinite horizon.  
    • Prediction when varied: Not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see each other’s payoffs)?
    • Discussion: The simulation does sort all players by payoff to apply taxes, but the paper does not specify whether (or how) each player sees everyone else’s payoff. No systematic variation is discussed.  
    • Prediction when varied: Not discussed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Discussion: The paper does not mention any feedback of who punishes whom; punishment is implemented centrally from the public fund.  
    • Prediction when varied: Not discussed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Discussion: Not applicable (the study does not use rewards).  
    • Prediction when varied: Not discussed.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   – The paper never uses the ratio “actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff,” i.e., it does not explicitly measure “efficiency.” Instead, it reports two main dependent variables: (1) fraction of cooperation (ρC) and (2) average payoff. These two measures differ in that:  
     • ρC indicates how many players choose cooperation over time,  
     • average payoff indicates how much payoff (on average) players receive in the final stationary state.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – Only one of the 15 parameters clearly appears in a form that the authors systematically vary: Parameter #8 (punishment magnitude, i.e., intensity p). Some partial reference is made to parameter #7 (punishment cost), but only to note that it is paid by a shared fund rather than individuals, and it is not systematically varied. None of the other parameters are substantively mentioned or manipulated.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   – Only parameter #8 (punishment magnitude p). They examine how changing p alters outcomes for fraction of cooperation and average payoff, comparing the “with-punishment” scenarios to “no-punishment” (p=0) scenarios. No other parameters are systematically explored in this way.

D. If you were to make predictions on how these 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency (solely based on this paper):  
   – The paper does not analyze 14 of the 15 parameters, so no predictions can be made from the paper about systematically varying them. The only parameter for which the paper provides testable results is the punishment intensity (p). From those results, one might infer that “slight intensity” or moderate p (rather than very severe p) generally yields higher fraction of cooperators and higher average payoff; presumably that would translate to higher efficiency if efficiency were measured. Beyond that, the paper does not offer information from which to predict how other parameters (like group size, round structure, chat, or knowledge of who punished whom) might affect efficiency.

For completeness, I note any other dependent variables (e.g., contribution levels) the paper does use.

1) Number of players
   • Discussed?

However, it does not label this as a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Rather, it shows how larger n can increase or decrease funds to enforcement and how that, in turn, changes public‐good contributions. Numerically, the paper shows (for certain functional forms) that per‐capita contributions to the enforcement fund can rise with n, especially under nonrival (γ=0) enforcement. Although the paper does not expressly compute “efficiency” as actual total payoff divided by the fully cooperative payoff, it does show (Proposition 8) that when n grows large, in some cases individual contributions to the public good remain bounded away from zero (nonrival enforcement) and in other cases go to zero (full rivalry, γ=1).

   • Discussed?

     No.

   • Discussed?  
     No. The theoretical model simply has each agent choose how much to contribute (gᵢ), without specifying how or whether any “default” is implemented.

     No.

   • Discussed?

Abstract: Why cooperation is well developed in human society is an unsolved question in biological and human sciences. Vast studies in game theory have revealed that in non-cooperative games selfish behavior generally dominates over cooperation and cooperation can be evolved only under very limited conditions. These studies ask the origin of cooperation; whether cooperation can evolve in a group of selfish individuals. In this paper, instead of asking the origin of cooperation, we consider the enhancement of cooperation in a small already cooperative society. We ask whether cooperative behavior is further promoted in a small cooperative society in which social penalty is devised. We analyze hawk-dove game and prisoner's dilemma introducing social penalty. We then expand it for non-cooperative games in general. The results indicate that cooperation is universally favored if penalty is further imposed.    • Discussion in paper?

   • Discussion in paper?

    • Discussion in paper?  
      Not discussed (rewards are not modeled).  
    • Systematic variation discussed?  
      No.

Summary answers:

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   – The paper does look at average payoffs in order to identify equilibria (e.g., WH, WD, WSil, WCnf) in hawk–dove and prisoner’s dilemma. However, it never frames outcomes as “group efficiency,” nor does it compare total payoff to a maximum possible payoff. Instead, it focuses on equilibrium frequencies of cooperation or defection and how these frequencies shift with an exogenous penalty.  
   – The dependent variables mentioned are (1) the expected payoff of each strategy, and (2) the equilibrium frequency of non‐cooperators vs. cooperators (i.e., the evolutionary stable strategy, ESS). These differ from “efficiency” because the authors do not measure how close total payoffs come to the theoretical maximum.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – Only parameter #8 (punishment magnitude) is clearly discussed. None of the other parameters (#1–7, #9–15) are mentioned in a way that maps onto the specific features listed above.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   – Solely parameter #8 (punishment magnitude) is systematically varied. The paper shows that as penalty (αH or αCnf) on non‐cooperation increases, equilibrium behavior becomes more cooperative. Although they compute payoffs, they do not specifically link this to “efficiency,” but rather to shifts in equilibrium strategies.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   – Because the paper never discusses most of these parameters, there is little basis to predict their specific effects on efficiency. The only parameter they analyze in detail is the magnitude of penalty (#8), which increases cooperation and thus may raise overall payoffs in their models. Beyond that, the paper does not provide direct discussion or numerical estimates for efficiency outcomes. Therefore, almost no predictions can be made for the other parameters solely from this paper’s content.

Author Full Names: Zu, Jinjing; Xu, Fanxin; Jin, Tao; Xiang, Wei
Article Title: Reward and Punishment Mechanism with weighting enhances cooperation in evolutionary games

Author Keywords: Cooperation; Evolutionary games; Reward and punishment; Social dilemmas; Weighting
Keywords Plus: PROMOTES COOPERATION; STRONG RECIPROCITY; MEMORY; POPULATION; DYNAMICS
Abstract: The essential of the human cooperative behavior is to find an effective mechanism to promote cooperation. In reality, there is a class of professionals who punish evil and promote good, such as police officers, judges, and volunteers. Their actions and respon-sibilities can profoundly affect the actions of other individuals by fines and bonuses. Motivated by this phenomenon, we propose a Reward and Punishment Mechanism with weighting (RPMW) for promoting cooperation. The core of RPMW lies in three aspects: (i) A subset of players are tagged as supervisors, who are generated by a random algorithm. If the supervisor chooses to cooperate, she/he acts as the doer of rewards and punishments, otherwise she/he is a general player. (ii) Each supervisor asks their neighbors in turn as well as rewards cooperators and punishes defectors. Bonuses (penalties) are calculated according to a weighting which is the ratio of the number of current evolutionary round cooperators (defectors) to the total of players. (iii) A factor alpha is added to control the intensity of rewards and punishments, and the /3 is denoted as the percentage of supervisors in the group. Furthermore, we do a detailed ablation study on the Reward Mechanism with Weighting (RMW) and Punishment Mechanism with Weighting (PMW) in three social dilemmas. The simulation results show that RPMW can effectively promote cooperation in prisoner's dilemma (PDG), snowdrift game (SDG) and stag-hunt game (SHG). We find that the frequency of cooperation reaches highest when the alpha is at its maximum and the /3 is in a positive impact on evolutionary cooperation. The results prove that RPMW is more effective than RMW and PMW on enhancing cooperation in PDG, SDG.(c) 2022 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER SCAN
-------------------------------------------------------------------

   • Mentioned?  Not at all.

   • Mentioned?  No.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor (here: game payoff parameters b or r)

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   • Mentioned?  No explicit cost to the punishing supervisor is ever stated.

Qualitative result: higher α ⇒ larger punishment ⇒ higher F_c and therefore a larger punishment-treatment effect.  Numerical illustration from PDG (Fig. 3a): with α = 1, cooperation persists up to b ≈ 1.44; with α = 0.25 it already collapses below b ≈ 1.18.  No efficiency numbers are given.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Three mechanisms are compared:  
     – RPMW (reward + punishment)

     – RMW (reward only)

Fig. 7 shows that the presence of punishment (PMW) generally outperforms reward alone (RMW) in PDG, whereas the reverse holds in a narrow α-range in SDG; combining both (RPMW) yields the largest cooperation effect in PDG and SDG.     • Mentioned?  No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
    • Mentioned?  No.  (The model is purely evolutionary; agents do not possess that information.)  
    • Systematic variation?  No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mentioned?  No.

14. Do punished players learn who punished them?  
    • Mentioned?  No (not modelled).

15. Do rewarded players learn who rewarded them?  
    • Mentioned?  No.

-------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
-------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables used  
   • The paper does NOT use group efficiency, total payoff, or average payoff.  
   • The sole quantitative dependent variable is the “frequency of cooperation” F_c.  
   • Visual “snapshots” of spatial strategy distributions are also provided but are descriptive.  
   • Hence, efficiency and cooperation are not interchangeable here; only cooperation is measured.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
   Mentioned: 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 9, 11  → 7 parameters.  
   Not mentioned: 3, 5, 7, 10, 12, 13, 14, 15  → 8 parameters.

C. For which parameters is the effect of systematic variation on the punishment-treatment effect discussed?  
   Discussed:  
     • 6 (b or r)  
     • 8 (α = punishment magnitude)  
     • 9 / 11 (presence or absence of reward; reward magnitude varies with α)  
   Count: 3 parameters (if reward presence and reward magnitude are taken together).  
   For none of these is efficiency analysed; only cooperation frequency is.

D. What predictions about the 15 parameters and their interactions can be made for their impact on the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency, solely from this paper?  
   • Because efficiency is never measured, the paper supports only very tentative, indirect inferences.  
   • If one assumes that higher cooperation translates into higher efficiency, then:  
       – Larger punishment/reward intensity α should raise efficiency.  
       – A higher share of supervisors β should raise efficiency.  
       – Including both reward and punishment (RPMW) should outperform either alone in PDG and SDG, with little difference in SHG.  
       – The beneficial effect of punishment (and thus of RPMW over RMW) grows as the basic game becomes more “tempting” to defect (larger b in PDG or larger r in SDG).  
   • No predictions can be made about any other parameter (1–5, 7, 10, 12–15) because they are either held constant or absent from the model.

Abstract: Social role theory posits that occupational gender roles give rise to gender differences in behavior, such that men and women engage in qualitatively different prosocial behaviors. Therefore, we expected that women who observed an unfair situation (involving a victim and a perpetrator) would respond by demonstrating communal prosocial behavior (by compensating the victim), whereas men would respond with agentic prosocial behavior (by punishing the perpetrator). The paper also discusses “fair vs. unfair” scenarios but does not translate those into efficiency measures.  

   • The paper’s main dependent variables are:  
     – Punishment transfers (Talers spent on punishing the perpetrator).  
     – Compensation transfers (Talers spent on compensating the victim).  
   • These are not treated as measures of efficiency; they are used as measures of “agentic” (punishment) vs. “communal” (compensation) prosocial behavior.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • The role structure (parameter 1: number of players) is explicitly stated as three players in a one‐shot or short scenario.  
   • The “punishment magnitude” (parameter 8) is discussed (1 Taler → 3 Talers deducted, or 1 → 5), and the “reward magnitude” (parameter 11, i.e., compensation triple) is also mentioned.  
   • They also mention the costs to the punisher (parameter 7) are always 1 Taler for each Taler of punishment.  
   • None of the other parameters are explicitly discussed as design factors (i.e., they are either absent or not varied, and the paper does not examine their impact).

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The paper does not actually employ a “punishment treatment vs. no‐punishment treatment” comparison that is typical of a public goods game.  

   • Although the paper varies the “punishment magnitude” (1:3 vs. 1:5) in Study 2, it does so only to see if men vs. women punish differently under different effectiveness levels. It does not report or discuss any effect on group efficiency or on a “punishment treatment effect” (meaning how payoff outcomes or cooperation rates shift in a with‐ vs. without‐punishment scenario).  

   • Consequently, there is effectively no discussion of how systematically varying any of the above parameters affects a “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency (or on any outcome akin to a standard public‐goods measure). The paper reports no numerical effect sizes tied to the 15 parameters in that sense.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not address efficiency or payoff maximization; it only discusses the amount of punishment and compensation in a third‐party scenario. There is no basis in the paper for predicting how those 15 parameters or their interactions would impact group efficiency in a public goods sense.  
   • Therefore, strictly from this paper’s content, one can make little or no prediction about how systematically varying the 15 parameters would influence a punishment treatment’s effect on group efficiency.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Answer concisely: the paper neither focuses on nor systematically varies any of these 15 parameters in the context of public‐goods‐type efficiency outcomes. It does measure punishment and compensation transfers, but it does not relate these to group efficiency, nor does it describe how parameter variations would affect a punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Author Full Names: Espin, Antonio M.; Branas-Garza, Pablo; Gamella, Juan F.; Herrmann, Benedikt; Martin, Jesus
Article Title: Culture and group-functional punishment behaviour
Author Keywords: Cooperation; punishment; Gypsy/Roma; culture; evolution
Keywords Plus: 3RD-PARTY PUNISHMENT; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; IN-GROUP; PAROCHIAL ALTRUISM; COSTLY PUNISHMENT; GROUP MEMBERSHIP; GROUP SELECTION; EVOLUTION; COOPERATION; PSYCHOLOGY
Abstract: Humans often 'altruistically' punish non-cooperators in one-shot interactions among genetically unrelated individuals. This poses an evolutionary puzzle because altruistic punishment enforces cooperation norms that benefit the whole group but is costly for the punisher. One key explanation is that punishment follows a social-benefits logic: it is eminently normative and group-functional (drawing on cultural group selection theories). In contrast, mismatch-based deterrence theory argues that punishment serves the individual-level function of deterring mistreatment of oneself and one's allies, hinging upon the evolved human coalitional psychology. We conducted multilateral-cooperation experiments with a sample of Spanish Romani people (Gitanos or Cale) and the non-Gitano majority. The Gitanos represent a unique case study because they rely heavily on close kin-based networks and display a strong ethnic identity. We find that Gitano non-cooperators were not punished by co-ethnics in only-Gitano (ethnically) homogeneous groups but were harshly punished by other Gitanos and by non-Gitanos in ethnically mixed groups. Our findings suggest the existence of culture-specific motives for punishment: Gitanos, especially males, appear to use punishment to protect their ethnic identity, whereas non-Gitanos use punishment to protect a norm of universal cooperation. Only theories that consider normative, group-functional forces underlying punishment behaviour can explain our data.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter summary, drawn strictly from the content of the paper you provided. Following that, you will find the requested four-point summary (A–D).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER‐BY‐PARAMETER ANALYSIS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1) Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The experiment always uses four‐person groups (p. 7, “Each four-person PGP group…”).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not vary group size.  
   • Any predicted effect on “punishment treatment effect” (or efficiency or any other dependent variable)? None. The paper does not discuss how changing the number of players would alter punishment or efficiency.

2) Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? Yes. It is a one‐shot public goods game (p. 4, “Participants only played one round”).  
   • Systematically varied? No. Only one round was used.  
   • Any predicted effect? No. The paper does not discuss what would happen if the number of rounds were altered.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned? The text indicates that participants made their decisions anonymously and did not communicate (p. 7, describing how each participant decided and submitted choices privately).  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no separate condition with or without communication.  
   • Any predicted effect? None in the paper.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned? Yes, they specify that contributions can be any integer from €0 to €10, so it is not “all or nothing” (p. 7).  
   • Systematically varied? No (they always allow a continuous contribution).  
   • Any predicted effect? None; the paper does not discuss how forcing “all or nothing” would influence punishment or efficiency.

5) Is the contribution default (e.g., forced/required)?  
   • Mentioned? No; the paper does not describe any forced or default contribution mechanism and does not explore toggling such a rule on/off.  
   • Systematically varied? Not applicable.  
   • Any predicted effect? None; not discussed.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each contributed euro yields €0.50 to each of the other three players (i.e., MPCR = 0.5), doubling total group contributions (p. 7).  
   • Systematically varied? No. It is always 0.5.  
   • Any predicted effect? None. The paper does not investigate how different MPCRs might alter punishment or efficiency.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? Yes. It costs €1 of the punisher’s funds to reduce another member’s payoff (p. 7).  
   • Systematically varied? No. This cost is a fixed 1:3 ratio (one spent to reduce three).  
   • Any predicted effect? The paper does not analyze how changing that cost might affect efficiency or punishment levels.

8) Punishment magnitude (the deducted amount per unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The “impact” is €3 for each €1 spent on punishment by the punisher (p. 7).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Any predicted effect? No predictions on how changing the magnitude would affect efficiency are given.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper only discusses punishment (no reward stage is implemented).  
   • Systematically varied? Not applicable.  
   • Any predicted effect? None; the paper does not address rewards.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Mentioned? No. Not relevant, as reward is never introduced.  
    • Systematically varied? Not applicable.  
    • Any predicted effect? None; not discussed.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward)  
    • Mentioned? No; same as above.  
    • Systematically varied? Not applicable.  
    • Any predicted effect? None.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    • Mentioned? Implicitly yes. It is a one‐shot game and participants know it is only one round (p. 4).  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Any predicted effect? None; the paper does not compare known‐ vs. unknown‐length settings.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much others gained/lost)?  
    • Mentioned? Yes. After contributing, participants see their partners’ contributions (p. 7).  
    • Systematically varied? No. All participants receive this same information.  
    • Any predicted effect? The paper does not discuss systematically varying the information display, only that it is provided.

14) When a player is punished, does that player know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Mentioned? Yes. Punishment is anonymous (p. 7).  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Any predicted effect? None. The paper does not discuss what would happen if the identity of the punisher were revealed.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Mentioned? No. Rewards are not used in the experiment.  
    • Systematically varied? Not applicable.  
    • Any predicted effect? None.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
RESPONSES TO THE FOUR SUMMARY QUESTIONS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper focuses on participants’ punishment decisions (how many points they spend punishing) and their contribution levels in a one‐shot public goods game. It also reports average individual earnings (e.g., “Mean earnings from the PGP were €13.34…,” p. 8).  
   • However, “efficiency” in the sense of “actual total payoff divided by maximum possible payoff” is not used as a principal dependent variable. The paper does not directly analyze how punishment affects group efficiency, nor does it introduce an explicit “treatment effect on efficiency.”  
   • The main dependent variables are generally punishment intensity (including altruistic vs. antisocial) and cooperation (contribution) decisions.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • The paper explicitly mentions or describes:  
     (1) Number of players = 4  
     (2) Number of rounds = 1 (one‐shot)  
     (3) No communication (implicit “chat disabled”)  
     (4) Continuous contributions (not all‐or‐nothing)  
     (6) MPCR = 0.5  
     (7) Punishment cost = €1 per unit  
     (8) Punishment magnitude = €3 deducted per unit  
     (12) One‐shot is known to participants  
     (13) Others’ contributions shown  
     (14) Punisher anonymity  
   • These total 10 parameters mentioned in some form. The remaining five parameters (#5, #9, #10, #11, #15) are not mentioned or not relevant to the design.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when systematically varied?  
   • None. Although several parameters (number of players, cost‐to‐impact ratio of punishment, MPCR, etc.) are specified, the experiment does not systematically vary them. The principal between‐subjects comparison is whether groups are ethnically homogeneous or mixed—this is not one of the 15 parameters listed. Consequently, the paper does not provide evidence or numerical effect sizes regarding how systematically changing any of the 15 parameters alters the “punishment treatment effect,” let alone its effect on efficiency.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • Because the study does not systematically manipulate or discuss changes in any of the 15 parameters (it keeps them fixed within a single design) and also does not emphasize group‐efficiency as a dependent measure, the paper offers essentially no direct basis to infer how varying these parameters might affect a punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency. One could note that the experiment uses a 1:3 punishment ratio and that punishing does alter payoffs, but it never extrapolates to how varying that ratio—or any other parameter—would affect group efficiency.  
   • Therefore, based strictly on what is in the paper, there is little or no information for predicting how changes in these 15 parameters would affect efficiency outcomes. The main focus is on how ethnicity and gender modulate punishment within a single unchanging design.

Abstract: Inequality reduces the ability of communities to work together. Recent policy proposals seem to presume that reducing inequality may allow groups to improve outcomes. We experimentally test if, after experiencing inequality, pure redistribution to eliminate inequality increases contributions to public goods. It does not; it fails to raise cooperation even to levels observed in groups that were always equal. The former rich continue to keep most of their resources for private consumption.
