Below we go through the 15 design parameters, one-by-one, extracting only what the paper says.  For every parameter we state  

(i) whether the paper explicitly mentions the parameter and, if so, the value(s) actually used; and  

(ii) whether the paper provides any prediction or numerical evidence on how a *systematic* change in that parameter would alter the **punishment-treatment effect** (i.e., the change that occurs when punishment is introduced, relative to a no-punishment baseline).  
Whenever a numerical effect can be backed out from a table or figure, we report it, but only for the variables the paper analyses (mainly group *contributions*, decision times, and punishment patterns—not efficiency).

-------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – fixed at 4 per group.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  No prediction about varying group size.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – always 20 repeated rounds.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  No prediction.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – “No subject identifiers were used … to minimise the possibility of reputation formation”; no chat facility was provided.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  No prediction.

4. All-or-nothing contributions?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – subjects could contribute any integer from 0 to 20; not all-or-nothing.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  No prediction.

5. Contribution default / take-back frame?  
   • Mentioned?  No; the game uses the standard “give” frame.  
   • No prediction.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – MPCR = 0.5 (each token in the GP yields 0.5 to each of 4 players).  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  No prediction.

7. Punishment cost per unit  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – sender pays 1 token for each punishment token.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  No prediction about changing the cost.

8. Punishment magnitude per unit  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – target loses 3 tokens per punishment token received (1:3 technology).  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  No prediction.

9. Reward option enabled?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – explicitly *not* allowed (only punishment).  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  No prediction.

10. Reward cost  
    • Not applicable (no reward option).  

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Not applicable.

12. Horizon known?  
    • Mentioned?  Yes – subjects were told they would play exactly 20 rounds with fixed partners.  
    • Systematically varied?  No.  No prediction.

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mentioned?  Yes – after the contribution stage each round, every player saw each group member’s contribution (in descending order) and total group contribution; after punishment, each subject saw the *total* punishment received.  
    • Systematically varied?  No.  No prediction.

14. Punisher identity revealed?  
    • Mentioned?  Yes – punisher’s identity was *not* revealed.  
    • Systematically varied?  No.  No prediction.

15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
    • Not applicable (no reward option).  

-------------------------------------------------
Numerical effect sizes that can be inferred (from Table 3):

For *LOW-instruction* sessions  
• Average group contribution without punishment (VCM-L): 25.98 tokens.  
• With punishment (Pun-L): 43.12 tokens.  
• Punishment-treatment effect on contributions: +17.14 tokens per round (≈ +21.4 percentage points of the 80-token group endowment).

For *HIGH-instruction* sessions  
• VCM-H: 31.01 tokens.  
• Pun-H: 60.02 tokens.  
• Punishment-treatment effect on contributions: +29.01 tokens (≈ +36.3 pp).

The paper does *not* convert these contribution gains into efficiency measures, nor does it vary any of the 15 listed design parameters.

-------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables used in the paper  
    – Decision/response times (proxy for comprehension)  
    – Group contributions to the public good  
    – Amount and targeting of punishment  
    – The paper does *not* analyse group efficiency, total payoff, or average payoff, although these can be computed ex post.  
    Contributions and efficiency are conceptually different: efficiency incorporates both payoff from the public good and the costs of (or losses from) punishment, whereas the paper focuses almost entirely on contributions and punishment patterns.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are at least mentioned?  
    10 of them: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14.  
    Parameters 5, 9, 10, 11, 15 are either not used or explicitly absent.

C.  For how many of the 15 parameters does the paper *systematically vary* the parameter and link that variation to the punishment-treatment effect?  
    Zero.  The only manipulated factor is *instruction format* (LOW vs. HIGH), which is *not* one of the 15 parameters listed.

D.  Predicting how the 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency, based solely on this paper.  
    • The paper provides no direct evidence or theory on any of the 15 parameters, because none of them is varied.  
    • All we can infer is that, *holding the entire game structure constant*, clearer instructions make punishment more effective at raising contributions and (by implication) should raise efficiency *if* punishment costs are not too large.  
    • Beyond that, the paper gives little to no basis for predicting how changes in group size, MPCR, punishment cost/magnitude, information revelation, reward options, etc., would modulate the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency.  Any such predictions would require information outside the scope of the paper.

Hence, based strictly on the content of this paper, virtually no quantitative or directional predictions can be made about the 15 design parameters listed above.

Abstract: Cooperation theories assume that interacting individuals can change their strategies under different expected payoffs, depending on their social status or social situations. When looking at sex differences in cooperation, the existing studies have found that the genders cooperate at similar frequencies.    • Systematically varied? No mention.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Discussed? No. The experiment does not include rewards.  
   • Systematically varied? No mention.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded by a reward)
   • Discussed? No. Again, there is no reward mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied? No mention.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
   • Discussed? Yes. The paper explicitly states that participants do not know when each interaction will end. They used a 75% probability of continuing.  
   • Systematically varied? No. They do not manipulate or compare known vs. unknown horizon lengths, nor make predictions about that variation.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost each round)?
   • Discussed? Yes. After each round, participants saw both players’ choices and their updated payoff scores.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not alter how feedback is displayed or analyze how doing so would affect punishment’s impact.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Discussed? The paper describes an anonymous two-player setting, but in a dyad it is necessarily clear who punishes whom. There is no explicit discussion of secrecy about the punisher’s identity for multi-person groups, since only pairs are used.

Summary of the Paper’s Dependent Variables and Parameters

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper does not use “group efficiency” (actual total payoff / maximum possible total payoff) as a reported dependent variable. Instead, the authors measure:  
     – Cooperation rate (frequency of choosing “cooperate”)  
     – Defection rate (frequency of choosing “defect”)  
     – Punishment rate (frequency of choosing “punish”)  
     – Individual final payoffs (monetary gains)  
   • They do not frame their outcomes in terms of efficiency as defined above; instead they focus on behavior frequencies and average payoffs.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned:  
     – (1) Number of players: A two-player setup is used (dyads).  
     – (2) Number of rounds: The game continues for a random number of rounds.  
     – (6) Payoff matrix (akin to an MPCR concept, though never called “MPCR”).  
     – (7) and (8) Punishment cost and magnitude (only in fixed form within the payoff matrix).  
     – (12) The number of rounds is not known (random termination).  
     – (13) Peer outcomes are shown each round.  
     – (14) In a two-player setting, the target of punishment sees the punisher’s choice.  
   • The rest (3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 15) are not mentioned as either part of design or systematically varied.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None are systematically varied in the study. All design features (e.g., payoff matrix, indefinite horizon) are fixed across sessions. The paper therefore makes no claims about how parameter variations would change the “punishment treatment effect.”

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of this paper, what would they be?  
   • Because the paper does not systematically vary any parameter and does not measure group efficiency (as total payoff / maximum possible payoff), no direct predictions can be drawn. The authors do note that punishing lowers individual payoff relative to cooperating or defecting, implying that with the same payoff matrix, punishment does not boost final earnings on average. However, they do not provide evidence or theory on how adjusting those 15 parameters (or their interactions) might alter that finding.  
   • Therefore, based on this paper alone, one can make little to no systematic prediction regarding how each of the 15 parameters (or their interactions) would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Authors: Wang, QS; Chen, XJ; Szolnoki, A

Article Title: Evolutionary dynamics in state-feedback public goods games with peer punishment
Keywords Plus: REPLICATOR DYNAMICS; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; COOPERATION; EMERGENCE; TRAGEDY; RISK
Abstract: Public goods game serves as a valuable paradigm for studying the challenges of collective cooperation in human and natural societies. Peer punishment is often considered an effective incentive for promoting cooperation in such contexts. However, previous related studies have mostly ignored the positive feedback effect of collective contributions on individual payoffs. In this work, we explore global and local state-feedback, where the multiplication factor is positively correlated with the frequency of contributors in the entire population or within the game group, respectively. Below, “punishment treatment effect” always means the **difference** between a condition with peer‐punishment and an otherwise identical condition without punishment.  
“Efficiency” is defined exactly as requested: actual total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff at full cooperation.

PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER EXTRACTION FROM THE PAPER
(“Yes” = the paper mentions the parameter; “Systematically varied” = the paper shows an explicit comparative analysis that allows one to infer the *direction* of change when the parameter is moved up or down.)

1. Number of players (group size, n)  
   • Mentioned? Yes – all analytical formulas contain n and all numerical illustrations fix n = 5.  
   • Systematically varied? No – every figure/table uses n = 5; no comparative plots for other n.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? No – the model is an infinite-time replicator dynamic.

3. Chat enabled  
   • Mentioned? No.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
   • Mentioned? Implicitly yes – strategies are “contribute c” vs “contribute 0”, but this is never varied.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Effect? Not discussed.

5. Contribution default (take vs give frame)  
   • Mentioned? No.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor (r or r0)  
   • Mentioned? Yes – baseline multiplication factor r0 and its feedback-augmented values are central.  
   • Systematically varied? Yes – Figs. 1, 2 and 4 change r0 over a wide range (e.g., 1.8 → 4.3).  
   • Observed qualitative effect (dependent variables reported in the paper):  
     – Larger r0 shrinks the basin of attraction of full defection and enlarges the basin of full contribution.  
     – Under *local* feedback this can make “full cooperation” the only locally stable outcome.  
   • No numerical efficiency difference between “with vs. without punishment” is provided, so the treatment effect on efficiency cannot be computed.

7. Punishment cost γ  
   • Mentioned? Yes – parameter γ.  
   • Systematically varied? Yes – Fig. 5 scans γ jointly with β.  
   • Qualitative effect shown: Smaller γ (cheaper punishment) produces a larger basin for the full-contribution equilibrium; extremely high γ (≥ β) erodes the usefulness of punishment.  
   • No efficiency numbers, no treatment effect computed.

8. Punishment magnitude β (fine)  
   • Mentioned? Yes – β.  
   • Systematically varied? Yes – Fig. 5 jointly with γ.  
   • Qualitative effect: Larger β enlarges the cooperation basin; very low β gives little effect.  
   • Again, no efficiency or treatment effect values reported.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Mentioned? Only in the Introduction as future work; never modelled or varied.  
   • Effect? None.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   • Both not modelled; no discussion.

12. Known number of rounds  
13. Peer outcomes shown  
14. Punisher identification  
15. Rewarder identification  
   • None of these appear anywhere in the model or prose.

DEPENDENT VARIABLES USED IN THE PAPER
The authors never compute “group efficiency”. They study:
   • Local stability of equilibria (types and locations).  
   • Size of attraction basins (fraction of the simplex S₃ leading to each equilibrium) – sometimes rendered as pie charts or heat-map colours.  
   • Whether “full cooperation” can become an absorbing state.

SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
   – Efficiency is **not** used.  
   – Reported DVs are: (i) equilibrium type (defection / coexistence / full contribution), (ii) local stability, (iii) size of attraction basins. These differ from efficiency because they say nothing about the *payoff level* once an equilibrium is reached.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   6 (MPCR / r0), 7 (punishment cost γ), 8 (punishment magnitude β), 1 (group size n as a constant), and 4 (binary contribution choice, fixed). Total mentioned: 5 of 15.

C. Which parameters are *systematically varied* and their effect on the punishment treatment effect is discussed?  
   Only 3: parameter 6 (r0), 7 (γ), 8 (β). Even for these, the paper reports effects on cooperation basins, **not** on efficiency and **not** on the difference between “punishment” and “no-punishment” conditions. So strictly speaking, the paper discusses *zero* parameters with respect to the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

D. Predicting the punishment treatment effect on efficiency using only this paper  
   • The paper does not compute payoffs with and without punishment, so almost no direct prediction can be made.  
   • Indirect inference: when the model predicts a larger basin for full cooperation (e.g., high r0, high β, low γ, or strong local feedback k), we may expect a higher likelihood that punishment raises efficiency, because reaching the fully cooperative state yields the maximum payoff.  
   • Conversely, if parameters place the system in a region where the all-defector equilibrium is still stable and attractive, introducing punishment may fail to improve efficiency.  
   • No numerical effect sizes (Δ-efficiency) can be extracted or estimated.

Hence, based solely on the paper, we can say little more than: “Higher r0, stronger fines β, lower costs γ, and especially the presence of local positive feedback k, *should* make punishment more likely to lift the group to the efficient full-cooperation equilibrium; otherwise, punishment may do little or nothing.”

Author Keywords: Public health emergencies; Evolutionary game; Governmental reward and punishment mechanism; Sustainable development
Abstract: Public health emergencies are critical to people's lives and health, economic development and social stability. Understanding how to respond correctly to public health emergencies is the focus of societal attention. This paper focuses on the tripartite entities of public health emergencies: local governments, pharmaceutical enterprises and the public. On the basis of the assumption of finite rationality, it delves into the game-theoretic interaction among these groups during such crises. By constructing an evolutionary game model, this paper analyses the dynamic adjustment process of the decision-making behaviors of these three parties, leading to the identification of evolutionarily stable strategies for the local government, pharmaceutical enterprises, and the public under different conditions. Moreover, MATLAB is used to carry out simulation experiments to analyse the influence of the local government's reward and punishment mechanism on the strategic choices of the involved parties in the game. Abstract: Understanding the emergence of prosocial behaviors (e.g., cooperation and trust) among self-interested agents is an important problem in many disciplines. Network structure and institutional incentives (e.g., punishing antisocial agents) are known to promote prosocial behaviors, when acting in isolation, one mechanism being present at a time. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter analysis of whether (1) this paper discusses the parameter at all (and, if so, what value it takes), and (2) whether the paper makes a prediction about how systematically varying that parameter affects punishment’s impact on outcomes. The paper’s outcome measures center on (i) whether the prosocial strategy (IT) evolves and (ii) the resulting population payoff (which the authors sometimes call “social welfare” or the “population‐mean payoff”). The paper does not explicitly define “efficiency” as “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff of a fully cooperative group,” although it does discuss average payoffs, social welfare, and how close the population is to full cooperation (IT). Hence below, “effect on punishment treatment” refers to what the paper says about how punishment influences which strategies evolve and/or the overall payoff.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Does the paper discuss it? No. The study uses an evolutionary model (replicator equations) and does not specify a finite number of players.  
   • Any prediction from systematic variation? No.  

2. Number of rounds
   • Does the paper discuss it? No. The formalism is of an evolutionary, infinitely repeated process with replicator dynamics, not a multi‐round laboratory game.  
   • Any prediction from systematic variation? No.  

3. Is chat enabled?
   • Does the paper discuss it? No.  
   • Any prediction from systematic variation? No.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Does the paper discuss it? No explicit reference to “all or nothing” contributions. The paper focuses on a binary (invest vs. not invest) trust game, but this is never discussed as a parameter to be varied.  
   • Any prediction from systematic variation? No.  

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much from public fund back to hand)?
   • Does the paper discuss it? No.  
   • Any prediction from systematic variation? No.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor
   • Does the paper discuss it? Yes, in the trust‐game setting, the parameter r (0 < r < 1) determines the payoff returns when trustees are trustworthy. This plays a role analogous to a “multiplication factor” in simpler public‐goods formulations.  
   • Any prediction from systematic variation? Yes. The paper systematically varies r and shows that for certain ranges of r, punishment can synergize more strongly with network structure (leading to full trustworthiness at lower penalty p). Figures 1 and 2 illustrate conditions under which “interference” vs. “synergy” emerges; for higher r (e.g., r > 0.5 or r > 2/3), synergy between punishment and network structure becomes more pronounced.  
     – Numerical effect sizes: The paper reports threshold values p₍1,b₎, p₍1,c₎, p₄, etc., that depend on r. There is not a single “effect size” but rather borders in parameter space. See, for instance, Fig. 2, where increasing r expands the parameter ranges in which synergy occurs and shrinks those in which punishment and network structure interfere.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Does the paper discuss it? No. The paper’s incentive is institutional, with a “tax” f shared by everyone, and a fine p imposed on untrustworthy actions. There is no mention of a separate cost that the punisher pays per unit of punishment (i.e., no peer‐to‐peer punishment cost).  
   • Any prediction from systematic variation? No.  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted per punishment)
   • Does the paper discuss it? Yes. The parameter p is precisely the penalty (or “expected fine”) for untrustworthiness. The paper systematically varies p.  
   • Any prediction from systematic variation? Yes. A primary focus of the paper is how varying p changes equilibrium strategy and payoff outcomes, especially in conjunction with varying r and the network structure (node degree k). Key insights include:  
     – For p below certain thresholds (p₍1,b₎, p₍1,c₎, etc.), the population remains stuck at mostly non‐investing strategies (NT‐NU). As p increases beyond those thresholds, the prosocial strategy (IT) takes over, raising the population’s mean payoff.  
     – The paper also highlights “synergy” effects when p is moderately sized and the network degree k is not too large or too small. Figure 2 shows regions of synergy vs. interference in the (p, k) plane across different values of r.  
     – Numerical effect examples: the paper derives closed‐form threshold expressions (e.g., p₍1,b₎ = (k(1 − r) − 3r + 1)/(k + 2)) beyond which full cooperation IT is stable. Several other threshold formulas (p₍4₎, p₍1,c₎ = 1 − r, etc.) appear in Figures 1–3.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Does the paper discuss it? No.  
   • Any prediction from systematic variation? No.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Does the paper discuss it? No.  
    • Any prediction from systematic variation? No.  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per reward)
    • Does the paper discuss it? No.  
    • Any prediction from systematic variation? No.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Does the paper discuss it? No. (Strictly an evolutionary model without explicit round‐knowledge.)  
    • Any prediction from systematic variation? No.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much peers gained/lost each round)?
    • Does the paper discuss it? No.  
    • Any prediction from systematic variation? No.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Does the paper discuss it? No. The model uses institutional punishment with no mention of identifying the punisher.  
    • Any prediction from systematic variation? No.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Does the paper discuss it? No reward mechanism is modeled.  
    • Any prediction from systematic variation? No.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   • The paper mainly uses (1) the population‐mean payoff (or “social welfare”) at the evolutionary stable state, and (2) which strategy composition is stable (in particular, whether the fully prosocial strategy IT takes over). They do not define “efficiency” as “actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff,” although they often discuss payoff improvements and label them “efficiency” in qualitative terms (e.g., synergy leads to “improved efficiency” by achieving high cooperation at lower cost).  

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Two parameters are explicitly mentioned and varied:  
     – #6 (the “return” r in the trust game, analogous to a multiplication factor).  
     – #8 (the penalty magnitude p).  
   • The paper does not discuss or vary the others.  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • For #6 (r): The paper analyzes how changing r alters the presence or absence of synergy or interference between punishment (p) and network structure (k). This ultimately changes equilibrium payoffs and how easily IT can emerge.

Article Title: The role of emotions in public goods games with and without punishment opportunities

Abstract: We consider the emotional correlates of activity in the Public Good game when monetary and non-monetary punishments are available, and when no punishment is possible. In our experiment, emotions are measured using Face Reading software that tracks the emotional content of facial expressions in real time. When no punishment is possible, greater anger and more negative emotional valence correlate with learning that one has contributed more than others. Lower valence and happiness, in turn, are associated with reducing one's cooperation in the next period. When non-monetary punishment in the form of expressed disapproval is possible, positive emotional valence is associated with cooperation, punishment of free-riders, and an increase in cooperation from one period to the next. Below I go through the 15 parameters, one at a time, and report exactly what the paper says about each of them.  
For every parameter I state  

(a) whether the paper gives its value (or range) and, if so, what that value is;  
(b) whether the paper varies that parameter systematically; and  
(c) whether the paper reports how such a variation changes the “punishment treatment effect’’ on ANY dependent variable (contribution, emotions, earnings, etc.).  Whenever a numerical effect can be read directly from a figure or table I cite it; otherwise I state that no effect size is reported.

----------------------------------------------------------------  
1. Number of players  
a. Mentioned: groups of 4 players.  
b. Not varied (always 4).  
c. No prediction or result about varying the group size.

2. Number of rounds  
a. Mentioned: 10 periods.  
b. Not varied.  
c. No prediction or result about varying the horizon.

3. Is chat enabled?  
a. Stated implicitly: no chat; decisions are private and computerised.  
b. Not varied.  
c. No discussion of enabling/disabling chat.

4. “All-or-nothing’’ contribution?  
a. Stated: subjects choose any integer amount from 0 to 20 ECU; hence it is NOT all-or-nothing.  
b. Not varied.  
c. No discussion of forcing all-or-nothing contributions.

5. Contribution “default’’ (i.e. refund frame)?  
a. Not used; subjects start with 20 ECU and decide how much to put in the public account.  
b. Not varied.  
c. No discussion of default vs. refund framing.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
a. Mentioned: MPCR = 0.4 (each ECU put in the group account yields 0.4 ECU to each of the four members).  
b. Not varied.  
c. No prediction or result about changing the MPCR.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
a. Mentioned.  
   • Monetary-punishment (MP) treatment: cost = 1 ECU per point.  
   • Non-monetary-punishment (NP) treatment: cost = 0.  
b. Varied across the two punishment treatments (costly vs. cost-free).  
c. Effects reported (relative to Baseline without punishment):  

   – Contributions (Fig. 1):  
     • Baseline final-period mean ≈ 3 ECU  
     • NP final-period mean ≈ 9–10 ECU  
     • MP final-period mean ≈ 14–15 ECU  
     Thus the same punishment magnitude is more effective (in terms of contribution levels) when it is costly to the punisher than when it is cost-free.  

   – Emotional correlates: costly punishment is accompanied by weaker emotion-behaviour links than cost-free punishment (see Sections 5.3 and 5.4).  
   – No efficiency measure is reported, so no numerical efficiency effect can be extracted.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss suffered per unit)  
a. Mentioned.  
   • MP: each point deducted 3 ECU from the target.  
   • NP: 0 ECU deducted (pure disapproval).  
b. Varied across MP vs. NP jointly with cost; not varied independently.  
c. Same empirical patterns as Parameter 7 (because the two parameters co-vary in the design). No separate manipulation, hence no isolated effect size is given.

9. Reward enabled?  
a. Not enabled in any treatment.  
b. Not varied.  
c. No discussion.

10. Reward cost  
(See 9.)

11. Reward magnitude  
(See 9.)

12. Is the number of rounds known?  
a. Subjects are told the game lasts 10 periods.  
b. Not varied.  
c. No discussion of making the horizon uncertain.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
a. Yes. After the contribution stage each subject sees every other member’s contribution; after the punishment stage each subject sees how many points they themselves received (but not the sources).  
b. Not varied.  
c. No discussion of hiding or revealing peer outcomes.

14. Do punished players learn the identity of the punisher?  
a. Not expressly stated, but the interface description implies anonymity (subjects see only *how many* points they receive, not who sent them).  
b. Not varied.  
c. No discussion of making punishment identifying vs. anonymous.

15. Do rewarded players learn the identity of the rewarder?  
a. Not applicable (no rewards).  
b. Not varied.  
c. No discussion.

----------------------------------------------------------------  
SUMMARY  

A. Dependent variables.  
   • The paper never reports or analyses “group efficiency’’ (total payoff / maximum payoff).  
   • Dependent variables actually analysed are:  
     – Individual contribution (ECU).  
     – Punishment sent / received (points).  
     – Real-time emotion measures (Happiness, Anger, Sadness, Fear, Disgust, Surprise, overall Valence, Arousal).  
     – Change in contribution from one period to the next.  
   These are conceptually different from efficiency because they ignore the cost of punishment and the lost group output.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   Seven: (1) number of players, (2) number of rounds, (4) contribution mode, (6) MPCR, (7) punishment cost, (8) punishment magnitude, (13) information on peer outcomes.  
   The remaining eight parameters are either absent or only implied as “not present’’ (3, 5, 9–12, 14, 15).

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the *effect of systematic variation* on the punishment treatment effect?  
   Only two: (7) punishment cost and (8) punishment magnitude, and even these are only co-varied jointly through the MP vs. NP comparison.  
   No other parameter is systematically varied, so there is no evidence on their interaction with punishment.

D. What predictions can be made—based solely on this paper—about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  

   • Because efficiency itself is never analysed, the paper provides little direct guidance.  
   • The only clear qualitative prediction is that allowing any form of peer punishment (monetary or non-monetary) will raise contributions relative to a no-punishment baseline, but monetary punishment (cost = 1, magnitude = 3) raises contributions more than cost-free symbolic punishment (cost = 0, magnitude = 0). Whether this translates into higher *efficiency* is unknown, because monetary punishment also destroys earnings through fines and costs.  
   • No prediction can be made from the paper about varying group size, length of play, MPCR, chat, visibility of punishers, rewards, or information structure, because none of those factors were manipulated or analysed.

In short, the paper gives us only one experimentally established lever—switching between “costly & consequential’’ punishment and “cost-free & symbolic’’ punishment—and even for that lever it does not compute efficiency. Consequently, almost no quantitative prediction about efficiency can be made for the 15-parameter space using this paper alone.
reference_APA: Noussair, Charles N., Tucker, Steven, Xu, Yilong & Breaban, Adriana (2024). The role of emotions in public goods games with and without punishment opportunities. JOURNAL OF ECONOMIC BEHAVIOR & ORGANIZATION.

Below, each of the 15 design parameters is treated in turn.  For every parameter I state
(1) whether the paper even mentions the parameter and, if so, the value(s) actually used, and  
(2) whether the paper contains any prediction or empirical evidence about how *changing* that parameter would alter the “punishment treatment effect.”  
Whenever the paper provides a numerical effect size I cite the relevant table/figure.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned.  All games have exactly three players (A, B, C).  
   (2) Not varied.  No predictions or evidence about changing the group size.

2.  Number of rounds (repetitions of the stage game)  
   (1) Mentioned and **systematically varied**.  Three treatments:  
       • 1-stage games (baseline, no scope for punishment),  
       • 2-stage games,  
       • 10-stage games.  
   (2) Effect of varying this parameter:  
       – Cooperation rate in *non-terminal* stages is .26 (1-stage), .25 (2-stage) and .63 (10-stage) – Table I.  
       – Thus moving from 1 to 10 stages raises the outcome that can be interpreted as “punishment-induced cooperation” by +.37 (37 percentage points).  
       – Moving from 2 to 10 stages raises it by +.38.  
       – The paper never reports efficiency, but if one assumes pay-offs map monotonically into efficiency, the authors’ conclusion is that “increasing the number of stages substantially increases cooperation” (p. 8).

3.  Chat enabled?  
   (1) Not mentioned; there is no indication that subjects could communicate.  
   (2) Not discussed or varied.

4.  All-or-nothing contribution decision?  
   (1) Yes.  B and C choose either B1/C1 (cooperate) or B2/C2 (defect).  This is indeed binary.  
   (2) Not varied; no predictions about changing from binary to continuous contributions.

5.  “Contribution default” framing (reverse public-goods)?  
   (1) Not mentioned.  
   (2) Not discussed.

6.  Marginal-per-capita-return / multiplication factor  
   (1) Pay-off structure is fixed: cooperating yields 50 points to B (or C) and 55 extra points to A relative to defection; defecting yields 70 to B (or C) and lowers A’s payoff by 55.  
   (2) The payoff parameters are *not* varied, so the paper offers no predictions about different MPCRs or multipliers.

7.  Punishment cost to the punisher  
   (1) Explicitly stated to be zero: A can switch partners “at no cost.”  
   (2) Not varied.

8.  Punishment magnitude (loss inflicted)  
   (1) The loss equals the foregone chance of being selected in future stages (maximum ≈ \$4.70 in the 10-stage game, p. 12).  
   (2) Held constant; no systematic variation.

9.  Reward enabled?  
   (1) Yes.  “Staying with” a cooperating partner is interpreted as a reward.  
   (2) Always enabled; not varied.

10. Reward cost to the rewarder  
    (1) Zero (keeping the same partner is costless).  
    (2) Not varied.

11. Reward magnitude (gain to the recipient)  
    (1) Equal to continued participation in the profitable relationship (not quantified separately).  
    (2) Not varied.

12.  Are subjects told when the game ends?  
    (1) Yes.  The number of stages in a block (1, 2, or 10) is common knowledge.  
    (2) Not varied independently of parameter 2.

13.  Are peer outcomes shown?  
    (1) The only information definitely revealed is one’s own pay-off; the paper notes (p. 4, footnote 6) that in the illustrative two-stage description “all players observe their own (but not others’) payoffs.”  
    (2) Not manipulated, and no claims about varying feedback.

14.  Do punished players learn who punished them?  
    (1) They trivially know because only A can punish and it is perfectly observable when A switches away.  
    (2) Not varied; no discussion of changing anonymity of the punisher.

15.  Do rewarded players learn who rewarded them?  
    (1) Same as #14: B or C sees that A re-selected them.  
    (2) Not varied.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY  

A.  Dependent variables actually used  
    – The paper reports: (i) cooperation rate, (ii) propensity of A to punish (switch) or reward (stay).  
    – *Group efficiency or total/average payoff is never reported.*  Efficiency would differ from the reported cooperation measure because payoffs include the chooser’s share and vary across stages.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
    10 of the 15: #1, #2, #4, #6–#12, #14, #15 are described in some form.  Parameters #3, #5, #13 (except for the oblique remark about own vs. others’ pay-offs) are essentially absent, and #7–#11 are only implicit and never manipulated.

C.  Which parameters are *systematically varied* and linked to the punishment treatment effect?  
    Only 1 parameter—#2 (number of rounds).  The paper provides numerical evidence that lengthening the repeated interaction from 1 to 10 stages raises cooperation by roughly 37 percentage points.  No other parameter’s variation is studied.

D.  What predictions about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency can be made *solely from this paper*?  
    • Longer repeated interactions (higher value of parameter #2) amplify the effectiveness of a zero-cost partner-switching punishment, so efficiency should rise sharply when the horizon is increased from very short (1–2 rounds) to moderately long (≈10 rounds).  
    • Because punishment is costless (#7 = 0) and highly salient (#8 large), any design that preserves those features should retain the cooperation gains.  
    • The paper offers *no* basis for predicting how changes in player count, communication, contribution granularity, MPCR, punishment/ reward costs or magnitudes, information revelation, or anonymity would affect efficiency; it simply does not study those dimensions.  Therefore, apart from saying “more rounds → larger positive punishment effect,” very little else can be predicted from the reported evidence.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter extraction of everything the paper “Power in economic games” says that is even remotely relevant for predicting how a punishment treatment will affect **group efficiency** in a Public-Goods Game (PGG).  No statements beyond the paper’s text are added.

-------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned once: the PGG is called an “N-person extension of the 2-person Prisoner’s Dilemma.”  
   • No value is given; no comparison of different N’s; no prediction about how changing N would alter the punishment treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Not mentioned.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Not mentioned.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Not mentioned.

5. Contribution default / withdrawal frame?  
   • Not mentioned.

6. MPCR or multiplication factor  
   • Not mentioned.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   • The term “costly punishment” is used repeatedly to indicate that punishers incur a cost, and that costs can vary across group members.  
   • No numerical value is supplied.  
   • The only qualitative remark about variation is: “If the costs of punishment differ, those group members with the lowest costs to punish may be the ones to exert their punishment power the most [30,31].”  
   • No outcome variable (contribution, efficiency, etc.) is linked to that variation, so no treatment-effect estimate is provided.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine per unit)  
   • Not mentioned.

9. Reward enabled (yes/no)  
   • The paper contrasts “punishment power” with “reward power,” saying that actors may prefer rewards to avoid harming others or harming their reputation and that “using rewards may be as effective as punishments [33].”  
   • No systematic manipulation, no numbers, no efficiency data.

10. Reward cost  
    • Not mentioned.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Not mentioned.

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
    • Not mentioned.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Not mentioned.

14. Do punished players know who punished them?  
    • Not mentioned.

15. Do rewarded players know who rewarded them?  
    • Not mentioned.


-------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables in the paper  
   • The review talks about “cooperation,” “free-riding,” “exploitation,” “collective welfare,” and “co-operation can back-fire,” but never formally defines or reports “group efficiency” (total payoff divided by the maximum attainable).  
   • Therefore, efficiency is neither measured nor analyzed; other constructs (e.g., contribution rates, retaliation, reputation) are discussed instead.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   • #1 (Number of players)  
   • #7 (Punishment cost – only qualitatively)  
   • #9 (Whether a reward option exists)  
   → 3 of 15 parameters.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of **systematically varying** that parameter on the punishment treatment effect for any dependent variable?  
   • Zero.  The paper provides no experimental contrasts, no effect sizes, and no directional predictions tied to systematic parameter variation.

D. Predictions one could make about the 15 parameters and their interactions—based solely on this paper  
   • The text is too general to support quantitative or even firm qualitative predictions about how any of the 15 parameters would modulate the influence of punishment on group efficiency.  
   • At most, one might hazard that (a) lowering punishment costs (#7) could increase the frequency of punishment, and (b) making reward available (#9) might substitute for punishment and thus reduce cycles of retaliation, but the paper supplies no data or theory explicitly linking these conjectures to efficiency.  
   • For the remaining 12 parameters, the paper gives no information that would allow even speculative predictions.

In short, the review is concept-mapping power in economic games; it does not supply parameter-level predictions needed to forecast how punishment will change efficiency in a public-goods setting.

Below each of the 15 design parameters is a concise statement of what can (and cannot) be learned from
Lowen & Schmitt (2013) about its influence on the “punishment treatment effect,” i.e. the difference between the
Expulsion-Only (EO) baseline and the Expulsion-plus-Punishment (WP) treatment.  
“Effect sizes” are reported whenever they can be read directly from the paper (usually Table 1).

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned: Yes – all sessions start with 16 subjects.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Predicted impact on punishment treatment effect? None – the paper never varies or models group size.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned: Yes – 15 periods in every session.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • No prediction about how changing the horizon would alter WP – EO efficiency differences.

3. Chat / communication allowed?  
   • Mentioned: No direct reference to any form of chat or face-to-face communication.  
   • Hence no discussion, variation, or prediction.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
   • Mentioned implicitly – subjects freely choose any split of their endowment (continuous choice, not all-or-nothing).  
   • Never varied, never analysed.

5. Contribution default / recommit option  
   • Not mentioned; not manipulated; no prediction.

6. Marginal Per-Capita Return (MPCR)  
   • Explicitly stated: each E$1 contributed yields E$0.20 to every player, i.e. MPCR = 0.20.  
   • Not varied; no analysis of alternative MPCRs or their interaction with punishment.

7. Cost to impose one unit of punishment  
   • In WP, a voter who is on the winning majority pays E$0.25.  
   • In EO the variable is effectively zero because punishment is unavailable.  
   • Thus the paper contains one discrete change in this parameter (0 → 0.25 when punishment is introduced).  
   • Observed effect on efficiency: EO = 58.07 %, WP = 57.13 % (−0.94 percentage points).  
   • No exploration of other cost levels, so no functional prediction beyond the single observed difference.

8. Magnitude of punishment  
   • In WP, a punished target loses E$40 once a majority votes for punishment; in EO magnitude = 0.  
   • Same comment as for parameter 7: only the 0 → 40 jump is observed; no systematic variation.  
   • The −0.94 pp change in efficiency combines the simultaneous changes in parameters 7 and 8, so their individual contributions cannot be disentangled.

9. Presence of a reward option  
10. Cost to reward  
11. Magnitude of reward  
   • Rewards are never available; the paper says nothing about them.

12. Do subjects know the number of rounds?  
   • Yes – all subjects are told the game lasts 15 rounds.  
   • Not varied; no prediction about alternative information conditions.

13. Are peer outcomes displayed?  
   • Yes – after every period each subject sees every other subject’s contribution and earnings.  
   • Not varied; no prediction.

14. Is the source of punishment revealed?  
   • Partially discussed – targets learn how many votes were cast against them but not which individuals voted.  
   • The anonymity rule is fixed; never varied.

15. Is the source of reward revealed?  
   • Not applicable – no rewards in either treatment.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––

Summary

A. Dependent variables.  
   • The authors report (i) individual and average contributions, (ii) average earnings, and (iii) efficiency
     (average earnings ÷ Pareto-optimal earnings, E$32).  
   • Contribution is a behavioral choice; earnings are monetary outcomes; efficiency normalises earnings relative
     to the social optimum. They are related but not identical.

B. Parameters mentioned (any value given, even if not varied): 9 of 15  
   – #1, #2, #4, #6, #7, #8, #12, #13, #14.

C. Parameters whose *systematic* variation is analysed for its effect on the punishment treatment effect: effectively 1 (or, counting costs and magnitudes separately, 2).  
   – The study toggles the availability of punishment, which simultaneously changes parameter 7
     (cost = 0 → 0.25) and parameter 8 (magnitude = 0 → 40).  
   – Reported impact on efficiency: −0.94 pp (58.07 % → 57.13 %).  
   – Impact on contributions: higher than EO in rounds 1-10, lower in rounds 11-15 (exact figures in Table 1 and
     Fig. 1).  
   – No other parameter is experimentally manipulated.

Below I go through the 15 design parameters one–by–one, always quoting exactly what the paper says (or does not say) and indicating whether the paper uses the parameter at all and, if so, whether it says anything about *systematically varying* that parameter and how such variation would alter the **punishment treatment effect**.  Whenever a quantitative expression is available, I reproduce it and point to the relevant equation, table or figure.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1. Number of players (size of the interacting group)  
   • Mentioned?  NO.  
   • The paper’s model has a *population size* N that is taken to the large-population limit, but no statement is made about varying the *interaction group size* and no link is drawn to the punishment treatment effect.  

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  NO.  The interactions are one-shot in an evolutionary model; no finite or infinite horizon is discussed.  
   • No predictions.

3. Chat between players  
   • Not mentioned; no predictions.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
   • Not mentioned; no predictions.

5. Contribution default / endowment moved back  
   • Not mentioned; no predictions.

6. MPCR or multiplication factor (i.e., benefit–to–cost ratio of cooperation)  
   • Mentioned?  YES.  In-group cooperation yields benefit b and cost c.  
   • Systematic variation?  YES, but only with respect to *emergence of parochial altruism*, never with respect to group efficiency.  
     – For a population split into T isolated groups and under low mutation, parochial altruism is favoured when  
       b > (T+1)/(T–1)·c + α – γ    (Eq. (4) in main text).  
       Hence increasing b (or reducing c) enlarges the parameter space in which punishment/cooperation emerges.  
     – No figure or table computes efficiency; the dependent variable is the stationary probability of the strategy.  

7. Punishment cost to the punisher (α)  
   • Mentioned?  YES.  
   • Systematic variation?  YES, again only for emergence.  
     – Threshold for two groups (T=2, low mutation): b > 5c + α – γ (condition (7)).  
       The coefficient on α is +1, i.e. every extra unit of punishment cost raises the benefit threshold by exactly one unit.  
     – For general T (low mutation): b > (T+1)/(T–1)·c + α – γ.  Same +1 slope w.r.t. α.  
     – No statements about efficiency or about the *difference* between a punishment and a no-punishment treatment.  

8. Punishment magnitude / fine to the target (γ)  
   • Mentioned?  YES.  
   • Systematic variation?  YES, by symmetry with α but with a negative sign.  
     – In all threshold expressions γ enters with coefficient –1.  For T=2: increasing γ by one unit *lowers* the b-threshold by one unit, thereby facilitating emergence.  
     – No efficiency results reported.

9. Whether a reward option is enabled  
10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   • Not mentioned; no predictions.

12. Whether the number of rounds is known  
13. Whether peer outcomes are shown  
14. Whether the punished player is told who punished  
15. Whether the rewarded player is told who rewarded  
   • None of these informational design choices appear in the model; no predictions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used in the paper  
   – The paper is concerned with “emergence” or “abundance” of strategies (parochial altruism, cosmopolitanism, selfish ethnocentrism, disloyalty) in evolutionary equilibrium.  
   – Efficiency, total payoff, average payoff, or any ratio of realised to maximum possible payoff is *not* reported as a dependent variable.  
   – Although payoffs are part of the derivations, they serve only to compute fixation probabilities; they are never analysed as an outcome in their own right.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   – 3 of 15:  
     (6) Benefit–cost parameters of cooperation (b, c)  
     (7) Punishment cost α  
     (8) Punishment fine γ  

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* that parameter on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable)?  
   – 3 parameters (6, 7, 8) are varied systematically, but only with respect to the probability that parochial altruism is favoured.  
   – No parameter is analysed with respect to *group efficiency* or to a *punishment vs. no-punishment treatment difference*.

D. What predictions about the 15 parameters’ impact on the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency can be made solely from this paper?  
   – Practically none.  The paper never computes efficiency and never compares a punishment treatment to a no-punishment baseline.  
   – All that can be inferred is that low punishment cost (α↓) and high punishment fine (γ↑) make parochial altruism more likely to evolve under certain mutation regimes.  Whether that would raise or lower realised efficiency is not evaluated.  
   – For the remaining 12 parameters the paper provides no leverage at all.

Hence, using only the content of this paper, one cannot construct a reliable predictor of how any of the 15 experimental design parameters (individually or in interaction) would change the *efficiency effect* of introducing punishment in a public-goods game.

Abstract: In a laboratory experiment we study how costly punishment behavior of second and third parties in a social dilemma situation is affected by monitoring costs. For every parameter I state  
(1) whether the paper says anything at all about it and, if so, the value(s) actually used in the experiment, and  
(2) whether the paper makes any prediction or reports any evidence on what would happen if that parameter were *systematically varied* with respect to the “punishment treatment effect.”  The only numerical effect sizes that can be inferred from the paper are taken from Tables 1–3.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
(1) Mentioned.  Stage-1 is a two–person Prisoner’s Dilemma (PD).  A *third* by-standing player can punish in the 3PP condition, so there are either 2 (2PP) or 3 (3PP) participants involved in a punishment relation.  
(2) Not varied.  No prediction made for different group sizes.

2. Number of rounds  
(1) Mentioned.  The PD and the subsequent punishment stage are strictly one-shot.  
(2) Not varied.  No prediction made.

3. Is chat enabled?  
(1) Mentioned.  “Direct communication among them was not allowed.”  Hence chat = No.  
(2) Not varied.  No prediction made.

4. Is contribution all-or-nothing?  
(1) Yes.  Subjects choose between “cooperate” (transfer the entire 10-token endowment) or “defect” (keep all 10).  
(2) Not varied.  No prediction made.

5. Is there a contribution default (reversal frame)?  
(1) Not used; the game is framed as giving, not as taking back.  
(2) Not discussed.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor  
(1) Stated implicitly: a 10-token transfer is tripled by the experimenter (MPCR = 3 for the *other* player).  
(2) Not varied.  No prediction made.

7. Punishment cost (cost to impose one punishment unit)  
(1) Fixed at 1 token for the punisher.  
(2) Not varied.  No prediction made.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss per unit inflicted on target)  
(1) Fixed at 3 tokens.  
(2) Not varied.  No prediction made.

9. Is a reward option enabled?  
(1) No.  Only punishment exists.  
(2) Not applicable.

10.–11. Reward cost / reward magnitude  
(1) Not implemented.  
(2) Not discussed.

12. Is the number of rounds known?  
(1) Yes – subjects know the interaction is one-shot.  
(2) Not varied.  No prediction made.

13. Are peer outcomes / actions shown?  (Information display to the punisher)  
(1) Central to the study.  The punisher can *buy* perfect information about the target’s stage-1 action.  The “monitoring fee” equals 0, 5 or 10 tokens in treatments M0, M5, M10.  
(2) Systematically varied.  Main findings (Tables 1–3):

    a) “Targeted” punishment (discriminating between C and D) falls sharply when the fee increases:  
       – Share of T-types (2PP): 68 % (M0) → 17 % (M5) → 17 % (M10)  
       – Share of T-types (3PP): 59 % (M0) → 11 % (M5) → 17 % (M10)

    b) Correspondingly, the *incentive to cooperate* (average punishment of D minus average punishment of C) falls:  
       2PP: 7.0 tokens (M0) → 2.2 tokens (M5) → 1.5 tokens (M10)  
       3PP: 4.6 tokens (M0) → 1.3 tokens (M5) → 1.3 tokens (M10)

    c) Second vs. third parties: “2P-overhead” (extra incentive created by second-party punishment) declines with the fee:  
       2.4 tokens (M0) → 0.9 tokens (M5) → 0.2 tokens (M10)

All reported differences are statistically significant at least at the 1 % level unless otherwise noted in Tables 1–3.  

These are the only systematic treatment effects the paper contains.

14. Is the identity of the punisher revealed to the punished?  
(1) Not discussed; anonymity appears to be maintained.  
(2) Not varied.  No prediction made.

15. Is the identity of a rewarder revealed?  
(1) Not applicable (no rewarding).  
(2) Not discussed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables used  
   – *Incentive to cooperate* = average punishment(defect) – average punishment(cooperate).  
   – Shares of behavioural types: Non-punishers (N), Targeted punishers (T), Blind punishers (B).  
   – Various punishment expenditures.  
   Group efficiency (total or average payoff) is *not* reported; thus all results are on punishment patterns, not on efficiency per se.

B.  Parameters mentioned (9/15)  
   1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13.  The remaining six parameters (5, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15) are absent.

C.  Parameters whose *systematic variation* is analysed (1/15)  
   Only parameter 13 (information availability, operationalised through the monitoring fee).

D.  Predictions one can make (for efficiency) from this paper alone  
   – Lower monitoring costs (i.e., easier or cheaper access to information about others’ actions) strengthen targeted punishment, increase the difference between how defectors and cooperators are treated, and therefore should raise cooperation incentives and ultimately *group efficiency*.  
   – When monitoring is costly, many punishers either abstain or punish indiscriminately; punishment then wastes resources with little cooperative benefit, so efficiency should fall.  
   – The cost-sensitivity of second-party and third-party punishment is similar, but second parties are slightly more prone to stop punishing whereas third parties are more prone to punish blindly; overall efficiency consequences are therefore expected to be roughly comparable across the two roles.  

For all other parameters the paper provides no basis for predicting how they would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

1. Number of players

   – Systematic-variation prediction?  NO.  n is kept fixed in all analyses; no comparative‐statics or simulations with other n are reported.

3. Chat enabled?  
   – Mentioned?  NO.  
   – Systematic-variation prediction?  Not applicable.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
   – Mentioned?  YES (indirectly).  x ∈ [0,1] is a *continuous* choice: members may sell any fraction outside the cooperative.  There is explicitly *not* an all-or-nothing restriction (Section 2.1).

   – Mentioned?  NO.  The cooperative *earns* the penalty revenue βy(q – p)(…) so the model contains no explicit cost term.  
   – Systematic-variation prediction?  Not applicable.

8. Punishment *magnitude* (impact on the target per unit imposed)  
   – Mentioned?  YES.  It is the scalar parameter β≥1 (“penalty parameter”) in payoff (3.1).  
   – Systematic-variation prediction?  YES.  Two cases are analysed:  
     • β = 1 (“limited penalty”): Theorem 2 proves that the attractive solution (full compliance) is *unstable*; Figs 2–5 show xᵢ and y diverging from (1,1).  
     • β > 1 (“effective penalty”): Theorem 3 proves that (1,1) is *globally attractive* for any initial y ≥ 1/β; Figs 6–9 show convergence when β = 1.15.  
     Numerical magnitude: no continuous response curve is given, only the qualitative threshold “β > 1 vs. β = 1”.

9. Reward enabled?  
   – Mentioned?  NO.  Rewards are not modelled.

    – Mentioned?  NO.

11. Reward magnitude  
    – Mentioned?  NO.

    – Mentioned?  NO.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    – Mentioned?  NO.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
    – Mentioned?  NO.  It is assumed common knowledge that the cooperative levies penalties, but no information treatment is manipulated.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
    – Mentioned?  NO.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables used in the paper  
    • Individual pay-offs fᵢ(t,x,y) and f_{n+1}(t,x,y)  
    • Strategy variables xᵢ(t) (member faithfulness) and y(t) (co-op punishment level)  
    • Resource state zᵢ(t) (fish biomass)  
    Group efficiency, total payoff, or “maximum possible payoff” ratios are *never* defined or reported.  Therefore efficiency—our target variable—is not analysed in the paper.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
    1 (number of players), 2 (continuous vs. discrete periods), 4 (contribution not all-or-nothing), and 8 (punishment magnitude β).  Four out of fifteen.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper *systematically vary* them and discuss their effect on the punishment treatment?  
    Exactly one: parameter 8, β.  No numerical dose–response is given, only the qualitative comparison β = 1 vs β > 1.

D.  If predictions about the punishment treatment effect on efficiency had to be made solely from this paper  
    – We can say with some confidence that raising the punishment magnitude above the threshold β = 1 should increase cooperative compliance (xᵢ → 1) and therefore *should* increase efficiency, because players end up at the cooperative solution that yields higher individual profits in the model.  
    – For all other parameters (1–7, 9–15) the paper provides either no discussion or no systematic variation, so no prediction grounded in the paper can be offered.  Any conjecture would be speculation beyond the text.

Hence the only evidence-based prediction we can extract is:

Higher punishment magnitude (β > 1) → stronger punishment treatment effect → higher compliance → presumably higher efficiency; limited punishment (β = 1) fails to improve outcomes.  For every other parameter, the paper is silent.

Abstract: Since social preferences towards individuals perceived as belonging to a different group are typically weaker, cooperation is more difficult in ethnically diverse settings. Abstract: We study the emergence of norms and their enforcement in a public goods game with private information about endowments. Subjects were randomly assigned a Low or High endowment and, across treatments, endowments were either Observed or Unobserved. In both treatments subjects could enforce contributions with peer punishment. We use punishment decisions to estimate contribution norms and then estimate the expected costs of noncompliance. In Observed, both Low and High types enforce a contribute-your-endowment norm, adjusting the costs of noncompliance to account for each type's en-dowment. When at least one High type pools with Low types (by contributing less than or equal to the Low endowment), contributions of zero are punished as if they come from a High type, while contributions equal to the Low endowment are not punished in expectation (in case they come from a cooperative Low type). This enforcement strat-egy prevents cooperation from unraveling, but it also enables High types to hide behind the Low endowment. Our results dovetail with results from bargaining games and suggest that in settings with incomplete information, norms can attenuate but not eliminate non-cooperative behavior. In this work, we explore the middle ground between the two from the perspective of strategy updating. As an intuitive idea, each agent selects the reference agent for learning by global selection with a probability. The results show that local selection favors cooperation more given a lower synergy factor, because cooperation can aggregate to defend against the invasion of defection. The results show that when global selection is frequently accessed by defectors but hardly accessed by cooperators, the system disfavors cooperation most: defection near the cooperation aggregation is hard to affect by cooperation around, while cooperation interacts locally and is invaded by defection around. (i) whether the paper even tells us the value of the parameter, and  
(ii) whether the paper contains any statement or evidence on what would happen if the parameter were *systematically varied* for the purpose of predicting the “punishment treatment effect” (i.e. the difference between a condition *with* punishment and the otherwise identical condition *without* punishment).  All numerical information is taken literally from the tables, figures or text of the article.

-------------------------------------------------
1.  Number of players  
(i) Yes – every game is played in *groups of three*.  
(ii) Not varied, no prediction.

2.  Number of rounds  
(i) Yes – one “one-shot” trial plus six further stranger-matched rounds (7 in total).  
(ii) Not varied; the authors never model how changing the number of rounds would change the sanctioning effect.  The only round effect they analyse is a *time trend* within the fixed seven rounds.

3.  Chat permitted?  
(i) Yes – explicitly ruled out: “no communication between participants was allowed.”  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction.

4.  All-or-nothing contribution?  
(i) Yes – binary choice: either place the whole 4-point endowment in the private or group account.  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction.

5.  Contribution default / “take game” framing?  
(i) The study does not employ a default withdrawal frame.  Each round starts with an empty public account and subjects choose where to *place* their 4 points.  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction.

6.  Marginal Per-Capita Return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
(i) Yes – each contributed point yields 2 points to *each* of the three players, so MPCR = 0.5.  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction.

7.  Punishment cost to the punisher  
(i) Yes – voting is *costless*.  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction on what would happen if the cost were positive or different.

8.  Punishment magnitude (loss per punishment unit)  
(i) Yes – a sanctioned player loses the 1-point bonus.  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction.

9.  Is a reward enabled?  
(i) A 1-point bonus is *initially* given to everybody; punishment can withdraw it.  No separate positive reward mechanism exists.  
(ii) Reward possibility is not systematically manipulated; no prediction.

10. Reward cost  
(i) Not applicable – there is no discretionary reward option.  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction.

11. Reward magnitude  
(i) The automatic bonus is 1 point.  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction.

12. Do players know the horizon?  
(i) Yes – after finishing the first (one-shot) round they are told that *exactly six more* rounds will follow.  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes displayed?  
(i) Yes – after every round subjects see each group member’s choice and pay-off.  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
(i) No – votes are anonymous; only the majority rule is announced.  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
(i) Not applicable (no active rewarding).  
(ii) Not varied; no prediction.

-------------------------------------------------
Summary

A.  Dependent variables used  
– Group *efficiency/total payoff* is never analysed.  
– The paper studies:  
  • Individual cooperation decision (binary).  
  • Empirical expectations about others’ cooperation.  
  • Personal normative beliefs and normative expectations.  
  • Use of exclusion votes.  
These variables are conceptually different from efficiency; e.g., high cooperation with a 0.5 MPCR still reduces efficiency relative to full defection.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are at least *mentioned*?  
Thirteen of them (everything except possibly 5, 10, 15) are explicitly described.  None is experimentally *varied* except the presence/absence of a sanctioning institution (which is not one of the 15 listed parameters, but rather a treatment dummy).

C.  For how many parameters does the paper study the *systematic* effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
Zero.  The article never changes any of the 15 parameters across treatments; hence it contains no estimates, coefficients or qualitative predictions for such variations.

D.  What predictions on efficiency can one make from this paper alone?  
Because efficiency is not reported and none of the 15 parameters is manipulated, the paper offers essentially no direct basis for predicting how changing any of those parameters – individually or in interaction – would alter the impact of punishment on efficiency. Abstract: The World Trade Center attack has shed light on the urgent need to implement preventing measures against terrorism and to enhance cooperation in the global security system for all countries. However, international coordination cannot be taken for granted. It is often ineffective and likely to fail for several reasons. Perhaps the more prominent reason to explain failure in coordination is that collective actions against terrorism may suffer from the well-known free riding problem. In this paper we experimentally investigate cooperation dilemma in counterterrorism policies by measuring to what extent international deterrence policy may suffer from free riding. In our game, contributions to the group account do not aim to increase the production of the public good but instead seek to decrease the probability that a stochastic event destroys the good. A country could choose to free ride by investing nothing in the international deterrence policy and instead invest all its resources in its own national protection or even choose to ignore totally terrorism by investing on alternative projects. We also look at the effects of institutions that allow sanctioning and rewarding of other countries to facilitate coordination on deterrence policy. We find that, in absence of institutional incentives and after controlling for risk aversion, most of countries defect by investing very weakly in collective actions against terrorism while largely investing to protect themselves. In contrast, the introduction of punishment/reward incentive systems improves significantly the contribution level to the collective security account.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what this paper says (or does not say) regarding each of the 15 listed parameters, followed by a summary (A–D) at the end. Per your instructions:

• I focus solely on what is stated in the paper.  
• Where the paper discusses outcomes or dependent variables other than efficiency (e.g., cooperation rates, amount contributed, final payoff), I explicitly note that.  
• For each parameter, I indicate (1) whether or where the paper mentions it (including any specific value used), and (2) whether and how the paper makes predictions about systematically varying that parameter on the “punishment treatment effect” (in particular, on any outcome measure, since the paper does not use the term “efficiency” in the formal sense of “actual total payoff divided by maximum possible,” but does examine payoff and welfare).  
• If the paper does not mention or vary a parameter or make predictions, I say so.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1) Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The design specifies that each group has 4 players (“n=4”).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how varying it would affect punishment’s impact? No. The experiment always uses groups of 4, and there is no discussion of how changing the number of players would affect punishment or efficiency‐related outcomes.

2) Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper uses 40 periods (rounds) in all sessions. Participants know that the game lasts for 40 periods.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how varying it would affect punishment’s impact? No. The number of rounds is fixed at 40, and there is no discussion of how a different number of rounds would affect the punishment treatment effect.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not describe any chat or communication among participants. They simply make decisions on their computer terminals.  
   • Any predictions about varying chat? No. This is not addressed.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned? Yes (indirectly). In the experiment, each player can invest any amount from 0 to 20 tokens in each of the three allocations (X, Y, or Z). Thus, it is not an all‐or‐nothing contribution.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how doing so would affect punishment’s impact? No. All players choose from 0 to 20 continuously. This parameter is not varied.

5) Is the contribution default (i.e., do players choose how much of their endowment to “take back”)?  
   • Mentioned? No. There is no “default” contribution or mechanism described. Players make an explicit choice of how many of their 20 tokens go into X, Y, and Z.  
   • Any predictions about varying it? No. Not discussed.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or similar multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? Only loosely. The paper does not use “MPCR” in the standard sense but instead uses a probability‐reduction approach (with parameter a = 0.16) to determine how total group contributions to X reduce the chance of a terrorist “shock.” The authors do not call this an MPCR, nor do they systematically vary it.  
   • Any predictions about varying a = 0.16? No. The value a = 0.16 is mentioned as fixed. There is no discussion of how changing it would affect punishment effectiveness.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Tables A3 and A4 (for sanctions and rewards) show the piecewise cost structure. For instance, punishing someone by 2 points costs the punisher 10 units, punishing by 9 points costs 125, etc.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary that cost or predict how changes in the cost would affect punishment’s impact? No. They fix one cost schedule and do not vary it across sessions or make predictions about varying it.

8) Punishment magnitude (the amount deducted from the punished player)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Again, Table A3 shows that, for example, 2 punishment points deduct 40 units from the target’s payoff, 9 points deduct 500, etc.

They do not vary the reward mechanism’s detailed parameters, but they do measure how having reward at all affects contributions and payoffs relative to the punishment or baseline conditions.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Table A4 lists a piecewise cost schedule (e.g., giving 2 reward points costs 10, giving 9 reward points costs 125, etc.).  
   • Is it systematically varied? No. The authors use one cost schedule in the reward treatment. No predictions on how changing that schedule would affect outcomes.

   • Mentioned? Yes. As in punishment, Table A4 describes how many additional tokens are gained by the target for each point awarded (e.g., 2 points yield +40 units to the target).

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Participants know from the start that there are 40 rounds.  
   • Does the paper vary this or predict changes? No. The 40‐round horizon is fixed.

   • Does the paper systematically vary how outcomes are displayed? No. There is one information‐display format. No direct predictions are made about varying that format.

   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper states that participants do not see individual punisher identities. Punishment is anonymous (“our experimental design…should prevent revenge effects”).

   • Is this parameter systematically varied? No. The experiment does not vary anonymity of the rewarder.

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   • The paper frequently reports “payoffs,” “earnings,” and “welfare” (final individual or group payoffs) as dependent variables. It also reports how frequently participants contribute to X or Y (“cooperation” or “contribution”).  
   • The paper does not use the explicit ratio “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff” as its primary measure. Instead, it focuses on:  
       – Amount contributed to the public account (X)  
       – Probability of an attack (and whether a participant is hit)  
       – Final or average payoffs (“welfare”).  

B) Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned explicitly:  
       1. Number of players (fixed at 4)  
       2. Number of rounds (fixed at 40)  
       4. Contribution method is not all‐or‐nothing (they use 0–20 tokens).  
       6. A parameter “a=0.16” that reduces risk (analogous to, but not called, an MPCR).  
       7 & 8. Punishment cost and magnitude (via a table).  
       9. Whether a reward is enabled (Yes/No across treatments).  
       10 & 11. Reward cost and magnitude (via a table).  
       12. The number of rounds is known (40).  
       13, 14, 15. Anonymous punishment and reward are mentioned, as well as limited feedback about peer contributions to X.  

   • Not specifically mentioned or not used as an experimental variable:  
       3. Chat between players (they do not mention chat at all).  
       5. Contribution default.  

C) For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, the only systematic variations in the experiment relevant to punishment are whether punishment is enabled vs. baseline (and whether reward is enabled vs. baseline). The cost and magnitude schedules for punishment/reward are given but not systematically varied.  
   • Thus, the paper only systematically varies:  
       – Parameter 9 (punishment or reward is enabled) relative to baseline.  
       – That is the key comparison from which they draw inferences about punishment’s and reward’s effects on cooperation and payoffs.  
   • Effect sizes mentioned:  
       – Punishment raises contributions to X relative to baseline but leads to lower final payoff than baseline (due to the heavy cost of administering punishment).  
       – Reward also raises contributions to X and, unlike punishment, leads to higher final payoffs than baseline since reward does not destroy resources overall in the same way.  

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not provide direct predictions for most parameters (1–8, 10–11, 13–15) when systematically changed; it holds those fixed in the experiment.
