Below I go through the 15 design parameters one by one.  
For each I state

• Whether the parameter is explicitly described anywhere in the paper and, if so, what fixed value(s) the authors used.  
• Whether the paper ever **systematically varies** that parameter and reports how the variation changes the *punishment-treatment effect* on any dependent variable.  
• The numerical effect size that can be directly read off the text / tables / figures (if any).

Because the paper never studies “group efficiency” (total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff), I refer to the two dependent variables the authors do analyse:  

– “Entrusted amount” in the Trust Game (TG) – a proxy for perceived trustworthiness.  
– “Partner choice frequency” – which punisher participants preferred as a future partner.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned: yes. Each Third-Party-Punishment (TPP) vignette involves exactly three players (Sender, Receiver/Victim, Observer/Punisher).  
   • Varied? No. Always 3; no prediction about changing this number.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned: single one-shot interaction in every experiment.  
   • Varied? No.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Not mentioned. No chat or communication channel is used or discussed.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution decision  
   • Partially mentioned. In Experiments 1A & 1B the Sender can either send 50 % of the endowment or send nothing, i.e., a dichotomous action.  
   • Varied? No systematic variation; the dichotomy is constant across conditions. No effect is reported.

5. Contribution default / “take” frame  
   • Not mentioned.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Not mentioned. The paradigm is not a public-goods game.

7. Punishment cost to punisher  
   • Mentioned and **systematically varied**.  
     – Exp 1A & 1B: cost is fixed (5 pence) whenever punishment is chosen.  
     – Exp 2A: four levels that covary with severity (cost = 3, 7, 11, 15 pence).  
     – Exp 2B: cost held constant at 3 pence while severity still varies.  
   • Reported effects (dependent variable = money entrusted in TG):  
     – Exp 2A (cost rises together with severity): significant main effect, F(3,1182)=28.42, partial η²=.067. Mean entrusted amounts rise from 9.94 pence (low cost 3p) to 12.38 pence (high cost 15p); high–low difference = +2.44 pence (Table 2, Table 3).  
     – Exp 2B (cost flat): no effect, F(3,678)=1.68, p=.17; max mean difference high–low = 0.55 pence.  
   • Interpretation offered by authors: higher **cost** (not severity per se) drives the signalling value; when cost is decoupled the effect disappears.

8. Punishment magnitude (severity)  
   • Mentioned and varied in parallel with parameter 7. Magnitude levels = 5, 10, 15, 20 pence taken from the punished player.  
   • Because magnitude and cost move together in Exp 2A and are decoupled in Exp 2B, the authors conclude that magnitude alone does **not** change entrusted amounts when its cost is held constant. (Same statistics as in parameter 7.)

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Not mentioned. No rewarding option exists in the design.

10. Reward cost  
    • Not mentioned.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Not mentioned.

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
    • Not relevant; only one round is played and this is common knowledge. Not varied.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Participants are shown (a) what the Sender sent, (b) how much the Observer spent and (c) how much the Sender lost – i.e., the entire payoff structure.  
    • This informational display is never varied experimentally; no effects are reported.

14. Punished player knows the identity of the punisher  
    • Not discussed; the punished party is a scripted vignette, so the issue is moot.

15. Rewarded player knows the identity of the rewarder  
    • Not applicable (no rewards).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
   – Group efficiency or total payoff: **Not used.**  
   – Used variables: (i) money entrusted to the punisher in a subsequent Trust Game; (ii) frequency with which a punisher is chosen as a future partner. These measure perceived trustworthiness, not efficiency.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   5 of them: #1 (players), #4 (binary contribution), #7 (punishment cost), #8 (punishment magnitude/severity), #13 (peer outcomes are displayed).

C. For how many parameters does the paper **systematically vary** the parameter and report its effect on the punishment treatment?  
   2 parameters:  
   – #7 Punishment cost (varied across 0, 5, 3, 7, 11, 15 pence).  
   – #8 Punishment magnitude (varied 5–20 pence).  
   Effect sizes are provided above; all other parameters are fixed or absent.

D. Predicting the punishment-treatment effect on group *efficiency* solely from this paper  
   The paper contains no efficiency data, no public-goods setting, and no test of aggregate pay-offs. All we can infer is:  
   • Higher punishment **costs** that accompany higher severities make observers trust the punisher more.  
   • When cost is held flat, higher **severity** alone does not raise trust.  
   Extrapolating to a real public-goods game’s efficiency is speculative. One could guess that punishment schemes that are *costly to the punisher* might increase subsequent cooperation (and hence efficiency) if, and only if, observers value the costliness; but the present study offers no direct evidence about contributions or payoffs, so any further prediction would be conjecture.

Author Full Names: Lie-Panis, Julien; Fitouchi, Leo; Baumard, Nicolas; Andre, Jean-Baptiste
Article Title: The social leverage effect: Institutions transform weak reputation effects into strong incentives for cooperation

Abstract: Institutions allow cooperation to persist when reciprocity and reputation provide insufficient incentives. Yet how they do so remains unclear, especially given that institutions are themselves a form of cooperation. To solve this puzzle, we develop a mathematical model of reputation-based cooperation in which two social dilemmas are nested within one another. The first dilemma, characterized by high individual costs or insufficient monitoring, cannot be solved by reputation alone. The second dilemma, an institutional collective action, involves individuals contributing to change the parameters of the first dilemma in a way that incentivizes cooperation. Our model demonstrates that this nested architecture creates a leverage effect. While insufficient on its own to incentivize cooperation in the first dilemma, reputation incentivizes contributions to the institutional collective action, which, in turn, strengthen the initially weak incentives for cooperation in the first dilemma. Just as a pulley system transforms minimal muscular strength into significant lifting capability, institutions act as cooperative pulleys, transforming initially weak reputational incentives into powerful drivers of cooperative behavior. Based on these results, we suggest that institutions have developed as social technologies, designed by humans to exploit this social leverage effect, just as material technologies are designed to exploit physical laws.

Below we map every one of the 15 design parameters onto the content of “The social-leverage effect: Institutions transform weak reputation effects into strong incentives for cooperation.”   
In each case we state (i) whether the parameter is explicitly present in the paper, (ii) the value(s) the authors actually use, and (iii) whether the paper says what would happen if the parameter were *systematically varied* for any outcome variable (note that the authors’ two focal outcome variables are “rate of cooperation” and “expected payoff,” not efficiency).

------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (i) Mentioned: Yes.  “n  ≫ 1” (large population).  
   (ii) No numeric value—only the inequality.  
   (iii) Never varied; no prediction for treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   (i) Mentioned: Yes.  The repeated game is infinite (“actors engage in infinitely many interactions”).  
   (ii) Infinite horizon is fixed.  
   (iii) No discussion of what would happen if the horizon were shortened or announced; therefore no prediction.

3. Chat enabled?  
   Not mentioned at all.

4. All-or-nothing contribution choice?  
   (i) Yes.  Both “contribute vs. free-ride” and “reciprocate vs. cheat” are binary.  
   (ii) Always binary; never contrasted with a continuous choice.  
   (iii) No systematic variation or prediction.

5. Contribution default / endowment returned?  
   Not mentioned.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   (i) There is an exact analogue: the “institutional efficiency” parameter ρ which multiplies every unit contributed to the institution.  
   (ii) Three values appear: ρ = 0 (baseline, no institution), ρ = 1⁄3 (labelled “inefficient institution”), and ρ = 3 (labelled “efficient institution”).  
   (iii) Systematic effect given:  
        • Increasing ρ sharply lowers the reciprocity-threshold δ̂₁(θ) and therefore raises the rate of cooperation (Fig. 6A vs 6B vs 6C).  
        • Fig. 7A shows the *difference* in cooperation rate between ρ = 3 and ρ = 0; Fig. 7B shows the corresponding change in expected payoff.  
        Numerical illustration (reading directly from Fig. 6/7): at μ ≈ 0.5 and δᵇ ≈ 1.5, cooperation is ≈ 0 with ρ = 0, ≈ 0 with ρ = 1⁄3, and ≈ 0.45 with ρ = 3 – a †45 percentage-point improvement.  
        These are the only explicit treatment-effect magnitudes provided.

7. Punishment *cost* (to the punisher) per unit  
   (i) The model replaces individual-level punishment costs with a pool-contribution cost c₂.  
   (ii) c₂ is set deterministically to c₁/3 throughout the numerical exercise.  
   (iii) Not varied independently; no treatment-effect prediction.

8. Punishment magnitude (deduction inflicted)  
   (i) γ ≥ 0 plays this role.  
   (ii) γ is not an exogenous parameter; it is endogenously determined by ρ: γ = ½ ρ c₂(1–q)n₂/(qn).  
   (iii) The magnitude therefore co-moves with ρ, but the paper never isolates γ itself for a comparative-static exercise.

9. Reward enabled?  
   (i) Yes – β ≥ 0 is defined.  
   (ii) All numerical results set β = 0 (pure punishment + monitoring).  
   (iii) The text notes that “a rewarding institution is obtained by setting γ = π₁ = 0,” but gives no outcome numbers, graphs, or comparative statics.  Hence no prediction.

10. Reward cost per unit  
11. Reward magnitude  
   Not parameterised or varied separately.

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
   Not discussed (the game is indefinitely repeated).

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
   (i) A related construct appears: probability that an action is observed (p₁ in trust games, p₂ in institution games, and extra π₁ supplied by the institution).  
   (ii) p₁ = 0.25, p₂ = 0.75 are fixed; π₁ is tied to ρ as above.  
   (iii) No separate manipulation, so no independent prediction for a punishment treatment effect.

14. Punisher identity revealed?  
15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
   Not mentioned.

------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables  
   • “Rate of cooperation” = probability a chooser trusts & the actor reciprocates.  
   • “Expected payoff” = average monetary payoff (actors’ lifetime + choosers’ one-shot).  
   Group *efficiency* (total payoff / maximum possible payoff) is never constructed explicitly, although “expected payoff” is closely related.

B. Parameters from the list that appear at all: 7 of 15  
   (1) number of players, (2) number of rounds (infinite), (4) binary contribution choice, (6) multiplication factor ρ, (7–8) punishment cost & magnitude (via c₂ and γ), (9) reward on/off, (13) observability probabilities (p₁, p₂, π₁).

C. Parameters whose *systematic* variation is analysed with respect to any treatment effect: only ρ (parameter 6).  No other parameter is independently swept through a range.

D. Predictions one can legitimately take from the paper for the punishment-vs-no-punishment effect on *efficiency* (total payoff)  
   • Higher institutional efficiency ρ leads to larger punishment magnitudes and/or monitoring probabilities, which in turn raise cooperation and average payoffs.  
   • If ρ is too low (e.g., ρ = 1/3), the institution is almost ineffectual; efficiency hardly differs from the no-punishment baseline.  
   • When cooperation is already easy (low δᵇ) and the population is very patient (high μ), introducing punishment/monitoring can slightly *reduce* payoffs because the extra contribution cost is “wasteful.”  
   • The model offers no other lever-specific predictions about chat, group size, finite vs. infinite horizon, identification of punishers/rewarders, etc.  Therefore, beyond the single robust insight about the multiplication factor ρ, the paper provides little basis for forecasting how the full vector of 15 parameters or their interactions would affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Authors: Wang, J; Liu, Z; Xu, Y; Li, XP
Author Full Names: Wang, Juan; Liu, Zhuo; Xu, Yan; Li, Xiaopeng
Article Title: Dynamic evolution in multi-player networked trust games with graded punishment
Keywords Plus: COOPERATION; PROMOTES; PHYSICIANS
Abstract: Trust holds a pivotal position in contemporary society. Yet, the question of how to elevate and sustain trust among selfish individuals poses a formidable challenge. To delve into this issue, we incorporate a graded punishment strategy into a networked N-player trust game, aiming to observe the progression of trust-related behavior. Within this game framework, punishers uphold a certain degree of trust among the participants by incurring an extra expense to exclude those who betray trust. By conducting numerous Monte Carlo simulation experiments, we uncover that the graded punishment strategy can effectively curtail untrustworthy conduct to a significant degree, potentially even eliminating such behavior, thereby fostering an improvement in the overall trust level within the population. However, to effectively deploy this strategy, it is imperative to strike a balance between the penalty cost and the penalty amount, ensuring that the natural evolution of the system is not unduly disrupted. This balance is crucial for preserving the stability and sustainability of the system while safeguarding trust. Broadly speaking, our study offers fresh insights and approaches for enhancing and maintaining trust in the networked society, while also highlighting the avenues and challenges for future research, particularly in the realm of applying graded punishment strategies.

Below, each of the 15 public-goods design parameters is dealt with in turn.  
For every parameter I state

• whether the paper says anything about it, and the value(s) used, and  
• whether the paper gives any prediction about what would happen to the *punishment treatment effect* if the parameter were systematically varied.  
(The paper’s dependent variables are mainly strategy frequencies such as the “investment group density” ρI+PI and, in one figure, total group wealth.  It never reports *efficiency* in the sense of “payoff divided by the cooperative optimum”.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned: Yes – the simulations use N = 1024 agents on a 32 × 32 regular lattice (average degree = 4).  
   • Systematic variation / prediction: No.  N is kept fixed.

2. Number of rounds (time steps)  
   • Mentioned: 20 000 Monte-Carlo steps (MCS), results averaged over the last 5000.  
   • Variation / prediction: None.

3. Chat allowed?  
   • Not mentioned.  No prediction.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution?  
   • The trust game assumes every investor (I or PI) puts in t = 1 each round; this is effectively “all-or-nothing”, but the paper neither labels it as such nor varies it.  
   • No prediction.

5. Contribution default / endowment retention?  
   • Not relevant, not discussed.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Closest analogue: the trustee return multipliers RT (set to 6) and RU (varied indirectly through rUT).  
     rUT ≡ (RU – RT)/RT is systematically varied from 0 to 1 in Fig. 5.  
   • Prediction given: Fig. 5 shows that as rUT increases the investment density collapses at a critical value rUT*, and rUT* rises with higher punishment magnitude β.  No numerical regression is provided; the figure indicates, e.g., at β = 0 the collapse occurs near rUT* ≈ 0.28, at β = 1.0 near rUT* ≈ 0.52.  
   • Effect on *efficiency* is **not reported** – only ρI+PI.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit (α)  
   • Discussed and systematically varied: α from 0 to 2 in steps of .05 (Fig. 1, Fig. 2, Fig. 6).  
   • Prediction: Higher α rapidly erodes the positive effect of punishment.  For each β there is a critical α* beyond which punishment no longer sustains investors; α* increases with β (≈0.50 at β = 0.4, ≈0.65 at β = 0.8, ≈0.85 at β = 1.0—read from Fig. 1).  Total wealth (Fig. 6) also falls with α.  No explicit efficiency ratio.

8. Punishment magnitude (β)  
   • Discussed and systematically varied (0, 0.4, 0.8, 1.0, etc.).  
   • Prediction: Larger β strengthens the punishment treatment effect – it raises α* (Fig. 1) and raises rUT* (Fig. 5).  It also increases final total wealth up to the point where α becomes prohibitive (Fig. 6).

9. Reward enabled?  
   • No reward option in the model.  Not mentioned.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   • Both not mentioned / not varied.

12. Finite horizon known?  
   • Not discussed.  The evolutionary simulations run indefinitely.

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
   • Not discussed.

14. Punishee sees who punished?  
   • Not discussed.

15. Reward recipient sees who rewarded?  
   • Not applicable (no rewards).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables used  
    – Investment group density ρI+PI (main outcome)  
    – Proportions of each strategy (ρI, ρPI, ρT, ρU)  
    – Total group wealth (Fig. 6)  
    – No explicit “efficiency = realised / maximal payoff”.

B.  Parameters from the list that are at least mentioned: 4 of 15  
    (1) number of players, (6) return multiplier/rUT, (7) punishment cost α, (8) punishment magnitude β.

C.  Parameters whose *systematic variation* is analysed for their impact on the punishment treatment effect: 3 of 15  
    (6) rUT, (7) α, (8) β.  
    – rUT: collapse point of cooperation shifts with β.  
    – α: higher cost undermines punishment’s effectiveness.  
    – β: stronger punishment enlarges the parameter space where punishment works and raises total wealth.

D.  Predictions for the 15 parameters’ influence on punishment-induced *efficiency* that can be made solely from the paper

   • Only α, β, and (indirectly) rUT are informative.  
     – Lower α (cheaper punishment) and higher β (harsher punishment) should improve efficiency until α exceeds a critical threshold; beyond that, efficiency collapses.  
     – Higher rUT (stronger temptation) lowers efficiency, but the negative impact can be offset by higher β.  
   • The paper provides no basis for predicting how the other 12 parameters (player number, round length, communication, reward options, information structure, etc.) interact with punishment to affect efficiency.  For these parameters the safest prediction, given the text, is “no clear prediction possible”.

Thus, the article offers useful quantitative guidance only for how punishment *prices* (α) and *strength* (β) – and, to a lesser extent, payoff multipliers (rUT) – condition the success of punishment in promoting cooperation and total payoffs; it is silent on the remaining design features.

Source Title: JOURNAL OF PERSONALITY AND SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY

Abstract: Cooperation underlies the ability of groups to realize collective benefits (e.g., creation of public goods). Yet, cooperation can be difficult to achieve when people face situations with conflicting interests between what is best for individuals versus the collective (i.e., social dilemmas). To address this challenge, groups can implement rules about structural changes in a situation. But what institutional rules can best facilitate cooperation? Theoretically, rules can be made to affect structural features of a social dilemma, such as the possible actions, outcomes, and people involved. We derived 13 preregistered hypotheses from existing work and collected 6 decades of empirical research to test how nine structural features influence cooperation within prisoner's dilemmas and public goods dilemmas. We do this by meta-analyzing mean levels of cooperation across studies (Study 1, k = 2,340, N = 229,528), and also examining how manipulations of these structural features in social dilemmas affect cooperation within studies (Study 2, k = 909). Results indicated that lower conflict of interests was associated with higher cooperation and that (a) the implementation of sanctions (i.e., reward and punishment of behaviors) and (b) allowing for communication most strongly enhanced cooperation. However, we found inconsistent support for the hypotheses that group size and matching design affect cooperation. Other structural features (e.g., symmetry of dilemmas, sequential decision making, payment) were not associated with cooperation. Overall, these findings inform institutions that can (or not) facilitate cooperation.

(a) whether the paper even mentions the parameter and, if so, the value(s) that were coded, and  
(b) whether the paper presents any evidence or prediction about how **systematically varying that parameter changes the “punishment-treatment effect”** (i.e., the difference between a Punishment condition and a No-Punishment control).  Effect sizes are given exactly as they appear in the article; note that all are expressed on *cooperation* (or contribution) and never on *efficiency*.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players (group size)  
– Mentioned?  YES.  Coded range = 2–324, Mdn = 3 (Table 3).  
– Any claim about how changing group size alters the *punishment* effect?  NO.  Group size was only analysed as a main effect on cooperation (meta-analytic d = -0.35 for larger vs smaller groups in the within-study analysis). No interaction with punishment is reported.

2. Number of rounds  
– Mentioned? NO.  The paper distinguishes one-shot vs. repeated (“matching design”) but never reports the exact number of rounds, nor analyses it.  
– Consequently, no statement on the punishment effect.

3. Chat / communication enabled  
– Mentioned?  YES (“Communication” variable: 208 of 2,340 cooperation rates allowed communication).  
– Any statement about how chat *modifies* the punishment effect?  NO.  Communication’s main effect (d = 0.46) and its interaction with conflict (K-index) are reported, but not its interaction with punishment.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
– Mentioned?  NO (the closest construct is “choice type: dichotomous vs. continuous,” but that is not an enforced “all or nothing” rule).  
– No prediction about punishment.

5. Contribution default (withdrawal frame)  
– Mentioned?  NO.  
– No prediction.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor (conflict of interest)  
– Mentioned?  YES.  They transform MPCR into the K-index (M = 0.44, SD = 0.17).  
– Any link to punishment?  NO.  K-index is treated as a predictor of cooperation and as a moderator of the *communication* effect, not the punishment effect.

7. Punishment *cost* to impose one unit  
– Mentioned?  NO.  The database only codes “sanction present vs. absent.”  No cost parameter is analysed.  
– No prediction.

8. Punishment *magnitude* (fine per unit)  
– Mentioned?  NO.  Not analysed.  
– No prediction.

9. Reward enabled  
– Mentioned?  YES (coded under “sanctions,” with separate meta-analysis for reward: d = 0.459 for reward vs no sanction).  
– Effect on *punishment* treatment?  NO.  Reward is analysed independently; no interaction with punishment is reported.

10. Reward cost  
– Mentioned?  NO.  
– No prediction.

11. Reward magnitude  
– Mentioned?  NO.  
– No prediction.

12. Do players know the final round (time horizon known)?  
– Mentioned?  NO.  
– No prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown each round?  
– Mentioned?  NO.  
– No prediction.

14. Do punished players learn who punished them?  
– Mentioned?  NO.  
– No prediction.

15. Do rewarded players learn who rewarded them?  
– Mentioned?  NO.  
– No prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary

A.  Dependent variables in the paper  
– The *only* dependent variable analysed is “cooperation” (either proportion of cooperative choices or proportion of endowment contributed).  
– **Efficiency (total or mean pay-off ÷ maximum possible)** is never reported, plotted, or analysed.  Thus, all numeric effects relate to cooperation, not efficiency.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
4 of 15:  
(1) Number of players (group size)  
(3) Communication allowed  
(6) MPCR/K-index (degree of conflict)  
(9) Reward enabled  
All other parameters are absent.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss their effect on *the punishment treatment effect* (for any outcome)?  
Zero (0) of the 15.  Punishment is analysed only as a **main effect** (punishment vs. no punishment: d = 0.602 on cooperation).  No moderation by any of the 15 listed parameters is tested or even suggested.

D.  What predictions can be made—based solely on this paper—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on *efficiency*?  
The paper offers almost no leverage.  It never measures efficiency and never studies moderators of the punishment effect.  The only cautious, paper-based expectations one could state are:  
• Punishment (presence vs. absence) tends to raise *cooperation* (d ≈ 0.60); if higher cooperation normally increases efficiency, then efficiency *may* go up.  
• The punishment boost appears larger when the same partners play repeatedly (partner matching), but partner matching is **not** one of the 15 parameters requested.  
Beyond that, the paper provides no data or theory that would let one infer how the 15 listed parameters—or their interactions—shape the impact of punishment on efficiency.  Any further prediction would require evidence outside the scope of this article.

In short, the current paper is largely uninformative for the specific forecasting task centred on *efficiency* and the 15 detailed design parameters of a punishment public-goods game.

Article Title: Exploring cyclic dominance in rock-paper-scissor strategies within the Optional Prisoner's Dilemma: A quantitative analysis with environmental feedback
Author Keywords: Optional Prisoner 's Dilemma; Rock -Paper -Scissor; Cyclic dominance; Environmental feedback
Keywords Plus: COOPERATION; PUNISHMENT; ALLELOPATHY; COMPETITION; DISPERSAL; EVOLUTION; TRAGEDY
Abstract: This research investigation delves into the concept of cyclic dominance and its interplay with environmental feedback within the framework of the Optional Prisoner's Dilemma (OPD) game. A quantitative model has been meticulously constructed to encompass both the OPD and RockPaper-Scissors (RPS) games, wherein the outcomes are contingent upon environmental feedback. The intricate relationship between player populations and their surrounding environment is elucidated through the utilization of replicator dynamics. The empirical findings of this study shed light on the existence of distinct equilibria contingent upon the prevailing environmental circumstances. Under scenarios characterized by resource depletion, an equilibrium state emerges wherein only solitary individuals (referred to as loners) persist. Conversely, under conditions of resource replenishment, an equilibrium is established where various strategic approaches coexist in equal proportions, akin to the dynamics of the Rock-Paper-Scissors game. Notably, cyclic dominance manifests itself during periods characterized by intermediate environmental conditions. Several pivotal factors have been identified as determinants of these dynamic phenomena, including the rate of environmental replenishment, the strength of the dilemma presented, the payoff for loners, and the reward for a draw. It has been empirically demonstrated that the presence of extreme values in the replenishment rate, irrespective of whether exceptionally high or exceptionally low, serves as an impediment to the emergence of cyclic dominance. This model underscores the substantial influence of environmental feedback on social dilemmas, particularly in the context of the OPD game, ultimately leading to the emergence of competitive cyclic dominance games reminiscent of the Rock-Paper-Scissors game. In doing so, it elucidates the intricate interplay between evolutionary game incentives and the dynamics of the surrounding environment.

Below, “punishment treatment effect’’ always means the difference between a punishment condition and the comparable no-punishment baseline.  “Systematically varying’’ means that the paper itself manipulated the parameter or at least compared two clearly different values of it within the same statistical analysis.  Everything that follows is taken verbatim or by direct numerical reading from the Shinada & Yamagishi paper and its figures / tables.

────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER–BY–PARAMETER CHECK
────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – every game is played by three people.  
   • Values?  Exactly 3 in both studies.  
   • Systematic variation?  None.  No prediction about changing group size.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – the game is explicitly “one-shot’’.  
   • Systematic variation?  None.  No prediction.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned?  Not mentioned; subjects were escorted to separate rooms and did not communicate.  
   • Systematic variation?  None.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – subjects could choose “some portion’’ of ¥800; hence NO all-or-nothing rule.  
   • Systematic variation?  None.

5. Contribution default / withdrawal frame?  
   • Not mentioned; the design is the standard “decide how much to give’’ frame.  
   • No variation.

6. Marginal Per-Capita Return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – each ¥1 you give yields ¥1 to each of the other two members; your own MPCR = 0, group MPCR = 2.  
   • No systematic variation; no prediction.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   • Study 1: cost = 0 (experimenter administers penalty).  
   • Study 2: cost = ¥1 paid by punisher reduces target by ¥2.  
   • Systematic variation?  YES – the paper directly compares zero-cost (exogenous) with positive-cost (endogenous) punishment across the two studies, but never in a single regression.  The authors note that the total punishment effect (direct + indirect) is smaller in Study 2 than in Study 1 (compare dark bars in Figs 1 & 2 and coefficients in Tables 1 & 2).  No numeric cross-study test is reported, so no effect size is given for “cost difference’’ per se.

8. Punishment magnitude  
   • Study 1: target loses 50 % of what she kept (max ¥400).  
   • Study 2: magnitude = 2 × (cost chosen by punisher) (max ¥400).  
   • Not manipulated; no prediction about changing magnitude.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • No reward option in either study.  Not discussed.

10–11. Reward cost & magnitude  
   • Irrelevant (see 9).

12. Is the number of rounds known?  
   • Subjects know the game is one-shot.  Not varied; no prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Only after all choices are over.  Not varied.

14. Does a punished player learn who punished them?  
   • Not stated explicitly, but description of feedback (“…by how much their earnings were reduced’’) omits identities; thus identity is concealed.  
   • Not varied.

15. Does a rewarded player learn who rewarded them?  
   • Not applicable (no rewards).

────────────────────────────────────────
DEPENDENT VARIABLES DISCUSSED
────────────────────────────────────────
• Primary: “Level of cooperation’’ = sum of contributions (¥).  
• Also: subjects’ expectation of others’ contributions (post-experimental survey).  
• Efficiency / total or average payoff is NOT used as a dependent variable; only a back-of-the-envelope welfare calculation is provided in § 3.2.2, not analysed statistically.

────────────────────────────────────────
DIRECT STATEMENTS ABOUT SYSTEMATIC VARIATION
────────────────────────────────────────
The ONLY parameter the authors purposely vary is Parameter 7 – “punishment cost / source’’ (exogenous vs. endogenous).  Even here, the comparison is across two separate studies and no formal cross-study statistical test of “cost’’ on the punishment treatment effect is reported.

All other parameters are held constant; therefore the paper makes no predictive or numerical statements about how varying them would change the punishment treatment effect on **any** outcome.

────────────────────────────────────────
NUMERICAL EFFECT SIZES THAT CAN BE READ
────────────────────────────────────────
(Values are in Japanese yen; “Pun–NoPun’’ denotes the treatment effect on contribution.)

Study 1 (zero-cost punishment)  
• Direct-effect condition vs. no-punishment: +¥105.79 (Table 1).  
• Combined-effect condition vs. no-punishment: +¥195.66 (105.79 + 89.87).  
• Indirect component (Combined – Direct): +¥89.87.

Study 2 (costly peer punishment)  
• Direct-effect condition vs. no-punishment: +¥85.91 (Table 2).  
• Combined-effect condition vs. no-punishment: +¥176.64 (85.91 + 90.73).  
• Indirect component: +¥90.73.

Those are the only quantitative “treatment effects’’ reported.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────
A.  Does the paper analyse group efficiency?  
    • No.  Main DV = individual (or group-sum) contribution.  
    • They also report expectations and a descriptive welfare calculation, but never run statistics on efficiency.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
    • Mentioned: 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14.  (9 parameters).  
    • Totally absent: 3, 5, 9–11, 15.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper study their *systematic* effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
    • Exactly ONE parameter (7: punishment cost / endogenous vs. exogenous).  
    • Even here no numeric cross-condition test on efficiency is provided; the only dependent variable tested is contribution.

D.  Predictions one could make for efficiency based only on this paper  
    • (i) Introducing punishment of either type (zero-cost or costly) raises contributions; therefore efficiency should rise unless punishment costs outweigh the extra public-good returns.  
    • (ii) When punishment is costless to the punisher (Parameter 7 = 0) the net contribution increase is larger (+¥195.66 vs. +¥176.64) and no resources are burned by punishers, so efficiency gains should be higher.  
    • (iii) Adding an “indirect-effect’’ channel (i.e., letting all players face punishment instead of only one) raises contributions by roughly ¥90 per player, regardless of whether punishment is costly or not (Parameters 7 & 8), so efficiency should increase further in the combined-effect setting.  
    • Beyond these three very narrow points, the paper provides no basis for predicting how any of the other 14 parameters, singly or in interaction, would influence the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.

Abstract: Social situations may vary in the severity of conflict between self-interest and collective welfare, and thereby pose collective action problems that might require different institutional solutions. The present study examines the effect of conflict of interests on beliefs, norms, cooperation, and choice of sanctioning institutions in social dilemmas across two experiments (total N =1304). In each experiment, participants interacted in a public goods game (PGG), and a modified PGG with institutional choice using a 2 (conflict of interests: low vs. high) x 3 (institutional choice: peer punishment/no sanction vs. centralized punishment/no sanction vs. gossip plus ostracism/no sanction) between-participants design. This pattern is pronounced over time in repeated interactions. We did not find that conflict of interests influenced the choice to establish a sanctioning institution. Taken together, the challenges arising from stronger conflicting interests can cause the collapse of cooperation, hinder the emergence of trust and norms of cooperation, but do not provide the impetus to support a sanctioning institution to promote cooperation.  • Normative expectations (second-order beliefs)

 • Group success in establishing an institution

Article Title: Why punish cheaters? Those who withdraw cooperation enjoy better reputations than punishers, but both are viewed as difficult to exploit
Author Keywords: Negative sanction; Punishment; Conditional cooperation; Reputation; Partner choice
Keywords Plus: 3RD-PARTY PUNISHMENT; STRONG RECIPROCITY; EVOLUTION; GENEROSITY; MEMORY
Abstract: Negatively sanctioning cheaters promotes cooperation. But do all negative sanctions have the same conse-quences? In dyadic cooperation, there are two ways that cooperators can sanction failures to reciprocate: by inflicting punishment or withdrawing cooperation. Although punishment can be costly, it has been proposed that this cost can be recouped if punishers acquire better reputations than non-punishers and, therefore, are favored as cooperation partners. But the evidence so far is mixed, and nothing is known about the reputations of those who sanction by withdrawing cooperation. Here, we test two novel hypotheses about how inflicting negative sanctions affects the reputation of the sanctioner: (i) Those who withdraw cooperation are evaluated more favorably than punishers, and (ii) both sanctioners are viewed as less exploitable than non-sanctioners. Sanctioners were also viewed as more difficult to exploit than non-sanctioners, with no difference between punishers and withdrawers. The results were the same when punishment was costly (US college sample, n = 203) with one exception: Costly punishers, who lost their payoffs by punishing, were viewed as more exploitable than withdrawers. Our results indicate that withdrawing coop-eration has advantages over punishing: Withdrawers are favored as cooperative partners while gaining a repu-tation as difficult to exploit. The reputational consequences of the three responses to defectors-punishing, withdrawing cooperation, and not sanctioning at all-were opposite to those predicted by group selection models.

────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
────────────────────────────────────────

1.  Number of players  
    (1) Mentioned: yes – always exactly two players (a duopoly, p. 3 & §4).  
    (2) No systematic variation; no prediction about how changing the group size would alter any punishment effect.

2.  Number of rounds  
    (1) Discussed: the game is *indefinitely repeated* with a continuation probability δ = 0.9 (p. 14).  Subjects do not know when it will end.  
    (2) Not varied; no prediction about round length and no link to punishment.

3.  Chat enabled?  
    (1) Not mentioned; there is no chat facility.  
    (2) Therefore no prediction.

4.  “All-or-nothing” contributions?  
    (1) Stage game offers just two discrete actions, L (cooperative low output) or H (non-cooperative high output) (Table on p. 11).  That is equivalent to an all-or-nothing contribution structure.  
    (2) The binary nature is fixed; no statement on varying the action space, let alone on punishment.

5.  Contribution default / “take” framing  
    (1) Not applicable; paper contains no default or “take-back” option.  
    (2) No prediction.

6.  Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
    (1) Not framed as a public-goods MPCR.  The PD payoff matrix is fixed (25,25; 15,28; 28,15; 16,16).  
    (2) Not varied; no prediction about altering that factor nor about punishment.

7.  Punishment cost to the punisher  
8.  Punishment magnitude inflicted  
9.  Whether a reward option exists  
10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
    (1) None of these appear anywhere in the experiment.  There is *no* peer-punishment or peer-reward stage.  
    (2) Consequently the paper gives zero information on how changing any of these five parameters would affect a punishment treatment.  Numerical effect sizes: none.

12.  Do subjects know the number of rounds?  
    (1) They know only the *continuation probability* (0.1 stopping chance) but never the realized end point (p. 14).  
    (2) That feature is not varied; no prediction relating it to punishment.

13.  Are peer outcomes shown each round?  
    (1) Subjects observe the same public signal z after every period; they do *not* observe the opponent’s action (unless β = 0, the perfect-monitoring treatment) and see their own accumulated payoff only at the end of a “cycle” (p. 14).  
    (2) Visibility of peer outcomes is held constant; no punishment-effect statement.

14.  Does a punished player learn the identity of the punisher?  
15.  Does a rewarded player learn the identity of the rewarder?  
    (1) No punishment or reward ever occurs, so these two information parameters are irrelevant to the paper.  
    (2) No discussion, no prediction.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────
A.  Dependent variables  
    – The *main* dependent variable is the *normalized average group payoff*  \bar{y}(β)  (actual average payoff minus Nash-equilibrium payoff, divided by the cooperative-surplus), shown in Table 2 and Fig. 2.  The paper labels this a measure of “cooperation” but it is numerically identical to *efficiency* as defined in the user prompt (actual total payoff divided by a maximum).  
    – Secondary variables: rate of the cooperative action L, rate of the efficient profile (L,L), period-1 cooperation rate.  These are distinct from efficiency because they do not include monetary penalties or cost/benefit ratios.

B.  Which parameters from the list are even mentioned?  
    Five:  
      1 (players = 2),  
      2 (indefinite rounds, δ = 0.9),  
      3 (no chat),  
      4 (binary/all-or-nothing actions),  
      12 (unknown horizon).

D.  If one had to predict how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would change the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency *using only this paper*, almost nothing can be said.  The study tells us:

    • Efficiency falls as the exogenous *noise* parameter β rises, even without any punishment stage.  
    • All other listed parameters were either fixed or not present.  
Hence, based purely on this source, the safest forecast is “insufficient information” for 14 of the 15 parameters.  The lone factual piece is that in a two-player indefinitely repeated PD without punishment, efficiency was lower when monitoring was noisier; whether adding punishment would amplify or mute that pattern is not addressed.

1. NUMBER OF PLAYERS  
(1) Mentioned: Yes. Groups of n = 5.  
(2) Systematic variation: No. All treatments use five players; no prediction or estimate for other group sizes.

2. NUMBER OF ROUNDS  
(1) Mentioned: Yes.  
• Stage-1 (VCM): 10 rounds in all sessions.  
• Stage-2 (with punishment): 10 rounds in the “Single-selection’’ treatments and 12 rounds in the “Multiple-selection’’ treatments.  
(2) Systematic variation: Partly. The Single vs. Multiple comparison incidentally changes the total number of punishment rounds from 10 to 12.  
Effect on punishment-treatment effect (contribution difference, Table 3-A, column “Single-Multiple’’):  
 Leviathan: +0.264 points (s.e. 0.772, p = 0.961)  
 Democracy: +1.114 points (s.e. 0.870, p = 0.195)  
So, within this narrow 10-vs-12 range the paper finds **no statistically significant impact**. No efficiency numbers are reported.

3. CHAT ENABLED?  
(1) Mentioned: No. There is no chat facility.  
(2) No discussion or prediction.

4. ALL-OR-NOTHING CONTRIBUTION?  
(1) Mentioned: Yes, implicitly. A “linear VCM’’ with a 0–20 continuous choice; therefore *not* all-or-nothing.  
(2) No variation, no prediction.

5. CONTRIBUTION DEFAULT / REFUND FRAME?  
(1) Not mentioned. Standard give-to-public-account frame is used.  
(2) No discussion.

6. MPCR / MULTIPLICATION FACTOR  
(1) Mentioned: Yes. Multiplier m = 2, MPCR = 0.4.  
(2) Held constant; no prediction about other values.

7. PUNISHMENT COST TO IMPOSE ONE UNIT  
(1) Mentioned: Yes. One management-pool point must be *assigned* for each punishment unit; those points are taken from a communal tax pool, not from the manager’s personal payoff.  
(2) No variation; no prediction.

8. PUNISHMENT MAGNITUDE  
(1) Mentioned: Yes. Convex mapping (Table in design): e.g., 1 assigned → 1 reduced, …, 10 assigned → 30 reduced.  
(2) Held constant; no prediction.

9. REWARD ENABLED  
(1) Not present in the design.  
(2) No discussion.

10. REWARD COST  
Not applicable.

11. REWARD MAGNITUDE  
Not applicable.

12. IS THE HORIZON KNOWN?  
(1) Mentioned: Yes. Subjects know the exact number of rounds in each stage (10 or 12).  
(2) Horizon length is not manipulated beyond the 10-vs-12 noted above; no separate prediction.

13. ARE PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN?  
(1) Mentioned: Yes. After every round all players see every participant’s contribution and profit, anonymously.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction.

14. IS THE PUNISHER IDENTIFIED?  
(1) Mentioned: Yes. Only the *total* punishment points used are revealed; victims do *not* learn who punished them.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction.

15. IS THE REWARDER IDENTIFIED?  
Not applicable (no rewards).

───────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used  
• Contributions to the public good  
• Several punishment metrics (probability of being punished; points assigned)  
• Profit (individual payoff after punishment)  
“Efficiency’’ (total payoff ÷ social optimum) is *never* reported.

B. Parameters mentioned (9 of 15)  
1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14.

C. Parameters whose *systematic variation* is analysed for their impact on the punishment-treatment effect (1 of 15)  
Only parameter 2 (number of rounds, via the Single-vs-Multiple condition). Even here the paper finds no significant effect, and no efficiency statistic is provided.

D. What can we predict—based solely on this paper—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions affect the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency?  
Very little. The study keeps every listed parameter except (trivially) the number of rounds fixed, therefore offers no direct evidence on how varying them would alter efficiency. The only actionable clue is that raising the punishment stage length from 10 to 12 rounds (accompanied by repeated elections) did *not* change the contribution-based punishment effect in a detectable way. For all other parameters the paper is silent, so any efficiency prediction would be speculative beyond the paper’s content.

Below each of the 15 parameters is treated in exactly the same way:

• “Mentioned?” = Does the paper contain the parameter (or an unambiguous equivalent) anywhere in the text, figures or tables?  
• “Systematically varied & linked to the punishment-treatment effect?” = Does the paper change that parameter over two or more values **and** report how the *difference* between a Punishment condition (γ > 0) and a Baseline condition (γ = 0) moves as the parameter is changed?  
Whenever a quantitative value can be read directly from a figure or equation it is reproduced; otherwise “n.s.” (not stated) is used.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   Mentioned? Yes.  The notation N is used throughout (e.g. N = 2 and N = 1024 are plotted).  
   Systematically varied & linked? No.  Formulas are written for any N, but the paper never shows how changing N alters the *difference* between γ > 0 and γ = 0 in any outcome.  

2. Number of rounds  
   Mentioned? No.  Only one-shot games plus Monte-Carlo steps for thermalisation are modelled.  
   Systematically varied & linked? No.  

3. Chat enabled?  
   Mentioned? No.  
   Systematically varied & linked? No.  

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
   Mentioned? Yes (each player either pays cost c or 0).  The parameter is fixed; it is never varied.  
   Systematically varied & linked? No.  

5. Contribution default (refund from the public fund)  
   Mentioned? No.  
   Systematically varied & linked? No.  

6. Marginal Per-Capita Return / multiplication factor (b)  
   Mentioned? Yes (symbol b).  Examples: b = 1 in most plots, and inequalities such as b > 2c.  
   Systematically varied & linked? Partly.  Eq. (21) shows β* = ln 2 / (2c − b); increasing b therefore lowers β* at which the punishment and no-punishment cooperation curves cross.  However the paper never translates that into a treatment effect on *efficiency*, only on cooperation density 〈n〉.  No numerical effect size on efficiency is provided.  

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   Mentioned? No—the model assumes punishment is cost-free for the punisher.  
   Systematically varied & linked? No.  

8. Punishment magnitude (γ)  
   Mentioned? Yes.  γ = 0 (baseline) vs γ = 1 and intermediate values are analysed.  
   Systematically varied & linked? Yes, for the dependent variable “average cooperation density 〈n〉”.  
   • Fig. 2a (b = 1, c = 0.3): at β = 3, 〈n〉(γ = 0) ≈ 0.33; 〈n〉(γ = 1) ≈ 0.97 → treatment effect on 〈n〉 ≈ +0.64.  
   • Fig. 2b (b = 1, c = 0.75): at β = 0.5, punishment raises 〈n〉; at β = 2 it lowers 〈n〉.  The crossing occurs at β* = 1.386 (Eq. 21).  
   For *payoff/efficiency* the only explicit statement is Eq. (11): average payoff change δ ε ≈ −γ b 〈n〉(1−〈n〉).  It implies any positive γ always *reduces* total payoffs, but no numerical magnitudes are given.  

9. Reward enabled?  
   Mentioned? No.  
   Systematically varied & linked? No.  

10. Reward cost  
    Mentioned? No.  

11. Reward magnitude  
    Mentioned? No.  

12. Finite/known horizon  
    Mentioned? No.  One-shot only.  

13. Peer outcome visibility  
    Mentioned? No.  

14. Punisher identity revealed  
    Mentioned? No.  

15. Rewarder identity revealed  
    Mentioned? No.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
   – Group efficiency / total or average payoff: referenced but **not used as an outcome variable**.  The paper does give analytical expressions for payoff (e.g. Eq. 11) but all figures and almost all text focus on “cooperation density” 〈n〉 and its variance.  
   – 〈n〉 (average fraction of cooperators) is the principal dependent variable.  
   – Fluctuation of 〈n〉 (variance) is also plotted (Fig. 5).  
   – These variables are distinct from efficiency; the paper notes that punishment lowers payoffs even while raising 〈n〉.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   Parameters 1, 4, 6 and 8 are mentioned (4 of 15).  The remaining 11 are absent.

C. For which parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* that parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
   One parameter: 8 (punishment magnitude γ).  
   – Effect reported on cooperation density 〈n〉 (see Fig. 2, Eq. 21).  
   – No parameter is linked to the treatment effect on efficiency.

D. Predicting punishment-treatment effects on efficiency using only this paper  
   • Because the model assumes punishment carries no cost for the punisher but always deducts γ b tokens from the *defector’s* share, Eq. (11) implies a negative direct effect on total payoffs (hence on efficiency) of size −γ b 〈n〉(1−〈n〉).  
   • At the same time γ can raise 〈n〉; whether net efficiency rises or falls therefore depends on the relative magnitudes of (i) the payoff loss term and (ii) the gain from more cooperation (which the paper never quantifies).  
   • No other of the 15 parameters is modelled in a way that allows a prediction about efficiency once punishment is introduced.  
   Consequently, beyond stating that “introducing punishment (γ > 0) always subtracts γ b 〈n〉(1−〈n〉) from total earnings while it may or may not raise 〈n〉”, the paper provides **too little information to make confident efficiency predictions as any of the 15 parameters are varied.**

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players

2. Number of rounds  
   • Discussed? Yes – 30 rounds (10 in Part 1, 20 in Part 2).  
   • Prediction under variation? None.

3. Chat allowed?  
   • Discussed? Implicitly – there is no mention of any communication channel and the software (z-Tree) did not allow chat.  
   • Prediction under variation? None.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution?  
   • Discussed? Yes – subjects choose any integer 0–20; hence NOT all-or-nothing.  
   • Prediction under variation? None.

5. Contribution default (Give vs Take frame)  
   • Discussed? Yes – this is the core manipulation.  
     – Give: move tokens from private to group fund.  
     – Take: move tokens from group to private fund (i.e. the “default” is that the tokens are in the public fund).  
   • Systematic-variation prediction? Yes.  The frame decisively alters the punishment treatment effect.  
     Dependent variables and numeric effect sizes that can be read directly from tables:  

       CONTRIBUTIONS (Table 2)  
       – Give-Pun – Give = +21.20 tokens per round (sd 19.34)  
       – Take-Pun – Take = +39.07 tokens per round (sd 14.00)  

       EARNINGS / EFFICIENCY (Table 5 & 6)  
       – Give-Pun – Give = +4.41 tokens per round (sd 30.29)  → not statistically significant.  
       – Take-Pun – Take = +25.30 tokens per round (sd 23.37) → statistically significant (Wald p = 0.0005).  

       In words: introducing punishment raises efficiency in the Take frame but not in the Give frame, and it raises contributions in both, with the gain almost twice as large in the Take frame.  

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Discussed? Yes – constant a = 0.5.  
   • Prediction under variation? None.

7. Punishment cost to punisher  
   • Discussed? Yes – 1 token cost per punishment point.  The theory section gives a threshold  \(c<\tilde c\)  for punishment to be individually rational, but the experiment never varies c, and no efficiency predictions are offered for different c’s.  

8. Punishment magnitude (damage to target)  
   • Discussed? Yes – every point sent reduces the target’s payoff by 3 tokens.  
   • Prediction under variation? None.

9. Reward institution present?  
   • Discussed? No – rewards are never available.  No prediction.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   • Both n/a.

12. Is the horizon known?  
   • Discussed? Yes – subjects were told the exact number of rounds in each part (Sec 2.3).  
   • Prediction under variation? None.

13. Are peer outcomes displayed?  
   • Discussed? Yes – after each round subjects saw every group-member’s contribution (in descending order) and own profit components (Sec 2.3).  
   • Prediction under variation? None.

14. Do punished players learn who punished them?  
   • Discussed? Yes – they do NOT; only the total punishment received is shown (Sec 2.3).  
   • Prediction under variation? None.

15. Do rewarded players learn who rewarded them?  
   • n/a – no rewards.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used  
   • Group contributions (tokens left in / put into the public fund).  
   • Punishment behaviour (frequency & amount).  
   • Group earnings = total monetary payoff after subtracting punishment costs.  This is the paper’s measure of efficiency.  Contributions and earnings are distinct: raising contributions need not raise earnings once punishment costs are counted.

Below I go through the 15 design parameters one‐by-one and report exactly what the Matsuzawa & Tanimoto paper says about each of them and, if applicable, what it says about how *systematically varying* that parameter changes the *punishment treatment effect*.  
(The authors always compare runs *with jealous punishment* to a “default” in which no punishment is allowed, so their graphs already represent a punishment-vs-no-punishment contrast.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned: Yes. They fix N = 10 000 agents for every simulation.  
   • Systematically varied? No. All results use the same N, so the paper makes no prediction about how changing N would modify the punishment treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Not reported. Simulations run “until the global cooperation fraction attains equilibrium”; no finite horizon is set or varied. No predictions.

3. Is chat enabled?  
   • Not mentioned. No predictions.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Not applicable; the study uses a two-action Prisoner’s Dilemma, not a continuous public-goods decision. No predictions.

5. Contribution default rule?  
   • Not applicable. No predictions.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Not used. The authors do vary the PD payoff parameters \(D_g\) and \(D_r\), but these are not MPCR-type public-goods parameters. No predictions relevant to MPCR.

7. Punishment *cost* (cost to impose one unit)  
   • Model component: the cost coefficient \(c_s\).  
   • Systematic variation: Indirectly, yes. They vary the *efficiency ratio* \(\beta=p/c_s\) (Fig. 5). Changing \(\beta\) while holding the penalty \(p\) constant necessarily changes \(c_s\).  
   • Reported effects (dependent variable = cooperation fraction \(P_c\))  
     – Lattice network: Higher efficiency (i.e., lower cost per unit penalty) → higher \(P_c\) (upper-left to lower-right gradient in Fig. 5A).  
     – BA scale-free network: *Lower* efficiency (higher cost) → higher \(P_c\) when \(p\) is already large (inverse gradient in Fig. 5B).  
   • Numerical effect size: Only visible as colour heat-maps; no exact coefficients are given, so magnitudes cannot be extracted.

8. Punishment *magnitude* (fine inflicted per unit purchased)  
   • Model component: the penalty coefficient \(p\).  
   • Systematic variation: Yes (Fig. 1 and Fig. 5 vary \(p\) from 0 up to ≈0.4).  
   • Effects: In both lattice and BA-SF networks, larger \(p\) (with \(\beta\) fixed at 1) strongly raises cooperation relative to the no-punishment baseline.  
     For example, on the lattice with \(D_g\!=\!0.7, D_r\!=\!0\) and \(\beta\!=\!1\) (Fig. 1A), increasing \(p\) from 0 to 0.4 moves average \(P_c\) from ≈0.08 to ≈0.55. (Visual estimate from the graph.)

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Not in the model. No predictions.

10. Reward cost  
    • Not in the model. No predictions.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Not in the model. No predictions.

12. Whether the number of rounds is known  
    • Not discussed. Infinite-horizon evolutionary updating is assumed. No predictions.

13. Whether peer outcomes are shown  
    • Not discussed. No predictions.

14. Whether the punished player sees who punished them  
    • Not discussed. No predictions.

15. Whether the rewarded player sees who rewarded them  
    • Not discussed. No predictions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used  
   – The study’s *main* dependent variable is the cooperation fraction \(P_c\) (percentage of agents playing “C”).  
   – “Total social payoff” or “efficiency” is mentioned qualitatively (e.g., heavy sanctions “inevitably suppress the total social payoff”), but it is *not* measured, plotted, or statistically analysed.  
   – Therefore, all quantitative results concern cooperation rates, not group efficiency.

B. Parameters *mentioned* in the paper  
   – 3 of the 15:  
     1. Number of players (fixed),  
     7. Punishment cost (embedded in \(\beta\)),  
     8. Punishment magnitude \(p\).

C. Parameters whose *systematic variation* is analysed with respect to the punishment treatment effect  
   – 2 of the 15: parameters 7 and 8.  
   – Both are varied jointly (Fig. 5) and individually (Fig. 1). The effect is reported only on cooperation, not on efficiency.

D. What can we predict—*solely from this paper*—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions will influence the punishment treatment effect on *efficiency*?  
   – Very little, because the paper does not measure efficiency. One can only infer indirectly:  
     • Larger penalties \(p\) and (on lattices) higher efficiency ratios \(\beta\) boost cooperation, which *might* raise efficiency if punishment costs are not too high.  
     • The authors caution that, especially on heterogeneous networks, heavy sanctions continue even in all-cooperator states and therefore *reduce* total payoff despite high cooperation.  
   – Consequently, the safest prediction from the paper is:  
     • “Increasing punishment magnitude \(p\) increases the punishment treatment effect on cooperation, but its effect on efficiency is ambiguous and may be negative when sanction costs are large.”  
     • “Changing the cost-to-fine ratio \(\beta\) has opposite effects in homogeneous (lattice) vs. heterogeneous (scale-free) networks, and the net impact on efficiency is not reported.”  
   – For the other 13 parameters the paper provides no information, so no prediction can be made.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
In short, the article gives detailed insights into how *punishment magnitude* and *cost-to-fine efficiency* shape cooperation, but it does not provide quantitative evidence on how any of the 15 listed design parameters, individually or in combination, affect the *efficiency* of a punishment treatment.

Abstract: Groups of individuals have social networks that structure interactions within the groups; evolutionary theory increasingly uses this fact to explain the emergence of cooperation (Eshel and Cavalli-Sforza, 1982; Boyd and Richerson, 1988, 1989; Ohtsuki et al., 2006; Nowak et al., 2010; Van Veelen et al., 2012). This approach has resulted in a number of important insights for the evolution of cooperation in the biological and social sciences, but omits a key function of social networks that has persisted throughout recent evolutionary history (Apicella et al., 2012): their role in transmitting gossip about behavior within a group. Accounting for this well-established role of social networks among rational agents in a setting of indirect reciprocity not only shows a new mechanism by which the structure of networks is fitness relevant, but also reveals that knowledge of social networks can be fitness-relevant as well. When groups enforce cooperation by sanctioning peers whom gossip reveals to have deviated, individuals in certain peripheral network positions are tempting targets of uncooperative behavior because gossip they share about misbehavior spreads slowly through the network. The ability to identify these individuals creates incentives to behave uncooperatively. Consequently, groups comprised of individuals who knew precise information about their social networks would be at a fitness disadvantage relative to groups of individuals with a coarser knowledge of their networks. Empirical work has consistently shown that modern humans know little about the structure of their own social networks and perform poorly when tasked with learning new ones. This robust empirical regularity may be the product of natural selection in an environment of strong selective pressure at the group level. Imprecise views of networks make enforcing cooperation easier. (C) 2016 Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved.

Below I go through the 15 design parameters one‐by‐one, reporting exactly what the paper says (or does not say) about each parameter and, when possible, whether the author derives a comparative-static prediction about *systematically varying* that parameter on the **punishment treatment effect**.  “Punishment treatment effect’’ is interpreted as “how easily punishment can sustain full cooperation (and therefore full group payoff / efficiency)’’ because the paper’s only outcome of interest is whether the in-group-policing strategy profile σ^NWIGP can support *full cooperation* in equilibrium.

------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Number of players  
    • Mentioned?  YES – denoted n.  
    • Value?  Variable, no specific numeric value fixed.  
    • Comparative-static prediction?  YES.  In Propositions 1–3 the critical discount factor that must be exceeded for punishment to sustain cooperation is proportional to (n-1).  Holding everything else constant, a larger n raises the right-hand-side of the incentive constraints, so a *larger group makes cooperation harder*, i.e. lowers the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

2.  Number of rounds  
    • Mentioned?  Indirectly.  The stage game is infinitely repeated; the author also introduces T, “the number of rounds an offender must suffer punishment”.  
    • Comparative-static prediction?  YES for T.  All incentive constraints contain δ^T.  Because δ∈(0,1), δ^T falls as T rises.  Therefore a longer punishment window (larger T) *tightens* the incentive constraint and makes cooperation harder to sustain.

3.  Chat enabled?  
    • Mentioned?  NO.  No direct mention of free-form chat among players.

4.  All-or-nothing contribution choice?  
    • Mentioned?  NO.  The paper analyses a binary Prisoner’s Dilemma (c vs d), not a continuous contribution PG game.

5.  Contribution default / give-to-self mechanism?  
    • Mentioned?  NO.

6.  MPCR / multiplication factor  
    • Mentioned?  NO.  The model does not contain a Voluntary Contribution Mechanism; payoffs are parametrised by α and β instead.

7.  Punishment cost to the punisher  
    • Mentioned?  PARTIALLY.  When a punisher plays d against an offender’s forced c, the punisher earns the payoff α (>1).  Because α>1, punishment is *not costly* to the punisher in this model (it is profitable).  No systematic comparative statics on varying α relative to the efficiency effect are provided except that all incentive constraints tighten as (α–1) grows (Propositions 1–2).

8.  Punishment magnitude for the target  
    • Mentioned?  YES – parameter β (>0) is the loss suffered by the punished player when the punisher plays d and the punished plays c.  
    • Comparative-static prediction?  YES.  In the incentive constraints the numerator contains β.  A larger β makes punishment more severe and therefore *easier* to sustain cooperation (i.e. raises the punishment treatment effect).

9.  Reward enabled?  
    • Mentioned?  NO.  The model has no rewarding stage.

10. Reward cost  
    • Mentioned?  NO.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Mentioned?  NO.

12. Horizon known?  
    • Mentioned?  Not directly.  The game is infinite with discounting, so the horizon is effectively indefinite; there is no discussion of subjects knowing a final round.  No comparative statics.

13. Peer outcomes displayed?  
    • Mentioned?  YES, but in the form of *gossip* that diffuses through the social network at speed r.  Players do *not* automatically see payoffs; they only learn what is communicated by others.  Comparative statics: the model uses the parameter r (degrees per period).  A higher r means gossip spreads faster and increases the size of the set K_{i,j,t,T}; this *loosens* the incentive constraint and therefore increases the punishment treatment effect.  The paper states this verbally; no numeric derivative is given.

14. Punisher identity revealed?  
    • Mentioned?  NO.  The model abstracts from identifying who delivered a sanction; only the act d vs c matters.

15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
    • Mentioned?  NO (and rewards are absent).

------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables  
    • The paper’s only real outcome is whether *full cooperation* can be supported in equilibrium.  “Total value experienced by the group” is monotonic in the number of cooperators and is interpreted as *group fitness*, but the paper never reports or analyses *group efficiency ratios* numerically.  No other dependent variables (e.g., contribution level, cooperation rate) are studied.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
    Parameters 1, 2 (via T), 7, 8, 13 are mentioned or have close analogues in the model (5 of 15).

C.  For how many parameters is a systematic effect on punishment derived?  
    • Number of players n – YES  
    • Punishment window T – YES  
    • Punishment cost/benefit α – partially (appears in constraints)  
    • Punishment magnitude β – YES  
    • Gossip-spread speed r – YES  
    → 5 parameters receive at least qualitative comparative-static treatment.

D.  What predictions can be made about the punishment treatment effect on *efficiency* using only the paper?  
    • Larger groups (higher n) → punishment becomes a weaker enforcement device; efficiency falls relative to smaller groups.  
    • Longer required punishment window T → harder to enforce cooperation; efficiency falls.  
    • Larger punishment benefit to punisher (α) and/or larger punishment loss to target (β) → punishment more effective; efficiency rises.  
    • Faster gossip diffusion (higher r) or larger average T-neighbourhood size (denser network) → punishment more effective; efficiency rises.  
    • Limited network knowledge (COARSE) vs precise knowledge (PRECISE) → for a given network structure, limited knowledge *increases* the punishment treatment effect by lowering the minimal discount factor needed for full cooperation.  
    • For the remaining ten parameters (chat, MPCR, rewards, anonymity of punishers/rewarders, etc.) the paper is silent, so no prediction can be made from this source alone.

Hence, using only this paper, one can confidently predict the direction of the punishment treatment effect for 5 of the 15 parameters; for the other 10 parameters the paper provides no information.

Authors: Arai, S; Tooby, J; Cosmides, L
Author Full Names: Arai, Sakura; Tooby, John; Cosmides, Leda
Article Title: Motivations to reciprocate cooperation and punish defection are calibrated by estimates of how easily others can switch partners
Keywords Plus: COMPETITIVE ALTRUISM; RELATIONAL MOBILITY; EVOLUTION; CHOICE; REPUTATION; TRUSTWORTHINESS; GENEROSITY; MECHANISMS; STRATEGIES; FAIRNESS
Abstract: Evolutionary models of dyadic cooperation demonstrate that selection favors different strategies for reciprocity depending on opportunities to choose alternative partners. We propose that selection has favored mechanisms that estimate the extent to which others can switch partners and calibrate motivations to reciprocate and punish accordingly. These estimates should reflect default assumptions about relational mobility: the probability that individuals in one's social world will have the opportunity to form relationships with new partners. This prior probability can be updated by cues present in the immediate situation one is facing. The resulting estimate of a partner's outside options should serve as input to motivational systems regulating reciprocity: Higher estimates should down-regulate the use of sanctions to prevent defection by a current partner, and up-regulate efforts to attract better cooperative partners by curating one's own reputation and monitoring that of others. We tested this hypothesis using a Trust Game with Punishment (TGP), which provides continuous measures of reciprocity, defection, and punishment in response to defection. We measured each participant's perception of relational mobility in their real-world social ecology and experimentally varied a cue to partner switching. Moreover, the study was conducted in the US (n = 519) and Japan (n = 520): societies that are high versus low in relational mobility. Across conditions and societies, higher perceptions of relational mobility were associated with increased reciprocity and decreased punishment: i.e., those who thought that others have many opportunities to find new partners reciprocated more and punished less. The situational cue to partner switching was detected, but relational mobility in one's real social world regulated motivations to reciprocate and punish, even in the experimental setting. The current research provides evidence that motivational systems are designed to estimate varying degrees of partner choice in one's social ecology and regulate reciprocal behaviors accordingly.

Abstract: Groupware is an effective form of media for knowledge sharing and active open communication. One remaining important issue is how to design groupware in which vast amounts of beneficial content are provided and active discussion is facilitated. The behavior of information in such a medium resembles public-goods games because users voluntarily post beneficial information that creates media values. Many studies on such games have shown the effects of rewards or punishments in promoting cooperative behavior. In this paper we show what types of incentive systems of rewards and punishments promote and maintain effective information behaviors or cooperative regimes in actual groupware. Our agent-based simulation demonstrates that a meta-reward system in which rewarders can gain other benefits for their own reward actions will probably encourage cooperation. Counterintuitively, our simulation also demonstrates that a system that applies sanctioning functions does not necessarily promote cooperation. Interestingly a first-order reward system-without any second-order incentives impedes the formation of cooperative regimes while this is not the case with first-order punishment systems without second-order incentives. These findings may elucidate how successful groupware operates.

The paper does not present an explicit efficiency calculation, but it does note “efficiency gains” in the sense that, in the lab, the (known) possibility of negative feedback led to more equitable offers. SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?

Where “efficiency” is mentioned, it is more a narrative comment about how higher offers or fewer rejections may lead to “efficiency gains,” but that is not tabulated in detail.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Of the 15 listed parameters for a public goods context, essentially only parameter (3) “Is chat enabled (i.e., is any form of feedback/communication present)?” is directly relevant in this paper’s design. Feedback is either absent (CONTROL) or present (KNOWN/UNKNOWN). No other parameters on the list are systematically discussed or manipulated.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?

Instead, non‐monetary negative feedback is possible in some treatments (KNOWN, UNKNOWN). The paper finds that, in the lab, if proposers know feedback is possible (KNOWN), they increase their offers; online, this knowledge has no effect. Numerically, in the lab, mean offers rise from roughly US$3.65 (out of US$10) to US$4.41 when feedback is known to be possible.

• The paper does not investigate multi‐player public goods, nor does it address varying costs or magnitudes of monetary punishment/reward, so almost no direct predictions can be made for the majority of the 15 parameters.

Authors: Wang, RY; Ng, CN
Author Full Names: Wang, Raymond Yu; Ng, Cho Nam
Article Title: Can Centralized Sanctioning Promote Trust in Social Dilemmas? A Two-Level Trust Game with Incomplete Information
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; POLITICAL TRUST; COOPERATION; RECIPROCITY; GOVERNANCE
Abstract: The problem of trust is a paradigmatic social dilemma. Previous literature has paid much academic attention on effects of peer punishment and altruistic third-party punishment on trust and human cooperation in dyadic interactions. However, the effects of centralized sanctioning institutions on decentralized reciprocity in hierarchical interactions remain to be further explored. This paper presents a formal two-level trust game with incomplete information which adds an authority as a strategic purposive actor into the traditional trust game. This model allows scholars to examine the problem of trust in more complex game theoretic configurations. The analysis demonstrates how the centralized institutions might change the dynamics of reciprocity between the trustor and the trustee. Findings suggest that the sequential equilibria of the newly proposed two-level model simultaneously include the risk of placing trust for the trustor and the temptation of short-term defection for the trustee. Moreover, they have shown that even a slight uncertainty about the type of the newly introduced authority might facilitate the establishment of trust and reciprocity in social dilemmas.

For each of the 15 parameters, I indicate whether the paper (1) discusses it (and, if so, what the paper says about its value) and (2) makes predictions about systematically varying it and how that might affect a “punishment treatment effect” on any dependent variable. 2. Number of rounds
   • Discussion: The paper studies a finitely repeated trust game (played for two periods in its formal analysis). The fact that there are two rounds is used to illustrate “end-game” effects.  
   • Systematic Variation or Effect on Punishment Treatment: The authors do not systematically vary the number of rounds (e.g., 2 vs. 5 vs. 10, etc.) and provide no quantitative or qualitative effect sizes about how changes in the number of rounds might alter punishment’s impact on any dependent variable.

   • Discussion: Not mentioned at all; there is no discussion of a default contribution or moving funds in or out.

   • Discussion: The paper does not mention an MPCR; the payoffs (R1, S1, T2, etc.) are from the trust game structure, not a public goods game.  
   • Systematic Variation or Effect on Punishment Treatment: Not addressed.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussion: The paper models a “punishment cost” C3 that the authority must bear to punish a trustee. This is part of the authority’s payoff functions.
