   • Discussion: Denoted ψ (psi), which reduces the trustee’s payoff from T2 to T2 – ψ if punished. ψ appears in several key inequalities.  
   • Systematic Variation or Effect on Punishment Treatment: The paper shows qualitatively that if ψ is larger, a B-type trustee is more inclined to honor trust (to avoid punishment), but it does not provide a numerical, systematically varied effect size or direct statements about how that transforms any “punishment effect” on group‐level measures (e.g., efficiency).  

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussion: The paper does not introduce a mechanism by which any player can reward others. The only mention of “reward” is R3, which is simply the authority’s own payoff received if trust is placed and honored.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)

    • Discussion: Yes. The paper states the game is finitely repeated (two rounds), and all players know the total number of rounds.

    • Discussion: The exposition does not mention displaying outcomes to all peers. It does note that each player observes whether trust was abused or honored (since that is part of the game structure and payoff), but there is no reference to systematically displaying payoff outcomes.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Discussion: By definition, only the authority punishes in the two-level trust game, and the trustee presumably knows if they have been punished. However, the paper does not discuss systematically varying whether the punisher’s identity is revealed.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Discussion: Not applicable, since the paper does not include a reward mechanism from others.

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?

   • The paper does not use the term “group efficiency” as “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff.” Instead, it analyzes:  
     – Trust (the probability that the trustor places trust),  
     – Reciprocity (the probability that the trustee honors trust),  
     – and how an authority’s centralized sanctioning or type (G or B) influences those behaviors in equilibrium.  
   • The paper sometimes references “group utilities” or scenarios that yield “the highest group utilities,” but it never defines or measures “efficiency” in the sense of a ratio (total payoff / maximum possible payoff).  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

   • Mentioned explicitly in the setup:  
     1. Number of players (3 players in the two-level game).  
     2. Number of rounds (2 rounds).  
     7. Punishment cost (C3 for the authority).  
     8. Punishment magnitude (ψ).  
     12. Whether the number of rounds is known (it is finite and commonly known).  
   • The other 10 parameters are not mentioned in the sense of either being manipulated or even defined in the text.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?

   • The paper does not systematically vary any of the parameters in an experimental design or in a set of comparative statics for “punishment treatment effects.” It derives analytical conditions (inequalities) involving C3 and ψ, but it does not provide effect sizes or an explicit measure of a “punishment treatment effect.”

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

   • The paper provides no direct measure of “efficiency,” and it never systematically varies those parameters. Its focus rests on conditions under which a trustee honors trust and the authority punishes.

Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; CULTURAL TRANSMISSION; COSTLY PUNISHMENT; DYNAMICS
Abstract: In this paper, we analyze a team trust game with coordinated punishment of the allocator by investors and where there is also a final stage of peer punishment. We study the effect of punishment on the reward and the investment decisions, when the effectiveness and cost of coordinated punishment depend on the number of investors adhering to this activity.  • Does the paper discuss it?  
   – The paper sets up an overlapping‐generations model (infinite horizon in discrete periods), but does not treat “number of rounds” as a design variable.  
 • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
   – No. The paper does not vary the number of rounds to see how that would affect outcomes.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
 • Does the paper discuss it?

 • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
   – No.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   – Yes, the model requires each investor to choose invest (I) or not invest (NI) in the project. That is effectively “all or nothing.”  
 • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
   – No. The paper treats this as a fixed feature of its “team trust game”; it is not varied experimentally or theoretically.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much of their endowment to move back into their hand)?  
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   – No. The paper’s investors simply invest or not; there is no partial‐contribution or “default” mechanism.  
 • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
   – No.

 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   – The paper’s “surplus” is fixed at 2 if both investors choose to invest. It does not describe this as an MPCR or a systematically varied multiplier, and there is no table or figure showing how changing that surplus would affect outcomes.  
 • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
   – No. They do allow the individual cost of investing, c, to lie in (0, 0.5), and remark that lower c makes cooperation (fully cooperative culture) easier to sustain; but they do not present effect‐size estimates or separate “MPCR” results. 7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
 • Does the paper discuss it?  
   – The model’s “z” is the cost of punishing unilaterally (z if one punishes alone, z/2 if both punish).  
   – They analyze ceteris‐paribus changes in z in their theory (e.g., see Assumption 1 and the discussion in Propositions 1–9).  
 • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
   – Qualitatively, yes: a higher punishment cost (larger z) makes it harder for cooperators to enforce high returns, reducing the likelihood of a fully cooperative outcome.

 • Does the paper discuss it?

Authors: dos Santos, M; Braithwaite, VA; Wedekind, C
Author Full Names: dos Santos, Miguel; Braithwaite, Victoria A.; Wedekind, Claus
Article Title: Exposure to superfluous information reduces cooperation and increases antisocial punishment in reputation-based interactions
Author Keywords: indirect reciprocity; game theory; experimental games; image score; punishment reputation; sanctions; cognitive constraints; helping behavior
Keywords Plus: INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; EVOLUTION; MEMORY; GAMES; CONSTRAINTS; GENEROSITY; MECHANISMS; BENEFITS
Abstract: Human cooperation is often based on reputation gained from previous interactions with third parties. Such reputation can be built on generous or punitive actions, and both, one's own reputation and the reputation of others have been shown to influence decision making in experimental games that control for confounding variables. Here we test how reputation-based cooperation and punishment react to a disruption of the cognitive processing in different kinds of helping games with observers. Saying a few superfluous words before each interaction was used to possibly interfere with working memory. In a first set of experiments, where reputation could only be based on generosity, the disturbance reduced the frequency of cooperation and lowered mean final payoffs. In a second set of experiments where reputation could only be based on punishment, disturbance increased the frequency of antisocial punishment (i.e., of punishing those who helped) and reduced the frequency of punishing defectors. Our findings suggest that working memory can easily be constraining in reputation-based interactions within experimental games, even if these games are based on a few simple rules with a visual display that provides all the information the subjects need to play the strategies predicted from current theory. Our findings also highlight a weakness of experimental games, namely that they can be very sensitive to environmental variation and that quantitative conclusions about antisocial punishment or other behavioral strategies can easily be misleading.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter review of what this paper does (and does not) say with respect to each of the 15 listed parameters, followed by the requested summary (A–D). Throughout, “punishment treatment effect” refers to the effect of introducing punishment on outcomes, and “efficiency” refers to total actual payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff under full cooperation. The paper itself does not measure efficiency in that strict sense but instead reports final payoffs (“accounts”), cooperation (helping) frequency, and rates of punishment (including antisocial punishment). These different dependent variables are noted wherever relevant.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Does the paper mention it?  
     Yes. Groups in study 1 consisted of 9 or 10 individuals; groups in study 2 consisted of 6 to 9.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     No. The paper never systematically varies group size nor predicts how changing it would alter any punishment‐related (or other) outcome.

2. Number of rounds
   • Does the paper mention it?  
     Yes. Study 1 had 24 rounds; study 2 had 16 rounds.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     No. The paper does not experimentally manipulate the number of rounds nor discuss how changing it would affect punishment or payoffs.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Does the paper mention it?  
     It indicates that participants made decisions anonymously and, in some treatments, heard superfluous words from experimenters (thus a “disturbance”), but there was no mention of enabling free-form chat among participants.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     No.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Does the paper mention it?  
     Yes. In both studies, a Donor can either “give something” (cooperate) or “not give,” making it a binary, all‐or‐nothing choice in each interaction.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     No. The paper does not explore what would happen if there were continuous (partial) contributions.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Does the paper mention it?  
     No. There is no discussion of any sort of “default” contribution; participants simply decide to donate (green light) or not (red light).

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor
   • Does the paper mention it?  
     It mentions the benefit and cost of donating: in study 1, donating costs the Donor 1 unit (the experimenter tops up to the Receiver’s benefit of 1 in the UK currency version); in study 2, donating costs 1 CHF and yields 2 CHF to the Receiver. However, there is no explicit term “MPCR” used, nor any systematic variation of these parameters.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     No. The cost‐benefit ratio is mentioned but not manipulated or discussed in terms of how varying it would affect punishment or payoff.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Does the paper mention it?  
     Yes. In study 2, punishing costs the punisher 1 CHF each time.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     No. The cost of punishing (1 CHF) is fixed; the paper does not explore changing that cost.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   • Does the paper mention it?  
     Yes. In study 2, each punishment subtracts 2 CHF from the punished player’s account.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     No. It is a fixed parameter in this experiment.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Does the paper mention it?  
     No. These experiments only involve cooperation (donation) or punishment; no separate reward mechanism (beyond donating) is tested.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     No.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Does the paper mention it?  
     No. Because no reward mechanism is introduced, this does not apply.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward)
   • Does the paper mention it?  
     No. There is no reward mechanism in the design.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
   • Does the paper mention it?  
     Yes. The paper explicitly states that “No information was given about the total number of interactions,” meaning participants did not know in advance exactly how many rounds would be played.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it (or revealing vs. not revealing the number)?  
     No. The design is the same across groups in that regard, and there is no stated manipulation of end‐round knowledge.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much peers gained or lost)?
   • Does the paper mention it?  
     The displays in both studies provided each player’s “image score” (in the generosity‐based experiment) or “punishment score” (in the punishment‐based experiment). However, the paper does not say that players observed exact monetary payoffs gained or lost by each other; they mainly saw arrows representing each other’s reputation.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     No. The study compares “disturbance vs. no disturbance,” but it does not otherwise vary how outcomes are displayed or hidden.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Does the paper mention it?
     The study design is meant to preserve anonymity, although the Receiver’s ID and “punishment reputation” are shown in the second study. The text does not indicate that punishers’ identities (as persons) are revealed.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?
     No. The paper does not manipulate whether the punisher’s identity is revealed or hidden.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Does the paper mention it?
     There is no separate “reward” mechanism in these experiments, so this is not covered.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?
     No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?

• The paper does not use “group efficiency” (i.e., actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff) as its explicit dependent variable.  
• It does measure:  
  – “Final payoff” or “final account” per individual.  
  – “Cooperation frequency” (helping) and “punishment frequency” (including “antisocial punishment”).  
  – Reputation (image score or punishment score) and how it correlates with final payoff.  

These dependent variables differ from “efficiency” in that the study focuses on either an individual’s accumulated payoff, or on behavioral counts of cooperation and punishment, rather than a ratio of actual to maximal possible group payoff.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

The paper explicitly mentions the following parameters in some form (though not necessarily systematically varied):  
• Parameter 1 (number of players): group sizes of 6–10 are stated.  
• Parameter 2 (number of rounds): 24 rounds (generosity study) or 16 rounds (punishment study).  
• Parameter 4 (all‐or‐nothing contribution).  
• Parameter 6 (benefit/cost of donating, effectively a multiplier of 2 in study 2).  
• Parameter 7 (punishment cost = 1).  
• Parameter 8 (punishment magnitude = 2).  
• Parameter 12 (players are not told how many rounds will be played).  
• Parameter 13 (some information display is provided, specifically the “reputation” on screen).

Most of the other parameters are either not mentioned or not relevant to the design (e.g., reward parameters). Of the 15, at least 8 get some mention (1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13), though none are systematically varied except for the “disturbance vs. no disturbance” treatment, which is not one of the 15 parameters.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?

None. Although the paper varies whether participants could punish (study 2) versus not (study 1), it does not systematically vary the 15 parameters you listed (e.g., cost or magnitude of punishment, number of players, etc.). The only main experimental factor was the presence or absence of “superfluous words” (disturbance), which is not among the 15 parameters. Hence there are no effect‐size estimates, numerical or otherwise, regarding systematically manipulating any of the 15 parameters.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

The paper provides little direct basis for predicting how changes in (1) number of players, (2) number of rounds, (7) punishment cost, (8) punishment magnitude, etc. would affect efficiency. It only documents that adding a mild cognitive disturbance changes cooperation and punishment patterns—sometimes undermining longer‐term payoff. Because the paper does not systematically manipulate any of the 15 parameters, one can say only that, if a given parameter were changed so as to make reputation tracking or memory demands more difficult, one might similarly see cooperation and payoffs fall. But there is no direct, quantitative guidance from this paper on how each of the 15 parameters or their interactions would affect “efficiency.”  

In short, the results here do not allow meaningful predictions about systematically varying any of the 15 parameters, beyond the general insight that anything that disrupts players’ ability to track reputations or plan strategically (as happened with superfluous words) may reduce prosocial punishment and cooperation (and thus reduce final earnings). There is no further detail for these 15 parameters.

Article Title: Punishment Effect of Prisoner Dilemma Game Based on a New Evolution Strategy Rule
Keywords Plus: LEADER-FOLLOWING CONSENSUS; FLOCKING; AGENTS
Abstract: We discuss the effect of the punishment in the prisoner's dilemma game. We propose a new evolution strategy rule which can reflect the external factor for both players in the evolution game. In general, if the punishment exists, the D(defection-defection) structure (i.e., both of the two players choose D-D strategy) which is the Nash equilibrium for the game can keep stable and never let the cooperation emerge. However, if a new evolution strategy rule is adopted, we can find that the D-D structure can not keep stable and it will decrease during the game from the simulations. In fact, the punishment mainly affects the C-D (cooperation-defection) structure in the network. After the fraction of the C-D structure achieved some levels, the punishment can keep the C-D structure stable and prevent it from transforming into C-C (cooperation-cooperation) structure. Moreover, in light of the stability of structure and the payoff of the individual gains, it can be found that the probability which is related to the payoff can affect the result of the evolution game.

Article Title: Fairness overrides reputation: the importance of fairness considerations in altruistic cooperation
Author Keywords: altruistic cooperation; mini ultimatum game; fairness; reputation building; future interaction; intentions

Abstract: Behavioral findings in several strategic games indicate that people punish others if they think they are being treated unequally, even at the cost of minimizing their own material payoff. We investigated the primary driving force behind such non-self-regarding behavior, so-called, altruistic cooperation. In all of our studies, a mini ultimatum game was played either one-shot (in Experiment 1a and 1b) or repeatedly (Experiment 2), and rejections of inequitable distribution were taken as a measure of altruistic cooperation. In Experiment 1a, we replicated previous findings indicating that the key mechanism contributing to the emergence of altruistic cooperation is fairness considerations. In Experiment 1b, we delved into the relative importance of two aspects of fairness considerations (i.e., outcome fairness and intentions) and showed that both aspects were effective in determining the level of altruistic cooperation, with the contribution of intentions being more important. In Experiment 2, we investigated the effect of the opportunity for reputation building and future interaction on altruistic cooperation. We found that these factors became influential only when fairness considerations were weakened, particularly, as a result of the removal of the possible intentions behind an offer.

SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?

The primary dependent variable is the Responder’s rejection rate for the (8/2) distribution in various Mini Ultimatum conditions. No parameter is systematically varied in the sense of multiple levels presented as separate conditions to see incremental changes in “punishment treatment effect” or in payoff efficiency. The paper does compare:

The paper offers little basis to predict changes in group efficiency as typically defined (total payoff / max payoff). It does suggest that repeated interaction with unknown endpoint can induce more “signaling” rejections in certain cases (particularly when fairness intentions are unclear)—which might imply lower efficiency under some conditions. Beyond that, there is insufficient discussion to predict how systematically altering any of the 15 parameters would raise or lower efficiency.

Authors: Langlois, CC; Langlois, JPP
Author Full Names: Langlois, CC; Langlois, JPP
Article Title: Provisions for noncompliance and treaty value: A game theoretic perspective
Keywords Plus: DILEMMA
Abstract: We present a game theoretic analysis of the prevention of noncompliance that deals with treaty violations whether they are intentional or not. Game theorists have developed probabilistic trigger schemes to handle such situations. We analyze dispute resolution procedures in subgame perfect trigger terms and suggest alternative designs for the handling of signatory breach. This paper shows that designs can be compared directly by evaluating their ability to keep signatories close to the cooperative goal in the long run. This criterion enables us to highlight the merits of generosity and redress for dispute resolution. Generosity avoids retaliation with certainty so that parties can settle before any retaliatory action is implemented. But if retaliation does come to pass, it is the cost to the victim of punishing the perpetrator that determines a design's value. Using a simple repeated prisoner's dilemma framework we find that, in most circumstances, a subgame perfect design that adds concern for the injured party's redress to the generosity built into a probabilistic trigger scheme yields better treaty value.

Author Full Names: Bond, Robert M.
Article Title: Low-cost, high-impact altruistic punishment promotes cooperation cascades in human social networks
Keywords Plus: CONDITIONAL COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; ENFORCEMENT; NORMS; BEHAVIOR; REWARD; GAMES
Abstract: Theoretical models and experiments suggest that social networks may significantly impact the emergence and stability of cooperation in humans. Similarly, theoretical models and experiments have shown that punishing behavior can significantly increase cooperative behavior in individuals. However, how punishing impacts the effects of social networks on cooperation is not yet understood. Here, I examine a set of laboratory experiments in which participants choose to cooperate or defect under differing punishment arrangements. Through analysis of the experiment as a network, I evaluate how institutional arrangements affect the degree to which social networks promote cooperative behavior. The results show that cooperative behavior spreads from person-to-person in all versions of the game, but that in versions of the game with low-cost, high-impact punishment the influence both endures for more rounds and spreads further in the network. These results show that the extent to which cooperative behavior cascades is affected by the institutional arrangements that govern game play.

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   No. The paper does not measure “efficiency” (actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible). Instead, it focuses on cooperation/contribution levels and their spread across the social network. The main dependent variables are:  
   • Individual contribution to the public good in each round.  
   • Degree to which these contributions “cascade” through network ties (e.g., how one person’s contribution affects another’s in subsequent rounds).

C. For which and how many parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   Only parameters 7 (punishment cost) and 8 (punishment magnitude) are systematically varied, and the paper provides analyses of how those variations influence cooperation (its main dependent variable). Specifically, “low‐cost, high‐impact” punishment produces the highest cooperation and most extensive “cascades.” No other parameter is systematically manipulated, so no other “punishment treatment effect” analyses exist for the other parameters.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   Because the paper does not measure or report efficiency at all—and focuses instead on contributions—it gives little direct basis for predicting how these parameters affect “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff.” The one clear result is that cooperation (and thus presumably total contributions) is highest and most enduring in the “low‐cost, high‐impact” punishment variation, which might hint at higher overall group payoffs. For impacts of the other parameters (group size, number of rounds, rewards, etc.) on efficiency, the paper gives no information. Therefore, the safest conclusion is that there is insufficient evidence to predict how varying most of the 15 parameters—or their interactions—would affect efficiency.

Abstract: Cooperation in collective action problems and resource dilemmas is often assumed to depend on the values of the individuals involved, such as their degree of unselfishness and tolerance. Authors: van Miltenburg, N; Przepiorka, W; Buskens, V
Author Full Names: van Miltenburg, Nynke; Przepiorka, Wojtek; Buskens, Vincent
Article Title: Consensual punishment does not promote cooperation in the six-person prisoner's dilemma game with noisy public monitoring
Keywords Plus: SOCIAL DILEMMAS; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; 2ND-ORDER PUNISHMENT; INSTITUTIONS; HUMANS; COMMONS; RULES; COORDINATION; METAANALYSIS; UNCERTAINTY
Abstract: We study the effects of different punishment institutions on cooperation in a six-person prisoner's dilemma game in which actors observe others' cooperation with some noise (i.e. imperfect public monitoring). Previous research has shown that peer punishment can sustain cooperation, if a certain proportion of group members punish defectors at a cost to themselves. However, in the presence of noise, co-operators will sometimes be mistaken for defectors and punished, and defectors will sometimes be mistaken for co-operators and escape punishment. Both types of mistakes are detrimental for cooperation because cooperation is discouraged and defection is encouraged. By means of a laboratory experiment, we study whether this adverse effect of noise can be mitigated by consensual punishment. The more other group members have to agree on punishing a defector, the less likely will a co-operator be punished by mistake. We compare a punishment institution in which each subject decides individually whether to punish another, with institutions in which punishments are only implemented if subjects reach sufficient consensus that a particular group member should be punished. In conditions without noise, we find that cooperation and subjects' payoffs are higher if more consensus is required before a punishment is implemented. In conditions with noise, cooperation is lower if more consensus is required. Moreover, with noise, subjects' payoffs are lower under all punishment institutions than in the control condition without punishment opportunities. Our results narrow down the conditions under which punishment institutions can promote cooperation if such cooperation is noisy.

1. Number of players
   • Mentioned? Yes. The experiment is conducted in six-person groups (the “six-person prisoner’s dilemma”).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The group size (n=6) is fixed throughout all conditions.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned? Yes. The experiment has 45 total periods, broken into three sequences of 15 rounds each.  
   • Systematically varied? No. All participants go through the same three 15-period sequences. There is no systematic variation in how many rounds are played.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned? No. There is no discussion in the paper of any kind of communication or chat channel between participants.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not mention, nor alter, any communication protocol.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each participant either contributes their entire endowment (20 points) or contributes nothing (p. 6). This is the structure of their one‐shot prisoner’s dilemma.  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no variation: the game always requires a binary choice (cooperate or defect).

5. Is the contribution default (where players decide how much to withdraw back)?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper never discusses any mechanism by which participants “move” part of the endowment back into their personal account once allocated; it is always a binary “contribute or not.”  
   • Systematically varied? No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Mentioned? Yes. They use a multiplication factor m=2.4 in the experiment (p. 6).  
   • Systematically varied? No. This value is the same throughout the experiment (no changes across conditions).

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment

   • Mentioned? Yes. Each punishment deducts b=6 points from the punished player (p. 6).

   • Mentioned? The paper states participants went through three sequences of 15 periods each, but does not explicitly say whether the participants knew in advance there would be exactly 15 periods per sequence. (From context, they likely knew, but this is not explicitly stated as “known or unknown.”)  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no manipulation of “knowing vs. not knowing” the number of rounds.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (how much others gained or lost)?

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Below is how (and whether) the paper links each parameter to any systematic predictions about the “punishment treatment effect” (i.e., how punishment affects outcomes). Remember that the paper reports only on differences between “no punishment” vs. “punishment” under three decision rules (IDR, CDR2, CDR3) and “noise” vs. “no noise.” None of the 15 parameters above are themselves systematically varied (except that the experiment inherently manipulates (a) whether punishment is possible at all; (b) the decision rule for implementing it; (c) presence or absence of observation noise). • For parameters 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12–15: The paper does give a fixed value or procedure (e.g., “n=6,” “a=2,” “b=6,” “m=2.4,” “punisher identity hidden”), but nowhere do they predict or measure how changing that value would influence the punishment treatment effect on cooperation, payoffs, or any measure akin to efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
• The authors do not use the term “efficiency = (actual total payoff)/(maximum possible payoff).” Instead, they measure:  
  – “Cooperation rate” (the fraction of players contributing in a period), and  
  – “Earnings” or “payoffs” (points each participant earns in the game).  
• They note that “earnings” can differ from maximum possible earnings, but they never formalize an “efficiency” ratio. Thus their two main dependent variables are (1) cooperation and (2) payoff. These differ because sometimes cooperation is high yet payoff is reduced by punishment costs.

(B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Mentioned explicitly in the setup (with specific values or procedures):  
  1. Number of players (n=6)  
  2. Number of rounds (3 sequences of 15)  
  4. Contribution choice is all or nothing  
  6. Multiplication factor m=2.4  
  7. Punishment cost to punisher: 2 points  
  8. Punishment magnitude to target: 6 points  
  13. Participants see (noisy) contributions and eventual punishments but not who punished.  
  14. Punisher identity is hidden  
• Not mentioned at all as factors to be manipulated or measured:  
  3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 15.  
• Hence 8 of the 15 are mentioned, and 7 are not.

(C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
• None of the 15 are systematically varied in the sense of the paper methodically changing that parameter’s value (except that “punishment presence” itself is manipulated, and the presence/absence of noise is manipulated—but these do not match 1–15 exactly). They do not, for example, vary (7) from 2 to some other cost or (8) from 6 to another level.  
• Consequently, the paper does not report numerical effect sizes for changes in any of those 15 parameters. All references to “effect sizes” in the results concern how IDR vs. CDR2 vs. CDR3 and noise vs. no noise affect cooperation and payoffs, not how changing a listed parameter (like the cost to punish) alters outcomes.

(D) If you were to make predictions solely based on the paper about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, what would they be?  
• The paper does not give any direct basis to predict how systematically varying, for example, the number of players, the punishment cost, or whether chat is enabled, would affect group efficiency in a noisy punishment environment.  
• It only establishes that when punishment is possible and there is noise in observing contributions, group earnings tend to drop below no-punishment baseline (because some punishment is wasted and cooperation does not rise enough to cover that cost). Also, more consensus-based rules reduce punishment error but suffer from too few punishers stepping forward under noise.  
• Since the authors never explore systematically varying the 15 parameters, there is “little to no prediction” that can be made from this paper alone about those parameters’ interactions with punishment for improving (or harming) efficiency.

Abstract: This study experimentally investigates how repeatedly-induced exogenous happiness and anger affect the dynamics of cooperation and punishment in a public good game with repeated trials, wherein costly punishment is available and stranger matching is used. The study finds that induced happiness may harm cooperation when the reactions of the punished are also considered. Abstract: Population growth and greater human well-being imply increased use of scarce resources, which makes innovative proposals for fair redistribution policies necessary. Abstract: Social norms for cooperation are often supported by positive and negative sanctions. After participating in the public goods game, they decide whether to use the sanctions. Below is a parameter-by-parameter analysis of what this specific paper says. In each case, I note (1) whether the paper mentions the parameter (and if so, the value used), and (2) whether the paper makes predictions (numerical or otherwise) about systematically varying that parameter and its effect on punishment or reward—especially with respect to any outcome measure (noting carefully that the paper does not itself use the term “efficiency” in the sense you specified).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper fixes groups of four players in all sessions (“We conducted a four-member PGG…”).  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect? No. The group size is always 4, and the paper does not discuss varying it or how that variation would affect punishment or any other outcome.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper uses 20 periods (rounds).  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect? No. They do not vary the number of rounds across treatments, nor do they offer predictions about changing it.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not describe any verbal or written chat among participants; it only says players observe each other’s contribution decisions and can subsequently choose whether to punish or reward.  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect? No. It is not varied or discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned? Indirectly. The paper allows participants to contribute any integer amount from 0 to 20 points to the public project, so contributions are not forced to be “all or nothing.”  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect? No. It is not manipulated, nor do they predict anything about “all or nothing” choices.

5. Is the contribution default (where participants move some or all of their endowment back into their own hand)?
   • Mentioned? No. Participants simply decide how many of their 20 points to contribute. No “default contribution” mechanism is described.  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect? No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Mentioned? Yes. The MPCR is 0.2, making any contribution “inefficient” in the sense that total benefit per contributed point is only 0.8 for the group.  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect? No. The MPCR is held constant; the paper does not discuss how changing the MPCR would alter the effect of punishment or reward.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned? Yes. Punishment costs 4 points (the punisher pays 4).  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect? No. The paper always uses a cost of 4 and does not predict how other cost values might affect outcomes.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted per unit of punishment)
   • Mentioned? Yes. The target of punishment loses 12 points.  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect? No. The magnitude is always 12 and not varied.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned? Yes. This is systematically manipulated across four conditions in Study 1: N(no social exchange), P(punishment-only), R(reward-only), PR(punishment–reward). In Study 2, similarly, certain treatments include both reward and punishment, while others have none.  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect for punishment’s impact?  
        – The paper does compare (P) versus (R) versus (PR) versus (N), but it interprets those in terms of overall contribution levels and final payoffs; it does not speak specifically of how varying reward “modulates” the punishment treatment’s effect on “efficiency.” Instead, it focuses on the effect of different sanction options on contributions and final payoffs. Numerical findings about final payoffs (Table 1) show that average payoffs are higher in the presence of reward (R or PR). However, these data are reported as comparisons across four treatments, not as a direct statement of how reward availability changes a “punishment treatment effect.”  
        – In short, yes, the presence/absence of reward is a major experimental factor, but the paper does not articulate a separate numeric “punishment effect on efficiency” as a function of reward presence.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Mentioned? Yes. It costs 4 points to reward another participant.  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect? No. They use 4 points as the cost in all relevant treatments.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward)
   • Mentioned? Yes. A rewarded player receives 12 points.  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect? No. The magnitude is always 12; the paper does not consider other values.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
   • Mentioned? Only implicitly in that participants consistently play 20 periods. The paper does not explicitly state whether participants knew from the start there would be exactly 20, but that is the usual procedure.  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect? No discussion about changing or hiding the number of rounds.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?
   • Mentioned? Partially. Participants see each other’s contribution decisions and see how punishments or rewards were allocated, but the paper does not highlight any separate or partial treatments that vary the information display.  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect? No. They do not manipulate whether or how peer outcomes are shown.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Mentioned? Not in detail. The experiment keeps participant IDs constant, and individuals choose whom to punish/reward. The writeup implies that players can link ID and behavior; however, the paper does not explicitly confirm whether the punished person knows precisely which ID punished them.  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect? No. No mention of systematically turning this information on or off.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Mentioned? Same situation as punishment. IDs are maintained, but the paper never describes a separate condition in which the rewarder’s identity is hidden versus shown.  
   • Systematic variation or predicted effect? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?

The paper does not present “group efficiency” in the sense of “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff if everyone fully cooperated.” Instead, it measures:  
• Contribution to the public goods in each period.  
• Usage frequency of punishments and rewards.  
• Final (individual) payoffs, which are also aggregated up to average group payoffs in Table 1.  
• Questionnaire-based measures of attitudes/norms.  

Hence, the paper’s main dependent variables are (1) contribution to the public goods, (2) punishment/reward usage, (3) final payoff, and (4) norm-related survey responses. “Efficiency” (as you defined it) is not explicitly measured.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

Mentioned in some form:  
• (1) Number of players (fixed at 4).  
• (2) Number of rounds (20).  
• (6) MPCR (0.2).  
• (7) Punishment cost (4).  
• (8) Punishment magnitude (12).  
• (9) Whether reward is enabled (yes/no across treatments).  
• (10) Reward cost (4).  
• (11) Reward magnitude (12).  

Not discussed or not varied:  
• (3) Chat  
• (4) All-or-nothing contribution  
• (5) Contribution default  
• (12) Whether the number of rounds is known (not manipulated)  
• (13) Display of peer outcomes (not manipulated)  
• (14) Knowledge of punisher identity (not manipulated)  
• (15) Knowledge of rewarder identity (not manipulated)

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?

• The paper systematically varies only two sanction-related parameters: (i) the presence of punishment vs. no punishment, and (ii) the presence of reward vs. no reward (Parameter #9).  
• However, it never frames any result specifically as the “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” It mainly reports (a) the effect of punishment on final payoffs (statistically significant but smaller than the effect of reward), and (b) the effect of reward on final payoffs and on sustaining contributions.  
• Thus, strictly speaking, none of the 15 parameters is systematically varied in a way that the paper explicitly ties to “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Instead, the authors discuss how enabling vs. disabling punishment or reward affects contribution levels and mean payoffs in the group.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

The paper does not offer explicit statements about “group efficiency” (as a ratio to a maximum possible payoff) nor does it examine each parameter’s systematic variations. Consequently, it is difficult to predict the punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency from this source alone. Its main findings are about:  
• The presence of a reward option leads to steadily higher contributions (despite the public goods being “inefficient”), which in turn correlates with higher final payoffs.  
• Punishment alone boosts contributions less reliably and yields lower final payoffs than reward alone.  

But there is no direct exploration of how modifying, for instance, the punishment cost or punishment magnitude, or the number of players, would systematically change “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Therefore, based solely on this paper, we can say little about how those 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment treatment effect on your defined notion of efficiency.

Authors: Sabin, N; Reed-Tsochas, F
Author Full Names: Sabin, Nicholas; Reed-Tsochas, Felix
Article Title: Able but Unwilling to Enforce: Cooperative Dilemmas in Group Lending
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC GOOD GAMES; COLLECTIVE ACTION; SOCIAL-STRUCTURE; LOAN REPAYMENT; GROUP SOLIDARITY; STRONG TIES; NETWORKS; CREDIT; COHESION; EMBEDDEDNESS
Abstract: It is known that greater social cohesion increases a group's ability to enforce cooperation. Despite this, defectors often go unpunished, and groups with social structures that are a priori favorable often fail. A critical distinction is required between the structural effect on ability versus willingness to punish. The authors develop a theoretical framework in which variation in a group's social structure generates a tension between ability and willingness to enforce cooperation. Structures that promote ability to punish also often reduce interest in carrying out sanctions, thus changing collective outcomes. The authors' empirical analysis involves a well-defined cooperative dilemma: group lending in Sierra Leone. They complement statistical modeling, based on a data set containing 5,487 group repayments, with ethnographic analysis. They find that (1) structural cohesion only increases economic cooperation between borrowers to a point, beyond which unwillingness outweighs increased ability to punish, reducing group repayments, and that (2) groups with disconnected subgroups perform worse on average. Although borrowers are more willing to punish defectors in the out-subgroup, they are unable to do so effectively.

Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS EXPERIMENTS; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; HUMAN COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; PROVISION; ECONOMICS; SELECTION; GOSSIP; GAMES
Abstract: Group cooperation is fundamental to human society. The public goods game is often used to describe the difficulty of group cooperation. However, there are other structures of institutions to maintain group cooperation such as Rotating savings and credit associations (ROSCAs). ROSCAs are informal financial institutions that exist worldwide, in which all participants contribute to a common fund and take turns to receive a return. ROSCAs are common in developing countries and among migrant groups in developed countries. There are various types of ROSCAs, and they share a crucial problem in that participants whose turn to receive a return has passed have an incentive to default on their contributions. We conducted a laboratory experiment to investigate the mechanisms that can prevent default in a fixed ROSCA, in which the order of receipt of returns is determined before starting and is also known to members. The findings are as follows. (i) Excluding low contributors from ROSCA groups by voting increased contribution rates both before and after the receipt of returns. (ii) ROSCA members exhibited reciprocity and a sense of revenge: that is, members contributed to the returns payments of other members who had contributed to them, and did not contribute to the returns payments of non-contributors. PARAMETER‐BY‐PARAMETER DISCUSSION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. Number of players  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter (and with what value)?  
     – Yes. Each group has 4 players. The experiment uses 20 subjects partitioned into five groups of 4.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying this parameter (for any dependent variable)?  
     – No. The study does not vary the number of players (it is fixed at 4). There is no discussion of how changing group size would affect any outcome, including punishment or payoffs.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter (and with what value)?  
     – Yes. Each session has 10 rounds, each round consisting of 4 periods. The paper mentions that subjects know there will be 10 rounds and observes end‐game effects in the final round.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying this parameter (for any dependent variable)?  
     – No. The paper does not alter the number of rounds experimentally; it is always 10. No quantitative effect sizes or modeling of different numbers of rounds are provided.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – No. There is no mention of any live chat, messaging, or communication channel among players.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying this parameter?  
     – No mention whatsoever.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter (and with what value)?  
     – Yes. Each non‐recipient in a period decides whether to contribute exactly 100 points or 0 points. No partial contributions are allowed.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying this parameter?  
     – No. Participants always face an all‐or‐nothing choice, and the paper does not investigate alternative contribution rules.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much to move from the public fund back into their hand)?  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – The design is such that players may either “contribute 100 points” or “contribute nothing.” There is no mention of a default mechanism, and no shifting from a public fund “back” to oneself.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying this parameter?  
     – No. The paper does not mention systematic variation of any default‐contribution mechanism.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – The payoff formula involves a discount factor δ = 0.3, but the game does not frame this as a “marginal per capita return” in the usual public‐goods sense. Rather, each recipient’s payoff depends on the number of contributors and on the factor (1 + δ)(n–4).  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying δ or any MPCR‐like factor?  
     – No. The discount factor is fixed at 0.3; there is no systematic variation of multiplication factors.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter and its value?  
     – They use what they call a “punishment rule” (also termed the “forfeiture rule”) in Treatments P and VP, but there is no per‐unit cost to the punisher. It is a costless rule: if you have not contributed in earlier periods, you cannot receive that round’s payout.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying the cost of punishment?  
     – No. The cost is always zero when punishment is in effect; there is no variation.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted for each unit of punishment)  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – The “punishment rule” removes the entire payout from a would‐be recipient who previously failed to contribute. It is not described in terms of discrete “units of punishment” or adjustable magnitude.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying punishment magnitude?

9. Whether a reward is enabled

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?

   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying whether or not the game end is known?

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained or lost)?  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?

   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying the display of peer outcomes?

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?

   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying whether punishment is anonymous or identified?  
     – No. The paper does not address this.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – There is no reward mechanism, so no such discussion.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying reward anonymity?  
     – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A–D SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Does the paper use “group efficiency” (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper primarily measures:  
     1) Individual and group‐level contribution rates.  
     2) Individual and average payoffs.  

   • Although the authors do not use the term “efficiency” per se, their “mean payoff” or “total payoff” is conceptually similar to “efficiency” in a public‐goods sense. They also examine how frequently participants contribute (“contribution rate”) both before and after receiving returns.  
   • Thus the paper’s main dependent variables are:  
     – Contribution rate: further subdivided into “before receiving the payout” and “after receiving the payout.”  
     – Payoff (both individual‐level and group‐level mean payoff).  

   • These are different from “efficiency” if one defines efficiency strictly as (actual total payoff) ÷ (maximum possible total payoff). The authors never formalize that ratio but do compare mean payoffs across treatments.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some capacity:  
     (1) Number of players (always 4).  
     (2) Number of rounds (always 10).  
     (4) Is contribution all or nothing? (Yes, always 100 or 0).  
     (6) Multiplication/discount factor (δ = 0.3) is somewhat analogous to an MPCR.  
     (7, 8) Punishment rule is costless and forfeits the entire payout; hence cost = 0, magnitude = total payout.  
     (12) Number of rounds is known to players.  
     (13) Players do see basic information on contributions and payouts.

   • However, the paper does not systematically manipulate any of those parameters; they remain fixed. The paper does not discuss chat (#3), default mechanism (#5), any reward aspect (#9–11, 15), or anonymous punisher identity (#14) in any systematic way.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, the paper does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters (e.g., group size always 4, number of rounds always 10, discount factor always 0.3, etc.).  
   • Because of that, it makes no direct predictions or measurements about how changing these parameters would modify the “punishment treatment effect.”  
   • Instead, the paper compares four treatments (B, P, V, VP) that differ in (a) whether a punishment rule is in force (B/V vs. P/VP) and (b) whether voting/exclusion is in force (B/P vs. V/VP). They do not treat punishment cost or magnitude as a parameter to be “varied” along a continuum.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper’s content, what would they be?  
   1) Because the paper finds that a simple “punishment rule” (forfeiture of the payout for non‐contributors) did not improve mean payoffs relative to “no punishment,” there is little evidence, within the confines of this study, that adjusting aspects such as punishment magnitude, punishment cost, or group size would improve efficiency—at least not without additional structural changes.  
   2) The paper does not discuss or vary contribution defaults, chat, or reward systems, so no direct predictions can be established.  
   3) The paper uses a specific discount factor (0.3) and does not analyze how different discount rates might change the outcomes; thus, no direct inference can be made about systematic variations of an MPCR‐like factor.  
   4) The authors do note that knowledge of the finite number of rounds leads to end‐game effects, but they do not model how drastically changing the number of rounds (or keeping it unknown) might alter the punishment treatment effect on total payoffs.  
   5) Overall, the paper strongly suggests that enabling group members to exclude free riders (voting) raised mean payoffs in a way that the punishment rule by itself did not. However, none of the 15 parameters were systematically varied enough in the study to yield effect‐size estimates for each parameter’s impact on “punishment treatment effect.”  

In short, the paper does not systematically manipulate any of the 15 parameters. Consequently, little or no prediction can be made, strictly from these data, on how each parameter would affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency. The standout finding from the paper is that adding a punishment‐type rule without additional social mechanisms (like voting and exclusion) did not boost payoffs or prevent free riding; it was the voting/exclusion mechanism that increased both contribution rates and mean payoffs.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
End of response.

Studies show that electing a community member to operate a centralized sanctioning institution further increases support for the public good. Summary of Key Questions

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?

   – Participants’ earnings (average or final token counts).  
   – Participants’ expectations of the monitor’s threshold.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
 • Parameters explicitly mentioned:  
   1 (Number of players), 2 (Number of rounds), 6 (MPCR is effectively 2/n), 7 (Punishment cost = 100 tokens), 8 (Punishment magnitude = 300 tokens), 9 (Reward is not enabled), 12 (Known number of rounds), 13 (Peer outcomes displayed), 14 (Single monitor identity is effectively known).

   – Whether the group had a centralized authority (punishment) at all.  
   – Whether that authority was selected randomly or elected.  
   – Whether the election gave equal votes, random votes, or votes based on past wealth.

   • None of the 15 parameters appear in the paper as formal, systematically manipulated public goods game parameters. Authors: Gillenkirch, RM; Kreienbaum, H
Author Full Names: Gillenkirch, Robert M.; Kreienbaum, Heike
Article Title: What guides subjective performance evaluation: Incentive alignment or norm enforcement?
Author Keywords: Subjective performance evaluation; Norm enforcement; Incentive alignment; Fairness
Keywords Plus: PERCEIVED FAIRNESS; MORAL HAZARD; DISCRETION; BIAS; DETERMINANTS; PERSPECTIVES; PREFERENCES; APPRAISAL
Abstract: This paper investigates the objectives guiding a superior's subjective evaluation of subordinate performance. In a laboratory experiment, we implement a team production setting under uncertainty, where subordinates contribute to the organization's output by choosing effort levels, but individual contributions are subject to random shocks. After observing joint output, the superior can invest into additional (perfect or imperfect) information about effort levels. We test two competing hypotheses about objectives guiding a superior's subjective performance evaluation. The incentive alignment hypothesis states that the superior is guided by the objective to establish financial incentives that align a subordinate's preferences with the organization's goals such that it is in the subordinate's self-interest to provide effort. In contrast, the norm enforcement hypothesis states that the superior has a focus on subordinate behavior and wants to enforce the norm of cooperation by rewarding high and punishing low effort. Our results reject the incentive alignment hypothesis and provide support for the norm enforcement hypothesis.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter accounting of what the Gillenkirch & Kreienbaum (2016) paper does—and does not—say about systematically manipulating each of the 15 features of a typical public‐goods game with punishment. Throughout, “the paper” refers solely to Gillenkirch & Kreienbaum (2016). If a parameter is not discussed, or if the paper does not analyze its systematic impact on any sort of “punishment treatment effect,” that is stated explicitly.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   – Yes. The experiment always has one “superior” and two “subordinates,” i.e., 3 participants per group (triads).  
 • Does the paper systematically vary this parameter or make predictions about how varying it affects a punishment treatment (or any dependent variable)?  
   – No. The number of players is fixed at three, and the paper does not explore changing this group size.

2) Number of rounds
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   – Yes. The experiment lasts for 16 rounds (grouped into four “cycles” of four rounds).  
 • Does the paper systematically vary the number of rounds or predict how it affects a punishment treatment effect on any outcome?  
   – No. The paper does not manipulate or vary the number of rounds; it remains fixed at 16. No prediction is made about changing the length of the game.

3) Is chat enabled between players?
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   – No. There is no mention of participants being allowed or disallowed to chat in real time.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary this parameter?  
   – No. It is not mentioned nor varied.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   – No. Subordinates choose integer effort levels from 0 to 10, and the paper does not treat this in terms of “forced all‐or‐nothing” decisions.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary “all or nothing” vs. continuous choice?  
   – No. No mention of such a design variation.

5) Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much to move from the public fund back into their hand)?
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   – No. The subordinates simply pick an effort level (0…10) at cost 0.7 per unit; there is no mention of a “default contribution” or a “default” mechanism.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary a default?  
   – No. Not mentioned or tested.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as a multiplication factor
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   – No. The study frames output and bonuses in terms of a linear relationship (joint output = sum of effort plus random shocks), not in the standard MPCR sense.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary the MPCR?  
   – No. There is no mention of any such factor being manipulated.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   – No. The “punishment” in the experiment is that the superior can allocate fewer points to a low‐effort subordinate—but the paper does not define a specific cost for imposing punishment.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary a punishment‐cost mechanism?  
   – No. There is no mention of it.

8) Punishment magnitude
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   – Only indirectly. “Punishment” is left to the superior’s reallocation decision: giving a subordinate less than that subordinate’s own contribution. There is no separate “units of punishment” or standardized “magnitude.”  
 • Does the paper systematically vary this parameter?  
   – No. The paper does not vary or quantify a uniform punishment‐token magnitude.

9) Whether a reward is enabled
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   – The superior can “reward” productive subordinates by giving them more than their own portion of output. However, there is no separate “reward” feature akin to an added mechanism; it is simply an outcome of the reallocation.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary whether “rewarding” is turned on or off?  
   – No. The paper does not treat “reward enabled vs. disabled” as a distinct parameter.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   – No. Any “reward” occurs by giving more of the existing joint output to a subordinate. There is no explicit cost for giving a reward.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary that cost?  
   – No. Not mentioned.

11) Reward magnitude (i.e., coins granted per unit of reward)
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   – No. The superior freely allocates points. There is no fixed ratio or discrete “reward‐unit” concept.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary the magnitude?  
   – No. Not mentioned.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   – Yes. Participants know there will be 16 total rounds (arranged in four cycles).  
 • Does the paper systematically vary or analyze how known vs. unknown game length affects outcomes?
   – No. The total round length is not manipulated.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (i.e., do players see how much their peers gained or lost each round)?
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
   – The subordinates see their own payoff and see what information the superior used, but the paper does not indicate that subordinates learn the other subordinate’s payoff.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary the display of peer outcomes?
   – No. The paper does not manipulate or highlight different rules for displaying peer outcomes.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who punished them?
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?
   – The identity of the “punisher” (the superior) is always common knowledge in the sense that there is only one superior. However, the study does not revolve around anonymity manipulations or an unknown punisher.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary knowledge of the punisher’s identity?
   – No. Not mentioned.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who rewarded them?
 • Does the paper discuss this parameter?
   – Similarly, the only possible person allocating payments is the superior. There is no separate variation of anonymity.  
 • Does the paper systematically vary whether the rewarder is known?
   – No. Not mentioned.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?  
   – The paper does not focus on “group efficiency” or “efficiency” in a public‐goods sense. Instead, its main dependent variables are (i) the superior’s willingness to pay for different performance‐information sets, and (ii) the superior’s subsequent allocation decisions (i.e., how the bonus pool is distributed), as well as (iii) subordinates’ effort levels in response to the superior’s behavior. “Efficiency” is not explicitly modeled or reported as a key outcome.

B. Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – The paper explicitly identifies or fixes two of the 15 parameters:  
     • (1) Number of Players: Always three (1 superior, 2 subordinates).  
     • (2) Number of Rounds: Always 16, known to participants.  
   – There is no explicit mention or variation of the other 13 parameters (e.g., cost or magnitude of punishment, reward mechanisms, “all‐or‐nothing” contributions, chat, etc.).

C. For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on a “punishment treatment effect” for each dependent variable, when systematically varied?  
   – None. The study does not systematically vary the number of players, the number of rounds, or any other parameter to gauge how it would affect a “punishment treatment effect.” There is no direct test of how changing any of the 15 parameters shifts total payoffs, efficiency, or “punishment” in a classic public‐goods sense.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, solely based on this paper’s content, what would they be?  
   – The paper does not give information to predict how varying the listed parameters would affect a standard public‐goods “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency. All results focus on the superior’s willingness to acquire performance information and enforce behavioral norms in a triadic team. Because the paper does not discuss or manipulate those parameters in the manner typical of a public‐goods‐with‐punishment experiment, one cannot draw meaningful predictions regarding how systematically changing them might affect group efficiency.  

In short, Gillenkirch & Kreienbaum (2016) do not investigate standard public‐goods parameters (e.g., marginal per‐capita return, cost/magnitude of punishment) or efficiency‐based outcomes in a direct way, so the paper provides no basis for projecting their separate or combined effects on efficiency.

Authors: Paál, T; Bereczkei, T
Author Full Names: Paal, Tuende; Bereczkei, Tamas
Article Title: Punishment as a Means of Competition: Implications for Strong Reciprocity Theory
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; HUMAN COOPERATION; BEHAVIOR; TOURNAMENTS; IMPACT
Abstract: Strong negative reciprocity, that is, sanctions imposed on norm violators at the punisher's own expense, has powerful cooperation-enhancing effects in both real-life and experimental game situations. However, it is plausible that punishment may obtain alternative roles depending on social context and the personality characteristics of participants. We examined the occurrence of punishing behavior among 80 subjects in a strongly competitive Public Goods game setting. Despite the punishment condition, the amount of the contributions decreased steadily during the game. The amount of contributions had no significant effect on received and imposed punishments. The results indicate that certain social contexts (in this case, intensive competition) exert modifying effects on the role that punishment takes on. Subjects punished each other in order to achieve a higher rank and a financially better outcome. Punishment primarily functioned as a means of rivalry, instead of as a way of second-order cooperation, as strong reciprocity suggests. These results indicate the need for the possible modification of the social conditions of punishment mechanisms described by the strong reciprocity theory as an evolutionary explanation of human cooperation.

Abstract: Sometimes we punish non-cooperators in our society. Such behavior could be derived from aversive emotion for inequity (inequity aversion) to make non-cooperators cooperative. Thus, punishing behavior derived from inequity is believed to be important for maintaining our society. Meanwhile, our daily experiences suggest that the degree of cooperation by the members of society (cooperation level of the group) could change the punishing behavior for non-cooperators even if the inequity were equal. Such effect of the cooperation level of the group cannot be explained by simple inequity aversion. Although punishment-related brain regions have been reported in previous functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) study, little is known about such regions affected by the cooperation level of the group. In the present fMRI study, we investigated the effect of the cooperation level of the group on the punishing behavior for non-cooperators and its related brain activations by a paradigm in which the degree of the cooperative state varied from low to high. Punishment-related activations were observed in brain regions such as the anterior insula, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC). The quantity of punishment in a high cooperation context was greater than in a low cooperation context, and activation in the right DLPFC and ACC in a high cooperation context showed greater activity than in a low cooperation context. This indicates that the cooperation level of the group, as well as aversive emotion for inequity, is the important factor of punishing behavior.
