Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter summary based strictly on what the paper by Kodaka et al. (2012) actually reports. Note that the paper focuses on how “the cooperation level of the group” (high vs. low) affects the severity of punishment decisions and associated brain activation. It does not systematically vary—or even discuss—most of the 15 parameters listed in your request.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The experiment involves three personas: two “cooperators” (B, C) and one “non‐cooperator” (A).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper always uses three, and does not examine how changing the number of players would affect punishment.  
   • Numerical effect size on punishment treatment effect? None provided.  

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not describe a repeated multi‐round structure (instead, participants saw multiple “events” within one scanning session but not in a repeated public‐goods‐game sense).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Numerical effect size? Not applicable.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Numerical effect size? Not applicable.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned? No. The “contributors” make amounts between 0 and 10,000 JPY, and the paper does not describe a forced “all‐or‐nothing” contribution.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Numerical effect size? Not applicable.  

5. Is the contribution default? (i.e., do players decide how much of their endowment to move back to themselves?)  
   • Mentioned? No. Participants only view pre‐set contributions for the three personas.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Numerical effect size? Not applicable.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not treat this as a standard public goods or linear MPCR game.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Numerical effect size? Not applicable.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? Not in a systematic, varied way. The study allows participants to choose “no punishment,” “moderate,” or “severe,” but does not report a graduated or monetary cost to the punisher that is experimentally manipulated.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Numerical effect size? Not applicable.  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned? Only in the sense that participants choose among three discrete levels (no punishment, moderate, severe), but this is not manipulated as an experimental parameter.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Numerical effect size? Not applicable in the sense of parametric variation; the paper simply reports overall differences in punishments chosen for the high vs. low cooperation conditions.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned? No. This study deals only with punishment, not reward.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Numerical effect size? Not applicable.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Numerical effect size? Not applicable.  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Numerical effect size? Not applicable.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Numerical effect size? Not applicable.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know others’ gains or losses)?  
   • Mentioned? Only in the sense that the subject sees each persona’s contribution. The paper does not describe a separate feedback phase with full payoff outcomes for all parties.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Numerical effect size? Not applicable.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Mentioned? No. There is no indication that the “non‐cooperator” sees who punished them.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Numerical effect size? Not applicable.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Mentioned? No. Rewards were not part of this design.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Numerical effect size? Not applicable.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What dependent variables does it use, and how do these differ from one another?  
   • The paper does not measure or discuss group efficiency, total payoff, or average payoff.  
   • The key dependent variables are (1) the behavioral measure of punishment levels (0 = no punishment, 1 = moderate, 2 = severe), and (2) neural activation (fMRI BOLD signal) in punishment‐related brain regions such as the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), anterior insula (AI), and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC).  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • The paper necessarily uses “number of players = 3” but does not systematically vary it. None of the other 14 parameters are discussed in a way that explicitly identifies them as design parameters or systematically manipulates them.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • None of the 15 parameters are systematically varied for the paper’s primary analysis. The paper only varies “cooperation level of the group” (high vs. low), but that is not listed among your 15 parameters. Consequently, there is no discussion of parameter‐by‐parameter effects on punishment (or on efficiency) within the framework of those 15 points.  

D. Based solely on the paper’s content, what predictions can be made about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
   • The paper provides no direct evidence or discussion about how manipulating these specific 15 parameters would affect a “punishment treatment effect” on group efficiency (and it does not use efficiency as a dependent variable). Since the paper’s focus is on how the group’s cooperation level (high vs. low) changes punishment decisions and fMRI activation, it furnishes insufficient information to predict how varying any of the 15 parameters in a standard public goods game would change efficiency outcomes.  

Thus, from the contents of this paper alone, we cannot make meaningful predictions about the influence of these 15 parameters on the punishment treatment effect regarding efficiency.

Authors: Hugh-Jones, D; Perroni, C
Author Full Names: Hugh-Jones, David; Perroni, Carlo
Article Title: The logic of costly punishment reversed: Expropriation of free-riders and outsiders
Author Keywords: Cooperation; Costly punishment; Group coercion; Heterogeneity
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS; COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; INSTITUTIONS; CONFLICT; POWER; WAR
Abstract: Current literature views the punishment of free-riders as an under-supplied public good, carried out by individuals at a cost to themselves. It need not be so: often, free-riders' property can be forcibly appropriated by a coordinated group. This power makes punishment profitable, but it can also be abused. It is easier to contain abuses, and focus group punishment on free-riders, in societies where coordinated expropriation is harder. Our theory explains why public goods are undersupplied in heterogenous communities: because groups target minorities instead of free-riders. In our laboratory experiment, outcomes were more efficient when coordination was more difficult, while outgroup members were targeted more than ingroup members, and reacted differently to punishment. Below, each of the 15 parameters is treated in turn.

For every parameter I indicate

(1) Whether the paper reports the parameter (and its value);  
(2) Whether the paper makes any prediction about what would happen if the parameter were systematically changed, specifically about the “punishment treatment effect” – i.e. the difference between a condition that contains a punishment (expropriation) stage and one that does not – on any outcome variable;  
(3) Whether the paper gives a numerical effect size that can be taken directly from a table or figure.

The expression “punishment treatment effect” is used in exactly the sense requested by the instructions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
(1) Mentioned.  All experimental groups have N = 4 (p 4, “Subjects were randomly allocated into groups of four”).  
(2) Not varied experimentally.  The theory treats N as a free parameter, but there is no systematic prediction about how changing N alters the punishment-minus-no-punishment difference in efficiency (or any other variable).  
(3) No numerical effect size.

2. Number of rounds  
(1) Mentioned.  Most treatments have 20 rounds; PX-Hist has 10+10 rounds.  
(2) Not analysed as an independent treatment variable.  No predictions made.  
(3) None.

3. Chat enabled  
(1) Never mentioned.  
(2) No discussion, no prediction.  
(3) None.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
(1) Not mentioned; the public–goods stage is continuous (0–50 ECU).  
(2) No prediction.  
(3) None.

5. “Reverse” contribution default (take from the public fund)  
(1) Not in the paper.  
(2) No prediction.  
(3) None.

6. Marginal-per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
(1) Reported once: π = 1.4 (p 11).  Not otherwise varied.  
(2) No systematic predictions.  
(3) None.

7. Punishment cost per unit (cost to the punisher)  
(1) The experiment sets k = 0 (p 11).  The model analyses both k > 0 and k = 0.  
(2) Theory predicts that if k rises above (f – l)/M punishment becomes unprofitable and disappears (Appendix 1, eq. 4 & discussion).  If k is low, punishment may become universal when M = 1.  No experimental manipulation, so no numerical effect size.  
(3) None reported.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine on the punished)  
(1) Fixed at f = 50 ECU (targets lose 50 ECU).  
(2) Theory: larger f relative to k and M makes expropriation more likely; too large an f with M = 1 yields “Hobbesian anarchy” and zero efficiency.  Not tested experimentally.  
(3) No numerical estimate.

9. Reward enabled  
(1) Absent from all designs.  
(2) No prediction.  
(3) None.

10–11. Reward cost / reward magnitude  
Not mentioned.

12. Whether the horizon is known  
(1) Not discussed; subjects are simply told the number of rounds in the instructions, but the authors never analyse or vary this factor.  
(2) No predictions.  
(3) None.

13. Whether peer outcomes are shown  
(1) Yes.  Baseline treatments give exact, public feedback on every player’s contribution and on how many people targeted whom (p 11).  Two systematic manipulations exist:  
 • PX-Noise adds independent noise to each subject’s observation of others’ contributions.  
 • All other treatments keep feedback exact.  
(2) Predictions / findings: In noisy feedback (PX-Noise-Het) minorities are no longer targeted more often than majorities and react less to punishment (Table 5, Table 4, Result 12).  However, the paper does not compute the punishment-minus-no-punishment difference in efficiency, so the effect on efficiency is not quantified.  
(3) No efficiency numbers; only mean contributions (17.39 vs 17.38 ECU, Table 8).

14. Whether punished players learn the identity of the punisher  
(1) They only learn the number of people who targeted each member (p 11).  Never varied.  
(2) No predictions.  
(3) None.

15. Whether rewarded players learn the identity of the rewarder  
Not applicable (no rewards).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables actually used  
 • Mean individual contribution (ECU)  
 • Number of successful expropriations and of expropriation attempts  
 • Probability of being expropriated  
 • (Occasional verbal use of the word “efficiency”, but no variable equal to total-payoff / maximum-payoff is ever calculated or reported.)  
Thus “efficiency” in the sense requested is never measured; the paper’s variables are not identical to efficiency.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
Seven: 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 13, 14.  (The remaining eight are never mentioned.)

C. For how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss effects of systematic variation?  
Three.  
 • 7 (Punishment cost) – only theoretically; no data.  
 • 8 (Punishment magnitude) – only theoretically; no data.  
 • 13 (Information on peer outcomes) – varied experimentally via the “Noise” treatment; effects reported on targeting patterns and contribution adjustments, not on efficiency.  
None of these discussions produces an effect size on efficiency.

D. What predictions about the 15 parameters and their interactions can be made for the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, using only the paper?

Given the paper’s content, very little can be said with confidence:

– If the punishment cost k exceeds (f – l)/M, punishment disappears; the punishment treatment effect on efficiency would then be zero (because there is no punishment).  
– If k is very small and M = 1, punishment becomes indiscriminate, contributions collapse, and efficiency is predicted to fall below the no-punishment baseline.  
– Increasing the noisiness of information about peers’ contributions (parameter 13) makes punishment less clearly conditional on free-riding, especially in heterogeneous groups; the authors observe that minorities then fail to raise contributions after punishment.  By implication, adding noise should reduce any positive impact of punishment on efficiency.  
– For all other parameters the paper offers no data-based or theoretical statements that map the parameter onto a change in the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

In short, the paper allows only narrow, qualitative predictions and provides no quantitative estimates of how any of the 15 listed parameters would change the punishment-versus-no-punishment difference in group efficiency.

Authors: Loukopoulos, P; Eek, D; Gärling, T; Fujii, S
Author Full Names: Loukopoulos, P; Eek, D; Gärling, T; Fujii, S
Article Title: Palatable punishment in real-world social dilemmas? : Punishing others to increase cooperation among the unpunished
Keywords Plus: REWARDS; FRAMES; IMPACT; MODEL
Abstract: Social-dilemma research has shown that imposing sanctions on defection may increase cooperation, a principle behind attempts to solve real-world social dilemmas. Yet sanctioning systems are often difficult to implement: They are unpopular and often have large surveillance and enforcement costs. A new sanctioning system, intentionally punishing defection intermittently for some but not all group members, is shown to increase cooperation among those not punished, a finding labeled the spillover effect. This study suggests that the effect cannot be attributed simply to cooperative tendencies, as factors affecting cooperation do not affect the effect's size. The benefits of such a sanctioning system, which preserves the characteristics of social dilemmas, could include minimization of surveillance and enforcement costs, and greater public acceptability.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what the paper does (and does not) say about each of the 15 listed parameters, followed by the requested four‐part summary (A–D). Throughout, please note that the paper’s central focus is on cooperation rates (and the “spillover effect” in those rates), rather than on efficiency (actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff), which it does not measure.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER‐BY‐PARAMETER ANALYSIS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1) Number of players  
   • Discussed? Yes. The experiment is conducted with six‐person groups (p. 9, “Position 4 in a six‐person group”; p. 8, “Participants were told that they would respond as Number 4 in a sequence of six group members”).  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no condition in which the group size is manipulated. The paper does not make predictions for changing the number of players.  

2) Number of rounds  
   • Discussed? The experiment presents repeated decision tasks (32 total trials per participant), but the paper does not treat the “number of rounds” as a systematically varied factor.  
   • Systematically varied? No. No separate conditions differing in round count are tested. No predictions are made about changing the number of rounds on any outcome.  

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not mention any communication/chat between participants.  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no mention of allowing or disallowing chat.  

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Discussed? In effect, the participant’s choice is binary (Option A vs. Option B), which is “all or nothing,” but this is not experimentally manipulated.  
   • Systematically varied? No. They do not compare an all‐or‐nothing design to one with continuous contributions; rather, the design always has a binary choice.  

5) Is the contribution default?  
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not mention default contributions or forced moves of endowments.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as a multiplication factor  
   • Discussed? No. The experiment uses a payoff matrix with fixed monetary amounts, not an MPCR mechanism typical of standard public‐goods games.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussed? No. This paper’s “punishment” (an intermittent cost to defect) is imposed by the experimental setup rather than by peers, so there is no discussion of how much it costs a punisher to inflict punishment.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Discussed? Partly—though not framed as “units” of punishment, the paper does vary the cost to defect (“no cost,” “low cost [SEK 1,000],” or “high cost [SEK 5,000]”).  
   • Systematically varied for punishment effect? Yes, but only in terms of comparing no‐punishment vs. punishment conditions. They find that when the cost to defect is high (SEK 5,000), cooperation rates increase substantially (from an overall 28.28% under no cost to 83.07% under “high cost to self,” see Table 1, p. 12–13). They also study an intermittent‐cost design where some group member (the “selected fee payer”) faces high cost while others do not. This leads to the “spillover effect,” in which those not currently paying the fee also cooperate more than they do in the “no cost” condition.  
   • Effect sizes for cooperation (not efficiency) when varying cost:  
     – No cost: 28.28% cooperation (overall mean).  
     – Low constant cost (SEK 1,000): 42.69%.  
     – High cost to self (SEK 5,000): 83.07%.  
     – High cost to others (i.e., another person pays the SEK 5,000 fee): 37.50%.  
     The “spillover effect” is specifically the increase in cooperation from 28.28% (no cost) to 37.50% (high cost to others), about a 9‐percentage‐point rise in cooperation. The paper does not present these changes in terms of group efficiency.  

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussed? No. This study involves no reward mechanism, only “punishment” (i.e., a fee for selecting the defecting option).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Discussed? No.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
    • Discussed? No.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    • Discussed? The paper does not discuss whether participants know in detail how many total trials there will be. It does not systematically manipulate that knowledge.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost each round)?  
    • Discussed? Not in terms of payoffs. Players are only told how many others cooperated or defected prior to their choice (the “33% prior cooperation” vs. “100% prior cooperation” manipulations). This is not systematically about revealing all payoff outcomes; the experiment states that participants see others’ choices but not specifically their monetary outcomes.  
    • Systematically varied? Partially yes for cooperation info, but not for payoffs. The study does manipulate knowledge of prior cooperation (p. 9–10). However, the paper does not tie that to a systematic discussion of “punishment treatment effect on efficiency”; rather, they examine how it affects cooperation overall and the spillover effect. They conclude that varying prior cooperation does not change the size of the spillover effect (p. 13–14).  

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Discussed? No. Punishment here comes via the experimenter’s cost assignment (not from another player), so there is no identification of a punisher.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Discussed? No. The paper does not involve any reward mechanism.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY (A–D)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?  
   • The paper does not use group efficiency as a measured dependent variable.  
   • The main dependent variable is the cooperation rate (i.e., how many participants choose “B,” the cooperative option). The paper also defines and measures the “spillover effect” as the rise in cooperation among those who are not currently forced to pay the cost of defecting.  
   • Thus, although the payouts are described, the critical outcome measure in the results is always the percentage of participants choosing to cooperate, not total payoffs or efficiency.  

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned explicitly or implicitly:  
     1) Number of players (fixed at 6; not varied),  
     4) All‐or‐nothing choice (binary A vs. B, but not varied),  
     8) Punishment magnitude (no cost, low cost, high cost),  
     13) Partial visibility of other players’ cooperation (33% vs. 100% prior cooperation).  
   • All other parameters (2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9–12, 14, 15) are not discussed or are irrelevant to this design in terms of systematic variation.  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The paper systematically varies only:  
     1) Punishment magnitude for defection (Parameter 8: no cost, low cost, high cost), and  
     2) Participants’ knowledge of prior cooperation (which relates loosely to Parameter 13, but is specifically “33% vs. 100% prior cooperation,” not payoff outcomes).  
   • Neither of these manipulations is analyzed in terms of “efficiency.” Instead, the dependent variable is cooperation rate.  
   • The only clear “punishment treatment effect” is the difference in cooperation between “no cost” (28.28% overall) and “high cost to others” (37.50%), about +9 percentage points. That difference is described as the “spillover effect.” Although “frame” (individual vs. group) and “prior cooperation” are varied, the paper reports that neither significantly alters the size of that spillover.  

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of this paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not link any parameter to changes in efficiency or total payoff. It provides no direct data on (or predictions about) how systematically varying group size, number of rounds, chat, the default mechanism, reward presence, or knowledge of punisher identity would affect efficiency.

       • f = 0.60 or 1.00 essentially eliminates dangerous strategies; the median payoff in all three networks exceeds 1.55 and often clusters around 2.1 (Fig. 9).  
       Approximate treatment-effect size that can be read from Fig. 9:  
       – Baseline without punishment on BA network: median payoff ≈ 1.05 (Fig. 3).  
       – Punishment with f = 0.60: median payoff ≈ 1.60.  
       → Punishment treatment effect on *average payoff* ≈ +0.55 (≈ +52 % relative improvement).  
       (The paper does not convert this to *efficiency*, but the maximum theoretical payoff is 3, so an average payoff of 1.60 corresponds to an efficiency of ≈ 0.53.)

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   Not mentioned.  No prediction.

10. Reward cost to rewarder  
    Not mentioned.  No prediction.

11. Reward magnitude  
    Not mentioned.  No prediction.

12. Is the number of rounds common knowledge?  
    Not discussed.  No prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    Not discussed.  No prediction.

14. Are punishers identified?  
    Not applicable; punishment is an imposed system-wide fine.  No prediction.

15. Are rewarders identified?  
    Not applicable; no reward is used.  No prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY (requested format)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables used  
   • Collective average expected payoff (sometimes called “collective benefits”).  
   • Density of “dangerous strategies” (strategies with p₄ ≈ 0).  
   These are *not* the same as group efficiency as defined in the user query (payoff divided by maximum possible payoff).  The authors never compute that ratio.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   3 parameters:  
     #1 Number of players (fixed at 10 000)  
     #2 Number of rounds (fixed at 2000)  
     #8 Punishment magnitude (varied)

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of **systematically varying** the parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
   Exactly 1 parameter – Punishment magnitude (parameter 8).

D. What predictions can we make—strictly from this paper—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
   • Increasing punishment magnitude (from 0.3 up to ≥ 0.6 in this model) monotonically raises average payoff and thereby efficiency; below about 0.6, punishment is too weak to eliminate low-p₄ “dangerous” strategies.  
   • For all other parameters (1-7, 9-15) the paper provides no evidence, so no prediction can be made solely on the basis of this text.

That is the full extent of what the paper allows us to infer.

Below I go through the 15 parameters one-by-one, quoting exactly what the paper says (or does not say) about each of them, and, when possible, extracting what the authors report about **systematically varying** that parameter and its influence on any “punishment-treatment effect.”  
(The authors never work with a public-goods game, never report group efficiency, and use “fraction of cooperators” and “payoff / payoff-distribution” as their dependent variables.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned: “Results … are obtained on 100 × 100 square lattices. … N=L² = 10 000.”  
   • Systematic variation? None. The lattice size is fixed, and no effect of changing N is reported.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned: “last 1 000 time steps out of 20 000 total time steps.”  
   • Not varied; no effect discussed.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Never mentioned.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule?  
   • Not applicable (the study uses 2-player PDG and SD, not a PGG).

5. Contribution default / retraction?  
   • Not applicable.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor (or analogous payoff parameters)  
   • Closest analogues are PDG temptation b (1.1 vs 1.3) and SD cost-to-benefit ratio r (0.4 vs 0.6).  
   • The paper shows that higher b (or higher r) lowers cooperation, but these comparisons are descriptive only; there is no regression or quantified “treatment effect.”  
   • No efficiency measure is reported, only ρ_c.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   • Cost is not attached to an individual punisher; instead the model introduces a *system-wide* proportional cost parameter p:  
     c = p × N × P_x / Σ_{φ_x} P_x.  
   • p is systematically varied (0 ≤ p ≤ 1).  
   • Reported effect: Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 show that, for any fixed β, increasing p monotonically raises ρ_c, eventually to full cooperation. Concrete numbers (from Fig. 1a, PDG, b=1.1, β=0.3): ρ_c≈0 at p=0, ≈0.3 at p=0.2, ≈1 at p≈0.6. No payoff/efficiency numbers given.

8. Punishment magnitude  
   • Strength of punishment β (0 ≤ β ≤ 1); f = β × P_x.  
   • β is systematically varied.  
   • Reported effect: For any fixed p, larger β increases ρ_c (Fig. 2 heat map). In payoff-distribution figures (Figs. 5 & 6) higher β moves mass from low-payoff to high-payoff intervals, implying a higher mean payoff, but no numerical averages or efficiencies are provided.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Not present.

10. Reward cost  
   • Not present.

11. Reward magnitude  
   • Not present.

12. End-game knowledge (finite / known horizon)  
   • Not mentioned (infinite-horizon Monte-Carlo simulation).

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
   • Not applicable; agents follow an imitation rule that uses neighbor payoffs, but there is no experimental display.

14. Punisher identity revealed?  
   • Not applicable.

15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
   • Not applicable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables used  
   • Group efficiency (total or average payoff divided by the maximum possible) is **not** used.  
   • Variables actually analysed:  
     – ρ_c (fraction of cooperators).  
     – Payoff distribution histograms (and occasional qualitative statements about “average payoff”).  
     These variables are not the same as efficiency; no efficiency ratio is reported.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   • 5 of 15: 1 (players), 2 (rounds), 6 (payoff parameters b or r), 7 (punishment cost parameter p), 8 (punishment magnitude β).

C. For how many parameters is there discussion of their *systematic* effect on a punishment treatment?  
   • 2 parameters: p (#7) and β (#8).  
   • The paper also shows two values of b or r, but does not systematically explore their interaction with punishment.

D. Predicting the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency solely from this paper  
   • The authors do not calculate efficiency, so any prediction must be indirect.  
   • Qualitatively, the paper shows that (i) higher p and (ii) higher β both raise the cooperation rate and shift the payoff distribution toward higher values. If efficiency were eventually computed as total payoff / maximum possible, one would expect efficiency to increase with p and β, at least until cooperation saturates.  
   • No statement can be made about parameters 3–5 and 9–15, and almost nothing about parameters 1, 2, or 6, because the paper neither varies them systematically nor links them to any efficiency-like outcome.

Article Title: The competitive advantage of sanctioning institutions revisited: A multilab replication
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; COLLECTIVE ACTION; COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; REPLICABILITY
Abstract: Is peer sanctioning a sustainable solution to the problem of human cooperation? We conducted an exact multilab replication (N = 1,008; 7 labs x 12 groups x 12 participants) of an experiment by Gurerk, Irlenbusch, and Rockenbach published in Science in 2006 (Gurerk o, Irlenbusch B, Rockenbach B. The competitive advantage of sanctioning institutions. 2006. Science. 312(5770):108-111). In GIR2006 (N = 84; 1 lab x 7 groups x 12 participants), groups that allowed members to reward cooperators and punish defectors were found to outgrow and outperform groups without a peer-sanctioning institution. We find GIR2006 replicated in accordance with all preregistered replication criteria in five of the seven labs we sampled. There, the majority of participants joined groups with a sanctioning institution, and participants cooperated and profited more on average than in groups without a sanctioning institution. In the two other labs, results were weaker but still favored sanctioning institutions. These findings establish the competitive advantage of sanctioning institutions as a robust phenomenon within the European context.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter summary regarding (a) whether the paper mentions each of the 15 parameters (and, if so, the value used in this study) and (b) whether it reports or predicts how systematically varying that parameter would affect the “punishment treatment effect”—in particular, its effect on efficiency (actual total payoff / maximum possible total payoff for a fully cooperative group) or on any of the other dependent variables the paper examines.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The experiment always has groups of 12.  
   • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No. The paper does not discuss changing group size or how changing it would affect the punishment treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? Yes. All sessions involve exactly 30 rounds (stated as such in the design).  
   • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No. There is no discussion of varying the number of rounds or how such variation might affect the efficiency of punishment.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned? Not in the sense of switching it on/off. The design does not include any chat/communication option, and the paper does not discuss it.  
   • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No. There is no mention of enabling or disabling chat, nor any prediction of how chat would alter punishment outcomes.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned? The paper describes a standard linear public goods game where each participant chooses any contribution from 0 to 20 tokens. So it is not “all or nothing.”  
   • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No. No discussion of making it all‐or‐nothing or potential impacts of that.

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., participants moving existing tokens back to themselves)?  
   • Mentioned? The paper uses a standard “contribute some portion of your 20 tokens” design. There is no discussion of a “default contribution” mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No. The study does not address or vary whether contributions are framed as “taking back” tokens.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The contribution is multiplied by 1.6 before being evenly redistributed. That implies an MPCR of 1.6 / (number of people in that institution).  
   • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No. They do not alter the multiplier or predict how changing it would affect punishment on efficiency.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each negative token assigned costs the punisher 1 token.  
   • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No. The paper reports only the single cost (1 token) and does not discuss how changing it would affect outcomes.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player per unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each negative token deducts 3 tokens from the target’s payoff.  
   • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No. No discussion of altering the 1:3 ratio or how that would impact efficiency.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Reward is enabled in the same institution that allows punishment.  
   • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No. The experiment always has reward and punishment together in the “sanctioning institution.” The paper does not discuss removing reward or systematically varying it.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Mentioned? Yes. It costs the reward‐giver 1 token.  
   • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No. The study does not explore changing that cost or how it would affect the punishment treatment effect.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. One positive token increases another’s payoff by 1 token.  
   • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No. As with punishment, the paper does not vary or discuss varying the 1:1 ratio.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Participants interact for 30 rounds, and the text indicates this is the known structure.  
   • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No. There is no commentary on what would happen if the game length were unknown or varied.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much others gained/lost each round)?  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Participants see everyone’s contributions, assigned tokens (positive/negative), and total round payoffs (although the order is randomized to avoid identification).  
   • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No. The paper does not vary the information that participants see or predict the consequences of changing it.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper explicitly states that the presentation order is randomized so that the punished cannot learn who punished them.  
   • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No. The paper keeps punisher identity hidden and does not discuss changing it.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Mentioned? Yes. As with punishment, the identity of the rewarder is also hidden (randomized listing).  
   • Systematically varied or predictions about varying it? No. The paper does not address making the rewarder identifiable or any effects that such an alteration might have.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Summary

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?

• The paper’s primary outcomes are individual and group “payoffs” or “profits,” and the proportion of participants choosing the sanctioning‐enabled institution. Although the word “outperform” is used, the study does not calculate “efficiency” strictly as (actual total payoff) / (maximum possible payoff). Instead, it tracks average or total earnings, cooperation/contribution levels, and institutional choice. Hence, “efficiency” in the precise sense of maximum‐possible‐payoff ratio is not reported, although the paper discusses payoffs/profits and cooperation rates.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

• All 15 parameters arise in some form in the design description (for instance, group size = 12; 30 rounds; no chat; continuous [0–20] contributions; MPCR = 1.6, etc.). However, the paper simply describes them as fixed design choices. It does not describe any changes to these parameters.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?

• None. The authors do not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters. They implemented the same protocol (same group size, same MPCR, same costs and magnitudes of punishment/reward, same number of rounds, same information format) in every location. There is no numerical effect size reported for how changing a parameter would alter outcomes.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

• The paper does not provide direct evidence or discussion about varying these parameters. The authors note that varying institutional features (e.g., other forms of sanctioning, different costs) is an important line for future research, but they do not supply new data or predictions for how changes would impact group efficiency. Hence, based only on what is stated, one cannot draw evidence‐based conclusions about how systematically altering each parameter would affect punishment’s impact on efficiency.
reference_APA: Lo Iacono, Sergio, Przepiorka, Wojtek, Buskens, Vincent, Corten, Rense, van Assen, Marcel & van de Rijt, Arnout (2023). The competitive advantage of sanctioning institutions revisited: A multilab replication. PNAS NEXUS.

Article Title: Sanctioned Quotas Versus Information Provisioning for Community Wildlife Conservation in Zimbabwe: A Framed Field Experiment Approach

Keywords Plus: THRESHOLD PUBLIC-GOODS; PROPERTY-RIGHTS; REGIME SHIFTS; COOPERATION; PUNISHMENT; DILEMMAS; COORDINATION; INSTITUTIONS; ENFORCEMENT; UNCERTAINTY
Abstract: We investigate the behavioural responses of natural common-pool resource users to three policy interventions-sanctioned quotas, information provisioning, and a combination of both. We focus on situations in which users find utility in multiple resources (pastures and wild animal stocks) that all stem from the same ecosystem with complex dynamics, and management could trigger a regime shift, drastically altering resource regrowth. We performed a framed field experiment with 384 villagers from communities managing common-pool wildlife in Zimbabwe. We find that user groups are likely to manage these natural resources more efficiently when facing a policy intervention (either a sanctioned quota, receiving information about a drastic drop in the stocks' regrowth below a threshold, or a combination of both), compared to groups facing no intervention. However, having information about the threshold also leads to higher efficiency and fewer depletion cases, compared to a situation without any intervention. The main contribution of this study is to provide insights that can inform policymakers and development practitioners about the performance of concrete and feasible policy interventions for community wildlife conservation in Southern Africa.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter account of what this paper does (and does not) say about each of the 15 parameters in your list, followed by the requested four-part summary.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. Each group in the experiment always consists of four players.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how varying it would affect punishment’s impact on efficiency (or any other dependent variable)?  
     – No. There is no indication that the number of players was altered across sessions or that the authors predict how changing the group size would affect the punishment treatment effect.

2) Number of rounds  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. The game continues for multiple rounds, and in practice ends either after 1 hour or if the elephant stock is depleted. The exact ending round is not known to participants.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how varying it would affect punishment’s impact on efficiency (or any other dependent variable)?  
     – No. They do not vary the number of rounds or analyze its systematic effect on punishment.

3) Is chat (communication) enabled between players?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. Players are always allowed to communicate face to face throughout the experiment (except at the instant of making their individual decisions).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how varying it would affect punishment’s impact on efficiency (or any other dependent variable)?  
     – No. In all treatments, communication is present; there is no “no-communication” treatment, nor predictions about systematically changing it.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. Participants can choose any integer amount of elephants to harvest, from zero up to the current stock. They are not forced to pick “all or nothing.”  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict how varying it would affect punishment’s impact on efficiency (or any other dependent variable)?  
     – No.

5) Is the contribution default (i.e., are participants forced to “take back” part of an endowment)?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. This is not a standard public-goods setting with a default contribution or endowment-reversal mechanism.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict any effect of such a design on punishment’s impact?  
     – No.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related “multiplication factor”  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – The paper uses a logistic growth function (or a thresholded variant) to model elephant and pasture stocks, but does not frame the payoffs in terms of an MPCR.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about how changing the multiplication factor would influence punishment’s effect on efficiency?  
     – No. There is no such systematic variation or explicit discussion.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Not in the sense of “peer punishment cost.” The experiment implements a “quota plus sanction” mechanism, where a top-down check (a die roll) may penalize offenders. There is no mention of a cost born by another player who punishes, because it is not peer-to-peer punishment.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary the cost of punishment or predict how changing this cost affects efficiency or punishment’s effect?  
     – No.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a punished player)  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes, but it is fixed. If the total harvest in a round exceeds the quota (i.e., if the elephant stock falls below 20), there is a 2/3 chance of someone being “controlled.” A caught player forfeits the harvested elephants of that round and is banned (cannot harvest) in the next round.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary that magnitude or predict how changing it would affect punishment’s effect on efficiency (or any outcome)?  
     – No. The magnitude is always the same (forfeit + temporary harvesting ban). There is no discussion of systematically altering it.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. There is no mention of a reward mechanism.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary a reward or predict its effect?  
     – No.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. As there is no reward mechanism, it is not addressed.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict an effect on punishment’s impact?  
     – No.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. Reward is not used in these experiments at all.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or predict an effect on punishment’s impact?  
     – No.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players? (Do they know when the game ends?)  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. Participants do not know exactly how many rounds will be played. This is done to minimize end-game effects.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary “known vs. unknown ending” or predict how that would affect punishment’s effect on efficiency?  
     – No. They keep the indefinite-horizon setup in all sessions.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players see each other’s payoffs or contributions)?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Participants see group-level total harvest, new stock of elephants, and new stock of pastures, but do not see individual harvest levels.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary how much outcome information is shown or predict how that would affect punishment’s effect on efficiency?  
     – No. It is the same across all treatments.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who specifically punished them?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. Punishment is instituted by a random check (dice) from the “experimenter/authority,” not by a specific peer. There is no mention that the identity of any punisher is known—indeed there is no peer punisher.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary that knowledge or predict how it affects punishment’s impact on efficiency?  
     – No, it does not.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who specifically rewarded them?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. There is no reward process in place.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary that knowledge or predict how it affects punishment’s impact on efficiency?  
     – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • Yes. The main dependent variables include  
     – Efficiency: defined as the ratio of the group’s actual joint earnings over the maximum possible joint earnings.  
     – Stock size of elephants (especially crossing or not crossing the threshold).  
     – Occurrence of resource depletion.  
     – Average (or total) payoff is also reported, but the paper usually refers to it in tandem with efficiency.  

   The paper also analyzes whether the resource stock dips below the threshold or is fully depleted, but that is a separate measure from efficiency. They usually focus on “efficiency” and on “stock levels” as the core outcomes.

B) Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
     1) Number of players (always 4, no variation),  
     2) Number of rounds (indefinite, not varied),  
     3) Chat (communication) is always present,  
     8) Punishment magnitude (they have a fixed “forfeit + ban” rule),  
     12) Number of rounds is unknown,  
     13) Peer outcomes (group-level) displayed.  
   • The paper does not mention or implement any systematic variation for the other parameters (4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15), nor does it discuss them in the sense of systematically varying them.  

C) For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect, specifically when that parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. The paper’s “punishment” is introduced via a sanctioned quota treatment (and that same punishment magnitude/rule is used whenever the elephant stock falls below the 20-unit threshold). However, the authors do not actually vary that feature (punishment cost or magnitude), nor do they vary any other game feature (e.g., group size, number of rounds known vs. unknown, presence vs. absence of communication).  

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of this paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not provide direct evidence for any systematic relationship between changes in those 15 parameters (other than the presence vs. absence of the sanctioned quota itself) and efficiency under punishment. The study only reports that introducing a sanctioned quota (with its fixed punishment scheme) plus (or minus) threshold information is associated with higher efficiency than no quota—and that combining quota plus threshold information does not outperform having just the quota alone. Beyond those comparisons, there is no discussion of how changing group size, altering chat, injecting a reward mechanism, changing punishment magnitude, or making the ending round known, etc., would affect efficiency. Therefore, based solely on this paper, one cannot make evidence-based predictions about how systematically varying those parameters (beyond the presence or absence of the sanctioned quota) would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Article Title: Two-layer network model of public goods games with intervention and corruption
Keywords Plus: PROMOTES COOPERATION; EVOLUTIONARY GAMES; EMERGENCE; STRATEGY
Abstract: Public goods games are widely used to model social dilemmas involving multiple agents. Though defection is the only rational choice for an individual in a public goods game, cooperative behavior is observed in a variety of social dilemmas, which is the subject of our research. Punishing defectors has been shown to be an effective mechanism for promoting cooperation, but it relies on the third-party umpire being fair. In this article, an umpire intervention model with corruption is proposed to explore the impact of corruption on punishment mechanisms. In our model, players and umpires operate in a multilayer network. The players play public goods games, which are overseen by umpires. Fair umpires punish defectors, whereas corrupt umpires take bribes from defectors rather than meting out a punishment. We separately explore the effects of the fraction of fair umpires rho(f), the spatial distribution, and the fine cost alpha and bribe cost beta. Our Monte Carlo simulation shows that the above factors have a significant impact on cooperation. Intervention by an umpire always improves social efficiency, even for an entirely corrupt system. Moreover, relatively developed systems can resist corruption. Staggered and centralized distributions always have opposite effects on cooperative behavior, and these effects depend on rho(f) and r. We also find that whether cooperators fully occupy the player layer depends only on whether beta reaches a certain threshold. Published under an exclusive license by AIP Publishing.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter review, following your numbered list of 15 parameters, indicating (1) whether the paper discusses the parameter (and if so, what specific value or setting is used), and (2) whether the paper makes predictions about how systematically varying that parameter would affect the “punishment treatment effect” for any dependent variable—especially efficiency (defined as total payoff / maximum possible payoff). When the paper instead reports effects on other variables such as the fraction of cooperators (ρc), that is noted explicitly.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   (1) Mentioned?  
       – Yes, the paper uses L×L=100×100 players (in one set of simulations) and also considers a scale‐free network with M=10 000.  
   (2) Systematically varied?  
       – No. The paper does not vary the number of players or discuss its effect on punishment or efficiency.

2. Number of rounds
   (1) Mentioned?  
       – The authors run each simulation for 20 000 steps to ensure stability, but “number of rounds” per se is not treated as a design parameter.  
   (2) Systematically varied?  
       – No. The paper does not investigate changes in the number of rounds.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   (1) Mentioned?  
       – No.  
   (2) Systematically varied?  
       – Not applicable.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   (1) Mentioned?  
       – Effectively yes. Each cooperator invests a cost of 1, while each defector invests 0, i.e., an all‐or‐nothing scheme.  
   (2) Systematically varied?  
       – No. There is no exploration of different contribution rules.

5. Is the contribution default?
   (1) Mentioned?  
       – No. The paper does not discuss any default mechanism whereby players “move” monies in or out of the public fund.  
   (2) Systematically varied?  
       – Not applicable.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   (1) Mentioned?  
       – Yes. The paper calls this “synergy factor” r. It is systematically varied (e.g., r from 1.1 to 4.5).  
   (2) Systematically varied and predictions for punishment effect?  
       – The paper examines how different values of r affect the fraction of cooperators (ρc). Although it sometimes refers to “social efficiency,” it reports results primarily in terms of cooperation levels rather than the payoff‐based efficiency ratio. Numerical “effect sizes” appear as thresholds for r above which cooperation thrives (e.g., a threshold of r ≈ 3.64 with no umpires; lower thresholds around r ≈ 2.92 or 1.52 when umpires—fair or corrupt—are introduced). The paper does not provide a separate quantitative measure of “punishment treatment effect on efficiency,” but it does show that higher r, together with the presence of punishment (even if partially corrupt), raises ρc.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   (1) Mentioned?  
       – No. In this model, the paper does not include a specific cost borne by the punisher.  
   (2) Systematically varied?  
       – Not applicable. The paper does not address punisher‐side costs.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from a punished player)
   (1) Mentioned?  
       – Yes. The paper’s parameter α is the (per‐defector) “fine cost,” i.e., how much a defector pays a fair umpire. This is the magnitude of the punishment.  
   (2) Systematically varied and predictions for punishment effect?  
       – Yes, α is systematically varied (e.g., 1.0 ≤ α ≤ 2.5 or higher). The paper shows that the fraction of cooperators (ρc) generally increases as α increases. They give one illustrative linear boundary 2 α + 3 β − 3.3 ≈ 0 dividing scenarios of higher vs. lower cooperation—though that refers to fraction of cooperators, not efficiency. The paper does not report a numerical “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” but does highlight that a larger α promotes more cooperation.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   (1) Mentioned?  
       – No. The model is strictly about punishing defectors (or taking bribes), with no reward mechanism.  
   (2) Systematically varied?  
       – Not applicable.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    (1) Mentioned?  
        – No.  
    (2) Systematically varied?  
        – Not applicable.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded per unit of reward)
    (1) Mentioned?  
        – No.  
    (2) Systematically varied?  
        – Not applicable.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
    (1) Mentioned?  
        – No. The paper does not discuss whether participants (modeled agents) know how many steps or rounds remain.  
    (2) Systematically varied?  
        – Not applicable.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?
    (1) Mentioned?  
        – Not explicitly. Players do use a Fermi‐type rule comparing payoffs locally, but there is no explicit manipulation of “outcome visibility.”  
    (2) Systematically varied?  
        – No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who punished them?
    (1) Mentioned?  
        – No. The paper does not discuss whether the identity of the punisher (fair umpire vs. neighbor) is displayed. Umpires are simply either fair or corrupt.  
    (2) Systematically varied?  
        – Not applicable.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who rewarded them?
    (1) Mentioned?  
        – No; the model does not include rewards.  
    (2) Systematically varied?  
        – Not applicable.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary:

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (actual payoff / maximum payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper occasionally uses the term “social efficiency” but does not formally measure efficiency as total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff. Its key dependent variable is the fraction of cooperators ρc (and sometimes payoff levels are mentioned locally). Thus, whenever “efficiency” is referenced, it is more an informal statement that higher cooperation can lead to higher collective benefit—rather than a specific ratio of total to maximum payoff.

B. Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Two parameters from your list are definitely mentioned and explored.  
     – Parameter #6 (the synergy factor r) is varied extensively.  
     – Parameter #8 (punishment magnitude, α) is also varied.  
   • All other parameters (#1, #2, #3, #4, #5, #7, #9, #10, #11, #12, #13, #14, #15) are either fixed, implicit without variation, or not addressed at all.

C. For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • The paper systematically varies #6 (r) and #8 (α). However, it does not report a formal “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Instead, it reports changes in the fraction of cooperators. No quantitative effect sizes are provided for an “efficiency ratio”; thresholds and curves are given for ρc.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper itself only gives clear evidence about synergy factor r and punishment magnitude α. It indicates that as r and α increase, cooperation is sustained more easily, and so presumably overall payoffs would rise. Even wholly corrupt oversight slightly raises cooperation relative to no oversight at all. For the remaining parameters (#1, #2, #3, #4, #5, #7, #9–#15), the paper provides no discussion, so no predictions can be made from the paper’s content alone.

Authors: Otten, K; Buskens, V; Przepiorka, W; Cherki, B; Israel, S
Author Full Names: Otten, Kasper; Buskens, Vincent; Przepiorka, Wojtek; Cherki, Boaz; Israel, Salomon
Article Title: Cooperation, punishment, and group change in multilevel public goods experiments
Author Keywords: Multilevel public goods; Cooperation; Punishment; Norms
Keywords Plus: CONFLICT; INFORMATION; STRANGERS; NORMS; CATEGORIZATION; COORDINATION; NEIGHBORHOOD; ENFORCEMENT; EVOLUTION; FAILURE
Abstract: Peer punishment is regarded as an important element in sustaining human cooperation for public good provision. Many behavioral experiments have shown that public good provision is higher if cooperation norms can be enforced by peer punishment. These experiments predominantly focus on single-group public goods, in which people have to choose between their private interests and the interests of their group. However, many societal problems comprise multilevel public goods problems, where multiple local groups are nested within a larger global group. We study experimentally how punishment affects cooperation and norms in multilevel public goods games. In our lab experiment, two local groups are nested within a larger global group. Participants have to choose between not contributing, contributing locally, and contributing globally. Local contributions would lead to a fragmented outcome where two separate local public goods are provided, whereas global contributions would lead to a unified global good that benefits all. Moreover, we study whether cooperation and punishment patterns depend on the type of public good participants are initially exposed to: single-group or multilevel. Participants either begin in a single-group public goods game and then shift to a multilevel public goods game or vice versa. We find that punishment is less effective in multilevel public goods games than in single-group public goods games. Punishment only promotes cooperation in multilevel public goods games if people have prior experience with solving single-group public goods games. Our results refine the boundary conditions for the effectiveness of punishment and suggest that 'starting small' by first solving single-group public goods problems is helpful for successful multilevel public good provision.

Below each of the 15 parameters we report exactly what can be learned from the paper and nothing more.

1. Number of players  
– Mentioned? Yes.  Groups always contain 4 players (two local sub-groups of two each in the multilevel game; four of the same colour in the single-group game).  
– Systematically varied? No.  All conditions use 4 players.  
– Prediction when varied? None.  The paper never analyses how changing group size would alter the punishment treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
– Mentioned? Yes.  Each part lasts 10 rounds; participants are merely told the part will last “between 8 and 12” rounds.  
– Systematically varied? No.  
– Prediction when varied? None.  The paper only reports the usual decay of contributions over rounds but gives no estimate of how a different round length or knowledge of the horizon would change the punishment effect.

3. Chat enabled?  
– Mentioned? No.  There is no communication and no discussion of its consequences.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
– Mentioned? Yes, implicitly.  Contributions are continuous (0–20 MU); nothing is forced to be all-or-nothing.  
– Systematically varied? No.  
– Prediction when varied? None.

5. Is the contribution “default” (reversible extraction)?  
– Mentioned? No.  Subjects allocate their endowment; there is no default pull-back stage.  No further discussion.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor  
– Mentioned? Yes.  Private: 1.0; Local: 0.7; Global: 0.5.  
– Systematically varied? No.  
– Prediction when varied? None.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
– Mentioned? Yes.  1 MU per punishment point.  
– Systematically varied? No.  
– Prediction when varied? None.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine to target)  
– Mentioned? Yes.  3 MU deducted per punishment point.  
– Systematically varied? No.  
– Prediction when varied? None.

9. Reward option enabled?  
– Mentioned? Yes, indirectly – there is no reward stage.  
– Systematically varied? No.  
– Prediction when varied? None (because rewards are never present).

10. Reward cost  
– Not applicable.

11. Reward magnitude  
– Not applicable.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
– Mentioned? Yes.  Players are only told a range (8–12); the exact number is concealed.  
– Systematically varied? No.  
– Prediction when varied? None.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
– Mentioned? Yes.  After each round players see every other member’s local and global contributions and, in punishment conditions, how many points they received.  
– Systematically varied? No.  
– Prediction when varied? None.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
– Mentioned? Yes.  Punishment is anonymous; targets see the number of points but not the source.  
– Systematically varied? No.  
– Prediction when varied? None.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
– Not applicable: there is no reward stage.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used  
– The paper does **not** report “group efficiency” (total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff).  
– Main behavioural variables: Local contributions (MU), Global contributions (MU), Total contributions (MU), Received punishment points, Assigned punishment points.  
– Additional variables: Personal normative views, Normative expectations, Empirical expectations.  These are conceptually different from efficiency because they measure amounts contributed or beliefs, not realised monetary pay-offs relative to an optimum.

B. Which parameters of the 15 are even mentioned?  
8 of 15:  (1) number of players, (2) number of rounds, (4) contribution not all-or-nothing, (6) MPCR, (7) punishment cost, (8) punishment magnitude, (12) uncertainty about horizon, (13) peer outcomes displayed, (14) punisher anonymity.  (Parameters 3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 15 are absent; 4 is implicit.)

C. Which parameters are *systematically varied* and analysed for their effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
None of the 15.  The only manipulated factors in the experiment are (i) whether punishment is available at all and (ii) the order of single-group vs multilevel play.  Neither factor is one of the 15 parameters on your list, so the paper contains 0 parameter-by-punishment interactions and 0 numerical effect sizes relevant to those parameters.

D. Predictions about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, based solely on this paper  
Because none of the parameters were varied or modelled, the paper offers virtually no leverage for forecasting how changing them would raise or lower efficiency.  At most, the text implies:  
– Keeping punishment anonymous (parameter 14 = “anonymous”) is compatible with punishment boosting cooperation in the single-group game and (when groups first experienced a single-group game) in the multilevel game; nothing is said about what would happen if anonymity were relaxed.  
– Showing others’ contributions (parameter 13) is a fixed design element; its importance is assumed but not tested.  
All other parameters are fixed and unanalysed.  Therefore, on the basis of this paper alone one can make **little to no prediction** about how systematic changes in any of the 15 parameters would alter the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Article Title: Collective minimum contributions to counteract the ratchet effect in the voluntary provision of public goods
Source Title: JOURNAL OF ENVIRONMENTAL ECONOMICS AND MANAGEMENT
Author Keywords: Global public goods; Climate change; Institutions; Ratchet-up mechanism; Minimum contributions; Laboratory experiment
Keywords Plus: COMMUNICATION; INCENTIVES; PUNISHMENT; COMMITMENT; ONLINE; EPAS
Abstract: We experimentally test a theoretically promising amendment to the ratchet-up mechanism of the Paris Agreement. The ratchet-up mechanism prescribes that parties' commitments to the global response to climate change cannot decrease over time, and our results show that its effect is detrimental. We design a public goods game to study whether cooperation is promoted by an amendment to the mechanism that stipulates that all agents must contribute at least a collectively chosen minimum based on the principle of the lowest common denominator. We find that binding collective minimum contributions improve the effectiveness of the ratchet-up mechanism. Non-binding minimum contributions, by contrast, do not encourage cooperation. Our data indicate that the difference is attributable to conditional cooperative dynamics. If other participants contribute less than the collective minimum contribution, even initially cooperative participants start to negatively reciprocate this form of non-compliance by contributing less.

   • Discussed? Indirectly, in that the authors use a piecewise linear fish‐stock function to define how the resource “replenishes.” This function is not framed as an MPCR.

Article Title: The cost of noise: Stochastic punishment falls short of sustaining cooperation in social dilemma experiments
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; STRONG RECIPROCITY; PROVISION; EVOLUTION; UNCERTAINTY; SANCTIONS; JUDGES; RISK; LAW
Abstract: Identifying mechanisms able to sustain costly cooperation among self-interested agents is a central problem across social and biological sciences. One possible solution is peer punishment: when agents have an opportunity to sanction defectors, classical behavioral experiments suggest that cooperation can take root. Overlooked from standard experimental designs, however, is the fact that real-world human punishment-the administration of justice-is intrinsically noisy. Here we show that stochastic punishment falls short of sustaining cooperation in the repeated public good game. As punishment noise increases, we find that contributions decrease and punishment efforts intensify, resulting in a 45% drop in gains compared to a noiseless control. Moreover, we observe that uncertainty causes a rise in antisocial punishment, a mutually harmful behavior previously associated with societies with a weak rule of law. Our approach brings to light challenges to cooperation that cannot be explained by economic rationality and strengthens the case for further investigations of the effect of noise-and not just bias-on human behavior.
