Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter analysis, based strictly on the content of the cited paper (“The combination of social reward and punishment is conducive to the cooperation and heterogeneity of social relations,” Chaos 32, 103104 [2022]). The paper studies a Prisoner’s Dilemma (PD) model on networks with coevolving structure and behavior, focusing primarily on the population’s “cooperation frequency” (i.e., fraction of cooperators in the population) as the outcome variable. It does not study a public goods game with a notion of “efficiency” (total payoff/max possible payoff) nor systematically compare punishment vs. no‐punishment in terms of efficiency. Instead, it emphasizes how varying a “punishment factor” (k₁), a “reward factor” (k₂), and the temptation to defect (b) influences long‐run cooperation frequencies. Below, each of the 15 parameters is checked against what the paper does or does not discuss, noting if the paper provides any systematic variation or if it makes any predictions about that parameter’s effect on punishment “treatment” with respect to any dependent variable (in this paper, the main dependent variable is cooperation frequency rather than efficiency).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1) Number of players  
   • Discussed?  
     – The paper does fix the number of individuals (N) in simulations. Common choices are N = 1000 (main text) or N = 100 (illustrations).  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. The paper does not report any systematic manipulation of N and does not link varying N to how punishment affects outcomes.  
   • Effect size or prediction about punishment treatment?  
     – None. No predictions about varying N are provided.

2) Number of rounds  
   • Discussed?  
     – The model is run for many time steps (up to 10⁴) until convergence, but these “time steps” are not analyzed in the sense of a finite‐round repeated game; they are simply steps of an evolutionary process.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. The paper does not explore how changing the total number of rounds/time‐steps would alter punishment effects.  
   • Effect size or prediction about punishment treatment?  
     – None.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. There is no mention of communication or “chat” between players.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Not applicable.  
   • Effect size or prediction?  
     – None.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Discussed?  
     – The paper analyzes a two‐strategy Prisoner’s Dilemma (cooperate or defect). It is indeed “all or nothing” in that sense, but the paper does not call it a public‐goods‐type “all‐or‐nothing contribution.”  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. They do not vary the strategy space; it remains a standard PD with binary choices.  
   • Effect size or prediction?  
     – None.

5) Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much of their endowment to keep)?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The paper’s PD model has only “C” or “D.” There is no partial or default contribution.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Not applicable.  
   • Effect size or prediction?  
     – None.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor  
   • Discussed?  
     – In the paper’s PD setting, the key “temptation to defect” payoff is b, which they vary from 1.0 up to 2.5. This is loosely analogous to how strongly a defector out‐earns a cooperator and can be seen as playing a similar role to a “multiplication factor.”  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Yes. The paper devotes extensive analysis to varying b in increments from 1.0 up to 2.5 and shows how the network’s cooperation frequency changes under different (k₁, k₂) values.  
   • Effect size or prediction about punishment treatment?  
     – The main dependent variable is cooperation frequency, not “efficiency.” They show that, as b increases (larger temptation), cooperation collapses to zero in the classic PD without reward/punishment; however, once punishment (k₁ > 0) and reward (k₂ > 0) are introduced, substantial cooperation persists for higher b. For instance, standard PD might yield ≈0% cooperators at b=1.4, whereas with moderate punishment and reward (e.g., k₁=0.6, k₂=0.6), cooperation can remain well above 0.5 or even near 1.0 in favorable parameter ranges (see Figs. 2–3). These numeric results concern the proportion of cooperators, not efficiency.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. In this PD setting, the “punishment” is cutting (severing) a link, controlled by k₁; there is no explicit “cost in coins” to the punisher. Hence the paper does not discuss or vary a punishment cost.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Not applicable.  
   • Effect size or prediction about “punishment cost”?  
     – None.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. In the paper’s model, punishment means that a cooperator may sever its link to a defector. No numeric “fine” or deduction is imposed.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Not applicable; the paper’s “punishment factor” k₁ is not a payoff deduction but instead a parameter that influences the probability links are cut.  
   • Effect size or prediction?  
     – None.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussed?  
     – Yes. The paper explicitly models a reward mechanism controlled by k₂. If k₂ > 0, there is a nonzero probability to create new links (“reward”), whereas k₂ = 0 turns off this mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – Yes. They vary k₂ from 0 up to 1.0 and examine how synergy with punishment (k₁ > 0) boosts cooperation.  
   • Effect size or prediction about “punishment treatment effect”?  
     – The paper’s dependent variable is cooperation frequency, not efficiency. They find:  
       – If only reward (k₂>0) is used (with no punishment), cooperation typically fails at high b.  
       – If both reward and punishment are present, cooperation can thrive, even for large b, often near 100% (see Fig. 3 and Table I).

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Discussed?  
      – No. As with punishment, this paper sets up a probability of forming new links (the “reward”), but there is no explicit cost to a “rewarder.”  
    • Systematically varied?  
      – Not applicable.  
    • Effect size or prediction?  
      – None.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
    • Discussed?  
      – No. The paper’s “reward” is the formation of a new tie; there is no direct numeric reward or payoff increment.  
    • Systematically varied?  
      – Not applicable.  
    • Effect size or prediction?  
      – None.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    • Discussed?  
      – No. The model runs for many discrete time steps in an evolutionary manner and does not address participants’ knowledge of game length.  
    • Systematically varied?  
      – Not addressed.  
    • Effect size or prediction?  
      – None.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?  
    • Discussed?  
      – The paper does state that each individual compares payoffs with neighbors for imitation decisions. However, there is no discussion about systematically hiding or revealing those outcomes.  
    • Systematically varied?  
      – No.  
    • Effect size or prediction?  
      – None.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Discussed?  
      – No. The paper’s link‐severing process does not address whether punished individuals “know” who cut the link.  
    • Systematically varied?  
      – Not applicable.  
    • Effect size or prediction?  
      – None.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Discussed?  
      – No. The paper does not discuss whether newly formed links reveal the “rewarder’s” identity.  
    • Systematically varied?  
      – Not applicable.  
    • Effect size or prediction?  
      – None.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   – The paper does not measure “efficiency” (total payoff / maximum possible payoff). Its primary outcome variable is the long‐run fraction of cooperators (“cooperation frequency”). The authors do sometimes examine individual payoffs in intermediate steps, but their main focus is on how many cooperators ultimately survive or dominate. They do not use “efficiency” in the sense commonly used in public goods experiments.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – (1) Number of players: Mentioned (N=100, 1000), but not systematically varied.  
   – (6) A PD temptation parameter b is systematically varied from 1.0 to 2.5 (analogous to a multiplier but not labeled as MPCR).  
   – (9) Whether a reward mechanism is present/absent is effectively turned on/off by setting k₂>0 or k₂=0.  
   – The paper does not otherwise align with or discuss the remaining parameters in the sense of typical public‐goods designs (e.g., no mention of penalty costs, reward costs in coins, known endpoints, or chat).

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   – The paper systematically varies three things: the temptation b (akin to #6), the punishment factor k₁, and the reward factor k₂. In the paper’s language, “punishment treatment” corresponds to “k₁>0,” with or without “reward” (k₂>0). That is not the same as a typical “punishment cost” or “punishment magnitude” in a standard public‐goods experiment, but it is indeed how that paper operationalizes punishment. The authors compare results with k₁=0 vs. k₁>0 (and likewise for k₂) across many values of b. They report large changes in cooperation frequency but do not speak of “efficiency.”

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper’s content, what would they be?  
   – The paper does not analyze efficiency (payoff‐maximization relative to a fully cooperative benchmark). All remarks pertain to cooperation frequency, not group efficiency. Beyond that, only (6) (temptation, b), (9) (presence/absence of reward), and their interplay with a punishment factor (k₁) are systematically studied. There is no direct discussion of how any of the other parameters—number of players, cost/magnitude of punishment, knowledge of rounds, or whether outcomes are visible—would affect a notion of “treatment effect on efficiency.” Consequently, the paper provides little or no direct basis for predicting changes in group efficiency with respect to any of the 15 parameters, other than noting that, when “punishment” (k₁>0) and “reward” (k₂>0) are added together, the fraction of cooperators often rises dramatically. If one extended their results to efficiency in a hypothetical public‐goods sense, the only clear inference is that reward plus punishment helps maintain high cooperation (which could imply higher payoffs). No further numerical or systematic predictions about efficiency can be made from the paper.

Authors: Doering, L; Ody-Brasier, A
Author Full Names: Doering, Laura; Ody-Brasier, Amandine
Article Title: Time and Punishment: How Individuals Respond to Being Sanctioned in Voluntary Associations
Keywords Plus: COLLECTIVE ACTION; SOCIAL-EXCHANGE; COOPERATION; NORMS; COMMITMENT; PSYCHOLOGY; ALTRUISM; POWER; ENFORCEMENT; FOUNDATIONS
Abstract: Little consensus exists on how group members respond when sanctioned by their peers. One school of thought suggests individuals become more cooperative, or prosocial, toward the group. Another line of research shows that individuals have negative emotional reactions to being punished and become less cooperative. We reconcile these seemingly conflicting viewpoints in the context of voluntary associations, where cooperation is crucial. Building on social psychological theories of dependence, we propose that responses to sanctions shift over time as individuals become increasingly dependent on other members to achieve valued outcomes. We draw on data from Colombian microsavings groups to develop this proposition, using qualitative data to flesh out the proposed mechanism and longitudinal, quantitative records to test our hypothesis. We find that individuals initially respond to sanctions by reducing prosocial contributions, but their responses become increasingly prosocial over time. This study generates a fresh vision of sanctions as temporally and relationally dependent.

Abstract: We define feasible, posterior individually rational solutions for two-person Bayesian games with a single informed player. Abstract: Current simulation practices in artificial societies typically ignore the contribution of sexuality as a driving force for the evolution of prosocial behaviours.    • Predictions about systematically varying it? No. The paper does not discuss altering these technological parameters.

   • Discussed? Yes, but not varied: the paper adopts a “standard 1:3 punishment technology,” meaning it costs 1 ED to reduce the target’s payoff by 3 EDs (p. 3).

8. Punishment magnitude
   • Discussed? Yes, again as part of 1:3 technology: one punishment point deducts 3 EDs from the punished person (p. 3).

Abstract: The public goods game is a famous example illustrating the tragedy of the commons (Hardin in Science 162:1243-1248, 1968). In this game cooperating individuals contribute to a pool, which in turn is distributed to all members of the group, including defectors who reap the same rewards as cooperators without having made a contribution before. The question is now, how to incentivize group members to all cooperate as it maximizes the common good. While costly punishment (Helbing et al. in New J Phys 12:083005, 2010) presents one such method, the cost of punishment still reduces the common good. The selfishness of the group members favors defectors. Here we show that including other members of the groups and sharing rewards with them can be another incentive for cooperation, avoiding the cost required for punishment. Further, we show how punishment and this form of inclusiveness interact. This work suggests that a redistribution similar to a basic income that is coupled to the economic success of the entire group could overcome the tragedy of the commons.

Abstract: Common resource dilemmas (CRDs) and public good dilemmas (PGDs) are distinct types of social dilemmas, yet they model the same underlying conflict between the collective interest and one's self-interest. Here, we study and interpret behavioral differences between these two main types of social dilemmas by applying a logic of appropriateness. In two experiments, we argue and demonstrate that CRDs, relative to PGDs, evoke higher levels of cooperation, because taking from collective property (in CRDs) is generally considered less appropriate than not giving from personal property (in PGDs). Importantly, these differential considerations of appropriateness are reflected not only in the willingness to cooperate but also in the willingness to punish and reward others' (non)cooperative behavior. Taken together, the findings reveal that CRDs and PGDs elicit different norms of appropriateness.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter inventory, based strictly on what this paper reports. Following that, you will find the required four‐part summary (A through D). In short, the paper does not study “efficiency” (i.e., total payoff relative to the maximum possible) at all, nor does it systematically vary most of the parameters below. Any numerical “effects” reported in the paper refer to how often participants choose to punish (or reward), or how much they cooperate—never to group efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER‐BY‐PARAMETER ANALYSIS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. Number of Players  
   • What the paper says: All sessions use four‐person groups (p. 4, p. 9).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary or predict effects of varying this parameter on the punishment treatment effect (whether on efficiency or on any other outcome)? No. There is no comparison across different group sizes.

2. Number of Rounds  
   • What the paper says: Participants face multiple “one‐shot” social dilemma games. In each experiment, they face 15 CRDs and 15 PGDs (pp. 6–7).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary or predict effects of varying the total number of these “one‐shot” decisions? No. There is no manipulation of “fewer vs. more rounds,” and the paper does not discuss how changing the number of rounds would affect punishment.

3. Is Chat Enabled Between Players?  
   • What the paper says: Not mentioned at all. There is no discussion of communication or chat.  
   • Does the paper predict how enabling/disabling chat would alter the punishment treatment effect? No.

4. Is the Contribution “All or Nothing”?  
   • What the paper says: No. Participants choose among six discrete percentage levels (0%, 20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, 100%) of their available points. There is no forced “all or nothing” contribution (p. 5, Figure 1).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary or discuss toggling between “all‐or‐nothing” versus partial contribution as it relates to punishment? No.

5. Is There a “Contribution Default”?  
   • What the paper says: Not mentioned. Participants simply decide how many points to take or leave (CRDs) or how many points to give or keep (PGDs). No default mechanism is described.  
   • Does the paper predict how introducing or removing a default would affect punishment? No.

6. Marginal Per Capita Return (MPCR) or Similar  
   • What the paper says: In both experiments, the “group account” is multiplied by 2 and split among 4 players, leading to an MPCR of 0.5 (pp. 5–6).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary or predict effects of changing this MPCR on punishment? No. MPCR is fixed at 0.5 in all sessions.

7. Punishment Cost to the Punisher  
   • What the paper says: In the “punishment” condition, imposing one “unit” of punishment costs the punishing player 1 point (p. 7).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary or predict how changes in the cost of punishment would affect outcomes? No. The cost is always 1 point.

8. Punishment Magnitude (How Much the Target Loses)  
   • What the paper says: The paper keeps the magnitude of each “decrement point” at 3 points (pp. 7–8).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary or predict how changing the 3‐point deduction would affect punishment? No.

9. Whether a Reward Is Enabled  
   • What the paper says: The paper has two separate between‐subjects conditions: “punishment” vs. “reward.” In the “reward” condition, one “increment point” can be assigned at the cost of 1 point to the rewarder, transferring 3 points to the target (pp. 7–8).  
   • Do they discuss “both punishment and reward simultaneously” or systematically vary enabling/disabling reward within the same game? No. The presence of reward is simply an either–or design (punishment‐only vs. reward‐only).  
   • Numerical effects: They do report the frequency of punishment vs. reward (e.g., in Experiment 1, punishment in CRDs is 34.78% vs. 25.60% in PGDs, reward in CRDs is 24.12% vs. 34.40% in PGDs). However, these are effects on cooperation or sanctioning decisions, not on efficiency.

10. Reward Cost to the Rewarder  
   • What the paper says: In the “reward” condition, each increment costs the granter 1 point (p. 8).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary or predict changes under different cost settings? No.

11. Reward Magnitude (How Much the Target Gains)  
   • What the paper says: The target always gains 3 points for each reward point assigned (p. 8).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary or predict the effect of adjusting that magnitude? No.

12. Is the Number of Rounds Known to Players?  
   • What the paper says: Participants do know they face a fixed set of 15 CRDs and 15 PGDs, but this is never manipulated.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary or predict differences between known vs. unknown round lengths? No.

13. Are Peer Outcomes Shown (Do Players Know Others’ Gains/Losses Each Round)?  
   • What the paper says: Not really. The design uses a “strategy method” in which participants specify what they would punish or reward for each possible choice by others, but they do not observe actual real‐time feedback from peers. The paper does not analyze or vary “peer outcomes disclosed vs. hidden.”  
   • No predictions about displaying peer outcomes and its effect on punishment are made.

14. When a Player Is Punished, Do They Know the Specific Punisher?  
   • What the paper says: Punishment assignments are anonymous, and the paper does not manipulate or even discuss revealing identities of punishers (p. 7: anonymity is maintained).  
   • No predictions about “known punisher identity” are made.

15. When a Player Is Rewarded, Do They Know the Specific Rewarder?  
   • What the paper says: The same anonymity and procedure as with punishment. No mention of revealing who gave the reward.  
   • No predictions about “known rewarder identity” are made.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY (A–D)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • No. The paper never reports on total or average payoffs, nor does it measure “efficiency” as “actual payoff / maximum possible payoff.” Instead, it focuses on:  
     – Cooperation decisions (how much people take or give).  
     – Punishment (likelihood/frequency of punishing).  
     – Reward (likelihood/frequency of rewarding).  
   • These are all conceptually different from efficiency. The paper does not investigate how total payoff might be altered by punishment or reward.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
     1) Number of players = always 4 in the experiments.  
     6) MPCR = fixed at 0.5.  
     7) Punishment cost = 1 point (to punisher).  
     8) Punishment magnitude = 3 points (deducted from punishee).  
     9) Whether a reward is enabled = yes or no (between‐subjects).  
     10) Reward cost = 1 point (to rewarder).  
     11) Reward magnitude = +3 points (to rewardee).  
     12) Number of rounds known = participants know they will face 15 CRDs and 15 PGDs, but it is not a formal variable of interest.  
   • Not mentioned, or mentioned only in passing with no variation or predictions: All the rest (Parameters 2, 3, 4, 5, 13, 14, 15) either do not appear at all or are never studied with respect to punishment.  

C. For which and how many parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when the parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, none of the 15 parameters above is systematically varied to see how it changes a “punishment treatment effect” relative to no‐punishment or baseline. Instead:  
     – The only major design contrast is punishment‐only vs. reward‐only (Parameter 9). Even then, the paper discusses how that contrast affects cooperation, punishment, and reward levels—not efficiency.  
     – The set cost and magnitude of punishment/reward (Parameters 7, 8, 10, 11) are always fixed; the paper does not manipulate them.  
     – MPCR (Parameter 6) is always 0.5, not varied.  
     – The number of players is fixed at 4, not varied.  
   • Therefore, the paper does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters to see how it alters a punishment‐on‐efficiency effect.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper never measures efficiency, so we cannot determine directly how any parameter shifts the punishment effect on efficiency. (The authors focus on how “punishment vs. reward” conditions affect cooperation rates—and they do not define efficiency or total payoff as a measured outcome.)  
   • Consequently, there is little basis for predicting how the 15 parameters would shape changes in group efficiency under punishment. One might speculate that increased cooperation could raise total payoffs (yet actual punishment also costs points), but the article itself does not discuss these trade‐offs, nor does it report net group payoffs or “efficiency.”  

In brief, the paper does not analyze efficiency or systematically vary the listed parameters to see how they might alter a “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency. It focuses on cooperation, punishment frequency, and reward frequency, without measuring total group payoffs or efficiency.

Authors: Chen, ML; Zhu, XL; Zhang, J; Ma, GP; Wu, YH
Author Full Names: Chen, Mingliang; Zhu, Xiaolei; Zhang, Jing; Ma, Ganping; Wu, Yuanhong
Article Title: Neural correlates of proposers' fairness perception in punishment and non-punishment economic games
Author Keywords: Proposers’ fairness perception; Punishment and non-punishment conditions; Ultimatum game and dictator game; Event-related potentials; Unfairness aversion; Guilty feeling
Keywords Plus: DECISION-MAKING; ULTIMATUM GAME; EMOTIONAL CONFLICT; ALTRUISM; DICTATOR; CORTEX; BRAIN; GUILT; COOPERATION; RECIPROCITY
Abstract: In economic games, people acting as responders always hope to be treated fairly; otherwise they may punish proposers even sacrificing own monetary gains. However, people often treat others unequally when they become proposers, especially in the absence of punishment mechanisms. Will people lose fairness perception when they become proposers? Previous researches mainly focused on the fairness perception of responders, few paid attentions to that of proposers. In present study, we used event-related potentials (ERPs) to record the neural activities of participants acting as proposers in the ultimatum game and the dictator game, corresponding to punishment condition and non-punishment condition respectively. In each trial, a participant could choose an offer from three categories: absolutely unfair, relatively unfair and fair. Behavioral results indicate that the proposers would choose more highly unfair offers that are beneficial to themselves in a non-punishment condition than in a punishment condition. However, no matter whether there was punishment mechanism, more highly unfair offers elicited larger MFN. This finding may reflect the existence of the proposers' unfairness aversion and guilty feeling triggered by intentional violations of social fairness norm and shows that the proposers do not give up the fairness norm in the cockles of the heart even in a non-punishment environment.

Article Title: Cooperation across multiple game theoretical paradigms is increased by fear more than anger in selfish individuals
Keywords Plus: SOCIAL VALUE ORIENTATION; DECISION-MAKING; GENDER-DIFFERENCES; DICTATOR GAME; ECONOMIC MAN; EMOTION; STRESS; PUNISHMENT; BEHAVIOR; MEN
Abstract: Cooperative decisions are well predicted by stable individual differences in social values but it remains unclear how they may be modulated by emotions such as fear and anger. Moving beyond specific decision paradigms, we used a suite of economic games and investigated how experimental inductions of fear or anger affect latent factors of decision making in individuals with selfish or prosocial value orientations. We found that, relative to experimentally induced anger, induced fear elicited higher scores on a cooperation factor, and that this effect was entirely driven by selfish participants. In fact, induced fear brought selfish individuals to cooperate similarly to prosocial individuals, possibly as a (selfish) mean to seek protection in others. These results suggest that two basic threat-related emotions, fear and anger, differentially affect a generalized form of cooperation and that this effect is buffered by prosocial value orientation.

Article Title: Group leaders establish cooperative norms that persist in subsequent interactions
Keywords Plus: STRONG RECIPROCITY; COLLECTIVE ACTION; PUNISHMENT; EVOLUTION; INCENTIVES; ALTRUISM; EXAMPLE; GAMES; POWER
Abstract: The temptation to free-ride on others' contributions to public goods makes enhancing cooperation a critical challenge. Solutions to the cooperation problem have centered on installing a sanctioning institution where all can punish all, i.e., peer punishment. But a new, growing literature considers whether and when the designation of a group leader-one group member, given the sole ability to administer punishment-is an effective and efficient alternative. What remains unknown is whether and to what extent these group leaders establish cooperative norms in their groups via their own contributions to the public good, their use of sanctions, or both. Nor has past work examined whether leaders' behaviors have lasting effects on non-leaders' cooperation in subsequent interactions, outside of the leader's purview. Here I show that leaders' contributions to the public good predict non-leaders' subsequent cooperation. Importantly, the effect is not limited to cooperation within the institution: the effect of leaders' contributions continue to predict non-leaders' contributions in a later interaction, where sanctions are removed. This process is mediated by non-leaders' increased contributions in the institution, suggesting that leaders have effects on followers that shape followers' subsequent behaviors. These effects occur above and beyond a baseline tendency to be influenced by non-leader group members; they also occur above and beyond the influence of peers in groups under a peer punishment institution. Results underscore how critical it is that groups install cooperative leaders: followers model their leaders' cooperation choices, even in decisions external to the original institution and outside of the leader's watch.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor  
• Mentioned? Yes. Contributions to the group fund are doubled (×2) and then split equally among four players, implying a marginal per capita return of 0.5.  
• Systematically varied? No. The paper uses the same doubling rule throughout and does not discuss how altering it would affect the punishment treatment effect.

• Systematically varied? No. The cost was fixed. The paper does not address how changing that cost would affect the punishment treatment effect.

Abstract: Numerous studies have demonstrated that sanctions can promote cooperation. However, it is important to know not only that sanctions can work but also under what conditions people are actually willing to sanction cooperation positively (i.e., reward) or noncooperation negatively (i.e., punish). In this article, we demonstrate that people use sanctions less often and sanction more mildly when they decide about sanctioning before (instead of after) the occurrence of others' (non)cooperation (Experiments 1 and 2), regardless of whether they decide directly afterwards or after a time delay (Experiment 2). Moreover, we reveal that beforehand (as compared with afterwards) people have not yet formed clear sanctioning preferences (Experiment 3). These findings corroborate our reasoning that the decision environment beforehand induces nonconsequential reasoning and thereby hampers people's willingness to sanction. We discuss the theoretical, methodological, and practical implications of our work.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter inventory and summary of how (if at all) this paper discusses each of the 15 specified public‐goods‐game parameters and any systematic variation of them. Throughout, “the paper” refers solely to Molenmaker et al. (in press) titled “The effect of decision timing on the willingness to costly reward cooperation and punish noncooperation: Sanctioning the past, the present, or the future,” and its reported experiments (hereafter “Experiments 1, 2, and 3”). Note that the paper’s main focus is on how sanction decisions (punishments or rewards) differ when made “before” vs. “after” others’ cooperative or noncooperative behavior. Nowhere does the paper measure or report a “group efficiency” (total payoff / maximum possible payoff) outcome; instead, the main dependent variable is “willingness to sanction” (choice and size of punishments or rewards).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER‐BY‐PARAMETER ANALYSIS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1) Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes, participants observe a four‐person public good game (with the participant as a neutral “fifth” person who can sanction).  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. The paper does not manipulate different numbers of players. All experiments keep the four‐player structure fixed.  
   • Does the paper predict or report any effect of systematically varying the parameter on the punishment treatment effect (for efficiency or any other variable)?  
     – No. The authors do not discuss how changing the number of players would alter willingness to punish/reward or any efficiency measure.

2) Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  
     – They describe one‐shot (single‐round) public good games.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. It remains a one‐shot interaction in the reported studies.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment?  
     – Not discussed. No predictions are made about multiple‐round vs. single‐round settings.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. There is no mention of any communication/chat condition in the paper.  
   • Systematically varied or effect size reported?  
     – No. Not discussed at all.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Experiment 1 used a dichotomous contribution (cooperate by contributing the full endowment vs. not cooperate by contributing nothing). Experiment 2 used a continuous contribution (how many euros out of 10 to contribute).  
   • Systematically varied with the intent of examining effects on punishment treatment?  
     – The paper changes from a dichotomous choice in Experiment 1 to a continuous choice in Experiment 2, but it does not analyze or discuss the effect of that manipulation on punishment’s impact for “efficiency” (nor does it systematically compare punishment outcomes across these two designs).  
   • Effect on punishment treatment (for efficiency or any DV)?  
     – No direct predictions or measurement about how switching from all‐or‐nothing to continuous systematically changes the “punishment treatment effect.” The authors simply changed the contribution format across experiments.

5) Is the contribution default (are participants forced to “opt out”)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Not discussed at all.  
   • Systematically varied or effect size reported?  
     – No.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes, but only in passing. In Experiment 1 (and generally), they state a 1.5× multiplication of the contributed amount in the public good game.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. It is used in all relevant tasks but remains fixed.  
   • Effect on the punishment treatment?  
     – Not discussed. The authors do not systematically investigate how changing the MPCR would alter punishment or reward decisions.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. In Experiments 1 and 2, it cost the sanctioner €0.10 per “decrement point.”  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. The cost was always €0.10 for each punishment point.  
   • Predictions about effect on punishment treatment (for efficiency or any DV)?  
     – They do not vary this cost or discuss how changing it would alter the results. No effect size or systematic variation is reported.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. Each “decrement point” subtracts €0.30 from the target.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. Kept constant at 3:1 “exchange ratio” (the punisher pays €0.10 to reduce the target’s payoff by €0.30).  
   • Predictions about effect if the magnitude changed?  
     – Not discussed. There is no systematic manipulation of punishment magnitude.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The paper explicitly compares “punishment” conditions (costly decreases) to “reward” conditions (costly increases).  
   • Systematically varied in the sense of toggling reward on/off?  
     – They do manipulate whether participants were in a reward or a punishment condition. However, they do not discuss “efficiency”; they measure only “willingness to sanction” (choice and intensity).  
   • Effect size or efficiency outcome?  
     – The paper reports the difference between punishment and reward in willingness to sanction but not how it impacts group efficiency.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes, it matches the punishment cost: €0.10 per “increment point.”  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No.  
   • Predictions about effect (for efficiency or other DVs)?  
     – Not presented.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted)  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes, awarding 1 “increment point” costs €0.10 and yields +€0.30 for the target.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No.  
   • Effect on punishment (or “reward treatment”) or efficiency?  
     – Not analyzed. They keep this ratio fixed.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – The tasks were always one‐shot, so participants knew there was only one decision.  
   • Systematically varied?  
     – No. Not discussed beyond one‐shot instructions.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Participants (in the “third‐party” observer role) do see or learn that “Person M” either contributed everything or nothing (Experiment 1) or contributed all €10 vs. kept €10 (Experiment 2). However, the display of comprehensive peer outcomes is not systematically varied.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment?  
     – Not discussed.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Not varied or discussed in any detail.  
   • Systematically varied or effect size reported?  
     – No.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Not varied or discussed.  
   • Systematically varied or effect size reported?  
     – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   – The paper does not measure or analyze any form of group efficiency, total payoff, or average payoff. Nowhere in the text do the authors report or focus on how punishment or reward decisions affect efficiency.  
   – Instead, the key dependent variables are: (1) choice to administer a sanction (yes/no), (2) how many “points” of reward or punishment are assigned (the intensity), (3) self‐reported emotional reactions, and (4) clarity of sanctioning preferences (in Experiment 3). None of these is the same as group efficiency.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – Mentioned:  
     #1 (Number of players): They consistently use four in the public good game.  
     #2 (Number of rounds): They specify a single‐round game.  
     #4 (Contribution all‐or‐none vs. partial): Experiment 1 uses a binary choice, Experiment 2 a continuous contribution.  
     #6 (Multiplication factor / MPCR): Stated as 1.5× in the public good.  
     #7 / #8 / #10 / #11 (Punishment/reward costs and magnitudes): They fix a 3:1 ratio—€0.10 cost per point to shift payoffs ±€0.30.  
     #9 (Reward is enabled?) The experiments compare “reward” vs. “punishment” conditions.  
   – Not mentioned, or at least not discussed in any meaningful sense: #3 (Chat), #5 (Default contributions), #12 (explicit knowledge about round endings—only a one‐shot is used), #13–15 (information disclosures).  
   – Even for those parameters mentioned, the paper does not explore systematic variations of them beyond the “punishment vs. reward” framing.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   – None are systematically varied except for “punishment vs. reward” (Parameter #9). However, even for that manipulation, the paper never analyzes changes in “group efficiency.” Instead, it only reports whether participants chose to sanction and how intensely they sanctioned.  
   – The authors do change the contribution format from all‐or‐none to continuous (Parameter #4), but they make no formal claims linking that change to any punishment “treatment effect” on payoffs or efficiency.

D. Based solely on this paper, what predictions can be made about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
   – The paper does not provide direct evidence or claims about efficiency or total payoff. It never measures any payoff‐based outcome. Therefore, one cannot meaningfully predict, from its text alone, how varying any of the 15 parameters would alter the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.  
   – Any such predictions would exceed what the authors actually discuss. The paper only shows that, when punishment or reward is contingent on future behavior (vs. past behavior), people are less willing to sanction (i.e., they do so less frequently and less intensively). No mention is made of how that, in turn, affects group payoff efficiency.

────────
End of answer.

Authors: Hajikhameneh, A; Rubin, J
Author Full Names: Hajikhameneh, Aidin; Rubin, Jared
Article Title: Exchange in the Absence of Legal Enforcement: Reputation and Multilateral Punishment under Uncertainty
Keywords Plus: CONTRACT ENFORCEMENT; TRUST; COOPERATION; INSTITUTIONS; RECIPROCITY; TRADE; NORMS; LAW; INFORMATION; ALTRUISM
Abstract: Principalagent problems can reduce gains from exchange available in long distance trade. One solution historically used to mitigate such problems is multilateral punishment, whereby groups of principals jointly punish cheating agents by giving them bad reputations. But how does such punishment work when there is uncertainty regarding whether an agent actually cheated or was just the victim of bad luck? And how might such uncertainty be mitigateduor exacerbateduby non-observable, pro-social behavioral characteristics? We address these questions by designing a simple modified trust game with uncertainty and the capacity for principals to employ multilateral punishment. Our experimental results indicate that a modest amount of uncertainty has little effect on overall welfare: while part of the surplus is destroyed by uncertainty, principals are also more willing to trust agents with bad reputations, thereby increasing the frequency of welfare-enhancing exchange.    • Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment?  
     – Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are they different?

• The paper frequently measures “total welfare” (the sum of principals’ plus agents’ earnings). That is its main analog to “efficiency.”  
• It also measures principals’ average payoff, agents’ average payoff, and behavioral measures such as the fraction sending (“Send”) or dividing (“Divide”). Thus, the paper’s primary dependent variables include:  
  – Total welfare (closest to “group efficiency”)  
  – Principals’ payoffs vs. agents’ payoffs  
  – Frequency of “Send” and “Divide” decisions  
• These outcomes differ from one another, because “Send” and “Divide” capture cooperation-like actions, while total welfare and payoffs capture monetary outcomes (an efficiency measure).

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

• The paper explicitly describes most of them in the sense of “how the game is set up,” but it does not treat 14 of them as systematically varied.  
• The only parameter from your list that is truly manipulated across treatments in the paper is parameter #7 (the punishment cost).  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?

• Only parameter #7 (punishment cost) is systematically varied (0 vs. 5), and the paper provides extensive results on how that variation changes behavior (Send/Divide), overall payoffs, and thus total welfare.  
• None of the other 14 parameters are manipulated, so the paper does not discuss their “punishment treatment effect” in a systematic sense.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper:

• The only concrete predictions come from the paper’s data on how varying the punishment cost (#7) affects total welfare. In short:  
  – When punishment is free (C = 0), principals punish more easily, potentially deterring bad behavior but also creating other strategic effects (e.g., some fear of being labeled “bad”).

Abstract: Third-party punishment is a common mechanism to promote cooperation in humans. Theoretical models of evolution of cooperation predict that punishment maintains cooperation if it is sufficiently frequent. On the other hand, empirical studies have found that participants frequently punishing others do not success in comparison with those not eager to punish others, suggesting that punishment is suboptimal and thus should not be frequent. That being the case, our question is what mechanism, if any, can sustain cooperation even if punishment is rare. The present study proposes that one possible mechanism is risk-averse social learning. Using the method of evolutionary game dynamics, we investigate the effect of risk attitude of individuals on the question. In our framework, individuals select a strategy based on its risk, i.e., the variance of the payoff, as well as its expected payoff; risk-averse individuals prefer to select a strategy with low variable payoff. Using the framework, we examine the evolution of cooperation in two-player social dilemma games with punishment. We study two models: cooperators and defectors compete, while defectors may be punished by an exogenous authority; and cooperators, defectors, and cooperative punishers compete, while defectors may be punished by the cooperative punishers. We find that in both models, risk-averse individuals achieve stable cooperation with significantly low frequency of punishment. We also examine three punishment variants: in each game, all defectors are punished; only one of defectors is punished; and only a defector who exploits a cooperator or a cooperative punisher is punished. We find that the first and second variants effectively promote cooperation. Comparing the first and second variants, each can be more effective than the other depending on punishment frequency.

Authors: Rauwolf, P; Bryson, JJ
Author Full Names: Rauwolf, Paul; Bryson, Joanna J.
Article Title: Expectations of Fairness and Trust Co-Evolve in Environments of Partial Information
Author Keywords: Trust; Partial information; Costly punishment; Fairness; Trust game; Negative pseudo-reciprocity

Abstract: When playing one-shot economic games, individuals often blindly trust others, accepting partnerships without any information regarding the trustworthiness of their partner. Consequently, they risk deleterious pacts. Oddly, when individuals do have information about another, they reject partnerships that are not fair, despite the fact that such offers are profitable-individuals costly punish. Why would one reject profitable partnerships on the one hand, but risk unknown offers on the other? Significant research has gone into explaining the contexts where blind trust or costly punishment provides an evolutionary advantage; however, both behaviours are rarely considered in tandem. Here we demonstrate that both behaviours can simultaneously be revenue maximizing. Further, given the plausible condition of partially obscured information and partner choice, trust mediates the generation of costly punishment. This result is important because it demonstrates that the evolutionary viability of trust, fairness, and costly punishment may be linked. The adaptive nature of fairness expectations can best be explained in concert with trust.

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?

   • They frequently interpret high payoffs as “revenue maximizing,” but do not present “efficiency” in the sense of “total payoff divided by maximum possible total payoff for the entire group.” Instead, they present average payoffs and fraction of maximum payoff for an individual.

     1) Number of players (they use 500 vs. 5000)  
     2) Number of rounds (set to 500 per generation, but not varied)  
     4) “All or nothing” is effectively how the trust game is structured, but not systematically varied  
     6) Multiplication factor b (varied systematically: 2, 3, 4, 5)

   • Trust-based partner choice plus partial information are crucial to the emergence of costly punishment (rejecting profitable-but-unfair offers). Abstract: The behavior decisions in social dilemmas are highlighted in sociological, economic, and social psychological studies. • Discussed? The paper states there was no communication between participants, but it does not systematically examine the presence or absence of chat.  
• Any prediction(s)? No.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
• Discussed? The paper uses a standard Prisoner’s Dilemma format in Experiment 1 (two discrete choices: cooperate vs. defect) and three discrete choices in Experiment 2 (cooperate, defect, or punish). Thus, de facto, the choice is “all or nothing” (there is no partial contribution).  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any prediction(s)? No.

5. Is the contribution default?
• Discussed? No. The paper does not mention any “default” contribution mechanism; there is no discussion of players deciding how much from the public fund to move back into their hand.  
• Any prediction(s)? No.

• Discussed? No. The paper’s payoffs are given in discrete payoff matrices (Prisoner’s Dilemma style), and no mention is made of an MPCR‐type parameter.  
• Any prediction(s)? No.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
• Discussed? Indirectly, yes. In the punishment conditions, the punisher typically loses 1 unit when choosing “punish.”  
• Systematically varied? No. The cost to the punisher (losing 1 unit) is the same in all punishing conditions (both symmetric and asymmetric).  
• Any prediction(s)? The paper does not examine or predict how varying the punishment cost would alter outcomes.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player who is punished)
• Discussed? Yes. The paper systematically varies punishment magnitude in a symmetric vs. asymmetric payoff matrix (in Experiment 2).  
   – Symmetric punishment: If a participant chooses “punish,” the punisher loses 1 unit, and the target loses 2 (or 3) units, the same for both players.  
   – Asymmetric punishment: One player’s “punish” option might make the target lose 4 units, while the other player’s “punish” option might make the target lose fewer (2 or 3).  
• Does the paper link this to a “punishment treatment effect” or to efficiency?  
   – The paper discusses only cooperation rate, defection rate, and punishment rate as dependent variables. It finds that asymmetric punishment magnitudes reduce cooperation more than symmetric punishment magnitudes do, especially among friends (i.e., those with smaller social distance).  
   – No “efficiency” measures (total payoff / maximum payoff) are reported.  
• Numerical effect sizes? For cooperation rates (Table 8), the symmetric‐punishment group’s mean cooperation rate is about 0.626, versus about 0.500 in the asymmetric‐punishment group (a difference of ~0.13). The paper does not frame these results in terms of efficiency changes.

• Discussed? Yes, but only in Experiment 1 (where “reward” means higher payoff if both cooperate). The authors compare symmetric‐reward vs. asymmetric‐reward payoff matrices, but they do not combine reward with punishment in the same design.  
• Systematically varied? They do vary whether the payoff for mutual cooperation is symmetrical (e.g., both get 3) or asymmetrical (e.g., one gets 6, the other gets 3). However, there is no condition with “no reward” vs. “reward,” and they do not relate reward to the punishment treatment effect.  
• Any prediction(s)? The paper finds that asymmetric reward structures lower cooperation rates. However, the authors do not examine or predict how reward presence or absence influences a separate punishment effect.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
• Discussed? No. The paper does not analyze any explicit cost to reward a partner (there is no separate “reward” choice equivalent to a “punish” choice). Instead, “reward” is built into the payoff matrix if both choose “cooperate.”  
• Any prediction(s)? No.

11. Reward magnitude
• Discussed? Yes. The paper systematically compares symmetric‐reward payoffs (both players get the same reward for mutual cooperation) versus asymmetric‐reward payoffs (one player gets a higher payoff than the other if both cooperate).  
• Any prediction(s) about efficiency or punishment?  
   – The paper looks only at how symmetric vs. asymmetric reward affects the cooperation rate. They do not measure efficiency and do not link reward magnitude to any punishment variable (punishment is absent in the reward experiments).  
   – Numerically, they report that shifting from symmetric to asymmetric rewards (Tables 1–3) reduces the cooperation rate by about 0.19 (Table 4).  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
• Discussed? Not explicitly. The paper does state that there are 50 trials in each block, but it does not say whether participants knew this exact total in advance, nor does it vary this.  
• Any prediction(s)? No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much others gained/lost)?
• Discussed? The paper indicates that participants could see their own scores. It is not entirely clear if they observed the partner’s payoff each round—only that the final total score for each individual was shown at the experiment’s end. The paper does not systematically manipulate or analyze the display of peers’ outcomes.  
• Any prediction(s)? No.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who punished them?
• Discussed? Because all interactions are dyadic, each player presumably knows if they were punished by the other. However, the paper does not explicitly analyze or vary anonymity of the punisher.  
• Any prediction(s)? No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who rewarded them?
• Discussed? The paper’s “reward” is simply the payoff for mutual cooperation in a 2‐player game. There is no separate “rewarding” action that one player can enact on another, so the paper does not discuss knowledge of a rewarder’s identity.  
• Any prediction(s)? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are they different?  
   • The paper does not report “group efficiency” or total (or average) payoff as a primary dependent variable. Instead, its dependent variables are:  
     – Cooperation rate (CR) – fraction of times a player chooses “cooperate.”  
     – Defection rate (DR) – fraction of times a player chooses “defect.”  
     – Punishment rate (PR) – fraction of times a player chooses “punish” (in Experiment 2 only).  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned (in the sense that a fixed value or condition is used or stated in the design):  
     1 (Number of players = 2),  
     2 (Number of rounds = 50),  
     3 (No chat/communication),  
     4 (Binary choice in Experiment 1, ternary choice in Experiment 2, but not varied),  
     7 (Punishment cost is 1, not varied),  
     8 (Punishment magnitude is varied: symmetric vs. asymmetric),  
     9 (A reward is effectively “enabled” in Experiment 1, though not toggled on/off),  
     11 (Reward magnitude is varied: symmetric vs. asymmetric).  
   • That is 8 parameters explicitly appearing in some form or another.  
   • The remaining parameters (5, 6, 10, 12, 13, 14, 15) are either not mentioned or not manipulated.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, the only systematically varied parameter directly connected to “punishment” is Parameter 8 (punishment magnitude: symmetric vs. asymmetric). The paper examines how this variation affects cooperation, defection, and punishment rates. Effect sizes are reported in terms of changes in cooperation rate (e.g., from ~0.626 down to ~0.500 under asymmetric punishment).  
   • The paper does not discuss efficiency as an outcome of that systematic variation.  
   • No other parameter is systematically varied to test its effect on a “punishment treatment” per se.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

Abstract: We propose a simple model of the emergence of equality before the law. A society can support effort ('cooperation', 'prosocial behaviour') using the carrot of future cooperation or the stick of coercive punishment. Community enforcement relies only on the carrot and involves low coercion, low inequality and low effort. A society in which elites control the means of violence supplements the carrot with the stick, and involves high coercion, high inequality and high effort. In this regime, elites are privileged by both laws and norms: because they are not subject to the same punishments as non-elites, norms are also more favourable for them. Nevertheless, it may be optimal-even from the elites' perspective-to establish equality before the law, where all agents are subject to the same coercive punishments and norms are more equal. The key mechanism is that equality before the law increases elites' effort, which improves the carrot of future cooperation and thus encourages even higher effort from non-elites. Equality before the law combines high coercion and low inequality. Factors that make equality before the law more likely to emerge include limits on the extent of coercion, greater marginal returns to effort, increases in the size of the elite group, greater political power for non-elites and, under some additional conditions, lower economic inequality.

  No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
• Discussed?

Section 4.3 analyzes what happens if “marginal returns to effort” increase (as in “defensive modernization”), but it does not present these changes in standard MPCR form.  
• Any prediction of (or measured effect on) punishment treatment effect?  
  The paper never uses the phrase “punishment treatment effect” specifically. It does say that if marginal returns to productive effort rise (holding overall average returns constant), then the elite are more likely to want higher effort and thus more likely to impose “equal” punishment on themselves (i.e., adopt equality before the law). 1. Number of players  
• Discussion in the paper: Yes, the paper discusses games in two‐player contexts (the Prisoner’s Dilemma) and in n‐player contexts (the Public Goods Game). For instance, in Section 2.1.2, it introduces an n‐person PGG.  
• Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment effect: The paper does not present any systematic variation (e.g., comparing different specific group sizes) nor does it forecast any punishment‐related impacts on efficiency across different group sizes. Most discussion focuses on whether players cooperate, defect, or reach certain equilibria, rather than on changes in total or average payoffs caused by varying n.

2. Number of rounds  
• Discussion in the paper: The paper contrasts one‐shot settings (e.g., one‐shot PGG or PD) with repeated, indefinite‐length settings. It mentions that if the number of rounds is known and finite, backward induction predicts defection in repeated PD games.  
• Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment effect: Although “repeated game” vs. “one‐shot game” is discussed, the paper does not systematically vary the number of rounds. It does not provide numerical predictions of how changing the number of rounds would alter a “punishment treatment effect” for efficiency or any other metric.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
• Discussion in the paper: Not mentioned at all.  
• Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment effect: Not applicable. The paper provides no discussion or data about communication or chat.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Discussion in the paper: The paper does mention discrete‐choice versions of the PGG (e.g., a two‐player PGG where each player either contributes his/her entire endowment or contributes nothing). It also discusses continuous‐strategy versions in a more general sense.  
• Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment effect: The paper does not quantify how moving from “all or nothing” to partial‐contribution or continuous strategies would systematically change the effect of punishment on efficiency. It mainly distinguishes that the PGG can be either discrete or continuous; no further predictive data are provided.

5. Is the contribution default?  
• Discussion in the paper: Not mentioned.  
• Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment effect: Not applicable.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor  
• Discussion in the paper: Yes, the parameter r>1 is introduced for the PGG multiplier, and PD games are sometimes described by b (benefit) and c (cost). These are used frequently to explain when cooperation vs. defection might evolve.  
• Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment effect: The paper does not specifically examine how changing r or b/c would shift a punishment‐based treatment effect for efficiency. Instead, it provides threshold conditions (e.g., r>1, or P>c for peer‐punishment to yield a cooperative equilibrium) but does not link these to “efficiency” measures or a quantitative punishment effect.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Discussion in the paper: Yes, it appears as C_I (the cost to the punisher) in peer and institutional punishment settings. The paper explains that punishment is costly, which can cause second‐order free riding issues or lower average payoffs.  
• Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment effect: No explicit or systematic variation is presented (e.g., the paper never says “we vary C_I and observe how it changes total payoffs”). Instead, it remarks qualitatively that if punishment is too costly, it may not evolve.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
• Discussion in the paper: Denoted as P in the two‐stage donation game with peer punishment. The text notes that if P>c, cooperation in a two‐person donation framework can become a Nash Equilibrium.  
• Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment effect: The paper does not report numerical effect sizes relating P to group efficiency or describe how systematically changing P shifts a punishment‐versus‐no‐punishment effect on average payoffs.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
• Discussion in the paper: Yes, the paper distinguishes punishment and reward as two incentive forms. Peer reward is mentioned (e.g., a bonus provided to cooperators), and institutional reward is also covered.  
• Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment effect: No direct analysis of “reward enabled vs. disabled” for the effect on group efficiency, particularly regarding a “punishment treatment effect.” Rather, the paper notes that reward alone often has less of a guaranteed effect on eliminating free‐riding than punishment, but does not quantify how toggling reward changes the punishment effect on efficiency.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Discussion in the paper: The paper denotes C_I as the cost for peer reward, or it denotes that the “institution” has a total budget proportionate to the sum of individual payments.  
• Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment effect: The paper does not systematically examine how changing the reward cost alters any measured effect on outcomes (efficiency or otherwise). 11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded per unit of reward)  
• Discussion in the paper: Denoted as R in the peer‐incentive game. The text also covers how, in institutional reward, the total reward is divided among cooperators.  
• Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment effect: The paper does not discuss systematically varying R, nor does it tie changes in R to changes in a “punishment treatment effect.”

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
• Discussion in the paper: It states that if the number of rounds is known and finite, backward induction leads to defection. However, the paper mostly focuses on indefinite repetition (with continuation probability) or one‐shot interactions.  
• Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment effect: Not discussed. No mention of systematic manipulations of “known vs. unknown horizon” for how punishment changes efficiency.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much their peers gained and lost)?  
• Discussion in the paper: The paper does mention that “players may know the historical behaviors of their coplayers” for indirect reciprocity, but does not specifically say they see their peers’ payoffs.  
• Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment effect: Not addressed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• Discussion in the paper: Not addressed. The paper discusses decentralized (“peer”) punishment and centralized (“institutional”) punishment but does not specify whether the target knows who administered it.  
• Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment effect: Not addressed.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
• Discussion in the paper: Not addressed.  
• Systematic variation and predicted effect on punishment treatment effect: Not addressed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
• The paper primarily examines cooperation or defection in terms of evolutionary stability (ESS) and Nash equilibria in repeated and one‐shot social dilemmas. It discusses “average payoff” in several places (e.g., that peer punishment can reduce the group’s average payoff if the punishment cost is large, or that repeated defection results in lower average earnings than repeated cooperation). However, it does not formalize “efficiency” as the fraction of the maximum possible payoff. Most of the discussion concerns whether cooperation will evolve, what strategies can be stable, and how payoff thresholds or costs lead to stable equilibria.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Mentioned in some form:  
1 (Number of players), 2 (Number of rounds), 4 (Discrete vs. continuous contributions), 6 (MPCR / multiplier r / b and c), 7 (Punishment cost), 8 (Punishment magnitude), 9 (Reward enabled), 10 (Reward cost), 11 (Reward magnitude).  
• Not mentioned (or only very tangentially alluded to but never developed):  
3 (Chat), 5 (Contribution default), 12 (Number of rounds known?), 13 (Peer outcomes displayed?), 14 (Punisher identity revealed?), 15 (Rewarder identity revealed?).  
In total, the paper explicitly touches on 9 of the 15 parameters in some manner, though not all in detail.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• The paper does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters to quantify how they change “the effect of punishment” (whether measured as efficiency or any other outcome). Although it mentions that “if P>c, a cooperative equilibrium may form,” or “if punishment is large enough, free‐riders are curbed,” it does not provide controlled parametric analysis (tables or figures) demonstrating how a measured punishment‐versus‐no‐punishment difference in payoff or efficiency changes with, say, group size or cost of punishment.  
• Hence, the answer is effectively zero: the paper does not provide any explicit numeric or systematic effect sizes for how varying these parameters affects the punishment treatment effect on any dependent measure.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
• The paper indicates in a broad sense that punishment can lead to higher cooperation frequencies but can also reduce average payoffs if the cost of punishment is significant. If “efficiency” were formally measured (total payoff / maximum possible payoff), the text suggests that adding a costly punishment option can, in many cases, lower overall welfare, especially in one‐shot or short‐run contexts, or if second‐order free riding is an issue.  
• However, the paper does not give enough details to make firm or numeric predictions for how systematically changing any of the 15 parameters would alter a punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency. Thus, beyond noting that severe punishment sometimes reduces group welfare and that reward alone is weaker in moving a population from all‐defect to all‐cooperate, there is effectively “little to no prediction” that can be made about specific changes in efficiency given parameter manipulations.
