Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter analysis of what the paper by Lois and Wessa (2019) does (and does not) say about each of the 15 listed public‐goods‐game parameters and how (if at all) they speak to systematically varying these parameters in relation to the “punishment treatment effect.” Note that in this paper, the authors use a repeated third‐party‐punishment version of the Dictator Game rather than a standard public‐goods game; as a result, much of the typical public‐goods‐game parameter variation (e.g., marginal per capita return, reward mechanisms) does not appear.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes, the authors explain that each participant was placed into a “team” of five third‐party punishers (plus a single dictator and a single recipient per round). Thus, effectively there are seven individuals involved in each round’s interaction (though only five serve as third‐party punishers).  
     – Exact value mentioned: 5 third‐party punishers vs. 1 dictator vs. 1 recipient.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No, the paper does not vary the number of punishers or the total number of players; there is no discussion of how changing team size or group size would affect punishment.

2. Number of rounds
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes, there were 49 rounds in total, divided into seven blocks of seven rounds each.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No, the number of rounds (49) was fixed and not manipulated. The paper does not predict how altering the total number of rounds would affect punishment.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No, there is no mention of any communication or chat function.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No mention at all.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – There is no “all‐or‐nothing” public‐goods contribution in this design. Instead, there is a Dictator Game action in which the dictator chooses among 0, 25, 50, 75, or 100 points to transfer.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No, the authors do not manipulate whether contributions must be all or nothing, nor do they discuss such variation.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. Because this is a third‐party‐punishment Dictator Game, there is no mention of a “default contribution” mechanism.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No mention.

6. MPCR (marginal per capita return) or related parameters
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No, there is no public‐goods multiplication factor. This game is not set up as a public‐goods game with an MPCR.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No mention.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes, the cost is explicitly 1 point for each punishment point the punisher allocates. The punisher could allocate up to 50 points from their own endowment in each round.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No, the cost remained fixed and was not varied across conditions.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes, the paper states that for each 1 point spent by the punisher, the dictator loses 3 points.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No, it was fixed at 3 points and not experimentally manipulated.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No, participants only had the option to punish dictators. There is no mention of a reward mechanism.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – No mention.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – No; as above, no reward mechanism was employed.  
    • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
      – No mention.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – No, again no reward mechanism.  
    • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
      – No mention.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – The text states the task “consists of 49 rounds,” but does not explicitly say whether participants did or did not know the game would last exactly 49 rounds. The authors do not systematically manipulate participants’ knowledge of the endpoint.  
    • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
      – No mention of systematically varying knowledge of the total rounds.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost each round)?
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – Participants see “feedback” about how many points each of their four peers used to punish in blocks 2–4, plus the average punishment. However, the paper does not say that participants see their peers’ payoffs or gains/losses—only how many punishment points peers allocated.  
    • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
      – They do manipulate the “content” of the peer‐punishment feedback (low vs. high vs. high & free rider), but not whether that information is shown or hidden. So they do not systematically turn “showing peer outcomes” on and off.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – No mention of whether the dictator learns who imposed the punishment or not.  
    • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
      – No mention.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – No, there is no reward mechanism at all.  
    • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
      – No mention.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Summary (A–D)

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper does not measure “efficiency” (actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff). Instead, the main dependent variables are:  
     – Average third‐party‐punishment points spent in response to different dictator allocations.  
     – Frequency of “free riding” (i.e., spending zero points to punish).  
   • Hence, the authors focus on how punishment decisions adjust over repeated rounds when presented with different peer‐punishment norms. They do not measure group efficiency or total payoff.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
     1 (Number of players), 2 (Number of rounds), 4 (Amount the dictator transfers), 7 (Punishment cost), 8 (Punishment magnitude), 12 (49 total rounds, though not clearly stated if that was known), 13 (Showing peer‐punishment feedback).  
   • Not discussed at all or not relevant in this design:  
     3 (Chat enabled?), 5 (Contribution default?), 6 (MPCR), 9 (Reward enabled?), 10 (Reward cost), 11 (Reward magnitude), 14 (Punisher identity revealed?), 15 (Rewarder identity revealed?).  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None of the 15 were systematically varied in the sense of toggling or changing the parameter itself (e.g., changing the punishment cost, number of rounds, or enabling/disabling chat). The design instead varied the content of peer‐punishment feedback (low vs. high vs. “high & free rider”), but that does not map onto one of the 15 listed parameters in a direct, systematic way.  
   • Consequently, there is no numerical effect size reported on how varying any of the listed parameters changes the punishment effect. The only systematic manipulation was the feedback about peers’ punishment (some had a free rider, some did not).

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would these predictions be?  
   • The paper does not address “efficiency” at all, nor do the authors manipulate those parameters in a way that would illuminate group payoffs. Consequently, there is not enough information to project how the paper’s findings would extend to efficiency. Predictions for most listed parameters (e.g., MPCR, number of players, reward presence, etc.) cannot be drawn from the authors’ data or arguments.  
   • If forced to speculate, the paper’s overarching finding is that social feedback (particularly the presence of a “free rider” in the group) reduces overall punishment and encourages free‐riding on punishment. In a typical public‐goods game, that kind of “bad apple effect” would likely decrease efficiency (by reducing sanctioning and thereby reducing cooperation). However, the article does not quantify this effect in terms of total or average payoffs, so no numerical estimate can be derived.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
reference_APA: Lois, Giannis & Wessa, Michele (2019). Creating sanctioning norms in the lab: the influence of descriptive norms in third-party punishment. SOCIAL INFLUENCE.

Below I treat each of the 15 design parameters in turn and report exactly what the paper tells us about them and about the way their **systematic** variation is predicted to influence the *punishment* treatment effect.  Throughout, “punishment treatment effect” = the difference in whatever outcome is plotted when consensual punishment is available versus when it is not.  Where the authors report numbers in figures or tables, I reproduce them; otherwise I merely note qualitative statements.  I make no statements that are not traceable to the text, figures, or tables.

----------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
----------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Number of players  
    • Mentioned?  YES.  Symbol N.  Typical values: N = 5 in Figs. 3–4, N = 10 in Table 1, N = 5,10,20,30 in Table 2.  
    • Systematic variation & prediction?  YES.  Table 2 shows how varying N alters the critical preference for punishment p_c (the p at which punishment becomes more effective than reward).  
        – For T = 1/2, p_c = 0.91 (N = 10), 0.94 (N = 20), “–” (not given for N = 30).  
      This means the *relative* effectiveness of punishment versus reward depends on group size, but no efficiency numbers are given.

2.  Number of rounds  
    • Mentioned?  NO.  The model is an infinite-time replicator dynamic.  
    • Therefore no prediction.

3.  Chat enabled?  
    • Not mentioned → no prediction.

4.  “All-or-nothing” contribution?  
    • Authors explicitly say their contribution rule is *not* all-or-nothing (“the contribution invested is not ‘all-or-nothing’ ”).  They never vary this feature.  
    • Thus no prediction.

5.  Contribution default (take-back)?  
    • Not discussed.

6.  MPCR / multiplication factor r  
    • Mentioned?  YES.  Symbol r.  Fixed at r = 3 in most figures; varied in Table 2 (r = 1.2,2,4).  
    • Systematic prediction?  YES.  Table 2 shows that increasing r lowers the critical p_c (T = 1/2 row): p_c = 0.68 (r = 1.2) → 0.73 (r = 2) → 0.89 (r = 4).  No efficiency data.

7.  Punishment cost to impose (α)  
    • Mentioned?  YES.  Symbol α.  Usually fixed at 0.3.  
    • Systematic variation?  NO numerical results; the text states qualitatively that “τ_c decreases as … the enforcement factor increases,” which implicitly refers to α, but no table or figure varies α.

8.  Punishment magnitude (β, the fine suffered per unit)  
    • Mentioned?  YES.  Symbol β.  Fixed at 1 in Figs. 3–4; varied in both tables.  
    • Systematic prediction?  YES.  
        – Table 1: τ_c falls as β rises (β = 0.3→0.7→1.5→3 gives τ_c = 8.0→5.0→4.0→3.0).  
        – Table 2 (T = 1/2 row): p_c increases when β rises from 0.0 to 1.5 to 3 (0 → 0.84 → 0.88).  

9.  Reward enabled? (binary)  
    • The model always allows *either* punishment or reward once a consensus is reached; there is no separate on/off manipulation of a reward institution, so this parameter is not present.

10. Reward cost (α for rewards as well)  
    • Same α as in (7); never varied.

11. Reward magnitude (β for rewards)  
    • Same β as in (8); therefore predictions identical to those already listed for β.

12.  Do players know the number of rounds?  
    • Not applicable; not discussed.

13.  Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Not discussed.

14.  Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
    • Not discussed.

15.  Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
    • Not discussed.

----------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
----------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables actually used  
    – The paper follows the replicator equation and reports:  
        (i)  the gradient of selection ẋ,  
        (ii) positions of stable/unstable fixed points,  
        (iii) “basin of attraction” (fraction of initial states that converge to full cooperation),  
        (iv) critical threshold values (τ_c, p_c).  
      There is **no measure of group efficiency or of total/average pay-off**.

B.  How many of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
    7 of them: 1 (N), 4 (all-or-nothing, only to say it is not used), 6 (r), 7 (α), 8 (β), 9–11 (reward institution, merged with punishment).  The remaining 8 parameters (2,3,5,12–15) never appear.

C.  How many parameters are *systematically varied* and linked to a punishment treatment effect?  
    3 parameters:  
      • N (Table 2),  
      • r (Table 2),  
      • β (Tables 1 & 2).

1. NUMBER OF PLAYERS (group size N)  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  All simulations draw N = 5 individuals from a well-mixed population of size M = 100 (Methods, stage 1; Fig. 1 caption).  
   • Systematic-variation prediction? No.  N is never varied; no statement or figure shows how changing N would alter the payoff gap between “no-punishment” and “punishment” conditions.

2. NUMBER OF ROUNDS  
   • Mentioned? Only that the model is run for 100,000 periods to let the system converge (Fig. 3 caption, etc.).  
   • Systematic-variation prediction? No.  The paper never varies, or even theorises about varying, the number of rounds.

3. CHAT ENABLED?  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Systematic-variation prediction? Not applicable.

4. ALL-OR-NOTHING CONTRIBUTION?  
   • Mentioned? Yes (Methods, second stage).  Individuals either contribute a fixed cost c or nothing.  c = 1 in most runs.  
   • Systematic-variation prediction? No.  This “binary” contribution rule is hard-wired; its alternative is never explored.

5. CONTRIBUTION DEFAULT (withdrawal from a public fund)?  
   • Mentioned? No.

6. MARGINAL PER CAPITA RETURN / MULTIPLICATION FACTOR (r)  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  Baseline r = 3; the paper systematically varies r (Fig. 5e) and r/N (Fig. 6).  
   • Systematic-variation prediction? Yes – for the frequency of altruistic punishers (not for efficiency).  
     – Fig. 5e: keeping all other parameters at their baseline values (α = 0.3, λ = 5, γ = 0.3, δ = 1), increasing r from ≈2 to ≈4 raises the long-run punisher frequency from ≈0 to ≈1.  Exact numerical values are not printed, but the curve is strictly increasing.  
     – Fig. 6a: When λ = 5 and ω = 0.5, a contour plot shows that a high r/N (> 0.5) sustains >40 % punishers even when costly-signalling efficacy α is as low as 0.2; if r/N < 0.3, punishers rarely exceed 10 %.  
   • Connection to “punishment treatment effect”? Implicit only.  The paper compares a zero-punishment baseline (γ = 0) with punishment conditions, but it never translates the resulting frequency differences into total pay-off (efficiency) differences.

7. PUNISHMENT COST TO IMPOSE (γ)  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  Baseline γ = 0.3; varied in Fig. 5f.

   • Mentioned? No.  The model contains no reward stage.

10. REWARD COST  
11. REWARD MAGNITUDE

   • Systematic-variation prediction? Not applicable.

12. ROUNDS KNOWN TO THE PLAYERS?  
   • Mentioned? No.  The model is evolutionary; the concept of “known horizon” never appears.

13. PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN?  
14. PUNISHER IDENTIFIED?  
15. REWARDER IDENTIFIED?  
   • Mentioned? No, No, and No.  Information feedback is not manipulated.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables in the paper  
   – The paper does NOT report group efficiency (total or average payoff / maximum ideal payoff).  
   – Reported dependent variables are strategy frequencies: proportion of punishers, cooperators, and defectors after 100,000 periods.  
   – “Cooperation established or not” is sometimes treated as a binary outcome.  These variables are conceptually different from efficiency because they do not incorporate punishment costs or earned payoffs directly.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   • Mentioned: 1, 4, 6, 7, 8.  (5 parameters)  
   • Not mentioned: 2, 3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15.

C. For which parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* the parameter on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable)?  
   • Only 3 parameters: 6 (r), 7 (γ), 8 (δ).  
   • Even for these, the outcome is punisher frequency, not efficiency.  No numerical treatment-effect sizes on payoffs are provided.

D. Predicted impact on *efficiency* (if one had to guess, using ONLY this paper)  
   – The paper gives almost no direct leverage: efficiency is never measured, and many of the 15 parameters (chat, information, rewards, number of rounds, etc.) are absent.  
   – A cautious projection would be:  
     • Higher r (parameter 6) → more punishers → likely higher contributions → efficiency probably rises.  
     • Higher punishment cost γ (parameter 7) → fewer punishers → lower contributions → efficiency likely falls.  
     • Stronger punishment magnitude δ (parameter 8) → more punishers (up to a point) → efficiency could increase, but only until over-punishment starts wasting resources (not modelled).  
   – For the remaining 12 parameters the paper offers no basis for any prediction.

In short, the article is almost entirely about how the *signal value* of punishment (captured in a separate parameter λ) interacts with the *efficacy* of costly signalling (α) to let altruistic punishment evolve. Below I go through the full list of 15 design parameters exactly in the order you gave them.  
For each parameter I state  

(1) whether the paper mentions/implements it (and, if so, its value), and  
(2) whether the paper says anything about what would happen to the *punishment-treatment effect* if that parameter were **systematically varied** (and, if numbers are available, I give those numbers).  
“Punishment-treatment effect” means the difference between a condition with punishment (10P or 20P) and the baseline (BL).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
(1) Yes. All groups contain 3 players.  
(2) No systematic variation; no prediction.

2. Number of rounds  
(1) Yes. The real game can last at most 30 rounds; subjects are only told it will not exceed 1.5 h.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction of how changing the number would alter the effect of punishment.

3. Is chat enabled?  
(1) Yes – the paper explicitly says that “the identities of group members were never revealed” and there is no communication. Value = “No chat”.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
(1) Mentioned implicitly: subjects may “extract fractions of tokens, not only whole numbers.” So the rule is *not* all-or-nothing.  
(2) Never varied; no prediction.

5. Contribution default / endowment retained unless moved out  
(1) Not applicable in this CPR design; nothing said.  
(2) Nothing.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
(1) Not applicable. The game is a CPR with logistic natural growth, not a linear public-goods technology. No MPCR stated.  
(2) Nothing.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
(1) Yes. To *enable* collective punishment, a player must pay a per-round tax that equals 0.50, 0.25 or 0.15 tokens when 1, 2 or 3 players respectively pay.  
(2) The tax size itself is fixed, but it *endogenously* changes with the number of taxpayers. The paper gives theoretical probabilities of paying the tax (q = 0.10 in 10P, q = 0.94 in 20P) and shows empirically that the sanctioning institution is virtually absent in 10P but present in ~80 % of periods in 20P. However, the experiment never *manipulates* the tax rate, so there is no systematic-variation prediction on efficiency.

8. Punishment magnitude  
(1) Yes. Whenever punishment is triggered, the punished player loses exactly 1 token.  
(2) Magnitude is fixed, but the paper exploits within-group variation in “Penalty/Harvest” (the share of a player’s harvest wiped out by the 1-token fine). Regression results (Table 4) show that a larger Penalty/Harvest ratio significantly *reduces* subsequent harvesting (coef ≈ –0.01 per 0.01 increase, p<0.01). Although efficiency is not calculated, lower harvesting in this CPR implies higher remaining resources and, ceteris paribus, higher pay-offs.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
(1) Not mentioned; there are no rewards.  
(2) Nothing.

10. Reward cost  
(1) Not applicable.  
(2) Nothing.

11. Reward magnitude  
(1) Not applicable.  
(2) Nothing.

12. Is the horizon known?  
(1) Yes. Subjects are told only that the session will not exceed 1.5 h; they do *not* know the exact number of rounds.  
(2) Not varied.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
(1) Yes. After each round each player sees every group-member’s harvest (in random order).  
(2) Display is not varied; no prediction.

14. Do punished players learn who punished them?  
(1) Yes. Under collective punishment the sanction comes from the “institution”; the specific voter is *not* revealed.  
(2) Not varied; no prediction.

15. Do rewarded players learn who rewarded them?  
(1) Not applicable (no rewards).  
(2) Nothing.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary  

A. Dependent variables  
– The paper never reports *group efficiency* (total actual pay-off ÷ maximum possible pay-off).  
– Reported dependent variables are:  
  • Fraction of harvested resources (per period, per player)  
  • Absolute harvest (tokens)  
  • Resources remaining in last period  
  • Probability of resource exhaustion (collapse)  
  • Frequency of establishing the sanctioning institution  
  • Frequency of sanctions  
  • Total pay-offs  
These variables capture extraction behaviour, sustainability and monetary earnings; none is identical to the efficiency measure requested.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are at least mentioned?  
Parameters 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 12, 13 and 14 (9 of 15) are described, although only 7 and 8 pertain directly to punishment design. The remaining six parameters (5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 15) are not mentioned at all.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the *effect of systematic variation* on the punishment-treatment effect?  
Strictly speaking, zero. No parameter is experimentally manipulated along more than one level aside from the treatment comparison “no second-order punishment (10P)” vs “second-order punishment (20P)”, which bundles several changes together (most notably parameter 7: effective cost of punishment).  
The regression analysis does show that higher *effective severity* (Penalty/Harvest) dampens extraction (parameter 8), but that severity is not an experimental manipulation. So only one parameter (8) receives any quantitative discussion of its marginal effect.

D. What predictions about efficiency can we make from this paper alone?  
– Moving from BL to 10P (collective punishment without a second-order tax penalty) does *not* change mean harvesting or collapse probability; hence we would predict essentially zero effect on efficiency.  
– Moving from BL to 20P (collective punishment *with* second-order punishment, i.e., higher effective punishment *cost*) *increases* harvesting, raises collapse probability (from 11 % to 56 %), and lowers total pay-offs. Therefore efficiency is predicted to *fall* sharply when the cost of establishing punishment is enforced through a second-order fine.  
– Within a punishment condition, making the fine more severe relative to the recent harvest (higher Penalty/Harvest) reduces subsequent harvesting. If efficiency were computed, it would likely *rise* with that ratio.  
Because no other parameter is varied, the paper provides little or no basis for predicting efficiency effects of changing group size, MPCR, communication, information conditions, reward options, etc.

In short, the paper only allows confident efficiency-based predictions about one composite manipulation (adding second-order punishment) and about the informal severity measure (Penalty/Harvest). All other parameters remain unexplored.
reference_APA: Schaefer, Alexander (2023). Polycentricity and adaptation: A multilevel selectionist approach. JOURNAL OF ECONOMIC BEHAVIOR & ORGANIZATION.

PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
--------------------------------------------------------------------

     • Mentioned?  Yes – 50 RWF (p. 12).

• Table 3, col. 2 (“Penalty”): regression of second-round contribution on conflict proxy and controls.  This is *within* the punishment treatment; it does not estimate a punishment-vs-baseline treatment effect.  No efficiency calculation is presented.

SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables used in the paper

    – Binary “Gave Penalty” and “Gave Reward.”  
    – Contribution in the risky PG version.  
    – Survey-based Risk-Aversion Index.

Below is a systematic walkthrough of each of the 15 parameters in your list, followed by the requested four‐part summary (A–D). Throughout, I refer only to the information contained in the Heller & Sieberg (2008) paper (“Functional unpleasantness: the evolutionary logic of righteous resentment”) as provided above. The paper is a theoretical evolutionary analysis focusing on three player “types” (Fair, Cheater, and Unpleasant) and examines under what conditions any of those three will persist in a population. It does not employ a standard public‐goods experiment design, nor does it measure “efficiency” (total payoff / maximum possible payoff). Instead, it evaluates whether various player types dominate or coexist, based on punishments, costs of punishing, and costs of being punished or cheated.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER‐BY‐PARAMETER DISCUSSION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1) Number of players
   • Discussion in the paper? No. The paper uses population‐level evolutionary models rather than specifying a finite number of players.  
   • Predictions from systematically varying it? No mention.

2) Number of rounds
   • Discussion in the paper? No. The model is not framed in discrete repeated‐game terms but rather in evolutionary‐game‐theoretic terms (differential survival of strategies).  
   • Predictions from systematically varying it? No mention.

3) Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussion in the paper? No.  
   • Predictions from systematically varying it? No mention.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussion in the paper? No.  
   • Predictions from systematically varying it? No mention.

5) Is the contribution default?
   • Discussion in the paper? No.  
   • Predictions from systematically varying it? No mention.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Discussion in the paper? No. The paper does not model a public goods production technology with an MPCR.  
   • Predictions from systematically varying it? No mention.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussion in the paper? Yes. The paper denotes the punisher’s cost as φ (“phi”).  
   • Predictions from systematically varying it? Yes, for whether or not “Unpleasant” (U) types or Cheaters (C) can invade or dominate the population. The authors examine two main cases: (1) φ > β versus (2) φ < β, where β is the cost of being cheated. They derive conditions under which Unpleasant types or Cheaters are evolutionarily stable.  
     – However, the paper does not report a numerical “effect size” on any dependent variable such as efficiency; it reports conditions (inequalities) under which each player type or combination of types will predominate.

8) Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from the punished player)
   • Discussion in the paper? Yes. The paper denotes the cost to the punished individual as γ (“gamma”).  
   • Predictions from systematically varying it? Yes, again in terms of whether Cheaters or Unpleasant types prevail or coexist under different parameter inequalities, such as γ > β, or cost conditions on φ and γ. But no numerical “effect size” is stated, and no separate measure of “efficiency” is given; the outcomes are evolutionary stability conditions (who dominates or coexists).

9) Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussion in the paper? No.  
   • Predictions from systematically varying it? No mention.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Discussion in the paper? No.  
    • Predictions from systematically varying it? No mention.

11) Reward magnitude (coins awarded to the rewarded player)
    • Discussion in the paper? No.  
    • Predictions from systematically varying it? No mention.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?
    • Discussion in the paper? No (there is no finite‐round or repeated‐game discussion).  
    • Predictions from systematically varying it? No mention.

13) Are peer outcomes shown?
    • Discussion in the paper? No. The theoretical analysis assumes that “Cheaters can be identified,” but not that full outcome information is revealed about payoffs or losses each round.  
    • Predictions from systematically varying it? No mention.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Discussion in the paper? No. The authors assume that Cheaters are “readily identifiable,” which allows Unpleasant players to punish them; they do not assume that the identity of the punisher is revealed to the punished.  
    • Predictions from systematically varying it? No mention.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Discussion in the paper? No (the paper does not include any mechanism for rewarding at all).  
    • Predictions from systematically varying it? No mention.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY (A–D)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A: Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   – The paper does not use “group efficiency” as defined by total payoff / maximum possible payoff. It does use “payoffs” in an evolutionary‐game sense, but these payoffs serve to determine which types survive rather than to measure how close the group is to a socially optimal outcome.  
   – Dependent variables in the paper are effectively the evolutionary stability of different player types (the proportion of Fair, Cheater, or Unpleasant players in equilibrium). These differ from group efficiency because they simply show which strategies can invade and persist, rather than how large or small the total payoff is relative to some maximum.

B: Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – Only two of your listed parameters clearly appear:  
     • Parameter 7 (punishment cost) appears as φ.  
     • Parameter 8 (punishment magnitude to the punished) appears as γ.  
   – None of the other 13 parameters are explicitly discussed.

C: For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when the parameter is systematically varied?  
   – Strictly speaking, the paper does vary φ and γ (Parameters 7 and 8), but it does so in order to determine whether Unpleasant players or Cheaters dominate. The authors do not discuss a “punishment treatment effect” on “efficiency.” Instead, they analyze how shifting φ or γ changes the evolutionary stability of each strategy (Fair, Cheater, Unpleasant).  
   – No numerical effect size is given; the discussion is in terms of inequalities (e.g., β > φ or γ > β, etc.).  
   – Hence, two parameters (7 and 8) are systematically varied, but not with respect to “efficiency” per se.

D: If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   – The paper does not provide direct statements about efficiency nor about any of the 15 parameters apart from φ (punishment cost) and γ (punishment magnitude). It also does not directly frame its results in terms of “public goods game efficiency.”  
   – Consequently, there is little in the paper to support predictions about how any of the 15 parameters—either singly or in interaction—affect group efficiency. The sole relevant takeaway is that changing φ or γ can shift the prevalence of punishing strategies in the population, which might, in a different model, indirectly affect overall cooperation or total payoffs. But the paper does not quantify those effects with respect to efficiency.

Abstract: Defector contributes nothing but gains benefit in public goods game. This phenomenon creates an incentive for free riding and causes inefficient equilibrium in which everyone is defector. Below I go through the fifteen parameters one‐by-one.  
For each parameter I state  

(1) Whether the paper explicitly mentions or sets the parameter (and, if so, what values are used).  
(2) Whether the paper **systematically varies** that parameter and, if it does, what the paper tells us about the *punishment-treatment* effect (i.e. the difference between a situation in which punishment is possible/used and a situation in which it is not). -------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players ( n )  
(1) Mentioned constantly; typical values: 20, 50, 64, 65, 80; in analysis n is allowed to vary from 20 to ≳80.  
(2) Yes, varied.  The paper does *not* supply efficiency figures, but it does show how n affects the *possibility* that punishment leads to more cooperation.  Key statements:  
   – Proposition 3: Same-strategy groups “solve the public-goods problem” (full cooperation) only when the cluster is *small*.  
   – Sect. 4.3, Fig. 6: When n is small at the start, punishment + fairness sustains growth; when n is large, punishment becomes too costly (because C=k₃ n²) and cooperation collapses.  
   Numerical example (Fig. 2 vs Fig. 1): With k₁=3 and C=10, full cooperation needs ≳30 players per same-strategy group when n=100, but only ≳7 per group when n=20.  No direct efficiency numbers are reported.

2. Number of rounds  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) Not varied; no effect discussed.

3. Chat enabled  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) Not varied.

4. “All-or-nothing’’ contribution rule  
(1) Yes: the model fixes q_c = 1 (cooperator) and q_d = 0 (defector).  
(2) Never varied, so no predictions about varying it.

5. Contribution default / endowment reclaim  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) Not varied.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor (k₁)  
(1) Yes: k₁ examined at 3 and 5 in Figs. 1–2, and allowed in [3,5] in simulations.  
(2) Varied systematically in Sect. 4.1.  Results relevant to punishment:  
   – Higher k₁ lowers the *minimum* group size needed for punishment to generate full cooperation (Fig. 1: with k₁=5 ≳4 players per same-strategy group are enough, whereas k₁=3 needs ≳7).  
   – Later the authors state that once the system has left the formation stage “no change is expected for strategies” when only k₁ changes, because it scales everyone’s profit utility equally.  
   Numerical effect sizes: not given in efficiency terms; only the thresholds (4 vs 7 players) are shown.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit ( C )  
(1) Central variable.  Fixed values 1–6 in Fig. 4; analytical treatment assumes C>0 and later sets C=k₃ n².  
(2) Varied systematically.  Analytical derivative: ∂F/∂C < 0 (Eq. (8)); i.e. lowering C increases the punishment advantage.  
   Simulation (Fig. 4-left):  
        C = 1 → equilibrium = full cooperation ( n_c ≈ 50 )  
        C = 6 → equilibrium = social dilemma ( n_c ≈ 0 )  
   Exact efficiency not reported, but qualitatively “lower C ⇒ larger punishment treatment effect”.

8. Punishment magnitude ( δ )  
(1) Yes: typical values 1.5, 2, 2.5.  
(2) Varied systematically (Fig. 4-right).  Theory: ∂F/∂δ > 0 (Eq. (8)) so, *holding everything else fixed*, a higher fine helps cooperators.  Simulation adds a caveat: too high δ makes both sides feel unfair, so cooperators may *stop* punishing, and cooperation falls.  In Fig. 4 a move from δ=1.5 to δ=2.5, with C=5, shows the equilibrium number of cooperators drop from ≈38 to ≈0.  Again, efficiency is not reported.

(2) Not varied.

(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) Not varied.

15. Rewarder identity revealed  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) Not varied.

-------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables used  
   – The paper never reports “group efficiency’’ (total payoff divided by the cooperative maximum).  
   – Reported variables:  
        • Individual total utility U_i (profit utility + fairness utility)  
        • Difference F = U_c – U_d with punishment, and f = U_c – U_d without  
        • Number of cooperators n_c at equilibrium  
        • Cluster size n at stabilization  
   These are conceptually different from efficiency because they do not normalise by the social optimum.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   5 parameters: 1 (n), 4 (all-or-nothing), 6 (k₁), 7 (C), 8 (δ).

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* the parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
   4 parameters:  
      – 1 (n) qualitative discussion through Propositions 2–3 and Figs. 5-6  
      – 6 (k₁) varied in Figs. 1–2  
      – 7 (C) varied in Fig. 4-left and analytically (∂F/∂C)  
      – 8 (δ) varied in Fig. 4-right and analytically (∂F/∂δ)  
   No numerical effect sizes on efficiency are given; only qualitative or threshold results.

D.  If we had to predict the punishment-treatment effect on **group efficiency** using only this paper:  
   – Small groups (low n) + low punishment cost C + moderate fines δ + high multiplication factor k₁ should raise efficiency because they lead to full cooperation under punishment, while the no-punishment outcome is defection.  
   – As n grows, C grows (model assumes C∝n²).  Eventually punishment becomes too expensive and cooperators stop punishing; efficiency would then fall back to the no-punishment level (social dilemma).  
   – Extremely large fines (high δ) can backfire, again lowering efficiency by making punishment unattractive.  
   – Changes in k₁ mainly scale everybody’s pay-off and therefore have little additional influence on whether punishment *changes* efficiency once cooperation is already established.  
   – For the remaining 11 parameters the paper gives no information, so no prediction can be made from this source alone.

PARAMETER–BY–PARAMETER SCAN

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Mentioned: 30 periods.

3. Chat enabled?  
   (1) Only anonymity is stated; no chat.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution?  
   (1) Players choose any integer out of 20 tokens; so answer = “no”.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

5. Contribution-default (withdraw vs. give)?  
   (1) Standard give frame; not described as a default.

   (1) Reported: every contributed token is multiplied by 1.6 and divided equally.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

   (1) Reported: 1 token.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

8. Magnitude of one punishment point  
   (1) Reported: recipient loses 3 tokens.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

9. Whether a reward option exists  
   (1) Reported.  Two main treatments:  
       • PN: players can choose a Punishment (P) community or a No-sanction (N) community.  
       • PR: players can choose a Punishment (P) community or a Reward (R) community.  
   (2) Systematically varied by treatment, and the paper *does* discuss how this alters the effect of punishment.  
       • Main qualitative finding: When the alternative is Reward (PR), the punishment community attains high contributions while *using on average only 4.5 punishment points per group in periods 1-15*, versus 10.7 points when the alternative is “No sanction” (PN); see Fig. 1.  
       • Consequently welfare losses from punishment are lower in PR than in PN (“sanctioning community avoids the initial stage of high punishment that is associated with high welfare losses”).  
       • Numeric efficiency measures are not reported, so no exact effect size is available, but the direction is clear: *introducing punishment is less efficiency-reducing when a competing reward community exists*.

10. Cost to give one reward point  
    (1) Reported: 1 token.  
    (2) Not varied; no prediction.

11. Magnitude of one reward point  
    (1) Reported: recipient gains 3 tokens.  
    (2) Not varied; no prediction.

12. Whether the horizon is known  
    (1) Not stated; no information.  
    (2) Not varied; no prediction.

13. Whether peer outcomes are shown  
    (1) Yes – before sanctioning, each player sees individual contributions of all others; after sanctioning they see contributions, payoffs, and sanctions for both communities.  
    (2) Not varied; no prediction.

14. Whether punished players learn the identity of the punisher  
    (1) Players interact anonymously and “changing player IDs … does not allow for reputation building”, implying identities are *not* revealed.  
    (2) Not varied; no prediction.

15. Whether rewarded players learn the identity of the rewarder  
    (1) Same anonymity; identity not revealed.  
    (2) Not varied; no prediction.

SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables used  
    • Contribution (tokens contributed).  
    • Profits / income (tokens earned after the public-good stage and after sanctions).  
    • Punishment and reward points sent/received.  
    • Inequality (income dispersion index used in a probit on migration).  
    “Efficiency” in the sense of *total payoff ÷ maximum possible* is *not* explicitly reported, although welfare losses and net profits are discussed.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
    11 of 15 (all except 3, 12, 14, 15 are at least implicitly described; 14 and 15 are actually implied but not parameterised).

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss the *effect* of systematic variation on the punishment treatment effect?  
    Exactly 1 – Parameter 9 (presence of a reward alternative).  
    No other parameter is varied across conditions, so no further causal statements exist.

D.  Predictions one could make **solely from this paper** about how the 15 parameters and their interactions shape the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency  
    • Presence of a competing Reward community (Parameter 9 = “yes”) mitigates the welfare loss normally observed when punishment is introduced, because fewer punishment points are actually used; hence efficiency *relative to a punishment-only setting* is predicted to be higher.

Below each of the fifteen parameters I report (a) whether the paper even mentions the parameter and, if so, with what value, and (b) whether the paper makes any prediction about what would happen to the **punishment-treatment effect on efficiency (or on any other dependent variable) if that parameter were systematically varied**.  “Punishment-treatment effect” in the present review means the *incremental* effect of allowing players to punish relative to a baseline without punishment.  
Because the study is a repeated employer–worker (gift-exchange) game—​not a public-goods game with an explicit punishment stage—​the vast majority of the fifteen public-goods design parameters simply do not arise.

────────────────────────────────────────────  
1. NUMBER OF PLAYERS  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Two variants are run: 1-on-1 (2 players) and 3-on-3 (6 players).  
   • Systematic predictions for punishment effect?  None.  The paper compares these two market sizes, but there is **no treatment that “turns punishment on or off,”** so no punishment-treatment effect can be extracted.

2. NUMBER OF ROUNDS  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Each game lasts exactly 5 periods; subjects play four such games.  
   • Predictions when varied?  None.  Horizon length is fixed; no systematic variation.

3. CHAT ENABLED?  
   • Mentioned?  No.  Subjects never have free chat.

4. ALL-OR-NOTHING CONTRIBUTION MECHANIC  
   • Mentioned?  No.  Not relevant to the employer–worker design.

5. CONTRIBUTION DEFAULT / ENDOWMENT BACK-TRANSFER  
   • Mentioned?  No.

6. MPCR / MULTIPLICATION FACTOR  
   • Mentioned?  No MPCR because there is no public-goods technology.  Instead, effort yields employer revenue b(e) = 5, 20, 40.  The paper never interprets that as an MPCR and never varies it.

7. COST TO IMPOSE ONE UNIT OF PUNISHMENT  
   • Mentioned?  No.  Punishment is never implemented via a dedicated stage; wage reductions are endogenous and costless to impose.

8. PUNISHMENT MAGNITUDE PER UNIT  
   • Mentioned?  No.  See #7.

9. REWARD ENABLED?  
   • Mentioned?  No explicit reward stage.

10. COST TO GIVE ONE UNIT OF REWARD  
    • Mentioned?  No.

11. REWARD MAGNITUDE PER UNIT  
    • Mentioned?  No.

12. IS THE HORIZON KNOWN?  
    • Mentioned?  Yes.  Subjects know each game lasts exactly 5 periods.  
    • Predictions when varied?  None—​the horizon is never varied.

13. ARE PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN?  
    • Mentioned?  Partially.  After every period each player sees a summary of *their own* and their partner’s pay-offs.  In the 3-on-3 market employers also see competing offers.  
    • Any systematic manipulation?  No.  Hence no prediction for punishment effect.

14. IS THE PUNISHER IDENTIFIED?  
    • Not applicable: there is no explicit punisher.

15. IS THE REWARDER IDENTIFIED?  
    • Not applicable: there is no explicit rewarder.

────────────────────────────────────────────  
SUMMARY

A.  Does the paper use “group efficiency” (total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • No.  Dependent variables are: wage offered, offer acceptance, effort level, “compliance” (giving at least the requested effort), employer earnings, worker earnings, and total surplus (employer + worker).  “Efficiency” as defined in public-goods studies is never reported.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   • Five: (1) number of players; (2) number of rounds (fixed at 5); (12) horizon known (yes); (13) some information display, though not varied; and, tangentially, (6) a benefit schedule b(e) that is *not* used as an MPCR.  The other ten parameters are not discussed.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss **their effect on the punishment-treatment effect** when the parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Zero.  There is no experimental factor in which “punishment” is introduced or removed, so the study never estimates a punishment-treatment effect, let alone how that effect changes with any parameter.

D.  If one had to forecast how the 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency using only this paper, virtually no prediction can be made.  The study neither manipulates explicit punishment nor measures efficiency in the public-goods sense, and therefore provides no quantitative or qualitative guidance about how introducing punishment would interact with any of the listed design parameters.

1. Number of players

2. Number of rounds (time steps)
   (1) Mentioned.  Simulations last T = 1 000 synchronous time steps; the last 25 % are averaged.
   (2) T is never varied, so no prediction.

3. Chat (communication) enabled?
   (1) Never mentioned.
   (2) No discussion, no prediction.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution?
   (1) Not discussed.  Players choose among three strategies C, P, D, but the paper never contrasts “all-or-nothing” vs. continuous choice.
   (2) No prediction.

5. Contribution default (take-back frame)?
   (1) Not mentioned.
   (2) No prediction.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor
   (1) The CRD is driven by risk probability r and cost c rather than an MPCR; no MPCR is reported.
   (2) No prediction.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit (pi_t)
   (1) Mentioned once: π_t = 0.03 (Section 2.3).
   (2) π_t is kept constant; no systematic variation or prediction.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine per unit) (pi_f)
   (1) Mentioned once: π_f = 0.30 (Section 2.3).
   (2) Never varied; no prediction.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
10. Reward cost
11. Reward magnitude
   (1) Rewards do not exist in the model; none of the three parameters is mentioned.
   (2) No prediction.

12. Are the number of rounds known to players?
13. Are peer outcomes shown?
14. Punisher identity revealed?
15. Rewarder identity revealed?
   (1) The model is purely computational; none of these informational parameters appears.
   (2) No prediction.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────
A. Dependent variables
   • Group efficiency (total or average payoff) is never reported.
   • Two dependent variables are used instead:
       – η_G  (group achievement): proportion of groups that reach the cooperation threshold.
       – η_I  (institution prevalence): proportion of groups in which enough punishers exist to run an institution.
     These are different from efficiency because they are binary group-level success metrics, not payoff sums.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?
   4 parameters: 1 (population size), 2 (rounds), 7 (punishment cost π_t), 8 (punishment fine π_f).

C. For how many of the 15 parameters is the effect of **systematically varying** the parameter on the punishment treatment effect discussed?
   Zero.  None of the four mentioned parameters is ever varied, so the paper contains no dose–response style prediction for any of them.

D. What predictions can be made—only from this paper—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?
   • Almost no direct prediction is possible, because efficiency is not measured and none of the 15 parameters is manipulated.
   • Indirectly, one might say that if punishment institutions (parameter family 7–8) exist at the fixed levels π_t = 0.03 and π_f = 0.30, cooperation (and therefore likely efficiency) is higher than without punishment when:
       – The population sits on a heterogeneous (scale-free) network,
       – Risk of failure r is low, and/or
       – A small fraction (≈ 6 – 10 %) of players are pre-committed to punishment.

Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS GAME; EVOLUTIONARY DYNAMICS; REPLICATOR DYNAMICS; COOPERATION; PUNISHMENT; REWARD; MECHANISM
Abstract: In this study, the effects of labor subsidy, taxation, and corruption mechanism on individual behavior are examined within the context of the public goods game. A specific focus is placed on the investigation of how individuals can obtain labor subsidies through the implementation of reward and punishment strategies based on taxation. The findings reveal that a moderate labor subsidy value fosters stable alliances between cooperators and executors, effectively excluding defectors, and this system remains robust under high tax levels. Additionally, it is noted that only the incentive provided by the reward mechanism can facilitate the invasion of defectors. Intuitively, the presence of a corruption mechanism exerts minimal influence on the average level of individual behavior when executors receive increased labor subsidies.

Below I go through the 15 parameters one‐by‐one, stating (i) whether the paper contains any information about the parameter and its value, and (ii) whether the paper makes any quantitative or qualitative prediction about the
effect of *systematically varying* that parameter on the “punishment-treatment effect” (i.e., the difference in group efficiency between a punishment treatment and a baseline without punishment).

Parameter-by-parameter inspection  
(Whenever a symbol appears in the quoted model I give it in parentheses.)

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  All derivations are done for a generic group size N; numerical illustrations set N = 5.  
   • Systematic variation?  No.  N is held constant in the simulations; no comparative-static results are reported for different N.  Consequently, no statement is made about how changing N would change the punishment-treatment effect (for efficiency or anything else).

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  No.  The model is an infinite-population replicator model, so “rounds” never enter.  
   • Systematic variation?  Not applicable.

3. Possibility of chat  
   • Mentioned?  No.  
   • Systematic variation?  Not applicable.

4. All-or-nothing contribution decision  
   • Mentioned?  Yes (cooperate = pay cost c, defect = pay nothing).  The action is binary in every specification.  
   • Systematic variation?  No alternate contribution rule is ever considered.

5. Contribution default (opt-out of a default contribution)  
   • Mentioned?  No.  
   • Systematic variation?  Not applicable.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  Yes: “synergy factor” F with 1 < F < N and F = 3 in all numerical examples.  
   • Systematic variation?  No.  F is fixed and never varied systematically; no prediction is given.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   • Mentioned?  Not directly.  In the model the cost of punishing is financed out of the tax pool, so there is *no* private cost to the punisher.  No free parameter is introduced for the punisher’s individual cost.  
   • Systematic variation?  None.

8. Punishment magnitude (deduction suffered per punishment unit)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes: γ_P = 1 is imposed “for comparative analysis”; never varied.  
   • Systematic variation?  None; therefore no prediction.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  A mixed system of reward and punishment is always available; its relative importance is governed by β (0 ≤ β ≤ 1).  Reward is never *absent* in the sense required to compute a treatment effect of “adding reward.”  
   • Systematic variation?  The paper *does* vary β, but β is not one of the 15 parameters in the user’s list; moreover, no comparison with a “no-punishment” baseline is offered.

10. Reward cost  
    • Mentioned?  Not as a private cost; the cost is pooled from taxes.  No free parameter attached, no variation.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Mentioned?  Yes, γ_R = 1 throughout.  Not varied.

12. End-period (number of rounds known)  
    • Mentioned?  No.  
    • Systematic variation?  Not applicable.

13. Peer-outcome visibility  
    • Mentioned?  No.

14. Punisher identity known  
    • Mentioned?  No.

15. Rewarder identity known  
    • Mentioned?  No.

==================================================================
SUMMARY
A.  Use of “group efficiency” as a dependent variable?  
    No.  The paper tracks expected pay-offs symbolically, but every result that is plotted or discussed uses *strategy frequencies* (ρ_C, ρ_D, ρ_E).  “Efficiency” (total or average payoff divided by the cooperative optimum) is never computed, reported, or used as an outcome.  Hence the dependent variables in the paper are *frequencies*, not efficiency.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters appear at all?  
    6 of them appear:  
       (1) number of players N (fixed),  
       (4) binary contribution rule (fixed),  
       (6) MPCR / F (fixed),  
       (8) punishment magnitude γ_P (fixed at 1),  
       (9) presence of reward (always on),  
       (11) reward magnitude γ_R (fixed at 1).

C.  For how many of the 15 parameters is *any* effect on the punishment-treatment effect discussed when the parameter is systematically varied?  
    Zero.  None of the parameters above is varied in a way that allows the paper to estimate or predict how “adding punishment” would change *efficiency*.

D.  What predictions about the 15 parameters and their interactions on the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency can be made solely from this paper?  
    Almost none.  Because the paper never (i) measures efficiency, (ii) contains a treatment without punishment, or (iii) varies any of the listed parameters in relation to an efficiency outcome, it provides no direct basis for forecasting how any of the 15 parameters—individually or in interaction—would alter the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency.  At best one can infer that parameters the authors *do* vary (tax T, subsidy α, reward-punishment weight β) influence *strategy composition*; but without an efficiency calculation and without separating out a “no-punishment” baseline, the paper yields no usable quantitative or qualitative estimate of a punishment-efficiency treatment effect for any of the 15 specified experimental design parameters.

In short, the paper as supplied offers no direct guidance for predicting how introducing punishment will change group efficiency as a function of the 15 parameters.
reference_APA: Han, Dun & He, Youxin (2023). The impact of labor subsidy, taxation and corruption on individual behavior. APPLIED MATHEMATICS AND COMPUTATION.

Authors: Mitsuishi, K; Kawamura, Y
Author Full Names: Mitsuishi, Kodai; Kawamura, Yuta
Article Title: Avoidance of altruistic punishment: Testing with a situation-selective third-party punishment game
Author Keywords: Altruism; Third-party punishment; Altruistic punishment; Reputation; Evolutionary psychology
Keywords Plus: NORM ENFORCEMENT; COOPERATION; IGNORANCE; EVOLUTION; BENEFITS; EMPATHY; IMAGE; ANGER
Abstract: Third-party punishment games have consistently shown that people are willing to bear personal costs to punish others who act selfishly, even as uninvolved observers. However, the traditional third-party punishment game places participants in contrived situations that mandate direct punishment decisions, potentially inflating the prevalence of such actions compared to those observed in more naturalistic settings. In light of this obligatory nature, one might speculate that if given the autonomy to step aside, people could be inclined to forgo punishment rather than penalize unfairness. The present study developed the Situation-Selective Third-Party Punishment Game (SS-TPPG), an experimental paradigm, to investigate whether avoidance of witnessing unfairness stems from a reluctance to make punitive decisions or a desire to avoid observing unfairness altogether. Three studies (total N = 810) consistently revealed that avoidance was driven by both a reluctance to witness unfair treatment and an aversion to administering punishments. Notably, participants who typically avoided observing unfair treatment were inclined to punish when forced to observe it. Furthermore, when given the opportunity to punish indirectly, participants were less likely to avoid observing unfair distributions. These results suggest that the elevated instances of direct punishment noted in the traditional third-party punishment game might be reflective of the game's structure, which constrains participants' ability to avoid witnessing unfair distributions.

Below, “punishment-treatment effect” (PTE) = (Outcome in a condition with peer punishment) – (Outcome in an otherwise identical control condition without punishment).  
The user asked specifically about **efficiency** (total group payoff / maximum possible payoff).  The paper never measures efficiency; all dependent variables are (a) “choice rate of the unfair deck / expected choice rate of the unfair deck” (i.e., avoidance of witnessing unfairness) and (b) “punishment rate.”  Wherever the paper reports an effect it is always on these two variables, never on efficiency.

I.  Parameter-by-parameter extraction

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  Implicitly 3 per interaction (distributor, recipient, 3rd-party observer).  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  No predictions or effect sizes.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  Yes. 30 trials in Study 1; 20 trials in Studies 2 & 3.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  The reduction (30→20) was purely procedural; no analysis of its effect on any outcome.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned?  No chat in any study; not discussed.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.

4. Contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Not applicable (there is no contribution decision).  Not mentioned; no variation.

5. Contribution default / rollback?  
   • Not applicable; not mentioned.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Not applicable; not mentioned.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  In the “direct-punishment” condition a cost is imposed through a real-effort typing task (length proportional to number of punishments; announced as 5-6 min in Study 1, 4-5 min in Study 2, ≤4-5 min in Study 3).  In the “indirect-punishment” condition and the “no-punishment” condition the cost is effectively 0.  
   • Systematically varied?  Only dichotomously (costful vs cost-free) via the three punishment-type conditions.  The paper reports that costful punishment leads to greater *avoidance* of unfair decks (Fig. 4; Study 3 ANOVA: ηp² = .06, direct < no < indirect).  No discussion of efficiency.

8. Punishment magnitude  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Each punishment deducts 300 yen from the distributor.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  Held constant; no predictions.

9. Reward enabled  
   • Not enabled.  Not discussed.

10. Reward cost  
    • Not applicable.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Not applicable.

12. Whether the number of rounds is known  
    • Mentioned?  Yes.  Participants were told in advance that there would be 30 trials (Study 1) or 20 trials (Studies 2&3).  
    • Systematically varied?  No.

13. Peer outcomes shown  
    • Mentioned?  Yes.  Every round the observer sees the distributor’s choice (100 yen or 500 yen to the recipient).  Not varied.

14. Punisher identified?  
    • Not mentioned.  Distributors are simply told they “may hear” an evaluation later (indirect condition) but the identity of any punisher is never revealed.  No variation.

15. Rewarder identified?  
    • Not applicable (no rewards).

II.  Numerical effect sizes reported (always for avoidance or punishment rate, never for efficiency)

– Direct vs No-Punishment (Study 1): choice rate of unfair deck  
  Welch t(252.1)=-6.34, p<.001, d=-0.79 (lower in costful direct-punishment condition).  
– Direct vs No-Punishment (Study 2): expected choice rate difference d=-0.48.  
– Direct vs Indirect vs No (Study 3): one-way ANOVA F(2,302)=10.38, p<.001, ηp²=.06.  
  Holm-adjusted pairwise:  
   • Direct < No  (d=-0.39)  
   • Direct < Indirect (d=-0.67)  
   • No < Indirect (d=-0.27)

III.  Parameters never mentioned or never varied with respect to PTE: 1,3,4,5,6,8,9,10,11,12,13,14,15.

IV.  Requested Summary

A.  Does the paper use group efficiency as a dependent variable?  
    No.  Two dependent variables are used:  
      (i) Choice / expected-choice rate of the unfair deck (an “avoidance” measure).  
      (ii) Punishment rate (fraction of observed distributions that are punished).  
    Neither equals efficiency; total payoffs are never reported.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are at least mentioned?  
    6 parameters: #1 (implicit 3 players), #2 (number of rounds), #7 (punishment cost), #8 (punishment magnitude), #12 (rounds known), #13 (peer outcomes shown).

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the PTE when the parameter is systematically varied?  
    Exactly one: parameter 7 (punishment cost, manipulated indirectly via punishment-type condition).  
    Even here the reported effects are on *avoidance* and *punishment rate*, not efficiency.

D.  What predictions about the 15 parameters (and their interactions) on the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency can be made solely from this paper?  
    Almost none.  Because efficiency is never measured, and because only punishment cost is manipulated, the only very tentative inference is:  
      – Introducing a *costly* direct-punishment option makes people avoid situations where punishment is possible; if similar avoidance occurred in a public-goods setting it could reduce the frequency of punishment and therefore (uncertain) effects on efficiency.  
    All other parameters are either fixed or unmentioned; the paper provides no basis for predicting their influence on efficiency.

Authors: Ünal-Kocaslan, O; Akgün, S
Author Full Names: Unal-Kocaslan, Ozge; Akgun, Serap
Article Title: Altruistic punishment in intergroup context
Author Keywords: Costly punishment; Norm enforcement; Social preferences; Social categorization; Third party
Keywords Plus: 3RD-PARTY PUNISHMENT; INDIVIDUAL-DIFFERENCES; SOCIAL CATEGORIZATION; STRONG RECIPROCITY; INGROUP; COOPERATION; MEMBERS; ENFORCEMENT; FAVORITISM; EVOLUTION
Abstract: Experimental studies in the literature have shown that individuals are willing to sacrifice their own resources to punish free-riders even if there is no possibility to get reward for this behavior. The aim of the current study is to examine whether individuals have preferences to punish violators when the punishment is costly for themselves and to test whether this preference is affected by social categorization (i.e., ingroup-outgroup settings). For these aims we conducted two experiments. In both studies the Third-Party Punishment Game was used. Study 1 in which a 2 (distributor's identity: ingroup vs. outgroup) x 2 (recipient's identity: ingroup vs. outgroup) x 2 (fairness: equal vs. unequal) within-subjects design was used consists of 38 participants and Study 2 in which a mixed design was used consists of 174 participants. It was found in both studies that participants spent higher amounts to punish unfair players than fair players. Additionally, in Study 2 participants were found to prefer to altruistically punish the perpetrator more harshly when the victim was an ingroup member. The findings suggest that individuals attempt to maintain cooperative behavior norms by engaging in costly punishment of selfish individuals, regardless of their group membership. However, the stricter reactions to unfairness directed to an ingroup member show that participants favor ingroup members over outgroup members in line with the social identity literature.

Below I go through the 15 parameters one‐by‐one, restricting myself strictly to what appears in “Altruistic punishment in intergroup context.”  
For every parameter I state  

(i) whether the paper even mentions or fixes a value for that parameter, and  
(ii) whether the paper provides any **systematic variation** of the parameter and any numerical effect size on a punishment-treatment effect (for any dependent variable).  
Whenever the paper discusses a dependent variable different from efficiency (e.g., “amount of punishment,” “anger”), I note that explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Number of players  
    • Mentioned?  Yes.  Every round involves exactly three players (Player A, B, C).  
    • Systematically varied?  No.  The game is always 3-player; no treatment compares 2, 4, or more players.  
    • No effect size with respect to varying this parameter can be extracted.

2.  Number of rounds  
    • Mentioned?  Yes.  Study 1 uses 20 rounds; Study 2 uses 8 rounds.  
    • Systematically varied?  No.  The round length differs between the two *separate* studies, but the paper never treats “# of rounds” as an experimental factor, never analyses its impact, and never links it to efficiency or any other outcome.  
    • No effect size available.

3.  Chat (communication) enabled?  
    • Mentioned?  No.  There is no chat or communication channel reported.  
    • No variation, no prediction.

4.  “All-or-nothing” contributions?  
    • Mentioned?  Indirectly.  Player A can choose *any* split of a 40-unit endowment; so contributions are *not* all-or-nothing.  
    • Systematically varied?  No.

5.  Contribution default / endowment returned to self?  
    • Not relevant to the third-party punishment design; not discussed.

6.  MPCR / multiplication factor (public-goods side)  
    • Not part of this design; not discussed.

7.  Punishment cost per unit  
    • Mentioned?  Yes.  In both studies Player C spends 1 unit (or 1 raffle ticket) for each punishment point.  
    • Systematically varied?  No.  The cost is always 1; no treatment compares different costs; no effect size.

8.  Punishment magnitude per unit  
    • Mentioned?  Yes.  Spending 1 unit removes 3 units from Player A (3:1 ratio).  
    • Systematically varied?  No.

9.  Reward option enabled?  
    • Not mentioned; no reward stage exists.

10. Reward cost per unit  
    • Not applicable.

11. Reward magnitude per unit  
    • Not applicable.

12. Are the number of rounds known to players?  
    • Mentioned?  Implied yes (instructions say the game “consists of 20 rounds” or “8 rounds”).  
    • Systematically varied?  No.

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mentioned?  Yes.  On the second screen each round, Player C is shown Player A’s actual allocation to B.  
    • Systematically varied?  No.

14. Punisher identity revealed?  
    • Mentioned?  Not explicitly, but by design Player C’s identity is *not* revealed and players never meet again.  
    • Systematically varied?  No.

15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
    • Not applicable (no rewards).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Use of “efficiency” (total or average payoff)  
    • The paper never measures group efficiency, total payoff, nor average payoff.  
    • Dependent variables actually analysed:  
        – “Amount of punishment” (how many units/tickets Player C spends)  
        – Emotional ratings (anger, guilt, “feeling good”).  
      These differ from efficiency because they capture individual spending or feelings, not overall material payoffs relative to a social optimum.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
    • 1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14 → 8 parameters are at least given a fixed value.  
    • The remaining 7 (3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 15) are not mentioned.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of **systematically varying** that parameter on any punishment treatment effect?  
    • None.  Zero of the 15 parameters are experimentally manipulated with multiple values in order to test their impact.  Consequently, no numerical effect sizes linking parameter variation to punishment (let alone efficiency) can be extracted.

D.  Predictions about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment treatment effect on *efficiency*, using only this paper  
    • The paper supplies no information on efficiency and never manipulates any of the parameters; therefore almost no predictive leverage can be gained.  
    • Only a descriptive guess is possible: with the fixed setting used (3 players, cost = 1, impact = 3, no rewards, full information about allocations, known finite rounds), third-party punishment does occur and therefore would *reduce* the punisher’s own payoff while reducing the perpetrator’s payoff even more; the net effect on *group efficiency* is unreported, and without knowing how often cooperation (fair splits) subsequently increases we cannot say whether efficiency rises or falls.  
    • Because no variation is studied, we cannot forecast how changing any of the 15 parameters would raise or lower efficiency under punishment.

In short, the article tells us that third-party punishment happens and is sensitive to ingroup versus outgroup *victim* identity, but it provides no data or theory that links any of the listed structural parameters to changes in efficiency.

Author Full Names: Loustau, Trystan; Glassman, Jacob; Martin, Justin W.; Young, Liane; Mcauliffe, Katherine
Article Title: The impact of group membership on punishment versus partner rejection
Keywords Plus: 3RD-PARTY PUNISHMENT; BIOLOGICAL MARKETS; PAROCHIAL ALTRUISM; INTERGROUP BIAS; COOPERATION; FAIRNESS; EVOLUTION; GAME; FAVORITISM; CHOICE
Abstract: People often display ingroup bias in punishment, punishing outgroup members more harshly than ingroup members. However, the impact of group membership may be less pronounced when people are choosing whether to stop interacting with someone (i.e., partner rejection). In two studies (N = 1667), we investigate the impact of group membership on both response types. Participants were assigned to groups based on a minimal groups paradigm (Study 1) or their self-reported political positions (Study 2) and played an incentivized economic game with other players. In this game, participants (Responders) responded to other players (Deciders). In the Punishment condition, participants could decrease the Decider's bonus pay. In the Partner Rejection condition, participants could reject future interactions with the Decider. Participants played once with an ingroup member and once with an outgroup member. To control for the effects of intent and outcome, scenarios also differed based on the Decider's Intent (selfish versus fair) and the Outcome (equal versus unequal distribution of resources). Participants punished outgroup members more than ingroup members, however group membership did not influence decisions to reject partners. These results highlight partner rejection as a boundary condition for the impact of group on responses to transgressions.

For every parameter I state:

(i) Whether the paper reports its value (or variation) in any of the 51
treatments contained in the meta‐analysis, and where in the text/tables this
appears;  
(ii) Whether the paper offers *any* prediction or empirical estimate for how
systematically varying that parameter changes the *punishment-treatment
effect* (i.e., the difference between a punishment treatment and its
baseline).  Whenever a numerical effect size can be read directly from
Table 2, Fig. 1 or the text, it is reproduced.

REMINDER: The only dependent variable analysed in the paper is the
percentage of the endowment contributed (“cooperation”).  *Efficiency* (total
or average pay-off divided by the maximum possible pay-off) is never
computed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
--------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Number of players (group size)  
(i) Yes.  Table 2 reports four categories (3, 4, 5, 8 players).  
(ii) No prediction about how changing group size *changes the
punishment-treatment effect.*  The table shows main effects on cooperation
(d = 0.29 / 0.41 / 1.08 / 0.14) but these combine *all* treatments, not only
punishment ones.

2. Number of rounds  
(i) Yes.  Table 2 lists nine categories (1, 6, 10, 12, 15, 16, 20, 24, 30).  
(ii) No statement linking the length of the game to the size (or even the
sign) of the punishment-treatment effect.

3. Chat enabled  
(i) Not mentioned anywhere.  
(ii) Consequently, no prediction.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
(i) Not mentioned.  
(ii) No prediction.

5. “Contribution-default” (withdraw from the public account)  
(i) Not mentioned.  
(ii) No prediction.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
(i) The canonical equation (p. 4) notes a factor G > 1, but no values are
given and the variable is never analysed.  
(ii) No prediction.

7. Punishment *cost* (to impose one unit)  
(i) Yes.  Table 2, row “Costly vs. free punishment”: ‘Costly’ k = 14, N = 2 022;
‘Free’ k = 7, N = 392.  
(ii) Yes.  The paper *systematically varies* this parameter and gives effect

  Costly punishment  d = 0.48 (95 % CI 0.23–0.74)  
  Free   punishment  d = 1.29 (95 % CI 0.73–1.85)  
  Difference (Q(1)=13.38, p=0.001).

These numbers are the *stand-alone* impact of punishment relative to the
baseline in each cost condition; the paper does not translate them into
efficiency.

8. Punishment *magnitude*  
(i) Never reported.  
(ii) No prediction.

9. Reward enabled  
(i) Yes.  Table 2, row “Reward”: ‘Present’ vs. ‘Absent’.  
(ii) The paper does give the main effect of allowing rewards
(d = 0.67 vs. 0.40) but does not report how rewards *interact* with
punishment.  Therefore no explicit statement about the punishment-treatment
effect.

10. Reward cost  
(i) Not coded separately.  
(ii) No prediction.

11. Reward magnitude  
(i) Not coded.  
(ii) No prediction.

12. Whether the number of rounds is known to players  
(i) Not discussed.  
(ii) No prediction.

13. Peer outcomes shown (information about others’ pay-offs)  
(i) The closest variable is “Information symmetry” (symmetric vs.
asymmetric).  Table 2: asymmetric information d = 1.17;
symmetric d = 0.32.  
(ii) The paper does not break this down by punishment vs. non-punishment
conditions, so no statement about the punishment-treatment effect.

14. Punished player learns the identity of the punisher  
(i) Not mentioned.  
(ii) No prediction.

15. Rewarded player learns the identity of the rewarder  
(i) Not mentioned.  
(ii) No prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables  
 • The paper *does not use* “group efficiency.”  
 • The sole quantitative dependent variable is “cooperation” (percentage of
the endowment contributed).  Sometimes the authors discuss “earnings,” but
no statistical analysis is performed on it.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  5 out of 15  
 1 (Group size), 2 (Number of rounds), 7 (Punishment cost),  
 9 (Reward enabled), 13 (Information symmetry as a proxy for peer-outcome
visibility).

when the parameter is systematically varied?  1 out of 15  
 Only parameter 7 (punishment cost).  Free punishment produces a much larger
cooperation effect (d ≈ 1.29) than costly punishment (d ≈ 0.48).

made solely from this paper  

The paper offers virtually no guidance because (i) efficiency is never
measured, and (ii) only one of the 15 parameters (punishment cost) is
systematically linked to the punishment-baseline contrast.  Therefore only
very cautious qualitative guesses are possible:

probably on efficiency *if* punishment is not excessively wasteful.  
 • Presence of punishment (versus absence) → sustained higher contributions;

alter the punishment-treatment effect on *group efficiency*.
