Abstract: Within the realm of complex systems, the examination of the evolutionary patterns inherent to natural resources represents a captivating and significant field of inquiry. Previous research, anchored in evolutionary game theory, proposed the logistic growth model to capture resource dynamics. However, these studies often overlooked a crucial reality - the resource growth rate is not static but varies with the current resource quantity. Herein, we extend the previous feedback -evolving game models by considering that resource growth is constrained by the current resource quantity and is influenced by individual decision -making. In such circumstances, ceasing exploitation to allow resource recovery is paramount for sustainable development. Furthermore, we find that coupled systems can exhibit bistability. Depending on initial conditions, the system either converges to a state where all individuals cooperate but resources are exhausted, or to a state where cooperators maintain a constant proportion, allowing for resource sustainability. Below each of the 15 design parameters I report exactly what the paper says and, when possible, what the figures/tables let us infer about the
“punishment-treatment effect” (i.e., the difference between a baseline without minority-rater punishment, M0, and the three punishment variants M1–M3).  
All statements are drawn only from the text, figures and tables reproduced in the paper.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players (group / population size)  
  • Mentioned? YES. Individuals are placed on an L×L lattice; the authors vary L = 50, 100, 200, 400 (Fig. 5).  
  • Systematic variation? YES.  
  • Effect on punishment treatment:  
  – M1 (fixed monetary fine c=0.25): Increasing L raises cooperation and keeps the M1–M0 gap large and positive. In Fig. 5A, at u=0.001 and r=2.6, w=0.5, F_C≈0.70 for L=50 and ≈0.95 for L=400; M0 collapses to ≈0.05 at all L, so the treatment effect grows from ≈+0.65 to ≈+0.90.  
  – M2 (share-reduction ρ=0.25): Mostly positive but one counter-example (r=2.6,w=0.5,u=0.001) where F_C(L=400) < F_C(L=200); the treatment effect therefore shrinks at that point.  
  – M3 (voice-reduction φ=0.25): little or no effect; the M3–M0 gap stays close to zero for every L.  
  No efficiency (payoff) numbers are reported.

2. Number of rounds  
  • Mentioned? NO. The evolutionary simulation runs until convergence; the horizon is not manipulated, nor is its knowability.

3. Chat enabled?  
  • Mentioned? NO.

4. Contribution “all-or-nothing” vs. continuous  
  • Mentioned? YES. Contributions are binary (1 or 0).  
  • Systematic variation? NO. The binary rule is fixed, so no treatment effect is examined.

5. Contribution default / endowment withdrawn  
  • Mentioned? NO.

6. Marginal Per-Capita Return (multiplier r)  
  • Mentioned? YES. r is varied between 1 and |G|; the paper repeatedly plots heat maps across r.  
  • Systematic variation? YES.  
  • Effect on punishment treatment:  
  – Without minority punishment (M0) two cooperation zones appear: Range (a) at medium r and Range (b) at high r.  
  – Adding monetary punishment (M1 or M2) enlarges Range (a) and makes it robust to random exploration; thus the treatment effect is largest at medium r (≈2.4–3.0 when w≈0.4–0.6).  
  – At very high r (≥4) M0 already yields moderate cooperation, so the incremental effect of punishment is small.  
  Exact efficiencies are not reported; figures give only F_C.  

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
  • Mentioned? PARTLY. In M1 the fine c is levied by a third party, so there is zero cost to the punisher; the parameter varied is the magnitude of the fine (see item 8).

8. Punishment magnitude (fine c in M1; ρ in M2; φ in M3)  
  • Mentioned & varied? YES. Fig. 4 gives heat maps of F_C as a function of punishment intensity and exploration rate u.  
  • Effect on punishment treatment:  
  – M1: For every u between 0.1 % and 10 %, cooperation – and hence the M1–M0 gap – peaks at a moderate fine c≈0.3; too small or too large c reduces the gap.  
  – M2: F_C and the treatment gap rise monotonically with ρ (0→1).  
  – M3: Varying φ does not lift cooperation above M0, so treatment effect ≈0.  
  Numeric example (Fig. 4A, u=0.001):  
   c=0  F_C≈0.05 (same as M0)  
   c=0.3 F_C≈0.95  → treatment effect ≈+0.90.  
   c=1   F_C≈0.15  → treatment effect ≈+0.10.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
  • Mentioned? NO. A “disguised” reward is always present in PRHDS, so its presence/absence is not varied.

10. Reward cost to grant one unit  
  • Mentioned? NO.

11. Reward magnitude (value of score-weight w)  
  • Mentioned & varied? YES. w∈[0,1] is the weight of peer scores in the redistribution formula; figures scan w from 0 to 1.  
  • Effect on punishment treatment: M1 and M2 enlarge the cooperation area mainly when w is in the middle range (≈0.3–0.6). The punishment boost disappears when w is very low (w≈0, almost no heterogeneity) or very high (w≈1, rating dominates). No efficiency numbers are provided.

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
  • Mentioned? NO.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
  • Mentioned? YES (ratings are fully public), but this is held constant; no systematic variation or treatment effect reported.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
  • Mentioned? NO. Minority punishment is executed by an anonymous third party.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
  • Mentioned? NO.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
– The paper never reports “group efficiency” (total payoff / maximum possible total payoff).  
– The main dependent variable is the fraction of cooperators F_C; secondary variables are the fractions of the eight strategy types. Payoffs are used only inside the evolutionary update rule, not as analysed outcomes.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
6 are explicitly present:  
(1) number of players, (4) binary contribution, (6) MPCR r, (8) punishment magnitude, (11) reward magnitude w, (13) public visibility of outcomes.  
Parameter 7 (punishment cost) is implicit (fixed at zero to the punisher in M1). All others are absent.

C. For how many parameters does the paper examine the punishment-treatment effect by systematic variation?  
4 parameters:  
(1) number of players L, (6) MPCR r, (8) punishment magnitude (c,ρ,φ), (11) reward magnitude w.

D. Predictions one could make for efficiency – based solely on this paper  
Because the paper gives no payoff or efficiency data, predictions must be indirect (higher cooperation ⇒ probably higher efficiency, except for the monetary fines that lower payoffs in M1). Hence:

– Moderate punishment magnitude (c≈0.3 in M1; any large ρ in M2) and medium values of r and w should give the largest positive effect on efficiency relative to no-punishment baseline.  
– Extremely large punishment, very low or very high w, very small populations, or the “voice-reduction” punishment (M3) are predicted to have little or even negative effect on efficiency.  
– Interactions: the positive effect of punishment magnitude is strongest at medium r and medium w; it weakens when r or w become extreme.  
Given the absence of efficiency numbers, these predictions are necessarily qualitative and modest in confidence.

Abstract: Altruism presents an evolutionary paradox, as altruistic individuals are good for the group yet vulnerable to exploitation by selfish individuals. One mechanism that can effectively curtail selfishness within groups is punishment. Here, we show in an evolutionary game-theoretical model that punishment can effectively evolve and maintain high levels of altruism in the population, yet not all punishment strategies were equally virtuous. Unlike typical models of social evolution, we explicitly altered the extent to which individuals vary in their power over others, such that powerful individuals can more readily punish and escape the punishment of others. In contrast, increased symmetry of power among individuals produced a more egalitarian society held together by altruism and punishment carried out by the collective. These extremes are consistent with the coercive nature of the powerful elites in social insects and egalitarian mechanisms of punishment in humans such as coalitional enforcement and gossip. Our overall findings provide insights into the importance of oversight, the consequences to changes in the power structure of social systems, and the roots of hypocrisy and corruption in human and nonhuman animal societies.

   i. Mentioned: yes. Ten “iterations” per generation (I = 10, Table 1).  
   ii. Varied: no.

3. Chat enabled  
   i. Not mentioned.  
   ii. Not varied.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
   i. Mentioned implicitly. Agents are either altruistic (contribute the whole endowment) or selfish (contribute nothing).  
   ii. Not varied (always all-or-nothing).

5. Contribution default (endowment automatically to public fund unless taken back)  
   i. Not mentioned.  
   ii. Not varied.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor  
   i. Mentioned: “contributions … are multiplied by m” (p. 7).  The actual m-value is not given in the tables, and it is never varied.  
   ii. Not varied.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   i. Mentioned: C = 5 (Table 1).  
   ii. Not varied; no predictions.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss inflicted on the target)  
   In the model the magnitude is captured by the “solitary value” S (a value of 0.05 ≈ very harsh, 1 = no real penalty).  
   i. Mentioned: yes.   S is varied from 0.05 to 1 in 0.05 steps.  
   ii. Systematically varied: yes.   
      – Figures 4 & 5 show the effect of S (together with power-symmetry x or power-distribution P) on the **equilibrium composition of strategies** and on “total altruism”.  
      – Numerical effect that can be read directly:  
        • When S ≤ 0.55 and symmetry is reasonably high (x ≥ 0.6) or power broadly distributed (P ≥ 0.30), altruistic punishment governs the group and total altruism ≈ 99 % (≈ maximal efficiency).  
        • When S > 0.55 the system collapses to pure selfishness, so efficiency drops to ≈ 0.  
        • In the intermediate zone (low x or low P but S ≤ 0.55) selfish punishers keep altruism at roughly 60–70 % (figures indicate ≈ 64 % altruists, ≈ 36 % selfish punishers).  
      The paper does not translate these frequencies into “efficiency”, but higher total altruism is the only proxy given.

9. Reward enabled  
   i. Not mentioned.  
   ii. Not varied.

10. Reward cost  
    i & ii. Not mentioned.

11. Reward magnitude  
    i & ii. Not mentioned.

12. Whether the number of rounds is known to players  
    i & ii. Not mentioned.

13. Whether peer outcomes are displayed  
    i & ii. Not mentioned.

14. Whether the punished player sees who punished them  
    i & ii. Not mentioned.

15. Whether the rewarded player sees who rewarded them  
    i & ii. Not mentioned.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used.  
   – “Total altruism” (frequency of players who contribute in the cooperation phase).  
   – Frequencies of each strategy (altruistic punisher, selfish punisher, altruistic non-punisher, selfish non-punisher).  
   – Occasional verbal reference to “group productivity” or groups that “flourish”, but no explicit efficiency measure (total payoff / maximum payoff) is ever calculated.  
   Thus the paper does **not** use “efficiency” as defined in the prompt; it uses strategy frequencies instead.

B. How many of the 15 parameters are actually mentioned?  
   Six: 1 (group size), 2 (rounds), 4 (all-or-nothing rule), 6 (MPCR/m), 7 (punishment cost), 8 (punishment magnitude).

C. How many are systematically varied and discussed for their treatment effect?  
   Only one of the 15—parameter 8 (punishment magnitude / severity S).  
   The paper also varies two model-specific variables that are **not** in the list (symmetry of power x and proportion powerful P) and analyses their interaction with S.

D. If we had to predict the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency from this paper alone:  
   – Stronger punishment (lower S, i.e., larger loss to the target) is predicted to raise efficiency, **but only** when power is fairly symmetric (high x) and reasonably widespread (high P).  
   – When punishment is weak (S > 0.55) efficiency is predicted to collapse regardless of other settings.  
   – The paper offers no basis to predict how changing any of the other 14 parameters would influence efficiency, because they are never varied and no conjectures are made.

Abstract: Cooperation is a ubiquitous trait among individuals of a species which interbreeds in nature and forms part of groups [1]. Various theories and models have been developed to explain the origins, maintenance, and continuation of cooperation within a generic population. Among these theories is the prisoner's dilemma (PD), which is a well-known framework for investigations on agents' behavior and strategies [2]. In a traditional PD game, pairwise players are assigned the same initial endowment, and they have no access to (nor knowledge of) the opponents' wealth throughout the course of the game. In real life, however, circumstances operate which (in most of the cases) unequally, asymmetrically or hierarchically distribute the income and resources, and the group members may be aware (completely or partially) of their opponents' power and capacity before making their own decision to cooperate or defect. We experimentally reveal the impact of inequality and visibility by means of comparing the results of four sessions where players (1) may have equal or unequal initial endowments and (2) may be visible or invisible to opponents as far as their wealth information is concerned. Our observations disclose that wealth information makes no significant difference to the promotion of cooperation when the initial wealth distribution is fair. In the case of initially unequal endowments, hiding the payoff information enhances the frequency of cooperation while visibility of the opponent's wealth harms group synergy. (C) 2019 Elsevier Ltd. Below I go through the 15 parameters in the exact order requested.  
For each parameter I state  

(i) whether the paper explicitly mentions it and, if so, the value actually used in the experiment;  
(ii) whether the paper ever varies the parameter;  
(iii) whether the paper says anything about how a systematic change in that parameter would influence the **punishment-treatment effect** (i.e., the difference between a condition with the possibility of peer punishment and an otherwise identical condition without that possibility) on any dependent variable, most importantly on group efficiency.  When an effect size can be read directly from a figure or table I report it; otherwise I report “not given”.

-------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
(i) Mentioned: yes.  All games are 2-player Prisoner’s Dilemmas.  
(ii) Not varied.  
(iii) No prediction about how changing the number of players would change the punishment-treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
(i) Mentioned: yes.  Subjects are told each round continues with 75 % probability (“indefinite horizon”); the exact number of realised rounds is not disclosed.  
(ii) Not varied.  
(iii) No prediction.

3. Is chat enabled?  
(i) Not mentioned (there is no chat).  
(ii) Not varied.  
(iii) No prediction.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution?  
(i) Not exactly applicable.  Subjects choose among the three discrete actions C, D, P.  
(ii) Not varied.  
(iii) No prediction.

5. Contribution default / “withdraw” frame?  
(i) Not relevant; never mentioned.  
(ii) –  
(iii) –

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor (or, here, the PD payoff matrix)  
(i) Mentioned.  Main matrix L shown in the text corresponds to “dilemma strength = 1”.   
(ii) Briefly noted that they ran a second, unpublished matrix (“dilemma strength = 2”) and obtained qualitatively similar results.  No systematic exploration.  
(iii) No prediction about how changing the payoff matrix would alter the punishment-treatment effect.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
(i) Implicit in the payoff matrix but never quantified as a separate parameter.  
(ii) Not varied.  
(iii) No prediction.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss per unit received)  
(i) Implicit in the matrix, not isolated.  
(ii) Not varied.  
(iii) No prediction.

9. Is a reward option available?  
(i) No.  
(ii) –  
(iii) –

10. Reward cost  
(i) –  
(ii) –  
(iii) –

11. Reward magnitude  
(i) –  
(ii) –  
(iii) –

12. Are subjects told when the game ends?  
(i) Yes: they are told only the 75 % continuation probability; horizon is unknown.  
(ii) Not varied.  
(iii) No prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes / wealth shown?  
(i) Yes.  This is the *only* parameter the authors manipulate:  
    • Visible wealth (“T1”, “C1”) versus  
    • Hidden wealth (“T2”, “C2”).  
(ii) Varied in a 2 × 2 design together with initial wealth equality vs. inequality.  
(iii) What the paper reports:  
    – Visibility lowers average cooperation when initial endowments are unequal (0.22 vs 0.49).  
    – Visibility has virtually no effect on the *frequency of punishment* (0.06 vs 0.03) and none on the *use of punishment by poor vs. rich players*.  
    – No statistic is provided that isolates “the punishment-treatment effect” because there is **no experimental condition in which punishment is removed**.  Hence the paper does *not* estimate how the *presence versus absence* of punishment interacts with wealth visibility on efficiency or on any other outcome.

14. Do punished players learn the identity of the punisher?  
(i) In a 2-player PD the identity is trivially known, but the paper never discusses it.  
(ii) Not varied.  
(iii) No prediction.

15. Do rewarded players learn the identity of the rewarder?  
(i) Not applicable (no rewards).  
(ii) –  
(iii) –

-------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY  

A. Dependent variables actually analysed  
• “Cooperation level” = frequency of choosing C  
• “Frequency of P” = frequency of choosing the costly punishment action  
• “Final wealth” (= individual cumulative payoff)  
The term “efficiency” (total payoff / maximum possible payoff) is never used, though final wealth is conceptually close.  Contributions and cooperation rate are therefore **not** interchangeable with efficiency in this paper.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
7 of them:  
(1) number of players; (2) number of rounds (unknown horizon);  
(4) discrete vs. continuous choice (implicitly “all-or-nothing”);  
(6) payoff matrix; (7)(8) punishment cost and magnitude (implicit);  
(12) horizon known; (13) visibility of peer wealth.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss *systematic variation* and its effect on the punishment-treatment effect?  
Zero.  
Only parameter 13 (visibility) is varied, but the experiment lacks a “no-punishment” baseline, so no punishment-treatment effect can be computed.

D. Predicting the impact of the 15 parameters on the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency **using only this paper**  
Because the study always includes the punishment option, it provides virtually no information on what would have happened had punishment been absent, nor on how any parameter modulates that hypothetical contrast.  The only cautious statements that can be made are:  
• Varying parameter 13 (showing vs. hiding wealth) affects cooperation and payoffs when wealth is unequal, but does *not* appreciably change how often punishment is used.  Whether this would translate into a larger or smaller *punishment-treatment effect on efficiency* cannot be inferred.  
• For every other parameter (1–12, 14–15) the paper gives no evidence whatsoever on their interaction with punishment, so no predictions can be drawn.

In short, the paper is concerned with visibility of wealth and initial inequality inside a *single* experimental setup where punishment is always available; it does not furnish data that allow one to predict how any of the 15 public-goods-game parameters would amplify or dampen the efficiency gains (or losses) produced by introducing punishment.

Below, each of the 15 parameters is treated in turn.  For every parameter I report  
(1) whether it is mentioned in the paper and, if so, the value(s) used;  
(2) whether the paper systematically varies the parameter;  
(3) whether the paper links systematic variation of the parameter to any “punishment-treatment effect” (i.e., the effect of adding a sanctioning institution on any dependent variable).  Numerical effect sizes are quoted whenever they can be read directly from the text, tables, or figures.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned.  Each group contains n = 3 members; two such groups are paired and share one “common-member”, so five subjects interact.  
   (2) Not varied.  
   (3) No prediction about how changing the group size would alter any punishment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Mentioned.  Exactly 20 rounds; subjects know this.  
   (2) Not varied.  
   (3) No discussion of how more/fewer rounds would change any punishment effect.

3. Chat enabled?  
   (1) Not mentioned; no chat was allowed.  
   (2) Not varied.  
   (3) No discussion.

4. “All-or-nothing’’ contribution rule?  
   (1) Not mentioned; the standard continuous VCM (0–20 tokens) is used.  
   (2) Not varied.  
   (3) No discussion.

5. “Contribution default’’ (withdraw-from-public-fund) framing?  
   (1) Not mentioned; standard contribute-to-public-fund framing is used.  
   (2) Not varied.  
   (3) No discussion.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   (1) Mentioned.  MPCR = 0.6 (a constant across all treatments).  
   (2) Not varied.  
   (3) No prediction concerning how a different MPCR would interact with punishment.

7. Punishment cost (per unit)  
8. Punishment magnitude (per unit)  
   (1) Costly token-deduction punishment is never implemented.  The only sanctioning institution is cost-free, one-round ostracism by majority vote.  Cost and magnitude parameters for monetary punishment therefore do not appear.  
   (2) Not varied.  
   (3) No discussion of varying punishment costs or magnitudes.

9. Reward enabled?  
10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   (1) Monetary rewards are never available, so none of these parameters are mentioned.  
   (2) Not varied.  
   (3) No discussion.

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
   (1) Yes.  Subjects are explicitly told the game lasts 20 rounds.  
   (2) Not varied.  
   (3) No discussion of uncertainty over the horizon and its interaction with punishment.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   (1) Yes, and this is the only parameter the paper systematically varies:  
       • CM: dedicated-members see individual contributions only within their own group.  
       • CM-Info: dedicated-members additionally see the common-member’s contributions in the *other* group.  
   (2) Systematic variation = information restricted vs. information widened.  
   (3) Effect on a sanction institution:  the only “punishment” in the paper is ostracism (CM-Ostracism).  Ostracism is *not* combined with varying information, so the paper gives no evidence on how changing information display moderates a punishment effect.  The information manipulation is studied only in the absence of ostracism.

14. Do punished players learn who punished them?  
   (1) Mentioned for ostracism: voting is anonymous; excluded players learn *how many* votes they got but not *who* cast them.  
   (2) Not varied (always anonymous).  
   (3) No discussion of revealing punisher identity and its effect on efficiency or any other outcome.

15. Do rewarded players learn who rewarded them?  
   (1) Not applicable—there is no rewarding institution.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Does the paper use “group efficiency’’ (total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
    No.  The paper’s outcome measures are individual contributions, group-level contributions, ostracism frequency, and their time trends.  Efficiency (payoff / maximum possible payoff) is never reported or analysed, and therefore is not equated with “contribution” in the article.

B.  Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
    Five parameters are explicitly described:  
    1. Number of players (n = 3 per group, plus 1 common member)  
    2. Number of rounds (20)  
    6. MPCR (0.6)  
    12. Horizon known (yes)  
    13. Peer-outcome visibility (varied across CM vs. CM-Info)  
    Parameter 14 is indirectly described (punisher anonymity) but never varied.

C.  For how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss *systematically varying* the parameter and tracing its effect on a punishment treatment?  
    None.  The paper conducts three main treatments: CM (baseline), CM-Info (information only), and CM-Ostracism (punishment only).  The information parameter (13) is varied, but only in the *absence* of the punishment institution; the punishment institution (cost-free ostracism) is introduced, but information visibility is held constant.  Hence the paper does not connect systematic variation of any of the 15 listed parameters to the effect of punishment on any outcome variable, let alone on efficiency.

D.  Predictions one could make—solely from the paper—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency  
   • Because the paper never measures efficiency, no direct quantitative predictions for efficiency can be extracted.  
   • The only sanction studied is cost-free, anonymous ostracism; it *raises* average contributions (≈ +5 tokens by common-members relative to no-ostracism) and equalises behaviour across groups.  If one *defines* this difference as a “punishment treatment effect”, then:  
       – The effect appears in groups of size 3, with MPCR = 0.6, 20 known rounds, anonymous votes, and no additional information about the other group.

Below I go through the 15 parameters one by one, quoting or paraphrasing only what is contained in the Klempt (2012) paper (including its references to the earlier Falk-Fehr-Fischbacher study, “FFF”).  I separate two questions for every parameter:

• “Mentioned?” – Does the paper give the value that was actually implemented?  
• “Systematically varied?” – Does the paper report what happens to the *punishment-treatment effect* when that parameter is deliberately varied across conditions?  When the answer is “yes,” I reproduce the qualitative or quantitative effect that the paper itself provides.  All effects refer to *punishment behaviour* (amount of deduction points or frequency of punishing), because the paper never reports group efficiency.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes – the game has 3 players.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  Only a 3-player game is run, so no effect of changing the group size is available.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? Yes – each subject plays exactly one round (“one shot”).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  Hence no evidence on how a different horizon would alter the punishment treatment effect.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned? No.  The paper gives no indication that any communication was possible.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution decision  
   • Mentioned? Yes – the first-stage action is a binary “cooperate or defect” Prisoners’ Dilemma choice.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  Only the binary version is used.

5. Contribution default / withdrawal frame  
   • Mentioned? No.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? No (the study uses a PD payoff matrix, not a linear public-good structure).

7. Punishment cost (to the punisher, per unit)  
   • Mentioned? Yes – in Klempt’s own experiment each deduction point costs the punisher 1 point.  
   • Systematically varied? No within the present study.  
   • HOWEVER, the paper summarises FFF where the cost-benefit ratio of punishment *was* varied (“low-sanction” vs. “high-sanction” treatment).  The qualitative findings reported from FFF are:  
     – Cooperators punish defectors equally in both sanction regimes.  
     – Defectors punish **only** in the high-sanction treatment and **never** in the low-sanction treatment.  
     (No numeric effect sizes on efficiency are given.)

8. Punishment magnitude (loss inflicted on target, per unit)  
   • Mentioned? Yes – each deduction point reduces the target’s payoff by 2.5 points.  
   • Systematically varied? Same remarks as for #7: not varied in Klempt, but varied in the earlier FFF study whose results are summarised (see above).

9. Whether a *reward* option exists  
   • Mentioned? Yes – indirectly; the paper says the second stage “allows them to punish,” with no mention of any reward possibility.  So the reward option is simply absent.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   • Mentioned? No – no reward mechanism is used.

12. Whether the number of rounds is known to players  
   • Mentioned? Yes – because the game is one-shot, the end is known.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Mentioned? Yes – after the game “subjects received feedback on their roles, others’ decisions, and payoffs.”  
   • Systematically varied? No.

14. Is the identity of the punisher revealed to the punished?  
   • Mentioned? Unclear but implied: roles are revealed in the final feedback, so punished players can in principle infer who punished them.  The paper does not discuss this design choice any further.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

15. Is the identity of a rewarder revealed?  
   • Not applicable – there is no reward stage.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables used in the paper  
    – Punishment *amount* (mean deduction points assigned).  
    – Punishment *incidence* (fraction of subjects who impose ≥1 deduction point).  
    The study never reports total group payoff, average payoff, or efficiency.  Hence “efficiency” is **not** a dependent variable in this paper.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are at least mentioned?  
    Eight: 1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14.  (Parameters 3, 5, 6, 9–11, 15 are absent.)

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss the *effect of systematically varying the parameter* on the punishment treatment effect?  
    Two (7 and 8), and only via the recap of the earlier FFF study: changing the punishment cost-benefit ratio alters *defectors’* willingness to punish (zero in the low-sanction condition, positive in the high-sanction condition) but leaves cooperators’ punishment unchanged.  No efficiency data are provided.

D.  Predicting the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency using only this paper  
    The paper contains no measurements of efficiency, so strictly speaking it permits almost no prediction.  The only indirect hint is the FFF finding that harsher punishment (relative to its cost) induces defectors to punish, which would obviously *lower* efficiency because punishment is wasteful.  Beyond that single qualitative inference, the paper offers no basis for predicting how any of the 15 parameters—or their interactions—would influence the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.

A. Dependent variables used

Throughout, “the paper” refers exclusively to the “Give and Take” manuscript you provided. Please note that, although the Give and Take game does include a “take” action that the authors sometimes describe as a “built-in punishment” and a “give” action that confers a bonus, the paper does not present these in the same way that many public-goods‐with‐punishment (or reward) experiments do. ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   (a) Does the paper discuss it?
       • Yes. The paper defines Give and Take specifically for two players and analyzes how they share a single indivisible resource.
   (b) Does it predict what happens if we systematically vary it?
       • No. Although the authors briefly mention the possibility of extending the game to more than two players in the future, they do not provide any systematic predictions or effect sizes about varying the number of players.

2. Number of rounds
   (a) Does the paper discuss it?
       • Yes, but the paper calls them “stages.” It examines both a finite number of stages l and an indefinite (or infinite) number of stages.
   (b) Does it predict the effect of systematically varying the rounds on punishment treatment or efficiency?
       • No. The paper analyzes how players’ strategies differ for finite vs. infinite horizons (e.g., backward induction arguments if l is finite), but it does not present a “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency nor give a numerical effect size.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   (a) Does the paper discuss it?
       • No. There is no mention of any communication or chat parameter in these experiments or simulations.
   (b) Does it predict any systematic effect?
       • No. Not mentioned at all.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   (a) Does the paper discuss it?
       • No. The resource is indivisible and can be either “kept” or “given,” but the paper does not frame this as an “all-or-nothing contribution.” It never uses that wording or systematically compares “all-or-nothing” versus other contribution schemes.
   (b) Does it predict any systematic effect?
       • No. Not mentioned.

5. Is the contribution default?
   (a) Does the paper discuss it?
       • No. The authors do not examine any default contribution, or have a parameter controlling how much is “moved back” by default.
   (b) Does it predict any systematic effect?
       • No. Not mentioned.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related factor
   (a) Does the paper discuss it?
       • No. The authors never refer to “MPCR” or a multiplication factor. The payoff structure is built around bonus for giving (b₍g₎) and costs for taking (c₍pt₎ and c₍st₎), not a typical public-goods MPCR.
   (b) Does it predict any systematic effect?
       • No. Not mentioned.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   (a) Does the paper discuss it?
       • Partly. The “take” action in Give and Take imposes two kinds of costs: c₍pt₎ is paid by the taker, c₍st₎ is paid by the one subjected to taking. Thus c₍pt₎ can be seen as a “cost to impose punishment.”  
   (b) Does it predict the effect of systematically varying c₍pt₎ on a punishment treatment or efficiency?
       • The paper does systematically consider c₍pt₎ ≥ 0 in many derivations and remarks that higher c₍pt₎ can deter taking. However, it does not speak of a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Nor does it quantify a numerical effect size for how varying c₍pt₎ changes group efficiency. The discussion concerns whether certain strategy profiles become equilibria, not how efficiency changes.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from the punished player)
   (a) Does the paper discuss it?
       • Partly. The parameter c₍st₎ is a cost paid by the one subjected to the “take” action, i.e., the “punishment magnitude” that the other player inflicts.  
   (b) Does it predict how systematically varying c₍st₎ affects any punishment‐treatment effect on efficiency?
       • The paper does analyze c₍st₎ ≥ 0 and shows that if c₍st₎ is large, it can deter non-cooperative actions. Still, it does not tie this discussion to “group efficiency” or provide effect sizes on a punishment‐treatment measure.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   (a) Does the paper discuss it?
       • No. There is no discussion of “enabling” or “disabling” a separate reward mechanism. The game’s “bonus for giving” (b₍g₎) is always part of the payoff structure, but the authors do not treat it as an optional parameter that might be removed.
   (b) Does it predict any systematic effect?
       • No. Not mentioned in the sense of toggling a reward on or off.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   (a) Does the paper discuss it?
       • No. While the game does have a bonus for giving (b₍g₎), there is no “cost to the rewarder” akin to a separate parameter for awarding that bonus.
   (b) Does it predict any systematic effect?
       • No. Not mentioned.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)
   (a) Does the paper discuss it?
       • Partly. One might interpret the “bonus for giving,” b₍g₎, as a “reward magnitude.” The paper frequently discusses b₍g₎ in [0,1) and remarks that if b₍g₎ ≥ 1, giving the resource dominates.  
   (b) Does it predict how systematically varying b₍g₎ affects a punishment‐treatment effect on efficiency?
       • The authors do examine b₍g₎ from 0 up to ≥1 in terms of equilibria. However, they do not frame it as “reward magnitude’s effect on group efficiency under a punishment treatment,” nor do they provide numeric effect sizes tied to efficiency.

12. Is the number of rounds known (do players know when the game ends)?
   (a) Does the paper discuss it?
       • They consider a finite-l game and an infinite-horizon game, but do not explicitly say whether players “know” l. They do not treat knowledge of game length as a separate experimental parameter.
   (b) Does it predict any systematic effect?
       • No. Not discussed in terms of variations or effect sizes.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?
   (a) Does the paper discuss it?
       • No. The paper does not discuss revealing payoffs or outcome information to the other player as a variable. In a 2‑player game, each sees who takes or gives, but there is no mention of systematically varying the visibility of payoffs.
   (b) Does it predict any systematic effect?
       • No. Not mentioned.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the punisher is?
   (a) Does the paper discuss it?
       • The game only has two players, so effectively each player knows who acted, but there is no separate discussion of anonymity or “known punisher.”
   (b) Does it predict any systematic effect?
       • No. Not mentioned as a variable.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is?
   (a) Does the paper discuss it?
       • Similarly, the paper never treats anonymity or identification of the giver as a separate factor.
   (b) Does it predict any systematic effect?
       • No. Not mentioned.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper does not use “group efficiency” in the sense of (actual total payoff) / (maximum possible payoff).    • None. Although c₍pt₎, c₍st₎, and b₍g₎ are each systematically analyzed, the authors do not frame any result as a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency,” nor provide effect sizes of how such variation influences group-level efficiency.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how these 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

Below, each of the 15 parameters is treated in turn.  
For every parameter I state  

(1) whether it is explicitly present anywhere in the paper and, if so, where and with what symbol/value;  
(2) whether the paper makes a quantitative or qualitative prediction about how **systematically varying** that parameter would change the “punishment treatment effect.”  
Because the paper never reports an experimental “treatment effect” (difference between a baseline game and a punishment game) and never reports group-efficiency data, I translate “punishment treatment effect” into what the authors do analyse: the conditions under which costly *sanctioning* (monitoring plus a monetary sanction, s) succeeds or fails in raising cooperation and total pay-offs relative to the no-sanction baseline.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Explicit.  The symbol n is the group size in all equations (e.g. Eq. 2, Eq. 3).  
   (2) No systematic‐variation results.  n is algebraically present but all key inequalities are written as proportions (e.g. n_M / n), so the authors never vary n to see how outcomes change.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Mentioned once (p. 10: “The process is then repeated for a number of rounds T”).  
   (2) No predictions; T drops out of all derivations.

3. Is chat enabled?  
   (1) Not mentioned.  
   (2) No discussion.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   (1) Yes.  The binary indicator ι_C ∈ {0,1} means “cooperate (=contribute) or defect.”  
   (2) The binary nature is assumed, never varied.

5. Contribution default (opt-out frame)?  
   Not mentioned; no predictions.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   (1) Present.  Parameter α is the amount of public good created by one contributor; C_C is the private cost of that contribution.  
   (2) α and C_C enter all core inequalities.  Example: For full cooperation to be an equilibrium when punishment is possible (Variant 2), inequality (13) must hold:  
          α β / δ  >  C_C / s.  
       Thus, increasing α (or decreasing C_C) lowers the monitoring investment β that is necessary for punishment to work.  No numerical effect sizes are given, only the algebraic condition.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   (1) Present.  A monitor pays δ per target, so C_M = p δ is the cost of imposing sanctions on p people.  
   (2) Appears in every inequality linking monitoring and cooperation.  Larger δ makes punishment harder to sustain (it raises the right-hand side of inequality (13) and therefore requires either more monitoring or a larger sanction s).  Again, only algebraic statements, no effect sizes.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine imposed on the target)  
   (1) Present as s in Eq. 3 and all later inequalities.  
   (2) Larger s makes cooperation easier to sustain (it lowers the required monitor frequency n_M/n in inequality (6) and lowers the right-hand side of (13)).  No numeric effect sizes beyond the symbolics.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
    (1) Not mentioned at all.  
    (2) No discussion.

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
14. Is the punisher identified?  
15. Is the rewarder identified?  
    (1) Not mentioned.  
    (2) No discussion.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY  

A.  Dependent variables used  
    • Individual utility u_i(t) (Eq. 1)  
    • Frequency of cooperation (n_C/n)  
    • Frequency of monitoring (n_M/n)  
    • No measure called “group efficiency” (pay-off relative to the cooperative optimum) is ever computed.  
    Hence efficiency is not a reported dependent variable, and all results are about cooperation/monitoring conditions.

B.  Parameters from the list that appear in the paper: 6 of 15  
    1 (group size n), 2 (rounds T, merely named), 4 (binary contribution), 6 (α, C_C), 7 (δ), 8 (s).

C.  Parameters whose *systematic variation* is analysed: 3 of 15  
    6 (α and C_C), 7 (δ), 8 (s).  
    For each of these the paper gives algebraic comparative-static results (no numeric effect sizes).

D.  What can be predicted, solely from this paper, about the impact of the 15 parameters (and their interactions) on the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
    • Because the authors never compute efficiency, predictions about efficiency are indirect: anything that pushes the system into the “full cooperation + adequate monitoring” equilibrium would, by implication, raise efficiency to its maximum; anything that leaves the system in the “no cooperation, no monitoring” equilibrium yields zero efficiency.  
    • According to inequalities (6) and (13)/(14), punishment improves outcomes when  
          – The fine s is large,  
          – Monitoring is cheap (low δ) or each monitor can check many partners (high p, although p is not one of the 15 listed parameters),  
          – The public-good technology is favourable (high α or low C_C),  
          – A sufficiently large fraction β of the public resource is earmarked for reimbursing monitors.  
      All other listed parameters are either fixed or absent, so nothing can be inferred about them.  
    • The paper provides no guidance on chat, information revelation, knowledge of the horizon, reward schemes, or identification of punishers/rewarders.  
    • Therefore, based solely on this paper, one can make only limited, sign-direction predictions for three parameters (α/C_C, δ, s) and for the collective-choice variable β; for the remaining parameters no prediction is possible.

A. Dependent variables actually analysed

Abstract: In this article, we study the problem of information sharing among rational self-interested agents as a dynamic game of asymmetric information.    (2) Systematic variation:  Fig. 3d reports that increasing f (with costly-signal amplification k = 6) “increases the proportion of punishers and decreases the proportion of defectors.’’  Again, the paper does not provide the no-punishment baseline for those f values, so the treatment-effect size on efficiency is not given.  Direction only.

8. Punishment magnitude / loss to the target (e)  
   (1) Values: e = 0 or 5; Fig. 6 varies e from 0 to 10 (x-axis).  
   (2) Systematic variation:  Fig. 6 shows *virtually no change* in the frequencies of any strategy when e increases.  The authors’ text: “the proportion of cooperation, punishment, and defection … does not change significantly due to the increasing loss from being punished.”  Therefore the paper predicts *little or no change* in the punishment treatment effect when e is varied (no numerical estimates).

9. Reward enabled?  
   (1) Never mentioned.  
   (2) No discussion.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   – not mentioned or varied.

12. Whether the number of rounds is known  
   – not mentioned.

13. Whether peer outcomes are shown  
   – not mentioned.

14. Whether the punished player learns the identity of the punisher  
   – not mentioned.

15. Whether the rewarded player learns the identity of the rewarder  
   – not mentioned.

────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A. Use of “group efficiency’’ as a dependent variable?  
   No.  The paper’s dependent variables are:  
   • Frequency (population share) of Cooperators, Punishers, and Defectors.  
   • Occasionally mean *payoff* or *fitness* (payoff after costly-signal transformation).  
   Efficiency—total payoff relative to a cooperative optimum—is never computed.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
   4 parameters: #1 (players), #6 (benefit b), #7 (punishment cost f), #8 (punishment magnitude e).

C. For how many parameters is a *systematic* variation linked to the punishment-treatment effect?  
   3 parameters (6, 7, 8).  Even for these, results are given only for conditions that already contain punishment, so the *difference* between punishment and no-punishment (i.e., the treatment effect) on efficiency cannot be extracted—only directional changes in strategy frequencies within the punishment regime are reported.

D. Predicting the 15-parameter influence on the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency, using only this paper’s evidence:  
   • Parameters the paper suggests *might* matter: higher cooperation benefit (b) and higher punishment cost (f) are predicted to raise the prevalence of punishers and lower defectors, which would normally raise efficiency *if* punishment were absent from the baseline.  Variation in e seems irrelevant.  
   • For every other parameter (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9–15) the paper offers no information, so no prediction can be made.  
   • Because the paper never measures efficiency, any numerical prediction of the treatment effect on efficiency is impossible on the basis of the reported results.

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Baseline sessions: 16 players (4 sellers, 6 buyers, 6 third parties).  Punishment sessions: 18 players (two extra observers).

SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables actually analysed  
   • “Group efficiency / welfare / total payoff” – yes, section 4.6 compares average earnings (≈ group efficiency).  
   • “Socially responsible behavior” – binary indicator of buying/producing the fair product (primary dependent variable).  
   • “Money-burning (anti-social behavior)” – whether subjects destroy partner income in the Joy-of-Destruction game.

B.  Parameters from the 15-item list that are even mentioned = 6  
      (1) # players, (2) # rounds, (7) punishment cost, (8) punishment magnitude, (12) horizon known, (13) peer-outcome visibility.

Article Title: Third-party punishers who express emotions are trusted more
Source Title: PROCEEDINGS OF THE ROYAL SOCIETY B-BIOLOGICAL SCIENCES
Author Keywords: third party punishment; trust; cooperation; emotion expression; anger; disgust
Keywords Plus: PUNISHMENT; DISGUST; COOPERATION; ANGER; REWARD
Abstract: Third party punishment (TPP) is thought to be crucial to the evolution and maintenance of human cooperation. However, this type of punishment is often not rewarded, perhaps because punishers' underlying motives are unclear. We propose that the expression of moral emotions could solve this problem by advertising such motives. In each of three experiments (n = 1711), a third-party punishment game was followed by a trust game. Third parties expressed anger or disgust instead of, or in addition to, financial punishment. Results showed that third parties who expressed these emotions were trusted more than those who didn't express (Experiment 1), and more than those who financially punished (Experiment 2). Moreover, third parties who expressed while financially punishing were trusted more than those who punished without expressing (Experiment 3). Findings suggest that emotion expression might play a role in the evolution and maintenance of cooperation by facilitating TPP.

Below, each of the 15 public-goods–game parameters is considered in turn.  For every parameter I indicate  

(1) whether it is mentioned or can be deduced from the methods of Kupfer & Tybur (2023), and the concrete value used, and  

(2) whether the paper reports (or allows one to infer) how *systematically varying* that parameter would change the “punishment treatment effect” (i.e. the difference that the possibility of punishment makes, here measured in the paper by trust or trustworthiness, not by efficiency).

Because the study is a one-shot **third-party punishment game (TPPG) followed by a trust game**, many of the 15 parameters that are standard in repeated public-goods games do not apply.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
--------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned.  A TPPG consists of three players (dictator, receiver, third party).  
   (2) Never varied; no predictions about varying group size.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) One round only; not hidden from participants.  
   (2) Not varied; no predictions.

3. Is chat enabled?  
   (1) Not mentioned; no chat.  
   (2) Not discussed.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule?  
   (1) Not relevant (there is no voluntary contribution stage).  
   (2) Not discussed.

5. Contribution default / endowment moved back?  
   (1) Not relevant.  
   (2) Not discussed.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   (1) Not relevant; there is no public good.  
   (2) Not discussed.

7. Punishment *cost* for each unit imposed  
   (1) Mentioned.  In Experiments 2 and 3 a third party can “pay 5 ¢”.  Cost is fixed at 5 ¢.  
   (2) Never varied; no predictions about other costs.

8. Punishment *magnitude* (damage to target per unit)  
   (1) Mentioned.  Paying 5 ¢ makes the dictator lose 15 ¢.  
   (2) Magnitude is fixed; no variation or predictions.

9. Whether a *reward* option exists  
   (1) No reward option in any experiment.  
   (2) Not discussed.

10. Reward cost  
    (1) Not present.  
    (2) Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude  
    (1) Not present.  
    (2) Not discussed.

12. Do players know the number of rounds?  
    (1) Only one round; nothing to vary.  
    (2) Not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    (1) Dictator’s selfish choice is revealed to the third party; the third-party’s response is revealed to the trustor.  These information flows are fixed.  
    (2) Not varied or analysed.

14. Does the punished player know *who* punished them?  
    (1) Not described.  The study never manipulates or analyses this.  
    (2) No discussion.

15. Does the rewarded player know *who* rewarded them?  
    (1) Not applicable.  
    (2) Not discussed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables  
   – The paper does *not* analyse “group efficiency” (total payoff / maximum payoff).  
   – Primary behavioural DV: amount (in cents) that a trustor sends to the third party in a subsequent trust game (“behavioural trust”).  
   – Secondary self-report DVs: perceived trustworthiness and perceived aggressiveness of the third party (7-point scales).  
   These variables differ in that behavioural trust is an actual monetary decision, whereas the others are subjective ratings; none equals efficiency.

B. Parameters *mentioned* (value stated)  
   1 (3 players), 2 (1 round), 7 (cost = 5 ¢), 8 (fine = 15 ¢).  
   Thus 4 of 15 are mentioned.

C. Parameters whose *systematic variation* is analysed for its effect on the punishment treatment effect  
   None.  The paper never varies any of the 15 parameters; therefore 0/15 parameters have estimated effect sizes on the punishment treatment effect for any DV.

D. What predictions can be made—using *only* this paper—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency?  
   Very few.  Because the study keeps all 15 parameters constant and never measures efficiency, it offers almost no leverage for predicting how changing any parameter would alter the efficiency impact of punishment.  The only indirect hint is that, with the fixed punishment cost (5 ¢) and magnitude (15 ¢), *adding* visible moral-emotion expression raises trust relative to punishment alone; but even this concerns reputation, not efficiency, and cannot be translated into quantitative efficiency predictions in a public-goods context.

In short, Kupfer & Tybur (2023) provides rich evidence about the reputational consequences of *emotion expression* in a third-party punishment setting, but it does not test, vary, or theorise about any of the canonical structural, incentive, or informational parameters that govern the efficiency effects of punishment in public-goods games.

Article Title: Cooperation and norm enforcement differ strongly across adult generations
Author Keywords: Cooperation; Third -party punishment; Norm enforcement; Intergenerational challenges; Experiment
Keywords Plus: 3RD-PARTY PUNISHMENT; INFORMATION; EVOLUTION
Abstract: Cooperation of different generations is crucial to meet many important societal challenges, including climate change or the sustainability of the welfare state. Little is known, however, about different generations' ability to cooperate in social dilemma situations, and their willingness to enforce social norms of cooperation. We present an experiment with two generations - juniors in their 20ies, and seniors who are 50 years or older, with an average age of 67. They play a repeated prisoner's dilemma (PD) game with third-party punishment. The third party is either a person from the same generation as the players in the PD game or from the other generation, and this is common knowledge. We find that seniors cooperate twice as much as juniors do, irrespective of the generation of the third-party. Moreover, seniors are much stricter as third parties and punish norm violations much more frequently than juniors do. However, the cooperation levels of both generations react hardly to third party punishment, which means that both generations differ strongly in their attempts to enforce norms of cooperation and in their reaction to norm enforcement. These differences across generations may pose a serious threat for the solution of intergenerational problems.

Below I follow the requested step-by-step format.  Everything is taken verbatim or inferred only from the text, figures and tables contained in the Praxmarer et al. paper.  No outside sources or conjectures are used.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK‐LIST
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Number of players  
    • Discussed?  Yes.  Two players interact in each Prisoner’s Dilemma (PD); one additional third-party punisher observes them.  
    • Systematically varied?  No.  It is always 2 players (+1 observer).  
    • Any stated effect of varying it on the punishment treatment effect?  No.

2.  Number of rounds  
    • Discussed?  Yes.  20 periods, known to all participants.  
    • Varied?  No.  Always 20.  
    • Predicted effect of variation?  None.

3.  Chat enabled between players  
    • Discussed?  Not mentioned.  (No chat was offered.)  
    • Varied?  No.  
    • Effect discussed?  No.

4.  “All-or-nothing” contribution decision  
    • Discussed?  The PD choice is binary (cooperate vs defect), so the contribution decision is indeed “all-or-nothing.”  
    • Varied?  No.  
    • Effect discussed?  No.

5.  “Contribution default” design (withdraw from the public fund)  
    • Not applicable / never mentioned.  

6.  Marginal Per Capita Return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
    • Discussed?  Payoff table of the PD is given (mutual C: 200 each; mutual D: 125 each; unilateral: 0/250).  An MPCR is not defined.  
    • Varied?  No.  
    • Effect discussed?  No.

7.  Cost to impose one unit of punishment  
    • Discussed?  Yes.  20 points to the third party.  
    • Varied?  No.  
    • Effect discussed?  No.

8.  Punishment magnitude (deduction per unit)  
    • Discussed?  Yes.  50 points are deducted from the target.  
    • Varied?  No.  
    • Effect discussed?  No.

9.  Reward enabled?  
    • No.  Rewards are never available.  (Hence 10 & 11 are irrelevant.)  

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
    • Not mentioned / not applicable.  

12. Whether the number of rounds is common knowledge  
    • Discussed?  Yes – participants are told the game lasts 20 rounds.  
    • Varied?  No.  
    • Effect discussed?  No.

13. Peer outcomes shown  
    • Discussed?  Yes.  After each period players learn the other player’s action and whether they were punished; third parties observe both actions and outcomes before punishing.  
    • Varied?  No.  
    • Effect discussed?  No.

14. Punisher identity revealed  
    • The players know there is exactly one third-party in their 3-person subgroup and also know that person’s generation.  The paper does not state that the individual’s ID is revealed beyond that.  The feature is fixed and never varied; no effect of varying it is discussed.

15. Rewarder identity revealed  
    • Not applicable (no rewards).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEPENDENT VARIABLES MENTIONED IN THE PAPER
• Cooperation rate (fraction of “Cooperate” choices).  
• Third-party punishment rate (frequency with which a defector is sanctioned).  
• Expectations about partner cooperation.  
• Overall welfare / per-capita earnings (Section 3.3).  
Efficiency – defined as actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible – is not explicitly used, although “overall welfare” (average tokens earned) is reported and is close in spirit.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
NUMERICAL INFORMATION THAT CAN BE DIRECTLY LIFTED FROM THE PAPER
(The numbers below come from Figures 2–5 and Section 3.3.  No systematic parameter variation accompanies them.)

• Average cooperation: juniors = 30.16 %, seniors = 60.89 %.  
• Average punishment of defectors in homogeneous groups: juniors 11 %, seniors 51 %.  
• Average punishment of defectors in heterogeneous groups: juniors 35 % (against seniors), seniors 34 % (against juniors).  
• Per-capita earnings: 3227 (J/J), 3026 (J/S), 3485 (S/J), 3398 (S/S) points.

None of those numbers isolates the causal effect of varying any of the 15 listed parameters; they reflect only differences in the generations of the subjects.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
A.  Does the paper use group efficiency?  
    – The authors report “overall welfare” / “per-capita earnings,” which is akin to efficiency but they never compute it as a ratio to the social optimum.  
    – Other dependent variables: cooperation rate, punishment rate, beliefs.

B.  Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
    – Mentioned: 1, 2, 4, 6 (payoff structure), 7, 8, 12, 13, 14.  → 9 parameters.  
    – Not mentioned / not applicable: 3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 15.  → 6 parameters.

C.  For which parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* the parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
    – None.  No parameter from the list is experimentally manipulated.  Therefore, 0 of the 15 parameters have an estimated or theorised causal impact on the punishment treatment effect in this paper.

D.  Predictions (restricted solely to what can be gleaned from the paper) about how the 15 parameters and their interactions will affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency:  
    – Because the study keeps every one of the 15 parameters fixed, the paper provides almost no direct basis for predicting how changing them would alter the efficiency impact of punishment.  
    – The sole qualitative hint is that, in the fixed environment used, costly third-party punishment did **not** raise cooperation for either generation; yet overall welfare was about 10 % higher in treatments with higher cooperation (the senior-player treatments) even though those treatments also had higher punishment rates.  From that we can tentatively infer:  
        • When baseline cooperation is already high, the welfare loss from punishment may be outweighed by the welfare gain from cooperation.  
        • Beyond that, the paper supplies no evidence to judge how altering any of the 15 parameters (e.g., lowering punishment cost, raising magnitude, introducing rewards, changing group size, etc.) would move efficiency.

In short, the article is informative about generational differences in cooperation and third-party punishment under one particular parameter configuration, but it offers virtually no leverage for forecasting how any of the 15 design features, singly or in interaction, would modify the efficiency effect of introducing punishment in a public-goods-type environment.

Authors: Feng, SN; Liu, XS

Article Title: Effects of three-faced strategy on the evolution of cooperation in social dilemma
Source Title: PHYSICA A-STATISTICAL MECHANICS AND ITS APPLICATIONS

Keywords Plus: PRISONERS-DILEMMA; GAME; PROMOTES; PUNISHMENT; DYNAMICS; REWARD
Abstract: Cooperative behavior can contribute to the development of society. Evolutionary game theory is a fundamental framework for studying cooperative behavior. This article explores the evolutionary dynamics of the three-faced strategy, which can demonstrate its different attribute behaviors according to different types of objects encountered by paying a certain role-switching cost. When three-faced individuals encounter cooperators, they will show defection behavior; when they interact with defectors, they will show punishment behavior; and when they meet the same kind, they will show cooperative behavior. The results show that the presence of three-faced individuals can effectively suppress defectors when the cost of role-switching is small or when the government gives relatively high incentives. Moreover, the moderate role-switching cost enhances the maintenance and emergence of cooperators. Additionally, as the system is in a stable state, which is full of three-faced individuals, the behavior displayed by the three-faced individuals at this time is consistent with that of the cooperators, which also promotes cooperative behavior in the population to some extent.

• whether the authors ever examine what happens when that parameter is **systematically varied**;  
• whether any numerical effect size on a *punishment treatment effect* is reported (none is).  
Whenever the paper talks about another dependent variable (e.g., fraction of cooperators) I point that out explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   – Mentioned only tangentially.  In the well-mixed model the population is “infinitely large”; in the spatial model it is a 100 × 100 lattice.  
   – Not varied; no predictions.  

2. Number of rounds  
   – Not mentioned (replicator dynamics are run until convergence; Monte-Carlo runs use 10 000 steps but this is never treated as a variable).  

3. Chat enabled?  
   – Not mentioned.  

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
   – Not mentioned; paper is a Prisoner’s Dilemma, not a public–goods game.  

5. Contribution default / refund rule  
   – Not mentioned.  

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   – The PDG’s temptation parameter b (1 < b ≤ 2) plays an analogous role.  
   – Systematically varied in Fig. 2 (b = 1.1, 1.2) and Fig. 5a (b from 1.1 up to 1.8).  
   – Reported effect: higher b raises the final fraction of three-faced individuals and lowers fractions of C and D (Fig. 5a).  No efficiency or punishment-treatment effect is calculated.  

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit (γ)  
   – Model parameter γ; values 0.4, 0.5, 0.8 are shown.  
   – Systematically varied in Fig. 5c.  When γ increases, the fraction of defectors rises sharply and three-faced + cooperators fall.  
   – No numbers on efficiency or on a “with- vs without-punishment” contrast.  

8. Punishment magnitude / fine on target (η)  
   – Model parameter η; varied repeatedly (0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.175, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8).  
   – Systematic results in Figs. 2, 4, 5b: larger η tends to reduce the share of three-faced individuals and (depending on b and δ) either raise both C and D or favour C over T.  
   – Again, no treatment-effect or efficiency figures.  

9. Reward enabled?  (binary on/off)  
   – The government subsidy α to the punisher is always present but its size can be 0.2, 1.5, 3.5, 4–6, etc.  Turning it completely off (α = 0) is never analysed, so a pure on/off comparison is absent.  

10. Reward cost to giver  
    – Not modelled; the reward is provided by an external “government,” not by peers.  

11. Reward magnitude to receiver  
    – The model has no peer-to-peer rewarding stage; α is a subsidy to the punisher, not a reward to a cooperator.  Hence no information.  

12. Do players know the number of rounds?  
    – Not relevant / not discussed.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    – Not discussed.  

14. Is the identity of a punisher revealed?  
    – Not discussed (there is no individual-level monitoring dimension in the model).  

15. Is the identity of a rewarder revealed?  
    – Not discussed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
REQUESTED SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Does the paper analyse **group efficiency** (total or average payoff)?  
    – No.  The dependent variables are (i) analytical stability of equilibrium points and (ii) simulated *fractions* of the three strategies (C, D, T) over time.  Although instantaneous pay-offs are written down, the authors never aggregate them into an “efficiency” measure, nor do they report total-payoff trajectories.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters appear at all?  
    – 4 of them:  
      6 (b, an analogue of MPCR), 7 (γ), 8 (η), 9 (presence/size of subsidy α).  

C.  For how many parameters does the paper study the **effect of systematically varying the parameter on the punishment treatment effect** (for any dependent variable)?  
    – Zero.  No separate “punishment treatment” (with- vs without-punishment) is introduced; punishment is embedded inside the three-faced strategy.

D.  Possible predictions about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) might influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency, *using only information from this paper*:  
    – The paper gives no direct leverage on efficiency, so only qualitative conjectures are possible.  If one equates “higher final share of cooperators or three-faced individuals” with “greater efficiency,” then:  
      • Lower punishment cost γ and higher fine η should strengthen the impact of embedded punishment, potentially raising efficiency.  
      • Larger government subsidy α suppresses defectors; thus, adding a reward element alongside punishment may improve efficiency.  
      • A higher temptation b makes three-faced players dominate but simultaneously lowers pure cooperation; the net effect on efficiency is unclear.  
      • Nothing in the text allows prediction for the other eleven parameters.  Hence, any further statement would be speculation beyond the paper.

In short, the article is rich on evolutionary-game dynamics but does not measure—let alone predict—the treatment effect of introducing punishment on efficiency, and it only touches four of the fifteen public-goods design variables listed in your prompt.

Below I go through the 15 design parameters one‐by‐one and report exactly what the paper says about each of them and, when possible, what the paper shows about how **systematically varying** that parameter changes the *punishment treatment effect*.  “Punishment treatment effect” is interpreted here as the difference in any outcome (e.g., cooperation fraction, total social welfare) between the situation with an institutional reward-and-punishment policy (p > 0) and the situation without that policy (p = 0).  All numeric effects are read directly from the figures or text; no outside knowledge is added.

---------------------------------------------------------------------
Parameter-by-parameter review
---------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned?  Yes.  The simulation fixes N = 1500.  
   (2) Systematically varied?  No.  The paper never changes N, so no prediction about how changing N would alter the punishment treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Mentioned?  Yes – 10 000 Monte-Carlo steps (MCS) with the last 1000 averaged.  
   (2) Systematically varied?  No.  The horizon is fixed; no prediction is made.

3. Chat enabled?  
   Not mentioned and not present; therefore no manipulation and no prediction.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   Yes – each player either contributes the full unit (c = 1) or contributes nothing.  
   This binary structure is never varied, so the paper gives no prediction about what would happen if fractional contributions were allowed.

5. Contribution *default* (refund frame)?  
   Not mentioned.  Players decide whether to contribute 1 or 0; no default reversal is studied.

6. Marginal Per-Capita Return / multiplication factor  
   (1) Mentioned?  Yes.  Each group’s multiplier is r_G = 1 + ω(|G| − 1).  The key parameter that is varied is ω.  
   (2) Systematically varied?  Yes.  ω is shown across wide ranges in Fig. 2 (and later figures).  
       • Effect on punishment treatment:  
         – When ω is small (≈0.1–0.2) introducing punishment (p > 0) frequently *reduces* total social welfare W_t; the additional cost of the policy (I_C) outweighs the modest cooperative gains.  
         – When ω is moderate to high (≈0.4–0.9) the same punishment policy increases W_t, and the gain is larger the higher ω is.  
         – Exact effect sizes depend on p and selection method; e.g., in Fig. 2, with ω = 0.8 and p = 0.3 the increase in W_t relative to p = 0 is roughly +0.35 (arbitrary units).

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   The model has *no per-punisher cost*.  Instead a fixed “cost of the policy” μ|G|² is borne by the central institution (or by the group if it self-adopts).  Therefore the parameter in the user’s list is absent; no prediction is possible.

8. Punishment magnitude (β)  
   (1) Mentioned?  Yes.  β is varied from 0 to 1.  
   (2) Systematically varied?  Yes (Fig. 6).  
       • For β = 0 there is no punishment; cooperation collapses and W_t is negative for all p.  
       • Increasing β monotonically raises cooperation and W_t up to about β ≈ 0.8; beyond that, further increases still help cooperation but create an *inverted-U* in W_t vs. p: at β = 1, partial intervention (p around 0.4–0.6) yields higher W_t than full intervention (p = 1).  
       • Quantitatively, with ω = 0.2 and μ = 0.1 (Fig. 6, bottom-left panel) moving from β = 0.2 to β = 1 raises the punishment treatment effect on W_t from roughly −0.1 to about +0.25 at p = 0.5.

9. Reward enabled?  
   “Reward” is automatically given—every deducted β is redistributed among cooperators.  The presence of reward is therefore *hard-wired*, never switched off, and never varied.  No prediction can be extracted about enabling vs. disabling reward.

10. Reward cost  
    Not modeled separately; the transfer β is budget-balanced, so cost = 0 in the model.  Not varied.

11. Reward magnitude  
    Not an independent parameter; it equals β divided by the number of cooperators.  Not varied separately, therefore no prediction.

12. Are the number of rounds known to subjects?  
    Not discussed; irrelevant in this simulation study.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    The model implicitly assumes full knowledge needed for strategy imitation (each player observes neighbours’ average payoff), but this visibility is never manipulated. No prediction.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
    Identities play no role; not mentioned; no manipulation; no prediction.

---------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary
---------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables used  
   • Fraction of cooperation (F_c) – proportion of players contributing.  
   • Total social welfare (W_t) – net total payoff of all players minus the central institution’s policy cost.  W_t is effectively an *efficiency* measure because it compares the realised total payoff to the resources consumed.  
   • Fraction of groups with the policy (F_g) and central-institution cost (I_C) are also reported.  
   Thus the paper *does* use an efficiency-type dependent variable (W_t); it also reports behavioural (F_c, F_g) and cost (I_C) outcomes which are conceptually distinct.

B. Parameters from the user’s list that appear at all  
   6 of 15 appear: 1 (N), 2 (rounds), 4 (binary contribution), 6 (MPCR via ω), 8 (punishment magnitude β), and—indirectly—7 (overall policy cost μ, though not a per-unit punishment cost).  The remaining 9 parameters are absent.

C. Parameters that are *systematically varied* and whose effect on the punishment treatment effect is examined  
   Only 3 of the 15:  
   • MPCR / ω (parameter 6)  
   • Punishment magnitude β (parameter 8)  
   • Policy-cost coefficient μ (closest analogue to parameter 7)  
   For none of the other 12 parameters is any systematic variation or effect reported.

D. If forced to predict the influence of the 15 parameters (and their interactions) on the punishment treatment effect *using only this paper*  
   • Higher MPCR (ω) ⇒ larger positive treatment effect on efficiency; when ω is very low, the treatment can be *negative*.  
   • Higher punishment magnitude β ⇒ stronger positive treatment effect on efficiency up to the point where policy cost begins to dominate (partial intervention optimal).  
   • Higher policy-cost coefficient μ ⇒ smaller (and eventually negative) treatment effect; with large μ the optimal fraction of punished groups p is well below 1.  
   • All other parameters (1,2,3,4,5,7 as “per-unit cost”, 9–15) are not addressed; the paper gives insufficient information to forecast their impact.

That is the full extent of what can be extracted from the article with respect to the user’s 15 parameters.

Abstract: In reality, leaders like to punish the employees who repeat mistakes in order to better manage their teams, and establish the prestige of the leaders. As the proverb goes, kill chickens and warn monkeys. This is also easy to promote cooperation among team members. Similarly, individuals who continuously make mistakes are less likely to be imitated by individuals around them. Motivated by those realities, based on PDG model, we propose the warning effect of persistent defection strategy evolutionary mechanism, in which discount punishment of the imitation probability is given to the player who imitates the neighbor player who continuously adopts the defection strategy. Here we set the discount punishment threshold H for the number of continuous defection strategy. If the number of continuous defection times of the imitated player reaches the threshold H , the imitating player will be given a discount punishment of imitation probability. The proposed evolutionary mechanism is more consistent with real-world situations. For instance, in the real world, people like to imitate the words and actions of their neighbors, however, when the imitated person has persistent bad behavior in the recent past, and especially when he/she is warned by the relevant department or agency, the probability of his/her words and actions being imitated decreases. Simulation and analysis show that the proposed evolutionary mechanism can better promote cooperation than the traditional PDG model. We also find that increasing the discount punishment factor alpha makes it easier to promote cooperation of evolutionary systems. Besides, the smaller the threshold H , the easier it is to promote cooperation of evolutionary systems. This also shows that the earlier the discount punishment factor acts on the evolutionary systems, the easier it is to promote the evolution of cooperation.

Any further prediction about how the listed parameters (alone or in combination) modulate the punishment treatment effect on efficiency would be speculation beyond the text.
