Abstract: Punishment and network reciprocity have profound implications for the evolution of cooperation. However, existing research on the consequences of cooperation under punishment in social networks has largely relied on agent-based models and laboratory experiments. Moreover, different from the majority of existing studies where punishment is always believed to be deterministic, the individuals' preferences for certain behaviors are always stochastic and vary with the environment. There is an urgent need to explore how cooperation evolves when punishment is stochastic and endogenous in social networks. In this paper, we propose a theoretical model of endogenous punishment in spatial public goods games. Cooperators each can stochastically choose whether to participate in the punishment for defectors. The choice to penalize defectors comes with a price. We analyze how cooperation evolves under endogenous punishment based on a regular network in the mean-field limit and outline the conditions under which endogenous punishment can support cooperation. When network reciprocity is unfavorable for cooperation, endogenous punishment can be effective in supporting cooperation. On the contrary, endogenous punishment no longer supports or even hinders the promoting effect of network reciprocity on cooperation. These findings illustrate that the effectiveness of endogenous punishment in fostering cooperation is dependent on the cooperators' willingness to pay for punishment as well as the topology of social networks.

Below I go through the 15 design parameters one‐by‐one.  
For each parameter I state

• Whether the paper mentions it at all (and the values that appear).  
• Whether the paper investigates what happens when the parameter is systematically varied and, if so, what it says about the punishment-versus-no-punishment difference (the “punishment treatment effect”).  
• Whenever the paper gives an explicit formula or a numerical illustration I cite it (using the equation, figure or table number that appears in the manuscript).  
Throughout, remember that the dependent variable the authors actually study is the **frequency of cooperation x (or the basin of attraction of full cooperation)** – not efficiency. Where that is the case I flag it explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players (group size, here = k+1)

• Mentioned? Yes. The population is laid out on a regular network of degree k, so each public-goods group has k+1 members.

• Systematically varied? Yes.  
  – Fig. 2b, Fig. 3b and Table 1 report results for k = 3 … 20.  
  – Qualitative statement (Results, p. 8): “There exists an intermediate degree k_c at which the attractive basin of cooperation is minimised. For k > k_c a larger k enlarges the basin; for k < k_c a smaller k helps cooperation.”  
  – Formal result: the critical willingness-to-punish above which punishment helps is  
    p_c = c k[(k+1)^2 – (k+3) r] / [(k+1)(β(k^3+k(k_c–2)–2) – α(k^2–k k_c+2))]        (Eq. in text).  
    With punishment absent (p=0) cooperation never spreads when r<r_c; with p > p_c it can.

• Effect size that can be read off: Table 1 shows how the interior unstable equilibrium x* changes with k and p (e.g. with p=0.5, x* falls from 0.365 at k=4 to 0.261 at k=20).  The difference x* (with punishment) – x* (no punishment) is therefore strongly k-dependent.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Number of rounds

• Mentioned? No. The paper is an infinite-horizon evolutionary model.

• Systematic variation? No.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Chat enabled?

• Not mentioned and not varied.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. All-or-nothing contributions?

• Mentioned? Yes. Players choose between “cooperate” (pay cost c) and “defect” (pay nothing).  
• Systematically varied? No – the binary structure is fixed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Contribution default / refund frame?

• Not mentioned.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor (r)

• Mentioned? Yes. Called the “enforcement factor” r ∈ (1, k+1).

• Systematically varied? Yes.  
  – Central threshold without punishment: r_c = (k+1)^2/(k+3) (Eq. 3).  
  – With punishment: r_o = r_c – Δ, where  
    Δ = (k+1)p[β(k^3+k(k_c–2)–2)+α(–k^2+k k_c–2)] / [c k(k+3)].  
    Hence punishment lowers the critical r by Δ.  
  – Fig. 1 contrasts r<r_c (no cooperation without punishment) with r>r_c (full cooperation even without punishment) and shows how introducing punishment helps in the former case and may hinder in the latter.

• Numerical illustration: For k=3, c=1, α=0.3, β=1, p=0.5  
  r_c = 16/6 ≈ 2.667; r_o ≈ 2.00 (Fig. 2a).  
  Thus the punishment treatment raises cooperation for 2.00<r<2.667 but can reduce it when r>r_c (see Fig. 4).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Punishment cost per unit (α)

• Mentioned? Yes (α>0).

• Systematically varied? Partially.  
  – Fig. 3a shows how the critical willingness p_c rises with α (higher cost makes punishment less effective).  
  – The unstable equilibrium x* increases with α (text, p. 7); hence cooperation (and any efficiency gains) decline as α increases.  
  – No direct efficiency numbers are supplied.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
8. Punishment magnitude / fine (β)

• Mentioned? Yes (β>α).

• Systematically varied? Yes.  
  – Fig. 3a: p_c falls as β increases, so punishment becomes effective at lower willingness-to-punish.  
  – x* falls with β (text, p. 7).  
  – Therefore the punishment treatment effect is strengthened by larger β.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
9. Is a reward option enabled?

• Not mentioned – the model contains no rewarding.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
10. Reward cost

• Not mentioned.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
11. Reward magnitude

• Not mentioned.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
12. Do players know the number of rounds?

• Not applicable (no discrete rounds).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
13. Are peer outcomes shown?

• Not discussed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?

• Not relevant – punishment is “endogenous and stochastic” but anonymity / identity is not modelled.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?

• Not relevant (no rewards).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
A. Dependent variables  
   – The paper analyses the *frequency of cooperation* x and the *size of the basin of attraction* of full cooperation.  
   – It also derives *critical thresholds* (r_c, r_o, p_c) but never reports **efficiency** (total or average payoff) directly. Hence efficiency-based treatment effects cannot be read off.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   5 of 15:  (1) number of players k+1, (4) all-or-nothing contributions, (6) multiplication factor r, (7) punishment cost α, (8) punishment fine β.

C. For how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss what happens when that parameter is systematically varied?  
   4 parameters: k (group size), r, α, β.  
   The effects are always expressed in terms of cooperation frequency or stability thresholds, not efficiency.

D. Predictions one could make (only using what is in the paper) about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on *efficiency*:

   • Because efficiency is proportional to average payoff, and average payoff in the model rises with the fraction of cooperators, any statement about efficiency can only be inferred indirectly from cooperation levels.  
   • Using that logic, the paper implies:  
     – Higher r, higher β and lower α enlarge the cooperation-boost produced by punishment when r<r_c.  
     – Very high r (r>r_c) reverses the sign: punishment can **lower** cooperation (and thus efficiency).  
     – Group size k has a non-monotonic effect: punishment is least helpful at an intermediate k=k_c and more helpful both below and above that point.  
     – No guidance is provided for the remaining 11 parameters, so no prediction can be made from this paper alone.

Hence, apart from the four parameters (k, r, α, β) the article gives no information that allows one to forecast the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Parameter-by-parameter inspection
--------------------------------------------------------------------

    • Systematically varied: yes (20, 100, 200; Fig. 9).

    • Mentioned: 20 000 Monte-Carlo cycles.

    • Not used.  The closest analogue is the “temptation payoff” T (default 3, varied in Fig. 8).

7.  Punishment cost to punisher

    • Reward never exists in the model, so “false” throughout.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
    • Not applicable (no rewards).

12. Number of rounds known to players  
    • Not discussed; agents are algorithmic learners and do not know the horizon.

13. Peer outcomes shown (payoffs revealed)?  
    • Stated that “players lack information about their neighbors’ payoffs” (Sec. 3.1).  
    • Not varied.

14. Punisher identity revealed?  
15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
    • Not mentioned; model only requires that punishment can be *observed* with probability S_i, but identity revelation is never discussed or varied.

Summary
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables  
    • The paper *does not* use “group efficiency” (total or average payoff divided by maximum) anywhere.

        – Counts of punishment and metapunishment acts (Fig. 4).

Abstract: Two mechanisms that have been used to study the evolution of cooperative behavior are altruistic punishment, in which cooperative individuals pay additional costs to punish defection, and multilevel selection, in which competition between groups can help to counteract individual-level incentives to cheat. Authors: Zhao, YK; Zhao, XB; Shen, ZJM

Author Keywords: Behavioral operations; Punishment game; Multi-round experiment; Strategy method; Experimental economics
Keywords Plus: STRATEGY METHOD; COOPERATION; COMPETITION; FAIRNESS; BEHAVIOR; CONSEQUENCES; RECIPROCITY; ECONOMICS
Abstract: We conduct a multi-round experiment on a punishment game using both the strategy method and the direct-response method. In the game, the sender may make decisions that are either favorable or unfavorable to the receiver, whereas the receiver may reward the favorable decision and/or punish the unfavorable decision. The hot-versus-cold effect is observed in both sender behaviors and receiver behaviors. Under the strategy method, the senders more often adopt decisions that are favorable to the receivers, whereas the receivers impose punishment more frequently than under the direct-response method. We suggest that in the multi-round experiment, the strategic value of punishment dominates the taste for punishment from the perspective of the receiver. According to our explanation based on mental accounting, the utility of imposing punishment is higher under the strategy method than under the direct-response method. Hence, the receiver is more likely to make punishment decisions. This difference in receiver behaviors prompts the sender to make receiver-favorable decisions more frequently under the strategy method.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
GAME STRUCTURE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1) Number of players  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. In Hsu’s sessions, each group has 4 players (n = 4). The broader session has 12 participants split into three groups of 4 each round, but it is always groups of size 4 making decisions.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying this parameter for any dependent variable?  
     – No. The group size is fixed at 4, and there is no analysis of how changing group size would alter the treatment effect. There is no discussion of systematically varying it.

2) Number of rounds  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. All sessions last 20 rounds. Subjects know there are 20 rounds.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying this parameter?  
     – No. It remains fixed at 20; there is no systematic manipulation of “number of rounds,” nor any direct prediction about changing the total rounds.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. The paper does not mention any communication or chat between players, so presumably there is no chat.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying chat?  
     – No, it is never discussed or manipulated.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – It does discuss how subjects may report any integer in [0, wᵢ] as “declared income.” This is not an all‐or‐nothing format; declarations are chosen continuously up to the subject’s income.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying an “all‐or‐nothing” requirement?  
     – No. All contributions/declarations are continuous, so there is no discussion of that design difference.

5) Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much of their endowment to move back to their hand rather than choose a contribution)?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. Each subject reports income and pays taxes, but there is no mention of a “default” mechanism.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying a “default” rule?  
     – No, not addressed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
MONETARY STAKES
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. Hsu sets m = 0.5 for the public good’s marginal per capita return.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying m?  
     – No. It is held fixed at 0.5; the paper does not examine what would happen to the punishment (endogenous audit) treatment effect if MPCR were increased or decreased.

PEER INCENTIVES
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Not in the usual “per‐unit punishment cost” sense found in Fehr & Gächter‐type experiments. Instead, each player can transfer some of the taxes they already paid into a group monitoring fund (Y account).    • Does the paper discuss it?

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?

   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Partially. In the endogenous‐audit treatment, each subject also sees whether they themselves were audited, how many group members got audited, and the total monitoring points contributed, but not who contributed how much.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying the exact information displayed?  
     – No. The display of peer declarations is always the same. The paper does not vary or compare different information‐feedback treatments.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes (indirectly). In the endogenous audit, punishment is collective (the group monitoring fund). No one knows which specific teammate contributed to that fund or triggered the audit.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying punisher‐identification?  
     – No, that is not manipulated.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. There is no reward.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying rewarder‐identification?  
     – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY (A–D)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A) Does the paper use “group efficiency” (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how do they differ?

• Hsu’s paper does not use the ratio of total group payoff to the “fully cooperative” payoff (what you called “efficiency”). The closest measures are:  
  – Individual compliance rate (reported income ÷ true income).  
  – Average (or total) reported income.  
  – Total taxes paid (and discovered).  
  – Average earnings per round.  
  – Several “productivity” indices (e.g., reported tax per audit, fraction of unreported income discovered).  

These differ from efficiency because they do not directly measure actual payoff vs. maximum possible payoff. Note also that “compliance” and “contributions” in the paper refer to fraction of income reported and taxed, whereas “efficiency” in your sense is not computed.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

• Mentioned explicitly (though not systematically varied):  
  1) Number of players per group (fixed at 4).  
  2) Number of rounds (fixed at 20).  
  4) Whether the contribution is “all or nothing” (the paper clarifies that it is not).  
  6) MPCR = 0.5.  
  8) Punishment magnitude (fine rate = 3 times the evaded tax).  
  12) Players do know there are 20 rounds.  
  13) Peer outcomes are partially shown (they see each other’s declared incomes).  
  14) Players do not learn who specifically punishes them (punishment is via the group fund).  

• Not mentioned / not in use:  
  3) Chat.  
  5) “Contribution default.”  
  7) Per‐unit punishment cost (in the standard sense).  
  9–11) Reward or cost of reward.  
  15) Rewarder identification.

Hence, the paper explicitly references (but does not vary) 8 of the 15: #1, #2, #4, #6, #8, #12, #13, and #14.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable) when each parameter is systematically varied?

• The paper never systematically varies any of the 15 parameters. The design uses fixed income distributions, 20 rounds, groups of 4, fixed fine rate = 3, MPCR = 0.5, etc. So there is no systematic variation of these parameters that Hsu then regresses or interprets for a punishment‐vs.‐no‐punishment effect.  
• Consequently, there are no numerical effect sizes in Hsu’s paper for systematically changing any of these parameters. The paper only reports results for whether including an endogenous‐audit (punishment) mechanism vs. not including it changes compliance and earnings.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

• Because the paper does not measure “efficiency” (in the sense of total payoff ÷ maximum payoff) and does not vary the 15 parameters, it offers little direct basis to predict how changing, say, the number of rounds, or the fine magnitude, or the presence of chat, etc., would alter a punishment mechanism’s effect on efficiency.  
• The only indirect hints involve the higher compliance and strong willingness to fund punishment (monitoring) observed under the endogenous‐audit scheme: participants pay about 20–30% of their already‐paid taxes to the monitoring fund, leading to significantly higher compliance. One might guess from the paper’s logic that:  
  – Increasing the fine rate (punishment magnitude) might further deter free‐riding (i.e., higher compliance), which might or might not improve overall payoffs if the cost of monitoring remains high.  
  – Increasing the group’s willingness or ability to invest in the monitoring fund (e.g., making punishment cheaper or letting players see more evidence of others’ under‐reporting) might strengthen compliance and thus possibly raise net payoffs, at least if the cost does not exceed the added benefits from reduced free‐riding.  
  – But the paper provides no numeric or direct modeling of “efficiency” or systematic parameter variations, so we cannot quantitatively predict how efficiency would shift.  

In short, the paper itself makes “little to no prediction” on how systematically altering those 15 parameters would affect efficiency, because it never manipulates them nor measures efficiency as you define it. Any further statement would go beyond what Hsu explicitly states. 

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(end)

Abstract: We consider repeated games with compact actions sets and pure strategies in which players commonly observe a public signal which reveals imperfectly the action profile. It is jointly rational if for all weights on players, the weighted average payoff is greater than or equal to the minmax level of the weighted average payoff function. PARAMETER–BY–PARAMETER CHECK

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned: yes.  The paper works with a set N={1,…,n}.  
   • Systematically varied and linked to a “punishment treatment effect”?  No.  n is kept completely general; nothing is said about how changing n would raise or lower efficiency (or any other outcome) once punishment is introduced.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned: the game is played for an indefinite number of periods with common discount factor δ.  
   • No systematic variation; no statement about a finite vs. infinite horizon effect on punishment.

3. Is chat enabled?  
   • Never mentioned.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule?  
   • Never mentioned.

5. “Contribution default” framing (withdraw from a public fund)?  
   • Never mentioned.

6. MPCR, multiplication factor, or any explicit monetary stake parameter  
   • Never mentioned.

7. Cost of sending one unit of punishment  
   • Not parameterized.  “Punishment” appears only as an equilibrium phase constructed by the theorists; no explicit marginal cost is modelled.

8. Punishment magnitude (deduction points per unit)  
   • Not parameterized or quantified.

9. Whether a reward option exists  
   • Conceptually yes: the equilibrium construction contains a “reward phase.”  
   • No numerical parameter, no systematic variation, no treatment-effect estimate.

10. Reward cost  
    • Not specified.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Not specified.

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
    • Yes: they know it never ends (infinite-horizon δ–discounted play).  
    • No systematic comparison with a known finite horizon.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • The only public information is a “public signal” f(x); individual payoffs need not be observable.  The paper never studies the presence vs. absence of payoff feedback as a treatment variable.

14. Is the identity of a punisher revealed?  
    • Not discussed; punishments are theoretical path-contingent strategies, not “actions with an identifiable sender.”

15. Is the identity of a rewarder revealed?  
    • Not discussed for the same reason.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
A – Dependent variables used in the paper  
• The paper’s dependent object is the vector of players’ discounted payoffs and the entire set of payoffs that can be supported in perfect public equilibrium as δ→1 (denoted 𝑉*, 𝑉(δ), etc.).  
• “Efficiency” in the public-goods sense (actual total payoff ÷ first-best total payoff) is never defined or measured.  When the authors use the word “efficient” they simply mean Pareto-efficient (surplus-maximising) action profiles.  
• Other notions introduced (admissibility, joint rationality, admissible min-max levels) are theoretical constraints on equilibrium payoffs, not outcome variables such as contribution rates.

B – Which of the 15 design parameters are even mentioned?  
Exactly three:  
   (1) number of players n;  
   (2) number of rounds, implicitly infinite;  
   (12) players’ knowledge of the horizon (they know the game is infinite).  
No numerical values are given, and none of the remaining 12 parameters appear in any form.

C – For how many parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the *punishment treatment effect* for any dependent variable under systematic variation?  
Zero.  No parameter is systematically varied, no treatment contrasts are reported, and no effect sizes (numerical or qualitative) are provided.

D – If forced to predict how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence punishment’s effect on group efficiency using only this paper, what can we say?  
Essentially nothing useful.  The paper is a purely theoretical characterization of equilibrium payoff sets in infinitely repeated games with deterministic public monitoring.  
• It provides no mapping from concrete experimental design parameters (punishment cost, punishment magnitude, chat, MPCR, etc.) to efficiency changes.  
• Even for the three parameters that are mentioned (n, horizon, horizon knowledge) the analysis is generic and does not compare alternative parameter values.  
Therefore any prediction about the direction or size of punishment’s effect on efficiency as these 15 parameters change would require information outside the paper, which the instructions prohibit.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account based strictly on what appears in the provided paper (Chapter 8, “Effectiveness of Coercive and Voluntary Institutional Solutions to Social Dilemmas,” by Samid and Suleiman). For each parameter, I note (1) whether it is mentioned in the paper (and if so, in what form), and (2) whether the paper makes any prediction about the effect of systematically varying that parameter on the “punishment treatment effect”—that is, how introducing punishment (fines) changes efficiency. “Efficiency” as defined in your request is not always the same as the various behavioral or payoff measures reported in this paper (e.g., the authors focus mainly on rates of authority support, cooperation, and payoffs rather than a strict “total payoff divided by maximum possible payoff” metric). Where the paper discusses other dependent variables (e.g., cooperation rate, support for authority), I will note that explicitly.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes, the paper always uses groups of six (6) players in all conditions.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – No. The study does not vary the group size or discuss how changing the number of players would affect punishment or efficiency.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes, each group played for up to 280 trials (or 1.5 hours).  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – No. The paper does not vary the number of rounds or describe how doing so might affect punishment’s impact on efficiency.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper does not report any form of direct communication or “chat” between participants.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – Not applicable.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes, in the modified NPD/APD setup, players either “defect” (keep entire endowment), “cooperate” (contribute entire endowment), or “join the authority.” There is no partial contribution.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – No. The paper does not vary whether contributions can be partial or must be all-or-nothing, nor does it predict how changing this design would affect punishment’s impact.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much to move from the public fund back into their hand)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper does not discuss or manipulate any default contribution setting.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – Not applicable.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes, the experiment multiplies each contributed 15 NIS by 4, then distributes it among all other players.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – No. There is no variation of the multiplication factor across conditions.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned?  
     – In the paper’s design, “punishment” is done by a central “authority” through fines, but there is no separate parameter tracking the cost borne by the punisher (as would appear in typical “peer punishment” designs). Instead, an “authority fee” is imposed on those who join the authority, but the study does not describe it as “the cost of punishing.”  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – No. The fee is varied in some conditions, but never as a specific “cost of punishment per unit.” The paper does not discuss how systematically changing a punisher’s cost might affect outcomes.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The paper systematically varies the “fine” that is imposed on non‐participants (defectors) in four “authority” games:  
       1) Non‐coercive (0% fine)  
       2) Moderately coercive (progressive 10% increases)  
       3) Exploitative (progressive 30% increases, plus an 80% fee)  
       4) Dominating (progressive 30% fine, plus a progressive fee)  
   • Systematic variation and effect on “punishment treatment effect”?  
     – The paper examines how these fines affect whether groups converge to one of the possible equilibria (e.g., all defect vs. partial authority support vs. full authority support).  
     – However, the paper does not give a numeric effect size linking fine increases to “efficiency” (in the strict sense of total payoff/maximum possible payoff). Instead, the authors mostly discuss:  
       • Rates of cooperation or “authority support.”  
       • Whether total benefits get eroded by fees/fines (cost‐effectiveness).  
       • Which equilibrium emerges (e.g., all‐defect, partial, or all‐authority).  
     – In short, while fines (punishment magnitude) are clearly manipulated, the paper does not translate that directly into an explicit change in “efficiency” as you defined it.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper focuses entirely on fines/punishment; it does not discuss adding or varying a reward.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – Not applicable.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. Not discussed at all.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – Not applicable.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. Not discussed.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – Not applicable.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – The paper states the game ends after 280 trials or 1.5 hours, but does not specify whether participants knew this exact stopping point in detail.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – No. There is no discussion of changing the knowledge or length of the game.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost each round)?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. This was explicitly varied:  
       • “Full feedback” condition: participants saw their own payoffs and other players’ payoffs each round.  
       • “Partial feedback” condition: participants saw only their own payoffs and how many players made each choice (cooperate, defect, authority) but not the exact payoffs of others.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on “punishment treatment effect”?  
     – The paper does not frame this in terms of “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” but does show that knowledge of others’ payoffs affected willingness to support authority and overall cooperation.  
       • In the non‐coercive authority condition, concealing others’ payoffs (partial feedback) boosted support for authority and, thus, boosted overall contributions compared to full feedback.  
       • The paper interprets this as partial feedback reducing the negative effect of social (unfair) comparisons.  
     – No direct numerical “treatment effect on efficiency” is provided, but the authors do report that under partial feedback, overall contributions (cooperation) were significantly higher in non‐coercive authority games.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. There is no indication that players ever learn the identity of who is imposing the fines, beyond knowing that “the authority” is administering them.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – Not applicable.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. Rewarding was not part of the study design.  
   • Systematic variation?  
     – Not applicable.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper does sometimes use the term “efficiency” or “cost‐effectiveness,” but its primary reported outcomes are:  
     – Rates of authority support (the fraction of players choosing “authority”),  
     – Rates of cooperation versus defection (i.e., who contributes vs. keeps), and  
     – Payoff patterns (particularly whether the group reaches a certain equilibrium: all‐defect, half‐authority/half‐defect, or all‐authority).  
   • Thus, the main dependent variables are authority support and cooperation rates, with some discussion of payoffs. The paper does not consistently frame these as “actual total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff,” so its “efficiency” notion is not always the same as the ratio‐based efficiency measure you described.

B. Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned (to some degree):  
     1) Number of players (fixed at 6),  
     2) Number of rounds (fixed at a maximum of 280),  
     4) All‐or‐nothing contribution,  
     6) Multiplication factor = 4,  
     8) Punishment magnitude (fines) – varied systematically,  
     13) Information display about peer outcomes – varied (full vs. partial feedback).  
   • The other parameters (3, 5, 7, 9–12, 14, 15) receive no explicit discussion or are simply not varied in the experiment.

C. For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   1) Punishment magnitude (parameter 8) is clearly varied across four “authority” conditions (non‐coercive/mild/exploitative/dominating). The authors do discuss how that variation changes outcomes (primarily in terms of equilibrium selection, support for authority, and overall cooperation). However, they do not present a numeric effect size specifically for “treatment effect on efficiency.”  
   2) Showing or hiding peer payoffs (part of parameter 13) is also varied (full vs. partial feedback), and they link it to changes in cooperation and authority‐support rates. Again, they do not present a direct numerical effect size on “efficiency,” but they do show significantly higher cooperation in the partial‐feedback versus full‐feedback version of the non‐coercive game.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, solely based on this paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper gives no direct quantitative estimates of “efficiency” in the strict sense you described. Instead, their findings suggest:  
     – When punishment (fines) is too low (non‐coercive), cooperation can remain low unless participants are shielded from explicit payoff comparisons. Even then, it may not induce the fully cooperative outcome.  
     – When punishment (fines) is moderate, some groups can achieve near‐full cooperation (and presumably moderate efficiency), but others remain stuck at low or mixed cooperation.  
     – For exploitative or dominating authority (very high fines, plus high or progressive fees on participants), groups often end up at all‐defect (i.e., no one cooperates) or all‐support (everyone cooperates but at harsh cost), which can undermine net payoffs (hence “inefficient”).  
     – Concealing others’ payoffs (“partial feedback”) can boost cooperation in some low‐punishment settings (non‐coercive), presumably by reducing envy or perceived unfairness.  
   • Beyond these broad tendencies, the paper does not offer numerical or formula‐based “efficiency” predictions for farther‐reaching variations (e.g., changing group size, changing MPCR, enabling rewards, etc.). Consequently, there is little basis in the paper to predict precisely how each of the 15 parameters would shape the effect of punishment on efficiency. The authors focus primarily on whether groups end in one or another equilibrium (defection or support for authority), and how that outcome relates to costs and payoffs—rather than giving detailed efficiency metrics for each parameter combination.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Authors: Greenwood, GW; Abbass, HA; Petraki, E
Author Full Names: Greenwood, Garrison W.; Abbass, Hussein A.; Petraki, Eleni
Article Title: When is altruistic punishment useful in social dilemmas?
Author Keywords: Altruistic punishment; Public goods game; Social dilemma
Abstract: It is not fully understood how cooperation emerges in a population of individuals with no connections or prior experience with each other. Strategy selection that is purely based on accumulated payoffs promotes free riders who put their self interests above that of any group. How could cooperation persist in these settings? Researchers have posited direct or indirect reciprocity as possible explanations but these theories fail if interactions are not repeated or reputations are ignored. Altruistic punishment may provide an answer. Punishers impose a penalty, such as a fine, on defectors. The idea is a sufficiently high enough penalty-or even the threat of a high penalty-will convince defectors that cooperation is more beneficial. The punishment is altruistic because punishers pay a cost to impose a penalty and expect nothing in return (including no future reciprocity). Empirical and human studies have shown when some individuals are punishers, and they are common, cooperation levels tend to increase. But it has never been specified exactly how large this majority of punishers must be to promote cooperation. Here we analyze cooperation, defection and punishment in a social dilemma, public goods game, and precisely identify the necessary conditions to make altruistic punishment an effective strategy for improving group cooperation levels.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of whether (1) the paper mentions each of the 15 parameters (including any specific value or range) and (2) whether it makes any prediction about how systematically varying that parameter would affect a “punishment treatment effect” (in particular, its effect on efficiency). Throughout, note that the article does not actually study “punishment” in the standard sense of paying a cost to reduce someone else’s payoff; instead, it studies a two‐stage game (a Public Goods Game followed by a Mutual Aid Game) in which “punishment” is metaphorically the refusal to aid defectors. The paper does not discuss a separate “punishment treatment” per se, nor does it measure “efficiency” as the ratio of total actual payoff to the maximum possible total payoff of a fully cooperative group. Consequently, it makes no explicit claims about how altering parameters would change a punishment‐versus‐no‐punishment difference in efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players
   • Mentioned? Partly. The paper uses n₉ to denote the global group size and nₗ for each local group, with a the number of local groups (so n₉ = a·nₗ).  
   • Predictions from systematic variation? No. The paper analyzes how different numbers of local groups (a) or different local‐group sizes (nₗ) affect stability of local vs. global cooperation, but it does not link this to any “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency, nor does it discuss a before/after “punishment” comparison.

2) Number of rounds
   • Mentioned? No. The article does not specify or vary the number of rounds, nor discuss whether individuals know the game length.  
   • Predictions from systematic variation? No mention.

3) Is chat enabled between players?

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

Keywords Plus: COSTLY PUNISHMENT; ANTISOCIAL PUNISHMENT; 3RD-PARTY PUNISHMENT; DECISION-MAKING; SOCIAL DILEMMAS; COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; ANGER; BEHAVIOR; POWER
Abstract: The existence of moral punishment, that is, the fact that cooperative people sacrifice resources to punish defecting partners requires an explanation. Potential explanations are that people punish defecting partners to privately express or to communicate their negative emotions in response to the experienced unfairness. If so, then providing participants with alternative ways to privately express or to communicate their emotions should reduce moral punishment. In two experiments, participants interacted with cooperating and defecting partners in a Prisoner's Dilemma game. After each round, participants communicated their emotions to their partners (Experiments 1 and 2) or only expressed them privately (Experiment 2). Compared to a no-expression control group, moral punishment was reduced when emotions were communicated to the defecting partner but not when emotions were privately expressed. However, moral punishment was only reduced but far from being eliminated, suggesting that the communication of emotions does not come close to replacing moral punishment. Furthermore, prompting participants to focus on their emotions had undesirable side-effects: Privately expressing emotions diminished cooperation, enhanced hypocritical punishment (i.e., punishment of defecting partners by defecting participants), and induced an unspecific bias to punish the partners irrespective of their actions.

Abstract: In this paper, we address the autonomic resource management problem for Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) in the presence of stochastic and selfish VPN operators. Resource management is one of the most important problems that faces Internet Service Providers. In the literature, the Autonomic Service Architecture is proposed to provide a resource management model that allows systems to manage themselves and aiming to utilize optimally the unused resources. Second, underloaded VPNs' operators might behave selfishly and refuse to lend their unused (spare) resources to other overloaded VPNs. PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1. Number of players  
   • Discussed?  Yes.  All simulation runs use a population of 12 “participants” (8 cooperative, 4 selfish).  Two benchmark counterfactuals (all 8 vs. all 12 cooperative) are shown in Fig. 1.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule?

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  No.  There is no public-goods technology; instead the model uses ad-hoc pay-off constants a, b, c, d.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   • Mentioned?  No explicit costly punishment mechanism exists.  “Punishment” in the paper simply means refusing future resource requests, which carries no defined token cost for the punisher.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine levied on target)  
   • Mentioned?  No.

9. Whether reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned?  No separate reward stage exists.

10. Reward cost  
    • Mentioned?  No.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Mentioned?  No.

12. Is the number of rounds common knowledge?  
    • Mentioned?  No.  The paper never says the agents know when play ends; the horizon is imposed by the simulation code.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mentioned?  No.  Agents keep personal histories or reputation counts but are not reported to observe others’ pay-offs.

14. Is the identity of a punisher revealed?  
    • Mentioned?  No.  As there is no direct punishment stage, the issue never arises.

15. Is the identity of a rewarder revealed?  
    • Mentioned?  No.  Same reason as 14.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables actually analysed  
   – “Total gain” of a subgroup (usually the eight cooperative VPN operators).  
   – “Number of victims” (instances where requests are rejected) in some figures.  
   – No measure called “efficiency” (total pay-off divided by the maximum possible) is computed.  “Total gain” is therefore not formally identical to the efficiency metric requested in the prompt.

B. How many of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   – 2 parameters: (1) number of players, (2) number of rounds.  The remaining 13 are not discussed.

C. How many parameters are analysed for **systematic variation** and its impact on a punishment treatment effect?

Article Title: Discriminatory punishment undermines the enforcement of group cooperation
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS EXPERIMENT; 3RD-PARTY PUNISHMENT; INGROUP FAVORITISM; PAROCHIAL ALTRUISM; GROUP MEMBERSHIP; PROMOTE; PSYCHOLOGY; DIVERSITY; EVOLUTION; CONFLICT
Abstract: Peer punishment can help groups to establish collectively beneficial public goods. However, when humans condition punishment on other factors than poor contribution, punishment can become ineffective and group cooperation deteriorates. Here we show that this happens in pluriform groups where members have different socio-demographic characteristics. In our public good provision experiment, participants were confronted with a public good from which all group members benefitted equally, and in-between rounds they could punish each other. Groups were uniform (members shared the same academic background) or pluriform (half the members shared the same academic background, and the other half shared another background). We show that punishment effectively enforced cooperation in uniform groups where punishment was conditioned on poor contribution. In pluriform groups, punishment was conditioned on poor contribution too, but also partially on others' social-demographic characteristics-dissimilar others were punished more than similar others regardless of their contribution. As a result, punishment lost its effectiveness in deterring free-riding and maintaining public good provision. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter summary, based strictly on what is stated in the paper “Discriminatory punishment undermines the enforcement of group cooperation,” by Molenmaker et al. (2023). Throughout, “the paper” refers only to that article’s text, figures, and tables. No content outside of the paper is introduced.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. NUMBER OF PLAYERS
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. Experiment 1 uses groups of four; Experiment 2 uses groups of six; Experiment 3 uses groups of three or six.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying this parameter’s effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
  – No. The paper does not systematically vary number of players to analyze its effect on punishment. No effect sizes, predictions, or conclusions are reported about how changing group size, in itself, would alter punishment’s effects.

2. NUMBER OF ROUNDS
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. Experiment 1 involves two blocks of 20 repeated rounds; Experiments 2 and 3 use a single‐shot (one‐round) public goods game.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying this parameter’s effect on the punishment treatment effect?  
  – No. Although the paper notes that Experiment 1 is repeated (40 total rounds) and Experiments 2 and 3 are one‐shot, it does not vary the number of rounds in order to study punishment effects, nor does it provide numerical effect sizes for round‐by‐round manipulations.

3. IS CHAT ENABLED BETWEEN PLAYERS?
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. There is no mention of any form of chat or communication among participants, apart from standard feedback about contributions and punishment points.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying chat?  
  – No. It is not addressed.

4. IS THE CONTRIBUTION “ALL OR NOTHING”?
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes, for Experiment 1. Participants there choose either to contribute their entire endowment (20 MU) or nothing, so that design is an all‐or‐nothing contribution. In Experiments 2 and 3, participants can contribute in increments of 10 MU (i.e., not strictly all or nothing).  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying all‐or‐nothing vs. partial‐contribution formats?  
  – No. Although the experiments use different formats (binary in Experiment 1; multiple‐level in Experiments 2 and 3), there is no additional analysis that explicitly compares or predicts how one format vs. the other alters punishment’s effects on outcomes.

5. IS THE CONTRIBUTION DEFAULT (E.G., DO PLAYERS MOVE FUNDS BACK TO THEIR HAND)?
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. The paper does not mention a default‐contribution mechanism or systematic use of a “take‐some” vs. “give‐some” default that is then reversed by the player.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying the default contribution to influence the punishment treatment effect?  
  – No mention.

6. MARGINAL PER CAPITA RETURN (MPCR) OR RELATED PARAMETERS SUCH AS MULTIPLICATION FACTOR
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. In Experiment 1, contributions are multiplied by 1.6 before being shared. In Experiments 2 and 3, the multiplier is 1.5.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying the MPCR and its effect on punishment?  
  – No. The multiplier is set in each study but never manipulated to study how it affects punishment. No numerical effect sizes for changing the multiplier appear.

7. PUNISHMENT COST TO IMPOSE A SINGLE UNIT OF PUNISHMENT
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. In all experiments, each Decrement Point (DP) assigned costs the punisher 1 MU. That 1:3 cost ratio (punisher pays 1 MU, target loses 3 MU) is stated.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying this cost?  
  – No. The paper does not vary or compare different punishment‐cost levels, nor is there an analysis of how changing this parameter would affect outcomes.

8. PUNISHMENT MAGNITUDE (THE COINS DEDUCTED FOR EACH UNIT OF PUNISHMENT)
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. Each DP deducts 3 MU from the target’s payoff, used in all three experiments.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying the punishment magnitude?  
  – No. There is no systematic variation or reported effect‐size analysis for altering the magnitude from 3 MU to another value.

9. WHETHER A REWARD IS ENABLED
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – It mentions reward only briefly in the general discussion (speculating that reward might similarly be prone to discrimination). However, the experiments do not implement reward at all.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying reward on the punishment treatment effect?  
  – No. Reward is not tested or systematically manipulated.

10. REWARD COST TO GRANT A SINGLE UNIT OF REWARD
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. Rewards are not part of the design.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying reward cost?  
  – No mention.

11. REWARD MAGNITUDE (THE COINS AWARDED FOR EACH UNIT OF REWARD GRANTED)
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. Rewards are not used.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying reward magnitude?  
  – No mention.

12. IS THE NUMBER OF ROUNDS KNOWN TO PLAYERS (DO THEY KNOW WHEN THE GAME ENDS)?
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Experiment 1 instructions note that participants did not initially know a second block would follow. However, the paper does not treat awareness vs. unawareness of the exact ending round as a systematically varied factor.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying round‐knowledge?  
  – No. The paper does not address how changing knowledge about the game’s final round would alter the punishment treatment effect.

13. ARE PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN (E.G., DO PLAYERS KNOW HOW MUCH THEIR PEERS GAINED AND LOST)?
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Participants see whether each group member contributed or not (Experiment 1) and receive feedback on how many decrement points everyone got (all experiments). The paper does not systematically manipulate this feedback.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying the amount or type of feedback on peer outcomes?  
  – No. It does not report any effect of varying such information on punishment.

14. WHEN A PLAYER IS PUNISHED, DO THEY KNOW WHO THE SPECIFIC PUNISHER IS?
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes, they explicitly design the study so that the identity of the punisher is never revealed — participants only see total DP received.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying punisher anonymity?  
  – No. The design keeps punisher identity anonymous, but there is no comparison of different identity‐revelation conditions.

15. WHEN A PLAYER IS REWARDED, DO THEY KNOW WHO THE SPECIFIC REWARDER IS?
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. Reward is not used at all in these experiments.  
• Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying reward‐giver anonymity?  
  – No mention.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   – The paper does not use “group efficiency” in the specific sense of “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff.” Instead, it measures:  
     • Cooperation (the fraction of players contributing).  
     • Free‐riding (the fraction not contributing when endowed).  
     • Punishment usage (frequency and magnitude of DPs assigned).  
     • “Wealth” or “group payoff” (final earnings).  
   These measures differ from “efficiency” because the paper never calculates the ratio of total payoff to its theoretical maximum. Rather, the article’s focus is on how punishment (vs. no‐punishment) affects cooperation, free‐riding, and total earnings, especially under “pluriform” vs. “uniform” group structures.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – The paper explicitly mentions or describes values/conditions for nine parameters:  
     (1) Number of players (groups of 3, 4, or 6),  
     (2) Number of rounds (20‐round repeated vs. single‐shot),  
     (4) All‐or‐nothing vs. partial contribution (binary in Exp.1 vs. multiple denominations in Exps.2/3),  
     (6) Multiplication factor (1.6 or 1.5),  
     (7) Punishment cost (1 MU per decrement point),  
     (8) Punishment magnitude (3 MU per decrement point),  
     (12) (Partial mention) that participants did not know about a second block in Exp.1,  
     (13) That contributors’ decisions and assigned DPs are shown in certain ways (though not systematically varied),  
     (14) That punisher identity is kept anonymous.  
   – The remaining six parameters (3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 15) are not implemented or are only mentioned in passing (reward is mentioned conceptually but never used).

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   – None. Although some parameters differ between experiments (e.g., repeated vs. one‐shot, or all‐or‐nothing vs. incremental contributions), the paper does not systematically manipulate any of these 15 parameters so as to isolate their impact on punishment. Thus, there are zero parameters that are varied for the purpose of measuring their effect on punishment’s outcomes, and no effect‐size estimates for parameter changes are provided.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper, what would they be?  
   – The paper provides virtually no direct guidance on how systematically changing any of the 15 parameters would alter the impact of punishment on group efficiency (the paper does not study “efficiency” directly, and none of these 15 parameters is actually manipulated to see how it affects cooperation or payoff). Its main finding is that punishment becomes less effective for cooperation (and thereby lowers group payoff) in “pluriform” groups, because discrimination creeps into the punishment decisions. Apart from that specific group‐structure finding, the paper does not offer predictions about varying the other parameters. Consequently, on the basis of the paper alone, there is little to no predictive information about how each of the 15 parameters or their interactions might affect punishment’s influence on efficiency.

Abstract: Costly signaling theory of religion has been proposed to explain the evolutionary adaptiveness of religion in general and, specifically, its prosocial effects, including the relative longevity of religious communes vis-a-vis their secular counterparts. This article focuses on two crucial aspects of this relationship: the features and functions of signals and the mechanism through which signaling translates into enhanced prosociality. It identifies some of the key factors of the costliness of behavior and distinguishes between religious and secular signals, arguing that only the latter serve to broadcast commitment. The role of religious signals, instead, might be to stimulate the supernatural watching (Under His Eye) mechanism: enhancing supernatural sanctions beliefs and providing a setting in which implicit prosocial responses are triggered. The relative absence of this mechanism in secular communities may explain their shorter life spans. A link is thus established between the costly signaling and supernatural punishment theories of religious behavior.

Authors: Zefferman, MR
Author Full Names: Zefferman, Matthew R.
Article Title: Constraints on cooperation shape hierarchical versus distributed structure in human groups
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; EVOLUTIONARY-THEORY; SELECTION; DESIGN
Abstract: Some human groups are organized hierarchically and some are distributed. Both types of groups occur in economic, political, and military domains, but it is unclear why hierarchical organizations are favored in certain contexts and distributed organizations are favored in others. I propose that these different organizational structures can be explained by human groups having different constraints on their ability to foster cooperation within the group. Human within-group cooperation is often maintained by monitoring and punishment. In hierarchical groups, monitoring and punishment are organized into tree-like command-and-control structures with supervisors responsible for monitoring the cooperation of their subordinates and punishing non-cooperators. By contrast, in distributed groups, monitoring is diffuse and punishment is collective. I propose that the organization of cooperative human groups is constrained by the costs of monitoring and punishment. I formalize this hypothesis with a model where individuals in a group cooperate to produce public goods while embedded in a network of monitoring and punishment responsibilities. I show that, when punishment costs are high and monitoring costs are low, socially-optimal monitoring and punishment networks are distributed. The size of these distributed networks is constrained by monitoring costs. However, when punishment costs are low, socially-optimal networks are hierarchical. Monitoring costs do not constrain the size of hierarchical networks but determine how many levels of supervision are required to foster cooperation in the hierarchical group. These results may explain the increasingly large and hierarchical groups throughout much of human history. They also suggest that the recent emergence of large-scale distributed organizations has been possible because new technologies, like the internet, have made monitoring costs extremely low.

Below, each of the 15 experimental‐design parameters is checked, one‐by‐one, against the content of Zefferman’s paper.  For every parameter I state  

(1) whether the paper mentions it at all and, if so, what value(s) or symbol(s) it takes, and  

(2) whether the paper says what will happen to the “punishment treatment effect” (PTE) – i.e., the difference in group efficiency with vs. without punishment – when that parameter is systematically varied.  Any numerical relationships that can be read directly from the text, equations, tables or figures are reproduced; otherwise I say “not given”.

Remember: the paper is a purely theoretical model of optimal monitoring/punishment networks; it never runs a *treatment* in the usual experimental sense (there is no “with-punishment” vs. “no-punishment” condition).  Consequently almost nothing in the paper can be mapped onto a classic “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”  I nonetheless follow the instructions literally.

------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Number of players (group size, N)  
   (1) Mentioned constantly (symbol N).  Examples: N = 6, 12 and 120.  
   (2) The paper gives no statement about how changing N alters a PTE.  
       All key equations (e.g., Eq. 1) contain N, but the author never 
       interprets this as a treatment effect of punishment.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Not mentioned.  One-shot Nash equilibrium only.  
   (2) No discussion, no prediction, no effect size.

3. Chat enabled  
   (1) Not mentioned.  
   (2) No discussion, no prediction.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
   (1) The model collapses equilibrium strategies into two discrete 
       possibilities (threshold contributor vs. pure free-rider, see 
       Table 2).  But no separate parameter switches this rule on/off.  
   (2) No prediction of its *variation* on any outcome.

5. Contribution default / rollback mechanism  
   (1) Not mentioned.  
   (2) No discussion, no prediction.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   (1) Present as “public-goods efficiency” b.  
   (2) Eq. (1) shows that universal contribution is socially efficient 
       only if  
          b > [N c_t] / [N c_t – K/m].  
       That inequality is a *threshold* condition; the paper never turns 
       b into a continuous treatment and never reports effect sizes for a 
       PTE.

7. Punishment cost to imposer  
   (1) Reflected in c_p (the amount each potential punisher must hold in 
       reserve).  
   (2) Eq. (2) implies that raising c_p increases the minimum in-degree 
       needed to deter free‐riding, but the paper does not follow through 
       to a quantitative change in efficiency or a punishment treatment 
       effect.  No numbers reported.

8. Punishment magnitude (or punishment efficiency, p)  
   (1) Central parameter; varied extensively in Figs. 4–6 and Eq. (2).  
   (2) Qualitative prediction: higher p (i) reduces the required number 
       of monitors, (ii) lets universal contribution remain optimal under 
       lower monitoring efficiency, and (iii) makes optimal networks more 
       hierarchical (graph-efficiency × graph-hierarchy composite rises 
       up to ≈1).  The paper still does **not** translate this into an 
       explicit treatment-minus-control efficiency gain, so no numerical 
       PTE is given.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   (1) Not discussed.  
   (2) No prediction.

10. Reward cost  
    Same as (9).

11. Reward magnitude  
    Same as (9).

12. Horizon known (finite vs. indefinite rounds)  
    (1) Not mentioned.  
    (2) No prediction.

    (1) Not mentioned.  
    (2) No prediction.

14. Punisher identity revealed  
    (1) Not mentioned.  
    (2) No prediction.

15. Rewarder identity revealed  
    Same as (14).

------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
------------------------------------------------------------------

A. Dependent variables actually used  
   • Social (group) efficiency Π_N (= total payoff)  
   • Two purely structural network indices: graph efficiency (E) and 
     graph hierarchy (H), plus their product E × H.  
   These are **not** the same as contribution levels or cooperation rates; 
   the paper never computes a “punishment treatment effect” in the usual 
   experimental sense.

B. Which of the 15 parameters appear at all?  
   4 parameters clearly appear:  
     1 (N), 6 (MPCR = b), 7 (punishment cost c_p), 8 (punishment magnitude/efficiency p).  
   One could argue that item 4 (all-or-nothing) is implicitly fixed, but it is never a variable.  No other parameter is mentioned.  So 4/15 at most.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of **systematic variation** on the punishment treatment effect?  
   Strictly speaking, zero.  
   If we relax “treatment effect” to “any efficiency consequence of changing a parameter in the presence of punishment,” then only parameter 8 (p) is systematically varied in the text and figures (and interacts with monitoring efficiency m).  No numerical effect sizes on payoffs are supplied.

D. Predictions one could make (and the limits thereof) when asked to forecast the punishment treatment effect on efficiency using *only* this paper:  
   • Higher punishment efficiency (larger p or lower punisher cost) should 
     enlarge the region of the parameter space where cooperation is 
     sustainable and therefore should *raise* group efficiency relative 
     to a no-punishment baseline.  
   • A sufficiently high MPCR (b) is a pre-condition; if b is below the 
     threshold in Eq. (1), punishment will not salvage efficiency.  
   • Group size N enters the threshold conditions but the paper gives no 
     comparative statics, so no clear directional prediction.  
   • Because none of the other 11 parameters are discussed, no prediction 
     can be made about their main or interactive effects on the PTE.

In short, the paper is informative about how *punishment efficiency* (p) and *monitoring efficiency* (m, not on your list) jointly shape the optimal *structure* of sanctioning networks, but it says almost nothing about classic experimental design factors such as round length, chat, anonymity, rewards, etc.  Therefore it provides only very limited guidance for predicting how the 15 listed parameters would modulate the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Author Full Names: Marco, Jorge; Goetz, Renan
Article Title: Public policy design and common property resources: A social network approach
Author Keywords: common property resources; cooperation; public policy; social networks; social norms
Keywords Plus: COOPERATION; RECIPROCITY; ENFORCEMENT; PUNISHMENT; EVOLUTION; PRESSURE; NORMS; GOODS; GAMES
Abstract: This paper analyzes the extent to which two factors-social networks and the severity of the scarcity of a common property resource-affect norm-complying behavior that favors cooperation. It assumes that those who comply with the social norm exercise social pressure on defectors. We develop an analytical framework that allows us to determine the minimum (maximum) share of norm-complying agents at which social networks start (stop) having an influence on cooperation. Knowing these shares allows policymakers to identify the conditions under which legal and/or informal enforcement policies for cooperation are effective and how different types of social networks affect the design of these policies. We find that stable steady states exist in which compliers and defectors coexist (partial cooperation), but the stability of such states requires that the costs of coordination among compliers to exercise social pressure are high. Full cooperation is another possible steady state but is unlikely to prevail if the agents do not perceive the scarcity of the common property resource as severe. A numerical study, empirically calibrated for an aquifer in Spain, shows that subsidizing the compliers' costs of exerting social pressure may impede the attainment of a steady state based on partial cooperation. Although social networks can promote cooperation, their influence is limited. The minimum share of compliers for attaining cooperation can be reduced by informal enforcement policies by not more than 26%. We show that combinations of different types of informal enforcement policies should be applied cautiously because they may cancel each other out.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter accounting of what the paper discusses and whether it makes any predictions—particularly about systematically varying each parameter—in relation to “punishment” (the paper’s counterpart is “social pressure”) and any dependent variable. Please note that the paper does not use the term “punishment treatment effect” or “efficiency” in the sense of actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff. Instead, it focuses on how “social pressure,” “sanctioning (punishment) costs,” and the “share of compliers” influence the eventual state of cooperation and resource extraction. Throughout, quotations in parentheses (“…”) mark close paraphrases of relevant paper content.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1) Number of players  
   • Discussed? Yes. The paper uses n ≥ 2 “agents” who extract from a common property resource.  
   • Value(s) if given? The paper sets “n >> 2” and treats the system as large, often normalizing per hectare.  
   • Systematically varied for a punishment treatment effect?  
     – The paper does include “Parameter 1” in Table 1 (the number of agents), but it does not analyze the effect on “punishment treatment effect” or “efficiency.” Instead, it notes that changes in n mainly re-scale the problem. There is no numeric effect given for how varying n might change any “punishment” impact.  

2) Number of rounds  
   • Discussed? No. The paper’s model is a dynamic system in continuous time (or discrete steps t = 1,2,… until T or resource depletion), but it does not treat “number of rounds” in the sense of a repeated public goods game.  
   • Predictions from varying it? Not mentioned.  

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not mention communication protocols (“chat”) or systematically vary it.  

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not mention forced binary contributions.  

5) Is the contribution default?  
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not analyze any default contribution choices or default allocations.  

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related group‐multiplication factor  
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not use an MPCR parameter (typical of public goods games).  

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussed? Partly. The paper’s counterpart is the “sanctioning costs” or “social pressure costs” function γi. That cost is not broken down as a “per‐unit” cost. Rather, costs depend on how many neighbors are defectors and on coordination among compliers (parameters α0, α1, α2, v).  
   • Value(s) if given?  
     – The paper uses α0, α1, α2 to define how sanctioning costs scale if many neighbors must be pressured.  
     – Tables show baseline values (e.g., α0=1, α1=1, α2=2.5, etc.) and how increasing/decreasing them changes the share of compliers at equilibrium.  
   • Effect of systematically varying on punishment treatment effect?  
     – The paper does not speak of a “treatment effect on efficiency”; instead, it studies how different levels (and cost structures) of social pressure produce stable full‐ or partial‐cooperation outcomes. There is no numerical “punishment‐treatment‐effect size” but rather a qualitative finding that higher punishment (social pressure) costs can favor stable partial cooperation.  

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted, per unit punishment)  
   • Discussed? Yes, under the label of “social pressure” ωi. It can be large or small, represented in part by the maximum social pressure parameter Υ (Upsilon).  
   • Value(s) if given?  
     – They set the maximum social pressure (Υ) = 2, meaning it can be “twice” the difference between defector and complier payoffs.  
   • Effect of systematically varying on punishment treatment effect?  
     – They vary Υ in their sensitivity analyses (Table 1) and note how that shifts the equilibrium share of compliers. They do not frame it as “punishment treatment effect on efficiency,” nor do they give a numeric effect size specific to a “treatment effect.”  

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not analyze rewards or positive transfers among agents.  

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Discussed? No. Not mentioned.  

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded, per unit reward)  
    • Discussed? No. Not mentioned.  

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    • Discussed? No. The paper does not model finite‐horizon repeated games with known end. There is a T that may end the game or resource can get depleted, but the paper does not treat “knowledge of T” as a systematically varied parameter.  

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained)?  
    • Discussed? Partly. The paper’s “Assumption A2” states that each agent is “perfectly informed about their neighbors’ actions.” However, it does not mention showing exact payoffs. Nor does it systematically vary whether this information is displayed.  
    • Effect of varying it? Not analyzed.  

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Discussed? No. The paper does not address the question of whether defectors learn who pressured them.  

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Discussed? No. The paper does not address rewards or identification of rewarders.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • No. The paper does not measure “group efficiency” = (actual total payoff) / (maximum possible total payoff). Instead, it models:  
     – The share of norm‐complying (cooperating) agents.  
     – Stability of full‐cooperation, partial‐cooperation, or no‐cooperation steady states.  
     – How social pressure and costs shape equilibrium “cooperation” and “resource stock.”  
   • These differ from “efficiency” because they do not quantify total payoffs as a fraction of the maximum possible payoff; instead, they track how many agents comply with a social norm and how the resource evolves.  

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   1) Number of players (mentioned)  
   2) Number of rounds (not discussed)  
   3) Is chat enabled? (not discussed)  
   4) All‐or‐nothing contribution? (not discussed)  
   5) Contribution default? (not discussed)  
   6) MPCR or multiplication factor? (not discussed)  
   7) Punishment cost? (addressed as “sanctioning cost” γi, though not per‐unit)  
   8) Punishment magnitude? (addressed as “social pressure” ωi, with a maximum of 2 × payoff difference)  
   9) Whether a reward is enabled? (not discussed)  
   10) Reward cost? (not discussed)  
   11) Reward magnitude? (not discussed)  
   12) Is the number of rounds known? (not discussed)  
   13) Are peer outcomes shown? (partially: neighbors see each other’s actions but this is not varied)  
   14) Identity of punisher revealed? (not discussed)  
   15) Identity of rewarder revealed? (not discussed)

In total: four parameters (1, 7, 8, and partially 13) are touched upon in some way.

C) For which and how many of these 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, the paper does not discuss any “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” The paper analyzes how changes in “social pressure” (akin to punishment) and its cost structure shape the share of compliers at steady states. It never uses the term “treatment effect” or the ratio‐based concept of “efficiency.”  
   • Still, Param. 7 (punishment cost) and Param. 8 (punishment magnitude) are systematically varied in the sense of different “sanctioning cost” functions and maximum “social pressure” strengths. The paper reports how these variations affect cooperation equilibria, not “efficiency.” There is no numeric “effect size” on “punishment treatment effect”; instead, it provides qualitative or percentage shifts in the share of compliers at equilibrium.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not mention “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” or measure payoffs as a fraction of the group optimum. It runs dynamic simulations to see whether the group ends up in partial vs. full cooperation (or resource depletion). Consequently, it offers little direct guidance regarding how each parameter would alter a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”  
   • From the paper’s discussions of social pressure, one could infer (in broad qualitative terms only) that more costly punishment (parameter 7) and lower possible punishment magnitude (parameter 8) could diminish cooperation outcomes. The paper also implies that if sanctioning costs are extremely high (7) and the resource is perceived as abundant, stable “partial cooperation” (or defection) may ensue. Absent more detail on payoff sums, no further prediction can be made.  

Overall, since the paper does not study “efficiency” (actual vs. maximum payoff) nor “punishment treatment effect” in the usual sense of experimental public goods models, only limited parallels can be drawn to the 15 parameters, and no numerical punishment‐treatment‐effect results on efficiency are provided.
