Authors: Isern-Mas, C; Gomila, A
Author Full Names: Isern-Mas, Carme; Gomila, Antoni
Article Title: A Second-Personal Approach to the Evolution of Morality
Author Keywords: Evolution; Feeling of obligation; Human morality; Moral motivation; Moral norms; Second-personal morality
Keywords Plus: COOPERATION; ALTRUISM; BEHAVIOR
Abstract: Building on the discussion between Stephen Darwall and Michael Tomassello, we propose an alternative evolutionary account of moral motivation in its two-pronged dimension. We argue that an evolutionary account of moral motivation must account for the two forms of moral motivation that we distinguish: motivation to be partial, which is triggered by the affective relationships we develop with others; and motivation to be impartial, which is triggered by those norms to which we give impartial validity. To that aim, we present the second-person standpoint of morality, first as Darwall conceives of it, and then as we reinterpret it from a naturalistic approach. Then we synthesize Tomasello's evolutionary account of morality, and Darwall's objections to it. To reply to those objections, building on Tomasello's proposal, we argue that the motivation to be impartial, and the feeling of obligation to comply with normative requirements, appeared when humans anticipated and, critically, internalized others' sanctions to the violation of social norms. Consequently, we posit that social norms and sanctions appeared first at the community level, and only after that were they internalized in the form of self-directed reactive attitudes. Finally, we derive some corollaries that follow from our proposal.

Author Full Names: Ozono, Hiroki; Nakama, Daisuke
Article Title: Effects of experimental situation on group cooperation and individual performance: Comparing laboratory and online experiments
Keywords Plus: SOCIAL PREFERENCES; PUNISHMENT; DISTANCE
Abstract: With the spread of online behavioral experiments, estimating the effects of experimental situations and sample heterogeneity is increasing in discussions of the generalizability of data. In this study, we examined how the experimental situations (laboratory/online) affected group cooperation and individual performances. The participants were Japanese university students, randomly assigned to laboratory or online experiments. For the group cooperation task, they were asked to perform the public goods game with or without punishment, but no effect of the experimental situation was found both for cooperative and punitive behaviors. For the individual tasks, participants were asked to perform tasks including a creative task and a dull task. We manipulated the presence or absence of an external incentive. As a result, there was no significant difference between the experimental situations with one exception: only in the laboratory situation was the performance of the difficult creative task lower in the presence of an external incentive. Furthermore, we conducted as an additional experiment using the same treatments for a Japanese online-worker sample. This sample was less cooperative in the public goods game than the student sample, both with and without punishment. In addition, the presence of external incentives facilitated performance of the online-worker sample only for the dull task. We discuss the similarities and differences with previous studies that examined the effects of experimental situations and sample heterogeneity, and the implications for remote work in the real world.

Authors: Amirova, I; Petrick, M; Djanibekov, N
Author Full Names: Amirova, Iroda; Petrick, Martin; Djanibekov, Nodir
Article Title: Investment traps and resilience to shocks: An experimental study of Central Asian collective water governance
Author Keywords: Central Asia; experiment; multiple equilibria; resilience; water management
Keywords Plus: POVERTY TRAPS; IRRIGATION; ASYMMETRIES; MANAGEMENT; SYSTEMS; POWER
Abstract: We theoretically and empirically investigate the investments of water users in a stylized local irrigation system. We model irrigation self-management as an interdependent interaction of users in an evolutionary game and study the resilience of the irrigation system. The theoretical model implies multiple stable equilibria at different efficiency levels. Users may be trapped in a low level of collective investment or succeed by being locked in a high collective investment level, implying an irrigation system resilient against external shocks. The study seeks to empirically identify such lock-ins in experimental interactions among Central Asian farmers. Furthermore, we inquire into whether a pre-play cheap talk opportunity with peer-monitoring or sanctioning treatments influence the self-reinforcing dynamic. Our findings revealed several stable states. Among these states, there are both low and high levels of efficiency, which we measure in the size of public good. Communication among users results in higher collective investment levels. However, this does not guarantee the complete elimination of inferior conventions from best-response play. Penalties crowded out the intrinsic motivation to cooperate as they reduced collective investment in both low- and high-level equilibria. Our findings imply that institutional settings tailored to each community can improve resilience to climate-driven perturbations in water resources.

   b) No predictions are made.

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?

However, it does not provide a ratio of actual total payoff to the maximum possible payoff. Rather, it treats “collective investment” (coupons invested in each round) as its main outcome. The authors also sometimes refer to the “size of the public good” or “collective payoffs,” but they never calculate efficiency as a strict payoff‐based fraction. Thus, “efficiency” is often treated as being synonymous with higher collective investment in this study, rather than that formal ratio.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Parameter 3 (communication/chat) and the broad idea of “penalty” (parameters 7/8) are mentioned. None of the other 12 parameters are explicitly discussed, nor do the authors provide numerical values for them.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• The paper implements two penalty (“punishment”) variants (“low penalty” and “high penalty”) but does not give any detail on how cost or magnitude is calculated. Hence, while there is some variation in penalty severity, the paper does not systematically link that variation to measured changes in an “efficiency” ratio.  
• No other parameters are systematically varied for the punishment effect.

D. Predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, based solely on the paper’s content:  
• The paper reports that introducing punishment (penalty) tended to reduce collective investment (i.e., reduce what they considered an efficiency‐like measure). Even in the “low” vs. “high” penalty comparisons, neither achieved higher average investment than the baseline with no penalty.  
• The paper does not analyze or mention the other parameters (1, 2, 4–6, 9–15) with respect to punishment’s effect on efficiency. Consequently, aside from noting that penalties (in general) appear to reduce voluntary cooperation, the paper offers little basis for additional predictions about those other parameters.

Authors: Wang, CQ; Perc, M; Szolnoki, A
Author Full Names: Wang, Chaoqian; Perc, Matjaz; Szolnoki, Attila
Article Title: Evolutionary dynamics of any multiplayer game on regular graphs
Keywords Plus: COOPERATION; POPULATION; STRATEGIES; PUNISHMENT
Abstract: Multiplayer games on graphs are at the heart of theoretical descriptions of key evolutionary processes that govern vital social and natural systems. However, a comprehensive theoretical framework for solving multiplayer games with an arbitrary number of strategies on graphs is still missing. Here, we solve this by drawing an analogy with the Balls-and-Boxes problem, based on which we show that the local configuration of multiplayer games on graphs is equivalent to distributing k identical co-players among n distinct strategies. We use this to derive the replicator equation for any n-strategy multiplayer game under weak selection, which can be solved in polynomial time. As an example, we revisit the second-order free-riding problem, where costly punishment cannot truly resolve social dilemmas in a well-mixed population. Yet, in structured populations, we derive an accurate threshold for the punishment strength, beyond which punishment can either lead to the extinction of defection or transform the system into a rock-paper-scissors-like cycle. The analytical solution also qualitatively agrees with the phase diagrams that were previously obtained for non-marginal selection strengths. Our framework thus allows an exploration of any multi-strategy multiplayer game on regular graphs. Evolutionary multiplayer games in structured populations illustrate a variety of phenomena in natural and social systems. This research provides a mathematical framework to analyze multiplayer games with an arbitrary number of strategies on regular graphs.

Article Title: Inequality averse and compassionate blood donor: implication for interventions

Abstract: Background and objectives Blood donors, compared to non-donors, are more likely to show a preference to help others either by sharing resources to directly compensate those in need or indirectly by punishing those who act unfairly. Authors: Riedl, A; Rohde, IMT; Strobel, M
Author Full Names: Riedl, Arno; Rohde, Ingrid M. T.; Strobel, Martin
Article Title: Free neighborhood choice boosts socially optimal outcomes in stag-hunt coordination problem
Keywords Plus: EFFICIENT COORDINATION; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; LOCAL INTERACTION; PATH DEPENDENCE; COOPERATION; PROMOTE; NETWORKS; MODEL
Abstract: Situations where independent agents need to align their activities to achieve individually and socially beneficial outcomes are abundant, reaching from everyday situations like fixing a time for a meeting to global problems like climate change agreements. Often such situations can be described as stag-hunt games, where coordinating on the socially efficient outcome is individually optimal but also entails a risk of losing out. Previous work has shown that in fixed interaction neighborhoods agents' behavior mostly converges to the collectively inefficient outcome. However, in the field, interaction neighborhoods often can be self-determined. Theoretical work investigating such circumstances is ambiguous in whether the efficient or inefficient outcome will prevail. We performed an experiment with human subjects exploring how free neighborhood choice affects coordination. In a fixed interaction treatment, a vast majority of subjects quickly coordinates on the inefficient outcome. In a treatment with neighborhood choice, the outcome is dramatically different: behavior quickly converges to the socially desirable outcome leading to welfare gains 2.5 times higher than in the environment without neighborhood choice. Participants playing efficiently exclude those playing inefficiently who in response change their behavior and are subsequently included again. Importantly, this mechanism is effective despite that only few exclusions actually occur.

Author Full Names: Okada, Isamu; Yamamoto, Hitoshi; Akiyama, Eizo; Toriumi, Fujio
Article Title: Cooperation in spatial public good games depends on the locality effects of game, adaptation, and punishment
Keywords Plus: SOCIAL-BEHAVIOR; EVOLUTION; NETWORKS; MAINTAIN; PROMOTES
Abstract: Despite intensive studies on the evolution of cooperation in spatial public goods games, there have been few investigations into locality effects in interaction games, adaptation, and punishment. Here we analyze locality effects using an agent-based model of a regular graph. Our simulation shows that a situation containing a local game, local punishment, and global adaptation leads to the most robustly cooperative regime. Further, we show an interesting feature in local punishment. Previous studies showed that a local game and global adaptation are likely to generate cooperation. However, they did not consider punishment. We show that if local punishment is introduced in spatial public goods games, a situation satisfying either local game or local adaptation is likely to generate cooperation. We thus propose two principles. One is if interactions in games can be restricted locally, it is likely to generate cooperation independent of the interaction situations on punishment and adaptation. The other is if the games must be played globally, a cooperative regime requires both local punishment and local adaptation.

• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. There is no mention of any in‐game chat or communication channel among subjects.  

• Effect of varying it on punishment?  
  – Not mentioned. No predictions are given.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. Contributions in the reported experiments can be any integer amount within a token endowment, not forced all‐or‐nothing.  

• Effect of systematically varying it?  
  – Not mentioned.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5) Is the contribution “default” (i.e., do people move tokens out of a public fund back into private)?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. The paper never mentions a “default” contribution mechanism. Subjects simply decide how many tokens to contribute to the public good.  

• Effect of systematically varying it?  
  – Not mentioned.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplier  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. They systematically vary the “return to the public good” in two ways: either 0.6 of a token (low return) or 0.8 (high return). Table 1 indicates that sessions 1–2 used the low return (0.6), and sessions 3–13 used the high return (0.8).  

• Do they make predictions or report numerical effect sizes regarding how that variation alters the punishment treatment effect?  
  – They do not frame it in terms of “efficiency” (actual total payoff ÷ maximum payoff). They do, however, report that “low returns” versus “high returns” change how people vote on punishment or no‐punishment institutions. In particular, under low returns (0.6), punishment tends to be less favored (the paper reports a 15‐percentage‐point increase in voting for the no‐punishment institution under low returns). This is discussed in the text where they run a reduced‐form probit model of votes (cf. Table 5).  
  – The paper reports no direct “punishment‐treatment‐effect‐on-efficiency” numbers, only on profits or voting patterns.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. Botelho et al. provide a punishment cost schedule in Table 2 (e.g., 1 token cost for 1 punishment point, 2 tokens cost for 2 punishment points, etc.). Fehr & Gächter (2000, 2002) also had different cost structures (convex vs. linear).  

• Is it systematically varied to learn how that change alone alters punishment’s effect on efficiency?  
  – No. Botelho et al. use a single cost schedule and do not manipulate it across sessions. No effect size is given regarding how cost variation alone changes the punishment treatment effect.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
8) Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from the punished player)  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. They specify that each punishment point reduces the punished player’s earnings for the round by 10%, up to 100%.  

• Is it systematically varied?  
  – No. A single 10%‐per‐point scheme is used. No effect size is given about how differences in punishment magnitude would change net payoffs or efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
9) Whether a reward is enabled  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Only in referencing other studies (e.g., Sutter et al., 2010), but Botelho et al.’s own reported experiment does not include a reward mechanism.  

• Is it systematically varied?  
  – No, the paper’s experiment only studies punishment vs. no‐punishment. They do not test reward.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. They do not implement rewards at all.  

• Effect of varying it?  
  – Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
11) Reward magnitude  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. Again, no reward mechanism is implemented in their own experiment.  

• Effect of varying it?  
  – Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
12) Is the number of rounds known to players?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes. They tell participants that there will be 20 rounds (two sets of 10) plus a final “round 21.” The final round pays 10× the normal rate.  

• Is it systematically varied so as to measure how that knowledge affects punishment?  
  – No. They do not alter whether the horizon is known or unknown. No effect size is given.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much peers gained/lost)?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – Yes, participants see some summary of others’ contributions and earnings. For example, near the voting stage they see a “review of (their) earnings across the periods.” Fehr & Gächter also show group members’ contributions.  

• Is it systematically varied?  
  – No. They do not run conditions where some see/no‐one‐sees. No numerical effect size is reported for such variation.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
14) When a player is punished, do they know the specific punisher?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – It is stated that the experiment is anonymous and does not identify counterparties personally. The paper does not describe a separate treatment in which the punisher’s identity is revealed.  

• Is it systematically varied?  
  – No. No analyses are reported on punisher identity disclosure.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is?  
• Does the paper discuss it?  
  – No. The experiment itself includes no reward mechanism, so this never arises.  

• Systematically varied?  
  – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

=========================================
SUMMARY  
=========================================

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   – They do not use “efficiency” in the sense of “actual total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff.” Instead, they primarily measure and discuss (a) average contributions and (b) profits (or “earnings”). They also mention voting outcomes. These are not identical to “efficiency,” so the paper often focuses on whether punishment raises or lowers participants’ actual monetary payoffs rather than on the fraction of a maximum possible payoff.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – Mentioned (but not always varied):  
     1. Number of players (2‐person groups, references to 4‐person groups in Fehr & Gächter)  
     2. Number of rounds (6, 10, 20 in references; 10+10+1 in their own design)  
     6. MPCR or multiplier (0.6 vs. 0.8)  
     7. Punishment cost (they show one cost schedule)  
     8. Punishment magnitude (10% per point)  
     12. Players do know the total rounds.  
     13. Peer outcomes are at least partly displayed.  
   – Not mentioned (or at most mentioned only in passing, but not used in the design):  
     3. Chat  
     4. “All‐or‐nothing” contributions  
     5. Default contribution mechanism  
     9. Presence of a reward  
     10. Reward cost  
     11. Reward magnitude  
     14. Identity of punisher known vs. unknown (not tested)  
     15. Identity of rewarder known vs. unknown (not applicable)

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable) when systematically varied?  
   – Only one: the MPCR (parameter 6). The authors switch between a 0.6 vs. 0.8 multiplier to see how it changes behavior in punishment vs. no‐punishment conditions. They provide regression estimates for how a “low return” (0.6) versus a “high return” (0.8) changes individual votes or profitability. They do not explicitly calculate changes in “efficiency,” but they do describe how lower vs. higher returns influence the likelihood that people will vote to keep the punishment option.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, solely based on this paper, what would they be?  
   – The authors do not explicitly analyze “efficiency” as “total payoffs relative to maximum.” They emphasize that when the net monetary benefit of punishment is negative, subjects do not want punishment, even if it increases contributions.  
   – From the one systematically varied parameter (the marginal return on contributions), we see no strong suggestion in the paper that an increased MPCR inevitably makes punishment generate higher overall payoffs. Instead, the authors find that actual profits often remain lower with punishment, even if contributions rise.  
   – Consequently, there is too little direct evidence in the paper to predict systematically how changing the other parameters (e.g., punishment cost, punishment magnitude, reward features, knowledge of punisher identity) would affect efficiency. Those topics are not formally tested by Botelho et al. in a way that yields numeric estimates of “punishment‐treatment‐effect on efficiency.”

Hence, based solely on the content of this paper, one cannot offer more than very limited predictions about how each parameter would shape the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.

Authors: Heine, F; Strobel, M
Author Full Names: Heine, Florian; Strobel, Martin
Article Title: Reward and punishment in a team contest
Keywords Plus: ECONOMIC SHOCKS; CIVIL CONFLICT; RENT-SEEKING; COOPERATION; COMMUNICATION; PREFERENCES; GAMES
Abstract: A team contest entails both public good characteristics within the teams as well as a contest across teams. In an experimental study, we analyse behaviour in such a team contest when allowing to punish or to reward other team members. Moreover, we compare two types of contest environment: One in which two teams compete for a prize and another one in which we switch off the between-group element of the contest. We find that reward giving, as opposed to punishing, induces higher contributions to the team contest. Furthermore, expenditures on rewarding other co-players are significantly higher than those for punishing.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter summary that focuses strictly on what Heine and Strobel (2020) say in their paper and whether (1) each parameter is explicitly mentioned (and at what value, if given), and (2) the paper makes any predictions about the effect of systematically varying that parameter on the “punishment treatment effect”—in other words, how adding punishment changes behavior or outcomes—particularly in terms of efficiency. Throughout, “mentioned” means that the authors at least state the parameter’s value or discuss it. “Discussed as systematically varied” means they explicitly compare or predict the consequences of changing that parameter itself (rather than having it fixed).

As a reminder:  
• “Efficiency” in your prompt is “the actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff of a fully cooperative group.”  
• The paper itself mostly measures payoffs via “mean income,” “rent dissipation,” or “over-investment,” and does not systematically vary most parameters. Instead, it focuses on whether each group is in a “contest” vs. “non-contest” environment and whether the group has “punishment,” “reward,” both, or none.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The experiment fixes groups of four players (p. 6, “Players are randomly sorted in groups of four.”).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not vary group size or predict any effect of changing it on the punishment treatment effect.  

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The experiment is run over 15 rounds (p. 6, “The experiment is conducted over 15 rounds. This is disclosed… to the participants.”).  
   • Systematically varied? No. They do not vary the number of rounds, nor do they predict how changing the round count would alter the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned? Indirectly. The authors note that participants “do not get to know from whom they get response… to circumvent that players react on response behaviour of particular co-players” (p. 8). No free-form or structured chat was used.  
   • Systematically varied? No. They do not implement chat in any treatment, nor do they make predictions about adding or removing chat.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned? Yes, in effect they do the opposite. Each player can contribute any integer amount from 0 to 100 tokens to their group’s “lottery tickets” (p. 6, “decides how much of [the 100-token endowment] to invest”).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper never discusses forcing an all-or-nothing contribution or predicts how that would affect punishment’s impact.  

5. Is the contribution default (as in a “remove from public fund” design)?  
   • Mentioned? No. The design is a straightforward “how many tokens do you invest” from 0 to 100. They do not present a default or endowment-withdrawal mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied? No. No mention of any default or changed rule of this kind.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? Only indirectly. The authors use a Tullock contest success function, with a prize “z = 100” (p. 7) and no explicit “MPCR” label.  
   • Systematically varied? No. “z = 100” is fixed. They do not experiment with or theorize how adjusting that prize systematically would alter the punishment treatment effect on efficiency (other than noting qualitatively that a higher or lower prize would shift Nash equilibria). There is no numerical test of varying this factor.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each punishment token costs the punisher 1 token (p. 8, “We apply a cost for response-giving of one…”).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The ratio remains 1:1 in all sessions. The paper does not predict how changing that cost would change the punishment effect.  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each punishment token removes exactly 1 coin from the target (p. 8, “if player ℓ punishes player k by 6, ℓ has to pay 6 for this action, and it is deducted from k’s account by 6”).  
   • Systematically varied? No. It is fixed at 1 token deducted for 1 token spent, and the authors do not vary it.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned? Yes. They have a “reward” treatment in which players can give positive tokens to teammates at cost 1-to-1 (p. 8).  
   • Systematically varied? Yes, in the sense that they run a separate “reward” condition, a “punish” condition, and a combined “reward & punish” condition. They do not systematically vary the cost or magnitude but do compare “reward present” vs. “reward absent.”  
   • Effect on punishment treatment? They do compare “punishment” vs. “reward,” but they do not directly test “varying reward magnitude or cost” on efficiency. Instead, they interpret that reward tends to raise contributions more effectively than punishment does (pp. 14–16).  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Granting 1 token of reward costs the giver 1 token (p. 8).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The experiment keeps it the same 1:1 ratio in all reward treatments. No separate predictions about changing the ratio.  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Same ratio of 1 coin for each 1 spent (p. 8).  
   • Systematically varied? No. They do not explore different reward magnitudes.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The design states that the 15-round horizon is common knowledge (p. 6).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The authors do not alter the knowledge or length of horizon in different sessions.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained or lost each round)?  
   • Mentioned? Yes, partially. Players see how much each teammate contributed and whether the team won, but they do not see individual payoffs of teammates beyond that data (p. 7–8).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The same feedback is given across all treatments. The paper does not link changes in that information display to punishment’s effect.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper explicitly states that punishment is anonymous within the group (p. 8: “participants do not get to know from whom they get response points assigned”).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The anonymity is fixed, and they do not compare what would happen if identities were known.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The same anonymity is maintained for reward (p. 8).  
   • Systematically varied? No. As with punishment, no variation.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary  
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • Yes. The paper discusses mean income per participant (“payoff” or “rent dissipation”) and notes that participants’ earnings are reduced substantially when they over-invest and punish each other (pp. 11–12, 21). However, the paper primarily treats “contribution levels” and “overspending” as key outcomes. They also report average income as a measure of how (in)efficient play became. Hence, “efficiency” in the sense of maximizing total tokens is indeed addressed, but much of the main analysis focuses on contribution levels, punishment, or reward behavior.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
     (1) Number of players (fixed at 4)  
     (2) Number of rounds (fixed at 15)  
     (3) Is chat enabled? (not used, but implied)  
     (4) All-or-nothing or incremental? (they used incremental)  
     (6) Contest “prize” as analogous to a multiplication factor (z=100)  
     (7 & 8) Punishment cost and magnitude (both 1 token)  
     (9) Reward presence (separate condition)  
     (10 & 11) Reward cost and magnitude (both 1 token)  
     (12) Number of rounds known (yes)  
     (13) Information about peer outcomes (partial knowledge)  
     (14 & 15) Anonymity of punisher/rewarder (yes)  
   • Not explicitly mentioned or used in their design:  
     (5) “Is the contribution default” is not discussed.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable) when systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, the paper does not systematically vary any of those parameters as the main experimental factor, other than whether “punishment” or “reward” is present at all (parameter #9). They do compare “punishment” vs. “no punishment,” “reward” vs. “no reward,” and “reward & punish” vs. “baseline.” They also compare “contest” vs. “non-contest” conditions. But they do not systematically vary cost-of-punishment or cost-of-reward, or group size, or number of rounds, etc.  

D. If you were to make predictions about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely from this paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper devotes most attention to the presence or absence of punishment, reward, and a rival group. They show that adding punishment alone tends not to increase payoffs in a “team contest,” because punishment can lead to over-investment and rent dissipation. Rewarding within a team can sometimes raise contributions, but in the presence of a contest, it can also lead to inefficiently high spending. From the text, they do not provide numerical predictions for other parameters (like bigger group size, unknown horizons, or chat). Thus, based strictly on this paper:  
     – Little can be concluded about how changing the group size, round count, communication, or the cost-magnitude ratio for punishment or reward would alter overall efficiency under punishment.  
     – They suggest that increasing the cost-effectiveness of either punishment or reward could change behavior, but they do not provide quantitative effects.  
     – In their specific design, punishment alone did not increase efficiency; adding punishment often led to costly overspending. Reward induced higher contributions than punishment did and sometimes improved payoffs—but only up to a point.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Hence, beyond the presence vs. absence of punishment or reward—combined with whether there is a contest or not—the paper stays silent on systematically varying the other parameters and does not provide numerical effect sizes for changes in them.
reference_APA: Heine, Florian & Strobel, Martin (2020). Reward and punishment in a team contest. PLOS ONE.

Authors: Selles, J; Bonhommeau, S; Guillotreau, P; Vallee, T
Author Full Names: Selles, Jules; Bonhommeau, Sylvain; Guillotreau, Patrice; Vallee, Thomas
Article Title: Can the Threat of Economic Sanctions Ensure the Sustainability of International Fisheries? An Experiment of a Dynamic Non-cooperative CPR Game with Uncertain Tipping Point
Author Keywords: Common-pool resources; Experimental economics; Fisheries management; International fisheries; Policy making; Tipping points
Keywords Plus: OPTIMAL MANAGEMENT; RESOURCE DILEMMAS; COLLECTIVE CHOICE; FISH STOCKS; HIGH SEAS; COMMONS; TRAGEDY; COOPERATION; AGREEMENTS; RISK
Abstract: Complex dynamic systems such as common-pool resource systems can undergo a critical shift at a given threshold, the so-called tipping point, which potentially requires substantial changes from the management system. We present in this research a framed laboratory experiment design to examine how the threat of economic sanctions influences the strategic management of a common-pool resource. We use the context of the East Atlantic bluefin tuna international fishery as it has been the archetype of an overfished and mismanaged fishery until a dramatic reinforcement of its regulations followed the threat of a trade ban. We consider endogenous threats and examine their effects on cooperation through harvest decisions taken in the context of non-cooperative game theory in which cooperation could be sustained using a trigger strategy. Our experiment results show that the threat of economic sanctions fosters more cooperative behaviors, less over-exploitation, and a more precautionary management of resources, reducing the economic rent dissipation. This result is exacerbated when the location of the tipping point that triggers the economic sanction is uncertain. In order to avoid free-riding behaviors and foster the emergence of a self-enforcing agreement, we suggest to introduce economic sanctions, such as trade restrictions, associated with uncertain biological limit reference points.

• Mentioned? Yes. The experiment uses an indefinite-horizon setup: participants do not know the exact stopping time. In practice, the authors analyze the first 15 rounds.  
• Systematically varied or its effect on the “punishment treatment effect” discussed? No. There is no comparison of different numbers of rounds; the paper does not study how changing the round count affects the sanction or any efficiency measure.

3) Is chat enabled between players?
• Mentioned? Yes, in the sense that the paper clarifies no face-to-face communication is allowed and only a “non-binding pledge” screen is provided.

• Systematically varied or its effect discussed? No.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor

10) Reward cost (to grant a unit of reward)

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward)
• Mentioned? No. There is no reward mechanism.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?
• Mentioned? Yes. The exact stopping point is intentionally unknown (an indefinite-horizon setup).  
• Systematically varied or its effect discussed? No. They only use this single approach of not revealing the total number of rounds.

13) Are peer outcomes shown?
• Mentioned? Yes. After each round, each subject sees the other subjects’ individual harvest decisions and can see profits.  
• Systematically varied or its effect on punishment or efficiency? No. There is no comparison with a scenario lacking that information.

14) When a player is punished, do they know the specific punisher?
• Mentioned? No. “Punishment” is a collective sanction (everyone loses) when the stock crosses the threshold, so there is no individual punisher identity to reveal.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know the specific rewarder?

  (13) Are peer outcomes shown? (yes, other players’ harvests and payoffs)

Abstract: Altruistic punishment of social norm violations plays a crucial role in maintaining widespread cooperation in human societies, and punitive behavior has been suggested to be related to the activity level of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER DISCUSSION

   • Systematic variation? No. The paper always fixes the number of players at three and does not manipulate or vary this parameter. No predictions are made about how changing the number of players would affect outcomes.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned? No. The experiment’s descriptions do not indicate any sort of direct chat or communication channel among participants.  
   • Systematic variation or effect? Not discussed in the paper.  

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not study a standard “public goods” setup. Instead, each participant chooses “Strategy A” (cooperate) or “Strategy B” (defect) in a Prisoner’s Dilemma. There is no mention of partial vs. all-or-nothing contributions.  
   • Systematic variation or effect? Not discussed.  

5) Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much of their endowment to move)?  
   • Mentioned? No. The design is a 3-player Prisoner’s Dilemma with a fixed payoff matrix per choice. There is no mention of any default contribution mechanism.  
   • Systematic variation or effect? Not discussed.  

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters (e.g., multiplication factor)  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper uses a Prisoner’s Dilemma payoff matrix (the “2 tokens added to defector, -4 tokens from each co-player” structure) but does not frame it in terms of an MPCR or a group multiplier.  
   • Systematic variation or effect? Not discussed.  

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? Partially. The paper states that each “token” spent by the punisher reduces the punishee’s payoff by three tokens. Hence the cost to the punisher is “1,” while the punishee loses “3” for each unit of punishment.  
   • Systematic variation or effect? The study always uses cost = 1 token (leading to 3 tokens of harm). It is not varied. No predictions are made about changing it.  

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. It remains fixed at “3 tokens lost by the punished player” per 1 token spent by the punisher.  
   • Systematic variation or effect? No. It is never manipulated, and the paper makes no predictions about systematically modifying this ratio.  

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper studies punishment only (costly punitive decisions). Rewarding or positive sanctions do not feature in the design.  
   • Systematic variation or effect? Not discussed.  

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Mentioned? No. No reward mechanism is present.  
    • Systematic variation or effect? Not discussed.  

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted)  
    • Mentioned? No. No reward mechanism is present.  
    • Systematic variation or effect? Not discussed.  

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?  
    • Mentioned? Not explicitly as a manipulation. The paper states there are 12 rounds, but does not say whether participants fully knew the exact final round in advance. There is no indication that this knowledge was hidden or varied.  
    • Systematic variation or effect? Not discussed.  

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much their peers gained or lost)?  
    • Mentioned? Partially. Players learn who cooperated/defected in the current round to make punishment decisions, but the paper does not systematically vary how much outcome information is provided.  
    • Systematic variation or effect? Not discussed.  

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Mentioned? The paper states that punishment choices are made anonymously. There is also random selection of the “punisher” whose punishing action takes effect, but the punisher’s identity is not revealed.  
    • Systematic variation or effect? Not discussed.  

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Mentioned? No. Rewards do not feature in the experiment at all.  
    • Systematic variation or effect? Not discussed.  

────────────────────────────────────────
FOUR-PART SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • No. The paper does not use group efficiency. It focuses on:  
        – Cooperation rate (“cooperation behavior”)  
        – Punishment amounts/types (second-party punishment vs. third-party punishment)  
     These are distinct from efficiency. The paper never reports “actual total payoff divided by maximum possible payoff.”  

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
       1. Number of players (fixed at 3)  
       2. Number of rounds (fixed at 12)  
       7. Punishment cost to punisher (1 token)  
       8. Punishment magnitude (3 tokens lost by punishee per 1 token spent)  
   • Not mentioned or not applicable: All others (3, 4, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15) are either absent or not varied.  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • None. The paper does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters listed. The only systematic manipulation they undertake is transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) over different regions of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex; the paper never manipulates number of players, cost of punishment, or any other of the 15 parameters.  

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper provides no direct information or analysis on efficiency (group payoff) or on systematically varying these parameters. Article Title: Inherited Institutions: Cooperation in the Light of Democratic Legitimacy
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS; SOCIAL PREFERENCES; FIELD EXPERIMENT; TAX EVASION; BEHAVIOR; ORGANIZATION; OBLIGATIONS; PUNISHMENT; SANCTIONS; AUTHORITY
Abstract: We experimentally investigate whether the procedural history of a sanctioning institution affects cooperation in a social dilemma. Subjects inherit the institutional setting from a previous generation of subjects who either decided on the implementation of the institution democratically by majority vote or were exogenously assigned a setting. In order to isolate the impact of the voting procedure, no information about the cooperation history is provided. In line with existing empirical evidence, we observe that in the starting generation cooperation is higher (lower) with a democratically chosen (rejected) institution, as compared to the corresponding, randomly imposed setting. In the second generation, we find no positive effect of the democratic procedural history on cooperation when the institution is implemented. Yet, the vote-based rejection of the institution leads to (marginally) less cooperation in the second generation.

As per your instructions, all statements refer strictly to the content of the paper itself; nothing is inferred from outside material.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players
• What the paper does:  
  – The study fixes groups of three players (p. 6).  
  – There is no systematic variation of the number of players.  
  – The paper does not discuss how changing the number of players would affect the punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency (or on any other outcome).

2) Number of rounds
• What the paper does:  
  – Each group plays a one‐shot public good game (p. 6).  
  – There is no systematic variation of the number of rounds.  
  – The paper does not discuss how varying the number of rounds would affect the punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency.

3) Is chat enabled?
• What the paper does:  
  – No communication/chat is mentioned or allowed.  
  – No discussion or variation of this parameter is provided.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
• What the paper does:  
  – Each participant can allocate from 0 to 20 points in integer increments to the public good; it is not all or nothing (pp. 6–7).  
  – No systematic variation of this “all or nothing” parameter is discussed.

5) Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much of the endowment to move back into their hand)?
• What the paper does:  
  – There is no mention of a “default” contribution rule. Players freely choose how much to contribute.  
  – No systematic variation of such a default is discussed.

6) MPCR or related multiplication factor
• What the paper does:  
  – The marginal per capita return (MPCR) is fixed at 0.5 (p. 6).  
  – This factor is not varied, and the paper does not discuss how systematic changes in MPCR would affect punishment or efficiency.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
• What the paper does:  
  – The experiment uses a central (“automatic”) sanctioning institution. There is no peer‐to‐peer punishment, so there is no cost that one player pays to punish another (pp. 6–8).  
  – Thus, the paper does not mention any punishment cost of the kind used in peer‐punishment designs, nor does it vary this parameter.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins/points deducted per punishment unit)
• What the paper does:  
  – If the centralized sanction is in effect and a player contributes less than 20 points, exactly 4 points are automatically deducted from that player’s payoff (p. 6).  
  – This 4‐point deduction is fixed; the paper does not systematically vary it or discuss how varying it would affect punishment effectiveness or efficiency.

9) Whether a reward is enabled
• What the paper does:  
  – There is no mention of any reward mechanism.  
  – The paper does not discuss or vary the possibility of rewards.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
• What the paper does:  
  – Not applicable, since no reward mechanism is included.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per reward unit)
• What the paper does:  
  – Not applicable, since no reward mechanism is included.

12) Is the number of rounds known?
• What the paper does:  
  – The paper describes a one‐shot game for each generation; there is no multi‐round repeated game.  
  – No systematic variation or discussion of hidden vs. known endpoint is provided.

13) Are peer outcomes shown?
• What the paper does:  
  – Second‐generation subjects do not learn the first generation’s actual contributions (p. 8).  
  – No systematic variation of the degree of outcome visibility is discussed.  
  – The paper does not describe any alternative treatments in which peer outcomes are displayed differently.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
• What the paper does:  
  – Punishment is automatic and centralized, so there is no information about “who” is punishing.  
  – There is no discussion about varying the transparency of punishment.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
• What the paper does:  
  – Again, no reward mechanism is present.  
  – The paper does not address any information reveal for rewards.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different from one another?  
• The paper does not explicitly analyze “group efficiency” (actual total payoff / maximum payoff) as its primary dependent variable.  
• The main dependent variables in this study are individual and group “contributions” to the public good (referred to as “cooperation”) and some follow‐up questionnaire measures (e.g., beliefs, satisfaction).  
• “Contributions” and “cooperation” are not the same as “efficiency.” While the authors do discuss payoffs in describing how the sanction operates, their formal analyses center on how much is contributed, not on total payoff relative to the theoretical maximum.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• The paper explicitly mentions and fixes:  
  – Parameter (1) Number of players = 3.  
  – Parameter (2) Number of rounds = 1 (one‐shot).  
  – Parameter (6) MPCR = 0.5.  
  – Parameter (8) Punishment magnitude = 4 points.  
• No other parameters are mentioned in a way that is systematically manipulated or discussed as a key design element.  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• The paper does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters.  
• Therefore, none of them are analyzed in the paper specifically with regard to how their variation would affect the punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency (nor on the paper’s main outcome of contributions).  

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
• The paper does not provide direct discussion or data on changing these parameters. It also does not present any treatment specifically designed to explore variations in group size, number of rounds, magnitude/cost of punishment, the presence of rewards, or information conditions.  
• Consequently, based on this paper alone, one cannot reliably predict how systematically altering any of the 15 parameters (or their interactions) would affect punishment’s impact on efficiency. The paper’s findings concern whether the sanctioning rule was adopted or rejected endogenously by vote (vs. exogenously) and how that history alone influenced cooperation in the next generation.

Abstract: The question of ethical conduct is key for professionals, such as lawyers, doctors, or experts of different kinds. We run a laboratory experiment aimed at investigating whether acting within a profession leads to more (or less) ethical, prosocial behaviour compared to acting outside of it. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of whether (and how) the paper discusses each of the 15 listed factors and whether the authors make (or report) any prediction about systematically varying these factors on the “punishment treatment effect.” Throughout, please note that the paper often focuses on cooperation rates, contributions, or payoffs, and only occasionally uses or reports something akin to “efficiency.” When mentioning effects on “payoffs,” the paper sometimes discusses outcomes that are closely related to efficiency but not always labeled as such.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes, occasionally. The authors give examples of experiments in which groups of four play repeated public goods games (e.g., Fehr & Gächter 2000). Some cross‐cultural work examines multiple participant pools of different sizes, but the core setup typically has four players in a group.  
   • Systematically varied or predicted effects on punishment treatment?  
     – No. The paper does not report (or make predictions about) varying the group size as a factor to analyze punishment’s impact on efficiency or payoffs.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The paper discusses 10‐round public goods experiments (e.g., Fehr & Gächter 2000) and also mentions 50‐period experiments (e.g., Gächter et al. 2008).  
   • Systematically varied or predicted effects on punishment treatment?  
     – Yes, in terms of payoff consequences. In shorter horizons (e.g., 10 or fewer rounds), punishment tended to lower net payoffs relative to no‐punishment conditions. By contrast, over 50 rounds, punishment eventually raised cooperation so much that average payoffs (which the paper sometimes treats as a measure of overall welfare) could surpass those in no‐punishment conditions. Numerically, the paper does not provide a specific effect‐size figure for efficiency, but it explicitly reports that with more repetitions (50 rounds) punishment may become payoff‐enhancing.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The paper does not describe any treatment in which participants can chat or communicate at will.  
   • Systematically varied or predicted effects on punishment treatment?  
     – No, not discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The typical design described allows contributions from 0 up to the entire endowment, but there is no mention of a forced all‐or‐nothing contribution format.  
   • Systematically varied or predicted effects on punishment treatment?  
     – No, not discussed.

5. Is the contribution default (do players “move” tokens back, etc.)?
   • Mentioned?  
     – No. The standard public goods framework in this paper involves deciding how many tokens from an initial endowment to put into the public good. There is no mention of a default mechanism reversed to “move tokens back.”  
   • Systematically varied or predicted effects on punishment treatment?  
     – No, not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Mentioned?  
     – Partially. The paper cites the standard linear public goods design in which α > 1 and α/n < 1, but does not give a wide range of different α values.  
   • Systematically varied or predicted effects on punishment treatment?  
     – No. The authors do not report or predict how changing α (or MPCR) systematically alters the punishment treatment effect.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. In Fehr & Gächter‐type designs, each unit of punishment typically costs the punisher 1 MU (money unit). Gürerk et al. (2006) also use the same punishment cost of 1 MU.  
   • Systematically varied or predicted effects on punishment treatment?  
     – No. The paper describes this cost as a fixed design feature, not something they vary across conditions.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from the target per unit of punishment)
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. A common implementation is that each punishment point deducts 3 MUs from the punished player (e.g., Fehr & Gächter 2000). Gürerk et al. (2006) uses a similar ratio (3:1 cost‐to‐damage).  
   • Systematically varied or predicted effects on punishment treatment?  
     – No. The paper treats this ratio as a constant in each design; there is no systematic variation reported.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. Some experiments discuss “positive sanctions” (i.e., rewards) in addition to punishments (e.g., Gürerk et al. 2006). Another example is Rockenbach and Milinski (2006), where indirect reciprocity can act like a reward system by conferring reputational benefits.  
   • Systematically varied or predicted effects on punishment treatment?  
     – The general presence or absence of rewards is a feature of certain designs, but the paper does not present a systematic reward/no‐reward factorial design with explicit effect sizes on punishment treatment. There is no direct quantitative effect reported for “varying reward presence” alone on efficiency.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Mentioned?  
     – Briefly. In Gürerk et al. (2006), each reward token costs the rewarder 1 MU and gives 1 MU to the receiver.  
   • Systematically varied or predicted effects on punishment treatment?  
     – No. There is no systematic variation of that cost in the paper.

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded per unit of reward)
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes, for positive sanctions, it is typically 1 MU awarded.  
   • Systematically varied or predicted effects on punishment treatment?  
     – No. As with punishment magnitude, the paper treats reward magnitude as fixed in each experiment; no systematic variation is reported.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. The paper notes that in some early work (e.g., Yamagishi 1986; Ostrom et al. 1992) subjects may not have known the exact endpoint. In Fehr & Gächter (2000), players know they will interact for 10 periods; in Gächter et al. (2008), they know there are 50.  
   • Systematically varied or predicted effects on punishment treatment?  
     – Not systematically. The paper notes that indefinite or known horizons can matter for cooperation, but does not provide new experimental manipulations across “known vs. unknown” within the same study.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (i.e., do players see others’ contributions and payoffs)?
   • Mentioned?  
     – Yes. In the standard punishment designs, participants see how much each group member contributed before assigning punishment (Fehr & Gächter 2000). In some designs, there is also mention of showing all participants’ final payoffs.  
   • Systematically varied or predicted effects on punishment treatment?  
     – The paper does not systematically vary “degree of feedback” to measure its standalone effect on punishment outcomes. In Rockenbach and Wolff (2010), some rules proposals limited information (e.g., only average contributions), but no direct effect‐size measure on punishment treatment is reported.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the punisher is?
   • Mentioned?  
     – Typically, the punishment mechanism is anonymous; the paper does not discuss conditions in which the punisher’s identity is revealed versus hidden.  
   • Systematically varied or predicted effects on punishment treatment?  
     – No. There is no discussion of systematically changing anonymity of the punisher.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is?
   • Mentioned?  
     – Not discussed in detail; as with punishment, the paper’s treatments generally involve anonymous interactions.  
   • Systematically varied or predicted effects on punishment treatment?  
     – No. The paper does not address this factor.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?

   • The paper primarily reports results in terms of contributions (cooperation rates) and average or total payoffs (sometimes called “net payoffs” or “wealth”) in various conditions. Occasionally, the authors label higher average payoff as higher “efficiency.” So “efficiency” appears in the sense of total group earnings minus costs.  
   • Other dependent variables include: cooperation rate (mean contributions), punishment frequency, payoff over time, whether participants choose or avoid a punishment scheme, and so on. These differ from efficiency in that they measure behavior or short‐run outcomes (like contributions) rather than the ratio of actual total payoff to a maximum possible payoff.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

   • Mentioned:  
     – #1 (Number of players) – only minimally referenced (often 4).  
     – #2 (Number of rounds) – discussed substantially (10 vs. 50).  
     – #6 (MPCR) – mentioned in the standard linear‐public‐good sense, but not varied.  
     – #7 (Punishment cost) – set to 1 MU in most studies.  
     – #8 (Punishment magnitude) – set to 3 MUs deducted from the target.  
     – #9 (Whether a reward is enabled) – yes, in some designs with positive sanctions.  
     – #10 (Reward cost) – commonly 1 MU.  
     – #11 (Reward magnitude) – commonly 1 MU.  
     – #12 (Is the number of rounds known?) – yes, known in many of their designs, but not systematically manipulated.  
     – #13 (Are peer outcomes shown?) – yes, in standard punishment designs.  
   • Not really discussed or varied: #3 (Chat), #4 (All‐or‐nothing contribution), #5 (Contribution default), #14 (Punisher identity revealed), #15 (Rewarder identity revealed).

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?

   • The only parameter that the paper explicitly varies (in a way that yields a clear systematic difference in punishment’s payoff effects) is the Number of Rounds (#2). Specifically, moving from a 10‐round to a 50‐round horizon eventually reverses the previously negative net‐payoff effect of punishment.  
   • None of the other parameters are systematically varied with direct effect‐size comparisons reported.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of this paper, what would they be?

   • The paper strongly suggests that extending the number of rounds (#2) can transform punishment from a payoff‐reducing mechanism into a payoff‐enhancing (and thus more “efficient”) one.  
   • Beyond that, the paper only fixes values for the cost and magnitude of punishment (#7 and #8), the possibility of rewards (#9–#11), or the group size (#1), without systematically varying them or measuring their standalone effect on efficiency. Hence, it offers little direct basis for predicting how those parameters would affect the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency if each were manipulated.  
   • Likewise, factors relating to communication (#3), all‐or‐nothing rules (#4), default mechanisms (#5), or revealing identities (#14, #15) are not addressed, so the paper provides no basis for predictions about their influence on efficiency.  

In short, the clearest takeaway is that increasing the time horizon (number of rounds) can shift punishment’s net effect from detrimental to beneficial, thereby improving group payoffs (and, in turn, efficiency). The paper contains little or no discussion enabling one to make systematic predictions about the other parameters’ effects on overall efficiency in a punishment‐based public goods setting.

Article Title: Combined effects of social pressure from the inside and outside of fishing communities promote cooperation for stock management
Author Keywords: Community-based management; Coupled socioeconomic and bioeconomic dynamics; Evolutionary game theory; Fisheries management; Social pressure
Keywords Plus: RESOURCE; BEHAVIOR; DYNAMICS
Abstract: We analyze a coupled socioeconomic and bioeconomic dynamics model for fisheries management in a local community. In the model, fishermen choose to cooperate with the fisheries management rule or not at each time step, depending on the utilities of each option. The social dynamics is coupled with the dynamics of the stock biomass. Fishermen's utility basically depends on their catch, and the utility function of the noncooperative option is penalized by a psychological punishment, social pressure, which is affected by both the fraction of cooperative players and stock abundance. We classify social pressure into two categories: pressure originating from the inside and from the outside of the community. We develop a utility function with these social pressures and analyze the coupled dynamics. Our results show that all fishermen can end up cooperating with the management rule if both sources of internal and external social pressure have sufficient effect. The results imply that psychological aspects on fishermen can have an important role for successful management of local fisheries.

Authors: Shinya, O; Yusuke, I; Hiroki, T

Article Title: The Condition for Generous Trust
Keywords Plus: TIT-FOR-TAT; EVOLUTION
Abstract: Trust has been considered the cement of a society and is much studied in sociology and other social sciences. Most studies, however, have neglected one important aspect of trust: it involves an act of forgiving and showing tolerance toward another's failure. In this study, we refer to this concept as generous trust and examine the conditions under which generous trust becomes a more viable option when compared to other types of trust. We investigate two settings. First, we introduce two types of uncertainties: uncertainty as to whether trustees have the intention to cooperate, and uncertainty as to whether trustees have enough competence to accomplish the entrusted tasks. Second, we examine the manner in which trust functions in a broader social context, one that involves matching and commitment processes. Since we expect generosity or forgiveness to work differently in the matching and commitment processes, we must differentiate trust strategies into generous trust in the matching process and that in the commitment process. Our analytical strategy is twofold. First, we analyze the modified trust game that incorporates the two types of uncertainties without the matching process. This simplified setting enables us to derive mathematical results using game theory, thereby giving basic insight into the trust mechanism. Second, we investigate socially embedded trust relationships in contexts involving the matching and commitment processes, using agent-based simulation. Results show that uncertainty about partner's intention and competence makes generous trust a viable option. In contrast, too much uncertainty undermines the possibility of generous trust. Furthermore, a strategy that is too generous cannot stand alone. Generosity should be accompanied with moderate punishment. As for socially embedded trust relationships, generosity functions differently in the matching process versus the commitment process. Indeed, these two types of generous trust coexist, and their coexistence enables a society to function well.

PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK  

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Throughout the paper the group size is n.  
   • Systematic variation & effect on a punishment treatment effect? Partially.  
     – Lemma 4.1 shows that the critical inequality for bilateral punishment contains the factor (1-p)^(n-2)/n.  
     – Proposition 4.2 and the surrounding text claim that when bilateral punishment works for some ranking profile it will also work for a Bilateral-Friendship-Form (BFF).  
     – No numerical treatment-effect on “efficiency” is provided; the result is stated as an existence/possibility statement (“can sustain” vs “cannot sustain”).  

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? No. The game is modeled as an infinitely repeated interaction with discounting.  
   • Systematic variation? No.  

3. Chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned? No.  

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule?  
   • Mentioned? No.  

5. Contribution default / withdrawal decision?  
   • Mentioned? No.  

6. MPCR or multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? No. There is no public-goods production technology; payoffs come from bilateral helping (benefit v, cost c).  

7. Punishment cost to impose a unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? Not in the sense of a monetary cost for actively punishing. The only “cost” a punisher bears is the future loss of receiving help from the deviator (grim trigger) but this is not parameterized.  
   • Systematic variation? No.  

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted)  
   • Mentioned? No explicit magnitude parameter exists; the “magnitude” is total exclusion from future help.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned? No.  

10–11. Reward cost / reward magnitude  
   • Mentioned? No.  

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
   • Mentioned? Not in the finite-horizon sense. The game is infinite with commonly known discount factor δ. No systematic finite-horizon comparison is made.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The model assumes perfect monitoring of all actions (Section 2.2).  
   • Systematic variation? No. Monitoring is assumed perfect and never varied.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who punished them?  
   • Mentioned? Yes, implicitly: punishment is executed only by the player who was refused help, so identities are common knowledge in the model.  
   • Systematic variation? No.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who rewarded them?  
   • Mentioned? No rewards are modeled.  


SUMMARY  

A. Dependent variables.  
   – The paper does NOT use group efficiency (total-payoff-divided-by-maximum) as an outcome.  
   – Outcomes studied:  
     1. Whether “full cooperation can be sustained” (binary existence result).  
     2. Minimum discount factor δ required for cooperation (= critical threshold).  
     3. Expected per-period costs and benefits for individual players under full cooperation.  
   These differ from efficiency because they do not measure realized payoffs relative to an upper bound; they measure feasibility or individual cost distribution.  

B. Parameters from the list that are mentioned: 1, 13, 14 (explicit) plus the implicit infinite-horizon analogue of 12. Total = 3 (or 4 if one counts parameter 12 in its “infinite undisclosed horizon” form).  

C. Parameters for which the paper gives any statement about how systematic variation affects a punishment treatment effect: only parameter 1 (group size) through the exponent (n-2) in Lemma 4.1. Even here, the paper does not quantify a treatment “effect” on efficiency, only on the feasibility of sustaining cooperation. No other parameter in the list is systematically varied. Hence: 1 of 15.  

D. Predictions one could make for the public-goods-style punishment-treatment effect on efficiency solely from this paper are extremely limited:  
   – Larger groups (higher n) make bilateral punishment harder because (1-p)^(n-2)/n becomes smaller, so the discount factor needed for cooperation rises; thus efficiency gains from introducing punishment should diminish with group size under bilateral punishment.  
   – Whether players punish individually (bilateral) or collectively (community) crucially changes outcomes; collective punishment is always at least as effective. However, the paper does not map this to any efficiency number.  
   – Balanced interaction structures (Latin squares; more specifically BFFs when n is even) maximize the parameter range in which punishment maintains cooperation. One might therefore predict that introducing punishment in balanced structures yields larger efficiency improvements than in unbalanced ones.  
Beyond these qualitative statements, the paper offers no data, figures, or effect sizes that let us quantify how any of the 15 listed parameters—or their interactions—change the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.

Parameter-by-parameter extraction from the paper (everything in square brackets comes verbatim or is arithmetically derived from formulas / figures in the paper).

────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? YES – always denoted N.  
   • Value(s)? General variable; examples N = 10 in Experiment 2; Figure 5 plots N from 2 up to ≈50.  
   • Systematic-variation predictions? YES.  
     – Tit-for-tat strategy sustains cooperation (and thus allows punishment to work) only if N < 6 [Proposition 3].  
     – For a finite-length punishment strategy the minimum punishing period must satisfy k > (N–1)²/(4N) (or, equivalently, N < 2k + 1 + 2√(k²+k)) [Proposition 3, Figure 5].  
     – Cooperative per-capita utility = c_l²/(4N); non-co-operative per-capita utility = c_l²/(N+1)² (Corollary in §4.1), so the *difference* (i.e., “punishment treatment effect” on pay-off/efficiency) widens as N grows.  These relations are presented algebraically but no single numeric effect size is tabulated.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? YES – the game is analysed as (i) infinitely repeated; (ii) finitely repeated with T stages (§3, §4.3).  
   • Systematic-variation predictions? PARTIAL.  
     – If the horizon is infinite (or unknown) cooperation enforced by punishment can be an equilibrium (Folk theorem ⇒ group optimal utility).  
     – If the horizon is finite *and* known, backward induction implies full defection in the last stage and, by induction, at every stage (Proposition 4).  
     – No quantitative gradient (e.g., marginal change per extra period) is provided; the result is binary: “finite & known” versus “infinite or unknown”.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned? NO.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Mentioned? NO.

5. Contribution default / endowment move-back design?  
   • Mentioned? NO.

6. MPCR, multiplication factor or similar public-goods technology parameter  
   • Mentioned? NO direct analogue.  The model employs a link-capacity parameter (c_l) but the paper never varies it systematically nor relates it to punishment.

7. Cost to impose one unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? NO explicit cost parameter.  “Punishment” is operationalised as other users reducing their own data rate; the cost to the punisher is implicit but never parameterised or varied.

8. Magnitude inflicted per unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? NO explicit parameter.  Again, only indirect, through the choice of flow rates.

9. Presence of a reward option  
   • Mentioned? A reward is *verbally* mentioned (“awarding rational behaviour”) but no formal model or parameter; not varied.

10–11. Cost and magnitude of reward  
   • Mentioned? NO.

12. Is the number of rounds known?  
   • Mentioned? YES.  Section 3.1 and Proposition 4 contrast the case where the end date is known (finite game) with the case where it is not (infinite game).  
   • Systematic-variation predictions? Binary as in Parameter 2: when the end is *known*, punishment cannot prevent final-stage defection and overall efficiency collapses; when *unknown* (infinite-horizon mindset) punishment can sustain the efficient outcome.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Mentioned? NO.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
   • Mentioned? NO.

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
   • Mentioned? NO.

────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
   The paper mainly analyses  
   – Individual utility U_i (a flow-rate/latency based monetary payoff)  
   – System (total) utility or “efficiency” (the authors use the terms “system optimal utility” and “low efficiency of equilibrium solutions”).  
   – Flow rate (x_i) and the auxiliary variable “punishment length” k.  
   Efficiency, contribution rate and flow rate are distinct: efficiency is the total payoff relative to the optimum; flow rate is an action variable; individual utility is a payoff component.

B. How many of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   • Explicitly discussed: 3 parameters (1, 2, 12).  
   • The remaining 12 are absent.

C. For how many parameters does the paper examine their *systematic* effect on the punishment treatment?  
   • Parameter 1 (Number of players): YES – analytic formulas and Figure 5.  
   • Parameter 2/12 (Number of rounds & its being known): YES – finite vs infinite horizon.  
   So 2 parameters receive systematic-variation discussion; none of the other 13 do.

D. Predictions one can make (and limitations)  
   1. Increasing the number of players makes it harder for punishment to sustain cooperation; specifically, tit-for-tat stops working once N ≥ 6, and with a finite-length punishment strategy the minimum punishment length must grow roughly with N² (k > (N–1)²/(4N)).  Hence, holding everything else equal, the positive punishment effect on efficiency attenuates as N grows unless punishment becomes longer or more severe.  
   2. If the horizon is infinite or the end is unknown, punishment can secure the efficient cooperative outcome; if the horizon is finite and known, punishment fails in the last period and, by backward induction, in all periods, so the efficiency gain disappears.  
   3. Beyond these two points, the paper supplies no information about chat, contribution format, marginal return, explicit punishment/reward prices, or information disclosure.  Consequently, no evidence-based predictions can be made about how those parameters or their interactions would change the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

In short, based solely on the paper: only the number of players and the time-horizon parameters have analysed links to the success of punishment in raising efficiency, and even these links are qualitative/threshold-based rather than precise marginal effect sizes.
