Below I go through the 15 requested parameters one‐by‐one.  For each I state (i) whether the paper explicitly mentions the parameter and, if so, what concrete value or assumption is given, and (ii) whether the paper makes any prediction about what would happen to the *punishment-treatment effect* (PTE) – i.e., the change in efficiency that would be caused by adding a punishment option – if the parameter were *systematically varied*.  All wording and numbers come only from the paper “Sticks and carrots: Two incentive mechanisms supporting intra-group cooperation.”  The paper contains one figure (Fig. 1) and no tables; it provides no numerical simulations or experimental estimates.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Number of players  
   (i) Mentioned.  The model *fixes* the group at “three agents” (p. 2).  
   (ii) No systematic variation is explored; hence no prediction about the PTE.

2.  Number of rounds  
   (i) Mentioned.  Interaction is “over an *infinite horizon (or… a finite horizon with *no known termination time*)” (p. 2).  
   (ii) Not varied; no PTE prediction.  Discount factors (δ) are discussed but are *not* one of the 15 parameters in your list.

3.  Chat enabled?  
   (i) Not mentioned.  
   (ii) No prediction.

4.  All-or-nothing contribution rule?  
   (i) Not mentioned; the strategic environment is a prisoners-dilemma, not a linear public-goods game.  
   (ii) No prediction.

5.  Contribution default / endowment retrieval?  
   (i) Not mentioned.  
   (ii) No prediction.

6.  MPCR / multiplication factor  
   (i) Not mentioned.  Payoffs are generic PD payoffs v(∙,∙).  
   (ii) No prediction.

7.  Punishment *cost* per unit  
   (i) Not specified.  “Collective punishment” means reverting to the stage-game Nash equilibrium; no explicit monetary cost parameter is defined.  
   (ii) Not varied; no prediction.

8.  Punishment *magnitude* per unit  
   (i) Same as (7); not specified.  
   (ii) No prediction.

9.  Reward enabled?  
   (i) Yes.  “We posit a *reward structure based on a transfer system*” (Abstract, p. 1).  Transfers τij≥0 are allowed.  
   (ii) The paper shows theoretically (Proposition 1, Lemma 2) that *allowing* transfers can enlarge the parameter region in which cooperation (and hence higher efficiency) can be sustained.  However, the paper does *not* vary the presence/absence of reward in a comparative-statics sense; it merely proves existence.  No numerical effect size on the PTE is provided.

10. Reward cost to grant one unit  
11. Reward magnitude per unit  
   (i) Neither parameter is given an explicit symbol or value; the model assumes transfers are costless to the giver except for the transfer itself.  
   (ii) Not varied; no prediction.

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
   (i) Yes.  The authors assume the horizon is *unknown* (“no known termination time”) or infinite.  
   (ii) Not varied; no prediction for PTE.

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
   (i) The paper says “Choices are *perfectly observable*, and players have perfect recall” (p. 2).  It never states whether players see each other’s *payoffs*, only actions.  
   (ii) Not varied; no prediction.

14. Punisher identity known?  
   (i) Not discussed; punishment is modelled as a *passive* switch to Nash reversion by *all* players rather than costly peer-to-peer targeting.  
   (ii) No prediction.

15. Rewarder identity known?  
   (i) Not discussed.  Transfers are bilateral and therefore trivially identifiable, but this is not analysed.  
   (ii) No prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables used  
   – *Group formation / sustained cooperation*: whether Nash-reversion strategies can support mutual cooperation in all dyads.  
   – *No* explicit measure of *group efficiency* (total or average payoff relative to maximum) is analysed.  Efficiency is only implicit; the proofs are about equilibrium existence, not payoffs.  Therefore “efficiency” in the sense you require is *not* a reported dependent variable.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   1 (number of players), 2 (number of rounds—assumed infinite/unknown), 9 (reward enabled via transfers), 12 (rounds unknown), and, by implication, 13 (actions are observable).  At most 5 of 15.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss the *effect of systematic variation* on the punishment-treatment effect for *any* dependent variable?  
   Strictly speaking, *zero*.  The paper never runs a comparative-statics exercise or presents data varying any of the 15 parameters.  It only proves that *given* certain values, punishment or reward can sustain cooperation.

D.  What predictions about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment-treatment effect on *efficiency* can be made *solely* from this paper?  
   • Introducing a *punishment* option that triggers collective Nash reversion can, in theory, move the group from a non-cooperative Nash outcome to sustained cooperation, thereby *raising* efficiency from its PD level to the cooperative level—*provided* each player has “incentive slack” in at least one relationship and δ is high enough.  
   • Introducing a *reward* (transfer) option can have a similar efficiency-raising effect if the external benefit β enjoyed by the rewarder is large enough to cover the necessary transfers.  
   • The model says nothing about how the magnitude or cost of punishment/reward, group size ≠3, finite known horizons, communication, or information disclosure would quantitatively change that effect.  Hence, for 13 of the 15 parameters, the paper allows little or no prediction.

In short, the paper is a theoretical existence proof rather than a parameter-sensitive analysis.  It offers essentially no empirical or numerical guidance for predicting how the listed parameters, individually or interactively, would modify the punishment treatment’s impact on group efficiency.

      – Snap-shots in Fig. 5 for b = 0.01, 0.05, 0.20.  
      – Heat-maps in Figs 6, 8, 9.  
   • Systematically varied effect? Yes (within punishment condition).  
      – There is an *inverted-U*: an intermediate b maximises cooperation.  Extremely small b cannot sustain punishers; extremely large b over-burdens cooperators.  
      – Again, no efficiency numbers and no direct baseline comparison.

12. Whether the horizon (# of rounds) is common knowledge  
   • Mentioned? No.

13. Whether peer outcomes are displayed  
   • Mentioned? No.

14. Whether the identity of a punisher is revealed  
   • Mentioned? No.

15. Whether the identity of a rewarder is revealed  
   • Mentioned? No.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used  
    – *Group efficiency / total or average payoff*: NOT used.  
    – Primary outcome: proportion (population share) of Cooperators, Punishers and Defectors.  
    – Secondary diagnostics: number of C-C, C-D, … links (Fig. 3) and transition counts between strategies (Fig. 4).  
    These variables are not equivalent to efficiency; high cooperation could coincide with lower (or higher) pay-offs, but the paper never reports that.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are at least mentioned?  
    9 of them: 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11.  Parameters 3, 5, 12, 13, 14, 15 are never discussed.

C. For how many parameters is their *systematic* effect on the punishment treatment effect analysed?  
    Strictly speaking, none of the parameters is analysed in terms of *efficiency-based* treatment effects, because efficiency is never measured.  
    If we loosen the criterion to “systematically varied and linked to any outcome inside the punishment condition”, then 4 parameters (6, 7, 8, 10/11) are varied.  Their effects are presented only for cooperation rates, not for efficiency, and not as differences to the baseline.

D. Predictions one can make (solely from this paper) about how the 15 parameters—and their interactions—would influence the punishment treatment effect on **efficiency**:

    • Because efficiency is unreported, all predictions below are *indirect*—they rely on the usual but untested assumption that more cooperation raises total pay-off when r > 1.  
    • r (MPCR) should increase the treatment effect most strongly when r is *below* the critical threshold (≈3.5) that is required for cooperation in the baseline game; for high r both treatments would already be efficient, so the incremental effect shrinks.  
    • Punishment magnitude (fine) and punishment cost (x) each have a non-linear influence; an intermediate region (fine moderate-to-high, x moderate) is predicted to maximise the efficiency gain.  
    • Reward/bonus b should again be intermediate; if too small, punishers collapse; if too large, cooperators are over-taxed, lowering efficiency.  
    • For the remaining 11 parameters the paper gives no basis for any efficiency prediction.

In short, the article gives rich qualitative (and some quantitative) information about how r, fine, x and b shape *cooperation rates* inside the punishment institution, but it never analyses pay-off efficiency and never varies the other eleven design features. Below I go through the 15 design parameters one-by-one.  For each parameter I state  

(1) whether it is explicitly mentioned in “Asymmetric social norms’’ and, if so, what concrete value or range is given, and  

(2) whether the paper says what will happen to the **punishment treatment effect** (i.e., the change in efficiency produced by adding a punishment option) when the parameter is **systematically varied**.  Whenever the paper contains a quantitative expression I copy it or point to the relevant equation/table/figure.  If the paper is silent, I say so and add nothing.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK‐LIST
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) YES.  The model is built for an economy with N players who are paired each period (“In every period N ≥ 4 players are paired …’’).  N is left as a free integer.  
   (2) NO.  Although the introduction notes that “large groups must be able to publicly monitor defections’’ (p. 2), the paper never contrasts a *punishment treatment* with a *no-punishment treatment*, nor does it derive how changing N would change that treatment effect on efficiency.  No numerical comparative-static result of ∂(punishment effect)/∂N is given.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) INDIRECT.  The game is *infinitely* repeated with discount factor β (Sec. 2).  A finite round horizon is therefore not a parameter in the model.  
   (2) NO.  Nothing is said about varying a finite horizon or about its impact on a punishment treatment.

3. Chat between players  
   (1) NO mention.  
   (2) Not applicable.

4. “All-or-nothing’’ contribution rule  
   (1) NO mention.  
   (2) Not applicable.

5. Contribution default / endowment-return stage  
   (1) NO mention.  
   (2) Not applicable.

6. Marginal Per-Capita Return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   (1) PARTIALLY.  The game is not a standard linear public-goods game, but pay-off parameters c, g, l and productivity α determine the incremental returns from actions C and D (Eq. (1), Fig. 1).  Those play the same structural role as an MPCR.  
   (2) NO systematic treatment-effect result.  The authors derive conditions such as c ≥ αg−l for the cooperative outcome to be globally efficient and give inequalities like “If c/g is sufficiently small then …’’ (p. 6), but never compare efficiency *with* vs. *without* punishment while varying c, g, or α.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   (1) NO explicit punishment-cost parameter exists.  “Punishment’’ in the model is “always play D”, which has no separate monetary cost to the punisher other than foregone cooperative gains that are already captured by c and g.  
   (2) Consequently, no statement on how changing an explicit punishment cost would affect the punishment treatment effect.

8. Punishment magnitude (how much the target loses per unit)  
   (1) NO explicit parameter of this kind.  The loss to the punished player arises endogenously from receiving D instead of C.  
   (2) No comparative-static result.

9. Reward enabled?  
10. Reward cost?  
11. Reward magnitude?  
   (1) These three are never mentioned.  
   (2) No results.

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
   (1) NO.  The horizon is infinite and common knowledge from the outset.  
   (2) No discussion of treatments that vary horizon knowledge.

13. Peer-outcome information (Do players see others’ pay-offs?)  
   (1) PARTIAL.  The public signal is extremely coarse: “At the period’s end players are informed if **everyone chose identically or not**’’ (Sec. 2).  They do **not** observe individual pay-offs.  
   (2) The paper does not vary the precision of that signal, so no treatment-effect prediction is given.

14. Is the identity of the punisher revealed?  
15. Is the identity of the rewarder revealed?  
   (1) Not applicable—the model contains neither a direct punishing action administered by a specific player nor any rewards.  
   (2) No results.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables  
    – The paper’s focal outcomes are (i) equilibrium continuation pay-offs (π*, vk, etc.) and (ii) whether “efficient play’’ can be sustained.  
    – *Group efficiency* as usually defined in public-goods experiments (actual total pay-off divided by the maximum possible total pay-off) is **not** directly reported.  
    – Contribution levels or cooperation rates are also not measured experimentally; they enter only as theoretical equilibrium actions.  Thus all dependent variables in the article are theoretical pay-offs, not experimentally observed efficiencies.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters appear at all?  
    • #1 (Number of players N)  
    • #6 (Return parameters c, g, α that together play the MPCR role)  
    • #13 (Some aggregate peer-outcome information, but only at a minimal yes/no level)  
    Total = 3 of 15.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss **how systematic variation affects the punishment treatment effect**?  
    – None (0/15).  The model studies equilibria that *already include* a punishment norm (contagious defection).  There is no baseline without punishment, so no treatment effect is ever computed, let alone linked to parameter changes.

D.  Predictive content for the 15 parameters, based solely on this paper  
    – Because the paper never contrasts “punishment’’ with “no-punishment’’, it offers virtually no leverage for forecasting a punishment treatment effect on efficiency for any of the 15 parameters or their interactions.  All that can be inferred is that sustaining high pay-offs with punishment requires certain inequalities (e.g., productivity asymmetry must be moderate, players must be patient, c/g must be low).  None of those results provide an estimate—numerical or directional—of how much **additional** efficiency punishment would create relative to a non-punishment baseline.  Therefore, any attempt to predict treatment effects for the listed parameters would have to rely on external evidence, not on this article.

In short, the paper is a purely theoretical analysis of equilibria that already embed a specific punishment norm; it does not contain the experimental or comparative-static material needed to link the 15 public-goods design variables to a punishment treatment effect on efficiency.
reference_APA: Camera, Gabriele & Gioffre, Alessandro (2017). Asymmetric social norms. ECONOMICS LETTERS.

   (2) No prediction about changing the magnitude.

9. Reward enabled?  
   (1) No; only punishment is available.  
   (2) Not discussed.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   (1) Not applicable; no reward option.  
   (2) Not discussed.

12. Is the horizon known?  
   (1) The paper never states explicitly whether subjects knew the game ends after 30 rounds.  
   (2) No analysis of varying horizon knowledge.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   (1) Study 1: No.  Only the punisher sees individual contributions; everybody else sees only own contribution and total group contribution.  
       Study 2 (“full information’’): Yes.  All players see every­one’s contributions.  
   (2) This is the **only parameter that is actually varied** (between Study 1 and Study 2).  
       Effect reported: the qualitative pattern of results is “surprisingly similar’’ (Section 4, Fig. 2, Table 2).  
       There is **no numerical effect on efficiency** (not measured) and no formal test on whether the punishment treatment effect differs between the two information regimes.  The authors simply conclude that the main findings “are qualitatively replicated.’’

   (1) Yes.  There is a designated punisher (“D”) known from the outset.  
   (2) Not varied and no predictions made.

   (1) Not applicable (no reward).  
   (2) Not discussed.

A. Dependent variables actually analysed  
   • Average individual contribution to the public good  
   • Difference between punisher and non-punisher contributions

Below I walk through the 15 pre-specified design parameters one by one and report exactly what the paper says (or does not say) about each of them and, whenever the authors **systematically vary** the parameter, how this affects the *punishment treatment effect* (as captured in the paper’s own dependent variables).  Throughout, the only dependent variables the paper actually reports are (i) the population fraction of the four strategies C, D, CP, DP and (ii) occasional snapshots of spatial patterns.  The paper never reports group efficiency or any aggregate payoff measure.

────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER–BY–PARAMETER CHECK
────────────────────────────────────────

1. NUMBER OF PLAYERS  
   • Mentioned?  Yes, indirectly.  The lattice size is fixed at l = 100 → N = 10,000 sites.  The *effective* number of players is n = ρ·N.  
   • Systematically varied?  Only through population density ρ (0 < ρ ≤ 1).  
   • Effect reported?  Fig. 1 varies ρ (together with dilemma strength r).  At ρ ≈ 0.55–0.65 and r≈0.4 the fraction of pro-social punishers (CP) reaches ~0.55, while at ρ = 1 (no migration possible) CP ≈ 0.  The paper calls this an “optimal population density” for altruistic punishment.  No efficiency data are given.

2. NUMBER OF ROUNDS  
   • Mentioned?  A simulation is run for > 50,000 Monte-Carlo steps, but that number is never varied.  
   • Effect studied?  No.

3. CHAT ENABLED?  
   • Not mentioned and not manipulated.

4. “ALL-OR-NOTHING” CONTRIBUTION MECHANISM  
   • By construction the donor-recipient Prisoner’s Dilemma has a binary choice (C vs. D), i.e. an all-or-nothing action.  The paper never varies this feature.

5. CONTRIBUTION DEFAULT (ENDOWMENT RETURN)  
   • Not applicable / not discussed.

6. MPCR OR MULTIPLICATION FACTOR (PUBLIC-GOOD RETURN)  
   • Closest analogue is the “dilemma strength” r = c/(b-1).  
   • Systematically varied?  Yes (0 ≤ r ≤ 0.5).  
   • Reported effect: Higher r lowers the stationary share of CP.  In Fig. 1 (with ρ fixed at 0.6) CP ≈ 0.8 at r = 0.2 but ≈ 0 at r ≳ 0.46.  Again, no efficiency numbers are given.

7. PUNISHMENT COST γ  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Baseline γ = 0.1; in Fig. 5 γ is varied up to ≈0.6 while keeping β/γ = 0.9.  
   • Effect reported: When individuals can move (ρ = 0.6) and r = 0.42, increasing γ (and therefore β proportionally) lets CP re-emerge (CP fraction rises from ~0 to ~0.5 at γ ≈ 0.5).  Without migration (ρ = 1) the same γ range keeps CP ≈ 0.  
   • No payoff/efficiency outcomes are shown.

8. PUNISHMENT MAGNITUDE β  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Fixed γ = 0.1; β varied in Fig. 4 from 0 to 0.3.  
   • Effect reported:  
        – r = 0.2: CP rises monotonically with β; at β = 0 CP ≈ 0.1, at β = 0.3 CP ≈ 0.85 (mobile population).  
        – r = 0.42: CP virtually absent for β < 0.18; jumps to ~0.55 at β ≳ 0.24 (mobile population).  
     Again, no efficiency data.

9. IS A REWARD OPTION ENABLED?  
   • No reward mechanism is present or discussed.

10. REWARD COST  
11. REWARD MAGNITUDE  
   • Not applicable.

12. ARE THE NUMBER OF ROUNDS KNOWN?  
13. ARE PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN?  
14. IS THE PUNISHER IDENTIFIED?  
15. IS THE REWARDER IDENTIFIED?  
   • None of these informational parameters are mentioned or manipulated.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────
A. Dependent variables actually used  
   • The paper never reports “group efficiency”, total payoff, or average payoff.  
   • Reported variables are the steady-state fractions of the four strategies (C, D, CP, DP) and spatial snapshots.  These are conceptually different from efficiency because they contain no direct payoff information.

B. How many of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   5 parameters:  
   (1) effective group size via ρ; (4) binary action; (6) dilemma strength r; (7) punishment cost γ; (8) punishment magnitude β.

C. For how many parameters is *systematic variation* linked to a punishment effect?  
   4 parameters: ρ (as a proxy for #players), r, γ, β.  In each case the paper shows how the stationary share of pro-social punishers changes, but gives no figures for payoff efficiency.

D. What predictions about the punishment-efficiency treatment effect can be made *solely* from this paper?  
   • Because the paper never measures efficiency, only indirect qualitative guesses are possible.  If one equates a higher CP fraction with higher expected group payoff, then:  
        – Moderate population densities (roughly 0.55–0.65 of lattice occupancy) should maximize the efficiency gain from introducing punishment; very sparse or completely full lattices should yield smaller or no gains.  
        – A weaker dilemma (smaller r) should increase the efficiency gain; at r ≳ 0.46 punishment ceases to sustain cooperation, so the efficiency effect would be zero or negative.  
        – Higher punishment magnitude β (with low cost) should increase the efficiency gain up to a threshold beyond which CP saturates.  
        – When β/γ is held below 1, simply raising both β and γ together (bigger absolute punishments) can still recover the efficiency gain in mobile populations.  
   • For the remaining 11 parameters the paper gives no information, so no prediction can be made.

In short, the article speaks only to four of the fifteen design parameters, reports outcomes in terms of strategy frequencies—not efficiency—and therefore allows only very limited, indirect predictions about how those parameters would affect the *efficiency* impact of introducing punishment in a public-good setting.
reference_APA: Guo, Tian, He, Zhixue & Shi, Lei (2023). Self-organization in mobile populations promotes the evolution of altruistic punishment. PHYSICA A-STATISTICAL MECHANICS AND ITS APPLICATIONS.

Authors: Philippsen, A; Mieth, L; Buchner, A; Bell, R
Author Full Names: Philippsen, Ana; Mieth, Laura; Buchner, Axel; Bell, Raoul
Article Title: Time pressure and deliberation affect moral punishment
Author Keywords: Cooperation; Punishment; Cognitive resources; Deliberation; Multinomial processing tree model
Keywords Plus: SOCIAL NORMS; COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; HONESTY; MODEL; RECIPROCITY; PREFERENCE; RESPONSES; DILEMMAS; BEHAVIOR
Abstract: The deliberate-morality account implies that moral punishment should be decreased with time pressure and increased with deliberation while the intuitive-morality account predicts the opposite. In three experiments, moral punishment was examined in a simultaneous one-shot Prisoner's Dilemma game with a costly punishment option. The players cooperated or defected and then decided whether or not to punish their partners. In Experiment 1, the punishment decisions were made without or with time pressure. In Experiment 2, the punishment decisions were immediate or delayed by pauses in which participants deliberated their decisions. In Experiment 3, participants were asked to deliberate self-interest or fairness before deciding whether to punish their partners. Different types of punishment were distinguished using the cooperation-and-punishment model. In Experiment 1, time pressure decreased moral punishment. In Experiment 2, deliberation increased moral punishment. So far, the evidence supports the deliberate-morality account. Experiment 3 demonstrates that the effect of deliberation depends on what is deliberated. When participants deliberated self-interest rather than fairness, moral punishment was decreased. The results suggest that unguided deliberation increases moral punishment, but the effects of deliberation are modulated by the type of deliberation that takes place. These results strengthen a process-based account of punishment which offers a more nuanced understanding of the context-specific effect of deliberation on moral punishment than the deliberate-morality account.

Below I go through the 15 parameters one-by-one, quoting only what is actually in the Philippsen et al. paper.  For every parameter I state  

(1) whether the paper mentions or fixes the parameter (and its value, if given), and  

(2) whether the paper says anything about what would happen to the *punishment-treatment effect* – i.e., the difference between No-Punishment and Punishment conditions – if that parameter were *systematically varied*.  Where numerical effect sizes can be read directly from the paper I cite them; otherwise I say “none reported.”  

Because the paper never compares a No-Punishment to a Punishment condition, it never reports a “punishment-treatment effect” on **efficiency** (or on any other outcome).  Consequently, for every parameter the answer to part (2) below will be “No discussion / No estimate.”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1. Number of players  
   (1) Yes – always exactly 2 players (a dyad).  
   (2) No discussion of varying the group size.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Yes – each participant plays 20 one-shot rounds with 20 different programmed partners.  
   (2) No discussion of varying the number of rounds.

3. Chat enabled?  
   (1) Not mentioned; there is no chat.  
   (2) No discussion.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule?  
   (1) Not applicable; game is a Prisoner’s Dilemma, not a public-goods contribution.  
   (2) No discussion.

5. Contribution default / withdrawal frame?  
   (1) Not applicable.  
   (2) No discussion.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   (1) Not applicable to a Prisoner’s Dilemma; pay-off matrix is shown but the paper never labels any MPCR-like parameter.  
   (2) No discussion.

7. Punishment cost (to the punisher)  
   (1) Yes – Experiment 1: participant can pay 1–5 cents to punish; Experiments 2–3: 1–3 points (1 point = 1 cent).  The cost was *fixed* inside each experiment; it was not manipulated.  
   (2) No systematic variation, no effect size.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss inflicted per unit cost)  
   (1) Yes – a cost–benefit ratio of 1 : 10 is used (e.g., pay 3 cents to deduct 30 cents).  Again, fixed, not manipulated.  
   (2) No discussion of varying it.

9. Reward enabled?  
   (1) No – there is no positive reward option.  
   (2) No discussion.

10. Reward cost  
   (1) Not applicable.  
   (2) No discussion.

11. Reward magnitude  
   (1) Not applicable.  
   (2) No discussion.

12. Is the number of rounds common knowledge?  
   (1) The paper does not state whether subjects were told there would be 20 rounds.  
   (2) No discussion of varying this information.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   (1) Yes – after every PD choice subjects see both their own and the partner’s pay-offs (Fig. 3 and text).  
   (2) No systematic variation, no effect size.

14. Is punisher identity revealed?  
   (1) The design is bilateral; a punished partner necessarily knows who punished them, but the paper never manipulates anonymity.  
   (2) No discussion of varying anonymity.

15. Is rewarder identity revealed?  
   (1) Not applicable (no reward option).  
   (2) No discussion.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used in the paper  
   • No measure of **group efficiency** (total or average pay-off / maximum possible) is analysed.  
   • The only DV’s are the five latent probabilities from the multinomial “cooperation-and-punishment” model:  
     – C: probability to cooperate  
     – P_Moral, P_Hypocritical, P_Antisocial: conditional punishment probabilities  
     – b: unspecific punishment bias  
   These are conceptually different from efficiency because they refer to behavioural probabilities, not to monetary outcomes.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   6 out of 15: #1, #2, #7, #8, #13, #14.  The remaining 9 parameters are never mentioned.

C. Which parameters does the paper *systematically vary* and link to a punishment-treatment effect?  
   Zero.  The study manipulates *time pressure vs. deliberation* (a cognitive-process variable) and the *content* of deliberation (fairness vs. self-interest).  None of the 15 structural parameters above is varied.

D. What predictions about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency can be made from this paper alone?  
   Very little.  Since (i) efficiency is not analysed at all, (ii) no parameter on the list is experimentally manipulated, and (iii) no statistical relationship is reported between any of the 15 parameters and pay-offs, the paper provides essentially no basis for predicting how changing any of the 15 parameters—individually or in interaction—would alter the impact of introducing punishment on group efficiency.  Any such prediction would require information that is not contained in the article.
reference_APA: Philippsen, Ana, Mieth, Laura, Buchner, Axel & Bell, Raoul (2024). Time pressure and deliberation affect moral punishment. SCIENTIFIC REPORTS.

Keywords Plus: SANCTIONS; MONETARY; GAMES
Abstract: This study conducts laboratory experiments to explore the effect of punishment on public good contributions when individuals have heterogeneous marginal per capita returns on the public good under different punishment networks. We also find that the complete punishment network leads to lower punishment severity and efficiency than the incomplete punishment networks.

Below, each of the 15 design parameters is considered in turn.

For every parameter we state  
• Whether the paper gives its value and, if so, what that value is.  
• Whether the paper makes any prediction (ex-ante hypothesis) or reports any ex-post result on how *changing* that parameter would influence the *punishment-treatment effect* — i.e., the difference in outcomes between a game **with** and **without** punishment.  
Because the experiment contains only punishment conditions (no baseline without punishment) and none of the 15 parameters is experimentally manipulated across treatments, the paper offers essentially no leverage on how systematic variation in those parameters would alter the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────

1. NUMBER OF PLAYERS  
• Stated: 4 players per group (Sec. 2.1).  
• No prediction or result about what would happen with a different group size.

2. NUMBER OF ROUNDS  
• Stated: 15 periods (Sec. 2.2).  
• Not varied; no prediction for other round lengths.

3. CHAT ENABLED?  
• Not mentioned; presumably no chat.  
• No discussion of varying chat.

4. “ALL-OR-NOTHING” CONTRIBUTION?  
• Contributions are continuous between 0 and 20 tokens (Sec. 2.1).  
• No discussion of forcing all-or-nothing contributions.

5. CONTRIBUTION DEFAULT / “OPT-OUT” FRAME?  
• Not used; no discussion.

6. MPCR (MARGINAL PER-CAPITA RETURN)  
• Stated: two MPCR types, 0.3 (“low”) and 0.7 (“high”), with two of each per group (Sec. 2.1).  
• Results: High-MPCR subjects contribute more than low-MPCR subjects; Tobit coefficients for “High MPCR” range from +3.21 to +6.39 tokens (Table 3). High-MPCR subjects also receive more punishment (Table 6).  
• However, MPCR itself is not manipulated between treatments, so the paper offers no estimate of how changing *group-average* MPCR or its distribution would alter the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency.

7. COST TO IMPOSE ONE UNIT OF PUNISHMENT  
• Fixed at 1 token to punisher (Sec. 2.1).  
• Not varied; no prediction about other costs.

8. MAGNITUDE PER UNIT OF PUNISHMENT  
• Fixed at –3 tokens to the target (Sec. 2.1).  
• Not varied; no prediction about other magnitudes.

9. REWARD OPTION PRESENT?  
• No reward stage exists.  
• No discussion of adding rewards.

10–11. COST AND MAGNITUDE OF REWARD  
• Not applicable.

12. ARE NUMBER OF ROUNDS COMMON KNOWLEDGE?  
• The paper does not say whether subjects were told the game lasts 15 rounds.  
• No discussion of varying this information.

13. ARE PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN?  
• Subjects observe contributions of *connected* members and, after punishment, the *number* of punishments they sent and received (Sec. 2.1). They never see anyone’s total pay-off.  
• Information structure is identical in all treatments; no prediction about changing it.

14. IS THE PUNISHER IDENTIFIED TO THE TARGET?  
• No. Targets only learn the *number* of punishments received, not who punished them (Sec. 2.1).  
• This anonymity is not varied; no prediction about revealing identities.

15. IS THE REWARDER IDENTIFIED?  
• Not applicable (no rewards).

────────────────────────────────────────
Summary requested by the user
────────────────────────────────────────
A.  Dependent variables actually analysed  
   – Group contribution  
   – Individual contribution  
   – Number of punishments received  
   – Punishment severity (punishments received ÷ potential punishers)  
   – Probability of being punished  
   – Group efficiency (group payoff / 160-token maximum)  
   These measures are conceptually distinct: contribution looks only at tokens invested; efficiency subtracts punishment costs and therefore can fall even when contributions rise.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters appear in the paper?  
   Parameters 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 13 and 14 (8 in total) are explicitly mentioned with concrete values.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss how *systematically varying* them would change the punishment-treatment effect?  
   Zero.  No parameter is experimentally manipulated among the 15 listed items, and no ex-ante hypothesis or ex-post analysis compares a punishment condition to a *no-punishment* benchmark.  MPCR (parameter 6) is correlated with behaviour, but its level is not varied between treatments, so the paper gives no estimate of its effect on the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

D.  Predictions one could make about the 15 parameters and their interactions, using only this paper  
   – Higher individual MPCR is associated with higher contribution and more punishment received; extrapolating, increasing the *share* of high-MPCR players in a group might raise contributions but could also increase punishment costs, making the net effect on efficiency ambiguous.  
   – Nothing in the paper informs how changing group size, round length, punishment cost/magnitude, information conditions, chat, rewards, etc. would influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency.  
   – Consequently, except for the tentative statement above on MPCR composition, the paper provides little basis for predicting how any of the 15 parameters—or their interactions—would alter the efficiency impact of adding punishment to a public-goods game.

In short, the study is valuable for showing that *network structure* matters when punishment is already available, but it does not vary or analyse any of the 15 parameters listed by the user, so it offers virtually no guidance about how those parameters affect the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency.
reference_APA: Peng, Hui-Chun & Fan, Yi-Hsuan (2023). Incomplete punishment networks, heterogeneity, and cooperation in public good experiments. JOURNAL OF BEHAVIORAL AND EXPERIMENTAL ECONOMICS.

Authors: Dewey, G; Ando, H; Ikesu, R; Brewer, TF; Goto, R; Nishi, A
Author Full Names: Dewey, George; Ando, Hiroyasu; Ikesu, Ryo; Brewer, Timothy F.; Goto, Ryunosuke; Nishi, Akihiro
Article Title: Punishment is slower than cooperation or defection in online network games
Author Keywords: Evolution of cooperation; Punishment; Decision time; Time pressure
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; DECISION TIME; EVOLUTION; INEQUALITY; RETALIATION; CONFLICT; BEHAVIOR
Abstract: Punishment serves as a balancing force that dissuades people from acting selfishly, which complements cooperation as an essential characteristic for the prosperity of human societies. Past studies using economic games with two options (cooperation and defection) reported that cooperation decisions are generally faster than defection decisions and that time pressure possibly induces human players to be more intuitive and thus cooperative. However, it is unclear where punishment decisions sit on this time spectrum. Therefore, we recruited human players and implemented two series of online network games with cooperation, defection, and punishment options. First, we find that punishment decisions are slower than cooperation or defection decisions across both game series. Second, we find that imposing experimental time pressure on in-game decisions neither reduces nor increases the frequency of punishment decisions, suggesting that time pressure may not directly interact with the mechanisms that drive players to choose to punish.

Below each parameter I list exactly what the paper says (if anything) and whether the authors vary the parameter in order to estimate a ​punishment-treatment effect – i.e., the change in any outcome that can be attributed to allowing punishment.  Whenever the paper reports an effect size I reproduce it; when it does not, I say so.  “Efficiency” (total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff) is never analysed, so no numerical efficiency results exist.

────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER EXTRACTION
────────────────────────────────────────

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Each session contained a mean of 14.9 players in Experiment 1 (range 9–25) and 14.8 in Experiment 2 (range 8–20).  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  The size variation is incidental; no analyses relate it to any outcome, so no effect size is reported.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  All sessions lasted 15 rounds (plus two practice rounds).  
   • Systematically varied?  No.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned?  No.  The paper never states that subjects could chat; all evidence points to “no chat.”  
   • Systematically varied?  Not applicable.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  A “cooperate” choice is binary: each cooperator “pays 50 points per connected player” or pays nothing (defect) or pays 50 to punish.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.

5. Contribution default (reversal decision)?  
   • Mentioned?  No.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  Implicitly.  A cooperator pays 50 and each neighbour receives 100.  That produces a cost-benefit ratio of 0.5 for the actor, but the MPCR is never labelled and is not manipulated.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.

7. Punishment cost per unit  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  The punisher “pays 50 points per connected player.”  
   • Systematically varied?  No.

8. Punishment magnitude per unit  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  “All connected players lose 100 points.”  
   • Systematically varied?  No.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – indirectly.  The authors state “No institutional/central punishment or sanctioning occurred,” and nothing in the design allows a positive reward option, so reward = “disabled.”  
   • Systematically varied?  Not applicable.

10 & 11. Reward cost / reward magnitude  
   • Mentioned?  No, because no reward option exists.

12. Are the number of rounds common knowledge?  
   • Mentioned?  Not stated explicitly, but players are told about “practice rounds” followed by the 15-round game, implying common knowledge.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  After every round subjects saw “the decisions made by other connected players … and an updated tally of in-game points.”  In Experiment 1 this “wealth visibility” (show vs hide) was randomly assigned across sessions.  
   • Systematically varied?  Yes – wealth visibility ON vs OFF in Exp 1.  
   • Reported effect on punishment-treatment outcomes?  The authors state that “there was no effect of wealth visibility on the frequency of punishment or decision times,” and therefore they kept wealth visible in Exp 2.  No numerical coefficients are printed in the main text; the only information is a qualitative “no effect.”

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Because every player’s choice (C, D, or P) is displayed, who punished is observable.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
   • Mentioned?  Not applicable—no reward option exists.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────
A.  Dependent variables used  
    • Efficiency or total payoff?  Not used.  
    • Main DVs:  
        – Decision time (response time).  
        – Frequency/proportion of choosing Punish, Cooperate or Defect.  
      These differ from efficiency because they measure speed or choice shares, not payoffs obtained relative to the cooperative optimum.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters appear in the paper?  
    Parameters 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 13, 14 (and arguably 12) are described.  That is 8 (or 9) of 15.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of systematic variation on any punishment-treatment outcome?  
    Only 1 parameter (peer-outcome visibility, #13).  The authors varied it and report “no detectable effect” on punishment frequency or decision time.  No parameter is analysed with respect to efficiency.

D.  Predicting how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency, using only this paper  
    • The paper provides almost no guidance, because efficiency was never measured and only one parameter was experimentally manipulated, yielding a null result.  
    • Therefore, based solely on the text:  
        – Altering wealth visibility (#13) is predicted to leave the punishment treatment effect on efficiency unchanged (null finding).  
        – For the remaining 14 parameters the paper makes no prediction; any effect on efficiency remains unknown.

In short, the article focuses on decision speed, not group efficiency, and it does not experimentally manipulate the standard public-goods design variables (MPCR, punishment cost, group size, etc.).  Consequently, it offers virtually no basis for forecasting how those parameters—or their interactions—would moderate the efficiency impact of adding a punishment option.

Authors: Deutchman, P; Aellen, M; Bogese, M; Bshary, R; Drayton, L; Gil, D; Martin, J; Pretot, L; Raihani, N; Santos, LR; Mcauliffe, K

Abstract: Across human and animal societies, punishment is used as a means of responding to cheating and modifying the behaviour of others. A growing body of work shows that human punishment decisions involve representing both the outcomes of transgressions as well as whether a transgressor chose to do wrong. Understanding whether and to what extent animals inte-grate information about choice into their punishment decisions can shed light on the selective pressures and cognitive mechanisms that shape punishment. In study 1, we investigate whether punishment in adult male cleaners is influenced by whether females had a choice to cheat. In study 2, we ask the same question of human adults, using a novel task inspired by the cooperative interactions between pairs of cleaners and their client fish. Our results support previous work finding that punishment of cheating in humans is sensitive to whether trans-gressors chose to cheat: they punished more when the alternative option was cooperation. However, we did not find a similar sensitivity to alternative options in cleaners. Our results provide a direct com-parison of the role of alternative options in punishment decisions in humans and a distantly related cooperative species. Below we walk through the 15 parameters one‐by‐one, sticking strictly to what is in the paper.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  
     – Cleaner-fish study: effectively 2 players (male and female; the “client” is a plate, not a strategist).  
     – Human study: 3 players (Player 1 = punisher, Player 2 = potential cheat, Player 3 = client).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Any prediction or effect size? None.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? Yes (fish: 8 blocks × 4 trials = 32 trials; humans: one incentivised decision plus hypotheticals).  
   • Varied? No.  
   • Predictions? None.

3. Is chat enabled?  
   • Not mentioned; there is no communication channel in either study.  
   • No variation; no predictions.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
   • Not applicable / not mentioned.  
   • No predictions.

5. Contribution default (withdrawal from a public fund)  
   • Not applicable / not mentioned.  
   • No predictions.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Not applicable; there is no public‐goods stage.  
   • No predictions.

7. Punishment cost per unit  
   • Mentioned? Yes, for humans: each \$0.01 spent reduces punisher’s endowment by \$0.01 (and cuts \$0.05 from the target).  
   • Varied? No (fixed ratio 1:5).  
   • Predictions? None.

8. Punishment magnitude per unit  
   • Mentioned? Yes: each \$0.01 removes \$0.05 from Player 2 (humans).  
   • Varied? No.  
   • Predictions? None.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Not mentioned / not available.  
   • No predictions.

10. Reward cost  
    • Not mentioned.  
    • No predictions.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Not mentioned.  
    • No predictions.

12. Is the horizon (number of rounds) known?  
    • Not discussed.  
    • No variation; no predictions.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Yes, descriptively:  
      – Fish: males watch females eat items.  
      – Humans: Player 1 is told how much Players 2 and 3 would earn.  
    • Not experimentally manipulated, so no predictions.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
    • Fish: always obvious (a chase).  
    • Humans: not stated; identity revelation not manipulated.  
    • No predictions.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
    • No rewards in either study.  
    • No predictions.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
   • Group efficiency / total payoff was NOT measured.  
   • Fish: binary “male punished (0/1)”.  
   • Humans: amount spent on punishment (0–10 ¢), plus moral “wrongness” and “responsibility” ratings (1–7).  
   These variables differ from efficiency because they track individual sanction behaviour or moral judgement, not total group earnings relative to a cooperative benchmark.

B. Which of the 15 parameters appear at all?  
   5 parameters: (1) number of players, (2) number of rounds (descriptive), (7) punishment cost, (8) punishment magnitude, (13) peer-outcome visibility.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss effects of systematic variation on the punishment treatment effect (for any DV)?  
   0 out of 15. None of the listed parameters were experimentally varied to test causal effects; therefore no effect sizes are reported.

D. What predictions about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency can be made from this paper alone?  
   The paper supplies almost no information that can be generalised to efficiency in a public-goods context. It only tells us that, holding all 15 parameters constant, humans punish more when the target “could have” cooperated, whereas cleaner fish do not. Because none of the parameters above were varied, we cannot credibly predict how changing any of them would alter the efficiency impact of punishment. Any further prediction would necessarily draw on literature outside this paper, which is not allowed.

Therefore, based solely on this paper, we can make little to no prediction about how any of the 15 parameters (individually or interactively) influence the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.

Author Full Names: Kido, Yuta; Takezawa, Masanori
Article Title: Coevolution of norm psychology and cooperation through exapted conformity
Author Keywords: Evolution; cooperation; social norm; norm psychology; cultural group selection
Keywords Plus: CULTURAL-EVOLUTION; NORMATIVE CONDUCT; FOCUS THEORY; PUNISHMENT; PEOPLE; TRANSMISSION; ENFORCEMENT; EMERGENCE; BEHAVIOR
Abstract: People willingly follow norms and values, often incurring material costs. This behaviour supposedly stems from evolved norm psychology, contributing to large-scale cooperation among humans. It has been argued that cooperation is influenced by two types of norms: injunctive and descriptive. This study theoretically explores the socialisation of humans under these norms. Our agent-based model simulates scenarios where diverse agents with heterogeneous norm psychologies engage in collective action to maximise their utility functions that capture three motives: gaining material payoff, following injunctive and descriptive norms. Multilevel selective pressure drives the evolution of norm psychology that affects the utility function. Further, we develop a model with exapted conformity, assuming selective advantage for descriptive norm psychology. We show that norm psychology can evolve via cultural group selection. We then identify two normative conditions that favour the evolution of norm psychology, and therefore cooperation: injunctive norms promoting punitive behaviour and descriptive norms. Furthermore, we delineate different characteristics of cooperative societies under these two conditions and explore the potential for a macro transition between them. Together, our results validate the emergence of large-scale cooperative societies through social norms and suggest complementary roles that conformity and punishment play in human prosociality.

Below I go through the 15 experiment-design parameters one by one, quoting only what is stated in the paper “Coevolution of norm psychology and cooperation through exapted conformity”.

----------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
----------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players (group size)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  They fix n = 16 for all simulations (Table 1 and throughout the text).  
   • Systematic variation / predicted effect?  No.  n is never varied, and no claim is made about how changing n would alter any punishment treatment effect (or any other outcome).  

2. Number of rounds the public–goods game is played  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Each generation agents “participate in collective actions for over 40 rounds”; later they say “cumulative number of cooperators across 40 rounds”.  
   • Systematic variation / predicted effect?  No.  The number of rounds is held constant; no prediction is offered about what would happen if it changed.  

3. Chat (communication) enabled?  
   • Mentioned?  Not mentioned anywhere.  
   • Systematic variation / predicted effect?  None.  

4. Contribution “all-or-nothing” versus continuous choice  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Cooperation (x) is explicitly binary: “Both are binary strategies” (Section 2.1).  
   • Systematic variation / predicted effect?  No.  The authors never compare binary to continuous contributions.  

5. Contribution default (endowment initially in the public fund)?  
   • Mentioned?  Not mentioned.  

6. Marginal Per Capita Return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  The payoff structure is referred to only in general terms; the actual MPCR value is relegated to the Supplementary Information, which is not reproduced here. No numerical parameter is given in the paper text provided.  
   • Systematic variation / predicted effect?  None in the text supplied.  

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   • Mentioned?  Indirectly.  They say punishment “incur[s] a cost for the actor”, but no symbol or numeric value is given in the excerpt.  
   • Systematic variation / predicted effect?  None.  The cost is fixed and unreported, and they never vary it.  

8. Punishment magnitude (deduction from the target)  
   • Mentioned?  Same as #7: punishment “harm[s] all defectors”, but the magnitude is not specified in the main text and never varied.  

9. Whether a reward option is available  
   • Mentioned?  No.  The model contains only cooperation and punishment; reward never appears.  

10–11. Reward cost and reward magnitude  
   • Mentioned?  Not mentioned.  

12. Whether the number of rounds is known to players  
   • Mentioned?  Not discussed.  (The model is evolutionary; “knowledge” of round length is not modelled.)  

13. Peer-outcome visibility (do players see others’ pay-offs?)  
   • Mentioned?  Not discussed.  

14. Punisher identity known?  
   • Mentioned?  Not discussed.  

15. Rewarder identity known?  
   • Mentioned?  Not discussed.  

----------------------------------------------------------------
A–D SUMMARY
----------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables used in the paper  
    • The paper never reports “group efficiency” (total realised payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff).  
    • Reported dependent variables:  
      – x : cooperation rate (binary 0/1, averaged).  
      – y : punishment rate (binary 0/1, averaged).  
      – α_i : degree of injunctive-norm psychology.  
      – α_d : degree of descriptive-norm psychology.  
      – Group fitness w_j (sum of cooperators across rounds) and individual fitness w_i (baseline fitness + mean payoff).  
    Efficiency is conceptually different from all of these and is not analysed.  

B.  Which of the 15 parameters appear at all?  
    • Mentioned: 1 (group size =16), 2 (40 rounds), 4 (all-or-nothing contribution).  
    • Possibly implied but with no values: 7 and 8 (punishment cost & magnitude).  
    • Not mentioned: 3, 5, 6, 9-15.  
    → 3 of 15 are clearly mentioned, 2 are only implicit, the remaining 10 are not mentioned.  

C.  Parameters whose *systematic variation* is analysed for their impact on the punishment treatment effect (or any DV)  
    • None of the 15 parameters are systematically varied in the paper.  
    • The only systematic manipulation the authors run is of two *injunctive-norm* parameters (v_x and v_y), which are outside the 15-item list.  
    • Therefore, 0 of 15 parameters have an analysed effect on the punishment treatment effect.  No numerical effect sizes exist for any of them.  

D.  What predictions (if any) can be made, relying only on this paper, about how the 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
    • The paper provides no direct evidence or theorising linking any of the 15 parameters to efficiency-based outcomes, let alone to the incremental effect of adding a punishment option.  
    • At best one could note that the authors’ entire model assumes:  
        – Small fixed groups (16) and many rounds (40).  
        – Binary (“all-or-nothing”) contributions.  
      Since cooperation evolved under those conditions when punishment norms were strong, one might *speculate* that holding those three parameters at those values is compatible with a positive punishment effect on cooperation (and hence perhaps efficiency).  
    • Beyond that, the paper supplies no basis for predicting how changing group size, number of rounds, punishment cost/magnitude, rewards, information conditions, etc. would alter the efficiency gain (or loss) from introducing punishment.  
    • Therefore, any quantitative or even directional prediction about the 15 parameters’ main effects or interactions on efficiency would be conjecture and would violate instruction #1.  The safe conclusion is that the paper does not allow meaningful predictions for these parameters.  

----------------------------------------------------------------
In short, the paper is a theoretical exploration of how different *norm-related* parameters (v_x, v_y, α_i, α_d) shape cooperation and punishment.  None of the usual laboratory design parameters listed in the prompt are analysed, and group efficiency is never used as an outcome measure.

Authors: Wang, XM; Zhu, HJ; Zhao, QY; Wang, YR
Author Full Names: Wang, Xiaoming; Zhu, Hongjin; Zhao, Qinying; Wang, Yaru
Article Title: The influence of social comparison on third-party altruistic behavior
Author Keywords: Social comparison; Anger; Empathy; Third-party punishment; Third-party compensation
Keywords Plus: INDIVIDUAL-DIFFERENCES; PUNISHMENT; JUSTICE; EMPATHY; IMPACT; OTHERS; PREFERENCES; ANONYMITY; MODEL; COOPERATION
Abstract: When faced with unfair events, people can choose to punish the violator (the first party who committed the unfair event) for the purpose of deterrence, or they can choose to compensate the victim (the second party who was harmed in the unfair event) for the purpose of restoration. So, when do people choose to punish, and when do they choose to compensate? Social comparison theory suggests that individuals can clarify their current environmental situation and make corresponding behaviors by comparing themselves with others. Therefore, this research investigated the influence of social comparison on third-party altruistic behavior and its psychological mechanism through three studies using a third-party punishment and compensation paradigm based the dictator game. The results showed that: (1) The direction of social comparison has a crucial influence on the behavioral strategies of third parties. Third parties in the upward comparison are more inclined to punish the violator, while third parties in the downward comparison are more inclined to compensate the victim. (2) Third parties generate higher anger emotions during upward comparison, which leads to a greater tendency to punish the violator, while they generate higher empathy during downward comparison, which leads to a tendency to compensate the victim. (3) Social contexts hardly influence the behavioral strategies of third parties, but it can regulate the cost that third parties pay for punishment or compensation. The research provided a new perspective for exploring third-party altruistic behavior and offered a new explanation and insight into issues of social fairness and justice.

Below, each of the 15 public-goods‐game (PGG) design parameters is checked against the contents of “The influence of social comparison on third-party altruistic behavior.”  
For every parameter I state

• Whether the paper even mentions or fixes that parameter (with the value, if given).  
• Whether the paper systematically varies the parameter and, if so, whether it reports the effect of that variation on any punishment‐related dependent variable. Numerical effect sizes are quoted whenever they can be read directly off the text, tables, or figures.  
• Whether anything in the paper links that parameter to *group efficiency* (total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff).  

Because the study is a third-party dictator-game paradigm (not a PGG) and never computes efficiency, most parameters are simply not addressed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1. Number of players  
   – Mentioned: YES. Each game involves three roles: Dictator (A), Recipient (B), Third party (C). Fixed at 3.  
   – Systematically varied: NO.  
   – Any effect on punishment treatment or efficiency: NO.

2. Number of rounds  
   – Mentioned: YES. Each participant faces three unfair allocations (60/40, 70/30, 80/20 splits).  
   – Systematically varied as an independent variable: NO.  
   – Any link to punishment treatment or efficiency: NO.

3. Is chat enabled?  
   – Mentioned: NO.  
   – No variation, no effects.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution format  
   – Mentioned: NO.

5. Contribution default / endowment back-transfer  
   – Mentioned: NO.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor of the public good  
   – Mentioned: NO (there is no public good in the design).

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   – Mentioned: YES. A third party “spends 1 token” to punish. Fixed ratio 1:3.  
   – Varied: NO.  
   – Effect of varying it: Not studied. Therefore no numbers.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss to target per unit applied)  
   – Mentioned: YES. Each token spent removes 3 tokens from the dictator (ratio 1:3).  
   – Varied: NO.  
   – Effect of varying it: Not studied.

9. Whether a reward option exists  
   – Mentioned: PARTIALLY. A “compensation” option for the victim is available, which functions like a reward (1:3 ratio). Its availability is never toggled on/off.  
   – Varied: NO.  
   – Effects on punishment treatment: Not tested.

10. Reward cost  
    – Mentioned: YES (1 token). Fixed. Not varied.

11. Reward magnitude  
    – Mentioned: YES (each token given raises the victim’s payoff by 3 tokens). Fixed. Not varied.

12. Do players know how many rounds remain?  
    – Mentioned: NO direct statement. Only three one-shot scenarios; knowledge was not manipulated.

13. Are peer outcomes displayed?  
    – Mentioned: YES (the dictator’s proposed split is shown to the third party).  
    – Varied: NO.  
    – Effect of varying: Not studied.

14. Does the punished player know the identity of the punisher?  
    – Closest construct in the paper: “Social context” manipulation (public vs. anonymous).  
      • Public: third party writes student-ID and is told that choice & amount will be posted on the university’s website.  
      • Anonymous: no identifying information is released.  
      • Whether the violator *personally* learns the identity is not clarified, but identifiability to outsiders is definitely varied.  
    – Systematic variation: YES.  
      – Main-effect results (collapsed over comparison direction):  
        ▸ Punishment rate: M_anonymous = .505, M_public = .424 (F (1,281)=8.372, η_p²=.029).  
        ▸ Punishment amount: M_anonymous = 7.724, M_public = 6.297 (F (1,281)=4.850, η_p²=.017).  
      – No efficiency metric is reported.

15. Does a rewarded player know the identity of the rewarder?  
    – Not discussed; the “compensation” option’s identifiability is not mentioned or varied.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Use of “efficiency” as a dependent variable  
   – NO. The paper never reports total group payoff or efficiency.  
   – Reported DVs: punishment rate, compensation rate, punishment amount, compensation amount, anger (self-report), empathy (self-report). These are behavioural or emotional measures, not efficiency.

B. Parameters that are at least mentioned (8/15)  
   1, 2, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13 (with parameter-14 being partially mapped through the “public vs anonymous” manipulation).

C. Parameters whose *systematic* variation is analysed for punishment-related outcomes (1/15)  
   – Parameter 14 analogue (public vs anonymous identifiability).  
     • Anonymous context increases both punishment rate (+0.081 absolute) and punishment amount (+1.427 tokens) relative to public context.  
   – No other parameter is experimentally varied.

D. Predictions about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment-treatment effect on *efficiency*, based **only** on this paper  
   – Because efficiency is never measured, the paper allows almost no direct prediction.  
   – One indirect inference: anonymity (our proxy for parameter 14) raises punishment frequency and magnitude; given the 1-to-3 cost-to-impact ratio, every unit of punishment lowers total payoffs by 4 tokens. Hence anonymity would be expected to *lower* group efficiency relative to a public context.  
   – For all other parameters (1–13, 15) the paper supplies no data or theory that can be converted into efficiency predictions. Any forecast for those factors would require assumptions beyond the article’s content.

In short, the article is almost entirely silent on how standard PGG design features affect the efficiency impact of adding punishment. The only relevant manipulation—public versus anonymous identifiability—shows that more anonymous settings elicit more punishment, which (given fixed costs and magnitudes) would mathematically reduce efficiency. No other parameter is explored.

Abstract: Cooperation is fundamental to human societies, and indirect reciprocity, where individuals cooperate build a positive reputation for future benefits, plays a key role in promoting it. Previous theoretical and experimental studies have explored both the effectiveness and limitations of costly punishment in sustaining cooperation. While empirical observations show that costly punishment by third parties is common, some theoretical models suggest it may not be effective in the context of indirect reciprocity, raising doubts about its potential to enhance cooperation. In this study, we theoretically investigate the conditions under which costly punishment is effective. This extension models a realistic scenario where defectors have a strong incentive to disguise their defection as cooperation. Our analysis reveals that when defection is difficult to detect, norms involving costly punishment can emerge as the most efficient evolutionarily stable strategies. These findings demonstrate that costly punishment can playa crucial role promoting cooperation within indirect reciprocity.

Below I go through the fifteen design parameters one‐by‐one and extract exactly what the paper says about each of them with respect to the “punishment treatment effect”, i.e. the difference in group efficiency when costly punishment is available (CP norms) versus when it is not (CD norms or DD norms).  References to equations, tables or figures from the article are given whenever the paper makes a quantitative or qualitative prediction.  No information outside the article is introduced.

-----------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
-----------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – an “infinitely large population” is assumed (Section 2).  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  The size is fixed, so the paper contains no prediction about how changing it would alter the punishment effect on efficiency.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  Only implicitly: interactions continue indefinitely with random matching.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  No prediction.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned?  Not at all.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Mentioned?  Not applicable; the underlying game is a donation game with discrete actions C, D, P.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.

5. Contribution default (take vs. give frame)?  
   • Mentioned?  Not at all.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Equivalent model parameters: benefit b and cost c of cooperation.  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – varied throughout the analysis.  
   • Systematically varied?  Yes.  
     – Key conditions for punishment to raise or lower efficiency:  
       • CP norms exist only if both q ξ (b+β) > c and q(b+β) > α (Table 3, Section 3.2).  
       • CP beats DD when  q > (−b+c+α+β)/(b−c+α+β)  (Eq. 31).  
       • CD norms (no punishment) already beat CP whenever they exist: π_CD > π_CP (Eq. 29 vs. 30).  
     Quantitative effect size that can be read directly:  
       dπ_CP/db = (1−μ) (Eq. 30) – so every one-unit increase in b raises efficiency under punishment by 1−μ coins; the treatment effect relative to the no-punishment DD baseline therefore increases by the same amount provided CP still satisfies the existence conditions.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher (α)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – varied.  
   • Systematically varied?  Yes.  
     – Appears negatively in efficiency with punishment: π_CP = (1−μ)(b−c) − μ(α+β) (Eq. 30).  
       ⇒ dπ_CP/dα = −μ (one-to-one negative effect).  
     – Also tightens the feasibility condition q(b+β) > α; larger α shrinks the parameter region in which punishment can ever improve efficiency (Table 3, Fig. 2).

8. Punishment magnitude on the target (β)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – varied.  
   • Systematically varied?  Yes.  
     – Direct payoff effect identical to α: −μ per extra punishment unit in Eq. 30.  
     – However, larger β simultaneously relaxes the two feasibility conditions q ξ (b+β) > c and q(b+β) > α, so it widens the parameter region in which punishment is admissible (Fig. 2 & 3).  
     – Net prediction from the paper: raising β makes the *existence* of a positive punishment effect more likely, but once CP is feasible it lowers efficiency by μ coins per extra β.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Mentioned?  No reward system is analysed.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.

10. Reward cost (to grant a reward)  
    • Not mentioned; no variation.

11. Reward magnitude (received reward)  
    • Not mentioned; no variation.

12. Do players know the final round?  
    • Not mentioned; infinite horizon is assumed.  No variation.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Reputations are *public* (Section 2), but the paper never discusses manipulating this.  No variation.

14. Do punished players learn the identity of the punisher?  
    • Not mentioned; therefore no prediction.

15. Do rewarded players learn the identity of the rewarder?  
    • Not mentioned.

-----------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
-----------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables used  
   • Average (or total) payoff at equilibrium: labelled π_CD, π_CP, π_DD (Section 3.3).  This is the paper’s efficiency measure.  
   • Cooperation level h* (fraction of good players / probability of cooperation) (Eqs. 15, 28).  
   These two variables are different: a treatment can raise cooperation yet lower efficiency if punishment costs are high, and such trade-offs are analysed.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
   6 (MPCR via b and c), 7 (α), 8 (β), and trivially 1 (population size is fixed and infinite).  So 4 of 15.

C. For which parameters does the paper discuss the *effect of systematically varying* them on the punishment treatment effect?  
   Exactly three: 6 (b,c), 7 (α), 8 (β).  For each of these the paper derives algebraic conditions and/or explicit derivatives showing how the efficiency gap between punishment and non-punishment regimes changes.  None of the other 12 parameters are varied.

D. Predicting the punishment treatment effect on efficiency using only this paper’s content  
   • Higher benefit-to-cost ratio (larger b or smaller c) increases the chance that costly punishment raises efficiency relative to DD; magnitude: +1−μ coins per extra unit of b in CP norms.  
   • Larger punishment cost α always decreases efficiency under CP norms (−μ coins per extra α) and shrinks the parameter space in which punishment can help.  
   • Larger punishment magnitude β widens the feasibility region for CP norms but, conditional on CP being in use, reduces efficiency at exactly the same −μ coins per extra β.  
   • All remaining parameters (1-5, 9-15) are either fixed or absent; the paper offers no guidance for their impact.  Therefore, little or no prediction can be made about their interaction with punishment effects on efficiency on the basis of this paper alone.

That exhausts every statement the article makes that is relevant to the fifteen pre-specified design parameters.

Abstract: Punishment of defectors is believed to be a key factor in sustaining cooperation among unrelated individuals. A. Dependent variables  
• The paper’s headline measure is η_G (population-average group achievement): the probability that a random group meets the cooperation threshold.  
• They also refer to the stationary frequency of each strategy and to the prevalence of reward or punishment institutions, but not to total pay-offs or an “efficiency” ratio in the sense of “actual / maximum group payoff”. Thus, efficiency is NOT the main dependent variable used.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
Five:  
1 (Group size N), 6 (institutional multiplication factor δ), 7 (punishment tax π_t), 9 (reward enabled / disabled), 11 (reward magnitude via Δ_RP).  (If one distinguishes cost and magnitude separately, parameters 7 and 10 collapse into the single tax π_t.)  

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of systematic variation on the punishment treatment effect?  
Only one—parameter 9 (presence or absence of reward).  Even here, variation is discrete (four institutional regimes) rather than a continuous sweep, but Fig. 3 and the surrounding text give clear comparative results.  No other parameter is varied.

D. Predictions one can legitimately make—restricted to the paper’s content  
• Adding a punishment-only institution (relative to no institution) shifts the defection-to-cooperation transition leftwards by ≈ 0.06 in risk space (r* ≈ 0.755 → 0.695) and lifts η_G by ~0.15 around r ≈ 0.70.  
• Adding a reward-only institution yields a larger improvement (Δr* ≈ 0.08; Δη_G ≈ 0.20) than punishment alone.  
• Allowing groups to choose between reward and punishment electorally produces the largest gain (Δr* ≈ 0.115; Δη_G ≈ 0.30).  
• Because no other parameters are explored, the paper offers no evidence‐based way to anticipate how changes in group size, tax size, punishment magnitude, δ, etc., would modulate the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.
