Below, each of the 15 parameters is considered in turn.  For every parameter I state  

• whether it is explicitly described in the article and, if so, its value(s);  
• whether the paper says anything about what would happen **if that parameter were systematically varied** for any dependent variable (including but not limited to efficiency), and—where possible—the numerical effect sizes that can be read directly from the tables or figures.  
If a parameter is absent or no predictions are made, that is said explicitly.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
• Mentioned: Yes – every group has 4 fishermen.  
• Systematic variation discussed? No – always fixed at 4. No prediction or effect size.

2. Number of rounds  
• Mentioned: Yes – 10 periods without sanctions, then 40 periods with sanctions (total = 50).  
• Systematic variation discussed? No – length is never manipulated; authors only speculate in the Discussion that “a longer game may be better able to measure … sanctioning mechanisms.” No numerical effect.

3. Chat enabled between players?  
• Mentioned: No – there is no chat functionality; players cannot communicate except through punishment decisions.  
• Systematic variation discussed? No.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution?  
• Mentioned: Indirectly – appropriation is continuous 0–50 units, not all-or-nothing.  
• Systematic variation discussed? No.

5. Contribution default (pre-set endowment left unless moved)?  
• Not applicable in this CPR design; players actively choose an appropriation level.  
• No discussion of varying it.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor  
• Mentioned: Yes – when the resource is full, each invested unit nets 3 (= 4 reward –1 cost). The factor declines with the stock level by formula (4/R0)·Rt-1.  
• Systematic variation discussed? No.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
• Mentioned: Yes   
  – Strict: cost = 5 points per unit.  
  – Graduated: cost = 1,3,5,7 depending on offender’s history.  
• Systematic variation discussed? Partly.  
  – Table 8 adds “Punishment Cost” as a regressor in a logit on the binary decision to punish (b = 0.046, s.e.=0.037, p > 0.1 in model 3).  That tests how cost influences the likelihood to punish, **not** efficiency.  
  – No results connecting different cost levels to group efficiency or pay-offs.

8. Punishment magnitude per unit  
• Mentioned: Yes – each cost unit is tripled for the target (strict: 15; graduated: 3,9,15,21).  
• Systematic variation discussed? No separate analysis; magnitude always tied to cost schedule above.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
• Mentioned: Yes – reward is **not** available.  
• Systematic variation discussed? No.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
• Both not applicable and not discussed.

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
• Mentioned: Yes – subjects were told the game lasts 40 sanctioning periods.  
• Systematic variation discussed? No, but authors note in Discussion that an unknown horizon could change behaviour.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
• Mentioned: Yes – at the end of each period players see every other player’s appropriation and the new resource size.  
• Systematic variation discussed? No.

14. Are punishers identified to the punished?  
• Implicitly yes (mutual monitoring, “the players are also the ones to decide on whom to sanction”), but never stated whether identities are revealed or only amounts.  
• Systematic variation discussed? No.

15. Are rewarders identified?  
• Not applicable (no rewards).

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables actually used  
• Efficiency (total pay-off ÷ maximum possible) is **not** used.  
• Macro level: Resource size, ΔResource size, Total group appropriation, Group profit.  
• Micro level: Individual appropriation, Individual profit, Punishing decision.  
  – Note: Resource size and appropriation are ecological/behavioural measures, not monetary efficiency; profit is monetary but not normalised to the cooperative optimum.

B.  Parameters mentioned  
8 of 15 are mentioned (1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14).

C.  Parameters whose *systematic variation* is analysed for its impact on any punishment treatment effect  
• None of the 15 is exogenously and systematically varied across treatments to predict differences in punishment effectiveness on the listed dependent variables.  
• The paper does include within-treatment variation of parameter 7 (cost) but only to explain the *decision to punish*, not efficiency.  Therefore the count is 0.

D.  What can we predict—solely from this paper—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
Because the study fixes almost all parameters and does not analyse efficiency, very little can be inferred.  The only qualitative hints are:  
• Larger groups (parameter 1) are not studied; no prediction possible.  
• Longer horizons (parameter 2) might make graduated sanctions look better, because in the experiment their advantage only appears late.  
• Higher punishment costs (parameter 7) slightly reduce the probability of punishing (Table 8) but the paper gives no link to pay-offs.  
• Endogenous choice of the sanctioning institution (not in the 15-item list) improved cooperation; parameters that increase perceived legitimacy (e.g., showing peer outcomes, parameter 13) might interact positively, but this is speculative.  

Beyond those qualitative observations, the paper provides too little evidence to form quantitative predictions about efficiency changes for any of the 15 parameters or their interactions.

Below I go through the 15 parameters one by one, always asking two questions:  
(1) Does the paper mention the parameter at all (and, if so, what value is used)?  
(2) Does the paper **systematically vary** the parameter and use that variation to make a quantitative or qualitative prediction about the *punishment-treatment effect* (any change that can be attributed to the introduction or magnitude of punishment) for *any* dependent variable?  When a numerical effect can be read directly from a figure or table I reproduce it; otherwise I simply state the qualitative result that is explicitly claimed.

──────────────────────────────────────────  
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned.  Replicator-dynamics section assumes “infinite” population; spatial simulations use a 100 × 100 lattice (N = 10 000).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction about changing N.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Not discussed (simulations run until a steady state).  
   (2) No variation, no prediction.

3. Chat enabled?  
   (1) Not mentioned.  
   (2) No.

4. All-or-nothing contributions?  
   (1) Not mentioned.  
   (2) No.

5. Contribution default / withdrawal framing  
   (1) Not mentioned.  
   (2) No.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   (1) Closest analogue is the PD benefit parameter b (they set b = 2, c = 1).  
   (2) Authors explicitly state that varying b “only affects the trajectory and velocity … but does not affect the properties of the equilibrium point” (Section 2.1).  They therefore *fix* b = 2 and do not relate it to any treatment effect.

7. Cost to impose one unit of punishment  
   (1) Not modelled.  A punisher receives exactly the same exit payoff as the punished player, so there is effectively zero cost.  
   (2) Not varied.

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted per unit)  
   (1) Represented by σ<0 (“exit punishment”).  In most simulations σ = –0.3; in Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 the analytical range –0.5 < σ < 0.  
   (2) Systematically varied only in Fig. 2 (σ on the vertical axis).  Result: for a fixed starting state, larger punishment (more negative σ) together with *low* asymmetry (k) moves the system to the all-loner equilibrium E₄, whereas the same σ with *high* k yields the all-defector equilibrium E₅.  No efficiency (payoff) numbers are provided.

9. Reward enabled?  
   (1) Yes.  σ>0 is called “exit reward”; most simulations use σ = 0.3.  
   (2) σ is not systematically varied on the reward side; only one positive value (0.3) is analysed, so no functional prediction is derived.

10. Cost to bestow one unit of reward  
11. Reward magnitude (coins received per unit)  
   (1) Not separately modelled; both fold into σ>0 and have no additional parameters.  
   (2) No systematic variation.

12. Finite horizon known?  
13. Peer outcomes shown?  
14. Punisher identity revealed?  
15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
   (1) Information-display issues are never mentioned in the paper.  
   (2) No variation, no prediction.

──────────────────────────────────────────  
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
   • The paper never reports **group efficiency** (total payoff divided by the cooperative optimum).  
   • Reported outcomes are (i) the *steady-state proportions* of Cooperators (SC + WC), Defectors (D) and Loners (L); (ii) occasionally time trajectories of those proportions.  These are behavioural variables, not payoff-based efficiency measures.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   4 of 15:  
   (1) Number of players (fixed),  
   (6) MPCR analogue (b),  
   (8) Punishment magnitude σ<0,  
   (9)/(11) Reward enabled / magnitude σ>0 (combined in σ).

C. Which parameters are **systematically varied** and related to the punishment-treatment effect?  
   Strictly speaking, none.  σ is varied (Fig. 2) but the authors only describe how it shifts the equilibrium mix of strategies, not how it alters *efficiency* or any other punishment-treatment contrast.  Therefore: 0 / 15.

D. What predictions about the 15 parameters and their interactions could be made for the *punishment-treatment effect on efficiency* based solely on this paper?  
   • Because efficiency is never calculated, the paper offers almost no direct guidance.  
   • Indirect hints: stronger (i.e., more negative) σ does not revive cooperation; it merely changes whether everyone ends up defecting or opting out.  Either way, efficiency would remain well below the cooperative optimum, so the predicted *treatment effect on efficiency* is likely negligible or even negative.  
   • Positive σ (reward) at low super-rationality leads to 50 % defectors + 50 % loners—again a low-efficiency outcome; only when super-rationality A is high do some cooperators survive.  Hence any positive impact of reward on efficiency is conditional on other psychological parameters, not on σ alone.  
   • None of the remaining 11 parameters are addressed, so no prediction can be drawn for them.

In short, the paper offers virtually no direct evidence for how any of the 15 experimental-design parameters would influence the punishment treatment effect on **efficiency**.

7 . Punishment cost α  
(1) α is fixed at 0.1 in all simulations.  
(2) Never varied; no predictions.

8 . Punishment magnitude β (fine)  
(1) Yes.  It is varied continuously in the β–γ phase diagrams (e.g. β from 0 to ≳0.15).  
(2) Main qualitative findings:  
    • When β < 0.087 (weak punishment), punishment cannot survive on its own; adding bribery (γ) can create R + G and R + D + G phases that raise contributions above the ALL_D baseline.  
    • 0.087 ≤ β ≤ 0.115: more complex sequences of phases; moderate bribery can either raise or lower contributions.

Rewards are not modelled; never mentioned.

10 . Reward cost  
Not applicable.

Not applicable.

Not part of the simulation; never mentioned.

Not part of the simulation; never mentioned.

Not modelled; never mentioned.

Not applicable.

A. Dependent variables  
• The paper does NOT use “group efficiency” (total or average monetary payoff divided by the cooperative optimum).

#6 (synergy factor r) and #8 (punishment magnitude β).  
α, γ (bribery fund) and r are explored jointly, but α itself is not varied.

Abstract: Social institutions are systems of shared norms and rules that regulate people's behaviors, often emerging without external enforcement. They provide criteria to distinguish cooperation from defection and establish rules to sustain cooperation, shaped through long-term trial and error. While principles for successful institutions have been proposed, the mechanisms underlying their emergence remain poorly understood. To address this, we introduce the evolutionary dynamical-systems game theory that couples game actions with environmental dynamics and explores the evolution of cognitive frameworks for decision-making. We analyze a minimal model of common-pool resource management, where resources grow naturally and are harvested. Players use decision-making functions to determine whether to harvest at each step, based on environmental and peer monitoring. After evolution, decision-making functions enable players to detect selfish harvesting and punish it by overharvesting, which degrades the environment. This process leads to the self-organization of norms that classify harvesting actions as cooperative, defective, or punitive. The emergent norms for cooperativeness and rules of punishment serve as institutions. The environmental and players' states converge to distinct modes characterized by limit-cycle attractors, representing temporal regularities in socio-ecological systems. These modes remain stable despite slight variations in individual decision-making, illustrating the stability of institutions. We measure evolutionary robustness of decision-making functions, defined as the capacity to keep dominance against invasion. It is revealed that plasticity, the ability to adjust actions to cope with diverse opponents, allows for such robustness. This work introduces foundational concepts in evolutionary dynamical-systems games and elucidates the mechanisms underlying the self-organization of social institutions.

   • Not applicable, never mentioned.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Not used.  Payoffs stem from logistic resource growth (parameter α) and from the harvest fraction β, but the term MPCR never appears and no treatment effect is attached to varying α or β.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   • Not parameterised.  “Punishment” here is indirect: the punisher over-harvests, which automatically reduces its own future pay-offs; no explicit cost parameter exists.  No systematic variation.

8. Punishment magnitude to the target  
   • Same as (7): not parameterised and not varied.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Rewards are absent.

10. Reward cost  
   • Absent.

11. Reward magnitude  
   • Absent.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
   • Not treated.  The model has no representation of player beliefs about horizon length.

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
   • Yes.  In the core model each player observes both her own richness and the opponent’s richness.  
   • Systematic variation: The Supplementary Appendix fixes either S or O to 0 so that *one* of these pieces of information becomes unavailable.  Result: when information on players’ states is hidden, cooperation collapses (“over-harvesting becomes dominant”, SI Appendix Fig. S11).  
   • However, this is still *not* framed as a punishment-vs-no-punishment comparison, so no punishment-treatment effect is given.

14. Is the identity of the punisher revealed to the target?  
   • Not modelled.

15. Is the identity of the rewarder revealed to the target?  
   • Not modelled.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY  

A.  Dependent variables.  
    • The paper’s main outcome is individual **fitness** (average payoff per step during one generation) and, by extension, group-level resource dynamics classified into “modes” (Sync4, Div6, etc.).  
    • “Efficiency” (actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff) is *not* reported.  Contribution rate is also not directly reported.  Hence efficiency sensu public-goods experiments never appears.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
    • 4 parameters appear at least once:  
      (1) number of players,  
      (2) number of rounds,  
      (4) all-or-nothing decision,  
      (13) visibility of peer outcomes.  
      The remaining 11 parameters are absent.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss the *effect of systematically varying* the parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
    • Zero.  The study never runs a “no-punishment” baseline, so no treatment effect of punishment—on efficiency or on any other outcome—is estimated for any parameter.

D.  Predictions one could nonetheless hazard (with extreme caution) if forced to forecast the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency solely from this paper’s contents.  
    • The paper implies that visibility of peer states (parameter 13) is necessary for punishment to emerge; removing that information destroys cooperation.  By analogy, in a public-goods setting we might expect that making peer outcomes invisible would strongly *reduce* any positive punishment-treatment effect on efficiency.  
    • Population size (parameter 1) and mutation rate (an analogue to strategy diversity) influence which institutional “mode” stabilises.  Larger, more diverse populations end up with modes that are slightly less efficient but more invasion-resistant, suggesting that the long-run efficiency gain from punishment might be smaller in larger groups.  
    • For every other parameter the paper gives no evidence that would allow even a directional prediction.

In brief, the paper is rich on endogenously emerging punishment but provides virtually no information that can be translated into parameter-by-parameter predictions about the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency in standard public-goods games.

Below, each of the 15 design parameters is treated in turn.  
For every parameter I report  

(1) whether the paper even mentions it and, if so, the value(s) used;  
(2) whether the paper systematically varies that parameter and, if so, what effect that variation is shown (or numerically implied) to have on the “punishment treatment effect”.  
The only outcomes actually analysed in the paper are the fractions of Cooperators (C), Punishers (P) and Defectors (D) and the distribution of exit‐probabilities θ.  “Efficiency” (total or average pay-off) is never computed.

PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER SCAN

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  Players are placed on an L × L lattice.  They run L = 100–500 (so N ≈ 10 000–250 000) “to exclude finite-size effects”.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  L is only a robustness check; no figure/table reports the effect of changing N on any outcome, let alone on a punishment treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Not mentioned as a variable.  Each simulation runs until a stationary state (>5 × 10⁵ Monte-Carlo steps); the horizon is not varied or used as an explanatory variable.

3. Chat enabled  
   • Not mentioned; not applicable.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
   • Not mentioned.  (The game is a binary spatial Prisoner’s Dilemma, not a continuous public-goods game.)

5. Contribution default / reversal frame  
   • Not mentioned.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor (in this paper: the benefit parameter b of the PD)  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  b is explicitly varied and called the “dilemma strength”.  
   • Systematically varied? Yes.  Figures 1–4 and the A–b phase diagram vary b from ≈1.0 up to ≈1.8.  
   • Reported effect: As b rises, the fraction of cooperative individuals (C + P) monotonically falls; various phase transitions (C+P ➔ C+D+P ➔ D+P ➔ D) are mapped (Fig. 2).  No pay-off efficiency numbers are supplied.  Quantitative slopes are not tabulated; only qualitative trends and state-boundaries are drawn.

7. Punishment cost (α)  
   • Mentioned? Yes: α = 0.1 in all main runs.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  α is fixed while β is varied through β/α ratios.

8. Punishment magnitude (β)  
   • Mentioned? Yes.  β is introduced via the ratio β/α (“sanction-to-cost ratio”).  
   • Systematically varied? Yes.  Fig. 4 shows β/α = 0.5, 1, 2, 3 while α = 0.1.  
   • Reported effect: Larger β/α shifts the tipping point at which punishers disappear to a higher b, enlarges the D+P or P phase, and “eliminates second-order free-riding” over a wider interval.  No numeric effect sizes on efficiency are given.

9. Reward enabled  
10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   • Not mentioned in any form; no reward mechanism is modelled.

12. Horizon known to players (finite/known vs unknown)  
   • Not discussed.

13. Peer outcomes displayed  
   • Players observe a randomly chosen neighbour’s cumulative pay-off when updating strategies, but the visibility of outcomes is not manipulated experimentally.  No systematic variation.

14. Punisher identity revealed  
   • Not relevant; the model assumes local knowledge but does not vary this.

15. Rewarder identity revealed  
   • Not relevant / not modelled.


--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
   • The paper never reports group efficiency, total pay-off or average pay-off.  
   • Reported DVs are:  
     – F_C, F_D, F_P: fractions of Cooperators, Defectors and Punishers.  
     – Mean or distribution of exit probabilities θ.  
   These measure strategy composition and behavioural propensities, not efficiency.

B. Parameters mentioned (of the 15)  
   • 3 parameters are explicitly present:  
     – #1 Number of players (L)  
     – #6 Multiplication factor / benefit b  
     – #7–8 Punishment cost α (fixed) and magnitude β (varied).  

C. Parameters whose systematic variation is analysed for its impact on outcomes that include punishment  
   • 2 parameters (#6 b, #8 β) are systematically varied.  
   • None of the variations are connected to any measure of efficiency.

D. Predicting the punishment treatment effect on efficiency from this paper alone  
   The paper contains no efficiency data and does not compare “with-punishment” to “without-punishment” treatments (punishment is always present; what is varied is adaptive exit and the aspiration parameter A).  Consequently, the paper offers almost no direct leverage for forecasting how any of the 15 parameters—or their interactions—would change the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.  The one indirect hint is that higher b and lower β/α both decrease the prevalence of cooperation; if one assumes (outside this paper) that more cooperation raises efficiency, then one would conjecture:  
   • Higher dilemma strength (b) would reduce the positive efficiency effect of punishment.  
   • Larger sanction-to-cost ratios (β/α) would enlarge that positive effect.  
For every other parameter the article is silent, so no evidence-based prediction can be made.

Below every parameter I stick to two questions:

(a) Is the parameter explicitly described anywhere in the paper?  
(b) Does the paper **systematically vary** that parameter and, if so, does it report how the punishment-vs.-control difference changes when the parameter is moved?  Whenever the paper gives numbers I quote them (always taken from the paper’s tables/figures).

────────────────────────  
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER REVIEW
────────────────────────  

1. Number of players  
(a) Yes. All groups contain exactly three players (A, B, C).  
(b) Not varied, therefore no prediction about its influence on the punishment treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
(a) Yes. Exactly 20 rounds; subjects know this.  
(b) Not varied; no prediction.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
(a) The instructions forbid any chat; the only messages are one-way numerical “recommendations” from the leader.  
(b) Not varied; no prediction.

4. All-or-nothing contributions?  
(a) No. Choices are continuous from 0 to 100 points.  
(b) Not varied.

5. Contribution-default (re-allocation) frame?  
(a) No. Players decide how many of their 100 points to contribute; there is no withdrawal frame.  
(b) Not varied.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
(a) Yes. Each contributed point is multiplied by 1.5 and shared equally, so MPCR = 0.5.  
(b) Fixed; not varied.

7. Punishment cost per unit  
(a) Yes. The leader loses one-third of the amount deducted from a follower. Example: to cut 3 points from a follower, the leader pays 1 point.  
(b) Cost is fixed; never varied, so no prediction.

8. Punishment magnitude per unit  
(a) Yes. For every point the leader spends, the target loses three points (3:1 ratio).  
(b) Fixed; not varied.

9. Is a reward option enabled?  
(a) No. The experiment contains no reward stage.  
(b) Not relevant.

10–11. Reward cost / reward magnitude  
(a) Not applicable (see #9).  
(b) Not varied.

12. Is the horizon known?  
(a) Yes. Subjects know there are 20 rounds.  
(b) Horizon length is not varied.

13. Are peer outcomes shown? (monitoring intensity)  
(a) Yes, and this is the **only parameter that the paper systematically varies.**  
 • Group Monitoring (GM): nobody learns individual contributions; only own payoff (which reveals the aggregate).  
 • Individual Monitoring (IM): the leader learns each follower’s individual contribution; followers still see only aggregates.  
(b) Effect of varying this parameter on the punishment treatment:  
 – Average follower contribution (Table 3)  
  Pun-GM = 53.52; Pun-IM = 81.16 → +27.64 points.  
 – Average leader contribution  
  Pun-GM = 54.95; Pun-IM = 73.89 → +18.94 points.  
 – Group-level efficiency (can be inferred):  
  Total contrib. in Pun-GM ≈ 162 pts ⇒ group payoff 300 + 0.5·162 = 381 → efficiency ≈ 381/450 = 0.85.  
  Total contrib. in Pun-IM ≈ 236 pts ⇒ payoff 300 + 0.5·236 = 418 → efficiency ≈ 0.93.  
  Hence raising monitoring from GM to IM increases the punishment treatment’s efficiency by roughly 0.08 (= 8 percentage points).  
 – Statistical results: The paper’s Mann-Whitney and regression tests show that punishment only raises cooperation significantly under IM (Hypothesis 3). Under GM, punishment does not outperform the recommendation treatment.

14. Do punished players know who punished them?  
(a) Implicitly yes: only the leader can punish, so identity is common knowledge.  
(b) Not varied.

15. Do rewarded players know who rewarded them?  
(a) Not applicable (no rewards).  
(b) Not varied.

────────────────────────  
SUMMARY
────────────────────────  

A. Dependent variables actually used  
– Main DVs: (i) individual & aggregate contributions (“cooperation”), (ii) intra-group correlation of contributions (“coordination”), (iii) punishment frequency/intensity.  
– Efficiency (total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff) is **never reported as a DV** – it can only be constructed from Table 3. Thus “efficiency” is conceptually different from the paper’s stated DVs.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
10 of them: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14.

C. Which parameters are both mentioned AND systematically varied with respect to the punishment-vs.-control comparison?  
Exactly 1 parameter: #13 (monitoring intensity). None of the other 14 parameters is varied, so their effect on the punishment treatment effect is not discussed.

D. What predictions can be made (only from this paper) about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?

• Parameter 13 (monitoring): Moving from group-level feedback to individual-level feedback for the leader is predicted to turn punishment from “ineffective” to “highly effective”, raising cooperation and (by extrapolation) efficiency by roughly 8-10 percentage points of the theoretical maximum.  

• For every other parameter (1–12 and 14–15) the paper contains no systematic variation, therefore it allows **no prediction**—except the trivial statement that if those parameters stay fixed at the values used in the experiment (3 players, 20 known rounds, MPCR = 0.5, 3:1 punishment leverage, etc.) the observed treatment effect holds.

In short, the only informative lever in this paper for forecasting punishment’s impact on group efficiency is whether the leader receives individual or only aggregate feedback about follower contributions. All other listed parameters are either constant or not present in the study.

Below I go through the 15 parameters in turn, referring only to what is written, graphed or tabulated in “Preference reversal and the evolution of cooperation”.  
For every parameter I state  

(i) Whether the paper mentions or instantiates the parameter (and the values used), and  
(ii) Whether the paper makes a prediction about what would happen to the *punishment-treatment effect* (difference between a punishment condition and a no-punishment condition) **when the parameter is systematically varied**.  
When numerical expressions that link the parameter to an outcome are given, I quote them; otherwise I say that no quantitative effect is provided.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------  
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION  

1. Number of players (group size N)  
 (i) Mentioned constantly. Values shown: N = 5 (Figs. 2, 3, 5) and N = 30 (Fig. 4); equations keep N symbolic.  
 (ii) Nowhere are different values of N compared side-by-side, so the paper gives **no systematic prediction** of how changing N alters the punishment treatment effect on any outcome.

2. Number of rounds  
 (i) Not mentioned. The model is an infinite-population replicator dynamic without discrete finite rounds.  
 (ii) No prediction.

3. Chat enabled  
 (i) Not mentioned.  
 (ii) No prediction.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution decision  
 (i) Yes. Each player either contributes the full amount c or contributes nothing (“cooperate or defect”). The setting is therefore binary (all-or-nothing).  
 (ii) The binary nature is fixed; the paper never varies it, so no prediction about varying this parameter.

5. Contribution default (re-allocation from the public pool)  
 (i) Not part of the model.  
 (ii) No prediction.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor (r)  
 (i) Present throughout as “synergy factor r (1 < r < N)”; numerically r = 3 is used in every figure.  
 (ii) A *formula* links r to whether cooperation can flourish without preference reversal:  
  Δπ(0)=−(N−1)pα+rc/N−c.  
  Because rc/N enters positively, increasing r lowers the cooperation-threshold on p. Nevertheless, the paper never plots or tabulates different r’s, so there is **no worked‐out numerical prediction** of how systematically increasing r changes the punishment treatment effect.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit (α)  
 (i) Appears in all payoff equations; numerical value α = 0.3 is used in every figure.  
 (ii) No figure or table varies α. Therefore no explicit prediction on the punishment treatment effect.

8. Punishment magnitude / fine (β)  
 (i) Appears in all payoff equations; β = 1 in every plotted example.  
 (ii) Qualitative prediction is given: “consensual punishment is beneficial … when the level of cooperators’ punishment preference is greater than a threshold which is *inversely proportional to the fine of punishment*”.  
  Mathematically: cooperation requires p > (c−rc/N)/[(N−1)β].  
  Hence increasing β lowers the p-threshold and should **strengthen** the punishment treatment effect. No numerical size is provided beyond the formula.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
 (i) Rewards are absent from the model.  
 (ii) No prediction.

10. Reward cost  
 Not present.

11. Reward magnitude  
 Not present.

12. Whether the number of rounds is known  
 Not applicable to an infinite-horizon evolutionary model. No mention, no prediction.

13. Whether peer outcomes are shown  
 Not discussed.

14. Whether the punisher is identified  
 Not discussed.

15. Whether the rewarder is identified  
 Not discussed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------  
SUMMARY  

A. Dependent variables used in the paper  
 • Fraction of cooperators (state variable x).  
 • Location and size of basins of attraction of full cooperation or full defection.  
 • Payoff difference Δπ(x)=π_C−π_D (used to locate equilibria).  
 Group **efficiency/total payoff is never used** as a dependent variable, although individual payoffs are written down for analytical purposes.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
 7 of 15: 1, 4, 6, 7, 8, (not rewards: 9-11), and the rest are absent.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when *systematically varied*?  
 Only 1 of 15 (parameter 8, the punishment fine β).  
 A formula shows that higher β lowers the cooperation-threshold on p, implying a larger positive punishment treatment effect on any cooperation-related outcome.

D. Predictions about the punishment treatment effect on efficiency that can be made *solely* from this paper  
 Because efficiency is never analysed, only indirect conjectures can be made:  
 • Increasing the punishment fine β (parameter 8) should enlarge the set of circumstances under which cooperation—and therefore efficiency—becomes stable, hence β is predicted to increase the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.  
 For all other 14 parameters the paper gives **insufficient information** to predict how they (or their interactions) would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

In short, beyond the qualitative statement that harsher fines (β) help cooperation, the article provides little that can be converted into predictions about how any of the 15 design parameters would change the effect of adding punishment on group efficiency.
reference_APA: Gao, Shiping & Li, Nan (2023). Preference reversal and the evolution of cooperation. APPLIED MATHEMATICS AND COMPUTATION.

Parameter-by-parameter extraction from the paper  
(numbers below correspond to the 15 parameters given in the prompt)

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Two sizes are fixed:  N = 200 × 200 = 40 000 for lattice/small-world runs and N = 40 000 for random networks.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  No figure or table varies N, and no prediction is offered about what would happen if it changed.  

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  Only implicitly: simulations run “until the system has reached steady state.”  
   • Systematically varied / prediction?  No.  

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Not mentioned.  No prediction.  

4. “All-or-nothing’’ contribution rule  
   • Mentioned?  Yes: every co-operator (punisher or not) “makes a contribution of 1,” defector contributes 0.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  The paper never considers continuous contributions, so no prediction.  

5. Contribution default / retraction rule  
   • Not mentioned.  No prediction.  

6. MPCR / multiplication factor (called r)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Values used: r = 3.5, 4.0, 4.5 (Figs. 2, 4, A12, A13).  
   • Systematically varied?  Yes – three discrete values.  
   • Stated effect on “punishment treatment effect”?  The paper reports how larger r enlarges the parameter region in which punishers (Ps) dominate and defectors (Ds) disappear.  No efficiency measures are reported, so the effect is on strategy composition, not on efficiency.  Numerical size: not given in coefficients, only visible in heat-maps (e.g., Fig. 2 shows P-dominated area expanding as r goes from 3.5 to 4.5).  

7. Cost to impose one unit of punishment  
   • Not explicitly parameterised; the model assumes “the fines imposed on defectors can be fully covered by the costs incurred to the punishers.”  No separate cost parameter is varied, so no prediction.  

8. Punishment magnitude (fine, α)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Main independent variable.  Typical values 2 ≤ α ≤ 6; critical value on lattices around α ≈ 4.0; several figures show α on the y-axis.  
   • Systematically varied?  Yes.  
   • Reported effect:  
       – Regular lattice (Fig. 2): when α > ≈4.0 and feedback sensitivity A is intermediate (≈0.235) DPs can survive; below that the system is CP-dominated or D-dominated.  
       – Random network (Fig. 4): only for large α (≥5–6) and A ≈ 0.2 do DPs out-compete Ds.  
       – Small-world (Fig. 6): higher α widens the window of network randomness p that maximises the DP share.  
     No total-payoff / efficiency figures are given.  

9. Reward enabled?  
10. Reward cost?  
11. Reward magnitude?  
   • Not in the model; the study deals exclusively with punishment.  No predictions.  

12. End-round information (finite-horizon knowledge)  
13. Peer outcome information  
14. Punisher identity revealed?  
15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
   • None of these informational parameters appear.  No predictions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used  
   – Group efficiency or total/average payoff is NOT used as an outcome in the results section.  
   – Reported outcomes are:  
       • Final fractions of three strategies (defectors D, co-operator-driven punishers CP, defector-driven punishers DP).  
       • Phase boundaries between “P-dominated” and “D-dominated” states.  
       • Occasionally mean payoff gaps between paired individuals (ΔDP-D etc.).  
   These variables capture evolutionary success, not efficiency.

B. How many of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   4 parameters are mentioned (1, 4, 6, 8).  The other 11 are absent.

C. How many of the 15 parameters are systematically varied AND their effect on the punishment treatment effect discussed?  
   2 parameters (6: MPCR r, and 8: fine α).  Even for these, the paper discusses their effect on strategy composition, not on efficiency or on a “punishment vs. no-punishment” treatment effect.

D. Predictions one could make – strictly from the paper – about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency  

   • Only tentative qualitative statements can be drawn because efficiency is never measured:  
     – Increasing the multiplication factor r should raise efficiency in any setting, and in the presence of punishment it also enlarges the region where punishers eliminate defectors; therefore the punishment treatment effect on efficiency would likely become more positive as r increases.  
     – Raising the punishment fine α strengthens the ability of punishment to remove defectors, up to a point; thus the treatment effect on efficiency should be positive for α above a network- and A-specific threshold (≈4 in the figures) but may level off (“saturation”) beyond that.  
     – Extremely high fines, while still wiping out defectors, do not further raise DP frequencies once saturation is reached, so additional gains in efficiency would probably be minimal.  
   • For any of the remaining 13 parameters (all the organisational, reward, or information variables) the paper gives no basis for prediction, so no evidence-based prediction can be made.

Article Title: Just ask? Preference revelation and lying in a public goods experiment
Author Keywords: Experimental economics; Public good provision; Collective action; Cooperation; Preference revelation
Keywords Plus: MECHANISM DESIGN; COOPERATION; PROVISION; PUNISHMENT; HETEROGENEITY; ENFORCEMENT; DISHONESTY; DEMAND
Abstract: This paper studies the extent to which simply asking group members to report their demand-type promotes cooperation in a public goods experiment with private, unobservable incentives. The design uses a simple public goods game, in which group members differ in both their dominant strategy contributions and socially optimal contributions. Treatments are conducted in which individuals either do not report their private payoff information, report only to group members, report to group members who can punish them, or report to a binding mechanism that charges them the socially optimal contribution for someone of their reported type. In all cases, messages are non-verifiable and participants are told that they are free to lie. When participants are able to report their type, either to their group members or to a binding mechanism, they contribute more. When reporting to a mechanism, there is a positive effect initially that fades with repetition, while reporting to group members is particularly effective at sustaining cooperation over time. Further, the misreporting of type is less frequent, considered more dishonest, and punished more harshly than free-riding. Consistent with work showing that weak punishment can backfire, the punishment mechanism is underutilized in this environment and its presence negates the positive effect of sharing information. Below we go through each of the 15 parameters exactly as requested.

-------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
-------------------------------------------------

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes – every group contains exactly 3 players (p. 10 “groups of three”).  
   • Systematically varied? No – the group size is fixed in all treatments.  
   • Any prediction for varying it? None.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? Yes – 10 periods (p. 10).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Prediction? None.

3. Chat enabled between players  
   • Mentioned? Yes – the design explicitly **disables** free-form chat; only the forced “I am a ___ type” message is allowed (p. 12–13).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Prediction? None.

4. All-or-nothing contribution choice  
   • Mentioned? No – subjects can contribute any integer 0–4.  
   • Prediction? Not discussed.

5. Contribution default (endowment initially in public fund)  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Prediction? None.

6. MPCR / multiplier  
   • Mentioned? Not in MPCR notation; instead a custom payoff table is used.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Prediction? None.

7. Punishment cost per unit  
   • Mentioned? Yes – a punisher pays 1 point to reduce a target’s earnings by 3 (p. 13). Value =1.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Prediction? None.

8. Punishment magnitude per unit  
   • Mentioned? Yes – 3-for-1 reduction (p. 13).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Prediction? None.

9. Reward enabled  
   • Mentioned? No – there is no reward option in any treatment.  
   • Prediction? None.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   • Both not mentioned and not used.

12. Horizon known (do players know when the game ends?)  
   • Mentioned? Yes – subjects are told there are 10 periods (p. 10).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Prediction? None.

13. Peer outcomes shown  
   • Mentioned? Yes – at the end of every period each player sees every other member’s contribution (and, when applicable, message and punishment) (p. 11-12).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Prediction? None.

14. Punishee knows who punished them  
   • Explicitly stated? Not stated; therefore unknown. No systematic variation, no analysis.

15. Punishee knows who rewarded them  
   • Not applicable – no rewards.

-------------------------------------------------
DEPENDENT VARIABLES DISCUSSED
-------------------------------------------------
The paper analyses four payoff-related measures:

1. “Cooperation” = (own contribution – dominant-strategy contribution) ÷ (social-optimum – dominant-strategy).  
2. Raw contribution (0-4 tokens).  
3. Group profits (used to measure efficiency) = actual group payoff compared to Nash payoff (Fig. 4, Table 3).  
4. Punishment received / imposed.

Cooperation and contribution capture behaviour; group profits capture efficiency.

-------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
-------------------------------------------------

A.  Does the paper study efficiency?  
    Yes.  Group profits above the Nash benchmark are repeatedly analysed (Fig. 4, Table 3).  Other dependent variables are Cooperation, contribution, message truthfulness, and punishment.  Efficiency (group profit) is distinct because it incorporates both the benefits of higher contributions and the dead-weight loss from punishment costs.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
    8 of them: 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13 (and 14 is touched on ambiguously).  

C.  For how many parameters does the paper examine what happens when that parameter itself is systematically varied?  
    Zero.  Every listed parameter is held constant across treatments.  The only treatment variation is the **presence** of punishment versus its absence, not the numerical values of punishment cost/magnitude or any other parameter.

D.  Predictions one can make about the 15 parameters’ effects on the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, using only this paper  
    • Introducing a punishment stage with cost = 1 and magnitude = 3 **decreases** efficiency relative to an identical game without punishment when types are private and only unverifiable cheap-talk messages are available (Tables 1 & 3).  
    • Because the mechanism fails through “under-utilisation,” one might conjecture (but the paper does not test) that lowering punishment cost or raising magnitude might reverse the negative effect; however, the paper gives no direct evidence, so no firm prediction can be made.  
    • All other parameters are not varied; therefore the paper provides no basis for predicting how changing them would alter the punishment effect on efficiency.

In short, the study tells us only that, in this particular 3-player, 10-period game with a 1:3 punishment technology and full post-round feedback, enabling punishment **does not increase—and may slightly reduce—group efficiency**.  No other parameter interactions can be inferred from the evidence presented.

Authors: Meiske, B; Alvarez-Benjumea, A; Andrighetto, G; Polizzi, E
Author Full Names: Meiske, Biljana; Alvarez-Benjumea, Amalia; Andrighetto, Giulia; Polizzi, Eugenia
Article Title: Nudging punishment against sharing of fake news
Author Keywords: Social norms; Social media; Fake news; Punishment; Norm-nudges
Keywords Plus: SOCIAL NORMS; MISINFORMATION; COOPERATION; ENFORCEMENT; TWITTER
Abstract: Corrective comments posted in response to misinformation shared on social media are not only effective in reducing belief in misinformation among those observing the interaction but also serve as a publicly observable social punishment against fake news sharing. We suggest that, by visibly displaying punishing behavior, corrective comments have the potential to function as a norm nudge, updating observers' perception of the norms regulating punishment, the socalled meta-norms. We conducted a preregistered online experiment in which participants joined discussions resembling an online forum and could comment on posts shared by previous users. We manipulated participants' possibility to observe corrective comments replying to a post sharing fake news and measured the effect of this variation on their propensity to leave a corrective comment. We show that participants exposed to posts corrected by other users are significantly more likely to reply with a corrective comment, even after controlling for participants' perceived accuracy of the shared post. Participants exposed to the corrections provided by previous users perceive replying with corrections as more socially appropriate. Our results suggest that social corrections work as a (meta) norm nudge, increasing the probability of punishing norm violations by increasing the social appropriateness of correcting. Our findings suggest that interventions targeting would-beenforcers could complement existing policies specifically directed at norm violators.

────────────────────────────────────────  
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION  
────────────────────────────────────────  

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  No.  The study is not framed as a multiplayer public-goods game; each participant reads a static forum page.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  No prediction or effect size.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  Indirectly, the task consists of 4 “pages,” but these pages are fixed and not framed as repeated rounds.

3. Chat enabled between players?

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule?  
   • Mentioned?  Not applicable.  No contributions are made.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.

5. Contribution default (withdraw vs. give)?  
   • Mentioned?  Not applicable.  No endowment decisions.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  Not applicable.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   • Mentioned?  Not monetised; writing a corrective comment is the “punishment,” and its cost is neither measured nor manipulated.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss to target per unit)  
   • Mentioned?  No.  No monetary deduction exists.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Mentioned?  No reward channel is available.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.

10. Reward cost  
    • Mentioned?  Not applicable.  
    • Systematically varied?  No.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Mentioned?  Not applicable.  
    • Systematically varied?  No.

12. Is the number of rounds known?  
    • Mentioned?  Not relevant; pages are simply read once.  
    • Systematically varied?  No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mentioned?  Participants can see peers’ comments, but never see any pay-offs.  The parameter in the sense of monetary outcomes is absent.  
    • Systematically varied?  No.

14. Punisher identity revealed?  
    • Mentioned?  Comments appear with some username (screenshot shows “User_...”), so the identity is visible but impersonal.  The paper never manipulates whether identities are hidden or revealed, nor links this to treatment effects.  
    • Systematically varied?  No.

15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
    • Mentioned?  No reward phase exists.  
    • Systematically varied?  No.

────────────────────────────────────────  
SUMMARY  
────────────────────────────────────────  

A. Use of “efficiency”?  
   • The paper never reports group efficiency, total pay-off, or average pay-off.  
   • Dependent variables used:  
     – Ic : indicator that participant leaves a corrective comment.  
     – Ie : indicator that participant leaves an endorsing comment.  
     – It : indicator that participant leaves any comment.  
     – Intensity of correction (1-5 scale).  
     – Normative expectations (appropriateness ratings).  
     – Empirical expectations (expected % who correct).  
     – Personal normative beliefs.  
   • These are behavioural and perceptual measures, not efficiency.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   • Parameter 13 (peer information) is implicitly present (others’ comments are displayed).  
   • Parameter 14 is implicitly present (commenter IDs visible), but not discussed.  
   • No other parameter is mentioned.  ⇒ 2 of 15 mentioned.

C. For which parameters does the paper discuss effects of systematic variation on the punishment treatment effect?  
   • None.  The experiment varies only one factor: presence vs. absence of corrective comments.  None of the 15 parameters above are manipulated.  ⇒ 0 of 15.

D. Predictions one could make about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, based solely on this paper  
   • Because the paper never studies efficiency, never manipulates any of the 15 parameters, and never reports pay-offs, it offers almost no direct guidance.  
   • The sole qualitative hint is that simply exposing participants to evidence of peer punishment (Parameter 13: visibility of peer behaviour) increases enforcement behaviour.  Extrapolating very cautiously, greater visibility of peer actions might raise enforcement and—if this were a standard public-goods game—could in turn increase efficiency.  
   • Beyond that, the paper is silent, so no further prediction can be justified.

Authors: Ibrahim, AM
Author Full Names: Ibrahim, Ahmed M.
Article Title: The conditional defector strategies can violate the most crucial supporting mechanisms of cooperation
Keywords Plus: DISPERSAL; EVOLUTION
Abstract: Cooperation is essential for all domains of life. Yet, ironically, it is intrinsically vulnerable to exploitation by cheats. Hence, an explanatory necessity spurs many evolutionary biologists to search for mechanisms that could support cooperation. In general, cooperation can emerge and be maintained when cooperators are sufficiently interacting with themselves. This communication provides a kind of assortment and reciprocity. The most crucial and common mechanisms to achieve that task are kin selection, spatial structure, and enforcement (punishment). Here, we used agent-based simulation models to investigate these pivotal mechanisms against conditional defector strategies. We concluded that the latter could easily violate the former and take over the population. This surprising outcome may urge us to rethink the evolution of cooperation, as it illustrates that maintaining cooperation may be more difficult than previously thought. Moreover, empirical applications may support these theoretical findings, such as invading the cooperator population of pathogens by genetically engineered conditional defectors, which could be a potential therapy for many incurable diseases.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter analysis of whether the paper (1) discusses each parameter (and, if so, what value it takes) and (2) whether it makes predictions about how systematically varying that parameter would affect punishment’s impact—specifically on efficiency (actual total payoff divided by maximum possible payoff), or on any other dependent variable that the paper examines (which, as noted below, are not necessarily measures of efficiency). References to “the paper” below refer solely to the text provided.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Discussed?  
     – The paper does mention the number of “agents” (e.g., 80 in the first model, 250 in the second model).  
   • Systematic variation / effect on punishment?  
     – The paper does not systematically vary the number of agents in order to test its effect on punishment or on any dependent variable. No predictions or effect sizes are given.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Discussed?  
     – The paper describes running simulations for a certain number of “ticks” (e.g., 15,000 or 30,000 steps). It does not refer to them as “rounds” in the sense of a repeated public goods game, nor does it discuss participants knowing the total length of play.  
   • Systematic variation / effect on punishment?  
     – Not systematically varied in the paper. No predictions or effect sizes are reported about how changing the simulation length would affect punishment’s impact on efficiency or any other outcome.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The paper does not mention any form of communication or chat among agents.  
   • Systematic variation / effect on punishment?  
     – Not applicable; no mention.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. While the paper discusses “cooperators” (harvesting half of a resource patch) and “greedy” agents (harvesting 99%), it does not frame these as forced, all-or-nothing choices in a standard public goods sense.  
   • Systematic variation / effect on punishment?  
     – Not applicable; no mention.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much of their endowment to move)?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The models focus on “harvest amounts” of patches, not on a default contribution to a common fund.  
   • Systematic variation / effect on punishment?  
     – Not applicable; no mention.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The paper does not describe a standard public goods game with a multiplicative factor on contributions; it deals with resource regrowth rates in patches, but not MPCR.  
   • Systematic variation / effect on punishment?  
     – Not applicable; no mention.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussed?  
     – The paper mentions “costs-punishment = 0.8” in the second model. Punishers also pay “costs-perception = 0.5.”  
   • Systematic variation / effect on punishment?  
     – The paper does not systematically vary the punishment cost or report how changing that cost alters punishment’s effects. No predicted numerical effect sizes are given.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted per unit of punishment)  
   • Discussed?  
     – The paper describes three types of punishment: (1) “kill,” (2) “pay fine” set at 5, and (3) “suspend harvest once.” These can be viewed as different punishment “magnitudes” in broad terms.  
   • Systematic variation / effect on punishment?  
     – The authors do run simulations under each type (kill, pay fine = 5, suspend harvest). However, they do not present results in terms of efficiency; instead, they track final frequencies of strategies (e.g., how often “greedy, non-punishing” wins). No direct effect sizes are given about how systematically varying punishment magnitude changes efficiency or even total payoffs. Instead, they observe that cheating agents can still dominate under all three punishment regimes.

9. Whether reward is enabled  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The paper does not mention rewarding or “positive” sanctions anywhere.  
   • Systematic variation / effect on punishment?  
     – Not applicable; no mention.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The paper does not mention any reward mechanism, so there is no discussion of reward costs.  
   • Systematic variation / effect on punishment?  
     – Not applicable; no mention.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward)  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The paper does not discuss rewards at all.  
   • Systematic variation / effect on punishment?  
     – Not applicable; no mention.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The text does not indicate that agents know how many “ticks” (iterations) the simulation will run.  
   • Systematic variation / effect on punishment?  
     – Not applicable; no mention.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost each round)?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. The paper does not describe any mechanism whereby agents see or react to specific peer payoffs.  
   • Systematic variation / effect on punishment?  
     – Not applicable; no mention.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Discussed?  
     – The paper does not mention knowledge of the punisher’s identity. It only states that punishing agents may “notice” or “perceive” greedy agents with some probability, not that the punished agent learns who dealt the punishment.  
   • Systematic variation / effect on punishment?  
     – Not applicable; no mention.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Discussed?  
     – No. Because the paper does not implement a reward mechanism, this does not arise.  
   • Systematic variation / effect on punishment?  
     – Not applicable; no mention.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are they different?  
   • The paper does not use “group efficiency” as an outcome in the sense of total payoff relative to a maximum achievable payoff. Instead, it tracks frequencies of strategy types (e.g., “greedy” vs. “cooperator”), average energy, and population sizes (e.g., how many agents go extinct). These outcomes are distinct from efficiency: they describe population composition and survival rather than payoffs relative to an ideal cooperative benchmark.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • The paper mentions (in some form) #1 (number of players/agents), #7 (punishment cost = 0.8), and #8 (punishment magnitude, e.g., “kill,” “pay fine,” “suspend harvest”). It does not discuss or mention chat, reward mechanisms, or the other standard public goods parameters (e.g., MPCR, knowledge of rounds, etc.).

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • The paper systematically switches among three “punishment magnitude” types (#8). However, it neither measures nor reports how these variations shift “punishment treatment effect” on total payoffs or on efficiency. Instead, it reports the final frequency of cheaters vs. cooperators. No numerical effect size is given for how a parameter shift influences the effect of punishment.  
   • No other parameter from the list is systematically varied to analyze punishment’s effect.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper gives very little direct information about how any of these 15 parameters would alter efficiency (in the public-goods sense). Its focus is on whether punishing or non-punishing cooperators survive against “conditional defector” strategies in an agent-based, resource-harvesting setting. Because it does not analyze total payoffs or maximum possible payoffs, it is not possible to derive clear, quantitative predictions on efficiency from the content of this paper. Any further statement would go beyond what the paper itself provides.

Authors: Webb, J; Foddy, M
Author Full Names: Webb, J; Foddy, M
Article Title: Vested interests in the decision to resolve social dilemma conflicts
Author Keywords: social dilemmas; institutional change; social inequalities; group processes
Keywords Plus: SANCTIONING SYSTEM; RESOURCE DILEMMAS; STRUCTURAL-CHANGE; COMMONS DILEMMA; PUBLIC GOOD; PROVISION; COOPERATION
Abstract: This exploratory study investigated the degree of correspondence between individual and group interests in the decision to adopt a sanctioning system to manage a shared resource with social dilemma properties. Fifty-two groups of four people accessed a free-running computer-simulated shared resource and had either equal or unequal resource access and experienced either an equitable or inequitable sanctioning system. Consistent with past research, a worse group outcome and greater voting for system change was found under the equitable than under the inequitable sanctioning system. However at the individual level of analysis, the results suggested that the sanctioning systems did not have the same implications for all group members and that some of those differences predicted voting for system change. The study suggests the need to investigate the various decision frames and inequitable implications associated with structural/institutional change and calls for further investigation of dependencies between micro- and macro-level units of analysis.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter survey of whether and how the study in the provided paper (Webb & Foddy) discusses each of the 15 listed features, and whether it makes any predictions about the effect of systematically varying them on the “punishment treatment effect.” Throughout, remember that:

• The paper itself never uses the term “punishment treatment effect on efficiency,” nor does it measure “efficiency” as actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff of a fully cooperative group.  
• Instead, the paper focuses on (a) whether “punishment‐rule” groups versus “equality‐rule” groups ended up with more or fewer resources remaining in a shared resource pool over time (“group outcome”) and (b) how often participants voted for each type of sanctioning system, depending on their own (inequitably or equitably) assigned access.  
• It does not provide direct numerical “effect sizes” in terms of raising or lowering efficiency, nor does it systematically manipulate most of the parameters listed below.  

With that in mind, here is the breakdown of all 15 parameters.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Yes. The experiment had exactly four players in each group (p. 9).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about varying group size?  
     – No. All groups in the study consisted of four participants (p. 9). There is no systematic variation or prediction related to different group sizes.  

2. Number of rounds  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Yes. Groups played for 25 trials (5 “blocks” of 5 trials), though sometimes a resource could collapse before 25 if overharvested (p. 10–12).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it or make predictions about the effect of changing the number of rounds?  
     – No. The paper does not manipulate the number of trials or examine how changing that number would affect punishment or efficiency.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Yes, implicitly: The paper specifically states that participants “were unable to see or verbally communicate” with one another (p. 10).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary messaging or chat?  
     – No. No chat was allowed for any group, and there is no manipulation or prediction regarding communication.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – The task was to harvest between 0 and a maximum quota (depending on one’s “access”), so it was not an “all or nothing” contribution (p. 10–11).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary whether contribution is restricted to “all or none”?  
     – No. Participants could choose any number of trees from 0 up to their maximum. The paper makes no predictions about changes in the “all or nothing” format.  

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., is there a default from which players must deviate)?  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – No. Participants simply chose how many trees to harvest each trial, with no mention of any default or forced “starting” level of contribution.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary this?  
     – No. No mention is made of default contributions being manipulated or studied.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as a multiplication factor  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – It does not mention a standard “MPCR,” but it does impose a 5% regrowth/regeneration rate on the shared resource (p. 10–11).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary that 5% growth factor or any MPCR?  
     – No. The 5% regeneration is simply used in all conditions; the paper does not investigate how changing that rate would affect outcomes or punishment.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
     – Not in the sense of a “peer‐to‐peer” punishment cost. In the study, the “punishment rule” automatically fines the single highest harvester $1.40 in each 5‐trial block. There is no cost borne by a “punisher.” (It is a structurally imposed fine, not an individual participant’s decision to punish.)  
   • Does the paper systematically vary or make predictions about changing the cost for someone to impose punishment?

   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?

   • Does the paper systematically vary or make predictions about changing that $1.40 amount?

   • Does the paper discuss this parameter?

  (1) Group outcome in terms of how many resources (trees) remained over time in the shared pool.  
  (2) Total or individual profit in currency terms, resulting from harvesting (minus fines).  
  (3) Voting preferences (willingness to keep or reject a given fining system).  

B: Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

  – (2) Number of rounds (25 trials, sometimes shortened by resource collapse)  
  – (3) Chat (explicitly disallowed)  
  – (4) Contribution format (participants could choose 0 up to a max quota, so not “all or nothing”)  
  – (6) A slight parallel to MPCR is the 5% regeneration/factor  
  – (8) Punishment magnitude is a fixed fine ($1.40)  
  – (12) Participants were not told how many rounds/trials in total  
  – (13) Partial display of group outcomes (only the average)  
• Not mentioned or not used:  
  – (5), (7), (9), (10), (11), (14), (15)  

C: For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable, when systematically varied?  
• The paper does not systematically manipulate or vary any of the 15 parameters specifically to test how those changes would alter “punishment treatment effect.”  
• It does compare “punishment rule” versus “equality rule” but keeps the fine $1.40 fixed. There are no manipulations of reward or chat or group size or known end round.  
• Hence none of the 15 parameters are tested in a way that can provide direct numeric effect sizes about how systematically altering each parameter would change outcomes.  

D: If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, solely based on the paper:  
• The paper does not give details that let us forecast changes in efficiency under systematically varied group size, round length, or fine magnitude, etc. The study keeps many factors fixed (4‐person groups, $1.40 punishment, partial information, no chat).  
• Thus, we can draw little to no direct prediction about how systematically altering any of the 15 parameters would affect efficiency as you define it. The study was not designed to vary those parameters in such a way.  
• At most, from the study’s findings, you could infer that having any “punishment rule” (fine on the highest harvester) can preserve more resources relative to a pure “equal‐fine” approach—but that does not quantify the group’s efficiency ratio, nor does it directly test variations of punishment cost, magnitude, or any other of the 15 elements in a systematic manner.

──────────────  
Hence, the paper provides only limited insights for predicting how systematically changing each of the 15 specific parameters would affect “efficiency.” It neither measures efficiency in the sense requested nor systematically manipulates most of these parameters. It does show differences in group‐level “resource remaining” and “profit” under a punishment‐rule versus equality‐rule for 4‐person groups, with a single fixed fine amount.

Throughout, keep in mind that the paper does not explicitly measure “efficiency” as “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff”; instead, it focuses on public‐goods (VCM) contributions, payoff differences between “Activists” and “Firms,” and frequencies of punishment‐stage outcomes.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. NUMBER OF PLAYERS  
• Mentioned? Yes. The paper consistently uses groups of four players (p. 6, “subjects are then randomly assigned to groups of four”).  
• Systematically varied? No. There is no indication that the number of players was ever changed.  
• Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

2. NUMBER OF ROUNDS  
• Mentioned? Yes. The VCM phase is played for 10 rounds, and the Stage Game is then repeated 10 times (pp. 6–7).  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

3. IS CHAT ENABLED BETWEEN PLAYERS?  
• Mentioned? No. The paper does not indicate any chat or direct communication between participants.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

4. IS THE CONTRIBUTION “ALL OR NOTHING”?  
• Mentioned? Not explicitly. The VCM is standard: subjects choose any integer amount of their endowment to contribute (pp. 6–7). There is no “all-or-nothing” constraint.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

5. IS THE CONTRIBUTION DEFAULT?  
• Mentioned? No. The paper does not refer to a “default contribution” mechanism.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

6. MARGINAL PER CAPITA RETURN (MPCR) OR RELATED PARAMETERS  
• Mentioned? Yes, it is the main systematic variation in the experiment: Low MPCR = 0.30 vs. High MPCR = 0.75 (p. 6).  
• Systematically varied? Yes, there are two between‐subject treatments (low versus high).  
• Effect on punishment treatment effect? The paper does not measure “efficiency” per se, but it does discuss how MPCR influences whether players go to the punishment node (“Nature”) in the Stage Game. The paper finds that with a higher MPCR (0.75), subjects “are more likely to reach the punishment node” (p. 10; Table 3) and punish the Firm. From figures in the paper (e.g., Figures 4–6), one can infer that the percentage of reaching the boycott/punishment node is roughly higher by about 5–10 percentage points in the high‐MPCR condition compared with the low‐MPCR condition, although no single numeric effect size is clearly reported in the text.

7. PUNISHMENT COST TO IMPOSE A SINGLE UNIT OF PUNISHMENT  
• Mentioned? Yes. The “boycott cost” is a fixed 10‐point cost to the Activist if the punishment stage is triggered (p. 7, Table 1).  
• Systematically varied? No (it is always 10 points).  
• Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed in terms of varying that cost.

8. PUNISHMENT MAGNITUDE (COINS DEDUCTED PER UNIT PUNISHMENT)  
• Mentioned? The Stage Game payoff tables show that if the boycott succeeds, the Firm must increase its public good contribution—effectively lowering the Firm’s payoff. The “magnitude” is not described as a per‐unit deduction; rather, it is a single forced move from, e.g., contributing 5 to contributing 15 in the public good (Table 1).  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

9. WHETHER A REWARD IS ENABLED  
• Mentioned? No. Only punishment (i.e., a boycott) is discussed.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

10. REWARD COST TO GRANT A SINGLE UNIT OF REWARD  
• Mentioned? No. There is no reward mechanism.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

11. REWARD MAGNITUDE (COINS AWARDED FOR EACH REWARD)  
• Mentioned? No.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

12. IS THE NUMBER OF ROUNDS KNOWN TO PLAYERS?  
• Mentioned? The paper states there are 10 rounds of the VCM and then 10 repetitions of the Stage Game, but does not explicitly discuss whether that was private or public knowledge. Typically, sessions do announce the total number of rounds, but the paper does not say it was varied.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

13. ARE PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN?  
• Mentioned? The paper indicates final payoffs and terminal nodes are revealed to participants at the end of each round (p. 9). Subjects also see others’ endowments in the VCM. However, there is no systematic comparison of “information displayed” conditions.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed in terms of changing that information display.

14. WHEN A PLAYER IS PUNISHED, DO THEY KNOW WHO THE SPECIFIC PUNISHER IS?  
• Mentioned? Not explicitly. Players know the roles (Activist vs. Firm) in a matched pair, so presumably the Firm knows it is the Activist who can punish. The paper does not systematically discuss or vary whether the punisher’s identity is hidden or revealed.  
• Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

15. WHEN A PLAYER IS REWARDED, DO THEY KNOW WHO THE SPECIFIC REWARDER IS?  
• Mentioned? No. There is no reward mechanism, so it is not addressed.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment effect? Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
• The paper does not explicitly use “group efficiency” (actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff) as a dependent variable. The main dependent variables are:  
  – Public good contribution amounts in the VCM (fraction of endowment contributed)  
  – Which terminal node (A1, A3, or Nature/punishment) is reached in the Stage Game  
  – Factors like “inequity aversion” (differences in VCM contributions) and “negative reciprocity” are also examined.  
• While payoff outcomes per node are shown, they do not frame it as “efficiency” or “efficiency gains.”

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Mentioned in some form (although not necessarily labeled in those exact words):  
  1 (groups of four), 2 (10 rounds), 6 (MPCR = 0.30 or 0.75), 7 (10‐point boycott cost), 8 (Firm is forced to contribute more if the boycott succeeds), 12 (10‐round structure, though not varied), 13 (payoffs revealed).  
• In total, 7 of the 15 are at least mentioned or used in the setup.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
• Only one parameter—MPCR (#6)—is systematically varied and explicitly discussed as influencing whether subjects go to the punishment/boycott node. No other parameter is systematically varied or tested with regard to its effect on punishment or any other outcome.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
• The paper gives no direct discussion of “efficiency” in the sense of total payoff relative to the maximum possible payoff. Hence, aside from noting that high MPCR sessions yielded more frequent movement to the punishment node (implying that a key monetary‐stake parameter can alter how often punishment is used), the paper provides little basis for predicting how any of the 15 parameters—either alone or in combination—would affect an “efficiency” metric. Most of the parameters (numbers of players/rounds, information displays, punishment cost, etc.) are held fixed or not mentioned, so no prediction can be made from the paper about systematically changing them. Only the discussion around MPCR suggests that higher returns might encourage more punishment usage; however, its direct effect on efficiency is not reported.
