Article Title: Watching Eyes Triggers Third-Party Punishment: The Role of Emotion Within the Eyes
Author Keywords: watching eyes; third-party punishment; emotion; reputation; eye cues
Keywords Plus: COMPETITIVE ALTRUISM; COUNTER-PUNISHMENT; ULTIMATUM-GAME; COSTLY SIGNAL; SOCIAL CUES; ANGER; COOPERATION; UNFAIRNESS; DOMINANCE; BEHAVIOR
Abstract: Third-party punishment refers to a behavioral phenomenon whereby people punish wrongdoers even if their sanction incurs personal costs but yields no direct benefits. Given the eye cues demonstrated ability to convey signals of being observed, its effect on third-party punishment, driven by virtue of its effects on others' perceptions, was investigated. In addition, emotional message featured in the eye region is crucial in social interaction, whether the emotion within the eyes serves this effect with varying degrees of influence has rarely considered. The present study aimed at exploring (a) the watching eyes effect on the third-party punishment and (b) whether this effect varies from negative eyes to positive eyes. By two experiments using a modified Third-Party Dictator Game, we displayed either eye images or control images above the question on whether to punish the dictators or not. There was no emotional diversity of eye cues in Experiment 1, and most participants tended to punish for unfair offer. However, the appearance of eye images increased the punishment relative to control images. In Experiment 2, the eye cues were subdivided into positive and negative. The effect of watching eyes on the third-party punishment was significantly stronger when the eyes were negative than positive. Results revealed that eye cues play a role in promoting the third-party punishment and offer a potential insight into the mixed findings, such that the emotion within the eyes, especially the negative expression in the eyes, may influence the watching eyes effect.

CP could consist of the lockout of workers, additional training units for football teams, increased control of athletes and firms, up to the shooting of fellow villagers of assassins. Abstract: Improving and maintaining cooperation are fundamental issues for any project to be time-persistent, and sanctioning free riders may be the most applied method to achieve it. However, the application of sanctions differs from one group (project or institution) to another. Abstract: This paper uses the framework of stochastic games to propose a model of emotions in repeated interactions. An emotional player can be in either a friendly, a neutral, or a hostile state of mind. The player transitions between the states of mind as a response to observed actions taken by the other player. The state of mind determines the player's psychological payoff which together with a material payoff constitutes the player's utility. In the friendly (hostile) state of mind the player has a positive (negative) concern for other players' material payoffs. This paper shows how emotions can both facilitate and obstruct cooperation in a repeated prisoners' dilemma game. In finitely repeated games a player who cares only for their own material payoffs can have an incentive to manipulate an emotional player into the friendly state of mind. Abstract: We investigate the effect of a full week of sleep restriction (SR) vs. well-restedness (WR) on contributions in a common public good experiment, the voluntary contributions mechanism (VCM). Abstract: It has been an old unsolved puzzle to evolutionary theorists on which mechanisms would increase large-scale cooperation in human societies. Thus, how such mechanisms operate in a biological network is still not well understood. This study addresses these questions with empirical evidence from agent based models designed to understand these network interactions. Repeated Prisoner's Dilemma games were designed to study how costly punishment, diversity, and density of connectivity interact to influence cooperation in a biological network. There were 1000 rounds in each game made up of 18 players engaged in pairwise relationship with their neighbors. This study shows three important interactions. (3) A synergy of diversity and decreasing density of connectivity favors cooperation in a biological network. Furthermore, this study also suggests a likelihood from empirical findings that spatial structures may not be favoring cooperation, as is the widely-accepted notion, but rather disfavoring defection in the global scale.

     – No. The modeling is of “make” vs. “take” vs. “sit” decisions, but not in the sense of “contribute all or zero tokens”; the paper does not use that terminology. 
   • Prediction from systematic variation?
     – None.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Mentioned?
     – No. There is no discussion of defaulting to a particular contribution level or pulling money back from a public account. 
   • Prediction from systematic variation?
     – None.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Mentioned?
     – No. The paper develops a Prisoner’s Dilemma–style payoff matrix (R, P, T, S) but never references MPCR or a “multiplier” on group contributions. 
   • Prediction from systematic variation?
     – None.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned?
     – No. “Punishment” in this manuscript is conceived as a probability π of being “caught” by some (possibly third-party) law enforcer. There is no discussion of a per-unit cost paid by a punisher. 
   • Prediction from systematic variation?
     – None.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted for each unit of punishment)
   • Mentioned?
     – No. The paper does not present a separate “punishment magnitude” variable. The “caught” outcome is simply modeled as the worst payoff. 
   • Prediction from systematic variation?
     – None.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned?
     – The paper discusses “empathic institutions” (θ) allowing partial alignment of utilities but does not treat “reward” as a costly or formal mechanism that one player grants to another. It never uses a “reward treatment” or “reward enabled” concept in the sense of typical experimental designs. 
   • Prediction from systematic variation?
     – None.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Mentioned?
      – No. As above, “reward” is not a variable with cost in this paper. 
    • Prediction from systematic variation?
      – None.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)
    • Mentioned?
      – No. The paper has no separate “reward magnitude” parameter. 
    • Prediction from systematic variation?
      – None.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
    • Mentioned?
      – No. The paper does not frame the model in terms of known or unknown horizons. 
    • Prediction from systematic variation?
      – None.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained or lost)?
    • Mentioned?
      – No. The paper does not discuss whether or how participants see one another’s payoffs. 
    • Prediction from systematic variation?
      – None.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Mentioned?
      – No. 
    • Prediction from systematic variation?
      – None.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Mentioned?
      – No. 
    • Prediction from systematic variation?
      – None.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

SUMMARY RESPONSES (A–D)

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?

   The paper does not use the specific ratio of “actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff” for a group. It instead focuses on:  
   • Whether the market (or exchange) collapses (“sit” = no trade) or thrives (“make” = trade) at equilibrium.  
   • The fraction of participants who select “make” vs. “take.”  
   • Overall “societal success,” which the authors describe in terms of wealth creation or payoffs at equilibrium.  

   These dependent variables are not labeled “efficiency” in the sense of typical public goods experiments, though the paper sometimes refers loosely to whether the market is “efficient.” Still, it is not the same formal measure as “actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff.”

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

   None of the listed 15 parameters (1–15) is explicitly mentioned or varied in the form that public goods‐with‐punishment studies typically do. The paper models only two key institutional parameters:  
   • π (probability of being caught if one “takes”)  
   • θ (empathic weight that aligns one’s utility with a partner’s)  

   These do not map onto the 15 enumerated experimental parameters from typical lab studies.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when that parameter is systematically varied?

   None. The paper does not discuss systematically varying any of the 15 parameters in order to measure how punishment treatments affect outcomes. Its theoretical analysis instead focuses on varying or combining π and θ.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

   Because the paper does not address any of these 15 parameters as they appear in a standard public goods experiment, it does not supply a basis for making predictions about how varying these parameters (e.g., “number of players,” “punishment cost per unit,” “reward magnitude,” etc.) might alter a punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency. In short, there is no direct information in the manuscript to support such predictions. The PDF focuses on a different modeling framework (the “theta-pi” model) rather than on a structured public goods–with–punishment design. Consequently, one cannot draw predictions from this paper on how those 15 specific features, or their interactions, would affect the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.

Authors: Christoforou, E; Anta, AF; Georgiou, C; Mosteiro, MA; Sánchez, A
Author Full Names: Christoforou, Evgenia; Fernandez Anta, Antonio; Georgiou, Chryssis; Mosteiro, Miguel A.; Sanchez, Angel
Article Title: Crowd Computing as a Cooperation Problem: An Evolutionary Approach
Author Keywords: Evolutionary game theory; Cooperation; Markov chains; Crowd computing; Reinforcement learning
Keywords Plus: LEARNING DYNAMICS; GAMES; PUNISHMENT; PLAY
Abstract: Cooperation is one of the socio-economic issues that has received more attention from the physics community. The problem has been mostly considered by studying games such as the Prisoner's Dilemma or the Public Goods Game. Here, we take a step forward by studying cooperation in the context of crowd computing. We introduce a model loosely based on Principal-agent theory in which people (workers) contribute to the solution of a distributed problem by computing answers and reporting to the problem proposer (master). To go beyond classical approaches involving the concept of Nash equilibrium, we work on an evolutionary framework in which both the master and the workers update their behavior through reinforcement learning. Using a Markov chain approach, we show theoretically that under certain----not very restrictive-conditions, the master can ensure the reliability of the answer resulting of the process. Then, we study the model by numerical simulations, finding that convergence, meaning that the system reaches a point in which it always produces reliable answers, may in general be much faster than the upper bounds given by the theoretical calculation. We also discuss the effects of the master's level of tolerance to defectors, about which the theory does not provide information. The discussion shows that the system works even with very large tolerances. We conclude with a discussion of our results and possible directions to carry this research further.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what this particular paper does (and does not) say, strictly following the content of the paper itself. The paper studies a repeated (“evolutionary”) principal‐agent setting—one master (principal) and n workers (agents)—where the master can audit, reward, or punish. However, it never uses the term “efficiency” (actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff) as a dependent variable. Instead, it focuses on individual‐level payoffs, probabilities of cheating, and time to “eventual correctness.” All references below are exclusively to what appears in the text, figures, and tables of the paper.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1) Number of players  
   • Does the paper discuss it? Yes. The paper always calls the number of workers n (required to be odd in their theoretical results).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it and predict how it affects the “punishment treatment effect” (i.e., how punishment influences outcomes)?  
       – They do vary n in simulations (e.g., 21, 25, 100 workers), but they do not measure “efficiency”; instead they study whether or not the system converges to correct reporting (and how quickly).  
       – There is no numerical effect size given in terms of “punishment treatment effect on efficiency,” only an examination of how larger n can degrade or slow down the convergence to correct answers when tolerance is high.  

2) Number of rounds  
   • Does the paper discuss it? The model is explicitly repeated over many rounds (the paper calls them “time steps” or “computing rounds”).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary it (as a design parameter) and predict effects on punishment or efficiency? No. They run simulations up to a certain cutoff (e.g., 1,000 or 100,000 rounds) to test convergence, but there is no systematic treatment of “number of rounds” as a parameter whose variation is reported, nor do they measure “efficiency.”  

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned or varied? No. There is no mention of real‐time communication or “chat” among workers.  

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned or varied? No. The paper’s setting is not a typical public‐goods format with discrete “all or nothing” contributions.  

5) Is the contribution defaulted (e.g., reversing the usual public‐goods decision)?  
   • Mentioned or varied? No. The paper does not discuss default contributions or a reversed contribution approach.  

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned or varied? No. This paper does not use a standard public‐goods game structure with an MPCR. Their “benefit to the master” from a correct solution is simply a payoff parameter, not an MPCR.  

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned or varied? Not in the sense of a cost to the punishing party. The paper states that the master’s act of punishing is assumed costless (the master’s main cost is auditing). There is no systematic variation or analysis of “cost per unit punishment.”  

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted for each unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Called W P₍C₎ in the paper.  
   • Systematically varied? Yes, the authors set W P₍C₎ either to 0 or 1 in their simulations to see how it affects cheating and convergence.  
   • Does the paper report any effect on “efficiency”? No. The paper reports that higher punishment magnitude leads to faster convergence to correct answers and reduced cheating probability, but it never assesses total‐group payoffs or efficiency.  

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The master gives a reward (benefit) W B₍Y₎ if a worker’s answer is eventually accepted as correct.  
   • Systematically varied (for punishment treatment effects)? The existence of a reward is central, but they do not remove it or systematically compare “reward” vs. “no‐reward” treatments for punishment’s sake. They assume a reward is always present. No data on efficiency.  

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Mentioned? Yes. M C₍Y₎ is introduced as the master’s cost to pay the worker’s reward.  
   • Systematically varied? No. They do not systematically vary that cost to measure changes in a punishment treatment. No efficiency analysis is provided.  

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Denoted W B₍Y₎ and usually fixed to 1 “by normalization.”  
   • Systematically varied? Not in a table or figure. The authors discuss that W B₍Y₎ must be high enough to cover workers’ aspiration + cost of computing, but they do not present a systematic parametric sweep to measure the punishment effect on efficiency.  

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
   • Mentioned or varied? No. The paper does not discuss whether players know in advance how many rounds will be played.  

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained or lost)?  
   • Mentioned or varied? No. The model assumes workers observe only their own payoffs. It never studies the effect of revealing others’ outcomes.  

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Mentioned or varied? No. Punishment comes from the master, not from peers, and the paper does not address whether the cheater sees who imposed it.  

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Mentioned or varied? No. As with punishment, the master’s identity is implicit; the paper does not discuss whether the worker explicitly sees “who” rewarded them or the effect of revealing that.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • No. The paper never analyzes “efficiency” as %(actual total payoff / maximum possible). It introduces payoffs only at the individual level to study cheating vs. correct reporting. The main variables of interest are:  
     (1) Probability of cheating (and how it evolves).  
     (2) Time to converge to “eventual correctness,” meaning that all answers are correct with probability 1.  
     (3) Master’s frequency of auditing over time.  
   • None of their dependent variables is described as efficiency or a ratio of total payoffs.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Explicitly mentioned:  
       (1) Number of players (n).  
       (8) Punishment magnitude (W P₍C₎).  
       (9) Whether a reward is enabled (they always enable it).  
       (10) Reward cost to the master (M C₍Y₎) is introduced but not varied in analysis.  
       (11) Reward magnitude (W B₍Y₎).  
   • These are five out of the 15.  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment (for any dependent variable) when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The paper varies (1) the number of players n and (8) punishment magnitude (0 vs. 1) in the simulations. Both affect how quickly the system reaches “correct answers” rather than “efficiency.” Numerical effect sizes (in terms of payoffs or efficiency) are not provided.

D) If you were to make predictions on how all 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not analyze efficiency at all and provides no data on total‐group payoffs. It focuses on the probability of cheating and eventual correctness. As a result, one cannot reliably predict how any of the 15 parameters would influence a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency,” because efficiency is never measured or discussed. We can only surmise that larger punishments (parameter #8) might help reduce cheating more quickly (which might help overall payoffs), but the paper does not quantify or even mention this as a group‐efficiency outcome.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Authors: McEvoy, DM
Author Full Names: McEvoy, David Michael
Article Title: Paying to punish on a free ride: member and nonmember punishments in voluntary coalitions
Author Keywords: coalitions; informal punishment; public good experiments
Keywords Plus: INTERNATIONAL ENVIRONMENTAL AGREEMENTS; PUBLIC-GOODS EXPERIMENTS; SANCTIONS; PROVISION; MECHANISM
Abstract: We explore public good experiments in which players have the opportunity to form cooperative coalitions. The decision to join a coalition is voluntary as is a member's decision to comply with the terms of the coalition. An informal enforcement mechanism is examined in which coalition members and nonmembers can impose costly punishments on one another. We find that when punishments are purely voluntary, coalition members and free-riding nonmembers are equally likely to punish noncompliant coalition members. Moreover, the extent to which nonmembers punish noncompliance does not change regardless of whether the members can credibly enforce compliance within their coalition.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter analysis of what the paper by McEvoy (2012) does or does not say about each of the 15 specified parameters, focusing on whether the paper discusses the parameter at all, provides any systematic variation of it, and/or offers predictions regarding its effect on punishment’s impact on efficiency. Throughout, “punishment treatment effect” refers to how introducing punishment changes outcomes (for example, total payoffs, cooperation, or related measures); however, the paper itself focuses on measures other than efficiency (in particular on participation in coalitions, compliance, and public good provision).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   (1) Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
       • Yes. The experiment uses 4-person groups.  
   (2) Does it systematically vary this parameter or predict how varying it affects punishment treatment effects?  
       • No. The paper uses only 4-person groups and does not vary group size.

2. Number of rounds
   (1) Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
       • Yes. There are 12 periods (rounds) in a strangers’ design.  
   (2) Does it systematically vary this parameter or predict how varying it affects punishment treatment effects?  
       • No. The paper sets the number of rounds to 12 but does not vary it or discuss how changing the number of rounds would affect punishment.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   (1) Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
       • No. There is no mention of any communication/chat feature in the experiment.  
   (2) Does it systematically vary this parameter or predict how varying it affects punishment treatment effects?  
       • No. It is not discussed at all.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   (1) Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
       • Partly. The paper indicates that “The decision to join a coalition is voluntary as is a member’s decision to comply with the terms of the coalition,” and each contributing member gives up their entire endowment of $7. Nonmembers keep it. Thus, compliance is effectively “contribute all or contribute nothing.”  
   (2) Does it systematically vary this parameter or predict how varying it affects punishment treatment effects?  
       • No. It is fixed as an all-or-nothing decision.

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much of their endowment to move from the public fund back to themselves)?
   (1) Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
       • No. The contribution is simply to forfeit one’s entire endowment ($7) if one complies, or keep it if one does not. There is no variable “default” mechanism described.  
   (2) Does it systematically vary this parameter or predict how varying it affects punishment treatment effects?  
       • No. It is not mentioned.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as the multiplication factor
   (1) Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
       • Indirectly. The public good has a total value of $3 per contributor (rather than a standard MPCR across individuals). Joint payoffs are maximized if all four players join and contribute, but the per-contributor calculation is not varied.  
   (2) Does it systematically vary this parameter or predict how varying it affects punishment treatment effects?  
       • No. The paper reports the private value ($7) vs. the public benefit ($3 per contributing member), but does not vary or analyze any explicit change in the multiplication factor.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   (1) Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
       • Yes, but in a specific way. Punishment is refusal to trade in Stage 3, which is costly because refusing to trade reduces both the punisher’s and the target’s payoff by $4 (each loses the $4 trade payoff). Thus, imposing punishment costs the punisher $4.  
   (2) Does it systematically vary this parameter or predict how varying it affects punishment treatment effects?  
       • No. The refusal-to-trade cost is fixed. The paper does not vary this $4 cost.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   (1) Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
       • Yes. If a player is punished (by someone refusing to trade), that player loses the chance at $4 from that trade.  
   (2) Does it systematically vary this parameter or predict how varying it affects punishment treatment effects?  
       • No. The $4 loss is fixed and not varied systematically.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   (1) Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
       • No. There is no provision for rewarding others; the experiment only includes punishment (refusal to trade).  
   (2) Does it systematically vary this parameter or predict how varying it affects punishment treatment effects?  
       • No. Rewards are not discussed at all.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   (1) Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
       • No. Rewards do not appear in the design.  
   (2) Does it systematically vary this parameter or predict how varying it affects punishment treatment effects?  
       • No. It is not present in the experiment.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted)
   (1) Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
       • No. There is no reward mechanism.  
   (2) Does it systematically vary this parameter or predict how varying it affects punishment treatment effects?  
       • No. It is not mentioned.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
   (1) Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
       • The paper states there are 12 periods in a strangers’ design, but it does not explicitly say whether participants were told in advance that there would be exactly 12 rounds.  
   (2) Does it systematically vary this parameter or predict how varying it affects punishment treatment effects?  
       • No. There is no mention of varying participants’ knowledge of the number of rounds.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?
   (1) Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
       • Partly. In Stage 3, participants “are provided with complete information regarding the other players’ decisions from the coalition and compliance stages” before they decide whether to trade (punish). But the exact net payoff of others is not clearly described in numeric detail. The paper does not mention displaying others’ full payoffs.  
   (2) Does it systematically vary this parameter or predict how varying it affects punishment treatment effects?  
       • No. The experiment does not vary information display in any systematic way.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   (1) Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
       • Indirectly. Because Stage 3 is bilateral between two players (they either trade or not), presumably one knows whether that specific partner refused to trade. Thus, in practice, it is clear who is punishing you in that interaction.  
   (2) Does it systematically vary this parameter or predict how varying it affects punishment treatment effects?  
       • No. That knowledge is not varied as a separate condition.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   (1) Does the paper discuss this parameter?  
       • No. The experiment provides no reward mechanism at all.  
   (2) Does it systematically vary this parameter or predict how varying it affects punishment treatment effects?  
       • No. There is no discussion of reward or awareness of reward.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
• The paper does not explicitly use group efficiency (= total payoff / maximum possible payoff) as a dependent variable.  
• The paper’s main dependent variables are (1) coalition participation (i.e., how many join the coalition), (2) public good provision (the total number of endowments contributed), and (3) instances of punishment (punishing noncompliance or nonparticipation). These differ from efficiency, since they measure participation, contributions, and punishment rather than actual total or average payoffs relative to some efficiency benchmark.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• The paper explicitly mentions or describes the following 9 parameters:  
  1. Number of players (4-person groups)  
  2. Number of rounds (12 periods)  
  4. Contribution is effectively “all or nothing” (must either keep or contribute the entire endowment)  
  6. A public good return structure ($3 per contributor), though not termed “MPCR,” is implicitly discussed  
  7. Punishment cost (the punisher forgoes the $4 trade outcome)  
  8. Punishment magnitude ($4 loss for the punished)  
  13. Players see who complied or not before deciding to punish (limited form of outcome visibility)  
  14. Because punishment is a bilateral refusal to trade, the target knows who refused to trade with them  
  2 (again) clarifies 12 periods, although it is only passively mentioned.  
• None of the other parameters (3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 15) receive explicit treatment in terms of definitions or systematic variations.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• The paper systematically compares three punishment conditions (no punishment, purely voluntary punishment, quasi-voluntary punishment). It does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters above (such as group size, number of rounds, or cost of punishment); these remain fixed across conditions.  
• Thus, strictly speaking, the paper does not vary any of these 15 parameters in a manner that would allow it to discuss or compute an effect size on efficiency or related dependent variables.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
• The paper provides no direct statements, data, or analyses about how systematically changing any of these parameters would alter punishment’s impact on group efficiency. It holds virtually all parameters constant while only changing the ability (and credibility) to punish.  
• Consequently, there is little to no direct guidance on how varying these 15 parameters, individually or in interaction, would affect punishment’s impact on group efficiency. All we learn from the paper is that when members can credibly punish noncompliance (quasi-voluntary punishment), public good provision increases; however, that result alone does not conclusively predict how systematically altering any of the 15 parameters would affect efficiency. Thus, based solely on this paper, one cannot reliably predict how the 15 parameters or their interactions might alter punishment’s effect on efficiency.
reference_APA: McEvoy, David Michael (2012). Paying to punish on a free ride: member and nonmember punishments in voluntary coalitions. APPLIED ECONOMICS LETTERS.

Authors: Watve, MG; Damle, A; Ganguly, B; Kale, A; Dahanukar, N
Author Full Names: Watve, Milind G.; Damle, Anuja; Ganguly, Bratati; Kale, Anagha; Dahanukar, Neelesh
Article Title: Blackmailing: the keystone in the human mating system
Keywords Plus: EXTRA-PAIR PATERNITY; LIFE-HISTORY; EVOLUTION; COOPERATION; STRATEGIES; PUNISHMENT; SEX
Abstract: Background: The human mating system is characterized by bi-parental care and faithful monogamy is highly valued in most cultures. Marriage has evolved as a social institution and punishment for extra pair mating (EPM) or adultery is common. However, similar to other species with bi-parental care, both males and females frequently indulge in EPM in secrecy since it confers certain gender specific genetic benefits. Stability of faithful monogamy is therefore a conundrum. We model human mating system using game theory framework to study the effects of factors that can stabilize or destabilize faithful committed monogamy. Results: Although mate guarding can partly protect the genetic interests, we show that it does not ensure monogamy. Social policing enabled by gossiping is another line of defense against adultery unique to humans. However, social policing has a small but positive cost to an individual and therefore is prone to free riding. We suggest that since exposure of adultery can invite severe punishment, the policing individuals can blackmail opportunistically whenever the circumstances permit. If the maximum probabilistic benefit of blackmailing is greater than the cost of policing, policing becomes a non-altruistic act and stabilizes in the society. We show that this dynamics leads to the coexistence of different strategies in oscillations, with obligate monogamy maintained at a high level. Deletion of blackmailing benefit from the model leads to the complete disappearance of obligate monogamy. Conclusions: Obligate monogamy can be maintained in the population in spite of the advantages of EPM. Blackmailing, which makes policing a non-altruistic act, is crucial for the maintenance of faithful monogamy. Although biparental care, EPM, mate guarding and punishment are shared by many species, gossiping and blackmailing make the human mating system unique.

Abstract: This work presents the results of framed field experiments designed to study the co-enforcement of access to common pool resources. The experiments were conducted in the field with artisanal fishers in Chile. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what the paper does (and does not) say about each of the 15 listed parameters, followed by the requested four‐part summary (A–D).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
• Discussed? Yes. The experiment always has 3 “insiders” and 3 “outsiders” (6 total players), but this number is not systematically varied across treatments.  
• Effect of systematic variation? Not discussed. The paper uses the same group size in all treatments and does not examine how changing group size would affect the punishment (co‐enforcement) treatment or any measure of efficiency or earnings.

2) Number of rounds  
• Discussed? Yes. Each part of the experiment lasts up to 15 rounds for each TURF (unless the resource is depleted earlier), but the number of rounds is not systematically varied as an experimental treatment.  
• Effect of systematic variation? Not discussed. The paper does not examine how changing the known or unknown horizon of 15 rounds would alter punishment outcomes.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
• Discussed? Yes. All insiders (blue‐group participants) can freely discuss harvest and monitoring strategies, whereas outsiders cannot. However, chat availability is not experimentally varied—insiders always communicate and outsiders never do.  
• Effect of systematic variation? Not discussed. The paper does not test any condition without insider communication or with outsider communication enabled.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Discussed? No. Harvest decisions in the experiment range from 0 to 6 units, and monitoring contributions are made in increments of 100 pesos (or by voting for one of several increments). The paper does not study forced “all‐or‐nothing” contributions and makes no predictions about such variations.

5) Is there a contribution default?  
• Discussed? No. The experiment does not use a “default” mechanism for how much of a participant’s resources go to a public/pooled fund. Players choose harvest and monitoring expenditures directly. No discussion of a default setting or how varying it would affect outcomes.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or a related multiplier/multiplication factor  
• Discussed? Not in terms of “MPCR.” The paper implements a stock‐growth CPR with a 10% growth rate each round, but it does not frame the design around the usual “MPCR” language from linear public‐goods games.  
• Effect of systematic variation? Not addressed. The paper does not vary the resource’s growth parameters experimentally nor reports how such variation would affect the punishment treatment effect.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Discussed? Partially. Insiders must buy “red chips” at a cost of 100 pesos per chip, which increases the probability of catching outsiders. However, this cost is the same across all co‐enforcement treatments; the paper does not vary the per‐chip cost systematically.  
• Effect of systematic variation? Not discussed. The paper does not examine how changing the cost of monitoring (i.e., punishment “cost”) would change outcomes.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player per unit punished)  
• Discussed? Yes. This is the central variation in “Low Fine” (650 pesos) versus “High Fine” (1300 pesos).  
• Effect of systematic variation? Yes, for outcomes such as poaching frequency, outsider earnings from poaching, and insider investments in monitoring. Numerically, the paper finds that higher fines (1300 pesos) allow insiders to achieve negative average poaching earnings for outsiders. However, the paper does not provide a specific “efficiency” measure or effect size on “efficiency.” Instead, it reports that higher fines tend to reduce outsiders’ net earnings from poaching more and help insiders “eliminate the average gains from poaching.”

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
• Discussed? No. The design is strictly about deterring poaching via monitoring and fines; there is no mention of a reward mechanism.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Discussed? No. There is no reward treatment in the design.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
• Discussed? No. Same as above—no reward mechanism is included.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?  
• Discussed? Yes. Subjects are told the game lasts for up to 15 rounds, but the resource can close earlier if depleted below a critical stock. There is no experimental variation of “known vs. unknown horizon.”  
• Effect of systematic variation? Not discussed.

13) Are peer outcomes shown?  
• Discussed? Partially. The total harvest from each zone and the total monitoring contributions are publicly announced each round, but individual decisions remain private. The paper does not manipulate “information display” in different ways; it uses the same announcement procedure in all treatments.  
• Effect of systematic variation? Not discussed.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• Discussed? No. Monitoring is announced only in aggregate (total chips). Outsiders who poach learn if they drew a “red chip,” but not the identity of which insider contributed it. The design does not vary the anonymity of punishers.  
• Effect of systematic variation? Not discussed.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
• Discussed? No. No reward mechanism is used, so there is nothing in the paper about identifying the rewarder.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?  
• The paper does not formally measure “group efficiency” as “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff.” Instead, it primarily reports:  
  – The amount outsiders poach (“poaching”).  
  – Insiders’ harvests and net earnings (including harvest revenue minus monitoring costs).  
  – Outsiders’ net earnings from poaching (including fines).  
  – The number of rounds (periods) before resource depletion.  
• While the authors sometimes refer to improvements as “more efficient,” they do not supply an explicit “efficiency” ratio or formula. Their main outcome variables thus differ from a formal efficiency measure.

B) Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• The paper explicitly mentions:  
  1) Number of players (always 6, no variation).  
  2) Number of rounds (up to 15, not varied).  
  3) Chat for insiders (always allowed, not varied).  
  7) Monitoring cost (100 pesos per “red chip”), but not varied across conditions.  
  8) Punishment magnitude (fines of 650 vs. 1300 pesos), which is systematically varied.  
  12) The horizon/length is known (up to 15 rounds).  
  13) Aggregate outcomes announced.  
• Discussed in passing but not really “varied or tested”: #1, #2, #3, #7, #12, #13.  
• Systematically varied only for #8 (and also whether insiders vote vs. individually contribute is varied, but that voting vs. individual contribution is not one of the enumerated 15 parameters above).

C) For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
• Only parameter #8—the punishment (fine) magnitude—is systematically varied and analyzed. The authors do present differences between “Low Fine” (650 pesos) and “High Fine” (1300 pesos) and show that the higher fine helps insiders drive average outsider poaching earnings below zero.  
• None of the other parameters on the list (1–7, 9–15) are systematically varied or analyzed in terms of their effect on co‐enforcement or punishment. The paper therefore does not provide numerical effect sizes for systematically varying any parameter besides the fine level.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
• The paper’s sole systematic variation relates to parameter #8 (fine magnitude). Higher fines (1300 vs. 650 pesos) reduce outsiders’ net gains from poaching significantly and can push those earnings below zero, indicating stronger deterrence.  
• Beyond that, the authors do not provide evidence on how systematically altering the other parameters (e.g., number of players, presence of communication, or information conditions) would affect “efficiency.” Therefore, the paper offers little to no direct basis for predicting how the other parameters or their interactions would shift the punishment treatment effect specifically on “group efficiency.”  

In short, almost all of the 15 parameters are not experimentally varied in this study, and the authors do not speak to how modifying them would change any “efficiency” ratio. The only systematic variation is the magnitude of the monetary fine (parameter #8), for which the study finds that increasing it reduces poaching gains and can eliminate outsiders’ average net earnings from poaching, but the paper does not track a formal efficiency measure.

Abstract: While all species are unique, only humans have been able to develop complex tools and technology, and to place energy and their environment under control. Social learning and extrasomatic storage of information enabled rapid development in recent evolutionary times. Our argument is that human uniqueness lies in human sociality. Keywords Plus: ULTIMATUM GAME; INFORMAL INSURANCE; FOLK THEOREM; EVOLUTION; INSTITUTIONS; ENFORCEMENT; PUNISHMENT; COOPERATION; REPUTATION; FAIRNESS
Abstract: While the threat of retaliation can stabilize cooperation, retaliatory cultures have also been linked to violence and war. There is little systematic evidence for cross-cultural variation in the use and consequences of retaliation in real-life settings. Analyzing a novel data set of foul play from three seasons of nine professional men's soccer leagues (n = 230 , 113), I show that players from a cultural background that places a higher value on revenge are more likely to retaliate for a foul during a game but are not more likely to commit fouls overall. I find that players are more retaliatory early on in a game, consistent with the use of retaliation as a deterrent to future transgression. Retaliation is indeed found to limit repeated offenses, as long as the perpetrator's cultural background also emphasizes retaliation. This informal conflict management interacts with formal sanctioning by the referee in several ways. Victims are less likely to retaliate if the foul was sanctioned with a yellow card, indicating a crowding out by the formal punishment mechanism. Both forms of sanction successfully reduce repeated offenses by the perpetrator of a foul, with sanctioning by a yellow card being around three times as effective as retaliation by the victim. These results provide unique evidence for cultural differences in establishing and maintaining cooperative equilibria and for the interaction of formal and informal punishment mechanisms for sustaining cooperation.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER–BY–PARAMETER CHECK  

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Only implicitly.  Throughout the paper the symbol n is used for “number of entities,” but this is never tied to an actual public-goods game or varied experimentally.  
   • Systematic-variation prediction? No.  

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? Not mentioned.  
   • Prediction? No.  

3. Chat / communication between players  
   • Mentioned? Yes, once.  p. 23 (sec. 3.2) cites Ostrom et al. (1992) and states that “individuals are more willing to engage in costly punishment when they are able to communicate and thereby coordinate their punishing behavior.”  
   • Systematic-variation prediction? A qualitative prediction is implied: enabling communication should strengthen punishment’s effectiveness (the paper does not quantify the effect).  

4. “All-or-nothing” contributions  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Prediction? No.  

5. Contribution default / take-back framing  
   • Mentioned? No.

   • Mentioned? No numeric MPCR or linear-public-goods formulation appears.  
   • Prediction? No.  

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   • Mentioned? Yes, conceptually: punishment is described as “costly,” and Bowles & Gintis (2011) are quoted to say that “the total cost of punishing a particular target declines as the number of punishers increases.”  
   • Systematic-variation prediction? No explicit parametric prediction; no numbers.  

8. Punishment magnitude (deduction per unit received)  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Prediction? No.  

9. Reward enabled or not  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Prediction? No.  

10. Reward cost  
    • Mentioned? No.  
    • Prediction? No.  

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Mentioned? No.  
    • Prediction? No.  

12. Are the remaining rounds publicly known?  
    • Mentioned? No.  
    • Prediction? No.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mentioned? No.  
    • Prediction? No.  

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
    • Mentioned? No.  
    • Prediction? No.  

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
    • Mentioned? No.  
    • Prediction? No.  


----------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary requested in points A–D  

A. Dependent variables actually used in the paper  
   • The paper never reports “group efficiency” (total payoff / maximum payoff).  
   • It works with theoretical constructs such as average individual fitness, group fitness, and “welfare,” none of which are operationalised with experimental payoff data.  
   • Hence “efficiency,” “contribution rate,” etc., are not empirically measured; they are conceptually distinct from the paper’s variables.  

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
   • Only 3 of 15 are even mentioned:  
       – Parameter 3 (communication / chat)  
       – Parameter 7 (punishment cost, only qualitatively)  
       – Parameter 8 (punishment magnitude) is **not** really mentioned; punishment’s “severity” is never separated from its cost.  
   • So either 1 or 2 parameters depending on how one counts punishment-cost vs. punishment-magnitude; conservatively, 2 parameters (3 and 7).  

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of **systematically varying** that parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
   • Zero.  
   • The single qualitative statement about communication does not constitute a systematic variation with an effect size, and no table or figure quantifies it.  

D. What predictions about the 15 parameters’ influence on punishment’s effect on efficiency can be made from this paper alone?  
   • Very little.  The only direct hint is that allowing players to communicate (enable chat) should make them “more willing to engage in costly punishment,” which, by usual logic, would increase cooperation and thus efficiency.  
   • The paper also argues in general terms that punishment will be more effective (and less individually costly) when many punishers can coordinate, implying that lower personal punishment costs (parameter 7) or mechanisms that spread cost over many punishers would help efficiency, but no explicit functional form is offered.  
   • For the remaining 13 parameters the paper provides no information, so no prediction can be extracted.  

----------------------------------------------------------------------
In short, the article is a high-level theoretical essay on multilevel selection and polycentric governance.  It is **not** an experimental study of public-goods games, does **not** manipulate any of the 15 design parameters, and therefore yields almost no usable quantitative priors for predicting how those parameters alter the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.

Keywords Plus: ITERATED PRISONERS-DILEMMA; EVOLUTION; DYNAMICS; PARTICIPATION; EXCLUSION; LONERS; OPTION; GAME
Abstract: Problems of cooperation have often been simplified as the choice between defection and cooperation, although in many empirical situations it is also possible to walk away from the interaction. We present the results of two lab-in-the-field experiments with a diverse pool of subjects who play optional and compulsory public goods games both with and without punishment. We find that the most important institution to foster cooperation is punishment, which is more effective in a compulsory game. In contrast to Rand and Nowak (Nat Commun 2(1):1-7, 2011), we find that loners are not responsible for anti-social punishment, which is mostly imputable to low-contributors (free-riders). Loners neither totally free-ride nor they significantly punish cooperators (or other types of players): they simply avoid all forms of participation whenever possible.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what this particular paper does—and does not—say about each of the 15 features, followed by a four‐part summary (A–D) as requested.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
• Mentioned? Yes. All sessions use groups of four players.  
• Systematically varied? No. The group size is always 4; the paper does not discuss how changing the number of players might affect punishment or efficiency.

2. Number of rounds  
• Mentioned? The paper describes repeated play and reshuffling of group members, but it does not clearly state the total number of rounds, nor whether participants knew any endpoint.  
• Systematically varied? No. There is no manipulation of “how many rounds” or any discussion of how changing the number of rounds would affect the punishment treatment effect.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
• Mentioned? No. There is no mention of players being able to communicate, nor any systematic variation of communication.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Mentioned? The paper clarifies that each player can contribute 0, 10, 20, 30, or 40 tokens out of 40, so it is not strictly “all or nothing.”  
• Systematically varied? No. The paper does not discuss any variation of this feature or any impact on punishment or efficiency.

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much of their endowment to move back)?  
• Mentioned? No. The paper does not refer to a “default” contribution regime.  
• Systematically varied? No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
• Mentioned? Yes. The common fund is doubled and split four ways, implying an MPCR = 0.5.  
• Systematically varied? No. The paper does not discuss changing the MPCR or how such a change would affect the punishment treatment effect.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Mentioned? Yes. Players choose either Option B (costing themselves 4 points) or Option C (costing themselves 8 points). However, these costs do not change across conditions.  
• Systematically varied? No. The paper uses the same cost structure in all sessions and does not predict how varying it would change outcomes.

8. Punishment magnitude (points deducted from the target)  
• Mentioned? Yes. Option B removes 12 points from the target, and Option C removes 24 points.  
• Systematically varied? No. The magnitude is fixed; the paper does not discuss what would happen if it changed.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
• Mentioned? No. The experiments involve punishment only; there is no reward mechanism.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Mentioned? No. As there is no reward, this parameter does not appear.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a rewarded player)  
• Mentioned? No. Same as above; not applicable.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
• Mentioned? No. There is no statement on whether participants knew precisely how many rounds they would play, nor any systematic variation of that factor.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much peers gained/lost)?  
• Mentioned? Some information is given: participants see how much each group member contributed (though not which individual contributed which amount) before punishment decisions. However, there is no full tracking of others’ payoffs, only contributions.  
• Systematically varied? No. The paper does not manipulate whether or how feedback is displayed.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• Mentioned? Yes. The paper states that punishment proceeds via the strategy method and that targets do not know the specific identity of their punisher.  
• Systematically varied? No. This feature is fixed, with no discussion of how changing it would affect the punishment treatment effect.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
• Mentioned? No. There is no reward mechanism, so this parameter does not appear.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (actual total payoff ÷ maximum possible total payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
• The paper does not measure or analyze “efficiency” in the sense of actual vs. maximum possible payoff. Instead, it focuses on (1) contribution levels (also described as “cooperation”), (2) optional vs. compulsory participation (who opts out versus who stays in and contributes), and (3) punishment behavior (both “normal” and “anti‐social”). These are distinct from efficiency measures because they do not directly assess total or average earnings as a fraction of the maximum possible.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Mentioned explicitly (but not varied):  
  1) Number of players (always 4),  
  2) Number of rounds (not really varied or clearly specified, but the design does involve repeated interactions),  
  6) MPCR = 0.5,  
  7) Punishment cost (4 or 8 points),  
  8) Punishment magnitude (12 or 24 points),  
  13) Partial information display of others’ contributions,  
  14) Punisher identity hidden.  
• Not mentioned or not used at all: 3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 15.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable, when systematically varied?  
• None. The paper does not systematically vary any of those 15 parameters (e.g., it does not change group size, does not change the punishment cost ratio mid‐experiment, does not remove or alter the feedback structure, and does not introduce or remove anonymity). The only experimental variation is (a) optional vs. compulsory participation and (b) the presence or absence of punishment. Neither of those appears in the 15‐parameter list above.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, solely based on the content of this paper, what would they be?  
• The paper does not provide systematic discussion or data on how varying group size, cost/magnitude of punishment, or any other of the listed parameters would affect efficiency (understood as total payoff ÷ maximal payoff). Accordingly, there is little basis in the paper’s text or tables for drawing clear, quantitative predictions about each parameter’s influence on efficiency. The main result is that adding punishment, as the authors implemented it, increases contributions compared to no‐punishment conditions, especially under compulsory participation. But how that relationship would change if any of the 15 parameters were varied is not addressed in the paper, so we cannot make evidence‐based numerical predictions.

Authors: Zhao, CY; Zheng, GZ; Zhang, C; Zhang, JQ; Chen, L
Author Full Names: Zhao, Chenyang; Zheng, Guozhong; Zhang, Chun; Zhang, Jiqiang; Chen, Li
Article Title: Emergence of cooperation under punishment: A reinforcement learning perspective
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS GAME; PRISONERS-DILEMMA; EVOLUTION; RECIPROCITY; PROMOTES; REWARD; BEHAVIOR; NETWORK; RULES
Abstract: Punishment is a common tactic to sustain cooperation and has been extensively studied for a long time. While most of previous game-theoretic work adopt the imitation learning framework where players imitate the strategies of those who are better off, the learning logic in the real world is often much more complex. In this work, we turn to the reinforcement learning paradigm, where individuals make their decisions based upon their experience and long-term returns. Specifically, we investigate the prisoners' dilemma game with a Q-learning algorithm, and cooperators probabilistically pose punishment on defectors in their neighborhood. Unexpectedly, we find that punishment could lead to either continuous or discontinuous cooperation phase transitions, and the nucleation process of cooperation clusters is reminiscent of the liquid-gas transition. The analysis of a Q-table reveals the evolution of the underlying psychologic changes, which explains the nucleation process and different levels of cooperation. The uncovered first-order phase transition indicates that great care needs to be taken when implementing the punishment compared to the continuous scenario.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter check, based strictly on the text, figures, and tables of the provided paper. Throughout, note that the paper focuses on the fraction of cooperators (fC) and on Q‐learning dynamics in the Prisoner’s Dilemma; it does not use the term “efficiency” (actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff of a fully cooperative group) as a dependent variable. Unless otherwise noted below, the paper provides no information about how systematically varying a parameter would affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency. References to any effect on “cooperation level” or “fraction of cooperators” should not be taken as statements about efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players
   • Discussed in the paper?  
     – The paper places N players on an L×L square lattice with periodic boundary conditions (typically L=100).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary this parameter or predict its effect on punishment treatment outcomes (for efficiency or any other dependent variable)?  
     – No. The paper fixes L (usually 100×100). It does not report any systematic variation of N or L, nor any effect sizes for changing the number of players.

2) Number of rounds
   • Discussed in the paper?  
     – The paper describes running the simulation for a large number of rounds (e.g., “a transient of at least 10^7 steps and then average over 500 steps”).  
   • Does the paper systematically vary this parameter or predict its effect on punishment treatment outcomes?  
     – No. The paper fixes a sufficiently large number of rounds to ensure convergence. No systematic variation is reported.

3) Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussed in the paper?  
     – No.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary this parameter?  
     – No mention is made of any communication or chat.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussed in the paper?  
     – The paper sets up the Prisoner’s Dilemma with two actions, Cooperate (C) or Defect (D). This is effectively a binary choice, but the paper does not use language about “all or nothing contributions.”  
   • Does the paper systematically vary this parameter?  
     – No. There is no mention of varying from partial contributions to binary contributions.

5) Is there a contribution default (e.g., do players decide how much to move from a public fund)?
   • Discussed in the paper?  
     – No. The paper describes a standard two‐choice Prisoner’s Dilemma; it does not describe any default or continuous contribution amount.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary this parameter?  
     – No mention.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor
   • Discussed in the paper?  
     – The paper does not use an MPCR or “public goods multiplier”; instead, it uses a Prisoner’s Dilemma payoff matrix with parameter b (0 < b < 1) that increases the temptation payoff T = 1 + b.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary this parameter or predict its effect on punishment treatment outcomes (for any dependent variable)?  
     – Yes, the paper systematically varies b from 0 to 1 (see Fig. 8a) to examine how cooperation (fraction of cooperators) changes. It finds that higher b (i.e., higher temptation) generally reduces cooperation. However, the paper does not express results in terms of group efficiency. No numerical “efficiency” effect size is given.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussed in the paper?  
     – Yes. The paper denotes this cost as c, which is subtracted from a cooperator whenever that cooperator punishes a defector.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary this parameter or predict its effect on punishment treatment outcomes (for any dependent variable)?  
     – Yes, the paper systematically varies c (usually 0 ≤ c ≤ 1) in Figs. 2 and 4 (and related text), focusing on its effect on the fraction of cooperators. They find that higher c typically lowers cooperation; for some parameter ranges, cooperation transitions can be discontinuous. The paper does not give a numerical effect size for efficiency.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
   • Discussed in the paper?  
     – Yes. The paper refers to it as punishment intensity p.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary this parameter or predict its effect on punishment treatment outcomes (for any dependent variable)?  
     – Yes, p is systematically varied (0 ≤ p ≤ 1) in Figs. 2–3, among others. Increasing p generally promotes cooperation if c is not too large, but the paper does not report effect sizes for efficiency.

9) Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussed in the paper?  
     – No. The paper mentions that “punishment and reward are also posed simultaneously” in some other works, but here they only study punishment, not reward.  
   • Does the paper systematically vary this parameter?  
     – No. No reward is used.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Discussed in the paper?  
      – No.  
    • Does the paper systematically vary this parameter?  
      – No.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)
    • Discussed in the paper?  
      – No.  
    • Does the paper systematically vary this parameter?  
      – No.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Discussed in the paper?  
      – No.  
    • Does the paper systematically vary this parameter?  
      – No.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?
    • Discussed in the paper?  
      – No. The paper does not describe any display of peer payoffs.  
    • Does the paper systematically vary this parameter?  
      – No.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Discussed in the paper?  
      – No.  
    • Does the paper systematically vary this parameter?  
      – No.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Discussed in the paper?  
      – No. (The paper does not implement reward.)  
    • Does the paper systematically vary this parameter?  
      – No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY RESPONSES

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   – The paper does not use group efficiency or total/average payoff as a primary outcome. Its main dependent variable is the fraction of cooperators, fC. It also analyzes Q‐table entries and “spatiotemporal patterns,” but not efficiency.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – #1 (Number of players) is mentioned but not systematically varied or studied for its effect.  
   – #2 (Number of rounds) is mentioned only as a large fixed number to allow convergence.  
   – #6 (MPCR or related) is replaced by the temptation parameter b in the Prisoner’s Dilemma; the paper does systematically vary b.  
   – #7 (Punishment cost c) is discussed extensively and varied systematically.  
   – #8 (Punishment magnitude p) is also discussed extensively and varied systematically.  
   – The remaining parameters (#3, #4, #5, #9, #10, #11, #12, #13, #14, #15) do not appear or are not varied in the study.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   – Strictly speaking, the paper’s “dependent variable” is the fraction of cooperators, not group efficiency. They systematically vary three main parameters that are relevant to “punishment treatment” in the context of the Prisoner’s Dilemma:  
       • b (the “temptation” payoff parameter, analogous to T−R in PD),  
       • c (the punishment cost),  
       • p (the punishment intensity).  
     They show how changing these parameters alters the fraction of cooperators and can yield continuous vs. discontinuous transitions in cooperation. There is no mention of numerical effect sizes on “efficiency,” only on fraction of cooperators.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   – Because the paper never analyzes group efficiency, it leaves us with no direct statements about total payoffs. We therefore cannot determine precise effect sizes or formal predictions about efficiency. We only know that, in terms of fraction of cooperators, (1) sufficiently large punishment intensity (p) can boost cooperation if cost c is not too large, (2) too high cost can make punishment backfire, and (3) higher temptation (b) undermines cooperation unless punishment is both intense and affordable. Extrapolating these insights to “efficiency” is speculative given the paper’s focus on cooperation levels rather than total payoffs. Accordingly, the paper provides little basis for definitive predictions about how systematically varying the 15 parameters, beyond p, c, and b, or any of their interactions, would affect a measure of efficiency.

Authors: Alvarez-Benjumea, A; Valentim, V
Author Full Names: Alvarez-Benjumea, Amalia; Valentim, Vicente
Article Title: The Enforcement of Political Norms
Author Keywords: political norms; political stigma; radical right; norm enforcement; social sanctions
Keywords Plus: 3RD-PARTY PUNISHMENT; SOCIAL NORMS; COOPERATION; PERSISTENCE; VIOLATION; SUPPORT
Abstract: Democracies generate norms prescribing what behaviours and preferences are deemed acceptable. But what keeps these political norms in place? We expect that they are enforced by observers who disapprove of norm-breaching behaviour and are willing to apply sanctions that make it socially costly. We test this expectation with a survey in Spain, where respondents were shown pictures of individuals with different political views. We focus on norms against radical-right preferences, one of the most established political norms. In line with our expectations, individuals disapprove of radical-right preferences more than other political preferences. This makes them more likely to socially sanction those preferences, which they do mainly in indirect ways that do not force interaction with the person breaching the norm. We provide evidence on the individual-level predictors of norm enforcement. Our findings highlight the micro-level mechanisms by which social influence affects the behaviour of democratic citizens.

Authors: Philippsen, A; Mieth, L; Buchner, A; Bell, R
Author Full Names: Philippsen, Ana; Mieth, Laura; Buchner, Axel; Bell, Raoul
Article Title: People punish defection, not failures to conform to the majority
Keywords Plus: ANTISOCIAL PUNISHMENT; SOCIAL NORMS; COOPERATION; RECOGNITION; EVOLUTION; MODELS; MEMORY; ENFORCEMENT; DILEMMAS; PROGRAM
Abstract: Do people punish others for defecting or for failing to conform to the majority? In two experiments, we manipulated whether the participants' partners cooperated or defected in the majority of the trials of a Prisoner's Dilemma game. The effects of this base-rate manipulation on cooperation and punishment were assessed using a multinomial processing tree model. High compared to low cooperation rates of the partners increased participants' cooperation. When participants' cooperation was not enforced through partner punishment, the participants' cooperation was closely aligned to the cooperation rates of the partners. Moral punishment of defection increased when cooperation rates were high compared to when defection rates were high. However, antisocial punishment of cooperation when defection rates were high was much less likely than moral punishment of defection when cooperation rates were high. In addition, antisocial punishment was increased when cooperation rates were high compared to when defection rates were high. The latter two results contradict the assumption that people punish conformity-violating behavior regardless of whether the behavior supports or disrupts cooperation. Punishment is thus sensitive to the rates of cooperation and defection but, overall, the results are inconsistent with the idea that punishment primarily, let alone exclusively, serves to enforce conformity with the majority.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
• Discussed?  
  – The paper uses a 2‐player Prisoner’s Dilemma (PD) setup. Participants always play in pairs.  
• Systematically varied?  
  – No. There is no variation in the number of players across conditions or any mention of changing group size.  
• Effect on punishment treatment?  
  – Not discussed at all.

2. Number of rounds  
• Discussed?  
  – The paper states there are 30 trials (with 5 training trials, and 25 “main” trials) per experiment.  
• Systematically varied?  
  – No. The number of rounds is fixed at 30 (5 training + 25 main).  
• Effect on punishment treatment?  
  – Not discussed. There is no reported manipulation of the number of rounds.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
• Discussed?  
  – Not mentioned. Participants had no direct communication channel other than the programmed feedback.  
• Systematically varied?  
  – No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment?  
  – Not discussed.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Discussed?  
  – The paper is about a standard PD choice: “cooperate” or “defect.” Although that is indeed a binary decision, the paper does not frame it as “all‐or‐nothing” in a public‐goods sense.  
• Systematically varied?  
  – No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment?  
  – Not discussed.

5. Is the contribution default (do players move endowment from the public fund to their hand)?  
• Discussed?

  – No.

  – Not discussed.

• Systematically varied?  
  – No. The monetary payoff structure is fixed.  
• Effect on punishment treatment?  
  – Not discussed.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Discussed?  
  – Yes. Participants can invest 1, 2, or 3 points to punish their partners, which subtracts 10, 20, or 30 points from the partner’s balance, respectively.  
• Systematically varied?  
  – No. The choice is between three fixed costs (1–3 points). There is no condition that changes these costs.  
• Effect on punishment treatment?  
  – Not discussed in terms of systematically altering the (1,2,3) cost structure.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted for each unit of punishment)  
• Discussed?

  – No.

• Systematically varied?  
  – No. Feedback is always provided.  
• Effect on punishment treatment?  
  – Not discussed in terms of changing that parameter.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• Discussed?  
  – Each round is a two‐player interaction (one partner’s picture is shown). Participants see if the partner punished them and for how much (in Experiment 1). They therefore know which partner imposed punishment in that round. However, the paper does not treat identity revelation as a systematically varied design feature; it is simply part of the two‐player setup.  
• Systematically varied?  
  – No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment?  
  – Not discussed beyond describing standard feedback.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
• Discussed?  
  – Not applicable. The paper does not use rewards at all.  
• Systematically varied?  
  – No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment?  
  – Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A: Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
• The paper does not report measures of “group efficiency” in the sense that you define it (actual total payoff relative to a fully cooperative ideal). The main dependent variables are:  
  – C: Cooperation rate (the probability that the participant cooperates).  
  – PMoral: “Moral” punishment of defection.  
  – PHypocritical: “Hypocritical” punishment of mutual defection.  
  – PAntisocial: “Antisocial” punishment of unilateral cooperation.  
  – b: A general punishment bias.  
• These differ from efficiency because they track how often participants cooperate or punish, rather than total outcomes relative to that of a fully cooperative group.

B: Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• In some form, the paper gives details about the number of players (parameter 1), the number of rounds (2), the punishment cost and magnitude (7 and 8), and the fact that peer outcomes are displayed (13). It also notes that participants know their total number of trials (12) and that no rewards are offered (9–11 not used). However, it does not systematically vary any of these parameters. The rest (3, 4, 5, 6, 14, 15) are either absent or only mentioned obliquely without any experimental manipulation or direct discussion.

C: For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• None. The paper does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters. The key manipulation in the paper is the proportion of cooperating vs. defecting partners (60% vs. 40%), but that does not correspond to any of the listed parameters (it is not the group size, not the number of rounds, not the cost of punishment, etc.). There is therefore no direct discussion of an effect of systematically varying any of the 15 parameters on punishment outcomes.

D: If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
• Because the paper does not discuss efficiency measures and does not systematically vary any of those 15 parameters, it provides little basis to predict how changing them would alter a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” The paper instead focuses on how the base rate of cooperation in a population (60% vs. 40%) affects types of punishment and cooperation. Consequently, there is effectively no guidance in the text for predicting how any of those 15 parameters might change group efficiency outcomes under a punishment regime. One could only say that if higher cooperation is induced (as was observed when most partners cooperated), average payoffs might rise; but the paper does not speak to your parameters or to efficiency per se.
