Article Title: Group membership and adolescents' third-party punishment: a moderated chain mediation model
Author Keywords: group membership; third-party punishment; unfair perception; anger; adolescents
Keywords Plus: COSTLY PUNISHMENT; GROUP BIAS; FAIRNESS; ANGER; COMPENSATION; COOPERATION; ENVIRONMENT; FAVORITISM; PSYCHOLOGY; CHILDRENS
Abstract: Third-party punishment (TPP) reflects people's social preference for fairness norms and is fundamental to maintaining fairness norms on a large scale. Several empirical studies have shown that the offender's group membership impacts TPP, but the detailed mechanisms have yet to be fully elucidated. The current study used the third-party punishment game task to explore the relationship between group membership, perceived unfairness, anger, and adolescents' TPP. A total of 306 teenagers aged 12 to 15 were chosen as subjects through cluster sampling. The results showed that group membership (classmate vs. stranger) and gender can affect adolescents' TPP together, which manifests as adolescents enacting significantly harsher punishments on strangers than on classmates, especially for boys. Group membership indirectly affects TPP through the mediating effects of perceived unfairness, anger and through a chain mediation of perceived unfairness and anger. Moreover, gender positively moderate the relationship between group membership and perceived unfairness. Specifically, group membership significantly affects boys' perceived unfairness, but cannot predict girls' perceived unfairness. The above results can be used to guide adolescents toward appropriate justice concepts and moral awareness, thus enhancing TPP.

Abstract: Two or more independent species lineages can fuse through an evolutionary transition to form a single lineage, such as in the case of eukaryotic cells, lichens, and coral. Below is a parameter-by-parameter analysis of whether and how the paper “The evolution of multispecies populations: a multilevel selection perspective” addresses each of the 15 public-goods‐game (PGG) design parameters and, in particular, how systematically varying those parameters would be predicted—based solely on the paper provided—to affect the “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency. As you will see, the paper does not refer to or analyze these 15 PGG-specific parameters at all, nor does it examine any form of “punishment treatment effect” or “efficiency” measures in a public-goods context. Consequently, there is no mention of effect sizes or any discussion of systematically varying these 15 parameters in relation to punishment.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Discussed? No. There is no mention in the paper of “players,” “group size,” or human-subject design comparable to a public goods game.  
   • Predictions about varying this parameter? No. The paper does not predict or analyze any relationship between number of players and a punishment treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not use a repeated-game or round-based framework.  
   • Predictions about varying this parameter? No. There is no mention of how changing the number of rounds would affect any punishment treatment effect.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussed? No. There is no discussion at all of communication between participants (or players) akin to a public-goods game with or without chat.  
   • Predictions about varying this parameter? No. The paper provides no analysis of communication effects on punishment or cooperation in a PGG sense.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Discussed? No. The concepts of forced/all-or-nothing contributions in a PGG do not appear in the paper.  
   • Predictions about varying this parameter? No. There is no mention of exogenously forcing either full or partial contributions nor any tie to a punishment effect.

5. Is the contribution default?  
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not address the notion of a default contribution or moving an endowment between private and public pools.  
   • Predictions about varying this parameter? No. No relevance to the paper’s multispecies-model discussion.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as multiplication factor  
   • Discussed? No. The paper deals with biological fitness and multilevel selection, not marginal per capita returns or multiplication factors in a standard PGG sense.  
   • Predictions about varying this parameter? No. No mention of any effect parallel to MPCR or a multiplication factor for a public good.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussed? No. The paper discusses “cheaters” in a biological sense but does not link this to a formal punishment‐cost structure or any PGG punishment mechanism.  
   • Predictions about varying this parameter? No. No numerical or qualitative discussion of how varying punishment cost would affect payoffs or efficiency.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted for each unit of punishment)  
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not describe or quantify anything akin to “punishment magnitude,” “coins deducted,” or analogous mechanisms.  
   • Predictions about varying this parameter? No. None.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussed? No. The paper describes “mutualistic benefits” biologically but does not analyze a reward mechanism as used in PGG reward treatments.  
   • Predictions about varying this parameter? No. No predictions or mentions of introducing or varying a reward system.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Discussed? No. Again, the paper does not reference any cost/benefit of financially rewarding cooperators.  
    • Predictions about varying this parameter? No. None.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward granted)  
    • Discussed? No. There is no reference in this paper to reward magnitudes or related payoff schedules.  
    • Predictions about varying this parameter? No. None.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players? (Do they know when the game ends?)  
    • Discussed? No. The paper does not examine typical repeated-game design features (e.g., known versus unknown endpoints).  
    • Predictions about varying this parameter? No. None.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know peers’ gains and losses)?  
    • Discussed? No. The paper includes no mention of revealing payoffs or outcomes across individuals in any sense comparable to a PGG.  
    • Predictions about varying this parameter? No. None.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Discussed? No. There is no concept of direct punishment or punisher identity in the paper.  
    • Predictions about varying this parameter? No. None.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Discussed? No. The paper never analyzes or even mentions a rewarder’s identity or knowledge of who provides a reward.  
    • Predictions about varying this parameter? No. None.
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Summary (A–D)

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper does not use “group efficiency,” “total payoff,” or “average payoff” in the sense of a public goods game. Instead, it examines the evolutionary conditions under which multispecies mutualisms arise, stabilize, or break down. The key outcomes (dependent variables) involve (i) the proportion of cooperators vs. cheaters and (ii) the presence vs. absence of mutualistic relationships in a metacommunity. These are clearly different from the traditional PGG notion of efficiency or payoffs measured in monetary units.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • None. The paper does not mention any of the 15 parameters (e.g., number of players, punishment cost, or reward magnitude) in a public-goods or formal game-theoretic framework.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. The paper makes no link at all to a punishment treatment effect and does not discuss systematically varying any of these parameters.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper offers no direct basis for making any predictions about these 15 parameters or their interactions in a public goods game. Consequently, there is no evidence in the paper to support any predictions—whether qualitative or quantitative—regarding changes in efficiency under punishment.

Authors: Li, Y; Mifune, N
Author Full Names: Li, Yang; Mifune, Nobuhiro
Article Title: Punishment in the public goods game is evaluated negatively irrespective of non-cooperators' motivation
Author Keywords: punishment; public goods; third-party punishment; fear; greed; reputation
Keywords Plus: INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; REPUTATION; EVOLUTION; ENFORCEMENT; ALTRUISM; BENEFITS; NORMS; FEAR
Abstract: The evolution of human cooperation toward strangers remains puzzling. While the punishment of non-cooperators is a possible explanation, whether punishments can help cooperation evolve depends on how people evaluate punishers. Thus, it is of vital importance to elucidate the perception of punishers. Previous studies have found that punishment is evaluated differently in different contexts; punishers are negatively and positively evaluated in the public goods game with punishment (PGG-P) and in the third-party punishment game (TPP), respectively. To disentangle the mixed evidence, our research focused on motivations for non-cooperation and examined whether different motivations for non-cooperation could explain the inconsistent findings. We hypothesized that people positively evaluate punishers when they punish those who non-cooperated to exploit others (greed), e.g., in a TPP situation. Contrastingly, people negatively evaluate punishers when they punish those who non-cooperated to avoid exploitation (fear), e.g., in a PGG-P situation. If so, in either game, punishers would be evaluated positively in situations where greed dominates, and negatively in situations where fear dominates the non-cooperation motivation. To test this, we conducted two online experiments with hypothetical scenarios in which the decision-making order was used to manipulate the motivations of non-cooperators. The results of Study 1 (N = 240) using only PGG-P and Study 2 (N = 602) using both PGG-P and TPP showed that the non-cooperation motivation did not have a significant effect on the evaluations of punishers and non-punishers. Punishers (vs non-punishers) were evaluated negatively in PGG-P and positively in TPP regardless of the decision-making order of non-cooperation. We discussed the role of higher-order information in the evaluation of punishment.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players
 • Discussed? Yes. The paper uses four players in a public goods game (PGG‐P) setting, plus an additional person as a punisher or third‐party observer, and two players plus an observer in the third‐party punishment game (TPP) setting.  
 • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not manipulate different group sizes; it simply sets group sizes for the PGG‐P (four players, or “four + one” in Study 2) versus the TPP (two players + one observer).  
 • Predicted effect on punishment treatment? None. The paper does not comment on how changing the number of players would affect punishment’s impact on efficiency (or any other outcome).

 • Systematically varied? No.

3) Is chat enabled between players?

 • Systematically varied? No.

 • Discussed? No.

 • Discussed? No. Although it is a one‐shot scenario, the paper does not specifically mention whether players are told about any horizon beyond the single‐round setting.

 • Predicted effect on punishment treatment? None.

 • Discussed? No. Rewarding is not part of the design.  
 • Systematically varied? No.  
 • Predicted effect on punishment treatment? None.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   No. The paper does not measure or analyze group efficiency or any payoff‐based measure of how “efficient” a group is. Instead, it examines how third parties or in‐group members evaluate “punishers” versus “non‐punishers,” measuring outcomes such as “impression evaluations” (e.g., trustworthiness, likability, kindness) and “intention to cooperate with the punisher.” These outcomes differ from efficiency (actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff).

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   The paper mentions the following nine parameters in passing or as part of the setup:  
   1) Number of players (they use 4‐person groups for PGG‐P, 2‐person plus observer for TPP),  
   2) Number of rounds (one‐shot),  
   4) All‐or‐nothing contributions (though not explicitly framed as such, in effect players either keep or contribute all),  
   6) Multiplication factor = 2 (the public good is doubled),  
   7) Punishment cost (punishers pay some of their 500 yen endowment),  
   8) Punishment magnitude = triple deduction (3× what the punisher pays),  
   13) The outcomes or decisions of peers are visible to the participants (though not systematically manipulated),  
   14) The identity of the punisher is known (to the extent that the scenario identifies who punished and who did not),  
   2) (again, number of rounds) was already stated but is indeed one‐shot.  
   The paper does not manipulate any of these, but it does refer to them in describing the experimental setup.

While the paper discusses punishment in both a public goods game and a third‐party punishment game, it does not systematically vary any of the 15 listed parameters (e.g., cost of punishment, group size, number of rounds, or multiplication factor) to examine how punishment’s effects would change. Consequently, there is no numerical effect size reported for these parameters’ influence on punishment outcomes.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

The authors do not provide any relevant data or interpretations that link these particular parameters to overall payoff or efficiency. Consequently, from this paper alone, there is little (or no) basis for making predictions regarding the effect of these parameters on efficiency.

Authors: Yan, MH; Mathew, S; Boyd, R
Author Full Names: Yan, Minhua; Mathew, Sarah; Boyd, Robert
Article Title: Doing what others do does not stabilize continuous norms
Author Keywords: social norms; norm evolutionary dynamics; cultural evolution; mathematical model
Keywords Plus: SOCIAL NORMS; EVOLUTION; PERCEPTION; TRANSMISSION; DYNAMICS; CULTURE; SPREAD; CUSTOM
Abstract: Differences in social norms are a key source of behavioral variation among human populations. It is widely assumed that a vast range of behaviors, even deleterious ones, can persist as long as they are locally common because deviants suffer coordination failures and social sanctions. Previous models have confirmed this intuition, showing that different populations may exhibit different norms even if they face similar environmental pressures or are linked by migration. Crucially, these studies have modeled norms as having a few discrete variants. Many norms, however, have a continuous range of variants. Here we present a mathematical model of the evolutionary dynamics of continuously varying norms and show that when the social payoffs of the behavioral options vary continuously the pressure to do what others do does not result in multiple stable equilibria. Instead, factors such as environmental pressure, individual preferences, moral beliefs, and cognitive attractors determine the outcome even if their effects are weak, and absent such factors populations linked by migration converge to the same norm. The results suggest that the content of norms across human societies is less arbitrary or historically constrained than previously assumed. Instead, there is greater scope for norms to evolve towards optimal individual or group-level solutions. Our findings also suggest that cooperative norms such as those that increase contributions to public goods might require evolved moral preferences, and not just social sanctions on deviants, to be stable.

• Does the paper discuss this parameter?

• Does the paper discuss any reward mechanism (i.e., a way to give additional positive points)?

• Does the paper systematically vary “reward on/off”?
  – No mention of any reward at all.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does the paper discuss this parameter?

• Does the paper systematically vary it?

• Does the paper discuss this parameter?

• Does the paper systematically vary it?
  – No.

• Does the paper discuss this parameter?

• Does the paper discuss this parameter?

• Does the paper systematically vary whether the punisher’s identity is revealed?

• Does the paper discuss this parameter?

• Does the paper systematically vary it?
  – No.

SUMMARY (A–D)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper’s main analyses focus on how many points senders send and how many points responders return. They also report individual and total payoffs—sometimes calling them “earnings” or “net earnings”—and note that net efficiency is diminished when punishment is used. So while “efficiency” (meaning total or overall payoff) is discussed, it is not the primary reported outcome; the authors are mainly interested in trust and trustworthiness (i.e., amounts sent and returned).  

   • In other words, the authors do use total payoff in places (especially to show that punishment actually lowered responders’ final payoffs), but they do not consistently label it as “efficiency.” They do remark on how punishment can reduce collective payoffs, effectively lowering efficiency.

B. Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned explicitly:  
     (1) Number of players = 3.  
     (2) Number of rounds = 6.  
     (6) Multiplier (3×).  
     (7) Punishment cost (1 point for each unit of punishment).  
     (8) Punishment magnitude (3 points lost by the responder).  
     (12) The number of rounds is known (6).  
     (13) Peer outcomes are shown at the end of each round.  
   • The other parameters (3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15) are either not used or only briefly clarified as absent (e.g., reward is never introduced, identity of punisher is not stated to be revealed, etc.).  

C. For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the “punishment treatment effect” for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • In the study, only two features are systematically manipulated: the presence/absence of punishment and the presence/absence of a justification requirement. None of the other parameters (like punishment cost level, group size, number of rounds, multiplier, etc.) is varied from one condition to another.  
   • Specifically:  
     – “Punishment on vs. off” is the key manipulation.  
     – “Justification on vs. off” is another key manipulation.  
   • Thus, only the presence or absence of punishment (parameters #7 and #8 as a single yes/no factor) is directly tested for its effect. However, the authors do not vary the numerical size of #7 or #8 (the cost or the magnitude)—they only have yes vs. no punishment. None of the other parameters is systematically varied.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper only manipulates punishment (vs. no punishment) and justification (vs. no justification). Based on those two factors, the authors find that adding punishment alone does not necessarily increase net efficiency (because the cost of punishing and the larger penalty to responders can reduce overall payoffs).  
   • The authors do hint that combining a justification requirement with punishment yields higher amounts sent and returned, but they also observe that the cost of punishing lowers responder payoffs enough to reduce their final earnings. Overall “collective” payoffs can drop under punishment.  
   • The paper does not provide enough direct evidence to predict how systematically altering any of the other parameters (e.g., the number of players, the multiplier, the known length of the experiment, etc.) would shape punishment’s effect on efficiency. They do not discuss or test such variations. Thus, little or no prediction can be made (from this paper alone) about how those 15 parameters would affect efficiency if they were individually or jointly manipulated differently than the authors did here.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Keywords Plus: FOCUS THEORY; ROAD SAFETY; PUNISHMENT; MONETARY; DRIVERS; COOPERATION; PROVISION; BEHAVIOR; IMPACT; SEAT
Abstract: We study policies aimed at discouraging behavior that produces negative externalities, and their differential gender impact. Using driving as an application, we carry out an experiment where slowest vehicles are the safest choice, whereas faster driving speeds lead to higher potential payoffs but higher probabilities of accidents. Faster speeds have a personal benefit but create a negative externality. We consider four experimental policy conditions: a baseline situation, a framing condition in which drivers are suggested that driving fast violates a social norm, and two punishment conditions, one exogenous and one endogenous. We find that the most effective policies use different framing and endogenously determined punishment mechanisms (to fast drivers by other drivers). These policies are only effective for female drivers which leads to substantial gender payoff differences. Our data suggest that these results arise from differences in social norms across genders, thus opening the way to designing more effective policies.

Throughout, note that the study uses a “driving-game” framing rather than a typical linear public goods experiment and does not explicitly measure “efficiency” in the sense of actual–to–maximum payoff. Instead, the authors focus on outcomes such as average speed, distribution of driving choices (Fast, Slow, Auto), earnings/payoffs, and social-norm beliefs.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
• Discussed?  
  – Yes, the paper’s theoretical model uses N = 10. In the actual experiment, sessions had between 8 and 12 participants, but the design did not systematically vary the group size.  
• Predictions about varying it?

2) Number of rounds

• Predictions about varying it?

• Predictions about varying it?  
  – Not discussed.

5) Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much to move back into their hand)?

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Discussed?

• Predictions about varying it?

8) Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
• Discussed?

• Discussed?

• Predictions about varying it?  
  – Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A: Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
• The paper does not measure “group efficiency” in the sense of actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff of a fully cooperative group. Instead, the main dependent variables are:  
  (i) Average speed (the mean of all players’ driving choices, which affects probability of accidents).  
  (ii) Distribution of driving choices: how many choose Fast, Slow, or Auto.  
  (iii) Payoffs/earnings from the game (distinct from a ratio-based efficiency measure).  
  (iv) Beliefs and normative expectations (participants’ guesses and normative views).  

B: Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• Mentioned explicitly:  
  – (1) Number of players: set to 10 in the model; 8–12 in the actual sessions (not systematically varied).  
  – (2) Number of rounds: random from 17 to 25; not systematically varied.  
  – (7) Punishment cost: in the Endogenous treatment it is £1 to contribute to the punishment fund, but not varied.  
  – (8) Punishment magnitude: set at £4 for Exogenous punishment and up to 2.5 times the number of punishers (with probability 25%) for Endogenous punishment; not varied.  

• Not mentioned or not used in the design:  
  – Parameters 3, 4, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15.  
  – Parameter 12 and 13 are partially described (rounds are only partially known; prior-round actions are shown) but not systematically varied in a way that the paper analyzes for punishment effects.

C: For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• None of the parameters are systematically varied to test how they would influence punishment’s effect on efficiency (or any outcome). Although the paper sets certain punishment parameters (cost and magnitude), there is no additional variation of them across treatments. The “Endogenous,” “Exogenous,” and “Framing” conditions are examined, but they do not individually manipulate any of the 15 parameters in multiple levels for a “systematic variation” design.

D: If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
• The paper does not provide direct evidence to predict how changing those 15 parameters would alter punishment’s effect on efficiency, beyond noting that declaring a punishment rule (whether exogenous or endogenous) changes behavior in ways that interact strongly with social norms and gender. Since no systematic variation of these parameters was performed, the study gives little foundation for numerical or directional predictions about how changes in, for instance, punishment cost, group size, number of rounds, or reward regimes would affect efficiency.  

In short, there is insufficient evidence in this paper alone to make robust predictions about how varying any of the 15 parameters might quantitatively affect the treatment effect on efficiency.

Authors: Milinski, M; Marotzke, J
Author Full Names: Milinski, Manfred; Marotzke, Jochem
Article Title: Economic experiments support Ostrom's polycentric approach to mitigating climate change
Keywords Plus: BOTTOM-UP; GOVERNANCE; COOPERATION; PSYCHOLOGY; TRAGEDY; DILEMMA
Abstract: The late Nobel laureate Elinor Ostrom envisioned a polycentric approach to mitigating climate change rather than a centralised solution. Debating about global efforts to solve climate-change problems has yet not led to an effective global treaty. Ostrom argued that instead of focusing only on global efforts, it is better to encourage polycentric efforts to reduce the risks associated with the emission of greenhouse gases. Many problems conceptualised as 'global problems' are the cumulative results of actions taken by individuals, families, small groups, private firms, and local, regional, and national governments. Ostrom and colleagues pointed to many examples of successfully managing a common good through interaction within a community. Energy-saving actions undertaken by individuals, families and actors at a small-scale pay off and, when multiplied, may reduce emissions globally. The incentive to achieve an individual net gain may trigger human investment decisions. Here we provide experimental support for Ostrom's basic ideas using methods of experimental economics. By subdividing experimental populations in subgroups that approach sub-goals of mitigating simulated dangerous climate change combined with incentives, the 'global' solution is achieved by combined subgroup contributions exceeding the 'global' threshold for averting simulated dangerous climate change. Incentives from refunded saved energy motivate reaching sub-goals, as Ostrom suggested. By contrast, coercing free-riding subgroups through sanctioning at a cost fails, because sanctioning also hits fair individuals who then reduce their contributions. However, the power of polycentricity with numerous successful units can help mitigate climate change.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what the paper says (or does not say) with regard to (a) whether the paper actually discusses the parameter (and its value, if given) and (b) whether it makes any predictions about how systematically varying that parameter would affect the “punishment treatment effect.” In this context, “punishment treatment effect” refers to what the paper calls the “sanction” or “sanctioning” condition (Treatment T3) relative to a comparable no‐punishment condition (Treatment T4). Note also that the paper itself does not use or report “efficiency” (actual payoff / maximum payoff) as a primary outcome variable; rather, it focuses on whether groups reach a threshold, on contributions, and on other payoff‐related measures.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
   • Discussed? Yes. All sessions use 9 players (sometimes subdivided into three groups of 3).  
   • Systematically varied? No; they always use 9.  
   • Predictions about varying it? No; there is no discussion or effect size regarding changing the number of players on punishment outcomes.

2) Number of rounds  
   • Discussed? Yes. All sessions last 10 rounds.  
   • Systematically varied? No; it is fixed at 10.  
   • Predictions about varying it? No; no effect size or discussion about how changing the number of rounds would affect punishment outcomes.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussed? Not mentioned at all. Subjects are separated by partitions and are anonymous; there is no in‐game chat.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Predictions? No mention.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Discussed? Not in the sense of being forced to contribute everything or nothing. Instead, players can choose 0, 2, or 4 each round.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Predictions? No discussion.

5) Is the contribution default (do players decide how much endowment to move back to themselves)?  
   • Discussed? Not in these terms. The design is a threshold game where one chooses 0, 2, or 4 each round; the article does not label any “default” policy.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Predictions? None.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Discussed? No. This is not a linear public‐goods design; it is a threshold (collective‐risk) design.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Predictions? None.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussed? Yes. In Treatment T3, each individual in a punishing subgroup pays €0.50 if they collectively sanction another subgroup.  
   • Systematically varied? No; it is always €0.50.  
   • Predictions about how varying it? No. The paper compares T3 (punishment available) to T4 (no punishment) but does not experimentally change the cost. No numerical effect size is given with respect to systematically changing this cost.

8) Punishment magnitude  
   • Discussed? Yes. In T3, each punished individual pays €2.00 out of their extra account if their subgroup is sanctioned.  
   • Systematically varied? No; always €2.00.  
   • Predictions about how varying it? No. The paper notes that punishment occurs frequently but does not systematically vary the magnitude. No numerical effect size for variations.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussed? Yes. T2 features an “incentive” or reward for subgroups approaching their €60 sub‐target.  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is a single “reward” treatment (T2), separate from the punishment treatment (T3).  
   • Predictions about how varying it? No. The paper does not alter the presence/absence or size of the reward across multiple levels in order to study its effect on punishment specifically.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Discussed? No. The “incentive” in T2 is distributed by the experiment rather than at a cost to peers themselves.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Predictions? None.

11) Reward magnitude  
   • Discussed? Yes. In T2, depending on the subgroup’s final total (≥€52 up to ≥€60), each member of that subgroup receives between €0.50 and €8.00.  
   • Systematically varied? It varies only within T2’s single treatment (from €0.50 up to €8.00), but there is no experiment‐wide design in which different sessions face different possible magnitudes of reward.  
   • Predictions about how varying it affects punishment? No. That condition does not overlap with punishment.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?  
   • Discussed? Yes. They know from the start there are exactly 10 rounds.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Predictions about varying it? None.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much others gained or lost)?  
   • Discussed? Partially. In T3, each subgroup sees the overall contribution of each of the other two subgroups in order to decide on punishing them; however, the paper does not systematically vary how much information is shown.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Predictions? None.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Discussed? The paper mentions that punishment is decided anonymously by at least two members of a subgroup. It does not say that punished subjects learn the specific identities behind the punishment vote.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Predictions? None.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Discussed? No. T2’s reward is administered by the experimenter as a subgroup bonus; it is not peer‐to‐peer.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Predictions? None.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use “efficiency” (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are they different?  
   – The paper does not report “efficiency = (actual total payoff) / (maximum possible payoff)” as its central dependent measure. Instead, the main dependent variables are:  
     • Whether the group(s) reach a required threshold (e.g., €180) to avert “dangerous climate change.”  
     • Total contributions by each group or subgroup.  
     • Frequency of different contribution levels (0, 2, or 4).  
     • Amount of monetary payoff outcomes (e.g., leftover money, “extra account” usage) but not expressed as a ratio to a maximum possible payoff.  
   – Thus “efficiency,” in the strict sense, does not appear. Their other measures focus on threshold success/failure and contribution patterns.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – Mentioned:  
     (1) Number of players (always 9)  
     (2) Number of rounds (always 10)  
     (7) Punishment cost (€0.50 per punishing individual)  
     (8) Punishment magnitude (€2.00 per punished individual)  
     (9) Whether a reward is enabled (yes for T2)  
     (11) Reward magnitude (€0.50 to €8.00 if subgroup contributions reach 52–60)  
     (12) Is the number of rounds known (yes, 10)  
     (13) Are peer outcomes shown (they see other subgroups’ total contributions in T3)  
   – Not mentioned in any detail or not used at all: parameters 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 14, and 15.  
   – In total, 8 of the 15 parameters appear in some form.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   – The paper never systematically varies any of these parameters in a way that would isolate their impact on punishment. Punishment cost and magnitude (Parameters 7 and 8) are held fixed in T3, and the paper compares T3 (punishment available) to T4 (no punishment). That reveals how punishment plays out in one specific design, but there is no systematic, multi‐level variation. The paper therefore gives no numerical effect sizes for how changes in these parameter values would alter the punishment‐versus‐no‐punishment difference.  
   – Consequently, none of the 15 parameters is truly varied across multiple levels in order to test how it influences the “punishment treatment effect.” The paper only compares one punishment treatment (T3) to one no‐punishment treatment (T4).

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   – The article does not report “efficiency” per se, nor does it investigate how varying any parameter (number of players, cost of sanctioning, reward magnitude, etc.) might systematically change the effect of punishment on total payoffs. It only shows that in its fixed design (T3 vs. T4), group‐level punishment does not raise contributions or final payoffs (and can in fact create side‐effects, such as discouraging fair contributors who also get “hit” by a group‐level sanction).  
   – Thus, the paper provides very little basis for predicting how changes in, say, the cost or magnitude of punishment (Parameters 7 and 8) or any of the other factors would alter a punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency. Its central finding is simply that under the single set of punishment parameters they tested, punishment did not improve group outcomes (as measured by whether they reached the threshold or how much was contributed). Extrapolating beyond that is not supported by the data presented.  

In short, the paper does not supply direct evidence or numerical effect sizes on how systematically varying any of the 15 parameters influences punishment’s effect on “efficiency.” It measures different outcomes (mostly threshold success and amounts contributed), uses fixed parameter values for punishment and reward, and does not study alternative levels of those variables. The reader therefore cannot infer detailed predictions about efficiency from the paper’s presented evidence.

Abstract: Game theory provides a powerful means to study human cooperation and better understand cooperation-facilitating mechanisms in general. In classical game-theoretic models, an increase in group cooperation constantly increases people's gains, implying that individual gains are a continuously varying function of the cooperation rate. However, this is inconsistent with the increasing number of risk-resistant scenarios in reality. A risk-resistant scenario means once a group does not successfully resist the risk, all individuals lose their resources, such as a community coping with COVID-19 and a village resisting a flood. In other words, individuals' gains are segmented about the collaboration rate. This paper builds a risk-resistant model to explore whether punishment still promotes collaboration when people resist risk. The results show that central and peer punishments can both encourage collaboration but with different characteristics under different risk-resistant scenarios. Specifically, central punishment constrains the collaboration motivated by peer punishment regardless of risk, while peer punishment limits the collaboration induced by central punishment only when the risk is high. Our findings provide insights into the balance between peer punishment from public autonomy and central punishment from central governance, and the proposed model paves the way for the development of richer risk-resistant models.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
   • Does the paper discuss it?

PEER INCENTIVES

INFORMATION DISPLAY

   • Does the paper discuss it?

   • Is it systematically varied whether participants do or do not know the number of rounds?  
     – No. Instead, the study compares a strictly one-round condition vs. a repeated condition in which participants do know from the outset that there will be multiple rounds. The paper does not manipulate “knowledge vs. ignorance” of the number of rounds.

   • Does the paper discuss it?

     – No.  

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – No. Rewards are not part of the experimental design.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY (A–D)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • No. The paper does not report any measure or analysis of total payoff, average payoff, or efficiency (i.e., the ratio of actual total payoff to the maximum possible payoff). Instead, it focuses on:  
     1) Punishment behavior (the amount participants choose to spend on punishing).  
     2) Impression evaluations of punishers vs. non-punishers (i.e., how positively or negatively punishers are viewed).  
   • How are these dependent variables different from one another and from efficiency?  
     – “Punishment behavior” concerns how much participants pay to inflict losses on a free-rider.  
     – “Impression evaluations” concern how punishers (or non-punishers) are rated (e.g., “very bad impression” to “very good impression”).  
     – Neither variable tracks total payoffs or efficiency measures.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form:  
     1) Number of players (fixed at four, not varied).  
     2) Number of rounds (varied: one-round vs. repeated).  
     6) Multiplication factor for the public good (always ×2, not varied).  
     7) Punishment cost (1 unit of punishment costs the punisher 1 and deducts 3 from the target).  
     8) Punishment magnitude (3×).  
     12) Whether there is one round or multiple (participants are explicitly told).  
     13) Some feedback is shown about others’ contributions (but not varied).  

   Thus, seven of the 15 parameters are at least mentioned/described.  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • The only parameter clearly and systematically varied in the design is parameter #2 (Number of rounds: one-shot vs. repeated).  
   • Even then, the authors discuss its effect on punishment decisions and impression evaluations—not on “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”  
   • They provide effect sizes for how a one-round vs. repeated context interacts with time pressure to influence the amount of punishment (for example, t(89)=2.51, p=0.01, d=0.54 in Study 1). But this is not an analysis of group efficiency.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not supply any direct data or models regarding how these parameters, including the number of rounds, would alter overall group efficiency. Its findings center on punishment behavior and the social evaluation of punishers.  
   • Therefore, based solely on Maeda et al. (2022), little to no specific prediction can be made about how systematically varying any of the 15 parameters would affect efficiency.  
   • The studies imply that certain factors (e.g., one-round vs. repeated game, time pressure vs. deliberation) change punishment decisions and how punishers are perceived. But the authors do not connect these changes to group payoffs or efficiency outcomes in any of their reported findings.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

In conclusion, Maeda et al. (2022) do not investigate group efficiency as a dependent variable, nor do they draw any link between systematically varied parameters and efficiency outcomes. They focus on how time constraints (intuitive vs. deliberative punishment) and whether the game is one-round or repeated (among other contextual factors) affect punishers’ behaviors and how observers evaluate them. No numerical effect sizes on efficiency or formal efficiency metrics appear in the paper.

Authors: Whitmeyer, JM
Author Full Names: Whitmeyer, JM
Article Title: The group control catastrophe
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; COLLECTIVE SANCTIONS; SOCIAL-CONTROL; NORMS; ENFORCEMENT; EVOLUTION; DILEMMAS
Abstract: This study elaborates a surprising finding by Heckathorn (1990). His simulation of group-mediated social control models a situation in which an agent outside a group tries to obtain compliance by group members through the administration of sanctions, In general, group compliance increases as the agents monitoring efficacy increases. The surprising finding is that under certain conditions group compliance collapses to zero for intermediate values of the monitoring efficacy. In this study I show this is part of a catastrophe, a bifurcation into two equilibria for intermediate values of the monitoring efficacy. Whether the group exists at a high-compliance or low-compliance equilibrium depends on the occurrence of simultaneous non-payoff-maximizing cooperation or defection. Cooperation pushes the group to the high-compliance equilibrium; defection knocks it to the low-compliance equilibrium. The catastrophe is robust: it exists for a range of parameter values and for different production functions for the public good (benefits from group compliance).

Below is a point‐by‐point analysis based solely on Whitmeyer’s paper (reproducing and extending Heckathorn’s 1990 model). I address each of the 15 parameters in the prompt, indicating (1) whether the paper mentions or uses that parameter (and any specific value), and (2) whether the paper makes any predictions about systematically varying that parameter and its effect on “punishment treatment” (or the effect of sanctions, collective or individual) on any dependent variable. Where the paper discusses dependent variables other than efficiency (such as compliance or payoff), I note that explicitly. If the paper does not discuss or vary a parameter, I say so and do not speculate beyond the paper.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper refers to this as “group size” (N).  
   • Value(s)? Primarily N = 10 (Heckathorn’s original setting), and the author also considers N = 50.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on outcomes? Yes, the paper examines whether the “group control catastrophe” (the collapse or survival of compliance under intermediate monitoring levels) holds for N = 10 and N = 50. The outcome variable is group compliance (and individual payoffs at equilibrium), not efficiency. The paper does not report a numeric “punishment treatment effect size” nor does it measure efficiency as a ratio of actual to maximum payoffs. It does conclude that the same qualitative collapse phenomenon (under certain parameter values) remains robust when N is increased to 50.  

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned? No. The paper describes a simulation process that iterates until equilibrium but does not treat this as a repeated public goods game with multiple discrete rounds known to the players.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned? No. There is no discussion of communication or chat among group members.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned? Yes. The model assumes each individual either complies or does not comply (and similarly, either enforces or does not enforce, and either opposes or does not oppose enforcement). The paper does not systematically vary this “all or none” assumption. It is simply built into the simulation model.  

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not discuss any “default contribution” or related mechanism.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Mentioned? No. Instead, the paper deals with “production functions” (accelerating, decelerating, S‐shaped, etc.) to describe how collective sanctions (or rewards) scale with group compliance, but it does not use a standard MPCR parameter from typical public goods games.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned? Not as a distinct parameter. Although the paper does discuss costs to the “agent” of sanctioning in aggregate, it does not break this out as “punisher’s per‐unit cost.”  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted for each unit of punishment)
   • Mentioned? Yes, as the “individual sanction” (Sᵢ) or “collective sanction” (S꜀). Examples include Sᵢ = 150, S꜀ = 75.  
   • Systematic variation and effect on outcomes? Yes, the paper analyzes various levels of Sᵢ and S꜀ (e.g., Sᵢ from 25 up to 350+, S꜀ from 25 up to 475+). The dependent variables are (a) equilibrium group compliance and (b) individual payoffs. There is no specific measure of efficiency (actual payoff ÷ maximum payoff). The paper does not provide numerical “effect sizes” for a “punishment treatment effect” but does show that certain values of Sᵢ and S꜀ influence whether compliance collapses or remains high under varying monitoring efficacy.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned? Yes, the paper notes that all results for “negative sanctions” (punishments) are formally symmetric if one uses “positive sanctions” (rewards). There is no separate systematic variation of “reward vs. punishment” conditions, only a statement that the sign of the sanction (positive or negative) does not change the model’s qualitative results.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Mentioned? No. While the agent can in principle use rewards or punishments, the paper does not treat the “cost of rewarding” as a separate parameter, nor does it systematically vary it.  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)
   • Mentioned? Only insofar as it is equivalent in magnitude to punishment “S” but with opposite sign. The paper does not give separate analysis of reward magnitude, nor does it systematically vary it independently of punishments.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not model knowledge of a game’s duration or any repeated‐game horizon effects.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown?
   • Mentioned? No. The model only shows how group members respond to sanctions and one another’s attempts at enforcement or opposition; there is no mention of revealing peer gains or losses.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not address the visibility or anonymity of who applies sanctions within the group.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Mentioned? No. Same as above; no discussion of identifying who applies the reward.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   The paper does not use “efficiency” as typically defined (actual payoff / maximum payoff). It primarily reports:  
   1) Group compliance (how many individuals comply) as the main outcome.  
   2) Equilibrium payoff to individual group members (as in Figure 3).  

   These are distinct from efficiency, which never appears as a ratio of actual to maximum possible total payoff.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   Four parameters clearly appear in the paper:  
   • (1) Number of players (group size).  
   • (4) “All‐or‐nothing” contributions/compliance (an assumption, not varied).  
   • (8) Punishment magnitude (Sᵢ and S꜀).  
   • (9) Whether a reward is enabled (mentioned as a symmetric alternative to punishment).  

   The remaining 11 parameters are either not mentioned or not dealt with explicitly.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   The paper systematically varies:  
   • (1) Number of players (N=10 vs. N=50) – It shows that the same “catastrophe” (compliance collapse at intermediate monitoring) can occur at both group sizes. This discussion concerns compliance and payoffs, not a defined “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”  
   • (8) Punishment magnitude (Sᵢ, S꜀) – It analyzes how different levels of individual and collective sanctions affect equilibrium compliance and payoffs. Again, not in terms of an explicit “treatment effect on efficiency,” but in terms of whether compliance collapses or remains high.

   The paper does not provide a numeric “punishment treatment effect size” for any measure of efficiency.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of this paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not measure nor model what it calls “efficiency.” It focuses on compliance and individual payoff.  
   • Of the 15 parameters, only group size (1) and sanction magnitude (8) are systematically varied, and even then, only with outcomes reported for compliance and payoffs—not efficiency as a ratio of actual to maximum total payoff.  
   • The paper notes that higher punishment (or reward) magnitudes and intermediate monitoring efficacy can lead to multiple equilibria (high or zero compliance). That might, in principle, translate to different total payoffs or “efficiencies,” but the paper itself does not compute or present that ratio.  
   • Consequently, the paper gives limited or no direct basis to predict how any of these parameters (or their interactions) would quantitatively shift a “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency. Any attempt to do so would go beyond what the paper explicitly reports.
reference_APA: Whitmeyer, JM (2004). The group control catastrophe. SOCIOLOGICAL PERSPECTIVES.

The study keeps all 15 parameters fixed and never measures efficiency, so it provides essentially no leverage for forecasting how changes in those parameters would alter the efficiency gain (or loss) from introducing punishment.  The only weak hints are:
   • A 4-player PGG with MPCR = 0.5 and a 1:5 punishment ratio permits children to punish at non-trivial levels; however, efficiency outcomes were not calculated.  
   • Younger children punished less efficiently than older children (they both punished and contributed less), suggesting that *age* (not on the parameter list) moderates efficiency more than any of the 15 design parameters.

In short, the article offers descriptive data on behaviour in a *fixed* game, but no systematic evidence useful for predicting how any of the 15 design variables would change the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency.

Abstract: Cooperation is the crux of many social problems, thus third-party sanction, as one of the most important ways to promote cooperation, is worth studying. In addition, we explored the characteristics of third-party sanctioning behaviors. A total of 280 students participated in the present study. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of (1) what the paper actually discusses (if at all), including any values used in the experiment, and (2) whether it makes any predictions about how systematically varying each parameter would affect the “punishment treatment effect” for any dependent variable (especially efficiency). Throughout, “the paper” refers strictly to the content in the provided excerpt (“Which is the ideal sanction…” by Hou et al.). No additional sources or conjectures are introduced.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – Yes, but only in the sense that the baseline treatment (B) had 4 players, while TP (punishment only), TR (reward only), and TP/R (punishment + reward) treatments involved 8 total participants (4 PGG-players + 4 third-party players).  
     – The paper does not systematically vary group size across treatments (e.g., comparing 4 vs. 6 vs. 8 players in the PGG). It simply keeps 4 PGG-players in each group (and adds 4 third parties in the sanction conditions).  
   • Predictions about systematic variation?  
     – No. The paper does not discuss how changing the number of (PGG-)players would affect punishment’s impact on efficiency or any other dependent variable.

2. Number of rounds
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – The game lasts 10 periods (rounds) in all conditions.  
     – The paper mentions that cooperation tends to decline over time in the baseline (B) and TR conditions, but the number of rounds is not manipulated.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation?  
     – No. The paper does not examine what would happen with fewer or more than 10 rounds. It does not relate changing the number of rounds to changes in punishment’s effect on efficiency or other outcomes.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – No. The methods section states that participants (PGG-players) “could not talk with each other,” but there is no condition in which chat is permitted.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation?  
     – No. The paper does not address enabling/disabling communication or its effect on punishment treatments.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – No. Contributions range from 0 to 20 tokens in any integer amount, meaning participants choose any amount in that interval. There is no mention of a forced “all or nothing” design.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation?  
     – No. The paper does not discuss forcing an “all or nothing” contribution.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – No. Participants directly decide how many tokens (0 to 20) to put into the common pool. There is no mention of a “return‐to‐hand” or “default" contribution mechanism.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation?  
     – No. Not discussed.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – The paper uses a total multiplier k = 1.6 for the group of 4 PGG-players. Effectively, each 1 token contributed becomes 1.6 tokens total, shared equally among 4 players, so each contributor recovers 0.4 tokens per token contributed.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation?  
     – No. The multiplier is fixed (1.6). The paper does not discuss systematically varying it or how that would affect the role of punishment.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – Yes: imposing 1 “punishment point” costs the punisher 1 token in the punishment (TP) and TP/R treatments.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation?  
     – No. The paper treats that cost as a fixed constant (1 token); it does not analyze what would happen if that cost changed.

8. Punishment magnitude
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – Yes: each punishment point reduces the punished player’s payoff by 3 tokens.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation?  
     – No. The ratio (3:1) is used consistently; there is no mention of systematically varying that ratio or how it would affect efficiency or other outcomes.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – Yes, explicitly. The paper compares three sanction conditions: (1) TP (punishment only), (2) TR (reward only), and (3) TP/R (both). However, it does not introduce intermediate variations (like “sometimes enabled, sometimes not” within the same design); it only tests presence/absence across the three treatments.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation?  
     – They do not separately manipulate “reward presence” as a continuous factor. Instead, they study distinct punishment-only vs. reward-only vs. combined. They do observe that TR alone has relatively weak influence on raising cooperation. But they do not speak of systematically manipulating reward presence to see how it shifts “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency.  
   – Numerical effect size? The paper does not provide a direct “efficiency” measure. It reports that, for average contributions, TR alone yields about 10.33 tokens (on average), whereas punishment (TP) yields ~12.36 and punishment + reward yields ~14.39, but those are contributions (cooperation), not efficiency measures.

10. Reward cost to grant one unit
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – Yes: similarly, 1 “reward point” costs the rewarder 1 token.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation?  
     – No. The paper holds this cost constant and does not discuss variations.

11. Reward magnitude
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – Yes: each 1 point of reward gives +3 tokens to the rewarded player.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation?  
     – No. The 3:1 ratio is fixed; the paper does not address how changes would alter punishment’s effect.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – The study was described as a “finitely repeated PGG for 10 periods,” and participants did play it for exactly 10 rounds. The text does not explicitly say whether participants “knew” it would end at round 10, but it is implied that it was a 10‐period game. There is no separate condition where players do not know the number of rounds.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation?  
     – No. The paper does not manipulate knowledge of the game length and does not predict how such knowledge would affect the punishment treatment.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (i.e., do players see how much their peers gained/lost)?
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – The paper states that at the end of each round, participants see contributions that everyone made and, in the punishment/reward conditions, see how many punishment/reward points were assigned to them. But there is no separate manipulation of the visibility or hiddenness of others’ outcomes.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation?  
     – No. The paper simply uses one feedback procedure.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – No. The paper does not mention that the identity of the third-party punisher becomes known to the punished player. It remains anonymous with respect to who actually imposed the sanction.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation?  
     – No mention of systematically varying punisher identity knowledge.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Discussion in paper?  
     – Same as punishment identity: it does not say that the rewarder’s identity is revealed.  
   • Predictions about systematic variation?  
     – No. Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables in the paper and how they differ.  
   • The paper measures:  
     – Level of cooperation (average contribution to the public good).  
     – “Dispersion” or “discrete trend” of cooperation (how contributions deviate from the mean).  
     – Final payoff (individual earnings).  
   • The paper does not explicitly use “group efficiency” = (actual total payoff) / (maximum possible total payoff) as a principal dependent variable. It mentions total/average payoffs in discussing how TP vs. TR vs. TP/R affects participants’ earnings, but it never provides an explicit efficiency ratio.  
   • Thus, “efficiency” is not directly investigated, whereas “cooperation” (contributions), “dispersion,” and “earnings” are the primary dependent variables.

B. Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned at least in passing:  
     – (1) Number of players: used a fixed set of 4 PGG-players (plus 4 third-party players in sanction conditions).  
     – (2) Number of rounds: always 10.  
     – (6) MPCR/multiplication factor: 1.6.  
     – (7) Punishment cost per unit: 1 token.  
     – (8) Punishment magnitude: 3 tokens deducted from the punished.  
     – (9) Whether a reward is enabled: yes/no across TP, TR, TP/R conditions.  
     – (10) Reward cost per unit: 1 token.  
     – (11) Reward magnitude: +3 tokens for the rewarded.  
     – (13) Peer outcomes: participants get feedback about others’ contributions, punishment/reward, and their own payoff.  
   • Not mentioned or used as a design variation:  
     – (3) Chat.  
     – (4) All-or-nothing contributions.  
     – (5) Contribution default.  
     – (12) Knowledge of the ending round is not manipulated as a separate condition.  
     – (14) Punisher identity known or not is not manipulated.  
     – (15) Rewarder identity known or not is not manipulated.  

C. For which (and how many) of these 15 parameters does the paper discuss effects on the “punishment treatment effect” when the parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, the paper does not systematically vary any single numeric parameter. Instead:  
     – Parameter 9 (Whether a reward is enabled) is varied in that the paper compares NO reward (TP) vs. reward (TR) vs. combined (TP/R). However, that is effectively comparing different forms of sanction rather than systematically varying a single dimension within the punishment condition.  
   • No other parameter is systematically manipulated (e.g., cost of punishment, magnitude of punishment, etc.).  
   • The paper therefore does not provide numeric effect sizes for changes along a continuum of those parameters; it only gives results from discrete conditions (B, TP, TR, TP/R).

D. Predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, if one relied solely on this paper’s content.  
   • Because the paper never tracks “efficiency” as total-payoff‐divided‐by‐maximum‐possible, we have little basis for specific quantitative predictions.  
   • It does indicate that adding punishment (TP) or punishment + reward (TP/R) raises cooperation more than a baseline with no sanctions or reward‐only; these changes also affect individual payoffs and distribution. But the authors do not connect that explicitly to an efficiency ratio or to systematic parameter variations (e.g., changing the number of players, the cost of punishment, etc.).  
   • In short, the study only directly compares:  
       – No punishment or reward (baseline)  
       – Punishment only (TP)  
       – Reward only (TR)  
       – Punishment + reward (TP/R)  
     and it focuses on cooperation levels, dispersion, and payoffs rather than efficiency per se.  
   • Hence, one can make almost no further predictions about how systematically manipulating the 15 parameters would affect the punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency, because the paper simply does not deal with most of those parameters or with efficiency as a distinct outcome.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Overall, the paper shows that third-party punishment alone or combined with reward increases cooperation (and changes payoff distributions), whereas reward alone has weaker effects on cooperation. However, it does not speak to parameter-by-parameter manipulations nor does it measure “efficiency” as defined by total payoff relative to the maximum possible. Consequently, if asked to predict how the 15 parameters would shape the punishment treatment’s impact on efficiency, the paper itself offers little direct guidance beyond noting that adding (third-party) punishment is more effective than reward alone in raising contributions.
reference_APA: Hou, Gonglin, Wang, Fei, Shi, Jieyan, Chen, Weijiang & Yu, Jie (2019). Which is the ideal sanction for cooperation? An experimental study on different types of third-party sanctions. PSYCH JOURNAL.

Keywords Plus: RANDOMIZED EXPERIMENTS; SOCIAL PREFERENCES; PUNISHMENT; DETERRENCE; SANCTIONS; FEEDBACK; COOPERATION; BEHAVIOR; CRIME; OBLIGATIONS
Abstract: Jeremy Bentham brought enlightenment to criminal policy. He argued that the primary purpose of criminal sanctions should be deterring future crime. To that end he advocated complete transparency. This article investigates Bentham's intuition in a public goods lab experiment by manipulating how much information on punishment experienced by others is available to would-be offenders. Compared with the tone that Jeremy Bentham set, the result is unexpected: when would-be offenders learn about punishment of others at the individual level, they contribute much less to the public project. This is due to an inevitable side effect. Information about punishment is only meaningful together with information about the infraction.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter summary of what the paper does—and does not—say about each of the fifteen parameters, followed by the requested four‐point summary (A–D).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
• What the paper says: It fixes groups of 4 “active” players (type A) plus 1 “supervisor” (type B) in every session of the experiment.  
• Systematic variation? No. All sessions use 4 contributors and 1 punisher. The paper does not discuss or predict how changing the number of players would affect any outcome (including efficiency).

2. Number of rounds  
• What the paper says: Each phase has 10 announced rounds; there are two phases, so the supervisor plays 20 rounds in total (10 rounds per group of type A players).  
• Systematic variation? No. The number of rounds is always 10 (per phase). The paper does not discuss or predict how varying the number of rounds would affect the punishment treatment effect on any dependent variable.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
• What the paper says: There is no mention of chat or communication.  
• Systematic variation? No mention, so none.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• What the paper says: Players decide how many of their 20 talers to contribute (from 0 to 20), so it is a continuous choice, not all‐or‐nothing.  
• Systematic variation? No, and the paper does not discuss the possibility of all‐or‐nothing contributions.

5. Is the contribution “default” (for example, are participants forced to “opt out”)?  
• What the paper says: Standard voluntary linear public goods game (no mention of a default or forced move).  
• Systematic variation? None.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
• What the paper says: The MPCR is fixed at 0.4; each taler contributed to the public good returns 0.4 talers per person.  
• Systematic variation? No. There is no discussion of changing MPCR or how that would alter the punishment treatment effect.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• What the paper says: The supervisor (type B) pays 1 taler to reduce a target’s payoff by 3 talers.  
• Systematic variation? None. It is always 1‐for‐3, and the paper does not discuss how changing the punisher’s cost would affect efficiency or any other measure.

8. Punishment magnitude (i.e., how many coins are deducted from the punished player)  
• What the paper says: Magnitude is always 3 talers deducted for each 1 taler spent by the punisher.  
• Systematic variation? None. The paper does not discuss varying it.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
• What the paper says: There is no reward mechanism at all.  
• Systematic variation? None.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• What the paper says: Not applicable (no rewards in the design).  
• Systematic variation? None.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
• What the paper says: Not applicable (no rewards in the design).  
• Systematic variation? None.

12. Is the number of rounds known to the players?  
• What the paper says: Yes, each group is told there will be exactly 10 rounds (and a second phase of 10 rounds if relevant).  
• Systematic variation? No. The paper does not discuss or predict how making the horizon uncertain would affect any outcome.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (i.e., do players see how much peers gained/lost)?  
• What the paper says: This is the core treatment variation. The paper systematically varies the precision/transparency of information given to contributors (“low,” “medium,” “high”). In “low,” participants see only average contributions and no direct information on others’ punishments; in “medium,” they additionally see average punishment imposed; in “high,” they see each individual’s contribution and individual punishment.  
• Systematic variation? Yes. This is the main treatment factor. The headline result is that greater transparency (i.e., moving from no or partial feedback to full individual‐level feedback) reduces contributions. The paper interprets this as “full transparency reduces cooperation” and thereby undermines the presumed deterrent effect. While the paper’s dependent variable is mainly “contributions,” it does note that lower contributions are typically detrimental to overall outcomes (and thus presumably to efficiency).

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• What the paper says: There is only one supervisor per group, so players presumably know that “player B” is the punisher. The identity of that same supervisor does not change across the 10 rounds of a phase. However, this is not systematically varied—no design condition conceals or discloses different punishers.  
• Systematic variation? None.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is?  
• What the paper says: Rewards are never used.  
• Systematic variation? None.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
• The paper does not present “efficiency” (actual total payoff / maximum possible total payoff) as a main dependent variable. The primary dependent variables are:  
  – Individual contributions to the public good.  
  – Punishment decisions, and how punishments shape subsequent contributions.  
  – Individuals’ payoffs (or “profits”), but mostly in the service of understanding contributions/punishment.  
• The authors do note that full contributions would maximize total payoff; however, they analyze whether and how punishment and feedback influence contributions rather than explicitly reporting group efficiency.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• The paper explicitly gives fixed values (but does not vary) for seven of them:  
  (1) Number of players = 4 + 1 punisher,  
  (2) Number of rounds = 10 (plus 10 more in Phase 2),  
  (6) MPCR = 0.4,  
  (7) Punishment cost = 1,  
  (8) Punishment magnitude = 3,  
  (12) Rounds known = yes (10 announced),  
  (13) Whether peer outcomes are shown = systematically varied (low / medium / high feedback).  
• The paper does not mention or does not implement the remaining parameters (chat, forced/all‐or‐nothing contributions, reward, etc.) or does not vary them in any way.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• Only one parameter—parameter 13, “Are peer outcomes shown”—is systematically varied.  
• The paper discusses how increasing feedback precision (i.e., showing precisely who was punished and how much) changes the “punishment treatment effect” on contributions. The main finding is that more information about who was punished can backfire and reduce contributions, thus reducing rather than improving cooperation.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
• Because only the feedback on peer outcomes (parameter 13) was actually varied, the paper provides evidence that “more transparency” about punishment tends to reduce contributions and thereby likely reduces overall efficiency. For the other parameters (1–12, 14–15), the authors do not offer any direct predictions or experimental findings about how varying them would affect efficiency or the punishment treatment effect. Consequently, on these other parameters, the paper provides little or no basis for prediction.

Abstract: Although conflicts typically lead to a waste of resources, organizations may still benefit from a corporate culture that tolerates or even encourages conflicts. The reason is that coordinated conflicts may help to enforce norms and foster cooperation. In this paper, we report results of a series of laboratory experiments designed to explore whether and under what conditions an efficiency-enhancing conflict culture can emerge. Using a principal-agent setup with subjective performance evaluation, we show that establishing a functional conflict culture is a delicate matter. If conflicts are encouraged in a careless hands-off manner, the destructive side of conflicts is likely to dominate. In our experiment, we find that conflicts have positive net effects on efficiency only if an explicit code of conduct is established and conflicts are institutionalized through a grievance process. Thus, providing workers with more power may be a necessary but not sufficient condition for improving productivity when performance evaluations are subjective.
