13. PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN?  
    • Paper states only that “participants learn their individual payoff after each round.”  It never says they see the partner’s payoff or the realized return.  Hence: not discussed, not varied.

14. PUNISHER IDENTITY REVEALED?  
    • Because interaction is one-to-one, the punished manager trivially knows the punisher.  Not manipulated or analysed.

15. REWARDER IDENTITY REVEALED?  
    • Analogous to (14); always known, never varied, no effect analysed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used  
   – Total surplus (= manager profit + worker profit)  
   – Worker effort (binary)  
   – Conflict (punishment) frequency and cost  
   – Bonus-payment frequency  
   Efficiency in the public-goods sense (actual payoff ÷ social optimum of an N-player public good) is never studied; the closest construct is “total surplus” of a two-person pair.

B. Parameters mentioned  
   10 of the 15 appear somewhere in the text: 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 15 (13 is only partly inferred).  The classical public-goods parameters 4 and 5 are entirely absent.

C. Parameters whose systematic variation is analysed for an effect on the punishment treatment  
   Only three parameters are ever **varied** across treatments and analysed:  
      • 3 (communication on/off)  
      • 7 (punishment cost: ∞ vs. 10, i.e., punishment off vs. on)  
      • The framing of the punishment stage (ordinary vs. grievance procedure); this is not among the 15 pre-specified parameters but effectively changes norm salience.  
   No numerical gradients for any of the other 12 parameters are provided.

D. What can we predict about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment-efficiency link, using only this paper?  
   • Reducing the *effective* cost of punishing from prohibitive to moderate (moving from no-conflict to conflict) can either harm surplus (baseline, communication, agreement) or mildly help it (grievance).  Hence: effect is context-dependent, not monotone.  
   • Allowing structured pre-play messages (parameter 3) does **not** make punishment more efficiency-enhancing; if anything, it shifts behaviour toward a PI norm and leaves surplus unchanged or slightly lower.  
   • Additional institutional framing (a formal grievance process) can flip the sign: with the same punishment technology, surplus becomes (slightly) higher.  Thus interactions between “punishment present” (parameter 7) and “institutional framing of information/legalities” (outside the 15-item list) are decisive.  
   • Because the paper never changes 1,2,6,8,9-15, and never studies 4-5, we can draw no prediction for their main effects or interactions.

In short, the paper demonstrates that the mere presence of a punishment option (parameter 7) is **not** sufficient for efficiency gains; its impact hinges on communication structure (3) and, especially, on whether the punishment is embedded in a grievance-style institutional frame.  All other listed parameters remain uninformative for predicting the punishment effect on efficiency within the confines of this paper.
reference_APA: Macleod, W. Bentley, Lara, Victoria Valle & Zehnder, Christian (2025). Worker Empowerment and Subjective Evaluation: On Building an Effective Conflict Culture. MANAGEMENT SCIENCE.

Below I go through the 15 public-goods-game design parameters one-by-one and relate them to the contents of the paper by Jia & Wang (“reputation-threshold trust game”).  I follow the required format as closely as possible.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned?  Yes.  Main simulations: L = 100 → 10 000 players; one robustness check: L = 500 → 250 000 players.  
   (2) Systematic variation & predicted impact on the punishment-treatment effect?  No.  The larger population is used only as a robustness test of the same model.  The authors do not (i) switch punishment on/off, nor (ii) report how a change in population size alters the incremental effect of punishment on any outcome (efficiency, contribution, etc.).

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Mentioned?  Yes.  10 000 discrete “time steps” in every run.  
   (2) Systematic variation?  No.  Time-horizon is fixed.

3. Chat enabled?  
   Not mentioned at all → no prediction.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   Not mentioned → no prediction.

5. Contribution default / endowment return?  
   Not mentioned → no prediction.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   Not part of the model.  The pay-off parameters are B, S, Temp, X instead.

7. Cost of imposing one unit of punishment  
   Not modeled.  “Punishment” is applied automatically by the platform;
   no player pays any cost.  Therefore no discussion of cost variation.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss per unit)  
   (1) Mentioned?  Yes, implicitly.  If a player’s reputation R < Z, every cell in the payoff matrix is multiplied by (R – Z)/Z, i.e. the further R lies below the threshold Z, the larger the penalty (“punishment magnitude”).  
   (2) Systematic variation?  Partly.  The authors vary Z from 0 to 20.  This simultaneously changes reward and punishment strength.  They report how strategy shares and total revenue change with Z (Figs. 2–3).  However:  
     • They never compare a “punishment treatment” to a “no-punishment control” while holding Z constant, so the paper contains no treatment effect in the usual experimental sense.  
     • No efficiency measure (total / maximum possible payoff) is reported.  
   Consequently, no numerical “punishment-treatment effect on efficiency” can be extracted.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   (1) Mentioned?  Yes.  If R > Z the same multiplier (R – Z)/Z is added, giving a reward.  
   (2) Systematic variation?  Z is varied 0–20, thereby strengthening or weakening reward.  No explicit on/off comparison; therefore no treatment-effect estimate.

10. Reward cost to grant a unit of reward  
    Not modeled (rewards are platform-provided).

11. Reward magnitude  
    As in parameter 8, magnitude rises with (R – Z)/Z and is indirectly varied through Z.  Same caveats: no punishment-treatment effect computed.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
    Not relevant in the simulation; not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    Not mentioned.

14. Do punished players learn who punished them?  
    Not modeled; punishment is not peer-directed.

15. Do rewarded players learn who rewarded them?  
    Not modeled; reward is not peer-directed.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables used  
   • Total revenue (aggregate pay-off).  
   • Proportions of the four strategies (TP, UP, TC, UC).  
   • Individual reputation heat-maps.  
   A specific “group efficiency” measure (actual / maximum possible total payoff) is never defined or reported.  Total revenue declines monotonically with higher Z, but the maximum possible revenue is never stated, so efficiency cannot be computed from the paper.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are at least mentioned?  
   6 of 15:  
   (1) number of players, (2) number of rounds, (7/8) punishment magnitude (implicit), (9) reward enabled, (11) reward magnitude.  The remaining 9 parameters never appear.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of systematic variation on the punishment-treatment effect for any dependent variable?  
   Zero.  Z is varied systematically, but this is done entirely inside the punishment/reward model; a “treatment effect” (difference between punishment and no-punishment) is not computed, and efficiency is not analysed.

D. What predictions about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency can be made solely from this paper?  
   • Very little.  Because the authors never report efficiency nor a control condition without punishment, no quantitative or even directional punishment-treatment effect on efficiency can be isolated.  
   • Qualitatively, one can infer that increasing Z (which strengthens both punishment and reward magnitudes) lowers total revenue while increasing the share of trustworthy strategies—so if one equates “efficiency” with total revenue, stronger punishment/reward appears to reduce efficiency.  If one equates “efficiency” with trustworthiness, the opposite holds.  The paper does not resolve this ambiguity.  
   • No statements whatsoever can be made about the other 14 parameters, because they are either fixed (players, rounds) or absent.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
End of analysis
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

Article Title: Cooperation in temporary partnerships
Author Keywords: Prisoner's dilemma; Random matching; Social norms
Keywords Plus: EQUILIBRIUM; REPUTATION; SHADOW
Abstract: The literature on cooperation in infinitely repeated Prisoner's Dilemmas covers the extreme opposites of the matching spectrum: partners, a player's opponent never changes, and strangers, a player's opponent randomly changes in every period. Here, we extend the analysis to settings where the opponent changes, but not in every period. In these temporary partnerships, players can deter some deviations by directly sanctioning their partner. Hence, relaxing the extreme assumption of one-period matchings can support some cooperation also off equilibrium because a class of strategies emerges that are less extreme than the typical grim strategy. We establish conditions supporting full cooperation as a subgame perfect equilibrium under a social norm that complements direct sanctions with a cyclical community sanction. Though this strategy less effectively incentivizes cooperation, it more effectively incentivizes punishment after a deviation, hence, can be preferable to the grim strategy under certain conditions.

Below I go through the 15 public-goods‐game design parameters one by one.  For each I state  

(i) whether it is mentioned in Camera & Gioffré (henceforth CG),  
(ii) the value(s) actually used, and  
(iii) whether CG says what would happen to the *punishment treatment effect* when the parameter is **systematically varied**.  Whenever CG contains an explicit comparative-static or a plotted relation I report the numerical or graphical information exactly as it appears.  Where nothing is said, I say so.

-------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
• Mentioned: Yes.  There are N = 2n ≥ 4 players; most numerical examples set N = 20 (p. 26, Fig. 1; p. 32, Fig. 2).  
• Systematic variation: Partly.  All algebra is written for any N.  Off-equilibrium incentives (e.g. σ₂ = (N-2)/(N-1) and the condition l ≥ N-2 for automatic credibility of punishment) explicitly depend on N, so CG derives the *direction* in which the critical discount factor δ₂ changes with N.  No figure sweeps N, and no efficiency numbers are given, but the paper does predict that increasing N (holding l fixed) makes punishment credibility easier (because (1-σ₂)/σ₂ = 1/(N-2) falls).  Numerical magnitude: not quantified.

2. Number of rounds (length of a partnership, T)  
• Mentioned: Yes.  Values analysed: T = 1, 2, 4 (Fig. 1).  
• Systematic variation: Yes.  CG shows that, as T rises,  
  – the lower equilibrium-existence bound δ₁ *increases* (cooperation becomes harder);  
  – the upper bound δ₂ *also increases* (punishment becomes easier).  
  These comparative statics are plotted in Fig. 1.  No efficiency outcomes are reported.

3. Is chat enabled?  
• Mentioned: No.  
• Systematic variation: Not applicable.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
• Mentioned: No.

5. Contribution default / endowment withdrawal  
• Mentioned: No.

6. MPCR or multiplication factor  
• Mentioned: No.  The game is a 2×2 Prisoner’s Dilemma with payoffs 1, 1+g, –l, 0, not a linear public-goods game.

7. Punishment cost to punisher  
• Mentioned: No.  “Punishment” here is simply choosing D; there is no costly punishment technology.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine imposed on target)  
• Mentioned: No (same reason as #7).

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
• Mentioned: No to all.

12. Whether the horizon is known  
• Mentioned: Indirectly.  The overall interaction is *indefinite* (infinite) and common knowledge; the within-partnership length T is fixed and common knowledge.  There is no discussion of varying this feature.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
• Mentioned: Yes, but only to state the monitoring structure: “private monitoring – players observe only their own pair.”  CG never varies this parameter.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
• Mentioned: No.

-------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
   • CG never reports *group efficiency* (total or average payoff divided by the first-best payoff).  
   • The paper’s key outcome measures are:  
     – Existence of a *subgame-perfect equilibrium* that yields full cooperation.  
     – Critical discount factors (δ₁, δ₂) that delimit where such an equilibrium exists.  
   These are logical/equilibrium conditions, not realised efficiency numbers, and therefore differ from contribution rates, cooperation frequencies or efficiency.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are **mentioned**?  
   5 of 15:  
   (1) Number of players, (2) Number of rounds/partnership length, (12) Horizon known (infinite), (13) Peer outcomes shown (private monitoring), and—very indirectly—(7)/(8) in the sense that “punishment” is just defection, not a designed cost or fine (but the paper itself does *not* introduce parameter values for them).

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of **systematically varying** them on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable)?  
   • Exactly 1: parameter (2) partnership length T.  
   • Parameter (1) is analytically present and enters formulas, so directionally its effect on δ₂ is derivable, but CG does not run an explicit comparative-static sweep or figure; therefore I do not count it as “systematically varied” under the authors’ own presentation.

D. Predictions one could make—*only* from CG—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency:  

   CG’s model is not a public-goods game, does not include costly punishment or rewards, and never computes efficiency.  The only credible, paper-based inferences one can make for a public-goods setting are therefore extremely limited:  
   • Longer partner stability (higher T) should raise the credibility of punishment off-equilibrium (easier to punish) but at the same time make cooperation on-equilibrium harder; whether efficiency rises or falls would depend on which margin dominates, something CG does not compute.  
   • Larger groups (higher N) slightly ease punishment credibility when punishment is done by switching to D (because each punisher loses proportionally less), but the paper gives no efficiency consequences.  
   • All other design features—chat, explicit fines and costs, rewards, information revelation—are not treated, so no prediction about their impact on efficiency can be extracted from CG alone.

In short, the CG paper supplies useful theory about how *partnership length* and, in formula, *group size* condition the set of discount factors for which a mixed direct-plus-community punishment can support cooperation, but it offers virtually no quantitative guidance about how any of the 15 public-goods-game parameters would change the *punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency*.

Author Full Names: Deng, Xiaoyang; Wang, Tao; Xue, Lian; Yang, Shuo
Article Title: Norm enforcement on minorities: Evidence from traffic violations
Author Keywords: Norm compliance; Social identity; Traffic violation; Compliance minority
Keywords Plus: GROUP IDENTITY; SOCIAL IMAGE; PUNISHMENT; DISCRIMINATION; COOPERATION; ECONOMICS; SELECTION
Abstract: Compliance with social rules is crucial for fostering cooperation in societies. Motivated by observational evidence from large-scale traffic violation data in a major city in China, we investigate the impact of social identity on rule-following behavior. We empirically showed that traffic violations are significantly less severe when individuals drive in foreign cities rather than the local city where the car is registered, a phenomenon we describe as the compliance minority effect. We next conducted a laboratory experiment with a street-crossing task, to further investigate the key drivers behind the compliance minority phenomenon. We found that participants exhibit more rule compliance when identifying as an outgroup minority than a local majority only when both observability and social sanctions are at play. Participants form the prior belief that being part of a minority in the community is associated with a higher chance of being monitored and punished than when they are part of the local majority, which is consistent with the posterior observations. Our results suggest that majorities can enforce augmented social norms on minority groups through an interplay of observability and punishment, which could lead to unintended consequences of local privilege that hamper the equality and efficiency of society.

Below I go through each of the 15 parameters in order.  
For every parameter I state  

(1) whether the paper ever mentions it and, if so, the value(s) actually used;  

(2) whether the paper says anything about what would happen to the *punishment-treatment effect* if the parameter were *systematically varied*.  
“Punishment-treatment effect” = the difference between a condition **with** peer-punishment opportunities and an otherwise identical condition **without** punishment.

When a numerical effect size can be read directly from a table or figure I reproduce it exactly as it appears; otherwise I write “n.a.”.  All references such as “Table 4” or “Fig. 4” refer to the tables and figures in the paper reproduced above.  No information beyond the paper is used.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned.  In the laboratory game each participant is matched with three others (group size = 4).  
   (2) Never varied, therefore no prediction.  Effect size: n.a.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Mentioned.  Five rounds of the street-crossing (rule-following) task.  
   (2) Never varied.  No prediction.  Effect size: n.a.

3. Chat enabled between players?  
   (1) Stage-1 “group-enhancement task” allows within-group text messages; the Stage-2 rule-following task (where punishment can occur) does *not* allow chat.  This setup is fixed.  
   (2) Not varied.  No prediction.  Effect size: n.a.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   (1) Not applicable; the decision is binary (wait 12 s or cross early).  
   (2) Not discussed.  No prediction.

5. Contribution default / give-back frame?  
   (1) Not applicable.  
   (2) No discussion.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   (1) Closest analogue is the externality of an early crossing: each violation costs every other group member 4 yuan.  This 4-yuan loss is fixed across all treatments.  
   (2) Never varied.  No prediction.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   (1) Mentioned.  A player can pay 1 yuan (or 2 yuan) to deduct 3 yuan (or 6 yuan) from the target.  This cost structure is identical in both punishment treatments (“Pun” and “EndogObs&Pun”).  
   (2) The *presence* versus *absence* of a punishment option is varied (Control & EndogObs: no punishment; Pun & EndogObs&Pun: punishment available) but the cost level itself is not systematically changed.  
       • Effect of “Pun” vs “Control”, Table 3: violation rate falls from .775 to .713 (−0.062).  
       • Effect of “EndogObs&Pun” vs “EndogObs”, Table 3: violation rate falls from .819 to .581 (−0.238).  
       • Logistic-regression marginal effect of EndogObs&Pun vs Control, Table 4 col (1): −0.175 (−17.5 p.p.).  
       Because the actual *cost per unit* is never manipulated, the paper makes no prediction about varying the cost itself.

8. Punishment magnitude (deduction inflicted per unit)  
   (1) Fixed at 3 or 6 yuan per unit as described above.  
   (2) Not varied.  No prediction.

9. Reward enabled?  
   (1) Not present in any treatment.  
   (2) No discussion.

10. Reward cost  
    (1) Not applicable.  
    (2) No discussion.

11. Reward magnitude  
    (1) Not applicable.  
    (2) No discussion.

12. Do players know the number of rounds?  
    (1) Implicitly yes—instructions say there are five rounds.  
    (2) Not varied.  No prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    (1) Yes.  After each round each player sees her own payoff; in observation treatments she also sees the chosen target’s waiting time and, if punishment is enabled, the net payoff after punishment.  
    (2) Not varied.  No prediction.

14. Is the punisher’s identity revealed?  
    (1) The paper never states that the punished player learns *who* punished them.  Therefore identity revelation is either “no” or unspecified, but it is constant across all punishment treatments.  
    (2) Not varied.  No prediction.

15. Is the rewarder’s identity revealed?  
    (1) No rewards exist.  
    (2) No discussion.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use “group efficiency” (total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper’s main dependent variables are  
     – Violation (binary) or waiting time (continuous),  
     – Punishment behaviour,  
     – Payoffs per person.  
   • “Efficiency” in the public-goods sense (actual payoff divided by maximum feasible payoff) is *not* the headline variable, but Section 3.3.4 does report average monetary payoffs and identifies the theoretical efficient benchmark (26 yuan) so an efficiency measure can be inferred.  Thus efficiency is implicit, not primary.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   10 of 15 are mentioned at least once:  
   1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14, (implicitly) 4 (binary action)  
   Parameters 5, 9, 10, 11, 15 are entirely absent.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* the parameter on the punishment treatment effect?  
   Zero.  
   The only dimensions that are varied experimentally are  
   • “Punishment allowed?” (yes / no) – this is a *binary presence* of punishment rather than a systematic variation of cost or magnitude,  
   • “Observability mode” (endogenous vs exogenous).  
   None of the 15 catalogued parameters themselves are varied over more than one level.

D. If one had to predict how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on *efficiency* based solely on this paper:  
   • Clear evidence: merely *enabling* peer punishment (with the fixed cost/magnitude used here) reduces violation rates slightly when observation is exogenous (−6 p.p.) and substantially when observation is endogenous (−24 p.p.).  However, average monetary payoffs *fall* once punishment is available (Section 3.3.4), implying lower efficiency under these fixed punishment parameters.  
   • The paper provides no information on how *changing* group size, number of rounds, MPCR, punishment cost/magnitude, information revelation, chat, etc. would alter that efficiency effect.  Consequently almost no further prediction can be made for the 15-parameter space.  The safest inference is that, in the environment studied, punishment improves rule compliance but at the parameter values chosen it does *not* improve average payoffs; whether different parameter values would reverse or amplify that trade-off is left completely open by the paper.

Article Title: Reconstruction of micro-dynamics characterizing human decision-making behavior in repeated social dilemmas
Author Keywords: Decision making; Bounded rationality; Evolutionary game; Repeated interactions

Abstract: Exploring evolutionary updating rules more consistent with individual cognitive processes is crucial to the study of human cooperation. A considerable number of dynamic models describing human decision-making behavior lack empirical evidence. We have conducted a behavioral experiment and proposed a hypothesis that human players make decisions based on proportional change rather than absolute difference of payoffs. Thus we can reconstruct the micro-dynamics, namely individual strategy updating rules, with a singular function considering the individual's choice to cooperate and defect separately. Our findings provide a novel framework for measuring human decision-making behavior with bounded rationality in repeated social dilemmas.

Below I go through the 15 parameters one‐by-one, restricting myself strictly to what is contained in “Promoting cooperation by punishing minority”.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  A 1000 × 1000 lattice (=1,000,000 players).  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  Only this single size is used, no results about changing it.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  None discussed.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  Yes, as Monte-Carlo steps: 10⁶ MCS with statistics taken over the last 10⁴.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  Not analysed.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Not mentioned at all → no value, no prediction.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  “Every cooperator contributes a unit cost… Defectors invest nothing.” (binary choice).  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  
   • Effect on punishment treatment effect?  None given.

5. Contribution default (endowment first in public fund)?  
   • Not mentioned.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor r  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  
   • Systematically varied?  Yes.  Figures 1–3 &  full α–r phase diagram (Fig. 2) vary r from ≈2.5 to 5.  
   • Effect reported?  
        – When α = 0 or small: ρ_c rises continuously with r (Fig. 1).  
        – When α is large (e.g., 0.8): a critical r ≈ 3.38 produces a discontinuous jump of ρ_c from 0 → 1.  
      All effects are reported for the dependent variable “fraction of cooperators”, not for efficiency.

7. Punishment cost to impose a unit of punishment  
   • Model: punishers “equally share the associated costs”. The numerical cost therefore equals α·(minority size)/(majority size).  
   • Systematically varied?  Not independently of α.  No separate results.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine) α  
   • Mentioned?  Yes—the paper’s key control variable.  
   • Systematically varied?  Yes (0 → 0.8).  
   • Effect reported?  
        – For any fixed r, higher α → higher ρ_c (Fig. 3).  
        – For α > 0.45, coexistence region C+D disappears (Fig. 2).  
        – Pay-off gap along cluster interface grows linearly with α:  P_C – P_D = 1.5 r + (17/24) α – 5 (Eq. 8).  
      Again, effects are on ρ_c and on payoff difference, not on efficiency.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Not mentioned.

10. Reward cost  
    • Not mentioned.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Not mentioned.

12. Finite horizon known to players?  
    • Not mentioned.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Not mentioned.

14. Is punisher identified?  
    • Not mentioned.

15. Is rewarder identified?  
    • Not mentioned.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables used in the paper  
   – Fraction of cooperators (ρ_c): main outcome plotted in Figs. 1, 3 and used in the phase diagram Fig. 2.  
   – Pay-off difference at the C–D interface (Eq. 8).  
   – Densities of the four group types G_cc, G_dd, G_cd, G_dc (Figs. 7–8).  
   Group efficiency (total or average payoff divided by the cooperative optimum) is NOT used anywhere.

B. Parameters mentioned (5/15)  
   1. Number of players (fixed 1,000,000)  
   2. Number of rounds (fixed 10⁶ MCS)  
   4. Binary contribution rule  
   6. Multiplication factor r (varied)  
   8. Punishment fine α (varied)

C. Parameters whose systematic variation is analysed for their effect on the punishment treatment effect (2/15)  
   – Multiplication factor r (Parameter 6)  
   – Punishment fine α (Parameter 8)  
   The paper compares α = 0 (no-punishment baseline) with α > 0, so a “punishment treatment effect” on ρ_c can be inferred for these two parameters only. No numerical efficiency effect is reported.

D. What predictions about efficiency can be made solely from this paper?  
   • Because efficiency is never calculated, only indirect conjectures are possible:  
        – Higher α raises ρ_c; if punishment costs do not overwhelm the benefit from cooperation, efficiency should also rise with α.  
        – For α > 0.45 the system ends up either in full cooperation or full defection, so efficiency would be either maximal or minimal; coexistence (and intermediate efficiency) disappears.  
        – At large α, a small increase in r around the critical value can trigger a jump from zero to full cooperation, implying a discontinuous jump from very low to very high efficiency.  
   • No predictions can be made for the remaining 13 parameters (1–5, 7, 9–15) because they are not varied or even mentioned in relation to punishment effects.

In short, the paper tells us only how varying the multiplication factor and the punishment fine shapes the **cooperation rate**; it gives no direct information about group **efficiency**, and it is silent on the other 13 design parameters.

Article Title: Evolutionary dynamics of cooperation in optional public goods games with loners' punishment
Keywords Plus: NETWORKS
Abstract: Volunteering is a common mechanism for promoting cooperation, characterized by the self-organized cyclic dynamics among cooperators, defectors, and loners. Although this mechanism protects cooperators from being overwhelmed by defectors, it does not guarantee their ultimate success. Defectors are motivated to exploit cooperators due to their contributions to public goods. This raises a question: Can punishing cooperators disrupt the balance of cyclic invasion among the three strategies, ultimately leading to their dominance? Based on experimental evidence of economic sanctions imposed by loners on cooperators, this paper introduces loners who punish cooperators into optional public goods games. We develop an evolutionary model of a four-strategy game within a structured population. By exploring the spatial dynamics of the system and the evolutionary patterns of specific strategy distributions, we study the properties of phase transitions and the underlying mechanisms. Our analysis aims to elucidate how cooperation evolves under such punishment. The results indicate that these punishers can create a three-strategy cyclic state with cooperators and defectors. Under specific conditions, the system can enter from this cyclic phase to a pure cooperator phase. Additionally, when loners have a high fixed income, the system may enter a coexistence phase, including cooperators and two types of loners. In this phase, traditional loners form protective enclaves to safeguard cooperators from severe punishment.

Below, each of the 15 meta-parameters is examined in turn.  For every parameter I first state whether it is mentioned in the paper and, if so, how it is operationalised.  I then say whether the paper **systematically varies** that parameter and, if it does, what the documented consequence is for the “punishment treatment effect.”  Throughout, “punishment treatment effect” means the difference between a baseline game without punishishing loners (the 3-strategy C+D+LN system) and the same game after the introduction of the punishing-loner strategy LP (the 4-strategy C+D+LN+LP system).  The only dependent variables actually reported are strategy frequencies and phase membership; the paper never reports efficiency, total payoff, or average payoff.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned: Yes.  The population is a square lattice of size L×L (L up to 320).  
   • Systematically varied: No.  L is increased only to rule out finite-size artefacts.  No quantitative effect on the punishment treatment effect is reported.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned: Yes (“no more than 10⁹ rounds”).  
   • Systematically varied: No.  The number of rounds is used only to ensure convergence.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned: No.  Not part of the model.  No effect reported.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Mentioned: Implicitly yes.  A co-operator pays a fixed cost c, a defector pays 0.  
   • Systematically varied: No.  c is kept constant; all decisions remain binary in every simulation.

5. Contribution default / endowment moved back?  
   • Mentioned: No.  Not modelled.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor (r)  
   • Mentioned: Yes.  r is the “synergy factor”.  
   • Systematically varied: Yes.  r is the x-axis in several r–δ phase diagrams (Figs. 1, 12).  
   • Reported qualitative effect: With the baseline (no LP) the system is C-poor for r<3.74, but after LP is added the location and width of the pure-C phase, the C+D+LN phase, and the C+D+LP phase shift.  No numeric efficiency gains are given; only phase borders are shown.

7. Punishment cost to punisher (α)  
   • Mentioned: Yes – cost incurred by each LP when punishing any C in the group.  
   • Systematically varied: Yes.  α is the y-axis in three α–β phase diagrams (Fig. 3).  
   • Reported qualitative effect: Larger α shrinks the region in which LP out-competes LN.  At high α and high β a new three-strategy phase (C+LN+LP) appears that temporarily raises the fraction of cooperators relative to the 3-strategy baseline, but no efficiency numbers are given.

8. Punishment magnitude / fine on target (β)  
   • Mentioned: Yes – fine levied on each punished C.  
   • Systematically varied: Yes.  β is the x-axis in Fig. 3 and the variable in Figs. 4, 8.  
   • Reported qualitative effect:  
        – Low β: LP is competitively weak; system behaves like the 3-strategy baseline (Fig. 5a).  
        – Intermediate β: a C+D+LP cyclic phase emerges (Fig. 5b; Fig. 6).  
        – Higher β: sequence of discontinuous transitions LP → C → LP (Fig. 4).  
        – Very high β (together with high α): C+LN+LP phase arises (Fig. 8).  
     Again, only phase membership and strategy fractions are reported, not efficiency.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Mentioned: No.  Not in the model.

10. Reward cost  
    • Mentioned: No.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Mentioned: No.

12. Finite horizon known to players?  
    • Mentioned: No.

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mentioned: No.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
    • Mentioned: No.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
    • Mentioned: No.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables  
    • The paper does NOT use group efficiency, total payoff, or average payoff.  
    • Dependent variables are: (i) asymptotic phase (e.g., C phase, C+D+LP phase, etc.); (ii) average fractions of each strategy in the stationary state.  These reflect cooperation levels but are not payoffs.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
    – Parameters 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8 are mentioned.  
    – Total mentioned: 6 of 15.

C.  Which parameters are *systematically varied* and linked to the punishment treatment effect?  
    – r (6), α (7), β (8) are systematically varied and their influence on strategy composition after introducing LP is mapped.  
    – Total: 3 of 15.

D.  Predicting the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency from the paper’s content  
    The article provides no efficiency or payoff data, so almost no direct inference about efficiency is possible.  All that can cautiously be stated is:  
    • High β combined with low α can eliminate defectors and therefore *might* raise efficiency if the fine and cost are not too large in payoff terms.  
    • Very high α or very high β can drive the system into an all-loner (L) phase, which would reduce efficiency relative to full cooperation.  
    • Low r values (<3.74) make cooperation fragile; adding LP under those conditions can either help (via C phase) or hurt (via LP phase) depending on α and β.  
    Because the model never reports total payoffs, these remain speculative; the paper itself offers “little to no direct prediction” about efficiency.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
End of analysis.

Below I go through the fifteen parameters one by one, strictly reporting what the Kim et al. (2025) paper says and, where possible, what it lets us infer about the *punishment‐treatment effect* (i.e. the behavioural change observed when moving from the ten periods **without** punishment to the ten periods **with** punishment).  “Efficiency” (total pay-off ÷ maximum possible pay-off) is **never** the main dependent variable in the paper; the authors mostly analyse *contribution levels*, *punishment levels* and, in an appendix, *average pay-offs*.  Whenever the paper is silent on a parameter or on systematic variation of that parameter I say so explicitly.

------------------------------------------------------------------
1. NUMBER OF PLAYERS  
• Discussed? Yes.  In NoR each “team” is a single person (k = 1); in RnoM and RM each team has three players (k = 3). Four teams form a “group”.  
• Systematically varied? Not in isolation.  Team size changes together with the representation manipulation, so the paper does **not** give a clean estimate of “more vs. fewer players” on the punishment effect.  No numerical effect on efficiency is provided.

2. NUMBER OF ROUNDS  
• Discussed? Yes.  Two blocks of ten periods each (20 periods total).  
• Systematically varied? No.  Nothing is said about what would happen with a different horizon.

3. CHAT / COMMUNICATION ENABLED?  
• Discussed? Yes.  In RM non-representatives can send *cheap-talk* numeric messages to the period’s representative; in RnoM and NoR no such channel exists.  
• Systematically varied? Yes (RM vs. RnoM).  
  – Effect reported (contributions, not efficiency):  
    • Later five periods of the punishment block: mean contribution = 11.50 points in RM vs. 9.64 in RnoM (Table 2).  
    • “Low contributors”: each additional punishment point raises next-period contribution by an extra 0.49 points in RM relative to NoR (Table 6, col. 6).  
  – No direct efficiency numbers are given, so no numeric efficiency effect can be extracted.

4. ALL-OR-NOTHING CONTRIBUTION?  
• Not mentioned.  Continuous choice 0–20 is used in every treatment.

5. “CONTRIBUTION-DEFAULT” (WITHDRAW FRAME)?  
• Not mentioned; standard “how much to *contribute*” frame is used.

6. MPCR (MULTIPLIER)  
• Discussed? Yes.  Total public contribution is multiplied by 0.4 per team.  
• Systematically varied? No.  Only the value 0.4 is used; no predictions about other values.

7. PUNISHMENT COST PER UNIT  
• Discussed? Yes.  A team pays 1 point for each punishment point it assigns.  
• Systematically varied? No.  No predictions for other cost levels.

8. PUNISHMENT MAGNITUDE PER UNIT  
• Discussed? Yes.  Each punishment point subtracts 3 points from the target.  
• Systematically varied? No.  No discussion of alternative magnitudes.

9. REWARD ENABLED?  
• Not present in any treatment; never discussed.

10. REWARD COST PER UNIT  
• Not applicable / not discussed.

11. REWARD MAGNITUDE PER UNIT  
• Not applicable / not discussed.

12. IS THE HORIZON COMMON KNOWLEDGE?  
• Discussed? Yes.  Subjects are told each part lasts exactly ten periods and that the experiment has two parts.  
• Systematically varied? No.

13. ARE PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN?  
• Discussed? Yes.  After the contribution stage every team sees every other team’s contribution and pay-off; after the punishment stage they also see every punishment allocation.  
• Systematically varied? No.

14. IS THE PUNISHER IDENTIFIED?  
• Discussed? Partially.  Within a period the punished team sees which *team ID* punished it, but team IDs are reshuffled every round and the individual representative is never revealed.  
• Systematically varied? No.

15. IS THE REWARDER IDENTIFIED?  
• Not applicable (no rewards).

------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables actually used  
   – Main: average *contribution* per team.  
   – Secondary: total punishment sent, prosocial vs. antisocial punishment, change in contributions across periods, average monetary pay-off (Appendix G).  
   – The paper never reports or analyses “group efficiency” as defined by the user (pay-off ÷ maximum pay-off), although Appendix G does compare average pay-offs across parts.

B.  Parameters *mentioned* (9/15):  1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14.  Parameters 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 15 are not mentioned.

C.  Parameters whose *systematic variation* is analysed for any dependent variable (1/15 clearly, possibly 2/15 if one counts the confounded team-size change):  
   – Parameter 3 (communication channel): RM vs. RnoM.  Effects reported on contributions and on the responsiveness of low contributors to punishment.  
   – No other parameter is cleanly varied; number of players (parameter 1) changes together with representation and therefore cannot be separated out.

D.  Predictions one could make **solely from this paper** about the punishment-treatment effect on *efficiency*:

   • Communication (parameter 3): allowing cheap-talk messages should *slightly mitigate* the efficiency loss that otherwise arises under representation, because it raises contributions (≈ +2 points in the late punishment periods) without noticeably increasing punishment costs.  
   • Representation / larger team size (parameter 1) seems to *lower* efficiency when punishment is available: representatives punish more (higher cost) yet end up with lower contributions than self-representing individuals.  
   • All the other parameters are fixed in the design; the paper gives no basis for forecasting how changing them would alter efficiency.

   In short, outside of “cheap-talk messages help somewhat”, the paper provides little or no guidance on how the fifteen parameters—or their interactions—would influence the punishment-treatment effect on *group efficiency*.

Abstract: Since Hardin (1968) emphasized the fundamental difficulties of common pool re- source (CPR) management, social scientists have been struggling to find a way of mitigating a free-riding problem in social dilemma situations. Below, each of the 15 design parameters is treated in turn.

For every parameter we state  

(1) whether it is explicitly described anywhere in the paper (and quote the value, wording, or figure/table where it appears), and  

(2) whether the paper makes any prediction or presents any evidence about what would happen if that parameter were **systematically varied** with respect to the punishment-treatment effect (and, if so, the numerical size of that effect).

Parameter-by-parameter inspection
-------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Yes. All groups consist of four players (Section 2.2 “Subjects are randomly assigned to experimental groups, each of which includes four players”).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Yes. Ten rounds: five without punishment, five with punishment (Section 2.2; Footnote 11).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

3. Chat enabled between players  
   (1) Indirectly: no face-to-face chat; only anonymous “dissatisfaction” cards can be sent (Section 2.3).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
   (1) Continuous choice: players decide “how much of their budget to invest” (Section 2.2).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

5. Contribution default / “take-back” frame  
   (1) Not used. Endowment starts in the player’s hand and can be put into the public fund (standard “give” frame).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   (1) One yen invested is doubled for the group of four, implying MPCR = 0.5 (Section 2.2: “the experimenter doubles the total amount … and distributes it equally”).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

7. Punishment cost  
   (1) Fixed at 10 yen per “dissatisfaction” message (Section 2.3).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

8. Punishment magnitude  
   (1) 0 yen – purely symbolic; no monetary deduction (Section 2.3).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

9. Reward enabled  
   (1) Reward is **not** enabled (no mention of any rewarding stage).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   (1) Not applicable; the paper never mentions any reward mechanism.  
   (2) No discussion.

12. End-round information (finite horizon known?)  
   (1) Subjects were told there would be 10 rounds; they were *not* told in advance that the punishment rule would start after round 5 (Section 2.3: “After the first five rounds, the experimenter gives additional instructions…”).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   (1) Yes. After each round the amounts invested by the other three group members are revealed, anonymously (Section 2.2, Footnote 10).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
   (1) No. Dissatisfaction cards are anonymous (“Recipients cannot identify who sent the messages to them”, Section 2.3).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
   (1) Not applicable (no reward stage).  
   (2) No discussion.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary  
A. Dependent variables  
   • The paper’s main outcome is the percentage of each subject’s endowment contributed to the public good.  
   • The authors also look at binary indicators such as “was punishment executed in the previous round” and at heterogeneous responses (punishers vs. punishees).  
   • Group efficiency, total payoff, or average payoff are **never** reported; contribution is **not** converted into efficiency figures anywhere in the text, tables, or figures.

B. Parameters mentioned  
   12 of the 15 parameters are at least mentioned or their values can be inferred (1-9, 12-14).  
   Reward-related parameters (10, 11, 15) are not present.

C. Parameters whose **systematic variation** is analysed  
   None. The paper varies only one factor—community “closedness”, a variable external to the 15 design parameters. No tables, figures, or regressions examine what would happen if any of the above 15 parameters changed.

D. Predicting punishment-treatment effects on efficiency using only this paper  
   • Because efficiency is never measured, the paper offers no direct basis for predicting how any of the 15 parameters would affect efficiency.  
   • Since none of the parameters are experimentally manipulated, the safest prediction is “insufficient information”.  
   • The only qualitative hint is that the punishment implemented here is **weak (cost = 10 yen, magnitude = 0)** and, in combination with a high-trust closed network, it *reduces* contributions. One might cautiously guess that:  
     – Making punishment *stronger* (changing parameters 7 or 8) could either counteract crowding-out or exacerbate retaliation, but the paper provides no evidence on direction or size.  
     – Allowing identification of punishers (parameter 14) might intensify peer pressure, yet the paper contains no data.  
   • Beyond that, the paper offers little or no guidance for forecasting efficiency responses to changes in player number, MPCR, reward availability, information structure, etc.

In short, the article is a study of community structure rather than of the 15 canonical public-goods-game design parameters, and it does not permit quantitative predictions about how altering any of those parameters would change the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.
reference_APA: Goto, Jun & Matsui, Takahiro (2025). Counterproductive punishment in closed communities: Experimental evidence from Japanese fishery. MARINE POLICY.

Article Title: Maintaining cooperation through vertical communication of trust when removing sanctions
Source Title: PROCEEDINGS OF THE NATIONAL ACADEMY OF SCIENCES OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
Author Keywords: cooperation; vertical trust; punishment; public good; experiment
Keywords Plus: COLLECTIVE ACTION; PUNISHMENT; FOUNDATIONS; MOOD
Abstract: An effective way to foster cooperation is to monitor behavior and sanction freeriding. Yet, previous studies have shown that cooperation quickly declines when sanctioning mechanisms are removed. We test whether explicitly expressing trust in players' capability to maintain cooperation after the removal of sanctions, i.e., vertical communication of trust, has the potential to alleviate this drop in compliance. Four incentivized public- goods experiments (N = 2,823) find that the vertical communication of trust maintains cooperation upon the removal of centralized (Study 1), third- party (Study 2a, 2b), and peer punishment (Study 3), and this effect extends beyond single interactions (Study 4). In all studies, vertical trust communication increases mutual trust among players, providing support to the idea that vertically communicating trust can be a self- fulfilling prophecy. Extrapolating our findings to natural environments, they suggest that authorities should carefully consider how they communicate the lifting of rules and sanctions.

Parameter-by-parameter extraction from the paper “Maintaining cooperation through vertical communication of trust when removing sanctions”

(1) Number of players  
• Mentioned? Yes – every study is a four-player public-goods game.  
• Systematically varied? No. No prediction or effect size on any dependent variable, including efficiency.

(2) Number of rounds  
• Mentioned? Yes – Studies 1–3 have two rounds, Study 4 has three.  
• Systematically varied? No. The extra round in Study 4 is not analysed as a treatment factor; no prediction about how changing the number of rounds would alter a punishment treatment effect.

(3) Chat enabled?  
• Mentioned? Yes – explicitly “The setup was completely anonymous” and no communication among players.  
• Systematically varied? No.

(4) All-or-nothing contribution?  
• Mentioned? Implicitly – contributions are continuous (0-10 tokens).  
• Systematically varied? No.

(5) Contribution default (back-transfer)?  
• Mentioned? No. There is no “take” or back-transfer frame in any study.  
• Systematically varied? No.

(6) Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor  
• Mentioned? Yes – tokens placed in the public pot are doubled (group return factor = 2, MPCR = 0.5 with four players).  
• Systematically varied? No.

(7) Punishment cost to the punisher  
• Mentioned? Partially.  
   – Centralised punishment: automated; nobody pays a cost.  
   – Third-party punishment: the punisher destroys tokens; no personal cost is described.  
   – Peer punishment: cost not reported.  
• Systematically varied? No prediction or test.

(8) Punishment magnitude  
• Mentioned? Yes – Centralised: 1.6 tokens taken per token under-contributed; Third-party: up to 15 tokens can be deducted; Peer: magnitude not specified.  
• Systematically varied? No.

(9) Whether a reward is enabled  
• Mentioned? Yes – no reward mechanism is ever present.  
• Systematically varied? No.

(10) Reward cost  
• Not applicable – never present.

(11) Reward magnitude  
• Not applicable – never present.

(12) Are the number of rounds known?  
• Mentioned? Yes – “all participants were informed about the total number of rounds”.  
• Systematically varied? No.

(13) Are peer outcomes shown each round?  
• Mentioned? Yes – “Players did not receive any feedback on payoffs before the very end of the study,” meaning outcomes were hidden.  
• Systematically varied? No.

(14) Is punisher identity revealed?  
• Mentioned? Implicitly – punishments (when they occur) are determined off-line via the strategy method and delivered after the game; identity is never revealed.  
• Systematically varied? No.

(15) Is rewarder identity revealed?  
• Not applicable – no rewards.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary requested by the user
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables  
   • Group efficiency (total or average payoff) is never reported.  
   • The paper analyses (i) individual contributions to the public good and (ii) self-reported trust; mood is measured but not treated as a main outcome. Contributions and trust are conceptually different from efficiency because they ignore the pay-offs lost through punishment costs and fines.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 12, 13, 14 (11 parameters) are at least described or fixed at a value. Parameters 5, 10, 11, 15 are not discussed.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of systematically varying that parameter on any punishment treatment effect?  
   Zero. None of the 15 parameters are experimentally manipulated; therefore no causal statements or numerical effect sizes are available.

D. Predictions one could make (solely from this paper) about how the 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency  
   • The paper gives almost no leverage: punishment magnitude, cost, MPCR, group size, feedback, anonymity, etc. are all held constant.  
   • The only actionable insight is that “vertical communication of trust” can substitute for continuing punishment and sustain high contributions even when the punishment institution is removed; but this pertains to communication, not to any of the 15 structural, monetary, incentive, or information parameters listed above.  
   • Consequently, based strictly on the paper, we can make little to no prediction about how changing any of the 15 parameters (alone or in interaction) would alter the efficiency impact of introducing punishment.

In short, the paper is informative about a communication intervention, not about how the usual design parameters of a public-goods game moderate the efficiency effect of punishment.

Abstract: We present a lab-in-the-field experiment with employees of the Addis Ababa Water and Sewerage Authority to understand how to improve coordination and collaboration in their daily work. Participants play a series of public good games under different rules: a standard game, a game with a threshold, and a game with a randomly selected anonymous monitor who has the power to punish. Below I go through the 15 design parameters one‐by‐one, always restricting myself strictly to what is written, tabulated or plotted in the paper “Motivating Public Sector Employees: Public Good Contributions in Addis Ababa Water and Sewerage Authority”.

────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
────────────────────────────────────────
(1) Number of players  
• Mentioned: Yes – every game is played in “groups of five”.  
• Systematically varied: No. All games use five players, so the paper contains no evidence on how changing the group size would change the punishment treatment effect (PTE).  

(2) Number of rounds  
• Mentioned: Yes – each subject plays four one-shot rounds (1 practice + 3 paid).  
• Systematically varied: No – always four rounds. No prediction supplied for other round lengths.

(3) Chat enabled?  
• Mentioned: Implicitly – no free communication is allowed; instructions are language-free and no chat channel is opened.  
• Systematically varied: No. No statement about what would happen if chat were added.

(4) All-or-nothing contribution?  
• Mentioned: Players choose any integer 0–10; so the game is NOT all-or-nothing.  
• Systematically varied: No.

(5) Contribution “default” (withdrawal from a public fund)?  
• Not mentioned.  

(6) MPCR / multiplication factor  
• Mentioned: Tokens contributed are doubled; with 5 players the MPCR is 0.40.  
• Systematically varied: No. Only that single value is used; no prediction for other MPCRs.

(7) Punishment cost to punisher  
• Mentioned: Cost = 1 token per punished target.  
• Systematically varied: No – fixed at 1. No results on other costs.

(8) Punishment magnitude (loss to target per unit)  
• Mentioned: 3 tokens deducted from target for each unit of punishment.  
• Systematically varied: No – fixed at 3. No prediction for other magnitudes.

(9) Reward enabled?  
• Not used.  

(10) Reward cost  
• Not used.  

(11) Reward magnitude  
• Not used.  

(12) Are the number of rounds known?  
• Not explicitly reported. No discussion about end-game knowledge and no variation.

(13) Are peer outcomes shown each round?  
• Mentioned: No. “No information on group return was revealed until the payment stage.”  
• Systematically varied: No.

(14) Does a punished player learn who punished them?  
• Mentioned: No. “The chosen monitor was known only by the experiment director and not by the group members or the monitor himself or herself.”  
• Systematically varied: No.

(15) Does a rewarded player learn who rewarded them?  
• Not applicable – rewards are not used.

────────────────────────────────────────
ANY NUMERICAL EFFECT SIZES REPORTED?
────────────────────────────────────────
Only one aspect that is directly related to “introducing punishment” is varied: the presence vs. absence of a (anonymous) monitor who can punish. All other parameters stay fixed. The paper therefore provides just one PTE estimate, associated with going from the baseline game (no peer punishment) to the monitor game (peer punishment enabled with cost = 1, magnitude = 3).

• Individual-level contributions (Table 3, col. 3): +0.788 tokens (SE = 0.179) relative to the no-punishment baseline.  
• Group-level aggregate contribution (Table 3, col. 5): +3.938 tokens (SE = 0.897) relative to the no-punishment baseline.

No efficiency (total pay-off / maximum possible) is reported, so no numerical effect on efficiency can be extracted.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────
A.  Does the paper use “group efficiency” (total or average pay-off) as a dependent variable?  
    • No. Dependent variables are:  
      – Individual contribution (0–10 tokens).  
      – Group outcome (sum of pay-offs that survive the threshold rule, expressed in tokens).  
      – Whether / how many group members the monitor punishes.  
      These differ from efficiency because they ignore both the costs of punishment (monitors’ 1-token payments and punished players’ 3-token losses) and the initial 10-token endowments kept by free-riders.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
    1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 13, 14  → 9 out of 15.  
    (Parameters 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 15 are not described.)

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when that parameter is systematically varied?  
    • None of the 15 parameters is systematically varied in the sense of taking multiple values. The only “variation” is the presence vs. absence of punishment itself, which is not one of the listed parameters (cost or magnitude). Therefore the answer is 0 parameters.

D.  If forced to predict how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the PTE on efficiency using only this paper:  
    • The paper offers just one data point: enabling an anonymous monitor (cost = 1, magnitude = 3) at MPCR = 0.40 and group size = 5 raises contributions but also destroys tokens via punishment. Because punishment costs (≈ 4 tokens per punished player) are not netted out in the contribution figures, we cannot tell whether overall efficiency rises or falls.  
    • With no additional evidence, the safest prediction about how changing any of the other 14 parameters (group size, MPCR, visibility, communication, etc.) would alter the efficiency impact of punishment is: “No clear prediction can be made on the basis of the reported results.”

Author Keywords: Inequality; Transparency; Secrecy; Public good; Experiment
Keywords Plus: TAX EVASION; BUSINESS; REDISTRIBUTION; INFORMATION; PERSPECTIVE; GOVERNANCE; FAIRNESS; BEHAVIOR; FIRM
Abstract: Across two studies, we examine the role of transparency and peer punishment in promoting cooperation and addressing economic inequality in public good contributions. With global inequality rising and the wealthiest few amassing a greater share of resources, its impact on social cohesion and business environments is increasingly significant. Financial secrecy further compounds these issues by allowing for income and wealth concealment at both societal and organizational levels. Our experimental findings reveal that transparency paired with peer punishment significantly boosts cooperation, particularly among advantaged individuals. In contrast, peer punishment alone proves insufficient to mitigate the adverse effects of inequality without the support of transparency. These results underscore the need for ethical governance structures that incorporate transparency, fairness, and accountability-principles essential for organizations committed to fostering trust and social responsibility in unequal settings.

Below, each of the 15 catalogue-parameters is examined in the order given.  For every parameter I state  

(1) whether it is explicitly described in the paper and, if so, its value(s) and location in the text/tables;  
(2) whether the paper **systematically varies** the parameter;  
(3) whether the paper says anything about how such variation alters the *punishment treatment effect* (i.e., the difference between a Punishment and a No-Punishment condition).  When any numerical effect can be read directly from a figure or table I quote it and say which figure/table it comes from.  Where the paper stays silent, I say so.

────────────────────────────────────────

1. Number of players  
   • Discussed: always 4 players per group (Methodology, Study 1; Table 1).  
   • Not varied.  
   • No statement on how changing the group size would alter the punishment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Discussed: 20 rounds (two blocks of 10) in both studies (Study-1 timeline Fig. 3; Study-2 timeline Fig. 5).  
   • Not varied.  
   • No prediction about changing the number of rounds.  Results across early vs. late rounds are reported, but round-number itself is never an experimental factor.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Not mentioned; no chat option appears in the procedures.  
   • Not varied.  
   • No prediction.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule?  
   • Discussed implicitly: subjects choose any integer amount from 0 up to their whole endowment (Instructions “You will decide how much… to contribute”).  So the game is *not* all-or-nothing.  
   • Not varied.  
   • No prediction.

5. Contribution default / “give-then-take” format?  
   • Not mentioned.  Standard “allocate from private account to public account” is used.  
   • Not varied.  
   • No prediction.

6. Marginal per–capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   • Discussed: MPCR = 0.4 for every player (Eq. 1).  
   • Not varied.  
   • No prediction about alternative MPCR values.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher (per point)  
   • Discussed: cost = 1 ECU per point (Eq. 2; Stage-2 instructions).  
   • *Systematically varied only in the trivial sense “punishment present (cost = 1)” vs. “punishment absent (cost not applicable)”.*  
   • Reported punishment treatment effects (dependent variables are *contributions*, not efficiency):  
     – Study 2, endowments *public*: introduction of punishment raises mean *relative contribution* by ≈ +22 p.p. (Fig. 6 left, difference between 0.38→0.60; χ²(1)=13.30, p<0.001).  
     – Study 2, endowments *secret*: introduction of punishment raises mean *relative contribution* by ≈ +13 p.p. (Fig. 6 left; χ²(1)=14.55, p<0.001).  
     – No efficiency measure reported, so no numeric effect on efficiency can be given.

8. Punishment magnitude to the target (per point)  
   • Discussed: 1 point deducted costs the target 3 ECU (Eq. 2; Stage-2 instructions).  
   • Held constant; not varied.  
   • No prediction about alternative punishment severities.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Not implemented, not discussed.  
   • No prediction.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   • Not applicable (no reward stage).

12. Are the total number of rounds known to participants?  
   • The paper never states whether subjects were told that the game would last exactly 20 rounds.  So status is *unclear*.  No variation.  
   • No prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (earnings and/or contributions)?  
   • Discussed: after each round subjects saw every group member’s contribution and their own payoff (Stage-2 feedback).  In punishment treatments they also saw any points received.  
   • Not experimentally varied.  What *was* varied is *whether endowments themselves became public after round 10* (Study 2) – but that is different from this parameter.  
   • No statement on how hiding or revealing peer *outcomes* (as opposed to endowments) would change the punishment effect.

14. Is the identity of a punisher revealed to the target?  
   • Not stated; default appears to be anonymous punishment.  
   • Not varied.  
   • No prediction.

15. Is the identity of a rewarder revealed?  
   • Not applicable.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used  
   – The paper never computes *group efficiency* ( realised total payoff ÷ socially optimal total ).  
   – Main DVs: absolute and relative contributions, individual/cumulative payoffs, Gini coefficient of earnings, and willingness-to-pay (WTP) for secrecy.  These differ conceptually from efficiency because they do not compare outcomes to the social optimum.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   7 parameters:  
   (1) players = 4; (2) rounds = 20; (4) continuous contribution choice; (6) MPCR = 0.4; (7) cost of punishment = 1; (8) punishment magnitude = 3; (13) peer contributions/payoffs are shown.  Parameters 3,5,9-12,14-15 are absent or only implicit.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss how *systematically varying* them influences the punishment treatment effect?  
   Effect sizes are reported only for the on/off manipulation of *punishment itself* (which touches parameters 7 & 8 in the sense “existent vs. nonexistent”).  No other parameter is systematically varied, so the count is **1 parameter pair (7&8)** out of 15, and even here the outcome measured is *contribution*, not efficiency.

D. Predictions one can make (and their limits) for the punishment-treatment effect on **efficiency**, based solely on this paper  
   – Because efficiency is never analysed, the paper offers almost no direct guidance.  
   – The sole relevant finding is that, when endowments are *public* (everything else fixed), introducing a punishment stage markedly raises contributions (+22 p.p. relative) and when endowments are *secret* the boost is smaller (+13 p.p.).  If higher contributions translate monotonically into higher efficiency (which they would in the present linear-PGBG), one could tentatively expect that “Punishment cost = 1, magnitude = 3” improves efficiency versus “No punishment”, and that the size of the gain depends on information about endowments rather than on any of the 15 catalogue-parameters themselves.  
   – For the other 14 parameters the paper provides no data or theory, so no prediction specific to them can be extracted.

In short, the study is rich on *transparency/inequality* issues but gives almost no leverage for forecasting how the usual design parameters of a public-goods game would moderate the punishment effect on group efficiency.

Author Full Names: Dato, Simon; Friehe, Tim
Article Title: Punishment for intentions or outcomes: the role of gender and social norms
Keywords Plus: DECISION-MAKING; TRUST; RECIPROCITY; FAIRNESS; EMOTION; BELIEFS; GAMES; PREFERENCES; COOPERATION; INEQUALITY
Abstract: Individuals often evaluate others' actions based on both their perceived intentions and their resulting outcomes, rewarding favorable actions and punishing unfavorable ones. This study aims to isolate the influence of these factors on punishment. We experimentally demonstrate that, when outcomes are held constant, second movers punish first movers who choose selfish actions more severely than those who select considerate ones. Conversely, when intentions are fixed, the severity of punishment does not significantly differ between fair and unfair outcomes on average. However, this average masks gender-specific variations. Men tend to prioritize punishing unkind intentions, while women are more sensitive to the perceived fairness of outcomes. Social norms help explain punishment choices and gender differences.

    • Discussed? No.  Not present.

Notably, when adapted indirect punishment outperforms direct punishment in promoting cooperation, defectors face stricter penalties without appreciably increasing punishers' costs, making it more efficient than direct punishment. Below we go through the 15 parameters one-by-one and state, strictly on the basis of what appears in Wen et al. (2025), (i) whether the parameter is mentioned and (ii) whether the authors systematically vary it and report how that variation changes the **punishment treatment effect** (PTE).  
For brevity, “direct-P” = direct punishment, “indirect-P” = their lattice-based indirect punishment, “PTE” = the difference between a punishment condition and its comparison condition (either “no punishment” or “other punishment form”).  Numerical values are copied verbatim or read directly from the figures.

-------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
-------------------------------------------------------------------

1 . Number of players  
 • Mentioned? Yes.  Simulations use square lattices of 100²–400² players (Model & Method).  
 • Systematically varied? No.  Different lattice sizes are used only for robustness; no results link lattice size to any change in the PTE.

2 . Number of rounds  
 • Mentioned? Implicitly. They run >10⁵ Monte-Carlo time steps and average over the last 2 000 steps.  
 • Systematically varied? No.  The length is fixed; no analysis of how varying it alters the PTE.

3 . Chat enabled  
 • Mentioned? No.  Not part of the model; therefore no prediction.

4 . All-or-nothing contribution decision  
 • Mentioned? Yes.  First-stage action is binary (cooperate vs defect in a Prisoner’s Dilemma).  
 • Systematically varied? No.  Binary choice is fixed; no comparison to continuous contributions.

5 . Contribution “default–withdraw” formulation  
 • Mentioned? No.

6 . Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
 • Closest analogue is the “dilemma strength” parameter r that shifts payoffs (r = 0.05 and 0.20 examined).  
 • Systematically varied? Yes, but only two points.  Fig. 2 shows that the four γ–β regions (where indirect-P > direct-P, vice-versa, parity, or neither effective) look qualitatively the same for r = 0.05 and r = 0.20.  No quantitative change of the PTE across r is reported.

7 . Punishment cost per unit (γ)  
 • Mentioned? Yes (core design variable).  
 • Systematically varied? Yes.  
  – Heat maps in Fig. 2 (γ on the x-axis) plus Fig. 3 left panels vary γ from ≈0 to 0.2.  
  – Main findings:  
   • For β = 0.2, indirect-P supports full cooperation at γ < 0.02 and still beats direct-P while 0.02 ≤ γ < 0.04.  
   • Cooperation under indirect-P collapses at γ ≈ 0.10; direct-P collapses only at γ ≈ 0.15 (Fig. 3).  
   • Thus, rising γ erodes the PTE of indirect-P faster than that of direct-P.  No payoff/efficiency numbers are given—only fractions of strategies.

8 . Punishment magnitude (fine β)  
 • Mentioned? Yes (core design variable).  
 • Systematically varied? Yes.  
  – Heat maps (Fig. 2) and Fig. 3 right panels vary β from 0 to about 0.7.  
  – At γ = 0.03:  
   • Direct-P eliminates defectors once β ≥ 0.26.  
   • Indirect-P needs β ≥ 0.66 to do the same.  
   • Between β ≈ 0.10 and 0.20, indirect-P yields higher cooperation than direct-P (still at γ = 0.03).  
  – Hence, increasing β benefits direct-P sooner (at lower fines) than indirect-P.

9 . Reward enabled  
 • Mentioned? No.  Only punishment mechanisms are modelled.

10–11 . Reward cost and reward magnitude  
 • Mentioned? No.

12 . End-round information (finite vs unknown horizon)  
 • Mentioned? No.  Evolutionary simulations run indefinitely; no player knows a “last round”.

13 . Display of peers’ outcomes  
 • Mentioned? No.

14 . Punisher identity visibility  
 • Mentioned? No.

15 . Rewarder identity visibility  
 • Mentioned? No.

-------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
-------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables  
 • No measure called “group efficiency” (total payoff / maximum possible) is reported.  
 • Reported outcomes:  
  – Fraction of cooperators (C N + C P)  
  – Fractions of each strategy type (C N, D N, C P, D P)  
  – Frequencies of punishment events, total fines on defectors, total costs to punishers (Fig. 5).  
 These are distinct from efficiency because they do not normalise total payoffs against the social optimum; nor do they present aggregate payoffs.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
 7 parameters: 1, 2, 4, 6 (as r), 7, 8, (4 is implicit) → strictly counted: 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8 = 6 distinct parameters.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* the parameter on the PTE?  
 Exactly 3 parameters:  
  • 6 (dilemma strength r) – two values compared; little effect on PTE.  
  • 7 (punishment cost γ) – full systematic exploration.  
  • 8 (punishment fine β) – full systematic exploration.

D. What predictions can be made—strictly from this paper—about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency?  
 • Efficiency as defined by total pay-offs is never computed, so only indirect, qualitative guesses are possible.  
 • Within the explored model:  
  – Low γ combined with low β (and β > γ) should make indirect-P more *efficient* than direct-P because it induces more fines on defectors without greatly raising punishers’ costs (authors’ verbal claim).  
  – High γ or very high β likely reduce efficiency for both punishment forms by adding cost without corresponding gains.  
  – Higher dilemma strength r does not qualitatively change which punishment form is superior, so no clear prediction on efficiency.  
 • For the remaining 12 parameters (number of players, time horizon, communication, reward options, information visibility, etc.) the paper offers no evidence, hence no prediction can be made.

In short, only punishment cost, punishment magnitude, and (to a minimal extent) the underlying payoff parameter r are systematically linked to the punishment treatment effect in the paper, and even those links are expressed in terms of cooperation rates, not efficiency.

As the use of AI becomes more pervasive throughout society, the need for socially intelligent agents capable of navigating these complex cooperative dilemmas is becoming increasingly evident. Direct punishment is a ubiquitous social mechanism that has been shown to foster the emergence of cooperation in both humans and non-humans. In the natural world, direct punishment is often strongly coupled with partner selection and reputation and used in conjunction with third-party punishment. The interactions between these mechanisms could potentially enhance the emergence of cooperation within populations. However, no previous work has evaluated the learning dynamics and outcomes emerging from multi-agent reinforcement learning populations that combine these mechanisms. This paper addresses this gap. It presents a comprehensive analysis and evaluation of the behaviors and learning dynamics associated with direct punishment, third-party punishment, partner selection, and reputation. Finally, we discuss the implications of using these mechanisms on the design of cooperative AI systems.
