Below we go through the 15 parameters in the order you gave.  
For each parameter we state  

(1) Whether the paper even mentions / sets a value for it, and what that value is.  
(2) Whether the paper tells us what *happens when that parameter is systematically changed* **for the punishment-versus-no-punishment treatment effect**.  When some systematic variation is reported but only for other outcomes (e.g., “co-operation per episode”) we say so explicitly.

────────────────────────────────────────

GAME-STRUCTURE

1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned.  Main text uses 5 agents; Appendix C additionally reports simulations with 10, 15, 20, 25, 30.  
   (2) Yes, population size is systematically varied, but only under *punishment* conditions.  Outcome reported: levels of co-operation and of “just-punisher selection”.  No baseline without punishment, so no direct “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” can be extracted.  Effect is small: with third-party punishment larger N gives *slightly* higher final co-operation; with direct punishment no clear trend (Fig. 12).  No efficiency numbers given.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Fixed at 10 rounds per episode and 2000 episodes; not varied.  
   (2) No discussion of varying it.

3. Chat allowed?  
   (1) Not present (no communication channel).  
   (2) Not discussed.

4. All-or-nothing contribution constraint  
   (1) Not applicable (binary C/D choice in a Prisoner’s Dilemma).  
   (2) Not discussed.

5. “Contribution default” mechanism  
   (1) Not applicable.  
   (2) Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────

MONETARY STAKES

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   (1) Prisoner’s-Dilemma pay-offs are fixed: R = 3, T = 4, S = 0, P = 1.  
   (2) Not varied.

────────────────────────────────────────

PEER INCENTIVES

7. Punishment cost (to punisher)  
   (1) Fixed at 10 units in all runs.  
   (2) Not varied.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss for target)  
   (1) Fixed at 3 units.  
   (2) Not varied.

9. “Reward enabled” (is there any bonus for punishing?)  
   (1) Yes.  A bonus is given to *just* punishers.  Two “schemes”:  
       – Scheme 1: bonus = +7 → net −3 (10 cost – 7 bonus)  
       – Scheme 2: bonus = +12 → net +2 (10 cost – 12 bonus)  
   (2) Bonus is **present** in both schemes; what is varied is its *magnitude* (see 11).  No run without any bonus, so the on/off aspect of parameter 9 is not studied.

10. Cost of granting a reward  
    (1) Not modelled; the reward is given automatically by the environment.  
    (2) Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude  
    (1) Systematically varied: +7 (Scheme 1) vs +12 (Scheme 2).  
    (2) Clear finding (Fig. 3a, Sec. 4.3):  
        – +7 → populations fail to learn punishment, converge to defection and very low societal reward.  
        – +12 → populations learn to punish, co-operate and obtain high “societal reward”.  
        Numerical effect size on *efficiency* is not given, but qualitative direction is unambiguous: larger bonus greatly improves outcomes.

────────────────────────────────────────

INFORMATION DISPLAY

12. Number of rounds known?  
    (1) Not stated; agents are reinforcement-learning models that simply experience 10-round episodes.  
    (2) Not discussed.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    (1) Agents observe the *previous actions* (C or D) of self and partner; that is always on.  
    (2) Not varied.

14. Does the punished know who punished them?  
    (1) Not specified.  In direct punishment the punisher is the partner (hence identity obvious); in third-party punishment identity may be unknown, but this is never manipulated.  
    (2) Not discussed.

15. Does the rewarded know who rewarded them?  
    (1) No explicit reward between peers, so not applicable.  
    (2) Not discussed.

────────────────────────────────────────

SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables actually analysed  
   – “Co-operation per episode” (percentage of C moves).  
   – “Punishment per episode”, “ratio of just to unjust punishment”.  
   – “Societal reward per episode” (= total payoff earned by the group, not normalised).  
   – “Societal reputation”.  
   “Efficiency” (payoff divided by the maximum possible) is *not* reported: societal reward is absolute, not relative to the cooperative optimum.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are at least mentioned?  8 of them: 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 13.

C. Which parameters are *systematically varied* and their effect on any outcome given?  
   – Parameter 1 (number of players): varied 6 values; effect described on co-operation, not on efficiency nor on a punishment/no-punishment contrast.  
   – Parameter 11 (reward magnitude for just punishment): two values; strong qualitative effect (only the high bonus lets punishment work).  
   No other parameter is varied.

D. Predictions one can make (only from this paper) about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency:

   • Larger groups are likely to show *slightly* higher co-operation (hence higher efficiency) when punishment is third-party; no clear trend under direct punishment.  
   • Increasing the positive bonus to just punishers (parameter 11) is crucial: a small bonus (net cost of punishing) eliminates the efficiency gain, whereas a larger bonus (net profit) lets punishment raise efficiency sharply.  
   • Changing punishment cost or magnitude, MPCR, information conditions, communication, etc., is not covered, so no prediction can be made.  
   • Because chat, contribution constraints, default options, and identity revelation are never studied, no prediction is possible for those.  
   • The paper gives no evidence on round-number knowledge, but because learning is long-run, one cannot infer an effect.

In short, the paper only lets us say with confidence that (i) the net profitability of punishing (implemented here through reward magnitude) must be positive for punishment to improve group payoffs, and (ii) population size has, at most, a modest modifying role.  For the other 13 parameters, the paper is silent.

Authors: Pedrazzini, S; Gurtner, LM; Aggrey, V; Moser, S
Author Full Names: Pedrazzini, Sabina; Gurtner, Lilla M.; Aggrey, Vincent; Moser, Stephanie
Article Title: Exploring individual and organizational factors influencing cooperation in commons: a scoping review
Author Keywords: commons; cooperation; social dilemma; individual perspective; commons' organization; social identity; trust; social norms
Keywords Plus: SOCIAL VALUE ORIENTATION; PUBLIC-GOOD EXPERIMENT; COLLECTIVE ACTION; GROUP IDENTITY; CONDITIONAL COOPERATION; DILEMMA ANALYSIS; PEER PUNISHMENT; CULTURAL NORMS; COLD-PRICKLE; STAKE SIZE
Abstract: Today, humanity faces multiple social and environmental crises that have arguably been caused by mainstream modes of economic organization. Against this background, commons represent a promising, viable alternative that enables people to self-organize to satisfy their needs in a more sustainable way. However, for commons to be successful, their members must cooperate. Despite the importance of cooperation for commoning processes, few studies in the scientific field of the commons have investigated cooperation using an individual-centered approach. To fill this knowledge gap, we conducted a scoping review to gather existing research about individual cooperation. We sought to identify factors that can impact cooperation in commons. We used a keyword search in three online databases to identify papers of interest. For inclusion, papers had to measure cooperation as an outcome variable, assess the impact of one or more factors on cooperation, use adult participants, and be written in English. The application of these criteria led to the inclusion of 135 papers. The included papers enabled us to identify nine factors influencing cooperation that could be divided into two categories. The first category includes individual factors, which depend on individuals' characteristics. These factors are: gender, social status, group identification, values and personality traits, and trust. The second category includes organizational factors, which concern the way individuals are organized as a group. These are: incentives, communication, social norms, and anonymity. We discuss these results vis-& agrave;-vis previous commons literature, showing that an individual perspective could significantly improve our understanding of how commons work. Moreover, we highlight the implications of the current review for future field research in commons.

9. REWARD ENABLED  
(1) Mentioned: Yes.  Rewards are compared to punishments.  
(2) Systematic-variation statement: The review notes that both reward and punishment “have a positive effect on cooperation” but that the literature is mixed on which is stronger.  No systematic manipulation within a single design is reported, and nothing is said about efficiency.

(1) Not mentioned.

13. PEER OUTCOMES SHOWN (feedback on others’ contributions/earnings)  
(1) Mentioned: Yes.  When talking about punishment the paper says that punishment is “more effective in improving cooperation when participants are informed about others’ *exact* contributions” (Grechenig et al., 2010; Ambrus & Greiner, 2012).  
(2) Systematic-variation statement: Qualitative only; no numeric estimate and no efficiency result.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
14. PUNISHER IDENTITY KNOWN  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) No statement.

15. REWARDER IDENTITY KNOWN  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) No statement.

A.  Dependent variables.  The review is almost always about “cooperation,” “contributions,” or “punishment frequency.”  Aggregate pay-offs or *efficiency* are occasionally mentioned (e.g., “group pay-offs are lower under costly punishment”), but efficiency is *not* a focal dependent variable.  Cooperation ≠ efficiency: higher cooperation under costly punishment can coincide with lower total pay-off because of punishment costs—a distinction the review itself highlights.

B.  Parameters merely mentioned (any context): 7 of the 15 – #1 (group size), #2 (rounds), #3 (chat), #7 (punishment cost), #8 (punishment magnitude), #9 (reward present), #13 (feedback on others).

• Accurate feedback on others’ contributions (#13) should raise the net benefit of punishment by preventing mis-directed fines, so it is likely to improve efficiency relative to a punishment regime with noisy information.

Authors: García, J; Traulsen, A
Author Full Names: Garcia, Julian; Traulsen, Arne
Article Title: Picking strategies in games of cooperation
Source Title: PROCEEDINGS OF THE NATIONAL ACADEMY OF SCIENCES OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
Author Keywords: cooperation; game theory; dynamics; agents; evolution
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; MAINTAIN COOPERATION; INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; SOCIAL NORMS; EVOLUTION; SELECTION; DYNAMICS; EMERGENCE; LEVEL; GO
Abstract: Evolutionary game theory (EGT) has been pivotal in the study of cooperation, offering formal models that account for how cooperation may arise in groups of selfish, but simple agents. This is done by inspecting the complex dynamics arising from simple interactions between a few strategies in a large population. As such, the strategies at stake are typically hand-picked by the modeler, resulting in a system with many more individuals in the population than strategies available to them. In the presence of noise and with multiple equilibria, the choice of strategies can considerably alter the emergent dynamics. As a result, model outcomes may not be robust to how the strategy set is chosen, sometimes misrepresenting the conditions required for cooperation to emerge. We propose three principles that can lead to a more systematic choice of the strategies in EGT models of cooperation. These are the inclusion of all computationally equivalent strategies; explicit microeconomic models of interactions, and a connection between stylized facts and model assumptions. Further, we argue that new methods arising in AI may offer a promising path toward richer models. These richer models can push the field of cooperation forward together with the principles described above. At the same time, AI may benefit from connecting to the more abstract models of EGT. We provide and discuss examples to substantiate these claims.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER–BY–PARAMETER CHECK

1. **Number of players** (group size in the public-goods stage)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  In the punishment example the authors use n = 5 and then **systematically vary n** in Fig. 2C.  
   • Does the paper link variation in n to the “punishment treatment effect”?  No.  
     – Fig. 2C shows the long–run **percentage of cooperation** (not efficiency) as a function of n for three different strategy sets, all of which already contain punishment.  
     – There is no baseline “no-punishment” condition, so no treatment contrast is reported.  
   • Numerical effect size?  None given; only qualitative trends (cooperation falls when n increases for the 4- and 9-strategy sets, is roughly flat for the 24-strategy set).

2. **Number of rounds**  
   • Mentioned?  No.  All evolutionary simulations are run until stationarity; an explicit finite number of rounds is never set or varied.

3. **Chat enabled between players?**  
   • Not mentioned.

4. **All-or-nothing contribution?**  
   • Mentioned implicitly.  The public-goods game allows only two first-stage actions: “Cooperate (contribute c)” or “Defect (contribute 0)”, i.e. an all-or-nothing rule.  
   • Systematic variation?  No.

5. **Contribution default (refund structure)?**  
   • Not mentioned.

6. **Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor**  
   • Mentioned.  In the punishment illustration the multiplication factor is fixed at r = 3 with cost c = 1 (so MPCR = 0.6).  
   • Systematic variation?  No.

7. **Punishment cost** (γ)  
   • Mentioned (γ = 1).  
   • Not varied.

8. **Punishment magnitude** (β)  
   • Mentioned (β = 1).  
   • Not varied.

9–11. **Reward system (enabled, cost, magnitude)**  
   • Not mentioned anywhere in the paper.

12. **Number of rounds known to players?**  
   • Not mentioned.

13. **Peer outcomes shown?**  
   • Not mentioned.

14. **Punisher identity revealed?**  
   • Not mentioned.

15. **Rewarder identity revealed?**  
   • Not mentioned.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
A–D SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used  
   – The paper never reports **group efficiency** (total payoff / maximum possible payoff).  
   – Reported outcomes are:  
     • “average percentage of cooperation” (Figs. 1B–D, 2B–C)  
     • Stationary abundance of strategies in evolutionary simulations.  
   – These are conceptually different from efficiency because they ignore the costs of punishment and the possibility that punishment could reduce total payoffs even while raising cooperation.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   5 out of 15:  #1 (group size), #4 (all-or-nothing), #6 (MPCR via r), #7 (punishment cost γ), #8 (punishment magnitude β).

C. For how many parameters is any **systematic variation** connected to the punishment treatment effect?  
   – Only 1 (#1, group size) is varied at all, and even there the comparison is **within punishment models**, so no effect on a “punishment vs. no-punishment” treatment is reported.

D. What predictions about the 15 parameters and their interactions can be made **solely from this paper**?

   – The only hint is that, with punishment already in place, larger groups (higher n) can undermine cooperation under some strategy-set assumptions (Fig. 2C).  Nothing is said about payoffs or efficiency, and nothing isolates the incremental effect of adding punishment.

Authors: Bühren, C; Dannenberg, A; Händel, P

Abstract: We use an experiment to study the demand for complete and incomplete formal punishment institutions and their ability to promote cooperation. Complete punishment institutions are implemented by the whole group and bind everyone. Incomplete punishment institutions are implemented by a subgroup and bind only the members of this subgroup. We distinguish between strictly incomplete institutions, in which only one subgroup can bind itself while the remaining individuals are unbound, and potentially incomplete institutions, in which two subgroups can bind themselves independently and separately in different institutions, potentially binding everyone. Theoretically, the demand for such formal punishment institutions should depend only on the benefit of cooperation within the group or subgroup bound by the institution. However, we hypothesize and the experimental results confirm that, in the case of incomplete punishment institutions, the benefit of cooperation has a much smaller impact on the demand than in complete punishment institutions. Instead, individuals' cooperativeness and coordination between the subgroups become important determinants.

1. NUMBER OF PLAYERS  
• Reported: All groups contain 6 players (three “red” and three “blue”).  
• Systematic variation: None. The number of players is held constant; no predictions are given for other group sizes.

2. NUMBER OF ROUNDS  
• Reported: 24 rounds, organised as six 4-round “phases”.  
• Systematic variation: None; no predictions.

3. CHAT ENABLED?  
• Reported: Only a *private* chat window with the experimenter for clarification. No chat between players.

5. CONTRIBUTION DEFAULT / “TAKE” FRAME?  
• Not mentioned; the usual “contribute to the joint project” frame is used. No discussion of default reversal.  
• Systematic variation: None.

6. MPCR (or MGR)  
• Reported and *systematically manipulated*: MGR = 0.75, 1.5, 2.5 (with 6 players this corresponds to MPCR ≈ 0.125, 0.25, 0.417).  
• Findings when MGR is varied  
  – COMPLETE institution (6-Vote): Raising MGR from 0.75→1.5 (or 2.5) pushes the mean implemented punishment rate from 6 % to ≈ 90 % (Table 2) and pushes mean contributions from ≈ 0 % to ≈ 100 % (Fig. 3).

A. Does the paper study **group efficiency**?

10. Reward cost?

Authors: Sparks, A; Burleigh, T; Barclay, P

Article Title: Expressed disapproval does not sustain long-term cooperation as effectively as costly punishment
Author Keywords: cooperation; punishment; sanctions; habituation; learning

Abstract: Punishment plays a role in human cooperation, but it is costly. Prior research shows that people are more cooperative when they expect to receive negative feedback for non-cooperation, even in the absence of costly punishment, which would have interesting implications for theory and applications. However, based on theories of habituation and cue-based learning, we propose that people will learn to ignore expressions of disapproval that are not clearly associated with material costs or benefits. To test this hypothesis, we conducted a between-subjects, 40-round public goods game (i.e. much longer than most studies), where participants could respond to others' contributions by sending numerical disapproval messages, paying to reduce others' earnings, or neither. Consistent with previous results, we observed steadily increasing contributions in the costly punishment condition. In contrast, contributions declined after the early rounds in the expressed disapproval condition, and were eventually no higher than the basic control condition with neither costly punishment nor disapproval ratings. In other words, costless disapproval may temporarily increase cooperation, but the effects fade. We discuss the theoretical and applied implications of our findings, including the unexpectedly high levels of cooperation in a second control condition.

Below, “punishment-treatment effect” always refers to the difference between the Costly-Punishment condition and any control condition (Nothing, Public Disapproval or Private Disapproval).  The term “efficiency” is interpreted as the total payoff the group actually earns; the paper does not compute the ratio of earnings to the theoretical maximum.

----------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER EXTRACTION
----------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  YES – fixed at 4 players.  
   • Systematic variation?  NO – no other group sizes tested and no prediction offered.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  YES – fixed at 40.  
   • Systematic variation?  INDIRECTLY – the authors split the 40 rounds into “early” (1-7) and “late” (34-40) periods.  
     – Early (1-7): Punishment lowered group earnings relative to Nothing by ≈14.2 L$ per group per round (SE ≈ 5.6).  
     – Late (34-40): The earnings gap disappeared (mean diff ≈ +6.1 L$, p = .80).  
     Predicted qualitative pattern: the longer the game, the more the initial efficiency loss from punishment is recouped.

3. Chat allowed?  
   • Mentioned?  NO – groups sat in silence; variable never discussed.  
   • Systematic variation?  NO.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
   • Mentioned?  NO – players could give any integer 0-20.  No manipulation or prediction.

5. Contribution default / “take” frame  
   • Mentioned?  NO.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  YES – total contribution multiplied by 1.6 (MPCR = 0.40).  
   • Systematic variation?  NO – fixed; no prediction.

7. Cost to impose one unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned?  YES – 1 L$ per 10 % earnings reduction of the target.  
   • Systematic variation or prediction?  NO – held constant.

8. Punishment magnitude (impact on target)  
   • Mentioned?  YES – each 1 L$ spent removes 10 % (up to 100 %) of the target’s earnings.  
   • Systematic variation or prediction?  NO – held constant.

9. Reward allowed?  
   • Mentioned?  NO – no reward option.

10 & 11. Reward cost / magnitude  
   • Mentioned?  NO.

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
   • Mentioned?  YES – they were explicitly NOT told the number of rounds.  
   • Systematic variation?  NO.

13. Are peer outcomes shown each round?  
   • Mentioned?  YES – everyone saw each player’s contribution and earnings.  Not varied.

14. Is punisher identity revealed?  
   • Mentioned?  YES – identity was concealed; only the aggregate punishment received was shown.  
   • Systematic variation?  NO.

15. Is rewarder identity revealed?  
   • Not applicable (no reward stage).

----------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
----------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables actually used  
   • Contributions (% of endowment)  
   • Group earnings (“profits”)  
   The paper never computes “efficiency” as the ratio of actual to maximal pay-off, so efficiency must be inferred from earnings; contribution rates are distinct from earnings because costly punishment can raise contributions while lowering earnings.

B.  Parameters from the list that the paper explicitly reports: 8 of 15  
   (1) Players = 4, (2) Rounds = 40, (6) MPCR = 0.40, (7) Punishment cost = 1 L$, (8) Punishment magnitude = 10 % per L$, (12) Rounds unknown to players, (13) Peer outcomes shown, (14) Punisher identity hidden.

C.  Parameters whose *systematic variation* (or time-based contrast) is analysed for its influence on the punishment-treatment effect: 1 of 15  
   • Parameter 2 (Number of rounds / game length): early vs. late comparison shows that punishment initially hurts efficiency but the disadvantage vanishes later.  No other parameter is experimentally varied or modelled.

D.  Predictions one can make about the 15 parameters and their interactions, *based solely on this paper*  

   • Game length (Parameter 2) is crucial: if the game is short (≈ 7 rounds), introducing costly punishment is predicted to *decrease* efficiency (-14 L$ per group per round vs. baseline); if the game is long (≥ 40 rounds) the net efficiency loss disappears and may eventually turn positive.  
   • All other listed parameters are either fixed or not discussed; therefore the paper offers no basis to predict how changing them would alter the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency.  Any further prediction would be speculation beyond the paper’s content.

In short, the only leverage this paper provides for forecasting efficiency effects is the expected number of repeated interactions: costly punishment is inefficient in the short run but pays off as the horizon lengthens; nothing in the article speaks to the other 14 parameters.

Abstract: The underrepresentation of women in top leadership positions may result in a potential loss in efficiency. In this study, we examine gender differences in leadership emergence and efficiency when a leadership task is framed as authority or responsibility. Below, each of the 15 parameters is taken in turn.  For every parameter I state  

(i) whether the paper mentions it (and its value, if given); and  

(ii) whether the paper makes any prediction or gives any quantitative evidence about how *changing* that parameter would alter the punishment-treatment effect (for efficiency or for any other dependent variable).  “Punishment-treatment effect” is understood as the difference between an environment **with** the peer-punishment option and an otherwise identical environment **without** it.

──────────────────────────────────────────  
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK  
──────────────────────────────────────────  

1  Number of players  
– Mentioned: Yes.  Groups of four (2 women + 2 men).  
– Systematically varied? No. Only four-person groups are used, so no prediction about varying group size.

2  Number of rounds  
– Mentioned: Yes.  Five rounds in every stage.  
– Varied? No.  No prediction about other horizon lengths.

3  Chat enabled?  
– Mentioned: Yes (implicitly).  Participants are explicitly told *not* to talk; no chat tool exists.  
– Varied? No.  No prediction about adding communication.

4  “All-or-nothing” contribution?  
– Mentioned: Yes (implicitly).  Subjects choose any integer 0–20; it is *not* all-or-nothing.  
– Varied? No.  No prediction about forcing binary choices.

5  Contribution default / “take” vs “give” frame  
– Not mentioned.  Contributions are always made out of a 20-token endowment (standard give frame).  No variation and no discussion.

6  Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplier  
– Mentioned: Yes.  Total contribution × 0.6 is equally shared, so MPCR = 0.6.  
– Varied? No.  No prediction about other MPCR values.

7  Punishment cost (cost per unit sent)  
– Mentioned: Yes.  Cost to leader = 1 token per point.  
– Varied? No.  No prediction about other costs.

8  Punishment magnitude (deduction per unit received)  
– Mentioned: Yes.  Each point makes the target lose 2 tokens.  
– Varied? No.  No prediction about other deduction factors.

9  Peer reward option enabled?  
– Mentioned: A *leader* bonus exists (0.4 × excess contributions), but ordinary group members cannot reward each other.  
– Varied? No.  Leader bonus level is fixed; peer reward is always absent.  No prediction about enabling/ disabling reward.

10  Reward cost (cost to give 1 reward unit)  
– Not applicable; there is no peer-reward mechanism.  Not discussed.

11  Reward magnitude (benefit per reward unit)  
– Mentioned only for the leader’s automatic bonus: bonus = 0.4 × (max(0, Σ c – 50)).  Not varied; no prediction.

12  End of game known?  
– Mentioned: Yes.  Subjects are told each stage lasts exactly five rounds.  
– Varied? No.  No prediction about making the horizon unknown.

13  Peer outcomes shown?  
– Mentioned: Partially.  After each round every subject sees *total* group contribution; only the leader sees individual contributions and incomes; individual-level data are hidden from ordinary members.  
– Varied? No.  No prediction about changing the visibility of peer outcomes.

14  Identity of punisher revealed?  
– Mentioned: Yes.  Punisher is always the single, known group leader; punished members know that the leader punished them (but never which *person* in treatments without a named leader because the leader’s personal identity is masked).  
– Varied? No.  No prediction about hiding / revealing punisher identity.

15  Identity of rewarder revealed?  
– Not applicable (no peer reward).  Not discussed.

──────────────────────────────────────────  
SUMMARY  
──────────────────────────────────────────  

A.  Dependent variables used in the paper  
– “Group members’ net income” (Table 9) – an efficiency / welfare measure.  
– Leaders’ and members’ contributions.  
– Punishment probability and amount.  
– Willingness to Lead (WTL) and votes received.  
These variables are *not* interchangeable: contribution measures cooperation; punishment measures enforcement effort; net income captures efficiency (pay-offs including punishment costs).

B.  Parameters from the list that are *mentioned* in the paper: 12 of 15  
(1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13, 14).  Parameters 5, 10, 15 are not mentioned.

C.  Parameters whose *systematic variation* is analysed with respect to the punishment-treatment effect: 0 of 15  
None of the listed parameters is experimentally varied; consequently the paper supplies no numerical elasticities or predictions for changing any of them.

D.  What can we predict – using *only* the information in this paper – about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency?  
Very little.  The study keeps every listed parameter constant and instead manipulates leader-selection mode and the *framing* of the leader’s role (authority vs. responsibility).  Therefore:  
– We have no within-paper evidence on how altering group size, horizon length, MPCR, punishment cost/magnitude, presence of rewards, information conditions, etc. would change the efficiency gain (or loss) from adding punishment.  
– The only qualitative hint is that, *given* the specific parameter constellation used (4-person groups, MPCR = 0.6, cost = 1, fine = 2, 5 known rounds, no chat), introducing a punishing leader raised average contribution from 10.6 to about 15 tokens and produced higher (though not fully quantified) net income relative to the no-leader baseline.  
Beyond noting that the punishment institution was beneficial under exactly those fixed parameters, the paper does not allow credible extrapolation to other parameter values.

Hence, if one had to forecast punishment-treatment effects on efficiency strictly from this paper alone, the honest answer is that almost no predictive leverage is available for the 15 design parameters.

Abstract: The mechanism of promoting cooperation in the public goods game has always been concerned by scholars. However, most of the existing studies are based on the premise that participants are self-interested. In order to explore why some sellers on e-commerce platforms voluntarily maintain the platform's reputation, we incorporate heterogeneous social preferences of sellers into the spatial public goods game. We find that heterogeneous social preferences can enhance cooperation by improving collective rationality. Specifically, the altruistic preference of sellers can greatly reduce free-riding behavior, while the inequality aversion preference has a little inhibitory effect. Furthermore, we propose a dynamic punishment mechanism to punish free riders. Parameter-by-parameter extraction from “Evolution of cooperation in spatial public goods game based on heterogeneous social preferences and dynamic punishment”

For every parameter:  
• “Mentioned?” – does the paper describe the parameter at all and (if yes) what value(s) are used.  
• “Systematic-variation & punishment-effect?” – does the paper vary that parameter and report how the **difference between a punishment condition and a no-punishment condition** (i.e., the “punishment treatment effect”) changes.  Whenever a numerical difference can be read from a figure/table it is given as a rough value (because exact numbers are not printed).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Scale-free networks with N = 100 are used throughout; Fig. 3b additionally shows N = 100, 200, 1 000 (only in the NO-punishment benchmark).  
   • Systematic-variation & punishment-effect?  No.  Variation of N is never crossed with the punishment treatments, so no statement about the punishment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  A simulation horizon T = 10^5 rounds is fixed; not varied.  
   • Systematic-variation & punishment-effect?  No.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned?  Not mentioned.  
   • Systematic-variation & punishment-effect?  Not applicable.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  The model is strictly binary: each player chooses C (contribute c = 1) or D (contribute 0).  Value = “true”.  
   • Systematic-variation & punishment-effect?  No.  The paper never contrasts binary with continuous contributions.

5. Contribution default / withdraw?  
   • Mentioned?  No.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Denoted r_e (“enhancement factor”) and varied in almost every analysis: r_e ∈ [1, 5.5].  
   • Systematic-variation & punishment-effect?  Yes.  Section 3.3 (Fig. 8a) plots cooperation under three conditions – No-punishment, Static-punishment, Dynamic-punishment – for each r_e.  The punishment treatment effect therefore changes with r_e.  Rough values extracted from Fig. 8a:  

        r_e   Coop(No)   Coop(Static)   Coop(Dynamic)   Dynamic – No
        1.0-1.5    0            0               0               0
        2.0       ≈0.05       ≈0.25          ≈0.35          ≈+0.30
        2.5       ≈0.60       ≈0.70          ≈0.80          ≈+0.20
        3.5       ≈0.95       ≈0.98          ≈1.00          ≈+0.05
        ≥4.5      ≈1.00       ≈1.00          ≈1.00             0

     The paper does not translate these cooperation levels into “group efficiency”, so only cooperation is reported.

7. Punishment cost (to the punisher)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Static mechanism: M1 = 1 (fixed).  Dynamic mechanism: expected average cost is also 1 by construction (m1 = M1/2).  
   • Systematic-variation & punishment-effect?  No.  M1 is kept constant.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine paid by the target)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Static: M2 = r_e.  Dynamic: average fine also equals r_e (m2 = M2/2).  
   • Systematic-variation & punishment-effect?  M2 covaries with r_e but is never varied independently of r_e, so there is no separate analysis of “holding r_e constant, change M2”.

9. Reward enabled?  
10. Reward cost?  
11. Reward magnitude?  
   • Mentioned?  None of the reward parameters appear in the model; no discussion.

12. Round number known to players?  
   • Mentioned?  Not addressed; players are simulated agents and no information conditions are discussed.  
   • Systematic-variation & punishment-effect?  Not applicable.

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
14. Punisher identity revealed?  
15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
   • Mentioned?  Not discussed anywhere.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
   – The paper does NOT report “group efficiency” as defined by the user (total payoff / maximum possible).  
   – Reported outcome measures are:  
        • Proportion of cooperators in the population (main measure used in every figure).  
        • Individual utility / payoff used internally in the evolutionary update rule, but averages are not graphed.  
   Cooperation rate, payoff and efficiency are conceptually distinct; only the first two are treated.

B. Parameters mentioned (any value given): 6 of 15  
   (1) number of players, (2) number of rounds, (4) binary contribution rule, (6) enhancement factor r_e, (7) punishment cost M1, (8) punishment magnitude M2.

C. Parameters whose **systematic variation** is linked to the punishment treatment effect: 1 of 15  
   Only parameter 6 (enhancement factor / MPCR).  Figures show that the extra cooperation generated by punishment is greatest at intermediate r_e (~2–3) and vanishes when r_e is very low or very high.  No numerical efficiency effect is provided.

D. Predictions you could make about punishment effects on efficiency using ONLY this paper  
   – Because efficiency is monotonic in cooperation in a binary-contribution, equal-sharing PGG, we would infer that efficiency differences will mirror the cooperation differences shown in Fig. 8a: dynamic punishment raises efficiency most when r_e is moderate (~2–3) and has little or no effect when the game is extremely hard (r_e ≤1.5) or trivially easy (r_e ≥4.5).  
   – For the other 14 parameters the paper provides no evidence, so no informed prediction can be made about their interaction with punishment on efficiency.

Authors: Rodrigues, J; Leipold, N; Hewig, J; Hein, G
Author Full Names: Rodrigues, Johannes; Leipold, Natasha; Hewig, Johannes; Hein, Grit
Article Title: The relationship of the source of punishment and personality traits with investment and punishment in a public goods game
Keywords Plus: EMPATHY; ANGER; ALTRUISM; COOPERATION; TENDENCIES; DYNAMICS; TRACKING
Abstract: In this study, we investigated the motivations behind punishing individuals who exploit common resources, a phenomenon crucial for resource preservation. While some researchers suggest punishment stems from concern for the common good, others propose it is driven by anger toward free riders. To probe these motivations, we developed a modified public goods game in which participants had the option to use their own money or the money from the common pool to punish free riders. The analysis included choice behavior, mouse trajectories, and personality traits like anger, empathy, and altruism. According to our results, investments were highest, and punishment was strongest if participants could punish using credits from the common pool, indicating that this is the preferred option to diminish free riding and maintain cooperation in public goods and common good contexts. Also, punishment was highest if the punisher's own investment was high, and the investment of others was low. Concerning traits, highly altruistic individuals tended to invest more and punish less in general but gave harsher punishments when they did choose to use the common pool punitively. Conversely, trait anger and trait empathy were linked to low investment while trait empathy also tended to be related to lower punishment. Taken together, these findings underscore the role of situational factors and personality traits in fostering cooperative behavior and shaping societal norms around costly punishment.

Below I go through the 15 pre-specified design parameters one by one.  
For each parameter I state (i) whether it is explicitly described in the paper and, if so, the value used, and (ii) whether the authors say anything about what would happen if that parameter were *systematically varied* – in particular, whether they report any numerical effects on the “punishment treatment effect” (i.e., the behavioural difference between a punishment and a no-punishment condition).  Whenever an effect size can be read directly from the reported regressions, I reproduce it.  I do **not** add anything that is not in the paper.

-------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
-------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  YES – always 4 (1 real participant + 3 computer-controlled “players”).  
   • Systematic variation discussed?  NO – number of players is fixed; no predictions made for other group sizes.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned?  YES – 50 trials per block, four blocks → 200 trials in total.  
   • Systematic variation discussed?  NO – authors only report that investment and punishment decline slightly over trials; they do not manipulate the number of rounds.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Mentioned?  NO – no chat function is described; the topic is not raised.  
   • Systematic variation discussed?  Not applicable.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Mentioned?  YES – contributions are **not** all-or-nothing; participants choose any integer from 0 to 20.  
   • Systematic variation discussed?  NO.

5. Contribution default / endowment “give-back” frame?  
   • Mentioned?  NO – only the standard “how much will you *put in* the pool?” decision is used.  
   • Systematic variation discussed?  NO.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  YES – the common pool is multiplied by 0.4.  
   • Systematic variation discussed?  NO – factor is fixed at 0.4 throughout; no predictions about different MPCRs.

7. Punishment *cost* to impose one unit  
   • Mentioned?  YES – two cost structures are implemented:  
        – “Own-money punishment”: 1 credit spent by the punisher costs the punisher 1 credit.  
        – “Pool-money punishment”: 1 credit spent *does not* cost the punisher anything (the participant is reimbursed as if no deduction had been made).  
   • Systematically varied?  YES – the entire design contrasts four blocks:  
        (a) No-punishment block (baseline)  
        (b) Own-money-punishment block  
        (c) Pool-money-punishment block  
        (d) Choice block (participant chooses either cost structure each trial)  
     Reported numerical effects (on *investment*, the only causal outcome analysed):  
        – Relative to the no-punishment block, average investment increased by  
          • β = 1.778 (z = 6.96, p < .001) when punishment was *cost-free* (pool block)  
          • β = 1.566 (z = 6.13, p < .001) in the choice block  
          • β = 0.092 (z = 0.36, p = .72) when punishment was *costly* (own-money block).  
     The paper does *not* translate these investment changes into efficiency changes.

8. Punishment *magnitude* (how many credits are removed from the target per unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned?  YES – 1 credit removed per credit spent.  
   • Systematic variation discussed?  NO.

9. Whether a reward option exists  
   • Mentioned?  NO – there is no reward mechanism in the design.  
   • Systematic variation discussed?  Not applicable.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   • Both parameters are not relevant to the study; neither is mentioned or varied.

12. Do players know the number of rounds?  
   • Mentioned?  NOT EXPLICITLY.  The instructions section reproduced in the paper does not state whether participants were told the game length.  
   • Systematic variation discussed?  NO.

13. Are peer outcomes shown each round?  
   • Mentioned?  YES – after every decision participants see (a) each other player’s contribution and (b) each player’s final payoff for that trial.  
   • Systematic variation discussed?  NO.

14. Is the punisher identified to the target?  
   • Not applicable: the only real human is the punisher and the “targets” are computer players.  The issue is not discussed or manipulated.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
   • Not applicable – no reward option.

-------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
-------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables used in the paper  
    • Group *efficiency* (total or average payoff divided by maximum possible payoff) is **not** analysed.  
    • The paper uses four behavioural variables instead:  
        1. “Investment” (credits contributed to the public pool)  
        2. “Punishment amount” (credits spent to punish in a given trial)  
        3. “Punishment source choice” (binary: pool vs. own money)  
        4. “Certainty of source choice” (mouse-trajectory area-under-curve)  
      These variables are conceptually different from efficiency; higher investment does not automatically imply higher group efficiency because punishment itself destroys resources.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are at least mentioned?  
    1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 13  →  7 parameters.

C.  For how many parameters does the paper *systematically vary* the parameter and report its effect on any punishment treatment outcome?  
    • Exactly one: Parameter 7 (punishment cost / source).  
    • No systematic manipulations or predictive analyses for the other 14 parameters.

D.  What predictions can be made—*solely* from this paper—about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) will influence the punishment treatment effect on **efficiency**?  
    • The paper gives direct evidence only about Parameter 7.  When punishment can be inflicted at *zero* personal cost (pool-money block) the authors find larger increases in contribution than when punishment is costly; however, because punishment in that block also directly depletes the common pool, the net effect on efficiency is ambiguous and not computed.  
    • For all other parameters the paper provides no data, no manipulation, and no theory-driven quantitative predictions.  Therefore, on the basis of this paper alone, essentially *no* predictive leverage is available for Parameters 1-6 and 8-15 with respect to efficiency.  Any attempt to predict their effects on group efficiency would require evidence that lies outside the scope of the study.

In short, the only parameter the paper actually manipulates is the *cost structure* of punishment (Parameter 7).  Even for that parameter the authors stop at contributions and punishment amounts, leaving the efficiency question unanswered.  Consequently, the paper offers very limited guidance for forecasting efficiency effects across the fifteen design dimensions.

Article Title: Effect of distribution of fines on evolution of cooperation in spatial public goods game

Abstract: In the realm of public goods game, punishment, as a potent tool, stands out for fostering cooperation. While it effectively addresses the first-order free-rider problem, the associated costs can be substantial. Punishers incur expenses in imposing sanctions, while defectors face fines. Unfortunately, these monetary elements seemingly vanish into thin air, representing a loss to the system itself. However, by virtue of the redistribution of fines to cooperators and punishers, not only can we mitigate this loss, but the rewards for these cooperative individuals can be enhanced. Based upon this premise, this paper introduces a fine distribution mechanism to the traditional pool punishment model. Under identical parameter settings, by conducting a comparative experiment with the conventional punishment model, the paper aims to investigate the impact of fine distribution on the evolution of cooperation in spatial public goods game. The experimental results clearly demonstrate that, in instances where the punishment cost is prohibitively high, the cooperative strategies of the traditional pool punishment model may completely collapse. However, the model enriched with fine distribution manages to sustain a considerable number of cooperative strategies, thus highlighting its effectiveness in promoting and preserving cooperation, even in the face of substantial punishment cost.

2. Number of rounds (time horizon)

   • NO systematic variation; nothing said about its influence on any treatment effect.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • NO. The model contains no communication channel.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • YES-value: being C or PC always means investing a fixed cost c = 1; being D means investing 0. Binary, not continuous.  
   • NO variation.

5. Contribution default / “take back” option?  
   • NO.

6. Marginal per-capita return / multiplication factor (synergy factor r)  
   • YES-varied: r examined at 2.0, 2.2, 2.4, …, 3.0 in Fig. 6.  
   • Effect described: Across all r the “punishment + fine-distribution” treatment yields a higher cooperation level (C+PC) than “punishment-only”, but the advantage narrows as r increases (“reduction in stabilisation points as r increases”, p. 8).  
   • No explicit efficiency numbers; only qualitative statements and heat-map shades.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit (β)  
   • YES-varied from 0 to 0.4 in Figs. 1–4 & 6.  
   • Effect on treatment difference:  
     – At low β (e.g., 0.15) the punishment-only model attains full cooperation (cooperation level = 1) while the fine-distribution model reaches ≈ 0.8 (Fig. 1, a₁ vs a₂).  
     – At high β (e.g., 0.40) punishment-only collapses to cooperation = 0 and zero total payoff, whereas the fine-distribution model keeps cooperation ≈ 0.6–0.7 and a strictly positive total payoff (Fig. 1, b₁ vs b₂; Fig. 4b).  
     – Hence the *incremental* effect of adding fine distribution on efficiency/cooperation is strongly increasing in β and even reverses sign between β ≈ 0.15 and β ≈ 0.40.  
   • No numerical regression coefficients are reported; effect sizes can only be read visually.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine)  
   • YES-varied jointly with β in Fig. 6 (fine shown along the vertical axes).  
   • Qualitative findings: when the fine is large, the fine-distribution model sustains cooperation for punishment costs that wipe out cooperation in the punishment-only model. Within a “small band” of fine values the reverse occurs: punishment-only reaches full cooperation (no defectors) whereas fine-distribution leaves some defectors and therefore a slightly lower cooperation level.  
   • No explicit numbers.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • NO. The model purposefully studies punishment, not reward. Parameters 9–11 are absent.

10. Reward cost  
   • NO.

11. Reward magnitude  
   • NO.

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
   • NO discussion; the model is an infinite-horizon evolutionary process.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • NO.

14. Do punished players learn the punisher’s identity?  
   • NO.

15. Do rewarded players learn the rewarder’s identity?  
   • NO.


--------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary requested by the user
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables used  
   • “Cooperation level” = fraction C + PC (most of the paper)  
   • “Total system payoff” (Fig. 4) – this is the closest construct to group *efficiency* although it is not normalised by the theoretical maximum.  
   • Counts of strategy transitions (Fig. 3) and spatial snapshots are also shown but are not outcome variables of interest here.  
   Cooperation level and total payoff are explicitly different: high cooperation does not always lead to the highest total payoff when fines are redistributed.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   6 of 15: (1) number of players; (2) number of rounds; (4) binary contribution rule; (6) synergy factor r; (7) punishment cost β; (8) punishment magnitude (fine).

C. For how many of the 15 parameters does the paper *systematically vary* the parameter and discuss its impact on the punishment treatment effect?  
   3 parameters: r (6), β (7), fine (8).  
   No other parameter is varied with respect to the treatment difference.

D. What predictions about the punishment treatment effect on efficiency can be made solely from this paper?  
   • Punishment cost β: The efficiency gain from adding fine distribution is *negative* at very low β, approximately zero at intermediate β, and *highly positive* at large β (β ≈ 0.4 in the paper).  
   • Punishment magnitude (fine): At moderate fines the fine-distribution treatment may slightly reduce efficiency (because some defectors survive), but at high fines it increases efficiency by allowing punishers to recoup costs and stay active.  
   • Synergy factor r: Raising r mitigates the difference between the two punishment variants; the fine-distribution bonus on efficiency shrinks as r grows from 2.0 to 3.0.  
   • For every other listed parameter (1–5, 9–15) the paper provides no evidence, therefore no prediction can be extracted.

In short, only parameters r, β and the fine itself are documented as moderators of the punishment-with-redistribution treatment; the direction of the effect is (i) strongly positive when punishment is expensive or the fine is large, (ii) weak or even negative when punishment is cheap and the fine is moderate, and (iii) diminishing as the public-goods multiplier r increases.

Abstract: The conservation of common-pool resources (CPRs), such as tropical forests, is a key challenge of development and environmental policies. • Mentioned: Yes – peer punishment operates under “perfect monitoring”; participants see every other player’s deforestation each round (Sect. 3.2.2); they also see how many punishment points they receive (Fig. 3 caption, Sect. 4.3).  
• Systematic-variation discussion: No. The monitoring regime is held constant.

14. IS THE PUNISHER IDENTIFIED TO THE TARGET?  
• Mentioned: Yes – players are represented by a rotating letter (Sect. 3.2.1). Thus the punished player can identify the letter of his/her punisher within the current stage.  
• Systematic-variation discussion: None. Anonymity level is fixed.

15. IS THE REWARDER IDENTIFIED?  
• Not applicable (no rewards).

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY  

A. Dependent variables used in the paper  
• Main variables:  
  – Forest plots converted (= deforestation) per round (first-order cooperation).  
  – Number of punishment points given/received (second-order cooperation).  
  – Change in deforestation from round t to t+1 (effectiveness of punishment).  
  – Expected monetary pay-off is calculated in Table 4, but **group efficiency (total pay-off ÷ maximum possible) is never used as an outcome variable.**  
These variables differ conceptually: deforestation measures resource extraction, punishment counts measure peer-enforcement activity, and efficiency would combine both costs and benefits into a single pay-off metric, which the authors do not analyse.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
Eight: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 13, 14 (parameters 4 and 14 are implicit but clear).  
The remaining seven (5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 15 plus the “reward” trio) are not discussed.

C. For which parameters does the paper discuss **systematic variation** and its effect on the punishment treatment?  
Zero. All eight mentioned parameters are **held fixed**. The only variables experimentally varied are (i) endowment inequality and (ii) country context; neither appears in the list of 15 parameters.

D. Predicting how the 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency, using only this paper  
Because the study never manipulates any of the 15 parameters, it provides almost no basis for quantitative prediction. Qualitatively:  
• Efficiency would almost certainly fall if the punishment cost (7) rises or if the punishment magnitude (8) falls, because Table 4 shows that only when the expected marginal loss from punishment exceeds the 6-point private benefit of deforesting does punishment deter free-riding.  
• Perfect monitoring (13) and identifiable punishers (14) appear to be prerequisites for the positive prosocial-punishment effect the authors observe, so weakening either would plausibly lower efficiency.  
Beyond these directional hunches, the paper offers **little to no guidance** on how varying any of the 15 parameters—or their interactions—would quantitatively shift the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency.

Below I move through the 15 public-goods-game (PGG) design parameters one at a time and report exactly what the supplied paper says (or does not say) about each parameter and about the consequences of changing that parameter for any **punishment treatment effect**.  I use the paper’s tables, figures and text only and do not import outside evidence or intuition.  Whenever the paper analyses variables other than “efficiency” (defined as total pay-off divided by the theoretical maximum) I flag that explicitly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
--------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Table 1 gives N = 100 agents.  
   • Systematic variation / effect?  No.  N is held fixed; the paper never investigates what would happen to any outcome (let alone an efficiency-based punishment treatment effect) if N changed.

2. Number of rounds (length of the repeated game)  
   • Mentioned?  Indirectly.  The model runs for 21 years at a daily time-step (≈ 7 700 rounds).  
   • Systematic variation / effect?  None.  The horizon is fixed.

3. Chat allowed?  
   • Mentioned?  Not as an experimental switch.  Agents are linked in static social networks but the paper never manipulates “chat/no-chat”.  
   • Effect predicted?  None.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule?  
   • Mentioned?  No.  Salt application (“contribution”) is a continuous proportion from 0 to 1.  
   • Effect predicted?  None.

5. Contribution default / “take” frame?  
   • Mentioned?  No.  
   • Effect predicted?  None.

6. MPCR (marginal per-capita return) or multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  No monetary public-good technology is modelled; instead, agents’ “energy” depends on de-icing benefits and water-quality damage.  
   • Effect predicted?  None.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher (per unit)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes indirectly.  Table 1 lists “Monitoring fee” MC ∼ U(0, 10), and monitoring costs are paid by all agents when an institution exists.  
   • Systematic variation?  No.  Although MC is heterogeneously drawn at set-up, the authors never vary its distribution across runs, nor report what would happen if MC changed.  No quantitative punishment-effect estimate is provided.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine imposed on target per unit)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Each agent has an initial “fine belief” F_i ∼ U(0, 1).  When an institution is voted in, the modal F_i becomes the system-wide fine F(t).  Figure 6(c) shows that across 100 baseline simulations the emergent F(t) hovers near 0.5 energy units.  
   • Systematic variation / effect?  None.  The fine emerges endogenously but is not experimentally manipulated, so no causal statement about “varying punishment magnitude” is made.

9. Presence/absence of a reward option  
   • Mentioned?  Yes.  Section 3.1.5 (ΔE_I term) describes an incentive pool funded by monitoring fees and redistributed to the θ_R = 25 % “best” cooperators.  
   • Systematic variation / effect?  No.  Reward is always on and θ_R is fixed; no simulations switch it on/off.

10. Reward cost to the rewarder  
    • Mentioned?  Indirectly via the shared monitoring fee M(t).  Not varied.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Mentioned?  Parameter α₃ converts the monitoring pool into pay-off; value never changed.  No effect estimated.

12. Whether the game length is known to players  
    • Not discussed.

13. Whether peer outcomes are shown  
    • Mentioned?  Yes; each agent knows the energy and defection history of agents in its social network.  
    • Variation / effect?  None.  The informational structure is fixed.

14. Whether the identity of the punisher is revealed  
    • Not discussed at all.

15. Whether the identity of the rewarder is revealed  
    • Not discussed at all.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PAPER’S DEPENDENT VARIABLES VS. “EFFICIENCY”
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The paper never computes “group efficiency” (total actual pay-off divided by the maximum possible pay-off under full cooperation).  The main outcome variables are:
   • Vadose-zone salt concentration (Fig. 3–11)  
   • Average agent “energy” (economic proxy)  
   • Institution application rate (analogous to group contribution norm)  
   • Number of defectors caught, fines, monitoring intensity, etc.

These are conceptually different from efficiency as defined in most PGG laboratory work.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
RECAP SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Does the paper analyse group efficiency?  
   – No.  Outcomes are salt concentration, agent energy, institution parameters, and behavioural counts.  None equal the efficiency metric requested.

B. Which of the 15 PGG parameters are even mentioned?  
   – 7 out of 15 appear in some form:  
     (1) Number of players; (7) punishment cost via monitoring fee;  
     (8) punishment magnitude (fine); (9–11) reward presence/cost/magnitude;  
     (13) visibility of peer outcomes.  The remaining 8 parameters are absent.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* that parameter on any punishment treatment effect?  
   – Zero.  No parameter from the list is experimentally or computationally manipulated with respect to punishment; hence no effect sizes (numerical or qualitative) are provided.

D. Ability to predict how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency, using only this paper  
   – Very limited.  Because the paper neither measures efficiency nor varies the listed parameters, almost no direct predictions can be drawn.  The only indirect hint is that some level of punishment (monitoring + fine) combined with a reward pool is part of every “institution” and is associated with lower salt concentration and higher (though still declining) average energy compared with runs without any institution.  But since costs to punishers and fine magnitudes were not experimentally varied, we cannot state how changing them would change efficiency.  Therefore, based solely on the provided paper, we can make virtually no quantitative or even directional predictions about how the 15 parameters—or their interactions—would modulate a punishment treatment’s impact on group efficiency in a standard public-goods game.
reference_APA: Armstrong, Kingston, Zhong, Yinman, Bhide, Shantanu, V, Grant, Stanley B., Birkland, Thomas & Berglund, Emily Zechman (2024). Simulating the emergence of institutions that reverse freshwater salinization: An agent-based modeling approach. JOURNAL OF HYDROLOGY X.

Below, each of the 15 parameters is examined in exactly the same order in which you listed them.

For every parameter I state  
(1) whether the paper talks about it and, if so, the value that actually occurred in the experiment, and  
(2) whether the paper **systematically varies** that parameter and therefore allows us to say anything about how changing the parameter would alter the *punishment-treatment effect* (the difference between a baseline public–goods game and an otherwise identical game that also contains peer punishment).  Whenever the paper reports a numeric effect that can be interpreted as a punishment-treatment effect I reproduce it.

Unless explicitly quoted, no statement goes beyond what is written in the paper.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   (1) Mentioned: fixed groups of three (one Small, one Medium, one Large).  
   (2) Never varied; no predictions or evidence on how changing the group size would alter the punishment-treatment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
   (1) Mentioned: exactly 30 finitely repeated rounds.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

3. Chat / communication  
   (1) Mentioned: “Communication between participants was not allowed.”  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
   (1) Mentioned: in every treatment the decision is binary—either contribute the whole 12-point endowment or contribute nothing.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

5. Contribution default (i.e., a take-back rule)  
   (1) Not used; every decision is framed as “where to put your 12 points,” never as retracting a default contribution.  
   (2) Not applicable; no prediction.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   (1) Mentioned: marginal aggregate return = 1.5.  Individual marginal private returns differ by size: 0.5 (S), 0.7 (M), 0.9 (L).  
   (2) Held constant; no prediction about changing the MPCR.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit  
   (1) Mentioned: fee φ = 1 point per punished target (a co-operator chooses “0, 1 or 2” points but the per-target fee is 1).  
   (2) Not varied; the paper contains no comparison with any other cost level, so no statement about how changing φ would affect the punishment-treatment effect.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine suffered by the target)  
   (1) Mentioned: 2 points (L), 5 points (M), 8 points (S) **per punisher**.  
   (2) Not varied.  The paper does note that because “the fine-to-fee ratio varies: the smaller is the nation, the more effective is the punishment,” Small players end up worse off than Large players in the Climate-Club treatment (Result 4), but that is a cross-player comparison, not a systematic variation of the parameter across treatments.  No econometric estimate of “what if the fine were different?” is provided.

9. Whether a reward option exists  
   (1) Mentioned only implicitly: there is **no** reward stage in any treatment.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

10-11. Reward cost and reward magnitude  
   (1) Not applicable; rewards are absent.  
   (2) No prediction.

12. Whether the horizon (number of rounds) is known to players  
   (1) Mentioned: players know the game is repeated exactly 30 times (“the interaction is finitely repeated and the whole setup is deterministic”).  
   (2) Horizon length/knowledge is not varied; no prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   (1) Mentioned: after every round participants “could observe the individual actions of their group members.”  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

14. Punisher identity revealed?  
   (1) The paper never states that punished participants are told *who* punished them; they only learn the *amount* of punishment.  Hence the safest coding is “identity not revealed/unspecified.”  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

15. Rewarder identity revealed  
   (1) Not applicable (no rewards).  
   (2) No prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Numerical punishment-treatment effects that can be extracted

The only treatment pair that cleanly adds punishment while keeping everything else unchanged is:

• Baseline PGG (no punishment) vs. PGGwP (punishment stage added)

Average **net earnings per person per round**  
PGG: 14.76  PGGwP: 13.59  Difference = −1.17 points  
(Standard endowment = 12, maximum surplus = 24 under full cooperation; the paper does not convert this into an efficiency ratio.)

Hence, with φ = 1 and fines = (2,5,8) the observed punishment-treatment effect on payoffs is negative (about −7.9 % of baseline payoffs).  The authors also report no statistically significant increase in cooperation (Result 2).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used  
   • Gross earnings (before punishment costs)  
   • Net earnings (after punishment and counter-punishment costs)  
   • Ex-ante cooperation rate (intended contribution)  
   • Ex-post cooperation rate (actual contribution)

   “Efficiency” defined as (actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff) is **not** used anywhere in the paper, although net earnings are a closely related payoff-based measure.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 12, 13 (10 parameters).

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the **effect of systematically varying** that parameter on the punishment-treatment effect?  
   Zero.  No parameter is experimentally manipulated across more than one level; only the *presence* of a punishment stage is manipulated, and “presence” itself is not among the 15 parameters listed.

D. If one had to make predictions about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency using **only** the information in this paper:

   • With the specific parameter bundle actually used (φ = 1; fines = 2,5,8; binary contributions; three players; 30 known rounds; full feedback; no rewards) adding punishment reduced efficiency (lower net earnings).  
   • There is no evidence about what happens if any single parameter (number of players, punishment cost, punishment magnitude, MPCR, information, etc.) is changed, so no reliable directional prediction can be made for any of them.  
   • The paper *suggests* (Result 4) that larger fines on the Small player make that player worse off, hinting that asymmetries in punishment magnitude can redistribute payoffs, but the aggregate effect on efficiency remains unclear.  
   • Because punishment costs created enough dead-weight loss to offset the (small) cooperation gains, any change that *lowers* punishment fees or *raises* the fine-to-fee ratio **might** improve efficiency, but this is conjecture—the paper provides no direct evidence.

In short, the experiment tells us that *with the one parameter constellation actually implemented* punishment hurt efficiency, but gives virtually no leverage for predicting how other parameter constellations would behave.

Below, each of the 15 design parameters is treated in turn.  For every parameter I report

• Whether the parameter is explicitly stated in the paper, and its value;  
• Whether the paper **systematically varies** that parameter;  
• Whether the paper offers any quantitative or qualitative prediction about how changing that parameter would alter the *punishment-treatment effect* on any dependent variable (and especially on group **efficiency** = realised total payoff ÷ maximum total payoff).

The phrase “punishment-treatment effect’’ refers to the difference in outcomes between conditions **with** versus **without** punishment (formal or informal).

------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
   • Stated: fixed at 5 (p. 13 “group of five”).  
   • Not varied.  
   • No prediction about varying group size.

2. Number of rounds (periods)  
   • Stated: 4 periods in Part 1; 6 phases×4 periods = 24 periods in Part 2 (total = 28).  
   • Not varied.  
   • No prediction.

3. Chat enabled?  
   • Not mentioned; chat is absent.  
   • Not varied.  
   • No prediction.

4. All-or-nothing contributions?  
   • Stated implicitly: subjects choose any amount 0–20 (so NOT all-or-nothing).  
   • Not varied.  
   • No prediction.

5. “Contribution default’’ (withdraw vs. give)?  
   • Not part of the design; subjects actively *contribute* to a public account.  
   • Not varied.  
   • No prediction.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Stated: MPCR = 0.4 (Eq. 1).  
   • Not varied.  
   • No prediction about changing MPCR.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher (per unit)  
   • Stated:  
     – IS (peer) scheme: punisher pays 1 for every 3 lost by target.  
     – FS (formal) scheme: each point deducted from the target costs the *group* 4⁄11 in total (1⁄11 to each of the 4 other members), giving the same 3:1 loss ratio.  
   • Not varied experimentally.  
   • No prediction about varying the cost.

8. Punishment magnitude to the target (per unit)  
   • IS: fixed at 3.  
   • FS: magnitude depends on the *sanction rate* that groups vote on (0, 0.4, 0.8, 1.2).  
   • Although the rate is *endogenously* chosen rather than exogenously manipulated, the paper does analyse outcomes for two categories:  
     – “Deterrent” rates (0.8 or 1.2)  
     – “Non-deterrent” rates (0 or 0.4)  
   • Predictions / effect sizes (Table 5):  
     – Voting-D treatment: deterrent FS raises individual contribution by ≈ +14.7 points and raises payoff by ≈ +10.7 points relative to the no-scheme baseline; non-deterrent rates have no positive effect (contribution −3.5, payoff −6.6).  
     – Voting-N treatment: deterrent FS raises contribution by ≈ +11.0 points and payoff by ≈ +4.6 points; non-deterrent rates increase contribution (+8.1) but not payoff.  
   • Thus, within the paper’s data, *greater punishment magnitude (moving to a deterrent rate) sharply increases efficiency*, but only when the magnitude is large enough.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • No rewards in any condition.  
   • Not varied.  
   • No prediction.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   • Not applicable (no rewards).

12. Horizon known?  
   • The instructions say subjects play a *finitely repeated* game, but the paper never states whether the exact end period was common knowledge.  
   • Not varied.  
   • No prediction.

13. Peer outcomes shown?  
   • Yes: after each round players see every member’s contribution, and under IS also the punishment points received.  
   • Not varied.  
   • No prediction.

14. Punisher identity revealed?  
   • Not reported; presumably anonymous (standard for Fehr–Gächter design).  
   • Not varied.  
   • No prediction.

15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
   • Not applicable (no rewards).

------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary

A.  Dependent variables  
   • The paper reports:  
     – Contribution (points contributed).  
     – Payoff / earnings (which the author also interprets as “efficiency”).  
     – Scheme choice indicators.  
   • “Efficiency’’ is used when total payoff is compared with the maximum possible (e.g., “achieved almost full efficiency”).  Contribution and payoff are distinct: punishment can raise contributions yet lower net payoffs because of punishment costs.

B.  Which parameters are mentioned? 7 of the 15: (1) group size, (2) rounds, (4) continuous contributions, (6) MPCR, (7) punishment cost, (8) punishment magnitude via sanction rate, (13) information on peer outcomes.

C.  Which parameters are *systematically varied* and analysed for their effect on the punishment-treatment effect?  Strictly speaking, none of the 15 are exogenously varied.  The paper does, however, contrast *different endogenously chosen punishment magnitudes* (deterrent vs non-deterrent sanction rates), giving us partial evidence for parameter 8 only (1/15).

D.  Predictions one can make about the 15 parameters—based only on what the paper contains:

   – Parameter 8 (punishment magnitude): Larger, deterrent punishment strongly increases efficiency; mild punishment can even lower payoffs once punishment costs are counted.

   – All other parameters: the paper offers no evidence or theory about their interaction with punishment beyond the single setting it used.  Therefore, no reliable prediction about how varying group size, MPCR, number of rounds, communication, reward options, information structure, etc., would change the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency can be drawn from this article alone.

In short, the article tells us that *if* punishment is sufficiently severe, it restores near-maximal efficiency, but it provides virtually no information about how the 14 other listed design features would moderate that effect.

Article Title: The evolution of cooperation in the unidirectional division of labour on a tree network
Author Keywords: cooperation in tree graph network; replicator equation of asymmetric games; sanction systems; supply chain
Keywords Plus: DYNAMICS; SPECIALIZATION; RECIPROCITY; PUNISHMENT; EMERGENCE; ALTRUISM; PROMOTES; GAMES
Abstract: Division of labour on complex networks is rarely investigated using evolutionary game theory. We investigate a division of labour where divided roles are assigned to groups on the nodes of a general unidirectional finite tree graph network. From the network's original node, a task flows and is divided along the branches. A player is randomly selected in each group of cooperators and defectors, who receives a benefit from a cooperator in the upstream group and a part of the task. A cooperator completes their part by paying a cost and then passing it downstream until the entire task is completed. Defectors do not do anything and the division of labour stops, causing all groups to suffer losses due to the incomplete task. We develop a novel method to analyse the local stability in this general tree. We discover that not the benefits but the costs of the cooperation influence the evolution of cooperation, and defections in groups that are directly related to that group's task cause damage to players in that group. We introduce two sanction systems, one of which induces the evolution of cooperation more than the system without sanctions, and promote the coexistence of cooperator and defector groups.
