Below, “paper” always refers to  
Nirjhor & Nakamaru (2023) “The evolution of cooperation in the unidirectional division of labour on a tree network.”  
The terms “punishment” or “sanction” in the paper correspond to a monetary deduction f that is imposed on a detected defector with probability ρ (defector-sanction system) or always on the premier if any defection occurs (premier-sanction system).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER–BY–PARAMETER SCAN
--------------------------------------------------------------------
(1) Number of players  
• Mentioned?  Yes – each node (group) contains an infinite population of players.  
• Systematically varied?  No.  The population size is fixed and never compared to any other size.  
• Numerical effect on punishment-treatment effect?  None reported.

(2) Number of rounds  
• Not mentioned (the model uses continuous-time replicator dynamics, not discrete rounds).  

(3) Chat enabled?  
• Not mentioned.

(4) “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
• Yes – an individual’s choice set is binary (cooperate vs defect).  This is built into the model but never varied; no comparison with a continuous contribution version exists.  Hence no treatment-effect estimate.

(5) Contribution default / endowment returned  
• Not mentioned.

(6) MPCR / multiplication factor  
• Not part of the model; pay-offs are defined by benefit b and cost x, not by a linear public-goods return.

(7) Punishment cost to the punisher  
• Not in the model.  No one pays to impose punishment; the only monetary transfer is the fine f borne by the punished party.

(8) Punishment magnitude (per unit fine deducted from target)  
• Mentioned?  Yes – parameter f (fine) with effective strength ρf in the defector-sanction system and f in the premier-sanction system.  
• Systematically varied?  Yes.  Figures 4-7 sweep ρf across many values.  
• Reported effects?  
  – Larger ρf enlarges the basin of attraction of the all-cooperator equilibrium and can destabilise the premier-defection equilibrium.  
  – Threshold conditions (Table 6): e.g. premierD is locally stable when  
    g_p – (1 – c_op) g_op + ρf < x_p (defector sanction)  
    g_p – (1 – c_op) g_op + c_op f < x_p (premier sanction)  
  – No efficiency measure is ever computed, so no numerical change in efficiency is given.

(9) Reward enabled?  
• Not included.

(10) Reward cost  
• Not included.

(11) Reward magnitude  
• Not included.

(12) Number of rounds known ex-ante  
• Not relevant / not mentioned.

(13) Peer outcomes shown  
• Not mentioned.

(14) Punisher identity revealed  
• Not discussed; the model is silent on whether punished players learn who punished them.

(15) Rewarder identity revealed  
• Not applicable (no rewards).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A.  Dependent variables used in the paper  
• Group efficiency (total or average payoff divided by the theoretical maximum) is never computed.  
• The authors analyse:  
  – frequency of cooperators in each group (continuous-time share i_c),  
  – local stability of four equilibria (all-C, premier-D, two types of mixed equilibria),  
  – conditions under which each equilibrium is locally stable as functions of parameters g, x, ρ, f.  
These variables are conceptually different from efficiency: they say nothing about aggregate realised pay-offs.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
2 of 15.  
• #4 (binary/all-or-nothing action) – fixed, never varied.  
• #8 (punishment magnitude f, implemented as ρf) – explicitly modelled and varied.  
No other parameter on the list appears.

C.  Parameters whose *systematic* variation is linked to a punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable)  
1 of 15 – parameter #8 (punishment magnitude).  
The authors sweep ρf and report qualitative regime shifts in the equilibrium configuration (Figures 4-7, Table 6).  All other parameters on the list are either absent or held constant, so no systematic effect is traced.

D.  Predicting the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency using only the paper  
Because efficiency itself is never calculated, very little can be said.  All that can legitimately be inferred is:

• Increasing the effective fine ρf raises the frequency of cooperative equilibria; under the usual assumption that full cooperation maximises total pay-off, one would *expect* efficiency to rise with ρf, but the paper does not confirm this.  

• No statements (and therefore no predictions) are possible for any of the remaining 14 parameters or for their interactions with ρf, because they are not analysed.

Hence, based strictly on the paper, predictions about efficiency must be limited to:  
“Larger punishment magnitude (parameter #8) should increase cooperation and therefore probably increase efficiency; for every other parameter we have no information.”

Article Title: Justice strategy can promote cooperation with the joint of dynamic aspiration in social dilemma
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; GAME; EFFICIENCY; EVOLUTION; REWARD
Abstract: - We investigate the concurrent effect of the justice strategy and dynamic aspirations on cooperation in evolutionary game theory. The justice strategy refers to a game in which players play the role of cooperators in the case of cooperation, the role of punishers in the face of defection, and receive the same payoff as their opponents. Players compare the payoffs with their own dynamic aspirations to decide whether to change their strategy. Through simulations, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our model in promoting cooperation and reducing or completely eliminating defections. A higher initial aspiration has a significant impact on reducing defection. Additionally, we find that diverse evolutionary dynamics arise from various initial settings. Remarkably, in specific situations, even a tiny initial fraction of justicers can rapidly retaliate and eventually dominate the entire system. Reflecting real-life scenarios, the influence of punishment typically lags behind the occurrence of defection, allowing justicers to gradually counteract defection upon its cluster emergence. Author Keywords: Authority; Collective actions; Insignia; Legitimacy; Political symbol

Abstract: The performance of government activities, including law enforcement and regulation, depends on whether citizens perceive them as legitimate. Although substantial studies have explored the institutional sources of legitimacy, how non-institutional factors affect perceived legitimacy remains unclear. Human societies have a long history of employing symbolic icons to enhance the legitimacy of a given authority. This study reports a laboratory experiment of public goods that investigates whether (and to what extent) symbolic factors enhance perceived legitimacy. In the contexts of various incentive schemes and transparency levels, an authority in each group decides whether to target a citizen for punishment after observing the contributions of citizens, and untargeted citizens then choose to support or hinder the authority. A symbolic scepter is issued to the authority in the treated group, whereas this symbol is absent in the control group. The experimental results suggest that the political symbol significantly enhances the authority's legitimacy regardless of the payment scheme and information transparency. A further analysis shows that the political symbol is not associated with the authority's choices regarding enforcement. Rather, the symbol's effect on perceived legitimacy is primarily driven by the citizens' side-that is, the increasing intrinsic tendency to support authority.

    • Effect on the punishment-related outcomes (no efficiency measure is reported):

      – Authority’s enforcement attempt  
      – Authority’s targeting style (resoluteness, perverse, predation)  
      – Individual contribution (binary)  
      – Profits are compared once in Appendix A7, but efficiency is never analysed.

Authors: Zhang, YQ; Zheng, ZH; Zhang, XM; Ma, JL
Author Full Names: Zhang, Yongqiang; Zheng, Zehao; Zhang, Xiaoming; Ma, Jinlong
Article Title: Dynamic punishment-reputation synergy drives cooperation in spatial public goods game
Author Keywords: Evolutionary game theory; Spatial public goods game; Reputation; Punishment
Keywords Plus: PRISONERS-DILEMMA; EVOLUTIONARY DYNAMICS
Abstract: In general, individuals with high reputation often leverage greater access to resources, influence, and opportunities, creating a differential advantage in societal hierarchies. Meanwhile, real legal systems impose stricter punishments on severe crimes to ensure proportional justice. In some social contexts, individuals who engage in punishment behavior may be perceived as more trustworthy or committed to group norms, potentially leading to an enhanced reputation. Motivated by these real-world observations, we incorporate a mechanism combining dynamic probabilistic punishment and reputation-driven cost reduction into the spatial public goods game, aiming to investigate their collective impact on the evolution of cooperative behavior in populations. Through extensive simulation experiments, it is proved that the mechanism of dynamic probabilistic punishment and reputation merging effectively promotes the evolution of cooperation. Critically, a larger reputation increment is more conducive to the emergence and promotion of cooperation. Notably, increasing reputation increments reduce cooperation's critical threshold toward lower bounds, resolving cooperation dilemmas while enhancing reputation-based strategy adoption that promotes cooperative prosperity. Even when the punishment cost exceeds the imposed fine, it still facilitates cooperation evolution to some extent, while increasing the initial punishment probability significantly enhances cooperative engagement and accelerates evolutionary dynamics, though adjustments to the reputation threshold demonstrate negligible impact on cooperative evolution within the population. These findings could be beneficial in our understanding of the combined effects of reputation and punishment on the emergence of cooperation.

For every parameter we state  

(1) whether the paper ever mentions or fixes the parameter and, if so, the value(s) used;  

(2) whether the paper ever systematically varies that parameter and reports what this does to the “punishment treatment effect”.  
(The paper never reports group-efficiency; the only dependent variables actually analysed are the cooperation‐rate ρC, phase boundaries between strategy mixtures, and speed-to-full-cooperation.  Numerical quantities therefore refer to those dependent variables.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players  
(1) Mentioned.  A 100 × 100 lattice is used, so N = 10 000.  
(2) Never varied; no predictions.

2. Number of rounds  
(1) Not mentioned; the evolutionary simulation runs until a stationary state.  
(2) Not varied.

3. Chat enabled?  
Not mentioned; no free communication channel exists.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
(1) Yes.  Cooperators and punishers always contribute 1 unit; defectors contribute 0.  
(2) Not varied.

5. Contribution default?  
Not applicable / not mentioned.

6. MPCR / multiplication factor (called the “synergy factor” r)  
(1) Mentioned.  Typical range explored: r = 1.0…5.0 in steps of 0.1 (Figs. 4–6).  
(2) Systematically varied.  Main results (all expressed in terms of cooperation rate):  
    • Higher r raises ρC.  
    • Critical r needed for ρC = 1 falls as punishment fine β increases and as reputation increment T increases.  
      – Example (Fig. 4c, reputation model, T = 5): with β = 1.0 full cooperation occurs already at r = 1.0.  
      – Example (Fig. 4a, traditional punishment): with β = 0.7 the same outcome requires r ≈ 3.0.  
    No efficiency figure is given.

7. Punishment cost to impose one unit (α)  
(1) Mentioned.  Varied from 0.1 to 0.6 (and up to 1.5 in Fig. 7).  
(2) Systematically varied.  
    • Higher α lowers ρC in both punishment regimes.  
    • With reputation the negative effect is strongly dampened; cooperation can survive even when α ≥ β (Fig. 7b-d).  
      – Example: With β = 0.92 and reputation (T = 3) ρC = 1 for every α ∈ [0,1.5]; without reputation ρC = 0 once α ≈ β.

8. Punishment magnitude (β, the fine paid by the punished)  
(1) Mentioned.  Varied 0.1…1.0 (Figs. 2, 3, 4, 6, 7).  
(2) Systematically varied.  
    • Higher β increases ρC and shifts the critical r-threshold for cooperation to smaller values.  
      – Example (Fig. 2b, reputation model, r = 3.2, f0 = 0.5): when α = 0.3 the switch from ρC≈0 to ρC≈1 occurs at β≈0.55; the corresponding switch without reputation needs β≈0.8.  
    • Interaction with α: when β is fixed, lowering α promotes cooperation (Fig. 2).

9. Reward enabled?  
Not mentioned; not present.

10. Reward cost  
Not mentioned.

11. Reward magnitude  
Not mentioned.

12. Horizon known?  
Not modelled; agents play indefinitely; no information about last round.

13. Peer outcomes revealed?  
Not discussed.

14. Punisher identity revealed?  
Not discussed.

15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
Not applicable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary requested in points A–D
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables  
   • The paper does NOT use group efficiency (total or average payoff divided by the maximum possible).  
   • Main dependent variables:  
       – Cooperation rate ρC (fraction of cooperators + punishers).  
       – Phase boundaries between different stationary strategy mixes.  
       – Speed (number of Monte-Carlo steps) required to reach full cooperation.  
     These are conceptually different from efficiency because they ignore the absolute size of pay-offs and the punishment costs actually paid.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   5 of them: #1 (group size), #4 (all-or-nothing), #6 (MPCR r), #7 (punishment cost α), #8 (punishment magnitude β).

C. For how many parameters does the paper give results obtained by systematically varying the parameter?  
   3 of 15: #6 (r), #7 (α), #8 (β).  No other parameter is experimentally manipulated in the paper.

D. Predictions one can legitimately make—restricted to what the paper says—about the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency  
   • Because efficiency is never reported, only indirect inferences are possible.  
   • If one assumes higher cooperation almost always yields higher efficiency, the qualitative predictions would be:  
       – Larger MPCR r → higher efficiency gain from punishment.  
       – Larger fine β → higher efficiency gain, with diminishing additional benefit once β is above ≈1.0.  
       – Larger punishment cost α → lower efficiency gain; however, introducing a reputation-based cost discount greatly cushions this loss and can even make punishment beneficial when α ≥ β.  
   • For the remaining 12 parameters the paper supplies no information, so no prediction grounded in the paper can be made.

In short, the paper focuses on how the synergy factor, punishment cost, punishment magnitude, and a separate “reputation increment” shape cooperation; it does not analyse, let alone quantify, their effect on group efficiency, nor does it address the other eleven parameters listed in the question.

Article Title: The Evolutionary Roots of Moral Responsibility
Keywords Plus: COOPERATION; PUNISHMENT
Abstract: Judging a person as morally responsible involves believing that certain responses (such as punishment, reward, or expressions of blame or praise) can be justifiably directed at the person. 5. Contribution default / endowment returned

6. Marginal Per-Capita Return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Not mentioned.  
   • No prediction.

7. Cost to impose one unit of punishment  
   • Punishment is repeatedly called “costly” or “risky” (because of retaliation), but the cost is never quantified.  
   • No prediction about how varying that cost would affect the punishment treatment effect.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine inflicted per unit)  
   • Never quantified or systematically discussed.  
   • No prediction.

9. Whether a reward option exists  
   • Rewards are mentioned only as one of several “responses” that can be directed at a person judged responsible.  
   • No prediction about what happens to efficiency when the ­presence/absence of a reward option is varied alongside punishment.

10. Cost to grant one unit of reward  
    • Not mentioned.  
    • No prediction.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Not mentioned.  
    • No prediction.

12. Whether the horizon (number of rounds) is known  
    • Not mentioned.  
    • No prediction.

13. Whether peer outcomes are displayed  
    • Not mentioned.  
    • No prediction.

14. Whether punished players learn who punished them  
    • Not mentioned.  
    • No prediction.

15. Whether rewarded players learn who rewarded them  
    • Not mentioned.  
    • No prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY  

A.  Dependent variables actually used in the paper  
    • The paper never measures “group efficiency,” “total payoff,” or any other PGG-style performance variable.  
    • Instead it discusses the *existence and evolutionary stability* of (i) punishment episodes, (ii) “moral responsibility judgment” in a demand sense (motivation to punish) and a permission sense (assessment of social support).  These are conceptual / psychological constructs, not payoff‐based measures.  

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are even **mentioned**?  
    – Parameter 1 (group size)  
    – Parameter 3 (communication / gossip)  
    – Parameter 7 (punishment is costly/risky)  
    – Parameter 9 (rewards exist conceptually)  
    That is 4 of the 15.  All others receive no mention at all.  

C.  For how many parameters does the paper discuss **systematic variation** and its effect on the punishment treatment effect for any dependent variable?  
    – Zero.  The author never manipulates, quantifies, or models how changing any of the 15 parameters would change the impact of punishment on efficiency, on cooperation, or on anything else.

    – No numerical effect sizes, no dose–response curves, and no interaction terms between any of the 15 parameters are provided.  Consequently, almost no actionable quantitative prediction about efficiency can be derived solely from this paper.

( i ) whether the paper ever mentions, fixes, or manipulates the parameter (and, if so, give the value(s) that appear in the text, tables, or figures);  

( ii ) whether the paper makes any prediction about what would happen to the *punishment treatment effect* (PTE) when the parameter is systematically varied.  
The PTE would normally be “outcome with peer-punishment – outcome without peer-punishment”, but the present paper never implements a ‘no-punishment’ baseline, and never reports efficiency; it only tracks contribution levels and prosocial / antisocial punishment expenditures.  Whenever no prediction is given in the paper, I explicitly say so.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players in a group  
   (i) Mentioned.  Group size n = 4 (Table 1 and §5.1).  
   (ii) Never varied; no prediction about the PTE.

2. Number of rounds  
   (i) Mentioned.  Construction stage: 300 (sometimes 500 or 1 000 in robustness checks, Appendix Fig. S7).  Expression stage: 10.  
   (ii) Never used as an experimental factor; no prediction about the PTE.

3. Chat enabled?  
   (i) Not mentioned at all.  
   (ii) No prediction.

4. “All-or-nothing” contribution?  
   (i) Not used.  Contributions are continuous integers 0–20.

   (i) Not discussed.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   (i) Fixed at μ = 1.6.  Not otherwise discussed.  
   (ii) No prediction.

7. Punishment cost (cost to impose one unit)  
   (i) Fixed.  Cost = e (1–10) chosen by a strategy mapping; cost-fine ratio is constant 1 : 3.  
   (ii) Never varied; no prediction.

8. Punishment magnitude (fine per unit)  
   (i) Fixed at 3 × e.  
   (ii) No prediction.

9. Reward enabled?  
   (i) No peer-to-peer reward option exists; central power redistributes collected fines but that is not an endogenous reward system among peers.  
   (ii) No prediction.

10. Reward cost  
    (i) Not applicable.  
    (ii) No prediction.

11. Reward magnitude  
    (i) Not applicable.  
    (ii) No prediction.

12. Do players know when the game ends?  
    (i) Never reported.  
    (ii) No prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    (i) Not reported.  
    (ii) No prediction.

14. Do punished players learn the identity of the punisher?  
    (i) Not reported.  
    (ii) No prediction.

15. Do rewarded players learn the identity of the rewarder?  
    (i) Not applicable.  
    (ii) No prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables actually used  
   • Antisocial punishment expenditure (cost per antisocial act)  
   • Prosocial punishment expenditure (cost per prosocial act)  
   • Contribution amount  
   • Composition of “basic individual types” (CE, FS, RB)  
   The paper never reports *group efficiency* (total payoff ÷ maximum possible).  Thus efficiency, PTE on efficiency, and related effect sizes are absent.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   5 of 15 are mentioned (1, 2, 6, 7, 8).  The remaining 10 are never mentioned.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* the parameter on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable)?  
   Zero.  None of the parameters are experimentally or computationally varied; therefore no causal statements, regressions, or effect sizes exist for any of them.

D. What predictions—restricted strictly to the information found in the paper—can be made about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency?

Article Title: Calculated Punishment
Author Keywords: Prosocial and antisocial punishment; Sequential sampling process; Computational modeling; Response times
Keywords Plus: SOCIAL VALUE ORIENTATION; RESPONSE-TIME; ANTISOCIAL PUNISHMENT; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; DIFFUSION-MODEL; DECISION-MAKING; COOPERATION; ORGANIZATIONS; COMPUTATION; ATTRIBUTES
Abstract: Punishment is fundamental to the evolution of cooperative norms in teams, organizations, and societies. Based on findings that people are faster when punishing others (relative to when withholding punishment), dual-process theories of punishment assert that humans have an intuitive tendency to punish, which requires effortful deliberation to overcome. Here, we propose an alternative single-process theory that models punishment decisions as a sequential sampling process. Below, each of the 15 focal design parameters is examined in turn.  For every parameter I indicate  

(1) whether the paper ever mentions the parameter and, if so, the exact value(s) used; and  
(2) whether the paper gives evidence or makes **predictions about what would happen if the parameter were systematically varied** to the *punishment-treatment effect* (defined here as the difference between a “with-punishment” and a “without-punishment” condition) on any dependent variable, especially group **efficiency**.  Numeric effect sizes are quoted whenever they can be read directly from tables or figures.

Because the experiment never contains a “no-punishment” control, the paper never measures a punishment-treatment effect on any variable (efficiency, contribution, etc.).  The only systematic manipulations are the *cost* and *impact* (magnitude) of punishment, and the outcomes reported are individual punishment decisions and their response times (RTs).

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned: Groups of 4.  
   • Not varied; no prediction.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned: 20 periods.  
   • Not varied; no prediction.

3. Chat between players  
   • Not mentioned; evidently absent.  
   • Not varied; no prediction.

4. Contribution “all-or-nothing”  
   • Mentioned implicitly: contributions in integers of 2 (0–20).  
   • Not all-or-nothing, not varied; no prediction.

5. Contribution default (endowment initially in public fund)  
   • Not mentioned; not implemented; no prediction.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned: Total contribution multiplied by 1.6 and split equally (MPCR = 0.4).  
   • Not varied; no prediction.

7. Punishment cost per unit  
   • Mentioned and **systematically varied**: 0 or 2 points.  
   • Effects reported on *punishment choice* (Table 1: prosocial β = −1.399; antisocial β = −1.755) and on RTs (Supplementary Table A5), but **no measurement of group efficiency and no “with-punishment vs. without-punishment” comparison**.  
   • Therefore, no information on punishment-treatment effect.

8. Punishment magnitude per unit (impact)  
   • Mentioned and **systematically varied**: 2 or 8 points.  
   • Effects reported on punishment choice (Table 1: prosocial β = +0.080; antisocial β = +0.056) and RTs, but again no efficiency or treatment effect.

9. Reward enabled  
   • Not present; no prediction.

10. Reward cost  
    • Not present.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Not present.

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
    • Mentioned implicitly: subjects were informed it lasts 20 periods.  
    • Not varied; no prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mentioned: after each contribution stage players see every member’s contribution and pay-off.  
    • Not varied; no prediction.

14. Punisher identity revealed?  
    • Mentioned implicitly: interactions are anonymous; identity not revealed.  
    • Not varied; no prediction.

15. Rewarder identity revealed?  
    • Not applicable; no reward.

────────────────────────────────────────

SUMMARY  
A.  Dependent variables in the paper  
   • *Group efficiency / total payoff*: **Not used.**  
   • Main outcomes: (i) binary punishment decision (punish = 1, withhold = 0); (ii) response time (RT) of that decision.  Other derived variables: “utility difference” (model-based) and model parameters from a drift-diffusion model.  These are conceptually distinct from efficiency.

B.  Parameters out of the 15 that are at least mentioned: 7 parameters (1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13; plus 14 implicitly).

C.  Parameters for which the paper studies **systematic variation** and its behavioral effect: 2 parameters (7 & 8).  Even for those, the paper reports only their influence on punishment decisions and RTs, **not** on a punishment-treatment effect, and certainly not on efficiency.

D.  What can be predicted (solely from this paper) about how the 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency?  
   • Very little.  The study never contrasts a regime with punishment to one without, nor does it track total group payoffs.  Consequently, no direct evidence links any parameter to changes in efficiency caused by introducing punishment.  
   • Indirectly, one might conjecture (from Table 1) that lower punishment cost (parameter 7) and higher punishment impact (parameter 8) increase the *frequency* of punishment; but without data on how those punishments alter subsequent contributions or pay-offs, their net effect on efficiency remains unknown.  
   • For all other parameters (1–6, 9–15) the paper provides no data or theory allowing any prediction about efficiency consequences of punishment.

Hence, if one had to forecast efficiency effects using only this paper, the honest answer is that the paper offers **insufficient information to make meaningful predictions.**

Abstract: This paper investigates theoretically and experimentally the social benefits and cost to have an endogenous punishment-enforcing authority in public goods game. An authority is chosen among members of a society via an imperfectly discriminating contest prior to a public goods game. Below I go through the 15 parameters one‐by‐one exactly as requested.  
For each I state  

(1) whether the paper ever specifies the parameter (and, if so, the value[s] actually used), and  
(2) whether the paper makes any prediction about how *systematically varying* that parameter would change the size or sign of the “punishment treatment effect” on **group efficiency** (or on any other dependent variable).  Numerical effect sizes are quoted whenever the paper itself provides them.

“Punishment treatment effect” = outcome in the condition **with** punishment/authority (A4, A8) minus the corresponding outcome in the condition **without** punishment/authority (NoA4, NoA8).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER

1.  Number of players (group size)  
   (1) Mentioned and *varied*: N = 4 and N = 8 in the experiment; N is a free symbol in the theory (results for any N, with limits as N → ∞).  
   (2) Systematic-variation predictions: YES.  
       • Theory (Table 2): efficiency gain 𝔅 increases from 70.91 % (N = 4) to 84.54 % (N = 8); social cost 𝔠 falls from 29.09 % to 15.46 %.  
       • Experiment (Table 4): efficiency gain rises from 40.86 % (A4) to 47.65 % (A8); social cost falls from 32.20 % to 18.95 %.  
       → Prediction: Larger N ⇒ larger positive punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

2.  Number of rounds  
   (1) Stated: 30 rounds (15 + 15).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

3.  Chat enabled between players  
   (1) Not mentioned.  
   (2) No prediction.

4.  “All-or-nothing” contribution constraint  
   (1) Mentioned implicitly: subjects choose any integer 0–50 → continuous choice, not all-or-nothing.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

5.  Contribution default / “take” vs “give” frame  
   (1) Not discussed.  
   (2) No prediction.

6.  MPCR (or multiplication factor)  
   (1) Stated: α = 0.75 in the experiment; α is a parameter in all formulae.  
   (2) α is *not* varied empirically and no comparative-statics result for changing α is reported; therefore no quantitative prediction for efficiency change.

7.  Punishment cost to the punisher per unit  
   (1) Fixed at zero: once the contest is over the administrator can punish at no additional individual cost.  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

8.  Punishment magnitude per unit (or punishment power)  
   (1) Upper bound parameter β = 3; condition β > α(1 − α) is imposed in theory.  
   (2) β is not varied; the paper only says “radical punishment is not necessary”.  No quantitative prediction of varying β.

9.  Reward enabled  
10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   (1) Rewards are never available.  
   (2) No prediction.

12.  Whether the number of rounds is known to players  
   (1) Yes, it is common knowledge (instructions).  
   (2) Not varied; no prediction.

13.  Are peer outcomes shown?  
   (1) Authority sees each individual’s contribution; all players see *group-total* RED investment but not individual peers’ contributions.  
   (2) This information structure is held fixed; no prediction for variation.

14.  Does the punished player know who punished them?  
   (1) The administrator’s identity is mechanically known (the “winning ticket” is announced), but anonymity is never manipulated.  
   (2) No prediction.

15.  Rewarder identity known  
   (1) No rewards exist.  
   (2) No prediction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
FINAL SUMMARY

A.  Dependent variables actually used  
   • “Efficiency gain” 𝔅 = 100 × (Total PG contribution)/(N ω).  
   • “Social cost” 𝔠 = 100 × [(ω − contribution of authority)+total contest spending]/(N ω).  
   • Individual contribution level, contribution rate, contest spending, punishment imposed, and individual income are analysed separately.  
   (Efficiency combines pay-offs and costs, whereas contribution level looks only at tokens given, and income looks only at private pay-off after all costs.)

B.  Of the 15 parameters, 9 are at least mentioned (1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14).  

C.  Only **one** parameter—Number of players (Parameter 1)—is both (i) mentioned and (ii) analysed for its *systematic* effect on the punishment treatment effect.  No systematic-variation results are provided for the other 14 parameters.

D.  Predictions that can be made *solely from this paper* about how the 15 parameters (and their interactions) influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency:

   • Increasing group size (Parameter 1) unambiguously increases the efficiency-improving impact of introducing punishment/authority and reduces the associated social cost.  
   • For all other parameters the paper gives either a single fixed value or none at all, so no further directional or quantitative predictions can be extracted.  Any claim about their effects on efficiency would go beyond what is stated in the paper.

Below I walk through each of the fifteen design parameters that you listed and ask two questions for each one:   

(i) Does the paper even mention or set that parameter, and if so what value (qualitatively or quantitatively) is used?  
(ii) Does the paper say what would happen to any *punishment-treatment effect* (on efficiency or on any other dependent variable) if the parameter were *systematically varied*?  When possible I quote or point to the relevant page, figure or equation.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK

1. Number of players  
   (i) Mentioned.  The model contains 2n players with n ≥ 3 (Section 3).  Results assume n is “large relative to p”.  
   (ii) No systematic-variation result.  The paper states that large n makes it less likely that a player is re-matched with the same deviator, but it never quantifies how changing n would change any punishment effect or any efficiency measure.

2. Number of rounds  
   (i) The game is infinitely repeated (discount factor δ).  No finite T is analysed.  
   (ii) No statements about varying the horizon length.

3. Chat between players  
   (i) Not mentioned at all.  
   (ii) No discussion.

4. All-or-nothing contribution rule  
   (i) Not applicable; there is no public-goods contribution decision in the paper.  
   (ii) Not discussed.

5. Contribution default / endowment move-back rule  
   (i) Not applicable.  
   (ii) Not discussed.

6. MPCR or multiplication factor  
   (i) Not applicable.  
   (ii) Not discussed.

7. Punishment cost to the punisher  
   (i) Not parameterised.  “Punishment” is modelled as the punisher switching to the min-max action mℓ; the cost is whatever payoff loss that implies, but there is no explicit cₚ parameter.  
   (ii) No statement about systematically changing that cost.

8. Punishment magnitude for the target  
   (i) Same remark as #7—implicit, not parameterised.  
   (ii) No systematic-variation discussion.

9. Whether rewards are enabled  
   (i) Rewards are never modelled.  
   (ii) Not discussed.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
   (i) & (ii) Not applicable.

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
   (i) Infinite-horizon setting; the issue never arises.  
   (ii) No discussion.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   (i) Players observe each partner’s *actions* in the past p periods and the corresponding modal actions (Section 4).  They do not observe pay-offs, only actions.  
   (ii) The paper does not explore varying the amount of information revealed; it simply assumes that this information set is available.

14. Do punished players learn who punished them?  
15. Do rewarded players learn who rewarded them?  
   (i) Identity disclosure is not modelled; punishers are not even explicitly labelled.  
   (ii) Not discussed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables  
   • The paper’s focus is on *equilibrium path payoffs* and the *ability to sustain cooperation* in an infinitely repeated random-matching game.  
   • It does **not** define or report “group efficiency” (total or average realised payoff divided by the first-best payoff).  
   • No other behavioural dependent variables (e.g., average contribution rates) are reported because the paper is purely theoretical.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned at all?  
   • Only 1 of the 15—parameter 1 (number of players).  
   • Parameter 13 (information shown) is partly related because actions are observable, but the specific item “peer outcomes shown” is not what the paper describes.  All other parameters are absent.

C. For how many parameters does the paper analyse the *effect* of systematically varying the parameter on any punishment-treatment outcome?  
   • Zero.  The paper never varies any of the 15 parameters in a systematic comparative-static way, and never computes a treatment effect (punishment vs. no-punishment) on efficiency or on any other outcome.

D. What predictions can be extracted—strictly from this paper—about how the 15 parameters and their interactions would influence the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency?  
   • Very little.  The only qualitative hint is that having a *large* number of players (parameter 1) relative to the players’ memory length p facilitates the functioning of the modal-action punishment mechanism.  One might therefore conjecture (again, within the paper’s logic, not from outside sources) that increasing the group size could make punishment *more effective* at sustaining cooperation and therefore improve efficiency, but the paper provides **no quantitative estimate**.  
   • For all other parameters the paper is silent, so no evidence-based prediction can be made.

Hence, on the basis of this paper alone, virtually no parameter-specific or interaction-specific predictions about punishment’s impact on group efficiency in a public-goods game can be formulated.

Below we go through each of the 15 public-goods-game parameters and check whether they are (i) explicitly mentioned in Mihm & Toth’s “Cooperative networks with robust private monitoring,” and (ii) used to generate **any** prediction about how changing the parameter would alter “the punishment treatment effect” on any dependent variable (efficiency, cooperation, contributions, etc.).  References to page numbers, figures or equations are omitted because the whole article was supplied in plain text.

────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER INSPECTION
────────────────────────────────────────

1  Number of players  
  • Mentioned?  Yes.  The paper uses the symbol I for the size of the player set and occasionally discusses “large” versus “small” populations (e.g., Sections 3.2, 4.1, 4.2).  
  • Systematic prediction?  No.  The authors never estimate or simulate how varying I would magnify or diminish a “punishment treatment effect.”  They sometimes note that certain existence conditions are easier to satisfy “for a sufficiently large population,” but that is a qualitative feasibility statement, not a treatment-effect estimate.

2  Number of rounds  
  • Mentioned?  No.  The model is an infinitely repeated game with discount factor δ; a finite horizon or an explicit “number of rounds” never appears.  
  • Systematic prediction?  Not applicable.

3  Chat enabled?  
  • Mentioned?  No.  
  • Prediction?  No.

4  “All-or-nothing” contribution rule  
  • Mentioned?  No.

5  Contribution default / endowment moved back  
  • Mentioned?  No.

6  Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
  • Mentioned?  No.  The paper studies bilateral Prisoner’s-Dilemma–type payoffs, not a linear public-goods payoff with an MPCR.

7  Punishment cost per unit  
  • Mentioned?  No.  “Punishment” in the paper is exclusively the act of severing ties, which is costless to impose in the model.

8  Punishment magnitude per unit  
  • Mentioned?  No.  (Again, punishment is simply losing the relationship.)

9  Reward option present?  
  • Mentioned?  No.

10  Reward cost per unit  
   • Mentioned?  No.

11  Reward magnitude per unit  
   • Mentioned?  No.

12  Do players know when the game ends?  
   • Mentioned?  No finite horizon; thus not discussed.

13  Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Mentioned?  No.  Information structure is captured only through the “radius of information” ρ (players see actions up to ρ network steps away), not through payoff visibility.

14  Is the punisher identified?  
   • Mentioned?  No.  Identity revelation of the deviator or punisher is never a parameter; players only know *what* edges are discontinued inside their radius.

15  Is the rewarder identified?  
   • Mentioned?  No.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────
A. Dependent variables used in the paper  
   • Total or average pay-off (“efficiency”) is discussed **only** in Section 3.1 as the first-best benchmark when commitment is possible.  
   • The work’s actual equilibrium analysis focuses on (i) whether a given *network structure* can be supported, (ii) individual net pay-offs on each link, and (iii) whether ties are continued or discontinued.  Thus “efficiency” in the public-goods sense (actual total pay-off divided by a cooperative maximum) is *not* the main dependent variable—in fact, efficiency is not reported for any treatment comparison.  
   • No variables such as contribution rates or cooperation probabilities in a public-goods game are reported.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   • Only one: parameter 1 (number of players).  
   • The remaining 14 parameters never appear.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss the effect of *systematically varying* that parameter on a punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable)?  
   • Zero.  Even for parameter 1, no treatment-effect estimate or direction is given.

D. What predictions—restricted to the content of the paper—can we make about how those 15 parameters (and their interactions) would influence the punishment treatment effect on group efficiency?  
   Given that 14 parameters are absent and the 1 that is present (number of players) is only used to state that certain existence conditions are easier to satisfy when the network is large, the paper provides virtually no leverage for predicting how introducing monetary punishment into a *public-goods* setting would change efficiency.  The model is neither a public-goods game, nor does it include costly punishment, rewards, or any of the display treatments listed.  Therefore, strictly from this paper, we can make **no quantitative or qualitative prediction** about the punishment treatment effect on efficiency as a function of the 15 parameters.

PARAMETER-LEVEL SCAN
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players

5. Contribution default / endowment retraction  
   • Mentioned?  NO.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  NO monetary returns or payoff functions are reported.

7. Punishment cost (per unit)  
   • Mentioned?  Costs are described qualitatively (“fines,” “asking members to leave,” “social pressure”) but never quantified.  
   • Systematic variation or prediction?  NONE.

8. Punishment magnitude (per unit)  
   • Mentioned?  Same as #7: qualitative only, never measured or varied.

9. Reward enabled?  
   • Mentioned?  NO discussion of positive rewards for cooperation.

10. Reward cost  
    • Mentioned?  NO.

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Mentioned?  NO.

12. Do players know the final round?  
    • Mentioned?  NO concept of rounds exists.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
    • Mentioned?  Indirectly—communities sometimes “don’t keep track,” but there is no formal disclosure variable and no test of its effects.

14. Do punished players learn who punished them?  
    • Mentioned?  NO.

15. Do rewarded players learn who rewarded them?  
    • Mentioned?  NO.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Dependent variables actually used  
   – Group efficiency or total/average payoff: **NOT used**.  
   – Variables actually analyzed:  
     1. Whether free-riding is perceived as a problem (binary).  
     2. Whether third-party punishment is ever implemented (binary).  
     3. Qualitative themes about contextual flexibility (“each according to ability”).  
   These differ from efficiency because they capture attitudes and institutional practices rather than realized monetary payoffs.

B. Which (and how many) of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
   – Clearly mentioned and given numeric values: 1 (Number of players).  
   – Mentioned only in qualitative passing: 3, 7, 8, 13.  
   – Not mentioned at all: 2, 4, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 15.  
   Total parameters touched in any way: 5 of 15; with quantitative information: just 1.

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss **their effect on the punishment treatment effect** when the parameter is systematically varied?  
   – Exactly ONE (Parameter 1: group size).  
     Result: No statistically significant effect on whether punishment is used.  
   – For the remaining 14 parameters, the paper provides **no** systematic tests or effect sizes.  

D. Predictions you could make about punishment’s effect on **efficiency** based solely on this paper  
   – Group size: the paper finds no link between size and the likelihood of punishing; therefore the safest efficiency prediction is “no clear effect.”  
   – All other 14 parameters: the paper is silent; no defensible prediction can be made.  
   – Interactions among parameters: impossible to forecast because no interactions were analyzed.

In short, the study is a qualitative field survey, not a controlled public-goods experiment. It yields virtually no data that can be translated into quantitative predictions about how varying the 15 canonical game parameters would change the **efficiency impact** of introducing punishment.

Parameter-by-Parameter Extraction from the Selterman paper

For every parameter the two questions required by the instructions are answered:

• “Covered?” = Does the paper tell us anything factual about the parameter (even a single fixed value)?  
• “Systematic-variation effect?” = Does the paper report, analyse, or predict what will happen to the punishment treatment effect when the parameter itself is varied across two or more levels?

1. Number of players  
   • Covered? Yes. Seven independent cohorts ranged in size from 29 to 244 (Table 2).  
   • Systematic-variation effect? Partially. In the “General Conclusion” the author notes that the 4 cohorts that succeeded in staying below the 10 % threshold were “smaller in total size” than the 3 cohorts that failed. No statistics are supplied, but the observation implies a (descriptive) negative association between group size and the cooperation benefit obtained from adding the punishment option. No explicit numerical effect size is reported.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Covered? Yes. All cohorts play a single, one-shot round.  
   • Systematic-variation effect? No. Only one round is ever used.

3. Is chat enabled?  
   • Covered? No. The paper never mentions any real-time communication or chat facility.  
   • Systematic-variation effect? Not applicable.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
   • Covered? Yes. Choices are discrete (0, 2, or 6 points). Continuous contribution is impossible.  
   • Systematic-variation effect? No. No alternative contribution format is studied.

5. Contribution default / “take” frame  
   • Covered? No mention.  
   • Systematic-variation effect? Not applicable.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplier  
   • Covered? Not mentioned.  
   • Systematic-variation effect? Not applicable.

7. Punishment cost (cost to assign one unit)  
   • Covered? Yes. By choosing 0 points a student forgoes the 2- or 6-point gain—i.e., an opportunity cost of up to 6 points for one “unit” of punishment.  
   • Systematic-variation effect? No. The cost is fixed and never compared with alternatives.

8. Punishment magnitude (loss suffered by target per unit)  
   • Covered? Yes. One punished 6-point chooser loses the entire 6 points.  
   • Systematic-variation effect? No. Magnitude is fixed.

9. Reward option enabled?  
   • Covered? No. No reward possibility exists.  
   • Systematic-variation effect? Not applicable.

10–11. Reward cost and magnitude  
   • Covered? No.  
   • Systematic-variation effect? Not applicable.

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
   • Covered? Implied yes: students are told the rules, and the decision is clearly one-shot.  
   • Systematic-variation effect? No.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Covered? Yes (after decisions). Aggregate counts of 0-, 2-, 6-point choices are announced.  
   • Systematic-variation effect? No alternative information treatments are studied.

14. Is punisher identity revealed?  
   • Covered? Yes. The ballot is designed to be anonymous; however, some punishers voluntarily reveal themselves in discussion.  
   • Systematic-variation effect? No. Anonymity level is constant.

15. Is rewarder identity revealed?  
   • Covered? Not applicable – no reward stage.  
   • Systematic-variation effect? Not applicable.



SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables actually used  
   • Group “success” (binary: cohort stays below/above the 10 % 6-point threshold).  
   • Counts or percentages of 0-, 2-, 6-point choosers.  
   • Three attitudinal factor scores (Understanding, Positive Feelings, Prosocial Motivation).  
   • Final-exam multiple-choice accuracy.  
   The paper never computes the usual efficiency measure (total actual payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff).

B. Parameters mentioned at all  
   9 of the 15: 1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14, and implicitly 3 (absence of chat is evident but not stated).  

C. Parameters whose systematic variation vis-à-vis punishment is discussed  
   Only 1 (Parameter 1, group size). Even here the paper offers only an informal, non-quantified observation; none of the other 14 parameters are analysed in a way that links their variation to the punishment treatment effect.

D. What can be predicted about the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, using only this paper?  
   • Smaller groups appear to gain more from adding the punishment option than larger groups; hence we might tentatively predict that the efficiency boost from punishment diminishes with group size.  
   • Because every other parameter is held constant, the paper supplies no direct evidence for how changing MPCR, punishment cost, punishment magnitude, communication, number of rounds, reward availability, or information conditions would alter the punishment–efficiency link.  
   • Consequently, aside from the very tentative group-size observation, the paper provides virtually no basis for predicting how the 15 parameters or their interactions would influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.

Abstract: We model group-separations in an n-player set. In the n-player set, every two players play an infinitely repeated two-player prisoners' dilemma game. 10. Reward cost to grant one unit

--------------------------------------------------------------------

2. Number of rounds

3. Chat enabled?  
(1) Yes – The instructions explicitly prohibited all interaction; so “chat” = *False*.  
(2) No – No variation, no discussion.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
(1) Mentioned implicitly. Subjects could choose any integer 0-20, so “all-or-nothing” = *False*.  
(2) No discussion of varying this.

5. Contribution default / endowment back-transfer?  
(1) Not used; the game starts with 500 units and only *adds* to a public pool.  
(2) No discussion.

6. Marginal Per-Capita Return (MPCR) / multiplication factor  
(1) Yes – The public pool is multiplied by 2 and then split equally, i.e. MPCR = 2/N. The factor “2” is fixed in every game.  
(2) No prediction about what would happen if the factor were systematically varied.

7. Punishment cost to punisher  
(1) Yes – Always 5 units.  
(2) No variation and no statement about how changes in this cost would affect anything.

8. Punishment magnitude suffered by target  
(1) Yes – A punished player forfeits the entire return from the public pool in that round (i.e., loses $\bar V$). The numerical size depends on others’ contributions but is *functionally fixed* by the rule.  
(2) No analysis of different punishment severities.

9. Reward enabled?  
(1) No – Only punishment exists.  
(2) No discussion.

10. Reward cost  
(1) Not applicable.  
(2) Not discussed.

11. Reward magnitude  
(1) Not applicable.  
(2) Not discussed.

12. Are the number of rounds known?  
(1) Yes – Players were told the game ends “randomly”; therefore “unknown”.  
(2) The paper gives no comparison with a “known-horizon” version.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
(1) Yes – After contributions, every player sees each peer’s contribution, current endowment, and rank.  
(2) No alternate information treatments were run, so no prediction.

14. Is the punisher identified?  
(1) No – Players only see *whether* they were punished (“at least one person punished you”) but not *who*.  
(2) No variation and no discussion.

15. Is the rewarder identified?  
(1) Not applicable (no rewards).  
(2) Not discussed.

Summary

A. Dependent variables actually analysed  
 • Contribution level per player per round (main outcome)  
 • Whether a player *chose* to punish (binary)  
 • Social Value Orientation (SVO) score (a trait covariate)  
 The paper never reports group efficiency, total payoff, or average payoff. Contribution is not the same as efficiency, so the paper does not analyse efficiency at all.

B. Which of the 15 parameters appear?  
 Eight: 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14.  
 The other seven (3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 15) are either fixed at a single value or absent.

 Zero.

Below I review each of the 15 requested design parameters and map them to what is (and is not) said in Shen et al. (2024).  “Punishment treatment effect” is interpreted exactly as in the instructions: the change produced when punishment is introduced, relative to a baseline.  The paper’s only outcome variables are the time-averaged proportions of Cooperators (C), Punishers (P) and Defectors (D); it never reports total or average pay-off (i.e., efficiency).  Wherever the authors vary a parameter and show what happens to those proportions, I report it.  If a parameter is merely mentioned but never varied, I say so.  If it is not mentioned at all, I also say so.  Page, figure and/or equation numbers refer to the PDF text that was provided.

────────────────────────────────────────
PARAMETER-BY-PARAMETER CHECK
────────────────────────────────────────

1) Number of players  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – the population is an L × L lattice (Sec. 2, first paragraph).  L itself is never stated nor varied.  
   • Systematically varied?  No.  No predictions.

2) Number of rounds (horizon)  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – Monte-Carlo simulation is run “at least 10⁷ iterations” until convergence (Sec. 2).  
   • Varied?  No.  No predictions.

3) Chat allowed?  
   • Not mentioned at all.  No predictions.

4) All-or-nothing contribution rule?  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – cooperators always contribute 1, all others contribute 0 (Sec. 2).  
   • Varied?  No.  No predictions.

5) Contribution default rule (re-allocation of a preset endowment)?  
   • Not mentioned.  No predictions.

6) MPCR / multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – the synergy factor r is fixed to r = 3 in every simulation (Sec. 2).  
   • Varied?  No.  No predictions.

7) Punishment cost to the punisher (one unit) – Gp  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – a central parameter, varied a lot.  
   • Predictions when varied?  Yes.  Key qualitative results:  
     – Case I (no compensation / fine distribution): with α = 0.5, cooperation first appears around Gp ≈ 0.20, peaks at Gp ≈ 0.38 (≈45 % of the population; Figure 3 text), then vanishes again at Gp ≈ 0.60.  
     – Case II (compensation + fine distribution): cooperation appears already at Gp ≈ 0.12, peaks at Gp ≈ 0.45 (>60 % cooperators; Figure 3 text) and survives until about Gp ≈ 0.84.  
     – Heat-maps in Figure 6 show the same non-monotonic pattern across a grid of (Gp, α) values.

8) Punishment magnitude (fine on the target) – α  
   • Mentioned?  Yes – single-punisher fine α is systematically crossed with Gp in heat-maps (Figure 6 and Figure 11).  
   • Predictions?  Qualitative only: higher α enlarges the region in (Gp, α) space in which cooperation survives (Figure 6).  No numeric marginal effect reported.

9) “Reward enabled?” (in the usual sense that peers can send positive transfers)  
   • The paper has no separate voluntary reward stage.  However, in Case II a share φ of the collected fine is *redistributed* to the punisher.  This is not a reward chosen by peers but it is the only positive transfer discussed.  I list it under #11 below.

10) Reward cost  
    • Not discussed (there is no costly prosocial reward action).

11) Reward magnitude – φ (share of the collected fine that the punisher keeps)  
    • Mentioned?  Yes – φ is explicitly varied while holding β = 0 in Figure 10 and in the heat-maps of Figure 11 (right-hand panels).  
    • Predictions?  
      – With r = 3, Gp = 0.5, α = 0.5 and β = 0, increasing φ from 0 to 0.3 monotonically raises the long-run fraction of cooperators from ≈15 % to ≈55 % (Figure 10 line plot).  
      – Heat-maps (Figure 11c vs 11d) show that higher φ widens the high-cooperation region when Gp is *high*; it has virtually no effect when Gp is low.

12) Do players know the number of remaining rounds?  
    • Not relevant in this evolutionary simulation; never mentioned.

13) Are peer outcomes displayed?  
    • Not mentioned.

14) Do punished players learn the identity of the punisher?  
    • Not mentioned (punishment is modelled as an automatic payoff deduction).

15) Do rewarded players learn the rewarder’s identity?  
    • Not applicable.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────
A.  Dependent variables  
    • The paper never reports efficiency (total or mean payoff).  
    • Reported outcomes are only: proportion of C, D and P in the stationary state, sometimes called “level of cooperation”.  These are strategy frequencies, not pay-offs.

B.  Which of the 15 parameters are mentioned?  
    – Mentioned: 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 11  (7 out of 15).  
    – Not mentioned at all: 3, 5, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14, 15.

C.  Which parameters are *systematically varied* and their effect on any outcome traced?  
    – Varied in figures/tables: 7 (Gp), 8 (α), 11 (φ).  
      So 3 of the 15 are experimentally varied; effects are given only on cooperation frequency, not on efficiency.

D.  If I had to predict the punishment-treatment effect on group efficiency using only this paper:  
    • I would base everything on Gp, α and φ.  Efficiency is likely to track the fraction of cooperators, so:  
        – Moderate punishment cost (roughly Gp ≈ 0.3-0.5) + moderate-high fine (α≥0.4) + some fine redistribution to punishers (φ ≈ 0.1-0.3) should *increase* efficiency the most.  
        – Very low Gp or very high Gp should *decrease* efficiency relative to no-punishment, because either punishers crowd out cooperators (low Gp) or defectors dominate (high Gp).  
        – All other listed parameters are either fixed in the model or unaddressed, so I have no basis for predictions about them.  Overall, beyond Gp, α and φ, the paper offers little to forecast efficiency effects.

That exhausts what can be extracted from the provided article without introducing outside information.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter account of what the paper actually did and did not say regarding each of the 15 listed parameters, focusing on whether (a) the paper mentions or uses the parameter at all (and, if so, the value adopted in the experiment) and (b) whether it systematically varies that parameter to assess the punishment treatment’s effect on “efficiency.” As instructed, “efficiency” is understood here to mean actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff of a fully cooperative group. Because the paper focuses instead on net tokens (a form of total payoff) and resource sustainability (often referred to as “cooperation”), any place where it discusses outcomes other than efficiency is noted. Effect sizes are provided only where the paper explicitly reports numerical details related to systematic variations.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players
 • Mentioned? Yes. The paper uses groups of four players.  
 • Systematically varied? No. All groups had exactly four players.  
 • Effect on punishment treatment (for any dependent variable)? None discussed.  

2) Number of rounds
 • Mentioned? Yes. The paper has 9 total rounds, split into 3 phases (3 rounds each).  
 • Systematically varied? No. All groups played exactly 9 rounds.  
 • Effect on punishment treatment? None discussed.  

3) Is chat enabled between players?
 • Mentioned? Yes, and systematically manipulated as a core part of the experimental design. Some treatment phases allowed real-time text chat (communication), and some did not (no communication).  
 • Systematically varied? Yes. The paper compares “no communication,” “unfacilitated communication with punishment,” and “facilitated communication with punishment.”  
 • Effect(s) on punishment treatment?  
   – The paper tracks how groups with communication (vs. those without) use or abandon monetary penalties, as well as the resulting cooperation (net tokens).  
   – For example, once a previously no-chat group was allowed to chat (Phase 2), net tokens approximately increased from a median of 211 to 378 (Mood’s Median Test, Z=5.78, p<.001, r(1)=0.82).  
   – However, the paper does not frame these results as “efficiency” (ratio of total payoff to maximum possible). It instead reports net tokens (a payoff level) and resource stability (cooperation).  

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
 • Mentioned? No. The study used a real-time foraging task with continuous harvesting and did not employ an all-or-nothing contribution scheme.

 • Systematically varied? No.

 • Systematically varied? No. All conditions used the same cost.  
 • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed in terms of how altering that cost would affect outcomes.  

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player per unit)
 • Mentioned? Yes. Each imposed monetary penalty deducted $0.04 (2 tokens) from the target.

9) Whether a reward is enabled

11) Reward magnitude
 • Mentioned? No. Rewards were not part of the design.  
 • Systematically varied? No.  
 • Effect on punishment treatment? Not applicable.  

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (i.e., do they know when the game ends)?
 • Mentioned? Not clearly stated. The paper does not say whether participants knew the exact total rounds.  
 • Systematically varied? No.  
 • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed.  

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much peers gained/lost each round)?
 • Mentioned? The paper notes that participants see how many tokens are harvested by everyone in real time, but this is not a manipulated factor.  
 • Systematically varied? No.  
 • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed.  

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
 • Mentioned? Not in detail. The paper says monetary penalties appear in real time, visible to everyone, but it does not systematically vary punisher anonymity or identity disclosure.  
 • Systematically varied? No.  
 • Effect on punishment treatment? Not discussed.  

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
 • Mentioned? No. Rewards are not used.  
 • Systematically varied? No.  
 • Effect on punishment treatment? Not applicable.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A) Does the paper use “group efficiency” (actual total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • No. The paper measures net tokens (a form of total or individual payoff) and resource sustainability (“cooperation”), as well as participants’ conceptual understanding of enforcement and social-psychological factors. These differ from “efficiency” as defined in the prompt.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • The paper at least mentions the following nine parameters:  
     (1) Number of players (fixed at 4),  
     (2) Number of rounds (fixed at 9),  
     (3) Chat enabled or not (actively manipulated),  
     (6) Each token’s basic monetary value,  
     (7) Punishment cost (fixed at 1 token),  
     (8) Punishment magnitude (fixed at 2 tokens),  
     (13) Some real-time feedback on harvest (though not varied),  
     (14) Real-time visibility of punishment events,  
     (15) Reward was never used, so effectively no mention beyond that.  
   • The study never discusses or implements parameters 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, or 12 as systematic manipulations.  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • Only parameter (3), “Is chat enabled?” is truly varied in conjunction with the presence/absence of punishment. The paper finds that having communication (especially “facilitated” discussion of punishment) changes how groups use punishment, with a roughly +48 median-token boost (Mood’s Median Test, p<.001) compared with unfacilitated communication. However, the study does not tie this back to a ratio-based efficiency metric.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely from this paper:  
   • The study provides insights only into systematically varying communication (chat and facilitation) combined with the presence or absence of punishment. Other parameters are either not mentioned, not varied, or not analyzed for punishment effects. The paper does not measure efficiency and thus provides little basis for predicting how each of the 15 parameters (especially those not manipulated) would affect punishment’s impact on group efficiency. The main finding is that adding communication—and especially guided (facilitated) discussion—improves how punishment is used and boosts payoffs in the game. For other parameters, the paper offers no direct evidence on their effect on “efficiency.”

Article Title: Lies and slander: truth-telling in repeated matching games with private monitoring
Keywords Plus: COMMUNICATION; NETWORKS; TRADE
Abstract: Incentives for cooperation may be enhanced substantially if a player can rely on the entire community to punish a partner who failed to cooperate. The ability of a player to report a defection to others can constitute a strong deterrent against defection if this report triggers a punishment imposed by the whole community. This paper studies the truth-telling problem in such a context. The paper presents a sequential equilibrium that supports cooperation in which a player unilaterally reports the play of a partner with strict incentives for truth-telling. It is shown, however, that desirable properties of equilibria described in the previous literature that assume truth-telling no longer exist. The implications of the results for practical examples, such as trading on eBay, are discussed.

Below is a point‐by‐point check of how (if at all) the paper by Kurt Annen (“Lies and slander: truth-telling in repeated matching games with private monitoring”) addresses each of the 15 parameters and any systematic effect on the “punishment treatment effect” (i.e., how adding punishment changes outcomes). Throughout, it is important to note that the paper focuses on a repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma with private monitoring, not a public goods game, and does not explicitly analyze “group efficiency” (total payoffs relative to a cooperative maximum). Instead, it discusses cooperation, discount factors, and the ability to sustain certain outcomes.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     Yes. The paper has n+1 players and examines how large n affects whether cooperation can be supported by personal vs. community enforcement. In particular, the paper notes that a larger number of players (larger n) makes personal enforcement harder to sustain (the required discount factor goes to 1), whereas with community enforcement the threshold discount factor does not grow as fast.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying this parameter on the punishment “treatment effect” (for efficiency or any other outcome)?  
     The paper does systematically vary n but frames the results in terms of whether cooperation is sustainable (via thresholds on the discount factor). It does not present a numerical effect size of “punishment treatments” on group efficiency. Instead, it shows that as n increases, community enforcement can still work while personal enforcement becomes harder. No direct results on efficiency measures or a “treatment effect” of punishment are provided.  

2. Number of rounds
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     No. The model is an infinitely repeated matching game (no finite-round discussion).  
   • Predictions about varying this parameter?  
     Not mentioned.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     No. The only “communication” is the one‐sided label‐reporting stage, not a free-form chat.  
   • Predictions about varying this parameter?  
     Not mentioned.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     No. The paper studies a repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma with Cooperate (C) or Defect (D); it does not vary a contribution level in a public goods sense.  
   • Predictions about varying this parameter?  
     Not mentioned.  

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     No. There is no concept of a default contribution in the study.  
   • Predictions about varying this parameter?  
     Not mentioned.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     No. The paper works with standard Prisoner’s Dilemma payoffs labeled a, b, c, and does not invoke a public-goods MPCR.  
   • Predictions about varying this parameter?  
     Not mentioned.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     No. Punishment is handled by future play of D or labeling a player as “guilty,” but the paper does not treat “cost to punish” as a separate, numerically varied parameter.  
   • Predictions about varying this parameter?  
     Not mentioned.  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted per unit punishment)
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     Not as a specific, numeric parameter. Punishment is conceptualized as being forced into low-payoff matches (e.g., “punishment path”), not as a configurable “magnitude” that is systematically varied.  
   • Predictions about varying this parameter?  
     Not mentioned.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     No. The models focus only on punishment and the possibility of “repenting” if one has defected, with no separate reward institution.  
   • Predictions about varying this parameter?  
     Not mentioned.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      No, same as above.  
    • Predictions about varying this parameter?  
      Not mentioned.  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per reward)
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      No.  
    • Predictions about varying this parameter?  
      Not mentioned.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      No. The setting is an infinite‐horizon repeated game, so there is no finite or known ending.  
    • Predictions about varying this parameter?  
      Not mentioned.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much others gained/lost)?
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      No. The game is deliberately set in private monitoring: outcomes in each match are perfectly observed only by the two matched players. Other players do not see these outcomes directly.  
    • Predictions about varying this parameter?  
      Not mentioned.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      No. The paper focuses on the fact that “the entire community” or “personal enforcement” can impose defection as punishment, but does not systematically discuss whether the punished party knows who is punishing them.  
    • Predictions about varying this parameter?  
      Not mentioned.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      No. There is no explicit rewarding in the model.  
    • Predictions about varying this parameter?  
      Not mentioned.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FINAL SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper does not use “group efficiency” as defined in typical public goods or punishing‐efficiency studies. Instead, it treats “cooperation” (C,C) and the maintenance of that cooperation under various discount factors as the main outcome. It also discusses players’ continuation payoffs and minimal discount factors under personal vs. community enforcement. These are different from an explicit “actual payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff” efficiency measure.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Only one of the 15 parameters—(1) the number of players—is clearly mentioned and analyzed. The paper focuses on n (the population size) in the repeated‐game setting. None of the other parameters appear as systematically varied or discussed.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable, when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, the paper does not frame the changes in n in terms of a “punishment treatment effect.” Rather, it shows how larger n influences the feasibility of supporting cooperation and how “community enforcement” can outperform personal enforcement. There is no explicit effect size on “efficiency.” So, there are zero parameters for which the paper provides a numerical effect size on a punishment‐treatment‐efficiency measure.

D. If you were to make predictions about how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper’s only relevant variation is that as the number of players increases, community enforcement (which relies on punishment via labels) remains feasible at discount factors below 1, while personal enforcement breaks down. However, because the paper never measures “efficiency,” it does not provide direct insights or effect sizes about how any of these parameters, or their interactions, would change a punishment treatment’s impact on overall efficiency. Accordingly, there is insufficient information to predict how the other 14 parameters would affect efficiency. We can say very little about them from this paper alone.

Authors: Calabuig, V; Jiménez-Jiménez, N; Olcina, G; Rodriguez-Lara, I
Author Full Names: Calabuig, Vicente; Jimenez-Jimenez, Natalia; Olcina, Gonzalo; Rodriguez-Lara, Ismael
Article Title: Coordinated and uncoordinated punishment in a team investment game
Author Keywords: Team investment game; Coordinated punishment; Uncoordinated punishment; Cooperation; Joint investment; Reciprocity; Efficiency
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS; WEAKEST-LINK; COOPERATION; TRUST; SANCTIONS; SPECIFICATION; RECIPROCITY; FADS
Abstract: Coordinated punishment occurs when punishment requires a specific number of punishers to be effective, otherwise, no damage will be inflicted on the target. While societies often rely on this punishment device, its benefits are unclear compared to uncoordinated punishment, where punishment decisions are substitutes. In this paper, we compare the efficacy of coordinated and uncoordinated punishment in a team investment game with two investors and one allocator. Our findings indicate that coordinated punishment results in higher levels of cooperation and reciprocity, as measured by the levels of joint investment and the return by allocators. Importantly, this does not translate into higher payoffs: investors use punishment more frequently when this is coordinated, which destroys the efficiency gains generated by the highest investment. In fact, our results suggest that the highest level of efficiency would be achieved if investors were not allowed to punish.
