Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what (if anything) the paper discusses about each of the fifteen parameters and whether it makes any prediction about how systematically varying those parameters would affect the “punishment treatment effect.” Note that “punishment treatment effect” here is understood to be the effect on efficiency (i.e., total payoff divided by the maximal possible total payoff) of being in a treatment where punishment is allowed, relative to a treatment where it is not. The paper also measures other outcomes—such as joint investment and amounts returned by allocators—but those are different dependent variables from efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
• Mentioned? Yes. The paper always uses two “investors” and one “allocator” in each group (3 players total).  
• Systematically varied? No. The number of players is held constant throughout all sessions.  
• Any prediction about varying it? No. The paper neither varies it nor discusses any efficiency effect of doing so.

2) Number of rounds  
• Mentioned? Yes. All groups play exactly 15 periods.  
• Systematically varied? No. It is always 15.  
• Any prediction about varying it? No. The paper does not analyze how changing the number of rounds affects any outcome.

3) Is chat enabled?  
• Mentioned? No. The paper does not refer to any communication or “chat” feature.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any prediction about varying it? No mention or prediction.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Mentioned? Yes. In the experiment, each investor’s decision is binary (invest 5 ECUs or do not invest).  
• Systematically varied? No. This binary (all‐or‐nothing) design is fixed.  
• Any prediction about varying it? No. The paper does not discuss how relaxing the all‐or‐nothing constraint would affect outcomes.

5) Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much to move back to themselves)?  
• Mentioned? No. The contribution is simply a fixed 5 ECU cost if the investor chooses to invest.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any prediction about varying it? No mention or prediction.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
• Mentioned? The “surplus” generated by a successful joint investment is always 30 ECUs, but there is no explicit reference to a public‐goods MPCR.  
• Systematically varied? No. The multiplier/surplus (30 ECUs) does not change across treatments.  
• Any prediction about varying it? No mention or prediction.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
• Mentioned? Yes. There is always a fixed 5‐ECU cost for an investor to choose to punish.  
• Systematically varied? No. The cost remains 5 ECUs in all punishment treatments.  
• Any prediction about varying it? The paper does not discuss what would happen if this cost were higher or lower.

8) Punishment magnitude (the amount deducted for each unit of punishment)  
• Mentioned? Yes. This is the central element that is systematically varied across three punishment treatments:  
  – Uncoordinated (UP₍30,60₎): if one investor punishes, the allocator loses 30% of payoff; if both punish, 60%.  
  – Coordinated (CP₍0,60₎): the allocator loses 0% if only one punishes, 60% if both punish.  
  – Coordinated with increasing returns (CP₍0,80₎): again 0% with one punisher, 80% if both punish.  
• Systematically varied? Yes.  
• Any prediction or measured effect on punishment treatment effect?  
  – The paper measures total payoffs (efficiency) across these different punishment‐magnitude setups. Although joint investment is highest in CP₍0,80₎, and allocators return more in CP‐style treatments than in UP₍30,60₎, the final efficiency (sum of total payoffs after punishment) is virtually the same under any punishment treatment (≈60 ECUs) and always below the no‐punishment benchmark (≈66.7 ECUs).  
  – Numerical points from the paper for final payoffs (i.e., after punishment) are about 59.67 (UP₍30,60₎), 60.20 (CP₍0,60₎), 60.05 (CP₍0,80₎), versus 66.67 in NP (no punishment).  
  – Thus, even though increasing the punishment magnitude increases joint investment, the final efficiency ends up no higher than other punishment treatments because more severe punishment also gets used more frequently.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
• Mentioned? No. Rewards are never introduced.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any prediction about varying it? None in the paper.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Mentioned? No. There is no reward option.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any prediction about varying it? None in the paper.

11) Reward magnitude (coins awarded for each unit of reward)  
• Mentioned? No. There is no reward option.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any prediction about varying it? None in the paper.

12) Is the number of rounds known?  
• Mentioned? Yes. Subjects know from the outset that the game lasts 15 rounds.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any prediction about varying it? No. The paper does not compare unknown‐length to known‐length horizons.

13) Are peer outcomes shown?  
• Mentioned? Yes, but only in a fixed way. Investors see the others’ decisions: who invested, how much the allocator returned, and who punished (if applicable).  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any prediction about varying it? No. The paper does not vary the information shown to see whether that changes punishment’s effect.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• Mentioned? The paper indicates that feedback was given about punishment decisions but does not detail whether identities are fully revealed.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any prediction about varying it? None.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
• Mentioned? No. Rewards do not exist in this design.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Any prediction about varying it? None.

────────────────────────────────────────
A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
• Yes, the paper explicitly measures total payoffs as “efficiency.” That is distinct from other measures it reports, including (1) the likelihood of joint investment, (2) the intended (or actual) amount returned by the allocator, and (3) frequency of punishment decisions.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• The paper explicitly mentions: (1) the number of players (always 2 investors + 1 allocator), (2) the number of rounds (always 15), (4) all‐or‐nothing contribution, (7) cost to punish (always 5 ECUs), (8) punishment magnitude (varied across treatments), (12) that subjects knew it was 15 fixed rounds, and (13) that certain outcome information was displayed.  
• Collectively, that is 7 parameters mentioned. However, only parameter 8 (punishment magnitude) is systematically varied in the experiment.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
• Only parameter 8 (punishment magnitude) is systematically varied across the three “punishment” treatments.  
• The paper does discuss, in detail, how different stipulations of punishment magnitude (especially 0% vs. 30% for one punisher, 60% vs. 80% for two punishers, etc.) lead to differences in joint investment, frequency of punishment, allocator returns, and ultimately efficiency. It also compares them to a baseline (no‐punishment) condition.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
• The only parameter clearly discussed and systematically manipulated is punishment magnitude (#8). Larger coordinated punishment magnitudes tend to raise cooperative investment and raise what the allocator returns, yet the efficiency difference among punishment treatments remains negligible or negative by the final payoff stage.  
• For the remaining parameters, the paper does not vary them or provide predictions about their interplay with punishment. Hence, we cannot infer how changes in (for example) the number of players, the number of rounds, or the availability of chat would alter the punishment treatment effect on efficiency. The paper simply does not address those parameters in a systematic way. Consequently, beyond parameter 8, there is little to no direct basis in the paper for extrapolating how these other factors or their interactions might affect efficiency.

Authors: Lec, FL; Matthey, A; Rydval, O
Author Full Names: Lec, Fabrice Le; Matthey, Astrid; Rydval, Ondrej
Article Title: Punishing the weakest link - Voluntary sanctions and efficient coordination in the minimum effort game
Author Keywords: Coordination; Minimum effort; Order-statistic game; Punishment; Sanction; Weakest link
Keywords Plus: CHEAP-TALK; PUNISHMENT; COMPETITION; FAIRNESS
Abstract: Using a laboratory experiment, we examine whether voluntary sanctions induce subjects to coordinate more efficiently in a repeated minimum-effort game. While most groups first experience Pareto inferior coordination in a baseline treatment, the level of effort increases substantially once ex post sanctioning opportunities are introduced, that is, when one can assign costly punishment points to other group members to reduce their payoffs. We compare the effect of this voluntary punishment possibility with the effect of ex post costless communication, which in contrast to the punishment treatment increases efforts only temporarily and fails to bring the players to higher payoff equilibria permanently. Our results indicate that decentralized sanctions can play an important role as a coordination device in Pareto-ranked coordination settings. Below is a parameter-by-parameter summary based solely on what is stated in the paper “Punishing the weakest link – Voluntary sanctions and efficient coordination in the minimum effort game.” The paper compares a Baseline (no sanctions) against two treatments: Punishment (costly punishment of others) and Disapproval (costless points that only signal disapproval). Its focus is entirely on a repeated minimum-effort game with 8 players and 16 rounds (8 rounds in Stage 1, followed by another 8 rounds in Stage 2). The paper does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters listed below, nor does it make predictions about how systematically changing these parameters affects the “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency. Instead, the paper focuses on whether punishment or disapproval helps groups move away from inefficient low-effort coordination, and on the net efficiency consequences of punishment.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The experiment always uses groups of 8 players.  
   • Systematically varied or predicted? No. The authors do not vary the group size and do not provide any prediction about changing the number of players.

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? Yes. There are 16 rounds total (8 in Stage 1, 8 in Stage 2).  
   • Systematically varied or predicted? No. The authors do not vary the number of rounds, nor do they predict how additional or fewer rounds would affect the punishment treatment effect.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned? Only indirectly. The paper does not allow free-form chat. Instead, there is either no communication (Baseline), costless “disapproval” (Disapproval), or costly punishment (Punishment).  
   • Systematically varied or predicted? No. They do not enable or disable chat as a separate treatment factor, so there is no discussion of chat’s systematic effect.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned? Not applicable. The core game is a minimum-effort game, and players choose integer effort levels from 1 to 7. There is no “all or nothing” format.  
   • Systematically varied or predicted? No.

5. Is the contribution default (whether players must actively opt out)?  
   • Mentioned? No. Starters always select an integer effort from 1 to 7. There is no notion of an “automatic” or “default” contribution.  
   • Systematically varied or predicted? No.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? The payoff function is 0.4 × (minimum effort) − 0.2 × (own effort) + 1.2, but the paper does not refer to this as an “MPCR,” nor is it varied.  
   • Systematically varied or predicted? No. There is no discussion of systematically changing those payoff parameters.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each punishment point costs the punisher 0.10 EUR.  
   • Systematically varied or predicted? No. They fix the cost at 0.10 EUR and do not study any variation of that cost.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each punishment point deducts 0.20 EUR from the punished player’s payoff.  
   • Systematically varied or predicted? No. The punishment magnitude is held constant at 0.20 EUR per point.

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned? No. The study only tests punishment or disapproval (no rewards).  
   • Systematically varied or predicted? No.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Mentioned? No. Rewards did not exist in the design.  
    • Systematically varied or predicted? No.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)  
    • Mentioned? No. Same as above—there is no reward mechanism.  
    • Systematically varied or predicted? No.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    • Mentioned? The paper explains that players know that there will be two stages of 8 rounds each, but this is not varied.  
    • Systematically varied or predicted? No. The authors do not analyze what happens if the horizon is unknown.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?  
    • Mentioned? Yes. After each round, players see the effort choices and payoffs (ordered from lowest to highest effort).  
    • Systematically varied or predicted? No. The feedback is not varied across treatments.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Mentioned? Yes. They do not know who the punisher is because effort and punishment information are displayed anonymously (ordered from lowest to highest effort).  
    • Systematically varied or predicted? No.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Mentioned? No. There is no reward mechanism in the paper, so this is not discussed or varied.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?  
   • The authors do measure payoff and “overall efficiency” (including punishment costs) as central outcomes. However, much of their analysis also examines effort levels (the Pareto-ranked equilibrium outcomes) as a dependent variable. They explicitly distinguish between (i) effort levels or minimum effort (their measure of “coordination”), (ii) payoffs within the game (before subtracting punishment costs), and (iii) total profit (payoffs minus punishment costs). They refer to group’s average or total payoff, as well as “efficiency” ratios (the fraction of the maximum possible payoff).  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some fashion: (1) Number of players (fixed at 8), (2) Number of rounds (fixed at 16), (6) The payoff function factor 0.4 (comparable to an MPCR-like parameter, but never labeled as such), (7) Punishment cost, (8) Punishment magnitude, (12) That there are 16 rounds total, (13) Players see each other’s efforts/payoffs, (14) The punisher is anonymous.  
   • The other parameters, including reward-related parameters, “all or nothing” contributions, or systematic manipulations of the cost/magnitude of punishment, are not employed or discussed in ways that vary them.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when the parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. The paper does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters. All design parameters (group size, number of rounds, cost of punishment, magnitude of punishment, etc.) are fixed. There is no analysis of how systematically changing these would influence the effect of punishment on efficiency or payoff.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not provide explicit predictions regarding variations of any parameter. The authors focus on a single fixed set of parameters. They only show that, with 8 players, 16 rounds, and a punishment cost of 0.10 EUR per point vs. a 0.20 EUR deduction per point, punishment opportunities eventually increase overall efficiency—once groups overcome initial inefficiency losses from paying punishment costs. Beyond that, the paper offers little basis for predicting how changing any of these 15 parameters (or their interactions) would alter the punishment effect on efficiency. Thus, one can make no further prediction from this paper alone.

Authors: Mohlin, E; Rigos, A; Weidenholzer, S
Author Full Names: Mohlin, Erik; Rigos, Alexandros; Weidenholzer, Simon
Article Title: Emergence of specialized third-party enforcement
Source Title: PROCEEDINGS OF THE NATIONAL ACADEMY OF SCIENCES OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
Author Keywords: evolution of cooperation; evolution of institutions; specialized reciprocity; third-party punishment; policing
Keywords Plus: SOCIAL NORMS; MAINTAIN COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; INSTITUTIONS; PUNISHMENT; DYNAMICS
Abstract: The question of how cooperation evolves and is maintained among nonkin is central to the biological, social, and behavioral sciences. Previous research has focused on explaining how cooperation in social dilemmas can be maintained by direct and indirect reciprocity among the participants of the social dilemma. However, in complex human societies, both modern and ancient, cooperation is frequently maintained by means of specialized third-party enforcement. We provide an evolutionary-game theoretic model that explains how specialized third-party enforcement of cooperation (specialized reciprocity) can emerge. A population consists of producers and enforcers. First, producers engage in a joint undertaking represented by a prisoner's dilemma. They are paired randomly and receive no information about their partner's history, which precludes direct and indirect reciprocity. Then, enforcers tax producers and may punish their clients. Finally, the enforcers are randomly paired and may try to grab resources from each other. In order to sustain producer cooperation, enforcers must punish defecting producers, but punishing is costly to enforcers. We show that the threat of potential intraenforcer conflict can incentivize enforcers to engage in costly punishment of producers, provided they are sufficiently informed to maintain a reputation system. That is, the guards are guarded by the guards themselves. We demonstrate the key mechanisms analytically and corroborate our results with numerical simulations.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter check of what the paper states, if anything, and whether it makes (a) any direct reference to the parameter and (b) any prediction about systematically varying that parameter on the “punishment treatment effect”—noting especially that the paper does not use the term “punishment treatment effect on efficiency” nor does it report “efficiency” (actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff) as an outcome measure.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • The paper does specify that there is a large population of agents (producers and enforcers) and uses, in simulations, a population size of N = 50. It also discusses limits as N becomes large.  
   (b) Predictions from systematic variation?  
       • No. The paper does not systematically vary the total number of players. There is no discussion of how changing the population size affects punishment or any “treatment effect.”

2. Number of rounds  
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • The model is an indefinitely repeated game with continuation probability δ. Thus, the number of rounds is random (geometrically distributed). The paper does not fix a finite round count.  
   (b) Predictions from systematic variation?  
       • Yes, in the sense that the paper reports results on differing continuation probabilities δ (Fig. 4J) and shows that cooperation is more difficult to maintain at lower δ. However, the paper does not phrase this in terms of a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Rather, they study whether cooperation‐with‐punishment can be sustained at different δ values.

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • No. The paper does not discuss communication or chat between players.  
   (b) Predictions from systematic variation?  
       • No mention, and no predictions are made.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • Yes. The paper’s prisoner's dilemma formulation gives each producer a binary choice: cooperate or defect.  
   (b) Predictions from systematic variation?  
       • No. The paper does not explore any alternative to the binary (all‐or‐nothing) move, nor does it compare how changing that might affect punishment.

5. Is the contribution default (e.g., do players choose how much to move from a public fund)?  
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • No. Producers have a simple binary choice between cooperate or defect.  
   (b) Predictions from systematic variation?  
       • No mention, and no predictions made.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters (e.g., multiplication factor)  
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • The paper’s prisoner's dilemma payoffs involve “b” (benefit) and “c” (cost) for cooperation, which together determine the net returns to cooperating or defecting. These are varied in Fig. 4 (panels D and E).  
   (b) Predictions from systematic variation?  
       • The paper analyzes how high or low b and c influence whether the population settles in a “cooperative” (punishing) or “defecting” outcome, in terms of fractions of cooperators and fractions of punishers. There is no explicit discussion of how varying b and c shifts a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency,” but they do show that raising the cost of cooperation c makes cooperation (and thus punishment that supports it) less stable.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • Yes. The paper denotes this “v” (the “variable cost of punishing”). They examine it in Fig. 4B.  
   (b) Predictions from systematic variation?  
       • They show that higher v reduces the likelihood of a cooperative/punishing equilibrium. However, the paper does not present a numerical effect size on “efficiency”; instead it shows how the fraction of cooperators/enforcers changes as v is varied.

8. Punishment magnitude (i.e., how much is deducted from the punished person)  
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • Yes. Denoted “p” in the model, representing the cost inflicted on defecting producers. It appears as a key parameter in both the theoretical discussion (threshold p > c(1 − τ)) and Fig. 4G.  
   (b) Predictions from systematic variation?  
       • The paper notes that punishment must be severe enough (p high enough) so that defection is deterred. Below that threshold, punishment can fail to sustain cooperation. It does not quantify any effect on “efficiency.”

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • No. There is no mention of rewarding or any positive transfer to cooperators from peers.  
   (b) Predictions from systematic variation?  
       • No mention, and thus no predictions.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • No. Not addressed in the paper.  
   (b) Predictions from systematic variation?  
       • No mention, and no predictions.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded for each unit of reward)  
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • No. Not addressed.  
   (b) Predictions from systematic variation?  
       • No mention, and no predictions.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?  
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • The paper’s model is an indefinitely repeated game with a probability δ of continuation in each round. There is no mention of players knowing (or not knowing) a specific final round.  
   (b) Predictions from systematic variation?  
       • They do not compare “known vs. unknown” horizon. Instead, they focus on the effect of δ. No separate predictions about “knowledge of the game ending.”

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players learn how much others gained or lost)?  
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • The paper discusses that producers do not gain large‐scale information about other producers (only enforcers can acquire broader info by paying the cost f). The text does not describe displaying “peer outcomes” or payoffs.  
   (b) Predictions from systematic variation?  
       • No mention, and no predictions.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • The paper does not explicitly say whether a punished producer knows the punisher’s identity. Punishment is modeled but not linked to any “known punisher” factor.  
   (b) Predictions from systematic variation?  
       • No. The paper does not vary this or discuss its effect.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   (a) Mentioned?  
       • No. As above, the paper does not feature inter‐player rewarding.  
   (b) Predictions from systematic variation?  
       • Not applicable. No mention of reward at all.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary:  
A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?  
   • The paper does not explicitly use “group efficiency” (understood as total payoff relative to the maximum possible). It does, however, compare payoffs in a “defecting” vs. “cooperating” equilibrium, sometimes describing the cooperative equilibrium as yielding higher payoff for both roles. In practice, the paper’s main focus is on (1) the fraction of producers that cooperate, (2) the fraction of enforcers that punish or do not punish, and (3) which equilibria—cooperative or defecting—are stochastically stable.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned explicitly or implicitly:  
       2 (they use an indefinitely repeated game, parameterized by continuation probability δ),  
       4 (the game is an all‐or‐nothing “cooperate or defect” choice),  
       6 (benefit b and cost c, analogous to changing returns in a public goods setup),  
       7 (punishment cost v),  
       8 (punishment magnitude p).  
   • All others (1, 3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15) are not systematically discussed.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The paper never frames its analysis as “the punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Rather, it shows how certain parameters (continuation probability δ, punishment cost v, punishment magnitude p, cost/benefit c and b, and conflict‐loss parameter l, which is distinct from the above 15) affect whether a punishing equilibrium with cooperation emerges. The paper provides no numeric “effect size” regarding efficiency. It does, however, show direction‐of‐effect on fractions of cooperators and punishing enforcers.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not speak of efficiency directly. It indicates only that cheap‐enough punishment costs (v), severe‐enough punishment (p), and a sufficiently large continuation probability (δ) favor cooperative states—implying higher payoffs than universal defection. No direct mention is made of systematic changes in the number of players, communication, known horizon, rewards, or knowledge about punisher identity. Consequently, there is little basis within the paper to predict how those unmentioned parameters would affect any “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” The most that can be inferred is that setting punishment to be sufficiently severe (p) and not too costly (v), together with a high probability of repeated interaction (δ), promotes a cooperative outcome, which in turn leads to higher overall payoffs than the defecting outcome. Beyond that, the paper does not analyze parameter interactions in terms of “efficiency.”

Authors: Muñoz-Herrera, M; Nikiforakis, N
Author Full Names: Munoz-Herrera, Manuel; Nikiforakis, Nikos
Article Title: Experimental evidence shows that ulterior motive attribution drives counter-punishment
Source Title: JOURNAL OF THE ECONOMIC SCIENCE ASSOCIATION-JESA
Author Keywords: Social norms; Counter-punishment; Altruistic punishment; Cooperation
Keywords Plus: 3RD-PARTY PUNISHMENT; NORM ENFORCEMENT; COOPERATION
Abstract: Evidence shows that the willingness of individuals to avenge punishment inflicted upon them for transgressions they committed constitutes a significant obstacle toward upholding social norms and cooperation. The drivers of this behavior, however, are not well understood. We hypothesize that ulterior motive attribution-the tendency to assign ulterior motives to punishers for their actions-increases the likelihood of counter-punishment. We exogenously manipulate the ability to attribute ulterior motives to punishers by having the punisher be either an unaffected third party or a second party who, as the victim of a transgression, may be driven to punish by a desire to take revenge. We show that survey respondents consider second-party punishment to be substantially more likely to be driven by ulterior motives than an identical, payoff-equalizing punishment meted out by a third party. In line with our hypothesis, we find that second-party punishment is 66.3% more likely to trigger counter-punishment than third-party punishment in a lab experiment. The loss in earnings due to counter-punishment is 64.6% higher for second-party punishers than third-party punishers, all else equal.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter accounting of what this paper says—if anything—about each of the 15 listed features of a typical public‐goods‐with‐punishment design, strictly according to the content of Jiang and Villeval’s paper “Dishonesty as a collective‐risk social dilemma.” The collective “punishment” in their study takes the form of an endogenous “collective sanction” (canceling the entire group’s payoff in a period with 60% probability) whenever a group’s total claims exceed a threshold. Where the paper does not discuss a parameter, or does not systematically vary it, that is stated explicitly below.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Discussed: Yes. The paper systematically varies small groups (3 players) versus large groups (6 players).  
   • Values used: 3 or 6 players per group.  
   • Effect of systematically varying on “punishment” (their collective sanction):  
       – Groups of 6 consistently had higher overall claims (e.g., Table 1 shows average 4.23 or 4.16 in large groups vs. 4.03 or 3.93 in small groups), reached the sanction threshold more often (about 71–73% of the time vs. 47–48% in small groups; see Table 2), and suffered more frequent actual collective sanctions.  
       – Consequently, large groups tended to end up with lower payoffs than if all had reported honestly.  
       – Numerically, for example, Table 2 shows that in small groups (SG‐INDI, SG‐COLL), the threshold was hit roughly 48% of the time on average, whereas in large groups (LG‐INDI, LG‐COLL), it was 70–73%.   

2. Number of rounds
   • Discussed: Yes. They ran 20 periods in both the “lying” and “no‐lying” versions of the game.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not alter the total number of rounds, so there is no discussion of how changing the round count would affect efficiency or sanctions.  

3. Is chat (communication) enabled between players?
   • Mentioned: They explicitly disallow communication (i.e., no chat).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not study enabling vs. disabling chat, nor any effect of communication on the collective sanction.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Not mentioned. In the experiment, participants report a number from 1 to 6 for each die roll (or directly choose 1–6 in the no‐lying version). There is no “all‐or‐nothing” format, and no variation of that format is discussed.  

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Not mentioned. Participants simply enter each claim (1–6); there is no default‐contribution rule that is manipulated.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Not discussed. Participants earn a linear payoff of 5 tokens per claimed point, minus a complete loss if the group triggers the collective sanction. The paper does not mention or vary a separate MPCR or group multiplier.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Not discussed. There is no individual‐level punishment‐choice mechanism and no cost borne personally by a “punisher.” The “punishment” in this study is a collective sanction caused endogenously by the sum of the group’s claims exceeding a threshold.  

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted per unit imposed)
   • Not discussed in the sense of per‐unit “punisher imposes X.” The collective sanction (if triggered) cancels everyone’s earnings for that period entirely. This severity was fixed; no systematic variation was studied.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Not mentioned. The design does not include any reward mechanism.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Not mentioned; no reward mechanism is present.  

11. Reward magnitude  
    • Not mentioned; no reward mechanism is present.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
    • Discussed: They do state the game lasts 20 periods, and participants are aware of that.  
    • Systematically varied? No. They do not vary whether the horizon is known or unknown.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown?
    • Discussed in the negative: players do not see individual claims or payoffs of peers. They only learn whether the group got sanctioned.  
    • Systematically varied? No. They do not study revealing vs. hiding peer outcomes.  

14. When a player is punished, does that player know who punished them?
    • Not applicable. No peer‐to‐peer punishment is imposed; the “punishment” is a blind, groupwide outcome.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who rewarded them?
    • Not applicable; there are no rewards in this design.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how do they differ?  
   • The authors do examine overall payoffs (and often compare them to the payoff that would arise under fully honest reporting). They also discuss payoff losses from collective sanctions as a “loss in efficiency.”  
   • However, they mainly report: (1) individuals’ average claims; (2) how often the group crosses the threshold (thereby risking “punishment”); (3) the actual frequency of sanction; and (4) individuals’ net payoffs. They label this overall outcome a “Tragedy of Dishonesty” when claims repeatedly trigger the group sanction.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned explicitly:  
       1) Number of players (systematically varied: 3 vs. 6).  
       2) Number of rounds (fixed at 20, not varied).  
       3) Lack of chat/communication (they do not vary it, but they mention that chat is disallowed).  
       12) The known horizon (20 periods).  
       13) Peer outcomes not displayed (they do mention that players only see group‐level sanction info).  
   • None of the remaining parameters (4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15) is varied; most are not applicable or are simply not discussed.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the “punishment treatment effect” for each dependent variable when the parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Only one parameter (#1, group size) is systematically varied. The paper shows that larger groups (6 members) report higher claims on average, reach the threshold more often, and suffer the “punishment” (collective sanction) more frequently. In that sense, it reduces group payoffs (i.e., lowers efficiency compared to smaller groups).  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency, solely based on this paper’s content, what would they be?  
   • The paper makes clear predictions only for parameter #1 (number of players): larger groups have worse outcomes (more sanctions, lower payoffs). For the other 14 parameters, the paper either does not mention them at all or does not systematically vary them, so no direct or quantitative prediction is provided.

Authors: Odouard, VV; Smirnova, D; Edelman, S
Author Full Names: Odouard, Victor Vikram; Smirnova, Diana; Edelman, Shimon
Article Title: Polarize, catalyze, and stabilize: how a minority of norm internalizers amplify group selection and punishment
Author Keywords: Norm internalization; Evolution; Group selection; Cooperation; Public goods game; Conformist transmission
Keywords Plus: CONFORMIST TRANSMISSION; CULTURAL TRANSMISSION; EVOLUTIONARY GAMES; SOCIAL-BEHAVIOR; COOPERATION; COEVOLUTION; RECIPROCITY; DEFECTORS; ENFORCEMENT; EMERGENCE
Abstract: Many mechanisms behind the evolution of cooperation, such as reciprocity, indirect reciprocity, and altruistic punishment, require group knowledge of individual actions. But what keeps people cooperating when no one is looking? Conformist norm internalization, the tendency to abide by the behavior of the majority of the group, even when it is individually harmful, could be the answer. In this paper, we analyze a world where (1) there is group selection and punishment by indirect reciprocity, but (2) many actions (half) go unobserved and therefore unpunished. Can norm internalization fill this observation gap and lead to high levels of cooperation, even when agents may in principle cooperate only when likely to be caught and punished? Specifically, we seek to understand whether adding norm internalization to the strategy space in a public goods game can lead to higher levels of cooperation when both norm internalization and cooperation start out rare. We found the answer to be positive, but, interestingly, not because norm internalizers end up making up a substantial fraction of the population, nor because they cooperate much more than other agent types. Instead, norm internalizers, by polarizing, catalyzing, and stabilizing cooperation, can increase levels of cooperation of other agent types, while only making up a minority of the population themselves.

Abstract: Institutions may rely on fundamental principles, e.g., of legal philosophy, but may also have evolved according to institutional fitness, as gauged by a society's well-being. In our stylized framework where two fundamental principles, equality and efficiency, conflict with each other, one of the three players is the third party who faces two symmetric co-players as culprits and determines whether to sanction the two culprits discriminatorily or treat them with parity. Authors: Goodman, JR

Article Title: The problem of opportunity
Author Keywords: Cooperation; Prisoner's dilemma; Cultural group selection; Free rider problem; Mimicry
Keywords Plus: TAG-BASED COOPERATION; STRONG RECIPROCITY; BIOLOGICAL MARKETS; PARTNER CHOICE; GAME-THEORY; EVOLUTION; STRATEGIES; SELECTION; COMPETITION; REPUTATION
Abstract: Cultural group selection theorists propose that humans evolved prosocial preferences. These claims revolve largely around the centrality of punishment in cultural groups, which helped to eliminate free riders. The purpose of this paper is to explore whether distinguishing between free-riding as an action, and free riders as entities, undermines or supports this view. I develop three individual-based models of the Prisoner's Dilemma. The first model shows that strong reciprocity removes overt freeriders from a population, and maintains a high rate of cooperation. In the second, I introduce individuals that mimic cooperative preferences, but who defect when they trick opponents into cooperating. I show that strong reciprocity is robust against this strategy, but not because individuals are replaced by strong reciprocators. Finally, I introduce a third strategy, covert mimicry, where some mimics may defect without detection. I draw attention to the problem highlighted in these models, which is that cooperation may be maintained in populations only because freeriders are not presented with the opportunity to defect. I discuss this problem in the context of cultural group selection and the human capacity for innovation, and suggest that hypotheses relying on prosocial preferences for maintaining cooperation require some revision.

Author Full Names: Duell, Dominik; Mengel, Friederike; Mohlin, Erik; Weidenholzer, Simon
Article Title: Cooperation through collective punishment and participation
Author Keywords: collective action; collective sanctions; imperfect; participation; public goods game
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS GAMES; EFFICIENT COORDINATION; LEGITIMATE AUTHORITY; SANCTIONS; ENFORCEMENT; INCENTIVES; INSTITUTIONS; EVOLUTION; COMMUNITY; DEMOCRACY
Abstract: We experimentally explore the role of institutions imposing collective sanctions in sustaining cooperation. In our experiment, players only observe noisy signals about individual contributions in finitely repeated public goods game with imperfect monitoring, while total output is perfectly observed as it is often the case in collective action problems in society. We consider sanctioning mechanism that allows agents to commit to collective punishment in case the level of cooperation among members of society falls short of a target. We find that cooperation is higher with collective punishment compared to both no punishment or punishment targeting individuals. Importantly, our results indicate that it is the combination of making a commitment to be punished and the collective nature of punishment which induces cooperation. Our findings show that punishing a group collectively for misbehavior of some of its members induces cooperation when individuals participate in setting up the sanctioning institution. The study contributes to the literature on institutional legitimacy and how to ensure good government performance when dealing with collective action problems, and, by considering commitment, improves enforcement methods criticized for their detrimental effects on some societal groups.

Keywords Plus: 3RD-PARTY PUNISHMENT; DICTATOR GAME; COOPERATION; ALTRUISM
Abstract: Although in everyday life decisions about losses are prevalent (e.g., the climate crisis and the COVID-19 crisis), there is hardly any research on decisions in the loss domain. Therefore, we conducted online experiments with a sample of 672 participants (mostly students), using third-party punishment dictator games (DGs) in the loss domain to explore the impact of losses and punishment threats on the conformity to the fairness norm. Subjects in the treatment condition have to divide a loss of -10 euro with the threat of a third-party punishment with different strengths (control: gains, no punishment). Overall, the statistical evidence seems rather weak, but when it comes to losses, subjects are more rational and straightforward with their words and deeds than with gains. Therefore, in the loss domain, subjects are more likely to believe that the fairness norm should be followed, and they subjectively perceive that the others do as well. Furthermore, although dictators' decisions are more selfish in the loss domain, dictators there react more strongly to the punishment threat by reducing their demands than in the gains domain. This holds as long as the punishment threat is strong enough, as judged from a rational perspective.

Article Title: Evolution of confrontation and cooperation in simple organisms as a function of environmental resources and cost of a conflict
Author Keywords: confrontation and cooperation; evolutionary algorithm; evolutionary game theory; Monte Carlo

Abstract: The root cause of human conflict needs to be understood but it is currently unknown whether the decision to engage in conflict is an inherited or acquired trait. This article reports two experimental simulations which demonstrate that the level of confrontation in a population of simple organisms can be explained by the evolution of a simulated gene pool. Game theory and evolutionary algorithms were combined in a novel way to examine how six variables influenced the decision to confront in the competition for resources. The main variable was how the genetically determined rate of confrontation evolved as a function of environmental resources and cost of a conflict. The additional modulatory effects of four other variables were also considered in the first round of simulations. Two variables were responsive to the difference between resources and cost. Two other variables were responsive to the organism's health status. Taking a systematic approach, we examined how a population of 1000 organisms were evolving in environments with different levels of reward and punishment. During each cycle, each organism was paired with another organism and thus needed to decide whether to confront or cooperate. We used a genetic algorithm to simulate the evolution of the gene pool over 500 cycles. The first series of simulations demonstrated that the baseline rate of confrontation was very responsive to environmental conditions. Our results also indicate that the decision to confront or cooperate depended not only upon the immediate competitive conditions, in which the organisms evolved, but were also responsive to their own health status. The second series of simulations used zero-sum games to explore how risk levels varied as a function of the potential cost of engaging in a confrontation. In the second round of simulations, a simple form of memory was implemented. The results indicated that memory had a limited, but significant effect, while the cost of a conflict was highly predictive of the level of risk taken by the organisms. Our two series of simulations show that AI could contribute to answering psychological and societal questions. Our unique combination of techniques has brought to light several new insights into the mechanisms that drive the population towards cooperation and confrontation. The degree of generalizability of our results and future avenues for deepening our understanding of these evolutionary dynamics are discussed.

Abstract: While people are surprisingly cooperative in social dilemmas, cooperation is fragile to the emergence of defection. Abstract: Formal enforcement punishing defectors can sustain cooperation by changing incentives. In this paper, we introduce a second effect of enforcement: it can also affect the capacity to learn about the group's cooperativeness. Indeed, in contexts with strong enforcement, it is difficult to tell apart those who cooperate because of the threat of fines from those who are intrinsically cooperative types. Whenever a group is intrinsically cooperative, enforcement will thus have a negative dynamic effect on cooperation because it slows down learning about prevalent values in the group that would occur under a weaker enforcement. We provide theoretical and experimental evidence in support of this mechanism. Using a lab experiment with independent interactions and random rematching, we observe that, in early interactions, having faced an environment with fines in the past decreases current cooperation. We further show that this results from the interaction between enforcement and learning: the effect of having met cooperative partners has a stronger effect on current cooperation when this happened in an environment with no enforcement. Replacing one signal of deviation without fine by a signal of cooperation without fine in a player's history increases current cooperation by 10%; while replacing it by a signal of cooperation with fine increases current cooperation by only 5%.

Abstract: We investigate how well firms can collude with partial communication in relation to full communication. We find that firms vary their communication strategies with network structures. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter accounting of how (and whether) the paper by Flannery and Wang (“Is the ‘smoke‐filled room’ necessary? …”) discusses or predicts anything about each of the 15 public‐goods‐game parameters in relation to “the punishment treatment effect” on efficiency. As you will see, the paper is about a two‐period Bertrand game with different communication networks, not a public goods game with a formal punishment mechanism. Consequently, most of the 15 parameters are not mentioned at all; where a parameter is mentioned (e.g., “number of players,” “is chat enabled?”), it is neither framed nor varied with respect to a punishment treatment or punishment costs/magnitudes. Below, “mentioned” means that some aspect of the parameter arises in the design (even if it is not systematically varied or related to punishment), and “not mentioned” means it does not appear at all in the paper.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned? Yes. The entire experiment is conducted with three players in each group (p. 4–5, 14–15).  
   • Effect of systematically varying it on the punishment treatment effect? Not mentioned. The paper does not vary the number of players, nor does it investigate how changing the number of players might affect any “punishment treatment” or efficiency measure.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned? Yes. They use a “two‐period” repeated game and run 16 rounds in total (p. 4, 14).  
   • Effect of systematically varying it on the punishment treatment effect? Not mentioned. They do not systematically vary the number of rounds (all sessions involve 16 rounds), nor do they address any impact on a formal “punishment treatment” or on efficiency.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned? Yes. Enabling vs. disallowing communication is the core of their four treatments: no communication (N0), one communication link (N1), two links with a leader (N2), and full communication (N3) (p. 5–6, 14–15).  
   • Effect of systematically varying it on the punishment treatment effect? Not mentioned in a public‐goods sense. They do examine how having no communication vs. partial vs. full communication affects collusion and total payoffs. However, they do not frame these comparisons as a “punishment treatment effect”; rather, they study how different communication networks influence cooperation and payoffs in a Bertrand‐type game.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not study a contribution game; it is a two‐price (Bertrand) game, so “all or nothing” contribution choices do not arise.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Mentioned? No. Again, the design does not involve a public goods contribution scheme, so there is no discussion of defaults for contributions.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Mentioned? No. The paper is about a Bertrand game with payoffs determined by setting prices, not a public goods game with MPCR. They do mention a discount rate of 2/3 for linking payoffs across two periods, but there is no systematic variation of a “multiplier” akin to an MPCR.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned? No. Although the term “punishment” sometimes appears when discussing “promise and threat” strategies (in the sense of switching to a lower‐payoff equilibrium in the second period if anyone deviates in the first), there is no explicit cost to impose punishment, no tokens or fees paid, and no parameter systematically varied for imposing punishment.

8. Punishment magnitude
   • Mentioned? No. Their “punishment” is simply choosing a lower payoff equilibrium in the second period after a first‐period deviation. There is no separate numeric “punishment magnitude” or dedicated mechanism for imposing punishments.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned? No. The study does not include any formal rewarding scheme. While they do speak of “pure promises” and “promise and threat,” they do not allow for an explicit reward mechanism akin to awarding tokens or cost‐based rewarding.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Mentioned? No. No reward mechanism is present in the design.

11. Reward magnitude
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not involve any separate “reward” parameter.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
   • Mentioned? Yes. Participants know there are exactly 16 rounds, and each round has two periods (pp. 14–15).  
   • Effect of systematically varying it on the punishment treatment effect? Not mentioned. While players do know the exact structure of the experiment, the authors do not vary whether that horizon is known or unknown, nor do they relate it to an explicit punishment treatment.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained or lost each round)?
   • Mentioned? Yes, in part. After each period, players see the price choices (and resulting payoffs) of others (p. 14). They do not systematically vary what is displayed, nor do they discuss efficiency or a punishment treatment in this context.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not implement a formal “punishment” assignment or identity revelation (e.g., no tokens or direct punisher identity). They only speak of mutual knowledge of who deviated in period 1, but that is not an explicit punisher identity revelation.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Mentioned? No. No formal reward mechanism appears in the experiment.

Summary of Findings from the Paper

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper’s main dependent variables are (1) whether or not each player chooses the “cooperative” (collusive) action in Period 1, (2) whether they choose the cooperative action in Period 2, and (3) total/average payoff over the two periods. The authors sometimes refer to higher payoffs or “more collusion” as greater efficiency but do not use “group efficiency” in the sense of “actual payoff divided by maximum possible payoff.”  
   • So their dependent variables are best described as (a) collusion rate in Period 1, (b) collusion rate in Period 2, and (c) total payoff. These differ from “efficiency” in a public‐goods sense.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • The paper explicitly mentions five parameters in some manner (1: three players, 2: two periods repeated for 16 rounds, 3: whether chat is enabled, 12: that the total number of rounds is known, 13: that peer choices and payoffs are shown). None of these, however, are discussed as levers in a punishment‐based public goods framework.  
   • The remaining parameters (4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15) do not appear at all.

C. For which and how many parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • None. Although “communication enabled” (parameter 3) is systematically varied, the study does not frame it in terms of a “punishment treatment” nor measure the change in “punishment treatment effect.” Their “no‐communication” vs. “partial” vs. “full” designs investigate how communication networks affect collusion and payoffs, not a dedicated punishment intervention.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not address formal punishment costs or magnitudes, nor do they consider standard “public goods efficiency.” They use a collusive Bertrand framework. Because of that, there is essentially no discussion of how systematically varying any of the 15 parameters might alter a punishment‐based treatment’s effect on efficiency. From this paper alone, one cannot make specific predictions about how those 15 parameters or their interactions would affect a “punishment treatment effect” for a public goods game.

In short, the paper studies the role of communication networks in a two‐period Bertrand game and reports how communication facilitates collusion or “cooperation” and thereby leads to higher average payoffs. It does not examine the introduction of a separate punishment mechanism, nor does it measure any “punishment treatment” effect on efficiency. Most of the 15 parameters relevant to a public goods and punishment framework simply do not appear.

Authors: Botta, R; Blanco, G; Schaerer, CE

Article Title: Discipline and punishment in panoptical public goods games
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; REPLICATOR DYNAMICS; EVOLUTIONARY GAMES; POOL PUNISHMENT; FREE RIDERS; COOPERATION; RETALIATION; INCENTIVES; PROVISION; OVERCOME
Abstract: In Public Goods Games (PGG), the temptation to free-ride on others' contributions poses a significant threat to the sustainability of cooperative societies. Therefore, societies strive to mitigate this through incentive systems, employing rewards and punishments to foster cooperative behavior. Thus, peer punishment, in which cooperators sanction defectors, as well as pool punishment, where a centralized punishment institution executes the punishment, is deeply analyzed in previous works. Although the literature indicates that these methods may enhance cooperation on social dilemmas under particular contexts, there are still open questions, for instance, the structural connection between graduated punishment and the monitoring of public goods games. Our investigation proposes a compulsory PGG framework under Panoptical surveillance. Inspired by Foucault's theories on disciplinary mechanisms and biopower, we present a novel mathematical model that scrutinizes the balance between the severity and scope of punishment to catalyze cooperative behavior. By integrating perspectives from evolutionary game theory and Foucault's theories of power and discipline, this research uncovers the theoretical foundations of mathematical frameworks involved in punishment and discipline structures. We show that well-calibrated punishment and discipline schemes, leveraging the panoptical effect for universal oversight, can effectively mitigate the free-rider dilemma, fostering enhanced cooperation. This interdisciplinary approach not only elucidates the dynamics of cooperation in societal constructs but also underscores the importance of integrating diverse methodologies to address the complexities of fostering cooperative evolution.

Abstract: This study explores the influence of migration costs and rewarding schemes on cooperation through the implementation of computational behavioral models in spatial public goods games. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter account of what this paper says (and does not say), strictly following only the information in the text, figures, and tables. Any mentions of “punishment” or “rewards” in this paper refer to the authors’ migration‐cost or discount‐factor mechanisms, and not to peer‐to‐peer punishing/rewarding in the usual sense. The paper’s main focus is on how migration costs and a “rewarding scheme” (implemented via a per‐round discount factor) affect average contribution (cooperation). No other parameters or systematic variations are explored in relation to efficiency.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players
   • Discussed? Only to the extent that each group starts with either 5 or 10 agents. The paper does not systematically vary the total number of players (or the group size k) to test how it would affect any “punishment treatment” or efficiency.  
   • Predictions upon varying? Not provided in the paper.  

2. Number of rounds
   • Discussed? The paper runs simulations typically over 800 rounds, and sometimes 2000 rounds (in Fig. 5). However, it does not systematically vary the number of rounds to analyze any changes in the punishment treatment effect.  
   • Predictions upon varying? No predictions are made about varying the number of rounds or how it might alter punishment or efficiency.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not mention any form of communication or chat between agents.  
   • Predictions upon varying? None stated.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned? No. In fact, the paper explicitly allows fractional contributions in increments of 0.25 up to a maximum of 1. This is not an “all or nothing” design.  
   • Predictions upon varying? None stated.  

5. Is the contribution default (where players decide how much to move back to their hand)?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper gives agents an endowment of 1 token each round and a discrete contribution choice, but does not discuss any “default” contribution mechanism.  
   • Predictions upon varying? None stated.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
   • Discussed? Yes. The paper’s “enhancement factor” r (r ≥ 1) plays exactly this role. They systematically vary r between 1 and 3.  
   • Predictions upon varying? The paper discusses how varying r (from 1 to 3) affects average contribution (and the fraction of “full contributors”), especially under different migration probabilities and with/without additional mechanisms like migration cost or the “rewarding scheme.” Numerically, the paper reports (e.g., Figs. 2, 3) thresholds around r ≈ 2 for cooperation to emerge. However, these discussions concern average contribution, not efficiency, and the paper does not provide a specific numeric “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency for different r values.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussed? Partly. The paper’s “punishment” is implemented as a migration cost cₘ = 0.2 whenever an unsatisfied agent switches groups. This is a single fixed cost and is not varied across multiple values. The only variation is whether that cost is “off” (baseline) or “on” (migration‐cost scenario).  
   • Predictions upon varying? The paper compares baseline versus the presence of a migration cost. It shows that imposing cₘ = 0.2 can foster cooperation even for relatively low enhancement factors. There is no separate numeric effect size provided for efficiency; instead, results focus on average contribution.  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player per punishment unit)
   • Mentioned? Not in the usual sense. The authors treat “punishment” purely as having to pay the cost cₘ = 0.2 to migrate. They do not describe any distinct “punishment magnitude” deducted from the target’s payoff (other than that single migration cost). No systematic variation is reported.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussed? Yes. They analyze two scenarios: “rewarding scheme on” versus “rewarding scheme off.” “Reward on” means that each agent’s payoff is multiplied by an individual discount factor δᵢ, which starts at 0.6 and automatically increases by 0.1 each round until reaching 1.0, provided the agent does not migrate.  
   • Predictions upon varying? The paper focuses on whether (yes/no) this discount‐factor reward mechanism is present. No numerical effect size is given for efficiency; rather, they show that the reward‐only condition can sometimes backfire, producing more free‐riders in spatial settings (Figs. 3(b), 5).  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Mentioned? No. The “rewarding scheme” does not entail a cost an agent pays to reward peers. Instead, it is an institutional mechanism that boosts each agent’s payoff if they stay put. There is no mention of systematically varying a “reward cost.”  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player per reward)
   • Mentioned? Indirectly, in the form of the discount factor δᵢ rising from 0.6 up to 1.0 each round an agent does not migrate. This is not separately varied or tested at multiple levels; it is a fixed mechanism. No quantitative effect size is discussed in terms of efficiency.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not address whether agents know the game length. The simulations are simply run for a specified number of rounds.  
   • Predictions upon varying? None stated.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown?
   • Mentioned? The opposite is stated: the paper uses a “blind model,” meaning agents do not see neighbors’ payoffs or contributions. This is not systematically varied.  
   • Predictions upon varying? None stated.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
   • Mentioned? No. Punishment is via migration cost imposed institutionally. There is no mention of identifying who caused the “punishment.”  
   • Predictions upon varying? None stated.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
   • Mentioned? No. The discount factor is likewise an institutional, automatic mechanism. No mention of personal identification of a rewarder.  
   • Predictions upon varying? None stated.  

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY

A: Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different from one another?  
   • The paper does not use “group efficiency” or payoff‐based efficiency measures. Its main dependent variables are (1) average contribution (cooperation level) of agents, and (2) the normalized number of migrations. The paper also refers to whether contributions converge to “full” (i.e., 1) but does not present efficiency = (actual payoff)/(maximum possible payoff).

B: Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • (1) Number of players: mentioned but not systematically varied for a punishment effect.  
   • (2) Number of rounds: mentioned (800, 2000) but not systematically varied for punishment effects.  
   • (6) MPCR/enhancement factor r: systematically varied (1 to 3).  
   • (7) Punishment cost (migration cost cₘ = 0.2): either off (baseline) or on (migration‐cost scenario).  
   • (9) Whether a reward is enabled (i.e., discount‐factor scheme): either off or on.  
   • (11) Reward “magnitude”: indirectly mentioned (δᵢ from 0.6 to 1.0) but not varied quantitatively.  

   Thus, the paper mentions six of the parameters (1, 2, 6, 7, 9, 11), though not all are tested in the sense of systematically varying them for punishment/efficiency effects.

C: For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • The paper systematically varies only three relevant features in ways that compare “punishment” (migration cost) versus no punishment:  
       – (6) Enhancement factor r (varied from 1 to 3).  
       – (7) Migration cost on/off.  
       – (9) Reward scheme on/off.  
   • Even for those, the paper discusses effects on average contribution and migration rates, not on efficiency.

D: If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not analyze efficiency in the sense of total payoffs relative to the maximum possible. Consequently, it provides no direct basis for making numeric predictions about how systematically varying any of the 15 parameters would affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency. Its findings only speak to how migration‐cost “punishment” and discount‐factor “rewarding” affect cooperation (average contribution), not efficiency. Therefore, one cannot reliably predict efficiency consequences from this paper’s data.

Authors: Nielsen, YA; Pfattheicher, S
Author Full Names: Nielsen, Yngwie Asbjorn; Pfattheicher, Stefan
Article Title: Separating individual and group-level cooperation in the Public Goods Game
Author Keywords: cooperation; intraclass correlation (ICC); Public Goods Game (PGG); variance partitioning
Keywords Plus: COMPETITION; PUNISHMENT
Abstract: Cooperation in the Public Goods Game (PGG) is determined by a mixture of individual differences (e.g. personality, social preferences) and group dynamics (e.g. reciprocation, social norms). However, to our knowledge, no thorough attempt has been made to separate individual and group levels of cooperation and to quantify the variance in cooperation that can be attributed to the group level. In an analysis of 10 open datasets (total N = 4,556, 1,003 groups, 7-50 rounds), we chart the trajectory of individual and group-level variance across rounds of repeated PGGs. We find that the portion of group-level variance increases initially and plateaus around the fifth round, typically at a level between 20 and 50%. In addition, we identify four factors that increase the portion of group-level variance: (i) punishment opportunities; (ii) detailed feedback including all group members' decisions; (iii) small groups (<= 4 players); and (iv) groups with homogenous social preferences.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1) Number of players  
   • Does the paper discuss it?

     – No.

     – No.

   • Does the paper discuss it?

   • Does it make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – They fix b = 5 and c = 1 in all examples and do not show how systematically changing these would affect punishment.  

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – The paper implements “pool punishment” with a population‐wide cost d (the “cost to maintain the punishment institution”). It is not modeled as a cost imposed per single unit of punishment but rather as a flat amount all cooperators must pay.  
   • Does it make predictions about systematically varying it?

       – If s is high enough (e.g., s = 5.6) and δ = 0.2, punishment deters defectors under both EUT (Figure 1a) and PT (Figure 2a).  
       – For intermediate s (e.g., s = 5.1), EUT predicts defection prevails, but under PT, cooperative strategies (AC or pay‐it‐forward S) can thrive (Figures 1b vs. 2b).

    • Does the paper discuss it?  
      – No, and the model does not feature any rewards.  
    • Does it make predictions about systematically varying it?  
      – No.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper does not use the term “efficiency” in the sense of “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff.” Instead, it focuses on:  
     – The proportion of each strategy in the population (AC, AD, S).  
     – The cooperation rate p (i.e., the probability of being helped).  
     – Expected payoff of each strategy.  
   • While “expected payoff” is sometimes discussed, the paper never refers explicitly to “efficiency” the way it is typically used in public goods experiments.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned explicitly:  
     – #7, if interpreted as “d” (the cost to maintain punishment), though not called “the cost to impose a single unit of punishment.”

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Only one parameter—punishment magnitude (s)—is plainly and systematically varied.  
   • The paper shows that raising s above certain thresholds can eliminate defection under either EUT or PT, although PT requires a lower threshold of s for cooperation to prevail.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • Because the paper does not analyze group efficiency at all—nor does it discuss most of these parameters—there is effectively no direct guidance for how 14 of the 15 parameters (1–6, 9–15) would shape efficiency outcomes under punishment.

Abstract: Cooperation is essential for the survival of human society. Understanding the nature of cooperation and its underlying mechanisms is crucial for studying human behavior.
