PARAMETER‐BY‐PARAMETER REVIEW
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1) Number of players  
   • Discussed? Yes. The paper uses groups of 4 players (p. 6 “In each team, all 4 participants completed the entire experiment…”).  
   • Systematically varied? No. All groups always have 4 players.  
   • Any prediction/effect on punishment treatment? No. There is no discussion of varying the group size and how that would affect punishment.  

2) Number of rounds  
   • Discussed? Yes. The experiment always involves 32 rounds (p. 6 “The experiment involved 32 rounds…”).  
   • Systematically varied? No. All sessions were fixed at 32 rounds.  
   • Any prediction/effect on punishment treatment? No. The paper does not analyze how changing the number of rounds affects the punishment treatment.  

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussed? No. No mention of any chat or communication option in the experiment.  
   • Systematically varied? No, not mentioned at all.  
   • Any prediction/effect on punishment treatment? None.  

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Discussed? Indirectly. Participants may contribute any amount from 0 to 20 tokens, so it is not an all‐or‐nothing format.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper never changes the contribution rule; it remains “any integer” from 0 to 20 tokens.  
   • Any prediction/effect on punishment treatment? None.  

5) Is the contribution default (do players decide how much to move back into their hand)?  
   • Discussed? No. There is no mention that participants face any “default” option or must choose “keep vs. move.”  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Any prediction/effect on punishment treatment? None.  

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
   • Discussed? Yes. The tokens contributed to the public fund are multiplied by 1.6 (p. 6 “The donated tokens in the public account would be multiplied by 1.6…”).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper uses a fixed factor of 1.6 throughout.  
   • Any prediction/effect on punishment treatment? No. There is no examination of what would happen if MPCR changed.  

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussed? Yes. In the Random Leader Punishment (RLP) condition, punishing another player costs the leader 1 token. For each token spent, the punished player loses 3 tokens (p. 7 “The cost‐benefit ratio for … punishment was 1:3”).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The cost ratio is always 1.  
   • Any prediction/effect on punishment treatment? The paper does not analyze what would happen if the cost changed; it uses the same 1:3 ratio throughout.  

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Discussed? Yes. Each token spent on punishment deducts 3 tokens from the target (p. 7).  
   • Systematically varied? No. It is always 3.  
   • Any prediction/effect on punishment treatment? The authors do not explore different punishment magnitudes; it is fixed at 3.  

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Discussed? Yes. The Random Leader Reward (RLR) group has reward power, the Random Leader Punishment (RLP) group has punishment power, and the standard RL group has no such power. Thus, “reward enabled” vs. “reward not enabled” is indeed one of the paper’s tested conditions (p. 6–7).  
   • Systematically varied? They compare a no‐reward condition (RL) to a yes‐reward condition (RLR).  
   • Any prediction/effect on punishment treatment (i.e., how having the option of reward vs. no reward might shape punishment’s effect)? The paper presents data showing that punishment’s effect (RLP) on average contributions is higher than reward’s effect (RLR) in sustaining cooperation. Specifically, Table 2 shows that the average contribution in RLP is 14.36 compared to 7.61 in RL (no reward, no punishment) and 12.81 in RLR. However, they do not describe a further “reward × punishment” interaction or how systematically varying reward alone would alter “punishment treatment” per se.  

     Numerical effect sizes that can be inferred (p. 9–10, Table 2 and Figures 2–4):  
     • Mean contribution in RL: 7.61; in RLP: 14.36; in RLR: 12.81.   
       → Punishment group’s average contribution is higher by 6.75 tokens compared to RL.   
       → Reward group’s average contribution is higher by 5.20 tokens compared to RL.  
     • Mean payoff in RL: 24.56; in RLP: 26.34; in RLR: 26.94 (second‐stage numbers in Table 2).  
       → Punishment group’s payoff is up by ≈1.78 compared to RL; reward group’s payoff is up by ≈2.38 compared to RL in that table’s snapshot (though note that after actual punishment or reward usage, the leader’s payoff changes).  

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
    • Discussed? Yes. Analogous to punishment, in RLR conditions, each token the leader spends grants the target an additional 3 tokens (p. 7).  
    • Systematically varied? No. The ratio is fixed at 1:3.  
    • Any prediction/effect on punishment treatment? They do not analyze whether changing the cost of reward would alter punishment’s effectiveness.  

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
    • Discussed? Yes, it is always +3 tokens per 1 token spent by the leader (p. 7).  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Any prediction/effect on punishment treatment? None. The paper only compares an enforced reward vs. punishment setting; it does not change the magnitude of either.  

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
    • Discussed? Yes. Participants know the experiment runs for 32 rounds (p. 6).  
    • Systematically varied? No, it is the same in all sessions.  
    • Any prediction/effect on punishment treatment? None.  

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained or lost each round)?  
    • Discussed? Partially. At the end of each round, players see (i) how many tokens they themselves contributed, (ii) the sum of tokens contributed by the entire group, and (iii) their personal payoff. Leaders additionally see each follower’s individual contribution (p. 7–8).  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Any prediction/effect on punishment treatment? No. The paper does not discuss changing the display of outcomes.  

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Discussed? Implicitly yes, because there is only one possible punisher (the leader). However, the paper does not vary whether this is revealed or hidden.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Any prediction/effect on punishment treatment? No.  

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Discussed? Same as (14)—they presumably know it is their group’s leader (only one person can give the reward). No variant condition is tested.  
    • Systematically varied? No.  
    • Any prediction/effect on punishment treatment? No.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FINAL SUMMARY (A–D)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
   • The paper does not present a formal “group efficiency” measure of (actual total payoff ÷ maximum possible payoff). Instead, it reports:  
     – Average payoff (sometimes referred to as “payoff” throughout).  
     – Contribution levels (often called “cooperation”).  
   • They also refer in places to “organizational efficiency” in a general sense, but their main dependent variables in the results are (1) average contribution per round and (2) average payoff.  

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned explicitly (in instructions or results, though not varied): #1 (4 players), #2 (32 rounds), #6 (multiplication factor = 1.6), #7 (punishment cost = 1 token), #8 (punishment magnitude = 3 tokens), #9 (reward is or is not enabled), #10 (reward cost = 1 token), #11 (reward magnitude = 3 tokens), #12 (participants knew there would be 32 rounds), #13 (players saw total group contributions and individual leader could see follower contributions), #14 and #15 (leader is the known punisher/rewarder).  
   • Not mentioned at all or not used: #3 (chat), #4 (all‐or‐nothing contributions), #5 (contribution default).  

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable, when systematically varied?  
   • The only parameter that the paper systematically varies relevant to punishment is the presence or absence of a punishment power (this is closest to “Parameter #9—whether a reward is enabled,” though strictly speaking the paper also has a separate treatment for punishment vs. no punishment).  
   • They do provide effect sizes for “punishment vs. no punishment” in terms of average contribution and payoff (see Table 2: average contribution in RL = 7.61 vs. RLP = 14.36; average payoff in RL = 24.56 vs. RLP = 26.34). They do not define these changes as “efficiency,” but note that punishment yields higher cooperation and higher payoff than the no‐punishment baseline (RL).  

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper itself only manipulates whether leaders can punish or reward. It does not provide evidence on how systematically changing the other parameters (e.g., changing the cost/magnitude of punishment, changing group size, introducing chat, etc.) would affect efficiency.  
   • The main inference is that enabling a punishment option increases cooperation and payoff relative to no punishment. Punishment is more effective than reward in sustaining high contributions. However, there is little direct information for how the other parameters, if varied, would influence efficiency or the punishment effect.

Abstract: This paper investigates the impact of cognitive load on the formation and maintenance of cooperation within a public goods game experiment featuring a punishment option. By integrating the experimental designs of prior studies and manipulating cognitive load through the memorization of numbers with varying digits, we reveal that high cognitive load accelerates the breakdown of cooperation, irrespective of the presence of a punishment system. Furthermore, under high cognitive load, participants are more likely to engage in antisocial punishment, while the punishment of free riders remains unaffected. These findings suggest that increased cognitive load depletes the cognitive resources needed for deliberative decision-making, leading to a higher propensity for antisocial punishment. Our study contributes to the literature by demonstrating the significant influence of cognitive load on cooperative behavior and providing new insights into the causes of antisocial punishment.

Abstract: How to maintain the sustainability of common resources is a persistent challenge, as overexploiters often undermine collective efforts by prioritizing personal gain. To mitigate the overexploitation of resources by violators, previous theoretical studies have revealed that the introduction of additional incentives, whether to reward rule-abiding cooperators or to punish those who overexploit, can be beneficial for the sustainability of common resources when the resource growth rate is not particularly low. Furthermore, when the rate of resource growth is moderate, we find that achieving this state cannot simply allocate all incentive budgets to reward. Article Title: Dynamic strategies for collaborative governance of rural environments: a simulation study on the most effective mechanisms
Author Keywords: Reward and punishment mechanism; Rural environmental governance; Evolutionary game; System simulation

Abstract: Rural environmental governance is one of the important tasks in China's rural revitalization strategy. Currently, relying solely on government governance cannot effectively solve the environmental governance needs of nearly 700 thousand administrative villages in China. Building a collaborative governance model of government regulation + villagers' supervision is the key to achieving successful rural environmental governance. Previous literature mainly used the evolutionary game model under the static reward and punishment mechanism (SRPM) to study the strategy evolution dynamics of village enterprises, the government and villagers. However, the simple model setting makes it difficult for the game system to accurately depict complex real-world problems, and it is concluded that the evolutionary stable strategy (ESS) of the game system can only be pure strategy Nash equilibrium (PSNE). In fact, it is difficult to see the stable strategy of either this or that, and most of the strategy combinations with asymptotic stability are mixed strategy Nash equilibrium (MSNE) rather than PSNE, which indicates that the model construction based on the SRPM is problematic. Therefore, this paper expands the SRPM and studies the strategic evolution dynamics of village enterprises, the government and villagers under the dynamic reward and punishment mechanism (DRPM). Theoretical research has shown that MSNE may indeed be the system's ESS under the DRPM, and a mathematical proof was provided. System simulation has shown that under the SRPM, village enterprises, the government, and villagers all exhibited a periodic strategy selection mode, and the strategies of all parties cannot achieve asymptotic stability. However, under the DRPM, the strategies of all parties eventually tend to stabilize over time, and MSNE is the system's ESS. This indicates that there is indeed a situation where MSNE is the system's ESS, and also confirms that the DRPM is indeed a stability improvement compared with the traditional SRPM. Finally, it is suggested that the government should focus on raising the upper limit of punishments for illegal emissions by village enterprises, and should carefully raise the upper limit of rewards for active supervision by villagers.

• Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment measured? No. The paper uses only two discrete fee levels (5 mild, 20 severe) and does not explore intermediate variations or how changing that fee level alone influences efficiency.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
• Mentioned? Yes, but only as two fixed levels in formal punishment: 50 (mild) or 90 (severe) tokens deducted from those who contribute below 100.  
• Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment measured? No. The paper compares “no punishment,” “mild,” or “severe” as three distinct states without offering a systematic manipulation of the penalty level.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
• Mentioned? No. The study’s experiment and simulation do not include any rewarding or bonus mechanism.  
• Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment measured? No.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
• Mentioned? No. Rewarding is not part of the design.  
• Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment measured? No.

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
• Mentioned? No. The paper’s design does not include rewards.  
• Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment measured? No.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
• Mentioned? Yes. In the underlying experiment [20], participants knew there were 24 rounds. In the simulation, the number of periods is also preset (e.g., 300).  
• Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment measured? No.

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much peers gained/lost each round)?  
• Mentioned? Partially. In the experiment’s second game, players see each other’s contributions in random order after each round. In the “Sorted-Info” condition, they additionally see the others’ earlier sorting‐game contributions.  
• Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment measured? The paper does compare “Sorted” vs. “Sorted-Info,” but does not systematically study the effect of displaying or hiding peer outcomes on punishment‐treatment efficiency. No numeric effect sizes isolating “information display” from other factors are given.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• Mentioned? No. The experiment uses a formal scheme (not peer‐to‐peer). Knowing the punisher’s identity is not part of the design.  
• Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment measured? No.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
• Mentioned? No. There is no reward mechanism, so this does not arise.  
• Systematically varied or effect on punishment treatment measured? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
• The article focuses on contribution levels and on payoffs (average or individual). While the authors do refer to the social optimum and net payoffs, they do not explicitly define or report “group efficiency” as (actual payoff / maximum possible payoff). Instead, they typically highlight “average payoff” and “contribution level” as dependent variables. Hence, efficiency (in the strict sense of that ratio) is not their primary measured outcome.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
• The following parameters appear in the text in some form (though not always extensively):  
  (1) Number of players (fixed at 5)  
  (2) Number of rounds (24 in the experiment, 300–1500 in simulation)  
  (6) MPCR (set to 0.3)  
  (7) Punishment “fee” (5 mild or 20 severe)  
  (8) Punishment “fine” (50 mild or 90 severe)  
  (12) Knowledge of the number of rounds (yes, but fixed)  
  (13) Display of peer contribution outcomes (yes, but not systematically varied)  
• The other parameters (3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15) are either not used in the design or not mentioned in any way relevant to varying punishment effects.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when the parameter is systematically varied?  
• None are systematically varied in this paper so as to measure their direct impact on the punishment treatment’s effect. The paper contrasts no punishment vs. mild vs. severe, but it does not do a parametric “sweep” or progressive variation of any single factor (number of players, MPCR, etc.). Hence, there are no reported effect sizes for systematic variations of the 15 parameters.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper, what would they be?  
• The paper does not give guidance on most of the 15 parameters. It only explores punishment/no‐punishment comparisons (mild vs. severe) in groups of five with a fixed MPCR of 0.3. As a result, little can be inferred about how systematically changing these other parameters would affect efficiency. The main snippet of insight is that “severe” (i.e., high) formal punishment can push rational free‐riders toward full cooperation (which in principle would raise group payoffs). However, for agents already prone to cooperate (e.g., “high cooperators”), that same punishment can reduce aggregate payoffs (thereby lowering efficiency) when the punishment cost is high. Overall, beyond that mild vs. severe observation, the paper offers no systematic predictions or numeric effect sizes regarding variations in the 15 parameters. Thus, one can make little to no further prediction from this source alone.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter accounting of what is and is not discussed in the paper regarding (a) whether the paper even mentions each parameter (and, if so, its value in the experiment), and (b) whether the paper makes any prediction about systematically varying that parameter and how it would affect the “punishment treatment effect” (i.e., how introducing punishment changes outcomes, especially efficiency). Where the paper does discuss numerical outcomes that relate to punishment, those are included. If the paper does not address a parameter or does not link it to any systematic variation of punishment, that is stated explicitly.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Discussed? Yes. The experiment consistently uses 8 players (p. 7, §2.1 and throughout).
   • Systematic variation or prediction about its effect on the punishment treatment effect? No. The paper never varies the group size (always 8) to see how it might change the effectiveness of punishment, so no effect size or prediction is provided.

2. Number of rounds
   • Discussed? Yes. Some sessions have 20 rounds (baseline protocol), others have 40 rounds (enforcement/treatment protocols).
   • Systematic variation or prediction about its effect on the punishment treatment effect? No. The paper notes that longer sessions allow for learning and convergence to different effort levels, but it does not systematically vary number of rounds in order to compare or predict a punishment-specific effect. No numerical effect size is provided regarding round-length changes and punishment.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussed? Yes. The “communication” setting (Setting C) and “communication with sanctioning” setting (Setting D) both allow player discussion (p. 10, §2.2.4). In the Treatment protocol, communication is enabled in Block 3 (no monetary penalties) and Block 4 (with sanctioning).  
   • Systematic variation or prediction about its effect on the punishment treatment effect? Partly. The paper does compare: (i) Baseline/Enforcement (no chat) vs. (ii) Communication (chat) vs. (iii) Communication + Sanctioning. However, it does not systematically isolate “chat alone” on the punishment effect; rather, chat-plus-punishment is introduced together in Block 4. No separate numerical effect size is stated for “chat alone affecting the punishment treatment effect,” so the paper does not isolate chat’s specific influence on punishment. Instead, the paper shows that introducing communication before punishment already boosts efficiency, and then in the next step it compares average net efficiency differences when adding sanctions.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussed? No. In the paper’s experiment, participants can freely choose integer hours (0 to 15) to allocate to fishing or construction. The design does not force “all or nothing” contributions, nor does it compare different styles of contribution choice. No predictions or effect sizes.

5. Is the contribution default?
   • Discussed? No. There is no “default” contribution level in this experiment. Participants choose hours of fishing (0 to 15) themselves. No discussion or predictions about varying a default.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters (e.g., multiplication factor)
   • Discussed? The paper does describe production functions for each area (pp. 6–7), but it does not systematically vary these functions or an MPCR-like factor. The two harbors (Alpha and Beta) have different parametric returns, but that is fixed.  
   • Systematic variation or prediction about its effect on the punishment treatment effect? No. There is no discussion about how changing the production/multiplication factor would alter punishment’s effect on efficiency, so no numerical effect size or prediction is given.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussed? Yes, briefly. Under the “communication with sanctioning” design (p. 10, §2.2.4), the experiment imposes no direct monetary cost on the punisher. Hence the “punishment cost to impose” is effectively zero.  
   • Systematic variation or prediction about its effect on the punishment treatment effect? No. This cost (zero for the punisher) is the same throughout; the paper does not vary it. No effect sizes or predictions are given about changing this cost.

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins/points deducted from a player per unit of punishment)
   • Discussed? Partially. The paper’s “sanctioning” has a stepwise effect: the first two sanctions against a given person are warnings (impose no penalty), while the third and subsequent sanctions trigger a 50-point penalty (p. 10, §2.2.4).  
   • Systematic variation or prediction about its effect on the punishment treatment effect? No. The experiment uses a single scheme (0 penalty for the first two, 50 points after). It does not systematically vary that magnitude. No effect-size comparisons are given for different punishments.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Discussed? No. The experiment does not include a reward mechanism, only sanctioning (p. 10, §2.2.4). No mention or prediction about rewards.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
    • Discussed? No. The paper does not use or discuss a reward mechanism. No mention or predictions.

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward given)
    • Discussed? No. Same as above—no reward mechanism is included, so no mention or predictions.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
    • Discussed? Yes. Participants are told how many rounds will occur (p. 9, “20 rounds,” “40 rounds,” etc.).
    • Systematic variation or prediction about its effect on the punishment treatment effect? No. The paper does not draw any separate, systematic punishment-effect predictions about known vs. unknown round lengths.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained/lost each round)?
    • Discussed? Partially. After each round, the total hours allocated to each area and each area’s average fishing payoff are announced, and subjects receive a card with their own total points (p. 9, §2.2.1). However, the paper does not systematically vary whether players see peer outcomes.  
    • Systematic variation or prediction about its effect on the punishment treatment effect? No. There is no separate manipulation of displayed information about peers. No effect size or predictions are provided.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
    • Discussed? Briefly. The paper states that punishers must identify the reason for punishment (p. 10, §2.2.4). However, it does not discuss systematically varying whether the target knows the identity of the punisher, nor does it measure how that variation would change punishment’s effect.  
    • No predictions or effect sizes are given.

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?
    • Discussed? No. The experiment does not include rewards, so nothing is said about anonymity or identification of a “rewarder.”

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary:

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   • Yes. “Net efficiency” or “appropriation efficiency” (actual total payoff minus a baseline, relative to the social optimum minus that same baseline) is a central outcome measure. The paper also tracks the frequency of “3–5 splits” across the two harbors, total effort levels, and individual defection events. These additional variables (e.g., whether the group hits the 3–5 allocation, how many hours are spent fishing, and how many times someone ignores a group agreement) are distinct from, though related to, efficiency.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned in some form: (1) number of players (always 8, not varied), (2) number of rounds (20 vs. 40, not systematically varied for punishment specifically), (3) chat (some sessions allow communication; others do not), (7) punishment cost to the punisher (zero), (8) punishment magnitude (50-point penalty after two warnings), (12) knowledge of number of rounds, (13) partial display of outcomes, (14) punisher identity is presumably known. That is 8 parameters.  
   • Fully absent or unmentioned: (4) “all or nothing” contributions, (5) default contribution, (6) systematically varying MPCR, (9) whether a reward is enabled, (10) reward cost, (11) reward magnitude, and (15) rewarder identity. That is 7 parameters not discussed in any systematic sense.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Strictly speaking, the paper only varies the presence or absence of sanctioning (punishment) alongside the presence or absence of communication. It does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters individually (for instance by increasing or decreasing punishment cost or magnitude in a controlled comparison).  
   • Hence, zero parameters in the list are “systematically varied” in the paper with explicit effect-size predictions for the punishment treatment. The one partial exception is that the paper reports a jump in efficiency from “communication only” to “communication plus sanctioning,” which can be read as the effect of adding punishment. Table 9 shows differences in net efficiencies across that switch (Block 3 to Block 4), but it does not come from systematically varying parameters 7 or 8 across multiple levels.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper’s discussion, what would they be?  
   • Little can be inferred for most parameters because they were not manipulated or discussed in the paper.  
   • The paper does suggest that allowing chat (parameter 3) plus adding sanctioning (parameters 7–8, fixed at no punisher cost and 50-point penalty after two free warnings) can boost efficiency and deter defection, but that sanctioning, if misapplied, can prompt “punishment wars” that slightly reduce efficiency in rare cases (Table 9). The effect size for going from “communication alone” (Setting C) to “communication + sanctioning” (Setting D) changes group net efficiency by anywhere from around −6% to +27%, depending on the group (Table 9).  
   • Beyond that, the paper does not enable predictions about varying other parameters (like number of players, reward mechanisms, exact punishment costs, or knowledge of future rounds) in relation to punishment’s effect on group efficiency.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Authors: Kanitsar, G
Author Full Names: Kanitsar, Georg
Article Title: Self-Governance in Generalized Exchange. A Laboratory Experiment on the Structural Embeddedness of Peer Punishment
Author Keywords: generalized exchange; peer punishment; cooperation; social networks; embeddedness; laboratory experiment
Keywords Plus: INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; COLLECTIVE ACTION; COOPERATION; REPUTATION; NETWORKS; GOODS; ENFORCEMENT; SOLIDARITY; EMERGENCE
Abstract: Peer punishment is widely lauded as a decentralized solution to the problem of social cooperation. However, experimental evidence of its effectiveness primarily stems from public good structures. This paper explores peer punishment in another structural setting: a system of generalized exchange. In a laboratory experiment, a repeated four-player prisoner's dilemma is arranged either in a public good structure or in a circular network of generalized exchange. The experimental results demonstrate that the merits of peer punishment do not extend to generalized exchange. In the public good, peer punishment was primarily altruistic, was sensitive to costs, and promoted cooperation. In generalized exchange, peer punishment was also altruistic and relatively frequent, but did not increase cooperation. While the dense punishment network underlying the public good facilitates norm enforcement, generalized exchange decreases control over norm violators and reduces the capacity of peer punishment. I conclude that generalized exchange systems require stronger forms of punishment to sustain social cooperation.

Below is a parameter-by-parameter review, drawn strictly from the paper by Kanitsar (2021). For each of the 15 parameters, I note whether the paper (a) discusses it at all (including any fixed value it assumes) and (b) makes predictions or reports findings about how systematically varying that parameter affects the “punishment treatment effect” (for instance, how punishment influences cooperation, earnings, or any other outcome). All statements refer only to what is actually reported in the paper’s text, tables, and figures; no additional sources or inferences beyond the paper are used.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Number of players
   • Discussed? Yes. The experiment uses groups of four players.  
   • Systematically varied? No. It is always four players, and the paper does not compare different group sizes. The effect of changing this parameter on punishment treatment effects is not analyzed.

2. Number of rounds
   • Discussed? Yes. Each group interacts for 16 rounds total, but participants do not know the exact number so as to avoid endgame effects.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper never changes the length of the experiment. No effect-size estimates or predictions for varying the number of rounds are provided.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Discussed? No. There is no mention of communication or “chat” features in the experiment.  
   • Systematically varied? Not applicable.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Discussed? Yes, though not in these exact words. The experiment is effectively a binary-choice prisoner’s dilemma (cooperate or defect), meaning each participant chooses one of two discrete options.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The experiment consistently uses a two-option choice (cooperate or defect) and does not explore partial contributions. No effect-size estimates exist for varying this.

5. Is the contribution default (players withdrawing from the public fund)?
   • Discussed? No. The design does not involve a default contribution mechanism or players “withdrawing” from a fund.  
   • Systematically varied? Not applicable.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor
   • Discussed? No direct references to “MPCR.” They fix the payoffs such that cooperating confers 10 MU to others (public-good case) or to the “next” person (generalized-exchange case), while defection yields 3 MU privately.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper keeps the same payoff structure throughout. No effect-size estimates for changing these payoff multipliers are given.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Discussed? Yes. This is a central treatment manipulation. The cost is either c = 1 MU (“costly punishment”) or c = 0 MU (“costless punishment”).  
   • Systematically varied? Yes.  
     – Findings for the Public Good structure:  
       • Moving from c = 1 to c = 0 raises cooperation substantially (from 0.59 to 0.92 in Table 1, p < 0.01) and also raises earnings (from 5.69 to 8.77 MU on average, p ≈ 0.05).  
       • Hence, costless punishment strongly increases the “punishment treatment effect” on cooperation relative to both the baseline (no punishment) and the c = 1 condition.  
     – Findings for Generalized Exchange:  
       • Changing c = 1 to c = 0 yields no significant difference in cooperation (0.66 vs. 0.59, p > 0.5) or earnings (7.32 vs. 6.54, p > 0.4).  
       • Thus, removing the cost of punishment does not enhance cooperation or payoffs in the generalized-exchange condition.

   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. The paper refers to the number of players as N (the “scale of the network”). They use N = 100, 200 (and a small example of N = 12 for illustration).  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it (and any effect on the punishment treatment)?  
     – Yes. They vary N (Figure 9) and observe that as N increases, the fraction of cooperators under the punishment‐and‐feedback mechanism declines, effectively weakening the mechanism’s ability to sustain cooperation.  
     – They do not discuss effects on “efficiency” in the sense of total payoff divided by maximum possible payoff; they only report how the fraction of cooperators changes.

2) Number of rounds  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – Yes. They define n as the number of PDG rounds in each block before links can be cut.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying it?  
     – Yes. They examine n = 1, 3, 5 (Figure 6). Once the punishment‐and‐feedback mechanism is in place, the fraction of cooperators does not change much as n varies.  
     – Again, no mention of efficiency; rather, they report outcomes in terms of cooperation fraction.

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not mention any form of communication or chat among players.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Discussed? No. This paper studies a Prisoner’s Dilemma, not a public goods game with forced all‐or‐nothing contributions.

5) Is the contribution default?  
   • Discussed? No. The paper does not mention or vary a “default” contribution mechanism.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters such as a multiplication factor  
   • Does the paper discuss it?  
     – They do not frame it as “MPCR,” but they do vary “b” in the payoff matrix A = [[1, 0], [b, 0]], 1 < b < 2. This b effectively serves as the temptation payoff, analogous to the parameter that drives defection’s profitability.  
   • Does the paper make predictions about varying b?  
     – Yes. They compare b = 1.1, 1.3, 1.5 (Figure 5) and find that larger b lowers the fraction of cooperators (though the punishment‐and‐feedback mechanism prevents cooperators from being entirely wiped out).  
     – No explicit mention of efficiency; they report the fraction of cooperators.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Discussed? No. In this paper’s model, “punishment” takes the form of cutting the network link with top defectors, but they do not treat that link‐cutting as having an explicit cost.

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Discussed? No. Likewise, the paper does not model a direct payoff penalty or “fine” for punishment. Instead, the “punishment” is that the defector loses links.

    • Discussed? No. Not applicable.

    • Discussed? No. Not applicable.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
    • Discussed? No. Not addressed.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
    • Discussed? No. There is no reward mechanism in this model, so this is not addressed.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?  
   – The paper does not measure or discuss “group efficiency,” understood as total payoff divided by the maximum possible payoff. Its central outcome is the fraction of cooperators over time. While the model does track individual payoffs (for the purpose of strategy updating), every result the paper reports is about how many cooperators remain in the population, not about overall efficiency.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   – Mentioned: (1) Number of players (N), (2) Number of rounds (n), and (6) Temptation parameter b (analogous to a multiplication factor in the payoff matrix).  
   – None of the other parameters (3–5, 7–15) are explicitly mentioned or varied. Thus, 3 of the 15 parameters appear in the paper.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   – The paper systematically varies:  
       • (1) N: they show that as N increases, the mechanism’s ability to sustain cooperation weakens.  
       • (2) n: increasing the number of rounds (in blocks) does not substantially change the fraction of cooperators when punishment‐and‐feedback is active.  
       • (6) b: increasing b (1.1→1.3→1.5) reduces the fraction of cooperators but does not wipe them out entirely if punishment‐and‐feedback is used.  
   – Their “dependent variable” throughout is fraction of cooperators, not efficiency. Hence, 3 parameters are varied and their influence on cooperation under punishment is discussed.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper, what would they be?  
   – Because the paper never examines total/group payoffs or efficiency (nor does it quantify “punishment cost” and “punishment magnitude” in payoff terms), it provides little or no direct basis for predicting how these 15 parameters affect efficiency. The only indirect clues come from how cooperation fares under different conditions. If one assumes higher cooperation implies higher group payoff—and thus higher efficiency—then one might guess that (a) smaller N, (b) lower b, and (c) the presence of a link‐cutting punishment rule favor higher efficiency, while the other parameters remain unaddressed. However, the paper itself does not link these parameters to efficiency metrics or to cost/benefit analyses of punishment, so any efficiency predictions would be speculative at best.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter inventory of what this paper does (and does not) say about each of the 15 features of a “public‐goods‐type” punishment experiment. All statements refer strictly to the provided paper and its figures/tables; no other sources are used.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes (implicitly). The paper models exactly two “players”: one top‐management‐team (TMT) from a state‐owned enterprise and one TMT from a private enterprise.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not explore changing the number of players.  
   • Any predicted effect on punishment treatment (for efficiency or otherwise)? No.  

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper uses a replicator‐dynamic/evolutionary‐game formulation but does not specify a finite or known number of rounds.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Any predicted effect on punishment treatment? No.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Any predicted effect on punishment treatment? No.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned? Yes, in the sense that each TMT chooses either “input knowledge” or “not input knowledge.” It is a binary (all‐or‐nothing) choice.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not examine alternative contribution formats.  
   • Any predicted effect on punishment treatment? No.  

5. Is the contribution default (do players decide how much of their endowment to move back)?  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Any predicted effect on punishment treatment? No.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? No. Although the paper has a parameter π for “excess profit” if both parties invest, it is not framed as a public‐goods MPCR.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Any predicted effect on punishment treatment? No.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? No. Punishment in the paper comes from a government penalty, not from peers bearing a cost to punish.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Any predicted effect on punishment treatment? No.  

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted for each unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned? Partially. The paper includes a lump‐sum government “penalty” p₁ or p₂ if a TMT fails to input knowledge. That penalty is not framed as “per unit” of punishment, but it does function as a punishment magnitude.  
   • Systematically varied? Yes, from 0.1 to 0.18 in the simulations (Section IV).  
   • Any predictions about its effect on punishment treatment effect for efficiency? No. The paper examines how changing p₁ or p₂ influences the final cooperative outcome (knowledge input), not “efficiency.” Numerical changes reported are in terms of speeding up or slowing down cooperation convergence (e.g., “the evolutionary steps shorten from 50 to 40”), rather than any effect on payoff efficiency.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned? Yes. A government‐provided reward r₁ or r₂ is given to TMTs that choose to input knowledge.  
   • Systematically varied? The fact that a reward is used is not itself “turned on/off,” but the paper does explore different magnitudes of r (see #11).  
   • Any predicted effect on punishment treatment? No. The paper does not link “enabling reward” to a “punishment treatment effect,” nor to efficiency, only to cooperation outcomes.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not analyze any cost to the rewarding party (the government).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Any predicted effect on punishment treatment? No.  

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded for each unit of reward)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Denoted r₁ or r₂.  
   • Systematically varied? Yes, from 0.1 to 0.18 in Section IV’s simulations.  
   • Any predicted effect on punishment treatment effect for efficiency? No. The analysis looks at how increasing r shortens or lengthens the evolutionary path to cooperative strategy. It does not discuss efficiency as a dependent variable.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Any predicted effect on punishment treatment? No.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players see one another’s payoffs)?  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Any predicted effect on punishment treatment? No.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Mentioned? No. All “punishment” is from a government entity, with no discussion of anonymity or identification of the punisher.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Any predicted effect on punishment treatment? No.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Mentioned? No. Likewise, the government‐based reward is not analyzed in terms of identification or anonymity.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Any predicted effect on punishment treatment? No.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY:

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   • The paper does not use “group efficiency” or “total payoff” or “average payoff” as a dependent variable. Its dependent variables and analyses revolve around (1) the final “input vs. not‐input” strategies that emerge under replicator dynamics, and (2) the speed/number of steps until those strategies stabilize. The authors call those outcomes “cooperative behavior” or “cooperation rate,” distinct from any explicit efficiency measure.

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Five are at least touched upon:  
       1) Number of players (#1) – exactly two (state‐owned TMT vs. private‐enterprise TMT).  
       2) All‐or‐nothing contributions (#4) – the paper’s model is a binary “knowledge input” or “not input.”  
       3) Punishment magnitude (#8) – a lumpsum government penalty p₁ or p₂.  
       4) Whether a reward is enabled (#9) – yes, it uses a government reward.  
       5) Reward magnitude (#11) – lumpsum r₁ or r₂.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?  
   • The paper does not use “punishment treatment effect” in the sense of a public‐goods experiment, nor does it measure “efficiency.” Punishment and reward (p and r) are systematically varied, but strictly for their effect on cooperation (probability of “input knowledge”). No parameter is discussed specifically in terms of “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”  
   • Numerically, the paper reports that increasing p or r tends to make the cooperative (input) strategy stabilize more quickly, but that discussion pertains to cooperation rather than to group efficiency.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not analyze efficiency at all and never reports a “punishment treatment effect” on payoffs or efficiency. Accordingly, there is little basis in the paper to predict how varying these 15 parameters would affect efficiency in a public‐goods sense. The authors focus throughout on evolutionary stability of knowledge‐input behavior and do not connect those findings to a measure of group efficiency. Consequently, one can make little or no prediction about efficiency solely from this paper.

Abstract: Punishment is crucial to maintain contribution and to prevent defection in societies. Abstract: Objective Stratified groups face at least two obstacles in solving collective action problems and producing public goods. Individuals face temptation to free ride, and high-ranking group members face incentives to protect their position at the group's expense. We introduce democratic competition for rank as a solution to the problem of cooperation in groups. We argue that democratic competition for high rank creates incentives for cooperation that are absent in nondemocratic groups. Methods In a small-group behavioral experiment, we contrast groups in which individuals compete for a valuable high-ranking position through democratic elections with groups in which individuals compete for high rank in resource-based competitions. However, high-ranking individuals in democratic groups exaggerate threats to the group at similar rates to high-ranking individuals in nondemocratic groups. Authors: Bica, A; Cretu, RZ
Author Full Names: Bica, Andreea; Cretu, Romeo Zeno
Article Title: The carrot and the stick: How guilt and shame facilitate reciprocity-driven cooperation
Author Keywords: Guilt; shame; reciprocity; cooperation; Ultimatum Game
Keywords Plus: EMOTION; APPRAISAL; FAIRNESS; EVOLUTION; SELF; CONFORMITY; PUNISHMENT
Abstract: Moral emotions (i.e. guilt, shame) and interpersonal processes such as fairness have been theorised to facilitate cooperation within society. However, empirical tests to support this association have yielded inconsistent results. The present research investigated whether guilt and shame have an impact on fairness-related decision-making and reciprocity-driven cooperation. College students (N = 94) were assigned to one of three experimental conditions (Guilt vs. Shame vs. Control) and instructed to complete an iterated Ultimatum Game against two anonymous partners. We manipulated social context so that one partner would appear as predominantly fair, and the other as predominantly unfair. For guilt, we found that participants (assigned as proposers) reciprocated fair partners with significantly larger amounts of money (i.e. positive reciprocity). For shame, we found that participants had higher rejection rates of unfair splits, and subsequently offered less money to unfair partners (i.e. negative reciprocity). We argue that both guilt and shame benefit fairness-related judgments, guilt by endorsing fairness, and shame by punishing unfairness. Our results also show that guilt and shame benefit reciprocity-driven cooperation, although they do so via different pathways. Our findings suggest that guilt promotes cooperation via positive reciprocity, whereas shame stabilises cooperation via negative reciprocity.

  – Migration decisions (whether participants move across groups in the “Moving Treatment”).  

• While the word “efficiency” appears when the authors mention that formal sanctions are “theoretically expected to generate high levels of efficiency,” the paper predominantly reports average (or total) payoffs, not an explicit “group efficiency = (actual sum of payoffs) / (maximum possible sum).” Thus, the main dependent variables are contributions, punishments, payoffs, and migration, with occasional references to higher payoffs as “more efficient.”

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

• Mentioned explicitly (though not systematically varied):  
  1) Number of players (fixed: 10 total).  
  2) Number of rounds (fixed: 30).  
  3) No chat is mentioned (they disallow it).  
  6) MPCR / multiplication factor (1.6).  
  7) Punishment cost to punisher (1 token).  
  8) Punishment magnitude (2 tokens in one set of instructions, 3 in the other).  
  12) Known number of rounds (30, fully disclosed).  
  13) Peer outcomes/information displays (they do see contributions of each group member in IS and average payoffs).  
  14) The identity of the specific punisher is hidden.  

• Not mentioned or not used at all:  
  4) All‐or‐nothing contributions (they use a continuous range 0–50).  
  5) Contribution default or reversed mechanism.  
  9) Whether a reward is enabled (it is not).  
  10) Reward cost (does not exist).  
  11) Reward magnitude (does not exist).  
  15) When a player is rewarded, do they know the rewarder? (no rewards are administered).

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?

• The authors do not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters (such as group size, punishment cost, etc.) to study their direct effect. Instead, they vary only whether participants can move between groups, keeping almost every other factor constant (e.g., always the same MPCR, same cost of punishing, etc.).  
• Consequently, none of the 15 parameters is “systematically varied” in the sense of analyzing how different values of that parameter alone alter the punishment treatment effect on efficiency or on any other dependent variable. The paper’s interest is in comparing “No Moving” vs. “Moving” and “Informal” vs. “Formal” sanctions, not in manipulating, for instance, punishment magnitude or the number of rounds.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

• The paper’s design does not speak directly to how changing each parameter would shift the effect of introducing punishment on efficiency. It focuses instead on whether participants can regroup endogenously (via “moving”) and how they vote for an informal or formal sanctioning mechanism.  
• Consequently, based only on this paper, one can say very little about how systematically varying each of the 15 parameters—beyond enabling vs. forbidding group movement—would alter the relationship between punishment and efficiency. The authors do show that formal sanctions (with an automatic fine) generally lead to higher contributions (and payoffs) than informal sanctions in the presence of low‐contribution newcomers, but that does not yield broad parametric predictions for changes in, for example, the punishment cost or the marginal per capita return.  
• In short, the paper provides no direct evidence on how to predict variations in efficiency for changes in any of the 15 parameters except that letting participants move across groups can undermine the popularity (and in some cases the payoff performance) of informal sanctions.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Authors: Shin, HC; Vallury, S; Janssen, MA; Yu, DJ
Author Full Names: Shin, Hoon C.; Vallury, Sechindra; Janssen, Marco A.; Yu, David J.
Article Title: Joint effects of voluntary participation and group selection on the evolution of altruistic punishment
Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS; COOPERATION; DYNAMICS; OPTION; EXIT
Abstract: It is puzzling how altruistic punishment of defectors can evolve in large groups of nonrelatives, since punishers should voluntarily bear individual costs of punishing to benefit those who do not pay the costs. Although two distinct mechanisms have been proposed to explain the puzzle, namely voluntary participation and group-level competition and selection, insights into their joint effects have been less clear. Here we investigated what could be combined effects of these two mechanisms on the evolution of altruistic punishment and how these effects can vary with nonparticipants' individual payoff and group size. We modelled altruistic punishers as those who contribute to a public good and impose a fine on each defector, i.e., they are neither pure punishers nor excluders. Our simulation results show that voluntary participation has negative effects on the evolution of cooperation in small groups regardless of nonparticipants' payoffs, while in large groups it has positive effects within only a limited range of nonparticipants' payoff. We discuss that such asymmetric effects could be explained by evolutionary forces emerging from voluntary participation. Lastly, we suggest that insights from social science disciplines studying the exit option could enrich voluntary participation models.

Below is an item-by-item look at the 15 parameters in your list, based strictly on what is reported in the Shin et al. (2022) paper. Throughout, please note that the paper’s primary focus is on the long-run frequency of cooperation (i.e., the proportion of cooperators in each group or in the entire population). It does not report group efficiency (actual total payoff ÷ maximum possible total payoff of a fully cooperative group) nor does it explicitly examine a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” Instead, the authors focus on how varying certain model parameters changes the proportion of cooperators/punishers over time.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
• Does the paper discuss it (value)?  
  – Yes. The paper sets the size of each group to n ∈ {20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120}.  
• Are there predictions about systematically varying it for the punishment treatment effect (for any outcome)?  
  – The paper does systematically vary n to see its effect on the long-run frequency of cooperation. However, it does not measure “treatment effects on efficiency”; rather, it reports that as group size increases, the option of voluntary participation can, under certain conditions, support higher levels of cooperation (Fig 1, Fig 2, Fig 3).  
  – No numerical effect size is given in terms of “efficiency” or “punishment treatment effect.” Instead, they show that larger n facilitates higher cooperation in certain payoff conditions, while smaller n reduces cooperation.  

2. Number of rounds
• Does the paper discuss it (value)?  
  – The paper calls each iteration a “time period” and runs simulations for 2,000 time periods.  
• Are there predictions about systematically varying it for the punishment treatment effect?  
  – No. The paper does not systematically vary the total number of time periods (rounds).  

3. Is chat enabled between players?
• Discussion?  
  – No mention of communication or chat features among players.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
• Discussion?  
  – The model allows an agent to be either a defector (contributes nothing) or a cooperator (contributes a fixed amount). There is no separate analysis or discussion of all-or-nothing mechanics beyond that standard binary choice. There is no systematic exploration of toggling all-or-nothing rules as a parameter.  

5. Is the contribution default?
• Discussion?  
  – The paper does not mention any default contribution mechanism (such as transferring an endowment back into a private account). No systematic variation of such a parameter is reported.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor
• Does the paper discuss it (value)?  
  – The parameter b = 0.5 is used as the group-benefit multiplier in the model.  
• Are there predictions about systematically varying b for the punishment treatment effect?  
  – They do not systematically vary b in the reported results; it remains at 0.5. No effect sizes are reported for variation in b.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
• Does the paper discuss it (value)?  
  – The parameter k = 0.2 is the “cost of punishing each defector.”  
• Are there predictions about systematically varying k for the punishment treatment effect?  
  – The authors do not systematically vary k in the paper’s main or supporting results. They fix k = 0.2.  

8. Punishment magnitude (coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)
• Does the paper discuss it (value)?  
  – The parameter p = 0.8 is the “cost of being punished” to a defector for each instance of punishment.  
• Are there predictions about systematically varying p for the punishment treatment effect?  
  – They include a “sensitivity analysis” where p is changed (see S1 File). In qualitative terms, the frequency of cooperation “significantly decreases when punishment is absent or inflicts less cost on defectors.” However, they do not provide a numerical effect size in terms of efficiency or a “punishment treatment effect.” They also do not frame these results explicitly as efficiency outcomes.  

9. Whether a reward is enabled
• Discussion?  
  – Not mentioned. No reward mechanism is included.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
• Discussion?  
  – Not mentioned; there is no reward treatment.  

11. Reward magnitude (coins awarded per unit of reward)
• Discussion?  
  – Not mentioned; there is no reward treatment.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?
• Discussion?  
  – Not addressed. Agents are in a simulation of 2,000 time periods. No mention of players’ knowledge of a final round.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?
• Discussion?  
  – The model is an evolutionary imitation model in which agents compare payoffs locally or with probability m to an agent in a different group. The paper does not describe any explicit information display to participants of peers’ detailed outcomes, only that agents imitate higher-payoff strategies with a certain probability.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?
• Discussion?  
  – Not mentioned.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the rewarder is?
• Discussion?  
  – Not mentioned (and no reward is studied).  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how do they differ?
• The paper does not use any explicit measure of group efficiency, total payoff, or average payoff as its primary dependent variable.  
• Instead, the main outcomes are:  
  – The frequency (long-run proportion) of cooperators (who may or may not punish) vs. defectors vs. nonparticipants.  
• These are different from efficiency because they measure how many are cooperating (and punishing) rather than how large the total payoff is relative to the maximum possible.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?
• Mentioned in some form:  
  1) Number of players (group size, n),  
  2) Number of rounds (the model runs for 2,000 time periods, but not systematically varied),  
  6) Multiplication factor (b = 0.5, though not varied),  
  7) Punishment cost k = 0.2 (mentioned but not varied),  
  8) Punishment magnitude p = 0.8 (mentioned and varied in a sensitivity analysis).  
• None of the other parameters in the list (e.g., chat, reward, knowledge of final round) are discussed in the paper.

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when systematically varied?
• Strictly speaking, the paper does not frame its analysis in terms of a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”  
• However, the closest analogs to systematic variation for their main dependent variable (frequency of cooperation) are:  
  – Parameter #1 (Group size, n): The paper systematically varies n from 20 to 120 and reports its effect on cooperation under voluntary vs. compulsory scenarios.  
  – Parameter #8 (Punishment magnitude, p): They perform a sensitivity analysis (with p lowered or absent) and note that cooperation drops when p is smaller or missing.  
• No other parameter from the list is systematically varied in the context of understanding how punishment changes a payoff- or efficiency-related outcome.

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the paper’s content, what would they be?
• Because the paper does not measure efficiency, it provides minimal direct insight into how these parameters affect a “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.”  
• The only solid inferences one might draw, strictly from the paper, are:  
  – Larger group sizes (parameter #1) can strengthen cooperation under certain payoff conditions. If one assumed that higher cooperation implies higher efficiency, then one might guess that large groups under altruistic punishment might yield a higher “efficiency” than small groups. But the paper does not quantify this as efficiency.  
  – Increasing the punishment magnitude p (parameter #8) is associated with higher frequency of cooperation, which might indirectly suggest higher efficiency. But no formal efficiency measure or numerical effect on total payoffs is given.  
• Beyond these broad connections, the paper provides little to no basis for predicting the other parameters’ effects on efficiency or on a “punishment treatment effect.”
reference_APA: Shin, Hoon C., Vallury, Sechindra, Janssen, Marco A. & Yu, David J. (2022). Joint effects of voluntary participation and group selection on the evolution of altruistic punishment. PLOS ONE.

Authors: Wang, Y; Fu, LY

Article Title: Analysis on the Evolution Mechanism of Open Environmental Protection Innovation among Equipment Manufacturing Oligopolistic Enterprises Based on Data Simulation
Keywords Plus: INDUSTRY
Abstract: The global economic environment is becoming increasingly complex with the variable change in the competition regulation and the merging of technological innovation. A single equipment manufacturing enterprise cannot achieve the realization of an intelligent strategy. With the help of open innovation, the enterprise can build an intelligent manufacturing innovation ecosystem based on promoting internal re-engineering of enterprises and mutual opening of internal innovation resource processes among enterprises to strengthen cooperation. However, since open innovation is a complex collaborative innovation of multiorganizational cooperation, this paper analyzes and discusses the green open innovation cooperation strategy among oligopolistic enterprises in the equipment manufacturing industry under the influence of environmental regulation by using relevant models and theories of evolutionary game theory. In addition, the optimal combination under the existing situation is selected by using the model to simulate and analyze the selection trends and results of oligopolistic enterprises several times. The study shows that the probability of choosing an open green innovation strategy among oligopolistic equipment manufacturing firms is positively proportional to the excess benefit of open green innovation and government subsidies and inversely proportional to the excess benefit of knowledge spillover, government penalties, and the cost of open collaborative innovation and knowledge spillover between two firms.

Abstract: Ostracism is one form of real-life punishment mechanism to penalize uncooperative individuals in many societies. Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter summary of what this paper actually says (and does not say) about each of the 15 features. Throughout, “systematically varying” a parameter means that the experiment itself varied that parameter across different treatment conditions (e.g., different values or on/off) in order to observe its impact on outcomes. If the paper merely states a fixed value for the parameter, or uses it in a single treatment only (without comparing multiple levels), then there is no systematic variation.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each group has 4 players.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The experiment always uses 4‐person groups; the paper does not vary group size or compare multiple group‐size conditions.  
   • Any stated effect on punishment treatment (ostracism) or efficiency? No direct testing; the paper keeps group size fixed.

2. Number of rounds
   • Mentioned? Yes. There are 6 rounds of the “standard public good game” and 6 rounds of the “public good game with ostracism.”  
   • Systematically varied? No. All sessions had 6 rounds in each condition. Although they note an “end‐game effect,” the paper does not compare different total numbers of rounds (e.g., 6 vs. 10 vs. 50).  
   • Any stated effect on punishment treatment or efficiency? Only that cooperation/ contributions drop in the final round (and punishment is not effective in that last round), but there is no systematic variation of the total round count.

3. Is chat enabled between players?
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper explicitly states that communication among participants was not allowed at any time.  
   • Systematically varied? No. They do not compare a “chat” vs. “no chat” treatment.  
   • Any stated effect on punishment treatment or efficiency? None. The paper does not examine how enabling chat would affect ostracism outcomes.

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?
   • Mentioned? Yes. The paper describes that players may contribute any integer amount from 0 to 10 baht. This is not “all or nothing”; it is a continuous (integer) choice.  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is only one contribution format (0–10).  
   • Any stated effect on punishment treatment or efficiency? Not tested.

5. Is the contribution default (i.e., do players move money from a public fund back to private, or vice versa)?
   • Mentioned? Not in the sense of “defaulting” from public to private. The design gives each player an endowment of 10 baht in their private account each round and they choose how many of those 10 to contribute.  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no alternative mechanism; the paper does not compare different “default contribution” formats.  
   • Any stated effect on punishment treatment or efficiency? None.

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters
   • Mentioned? Yes. MPCR is set at 0.625 for all sessions.  
   • Systematically varied? No. They do not run multiple MPCR values; the paper only explains that 0.625 was chosen to exceed 0.5.  
   • Any stated effect on punishment treatment or efficiency? No direct test of varying MPCR. The paper simply notes that the higher‐than‐0.5 MPCR helps ensure the public good still has non‐trivial returns even if group size shrinks due to ostracism.

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment
   • Mentioned? Yes. The cost of voting to ostracize is 0.10 baht (1% of the 10‐baht endowment) each time a player casts a vote.  
   • Systematically varied? No. They use only that single cost.  
   • Any stated effect on punishment treatment or efficiency? The paper does not compare multiple cost levels, so no estimates of how changing the cost would affect outcomes.

8. Punishment magnitude (the deducted amount per unit of punishment)
   • Mentioned? Yes, but in the form of ostracism: if a player receives ≥50% of votes in a period, that player is excluded (“moved to the red zone”) for two subsequent rounds (earns zero, cannot vote, and does not observe information during those two rounds).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The ostracism rule is fixed: two rounds of exclusion, no alternative durations or intensities.  
   • Any stated effect on punishment treatment or efficiency? The paper shows that ostracism (compared to no punishment) increases contributions and raises average payoff by about 23%, but it does not vary the length or severity of ostracism.

9. Whether a reward is enabled
   • Mentioned? Yes, in the sense that the paper focuses on punishment only (ostricism) and does not implement any reward mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied? No. No reward treatment is included.  
   • Any stated effect on punishment treatment or efficiency? None, because no reward option is present.

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward
   • Mentioned? No. Rewards never appear in the design; the paper does not discuss any cost for rewarding.  
   • Systematically varied? Not applicable.

11. Reward magnitude
   • Mentioned? No. Rewards are never used; the paper does not address awarding extra coins.  
   • Systematically varied? Not applicable.

12. Is the number of rounds known to players?
   • Mentioned? Yes. Participants know from the start that each public good game has exactly 6 rounds.  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Any stated effect on punishment treatment or efficiency? They discuss end‐game effects (the collapse of cooperation in the final round) but do not systematically vary the knowledge of round length.

13. Are peer outcomes shown (e.g., how much each other player gained or lost)?
   • Mentioned? Yes. After each round in both the standard and ostracism treatments, participants see each other’s contribution amounts (but not personal identities).  
   • Systematically varied? No.  
   • Any stated effect on punishment treatment or efficiency? The paper does not test alternative information displays—only this single design in which everyone sees contributions.

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?

Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS; EVOLUTION; COMMUNICATION; COOPERATION; ROBUSTNESS; PUNISHMENT; BEHAVIOR; TRAGEDY
Abstract: Multiple biological groups, such as ant colonies, appear to have a noteworthy inefficiency: they contain vast amounts of redundant members that are not strictly needed to maintain the group. Philosophers and biologists have proposed that such inefficiency is illusory because redundancy enhances the resilience of groups when living under harsh conditions. Still, this proposal is unsatisfactory in different respects. First, it is too vague to account for when redundancy is selectively advantageous. Furthermore, it overlooks cases in which redundancy fails to increase the resilience of groups. This paper offers an account of group redundancy that addresses these difficulties. Specifically, it advances the hypothesis that the mere presence of harsh conditions is not what drives the evolution of redundancy; rather, it is the fact organisms are often unable to predict when they will face harsh conditions. Redundancy enables groups to properly respond to unpredictable circumstances without resorting to the unreliable detection systems of their members. A better understanding of the phenomenon of redundancy is likely to impact other key issues in philosophy of science, including the evolution of cooperation and transitions in individuality, and the role of redundancy in complex systems, be they biological or not.

Abstract: Ostracism, or exclusion by peers, has been practiced since ancient times as a severe form of punishment against transgressors of laws or social norms. The purpose of this paper is to offer a comprehensive analysis on how ostracism affects behavior and the functioning of a social group. • Consequently, the paper does not allow for firm predictions about the 15 parameters’ influence on a punishment treatment’s effect on efficiency (understood as actual / maximum payoff). Any such predictive statement would go beyond what the authors actually test. The only general note is that in their comparison of “no‐exclusion” vs. “exclusion” treatments, they find that total earnings remain roughly similar across these two conditions, indicating that exclusion did not greatly harm (nor boost) overall payoffs under the specific, fixed settings they used. However, that result is not tied to systematically varying any of the 15 parameters.  

Overall, therefore, the paper does not provide direct guidance on how to adjust or design any of the listed parameters to increase or decrease the “punishment treatment effect” on efficiency. Any such predictions would be outside the scope of the data and analyses reported in this study.

Abstract: Standard public goods games often assign group members the same marginal per capita returns to public goods production, but in reality group members facing differential individual returns often must collaborate to produce a public good. This paper uses a laboratory experiment to investigate the comparative efficacy of punishment and reward in heterogeneous groups. Contrary to the common belief that punishment is more effective than reward, I find that reward increases group contributions and efficiency, but punishment does not.
