Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter inventory of what the paper does (and does not) say about each of the fifteen features you listed. Throughout, “the punishment treatment effect” refers to how adding a costly‐punishment stage (versus no punishment) influences efficiency (the group’s actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff). In the paper, there is a “punishment” condition, a “reward” condition, and a “control” condition (no punishment or reward). However, none of the 15 parameters is systematically varied within the punishment condition to test how changes in that parameter alone would alter the punishment effect on efficiency. Instead, those parameters are either held fixed or discussed only in passing. Consequently, there is no numerical “effect size” reported for changes in any parameter on the punishment treatment effect in particular. Below are the details.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
1) Number of players  
• Discussed? Yes. The paper always uses three‐person groups.  
• Systematically varied? No. There is no manipulation of group size (it stays at three).  
• Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency)? Not discussed.  

2) Number of rounds  
• Discussed? Yes. Each session features public‐goods play over 10 periods (and then another 10 in a second block).  
• Systematically varied? No. They keep it at 10.  
• Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency)? Not discussed.  

3) Is chat enabled between players?  
• Discussed? The paper states that participants cannot communicate with one another.  
• Systematically varied? No. There is no condition allowing chat.  
• Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency)? Not discussed.  

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
• Discussed? Only implicitly. In the experiment, each participant can contribute any integer amount from 0 to 20 tokens, so it is not “all or nothing.”  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency)? Not discussed.  

5) Is the contribution default (do players “take back” a chosen amount)?  
• Discussed? Not mentioned at all. Participants simply decide how many tokens (0–20) to contribute.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency)? Not discussed.  

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR)  
• Discussed? Yes. One “high‐benefit” group member has MPCR = 0.9; the other two have MPCR = 0.4.  
• Systematically varied? No. There is no experiment‐wide manipulation of MPCR levels (0.9 and 0.4 remain fixed).  
• Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency)? The paper does compare behavior of high‐MPCR versus low‐MPCR players, but does not discuss how changing MPCR values would affect punishment’s impact on efficiency.  

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit  
• Discussed? Yes. It costs 1 token for a player to allocate 1 “punishment point.”  
• Systematically varied? No. Always set to 1 token.  
• Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency)? Not discussed.  

8) Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
• Discussed? Yes. Each punishment point deducts 3 tokens from the punished player.  
• Systematically varied? No. Always 3 tokens.  
• Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency)? Not discussed.  

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
• Discussed? Yes. There is a separate “reward” condition. Reward was not combined with punishment; it is a different treatment.  
• Systematically varied with respect to punishment? No. The paper simply compares (1) a control (no punishment/reward), (2) a punishment‐only condition, and (3) a reward‐only condition. It does not systematically toggle reward “on” or “off” inside the punishment treatment itself.  
• Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency)? Not specifically addressed, because the paper never mixes reward into the punishment treatment nor isolates how “adding reward” would change punishment’s effect on efficiency.  

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit  
• Discussed? Yes. It costs 1 token to give 1 “reward point.”  
• Systematically varied? No. Always 1 token.  
• Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency)? Not discussed.  

11) Reward magnitude (the coins awarded per unit of reward)  
• Discussed? Yes. Each reward point confers +3 tokens to the rewarded player.  
• Systematically varied? No. Always 3 tokens.  
• Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency)? Not discussed.  

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?  
• Discussed? Yes. Each session has a fixed known horizon of 10 periods (twice).  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency)? Not discussed.  

13) Are peer outcomes shown (do players see how much peers gained/lost)?  
• Discussed? Yes. Each period, everyone sees each group member’s contributions and earnings (including total reward/punishment points received).  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency)? Not discussed.  

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
• Discussed? Yes. The paper states that participants only see the total combined points assigned by the two teammates; they do not learn exactly who punished them.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency)? Not discussed.  

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
• Discussed? Yes. The paper similarly states they only see the total combined reward points from the other two players; the specific rewarder is not revealed.  
• Systematically varied? No.  
• Effect on punishment treatment (including efficiency)? Not discussed.  

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Summary of Key Points

A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable?  
Yes. The paper reports both (i) contributions (how many tokens participants contribute to the public good) and (ii) efficiency or “final earnings” after the second (punish/reward) stage. These are different: contribution is how many tokens go into the public good, whereas efficiency is the total (or average) payoff group members keep by the end of each period.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
All 15 can be identified or inferred in the design (e.g. 3‐person groups, 10 rounds, no chat, MPCR values of 0.9 vs. 0.4, punishment cost 1 / magnitude 3, reward cost 1 / magnitude 3, known number of rounds, feedback on contributions, etc.). However, none of these is actually manipulated in a way that “systematically varies” the parameter across different punishment treatments.

C) For which (and how many) of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect (for any dependent variable) when each parameter is systematically varied?  
None. The paper does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters in the punishment condition. There are only three conditions: punishment, reward, or neither—hence no within‐punishment manipulations of cost, magnitude, group size, and so on. As a result, there is no reported numerical effect size of changing a parameter on punishment’s impact on efficiency.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on this paper, what would they be?  
The paper provides virtually no guidance for how changes in any of these 15 parameters might alter the relationship between punishment and efficiency in heterogeneous‐MPCR groups. The main finding is that, under the single fixed version of punishment (cost = 1, magnitude = 3, in 3‐person groups over 10 known rounds), punishment does not reliably improve efficiency relative to the control condition. The paper does not speculate on how altering those parameters may (or may not) change that result. Hence one can say little to nothing beyond the experiment’s conclusion that, in its specific setup, punishment fails to raise efficiency while reward does.

Article Title: Negative Feedback Punishment Approach Helps Sanctioning Institutions Achieve Stable, Time-Saving and Low-Cost Performances

Keywords Plus: PUBLIC-GOODS; ECONOMIC SANCTIONS; POOL PUNISHMENT; EVOLUTION; SYSTEMS; THREATS; WAR
Abstract: Sanctioning institutions widely exist in human society. Although these institutions play an important role in the management of social affairs, sanctions are often seen to be costly in terms of both time and money. To enable sanctioning institutions to develop effective sanctions, we propose a negative feedback punishment approach for these institutions that combines the feedback control principle and the negative correlation principle. In the negative feedback punishment approach, the punishment intensity imposed on the group is negatively correlated with the current group cooperation proportion. Through evolutionary simulation and theoretical analysis, we found that the negative feedback punishment approach facilitates more stable, time-saving and low-cost performance by sanctioning institutions than other punishment methods. This work offers a feasible solution for sanctioning institutions to solve social dilemmas and provides a possible theoretical starting point for investigating effective pool punishment measures.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter analysis of whether, and how, this paper addresses each of the 15 listed parameters, together with any predictions about the effects of varying those parameters on punishment and group outcomes. Throughout, please note that the authors’ measured outcomes and discussions focus on cooperation rates, “time cost,” “monetary cost,” and the stability of cooperation under different “negative feedback” vs. “constant” punishment rules. The paper does not explicitly use the term “efficiency” (as in total payoff / maximum possible payoff) for its performance measures, so no direct statements connect the paper’s results specifically to group “efficiency.” Where the paper is silent on a parameter or on systematic variation of that parameter, that is stated explicitly.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The authors fix the number of players at 100 in their simulations (Appendix A.1).  
   • Systematic variation? No. The paper does not discuss the effect of varying the number of players on any outcome.  

2. Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? Yes. They gradually evolve the population over 300 rounds (and discuss the group’s convergence behaviors in figures).  
   • Systematic variation? No. The paper does not vary the number of rounds or study its impact.  

3. Is chat enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not discuss whether players communicate.  
   • Systematic variation? No.  

4. Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned? The model allows two strategies, “C” (contribute 4) or “D” (contribute 2), so it is not a pure “all or nothing” contribution game.  
   • Systematic variation? No. There is no discussion of varying this feature.  

5. Is the contribution default (if true, do players decide how much of their endowment to move from the public fund back into their hand)?  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper frames contributions as fixed amounts for each strategy (C or D) with no mention of defaults or endowment reallocation.  
   • Systematic variation? No.  

6. Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
   • Mentioned? The paper uses a synergy coefficient μ = 3.  
   • Systematic variation? No. The authors do not systematically vary μ or examine how changing μ would affect outcomes.  

7. Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? Not in the narrower sense of “cost to the punisher.” This is a “pool punishment” model in which punishment is institutionally applied as a fraction t of a defector’s resources, but the paper does not discuss or vary the cost borne by whoever enforces punishment.  
   • Systematic variation? No.  

8. Punishment magnitude (the coins deducted from a player for each unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. In each round, a defector with resources Rᵢ(p) is punished an amount Rᵢ(p) × t(p), where 0 ≤ t(p) ≤ 1.  
   • Systematic variation? Yes. The central focus is on how “punishment intensity” t changes with “punishment intention” k (varied from 0 to 1) under different punishment methods (constant vs. negative feedback).  
   • Effect size or predicted directions? The authors report that whether t is set to be constant or determined by negative feedback drastically affects cooperation rates and the “time” and “monetary cost” to the group. However, the paper frames these effects in terms of cooperation proportions, not “efficiency.”  

9. Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned? No. Only punishment is modeled (there is no mention of exogenous or endogenous rewards).  
   • Systematic variation? No.  

10. Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Systematic variation? No.  

11. Reward magnitude (the coins awarded to a player for each unit of reward)  
   • Mentioned? No.  
   • Systematic variation? No.  

12. Is the number of rounds known to players (do they know when the game ends)?  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not address what is known to participants about timing or the game’s end.  
   • Systematic variation? No.  

13. Are peer outcomes shown (do players know how much their peers gained and lost each round)?  
   • Mentioned? The authors model individuals learning from each other’s payoffs in an evolutionary sense, but they do not describe any explicit “display” or “knowledge condition” from a real‐world perspective. Their game‐theoretic approach simply updates strategies probabilistically using payoffs.  
   • Systematic variation? No.  

14. When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper treats punishment as a “pool punishment” by an institution. No mention is made of revealing punisher identity.  
   • Systematic variation? No.  

15. When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not include reward.  
   • Systematic variation? No.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different?  
   • The paper does not measure “efficiency” as in actual total payoff divided by the payoff of a fully cooperative group. Instead, the authors focus on:  
     – Cooperation rate (final proportion of cooperators).  
     – Time cost (how many rounds the group/institution needs to converge).  
     – Monetary cost (an aggregate of how intensively punishment was used).  
     – Stability of outcomes (the variance in cooperation level and punishment intensity).  
   • These differ from efficiency because the authors do not normalize group payoff by the theoretical maximum payoff.  

B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?  
   • Mentioned:  
     (1) Number of players (fixed at 100).  
     (2) Number of rounds (fixed at 300 evolutionary rounds).  
     (4) Contribution amounts for cooperators vs. defectors (but not systematically “all or nothing”).  
     (6) Multiplication factor (synergy coefficient μ = 3).  
     (8) Punishment magnitude (expressed as fraction t).  
   • Thus, five of the parameters appear in some form.  

C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?  
   • Only Parameter #8 (punishment magnitude) is systematically varied (via “punishment intention” k from 0 to 1, which shifts punishment intensity).  
   • The authors do not systematically vary or analyze the effect of 1, 2, 4, or 6 on the outcomes; those remain fixed in the simulations.  

D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?  
   • The paper does not directly address “efficiency” as defined above, nor does it vary most parameters, so there is little basis to predict how changing (1), (2), (3), (5), (6), or the others would affect efficiency.  
   • The only systematic variations are in punishment intensity (#8), which the authors link to higher cooperation proportions and lower overall “monetary cost” if negative‐feedback punishment is employed—but they do not directly measure group efficiency.  
   • Accordingly, we can make almost no direct predictions on efficiency, as defined in the question, from this paper alone. The text focuses on cooperation rates and cost/time metrics rather than actual payoffs versus the maximum possible.

Authors: Li, YZ; Luo, J; Niu, H; Ye, H
Author Full Names: Li, Yuzhen; Luo, Jun; Niu, He; Ye, Hang
Article Title: When punishers might be loved: fourth-party choices and third-party punishment in a delegation game
Author Keywords: Third-party punishment; Costly signaling; Delegation game
Keywords Plus: ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; STRATEGIC DELEGATION; BIOLOGICAL MARKETS; INDIRECT RECIPROCITY; PARTNER CHOICE; COSTLY SIGNAL; COOPERATION; EVOLUTION; ENFORCEMENT; REPUTATION
Abstract: Third-party punishment (TPP) has been shown to be an effective mechanism for maintaining human cooperation. However, it is puzzling how third-party punishment can be maintained, as punishers take on personal costs to punish defectors. Although there is evidence that punishers are preferred as partners because third-party punishment is regarded by bystanders as a costly signal of trustworthiness, other studies show that this signaling value of punishment can be severely attenuated because third-party helping is viewed as a stronger signal of trustworthiness than third-party punishment. Third-party helpers donate their payoffs to victims of defection in games instead of punishing defectors as third-party punishers do. Then, under what circumstances can third-party punishment be maintained by costly signaling when helping is also present? We show that punishers are preferred over helpers by fourth-party individuals as their delegates to deter potential exploitation. This suggests that costly signaling can facilitate the maintenance of third-party punishment in partner choice with delegation interactions.

     – Similarly, when “help” is given, it is known that the third party was the one who helped; the paper does not address any changes in anonymity or visibility of the rewarder.  

   • Does the paper make predictions about systematically varying rewarder visibility?
     – No. There is no mention of systematically varying that factor.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

▌ A. Does the paper use group efficiency (or total/average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables, and how are these different?

• How trusted or preferred punishers/ helpers are afterward (e.g., amounts sent in a trust game, amounts offered in an ultimatum, or frequency of partner/delegate choice).  
• Actual individual payoffs in the ultimatum or trust games, not framed as an overall group‐efficiency ratio.  
• The paper does sometimes compare average incomes of punishers vs. helpers vs. those who do nothing, but it never frames that as an “efficiency” measure relative to a cooperative maximum.

▌ B. Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

The paper explicitly uses fixed values for:  
• Punishment cost (Parameter 7 = 5 RMB).  
• Punishment magnitude (Parameter 8 = 5 RMB).  
• Reward/help cost (Parameter 10 = 5 RMB).  
• Reward/help magnitude (Parameter 11 = 5 RMB).  
• Multiplication in a trust game (Parameter 6) = triple.  

None of the other parameters are changed or systematically varied. A total of five parameters (6, 7, 8, 10, 11) are at least mentioned in passing or used in a fixed design; the other parameters either do not appear or are not manipulated.

▌ C. For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?

None. Although the paper “uses” certain values for punishment and help costs/magnitudes, it never systematically varies any parameter (including cost or magnitude or the multiplier) to see how that variation would change the punishment treatment effect. No effect‐size estimates are given for changing those parameters, and the paper does not present predictions of how altering them would shift outcomes.

▌ D. If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of this paper, what would they be?

Because the paper does not measure efficiency (in the sense of total payoffs relative to a cooperative maximum) and does not vary or even discuss most of the 15 parameters in a systematic way, it provides no basis for specific predictions about how changes to those parameters would affect the “punishment treatment effect on efficiency.” The evidence and discussion revolve around trust game offers, ultimatum offers, and partner‐choice frequencies, not group efficiency. Abstract: This paper addresses the question of the effectiveness and permanence of temporary incentives to contribute to a public good. Using a common experimental framework, we investigate the effects of a recommendation that takes the form of an exhortative message to contribute, a monetary punishment and a non-monetary reward to sustain high levels of contributions. Below is an item-by-item account of whether and how the paper by Nakagawa et al. (2022) addresses each of the 15 parameters and what, if anything, it says about systematically varying them in relation to a punishment treatment’s effect. Throughout, it is important to keep in mind that the paper reports on one particular experimental design: a repeated public goods game with groups of four subjects, 30 total periods, and three treatments (Monetary Punishment, Non-monetary Reward, and Recommendation). The paper’s main focus is on contribution levels (and sometimes beliefs about others’ contributions), not on group efficiency—which the user defined as “actual total payoff divided by the maximum possible total payoff.” Any references to “efficiency” or “cost-effectiveness” in the paper do not match the user’s specific definition (ratio of realized payoffs to the fully cooperative payoff).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Number of players  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The experiment uses groups of four players.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not vary group size, nor does it predict how changing group size would affect the punishment treatment effect on efficiency or any other dependent variable.

2) Number of rounds  
   • Mentioned? Yes. Each group plays 30 periods (rounds).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The total of 30 periods is fixed, with no manipulation across treatments or sessions. The paper does not discuss how changing the total number of rounds would affect the punishment treatment effect.

3) Is chat (communication) enabled between players?  
   • Mentioned? No. The paper does not describe any text-based or verbal communication among participants, other than the ability to punish or reward in the relevant treatments. There is no “chat” feature.  
   • Systematically varied? No—nor is it discussed as a factor to vary.

4) Is the contribution “all or nothing”?  
   • Mentioned? No. Subjects may contribute any integer amount from 0 to 20 tokens. No “all-or-nothing” rule is imposed or analyzed.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

5) Is the contribution default (i.e., do players decide how much to move from the fund back into their hand)?  
   • Mentioned? No. Participants simply choose how many of their 20 tokens to contribute; the paper does not provide or analyze any “default” contribution mechanism.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

6) Marginal per capita return (MPCR) or related parameters (e.g., multiplication factor)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. The MPCR is 0.4 for each token contributed.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper sets MPCR = 0.4 and does not discuss changing it, nor does it relate changes in the MPCR to the punishment treatment effect.

7) Punishment cost to impose a single unit of punishment  
   • Mentioned? Yes. In the Monetary Punishment treatment, each punishment point assigned costs the punisher 0.25 tokens.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The cost is fixed at 0.25 tokens per point. The paper does not analyze how changing that cost would affect outcomes.

8) Punishment magnitude (how many tokens the target loses for each unit of punishment)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. In the Monetary Punishment treatment, each point of punishment reduces the punished player’s payoff by 1 token.  
   • Systematically varied? No. It is fixed at 1 token deducted for each point. No discussion of varying it.

9) Whether a reward is enabled  
   • Mentioned? Yes. There is a Non-monetary Reward treatment.  
   • Systematically varied? The paper contrasts a “reward” treatment vs. “punishment” vs. “recommendation,” but it does not systematically vary reward “on” versus “off” within the punishment treatment. There is only a single Monetary Punishment treatment and a separate Non-monetary Reward treatment.

10) Reward cost to grant a single unit of reward  
   • Mentioned? Yes. In the Non-monetary Reward treatment, assigning approval points has no monetary cost (0 tokens).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The cost is always zero; there is no analysis of changing it.

11) Reward magnitude (how many tokens the target gains for each unit of reward)  
   • Mentioned? Yes. In the Non-monetary Reward treatment, the reward is purely symbolic; it does not alter payoffs in tokens.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper never introduces a different magnitude or monetary gain for receiving points.

12) Is the number of rounds known to players?  
   • Mentioned? Yes. All subjects know from the start that there are 30 total periods.  
   • Systematically varied? No. The paper does not examine changes in whether or not the game length is known.

13) Are peer outcomes shown?  
   • Mentioned? Partially. After each period, subjects see how many tokens each of the other group members contributed (but in ascending order, so no one is individually identified). They also see total points of punishment or reward they received (when relevant).  
   • Systematically varied? No. The same feedback format is used throughout the sessions, and the paper does not predict how changing that informational display would alter punishment’s effect.

14) When a player is punished, do they know who the specific punisher is?  
   • Mentioned? Yes. They do not know the identity of the punisher. The experiment keeps punishment anonymous.  
   • Systematically varied? No. There is no manipulation of anonymity.

15) When a player is rewarded, do they know who the specific rewarder is?  
   • Mentioned? Yes. They do not know who assigned reward points. As with punishment, the rewarder’s identity stays anonymous.  
   • Systematically varied? No.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A) Does the paper use group efficiency (or total or average payoff) as a dependent variable? What are the dependent variables and how are these different from one another?

• The paper does not report “efficiency” as defined by actual total payoff / maximum possible payoff. Instead, it measures and analyzes:  
  – Contribution levels (the share or number of tokens contributed to the public good).  
  – Frequency of zero or full contributions (binary indicators).  
  – Beliefs about others’ contributions.  
• Although the paper mentions earnings, it does not center on efficiency in the sense requested here. Contribution rate (and sometimes beliefs) is the main outcome, which differs from payoff-based efficiency.

B) Which and how many of the 15 parameters are mentioned in the paper?

• Mentioned in some form:  
  1) Number of players (groups of 4).  
  2) Number of rounds (30).  
  6) MPCR (0.4).  
  7) Punishment cost (0.25 tokens per point).  
  8) Punishment magnitude (1 token deducted).  
  9) A reward is enabled in one treatment.  
  10) Reward cost (0 tokens).  
  11) Reward magnitude (0-token, purely symbolic).  
  12) Rounds are known (30).  
  13) Limited peer information is displayed (others’ contributions are shown in ascending order; total punishment/reward points are displayed).  
  14) Who punishes is unknown.  
  15) Who rewards is unknown.  
• Not really discussed or not used at all:  
  3) Chat.  
  4) All-or-nothing contribution.  
  5) A default contribution mechanism.

C) For which and how many of the 15 parameters does the paper discuss their effect on the punishment treatment effect for each dependent variable when each parameter is systematically varied?

• The paper does not systematically vary any of the 15 parameters within the punishment treatment. All key parameters (e.g., punishment cost of 0.25 tokens, punishment magnitude of 1 token) are held constant.  
• Therefore, the paper provides no numeric effect sizes or predictions about how systematically changing any parameter would alter the punishment treatment’s effect on outcomes. It only reports how the single chosen punishment scheme affected contributions, compared to the other treatments.

D) If you were to make predictions on how the 15 parameters and their interactions influence the punishment treatment effect on efficiency solely based on the content of the paper, what would they be?

• Because the paper does not study efficiency per se (nor systematically vary these parameters), there is very little direct basis for any quantitative predictions about changing group size, number of rounds, punishment cost, etc. The authors do note that having a “low cost–high impact” punishment can be effective in increasing contributions, but they give no formal predictions on how variable cost-to-impact ratios would shift efficiency.  
• Likewise, for the other parameters (such as whether the number of rounds is common knowledge, or whether punisher identity is revealed), the paper does not supply systematic discussion or data.  
• Overall, there is “little to no prediction” that can be made about how changing these 15 design factors would affect the punishment treatment’s impact on group efficiency, based on the paper alone. The paper confines itself mainly to how punishment, reward, or recommendation compares with no intervention, when all other design factors are held fixed.
reference_APA: Nakagawa, Maho, Lefebvre, Mathieu & Stenger, Anne (2022). Long-lasting effects of incentives and social preference: A public goods experiment. PLOS ONE.

Article Title: Optimizing the social utility of judicial punishment: An evolutionary biology and neuroscience perspective
Author Keywords: punishment; evolution; society and culture; ethology and behavioral ecology; justice
Keywords Plus: ULTIMATUM GAME; ALTRUISTIC PUNISHMENT; 3RD-PARTY PUNISHMENT; DECISION-MAKING; MIRROR-NEURON; COOPERATION; MECHANISMS; DETERRENCE; FAIRNESS; EMOTION
Abstract: Punishment as a response to impairment of individual or group welfare may be found not only among humans but also among a wide range of social animals. In some cases, acts of punishment serve to increase social cooperation among conspecifics. Such phenomena motivate the search for the biological foundations of punishment among humans. Of special interest are cases of pro-social punishment of individuals harming others. Behavioral studies have shown that in economic games people punish exploiters even at a cost to their own welfare. Additionally, neuroimaging studies have reported activity during the planning of such punishment in brain areas involved in the anticipation of reward. Such findings hint that there is an evolutionarily honed basic drive to punish social offenders. I argue that the transfer of punishment authority from the individual to the group requires that social offenders be punished as a public good, even if such punishment is not effective as retribution or deterrent. Furthermore, the social need for punishment of offenders has implications for alternatives to incarceration, publicity of punishment, and judicial structure.

Below, each of the 15 public-goods-game (PGG) design parameters is treated in turn.

For every parameter I report  
(1) whether the paper makes any explicit mention of it (and, if so, what concrete value or description is given), and  
(2) whether the paper says what would happen to the “punishment treatment effect” if the parameter were **systematically varied**.  
When the paper speaks of outcomes other than efficiency (e.g. “level of solidarity” or “percentage of strategies in the population”) I note this explicitly.  No numbers are invented and no outside sources are used.

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Number of players  
(1) Mentioned only qualitatively.  Two‐person (dyadic) interactions and an n-person “Volunteers’ Dilemma” are contrasted, but no concrete group sizes are given or varied.  
(2) No systematic variation; no prediction about the punishment effect.

2. Number of rounds  
(1) Not mentioned.  Evolutionary replicator dynamics are used instead of a finite repeated game.  
(2) No discussion, no prediction.

3. Chat enabled?  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) No discussion, no prediction.

4. All-or-nothing contribution?  
(1) Yes.  Every game is strictly binary: “cooperate” (help/contribute) or “defect.”  
(2) This binary form is fixed; the paper never varies it, so no prediction.

5. Contribution default (endowment first put in public fund)?  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) No discussion, no prediction.

6. Marginal per-capita return (MPCR) or multiplication factor  
(1) Not used.  Instead the author works with Prisoner’s-Dilemma and Altruists-Dilemma pay-off orderings (T, R, P, S) and defines “solidarity gains.”  
(2) No systematic MPCR manipulation; no prediction concerning punishment.

7. Punishment cost to imposer  
(1) Yes.  Called “costs of sanctioning.”  Several qualitative statements:  
    • “If costs of sanctioning are not too high, a very few Hypocritical Cooperators (DC) are able to outperform all bad guys (DD)….”  
    • “If sanctioning costs are too high nobody voluntarily cooperates or tries to influence others; DD takes over.”  
(2) Qualitative prediction only: lower costs → stronger punishment effect (higher cooperation/solidarity); very high costs → punishment ineffective.  No numerical effect sizes.

8. Punishment magnitude (effectiveness of sanctions)  
(1) Yes, referred to jointly with sanctioning costs as “costs and effectiveness of sanctioning.”  No concrete values given.  
(2) Qualitative statement that outcomes “crucially depend on the ratio of gains … and costs and effectiveness of sanctioning,” but no systematic variation or quantified effect.

9. Reward enabled?  
(1) Not mentioned.  
(2) No discussion, no prediction.

10. Reward cost  
11. Reward magnitude  
(1-2) Neither is mentioned; no prediction.

12. Is the number of rounds known?  
(1) Not mentioned; game is not framed as a finite repeated PGG.  
(2) No discussion, no prediction.

13. Are peer outcomes shown?  
14. Is punisher identity revealed?  
15. Is rewarder identity revealed?  
(1-2) None of these information variables is discussed; no predictions.

────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY

A. Dependent variables used  
   • Group efficiency (total or average payoff relative to maximum) is **not** used.  
   • The paper reports (i) “level of solidarity” (L) – the average probability of cooperation/help, and (ii) the percentage representation of each strategy (CD, DD, TFT, CC, DC, DO, etc.).  
   • These variables differ from efficiency: e.g., in an Altruists’-Dilemma higher solidarity can actually reduce aggregate pay-offs.

B. Which of the 15 parameters are even mentioned?  
   3 parameters:  
   – Parameter 4 (binary contribution rule)  
   – Parameter 7 (punishment cost)  
   – Parameter 8 (punishment magnitude/effectiveness)  

C. For how many parameters does the paper discuss their *systematic* effect on a punishment treatment?  
   Only 2 (punishment cost and punishment magnitude/effectiveness), and only qualitatively.  No tables or figures give numerical gradients or effect sizes.

D. What predictions about the 15 parameters’ influence on the punishment-treatment effect on efficiency can be made **solely from this paper**?  
   • Lower punishment costs and/or higher punishment effectiveness should increase solidarity; in a Prisoners’-Dilemma this would plausibly raise efficiency, while in an Altruists’-Dilemma it may create “over-compliance” and could reduce efficiency.  
   • All other listed parameters are either fixed or not discussed, so no additional prediction can be extracted from the paper.

In short, the paper offers qualitative insights about the importance of sanction *costs* and *effectiveness*, but provides no quantitative mapping—and no information at all—about the other 13 design parameters in the standard laboratory PGG framework.
